*Patrologia Latina*, vol. 170

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … Second Series.*

## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology,**

or a universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the Church’s first twelve centuries, most carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other, an index of Holy Scripture, through which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each passage in each book of Scripture, and in what places in their works.

A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to every other if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient form of the volumes, uniformly maintained throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and shorter works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series,**

in which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Universal Clerical Library*, or *Complete Courses in the Individual Branches of Ecclesiastical Learning*. The *Patrology* has been published in two editions: one Latin, the other Greco-Latin. — The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition sell for one thousand francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greco-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. — The purely Latin edition includes all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

## [The complete works of Rupert of Deutz]

[Col. 0009]

### Letter of the Right Reverend Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, to the venerable Cuno, Bishop of the Church of Regensburg, concerning the book *On the Divine Offices*

[Col. 0009]

I now offer, according to the command of the holy and mystical Law, the first fruits of the produce of the land which the Lord gave me (Deut. 23): that is, I send you, Father Cuno—hitherto abbot of the monastery of Segeberg, but now, through the increase of the Lord’s grace upon you, bishop of the Church of Regensburg—this present little work which I wrote on the divine offices and which you have long desired.

For these are the first fruits of all the works which, you rejoiced, have come to me from the Lord, and which you read willingly, not hesitating to commend them and to testify that they are truly produce of the land which the Lord gave: that is, the true sense of Holy Scripture, composed by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1). I dedicated many of those works under your name, and some under the name of Lord Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne. But this work, which was the first, and a few others, I had left without the distinction of any title, as you yourself know.

Thus I had offered the first fruits of the produce and left them in the presence of the Lord God; and, after worshipping the Lord, I feasted upon the Scriptures, as the holy Law immediately says in the same place: “After worshipping the Lord your God, you shall feast upon all the good things which the Lord your God has given you” (Deut. 26).

Yet I had offered these first fruits in the presence of no priest, though the Law ordained that this should be done in the following manner:

> “You shall take the first fruits of all your produce and place them in a basket; you shall go to the place which the Lord your God has chosen for his name to be invoked there; you shall approach the priest who is in office in those days and say to him: ‘Today I profess before the Lord your God that I have entered the land which he swore to our fathers that he would give us.’ And the priest, taking the basket from his hand, shall set it before the altar of the Lord your God” (Deut. 26; Num. 34; Ps. 77).

Why I did not approach a priest according to this mystical rite, I shall explain. I was not yet known to any bishop; and the priest who was in office in those days would neither care for me nor admit me to such a profession. He would not even believe that anything at all of this land within the tribes of Israel had, by the measuring-line of distribution, been allotted to me in so small a share.

But I knew that neither Moses nor the priests, but Jesus alone, had apportioned by lot the land beyond the Jordan among the tribes of Israel (Josh. 15). Therefore, caring little for priestly patronage, I held my basket, gathered into it such first fruits, and set them before the altar of the Lord God. For I had this intention and desire: that my offering might be pleasing in the sight of the Lord.

Meanwhile I heard something that recalled for me the following passage from ancient history. When the Lord had spoken to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel that they take for me first fruits; from every person who offers freely you shall receive them” (Exod. 25), and they were offering eagerly in rivalry, the craftsmen came and said to Moses: “The people are offering more than is necessary; the offerings suffice and overflow” (Exod. 35–36).

I heard something similar, for people said against me: “This man writes what is unnecessary. The saints have written; the writings of the saints suffice and overflow. We are unable to read what the saints have written, much less these things which this unknown man writes from his own heart without authority.”

Passing by these and many far graver things with a deaf ear, because I was wholly possessed by that love of the Word of God which would not allow me to be silent, I gathered these first fruits and certain other things into my basket until you came—my faithful friend and patron—through whom I might become known to the priest of the Lord, the Archbishop of Cologne.

But behold: you are a priest by the Lord’s gratuitous calling; you have become a bishop through the voluntary election of clergy and people. To you I may confidently approach with these first fruits—indeed, with all produce of this kind—and say: “Today I profess before the Lord your God that I have entered the land which he swore to our fathers that he would give us” (Deut. 26).

For I know that you willingly receive this profession. I may say that the Lord Jesus, who, after bringing his people through the waters of the Jordan, apportioned the land by the measuring-line of distribution—that is, who distributes varieties of graces to those who believe and are justified by his grace through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit (Tit. 3)—has also recognized my smallness in that distribution according to this measuring-line (1 Cor. 12). The Evangelist expresses it thus: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

I have said too little in stating that you willingly receive such a profession. Indeed, I can truthfully say that, urging me very strongly and more than I wished, you even adjured me not merely to tell you, but also to write, how I entered into this portion of the excellent land. Why I have not yet dared to obey that adjuration, God knows, and you, as one privy to it, know in part.

> [Note: [Col. 0009] Elsewhere the author himself admits that he occupied himself with the Scriptures through divine revelation.]

Therefore, O priest of the Lord, receive the basket from my hand and set it before the altar of the Lord with greater authority than you have hitherto exercised. And I shall speak in the Lord’s presence whenever either you or anyone following your example deigns to reread my writings as the produce of the land which the Lord gave and upon which he bestowed his blessing.

The little books containing these present first fruits number twelve. I have also taken care to append a list of all the other works I have offered:

- Ten books of commentaries on Job, abridged from the abundance of the insights and sayings of Blessed Gregory.
- [Col. 0011] Fourteen books of exposition on the Gospel of John.
- Forty-two books on the works of the holy and undivided Trinity.
- Twelve books on the Apocalypse of John.
- Thirty books on the twelve Minor Prophets.
- Twelve [thirteen] books of the short work *On the Victory of the Word of God*—which is almost your own work.
- A work on the glory and honour of the Son of Man according to the Gospel of Matthew, to which you urged me in your customary manner.
- A work from the Books of Kings, on the glorious King David, to which my lord, the Archbishop of Cologne, urged me with great force. In one of these I have proceeded to the eighth book, and in the other to the eleventh.

> [Note: [Col. 0011] He later completed twelve books on Matthew and fifteen on David.]

I am now occupied with these works; when, life accompanying me, I have completed them, I shall leave these also through your hand in the Lord’s presence. And, having worshipped the Lord, I shall feast upon all the good things which he has given me.

I have also expounded the Song of Songs in seven little books. You read this all the more gladly because you love more faithfully and devoutly the Blessed Virgin Mary, mother of the beloved Son of God, to whose honour I have endeavoured to dedicate that entire work. In mentioning this I greatly rejoice with you that you have already received some fruit of your great love; for I know very well that you have always loved, and still love, the Word of God.

This Word is your flame; it is your light. Having it in your heart and on your lips, you are a lamp which God, who kindled it, willed not only not to remain hidden, but to be placed and to shine on a lampstand greater than that on which it formerly stood in the house (Matt. 5). Nor do I doubt that every single eye which sees you rejoices with you because of the light of the Word shining from your mouth, and, I believe, all the more abundantly because there are more persons in the house in which you must minister such light.

I especially ought to rejoice in your light. Yet I neither wish nor ought to rejoice in your light merely for an hour; I am pressing on toward everlasting rejoicing, and I know that you too are pressing toward it. For true rejoicing consists not in your having become richer or more glorious in this world, but in the fact that the abundance and perfection of present riches and glory await in heaven, while present riches fill the hand for almsgiving to one who desires to lay up treasure in heaven (Matt. 6).

And present glory, because it is according to God, becomes material for greater love and thanksgiving, since hope, the companion of truth, confirms this mercy, according to the words: “Mercy and truth shall go before your face, O Lord” (Ps. 88). Mercy has exalted you here; truth will make you blessed there. You now know, and will then know more perfectly, the rejoicing of the saints, of whom it is said: “O Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance; in your name they shall rejoice all day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted” (ibid.).

## Twelve books of the Right Reverend Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, on the divine offices throughout the course of the year

### Prologue

[Col. 0011]

Those things which are performed in the divine offices throughout the cycle of the year, in an established order, require an attentive listener and a learned teacher and interpreter of the venerable Scriptures if they are to be properly expounded. For they are signs of the loftiest realities and contain the greatest sacraments of heavenly mysteries; no one but a learned and devout person is fit to aspire to contemplating their majesty.

Indeed, these things were ordered and instituted by such men for the service of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the head of the Church (Eph. 1). They both understood profoundly the mysteries of his incarnation, nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and took care to proclaim them faithfully and wisely by voice, by writings, and by signs of this kind.

In this respect they imitated the blessed sons of Noah, Shem and Japheth, who, when Ham mocked and cursed their father’s nakedness, took a cloak behind their backs and covered it with reverent care (Gen. 9). For what else did Noah, planting his vineyard (Ps. 79), becoming drunk and sleeping, and lying exposed in his tent, prefigure but the Lord Jesus Christ? From his vineyard, which he transplanted and planted from Egypt, he was made drunk with the vinegar of sufferings (John 19), lulled into the sleep of death; that is, being found in appearance as a man, he openly appeared subject to suffering and death.

But let Ham go out and report it abroad, accusing him of weakness. Ham means “hot”: namely, every heretic, hot for quarrelling, contentious and impatient. But illustrious Shem and enlarged Japheth—that is, the Catholic and apostolic Fathers—adorn and venerate with the honourable cloak of the sacraments the weakness assumed for our sake; and they do this behind their backs, because those weaknesses have rightly passed away and were not seen by them while present.

To celebrate these sacraments while not understanding their causes is like speaking in a tongue and not knowing its interpretation. “He who speaks in a tongue,” says the Apostle, “should pray that he may interpret” (1 Cor. 14). Among the spiritual gifts of grace by which the Holy Spirit adorns his Church, he urges us especially to seek this: that we may prophesy—that is, that we may grasp with the understanding of the mind those things which we pray or sing in the Spirit.

Yet we should not altogether judge of these matters as we do when “I pray in a tongue: my spirit indeed prays, but my mind is unfruitful.” [Col. 0013] For those who faithfully and devoutly observe the mysteries or signs of the Church are not without fruit even if they cannot know their causes. These things were instituted precisely so that the secrets of God, which can be understood by few, might in a wonderful way be performed by almost all.

Do the other members, which do not see but nevertheless work, lack fruit because only the eyes see in working? But every member has its own dignity. The eyes, however, excel because they lead and direct the rest. Therefore I call upon the Holy Spirit, the maker of all sacraments, that by the grace through which he ordered these things through the holy Fathers, he may deign to reveal them to me according to the meaning and authority of the Scriptures.

It seemed good to arrange this little work so that I should first set forth those matters which are almost daily, and then those which vary according to particular times and reasons, with the help of Christ himself. By his gracious blood the whole earth has been made purple; heaven flourishes through his victories; the seasons are marked by his mysteries; days and hours are adorned by his remembrance.

The merit or worth of this study ought to obtain from all good people this result: although they are accustomed to drink old wine with delight, they should not judge our new wine worthy of rejection. For we detract nothing from the authority of the ancients—Amalarius, certainly, and any others who may have written on such matters. Rather, it has been and always will be permitted to anyone, while preserving the faith, to state what he thinks.

We must first discuss whence the seven hours of the day—the first daily duty of our service, which we call canonical, that is, regular—have derived the reasons for their institution.

# Book One

[Col. 0013]

## Chapter I. On the canonical hours

[Col. 0013A]

No one who does not wish to appear empty and ungrateful before God may negligently pass over the seven canonical hours of the day. For they offer praises to our Creator and are, as it were, tributes of thanksgiving for his certain and great benefits. Christ, the true sun and eternal day, has twelve spiritual hours standing eternally with him; these seven hours that move in time he has illuminated and consecrated by the brightest rays of his mercy. We shall draw the reasons for each one from the treasury of Scripture.

## Chapter II. On Prime

[Col. 0013B]

At the first hour we ought to render praise to our Creator before every concern for the body. At that hour our Lord, already spat upon, mocked, and struck with blows, and still to be filled with reproaches, stood bound before Pilate for our sake (Matt. 27). At the same hour, restored to life and standing on the shore, when by the catch of fish, from which the nets were not torn, he had signified what the Church would be like in the resurrection of the dead, he held a honeyed meal with seven disciples (John 21).

Therefore, since the kingdom of God must be sought first and all other things will be added to us (Matt. 6), and since in the Law the Lord commands that every first thing be offered to him (Exod. 13, 23), let us offer the first hour of the day to our Redeemer and seek the kingdom of him “who was delivered up for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4).

## Chapter III. On Terce

The third hour shines with a twofold distinction. At this hour the Lord Jesus was crowned with thorns and crucified by the tongues of the Jews (Matt. 27), according to the words: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). For when Pilate judged that he should be released, “they strengthened for themselves an evil word” (Ps. 63), persistently crying, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19).

And the Holy Spirit, who had not been given for the remission of sins before Jesus was glorified, was poured out upon the Church at its birth in tongues of fire; and the Lord’s promise to the disciples was fulfilled: “You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1).

## Chapter IV. On Sext

At the sixth hour Christ the Lord was lifted up upon the cross for our sake, that he might draw all things to himself. The small light of the Jews was extinguished—the light concerning which the true Light itself had said: “Yet a little while the light is among you; run while you have the light of life, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12). As bodily darkness likewise rushed over the earth, the true light passed to the illumination of the Gentiles.

## Chapter V. On None

At the ninth hour also, with good reason, we cry out in praise of God, when the Lord Jesus, “crying with a loud voice, gave up his spirit”; the thief was admitted into paradise (Matt. 27; Luke 22; Mark 15), forgiveness was consecrated for those who truly repent and confess, even though late, and the veil of the Law and the Prophets was torn, so that we began with unveiled face to contemplate the glory of the Lord.

Then also, when his side was pierced, there flowed out the elements [sacraments] for the Church’s formation: blood, by which we are redeemed, [Col. 0013C] and water, by which we are washed (John 19).

## Chapter VI. On the morning and evening synaxis

The sacrifice of evening and morning praise has been consecrated for us by great mysteries. I omit the fact that, under the shadow of the Old Testament, the holocaust was continually offered morning and evening, concerning which the Law says: “It is a sacrifice to the Lord, an odour of sweetness, a perpetual offering throughout your generations” (Exod. 20). I hasten rather to evangelical grace; thence the splendid dignity of these hours becomes evident.

In the evening the Lord takes bread and wine and represents the reality of his body and blood (Matt. 26; Luke 22). Carried in the hands of his own people, he writes a testament for his heirs (Heb. 9); by washing the disciples’ feet he especially commends humility and charity; and reclining again, soon to die, he bids his friends and little children a final farewell through the solemnity of a long discourse (John 13). He is also buried in the evening (Matt. 27).

Likewise, in the evening, appearing alive in the guise of a traveller, he is recognized in the breaking of bread and kindles the hospitable hearts of the disciples with the fire of his charity cast into them (Luke 24).

At morning, the cock’s crow rebukes Peter, who had denied three times; the Lord looks upon him, and the penitent denier has recourse to tears (Matt. 26; Luke 22). Likewise, at dawn, when the Lord’s resurrection is announced to the holy women by angels in white garments, the sadness of the faithful already begins to be turned into joy (Matt. 28). The Living One is sought among the dead; he shows himself alive, and deigns also to be touched and worshipped (Luke 24; John 20).

It should be noted that the other hours have seven parts: the verse, “O God, incline to my aid,” with the *Glory be to the Father*; a hymn; psalms; a reading; a responsory or verse; the petition of the litany; and the concluding prayer. To these hours an eighth item, the canticle from the Gospel, is added, because they are sung for the eighth day: they look toward the blessedness of the resurrection, by which they are especially marked, according to the meaning of the Gospel text: “On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath” (Matt. 28).

## Chapter VII. On Compline

The hour of Compline recalls to us that event in the Lord’s passion when Judas had already departed and he “began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14). Having entered into agony, he prayed more earnestly and, with his body prostrate, sweated drops of blood (Luke 22), then treading the winepress alone (Isa. 63) and prefiguring the blood of martyrs which would later be shed according to their ability.

It likewise recalls that event of his resurrection when, after making peace between God and human beings (Eph. 2), he returned as a faithful ambassador and proclaimed the Gospel to us, standing in the midst of his disciples and saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20).

## Chapter VIII. On the night vigils

The splendour of evangelical grace has instituted more magnificently the night vigils, of which the Prophet says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118). For our Lord was born of the Virgin at midnight (Luke 2); likewise, like Samson formerly besieged by the Philistines (Judg. 16), he rose from the dead at midnight after breaking down the gates of hell (Matt. 28).

He is also said to be coming at midnight (Matt. 25), in likeness of the Egyptian time when the Passover was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts were consecrated with the blood of the lamb as a type of our foreheads (Exod. 12).

“Therefore,” says Blessed Jerome, “I think that the tradition of the apostles has remained: that on the day of the Paschal vigil the peoples awaiting Christ’s coming may not be dismissed before the middle of the night; and, after that time has come, they may, in the confidence thus assumed, all celebrate the festival day.”

## Chapter IX. Why Vespers and Matins differ in order from the other hours

Although, apart from the night vigils, these are the seven hours of the day—Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline—Matins and Vespers rightly differ from the other hours both in the number of psalms and in the order of the hymns. For they also derive ancient authority, as stated, from the Old Testament.

That ancient practice of morning and evening sacrifice must indeed have had considerable weight in these offices; likewise, to repeat what was said above, the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, which occurred in the evening (Exod. 12), and the event in the morning watch when the Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians, destroyed their army, overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were swept into the deep (Exod. 14). So too, in the creation of the world, with the other hours unmentioned, evening and morning are commemorated in the sixfold division of divine works (Gen. 1).

Therefore, at these hours alone, psalms of ancient authority precede the hymn, which is of evangelical joy, after the example of the Lord, who, after a hymn had been sung, went out to the Mount of Olives (Matt. 26; Mark 14). And because they commemorate the greatest mysteries from the Gospel and are for that reason adorned with Gospel canticles, they have hymns almost joined to them. Compline also, since among some it has a canticle from the Gospel, has a hymn immediately after the psalms together with that canticle.

This is unsurprising, since even in the titles of the psalms one finds now “Psalm of a Canticle,” now “Canticle of a Psalm” (Pss. 24, 65), and the alteration itself is not without reason. The common dignity of all the hours is also shown by the fact that we refer both their beginning and their end to God. At the beginning we invoke God for help; at the end we render thanks to God.

## Chapter X. On the order of the hours on feast days

Whenever we have material for praise drawn from the time of grace—for example, on Sundays and the feasts of saints—we do not bend the knee during the hours. We stand, displaying the liberty and grace (Gal. 4; Eph. 2) which has broken the iron yoke from the necks of us who were bent over (Jer. 28), so that we might walk upright (Isa. 45).

Then we divide the vigils into three nocturns, so that we may proclaim not only in word but also in deed the three watches of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching; and if he comes in the second watch, and if in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke 12).

Then the offices of reading and singing, instituted for the building up of the Church, resound more numerously, so that we may prepare ourselves to open to the Lord at whatever hour he knocks (Rev. 3), after the pattern of the two trumpets of the Old Testament, which were commanded to sound more frequently and in shorter blasts when the camp was to move (Num. 20).

The plurality of readings is not identical in every order. Clerics read nine; monks, twelve. For the number nine among the former is square—that is, a quadrilateral with sides equal on every side—and indicates that the word and deed of preachers ought always to be equal. The number twelve among the latter consists of unequal sides: three times four, or four times three, makes twelve. This indicates that they ought to extend themselves more in one respect and, following the example of Jacob, limp while wrestling with the Lord (Gen. 32): that is, they should work less in order to meditate more deeply, these men who preach the faith of the Trinity to the world’s fourfold extent.

In both orders, the plurality of readings signifies the plurality of preachers sent into the world from the time of grace. For in deep night the cock usually gives fewer and more prolonged calls, whereas near day it gives more frequent and quicker calls. Thus before the Lord’s incarnation the heralds of life were few and infrequent; afterwards they were many and frequent. We signify the small number of the earlier preachers by the three readings of ordinary nights, and the multitude of the later preachers by the readings on the feasts of the Lord or of saints of the New Testament.

This reason was considered so compelling that the Roman order, which has laudably carried out the reasons of divine matters according to apostolic faith, decreed that the Paschal night itself should have no more than three readings. For on that night the holy preachers—the apostles—were few in number, silent through fear of the Jews, and sorrowful over the Lord’s death; they avoided being seen and feared being heard. At the very twilight, when the holy women reported that the Lord had risen and had appeared to them, they did not believe; these words seemed to them like nonsense (Luke 24).

Nor does this same reason regard only that night, but also the period thereafter until Pentecost, in the small number of readings: at Pentecost the holy preachers were both more numerous and eloquent through the fervour of the Holy Spirit. Yet those who, considering the majesty of the solemnity, keep the complete and solemn number of readings come no less close to reason. For even if the apostles were silent (Matt. 28), the addresses of angels and the frequent visitation of the Lord himself (John 20–21) constitute a proclamation most celebrated and worthy of imitation.

## Chapter XI. Why we precede readings with prayer

We precede the aforementioned readings with prayer because we ought to ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest (Matt. 9), and to open our hearts to his Law and commandments (2 Macc. 1), lest the seed of the Word of God which we are about to hear should be eaten by birds, choked by thorns, or overthrown by the hardness of rocky ground where it has found no root (Matt. 13; Luke 8).

## Chapter XII. On “Command, O Lord”

The person about to read, by asking for a blessing, signifies that no one should presume to undertake the office of preaching unless sent or permitted. For “How,” says the Apostle, “shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10).

## Chapter XIII. On “But you, O Lord”

The reader’s words at the end, “But you, O Lord, have mercy upon us,” signify that not even the good office of preaching can be carried out without the dust of some fault, however slight. For, as Blessed Augustine says: “The word of preaching is heard more safely than it is spoken.” For when a preacher senses that he is blessing others, it is exceedingly difficult for him not to be touched, however slightly, by a spirit of self-exaltation. Since he walks, as it were, upon the earth, and his feet are dirtied by some dust, he needs God’s mercy to wash this part of him, even if he is otherwise wholly clean.

## Chapter XIV. On “Thanks be to God”

When the choir responds, “Thanks be to God,” it refers not to the reader’s final prayer, but to the entire reading. For we give thanks to God because he deigns to break for us the bread of his teaching, lest we perish through hunger for hearing the Word of God (Isa. 14; Luke 15). Thus, even after those readings at whose end “But you, O Lord” is not said—namely the little chapters of the regular hours—we cry, “Thanks be to God,” because it is the Word of God in which every human being lives (Deut. 8; Matt. 4).

## Chapter XV. On responsories
Responsories, which we sing after the readings, indicate to us that we ought to respond in action to God’s holy admonitions, lest we be like children sitting in the marketplace, playing and saying: “We played for you, and you did not dance; we lamented for you, and you did not weep” (Luke 7). For they are so called from responding. Thus we ought to sing sad things in response to sad readings, and joyful things to joyful readings [Col. 0018D]. For it is neither customary nor fitting that, when the reader has spoken sorrowful matters—for example, matters of repentance or some lament over the Lord’s Passion—the choir should dance in the responsory with joy over the kingdom and the glory of the Resurrection. Rather, while the reader, like “John, neither eating nor drinking” (Matt. 11), preaches repentance, we likewise weep in the responsory; while he, like “the Son of Man, eating and drinking” (ibid.), sings to us of the joy of the kingdom, we fittingly dance as we answer him in song. And the fact that, with one leading, the choir follows in harmony both in these and in other such chants establishes what the Apostle urges: that we all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among us (1 Cor. 1).

## CHAPTER XVI. On Bells

That there should be sounding instruments in the Church, by which the people are stirred to the praise of God, rests upon divine authority and ancient custom. For formerly trumpets or bells—different indeed in form, but understood according to the same rationale—were used. We read in Leviticus that trumpets were made at the Lord’s command, to be used at the Jubilee (Lev. 23, 24; Num. 10), and of such power that at their blast Jericho fell (Josh. 6). And in Chronicles, among the singers chanting mysteries with harps, and among the Levites singing for the octave, David sang and leapt, while the sounding of seven trumpets rang out before the ark of the Lord’s covenant (1 Chron. 15).

But now, for confessing the Lord and for proclaiming his mercy in the morning and his truth in the night (Ps. 91), bronze signals also resound; and at every hour of the divine office, as though at the beginning of an illustrious discourse, they serve to make the hearers of divine praise attentive, receptive, and well-disposed [Col. 0019B]. These signs of the Church, therefore, and those legal trumpets signify one and the same thing: namely, the holy preachers of the Church, who summon and prepare the people for “Mount Zion and the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the gathering of many thousands of angels” (Heb. 12), and for God’s future judgment. They strive, insofar as they can, to express the greatness of the matter by grandeur of speech, so as to strike the inwardly stored ears of the heart and to bend and overcome the understanding of the deaf hearer toward hearing [Col. 0019C].

Although the discourse hastens toward higher matters, it should not be passed over how the perfect preacher is fashioned in a certain likeness of this sign. Let him imitate the hardness of the metal by strength of mind, and the iron striker by which the sound is struck out by constancy of speech. “Behold,” says the Lord, “I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and flint I have made your face” (Ezek. 3). Fleeing also earthly dwelling and saying, “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3), let him suspend his heart on high; and, hanging from the tower of strength which stands before the face of the enemy (Ps. 60), let him remember that he has been set as a watchman over the house of Israel [Col. 0019D] (Ezek. 3).

Let him bear the wood of the Cross upon his head—that is, in his ruling faculty, which is the mind—and let him extend from it, as far as weak brethren, as though to the ground, the rope fastened there: that is, the bond of charity. Thus admonished, let him never cease to ring out and open wide his mouth, saying: “For the charity of Christ presses us” (2 Cor. 5). Thus, set as a watchman upon the walls of Jerusalem, let him not be silent, but announce whatever he sees or hears, according to the saying: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no rest, all day and all night” (Isa. 62); being urgent in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4). To those who sleep on ivory beds and luxuriate upon their couches (Amos 6), let him not cease to praise the Lord’s name, lest they sin in a sleep wickedly buried in sin until the morning—that is, until the dreadful judgment of God [Col. 0020A].

Finally, this should be noted: just as more preachers were sent in the age of grace, and they ring out more frequently with theological symbols, having gifts differing according to the grace given them (Rom. 12), so the aforesaid bells also differ in size and sound. Whenever some festal commemoration of evangelical grace is observed, they ring more tumultuously, thunder more often, and resound more prolongedly, in order to rouse, as if forcibly, those who sleep in the night and those who are drunk—“for those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night” (1 Thess. 5)—to the praise of God. And if they do not prevail so as to compel them to rise and pray lest they enter into temptation, at least they do not permit them to sleep securely.

Therefore let the evangelical choir of preachers imitate the threefold signal of a solemn day—the morning signal, the evening signal, and that rung at the beginning of Mass—in such a way that it always preaches the lamentations of the present life, the song of the life to come, woe, and Gehenna [Col. 0020B].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Ministry of the Altar

Now the order of the daily course requires that we approach the treasury of the highest sacrament, namely the sanctuary of the Mass. If the Treasurer of salvation and Ordainer of charity makes it accessible to me; if he opens with the key of David—he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3)—my soul may rejoice and sing that the King has brought her into the wine-cellar (Song 2). For this is the sanctuary of propitiation; this is that mercy-seat upon which two cherubim, with faces turned toward one another, gaze mutually—namely, the two Testaments [Col. 0020C] (Exod. 25). For what was promised, prefigured, and greeted from afar in the Old Testament, but given, revealed, and made manifest in the New, is here presented in its presence: not in shadow but in truth, not in figure but in reality (Heb. 9–10).

Here that takes place in which our David seemed mad to King Achish: when, hanging on the Cross, he beat the drum and struck against the gates of the city (1 Sam. 21)—that is, against hearts shut against belief in him; when he was borne in his own hands, holding bread and wine and saying, “This is my body; this is my blood, the new covenant” [Col. 0020D] (Matt. 26; Luke 21); when his saliva ran down upon his beard—that is, when he seemed to speak childish things, saying, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

For he fled from that people whom he now calls Achish, that is, “How is it?” because they said, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid.). But earlier he called him Abimelech, that is, “the kingdom of my father.” Having received the kingdom over the true Judah and the true Israel, he now, in the mystical sense of Chronicles, “clothed in a linen robe, dressed in a linen ephod,” as the illustrious precentor leads the choirs in sacrifice and leaps before the ark of the Lord’s covenant (1 Chron. 15). O king, O prince of sacred things! What can so great a dance of so illustrious a head mean, while he pitches the tabernacle for the ark of God, and, clothed in the ephod, offers a burnt offering and blesses the people in the name of the Lord—though the priesthood did not belong to him, since he was of the tribe of Judah? (1 Chron. 16.)

But the Lord rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh; and, after the priests of Shiloh had been slain, he chose the tribe of Judah, chose David his servant (Ps. 77). Behold, the king chosen beforehand from the tribe of Judah [the printed text has: *praegesti de rex tribu*; perhaps *praeelegit rex de tribu*, “the king chose beforehand from the tribe,” etc.] confidently acts in matters which he knew were due to his Son, his Lord, of whom he said: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Matt. 22; Ps. 110). Behold, he commands the priests, directs the Levites to sanctify themselves, appoints singers, chooses those who sing mysteries, who sing for the octave, who sound the trumpets, who ring the horns, who make music with lyres, cymbals, harps, and instruments [Col. 0021B] (1 Chron. 15). In all these things he looks to the Son. “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. 68; Eph. 4).

For it should be known that the ark of the Lord, which is sometimes understood as any ruler of the Church, much more fittingly signifies the humanity of Christ the Savior. It has a window in its side—that is, the lance-wound from which water and blood flowed (John 19); within it contains manna—that is, the Word of God united to it—and the tablets of the covenant (Heb. 9), because “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2), as well as the rod of priesthood and royal power. Therefore our David, after the rule of Saul—that is, the dominion of death—has been destroyed, brings the ark of God into Jerusalem and sets it in the tabernacle of heaven which he himself stretched out [Col. 0021C] (2 Sam. 6).

Looking upon this during the days near the holy Resurrection, the Church stirs itself up, after the example of the former people, to sing to its David when it chants this responsory: “The people in Israel sang *alleluia*” (1 Chron. 15). Thus the whole multitude of Jacob sings lawfully, and David himself strikes the harp with the singers in the house of the Lord. Whatever Israel sings, it has learned from this Master, from this Precentor, who strikes the harps of hearts with God’s finger. The jubilation stirred up by him breaks forth through strings into bodily voices and the harmony of the choir—now low, now high or exalted—and the song of the great body of the Church, spread among all nations, because it resounds with one faith, is at once manifold and one, everywhere and from every side, and is sweetly heard by him [Col. 0021D].

Let us therefore now touch upon the order of the altar, the order of a great and unending mystery; and, with him opening the way, let us come to know at least in part the imitation in the members of the body—the priests—of the sacred things that preceded in the Head, namely Christ, the Prince of priests. First, then, we must speak of priestly vestments.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Priest’s Attire

That there is nothing in priestly attire devoid of reason was also established among the ancients, as blessed Jerome testifies in writing to Fabiola. Therefore, among us, the more worthy Christ’s priesthood is than the ancient priesthood, the more worthy reasons are shown to belong to priestly attire. For they referred the sacred vestments, according to the colour, material, and position of each, to the four elements of the world, the two hemispheres of heaven, the divisions of the Zodiac, and heaven itself. Finally, by the ineffable name of God inscribed on the golden plate which was on the high priest’s forehead [Col. 0022A] (Exod. 28), they wished to signify that all things below are governed by God’s will; and they maintained that it was fitting for the high priest to pray to the Creator not only for Israel but for the whole world—although our writers, and blessed Jerome, according to their custom, also tend in these matters to draw back the veils of spiritual understanding.

Therefore, since even the old things were not without rationale, let us, having gone beyond the copies of heavenly things, contemplate rather the heavenly things themselves in the true priesthood [Col. 0022B].

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Amice

In the ministry of the altar the priest bears the person of his Head, namely Christ, whose member he is. Some cover their head with the amice until they fold it back over the mouth of the chasuble and fit it to themselves like a head-covering or crown. This is what we read in the Apocalypse: that a mighty angel came down from heaven, clothed with a cloud (Rev. 10); and in Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord comes riding upon a white cloud” (Isa. 19). For when the Son of God, the Angel of Great Counsel, came for the salvation of the world, he was clothed with a cloud, when he hid his divinity—which is head and principle—in our flesh [Col. 0022C]. Therefore the first garment of the priest, the amice, signifies this hiding-place of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Alb

The alb is a close-fitting linen garment which, as Jerome says, is called in Hebrew *ephobad* [perhaps *ephod*], and belongs from ancient times to the priestly and Levitical order. It stands at the greatest distance from the tunics of skins, which are made from dead animals and with which Adam was clothed after sin (Gen. 3). Since it has nothing of death, but is wholly white, it signifies the new life of Christ’s priesthood, which he taught and bestowed in baptism, so that, rising from baptism, we may gird our loins in truth (Eph. 6) and the entire shamefulness of former sins may be covered [Col. 0022D]. Hence David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 32).

The tongue of this same garment, fastened above, intimates his heavenly teaching. Hence John says: “He who comes from heaven is above all; whoever receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Stole

The stole, which rests upon the priest’s neck over the amice, signifies the obedience of the Son of God and the servitude which the Lord of all undertook for the salvation of the ages (Gal. 4). For—something to be contemplated with great reverence—the Son of God obediently suffered and died (Phil. 2). Yet he neither contracted the cause of mortality, namely sin, by origin nor committed it by act; therefore he owed nothing to death [Col. 0023A]. But the Father gave him the cup, not as judge but in love; not in wrath but by will; not from necessity but by grace; not for vengeance.

And as Jacob, free and nobly born, obeying the command of his father Isaac and the counsel of his mother Rebekah, served Laban in order to take Rachel and Leah in marriage (Gen. 38, 39), so the Son of God, obedient to the command of the Father and the counsel of the Holy Spirit, served the world, bearing sins on his subjected shoulders, in order to take to himself the Synagogue from the Jews and the Church from the Gentiles. Therefore, when the priest receives the stole, he ought to remember and know that he takes upon himself a great yoke—sweet indeed, yet great; light indeed, yet great (Matt. 11).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Chasuble

The chasuble, the garment of our great priest Christ, signifies that garment of the true Aaron upon whose hem descends the ointment that is upon the head, first descending upon Aaron’s beard (Ps. 133). What is that garment? The holy catholic Church. For Aaron’s beard—Aaron being interpreted “mountain of strength”—that is, Christ’s apostles and apostolic men, are strong and perfect. The royal and priestly ointment is the Holy Spirit, whose whole fullness is in the Head, namely Christ (Col. 2); from there it first descends upon the apostles, as upon the beard, then upon the whole Church, and even to the furthest members of the Church, as to the hem of the garment [Col. 0023C]. Therefore the chasuble signifies Christ’s garment, which is the Church.

It is whole and closed on every side, in order to show the unity or integrity of the true faith. The amice, which previously covered the priest’s head, is placed over it and fittingly encircles its opening. We have already said that it signifies the cloud of his humanity, in which divinity lay hidden; for the humanity of Christ is the head, crown, and glory of the Church, while God is the head of that humanity (Eph. 1; 1 Cor. 11). But in that the chasuble, although one and wholly entire, is by the adjustment of the hands—aptly depicting the extension of the crucified Lord’s hands—divided, as it were, into a front and a back, it is a sign of the ancient Church which preceded the Lord’s Passion and of the new Church which follows it [Col. 0023D].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Tunic

The things said thus far are common to presbyters and bishops; those which follow belong properly to bishops. The tunic worn by the pontiff beneath the chasuble was, in the ancient priesthood, hyacinth-blue in colour, with little bells and pomegranates hanging from its lower part, so that the pontiff might proceed wholly vocal and not die (Exod. 28). As Jerome says, it signifies the knowledge of high things, which is not open to all but to the greater and more perfect. Moses, Aaron, and the prophets possessed it, as did all to whom it is said: “Go up to a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion” [Col. 0024A] (Isa. 40).

Above all, Christ the Lord, the Wisdom of God and weaver of evangelical doctrine, possessed this tunic, and gave it to his apostles. “For all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father,” he says, “I have made known to you” (John 15). But they could not put it on or bear it except when the Holy Spirit came upon them. This tunic was also signified by the Lord’s garment, which the soldiers would not divide because it was seamless, woven from above throughout (John 19), thereby signifying the exceedingly great harm that would befall those who attempted to rend with heresies the Scripture of Christian faith.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Sandals

The sandals of the pontiff signify that footwear of the Lord’s Incarnation concerning which he says in the psalm: “Into Idumea I shall stretch out my shoe” (Ps. 60), that is, “I shall make my Incarnation known to the Gentiles.” For in order that the Son of God might exercise priesthood for us, he came into this world shod, as it were, with our flesh. Therefore, as has been said, the pontiff’s sandals signify the Incarnation of the Son of God [Col. 0024B].

It is fitting that the same thing should be signified in the covering of the head and in the footwear of the feet: for divinity lay hidden in the flesh, and through his flesh knowledge travels throughout the whole world. By the straps with which the sandals themselves are fastened to the feet, we understand the same thing which John the Baptist is shown to have signified by the sandal-strap when, speaking of Christ the bridegroom, he said: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark 1; Luke 3). Therefore, by the straps of the sandals we understand to be signified that ineffable union, that immeasurable charity, those indissoluble bonds of the Holy Spirit by which the divinity of the Word joined itself to our flesh [Col. 0024C].

Moreover, when the pontiff looks upon so sacred and mystical an adornment of his foot, he ought to remember and know that he too is a beautiful foot, according to the saying: “How beautiful upon the mountain are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace” (Isa. 50), etc.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Ring

The ring on the finger signifies the house of the Holy Spirit, with which the Son of God descended to his Church, rich and adorned; it also signifies what he distributes to those who believe in him through many and varied gifts according to his good pleasure, giving to one a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge (Rom. 12; 1 Cor. 17), etc. The Catholic pontiff, as Christ’s vicar, visibly imitates these invisible distributions of graces through the divisions of sacred orders, appointing some in the Church as priests, others as deacons, and the rest as ministers of the sacred altar [Col. 0024D].

But the meaning of the aforesaid ring extends more broadly: when he preaches sound doctrine and whole faith to the entire Church, he betroths her to Christ as a bride pledged with a ring. Therefore it is not without reason that a jeweled ring gleams upon his finger, through whose ministry Christ the Lord distributes such splendid gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0025A].

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the Golden Plate Has Given Way to the Sign of the Cross

The golden plate of the ancient high priests has yielded place to the sign of Christ’s Cross. Formerly it gleamed upon the forehead as the eighth ornament of the high priests (Exod. 28); now the almost identical ineffable majesty of the Name is inscribed there. There was the ineffable name of God; here is the inestimable mystery of the Cross. For the Cross is an inestimable sign, a wondrous power. The Cross is the hope of Christians, the resurrection of the dead, guide of the blind, staff of the lame, destruction of the proud, consolation of the poor, support of the needy, hope of the despairing. The Cross is the magnificence of kings and the glory of priests [Col. 0025B]. Therefore the Cross is a more sacred ornament than the golden plate.

Nor should it at once occur that this ornament does not belong especially to the pontiff because it is also common to the whole people with him. For his dignity has in this something which is not shared even by priests of lower rank. Thus the standard-bearer of Christ’s worshippers bears this banner on his own forehead in such a way that he alone is permitted to mark it upon the foreheads of the people subject to him with sacred chrism. As it belonged to the apostles to lay hands upon the baptized so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, so this practice, effective to this day, belongs properly to bishops.

See what and how great an ornament that prodigal son received in his priests: he who, returning from the distant country where he had fed swine, was met by his gracious father, who ordered the fatted calf to be killed. The entire household of the father rejoices in the glory of the penitent son; but his elder brother, that tiller of the field, stands outside, tormented by envy, and refused to share in the banquet of his brother’s salvation [Col. 0025C] (Luke 15).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Archbishop’s Pallium

Yet archbishops have an eighth garment in place of the golden plate, called the pallium, given from the apostolic see. Hanging from the neck around the breast, its arrangement openly signifies the collar of humility or wisdom, which very greatly befits the office of bishops and the head of their council. The rationale of this privilege should not be passed over.

After the twelve apostles had been dispersed throughout the whole world and presided over individual cities, both they and their successors sent preachers into the provinces adjacent to their sees, and ordained them bishops, so that wherever they were received they might perform all the sacraments of Christianity as the apostles themselves did, and might ordain bishops in the cities of their province. The successors of some apostles were called patriarchs. But Peter’s successor, on account of the preeminence of the prince of the apostles, is called the Apostolic One. Those sent by them through the provinces, both they and their successors, are called archbishops; and those ordained by these in provincial cities, together with their successors, are called simply bishops even to the present day [Col. 0025D].

Therefore those who have received the beginning of faith from the apostolic see observe this rule for metropolitan churches: they are to have no pontiff except one sent from the same see from which the first preacher of faith was sent to them. That mission is the bestowal of the aforesaid pallium, which, as was said, hangs from the neck and signifies the humility of the Lord, who says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20).

Among the other archbishops of Gaul, the archbishop of Rheims preeminently possesses authority by right, because, besides being an ancient metropolitan see, its bishop, blessed Remigius—what is a great matter—was sent by God himself and magnificently promised before he was born; he first brought the Frankish peoples, together with their king, to the Catholic faith. Pope Hormisdas, the fifty-third from St Peter, duly approving this mission, delegated his own authority to the same bishop of Rheims throughout the entire kingdom of Louis; and, increasing the primacy of the Church of Rheims, confirmed it by supreme authority [Col. 0026B].

For the Church of Trier, Maternus, sent by the apostle St Peter, left the inheritance of the pallium to his successors. Crescens, the disciple of the apostle Paul, preached to Mainz. At Utrecht, St Willibrord was sent by Pope Sergius.

But the metropolitan see of Cologne obtained primacy, chiefly because the aforesaid Crescens first brought to Cologne also an apostolic visitation of the Word of God. At Canterbury, the noble metropolitan see of the English, Augustine was sent as its first bishop by St Gregory [Col. 0026C], and with vigorous ministry of preaching aided the whole English people toward knowing Christ. Concerning sacred vestments, then, enough has been said for the present, as far as ability permits.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Entrance Antiphon

When at last the priest is about to enter the holy altar, both the priest himself and the entire Church present ought to expand their souls and hold within the ample bosom of faith the remembrance of the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the remembrance of all the saints who, from the beginning of the world, awaited these things in hope, prefigured them in deeds, and prophesied them in speech or writing. In contemplating them, they should break into song by leading the antiphon called the Entrance Antiphon [Col. 0026D].

For just as the priest’s entrance signifies the coming of the Son of God into this world, so the antiphon said at the Entrance expresses the voices and expectation of the patriarchs and prophets. The aforesaid antiphon enters, then, having been sung not less than once, with such solemnity as most fittingly corresponds to the reality signified. Flaming tapers proceed, namely as a sign of the joy that shone out upon the whole world at the Savior’s birth, concerning which the angel said to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy” (Luke 2), etc.

Two ministers precede the priest, not walking side by side or at his flank, but before the subdeacons. These two signify the Old and New Testaments—that is, the Law and the Gospel—of which the Law is earlier in time, while the Gospel is greater in dignity [Col. 0027A]. For the Savior introduced these ministries of salvation: he brought the Gospel, but came not to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it (Matt. 5). These are the two feet of the angel of whom it was said above: “He came down from heaven clothed with a cloud, and placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth” (Rev. 10).

For legal morality, taught by John the Baptist or by the Lord himself, was heard more peacefully (Luke 3); but at evangelical dignity—that is, the manifest doctrine of faith—when, for example, he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and, “Before Abraham was made, I am” (John 8), hearts unstable and false swelled like the astonishing surges of the sea (Ps. 93). The subdeacon also carries before him the text of the Gospel because the Law indeed contains testimonies concerning Christ, as he himself says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote concerning me” [Col. 0027B] (John 5). He carries it closed because, before the Lamb slain opened the seven seals, the sacrament of Christ’s Passion was closed in the book of the Law (Rev. 5).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Incense

When the priest has entered and stands at the holy altar, a censer is placed in his hand for burning incense. For the aforesaid “angel,” as we read in another passage of the Apocalypse, “stood beside the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand” (Rev. 8), when the Son of God manifested himself in the sight of the Church, having an immaculate body which he also filled with fire, because the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit rested bodily in him [Col. 0027C] (Col. 2).

Meanwhile the choir sings *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy,” which signifies all the universal prayers of the Church. These are the true incenses, of which it is there said: “Much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne of God” (Rev. 8).

## CHAPTER XXX. On “Glory in the Highest”

There immediately follows the hymn *Gloria in excelsis*, “Glory in the highest,” which the holy Church seized from the mouths of angels. This hymn belongs both to angels and to human beings. First, it is the hymn of angels rejoicing that, with the Lord’s birth, the brightest lamp had now been kindled [Col. 0027D] (Luke 2), by means of which eternal Wisdom would undoubtedly find the lost drachma (Luke 15). Hence, already anticipating the event, they say: “And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2), because no one among all who are in heaven or beneath the earth (Rev. 5) could make peace between God and human beings; but this Maker of all, God made man for human beings, was now about to make it in his flesh, having broken down the wall of enmity (Eph. 2).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Collect

The prayers which follow, said by the priest after the greeting by which the hearers are made attentive, are said in accordance with the prayers of the Lord himself [Col. 0028A], whose entire life was a continuous and unceasing prayer for us. This too is signified in the Apocalypse by the smoke of aromatics rising before God from the angel’s hand (Rev. 8). For the true man, destined to suffer for us, whose voice is this—“You did not ask for burnt offering for sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 40)—always prayed for us to the Word of the Lord united with himself, and to the Father and the Holy Spirit; and, as the Apostle says, “in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications to him who could save him from death, with strong crying and tears, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

Psalm 7 well indicates this prayer of his; its title reads: “A psalm of David himself, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush,” that is, the Ethiopian, namely the malicious people who, with Herod or after Herod, persecuted him, especially the Pharisees [Col. 0028B] (Luke 13). Like the wicked tenants of the Lord’s vineyard, they said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21).

The addition at the end of the prayer, “Through our Lord,” is made because our Lord Jesus Christ is mediator between God and human beings, and it is impossible for the eternal benefits of God to come down to us by any path other than through him. Therefore through him we ask and obtain, just as we often draw heavenly fire from the distant sun through an intervening crystal stone onto material set beneath it. Thus far the beginning of Mass, called the Entrance, has recalled to us the Savior’s entrance into this world: that is, from his birth until John’s preaching, when he himself, baptized and praying, observed the forty-day fast [Col. 0028C] (Matt. 4).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Epistle

The Epistle, representing the person of the Law and the Prophets, performs the office due to a forerunner before the holy Gospel of Christ. For the Law, receiving the infant people of God through the hand of Moses as a pupil to be guarded, taught it to await Christ’s coming; and through the mouth and finger of John, it pointed out Christ now present to this same pupil, now grown, so that it might follow him (Matt. 3; John 3). For the Law preceded the Gospel as the rod precedes the Spirit of gentleness, fear charity, beginning perfection, and the command of a ruler the counsel of one who loves [Col. 0028D].

The Epistle, however, is the voice of the Law, professing its own imperfection in John and sending its hearers onward to evangelical perfection. Although it is often taken from apostolic letters, it remains in the same rank as though it were always from the Law and Prophets. For apostolic reading, too, always teaches and administers morality and the active life rather than the sublimity of the contemplative life which shines in the Gospel.

Now *epistola* is Greek; in Latin it is called *supermissio* or *supererogatio*, “a sending beyond” or “an over-and-above contribution.” This name fittingly agrees with apostolic letters, because they were added over and above to Christ’s Gospel. For the apostolic order is that innkeeper to whom our Samaritan—that is, our guardian, the Lord Jesus Christ—entrusted the man whom he found stripped, wounded, and left half-dead by robbers. Producing two denarii, that is, the Law and the Prophets, and saying to him: “Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I shall repay you when I return” [Col. 0029A] (Luke 10). Therefore the letters which the apostles added over and above to Christ’s Gospel are aptly called epistles.

They differ almost equally from the majesty of the holy Gospel as do the Law and the Prophets, because both alike treat of morals. The latter announce the future mysteries of the Gospel; the former recall them now as past. Therefore, as was said above, the Epistle performs the Law’s moral office, differing from that which in the order of Mass precedes the holy Gospel by as much as a servant differs from a lord, a herald from a judge, and an envoy from the one who sent him. Accordingly, when it is read, we sit without impropriety; but when we hear the holy Gospel, we stand with eyes reverently cast down, as before our Lord.

In preceding the holy Gospel, it imitates the ministry of John the Baptist, who, correcting transgressors of the Law and preparing their morals to receive evangelical faith (Luke 3; Matt. 3), fulfilled what the angel had said of him: “He himself will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” [Col. 0029B] (Luke 1).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Maniple

The maniple which the subdeacon wears upon his left arm, leaving his right free and ready for service, indicates to us that if, fearing the axe of eternal judgment, which has already been laid to the roots of the trees so that every tree not producing good fruit may be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 3), we embrace the aforesaid repentance and bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, we shall carry back sheaves of righteousness, according to the saying: “They went forth and wept, scattering their seed; but they shall come again with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” [Col. 0029C] (Ps. 126).

The fringes of the maniple, stole, or any sacred garment signify perseverance in those same good works, or the completion of moral conduct, because a fringe is the outermost part of a garment. With such fringes the glorious daughter of the king is clothed about in the psalm (Ps. 45), just as Joseph, growing up and comely among his brothers, wore a long tunic (Gen. 37) [Col. 0029D].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Gradual
The Gradual looks to the lament of repentance: a harsh and weighty chant, so much so that it is neither customary nor fitting to render it in exalted voices. For it signifies not yet the rest of those rewarded, but the labor of those at work. For this reason it is omitted from the office on the days after Pentecost, since those days signify the future happy state of holy Church in the kingdom of God, when Christ’s threshing-floor, purified by the winnowing-fan which is in his hand, will leave no remaining grain fearing that it must be cast out of the Lord’s granary into the unquenchable fire of the chaff [Col. 0030A] (Matt. III; Luke III). Nevertheless, it is customarily sung in the first week of Easter; the reason for this custom will be given more suitably in its proper place.

It is called the Gradual from the steps of humility, as being fitting for one who has not yet ascended from virtue to virtue, but, set in the valley of weeping, has nevertheless already ordered ascents in his heart (Ps. XLIII). Although an account of these may be found in many places, it is most especially set forth in the fifteen Songs of Ascents. Indicating the beginning and completion of such an ascender, the cantor often stands upon a step; and one lower than he customarily stands there to sing the following Alleluia.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Alleluia

[Col. 0030B] Alleluia is a name foreign to the Latin language. Its mystery, like a drop of joy from the riches of the heavenly Jerusalem, first descended through the Holy Spirit into the minds of the patriarchs and prophets, and afterward more fully into the mouths of the apostles. For it signifies the eternal feast of angels and blessed souls: ever to praise the Lord, and ever to sing, without end, the new miracle of beholding the present countenance of God.

The poverty of this present life can in no way deserve to attain this; but to know where it is and to taste it beforehand in the joy of hope, to thirst and hunger for that which one has tasted—this is that perfection of the saints in this life which is so called. Therefore this Hebrew name has remained untranslated, so that, being a foreign word, it might indicate rather than express a joy foreign to this life [Col. 0030C] as well.

Since, then, it is, as it were, the proper name of future blessedness, it is rightly used more frequently at the time when the Lord, rising again, offered and promised us the hope of that blessedness. Yet it was not formerly the custom of the Roman Church for it to be sung at Mass in other seasons also; this was instituted—or rather restored—by Blessed Gregory. For from the time of Pope Damasus, though the same custom had previously existed, it had fallen into disuse. Finally, when he perceived some murmuring about this and certain other matters, as though he were steadily following the customs of another Church, he did not disdain to give the reason, saying: “In none of these matters have we followed another Church.”

[Col. 0030D] “For the practice of saying Alleluia here is said to have been brought from the Church of Jerusalem, according to the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory. And therefore we have cut off the custom of Alleluia more especially in this see, because it had been handed down here by the Greeks.”

Alleluia, therefore, is sung after the Gradual: a song of joy after the mourning of repentance. And, striving with all our might to express the magnitude of the consolation laid up for those who now mourn, we jubilate rather than sing; and we draw out the one short syllable of this worthy utterance 15 into many neumes, or divisions of neumes, so that the mind, astonished and filled by the pleasant sound, may be caught up to that place where “the saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. CXLIX).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. [Col. 0031A] On the Gospel

Up to this point the priest sat apart: victorious over evil thoughts, and by sitting signifying the victory of the Lord. For, when the tempter had been conquered, angels ministered to him as he sat and ruled, as it is written: “The tempter left him, and angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV).

At last he rises and approaches the altar, so that the Lord Jesus may fittingly come to our mind: after John had prepared for him a way into human hearts, he returned from the desert to teach in person and, choosing his disciples, to send them out to preach. For the priest sends the deacon to read the holy Gospel, giving him the requested blessing, which he had not given earlier to the subdeacon who was to read the Epistle.

[Col. 0031B] For he sent the Law and the Prophets invisibly and in an invisible manner; but the apostles and evangelists, whose person the deacon bears, he sent and taught visibly when he had become visible, kissing holy Church, namely his bride, with the kiss of his mouth (Song IV). The deacon receives the text of the holy Gospel; carrying it to the reading-desk, he becomes Christ’s foot.

Torch-bearers proceed before him with the censer, by which joy and good repute are signified. For joy is always present in good news. Those who carry this good news also know themselves to be of good repute; and they confidently say: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God in every place” (II Cor. II). Therefore incense, the sign of good repute, is sprinkled over the very place where the Gospel is to be read.

If that place is a feast-day [Col. 0031C] gathering-place, where the people customarily assemble, it is higher, so that its very position may remind the deacon that he who invites the slothful people upward to the Lord ought to stand on the mountain of virtues, according to the words: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem” (Isa. XL).

His stole also proclaims this strength. It is placed over the shoulder and hangs down from there as far as the girding of the loins; this signifies that he will have the strength to lift up his voice if he is strong in action and girded against the battles of lust. For evangelical preaching, which is “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” (Song IV), does not flow with force from elsewhere [Col. 0031D] than Lebanon—that is, from a pure heart and a clean mouth. For the filth of vices, while it constricts the conscience, also narrows the mouth, lest living waters flow forth in a torrent.

That he wears the dalmatic only on feast-days signifies that the disciples could bear the meaning of sublime mysteries only after the Lord Jesus had been glorified and the Holy Spirit had come. For, on the authority of blessed Jerome, we said above that such a tunic signifies the meaning of sublime things [Col. 0032A]. It is closed around the neck so that the breast is covered, because, as the Apostle says, the Gospel is veiled in those who perish (II Cor. IV).

The subdeacon goes before the deacon, carrying the cushion upon which he places the Gospel, because for everything the Gospel says the Law supplies appropriate testimony. The highest reverence is due in hearing the Gospel, which is preeminently the Word of God. The deacon fittingly demands this reverence in the first words he utters, saying: “The Lord be with you.” For whose presence more fittingly than the Lord’s should hearers, reverent and devout, render the requested silence? At once attentive and favorably disposed, their hearts and faces turned toward him, [Col. 0032B] they answer: “And with your spirit.”

He immediately makes them receptive as well, saying: “The continuation of the holy Gospel.” We say this not because the majesty of the Gospel has ever deigned to submit to the rules of rhetoricians, but because what the study of eloquence strives to accomplish among human beings, the supreme nature of wisdom accomplishes more perfectly in its Church. “For,” as blessed Augustine says, “eloquence is wisdom’s companion; and wherever this mistress goes, eloquence follows as her handmaid.”

We answer, “Glory to you, O Lord,” glorifying the Lord because he sent us the word of salvation, according to what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And they glorified the Lord, saying: Therefore God has granted repentance unto life even to the Gentiles” (Acts XI).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 0032C] Further on the Gospel

The holy Gospel is the principal element of all that is said in the office of the Mass. For just as the head takes precedence over the body and the other members serve it, so the Gospel takes precedence over the whole office, and all that is read or sung there accords with it by an intelligible rationale.

For example, on the first Sunday of the Advent of the Lord this Gospel is read: “When the Lord Jesus drew near to Jerusalem” (Matt. XXI), etc. In order to understand how the other members of the office harmonize with this Gospel reading, let us first ask how that reading suits the season [Col. 0032D]. A brief argument gives the following answer.

The Son of God came in order, in compassion, to free the human race, bound by the devil in the chains of sins, and to lead it back into the heavenly Jerusalem—from which captive humanity had been carried away—by teaching it his ways and becoming the gracious assessor of hearts. Without doubt, this is the mystical meaning contained in this same Gospel.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0033]

## 16 CHAPTER I. On the Creed: “I believe in one God”

[Col. 0033A]

After the Gospel has been read, what follows requires greater attention, since it contains the greater mysteries of our salvation. For just as, after the Lord’s Passion, greater gifts of charisms were poured out through the generosity of grace than before, so greater mysteries were ordained after the reading of the Gospel.

Therefore, if it is Sunday or a day adorned by some fitting feast, the Creed is sung, namely: “I believe in one God.” For this exultation of faith especially concerns the mystery of the Lord’s Resurrection on Sunday, or that of Pentecost, when the new offspring of the Church, about to enter the cleansing bath of the life-giving font, recited the Creed [addition: “of faith”] which it had learned in catechesis.

Thus, in this harmony, the Catholic choir fittingly and consonantly responds to evangelical teaching; and lest the chosen child, the teacher of the heavenly song, the joyful musician, should say to it, “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matt. XI), it shows, by singing and dancing with a cheerful mind, how well it has retained the sweet measure of his song.

Meanwhile, the subdeacon carries around the open book of the Gospel for all to greet with a reverent kiss. He had carried it closed at the Introit, because, after Christ’s preaching, the Law began to display openly to believers the evangelical faith which it had previously carried closed.

## CHAPTER II. On the Offertory

After the Creed, the Offertory is sung. The Offertory is the Church’s chant, having this name from offering, because it is sung when we offer or prepare for our almighty Creator an incorruptible sacrifice of praise [Col. 0033C] (Ps. XCIV).

Here the door of faith must be opened ever more widely and the chambers of the soul must be laid open, so that the work of truth may enter, by which bread and wine are transformed into the true body and blood of the Lord; lest we become like that Achish (I Sam. XXI) mentioned above. For many, having no eyes of faith and seeing nothing beyond bread and wine in the holy Sacrifice, murmured when it was said to them, “It is the body and blood of the Lord,” saying, “How can it be?” For they did not know what words the seven thunders had spoken [Col. 0033D] when that mighty angel cried with a loud voice “as when a lion roars” (Rev. X), nor that those words in any way pertain to the mystery of sacrifice, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “I will go around and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of loud acclaim” (Ps. XXVI; II Cor. IV).

But we believe, and therefore we speak: whatever that angel cried out in the great cry of the eternal Gospel (Rev. XIV), whatever the Holy Spirit spoke to his Church after that cry through the sevenfold thunder of his gifts, the holy Catholic Church offers to its Creator the true Word of God, the true Son of God [Col. 0034A], believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth (Rom. X), and together with him offering bread and wine with its hands, as the Savior himself handed them on to it by offering them (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII).

For what portion of his benefits would the Church be thanking its Creator, Savior, and Enlightener for, if it offered him nothing but bread and wine? Is only the earthly body nourished and sustained by such fruits?
