Even before the Church had grown and reached the time of marriage, before it had been joined to its husband and conceived from him a son whom it could offer as an acceptable sacrifice, its sacrifice was not so empty as to contain nothing beyond what appeared outwardly.

For it had invisible grounds for offering invisible victims: namely, memorable works of God—for example, the hand which the Lord stretched out over the firstborn of Egypt; his passing over the dwellings of Israel marked with the blood of the lamb; his passing over and saving, protecting and delivering them; Israel’s crossing of the Red Sea; the drowning of Pharaoh, his army, and his chariots; and the other mighty works of God [Col. 0034B] (Exod. XII). Yet all these were shadows of things to come, which happened to them as figures. Therefore the sacrifices themselves, offered for these reasons, were indeed holy, but shadows of holier things; indeed good, but figures of better things. Such as were the grounds, such were the memorials of the grounds.

The holy Church therefore offers not only the bread and wine seen bodily [Col. 0034C], but also that which is seen only with the eyes of faith—the Word of God, the Son of God—offering a new and true sacrifice. For it now conceives by believing with the heart unto righteousness, and now gives birth by confessing with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X).

For it is that great woman seen in the Apocalypse, clothed with the sun—that is, Christ, whom it put on in baptism—with the moon under her feet (Rev. XII), that is, trampling all mutable things. For the moon is changeable (Ecclus. XXVII), and therefore signifies the changeable world. And it wears upon its head a crown of twelve stars, that is, the choir of the twelve apostles who shone forth at its beginning; and it has in its womb, and cries out in travail and is tormented in order to give birth.

The weighty and grand-sounding chant of the Offertory of which we speak imitates this saving anguish of the woman who has in her womb, cries out, and gives birth [Col. 0034D]. Extended in frequent neumes and fruitful in its verses, it cannot adequately express what it signifies, even by however long a jubilation. Therefore do not say in your heart, “Who shall ascend into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down from there” (Rom. X), so that he who, having risen from the dead in himself, now dies no more, may nevertheless be again immolated for us in his mystery through the victim of the sacred altar.

“For the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. [Col. 0035A] VI), that is, “the word of faith which we preach,” says the Apostle (Rom. X). Since, therefore, the Word of God—the Word of the cross, Christ the Lord—is near in your mouth and heart, if you pour the river of this word over the bread and wine, and utter in the order established by him the truth of this word, he immediately receives from the holy altar that same bread and wine, transforming them into his body and blood, by the same power, the same might or grace by which he was able to assume our flesh from the Virgin Mary in whatever manner he willed.

Nor are there said to be, or are there, two bodies: that which is from the altar and that which was received from the womb of the Virgin. For the one and same Word, the one and same God, is above in the flesh and here in the bread. Otherwise, the bread which we sacrificed yesterday and that which we sacrifice today [Col. 0035B] or tomorrow are several bodies; nor would we rightly say that the body of the Lord is offered by the Church. We would more properly say “bodies,” because almost as many loaves are offered daily as there are priests in the Church. But the cause forbids this, reason refutes it, and religion rejects it. For the unity of the Word brings about the unity of the sacrifice.

For the one Word both once took flesh from the Virgin Mary and now receives from the altar the saving victim. Thus there is one body: both that which was born of Mary and hung on the cross, and that which, offered upon the holy altar, daily renews for us the Lord’s very Passion.

Since the Church also is the body of Christ through the unity of the same Word or Spirit—for the Word of God that united itself to flesh from the flesh of the Virgin Mary has the same Spirit of Christ dwelling and abiding in itself—it should be understood that not only so much of the Word of God comes to the sacred victim as is the grace of that same Word possessed by any individual priest who stands to sacrifice. For each person has his own distributive grace or gift of the Word or of the Holy Spirit.

But into the sacred victim there is poured such fullness of divinity as descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary, and such fullness as distributes itself throughout the body of the Church by the divisions of graces [Col. 0035C]. For just as that God-bearing bread is made not from one grain but from many, and that most holy wine has flowed together not from one grape but from many clusters, so likewise it does not possess merely as much of the Word of God as is the grace of one human being, but as much as is the fullness of the entire body of Christ, which is the Church (Eph. I). The Church consists of many people and, through each individual person of Catholic faith, is present in its entirety at the holy altar in every place and at every time.

But let us now continue the order we have begun, and let us consider, so far as we can with faith brought near, how these things take place—not as the aforementioned Achish, who always says, “How can it be?” (I Sam. XXI), but as the true Abimelech, that is, “the kingdom of my father,” to whom it is truly said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

## CHAPTER III. Again, on the Oblation

With the aforesaid chant, the sacred oblation of bread and wine, having been received, reaches the holy altar in such a way that the subdeacon bears it to the deacon, and the deacon bears it to the hands [Col. 0036A] of the priest; or, as is done among the more careful, places it upon the altar itself. For the Law, which, as we have already said, is signified by the subdeacon, only prefigured in Melchizedek the sacrifice of our salvation; but through evangelical tradition it came to the altar—that is, to the solemn rite of the Church (Ps. CIX; Heb. VII).

## CHAPTER IV. On the Silence after the Offertory

After this the priest seeks the solitude of silence, as the memorial of the Lord’s Passion approaches. Turned toward the altar, he does so when the choir’s chant has ended and the whole Church has become silent. This signifies that our Lord no longer walked openly among the Jews when they were plotting to kill him, “but went away into the region near the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim [Col. 0036B], and stayed there with his disciples” (John XI).

“Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council, saying: ‘What are we doing? You see that we are accomplishing nothing. Behold, the whole world is going after him.’ And one of them, named Caiaphas, high priest that year, prophesied that it was expedient for one man to die for the people; and from that day they planned to kill him” (John XII).

This too is not devoid of mystery. For he who came in order to suffer did not hide himself through fear of the Passion, but outwardly displayed what was inwardly taking place in their hearts. For he was truly about to go into the region of the Gentiles by the feet of those who preach the Gospel—a region near the wilderness of those to whom he already then said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you [Col. 0036C] desolate” (Matt. XXIII)—not into the wilderness itself, which for him was the unbelief of the Jews.

Therefore, as the priest stands in silence and silently says the prayer over the offerings, he prepares the holy sacrifice. For our Lord, even while hiding himself and not walking openly among the Jews, was meditating for us the saving mystery of his Passion.

But since Passover was already near, and many had gone up to Jerusalem to sanctify themselves before Passover and sought him, saying: “What do you think? Will he not come to the feast day?”—while the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they might seize him—the Lord Jesus came to Bethany six days before Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he had raised. “And they made him a supper there, and Martha served,” because he then again walked openly, so that Lazarus was one of those reclining with him [Col. 0036D] (John XI, XII).

The priest again raises his voice, saying: “Through all ages of ages.” Since he is about to say something deserving attention, he first offers a greeting, wishing us also to be such persons as the Lord may deign to remain with and to make a feast among.

For then the Church ought to keep in mind that beautiful woman who brought to that feast “an alabaster jar of costly pure nard ointment and poured it upon the head of him reclining” (John XII), and ought to hear what the priest begins to say: “Lift up your hearts.” “We have them to the Lord.” Thus it too, like a true woman bearing ointment, may lift its heart upward to the very divinity of the Son of God [Col. 0037A], and, touching by faith that head equal to God the Father, anoint it with the ointment of Catholic confession, which the priest then sings.

For we ought to give thanks to our almighty God through Christ our Lord, believing and confessing that through him angels praise his majesty, dominions adore it, powers tremble, and so forth. Certainly this is to touch the hidden beginning of his divinity and to pour fragrant ointment of devotion upon his head.

This ointment is made from the essence of evangelical spice, namely from what John says of the Word: “In the beginning was God with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I). The house of the Church is now filled with this fragrance; but dying flies have ruined its sweetness [Col. 0037B] (Eccles. X)—that is, all heretics wrapped in filth, whom the dung of error feeds with stench and whom the words of truth kill by their good fragrance.

Therefore the priest, after the intervening silence mentioned above, raises his voice as though after the Lord’s hiding, and in some manner represents him openly coming to Bethany, openly feasting, and anointed with ointment. And the great woman, holy Church, completes that anointing of sacred confession in such a way that, together with the angels and the children who came out to meet the Lord on the following day, singing and raising palm branches (Matt. XXII), she sings this hymn of the devout heart: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Hosts [Sabaoth]” (Isa. VI), etc.

Where it says, “Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” she lets the aforesaid ointment of devout confession flow down, so that it may anoint not only the Lord’s head but also his feet: faithfully contemplating the Passion of the mortal man, to which he came blessed amid the aforesaid praises of the great crowds.

## CHAPTER V. On the Secret

After the joyful acclamation of the people follows the history of secret sorrow and the reason for deep silence. For the Secret is a memorial of the Lord’s Passion, and it enjoins silence upon the choir for as long as the course of the week before Easter continues in this order.

On the same day on which praises were cried out to the Son of David—the tenth day of the month, when that typical Paschal lamb was brought into the houses of the Jews [Col. 0037D] (Exod. XII)—this Lamb of God entered the city of Jerusalem. Beset by most wicked butchers, he was sought for death by many plots; delivered up by God the Father, “who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII); and likewise delivered up by himself, because “he loved us and gave himself up for us” (Eph. V).

On the second and third days they accomplish nothing (John XII), while the people do not dare to lay hands on him for fear (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXI), since a great multitude was around him, wholly occupied with hearing him. On the fourth day Judas, one of the twelve, overthrown by the devil, sold him to the Pharisees and promised to hand him over, so that they might seize him without the crowds (Mark XIV). On the fifth day, with the contest now near, he writes his testament for his heirs [Col. 0038A], entrusting to them the treasure of his body and blood (Luke XXII). That same night he is seized, bound, and mocked (ibid.). On the sixth day he is crucified: first by the tongues of the Jews, then by the hands of the Gentiles; finally, at the ninth hour, when an earthquake occurred, he gave up the spirit (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV; Luke XXIII). On the Sabbath he rested in the tomb. Rising from the dead on the first day of the Sabbath, he announced peace to his disciples and peace to the whole world (Matt. XXVIII; John XX).

The true form and appearance of all these events is represented so secretly in the Canon, and, through their course flowing over bread and wine as a truly living stream, we receive the true divinity and true humanity of Christ seated and reigning in heaven as truly as we may almost daily obtain the true substance of fire from the sun by placing a small crystal sphere beneath it [Col. 0038B].

The hands of Christ perform this through that sun: hands shaped like gold, full of hyacinths (Song V), the hands of him who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). The hands of Christ, I say, perform this through the priest’s hands, strengthened by his hands; especially because, in order that they may be able to perform this with him, through him, and in him, they have been marked with holy oil for the nails of his Passion.

Therefore it is not difficult to discover at what places in the Canon each of the matters set forth above is commemorated, especially since some of them are sufficiently evident in themselves.

## CHAPTER VI. “Therefore, you”

From the beginning of the Canon, namely “Therefore, you, most merciful Father” [*Te igitur clementissime Pater*], to the place, “The day before he suffered,” the meanings of four days are noted. On the first of these, the true Lamb—delivered up by God the Father or by himself, as was said (Rom. VIII; Eph. V)—was brought into the houses of Israel by coming into the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0038C]. This bringing in, or delivery, is marked by a threefold sign of the cross, in the words: “that you may accept these gifts, these offerings, these holy, unblemished sacrifices.”

On the fourth day he was handed over and sold by Judas; this sale, or betrayal, is likewise marked by three crosses in the words: “blessed, enrolled, ratified.” There the Church, which earlier, in its extreme poverty, had no victim to offer, said: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV). It gives thanks to the Holy Trinity because it has merited to receive the cup of salvation and call upon his name.

“These gifts,” it says, “these offerings.” The same sacrifices are gifts and offerings: gifts because they are given to us by him; offerings because they are offered to him by us. For a *donum* is given by one above; a *munus*, by one below.

There, I say, in the very first action, commemoration is made of all those to whom the same sacrifice belongs, and who correspond to it by a true likeness: though many, they are joined through one faith and one spirit into the one body of the Church, just as that bread is made from many grains and that wine has flowed together from many grapes. These are not only apostles and martyrs, but all the faithful who, trusting in their merits, hope that this will benefit them for salvation—those for whom it already benefits toward honor [Col. 0039A].

Therefore, as [or: since, *quoniam*] it is written: “No stranger shall eat of them, because they are holy” (Exod. XXIX), we receive for eating of this Lamb only one who is joined to our household (Lev. XXII): namely, every member of the household of faith (Gal. VI), from prince to commoner, from apostle to publican.

## CHAPTER VII. “This oblation, therefore”

In the following section of the prayer, we ask that the sacred oblation may be blessed, enrolled, ratified, and reasonable, as is a conscientious embassy seeking the public welfare. For it is the embassy of that king “who, unable with ten thousand to meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand, sends and asks for terms of peace” [Col. 0039B] (Luke XIV).

Since we are unable to be justified before him by deeds alone—he who will exact an account not only of deeds but of thoughts, and who comes as it were with a double army—we send the embassy of the present sacrifice and ask for terms of peace. It is a matter of great praise, however, to conduct this embassy in such a manner that the utterance of the Church may merit blessing from him to whom it is sent, just as David blessed the wise Abigail, saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, and blessed be your speech, and blessed be you, who have kept me today from going to bloodshed and avenging myself with my own hand” (I Sam. XXV).

For Abigail, whose name is interpreted “the exultation of my father,” namely holy Church—once the wife of Nabal, that is, “the fool,” namely the devil—anticipates, by the embassy of the present sacrifice, the Word David, that is, Christ, “strong of hand” or “beloved.” As he endures the persecutions of Saul—that is, struggles toward the Passion of death [Col. 0039C]—she asks him for peace, lest he avenge himself by his own hand against foolish Nabal, in such a way that she too should perish with him in eternal damnation.

Since she hastens without the counsel or knowledge of that fool, follows the gifts sent beforehand with prayer, and, worshipping, wisely speaks words of peace, she makes the oblation blessed when her utterance is blessed; enrolled, when no oblivion erases it; and ratified, when the forgiveness of sins having been granted cannot afterward be undone by any alteration of judgment.

## CHAPTER VIII. “The day before he suffered,” to “Do this in remembrance of me”

The miracle of such novelty is made whole anew, and whatever we attempt to say, speech, compared with the thing itself, appears scarcely to possess any weight at all. For especially when the summit of the highest mystery has been reached—when one has come to the very heart of the holy sacrifice—speech fails, the tongue gives way, and uncircumcised lips accuse the equally uncircumcised mind of rashness and insolence in its undertaking.

“For who knows the order of heaven, or will set forth its reasons on earth?” (Job XXXVIII). For the order of heaven has shone upon us from this present chapter; its brightness could not be borne by the often-mentioned and still-to-be-mentioned Achish (I Sam. XXI). The supreme priest, about to depart from here into the sanctuary of heaven by the way of the Passion [Col. 0040A], now performs sacrifice in a wondrous manner according to his own order, according to the rite of the heavenly sacrifice: taking bread into his holy and venerable hands and saying, “This is my body”; taking the splendid cup of wine and saying, “This is the cup of my blood” (Matt. XXVI).

What then? Shall we be silent, and by our silence seem to agree with those whose polluted lips the Seraph did not touch with the glowing coal (Isa. VI) which it brought from the altar, and who always say: “How can it be? How can it be?” On the contrary, let us cry out. And lest we lack what to cry, let us knock at the door of the friend who customarily lends three loaves (Luke XI): that is, faith, hope, and charity, which are especially necessary in this matter. For he permits us, not to contradict, but to desire knowledge.

Therefore, lest we be altogether ignorant of how this is, let us now consider, in the order of so wonderful a sacrifice, the three things which we customarily seek in the work of any distinguished author: its matter, its intention, and its final cause or usefulness. When the chamberlain of truth has opened each of these to us with the little key of grace, as we knock with the hand of faith, “even if not yet face to face, at least through a mirror and in an enigma, we shall see how it is” [Col. 0040B] (II Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER IX. Matter
The matter or substance of the sacrifice, which was then and now is in the hands of our high priest, is not simple, just as the high priest himself is not of divine substance alone or human substance alone. For both in the high priest [Col. 0040C] and in the sacrifice there is a divine substance, and there is also an earthly one. In each, the earthly element is that which can be seen bodily or locally; in each, the divine element is the invisible Word, “which in the beginning was God with God.”

For when that same great high priest, holding bread and wine, said, “This is my body; this is my blood,” it was the voice of the Incarnate Word, the voice of the eternal Beginning, the word of the ancient counsel. The Word which had taken human nature—that is, while remaining in flesh—received the substance of bread and wine as an intervening medium, joining bread to his flesh and wine to his blood.

Just as, in bodily perception, the tongue intervenes between the mind and the corporeal air, and, joining the two, produces one utterance, which, once sent forth [Col. 0040D] into the ears, is quickly consumed and passes away insofar as it is audible, while the meaning of the utterance remains whole and unconsumed both in the speaker and in the hearer: so the Word of the Father, intervening between the flesh and blood which he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb, and the bread and wine which he took from the altar, makes one sacrifice. When the priest distributes this sacrifice into the mouths of the faithful, the bread and wine are consumed and pass away; but the Virgin’s offspring, united to the Word of the Father, remains whole and unconsumed, both in heaven and among human beings.

But to one in whom faith is absent, nothing of the sacrifice comes except the visible appearances of bread and wine. As an ass at a lyre, when it raises its irrational ears, hears the sound indeed but does not perceive the measure of the melody. Such persons are compared [Col. 0041A] to the Jews or to their fathers, of whom the Lord says: “Your fathers ate manna and died” (John 6). But those who receive with faith are compared to those of whom the Apostle says: “Our fathers all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10). For some, through unbelief, are the fathers of Jews and heretics; others, through faith, are the fathers of apostles and believers.

The invisible bread, which came down from heaven, is life. The visible bread, which grew from the earth, is nevertheless one bread; just as he who came down from heaven, and he who was conceived and born from the Virgin’s womb, is one Christ. Therefore, whoever eats the visible bread of the sacrifice yet, through unbelief, rejects the invisible bread from his heart [Col. 0041B] kills Christ, because he separates life from that which has been made alive, tears with his teeth the dead body of the sacrifice, and thereby is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 11).

But the adversary says: God-and-man Christ is living, sentient, and movable in his own body. But the body of the sacrifice has no life, no sensation, and is not movable. From this premise he concludes: “Therefore it is not the body of the Lord; it is not Christ.”

To this I say: I beg you, what sort of life do you seek in the Lord’s body? There is animal life, and there is spiritual life. Animal life operates through the five senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. This is animal life; it is fleshly life; it is flesh. “But the Lord says that the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). If the Jews [Col. 0041C] had wished, or had been able, to cut up and devour the flesh which they crucified as they would the flesh of a lamb, or to swallow it whole and alive, as the sea-monster swallowed Jonah alive (Jonah 2), it would have profited them nothing; indeed, they would have defiled their consciences by a greater sacrilege.

Therefore, if animal life, because it is flesh, were present in the Lord’s body, it would profit us nothing; and for this reason it is superfluous to seek it. For what would the heavenly man administer to us through this heavenly sacrifice that we did not lack? It is not his wisdom to feed our curiosity with unnecessary miracles. Curious Herod sought this when he had long desired to see Jesus, because he hoped to see some sign performed by him (Luke 23). Because Jesus did not do this, Herod despised him and sent him back clothed [Col. 0041D] in a white garment.

Therefore his wisdom ought to administer to us in the sacrifice spiritual life alone. This was also fitting for our need: namely, sanctification and blessing, mercy and truth, justice and peace. His spiritual life is present in the body of the sacrifice without his animal life, as the light of the sun is represented to us in the body of the moon without its heat. Therefore the supreme high priest constituted this sacrifice for us from those things by which the whole human being is nourished: from the Word of God, in which the human being lives (Deut. 8), and from the fruits of the earth, by which the body alone lives—namely, from those which are foremost among all such things. Bread is foremost among things pertaining to food; wine, among things pertaining to drink.

### Chapter X. [Col. 0042A] Intention

While we seek the intention of so great a work, the utterly pure eye of so luminous a body, our own eye too must be single and our body luminous: that is, we must be led by the desire to learn, not by a purpose of contradiction. Where, then, shall we find the admirable eye of this beauty—that is, the end toward which the sacrament of so beautiful a work tends? In the very head itself: in that same word of truth which sounded forth to us.

For he says: “As often as you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me. Whoever has ears to hear” (Matt. 26) receives this saying as the grief-stricken affection of a father dying for his children; as the utterance of genuine devotion; as the sharply pointed dart of wounding love. [Col. 0042B] “Because his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father,” because what he said to the disciples was true: “Where I am going, you cannot come” (John 13). And when Peter said, “Lord, where are you going?” he replied, “Where I am going, you cannot follow me” (ibid.). Because, I say, Peter could not then follow him, Christ, drawing up for them the inheritance due to them, entrusted to them a visible memorial of himself.

For he judged the reminder of the Scriptures alone insufficient for this purpose. He had undertaken to cure a sick person prone to forgetfulness and in large part incapable of learning: namely, the human race. Behold the difficulty of that medicinal discipline which is in the sacred Scriptures. What portion of us is capable of receiving that antidote, fragrant in the holy Gospel with the finest ointments: [Col. 0042C] “In the beginning was the Word,” God with God, through whom all things were made, and who was made flesh? (John 1). To chew this over is indeed a most approved remedy, sweet to the palate of the loving soul; but so great a food belongs to very few.

Moreover, this meditation is nourishment for the mind alone and sanctification for the soul alone. But he ardently desired to bind both elements of us, body and soul, to himself; he hastened to heal both, both infirm—indeed, both dead—by the medicine of immortality. Therefore, by a great art of love, the Wisdom of God compounded his remedies, so that by the daily renewed remembrance of its salvation he might strike the lethargic mind of the great sick man; and so that he might accustom the toothless infant multitude of souls, which [Col. 0042D] could not grind and chew the solid food of the Word, the ancient and eternal Beginning, to drink, in this most sweet liquid prepared for them, the divinity of that same Word in the sacrament of bread and wine.

Take from the assembly of the Church these daily funeral rites of our Savior, and see whom the Savior himself might rightly call out to: “What profit is there in my blood?” (Ps. 29). For as the memory of him, now glowing everywhere in this manner, grows cold, all charity will grow cold; faith will become mute; hope will limp; the great cry of the blood of righteous Abel will fall silent (Gen. 4). Through the rite of so great a sacrifice handed down to us, that blood daily restores its voice, daily opens the mouth of the drinking and crying earth—that is, the Church—rebuking the accursed Cain and demanding the due vengeance for blood shamefully shed. [Col. 0043A] Therefore, while this memory remains warm through so great a celebration, Christ’s charity grows warm, the edifice of faith stands firm upon its foundation, and hope is revived through the daily remission of sins (Matt. 24).

### Chapter XI. Usefulness

This is the usefulness contained in the power of this sacrament: by its aid it becomes possible for those who are on earth to ascend to heaven. Otherwise this is impossible; for the Savior says: “No one ascends into heaven except the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 5).

To the one and only Son of Man who descended from heaven—because he is one person with the Son of God, with the Word of the Father, which descended from heaven and came from the Father’s heart into the Virgin’s womb—to this one and only Son of God [Col. 0043B] and Son of Man, as to their head, all the members of the body are joined (Col. 2): all who are received in faith in this sacrament and in the fullness of this charity. Thus one body, one person, one Christ—the head with his members—ascends into heaven (Eph. 5), and, joyfully ascribing a glorious Church to God, says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2). And showing that he and she have come together into unity of person, he says: “The two shall be one flesh.” This is a great sacrament.

The flesh of Christ, which before the Passion was the flesh only of the Word of God, through the Passion so increased, was so enlarged, and so filled the whole world, that through the new mixture of this sacrament it makes all the elect—those who have existed from the beginning of the world and those who will exist until the last elect person at the end of the age—into one Church, joining God and human beings together eternally. [Col. 0043C] That flesh was one grain of wheat; before it had fallen into the earth and died, it was one grain, but now, after it has died, it grows upon the altar, bears fruit in our hands and bodies, and when the great and wealthy lord of the harvest ascends, he carries with him into the granaries of heaven the fruitful earth in which it grew (John 15).

### Chapter XII. “Wherefore, O Lord, we thy servants”; through “and the chalice of everlasting salvation”

Since, then, the usefulness of the memorial entrusted to us is so great, blessed Church next sets before herself three emblems of that same memorial: namely, so blessed a Passion, also the resurrection from the dead, and likewise the glorious ascension into heaven. The first wounds the Church’s charity, the second strengthens faith, and the third gladdens hope.

For when, in saying “a pure offering, a holy offering, an unspotted offering, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” she impresses upon the substance of bread and wine the fivefold sign of the cross, she directs the instructed contemplator of these realities to that blessed Passion—to Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father and, as has been said, truly incorporated with it. [Col. 0043D] For from this point until he removes the corporal covering from above, the agony and Passion of him hanging on the cross are breathed forth. These, therefore, are the clefts of the living rock in which the beautiful and unspotted dove—that is, the Church—dwells; and in them she makes her nest most securely when, within the aforesaid words or the five signs of the cross, she holds and contemplates in faithful memory the five wounds of her beloved: two of the hands, as many of the feet, and one of the side. [Col. 0044A]

### Chapter XIII. “As thou hast deigned to accept the gifts of Abel,” and the rest

The comparison concerns likeness, not degree. For this sacrifice is far more acceptable to God than that which Abel offered, that which Abraham offered, or that which Melchizedek offered. For the reality is more powerful than the shadow, truth than the figure. Therefore let us seek the likeness itself rather than equality in the degree of acceptance.

By offering, we are like Abel if, while offering rightly [Col. 0044B], we also divide rightly. Because Cain did not do this, he sinned (Gen. 4). He rightly offered to God what was due to God; but, keeping himself for himself and withholding his heart from God, he divided wrongly. Abel, however, offered the sacrifice of righteousness inwardly in his heart, because he did not keep himself for himself but subjected himself to God; and therefore the Lord looked graciously upon his outward gifts. Likewise Abraham first offered his whole self in outstanding faith; and therefore, when he offered what was his, he offered acceptable sacrifices (Gen. 22). So that we might know and imitate this, God demanded of him a father’s affection and commanded him to sacrifice [supply: his son] to him; and immediately found his spirit ready—or rather, displayed it to us.

Nor could Melchizedek, unless he had first offered himself [Col. 0044C] and laid up his heart upon the high altar of God, have foreseen the reasons for which he first offered, without precedent, a sacrifice of bread and wine (Gen. 14). Therefore we too, if, standing ready to offer, we divide rightly as has been said—that is, first offering ourselves, slaughtering and mortifying the ram-like spirit because of the way, the bull-like fierceness, and the goat-like lust, in accordance with what we sing in the psalm: “I will offer to thee fat burnt offerings with incense of rams; I will offer to thee bulls with goats” (Ps. 65)—have divided rightly. Therefore the Lord deigns to accept our sacrifices as he accepted the gifts of Abel, the sacrifice of Abraham, and the unspotted offering of Melchizedek. [Col. 0044B]

And, in accordance with the following prayer, he commands that these be borne by the hands of his holy angel to his high altar and into the presence of his divine majesty, in a non-local and invisible manner. For his majesty is everywhere non-local and invisible; everywhere is his high altar, which is the faith of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0044D]

### Chapter XIV. “To us also, thy sinful servants”

It is the practice of many churches, when they come to the words, “To us also, thy sinful servants,” to break the silence by raising the voice a little. For at that moment of the Lord’s Passion, the confession of the thief ought to come to our minds (Luke 23), together with the Lord’s response from the tribunal of the cross, assigning him to paradise.

### Chapter XV. [Col. 0045A] “Through whom, O Lord, thou dost always create all these good things”

Finally, with the three crosses by which the priest declares, “Through whom, O Lord, thou dost always create all these good things, sanctify, give life, and bless,” the Passion of the Lord is brought to completion; and we are reminded of the fact that, crying with a loud voice, he gave up his spirit (Matt. 27).

Therefore the corporal covering is immediately removed, because the veil of the temple was torn; indeed, because those things written concerning him, which until then had been closed and covered, and whatever he had foretold concerning his Passion had been a word hidden from them, were now, when all had been accomplished (Luke 28), also revealed. And when, with the chalice uncovered, the threefold sign of the cross is made with the offering above [Col. 0045B] the chalice, with the words, “Through him, and with him, and in him,” it expresses the confession made in the words of the centurion, who, seeing the earthquake and the things that occurred, cried with a loud voice: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27).

The two crosses made at the side of the chalice, with the words “all honor and glory,” represent for us the sacraments of blood and water which, when the soldier’s lance opened the Lord’s side, flowed forth for the redemption of our salvation. Then the deacon approaches, and both he and the priest reverently set down again upon the altar the sacrifice which had been raised a little, because Joseph of Arimathea came with the centurion, and Nicodemus also; and, having obtained Jesus’ body from Pilate, they took it down and buried it. They buried it, I say, as is signified for us by the chalice’s being covered again with the corporal. [Col. 0045C]

At this point blessed Gregory fittingly decreed that the Lord’s Prayer should be said, maintaining that it was incongruous that, while a prayer composed by a schoolman was said over the Eucharist, the prayer which our Lord himself had personally taught should not be said. Although he seems to have received this practice from the Greeks, he nevertheless wished it to differ in this respect: among the Greeks it is said by all the people, while among us it is sung by the priest alone.

Therefore, because Jesus, as has been said, gave up the spirit crying with a loud voice; because the centurion cried, “Truly this was the Son of God”; and because the women lamented, weeping for the Lord, the priest raises his voice, saying, “For ever and ever,” and then says the Lord’s Prayer. Likewise the choir responds, imitating [Col. 0045D] the few faithful persons who mourned the Lord with hearts crushed and broken—just as once, when Abel was slain by the envious fury of his wicked brother, a few kinsfolk lamented in impatient grief and unaccustomed anguish of heart. After this, a brief silence is again observed, signifying the Sabbath on which the Lord rested in the tomb.

### Chapter XVI. “The peace of the Lord be always with you”

Then the raising of the voice again signifies the good news of the Lord’s resurrection, when the priest says: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” This commends to us the fact that our Lord, standing in the midst of his disciples, said to them: “Peace be with you” [Col. 0046A] (John 29; Luke 24). Meanwhile, holding the body of the Lord, because he was made known in the breaking of bread, he assigns his offering, by a threefold breaking, to the holy Trinity; and he immerses one particle, signifying the person of the Son, in the sacred blood.

### Chapter XVII. “Lamb of God, who takest away”

Immediately the rejoicing Church’s memorial passes on to the glory of the ascension, saying: “Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. Thou who sittest at the right hand of God the Father, have mercy upon us.” For God raised him up to grant repentance and the remission of sins (Heb. 10; Acts 5), and exalted him as Prince and Savior.

### Chapter XVIII. [Col. 0046B] On Communion

Then, by a religious custom, we give and receive from one another the kiss of peace entrusted to us by the priest, rejoicing and recalling that “we have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5), and signifying by the kiss of peace that we ought to be bound together (Eph. 4), which is the bond of perfection (Col. 5).

The chant which we call the Communion, and which we sing after the saving food, is a thanksgiving, according to the words: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 21).

### Chapter XIX. On the Post-Communion Prayer

[Col. 0046C] The prayers called the *collectae*, said to conclude the rite, signify the prayers of our head, Jesus Christ, seated in heaven. As the Apostle says: “He died—rather, he also rose again” (Rom. 14); “he is at the right hand of God; he also intercedes for us.” For the supreme high priest intercedes for us, because through that in which he is like us he reconciles us, and through that in which he is equal to the Father he absolves us.

### Chapter XX. On “Let us bless the Lord”

The deacon adds the final portion, namely, “Let us bless the Lord”; and by this saying he urges the people to give thanks to God for the benefits received. For surely, with the Redeemer seated at the Father’s right hand [Col. 0046D] and interceding for us, his apostles persist in saying to us: “Give thanks always; pray without ceasing” (Eph. 5; 1 Thess. 5).

But if there is a festival, looking toward the time when the sending of our salvation was celebrated, the deacon, clothed in a dalmatic and signifying the perfection of future blessedness, then says: “Go, the dismissal is made.” For this is the solemn dismissal of the people, relying on the reverent modulation of its utterance to express the dignity of the event and, as it were, to fix its memory in the hearts of the departing people with a final touch.

This most holy mystery of the altar is called *missa* (“dismissal” or “sending”) because it is the one sending able and sufficient to bring about the appeasement and dissolution of the enmities (Eph. 5) that existed between God and human beings.

### Chapter XXI. [Col. 0047A] How, and by whom, the Office of the Mass was arranged

Formerly the solemnities of the Mass were not celebrated with so great an outward display of beauty, nor was all this glory of religious observance completed and polished by any one person. Rather, the sacred pontiffs, splendid lights of the Roman See, as they shone forth in different times, gradually perfected by the brightness of their zeal the beauty of this saving office.

And just as David and Solomon in particular enlarged more splendidly the order of the old sacrifice handed down by the Lord through Moses—by the ministry of priests and Levites (1 Chron. 23), the great number of singers, the festive music of divine psalms, the splendid magnificence of temple and altar, and the multitude of sacred vessels (3 Kings 7)—so the holy Roman Church, receiving through the first apostles the wondrous rite of the new sacrifice handed down by the Lord, embraced it in religious faith, preserved it with faithful care, and adorned it with diligent provision.

We shall now state, then, what each of them contributed, following rather the order of the things which were arranged than that of the persons who arranged them.

### Ordinance of Pope Celestine

Celestine, the forty-first pope, established that all one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice. Previously this had not been done; only the epistle and Gospel were recited. As a result of this ordinance, Introits, Graduals, Offertories, and Communions selected from the psalms began to be sung with musical settings at Mass in the Roman Church. [Col. 0047C]

### Gregory

Gregory, the sixty-first [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, the sixty-first pope from Blessed Peter.], systematically compiled and arranged the Antiphonary. He ordered that the clergy should sing *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) at Masses, whereas among the Greeks it was sung by all the people. He caused *Alleluia* (“Praise the Lord”) to be said at Masses outside Pentecost. In the Canon he added three words over the offering: “And order our days in thy peace, command that we be delivered from eternal damnation, and numbered in the flock of thine elect.” He also decreed that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited after the Canon over the offering.

### Symmachus

Symmachus, the forty-ninth pope, established that “Glory in the highest” should be sung at Mass every Sunday [Col. 0047D] and on the feasts of martyrs. Pope Telesphorus, the seventh from Blessed Peter, had established that this hymn should be sung at Masses on the night of the Lord’s Nativity only—Masses which he himself instituted on that very night—and added to it the words that follow the words of the angels.

### Gelasius

Gelasius, the forty-seventh pope, composed tracts and hymns, and dictated the prefaces of the sacraments in a careful and polished style.

### Innocent

Innocent, the thirty-eighth pope, decreed that the kiss of peace should be given before Communion.

### Leo

[Col. 0048A]

Leo, the forty-third pope, who was very powerful in delivering homilies, added to the Canon: “a holy sacrifice, an unspotted offering.”

### Damasus

Damasus, the thirty-fifth pope, instituted the singing of “I believe in one God,” in accordance with the decree of the holy universal synod held at Constantinople by one hundred and fifty bishops.

### Alexander

Alexander, the sixth pope, established at the consecration of the Eucharist that, just as blood and water flowed from the side of the crucified Lord (John 19), so water should be mixed with wine in that consecration. He decreed that neither wine without water nor water without wine ought to be offered.

### Sixtus

[Col. 0048B]

Sixtus, the seventh pope, instituted the singing of the hymn: “Holy, Holy, Holy.”

### Sergius

Sergius, the eightieth pope, made this final ordinance: that during Communion the clergy should sing “Lamb of God.” Thus the Roman Church, zealous for the divine law, gradually brought forth from its treasury new memorials of devotion, and fashioned for the holy sacrifice a kind of diadem of religious office, as though from gold and precious stones.

Yet the sacrifice is not thereby holier than it was before, [supply: when] it was consecrated with the Lord’s words alone and the Lord’s Prayer alone. But it was especially fitting that faith, which [Col. 0048C] at that time was still unformed and, as a certain writer both learned and faithful says, “dishevelled in rustic dress, with bare shoulders, unshorn hair, and exposed arms,” should, where it could be adorned, be gilded especially in this respect, as though in its head, and should shine with the venerable symbolism of the matters set forth above.

### Chapter XXII. On Unleavened Bread
Why the holy Roman Church has never admitted leaven into the sacrifice is a question neither idle to ask nor useless to know, especially since all Greece has hitherto opposed this custom. For the Greeks offer sacrifice with leaven, and, supported by some authority—I know not what authority, certainly one never derived from the authentic Scriptures—they most obstinately reject the Roman Church’s practice, both legal and [Col. 0048D] evangelical. They have very often been defeated by sound arguments; yet the arrogance of the see of Constantinople, mother of many heresies, has disdained to yield.

Pope Leo IX, the 148th of this name from blessed Peter, conciliated the mind of Emperor Constantine by a letter written to him, and sent to Constantinople his legates: Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida; Peter, archbishop of Amalfi; and Frederick also, a levite and chancellor. He refuted many Greek heresies. Among other things, they called the Latins “Azymites,” that is, users of unleavened bread; and, persecuting them severely, they closed their churches. He also struck Michael [Col. 0049A] the patriarch—removed from the emperor’s favour and court—with the sword of excommunication.

Greece, however, has been so leavened with great heresies that it should not seem surprising that it offers sacrifice with leaven. Holy Roman Church, by contrast, has always possessed such purity that, even for one lacking knowledge of the Scriptures or the ability to argue, her authority alone ought to suffice regarding unleavened bread against the Greeks. For Constantinople has produced not only heretics but many heresiarchs. But the Roman Church, more deeply founded upon the rock of apostolic faith, has stood firm; it has always refuted the heretics both of Greece and of the whole world, and, from the lofty tribunal of faith, has rendered judgment.

Nevertheless, scriptural support ought not to be lacking, lest so pure an authority seem to have suffered any loss [Col. 0049B] at all. Such support could be sought more certainly and conveniently if it were established in writing or by a reliable author what reasoning the Greeks think they possess in favour of leavened bread. For the Roman Church’s custom accords with legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic reasons.

Some report that they have heard this argument from Greeks who use leavened bread: Mary was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, and therefore Christ’s incarnation and the manifest swelling of the virgin womb are rightly signified by leavened bread. Whoever among them relies on this reasoning is farther from the rule of sound teaching than if he gave no reasons whatever for the practice in question. For why do they offer leavened bread in order to signify Mary’s pregnant and swollen womb? On this account, plainly, they wish the bread of sacrifice to be Mary, while the bread’s defect—namely, leaven—is Christ her Son.

This reasoning is rejected as unsound on two evident grounds. First, because we must offer not Mary’s body, but the body of Christ alone, who alone was crucified for us. Second, because no authority whatever in Sacred Scripture, whether Old or New Testament, supports leaven as signifying anything good. We recall the memory of the Lord’s incarnation more beautifully and rationally from the holy Gospel. For when the Lord said of the bread which he took, “This is my body” (Matt. 26), as often as we repeat that most sacred action, we renew his incarnation for ourselves in such a way that, for this purpose, we require not the womb of blessed Mary, but her faith alone, [Col. 0049C] by which she conceived.

The visible altar is the sign of that faith, as the teachers of the Church rightly hold. Therefore, when the Word of God, descending through the faith of the Church, takes bread from the sign of faith, which is the altar, there is renewed for us that event in which the same Word of God, descending through the Virgin’s faith into her womb, assumed flesh. Thus we renew the Lord’s incarnation, not as leaven in bread signifies Mary, but as the Word of God in bread signifies the Catholic Church: for just as the one bread is made from many grains, so the Church is one body constituted from many persons through unity of faith.

I have said that the Church is signified by that bread, not insofar as it [Col. 0049D] is offered and consecrated, but insofar as it is made, as stated, from many grains. For insofar as it is consecrated, it does not signify even the individual body of the Lord, but is a transfusion into itself of the Word of God through faith in the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension. For the Lord does not say, “This signifies my body,” but, “This is my body.” Therefore the aforesaid argument from leaven is weak and deservedly contemptible.

Unleavened bread, however, derives from both evangelical and legal authority. For the Lord, both in the Law—where he commanded the typical sacrifice of Passover—ordered leaven to be cast out (Exod. 12; Deut. 16), and in the Gospel—where he himself first celebrated the new sacrifice—likewise consecrated unleavened bread. And lest perhaps you suppose otherwise: at that time leaven was not to be found in the houses of Israel, [Col. 0050A] for this had been established by the law of the Lord. Therefore, when moving from the old sacrifice to the new, he did not leave aside unleavened bread, but blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Mark 14; Luke 22). Did he say anything about leaven, or complain that leaven had been lacking to him because the custom of the Law compelled it? Rather, he who commanded unleavened bread in the Law ought not, under grace, to establish its opposite.

It must be noted and remembered that none of the practices of the ancient Law has been destroyed by the arrival of contrary decrees from the Gospel. Those practices which have been abolished or superseded gave place to better things, not contrary things—as circumcision gave place to baptism. Circumcision is indeed good, but baptism is better. Nor did God act changeably when he preferred what is better to what is good, especially since that people had made the good thing void, as God himself reproaches them through the prophet, saying: “And you have made my covenant void” (Mal. 2), and so forth.

Rather, uncircumcision seems opposed to circumcision, as possession is opposed to deprivation. Yet the Lord said nothing concerning uncircumcision; indeed, he was silent about both. “For circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing,” says the Apostle, “but faith working through love” (Gal. 5). Unleavened bread and leaven, however, are plainly opposed as immediate contraries. Therefore it did not befit God, as though laying down things contrary to himself, to reject unleavened bread and prescribe leaven, which he had formerly prohibited when he said: “You shall not sacrifice the blood of my offering upon leaven” (Exod. 23).

God approves unleavened bread [Col. 0050D] not for its own sake, but for the sake of that of which it is a sign. For it signifies that we who sacrifice should feast at the Paschal banquet “not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

Nor should this signification of so necessary a matter be rejected because it is known to have come from the ceremonies of the ancient Law. For we have not rejected all the significant practices of that Law (Exod. 12). We still observe the full face of the moon and never celebrate Passover during its waning; daily we burn sacred incense to the Lord as a sweet savour; we possess holy anointing oil (Lev. 2; Exod. 10); in place of trumpets we have bells; and there are many other such things [Col. 0051A] (Num. 10). For the things signified are good moral things; accordingly, we celebrate all their signs in reading, and some also in action, so that the things signified themselves may be impressed upon our senses in season and out of season. Who would dare disapprove this?

Following the example of the apostles and teachers, we also customarily take from the Gentiles whatever has been rightly said or done by others, and cut away the superfluous nails and hair of the captive woman (Deut. 21), so that the thought, cleansed of foreign falsehood, may be worthy to enter the bridal chamber of truth. How much more naturally and justly, then, does the Church remember her own antiquities? She boasts in the Song of Songs and says: “All manner of new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Song 7).

Therefore unleavened bread was not to be rejected because it had been handed down in the ancient Law for the sake of signification; rather, it was to be retained precisely because what it signifies is best and more fitting for this time of grace. For it signifies what the apostolic trumpet declares should rightly be understood: namely, that between Christ—who from the sinful mass assumed sinless flesh, as unleavened bread from leavened—and the Christian people, there should be no malice or wickedness, just as in unleavened bread with leaven and water there enters nothing of the old mass or of an alien mixture [Col. 0051B] (1 Cor. 5).

Water signifies the people, according to the words: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32). That Christ is signified by wheat can be proved by no better authority than his own: predicting figuratively that he would be put to death by the unbelief of the Jews and multiplied by the faith of the peoples, he says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 15 [sic]). Water mixed with wheat without leaven signifies that the peoples, joined to Christ by faith, ought to be simple.

Since, therefore, it is a memorial of the sincerity and truth in whose unleavened bread the Apostle exhorts us to feast after the old leaven has been purged away (1 Cor. 5), so that we may be a new dough, unleavened bread has rightly been preserved among the useful signs of the ancient Law. Christ, the great high priest, is its author; and through blessed Peter, his successor, it was faithfully entrusted to the Roman Church. Blessed is that Church, because it received in its foundation [Col. 0051C] the rock which Truth praised and declared blessed from his own mouth (Matt. 16). It has been built upon that rock with such construction that it has stood as an unconquerable wall against all heresies. From whatever quarter of the world faith has been endangered, it has fled to her and found hanging from her, ready and prepared, “a thousand shields and all the armour of the mighty” (Song 4), with which it might defend itself.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the adornment of the altar or church

The most holy ministry of the altar is called the *missa*, as was said, because it is the sole effective and fitting embassy sent to reconcile the enmity that existed between God and humankind. Although its divine rationale possesses unceasing splendour, its outward observance—in the sacred vessels, the furnishing of the altar, and the vesture of its ministers—is always holy, but, according to the differing character of days and seasons, sometimes more splendid [Col. 0052A].

Gold and silver, precious stones, and, according to the ability of the faithful in each place, festive devotion shine forth. In worldly matters such things are emblems of ambition; in ecclesiastical and divine matters they are offices of piety. This is not because golden rather than earthen vessels, jewelled rather than bare ones, delight God, who is spirit, more greatly; it is because people willingly offer to God what they love, and by the love of God through which they separate it from themselves, whatever it may be is made precious to God.

For they love gold, which is pre-eminently the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes (1 John 2). Therefore, when they offer it to God, who does not need it, as David poured out to the Lord the water for which he had longed, beyond doubt what they offer is holy and pleasing to God (2 Sam. 23). It would be most blameworthy to anoint the feet of luxurious and wicked people as ointment was poured over the Lord’s feet—ointment which could have been sold for much and given to the poor (Matt. 26; John 12). Yet the devoted woman laudably did this for the Lord because the Lord, who had no need of this act, weighed against a pound of precious ointment a pound, rather, of piety and faith. Therefore, in return for the fragrance spread through one house, he caused the woman’s memorial to be proclaimed throughout the world [Col. 0052B].

Thus, when Christ is honoured in the furnishings of the altar by gold, stones, and silken vestments, these too might be given to the poor; but the adornment of the Lord’s table is not therefore rightly condemned. When its condition is uncared-for, it is not without blame on the part of those who seem able to adorn it.

For when the Lord rebukes the people through the prophet for saying, “The table of the Lord is defiled” (Mal. 1), he seems to do so because what was thought to be the altar’s defilement—its bare poverty—was then without blame. On returning from Babylon, the people had made only an altar from chance and unworked stones, as Jerome says: without a temple, without buildings of the city, and without constructed walls. They supposed religious worship lessened because the temple’s ornament was lacking; nor did they understand that almighty God seeks neither gold and gems nor a multitude of sacrifices, but the disposition of those who offer.

But where opportunity and resources were not lacking, the Lord himself commanded works of gold and silver to be made for him with the highest craftsmanship [Col. 0052C] (Exod. 25, 26, and 27). Nor should that saying of blessed Jerome immediately be objected to us: if we receive these things from the Old Testament, then consequently we should also receive the rite of sacrifices, the law of the Sabbath, and similar matters. For his statement argues only that ornaments of gold or gems for divine worship should not be demanded as necessary. Writing against Vigilantius, and likewise to the virgin Demetrias, he does indeed prefer almsgiving to the poor; yet concerning such matters, he says, “Let each one abound in his own judgment; I neither condemn nor censure” (Rom. 14).

By a clear argument we also conclude that such figures as blessed Gregory morally expounds concerning the construction of the tabernacle are not so dissolved by the presence of truth that they ought not even now to be set forth in the outward worship of the Church on a similar, or the same, rationale—so that from that tabernacle may shine forth to us what ought to be the adornment of God’s inner house, which we are.

Although the author of the figurative promises, both old and new, changed the sacraments because he fulfilled the promises and, as great Leo says, put an end to the announcements, since the one announced had come, nevertheless in moral precepts or figures [Col. 0053A] (1 Cor. 3) no decrees of the former Testament have been rejected; rather, many have been augmented by evangelical teaching. The Gospel sets forth sayings and deeds, parables and allegorical likenesses, more beautifully than the Law, and Christ does so more frequently than the prophets. Following his teaching, the Church imitates invisible things by the arrangement of visible things—not only in the sacred vesture of those ministers discussed above, but also in the other adornment of church and altar.

For if no spiritual realities are signified in these things as well, why are costly cloths and wholly silken hangings suspended on the walls, and why is the most holy body of the Lord covered when placed upon a linen corporal? According to its dignity, we would rightly place around it whatever most precious thing we could possess. Therefore certain mysteries worthy of inquiry and understanding have been perceived in these things, with due discrimination.

The linen corporal, on which we celebrate the memorial of the Lord’s passion, signifies his tribulation and the singular purity of his flesh. Linen is born from the earth and, worn down by many pressures, attains the dignity of snowy whiteness and fine smoothness. It rises from the earth coarse and undistinguished, but under the hands of pressing workers it is refined and made white. Thus we perceive the Lord’s tribulation in the linen corporal. “For he grew up like a shoot and like a root from thirsty ground, having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53) [Col. 0053B]; but because of the purity of his soul, which he gave for our sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.

More attentive observers ensure that the corporal is double, signifying the linen cloths for the Lord’s head in which Joseph wrapped his body after anointing it with spices (Matt. 23 [sic]; Luke 23). The cloths which, as stated, are solemnly hung on the church walls signify the future glory of the holy Church in Christ’s kingdom, which the present solemnities recall to us: the kingdom “where Christ will present to himself a glorious bride, without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5).

The Gospel books too are deservedly adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones: in them gleams the gold of heavenly wisdom; shines the silver of faithful eloquence; and flash the precious stones of miracles, fashioned by the golden hands of Christ, worked with hyacinths. By these and other such ornaments, the queen standing at the right hand of the most beautiful and mighty king speaks, as it were, so that we may ponder and recall her gilded clothing, the varied colours with which she is clothed, and all her glory [Col. 0053C] which is within, amid golden fringes (Ps. 44)—that is, in perseverance in good works. Admonished by visible things, we may eagerly contemplate invisible adornments and her glory laid up in heaven.

Then it is customary for the singers—and indeed for the whole choir of psalmists—to take costly vesture from the sacristy and celebrate the joyful banquet of the sacred sacrifice with loud voices and amplified chants. The subject requires that I not pass over something proper to our order, that is, monks. At festivals of this sort we customarily all stand or process in white garments; it was explained above that this vesture signifies the new life of the saints. For then we are set in contemplation of that newness concerning which the Apostle exhorts us: “As Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

Therefore, though we are those locks of hair of which it is written, “His locks are like lifted palm branches, black as a raven” (Song 5)—because, being attached to our head, we ought, with humble conscience, to be black and, having conquered the world, to tend upward—nevertheless, when the state of that age is commemorated in which the bridegroom is always with his children, we suitably display joy and cover the daily blackness of salutary sorrow with glad whiteness, according to the saying: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 5 [sic]) [Col. 0054A].

Suitably, therefore, when we process in white, all alike, from elders to infants, carry sheaves, because in that life signified by white garments “each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour” (1 Cor. 3), and “they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On copes

At the greater feasts we also put on copes, that we may glory more abundantly in God, looking toward the future resurrection, when all the elect—who now, after laying aside the flesh, are rewarded only in the soul, each being given a white robe (Rev. 6)—will receive two robes: namely, the rest of souls and the glorious immortality of resurrected bodies [Col. 0054B] (1 Cor. 15).

These copes are rightly open on the inner side and entirely unsewn except for the single necessary clasp, because bodies then transformed and immortal will certainly confine the soul within no narrownesses; they will not cover the heart or impede inward contemplation of the holy Trinity. They are also adorned below with fringes, because then nothing will be lacking to our perfection; rather, what “we know in part and prophesy in part,” we shall know as we are known, because we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXV. On the shaving of heads

Yet, though thus adorned, we leave the head uncovered and cover with no ornament the shaving which we call the crown. For our joy is not yet complete, because we rejoice not in a present possession but in hope of future things.

We are shaved because we are sons of Core—that is, “the bald one,” namely our Lord Jesus Christ—who was crucified at the place of Calvary. And to him, that is, to the true Elisha, foolish and senseless boys said mockingly: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (4 Kings 2). Thus, with shaven heads, we have changed the ancient law of the Nazirites [Col. 0054C] (Num. 6). Formerly Nazirites grew their hair; we, on the contrary, cut our hair, because Christ the Lord, prince of the Nazirites, was made bald—that is, crucified in the place of Calvary, where the heads of the condemned were cut off.

Delilah—that is, the synagogue, poor and lacking understanding—shaved the head of the most mighty Samson, that is, of our sun, and handed him over into the hands of the Philistines (Judg. 16). But he, captured and seemingly conquered, conquered those who captured him; and, dying, killed more enemies than he had killed while living. For by dying the Lord shattered hell, conquered death, and restored life.

Although in the adornments mentioned above we rejoice in his victory, in shaving our heads we mourn his baldness in compassion. Yet we call this emblem of humility a crown—that is, victory—because that faithful baldness of the Lord, of which this shaving is a sign, is beyond doubt our victory, triumph, honour, and glory. “But far be it from me to glory,” says the vessel of election, “except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). But this glory has not yet appeared what it shall be, and it still bears the appearance of sorrow, until sorrow [Col. 0054D] is turned into joy and our joy is full (John 16).

# BOOK THREE. ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER FROM THE LORD’S ADVENT

[Col. 0055]

## 26. PROLOGUE

[Col. 0055B]

The discourse has sailed through narrower and deeper waters. While above it ventured to test rather than fully explore the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, it encountered no peril to faith; and now, with faith sufficiently mature or exercised, it confidently trusts in God that whenever it must sail through this deep, it will suffer shipwreck against no obstacle of rock.

Now, according to our purpose, as we enter upon the order of the year which is arranged around that sacrament itself, we ask the Holy Spirit who governs us not to cease filling our sail with the gentle breeze of his favour, until he brings the proposed work to the harbour of its desired completion. Beginning with the Lord’s Advent, we must first ascertain by consideration of causes why that season is so called, and what is signified by this term.

## 27. CHAPTER I. On Advent

The season preceding the memorial of the Lord’s nativity is called Advent because its entire ecclesiastical order is arranged according to contemplation of the Lord’s coming. The Lord is rightly said to come, though he is everywhere present through the invisible presence of his majesty, when, having assumed that which is visible and ours, he shows himself visible to bodily sight [Col. 0055C].

This happened then, when the Word through whom all things were made, who was in the world and through whom the world was made, though the world did not know him, became flesh so as visibly to dwell among us (John 1). It will happen likewise in the future, when he who now sits at God’s right hand—and although he is with us until the consummation of the age (Matt. 24 [sic])—will not assume something else, but will present again to us what he assumed once for all; and, as he himself said, “We shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Luke 21).

Therefore the season preceding the memorial of the Lord’s nativity is called Advent because these things which have been stated are commemorated partly as past and partly as future. For on the first Sunday the first coming, now past, is commemorated as though future in the person of the ancient Church. On the second and third Sundays, the second coming is announced by prophetic and apostolic trumpets as now imminent to those who await and desire it.

The second coming is proclaimed on two Sundays because the first coming was awaited as promised only by the Church which preceded the Lord’s incarnation; but both the Church before and the Church after heard of the second. The former was instructed only by prophetic proclamations, the latter by prophetic and apostolic proclamations alike. Hence on the second of those Sundays the prophetic office sounds forth, namely, “People of Zion”; but on the third the apostolic: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Phil. 4).

The fourth Sunday, which always looks immediately toward the day of the Lord’s nativity, commemorates the time when the Virgin’s womb was already pregnant and swollen, the Lord was near, [Col. 0055D] and the Godhead, kicking within, bound itself in that thong of its incarnation (Matt. 3), which John, in the Gospel of the same Sunday, professes himself unworthy to untie (John 1).

## CHAPTER II. On the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent

That these things are so may plainly be known from the offices of those Sundays themselves. For on the first Sunday the human race seeks not yet recompense but the beginning of righteousness. It has not yet reached its homeland, but asks that the way be shown to it; for it says: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. 24).

This is the voice of the old human being, bound by the chains of original sin, neither knowing nor able to return to its heavenly homeland. Accordingly, the Gospel reading is then recited in which those ways of the Lord by which humanity ought and can return to that place from which it fell are especially commended: namely, obedience, meekness, humility, and supreme love. Obedient to the Father in suffering for us, he willingly came to the place of his passion, meek and humble, as the prophet foretold of him: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, seated upon the colt of an ass” (Zech. 9). And that love was love than which none is greater, as he himself said: “No one has greater love than this” (John 15), and so forth.

Furthermore, the whole cause of the first coming is typologically contained in that reading of the holy Gospel. But this was discussed above, where, in order to demonstrate that the other parts of the office adhere and accord with the Gospel as a body with its head, the office of this Sunday was put forward as an example.

We know that the tethered ass or its colt signifies the human race, for whose release the Lord plainly came, so that, becoming our rider and possessor, he might lead us back by the paths of salvation, riding upon us, into the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the office establishes that the first Sunday regards the first [Col. 0056A] coming of the Lord. The intention of that office is plainly this: that upon those to whom the Lord has not yet come—for he has not yet come to those who have not yet received faith in his incarnation; to those, I say, who have not yet believed in his coming—there may come through faith such great salvation that, trusting in the Lord, they may not be put to shame, nor may their enemies—that is, demons—continue to mock the ass which they bound in the chains of sins. Rather, once released, may the Lord show it his ways and teach it his paths (Ps. 24).

This is clearly proclaimed in the introit, gradual, and alleluia. The apostle Paul intervenes and, in the Epistle reading, shows the ass which ways it ought to walk and which it ought not to walk. He begins this instruction: “Knowing that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13). Saying this and what follows, he plainly acts like a faithful charioteer, bridling the ass so that, when the Lord mounts in order to complete his journey, it may keep to straight paths. Finally he says, “Put on our Lord Jesus Christ”—which is as though he said to that same ass: Receive as rider the king of Zion.

That after the Gospel the offertory repeats what the introit antiphon declares indicates that even after the ass has received the Lord as its rider, it ought not to be secure before it arrives with its rider in the heavenly city of Jerusalem. For it may happen that the offended rider wishes to change his vehicle, which he had seemed formerly to approve. Therefore the Church continues in the offertory to say what it had said in the introit, adding: “Direct me in your truth,” and so forth.

The communion chant likewise—“The Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit” (Ps. 84)—is plainly the voice of the ancient Church awaiting the Lord’s first coming: when, by the gracious gift of the Holy Spirit, our land—that is, the Virgin’s womb—conceiving, yielded its fruit, bringing forth God and man, blessed for ever [Col. 0056B]. The collect said at the introit, that over the offerings, and that after communion all plainly look to the same thing, namely the Lord’s first coming.

### Why the station is held at Saint Peter’s

It should also be noted that, according to the most sacred arrangement of the most vigilant Pope Gregory, the station on this Sunday is rightly held at Saint Peter’s. He is one—indeed the first—of the disciples sent to release that great ass. For God worked through him in the apostleship of the circumcision (Gal. 2), and, carrying out the same embassy among the Gentiles with his companion blessed Paul, he entered Rome for Christ. Thus he released the empire of the world as the head, so to speak, of the aforementioned ass. The two who were sent from the Mount of Olives to release that animal ass therefore seem beautifully to be represented, as a type of all preachers, in these two men, Peter and Paul. They made Rome, the head of the world, the vehicle, dwelling-place, chariot, and throne of Christ the Lord, the eternal King.

### Why the deacon and subdeacon do not use their customary sacred vestments in Advent

From then until the sacred night of the Lord’s nativity, the deacon and subdeacon proceed in reduced vesture. The deacon wears no dalmatic, nor does the subdeacon wear [Col. 0056C] a tunic. The subdeacon represents the Law, which before the Lord’s incarnation lacked the adornment of the Gospel; the deacon represents the Gospel itself, whose brightness had not yet appeared before the mysteries of the Lord’s nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension. For that season signifies not their presence, but their expectation; hence, as was said, it is called the Lord’s Advent.

At times they use chasubles, the garment which, when discussing its dress, we said belonged to the priest. This should trouble no one. The subdeacon and deacon do not use chasubles so as to read or minister in them; rather, when about to read or minister, they take them off, clearly professing that this is not their own garment, nor one owed them by reason of their order, but that they receive it on loan because of reverence for the Lord’s feast or some other feast, in order to console their poor and unbecoming lack of vesture.

For the same reason, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is not then said, and *Ite, missa est* is omitted, because that season signifies, as stated, the time when the joy of peace and that consummation of our salvation which we still anxiously await were as yet expected.

## CHAPTER III. On the second Sunday
The station for the Second Sunday is at holy Jerusalem. For the whole office of this Sunday is sung to gladden the heart of her who first received the coming of the Son of God, and who, justified by faith [Col. 0059A] (Rom. V) and having peace with God, longs at his second coming to behold her glorious king. For she is a chaste woman who mourns her husband’s absence and desires his presence; and thus she sighs for the bridal chamber of her only bridegroom, “as the deer longs for fountains of waters” (Ps. XLI).

To her, therefore, longing, hastening, and panting, the present office foretells joy, impresses hope, and proclaims patience. Let us first consider the saying of the Gospel, with which the remaining parts of the office—full of joy, consolation, and peace—are shown to harmonize, after the signs that are to precede that glorious coming have been set forth. “When these things begin to happen,” says the Lord, “lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke XXII).—“Lift up your heads,” says blessed Gregory, [Col. 0059B] “that is, make your hearts glad.” In accordance with the consolation of this truthful promise, the prophetic trumpet sings beforehand at the Introit to the people of Zion: “Behold,” it says, “the Lord will come to save the nations, and the Lord will cause the glory of his voice to be heard in the joy of your heart” (Isa. XXX).
