For the people of Zion are a little child and an orphan, born in this exile of a mother who is a stranger, and of a father whom they have never seen; seeking their absent father with groans and continually striking heaven with cries, because, as their mother tells them, they have heard that their father has gone there, and have scarcely understood it in their infancy. Taking pity on this child as it weeps and cries in prayer, the mother sings this entire office (Acts I), testifying that the return of the father is now close at hand for the one who longs for it, and that the glory of his voice will be heard when [Col. 0059C] he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom in the joy,” he says, “of your hearts” (Matt. XXV). This joy will be complete, so that, when his signs begin to occur, we ought, according to the Lord’s saying, to lift up our heads (Luke XXII), that is, to make our hearts glad.

Since this cannot be accomplished by us unless he himself makes us glad with the joy of his Spirit, we rightly pray in the Collect, saying: “Stir up, Lord, our hearts”—that is, raise them and make them glad—to prepare the ways of your Only-Begotten Son; namely, that they may be ready to meet him, not fleeing through fear but welcoming his coming in love.

To this purpose this apostolic reading is fittingly recited to us: “Whatever things were written were written 29 [Col. 0059D] for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. XV), and what follows. For it avails to correct the impatient soul, excessively distressed and desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ; while it wishes us abundance of hope, it urges us to endure, with peace and joy, the delays of our Lord’s coming (Phil. I).

The Gradual, plainly singing of him who is to come, “whose beauty of splendor is from Zion” (Ps. XLIX), in accordance with the saying that salvation is from the Jews, proclaims the same joy to his saints (John IV); they are to be gathered at his right hand because they have established his new covenant above the former sacrifices (Ps. XLIX). The Alleluia, with two verses, in its first verse proclaims the joy of hope of him to whom it is said: “We shall go into the house of the Lord,” and the joy arising from that future event [Col. 0060A] (Ps. CXXI), where his feet shall stand in the courts of Jerusalem.

After the Gospel mentioned above has been read by the herald of joy, and the promise of truth confirmed where it says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke XXI), the people of Zion, as though they had received consolation, rejoice and, believing the truth, say: “O God, by turning us you will give us life, and your people shall rejoice in you” (Ps. LXXXIV). “You will give us life,” that is, through the resurrection, turning us now through faith; “and your people shall rejoice in you.” The children of the bridegroom shall rejoice when his presence is restored to them, and their former sorrow has been changed into joy; they shall rejoice with full joy.

It would be excessively long, and is not our purpose, to pursue everything in the manner of an expositor. Our purpose is only to seek the harmony of each office, like [Col. 0060B] the structure of each body. The sum of this office, therefore, is that pilgrim Jerusalem—that is, the present Church—should endure this life’s exile with most patient hope; and, when according to the prediction of the Gospel already cited it recognizes that the ruin of the world is imminent, should lift up its head and, in accordance with the exhortation of the Communion, rise and stand on high, rejecting earthly things and loving heavenly things, as the Collect said at the conclusion asks; and should behold the delight (Baruch V) that will come to it from its God, and, as summer draws near, should disperse the clouds of its sorrow, because the days of eternal life shine with the brightness of the sun (Apoc. XXI).

## CHAPTER IV. On the Office of the Third Sunday.

[Col. 0060C] The whole office of the Third Sunday sings consolation, especially for rulers of churches. The higher their rank, the more their life is subject to human judgments; and the more brightly their merit shines in the divine judgment, the more often their reputation is torn to pieces among men. For it announces to them that he will come who shall illumine the hidden things of darkness; for he is their judge and witness of their consciences, who cannot err at all in judgment.

That they may rejoice in the prospect of so great a witness and judge, and may know what to hope from him, that famous and illustrious testimony which he bore concerning John the Baptist is fittingly recited: “Amen, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. [Col. 0060D] XI). A great testimony, a weighty proclamation. God denied that he was a man clothed in soft garments; he denied that he was a reed shaken by the wind; he declared that in office or merits he was an angel. In one man he showed what he will do in all: when he comes to judgment before the Father and the holy angels, he will render to each a testimony appropriate to that person.

Who, then, will not blush to weep because he has no testimony from men corresponding to his merits, when so great a herald of his merits is reserved for him in heaven? “Rather, rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice,” says the Apostle—this is sung at the Introit—“let your moderation be known to all men” (Phil. IV). But if they shut their eyes and refuse to see your light shining before them, be anxious [Col. 0061A] about nothing: the Lord is near, who will bring your light before those unwilling to see it. Only let your petitions be made known to God; for that one witness will prevail against all accusers.

The following Collect asks that this promised consolation be fulfilled, saying: “Incline your ear, O Lord, to our prayers, and illumine the darkness of our mind by the grace of your visitation.” For his coming, which we pray may not be delayed, will illumine the darkness that we suffer when we are falsely judged by those in error and ourselves judge falsely. As the same Apostle says in the following Epistle reading: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illumine the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV).

For this entire reading tends to this end: that it may seem a very small matter to us to be judged by a human day, as it was for John, whom, as stated above, the Lord proclaims in the Gospel not to be a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. XI). [Col. 0061B] The Lord is sorrowfully entreated concerning the same matter in the Gradual, after fitting praise has been offered: “You who sit, O Lord, upon the Cherubim” (Ps. LXXIX), etc. For in that he sits upon the Cherubim—that is, upon the fullness of knowledge—he knows and is able to penetrate the hidden abyss of our hearts, and to bring whatever lies hidden there into public view by true testimony. For this purpose, in accordance with the voice of the Psalm which sounds in the Alleluia, he will stir up his power and come.

And just as in the Offertory, as though it had already happened because it will undoubtedly happen, we confidently say: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land; you have turned away the captivity [Col. 0061C] of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXIV), so the elect, standing at the right hand after testimony has been given to them by the true Judge, shall rejoice and receive the liberty of the children of God (Rom. VIII), according to what is written elsewhere: “When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice” (Ps. XIII).

The prophetic trumpet strengthens the fainthearted with hope of this liberty in the Communion: “Say to the fainthearted: Be strong, and do not fear” (Isa. XXXV). They often tremble greatly when they have heard human prejudgments against themselves, though they ought to be consoled by the treasure stored in their conscience; for they do not yet know in what condition they will be found in that dreadful judgment of God. Hence blessed Gregory, wearied by many human prejudgments and more experienced than many others in what [Col. 0061D] rulers of churches suffered and how much consolation they needed in these matters, dedicated this office to them at this celebrated station. Writing to the Emperor Maurice, he says among other things:

> “But as for the fact that the piety of my lords threatens me with that fearful and terrible judgment of almighty God, I beg, by that same almighty Lord, that it do so no further. For we do not yet know what each person is like there.”

And Paul, the eminent preacher, admonishes us, saying: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illumine the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts” (I Cor. IV).

### Why the Station Is at Saint Peter’s.

It should be understood that the station is fittingly held at Saint Peter’s for the office of the present Sunday, because he is the first and chief of the rulers of the Church. To them this same office proclaims joy and patience amid tribulation, long-suffering in hope. How great is the pressure upon their mind, “and besides those things which are outward, how great is the daily burden” (II Cor. XI), how great the concern for the souls entrusted to them—30 [Col. 0062A] no one except those who have experienced it can know fully and clearly, although diligent and thoughtful readers may learn something of it through frequent reading, especially from the books of blessed Gregory.

Blessed Gregory himself, the eminent glory of the Roman see after the Apostle Peter, who was, as stated, thoroughly aware of this anguish, consoled himself with them through this office. [Col. 0062B] For, as we read in the book of his life, he carefully arranged the stations among the basilicas or cemeteries of the blessed martyrs, through which the Roman people still hasten eagerly, as if he were living among them; and, travelling through them himself while still able to speak, he delivered twenty homilies on the Gospel at different times. He dictated the remaining twenty, but, as his stomach grew weak through continual illness, entrusted them to others to pronounce. As a truly most sweet instrument of the Holy Spirit, he conceived whatever he wrote at the dictation of God’s finger; so he established the same stations not without that same Spirit, and likewise these and his other works, as it were, for the Church.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 0062C] On the Fasts of the Four Seasons.

Among the other weekdays, Wednesday and Friday are especially assigned to fasts because they are distinguished above the others by the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. For on Wednesday the Lord was sold by Judas the betrayer, and on Friday he was crucified by the Jews (Matt. XXVI). Thus, each Sunday has its own readings from the Gospels and Epistles; and these days were judged more suitable for fasts, litanies, and the abstinences of penitents, so that on the days when the innocent Lord was sold and suffered for his servants, the sinful servant might weep and fast, and more solemnly hear the holy reading, which is food for the soul.

For this reason the fasts of the four seasons were instituted to be celebrated on these same weekdays, with the day of the Lord’s burial added—namely Saturday—so that there might be three days of fasting. Thus, by a salutary exchange, we may obtain the good temperateness of each season’s three months through the three days on which we fast; and, offering the Lord one day for each month, may pass this tranquil and peaceful life beneath the elements of the world, protected from spiritual wickednesses (Eph. VI) and from the malice of severe storms.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Fast in the Advent of the Lord.

Therefore, in the third week of the Lord’s Advent, the fast of the winter season is appointed on Wednesday. Because of the coming of the Lord, it is more solemn than the fasts of the other seasons, and it has a fuller office both by day and [Col. 0063A] by night, pertaining to the coming of the Lord itself. Thus, while the flesh is afflicted by fasts, the soul may rejoice more abundantly in testimonies of its redemption drawn from the sacred reading or from the Church’s song.

On the first day of the fast, namely Wednesday, the station is fittingly appointed at Saint Mary’s. For the entire office of that day plainly pertains directly to that temple of the Lord, that sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, in which the whole God, dwelling for nine months, deigned to become man (Luke I). For from the Gospel is recited the announcement, or incarnation, which was proclaimed beforehand by prophetic trumpets, brought in person by the angel, received by the faith of the blessed Virgin, and completed and brought forth through her incorrupt womb.

[Col. 0063B] The prophetic sound briefly sings all this in the Introit: “Drop down dew, ye heavens” (Isa. XLV), it says, and what follows. In saying, “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above,” it expressed the ministry of the angelic address, through which God the Word descended into the inward ear of the believing Virgin, like rain upon the fleece (Judg. XVI). By saying, “Let the clouds rain the Just One,” it denotes itself and the other prophets, who, as clouds, rain down the Just One—namely Christ—and his faithful upon the earth of our heart by heavenly teaching. “Let the earth be opened,” it says (Isa. XLV), receiving the Word and saying, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word” (Luke I); and let it bring forth the Saviour, blessed forever, bringing forth for us God and man.

Everything that follows likewise accords with the Gospel sense. The Epistle reading refreshes the souls of those who fast in two ways. First, it proclaims that mountain which, in accord with the Gospel, receiving the throne of David its father, and growing from a little stone into a mountain (Dan. II) and filling the whole earth, shall reign in the house of Jacob forever (Ps. LXV). The following verse of the Gradual beautifully answers this reading: “Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. XXIII), etc. For only one innocent in hands and clean of heart, and whose life agrees with faith, shall have a share in that incarnation of the Lord.

The remaining parts of the office plainly pertain to the same Gospel sense; there is no need to dwell upon proving this, since it is evident. Therefore, according to such an office, the station is fittingly appointed at Saint Mary’s on this day.

## CHAPTER VII. On Friday of the Fast.

[Col. 0063D] The station on Friday is appointed at the Holy Apostles. Its reason is indeed more hidden, but for those who seek it, it quickly becomes clear from a small spark. For in the Gospel of the present day, in the canticle of the Blessed Virgin, that memorable saying is found which plainly concerns the Apostles themselves: “He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke I). For from the seat of spiritual teaching, from the chair of Moses, he has put down the mighty from their seat—that is, the proud scribes and Pharisees—and has exalted the humble Apostles to that same seat.

As elsewhere the Lord himself says: “I confess to you, [Col. 0064A] Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI). Because this was done in the truth of judgment, and because, when the blessed Virgin spoke these words, the Lord himself was near—namely, in her womb—this Introit is fitting: “Be near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth” (Ps. CXVIII).

And because, while the rod from the root of Jesse was then flowering, the Spirit of the Lord already rested upon its flower, so that John, receiving from his fullness, leaped in Elizabeth’s womb (John I; Luke I), this Epistle aptly accords with the Gospel: “There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI), etc. To go through every detail would be too long, and because it is evident in itself that they pertain to the same matter, it would be tedious. Finally, the Communion: “Behold, the Lord shall come, and all his saints with him” (Zech. XIV), plainly concerns the glorification of those same Apostles, who shall come with him at his second coming for judgment.

## 31 CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0064B] Why Only One Reading Is Read at Mass.

It may be asked why on Wednesday—the first day of the fast—there are two readings and two Graduals appointed, while on Friday only one reading is used, but on the following Saturday six are read. The answer is that, since two are read on Wednesday, according to the progress of the fast we ought to read three on Friday and four on Saturday. But because ordinations are customarily held on Saturday, two readings transferred from Friday were added to the four Saturday readings, so that the abundance of the sacred office might be reserved especially for those who are described as [Col. 0064C] both fasting and novices in holy orders.

### Why Twelve Readings Are Designated for the Saturday Fast, Though Only Six Are Read.

It should also be understood that, although only six readings are to be read on Saturday, twelve readings are indicated in the headings because, when the Roman Church was composed of Latin and Greek speakers, each reading was recited in both languages. For when they were recited in one language, they could not be understood by the people of the other language. Thus, as each one was read twice, twelve are counted by doubling the number of six readings.

Furthermore, it should be noted that the sacraments of ordination are assigned to Sunday, on whose eve they are performed; and both Saturday evening and the first morning of Sunday may lawfully be celebrated by fasting persons while fasting.

## CHAPTER IX. The Judgment of Pope Leo: Ordinations Performed on Saturday Evening Belong to Sunday.

For the great Leo says, writing to Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria:

> “What we know to have been observed by our fathers with more careful concern, we desire to be observed by you also: that priestly or levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but should be instituted under the law of the divine office after the day of Saturday—that is, after the beginning of the night that dawns upon the first day of the week—so that sacred blessing may be conferred upon those to be consecrated by fasting men while they are fasting. The same observance will be maintained if it is celebrated in the very morning of Sunday, while the Saturday fast continues, since the beginning of the preceding night does not depart from that time; and there can be no doubt that it belongs to the day of the resurrection, as is also shown in the Lord’s Passover.

> “For besides the authority of the custom which we know has come from apostolic teaching, Sacred Scripture itself makes plain that, when the Apostles, by command of the Holy Spirit, sent Paul and Barnabas to evangelize the Gentiles, they fasted and prayed and laid hands on them [Col. 0065A] (Acts XIII), that we may understand with how great devotion on the part both of those giving and those receiving it care must be taken lest the sacrament of so great a blessing appear to have been performed negligently.

> [Col. 0065B] “Therefore you will act piously and commendably in accordance with apostolic institutions if you yourself observe this form of ordaining priests throughout the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside: namely, that blessing should never be given to those who are to be consecrated except on the Sunday of the Lord’s resurrection, whose beginning is known to be assigned from Saturday evening, and which has been consecrated by such great mysteries of the divine dispensations that whatever has been established as more eminent for the Lord has been accomplished in the dignity of this day.

> “On this day the world received its beginning; on this day, through Christ’s resurrection, death received its destruction and life its beginning. On this day the Apostles receive from the Lord the trumpet of the Gospel to be preached to all nations, and receive the sacrament of regeneration to be carried into the whole world. On this day, as the blessed Evangelist John testifies, when the disciples had assembled together, with the doors shut, the Lord entered to them, breathed upon them, and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained’ (John XX). [Col. 0065C] On this day, finally, the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord came to the Apostles (Acts II). Thus let us know that, by a certain heavenly rule, the mysteries of priestly orders are to be celebrated by us on the day on which all gifts of graces have been gathered together.”

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 0065D] Again, on Saturday, and Why the Station Is at Saint Peter’s.

On this Saturday, and on all the Saturdays of these four seasons, the station is fittingly celebrated at Saint Peter’s. For since the supreme pontificate of the Church after Christ was first conferred on him, and since he was the first and chief to celebrate holy ordinations in the Church, and since the Roman pontiff especially acts in his place when he ordains ministers necessary to the holy Church and pastors for Christ’s sheep, it is fitting that the station should be celebrated at his church, as though recourse were being had to the supreme authority.

Therefore Mother Church, gathering her fasting children at Blessed Peter’s, refreshes them, as though from Peter’s own mouth, with manifold sacraments in their soul, and by his authority distributes the spiritual distinctions of ministries. Here it should be observed that the fifth reading, which is the last of the additional instruction, is never changed, and is always that in which it is read that the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace of fire (Dan. III). This is not without a great and mystical reason.

[Col. 0066A] For just as heavenly grace came to the aid of the youths cast by the Babylonian king into the fiery furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew, so the urgency of fasts and prayers delivers us when we are assailed by the flames of lusts sent by the devil, the king of confusion. “This kind is not cast out except in prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII).

After this reading has been read, the hymn of the same youths follows, by which every creature is urged to bless the Creator, before priests are ordained. Thus we may recognize that those whose mouths and hands are admitted by right to pronounce blessings and, what is greatest, to consecrate the body and blood of the Lord, are those who have overcome by strong faith the furnace of vices kindled by the king of confusion.

[Col. 0066B] What follows now plainly proclaims the Lord’s coming and accords with the voice “crying in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord’” (Isa. XL; Matt. III), etc. For this Gospel is the beginning of that day: namely, the preaching in which John strikes the hearts of sinners and calls them to repentance, calling them a brood of vipers, saying that the axe is already laid to the roots of the tree and the winnowing fan is in the Judge’s hand, so that, cleansing his threshing-floor, he may gather the wheat into the barn but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. III).

The Epistle likewise anticipates this Gospel in the same sense, namely by preaching the second coming of the Lord, when, after the man of sin, the son of perdition, has first been revealed, he will kill him with the spirit of his mouth (II Thess. II) and destroy him by the brightness of his coming. But the Introit antiphon also—“Come and show us [Col. 0066C] your face, O Lord, who sit upon the 32 Cherubim, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX)—plainly looks to that time when, as we sing also in the Offertory, the daughter of Zion exultantly hears: “Your king, the holy one and Saviour of the world, shall come” (Zech. IX). And, as was set forth in the Tract, “He shall come, stirring up his power” (Ps. LXXIX); and the one whom he leads—Joseph, like a sheep—separated from the kids who will be at his left, he will place at his right hand (Matt. XXV).

Meanwhile, however, we must weep before him who made us (Ps. XCIV), lest he who is mighty and terrible, who, according to the Communion, “rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII), no hostile little ones being able to withstand him—for it is written of them, “The arrows of little ones became their wounds” (Ps. LXIII)—when [Col. 0066D] he comes, should likewise be a giant to us, contend with us in judgment in his great strength, and crush us beneath the mass of his greatness.

## CHAPTER XI. Why the Fourth Sunday Is Unassigned.

The office for the Fourth Sunday is marked *Vacat*—that is, it is not assigned by apostolic ordinance as a station to any saint. How rightly this was established can be understood by considering the rationale of the same office.

In the Gospel of this Sunday, while the wind of the Pharisaic question is blowing, this spark of shining truth flashes forth from the flame of divine fire which burned, burning and shining (John V), in the holy mind of John: “He it is,” he says, “who is to come after me, who was made before [Col. 0067A] me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John I). Upon this sentence of trustworthy testimony, grave and worthy of the heart and mouth of so great a forerunner, depend all the parts of the sounding office.

That Idumaea, which had heard the prophetic promise of its visitation, “I will stretch out my sandal over Idumaea” (Pss. LIX, CVII), stands and, looking to that time when the king who had made this promise came forth from his reclining-place—that is, from the bosom of the Father—and was now being shod in the Virgin’s womb, enclosing his steps in that wonderful and insoluble strap of the Incarnation. Looking, I say, to this, Idumaea—that is, the alien Gentile people—cries in the Introit: “Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people” (Ps. CV), namely, in your Son, in whom you have been well pleased—[Col. 0067B] the sole one out of the thousands of peoples who has been yours from the beginning of the world. Visit us in this same salvation of yours, as a physician visits a sick man lying helpless, by gratuitous condescension (Matt. III, XVII).

What follows—the Collect, Epistle, Gradual, and Alleluia—all alike declare, in accordance with contemplation of the Virgin’s pregnant womb, that the Lord is near and his coming swift. In the Offertory, moreover, it is plainly proclaimed—not by the example of an angel—that it is the saving temple of the Lord, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the bridal chamber of holiness, the banquet-hall of divine counsel, in which, as stated, the divinity coming for our salvation was shod with our flesh.

[Col. 0067C] To which of the saints, all of whom are his servants, was this great mystery of Christ the King entrusted in such a way that this office could rightly be sung at a prescribed station in that saint’s church? For if the offices assigned to each saint at the solemn stations are rightly considered, they are found to accord with the virtues or merits of each. Thus the station is held at Blessed Peter’s, who principally possesses the power of binding and loosing (Matt. XVI), when, as stated, the loosing of the ass is proclaimed to us as a type of the Church (Matt. XXI); and when we conduct the scrutinies and the catechumens are signed, the station is celebrated at Paul’s, the teacher of the Gentiles.

Yet John himself declares that he is unworthy to loosen this binding of the strap—that is, to unveil the mystery of Christ’s holy Incarnation—although none greater has arisen among those born of women (John I; Matt. XI). For who can investigate how the Word is made bodily, how the highest and life-giving Spirit is animated within a mother’s womb, how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived? [Col. 0067D] Therefore this mystery was entrusted to none of the saints in such a way that this office ought to be assigned to him at a proper station.

Accordingly it is *vacat*, not because, as some suppose, it is less authoritative, but because it is reasonably excepted from the most orderly arrangement of the stations. For it has a subject matter which effects all salvation and holiness, yet is unsearchable by any saint; bestowed upon all, yet administered through the Holy Spirit alone, who, in the banquet-hall of the Virgin’s womb, was alone the mediator, alone privy to the mystery, and the sole heavenly steward of the wedding feast (Luke I).

[Col. 0068A] We pass over the nocturnal offices, to avoid prolixity, especially because they themselves make sufficiently clear that they do not differ from the daily ones. It should be noted, however, that by the ancient and universal custom of holy Church, the prophet Isaiah is fittingly read during this season. He is a noble prophet, eloquently plain and plainly eloquent concerning both the first and second comings of the Lord—indeed, a great and true evangelist who announces them. For throughout the year the sacred readings have been plausibly ordered according to the rationale of occasions or seasons, as will become clear in their respective places below.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Office at the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

At the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, that beautiful oracle of divine consolation is frequently and most solemnly on the Church’s lips: “Today you shall know that [Col. 0068B] the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory. Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear” (Exod. XVI), etc.

By this the Church sends each one of us to the history in the book of Paralipomenon, when, in the reign of Jehoshaphat, the children of Ammon and Moab, together with the inhabitants of Mount Seir, gathered against Judah (II Chron. XX). And all Judah assembled at Jerusalem and in the temple of the Lord to implore his face. While they stood before the Lord with their wives and little children or offspring, and cried aloud to the Lord, Jahaziel, son of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, a Levite, cried out from the midst of the multitude when the Spirit of the Lord came upon him: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear; tomorrow go forth, and the Lord shall be with you,” etc.

To that passage, as stated, the Church directs each of us, earnestly seeking [Col. 0068C] to stir up our hearts, that through this likeness we may vigilantly recognize how fittingly the Nativity of the Son of God according to the flesh came to our aid. For the resemblance is not slight. Just as visible enemies had then visibly gathered against Judah—namely, the children of Ammon and Moab (Jer. XLVIII), and the inhabitants of Mount Seir (Ezek. XXXV), who are frequently used in Sacred Scripture as figures of sins, vices, and evil spirits (Gen. XVI), with names also suited to that very purpose: Ammon means “a troubled people”; Moab, “from the father,” namely the devil; Seir, “hairy” or “rough”—so our sins and vices were gathering for our destruction, and there was no one to help.

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 0068D] On the Office of the Same Day.

The very name that is called the Vigil ought to awaken us, so that we may attentively consider the things gathered into the office of this day. When we have seen from what passages of Scripture these have been collected, there will present itself to us not so much an obvious expression as a wondrous signification of the profound intention by which the composer of the office seeks, through such an office, to occupy our minds in divine meditation. First, then, we must speak of the Introit: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come.” This is taken, with a slight alteration, from Exodus. For when the Lord had said to the children of Israel, “Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you,” Moses and Aaron said to them: “In the evening you shall know [Col. 0069A] that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see his glory” (Exod. 16).

Therefore, when this is sung to us in the Introit as we keep watch in mind while awaiting the Lord’s Nativity—the words spoken to those then receiving bread from heaven, that is, manna—the instructed choir readily perceives what the warm eye of devout intention indicates; that is, toward what the truly wise composer of the office directs us, or to what he invites our thoughts—he who is a learned scribe conscious of his great treasure (Matt. 13). In short, he invites us to reflect that the manna given to the children of Israel as they left Egypt and journeyed toward the promised land was a figure of the Word of God. Assuming flesh through the Virgin, he came to feed us who believe in him, we who had been fasting from God, swollen and surfeited with the vices of the flesh, as though with the flesh-pots of Egypt.

The interpreter of this likeness is not any ordinary man, but he himself who said: “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died. This is the bread descending from heaven, that if anyone eats of it, he may not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). Understanding this, and exulting magnificently, we are further enlarged in spiritual joy through the addition from the psalm, saying: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23). The Offertory likewise, with its verses, is taken from this psalm. For this psalm agrees in every respect with the day and with its subject, since the intention of the whole present office and of this psalm is almost one and the same.

For on this present Vigil we are commanded to contemplate [Col. 0069C] not merely that Christ was born, but also why he was born and when he was born, just as we sing: “Consider how great and glorious he is” (Heb. 7). And in the psalm, according to its title, which is: “A Psalm of David on the first day of the Sabbath,” the Prophet treats of Christ’s victory, accomplished in the resurrection on the first day of the week (Luke 24), exhorting the faithful to prepare themselves, as is fitting, for the coming of so great a king: to lift up, as we sing in the Offertory, their gates—the gates of death, that is, vices—or to raise the gates of righteousness, the virtues, so that the King of glory, the Lord of hosts, may enter, to overthrow the strong man armed. The world is his, because he founded it upon the seas (Ps. 23): just as of old “he divided the Red Sea into divisions” [Col. 0069D] (Ps. 135), so now, leading forth the world—that is, the Christian people—amid the dissensions of embittered peoples, he has founded it in faith and established it upon the rivers, that is, upon the rulers of this age.

Likewise, the fact that this verse is added to the same Introit, transformed into the Gradual—“Give heed, O Shepherd of Israel” (Ps. 79)—builds up the vigilant understanding. For that psalm is a prayer for Jews and Gentiles, who were soon to be changed into him when the Lord Jesus appeared. The faithful also pray in that psalm for the unbelieving Jews, who in the title are called Assyrians—that is, those directing themselves according to their own judgment, “who, seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10)—that at last [Col. 0070A] they may be converted, as they themselves foresee will eventually occur. In the aforesaid verse, the Jewish people are signified under the name Israel; under the name Joseph, which means “increasing,” is signified the multitude of the Gentiles added to them, according to the saying: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also” (John 10), etc.

It is plain concerning the Gospel and Epistle that the aforesaid Introit agrees with them: for the sense of each chiefly seeks to attest what manner of manna the Lord has rained upon us through the gate of heaven, namely through the Virgin. The angel says in the Gospel: “For that which is born of her is of the Holy Spirit; and she shall bear a son” (Matt. 1), etc. Paul says in the Epistle: “Who was made to him from the seed of David” (Rom. 1). For Mary was the greatest of the gates of heaven which the Lord opened to us in order to rain this manna: through her the Word of God, made flesh, descended from heaven to us.

Indeed, the other gates—that is, all the souls of the saints who from the beginning deserved to receive that Word into the bosom of faith—brought forth with their mouths the word of salvation; that is, they preached and composed Holy Scripture, saying: “From fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26). But she conceived that Word, full of grace in such a way, that she gave birth to him made a visible human being, in the reality of flesh, while the same Holy Spirit spoke this Word through the mouths of the prophets and worked his conception in the Virgin’s womb.

This also was signified from heaven [Col. 0070C] in what is written concerning the aforesaid manna: “When the dew descended upon the camp in the morning, the manna descended with it” (Exod. 15 [apparently 16]). For the dew signifies the Holy Spirit, of whom it has now been said, “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit”; while the manna, as has often been said, signifies the Word of God, united to human nature through his operation. And the disobedient people’s keeping back some of what they had gathered, not eating it all as they had been commanded, signifies that they were unwilling to believe everything they received from the holy prophets concerning the Word of God. But what became of the manna that was kept back? “It decayed,” he says, “and began to swarm with worms” (Exod. 16).

Surely this means that to this day Judaea refuses to eat the manna—that is, to believe in the Word of God—because he assumed decay, that is, our flesh, and truly became a worm: he who had been pure manna, that is, he who was God, indeed the Word of God, truly became a mortal human being. But because on the Sabbath it did not decay and no worm was found in it, this beautifully signifies what the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Rightly, therefore, we sing in the Introit: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see,” etc.; because today, that is, in the present life, we know and believe that the living bread came down from heaven, while in the morning, that is, in the glory of the resurrection, we shall see not only his human form but also the glorious form of his divinity. And, as we sing in the Communion: “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God” [Col. 0071A] (Isa. 40).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the question commonly asked: why God permitted the Fall of man, for which his Incarnation became necessary

This troublesome question is often pressed upon us by some: Why did God permit the Fall of man to occur, when, being almighty, he could certainly have prevented it, at least by keeping the tempter himself far from the entrance to Paradise? Why did he prefer that his Incarnation should become necessary for the human race rather than, by a short way, drive the serpent away from converse with man? The Apostle says that this is a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles; but if we are governed by the spirit of devotion, so that we are gentle and therefore seek in order that we may find, we shall knowingly profess that this foolishness of God is wiser than men (1 Cor. 1).

In order that this may more easily be proved, I wish first to introduce some likeness of a matter of such majesty. Since weak eyes cannot behold divine justice or wisdom shining in itself, let them understand its beauty by its image, as though contemplating it in a mirror placed before them. We may therefore take a fitting likeness from what is written: “He called a famine upon the land and broke all the support of bread,” and shortly afterward: “And Israel entered into Egypt” (Ps. 104), etc.

We ask those who are accustomed to be troubled by the aforesaid question why God wished Israel [Col. 0071C] to enter Egypt, whence afterward they were led out through Moses and Aaron by signs and wonders, after great labor on their own part (Exod. 7–8). For the covenant which he made with Abraham, which he swore to Isaac, which he established as a commandment for Jacob—saying, “To you I shall give the land of Canaan” (Ps. 104)—while they were inhabitants of it, namely the land of Canaan, he could have made that covenant stand without calling famine upon the land or allowing Israel to enter Egypt. There, that is, within Canaan, he could have greatly increased his people and strengthened them against their enemies, permitting no one to harm them and reproving kings on their account (ibid.). Yet, as was said, he preferred that the cause should arise for Israel’s entering Egypt, and that Moses [Col. 0071D] his servant and Aaron should be sent there; that he should put the words of his signs in them; rebuke the Red Sea so that it was dried up; lead them through the wilderness for forty years after their enemies had been overthrown; bear with their ways; and meanwhile rain down manna for them to eat and give them bread of heaven (Ps. 105).

Let the person who seeks higher matters answer, then, why God permitted them to enter there, from which they were to be brought back at such expense of delay and labor. Perhaps he will give the obvious and true answer: in order to make his power known among the nations, so that there might be works of his that could profitably be proclaimed among the nations (Ps. 76); so that we might know that he is the Lord our God (Ps. 104), and prove by experience that “his judgments are in all the earth” [Col. 0072A] (ibid.); in short, so that God might become known, without knowledge of whom no human being lives. For this reason he permitted the things mentioned above to be done. And this is right, good, and beyond reproach.

For if a human being ought not, when an occasion is offered, fail to bring forth the useful thing within him, because it is written: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20), how much more ought the benevolence of God to embrace the occasion offered to him—namely, to send Joseph to be sold as a slave (Gen. 37; Ps. 104)—so that he might display the useful treasures of his wisdom, since that sale was the cause or beginning of their captivity. The beginning of that captivity is not to be imputed to God because he called famine upon the land, but to those by whom Joseph was sold [Col. 0072B] into slavery. There is therefore no doubt that whatever God permitted or did there was beyond reproach.

Accordingly, when they went down into Egypt, Jacob alone, their father, who had been free from that guilt, was revived by hope of the promise. For he heard God saying to him: “Do not fear; go down into Egypt. I shall go down there with you, and I shall bring you back from there” (Gen. 46). But these earthly events are an image of that divine justice proposed above, and were done as a pattern of heavenly things. With the same simplicity of eye—that is, the intention of doing what is beneficial—God permitted Adam, who was willing, to descend into this Egypt, that is, into the darkness of sin, when he had placed him in the pleasantness of Paradise; the land in which he commanded Abraham, Isaac, and [Col. 0072C] Jacob to dwell as sojourners, promising it to them, was a type of that Paradise.

And all the benefit arising from his permitting Israel to enter Egypt is as much less than that arising from Adam’s sin as a figure is less than truth, a likeness than the thing itself, a shadow than a body. For, to omit now the other matters, whose meanings are indeed very extensive but must be applied at other times or places: the fact that he rained manna for them to eat and gave them bread of heaven (Ps. 77), though truly a great and wonderful good, is far inferior to that bread of angels which it signified—the Word of God, God the Word, the Word made flesh. Not only does the Lord himself testify in the Gospel that the manna was a sign of this incarnate Word, when he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” [Col. 0072D] (John 6); Moses also sets this down in Deuteronomy. Having said, “He gave you manna as food, which neither you nor your fathers knew,” he immediately adds: “that he might show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8).

And so that you may perceive more clearly, in both cases, the aforesaid simplicity of the divine eye—that is, purity of intention—it is easy to prove by clear testimonies that these things had to occur for the instruction not only of the human but also of the angelic creature. For after Moses had said concerning the manna what has been quoted above, he added shortly afterward, speaking indeed to human beings: “For as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God has disciplined you” [Col. 0073A] (Deut. 8). But concerning the mystery of the incarnate Word, Paul writes to the Ephesians: “That through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

Thus, as appears in the mirror, the brightest Sun of justice—most pure of everything that might be worthy of reproach or the mark of foolishness, as it seemed to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1)—proceeds in the dispensation of his Incarnation. Of all the methods by which worldly wisdom, which God made foolish, asserts that the Almighty could or should have overthrown or rendered futile the devil’s wickedness, this method that pleased God is the best of all: that the devil should be permitted to deceive man, thereby adding to the measure of his own condemnation; and that, having gained the result of his fraud, he should then be brought to judgment through the man.

And the king of Egypt, seated in the principality of pride—that is, the prince of darkness—was first to be crushed by the ten plagues, that is, by the scourges of the ten commandments of the Law. Then, as we hasten through baptism to eat this manna, he, the pursuer, is drowned in the waves of that same sea. And when we have been refreshed and strengthened by the manna of the incarnate Word and have entered upon his land—that is, the heavenly fatherland, which he lost through pride—he himself, with his attendant hosts, namely the spiritual Canaanites, shall be slain. This will occur on the day of judgment, when, in a wondrous and most beautiful ordering, this God-and-man will punish both what was done against God and what was done against man: both the pride by which he swelled against [Col. 0073C] God and the envy by which he deceived man.

God foresaw and predestined all these things before he created man. But he foresaw man’s Fall without predestining or willing it; indeed, he forbade it under threat of death (Gen. 2). For God foresaw and predestined only good things; evil things he foresaw only, not also predestined, though he justly assigned fitting places to them.

Someone may ask further: Since there is no transgression if there is no commandment or law, why did God give man a commandment which he foreknew would not be kept? Clearly because he was the Creator and man the creature; and the creature had to be instructed by the Creator. For the creature could not have been so created that it was perfect by its own nature, which belongs to the divine nature alone; nor could it have come to know that God is “gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11) except by making progress through instruction. A commandment is, moreover, the beginning of every discipline of instruction. Therefore a commandment had to be given—especially one that would dispose the creature toward humility, by forbidding it to wish to know more than it ought to know [Col. 0073D] (Rom. 12). Because of this fault the devil fell; and for this reason in Ezekiel he is called, with reproach and irony, a cherub (Ezek. 28), that is, “fullness of knowledge.” But he ate of the tree in order to have the knowledge of good and evil—that is, all knowledge—like God; and thus it is thereafter called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because it truly was so, but because, through the devil’s deception, the woman believed this of it (Gen. 3).

These matters have been briefly set forth only for those who seek the knowledge of God with us in humility of heart, not for those who act deceitfully, to whom the Apostle says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Rom. 9). To answer the captious little questions of such persons belongs neither to our capacity nor to our present purpose. With these matters, I say, prefaced, we proclaim the glory of the same Lord’s Incarnation: praising God the Father, who through it showed us his face; glorifying the Son, our salvation, who assumed our flesh; and giving thanks to the Holy Spirit, whose proper work was that wondrous conception of the new man.

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 0074B] Why two Epistles are read at Mass on the Lord’s Nativity

It is worthy of inquiry why, at this solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, two Epistles are read for the solemnities of Mass, both by day and by night, whereas this does not occur in this manner at any other time during the year. Most importantly, the first is always taken from the Old Testament and the next from the New. As we investigate this, the splendid teaching of blessed Gregory immediately opens the way of understanding:

“For good reason the two cherubim which cover the propitiatory look at one another, with their faces turned toward the propitiatory. For *cherub* means ‘fullness of knowledge.’ And what is signified by the two cherubim but the two Testaments? What, indeed, is figured by the propitiatory but the incarnate Lord? Of him John says: ‘For he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2). And when the Old Testament announces that this must be done, which the New Testament proclaims has been done in the Lord, the two cherubim, as it were, look at one another while turning their faces toward the propitiatory. For, seeing the incarnate God placed between them, they do not differ in their gaze, since they agree in recounting the mystery of his dispensation.”  
[Note: [Col. 0073D] St Gregory, *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 25, no. 3, Migne edition.]

Therefore we understand the same likeness to be presented to us when, just as the two cherubim look mutually upon one another with their faces turned toward the propitiatory, so the two readings from the two Testaments look, with harmonious testimonies and one and the same meaning, toward the Gospel reading, in which our propitiatory—that is, the incarnate Word—is preached. The reason why the station is celebrated at Saint Mary’s in this office is plain: namely, because from her womb this salvation awaited and received by Judah and Jerusalem came forth.

## CHAPTER XVI. That Christ was born at night

It is probable that Christ was born on the Lord’s night, although the sacred Gospel narrative is silent on this matter. For if you trace backward according to the rule of computation, you will find that the concurrents of the year in which he was born were five. Adding these to the seven regulars of December [Col. 0075A]—or, more briefly, to the three regulars of January—you will find that the day with which we begin December was the fifth feria, and that with which we begin January was the first, that is, Sunday, after subtracting seven from the number produced by combining the regulars and concurrents. Now, when December begins on the fifth feria, or January on the first, it necessarily follows that the day of the Lord’s Nativity, which is the twenty-fifth day after the Kalends of December and the eighth before the Kalends of January, is the first feria, that is, Sunday.

Therefore Christ was born on Sunday night, in harmony with the ordering of his wonders: on the night of the same day on which he said, “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. 1), light rose in darkness for the upright in heart, and the Dayspring from on high visited us, “to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” [Col. 0075B] (Ps. 3; Luke 1). He was fittingly born at night so that, at the very time of his rising, he might signify that he came to illuminate our night.

## CHAPTER XVII. Why two Masses are celebrated on that night

For this reason two Masses, instituted by Pope Telesphorus of holy memory, honor the most sacred commemoration of that night with most fitting veneration. Truly apostolic is the faith of the holy Roman Church, which decreed that, on the annual night of the one Nativity of the Son of God, the glory of the twofold Nativity—divine, namely, and human—should thus be commemorated by solemn vigils: that it should appoint the first Mass in honor of that Nativity by which God the Father begot him from his own womb, that is, from the secret place of his proper substance, “before the morning star” (Ps. 109; Prov. 9), that is, before angelic nature and before he made anything; and should chant the second, praising and exulting, in veneration of him who came blessed in the name of the Lord through the Virgin’s womb.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why the Book of the Generation is read before the first Mass

On this night, before the solemnities of Mass, the *Book of the Generation of Jesus Christ* (Matt. 1) is read to us. This has been handed down by the holy Church in a most beautiful order and mystical institution. For behold: the truly divine architects of the order set before us, through the sequence of this reading, that ladder which Jacob saw while sleeping at night in the deep darkness. The Lord, resting upon its summit which touched heaven, appeared to Jacob and promised the land as an inheritance to him and to his seed, when Jacob, at his father’s command, was going to take a wife from the household and kindred of his father and mother for the propagation of that seed.

For, to say nothing now of mortality—according to which, “all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10)—what did that ladder prefigure, upon which the Lord rested, as has been said, and appeared, if not the generation of Jesus Christ? The holy Evangelist so wove it together by divine utterance that he came through Joseph to Christ. Upon Joseph, namely, the highest [Col. 0075D] rung of the ladder, the little Lord rested. Did he not rest upon that blessed man when, born in this world an orphan—that is, without a fleshly father—he deigned to be sustained, together with his mother who had given birth, by Joseph’s support? And, to omit other things, did he not most especially rest upon him when, so that he might not be found by the enemies Herod and the others who were seeking his life, he was carried into Egypt by that same foster-father, and after Herod’s death was brought back again into the land of Judah? [Col. 0076A] (Matt. 2).

When, therefore, in the middle of the night we hear that book of Christ’s generation, we are asleep not with bodily sleep but in contemplation of heavenly things, according to the Bride’s saying in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5). When, I say, we hear that generation, then we do not so much dream as see, with a wakeful mind and sure faith, the aforesaid ladder. We hear our little Lord, made little for us, coming forth through the gate of heaven—which the highest rung of the ladder, namely blessed Joseph, touches by the dignity of his espousal; through the gate of heaven, I say, that is, through the blessed Virgin—coming forth little and crying, and resting upon the ladder in the manner already described, promising our salvation, that is, the salvation of the Gentiles, as a great blessing; indeed, fulfilling the promise.

For what Jacob heard the Lord say in that sleep—“And in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 28)—is fulfilled in this generation of Christ. The truly divine Evangelist, seeing this, expressly inserted Rahab the harlot and Ruth the Moabitess into this genealogy, because he discerned that Christ came according to the flesh not only for Jews but also [Col. 0076C] for Gentiles. Indeed, he deigned to have mothers from the Gentiles, as the prophets had previously testified. David says: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon” (Ps. 86), that is, the breadth of the confused nations. For *Rahab* means “breadth,” and *Babylon* means “confusion.” Isaiah says in the oracle concerning Moab: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). This is as if he plainly said: You shall send forth, Lord, your Lamb, Christ, from among the Gentiles, so that carnal Israel may not boast that Christ belongs peculiarly to it. The very fact that you shall send this same Christ from the Gentiles to the mountain of the daughter of Zion openly contradicts that estimation.

For by the rock of the desert is signified Ruth the Moabitess, who, standing [Col. 0076D] firm upon the rock of solid faith, forgot her ancestral gods and her own people; she came with Naomi, was joined to Boaz the Bethlehemite, and bore Obed, grandfather of King David (Ruth 4), thereby becoming also an ancestress of the Savior. Thus, with forefathers produced from two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, as two sides of the ladder, and with diverse rungs inserted, they support Christ the Lord coming forth from the summit of heaven. All the holy angels descend and ascend by it; and all the elect first descend by being humbled to receive faith in his Incarnation, and afterward are raised to see the glory of his divinity.

Thus elsewhere the Lord himself says: “Amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending [Col. 0077A] upon the Son of Man” (John 1): that is, supported and raised by the Son of Man, you shall see all the saints ascending to God, the barriers of heaven having been opened to them through the redemption of the Son of Man. And in order that they may afterward ascend, they must first descend to the prayer of his cross or Passion in the spirit of humility. Matthew and Luke appear to indicate both this ascent and descent: one of them traces Christ’s generation by descending (Matt. 1), the other by ascending (Luke 3). For God made man, while crying in the cradle, invites us to humility through the example of his humility; but when baptized, as he begins to shine forth with heavenly miracles, he raises the humble to understand the glory of his divinity.

When at last that aforesaid generation of Christ has been read, the choir of the Church immediately resounds, chanting solemn praise to God. And rightly so. For if Jacob, when he awoke from sleep, said, “Truly the Lord is in this place” [Col. 0077B] (Gen. 28), etc.—if, I say, he was so amazed at the shadow or figure of future things which he had seen in a dream—how much more ought we, beholding the reality of the accomplished matter, to be stirred up to praise and to call this place, that is, the holy Church, Bethel, that is, “house of God,” where truly there is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven, namely the blessed offspring and the glorious Virgin who bore the King of heaven? And if Jacob, “rising at once, took the stone which he had placed beneath his head and set it up as a pillar, pouring oil upon it” (ibid.), how much more should we, as soon as this genealogy has been recited to us, lift up with the highest praises the supreme, precious cornerstone (1 Pet. 2), which we have placed beneath our head, that is, our heart, as a stable foundation, and pour upon it the oil of devout confession and thankful devotion?

Therefore we rightly celebrate the solemnities of Mass immediately; and just as the angels were seen ascending and descending, so we too ascend through faith, singing the first Mass, as has been said, in praise of the divine Nativity, and the second in confession and honor of the human generation which he underwent for us.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why the Evangelist arranged Christ’s genealogy so as to carry it to Joseph rather than to Mary

[Col. 0077D] Perhaps someone now asks why the Evangelist, although he could have traced from Abraham or David that line of descent by which he might reach the fleshly father of the blessed Virgin, and the Virgin herself as mother, and the son born from her, preferred to arrange it so as to descend to Joseph, who without doubt is not Christ’s fleshly father. The answer is that this would rightly have been done had the Evangelist intended to show through which fathers, or what sort of fathers, Christ’s flesh was connected to the fleshly descent of David or Abraham. But this is not what he intends, since to be Christ’s fleshly kinsman is not so great a thing that it should need to be proclaimed by the evangelical voice throughout the world. Many of his fleshly relatives could indeed have been evil, of whom he says: “My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me” [Col. 0078A] (Ps. 37).

What, then, does he rather intend? Certainly this: to trace the lineage of those gods of whom the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81). The Lord himself testifies in the Gospel that they were called gods because the word of God came to them (John 10). It is clear that the word of God which came to them is none other than this Word which was made flesh. They either heard of his Incarnation through the Holy Spirit—as Abraham and David did—or through prophets sent to them, as Ahaz did. To him, when the prophet had said, “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord,” he shortly afterward added: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7), etc. Therefore the Evangelist arranged this genealogy for that reason: because through them, or to them, the promise of this Incarnation was made.

There is no doubt, moreover, that Abraham was the first and blessed Joseph the last of all these. For the same word of God came to Joseph when he was told: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear [Col. 0078B] to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1). We must carefully observe what is said when David and Abraham are more conspicuously named than the others in this genealogy, the Evangelist saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (ibid.). Blessed Joseph too is called no less eminently father of the Lord, not by the nature of flesh but by affection and office, when in that same genealogy he is called “the husband of Mary.” Here, moreover, the angel says to him: “Joseph, son of David,” etc.

Since, then, there are these three foremost and most distinguished persons—Abraham, David, and Joseph—named, I say, among all those to whom the promise was made, we must especially inquire why the Evangelist intends to name these more eminently. Clearly, he considered the successive enlargements of the promise by which Christ was promised at different times to these three as man, king, and God. For the promise made to Abraham declared Christ to be a true human being: “In your seed,” he says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). The promise made to David signified that he would be not only man but king: “From the fruit of your womb,” he says, “I shall set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). But the promise made to blessed Joseph plainly declares him God: “You shall bear [Col. 0078D] a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). For to save from sins belongs to God alone.

The three Magi later attested these same three things—mortal human being, king, and God—by their mystical gifts, through the wondrous working of the Holy Spirit’s grace. Thus the Gentiles, formerly brutish and unlearned, suddenly learned all the things which at different times he had promised to the Jewish people. Therefore Christ’s sacred genealogy was rightly woven together, and in the manner fitting for one who observed heavenly mysteries, so that it should be brought down to Joseph, to whom, as has been said, the final indeed but best promise was made, ending thus: “For he shall save his people from their sins.”

[Col. 0079A] It is especially pleasing, moreover, that this same genealogy, like a fisherman’s long line cast into the waves of this age, bears at its upper end an iron hook within its bait: that is, the true God in true flesh, to catch Leviathan, the great serpent, who devours human souls like little fish (Job 40; Isa. 27). It is evident, however, that a fisherman’s line is attached not to flesh but to iron. The beauty of the comparison is therefore complete in this: the often-mentioned ancestry of the Savior is not brought down according to fleshly descent to Mary, but reaches Joseph according to divine kinship. Since Joseph is not Christ’s fleshly father but the next-to-last heir of faith and of the aforesaid promise, it is as though the line were tied not to flesh but to an iron hook.

It has already been said above that Christ was born on Sunday night, so that on the day when God said, “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. 1), the true light might rise for us amid darkness. Let us now add that this same wondrous Creator of ours, who, as has been said, was born on Sunday night, was conceived on the sixth feria. For if you add the five concurrents of that year mentioned above to the one regular of April, the result is six. And when the month of April begins on the sixth feria, the eighth day before the Kalends of April is likewise certainly the sixth feria, on which we observe the Lord’s Annunciation. Therefore, admiring and revering the devout and beautiful order and provident arrangement in the author of our salvation, we see that on the day on which he formed the old Adam from the clay of the earth, he began to remake for himself the new human being [Col. 0079C] from the true flesh of the Virgin Mary (Gen. 2; Luke 1), and on that same day was nevertheless to redeem him by the Passion of his death.

## CHAPTER XX. On the office of the first Mass.

The office of the first Mass, namely, “The Lord said unto me: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps. II), plainly commemorates throughout almost all its parts the divine birth of the Son of God. “For ‘today,’” says Blessed Augustine, “because it signifies presence, and because in eternity there is neither anything past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it were not yet, but only the present, since whatever is eternal always is—for this reason the saying, ‘This day have I begotten thee,’ is understood in a divine sense: it proclaims the everlasting generation of the power and wisdom of God, which is the only-begotten Son” [Col. 0079D] [Note: Col. 0079D. St Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm II*].

Therefore, since this venerable saying is so often repeated in the person of God the Father—in the introit, the gradual, the alleluia, and the communion—the offertory, “Let the heavens rejoice” (Ps. XXV), joins in with the rejoicing angels who sing “Glory in the highest.” In the collects, indeed, the Lord’s Nativity is commemorated; yet the incarnation of the Word is not yet expressed even there. Rather, the service chiefly venerates, through the brightness of the true light, the divine generation of the Son of God. How, then, does it accord with the Gospel, which plainly recounts his human birth?

[Col. 0080A] Clearly, through that single expression of splendid and venerable dignity which the impure Helvidius, with blind eyes that did not see and without knowing how to venerate it, turned into an insult against the undefiled and perpetual Virgin. For there one reads: “And she brought forth her firstborn son” (Luke II). Helvidius argued foolishly that blessed Mary had other children by Joseph, who were called the brothers of the Lord, because the Evangelist called him “firstborn.” He maintained that one who has no brothers is not called firstborn, and that the preceding statement consequently requires this conclusion. Blessed Jerome gave an apt and eloquent reply: everything that opens the womb is firstborn, and every only-begotten child is firstborn; but the proposition is not reversible, for not every firstborn is also an only-begotten child [Col. 0080B] [Note: Col. 0079D. St Jerome, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*, no. 10, Migne edition].

Yet it should be understood more reverently: the most eloquent Evangelist did not insert “firstborn” so superfluously as to refer merely to the fact that she was a mother—a Virgin Mother, which the preceding whole narrative had already established, and which is far greater than for any mother to bear a firstborn child. Bede likewise holds the same view in his commentary on Luke.

For Christ the Lord is “the firstborn of every creature,” the power and wisdom of God (I Cor. I), which says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. XXIV). He who, according to his human nature, came after John and after many other saints, is, according to the higher glory and the privilege of grace poured out upon his lips, “firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. VIII). Thus it should be understood and distinguished [Col. 0080C]: “And she brought forth her firstborn son”—that is, firstborn before every creature. “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII). Therefore it cannot be that, according to the tenor of the order mentioned above, the divine birth which is praised or recalled in the chant should be narrated in the readings.

## Chapter XXI. On the Office of the Second Mass

The office of the second Mass wholly accords with the words of the shepherds, who say: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word,” etc. (Luke II).

The shepherds of souls—whose cry is, “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIV)—these holy shepherds, I say, who keep vigil and guard the watches of the night, that is, of the present life, over the Lord’s flock [Col. 0080D], instruct its souls by reading and singing. They report to the same flock what they have seen at Bethlehem, that is, in the house of bread: namely, him who came down from heaven (John VI). Rejoicing, they say: “A light shall shine upon us this day,” etc. (Isa. IX). And there follows: “The Lord hath reigned; he is clothed with majesty” (Ps. XCII).

For when the Lord God became man, he reigned over us, clothed in that beauty of which it is elsewhere said: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the beauty wherewith his mother crowned him” (Cant. V). That very humanity which, because of his exceeding love wherewith he loved us [Col. 0081A] (Eph. II), the Godhead put on, is adornment: the adornment of compassion, the diadem of loving-kindness, the crown of glory, the beauty of grace, the loveliness of charity.

Everything that follows has the same meaning. The two readings, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isa. LXI) and “The goodness of God appeared” (Tit. III), are like the two cherubim mentioned above. With bright and open faces—that is, meanings—they look toward what is in the Gospel: God incarnate, the mercy-seat (Exod. XXIII). In the gradual he is blessed; in the alleluia he is proclaimed as clothed with the beauty mentioned above; in the offertory he is praised for establishing the world (Ps. XCII). He is the same one who in the Gospel is figured by Bethlehem, that is, by the house of bread: namely, the holy Church, which he established by being himself born as man within it—he whom the Most High founded [Col. 0081B] (Ps. LXXXVI); and from that time his throne has been made ready (Ps. XCII), from the time when he who is God from eternity was born as man in her.

This same Bethlehem is his house, which holiness adorns for length of days (Ps. XXII). And because the first wall is from the Hebrews (Eph. II), whose firstfruits were the shepherds mentioned above (Luke II), the communion is appropriately: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion” (Zech. IX). For the Church which is from the Hebrews is properly called the daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem, especially because in Zion, which is also Jerusalem, were their Temple and their holy things.

Both Mass stations ought to have been held at Saint Mary’s; but an intervening cause required that one be celebrated at Saint Anastasia’s: namely, her passion. She was one of the noblest Roman matrons, and under the Emperor Diocletian, after the long labor [Col. 0081C] of chastity and service to the saints, after prolonged squalor in prison, was at last stretched out by hands and feet, bound to stakes, and burned by fire placed round about her. On the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, she was born into heaven.

## Chapter XXII. On the Office of the Greater Mass

On the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity resounds that chief trumpet-blast of the Gospel, which the Holy Spirit, breathing through it, quickened with greater grace, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

This is that wondrous trumpet which, sounding in Zion, called the nations, proclaimed to peoples, and announced to the ends of the earth and the islands [Col. 0081D] (Isa. LX)—which were far off because they had departed far from the Lord (Eph. II)—that our Lord and Saviour was coming. This, I say, is that great sound of the heavens declaring the glory of God, which went forth into all the earth (Ps. XVIII); this thunder proclaiming the works of his hands in the firmament, which made the words of the speaking heavens heard unto the ends of the earth: namely, that God the Word, God hidden (Isa. XLV), “hath set his tabernacle in the sun, and goeth forth as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII; Rom. X).

For it announces to all nations, with beautiful feet bearing good tidings, the preaching of peace and the proclamation of salvation (Isa. LII). It burst forth from the narrow confines of Judaea, where God alone was known, and from carnal Israel, in whom alone his name was great [Col. 0082A] (Ps. LXXV); and the evangelical trumpet spoke this salvation of God to all nations. No longer are there languages or speeches in which the aforesaid voices of the heavens are not heard (Ps. XVIII).

This is what we sing in the introit according to the prophet: “Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given” (Isa. IX). These are the wonders for which we ought, in the following words, to sing a new song to the Lord. This is the arm which, according to the prophetic reading of this day, “the Lord hath prepared in the sight of all nations” (Isa. LII). This is the salvation of our God, which all the ends of the earth have seen (ibid.). This is that of which the following apostolic reading speaks: “In these last days God hath spoken unto us in his Son,” he who of old spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways by the prophets [Col. 0082B] (Heb. I).

Thus, according to the gradual, all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God, and God has made known his salvation (Ps. XCVII). Thus, according to the alleluia, a great light has come down upon the earth, because God the Word, God the true light, who enlightens every person coming into this world, came down through the cloud of flesh, came down upon our earthly life. All this is sufficiently clear in itself: it accords with the Gospel that is its head.

One point deserves inquiry: namely, the offertory, in which the dominion and power of our Lord Jesus Christ, the great and dreadful judge and victorious king, are proclaimed, especially in this verse: “Thou hast humbled the proud one as one wounded” (Ps. LXXXVIII). We might suppose that this whole office refers solely [Col. 0082C] to the night in which the Lord was born. But on that night the child born unto us did not yet know, by reason of the age of the flesh he had assumed, how to call father or mother (Isa. VIII).

Yet in this offertory, and especially in the verse just quoted, that strength is praised by which, according to his prophetic name, “Make haste to take the spoils; hasten to seize the prey” (ibid.), he humbled the proud devil like one wounded, ascending on high and leading captivity captive (Ps. LXVII). In the power of his arm he scattered his enemies; and this pertains to the final clause of the Gospel cited above: “And we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I). For this is the glory of the incarnate Word: that he stripped away the spoils [Col. 0082D] and swiftly plundered hell.

Therefore this office concerns not only an infant’s crying and a hidden manger. It is the sound of the apostles, which went forth into all the earth, saying: “He hath set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII), and proclaiming the whole acceptable year of the Lord, announcing the whole salvation wrought by the Word made flesh. Hence, both because of the excellence of so great a day and because blessed Peter the Apostle first saw and first confessed this salvation of our God—when the Father who is in heaven revealed it to him (Matt. XVI)—and as prince first brought the good tidings to the Roman citadel, the station is rightly held at his church.

O truly “great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared unto angels, was preached unto the nations, believed on in the world, and received up into glory” [Col. 0083A] (I Tim. III).

When this Gospel, or nearly any Gospel containing something holy concerning Christ, is read, an ancient custom prevails in almost all churches: the deacon, as though coming from the south, stands turned toward the north. “For behold, I come from the south,” says the Lord; and Habakkuk says: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. III). For he came from the south because the Son of God came and was incarnate through the operation of the Holy Spirit; and through the Holy Spirit “offered himself as a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour” [39] (Eph. V).

The deacon, therefore, when he is about to recite so great a salvation, fittingly turns toward the north, in order thereby to indicate that, when this salvation of God was sent to the nations [Col. 0083B] (Isa. LII), a mighty embassy was directed against the devil, according to God’s saying: “I will say to the north: Give up” (Isa. XLIII).

## Chapter XXIII. On the Office, “When Deep Silence”

The office of the Lord’s Nativity is, as we have said, the joy of the nations, who have all seen the salvation of God, and whose reception is life from the dead, namely for the Jews (Rom. XI). But this office has no fixed place on a particular day and is almost a bereaved proclamation of the Jews who are to be recalled at the end of the age.

For the wild olive ought not to boast against the branches of the good olive, because they were broken off and fell through unbelief. It was itself grafted in contrary to nature and stands by faith (ibid.).
