Nor is it fitting that the younger brother should rejoice because, having been received and feasting with his father, the elder brother angrily refuses to enter; rather, amid the festivities he entreats his father to go out and bring him in, softened by gentle words [Col. 0083C] (Luke XV).

That this is so appears sufficiently even from the communion of the present office: “Take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Judah; for they are dead who sought the child’s life” (Matt. II). For now that child, namely God incarnate, has left his house and forsaken his inheritance (Jer. XII), because, as it is written, ascending upon a white cloud he entered Egypt: he went to the nations, which had been the kingdom of the ancient Pharaoh, that is, the devil (Isa. XIX).

But then, when those who sought his life are dead—that is, when the flame of modern envy by which they sought the souls of his saints and shed blood upon their land, that is, before their own people, has been lulled to sleep—he will return. Then, I say, according to the mystical sense of the Gospel, when Jesus has been brought into the Temple, that is, into the synagogue of the Jews through faith, “his father and mother,” namely, all his kindred according to the flesh, “were marvelling at those things which were spoken concerning him. And Simeon blessed him” [Col. 0083D] (Luke II): that is, that people, then righteous and God-fearing. Thus he who is now “set for a fall” will then be set “for a resurrection in Israel” (ibid.).

Since the time of his coming cannot be known by us, it is rightly compared to night; and therefore in the introit, “When deep silence” (Wis. XVIII), that which is past is sung because of this similar future event. Then he will fulfil that for which “God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV); and the heir will be set free, who is still held in servitude under the elements—that is, under the literal sense—because he is a child in understanding. At last he will obtain the kingdom and throne of David his father: he of whom the gradual sings, “Fairer in beauty” [Col. 0084A] (Ps. XLIV).

## Chapter XXIV. On the Holy Day of Epiphany

The holy day of Epiphany is celebrated for three reasons. On that day the Lord was adored by the Chaldaeans [Col. 0084B] (Matt. II); likewise, having now begun to be thirty years old, he was baptized by John (Luke III); and, when the year came round again, he made wine from water at the wedding (John III). Since, then, it is celebrated for these three reasons, it rightly takes the first of them according to the solemnity of the daily office.

Among these three, the Lord’s baptism by John appears to surpass the rest; and for this reason the Greeks are said to celebrate the sacrament of baptism more numerously and solemnly on this day. Yet the holy Roman Church, ever illuminated by that revelation through which Peter knew Christ as the Son of God, declares in explicit writings that this practice must be avoided.

For Leo the Great, writing to all the bishops established throughout Sicily, says among other things: “I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have adopted so irrational an innovation as to believe, through confusion of the mysteries belonging to the two times, that there was no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which he rose from the dead” [Col. 0084C] [Note: Col. 0083D. Letters of St Leo the Great, Letter 16, to all the bishops throughout Sicily, chapter 1].

And subsequently he says: “Properly speaking, it is in the death of the Crucified One and in the resurrection from the dead that the power of baptism makes a new creature from the old, so that in those who are reborn both the death of Christ and his life may work, as the blessed Apostle says: ‘Do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death’” (Rom. VI) [Note: Col. 0084D. Ibid., chapter 3].

And shortly afterward: “The very character of the work, therefore, teaches that the lawful day for the general celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. For confirmation of this, it is of great importance that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he rose from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the bishops of the Churches were instructed—both the form and the authority to baptize, saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’” [Col. 0084D] (Matt. XXVIII). “He could indeed have instructed them in this even before his passion, had he not intended it to be understood particularly that the grace of regeneration began from his resurrection” [Note: Col. 0084D. Ibid.].

Again, after some further remarks: “But if anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany, which in its proper order is to be revered with due honour [Col. 0085A], possesses a privilege for baptism because some suppose that on that day the Lord came to the baptism of Saint John, let him know that that baptism had a different grace and a different rationale, and did not belong to the same power by which, through the Holy Spirit, those are reborn of whom it is said: ‘Who were born, not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God’” (John I).

“But the Lord, needing no remission of any sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, chose to be baptized (Matt. III), just as he chose to be circumcised and to have an offering for purification made for himself (Luke II), so that he who had been made of a woman, as the Apostle says, might be made under the law (Gal. IV)—a law which he had not come to destroy but to fulfil (Matt. V), and, by fulfilling it [Col. 0085B], to bring it to an end. As the blessed Apostle proclaims: ‘Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes’” (Rom. X).

“But he established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he taught that he himself was the beginning” (Col. I). “And he ordained the power of regeneration when from his side flowed the blood of redemption and the water of baptism” (John XIX) [Note: Col. 0085D. Letters of St Leo the Great, Letter 16, to all the bishops throughout Sicily, chapter 3].

Therefore, among the three reasons, the Lord’s baptism by John is not the preeminent one, because he established for us the sacrament of his baptism not then but when blood and water flowed from his side. Rather, preeminent and chief is the fact that he was adored by the Magi, who were certainly Gentiles; this provides great matter for spiritual joy to the hearts of the enlightened nations [Col. 0085C]. For in them the firstfruits of the nations were then received. Our peace received them—the one who made both peoples one, being God and man, one Christ in himself, and joining Jews and Gentiles into one people (Eph. II).

Thus the whole office of the Mass is worthily composed concerning this: in it the holy Church, chosen from the nations, offers to God a grateful proclamation of praise for the beginning of her calling and for her salvation. The entire theme of praise is the gifts of the kings: gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. II). These gifts were offerings produced by faith, deposited through heavenly instruction, and understood through the Holy Spirit [40]. For what could be more fitting to heavenly instruction than to confess, by gold, a king; by incense, God; and by myrrh, one who is mortal?

The neighbouring wall contributed nothing of the sort: that wall which came from the Jews and first joined itself, in the shepherds, to the cornerstone. Nor is this surprising. The angelic teaching instructed those shepherds, that is, the Jews [Col. 0085D] (Luke II); but the divine oracle alone, through the invisible instruction of the Holy Spirit, taught these, namely the Gentiles, when they received the new star (Matt. II).

Therefore the whole office of this day, by prophetic testimonies and praises, resounds with, venerates, and honours the gifts of the kings, which bear witness to the entirely sound faith of the holy Church.

Concerning the third cause of the feast mentioned above—namely, that the Lord made wine from water—it is commonly asked how it can fit that this occurred on the same day on which the Lord was baptized. For on the day on which the Lord was baptized, he neither chose disciples nor performed miracles, but was immediately led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; there he observed a fast of forty days, and, returning from there, only then chose disciples, whom he would instruct by teaching and confirm by miracles [Col. 0086A] (Matt. IV).

Did he, then, spend the entire thirtieth year of his age—at the beginning of which he was baptized—without disciples, and so, when the year came round, perform on that same day this wonderful first sign before his disciples? It must indeed be believed so, since, according to the authority of holy Church, we cannot deny that these three things mentioned above were celebrated on one day.

For before John was delivered up, Christ neither preached publicly nor chose the twelve apostles. It is also plainly clear from Luke’s narrative that, after going forth in the power of the Spirit into Galilee and preaching publicly, he did not immediately choose disciples. Instead he taught in the synagogues of the Jews and was glorified by all: “And all bore him witness, and wondered at the words of grace which proceeded from his mouth” [Col. 0086B] (Luke IV [the source reads XIV]).

Before choosing them, he had suffered persecution so that he was led to a precipice; fleeing from city to city, he taught in the synagogues on Sabbaths (ibid.). Before this, too, he healed Simon’s mother-in-law, who was suffering from severe fevers, and did several other things. Thus his fellow-citizens said to him when he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: “Whatever things we have heard done in Capernaum, do here also in thy country” (ibid.).

We therefore celebrate the holy day of Epiphany adorned with three miracles. For, as we have sung: “Today the star led the Magi to the manger; on this day Christ was baptized by John; on this day, at the wedding, wine was made from water.” Thus, in a short space—that is, thirteen days—his age of thirty years is commemorated. The remaining three years, during which he preached and declared his divinity by miracles, are commemorated in the offices of the three Sundays following Epiphany.

These pertain to Epiphany—that is, manifestation—because whatever heavenly mysteries of his divinity he taught during the three years of his preaching, and whatever he performed with his “rounded and golden hands” [Col. 0086C] (Cant. V), that is, hands acting easily and divinely, were proofs by which his true divinity became known through flesh.

Therefore on the first Sunday is set the Gospel in which he first testified that God was his Father, saying to his parents: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” (Luke II).

On the second, however, the Gospel is read in which, invited to a wedding, he turned water into wine (John II). This was truly a great sign of divinity; for God alone can change nature. It was also a venerable sign of our restoration, by which our mortal nature will put on immortality and corruption will possess incorruption (I Cor. XV); and it was a beautiful and fitting beginning of his signs.

Likewise on the third Sunday, when we say, “And, to protect us, stretch forth the right hand of thy majesty,” his true divinity shines forth, according to the stretching forth of the hand [Col. 0087A] with which he touched the leper, saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII). It shines forth also through the centurion’s faith, for by healing the centurion’s servant while absent in body, he showed himself to be God, who is present everywhere. Thus, in the three Sunday offices, the manifestation of the Lord—that is, the whole of his preaching during the three years—is commemorated.

## Chapter XXV. Why We Carry Candles at the Purification of Saint Mary

At the Purification of Saint Mary we carry candles in order that we may in some measure share in the blessed joy of righteous Simeon, who, carrying the infant Christ in his arms, recognized him and confessed that he was prepared “before the face of all peoples, a light for revelation to the nations” [Col. 0087B] (Luke II).

Admonished outwardly by this sign, we more closely embrace in the arms of faith within our minds that true light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I); and, with desires rising upward, [Col. 0088A] grieving, we seek his bodily absence, and seeking, we grieve.

For he departed into heaven. Before leaving here, already beyond the infancy in which he was carried by Simeon, he had increased in age and wisdom (Luke II). Therefore we all bear in our hands his visible sign, though we neither need nor can visibly bear him, as Simeon did.

Consecrated candles suitably signify to us that which was visible in Christ. For as the bee produces wax and honey by a virginal work, so the Virgin Mary brought forth Christ, God and man, while the integrity of her womb was preserved. For bees neither mingle in sexual intercourse nor are dissolved by lust; they are shaken by none of the pains of childbirth, but suddenly send forth a great swarm of offspring, gathering their progeny with their mouths from leaves and herbs [Col. 0088B].

Therefore, by a fitting sign, we represent as far as we can the carrying of the infant Christ, proclaiming with heart and mouth the blessedness of him who lived so long that he saw Christ the Lord, saw him in order to adore him, adored him in order that, dismissed in peace, he might happily depart from here (ibid.).

# Book Four

[Col. 0087]

## Chapter I. On Septuagesima

In this chapter many matters must be investigated: why it is called Septuagesima and why it bears this name; on what grounds it is celebrated before the Lord’s Passion; and why alleluia is removed from the mouth of the Church. All these have reasons so true and so certain that, whatever else one may say, secure truth will resist it on every side and will strike the needy and failing conscience with a multitude of opposing or contradictory considerations.

For example, suppose one says that it is called Septuagesima because seventy days are counted from this Sunday until the Saturday on which the white garments are laid aside, and that these days signify our captivity, in which we wander from God in this world (II Cor. V). Immediately an objection strongly opposed to our calculation arises: the day of the Lord’s Resurrection—the nobility of the year, the glory of the months, the armour of the days—is counted within this number. What day could seem less fitting to signify captivity than that upon which the Lord rose again after conquering the captor? [Col. 0087D] (Eph. IV). What day will deserve to signify freedom, if the first day of the Lord’s Resurrection occurs as the sixty-fourth in the number of days signifying our captivity, formerly signified by the same number of years when the people of God were exiles under Nebuchadnezzar in the land of Babylon? (Jer. XXV).

Likewise, there is this objection: although this Sunday called Septuagesima is the seventieth from the Saturday mentioned, the following Sunday—called Sexagesima—is by no means the sixtieth; Quinquagesima is by no means the fiftieth; and Quadragesima is by no means the fortieth [Col. 0088C]. What, then, should we call Septuagesima? This must be explained more deeply and more firmly.

## Chapter II. What We Call Septuagesima

We call Septuagesima the seven consecutive Sundays distinguished by great and mystical offices. On the first, man, cast out from the happiness of paradise and from the face of his Creator, cries: “Groanings have surrounded me,” etc. (Gen. III). On the seventh, returning from this pilgrimage and valley of tears, it is said in the prophetic voice: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep a feast, you who love him” (Isa. LXVI), etc.

## Chapter III. Why We Call It Septuagesima

We call the first Sunday, which is the seventh from the last, Septuagesima rather than otherwise; the sixth, Sexagesima; and the fifth, Quinquagesima, because the offices commemorate the same thing that was signified by the seventy-year captivity of the people of God, who literally sat and wept by the rivers of Babylon [Col. 0088D] (Ps. CXXXVI).

And what is that thing? It is the sevenfold division of the ages of the world. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham—or, according to some, to Moses; the third from Moses to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth from the Babylonian deportation to the coming of the Lord; the sixth from the coming of Christ to the end of the world. The seventh age of the world is already that rest to which the souls of the elect daily pass, resting between the breasts of their rejoicing mother, the heavenly Jerusalem (Isa. LXVI).

Because, therefore, through these seven Sundays the same thing is commemorated that was signified by the seventy years of Babylonian captivity, this first Sunday of the seven is rightly called Septuagesima. How sound this is will become clearer below from the offices of the Sundays themselves [Col. 0089A]. Now we must say on what grounds they were appointed before the Lord’s Passion.

## Chapter IV. Why the Seven Sundays Were Thus Appointed before the Lord’s Passion

Blessed Pope Gregory—who, as we have already said above, is described in the book of his life as a most diligent arranger of the offices and stations—understood, by that meaning which the Holy Spirit revealed to him, that the worthy commemoration of Christ’s saving Passion required that testimony be rendered to him by all the saints and elect who had existed from the beginning of the world, as though common funeral rites were being rendered to him through the mouth of the present Church.

For all the saints from the foundation of the world had one salvation and expectation: the Passion of the Redeemer. It was foretold in their harmonious utterances and prefigured in their deeds. As many mirrors, though situated in different places, reflect the same image when set before a single sun, so many saints, coming beforehand at different times and with different merits, prefigured in diverse figures the one and same Passion of the Saviour.

Therefore, after the aforesaid arranger of the offices had commemorated Christ’s Nativity and manifestation, and the three years of his preaching had been made known, he made a praiseworthy digression in our year [42] [the text probably reads: “in our mind”], returning to the beginning of the world. Gathering from the different ages voices suitable to the Church, he brought forward, as though from different places, seven choirs in a rational and venerable order [Col. 0089C]. How and in what manner the individual choirs sing in harmony with the present Church will be explained shortly. First, however, it seems necessary to say why alleluia, which is the praise of God, is removed from the mouth of the Church during these days.

## Chapter V. Why Alleluia Is Omitted
If we rightly consider what praise of God *alleluia*—a name of ancient dignity and authority—signifies, it appears most beautiful and reasonable, as indeed it is, that this voice has customarily been removed from the mouth of the holy Church during these days [Col. 0089D]. For it does not signify just any praise of God—not the praise of the greater or lesser creatures of heaven, earth, and sea, and of all things in them. Otherwise, if *alleluia* signified every kind of praise of God, it would be pointless for it to be removed from our mouths at this season, when, never ceasing from God’s praises, we praise Him who in the beginning made heaven and earth; who divided light from darkness; who made the firmament and set it amid the waters; who at His command caused the earth to bring forth green herbage and trees bearing fruit according to their kind; who made the heavenly lights and placed them in the firmament; who commanded fishes, birds, and beasts to come forth; and finally, who created man in His own image (Gen. I).

[Col. 0090A] What praise of God, then, does *alleluia* signify? Surely that praise—indeed, that very one—to whom God the Father says in the Psalm: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. LVI [57], CVII [108]). The glory of the Father, the Son of God, is perfect praise and everlasting music: namely, the supreme Wisdom, born from the heart of that same Father, the eternal musician. He assumed the harp of our humanity; and when that harp had been broken by envious and foolish children, who ought to have danced at His song (Matt. XI), He restored it again through the glory of the resurrection and made it an unviolated psaltery. That glory, I say—that harp or psaltery—is our *alleluia*.

For whatever heavenly delight He displayed to His hearers—whose eyes were blessed because they saw, and whose ears because they heard (Luke X)—whatever, I say, the Lord Jesus Christ sang beforehand with His own mouth concerning heavenly joys, is *alleluia*: it is the new song; it is sweet praise. Yet neither did the ancient saints see or hear this, of whom the Lord Himself says: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X; Matt. XIII). Nor can we, so long as we are in the body—for He has withdrawn into heaven—see it or deserve to hear it. For “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V).

But when we commemorate the probable condition of the ancient Church, not yet redeemed, and lament our own sojourning because it has been prolonged, *alleluia* is quite fittingly removed from our mouths. For He whom it signifies “had not yet come; He has now withdrawn from us; and the bridegroom has been taken away [Col. 0090C] from His children” (Matt. IX). He who sang the responsory *Alleluia: While she is present, they imitate her, and they desire her when she has led herself forth*, understood this rightly. For in saying here concerning *alleluia* what is written about Wisdom—which is without doubt Christ—he plainly intended Christ to be understood by *alleluia*: while He was present, they imitated Him; when He led Himself forth, ascending into heaven, they desired Him, and He “triumphs, crowned for ever” (Wis. IV) before God the Father (Eph. IV), as it is written: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour, O Lord, and hast set him over the works of thy hands” (Ps. VIII [9]).

He did not deal in trifles or string together childish absurdities when he said: “Alleluia, return to thy treasures; the angels shall bless thee.” For Christ the Lord has returned [Col. 0090D] to His treasures—that is, to the hidden places of heaven—where He is blessed by angels and desired by His children who are pilgrims here below.

Yet not only the glorious Bridegroom of the Church, Christ the new man, is proclaimed under this name; His new Bride, the holy Church—for she is His body—may also rightly be proclaimed by the same name. For she too is an instrument of that music, that is, of divine Wisdom, whose whole fullness dwells bodily in the man Christ (Eph. I; Col. II). Therefore, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, when the new offspring is reborn and the young lambs who have come to the fountains are filled with brightness, we rightly address the new Church herself—wholly new, announcing new joys—by this name, *alleluia* [Col. 0091A]. She answers us with a gentle countenance and sweet voice, because the whole office of that day, and of the entire Paschal week, is the exultation of those who were then born anew through water and the Spirit. But we shall speak better of this in its proper place; now let us return to what precedes.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Office of Septuagesima, and Why the Station Is Held at Saint Lawrence

Since it was said above that the seven Sundays signify the seven ages of the world, we must now say how the office of the first Septuagesima Sunday suits the first age. First, it must not be passed over why the station is held at Saint Lawrence. The reason is fitting and apt [Col. 0091B]. For as, in the Church of the first age, the righteous blood of the protomartyr Abel cries from the ground to God, which opened its mouth and received it from the hand of Cain his brother, so in the Roman Church the precious death of blessed Lawrence, by a new and unheard-of kind of martyrdom, cried out to heaven—cried out and was heard throughout the whole world. Foreseeing this cry of his, the holy martyr himself said to Hippolytus: “Hide Christ still more in the secret places, in the inner man; and afterward, when I cry out, listen and come.”

Thus the voice of the first Church, with Abel as its precentor, is fittingly: “They surrounded me” (Ps. XVII [18]). For the sorrows of death had surrounded him, since the joys of life had been lost through the first parents. Indeed, the sick man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, was stripped, wounded, and left half dead by them, had begotten him in his own pains: sick, one sickly; wounded, one diseased; dying, one mortal (Luke X). “And in my distress,” he says, “I called upon the Lord, and He heard my voice from His holy temple” (Ps. XVII [18]). By the certainty of hope he faithfully assumes as already accomplished what was to occur much later, for he had already received the divine oracle concerning the restoration of his salvation, when the Lord said to the serpent: “I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed” (Gen. III).

For the victory of our Redeemer was already then promised: though He is the woman’s seed, He exercised hostility against the ancient dragon so completely that He crushed its head [Col. 0091D] and took away all its power. Let him therefore say: “He heard my voice from His holy temple.” But how great was the expectation! How great the delay of salvation! For there are seventy-seven generations from Adam to the birth of Christ; so we find in the Gospel according to Luke (ch. III). Thus those who, according to the Gospel of the present day, were hired early in the morning murmur fittingly: “These last have worked one hour, and thou hast made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Matt. XX). For those who have lived from the beginning of the world, because they had to live here for a long time, necessarily bore the longer trials of the flesh as well.

This, then, is that very long course of which the Apostle says in the Epistle, in harmony with the Gospel just mentioned: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run indeed, but one receives the prize?” (I Cor. IX). Yet they comforted themselves in their exceedingly long hope, as it were saying what we sing in the gradual: “For the poor shall not be forgotten for ever; the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. IX [10]). Likewise the tract, like the collect in which we say, “That we who are justly afflicted for our sins may mercifully be delivered for the glory of Thy name”—the tract, I say, *Out of the depths*—is the voice of a man groaning beneath the just hand of God amid blows and saying: “If Thou, O Lord, wilt mark iniquities, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. CXXIX [130]).

In these tracts, moreover, it must be noted that nearly all are composed in the graver tones and are never raised into the modes called authentic [Col. 0092B]; rather, all are content with the lower limits of the plagal modes, declaring weeping and sorrow in the lowliness of their sounds. This has been observed very fittingly. For a time of sorrow demands that *alleluia*, the song of those who rejoice, should be omitted. Thus the tract, which meanwhile is sung in place of *alleluia*, turns aside the height and excellence of joy through its grave resonance and restrained movement.

In the offertory, “It is good to give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. XCI [92]), the voice is similarly that of one under the scourge, confessing amid blows the justice of Him who strikes. That verse especially suits the beginnings of the infant Church: “My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn, and my old age in rich mercy” (ibid.). For not in her infancy, when she was glorified by righteous Abel’s sacrifice and made purple by his first blood (Gen. IV); not in her childhood, when, with God speaking to Noah or Abraham, she received the first rudiments of saving teaching (Gen. VI; XII); not in her adolescence, when she received the schoolmaster—that is, Moses’ law—lest she become wanton (Exod. XXIV); not in her youth, when she was crowned with holy kings beginning with David; but in her old age, when she had already grown feeble through kings and prophets, “her horn was exalted like that of the unicorn”—that is, Christ, the king of singular power—and “her old age [was] in rich mercy,” because in the abundance of mercy the blessed King of Israel came (Gal. III).

The communion also, “Make Thy face to shine upon Thy servant” (Ps. CXVIII [119]) [Col. 0092D], is the voice of that same Church according to the first age of the world: the voice, I say, of a man stripped of the glory of God’s countenance, asking that the wall of hostility (Eph. II), interposed between them, be dissolved and torn down—a wall by which the mirrors of human souls had lost the face of the true Sun.

Up to this point, from the day of the Lord’s Nativity, whatever was read in the night vigils had been from the New Testament—fittingly, of course, because of the present life of Christ the same new man, which those days signify. And Paul, the great herald of holy newness, comparing the new grace with the old law, humbled the law of works and raised up the law of faith with the palm of righteousness (Rom. V). But now, according to the reason stated above, ancient history is repeated, in which are narrated the miseries of the old life, lamented by the holy Church in the office already set forth [Col. 0093A].

## CHAPTER VII. On Sexagesima

The distinguished office of this Sunday looks to that time of the second age when He who sows went out for the first time to sow His seed: when Noah first spoke, beginning to prepare the reconciliation of the world, and when He began to imbue the Church, now past her infant years, with the first rudiments of His gentle commandments. For from the time when she was cast out from the calm and peaceful womb of Paradise and born into this misery—whose birth blessed Job, in the person of the same Church, as blessed Gregory says, laments in saying, “Let the day perish in which I was born” (Job III), and so forth—He is read to have handed down no discipline of commandments to her.

But when He spoke with Noah, saying, “For behold, I establish my covenant with you” (Gen. IX), and, by a repeated blessing, began to remove the curse brought upon them, He gradually subjected the childhood of the world to His instruction, giving certain commandments, first to Noah and then to Abraham, and in those first fathers initiating the righteousness of faith. He completed these things in the fullness of grace when, taking the form of a servant, He went out into this world (Phil. II) to sow His seed, in person among the Jewish people and through the holy apostles among all nations.

Accordingly, on this Sunday is read the Gospel: “He who sows went out to sow his seed” (Luke VIII); and the station is held at Saint Paul, for a worthy and evident reason. For he is the chief leader of the word [Col. 0093C], indeed the true sower of words, through whom all nations came to know the grace of God. Therefore, before the priest enters—just as before that sower goes out to his work (Acts XIV), while he is still reclining and rests in the bosom of God the Father—the choir cries aloud: “Arise, why dost Thou sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XXIII [44]). For by arising and sowing His seed He was to bring it about that His face, which He had turned away on account of sin—that is, the knowledge of Him—would once more shine upon the human race. Ignorance of God was the barrenness of our earth.

The sower of heavenly wisdom, therefore, going out to His work, as has been said, and employing His ploughmen, that is, the holy apostles, had as a useful labourer especially blessed Paul, who laboured more than all of them. He sent him to the nations; and, splitting hard hearts with the sharp ploughshare of his tongue, He poured in the abundant seed of faith and morals (I Cor. XV). Upon entering, the priest immediately in the collect, “O God, who beholdest,” sets forth the solemn commemoration of this same Doctor of the Gentiles (II Cor. XI), so that the proper character of the station, suitably assigned, may more clearly commend it. The following Epistle is further relevant to this, in which that same mighty labourer of the heavenly farmer recounts his true labours and the dangers inflicted upon him by those who had invaded his Lord’s fields and would not permit them to be ploughed.

The gradual concerns both classes of people: those who, like good ground, received the seed of the Word of God [Col. 0094A] and yielded the fruit of righteousness; and those who, rebelling against the Lord of the whole earth, broke His plough and slaughtered the innocent oxen. For once the Word of God had been scattered abroad, what He says came to pass: “Let the nations know that Thou, whose name is God, art Thou alone the Most High over all the earth” (Ps. LXXXII [83]). And those who rejected it were made like a wheel: that is, in that, rising in things behind—that is, carnal things—they fall in the forepart, that is, in intellectual things. And as stubble is scattered before the wind, so they perished when the spirit of God’s wrath blew.

In the tract, the Church gives thanks to the oft-mentioned sower: “The earth is moved and troubled” (Ps. LIX [60]); that is, all sinners. When they realized that their own tillage was hateful to God, they were moved to repentance; and, beginning through the significance of preaching to fear, they flee from the face of the bow—that is, from the day of judgment—when the rebels against the divine Word will be struck by the arrow of eternal condemnation from the two Testaments, as it were from two bent horns. Finally, when the Gospel has been read, the corresponding offertory follows: “Perfect my steps in Thy paths” (Ps. XVI [17]). For we must fear lest, having received the seed of the Word of God, we should be laid out beside the way and wander in outward things, be snatched away by birds—that is, unclean spirits—or be choked by the cares and thorny riches of the world; or lest, lacking moisture—that is, the richness of charity—the good seed should wither in us, and so our steps should not be perfected.

He makes His mercies wonderful when He keeps the mercifully implanted seed as [Col. 0094C] the pupil of the eye (ibid.), lest it be pricked by choking thorns; He protects it beneath the shadow of His wings (ibid.), lest it be dried up by the sun’s heat; and He delivers it from the wicked, lest he take the word from our hearts—so that the good ground, bearing fruit in patience, may say: “But I shall appear in righteousness before Thy face” (ibid.). And, as we sing in the communion: “I will enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. XLII [43]). Thus the seed of God bears our earth, in which it has grown—wondrously!—up with itself into the barns of heaven. For though we are earth, unless we are carried by the Word of God, which is Christ, we do not ascend into heaven, as He Himself says: “No one ascends into heaven except the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John V). Therefore with Him and through Him we shall be raised up, carrying sheaves of righteousness, while God makes glad our youth in the strength of eternal newness [Col. 0094D].

## CHAPTER VIII. On Quinquagesima

This Sunday signifies the third age of the world. God looked upon the Church as a young woman reaching maturity, when her time, according to the prophet, was the time of lovers (Ezek. XVI); He rescued her from among fornicators, sending Moses and Aaron and bringing the children of Israel out of Egyptian slavery through great signs and wonders. The office of the present Sunday fits this event very closely, as does the Gospel read on this day. For as the blind man sitting here begged for the light of the way, but was rebuked by the crowds and told to be silent (Luke XVIII), so there the children of Israel, holding to the faith of their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and crying to the Lord to bring them out of Egypt—a word which in our language means “darkness”—and to teach them the worship of His name, which is true and necessary illumination, were rebuked by the Egyptians who oppressed them and said proudly: “You are idle, and therefore you say: Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord” (Exod. V).

Therefore, when the Lord, sending Moses and Aaron, commanded His people to be brought to Him, performed before them miracles by which the true God could be recognized, and gave them a written law, commandments of life, and a rite of worship, then that great blind man—that is, the human race—began to be enlightened, and is enlightened more and more even now, though the crowds, always invisible and sometimes visible too, oppose and rebuke him [Col. 0095B].

This is what the office of this Sunday expresses. For as the priest is about to enter, the blind man mentioned above, as it were, anticipates his illuminator’s coming with cries while the choir sings: “Be Thou unto me a protecting God” (Ps. XXX [31]). Certainly the words, “For Thy name’s sake Thou wilt be my guide and nourish me” (ibid.), concern the way beside which the blind beggar sits. Christ is at once both the Way and the Guide. Likewise, the following collect, “Mercifully hear, we beseech Thee, O Lord, our prayers,” is the cry of the blind man clamouring ever more earnestly to be heard. For when it says, “And, loosing us from the bonds of sins, keep us from all adversity,” it strikes at the crowd of phantasms suffered in prayer, just as the blind man in the Gospel faced the rebuking crowd, and as the children of Israel faced the Egyptians who obstructed and violently detained them lest they go to sacrifice to the Lord God of their fathers (Exod. V).

The reading of the Epistle also—“Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels”—looks to the illumination of this same blind man, not merely from the place where it says, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII), but from its entire course, when it shows charity as the way surpassing all charisms. For charity is the eye of the heart. Whoever lacks it is blind, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going (I John II). Indeed, when God began, as was said, to enlighten humankind by giving the law to the children of Israel, He first anointed its eyes with this collyrium, saying: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy soul, with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself” (Deut. VI).

Although the gradual seems in almost every phrase to sound only the deliverance of the children of Israel discussed above, nevertheless, in saying, “Thou hast made known Thy power among the nations” (Ps. LVII [58]), it concerns the illumination of that same great blind man. So too, in the tract, the words “Enter into His presence” (Ps. LXLIX [50]), and the rest, are the same as saying: “Approach Him and be enlightened.” And when, after the Gospel mentioned above has been read, we say in the offertory, “Blessed art Thou, O Lord; teach me Thy justifications” (Ps. [Col. 0096A] CX [119]), the blind man plainly asks in other words to be enlightened. Immediately he takes up the praises of the way beside which he sat begging and was enlightened; and with such harmony, with such loud proclamation, he repeats “the way of Thy testimonies,” “the way of truth,” and “the way of Thy commandments,” that he can even rouse the hardness of stones to glorify his illuminator.

But because it is not enough to have reached the way and received the illumination of knowledge unless we cast away the desires of the flesh, we are fittingly alarmed by the example of those of whom we say in the communion: “They ate and were exceedingly filled.” For because of the incontinence of their desires they were laid low in the wilderness and did not reach the land of promise (Ps. LXXXVII [88]; Num. XIV). Paul also makes us watchful by their example: “So run,” he says, “that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX).

But whom should we believe to have been guide or shepherd when the Lord again brought His people, the sheep of His pasture, out of the land of Egypt, dividing for them through distributions of grace the Red Sea of baptism, which flowed from His side as He hung upon the cross? Surely blessed Peter the apostle. In the great body of this oft-mentioned blind man, he too was the first to be enlightened, when Christ, Son of the living God, said to him: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to thee, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI). Accordingly, the station of this Sunday is held at the same apostle, so that all the people, seeing, may glorify God after his example and say: “People of acquisition, proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness [Col. 0096C] into His marvellous light” (I Pet. II).

## CHAPTER IX. On the First Sunday of Lent

The office of this Sunday uniformly resounds and repeats the prophetic oracle of the Holy Spirit, without changing subject or persons: an oracle in which most high and fitting aid is promised to the holy Church as she fights against the ancient dragon. This Sunday concerns the fourth age of the world, when the world was strengthened in full youth, and the people of God, as though entering manhood, were crowned with the diadem of kings and adorned with the wisdom of holy prophets. For the patriarch David, chosen according to the Lord’s heart after Saul had been removed, the first of kings and foremost of prophets, prefigures by his name Christ, strong of hand or desirable [Col. 0096D] (I Sam. XVI); he prefigures Him by his victories and announces Him through prophetic utterances and spiritual songs.

And because the Scripture of this prophet and of the others was closed until Christ’s coming, and because hidden knowledge was darkened in the prophets like dark water in the clouds of the air, until the Lamb of God—the only one worthy to receive the book and open its seals (Rev. V)—should, by fulfilling the prophetic voices in His Passion, open them: therefore from this Sunday onwards veils hang before the holy altars of the Church, so that the people may not see the Holy of Holies. In the week before Easter, by the removal of the veils, the same signification is renewed that was effected when the veil of the temple was torn as the Lord gave up His spirit (Matt. XXVII).

Accordingly, on this Sunday the Gospel is appointed in which Christ, the head of the Church, fasting in the wilderness, is said to have overcome the snares of the tempter (Matt. IV), and thus to have walked upon the asp and basilisk and trampled the lion and dragon (Ps. XC [91]). The prophetic trumpets sound throughout the entire office, promising the same victory to all the members of this Head and to the whole body of the Church. The station prescribed for this office, at Saint John Lateran, is highly fitting. For as this entire office sings of the true blessedness of the Saviour, who before all and for all walked upon asp and basilisk, and as it is wholly prophetic, so the Lateran church itself was built by Emperor Constantine in the name of the same holy Saviour and in honour of John, prophet [Col. 0097B] and more than prophet (Matt. XI). Thus prophetic praises are fittingly celebrated there at the apostolic station.

Not only is this Sunday called Quadragesima, as those preceding were called Quinquagesima, Sexagesima, and Septuagesima; the entire period extending from this day to the most sacred solemnity of Easter is also called Quadragesima, namely because we extend through these days an imitation of the Lord’s fast. Yet four days are found lacking for this calculation. For although forty-two days are counted from here to the holy night of Easter, Christian devotion presumes to dedicate only thirty-six to abstinence. Canonical authority forbids the first day of the Sabbath, made bright by the splendour of the Lord’s resurrection, ever to be darkened by any cloud of public fasting.

Therefore, in order that the solemnity of our fast may be fitted more closely to the Lord’s example, the four days preceding this Sunday were added to the aforementioned tenth of the whole year. For thirty-six, the number already mentioned, is a tenth of the whole year—that is, of three hundred and sixty days. With four added, forty is produced: that is, four with ten. And this is the truer etymology of the name; otherwise only one day—namely the third weekday of this week reckoned from Easter—is “fortieth.”

Pope Telesphorus of holy memory, seventh from blessed Peter, established this saving preparation before holy Easter so that the Christian people, unable to maintain the rule of apostolic abstinence, might not abandon it altogether [Col. 0097D]. For the apostles, the first children of the Bridegroom who had been taken away, loved fasting and weeping throughout their whole life; their soul refused to be comforted, and they took such delight in remembering Him. But after the number of believers began to increase, and the nets of faith drew in fish so undiscriminating that, together with those who abstained, a multitude of drunkards entered as well, the teaching of ecclesiastical discipline came to the rescue. Like a strict mother, it moderated the intemperance of gluttonous children, so that, since they could not be compelled to observe the whole, they might at least observe a portion and dedicate the tithes of their life to abstinence.

Therefore, although the Apostle says of the whole time of grace, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI), and the rest, on this Sunday is recited that Epistle-reading by which the temporal observance of fasts, which as said ought to have been continuous, is begun [Col. 0098A].

## CHAPTER X. Why We Place Ashes upon Our Heads

If we all possessed the knowledge of mourning, and if the prophet’s lament were equally meaningful to all: “The crown of our head has fallen; woe to us, for we have sinned” (Lam. V); and if it were readily within everyone’s power to do what is likewise said to us: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II), then we would have no need either to sprinkle our heads with ashes or to walk barefoot.

But now most of us neither remember of our own accord what adornment of the head—that is, of the heart—we lost by offending God, nor can stony hearts easily be rent unless we are assisted by outward instruments. Therefore, that our calamity may be recalled to our minds and that we may remember that we are dust—which our father Adam had forgotten when he cast God, his crown, away and thereafter perceived his nakedness—we sprinkle our heads with ashes and uncover the highest parts of the body, namely the feet. In this attire we confess that we are neither gods nor from heaven, but are human beings and have our beginning from the earth; and that, stripped of our glory through sin and set naked among enemies, we need the adornment of God’s grace [Col. 0098C].

## CHAPTER XI. On the Second Sunday of Lent, Why It Is Vacant

The second Sunday of Lent, which in the sequence and arrangement of the seven Sundays mentioned above is the fifth, is, by a beautiful and rational ordering, vacant: as though the bishop of the Church, now a weary singer, had nothing, or no one, or nowhere upon which to sing the words of the Lord’s songs; or as though, weary of unfruitful hearers, he had hung up the instruments upon the willows.

For it signifies the fifth age of the world, when the temple of the Lord had been destroyed and the people of God carried off into Babylon. The Church of God groaned under a double captivity: a stranger in this world and captive beneath Nebuchadnezzar (Ps. CXXXVI [137]; Jer. LII) [Col. 0098D]. At that time the people of God had neither temple nor altar, and were forced to worship the Babylonian gods and the statue of King Nebuchadnezzar, who bears the type of the devil, under threat of the furnace set before them (Dan. III).

It was therefore not without reason, and was arranged with rational care, that, while all the private weekdays of this time are enriched with their own offices and marked by fixed stations—except the Saturday before Palm Sunday, for which a reason must also be sought in its proper place—this Sunday alone should be vacant and should have no office except one borrowed from elsewhere. Yet it does have a Gospel reading, wholly consonant with that aforementioned captivity of the people of God. For what that captivity had signified, when Nebuchadnezzar tyrannically dragged God’s people from noble Zion and the temple of the Lord, forcibly oppressing them under the command of a barbarous goad, is likewise signified [Col. 0099A] in the Gospel of the present Sunday: the daughter of the Canaanite woman tormented by a demon signifies human souls wickedly inflamed by the devil with the passions of evil desire and violently dragged by the long rope of sins, through evil habit, into the wretched servitude of his will.

The Canaanite woman cried after the Lord (Matt. XV); the faith of the patriarchs and the merit of Daniel and his companions intervened so that the Babylonian captivity might be loosed (Dan. IX). And now our heavenly mother Jerusalem cries that penitents may be granted the power to resist sin. It also has its own Epistle, in which the Apostle says: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour” (I Thess. IV), and the rest. We are summoned to escape that slavery which was signified, as stated, by the vessels of the Lord’s house being carried away and defiled in the Babylonian captivity, so that the king of Babylon drank from them, together with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines (Dan. V). The same is also signified in the Gospel by the fact that an unclean spirit had invaded the Canaanite woman’s daughter, a vessel indeed of the Creator.

Though the remaining texts are borrowed, having been taken from the Wednesday of the fast, in every sense they agree with what has been said. For in the introit we ask the Lord to remember His mercies, lest our enemies ever rule over us (Ps. XXIV [25]); and in the collect, that we may be defended against all adversities in body and cleansed from evil thoughts in mind. In the gradual the Church asks to be delivered from her necessities: “To Thee,” she says, “have I lifted up my soul” (ibid.). In the offertory verse: “Have mercy on me according to Thy word” (Ps. CVIII [119]). Likewise in the communion: “Understand my cry” (Ps. V). All these are the cries of that great woman (Rev. XVII)—namely, the Church our mother—unceasingly crying after the Lord on behalf of every sinful soul, that is, her own soul [Col. 0099C]. These texts are suitably borrowed from a fasting day because the passions of evil desire, signified by the demon-possessed daughter of the Canaanite woman and likewise by Nebuchadnezzar, captor of God’s people, are not cast out except by prayer and fasting (Matt. XVII).

## CHAPTER XII. [Col. 0099D] On the Third Sunday of Lent
After the mystical commemoration of that captivity, in which the king of Babylon carried off the vessels of the Lord’s temple—bearing, as has been said, the type of the devil—on this following Sunday, which signifies the sixth age of the world, the Gospel is appointed in which a strong man, armed, guarding his court, is said to lose the vessels or weapons in which he trusted when one stronger comes upon him; and the unclean spirit, which had gone out of a man, seeking rest and not finding it, says: “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Luke XI; Matt. XII).

For in the sixth age of the world the Son of God came into this world through the mystery of the Incarnation, and, fighting [Col. 0100A] by the finger of God, cast out a dumb demon; and the dumb man spoke, who, according to another Evangelist, was also deaf. For then, when the demon had been cast out, the deaf man heard and the dumb man spoke: when the prince of this world had been driven out, the world heard the words of God and spoke the praise of God. Thus were plundered the vessels of that armed strong man, namely the devil, which he had transferred from the honour of Paradise (Gen. III), just as the aforementioned Nebuchadnezzar transferred the children of Israel and the vessels of the Lord’s temple to the insults of Babylon.

But behold, the unclean spirit which had gone out of the man (Matt. XII), that is, out of the Jewish people, has now returned into him again, taking with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself; for the Jews now sin more grievously, cursing Christ in their synagogues, than formerly when they served foreign gods in Egypt.

Therefore, in the office of this Sunday, at the Introit this dumb man, now speaking because the demon has been cast out, says triumphantly: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. XXIV); and he gives the reason, which he who had been deaf heard from the holy preachers: “For he,” he says, “will pluck my feet from the snare” (ibid.). The eloquence of the dumb man continues, whose mouth wisdom opened: “Look upon me and have mercy on me”; and likewise he supplies a highly rhetorical reason by which he may move God as hearer and make mercy his advocate: “For,” he says, “I am alone and poor” (ibid.).

And what we say in the Collect, “Stretch forth the right hand of thy majesty for our defence,” is an invocation of that same stronger one who, as was said, came upon the armed strong man (Luke XI). In the Epistle Paul, the distinguished soldier and helper of the stronger one just mentioned, addresses those vessels which were plundered from the conquered and [Col. 0100C] bound strong man, so that, cleansed from their former stains by holy baptism, they may not be defiled again, when he says: “But fornication and all uncleanness must not even be named among you” (Eph. V), etc.

The Gradual, “Arise, O Lord” (Ps. IX), is the cry of every chosen vessel against that same armed strong man, guarding his court and possessing it in peace before the coming of the stronger one. The Tract also, “To thee have I lifted up my eyes” (Ps. CXXII), is the eloquent voice of the dumb man so often mentioned, asking for his eternal salvation in a most expressive prayer and adorning that same prayer with a fitting comparison.

In the Offertory the same dumb man, now eloquent, proclaims the righteous judgments of the Lord: namely, that after the demon had been cast out from him, he was permitted to return again to that man from whom he had formerly gone out, that is, to the Jewish people, because this was done in the truth of God’s judgment: “The judgments,” he says, “of the Lord are true” (Ps. XVIII). Giving thanks for the opening of his own mouth, he says: “And let the words of my mouth be pleasing” (ibid.), etc.

In the Communion the same man, restored from dumbness to speech, rejoices that, like “a sparrow, he has found himself a house, and like a turtledove a nest,” namely, “thy altars, O Lord of hosts”: that is, the holy Church of the patriarchs, so that, with “the blessed who dwell in thy house, O Lord,” he may praise thee “for ever and ever” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Moreover, the foregoing explanation of this office commends what is written [Col. 0101A] concerning the station at Saint Lawrence. For by whose battles, if not those of the holy martyrs, and especially of this saint, was the armed strong man of whom we have spoken driven from his court—that is, Rome? For Prudentius says:

> Now Rome, devoted to Christ,  
> Victorious under Lawrence as her leader,  
> Triumphs over the barbarous rite.

PRUDENTIUS, *Peristephanon*, hymn II, 2–3.

And elsewhere above, in the person of the same martyr:

> Depart, adulterous Jupiter,  
> Forgetful of your sister’s violation;  
> Leave Rome free.

Ibid., 465–467.

Rightly, then, we sing of the conquered strong man to the soldier of the victor.

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 0101B] On “Laetare, Jerusalem” and Mid-Lent Sunday

This Sunday is the seventh from that called Septuagesima. It signifies the Sabbath of the world, that is, rest, in which the souls of the saints and elect, having laid aside the burden of the flesh and, like victors after battles, laid down their arms, rejoice in repose. And now these same elect, endowed with single robes—that is, with the blessedness of the soul—await the resurrection, in which they will receive double robes (Apoc. VI), namely the immortal glory both of souls and of bodies.

There that Jerusalem which is above, which is free, which is the mother of us all (Gal. IV), rejoices; and, keeping feast because of the number of her children, 47 returning from the pilgrimage of this world, she pours forth her reserved banquets and presses from her breasts the delights of motherly consolation. There, I say, God, the ancient Father, and the Son of God, the new Bridegroom, console their returning children, as he promised through the prophet, saying: “Their children shall be carried upon shoulders, and they shall be comforted upon knees; as a mother comforts her children, so will I comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted” (Isa. LXVI).

Therefore, on this Sunday, which, as has been said, is a sign of that Sabbath, its whole office is a proclamation of that rest and that consolation, by which those children of so great and so free a mother who are now pilgrims are reminded to overcome their present sorrow [Col. 0101D] by the hope of future consolation, so that they may be, according to the Apostle, “rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII), since they are to drink from the breasts of consolation in the heavenly Jerusalem.

And first it must be said that the evangelical banquet in which the Lord satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes (John VI) accords very well, in a mystical sense, with the stated significance of this Sunday. For it signifies, as ecclesiastical authority hands down, that life-giving banquet of the holy Scriptures, by which, from the few books of Moses and the prophets, as the abundance of the divine blessing increases among the mouths of those eating—that is, among the studies of those expounding them—the world, once fasting from the knowledge of God, is abundantly refreshed; and when the storehouses have been filled with an abundance of sayings and meanings, we guests withdraw weary and overcome.

This banquet of divine knowledge begins here, but will be perfected in the everlasting glory of that Sabbath of which we speak. “For now I know in part,” says the Apostle, “but then I shall know as I also am known” (I Cor. XIII), etc. For, according to the prophet: “No longer shall a man say to his brother, ‘Know the Lord’; for all, from the least to the greatest, shall know me, says the Lord” (Jer. XXXI). Therefore this satisfying of the five thousand men, recited from the Gospel on this Sunday, signifies that abundance of divine knowledge and vision.

Then Jesus, who truly crossed over the Sea of Galilee because, rising from the dead, he passed beyond all the bitterness of this stormy and restless age, will satisfy with a great banquet the crowd of believers who follow him—all the children of the heavenly Jerusalem, now grown and weaned. As its type, the father Abraham is recorded to have made a great feast on the day of the weaning of Isaac, the only son of the free woman, when he had been weaned (Gen. XXII).

Therefore that joyful address of the Holy Spirit, set forth beforehand by the prophetic mouth—“Rejoice, O Jerusalem”—and the rest of the consolation sung here, “And you shall be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation” (Isa. LXVI), clearly accords with such a banquet. It is the very consolation which we seek in the following Collect when we say: “That we who are afflicted through the deserts of our iniquity may be revived by the consolation of thy grace”: namely, when, panting pilgrims after the toil of this captivity, we shall sit [Col. 0102C] in that heavenly Jerusalem, saying: “We have become like those who are comforted” (Ps. CXXV).

It is the consolation of freedom of which we likewise rejoice in the Epistle, as the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.” It is also that same “peace in her strength and abundance in her towers” (Ps. CXI), concerning which we sing in the Gradual: Rejoicing in those things which have been said to us by our holy apostles and doctors, “we shall go into the house of the Lord.” When we have reached it, what is said in the Tract will also be fulfilled: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. CXXIV), when the rod—that is, the power of sinners—has been taken away; for though the Lord permits it for a time as a trial, “he will not leave it upon the lot of the righteous” [Col. 0102D] (ibid.).

In the Offertory also we call blessed the guests of that same consolation, rejoicing in the feasts of praise; and we bless the Father of the banquet from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem (Ps. CXXXIV), so that from the present Church, which is called Zion—that is, “watchtower”—where, being placed as watchmen, we now see “through a glass darkly” (I Cor. XIII), we may begin to sound forth praise, offering, and blessing, and may perfect them in that heavenly Jerusalem in which he dwells.

This is the Jerusalem which, according to the true and mystical meaning of the Communion, is not yet completed, and is still being built as a city from living and chosen stones, in which “the tribes ascended, the tribes of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI): noble tribes, royal tribes, priestly tribes. The very church to which the station is prescribed for the present office likewise designates that same heavenly city of God by its name, Jerusalem. For it too is called Holy Jerusalem, so that by its very name it may awaken the memory and desire of that city among citizens of heaven who are pilgrims in this world, having here no abiding city but seeking the city to come (Heb. XIII), and who greet it from afar as pilgrims.

The rationale of this station differs from that of the Second Sunday of the Advent of the Lord, because that is an announcement of future blessedness, whereas this is, as it were, its present contemplation. Hence we celebrate more festively, because it is the solemnity of our hope. The Christian people rejoice; and, as on a solemn day the Christian emperor is crowned, he is admonished by innocent games to meditate upon the peaceful leisure which we shall enjoy in the bosom of that mother above.

The magnitude of this solemnity is also shown by the fact that, in order to complete it, two Collects are said by the authority of the Roman order; likewise, at the Annunciation of the Lord, two prayers are prescribed at the Introit, so that we may seem to have performed, as it were, a double office in keeping with the dignity of solemnities of this kind. And lest anyone object: Why, then, is nothing of this sort observed in the greatest solemnities of the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord and in the other principal feasts? The answer is that in those solemnities there is no need of this duplication, because they are extended through their octaves and their observance is not confined to the compass of one day.

After the most orderly arrangement of the seven Sundays, by which, as has been said, the seven ages of the world are figured—ages all redeemed by the Passion of the Lord and sprinkled with his blood—the celebration of the Lord’s own Passion begins. And, as though a long funeral procession had gone before, the very victim of our salvation follows, setting before the eyes of our minds the wounds that he endured for our sake.

It begins, moreover, with our catechumens, namely on Wednesday, when we celebrate the scrutinies. What rationale these have, and why they are celebrated especially on that day, we shall say later, as the Lord grants. But now, lest the weekday offices of Lent be left altogether untouched, let us consider only, under the guiding light of the Holy Spirit, the harmony of the Gospels and Epistles—a harmony so great and so useful that it should by no means be passed over without consideration. For to pursue the rest would be too long and tedious, especially since, once these things have been examined, the others may also become sufficiently clear to those who inquire into them on their own.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Gospels and Epistles of the Weekdays of Lent, and How They Agree with One Another

On Monday in the first week, this Gospel is read, in which the Son of Man declares with his own mouth that he will come in his majesty and will separate all nations gathered before him, 48 “as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats; and,” he says, “he will place the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on his left” (Matt. XXV), etc. Surely the prophetic discourse, the forerunner of the Gospel, anticipates this in the same sense, when the Lord says: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock” (Ezek. XXXIV), etc. “I will bring them out,” he says, “from the nations,” namely, “as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats”; “I will feed them in most fertile pastures.” These are certainly none other than the kingdom of which he says: “Come, ye blessed” (Matt. XXV), etc.

On Tuesday, in the Gospel, after those who bought and sold in the temple had been cast out, and after the Lord had answered the calumniating and questioning Pharisees, “and, leaving them,” says the Evangelist, “he went out of the city into Bethany, and remained there” (Matt. XXI). But this, as blessed Jerome says, prefigured that he was about to leave them because of their unbelief and to pass over to the salvation of the Gentiles, who are designated by Bethany, that is, “the house of obedience,” because they became obedient to the Word of God, according to the words: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII).

Therefore the prophetic reading appropriately begins: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV), followed by the rest, which is fitted to seek the Lord and effect his finding. For when the Prophet said these things, he surely foresaw the time when the Lord could not be found by the Jews and, passing over to the Gentiles, as to the house of obedience, would no longer be near to those who disobeyed.

On Wednesday, when the fast’s solemnity is doubled, the Gospel is read in which the unclean spirit who has gone out of a man is said to walk through waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it (Matt. XII). For undoubtedly, according to blessed Job, it rather lies down in moist places (Job XXXIX), while it shuns bodies dried up by fasts. Before this evangelical teaching are placed the examples of Moses and Elijah, each of whom, in the respective readings, is reported to have fasted forty days and forty nights (Exod. XXIV; III Kings XIX).

On Thursday the Lord, in the Gospel, convicts the Jews who boast and say, “Our father is Abraham,” because they do not perform the works of Abraham; and he concludes that they are rather of their father the devil, because they do the works of the devil and seek to kill him, which Abraham did not do (John VIII). Or, as some customarily read on this day, the rich man tormented in hell, calling Abraham his father and entreating him, is not heard as a son (Luke XVI). To this plainly pertains the prophetic passage placed before it in the Epistle: that if a righteous man begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood and doing every abominable thing, the righteous man himself will live in his righteousness, but his son, who has worked iniquity, will die by death (Ezek. XVIII).

On Friday the grace of baptism is signified in the Gospel, by which the youth of the soul is renewed like that of an eagle, its life is redeemed from destruction, and it is crowned in mercy and compassion (Ps. CII). For the angel who descended into the pool signified Christ, the Angel of great counsel; while the water of the pool, which was stirred, signified the Jewish people, who were stirred by seditions when that same Angel of great counsel descended upon them by assuming flesh (Isa. IX), and thus the movement of the water became troubled so that they crucified him.

The one man who descended into the water and was healed prefigured the one holy catholic Church which, descending into Christ’s baptism, is healed from infirmities. But the man who had lain there thirty-eight years represented the whole body of those who languish under grievous crimes; they too nevertheless are healed through faith in Christ. The Jews criticize this as though it were unjust; for they have always hated the salvation of the Gentiles. Therefore the prophetic reading appropriately comes before it, in which, when the Lord says, “If the wicked man turns from his wickedness and does judgment” (Ezek. XVIII), and the rest, “on whatever day he groans, he shall be saved,” they murmur and say: “The way of the Lord is not just” (ibid.).

Yet it is not casually true that if anyone groans he will be saved; rather, if a sinner groaning over his sins hastens to Christ’s baptism, he will immediately be saved, because none of his former injustices will be remembered. Private penance, however, is laborious and, amid its labours, does not make the penitent so secure of pardon.

On Saturday, when priests and the other ministers of Christ’s altar are ordained, this Gospel is appropriately read: “Jesus took Peter and James and John, led them up a mountain, and was transfigured before them” (Matt. XVII). For priests and the other ministers of the altar, when they are advanced to so great a ministry, as it were ascend with the Lord to a very high mountain, so that with unveiled face they may behold his glory (II Cor. III), understand what Moses and Elijah—that is, the Law and the Prophets—speak with him or about him, proclaim it to the people below, and, possessing legal morality and prophetic teaching together with faith in Christ, may be ready to render an account to everyone who asks (I Pet. III).

Therefore the reading of the Apostle is aptly placed before it: “We beseech you, brethren, correct the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted” (I Thess. V), etc. For this is the office of those ordained to be shepherds of souls.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Weekdays of the Second Week

On Monday of the second week is read that Gospel passage in which the Lord threatens the Jews that, because of their faithlessness, he will depart from them, saying: “I go away, and you shall seek me, and you shall die in your sin” (John VIII). In saying this, he of course signified that he would pass over to the Gentiles. Hence they too, as though divining, say: “Will he go into the dispersion of the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?” (John VII). The prophetic prayer of Daniel placed before it (Dan. IX), by which he asks that the Lord’s fury and wrath may be taken away from that people, fittingly accords with this Gospel. For it is this fury and this wrath that the Prophet’s most tearful lament especially bewails.

On Tuesday the Lord, in the Gospel, rebukes the scribes and Pharisees because, sitting in Moses’ chair, they vainly claim the teaching office for themselves, saying but not doing; because they love greetings in the marketplace and to be called Rabbi by men. At last he strikes them, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XVIII). That is, because those proud men were to be removed from the teaching office of the knowledge of God, and humble teachers of the Church from among the Gentiles would receive their chair.

This was prefigured by the widow of Zarephath, of whom the preceding reading speaks, to whom Elijah went by the Lord’s command when there were many widows in Israel (III Kings XVII). Thus the Church from among the Gentiles received in the hospitality of faith the teaching of the Law and Prophets sent to her from God, while drought and sterility remained with the Synagogue. For, as the Lord had elsewhere threatened her, he had commanded his clouds—that is, the holy preachers of his grace—not to rain upon her (Isa. V).

And so this Church, humbling herself, was exalted by Christ while she gathered two pieces of wood for the cross in order to make for herself an ash-cake, the bread of repentance. With her, the jar of flour did not fail, 49 nor was there any diminution in the cruse of oil (III Kings XVII): that is, the knowledge of the Law endured together with the grace of the Gospel. But that other people, exalting itself, was humbled so greatly that its Pharisees, millers of the Law, do not know how to grind even the Law’s flour, nor can they find the oil of the Gospel while walking in their phylacteries and enlarged fringes (Matt. XXIII).

On Wednesday is appointed the Gospel passage in which the Lord reveals his plan secretly to his disciples, saying: “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered to be crucified” (Matt. XX), etc. By these things the devil, our enemy and foe, was to be captured and judged. Therefore the reading in which Esther implores God’s help against Haman (Esth. XIX) is appropriately placed before it. For Haman bore the type of the devil in that, desiring to be worshipped, he wished to hand over the people of God to death and prepared a cross for Mordecai. And as he was cast upon the very cross which he had prepared, so Christ, as the Apostle says, “openly made a display, confidently in himself, and removed the very handwriting from the midst, fastening it to the cross” (Col. II).

Therefore only Esther’s prayer is set forth here, because to narrate the whole history, which, as has been said, is a type of the Lord’s Passion, would be too long and burdensome. Moreover, from the incident of the two sons of Zebedee, the Lord indicates to us that we too can conquer the devil only through participation in that same Passion.

On Thursday the Lord, by his own example, teaches in the Gospel that trust should be placed not in human testimony but in that of God alone. Speaking according to the frailty of the flesh, he says: “And if I bear witness of myself, my witness is true; there is another who bears witness of me” (John V). And he adds: “The Father who sent me bears witness of me. You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth; but I have a greater testimony than John” (John V). And again: “I do not receive testimony from men” (ibid.). The prophetic reading placed before it undoubtedly accords with this, from Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from God; for he shall be like a tamarisk in the desert” (Jer. XVII). And a little later: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord” (ibid.), etc.

On Friday is read the parable which the Lord spoke against the evil Pharisees, the evil cultivators of the divine Law who were to be miserably destroyed, because they were planning to kill the only son of the householder sent by him—that is, the Lord himself—whom they should have revered, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI). Therefore the kingdom of God was to be taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruits.

The reading placed before it from the book of Genesis beautifully accords with this parable. In it Joseph’s brothers, seeing him coming to them from afar, spoke to one another, saying: “Behold, the dreamer comes; come, let us kill him, and see what his dreams will profit him” (Gen. XXXVII). For Joseph, in that he was sold and cast into prison, bore the type of the Lord himself, who was sold, delivered to death, and buried; and thus, cast out from his vineyard, like the useless stone rejected by the builders, he passed over with the kingdom of God to the Gentiles who produce its fruits, just as Joseph, sold and cast out by his own people, fed the Egyptians.

On Saturday, both the Gospel and the Epistle contain the figure of the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile. The former—the Jewish people, in respect of the worship of one God—is, as the merciful father receives the repentance of the younger people, that is, the Gentiles, tormented by envy as it stands outside; yet it ought to rejoice because its brother had been dead and came to life, had been lost and was found (Luke XV), because, as we sing on the same day, “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls and giving wisdom to little ones” (Ps. XVIII).

The Epistle that precedes therefore accords well with the Gospel: there the younger brother feasts with his father while the elder remains outside in the field (Luke XV); here Esau, while his brother Jacob offers a meal and hastens toward the blessing at the counsel of his mother Rebecca—who signifies the Holy Spirit—is delayed outside, occupied in hunting (Gen. XXVII). For the Jewish people, held fast by earthly thoughts and carnal observances, loses spiritual grace.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Weekdays of the Third Week

On Monday of the third week the Lord foreshadows in the Gospel that he will have no honour in his own country, namely Judaea, and will pass over to the Gentiles, where he will be honoured. For when the Pharisees say, “What great things we have heard you have done at Capernaum, do also here in your own country,” he answers: “Amen I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country” [Col. 0108A] (Luke IV).

Again, by that terrible and venerable oath of his, he teaches through a comparison—not merely implicitly but altogether expressly—that, setting them aside, he would rather heal the Gentiles from their sins: “Truly,” he says, “I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Zarephath of Sidon. And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (ibid.).

Further, in that they rose up, threw him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built in order to cast him down (ibid.), it is signified that salvation would pass away from them, when it is said: “But Jesus, passing through the midst of them, went away” (ibid.). For when the Jews, crucifying him, wished to cast him into the depth of oblivion, he turned away and, passing through their midst, went to the peoples of the Gentiles by his feet—his beautiful feet, that is, the holy preachers.

Therefore the reading concerning Naaman the Syrian is appropriately placed before this Gospel. Elisha signifies Christ, while Naaman the leper signifies the Gentile people, unclean and idolatrous.
