In that Elisha himself did not go out to him but sent him word, saying, “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and you shall be cleansed” (IV Kings V), he prophetically indicates what occurred: Christ did not himself preach to the Gentiles, but, sending others, commanded that they be baptized: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

The leper is washed seven times because in baptism is the distinctive operation of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, from whom we are reborn and, receiving forgiveness of sins, restored anew.

On Tuesday the Gospel commends the bright work of mercy. The Lord says: “If thy brother sins against thee,” that is, with thee knowing it, “go, rebuke him between thee and him alone” (Matt. XVIII), etc. And because, where two agree—namely, the corrector and the hearer—there is no need either to bring in another person or to tell the Church, since the person rebuked between thee and him alone listens willingly, pardon, I say, is then at once obtained from the Lord, being ready at hand. “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, if two of you agree concerning anything whatsoever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father” (ibid.).

And that he spoke about obtaining pardon, he himself testifies when he first says: “Amen I tell you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (ibid.). It concludes thus: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against 50 me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” And Jesus says to him: “I do not say to thee, Peter, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (ibid.).

The reading placed before it harmonizes beautifully with these words. For the woman who cries to Elisha for her two sons, whom a creditor is trying to take into slavery (IV Kings IV), is the Church herself, concerned for the sins of the children whom she bore in baptism, lest the exactor, the devil, draw debtors into the condemnation of everlasting death for the coin of evil pleasure which he lent them.

The true Elisha, that is Christ, commanded her to pour oil into vessels with the door shut (ibid.), because, when sinners have been confronted by private reproof, he commands that remission and absolution be granted them, authority having been given to bind and loose, as he promised in the Gospel just cited and confirmed the promise with the truth interposed, that is, *amen*. Therefore, when the door is shut and the vessels are filled, the oil overflows, because through private correction forgiveness of sins immediately flows abundantly to penitents. But when one who has been rebuked secretly between thee and him alone does not listen, after the matter has been told to the Church he is not to be treated with the gentle oil of such easy indulgence, but must fittingly be cut by the cautery of penance.

On Wednesday, when the Pharisees accuse the disciples of the Lord of transgressing the traditions of the elders by not washing their hands while eating bread, the Lord rebukes them and turns the point of accusation back upon its authors: “Why,” he says, “do you transgress the traditions of God for the sake of the traditions of men? For God says: ‘Honour thy father and thy mother.’ But you say: ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “A gift: whatever comes from me will benefit thee,”’” (Matt. XV), etc.

For the avarice of the Pharisees had taught the young men, whose snare they had all become, to bring gifts to the temple without their parents’ command—indeed, having snatched them from their parents. When the parents protested that they were dishonoured by their children in this way, although God says, “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Exod. XX), the young men would object: “Rather, we honour our father in this way. For God is our Father, and we bring these things to his temple; and what we, his sons, offer to him will benefit you, our parents.”

The Lord condemns these and similar things among the traditions of men, which they preferred to the traditions of God; and he teaches at the same time that transgression of God’s commandments alone defiles a person (Matt. XV). Therefore in the reading from Exodus God’s commandments themselves are set forth: “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Exod. XX), etc. By these the hypocrites are convicted in the Gospel: outwardly clean through observing the traditions of men, but inwardly defiled through transgressing the traditions of God, because it is not what enters the mouth but what proceeds from the heart that defiles a person (Matt. XV).

On Thursday, when crowds come to him to make him king because they had eaten of his loaves and were filled, the Lord exhorts them: “Labour not for the food which perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John VI), etc. For he had said to them: “Amen I tell you, you came to me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” (ibid.).

In this he also rebukes the multitude of priests, because they come in crowds to the Lord’s altar not because they delight to contemplate the mysteries there commemorated—of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ—but because they eat of his loaves and are filled, namely from the tithes and offerings of the faithful, seeking only the wages of the body.

For this reason the reading is suitably placed before it in which the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and preach there this word” (Jer. VII), etc. Thus those also who entered the gates of the Lord’s house with pomp, feeding their desires and applauding themselves as they said, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this” (ibid.), were more intent upon making plunder from the people through it than upon making their ways good and directing them rightly, as they are commanded in the same reading.

On Friday, the Gospel is read in which the Lord Jesus, weary from his journey, sat at the well about the sixth hour and spoke with the Samaritan woman who had come to draw water: “If you knew,” he says, “the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4), etc. The mystery of this reading is well known and celebrated in the faith of the holy Church: namely, that our Lord Christ, wearied by the journey by which he came for our salvation—even unto death, indeed death on a cross (Phil. 2)—sat upon the well; that is, he overcame the depth of worldly wisdom. And the Samaritan woman, that is, the Church from another people, accustomed to draw dead water from the deep—indeed, dark—teachings of the philosophers, water by which she could not satisfy the thirsty soul so that it might not thirst again, learned that “whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water which he gives,” that is, of the Holy Spirit, “shall never thirst, but it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

The reading placed before this Gospel is highly fitting. In it, when the children of Israel had assembled against Moses and said, “Give us water” (Exod. 17), the Lord commanded him and led them to water, to the rock of Horeb; and, though distrustful, Moses struck the rock twice with his staff, and most abundant waters came forth, so that the people and their cattle drank (Num. 20). In this matter Moses signifies the unbelieving Jewish people; the thirsty people, the expectation of the human race; and the rock, Christ. Moses struck the rock twice with his staff: that is, the Jewish people fastened Christ to the two pieces of wood of the cross. And most abundant waters came forth—the living waters which, in the Gospel mentioned above, the Lord declares that he has for the Samaritan woman. This water is the Holy Spirit, who was given when Christ the rock was struck by the staff of the cross—or rather, after that striking, was glorified by resurrection and ascension.

On Saturday we read in the Gospel of the woman caught in adultery, brought to the Lord Jesus by the Scribes and Pharisees, who were testing him and thus concealing the double-edged dagger of their brigandage: so that, whatever he answered, they might accuse him calumniously (John 8). That is, if, as merciful, he said she ought to be dismissed, he would be accused as unjust and an adversary of the Law; if she should be punished, he would be defamed as unmerciful. Meekness met justice in such a way that, when the accusers withdrew, since their own consciences had drawn them away, only two remained: misery and mercy.

The reading from Daniel which precedes it accords with this Gospel: although, as Blessed Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0111D] Jerome, *Apology against the Books of Rufinus*, book II, 33, Migne edition.], it is not found in the Hebrew text, it tells how Susanna was delivered by God’s help from the false charge of adultery (Dan. 13). The one escaped through mercy, the other from stoning through justice. Thus in the office of the same day, in a manner of speaking, “mercy and truth meet each other” (Ps. 84), in corresponding persons and under the same aid of mercy, though in differing cases.

## Chapter XVII. On the ferias of the fourth week

On the second feria of the fourth week, when the Pharisees ask and say in the Gospel, “By what authority do you do these things, and what sign do you show us?” (John 2), the Lord answers: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He spoke of the temple of his body (ibid.). Shortly afterwards the Evangelist adds: “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all men, and because he had no need that anyone should bear witness concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man” (ibid.).

The reading concerning the two harlots, who disputed before Solomon concerning the living child, is rightly set before this Gospel. To the one who said, “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but divided” (3 Kgs. 3), the supremely wise Solomon did not entrust the living child. Those women bore the figure of the Synagogue and the Church; the child, however, signifies Christ, whom the Synagogue neither conceived nor bore in the womb of faith, but even desired to have killed, and still wished his memory to be extinguished, so that he might live neither among her nor in the Church of the Gentiles. Therefore the true and truly most wise Solomon, as the Evangelist says, did not entrust himself to the Jews, but turned toward the Church from among the Gentiles, saying in a manner to his apostles: “Give her the living child, for she is its mother” (ibid.).

On the third feria, the Lord speaks to the Jews and rebukes them as murderers and impious men. He removes Moses, who formerly prayed for them when they made the calf at Horeb, and to whom he had said: “I have forgiven according to your word; nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs” (Exod. 32). Moses, I say, hitherto praying for them, he angrily removes, saying: “Did not Moses give you the Law? Yet none of you keeps the Law” (John 7). For by every manner of transgression separating them from Moses, he shows that the one he removes no longer belongs to them.

Immediately, once Moses the intercessor has been removed, he convicts them of their crime: “Why,” he says, “do you seek to kill me?” (ibid.). But they, raging according to their custom, say: “You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?” (ibid.). He, however, mentioning Moses a third time—the Moses whom they were rejecting—convicts them all the more. Thus the reading is aptly placed first in which Moses is told: “Go down from the mountain; your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have sinned. They have quickly departed from the way which you showed them, and have made for themselves a molten calf” (Exod. 32). And when the Lord says, “Let me alone, that I may destroy them” (ibid.), it follows: “But Moses prayed to the Lord his God, saying: ‘Why, O Lord, are you angry with your people?’” (ibid.), etc.

Moses’ prayer availed for them until the time came when they would commit so great a murder by crucifying the Son of God, who now says to them: “Why do you seek to kill me?” Therefore Moses the intercessor was now to be removed, just as God had then said when appeased: “I have forgiven according to your word. Nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs.”

## Chapter XVIII. On the fourth feria of the scrutinies

On the fourth feria the sacraments proper to the new Church begin, by which the most holy Passion of our Redeemer is figured in the venerable rite of the holy Church, working through the children of adoption the holy newness of the Spirit. For on this day our catechumens, according to the ancient tradition of the holy Roman Church, are signed, that in the most holy solemnity of our Redemption they may be born again from water and the Holy Spirit (John 3), dying with Christ and rising with him in baptism, according to the Apostle, who says: “As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

For it was once the custom in the holy Church for the sacrament of this regeneration to be celebrated at no other time, except for those upon whom illness or sickness unexpectedly came, so that danger of death was imminent. Almost all the offspring of the Church, whom she could give new birth during the year through the word of preaching, gave their names on this day as the Paschal solemnity drew near. During the following days, until the solemnity of Easter itself, each heard the rule of faith—whence the name *catechumen*, for *catechumenus* means “hearer”—and, nourished and growing, finally, in the fullness of time, after the moon had become full, returned the Creed in the solemnity of the holy baptistery with full faith, died with Christ, and rose with him.

But after Christianity had grown and that net of the Word of God had been filled with fish (Matt. 13), it seemed dangerous to defer so great a multitude because of the many occasions of death among a multitude of people, especially because of the throng of infants growing up from Christian parents, whose tender life is very often cut short by a slight occasion. Therefore it seemed good to the holy Church, with permission—indeed, an offer—of baptism everywhere extended, to forestall every danger, while nevertheless celebrating the solemnity of baptism, at least for some, with the Lord’s resurrection, to which it is analogous.

Thus on the fourth feria the beginnings of the new Church are celebrated, called the scrutinies. They are called *scrutinies* from *scrutinizing*, because those who approached had to be examined lest some root of bitterness lie within them, as it did in Simon Magus (Acts 8), and in very many heretics and founders of heresies; so that holy things might not be given to them unless Christian faith had first put down deep roots in their minds. Why they are celebrated especially on this day, and whether the number of the following days up to the day of the Lord’s Passion contains a mystery, must now be explained.

## Chapter XIX. Why the scrutinies are held on the fourth feria

The great scrutiny is celebrated on the fourth feria rather than the fifth or sixth, so that those who fast and prepare their vessels to receive grace may have fifteen days of fasting until the day on which the Lord was crucified, because our Lord, the true Lamb, was sacrificed on the fifteenth moon. This is not without a great mystery.

For the Paschal moon, concerning which the Lord said to Moses, “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first in the months of the year. On the tenth day of this month each of you shall take a lamb, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day” (Exod. 12; Lev. 23)—this Paschal moon, I say (for the Hebrews know and reckon only lunar months), signifies the holy Church, illuminated by that same Sun. Receiving his Passion in the fullness of faith, she dies with him and is buried with him in the sacrament of baptism.

Therefore, whenever the new offspring of the Church is prepared to die with Christ, the scrutinies are celebrated on the fourth feria, so that the number of days of its preparation—that is, of stricter fasting—may equal the age of the moon which signifies it. For if they were celebrated rather on the sixth feria, which is the fifteenth day of the Lord’s crucifixion, only thirteen days of fasting would remain for their preparation; for two Sundays intervene, and fasting is not permitted on Sundays. Therefore, while the scrutinies are celebrated on the fourth feria and the following fifteen days are spent in fasts and instruction in the faith, the new Church, “fair as the moon” (Song 6), advances to fullness, so that, dying and rising with Christ crucified at the full moon, she may be joined to him in baptism.

## Chapter XX. That this scrutiny is the principal one of the seven scrutinies

It should be known that this ancient custom was not merely a scrutiny, but the principal one of all. For according to the Roman order, seven scrutinies were held until Holy Saturday in the vigil of Easter, so that, when the catechumens had been completed by the sevenfold number, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit might be given to them. The first was on the second feria of the third week of Lent, when the great scrutiny of this day—the fourth feria—was announced to the catechumens in this way:

“The day of scrutiny, most beloved brethren, on which our elect are to be divinely instructed, is at hand. Deign therefore to assemble in the same place on the following fourth feria, about the third hour, with attentive devotion, so that we may perform with blameless ministry the heavenly mystery by which the devil with his pomp is destroyed and the gate of the kingdom of heaven is opened.”

Likewise on the fourth feria, after the solemnities of the Masses had ended, the priest announced that they were to return for the scrutiny in that week, saying: “When Saturday comes, assemble early at that church.” Again and again the priest announced whichever day he wished in this manner: “When that feria comes, assemble early at that church,” until, as stated, the seven scrutinies were completed.

## Chapter XXI. On the office of the same fourth feria

How holy, devout, and mystical is the office of the Mass that follows on this feria, according to what has been said. First, in the Gospel—which, as has often been said, is the principal part of the entire office—the sacrament both of catechetical instruction and of baptism is beautifully prefigured by the beautiful maker of our salvation, the Son of God.

For the man blind from birth (John 9) signifies the human race: certainly a great blind man, and very blind, who in the first parent, looking toward the prince of darkness, lost the beautiful eyes implanted in the mind to see the Creator, where the image of the Maker shines; and therefore he is fittingly signified by a man blind from birth. When this man is recalled to the light of truth, and the ministers of Christ preach the incarnation of the Son of God himself and the other mysteries which he performed in the flesh for our salvation, the Lord makes mud from his own spittle and puts it upon the blind man’s eyes (ibid.).

For the spittle from his mouth and lips, in which “grace is poured forth” (Ps. 44)—the spittle, I say, which descends from the head—signifies the divinity of Christ the Son of God, the good Word which the heart of the Father uttered forth (ibid.); the Father, as the Apostle says, is the head of Christ (1 Cor. 11). For God the Head spat upon the earth and united his spittle to the dust which every wind tossed and carried about, when his heart uttered forth his Word into the earthly womb of the Virgin and joined it to the dust of our nature in one person, so that this tiny dust, receiving from such great spittle a stable form, appearance, and beauty, might be preserved.

Therefore, while faith in this incarnation is preached to the human race, the eyes of the great blind man, as stated, are anointed with the mud which the Lord made. But when, having thus been catechized, this same blind man comes to the sacred fonts, is washed with a visible spring, and is purified by an invisible power, he does precisely what the Lord commanded: “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash” (John 9). For the visible spring, once the power of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, becomes the pool of Siloam, that is, “of the Sent One,” whom the Son of God, ascending to the Father, said that he would send and did send to his disciples. That Sent One descends into his pool and, by his forgiveness, washes from sins the eyes anointed with faith in Christ, illuminating them with the knowledge of God.

Upon this as upon a head all the members of the office depend. First, at the Introit, the prophetic voice says: “When I have been sanctified in you, I shall gather you from every land, and pour clean water upon you” (Ezek. 36), etc. For the Lord is sanctified in catechumens when they hear and believe that he is holy. Therefore, clean water is poured over them—that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom this visible water is cleansed and cleanses—and, purified from all their defilements, they then live in such a way that they may bear witness that he is holy, at whose command they too are holy (Lev. 20, 21).

This is repeated in both readings in different words but with the same meaning. For in the first, from the prophet Ezekiel, the same words sung at the Introit are read, and this is added: “I shall take away the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36), etc. Our catechumens have a heart of flesh: that is, a soft and tender heart, readily yielding to the finger of God as he writes the new Law. They receive into themselves the written doctrine of faith which the stony hearts of the Jews do not receive, but by which they are broken. The earlier tablets which Moses broke were broken as their type (Exod. 32), while other tablets were cut out as a type of the Gentiles (Exod. 34).

In the second reading Isaiah says: “Wash yourselves; be clean. Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; though they be red like the worm-dye, they shall be as white wool” (Isa. 1). This equally commends the forgiveness of sins received in baptism. The gradual chants too sing beautifully and harmoniously to the same sense. For whose voice is this, if not that of one catechizing the new offspring of the Church: “Come, children, hear me; approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33)? Indeed, to alter only a few words in accordance with the Gospel, it is as though he said: “Come, blind men, that your eyes may be anointed with the mud which the Lord made from spittle; come to the pool of Siloam and be enlightened.”

The fact that the present office joins two readings and as many graduals arises from the solemnity of the sacrament: namely, that because of the increase of children it may also have an increase of spiritual foods. After the Gospel has been read, in which the often-mentioned blind man, enlightened and cast out of the synagogue, finds the Son of God outside—or rather, is found outside by the Son of God—and falls down and worships him (John 9), the Offertory fittingly follows this meaning: “Bless, O nations, our God” (Ps. 65).

For in that psalm, from which it is taken, according to the sacred exposition of venerable doctors, the apostles speak, exhorting the Gentiles by inexpressible praise, in deed and voice, to praise God; and inwardly to tremble and fear because of his hidden and terrible judgment, by which he received them and rejected the people formerly his own peculiar and chosen possession. They are to fear lest, perhaps, since he did not spare the natural branches because they were disobedient—indeed, because they cast the enlightened blind man out of the synagogue, that is, refused communion with the falling Gentiles—he may not spare them either if they become proud (Rom. 11).

This Offertory with its verses therefore aptly agrees with its subject, especially in the words, “Because of the greatness of your power, your enemies shall lie to you” (Ps. 65), etc. For his enemies lied when they said, “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 12), whereas he cast them out by the finger of God. This anticipated what had to be done in catechesis: the unclean spirit had to be cast out from persons possessed through idolatry, whom that strong armed one guarded in his ill-secured court (Luke 11).

Therefore we fittingly and reverently sing on this day—on which his Jewish enemies lie even now concerning the casting out of that dumb demon, asserting that it does not occur by the Spirit of God. But in vain. For while they blaspheme, that which follows comes to pass: “Let all the earth worship you. Come and see the works of God: how terrible he is in his counsels toward the children of men” (Ps. 65), namely, in the rejection of that former people and the reception of the Gentiles.

The Communion chant also, raising high notes in melodious and sweet modulation, is the joyful proclamation or testimony of the human race confessing the incarnation of the Son of God, according to the words: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115). And just as that man did not keep silence when the Pharisees were indignant, cursed him, and cast him out of the synagogue, but said: “That man called Jesus made mud from spittle, anointed my eyes, and now I see” (John 9), so those to whom the Lord says, “Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man” (Luke 6)—the more Christ’s enemies curse them and shut their mouths, the more they preach, knowing and understanding that this mud, that is, Christ’s incarnation, is the illumination of all who see.

### At the Introit

Where scrutinies are performed, collects are also properly said for the catechumens.

### Prayer

[Col. 0116C]

Almighty and everlasting God, multiply your Church by spiritual fruitfulness, so that those who are earthly by generation may become heavenly by regeneration.

### Secret

Lord, rejoicing, we offer the gifts of everlasting remedy, humbly beseeching you to enable us both to venerate them worthily and to present them fittingly for the salvation of others; through Christ.

### Postcommunion

We beseech you, Lord: in your kindness always raise up your household; order it when corrected; mercifully protect it when subject to you; and govern it by your everlasting goodness unto salvation, through our Lord.

### Why the station is at St. Paul’s

[Col. 0116D]

When the rationale of the scrutinies has been considered, as stated, it is evident that the station appointed at St. Paul’s is highly appropriate. For he was the great and wondrous catechizer of the whole world and, as he himself says, “a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth” (1 Tim. 2). He himself was also catechized magnificently and wonderfully, because, as he says to the Galatians: “My Gospel, which has been preached, is not according to man. For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

For with the voice which he heard bodily from heaven, by which his carnal understanding was struck down and slain (Acts 9), he also received the incorporeal voice of heavenly instruction. Hearing it for three days, through the most effective power of the catechizing master, this wondrous catechumen was himself made a perfect teacher of the Gospel. Nor was he far unlike the blind man of the Gospel: being bodily blind, he was sent to the pool of saving baptism, where, enlightened both in body and soul, he did not cease, while Pharisees and all enemies of Christ opposed him, to tell what the man called Jesus had done for him, how his eyes had been opened, and to show everyone that very mud which the Lord made from spittle—that is, the incarnation of the Word of God (Acts 18). For this reason they cursed him and cast him out of their synagogue, after he had been beaten five times with one less than forty lashes (2 Cor. 12).

## Chapter XXII. On the fifth feria

On the fifth feria, in the Gospel where the Lord says, “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5), to show us how he works and that Scripture, administered through Moses, did not speak falsely when it says, “God rested from all his works on the seventh day” (Gen. 2)—to show, I say, that he then worked when he made the world and works until now when he governs the world—he shortly adds: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5).

Showing that he said this concerning the resurrection which now occurs, “by which men pass,” as most blessed Augustine says, “from the death of unbelief to the life of faith, from the death of falsehood to the life of truth, from the death of iniquity to the life of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0117D] St Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 19, §8; *Patrologia*, vol. 35, Migne edition.], he says: “Amen, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (ibid.). “And attend to this,” says the same Augustine: “He does not now pass, but has already passed from death to life” [Note: [Col. 0117D] Ibid., §7.].

And then: “Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live.” “It is not,” he says, “because they live that they hear; but because they hear, they come to life again” [Note: [Col. 0118D] Ibid., §10.]. By this it is yet clearer that this is said concerning the resurrection in which those dead in unbelief and ignorance of God rise in such a manner that they first hear, and by hearing come to life again. If we believe rightly, we too have risen by this resurrection, and, having already risen, await another resurrection at the end.

The reading from the Book of Kings concerning the son of the Shunammite is rightly placed before this Gospel. The boy sent by Elisha with the staff did not raise him. But Elisha himself came, stretched himself upon the dead body, conformed himself to its limbs, walked back and forth, and breathed seven times into the boy’s mouth; and straightway, through the mystery of compassion, restored him to living light (4 Kgs. 4). For this raising of the boy signified the same resurrection of the human race which occurs through faith, of which the Gospel has spoken above, as Saint Gregory attests:

“The Creator of the human race, God, grieved for the dead boy when he looked in compassion upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he set forth the terror of the Law, he sent, as it were, the staff through the boy. For God held the staff through the Law when he said, ‘If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.’ Thus fear could not raise from the death of sin, but grace, prepared in meekness, raised the dead to the state of life. Yet the boy with the staff could not raise the dead, because, as Paul attests, ‘the Law brought nothing to perfection’ (Heb. 7). But he himself came in person, humbly stretched himself upon the corpse, and conformed himself to the limbs of the dead, ‘because though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man’ (Phil. 2). He walked back and forth because he calls both Judea and the nations near at hand and far away. He breathes seven times upon the dead because, through the operation of divine grace, he breathes the sevenfold Spirit into those lying in the death of sin. And immediately the young man rises, because the boy whom the staff of terror could not raise returned to life through the Spirit of love.” [Note: [Col. 0118D] St Gregory, *Morals*, book 9, ch. 4, on Job 10; *Patrologia*, vol. 75, Migne edition.]

## Chapter XXIII. On the sixth feria

[Col. 0118C] On the sixth feria the Gospel of the raising of Lazarus is read. The mystery of this miracle is well known and celebrated by nearly all teachers: namely, that Lazarus, whom the Lord loved, of whom he himself said, “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps; but I go to awaken him from sleep” (John 11), and whose sisters had often ministered to the Lord, bore the figure of a man already faithful and placed within the Church. Although he is the friend of our Lord Jesus Christ through faith, he dies to him through wicked conduct; buried in the tomb of an evil conscience under the habit of crimes and already stinking through disgrace, he finally, through God’s hidden inspiration and the great fear of future judgment—as though shaken by the Savior’s great cry—springs back to life through repentance. Opening the tomb of his evil conscience by voluntary confession, he deserves to be loosed from the bonds of sins because he lives.

This was prefigured in the son of the woman of Zarephath, to whom Elijah went by the Lord’s command, leaving drought and famine among carnal Israel. For that woman too, as has already been said, mystically signified the Church from among the Gentiles, which received in the hospitality of faith the Law and the Prophets—indeed Christ, whom they acknowledge—as Elijah. The son of this widow is every faithful person, who dies when he commits a sin worthy of death.

What was signified in the Lord’s cry calling Lazarus, in whose house he himself was fed by Lazarus’s sisters, was anticipated in Elijah’s cry when he cried to the Lord and said: “I beseech you, Lord, have you even afflicted the widow with whom I am somehow sustained, so as to kill her son?” (3 Kgs. 17). The Lord’s calling Lazarus his friend also accords beautifully with the statement that this was the son of Amathi, that is, “truth.” For the Jews maintain that Jonah was the son of this widow of Zarephath, whom Elijah raised; afterwards his mother said to Elijah: “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of God in your mouth is true” (ibid.). For this reason, they say, the boy was called Amathi. For *Amathi* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as *veritas*, “truth”; and because Elijah spoke the truth, he who was raised was called the son of truth.

Nor is it without mystery that Elijah, in order to raise the dead man, laid him upon his own bed. Elijah’s bed signifies the catholic Church of Christ, in which alone dead souls live again through the forgiveness of sins. For of this Church it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold Solomon’s bed, sixty valiant men surround it” (Song 3). Thus this reading from the Book of Kings fittingly and harmoniously precedes the Gospel reading mentioned above.

## Chapter XXIV. On the seventh feria, Saturday

On this Saturday the Gospel is appointed in which, after the Lord had said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8), the Jews oppose him, saying: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (ibid.). He refutes them with a firm and true argument, saying: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true” (ibid.).

He immediately puts forward what must necessarily be granted: “It is written in your Law that the testimony of two men is true” (ibid.). At once he adds: “I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid.). This too must be conceded. For the audible testimony of the Father is plainly known: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). The dead whom he raised, and so forth, and the good works which he showed them from his Father, were testimonies concerning him, both of the Father and of the Son. Thus they falsely calumniated testimony that was true and trustworthy, transgressors of the Law against their own Law.

The prophetic reading which precedes this agrees beautifully with these words: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know”—namely, your own witness—and “nations which did not know you shall run to you because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you” (Isa. 55); namely, in accordance with the words which you say concerning him: “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.” For the nations unknown to the Son run to him in faith because they establish the Son himself and God the Father—who are two witnesses because they are two persons, but not two gods—to be faithful and competent witnesses, whose testimonies they receive, from the words and deeds of each, holding certain that the Son himself was sent from the Father for their salvation.

There is also the fullest harmony between the beginning of the Gospel reading, “I am the light of the world” (John 8), etc., and the opening of the prophetic reading, “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55), etc. For that light makes drunk, and this water of wisdom enlightens those who drink it, as the Psalmist testifies. Having said, “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35), he immediately adds, “And in your light we shall see light” (ibid.). One and the same Wisdom of God the Father is the fountain of life and light from light. And of both it was said above: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” (ibid.).

## Book V

### Chapter I. On Passion Sunday
On the evening preceding this Sunday, the annual celebration of the Lord’s Passion begins. Why it begins so many days before the day on which the Lord was crucified may be observed from the Gospel of John. For he says: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus and said: What are we to do, since this man performs many signs?” (John 11). And when one of them, named Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, had prophesied that it was expedient for one man to die “for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (ibid.), the Evangelist immediately adds: “From that day therefore they planned to put him to death” (ibid.). And afterwards: “Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews; but, leaving them, he went into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples” (ibid.).

The time when that council was held may likewise be inferred from what follows. For it continues: “Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, in order to sanctify themselves” (ibid.). Clearly, this indicates that the beginning of the first month had then occurred when Lazarus was raised, on account of which sign the council was held not long afterwards. For it was the Jews’ custom, by command of the Law, to sanctify themselves before Passover and to begin this sanctification on the first day of the first month. On that day the tabernacle was also dedicated, as we read in Exodus, when the Lord spoke to Moses: “In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall set up the tabernacle of the testimony and place the ark in it” (Exod. 40), and so forth. And shortly afterwards: “Taking the oil of anointing, you shall anoint the tabernacle with its vessels, so that they may be sanctified” (ibid.), and so forth.

Nor should this be passed over: the beginning of that month, that is, the first moon, fell that year on a Friday. For the Friday on which the Lord was crucified was the fifteenth day; and therefore, as has been said, it must have been so—no one doubts it. For the fifteenth always falls on the same weekday as the first. Therefore, from what has been said, since the composer of the ecclesiastical office did not without reason wish the Gospel concerning the raising of Lazarus to be read on Friday, which is the fifteenth day before that on which the Lord was crucified, it is to be understood that the Lord raised Lazarus on the very day of the new moon.

This lawful progress of our King is exceedingly delightful: this lawful and holy trumpet-blast of our supreme Priest on this day of the new moon. He who once commanded the children of Israel through Moses, saying: “When you go out to war against enemies who fight against you; whenever you hold a feast, and on festival days and at the Kalends, you shall sound trumpets over the burnt offerings and peace-offerings” (Num. 10)—he, our King, about to go forth to the warfare of his Passion against the devil, prince of this world; he, our supreme Priest, about to hold the feast of his body and blood, when, in giving it to his disciples, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22); about to hold the feast-day of his most holy resurrection; having, I say, the Kalends, that is, the beginning of the month or moon, at whose full he was to accomplish these things—he sounds the trumpet of so great and excellent a miracle. By it he both struck his enemies with astonishment and encouraged the hearts of the devout more and more to believe.

For his enemies too, disturbed, say: “If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him” (John 11); and the people, especially animated to faith by this sign, afterwards went out to meet him when he came to Jerusalem, with palms and praises. Now, after Lazarus had been raised, it was not long before the Pharisees heard of it. For Bethany is only fifteen stadia from Jerusalem—that is, less than two full miles. And of the Jews who had been with Jesus when he raised Lazarus, “some,” says the Evangelist, “went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done” (John 11). Nor was there any delay in assembling the council after this. For the Evangelist immediately links the events thus: “Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council.”

Again, it was neither long nor difficult to assemble it then. For since, as the Evangelist says, “because the Passover of the Jews was near, many went up to Jerusalem in order to sanctify themselves,” then especially the chief priests and Pharisees, who were the clergy of the Jews, if any of them happened to be far away, had gathered solemnly. Moreover, the consecutive observance of two solemn days, namely the Sabbath and the new moon—which, as was said above, had been on the preceding day—had made them more numerous and more available for conducting the council. Nothing, therefore, prevents the conclusion that on that same Sabbath—whose evening we mark by beginning the annual commemoration of the Lord’s Passion—that council of the impious was assembled. And because from that day they planned to put him to death, the Church, sharing in every respect the suffering of her Lord as a body shares that of its head, begins public mourning in the evening, as though after the hour of that council.

Therefore, once this commemoration of the Lord’s Passion has begun, as stated, a spectacle worthy of beholding unfolds. For after the seven Sundays previously arranged above have been set before us as though a funeral procession, and after the Church, according to the rite of the office, has proceeded in her order through an equal number of ages of the world, at last the very death of Christ—to which all that procession was ordered beforehand—is borne before the eyes and impressed upon the devout minds of the faithful: the wounds and every token of death borne for all by the one salvation, Christ, God and man, the only-begotten Son of God.

For nothing is more frequent than the royal standards going forth and the radiant mystery of the cross. We meditate, both in nocturnal and diurnal chants gathered from the authoritative Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments alike, on vinegar, gall, and reed; on the nails and spear piercing the body. Thus the tresses of the Church’s head—that is, the thoughts of her heart—become “like a king’s purple bound in channels” (Song 7), while she meditates on the Passion of the Redeemer and applies her understanding to the authoritative Scriptures: that is, to the precious purple dyes which flowed forth through the mouths of prophets and apostles, as through certain channels, by the working of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter II. Why We Do Not Say “Glory Be to the Father”

Yet on this Sunday and throughout the whole week the mourning is less intense, because the Lamb was not immediately, after the council had been held, handed over into the hands of impious executioners to be led to sacrifice. Rather, from that time he began to be sought; and the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it so that they might seize him (John 11); and “Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews” (ibid.). We too, therefore, in a certain manner withdraw with him, since we somewhat suppress the voice of joy and praise.

For we omit “Glory be to the Father” from the responsories, and among some it is not said at Masses either with the introit of the office. For although it is a brief verse, because it is the more explicit and more proper praise of the Holy Trinity, its omission fittingly signifies the solitude and silence of our head, who was not walking openly.

## Chapter III. Why Jeremiah Is Read on This Sunday

The prophet Jeremiah is also suitably read at the night vigils during these days. For he prefigured the Passion of our Redeemer not only by his words but also by his own sufferings. Likewise, amid those same tribulations he did not perish, but survived the fall of the city or Temple. Although after these things the Jews are said to have stoned him when the people went down into Egypt, and although, in accordance with his prophecy, Zedekiah was captured and, after his sons had been killed, the king of Babylon put out his eyes—nonetheless all this signifies the Redeemer.

For our Redeemer also, when he was thought and desired to be extinguished and crushed out of the land of the living, according to the words, “My enemies spoke evil against me: When will he die and his name perish?” (Ps. 40), emerged victorious from all his tribulations, from death, and from hell; and he survived—indeed, he is and shall be—the sinful city. Though it was called Jerusalem, it has by its merits become part of that city “which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt” (Rev. 11).

And according to his prophecy, when he said: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9), the Jewish people were captured in their pride. After their sons—that is, the carnal works of the Law, in which no living grace of God remained—had been killed, the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar, namely the devil, furthermore put out their eyes. “Their eyes were darkened so that they might not see, and their back is always bent” (Ps. 68).

Thus Jeremiah the prophet is appropriately read during these days: in his afflictions he signifies the Passion of Christ the Lord, and with tearful laments bewails the future rejection of the Jewish people under the figure of the captivity which then occurred.

## Chapter IV. On the Office of the Same Day

The whole office of the Mass proclaims what was to come about through the Lord’s Passion: namely, that the old priesthood of the Jews was to be abandoned by the mediator of the New Testament himself, the high priest of the new sacrifice. The holy Gospel signifies this mystically, while the preceding apostolic reading declares it openly.

For when the Evangelist had said, “The Jews took up stones to throw at him,” he immediately added, “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple” (John 8).

“And what,” says Blessed Gregory, “does the Lord signify by hiding himself, except that Truth itself is hidden from those who disdain to follow his words? Truth flees the mind which it does not find humble.”  
[Note: [Col. 0123D] St Gregory, *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 18.5, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, ed. Migne.]

This indicates, therefore, that he was about to abandon the Temple and all the holy things of the Jews because of their pride and hardness of heart. The guardian powers of the Temple—whom Josephus testifies were heard saying, “Let us depart from these dwellings”—were about to go to better dwellings, which they would themselves protect while the Lord inhabited them.

But in the Epistle reading the Apostle says: “Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hands” (Heb. 9), and so forth. By these words he clearly declares to what better realities our high priest departed when he went out from the Temple.

The introit, moreover—“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people” (Ps. 42), and so forth—and likewise the gradual, “Deliver me from my enemies” (Ps. 17), are the words of him who goes out of the Temple and, in his humanity, prays that his cause—that is, the faith of the Gospel—may by a manifest distinction be distinguished from the justifications of the Law. And this occurred when the Temple was destroyed and the sacrifices of the Jews abolished.

For if the power of the Jewish kingdom and the worship of the old Temple had remained, they would have been a greater hindrance to Christian faith. Carnal and weak persons could not readily distinguish the emptiness of the old priesthood if it were supported by temporal prosperity and glory. Therefore, just as Moses first died and afterwards the children of Israel, led by Joshua, crossed the Jordan, so it was necessary that the Temple and old priesthood first be destroyed, so that we might pass without scruple to the saving baptism of Christ.

The following words in the gradual, “Teach me to do your will” (Ps. 142), refer to what he said in prayer when the moment of death was at hand: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). He asked this not from fear of suffering but from mercy toward the former people, lest he drink the cup offered by them. Therefore he pointedly did not say, “Let the cup pass from me,” but, “Let this cup pass from me.” When, I say, he had prayed this, returning into himself, he confirms from the person of God and Son what he had tremulously refused from the person of man: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.).

Then, as though one were to ask why he left the Temple turned away and angry, the tract follows: “Often,” he says, “have they assailed me from my youth” (Ps. 128)—that is, from the beginnings of the Church, “from the blood of righteous Abel” (Matt. 24). Often, I say, they have assailed me in my members, in my body, which is the Church, by killing the prophets and stoning those sent to them (Matt. 21); and “they prolonged their iniquity” (Ps. 128), perseveringly killing even unto myself, of whom they now say: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21).

In the offertory, “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart” (Ps. 110), he asks for the reward of obedience—having “become obedient unto death” (Phil. 2)—when he says in the form of a servant: “Reward your servant, that I may live” (Ps. 118), that is, that I may rise again; “and then I shall keep,” that is, I shall cause to be kept, “your words. Give me life according to your word” (ibid.), that is, through the power of your Word dwelling in me.

The following verse, in accordance with the Gospel words quoted above—“Which of you convicts me of sin? Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (John 8)—calls blessed the spotless, “who walk in the Law of the Lord and search out his testimonies” (Ps. 118). Another verse, “I have chosen the way of truth,” wholly vocal, elegant in its words and melodious in its neumes, is the voice of devout faith, frightened and stirred by what it heard shortly before: “If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” (John 8).

For when the choir of the Church raises this cry aloud, it seems to leap out from the company of those reproved for not believing one who speaks the truth, and who therefore do not hear the words of God because they are not of God. Seizing the standard of truth, it says: “Give me understanding” (Ps. 118), and so forth—just as the apostles say elsewhere: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17).

Communion: “This is my body, which shall be given for you” (Matt. 26). This is the well-known and most celebrated utterance of Christ, the supreme Priest and mediator of the New Testament, who has gone out from the Temple so often mentioned, and who, according to the words of the preceding Epistle, enters once into the holy places “not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood” (Heb. 9). Since Blessed Peter is the first heir of this priesthood and, after Christ, the first high priest both in time and dignity—he who followed the one saying, “Follow me” (John 21), likewise girded in the same manner and led away where he did not wish—it is fitting that the station appointed for the present office should be at his church.

## Chapter V. On the Harmony of the Weekday Readings

On Monday is read the Gospel in which it is said: “The chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize Jesus” (John 7). It continues: “But Jesus said to them: Yet a little while I am with you, and I go to him who sent me” (ibid.). He then adds what would happen to them: “You will seek me, and where I am you cannot come” (ibid.), namely, because the wall of unbelief stood in their way. By this saying he plainly threatened that, having left them, he would migrate to the Gentiles. Hence they too, as though divining it, say: “Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, to teach the Gentiles?” (ibid.).

The reading of Jonah, who, unwilling to preach to the great city Nineveh, fled to Tarshish and gave himself up to the waves of the sea (Jonah 3), is rightly set before this Gospel. He feared, as Jeremiah says, that the abandonment of his own people would follow when God became known among the Gentiles. For Jonah, whose name means “dove,” sent to preach the grace of God to the city of Nineveh, signifies Christ the Lord, sent by God the Father for the salvation of the whole world.

For as Jonah, unwilling to approach great Nineveh, gave himself instead to the waves of the sea, so our Lord, unwilling to approach the Gentiles in bodily presence, remained amid the tumults of the Jews who persecuted him (John 8). “The sea boiled, and the sailors were afraid” (Jonah 1). For when Pilate heard the accusation that he “made himself the Son of God, he was more afraid” (Matt. 27). At last, as the grave tossing continued because they cried, “Crucify, crucify” (ibid.), he washed his hands in the manner of the sailors, who said, “We beseech you, Lord, do not lay upon us the blood of an innocent man” (Jonah 1), and said: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27). He handed Jesus over to them to be crucified, as though casting him into the sea.

And the great fish swallowed him—that is, death—but its belly was burned by the fire of his divinity, and on the third day it vomited him forth alive again. Then at last great Nineveh, that is, the world, terrified by his preaching, is saved through the threefold immersion of baptism, as by a three-day repentance. And the ivy which shaded Jonah’s head—that is, Judaea, once Christ’s dwelling-place—withered.

On Tuesday, where the Gospel says: “Jesus walked in Galilee; for he did not wish to go into Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him” (John 7), and shortly afterwards nevertheless says: “He himself went up to the feast, not openly but, as it were, in secret” (ibid.), it continues: “Therefore the Jews were seeking him at the feast and saying: Where is he? And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said: He is good; others: No, but he deceives the crowd.”

To this Gospel, with a certain resemblance, accords the preceding reading concerning the prophet Daniel, although it is not found in the Hebrew text: the Babylonians, gathering against the king, said: “Hand Daniel over to us, for he destroyed Bel and killed the dragon” (Dan. 14), and so forth. For the Jews too, truly and spiritually Babylonians (1 Pet. 5), who were now seeking Jesus, eventually gathered against Pilate, governor of Roman power. Rome is written and spiritually is Babylon (Rev. 18); and, having stirred up a sedition, they demanded that he hand Jesus over to them. They did as he complains through the prophet: “They brought my life down into the pit of death, and set a stone upon me” (Lam. 3).

And when the conqueror of lions, that is, of malicious spirits, had again shown himself alive, “the king of Babylon cried out” (Dan. 14)—that is, the Roman Empire—with a loud voice: “Great is the God of Daniel” (ibid.). With a loud voice, I say. For a great sound was made when the first emperor of the Roman city, that great Babylon, received the faith of Christ. “The church which is gathered in Babylon greets you,” says the apostle Peter (1 Pet. 5), referring figuratively to Rome.

On Wednesday, in the Gospel, the Jews surround the Lord and say: “How long will you take away our life? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10). And Jesus answers: “I tell you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in the name of my Father, these bear witness to me” (ibid.). And after some words he adds: “I and the Father are one” (ibid.). Let Arius hear, “We are one”; let Sabellius hear that he did not say, “one person,” but “one thing.”

When they wished to stone him and accused him of blasphemy, he said: “If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works” (ibid.). Here, since he declared himself not only to be Christ, whom they sought, but also God—which the heretics refuse to understand, though the Jews understood it when they said, “Though you are a man, you make yourself God” (ibid.)—the reading is rightly set before it in which the Lord declares himself to be Lord and God to their fathers in nearly every precept, as though crushing the hard neck of a contumacious servant (Lev. 19).

For these also, sons of rebellious, unbelieving, testing, and murmuring ancestors, testing him and hardening their necks, deserved that just as the bodies of those ancestors were laid low in the wilderness (Num. 14), so they themselves should be driven far from the promise, standing against the blood of their neighbour and transgressing every precept of the aforesaid reading.

On Thursday the whole mournful office laments the barrenness of the Jewish people. Like willows, they possessed manly strength through knowledge of the Law but bore no fruit of faith or good works. For they were especially the Jews who had become deaf while the Lord preached, to whom he had said: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matt. 17). They are the willows of which, on that same day, there is mournful singing in the person of the ancient and new saints: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136), and so forth.

For ever since they shattered upon the wood of the cross that precious instrument of Christ’s humanity—to which the Father says in the Psalm, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56)—the holy Fathers and prophets have hung their instruments upon those willows. For no prophet has since been sent to the Jews, and the books of the prophets which they read, because they do not understand them, they allow to lie idle like instruments hung up.

We must therefore see what accords with so mournful an office in the Gospel of that same day. The officers whom the chief priests and Pharisees had sent to seize Jesus returned. They returned, I say, without charge against him and full of amazement; when those men said to them, “Why have you not brought him?” they answered: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 7). By saying this, they truly preferred his most sweet song—that is, his teaching—to every instrument and every singer who from the beginning had sung to us a hymn from the songs of Zion (Ps. 136).

But those others, envious and quarrelling among themselves—consider what they finally did. “Each one,” says the Evangelist, “returned to his own house” (John 7). O fruitless willows! The contempt of the supreme and saving song could not have been more clearly signified. Rightly, therefore, they have thus far remained shut up [or: enclosed] in their own houses, which they could not distribute, though those who distribute the houses of Zion are commanded in the Psalm: “Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses” (Ps. 47).

Shut up in their own houses, that is, enclosed in evil consciences, they do not deserve to be called out in public to hear the instruments of the Scriptures, which are hung up for them but sing sweetly and clearly for us. Yet joined to the sons of Edom—indeed, having become their head—mingled, I say, with the earthly and bloodthirsty persecutors of holy Zion, of whom we sing that same day, “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem” (Ps. 136), they first shattered in the punishment of the cross that proper instrument of divinity. Then they killed, scourged, stoned, and persecuted from city to city the wise men and scribes sent to them (Matt. 23); and also in the cities of the Gentiles they raised persecution against the apostles by stirring up sedition (Acts 13–14).

In a manner, they said: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundations” (Ps. 136), so that, if they could, they might then overthrow the rising Church utterly. And, as we read in ecclesiastical histories, when the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—compelled Christians to idolatry, these men sometimes pressed them even more vehemently.

Thus the aforesaid Gospel is suitably preceded by the reading from the book of the prophet Daniel: the prayer of the three children. According to the history, seated and weeping beside the rivers of Babylon, they sorrowed that they sang the praise of God in vain among its willows, that is, among fruitless people. Ordered besides to worship the golden statue, and cast into the furnace because they refused, they foreshadowed the martyrdoms and victories of the Church (Dan. 3). This office is especially fittingly placed on this day because after this day no Gospel reading is read concerning the Lord’s public preaching to the Jews. Behold, therefore, that instrument of divinity has been hung upon those Babylonian willows.

On Friday this Gospel is read: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus and said: What are we to do, since this man performs many signs? If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him” (John 11). And, adducing the cause of their anxiety as though it were reasonable, they say: “The Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (ibid.). For they were under Roman rule, because the sceptre had already been taken away from Judah and the ruler from his thigh (Gen. 41); and they had Pilate, governor of Roman power.

But because they thus feared frost, snow fell upon them (Job 6), and they were crushed with a double destruction (Jer. 17). For they lost both their place and nation; and, blotted out from the book of the living (Ps. 68), they were written in the earth. Thus the reading from Jeremiah the prophet is fittingly set before the account of those dogs who surrounded the Lord, that council of evildoers which besieged him: “O Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded, and those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17). And shortly afterwards, observing their perverse anxiety when they say, “The Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11), he says: “Let them be afraid, but let not me be afraid. Bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17).

This was done through Titus and Vespasian, when, having already lost the kingdom of God, they also lost their place and nation. Although the Jews often sought to kill the Lord—for more than once they took up stones to stone him, and the chief priests and Pharisees also sent officers to seize him—the Evangelist rightly said concerning this council: “From that day therefore they planned to put him to death” (John 11). For now they seemed to themselves to be acting, not by a tumultuous or popular sedition, nor with prejudgment, but by a lawful judicial session; as has been said, they alleged their anxiety lest, since he was called king, they themselves should be accused of treason against the Roman Empire under which they lived.

## Chapter VI. Why There Is No Office on the Saturday before Palm Sunday

On the Saturday when the lord pope gives alms, the Saturday is that on which the Lord came to Bethany and had supper in the house of Lazarus, whom he had raised, as the Evangelist relates: “Jesus therefore, six days before the feast of Passover, came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he raised. Therefore they made him a supper there. Lazarus was one of those reclining with him. Then Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped them with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12).

There, by a celebrated mystery, the fragrant work of almsgiving was commended. For Mary bore the type of the Church, while the Lord’s feet are the poor who are weak: although they are his extremities, they are nevertheless his members through the union and unity of faith. A woman anoints the Lord’s feet and wipes them with her hair, which is certainly superfluous to the body, whenever the rich who are in the Church comfort poor believers with the gentleness of mercy and supply their need from their own abundance.

Thus, in order that the Roman pope may offer the Lord a celebrated supper with Mary, he gives alms on this Saturday; and since he is occupied about the Lord’s feet, the Saturday is left free.

## Chapter VII. Palm Sunday

On this Sunday, when the Lord came into the city of Jerusalem in order to suffer, the moon was in its tenth day. Concerning this day the Lord commanded the children of Israel in the Law: “On the tenth day of the first month, each shall take a lamb for his families and houses, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening” (Exod. 12).

The history of the wonders previously performed is familiar and celebrated: Moses struck Pharaoh and all Egypt with ten plagues by the rod in his hand. Yet though Pharaoh was afflicted, he was not conquered until the lamb was sacrificed in the houses of Israel. But what this signified—how “all these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. 10)—and how it pertains to the present matter must not be passed over.

Pharaoh bore the type of the devil; Egypt, of the world; and the children of Israel, of all who are foreordained to life and are called the people of God. The captivity and bondage of the children of Israel signify the captivity in which the devil, by transgression, enslaved in the darkness of this age humankind created in the freedom of Paradise and made it subject to death.

Moses stood with Aaron before Pharaoh and, holding the rod in his hand, said: “Thus says the Lord: Let my people go” (Exod. 7). In the rod of Moses we recognize the discipline of the Law; in Aaron, the priesthood of that same Law. These two were given so that they might deliver God’s people from the slavery of Pharaoh, that is, of the devil. The ten plagues with which Pharaoh was struck foreshadowed the ten commandments of the Law, by which the people of God were commanded to resist the devil, captor of the human race.

For then death, “which reigned from Adam until Moses” (Rom. 5), first began to hear contradiction in its kingdom, when God demanded from humanity the worship due to him and obedience to his commandments. But just as Pharaoh was not so overcome by the ten plagues that he let the children of Israel go, so the devil was not so overcome by observance of the ten commandments of the Law that humanity returned to Paradise.

Therefore, as after the ineffectual rod of Moses the lamb was finally commanded to be sacrificed, and then the firstborn of Egypt died; and as, struck by that one plague, Pharaoh released the people, while he himself and the remaining Egyptians, pursuing those who crossed over, were drowned in the Red Sea—so, after it had become clear that the Law “brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7), Christ, the Lamb of God, was sacrificed. In his death the firstborn, that is, original sin, was destroyed; and in the Red Sea of baptism, made red by Christ’s blood, actual sins also were utterly swallowed up together with the devil (Col. 2; 1 Cor. 10).

Therefore, on the tenth moon, as has been said, Christ the Lord, the true Lamb, obedient to the command of the Father, entered the city of Jerusalem in order to suffer. Yet his entry too is not devoid of mysteries. For wherever this true Sun proceeds, he casts, as it were, shadows resembling the body set between, of the salvation whose image he effects.

Coming, therefore, to his Passion, let us see what shadows he casts of radiant mercy, in the abundance of which he comes blessed. First, from the Mount of Olives he sends two disciples into the village opposite them, that they might untie there an ass tied up and her colt and bring them to him (Matt. 21), and so forth. In these things he mystically foreshadowed the benefit contained in his blood and the fruit of the Passion to which he was coming.

For, because of the Passion of death, he was to ascend, crowned with glory and honour (Heb. 2), to the right hand of the Father, who is the Mount of Olives: that is, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1), God of peace, fountain and source of light. From there, giving gifts to human beings, he would send his apostles. Having received the power to bind and loose, they would free the ass and her colt—that is, both peoples, Jewish and Gentile—from the folly of error and the burdens of sins. And when the human race had been brought to him through faith, he himself, sitting upon it, as it is written, “Your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3), would lead souls into the heavenly Jerusalem, while crowds of angels came with praise, raising palms of victory and olive branches, the emblems of peace.

## Chapter VIII. Why the Sunday Procession Is Not to Be Omitted Because of the Procession of Palms

Those who carefully examine evangelical authority have rightly determined that the ordinary Sunday procession, by which on every Sunday we commemorate the glorious resurrection of the same Redeemer, should not be counted together with today’s procession of palms, by which beyond doubt we recall his Passion. For it is certain that contrary or opposing things cannot suitably be displayed at the same time in one and the same act. But these plainly differ and are opposed to one another. What is more contrary than joy to sorrow, life to death, resurrection to setting?

On every Sunday, consecrated from the first day after the Sabbath on which the Lord rose, we signify by the order of this procession that we ought to go out into Galilee—that is, into migration—with his apostles in order to see the Lord. That is, we ought not to remain the old people we once were, but to “walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). Therefore, in such processions we always follow our prelates as they go before us, as though following the Lord into Galilee; and the place where we conclude the procession at its final station is rightly called by us Galilee.

But no one is unaware that this annual procession of palms is a proclamation of the Passion, and that what the Hebrew children did—meeting the Lord with olive branches, crying out and saying, “Hosanna in the highest”—is renewed in action for the refreshment of devotion. Therefore those from whom we received this practice act more correctly: before Terce, they perform the memorial of the Lord’s resurrection which recurs throughout the year, as on other Sundays; and after Terce, with the procession of palms, they set forth the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion.

## Chapter IX. That This Greater Week Corresponds to the Week of the World’s Creation
It is a great and admirable thing that on the Lord’s Day, which is the first day, on which God began to work the creation of the world, the Savior enters upon the labor of the Passion; and, having wrought our salvation throughout this whole week, which is called the Great Week, on the seventh day he ceased and rested in the tomb. He wrought humanity’s salvation in as many days as he arranged in the world the human being and all that he created for humanity’s sake. [Col. 0131C] And according to the creation of diverse works, some days were consecrated more, others less, by the differing quantity of things and offices.

This first day, on which he enters with such brilliance upon the work of the saving Passion, corresponds in dignity to that day on which he said: “Let light be made, and light was made” (Gen. 1). Of the individual remaining days something will be said in its place; for now let us briefly consider the office of this day.

## Chapter X. On the Mass of the same day

That handing-over of ours, by which the Father handed him over, as the Apostle says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8), that handing-over, I say, is the material or cause of so great [Col. 0131D] and solemn an office. For on this day the Father handed him over, in that he came into the hands of his enemies by the Father’s will—he who previously, though often sought amid tumult, had frustrated all their attacks. Obedient to the Father’s will, he came to drink the cup of the Passion; and, though the flesh was weak for drinking it, being ready in spirit (Matt. 26), he said: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22).

Therefore, because the Father handed him over on this day and gave him the cup of the Passion, the Passion is rightly read with those same palm branches by which he was received; and it supplied the venerable matter for the entire office. For from what he said while hanging upon the cross—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27)—it is evident that the whole twenty-first Psalm [Psalm 22] [Col. 0132A] was composed in his own person. For this reason, on this very day, nearly the whole Psalm is nevertheless sung in that same person.

First, in the Introit, “O Lord, do not make your help far from me” (Ps. 21 [22]), he himself prays—the one who, “like a worm and not a man” (ibid.), was lightly trampled underfoot without any regard, abandoned for our sake for a time. He prays, I say, to the Father not to delay his help, that is, to hasten his resurrection and deliver his lowliness from the power of those who are unicorns, that is, of singular pride (ibid.).

Then, in the Tract, our David himself treats this more fully, according to the title of the same Psalm: “unto the end,” that is, unto victory; “for the morning taking up,” that is, for the resurrection, so that it might happen “very early in the morning,” as indeed it did, “while it was still dark” at the tomb (Mark 16; John 20).

The Epistle too undoubtedly precedes the reading of the Passion with its proclamation. For the Lord’s second prayer in the Passion, when he says, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it” (Matt. 26); the fact that the supreme God is mocked in the supreme humility of humanity, spat upon, gives his back “to those who strike, and his cheeks to those who pluck them” (Isa. 50), and patiently endures the rest, obedient to the Father’s will unto death on the cross (Phil. 2)—all these things Paul plainly sets before us in the Epistle for imitation, saying: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus” (ibid.), etc.

Likewise, in the Gradual, while it says, “You held my right hand, and led me in your will” (Ps. 72 [73]), it most beautifully suggests that God the Father, as though with his left [Col. 0132C] hand, held Christ’s right hand—that is, restrained in some manner his divine power, lest he defend himself—and led him, according to his will, into the power of his enemies, that is, into the city of Jerusalem.

It may be asked why this Gradual is sung on this day, since not all of it suits his person. For it does not apply to him to say: “But my feet were almost moved, and my steps almost poured out” (ibid.). Yet one must know that the Psalm from which it is taken reproves those who praised God only for bodily safety and for the prosperity or abundance of temporal things. Such praises had not ceased before our Lord, King of all ages, came and, through what he suffered, strengthened us [Col. 0132D] so that we should not be scandalized when we see the wicked prosper while things do not go rightly for the good.

For what righteous person, seeing Justice itself crucified by those whose iniquity “came forth as from fat,” who “were not in the labor of men, nor were they scourged with men” (ibid.)—what righteous person, I say, when something similar happens to him, would now say: “Therefore I have justified my heart in vain and washed my hands among the innocent” (ibid.)? For if he tells it thus, behold, he has rejected the nation of God’s sons—indeed, the Passion of the Son of God himself (ibid.). Therefore, when the scourged and crucified Righteous One is displayed, it is fittingly sung: “How good is the God of Israel to those upright in heart” (ibid.), so that our feet—that is, our reason and judgment—may not be moved when we see the peace of sinners (ibid.).

The Offertory also, with verses taken from the sixty-eighth Psalm [Psalm 69], which was wholly composed in the person of the Savior praying in the agony of the Passion, indicates with how great a desire of love he accepted those things which were read beforehand in the course of the Passion. For it says: “My heart expected reproach and misery”: it expected reproach, namely, in words—that is, my heart desired it—and misery, namely, in deeds. “And I waited,” that is, I expected one who would grieve with me, namely, who would mourn with me over his own destruction; and there was none—understood: none who would do this. “I sought one to console me,” that is, one acting rightly through repentance, “and I found none. And they gave me gall for my food”: that is, they made themselves bitter to me, etc.

## Chapter XI. On Monday of Holy Week

[Col. 0133B] Monday seems less adorned than the other days of this week, whose offices are all purpled by the reading of the Passion or by other marks of the Lord’s death. Nor is this surprising. For in that first week, in which all things were created, and to which this one is similar, as was said above, the second day is commended somewhat less than the others by the Creator’s approval.

For when he had said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. 1), there was not added, as in the works of the other days, “and God saw that it was good” (ibid.). This is indeed added in the Septuagint, but it is not found in the Hebrew.
