Moreover, as Jerome says, the number two is thereby disgraced, because it is the first to fall away from unity and is the initiator of division. [Note: [Col. 0133D] St. Jerome, Epistle 69, §6.]

[Col. 0133C] And because the division of the upper and lower waters signifies the division of good and evil—though just, yet evil on account of the punishment of those who are divided—and because that division was made on the second day, and because what we call “second” proceeds from the binary number not in sound but in meaning, it was rightly not added, according to the Hebrew truth, concerning the work of the second day: “and God saw that it was good.”

Therefore, since the second day of the world’s creation is less distinguished by praise of its work, it is not surprising that the second day of this week, which corresponds to it, should be less purpled by the office of the Passion.

The Gospel of this day relates that, having been received with palm branches, he entered the city of Jerusalem. And when the Gentiles wished to see him (John 12), as their salvation—of whom Jacob had long before prophesied, saying: “And he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49)—and when, on that account, he had figuratively called himself a grain of wheat, to be put to death by the unbelief of the Jews and multiplied by the faith of the peoples; when, I say, he asked that his glorification might dawn for the salvation of the Gentiles, praying to the Father and saying, “Father, save me from this hour. Father, glorify your name,” a voice came from heaven saying: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12).

And because, obedient to the will, he gave himself into the hands of those seeking his life when he came into the city already mentioned, this prophetic reading is fittingly prefixed: “The Lord God opened [Col. 0134A] my ear,” namely, so that I might obey his will; “but I do not resist; I did not turn backward. I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them” (Isa. 50), and the other words agreeing with this: that, not refusing to suffer, he gave himself up for the world’s salvation. But all the members of the office correspond to his prayer in the Gospel that he be glorified, namely by the glory of the resurrection, in which he asks to be delivered and his harmful assailants to be judged and conquered.

## Chapter XII. On Tuesday

Tuesday is fittingly preceded by the reading from Jeremiah before the Passion is read, because he says in Jeremiah’s person: “You, O Lord, showed me, and I knew; you revealed to me their devices. And I was like a lamb led to the victim, and I did not know that they had devised plans against me, saying: ‘Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us destroy him from the land of the living.’ You, O Lord of hosts, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, let me, I pray, see your vengeance upon them” (Jer. 11).

For during these days until Wednesday, these devices and their plans grew more and more heated; but, being afraid “lest perhaps a tumult arise among the people” (Matt. 26), they lacked opportunity. For our Lord himself, “by day,” as Luke the Evangelist says, “was teaching in the temple, but by night he went out to the mountain called Olivet, and the people extolled him in the temple” (Luke 21).

And he was so far from flattering anyone, as Jerome says, that in a great and populous city he never had even the lodging of one night. And just as the most arrogant Haman, having erected in his own house the cross which he had prepared for Mordecai, sought an opportunity to petition the king about him in the morning so that he might be hanged (Esther 11), so the devil, having formed a plan in his own house—that is, in the hearts of the Jews—saying, “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” that is, the cross into his body, sought an opportunity to hand Jesus over to Roman authority.

Therefore, seeing vengeance upon them, as was said in the Epistle, “We glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). For he from whom they took counsel to put wood into his bread was pierced and despoiled by that same wood, so that Christ’s glorious cross, lifted from the punishment of the guilty, was raised upon the foreheads of emperors. Thus in the Introit [Col. 0134D] we sing: “We ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The other things that follow in the office are plainly words of his person while he is in agony and praying for his resurrection.

## Chapter XIII. On Wednesday

Wednesday, the sale of our Head, is the beginning for the whole body of the Church of unprecedented contrition and humility. For on this day “Judas went away and spoke with the chief priests and magistrates about how he might hand Jesus over to them. And they rejoiced and agreed to give him money. And he promised” (Luke 22).

Therefore, because on this day the Church was deprived of her Head, she lays aside on the same day the customary observance of her procession and darkens the customary joy of all nocturnal and diurnal psalmody after this day. Moreover, throughout the year’s cycle, in the penitential observance of fasts, for the reason stated above, Wednesday holds second rank after Friday, on which our Lord was crucified.

Now, because the office of this Wednesday shines forth above the others by its sacred arrangement—indeed, because it is almost wholly the mournful voice of our sold Head—it is pleasing to linger briefly over it. And first this must be said: the office of the present day deserved two readings and a long, mournful Tract in place of the second Gradual because of the Lord’s sale just mentioned; and all the members of the office reverently serve the reverence due to the Lord as he prays [Col. 0135B] and lies prostrate upon his face. Of him, on this day, the Passion according to Luke reads thus:

“And he was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw; and, kneeling down, he prayed, saying: ‘Father, if you will, remove this cup from me.’ And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the earth. And an angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him” (Luke 22).

The other Evangelists also report that he prayed to the Father, whom he is unquestionably less than according to his humanity, in which he was also “made a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). But this eloquent Ox, namely Luke, more elegantly pursuing the sacrificial offering of the saving calf, presents to the world, angels, and human beings a more wonderful spectacle in Christ’s bearing as he prays in our weakness.

Hence the Church, contemplating such great marvels, trembles; and in the Introit, as though stunned, bursts out in a sudden cry: “At the name of the Lord let every knee bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2), etc. Truly, seeing the Lord of all angels and human beings fall down and struggle in a sweat of blood, it strikes human hearts with this terrifying cry, lest anyone dare remain stiff and exalted when he, so great, in such great humility for our sake cast himself down and bent his knees.

Great, devout, and worthy of the contemplation of our minds is the office of this day: holy Church labors to bring the hearts of each of her children, by contemplation, into the presence of so great an event, and by the voices of the apostles [Col. 0135D] and prophets, as though they were present and standing around the agonizing Lord, to arouse them to awe and compassion.

Once the Introit antiphon has been proclaimed, as stated above—taken from the Apostle, something very rare, for few are drawn from the New Testament—Isaiah the prophet, the most eager spectator and herald of this Lord’s Passion, immediately hastens forward as though present, summoning us by the reader’s voice to behold that agony and saying: “Say to the daughters of Zion: Behold, your Savior comes” (Isa. 61). And he adds: “Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him” (ibid.).

In this very brief statement he fittingly commends both the work of the Passion toward which he was directed and the reward of glory or honor with which he was to be crowned through the divinity that is with him—namely, in the unity of one and the same person. Then, marveling at his appearance, he says: “Who is this that comes from Edom,” that is, from the bloody or earthly Jews, “with dyed garments,” that is, with the members of the body, which are the garments of divinity, dyed with the purple of blood—“with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (ibid.).

Bozrah means “strong” and “fortified,” and signifies the city of Jerusalem, which the Lord who was bloodied by it had once made strong and fortified more by his own help than by its circuit of walls. But it is a city in Moab; by this name he strongly strikes at the Jews of Jerusalem. For it follows that they are Moabites, as indeed they are; for Moab means “from the father.” And when the Lord said to the Jews: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham; but now you seek to kill me: Abraham did not do this” (John 8), he added: “You are from your father the devil” (ibid.).

Therefore, after he had said, “Who is this?” and the other replied, “I who speak justice and am mighty to save” (Isa. 61), he again asks: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one treading in the winepress?” (ibid.). That is: since you speak justice, why are you bloodied by the pressure of the cross? But he replies: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (ibid.), understood: for all, so that all might be set free.

Having heard these things, the choir of the Church, knowing that the Lord’s agony, sweat of blood, and prayer are for her—indeed, are hers—adds its voice. Yet it does not speak [Col. 0136C] in the plural, because it is one person with Christ, as a body with its head; and it sings the Gradual: “Do not turn your face away from your servant,” that is, from me, who am your servant; “for I am troubled,” namely for you; “hear me quickly,” that is, raise me up. “Save me, for waters”—that is, the Jews, who are always in the motion of envy—“have entered even unto my soul,” that is, so far as to kill me; while dwelling among them, “I am fixed in the deep mire, where there is no substance” (Ps. 68 [69]), because they have lost the True One.

Then, after the other reading from the same prophet has been proclaimed, in which, while speaking, he foresaw with spiritual eye Christ in the same form in which he is now represented by the Evangelist—namely, having no form or beauty; rising like a shrub and as a root out of thirsty ground; despised and the lowest of men; a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity; wounded for our iniquities and bruised for our crimes; reckoned among the wicked and praying for transgressors (Isa. 53)—after this reading is pronounced, there occurs what is done on no other day in the year except this Wednesday, the great day of Parasceve [Good Friday], and the Saturdays of the Four Ember fasts: namely, that the Epistle is followed not by a Gradual but by a Tract.

For apart from the aforesaid days, the Epistle is always followed by the Gradual, or by Alleluia if the season excludes the Gradual, as happens during the days of Pentecost. The reason is that the musician who said: “We played for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep” (Matt. 11)—to whose music Alleluia corresponds as it were to dancing, and to whose lament the Gradual corresponds as it were to penitential weeping, as has already been said in its place—that musician, I say, is taken away on these days. For on Wednesday he is sold, and on the following Friday he is crucified.

But on the day of Parasceve each reading is followed by its own Tract. On this day, however, because though sold he was still with the disciples, only one Tract is used in place of the Gradual, as though the mourning were not yet complete. That the Tract belongs to mourners and is more suited to mourning than the Gradual, which is the lament of penitence, is shown by this: it is sung not with Alleluia, as is the Gradual, but in place of Alleluia on those days on which we mourn death, which entered the world through the envy of the devil (Wis. 2)—that is, from Septuagesima until Easter.

This Tract is from the one hundred and first Psalm [Psalm 102], which suits the subject and time very well. For its title too concerns the moment when, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, wet with bloody sweat (Luke 22)—a sign of the abundant blood to be shed in the slaughter of martyrs—or the time when he prayed for transgressors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23); and again: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (ibid.). For the title reads: “The prayer of the poor man, when he is anxious and pours out his petition before the Lord” (Ps. 101 [102]).

This poor man is he who, as the Apostle says, “though he was rich,” by his grace “became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8). Therefore, while this poor man prays for us, all the poor in spirit, who are one body with him, pray together as he prays before them. And to this highest angel, holding the golden censer of his immaculate body and offering the incense of his prayer (Rev. 1), our choir likewise eagerly adds together the incense of its prayers, saying and repeating: “Lord, hear my prayer” (Ps. 101 [102]), etc.

After the Passion has also been read, the Offertory sets forth the sacrifice of that same reiterated prayer. The Communion too is from the same Psalm: “I mingled my drink with weeping” (ibid.), so that you may see that this whole Psalm was written in his person: he “who,” as the Apostle says, “in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications, with loud crying and many tears, to him who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

Finally, this must not be passed over: on this day the Sun of Justice was fittingly sold for our salvation, because in that week of the world’s creation this visible sun was formed to shine upon the world. O truly wondrous ordering of divine grace! Great and marvelous condescension of unique love! Thus he deigned to suffer for us who were lost, so that he did not disdain also to be sold for us who had been sold. For we had been sold in a miserable sale, as the Lord himself says through the prophet: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isa. 62). A true saying, bearing divine weight. “You were sold for nothing,” he says, that is, deceived by false promises. For what even of temporal profit did miserable man obtain by departing from God and handing himself over to the devil? “And you shall be redeemed without silver.” For what, captive daughter of Zion, did you give for your redemption? With no preceding merits, but by grace alone, Christ was sold and redeemed those who had been sold.

## Chapter XIV. On Thursday, which we call the Lord’s Supper

Thursday, which we call the Lord’s Supper, is varied by the commemoration partly of joyful and partly of sorrowful events. In accordance with the difference between these two dispositions, joy and sorrow, it also retains diverse and almost contrary characteristics in the regular offices. For the Mass has a complete and most festal office—indeed, more than customarily festal—whereas during the canonical hours we render to God a service neither festal nor complete in the customary manner: at each hour we cut off the heads, that is, the beginnings, and conceal their endings in silence.

But the Mass is carried out fully and solemnly, and through the hands of the bishop it is uniquely made fruitful by many sacraments of mercy. And just as, on the fifth day in the week of the world’s creation, the race originating from the water was partly returned to the deep and partly raised into the air, so that creatures sprung from one stock should take different places, so on Thursday of this week, in which we have been renewed, the sacraments of one and the same salvation partly press us down into sorrow and partly lift us into joy, so that mysteries brought forth for one salvation are celebrated with very different worship or disposition. Let us therefore seek the reasons according to the Gospel narrative, beginning with the joyful matters.

## Chapter XV. Why the Mass of this day is solemnly celebrated

The reason why the Mass of the aforesaid day rejoices amid sad hours, as the sun sometimes glows through clouds, is that the Lord Christ, the Holy of Holies, to whom the Father said with an oath: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [110])—he himself priest and himself victim—instituted for us the rite of the new sacrifice on the night when he was handed over. Taking bread and the cup of wine, blessing them and saying, “This is [Col. 0138D] my body; this is the cup of my blood” (Matt. 26; 1 Cor. 11), he then first performed the office of his priesthood, putting an end to the old priesthood; and, after the eating of the typical lamb, offered himself, who is the true Lamb, to God the Father with his own hands.

This is what the Apostle says: “Not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9). For the very body which was slain by the ungodly, and the same blood which was poured out upon the cross, that eternal priest then offered. And he of whom it was said elsewhere, when the Jews wanted to stone him, “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 18), now truly went out of the Jews’ temple, abandoned their sacrifices, and hid himself in the sacrifice of bread and wine in such a manner that the ungodly could not recognize at all what is there.

Therefore, because today he handed down the true sacrifice (Heb. 9) and, about to die, wrote the new testament in his blood for his heirs, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart—as he himself says, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26)—the Mass alone fittingly deserves a solemn chant and the joyful adornment of the ministers of the altar amid the sorrow signified through all the hours.

And lest anything of beauty be lacking to the holy sacrifice, on the day of its institution the bishop also sings the *Gloria in excelsis*. Every bishop should on this day completely perform everything belonging to his office. Thus he reconciles the Church’s penitents, blesses oil, and prepares chrism, by which, sealed, we receive the testimony of the Holy Spirit (Eph. 4), saying to God: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

The order of consecration is venerable and devout; but if you examine, however slightly, the reasons for the things done in that consecration, you will delight much more deeply in the inward beauty of devotion. The order itself is visible to everyone; but according to our purpose, we shall seek its reasons. What, then, chrism signifies; what is effected for us in it; why it is consecrated on this day; and what mystery the order of its consecration contains—these we desire to consider, with the giver of true light going before us.

## Chapter XVI. [Col. 0139C] On Chrism

*Chrisma* is Greek; in Latin it is called *unctio*, “anointing.” From this name our Lord is called Christ, that is, “the Anointed One.” Moses was the first to institute anointing with chrism in Exodus (Exod. 30): by the Lord’s command he compounded it, and Aaron and his sons were the first anointed with it (Lev. 8). At that time this mystical anointing belonged only to kings and priests, by which Christ, the supreme King and true Priest, was prefigured.

But after Christ the Son of God came in person and was anointed by God the Father with heavenly and true ointment, not only bishops and kings but the whole Church is consecrated by the anointing of chrism through the laying on of hands.

That it belongs to bishops alone to seal and bestow the Paraclete Spirit is shown not only by the Church’s custom but also by that reading from the Acts of the Apostles which affirms that, when certain persons had been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the hands of the Apostle Paul. Thus it is read: “And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them” (Acts 19), etc.

Likewise, elsewhere it is written that the apostles in Jerusalem sent Peter and John to Samaria to give the Holy Spirit to those already baptized: “Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8). Here it is plainly understood that it belongs to bishops alone, as the successors of the apostles, to seal and bestow the Paraclete.

It is read in the papal records [*Gestis pontificalibus*] [Col. 0140A] that Pope Sylvester decreed that the priest should anoint with chrism a baptized person raised from the water, because of the risk of a sudden death, lest baptized persons should die without the laying on of hands because the bishop is absent and difficult to reach. Priests may therefore anoint the baptized with chrism, but only chrism consecrated by a bishop; yet they may anoint not the forehead, which belongs to bishops alone, but the crown of the head.

Perhaps someone may say: “What profit is the mystery of confirmation to me after the mystery of baptism? For if, after the font, we need the addition of a new kind [of gift], then, as I see it, we did not receive everything from the font.” This must not be understood so. For what benefit is it if any parent grants a great inheritance to a little child unless he provides that child with a guardian? (Gal. 4).

The Paraclete is the guardian, comforter, and tutor of those reborn in Christ. At the devil’s prompting they might, like children, lose the benefit of baptism as they might lose their property, if they did not have this guardian. Chrism, therefore, is the sign of the Holy Spirit and contains his power.

It was fitting that the Holy Spirit should give us grace through this visible form of his own. It is the fruit and richness of the olive, a tree that ministers peace and light, mixed with balsam, whose tree is fragrant and foremost among aromatic trees. The Holy Spirit is the richness of the divine substance, so that whoever has been refreshed by him may say: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22 [23]).

The fragrance of balsam in the oil signifies the sweetness of the same Holy Spirit, by which he attracts with a good odor all who have a nose—that is, the faculty [Col. 0140C] of discernment—and makes them desire himself. Whoever receive him say with the Apostle: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2; Heb. 13). The Holy Spirit, therefore, who acts visibly for our sake so that through visible things we may more easily grasp invisible things, fittingly pours into us through this likeness his sweet and fragrant grace.

## Chapter XVII. Why chrism is fittingly consecrated on this day

It is known that this day represents the fourteenth day of the first month, on which the lamb was commanded to be sacrificed in the evening; and with its blood both doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which it was to be eaten were to be marked, so that, when he saw that sign, the destroyer of Egypt might pass untouched over the houses of the sacred feast.

It is clear that the sign of Christ’s cross is therefore impressed upon our foreheads from this chrism: so that the destroying devil may have no right to harm in the houses of our souls and bodies. This was prefigured by the blood of that typical lamb with which the doorposts were marked. Therefore it is fitting that, on the day when that merely figurative act was performed, this sacred rite of the present reality should be solemnly prepared for us.

In accordance with this likeness, it would seem consequent that on this very night the houses in which the lamb is to be eaten—that is, the foreheads of those in whose minds faith in Christ, the Lamb of God, is stored—should be marked with holy chrism. This would rightly seem so if on this same night it were fitting to celebrate the Paschal feast together with the crime of the Jews that we mourn.

But now, although the Lord’s Passion is the summit of our salvation, holy Church nevertheless reasonably dedicated the day on which he suffered rather to mourning and silence. She judged that the joy of that solemnity by which we were redeemed should be deferred until the third day, on which that Victor rose again. Then at last we celebrate the banquet of the Paschal Lamb in our houses, both for the salvation of souls recovered, accomplished on Friday, and for the future resurrection of bodies granted to us when he rose again on the first day of the week, saying: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity [Col. 0141B] and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore, having received that by which we mark the doorposts of our foreheads, we wait until the evening of Saturday, which is for us the evening of the Paschal banquet. Then, after the foreheads of the baptized have been marked—those who, fleeing the true Pharaoh, namely the devil, are hastening toward him through the Red Sea of baptism—we begin that banquet of ours “with the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41 [42]).

And if you ask why the consecration of chrism itself is not also deferred, the reason is that from this Thursday until the evening of Saturday, when chrism must be used, we are free from the solemnities of Masses; and it is permitted to consecrate it in the place where we receive peace. Moreover, reason requires that baptism be celebrated before these things on this Holy Saturday; this will be discussed in its place, namely in the great office of Holy Saturday. Therefore the consecration of chrism too ought not, nor could, be deferred.

## Chapter XVIII. What mystery the order of consecrating chrism contains
In the place where we are accustomed to bless grapes, the oil for the sick is consecrated, and it is concluded with the conclusion: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” etc. For it has no proper office: that is, neither the words of greeting—“The Lord be with you”—at the beginning, nor is it concluded, like the other prayers, “through our Lord.” But the consecration of the oil of chrism, called the principal consecration because at its anointing the principal Spirit is bestowed—that is, the sevenfold Paraclete—has an office of its own. First it is exorcized; then, at “The Lord be with you” and “Lift up your hearts,” [Col. 0141D] its blessing begins and is ended through “our Lord.” It is consecrated in the place where we are accustomed to give one another the peace; and this is the work of divine grace, that peace and concord may reign in us.

The twelve priests who stand around the bishop, as witnesses and hearers of this same mystery, signify the twelve apostles, in whose presence Christ, the supreme pontiff, today drew up the testament and displayed the whole inheritance of salvation and the fruit of his departure—that is, the Spirit, the Paraclete—saying: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16). For chrism contains the sacrament of his grace; and, from the time when he was in some manner purchased and acquired by the price of Christ’s death, he began—something that had not previously occurred—to be given for the remission of sins. Hence the name Paraclete was first applied at that time: for us, condemned in our first parent, the remission of sins is the sole *paraclesis*, that is, consolation; and this could never have been acquired for us except by Christ’s departure, that is, his death.

The booklet of the Roman Order says concerning the consecration of chrism: “Immediately two acolytes shall hold on their right arms the vessels, wrapped in a white silk cloth, so that they may be seen from the middle. Before the vessel comes before the bishop at the altar, one half of it is covered and one half left uncovered.” The vessel containing chrism in some manner signifies Christ’s body, assumed from the Virgin, in which the fullness of the Holy Spirit dwells bodily [Col. 0142B] (Col. 2). Before it passed to the altar of the cross, it was for a time covered and for a time uncovered. In its earliest period it was covered, when he fled into Egypt (Matt. 2) as though he were not King of kings; when he was carried to the Temple (Luke 2) as though he were not almighty; and when he was subject to his parents (ibid.) as though he were not the author of parents. In these and similar matters it was covered, hidden away. It was uncovered after he began to work miracles, to preach at the same time, and to show himself to be God, as when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). In these and other respects it was uncovered.

But after the vessel has been blessed and returns from the altar, it is visibly and openly saluted by the pontiff and the ministers of the altar. This signifies that Christ, after passing from the altar of the cross, gave his bodily presence to those whom he wished to be witnesses of his resurrection [Col. 0142C] (Luke 24). Its being carried for salutation to the others, invisible and covered, signifies that Christ, returning to heaven, became invisible to humankind, as he himself testifies: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16). Yet although we do not see his bodily presence, we salute him daily in veneration.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why penitents are rightly restored to the Church on this day

At every time bishops ought to exercise that embassy for the reconciliation of sins of which the Apostle speaks. After saying, “God was in [Col. 0142D] Christ reconciling the world to himself, and placed in us the word of reconciliation” (2 Cor. 5), he immediately added: “Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (ibid.).

Yet it is especially fitting for such ambassadors on this day solemnly to exercise that embassy: to call back freely into the bosom of their mother those sinners who, having lost baptism through superadded crimes and consequently been sent outside the Church, have become “like a weaned child upon its mother” (Ps. 130), reconciliation having been offered to them; and, by going out publicly and solemnly, to beseech them to receive that reconciliation with willing assent. For on this day Christ, the supreme High Priest, “appeared before the face of God for us” [Col. 0143A] (Heb. 9) in the abundance of mercy. As was said above, he performed the priestly office once, delivering the sacrament of his body and blood; and immediately the priest himself, who was also the victim, was seized, bound, and led to his Passion.

For why was mercy bound, except that the merciful one might loose penitent sinners? Why did Christ die, except for the ungodly? “But,” says the Apostle, “God commends his love toward us, in that, while we were enemies, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5). Although the riches of God’s goodness are never at any time inactive, nevertheless at this season forgiveness of sins is more generously bestowed through pardon, and the reception of those reborn is more abundant through grace. We are enlarged by those renewed; we grow by those who return. Waters wash; tears wash. Hence there is joy over the reception of those called, and gladness over the absolution of penitents.

What sinner’s heart has been so hardened by the cold of crimes that it is not melted by the warmth of compassion when it hears the voice of Christ’s oft-mentioned priest, saying outside the doors of the Church through his rational trumpets: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord”? For, to demonstrate that this is his voice, these words are taken from Psalm 33, whose title reads: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and was borne in his hands, and dismissed him and went away.”

It is very well known in the Holy Scriptures, and has already been stated by us, that David—whose name means “strong of hand” and “beloved”—when fleeing Saul’s persecution came to Achish, here called Abimelech, changed his countenance before him, and “was borne in his hands” [Col. 0143C] (1 Sam. 21), signified the Lord Jesus. Before Abimelech, whose name means “the kingdom of my father”—that is, before the Jews—he changed his countenance, namely the rite of sacrifice, when, after the lamb of the old Passover had been sacrificed, he took bread and wine and was borne in his hands, saying: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). This occurred on this day of remission and grace.

Therefore, when so great a High Priest stands before God the Father, holding bread and wine and inviting all to the banquet of his body and blood, excluding neither righteous person nor sinner, and saying through the mouths of pontiffs: “Come, children, listen to me,” what sinner’s heart, even if made of stone, will not be softened to the lament of repentance? Great is the voice of the one who invites; great and capacious is the bosom that receives. All the gates of the churches stand open, so that you may understand that neither those coming from the south nor those from the north—that is, neither righteous persons nor sinners—ought to be forbidden from approaching the opened fountains of divine mercy.

## CHAPTER XX. On the washing of feet together with its office

That the Lord and God of all washed the feet of his disciples instructs us in two ways: morally and allegorically alike. “If,” he says, “I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, how much more ought you [Col. 0144A] to wash one another’s feet? For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (John 13). How can we, who are dust and ashes, not blush to raise in contempt of those like ourselves our stiff necks and a stature to which no one of us, even by thinking, can add one cubit (Matt. 6; Luke 12), when we have heard that the Maker of the human creature, bending to the ground with knees bent, applied himself to washing his disciples’ feet? By this act, therefore, he set before our pride a powerful example of his humility.

He did this when he was about to die, so that it might cling more closely to the minds of those whom he was naming as his heirs. For sayings and deeds that a father says, commands, speaks, requests, or enjoins at the end when dying are accustomed to adhere more closely to dutiful and loving children. Moreover, by this work of humility he mystically signified something greater, which must not be passed over because the whole office of today’s Mass depends upon it.

For by this he in some manner declared that he had risen from supper—that is, from the banquet of paternal glory—and had laid aside his garments: “for he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2). Girded with our earthly flesh, as it were with a linen cloth—whose material, of course, springs from the earth—he poured out his blood as water into a basin; and from it he daily washes our feet when we receive him for the remission of our sins. For our feet, that is, our actions, must daily be washed, although once washed through baptism, we are wholly clean through faith. [Col. 0144C] “If we say that we have no sin,” and thus refuse to have our feet washed, “we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Although Peter had been washed and was clean, the Lord said: “If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me” (John 13). Parallel to this is what he says elsewhere: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). In accordance with this true sense of the Gospel reading, approved by the Fathers, the reading from the Apostle is rightly prefixed: “When you come together, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper” (1 Cor. 11), etc. There it is shown how we are washed by this sacrament and do not eat and drink judgment upon ourselves: namely, that each one of us should examine himself and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup (ibid.).

For in no other way are we better purified from the defilements of earthly actions than by approaching this table not cherishing our sins, but hating them and fleeing from them with our whole heart. Whenever we stand at the holy altar, we indeed bear Christ’s person and act in his stead, as has already been said in its place. For the Apostle also says: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Whenever we utter his words over the bread and wine—“This is my body; this is the cup of my blood” (1 Cor. 11), etc.—he himself, the beautiful and gracious minister, who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20), having in some manner put aside and folded up the purple robe of his sovereignty, girded with a linen *birrus* [cloak], and wholly ready after the manner of servants, as he is about to offer us the cup of salvation with the bread of life, pours upon it the golden, liquid spice of his divinity. Thus, ministering to each person as we drink joyfully, he pours it into the inner faculties of the soul and purifies those who, occupied with earthly matters, even if they do not wholly tread them underfoot, nevertheless cannot altogether escape being defiled by them in some part, however slightly.

That we might know with how great love and humility he does this, before delivering to us the sacrament of his body and blood he first washed feet, as has already been said, thereby most fittingly commending that comparable purification. Thus such an apostolic reading is rightly placed before the aforementioned Gospel. [Col. 0145B] But because, after he had washed their feet, he took his garments and reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done to you?” (John 13), etc., this offertory fittingly follows: “The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me. I shall not die but live, and shall proclaim the works of the Lord” (Ps. 117).

For after he had completed every ministry of our salvation, he received again the garments and brightness of glory concerning which, praying in the form of a servant, he had said: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17). Reclining again at the right hand of God, he “opened their understanding,” after giving the Holy Spirit, so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24) and know what he had done to them. Then was fulfilled what had long before been prophesied and is now sung with reference to this, as stated. For what is said here, “I shall not die, but live,” is what the Apostle says: “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6)—from that reclining again of his. “I shall proclaim,” he says, “the works of the Lord” (Ps. 117), and, through his interpreter the Holy Spirit whom he gave us, says: “Do you know what I have done to you?” The rest plainly pertains to the same meaning.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why prelates ought to wash the feet of their subjects

Meanwhile, we should carefully observe how truly and wisely he provided for us also in what he did outwardly, when he willed that his apostles and all prelates of the Church should be, as it were, liable for such service: that in solemn custom they ought, following his example, to wash the feet of their subjects. For by this he yearly impresses and repeats what he says in Luke 22: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors; but it shall not be so among you. Rather, let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the leader as the servant.”

For it is greatly contradictory both to rule as the kings of the Gentiles do and, by the obligation and command of the evangelical rule, to wash feet in the manner of servants. Hence one of the great apostles says: “We preach not ourselves, but Jesus Christ; and ourselves your servants through God” (2 Cor. 4). Yet subjects may not use this freedom in their vices. For when persons live viciously, they become beastly, that is, like beasts. And in order that prelates of the Church may rule over beastly persons, they also have the support of the ancient authority by which the first human beings, when created, were commanded to rule over the beasts of the earth (Gen. 1). Therefore, where subjects become like beasts, there the evangelical man recognizes that he ought rightly to rule.

Accordingly, when prelates wash the feet of their subjects on this day, when they reverently offer food and mix drink, the authority to rule disappears, and the whole arrogance of the kings of the Gentiles and of those who, possessing power, desire to be called benefactors is humbled within them. But that after washing his disciples’ feet the Lord opened his mouth and delivered that most splendid discourse in which he so earnestly promises the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit—and that we too, after feet have been washed according to his example, read or hear the same discourse—signifies that the grace of the Holy Spirit is shown only to the washed and clean.

Thus in the Apocalypse, when the angel had said to John: “Nothing defiled, nor anyone doing iniquity and falsehood, shall enter into it” (Rev. 21), there immediately follows: “And he showed me a river of living water, like crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (ibid.). Of this river we also read in Ezekiel: “I saw water coming out from the Temple on the right side, and all to whom this water came were made whole” (Ezek. 47). For not all to whom the visible font of baptism comes are saved; otherwise salvation would not have passed Simon Magus by when he entered the visible waters of baptism (Acts 8). [Col. 0146C] But this was said of that fountain of life and river of peace, with whom lies all authority over salvation, whom the Lord promises in the discourse that follows to give to those purified in the manner stated above.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the mandatum of the poor

The *mandatum* performed among the poor is not wholly of the same rationale. The former is Christ’s; this is the Church’s. The former belongs to the present day; this looks to the history of the preceding Sabbath. For on the Sabbath, when the Lord Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead and whom he raised, Mary took a pound of precious genuine nard ointment, anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped his feet with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John 12).

The Church imitates that woman, anointing the Lord’s feet—that is, refreshing the poor with alms. Although they are the lowliest members, they are nevertheless his members and, like feet, are reckoned the extremities of his great body. She wiped these feet with her hair—that is, she supplied them from the superfluities of her possessions—as the Apostle says: “Let your abundance supply their need” (2 Cor. 8). Therefore this *mandatum* is the Church’s service; and consequently the whole congregation washes the poor’s feet, whereas in the other ceremony, as stated, the prelates alone serve in Christ’s place.

In this the Church beautifully goes before her Lord: before Christ washes the disciples’ feet, the disciples themselves wash the feet of Christ—that is, of the poor—and anoint them with the ointment of almsgiving. Thus the house in which Christ is to be present is prepared, filled with the fragrance of this ointment, at the hour when he himself will wash our feet through our prelates [Col. 0147A]. That this is so is also clear from what we sing on those days: “Then Mary anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”

For this reason, a reasonable custom instituted by those among whom zeal for religious observance is more fervent is observed as follows. First, poor people are brought inside the monastic workshops; and before the brethren render them the charitable service owed in washing their feet, they recline at a meal and are refreshed with sufficient dishes. Surely then Christ is received into Bethany—that is, the house of obedience—and faith rejoices not vainly that it has made supper for him there (Matt. 10; 25). Then the whole congregation rises like that woman of the Gospel—for Mary indeed bore the type of the Church—rises, I say, from the table at which, trusting and tasting moderately, it had broken its fast for so great a guest, who is without doubt received in the poor. It gathers before the poor, bearing a pound of ointment—that is, the intention of almsgiving, sweetly fragrant before Christ—and, prostrating itself before them, serves them in every respect as though serving Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Why during the hours of three days the Church does not maintain her order

When the solemnities of the Masses have been completed—celebrated festively for the reasons stated above and, as has been said, shining like the sun amid clouds of sorrow—deeper silences of that same sorrow immediately follow and increase. For the Church does not maintain her order, which she had already begun to alter and diminish from the nocturnal vigils of the same day. Beginning, therefore, from the nocturnal vigils, we wish briefly to set forth the reasons for so great an alteration or diminution.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the unusual vigils of the three nights

First, it must be said that the vigils of these three nights, which we chant in an unusual order and complete in darkness, are the obsequies of the Lord’s death of three days; and therefore the vigils of Thursday are assigned to mourning for that death, because the evening of the Sabbath and the night itself, “which dawns toward the first day of the week” (Matt. 28), ought not to be devoted to the lament of obsequies. For the Lord, rising in its midst, illuminated that whole night and the preceding evening with the joys of his victory.

From that time it began that, in every solemnity, the night should precede the day and the evening should always shine beforehand with the brightness of the coming day. Therefore, that we may celebrate the obsequies of the Lord’s three-day death over three days, we have also included the night of Thursday, because the Lord had already been sold by the infamous bargain of the most wretched Judas. Thus, what secular canons never customarily do on ordinary days, and monks never do either on ordinary or solemn days, both orders perform: they distribute the vigils among nine lessons, in such an order and form that they seem little or not at all different from the office of the dead. [Col. 0148A]

## CHAPTER XXV. Why we omit beginnings and endings

Moreover, all the hours of the day are conducted so that they have neither beginning nor ending in the customary manner. And rightly so: for our Lord, who is beginning and end, as he himself says, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8), and elsewhere, “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1)—he, I say, who is our head and beginning, Jesus Christ, has in these days been taken away from us, delivered into the hands of the ungodly and cast among the iniquitous. Therefore we rightly cut off the beginnings of the praises of our joy—that is, the regular hours—and conceal their endings in silence; and while chanting psalms we wholly omit the *Gloria Patri*.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why the candles are extinguished

The extinguishing of the candles signifies that, when the Lord was crucified, “darkness came over the land from the sixth hour until the ninth hour” (Matt. 27). Indeed, the extinguishing of the candles signifies what that darkness signified: namely, the blinding of the Jewish people, who, having first killed the prophets and stoned those sent to them, finally killed the very Lord of the prophets (Matt. 21), and were deservedly cast into the darkness of unbelief and abandoned by the light of his countenance.

The many lights which we find burning when we rise for the vigils signify all the saints, who shone with prophetic speech and, like foretelling stars announcing that the sun of righteousness would arise and suffer, were sent at different times to pour the light of divine knowledge into that people. But by extinguishing their bodily life, they brought spiritual blindness upon themselves, and finally deserved to hear that “upon them may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel” (ibid.), etc. Therefore the candles, insofar as they are extinguished one by one after successive psalms, signify the prophets, each of whom, after completing the ministry of his prophecy, was killed by them.

The final candle, likewise extinguished—not larger than the others—signifies the Lord himself, who, reckoned as though one of the prophets, was finally killed [Col. 0148D]. After him no prophet arose among them, and when he was extinguished he left them in the deep darkness of error and unbelief.

## CHAPTER XXVII. What the tropes signify

It is customary in many places, once the lights have been extinguished, to chant mournful tropes in the darkness itself, with the singers leading and the choir responding in plaintive melody, beginning with *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.” They signify the laments of the holy women who, as we read in the Gospel, mourned the Lord, “sitting opposite the tomb” (Matt. 27).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the new fire

When the fire that is extinguished at Matins, as stated, has been lost, during these three days we have recourse to stone: either striking the stone to draw hidden fire from its concealed veins, or setting a transparent crystal stone in the sun’s rays under a clear sky and receiving, by the visible wonder of the ray passing through the crystal orb, its heat into tinder placed beneath it. By this we fittingly portray that God, who “commanded light to shine out of darkness,” may shine in our hearts for the illumination of his glory (2 Cor. 4), through the death of Christ. As was prefigured at Matins, the Jews extinguished him for themselves, and darkness came about.

For when we receive fire from it in this way, the stone signifies Christ, “the stone rejected by the builders, which has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117). Hence the prayer at the blessing of the same fire is as follows: “O God, who through your Son, namely the cornerstone, bestowed the fire of charity upon your faithful, sanctify this new fire, produced from flint, for the benefit of our uses,” etc. Prudentius too, in his hymn sung on Holy Saturday [Note: [Col. 0149D] Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* V.7–8; *Patrologia*, vol. LIX, ed. Migne], after saying:

> Yet you show us  
> to seek lights from a stone-born seed,

immediately added, to show that this is done in commemoration of the fact that the fire of the Holy Spirit proceeds to us from Christ the stone [Note: [Col. 0149D] Ibid., 9–12]:

> Lest humanity should not know that its hope of light  
> is stored in Christ’s solid body—  
> he who wished himself to be called the steadfast rock—  
> from which the race of our little fires has come.

[Col. 0149C] Therefore the stone from which we strike fire signifies Christ, who, struck by the blow of the cross, poured out the Holy Spirit upon us. But if we set a crystal stone before the sun and place tinder beneath it, so that through the crystal the extinguished coals may be rekindled by the sight of Phoebus’ lamp, we should most gladly be reminded that “the man Christ Jesus is mediator between God and men” (1 Tim. 2). Intervening as the middle one between God and extinguished humanity, and drawing near even unto death to our weakness, he pours into us the fire hidden far from us: that is, the most exalted divinity of the Holy Spirit—the fire of the Holy Spirit which, as he himself testifies, he came to cast upon the earth and ardently desired to be kindled (Luke 12).

Nor is it empty religion to go out in solemn procession for the blessing of the new fire. “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach,” says the Apostle (Heb. 13). For as we proceed to that fire, we ought to remember that we must go out to him whom the Jews cast outside their camp and city, so that through the fire of the Holy Spirit we may have eternal life, believing in him whom they extinguished from this present life.

Thereafter, as evening approaches, greater intensifications of sorrow follow. The altars are stripped, washed with wine and water; the bells fall silent; sorrowful silence swallows up all the regular hours except the nocturnal vigils [Col. 0150A]. We know the practice; let us seek its mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why the bells do not ring

The signs of the Church, which we call bells, signify Christ’s holy heralds, as has already been said in its place. Fired by the fire of charity and formed by divine instruction, remaining under the protection of the God of heaven as in a tower of strength (Ps. 60)—indeed, hanging with minds suspended by a certain cord of brotherly love—they are moved all day and all night so that they may not cease to preach the Lord’s name, saying: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no rest” (Isa. 62).

Now it is known that the first such heralds, namely the holy apostles, not only fell silent but “all fled, leaving him” (Matt. 26). Peter also, leader of the others, from whose mouth the proclamation of truth first “went out into all the earth” (Ps. 18)—he who said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16)—suppressed that most clear voice, fell silent, left Christ, fled, and denied him (Matt. 26). Therefore, at the hour when the Lord was handed over, we rightly impose silence on the Church’s signs, and signify Christ alone treading the winepress; alone on the wood of the cross, beating as a drum with his outstretched body; bearing witness to truth in a humble and solitary voice; and, like a wooden mallet suspended and sounding upon a board, inviting the people to the Church. [Col. 0150C]

## CHAPTER XXX. Why the altars are stripped

For those wishing to know why the altar is stripped, the matter becomes clear if they first observe what the altar itself signifies. It signifies Christ, because in the Temple it stands above the whole body of the Church in dignity and honor just as Christ does. If authority is also desired, the Lord’s saying through Moses is at hand: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. 20). Blessed Gregory expounds this as follows: “To make an altar of earth is to place hope in the incarnation of the Mediator. For our offering is then received by God when our humility, that is, whatever it works, has been laid upon this altar, upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation. Therefore we place an offering upon an altar of earth if we establish our acts firmly in faith in the Lord’s incarnation” [Col. 0150D] [Note: [Col. 0150D] St Gregory, *Moralia*, book III, ch. 26, §51, on Job 2; *Patrologia*, vol. LXXV, ed. Migne].

Therefore, when we behold the altar bare, that which the prophet magnificently and mournfully laments ought worthily to resound in our inmost ears and to appear immediately before our inward sight: “Behold, we saw him, and there was no form or beauty in him; and we considered him despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity. Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sins” (Isa. 53). Clearly these words were spoken of his Passion.

For he who was “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44), who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2), was seen especially in his Passion as having neither form nor beauty, his face as though hidden. Earlier, indeed, he went about comely and was magnified by all; for, as he is praised in the Song of Songs, “His belly was ivory, set with sapphires” (Song 5): that is, the weakness of his nature sometimes shone forth in him with heavenly miracles. But now, because “the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all, he rose up before him as a shrub and as a root out of thirsty earth” (Isa. 53), that face and those eyes from which, as Jerome says, something fiery and star-like shone forth—for example, when he drove sellers and buyers out of the Temple (Matt. 21), something an infinite army could not have done—were now despised, struck with slaps, veiled, and spat upon.

His cheeks were plucked, cheeks which, like beds of spices, breathed a pleasing fragrance upon those approaching and expressed to those looking upon them his kindness and gentleness. His hands, so ready to work miracles of divine beneficence that they were deservedly called “rounded, golden, full of hyacinths” (Song 5), were bound with fetters and pierced with nails. Because of such things it was said: “There is no appearance in him, nor form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). Further, this too pertains to the reason for the stripped altar: the same Lord was stripped of his garments. “For when the soldiers had crucified him, they divided his garments among themselves and made four parts, a part for each soldier” (John 19). And they said of the tunic: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it shall be” (ibid.).

Our Noah—whose name means “rest,” namely the Lord Jesus, in whom we find rest for our souls (Matt. 11)—drank such wine from his vineyard, which he planted, that is, from the Jewish people whom he transplanted from Egypt (Ps. 79). He was intoxicated with every bitterness, fell asleep in the sleep of death, and appeared for a time stripped in all things of the glory of his divinity. Therefore, since the altar signifies Christ, it is rightly stripped of its covering and ornament in remembrance of these things.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why they are washed with wine and water

The reason why the altars are washed no less delights one who understands than the matters already stated. They were established to be washed because our Lord, whom the altar signifies, as stated, poured out blood and water from his side when it was pierced by a soldier’s lance (John 19). Therefore they are washed with wine and water. For wine, by the authorizing act of the Lord himself, has been adopted in the sacrament of sacrifice in place of blood.

From his side the supreme maker of our salvation poured out blood and water, the first elements of that salvation. By blood we are redeemed; by water we are washed. This water was the first origin of that baptism by which we are baptized. He received it from no one, but himself became its first author. We say this lest we suppose that he received his baptism from John—something which Roman authority does not allow, opposing the tradition of the Greeks, according to which baptism is celebrated on Epiphany as on the Paschal night. This too was said above where mention was made of Epiphany. But we shall speak more fittingly about the origin of baptism when the treatment, or the order of subjects, requires it in discussing the Lord’s death on the following Parasceve, or in the office of Holy Saturday.

It should be known, however, that those whom we also imitate act more rightly, and their custom comes closer to the Gospel order: they strip the altars today, that is, Thursday, but wash them on the day of Parasceve itself. For on Thursday the Lord indeed began, toward evening, to enter his agony; but on Friday, pierced by the lance, he poured blood and water from his side. Therefore we customarily wash them with singing pertaining to the Passion or with penitential psalmody [Col. 0152B]. The rough little branches with which they are washed signify the scourges that cruelly cut that sacred breast, capable of containing God. For the divinity dwelling within had not excluded the capacity of the flesh to suffer; rather, in him our flesh endured real pains and the genuine welts of rods.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Why we chant the hours in silence
That not only the ringing of bells falls silent, but that our choir also wholly suppresses the regular harmony of the Hours, signifies that Christ’s apostles not only ceased preaching, as they had been accustomed to go about “through the villages, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere” (Luke IX), but also that on this night, after they had sung the hymn and gone out with him to the Mount of Olives [Col. 0152C], fleeing and overwhelmed by sorrow, they all fell silent from their common praise. This profound silence begins after Compline because at about this hour, when he had said to the disciples, “Behold, he who will betray me has drawn near” (Matt. XXVI), they began to be heavy and slept from sorrow; and finally, when the crowd came, and he who was called Judas, and they seized him, “leaving him, they all fled” (ibid.). Nor did any of them thereafter approach him more closely, except that disciple who, as John says, “was known to the high priest, and spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in” (John XVIII). Jerome maintains that this man was John himself.

## Chapter XXXIII. [Col. 0152D] Why We Do Not Say Matins, Like the Hours, in Silence

Here one may ask why, when mournful silence covers the daytime Hours, uncovered melody gives utterance to the night watches or praises. To this it must be said that one time is signified by day, another by night. For by the daytime Hours we signify the presence of the Lord’s Passion, but by the nocturnal watches the earlier times through which the prophets foretold that same future Passion. Since they were not slain in silence, when we bring forth their voices the candles, as was said above, are extinguished; the last of these, extinguished at the Evangelical Canticle, signifies the Lord himself, who was slain while bringing good news.

# Book Six

[Col. 0153]

## Chapter I. [Col. 0153A] On Preparation Day

The sixth day from that on which our Lord entered the city of Jerusalem in glory (Matt. XXI)—glory which envy would soon follow—more clearly confirms what was stated above: namely, that this week of humanity’s restoration corresponds, in the order of its mysteries, to that first week of the world’s creation. For on the sixth day of that week the Creator wondrously made the human being; on the sixth day of this week the same Savior restored him still more wondrously.

This day is called *Parasceve*; and *parasceve* means “preparation.” By this name the Jews living among Greeks called the sixth day before the Sabbath, which is now called by us Friday, because on that day they prepared what would be necessary for the Sabbath, in accordance with the ancient command concerning manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather double” (Exod. XVI), etc. But Jews living among Romans more commonly called it in Latin *coena pura*, “the pure meal.”

Since on the sixth day the human being was made and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—whence he commanded that this day be called Sabbath, that is, “rest”—the Lord was rightly crucified on this same sixth day, accomplishing the mystery of humanity’s restoration. Thus, when he had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished” (John XIX): that is, on the sixth day the entire work which he had undertaken for the renewal of the world was perfected.

## Chapter II. [Col. 0153C] Why Mass Is Not Sung on This Day

The first question concerning this day is why it has no office, or rather—what seems especially remarkable—why it is free from the solemnities of Mass, although the Lord’s Passion, celebrated on this day, is the beginning of sacrifice and the sum of our salvation. For so great an event seems rightly to deserve celebration with the highest solemn joys.

If the annual day of any martyr, on which through the Passion of death that martyr passed to the glory of immortality, is honored with festal joy—and rightly, since “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV)—why is this day deprived of the instruments of solemn joy? On this day the King of all martyrs and saints opened paradise by his death to all the saints, ancient and new [Col. 0153D]; and on this day was paid even for the thief to whom he said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII), that wondrous price by whose weight, as we sing, the captivity of the world was redeemed, the barriers of hell were broken, and the gate of the heavenly kingdom was opened to us.

Why then [Col. 0154A] is it so excluded from public joys that the authority of ecclesiastical order has not assigned to it even the gladness of Mass? Therefore, having consulted the oracle of heavenly grace, something brief must be said concerning this matter.

“We ought indeed,” as the Apostle says, “to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI), and faithfully to exult, setting all other joys aside, in the grace of so great a price given for our redemption. Yet there are certain things which very greatly darken this glory and exultation of ours.

First is the consciousness of our guilt, on account of which the commanding love of the Holy Trinity delivered to death a man of such reverence and dignity—one person with God the Word, a man invoking God and owing nothing to death. As the Apostle says: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). We ought not so to rejoice in the grace of him who delivered him, or in the love of him who died, that we do not also grieve because we were the cause of torments and death to so great a Lord. For not to rejoice is ingratitude; but not to grieve is cruelty.

Let us not be such unthinking praisers of God’s providence or foreknowledge as to suppose that his foreknowledge and his ordination are the same. For these—that is, God’s foreknowledge and ordination—are neither equal nor interchangeable. God foreknew all that he ordained, but he did not preordain or predestine that everything he foreknew should happen. For concerning the human being, when he made him, he foreknew two things: namely, both how he would be deceived through the devil’s fraud, and how God could restore the deceived and ruined man through his omnipotence [Col. 0154C]. These two things, I say, he foreknew; but one of them—the human fall—he permitted to occur, adding to the devil’s deserved condemnation; while the other—humanity’s restoration—he preordained, so that, as the Apostle says to the Ephesians, “the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. III).

Thus Jerome, in his commentary on the same Epistle [Note: [Col. 0153D] St Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, book II, chapter 3, verse 10, *Patrologia*, vol. XXVI, Migne edition], says:

> “If the manifold wisdom of God, now revealed to them through the Church, was unknown to the principalities and powers in heaven—whom we must understand to be holy servants of God—how much more was it unknown to the patriarchs and prophets. Above we showed not that they were ignorant of the mysteries of Christ, but that they did not know them as the apostles [Col. 0154D] did. For the manifold wisdom of God has now been revealed through his Church both to the principalities and powers; this wisdom God had formerly decreed in his mind would come to be, and we now recognize it as perfected from what we see. Therefore Christ’s cross benefited not only us, but also the angels [Col. 0155A] and all the powers in heaven, and disclosed a mystery which they had not previously known. Finally, they marvel at him returning bodily to heaven and say: ‘Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one beautiful in his robe’ (Isa. LXIII). And elsewhere: ‘Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts: he is the King of glory’ (Ps. XXIII).”

Therefore let us not suppose that both the human fall and its restoration belonged to the divine ordination. Rather, God foreknew the fall and permitted it to occur for the devil’s condemnation; but he preordained the restoration for the manifestation of his manifold wisdom.

“And not, as we are slanderously reported, and as some assert that we say, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come’—whose condemnation is just” (Rom. III). For he had said: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V). Certain people, rightly deserving condemnation, distorted this statement so as to assert that he had said that we ought to do evil so that good might come.

Why say these things? Clearly, so that we may observe that God, when he made humanity, much less either willed or in any way said, “Let evils happen so that good may come.” Rather, though God did not will it, forbade it, and threatened death, the human being, consenting to the devil, committed evil (Gen. III); but through God’s ordering, good came. And “where sin abounded,” grace so “abounded still more” that, since no one owed satisfaction for guilt except a human being, and no one could make payment except God, merciful God became human, so that, though he owed nothing to death for himself, by dying he might pay our debt for us [Col. 0155C].

Therefore, as was said above, awareness of our guilt checks our joy, so that we do not exult on this day but walk with bowed head: for our crimes made those wounds; we, rebellious servants, committed the deed for which he, Lord of all, is scourged; what he repaid, we had stolen (Ps. LXVIII).

Moreover, evangelical authority and the Lord’s own sayings teach us to leave joy to the Jews on this day and ourselves to grieve. For after saying, “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me” (John XVI), he added: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (ibid.). He further confirms by a persuasive example that sorrow befits this great event: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (ibid.).

He compares his Church to a woman. Because she loves Christ, whom, begotten of God the Father, she received into our nature, she rightly has sorrow on this day when he dies by death, as though he were passing through birth into eternal life and the glory of immortality; and she cries out “as one with child, crying out in travail” (Rev. XII). And because, after he rose, he was born into his eternal kingdom, “the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John XX). As he himself had said [Col. 0156A], “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI). Thus the preceding comparison of the woman is most beautifully fulfilled: after she has given birth, “she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world.”

## Chapter III. Why the Celebration of Our Redemption Is Transferred from Friday to Sunday

The joy of so great a salvation, so great and necessary a redemption, and so great a price—by whose weight the captivity of the world was redeemed, the barriers of hell were broken, the gates of heaven opened, and the thief, an example to penitents, entered paradise with the Lord [Col. 0156B] (Luke XXIII)—must therefore be deferred, I say, until the third day. On that day so great a victor rose again, announced his victory to us, and showed us in himself what we may hope concerning ourselves. Then, for the redemption of souls accomplished on this day and for the resurrection of bodies established by that light, this twofold gift of an ineffable, immeasurable, and infinite solemnity and dignity must be celebrated with all heart, voice, and strength.

Meanwhile, let sorrow reign on this day. On this day called *tristitia*, “sorrow”—that is, on this sorrowful day—let us grieve in repentance. Let the Friday of the Lord’s Passion pass through our soul; let the nails in his hands and feet fasten our flesh; let his cross suspend our desire. “Let us suffer with him, that we may also reign with him” (Rom. VIII).

Today let us not sacrifice while the victim is taken from our hands. Let not friends sacrifice while enemies slaughter him. “The Lord,” says Moses, “will fight for you, and you shall be silent” (Exod. XIV). Therefore, as long as he alone treads the winepress and his garment is sprinkled with blood (Isa. LXIII); as long as, bound, he is mocked, struck with fists while his face is veiled, slapped, and spat upon; as long as he is ridiculed while clothed in a white garment, and again while receiving a reed in his right hand, a purple garment, a crown of thorns, and the piercing of nails—by which, hanging on the cross, he was made a curse under the law and drank the cup of vinegar; as long as he is glutted with so many reproaches (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXIII; John XIX; Deut. [Col. 0156D] XXI)—so long let us, that is, from morning until the ninth hour, keep continual and profound silence, suited to mourning.

Entering the inward solitude of meditation, and taking off the sandals from our feet with Moses, let us hear him speaking as though from the midst of the bush: “I have indeed seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them” (Exod. III). For now he clings as though in a thorn-bush: nailed fast, crowned with thorns; and the shrub of the cross puts forth, as it were, reddish mulberries with drops of blood, so that, as one writer says:

> Sins are cleansed in sorrow by the blood  
> Which the twisted bush brings forth amid dense torments.

## Chapter IV. [Col. 0157A] Why We Assemble at the Ninth Hour to Adore the Cross

At about the ninth hour (Matt. XXVII; Mark XVII; Luke XXIII), when he was soon to yield up his spirit, he cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). Seeing what had happened, and that he had breathed out his spirit with this cry, the centurion—the precentor of our faith—also cried out, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII; Mark XXIII). Pilate then ordered the body to be given to Joseph at his request; Nicodemus came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, and they took Jesus’ body and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices (Matt. XXVII; Mark XVII; Luke XXIII; John XIX).

Then, I say, it was permitted to these and the other disciples [Col. 0157B] to draw near and express their grief over so great a funeral, as the persecutors gradually withdrew: either because they had departed, sated by the prolonged spectacle of the Lord’s death; or because, seeing the earthquake by which the veil of the Temple was torn, the rocks split, and the tombs opened, they fled in terror (Matt. XXVII). Therefore let us too assemble about the ninth hour, and offer at that supreme funeral not so much an office of Mass as a funeral lamentation, which we perform in this order.

## Chapter V. On the Office or Order for Adoring the Cross

The account of the sacred Passion is preceded by those two animals of which we also sing: “You will be made known in the midst of two animals”; namely, the Law and the Prophets [Col. 0157C], which bear harmonious witness to him, just as Moses and Elijah appeared with him on the mountain at his Transfiguration, speaking with him (Matt. XVII).

For the first reading is from the prophet Hosea: “In their tribulation they shall rise early to me. Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has begun and he will heal us; he will strike and he will cure us; he will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us” (Hos. VI). The second is from Exodus: “Moses said to the children of Israel: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year. On the tenth day of this month let each take a lamb according to your houses and families, and you shall sacrifice it on the fourteenth day of this month in the evening” (Exod. XII), etc.

The first, certainly, is a proclamation of the Resurrection; the second, of the Passion. It is particularly suited to the Passion which is to be read today according to John, especially because this evangelist himself drew from it the testimony: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John XIX). Each reading is followed by its own tract, a chant proper to those who mourn, as was said long above in connection with Septuagesima.

The first tract endeavors to stir us to trembling, as Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. III). For Habakkuk, since he here enters into conflict and wrestling, so to speak, with God in an embrace, received the name of one embracing—that is, wrestling. “For no one,” Jerome says, “has dared with such bold speech to summon God to a disputation concerning justice and to say to him: Why is there such great injustice in human affairs? How long, O Lord, shall I cry and you will not hear?” (Hab. I), etc.

If, I say, this strong and stern wrestler with God, standing upon his watch and fixing his step upon the fortification, when he contemplates Christ on the cross and sees the horns in his hands and there his strength hidden, says, “I was afraid,” and is terrified—what shall we do, far inferior as we are and possessing far less confidence for the day of judgment, when we see manifest in the clouds of heaven that strength which he here fears hidden in the horns of the cross that were in his hands? What will the planks do if the columns tremble? Rightly, therefore, so that this tract may increasingly stir our fear, it is sung in many churches worthy of imitation in such a way that after every verse the first is repeated alternately, now from the beginning, now from the middle [Col. 0158B].

The following tract, “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man” (Ps. CXXIX), according to the title of that psalm, “Unto the end, a psalm of David,” is the voice of that same mighty-handed champion, our defender, fighting in his Passion for our salvation. This prayer is attributed to him for this reason: that we too, following a similar example when in danger, may deserve to be delivered by the Lord through devoted prayer.

## Chapter VI. Why the Passion According to John Is Read on This Day

Although the order of composition itself seems to have required that on this day, after the other evangelists, the Lord’s Passion according to John should be read—for it is established that, after returning from the island of Patmos, where he had been exiled, John wrote his Gospel last, after all the others—there is also this further and greater reason: he was personally present. When the others did not dare to be present, he, because, as he says of himself and as Jerome attests, was known to the high priest (John XVIII), followed more confidently and stood beside the cross.

For, when Jesus’ mother and his mother’s sister were standing beside Jesus’ cross, Jesus, seeing his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing there, said to his mother, “Woman, behold your son”; then he said to the disciple, “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into what was his own (John XIX). A little later he says of himself: “He who saw has borne witness, and his testimony is true” (ibid.).

## Chapter VII. [Col. 0158D] Why the Evangelist Inserted His Own Testimony

The mystery of this great event, for which the holy evangelist so carefully inserted his own testimony and added appropriate examples from Scripture, must not be passed over.
