He had said that the soldiers broke the legs of the thieves; but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.

“These things,” he says, “were done that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says concerning him: ‘You shall not break a bone of it.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They shall look upon him whom they pierced’” (John XIX).

Why did the lamb who was sacrificed not will that a bone of him should be broken? This did not happen by chance, but because he willed and ordered it. For he endured at the hands of those who killed him through their own will or wickedness no torments other than those which he himself willed and arranged [Col. 0159A]. In one respect he spoke of a likeness to us: namely, that like us he was born a mortal and passible human being. In all other respects he spoke of dissimilarity from us, because he was born when and how he willed, and died when and how he willed.

Why, then, did he not will that his legs should be broken, like those of the criminals among whom he was numbered? Clearly, because the breaking of bones nowhere commends any good thing through its likeness.

## Chapter VIII. That Each of the Things the Lord Suffered Mystically Signifies Something

Let us consider what our Lord suffered in his Passion, and we shall find that certain other matters are signified through these things, which spiritually edify us more deeply. For he so ordered not only what he did but also what he chose to suffer that, if you behold the inward things while attending to the outward ones, you will find a corresponding resemblance in both, just as from the shape or distinctive quality of letters or strokes you recognize the same hand of a writer in different places.

## Chapter IX. What the Form of the Cross Signifies

Does not the very form of the cross first signify something mystical? I pass over the fact that no one can deny that it was most fitting for the salvation of humankind to be established upon the wood of the cross: so that life might rise again from the place whence death arose, and he who conquered on a tree might also be conquered on a tree.

And, as one writer says:

> Let no one fail to know that the form of the cross is to be venerated,  
> Which bore the Lord, triumphing in mighty power;  
> From it he gathers the four regions of the squared world.

I shall not pass over the fact that he signified in the form of that very cross on which he hung the first gateways of the salvation he was accomplishing: faith, hope, and love, and the fourth among them, perseverance. For the cross has length, breadth, height, and depth—that is, its point by which, fixed in place, it is set in the earth. Its length extends as far as the arms; its breadth lies in the spreading of those arms; its height rises upward from the arms, where the head is above.

These four dimensions signify the virtues just mentioned [Col. 0159D]: depth, faith, which is laid first in the depths of the heart through the hidden calling of God’s will, like a foundation in a building; length, perseverance; height, hope, which is laid up for us in heaven; and breadth, love. For Augustine says that he understands the Apostle to have spoken of these: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. III). Thus our Savior proclaimed the first approaches to salvation in the form of his instrument of punishment.

## Chapter X. What It Signifies That, Having Tasted the Cup of Vinegar, He Did Not Wish to Drink

By tasting but refusing to drink the vinegar mixed with gall offered to him (Matt. XXVII), he signifies the rejection of his vineyard, namely the Jewish people. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). But that vineyard, which he had expected to produce grapes and which produced wild grapes instead (ibid.), at last mixed for him the bitterness of death. Having tasted it only slightly—that is, for three days—he no longer wishes to drink from the fruit of that vine (Matt. XXVI). “For having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

## Chapter XI. Why He Permitted a Scarlet Cloak To Be Placed around Him

Likewise, does the fact that, when he was mocked, he did not disdain to have a scarlet cloak put around him (Matt. XXVII) not accord with the ministry of love which he was performing for us in his Passion? Scarlet (*coccus*) is a fiery color; in the Lord’s tabernacle it was commanded to be offered, and in the priestly garment to be used twice-dyed (Exod. XXVI). It signifies the twofold love of God and neighbor, through which whatever we offer becomes burning and, as it were, beautifully colored in the sight of God.

For he himself, “because of the exceeding love with which he loved us” (Eph. II), drank the cup of the Passion, as he himself says: “So that the world may know that I love the Father” (John XIV); and, “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). Therefore the scarlet cloak was entirely fitting for this our King, so that by this very garment he might show himself to be the one signified in the Law by the red heifer, whose body was commanded to be burned outside the camp for sin, and whose ashes were to be sprinkled upon the people in water with hyssop [Col. 0160C] (Num. XIX).

## Chapter XII. Why He Received a Reed into His Hand

He did not refuse to receive in his hand from those mocking him a reed or pen, “with which,” as Jerome says, “he might write the sacrilege of the Jews or kill poisonous animals.” [Note: [Col. 0159D] Jerome, *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, book IV, chapter 27, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVI, Migne edition.]

For he had in his hand a rod—that is, his own life under his own power—so that he might lay it down willingly and take it up again. And just as Moses cast down his rod before Pharaoh, and it became a serpent, devoured the rods of the magicians when they too had been turned into serpents, and then became a rod again (Exod. VII), so he himself was now, as it were, about to lay down his life, descending into death, which entered the world through the serpent (Wis. II), in order to consume the serpents of the Egyptians—that is, the deaths of sinners—and to return again into the rod, that is, into his former power.

## Chapter XIII. Why He Wore a Crown of Thorns

By the crown of thorns he visibly signifies what the prophet foretold concerning him: “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. LIII). For thorns signify sins, which prick and tear the soul. They were also given to the human being because of sin, when the Lord said to Adam: “When you cultivate [Col. 0161A] the ground, it shall not yield its fruits to you, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III).

All the other things he suffered and by which he was mocked contain both mysteries and moral instruction. For when his face is veiled and he is then struck with fists, that veil signifies the covering spread over the hearts of the Jews, so that they do not deserve to see him whom even now they strike with insults and buffet with curses in their synagogues.

But in all these things he provides us with a most powerful example of humility. Who would not be ashamed to raise the neck and arm himself with a fat neck (Job XV), when God and Lord of all has been struck with fists for us by those mocking him? For we might disdain to imitate the humility of a human being; yet, with God humbled beneath so many insults, let us be ashamed to be proud.

## Chapter XIV. Why He Did Not Wish His Legs To Be Broken

Therefore, he who endured the other things with purpose did not, without reason, refuse to have his legs broken; rather, it was by his ordering that he refused it. For bones, which everywhere in Scripture are mystically understood as virtues, would proclaim no mystery to us in being broken. On the contrary, his legs, preserved unbroken, mystically signify for us that all his ways are straight and inviolable (Ps. CXVIII).

For his legs signify his ways; hence the Song says: “His legs are marble columns, founded upon bases of gold” (Song V): that is, his beautiful paths, established in uprightness upon the wisdom of divinity. What, then, did he choose to happen instead of the avoided breaking of his legs?

## Chapter XV. Why He Poured Blood and Water from His Side

“But one of the soldiers,” says the evangelist, “opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX). Why, then, did he choose that this should happen? Clearly, so that he might pour out upon us that water together with his blood, concerning which, when commending it, he said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III).

Indeed, the sacrament of this water took its beginning from this miracle. Therefore the Lord, baptized in his Passion (Luke XII), when already dead sent forth to us this participation in his saving death. It is neither new nor strange that we say that he was baptized in his Passion. When the mother of the sons of Zebedee made her request, saying, “Teacher, say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (Matt. XX), he replied: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (ibid.). When they answered, “We can,” he said, “You shall drink my cup, and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized” (ibid.), etc.

By the name of cup or baptism he meant to designate the Passion of martyrdom, by which it befitted both him and them to be perfected. Hence elsewhere he says of his Passion: “But I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke XII). In Greek, however, *baptismus* means in Latin *ablutio*, “washing” [Col. 0162A].

What uncleanness, then, did the Lord have that he should be washed by the baptism of the Passion? Clearly, our mortality and passibility, on account of which he appeared filthy and contemptible to human beings, as we read in Zechariah: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments. And the angel said to those standing before him: Remove the filthy garments from him” (Zech. III).

Jerome says: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments, he who had committed no sin but was made sin for us, and himself bore our infirmities” (Isa. LIII; 2 Cor. V). And we read in the Apostle: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. III). In the twenty-first psalm he says: “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.” And in the sixty-eighth: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my sins are not hidden from you.” “All these,” he says, “are called filthy garments, and are removed from him when by his death he blots out our sins.”

Therefore, when “we see the Lord Jesus crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II), and washed from the sins which he himself had borne, we rightly understand that he was baptized by his own baptism in his death, and that, so as to transmit that same baptism to us, he poured forth blood and water from his side when already dead. It has been said elsewhere that the baptism by which he was baptized by John did not belong to the same power.

## Chapter XVI. Why Neither Blood Alone nor Water Alone Came from His Side, and Why Water Was Joined to Blood

Neither blood alone nor water alone flowed from the Savior’s side because the divine order of our salvation required both. By blood we are redeemed; by water we are washed. Nor were we redeemed merely so that he might possess us as we were before. Thus the Apostle says: “God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification in Christ Jesus” (1 Thess. IV). And elsewhere, after recalling their former sins: “And such were you,” he says, “but you were washed; but you were sanctified” (1 Cor. VI), etc.

Therefore, so that there might be a means by which we could be washed from sins, water—which could wash only bodily filth—was joined to blood, the price of our redemption. From this union it received the power and authority to cooperate worthily with the Holy Spirit in cleansing the invisible filth of sins [Col. 0162D].

It received this through its union with living and precious blood, so that by a true analogy it may be compared with the Red Sea, through which the saved people passed, while Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. XIV). For it conveys those fleeing the Egypt of this world, cleansed, into the true land of promise; and it wholly swallows the pursuing devil together with his former works and pomps.

Therefore, as was said above, it was far more fitting that the soldier’s spear should open the Lord’s side than that his legs should be broken. It was more fitting, I say, and more becoming for so great an artificer of salvation; and it greatly contributed to the beauty [Col. 0163A] of the work that, when dead, he should draw from his side that from which the Church would be born—he who drew a rib from sleeping Adam, from which Eve might be formed (Gen. II). What could be more beautiful, elegant, or sweet than this analogy? For that first Adam fell asleep; this second Adam, as was said, died in order to rise again. The Lord caused sleep to fall upon the former; the Father gave the cup of the Passion to the latter.

“Go forth, therefore, and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy” (Song III). Go forth, I say, from those darknesses “which came over the earth from the sixth hour until the ninth hour” (Matt. XXVII); indeed, from those darknesses signified by them, which even now cover [Col. 0163B] the face of the hearts of the Jews. Go forth from these darknesses and behold in attentive contemplation him “who called you into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. II): the great King, the peaceful King, in his diadem of thorns, the ornament of love and great compassion, with which his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him on this day of his betrothal. On that day, as was said, he brought forth for his bride, the Church, then to be born, the first elements in the joy of his heart.

## Chapter XVII. Why Solemn Prayers Are Made on This Day for the State of the Church
For the state of the holy Church, faithful prayer should indeed be made at all times; but on this day especially the solemn prayers for her, to be pronounced by the priest according to the orders and distinctions of ranks or dignities [Col. 0163C], have reasonably been instituted. For on this day our Savior prayed for all, and became the common sacrifice for all; and, as he drew near to his Passion—or rather, as he already stood almost at the altar of the cross—when praying for his disciples, he said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John XVII). Clearly, this was that Angel of great counsel (Isa. IX), of whom we read in the Apocalypse: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand” (Apoc. VIII). Today, standing beside the altar of the temple—that is, in the sight of the Church—he lifted up before God the golden censer of his immaculate body, hanging upon [Col. 0163D] the cross; and for us he kindled the worthy incense of prayer with “a loud cry and many tears,” as the Apostle says (Heb. V). Rightly, therefore, we too offer solemn prayers with him, for ourselves and for all, according to what is added there: “And much incense was given to him” (Apoc. VIII), etc.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why we do not bend the knee for the Jews

Here it should be observed that, although in each of the prayers we bend the knee at the deacon’s proclamation, we do not do so only in that which is said for the Jews. This is because, until the fullness of the Gentiles shall enter in, the blindness which has happened to Israel (Rom. XI) cannot be driven away or expelled by the hand of any prayer. Thus, professing that we neither ought, nor wish, nor are able to resist the divine judgments [Col. 0164A], we indicate that at present earnest attention ought not to be directed toward them, by not bending the knee; yet in some fashion we pray even for them, because it will come to pass that he will draw them also to himself—he who was therefore lifted up upon the cross, that he might draw all things to himself (John XII).

## CHAPTER XIX. Why those who carry the cross sing “My people,” and the other antiphons; and why, after each, *Hagios* is answered in Greek and “Holy God” in Latin

These three antiphons—“My people,” “Because I led you out,” and “What more ought I to have done?”—which are sung while the cross is being carried, differing little or not at all in meaning and alike also in words and melody, signify the threefold writing of the title and accord with its sense [Col. 0164B], which was written over the Lord’s head in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John XIX).

For, because “Jesus of Nazareth” was written there, at the end of each antiphon is added, “to thy Savior,” in accordance with the interpretation of that name. And because he truly is “King of the Jews,” although they denied this of him and wished even to alter the title, saying, “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said, I am King of the Jews’” (ibid.), this is affirmed in those same antiphons from his deeds, by setting forth the true and ancient office of a king: namely, that he led them out of the land of Egypt, guided them through the wilderness for forty years, fed them with manna, and brought them into a very good land.

And because this title, “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,” [Col. 0164C] was, as has been said, written threefold—in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—after each antiphon, to which “to thy Savior” is appended at the end, that which in the title is *Jesus* is answered in Greek and Latin by *Hagios, hagios*—“Holy, holy”—that which in the same title is *Nazarenus* in Hebrew. But no answer is made in Hebrew, because that people still denies its king and, with averted heart, curses and detests that title.

Thus the cross is borne while the aforementioned antiphons are sung, and it is faithfully answered in Greek and Latin, because the crucified Lord, withdrawing himself from the Jews who deny him, advances toward the confession of the Gentiles. The apostles draw near and sing—that is, with all their strength they preach the reproach of the cross (I Cor. I), of which [Col. 0164D] they are not ashamed (Rom. I)—and at times endure much and are wearied beneath the heavy burden of persecutions. This too is fittingly signified by the fact that the bearers of the same cross now proceed and now halt as though weary.

## CHAPTER XX. What it signifies that the cross, hitherto covered, is now uncovered

The veil by which this same cross was hitherto covered, and which is removed when it is said, “Behold the wood of the cross,” signifies that veil beneath which the Lord hid himself from the Jews, and which is laid over their hearts. But it is revealed to us because, as the Apostle says, it is removed in Christ (II Cor. III).

For he showed himself to us in the prophets and opened the meaning, so that we might understand [Col. 0165A] the prophets—not as Moses placed a veil over his face (Exod. XXXIV), while “the children of Israel could not gaze upon his face” (II Cor. III)—but he reveals his face to us, “so that, beholding his glory, we may be transformed into the same image from the brightness of the Law into the brightness of the Gospel, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (ibid.).

This revelation was first signified by the fact that, when he gave up the spirit, “the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom” (Matt. XXVII). From that time all the mysteries of the Law lay open, and the secrets of the Jews passed over to the faith of the Gentiles. In the Gospel according to the Hebrews, Jerome says, we read that the lintel of the temple, of immeasurable size, was broken and split apart. Moreover, Josephus reports that the angelic powers, [Col. 0165B] formerly the rulers of the temple, then cried out together: “Let us depart from these dwelling places.”

And in this also—that “the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened” (ibid.)—there is, according to the letter, the greatness of the signs: heaven, earth, and all things tremble at the crucified Lord. Mystically, however, it signifies the trembling of believers: having abandoned their former errors and had the hardness of their hearts softened, they who had formerly been like the tombs of the dead afterward came to know their Creator. Hence also in the psalm: “You have moved the earth, O Lord, and troubled it” (Ps. LIX). And again: “The earth was moved and trembled” (Ps. XVII).

## CHAPTER XXI. Again, concerning the cross

[Col. 0165C] Therefore this revelation of the cross to be adored, like that rending of the temple veil, mystically signifies that the mysteries of the Scriptures, formerly closed, are opened to those who believe in the Crucified One. For through the Passion or cross of Christ, once believed, we now understand the sacraments of the Law and the secrets of the prophets: for example, why Pharaoh or Egypt, though struck by ten plagues, did not yield, yet, conquered by the blood of the lamb alone, dismissed the children of Israel; and who he is in the prophets “whose government was made upon his shoulder” (Isa. LV); or who “was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. IX). These things and the rest, formerly hidden, are now opened to those who receive the cross of Christ.

Thus it has come about [Col. 0165D] that we can now drink from the waters of Marah, which, as we read in Exodus, the people could not drink until Moses cried to the Lord and “the Lord showed him a piece of wood; and when he cast it into the waters, they were changed into sweetness” (Exod. XV). For the waters of Marah signify the Law, which has no small bitterness in itself when it says, “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Deut. XIX), and the like. But it is made sweet by the wood when, setting before yourself the example of the Lord’s Passion, you offer the other cheek also to him who has struck you on the cheek (Matt. V), etc.

Therefore, in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ we adore timely glory, as Paul says; salvation won; life restored; perfect salvation; perpetual deliverance. We adore the cross: the defense of faith, the support of hope [Col. 0166A], the throne of charity, the title of mercy, the proof of godliness, the vehicle of grace, the standard of peace. We adore the cross, which cut down pride, crushed envy, corrected guilt, and destroyed punishment. The cross of Christ is the gate of heaven, the key of paradise, the overthrow of the devil, the raising up of humankind, the consolation of our captivity, the price of freedom. The cross is the expectation of the patriarchs, the promise of the prophets, the triumph of kings, the dignity of priests. The cross rebukes tyrants, bends the powerful, raises up the afflicted, and ennobles the poor. The cross is the destruction of darkness, the infusion of light, the escape from death, the vessel of life, the command of salvation. Whatever progress we make toward God, whatever we gain, whatever we hope for, is the fruit of the cross to be adored. Through the cross Christ drew all things to himself (John XII). It is the kingdom [Col. 0166B] of the Father, the scepter of the Son, the seal of the Holy Spirit, the testimony of the whole Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXII. Why the Lord’s body is reserved on the preceding day for the present day

Reason would seem to require that, having consecrated the Lord’s body on this day and reserved it from then until Saturday, we should remain, throughout that whole Saturday, hushed in unbroken silence, abstaining until the first day of the week from all daytime psalmody and every ministry of the holy altar. For thus we might be thought to approach the reality more closely, because on this day our Lord was sacrificed, rested in the tomb on Saturday, and his disciples spent the whole following night in sorrow, until the women returned from the tomb at dawn and, reporting what they had heard and seen [Col. 0166C], gradually began to breathe again and revive into joy.

In this way we would seem more truly to observe the Lord’s death of three days and to preserve more properly that analogy from the ancient history, in which it was said concerning manna, given to the children of Israel as a figure of the Lord’s body: “On the sixth day let them gather what they are to bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather on each of the other days, because it will not be found on the seventh day” (Exod. XVI).

But now, conversely, it is found among us on the seventh day, because after noon we solemnly consecrate the body amid the voice of exultation and praise. On this sixth day, however, it is in a manner not found, because it is not consecrated, but was brought in and reserved the day before—that is, on Thursday—for us to receive today. Why this is done deserves attentive consideration, for it is not without reason.

[Col. 0166D] Our Lord was not sacrificed only then, or first then, when he was suspended on the cross by the Jews; but also on the day before he suffered, when, taking bread and the cup, he blessed them and gave them to his disciples, saying: “This is my body; this is the cup of my blood” (Matt. XXVI). He was sacrificed by his own hands; by his own hands he himself entrusted to us the lamb, that it might be continually sacrificed.

From that sacrifice, the first day of the week is the third day; but from this sacrifice, Saturday itself is likewise the third day. It is clear, however, that, as was said above, the powerful reason which draws the night or evening of Saturday away from the silence or sorrow required by the repose of the tomb is that, during part of that same night, the Lord rose [Col. 0167A] and the true sun illuminated all of it with the radiance of incomparable joy.

Therefore the three days of the Lord’s death, which could not be completed when reckoned from his slaughter by the Jews, are fittingly and reasonably transferred to this reckoning, according to which he was sacrificed by his own hands. A very great proof of this is that on these three nights we sing shortened vigils with the lights extinguished, in likeness of the darkness which came over the earth while the Lord suffered—signifying, as was said above, the blindness which from that time happened to Israel (Rom. XI). Thus the new sacrifice, which preceded the Lord’s death on the previous day through his own hands, solemnly coincides likewise with the previous day of his resurrection, namely the evening of the most holy Saturday.

Accordingly, just as on this day, which is Friday, on which Christ, the saving victim, is slain by his enemies, the glory of sacrifice and that heavenly manna are rightly, as it were, buried by us because they are not found today (Exod. XVI), so on Thursday we prepared and brought in what we receive on this day; and it was double what we were accustomed to gather on each of the other days (ibid.) [Col. 0167B].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the fact that two priests carry the Lord’s body from the place in which it was reserved the preceding day, and that only the Lord’s Prayer is said over it

At last, after the cross has been saluted, two priests carry to the altar the Lord’s body which was reserved the preceding day; and the officiating priest, after the prayer has been said, begins thus: “Let us pray, instructed by saving commands.”

[Col. 0167C] It is clear that this place is in the Canon, where, after the chalice with the Lord’s body has been elevated, it is said, “Through all ages of ages,” and, after the Lord’s Prayer follows, the chalice is covered again. By this there is represented to us, from the Lord’s Passion, the fact that his body, taken down from the cross, was buried. But this has already been discussed in the second little book of this work, where the other things which were to be said in the Canon according to the order of the Lord’s Passion were also noted.

Now it must be said that the two priests who carry the Lord’s body to the altar signify Joseph the righteous man of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who carried away for burial the body of Jesus, requested and granted to them by Pilate (John XIX). We, however, communicate in silence [Col. 0167D]; but the blood which we receive cries to God from our mouth, as it is written: “Behold, the voice of the blood of your brother Abel cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). For we—that is, the Church—are the earth which opens its mouth and faithfully drinks the blood of Abel (ibid.), that is, of Christ, which Cain—that is, the Jewish people—cruelly poured out.

But he was cursed upon that same earth and became a wanderer and fugitive upon it (ibid.), as it is written in the psalm: “Scatter them in your power” (Ps. LVIII). Cursed, I say, by that curse which he freely invoked upon himself and his descendants, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

## CHAPTER XXIV. [Col. 0168A] The beginning concerning Holy Saturday

On Saturday, after the profound night of sorrow, it grows light for us after noon into the supreme brightness of joy, as the evening of that night approaches in which Christ, the true sun, rose victorious from the lower world. Every Christian soul, watchfully attentive and rejoicing beforehand, applauds itself and says: “And night shall be illuminated as day, and night shall be illumination amid my delights” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

Therefore, all of us who belong to the priestly or levitical order rightly sound the saving trumpet for the victory of so great a king, according to that saying in the psalm: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast” (Ps. LXXX). For what day is more notable than this night? What solemnity more excellent than this victory? What other new moon is ours except that in which, on this night, the new Church is reborn in Christ through baptism? Rightly therefore the angelic trumpet of heaven now exults, resounds with the saving trumpet; the earth rejoices, Mother Church is glad, and the entire court of the divine name echoes with the mighty voices of the peoples [Col. 0168B].

## CHAPTER XXV. Why this Saturday is called holy

This Saturday has surpassed the common meaning of its name, namely *vigil*—the attentive expectation or preparation for any great festival to be received with devotion. It is called Holy Saturday, both for many other reasons and especially because the new Church is sanctified in the sacred font of baptism in preparation to receive so great a brightness of light [Col. 0168C].

For on this day, according to the true and evangelical tradition of the Fathers, it is customary for the fonts to be blessed and for the vessels of believers, both body and soul, prepared through faith, to be sanctified by new regeneration. Souls that had been dead are prepared for victorious life, death having been conquered (Hos. XIII; I Cor. XV), as it returns from battle, so that in the great court of King Christ there may be no native-born servant or purchased slave who is not clothed, for the entry of the triumphant Lord, in the silk of grace and the gold of chastity. But we shall speak of this in its proper place below.

## CHAPTER XXVI. For how many, or for what, reasons the paschal solemnity shines forth

Now, before discussing the order or rationale of the office, it must be said for how many, or for what, reasons the solemnity of Easter is held so illustrious and celebrated. For many consider in it only this: that the Lord rose “on the first day of the week” (Matt. XXVIII), whence the day is called the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection. This is indeed a great ground for solemnity and joy of heart: because, while we believe that there is a resurrection of the dead by his rising, we rightly rejoice in hope that we too shall rise.

Yet in contemplating this solemnity, the eye of our memory must never pass over that joy concerning the redemption of our souls which, as has been said above, was deferred to this day from Friday, on which our Savior accomplished it through his cross and blood [Col. 0169A]. For these are the paschal feasts in which that true lamb is slain and the doorposts are consecrated by its blood. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed (I Cor. V): by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising he restored life.

There are two great and innumerable causes of this paschal feast: the redemption of souls, won on the day of Preparation by Christ’s death; and the resurrection of bodies, given and confirmed on the first day of the week when Christ rose (I Cor. XV). A third necessary solemnity, that of baptism, is added to these, conferring upon us all their benefit and fruit; and, because it took its beginning and the whole rationale of its sacrament from them, it is rightly added amid these same paschal joys [Col. 0169B].

Therefore for three reasons this night, illuminated as day, shone in our delights. O truly festal day, truly blessed night: nobility of the year, ornament of the month, strength of days, splendor of hours—the night in which hell was desolated and paradise opened. This night is the departure of death and the return of life: the light of grace, the splendor of glory, the cup of sweetness, the river of delights, the flood of peace, the gaining of strength, the praise of the divine counsel. On this night the tax-collector ceased, tribute rested, captives were restored, the weary took breath, the rod of persecutors was broken, and the yoke of rulers rotted away. By the beauty of this night paradise flowered anew, heaven was clothed in purple, angels became radiant, and human beings were made glad.

This night is called Passover. *Pascha* in Hebrew is called in Latin *transitus*, “passing over.” Who, then, passed over? From where and to where did he pass? Christ the Lord passed from this world to the Father, from death to life, from lowliness to glory, from servitude to kingship, from insults to honor, from the waves of the age to the harbor of heaven, from the midst of thieves to the Father’s seat [Col. 0169C].

And we too have passed over. “For Christ is our Passover”: Christ sacrificed is our passage. To where, then, have we passed? From how great a distance? We have passed from a double destruction to a double salvation of body and soul; from the devil to God, from the enemy to the Father, from the tyrant who is neither God nor human to our King, who is God and human. We have passed, I say, from darkness to light, from weariness to rest, from mourning to song [Col. 0169D], from nakedness to clothing, from poverty to abundance, from guilt to grace, from punishment to glory.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Why Easter is not celebrated before the first full moon occurring after the vernal equinox

Every sex ought to recognize so joyful a solemnity, so wonderful a brightness of true light, so splendid a height of grace; every age ought to hold it in mind; every condition ought to receive it. For not to know it belongs to misery; not to possess it, to captivity; not to need it, to condemnation. Thus the pagan is miserable because he does not know it; the Jew is captive because he does not possess it; the heretic is condemned because he does not love it.

That this good, therefore, may delight the wisdom of elders, gladden the childhood of the young, and build up the progress of those in between [Col. 0170A], divine authority lends support, the nature of the elements concurs, and ecclesiastical practice likewise strives toward it. For it belongs to divine authority, and was handed down from the ancient law of Moses, that it should not be celebrated before the full moon of the first month (Exod. XII), namely, where the first full moon occurs after the vernal equinox.

This greatly delights the minds of the wise, because it contains within itself a great and beautiful mystery. For the moon, which possesses no light of its own but borrows it from the sun, signifies the holy Church, which has not from itself but has received from Christ, the true sun, the grace of inward light. The equinox, moreover, after which day now exceeds night and, cutting away the hours of night, diminishes it and adds to itself, signifies that after the night of ignorance the day of the knowledge of God has begun to extend in long serenity, and that the zeal and labor of those who know God’s truth diminish the multitude of the ignorant [Col. 0170B].

Therefore, when the paschal lamb is sacrificed and the people of God, Pharaoh and his army having been drowned, are freed from servitude, there is a full moon (Exod. XIV), and night is overcome by victorious day. For while Christ, the Lamb of God, suffers, the fullness of grace illuminates the holy Church, so that, like the moon with unveiled face, she may contemplate the glory of the true sun and, now fit and now pleasing, prepare to enter his bridal chambers. Thus day overcomes night, as it is written: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V).

The elements also gladden us in this, and nourish the infancy of our understanding: after the harshness of winter, the gentle air breathes forth springtime mildness [Col. 0170C]; the earth, lately aged by barren cold, grows young with green grass; flowers and crops bloom again with renewed fruit; and the birds of heaven, sad frost having been cleared away, sing sweetly. For amid the joys which we celebrate while seeing these things, we ought to be reminded by an appropriate likeness from the visible things themselves how greatly we have advanced in invisible things through Christ’s resurrection: namely, because, once the frost of unbelief and the showers of vices have been driven away, the world has flowered anew in the beauty of faith and virtues. Hence it is said also in the Song of Songs: “For now the winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared, flowering vineyards have given their fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Cant. II). Thus the observed character of the season or of the elements somewhat enlarges the joys of devout contemplation [Col. 0170D].

Furthermore, with respect to recognizing the grace of this solemnity, ecclesiastical practice aids even the carnal-minded. For because they are unable to open the eyes of the mind to behold spiritual things unless they are aroused by a stronger force of bodily occurrences, causes have been sought by whose impulse they might be powerfully stirred and struck. The forty-day fast, which, as has elsewhere been said, is offered to God as a tithe of days, has been arranged and fixed so that it may in no way end before this most sacred night; and then a continuous number of fifty days follows, during which fasts are wholly relaxed.

Thus, while the body is worn down by abstinence [Col. 0171A] and relaxation is hoped for from no source except this paschal night, this blessed night is thereby embraced and received with expectation even by the carnal-minded; and before it comes, all the intervening days of Lent are almost daily counted diligently like the daily stages of a longed-for journey. Therefore, as has been said, this sacred solemnity is sweet to all, dear to all, desirable to all: like light to those walking in darkness, like a fountain of water springing from a rock to the thirsty, like “the tabernacle which God pitched” to those on pilgrimage (Heb. VIII). But let us now take up the office itself, that at last we may loosen our joyful mouths after sorrowful silence.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the paschal candle

[Col. 0171B] A distinctive ornament of this great solemnity is the candle, which Zosimus, the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church, instituted to be blessed throughout the churches. From its sweetly sounding blessing begin the praises of Christ’s holy resurrection. It signifies our same Lord rising again and brightening the sorrow of his disciples—indeed, of the whole world—with the brightness of fitting joy. This is truly fitting, and the force of the symbolism itself requires it: just as on the preceding nights extinguished lights made the face of the Church sorrowful, so on this same night the illuminated candle makes it glad with the radiance of its dancing, unceasing flame.

## CHAPTER XXIX. What the candle signifies

[Col. 0171C] It has been stated above that the candles which were extinguished signify the deaths of the prophets and righteous persons who were slain from the blood of righteous Abel to Christ; and that the candle which is extinguished at the Gospel, no larger than the others, signifies the Lord himself, who, while preaching the Gospel, was killed and reckoned as one of the prophets. It is clear, however, that God raised up him who was killed in contempt and humility, and “exalted him as Prince and Savior, to give repentance for the remission of sins” (Acts V).

Therefore the order of symbolism proceeds fittingly when the conspicuous size of the candle signifies the bright greatness of the risen one. The candle especially resembles Christ because the little mother bee, which produces the substance of wax [Col. 0171D], conceives and gives birth without intercourse. The Virgin Mary, Mother of God, is rightly compared to her: she, inviolate, brought forth for us God in flesh, as honey in wax. Therefore, since it fittingly bears the likeness of Christ’s humanity, the year is consequently inscribed upon it from the Incarnation of the same Lord Christ. And because he was crucified, the figure of the cross is likewise suitably engraved upon it.

Moreover, the blessing of the same candle confirms what has been said. First, when the one blessing it prays in the Preface: “May he who has deigned to gather me, not by my merits, into the number of Levites, command me, by pouring in the grace of his light, to complete the praise of this candle.” For the praise of the candle could in no way be mentioned unless it signified Christ the Son, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0172A], is the one and only God to be praised—especially since that praise of the candle is the delightful and most sweet proclamation of this night, and sounds forth, like a most clear trumpet, the grace and victory of the risen one by comparing the old things with the new.

“But now,” it says, “we know the praises of this pillar, which blazing fire kindles in honor of the Lord; though divided into parts, it nevertheless knows no loss of its borrowed light.” From these two verses also the often-mentioned significance of the candle shines forth more and more clearly. For when it says, “We know the praises of this pillar,” it plainly indicates to us that by this precious lamp we should understand the same thing which was prefigured by that pillar which went before the camp of the children of Israel as they departed Egypt through the Red Sea [Col. 0172B] (Exod. XIII, XIV).

That pillar of cloud signified the cloud, well known to us, of Christ’s humanity, in which the wisdom of God properly placed its throne, as wisdom itself says: “My throne is in the pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. XXIV). For now that pillar of cloud goes before its people, freed from the devil’s slavery and crossing the Red Sea of baptism, as guide of the way, in order to bring them into the true land of promise, the land of the living, which, as Moses says, “the Lord our God watches day and night” (Deut. XI): now showering it with heavenly teachings, and thus truly a pillar of cloud; now setting it aflame with the fire of his Spirit, and thus truly a pillar of fire. We therefore now know the mysteries of this true pillar.

But when it adds concerning the nature of fire, saying, “Though divided into parts, it nevertheless knows no loss of its borrowed light” [Col. 0172C], this likewise serves the same argument. For we see many lights kindled from one, and yet that one light does not thereby diminish itself. Did he wish to teach us a fact so familiar to everyone, especially in such a place, for any reason other than its own significance? For it would have been absurd to insert this among such great praises without a mystery.

Therefore, while blazing fire kindles the waxen pillar and is praised in this way for the abundance natural to it, another most beautiful and devout spectacle is presented to the eyes of our minds. In short, it is suggested that the fiery power of divinity, breathing from above, restored to life the substance of Christ’s humanity, lying extinguished in the tomb; and, like truly blazing fire, the glory of the blessed resurrection happily shone forth for us on this night unto everlasting joy [Col. 0172D].

Likewise, all the little candles in the Church ought to be lighted from the flame of the consecrated candle. When this is done, the following fittingly comes to mind: on the day on which our Lord rose, when evening had come, he stood in the midst of his disciples, showed them his hands and side, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). For there began to be given to human beings that fire which is clearly signified by this visible fire, which he himself came to cast upon the earth and greatly desired to be kindled (Luke XII).

## CHAPTER XXX. [Col. 0173A] Why the deacon blesses the candle

Here the novelty of the rite itself prompts the question why the deacon pronounces over the candle a blessing of such great matter and dignity while the priest, or even the bishop, is present and clothed in sacred vestments. The reason is readily apparent to those who inquire.

For it is clear that the good news of Christ’s holy resurrection was proclaimed to the holy apostles as they wept and mourned by the lesser sex—that is, by women (Luke XXIII). This was done by so rational a disposition of divinity that it ought by every right to have its memorial among those things which are performed symbolically in the Church. For since a woman, sent by the devil, offered death to a man, fittingly the same sex, sent by the Christ restored to life [Col. 0173B], proclaimed life to the male sex. Therefore the minister of the lower rank begins the joy of our great solemnity with the candle’s blessing, so sweet, beautiful, and honeyed, because through the lower sex the miracle of the Lord’s resurrection, so joyful and devout, was announced not to just any men, but to the apostles themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why incense is also carried for blessing the candle

When the deacon approaches with the other assisting ministers to bless it, pieces of incense are also carried, so that, in presenting them, he may affix them to the little cross engraved upon the candle. This too relates to the aforementioned reason. For the women who sought the Lord dead and deserved to see him alive carried spices, as the Evangelist relates: “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark XVI) [Col. 0173C].

## CHAPTER XXXII. Why it is called, or is, an evening sacrifice

Therefore, while offering incense, he says: “In the grace of this night, then, receive, holy Father, this evening sacrifice of incense.” It is clear that the sacrifice is evening sacrifice, and that the entire office of the present day belongs to the evening of Saturday, “which dawns toward the first day of the week” (Matt. XXVIII).

Why, however, this most holy solemnity has both a morning and an evening sacrifice may be gathered from the reasons stated above. For it was said above that the present solemnity shines for two reasons: the redemption of souls, won on the day of Preparation by Christ’s death, and the resurrection of the dead, confirmed on the first day of the week by his rising. It is clear that the same author of our resurrection, when evening was drawing near, bowed his head and gave up the spirit (John XIX). At the hour when the first Adam, sought by the Lord crying and saying, “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. III), was found disobedient, this second Adam, having completed his Passion, was found obedient, crying and saying, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII).

Therefore we offer the morning sacrifice because this Morning Star, the firstborn of the resurrection, by rising opened for us the day of eternity [Col. 0174A]. We first offer the evening sacrifice also because, as has been said, when evening drew near he gave up the spirit and by his death made that evening memorable; but its celebration was deferred, as has been said, and fittingly transferred to this time.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On baptism
The law of victory among men is equitable: whoever had been conquered before the war must, after the war, yield to the right and dominion of the victor. Envoys are sent throughout the conquered realm to announce that the former tyrant has been defeated, to display the titles of the victor that must be acknowledged [Col. 0174B], and to proclaim his rights. Thus the Lord himself, who came to wage war upon the enemy of the human race, says in the Gospel: “When a strong man, armed, guards his court, all that he possesses is at peace; but if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted, and distribute his spoils” (Luke 11).

On this night the Son of God, coming as one stronger against that armed strong man, namely the devil, and bringing the banner of his cross as a warrior, seized him, bound him, took away his weapons, and restored his spoils to paradise. That one so strong, who trampled down the whole earth, was caught upon the hook of the cross; for, while he sought to attack in Christ the frailty of flesh by death, he was pierced by the sting of divinity. Rightly, therefore, on this same night is celebrated the sacrament of baptism [Col. 0174C], by which our priests go boldly against the unlawful dominion of the conquered power, as envoys, indeed, of Christ the victorious king. Bringing forth the tokens of victory, they require from men renunciation of the conquered one and confession of the victor.

The time and the order of this office now require that something be said concerning the greatness of this sacrament; and first it seems necessary to say how, or what, the death of Christ accomplishes in us through baptism. For it would seem to follow that, just as we became mortal through sin and are baptized for the remission of sins, so after baptism we should now be immortal.

## Chapter XXXIV. [Col. 0174D] How, or what, the death of Christ accomplishes in us through baptism

The Apostle Paul says: “Do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

Here he plainly shows that a profitable exchange has been made for our twofold and everlasting death, to which we had justly been bound: namely, that by dying through baptism with Christ, who was subjected to an unjust death, we ought no longer to die. For this reason Christ, dead, poured forth from his side the stream of his death—namely blood and water—that we might not lack that by which we could become participants in that same death [Col. 0175A] and thus be freed from our own. For it is greatly contrary to justice both to die with righteous Christ and to be condemned with sinful devil.

Yet the same justice does not likewise permit that all of us “who have been baptized into the death of Christ Jesus” should immediately also be free from bodily death. For in baptism there is the likeness of the one simple death that Christ underwent. But we, liable to a twofold death, that is, of body and soul, undergo the remedy of baptism. Therefore, because of Christ’s one death, to whose likeness we have been united in growth (ibid.), grace has driven away from us one death, that which was the saving of the soul; but the judgment of justice has reserved the other, that of the body. “Indeed the body,” says the Apostle, “is dead,” that is, most certainly destined to die [Col. 0175B], “because of sin; but the spirit lives because of justification” (Rom. 8).

But the bodies of the baptized also have consolation in their hope: because those whose spirit now lives “because of justification” will themselves also be changed through the resurrection—that is, they will become incapable of suffering—when what is mortal is swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5). This is not said as though resurrection follows because we have been baptized; otherwise, whoever are not baptized would not rise again. Rather, because we have been baptized, faith will receive its reward: when all the dead rise, believers alone will be changed. “We shall indeed all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed.” For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, “that is, made immortal,” and we shall be changed (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0175C]; that is, we too shall obtain impassibility, which the unbelieving will not possess. For “those who have done evil shall come forth to a resurrection of judgment” (John 5).

Therefore, in baptism we have now received the present justification of the spirit, but the hope of a future transformation. And just as the preceding death of the soul became the cause of bodily death and of all the corruptions of the flesh, so now the life or justification of the spirit, by which we are revived in baptism, will be the effective cause that, in the resurrection, we are transformed—that is, made incapable of suffering.

No argument ought to be drawn from bodily death, as though the power of baptism should consequently have swallowed it up as well. Although this too took its beginning from original sin, which is abolished in baptism, nevertheless the two deaths befell sinful man in different ways. For a stubborn desire for divinity brought death upon the soul; but God took from the body the means of living forever, acting to assist rather than to punish: “Behold,” he says, “Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore see lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3) [Col. 0175D].

These words seem to sound like anger or vengeance; but, rightly considered, they are words of fatherly providence and a certain preparation, already then, of mercy hovering over us from afar. For what would eternal life have been to a man already corrupted except eternal misery? Plotinus also, a certain philosopher among the Gentiles, is praised by Augustine for having understood this correctly. For, when he was speaking of human souls, he said: “The merciful Father made mortal bonds for them.” Thus, Augustine says, he judged that this very fact—that men are mortal in body—belongs to the mercy of God the Father, lest they be held forever in the misery of this life [Col. 0176A].

For what then would distinguish them from demons? But now they differ greatly, because God’s eternity is blessed—or rather, is eternal blessedness—whereas the eternity of demons is miserable, or rather, is eternal misery. Man, whose misery is mortal or whose mortality is miserable, has fallen from God’s blessedness, but has not reached the misery of demons, through the providence of the merciful God who says: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever.” Therefore we judge that there should be no complaint as to why our bodily death is not abolished in baptism. Rather, the faithful person ought to desire that it come, and that, as an advance of mercy, it may release the soul from the misery of this present life. “For he is not as a man, that he should lie; nor as a son of man, that he should change” (Num. 23). The purpose of one and the same grace, which began then, when he forbade man to be immortal, he now displays in the faith of baptism, and will bring to completion on the day of resurrection.

## Chapter XXXV

That, according to the Lord’s pronouncement, no one has ever entered the kingdom of God unless reborn of water and the Holy Spirit; and that, at the hour when our Lord poured blood and water from his side, the entire Church—already existing or having existed from the beginning of the world down to the thief who confessed upon the cross—was baptized.

[Col. 0176C] The sacrament of baptism is so great and so necessary that without it, according to the Lord’s pronouncement, no one can see the kingdom of God (John 3). Here one may raise the question of that thief to whom, when he confessed on the cross and said, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom,” the Lord replied: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). For he was not baptized according to the rule by which each of us is baptized. How, then, is the Lord’s pronouncement defended, which says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God?” (John 3).

But if such matters disturb us, the understanding of our heart is still narrow, and we do not yet behold with sufficiently opened eyes the clear majesty of holy baptism. We attend only to the stream which Christ sent forth to us who were outside, when he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). We attend, I say, only to the stream of holy baptism that came forth to us; we observe less carefully where, when, and how abundantly the fountain of the house of David itself (Zech. 13) overflowed before it was conveyed to us [Col. 0176D].

But that saving fountain cleansed the whole Church—gathered from the beginning through the six ages of the world, and shut out from entrance into paradise because of original sin—and all who were then still alive in the body and belonged to that Church, hearing our Lord himself and faithfully following him. That saving fountain of baptism cleansed, I say, the whole Church from Adam down to the aforesaid thief, at the hour when the side of Christ was opened by a soldier’s spear and blood and water burst forth (John 19). There Christ likewise washed in his blood from its sins the whole Church which then existed or had existed from the beginning of the world, in order to present to himself a glorious bride, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5) [Col. 0177A].

For from the time it was stained by the sin of the first parent and, because of this, grew old and wrinkled amid corruptions—or, to use Isaiah’s words, “from the time it drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath, and drank the cup of stupor to its dregs, and drank it down to the sediment” (Isa. 51)—there was not, as the same prophet says, one of all the sons whom it bore to raise it up; nor was there one of all the sons whom it nourished to take it by the hand. “Your sons,” he says, “have been cast down; they sleep at the head of every street, like a beast caught in a snare” (ibid.).

Although circumcision under the Law then provided against the wound of original sin the same assistance of saving healing which baptism customarily provides now, in the time of grace revealed, this remained wholly excepted: they were not yet able to enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom. They waited after death, comforted only in Abraham’s bosom by blessed hope, for the happy entrance into the peace above, until he should come who soon afterward speaks in the same prophet: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who spoke—behold, I am present” (Isa. 52). And a little later the same prophet says of the same one: “He shall sprinkle many nations” (ibid.) [Col. 0177B].

Of this sprinkling the Church speaks through the mouth of David, who was one of the aforesaid ancient sons of the Church: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). By hyssop—a lowly herb, growing in rocky places, which when drunk reduces swelling of the lungs, and concerning which the Law also commanded that lepers be sprinkled with a bunch of hyssop dipped in the blood of a victim, and thus cleansed (Lev. 14; Num. 19)—by hyssop, I say, the lowly and health-giving herb, he signifies the humility of Christ’s passion. With this the Church that speaks through David was to be sprinkled, washed, and made whiter than snow.

Thus too the prophet Zechariah, after speaking of his entrance into the city of Jerusalem to suffer: “He himself is poor and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. 9), shortly afterward turns to him and says: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (ibid.) [Col. 0177C]. That is: in the blood of your passion, by your clemency you freed those who were held bound in the prison of hell, in which there is no mercy. And this stronghold, to which the Lord exhorts the same prisoners through the same prophet, immediately adding, “Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope” (ibid.), we must understand as none other than the dwelling-place of paradise, into which the first thief entered with the Lord.

[Col. 0178A] Therefore Jesus, baptized in his passion—of which he himself said, “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12)—at the hour when he poured forth blood and water from his side, baptized at once and together his whole body, which is the Church, however much it had grown from the beginning of the world up to that same hour. It was sprinkled with hyssop, as stated above, cleansed, and wholly made whiter than snow.

But because of those who were outside and were not yet united by faith to the body of that Church, that wave did not touch them. For no one is baptized before having faith in that baptism. For their sake, I say, the sacrament of baptism was placed, as it were, conveyed before the doors of that Church, so that all Jews or Gentiles wishing to enter the Church may be baptized, because the Church itself was baptized. Hence we read that Paul alone was baptized (Acts 9), because when the Church was baptized universally, as stated, he was not yet in the body of that Church, but in the synagogue of Satan, which had crucified Christ, the head of the Church [Col. 0178B].

We do not read that Peter, or any of the others who had adhered to Christ, was baptized individually; nor could Augustine himself find this, in the letter he wrote to Seleucia when asked about the baptism of the apostles. For before his passion, the Evangelist says, Jesus did not baptize, but his disciples did (John 4). But how did his disciples baptize except in the manner in which John’s disciples did, namely, unto repentance? Indeed, the authority of Leo, pope of Rome, demonstrates from the Gospel narrative that the rule for baptism had not been given before the Lord’s passion, but was given by him after his passion and resurrection, when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28) [Col. 0178C].

Let each person judge for himself concerning these matters, whether he should maintain that they were rebaptized. But concerning the aforesaid thief, no one doubts that he entered paradise with the Lord; yet he was baptized visibly only in the universal Church, together with that stream which flowed from the Lord’s side. For, as has often been said, then the whole Church which was upon earth or beneath the earth was baptized; and thus it was reborn from the side of dead Christ, just as Eve was made from the side of sleeping Adam (Gen. 2). For just as Adam’s rib was the material cause from which Eve was formed, so that stream which flowed from Christ’s side was the effective cause by which the holy Church, his bride, was reborn for paradise or heaven and for Christ’s spiritual marriage.

Indeed, no one yet, from the whole human race, had seen the kingdom of God. Yet he himself had declared, without any exception of those past, present, or future: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3) [Col. 0178D]. Therefore all had to be reborn: the whole Church, of ancient and new alike, because it had been begotten in the transgression of the first Adam, had to be regenerated in faith in the second Adam, so that it might see the kingdom of God.

## Chapter XXXVI

Why none of the saints of old could, by his own sorrow, be restored without the baptism of Christ’s blood to that place from which the first human being fell.

Someone may wonder why, until then, none of the righteous—none of the holy patriarchs or prophets, not even father Abraham, whose faith was first reckoned as righteousness when he believed against hope in hope (Rom. 4), and who, by the merit of that same faith, was called the friend of God (Jas. 2)—could by commendable righteousness at least in himself erase original sin and restore himself to paradise. Yet anyone who has knowledge of divine or even human law is by no means surprised at this. For how can the slave of one liable to capital punishment and condemned redeem his own head, if he adds nothing to his service, or even diminishes what he owed before incurring guilt? Greater debts are not discharged by other and lesser debts.

For example: that man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke 10) owed ten thousand talents to his king in Jerusalem—for who can estimate how much a creature owes the Creator? He was rich and illustrious in that city, and he did not lack the means of paying so great a debt. He had been warned by his lord to be faithful and obedient; he had received a command that was not difficult to keep, after whose observance he would deservedly be advanced to the rank of higher dignity. But induced by the accursed prince of Jericho, the enemy of his lord, with hope of reigning, he went down [Col. 0179B], despising service as though fit to reign, and carried away with him his lord’s entire due. Immediately he was stripped by that deceiver, beaten, and left half-dead.

As this traitor lay in Jericho—he who before defecting owed ten thousand talents—if he offered one hundred denarii in satisfaction, would he pay the entire debt, heal his wounds, and wipe away the disgrace of treason, so that, infamous among illustrious nobles, he might sit in that royal court? Certainly not. Rather, he would be treated well and mercifully if, merely not admitted into that city or court, he were not also burned by fire or altogether expelled from the life of which he is unworthy by some other punishment.

Therefore merciful Divinity dealt well with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and any righteous person: excluded from paradise, they were nevertheless not tortured by the fires of hell; placed in peace, they waited for that lawgiver who, when he came, would give blessing, “that the God of gods might be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83) [Col. 0179C]. Whatever faithful service any righteous person offered to God was, compared with the praise and glorification which a human being created in paradise owed to the Creator, as one hundred denarii compared with ten thousand talents. How then could he also redeem original sin? Moreover, this miserable life could not then any more than now be lived wholly without actual sins, at least slight ones.

Therefore it did not accord with the supreme justice of God—who forbids any stained thing to be offered to him in this earthly sanctuary—that he should receive anything but the spotless in those heavenly holy places, and should make corrupted human nature altogether equal to angelic dignity, wholly incorrupt. He would become unjust as well as just, and the most glorious commonwealth of heaven would be thrown into confusion by such disorder [Col. 0180A].

And lest, which God forbid, we should criticize God’s judgments with those who, according to Ezekiel, turned over within themselves the proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezek. 18), it is pleasing to pursue the proposed comparison further according to the equity of human law, since it is human beings who criticize God’s judgments. Let fair judges of worldly law and unjust critics of divine judgment hear this and reply.

After the aforesaid man went down to Jericho, he begot, as Scripture relates, sons and daughters in his own image and likeness (Gen. 5). For what is meant by the statement, “Adam begot in his own image and likeness”? It plainly means that, stripped by robbers as stated above, he begot children naked, wounded and sickly, himself half-dead and they also half-dead. The sap of a corrupted root likewise broke forth corruptly in its fruits. And, what is especially lamentable, though stripped and half-dead, he begot far more than he would have begotten had he remained in his original health as the faithful and obedient guardian of paradise [Col. 0180B].

For then from him only those would have been born who were predestined to life, since they are now recalled to that same life through Christ’s grace. For because of sin God says: “Cursed is the earth in your work: when you cultivate it, it shall not yield its fruits, but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 5). To this earth, that is, to the woman, he says: “I will multiply your pains and your conceptions” (ibid.). Thus multiplied conceptions from the earth of the flesh—which, because of the pride by which it desired divinity, was subjected to lust—grew beyond measure like a dense growth of thorns and thistles. So many reprobate are born that, in comparison with them, the elect are few (Matt. 20).

Let the sons of that man now speak, all who were born in Jericho: of that man, I say, who justly lost the city of Jerusalem because he abandoned it willingly [Col. 0180C]. Let them say whether they may claim by hereditary right that same city, lawfully awarded to their father. Let legal experts say in which court, Roman or barbarian, they would venture to give a similar judgment.

But someone will say: The Lord himself, in whose mouth is the law of mercy, says, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. 18). Quite so. But again another prophet says: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we have borne their iniquities” (Lam. 5). And Moses says to God: “You repay the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20) [Col. 0181A].

Therefore the harmony of these pipes must be sought; for, since one and the same Spirit breathed through them, no discord should be understood in them. Clearly, children bear the iniquity of their fathers when they follow them. You say to me, then: Abraham, Isaac, and the other righteous did not follow the iniquity of their first parents, but were found proved by every testimony of faith (Heb. 11). Let us therefore grant that they ought not to bear it insofar as they did not follow it. And he who did not follow it at all—Christ God, possessing flesh from Adam’s flesh and bones from Adam’s bones—ought not to bear it at all.

But how far they were from that iniquity of their parents, even though they had advanced to the height of righteousness! Isaiah, one of the foremost, says: “We have all become as unclean persons, and our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 6). It was therefore not fitting that their righteousness, since it was menstruous, should enter the heavenly sanctuary until that fountain of the house of David—the fountain of baptism of which we are now speaking—should be opened, according to the prophet Zechariah, for the washing of the menstruous woman (Zech. 13), namely when the spear opened the side of the crucified Lord [Col. 0181B].

Meanwhile, for them a great reward, exceeding all their righteousness, was present rest among the dead and the sure, blessed hope of future glorification through Christ. Thanks be to the merciful justice of God and the just mercy of God, who so opposed in order to assist, so struck in order to heal (Isa. 19), and, according to the Psalmist’s words, “Mercy and truth have met together; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). Thus he exercised truth and justice against guilt, while reserving mercy and peace for humanity. For since satisfaction for guilt was owed only by a human being, yet could be accomplished only by God, God became human, so that the one and same Christ, as true God, might demand it from humanity and, as true human, might pay it.

Therefore, as we began to say above, that we might be justified by participation in Christ’s death, “we were baptized into his death [Col. 0182B], buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 8). Concerning the sacrament or order of this renewal, which is celebrated after the above-mentioned consecration of the candle, something has already been said.

# Book Seven

[Col. 0181]

## Chapter I. On the order of this same baptism

[Col. 0181C]

Those things celebrated in baptism, those things spoken and done, were the alleged crimes on account of which martyrs were accused as evildoers, seized, and killed. For the devil, renounced in the sacred font through the profession of the Christian faith, against whom judicial sentences are pronounced, having great wrath, raged in the hearts of the ungodly. Offended by the trumpet of the divine name, he used their blindness and madness as his weapons against God; and, as is read in the Apocalypse (Rev. 8), like a great mountain burning with wrath when the trumpet sounded, he fled into the depths of ungodly hearts and, fabricating a charge of sorcery from the divine exorcisms by which he had been expelled, dictated laws in opposition [Col. 0181D].

“But you are my witnesses” (Isa. 43), says the Lord; that is, you know very well that we have learned no evil art from a good teacher. Therefore, in what is said or done, let us contemplate, by applying the mirror of faith, the power by which the devil is condemned and pierced through.

## Chapter II. That the readings and chants of the present day pertain to the sacrament of baptism

First, readings are recited from the Old Testament that pertain to this New [Testament] sacrament; and likewise chants, that is, tracts corresponding to it, are sung in response. For it is difficult to number how customary and frequent it was for the Holy Spirit, even before Christ’s coming, to work especially through waters and to prefigure the grace of baptism in mystical words or deeds. Therefore sacred readings suited to baptism are solemnly recited for the instruction of the candidates for baptism.

And just as Abraham’s servant, sent to obtain a wife for his master’s son Isaac after Isaac’s mother Sarah had died, found Rebecca at a fountain of water, gave her earrings to adorn her face and bracelets for her hands, and so brought her, adorned beforehand, to Isaac (Gen. 24), so the envoys of God the Father—that is, his priests—coming to the fonts of baptism acquire through the teaching of faith a new bride, that is, a new people, for Christ the Son of the Ancient of Days [Col. 0182C].

For God the Father bound them by a great oath of love, presenting the incarnation of the Word coeternal with himself. As a type of this, the old man Abraham made the aforesaid servant swear upon his thigh. They also possessed with them all the good things of their lord, because they had been made rich in word and in all knowledge (1 Cor. 15), and in the working of great powers. God the Father, I say, bound them by oath to take for his Son, the true Isaac—that is, our laughter or joy—a new bride, the Church from among the Gentiles; because his mother, the Synagogue, which bore him according to the flesh, is dead, and has been slain by the blood of her own son whom she killed, because she said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27) [Col. 0182D].

Therefore, while we recite sacred readings to the candidates for baptism, Abraham’s servant, as it were, addresses Rebecca at the fountain of water—Rebecca meaning “obedience”—and gives her earrings, that is, the teaching of faith, which adorns well the obedient ear. She also receives bracelets upon her hands when she works in the mortification of her flesh what she believes, and for this reason remembers herself to have been baptized into Christ’s death. Without delay she gladly hastens to Isaac, forgetting her people and the house of her father (Ps. 44), and presenting herself wholly prepared for the heavenly marriage.

## Chapter III. What in the first reading pertains to baptism

Someone may perhaps ask what relation to the sacrament of baptism has the first reading, from the book of Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Whoever is such a person is like a sealed sack: before it is shaken out, what it contains does not appear [Col. 0183A]. But the prophets, of whom Moses is the first or greatest, have now been shaken out, so that the sacraments they contained, closed and covered, may come forth revealed. Since the apostles first did this—for they were the first after Christ to open the prophets for us, as it were, by shaking them out—they are therefore called in the Psalm “sons of those shaken out” (Ps. 126).

This reading especially has already been shaken out and expounded by great and mighty men, by whom it is also called the *Hexaemeron*, that is, the work of six days. If everything they said that pertains to the sacrament of baptism were gathered together, excessive length would bring great weariness in the present place. Therefore it must be said briefly that this reading bears especially splendid testimony to Christ’s baptism because it says: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” while at the same time the evident oracle of the divine name in which we are baptized—that is, of the Holy Trinity—sounds forth once and again [Col. 0183B].

It says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). What other beginning should we understand than the Son? For he himself, when the Jews asked him who he was, said: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). Therefore the Son is the Beginning. Through the Son God made heaven and earth. “All things were made through him,” as John the Evangelist relates, “and without him nothing was made” (John 1). Without doubt, then, the Father is to be understood in the name God, and the Son in the name Beginning. Indeed, after he had said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), he immediately added: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (ibid.) [Col. 0183C]; this Spirit is the third person in the Trinity.

Likewise, in the same reading: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid.). Hence Gregory says: “God spoke all things, and they were made.
