But when he determines to make man, he first sets forth this, which must be reverently considered, saying: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ Thus, since a rational creature was to be created, he appeared to be made as though with counsel, as though formed from earth with deliberation and raised by the inspiration of the Creator into the power of a living spirit; so that he who was made in the image of God might come into being, not through the sound of a command, but through the dignity of the operation.”

Something further must be said, appropriate to the present subject, about the words mentioned above, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” and about the likeness here stated: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” For truly the Holy Spirit is now borne over the waters for this reason: that he may restore through the regenerating grace of baptism the likeness of God which had been abolished in man through sin [Col. 0183D]. To make this clearer, it must first be explained what difference there is between the image and likeness of God.

## Chapter IV

What the difference is between God’s image and likeness; and that by sinning man lost not the image but the likeness, to which he is re-formed through Christ’s baptism.

Man was made in the image of God insofar as he is rational; but he was made in the likeness insofar as he was created an imitator of divine goodness. For the image of God, or “the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1), as the Apostle says, is the Son; but the goodness or charity of God and of his image is the Holy Spirit. Therefore it was not said: “Let us make man in my likeness and image,” but “in our image and likeness,” because likeness belongs not to one person only but to two persons, namely Father and Son; whereas image belongs not to two but to one, namely the Father. For the Son is the Son of the Father alone, not also the Son of the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit is the Spirit not only of the Father but also of the Son [Col. 0184A].

Now a rational creature could lose that by which it was made in the likeness of God, but it could not be deprived of that by which it was created in the image of God. Why? Because imitation of divine goodness, through which God’s likeness is retained, also requires the creature’s will; whereas rationality, which is engraved upon the human soul by the impression of God’s image, proceeds from the skill of the Creator alone.

Therefore, so that we may recover by our own will the likeness of God which we lost by our own will, the goodness of God, the Holy Spirit, descends as far as we can readily reach: he is borne over waters that are at hand, asking of us only our will and freely providing everything else. For he himself created the water which flowed from Christ’s dead body—he who caused the body of Christ itself to grow together from the womb’s moisture of our nature, as we have in the Creed, “And he was incarnate by the Holy Spirit,” or in the Gospel: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1) [Col. 0184B].

And he who, at the creation of the world, as is written in the present reading, was borne over the waters in the manner of a bird—warming its eggs with the heat that gives life, as Jerome says—is now borne over the waters of baptism, that, cherishing beneath his grace those who enter, he may regenerate them into true life, spreading his wings, taking them up, and carrying them upon his shoulders (Deut. 32).

And if there is need for him to draw nearer to someone—that is, if someone is kept away from the waters though wishing to reach them, as Cornelius was prevented when Jews prohibited Gentiles from being received (Acts 10), or as many confessing Christ during persecution could not reach the waters because they were held back by prisons and bonds [Col. 0184C]—if, I say, there is need because of anything of this kind, then the mother of God’s grace flies to them and extends her wings beyond the nest of waters. Thus, while Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word; and they spoke in tongues and magnified God (Acts 10).

## Chapter V. That martyrs who did not receive baptism may rightly be said to have been baptized in their own blood and death.

But Peter commanded those men, protected by so great a defender, to be baptized in water in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Many others, however, overtaken by the crisis of persecution, suffered punishments without baptism in water and were brought to completion for [Col. 0185B] Christ’s sake. What then? Were these baptized? Indeed, they attained a grace greater by so much than those who die in the Church’s peace as they shared, at greater cost, in Christ’s death and blood. For in ordinary baptism there is only a likeness of death, as the Apostle says: “For if we have been made one with the likeness of his death, we shall also be [one with him] in the resurrection” (Rom. 6); but in martyrdom there is death itself. If martyrdom were not baptism, the Lord would never have said of his Passion—as was recalled above—“I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12).

But, excepting those whom such a crisis overtakes, the Holy Spirit comes to no one outside the font, and contains the whole remission of sins within the waters, extending it no further. Above all from the passages already mentioned, the reading in question accords with the sacrament of baptism. Otherwise, were there not a reason to avoid wearisomeness, it could be shown from the authoritative treatises of the doctors that the entire sequence of the world’s creation, set forth in that same reading, bears likenesses of our renewal effected through baptism.

For he who “in the beginning created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), and performed the other works of the six days, now says: “Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isa. 65): that is, new saints and a new people of the Church. “And he divides the waters from the waters” (Gen. 1); and the firmament of apostles and prophets was set in place (Eph. 2), dividing the waters of divine wisdom, which it contains, from the waters of human or carnal prudence. Of this the Psalmist says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103 [104]). And when the waters had been gathered into one place, “God set bounds to the sea” (Job 38), that is, to the storms of this age: he set its bar and doors, and said, “Thus far shall you come, and here shall you break your swelling waves.” Thus the earth of the Church, delivered from shipwreck, brought forth: the fields of the wilderness—that is, the broad expanse of the Gentiles—brought forth the fragrant shoot of Israel, because the faith of the patriarchs and prophets blossomed among the Gentiles.

And in the firmament of prophetic or evangelical Scripture—for, Augustine says, God wished to set the firmament in the Scriptures against the more treacherous errors—in the firmament, that is, of Holy Scripture, were set the sun and moon and the multitude of the stars: that is, the greater, lesser, and intermediate lights of teachers. Some of the baptized unfold themselves through contemplation, saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3); others float amid worldly cares; and, as the cultivation of Christianity advanced, even the four-footed animals (Acts 10), that is, crowds of carnal people, crept forward into faith in Christ. And the Lord of such a creation is the new Adam, guardian and possessor alike of earth and of the heavenly paradise: he whom the serpent did not deceive, whom woman did not seduce, who committed no sin, and therefore owed nothing to death.

But the very first season of the year, namely spring, [Col. 0186B] accords with the same likeness; for not only in Israel’s departure from Egypt was the blood of the lamb the restoration of freedom, but the whole world also took the beginning of its creation then. Hence great Leo said: “Now the sacred new month has shone forth for the festival foretold above all festivals, so that in the same season in which the world received its beginning, the Christian creation might have its origin.”

Of this new creation the Apostle Paul said: “For we know that every creature groans and is in labour pains even until now” (Rom. 8), namely, until the revelation of the sons of God, which he had previously mentioned when he said: “For the expectation of the creature awaits the revelation of the sons of God” (ibid.). And then he continues: “And not only it, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit,” that is, we who first received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, “we ourselves groan within ourselves” (ibid.), and so forth. For although we may seem perfect, nevertheless, while we are corruptible, we do not live securely, nor do we consider that we have already attained it (Phil. 3).

## CHAPTER VI. On the second reading

The second reading is that from the book of Exodus: “It came to pass in the morning watch, and behold, the Lord looked upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of cloud and fire; he destroyed their army and overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were carried into the deep” (Exod. 14).

Without doubt, not merely in part but manifestly throughout, this whole reading presents a type of Christ’s saving baptism; and it is well known that the mystery of this reading has been repeatedly celebrated by teachers throughout the sacred Scriptures. Thus it is said in the above-mentioned blessing of the candle: “This is the night in which you first led our fathers, the children of Israel, out of Egypt; afterwards you caused them to pass dry-shod through the Red Sea.” How this is accomplished now, in individual persons, through Christ’s baptism, faith alone beholds with its own eyes; and therefore it sings to the Lord the Song of Moses, that is, the following tract: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15).

But how this was accomplished in the holy Fathers and in all the elect who awaited this passage in the underworld—what a host of blessed souls, led by the mighty soul of Christ, passed through that sea which flowed from his side, divided into water and blood; what exultation of those coming forth from darkness; what joy of those entering paradise—“eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

## CHAPTER VII. On the third reading

The third reading: “Seven women shall seize one man on that day, saying: We shall eat our own bread and wear our own clothing” (Isa. 4), and so forth. This too plainly pertains to the sacrament of baptism and to the instruction of those to be baptized.

But we must now say why four readings are read, taken from the Law and the Prophets. The first reading is read because, as has been said, while recounting the creation of the world and the formation of humankind, it introduces also the mysteries of the waters with the authority of God’s Spirit. The other three, however, look to the three ages of the world: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. In all these times the necessity of baptism’s remedy is commended.

Concerning those who were before the Law, it is clear because, as was already said in the second reading, they prefigured Christ’s baptism in that they crossed the sea; and, as the Apostle says, “All were baptized under Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10). For the Law had not yet been given. But concerning those who were under the Law, Isaiah says in the third reading: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanse the blood of Jerusalem from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4). Of this burning John the Baptist says in the Gospel: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John 3).

That one man is Christ, whom, according to this reading, seven women shall seize—that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. Of them the same prophet says elsewhere: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). These seven graces seized Jesus, whom, as Jerome says, they had long desired, because they could find no other in whom they might rest in everlasting abiding. That the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things needs no exposition. Therefore, they say, “We shall eat our own bread and wear our own clothing.” But because reproach is always found among human beings, since no one living sought the gifts of the Holy Spirit, they desire Jesus’ name to be invoked upon them, so that what was imperfect in the Law might be fulfilled in the Gospel.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fourth reading

The fourth reading: “Moses wrote the song” (Deut. 31); or: “This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord” (Isa. 54). For these are read alternately at Easter and Pentecost, and both express this time of grace more plainly.

In the reading, “Moses wrote the song,” Moses himself says: “For I know that after my death you will act wickedly,” and so forth. Almost all the holy doctors understand Moses’ death as the end of the Law, that is, Christ’s coming. His grace succeeded the Law as Joshua succeeded Moses: Joshua, a victorious leader, brought God’s people, having crossed the Jordan, into the promised land through mighty battles, prefiguring Jesus Christ both in name and deed. Jesus Christ, fighting against the devil by his blood and victorious over death, restored to paradise through baptismal grace the whole people of the elect, none of whom the Law had brought to perfection.

Certainly in this time, according to the song written by Moses, “They sinned against the Lord; they are not children”—namely, the Jews—“a crooked and perverse generation, a foolish and unwise people,” whom the Lord and their Father had established “upon a high land” (Deut. 32): that is, upon knowledge of the Law and Prophets, so that they might suck honey of heavenly teaching from the rock, which was Christ, and oil—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—from the same exceedingly hard rock, made imperishably firm by the power of the resurrection. And behold, by contrast: “From the vineyard of Sodom and from the suburbs of Gomorrah is their grape: a grape of gall and a most bitter cluster” (ibid.). “And because of these things,” he says, “I shall hide my face from them” (ibid.), and so forth.

But truly the heavens and earth of which he says elsewhere through the Prophet: “I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isa. 65)—the new heavens, I say, and the new earth of the Church—heard the words of his mouth. As we sing in the following tract: in them the Lord’s teaching thickens like rain, and his utterance flows like dew, like a shower upon the grass and like drops upon the herbage, because the name of the Lord is invoked over us: the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28), which contains the whole power of our regeneration accomplished through baptism.

No less does that reading of Isaiah, “This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord,” look to the same time of grace, as has been said above, summoning believers and saying: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55): that they may come to God’s river, which is filled with waters (Ps. 64 [65]), and whose “rush makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45 [46]); that they may drink “waters from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). He speaks to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water; and the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). But it should be known, as Jerome says, that a human being supplies water, whereas God supplies the Holy Spirit, by whom stains are washed away and sins cleansed.

## CHAPTER IX. On the tracts which we sing after these readings

Each of the chants that the choir sings after these three readings indicates the great exultation of those reborn: they rightly ought to exult because, with all sins submerged, they themselves pass through the sea of baptism delivered. Yet this exultation must be in fear and trembling, and joined with the laborious and necessary mortification of the flesh, for as long as we stand in the body—like those whom we read of in the Apocalypse (chap. 15), standing above the sea of glass—which cannot bear those made heavy and again burdened with sins.

Therefore, having cast aside the burdens of the age and being content with a simple tunic, we ought to remain or walk upon this glassy sea of baptism mingled with the fire of the Holy Spirit, holding, as is read there, the harps of God: that is, wholly mortified in the flesh and stretched out in God’s praise, trembling as we sing and singing as we tremble, according to: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). Rightly, therefore, we render as tracts the words of the songs of Moses and of the prophets which we sing after the readings; for it has already been said that the tract is the song of mourners and accords with the misery of the present exile.

The fourth tract differs from the others in that it is sung without any preceding reading. Nor is this surprising. In the present office it is not the voice of the universal Church, as the others are. It is rather the voice solely of those present who are to be baptized, still infected by the poison of original sin, and who therefore hasten to baptism that they may become young again, “as the deer longs for fountains of water” (Ps. 41 [42]). This is especially confirmed by the following Collect: “Almighty everlasting God, look graciously upon the devotion of the people being reborn, who, like a deer, longs for the fountain of your waters.”

By contrast, the first reading ends with no following chant, because, once all the works of the world had been created and completed, ungrateful humanity did not sing worthy thanks to God the Creator. Rather, it fell silent in the praise of God; and, listening to the serpent, it became deaf against the command it had received. Hence *Ephphetha*—that is, “to open”—is said also to the person being baptized, taken from the Gospel in which our Lord signified, in the deaf and mute man whom he healed, the healing of the human race, which, as has been said, had become deaf and mute (Mark 7).

Nor should it be passed over that neither the greeting before the Collects—namely, “The Lord be with you”—nor any superscriptions, that is, titles, are prefixed to the aforesaid readings. For from the day before yesterday we have cut off these titles, like heads from bodies, from all readings, until Christ our head is restored to us by his resurrection. The likeness of that resurrection is represented to the eyes of faith in those who, clothed with Christ, ascend from the fonts after baptism, as the Apostle says (Gal. 3). Nor before this do the Church’s bells ring out, for the reason already stated above.

## CHAPTER X. On the consecration of the font

The consecration of the font is accomplished in the name of the Holy Trinity, and especially by the invocation of the Holy Spirit. This is rightly done because the whole regeneration of humankind, though it is the work of the whole Trinity, is nevertheless the particular operation of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Trinity, as Leo the Great says, so divided among itself the work concerning humanity that the Father created, the Son redeemed, and the Holy Spirit regenerated or kindled. Yet the Father created with the Son and Holy Spirit; the Son redeemed with the Father and Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit regenerates and enlightens with the Father and Son.

For when the Father created, he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). And when the Son redeemed, the Father gave him the cup of the Passion, and the Son himself drank it through the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle Paul says (Heb. 9): “The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself to God,” and so forth. And for the Holy Spirit to regenerate, the Father gives that same Paraclete Spirit, while the Son baptizes in the same Spirit, as John the Baptist indicates in the Gospel that it had been said to him: “He upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

The Holy Spirit, then, sanctifies the waters; the Holy Spirit is the sanctification of our font; indeed, the Spirit is the fountain of life (Ps. 35 [36]), the river of peace. The Holy Spirit is that gracious stream from the Father’s heart, from which abundant mercy runs forth to us like an overflowing river. The Holy Spirit is the love of God, the torrent of God’s delight. He moved the father of the two sons with inborn pity toward the younger son, that is, the Gentile people, who by living dissolutely had consumed his share of the paternal substance and had fed foreign swine in a far country—that is, had worshipped unclean demons. When he returned, the father received him, proclaimed a feast-day to all his friends, that is, to the angelic assemblies, and ordered the first robe to be brought forth together with a ring (Luke 15).

What, indeed, do we understand by the ring except the seal of faith? For when the catechumen who is to be baptized recites the creed of the sacred faith which he firmly holds, he has surely inscribed it upon the tablets of his heart and has given him a fitting ring upon his hand. And in being sealed with the cross of Christ, he may say with the Apostle: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2); and in being immersed three times, he may be conformed to Christ’s three-day death. By this wonderful service of mercy, while alive and unharmed, he is fastened to the Crucified, dead, and buried One; he dies with him and is buried with him. Without doubt, he receives sandals on his feet. Sandals, after all, are made from dead animals. These are plainly signs of the Lord’s death, which he receives so that, following the example of him who was crucified for us, he may henceforth crucify his flesh with its vices and desires, and, mortifying his members which are upon earth, may say: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 5).

But when he receives the white garment, which indeed signifies Christ’s new consolation, as the Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Col. 3), the Father surely clothes him in the first robe and says: “Let us eat and drink, for this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Mass of the same day, and why it lacks the customary chant, namely the Introit and Communion

Immediately the paschal banquet of the evening sacrifice is prepared, the threefold litany preceding in honour of the holy and undivided Trinity (Gal. 3). In the threefold name of this Trinity the son of whom we speak was baptized—the son who “was dead and has come to life; was lost and has been found” (Luke 15). The bells, hitherto silent, ring out, and the choir exults as harmony resounds.

The angels rejoice with us, and because of their rejoicing we repeat their hymn, omitted since Septuagesima: namely, *Gloria in excelsis*. That fattened calf is brought: namely, Christ, God and man, whose flesh we ought to eat and whose blood we ought to drink. He is called a calf because, as man, he was sacrificed for us; fattened because in him “the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 2).

But the elder brother—that is, the Jewish people—will not take part in this banquet. Standing outside and hearing the music and chorus, he speaks ill of his brother, tormented by envy and hatred; reproaching the father’s mercy, he prefers to be consumed by grief and hunger rather than to rejoice and feast with his brother. Yet at some time the father will go out and, graciously showing a cheerful face to his estranged and sorrowful son, will persuade and entreat him to share in the fitting joys and feast, holding his hand and counselling him with tender words; and then the remnant of Israel will be saved.

Meanwhile, until that happens, the joy of the Father’s house, that is, of the present Church, will not be full or complete. For although the Jewish people have always hated the salvation of the Gentiles (Rom. 11), the Church of the Gentiles nonetheless grieves that that people stands outside, and that its own salvation is an occasion of stumbling to them. Accordingly, certain ornaments have suitably been removed from this evening sacrifice, so festive and joyful: namely, the Introit, Gradual, Offertory, and Communion. These were excerpts from the Psalms, first appointed to be sung before the sacrifice by Pope Celestine, the fortieth from Peter, and instituted to be sung with sweet melody in the Roman Church.

Meanwhile, as the calf is brought and the banquet is prepared, Paul, that foremost and most faithful of servants, comes before the son who has returned. Finding him already wearing a ring on his hand, already shod, and already clothed in the best robe, he joyfully addresses him in the present Epistle, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on things above, not on things upon earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

O the graceful eloquence and dutiful diligence of a faithful steward! “You have died,” he says, because everything in you that had its mind upon earthly things has died. What else had that son, who deserted his father, who was wanton and prodigal, previously desired except to arrange banquets with prostitutes, squander his own goods, covet those of others, and feed foreign swine? (Luke 16.) All this is dead and buried in Christ’s baptism. But the new life which rose from that same baptism, which made such a son wholly different—the new life, I say, hidden with Christ in God—is Christ himself, the same new man, whom the white garment of the baptized person also signifies. “For when Christ,” he says, “your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3).

The angel’s garments in the following Gospel, white as snow, likewise signify this same life created by divine newness. Behold, meanwhile, heavenly harmony sounds forth, to gladden the guests: the *alleluia*, as though sent down from heaven and restored to our mouths. Since Septuagesima, our instruments had not sung it, because in those days the captivity of the present life was signified; thus the *alleluia*, which signifies the joy of the future life, hung silent as though upon the willows of this Babylon while we mourned. But now, because that most sacred night is already at hand in which Christ, the author of liberty, rose again, and in which, as has been said, the new children of the Church who are baptized rise in the first resurrection, our instruments, as though snatched from the willows, hasten to resound with *alleluia* and say: “Give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. 117 [118]); and they add the reason: “for he is good” (ibid.), proved by its effect; “for his mercy is unto the age” (ibid.), understood as displayed in the remission of sins which he has granted in baptism. And the *alleluia* rightly takes up this verse first.

For Psalm 117 [118], whose first verse is this *alleluia*, commends in its title this great mercy and this solemn day which the Lord has made, so that we may exult and rejoice in it. This *alleluia*, like the rest of this day’s office, is especially the exultation of the baptized, because, as has been said, they have already risen with Christ in the first resurrection. Yet a great labour remains for them, that they may have a share in the second resurrection; and amid this labour of good works there remains fear, there remains weeping, whether because of the danger of Gehenna or the longing for eternal life.

Rightly, therefore, because the joy of the hope of those who have been called is not yet complete, diminished as it is by the anxiety of those still dwelling away from God, a Tract is sung together with the *alleluia*—a chant which, as has already been said, belongs to mourners. Likewise, throughout the whole Easter week until Saturday, on which they themselves lay aside their white garments, the Gradual is sung for the same reason. It is the chant of those who labour, and it would not pertain to the days of Pentecost except because that season is a sign of future rest, peace, and glory.

For in the Canon, throughout this week, this is added on their behalf: “Therefore, Lord, accept this offering of our service, and of your whole family, which we offer to you for those whom you have deigned to regenerate from water and the Holy Spirit, granting them remission of all their sins.” And from this evening, on which they were baptized, at each Vespers of this week the clergy proceed to the fonts, celebrating, together with Christ’s resurrection, the solemnity of the holy baptistery.

## CHAPTER XII. Why the kiss of peace, omitted since the day before yesterday, is now restored

Why the kiss of peace, which Pope Innocent, the thirty-eighth after blessed Peter, established to be given, was omitted from the day before yesterday and is restored today, is more quickly learned from the very place in the Canon where it is given. For it is given at the point at which we uncover the chalice for the second time and say: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

This place, as was said in the exposition of the same Canon, signifies that our Lord rose from the dead and, standing in the midst of his disciples, said to them: “Peace to you” (John 20). By this he showed us that the wall of enmity erected between us and God (Eph. 2), namely sin, had been destroyed—a wall which our Lord went forth through the passage of death to dissolve. Having accomplished this, he returned in the resurrection and announced the peace he had won for us by the first words he uttered in the midst of his disciples: “Peace to you.”

Rightly, therefore, from the time when he went forth to establish that peace until he returned and said, “Peace to you,” we omitted “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” and did not give the kiss of peace. At the same time we execrated and anathematized the shameful kiss of Judas the betrayer, by which, in handing over the Son of Man, he disgraced the holy and innocent fellowship of the apostles before outsiders, giving them occasion to curse and detest those whose holiness had been held in great esteem, so that they might repeatedly sing concerning them something like this:

> … And from one crime  
> Learn all from one crime.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* II.65–66)

## CHAPTER XIII. On the day of the Lord’s resurrection

This sacred day looks to that eighth day which is found in Chronicles (2 Chron. 7) and in the superscriptions of certain Psalms (Pss. 6, 18 [19]); the Lord made it the solemnity of solemnities, just as, because of their greatness, things are called Holy of Holies and Song of Songs. For as those surpass other holy things or songs, so the dignity of this most holy solemnity surpasses other solemnities.

That eighth day will be the glory of the perfect and consummated resurrection. In it all the elect, who now after laying aside the flesh enjoy the one and simple blessedness of the soul alone—as we read in the Apocalypse, “white robes were given to each of them” (Rev. 6)—will be rewarded with a double happiness, that of body and soul, and so will receive two robes of everlasting glory.

As the seven ages of the world precede that eighth in their order—the sixth of which is now unfolding from Christ’s advent, while the seventh is the rest of souls that have laid aside the flesh, as has already been said elsewhere—so too seven Sundays have preceded this most sacred solemnity. On the first of them we sang, “The sorrows of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17 [18]); on the seventh, “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (Zech. 2). Each corresponds, in the character of its office, to the corresponding age, as has already been said in its proper place and order. Between them the memorial of the Lord’s Passion has been inserted for two weeks, and why this is done has already been explained.

There follows this feast of the eighth age, which lies beyond seven because it is eternal, commended by the glorious resurrection of Christ: noble, wonderful, beautiful and sweet, splendid and desirable. For what is laid up for us in that eighth age is no small thing. As the eighth day is the same as the first, so in that age humanity is restored to that very end for which it was created, and will be immortally happy in body and soul, and happily immortal like the angels of God—indeed, restored above the dignity of its first origin, because it will behold its own nature, in the unity of the person of the Son of God, a person set above all the works of the Father’s hands, worshipped, praised, and glorified by angels in the coessentiality of the supreme and undivided Trinity.

Therefore, when we commemorate the heavenly birthdays of the saints, concerning whom there is no doubt that, having departed their bodies, they have already obtained eternal glory, we also celebrate the eighth day, calling them blessed also because in the future, when they receive their bodies again, they will happily obtain glorious immortality.

This is also signified by the eight evangelical beatitudes, in which the eighth returns to the beginning. For the same declaration of blessedness occurs in both the first and eighth: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Hence Augustine: “The eighth statement,” he says, “which returns to the beginning and reveals the perfect human being, is perhaps signified also by circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament, by the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath—which is indeed the eighth, that is, the first day—and by the celebration of the octave days which we observe in the regeneration of the new human being.”

Concerning that eighth day, then, which is the resurrection—already fulfilled in our head, namely Christ—something must now be said according to the office and mystical order of the present day, on which he rose.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why the Lord did not wish to rise before the third day

The number three is held notable even among secular philosophers, because it is the first of the odd numbers and of those which, apart from unity, admit no further division. Among us it is of far more illustrious repute—indeed, of primary and divine authority—both because of the very essence of the holy and undivided Trinity and because our Saviour rose from the dead on the third day.

And certainly this third day looks to that same mystery of the holy Trinity. For the Lord did not rise before the third day because it was fitting that Christ’s death in the flesh should obtain for us the propitiation of the holy Trinity by enduring three days. Otherwise, why, when we are baptized by a threefold immersion in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are we said to be planted together—indeed, truly “made one with the likeness of his death” (Rom. 6)—unless because he himself endured that same death, which before his baptism he had called his baptism, for three days in the name of and in obedience to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

For the Father, as the Son himself testifies, gave the cup of the Passion to the Son; the Son himself drank it, having power over his own soul, as he says: “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10); and the Holy Spirit caused it to be given to him to drink, as the Apostle says: “Christ through the Holy Spirit offered himself” (Heb. 9). Fittingly, therefore, the Lord’s death lasted three days: the Holy Trinity ordained it, and our nature in him alone bore it in order to obtain for the human race the propitiation of that same holy Trinity.

Moreover, the entire number of years of his life indicates that he rendered service to the holy Trinity and obeyed its command. For in the thirty-three years during which he walked upon the earth, the number three is repeated, with this difference alone: one three rises to the limit of ten, making thirty, while the other remains within the single unit, so that it is simple. As a type of this, Isaac too was led to be sacrificed over the course of three days (Gen. 22). For from Gerar, where Abraham was then living, to Mount Moriah—that is, the site of the Temple—is three days’ journey, as Jerome says; accordingly he arrived there on the third day, as the narrative relates: “And on the third day he came to the place which God had told him.”

But to return to what I began: wondrous swiftness, that marvellous course of saving grace, by which in three days he might wipe away the sins of the three ages of the world, and by Christ’s one death alike release all who had lived before the Law, all who had lived under the Law, and all who were to come under grace—assigning one day of that death for each of the several times. The Holy Spirit indicated the whole of that swiftness when, commanding the Prophet, he said: “Call his name: Hasten to strip the spoil; make haste to plunder” (Isa. 8).

## CHAPTER XV. Again, on the celebration of the resurrection
Concerning this, the Song of Songs also says: “Return; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel, my beloved” (Song 2). For he hastened to strip Hell of its spoils and hurried to seize booty; and, returning like a gazelle or a young stag—that is, like the son of the patriarchs, most swift in coming to save—he appeared upon the mountains of Bethel, that is, he was seen by the apostles, so as quickly to turn their sorrow into joy. They are the princes of Mount Bethel, that is, of the house of God, which is the Church, eminent in the highest virtues. He hastened, I say, [Col. 0195D] to strip Hell of its spoils—that is, to lead away, by the right of a conqueror, all the elect. For what delay could there be in stripping it, or what difficulty in distinguishing them? He was the sun; but those whom he sought were, as it were, mirrors. Their faith was a mirror, sufficiently capable of reflecting the sun’s appearance by its ray; but it had not hitherto shone, because the intervening wall of enmity stood opposed to the sun (Eph. 2), namely original sin. But Christ, dying in his flesh, had dissolved and torn down that wall which, by an adverse shadow, held in darkness those mirrors of souls awaiting the true sun. What delay, then, could there be, once the wall had been demolished and the true sun had descended into Hell, before those receptive vessels of light—that is, the souls of the elect—immediately shone forth? As soon as this sun descended there—[Col. 0196A] that is, the most powerful soul of Christ, flashing with the divinity of the omnipotent Word inherent in it—they shone brightly, and the princes of darkness were scattered “like smoke, and as wax melts before the fire” (Ps. 67 [68]). And the righteous, coming out from darkness and received into Paradise, began to feast and rejoice in the presence of God. The thief feasted with them, he to whom the Lord, hanging upon the cross, had said: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23). Throughout the whole Sabbath the Lord Christ rested from every work with them, and the Beloved fed among the lilies (Song 2), until the third day should breathe and the shadows decline.

Therefore on the third day, the divinity of the Trinity having been made propitious to us, he swiftly cast away from himself the death which he had tasted, as he had signified when, thirsting upon the cross for our salvation—and therefore saying truthfully that he thirsted—he refused to drink the vinegar offered to him. For he tasted a little of death’s vinegar, which he would soon—that is, on the third day—reject, and would drink no more. “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

## CHAPTER XVI. What it signifies that our Lord rose at night

Christian faith firmly maintains that our Lord, who became a mortal man in order to be judged, will come at the end in order to judge; and that he will show to those whom he judges, for the increase of their condemnation, that same form of a servant in which he was judged, bearing the scars of his wounds, so that they may see him whom they pierced (Zech. 12); but to his lovers he will show them as an everlasting memorial of charity. That day, however, [Col. 0196C] will come not with expectation, but like a thief in the night, as happened in the days of Noah and in the days of Lot, when all were selling and buying, planting and building, taking wives and giving them in marriage, and sudden destruction came upon them (Matt. 24). So it will be when the Son is revealed.

Appropriately, therefore, when the Judge, who was to come with judicial power, rose again, he chose the time of night, so that, just as in his other outward deeds and sayings he was accustomed to signify something else, so also in this he might signify the time of his second coming, which cannot be foreseen. Thus, just as Samson—whose name is interpreted “their sun”—besieged by enemies, rose by night, carried away the gates, [Col. 0196D] and ascended to the summit of the mountain (Judg. 16), so Christ our true Sun, surrounded by guards and weapons, rising at midnight from the sleep of death, carried off the gates of Hell—that is, every right of death—and ascended to the right hand of Majesty on high. By that very time he indicated that we must always be ready, because, just as he then rose at night while all rested, so he foretold that he would come at an hour when we do not expect him (Luke 12).

## CHAPTER XVII. What it signifies that he rose with an earthquake

The great earthquake which occurred likewise contributes to the signification of that same second coming. For there will be distress from the sea and its waves; and not only the earth, but also “the powers of heaven shall be shaken, and then [Col. 0197A] we shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24; Luke 21). When he came to suffer, indeed, he came hidden; but then, when he comes to judge, our God will come manifestly, and then he will not keep silence: before him is fire, a mighty tempest (Ps. 49 [50]). And because then the reprobate will wither from fear, while the righteous will raise their heads—that is, their hearts will be made glad—both are beautifully prefigured here by the appearance of one and the same angel, whose “countenance was like lightning, but whose garments were like snow.” For the wicked guards, terrified by the brightness of his appearance, became as dead men (Matt. 28); but the women who devoutly sought the Lord were comforted by his snowy garments and his gentle words: “Do not fear” (ibid.), and so forth.

Hence [Col. 0197B] we sing on this day: “The earth trembled and was still, when God arose in judgment” (Ps. 63 [64]). For this was said concerning that day when he will make judgment heard, saying to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25); but to those at his left: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid.). For when God, who now seems asleep or not to care for what is done under the sun, rises in judgment (Job 22), the earth will tremble and be still—that is, the wicked, who are earthly, will fear and become still because they will cease to harm others. This day, therefore, upon whose night our Lord rose with an earthquake, signifies that day of eternity, the day of the future resurrection, at whose dawn our same Lord will unexpectedly appear, as has been said, while the heavens burn and the powers of heaven tremble [Col. 0197C] (Luke 21).

## CHAPTER XVIII

That Matthew does not disagree with the other Evangelists when he says “the women at the evening of the Sabbath”; that they truly began to come in the evening and arrived at dawn; and why they acted thus.

It also mystically suggests something to us that the women devoted to Christ, who had loved him alive and longed for him dead, came to the tomb while walking through the night, aided by the moon. For they walked through the night, since they were at the tomb at dawn. Otherwise, unless they had come by night, how could they have been present at the sepulchre so early? For example, how could Mary Magdalene, whose home was at Bethany (John 20), a village fifteen stadia [Col. 0197D] from Jerusalem, have come, according to John, first among the others, on the first day of the week, to the tomb very early, while it was still dark?

For after the Lord’s burial the women who had followed him did not remain in Jerusalem. But when they had seen where he was laid, “returning,” Luke says, “they prepared spices” (Luke 23). Mark indicates more clearly when they prepared or bought them: “And when the Sabbath had passed,” he says, “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16). For on the Sabbath, as Luke says (Luke 23), they rested because of the commandment—understood to be that of the Law—because the Law forbids work on the Sabbath (Exod. 20).

It is therefore evident that, wakeful in tears through love, [Col. 0198A] and wearied by the overly long delay of the holding-back Sabbath, on which Jews were permitted neither to work nor to walk more than a thousand paces, as soon as that burdensome Sabbath had gone, departed, passed away, they did not rest or give sleep to their eyes (Ps. 131 [132]); nor did they wait for the morning star in order to set out. They took night for day, desire for guide, and the moon for sun. The moon did not fail the night, for it was then in its seventeenth day. The seventeenth-day moon rises shortly after the close of evening—that is, about half an hour afterward—and thereafter supplies its light throughout the whole night.

Some, therefore, have wrongly accused the Evangelists of saying contradictory things when Matthew says that the women came to the tomb at the evening of the Sabbath, while the others say that they came at dawn on the first day of the week. Matthew [Col. 0198B] stated when they began to come, in order to commend their longing; the others stated when they arrived.

What, then, does it mystically suggest to us that those women came in this way, except that faithful souls, ready—as 1 Thessalonians 5 says—that is, watchful in mind, loving and seeking the Lord, strive eagerly and swiftly to come to that advent of the Son of Man which, as stated above, will come like a thief in the night (John 19), not only with an earthquake but with the powers of heaven trembling, so that they may find consolation when the wicked will become not merely as, but truly, dead? Thus they now prepare and carry with them spices: that is, testimonies of the Lord’s resurrection, gathered from the garden-beds of Scripture together with the fragrance of virtues—namely, that his soul was truly not abandoned in Hell and that “his flesh [Col. 0198C] did not see corruption” (Ps. 15 [16]).

And just as it was not enough for those women that the righteous Joseph and Nicodemus had embalmed him with linen cloths and spices (Luke 23), while they themselves were present and watching, unless they too added something of their own to so great a work of devotion; so it is always desirable to holy and faithful minds to add some labor of their own to what the apostles or apostolic men wrote concerning faith in the resurrection. Almost all do this in speech or deed, and a few also in writing. Therefore, just as he showed himself alive to them, and, that he might be recognized, called Mary by her own name (John 20)—a great indication of his love; hence he says to Moses, “I know you by name” (Exod. 33)—so then he will be close to all who now seek him in truth [Col. 0198D] (Ps. 144 [145]), and will show them their names written in the book of life (Rev. 3).

## CHAPTER XIX

How much more rightly holy now is the first day of the week, on which the Redeemer of the world rose from the dead, than formerly was the Sabbath, on which the same Creator of the world ceased from his work.

How far the sanctification of the first day of the week, given to us, outweighs that sanctification by which the Sabbath was consecrated for the Jews may be perceived by comparing the causes and times of each sanctification. For from different and very unequal causes our Creator blessed the Sabbath, and our same Savior consecrated the first day of the week. [Col. 0199A] The cause of the Sabbath’s blessing was that God rested on it from every work which he had made (Gen. 2); whereas the cause of the first day of the week was that God, having become man, rose from the dead on it. Who does not see how widely different these are from one another?

For if God’s rest is the cause of a day’s sanctification, then where his rest is greater and truer, there the sanctification is more abundant. Likewise, where we observe greater labor in the worker, we recognize correspondingly greater rest in one who ceases from work. It is clear that he was not wearied while creating the world, since he worked all things through his Word and, ordering the universe, said of each thing, “Let it be,” and it was made. But the same one, when, to redeem the world, he became man (Heb. 2)—Christ, one and the same, God and man—suffered, was crucified, [Col. 0199B] and was buried, was beyond doubt afflicted with no slight weariness. Therefore, on the day on which he rose, crowned with glory and honor (Ps. 8), he entered into true rest, and rested far more excellently than when he ceased from the creation of the world.

For God rests not in the visible mass of worldly creation but in intellectual heavens, that is, in holy souls. Now the Bridegroom rejoices over the bride whom he purchased with his blood; God our God rejoices over us; and the daughters of kings delight him—or rather, because the Church is one, that queen delights him who stood at his right hand (Ps. 44 [45]), whom he prepares in the present and calls his friend, and whom in the future he will make drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35 [36]). No one, therefore, can doubt that the first day of the week was sanctified so much more abundantly as [Col. 0199C] Christ, God made man, rising, entered more truly into his own rest, which is the cause of sanctification.

Let us therefore leave to the Jews the old joy of their final Sabbath, which they find in the creation of the visible world. They have always delighted only in its passing fruit, always desired to rejoice only in its prosperity, and seemed to worship its Creator in servile fear only to obtain it. For they have always clung so closely to earthly things that whatever heavenly things were promised to them had always to be veiled beneath the names of earthly things which they love, as in this: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of the Lord; write them in your heart as though in a book, and I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. 6). Indeed, even God himself and the Lord through whom the world was made, coming unto his own, was not received by those who were his own; nor were they willing to understand that he was the King of the Jews, because, contrary to the expectation of their carnal understanding, he proclaimed blessedness to the poor and woe to the rich. They thought—[Col. 0199D] as they still dream now while Christ reigns—that they would possess on earth a golden, jeweled Jerusalem, with streets paved in pure gold.

Our Sabbath observance is transferred on this day from the seventh to the eighth, which is also the first. It is rightly transferred to the eighth because, as has been said, our joy is taken from a work other than the creation of the world. For God’s operation is twofold: first, the creation of the world; second, the salvation of the world. According to creation, “nothing new is done under the sun” (Eccl. 1), because he who lives forever created all things at once. According to salvation, Christ says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 8). Lovers of the world keep Sabbath from the creation of the world; but we ought to rejoice in the salvation of the world, for our life and rest are hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3).

## CHAPTER XX

By what rationale or authority, from this day of the Lord’s resurrection onward, a procession with the blessing of water is conducted on every Sunday throughout the year.

This day which the Lord made has this distinctive feature, and every first day of the week received it from this day: a solemn procession is conducted while the people are sprinkled with blessed water. [Col. 0200B] Yet on this first and chief of all Sundays itself, nor on holy Pentecost, is the water blessed, because it was taken on the preceding Sabbath evening from the sacred font of baptism, before anyone is immersed and before chrism has been put into it. For we are not sprinkled in order to be rebaptized; rather, with this memorial of our baptism, we ought frequently to invoke over ourselves the grace of the divine name. And we are sprinkled on each Sunday because, on the sacred evening of this first Sunday, the holy Church universally celebrates baptism, for the reason mentioned above.

Hence, while sprinkling on this day, we sing: “I saw water flowing from the temple’s right side, alleluia” (Ezek. 47), and so forth. This is taken from the prophet Ezekiel. The hand of the Lord, coming upon him, had shown him a city [Col. 0200C] built upon a high mountain and sloping southward, and in it a wonderful temple established (Rev. 1). That city signified the Church, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). What, then, is the temple but that of which he himself says: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will raise it,” speaking of the temple of his body? (John 21.) And John also, when speaking in the Apocalypse of that same city shown to him, says: “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

What water did he see flowing from this temple [Col. 0200D] if not the life-giving font of holy baptism? For when the Jews had destroyed it, blood and water, as stated above, came forth from his side. And rightly water came forth from the right side, of which it is said: “All to whom this water came were made whole.” For this temple, not made with hands, also has two sides. Its right side is the divine nature, its left side the human nature. It was therefore deliberately necessary to say from which side that water came forth, to all whom it came and they were made whole: “from the right side,” he says. And rightly so. For from Christ’s divine nature the Holy Spirit, the invisible water, proceeds; he gives saving power to the visible water which flowed from the left side—that is, from the humanity pierced by the lance.

Therefore, on this day of the Lord’s resurrection, also made solemn by the celebration [Col. 0201A] of the sacred baptistery, we rightly sing during the sprinkling that praise of this river, through whose flood we have been restored to life by Christ’s death. But on the other Sundays after Pentecost we sing: “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]). This too the Prophet foretold concerning faith in baptism: by hyssop, a lowly medicinal herb which reduces swelling of the lungs, signifying faith in Christ’s humility or passion; and by the phrase concerning the washing that whitens beyond snow, more clearly expressing baptism itself.

Then, with crosses and banners, which are the insignia of Christ’s victory, all clad in white and rejoicing in praise of the holy resurrection, we proceed amid such expectant joy of the assembled people, men and women, old and young alike, that even bodily that prophetic saying seems to be fulfilled in us: “You shall go out with gladness and be led forth with joy; for the mountains and hills shall leap, awaiting you with joy” (Isa. 55).

## CHAPTER XXI

Why the Lord summoned the disciples to Galilee to see him, although he was also seen in Jerusalem; and why a procession is held every Sunday.

That a procession is conducted is derived from the mystical authority of the Gospel: namely, from the fact that the angels command the women, saying, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee” (Mark 16); and that the Lord himself, meeting them as they came out from the tomb, when they had taken hold of his feet and worshiped him, said: “Go, tell [Col. 0201C] my brethren to go into Galilee; there they will see me” (John 20).

If we recognize the reason for this first command—that the risen Lord gives through his angels and in his own person to his disciples, that they should go into Galilee, “and there,” he says, “they shall see me”—we shall surely confess that it is fittingly done that we celebrate the remembrance of that command on this day and on every Sunday throughout the year by solemn observance, that is, by a procession. For not without cause or without the weight of divine counsel does he promise that he will be seen in Galilee, although he could have shown himself to them in Jerusalem; indeed, he was seen there five times on the very day on which he rose. If he intended to show them nothing in Galilee but his side, hands, and feet for touching and handling, this would seem to be done in vain or [Col. 0201D] without weighty reason—something wholly unfitting to divine majesty.

For according to both John and Luke he did this in Jerusalem on that very day, when the two disciples to whom he had appeared while going to Emmaus returned to Jerusalem and related what they had seen, and, as those with them wondered, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace be with you.” When he had said this, he showed them his hands and side (John 20; Luke 27). What, then, did he show in addition when he summoned them into Galilee? Surely this: what was hostile to earthly Jerusalem. Calling them away from that city and from the temple and old priesthood, he disclosed to them his purpose—or rather, the counsel of the whole Trinity: “All power,” he said, “has been given to me in heaven and on earth. [Col. 0202A] Going therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Behold, this is that great migration which Galilee itself commends by its name. Great, I say, was the migration commanded to Christ’s disciples: to migrate from the Jews to teaching and baptizing all nations, although he had previously said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10); and to migrate from the oldness of circumcision to the new grace of baptism, whose rule he then prescribed, though he had nowhere previously handed it down to them. A great cause indeed, and worthy for the Lord not only to declare in words but also to prefigure by a present deed. For just as before his passion he was accustomed to employ resemblances in many of his sayings or deeds—for example, just as, eight days before this, coming to suffer in order to redeem humankind, he signified that redemption of humankind by the loosing of the ass and her colt (Matt. 21)—so then, when he said to his apostles, [Col. 0202B] “Going, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), he wished to signify the same migration of his grace by Galilee, whose name is rendered in Latin as “migration.”

All this concerns us—that is, the Church from among the Gentiles—to which salvation migrated from the Jews through this command. Therefore, rightly and deservedly, in commemoration of this first command, which our Lord gave as soon as he was seen after the resurrection—“Tell my brethren,” he said, “to go into Galilee; there [Col. 0202C] they will see me” (John 20)—we hold a solemn procession and sprinkle ourselves and our places with blessed water, in honor of this day on which we were commanded to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXII. On what day the disciples, seeing the Lord in Galilee, worshiped him, according to Matthew

No one can doubt that on the day upon which the Lord rose—that is, on the first day of the week—he summoned the disciples into Galilee. But it is not entirely clear in itself on what day, according to Matthew (Matt. 28), they went there, saw him, and worshiped him. Jerome, however, maintains that this happened again on the first day of the week—that is, on the eighth day—and that it is the same appearance of which John says: “And after eight days his disciples were again within, and Thomas with them” (John 20). For Jerome says on Matthew: “After the resurrection the Lord is seen upon the mountain of Galilee and is there worshiped; although some doubt this, then he is shown more plainly to Thomas and displays his side wounded by the lance and his hands fixed with nails.” Therefore, although some who count the occasions on which the Lord is described as appearing after his resurrection may seem to think otherwise, we nevertheless judge that this interpretation of the aforementioned teacher should not be rejected.

Reason itself admits that the disciples, commanded so many times on the very day on which the Lord rose to go into Galilee, did not delay beyond eight days, especially since, when they saw him that evening, while Thomas was not with them, they could have conceived a most urgent hope and an even more burning desire to see him again. [Col. 0203A] Nothing in evangelical authority opposes Jerome. For John’s statement that “after eight days the disciples were again within” does not compel us to confess that they were within in the same place. They were indoors, but on the mountain—that is, in the city of Nazareth, situated upon a mountain in Galilee.

For thus we have it in Luke: after he had said that the Lord, having fasted forty days and forty nights, returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and, already renowned in Capernaum, came to Nazareth where he had been brought up; and after they said to him, “What great things we have heard done by you in Capernaum, do also here in your own country,” and he answered them, “Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel, and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow in Zarephath of Sidon” (1 Kings 17; Luke 4)—after, I say, the Evangelist had said these things, he immediately continued: “Filled with anger, they rose up and cast him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain upon which their city was built, that they might throw him down” (Luke 4).

We must not suppose, therefore, that the Lord went beforehand to any mountain other than Nazareth, which was situated upon a mountain, and summoned his disciples there. Thus, as has been said, no evangelical authority conflicts with Jerome. After eight days they were indeed indoors, but not in the same house or the same city. And fittingly, in the place where he endured his first persecution and first prefigured the Jews’ rejection and the passage to the Gentiles—as is written after the words cited above, “But Jesus, passing through their midst, went away” (ibid.)—there, after all persecutions, he abandoned the Jews and changed their rite, abolishing circumcision and commanding all nations [Col. 0203C] to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIII

That it was prophetically said concerning our Redeemer: “Naphtali, a hind sent forth, giving words of beauty.”

At the same time it should be noted that where he preached most before his passion, in the borders of Zebulun and [Col. 0203D] Naphtali, as we have in the Gospel, beyond the Jordan in Galilee, there after his resurrection he completed the same teaching by giving the command to baptize and teach. Thus, as the Evangelist himself subsequently applies the testimony of the prophet, “the people of the Gentiles, who walked in darkness, saw a great light” (Isa. 19), he also fulfilled that prophecy which says: “Naphtali, a hind sent forth, giving words of beauty” (Gen. 49).

For, sent forth by divine power from the pursuit of the dogs, of whom he himself says through David’s mouth, “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. 21 [22]), sent forth, I say, into full safety, he hastened back with the swiftest leap of resurrection to the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, where he had first begun to teach. He himself became Naphtali—that is, “expanded”—namely through the expedition of charity; and he gave those words of beauty already mentioned concerning us Gentiles who were to be baptized, concluding thus: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt., final chapter).

## CHAPTER XXIV. Again, on the procession, according to its variation among different orders of monks and canons

The aforesaid procession is conducted so that we always find before us, at the place where we stand for the final station, the priest going ahead and visiting the offices, with a cross. This also depends upon the same authority of the Gospel. For our Lord, whose person the priest bears in his office, as has already been said elsewhere, stated both before his passion and after his resurrection that on this day he would go before his disciples into Galilee. For on the night in which he was betrayed he said: “But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee”; and when he had risen, as we read on this day, the angel said: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26; Mark 16).

In beautiful accord with this signification is also the prayer which the priest says there—that is, at the final station—addressed to the person of the Son: “Lord Jesus Christ, who sanctified the gateway of the gates of Jerusalem,” and so forth. For it is directed to the person of the Son; under the name Jerusalem, the Church is mentioned, built from all baptized nations; and under the name of its gates [Col. 0204C] is signified the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, in which they are baptized. This accords with the Apocalypse, where, as a signification of that same divine name, the city—which signifies the Church—has “three gates from the east, three gates from the west, three gates from the north, and three gates from the south” (Rev. 21), because, at whatever age they come to faith in Christ—whether in childhood, adolescence, youth, or old age—“the name comes fourfold to the crossroads,” as Prudentius says.

Thus it comes about that this entire procession is nothing other than thanksgiving because the risen Lord, immediately mindful of us who were without God (Eph. 2), summoned his disciples into Galilee for the purpose of baptizing us in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0204D] Hence we also call Galilee the place where we end the procession in the final station; and in a procession of this kind—that is, a Sunday procession—the chief persons after our prelate always follow the priest who goes ahead, just as the more worthy members follow the head. Taught also by the examples of our elders, and because it agrees with the matter already stated, we observe that on no Sunday do we ever sing in this procession anything belonging to the Old Testament history, but always something from the New Testament and sounding forth the glory of the Gospel.

But the present discourse concerns this chief day of Easter, by which every first day of the week was distinguished and called the Lord’s Day: the day on which our Lord deigned, as stated, to summon our fathers, the apostles, into Galilee to hear the counsel of grace. The station of this day, at which the procession ends, splendidly arranged in the middle of the church, beautifully commends the matter under discussion, while the whole sacred choir of the Church in festal array, with people of both sexes standing around, happily bursts forth with all its strength into a voice of exultation and salvation, singing the antiphon: “The angel sat at the Lord’s tomb” (Mark 16).

For this antiphon plainly expresses the very matter which the apostles were commanded to teach to all nations: namely, that God, having become man, conquered our death by dying and restored life to us by rising again. The melody joined to the words accords greatly with this matter: the chant, harmoniously composed in the lively manner of the fourth mode (*tetrardus*), repeatedly dances with nimble return, suspending the festal words; and, uttering joyful sounds, flits repeatedly like a morning lark among the high points of its voices. This station, therefore, commemorates to us in festive harmony what the heavens, commanded in Galilee by their Creator, declared: the glory of God (Ps. 18 [19]), the glory of Christ’s resurrection, as we read that “with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” (Acts 4). This must therefore be sung with all our strength and proclaimed with all heart and mouth in the hearing of the people who stand around, because “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0205C]

That we rightly place blessed Mary at the beginning of our joy in this procession, turning aside at the first station on every Sunday for her commemoration; that it should not be believed that she did not see the risen Lord; and that the mother ought not to have been written among the witnesses.

Rightly and laudably our elders—that is, those of our monastic order—handed down, and it has hitherto been kept as a fixed and inviolable law, that in processions of this kind, on every Sunday throughout the year, we visit in the first station the memorial of the blessed Mother of God, singing whatever belongs especially to her; and, after greeting her and saying the prayer, only then perform the procession in the order described above. [Col. 0205D] Thus, through the fervent zeal of holy religion, provision has been made that within the cloister there should be a chapel of this blessed Virgin, consecrated in her honor—above all, indeed, this particular oratory bearing her name.

What more fitting thing could Christian devotion devise in keeping with the Gospel faith? What more beautiful, what more venerable, than to rejoice with the Virgin Mother over the resurrection of her only-begotten Son, who will die no more, and in whose Passion a sword pierced her soul? (Luke 2.) Christian devotion delights to consider how great a torrent of joy, suddenly overflowing and filling the place of the wound, intoxicated her soul, pierced by the sword of grief, when her Son returned alive and—perhaps before all other mortals, not depriving the Virgin of her maternal honor—announced to her his victory [Col. 0206A] and offered for her kisses the sweet wounds of his flesh: that flesh which she had conceived as true flesh from her own flesh and borne.

What then? Will this seem to conflict with the Gospel, which relates that the risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene? Far be it. But we except the blessed Virgin Mother from the witnesses appointed beforehand—those alone whom it belonged to the Evangelists to name, or whom it was fitting to announce Christ’s resurrection. Was it fitting that she should announce it, so that her words might appear as nonsense before the apostles? For if the words of women who were strangers appeared to them as nonsense (Luke 24), how much more would they have believed that the mother was raving through love for her Son? Most truly, therefore, the risen Son appeared to his Mother; but she, as she had begun from the beginning, so now too “kept [Col. 0206B] all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2).

If this does not seem true for the reason that none of the Evangelists attests it in writing, it follows that after his resurrection he was never seen by his Mother, since none of them expressly says when or where he appeared to her. But far be this from him who commanded in his law that father and mother be honored (Exod. 20); far be it, I say, that such a Son should have dishonored by such harsh neglect the Mother who, on his account, had been pierced through by the sword of grief (Matt. 15). The apostolic truth of the holy Roman Church did not think so; it set this blessed Jerusalem at the beginning of its joy. For when, on this first day of Easter, it prescribed the station at this Holy Mary of whom we speak for the office of Mass, what else did it do than set [Col. 0206C] Jerusalem at the beginning of its joy?

For if every soul fearing the Lord is thus blessed, “that it may see the good things of Jerusalem, and see its children’s children, peace upon Israel” (Ps. 127), and therefore is itself called and is Jerusalem—that is, “vision of peace”—how much more should this thrice- and four-times-blessed Virgin be called Jerusalem, who, “blessed among all women” (Luke 1), saw her Son, peace above all true Israel: namely, Christ, of whom the Apostle says, “For he himself is our peace, who has made both one” (Eph. 2). She above all others, she before all others, saw this peace of ours. She is Jerusalem: beautiful, chosen, sweet, and fair, whom the daughters of Zion saw (Song 6), [Col. 0206D] called blessed, and whom queens praised.

Therefore, when the holy Roman Church, in today’s station, as has been said, set her at the beginning of its joy, it did not suppose that she had not seen peace coming upon Israel—that is, her Son rising for our justification (Rom. 4). But let the discourse return to the particular reason, mentioned above, for today’s procession and for all Sunday processions. At the time when the eleven disciples went away into Galilee (Matt. 18), to the mountain appointed for them by the Lord Jesus, did they pass by this blessed Mary of whom we speak, and see and worship him without her? Certainly not. They went to no house other than hers, and to no mountain other than that upon which [Col. 0207A] her city Nazareth stood, as has already been said, when they saw him.

Accordingly, it was beautifully and laudably handed down by our elders, as we said above, that in today’s procession and in all Sunday processions throughout the year we visit the memorial of the blessed Mother of God in the first station, for the same reason for which the station at Saint Mary is prescribed for the office of today’s Mass: that we may set her, as has been said, at the beginning of our joy, recalling the words of the Song of Songs and not vainly judging that the new Bridegroom of the new Church, as soon as he rose, said: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” (Song 4).

For in what part of his body did the eminence of the Church rise more highly, after Christ himself, its head, than in the singular merits of this queen of angels, from whose flesh Christ was brought forth without a man, [Col. 0207B] “like a stone cut from a mountain without hands” (Dan. 2)? And on what mountain summit could so much myrrh—that is, mortification—together with the fragrances of incense—that is, devout prayer—[Col. 0208A] be found as in the soul of this blessed Virgin, uniquely pierced by the sword of the Lord’s Passion?

To this mountain of myrrh, therefore, we too go, turning aside in the oft-mentioned station at Saint Mary. On this day, rejoicing mystically, we bring forth in song those same words of the released stag, mentioned above—“words of beauty” (Gen. 49)—by which he there commanded that all nations should be baptized: “You are wholly beautiful.” For it is the familiar judgment of nearly all teachers that by these words the new Church is invited to rise and hasten, the apostolic Church, which was then small in number, to come from Lebanon (Song 4)—that is, to bring the nations to Christ through the whitening of baptism—with Mary, the Mother of our faith, helping; that is, now revealing “all these words which [Col. 0208B] she had hitherto kept in her heart” (Luke 2).

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0207]

## CHAPTER I. On the Mass of the Same Day

The whole office of the present day, in all its parts, looks toward that day of eternity, access to which God opened for us through his Only-begotten Son, after conquering death; there “the righteous shall feast and exult in the presence of God” (Ps. 67), who now feast, as we sing and read, “on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5), and “shall drink the good wine” which was made from water at the heavenly wedding (John 2): that is, they shall delight in the glory of immortality and impassibility, wholly transformed from mortal corruption.

And rightly so: since Pascha means “passage,” the Paschal chant of this present day looks toward that place where a homeland has been established for those who pass over. Then the holy city Jerusalem will shine with eternal newness, and, itself new, “having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5), will sing a new Song. The teacher and precentor of that eternal Song will be her new Bridegroom, who rose first. When the Father said to him, as we have in the Psalm, [Col. 0207D] “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp,” he answered, “I will arise at dawn” (Pss. 56, 107).

Rightly, therefore, in the Introit of today’s office, he who rose first utters the first voice, saying: “I have risen, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138). Paul invites and instructs us toward the newness of this Song in the following Epistle reading: “Purge out,” he says, “the old leaven, that you may be a new lump” (1 Cor. 5), and so forth. By an evident comparison he teaches the baptized, exhorting us to be a new lump—that is, without leaven—because the one body of the Church is made from many human beings as one loaf is made from many grains.

From what sort of thing this bread is leavened and rendered unworthy of the Paschal table, we clearly learn from what he had said above to the Corinthians. For he had said: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such immorality as is not even among the Gentiles: that one should have his father’s wife” (ibid.). And shortly after: “Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven” [Col. 0208C] (ibid.), and so forth.

Thus, by this reading, the composer of the Church’s office intended to impress upon Christ’s Church that it should preserve unstained the bridal garment received in baptism, since Christ desires to present her to himself as a glorious bride, “having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5). For sexual immorality, on account of which this reading was written, as was said above, or any other condemnable vice, is the old leaven: the disease of the old man, the stain of the old life.

Therefore, since this day proclaims newness of life and announces eternal youth, the diligence of the Roman Church is indeed to be admired and praised also in establishing that the Gospel according to Mark should be read in the present office. For, besides being likened to the lion in the wondrous figure of the four living creatures, and besides the appropriateness of reading his Gospel so that the lion might proclaim the roar of the risen lion, of whom it had been foretold: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have ascended.
