Resting, you have lain down as a lion and as a lioness; who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49)—besides this, I say, his Gospel is especially fitting to the office of this day because he calls the messenger of the holy Resurrection, whom the others simply call an angel, by the more profound mystery, a young man: “They saw,” he says, “a young man sitting at the right, clothed in a white robe” (Mark 16).

These two expressions I have cited—“a young man” and “clothed in a white robe”—proclaim likewise the two things said by the Apostle in praise [Col. 0209A] and honor of the glorious Church: namely, “having no spot” and “having no wrinkle” (Eph. 5). For because the glorious Church, for which Christ died and for whose justification he rose (Rom. 4), will have no wrinkle of the old man whom she put off in that glorious resurrection for which she now prepares herself by purging out the old leaven, as has been said, the holy Evangelist rightly calls the angel, herald of that same resurrection, a young man. And because she will have no stain—the stain from which her Bridegroom washed her in his blood, from her sins (Rev. 22)—he fittingly and carefully described him, as he truly was, as clothed in a white robe.

Therefore, with most careful design, the Gospel of Christ’s Resurrection according to Mark is read on this day, in which the young man seated at the right side of the Lord’s tomb and clothed in a white robe proclaims by his very appearance to our baptized people—whose youth “has been renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102)—what they have received and what they should hope for. All the parts of the office harmonize in this proclamation, most especially and unanimously crying out that, having purged away the old leaven, feasting “on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5), we should so preserve the first resurrection of baptism that we may be prepared for the eternal youth of the second resurrection.

Then, as we sing in the Offertory, when God rises in judgment—he who is now thought to sleep and not care for human affairs—the earth will tremble and be at rest (Ps. 75): that is, the wicked will be terrified, and, handed over to Gehenna, will cease to do harm; and the place of the Lord, namely the Church, will be in peace. And in Zion, now young and [Col. 0209C] white, as the appearance of the aforementioned angel proclaims, all opposing powers—the bow, shield, sword, and wars of vices—will be broken.

The Gradual, which is the chant of those laboring in this pilgrimage, has already been said not to belong to these days of the Resurrection until Pentecost, but to have been added to the offices through this week on account of the baptized. Yet, just as present joy from the recent remission of sins relieves the toil of the warfare which those for whom it was added have undertaken, so the words customary to the neumes of the Gradual brighten the day, daily resounding: “This is the day which the Lord has made.” That we must exult and rejoice in it we receive both from the verse itself and from its verses, taken from the same Psalm and distributed throughout the week.

## CHAPTER II. On the Unusual Order of Evening Praise, the Reason for Which Is the Solemnity of the Holy Baptistery During This Week

[Col. 0209D]

Although all the regular hours mentioned above display tokens of newness and joy, the evening synaxis is nevertheless adorned more splendidly by the brightness of this feast, according to the Roman order. Since baptism was celebrated on the evening of Easter Saturday, that same hour retains throughout the festive week the joy of regeneration in the following manner.

First, because in the rite of baptism the *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—was begun and the litany was sung three times in honor and reverence of the adorable name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whose name baptism is performed: [Col. 0210A] therefore the office begins, not as usual with the verse, “O God, attend to help me,” but with the festive harmony of *Kyrie eleison*.

For the same reason there follow three Psalms, to be sung under one *alleluia*, which do not change throughout the week: both because this whole week is counted as one day, because it looks toward the universal day of Resurrection; and because both these psalms and the others reserved for the processions of which we must speak are marked with the eminent title *alleluia*, which we know is fitting—indeed, proper—to the subject and season.

Nevertheless, the first—namely, “The Lord said” (Ps. 109)—alone does not have *alleluia* in its title. It is sung most especially in praise of Christ, both according to his divinity and according to his humanity, on the authority of God the Father; throughout its course it treats of his glorious and ineffable exaltation, by which, having drunk from the torrent of death, he today exalted his own head.

After the three Psalms, in place of the chapter, the canticle is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made,” as it is at all the regular hours; nevertheless, because of the greatness of the joy to be signified, it is sung in place of the chapter. Then *alleluia* with its verse is sung in place of a hymn, because *alleluia* is the proper hymn of the heavenly homeland. After the Gospel canticle with its antiphon and after the prayer has been said, they proceed to the fonts with the Psalm, “Praise, O servants, the Lord” (Ps. 117), which, itself marked *alleluia* in its title, plainly suits those for whom it is reserved: the sacred fonts.

For it is an exhortation to divine praise addressed to children—that is, to the new children of the Church, who through baptism have become children, that is, pure from vices. This whole Psalm is directed only to believers from among the Gentiles, as is easily seen from its saying: “Who makes the barren woman dwell in the house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112). That is, he makes Gentile humanity, formerly barren but now a mother of children according to faith, dwell in the house—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem—fulfilling the prophecy: “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear” (Isa. 54; Gal. 4).

Therefore now, at the fonts, the Church our mother exults rejoicing in praise of that grace through which she merited to become, as she heard in the Song of Songs: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing in force from Lebanon, so that [Col. 0210D] its shoots may be a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard: cypress with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, myrrh and aloes, with all the trees of Lebanon” (Song 4). All these things, by their various properties, signify the different merits or spiritual advances of those who have been planted into the likeness of Christ’s death in the font of baptism (Rom. 6); but it is not now the place to discuss them individually.

When this station is finished, one proceeds thence to the oratory of Saint Andrew the Apostle, singing: “When Israel went out.” This signifies the departure of those who, reborn as Israel—that is, “those seeing God”—go out from the Egypt of this world and from the barbarous people of unbelievers, from the sea—that is, the depth of the Gentiles—and from the Jordan, that is, the Jews; for the Jordan is the river of the Jews’ land, and it is interpreted as “flowing backward.” The Gentiles and Jews, I say, see the wonders worked through those who depart, [Col. 0211A] and flee backward from unbelief to faith, from flesh to spirit, from the devil to God, whom they had abandoned.

Hence the mountains—that is, the apostles—and the hills—that is, their disciples—leap like rams and lambs of sheep, rejoicing and saying: “What ails you, O sea, that you fled? And you, O Jordan, that you turned back?” Thus every evening of the Paschal week is completed by a threefold station at the hour when baptism was celebrated on Saturday in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Perhaps this is why nearly every evening ends at Saint Andrew: because blessed Gregory, who arranged the stations as they have hitherto been observed, was especially devoted to that Saint Andrew. Near his basilica and the basilica of Saints John and Paul on the Clivus Scauri, he established a monastery in his own house, [Col. 0211B] in which, leaving everything behind, he escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world and put on the long-desired monastic garment.

Nor is it surprising that, out of devotion, he consecrated this evening station to so great an apostle, since he also made more distinguished the station at Saints Cosmas and Damian, on the day when “I am the salvation of the people” is sung. He dedicated it to those same saints with its own solemn collects, as many observe even now, because his great-grandfather Felix IV, bishop of the Apostolic See, a man held in great reverence in Christ’s Church, most beautifully built the basilica of these saints on the Via Sacra beside the temple of Romulus, as may still be seen.

Possibly also the fact that only three readings are read at the night vigils according to the Roman order refers to the majesty of the divine name—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—in whose name baptism was celebrated. For for what reason would the readings be multiplied beyond this number? Our preachers, whom, as has already been said elsewhere, the larger number of readings in solemnities signifies—for under the time of grace more heralds of truth began to be sent—those preachers of the Gospel, that is, the apostles, were then silent and hidden. Nor did they, as was their custom while the Lord dwelt with them, go about the villages, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere (Luke 9).

Let no one object that more readings were read on the three mournful nights preceding. For a different rationale for those has been set down in its place. Thus the number three, made illustrious by the authority of the divine name in baptism, fittingly takes first place in this feast both in Psalms and in readings.

## CHAPTER III. Why Monks, No Less Than Canons, Ought Not Alter Their Customary Rule During These Days

Although the matters mentioned above have a theoretical rationale, our own order—that is, the monastic order—must not alter its equally authoritative rule. For example, it must not reduce the night vigils of any Sunday to three readings, nor remove the litany prayers from the regular hours and make joyful *alleluia* resound in their place, on the ground that in that blessedness signified by this Paschal solemnity there will be no supplication of the wretched but only [Col. 0212A] the praise of the blessed.

Nor should they, because they do not have fonts, devise in their own places the evening stations said to be held on account of the solemnities of the fonts. For these are pontifical traditions belonging to the shepherds of the people. And although blessed Gregory, who arranged the stations and, taught by the finger of God, refined almost all the splendor of the clergy, excelled in monastic dress, such customs must still not be maintained by the monastic order. In transmitting them for pontifical office, he instituted them for the ministers of the lower—that is, active—life.

For the holy Fathers never had such a practice of commanding contrary or conflicting things. Blessed Benedict had, before Gregory, commanded—as blessed Gregory himself asserts, Benedict was full of the spirit of all the righteous—that on Sunday never fewer than twelve readings be read at the night vigils. Likewise, for the other regular hours, he had prescribed a universal rule for his order without any exception.

Therefore one must not believe that blessed Gregory, when instituting the order of active life—to which, in his letters, he laments that he had descended—wished in any respect to turn the higher order, that is, the order of contemplative life, in the opposite direction. Each order, then, more rightly keeps its own rule, according to the words: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Jer. 31; Hab. 3).

They agree only in this: that until Pentecost, not bending the knee but praying while standing, we confess by this sign the freedom which Christ acquired for us by rising; that we say *alleluia* without interruption; and that we, the children of the Bridegroom, do not fast because the Bridegroom is with us. Otherwise, whoever in the monastic order cuts from the regular hours during this week the litany’s supplication—that is, *Kyrie eleison*—for the reason stated above, must consequently not restore it until Pentecost. For not this week alone, but all these fifty days signify the eternal Jubilee of the future Resurrection, in which nothing will any longer be supplicated, but there will be exultation and rejoicing only in perfect salvation.

## CHAPTER IV

How Appropriately Faith in the Resurrection Was Confirmed Through Forty Days; Together with an Account of a Miracle Shown to a Certain Brother in This Year, 1111 from the Incarnation of the Lord

[Col. 0212D]

Truly wonderful and worthy of proclamation is the diligent love of our Savior. Though he suffered for our offenses and rose for our justification (Rom. 4), nevertheless, for our instruction, he delayed the glory of his ascension for forty days, during which he presented himself alive by many proofs to his apostles, whom he chose to be witnesses of his resurrection (Acts 1).

For on the very day on which, rising, he ascended above the west (Ps. 67), he could also have made the cloud his ascent (Ps. 103), and, having once shown his true humanity to his witnesses, the true divinity of the Word could with the same swiftness with which he had raised it have placed it at the right hand of the Father’s majesty after three or a few more days. Great, therefore, was that love—and truly not seeking its own things (1 Cor. 13)—which, to assist those slow to believe, delayed Christ’s triumphant ascension (Luke 24), and, in order to show grace brought to completion, postponed the glory prepared for the victor.

Woe, then, to faithless heretics, whom this lawful number of forty days, after they have been awaited and remain uncorrected, at last subjects to a just sentence. For forty days is also among human beings the legitimate period for prolonging deliberations, so that a person whose counsel is sought, even if he is lunatic—that is, foolish, since “the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27)—if, after waiting so many days, he has not accepted sound counsel, may be judged justly; because within forty days the moon changes. Thus he is more than a fool who has not changed through so many days.

But it is pleasing to prove by another parallel from the ancient Scripture of divine authority that those who disparage the resurrection of the dead rightly deserve never to attain the glory of that same resurrection, which, examined through forty days, they still slander with stubborn impiety.

We read in the book of Numbers that the Lord, speaking to Moses in the wilderness of Paran, said: “Send men to examine the land which I will give to the children of Israel, one from each tribe of the leaders—that is, twelve men. When they had gone up, they explored the land; and they went up toward the south, proceeding to the torrent of the Cluster, and cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole,” [Col. 0213C] and so forth.

When the scouts returned after forty days, having gone around the whole region, some of them disparaged before the children of Israel the land they had inspected, saying: “The land which we have surveyed devours its inhabitants.” But Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh said: “The land which we have surveyed is very good. If the Lord is favorable to us, he will bring us into it and give us that land flowing with milk and honey.” And when the whole multitude cried out and wished to crush them with stones, the Lord appeared and said: “All the men who have seen my majesty and the signs which I wrought in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have now tested me ten times—none who has disparaged me shall see the land concerning [Col. 0213D] which I swore to their fathers” (Num. 13–14).

The apostle Paul too bears witness that these things happened to them as a figure. For when, speaking of this sacred history, he had said: “Our fathers all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ—but God was not pleased with most of them; for they were struck down in the wilderness.” And because they tested Christ, “they perished by serpents”; and because they murmured, they perished “by the destroyer”; he immediately adds: “Now all these things happened to them as figures, but they were written for our correction, upon whom [Col. 0214A] the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10).

They happened as a figure, plainly, of what other things than those done in this end of the ages—that is, in this sixth age of the world? Christ the Lord, having defeated the king of Egypt—that is, the prince of darkness—led his people through the Red Sea of his baptism; and now governs them through the wilderness of the present life, that he may bring them into the promise of the eternal inheritance: namely, into the blessed glory of resurrection of which we now speak.

For what “land flowing with milk and honey” should we hope from him, if not conformity to the body of Christ which rose, “in whom dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2), so that through it, as the Apostle says (Phil. 3), he may refashion our body of humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory? Therefore those who deny the truth of that resurrection, like scoffers, tempters who desire evil things, and murmurers, are justly struck down in the wilderness, perish, and are destroyed by the destroyer.

For the Gospel Scripture reports that the land of Christ’s flesh was examined by many proofs for the same number—that is, forty—days, establishing that he truly rose from the dead (Acts 1), so that we may truly know from it what the condition of our future resurrection will be. The scouts of faith went up toward the south—that is, where Christ, the true Sun, was lifted up through the most high resurrection—and brought us the cluster with its branch, borne by two men: Christ himself, to whom the Bride says in the Song of Songs, “My beloved is a cluster of cypress to me” (Song 1). They bear him, I say, [Col. 0214C] on a pole, two men: that is, hanging upon the wood of the cross in the true body in which he rose.

Two men bear this one whom they have taken up, that is, the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile. And just as the one in front among those carrying the cluster bore it indeed but did not see it because his back was turned, while the one behind both bore it and saw it, so the first people, the Jewish people, bears in the Scriptures the testimonies of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, but does not believe with a turned-away heart and therefore does not understand. The latter people, the Gentile people, both bears and sees, because what it reads it understands by believing, and believes by understanding.

Bringing this cluster, therefore, the scouts of truth—that is, those proclaiming Christ—the apostles, faithful witnesses, tell us in writings (1 Cor. 5) and tell us by miracles concerning the glory of the resurrection for which we hope: “The land which we surveyed is good, as may be known from these fruits” (Num. 13). For how is it unlike this which they announce to us: that the incorruptible glory of resurrection is put upon flesh, and that the true, same nature of that flesh remains? “We surveyed it,” they say, “we saw and examined it; our hands handled the Word of life” (1 John 1). For we put forth our hands and felt his side; we handled the scars of his wounds in his hands and feet, as he said: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” And “we ate,” they say, “and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (John 20).

But those who likewise went up to explore Scripture, filled with an alien spirit, false and deceiving, deny that the true nature of bodies will rise and suspect that the Lord’s body after the resurrection was phantasmal—that is, more subtle than winds and air. How are these unlike those murmurers who disparaged the land they had inspected, saying: “This land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants” (Num. 13)? For the life we hope for devours its inhabitants if it admits us in no other way than with the true nature of bodies perishing in those who rise.

They argue and say: How was the Lord’s body true after the resurrection, when he entered to the disciples through closed doors? (John 20.) I would seem to fling words into the wind if I wished to hurl many argumentative shafts of reply against these enemies of the Christian faith. For those little foxes have long since been terrified by the thunder of heaven—that is, by the voice of the thundering Church—and wherever they are they hide in underground dens. They do not dare to come out, according to their foul custom, to destroy with their rotten teeth the flowering, fruit-bearing vineyards (Song 11 [perhaps OCR for Song 2]).

But behold: while we write these things, the grace of the risen one smiles upon us through a joyful miracle involving one of our brothers. I call to witness that blessed and delightful night in which Christ rose victorious from the lower world: I am telling no lie concerning this, unless he is so sacrilegious as to have dared to invent anything in such a matter—something which his life and profession wholly forbid even us to suspect. Yet his name will be concealed, because he earnestly asks this also. For he desires that the event should shine before people, so that the Father in heaven may be glorified (Matt. 5); but he does not wish himself to be seen, nor does he attribute the miracle to his own merits, since God’s grace alone is its agent, by a judgment we do not know. For many will come on that day saying: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and work many mighty deeds in your name?” And he will answer them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know where you are from” (Matt. 7).

The matter is this. On this holy Easter Saturday, when the year 1111 from the Incarnation of the Lord was inscribed on the candle—of whose proclamations we have also said something above—at the church of Saint Lawrence, at the preceding Matins of that day, after all the lights had been extinguished according to custom, while the last of them was being put out and Lord Abbot Berengar was beginning this antiphon for the Gospel canticle—“The women sitting at the tomb”—the belt with which this brother was tightly girded suddenly fell before his feet as though thrown down.

He thought it had come loose and fallen; yet this would have been remarkable, since it had not slipped down or descended around his legs and feet, but had sprung out before his feet as though thrown down, as was said. He bent down to pick it up and gird himself again. But when he put his hands to it to wrap it around himself, he was beyond measure astonished that it did not yield to him, still being as tightly bound as it was. As he looked closely and reflected to himself in great amazement what this might mean for him, behold, there came a voice, and he heard a whisper like a gentle breeze saying to him:

> Thus Christ could come forth from the closed tomb.

Indeed, as he himself testified in recounting it, this question often came into his mind: how the true body of the Lord—of which he did not in the least doubt—could rise from a closed tomb and enter to the disciples through closed doors. At once he recalled that similar incident which Augustine recounts in the *City of God*, concerning a certain Petronia, a woman of very high rank, who was miraculously cured of a severe and prolonged pain, when every medical remedy had failed. She said that a Jew had persuaded her to insert a ring into a thread-like binding, so that it should be tied around her naked body beneath all her clothing; and that the ring had, beneath its gem, a stone found in the kidneys of an ox. Bound with this supposed remedy, she was coming to the threshold of the holy martyr Stephen. But having set out from Carthage, when she had stayed on her estate near the river Bagrada, she rose to continue her journey and saw the ring lying before her feet. Amazed, she examined the thread-like band by which it had been tied. When she found it still fastened exactly as it had been, its knots wholly intact and very firm, she supposed that the ring had burst forth and sprung out. Since the ring itself too was found entirely unbroken, she presumed that she had received, through so great a miracle, a kind of pledge of her future healing; and, untying the binding, she threw it together with the ring into the river. “Let not those believe this,” says Augustine himself, “who do not believe that the Lord Jesus was brought forth through the intact virginity of his mother, and entered to the disciples while the doors were closed.”

Let these two outstanding miracles of divine mercy now be compared: this recent one, in which a man’s belt, firmly fastened about his loins and still unloosed, passed through him and sprang away; and that more ancient one, in which a ring set into a girdle burst out while the knot remained intact. I do not know what I should wonder at more, except that here likewise, as stated above, a voice was heard from heaven:

> Thus Christ could come forth from the closed tomb.

When I received this account—namely, in the morning, at the first opportunity for speaking, when that brother, still astonished, related the event to only two brethren, one of whom was myself, earnestly begging that we should never disclose the secret entrusted to us together with his name—when, I say, I received it, I eagerly embraced it as a miracle offered by God especially for my own purposes. For on that same night, and a little before the very hour at which this occurred, I had begun to ponder the aforesaid comparison: namely, that those who disparage faith in the resurrection, and therefore do not believe that the true nature of flesh will rise again, because the Lord rose from a closed tomb or entered to the disciples through closed doors, are like those who disparaged the land which they had inspected before the children of Israel, saying: “The land which we have explored devours its inhabitants.”

[Col. 0217A] It is therefore not inopportune that this discourse on the glory of the resurrection is now drawn out at greater length, since heavenly miracles, freely presenting themselves, add material to what has been begun. Even if these things were lacking, Christian faith could not catch the wise in their own cunning: while they avoid believing that a true body could enter through closed doors—which is above nature—they escape into that judgment which says that it became subtler than winds and air—which is against nature. For they not only do not help themselves at all, but entangle themselves still more: in defending nature from what is above it, they reduce it to what is contrary to it. Both are miracles; but the former, as said, is above nature, whereas the latter, imagined by heretics—namely, that a tangible body became intangible—is indeed a greater miracle, but a useless miracle and one contrary to nature. What Divinity preferred, whether what is contrary to nature or what is above nature, he plainly shows in the Psalm, saying: “You have laid your hand upon me” (Ps. 138). But now, by setting forth the examples mentioned above—that a true human body passed beyond the true body of its belt, that is, a deer-skin girdle firmly bound with a knot, and that of old a ring sprang forth while the knot remained unloosed—Divinity proposes:

> Thus Christ could come forth from the closed tomb.

Reason takes up the argument: “But those things occurred above nature.” Faith concludes: “Above nature, therefore the true body of Christ could come forth from the closed tomb and enter to the disciples through closed doors.” And this truly befitted God: to use his power in such a way that he did not destroy the nature which he had made, but conveyed or brought it, while it remained the same—indeed, perfected—to whatever place and from whatever place he willed. Whoever does not grant this must, still less, grant that the Apostles, still corruptible and mortal, were brought out in the manner written in the Acts of the Apostles: “We found the prison indeed closed with all care, and the guards standing before the doors; but when we opened the prison, we found no one inside” (Acts I [cf. Acts 5:23]). If he accepts Holy Scripture, he must assert that these men too, who had not yet risen, vanished into winds and thin air so that they could be breathed out through open cracks. Those who do not accept it are not to be heard, but are wholly to be avoided as unbelievers.

For us who believe, this suffices as proof: God created all things from nothing, and all things are accounted by him as if they were nothing and emptiness for doing whatever he wills, for conveying anything wherever he wills. Indeed, it would be more marvelous if he could not do so, since scarcely any craftsman is so unskilled that he cannot himself penetrate or open what he has made. But when he willed, “the earth opened and swallowed Dathan” (Num. 16), and immediately, closing its mouth, covered the assembly of Abiron [Abiram], who had become leaders of sedition, disparaging God’s promises and saying mockingly: “So indeed you have brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey!” (ibid.). Those who dared, as stated above, to disparage faith in the resurrection should have avoided their example; for they too belong to those of whom the Lord says: “I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. 94). None of them shall enter into the inheritance promised to believers. For he swore to them in his wrath, provoked by their wickedness.

## CHAPTER V

Why this holy Paschal solemnity has an octave, although it is itself the eighth—that is, although it looks toward the eighth age of the world, which is the universal resurrection.

Now, as I am about to speak of the remaining offices of the Paschal week, I think it fitting first to say something generally about the Octave of Easter itself. For one may ask why this holy solemnity, although it signifies that eighth age—as stated above—which, eternal and unchanging, will succeed the seven passing ages of this world, nevertheless itself has an octave. Concerning other solemnities, nearly everyone knows that they have octaves because, considering together that their beginning is already present and that their end—that is, the consummation of blessedness in the resurrection—is still to come, we rightly extend the joy of the celebration through the eighth day. But this solemnity, because it is that of the resurrection, looks toward the whole eighth age itself, and its celebration is extended beyond eight days, that is, until Pentecost. Why then does it also have an octave? The question is rightly asked.

It must therefore be understood that our resurrection, which we await and already celebrate in anticipation through the arrival of this solemnity, will be the true and perfect circumcision, signified by the circumcision of the eighth day commanded for carnal Israel under the Old Law (Gen. 17). Now this true circumcision has eight beatitudes; and Jerome says: “Consider that the eighth beatitude of true circumcision ends in martyrdom: ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matt. 5). We therefore rightly celebrate the true circumcision of resurrection with solemn offices over eight days. To show its greatness, the Lord himself commended it, as it were, as a full and solid body, by measuring it with the number eight of the beatitudes—a number which geometers consider such that it first produces a full and solid body. For it is familiar to him to employ our numbers—or rather, his own—to whom it was truly said: “You have ordered all things in number, measure, and weight” (Wis. 11).

Yet since it is more worthwhile to recognize in Holy Scripture not so much geometrical doctrines as the melodies of the eternal musician, God—who indicates that he has a lyre, when he says in the Psalm: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56)—let us consider the melody of that lyre, or rather the lyre itself, in these eight sentences of the beatitudes as in eight strings which render a complete octave (*diapason*). This should especially please musicians: since, as writers on musical art relate, lyres were anciently customarily made with eight strings for the octave, the heavenly musician God presents to them in his lyre—that is, in the humanity which he assumed from the wood of flesh like ours—a likeness of this. For, modulating the melody of eternal joy through the complete octave, that is, through the eight strings of the beatitudes (Matt. 11 [probably Matt. 5]), he stirs skilled children to dance, that is, obedient disciples to act well.

It is certainly most familiar in our faith that this lyre lacks none of the seven distinctions of notes. For what are the seven spirits of God, of whom the Lord’s human nature is the unique resting-place, except seven distinctions of spiritual notes, from which the whole teaching of our same Lord is woven? Nor should this be passed over: just as there are only seven distinctions of notes, and therefore in an octave the eighth is always the same as the first, so, according to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, while this lyre of eight strings—that is, of eight beatitudes—sounds its heavenly octave for us, the eighth beatitude is the same as the first: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Lest this seem contemptible to anyone because it is unsupported by the authority of any writer, we have a judgment of blessed Augustine not far different concerning these same spirits of God and the same beatitudes. Distinguishing in his book *On Christian Doctrine* the seven steps by which one may ascend to divine contemplation, he adapts the seven spirits of God to the seven aforementioned beatitudes in this way, setting the eighth aside for the moment because it is the same as the first.

Concerning the spirit of the fear of the Lord, he says: “This fear necessarily impresses upon the mind the thought of our mortality and future death, and, fastening every movement of pride to the wood of the cross as with nailed coals, makes men poor in spirit, that is, humble.”

Then concerning the spirit of piety he says: “It is necessary to become gentle through piety, and not to contradict Holy Scripture, whether understood when it rebukes our vices, or not understood, as though we could think something wiser.”

Concerning the spirit of knowledge, he says: “Then that fear by which one thinks of God’s judgment, and that piety by which one can do nothing but believe the authority of the holy books, compel him to mourn for himself. For this knowledge makes a person of good hope not boastful but lamenting.”

Concerning the spirit of fortitude, he says: “By this disposition he obtains through diligent prayers the consolation of divine help, lest he be broken by despair; and he begins to be at the fourth step, namely fortitude, by which one hungers and thirsts for righteousness, and the mind, resolutely turning itself away from every deadly pleasure of passing things, is drawn forth.”

Concerning the spirit of counsel, he says: “When he has seen, so far as he can, the unchangeable Trinity and the same Unity shining in the distance, and has perceived that through the weakness of his sight he cannot endure that light, then at the fifth step, that is, in the counsel of mercy, he purifies his troubled soul; and, earnestly exercising himself in love of neighbor, he is perfected in it.”

Concerning the spirit of understanding, he says: “When in this manner he has reached love of his enemy, he ascends to the sixth step, where he now purifies the very eye by which God can be seen, as far as he can be seen by those who die to this world, namely, ‘through a mirror and in an enigma’” (1 Cor. 13).

Concerning the spirit of wisdom, he says: “Thus purifying the eye of the heart, such a son ascends to wisdom, which is seventh, and enjoys it in peace and tranquillity: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’” (Ps. 110). For from that fear one strives and comes to wisdom itself through these steps.

But let us now turn to considering the rationale of the offices; and, by the authority of so great a doctor, let us establish that the same offices which mystically proclaim the eight beatitudes do not differ from the stages or order of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, in these Paschal offices of the present week, the harmony of the eight beatitudes is so observed that, if carefully examined, the sense and order of the offices are found to agree with the meanings and order of the sayings by which the Lord composed those beatitudes. This was not stated above in the office of the first day, but was suitably reserved until now, because the long interruption concerning new customs, of which it seemed necessary to speak, might have tired the reader’s memory or even deprived it of this point. Now, therefore, when the rationales of the Paschal offices must be continued, what was left unspoken there will be stated more appropriately.

## CHAPTER VI

Again concerning the office of the first day, the Sunday of the Resurrection: how both it and the other offices of this week are ordered as ascents according to the eight beatitudes and according to nearly as many gifts of the Holy Spirit: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

It was said above that the office of the first day, the Sunday of the Resurrection, looks toward the day of our universal resurrection; and this was demonstrated by plain and spontaneously occurring arguments, especially since the Offertory plainly corresponds to the argument: “The earth trembled and was still, when God arose in judgment” (Ps. 75). This undoubtedly requires those who have entered the warfare of Christian faith to become poor in spirit, that is, humble, considering that there will be great fear and trembling when the King and Judge of all says to the Father, “I have risen, and I am still with you,” to the humiliation of his enemies, who said: “For he shall die, and his name shall perish” (Ps. 40). For none of us knows who will then be placed at the right hand and who at the left.

Although we feast on unleavened bread and Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5), although the flesh of the Lamb is precious, the wild lettuces with which we eat it are exceedingly bitter; and because of that flesh, we eat with staffs in our hands and in haste (Exod. 12), being fearful throughout the whole night. This is the spirit of the fear of the Lord, placed as a foundation in the depth of the heart so that all that is to be built upon it may be firmly supported. This is that poverty, that is, royal humility, which, set in front, preserves the whole abundance of blessedness to follow, lest it be puffed away by the wind of pride. This is the first of the seven steps by which, according to Ezekiel, one ascends to the eastern gate (Ezek. 40).

And lest anyone be disturbed that these steps are ordered differently by the doctors than by the prophet: the spirit of fear, which we place first, is placed last by Isaiah (Isa. 11). Gregory’s statement must be given: “Because the prophet spoke from heavenly things down to lowly things, he began rather from wisdom and descended to fear. But because we proceed from earthly things to heavenly, let us count the same steps in ascent, so that we may be able to arrive from fear at wisdom.”

But to return to the preceding point: what else is signified in the same office by the young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe (Mark 16), except that “the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5), ascending from the fear of the Lord, will obtain the kingdom of heaven, and from them gathered together the “queen shall stand at his right hand in garments of gold” (Ps. 44)?

That the station at Saint Mary also accords with these matters, in addition to the reasons mentioned above, is abundantly proved by arguments already sought out. For we all know her to be the queen of the humble. Her soul magnifying the Lord and her spirit rejoicing in God her Savior give the reason: “For he has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid”; because “he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts,” because “he has put down the mighty and exalted the humble” (Luke 1). Truly and faithfully. For “he has set the world upon them.” Where we have in the song of Hannah, “For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them” (1 Sam. 2), in Hebrew we have: “For the afflicted of the earth are the Lord’s.” “The afflicted of the earth,” says Jerome, the Hebrews understand as the poor in spirit and humble in heart; and they say that the Lord set the world upon them because they judge that the earth stands through their merits. But we know that the world—that is, the Church—has been set upon the foundation of the humble Apostles and prophets (Eph. 2); and we know that the stone which became a great mountain (Dan. 2) fills and supports this world, and was taken from the womb of the humility of Mary, of whom we speak.

We have now recapitulated the office of the first day in order to continue the eight beatitudes. Henceforth, so that their mystical sequence may appear more clearly, we shall make our way through the offices individually according to our plan.

## CHAPTER VII. On the office of the second feria: “Blessed are the meek.”

[Col. 0221D]

It has often been said that the Gospel of each office is its head, and that its other parts adhere to it as limbs to a head, in harmonious meaning. Now the Gospel of the present day is this: two of the disciples of the Lord Jesus, going to a village named Emmaus, recognized at last, in the breaking of bread, the Lord who had appeared to them on the road but in another form (Luke 24). “And when he vanished from their eyes, they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus, while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?’” (ibid.).

We must first see how the other parts of the office agree with this Gospel, especially the Introit: “The Lord brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey” (Num. 14), and so forth. Then it will be evident that the entire office corresponds to the meaning of the second beatitude: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). This would indeed be difficult unless the doctors before us had called the tearful compunction by which these men said that their hearts burned an earth watered with waters. And rightly so: because when compunction stirs up tears, the faithful soul, refreshed as though by the good grain of its land, says: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41).

Blessed Gregory elegantly compares this soul to Achsah, daughter of Caleb, who, sitting upon an ass, sighed and was asked by her father: “What do you have?” “Behold,” she said, “you have given me a dry land; give me also land watered with waters.” And her father gave her the upper spring and the lower spring (Josh. 15). “For every faithful soul,” he says, “sitting upon an ass, that is, ruling over the motions of its flesh, is first pierced by fear, which is the ‘lower spring’; afterwards by love, which is the ‘upper spring.’ Having first wept lest it be assigned to punishments, it afterwards begins to weep most bitterly because it is delayed from the kingdom.”

And this comparison presented itself fittingly: while it is invisibly fulfilled in each of the elect, it was visibly accomplished also in these two of whom we speak. For while they were walking together and speaking sadly about what had happened (Luke 24), what else was their soul doing but sighing like Achsah seated on an ass? And when Jesus approached and joined them on the road, saying, “What are these words that you are exchanging as you walk and are sad?” (Luke 24), how unlike this is what Caleb said to his sighing daughter: “What do you have?” Indeed, the very name Caleb is appropriate to the Lord Christ, for it is interpreted as “as if heart.” Christ God, the Word of God, was uttered from the heart of the Father (Ps. 44), and is in every respect like the Father’s heart from which he was uttered.

The Lord was also “as if heart” in this respect: he conformed himself to the hearts of the disciples so that, because inwardly among themselves they loved and doubted, the Lord might be outwardly present with them and yet not answer who he was. But when he enriched their hearts with such love that, astonished by the greatness of that love’s riches, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24), who does not perceive that he gave their souls the “upper spring,” namely, that they might be pierced by a deep wound of heavenly love?

Thus no doubt remains that, in such a Gospel, this Introit agrees: “The Lord brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey.” Consequently it is certain and proved that the office of this second feria proclaims the second saying of the beatitudes: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” The spirit of piety produces meekness, as both the matter itself indicates and Augustine’s statement cited above confirms. Therefore both the second saying of the beatitude and the second stage among the gifts of the Holy Spirit supply the material theme of the present office.

The reading from the Acts of the Apostles, which is set before it through the mouth of the Apostle Peter, also echoes this Gospel in accordance with its role of preceding it, especially where it says: “To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name” (Acts 10). For after the Lord had rebuked the aforementioned disciples because they were slow to believe, “beginning,” says the Evangelist, “with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24). Likewise the Offertory, “The angel of the Lord descended from heaven,” agrees with the Gospel words in which the disciples, reporting to the Lord whom they suppose to be a stranger, say among other things: “But certain women of our company terrified us. They were early at the tomb, and, not finding his body, came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he lives” (ibid.).

Alleluia. Does not “Was not our heart burning within us” cry out to us of that future time when all whose heart now burns concerning Jesus on the way, while he speaks to us through the Scriptures, having recognized him in the breaking of the bread of which it is said, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14), will then in an eternal acclamation remind one another of the desire with which we now burn and marvel at our satisfaction, then full and without weariness, having at last experienced in reality what we now believe with sighs?

### Why the station is at Saint Peter

According to what has been said, it is also most fitting that the station at Saint Peter is prescribed for the present office. Let us recall what was done to him, and it will appear more clearly to whom God, the Father of all, gave more generously the “upper spring and lower spring.” As soon as he fell by the threefold denial, “the Lord turned,” says the Evangelist, “and looked upon Peter; and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, who had said to him: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’; and he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22). Then, truly pierced by fear, he began, blessed among all the meek, to possess the earth; this was to receive the “lower spring.” But when the Lord rose—and, as we read in the Gospel (Luke 24) and sing in the Communion on this day, “The Lord has risen and has appeared to Peter”—what a great groan of mercy, pierced by true love, do we think responded to him as he ran inward to meet the Lord? This was to receive the “upper spring.”

Therefore, because he too is set forth as an example to all the meek, while the blessed Mother of God is queen of all the humble, we rightly proclaim in today’s station at Saint Peter, after his example, the blessed “meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5), just as in yesterday’s station at Saint Mary we proclaimed after her example the blessed “poor in spirit,” that is, humble, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the office of the third feria: “Blessed are those who mourn.”

How the office of the third feria agrees with the third saying of the aforementioned beatitudes could not readily be proved unless the discourse were supported by the authority of Scripture favorable to the matters written above. For it is clear that there is no contradiction, nor any diversity of meaning, but there is manifest dissonance in the words. In the saying of the third beatitude, those who mourn are called blessed: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). But in the Introit of this office, blessed men are said to have drunk the water of wisdom. In the Offertory, when the Lord thundered from heaven and the Most High gave his voice, springs of waters are remembered as having appeared (Ps. 17). In the Communion, too, those who have risen with Christ are commanded to set their minds on things above (Col. 3). Thus nearly the whole office commends divine knowledge to us, nowhere declaring in its own words the mourning of the blessed.

Here, therefore, we must necessarily retain Augustine’s statement—one among the others cited above—as our support: “Then that fear,” he says, “and that piety, which cannot but yield to the authority of the holy books, compel him to mourn for himself. For this knowledge makes a man of good hope, not boastful but lamenting.” Let us therefore direct our attention to that third stage and prove that this office, in which the knowledge of God is proclaimed under the name of waters, does not differ from the beatitude of those who mourn.

First, it must be understood that this mourning, of which it was said, “Blessed are those who mourn,” is not for the dead under the common law of nature, but for those dead in sins and vices. Thus the Apostle Paul says that he weeps and mourns for those who have not repented after fornication and impurity (2 Cor. 11 [cf. 2 Cor. 12:21]). They are to be mourned because they have not mourned. This mourning is commended in today’s Gospel, where the Lord says to the disciples to whom he had appeared: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24). For to repent is to mourn for sins.

Nor does this same Gospel reading entirely omit the cause that produces this mourning. For when the Lord had said to his disciples, “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled,” then, says the Evangelist, “he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (ibid.). The other parts of the office proclaim both the effect itself—namely, the mourning of repentance—and its effective cause—namely, knowledge. For the understanding of the Scriptures effectively causes lamentation or mourning, because, just as hardly any traveler is so cruel and foolish that, if he should pass through the midst of slain persons, he would not at least stop with a certain compunction, restraining his laughter and loud mirth; so there is no one who is not wounded by some measure of grief when, being occupied with the Scriptures rightly understood, he considers the prophets killed, the Lord of the prophets crucified, and all the heralds of truth sent by him suffering tribulation—men who bore witness, by weeping and dying, that every joy of this present life is vanity and deception.

The composition of this office is so intent on proclaiming the knowledge of God that, although all the verses of the Gradual throughout this week are taken from one and the same Psalm, the one hundred seventeenth, it chose for today’s verse, “Let those now say who have been redeemed by the Lord,” to be taken from another, namely Psalm 106. That whole psalm is an exhortation to all the faithful to praise the Lord because through the knowledge of himself he delivered us from a fourfold temptation: because “he rescued them from their necessities,” that is, from the danger of unbelief; because “he delivered them from their necessities,” that is, from the weakness of evil habit; because he delivered them from weariness in good action; because he brought them out from the assaults and cunning of heretics, who had previously wandered in a waterless wilderness—that is, in dryness of teaching, through poverty of the sacred Scriptures—before, as we sing in the Introit, “the water of wisdom” gave them drink (Ecclus. 15); before, as we sing in the Offertory, when the Lord thundered from heaven, “the springs of waters appeared” (Ps. 17), that is, the Apostles, through whom the Most High “gave his voice” (ibid.), that is, made known the knowledge of his ways of which we now speak. Plainly, therefore, the office of the third feria commends the third saying of the beatitude by proclaiming that knowledge which makes people not boastful but lamenting.

### Why the station is at Saint Paul

The station at Saint Paul is fittingly prescribed for this office, according to all the matters stated above or that can reasonably be said. For to him the Lord opened the understanding, by a singular grace, so that he might understand the Scriptures, as was said shortly before concerning the other Apostles. Hence he himself says: “My Gospel which was preached is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from man nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1). Moreover, what is said in the same Gospel (Luke 24), that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, was fulfilled especially through him: through him all nations came to know the grace of God; through him the nations drank the water of wisdom; and especially through him the sorrowful knowledge of God was added in speech and writing, as may be found more fully in the Epistles to the Corinthians.

For he says to those among whom fornication had been reported: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” (1 Cor. 5), and so forth. Again: “You were made sorrowful unto repentance; you were made sorrowful according to God” (2 Cor. 7), and the rest. He so required mourning from those to whom he had preached that, if they did not mourn, he himself lamented that God would humble him among them and mourned for those who did not mourn. Thus he says to the same Corinthians: “Lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many who have sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and licentiousness which they committed” (2 Cor. 12).

Thus too blessed Job, after he had said concerning the knowledge which he had before the Lord spoke to him from the whirlwind, “I have heard of you by the hearing of the ear,” and had added concerning the increase of that knowledge which he received from God’s conversation, “But now my eye sees you,” immediately showed that multiplied knowledge is the effective cause of mourning and repentance: “Therefore,” he says, “I rebuke myself and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42). Let us therefore remove from Paschal joys our unsuitable merriment, and let us not eat the flesh of the Lamb without wild lettuces, because “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the office of the fourth feria: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.”

It is not laborious to prove how the office of the fourth feria agrees with the fourth saying of the beatitudes. Rather, the question would be how this fourth beatitude, in which it is said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” corresponds with the fourth stage of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely fortitude, unless Augustine’s words cited above made it clear that the work of fortitude is to tear the mind so far away from every deadly pleasure of passing things that it may be free to hunger and thirst for righteousness.

But what has been stated beforehand—that the present office is a proclamation of the fourth beatitude—is plainly evident because, through the meal which our Lord celebrated after his resurrection with the seven disciples according to today’s Gospel, that satisfaction is signified which, as blessed Gregory explains, is reserved at that eternal banquet for those who hunger and thirst for righteousness here. It remains only that, with the mystical meaning of the Gospel leading the way, we see how the other parts of the office follow it.

By the truthful exposition handed down by the doctors, we have been taught that when our Lord, after his resurrection, stood on the shore while his disciples were toiling at sea (John 21), this signifies that he “having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6), as though he were speaking through the facts themselves: established in the solidity of eternity, “I no longer appear to you on the sea, because I am not with you amid the waves of disturbances.” That, when morning had come, he stood on the shore and the disciples did not know that it was the Lord, and said, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat and you will find” (John 21), signifies that in the morning—that is, on the day of judgment, after the night of this present age has passed—he will gather all his elect by the universal resurrection at his right hand. [Col. 0226D]

For the great fish, all numbered, one hundred and fifty-three, signify all the elect, who are great through their merits and perfected by faith in the Holy Trinity, and who are then to be gathered to the shore of the sea, that is, to the end of the age. There he invites the seven disciples to a meal, because the perfect Church, then wholly built up by the sevenfold Spirit, having received their bodies, will recline with him at eternal feasts. What, then, is meant by what we sing in the Introit, spoken of the day of judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25), unless that this very thing is signified in the aforesaid Gospel, where, when the disciples had come out onto the shore and were drawing such a number of great fish, the Lord said: “Come, dine” (John 21)? [Col. 0227A]

For that kingdom is one eternal dinner, one single and perpetual supper. There all the elect will be found, whom here he calls blessed of his Father and who are signified by those great, numbered fish. There, I say, on that shore—that is, at the end of the age—they will find coals and a fish laid upon them: a roasted fish, that is, Christ, God and man, who suffered, then set upon a fire not of suffering but of love. Isaiah speaks of this love: “The Lord says, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). That is, the fire of love which is now small in Zion, that is, in the present Church, will then be an everlasting and unquenchable furnace in Jerusalem, that is, in that vision of eternal peace. [Col. 0227B]

They will also find bread set out: that is, God, the true nourishment of eternal life, the food of angels, whom he feeds immortally. The Epistle taken from the Acts of the Apostles, concerning the preaching of the blessed Apostle Peter, according to its custom precedes the Gospel which follows with its testimony, touching especially on the place where it is said: “Simon Peter went up and drew the net onto the land, full of great fish.” “I think,” says Gregory, “that your charity already perceives what it means that Peter draws the net onto the land. For the holy Church has been entrusted to him; to him it is especially said: ‘Feed my sheep’ (ibid.).” He does this by his words; he does this by his Epistles; and, to return to the matter begun, he did this in that second discourse from which the foregoing reading was taken from the Acts of the Apostles, when five thousand men were enclosed in the nets of faith. [Col. 0227C]

The verse of the Gradual, “The right hand of the Lord has wrought mightily” (Ps. 117), fittingly accords with the saying: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find.” To those who look more deeply, it is also clear that this is a suitable utterance of the Lord’s human nature itself, standing upon the shore, as stated above, and having escaped all the fluctuations of our mortality through the power of the resurrection: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought mightily,” that is, the power of the Word united to me made me conquer death; “the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (ibid.), that is, has made me worthy of praise. And by repeating, “The right hand of the Lord has wrought mightily,” he shows the quality of that same resurrection: namely, its eternity, as follows in the same Psalm: “I shall not die, but live” (ibid.). 102 In accordance with this sense, we sing with the Apostle in the Alleluia, at the Communion: “Christ, having risen from the dead” (Rom. 6). [Col. 0227D]

The Offertory, “The Lord has opened the gates of heaven,” etc., impresses and repeats to us a third time what that bread signifies which our fishermen, having come ashore with the abundant multitude of great fish, found with the roasted fish and to whose dinner they were invited. Namely, it is that same bread laid up for us in our homeland, which we now taste on the way, that we may see that “the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 28), and which we receive in the sacrament of the altar. For the Lord opened the gates of heaven and rained down this bread upon us: the gates of heaven, I say, being the prophets who foretold, the angels who announced, Mary who conceived and bore him, the apostles [Col. 0228A] and other doctors, who by preaching sent the word of God into the mouths of our needy souls, panting in their poverty, so that we might taste and know, and, as we make for the homeland where the fullness of this bread is found, might not fail on the way.

## CHAPTER X. Why the Station Is at Saint Lawrence’s

Blessed Lawrence, one of those great fish and well known among them, was a great fish and himself roasted; the fragrance of his roasting sweetly fills the whole Church of Christ. In that prolonged death, in those tortures, because he had eaten well and drunk well, Augustine says, being fattened, as it were, by that food and made drunk by that cup, he did not feel the torments. For he was there who said: “It is the Spirit that gives life” (John 6). The flesh was burning, [Col. 0228B] but the Spirit sustained the soul. He did not yield, and he entered into the kingdom.

Therefore, from among all the same fish which Simon Peter draws onto the land, this one was fittingly chosen here, whose greatness the station of this day displays for us to behold. For in this most valiant defender of the Christian faith especially shines forth what has above been shown by the authority of Scripture: that the fourth beatitude, namely to hunger and thirst for righteousness, corresponds to the fourth degree of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, that is, the spirit of fortitude. For this notable martyr, hungry in fortitude and strong in hunger, was so filled by the first taste of that bread that he did not thirst for torments; because, as Augustine says, “thirsting to follow the bishop Sixtus who went before him, he received the oracle, conquered the devil, and attained triumph.” [Col. 0228C]

## CHAPTER XI. On the Office of Thursday: “Blessed Are the Merciful”

How the Office of Thursday corresponds to the fifth saying of the Beatitudes, in which it is said, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5), will be easy to recognize if we first set forth the mystical sense of the Gospel reading concerning Mary Magdalene. She had been a sinner in the city; and, loving truth, she washed away the stains of sin with tears. She bore the type of the Church from the Gentiles, which, once it had recognized truth, abandoned the crowds of errors to which it had prostituted itself and ran to the fountain of grace to be washed; and the utterance of Truth is fulfilled, which says: “Many sins are forgiven her” (Luke 7).

While the Jewish people was jealous—the Pharisee being its type, reproaching the fountain of mercy, saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know who and what sort of woman this is who touched him, because she is a sinner” (ibid.)—this same woman, as we read in today’s Gospel, stood outside the tomb weeping. After the angels spoke to her, she turned back and saw Jesus; and, having first been called by him by her own name, she in turn calls him Teacher [*Rabboni*] (John 20), etc. [Col. 0228D]

In these matters too she bears the type of that same Church. Thus the Church from the Gentiles stood outside, because it had not entered into the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets; yet it sought the Lord, like the most blessed centurion Cornelius (Acts 10), or like that Ethiopian eunuch who “had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning while reading the prophet Isaiah,” whose entrance into understanding he could not find (Acts 8). Thus also many Gentiles seeking God stood outside, because they could not find the one through whom they might enter into knowledge of the truth. It was to come about—but not before the Lord’s ascension—that truth would shine upon them and that they would make known their faith to the apostles, confessing that Christ had ascended to God his Father: that is, that according to his divinity he is equal to God the Father, though according to his humanity he is less.

Therefore, to Mary, who wished to hold his feet, he says: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and tell them: I ascend to my Father” (John 20), etc. [Col. 0229A] It is as though he said to the Church from the Gentiles which sought him, as mentioned above and as we read that the Gentiles had sought him before his passion, Philip saying: “Lord, we wish to see Jesus” (John 12): “Do not hold me now; but after I have ascended to the Father, show my apostles, who are my brothers, that you believe in my very ascension—that is, that through me they can confer upon you the same thing that I can.”

Thus the Gospel of the present day corresponds to that Beatitude: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” For in Hosea the Lord says of the same Church: “I shall call ‘Not my people,’ ‘My people’; and ‘She who has not obtained mercy,’ ‘She who has obtained mercy’” (Hos. 12). And this fifth Beatitude—or rather, the cause of beatitude, namely being merciful—is rightly assigned, according to Augustine, as stated above, to the fifth upward degree of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, that is, to the Spirit of counsel. For as counsel directs the mind, so mercy and compassion, by which the aforesaid woman was pierced as she wept at the tomb, helped her to see the Lord first. Likewise Cornelius’s works of mercy (Acts 10), namely the alms which he gave, helped him, under the angel’s guidance, to come to the Lord. Indeed, the counsel of mercy cleanses the eye of everyone seeking God. [Col. 0229B]

But now let us fit the remaining members of the Office to their head, namely to the Gospel sense. First, we marvel that nearly the same mystery appears in the eunuch, of whom the preceding reading from the Acts of the Apostles speaks. For what is signified in the Gospel by the sinful woman is narrated in the Epistle as beginning to be accomplished through the Ethiopian (Acts 8). Both signify the Church whose sins are to be justified: she through the name of sinner, he through Ethiopian blackness. There the sinner, seeking the Lord, surpassed the apostles themselves in love; here Ethiopia was beforehand in giving its hand to the Lord God. She wept as though the Lord were dead; he read in Isaiah the prophecy of the Lord’s passion, sympathizing with it. There were darknesses for her at the tomb; he lacked the lamp of knowledge for understanding. Seeing the Lord, she did not recognize him; reading of him the comparison of a sheep and a lamb, he did not know of whom it was spoken.

In short, her eyes and mouth were opened so that she said, “Rabboni” (John 20); his were opened so that, agreeing with the teaching of truth as Philip preached, he said: “What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts [Col. 0229D] 8). This is the mute man signified by Mary and received in the eunuch as in firstfruits: this, I say, is the mute people of the Gentiles; and these are the 103 infants, namely idolaters, who did not know how to speak of God. Of them we sing in the Introit: “They praised together your victorious hand, O Lord, because wisdom opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10). For what reason did they praise? Clearly because, as was stated earlier in the same book of Wisdom, “the sea covered their enemies”—namely the sea of baptism—“and they were brought up from the depths of hell” (ibid.), because through baptism they rose in the first resurrection, which is that of the soul.

That these things are so is more clearly demonstrated by the following Collect: “O God, who hast united the diversity of the nations in the confession of thy name, grant that those reborn from the font of baptism may have one faith of minds and godliness of deeds.” [Col. 0230A] The verse of the Gradual likewise accords with this when it says, “The Lord is God and has shone upon us” (Ps. 117), because for Mary, seeking the living among the dead, there were darknesses at the tomb. Through them was signified ignorance of God in the hearts of the Gentiles, which was even more clearly expressed through the Gentile and Ethiopian eunuch. Nor does any Alleluia better suit this sense than: “Christ has risen and has shone upon his people.”

The day of our solemnity, of which we sing in the Offertory, “On the day of your solemnity, says the Lord,” etc., is the great day, the splendid day: Christ himself, day from day, light from light. In him we came forth from the land of Egypt, that is, from the darkness signified by the darkness which Mary had at the tomb or by the aforesaid Ethiopian blackness of the eunuch. It is the day in whose light we walk and make for the land which truly flows with milk and honey, because there God and man, Christ, is present: ever sweet to angels through his divinity and pleasant to human beings through his humanity; ever present, ever desirable. He has shone upon us from the time when he ascended to the Father—that is, from the time when we recognized and believed him to be equal to the Father. We, therefore, “a people of acquisition” (1 Pet. 2), are rightly commanded to proclaim his mighty acts in the Communion, because, according to what has been said, “he called us from evil and profound darkness into his marvellous light” (ibid.). [Col. 0230C]

## CHAPTER XII. Why the Station Is at the Holy Apostles

[Col. 0230D]

The station at the Holy Apostles clearly accords with the mystery described above. It was through the ministry of the apostles that the mouth of the mute was opened; that the tongues of infants became eloquent; that the dreadful Ethiopian was clothed in the white fleece of the Lamb; and that every sinful soul found the opening of the cross in the jaw of Leviathan (Job 40), through which it may escape and, seeking the Crucified One not now in the tomb but in heaven, find mercy. Therefore in the aforesaid Gospel the Lord calls these same apostles his brothers (John 20), because through their labours it was accomplished that the Church of the Gentiles should lack nothing on account of the Lord’s not having illumined it by his bodily presence. [Col. 0231A]

Moreover, Philip, who as stated above clothed the Ethiopian in the whiteness of faith, mystically signifies all the apostles by his name. For *Philippus* is interpreted “mouth of the lamp.” The lamp, that is, the light, is the Saviour of the world, as Isaiah says concerning him: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her Righteous One goes forth as brightness and her Saviour is kindled as a lamp” (Isa. 62). The apostles, or any holy preachers, are rightly called his mouth, because they separate truth from falsehood, as it is said elsewhere: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be my mouth” (Jer. 15). Philip, therefore, as has been said, signifies by his name all the apostles, who even to this day do not cease by their writings to make Ethiopian souls white. Moreover, they rebuke the Synagogue which murmurs against the Lord on account of the Church of the Gentiles, just as Miriam once murmured against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife (Num. 12). [Col. 0231B]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Office of Friday: “Blessed Are the Pure in Heart”

The Office of Friday plainly answers to the sixth saying of the Beatitudes: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). For it treats of the blessedness of those who pass over—that is, all who, passing from the oldness of the flesh to the newness of the Spirit (Rom. 7), after the eye of the heart has been cleansed, shall at last see through long desire the glory of the supreme Trinity. As their type, our fathers the apostles [Col. 0231C] were summoned and went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, as today’s Gospel relates; and, seeing him, they worshipped him (Matt. 28). At the same time they received the command how they should cleanse all the vessels which one stronger than the strong man armed, coming upon him, had taken away (Luke 11), the Lord saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

No one can doubt that, when he says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” understanding is obtained through purity of heart; and therefore Augustine’s aforesaid judgment holds in this case also: that the sixth saying of the Beatitudes corresponds, in the ascending order, to the sixth degree of the gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely, that purity of heart is never absent from understanding. It remains, therefore, to fit the other parts of the Office to their head, namely to the Gospel sense. [Col. 0231D]

First, in the preceding Epistle reading, the blessed Peter, after saying, “In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water,” immediately adds: “The like figure whereunto baptism now saves you also, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the inquiry of a good conscience toward God” (1 Pet. 3). It need not be asked in what respect this reading accords with the aforesaid Gospel, in which the rule of saving baptism was first handed down. For it is well known and customary in the authentic writings of the doctors that baptism, as the Apostle Peter says in this Epistle, is a “like figure,” and that its type was preceded by the salvation through water of the few—that is, eight souls—in the ark in the days of Noah. [Col. 0232A]

For Noah prefigured Christ both in deed and in name, since *Noe* is interpreted “rest.” This name was given him by his father Lamech, who said: “This man shall comfort us” (Gen. 5); or, as it is found in the Septuagint: “He shall give us rest from the works and labours of our hands in the earth which God has cursed.” For Christ is our rest, as he himself said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Therefore, when Noah guided the ark over the waters of the flood, by which sinners were destroyed while those who were with him were saved through faith, since, believing in God’s righteousness, they separated themselves from unbelievers, he also prefigured Christ in deed, as stated above. Christ now guides the Church over the waters of baptism, by which those who do not believe are condemned, while those who believe and are baptized are saved with him (Mark 16). The Holy Spirit brings them peace, that is, remission of sins, of which the dove once bore the figure when it brought to the ark in its mouth a green branch of olive (Gen. 6). [Col. 0232B]

That number eight of souls which were saved in the ark, because it proceeds from the first even number, namely two, produces a solid body—that is, one having length, breadth, and height. For twice two twice is eight, as is customary among geometers and arithmeticians. This number eight, I say, of souls signifies the perfection of the body of the Church, which, while the world of unbelievers goes before it into judgment by water—a judgment by which believers are now separated from unbelievers—saves itself through faith and floats upon the wood of the cross. And that ark fittingly had a window in its side through which those who were to be saved entered, because Christ was wounded in the side by the soldier’s lance, and through the sacrament of that wound all believers enter the Church. [Col. 0232C]

And because the Church consists of human beings, the ark, which signified the Church, fittingly displayed in its very shape a certain likeness of the human body. The human body is so proportioned that it has one sixth of its length in breadth and one tenth of that same length in height. The ark was unquestionably constructed in the same proportion: it was three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty cubits in height (Gen. 6). [Col. 0232D]

Therefore, since in every respect the Epistle reading accords with the Gospel, it is easy to fit the other members of the Office to it. The Introit, “The Lord brought them forth in hope, and the sea covered their enemies” (Ps. 77), and likewise the Offertory, “This day shall be a memorial to you,” with its verses, are joined by familiar and closely related meanings to both the Gospel and the Epistle. For they send us back to the most celebrated history of the fathers, who, as a type of our baptism, “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10). [Col. 0233A]

For just as the Lord brought them forth in hope—namely, hoping to be delivered, though Pharaoh with his people pursued them—and the sea covered their visible enemies, so all who believe in Christ, though they remember having committed very great sins, go forth to him with a sure hope of forgiveness; and all their sins are covered in the sea, that is, in the waves of baptism. Therefore this day, namely Christ, in whose light we came forth from darkness, is commanded to be a memorial: Christ, I say, who is our day, that is, our Passover, festive and solemn for us, ever to be celebrated and held in mind. He alone fought for us while we were silent, because, dying alone for all, he poured forth from his pierced side that sea in which our enemies—that is, our sins—are covered.
