The verse of the Gradual, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117), corresponds with the saying in which our Lord expresses the glory and honour with which, because of the suffering of death, he was crowned (Heb. 2), saying in the same Gospel: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). This prophetic testimony is rightly joined to the aforesaid Gospel saying as a rebuke to those who rejected such a stone. This is what he meant when, despised before the chief priests, he patiently endured: “Nevertheless I say to you: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God” (Mark 14). [Col. 0233B]

## CHAPTER XIV. Why the Station Is at Saint Mary’s

What was stated above, on the not unreasonable judgment of Jerome—that the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain, as today’s Gospel reading relates (Matt. 28), and saw the Lord in Nazareth, which is situated on a mountain, and in Mary’s house—is further confirmed to some degree by the fact that the station prescribed for today’s Office is at Saint Mary’s. For the care of the Roman Church is shown to have understood the same. And this Office, which, according to the Gospel reading, as stated above, wholly concerns the sacrament of baptism, is fittingly appointed to be sung at the apostolic station in the very place where the disciples were indoors and Thomas with them, according to Jerome; for in today’s Gospel reading the one rule for baptism is handed down. [Col. 0233C]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Office of Saturday: “Blessed Are the Peacemakers”

[Col. 0233D]

The seventh saying of the Beatitudes is: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5). Truly peacemakers are those who, having received peace among themselves and with God, now admit nothing that opposes God, and likewise strive to walk in peace with every person on the way of this present life, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “If it be possible, as much as lies in you, live peaceably with all people” (Rom. 12). The Office proclaims an example of this in the principal subject of the present Saturday.

To make this clearer, let us first set forth the mystical meaning of today’s Gospel. “Two ran together,” says the Evangelist (John 20), namely Simon Peter and that other disciple whom Jesus loved, etc. The familiar exposition of the doctors is that John, who came first to the tomb but did not enter, signifies the Synagogue, which, possessing the Law and the Prophets, first read of the Lord’s passion but refused to believe in one who had died. Peter, however, who came later but entered first, signifies the multitude of the Gentiles, which later came to knowledge of the same Lord’s passion but came first to faith. [Col. 0234A]

But the matter now at hand, on account of the aforesaid saying of the Beatitudes, is to ask what relates to the Church in its being peaceable. Faithful inquiry can more quickly discover this from the preceding Epistle reading. For after the Apostle Peter had said of Christ the stone: “Coming to him, the living stone, indeed rejected by men but chosen and honoured by God” (1 Pet. 2), he shortly adds: “To you therefore who believe, honour; but to those who do not believe, the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, in which also they were placed” (ibid.).

Such stumbling or offence is plainly opposed to peace, through which the Jews are charged with rebellion and unbelief: for, tormented by hatred of the converging Gentiles, who, as stated, are signified by Peter, they are so distressed that, as John figures it, they preferred to perish standing outside rather than enter with the fellowship of the Gentiles into faith in Christ’s passion. Therefore, when these sons of wrath and strife have been disinherited, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God,” as Peter adds in the same Epistle reading: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (ibid.), etc. [Col. 0234B]

Such a son of peace, because he is not offended by fellowship with any person tending toward God, “ascends,” Augustine says, “to wisdom,” which is seventh in the ascending scale of degrees, namely of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and he enjoys that wisdom in tranquillity and peace. For it was said above, according to the same Augustine, that the seven Beatitudes—for the eighth is the same as the first—are fitted in ascending order to the seven degrees of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first or lowest of these is the spirit of the fear of the Lord, while the highest is the spirit of wisdom, to which, as has just been said, the “blessed peacemakers, sons of God,” ascend. [Col. 0234C]

In accordance with what has been said, the Introit appropriately begins: “The Lord brought forth his people in exultation and his elect in gladness” (Ps. 104). By this we are directed to another ancient likeness in which what we now understand as signified in the Gospel by Peter and John was prefigured: namely, the history of the fathers, in which those who first received the promises are related to have been rejected for unbelief. Of them the Psalm says: “For forty years I was offended with that generation” (Ps. 74); and afterward: “To whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (ibid.). The children, however, who arose after them, being introduced into that promised land, signified the same people of the Gentiles who are now represented by Peter, coming later but entering the tomb first.

For of those who, after their fathers had been rejected, entered into that promise, it is said in Psalm 104: “And he brought forth his people in exultation and his elect in gladness.” He brought them forth, namely, from the wilderness. For concerning their coming forth from Egypt he had said earlier: “And he brought them forth with silver and gold, and there was not one feeble among their tribes” (Ps. 74). What follows likewise indicates that this is so: “And he gave them the lands of the Gentiles, and they possessed the labours of the peoples” (ibid.). [Col. 0235A]

The aforesaid Introit, therefore, is thanksgiving because, while the Jewish people delayed, the Gentiles were admitted, in accordance with the mystical sense of the Gospel and the Apostle’s saying: “Blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11). The Gradual, moreover, has now from this day been changed into Alleluia; indeed, after this day it is omitted until Pentecost, because those for whose acquisition and new enrolment this laborious chant was sung, when the white garments were laid aside, now from this day are made our equals and keep festival with us in contemplation of that octave so often mentioned.

What follows—“Alleluia, praise the Lord, children” (Ps. 112), with a double verse—is an exhortation to those who, through recent baptism, have become children, that is, have been made pure from vices, to praise the Lord in voice and deed. For, just as Peter was figured as entering first into the tomb and seeing the linen cloths laid there and the cloth for the Lord’s head (John 20), so they too, having entered into faith—though formerly without God (Eph. 2)—received knowledge of Christ’s humanity and divinity. The entire Psalm is directed to the election of the Gentiles; this is especially proved by what is said at its end: “Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house” (Ps. 112), etc. [Col. 0235B]

The Offertory also, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117), plainly suits these same children of God. For that verse of Psalm 117 was sung also by the children who met the Saviour as he came to his passion, carrying palm branches in their hands (Matt. 21). Mother Church also adds, saying to her children: “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord”; that is, we who are the household of the Lord mark you with holy baptism, because “the Lord is God and has shone upon us,” as another prophet says: “The people of the Gentiles, who walked in darkness, saw a great light” (Isa. 9): the Gentiles, I say, whose figure Peter bears in the present Gospel, as stated above.

The following two verses also concern the same matter. The first, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” concerns the joy of the Gentiles, whose type Peter was when he entered the tomb; the second, “The stone which the builders rejected,” rebukes the Jews, to whom Christ is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (1 Pet. 2). John signifies them, when, having come first, he halted as though offended and was forestalled by Peter, who came later. [Col. 0235C]

The Communion, “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3), plainly accords with the aforesaid saying of the Beatitudes: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” For the Apostle Paul had previously said to the Galatians, whom certain Jews were troubling, and to whom Christ was a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence: “You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (ibid.). He then immediately gave this reason: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” This concerns the baptized altogether: they are not to seek circumcision of the flesh, but are to keep only the true circumcision of the Spirit which they have received, nor are they to be moved further by the scandal of the Jews. Peter paused because John did not enter the tomb before him or together with him.

## CHAPTER XVI. Why the Station Is at Saint John Lateran

[Col. 0236B]

Not only on this Saturday, when the white garments are laid aside, but also on the eighth day mentioned above, that is, on Holy Easter Saturday, the maternal privilege of the Lateran Church requires that the Pope proceed nowhere else, but that in the same Church which is the apostolic seat he complete the octaves of the holy baptismal font which it has begun. It was built by Emperor Constantine in honour of the holy Saviour and of Saint John the Baptist, who said: “Let it be known to all that we have become such worshippers of Christ that we build within our palace a temple to his name, in which the Christian people, assembling there together with us, may render thanks there to the divinity.”

The very name “at the Laterans” recalls the ancient disgrace of filthy Nero, who shamefully used magical potions there and, as is reported, while hiding there vomited up frogs. But “where iniquity abounded, grace superabounded” (Rom. 5): now there is there the mother Church of the Roman Empire, which, having borne children on Holy Saturday and clothed them in Christ’s brightness, likewise circumcises them on this eighth day with the spiritual stone. In today’s Epistle, Peter, as mentioned above, calls this stone a stone of stumbling for the Jews, but for us who believe a stone of honour and the head of the corner. [Col. 0236C]

The spiritual and true circumcision is that of which he had already said in the same Epistle reading: “Brethren, laying aside all malice, all guile, hypocrisies, envies, and every detraction, as newborn infants desire the rational milk without guile” (1 Pet. 2), etc. This is the true and truly holy, indeed the only necessary, circumcision: that by which all the senses of our body and our ruling principle itself—that is, the mind—are circumcised. Without this circumcision Christ dies in us, that is, faith in Christ dies, and Paul’s jubilant address to us at the Communion does not benefit us: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3), just as the Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). [Col. 0236D]

This was fittingly prefigured by the event in the ancient history: “When Moses was on the journey at a lodging place, the Lord met him and wished to [kill] him. Zipporah immediately took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son; she touched his feet and said: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me.’ And he let him go, after she said to him: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me because of the circumcision’” (Exod. 4). Moses, in having Zipporah, a foreign woman, as his wife, signifies Christ, who received as wife the Church from the Gentiles, a foreigner. Hence our doctors refer mystically to this what is said, that “Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses because of his Ethiopian wife” (Num. 12): namely, that the Synagogue and the old priesthood, envying the salvation of the Gentiles, blaspheme Christ to this day. [Col. 0237A]

“Therefore, when Moses was on the journey at a lodging place,” and his sons had not yet been circumcised, “the Lord met him and wished to kill him,” because while Christ, walking among us through faith on the journey of the present life, is at a lodging place—that is, turns aside to those who are now baptized—unless his children are circumcised as stated above, his faith will quickly die in them. [Col. 0237B]

What prevents this, Zipporah—that is, Mother Church—quickly takes a very sharp stone and circumcises the foreskin of her sons: namely, by that circumcision of which it was said above in the Epistle reading. That stone, which is Christ himself and of which the same reading spoke, carefully and swiftly cuts off the flesh—that is, the works of the flesh. And she touches his feet—that is, follows his footsteps—and says to these same sons: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).—“You are,” she says, “[Col. 0237C] a bridegroom of blood to me,” because, in betrothing me to yourself, you shed your blood as a dowry; and, when the exigency of the cause demands that I suffer for you, you require in return my blood; and meanwhile now you require that I crucify my flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5). Therefore, as was said above, the station is rightly held on this eighth day at Saint John Lateran, because that Church is the mother and apostolic see, and she herself circumcises by spiritual circumcision those whom she has begotten as children for Christ.

## Chapter XVII. On the eighth day: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

The eighth beatitude returns to the beginning; that is, it is the same as the first: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0237D] (Matt. 5). Yet it differs slightly, namely in that the preceding ground of blessedness is one thing here and another there. There, that is, in the first, it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (ibid.); here, that is, in the eighth, it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (ibid.). Hence Jerome says: “And observe that the eighth beatitude of true circumcision is brought to its close by martyrdom.”

Therefore, although on the eighth day the same office is sung as on the first, because the eighth beatitude returns to the beginning, as has been said, nevertheless, because the preceding grounds of blessedness in the first and eighth differ, those who are more diligent rightly retain in the same office another item: the Gospel of the following week, namely that according to John: “When it was evening on that day” (John 20), etc. For the letter of this reading also mentions the eighth day: “And after eight days,” it says, “the disciples were again inside” (ibid.); and its inner sense does not pass beyond the ground of the eighth beatitude.

For what does it mean that the Lord stood in the midst of the disciples, who remained indoors with the doors shut, bringing the good tidings of consolation and peace, except that to those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake—and whom, according to another Evangelist, people hate and exclude (Luke 6), as the apostles had already been excluded, not daring to go forth publicly before them—their Lord and God graciously makes himself available for contemplation? Thus they may already taste, amid their tribulations, and see how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33), and so a more assured hope may console them as they walk in the midst of tribulation, recalling what the saying of which we speak strives repeatedly to impress: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

But the Epistle always owes a service of anticipation to its Gospel; and therefore the Epistle reading of this Sunday too is not omitted: “Everything born of God conquers the world” (1 John 5). For in this reading our victorious faith is proclaimed, and that faith itself is called the victory over the world. Supported by three witnesses—for Father, Word, and Holy Spirit bear witness in heaven, and likewise there are three witnesses on earth, namely the same Spirit, the water of baptism, and the blood of Christ and of his martyrs, which attest his truth—[Col. 0238C] defended, I say, by three witnesses in heaven and on earth, it awards the kingdom of heaven to those whose right it is by the law of war: namely, “those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

The Introit, “As newborn infants” (1 Pet. 2), is to be sung during the following weekdays. It too agrees with the Gospel just mentioned, though not in the same sense already stated—namely, that through fear of the Jews the Lord’s disciples were within with the doors shut, beginning to suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, which, as we have said, is the ground of the eighth beatitude. Rather, it refers to another saying which the Lord uttered concerning future believers: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20).

For, lest we suppose faith alone sufficient for us, the rule of life without [Col. 0238D] which faith is dead is fittingly set forth beforehand by this Introit. For we are indeed marked out by what he says, “Blessed are those who have seen and believed,” but only if we follow our faith with works. For he truly believes who keeps in action what he believes. Accordingly Paul says of those who retain faith merely in name: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1). And James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). Thus this brief portion of apostolic speech in the Introit rightly shows what manner of life makes faith beneficial, lest, upon hearing the words spoken of us, “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed,” we deceive ourselves.

The final sentence of the preceding Epistle is consonant with the same point and should be understood similarly [Col. 0239A]: “He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself” (1 John 5). The Communion, “Put forth your hand,” in its plain literal sense edifies us; but to those who look inwardly it is clear that it concerns the Jewish people, which persists in unbelief to this day. Thomas the Apostle, long doubtful, at last saw, touched with his hand, and believed, as a type of that people.

For if we follow the letter alone, its sense cannot stand in every respect. Those who have not seen and yet have believed are indeed blessed, but not in the comparison or sense expressed by the wording: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20). Therefore, in the person of Thomas, the remnant of Israel who will be saved are reproved as having a lesser faith than the Gentiles, because the Gentiles have not seen and yet have believed. But Israel will not believe unless the event appears openly, with Elijah and Enoch going before; whereas Paul says that faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen (Heb. 12). Therefore we possess a more praiseworthy faith, since we faithfully believe in a thing not yet appearing.

# Book Nine

[Col. 0239]

## 107 Chapter I. On the second Sunday after the albs.

[Col. 0239B]

Because this Sunday is a solemnity of the holy Roman Church, the office of the same Sunday suitably commends to those engaged in deliberations what pattern pastors of souls ought to follow. Through the Gospel, most plainly this is done: he who is good substantially, not by an accidental gift, says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10), etc. Then, by the contrasting description of the hired servant and by his repeated commendation of his own goodness, he gives the sheep a clear judgment whereby they may discern whom to flee and to whom they ought to entrust the care of their souls.

The remaining parts of the office praise the pattern of the good shepherd. First, at the Introit we sing of him: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” [Col. 0239C] (Ps. 30), so that, just as he not only loves judgment but also mercy—and puts mercy first and judgment second, as is set forth earlier in the same psalm in one and the same verse, “He loves mercy and judgment”—so all who are appointed judges of souls may always let mercy triumph over judgment, in order that they themselves may obtain the same.

And what follows, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (ibid.), indicates that apostles or apostolic pastors are made such not by their own strength but by the power of God’s word: seeing the wolf come, they do not flee or abandon the sheep, as hired servants do.

The Epistle unmistakably fulfills its office of anticipation, when, after the statement concerning that uniquely good shepherd who laid down his life [Col. 0239D] for his sheep—“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps”—it adds at the end: “For you were once like wandering sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (1 Pet. 2).

The Offertory indeed proceeds not quite so plainly, but no less harmoniously, with the same sense as the Gospel: “O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn” (Ps. 62). For that psalm bears this title: “A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea”; that is, this psalm is to be attributed to Christ according to what he did or endured among the Jews. They are called a wilderness because, having forsaken God, they too were justly forsaken by God [Col. 0240B]. They are also called Idumaeans, “earthly” or “bloody,” because they shed the blood of the prophets and of the Lord himself. Yet this good shepherd laid down his life for his sheep in that wilderness. Therefore those who ought to do the same by his example are rightly stirred by his voice to watch for God from the dawn over their flock: for God, not for temporal wages; to thirst for him with soul and body in many ways; and, rejoicing in the shelter of his wings—that is, in the hope of his consolation (Ps. 62)—not to fear the wolf or flee after abandoning the sheep.

## Chapter II. On the third Sunday.

The remaining Sundays that follow until the Ascension of the Lord celebrate in their offices the fulfillment of his promise that, after the sorrow occasioned by his death, the hearts of his disciples would be made glad by his resurrection. He spoke this promise to them at supper on the night when he was betrayed. Hence on this Sunday we fittingly sing at the Introit: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name” (Ps. 65). For a title corresponding to the meaning of this psalm is prefixed: “Unto the end: a canticle, a psalm of the resurrection.”

The cause or matter of the rejoicing commanded here is that which the Lord adds in the following Gospel after announcing sorrow: “But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16). And in order that the comparison previously given to the apostles, of a woman who is sorrowful when she gives birth, may be fitting for us too—for so it is expedient—the reading from the Apostle appropriately precedes this very Gospel: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2), etc.

For in this abstinence there is labor, as the Psalmist says: “There were pains as of a woman in labor” (Ps. 74). He had indeed said before: “They were troubled, they were shaken; trembling seized them” (ibid.), speaking of those who, according to the Apostle, were made sorrowful unto repentance (2 Cor. 7). But just as the pain of a woman in labor is fruitful—“for when she has given birth, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16)—so too what [Col. 0241A] they disparage concerning us, as concerning evildoers (1 Pet. 2), will not be without consolation. For at last, considering us from our good works, they will glorify God on the day of visitation.

This was well prefigured by Tamar in the ancient history. When they accused her, saying, “Tamar has committed fornication, and her womb appears to be swollen” (Gen. 38), she brought forth the ring, bracelet, and staff which Judah had given her as a pledge, saying: “By the man to whom these belong I have conceived” (ibid.). Judah, whose name means “confession,” signifies Christ; Tamar, whose name means “bitterness,” signifies the Church from among the Gentiles, in which is the bitterness of repentance, by which “Peter too went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26).

Tamar therefore, covering her face—that is, the Church from among the Gentiles, blushing for former [Col. 0241B] errors—sat on the road by which Judah was going to the washing-place to shear sheep (Gen. 38); that is, she met Christ at baptism, as the deer longs for springs of water (Ps. 41). Having conceived faith in Christ the true God through the Holy Spirit, and having received that same faith as a ring, works of faith as a bracelet, and justification of the spirit as a staff, as an earnest—that is, as a pledge—she is accused by both Gentiles and Jews of having committed fornication with falsehood and of being defiled by a spirit of error. But patiently enduring their deceitful accusations, she will at last silence the ignorance of foolish people (1 Pet. 2), proving by the aforesaid pledges that she has conceived by the true God; and she will be glorified with that same God on the day of visitation.

The Offertory, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 145), concerns the joy, mentioned above in the Gospel, of this woman over Christ’s resurrection. For this psalm also has *Alleluia* in its title. And what we sing in the verse, “The Lord raises up the fallen; the Lord frees those in bonds” (ibid.), is the rejoicing of those whose sorrow, according to the Lord’s promise, was changed into joy when he rose again (John 16).

## Chapter III. On the Gospel of the fourth Sunday, which says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” etc.

To some, the common exposition of this statement seems weak and inadequate: namely, that it was expedient for the apostles that our Lord should depart from here because, unless he had taken away his bodily presence from them, they would not know how to love him spiritually; and that this is why he said: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16).

For this exposition seems less than the majesty of the gift of the Holy Spirit requires, especially because the Lord himself calls the coming of that same Holy Spirit a baptism, saying in the Acts of the Apostles: “For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1). To be baptized in the Holy Spirit is nothing other than to receive through the Holy Spirit remission of original sin and of all actual sins, and to have the entire old human being transferred into newness of life. In this sense, the exposition mentioned above is undoubtedly insufficient.

For loving God spiritually and being baptized in the Holy Spirit are not equivalent. Otherwise the holy persons of old, who undoubtedly loved God spiritually and indeed received great gifts of that same Holy Spirit in prophesying and working signs, would have been baptized in the Holy Spirit—that is, would have received remission of sins—and would not have been held in hell because of original sin until Christ’s coming.

Moreover, it conflicts with the fact that the apostles did love the Lord spiritually while he was present, though not so strongly; for example Peter, who, when he confessed his love for the third time, was told: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21). For flesh and blood did not reveal this love to him, but the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 16). Therefore we should not suppose that we have found the proper sense in these words [Col. 0242B] of the Lord unless we make his two statements equivalent: namely, “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” as though he had said, “For if I do not go away, you will not be baptized in the Holy Spirit.”

This is easy to establish if we first consider when, or how, he went away. Many recall that he first went away when, in the apostles’ sight, he ascended into heaven. But when he ascended, the apostles rejoiced, and, as we sing, with joyful light they accompanied him as he sought the stars; indeed, as Luke says: “And they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24). Yet the Lord had foretold that they would be made sorrowful when he went away: “Sorrow,” he says, “will fill your heart” (John 16). And shortly afterward: “Amen, amen, I say to you, that you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you shall be sorrowful” (ibid.), etc.

Therefore, evangelical authority makes it clear that he did not first go away when he ascended into heaven, but when, dying, he left the world and went to the Father. For John the Evangelist was speaking of his death when he said: “Knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John 13), etc. For on the very night when he was to be betrayed, he delivered the discourse to his disciples from which this reading is taken, and near the end of the prayer he says: “And now I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world, and I come to you” (John 17). For this reason his Passion is called *pascha*, that is, “passage.”

Accordingly, we infer in this way that the Paraclete, namely the Holy Spirit insofar as he is Paraclete, was given because of this departure. The Holy Spirit is called Paraclete, that is, Comforter, because through the regeneration of baptism he makes the captive children of Adam children of God (Rom. 5), and comforts them while they are pilgrims in this age, bearing witness “to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8), when he is given not only for the grace of prophecy but for the remission of original sin and of all actual sins through faith in Jesus Christ.

But this would not have happened unless Christ, one for all of us, had paid Adam’s debt to the eternal Father and had washed away the bond of the old guilt by his gracious blood. Nor had anyone previously received the Holy Spirit in that grace, as John testifies and says in the Gospel: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” [Col. 0243A] (John 7). Nor did we receive reconciliation in any other way than through Christ’s blood (Eph. 2), in whose death, according to the Apostle, we were baptized and received the Holy Spirit, who is the true remission of sins (Rom. 6).

Therefore, when he says, “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” it should be understood as though he had said: “Unless, then, I am handed over to death, the necessary *paraclesis*, that is, remission of sins, will not be given to you.” For if it is understood of the Ascension, it also conflicts with the fact that before he ascended—indeed, on the very day on which he rose—he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20), namely for remission of sins. For it immediately follows: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (ibid.).

Finally, nobody can doubt this either: if Christ, exempt from death, had ascended into heaven, this Paraclete would not have been given to us. For he said: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12). Thus we understand this, and whatever he said at that supper concerning his departure, more truly, more correctly, and more consistently of death than of the Ascension. And when he says, “I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” (John 16), it can in no way be understood better than as referring to what he says afterward: “The hour is coming when you shall be scattered and leave me alone” (ibid.), with the same complaint with which he said through the prophet: “I have trodden the winepress alone; I looked around, and there was no helper” (Isa. 63).

Likewise, what he says, “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14), is more evenly understood of the Passion than of his sitting at the Father’s right hand. For Paul affirms that he prayed on the cross and cried out in death, saying of him: “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and many tears to him who could save him from [Col. 0243C] death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5). For after he ascended into heaven he does not cry out to be saved from death; therefore neither does he ask that the Paraclete be given to us, but gives him, now exercising the authority given to him in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28). But on the cross he asked, being for a little while made lower than the angels (Ps. 8); when ascending into heaven, however, he says: “I will send upon you the promise of my Father” (Luke 24).

But perhaps what the Apostle says—“At the present time Jesus Christ intercedes for us, who died, indeed who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8)—may seem to conflict with this and to establish that even now he asks for us in the sense stated above. But when the mode of intercession is properly considered, it is found rather to support firmly what has been said. For that intercession, by the true assertion of all doctors, is not a humble petition [Col. 0244A], but the eternal commemoration of his Passion, once undertaken and once offered for us as a sacrifice (Heb. 10): the once-admitted cry of his innocent blood in the sight of the Holy Trinity, convicting the murderers who shed it, but defending us who drink it in the ministry of the altar by an intercession not needy but powerful.

Otherwise, how could he say even before ascending, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” and then, after ascending, intercede or ask that the Paraclete be given to us? But someone says: “He asks through his humanity, who gives through his divinity.” This is altogether true: then, dying and made for a little while lower than the angels (Heb. 2), he asked through his humanity; but now, crowned with glory and honor and set over all the works of the Father [Col. 0244B], he gives through his divinity, having all authority, as one seated at God’s right hand. Hence, just as “having risen from the dead, he dies no more” (Rom. 6), so no Catholic invokes him now in order that he may ask the Father.

Furthermore, what has been said can be established if the Lord’s own statements are compared. Unless they are distinguished, they will seem contrary to one another: namely, “I will ask my Father and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14), etc., and what he says later in the same discourse: “In that day you shall ask in my name; and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you” (John 16). Giving the reason, he says: “For the Father himself loves you” (ibid.). And immediately he confirms the same thing, saying: “Because you [Col. 0244C] have loved me and believed that I came forth from God” (ibid.).

For what is meant by “I will ask” and “I will not ask”? It means, of course, that in his Passion he was to become a sacrifice and ask that we might receive the Paraclete—that is, the Spirit of remission of sins—and thus that the wall of enmity standing between God and human beings might be destroyed in his flesh (Eph. 2). Once that wall was destroyed, “on that day,” he says—the day of peace and grace that follows—“I will not ask the Father concerning you.” Why? “For the Father himself loves you,” he says: that is, by dying once, I reconciled you to God in my blood; and, as I said above, I left peace to you, I gave you my peace—that is, peace restored through me between God and yourselves. And this is through your faith and love: “because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.”

Thus when he says, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” it can in no way be understood better than that he asked on the cross and cried out in his death, according to the Apostle’s statement cited above. Nevertheless, because from the day of the Ascension the apostles, made certain of his power, awaited the same Holy Spirit whom he had promised, we rightly sing and read how he promised him when about to die, and likewise promised him again when ascending into heaven—so that we may know that his death was the effective cause of the gift, while his Ascension effected the authority to give it. But now let us return to what went before.

The Apostle’s reading is appropriately placed before the Gospel of this fourth Sunday: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” [Col. 0245A] (Jas. 1), etc. The Holy Spirit is God’s good and perfect gift, without whom both angelic and human nature are wretched and pitiable, blind and naked (Rev. 3), as is most evident both in demons and in lost human beings. For Michael does not differ substantially from the devil, Moses from Pharaoh, or Peter from Nero; they are distinguished solely by this Spirit, whom the former deserved to receive while the latter were judged unworthy.

This gift, so great and so necessary, comes to the aid of human need in a twofold operation. By the first bestowal, our sins are forgiven; by the second, distributions of graces are apportioned. By that benefit—namely remission of sins—this gift, that is, this Spirit, is poured out universally and uniformly upon all; but by this addition—namely the division of graces—it is given particularly and in diverse ways, differently to different persons. Hence, after the Apostle had enumerated some of these divisions, he says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Both bestowals were poured out upon the holy apostles in a marvelous manner at definite times and on definite days: on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, for remission of sins (John 20); but on the day of Pentecost, in an abundant outpouring of graces, for the instruction of all nations soon to follow (Acts 2). For on the day when the Lord rose, having died for our offenses in order to show that he rose for our justification (Rom. 4), standing in the midst [Col. 0245C] of his disciples, he announced for the first time the peace he had made between us and God, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20). Immediately he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid.), thereby showing that he was giving the remission of sins which he had acquired by his blood, not only to them but also to all who were to believe in him.

And immediately he added: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (ibid.), so that they might be fit to preach and bear witness to the whole world concerning the remission of sins which they had received. On the day of Pentecost that same Holy Spirit granted them the gifts of charisms, and by these, as was read in today’s Gospel, “he will convict [Col. 0245D] the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16).

Therefore, as was said above, this reading from the Epistle is rightly placed before this Gospel, because the good gift and perfect gift is none other than this Holy Spirit. Since this Spirit is given freely—indeed, is grace itself—it fittingly adds concerning the giver of this gift: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (ibid.). This is no different than if he had said: “He begot us through the grace of the Holy Spirit,” because by the Holy Spirit he infused his seed—that is, his word—into our minds so that we might be born again.

Likewise, what he says, “You know, my most beloved brethren: but let every person be swift to hear and slow to speak” (ibid.), can instruct us by a magnificent example if we consider that statement of the Gospel reading at which the diligent composer of the ecclesiastical office aims. For it is fitting to rebuke the presumption of human vanity by the example not of just anyone, but of the Paraclete himself, when he places this reading from the Apostle before the Gospel mentioned above. For the Lord declares that the Paraclete will be such as he wants us to be in speaking, saying: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16).

This is the strongest ground of the preceding statement which he had proposed when he said: “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth” (ibid.). For he removes the opposite, namely speaking from oneself, under which is contained every falsehood, undoubtedly contrary to truth. To make this clearer, let us define both opposites: to speak from oneself and not to speak from oneself.

To speak from oneself is to invent things that do not exist. The Lord charges the devil with this sin in the Gospel, saying: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources; because he is a liar and its father” (John 8)—that is, father of the lie. Not to speak from oneself is to utter things that exist, even if one utters them unknowingly, as Caiaphas did when, unknowingly—indeed while intending something else—he said that it was expedient that one man should die for the people.

All the more, therefore, one who knowingly utters what exists does not speak from himself, as Christ himself does. Though knowingly uttering what exists, he says: “The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself” (John 14): namely, not falsehood but the truth which I heard and received before the human nature which you see as mine came to exist. Thus elsewhere he says to the Jews: “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from my Father” (John 8).

The Holy Spirit does this as well. For he speaks to us the truth which he heard from God: the uncreated truth, consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father; a truly existing truth, a truthful essence remaining unchangeably. Thus the statement, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak,” rightly proves what he had proposed when he said, “He will teach you all truth.” He confirms this again by adding: “He will glorify me, because he will receive of mine and declare it to you” (John 16). [Col. 0246D] And he gives the reason why he said “of mine”: “All things which the Father has are mine” (ibid.).

For whatever the Father has, whatever he knows, whatever he can do, he gave to this Lordly man who speaks these things, as he says in the psalm: “I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 44), showing what he had meant by saying: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (ibid.). The Father poured forth into the Virgin’s womb all his wisdom, all his power, and, in short, his whole Word; and he united it to human nature. Therefore he now says: “All things which the Father has are mine.”

And he did not say, “He will receive mine,” but “He will receive of mine and declare it to you” (John 16). For the Holy Spirit did not make the apostles comprehend all that wisdom, but taught them those things necessary for faith: namely the mysteries of the incarnation, [Col. 0247A] birth, Passion, and resurrection, which the disciples had not yet been able to bear so long as they saw him to be corruptible and mortal. Nor would it have been fitting for this teacher to be given before the human race had first been reconciled to God through Christ’s death.

Therefore, as the ecclesiastical office teaches by commendably placing the aforementioned reading before this Gospel, let a human being not speak from himself, but be swift to hear and slow to speak: that is, let him first hear what the Lord God speaks within him, and speak peace according to him (Ps. 84). Arius refused to do this, and therefore spoke wars and scandals, as do all who speak from themselves while seeking their own glory.

According to this gift, according to the Paraclete, we put off the old human being with its deeds and put on the new (Col. 3); this is to sing a new song. Therefore we rightly sing this very thing in the Introit and rejoice in the Offertory, because this gift is the effective cause of eternal rejoicing, which begins here and will be completed in the world to come.

## Chapter IV. On the Sunday before the Ascension of the Lord.

On the Sunday before the Ascension of the Lord, this reading from the Gospel is fittingly appointed: “Until now you have asked for nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16). For the Lord said this concerning the glory of his Ascension, through which his disciples, made certain of his omnipotence, began to ask in his name, so that their joy might be full; and, persevering with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary his mother and his brethren, they received the Holy Spirit on the tenth day (Acts 1). Therefore this reading aptly urges us to ask confidently in his name, recalling in his Ascension what the Apostle John says: “Because we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for sins” (1 John 2).

For, to encourage our hope in asking, as he was about to depart to heaven by the way of his Passion, near the end of the discourse which he gave at supper, he deigned to impress and repeat this, immediately appending the prayer which, once completed, he was immediately betrayed. Yet we should not suppose, whatever sort of persons we may be, that the opportunity of asking offered to the apostles is to be seized by us on equal terms with them. Unless we are like those who deserved to hear these words—those to whom, above, according to Luke, he had said: “You are they who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22)—unless, I say, we are like them, we cannot use the same confidence in asking.

Accordingly, this apostolic reading is suitably placed beforehand: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1). For a soldier deceives himself if, though a hearer and not a doer of the command, he demands generous rewards merely because he has heard it. The same writer says a little later: “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that man’s religion is vain” (ibid.). Certainly, when we ask, the tongue performs a kind of personal embassy. If, without a bridle and the guard of the mouth, it readily strays through idle or even harmful words, it is heard with difficulty when it asks, because the distance from vanities, to which it is accustomed, to the ears of the Lord of Hosts is so great that it does not easily deserve to be heard.

To such persons the same apostle says elsewhere: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). But to those who, as he says at the end of this reading, keep themselves unstained from this world, the Lord says familiarly, after the example of the apostles: “Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.” Elisha, who followed his master not only in body but also in heart, was a type of these men and deserved to hear: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken from you” (4 Kings 2). And what he asked was deservedly granted, when with the confidence of great faith he said: “I beseech you, let your spirit be doubled in me” (ibid.).

For Elijah, the chariot of Israel and its driver, signifies in the present chapter our Lord, who, as a charioteer, governs his Church by the word of his teaching and, as a chariot, conveys it to heaven by the vehicle of his divinity. Elisha, however—who, although permitted once, twice, and three times to remain behind for himself, refused through love of his master to use that permission—represents the apostles and apostolic men. Through love of Christ, refusing even to use what is permitted, they follow him beyond the limit of commandment, voluntary observers of counsel. The rich young man in the Gospel, unwilling to do this, went away sorrowful (Matthew 19).

Therefore, to one of this kind who asks and says, “I beseech you, let your spirit be doubled in me,” the Lord Jesus, who ascends to heaven, says: “If you see when I am taken from you, what you ask shall be granted” (4 Kings 2). “If you see”—that is, if you do not turn the eyes of your mind down to earthly things, but long only for heavenly things—what you ask shall be granted. For in such persons Christ’s spirit becomes double: since he walked meekly among men, as the Holy Spirit signified when he appeared above him in the form of a dove (Matthew 3), that same Spirit makes these persons at once meek and fervent in zeal. For, toward those subject to them, as cause or time requires, they come now with a rod, now in a spirit of meekness (1 Corinthians 4).

This is that joy whose message we are commanded in the Introit to proclaim to the ends of the earth [Col. 0248D]. This is the benefit for which, in the Offertory, the nations are urged to bless God, and at Communion to sing and proclaim his salvation (Psalm 95), because we have as advocate one who shares our nature (1 John 1), and by asking in whose name we may deserve to receive full joy.

## CHAPTER V. On the Rogation Days Instituted by Saint Mamertus

Mindful of this promise and placing his hope in it, Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted solemn rogations before the day of the same Sunday of the Lord’s Ascension, when the Christian people were oppressed by prolonged and grievous affliction. Wolves, daring even to contend in packs with densely gathered human beings under divine judgment, inflicted the rabid slaughter of their teeth not only upon villages but even upon crowded cities [Col. 0249A]. The purpose was that, as the Lord was departing to heaven and saying, “Ask, and you shall receive” (John 16), the remembrance of human misery might be more urgently presented in three days of supplication; and that, with the power of the promiser recalled, the hope of those who ask in faith might be strengthened.

In these same processions the emblems of the conqueror ascending into heaven, namely crosses and banners, are carried before them. Their use in the Church began in the time of Constantine. When he had seen in a dream the sign of the cross splendidly displayed in heaven and had been told, “O Constantine, by this you shall conquer,” he ordered skilled men to fashion, from gold and precious stones, the sign of the holy cross into a banner called the *Labarum*. This military emblem was more precious than the others because it was customary for it to go before the emperor and to be adored by the soldiers.

It should be known that these three-day rogations are older than the Greater Litany instituted by blessed Gregory. Indeed, from the twentieth year of Zeno’s reign, when Bishop Mamertus instituted the aforesaid rogations, until the new year of Emperor Maurice, when a great flood occurred in the regions of Venetia, Liguria, and Italy—such as is not believed to have occurred after the time of Noah—and was immediately followed by a plague in the groin, during which the Roman people was almost destroyed and Pope Pelagius died of the same plague, Gregory, still a deacon, proclaimed the Greater Litany: the chronographers find a little more than one hundred years [Col. 0249B].

The salutary and timely traditions of both are celebrated in the same office, in which we are urged by the Gospel parable to persevere in knocking at the door of the friend (Luke 11), namely our Lord Jesus Christ. His door is now shut and his children are with him in bed (ibid.), because, having ascended on high, he led captivity captive (Psalm 67); received into his temples as into a bedchamber, he rests there after the labor of his Passion upon the couch of consummated glory, together with his children—that is, the saints who have departed from the labors of this world.

And from there, as we sing in the Introit, “He heard our voice” (Psalm 17), if, as we say in the Offertory, “We confess the Lord exceedingly with our mouth” (Psalm 118): “exceedingly,” I say, meaning even to importunity, so that that Gospel friend may rise and give his friend as many loaves as he needs (Luke 11). The Epistle aptly encourages the one knocking at the friend’s door to persevere, offering the example of Elijah, so that we may argue from like to like that a friend can be overcome by the persistence of knocking.

Let no one who knocks despair because he is a sinner and the proposed example concerns a righteous man. For it is set before sinners. The same apostle indicates that he speaks to sinners when he begins: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 3). Yet this is the beginning of righteousness. “For the righteous man is the first to accuse himself” (Proverbs 18); that is, he begins to be justified by accusing himself. Thus the universal statement includes the sinner who has been justified by his self-accusation: “For the persevering prayer of a righteous man avails much” (James 5). Therefore he too may use the example proposed from righteous Elijah, so that, in knocking, if not on account of friendship, as the Gospel says, he may at least overcome through the persistence of importunity (Luke 11).

## CHAPTER VI. On the Mass on the Vigil of the Lord’s Ascension

On the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, the Gospel reading is appointed in which the Lord Jesus, about to be betrayed, “lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17). The reason why it is read in anticipation of this solemnity is this: what he then prayed while about to suffer became known to men when he ascended; namely, that in dying, as he says in the Song of Songs, he “ascended the palm tree,” and in rising again “seized its fruits” (Song 7).

Since this became known to men through the Ascension, as has been said, for their salvation—for men could not be saved without knowledge or faith in it—this prayer is rightly read, in which he prayed this very thing, being now about to go by the way of his Passion, by drinking the deadly torrent, to that glory. It should be noted, however, that when he said, “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you,” he immediately added: “As you gave him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17). He did not say, “and give him,” but, “as you gave him power.”

For although the Lord Jesus was crowned with glory and honor because of the Passion of death (Hebrews 2), and God therefore exalted him because “he became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2), nevertheless, before that death itself and before that cross itself, the Father had given him the kingdom and power over all flesh. But it was not yet the time for him to be glorified in that kingdom or power while he was still mortal.

To demonstrate this more plainly, it is pleasing to offer an authoritative comparison from ancient history, known to almost all students of venerable letters. Behold Saint David, who signified by his own name this desirable and strong-handed Christ, foreshadowed him by deeds, inherited him by promise, and sang of him in prophetic psalms: he was glorified in one way, and at another time, by God’s gift, received royal power [Col. 0250D]. For he was glorified with his glory when Saul had died and he went up to Hebron, being received first by the tribe of Judah and then by all Israel (2 Kings 2). But God gave him this same authority when he took him from the flocks of sheep and, through the hand of Samuel, anointed him king among his brothers (1 Kings 16).

Oh, with how many bitterness-filled draughts was he made to drink from receiving authority until he enjoyed the kingdom! With how many labors did God, as Saul persecuted him, instruct him while fashioning his crown? By this comparison the proposed matter is readily understood. Thus our Lord too, before he was glorified with that glorification for which he now prays, saying, “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17), had received royal dignity, having been anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Psalm 44). This occurred not for the first time when the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove (Matthew 3), but already when true man was assumed in secret in the virginal womb by the true God, God the Word, through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

The whole fullness poured out into that Incarnation is aptly signified by the horn of oil with which David was anointed secretly in his father’s house, so that Saul might not know. And as the calf which Samuel, at God’s command, took with him deceived Saul, so that he might not know what was happening in the house or suspect anything except what the preparation of the calf seemed to indicate, namely the intention of sacrifice (2 Kings 16), so the mortal nature of man that appeared in the world deceived the devil. He did not know what had been done in the Virgin’s womb, nor did he suppose anything else about Christ except what the suffering flesh outwardly showed: namely, a mere man, subject in every respect, as he supposed, to our corruption, and flesh of sin.

Yet in the course of time he perceived that Christ could resist his tyrannical dominion; just as Saul, possessed by a demon, understood from David’s mighty deeds that something was being done against his throne in him, through the Spirit of the Lord which had departed from Saul and was directed toward David (ibid.) [Col. 0251B].

Therefore, what our Lord says when the hour of death is at hand—“Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you”—and immediately adds, “as you gave him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17), is like David, while Saul pursued him in the wilderness of Ziph or in the wilderness of Maon at the Rock of Division, when he despaired of escaping Saul’s presence (1 Kings 23), saying to God, who hears all: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope” (Psalm 118); or, “As you swore to David in your truth” (Psalm 88)—that is, when you took me from my father’s sheep and anointed me with the anointing of your mercy (1 Kings 16).

But what he says afterward—“And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17)—must be understood in such a way that we should by no means suppose the divinity of the Word to have been obscured from the glory which God had in the beginning with God. For Christ does not pray according to his divine nature, but according to the form of a servant which was about immediately to die. How, then, does the nature of a servant ask to be glorified with a glory previously possessed, or how did it possess this glory before the world was?

Plainly, because of the unity of his person, the form of a servant truly affirms that its own glory is that which the form of God united to it had with the Father before the world was. Thus the form of a servant must firmly be said to have possessed that glory then in the same way as the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven. For he says: “And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3) [Col. 0252A]. The man visible to sight did not descend from heaven, but he who was conceived and born from the flesh of Mary the Virgin.

Likewise, the man, the Son of Man, who, as has been said, was conceived and born from the earthliness of flesh and who spoke these things while standing on earth, was not in heaven but walked on earth, soon to be seized, crucified, and buried in the earth. Therefore, just as, because of the unity of person, the Son of Man descended from heaven because the Word united to him was in heaven and everywhere, so, because of that same unity of person, the praying human nature now says: “Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was.”

But now let the discussion turn to those parts of this Gospel reading upon which the remaining elements of the office depend [Col. 0252B]. A little later, where he says, “I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me” (John 17), he immediately adds: “Because they are yours; and all mine are yours, and yours are mine; and I have been glorified in them” (ibid.). Near the end of the same prayer he says: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they may be one in us” (ibid.), and so forth.

“Let them be one in us,” he says, “as we are one,” in the manner stated above: those whom you gave me are yours, and by passing into my possession they did not cease to be yours; and all mine are yours, and yours are mine—indeed, more truly yours because they began to be mine. It is pleasing to examine this mode of sharing more closely, so that we may understand how those things which belong to the Father are more truly the Father’s from the fact that they were given to Christ the man.

This should therefore not be passed over: before this Son of Man was brought into the commonwealth of God the Father and, as Daniel saw in the vision of the night, brought even to the Ancient of Days—who gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, so that all peoples, tribes, and languages might serve him (Daniel 7)—the whole universe was unprotected and unjoined to its Creator, because there was no mediator between Creator and creature. For whatever existed was either Creator or creature.

Therefore, in order that there might be found a middle bond of perfect fellowship, this one was introduced, who might bind Creator and creature more firmly together because one and the same Christ is both: Creator, namely because he is God; creature, because he is man [Col. 0252D]. And although the Apostle says, “For nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Hebrews 1), nevertheless angels are not deprived of this condescension. Since man is every creature in some respect—having being with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and discernment with angels—and since God assumed man, it follows that angels too rejoice because he who was Creator above them is also a creature together with them.

Moreover, this too pertains to the matter: man, according to the body alone, visibly bears a kind of likeness to the world, being composed of four elements. Hence the Greeks call him *mikrokosmos* (μικρόκοσμος), that is, “the lesser world.” According to the soul alone, however, he is of angelic substance, namely rational and immortal; like an angel, he differs from the Creator only by the substantial difference that he is created [Col. 0253A]. Thus the fact that God became man pertains also to the rejoicing of the angelic creation.

Therefore, as has been said above, in order that there might be one through whom Creator and creature could be bound together more firmly, this mediator, the Son of Man, was introduced into the commonwealth of the Creator. Receiving in human nature what he had not possessed, he would not usurp authority for himself but, according to the Apostle, would hand over the kingdom to God and the Father (1 Corinthians 13), saying, as was set forth above: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.” This is the mode of fellowship and likeness which he has in view when he says: “That they may be one in us, as we are one.”

The composer of the sacred office, holding this truth most faithfully, appointed before this Gospel the reading from the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and none of them said that anything which he possessed was his own. But distribution was made to each as anyone had need” (Acts 4). By this he plainly indicates how we should understand what the Lord says in prayer, “that they may be one as we are,” and what he had earlier declared: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.”

If, because of the weakness of our eyes, we cannot behold the sun in its own height, let us observe its course in the lower steps. That is: if we cannot discern in himself the deified man, admitted into communion with the Trinity without any multiplication of persons, saying with awareness of what fullness, “All mine are yours, and yours are mine,” let us look to his imitators, of whom it was said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul,” and so forth [Col. 0253C]. Let us argue in this lesser instance from that greater one.

We must necessarily grant that there is less fellowship, less agreement or charity, and less grace of the Holy Spirit in many human persons, in a multitude of human beings—even believers, even righteous people, even those walking in truth and charity—than there is in the Father and Christ the Son, God and man. In him human nature is so united to divine nature that it cannot divide that person into two; his agreement and charity are so fruitful that the grace of the holy sevenfold Spirit has never been lacking to him.

Yet behold: among these many persons, who possess far less, there is such fellowship and such harmony of charity that in spiritual things they have one heart and one soul, while even in bodily possessions nothing is private, but all things are common. The charity of their fellowship in bodily things is clear, because they came forth from baptism such persons that they are elegantly compared with “a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Song 4), stripped of the fleeces of those possessions which they laid at the apostles’ feet [Col. 0253D].

We have everywhere in Scripture, and especially in the Apostle, a clear and evident indication of unity in spiritual things as well. After saying, “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord” (1 Corinthians 12), he adds a little later: “For as the body is one and has many members, but all the members, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (ibid.) [Col. 0254A]. For as in one body we have many members, but all members do not have the same activity, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

Something similar is found in the replies of blessed Lawrence. When he showed Decius the poor, he said—not concerning their rags or diseased bodies, but concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit which believers had received: “Behold, these are the eternal treasures, which are never diminished nor decreased, which are scattered among individuals and found in all.” For Christ’s poor receive divisions of graces, and each performs his own gift; yet each shares with all his own particular grace.

For example, the spirit of knowledge and the spirit of piety (Isaiah 11), good portions of the heavenly treasury, were scattered among the individual persons Peter and Paul, but are found in all: while knowledge flows from Paul’s mouth to all hearers according to their capacity, Peter’s piety, instructed by his own fall, opens to all sinners who rightly knock the doors of fitting mercy [Col. 0254B]. Thus the eye sees and the ear hears for the whole body; nor can the eye say to the hand, “I have no need of your works,” nor the head to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.”

Therefore, the fellowship of the Trinity with the assumed human nature is a bond of unanimity far stronger than this, on account of which he says: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.” Though we cannot now see it as it is, we nevertheless behold it in some measure through the mirror of this likeness of our own (1 Corinthians 13).

And behold something great and wonderful, visible to the heavens and the powers of heaven, appears in that nature of the blessed Son of Man, with whom all things are common with the Father: both those which he naturally possesses in himself and those which he potentially created beneath himself. The Father naturally has within himself the Word born from himself; but because the Father uttered him, that man has the incarnate Word within himself. The Father likewise has the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself; that man has the Holy Spirit always resting in himself.

The Father potentially created beneath himself heaven and earth and all things in them: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim and seraphim, and the tenth drachma, that is, man (Colossians 1) [Col. 0254D]. But this true man Christ joined and reconciled all these things in himself; he was set over all things, and all things are subjected under his feet (Psalm 8). That Father, the Ancient of Days, sits upon the throne; and this Lamb, the Son of Man, also sits there. Indeed, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5); and, as is said elsewhere, “he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (ibid.).

Therefore all nations, as we sing in the Introit, clap your hands; rejoice to God with the voice of exultation (Psalm 49), while the devil’s envy weeps and consumes itself in grief because it has been frustrated—or rather because it has brought benefit while desiring harm. For before man fell, he was nevertheless merely man; but now, while he repairs the fall and ascends, he is God and man [Col. 0255A]. Now he is “Lord, now exalted, terrible, a great king” (Psalm 46).

He is Lord, I say, and his name is wonderful in all the earth; exalted, because his magnificence has been raised above the heavens (Psalm 8); terrible, because as he ascended, so he will return to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1). This great king now sits victorious in that court at the Father’s right hand, crowned with honor and glory: a beautiful and awaited king in his blessed commonwealth; heir of a Father not dead but never to die; himself dead once and now never again to die; possessing all the treasures of the ancient imperial Father, stored in the treasury of his breast. From these he gives gifts to men (Psalm 76): to one a word of wisdom or knowledge, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of words, to another workings of powers (1 Corinthians 12), and things like these.

Therefore, as has been said, all nations, clap your hands—that is, clap with joy; do good works. Nothing could have been more elegantly prefixed to the Introit, according to the stated sense of the Gospel or the reading from the Acts of the Apostles. For in “clap your hands,” both action and the aforesaid sharing of charity are briefly commended. In clapping there is joy and the striking together of hands. Thus we are commanded to clap our hands so that, with joyful charity, we make common whatever we have, whatever we know, whatever we can do; and by this agreement may be one, cleaving to Christ as a body through the harmonious fitting together of its members [Col. 0255C].

## CHAPTER VII. On the Office for the Day of the Lord’s Ascension

The office for the day of the Lord’s Ascension sings joy to all who love him. For while we believe that our Redeemer himself has ascended into heaven, we too dwell in heavenly things in mind; and with the certainty of hope we already possess the thing to which we rejoice that he has attained. For, as he himself says, “Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Matthew 24): that is, the true beholders of the sun and lovers of its brightness will follow him to where he is [Col. 0255D]. Their souls fly upward to heavenly things on the wings of virtues, despising earthly things, and do not fall back again to earth on account of corpses.

For the body upon which alone eagles of this kind feed is in heaven: the body, I say, of Christ, “in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2), which feeds angels and is the food and eternal life of every rational creature (John 6). This joy, I say, the office of the present day proclaims; but this very joy is troubled by what we also sing in the voice of the angels saying: “So shall he come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1).

For God indeed ascended in jubilation, namely that of the apostles, “who, worshipping, as Luke relates, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24) [Col. 0256A]. Those chiefly share in this joy who, possessing the perfection of charity within themselves, have confidence on the day of judgment. God, I say, ascended in the jubilation of such persons; but he ascended also “with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 46), that is, with the terrifying proclamation of that same judgment, when the angels say: “So shall he come as you saw him going into heaven.”

Among those who end their lives in the peace of the Church, surely few fight so well and contend so lawfully that they can look securely upon the insignia of the coming king—namely the cross and the marks of the nails—and kiss them with an unrebuked conscience. Few, I say, have so borne their own cross and followed him that they may justly claim the generous rewards of so great a conqueror for their laborious military service. Indeed, according to the parable which he himself set forth, few return with due profit the talents entrusted to them by the man departing into a far country (Matthew 25): that is, the gifts which he gave to men when he ascended on high and led captivity captive (Psalm 67; Ephesians 8), namely the flesh by whose nature our minds are held captive in this world [Col. 0256B].

Few expend those gifts for their neighbors’ benefit so that they permit none of them to lie buried in the earth—that is, to be perversely turned to earthly uses—and none to remain without spiritual gain. But let it be so: sometimes persons are found who have strengthened their arm rightly and manfully in pursuits of this kind. Such a person is deservedly praised, because while others are sluggish, with their sides bare and deserted, he advances attended by a great army; and he is about to meet that king with ten thousand for battle—that is, for the contest of judgment (Luke 14).

But, according to the Gospel parable, that king comes with twenty thousand (ibid.), because while this good and faithful servant can scarcely render an account even of his deeds, his Lord, when he returns, demands an account from him also of his thoughts. Thus, terrified by the double army of interrogations, he must necessarily distrust his simple and half-complete answers [Col. 0256C].

Therefore, while we are concerned about sending an embassy and asking for peace, and await the response of that peace, we do indeed rejoice in hope, as has been said; but fear greatly diminishes this very joy of hope. Because this anxiety is salutary, the final sting of the Epistle is repeatedly used both in the Introit and in the Offertory: “So shall he come as you saw him going into heaven” [Col. 0256D].

The entire force of the sentence, almost the entire spirit-stirring blast of this Gospel trumpet, sounds especially in the little phrase added to the verb: “So shall he come.” For it sharply strikes the unhappy pride of those who pierced him; it strikes the lost wisdom of the world and reprobate prudence with lightning. Then truly what is weak in God will be stronger than men, and what is foolish in God—for they considered Jesus Christ crucified to be folly—will be wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1), as they themselves confess with grief.

Then Isaiah’s terrifying prophecy will be fulfilled in them: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, that they may not see” (Isaiah 26)—that is, that they may not see the glory of the Lord [Col. 0257A]. For the wicked will not see the glory of the Lord, that is, the divinity of the man Jesus Christ, the sight of which will be salvation to those who see it; but they will see the flesh which they despised, mocked, spat upon, scourged, crowned with thorns, and pierced. For the same prophet continues: “Let them see and be confounded” (ibid.). Expressing how great this shame of an evil conscience is, he says: “And let fire devour your enemies” (ibid.).

Then angels and archangels will tremble; where then will the wicked appear? (1 Peter 4.) Angels, I say, will tremble and, as the Lord says to blessed Job, “being terrified, they shall be purified” (Job 41), when Behemoth, who was made to fear no one, “who is king over all the children of pride” (ibid.), wonderfully created and fearful in his own nature, malice, and conspicuous ferocity, is brought before the strength of the Son of Man; when the entrails of hell are laid open, “he shall be cast down while all behold” (Job 40) [Col. 0257B].

Certainly the holy angels are proved not to undergo judgment through purgatorial terror. They have been made firm as a solid body, just as the softness of waters is said to turn into solid crystal. After that prince of sin sinned, they, refusing to sin, received this as their reward: that now they cannot sin. Yet because they were of the same condition, they too could have sinned; perhaps, at the sight of the present wrath, they will fear that they once had that same possibility, which they too could have incurred had they been abandoned by grace.

For Lord Ephrem says that the very ranks of angels will be afraid and tremble on the day of his coming. But concerning holy human beings, who imitate the ministries of heavenly spirits by proclaiming the truth of God and therefore receive their common name, being called angels—for *angel* is the name of an office, not of a nature—there is no doubt that they tremble and are pierced with fear. If, then, holy angels will tremble, where will the wicked appear? That day will be for them a day of wrath, a day of calamity and misery, a great day and exceedingly bitter.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Statement: “And He Sits at the Right Hand of God.”

This concern, then, renders our present joy incomplete; Mark alone records its climax in the Gospel. For after he had said, “And the Lord Jesus indeed, after he had spoken to them, ascended into heaven” (Mark 16), he added this: “And sits at the right hand of God” (ibid.). For the height of our joy is that the true nature of our flesh, going before us in that Son of Man, sits at the right hand of God. Today that venerable Ancient of Days, with thousands of thousands ministering to him and ten thousand times a hundred thousand standing before him, received him, coming according to Daniel in the clouds of heaven, upon his fiery throne (Dan. 7), and, uttering from his hoary head a fitting decree, said to him—as David, his father according to the flesh, had said—“Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109 [Vulgate 108]), etc.

This must not be understood as the Anthropomorphites think: that God, like us, has a right hand on one side and a left hand on the other, and is bounded by a human form; nor should we suppose that God’s sitting means that he does so with bent knees.
