Nor, Augustine says, should we fall into that sacrilege in which the Apostle denounces those “who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man” (Rom. 1). For it is sinful for a Christian to set up such an image of God in a church, and far more sinful to set it up in the heart, where the true temple of God is.

Therefore, God’s “sitting” signifies not a position of limbs but judicial power. And what he says to Christ the Lord, “Sit at my right hand,” means: be equal with me; which is the same as if he had said, “Reign with me.” This was said to him according to his human nature, since according to it kingdom and honour were given to him, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him (Dan. 7). Hence in the Communion we sing: “Sing to the Lord, who ascended above the heaven of heavens toward the east” (Ps. 68 [Vulgate 67]).

For Christ’s human nature, through the dignity of every virtue and holiness, surpassed every spiritual creature so completely that it ascended even to the East—that is, to the Son personally united to it—leaving nothing beyond itself except God. Here it should be noted that it did not say “to the rising” or “to what will rise,” but “to the East.” For that ineffable generation is not considered in terms of past and future: the Son is generated from the Father in an everlasting present.

Yet this must also be understood locally, because he ascended above the firmament of heaven, and this toward the eastern region. For the statement “even to the East,” that is, “even to the Son personally united to it,” is not said with reference to place, but to the transformation of human nature—a transformation in which we too, according to the Apostle, shall be transformed according to our measure (1 Cor. 15). Nor was it transformed in such a way that the true substance of flesh passed over into that substance of the East; rather, glory was added, while nature was not taken away. Passibility was absorbed; impassibility succeeded it. Mortality perished; the flesh acquired coeternity with the Word.

Thus water hardens into the likeness of stone. For crystal has the appearance of a stone, but is not by its own nature stone, because, as natural philosophers say, the substance of water hardened by frost produces this appearance. Gregory, in his exposition of Ezekiel, relates this by an apt comparison to the aforesaid transformation of the flesh.

> **[Note: Col. 0257D]** St Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 7, §19, *Patrologia*, vol. 76, ed. Migne.

For he says:

> “The body of our Redeemer, because it was subject to suffering even unto death, was in one respect like water, since by being born, growing, becoming weary, hungering, thirsting, and dying, it ran through the successive moments of time until his Passion. But because through the glory of his resurrection it gained strength from corruption into the power of incorruption, because, after the manner of crystal, it hardened from water, so that in him there might remain both that same nature and yet no longer the mutability of corruption which it had possessed. Water, therefore, was changed into crystal when the weakness of its corruption was strengthened by his resurrection into the firmness of incorruption.”

And it should be noted that, although crystal is a most beautiful substance, in this sense there is said to be, as it were, a terrible appearance of crystal, because our Redeemer, one and the same, will appear serene to the righteous but terrible to the unrighteous, as was said above.

Therefore, just as water, without the substance or quantity of its substance perishing, but with only its fluid quality passing into solidity, hardens into the likeness of stone, so the manhood of the Lord, to whom we sing, did not lose the substance of its members, which, its number or quantity being preserved, ascended. First, because he rose, it ascended—namely, not locally, into conformity and coeternity with the East, that is, with the divinity of which it was said above—while the unstable quality alone was wholly absorbed, the quality by which he feared and could be sorrowful and afraid, and said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26; Mark 14), and other such things. Second, on this day, in the sight of the apostles, it ascended locally above the firmament of heaven, as was said above, toward the east, that is, toward the eastern region.

But where and how the Lord’s body is in heaven is, Augustine says in his book *On the Catholic Faith*, a most curious and superfluous question. It is enough to believe that it is in heaven. For it does not belong to our frailty to investigate the secrets of heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. That a procession is held on the day of the Lord’s Ascension by authority of the Gospel

That we hold a procession on this day commends to us the fact that we ought to follow our Lord into that very heaven into which he himself entered as our forerunner, by the same path of obedience which he, becoming obedient unto death (Phil. 2), displayed beforehand by his example.

For he himself, just as he was about to ascend into heaven, deigned to signify this very thing, as Luke the Evangelist relates. For after the Lord had said, “And I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24), Luke continues: “And he led them out as far as Bethany” (ibid.). By that leading-out he signified that we ought to follow him, as was said above; and by the name Bethany, which is interpreted “obedience,” he signified that, by imitating his obedience, we may become his members and may ascend with him who bears all things by the word of his power.

Accordingly, the more careful orders of the Church rightly sing in this procession, among the responsories which especially concern that same leading-out, the responsory: “The Lord Jesus led his disciples out to Bethany and blessed them,” which is taken from Luke’s Gospel. For in singing and processing in this way we speak to one another and recall the very thing which the Lord signified by that leading-out: namely, that his followers ought to go out from the world, as he had already told them: “I chose you from the world, that you may go and bear fruit” (John 15).

Where are you to go? Surely into the whole world. For this is what he then said to them according to Mark: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). In this he openly rebukes the Jews, who vainly glory that they alone are the peculiar people of God. For apart from the fact that, in one respect, as blessed Gregory says, every human being is a creature—for one has existence with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and discernment with angels—apart from this, I say, he rebukes the Jews by saying “to every creature.”

For he used a concise expression, saying “to every creature” in place of “to every human being.” Had he said “to every human being,” an explanation would have been required as to why not to the Jew alone. And what better explanation could be given than that, just as the Jew is God’s creature, so also is the Gentile? Hence the Apostle says: “Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, also of the Gentiles” (Rom. 3). Beautifully, therefore, he used the concise phrase “to every creature,” by which he both denotes every human being and supplies the just reason for his command.

> **[Note: Col. 0259D]** St Gregory, *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 29, §2, *Patrologia*, vol. 76, ed. Migne.

## CHAPTER X. Why the same procession is held not before but after Terce

Since, therefore, we reasonably hold a procession on this day, it is likewise reasonable that it is celebrated not, as on Easter Day or other Sundays, before Terce is sung, but after it has been sung. For only the Sunday procession, because water is then blessed in memory and veneration of holy baptism, as has been said elsewhere, precedes Terce. At that hour the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles; thus, just as we are baptized and thereby receive the Holy Spirit, so we first sprinkle ourselves and our places with blessed water, and then sing the memorial of the coming of the Holy Spirit, namely, Terce.

Why the memory of holy baptism is thus renewed for us on Sunday has been said above, where we spoke as far as we were able about the holy solemnity and order of Easter. Therefore this procession and the other processions which are held without the blessing of water rightly follow Terce when it has first been said, and are joined without interruption to the ensuing office of Mass.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Sunday after the Lord’s Ascension

The office of this Sunday is the voice of the apostles, who, in obedience to the command of the ascending Lord, remained in the city until they should be clothed with power from on high (Luke 24), being of one accord in prayer with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1).

But it is not only their voice; it is also ours, to be uttered from heart and mouth into the ears of the Lord, that by grace his Spirit may deign to descend even upon us. For we too, although the lowest, are members of that same body in which the apostles hold preeminence. Let that ointment descend upon us which, overflowing in fullness upon the head—that is, upon Christ—first descended upon Aaron’s beard (Ps. 133 [Vulgate 132]), that is, upon the mountain, namely our same Lord Christ, exalted above the mountain of heaven; upon the beard, I say, that is, upon strong and perfect men, our fathers the apostles; and let it descend even to the hem of his garment (Ps. 133 [Vulgate 132]), that is, to those chosen from the Jews who were close to the apostles. And as dew, let it descend upon Mount Zion (ibid.), that is, upon every believer among us from the Gentiles.

Accordingly, the Introit of the present office is most suitable to this expectation: “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you.” For this is described in Psalm 27 [Vulgate 26], which bears the title: “A psalm of David before he was anointed,” that is, before he was anointed king. This title also directs us to the history. While David was still a boy in the house of his father, namely Bethlehem, he was anointed by Samuel (1 Sam. 16), the Holy Spirit thereby foreshadowing that he would be king. Then he was anointed at Hebron and yet reigned only over the tribe of Judah after Saul’s death (2 Sam. 2). Later he was anointed a third time, when he received the dominion of the whole Israelite people.

These anointings signify something mystically for us. For as David was anointed three times, so every believer ought to partake of a threefold anointing: first, in baptism, where they are renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit; second, when through the laying on of the bishop’s hands they are increased by the gifts of that same Holy Spirit; third, on the day of judgment, when they will attain the perfect sweetness of that same spiritual grace.

But we should not suppose that David composed this psalm before he was anointed in his father’s house. Whether he composed it immediately after that anointing or after the second is uncertain. We, however, sing this office after the second anointing, while awaiting the third; for we have already received the laying on of hands from bishops. But the apostles, whose expectation this office imitates, were awaiting the second anointing after the first. For after the remission of sins which they had received at Christ’s death—when he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20)—they were awaiting from heaven the laying on of hands by the same great High Priest, Jesus Christ, who has passed through the heavens (Heb. 4). This was their second anointing.

But we, having received this second anointing from bishops with holy chrism through their ministry, await grace upon grace: the third grace which we shall receive in that heavenly Church in such fullness that it is deservedly called intoxication and overflowing delight, as the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 36 [Vulgate 35]). And Isaiah says: “The Lord says, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). For the gift of the Holy Spirit in Zion—that is, in the present Church—is fire, however great; but in Jerusalem—that is, in the heavenly homeland—it is a full and unfailing furnace.

Therefore, in accordance with the aforesaid expectation, we sing at the Introit: “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you” (Ps. 27 [Vulgate 26]); and because the voice of the body is not enough, we add: “My heart said to you: I have sought your face,” etc. The Epistle teaches how we ought to pray this very prayer, saying: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (1 Pet. 4), etc. The Gospel, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father” (John 16), is therefore fittingly read, because the apostles were awaiting that same promise and undoubtedly held in both mind and speech the prayer which, at the end of his discourse, he prayed to the Father for them and for us who were to believe through their word. Hence the Communion is also fitting: “Father, when I was with them” (John 17). The Offertory likewise, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 146 [Vulgate 145]), is not out of keeping, because Luke writes: “And they were in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke 24).

## CHAPTER XII. Why the apostolic writings have thus far been read at the night vigils

For this reason, throughout these days of the Lord’s resurrection—that is, from Easter until Pentecost—the apostolic writings have been read in the night vigils: namely, the Acts of the Apostles, the Apocalypse, and the seven Catholic Epistles. For they proclaim testimony to that same resurrection, as it is written: “With great power the apostles gave testimony”—that is, both by voice and by writings—“to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 4).

But on those days which signify the period during which the Lord lived in this world before his Passion, the Apostle Paul is read, because almost everywhere his entire purpose is to prove that grace was necessary for the whole world—that is, for Jews as well as Gentiles—and that no one can be saved by works of the Law but only by faith in Christ. Thus, throughout the whole time in which the presence of our Lord is commemorated, whether before or after his Passion, the heralds of the New Testament fittingly speak, so that his children may, as it were, drink the milk of consolation from the breasts of the Bridegroom who is present.

These breasts, indeed, are those of Scripture, of which the Church says to that same Bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song 1).

# BOOK TEN

## CHAPTER ONE. On the coming, divinity, and operation of the Holy Spirit

How venerable and worthy of embrace the solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit ought to be for holy mother Church and all her children is clearly shown by considering both the dignity of the person who comes and the purpose of his coming.

For he himself is God and Lord, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son, uncreated and immeasurable, as the third person of the creative Trinity. Without his grace no rational creature remains steadfast in the order of heaven. The angel who departed from him became a devil; the human being who approaches him is made like God.

The purpose of his coming is this: since the Bridegroom has been taken away, he may assume the care and guardianship of his orphaned children and defend, by lawful advocacy, the inheritance bequeathed to them in the Father’s testament—indeed, written out in his blood—in every court, before whatever judge, king, tyrant, or rulers of the earth. For a lawsuit concerning the boundaries of the paternal possession was to be brought before the court. Although the Ancient of Days said to the Bridegroom of whom we speak, the Father of the orphans, “Ask of me, and I shall give you the Gentiles for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2), there were nevertheless to be those who wished greatly to narrow, or even nullify, his inheritance: the Jews, who confined it to their Synagogue alone; Donatus, who sought to confine it to Africa alone; and the pagans, who wished that none of his possession should exist anywhere.

Moreover, since the sons could claim the estates of heaven as bequeathed to them by the aforesaid testament of their Father, it was necessary that this most faithful guardian should be present against the snares of evil spirits, in order to instruct and protect them and to intercede for offenders. “For,” the Apostle says, “we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8).

Therefore, in proportion both to the dignity of the person who comes and to the cause of his coming, this solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit is glorious, splendid, venerable, and sweet to the household of holy Church, equally with that most sacred feast of the Lord’s resurrection. For just as our birth would have profited us nothing unless redemption had profited us, so our redemption would have profited us nothing unless we had been enlightened by the Holy Spirit and received remission of sins.

## CHAPTER II. By what authority baptism should be administered on the Saturday of Pentecost, as also on the Saturday of Easter

For this reason these two seasons, Easter and Pentecost, were appointed by the Roman pontiffs for baptism. Hence the great Leo, writing to all those established throughout Sicily, after speaking of Holy Saturday of Easter, on which baptism should be administered, added:

> “To this observance is added also the solemnity of Pentecost, from the coming of the Holy Spirit. It depends upon the point of the Paschal feast; and whereas the other feasts belong to other days, this one always falls on the day distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace and inviting those whom illness, the length of a journey, or the difficulty of navigation has prevented from attending on Easter Day, so that, though hindered by whatever necessities, they may obtain the fulfilment of their desire through the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

> **[Note: Col. 0263D]** St Leo, Epistle XVI, to all bishops established throughout Sicily, ch. 3, *Patrologia*, vol. 54, ed. Migne.

And shortly afterward:

> “But we defend this not on the basis of our own persuasion, but prove it by a sufficiently apt example of apostolic authority, following blessed Peter the Apostle. On that very day on which the coming of the promised Holy Spirit filled the number of all believers, he consecrated by the laver of baptism a people of three thousand converted by his preaching, as the holy Scripture which contains the Acts of the Apostles teaches in a trustworthy history (Acts 2), saying: ‘When they heard this, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles: What shall we do, brethren? And Peter said to them: Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,’” etc.

> **[Note: Col. 0263D]** St Leo, ibid., ch. 4.

Indeed, such reverence for so great a Lord is worthy and just, since equity requires equal laws in equal cases: because the Son, not except through the finger of God, conquered the strong man armed by rising again, and plundered and cleansed his goods (Matt. 21; Luke 11), so likewise, when this finger of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—comes, there should be presented to him, as to the rising Son, his own work: namely, the effect of holy baptism. This is especially so because the regeneration effected by that baptism is the proper operation of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning the sacrament of this regeneration, some matters have been set out above under Holy Saturday of Easter, together with the readings and chants belonging to that sacrament, insofar as the intended brevity allowed and as seemed worthy of investigation.

## CHAPTER III. What the reading “God tested Abraham” has to do with the grace of the Holy Spirit

Nevertheless, we must not now pass over what the reading appointed for this day, “God tested Abraham” (Gen. XII), has to do with the grace of baptism. The answer is easy and plain to those who ask. In the outpouring of the Holy Spirit which we celebrate, there was fulfilled what the Lord said to our father Abraham in this reading: “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son, I shall bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand which is on the seashore” (ibid.).

Above all, he added: “Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice” (ibid.). This, I say, began to be fulfilled when the Holy Spirit, invisibly penetrating the breasts of the apostles, gave a new sign of sanctification, so that every kind of language was born upon their lips (Acts 2).

For the Holy Spirit then began to be given to all nations, coming openly upon the Gentile Cornelius and certain others by a sign. He is the one and only blessing of God, by whom all nations are blessed in the seed of Abraham, who is Christ. In the Virgin’s womb, the same Holy Spirit anticipated Christ in blessings—that is, in outpourings of all his graces—so that we all might receive from his fullness.

No tract follows this reading because it is not written that father Abraham sang any song for this deed. For he had no one to whom, or with whom, he might sing: he was one and almost the sole worshipper of God, and likewise a pilgrim in a foreign land. The rest, as said above, has been discussed as far as possible in the office of Easter Saturday.

## CHAPTER IV. That there are seven offices in honour of the sevenfold Spirit, with Thursday left vacant

In all the offices of this most sacred solemnity, the authority of the Holy Spirit is preeminent. His majesty provides their subject matter. This is particularly clear in the Epistles taken from the Acts of the Apostles. Yet in certain Gospels, and in texts used for the Introits or said at the Offertories, it is not so evident on the surface of the letter that they proclaim the person or proper operation of the Holy Spirit. But if we search more deeply, and rub the ears of grain in our hands so as to reach the hidden kernels, it will become clear that all of them concern his operation and the fitting instruction of the baptized.

From this Saturday until the following Saturday there are seven offices, one day—Thursday—having no office of its own but borrowing the Sunday office, in honour of the seven gifts of that same Holy Spirit. Yet we shall not be content merely to seek, in accordance with our purpose, the harmony of the parts in these offices. Rather, by seeking the artisan of our salvation, we shall venerate the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

For it is fitting that, by weighing the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic utterances gathered in these offices, we should recognize God as the ancient, not a recent, player of the organ through his own voices. This is especially so because even in those passages which seem less clearly to sound this in their letter, it is sometimes demonstrated more magnificently when their inward meaning is faithfully weighed; as in the words: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. 81 [Vulgate 80]).

## CHAPTER V. Why the Apostle Paul nevertheless caused those baptized in John’s baptism to be baptized

The reading from the Acts of the Apostles: “It happened while Apollos was at Corinth” (Acts 19), etc.

On every day of this week, the readings taken from the Acts of the Apostles plainly proclaim both the power and the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which he nourished the tender infancy of the Church at its birth with such sweetness that believers spoke in tongues and prophesied when the apostles laid hands upon them.

But today’s reading, that of Saturday, commends the unique dignity of Christ’s baptism by recording that Paul rebaptized—or rather, because they had not been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, baptized—the disciples who had been baptized with John’s baptism. The reason is plain: John’s baptism did not belong to the same power as that which Christ’s baptism works in us.

First, John baptized unto repentance, whereas Christ baptized unto the remission of sins. Then, and this is most important, John did not baptize in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is the sole and unique rule of baptism, which the Savior, having written it in his blood, delivered to his disciples after his resurrection, and not before.

Its power and authority are so great that, whatever someone may say during the immersion—even if he recites in order all four Gospels and sings the whole orthodox exposition of the Catholic faith—if he alone omits this rule, the concise but consummating word, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” then, I say, he has not performed the work of baptism. Consequently, the person thus immersed has received nothing and still needs baptism.

But if these words alone have been uttered, whoever the minister of word and water may be, and whoever performs the baptism—whether dove or raven, that is, whether chaste or adulterous or drunken; whether Catholic or heretic; or even if someone happens to baptize in play—it is in no way permissible for the baptism to be repeated, lest the invocation of so great a name seem to be nullified.

Although almost no one doubts this, it is pleasing to insert something relevant which ecclesiastical history relates concerning the beginnings of Athanasius.

At the time when Bishop Alexander was observing at Alexandria the feast-day of the martyr Peter, and after the customary solemn observances was awaiting the clergy who would assemble for his banquet, he saw from afar, at a place near the sea, children playing on the seashore. As often happens, they were imitating a bishop and the rites customarily performed in churches. But while he watched the children attentively for a long time, he saw them performing certain more secret and mystical acts as well.

At once disturbed, he ordered the clergy to be summoned to him and showed them what he himself saw from afar. Then he commanded them to go and bring all the children, once seized, to him. When they were present, he asked what their game was, what they had done, and how. At first, frightened as children of such an age are, they denied it; then they disclosed the affair in order and confessed that certain catechumens had been baptized by them through Athanasius, who had played the part of bishop in that childish game.

Then Alexander carefully asked those said to have been baptized what they had been asked and what they had answered; he likewise questioned the boy who had asked the questions. When he saw that all was in accordance with the rite of our religion, it is reported that, after consulting the council of clergy, he decided that baptism ought not to be repeated for those upon whom water had been poured with the questions and answers intact, but that those things should be completed which are customary for priests.

It is clear, therefore, that John’s baptism was of power far inferior to Christ’s baptism, and no question is needed as to why the Apostle Paul nevertheless had those baptized who had been baptized only with John’s baptism. For when asked, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” they answered, “But we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit” (Acts 19). This sufficiently shows how imperfect John’s baptism was, since he in whom alone the power of baptism subsists was not even named: the Holy Spirit, in whom Christ baptizes, as John himself says: “I baptize you in water; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3). And again: “He who sent me,” he says, “to baptize, told me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VI. On the particular character of consolation, according to which the Holy Spirit is given as another Paraclete

Just as the Holy Spirit is a person other than the Son, so, in the particular character of his consolation by which he consoles us, he is another Paraclete. Therefore the Son of God, having said many things concerning himself, says in today’s Gospel reading: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14).

For this to become clearer at last, careful distinction is needed in order to know what the Son properly accomplishes in creatures, and what the Father properly accomplishes through the Holy Spirit.

The substance of all creatures was created through the Son, as the Evangelist testifies, saying: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). But setting aside everything that does not pertain to the present subject, we must speak only of angelic and human substance.

Every human or angelic creature, and all the substantial qualities without which no substance can anywhere even be conceived—namely, being, living, sensing, and discerning—which belong naturally to it and therefore cannot be absent from the same substance, were created through the Son together with that substance itself [Col. 0267C]. But to be well, to live holily, to sense rightly, to discern prudently, or to understand wisely: these are accidental qualities bestowed through the Holy Spirit. It is clear that they are accidental because they are present in a good person or angel and absent from an evil one, while nature or substance remains. And lest any opening for cavilling seem to be given: these qualities are called accidental, although the Holy Spirit himself, whose gifts these are, is a substance—just as it is undoubtedly accidental to a woman to be pregnant, although the seed by which she is impregnated, or that from and through which the seed is transferred into her, is a substance.

But, to return to my subject: those suffer excessive poverty who, having attained only the benefit of creative power and using only nature’s goods, which were created through the Word, have not yet deserved to be adorned with the higher goods given by the Father and the Son through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0267D]. More wretched still are those who never deserve to receive them; to such persons the Lord says: “Woe to you, for you have your consolation!” (Luke 6). The Apostles, however, were not such as never deserve to receive them; nevertheless, the order of divine dispensation did not yet require that they should receive them and be perfected already. And the fact that the Son of God was among them, that before the Spirit had been given he was speaking and walking among them, was a preparation for the time when he would be united to their minds through that same Spirit [Col. 0268A], through whom he had been united to human nature in the Virgin’s womb.

And when he said to them, “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever,” it is as though the mouth of a friend, standing behind the wall and looking through the window (Song 2), said amid kisses to his loving bride, who had said, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1): “I shall tear down this wall, which scarcely admits our kisses through windows, which separates you from my ivory belly adorned with sapphires; and soon we shall be two in one flesh, and through the infusion of seed it shall come about that you shall no longer be barren.”

For when the Lord spoke these things before his Passion, the wall of enmity still stood (Eph. 2), that is, original sin between human beings and God. But Christ’s bodily presence was like the mouth of the Beloved, who drew his friend with as many kisses as he invited the Church, still small in a few disciples, to faith by teachings or miracles [Col. 0268B]. Yet just as the beloved never conceives by a kiss alone, so their souls could not be impregnated by the power of the Word, which is the seed of God the Father, unless through the coming of the Holy Spirit the union of God and our souls were accomplished, and through him the seed which is the Word of God were carried even into the innermost parts of their womb.

When this had happened, their soul at once refused to be consoled by the temporal or natural goods of human creatures; and therefore they rejected every consolation of worldly things, because they remembered God (Ps. 76), that is, they understood that God is an incomparably worthier and higher good, and, understanding this, they delighted in him [Col. 0268C]. Concerning this knowledge of the Father and himself, the Lord had said a little earlier: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also” (John 14). For of what knowledge did he speak, if not of the experience of love? Indeed, in Holy Scripture, both properly and with complete propriety, a man is customarily said to have “known” his wife, or a wife her husband, for the experience of natural union.

By this likeness, because God was to be known by the Church acquired through the Passion of the Son who spoke these words, he immediately added: “And from now on you shall know him” (ibid.). And because to know in this way is to see, he at once added: “And you have seen him” (ibid.), using the past for the future, which is most certainly to occur; by that manner of speaking by which a little later he will say: “And now I am no longer in the world” (John 17) [Col. 0268D]. If this displeases anyone, let him show how God can be truly or profitably known otherwise than through love of him, or how they had already seen the Father when the Son himself now says: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father.”

The disciples judge the antecedent and consequent in this statement not to cohere. Thus Philip says: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (ibid.), as though saying: “You have shown yourself, and we see only you; show us the Father.” But he does not approve their understanding, because they thought that nothing remained in the Son which they had not seen—although he too is God, who is seen in the heart equally with the Father, as he said elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5) [Col. 0269A]. He says: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?” (John 14). For you have not known me if, seeing me according to my humanity, you think you have seen me wholly. “He who sees me sees the Father also” (ibid.). But you have not seen the Father, as you yourselves confess; therefore neither have you seen me, “because I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (ibid.).

This must not be understood locally, nor can it be so; rather, it means what he says: knowledge of the Father is in knowledge of the Son, and knowledge of the Son is in knowledge of the Father. This knowledge of both comes through the Holy Spirit, and it alone is the consolation of the saints who are pilgrims in this age: strengthened by it, they patiently—indeed gratefully—endure the world’s hatred, reproach, expulsion, persecution, scourging, and killing; and, alike in prosperity and adversity, while this Spirit intercedes for them with inexpressible groanings, they count weeping as refreshment (Rom. 8), as it is written: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41), and so forth [Col. 0269B].

Therefore, because this is the Holy Spirit’s proper operation, he is rightly called another Paraclete. The following offertory follows: “Send forth your Spirit” (Ps. 103), etc. For when this other Paraclete is given, when this Spirit is sent forth, new human beings are created, and thus the face of our earth is renewed—the earth which was cursed in Adam’s sin and condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles as the lust of the flesh sprouts (Gen. 3). It is renewed, I say, and brings forth a new creature, “whose expectation,” as the Apostle says, “awaits the revelation of the sons of God; it groans and labours in birth” (Rom. 8) [Col. 0269C], until, in that revelation of the sons of God, it reveals the seed of God which it first conceived through this Spirit by the grace of baptism.

Then, in the following verse, the pregnant soul exhorts itself to bless the Lord for his mighty magnificence. If such blessing or thanksgiving is made only with the lips, it is flattery before God; but if it proceeds from a loving heart, the goodwill by which it loves the magnificence it praises is judged worthy of reward before him. Therefore it rightly exhorts the inward breath of the soul rather than the plectrum of the tongue to bless the Lord. Such confession is a fitting adornment which the Lord puts on, clothing himself with it as with a radiant garment. The reason for blessing the Lord is expressed more fully in this verse: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin” (Ps. 103) [Col. 0269D]. For through this Holy Spirit of whom we speak, heaven—that is, the Scripture of the prophets—is stretched out. It is stretched out like a skin, in which nothing lies hidden once it has been spread open. “You cover its upper parts with waters,” he says: that is, over them you pour the excellent way of charity in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Communion: “On the last day of the feast,” it is clear, pertains to the gift of the Holy Spirit, of whom he said: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” For he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive (John 7).

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0270A]

**On the procession of the same Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.**

But since our purpose now is to seek not only the harmonious parts in the offices, but also the divine power of the Holy Spirit, this saying of the Saviour must not be passed over. It is commended not merely by the dignity of its meaning but also by the venerable authority of the one who spoke it—especially since he uttered it with a cry, in order to make his hearers attentive. For it is written thus: “Now on the last, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7), etc.

Therefore, if we are hearers who are not ungrateful and are worthy of such an orator, let us consider with goodwill, teachableness, and attention not only what he said but also at what time he said it—for this too pertains to the matter [Col. 0270B]. It was the Jewish feast-day of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*). “Those who have read the Scriptures,” Augustine says, “know what Scenopegia is. On the feast-day they made booths, after the likeness of the booths in which they had lived when, having been brought out of Egypt, they journeyed in the wilderness. This was the feast-day, a great solemnity. The Jews celebrated it as though remembering the Lord’s benefits—those who were going to kill the Lord.”

> [Note: [Col. 0269D] St Augustine, *Tractate XXVIII on the Gospel of John*, ch. 7, §3; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, Migne edition.]

On the last day of this feast Jesus stood and cried out, inviting to drink not any sort of persons, but all who thirsted. Aptly so. While they were remembering, as has been said, God’s benefits, the cry of the one inviting them to the gift of the Holy Spirit was directed toward the people.

But we, brought out of the Egypt of unbelief, freed from captivity and the service of spiritual Pharaoh, and conveyed through the sea of baptism, now dwell as pilgrims in the wilderness of this present life in booths, namely churches or monasteries in which we serve, until we attain the kingdom of the heavenly inheritance [Col. 0270C]. If, therefore, remembering God’s benefits, we celebrate feasts by abstaining from evil works and rejoicing in contemplation of divine goodness—because through the Passion of his only Son he accomplished our salvation—we hear the cry of the one inviting us; in thirst we run and drink, because thus the gracious vein of divinity, namely the Holy Spirit, is opened to us.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0270D]

**In what order the same procession of the Holy Spirit takes place.**

Great is the matter, and one to be hoped for from God, which we have undertaken to consider: namely, in what order the Holy Spirit comes to his creature. Once this has been clearly perceived, it will also become clear how rightly he is called “proceeding” in the Gospel.

This order is necessary: first, in the rational creature good will toward the Creator must be aroused by consideration of his benefits. And lest those benefits should be lacking, “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). “How,” asks the Apostle, “has he not also given us all things with him?” But there are ungrateful people who, just as in the works of the world they offer no grateful praise to God the craftsman—those whom the Apostle rebukes when he says: “Although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks” (Rom. 1) [Col. 0271A]—so also, when the great love of God is preached to them, that he delivered up his Son for us, do not reverence the greatness of the benefit but ridicule the word of Christ’s cross as folly (1 Cor. 1).

The Spirit never deigns to visit such people, because, hateful to God, they transgress the natural law through excessive ingratitude. For it is natural to a human being to return love to one who loves, and to be able to distinguish what work is worthy of praise and what is unworthy. Because by their own fault—namely, because they are ungrateful toward God—they refuse to do this, the Spirit of God rightly does not entrust himself to them, but leaves them delivered up, as the Apostle says, to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, to dishonourable passions, and to every reprobate mind (Rom. 1) [Col. 0271B].

But those whose perception has not been blinded by the devil’s dart of envy, recognizing the Maker from the works of the world, reverence him and gladly praise his wisdom in the equity of his works. Much more, when they hear of the incarnate One who suffered for all—the Christ who is God’s power and God’s wisdom (1 Cor. 1)—they love, approve, embrace, and honour him. Hence that saying in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you” (Song 1).

Thus, as at betrothals the bridegroom is first shown to the bride, his lineage praised, his courage proclaimed, his riches enumerated, and his beauty commended—by all of which her reciprocal affection and voluntary assent are sought, and finally, through the encounter of love, he who pleased her in his possessions is known wholly in himself—so our Creator first arouses the affection of our souls toward himself by the manifestation of his works, by faithful preaching of his all-powerful divinity and his most holy incarnation [Col. 0271C]. Then, when he sees that he has pleased her, he approaches confidently, as it is written of the strong woman: “The heart of her husband trusts in her” (Prov. 31), and pours into her the fullness of his love, that is, the Holy Spirit.

There he manifests himself; and this never happens by anything other than this Holy Spirit of whom we speak. Therefore, when the Lord was soon to suffer and, after that Passion, to give this Spirit, he commended love more earnestly (John 11), so that love in the human heart might meet the love of God, who is the Holy Spirit, and prepare a place for it [Col. 0271D].

Now, to return to what was said above: he sought such a thirst of love when, standing and crying in the Temple, he said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink.” The feast of Tabernacles also—when, as stated above, they made booths in remembrance of God’s benefits, after the likeness of the booths in which they lived in the wilderness after being brought out of Egypt—this great feast of its solemnity was a type of the feast which ought to shine in our minds as we contemplate the benefits which God has magnificently wrought for us through his Son, our Redeemer; and, consequently, as we thirst to behold in himself the one whom we have experienced in such great benefits of his [Col. 0272A].

In such persons, surely, the Lord’s cry, “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink,” does not find deaf ears. Explaining what thirst he seeks and what drink he offers, he adds: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). “He who believes in me” is the same as though he had said, “He who thirsts for me.” For what is it to believe in Christ except to thirst for Christ?

To believe *in* Christ is much more than to believe Christ, or to believe that Christ exists. To believe Christ means, implicitly, to believe that what he says is true; to believe Christ means, implicitly, to believe that he exists. This is no great thing, since even demons believe and tremble (Jas. 2). But to believe in Christ means, by walking in faith, to press onward into Christ: to revere and love the Word through whom all things were made; and, still more, the Word made flesh who dwelt among us (John 1) [Col. 0272B]. Whoever thirsts in this way is given to drink of the Spirit of Christ.

O how greatly the creature is raised from poverty, so as to have one and the same Spirit with its Creator—the one Spirit who alone is the abundance of eternal riches. By him the belly of the soul is so inebriated and filled that living waters flow from it, namely, the teachings of divine wisdom; so that it is deservedly called “a fountain of gardens, a well of waters” (Song 4).

Therefore, as has been said above, this is the customary order and fitting preparation before the coming of the Holy Spirit: first, good will in the creature toward the Creator must be stirred up by preaching his benefits. For, as Scripture testifies when it says, “It belongs to a human being to prepare the mind, but to the Lord to govern the tongue” (Prov. 16); and again, “It belongs to a human being to plan his way, but to the Lord to direct his steps” (ibid.) [Col. 0272C], this Scripture testifies, I say, that it is natural for human affection—that is, good will—to be moved by the Creator’s good deeds. Where this does not occur, it is the fault of ingratitude and the contempt of a proud mind.

For what the Apostle says, “God is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing for good will” (Phil. 2), does not conflict with the foregoing statement. It belongs to a human being to prepare the mind, that is, to will what is good, while by rational perception one discerns and approves what is good, as the same Apostle says: “For willing lies close at hand to me” (Rom. 7). But God himself works this willing when, by his grace, he deigns to bring about and show to a human being the causes by whose consideration that person’s will is aroused to love God [Col. 0272D].

For example, it belonged to the Apostle Peter to will to be ready to go with the Lord to prison and to death (Luke 22); but the Father had wrought this willing in him, because he had sent his Son Christ into this world and revealed him to Peter. And because Peter and the other Apostles, while the Jews were envious and persecuting them, had, as was said, conformed their own will to God’s, God therefore accomplished what belonged to him, by sending them the Holy Spirit. Once he received that Spirit, Peter, who already had the will, might also have the power to accomplish it—namely, to go mightily for Christ to prison and death.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0273A]

**Why the Holy Spirit is properly called “proceeding,” although the Son proceeded from God, as he himself says: “For I proceeded from God and came.”**

Since the Son too proceeded from the Father, as he says to the Jews: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me; for I proceeded from God and came” (John 8), one rightly asks why the Holy Spirit is properly called “proceeding.” The ready and easy answer is this: the Son, having been sent once, came once to redeem the world through the mystery of the Incarnation; and just as all things were made through him once and all at once, so too all things were restored through him once and all at once. Therefore he does not say in the present tense, “I proceed from God,” but in the past: “I proceeded,” he says, “and came” [Col. 0273B].

But the Holy Spirit does not visit all the hearts of the elect once and all together; rather, coming at diverse times, he visits in diverse ways. That is, the one and same God and Lord variously dispenses the divisions of graces (1 Cor. 12). Of this sanctifying activity the Son says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). For God’s operation is twofold. And concerning the other work of God, which he performed through the Son—namely, the creation of all things—it is written: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Sir. 18).

Therefore, when the Son spoke of the Holy Spirit, saying, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth,” he says in the present tense: “who proceeds from the Father” (John 16) [Col. 0273C]. As the body of the moon was fully formed in heaven once, but always needs the sun’s benefit in order to be illuminated by it, because it does not shine with its own light, so the holy Church was born once in baptism, yet amid the failings and various labours of the present life it always needs to be visited and refreshed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore it strives to stand before the face of divinity, whenever it daily gives thanks to its Creator for his benefits: for example, when in the consecration of the Eucharist it confesses it worthy and just always and everywhere to give him thanks, praying that its own voices too may be admitted with the powers of heaven and of the heavens, because through Christ our Lord it was both created, and redeemed through that same one who is blessed and comes in the name of the Lord [Col. 0273D]. For especially by this remembrance of his benefits it comes before the face of its Creator and, like the moon, sets the face of its heart before the true Sun. Thus, by the Spirit of sanctification, it is initiated in those who perhaps have not yet received him, and in those who have already received him it is perfected through the addition of a gift.

Therefore the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, is rightly alone called “proceeding”; but the Son, because he says not “I proceed” but “I proceeded and came,” is declared not proceeding but begotten, as he truly is. For he proceeded before all times, born from the Father’s heart; he came in time, incarnate from the Virgin Mary.

## CHAPTER X

**Again, from the foregoing: that the Holy Spirit can be received by the human soul, which belongs properly to divine substance.** [Col. 0274A]

If we carefully attend to the Lord’s words set out above, when he spoke of the Spirit whom believers in him were to receive—“If anyone thirsts,” he says, “let him come and drink” (John 7), etc.—we recognize in these words too the true and perfect divinity of the Holy Spirit, of which dry and empty Macedonius never drank anything, along with all others whatsoever who, by blaspheming the Holy Spirit, are convicted as guilty of an eternal sin.

To make this evident, we must first state what no one doubts: this drink is received not by flesh but by spirit, discerned not by the mouth but by the heart, not by the palate but by reason. What is drunk certainly penetrates the inward parts of the drinker; and, being subtle enough to be received, it fills the denser vessels which are therefore able to receive it. It is therefore clear that the Holy Spirit can be received by the human soul and penetrates its inward parts, since the soul drinks him—that is, receives him into the inward parts of its substance [Col. 0274B].

But this belongs properly to divine substance; and no human or angelic spirit can penetrate another except God, the creator of each and of all, to whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (Acts 1). This Spirit alone, I say, fills the soul. When someone is said to be full of a possessing demon, this must not be understood as though the evil spirit had substantially entered the human spirit. Both are created; neither is so much subtler than the other that one can be received by the other or contain the other. But someone may be full of a demon in the same way that a person is sometimes not improperly said to be full of wine or fever [Col. 0274C]. This is certainly understood in relation to the body: fever or drunkenness, having entered the veins, sinews, and all the hidden passages of the body—but not the substance of the soul—afflicts the soul dwelling there in its own abode.

Therefore the Holy Spirit is God, because he can be received by the human spirit, as has now been said, on the authority of Christ, who invites thirsty souls to drink him. In this sense we also understand the Apostle’s words: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4), and very many similar passages.

## CHAPTER XI

**Again, on the procession of the Holy Spirit in a lesser or greater visitation, according to the saying: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.”**

[Col. 0274D] When that same Spirit searches the depths of the human heart, no one knows it except the one who receives him. But those who drink recognize from the taste the greatness of the infused gift, when rivers of living water consequently flow from his belly (John 3). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (ibid.).

For the river of living water—that is, the abundance of saving teaching which flows from the belly of one who believes in Christ—is the voice of the Spirit who breathes where he wills. Wherever he has breathed, passing through the womb of the mind, he produces a fountain of living water, that is, understanding of truth; directing its stream to the mouth, he clothes it in bodily speech, sends it into your ears, and through the ears carries it to the soul of the one drinking. The quality of its taste testifies truly that it is the voice of the Holy Spirit: namely, when, poured into a heart, he orders in an elect vessel grace that will benefit many [Col. 0275A].

Indeed, even the one who receives him does not know where he comes from or where he goes, although he knows and feels when he comes and when he departs, once the perceptible visitation has been completed. “For suddenly,” as Gregory says, “he perceives something like the whisper of a gentle breeze, and this is what he beholds of the incomprehensible substance of eternity.”

> [Note: [Col. 0275D] St Gregory, *Morals*, book V, on Job 3, ch. 36, §66; *Patrologia*, vol. LXXV, Migne edition.]

But by that whisper of a gentle breeze in Elijah is signified the more frequent visitation (3 Kings 19), by which the mind tastes the savour of divinity whenever it is raised in the height of contemplation. The present work pertains more particularly to that greater visitation in which the human mind is far more excellently illumined when someone is to be sent forth publicly, so that rivers of living water may flow from his belly for the salvation of many [Col. 0275B]; or, as it is written elsewhere, so that, conceiving from the fear of the Lord, one may give birth and bring forth the spirit of his salvation upon the earth (Isa. 26).

Thus our fathers the Apostles, or apostolic men, were sent; likewise those who, more by the task of writing than by bodily access or presence, poured out for us living water which they happily drew from this Saviour’s fountain, from the abundance of this Holy Spirit (Isa. 12). In such persons that saying from the Song of Songs is more magnificently fulfilled: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (Song 5).

For suddenly, and without being known, the Holy Spirit leaps in and, as if through an opening, glides into the inner enclosure of the soul. At his entrance the weakness of the human spirit immediately trembles because of the unfamiliar strength and weight it feels [Col. 0275C]. But he who has entered first consoles the fearful soul with the familiar caress of his sweetness, as though with a kiss. Then, according to the work for which he prepares that soul, he rises up. For example, if his purpose is, as has been said, that living waters should flow from its belly—that is, more abundant teachings of life—then, rising up, he traverses the womb of the soul and expands it as he goes around it. By the marvellous increase of his own circuits, he signifies its future progress in divine knowledge, though it was formerly small and narrow; sometimes he floods it with such greatness as though one of Paradise’s rivers were flowing through the widened channel of that soul.

Meanwhile the soul marvels at its own magnitude and the vast ambulatory space of its bosom—truly three and four times blessed, since, as it is written, “because she loved purity of heart, for the grace of her lips she has the king as a friend” (Prov. 22), namely Christ, from whom she receives such a gift [Col. 0275D]. When the measure which this Spirit wishes to give has at last been filled—for as he breathes where he wills (John 3), so he distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12)—and the miracle ceases and the soul returns to itself, then it cannot refuse to rise and open to the Beloved. That is, it must undertake the ministry of teaching and open to Christ, always by speech and sometimes also by writings, hearts closed to him, striving to remove the bolt of unbelief [Col. 0276A]. Thus, going forth publicly, it fulfils the command it heard within: “Let your fountains be poured forth abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5).

## CHAPTER XII

**On the day of Pentecost: how the day on which the Law was given is reckoned as the fiftieth from the day on which the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt, on the anniversary of which the Holy Spirit was given.**

First, this must not be passed over: the day on which the Law was given, in whose remembrance Pentecost was a great solemnity—the day, I say, on which after the crossing of the Red Sea the Law was given to the children of Israel on Mount Sinai—was plainly the fiftieth day from the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb. For some, especially those devoted to the science of calculation, when they read that the lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month (Exod. 12), while in the third month the Lord descended before all the people upon Mount Sinai on the third day of the month (Exod. 19)—for, Scripture says, the third day had now come, the morning had grown warm, and behold, thunder began to be heard (ibid.), etc.—when they read this, they are astonished and perplexed, proving that the number fifty does not hold from the fourteenth day of the first month to the third day of the third month [Col. 0276B].

For since the Hebrews have lunar months only, and the moon of the first month has twenty-nine days while that of the second has thirty, the question must not be passed over. It is resolved as follows. The Lord indeed descended upon Mount Sinai on the third day of the third month, as was stated; but observe what follows. He also said to Moses: “Go up to the Lord, you and Aaron” (ibid.), etc. “Moses alone went up to the Lord, and they did not approach him.” “So Moses came and told the people all the words and judgments of the Lord” (Exod. 24). Then afterward: “In the morning,” it says, “rising up, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain” (ibid.). And a little later: “The Lord said to Moses: Go up to me on the mountain and remain there; and I shall give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written, that you may teach the children of Israel” (ibid.).

Thus the Law was given not on the third day of the month, when the Lord came down upon the mountain, but on the fourth day, when he gave the tablets and his written law [Col. 0276C]. Therefore it is clear that the day on which the Law was given was the fiftieth from the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb. Since the Holy Spirit is given on that day, the wonderful harmony of his works is commended to us, concerning which the holy doctors have treated sufficiently.

One should also know that, by the command of the Law, these fifty days began to be counted not from the Paschal evening itself, when the lamb was sacrificed, but from the following first day of the Sabbath. Thus it is written in Leviticus: “You shall bring to the priest sheaves of ears of grain, the firstfruits of your harvest. He shall raise it before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath, and shall sanctify it. Therefore you shall count from the very day on which you offered the sheaf of firstfruits seven full weeks, until the day after the completion of the seventh week; and thus you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwellings, two loaves of firstfruits” (Lev. 23), etc. [Col. 0277A].

Thus fifty days began to be counted from the first day of the Sabbath, which we call the Lord’s Day—that is, after the great day of the Paschal Sabbath had passed. But our Lord rose on that day, and, as the true priest, he raised and sanctified before the Lord God his Father his own body, the true sheaf of the earth’s new fruits. Therefore no question remains as to why the day on which the Holy Spirit was given—certainly the fiftieth from the day on which he rose—was also the Jews’ Pentecost; because, as has been said, the days of Pentecost began to be calculated not from the Paschal evening itself but from the subsequent first day of the Sabbath.

Therefore let us offer to the Lord on this day two loaves of firstfruits, that is, let us give thanks for those two benefits: namely, that by one and the same Spirit he formerly wrote the Law and commandments for the ancients on tablets of stone, as Moses says in Deuteronomy: “He gave me two tablets of stone written by the finger of God” (Deut. 9)—for the finger of God is the Holy Spirit—and that now he has written grace for the new, that is, evangelical, fathers on tablets of flesh (2 Cor. 3) [Col. 0277B].

Let us celebrate the solemn day which shines forth after seven weeks and by its number, fifty, signifies jubilee—that is, release (Lev. 25)—whereby, released from every debt, we return to the ancient possession which we lost when sold under sin (Rom. 7). For as this festal day breaks forth after seven weeks, so, after the cycle of the world in which we now labour, that eternally festal day will shine forth, when we shall labour no more but, settled in blessed leisure, shall behold, marvel at, and praise the true Sun crowned with a festal diadem.

Now, according to the office of this same day, let us continue, as begun, concerning the same Holy Spirit, setting at the head the Epistle in which his coming is narrated.

## CHAPTER XIII

**What was signified by the sound made from heaven at the coming of the Holy Spirit.**

The sound suddenly made from heaven at the coming of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2) was a sign of the sound which was to go forth into all the earth, when those heavens, whom he was now coming to strengthen, declared the glory of God, and the firmament of their most steadfast faith announced the works of his hands (Ps. 18), with the magnificent thunder of the word and flashes of miracles [Col. 0277D].

For it was soon to happen, when this Spirit thundered the proclamations of Christ through their mouths, that the earth would be moved to repentance and would tremble; and the foundations of the mountains—that is, the hearts of the proud—would be troubled and shaken when they heard that he was angry with them (Ps. 17), unless they repented. Thus also in the Apocalypse, when the angel had taken the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and cast it upon the earth, “there came thunderings, voices, lightnings, and a great earthquake” (Rev. 8) [Col. 0278A].

That fire was now sent, and divided tongues as of fire appeared to the Apostles: that fire, I say, with which the Angel of Great Counsel had long before filled the golden censer of his immaculate body, and, now taken up into heaven, was doing what he had said: “I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I will except that it should burn?” (Luke 12).

## CHAPTER XIV

**Why the Holy Spirit, whose nature is invisible, displayed visible fire outwardly.**
For the visible fire that was also manifested outwardly was certainly not the substance itself of the Holy Spirit, whose nature is invisible. That visible fire, I say, was a sign for us of his divine activity, [Col. 0278B] so that through the effects of this fire of ours, which we know, we may understand what this fire—this God, this Holy Spirit—works in us. In visible nature, moreover, visible fire has manifold usefulness. It adorns the heaven with splendid embellishments in sun, moon, and stars; it not only gladdens the earth by light poured down from above, but also stimulates it to bring forth by the benefit of heat, and nourishes in its bosom the seeds it has received. Furthermore, drawn from veins of flint and fed with suitable fuel, it lightens our night; in rivalry with the absent day, light performs innumerable services for mortals, by which the want of this present life is relieved. Add also that at that time, by the Lord’s command, it always burned upon the altar, while the priest continually supplied wood; and it consumed the holocaust, [Col. 0278C] the sacrifice so called because it was wholly burned (Lev. VI; Num. XXVIII). But among its other natural excellences, fire has this remarkable property: when divided into parts, it suffers no loss of its borrowed light. Those who read the Scriptures know that the meanings of all these things are referred to the Holy Spirit and his works are likened to these qualities. Therefore, the fact that the Holy Spirit was manifested in fire was a sign—not for himself, but for us, to whom the divine majesty has been accustomed from the beginning to speak through such signs.

## CHAPTER XV. Why, though the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, the Holy Spirit is more particularly called fire

Nor should we omit why, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, it is more especially, indeed [Col. 0278D] almost solely, the person of the Holy Spirit who is called fire, and sometimes “the fire of the Lord,” as there: “For in the fire of the Lord the whole earth shall be devoured” (Zeph. I). Yet this will not seem strange if you recall that this Spirit is properly and naturally love. This love, I say, or charity, by which the Father loves the Son or the Son loves the Father, is the Holy Spirit; he is called, and is, the goodness of both.

“For if you ask,” says Augustine, “who made all things, I answer: God. If you ask through what means: through his Word. If you ask why: because he is good, he made all things. And this Trinity is one God.”

Thus the love of God is the Holy Spirit. Love, both spiritual and carnal, is truly called and is fire—so perceptibly hot [Col. 0279A] that no one in love is ignorant of its heat. But since God’s own love is consubstantial with him, God is so enkindled by this same love of his that, without distinction of persons, God is called and is an invisible and incorporeal fire, according to the Apostle: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. XII).

Nevertheless, where a distinction of persons is needed, when we distinguish what is proper to each person, just as we call God the Father life living immortally in itself, and his Son the true and unchangeable wisdom through whom he created the whole creation, so we call the Holy Spirit his love, through whom he desires and longs to inhabit the rational creature. This love, like fire—or rather, truly as fire—tends toward the rational creature placed before it, just as visible fire always tends toward the material suited to it and set before it. Yet the creature which is melted by that fire is not consumed, just as wood, hay, and straw are consumed by this visible fire; rather, as gold and silver melt in this fire and are not consumed, but remain and become purer, so it is in that fire, in that furnace which, Isaiah says, is in Jerusalem (Isa. XXXI). Blessed is the rational creature: it melts without being consumed in the blaze of this love, in the torrent of this delight—always pure, always liquid, always burning with love, always enjoying God who loves it; needing nothing in its desire, and never becoming sated in its enjoyment.

## CHAPTER XVI. Why the Holy Spirit appeared in fire in such a way as also to deign to form tongues from [Col. 0279C] that fire

Since, then, it is clear that the Holy Spirit rightly appeared in fire (Exod. III; Acts II), because this our God is a consuming fire (Deut. IV; Heb. XII), there is also the question why he appeared in fire in such a manner as to deign to form tongues from the same fire. But in this sign too the activity of the same Holy Spirit is splendidly commended to us.

For the Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, by means of the tongue—which has the closest kinship with the Word—not only expressed that he is of the same substance as the Word of God, but also that through him God the Father speaks his Word to us, as he himself says in the Psalm: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” [Col. 0279D] (Ps. XLIV).

Now, so that we might perceive that this very Spirit is expressed by that verse of the Psalm, he who accomplished the incarnation of the Son of God—and that Psalm is an epithalamium of that incarnation—he, I say, who united to the womb of the Virgin the good Word uttered from the Father’s heart to human nature, now appeared in a tongue as the Holy Spirit, in order to inscribe that same Word upon the minds of the apostles; and thus he too is compared to the pen of a swiftly writing scribe. Therefore the verse “My tongue,” together with the preceding “My heart has uttered,” is fittingly sung in the offices of the apostles, though it occurs more frequently in the offices of Virgins. And rightly so: for this Word was uttered more fully and excellently into the bosom of virginity, namely so as to assume flesh from it; but into the hearts of the apostles it was uttered so as to become audible and intelligible to us through bodily speech.

Therefore, because the Holy Spirit is that tongue of God the Father by which, as by the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, he swiftly inscribed his good Word whole into human nature, as he willed, declaring his works to the king—that is, to the assumed man—so that he might know and be able to accomplish entirely what God himself knows and can accomplish, he rightly appeared over the apostles in a tongue. To them he came to inscribe, with that same speed of the pen, knowledge of the same Word and of his incarnation, so that men hitherto unlearned might know how to preach it eloquently according to the Scriptures.

By this it especially agrees and coheres with the Gospel, since what is said there was fulfilled here: “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you” [Col. 0280B] (John XIV). For see: immediately upon being sent, he declares himself to be that teacher who, according to the promise of the bridegroom struggling in death, would come as Paraclete—that is, Comforter—to his orphaned children. I say, he declares himself the teacher who is to teach them all things by this sign, when he is shown in a tongue and at the same time teaches them the languages of all nations, so that they might speak to all people of those mighty works of God concerning which they alone were inwardly taught.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0280C] That the apostles did not, as some suppose, speak only one language, namely Hebrew, so that to each nation it seemed to be its own language; for that miracle, as Bede says, would have belonged not to those speaking but to those hearing.

And it was not—as some suspect—that all languages and forms of speech were heard in their voices while they themselves spoke only one language, namely Hebrew, and each man of every nation merely thought it his own language. For that, as Bede says, would have been a miracle not of the speakers but of the hearers: that is, the real power would not have belonged to those who spoke, but the prodigy—or rather, the error, the perception of something not actually existing—would have been in the ears of the hearers. No, I say: the Spirit of truth did not act thus; nor can anyone who prudently discerns what that teacher teaches think this of him, since he came to teach all truth (John XVI).

[Col. 0280D] It would remain for those holding this view to assert that the apostles, scattered throughout the whole world and writing to people of diverse languages, wrote their books in the letters of one language only, namely Hebrew; and that every person of whatever language who saw their Hebrew characters, by the same miracle, supposed them to constitute writing in his own language. This is quite ridiculous. At least let them except us Latins. For we know with certainty that we cannot read without translators the Scriptures which they wrote in Hebrew or Greek. It would also follow that whatever language they heard, they thought Hebrew, and whatever writing they saw, they believed to be Hebrew. As has been said, this is utterly frivolous, foolish, erroneous, and in every respect unworthy of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it difficult to refute this presumptuous suspicion by the authority of Scripture: “And they were all filled,” it says, “with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” [Col. 0281A] (Acts II). “They began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance”: these are the words of Scripture, wholly opposed to what the aforesaid conjecture imagines.

They therefore spoke, and did not merely seem falsely to speak; and the Holy Spirit truly gave them utterance. Thus, as we sing, he instituted this new song, setting forth a sign of sanctification, so that every kind of language might arise in their mouths. A new sign, I say: for it signified that the Church would thereafter speak of God—hitherto known to it in Judaea alone (Ps. LXXV)—in the languages of all nations. Indeed, it was such a sign that it was also the efficient cause and beginning of the future reality. For how could they become teachers of the nations unless, through knowledge of languages, they had an abundance of speech by which to converse with them? How, I say, could we even answer “Amen” to their blessing if we did not know what they were saying? (I Cor. XIV).

These men were about to build a tower—now in an acceptable and divinely appointed time—a tower whose summit would touch heaven (Gen. V), through which anyone fearing the coming judgment might flee into heaven. But those who formerly wished to erect a tower for themselves, without God’s teaching and by human work alone, with pride as their guide, by which they might ascend into heaven, were, when their languages were confused—though the earth had previously been of one speech and the same words—divided against one another and scattered [Col. 0281C] (Gen. VI).

Therefore now, when by God’s counsel the tower of Christ’s body, which is the Church, is duly and orderly built from living and chosen stones throughout the world (I Pet. II), all languages are rightly restored to the mouths of these builders. And it is not as it was there, when one man asked for a stone and another offered bitumen, or when one asked for water and another held out a trowel; so here, when our builders proclaim peace, we do not suppose that they mean war, and when they preach the kingdom of God, we do not imagine the glory of the world.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How fittingly the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles at the third hour

[Col. 0281D] The Holy Spirit, arbiter of all mysteries, fittingly came upon the apostles at the third hour and consecrated that same hour with life-giving mysteries, at which human beings, still sober and still fasting from bodily food, ought first to seek the kingdom of God. For because our Lord, on the night when he was betrayed, after the typical supper of the lamb, handed down the sacred Eucharist of his body and blood (I Cor. XI), perhaps we might judge that it mattered little or nothing whether we approached that banquet of life fed or fasting. But he was constrained by reason and by the critical moment of time not to delay instituting that sacrament at such an hour.

By reason: because the order of the new sacrifice was not to be begun before the old was completed. By the critical moment of time: because he was immediately to be seized and led to his passion, and had no other opportunity to draw up this testament for his heirs before his death. Hence, when he gave them the cup of his blood and said, “Drink all of you from this; for this is the cup of my blood” [Col. 0282A] (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXIV), etc., he immediately added: “But I say to you, I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (ibid.).

And indeed, in the kingdom of the Father—that is, once made immortal—after his resurrection he ate and drank with his disciples (John XXI), and could then first have handed down to them his body and the cup of the new and eternal testament. But he acted more fittingly now, because a testament was not valid unless, as the Apostle says, the death of the testator had intervened (Heb. IX). Therefore the Holy Spirit, who is the author and power of this and all mysteries, fittingly deigned to be given at the third hour, so that the time might indicate when it is most suitable for his own mysteries likewise to be given or celebrated.

Hence the assembly of the universal Church is rightly accustomed to gather especially at this hour, unless it is a fast day; and at the appointed third hour, more illustrious than the others because of the honor of the same Holy Spirit, the solemn rites of the Mass are celebrated in the presence of choirs, with common psalmody. Nor are these divine mysteries given to anyone after bodily food, unless the unavoidable urgency of imminent death compels it.

## CHAPTER XIX

That the Holy Spirit visibly showed the aforesaid signs, yet worked invisibly as invisible, and inwardly filled their hearts.

[Col. 0282C] These things, indeed, which have been mentioned were seen or heard outwardly; but all the glory was inward, and these outward manifestations were its signs. For inwardly the blessed apostles would see God with a pure heart, entering the secret places of their souls with great majesty and tempering his strength with overflowing sweetness, so that he might not so much terrify the still-fragile breasts of mortal men by a miracle of power as gladden them by an inward awareness of grace. For there was he of whom it is said: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). Again: “For my spirit is sweeter than honey” (Ecclus. XXIV).
