Again: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” [Col. 0282D] (Ps. CIII). Of him the Jews said, as if divining: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II).

There, I say—that is, into the new wineskins of their hearts—was poured the fervent new wine of the divine substance (Matt. IX), the Holy Spirit, just as the Lord Christ said when promising him to them: “But you shall know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John XIV).

## CHAPTER XX

That the Holy Spirit is not lesser because he can be contained by the human spirit, since the same must be understood of the Father and the Son.

“He will be in you,” he says. For the Holy Spirit, as has already been said above, can be contained by a human or angelic spirit. Though this can suffice to prove his true divinity, some heretics have turned it instead into an argument for their own faithlessness. For, while asserting that the Son is less than the Father, they also wished to assert that the Spirit is less than the Son because he is in us and suffers the contaminations of human souls. But in saying this, sinners have gone astray and spoken falsehood [Col. 0283A] (Ps. LVII). For it follows for them that they do not confess either the Father or the Son to be God.

For parallel—indeed identical—statements have been made, as today’s Gospel proves by example. When the Son had said, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV), he immediately added: “And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid.). Therefore, when they deny that the Holy Spirit is God because it is said, “He will remain with you and will be in you” (ibid.), it follows that they must deny that the Father and the Son are God because the Son says of the Father and himself, “We will come and make our dwelling with him.”

But once these people have been driven away and scattered with their smoke, like locusts issuing from the pit of the abyss (Apoc. IX), Catholic faith rather takes this as an argument of truth in proving that the Holy Spirit is God: namely, that he can be contained by the human spirit. This belongs properly to the divine substance and is common to the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, who are one and the only God: capable of no one, yet capable of his rational creature.

## CHAPTER XXI

That although it was said to the apostles of the Holy Spirit, “He will remain with you,” nevertheless the sign proper to the Son of God was what was said to John: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining.”

It must be understood that when the Lord said to his disciples concerning the Holy Spirit, “He will remain with you and will be in you” (John XIV), reason requires us to understand a mode of remaining very different from that in which the same Spirit remained in the only-begotten Son of God, of whom it was said: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining—this is he who baptizes” [Col. 0283C] (John I).

If this difference in remaining is rightly observed, it will at the same time become clear why, although the whole Trinity makes its dwelling with the one who loves it, Holy Scripture more often, and as though uniquely, affirms this of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0283D] We understand the Holy Spirit to remain in his creature in two ways. One manner of remaining is when that creating substance, filling the creature’s substance through itself, always indwells it. This must not be doubted of the blessed angels and of the spirits of holy people who are already with God, released from the flesh. But the same must not be thought of those who are still in mortal flesh. For as long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX), it is subject to many variations: now, indeed, if they are very perfect, with heart enlarged they merit that visitation which, as Gregory says, is signified in Elijah by the gentle whisper of a breeze; and they recover strength, like the same Elijah who, after that whisper, overturned kingdoms, anointing other kings and the prophet Elisha (III Kings XIX). Yet at another time they tremble when courage fails, like that same Elijah who, shortly before, had shut heaven by a word and now fled through the wilderness because of a woman’s words.

But another manner of remaining is when, beginning to dwell through faith, he never leaves his Church in unbelief, or, once he has bestowed the other gifts of grace, never afterwards withdraws them. For example, he did not so distinguish wisdom granted to the Apostle Paul by periods of time that, when the gift overflowed, Paul was wise, and when it receded, he became foolish. Of this manner, indeed, he says: “I will not leave you nor forsake you” [Col. 0284A] (Heb. XIII). But of the manner mentioned above: “Turn away your eyes,” he says, “for they have made me fly away” (Song VI). And again it is written of this manner: “Because the four living creatures, when moving, did not turn back, but each went straight before its face” (Ezek. I), that is, each remained in its purpose. But of the manner mentioned above: [Col. 0284B] “They went,” he says, “and returned in the likeness of flashing lightning” (ibid.).

No mortal ever existed in whom this Spirit, who is the substance of divine love, rested in unending abiding, except that one man whom seven women—that is, the seven graces of this Spirit—seized once and held always (Isa. IV). Therefore it was said: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining” (John I). This does not mean that the Spirit first descended upon him at that time, since from his very conception he had the whole fullness dwelling bodily in him [Col. 0284C] (Col. II), as it is written: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Prov. IX). That is, the wisdom of God the Father, in the building or conception of his body, immediately employed the seven graces of his Spirit. Rather, an appropriate sign was given to the forerunner and witness of his faith, so that he might know what testimony he ought to bear concerning him.

But according to faith, and the other gifts of grace divided among individuals as he wills, the Holy Spirit always dwelt, as has been said, in his Church. Since these gifts are properly works of the Holy Spirit, Holy Scripture therefore more frequently and almost uniquely, as stated above, commends the Holy Spirit’s dwelling in us. [Col. 0284D] The whole Trinity can be contained and makes its dwelling in us, because now, while we are pilgrims, the Holy Spirit dwells in us through those gifts of his; but in the future the very substance of the Trinity will dwell in us in eternal embraces.

## CHAPTER XXII

That no one but God can be everywhere; hence the Spirit of the Lord, who filled the whole world, is God.

[Col. 0284D] Likewise, through what we sing at the Introit, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. I), the Catholic Church proclaims his divine power. For who but God could he be, if, after the apostles had been dispersed through the world, he could be present with all of them at one and the same time? For example, with Thomas in [Col. 0285A] India, and with Peter or Paul in Rome. Indeed, when each year, both on Holy Saturday of Pentecost and on Holy Saturday of Easter, the Church celebrates the holy mysteries of baptism—which are known to possess no efficacy without the Holy Spirit—how could he be present throughout the whole world, wherever the Church has now spread, so that his fullness might everywhere descend into the fonts and everywhere overwhelm with waves the spiritual cavalry of Pharaoh, that is, the throngs of all sins?

We say that he fills that whole world in such a way that we should understand the universal Church, spread throughout the world. For divinity is not contained by the elements of the world or by inanimate bodies; but it is rightly believed to fill the holy Church everywhere. And, what is a more worthy and true sign of his divine majesty, he fills the head of that same Church itself, as it is written: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” [Col. 0285B] (Luke IV).

Therefore we bear witness to his divine presence everywhere when we sing at the Introit, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.” In the sense already stated, this phrase looks back to what follows in the same passage: he filled the Church, still small but destined to spread through the whole world—that is, Christ’s disciples—when, as a sign, all the languages of the world were brought forth in their mouths. What follows, however—“And that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. I)—why Wisdom said it is clear from what it adds: “Therefore he who speaks unjust things cannot be hidden” (ibid.); or from what it said before: “And no curse shall be delivered from his lips, because God is witness of his inner parts, a true searcher of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue” [Col. 0285C] (ibid.). From this it is evident that “has knowledge of speech” is said as though it meant: he knows with what mind each person speaks.

Nevertheless, in the logic of the present office it refers to knowledge of languages. By giving their diversity to his faithful, he magnificently proved that he possesses knowledge of every form in which human speech can vary.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is the confirmation of the whole divine work

The Offertory set forth above fittingly accords with the work of the Holy Spirit: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Ps. LXVII). [Col. 0285D] For, that we may know that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is the confirmation of the whole work of divinity, we must first state what the Lord worked in his apostles before the coming of that same Holy Spirit. He worked faith in them, namely the faith which sounded from Peter’s mouth on behalf of all: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). But how weak it was before the Holy Spirit came is plain to all who know that Peter, the chief of the apostles, terrified by the voice of a single maidservant, denied that he knew him whom, as has been said, he had confessed to be Christ, the Son of the living God (Luke XXII). But when he received the gift of this Spirit, he did not fear even the authority of the Roman ruler; rather, confessing Christ unto death, he glorified Christ by that very death of his.

The Holy Spirit therefore confirmed faith in the apostles; and so, as has been said, we fittingly sing in the Offertory: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us,” that through the same Spirit this same faith may be confirmed in us, adding, “from your temple, which is in Jerusalem” [Col. 0286A] (Ps. LXVII), that is, from the apostolic Church, which certainly began from Jerusalem (John XXI), that is, from Judaea; as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “For salvation is from the Jews” (John IV). Through the same Spirit, I say, we ask to be confirmed, because apart from him whatever we believe, whatever baptism we receive, whatever we undertake, is proved weak and empty.

For the heavens, namely the orders of the higher spirits, were indeed made firm by the Word of the Lord so that they might be rational and eternal in their nature; and “by the Spirit of his mouth all their power was made firm” (Ps. XXXII), by which they remain in the likeness of God, that is, in holiness. Hence elsewhere it is written: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job XXVI).

[Col. 0286B] In the remaining offices of the present week, although almost all resound with the name and grace of the Holy Spirit, the Gospels alone may raise the question what they have to do with the solemnity of his coming. Therefore something brief must be said about them, only so that their agreement with the individual offices to which they are assigned may appear.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the office of Monday

On Monday this Gospel is read: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” [Col. 0286C] (John III), etc. Taken by itself, what is said here does not immediately make clear what it has to do with the present solemnity. But when the preceding reading from the Acts of the Apostles is considered, it at once illuminates its reason like a ray of light.

“While Peter was speaking,” it says, “the Holy Spirit fell upon the Gentiles who heard the word. And the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the nations” (Acts X), etc. The aforesaid Gospel is therefore placed with this reading from Acts so that it may be demonstrated that this work of the Holy Spirit, by which “he gave repentance unto life to the Gentiles” (Acts XI), was not done through a change of plan. For the Son had willed the same before he suffered, [Col. 0286D] though at that time he had not wished to preach to the Gentiles in person; indeed, when sending the disciples, he said to them: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X).

For what Peter says here, “In truth I have learned that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X), the Son of God bears witness to in the Gospel, saying that he was sent not for judgment but for the salvation of the whole world (John XII), and adding, without distinction of Jew and Gentile: “that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life,” and the rest that follows. Thus, though Christ himself did not preach at all to the Gentiles, he foretold much concerning their salvation and his glorification among them.

[Col. 0287A] So Isaac did not himself instruct his younger son Jacob concerning the food to be brought to him; but Jacob was introduced through Rebecca, who was of one body with Isaac, when Isaac was preparing to give the blessing to Esau, his firstborn (Gen. XXVII). For Isaac signifies Christ; Esau, the Jewish people; Jacob, the Gentiles; and Rebecca the mother signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. For with Rebecca advising—that is, with the Holy Spirit of counsel providing—the younger son, namely the people of the Gentiles, enters to Isaac, that is, to Christ, while Esau lingers outside and is occupied with hunting—that is, while the former people attend to carnal ceremonies.

The younger people enter, I say, observing the Ten Commandments of the Law which had been given to the former people; they are adorned with the knowledge of the Law and Prophets, just as Jacob was clothed by his mother in Esau’s very fine garments [Col. 0287B]. They have skins of kids about hands and neck, that is, they make an open confession of sins; and offering food—that is, faith “working through love” (Gal. V)—they receive first the same blessing which descended upon the apostles, as we heard in the reading mentioned above: “While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word, and they were speaking in tongues and magnifying God.”

This Introit indicates the greatness of so great a blessing: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX). For by this is indicated the blessedness of the Gentiles, who through the Holy Spirit, as rational people, receive the inward marrow of Holy Scripture, [Col. 0287C] whereas the carnal Jews, like irrational cattle, pursue only the outer husk. For the divine word is wheat: its surface of letters is the husk, but the spiritual sense which we seek is the marrow. Hence it is clear that the Holy Spirit is, as it were, the richness of the divine substance, of whom the Psalm says: “As with fat and richness let my soul be filled” (Ps. LXII), because his inspiration implants in our souls the richness of the Word of God.

He fed, I say, the Church from the Gentiles with the fat of wheat, as stated. He also satisfied them with flowing honey from the rock, that is, with the teaching, wisdom, and explanation of mysteries which proceeded from the Lord Jesus, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II). [Col. 0287D] Therefore the Communion says of the same Spirit: “The Holy Spirit will teach you whatever I have said to you” (John XIV). The Offertory, “He thundered” (Ps. XVII), undoubtedly agrees with this very point, because through the Holy Spirit “the fountains of waters appeared” (ibid.), that is, the Scriptures of the prophets were understood.

## CHAPTER XXV. That the Holy Spirit is not given outside the Catholic Church

In the office of Tuesday, it is preached to us that the Holy Spirit cannot be given outside the Catholic Church, and that it has been given only to the bishops of apostolic faith, so that those who approach to be confirmed or ordained may receive the gift of that Holy Spirit through the laying on of their hands. For the reading from the Acts of the Apostles appointed in this office says:

“When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. For the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0288A] (Acts VIII).

And so that we may know that one must enter the holy Church only through the gate of apostolic faith, and that the grace of the Holy Spirit is received in no other way, this Gospel is fittingly joined to the reading: “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter the sheepfold through the door but climbs in another way, he is a thief and a robber” (John X), etc.

[Col. 0288B] Everywhere in the books of the Fathers are found statements confirming that the sacraments of such persons have indeed an appearance of piety but deny its power (II Tim. III). It is as when a branch has been cut from the vine: it is still a branch, but it can no longer bear fruit (John XV); or when a hand has been cut from the body: it is still a hand, but it cannot retain within itself the body’s life and sensation. Therefore, when those baptized by such persons return to the Catholic Church, the washing of the flesh is not repeated in them, if they have been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—for many heresies baptize in this manner too—but by the laying on of hands they receive the Holy Spirit, whom, as stated, they could not receive outside.

Therefore this office proclaims, as has been said, that the Holy Spirit is not given outside but [Col. 0288C] within, through bishops, whose office it is to lay hands by succession from the apostles. Their voice is also heard in the Introit, the voice of those laying hands and saying: “Receive the joy of your glory, giving thanks to God, who has called you to the heavenly kingdoms.” This is taken from the apostolic epistles, with a modest alteration from the letter. For instead of what the Lord said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX), they, reverently acting in his stead, say: “Receive the joy of your glory.”

For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, who had been variously led astray by such thieves and robbers as the Lord condemns in the Gospel cited above—that is, by false apostles—says: “You are our glory” (II Cor. I). And elsewhere: “Giving thanks to God” (Eph. V), etc. For this is the glory of Catholics and orthodox believers: that they entered the sheepfold through the door, that is, through the faith of those who seek not their own glory, as heretics do, but God’s glory in the Holy Spirit. Hence in the Communion we sing: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will glorify me.” This is as though it said: whoever gives or receives the Spirit proceeding from the Father will seek not his own glory or glorification, but God’s.

The Offertory too, “The Lord opened the gates of heaven” (Ps. LXXVII), proclaims the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom the sacred Scriptures were opened to the apostles and, through the apostles, to us, so that the Lord might rain down upon us in abundance the manna of the Word of God (ibid.). By their authority the Catholic Church is exalted against the heretics rising up against it, as we sing in the following verse [Col. 0289A].

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the summer fast ought to be observed in the very week of Pentecost
In the office of Wednesday we proclaim the manifold knowledge given to the Church through the Holy Spirit, in close harmony especially with the Gospel and prophetic readings assigned to the fast. For the readings of the three fast-days correspond more closely to the remaining parts of the offices, not only in meaning but sometimes even in wording; as does that Introit: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5), which is taken from the Epistle reading assigned to the fast. Hence, quite in accordance with ecclesiastical practice—and this is also the judgment of Roman authority—the solemn observance of the fasts is always celebrated in this sacred week of Pentecost, whether the seasonal dates fall later or earlier. The very writings of the ancient apostles unquestionably testify that this too was established by them.

For this is not the new allegory handed down by them, according to which some of our contemporaries have thought fit to observe, from the first week of March until the Nativity of the Lord, three fourteen-week periods (*tessarakaidekadas*, τεσσαρακαιδεκάδας), after the likeness of the three fourteen-generation periods which Matthew arranged in Christ’s genealogy. Rather, because the first fast belongs to spring and the second to summer, and because the end of Lent never occurs before the beginning of spring, while Pentecost never occurs before the beginning of summer, it rightly pleased the venerable mother Church of Rome to appoint the offices of these fasts in the first week of Lent [Col. 0289C] and in the very solemnity of Pentecost, and never to confuse them because the seasonal dates come early or late.

Nor does the observance of fasts sadden or darken that solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit; rather, it makes it brighter. For the delights of the Holy Spirit produce in the minds of the elect a distaste for bodily pleasures; and, because the bridegroom has been taken away, his sons must fast (Matt. 9). Thus the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, dispenses his grace and consolation in such a way that they delight in unutterable groanings (Rom. 8), “groaning like doves” (Nah. 2), and regard groaning as their song. Therefore it must briefly be explained how these offices accord, in their respective parts, with the fast.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Office of Wednesday: that manifold knowledge has been given to the Church through the Holy Spirit

First, the office of Wednesday proclaims the Church’s manifold knowledge, as was said above. For, as Daniel says, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). Through the zeal of eminent men enlightened by the Holy Spirit, from the books of Moses and the writings of a few prophets such an abundance of books has grown that we who do not read them seem, like weary guests at a banquet, to withdraw while leaving much untouched.

The holy Gospel mystically suggests this to us in the five loaves and two fish, with which five thousand men were satisfied, while twelve baskets were filled from the fragments (John 6) [Col. 0290A]. For they were increased by the Lord’s blessing, signifying the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Once he had been given, the Law and the Prophets were multiplied among the studies of their interpreters, just as those loaves were multiplied among the mouths of those eating.

Of this Spirit Wisdom says in the first reading: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1), etc. And Isaiah in the second reading: “Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and Most Upright One, whom I have chosen. For I shall pour water upon the thirsty land, and streams upon the dry ground” (Isa. 44). Explaining what he meant by “I shall pour,” he says: “I shall pour out my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring” (ibid.).

In harmony with these the Introit sings beforehand: “O God, when you went forth before your people, making a way for them, dwelling among them” (Ps. 67). This is indeed taken, section by section, from the sixty-seventh Psalm; and that whole psalm concerns Christ’s exaltation and the Church’s glorification. For through the aforesaid knowledge and the other charisms of the Holy Spirit, God went forth—that is, he became known in the sight of the Christian people—making for them a prosperous way (ibid.), namely by removing their former snares of error.

And because the aforesaid holy teachers—whose voice may also be that in the Offertory, “I meditated upon your commandments, which I loved exceedingly” (Ps. 118)—have diligently expounded the sacred Scriptures through meditation, all say the same thing and there are no schisms among them (1 Cor. 1). Accordingly, in the Communion is recited to them that saying of the Lord which they themselves embrace: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Office of Friday: that the Synagogue is to be raised through faith

On Friday, by a beautiful and wonderful mystery, the Gospel signifies for us what we hope will happen to the Synagogue: namely, that at last it will be raised through faith in Christ. It is now dead through envy, since the grace of the Holy Spirit received the Church coming from the Gentiles.

For the woman healed of an issue of blood by touching the fringe of the Saviour’s garment signifies the Church from the Gentiles; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom the same Lord raises, signifies the Synagogue, now dead, as was said, through unbelief [Col. 0290D]. In this there is something deeply wonderful and mystical: when the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was born, this woman began to be ill; and when this woman was healed, the girl died. Thus it is written in the Gospel that the girl was twelve years old (Mark 5), and that the woman had suffered the issue of blood for twelve years (Matt. 9).

What could be more beautiful or fitting? For when the Synagogue was born in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Gentile society began to languish in the filth of idolatry, as though through an issue of blood. And when, through the drawing and reception of the Holy Spirit, this woman was healed—as the Spirit bore witness in Cornelius (Acts 10)—then the Synagogue, moved by envy and judging itself unworthy of eternal life, died. But it shall live again after “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in” (Rom. 11), a future event proclaimed by the present grace of the Holy Spirit.

To it, under the name of its city Zion, the preceding prophetic reading says: “Rejoice, children of Zion, and be glad in the Lord, who has given you the teacher of righteousness; he shall cause the early and latter rain to descend in the beginning” (Joel 2) [Col. 0291A]. By the early and latter rain he signifies Gospel teaching: sent to them in the first age like early rain, and to be sent in the last age like latter rain. “And you shall eat,” he says, “eating and being satisfied, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonderful things with you” (ibid.).

You shall eat, I say, “not food which perishes, but that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6), concerning which, in the Introit, we say in the person of her who is to be raised: “Let my mouth be filled with your praise” (Ps. 70), etc. Therefore neither is it devoid of mystery that, when the Lord had raised the girl, it was added: “And he commanded that something be given her to eat” (Mark 5). For, inwardly refreshed, she will say what we sing in the Offertory: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 102), etc.

Then, more universally, will be fulfilled what we sing in the Communion: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3), having power, namely, when he wills, to go to the Gentiles and again to return to the Jews, making himself known everywhere by his voice; for no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Office of Saturday: that the two peoples, Gentile and Jewish, shall have peace and concord

The office of Saturday foreshadows the concord of the two peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile. At last, both confessing themselves enlightened by one and the same Spirit, they will follow Christ, whom they have recognized, without dispute.

For the two blind men reported in the Gospel to have received sight (Matt. 20) signify these two peoples, as is evident from the preceding Epistle reading. To what two peoples, if not to Jews and Gentiles, contending against one another, does Paul say: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5)? This is clear to those who read and understand what precedes, where by a long and powerful argument he maintains that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin; that the latter are not excusable because of ignorance of God; that the former could not be justified by works of the Law; and that Christ’s grace is equally necessary to all. Having shut all under sin, he finally concludes: “Therefore, having been justified by faith” (ibid.), etc.

Thus the two blind men who receive sight mystically signify the two peoples. Their voice too is that of the Introit, taken from the aforesaid Epistle reading: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through his Spirit dwelling in us.” Both reason and authority require fasting in the present week, so that the readings and Gospels pertaining to the fast may be especially consonant with the offices.

And if the five readings are considered, they all bear witness to the grace of the Holy Spirit: all indeed by signs suited to the matter [Col. 0292A], but some in explicit words, such as this first reading from the prophet Joel: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2), etc. The second reading also, in which it is said, “You shall count seven complete weeks until the day after the completion of the seventh week” (Lev. 25), concerns the present solemnity, which we celebrate after counting seven weeks from Easter Day for the coming of the Holy Spirit. Among the ancients it was the great feast of weeks, instituted in remembrance of the giving of the Law; among us it is the joyful jubilee in remembrance of grace, that is, of the remission of sins.

And because, after the concord of the two peoples has been effected, the Lord will soon come, we rightly sing in the Communion, to the sons who mourn the bridegroom’s absence and await his return with longing, those consoling words: “I shall not leave you orphans; I shall come to you again, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 14).

## CHAPTER XXX. That each of the aforesaid offices corresponds to one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit

We must now briefly indicate how the individual offices correspond to the individual gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The first two offices, those of Saturday and of the following day of Pentecost, proclaim the spirit of wisdom and understanding. For he gave wisdom and understanding to the apostles, so that, as we sang on Saturday, “Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 17), and so that they might understand the Scriptures, as we read on the very day of Pentecost [Col. 0292C], the Lord promising: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 14). Heavenly instruction made them both wise, so that they knew when they ought to speak, and understanding, so that they did not remain ignorant of the mysteries of the Scriptures—though until then they had been unlearned and without letters.

The office of Monday pertains to the spirit of counsel, because they praise God for the calling of the Gentiles. While their salvation lay in the hidden will of God, the apostles themselves did not know that counsel, until it was said to Peter in an ecstasy of mind: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10). Afterwards, as he spoke, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word [Col. 0292D]; this is why, as stated above, the office commemorates it.

The office of Tuesday commends the apostles and their successors because, against thieves and robbers who climb into the sheepfold by another way (John 10)—that is, against false apostles or leaders of heresy—they dare, when the cause demands it, to be strengthened by the spirit of fortitude and to say: “For we are your glory” (2 Cor. 1). They glory, not foolishly, but by speaking the truth. Therefore this office pertains to the spirit of fortitude.

The office of Wednesday proclaims the spirit of knowledge, as is especially clear from the Gospel, in which the loaves are reported to have been multiplied by the Lord’s blessing (John 6) [Col. 0293A]. The mystical meaning of this has already been explained above.

The office of Friday looks to the spirit of piety. For it is a work of piety that the Lord raises the girl and commands that food be given her (Mark 5); indeed, so too is that which is signified thereby: that at the end, raising by faith the Synagogue now dead, he will fill her mouth with praise, so that she may utter a devout confession of God’s just judgment (Ps. 70).

The office of Saturday pertains to the spirit of fear; for when the two aforesaid blind men—that is, the two peoples—have together recognized their illuminator, the day of judgment will be near, a cause of fear and trembling even for the elect (1 Pet. 4) [Col. 0294A].

Nor is it surprising that this order of offices proceeds downward from the spirit of wisdom to the spirit of fear, while the offices of Easter week proceed upward from the spirit of fear to the spirit of wisdom. For in these the descent of the Holy Spirit to us is set forth; in those, our ascent to him. This has been explained more fully in those same Easter offices.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0293]

## CHAPTER I. Why, after the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, an office concerning the Holy Trinity is appointed

[Col. 0293B]

Once the solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit has been celebrated, we immediately thereafter sing, in the office of the following Sunday and by a fitting arrangement, the glory of the Holy Trinity. For after the coming of that Holy Spirit, faith in and confession of the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at once began to be preached, believed, and celebrated in baptism.

For while the Lord was previously present in the flesh, we nowhere read that the distinction of this name was openly handed down or observed, except when, after his resurrection, he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Yet the rule was then handed down; now, however, it was first put into practice, when on the very day of Pentecost baptism was first celebrated in the Church for three thousand persons.

Thus the name of the Lord’s power began to become known throughout the earth, as the leaders of Christ, the great King David, fought on his behalf. He was bodily absent, but by the presence of his divinity he directed and ordered the whole course of the battle. His most faithful leaders laboured with the utmost care, when the opposing city was being taken, that victory might be attributed not to their own name but to his. So we read that David was told by his commander, while he was besieging Rabbah of the Ammonites: “Gather the people and besiege the city, for the city is about to be taken, lest, when it has been taken, the victory be attributed to my name” (2 Sam. 12) [Col. 0293C].

Concerning this it is further said that he took the crown of their king from his head, and it was placed upon David’s head. Instead of “their king,” the Hebrew has *Melchom*. Hence Jerome says:

> “Their king is called their idol, which is here called Melchom.”

[Note: [Col. 0293D] St Jerome, *Commentary on Amos*, book I, chapter 2, verses 14–15, *Patrologia*, vol. XXV, Migne edition.]

David is said, according to the Law, to have melted down and purified the gold of that crown and to have made a crown for himself from it (1 Chron. 20), which is said here to have been placed on his head (2 Sam. 12). Thus our David took away idolatrous worship and, from the chief rulers who worshipped idols, as though from their crown, crowned himself and his Church [Col. 0294B]. Hence he says to this same Church in the Song of Songs: “You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4).

For then too the same David took the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and had Uriah himself killed while he carried in his hand the written sentence of his own death (2 Sam. 11). In the historical event he committed a grave crime, yet he foreshadowed a great mystery to be accomplished in its time through Christ the King, truly strong of hand and desirable.

For this true David, our Lord, when he walked upon the roof of his house—that is, when he was already reigning on the throne of paternal majesty—after midday—that is, after the burden and heat of his passion—and had already sent his apostles to preach to all nations (Rom. 7), which are here prefigured by Rabbah, the city of the Ammonites [Col. 0294C], saw the Law which he had given through Moses. It was indeed holy and good, but attached uselessly to a carnal people, as Bathsheba, most beautiful indeed but barren, was joined in an unfruitful marriage to Uriah the Hittite.

Taking that sacred Law, then, and joining its meaning to his Spirit, he kills its proud husband, namely the Jewish people. Their pride is signified by the name Uriah—for Uriah is interpreted “my light is God”: that people regarded God’s light and knowledge as their own possession, as though God were God of the Jews only and not also of the Gentiles (Rom. 3). He kills that carnal people in this manner: by taking from its heart the inner meaning of his Law, he leaves in its hand the letter alone, so that, accused by it, it may be held guilty, as the Lord himself says: “There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5) [Col. 0294D]. This is aptly prefigured by the fact that Uriah himself is commanded to carry the death sentence written by King David (2 Sam. 11).

Therefore, after the solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit has been celebrated, as was said above—and after receiving him the apostles at once began to preach the faith of the Holy Trinity—we rightly proclaim, in both the night and day office of the following Sunday, the name and glory of that same holy and undivided Trinity.

Concerning the unity of its substance and the Trinity of its persons, great and Catholic Fathers have written great and worthy things and, as it were harvesting their own vintage, have filled their presses. We, as those gathering grapes after the harvesters, and ourselves hoping in God’s blessing, wish, though last of all, to speak words of Catholic peace for that same faith.

## CHAPTER II. That the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the proper description of the true God

The name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the perfect and complete definition of the one true God. It excludes the entire multitude of all who are called, or have ever been called, gods, whether in heaven or on earth [Col. 0295B]. Of these, some were falsely called gods, worshipped by Gentile peoples deceived by various errors; others were not gods by nature, but were made gods by an accidental gift from the true God, according to the saying: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

For human presumption attached to false gods the other names proper to the supreme and one Godhead, calling them creators and rulers of the world, immortal and everlasting, heavenly and almighty, and giving them similar titles—titles inserted also into poetic fictions, by which demons have customarily fed themselves. But this name has not been heard from the beginning of the world, nor could human beings devise it from their own hearts; for its meaning “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64).

For things are first understood, and names are afterwards assigned to them at pleasure, as even the great pagan philosophers say: things in speech are signs of the affections in the soul. But no one who fashioned for himself whatever gods he wished knew the meaning of the aforesaid name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore they could neither devise nor impose this name upon the things which they called gods.

God alone imposed this name upon himself when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28) [Col. 0295D]. Although the prophets somehow knew its meaning, they ought not to have uttered the name itself, because the world, still an infant, could not have grasped the meaning of that name.

Therefore, as stated above, this name of the living God is the perfect and complete definition of the true God. It makes manifest the distinction by which those are identified who have that writing on their foreheads, concerning whom the angel ascending from the rising of the sun and bearing the seal of the living God cried in the Apocalypse: “Do not harm the earth, or the sea, or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (Rev. 7). For then that Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. 9) cried out to the four angels—that is, to the four principal kingdoms—when, through the victorious cry of preaching, kings and emperors themselves were converted to the faith and did not hinder those who taught and baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0296A].

## CHAPTER III. On the meaning of the same name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit

To understand the meaning or mystery of this great name, the eye of the heart, by which alone God can be seen, must be cleansed; just as, when we wish to look upon this sun, we must cleanse the bodily eye of dust if any has entered it.

For even the carnal persons in the Church, and many heresies too, not only dim-sighted through the dust of the flesh but groping in the darkness of impiety, retain and confess this name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by memory, because they in some fashion hold to the authority of the Gospel handed down in the Lord’s own voice. Yet the meaning of the name is seen only by those who have cleansed the eyes of their hearts: now through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face, when that which is perfect has come (1 Cor. 13) [Col. 0296B].

Those who are such understand, through these reverent names of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the true and single glory of the supreme Godhead: namely, that now, and before he made anything, God was one and the same and alone, yet not deserted or solitary—alone, that is, in substance; alone and one, but not in person.

## CHAPTER IV. That God’s nature is signified more by these relative names than by substantial names

The mystery of the divine nature itself is expressed more by these relative names than by any substantial names. We call “substantial names” those which are equally common to the three persons, such as God, Almighty, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and the like. But these names are relative, because the Father is father of someone, the Son is son of someone, and the Holy Spirit is spirit of someone.

It must be understood, however, that relation is not reciprocal in every respect. The Father is related and reciprocally referred to the Son, because the Father is Father of the Son and the Son is Son of the Father [Col. 0296D]. But the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, and the relation is not reciprocal. For the Father is not Father of the Holy Spirit, nor is the Son Son of the Holy Spirit. Yet the same Holy Spirit is called, and is, a gift; and under this name relation may rightly be reciprocal. For a gift is the gift of a giver, and a giver is the giver of a gift.

By these relative names, rather than by substantial names, we are shown what we ought to love, praise, and glorify. For what could a creature’s goodwill toward its Creator desire more than that for which he chiefly glories, saying: “Shall I, who cause others to bring forth, not myself bring forth? Shall I, who give generation to others, be barren?” (Isa. 66). Though this appears to have been spoken of adopted sons, the beginning of praise comes from the generation of that Son who alone is natural, by participation in whom others become adopted sons. For the Father who speaks these things begot him alone (Ps. 2); the others he created, and did not beget them from his own substance, but regenerated them by his grace (Titus 3) [Col. 0297A].

## CHAPTER V. Why, though we confess three persons, we are forbidden to say three gods

Though we confess three persons, we are nevertheless forbidden to say three gods, because even the relation mentioned above does not happen to God accidentally, nor does any other accident attach itself to the divine substance.

For in these three persons there is no difference of quantity, quality, time, place, action, passion, position, or possession. There is no difference of quantity, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each equally immeasurable in substance; none of quality, because each is likewise equally holy, just, and good in substance; none of time, because each is equally without beginning; none of place, because each is equally uncircumscribed and in every place; none of action, because the operation of the Trinity is equally unchangeable; none of passion, because each is equally subject to no passion; none of position, because none is held in a local posture of lying or sitting [Col. 0297B]. Nor is there a difference in the category called possession, because nothing such as being shod, armed, crowned, and the like is ever predicated of God except figuratively.

How then can a number of gods be asserted in the Trinity, where there is absent the multiplicity of accidents which alone produces number among individuals belonging to the same species? For example, since “man” is one species and all men are one in species, as the pagan philosophers themselves also maintain, examine whatever produces number among individuals, and you will find absolutely nothing except a mere multiplicity of accidents. But these, as has been said, are wholly foreign to the Godhead. Therefore there is neither reason nor basis for saying that there is a plurality of gods.

## CHAPTER VI. That, because of its simplicity, the divine substance is subject to no accidents

The reason why the creating substance does not receive accidents is evident if you first consider why created substance is subject to them. It is subject to accidents because, whatever it may be, it consists at once of matter and form.

For example, when an artisan makes a statue by the craft of sculpture, its matter is the substance of bronze; its form is whatever image is imposed upon it through art—an emperor’s likeness, for instance, or, if he prefers, an image of Jupiter. Thus what we call a statue is not simply what it is, because it is not one simple thing. Nor is bronze itself, before anything is formed from it, a simple thing, since its matter is earth, which differs greatly from what appears under the form of bronze [Col. 0297D].

If you consider the earth itself, it too is not simply what it is, since it has this name from form. For it is called earth because it is heavy and dry. But it receives its being from *hyle*, what they call unformed created matter. Likewise, a human being is not simply this or that, because he consists of parts, soul and body, which death undoubtedly separates though bound together by a dissoluble bond.

So too all other things consist, as was said, of matter and form; therefore they are subject to a multiplicity of accidents and are mutable. But God’s substance is simple: not formed, but form alone; form, I say, lacking matter. Hence I know not what instrument of the Holy Spirit sang the foregoing:

> “The heart of the Virgin was made steadfast, in which she conceived divine mysteries at the angel’s announcement,”

and immediately added:

> “Form, more beautiful than the sons of men, received you in a chaste womb.”

This a truly Catholic precentor of the Church foretold. For the blessed Virgin received Form—that is, God—in her chaste womb, and that same Form brought forth for us a man more beautiful than the sons of men [Col. 0298B]. This is the one thing which is not formed. How then could it be subject to accidents?

For all other things derive their mutability from their matter, as was said. This one alone is without matter, and therefore truly is; it rests upon nothing, and is most solid above all things, beautiful beyond all things. Nothing can be in it other than what it itself is; nor can it be subject to accidents. Although it is substance, it is not receptive of contraries—though the wisdom of the world, which this same God has made foolish, does not grasp this (1 Cor. 1).

## CHAPTER VII. That the relation of the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is in no way an accident in God, although relation is one of the accidents

Therefore, though we confess three persons, as stated above, we are rightly forbidden to call them three gods; nor ought we to predicate in the plural number whatever are names of substance. We multiply persons only, because we are rightly compelled to do so by manifest relation—that is, by the relative names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Yet although this relation is rightly counted among the multitude of accidents in the case of human beings, it must be understood that we do not concede that it is in any way accidental to God. For it did not happen to God in time that he should be Father, or that he should beget a Son, as it does to a human being, who is fully complete in his substance long before he becomes a father or begets a son [Col. 0298D].

All this mist of our mutability must be passed beyond; and, with the eye of the heart cleansed, as was said at the beginning, we must see at least through a mirror in an enigma that God is born from God in a manner far different from that in which a human being is born from a human being, through the flow of flesh, in time and place. It is of no small help toward this if for the moment we express Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in other, substantial terms.

Accordingly, we say that the Holy Trinity is life, wisdom, and love. We call God the Father life, living immortally in himself; we call the Son of God the Father his wisdom, ineffably begotten from his heart, consubstantial and coeternal; and we call the Holy Spirit the love of the Father and the Son, likewise consubstantial and coeternal [Col. 0299A]. These are names of substance.

For the Father is life substantially: not something made alive, as a human being or an animal is a body made alive; nor like the soul, which, though living, is not life itself, and is consequently subject to many disturbances and unworthy of the higher life. Rather, he is the very substance of life: a subtle, luminous, mobile, keen substance, subject, as stated above, to no accidents, needing nothing, capable of being received by every rational life, yet himself capable of receiving none.

For what is capable of containing another is necessarily coarser, denser, and more bodily than that which it contains. A vessel is capable of containing water because its material is earth, which is certainly denser and more bodily than the element of water. But this life of which we speak is so much subtler and purer than all things that it becomes form itself or matter itself for all things compounded of matter and form, as has already been said. Therefore it is simple and remains what it is without any mutability: good form, light not illuminated but illuminating; true light, the fountain and source of everlasting light.

Therefore this life is capable of containing nothing, yet is capable of being contained. In comparison with it, all other things are dense and bodily vessels, even spirits; yet, formed by this life—the God living in himself—with a rational capacity, they are capable of it, and therefore live blessedly and holily [Col. 0299B].

The Son likewise is wisdom substantially: that is, not merely wise, which can also be said of someone who participates by an accidental gift in wisdom, but the very substance of wisdom. Nor do we employ the terms of dialecticians because we think that the Holy Trinity should in any way be subjected to their vanity, but in order to express more clearly and briefly, through familiar and more significant signs, what must be signified.

We grant them, indeed, their division of all things into two, substance and accident; but that which is above all things, beyond all things, and apart from all things—namely this wisdom, indeed the whole blessed Trinity—we do not submit to their definitions. For this substance is in no way receptive of contraries, although God, in accordance with our manner of speech, is now said to be angry and now to be pleased.

And this wisdom of God is an accident in a human being, because it may be present or absent without corruption of the subject—that is, without diminution or destruction of human substance. But in itself it is truly substance: more mobile than all movable things, reaching everywhere, working all things, ordering all things, beautiful, sweet, radiant, noble, rich, the artificer of all things (Wis. 7–8) [Col. 0299D].

We have learned, believe, and confess that this wisdom of God is the Son, naturally begotten from him. Naturally, I say, not imaginatively or by resemblance, as we sometimes call a blessed man’s deeds his children. Rather, just as naturally as a human being begets a human being, so we understand God to be naturally begotten from God, light from light: begotten, I say, not made; born, not adopted; coequal, coeternal, consubstantial.

It does not follow, therefore, that when this same wisdom is given to a human being, it is called the son of that person’s heart, except figuratively, as the Lord says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12) [Col. 0300A]. This wisdom is not the son of the person to whom it is given, but of him from whom it was truly born and by whom it is given. For the ray by which our eyes are illuminated is not our ray, but the sun’s ray. This wisdom is the Son of him who received it from nowhere else, from whose heart it was born: as brightness from the sun, a stream from a fountain, or vapour from fire.

[Col. 0300B] The Holy Spirit is likewise substantially love: that is, not merely one who loves, which can also be said of someone who, sharing by an accidental gift in that same Spirit, begins to love according to the measure of that participation; rather, he is the very substance of divine love. Nor should our understanding therefore suffer any obscurity that would keep us from judging this love to be true and perfect substance, because this divine love may be present to, or absent from, human substance without any diminution of that same substance of ours; for this love is indeed an accident in a human being—that is, an accidental gift. But in himself he is true substance, living nature, true God. For this reason he is properly called the Holy Spirit, although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy. For just as an airy wind—for example, the south wind at midday (for it signified the Holy Spirit because it is warm)—just as, I say, the south wind at midday runs from its own quarter toward the opposite north [Col. 0300C] and carries timely rains to parched lands, so this Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Creator through his own proper operation, pours into the rational creature, according to his will as God and Lord, the aforesaid wisdom into its needy nature. Hence he is also called the Spirit of wisdom, even apart from the arrangement or order in which his seven graces are enumerated: “The Spirit, I say, of wisdom—holy, unique, manifold, subtle, eloquent, swift-moving, undefiled, sure, gentle, loving what is good; keen, humane, kindly, steadfast, secure, possessing every power, beholding all things” (Wisdom 7).

By these substantial names, therefore, as was said above—life, wisdom, love, or charity—by these, I say, we are aided in understanding that the relation consisting in the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did not in any way begin in time. For since the Father, as was said, is life, and the Son wisdom, whoever contends that the name Father, or the generation of the Son, began in time must consequently admit that God was at some time without wisdom—God, I say, was unwise, which it is wicked even to say. But faith recoils from this, piety anathematizes it, and every creature detests it. Thus God is Father not from time onward, but before all ages, because the Son—that is, his wisdom—is with him without beginning. Hence Wisdom herself says: “Before God made anything, I was present, arranging all things with him, playing with him at all times, playing in [Col. 0301A] the circle of the earth. And my delights were to be with the children of men” (Proverbs 8). Equivalent or identical with this is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), etc. Again, since the Holy Spirit is love, whoever contends that the Father and Son existed before the Holy Spirit must consequently hold that there was a time when neither the Son loved the Father nor the Father loved the Son. To suppose this is utterly foolish and impious. For us, however, it is superfluous to establish by testimonies that the Father loves the Son—indeed, that, as he himself says, he loved him before the foundation of the world (John 17)—because it is sufficiently probable, indeed necessary, that such a Father has always loved such a Son.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0301B] That Wisdom’s saying, “I was playing before him”—that is, before God—“in the beginning,” is the same as what is said of the Word: “What was made, in him was life.”

Yet, lest we seem to have left the foregoing chapter under a cloud, what other play can we understand in Wisdom’s saying, “I was playing before him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth” (Proverbs 8), except the joy of the love of which we are speaking? For it was a delightful play to God the Father to behold in his wisdom what he was to make: first, the blessed court of heaven and the beautiful commonwealth, whose glory was to be distinguished by ten orders of angels; then the visible structure of this world—the spherical vault of heaven, the sun and moon, the shining stars, the upper waters, the lower waters, all [Col. 0301C] abysses, snows and hail, mountains and hills, the whole expanse of the earth, the sea and everything in it, whatever flies above, whatever creeps or walks below, beasts and all cattle, kings of the earth and all peoples. For of all these the Evangelist says: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1). And what is meant by the addition, “And my delights were to be with the children of men” (Proverbs 8)? What, I say, except that even then it was foreseen in that same Wisdom that it would rest in human nature, and, having become the head of humankind, would join to itself in its delights companies of saints and wise persons? To behold these things before they were made was play to God and to his wisdom: festive play, joyous play, delightful play. But to rejoice in such things, to behold all these things [Col. 0301D] with gladness and in largeness of heart, is Wisdom’s love: a devoted love, a holy love, which we said above is the Holy Spirit. Therefore what Wisdom, who is the Son, says concerning her eternal antiquity, must also necessarily be granted concerning this love, which is the Holy Spirit: namely, that “the Lord possessed him at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning, from eternity, from of old, before the earth was made” (ibid.), etc.

## CHAPTER IX

That the Catholic faith neither separates the substance, as Arius did, nor confounds the persons of the Trinity, as Sabellius did.

Thus we neither separate the substance, as Arius did, nor confound the persons in the Trinity, as Sabellius did [Col. 0302A]. Rejecting with abhorrence the whirlpool of each error, and traveling the royal road, we spread the marked sails of the Catholic confession. For one of them, maintaining that the Son is less than the Father, a creature, and changeable, impiously and most wickedly attempted to take from the Creator what he graciously deigned to grant to all creatures made by him that live, whether they merely live or both live and have sensation. For he distinguished each according to its kind, so that they might reproduce in their species and not degenerate: “Let the earth bring forth green grass, bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree bearing fruit, each having seed according to its own species” (Genesis 1). Likewise: “God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which [Col. 0302B] the waters brought forth according to their species, and every winged creature according to its kind” (ibid.). And afterward: “Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind” (ibid.), etc. Finally, he formed even humanity so that it might reproduce, as it is written, according to his image and likeness (ibid.). Thus that fool fails to see what a great insult he offers to the Creator, and what barrenness and poverty he charges upon his nature: that the creatures made by him should bear seed in their own kind, while the Creator himself should have no seed of his own kind; that he himself should lack the very good which he bestowed upon others, barren, deserted, and solitary. Does he not therefore rightly complain against such detractors in the prophet, saying: “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth? And shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” (Isaiah 66). From where did he take the pattern by which he gave fruitfulness to his creatures, if he himself is dry in barrenness, if, while creating so many things, he could generate nothing from himself? Why does he so earnestly go round the doors of maidens throughout the whole night of this present life, asking that they be opened to him, if he does not burn with love naturally implanted within him, if he does not flourish with genuine seed? For he presses upon them from within, breathing forth the vehement love which we call the Holy Spirit, the communion of his own nature; and his own Word—already Son, born already from the beginning and from eternity—yet, as seed truly implanted in himself, scattering itself among many brides, that is, many souls, daily multiplies the race of gods, to whom the Prophet says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” [Col. 0302D] (Psalm 81). Likewise the Evangelist, speaking of that one Son of God and Word of God, says: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1).

But that unhappy Arius mentioned above, and everyone like him—a merely animal man, not perceiving the things of God and savoring only the things of the flesh (1 Corinthians 2)—hearing that a Son was born to God, clings with his entire mind to images of the flesh. He contends that it follows that, if a son were generated or born, the father’s substance must have flowed out, and that the son must have been drawn locally from that substance of the Father; and by this calumny of passibility he reproves us as though it followed necessarily. Again he adds concerning the Son: “If he was born, then assuredly there was a time when he was not.” And [Col. 0303A], as though necessarily inferring temporality, he strives, as far as lies in him, to remove the Son’s coeternity with the Father. But coeternity and consubstantiality have already been discussed above. As for the argument of an outflow or diminution of the Father’s substance, which he claims necessarily follows in the generation of the Son, it must be said that they have grossly deceived themselves by an excessively carnal understanding. They ought not to have drawn an argument from flesh, which flows forth passibly in propagation, in reasoning about the divine generation. The same properties do not belong to unlike things. And what is more unlike than spirit and flesh—and not merely any spirit, but the Spirit who is Creator of all spirits? For God is spirit, and one who worships him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4). [Col. 0303B] Therefore they ought not to object to us, who confess that the Son of God is naturally born from the Father, that our confession entails a passibility of the divine substance which is not absent in fleshly generation—that is, an outflow or diminution. There is indeed some likeness drawn from flesh to God, who is spirit, and introduced into the sacred Scriptures, as in the Song of Songs and the mystical books of the prophets, under the names of bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife; but this is wholly figurative—that is, so that in what the letter says you understand something far different: namely, God in the husband; the Son, that is, his Word, in the seed of God; the Holy Spirit in love; and the rational creature—that is, the human soul or angelic substance—in the wife. But there is a truer likeness, drawn from the inner human being, which strikes the enemy back with his own weapons. For if a likeness to God is sought from humanity, let it be drawn from the place where the image of God is shown to shine.

[Col. 0303C] The human body, however, was not formed according to the image of God, as those called Anthropomorphites supposed; imagining God to have human shape, they set up an enormous image in the temple of their heart. For since it is written, “Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66), their view would entail that God sat in heaven so vast that he touched the earth with his feet. Therefore one may argue, on the contrary, from the inner human being that the generation of the Son of God compels us to admit no diminution or outflow of the Father’s substance.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0303D] By what likeness it may be understood that the Son could be born without an outflow or diminution of the Father’s substance.

It is worth observing the intention or skill situated in a human soul, and how it passes from the soul to some hearer or into action without diminution of the soul. If you set forth your plan to all who can be present or hear, or if, as a diligent teacher, you pour your knowledge into the ears of many by speaking and teaching, filling the minds of learners whom you had received empty, has your understanding thereby flowed away, been diminished, or suffered any loss of itself? Again, if you are a craftsman and conceive some excellent work, first sketching in your mind the design of its construction and afterward bringing it into existence in a work admirable and praiseworthy [Col. 0304A], does the spring of your talent immediately dry up, so that it no longer retains what it has produced? How much more, then, is the wisdom of God—which is God, the Son of God, the maker of all things, beholding all things, reaching from end to end (Wisdom 8)—not so born as to flow out, nor so generated as to diminish the Father’s substance? Not even when it first shone forth to construct the fabric of the world and created all visible and invisible things, nor when, assuming flesh in the Virgin’s womb, it was wholly inscribed upon human nature, did the Father have any less in his heart; nor was the Word thereby erased or worn away in his nature because he transcribed it whole upon the skin of our nature. Therefore let Arius, and all who do not confess the consubstantial Trinity, be anathema, says the holy Council of Nicaea [Col. 0304B]. But for those who proclaim the consubstantial Trinity, let the kingdoms of heaven be prepared.

## CHAPTER XI

That the Sabellian heresy, by confounding the persons, was consequently called Patripassian.

The other, namely Sabellius, though by a different yet no less detestable error, confounds the persons of the Trinity and asserts that there is one person: namely, that he who is Father is himself Son, and himself Spirit. He is so blind in mind as not to attend to these most splendid and manifest testimonies of the Lord, who says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). Likewise, when he was baptized in the Jordan, a voice from heaven said: [Col. 0304C] “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3), and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. We consequently call this heresy Patripassian. For if the Son who was incarnate and suffered is the very same person as the Father, then without doubt the Father himself was incarnate and suffered. Hence we rightly call this heresy Patripassian, as was said. But, execrating this error, we believe and confess that the Word which was in the beginning with God—the Word, I say, which was God, is not himself the one with whom this Word was—we believe and confess that this Word became flesh; that is, we confess that he who begot is one, and he who was begotten another: another in person, not another in substance. Hence the Son himself says: “I and [Col. 0304D] the Father are one” (John 10). We are one, certainly, in substance; yet we do not doubt that he spoke according to a plurality of persons.

## CHAPTER XII

That in a rational creature, rightly constituted in good and perfect beauty, the Holy Trinity may be recognized through the distinction of its works.

In the rational creature likewise, established in good and perfect beauty, it appears in some measure as in a translucent mirror that the divinity which is to be worshiped subsists not in one person alone, as the aforementioned Sabellius errs, but in three persons. For behold: as was said above, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—relative names—are also called, or are, by other substantial names: life, wisdom, and love. So in a human being or holy angel we count these three: spirit or soul, rationality, and love [Col. 0305A]. These are three. And it is manifest that spirit or soul is not itself rationality; otherwise no soul would lack reason. But the soul of a beast is brute, and, as it lacks reason, so it lacks eternity; and as it performs only the senses of the flesh, so it dies with the flesh. Likewise rationality is not itself love; otherwise nothing rational would be without love. But every human being and every angel is rational, though not every human being or angel possesses in himself the love of God. Hence Ezekiel rebukes the devil, who first despised it within himself: “Gold,” he says, “was the work of your adornment, and your settings were prepared on the day [Col. 0305B] when you were created” (Ezekiel 28). And shortly afterward: “Your inward parts,” he says, “were filled with iniquity” (ibid.). He calls the rationality with which the devil was created his settings, because as a precious stone is set in gold, so he could have been bound by the Holy Spirit, who is indeed love, and joined in the unity of the heavenly order, but refused. So too is every proud human being who imitates his pride. Therefore, as has already been said, love is not itself rationality, nor rationality itself soul or spirit; rather, the three together show one perfect work, like its Creator. Therefore contemplate the Creator God in this, as in a mirror, as existing not in only one but in three persons. Whoever denies any one of them does not have God, just as, if you remove any one of the three things mentioned above from a rational creature, no work of any worth remains. [Col. 0305C] For having lost love, the angel who had been created an angel of light became the devil, prince of darkness. Likewise, a human being without love is evil and is a son of that same devil. But if rationality is lacking, everything that lives and feels is brute. If soul or spirit is absent, still more certainly neither rationality nor love is in any creature. If, I say, you deny any one of the three persons, you do not have God; for if you deny the Holy Spirit while confessing the Father and Son, since that same Spirit is love, you have made God for yourself without love—that is, your enemy and foe. If you deny the Son, since the Son of God is wisdom, you have fashioned for yourself, in a phantom error, a brute and foolish God. For the faith of the Council of Nicaea proves that those who think wrongly concerning the Son [Col. 0305D] are like the gentiles. Thus Catholic faith rightly, as was said above, anathematizes in Arius the separation of substance and in Sabellius the confusion or destruction of the persons.

## CHAPTER XIII

How the number of the three persons was not increased by the Son of God’s becoming human, and why, accordingly, it is neither called nor is a quaternity, but nonetheless a Trinity.

Although the Son was incarnate and is the same both God and human, the plurality of persons does not thereby increase, so that the Trinity which existed before his Incarnation should afterward be called or be a quaternity. For the Catholic Church does not receive two sons; indeed, it anathematizes [Col. 0306A] Nestorius and all who profess one Son before the ages and another after the assumption of flesh. For we preach two things, that is, two substances—two, I say, in the neuter gender, not the masculine—not two persons in Christ. And just as a person sitting on a horse is not two, but one rider, so God in a human being is not two Christs but one Christ. For how will you predicate “two” or “three” of individual things belonging to different species when you cannot supply one name of substance? For example: this human being and this horse are individuals of different species, namely, the human and the horse. If, then, speaking of this horse and this human being, you say “two,” you will predicate the mobile term improperly, since there is no fixed substantial term which you can supply; reason does not permit you to say either “humans” or “horses” of one human being and one horse. [Col. 0306B] No less improperly will you predicate “two” concerning Christ. For as this rider consists of this human being and this horse, so Christ consists of this individual of God, which is the Word of the Father, and of this individual human being, which began by being born from the Virgin Mary. There is no doubt that God and human being are different species, far distant from each other by wholly substantial differences, from the first division under the most general genus, which is substance. For the human being is contained far below under the corporeal, whereas the true God is under the incorporeal. If, then, speaking of Christ you say “two,” you will predicate improperly, because there is no fixed substantial term that you can supply fittingly. Nor would you speak correctly if you supplied “Christs,” because “Christ” is not a substantial name but the name of an office; nor can you more rightly predicate two Christs of God and a human being than two riders of a human being and a horse. [Col. 0306C] Indeed, you say “two Christs” of God and a human being even less appropriately than “two riders” of a human being and a horse, because God, united to a human being, will never be separated; but a person sitting on a horse is separated whenever he dismounts. Nor is this likeness taken as an argument incongruously, since in Christ divinity used humanity as a rider uses a horse. Hence a red horse is shown in the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1), and in the Gospel the Samaritan is said to have placed on his own beast the man wounded by robbers (Luke 17). Thus, just as [Col. 0306D] your son, if he went out on foot and happened to return to you seated on a horse, does not thereby make three persons with you but only two as before—for it is not fitting that, along with your son, the son of the beast should double the number of persons—so the Son of God, the Word of the Father, uttered in divinity alone into the Virgin’s womb, when he returns with humanity to the Father’s right hand, does not cause the number of persons to increase. For it is not fitting that human nature should double the number of persons alongside the nature of God, since it differs from that substance by differences more numerous and greater than those by which a horse differs from a human being. For rationality separates a human being from a horse; but very many substantial differences, too many to enumerate, separate a human being from God.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0307A] Why, before the Lord’s Incarnation, faith in the Holy Trinity ought not, or could not, have been required of the common people.

Therefore, in generations past before Christ’s coming, the mystery of this great divine name—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—was kept silent from the common people, because the excessively fleshly infancy or youth of the world could not yet grasp it. Even now, when the world has grown old and gray-haired after Christ’s coming, it has not been able to understand without great labor by its preachers; and likewise because the blessed Trinity had not yet performed that mercy toward us which we confess in this faith. I say, it had not yet performed for us the mercy for which it is now rightly worshiped: that mercy by which the blessed Trinity allotted to itself a threefold operation [Col. 0307B] concerning our salvation—so that the Son might redeem the human being whom the Father had created, and the Holy Spirit might set him aflame. This is not because the Father created anything without the Son and Holy Spirit, or the Son redeemed without the Father and Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit enlightened or cleansed by forgiveness of sins without the Father and Son; but because, although the operation of the supreme and one divinity is common and inseparable everywhere, the distinction of the persons is nevertheless manifest in the proper character or order of the work and must not be unknown to any of the faithful. For the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1), are the Father’s words to the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the flesh which was taken from the Virgin, died, was buried, and rose again is the Son’s flesh; and the dove which descended upon the Lord [Col. 0307C] (Matthew 3), and the fire which appeared over his apostles (Acts 2), visibly displayed not the substance but the present power of the Holy Spirit. Therefore in former ages faith in the Holy Trinity was rightly not required of the common people, because, as was said, this same Trinity had not been disclosed, in a manifestation for worship or in a distinction of operation, to the people of God still in infancy and serving under a pedagogue (Galatians 3).

## CHAPTER XV

That the Old Testament did not keep silent concerning the same faith of the Trinity, and that the saints of old did not please God without it.

Nevertheless, the ancients did not please God wholly without faith, because those from whom, as from their roots, many branches were borne—the great Fathers, that is—did not lack the richness of this divine name by which we now are nourished. For when we were a wild olive, the natural branches having been broken off because of unbelief, we were grafted through the same faith into a good olive tree (Romans 11).
