Indeed, their books supply Christ’s Gospel with very many testimonies to the Trinity. Hence these two Testaments are rightly signified by the two seraphim in Isaiah, whose cry is: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory” (Isaiah 6). And because the Jewish people, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, were blinded by unbelief when they heard this cry through the mouths of the apostles, this too is fittingly shown to the prophet by the Lord’s house being filled with smoke (Isaiah 6). For that smoke signifies the blindness of the Jews, just as shortly afterward the same prophet is told: “Blind the heart of this people” (ibid.), etc. But we, having the eyes of our hearts opened through faith to the book which the Lamb opened, say with the aforementioned seraphim, and likewise with the four living creatures: “Holy, holy, holy” (Revelation 5), adding: “Salvation to our God who sits upon the throne [Col. 0308A] and to the Lamb” (ibid.). That is, the Lamb, in opening the book already mentioned, has shown the mystery of the Trinity written in it, which had not been known. For when, in answer to the Jews who asked and said, “Who are you?” he replied, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8), he opened to us that, as he also says in the psalm, “At the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Psalm 39), Moses intended no other “beginning” when he said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1)—no other beginning, I say, than the Son, since John also says, “All things were made through him” (John 1). God created heaven and earth in the beginning: that is, the Father in the Son. Add what follows: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1), and behold, at the head of the book which the Lamb opened, the blessed Trinity shines forth. Having entered Holy Scripture through these threefold gates, you then find scattered everywhere its golden titles of that same divine name.

## CHAPTER XVI

How the Trinity is set forth in each of the works of the six days.

First, in the work of the six days, if you attend carefully, the same Trinity is set forth. For example: “God said: Let there be light” (Genesis 1). Then: “God saw that it was good” (ibid.). In the words, “God said,” we recognize, with the Father, the Word through whom all things were made. And in the addition, “And God saw that it was good,” we understand the great diligence and benevolence of the worker, which is undoubtedly none other than the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity. We ought not to suppose that the phrase, repeated in each case, “God saw that it was good,” was placed there by chance or superfluously. Rather, let us faithfully perceive that great diligence of the Creator is commended to us. And so that you may know how much that diligence of which we speak contributed to God’s work, [Col. 0308D] turn to your own heart, whoever you are who are a craftsman or maker of some praiseworthy work. So that you may know how much diligence—which is the Spirit—contributed to his work, look at how much your own diligence contributed to yours. Certainly you possessed the art in your mind in some fashion as the Word was in the beginning with God. Conscious of that art, you did not allow yourself to remain idle. Why? To adduce, among many possible causes, the best reason: love of usefulness—that is, the intention of benefiting many—made you unable to tolerate idleness. This one cause distinguishes you from that servant who is reproved as wicked and slothful, whereas you are praised as a good and faithful servant (Matthew 25). In other respects you were alike, since the talent of good skill was entrusted to the mind both of that servant and of you. But see [Col. 0309A] how great a difference diligence or benevolence in you has made between you and him. While he digs into the earth and hides his lord’s money (ibid.), you, by employing the talent entrusted to you, gain double; and, seeing in each advance that the gain is good, you thirst for more, and because of the greatness of your desire do not feel the labor in the work. The gain grows; the desire for gain grows. By this likeness, then, consider how much God’s diligence or goodness accomplished in his work, since it is shown to have taken magnificent delight in it by the repeated statement: “And God saw that it was good,” and by his saying: “Let there be” (Genesis 1), etc. Only in the work of the second day was that phrase not added, certainly through the grace of a mystery discussed elsewhere. But that diligence or goodness is to be understood as none other, as has been said, than the Holy Spirit [Col. 0309B]. “For if you ask,” says Augustine, “who made all things, I answer: God. If you ask through what, I say: through the Word. If you ask why, I answer: because he is good. And this Trinity,” he says, “is one God.”

## CHAPTER XVII

That in the formation of the human being the proper work of each person of the Trinity must be distinguished.

Accordingly, in the work of the making of the world and of every created thing, the gracious Trinity—almighty and knowing all things—is commended to all. Yet more especially, in the one whom it determined to set over all things, that is, in man, it deigned to express itself, saying: “Let us make man” (Gen. 1). For in the word “let us make” the plurality of persons is plainly indicated, and in [Col. 0309C] the counsel thus prefaced, that same diligence of which we have already spoken is more magnificently commended.

In this work, moreover, the fashioning is the proper operation of the Father. But the two things added in this formation beyond the other living creatures already created—namely, that man should be made after the image of God, and after the likeness of the other persons, that is, of the Son and the Holy Spirit—are marks of those persons. For man was made after the image of God, which is the Son, as the Apostle says, speaking of him: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1); and elsewhere: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1). After the image, I say, of God, or the figure of his substance, man was created insofar as he is rational; but after the likeness, insofar as he was created an imitator of [Col. 0309D] divine goodness—which is properly the work of the Holy Spirit. For the goodness or charity of God is the Holy Spirit.

And when, as was said above, he had stirred up the Father to work all things through the Word, then, in the fashioning of man, he made him so zealous that he withheld none of those things which he could bestow. For what did man, thus created, lack besides natural divinity? Yet God could indeed generate that which is God by nature; for the Word whom he generated is God. But to create or fashion such a thing, although omnipotent, he could in no way do so. Nor is anything thereby detracted from omnipotence when God, who is beyond all things, outside all things, and above all things, is said not to have been able to create one equal to himself.

Therefore, in the fashioning of man, as has been said [Col. 0310A], the benevolence of God, which is the Holy Spirit, especially applied its work, when it bestowed upon him who, as created, could not naturally be God, by grace the likeness of God. And so that this likeness of God might have a seat or receptacle, the image or figure of the substance of God, which is the Son, was impressed upon the human soul, so that through its Holy Spirit it might receive the aforesaid likeness—as a hole is opened in a precious stone so that it may receive a slender rod of gold by which it is bound and held.

The same must be understood concerning the angelic creature. Hence that angel is rebuked in Ezekiel, as was said above: “And thy openings,” he says, “were prepared on the day when thou wast created” (Ezek. 28). Because he was created rational, yet through the opening of that same reason he was unwilling to admit gold—that is, [Col. 0310B] the holy spirit of love. Therefore it follows: “Thine inward parts were filled with iniquity” (ibid.).

But to return to man: especially in the fashioning of man, the great and profound counsel of the Trinity had to be signified, namely, because man was not only created, but is also the unique material through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known to principalities, powers, and heavenly beings, as the Apostle says (Eph. 5). For besides what these words declare—“Let us make man in our image and likeness”—this too was determined in the same counsel: how the same Trinity which fashioned man would recover him after his loss through the proper and distinct operation of each person. This is evident from the plain distinction of that operation.

For after the fashioning—indeed, after the fall—of man, the Trinity which created him set itself in this order to recover him. First comes the Father, who, uttering this statement: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3), immediately adds: “Now therefore see lest perhaps he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever,” and “he cast him out” (ibid.), etc.

Here the Father of mercies made a way—a way, I say, for his mercy—because he was unwilling that man should live for ever after sin. For since man’s life after sin is miserable (Job 7), if it were eternal, what would it be but eternal misery? Such is the lot of demons: eternal misery, or [Col. 0310D] miserable eternity, in opposition to God, whose own is eternal blessedness, or blessed eternity.

Therefore the first and great work of mercy is that of which Augustine records that even Plotinus, a certain pagan philosopher, rightly said: “The merciful Father created mortal bodies for us.” In this way the guardian of men not only set man in a condition contrary to himself, but also made him far different from demons, so that his might be temporal misery, or miserable temporality. Thus the proper work of the person of the Father is the infliction of mortality; the proper work of the person of the Son is the redemption of souls, together with the resurrection of bodies; and the proper work of the Holy Spirit is the reviving of souls, together with that transformation of bodies of which the Apostle says: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. [Col. 0311A] 13), that is, we shall be incapable of suffering. For only those who have received the Holy Spirit will be incapable of suffering after the resurrection.

Thus, both in the creation and in the re-creation of man, the Trinity is proved to have acted distinctly, as was said above. And that this whole work was foreseen by him whose providence is not deceived in its ordering is testified by that reverent expression of the divine counsel: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Therefore, as was said above, in Isaiah the two seraphim are rightly understood to be the two Testaments, which cry to one another in harmonious voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6), while the Old Testament likewise gives concordant witness to the glory of the same Trinity revealed in the New Testament, as we have already briefly said appears in the very doors of ancient Scripture. But if, having entered, we should wish to search everywhere for testimonies to the same Trinity, the length would exceed all bounds and would produce excessive weariness, especially since another subject is proposed. Therefore, hastening to our purpose, it is pleasing to consider only why it was fitting that, to obtain propitiation from God the Father for the human race, the Son alone—or above all the Son—should assume flesh.

## CHAPTER XVIII

How fitting it was, although there are three persons of the Godhead, that the assumption of flesh and the redemption of man should belong to the person of the Son alone.

The divine arrangement by which it pleased God that the person of the Son rather than that of the Father or the Holy Spirit should be incarnate is especially wonderful because the sin of the first man was committed chiefly against that same Son, for whose expiation the Son himself deigned to become man. Moreover, the pride of the devil, the ancient sinner, swelled against the Creator chiefly on account of the Son. This may readily be seen from his words. For he says: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

Certainly, when he said these things, he was tormented by the envious malice of a slave-like contumacy against the Son, because to the one and only begotten—not made—being, the whole court of heaven rightly rendered service, equally with the Father, in view of so great a difference. He resented being separated by a great difference from the One who was in the bosom of the Father, when he saw himself, among the other creatures, made by God the artificer, but that One alone begotten from God the Father, born above [Col. 0311D] all things. Then his servile pride attacked that same only-begotten Son, far more wickedly than Ishmael, born of a slave-woman, persecuted his lord Isaac, born of the free woman, as the Apostle testifies—more wickedly, I say, inasmuch as both the malice was far subtler and the difference of condition that provoked the proud one’s hatred was far greater.

Because of this hatred he was already a murderer, as the same Son of God testifies in his Gospel, saying: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8). But he could not then accomplish that murder in act, since the Son of God did not yet possess a human nature capable of being killed. He accomplished it, however, when, recognizing that he had descended to earth and become a mortal man—for, says the Evangelist, “demons went out from many, crying and saying, ‘We know that thou art the Son of God’” (Luke 4)—when, I say, the ancient sinner recognized that he had come in the flesh, he rose up and fastened him to the cross through his own agents.

For, as the Apostle says, “none of the rulers of this age knew his wisdom,” that is, the arrangement by which he was to redeem the human race through his death: “For had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). Yet by the very weakness of death, through which he imagined himself victorious, he persists in his implacable hatred of that Son of God: through the mouths of Jews who deny him, through the blasphemies of heretics who assert that he is a creature.

But to return to the sin of the first man: it must be known that, before the devil persuaded the woman through the serpent to eat of the forbidden tree, both man and woman had, through the hidden instigation of that enemy, desired to be like gods. Otherwise he would have used this promise in vain to induce the act he urged, saying: “And you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3). For no one promises as the fruit of some action anything except what he judges to be desired.

And against which person of the Trinity human pride here chiefly directed itself appears from what he added: “Knowing good and evil” (ibid.). Certainly they proudly emulated the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father; that is, they thought that they would be equal to him by possessing knowledge of all things. Hence the tree of transgression received its name ironically, so that it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, although the writer of the history calls it so even before man’s sin. This plainly occurs by anticipation. In the same irony, the Trinity itself, which is one God, says: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil” (ibid.). “As one of us,” that is, as the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father, whose equality he desired—that is, knowledge of good and evil.

For the knowledge of good and evil belongs to God alone, who knows all things and also knows well how to use evil for good. Therefore, after it had been said, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” it was immediately added ironically wherein this consisted: namely, in his being “knowing good and evil.” Likewise, the devil too is ironically called a cherub in Ezekiel, which is interpreted “fullness of knowledge” (Ezek. 28).

Therefore, the devil swelled up more particularly against the proper person of the Son of God, and raised man up likewise, since each desired equality with the wisdom of God, which is the Son, and despised to be subject to him. Hence, as was already said above, the dispensation of the Godhead is wonderful—its condescension wonderful—that he against whom sin had been chiefly committed, namely the Son, should approach as intercessor before the Father, having become man and, out of voluntary charity, given over to death for his enemies. It is as if Isaac should submit to being sacrificed for this reason: that Ishmael might return into the favor of father and mother and become his co-heir—Ishmael who had been cast out because he persecuted not the father himself, but Isaac (Gen. 22; 21).

Yet sacred history records neither Isaac nor anyone else as having undergone voluntary death by interceding for enemies. For scarcely does anyone die for his friend, or, as Paul says, “scarcely for a righteous man does anyone die” (Rom. 5). Therefore the Son of God commends his love toward us because, although by sinning against him we had offended the Father, he deigned to assume the nature in which he might die for us (ibid.).

In this love, whoever imitates him can ascend to that likeness of God which the devil through pride, and man himself, desired. For after he had said: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5), he immediately added: “That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). As though he said: It is not the magnificence of knowledge, through confidence in which Satan said in his heart, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), nor that knowledge which, promising it to your parents, he said, “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). It is not knowledge, I say, but charity surpassing knowledge (Eph. 3), which is the effective cause of your becoming like the Most High. Nor do I begrudge you the dignity of sons of God; for I did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized (Phil. 2). But I reject the ascent of pride by which, when Satan ascended, “I saw him fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11).

Seeing this miracle of divine dispensation, the Prophet said: “O God, give thy judgment to the king, and thy righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71). Great and wonderful is this: that the Son, although equally God with the Father in relation to his creature, deigned also to be called and to be its king, and this according to the judgment and law of righteousness. This may readily be perceived as follows.

It was fitting that this very Son, through whom all things were created, should be lord and king of all, and that they should not be ruled through some other being, who, since he was created, was certainly not their Creator. Now it is the due and lawful office of a king that he himself first fulfill in deeds the commands which are to be given or have been given to his subjects, lest, while he commands his soldiers to perform arduous service, he himself, abusing his power, should live in delights and provide ground for their murmuring. They would undoubtedly say that a commander is luxurious who commands his subjects to do what he himself avoids doing or cannot do.

Therefore it was fitting also that, as God, he should himself especially fulfill in action what he had commanded or would command; as king, that is, he should fulfill the work of every kind of humility, such as this: “The greater thou art, humble thyself in all things” (Ecclus. 13). Great and wonderful, as was said above, is this: that although he could rule over his creature by the mere excellence of his power, he preferred to submit with it equally to the judgment and law of righteousness.

Therefore, before he underwent in his own form the warfare of human life, he gave men lesser commandments; but after he had become man, he imposed higher ones, after the manner of a good and vigorous king. When such a king has engaged the enemy in the first line of battle, exhausted by sharp conflict and distinguished by bloody wounds, and has delivered all men at peril to himself, then at last he gives commands of courage more confidently, more justly, and more steadfastly, since his deeds support his words. His soldiers, seeing their leader’s blood, dare not murmur at toil or seek luxuries.

Thus, before the Lord of hosts was clothed with weakness, it was said to the ancients: “Thou shalt not kill” (Exod. 20). But when that same King of glory had been tempted in all things in like manner without sin and had learned obedience without defending himself, he said: “But I say unto you, that everyone who is angry with his brother” (Matt. 5), etc. Rightly, therefore, as was said above, the Prophet says: “O God, give thy judgment to the king, and thy righteousness to the king’s son,” because the greatness of righteousness is in no way less than the immensity of divine power.

And we also, who were held guilty under our ancestral transgression, receive that righteousness in him, as is immediately added in the same Psalm: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71). We receive it in him because him whom our first parents despised as God shining in his glory, we adore as born in our flesh and dying on his cross. For by this we are justified: beyond the ancient obligation of service, which is to worship God—which the human race would have owed even had it never sinned—there is added that we worship a crucified man. By this satisfaction it is brought about that the righteous God, while preserving his justice, restores us to our ancient state.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Office of the Same Holy Trinity

In the office of that same holy Trinity, the Gospel reading is rightly appointed in which the most necessary remedy of saving baptism is especially commended (Matt. 28): namely, because without the power of this name, whatever else one may say, the washing is ineffectual; no one can be reborn through water; and we are not marked by this name otherwise than when we receive with it the sacrament of baptism.

The reading from the book of the Apocalypse which precedes it accords with this Gospel, especially in what it says: “And round about the throne was, as it were, a sea of glass like crystal” (Rev. 4). For the glassy sea like crystal signifies the baptism of pure confession and firm faith. And what is said in the Gospel, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3), is signified here by the sea being shown round about the throne. For because the sea is round about the throne, it is certainly necessary to cross the sea in order to reach that throne.

There are also “seven burning lamps before the throne” (Rev. 4), that is, the seven spirits of God; for it was not said, “Unless one is born again of water alone,” but “of water and the Holy Spirit.” And “in the midst of the throne and round about it” are four living creatures, saying day and night: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who wast, and art, and art to come” (ibid.). These are Catholic teachers, who, distinguished by the quality of their merits as by differing faces, and full of eyes both around and within—that is, in bodily and spiritual matters—by the illumination of [Col. 0315A] the Holy Spirit, do not cease to preach the faith of the Holy Trinity in adversity and prosperity alike, in order to guard against the unbelief of heretics and to provide for the salvation of their subjects and themselves; and they invite the peoples to that sea of baptism.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0315]

## CHAPTER I. The First Sunday after Pentecost

The office of the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost gives voice to that poor man figured by Lazarus in the Gospel (Luke 16), namely, the Gentile people. Fleeing to faith in the Trinity through the preaching of the apostles, as was said above, it desired to be refreshed from the inward meaning of the Law, as though from crumbs falling from the rich man’s table—that is, the Jewish people, which, because it held the teaching of the Law not for charity but for self-exaltation, swelled as though from received riches.

But that other people, namely the Gentile people, when converted to God, was not ashamed to confess its sins, and so was full of sores; its wound was upon the skin. These, I say, are the words of the beggar, as is especially clear in the gradual: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee” (Ps. 40).

The Epistle, “God is charity” (1 John 4), is first directed against the envy of the Jewish people, which contends that the poor man just mentioned ought not to be admitted, according to the words: “Why didst thou enter in to men having the foreskin?” (Acts 11). For it is plain that the Jews have always hated the salvation of the Gentiles.

At the same time, because the moral sense is not absent from this Gospel, we are usefully warned by this example not to turn our face away from any poor person. The charity commended in the aforesaid Epistle can readily be understood in the same, that is, moral sense, especially where it says: “For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

## CHAPTER II. The Second Sunday after Pentecost

On the second Sunday this Gospel is read: “A certain man made a great supper, and invited many” (Luke 14). It is well known that by the many who were invited and began to make excuses at the hour of supper are signified those who despise the invitation, loving earthly things more than heavenly and being occupied more with bodily than spiritual concerns.

And in that each of them says: “I pray thee, have me excused” (ibid.)—that is, he says, “I pray,” yet despises to come—humility in speech but pride in deed is clearly expressed. For when any carnal person is told, “Turn back; follow God; leave the world,” he is accustomed to reply: “Pray for me, for I am a sinner; I cannot do this.” In saying, “I am a sinner,” he suggests humility; in adding, “I cannot be converted,” he displays pride.

Therefore in the gradual we ask to be delivered from these wicked lips and this deceitful tongue (Ps. 119). Rightly, beautifully, and harmoniously, the excellent servant who invites us says in the preceding Epistle: “My little children, let us not love in word nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3).

Whoever despises their wicked lips and deceitful tongue—for they commonly call back those who desire to be converted, first by censuring their holy purpose, which is to have wicked lips, and then by excessive praise and by alleging the excessive difficulties of the narrow way or strait gate (Matt. 7), which is to sharpen a deceitful tongue—whoever, I say, despises such discouragers and will not listen to them, strengthens his soul and says what we sing in the Alleluia: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient; will he be angry every day?” (Ps. 7). For elsewhere he says: “Him that cometh to me I will not cast out” (John 6).

And finally, recovering from weakness and running with an enlarged heart in the way of the Lord’s commandments, which had begun with a narrow entrance, he says what was sung at the introit: “The Lord became my protector, and brought me forth into a broad place” (Ps. 17).

## CHAPTER III. The Third Sunday after Pentecost

In the Gospel of the third Sunday, we are taught how great is God’s care for converted sinners through the parable of the hundred sheep and of the one that was lost. The good shepherd, having found it, lays it rejoicing upon his shoulders and thus brings it back to the flock. Likewise, in another parable, a woman diligently lights a lamp, seeks, and finds one lost drachma out of ten (Luke 15).

The warning in Peter’s Epistle, that we must keep watch, surely looks to this meaning: “For your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). He had indeed devoured that hundredth sheep and, grieved that it has now been found, goes about again and roars more loudly. Therefore Peter also said beforehand: “Casting all your care upon him, because he careth for you” (ibid.). The gradual accords with this sense: “Cast thy thought” (Ps. 54); so too the offertory: “Let all hope in thee” (Ps. 9). And because the aforesaid Gospel concerns a sinner, over whose repentance there is joy among God’s angels, the solitary poor man rightly cries in the introit: “Look upon me, and have mercy on me” (Ps. 24).

## CHAPTER IV. The Fourth Sunday after Pentecost

The Gospel of the fourth Sunday is: “Be merciful, because your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6). The Epistle reading which precedes it plainly agrees, repeatedly asserting that creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God (Rom. 8), whose Father the Lord declares him to be in the present Gospel: “Be merciful,” he says, “as your heavenly Father [Col. 0317A] is merciful.”

The introit, “The Lord is my illumination” (Ps. 26), and likewise the offertory, “Enlighten my eyes” (Ps. 12), are fitting for this reason: when the Lord, the illumination of the heart, expels by the grace of the Holy Spirit the beam or speck of sin from the eye—that is, hatred, which the Gospel shows must be cast out—the eyes of those who are to see God are enlightened. Thus, as we sing in the gradual, “May a clean heart see the will of the Lord, and visit his temple” (Ps. 26); and this is not by their own strength but by his, to whom we say in the communion: “The Lord is my strength” (Ps. 17), etc.

## CHAPTER V. The Fifth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Gospel of the fifth Sunday it is related that, when the nets were cast at the Lord’s command for a catch and a great multitude of fish had been enclosed, both the nets broke and the boats were filled so that they began to sink (Luke 5). This signifies that, when crowds of carnal people fill the Church and multiply beyond measure, tumults and dissensions arise; and the little boat of the Church is pressed down not only by the evil habits of drunkards and robbers who enter it, but the net of faith is also torn apart by the disputes of heretics.

For this reason the reading of our great fisherman, the Apostle Peter, is fittingly read beforehand, exhorting his fish to unity and peace: “Be ye all of one mind, patient, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble, not rendering evil for evil, nor cursing for cursing” (1 Pet. 3), because through this tumult grows and sedition gains strength. And after a few words: “But if ye suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, blessed are ye” (ibid.), etc.

The other parts of the office are the words of the Church placed amid dangers of this kind. The introit: “Hear, O Lord, my voice” (Ps. 26). The gradual, however, “Our protector, behold, O God” (Ps. 83), accords with the meaning stated above. For it is taken from a psalm entitled “For the winepresses.” There can be no doubt that this name signifies the present Church, in which the elect suffer so many scandals from the reprobate that, according to the Gospel comparison, the net seems almost to be torn by the tumult of fish.

Whoever avoids their schisms says in the offertory: “I will bless the Lord who hath given me understanding” (Ps. 15); and in the communion: “One thing have I asked of the Lord” (Ps. 26), that is, not divisions of minds but unity of faith.

## CHAPTER VI. The Sixth Sunday after Pentecost

On the sixth Sunday, when the Lord says in the Gospel, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Thou shalt not kill’; but I say unto you” (Matt. 5), etc., he plainly impresses upon us that necessary newness which is everywhere commended in the sacred Scriptures: “That we be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and putting off the old man, put on the new, which according to God is created” (Eph. 4).

For we who are called new ought to surpass for the better what was said to the ancients. Therefore the reading is rightly placed first, that we might put on the new man, Christ, as the Apostle says: “All we who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized in his death” (Rom. 6), etc. Thus, in saying, “And let us walk in newness of life” (ibid.), he testifies that we owe more than what was said to the ancients.

The other parts of the office—the introit, “The Lord is my strength” (Ps. 17); the gradual, “Return, O Lord” (Ps. 89); and the offertory, “Perfect my steps” (Ps. 16)—are the words of the Church striving toward the evangelical perfection mentioned above and imploring help, because no one can attain true and perfect righteousness by himself.

And the one whose righteousness has so abounded that, according to the same Gospel, if he brings his gift to the altar and there remembers that his brother has something against him, leaves his gift there and goes first to be reconciled to his brother (Matt. 5), is the one who says in the communion: “I will go round about, and will offer in his tabernacle a sacrifice of rejoicing” (Ps. 26).

## CHAPTER VII. The Seventh Sunday after Pentecost

On the seventh Sunday this Gospel is read, in which the Lord, intending to feed the people, says: “I have compassion on the multitude” (Mark 8), etc., and gives this reason for his compassion: “For some of them have come from afar” (ibid.).

Now those who have come from afar signify those who, converted from criminal sins or even from the worship of demons to the true God, hunger and thirst for the righteousness from which they have been fasting. Therefore the reading in which such persons are told is appropriately placed first: “For when ye were servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness. What fruit therefore had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed? For their end is death” (Rom. 6).

To such persons the Church as mother says in the gradual: “Come, children, hear me” (Ps. 33), etc. And because they are sinners, they say in the offertory: “As in a holocaust of rams,” etc. Nevertheless in the introit the saving call is made to them: “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. 46), as those elsewhere, when fed, said: “Truly this is the prophet—indeed, the Lord of the prophets—who is to come into the world” (John 6).

## CHAPTER VIII. The Eighth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Gospel of the eighth Sunday the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7), etc. This can indeed be understood of all who promise one thing by their dress and speech but show another in their deeds; yet it must especially be understood of heretics, who appear to clothe themselves with a certain garment of piety—continence, chastity, fasting—while inwardly possessing a poisoned mind and deceiving the hearts of simple brethren.

The Epistle reading, “We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh” (Rom. 8), agrees with this Gospel, which says: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7). For a little earlier the Apostle had said: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8); and now he says: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (ibid.). And the works of the flesh, of which he says, “But if by the Spirit you mortify the works of the flesh, you shall live” (ibid.), are the fruits by which false prophets are known. From them the Spirit of God distinguishes the sons of God, bearing witness to their spirit (ibid.).

This Spirit is the mercy of which we sing in the introit: “We have received, O God, thy mercy in the midst of thy temple” (Ps. 47), that is, in ourselves, who are thy temple (1 Cor. 3), and this “in the midst,” that is, manifestly. For the Holy Spirit came manifestly upon the Apostles (Acts 2).

To this Spirit, I say, the Church cries in the gradual: “Be thou unto me a protecting God” (Ps. 30); and in the offertory: “Thou wilt save the humble people, O Lord” (Ps. 17), according to the words: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. 66). For he has hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones (Matt. 11). Hence they are addressed in congratulation in the communion: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

## CHAPTER IX. The Ninth Sunday after Pentecost

The Gospel of the ninth Sunday instructs pastors of souls to mercy: in compassion they should impose measured penance upon those who confess, according to what they owe or according to the gravity of the sins they have committed. For the Lord praised the unjust steward because he had prudently done the things narrated of him in the proposed parable (Luke 16).

The Apostle’s reading, placed beforehand, accords with this purpose by recounting those who had crossed the sea and tasted God’s gifts, yet nevertheless, through lust and fornication, perished by serpents or by the destroyer (1 Cor. 10); and immediately adding: “Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (ibid.), etc.

For just as these persons, though already glorified, perished, and that steward in the Gospel had possessed his lord’s favor, from which nevertheless he fell, so every prelate must remember and know that he too has either sinned, or, if he has not sinned, is nevertheless of the same frailty, so that he could have sinned or may yet sin. Warned by his own condition, he should reflect that he has accepted the care of weak souls, not tyranny over sound ones.

The introit, “Behold, God helpeth me” (Ps. 53); the gradual, “O Lord our Lord” (Ps. 18); and the offertory, “The righteousnesses of the Lord,” are the words of the aforesaid steward, giving thanks to the Lord his God, who shows mercy to the merciful. The communion, “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Matt. 6), commands the same as that saying of the Lord from the Gospel already mentioned: “Make for yourselves friends of the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16), etc.

## CHAPTER X. The Tenth Sunday after Pentecost
On the Tenth Sunday the Gospel is read in which the Lord is said to have wept over the city of Jerusalem. And, entering the Temple, he began to cast out those who were selling therein [Col. 0320A] (Luke 19). It is well known to almost everyone, both from the Scriptures and from common usage, that this signifies that the Lord casts out of his Church those who buy or sell sacred orders, since such traders make even the doves—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—objects of sale. Therefore, fittingly and aptly, the reading from the Apostle is first set forth, which quite openly indicates that no spiritual gift can be given by man, much less sold, but is freely given by the Spirit of God alone, who apportions to each as he wills: to one the word of knowledge, to another the word of wisdom, to another kinds of tongues, to another faith, to another prophecy (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

And he who awaits the choice of this Spirit—that is, of the Holy Spirit—rather than that of human beings, is addressed in the Introit: “Cast [Col. 0320B] your care upon the Lord, and he himself will sustain you” (Ps. 54). “Cast your care upon the Lord,” he says, not upon yourself; saying what is written elsewhere: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. Nor have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130). Thus, lest he be like Simon Magus, who thought that God’s gift could be possessed with money (Acts 8). “And he himself will sustain you,” he says—namely, you who say what is sung in the Gradual: “Keep me, O Lord, as the apple of your eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16), lest through pride and wandering I become like a weaned child upon its mother (Ps. 130). Rather, “let my judgment”—that is, my election—“come forth from your presence” (Ps. 16), than that I should commend myself through my own presumption.

The same person says in the Offertory [Col. 0320C]: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; for all who wait for you shall not be put to shame” (Ps. 24). But to those who await things from human beings or buy them, the Wisdom of God says: “An inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20). And that God does not accept the sacrifice of such priests, because their sacrifices are sacrifices of injustice, is shown by the contrary in the Communion: “You shall accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. 50), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XI. The Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost

On the Eleventh Sunday this Gospel is appointed: “Two men went up into the Temple to pray” (Luke 18), and so forth. The reading from the Epistle which precedes it plainly agrees with this [Col. 0320D]: “I make known to you the Gospel” (1 Cor. 15). For Paul admirably imitates in this Epistle the example of the tax collector in the Gospel, who accuses himself and says: “I am not worthy to lift up my eyes to heaven” (Luke 18), when he says: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15), and so forth.

And because such humility preserves the unity of God’s household, so that one may not be puffed up against another, this Introit is rightly prefixed: “God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. 67). And what is said in the Gradual, “And of my own will I will give thanks to him” (Ps. 27), and likewise in the Offertory, “O Lord, I have cried [Col. 0321A] to you, and you have healed me” (Ps. 29), agrees with the words of the tax collector standing afar off and confessing his sins. To such a one—not one who glories Pharisaically that he gives tithes of all that he possesses, but one who first offers himself in humble confession—it is said in the Communion that he may then offer what is his: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. 3), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XII. The Twelfth Sunday after Pentecost

The Office of the Twelfth Sunday in some parts looks to those who bring the deaf and mute man to the Lord and beseech him to lay his hand upon him; in other parts, to the mute man himself, who speaks rightly when his mouth has been opened. For that deaf and mute man signifies the human race, which in its first parents became deaf to the precepts of its Creator [Col. 0321B] and mute in proclaiming his praise. Those who bring him and entreat the Lord for him signify the whole choir of preachers, who never cease to invite the human race, by speech and writing, to Christ’s grace.

The voice of this deaf and mute man is very fittingly the Introit: “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. 69): as though, after the paralysis which had suddenly bound his tongue had been healed, at the first movement of that tongue he should suddenly invoke the name of God for aid. The same speaker rightly says in the Gradual: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). The Epistle, “We have such confidence through Christ toward God” (2 Cor. 3), and so forth, concerns those who bring him [Col. 0321C]: they have confidence not in themselves, as though they could by themselves open his mouth or ears, but “our sufficiency is from God” (ibid.), and so forth.

And this Offertory is beautifully appointed: “Moses prayed” (Exod. 23 [probably Exod. 32]). For after the example of him “who in the time of wrath was made reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44), all rulers ought to set themselves against the sins of their subjects and beseech the Lord to lay upon them the hand of mercy. For the Lord was angry because of the calf which Aaron had made, and had said that he would destroy them. By Moses’ example, I say, all rulers should act.

And because those same preachers are that earth which, as we read in the Psalm, being filled with the fruit of the Lord’s works—that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—brings forth grass for cattle (Ps. 103), that is, teaching for carnal peoples who did not know God, this also is rightly sung in the Communion: “The earth shall be filled with the fruit of your works, O Lord” (ibid.) [Col. 0321D].

## CHAPTER XIII. The Thirteenth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Office of the Thirteenth Sunday, all the parts concern that Gospel passage in which the Samaritan—whose name means “keeper,” namely our Lord Jesus Christ—draws near to the man stripped and wounded by robbers. Priest and Levite—that is, the entire Old Testament—had passed him by. He drew near to the human race, which could not be reconciled—that is, he assumed our humanity—poured the oil of consolation and the wine [Col. 0322A] of penitence into the wounds of sins, placed him upon his own beast—that is, bearing our sins in his own body upon the wood—brought him to the inn of the Church; and, going away to heaven, entrusted in his own stead the care and provision for us to his innkeepers, that is, the apostles and apostolic men (Luke 10).

As stated, the other parts of the Office concur with this Gospel. First, the Epistle, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. 3), is greatly opened to understanding by being prefixed to such a Gospel, together with almost the whole of Paul’s argument to the Galatians, from which this reading is taken. For by the fact that both priest and Levite passed by when they saw that man, it is intimated what the Law contributed, which was given four hundred and thirty years after the covenant of God, confirmed by promise with faithful Abraham: namely, that the Law itself was not contrary to God’s promises, but that no one could be justified before God by works of that Law.

Accordingly, we understand from the fact that, as stated, both priest and Levite passed by the man when they saw him, that the Law entered in as a physician’s servant sometimes enters the room of a sick man: he knows the causes of the disease, but cannot prepare the antidote to apply. He knows only how to tell the sick man from which foods and drinks he must abstain, lest the disease grow worse [Col. 0322B] and make one who is half-dead altogether dead. This is what the Apostle says in the aforementioned Epistle: “Why then the Law? It was added because of transgressions” (ibid.), and so forth.

For man is born half-dead through the wounds of original sin. But through actual transgressions—on account of which the Law was given—if he does not abstain, as from harmful foods, he dies altogether. Therefore, according to these things, the Introit is well prefixed: “Look, O Lord, upon your covenant” (Ps. 73), which is repeated in the Gradual. This was the voice of the ancients demanding Christ’s coming to the infirmity or imperfection of the Law: as though, while priest and Levite passed by, that wounded man begged the aforesaid Samaritan to draw near, and said to him what is sung in the Offertory: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. 30), and so forth. And because the body of Christ which we receive especially heals those wounds, we fittingly sing in the Communion that passage from the Book of Wisdom: “You gave us bread from heaven” [Col. 0322C] (Wis. 16).

## CHAPTER XIV. The Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Gospel of the Fourteenth Sunday, ten leprous men are said to have been cleansed by the Lord; and only one of them, bearing the figure of the one Church, while the others are ungrateful and prefigure heretics, returned and gave thanks. He is praised by the same Lord for the faith by which he was saved (Luke 17). The voice of the same Church, signified by that one man, is the Introit: “Behold, O God, our protector” (Ps. 83), especially the words: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (ibid.). For this is the same as saying: It is better “to have one heart and one soul” [Col. 0323A] (Acts 4), and to think and speak the same thing, than to be divided by diverse—indeed, contrary—opinions and to make schisms (1 Cor. 1). Since the holy Church observes this, and is therefore called the one dove (Song 6), she is well represented in the Gospel by the one man, as stated.

The Epistle agrees with the aforesaid Gospel in that it openly expresses what was signified by their leprosy when it says: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust” (Gal. 5), and so forth, among which are listed sects—that is, heresies. Cleansed from these, the Church gives thanks in the Gradual: “It is good to trust in the Lord” (Ps. 117), and so forth; namely, because no human being—not the rulers of carnal sacrifices, of whom the Lord spoke to those same lepers [Col. 0323B]—can take away the leprosy of sins, but the Lord alone.

But the words in the Offertory, “The Lord will send his angel around those who fear him, and he shall deliver them: taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33), concern those fruits which are expressed in the Epistle: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience” (Gal. 5), and so forth. To taste these is to be healed from the aforesaid leprosy. And because the Lord commanded the one who gave thanks: “Go and offer the gift which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Matt. 8), we fittingly sing in the Communion: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6), namely, because flesh and blood are the gift which the one Church of Christ continually offers for its cleansing.

## CHAPTER XV. The Fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost

[Col. 0323C]

The Office of the Fifteenth Sunday, if it is rightly considered, clearly appears to be sung chiefly against pride and vain glory. For Luke testifies that the saying in this Sunday’s Gospel—“Do not be anxious, saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we drink?” (Matt. 6), and so forth—pertains to this, since when he reports the same words he adds: “And do not be lifted up on high” (Luke 12). Indeed, according to the same Luke, before these words the Lord told the parable of the rich fool whose field brought him abundant crops, and who said: “I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul [Col. 0323D], you have many goods stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.” But God said to him: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (ibid.).

Therefore, against the rich, who must be commanded “not to think proudly, nor to hope in uncertain riches” (1 Tim. 6), this is commanded in the aforesaid Gospel: “Do not be anxious,” and so forth. The preceding Epistle agrees with it where it says: “Do not become desirous of vain glory” (Gal. 6); and again: “Whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap; and he who sows in the flesh shall also reap corruption from the flesh” (ibid.).

The voice in the Introit belongs to the person who faithfully embraces this precept: it is addressed to our Father, who knows all things that we need, as was said in the same Gospel [Col. 0324A]. That voice, I say—“Incline your ear, O Lord, to me” (Ps. 84)—is the voice of a poor man who humbly seeks first from God’s hand the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and then the necessities of the body which are to be added. He also says in the Gradual with the same meaning: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. 91), that is, to seek necessities from the Lord, and in that hope to sing psalms—that is, to do good works—in your name, that is, for the honor of your name, O Most High. “To proclaim his mercy in the morning” (ibid.), that is, first to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

The same man, rejoicing that he has received necessary sustenance from the Father, tells others in the Offertory: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord” (Ps. 39); that is, seeking not elsewhere but from the Lord his kingdom, I waited [Col. 0324B] for the things to be added, “and he looked upon me” (ibid.), that is, he added what is necessary for this life. The Communion clearly expresses the food of that kingdom of God which must be sought first: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). For what is the kingdom of God except his dwelling in us? And this dwelling in us is brought about by eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Therefore this too is rightly appointed in the Communion.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost

On the Sixteenth Sunday this Gospel is read, in which the Lord restored alive to his weeping widowed mother her only son who was dead, and fear came upon them all and they magnified God (Luke 7). This widow signifies the holy mother Church [Col. 0324C], that is, the whole order of prelates, who have the care of souls to be regenerated in Christ, and who follow the death of each soul, whenever it appears in manifest crimes, with great weeping. For the widow’s son dies when someone is separated through some crime from the body of the Church, which is a widow because Christ her bridegroom is not presently remaining with her.

Therefore, the reading from the Apostle is well prefixed to this Gospel: “Brethren, I beseech you not to faint at my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For this reason I bend my knees” (Eph. 3), and so forth. He who says, “My little children, whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4), beautifully expresses in the Office, in both person and words [Col. 0324D], the widow Church who with great groanings seeks the life of her children. The Introit, “Have mercy upon me, O Lord, because I have cried to you” (Ps. 30), and likewise the Offertory, “O Lord, look to my help” (Ps. 70), are the voices of this widow, namely the holy mother Church, which she ought to utter for the resurrection of her children who have perhaps fallen into the death of sin.

The Gradual, “The nations shall fear your name, O Lord” (Ps. 101), agrees with what was said in the aforesaid Gospel: “And fear came upon them all.” For how does the Lord build Zion, according to the verse of the same Gradual, except by providing life and preservation for the souls of his spiritual children? Because he accomplishes this through the food of his body and the drink of his blood, a thanksgiving is rightly placed in the Communion [Col. 0325A], with that same widow, namely the holy Church, saying: “O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Office of the Seventeenth Sunday we are taught how we ought to strive to be judged great and worthy of honor in the eyes of the Lord, and how, in the house which is the Church, we ought not to seize the highest places at table by our own presumption, but await them from his election. The parable in this Sunday’s Gospel says: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place” (Luke 14), and so forth, indicating that in his heavenly banquet there will be what he finally adds: “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.”

Hence the Apostle says in the preceding reading from the Epistle: “I therefore beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling by which you have been called” (Eph. 4), and so forth. This is the same as if he said: I beseech you that, invited to the wedding of Christ and the Church, you enter and recline as did he who invited you, who also said: “But I am in the midst of you as one who serves” (Luke 22). And he served until the Father said to him, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14); that is, until to him who was obedient unto death he gave “the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2).

The Introit, “You are righteous, O Lord” (Ps. 118), openly commends that saying in the Gospel: “Everyone [Col. 0325C] who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14). At the same time it is a prayer for him who humbles himself: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy” (Ps. 118)—namely, with this mercy, that you may say to him: “Friend, go up higher.” The Gradual, “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 32), is the universal blessedness of the gentile people, who, while the Jewish people was proud, humbled itself under the sign of Christ’s cross and deserved to go up higher: that is, above that people which sat in the first place, indeed which was proud of sitting in the first place.

The Offertory sets forth a most efficacious example: he who, having humbled himself, said, “We have sinned, we have done iniquity, we have acted wickedly” (Dan. 9), and so forth, deserved to be so exalted that, while he prayed—as he himself testifies in the same Offertory, saying, “I prayed to my God, I, Daniel” (ibid.), and so forth—the archangel Gabriel, herald of things to come, was sent to him, as the following verse has it: “While I was still speaking” (ibid.), and so forth. By that vision he was so exalted that he not only foresaw the Christ who would come for our salvation—which is common to the other prophets—but by a certain special grace also learned beforehand the exact times of his coming, the angel saying to him: “Seventy weeks are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, and transgression shall be ended” (ibid.), and so forth.

The Communion also—“Make vows and render them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75)—seems chiefly to command that we recline in the last place where it says: “terrible to him who takes away the spirit of princes,” that is, of the proud. By converting or casting them down, he says in effect to each of them: “Give place to this man” (Luke 14) [Col. 0326A].

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost

Therefore the aforesaid Office teaches that whoever is invited to Christ’s wedding should recline in such a place that he may deservedly be told, “Go up higher” (Luke 14). The Office of this following Sunday, with great and wonderful force of exhortation, shows the same person who has been called higher—that is, who has been set over Christ’s household and has received the care of souls—how he ought to conduct himself in that higher position: namely, that, according to the Gospel of the same Office, he may not be like the Scribes and Pharisees, who [Col. 0326B] sat upon Moses’ seat (Matt. 23), but like Moses himself. From Moses’ example—an example which ecclesiastical rulers ought to follow—a long and powerful exhortation is found in the Offertory, “Moses sanctified,” and its verses.

For rulers of souls ought not to be ignorant for what task they have been summoned to a higher place: namely, not so much to seek to rule as to be useful; and, sitting in Moses’ seat, to say and do—indeed, first to do—that which they say with authority. Nor should they wish to be called Rabbi; rather, they should strive to bear the sins of the people and to turn away God’s wrath from their subjects. Therefore Moses’ example is rightly placed in the Offertory together with this Gospel: Moses sat so upon the chair of teaching that, through exceeding humility, he could intercede for his subjects and even hold back God when he said: “Let me alone, that my fury may be kindled against them” (Exod. 32).

For they had made a calf when, as we sing in the verse of the Offertory, “Moses, seeing it, fell down and worshipped, saying: I beseech you, O Lord, forgive the sins of your people.” And the Lord said to him: “I will do according to your word” (ibid.). This is the faithfulness of the servant whom the Lord has set over his household (Luke 12), which they themselves ask for in the Introit, that your prophets may be found faithful: “Grant peace, O Lord, to those who wait for you” (Ecclus. 36); that is, forgive the sins of those whom you have entrusted to us. For the peace of God is the remission of sins. “That your prophets may be found faithful”: that we may be found faithful servants, while we not only rule over your household [Col. 0326D], but also profit them by usefully interceding for them.

To such persons the Apostle says in the present Epistle reading: “I give thanks to my God for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you, because in all things you have been made rich” (1 Cor. 1), and so forth. These same persons say in the Gradual: “Let peace be in your strength” (Ps. 121), that is, remission of sins in your Holy Spirit. To them likewise it is said in the Communion: “Take victims and enter into his courts” (Ps. 95), namely because it is your office to intercede for your subjects, following Moses’ example, standing before the Lord in the breach of heart (Ps. 105).

## CHAPTER XIX. The Nineteenth Sunday after Pentecost

In the Gospel of the Nineteenth Sunday the Lord says to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9). And when those who heard him thought evil in their hearts and said, “He blasphemes,” and so forth, he said: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”; then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (ibid.).

This paralytic signifies a person weakened and slackened from every good work. When he is healed by the Lord and, according to the preceding Epistle, renewed in the spirit of his mind, he fulfils the apostolic command which follows in the same Epistle: “He who stole, let him steal no more; but rather let him labor with his hands, so that he may have something to give to one who suffers need” (Eph. 4). For while he was weakened by paralysis, he did no good work; indeed, he stole the labors of those who worked [Col. 0327B].

The following Office therefore expresses how prelates or rulers of souls ought to procure the salvation of their subjects, as was said in the preceding Office. For it is their task to offer the paralytic lying in bed: that is, to pray for those whose sins keep their souls, languishing in an evil conscience, numb toward good work; and to intercede for them in such a way that, seeing their faith, the Lord may say: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9).

In the Introit, when the Lord says, “I am the salvation of the people,” he bears witness concerning himself to the very thing that is proved in the aforesaid Gospel by the healing of the paralytic against the Pharisees’ murmuring: namely, that he has power on earth to forgive sins. In the Gradual, the same paralytic, now healed and working with his hands at what is good—hands which had formerly been weakened—says: “The lifting up of my hands” (Ps. 140). Strengthened in faith by this experience of power, and trusting that he will obtain forgiveness of sins, he says in the Offertory: “If I walk in the midst of tribulation” (Ps. 22), and so forth. Likewise, strengthening knees once weakened, he says in the Communion: “You have commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly. Would that my ways might be directed to keep your ordinances!” (Ps. 118) [Col. 0327C].

## CHAPTER XX. The Twentieth Sunday after Pentecost

The Office of the Twentieth Sunday consists partly of the voices of those who entered into the wedding, and partly of the voices of the Fathers mourning for those who, invited to the same wedding which the king made for his son, not only refused to come, but also seized his servants sent to them, abused them, and killed them (Matt. 22). It is known that the Jews first did this: they persecuted the prophets and wise men sent to them, and abused Christ’s apostles.

The prophets therefore foresaw that these murderers would justly perish and that their city would be overthrown. Their voice is that which is sung in the Introit from Daniel’s words: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment” (Dan. 5), and so forth. Likewise in the Offertory: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136). For in this Psalm, or in its verses, they lament that they hung their instruments upon Babylon’s willows: that is, because of unfruitful and barren hearers, the voices of preachers fell silent [Col. 0328A]—because of those, I say, who, invited to the wedding, as stated, refused to come, because they were not worthy.

But in the Epistle reading Paul the Apostle fittingly admonishes those gathered from the ends of the roads, so that the wedding might be filled with guests reclining at table: “See how you walk carefully, not as foolish persons but as wise” (Eph. 5), and so forth. His purpose is that no one may be found drunk with wine, in which is dissipation, and without a wedding garment when the king enters to see the guests; but that, on the contrary, you may “be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (ibid.). These are the true banquet-dishes of this wedding, for which in the following Gradual we give thanks, saying: “The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord” (Ps. 144), and so forth; or which one of us seeks in the Communion, saying: “Remember your word to your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 118) [Col. 0328B].

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Twenty-First Sunday after Pentecost

The Office of the Twenty-First Sunday contains the voices of a person set in the conflict of virtues and vices. Sometimes, when he begins to flourish in holy virtues, and in accordance with the blessing of the person who fears God, his wife—that is, the house of God over which he perhaps presides—has grown like a fruitful vine along the sides of his house, that is, in the breadth of the holy Church; and his children, like olive shoots around his table [Col. 0328C] (Ps. 127); when, I say, he has thus advanced, the tempter, the devil, suddenly being permitted by God’s hidden dispensation, shakes and overturns his house, that is, the condition of his conscience, and, with consciousness disturbed in its knowledge, nearly crushes his children, that is, the virtues of the soul.

This is proved more clearly than daylight from the Offertory: “There was a man in the land, named Job” (Job 1). For in such a person there are morally enacted those things which are historically recounted as happening in the temptation of blessed Job. The shaking or danger of this noble and combative soul is signified in the Gospel by the fever which had nearly destroyed the royal official’s son (John 4). But the preceding Epistle strengthens and consoles him, surrounded by temptations, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (2 Cor. 2), saying: “Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph. 6), and so forth.

The Introit, “In your will, O Lord” (Ps. 72), and so forth, is the voice of the same soldier, who with humble conscience falls to the ground with blessed Job—that is, acknowledges himself to be earth—and says: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). After this confession, surrounded by temptation, he asks for escape, saying in the Gradual: “O Lord, you have been our refuge” (Ps. 89). And in the Communion: “My soul has hoped in your salvation and in your word” (Ps. 118) [Col. 0328D].

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Twenty-Second Sunday after Pentecost

[Col. 0329A]

In the Office of the Twenty-Second Sunday we say in the Introit: “If you should observe iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129). Certainly, in the person of that servant of whom the Gospel speaks, each one of us humbly recognizes himself: he owed ten thousand talents to his king, and falling down begged, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you all” (Matt. 18). Therefore, considering the greatness of his debt—that is, of his sin—each one of us says: “If you should observe iniquities, O Lord,” and so forth.

But for each one of us to obtain release, we must do what Paul says in the preceding Epistle: “And this I pray, that your charity may abound more and more in knowledge and in every understanding” (Phil. 1), and so forth. It is understood: so that each of you may forgive his brother from your hearts (Matt. 18). Where this charity abounds, as has been said, that exultant utterance is fittingly produced according to which we say in the Gradual: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132).

And if you ask how great or what kind of a good unity is—that is, the charity of brothers dwelling together—the verse continues: “Like ointment upon the head” (ibid.), and so forth; that is, like forgiveness of sins poured out through the Holy Spirit, which descends from our head, namely Christ, to Aaron’s beard, that is, to Christ’s strong and perfect apostles, and from them even to us. For then the dwelling together of brothers is like that ointment, when we forgive one another if we have anything against another (Matt. 18): brothers and fellow servants, just as Christ, the King of the Gospel, forgave us. For he “commanded blessing” (Ps. 132), that is, the same charity of forgiveness, that we may forgive one another; and life for evermore—understand that perhaps he promised the reward of this charity [Col. 0329C].

But in the Offertory, “Remember me, O Lord” (Esther 14), taken from Esther’s prayer, we are most strongly moved to take care and pray that our words may please in the sight of the prince—namely, of that same great king who settled accounts with his servants—our words, I say, when we say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6). For these words will not please in the sight of the prince, when he settles accounts, if we too do not forgive our debtors. But what we sing in the Communion from the authority of the Gospel, “I tell you, there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15), must be understood of that debtor who so repents and so asks forgiveness for himself that he first forgives his fellow servants.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Twenty-Third Sunday after Pentecost

So fully does the most holy Church, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, make supplications, prayers, and thanksgivings (1 Tim. 2) for all, that she gives thanks also for the future salvation of the children of Israel, whom she knows are at some time to be united to her one body. For because their remnant shall be saved at the end of the world (Rom. 3), she rejoices concerning them in this final Office [Col. 0330A] of the year, as future members of herself.

Therefore, in the Introit she declares continually what was prophesied concerning them: “The Lord says: I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction” (Jer. 29). For he thinks thoughts of peace and not of affliction who promises that he will make a banquet of his grace with those who are his brothers according to the flesh, as was prefigured in the patriarch Joseph. For just as his brothers who had sold him came to him—he who ruled throughout all the land of Egypt—compelled by famine, and were recognized and received by him, and he held a banquet with them (Gen. 13 [probably Gen. 43]); so the remnant of the children of Israel will return to our Lord himself, who rules over the whole world and abundantly nourishes with the bread of life the Egyptians, that is, the Gentiles, who had been in the darkness of sins. They will be received into grace by him whom they denied and killed; then he will share his table with them, and this Joseph will be intoxicated with his brothers.

The grace of this table is signified by the Gospel in the Sunday Office in which he is said to have satisfied five thousand men with five loaves (John 6). For then he will open to the Jews the five books of Moses, which the child—namely, the same people, childish in understanding—now carries like whole loaves. Then they too shall eat and be satisfied, and, seeking him, shall praise the Lord (Ps. 21). Then the prophecy of Jeremiah, rightly prefixed to this Gospel, shall be fulfilled: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they shall no longer say [Col. 0330C], ‘The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt’; but, ‘The Lord lives, who brought out and led back the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands into which I had cast them, and they shall dwell in their own land.’”

Released, therefore, from the captivity of souls in which they are now held, they will cry aloud in thanksgiving, as the following Gradual indicates: “You have delivered us, O Lord, from those who afflict us” (Ps. 43), and so forth. The supplication in the Offertory, in which we say, “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. 129), also plainly agrees with the same matter or time. For their brothers will say to this great Joseph on that day: “We beseech you that you forget the crime of your brothers” (Gen. 50). The Communion also—“Amen I say to you, whatever you ask in prayer” (Mark 11), and so forth—is the reply of that same Joseph, saying: “Do not fear. You devised evil against me, but God turned it to good, in order that he might exalt me, as you now see, and save many peoples. Do not be afraid; I will feed you and your little ones” (Gen. 50) [Col. 0330D].

## CHAPTER XXIV. Again, concerning the nocturnal readings during the summer
The night readings throughout the summer, by their variety and sequence, portray the course of the ages, or the progress of holy Church. First, the history of Kings, which is appointed immediately after Pentecost, is mystically likened in its first two books to the earliest times of Christianity, when, as faith in Christ gradually increased, the old idolatry fell away. For just as, upon the reign of Saul, whom the people had desired against the will of God (1 Sam. 10), there followed the election of David (1 Sam. 16), whom the Lord says that he found after his own heart; and at last, when the whole kingdom had been wrested from the house of Saul, it submitted itself to that same David (2 Sam. 5): so, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the worship of God came into the world in place of the worship of demons; and at last the Christian faith, victorious through the wars of the martyrs, took its seat upon the throne of the Roman Empire, and thereafter the whole world submitted itself with a strong hand to Christ.

In the following two books, in which the kingdom was divided away from the house of David, when Jeroboam seized the schism of the kingdom—as had been signified to him through the hand of Ahijah the Shilonite—and, despising the temple of the Lord, made two calves (1 Kgs. 12), were signified those times in which the madness of heretics tore the Church apart and, despising Christ’s altar and rejecting the worship of truth, fashioned diverse images of their own falsehoods.

Then follow the books of the most wise Solomon: that is, just as, after the conflicts with heretics, the talents of teachers shone forth in the Church, who, stirred up by their disputes, did not sleep but devoted themselves to wisdom and knowledge, and in a manner also debated, as is read of Solomon: “Concerning the trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that springs from the wall” (1 Kgs. 4). That is, they allowed no word at all of Holy Scripture, whether small or great, to lack allegory or some useful moral meaning.

After this the book of Job likewise appropriately follows, since especially in the peace of the Church there are not lacking those temptations directed against men striving after virtue, which, in all the blows and consolations of that same holy Job, are morally represented, according to the blessed Gregory. For then inwardly press upon them the temptations of spiritual vices; and the more hidden the struggle, the more difficult the victory.

## CHAPTER XXV. Likewise, concerning the night readings from the month of September

Thereafter, beginning in the month of September, four books are appointed: Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Ezra. How fittingly their consideration expresses the four cardinal virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—is plain.

Tobit, indeed, is not inappropriately taken as a figure of prudence. Though his outward eyes were blinded, he gives his seeing son precepts for living, so that Solomon’s saying may be fulfilled: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2). For by the head is understood the resourcefulness of the mind, but by the eyes, foresight, which is the same as prudence. Therefore he rightly stands at the head under the title of prudence, who provides a safeguard for that mind whose guidance he himself needs outwardly.

Judith, moreover, clearly presents the image of fortitude in that she opposed herself for the liberation of her country to the most savage tyrant when fighting men were afraid, and, an unarmed woman, overcame the commander of the army with God’s help. For her strength was from God, as she herself says in prayer: “And now, O Lord, help me, a widow, that I may accomplish what I believed I could do through thee” (Judith 13). How truly strong she was she showed when, about to cut off with her own sword the head of Holofernes, overcome by drunkenness, she said: “Strengthen me, my God, in this hour.” And she cut off his head (ibid.).

Yet these two books are not in the Hebrew canon, but came to be used for the instruction of holy Church by the authority of the Nicene synod.

Esther, however, is assigned to temperance: when Queen Vashti is repudiated because of her arrogance, Esther is put in her place in the kingdom. For this is a distinctive proof of temperance: that she turned into gentleness that lion of whom she herself says to the Lord, “Grant me favor in the sight of the lion” (Esth. 14)—that is, King Ahasuerus—and transformed the decree prompted by Haman, who most intemperately swelled with pride and desired to destroy the Jewish people, into consolation for her own race.

Ezra, who is joined to these, is shown to possess the privilege of justice in word and deed. For as justice restores what injustice has destroyed, so he restored the temple and city, ruined because of the people’s sins. Likewise, just as he is one work divided into two volumes—for Nehemiah is joined with him in the same work—so the two precepts of justice correspond to him: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7), and “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4). These four books, then, distinguished by the aforesaid virtues, rightly follow the book of Job, which, according to the testimony of blessed Gregory, expresses the afflictions of holy Church; for after temptations have been vigorously overcome, the glory of virtues is granted to the elect.

But because, so long as we are away from the Lord in this world (1 Cor. 5), we suffer wars of vices amid virtues, the books of the Maccabees are read immediately afterward. In them that great enemy Antiochus is said to prevail against the continual sacrifice and to persecute God’s martyrs (2 Macc. 4). Yet he is conquered by the labor of Judas and his brothers, because, by confession of evil deeds together with the practice of good deeds, he is at times overcome when God grants it.

Afterward the books of the prophets resound until the coming of the Lord, now proclaiming the terror of the strict Judge, now the consolations of the merciful Creator. Of these, Ezekiel, whose name is interpreted “strength of God,” and Daniel, which signifies “judgment of God,” are the greater and first prophets, because hope arising from the strength of divine assistance and fear arising from the judgment of God alike teach the mind to use present things rightly, lest it either fail by despairing of God or fall by presuming upon itself.

We refrain from speaking of the remaining twelve prophets, gathered into one volume, because we know that the holy Fathers have discussed them abundantly.
