They are read until the coming of the Lord so that, amid the darknesses and conflicts of this age, until Christ’s return, the Scriptures may enlighten and console us. Through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0333]

[NOTE.]

After the books on the divine offices, in the edition printed at Venice in 1751 by Michael Pleunich, which we follow, is read the Apology of Dom Gerberon against the assailant of Rupert’s doctrine. In our edition it has a more suitable place among the Prolegomena to the first volume of Rupert’s Works.  
*(Editor of the Patrologia.)*

[Col. 0333]

THE GOLDEN BOOK OF THE REVEREND LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, CONCERNING THE BURNING OF THE TOWN OF DEUTZ, WITNESSED IN HIS OWN TIME.

[Col. 0333]

149–225. CHAPTER I

[Col. 0333A]

See how Satan the accuser has also considered our negligence in sin—or, shall I say, the innocence of holy Job—while, according to his custom, he restlessly goes about the earth and walks through it (Job 1). You know these things, most beloved brothers, who together with me serve the Lord in this monastery of Deutz and have marvelously experienced both his wrath and his mercy amid the flames, as the prophet said to him: “When thou art angry, thou wilt remember mercy” (Hab. 3).

You know, I say—or you ought to know—that unless he in his mercy had denied power to him who asked wickedly, unless he had commanded that we be spared, even today our friends, seeing our wound, would be afraid, and some would judge us ill, after the likeness of the friends of blessed Job (Job 13). Yet he was not merely restrained from stripping away our whole skin by burning it, as he had begun to do; rather, as the Lord says of him to Job: “Will he make a covenant with thee, and wilt thou have him as an everlasting servant?” (Job 40). And, as the Apostle says, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8): so it happened now also.

I desire to relate the event as it occurred, with this purpose: that our descendants too may know it, and that no antiquity of time may be able to erase from our hearts the memory of the glorification by which, in so great a fire, the sacrament of the Lord’s body was glorified, as our eyes saw; and of the deliverance by which this church, in which we invoke the name of the Lord, was delivered from the pressure of the flame. For many saw the presence of divine protection: namely, what seemed to be the form of a most beautiful man leaning down from above and repelling with an outstretched hand the assault of the surrounding flames.

When I have related these things more carefully in writing, may this be my reward from the Lord: that he may not accuse me of ingratitude, as he rebuked those of whom he said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” (Luke 17). For likewise we too would deserve rebuke unless we offered both heart and mouth in thanksgiving; as if he himself should say: “Was not the holy and life-giving sacrament, by which undoubtedly the leprosy of sins is cleansed, preserved for these by the manifest power of God from so great a fire? And where are the thanksgivings?” Thus the event occurred.

## CHAPTER II

In the present year, which is the year 1128 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [25 August], in the first watch of the night, a fire suddenly arose and seized the middle of the village street. Driven by the wind, it quickly grew beyond measure.

There had been an exceedingly great and long-lasting drought; and all around, the houses and barns were abundantly filled with crops recently gathered and carried in. Thus the blaze, suddenly kindled, grew without delay. Not only did the flowing Rhine shine with its light and nearby Cologne glow, but this entire region and almost the whole province beheld on every side a grim and terrible brightness. Indeed, for almost two hundred stadia and farther the fire blazed, and those who did not know of it along the Rhine thought that the sky was burning.

What courage had you then, dearest brothers, and I as well, when through the towers and between the towers you saw the mad armies of flame drawing near and threatening, and the battalions of great sparks leaping and rushing upon us? The victorious flame, with astonishing speed, seized the surrounding towers, hateful to us; and in one assault swept over our houses and workshops as far as the very entrance of the monastic cloister. It made this whole fortress—marvelous to say!—as it were one furnace, so that thousands of people looking on from the nearby city saw what was indeed true: that this whole monastery was surrounded and covered with flames. Later I shall state why I called, and call, the aforesaid towers hateful to us.

What, then, was our state of mind? Did not the sight shudder? Did not hearing grow terrified? Did not hearts tremble, and all bodily senses flee in astonishment? As I examine myself, recalling what I was found to be in that trial, I rebuke myself all the more.

For almost what the aforesaid Job says to his friends happened to me: “As soon as God moves himself, he troubled you, and his terror shall rush upon you” (Job 3). For what is this? Is it characteristic of the righteous and of those of perfect faith to be troubled as soon as he moves himself, and to be overwhelmed by the ruin of his terror? Is it not rather theirs, as soon as they perceive that he is moved, to rise up and hold him fast?

The prophet Isaiah mourns that such persons were lacking, or are lacking, in the sinful nation: “There is none,” he says, “that calleth upon thy name; there is none that riseth up and holdeth thee” (Isa. 64). This, I say, belongs to the perfect; and such perfection is rightly required above all of us who are called prelates: that we should wrestle against the wrath of God, following the example of the first prelate, Moses, who wrestled with and held God when God said to him: “Let me alone, that my wrath may grow hot” (Exod. 32).

And how did he wrestle? Surely by weeping and praying to him; or, as the Psalmist says, by “standing in the breach” (Ps. 105), that is, in the deepest humility of mind before him. Before Moses, holy Jacob too wrestled with him (Gen. 32), namely by weeping and entreating him, as the prophet Hosea clearly and briefly teaches: “In his strength,” he says, “he directed himself toward the angel, and prevailed over the angel; he wept and entreated him” (Hos. 12).

But we who come last, I and those like me, while the Lord is calm and does not move himself, stand before him; and sometimes we even dare to flatter him and in some manner to smile with the heart’s smile, through the confidence of faith by which we believe in him. But when he moves himself even a little and indicates that movement by even a slight storm, or by the single stroke of lightning darting past with a sudden thunderclap, immediately we are troubled and almost lose confidence. We stand far off like fugitive retainers: steadfast in peace, flighty in war; high-minded in prosperity, small-minded and fearful in adversity. We scarcely hope that anyone will answer when we call upon him (Job 5); scarcely do we turn to one of his holy friends that he may hold him, because we are troubled in conscience.

I, indeed, was especially troubled. For I fled almost naked and sat far from the fire, far from this endangered house, remembering holy David, who, though he was a man of such great merits, nevertheless, troubled by a sudden report, hastened to depart: “Lest,” he said, “Absalom come and seize us.” And having gone out on foot, he stood far from the house: “And if,” he said, “I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and show me his ark and his tabernacle” (2 Sam. 15).

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile, while the swift fire was still devouring the first portions of the prey granted to it, stretching its tongue farther and terrifying all with its baleful light, one of the brothers, carrying from the sacristy a corporal cloth of the Lord tied aloft to a long pole, stood before the flames. He hoped that the fire and all the enemy’s power would yield to so sacred an object.

When the fire did not yield in this manner, he persisted with unfeigned faith and with a boldness not to be condemned. He thrust the pole itself, with the corporal, forcefully into the midst of the flames, shaking it for some time as though he were piercing the raging fire, until the rebellious flame burst out even toward him and almost scorched him with its breath.

At last he withdrew, quickly drawing out the pole he held, partly burned, but the corporal—marvelous to say!—unharmed and uncontaminated by fire. He rolled it up and threw it as high as he could into the flames, desiring and hoping that, by its casting in, the fire might be overcome by the Lord’s will and fail as though strangled.

But that great fire, permitted by God, in a marvelous fashion cast the intact corporal out of its midst by a hidden and unknown force. It drove it farther off into that part of the town which had not been granted to it and where, as was plain, it would do no harm. Who would not delight to have seen, or to see, so great a miracle?

The aforesaid corporal was brought back so whole and unharmed that it nevertheless bears a not unseemly mark: namely, a reddish line, whereas it remains, as it was before, entirely white. This pleases more, surely, than if no trace whatever of the fire had remained upon it; for thereby it is a clearer memorial and ought to be recognized among all sacred objects of this kind.

## CHAPTER IV

Accordingly, when the fire, with its reins loosed, possessed the whole fortress, within and without, as has already been said, I sat at a distance among houses untouched by the fire, though still able to watch that mournful spectacle—the surging crests of the flames. Someone stood upon a higher roof and said that the Basilica of Saint Urban was burning: that is, the parish church situated before the gates of the monastery.

I thought all was over and almost despaired of the monastery’s deliverance, except that my spirit sang within me: “In wrath thou wilt remember mercy” (Hab. 3). Then, after no small delay, the inward man also began to sing within me: “I bless thee, Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, because through thy Son the fire has been extinguished from beside me.” And so it had been.

For people immediately came to say that the fire had fallen away and left the monastery safe and unharmed with its cloister; only the adjoining houses and workshops, with their yards, had all been reduced to ashes and cinders. Who could have hoped for this? Who except God could have done it, whose help the multitude of people of both sexes, looking on from the farther bank of the Rhine, called upon most humbly and devoutly?

For many of them saw—and publicly confess that they saw—a most handsome man above the roof of the monastery, leaning upon his left side or elbow and driving back with uplifted right hand the attack of the fire which had already seized the bell tower inwardly. When I heard this good news, I returned after that mournful night, once daylight had come. And behold, the parish priest of the aforementioned church, Stephen by name, was spreading abroad—and was especially eager to tell me—the sweet and joyful miracle, a very good sign and a great, evident proof of God’s watchful mercy toward us.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0337A]

He had placed beside the altar, according to custom, a wooden pyx containing the body of the Lord, in a window or inner wall-recess constructed of wooden shingles, with a little door and bolt. With the said pyx were other vessels belonging to the sacred ministry: another pyx containing unconsecrated hosts; a pewter wine-flask; a vessel for incense; candles; and some linen—all of which must be mentioned because of so great a miracle.

For in the violence of that mighty fire, when not only the basilica itself but the entire space of the fortress was like one furnace—much greater than that Babylonian fire whose flame rose forty-nine cubits above the furnace (Dan. 3)—when fragments of burning beams were falling, and metal bells, marvelously ringing of themselves as they burned and burning as they rang, had fallen from the height of the burning bell tower, not merely shattered but almost melted; and when the fire, thus fallen, raged more fiercely within the walls of the basilica, confined by all that material: the recess itself burned, with everything aforementioned stored within it, being consumed lightly and quickly, considering the greatness of the fire, like straw or a small quantity of hay. Only that pyx containing the body of the Lord remained safe and untouched.

As soon as the aforementioned priest was able to gain access, he quickly removed the heap of burning wood and ashes. He was grieved, as he confessed, because, in his agitation at the pressing fire, although he carried out certain things or had them carried out, he had forgotten to take the body of the Lord. Looking within, he found this remarkable miracle.

Immediately taking it up, displaying and proclaiming to all who were present that sacrament of our faith, he came rejoicing to me. Through the abundance of his joy he had forgotten his negligence, although not without a cloud of sorrow over the damage that had occurred. For throughout that day a kind of night still lay in our hearts; and, as though pressed by heavy sleep, the eyes of our mind were not yet able to behold the rising sun—that is, the brightness of the divine presence shining around us, or in our midst—through the three miracles: this very great one, and the other two which I narrated above.

The following day was Sunday. At about the third hour I went there, with many following or present, and I looked upon the place and considered the deed of power worthy of admiration. To the joy was added this also: we saw that the altar was unharmed, although the great stones joined to the altar, which lay spread out in front of it, had been broken and divided into pieces by the great masses of fragments—that is, beams broken by the fire and falling while burning.

## CHAPTER VI

We ought therefore to have praised God and openly proclaimed in speech the greatness of his mighty works. But are we sufficient to praise him worthily? For these, O Christ, are thy miracles, not unlike in glory to that by which thou wast glorified with thy three youths in the midst of the Babylonian furnace, when King Nebuchadnezzar declared: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3).

Truly, I say, this glory is not far unlike that glory. For what that great furnace, fiercely kindled by the command of that king who bore the type of the devil, was there, that was on that night this whole fortress kindled into one fire and made, as we have said, like a single furnace. Our yards or barns and other buildings, filled with the new harvest, increased the flames of the structures beyond measure; yet, though surrounded on every side and covered by the height of the flames, the monastery was not harmed.

Did not thy children, O Lord—namely, all the brothers and many poor persons who had taken refuge within—walk in the midst of the fire? For thou, Son of God, didst walk with them in ready grace; and thou gavest three signs as witnesses of this thy condescension. Two of these were seen by those who wished to see or came near in order to see: namely, thy body together with the vessel in which it had been placed, and the unchanged corporal, just as the trousers of those youths were not changed or scorched. The third, which was the appearance of a man leaning over the monastery, was not seen by all who were present or looking on; but so many credible and trustworthy persons confessed that they had seen it that we should think it sinful not to believe them, or even to doubt.

Otherwise, why should we inquire after the sight of men? Nothing could have resisted or survived so great a fire unless thy power, O God, had been present in action. Accordingly, we praised thee and we praise thee; and our mouth shall yet speak thy praise, and we shall bless thy holy name.

When, in procession, we carried around the body of the Lord—for, as I said above, it was Sunday, on which a procession is customarily held in solemn observance of the Lord’s resurrection—the people also cried out in a clear, rejoicing chorus. The above-mentioned priest confessed his guilt with tears before all: because, although he rescued from the fire the other things that he could, he had forgotten to take this one sacrament of our redemption and salvation.

Together with you, dearest brothers, I judged it fitting to transfer the aforesaid corporal and that pyx to the high altar as supreme relics, and to inscribe this single verse above them:

> This body of the Lord conquered the flames within its pyx.

## CHAPTER VII

What room remains, then, beloved, for anyone to say or suppose that the evil of so great a fire occurred by chance or accident, rather than by God’s judgment or providence? For there have been and still are many unlearned people who think that all things done under the sun are governed by chance and that the world is not at all ruled by God’s providence. This is especially because prosperous things often happen to the unjust, and adverse things frequently happen to the just; and concerning this they murmur in their hearts.

Against such persons the prophet Jeremiah speaks in lamentation: “Who is he that spoke, and it came to pass, the Lord not commanding? From the mouth of the Most High proceed neither evil nor good. Why has a living man murmured, a man because of his sins?” (Lam. 3). For it is the mark of an unbelieving mind to say that evils and goods—that is, adversities and prosperities—do not proceed from the mouth of the Most High. For example, that Jerusalem should be burned by the Babylonian fire, which occurred when Jeremiah spoke these lamentations; and again, that after seventy years the captivity of that people should be released.

It is, I say, the mark of an unbelieving and murmuring mind to say or suppose that none of these things was done at the Lord’s command, but that all happened by chance, when another prophet also said: “Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord hath not done?” (Amos 3).

Such unbelief, beloved, must be avoided by us. Let us rather hear what immediately follows in the same passage of Jeremiah: “Let us search our ways and examine them, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands unto God in heaven” (Lam. 3). For if we truly search our ways and knowingly say what we often say, “We have sinned, acted unjustly, committed iniquity” (Bar. 2), we shall find that we have received less than we deserve. We deserved indeed to be struck by the rod of judgment, but, as mercy exalts itself above judgment, we have been touched only a little by the fatherly rod of discipline.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now I wish to state why the victorious flame seized with astonishing speed the towers of this fortress, hateful to us. For I promised this when I added above (ch. 2): “Later I shall state why I called, or call, the aforesaid towers hateful to us.”

Attend, therefore, dearest brothers, how rightly I grieved over them in sorrow, and with how perfect a hatred I hated—not the stones or walls, but the injustice dwelling in them. For the whole enclosure of this fortress ought to have been legally holy, since it is written thus in the law of the Lord: “Whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to the Lord, and property consecrated belongs by right to the priests” (Lev. 27).

Who does not know that the possession of this fortress had been consecrated to God, to our Lord Jesus Christ, and to his holy mother, the perpetual virgin Mary? For the book of the Life or Acts of our father blessed Heribert relates that, when he desired to build a monastery in honor of the Lord and of his aforesaid mother, blessed Mary ever Virgin, in accordance with a vow—Emperor Otto having urged him to do so—and desired also to know in what place it would please that holy Mother of God for this to be done, she appeared to him in a vision and said:

> “Arise, and go to the fortress of Deutz. Command that a place be cleared within it, and there establish a monastery for God, for me, and for all the saints, so that where sin and the worship of demons once dwelt, there justice may reign and the memory of the saints.”

[Note: [Col. 0339D] See below, in the *Life of St. Heribert*, ch. 13.]

At that time there was in the same fortress a manor belonging to the bishop’s service. Concerning the building of the fortress, however, there are different opinions. Some suppose it to have been the work of Julius Caesar; others maintain that it was built by Constantine himself after he had conquered the Franks, at the time when Emperor Constantius and his son Constantine conducted an expedition in Gaul.

An inscription, found not many years ago on a stone tablet among fragments of the walls, itself broken into pieces but in such a way that the pieces could be joined together, asserts that the latter opinion is the stronger. It read as follows:

> “Constantine, pious Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, having conquered the Franks, ordered the fortress of the Deutzians to be built in their lands. The soldiers made the tower with the intervening tower-space. These eighteen made vows.”

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The same Lord Surius communicated this to me from a certain ancient book in this form: “By the power of the Lord Constantine the Great, most pious, most fortunate, unconquered Augustus, after the Franks had been subdued and conquered, they made the fortress of the Deutzians in their lands, in the presence of their prince, in devotion to the divine power and majesty: these eighteen made vows.”]

And indeed it is well known historically that Constantine magnificently defeated the Franks and Alemanni and gave their kings to the beasts. But because Julius Caesar’s achievements in Gaul are more famous, the opinion has become more widespread that he too was the founder of this fortress, although it is supported by no documentary testimony of writers.

This fortress remained remarkable for beauty and strength until Emperor Otto I. His brother Bruno, Archbishop of the Church of Cologne—the twenty-fourth after Saint Severinus—equally illustrious for great nobility, excellence of character, and outstanding piety, destroyed it. He did not fear the wrath of his aforementioned brother, the emperor, which is reported to have been so fierce that it would have compelled Bruno, much against his will, to rebuild it, had not the emperor himself been quickly overtaken by death.

The sixth archbishop after that Bruno of blessed memory, Saint Heribert, consecrated the same town to the Lord in the manner already stated—indeed, the ruined fragments of the town, so to speak—by building a monastery in its midst for God, in honor of our Lady Saint Mary, perpetual virgin. He cleared the whole place for this work in such a way that he left no secular dwelling there. He gave those whom he ordered to leave dwellings outside, adjoining the exterior wall, as very many people know and testify even today, especially their descendants, who hold the same beneficed houses and are subject to the right and lordship of this church.

## CHAPTER IX

Therefore, in accordance with the aforementioned decree of sacred law, the whole area of this fortress ought to have been holy to the Lord—that is, it ought to have suffered no contamination from common or secular affairs, of the kind which we have seen and heard has often brought great offense or scandal, in very many places, upon brothers consecrated to God and bound to the prescribed purity of monastic religion.

Until almost our own times, as you know, some trace of the ancient right remained to this monastery: the prior or provost of the monastery held, without anyone objecting, the keys of this fortress; and the gates, once closed, were not opened throughout the whole night until the proper hour of day.

But now, through the long negligence of our predecessors, while they accommodate themselves too much to secular persons, such license has grown that it is fitting for us to say that prophetic utterance—especially we for whom religion is desirable and welcome, and who are zealous for the Lord with good zeal: “Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners” (Lam. 5).

For people have occupied the fortress, and have restored for their own habitation not only the towers and spaces between towers, men respectable indeed according to the world; but they have also let the under-tower chambers, which they call cellars—like dark caves and almost hidden corners—to persons whose life is doubtful, condition unknown, and reputation obscure. Thus serious people in our neighborhood have such an opinion of these dwellings, and judge them as certain workshops of uncleanness. Therefore they say: “They ought not to doubt that this fire happened justly, not only to those inside who committed such things, but also to those outside who consented to their commission; and they either suppressed me, though protesting, by litigation or left me unsupported through silence.”

Certainly, even if there were other causes of the fire, I do not hesitate to say that this was a very great cause and that it occurred by the Lord’s judgment. For before it happened I saw it in a dream, and several times reported such fear to some of you with astonishment. There was present and impending before us, as we watched, something like the day of judgment, while we seemed to stand as if in the eastern part of a certain monastery, turned toward the west.

Meanwhile the bells hanging from a tower rang with a terrible crash, and this seemed to be an announcement of the approaching Judge. We saw no person in that vision; but suddenly, from the north, through open windows, a horrible crackling fire, sparkling in many directions, leapt in and fell scattered before our faces. Yet it did not touch us—that is, me and those who seemed to be standing with me—except that in that vision the magnitude of the fierce terror was immense.

But do we need arguments or conjectures to know or believe that this occurred not by chance but by the judgment of the Lord who corrects, especially when the Apostle says: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11)? Oh, would that those who, presuming to invade a place consecrated to God, have, insofar as lay in them, broken—nay, I will not say rendered void—the vows of the aforesaid blessed bishops, might through this present judgment, this moderate and bearable correction, fear and escape the sentence of the future universal judgment. For the devotion of saints, built upon the foundation of the apostles (Eph. 2), cannot be rendered void: they did not judge it fitting to build upon the foundation of pagans, nor indeed upon that of any dead human beings.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0342A]

It is strange: whence comes to mortal minds so great a desire for earthly height, or for a stronghold resting on an earthly foundation, when their life is short—far shorter than was the life of ancient human beings, the first of whom, Cain, built a city (Gen. 4)? And what shall I say? Was there ever anyone among the whole number of saints or praiseworthy men who, Scripture bearing witness, built an earthly city or a fortress on an earthly foundation—men whom the wise man, Jesus son of Sirach, proposes for praise when he says: “Let us praise glorious men, and our fathers in their generation” (Ecclus. 44)?

Indeed, that it might be clearly marked by testimony that earthly fortifications—of which Cain, as has already been said, was the first author—have never pleased God, the first of all the cities which the children of Israel, after crossing the Jordan, possessed (they being children of pilgrims, that is, of the holy patriarchs, who did not wish to have here an abiding city but sought the one to come [Heb. 13]) utterly fell by God’s will or judgment. No engines of war struck it; sacred trumpets alone sounded, Joshua proceeding, in whom was the Spirit of the Lord, and saying: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up and builds Jericho. In his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and in the last of his children shall he set up its gates” (Josh. 6).

And this came to pass. “For in the days of Ahab king of Israel,” says Scripture, “Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. In Abiram his firstborn he founded it, and in Segub the last of his children he set up its gates, according to the word which the Lord had spoken through Joshua son of Nun” (3 Kings 16). Such judgment did that city undergo which first opposed the people of God, or the ark of the Lord, as they crossed the Jordan. Were the other cities of the Canaanites of better merit, then, that they too did not likewise fall at the entrance of that same people of God? Certainly not; but the time had not yet come, and in one earthly city it was sufficient to signify what the other enterprises of the nations also deserved.

## CHAPTER XI

My brothers, according to the Scripture which says, “Affliction alone shall give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28), something very nearly happened to me. For the affliction which you saw me endure, which you heard in the pain of a voice like that of a woman in labour throughout an entire year—indeed, for almost two full years before the scourge of this fire overflowed—gave understanding to the hearing. It gave me occasion to understand more clearly the truth that builders of earthly cities are denounced in Holy Scripture, both before and after the Flood, as architects or citizens of the adverse city, which is opposed to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Before the Flood, it says: “Cain built a city and called it by the name of his son Enoch” (Gen. 4). After the Flood, it says: “Nimrod began to be mighty on the earth; and the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon. From that land Asshur went forth and built the city Nineveh and the streets of the city” (Gen. 10). On account of such powers the Lord called this world “the court of a strong man armed” (Luke 11).

For by that same power through which Nimrod began to be mighty upon the earth—and on account of which he was called in the proverb, “a mighty hunter before the Lord”—idols too began to be worshipped, and were commanded to be worshipped as God: ostensibly for the beauty and defense of the city, but especially at the beginning in remembrance of their illustrious name. Thus Scripture says in the Book of Wisdom: “A father, grieving in bitter sorrow for a son suddenly taken from him, made an image of him; and him who then was as a dead man, he now began to worship as a god, and established sacred rites and sacrifices among his servants” (Wis. 14). Then, as time intervened and wicked custom grew strong, this error was observed as though it were law, and images were worshipped at the command of tyrants.

This was plainly the reason why this world became such that it was rightly called the court of a strong man armed: while the devil, who ought by right to have possessed nothing in the world, was enlisted through idolatry to support tyranny by lovers of the world, who hastened to exercise tyranny in the world. Of these Nimrod, mentioned above, was the first, a tyrant according to his name. For *Nemroth* is interpreted “tyrant,” or “fugitive,” or “transgressor.”

It should be understood, moreover, that when “the court of a strong man armed” is spoken of, his house also must be understood together with the court. An *atrium* is called the first entrance of a very spacious house, where the inhabitants, acting according to their own judgment, were known to make hearths to drive out the cold; and, antiquity relates, *atria* were so named from the very dark cloud of smoke, as though from *ater*, “black.” And what is his house but hell? Therefore cities founded upon earth—such as those in the greatest or best-known of which King Nimrod exercised tyranny, and to which Asshur set himself—when they display idols publicly and gather the thickest smoke of sacrifices, are rightly called, and are, the foulest courts of that exceedingly vast house, namely hell; since they are courts, or one court, of the strong man armed—that is, the devil.

Yet in “the courts of the house of the Lord” (Ps. 133), in which we stand or ought to stand, this etymology almost fails; for there is no black smoke in them—unless one reasonably considers that the weeping grief of penitents is indeed smoke, but smoke destined to bring forth true light, just as, conversely, the smoke of blindness and ignorance in that court of the aforesaid strong man armed brings forth the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XII

Since these things are so, does not the cause of the pilgrims—the holy Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the rest who did not build cities or castles, but rather left built cities and lived in huts, confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth—shine forth more and more? “For they awaited a city having foundations,” says the Apostle, “whose architect and builder is God” (Heb. 11).

They did not build cities and castles; rather, they built that which is contrary to cities and castles, namely an altar to the Lord. Abraham, the first or best-known of pilgrims, is recorded to have done this three times. First, where God appeared to him as he entered the land of Canaan and said: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. 12). Secondly, where, traversing or advancing through the land, he pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai (Gen. 13). Thirdly, where, commanded to offer his only-begotten son as a burnt offering, he obeyed praiseworthily (Gen. 22).

Therefore this was, is, and ought to be until the consummation of the age the reason for the pilgrimages in this world of the children of God: they ought to be God’s helpers, helpers in God’s building work, in order to cast the strong man armed out of his court—the one whom the Son of God conquered. How are they to cast out that strong man armed? Certainly, first by attacking and destroying every fortification of falsehood, or contrivance of fanatical error, through the most steadfast preaching of truth; and then by uprooting, insofar as possible, or obscuring the lofty titles of the proud men of this age. Of such it is written in the Psalm: “Their tabernacles are from generation to generation; they called their names upon their lands” (Ps. 48).

For example: where the lofty tomb of Romulus had been raised, there should rise above it the basilica of the apostle Peter; and where his discordant brother Remus, crushed by a tomb nearly equal to that of his brother Romulus, lies buried, there Paul, Peter’s companion and the standard-bearer of Christ’s cross, should rule in his own house, to the honour of his King, Christ himself.

It is beyond doubt that the pious intention of the blessed bishops Bruno and Heribert, mentioned above, belongs to the lot of pilgrims who build such things in such a manner. They cast out from this court—or portion of the court—of that strong man armed some rogue, one of his attendants (and he has many such): the one by destroying the castle, the other by building this monastery in honour of the Stronger One who conquered that strong man.

What more does a citizen of heaven and pilgrim upon earth, according to his profession, possess to do than build, insofar as he can, upon the foundation of the holy Fathers—of whom Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were the foremost or best known—who built no earthly city but sought the city above, or heavenly city?

Perhaps you say: David took the stronghold of Zion, and “this,” Scripture says, “is the city of David” (2 Sam. 5). And it is written in praise of the Fathers concerning Hezekiah that “he fortified his city and brought water through the midst of it” (Ecclus. 48). The ready answer is that taking or fortifying a city is far different from founding or building one. Thus it should be noted that, under the leadership of Moses and Joshua, it was granted or permitted to take walled cities and dwell in them; nowhere, however, were they commanded to build them. Indeed, God chose to cast down one city above all others—namely Jericho, as mentioned above—by the miracle of his power, in order to indicate to us by this sign that his will neither was nor is in structures of this kind, which mortal presumption has devised. Before the Law he showed the same thing by another miracle at the tower of Babel, where he confused their tongues (Gen. 11).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the fortification with which Hezekiah fortified his city—so that we may rightly venerate it in the praises of the Fathers—must be understood spiritually. That fortification was most powerful prayer; and the water which he led through the middle of the city was mercy, which so descended from heaven that in one night the angel of the Lord slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand men from Sennacherib’s army (4 Kings 19).

Likewise, when David took the stronghold of Zion and expelled the blind and the lame, who hated David’s soul, he intended to make there a place for the name of the Lord (2 Sam. 5). And he did so by bringing there the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and by setting about building there a house of prayer, which God willed to be completed through his son Solomon. Hence he sang with rejoicing: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim, but chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion which he loved” (Ps. 77)—and other things, of which a fuller discourse would present itself, were it not necessary to pursue brevity and avoid weariness.

## CHAPTER XIII

With what voice, with what words, shall I at last be able to express the greatness of the affliction which, as I have already said above, gave and increased this understanding to the hearing? For I was violently afflicted; and, to say it briefly, I almost happened to pluck out my right eye and cast it from me; I almost happened to cut off my right hand and foot and cast them from me. For it offended me so that I nearly resolved to leave this place, when he began to rebuild a tower and construct a solid house, with such importunity of the site and such unhappiness of this cloister as no religious soul could ever patiently endure—or even behold—if the work had been brought to completion.

The tower stands at a corner: that is, it stands in the angle joining two walls of the cloister which approach from different directions. Strange! My right eye, while it undertook such work, did not see—or was unwilling to see—that this very undertaking would become the beginning of destruction for our profession, although it had been accustomed to revere and advance that profession. For what else could be expected? For men and women of spiritual purpose, the silence, freedom, security, and a certain protection of solitude are essential; against them, such noise is a kind of captivity.

Hence comes the title of the seventieth Psalm: “A Psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab, and of the first captives.” The literal sense of this title is that Jonadab the priest commanded his sons to abstain from wine and to dwell in tents (Jer. 35). But when the Babylonian attack threatened, they were compelled to depart from their rule of life and, torn away from their tents, entered the city; therefore they were rightly called the first captives. For, when shut within the walls of the besieged city, they were made captive before the other people of the same land were led to Babylon after the city’s capture—which was their captivity.

In the spiritual sense, we too become captives when we are enclosed, with the aforesaid kind of importunity, by fortifications which are not within our jurisdiction or whose way of life we are unable to regulate. Just as Jonadab—whose name means “the voluntary one of the Lord”—a priest himself, commanded his priestly sons to live in tents, so the Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal priest, who became ours by voluntary charity, does not wish his priests to delight in cities and castles; especially not us, whose priesthood is adorned by our religious purpose and whose purpose is adorned by priesthood—that is, those of us who both profess the monastic life and serve at the sacred altar.

But what need is there of subtler arguments? My own eye knows it, and you, my brothers, know that as water suits little fishes, so a quiet dwelling suits and is desirable to persons of our profession. If any one of you perhaps thought otherwise at that time, he certainly had not yet wiped from the eye of his mind all the dust of earthly-mindedness.

## CHAPTER XIV

Thus I almost then, as I said above, became one-eyed, maimed, and lame because of such offense—except that that eye spared me, that hand restrained itself, and that foot ceased to run, at the swift pace of the work which it had begun; though not without offense, not without an outburst, not without disturbance of its own purity. For it preferred to be overcome by reason by ceasing from the work rather than, by persisting in the work, to continue altogether to offend me. Yet it was unwilling at the same time to judge that I had been offended so simply as one of the little ones, of whom the Lord says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18).

What or how great were the things I suffered in consequence, I might insert in the present writing, except that lean or slight matters are not easily adorned with carefully sought words; and, as one of the wise or eloquent secular authors says, for someone to commit his thoughts to writing when he can neither arrange nor illuminate them, nor attract the reader by any delight, belongs to a man intemperately abusing both leisure and letters.

For the present I can say this truthfully: through no small experience I learned to sympathize with him to whom the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Ps. 80). He is Joseph, whose calamity the preceding verse proclaimed in words both brief and wondrous: “He heard a language which he did not know” (ibid.).

According to the history, this is a recapitulation or parenthesis—that is, an insertion. For it was not when the tribe of Joseph left the land of Egypt, but when Joseph himself entered Egypt as a young man and served there, that he heard a language which he did not know; and his hands served in the basket, until God turned his back away from burdens (ibid.).

The full discourse or meaning, therefore, is this: when Joseph—that is, the tribe of Joseph, or all Israel—departed from the land of Egypt, where the children of Israel had served because of sin, since Joseph had been sold by his brothers; where Joseph himself, the first to serve, heard a language he did not know, and for this reason it was justly repaid to them that they too should serve; when, I say, Joseph—that is, Israel, carrying Joseph’s bones from the land of Egypt—went out, God our helper, the God of Jacob, set this testimony in him: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm,” and so forth to the end of the Psalm.

To what end is this? Certainly, that I may confess that from my own experience I have discovered that no small part of Joseph’s calamity was precisely this: in serving and bearing burdens upon his back, he heard a language he did not know, and he was long afflicted before he became accustomed to communication in the language of those whom he served.

Moreover, while he lived in his master’s house—a master who knew very well that the Lord was with him, and that all that he did was directed by the Lord into his hands, so that he, set over the household, administered the house entrusted to him (Gen. 39)—did he easily or without effort overcome envy by virtue? Do you suppose there was no malicious eye there, troubled that a resident alien—indeed, a purchased slave—was preferred by so great a favor of his master above all his household servants and over all his estate?

A certain wise man truly says: “He who has not been tested, what does he know?” (Ecclus. 34). For trial instructs the tested person concerning similar matters, even when they are far greater; and it instructed me, I confess, to understand better the tribulation in which Joseph called upon the Lord, and the hidden place of the storm in which the Lord heard him.

For when, through the occasion of the scandal mentioned above, the waves of temptation rose more greatly than usual against me, I was in such tribulation and endured such a storm in the hidden place—that is, in my mind—that I almost, defeated, resolved to lay down the burden of the care of this monastery. I was very forgetful of that virtue, and undiscerning with respect to the memorable constancy of that victor, of whom I now remember better: however great his tribulation, however great the storm he endured in secret, he did not himself cast the burdens from his back; rather, “God,” Scripture says, “turned his back away from burdens.” He endured commendably and waited patiently until God should turn them away. My inner sense was disturbed, and therefore it had almost lost the power of discernment, so that the memory of so great an example, or of similar ones, was shut out.

## CHAPTER XV

But the guardian of Israel, who neither sleeps nor slumbers (Ps. 120), anticipated me by his ever-watchful guardianship, and corrected me by a correction perceptible indeed but ineffable: namely, by a certain sign. Once you have perceived it, you need not be taught by a human being that it is most powerful, according to the saying of Moses: “Most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh” (Num. 16); and according to the Psalmist: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. 103).

How swiftly that sign of his runs! For the same Psalmist says: “He sends forth his word to the earth; his word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147). Although his word runs in very many other and indescribable ways, it also runs swiftly in this way, when he strikes someone by a perceptible sign, so that the entire person, inward and outward at once, trembles and is shaken indescribably in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.

You may think that this belongs to what the Beloved in the Song of Songs says: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (Song 5). Perhaps I may be accused of folly because I have brought this secret into public by writing it down, when one of God’s confidants says concerning greater things: “My secret is for myself; my secret is for myself,” adding, “Woe is me!” (Isa. 24). Why, then, have I become so foolish, unless some necessity compelled me?

For many people, whose eye is not single, disparage the labours of us or of persons like us, and ascribe it to presumption or empty glory that we write and diligently treat the mysteries of Holy Scripture, and consequently receive some honour in Christ’s Church. Yet the Apostle says: “Let elders who rule well be held worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and doctrine” (1 Tim. 5).

But I have this witness in my soul: he who, as I mentioned above, sends forth his word to the earth and whose word runs swiftly, or who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. For I received the ability or ministry of writing from the perceptible infusion of his gift or grace.

> [Note: Col. 0347. Rupert says the same at the beginning of Book VII on Matthew and of Book XII.]

And more than once, when I wished to desist, yielding to certain envious persons who said, “Books are enough for us,” or something similar, he struck me and, by the sign mentioned above, shook me as I trembled, as though beneath a master’s rod.

## CHAPTER XVI

What acts of thanksgiving, then, can I offer him as my due? For unless he had anticipated me in the manner now stated and, understanding my thoughts, corrected me by such a touch—as though saying, “Who are you, that you should fear a mortal man?”—perhaps today I might be thought not Joseph, whose back the Lord, as I mentioned above, turned away from burdens, but in some manner like Esau. In a certain impatience he despised or thought little of his birthright: “Behold, I am dying,” he said; “what will the birthright profit me?” (Gen. 24).

Those birthrights were certain privileges, and above all the dignity of priesthood. The garments of that priesthood were Esau’s exceedingly fine garments, which Rebekah, Scripture says, had with her at home (Gen. 27). Their meaning according to the mystical interpretation is clear and well known: they signify Christ’s gifts, the diversities of the graces of the Holy Spirit, bestowed upon us publicly and privately. Publicly, because they were taken from the Jews and given to the Gentile people; therefore we, all nations, say in the Psalm while clapping our hands: “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. 46). Privately, because in any house of God one person who follows bodily exercise is often passed over, while the one who exercises himself unto godliness (1 Tim. 4) is more abundantly adorned by the grace of the Holy Spirit—signified by Rebekah in that action—who apportions to each as she wills (1 Cor. 12).

Certainly, pastoral care and the teaching of wisdom are no small portion of such garments or ornaments. Hence the Apostle says: “And he gave some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4).

Therefore, whoever, having no reasonable cause, despises and rejects as useless the pastoral care once undertaken, because of impatience at any adversity or difficulty, is certainly not far unlike Esau, who, because of the impatience of hunger, cast away his birthright and said: “Behold, I am dying; what will the birthright profit me?” Consequently, whoever he may be, he is greatly disordered if, after recognizing his foolishness, he strives again to rise to his former position and recover the honour. In this matter he is not at all to be heeded, according to the subsequent example of the same Esau, of whom the Apostle says: “For know that even afterwards, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, though he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12).

Nevertheless, although it says that “he found no place for repentance,” no one of this sort ought to despair of salvation, although he may be compelled to despair of recovering his office of honour.

## CHAPTER XVII

Thus strengthened, I returned, as one who now understood better the counsel of Wisdom, saying: “If the spirit having power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Wis. 10). But did that spirit having power—certainly from the Lord, who gave him power to test holy Job, whom I mentioned at the beginning, whose power is indeed just but whose will is always unjust—cease to rise against me? Rather, he rose persistently. It seemed that little good had been done for us by the cessation of the construction of the aforesaid fortification, because some friends of ours, abusing an opportune time (for they knew the displeasure of one higher in rank, to whom our soul ought to have been subject according to God), had received permission without our knowledge and were building other towers and houses within. We opposed them, indeed, but could not prevent them.

Throughout that whole time, throughout that whole year, when I remember it, what judgment am I to make of myself? In what state did that storm find me? What did it show me about myself? Certainly, unless the Paraclete had suggested among other things also what the Saviour says to us: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light, and like a shining lamp it will enlighten you” (Luke 11), today I should fear exceedingly that perhaps I exceeded measure in my words and did not moderate the vehemence of my most bitter grief.

Do you wish to know the sum of it? I, so insignificant a man, did not hesitate to employ partly the example of so great a leader, Joshua, who, speaking in the Spirit of God, pronounced a severe curse upon anyone who should rebuild the walls of Jericho, as mentioned above (Josh. 6). But how can I know whether this pertained to the example of him whose entire imprecation was as just as it was mystical? This was why, in my exasperation, I said: “Let it be done to those who build in such a manner, nearly besieging us and not allowing us to live in peace, according to Joshua’s imprecation.”

My tongue indeed satisfied an anger that was not unjust; but my mind was not wholly deprived of love. Within, love still lived, at least as a spark of fire usually preserves beneath piled ashes some slight power of its heat. Let that anger, therefore, have been to me like a splinter in the eye (Luke 6). But does it rarely happen, or happen only to us, that people like us suffer such a splinter rushing into the eye—a splinter which even some ill-disposed person may criticize, while failing to consider the beam in his own eye (ibid.), precisely because he is ill-disposed or envious?

Rather, it very often happens that those who have a sweeter love of God are more grievously offended and, through exasperation, become or appear far different from themselves. Therefore the Lord, the examiner of their most tender heart, says to them: “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2).

For example, was not Moses, as Scripture says, “the meekest of all men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12)? Yet he could be exasperated, and his eye was troubled by anger because of the stiff-neckedness of the people subject to him. The Psalmist, who understood this well, says: “Moses was vexed because of them, for they provoked his spirit, and he spoke rashly with his lips” (Ps. 105). How, you ask, did he “speak rashly with his lips”? Namely, by speaking in a manner other than he was accustomed to do. For he said: “Hear, you rebels and unbelievers: can we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Num. 20).

Therefore we who are lowest are not, whenever we are disturbed and, inflamed by excessive zeal, seem to exceed measure in words, immediately to be judged on account of the splinter, as though we were those who carry a great beam of hatred in their eye. For perhaps we do not wish all that we invoke in curse to come to pass, intending only, by whatever means, to be delivered from troublesome people while their life or soul is preserved, although we may appear to curse otherwise.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Why say more? At last, after prolonged affliction, the counsel which one of the friends of blessed Job spoke took hold in my mind—rightly indeed, if only he had prudently considered the person to whom he spoke: “Call, then,” he said, “if there is one who will answer; and turn to some one of the saints” (Job 5).

The wife of the man whose work or building especially grieved us died, and on this occasion, I think, he began to act more gently, so as to enter into an agreement of this kind with me: he would cede to us the house which he had begun to build beneath the tower which he had rebuilt as his own, partly for the sake of his soul and partly upon receiving money. For that house, situated beside the entrance of the castle gate, seemed suitable for distributing alms.

Thus, long afflicted, I thought that I should turn to one of the saints: namely, by building in his honour an oratory above the same gate, so that the aforesaid hospitable house might stand adjoining it. I turned to blessed Lawrence, certainly one of the saints, and especially suited by a special grace to this purpose in accordance with his end. For this was his end: he washed the feet of the holy poor, dried them with linen cloths, and faithfully ministered to them from the treasures or resources of the Church which he had received to dispense, shortly thereafter to accomplish the glorious triumph of martyrdom. Thus his memory is in blessing, in these venerable words of the ancient Scripture: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111).

Judging him a suitable and faithful protector, I immediately laid the foundation of the future oratory. As time allowed—for the severity of winter was approaching—the vaulted structure rose to the height of the gate. In order that it might be protected from snow and winter rains, it had at once to be covered with light material and straw. What event followed such roofing, my brothers?

For when, as was said above, the fire began to rage outside the walls, and those who, as has already been said, had transferred the towers into one legal ownership rushed competitively to them, carrying their movable goods up to the height and fortification which they hoped would be inaccessible or impenetrable to fire, sparks suddenly flew in and, falling upon the straw which covered the aforesaid work, burst into a huge flame. This flame, far more effectual than any engine of war, entered the adjacent tower through its high windows and narrow cracks; then leapt swiftly into a second and third tower; finally, seizing the whole castle and all the timber in the towers as fuel granted to it, it made a dreadful spectacle for all, so that it not only surrounded but actually covered the entire monastery.

## CHAPTER XIX
To you, therefore, may our turning be made firm, O blessed Lawrence; and may you be the one who answers when we call upon you, in accordance with the foretokening of that memorable fragrance by which you seemed to give me a kiss in the presence of the Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal King—as though He were already coming with the clouds, that every eye might see Him, and with Him the thousands of saints, among whom you appeared fiery, and yet like a clear flame, gleaming alike in countenance and clothing.

When He comes, will not the world be examined according to the likeness of this fire which I have recounted—especially since, from the midst of so great a conflagration, [Col. 0351D] from the burning heat of so vast a furnace, the Lord’s body came forth safe and unharmed? Or do we foolishly compare the event that befell us with that great judgment which is to come? By lesser things indeed, on the Lord’s own authority, that same judgment or the kingdom of heaven is compared. Thus it is compared to a harvest of wheat (Mark IV); it is compared to a dragnet or fisherman’s net (Matt. XIII); it is compared to a little leaven in three measures of meal (Luke XIII); it is also compared to a mustard seed (ibid.). In what respect was the judgment enacted by this fire inferior to these or similar things, so that we should not judge ourselves warned, through its likeness, of the wrath to come—that is, the fire of the universal judgment—especially where the presence or providence of that same Judge worked in so many ways, [Col. 0352A] He who will then judge all things together?

For just as that great and final judgment will be conducted in four divisions: one division will be of those who will be judged and saved through judgment; another, of those who will be judged and condemned through judgment (Matt. XXV); likewise one division will be of those who will not be judged but will judge with the Lord (Matt. XIX); and another, of those who will not be judged but will perish without the Law, because they did not receive the Law and sinned without the Law (Rom. II), and therefore have already been judged—so something similar happened now.

One woman, surrounded by the flames of this fire and unable to escape, was miserably burned to death. Some of our possessions, however, were burned, but we ourselves were not; while the Lord’s body, bodily and corporeal, suffered nothing from the fire. [Col. 0352B] The towers, moreover, though they felt nothing, were consumed in a dreadful spectacle—those towers that had been a burden to us.

Therefore, in ourselves, whose possessions partly perished while the place itself was preserved with us, we rightly perceive a likeness of those who will then be judged and saved through judgment, according to the Apostle’s words: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III). Alas, how I feared that my work might burn—that work which is my greatest consolation in this life: namely, the work of the books which I had produced, especially those of which copies existed nowhere else outside this place.

One of them was a little work which I had very recently composed, on the glorification of the Trinity and the procession of the Holy [Col. 0352C] Spirit, in nine volumes or books. For it I was nearly as anxious as a merchant who, having lost all else and despaired of everything, would wish to preserve the one pearl which he had perhaps only lately purchased.

Furthermore, in the burning of the woman—although one ought not to despair concerning her—there is some likeness of those who will be judged and condemned through judgment: that is, the damnation which she endured in her body, they will endure alike in body and soul. In the Lord’s body, bodily and corporeal, which suffered nothing from the fire, is there not some likeness of those who will not be judged but will judge with the Lord? And in the towers, which felt nothing and were burned, is there not some likeness [Col. 0352D] of the proud, who, not possessing the Law, as stated above, will perish without the Law because of their tower-like pride?

Indeed, we assign the likeness of the condemnation of those who perish without the Law more suitably to human towers than to any kind of Christian people, because they sinned without the Law and therefore will perish without the Law—especially since the towers are said to have been the works of such people as sinned without the Law; for they were pagans.

## CHAPTER XX

In what, finally, do we desire the turning by which we turn to you, O most blessed martyr, to be made firm? For we do not take lightly, nor ought we to make little of, the sentence quoted above, even though it was uttered without discernment: “Call then, if there is anyone who will answer you; and turn to one of the saints.” [Col. 0353A]

God Himself, the advocate of blessed Job, against whom this sentence had been strangely uttered, both approved the sentence and, according to that very sentence, honored blessed Job as one of the saints, so that the man who had first spoken to him in this way was made to turn to him. That man had judged the holy man wrongly, thinking that, unless he were wicked, it could by no means happen that he should be struck by so great an affliction.

For Eliphaz the Temanite, beginning first in this manner, said: “Remember, I pray you: who ever perished being innocent? Or when were the upright destroyed?” (Job IV). The implication is: “You have perished and been destroyed.” Proceeding as though Job were a sinner, he said among other things this sentence: “Call then, if there is anyone who will answer you; and turn to one of the saints.” Was he not especially rebuked and commanded to turn to holy Job?

For at the end of the book Scripture relates thus: “After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My wrath is angry against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before Me as My servant Job has. Take therefore for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams; go to My servant Job and offer 234 a burnt offering for yourselves. But My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his person, lest your folly be imputed to you; for you have not spoken rightly to Me as My servant Job has.” So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite departed and did as the Lord had spoken to them; and the Lord accepted Job’s person. [Col. 0353C] “The Lord also turned to Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends” (Job XLII).

We ponder this report in our minds, confessing that we cannot sufficiently marvel at God’s ordering: for to the man who said to so great a man, “Turn to one of the saints,” God said: “You yourself, turn to the holy righteous man to whom you are speaking.” And were you not, O blessed martyr, a kind of Job in your own time?

Indeed, the one holy Catholic Church—the whole body together with its head, Christ—is one Job, according to the likeness or type borne by that blessed man Job. And just as his friends thought wrongly of him when he was grievously afflicted, as though for his crimes, so heretics judged the holy Church wrongly whenever the tempter Satan, having received permission and gained possession of the hearts of impious rulers, struck her from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head (Job II), cruelly persecuting great and small alike. [Col. 0353D]

Yet, just as in one body all members do not have the same function (Rom. XII), so in such a striking all the members of the Church’s body neither underwent the same experiences nor endured equal suffering. You are one member of this body; and while you suffered, all the members rightly suffered with you (I Cor. XII), hearing your cry—the cry of your passion—O most true Job, that is, “the suffering one.” You too, fully understanding this through spiritual knowledge and mystical perception, said to your most faithful companion, who was deeply grieving, with tears and sorrow, over your sufferings: “Rather, be silent, and hide [Col. 0354] Christ in the inner person; then, when I cry out, hear and come.”

For he had said, weeping and sorrowful because of you, when another cried out—namely, a Roman soldier—“I am a Christian,” and for this had died: “Why should I not also cry aloud that I am a Christian, and fall with you?” O how reverently instructed ears receive that saying which you took from his mouth, so as to say, with a subtler meaning of your own: “When I cry out, hear and come.” For you truly said this with that meaning by which it is fitting for the whole Church, together with blessed Job, to say concerning her martyrs: “Earth, earth, do not cover my blood; and let my cry find no hiding-place” (Job XVI), and the words that follow.

## CHAPTER XXI

But you, blessed martyr, as I had begun to say, [Col. 0354B] were a kind of Job in your own time; and now, and unto the end of the age, Christ hears your cry—the great cry of your passion—and so does Christ’s Church. For the earth could not cover it, nor did it find in her any place of concealment.

And what, or what kind of earth, is that? Surely it is that very earth from which the blood of Abel, the first martyr, cries to God (Gen. IV)—indeed, the blood of Christ, of whom that righteous Abel bore the type. This earth is the universal Church. She first heard your cry and first cried out with it; and she taught us to cry out with her in words of this kind. These were first the words of the often-mentioned Job, but they are no less the words of the holy Church in her afflictions, and they are most fittingly applicable to you:

“My prayer is pure; and therefore I ask that a place be given to my voice in heaven, because there [Col. 0354C] is my Judge and my Witness on high” (Job XI).

And again:

“He tested me like gold which passes through fire. My foot followed His steps; I kept His way and did not turn aside from it. I did not depart from the commands of His lips, and I hid the words of His mouth in my bosom” (Job XXIII).

Because of such a cry, we turn to you; and while we hear also the clarity of your own voice—the words of your mouth—spoken in that most noble and splendid contest of yours, in which you confessed and praised God our Savior amid the fire, under the pressure of the flame surrounding you, we weigh the words of that confession of yours, truly worthy of being weighed as in a balance.

What do we see in you, O most blessed soul, except that Shulammite whom the Beloved loves, crying and saying: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, [Col. 0354D] that we may behold you” (Song VI)? Who is this Shulammite except faith? She was awaited in order that she might return, because she had almost disappeared among humankind. For nearly all gloried not in Abraham’s faith but in the flesh.

Just as formerly free Sarah, because she was barren, was despised, while Hagar the slave woman, because she was fruitful, was chosen (Gen. XVI), so the faith by which Abraham was justified was neglected, and nearly all gloried in the Law according to the flesh. Freeborn faith was regarded as contemptible, according to the name *Sunamitis* [Shulammite], which is interpreted “captive” or “despised.” But she returned and appeared upon the earth—this free woman, this noble woman, this daughter of the prince, namely God—when the believing Virgin, receiving the Word, conceived [Col. 0355A] and bore the Son, the prince of freedom, the firstborn of the children of faith, who from that time were multiplied throughout the world and will be multiplied until the end of the age.

She spoke in you, and Christ beheld her in you. But the tyrant did not see her; he could not seize her with his hands. When you walked in the fire, she was not burned (Isa. XLIII); hence it is most truly written: “And the flame shall not burn in you” (ibid.), because the flame did indeed burn outwardly, but wrought no injury inwardly.

How, then, do we see this Shulammite in you? Truly, as the strong woman in whom her husband’s heart trusts (Prov. XXXI), and who, among her other works of strength, also gave a girdle to the Canaanite (ibid.): that is, she magnificently strengthened you, who were lowly in your own eyes and humble in spirit.

[Col. 0355B] Otherwise, O most blessed one, why did you weep when Sixtus departed with his other deacons, unless you regarded yourself as a kind of Canaanite—that is, a base and sinful person, unworthy of the same or a similar glory of martyrdom? Had you not regarded yourself as unworthy, you could have cried out that you were a Christian without awaiting the blessing of a man, however holy, however much a bishop and teacher.

Therefore she rightly gave you a girdle; and by girding you, because you were humble in your own eyes, she showed and made known that you were great in the eyes of the Lord: that is, not a Canaanite but a son of the kingdom. What did she do, by contrast, to kings or sons of the kingdom—namely, to those who are great in their own eyes? She certainly did not give them a girdle; rather, she took away the belt which they seemed to possess, according to the words of the often-mentioned holy Job: “He loosens,” he says, “the belt of kings [Col. 0355C] and girds their loins with a rope” (Job XII).

## CHAPTER XXII

Behold, my mouth has spoken these things from the abundance of my heart, turned toward you (Matt. XII), because abundant in that heart is the anxiety of one walking between hope and fear. For I set out upon the road of all flesh, knowing that we must all be made manifest before Christ’s tribunal (II Cor. V). And, to express this in the words of the same blessed Job: “Behold, my brief years pass away, and I walk the path by which I shall not return” (Job XIV).

O how dreadful is this departure! A Christian is neither permitted—indeed, has no leisure—to ignore or disguise this dread, since not only does meditation seize him when awake, but a wakeful trembling also takes hold of him when asleep; so that his soul continually refuses consolation and remembers God (Ps. [Col. 0355D] LXXVI), and, before it sees His face, can never be secure.

I confess that I would not say these things except from experience; nor, unless taught by experiences, would I clearly understand what the aforementioned holy man also says: “If I say, ‘My bed shall comfort me, and I shall be relieved while speaking with myself upon my couch,’ You terrify me through dreams, and strike me with horror through visions” (Job VII).

Why should I be ashamed to confess that such terror or horror has sometimes happened to me? During the night I saw myself proceeding to Christ’s tribunal. From the face of Him seated upon the throne, many wretched people appeared to flee so horribly that, after that vision, I no longer need to be taught by a human being or through a human being what or how great is that which says: “Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered; and let those who hate Him flee from before His face” (Ps. LXVII). [Col. 0356A]

As far as I can remember, I walked with great fear and in a spirit of humility: greatly fearing indeed, but also possessing much hope. I feared that, when I had come to the point of needing to stand before that tribunal and see His face, I might recoil in terror; yet I hoped that I would find that same face gracious—the face from which, as I have said, many tried with unspeakable flight to flee, though they could not escape.

Behind my back followed exceedingly foul spirits in an innumerable multitude, waiting for me to turn back and flee from the face of Him seated upon the throne, so that they might immediately seize me and carry me away into the condemnation allotted to their party. Before that, they did not dare touch me at all. [Col. 0356B]

As I have said, they followed behind my back and walked likewise on my right and left; nevertheless, no crowd pressed upon me. On every side there was spacious room for my solitary advance, and before my face an unobstructed view, with none running before or going ahead.

In such a procession I seemed to enter the Lord’s temple, in which there was an image of a throne and of Christ, our Judge and Savior, seated upon it; around Him sat, as it were, the senators of judgment and princes of God’s kingdom. With what voice, in what words, could I express the horror of the many fleeing but not escaping from His face, as I have said?

Having entered before His face, I immediately sat down, exceedingly frightened, among many who were upon the face of the earth—that is, upon the pavement—received as though into a house of refuge. And looking back, I saw none of those who had pursued me, except that one serpent, creeping over the ground with its whole body, raising only its head and stretching out its tongue, seemed, I know not how, to be devising occasions against me. When I had seen these things, I immediately awoke from sleep. [Col. 0356C]

## CHAPTER XXIII

Whatever these things may be, O thrice and four-times blessed martyr, who does not know that we must all stand before Christ’s tribunal? (I Cor. V). There indeed, whoever loves Christ will have confidence. Thus John says in his Epistle: “In this love has been made perfect with us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgment” (I John IV). Likewise: “And now, little children, remain in Him, that when He appears we may have confidence and not be put to shame before Him at His coming” (I John II). [Col. 0356D]

So that you may be a helper to me in attaining such confidence, I turn to you with a sacrifice of good will; and if it is willing, says the Apostle, it is accepted according to what it has, not according to what it does not have (II Cor. VIII). And indeed, if life accompanies me, I hope that this will may have its effect: that it may fulfill the vow which it began concerning the work mentioned above—that you, who rest in the heavenly kingdom as worthy chancellor of Christ the King and of His most mighty mother, the Queen, may also be the special patron and guardian of this place dedicated to God and to that same perpetual Virgin.

And may no secular power be free to preside over these fortresses, long half-ruined and now half-burned; for it is in no way expedient for monastic profession to endure cohabitation with, or so [Col. 0357A] close a bordering upon, an alien manner of life.

Nevertheless, however the end or completion may turn out of this man-made foundation which I have made, I hope that the will—which, as I have said, is willing—will be accepted. And just as, in the burnt offering of seven bulls and seven rams, the friends of blessed Job were accepted when the Lord said: “But Job my servant will pray for you, and I will accept his person, lest your folly be imputed to you; for you have not spoken rightly to Me [Col. 0358A] as My servant Job has” (Job XLII), so we too shall be accepted through you in good will—provided that we sacrifice that hardness which most needs slaughter, like the neck of a bull, and that presumption like the head of a ram: that is, presumptuous mastery or leadership in the flock of the Christian people. Then the Lord will turn to you, O blessed man, and accept your person as you pray for your friends.

Alas, what an uncertain course we run; but you, Lawrence, bear the laurel, tested by fire as gold.

[Col. 0357]

**Of the Reverend Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz: On the Meditation of Death**

**Book One**

### Chapter I

[Col. 0357B]

What now, O soul? At least from this point be more instructed, and for the time that remains live according to the life of the wise, which is meditation upon death. For now is especially your time for weeping and mourning (Eccl. III), after the empty months which you possessed have swiftly passed, and the laborious nights which you counted for yourself; so that, in truthful regard to your conscience, you can say: “The fear which I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened” (Job III).

When the Apostle spoke of his pressures or tribulations, he said: “We ourselves had within ourselves the answer of death, that we should not trust in ourselves” (II Cor. I). We neither can nor wish to compare our small matters with those great matters of so great an Apostle. Yet there is sometimes some likeness between small and great things, though they are unlike: thus, a little ant gathering grain at harvest is rightly said to resemble a great and wise man who provides for himself by good deeds for the life of the age to come. [Col. 0357C]

Thus, by a certain likeness, we small people may use the words of the great Apostle now before us, because many lesser persons have experienced enough to say with him: “But we ourselves had within ourselves the answer of death, that we should not trust in ourselves.” Therefore, O little soul, train yourself in the life of the wise, which, as I have said, is meditation upon death. Remember how often you too have received the answer of death, so that you ought not to take delight in any delay or lengthening of this present life.

### Chapter II

[Col. 0357D]

But when you, O human being, are invited to the meditation of death, is this alone said to you: that you should remember you are going to die? Indeed, even this alone is useful to meditate upon, because of the care, anxiety, and fear of rendering an account at the hour of your departure. For this reason Wisdom says: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII). Yet the whole meditation of death is not exhausted in this alone, nor is the life of the wise thereby perfected—just as the fear of the Lord, which Scripture calls holy and enduring for ever and ever (Ps. XVIII), is not full or perfect when someone avoids sin solely through fear of Gehenna.
