In what, then, does the fuller meditation of death, which perfects the life of the wise, consist? Surely in faithfully believing and firmly knowing that God most beneficially inflicted bodily death upon the human being, because that human being was dead in soul through sin, and forbade him to live forever. And in knowing that from death comes the treasure of life and salvation through Jesus Christ, who deigned to become a participant in our mortality.

Concerning this treasure, [Col. 0358C] the Lord’s words to blessed Job are rightly understood: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or seen the treasuries of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?” (Job XXXVIII). For, besides the moral meaning, by the names of snow and hail are rightly understood all the afflictions which God justly brought upon the human race, including death itself, the sum of all afflictions.

Who, I ask, except God alone, or God’s Son alone, entered such snow and saw such hail in such a way as to bring forth treasures from them? That is, who endured all afflictions and death itself among impious people, built up in the coldness of unbelief, in such a way that, through the very fact that He suffered death, He stored up for us the delight and exultation of eternal life?

[Col. 0358D] “And indeed, I prepared this snow and this hail,” He says, “for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war”: that is, because of the enmity of the ancient serpent and the opposition or rebellion of the human being who consented to him, God brought in affliction and death, saying, “Cursed is the earth in your work,” and the rest, down to “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return,” or down to “lest he eat of the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. III). [Col. 0359A]

But these things, thus imposed upon humanity, in turn became instruments of life and salvation through the grace of God, who knows in a wondrous and ineffable way how to make good use of our evils. This is our proposition, and upon these matters we wish to dwell diligently in this little work which it pleases us to call *Meditation on Death*. The occasion for writing it was the danger of fire which I recounted in the preceding little book, in which the Lord’s body—the memorial of that same Lord’s death—was marvelously preserved, as the Apostle says: “As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes” (I Cor. XI).

### Chapter III

Let all the dead, therefore, whose resurrection shall be unto life, [Col. 0359B] first give thanks to their God and bless Him because He devised such a plan concerning them: since the human being was dead by the death of the soul, which is the commission of sin, he was not allowed to live forever in the life of the flesh or body.

We too, who now live—or rather are dead, that is, are certainly going to die—of whom the Apostle says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification” (Rom. VIII): we, I say, knowing and considering how useless it would have been for the sinful human being to eat of the tree of life and live forever, and at the same time knowing and beholding by faith how great a benefit has come through death, because life has wonderfully been drawn from death, open our mouths and draw breath to bless you [Col. 0359C] and give thanks to you, O God, according to our measure.

And because none of us is sufficient for this, behold, I, “the refuse of all” (I Cor. IV), strive to invite every power to aid this desire of blessing, and I say with such cry of heart as I can: “Let heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them bless You for this discovery which You discovered, and which You alone could discover through Your wisdom” (Dan. III), as is plainly written in Job: “I have found whereby I may be merciful to him” (Job XXXIII).

What is that which You have found, whereby You are merciful to the human race, except the discovery of such death—not the death of the soul but of the body? It follows: “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth” [Col. 0359D] (ibid.). How true this is—how great and wretched is the wasting by which human flesh has been or is consumed—the graves of the dead most clearly answer when, sometimes opened by some accident, they cast out bones which the earth had received clothed in skin and flesh, as the same Scripture says a little earlier: “His flesh will waste away, and the bones which had been covered will be laid bare” (ibid.).

And indeed, in this there is mourning, or cause for mourning; but consolation softens that same mourning in the wise person’s heart, whose whole life, as I proposed above, is the meditation of death. For the fruit of such wasting is this, which God Himself, having been made merciful, says: “Let him return to the days of his youth.” You must understand that a human being had to die or be consumed for this reason: so that, through a mercy not unjust, he might be renewed [Col. 0360A] into that for which he had been created—namely, eternal life. This life is beautifully signified by days of youth because it will never wither or fail through any old age; it will never be dried up by any antiquity, nor, when restored—indeed, repaired to a state far better than before—will it lose the beauty of its vigor.

### Chapter IV

Where, when, and with what intention, O God, did You discover this discovery? For we perceive that what You said—“I have found whereby I may be merciful to him”—is not of small weight. Let the diligent soul therefore stand here longer in meditation, remembering what Wisdom said: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. VII). For there the end of all is recognized, and the living human being considers what he will become. [Col. 0360B]

And indeed the Lord Himself speaks of such people: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). Therefore, so that I may more delightfully discover the things I have asked—namely, where, when, and with what intention God discovered this, so that human flesh should be consumed by death, and how or how many times He brings about that same consuming—I wish to set down here the entire chapter from which I took this verse: “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth.”

This is the chapter:

> “Through a dream, I say, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon human beings and they sleep in bed, then, opening the ears of men and instructing them, He trains them by discipline, that He may turn the human being away from what he has done and free him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption [Col. 0360C] and his life from passing into the sword. He also rebukes through pain upon the bed and causes all his bones to waste away. Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food formerly desired by his soul; his flesh will waste away and the bones that had been covered will be laid bare. His soul will draw near to corruption and his life to mortal things. If there is an angel speaking for him, one among like beings [Vulgate: one among a thousand], to declare the human being’s righteousness, He will have mercy on him and say: ‘Deliver him, and let him not descend into corruption; I have found whereby I may be merciful to him.’ His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth. He will pray to God, and God will be gracious to him; he will see His face with joy, and He will restore to the human being his righteousness. He will look upon people and say: ‘I have sinned and truly transgressed, and I did not receive what I deserved. I have delivered his soul from going into destruction, but living he shall see the light.’ Behold, God does all these things three times for each person, to call back their souls from corruption and illuminate them with the light of the living” (Job XXXIII). [Col. 0360D]

Nearly all these things must be understood according to the literal sense, which is most weighty and most sacred, in keeping with the purpose before us, namely the meditation of death—except for what was first said: “Through a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon human beings and they sleep in bed.”

For these things must be understood anagogically: by dream, vision of the night, falling sleep, and sleep in bed—a manifold circumlocution—you are to understand the holy leisure of sacred meditation. That is, the ears of the heart are opened only to those whose minds are at rest: whom love of this world does not disturb; whom the enticement of this present life does not delight; whose heart does not wake in avarice. Such people clearly hear and rightly understand that the saying, “lest he also eat of the tree and live forever” (Gen. III), and elsewhere, “My Spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI), is not so much the sentence of an avenger’s wrath as the providence of advising mercy; not so much the vengeance of a judicial sword as the discipline of a fatherly rod. [Col. 0361A]

Nevertheless, let it be called wrath; let this discipline be called anger. “Behold,” says the prophet, “You were angry, for we sinned; and we all fell like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, carried us away” (Isa. LXIV). And when the Psalmist had yielded to this discipline—that is, mortality or death—saying, “In the morning let it pass like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither” (Ps. XCIX), he immediately added: “For we have failed in Your wrath and have been troubled in Your anger” (ibid.).

In another prophet also, God Himself calls this discipline, or these sufferings of which it is written here, “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings,” not merely wrath but even “most grievous judgments,” when He says: “Even if I send my four most grievous judgments—sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—upon Jerusalem, to destroy from it human being and beast, yet there shall remain in it a remnant bringing forth sons and daughters” (Ezek. XIV). [Col. 0361C]

So let it be called thus. For this opinion does no harm; indeed, it greatly benefits and cooperates with God’s intention or purpose—just as, if a boy, while being sharply beaten by his father, imagines it to be anger, though his father strikes out of love and loves in striking, knowing what is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. XIII).

### Chapter V
Accordingly, with what purpose God the Father has struck his children with this rod, so that according to the flesh they might be consumed by sufferings, this Scripture plainly states when it says: “That he may turn man away from the things which he has done, and free him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption and his life from passing into the sword.” [Col. 0361D] Truly a great saying. For this reason, it says, that he may free man from pride and prevent his life from passing into the sword, he instructs him by such discipline. First he rebukes him through pain upon his bed, and causes all his bones to waste away. This often happens from a slight fever: one who shortly before seemed strong to himself soon has his limbs dried up, cannot even stand upon his feet—indeed, has no strength even to sit—and lies wholly unable to bear his pain upon his bed. Bread, or every kind of food previously desirable, then becomes so abhorrent to him that, forcing himself to eat while his stomach resists, he often casts it up in vomiting. He is shaken all over with trembling, though shortly before he delighted in mounting a horse or being carried about, whether he was a most powerful king [Col. 0362A] or a noble commander. Hence one of the mightiest kings, while he was fiercely pressed by a violent fever toward imminent death, is reported to have said: “Woe, woe! How great is that king who so powerfully binds mighty kings!”

Further, if you have not yet sufficiently learned how truly a dead body wastes away, as he says, “His flesh shall waste away, and the bones that were covered shall be laid bare,” go, whoever you are, to the tombs of the dead. As I said above, they themselves will answer you and show you, to the full satisfaction of your eyes; and if the corpses are more recent, so that some moisture remains, they will show you, to the full satisfaction of the stench—more than your nostrils can endure. In order, I say, to free him from pride, to rescue his soul from corruption, and to prevent his life from passing into the sword, he thus rebukes him; for this reason he will thus cause his flesh to waste away, the following sentence having been pronounced: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III). Thus the bones that had been covered with skin, flesh, and all the sinews are laid bare. In what other way could he be freed from pride? Even now the frivolity of this creature is scarcely brought down to the weight of humility. Every day we die, and the dead are buried by the living, who are themselves certainly to die; yet meanwhile most people are so puffed up by the presumption of a proud heart that they eagerly forget that they are human beings. Such persons are gravely censured in the Scriptures: Assyria, Pharaoh, Tyre or the king of Tyre, and also the king of Babylon. Under their names Scripture reproves above all the devil, because he “set his heart as the heart of God,” saying, “I am God, and I have sat on the throne of God” (Isa. XIV), since such [Col. 0362C] men, through the vice of such ambition, were like him.

For what would they be reproved if they could hope that what is said here would not come to pass: “His flesh shall waste away, and the bones that were covered shall be laid bare”? What, I say, if man did not die, just as the devil does not die? By what, or through what, are they freed from pride, so that his soul may not descend into corruption and his life may not pass into the sword—understood as that sword into which the devil passed, namely, into the judgment of eternal damnation? For he passed into that sword because of pride. It must be carefully observed that the text does not say that the sword passed into him, but that he “passed into the sword.” The sense is entirely different when the sword is said to pass, as there: “And if I say to the sword, ‘Pass through the land’” (Ezek. XIV), and here, where a man is said to pass, or not to pass, into the sword. The passage of the sword through the land signifies a transitory punishment; the passage of the proud man into the sword indicates everlasting damnation.

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore your purpose, O God, is praiseworthy and worthy of every thanksgiving: for this reason you willed us to be mortal, so that we might be freed from pride and, consequently, might not pass into that evil sword. It is indeed remarkable that the devil, although he has passed into that sword, is still proud. But is it not less remarkable in men, the sons of pride, who still act proudly while knowing and confessing that they are mortal and soon to die? For they say:

> “Short and wearisome is the time of our life,  
> because we were born from nothing,  
> and after this we shall be as though we had not been.  
> For the time allotted to us is the passing of a shadow,  
> and there is no return from our end,  
> because it has been sealed, and no one returns.  
> Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that exist,  
> and make swift use of creation as in youth.  
> Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments,  
> and let not the flower of time pass us by.  
> Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither;  
> let there be no meadow which our revelry does not traverse.  
> Let none of you be without a share in our revelry.”  
> (Wis. II)

When they say these things and others like them, is their hardness less astonishing than that of their king, Satan, of whom the Lord says to blessed Job: “He himself is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI)? [Col. 0363B] For from the very thing by which they should have been humbled—namely, the certainty of death—they become more proudly desperate, plainly in imitation of the devil. Though he knows himself to be condemned and to have passed into the sword irrevocably, he is nevertheless still proud.

Scripture intends us to marvel greatly at the hardness of so great a rebellion when it says in the book of Revelation: “One of the heads of the beast was as though slain unto death, and the wound of its death was healed” (Rev. XIII). Again: “It made the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed” (ibid.). And afterwards: “Let them make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived” (ibid.). For the devil, who dwelt wholly in Antichrist, is that blood-stained beast which has the wound of the sword and lives, and whose wound of death [Col. 0363C] was healed. Certainly he lived, or lives, falsely, and the wound of his death was falsely healed; for in truth he is dead, and the wound of his death cannot be healed. Yet he wishes to be regarded as living and the wound of his death to appear healed—that wound of the sword, namely, the sentence of eternal damnation which he received in heaven, from which he fell irrecoverably.

In what respect does he wish himself to appear alive, or the wound of his death to appear healed? Clearly in this: that, while his ambition for divinity remains—the ambition by which he swelled with pride in heaven—he presents himself as God to deceived human beings and strives to be worshipped as the living God, although he is the dead devil. In imitation of him, I say, these men are proud in this manner: while professing that they know that they will soon die, they say, “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither,” and the rest, adding, “For this is our portion and this is our lot” (Wis. II). Even if some such persons sometimes mourn, they perceive no true reason why they ought to mourn.

## CHAPTER VII

Against such people the holy man says: “What is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should be patient? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job VI). Certainly the strengths of these things—stones and bronze—differ in sound when struck, but both are without sensation. Their sounds differ so greatly that bronze, when struck, not only rings more clearly than stone, but also produces sweet and pleasing harmony when the proper numerical proportions are observed in its weight. Yet, as has already been said, both are without soul and feel absolutely nothing.

By this comparison, are not those whose words we set forth above stones? They refuse to feel the pains of death; indeed, precisely because they know they will die, they speak most harshly and proudly, and because they are going to die they strive hurriedly to seize every pleasure beforehand. Plainly they are stones, and their strength is the strength of stones, because not only do they not utter a groan, but they are even said to count it praise and glory that they disdain to utter one.

But those who read or chant words of groaning, yet do not care to grasp or attend to their meaning—for example, “The groans of death surrounded [Col. 0364B] me; the pains of hell surrounded me” (Ps. CXIV), and many other such sayings in the Scriptures—differ from the persons just mentioned in this regard only as the sound of bronze differs from the sound of stones. Of such people you may rightly say that their flesh is bronze. Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. XIII).

Therefore you also, O my soul, make it possible for yourself to say truthfully: “My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze.” How? By doing this: not merely allowing the groans of death to surround you and the perils of hell to find you, but finding the pains themselves, as the passage says. For after first saying, “The pains of death surrounded me; the perils of hell found me,” it immediately adds: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXIV). Have this additional thing, O sensitive soul; have this more than the strength of stones and the ringing of bronze or cymbals. For the pains of death surround all human beings because of the sin of one, and the perils of hell find them; but not all find tribulation and sorrow, because very many have been and are insensible. Only the perceptive, only the faithful and elect, have found tribulation and sorrow and called upon the name of the Lord. That is, they felt and understood the unhappiness of their condition, which befell them in Adam; and they turned to the Lord God, hoping, desiring, [Col. 0364D] and with tears entreating him for the twofold resurrection of the dead.

## CHAPTER VIII

How did they find tribulation and sorrow? How did they call upon the name of the Lord? Abraham was the first to say: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.” The first, I say. For although some righteous persons, of whom there were a number before him, may have been able to say the same, he is nevertheless the first in Scripture to have the testimony of this devout confession. Likewise, according to the narrative of Scripture, he was the first to lament and weep for the dead. “Sarah died,” it says, “and Abraham came to lament and weep for her. And when he rose from the funeral observance, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying: ‘I am a stranger and sojourner among you; give me a right to a burial-place among you, that I may bury my dead’” (Gen. XXIII).

Even if others before him lamented and wept for their dead and dutifully buried them, nevertheless, since Scripture mentions none of them, we should recognize that it judged Abraham first worthy of recording his lamentation, weeping, and care for burial. In the latter respect, namely, his diligence concerning burial, there is no doubt that he possessed faith in the resurrection, as the Apostle testifies concerning him: “He who had received the promises offered up his only-begotten son, to whom it was said, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called,’ judging that God is able to raise even from the dead” (Heb. XI). In the former respect, however—that is, lamentation or weeping—we may say that this faithful man, being wise, had found, that is, understood, tribulation and sorrow: the tribulation of the soul’s death and the sorrow of bodily death. These two are alike, and there is much to say about them according to the same understanding of faith possessed by that father of believers, especially because in the chapter taken above from the book of blessed Job it is written: “If there shall be an angel speaking for him one thing of the like things, to declare man’s righteousness” (Job XXXIII), and so forth.

These two, I say, are alike: the death of the soul and the death of the body, although they differ greatly in the magnitude of their tribulation and sorrow. In what are they alike? Namely, in this: just as a body abandoned by its spirit is a corpse, and rots, stinks, is dissolved into mud, and becomes useless ashes and insignificant dust, so the soul, abandoned by its Creator because of sin, is dead and becomes a kind of corpse and the tomb of a certain corruption. Thus the Lord speaks in Ezekiel concerning the multitude of the reprobate, and the devil, their prince and author of their death: “There, namely in the pit of hell, are Assyria and all its multitude; their graves are around it, all slain, who fell by the sword, whose graves have been given in the furthest parts of the pit” (Ezek. XXXII).

## CHAPTER IX

The wise person is always mindful of that death, and its remembrance is bitter to him: the death in which the transgressing soul, abandoned by the Spirit of the living God, becomes the tomb of the dead one, namely the devil. Yet when he sees before his eyes the likeness of that death—that is, the bodily death of someone dear to him—for he sees what the body has become when the soul is absent, [Col. 0365D] then he recalls that great death more fully and appropriately, affected in two ways: on the one hand by the loss of a beloved person, whose companionship had in some measure comforted him; on the other, by contemplation of that person’s soul and also, without doubt, of his own, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Have pity on your own soul, pleasing God” (Sir. XXX).

For who now knows concerning his own soul whether it is worthy of love or hatred, of life—which is God—or of death (Eccl. IX)? Therefore it was neither done vainly nor written without purpose that an old man lamented and wept for an old woman, Scripture saying: “Abraham came to lament and weep for her.” It must be carefully noticed that it says Abraham “came to lament and weep for her,” and does not say whence he came. For it cannot be inferred from this passage of Scripture that Abraham was absent when she died. Therefore, when he is said to have come, the reference is not so much to bodily movement or the walking of feet as to the attention of the heart and the application of the senses to meditation upon so great a matter.

Already, without written instruction, he understood what Wisdom said and wrote much later through Solomon: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Sir. VII). “For there the end of all human beings is brought to mind, and the living person considers what he shall become.” Such mourning or weeping truly befitted Abraham’s old age. By his gray head—indeed, by the grayness of his mind—he left to his children, that is, to all who seek wisdom, an example worthy of them: he preferred to go to the house of mourning rather than the house of feasting, with the purpose that they might be willing [Col. 0366B] to be reminded what the end of all human beings is, and that the living person might consider what, and of what kind, he shall become.

This is indeed a great instrument of that deliverance of which we began above to treat according to these words of Scripture: “That he may turn man away from the things which he has done, and free him from pride.” But who is sufficient for these things by himself? For it is God’s gift, God’s grace, to have a tender or soft heart, able to bend to such lamentation or weeping, according to the words of holy Job: “God has softened my heart” (Job XXIII). That this might abound more and more, the same man says: “Release me therefore, O Lord, that I may weep a little for my sorrow before I go and do not return, to a dark land covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job X).

For what does it mean to say, “Release me,” except as if he said: “Do not harden my heart as the hearts of those are hardened whose strength, as we mentioned above, is the strength of stones and whose flesh is bronze, so that they do not feel their sorrow”? Finally, God is rightly said not to release but to shut in those who are of this kind, as the same man says later: “If he shuts in a man, there is none to open” (Job XII). By “shutting in” a person he means hardening him: he does not judge him worthy to receive the grace of tears or the perception of sorrow, so that he may say what I recalled above: “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. CXIV); or: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. XLI).

For the text continues: “If he holds back the waters, all things shall dry up” (Job XII). Its meaning is this: where his grace does not work—the grace which alone can give the weeping of which we speak—human hearts are hardened. And immediately it adds: “If he sends them forth, they will overturn the earth” (ibid.). That is to say: if he who alone can give sends forth the waters of tears, they will soften the hardness of those same hearts, or overturn our earthliness.

## CHAPTER X

We must now proceed more deeply in this meditation upon death, and meditate in such a way that, through the merit of faith, the meditation may be worthy before the sight of the Lord, as it is written: “And the meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. XVIII). How? Surely by meditating not only on our own death, which the first man incurred through pride and disobedience and left to us all as an inheritance, but also—and above all—on the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, who by dying conquered our death and by rising restored life.

Let us therefore follow the chapter written above. After it said, “And instructing, he teaches by discipline, that he may turn man away from the things which he has done and free him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption and his life from passing into the sword,” it adds: “He rebukes also through pain on the bed, and causes all his bones to waste away. Bread becomes abhorrent to him in his life, and food previously desirable to his soul. His flesh shall waste away, and the bones that were covered shall be laid bare. His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to deadly things.” Then at last it adds: “If there shall be an angel speaking for him [Col. 0367B] one thing of the like things, to declare man’s righteousness, he will have mercy on him and say: ‘Deliver him, that he may not descend into corruption. I have found that whereby I may be gracious to him,’” and so forth. “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth” (Job XXXIII).

I have already said that the two like things are two deaths, one of the soul and the other of the body; and this one verse of Scripture briefly indicates both. “His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to deadly things.” Here corruption is rightly understood as death, to which the soul even of every elect person has drawn near, but has not descended into that same corruption, namely death: although set apart in darkness, it was freed from the punishments of eternal damnation through faith in Jesus Christ, whose coming all the saints from the beginning of the world awaited.

The devil himself is corruption, for death is his name. But “deadly things” are all the sufferings of his death, which is the dissolution of the body. To these deadly things the life by which a human being lives in the body has so drawn near that he has not only been prevented from eating of the tree of life, by which he might live forever, but his days are also shorter than they were in the early age of the world. For, as the Psalmist says: “The days of our years are seventy years; but if in the strong, eighty years, and what is beyond them is labour and sorrow” (Ps. LXXXIX).

And in what these two are alike—the death of the soul and the death of the body—has already been said: namely, just as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and just as the body rots and returns to dust when the soul departs, so the soul becomes dark when God abandons it because of sin, and becomes the tomb of eternal corruption, namely, the devil. It remains now to say who or what sort of angel spoke one of these like things, what or what sort of thing that one was, and what or what sort of speech declared man’s righteousness.

## CHAPTER XI

This Angel is the Son of God. He differs—and it is not unknown, or ought not to be unknown, to anyone—that this Angel differs greatly from all other angels, both holy spirits and holy human beings, who themselves are called and are angels on account of a certain dignity of spiritual office, as in this passage: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). It differs greatly, I say, because this Angel is by nature God and Lord, and is an angel by the condescension of his office; for all others are his creatures and servants.

Therefore this Angel, on account of his own excellence, is fittingly called simply and without qualification “angel,” when Scripture says: “If there shall be an angel speaking for him one thing of the like things.” But all the others are called angels *of the Lord*. For this Angel, as has already been said, is the Lord himself; he has become the angel, that is, the messenger, not of some lord above himself, but of his own word, as it is written concerning him in the prophet Amos: “For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, declaring his word to man—the Lord God of hosts is his name” (Amos IV). Of which angels, that is, messengers, was such a description ever spoken, or ought it to have been spoken—“declaring his own word to man”—except of this one, whose name is the Lord God of hosts? [Col. 0368B]

For all angels, whoever have been sent to announce—on which account they are called angels, or, as the Apostle says, “ministering spirits sent forth for service on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation” (Heb. I)—all of them, I say, announced another’s word, namely God’s. But this one alone announced his own word, for he is God. He who similarly wished to announce his own word, and presumed to speak from himself, announced not truth but falsehood; this is the fallen angel—indeed, not an angel but the devil.

Therefore, when it says, “If there shall be an Angel speaking for him one thing of the like things,” it is the same as if it said: “If God shall take upon himself for man one of man’s two deaths,” which two deaths are the two like things in the likeness mentioned above. But how could this happen unless God first became man? For God was and is in his own nature immortal, impassible, incomprehensible, and invisible. Thus, in the saying “one of the like things,” it is rightly understood that God foretold that he would become man and die for man. Who could bear to hear it if that prophetic Spirit had expressed this meaning in common and explicit words? Therefore he necessarily enclosed and sealed the meaning, calling God—the Son of God—“Angel,” and saying “one of the like things” in order to say “the death of the flesh,” by which every human being dies.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0368D]

Here is weight in meditation, or meditation in weight. For when this Angel had become man and wished it to be known that he had come as the world required, having in view that one of the like things, he said: “Blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me” (Matt. XI). What is it to be scandalized in him except to refuse to believe in him because, as a mortal man, he was seized, could die, and could be crucified? Hence the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. I).

To what end is this? Clearly, we marvel at the blessedness of the grace which this Angel bestowed upon us through the Holy Spirit: because not only are we not scandalized in him on this account, but we are all the more firmly established in faith in him. For unless this Angel were God, he could by no means have become the man who would truly die according to the reality of our nature. What then? Could a created angel, who certainly is not God, have assumed human nature? Angels could indeed appear, and are recorded as having appeared, in the form of human beings, as here: “When Abraham lifted up his eyes, behold, three men appeared to him, standing near him” (Gen. XVIII). But none of them ever appeared in the reality of human nature except this one, who assumed the reality of our nature in such a way that he also spoke one of the like things—that is, died a real death of the flesh.

Therefore we are not scandalized in him; rather, we are more firmly established in faith. For since he truly died, it is evident that he is truly human; and since he was able to assume true human nature, it is evident that this Angel alone is God. For God alone is so subtle that a rational creature can be capable of receiving his substance. Neither human creature is capable of angelic creature, nor angelic creature of human creature, because neither is more subtle than the other—namely, neither angel than the human soul, nor human soul than angel. God alone, as has already been said—the Creator of both, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is far more subtle than either angel or human being, and consequently is capable of both angel and human being. Of these three persons, this one, namely the Son of God, who is the Angel, willed human nature to be capable of himself in such a way that, becoming one person with humanity, he became so truly human as to speak one of the like things, that is, to die.

## CHAPTER XIII

What sort of speech is this? Or why is the death of this Angel called speech when it says, “If there shall be one speaking for him”—that is, for man—“one of the like things”? It is because he is God to whom he spoke or speaks, and to whom all things speak through their movements, for he understands all things. Yet the passion of this Angel, namely his Son, is especially speech. For if the blood of the saints cries out to him—as he himself says to Cain, “Behold, the voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV)—how much more does his blood speak to him? Hence the Apostle says: “You have come to Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and to the sprinkling of blood which speaks better than Abel” (Heb. XII).

Therefore the death of this Angel is truly speech; and, if it pleases you to hear it, it is also the writing of a testament. Let us go to that Scripture to which this same Angel sent us in the passage mentioned above, after he had said, “Blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me.” “What,” he says, “did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face’” (Mal. III). Let us go there, I say, and see what follows. It says: “And immediately the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (ibid.).

This was said concerning John the Baptist by the person of God the Father, or by the person of the Holy Spirit who spoke through the mouths of the holy prophets, to this Angel, the Son of God and son of man: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.” Then, by the figure called *apostrophe*, that is, a turning of address, the speech is at once directed to all those who awaited this special or proper Angel, who is called Angel in the antonomastic sense, and it says to them: “And immediately the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire.”

Certainly, he whom all the saints from the beginning of the world awaited, sought, and desired is the Messiah and Christ. He calls this one “Ruler” rather than “the Angel of the Ruler” or “of the Lord”; not “Angel of the Lord,” a designation common to very many, but “Angel of the covenant,” a name or description proper to him who became Angel in such a way that he alone could die and did die according to our nature which he assumed, and, by dying, could write for us the testament of an eternal inheritance. That this may become clearer, let us pursue the last of the four clauses set forth above: “to declare man’s righteousness.”

## CHAPTER XIV

This is the sum of his speech; this is the fruit of his death, which is his speech; this is the voice of his blood speaking better than Abel: to declare man’s righteousness. And what is it to declare man’s righteousness except to stand against man’s accuser, persuader, and prosecutor before the judging Trinity, and to defend man in the office of advocate by a lawful defence? On what ground?

For if, says the Apostle—indeed, Christ himself speaking in the Apostle—“if by the offence of one death reigned through one, much more those receiving the abundance of grace and of the gift and of righteousness shall reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, as through the offence of one came condemnation upon all human beings, so through the righteousness of one came justification of life upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous” (Rom. V). Is this not just?

Give ear, O faith that dwells in us, or through which Christ dwells in our hearts. Give attentive ears, and understand here the true and steadfast declaration of our righteousness: if it was just that we should be condemned because of the sin of one man, because we were born from him like worthless fruit from a diseased root, it is much more just and equitable that through the righteousness of one man we should all be justified, because we have been willingly reborn from him as from a good root, into which we are grafted through faith.

Truly blessed is the man “who has fulfilled his desire from these” (Ps. CXXVI): who, desiring such a declaration of so great an equity, held firm to the end of life in faith in the promise of this eternal inheritance. Truly blessed, I say, because “he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (ibid.). Rather, he shall be glorified by the glorious victory of righteousness, saying to his enemies in that gate, at that doorway of eternal life, when the soul departs, released from the body: “Behold the declaration of righteousness which this Angel of the covenant, who speaks for me, declared—this Angel who, becoming man, wrote for me in his own blood the testament of eternal inheritance. Thus I am now no longer mortal, belonging to him who begot me mortal according to the flesh, but to him who regenerated me according to the spirit after the death which he wrote from me, having become immortal. Regenerated and made alive by his single death, I have rightly escaped both deaths, now living through his justification in spirit and in the body, which is dead because of sin and will without doubt live again through him.”

What are those things, O most prudent faith, from which your desire must be fulfilled, so that you may not be put to shame when you speak in the gate to your enemies, or to my enemies? For it says: “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them.” From which “them,” then? What are “they”? The verse set before it is this: “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those cast out” (ibid.). Before this another verse came first: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, sons are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb is the reward” (ibid.). Again, before this verse comes another: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (ibid.).

Behold, these truly are the things from which the man who has desire, and from which he fulfills his desire, is blessed and shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate. For the sitting of which it says, “Rise after you have sat down,” is humility, which the king of all the sons of pride (Job XLI), the devil, did not know. The bread of sorrow is the sweetness of holy compunction; and the eating of this bread is perseverance in that same compunction. In it the soul possessing the spirit of humility is refreshed and delighted by such and so great a refreshment as no one knows except the one who receives it. Such a person may indeed say something like this: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. XLI); but he cannot tell how the bread of those same tears tasted to him—the bread which he deserved to eat.

But let us return to the chapter.

## CHAPTER XV
“If there should be an angel speaking for him, one like him, he will have mercy on him and say: ‘Deliver him, lest he go down into corruption. I have found a means by which I may be propitious to him. His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth’” (Job 33).

Whatever has hitherto been said by us to this man, or is still to be said, receive it thus, whoever you may be who deign to be present: as the title of the work promises, namely, not so much as the exposition of one teaching as the sitting of one seated in meditation upon death, according to the custom of those who eat the bread of sorrow. To them it is sweet not only to speak, but also to meditate longer upon that very thing which they have already spoken; and, to use language in accordance with the majesty of the divine word, not only to eat, but also to chew the cud upon the bread of sorrow.

What, then, do you chew over, O soul? What do you meditate upon? I hear what you say to me; I perceive the answer of your sorrow, but I cannot easily grasp its meaning in words or adequately express it. Yet behold: at the same time I hear this same Angel giving utterance in the prophet to words of this kind: “You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed” (Isa. 52). This voice, O my soul, helps my tongue to find words by which I may express, at least somewhat, the meaning of your sorrow.

Let us consider where, when, and how we were sold, and again where, when, and how we were redeemed. Behold, in these very few words there is truly great, lofty, and resounding utterance. For truly in the saying, “You were sold for nothing,” there is a great, grave, and astonishing reproach; and truly in the saying, “and without silver you shall be redeemed,” there is great, sweet, and astonishing consolation.

Let the first consideration concern the sale, less gratuitous than the phrase “you were sold for nothing” suggests. Where were we when we were sold, or as we were being sold? In Adam’s loins. O lamentable offspring! Were you then sold when you did not yet exist? And how were you sold? By aspiring to the height of divinity and awaiting the fulfillment of this ambition, according to the serpent’s words: “Eat, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). But what he said did not come to pass. Therefore it was truly said: “You were sold for nothing,” because neither you nor he in whom you transgressed received the hoped-for or promised price of transgression.

The reproach, then, is great; yet in fact it is much milder, and far gentler in comparison with the intention of so evil a bargain. For in relation to the purpose of him in whom we were sold, it was too little to say, “You were sold for nothing”; it would have been more to say what is true: “You were sold most ruinously,” because not only were you not made like the Lord, but you also died to God.

The redemption of which he says, “and without silver you shall be redeemed,” demands a consideration greater than mortal speech can unfold in words. What, then, does it mean that you shall be redeemed without silver? We know where and when we were redeemed: namely, we were redeemed there where we were not present, nor did we negotiate anything with the Redeemer concerning the price of redemption. As it is written in the prophet, from the person of that Redeemer who looks upon the mystery of this our redemption: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me” (Isa. 63 [the citation prints Isa. 6]).

We were redeemed when this Angel spoke thus, one among a thousand like him, so that, when he died and was pierced by the lance, blood and water flowed from his side. There silver was not the price of redemption. What, then, or how great a thing is meant when he says, “and without silver you shall be redeemed”? For just as he had said, “You were sold for nothing,” so he neither ought nor intended to say, “You shall be redeemed for nothing.” What then? Because he said, “and without silver you shall be redeemed,” is this the same as saying, “You shall be redeemed for nothing”? Certainly not; nor did it happen thus. For we were redeemed not freely, but at a price—and that from what was ours. Therefore this proclamation is true and just, the proclamation of which we are speaking according to the present chapter, where it is said that he may “declare man’s righteousness.”

## CHAPTER XVI

O truly marvelous exchange: we were redeemed, I say, from what was ours! From what of ours? What was ours? Was it silver? Was it gold? And even if we possess silver or gold, was it ours? Did we bring any of these things into this world? Indeed, O man, you can rightly call only that yours which you brought into this world. But what did you bring into this world when you were born, except the burdens of two deaths? For you were born already dead by the death of the soul, and soon to die by the death of the body.

You acquired gold; you acquired silver. But this was surely acquired from what was not yours, and therefore is not yours—leaving aside the case of any violent king or tyrant. Even one of those who reign lawfully possesses gold and silver lawfully and spends them by the use proper to ownership; nevertheless, they are not his. They are God’s gift.

[Col. 0373B] Faithful David knew this. When he had prepared for the work of the house of the Lord gold and silver, bronze and iron—gold for golden vessels, silver for silver ones, bronze for bronze, iron for iron, wood for wooden things, every precious stone, and Parian marble in greatest abundance—he said: “I give these things to the temple of my God” (1 Chron. 29). Afterwards, blessing the Lord, he said: “Yours, O Lord, is the kingdom; yours are riches, and yours is glory. Who am I, and who is my people, that we should be able to promise all these things to you? All things are yours, and we have given you what we received from your hand. For we are strangers and sojourners before you, as were all our fathers. O Lord our God, all this abundance which we have prepared, that a house might be built for your holy name, is from your hand, and all things are yours” (ibid.).

Therefore, O faithful David, let gold and silver in some fashion be yours, because they have been given to you by him whose all things are, if indeed, as you yourself confess—and as all of us confess who examine the truth—they are not altogether yours, nor any one of ours. “For we brought nothing into this world” (1 Tim. 6). Consequently, gold or silver given by a human being to God the Judge for the redemption of a human being would not suffice to declare human righteousness; for justice would object to the accuser’s contrary assertion: “What you give is not yours.”

It is indeed written and true that “the redemption of a soul is a man’s true wealth” (Prov. 13); but this is rightly understood not of original sin, but rather of actual sins. And redemption of this kind is of little value to a person unless that person has first been freed from original sin.

For example, Daniel says: “Therefore, O King Nebuchadnezzar, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercies to the poor; perhaps he will pardon your offenses” (Dan. 4). Had this counsel pleased him, perhaps the Lord would have pardoned him in this respect: that all those things would not have come upon him—namely, that his kingdom passed from him, that he was driven out from among human beings, that his dwelling was with beasts and wild animals, and that he ate grass like an ox. But how much would this redemption have availed him if he was not to possess redemption in the world to come?

Therefore, since for the declaration of human righteousness it was necessary that a human being be redeemed from what was his own, yet he could call nothing his own except these two things which alone he brought into this world—the death of the soul and the death of the body—behold the truly marvelous exchange: this Angel took upon himself one of these two, namely bodily death, and by such a price acquired for humanity the life both of soul and body.

## CHAPTER XVII

When did God devise this exchange? When did this Angel find this plan? For, declaring human righteousness, he says: “I have found a means by which I may be propitious to him” (Job 33).

Did God first discover this only when the first human being seized what belonged to another by eating the forbidden tree and, by aspiring to the height of divinity, sought to seize it? Did he then say, “Lest perhaps he also take of the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3), and, saying this, send him from paradise, intending to make from the one death of the body an antidote of life against the one death of body and soul? No: before he made either humanity itself or any creature, he had found this and kept it hidden with himself—that is, no angel knew it; he alone knew it.

The Apostle bears witness, writing to the Ephesians: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace has been given: to preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

What are the “unsearchable riches of Christ” of which he speaks? What is the “mystery hidden from the ages in God who created all things”? Is it not this discovery of which we are speaking here, as that Angel declares human righteousness and says, “I have found a means by which I may be propitious to him”?

O truly unsearchable riches of this Angel—the riches of Christ! Who else could search out, who else besides him could discover, such riches: the riches of this propitiation? With the Apostle I would truly call them great riches: riches of charity and mercy, riches of good will and great power. For this Angel, Christ the Son of God, possesses such charity, such good will, and such abundant mercy that, taking from us as a price one of our two deaths—the only things, as has already been said, that we brought into this world—he made this price, burdensome to himself but life-giving to us, an antidote for our poverty; he made it for the needy human race a most marvelous seed-bed of salvation and of his riches.

Speech fails, and the mind, considering the greatness of the mystery, judges its tongue to stammer rather than speak. Perhaps someone says in reply: If this Angel did not newly discover this mystery, or the riches of this unique propitiation, but kept hidden with himself before the ages all that has now been done, why did he first make it known only now, after so many ages, both to angels and to human beings? Why did a plan first please him which afterwards had to be changed?

For when he could have foreseen it and said concerning Adam, “If we take him and place him in paradise, he will aspire to become like one of us; therefore now, lest he be lifted up in pride by the great happiness of paradise and think himself Lord, let us leave him here to till the earth from which he was taken”—when, I say, he could have foreseen and said or done this, he delayed excessively. Having placed him in paradise, an occasion arose such that, as though his plan had changed and he had repented of his former counsel, the blessed Trinity said with most grave irony: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

For Adam had not become like God; rather, he had lost the grace and honor of the God who was to make him so. And Adam was driven out, “lest perhaps,” he says, “he stretch out his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever” (ibid.), accompanied by the sentence: “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid.).

People who appear to themselves highly ingenious, but are in truth exceedingly troublesome, commonly advance these or similar arguments, so that the prophetic rebuke almost reaches them: “Is it too little for you to weary human beings, that you also weary my God?” (Isa. 7). For they say: We have heard that God willed Adam’s sin to occur, through which we were all ruined—which amounts to saying that God himself did it, for “the Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 134).

## CHAPTER XVIII

Here, then, I would like briefly to speak of the order of judgment or justice, so that it may be clear that God before the ages, as has already been said, both foreknew humanity’s sin and found a means by which he might be propitious to humanity; and yet that, while the human being was not immediately committing it or had not committed it, God ought to have sentenced him guilty to death.

The order of judgment or justice in every criminal case is such as the Lord of judgment himself prescribed by his own mouth in the case of the greatest crime, namely fraternal hatred. “I say to you,” he says, “that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5), namely, divine judgment.

For as long as one who is angry with his brother—that is, who hates his brother, like Cain, of whom it is written that “he was exceedingly angry and his countenance fell” (Gen. 4)—covers over that anger in such a way that he reveals it by no deed or sign subject to judgment, so that he may be accused in the assembly of the Church or convicted by witnesses of hating his brother, he is liable to God’s judgment alone.

But if by some audible or visible sign of voice or mockery he has revealed that hatred, he is now liable not only before God but also before persons who hold the office of judging. Thus he says: “Whoever shall have said to his brother, *raca* [a contemptuous, inarticulate sound], shall be liable to the council” (Matt. 5). The council is the assembly of the Church sitting in judgment; and undoubtedly it belongs to the council to judge concerning such a sign of hatred as *raca*, even if it is not an expressed articulate or written word. For there are many signs of hatred without an evil word: for example, when someone, with wrinkled nostrils or a pale face, withholds from a brother the kiss of ecclesiastical peace.

But “whoever says, ‘You fool’”—that is, whoever perseveres full of the bitterness of insatiable hatred, so that he does not cease even in his brother’s distress to insult him to the point of death—“shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (ibid.), unless he does what follows: “If therefore you offer your gift at the altar,” and the rest, through “go first and be reconciled to your brother” (ibid.).

Certainly God is now such as he was in ancient days; and he held then, as he holds now, the same order of judgment. Not only has he never supplanted judgment or overturned what is just, but in judging he has always acted with forbearance, so that he has never rushed—that is, pronounced too hastily—the sentence of judgment that a person is liable to the fire of Gehenna. He always willed to maintain this intermediate stage as testimony to his just judgment: that one to be condemned should first be declared liable to the council.

Therefore I wonder that some have said, or even written, that the first angel fell immediately where he was created. For if he fell immediately, what will they say when asked when he was placed in heaven? [Note: [Col. 0375D] See the same author, chapter 8, book III, on Genesis.] For the truth of prophetic Scripture reads thus: “Gold,” it says, “O Lord God, was the work of your beauty, and your openings were prepared on the day on which you were created. You were an outstretched and protecting cherub” (Ezek. 28). Then it adds: “And I placed you upon the holy mountain of God” (ibid.). Without doubt, by God’s holy mountain it means heaven.

But is it permissible even to say that he fell immediately where he was placed upon God’s holy mountain? For it follows: “You walked in the midst of fiery stones, perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you” (ibid.). Here one must observe that it did not say, “until I found iniquity in you,” but “until iniquity was found in you.” And after a few words are inserted, “In the multitude of your trade your interior was filled with iniquity, and you sinned” (ibid.), it finally adds: “And I cast you from the holy mountain of God and destroyed you, O cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones” (ibid.).

We say this concerning the most ancient order of judgment: God had indeed long ago found—indeed foreknown—the iniquity of that angel, but he did not at once prepare to pronounce the sentence upon him that he was liable to judgment. Rather, he patiently endured until he also became liable to the council; that is, until the iniquity which he alone had found in the angel was also found by the holy angels. Then at last he pronounced this sentence: “He is liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

Does not this same order shine forth more and more in the following words? “Your heart was lifted up,” he says, “in your beauty; you destroyed your wisdom in your beauty” (ibid.). But the fiery stones, the holy angels in whose midst you walked “perfect in your ways”—that is, through hypocrisy—did not yet see this; for God alone, of course, sees the heart. Therefore it came to pass, and ought to have come to pass, that since you were liable to divine judgment, you should also become liable to the council of holy angels.

It follows: “I cast you upon the earth; I gave you before the face of kings” (ibid.). This happened: those kings, noble angels, saw you—noble because humble; but you, by pride, were made ignoble. Then at last, he says: “Therefore I shall bring forth fire from your midst, which shall devour you” (ibid.). What is this but to say: “You shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna”?

## CHAPTER XIX

Having briefly set these matters before us, many things open themselves and press themselves upon this meditation—this meditation upon death which you, O soul, have undertaken for the purpose of instruction.

First, then, concerning the things divinely done with respect to humankind, an account must be rendered according to the same order of judgment to those who, in the manner mentioned above, raise questions about human death. They wish it to follow that God willed the cause of death—namely sin—to occur, because, when he placed Adam in paradise, he surely foreknew future events and knew beforehand that this would happen.

If you have rightly considered this gradation—first, the guilt by which a person is liable to judgment; then, the guilt by which he is liable to the council; and thirdly, the guilt by which he is liable to the fire of Gehenna—truth will wholly free you from a suspicion of this kind, because of your single eye, which intends to do what Wisdom teaches or commands: “Think of the Lord in goodness” (Wis. 1).

For the Lord is just; the Lord our God is upright; he is a faithful God and without any iniquity. When he placed humanity in paradise, he already held humanity liable to judgment, because he saw the swelling of its ambition. But humanity was not yet liable to the council; therefore he did not pronounce sentence upon it. Rather, with the same goodness, patience, and forbearance by which he still waits for individual sinful people—as the Apostle says, “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and forbearance? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2)—with that same goodness, I say, he waited for humanity and bestowed his benefits upon it more abundantly.

But humanity, as God immediately says there through the Apostle, “according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, treasures up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God” (ibid.), came to the deed of sin when it ate with malicious intention the fruit of the forbidden tree. By this it became liable to the council, though it had long been liable to judgment.

By what guilt had it long been liable to judgment? Clearly, by the guilt of ambition, whereby it desired to be like God. This swelling, before it was outwardly detected in the deed of sin, was known to God the Judge alone. Therefore, when it was outwardly tempted, it fell so easily into the serpent’s suggestion: “Eat, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3), because the swelling of this ambition was already within. Hence it has been truly said before us that, unless it had first swelled inwardly, when tempted outwardly it would not so easily have fallen.

It therefore became, as has been said, liable to the council (Matt. 5), because it had first been liable to judgment. For just as its guilt is now known to the whole assembly of human beings, so then it became known far more clearly to the assemblies of angels. And by the testimony of that council it received its sentence, as is written there: “And he cast out Adam, and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and a flaming sword” (Gen. 2 [the citation prints Gen. 2]).

The common crowd would be astonished if it heard that for so small a food a person was made liable to so great a council; yet no wise person is astonished that even today anyone is liable to the council for so slight a sound as *raca*. But we are not at all astonished. Rather, praising and reverencing the just judgment of God, we seek mercy. For we know that just as the brief sound *raca* is a sign of great hatred, and for that reason rightly makes a person liable to the council, so much more was the bite of a single apple, however small, a sign or testimony against humanity of great ambition. Therefore humanity was rightly held guilty and inexcusable before the entire council of heaven and earth—already dead in soul, mortal in body, and in respect to both liable to the fire of Gehenna.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0377]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0377C]

In the preceding book it was shown, according to the words of the chapter undertaken from the book of Job, that afflictions avail to free a person from pride, as does bodily death. The discussion extended from the saying, “Then he opens the ears of men, and instructing them he teaches them by discipline, that he may turn a person away from the things which he has done and free him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption and his life lest it pass into the sword” (Job 33), to the saying: “Behold, God works all these things three times with each person, that he may recall their souls from corruption and enlighten them with the light of the living” (ibid.).

Certainly, in taking up this chapter I dug deep and laid foundations upon the rock: the foundations of this building or work, at its entrance or doorway, so that this first title may fittingly meet the reader—*Meditation upon Death*. I dug deep, I say, and I myself wonder more and more at the magnitude of this depth. For how much discourse has now been built in this depth upon this rock of sacred Scripture? Yet this superstructure scarcely rises to the level ground of the reader’s understanding; it scarcely appears and does not yet stand forth. Therefore, while building must still continue until a little house is made, more laborious work and more subtle meditation are necessary, with God’s help.

What then shall I do, that this Scripture may rise more quickly and proceed more effectively? I shall dig more broadly into that same depth, and shall inspect more attentively this very rock upon which I have laid the foundation—the Scripture, or chapter of Scripture, upon which I have hitherto founded the discourse begun—so that neither the meaning of that arrogant speaker who uttered these words may escape me nor the cause or patience of blessed Job, against which he uttered these very good words in no blessing.

An attentive survey of it will furnish the builder with richer material: material of gold, silver, and precious stones—namely, “your wonderful testimonies, O Lord”—which the Christian soul searches out, or ought to search out, from the Scriptures of truth, all of which accord with this Scripture. For all Scriptures tend toward that Angel who was to speak, and has now spoken, for humanity, “one like him,” mentioned above; and they concern the propitiation now accomplished through the same Angel speaking and saying: “I have found a means by which I may be propitious to him” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER II

Elihu, son of Barachel Buxetes, who in anger and indignation spoke so many and such great things against Job, is Balaam—the man first called prophet and afterwards diviner because of the fault of avarice—whose dumb beast of burden, namely the she-ass, as is written in the book of Numbers, rebuked his folly.

Why was he angry and indignant against Job? Because, he says, Job seemed righteous to himself, because he said that he was righteous (Job 32). On this account he was exceedingly angry; and, like a vigorous champion, as though contending for the Lord, he attacked him thus: “You said therefore in my hearing, and I heard the sound of your words: ‘I am clean, without offense, undefiled, and there is no iniquity in me’” (Job 33).

Beginning thus, he pursued many matters most arrogantly—indeed, with much knowledge, but also with much folly: knowing what he said, but not considering to whom he said it. He was an example of all arrogant persons, such as those against whom the Apostle speaks: “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?” (1 Cor. 10). He judged the holy man wrongly, perversely asserting that Job had said he was righteous before God, clean and without sin.

Job had not said that evil thing; rather, this man had heard a good thing wrongly. The good words of the blessed man are wholly opposed to this evil hearing: “If I should wish to justify myself, my own mouth would condemn me. If I should show myself innocent, he would scarcely approve me, and my garments would abominate me” (Job 9). Who could have passed over words like these?

But among other things Job had also said: “At least now understand that God has afflicted me not with equal judgment and has surrounded me with his scourges.” Elihu had not heard, seen, or understood this or anything like it well. Why had he not seen well? Clearly, because he had lofty and elevated eyes.

For when they heard of every evil that had happened to him, came together to visit and console him, was it said or written without reason: “When they lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him” (Job 2 [the citation prints Job 3])? Certainly not without reason; rather, with great weight, this was said in accordance with the truth and nature of the matter.

For the eyes which they should have fixed upon their neighbor or friend—the eyes of the heart, which ought to be opened by understanding of God and of one’s neighbor—they lifted up afar off and raised on high; and thus they did not recognize him. For, not knowing the secret of the temptation by which Satan tested him, they supposed him impious: harsh conjecturers, reasoning as if from effects that he was truly impious because God had struck him in this fashion. God, they held, strikes no one unjustly—or, to use their own words, “never supplants judgment or overturns what is just” (Job 8).

Thus Elihu and Job’s three friends thought that they knew him, but did not know him, as the whole course of their disputation proves. This was a labor before them until they entered into the sanctuary of God and understood “in their latter end” (Ps. 72), when the Lord said to them—though excluding this arrogant one—“My wrath is kindled, because you have not spoken rightly before me, as has my servant Job. Take therefore for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job” (Job 42), and so forth.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0380B]

But whence did they suppose that they knew him? “For,” Scripture itself says, “they saw that the sorrow was very great” (Job 2). In a remarkable way, Job did not envy the wicked when he saw the peace of sinners (Ps. 72). He did not, I say, envy them, so as to say: “Therefore I have cleansed my heart in vain and washed my hands among the innocent, and I have been scourged all day long” (ibid.), while they were scandalized by him so as to say: “This man was not innocent; this man was not upright. Who innocent ever perished, or when were the upright destroyed? Rather, we have seen those who work iniquity and sow sorrows reap them: by the breath of God they perish and by the spirit of his wrath they are consumed” (Job 4).

Therefore this man was not innocent or upright; rather, he was in God’s sight a worker of iniquity, sowing sorrows and reaping them, since by the breath of God he perished and by the spirit of God’s wrath he was consumed. He was a hypocrite, and his hope perished (Job 8).

They began to say these and similar things because they saw that the sorrow was very great. For from the greatness of the pain they inferred an antecedent greatness of iniquity. It is indeed true that they saw the pain to be severe. But did they know the quality or root of that pain? Certainly not. For they must not be thought to have understood even then, when after seven days he opened his mouth and said, “Let the day perish in which I was born” (Job 3), and so on, through “and indignation came upon me” (ibid.).

For they said: “Behold, you have taught many and strengthened weary hands; your words strengthened the wavering, and you strengthened trembling knees. But now the plague has come upon you, and you have failed; it has touched you, and you are troubled” (Job 4).

They thought that the whole cause of the pain which they saw to be a severe evil was that which had then befallen him, on account of which they had come together to visit and console him. But beyond that particular pain which appeared outwardly, he had inwardly a more rational sorrow, common to all saints and perfect persons. One of these, Isaiah, said: “My secret to myself, my secret to myself; woe is me” (Isa. 24).

What, above all, do holy men grieve over? Is it the day of death, which awaits all living beings? Rather, it is the day of birth. This is the place of understanding, whose price humanity does not know and which is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly.

The person living pleasantly blesses his own day and wishes the day of his birth to be blessed—so much so that he even dares to celebrate it with festive banquets, as Herod did in the Gospel and as Pharaoh did in a much more ancient age, at a time when this blessed Job is known to have lived. For Job was Joseph’s contemporary; indeed Philo relates that Job’s wife was Dinah, Jacob’s daughter.

Against the presumptions of people of this kind, who thus blessed the day of their birth, this blessed and wise man rightly, opening his mouth, cursed his day and prayed for a swift end to his most miserable condition, saying: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived’” (Job 3).

For what reason? Clearly because a person is born, in respect to the soul, full of the death of sin, and, in respect to the body, soon to die; from birth itself he is filled with many miseries (Job 14). Those who love the vain glory of this world call such a condition a day—though it is not one; but he calls it a night, as it truly is.

Did he first begin, then, when he opened his mouth and spoke in this way, to meditate upon death? Did he first then know what Wisdom wishes all of us to know when it says: “The day of death is better than the day of birth; it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, for there the end of all people is brought to mind, and the living person considers what he shall become” (Eccl. 7)?

No. Before that evil befell him, or that pain which alone his friends saw, the holy man already possessed this meditation or knowledge. Yet the present cause added something to the same knowledge or sorrow. For holy men are accustomed to be instructed by the adversities of this life and to advance toward weariness of the present world and love for the world to come.

For example, when Elijah was afraid and fled because of Jezebel’s threats, he asked for his soul that he might die and said: “It is enough for me, Lord; take away my soul. For I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19). Likewise another says: “And now, Lord, take my soul from me, because death is better for me than life” (Ecclus. 30). Moses also says to the Lord: “I cannot bear this people alone, because it is burdensome to me. But if it seems otherwise to you, I beg you, kill me, and let me find grace in your eyes, lest I be afflicted by such great evils” (Num. 11).

247 ## CHAPTER IV
They therefore understood the words of blessed Job wrongly, when, beginning to speak, they said to him: “But now a scourge has come upon you, and you have failed; it has touched you, and you are troubled” (Job 4). For he had not failed; rather, he had advanced. He was not troubled; rather, he possessed a most clear understanding. Hence arose the wondrous contest: he, while afflicted, vigilantly sees the truth, whereas they, living pleasantly, dream, as it were, an account of truth. Thus it is conducted and carried through with the darts and most sharp little spears of arguments that run to and fro, so that exceedingly few are the spectators of this battle who certainly know with what intention such missiles are launched from their quivers, and in what different directions the arrows of manifold discourse run: here toward the side of the Spirit of God, there toward the sides of the contrary spirit, the spirit of this world. In short, how difficult this book is to understand or expound in its several parts. For, as blessed Jeremiah says, it is transmitted as wholly oblique even among the Hebrews; and it is slippery, speaking one thing while doing another, so that, if you wish to hold an eel or little moray in tightly clasped hands, the more firmly you press it, the more swiftly it escapes.

Someone says: “What need was there for such a contest, or for so great a contest? Why did blessed Job wish to contend, and by contending allow the tranquillity, or peace, of his mind to be disturbed? If his friends attacked him without cause, why was he not likewise peaceable with them, and by his silence deprived them of the opportunity to contend?” To this I say: It is indeed written, “The wise man will be silent” (Ecclus. 20); but it is added, “until the time” (ibid.). Again: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccles. 3). Blessed Job remained silent so long as it was the time for silence, as Scripture says once and again: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips” (Job 1). He himself also says: “Did I not dissemble? Did I not keep silence? Did I not remain quiet? And indignation came upon me” (Job 3). As though he said:

A messenger came to me saying: “The oxen were ploughing and the she-asses feeding beside them; and the Sabeans rushed in, took everything, and struck down the servants with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job 1). Did I not dissemble?

Another came and said: “The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and servants it touched; and I alone escaped to announce it to you” (ibid.). Did I not keep silence?

Another came and said: “The Chaldeans formed three bands, attacked the camels and took them; moreover they struck down the servants with the sword, and I alone fled to tell you” (ibid.). Did I not remain quiet? For in all these things I did not open my mouth (Job 2).

And what followed? Indignation came upon me—that is, an affliction so great that, in comparison with it, whatever had happened before did not seem indignation: “While my sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind came from the region of the desert and struck the four corners of the house; it fell and crushed my children, and they died” (Job 1). At last I myself too, struck by a most grievous ulcer from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head, behold, scrape away my discharge with a potsherd while sitting on a dung-heap (Job 2).
