Now at last I sigh, and “my roaring is like overflowing waters” (Job 3). Now at last I opened my mouth and spoke in groaning. Why do you wonder? Why do you not rather pity me—at least you, my friends? (Job 19). Why, behold, have you sat for seven days and seven nights, and none of you speaks to me a word of consolation? Indeed, instead you compose words of rebuke. For it displeases you exceedingly, when you see the violent grief of your sighing and roaring friend. Do you wish me not to grieve? Do you demand from me such patience or strength that I should not groan? Surely this is impossible according to nature. “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, since I am flesh, that I should act patiently? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job 7).

## CHAPTER V

In saying these things and others like them, and much greater lamentations, he certainly had not failed, nor was he disturbed; rather, he had gained great strength and acted in great serenity of heart, with that strength by which holy Jacob prevailed while wrestling with the angel, and with that serenity by which the same man was glorified when he saw. For this man too was to be glorified to such a degree that the Lord would speak to him and show him still greater mysteries.

For by what strength was Jacob strong against the Lord? How did he prevail? Surely weeping was his strength; by weeping he prevailed, as the truthful Scripture in Hosea expresses more plainly. For after it had said, “In his strength he was directed with the angel, and he prevailed over the angel; he was strengthened” (Hosea 12), it immediately adds: “He wept and entreated him” (ibid.).

These friends of blessed Job, when first he opened his mouth and uttered lamenting words, interpreted his weeping or groaning as a failure of strength; and they rebuked him as though he were impatient and had never truly possessed the fear of the Lord. For they said: “Where is your fear, your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?” And what was it to find immediately thereafter and say thus, “The tiger has perished because it had no prey, and the lion’s cubs are scattered” (Job 4), unless they were saying, as it were: You were not a man but a savage tiger, and your children were not human beings but lion’s cubs. “The tiger has perished because it had no prey”; that is, you have fallen away from God because you lost your former substance.

And who does not know that blessed Job had a greater cause for grief than blessed Jacob? Jacob had lost one son, Joseph, whom he thought devoured by a wild beast; but Job, after the loss of all his goods, received in one day the news that seven sons and three daughters had all died together, and afterwards, struck by a most grievous ulcer, sat on a dung-heap. Yet when Jacob, indeed, tore his garments, mourned for his son, and refused consolation, saying, “I shall go down mourning to my son in hell” (Gen. 37), no one interpreted his tears or these words so maliciously as to say to him: “Where is your fear, your strength, your patience?”—and the things said to Job were far harsher still.

Therefore Job was not to be blamed for his groans as though for impatience. Rather, Satan had perverted his judges—who ought to have been his friends, so that they might judge lovingly—Satan who had sought permission to tempt the innocence of the blessed man, which God had praised. Hence Job himself says among other things in one place: “The earth has been given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the face of its judges” (Job 9). By “earth” he means himself; by “the wicked,” the devil or Satan; by “the judges of the earth,” his friends; and by “the covering of their face,” their ignorance or error.

And it should be noted that the conflict with his friends was the seventh assault of that same Satan who had sought to tempt him. For there were four messengers, whose words he heard and patiently endured. The fifth was the contrivance by which Satan himself struck him with a most grievous ulcer. The sixth was the foolish speech of his wife. The seventh, as has now been said, was the perverse judgment concerning him held by his friends, who slandered and reproached him.

## CHAPTER VI

But now we must return to the chapter of the question set forth above, which was this: Why did blessed Job wish to contend, and by contending allow the peace or tranquillity of his mind to be disturbed, rather than by his silence take from them the opportunity to contend? For perhaps someone thinks this might have increased the praise of a patient man, the Apostle also saying: “Do not contend in words, to no useful purpose but the ruin of the hearers” (2 Tim. 2).

The answer here is plainly easy: no wise man ought to be so patient that, hearing something against the truth, he remains silent and does not defend the truth. A faithful soul can by no means permit this; indeed, it cannot. It can die; it cannot be silent. And if at some time it resolves within itself to keep silence, it does not persist in that resolve.

For example, when the prophet Jeremiah said: “The word of the Lord became to me a reproach and a derision all day long; and I said: I shall not remember him, nor speak in his name” (Jer. 20), we should carefully note what he immediately said: “It became,” he says, “as a burning fire in my heart, shut up in my bones; and I failed, unable to endure it” (ibid.). In the same sense, when the Psalmist said: “I set a guard upon my mouth while the sinner stood against me; I was dumb and humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 38), he immediately says: “And my grief was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall burn” (ibid.).

Was not blessed Job such a man, and was he not most clearly known to be such by the testimony of the Lord himself? For once and again He thus declared concerning him: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil?” (Job 2). Satan answered Him: “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced in him and his house and all his substance round about? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. But stretch forth your hand and touch all that he has, and you will see whether he blesses you to your face.” God said: “Behold, I give into your hands all that he has; only beware lest you touch him” (ibid.).

> [Note: [Col. 0383D] St Prosper, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, part I, ch. 22, *Patrology*, vol. LI, ed. Migne.]

A great contest takes place. The faithless and apostate angel attacks the faithful servant of God; and, full as he is of self-generated malice, he lays waste, drives away, and destroys all the innocent man’s possessions, and together with his entire inheritance consumes every heir. Yet though so many darts have been launched, Job remains unharmed. As a soldier of God, he strikes the devil down with one stroke—God’s stroke:

> “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, and the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

Overcome in this contest, Satan proposes another and greater one: “Stretch forth your hand,” he says to God, “and touch his flesh and bones, and you will see whether he blesses you to your face.” “Stretch forth your hand” means nothing other than: Give permission. For the devil did not have even this power over the swine (Matt. 8), unless it had been given by Him who, under this authority, handed Job over to him too, so that he should not exceed the limit of the command. “Behold,” says God, “I hand him over to you; only preserve his life” (Job 2).

When Job was struck by a grave wound, when the entire frame of his body was decaying, all his limbs disjointed, discharge flowing, and worms boiling forth, while his mind stood intact in an uncorrupted body, and the devil perceived inwardly strong the man whom outwardly he judged weak—he armed the woman, that instrument whom he had left as necessary for himself; and through his wife he strikes the strongest man at his side. And when the woman poured in the poisoned darts which she had received from the enemy, she said among other things: “Say some word against the Lord, and die” (ibid.). Immediately Job, remembering the fall of the first man, said to this new Eve—and in her to the enemy who fought in order to conquer: “You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (ibid.).

The enemy was cast down by these divine darts; the perverse angel was overcome through grace by a human being; and the piety of humble patience defeated every assault of pride (ibid.).

But when Job’s three friends had heard of the most lamentable disaster of his fortunes, they came to him together, so that by their consolation they might in some way heal these boundless miseries—might either take away or at least lessen the excessive grief already conceived in his mind. Seeing him now exceedingly foul with mourning and horror, they were so disturbed that they scarcely recognized him; crying aloud, they wept, tore their garments, sprinkled dust upon their heads, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him.

When these days and nights had passed, Job saw his friends, whom he knew had come for the sake of consolation, sitting on the ground as though mute; and he saw that in this manner they were not healing his most bitter grief, but increasing it more and more. He therefore performed the office of a wise man, carefully observing that saying of Ecclesiastes: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” Seeing them silent, he himself broke silence, opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth (Job 3).

## CHAPTER VII

If it pleases us to retain the simple meaning of this history and seek no other, we find in it a most illustrious example of patience supplied to us. But if we wish to revisit it somewhat more deeply according to the anagogical sense, we shall see hidden in it not so much an example of patience as a judgment most fitting to this subject.

For Job,

> [Note: [Col. 0385D] Rupert, book VI on Genesis, ch. 34; and book II, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, chs. 3 and 4.]

who sprang from the stock of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, bore the type of Christ. For as Job, struck with a most grievous ulcer, sat on a dung-heap and scraped away his discharge with a potsherd, so Christ was struck with a most grievous ulcer when, according to the testimony of the Wise Man, the wicked men—whose hearts Satan surely possessed—said: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2).

Satan struck Job, envying the simplicity and uprightness of the innocent man who feared God; but he caused Christ to be struck because he could not endure the torments he suffered from Christ’s presence, as he confessed many times. For example, when he said through the mouth of a man into whom he had sent an entire legion: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the most high God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me” (Mark 5). For Satan was more pressed in this man; in this man more than in Job, he was summoned to judgment and trial.

There, when asked by the Lord, “Whence do you come?” (Job 2), he replied: “I have gone round and walked through the earth once and again.” No judgment was demanded; there was no one to say: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall you, Satan, the roamer of the world and walker through the earth, be cast out.” No one, I say, was there to say these things. Therefore he gloried that, no stronger one coming upon him, the conqueror was free to go round and walk through the earth. But here there was one who said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12).

Therefore, when this One, once rich and truly king, sat grieving, surrounded by the army of angels, but was cast outside the gate and struck by a most shameful death, he truly sat, like Job, upon a dung-heap, covered with discharge and regarded as a leper; for “the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all” (Isa. 53). Yet by the power of his resurrection he was to blot out these same iniquities of ours, all corruption, and our very mortality. Therefore it is rightly said that Job scraped away his discharge with a potsherd (Job 2). For a potsherd is first soft clay, but afterwards becomes hard when baked by fire. So too Christ’s flesh was first passible and mortal, being our clay; but afterwards, through the fire of the Passion, it was made firm in the resurrection so that it would no longer be dissolved by death or by any corruption for ever.

## CHAPTER VIII

When Job’s three friends, who had gathered to console him, beheld him most miserably afflicted and sitting upon a dung-heap, and had sat upon the ground with him in silence for seven days and as many nights, at last he opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth, saying: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night wherein it was said: A man is conceived” (Job 3), and so forth.

That Job is said here to have cursed the day of his birth seems a sign of impatience. But when we consider these things more carefully and examine somewhat more diligently the anagogical meaning of this curse, it will become clear that not Job alone, but all the elect, even now curse this day.

> [Note: [Col. 0386D] Rupert, book XXVII, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 5.]

Seek this out, then, O faithful soul, so that you may be able more profitably to meditate upon death. “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night wherein it was said: A man is conceived,” and so forth.

The day of birth—or the night—which it was the part of a wise man to curse was the sin of the first man: a day, I say, ironically, but truly a night. For in that seeming day, the deceiver promised that our eyes would be opened, saying: “Eat, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). But when he was believed, the wall of enmity rose between us and God, and thus we were badly conceived in night—that is, unable to see God.

Job cursed that day—or rather, that night—as far as he could; and so did every other person from the beginning of the world who condemned that sin of the devil and sighed for God’s righteousness. But no curse of theirs could condemn it with sufficient effectiveness. He then adds the causes of this same impossibility: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish immediately upon coming forth from the womb? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I nursed at breasts?” (Job 3).

Far be it from us to believe that so great a man, endowed with such knowledge of the Spirit and meanwhile praised by such testimony of the Judge, wished that he had perished as an abortive child. Rather, as is known also by the reward, he has within himself the witness of his strength; the weight of his speech must be assessed inwardly.

Therefore, as Job cursed the day of his birth, so Christ also cursed his. For Christ was born on that day of sin and conceived in that night of unhappiness. Yet this new man and that new man were new in very different ways. For the former was born or conceived in the manner described, so that he who was a man and was good might become a sinner and become evil. The latter, however, was conceived and born so that he who was God, impassible and immortal, might become man and become passible and mortal.

Both, indeed, were in the day or night of sin: the former in order that sin might come to be, the latter because sin had come to be. The former, deceived by wicked suggestion and born—that is, degenerated—through corruption of his own substance, was born to the devil both for guilt and punishment. The latter, conceived of the Virgin by the will of the Father and his own will, and made man by the assumption of another substance, was born to God without guilt, for the penalty of guilt.

Here is a matter of wisdom; here attention must be paid to what the spirit of wisdom says or indicates. Behold, a man—Christ, a righteous man—owes much to sinful human beings. “Let the slack hands be strengthened, and let the feeble knees of sinners be made firm” (Isa. 35), because, if they are instructed by faith and piety, if they are wise advocates or learned in the law, they have grounds on which to bind their Judge.

Let the Judge say: “Because of your day of sin I was born; because of your night of iniquity I was conceived; and I, who was the immortal Lord God, became mortal man.” Let faithful sinners, penitent sinners, reply: “And although we owe you much, God Christ, because you became man, yet you, man Christ, owe much in return to us, because for our sake you were assumed into God. For unless we had been sinners, there would have been no reason why you should be assumed into God.”

Let them be strengthened, I say. For they ought not only to consider that the Lord of such great dignity suffered such injuries—even death, and death upon a cross—for the sins of persons so unworthy as servile beings. They should also consider that, unless the servants had sinned, the servile nature would not have been assumed into the Lord God. For that Lord did not receive more injury than glory for his rebellious or criminal servants. For those for whom he hung upon the cross are the same persons for whom he now sits at the right hand of God as intercessor.

Here the king of God’s kingdom, accepting the argument of truth from whomever he receives it, whether Jew or Gentile, gladly suffers violence, so that violent persons may seize the kingdom itself; and, as though overcome by their argument, he opens his mouth and says to them: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night wherein it was said: A man is conceived.” That is to say: Let the day of sin, which according to the falsehood of the serpent saying, “Eat, and your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3), was thought to be day but is in truth night, perish for you—the day or night on account of which I, who was God, was born as man.

How is it to perish? “Let not God seek it from above, and let it not be illuminated by light.” Let this be your blessedness, of which the Prophet also speaks in the Psalm with longing: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31). For this is what it means for that day not to be sought out and not illuminated by light: that iniquities are forgiven and sins covered.

For this reason blessed Job cursed—that is, condemned—the day of his birth. Christ, however, did not so much curse that day as remove it from the number of days, since he was born not merely to condemn our sin, but to take it away, as John testifies, saying: “He appeared in order to take away our sins” (1 John 3). By his Passion he not only cursed sin, but utterly removed it; and he blotted out the bond which the devil held against us, fastening it to the cross itself (Col. 2).

Therefore, just as upright and devout Christians ought to flee sins and keep themselves free from every appearance of evil (1 Thess. 5), so too it is fitting that they curse or condemn those sins; for this condemnation follows their flight from them. Blessed Job, therefore, should by no means be accused of impatience because, when his friends were silent, he opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. We should believe that he did this not because he was moved by the bitterness and weariness of immeasurable grief, but for the sake of defending and explaining the truth.

For just as excessive speech is unfitting for wise men, so, conversely, silence while it is the time to speak is in no way fitting—especially when speaking ought to occur for the sake of defending the truth. Whoever does this acts like one who denies the truth, concerning whom the Savior says: “Whoever confesses me before men” (Matt. 10), and so forth; “Whoever denies me,” or, as Mark says, “whoever is ashamed of me and of my words” (Mark 8), and so forth.

Let these remarks on blessed Job suffice. If anyone perhaps desires more, let him consult the expositions of Pope Gregory on the book of Job. What we have here explained briefly, he sets forth more fully, more sweetly, and more clearly.

## CHAPTER IX

Since God the Father, then, in his immense mercy wished us to be freed from our sins, sending us his only-begotten Son, who by assuming mortal flesh would take away our sins and, suffering for us a most shameful death, would free us from the death of the soul, it is surely fitting that you, O soul, live the remainder of your time according to the life of the wise man, which is meditation upon death.

> [Note: [Col. 0389C] Rupert, book XXIX, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 26; and book II on Revelation.]

For this bodily death, which all of us must undergo—indeed, from which no mortal person is free—was devised by God for this reason: that through it we might be freed from the death of the soul. The latter is first in act, but is called second in experience. For man died in soul before he died in body. On the very day Adam rashly violated the forbidden tree, he died the death of the soul; but he then first experienced that death of the soul when dust returned to dust—which is the death of the flesh—and the soul descended to the wretched.

Therefore, in order that we might be freed from this death, we had to undergo bodily death, so that, with earth thus restored to earth, at some time in the resurrection of the dead, when we all stand before Christ’s tribunal (2 Cor. 5), we may put off the corruptible body and put on incorruption; clothed with it, we may rejoice in glory with Christ for ever.

Through this death we have been freed from the death of the soul, and this not from ourselves but through the intervening Passion of Christ. For we could neither make satisfaction for ourselves nor enter the kingdom of heaven; rather, Christ first had to come and undergo the second death for us—he who “did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2)—so that, freed from the death of the soul, we might be made participants in the heavenly kingdom.

But perhaps someone will say: “Since, reborn in Christ, we have escaped the guilt of our earthly parent, why do we still bear the penalty of that guilt? Why do we still die? Why do we not pass into a better life without the affliction of death? Why are we stripped, rather than further clothed?”

> [Note: [Col. 0389C] Rupert, book XXVII, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 27. He resolves this same question in book XXIV on Genesis, ch. 25, and book III on the prophet Nahum.]

To this, groaning, we may say: We have been sought out not through mercy alone, but through justice also, the companion of mercy. Indeed—and this too must be considered with great reverence—we were made mortal in our first parents and expelled from paradise not through justice alone, but also through the mercy that flies about us.

For it must be understood that, although the cause was the same, it was not by the same hand that we suffered death in the soul and were subjected to mortality in the body. The death of the soul was devised for us by the devil; the mortality of the body was imposed upon us by God’s provident wisdom, or wise providence. For if after sin we had been allowed to live the life of the body and remain immortal, we would be like demons, because for us, as for them, eternity would be miserable, or misery eternal.

Therefore God, making good provision for us, said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore, lest he stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life and live for ever” (Gen. 3), and so forth. These words may perhaps seem to breathe great wrath to someone, but to those possessing instructed discernment they surely breathe great mercy.

Since, then, bodily death possesses such great and excellent usefulness that through it we have also been freed from the death of the soul, before all else do you, O faithful soul, “always remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). For this reason I do not at all doubt that, made more secure through Christ’s death and freed from the death of the soul, you shall overcome all the labours of this life and inherit eternal life with all the saints. So be it!

[Col. 0389]

# THE LIFE OF ST HEREBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, BY RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ

## 251 AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0389D]

You, venerable Father Marcward, imposed this work upon me as a compulsory service: that I should rewrite in a new style, for the glory and praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, the life of the holy archbishop Herebert, resplendent in virtues but, as it seemed to you, somewhat obscured by the rust of its former style. For otherwise I was going wherever the ardour of study led me as I wrote, and therefore I judged that in obeying you I was serving, surely, as under compulsion.

But when I was long distressed both by your continual urging and by my own will tending toward other things, at last there came to mind what the supreme and truly master teacher of love fittingly said upon the mountain among the other precepts of evangelical perfection: “If anyone compels you,” he says, “to go a thousand paces, go with him another two” (Matt. 5). There also came to mind Simon the Cyrenian, whom, as the Evangelist testifies, they compelled while he was passing by to carry Jesus’ cross (Matt. 27).

Finally, the example of that same man—who indeed carried Jesus’ cross, yet was not himself crucified—and the very fact that he carried a cross not his own, unwillingly and under compulsion, strongly rebukes any Christian who proclaims the labours of Christ or his saints in such a way that he does not cooperate by imitation; and who does what he proclaims more from the necessity of a command than from the devout desire of his mind.

I therefore consented. Setting aside for the present the course I had proposed, I turned aside to this task, no longer unwilling, but now with a good will, if the Spirit of God our Father should deign to suggest what or how I ought to speak. Behold, you have what you commanded—or rather, what you compelled me to undertake more by asking than by commanding. Judge yourself whether, by bringing it about, you have made any progress; that is, whether this later writing is more or less suitable for edification than the earlier writings that did not satisfy you.

Moreover, my conscience as witness before God, and this present letter before those who deign to hear or read it, may excuse me: not because I was pleased with myself did I set myself above the earlier writers by writing, but because I wished to please your charity by obedience, I submitted myself to your request. For I considered you worthy of my obedience, although I have not professed the monastic warfare under your rule.

For you, taken from the monastery of Siegburg and, like a green shoot, transplanted from that garden of delights into the Church of that same blessed confessor of Christ, brought forth anew the fruit of holy religion, which had there almost withered away. Thus, with God’s favour, you deserve to say that Davidic saying: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God” (Ps. 51).

## CHAPTER I. On the birth of blessed Herebert, and the divine signs that appeared at his birth

[Col. 0391C]

In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 990, on the sixteenth day of March, when Otto III ruled the Roman Empire, St Herebert was given by God as bishop to Cologne Agrippina, the distinguished metropolitan city of Germany; and he lived commendably in that see for twenty-three years, two months, and nearly twenty-two days.

The Ascender into heaven—of whom it is written, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67)—deigned to foreshadow at Herebert’s very birth the gift of grace that he was to give him. For when the child was being brought forth by night from his mother’s womb, an immense light shone from heaven in that place; some who slept saw it with the eyes of the heart, and others who were awake saw it with bodily eyes.

The father of that infant was sleeping, and with him was a certain friend, a Jew, who had come to him at that time, according to their custom, for familiar conversation or business. Both of them, sleeping at the very hour in which the blessed birth came forth into light, saw one and the same dream. Upon waking, they immediately spoke to one another, each intending to relate his own vision, since they did not know that it had been common to both, or one single vision. The one who had come because of friendship, as already said, told his dream first; then the master of the household himself testified with great astonishment that he had seen exactly the same thing, and nothing else.

The dream was as follows: the chamber in which the woman was known to be lying down and near childbirth opened at its front, and a radiance entered and shone forth like the midday sun. Meanwhile, at that same hour, attentive women were, according to custom, present around the woman giving birth; and they too, as already said, saw with bodily eyes the miracle of heavenly brightness poured forth.

While the two men were still speaking in wonder of the dream which they had seen, and making no idle conjectures concerning the happiness of the birth, behold, one of the women, astonished at once with joy and fear, brought the father the good news: namely, that an excellent son had been born, and that at his birth there had appeared a divine miracle of wondrous sweetness and a great light shining around him.

## CHAPTER II. That the visible light which shone in the house at his birth was a sign of the invisible light by which he was to be illuminated
This, then, who could doubt was a sign of the grace to be bestowed upon him, signifying that the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, would illuminate him more abundantly? (John 1.) And indeed, if spiritual light alone—the grace unknown to Jewish blindness—were to have been granted him, it might perhaps rightly have seemed incredible or unfitting that a Jew should have shared in the same luminous dream which his Christian father was worthy to see. But this chosen and glorious son of light was to shine both through the inward gift of eternal light, which upright Jacob especially desired, and through the outward attainment of temporal glory, which Esau the hunter alone sought among his father’s blessings (Gen. [Col. 0392C] 27). For who does not know how brightly the great Church of Cologne shone, especially in those times, even in the resources and honours of this world?

Since, therefore, he was to preside over so great a see, and this lamp of the Lord was to be raised upon such a great lampstand—having such resources, and possessing also exceptional standing and right at the summit of the earthly empire, as the following narrative will show—it should not seem unworthy that a Jew too received a presage of his future splendour. For he said to his father: “Know most certainly that the child born to you will fill you with joy and make his birth illustrious through the great splendour of his own name.” That man could say this while looking only to the light or glory [Col. 0392D] of the world; but Christ, the true light and the glory of the heavenly homeland, wonderfully fulfilled his wonderful prediction.

For on the night when He was born of the Virgin, “light arose in the darkness for the upright” (Ps. 111 [112]), and the glory of God shone around shepherds watching over their flock (Luke 2): on that same night—indeed, at the very dawn of the following day—during the sacred solemnities of Mass, whose opening words are, “Today light shall shine upon us,” the bishop was consecrated, bearing the true light and receiving the ministry of those to whom it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5), and so forth. Who can doubt that this occurred by the Lord’s providence or ordering, through the same care or grace by which He had previously sent the aforesaid sign at his birth? But this matter must be discussed more fully in its proper place.

## CHAPTER III. On his maternal lineage, and how the stock from which so great a man was to be born was, by God’s providence, redeemed from captivity.

[Col. 0393A]

With such a presage, as has been said, this boy, a son of blessed predestination, was born in the Gallic city of Worms. His maternal family, moreover, had been carried there—namely, into the Gallic territory of Worms—from its Alemannic source by adverse fortunes. For his maternal grandmother, named Emma, was the daughter of Regimbold, a most noble count of the Alemanni. When the Huns were plundering, she was taken from her father’s castle with her two sisters and forcibly carried away captive into the territory of the aforesaid city.

When a certain nobleman saw her, he immediately, at God’s prompting—without whom not even one sparrow falls to the ground (Matt. 10)—pitied the captive girl’s noble appearance and redeemed her. Why say more? By God’s providence, so that the root from which the fruit enduring unto the acquisition of salvation was to be born might be preserved, the girl’s father, while he happened to be travelling to the emperor’s court, lodged in the house of that same nobleman. There, amid much conversation, he recognized his daughter; he rejoiced, and gave her, with a large dowry, in marriage to the man who had redeemed her and asked for her hand. From that marriage was born the mother of this saint.

I have not wished to pass this by, because it contributes somewhat to the praise and glory of God that this bitterness was overcome by such great blessings of sweetness: redeemed captivity gave birth to such a great citizen of heaven.

## CHAPTER IV. How, under Hildebald, bishop of Worms, he advanced by God’s grace in the sacred studies of ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0393C]

Thus, according to the foreseeing purpose of God—who before the ages of the world foreknew and predestined all the saints to be conformed to the image of His Son (Rom. 8), and called, justified, and glorified each in his own time—this saint was foreknown in order that he might be born, and was called not only that he might be justified through the grace of baptism, but also that he might be glorified with the honour of pontifical grace. The preparation for this distinction lay in his being entrusted, in the same Church of Worms, to liberal studies.

For with such ease did he drink in the streams alike of divine and human philosophy that there could be no doubt that inwardly he had as teacher Him of whom the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase” (1 Cor. 3). This was especially evident because, together with the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of piety and fear of the Lord shone in him—the fear by which every saint begins to ascend to wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110 [111]).

Observing this, the venerable Hildebald, then bishop of the same Church of Worms, and recognizing the prudent young man from his studies—as Scripture says, “A child is known by his pursuits,” whether his works are pure (Prov. 20)—rejoiced in him, holding a good hope that this man would be useful [Col. 0394A] to holy Church. For that bishop possessed the benevolence which the Holy Spirit expresses in the prophet: “Say to the righteous that it is well, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds” (Isa. 3). He also knew that the Lord had said in the Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest” (Luke 10).

Desiring, therefore, to provide for holy Church, and hoping that in the see over which he presided God had already prepared for him a successor, he endeavoured to encourage the young man’s good conduct with worthy praise. Accordingly, when the provost of that Church died at that time, he immediately appointed him in his place. But He who is holy and true, who has the seven stars and walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands (Rev. 1), determined to fix this star in another place of His firmament and set this lamp upon the lampstand of another Church [Col. 0394B].

## CHAPTER V. How, through his good reputation, he became known to Emperor Otto and was made archchancellor; and how, persuaded by him, he entered the rank of the priesthood together with Bruno.

Accordingly, so that one who was to be sought from farther away might become known more widely, Otto III, emperor of the Romans, heard of the illustrious man—who and what manner of man he was. And as God inclined the emperor’s heart, as it is written, “The king’s heart is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21), the man’s excellence so pleased him that he associated him with his own court and first made him his chancellor.

Persuaded by him, this blessed man cheerfully took upon himself the Lord’s yoke, namely the honour of the priesthood, together with Bruno, who later exercised the dignity of the Roman pontificate. Yet Bruno himself did not then readily consent to become a priest, humbly excusing himself as though he were receiving a grace greater than his merits. Both, certainly, were praiseworthy: this man, who readily consented with a willing mind; and that one, who at first was astonished and tried to decline a task so arduous.

For the centurion, when the Lord said to him, “I will come and heal your child, lying paralysed in the house,” answered: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof; but only speak the word, and my child shall be healed” (Matt. 8). He was immediately praised by the same Lord for the humility of his faith. And Zacchaeus, when He said, “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must remain in your house,” immediately came down quickly and received Him joyfully (Luke 19); according to the joy of his charity, he was judged worthy to hear the Lord say: “Today salvation has come to this house” (ibid.).

Yet this man also, who, when asked, had promptly undertaken the office of priesthood, as has been said, later humbly refused the still more excellent rank of bishop when it was offered him. For shortly afterward the bishop of the Church of Würzburg died, and the emperor wished him to be appointed in his place. He refused, declaring himself unworthy; and he at once secured the transfer of that election to his brother Henry, whom he considered far more worthy than himself. [Col. 0395A] Thus his brother presided over the aforesaid Church, while he himself was preserved in humility and love for the time and place appointed him by God.

Meanwhile, when the Roman pontiff died, the aforesaid Bruno received the apostolic see, taking the additional name Gregory V. He lived in it for almost two years and nine months, the eleventh after the other Bruno, who was also called Leo IX. Since the manner in which he was first expelled by the Romans rebelling against the emperor, and then killed by poison, is of less relevance to the present subject, let us omit it for now and pursue our purpose instead.

## CHAPTER VI. How, after harmony was achieved among the people of Cologne, he was elected archbishop.

[Col. 0395B]

Not long afterward the metropolitan church of Cologne was widowed by the death of Everger, archbishop of that city. But when they sought to elect a successor, their unanimity was torn apart, and clergy and people bitterly disagreed with one another. The clergy demanded one man by their election, the people another; and the conflict between the opposing parties went so far that they nearly took up arms. Thus, as though Jesus were absent, the little ship was tossed by waves in the midst of the sea (Matt. 14).

But He swiftly came to the aid of those in distress and came to them walking upon the sea. For the man whom the clergy elected without the people’s approval, namely Wezelin, provost of the house of Saint Peter, suddenly called for silence and addressed them all in this manner, according to God’s will:

> “In this matter, fathers and lords, let us all together seek not our individual interests but those of the Lord, and let us take the best counsel we can. For I neither desire to preside over you myself nor envy another the office. Free in this matter from both envy and ambition, I designate for you another man, well known to you and worthy: the illustrious Heribert, strong in relation both to God and to the world, devoted to Christ and dear to the emperor. Let us therefore end the dispute by agreeing to elect this most worthy man.”

He had scarcely spoken these words when the entire crowd swiftly cried out Heribert’s name from his mouth. One voice and one will possessed all those whom the bond of peace now, in a marvellous manner, united in one absent man, though they had until then been divided by discord. Thus, at the Lord’s command, the wind ceased and there was calm (Matt. 8).

The swiftness of this calm is made more memorable to us by storms in other times or places that have sometimes been heard of or seen, in which, as though Jesus slept or were absent, the sea’s disturbance was not calmed before a great number of souls—indeed, of bodies and other things besides—perished and were destroyed. Where such things occur, they must surely be ascribed to the just judgment of God on account of the sins of the inhabitants. But the fact that help came so swiftly to the little ship of the Church of Cologne, while it was tossed by those waves of discord, lest matters come to arms, must be ascribed to divine mercy.

Moreover, the blessed man’s merits were evidently confirmed also in this: when his name was proposed for election, the fierce discord of clergy [Col. 0396A] and people ceased, and peace was restored. For to attentive minds the event itself declared that the Prince of Peace (Isa. 9), the cornerstone, and Christ our peace—who made both one, destroyed enmities in Himself (Eph. 2), and through His blood made peace in all things in heaven and on earth (Col. 1)—was sending him.

## CHAPTER VII. How the emperor rejoiced at his election, and how wisely he received the favour of that election.

Thus the election of the faithful servant was memorably celebrated in the Lord’s presence, and it immediately merited testimony and praise both from God and from men. For the hand of the Lord had already touched the heart of the aforesaid emperor, so that through this man he might calm the disturbances in that divided city, disturbances already known to him by report.

When he was being tempted with money by another man, whom—as has been said—the people’s dissension had acclaimed, he delayed his answer and concealed his contempt for the money offered. Meanwhile, from the territory of Benevento, where he was then residing, he wrote with his own hand to the blessed man, who was then at Ravenna conducting, with the bishop of that city, business ordered by the emperor:

> “Otto, Augustus and emperor by the grace of God alone, to Heribert, arch-logothete: greetings, Cologne, and one ell of pallium.”

When the delegation of the people of Cologne arrived—many honoured men from both clergy and people, those regarded as most eminent in each order, together with certain leading princes of the land—they presented before him the election of such a man. The emperor was greatly delighted by this and gave no small thanks to the city for its prudent decision: they thought and chose, in one and the same spirit with him, what he himself desired and regarded as best.

Thus the gatekeeper plainly opened the way for one entering the sheepfold, reconciling all in his election so that no obstacle arose. The venerable man truly received all this wisely. Going meanwhile to a church, he prostrated himself on the ground and with his whole heart gave thanks to the Lord God, giver of heavenly graces. He did not rejoice, of course, in temporal glory, but adored the gift of heavenly blessing. For how could he fail to rejoice when he perceived from such evident proofs that he was an object of God’s care?

For he imitated the holy king and prophet David. When David heard the word of the Lord spoken through the prophet Nathan: “When you have fulfilled your days and go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, one who shall be of your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne for ever” (2 Sam. 7), and so forth, he went in and sat before the Lord and said: “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you should grant me such things?” (ibid.). And he added: “Now, therefore, Lord, let the word which you have spoken concerning your servant and his house be confirmed for ever, and do as you have spoken” (ibid.).

When the strong, wise, and humble king said these things and the rest, he rejoiced not in the temporal memorial of his house or of the handmade temple which his son Solomon was to build for the Lord’s name, but in the eternal glory of Christ, his descendant according to the flesh, and of the Church—a glory which, by the prophetic Spirit, he understood in the figure of his Solomon-like son and that son’s temple [Col. 0397A].

By this example the blessed man acted; and so must everyone act who is called by the Lord to preside as ruler over God’s house or shepherd over Christ’s sheep: he must embrace not human glory but divine grace. For it is indeed a great grace to be shepherd and bishop of souls, to be counted among the greatest gifts which Christ, ascending on high, gave to humanity (Eph. 4). For after the Apostle had said, “He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things; and he gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists” (ibid.), he went on to say: “Others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints” (ibid.). Rightly, therefore, and wisely he gave thanks for the bestowed, or to-be-bestowed, gift of blessing and pastoral grace.

## CHAPTER VIII. How free he was from ambition, and concerning the death of the bishop of Strasbourg.

Although his whole life shows how free he was from the vice of ambition, there was also this memorable testimony: when an archbishop was to be created on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July], a day famous for the martyrdom of Saint Kilian, he preferred that it be deferred until the following day because the mournful funeral rites of the bishop of Strasbourg were then being held there. He did this lest, while others were mourning and weeping, he should seem to be rejoicing with his own people, mindful of Scripture’s saying: “An inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning will lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20).

And indeed the death of that bishop was to be mourned, because it had occurred in a terrible manner, preceded by a sign of ill omen. For when, crowned with his mitre, he began to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, and turned toward the people to say, as customary, “Peace be with you,” he looked at the emperor and burst into such laughter that he seemed utterly to have forgotten why he had turned. Then, when they came to dinner and all were seated together, he was struck by a pleuritic illness; carried in men’s arms to his lodging, he gave up [Col. 0397D] his spirit on the fourteenth day.

Seven years before, as he was accustomed to relate, he had seen a vision: an old man stood before him, clothed in purple and crowned with a bishop’s mitre. Declaring himself to be Bishop Kilian, he uttered to him this oracle: “Act during these seven years in a manner worthy of a bishop; for no longer span of life has been appointed for you by the Lord.” However he received the vision, whatever preparation he made, and whatever state he was found in at the hour of death, that man’s end, as described, rightly renewed or increased in this wise man the meditation upon death. And it was a great proof of his self-restraint that, because it was a time for weeping, he chose by deferring the event to be present, bereft of any time of rejoicing for himself or his followers, at the sorrowful funeral rites [Col. 0398A].

## CHAPTER IX. With what humility he came to Cologne, and when he was consecrated.

Indeed, the episcopal honour was conferred upon him at Benevento on the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June]. From there he proceeded to Rome and received the pallium from the bishop of the apostolic see. Yet he entered the city of Cologne and took his seat in his see on a day not unknown among Christians: namely, the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

As he approached and was already near at hand, it is worthy of remembrance how he recalled the apostolic teaching which says: “I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility [Col. 0398B] and gentleness” (Eph. 4). For, truly humble and gentle, he sent the pallium of his apostolic mission before him, while he himself, clothed in linen and barefoot, followed with slow step, although the winter cold at that season was exceedingly burdensome even to those wearing shoes.

He considered also his calling: that he was summoned not to the kingdoms of the nations, but to minister to Christ’s holy disciples. And although he was now coming to his distinguished city of Cologne, by such attire he confessed with the blessed patriarchs whom the Apostle mentions that he was a stranger and pilgrim upon earth, signifying that he sought a better homeland (Heb. 11), that is, the heavenly one, and the city which God had prepared for them.

Thus he came, led by the Holy Spirit, in a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart, yet not without holy and spiritual joy. And, as was mentioned above, on that very night of our joy—namely, the Lord’s Nativity—he was consecrated during the solemnities of Mass which, according to custom, were celebrated a little before or around daybreak. Several bishops had come with him for this very purpose.

Who would not marvel at the divine ordering in that consecration? Who would not revere here the height of the divine counsel, by which it pleased God that it should occur thus? For the Holy Spirit composed the whole of that matins office for the holy shepherds of Christ’s sheep, of whom those shepherds were the mystical pattern: on that night, as they watched and kept the night watches over their flock, the glory of God shone around them, and they were worthy to be the first to hear from holy angels the good news, the great joy, of the Saviour’s birth, as the holy Gospel of that Mass recounts (Luke 2) [Col. 0398C].

Certainly all parts of that office are the voices of the Church’s shepherds, such as ought fittingly to resound to the rational sheep entrusted to their care, proclaiming the Saviour born of a Virgin for the world’s salvation. If the reader’s weariness were not to be avoided, it would readily be possible to expound every part according to this sense. Yet there is one matter which ought not rightly to be passed over: the prophetic chapter which, in that office, customarily precedes the apostolic reading—especially because that passage was marvellously suited to the person of this holy shepherd.

For when, in consecrating him, two bishops held the book of the Gospels over his head and neck, and the same book was immediately opened, this first verse appeared:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to bring good news to the poor” (Isa. 61).

For this prophetic chapter of Isaiah is inserted in the Gospel text in this manner: “Jesus,” says Luke, “returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And according to his custom he entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day and stood up to read. And the book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him. When he opened the book, he found the place where it was written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. He sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord [Col. 0399A] and the day of recompense.’ And when he had closed the book, he gave it back to the minister and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. Then he began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing’” (Luke 4).

It is clear, therefore, that it is Christ’s person who speaks these words concerning Himself in His prophet. But He is not merely anointed: He is anointed above all others, as another Scripture says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44 [45]). For all the saints—every participant or companion of that beautiful and gracious king—have been anointed with the same Spirit and the same oil of gladness. Indeed, no one can in any way be holy without this anointing.

Since, then, it is clear that all His participants are anointed with the same Spirit of the Lord, of whom that supreme and most mighty one says, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” and so forth, declaring, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing,” undoubtedly the bishops of the Churches, whose office it is to bring good news to the poor and proclaim release to captives, and who are anointed with holy chrism for this purpose, ought each to know, and may say of themselves after Christ: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me,” and so forth.

Thus, while in the anointing of this blessed bishop, with the Gospel book opened above his head, Holy Scripture uttered this first declaration, all who were present rightly received the saying reverently as a true oracle of divinity: believing that the Lord had sent him, and not doubting [Col. 0399D] that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him.

Together with this prophetic reading, in accordance with the order of that matins office, as the choirs sang in harmony and alternation, divine utterances rang forth—sacred proclamations of the light and glory with which the Prince of Shepherds, our God and Lord, was clothed, He who shone upon us on that night. Their exposition need not now be continued, lest, as already said, prolixity breed weariness. This alone I shall say without hesitation: these were certain signs of God’s purpose continuing in its course. When this blessed man was born, God marvellously produced the brilliance of light as a sign; and when he was consecrated, He so ordered that consecration that proclamations should be heard around him in the solemn rites concerning the true light, of which all shepherds of souls ought to be messengers, following the example of those shepherds whom the glory of God shone around on that night [Col. 0400A].

## CHAPTER X. How he endured the envy of certain persons and began to be suspected by Emperor Henry.

This is Your work, Christ, whose word is true—or rather, who are Truth itself (John 14)—whose saying must stand: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). Again: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in hiding, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those entering may see the light” (Luke 11).

But what city, ever so placed upon a mountain, has not suffered envy and been attacked by Cain’s earthly city, set in the valley, whose prince is Satan? Or what lamp, ever so set upon a lampstand, has had no wicked eye envy it? To speak more plainly: what saint, built upon the mountain of virtues and shining in word and example for the edification of those who see and hear, has suffered no tribulation from the ungrateful and envious? Who, amid the joyful gifts of heavenly grace, has not had his own measure of such tears as the inhabitants of Cedar—that is, of darkness—cause to the children of light?

For this is what each groaning person says in the Psalm: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar. My soul has long been a sojourner. With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119 [120]). Yet although they are afflicted, they are not permitted to be afflicted without measure—that is, beyond what they can bear. Again, they say: “Lord God of hosts, you will feed us with the bread of tears and give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 79 [80]).

Therefore this saint also had to suffer adversity amid the prosperity of virtues, by which he burned as he advanced inwardly, and amid the rays of miracles by which outwardly he shone for God’s glory. His soul was a city of God the King set upon a mountain; he was a lamp placed upon the lampstand of a distinguished Church. The ensuing course of the narrative will at once show this [Col. 0400C].

But how, or upon what occasion, did adversity find an entrance against him? Through the collapse of a great wall or a very high tower: that is, through the death of the oft-mentioned emperor. While he still lived, his friendship could be a wall for Heribert against the adversaries whom envy afterwards stirred up against him.

If that emperor had heeded the blessed man’s counsel in this matter, as in other things, he would have come much nearer to wisdom and would not have regretted it, according to Wisdom’s own saying: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclus. 32). But because he did not do so, he fell into the snares of an evil woman: namely, the wife of Crescentius, who had rebelled against him and whom he had ordered, once captured, to suffer capital punishment. Not guarding himself against her, although he had often been warned by the holy man, he was poisoned while sleeping in his chamber.

Thus he died at Rome in the third year after the blessed man’s ordination [Col. 0401A]. The saint had gone with him on that occasion too, being indispensable for the management of the kingdom’s most important affairs. On the following day, when the emperor had confessed to him the poison he had taken and sensed that he was dying, he also made this final request of him: that he should arrange for his body to be transferred for burial at Aachen.

While the faithful man was occupied in carrying this out, he also held the regalia in his possession and was not present at the election of the new ruler, Henry, then duke of the Bavarians. The princes of the realm chose him as their king, a man most wealthy by worldly rank and not slightly trained in literary studies. This gave the adversaries their opportunity against Heribert—such adversaries as have never been lacking in the Church since Abel and Cain first offered sacrifices to God (Gen. 4): false brethren, of whom Scripture says, “They have gone in the way of Cain” (Jude 11), and whose oppression the Apostle likewise laments among the chief of all his perils (2 Cor. 11).

He promptly returned the regalia when they were demanded. Yet because, as has been said, he had not been present at the new ruler’s election, Henry thereafter regarded him with suspicion. For this reason the king more readily gave ear to the saint’s detractors; indeed, he persecuted him with implacable hatred until, shortly before the saint’s death, he deserved to be rebuked by the Lord—a matter which the present narrative will not omit in its proper place. Now let us proceed through the miracles of his memorable works to the Lord’s praise.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the drought, and how the grace of the Holy Spirit appeared over him in the form of a dove, so that by his tears he obtained sudden rain from heaven.

The event now to be narrated makes sufficiently clear that what we mentioned above happened not by chance but by divine ordering: namely, that at the consecration of the holy bishop there first presented itself from the book of the Gospel that utterance of Christ, the merciful high priest: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61).

For the drought that followed afterwards sternly reproved the sins of the peoples: almost every blade of grass had withered away, every field was scorched, and it threatened not merely some ordinary famine, but a deadly famine already at hand. Indeed, along with the drought, pestilence also raged: many were dying, and many still scarcely dragged about their afflicted bodies. [Col. 0401D] Thus the most compassionate bishop’s concern was no small or commonplace one; and with his concern came the anguish of a sympathetic heart, and with his anguish continual, tearful prayer. Since a sword pierced his soul and the Holy Spirit groaned in his heart, as the Apostle says: “For we do not know how to pray as we ought; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8), he deserved both to reconcile the people to God—as a certain wise man said of the great and worthy Priest: “In the time of wrath reconciliation was made” (Ecclus. 44)—and, while effecting that reconciliation, to be glorified by a glorious miracle.

A three-day fast was proclaimed. The grieving people went through the city, made fruitful by so many thousands of saints, faithfully and humbly pouring forth tearful prayers at the shrines of each one, [Col. 0402A] that they might be delivered from the evils now imminent, indeed almost present. There was a public procession of clergy and people, monks and nuns as well; from every rank and from both sexes they resounded—diverse in language, yet one in intention and the same in meaning—with *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), and struck against the height of heaven.

Among them all, and before them all, the archbishop went forth, sad and supplicating: the hope of his sorrowing children and father of his country. His heart was so wounded, and his groans so great, that in a wondrous way the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, judged him worthy of consolation. When, therefore, the solemn litany had left the oratory of Saint Severinus and was approaching the oratory of Blessed Pantaleon, behold: a dove of snowy whiteness, seen by many, flew about his head; then suddenly vanishing, it appeared again visibly. [Col. 0402B] Many saw it, though not all, because it was not an earthly apparition but heavenly grace, granted to some to behold.

When they reached the place where the aforesaid confessor of the Lord, Severinus, had deserved to hear the voices of angels chanting psalms at the passing of blessed Martin, they saw from a distance the same dove circling the holy man’s head for the third time. Immediately it rose aloft, sought the heavens, and appeared no more. Who, then, could doubt that the grace of the Holy Spirit—such as dwelt within the chamber of his heart—appeared outwardly, especially at so mournful a time?

For the dove, like the turtledove, is a bird of mourning, accustomed to utter a groan instead of song. And just as the turtledove wanders alone, so the dove is accustomed to mourn in flocks. Most truly, therefore, the grace of the Holy Spirit marked out this man, praying and groaning beyond all others, by such a sign; and concerning him it said, in a certain manner, the very words which sacred Scripture records as spoken of another prophet, not unknown but eminent: “This is the lover of his brethren and of his people; this is he who prays much for the people and for this city” (2 Macc. 15). [Col. 0402C]

Certainly this man also showed himself most gentle among his people, after the likeness of the gentle and simple dove, overflowing with the holy spirit of compassion. Therefore his groaning and prayer could not perish. When the time for the meal came, he himself, though food had been set before him, almost kept a fast—yet, as was his custom, and especially then, concealed his fasting. Some looked toward him and spoke sorrowfully, saying that, despite the tears shed by so many that day, heaven had not yet opened because the Lord had not been propitiated. This blessed man answered with words worthy of remembrance, truly gentle and truly meek:

“Beloved ones, it is your shepherd’s fault that heaven above is so like iron, that the abundance of the Lord’s compassion and mercies has restrained itself from you. For unless the Lord were angry at my sins—I who ought to stand as mediator between him and you—he would already have torn open heaven, and his benefaction would have descended and rain would have fallen upon you.”

As he said these things, tears flowed from the wounded souls’ eyes, [p. 257] as though they were blood; and although he wished to restrain them as they burst forth and ran with force before many people, he could not. [Col. 0402D] Overcome by tears, he bowed his head upon the table in his hands and wrestled, in the strongest spirit, with the mighty God through humility and burning prayer.

At that very hour the sky was so clear that no cloud appeared in the air. But behold: suddenly, with a great crash, a vast outpouring of rain burst forth in a flood, so that the sound of the rain was heard before the holy man lifted his head from prayer. All who sat around immediately sprang away from the table and tried to rush out, so that they might resound with hymns in praise of Christ and of so great a bishop, and make the church bells ring. But that prudent man, most watchful guardian of his humility, sternly adjured them and forbade this; he barely obtained that for the moment they should be silent concerning himself, though they should never cease to praise God and give thanks to Christ. [Col. 0403A]

Nor was the rain then inadequate; rather, it watered the earth so abundantly that it restored the nearly dead roots of the crops to fruitfulness.

## CHAPTER XII. How he and Emperor Otto, by their common resolve, determined that whichever of them survived should build a monastery.

Meanwhile, while the father of the poor, the daily provider for widows and orphans, devoted himself to many great works of mercy, his mind was occupied by a continual concern to build a monastery for monks who would serve God. Their order professes that they are poor—voluntary poor people—having nothing of their own in this world.

While Emperor Otto was still alive, he had encouraged him in this undertaking. For when, on his final expedition, [Col. 0403C] Otto was entering Italy to settle the affairs of the realm, having the blessed man in his company, and all things were prospering, he discussed with the man of God the salvation of his soul and said, as it were: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 65). He received this counsel: that, for his salvation, he should construct a monastery of monks in honour of the holy Mother of God and of all the saints.

Having adopted this saving counsel, he immediately assigned to Christ the estates necessary for this undertaking. He handed them over to the blessed man, upon this pledge or covenant: since human life is uncertain, should the necessity of death overtake either of them, whichever one remained alive should fulfill the vow. [Col. 0403D] Such was the agreement made between them, with Christ as mediator. Thus these eminent men remained mindful of the poor, heirs of eternal greenness, such as those of whom the prophetic Spirit says in the Psalm: “The trees of the field shall be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon, which he has planted” (Ps. 103).

Under the names “trees of the field” and “cedars of Lebanon,” this proclamation mystically promises, through the Holy Spirit, the rich and powerful of this world who are to be hospitable to the poor; likewise, the spiritual children of the Church, of whom it immediately adds: “There the sparrows will make their nests; the heron’s home is their leader” (*ibid.*)—that is, Christ, signified by the bird called the heron, is the provider for those who become poor for his sake. He prepares the hearts of worldly rich persons so that, just as sparrows nest in the branches of the trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon, so these persons may receive, on the estates of those rich people and without possessions of their own, the necessities of this life prepared for them. [Col. 0404A]

I have wished to recall this so that everyone who lives from the provision of such persons, while professing Christ’s spirit and the holy poverty taught by Christ himself, may reflect that he ought, like sparrows, to fly—that is, to think heavenly thoughts—so that he may be worthy of the hospitality or provision prepared for the spiritual life of sparrows, that is, of the poor or humble. For this is why the same Lord Christ, instructing his poor, says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6). And again: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For your heavenly Father knows what you need. Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (*ibid.*). [Col. 0404B]

This is as though he were saying: “Come to me securely, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). Come securely and confidently to the rest of the contemplative life, taking no thought for tomorrow—that is, because your heavenly Father, knowing already what you need, has long ago promised and prepared food and clothing for you, saying through the Prophet: “The trees of the field shall be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon, which he has planted; there the sparrows will make their nests.”

But let us leave these matters and return to our subject. For it was not our purpose to teach monks that they should not receive established provisions unless they wish to fly by the wing of contemplation and be free from the servile work of sin, but to weave the narrative of the blessed man’s deeds. [Col. 0404C]

## CHAPTER XIII. How the holy Mother of God appeared to him and indicated the place where he ought to build the monastery.

When, therefore, blessed Heribert desired to build the monastery in a chosen place but nowhere found a site that he judged sufficiently fitting and suitable, he turned to the Lord and to his holy Mother. Through fasts and prayers he asked that her will might be revealed to him. He did this persistently, and, as is written of the holy prophetess Anna, “her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1); he did not cease until he received from heaven an answer proportionate to his merits.

One night, [Col. 0404D] after the vigils, when his weary limbs had yielded to sleep, behold, in a vision there came that blessed Queen of angels and of all saints. Seated upon a starry throne and possessing with her Son the broad and spacious kingdom of heaven, she did not disdain even this small dwelling offered to her on earth in faithful devotion. Standing by him, she said:

“Know, Heribert, that your prayers have been heard. Behold, I have now come to you to tell you in what place you are to fulfill the vow which you bear in your mind. For I am Mary, the Mother of the Lord. Rise, therefore, and go to the fortress of Deutz; command that a place within it be cleared, and there establish a monastery for God, for me, and for all the saints, so that where sin and the worship of demons once abounded, righteousness may reign in a multitude of saints.”

Having spoken these words, [Col. 0405A] the Mother of Mercy disappeared, while the blessed man awoke and thus fell back from the sweetness of so great a vision.

Within the same fortress there was an estate belonging to the bishop’s service. Rising, therefore, and giving most devout thanks to God in heart and speech, and not proving ungrateful to her who had deigned to appear to him, the Mother of everlasting salvation, he immediately summoned the steward of the aforementioned estate. He ordered him to have the estate cleared as quickly as possible, since it was now to become the court of the King of Heaven and his Mother: all its household goods were to be carried out, making room for the name of the Lord, which was coming to dwell there.

This was done. When the abundance of all the goods had been removed, the place was cleared more quickly than could have been expected. Why say more? Once the foundations had been laid, a beautiful structure rose rapidly and eagerly. [Col. 0405B]

[p. 258]

## CHAPTER XIV. How the church structure collapsed, another structure arose, and what example may fittingly be drawn from this.

But what shall I say? When the work was almost completed, and the community of monks serving God had already been gathered, as intended, one night after the solemn offices of Matins had ended and everyone had gone out, the whole building suddenly collapsed so completely that not one stone remained upon another, except for one small wall, which alone was found standing amid the ruins.

What should a wise reader think of this occurrence? Had the structure not arisen by heavenly authority; had not the dignity of such an exalted person as she who appeared, as already stated, commanded that the work be done in such a place; and had not this bishop, the founder of the work, been of acknowledged holiness—we might judge it an accident. [Col. 0405C] But now, considering the character of the events and persons, we may judge that this was done by divine and just ordering.

Since we cannot perceive the depth of the divine counsel, I wish to say only this: a fearful sign was given to all those who inhabit holy places, and especially to those who were thereafter to undertake holy service in that same place. For what was truly said of the Virgin’s Son—“Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke 2)—may not unfittingly be said of this place, the oratory of that same Virgin, and every place of the saints: it is set for the fall and rising again of many. For whose fall, except that of those who lead a ruined life in a holy place and will therefore bear a greater judgment? And for whose rising, except that of those who depart from the wicked world, flee past sins, take refuge in a holy place to do penance, and thus rise again to the state of righteousness? [Col. 0405D]

Certainly, it is not absurd to understand the fall of the former in the aforesaid collapse of stones, and the rising of the latter in the renewed building, which immediately arose in improved form. The man of God indeed grieved deeply over what had occurred. But soon recovering the strength of holy desire, he excavated the whole site for building the monastery to the depth of a ship’s mast, laid the foundations again, and, when it had quickly been completed, dedicated the monastery on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May]. From the stones of the former structure he built the cloister and its associated buildings.

Therefore, whenever you read or recall such an event, you who delight with an attentive mind to investigate examples of spiritual things through the likeness of any bodily things, not caring from what humble matter you obtain instruments of salvation, provided that you can be usefully built up—at the same time you may fittingly remember what is manifestly written with divine authority, where the Lord says to the Prophet: “Rise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you shall hear my words.” “And I went down,” he says, “to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel. And the vessel which he was making of clay with his hands was spoiled; and he turned it and made it into another vessel, as it pleased him in his eyes to make it” (Jer. 18). [Col. 0406A–B]

The purpose of the present narrative does not allow us to pursue or expound these matters and others like them. It seeks only briefly to recall here that, in every order, the proud fall or are broken because of their hardness, while the humble, converted to repentance because of their gentleness, are restored.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the Lord’s cross, which could finally be made not from just any wood but from a single tree; and what it also exemplifies.

Another event occurred which likewise ought not to be passed over or thought devoid of meaning. As soon as the man of God had laid the church’s foundations, he ordered that a cross of the Lord, which they were to erect there, be made. [Col. 0406C] The craftsmen laboured diligently to fulfill the command, but their diligence produced no result. Every day, rejecting one piece of timber after another, they cut other woods; yet they could by no means execute their craft from any kind of wood, however carefully selected. Worn out by much labour and even greater weariness, they decided to abandon that work altogether.

One day, however, the blessed man had come to an estate belonging to him, and at his command a table was prepared for him in an orchard adjoining his house. Opposite stood a pear tree, stretching high upward. Its branches were spread apart—indeed, like outstretched arms—so that it seemed in some manner to imitate the image of the Lord extending his hands upon the cross. As he sat at table and casually let his eyes wander while eating, behold: the tree suddenly presented this image to him; and in a wonderful way, at first sight it struck his mind with a certain divine awe. [Col. 0406D]

Without delay, making before his eyes the sign of the cross, familiar to him, he came fully to himself and wisely understood that this had been divinely foreseen and set before his eyes. Immediately summoning a craftsman, he ordered that tree to be cut down and that the Lord’s cross and the image of the Saviour upon it be carefully made from it. The craftsman obeyed, and the elegance of the work quickly and quite effectively followed the skill of the art.

What may be inferred from such an event? Does God concern himself with timbers or trunks, so as to indicate to the craftsman which wood, or what kind of wood, he ought to choose? No; there is truly another matter about which God is concerned, and which the prudent reader may profitably contemplate through this likeness. For the sign of the cross or image which the Christian people venerate in remembrance of the Saviour, lifted up before their eyes just as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness as a sign (Num. 21), ought to be imitated in a subordinate honour by shepherds whom the Holy Spirit has appointed to govern the Church of God (Acts 20), which he acquired by his own blood. [Col. 0407A]

Those who are known to act in Christ’s place ought to be honoured in Christ’s stead. They must not be thrust into the stewardship of God’s house by human presumption, but called by God’s election: that person should be appointed whom God has chosen, whom God has deigned to show worthy of presiding as his own worker, worthy through the Holy Spirit. Thus the event itself, which occurred almost in the same way, rightly reminds us of this truth, of this divine election: not just any wood, not whatever the human craftsmen wished, but that which divine will pointed out could be brought to the completion of such a work. [Col. 0407B]

[p. 259]

## CHAPTER XVI. How, while working miracles, he always fled reputation and glory; and why Elisha wished to perform twice as many miracles as Elijah, saying, “I pray that your spirit may be doubled in me.”

This blessed man possessed from the Holy Spirit, who “distributes to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12), the grace of working miracles; yet he always fled glory. As an outstanding guardian of humility, he did not wish—indeed, he avoided—having his righteousness seen by human beings.
