For it is especially by the light of such works that the life of saints becomes known before men. [Col. 0407C]

A sufficiently clear and evident indication of this is that, although he possessed this grace, as has been said, he is never found to have poured out prayer to the Lord for the working of any miracle. Nevertheless, some miracles of this kind were performed through him: at times against his will, and at times without his knowledge, as the following account will show.

Yet in this praise of his humility, nothing is detracted from the authority or glory of great saints who are recorded to have obtained the work of this grace through prayers often poured out. “Everything has its time,” says Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 3). For just as the Apostle says concerning kinds of tongues, which are given by the same Spirit: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14), so one may rightly say concerning miracle-working that miracles are for a testimony, not to believers but to unbelievers. They are especially to be desired by saints where a people ignorant of the true God is being instructed in faith. [Col. 0407D]

Accordingly, we observe that holy Elisha acted praiseworthily when Elijah said to him, “Ask what you wish before I am taken from you” (4 Kgs. 2), and he immediately asked: “I pray that your spirit may be doubled in me” (*ibid.*). He saw unhappy Israel following the fornications of the utterly wicked Jezebel, “limping between two sides” (3 Kgs. 18), following Jezebel’s idol Baal while wavering after the God of their fathers, who alone is the true Lord God. He saw that the people could not be restored to their proper state except through the working of many miracles. [Col. 0408A]

He therefore asked for a difficult thing; yet because he sought not his own glory but God’s glory and the common salvation of the people, what he asked came to pass, and the double spirit of Elijah rested upon him. For he received a twofold gift of the Spirit in the working of miracles. If you consult Scripture and calculate carefully, Elijah performed eight miracles, while Elisha performed about sixteen.

Thus those saints also are worthy of praise who, through charity or for the edification of unbelievers, worked miracles by prayers poured out to God. And this man and the others are rightly honoured who, for the preservation of humility, endeavoured in some manner to flee that grace of miracles which had been granted them from heaven and pursued them of its own accord. But let us now begin the narrative of this saint’s miracles. [Col. 0408B]

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning a demoniac who was set free while he was preaching.

On a feast day this holy man of God was, as usual, preaching to the people. It was the day which Christianity calls Palm Sunday, on which the King of Heaven entered the holy city Jerusalem, seated upon an ass’s colt (Matt. 21), plainly in contempt of the pride of earthly kings, of whom the Psalmist says: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses”; immediately adding, “But we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19).

In that name he then came to suffer, while the crowds cried: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21). [Col. 0408C] His sermon, therefore, was suited to the day and subject: how the devil, through the seduction of the first man, had occupied the court of this world as a strong man armed; and how the stronger Son of God, coming upon him through the humility of his cross and passion, conquered that strong man and took away all his goods—that is, ourselves, human beings—from him by right of conquest (Luke 11).

But behold: in the vast crowd of hearers was a certain man bodily possessed by that same strong man and prince of darkness, and therefore bound with hard chains. He had already been taken through many holy places in order that he might be freed through the merits of saints, but the desired healing had not come to him, because his deliverance was reserved by God’s providence for the merits of this most blessed man. [Col. 0408D]

As such a sermon flowed from the blessed man’s mouth, the enemy’s strength could not endure the power of truth. At every statement, as at so many blows, he howled more fiercely and, through the teeth of the wretched man, as though they were his own, gnashed at himself when he heard the accounts of his defeat by Christ. Thus the captive man, already known to many, became known to all, disturbing everyone’s silence with his cries and alone unsettling the whole region’s multitude, intent upon hearing the word of God.

At his cries, above all, that man, the son of mercy, directed all his attention. He could not continue the sermon which he had on his lips, because he was overcome by the greatness of his compassion. In silent thought he prayed that in one man might be made manifest the power of the Liberator who had freed the whole world. [Col. 0409A] While praying silently, he deliberately repeated again and again the passage recounting the glory of the victorious Christ and the ruin of the conquered devil. He seemed to have passed beyond conscious awareness, repeating the same sentence so many times, weeping at the same time and adorning the eloquence of his speech with most abundant, and most beautiful, tears.

The ancient enemy, as already stated, could not endure this, but was forced out by the power of the almighty Word. He fled, leaving free the man whom he had long possessed. When he had been driven out, the man who had been held bound by many said in a calm voice: “I beg you, release me, so that I too may quietly hear what that blessed bishop is saying.”

When he first said this, people thought that the wicked enemy was still deceiving them within him. But the man spoke more firmly, again and again declaring that he had been freed through the merits of the blessed bishop and speaking sound words. They therefore released him. He stood of sound mind, listening with the other hearers ever more attentively to the remainder of the sermon. [Col. 0409B] As many witnesses and admirers of the miracle performed toward the blessed man arose as there were people standing around him while he preached in that place. They had closely observed his expression and tearful bearing: although he said nothing with his lips for the captive’s deliverance, he nevertheless accomplished it through the power of silent prayer.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Abbot Volbert: warned in a vision, he recovered health through water in which the holy man washed his hands after Mass.

At the same time another proof of his miraculous power occurred, in which he shone more brightly from above, though through his pursuit of humility he kept himself low in his own estimation. [p. 260] [Col. 0409C] Three persons suffering illness were directed to him by heavenly visions, as to a physician of salvation, for testimony to his merits.

The first was a venerable man named Volbert, abbot of the already mentioned monastery which the saint himself had built. He was afflicted by a severe and long-lasting disorder of the head and eyes. One night it was divinely intimated to him in a vision that he should bathe his head and eyes by pouring over them water in which the holy bishop of God had, according to custom, washed his hands after the celebration of Mass. He was to believe without doubt that he would immediately recover health.

He believed, since more than most others he was personally acquainted with that most holy life. He came, having first been summoned by the bishop himself—as he was often summoned and consulted concerning the necessary affairs of the aforesaid monastery. [Col. 0409D] When the bishop was preparing in his customary manner to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, Volbert approached him more closely, as a familiar associate, related the vision, and asked that, as he had been shown, water from the bishop’s hands be given him by his command.

But the bishop, as though deeply offended and in some manner forgetting his gentleness—by which he could truly say, “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great things nor in wonders above me” (Ps. 130)—drove the man away as delirious and mad. Did he not know, or had he not seen, the Rhine flowing past his very doors, in which he could wash not merely his head and eyes but his entire body as much as he pleased?

Though rejected, Volbert did not lose faith in the vision. He obtained from the bishop’s attendants, secretly, that what he requested should be saved for him. As soon as he poured that water over his head and eyes, he recovered full health. [Col. 0410A]

## CHAPTER XIX. How a blind woman, warned in a vision, dipped her eyes in the wine in which he had washed his fingers after Mass and was enlightened.

After him, a woman who had long been blind saw almost the same vision. She was told that if she dipped her eyes in the wine in which the same holy man of God had customarily washed his fingers after receiving communion of the Lord’s body and blood, [Col. 0410B] she would immediately recover her lost sight. She believed; and taking care to obtain the remedy shown to her, she dipped her eyes in the wine and immediately received the desired light.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning a paralysed woman: similarly warned in a vision, she asked him for a blessing and was healed.

Then another woman, long paralysed, was warned in a vision to seek the blessed man’s blessing, trusting in Christ’s power that, through the merit of the blessed bishop, once her illness had been driven away, health would immediately follow. Without hesitation she asked to be carried by men and placed beside the road along which the man of God would pass.

Thus, as he passed, [Col. 0410C] she cried out and asked for a blessing in the Lord’s name. He paused briefly; when those present told him that she was paralysed and sought a blessing, he stood at a distance, raised his hand, and made the sign of the cross. Immediately restored health made her loosened limbs strong; and she who had been carried by the hands of others rose and returned home unharmed.

Thus, in a wondrous way, he who wished to remain hidden in his own eyes became more and more renowned through God, and the voice of truth was fulfilled which says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5); and, “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke 11).

## CHAPTER XXI. How a familiar cleric, visited by him, suddenly recovered from the burning of fevers.

At one time a cleric close to him, indispensable in his daily service, was seized by a severe fever and grievously tormented, so that nearly everyone despaired of his life. [Col. 0410D] At that time the holy bishop was travelling with the emperor, proceeding with him from the city of the Vangiones [Worms] to Mainz. He had the aforesaid cleric with him on the journey, as he customarily used his service both outside and within.

When the fever seized him on the journey and wore him down almost to death, concern arose in the father—who always had a loving disposition toward the afflicted—both from that same compassionate affection and, in the circumstances, from no small concern for his familiar attendant’s service. He went to the bed, leaned over and visited his sick man, asking him paternally whether he wanted anything, or whether he could manage at least to taste something. [Col. 0411A] Burning with the fierce heat of fever, the cleric declared that he desired nothing but water.

When this was granted with a blessing, the bishop himself entered, as customary, upon the solemnities of Mass. He did not pray aloud, so that those outside could hear, for the working of a miracle to grant health to the sick man. As has been stated above, he never offered an open prayer for miracles or signs of this kind. Yet he prayed—speaking to God but silent toward people—and especially in such cases observed the Gospel counsel of the Lord: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6).

For, having shut the door of his mouth, he prayed in such cases so that, when the effect of the miracle followed, he might be thought to have done nothing and thus his righteousness would not be seen by men. [Col. 0411B] Why say more? Once the Mass solemnities had been completed, when he again visited his sick man, the latter—without doubt rescued through the bishop’s merits from the great fires of fever and from the fear of approaching death—had recovered so fully that, now having an appetite for food, he asked that a dish from the bishop’s table service be sent to him.

This was done. Refreshed from it until he was satisfied, he recovered so fully from his illness that on the next day he went ahead to Mainz with the others on their intended journey and once more performed in full the duties of episcopal service as he had been accustomed to do.

## CHAPTER XXII. How, while praying amid the darkness of night, he was made radiant by divinely surrounding light; and how this happened many times.

The same familiar cleric, afterwards provost of the house of Saint Peter, knew and was accustomed to recount many great and magnificent things concerning that same father. Although most of these have been passed over for the sake of brevity, there is one which I have not wished to pass over in silence. It is truly a great and evident sign that his prayer was indeed fire and that his charity stood before the eyes of the Godhead like a burning and shining lamp. [Col. 0411C]

One night, while all those around him slept, the lamp that had customarily been placed before him to shine throughout the night was extinguished. [p. 261] The aforementioned familiar cleric suddenly awoke from sleep, rose, and looked about here and there in the somewhat dreadful silence. Anxiously disturbed about restoring the light, he beheld a divine and memorable sight, as he himself testified under oath. For in the very darkness of night, behold, an immense light shone from the bed on which the blessed bishop prayed wakefully with his hands outstretched. As its brilliance continually increased, he could not, as he confessed, see or distinguish those hands themselves. [Col. 0411D]

This sign made sufficiently clear that he was truly a son of light and of that day; and that his prayer truly consumed sins like fire and conquered the powers of darkness. Nor did this happen only once. Many times, after the hymns of Matins and the continuous chanting of psalms, when a material light had been put away somewhere, spiritual light surrounded the holy bishop as he prayed more secretly, so that the presence of the midday sun seemed to be at hand. [Col. 0412A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning his humility, by which, though despised by all the priests, he baptized the son of one of his poor dependants.

Already glorious signs of his humility have been set forth: in working miracles he sought the glorification of the Father who is in heaven, and avoided being known or seen by people. The virtue of humility itself, moreover, is only then sweet and praiseworthy in its perfection, when one who inwardly submits himself to God his Creator in contrition of heart also outwardly lowers himself, in accordance with circumstance and occasion, to the condescension due to the lowliest of people—the greater he is, the more deeply he humbles himself.

I am therefore pleased to insert into this narrative [Col. 0412B] an event that affords an example of great humility and a useful testimony: especially that in sacred matters no ecclesiastical dignity should despise any faithful poor person. And since very many ministers of the saving sacraments grievously sin by selling holy things and doing everything for gain, this example ought readily to be pressed upon them; for the event sharply rebukes their sin as well, whereas this saint shone forth, as has been said, in the great praise of humility.

A little child had been born to one of those poor persons whom the holy father supported with daily assistance. Because he was poor and had nothing profitable in hand, he was despised by the priests as he carried the little boy through the whole city of Cologne, asking that the grace of regeneration be bestowed upon his son. [Col. 0412C] Worn out and scorned, he therefore fled to the holy bishop and complained loudly and tearfully that he had been despised in such a matter.

The bishop, being truly wise, said at once: “Bring him to me, for I will baptize him.”

But the man said: “Then receive him yourself also from the sacred font, and deign to become my co-godfather.”

Accordingly, he baptized the poor little child, not weighing the sacrament of our salvation according to persons. By his deed and example he rebuked so many priests of so great a city because they had dared to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality, judging among themselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts, as the Apostle says:

> “If a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also enters, and you pay attention to the one wearing splendid clothing and say to him, ‘Sit here in a good place,’ but say to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool,’ do you not judge among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?” (James 2)

If in any judgment this apostolic authority rightly rebukes those who show partiality, how much more ought the holy man, in the dispensing of sacraments freely bestowed from heaven, to have rebuked by his example contempt for poverty? Thus, rightly walking according to the rule or counsel of Wisdom, which says, “If you do good, know to whom you do it, and there will be much gratitude for your good deeds” (Ecclus. 12), he bestowed [Col. 0413A] the sacrament of salvation, giving heed not to the person but to the creature formed in God’s image. He himself received the boy from the sacred font, became his co-godfather, and gave the father something with which to feed him.

On a later day, after celebrating the station at St. Severinus, he was returning, accompanied by a great crowd of clergy and people, and unknowingly passed the tiny hut of the poor man just mentioned. When the man saw him going by, he boldly sprang forward, seized the horse’s bridle, and cried out, adjuring him by the name of Christ and by the majesty of divine charity to stop a little and take at least something small from the provisions of his co-godfather, remembering the covenant he had made with him at the aforesaid regeneration or reception of the little son.

Let those also hear this example who, as though by priestly right, gladly take provisions from the poor—indeed, even exact them by force. To such men the Lord spoke through the prophet: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion” (Amos 6), and added: “You who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd” (ibid.). [Col. 0413B] Let them, I say, hear and imitate this example: the great bishop turned aside to the hut of such a co-godfather and took an excellent meal—a piece of bread, a young chicken, and a cup of thin beer. Let this be the cause, this the safeguard of piety, this the charity, whenever and wherever priestly dignity lowers itself toward the poor in order to receive a gift. Let these things suffice as a testimony or example of his humility.

## CHAPTER XXIV. [Col. 0413C] On his mercy: how he freed from hanging a cleric condemned for sacrilege.

As for mercy—how great a dwelling it had built for itself in his breast, and how truly he was merciful and a son of mercy—the witnesses were the crowds of poor people and the almost countless bands of the hungry. During famine raging throughout almost the entire world, he received with fatherly affection and motherly compassion those who flocked from many regions, not merely during one season or one year but through several years of his episcopate. In the wide generosity of his most kindly heart, he distributed them among the estates of his bishopric according to what he judged each property capable of sustaining.

Yet besides these daily manifestations of his compassion, he once performed a memorable deed [Col. 0413D] in which, because of the abundance of his mercy, he might seem nearly to have incurred the fault of lying, pretence, and duplicity. But as we recount such an action, let us recall at the same time the saying of the Wise Man: “The wrongdoing of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42).

The matter occurred as follows. A certain cleric among the poor people who, as has been said, had gathered under the care and almsgiving of the blessed bishop, was not content with the charitable allowance daily given him there. He had gone off as far as Saxony and, pursuing idleness—which, as Wisdom says, “has taught much wickedness” (Ecclus. 33)—had committed theft. Breaking into three churches by night, he took from them sacred vessels and vestments, and, as a sacrilegious man, made his way back toward Cologne. [Col. 0414A] There he was caught—or rather, pursued immediately by those who had suffered the loss, he was brought as an accused man before the judge of that city. There was no doubt about the sentence: according to civil law, a convicted sacrilegious thief was to perish at once by hanging.

The holy father happened then to be present in the city. On hearing what had happened, he immediately summoned the judge to himself and ordered him, as though he were an indignant avenger of theft, to bring the thief into his presence.

“I shall take no food or drink today,” he said, “until that man guilty of death appears before me.”

This was done; and when the man was brought before him, the bishop looked at him with stern eyes and said: “It is not lawful that you should live, since death, deserved and already prepared, has been acquired by so great a crime.”

After uttering these threats publicly before everyone, [Col. 0414B] he entrusted the accused man to an excellent officer—namely, the provider for the poor—but privately ordered that he be abundantly refreshed with necessary provisions.

When he himself reclined for dinner—the sole apparent reason for postponing the man’s punishment—and the whole gathering was seated and intent upon the meal, he did not forget his purpose. Secretly summoning the aforesaid provider for the poor, and secretly giving him gold, he whispered: “Lead out the cleric; saddle my horse for him as quickly as possible, ride alongside him, take him beyond the nearest forest, and, having given him a pound of silver, release him to safety. Then return as quickly as you can and stand before me.”

It was done as he commanded. When the servant had returned and stood before him, the bishop said with feigned severity: “Well then, where is that accused man?” In saying this, he appeared—or rather wished to appear—to be deliberating about the imminent execution of the punishment. [Col. 0414C] But the man, knowing both his will and his deed, feigned grief and fear.

“He has escaped, my lord,” he said.

Then the bishop too rushed about, displaying his pretended alarm in words and complaints, and threw all those present into astonishment. Rebuking and scolding the man as though intensely angry, the holy bishop turned to the people who had gathered for the spectacle:

“Look! That accused man has escaped; he has got away. Go, run, so that he may be brought back from flight and quickly pay the punishment due.”

This remarkable act of compassion was performed by this memorable craftsman of a brother’s salvation: a faithful dissembler and, if the expression may be used, a splendid liar. If anyone should think that such a contrivance cannot escape the charge of lying, he may sing again and again what has already been said: “The wrongdoing of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42). For “man” is he who strives toward virtue and, in all that he does, is intent upon the kingdom of charity. But “woman,” that is, the soft or effeminate person, is judged to be anyone of either sex who intends evil and is devoted to the kingdom of greed. Therefore, although in this deed he may seem to have incurred the fault of pretence, he is a “man”; and this wrongdoing of his is better than the good deed of one who feigns zeal for justice while practicing cruelty.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the persecutions of the holy man.

Amid so many and such great works of compassion, the servant of Christ, as though an evildoer, was not free from persecutions, as was mentioned above [Col. 0415A]. Nor is this surprising. For the Apostle says—or rather Christ, who speaks in his Apostle: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

And prophetic truth, in the psalm, after speaking of the holy rulers of the Churches, says:

> “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work in great waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” (Ps. 106)

It immediately adds:

> “He spoke, and a stormy wind arose, and its waves were lifted up. They rise to the heavens and descend to the depths” (ibid.),

and so forth.

Therefore this man too, because he lived piously in Christ, had to suffer persecution; and because he had undertaken to govern a ship upon the sea—that is, the Church in this world—he had to be troubled and tossed by waves.

He suffered persecution from envious people, namely those whose way of life was utterly unlike his. For he was burdensome to them even to look upon; and wherever he moved or stood before the Lord more holy and reverent, humble and little in his own eyes, there he displeased the envious all the more. His appearance was indeed most venerable, and a certain majesty of the virtues reigning in his mind was somehow visibly perceived outwardly in his face, especially when he stood at the holy altar intent upon the sacred solemnities of the Mass. Then he appeared so venerable that those wishing to look upon his face were frightened as subjects by something like the dignity of a master—unless they were strengthened by love, which alone is worthy of the sight of God and his saints.

The envious, angered all the more by this, cursed him, insolently saying to one another [Col. 0415C] that he was a demon, though it was clear that he was an angel of the Lord, according to the truth of Scripture:

> “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” (Mal. 2)

“Look,” they said, “at the demon, how he transforms himself into the likeness of an angel, so that none of us can look upon his face.”

And what wonder if Truth spoke truly, and the household of falsehood spoke in accordance with his saying? For he said: “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household” (Matt. 10).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On St. Henry the Emperor, who, badly persuaded by the envious, was hostile to the holy man.

A contrary wind raised greater waves in the emperor’s mind [Col. 0415D], because the envious men already mentioned constantly strove, by whispering slanders, to increase the suspicion that he had conceived against the holy man at the beginning of his reign, as has been said above. The matter advanced so far that the emperor, inflamed with excessive fury against him, set out for Cologne, intending either to remove him from the episcopate or, if this could not reasonably be done, to treat him in some way dishonorably and indignantly.

But God, Lord of sea and waves, who spoke mystically to blessed Job:

> “I surrounded the sea with my boundaries; I set bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far shall you come, and here you shall break your swelling waves’” (Job [Col. 0416A] 38),

did not permit this storm to proceed so far that the emperor might accomplish what he intended. Instead, he intervened and helped both: the man who suffered undeservedly, and the man who, thinking ill of an innocent conscience, sinned through deceived error.

The reason for which the emperor was hastening to Cologne in such a state of mind was as follows. Having raised an army, the emperor had besieged a certain Count Otto, eminent in worldly rank, in the castle called Hammerstein, situated above the bank of the Rhine. This Otto had repeatedly ravaged the bishopric of Mainz with much violence, laying it waste with fire and sword, fiercely inflamed by great hatred against the bishop of that city. For he had been anathematized by that bishop, by judgment of a general council, on account of an unlawful marriage.

When the emperor, stirred by the complaint of that bishop, had besieged Otto in the aforementioned castle, he ordered this venerable man also to come quickly with his own men for the affair. But at that time the bishop was afflicted by severe fevers and therefore could not fulfill what was commanded. [Col. 0416B] When the emperor heard this explanation of his inability, he did not believe it, being possessed by his former suspicion and thinking that the bishop had always found the times of his rule hateful. He therefore replied in anger and with great heat of wrath:

“If he disdains to come to me, I myself must visit him because he is ill.”

And with this anger, as soon as he had defeated his enemy, he hastened to Cologne, as has been said. The envious men mentioned above pressed urgently forward and intruded themselves excessively, fanning ever more fiercely the already burning fire of his rage by their malevolent tongues, slandering the innocent man of God.

But because the time had come for consolation and for placing an end to those waves and to the long storm of adversity, the Lord looked down from heaven, “made his storm into a gentle breeze, and its waves were stilled” (Ps. 106). For on the very night when he entered Cologne and was most dutifully received by the man of God, after he had given himself to sleep, he saw in a dream a certain man of venerable appearance, clothed in pontifical vestments, who addressed him thus:

“Beware, Emperor, lest hereafter you sin any further against my fellow-servant Herebert. Know that this man is acceptable to God; whatever you commit against him, you shall without doubt bear judgment for it.” [Col. 0416D]

Surely, by thus forewarning the emperor, the grace of merciful God spared his ignorance. For in holding such a man under suspicion, he sinned not from malice but from ignorance. Indeed, fear of the Lord possessed the emperor’s soul; nor did he knowingly wish to arrange or judge anything in the kingdom by which the heavenly Majesty might be offended. Whenever he intended to determine or judge any business of the realm, he preceded all his decisions and judgments with prayers and alms, so that his mind and actions might be governed by heavenly rule and he might not at any time go astray in acting or judging contrary to divine laws.

Therefore, in accordance with his intention, he was rightly forestalled and preserved by the divine oracle, as has been said, lest, by wronging a bishop of such great merits as he intended, he himself should become liable to the judgment of the Divinity.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the emperor, while his rivals looked on, kissed the holy man three times.

Why say more? When morning came, the emperor, now changed in mind, summoned the man of God. The holy man still did not know what had happened from heaven—that the king had been pierced by a heavenly visitation—and accordingly, with tearful eyes, he brought forward his complaint, asking why the emperor had for so long been hostile to him. Suddenly, beyond expectation, the emperor rose and embraced the man of God.

In his astonishment, the holy man received these words of consolation from him: [Col. 0417B]

“Since I ascended, by God’s gift, to the height of royal power, I confess, venerable Father, that I have been excessively credulous toward slanderers’ tongues. I hated you; carrying this beam of hatred in my own eye and therefore seeing nothing, I judged you unjustly and did not deserve to see your righteousness—indeed, the grace of God shining in you.

“Yet while you say nothing, heaven cries out for you and defends your cause before me. For he who always has cared and does care for his saints, as it is written, ‘did not permit anyone to harm them, and rebuked kings on their account’ (Ps. 104), saying, ‘Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act maliciously against my prophets’ (ibid.)—he himself rebuked me on your behalf, that I might know you to be numbered among his elect.

“Forgive, therefore, I pray, the malice I have committed against you, or the intention I had to touch you, the servant of God. For I acknowledge my sin and will no longer add to it by opposing your holiness.”

After these words he kissed the holy bishop once, then again, and a third time, thus tying the threefold knot of love of which the Wise Man speaks: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclus. 4). It may certainly be thought that the emperor—an upright and ecclesiastically minded man, as he was learned and perfectly accomplished in literary knowledge—remembered the Gospel, where Peter, first of the apostles, wiped away the guilt of his threefold denial by a threefold confession of love, answering the third time: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21).

Beautifully and fittingly, therefore, he gave the threefold kiss of love and peace under the testimony of the Holy Trinity; and by this sweetness of grace and honor he overcame the bitterness of his former hostility. Without delay, now as a friend receiving a friend, he seated the man of God near himself. Seeing this, the adversaries who had assembled against him as though they had found an opportune time, and had long sharpened their tongues for accusation, were confounded and immediately turned to flight. But the rest blessed the Lord, magnifying the truth of Scripture: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How, when the emperor again humbly sought pardon, he foretold his own death.

The religious king was not content with this reconciliation, but remained anxious about divine judgment. For the person against whom some sin has been committed indeed has the evangelical command or counsel to forgive from the heart one who sins against him (Matt. 18); yet he who gave the law must still be feared, who said through the prophet, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 1), and of whom it is likewise written, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12).

Therefore, rightly anxious and not content with the reconciliation already made, on the following night, after the conclusion of the matins solemnities, [Col. 0418A] the same emperor took one of his clerics and went to the chamber of the holy bishop. He did not find him resting there, however, but keeping vigil, as was his custom, and persisting in prayers in the nearby chapel of St. John.

Immediately casting off his cloak and prostrating himself on the ground before the bishop’s feet, he asked to be received in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, and to be granted, through the authority that the Lord had bestowed upon his priests, pardon for all that he had committed against him.

Without delay the servant of almighty God lifted the prostrate emperor from the ground; and through Christ standing between them, who said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. 18), and then, “Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (ibid.), absolution from guilt was effected in heaven and on earth according to the king’s faith.

But for the servant of God this was the beginning of everlasting consolation, since he was soon to ascend from this valley of tears to the joy of the divine vision, as the Psalmist says:

> “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears.” (Ps. 83)

And soon afterward:

> “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” (ibid.)

For this same man of God, taught beforehand by a revelation of the Spirit, knew this and said, among other things, in that private meeting to the same emperor: “Know with certainty that after your departure, by which we are now to be separated, we shall never again see one another’s faces in this world.”

The emperor, all the more pierced in heart, again threw himself into embraces and kisses, weeping and caressing almost every part of him—his hands, eyes, and neck—with lingering kisses. After doing this, he returned secretly to his chamber, carrying away the sorrowful recollection of the blessed man’s prophecy. Later, when that man’s death followed, he learned it to have been true and, as he had heard it, recounted it himself in his own words. Nor was this saint of God prophetically foreknowing only of his own death; he also foresaw the emperor’s death, as the present narrative will not fail to tell in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The holy man is seized with fever and fortified by the Church’s sacraments.

Therefore, after the emperor’s departure, blessed Herebert, a citizen of heaven, wearied by his long pilgrimage in this world, gazed with longing upon the everlasting dwelling of his heavenly homeland. At last he was seized with fever; and behold, the servant of the Lord, watchful because of this expectation, thought that he felt the Lord already coming and knocking, that the door might be opened to him. [Col. 0419A]

At that time he was in a village of his diocese called Neuss. As he was troubled by the urgent and worsening illness, he quickly sent to Cologne and summoned Abbot Elias. When Elias arrived, Herebert was anointed with holy oil in the name of the Lord according to the Apostle’s command (James 5), and at the same time fortified with the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. Only then was he carried aboard a boat to be conveyed to Cologne.

By his order he was brought into the chapel of the prince of the apostles and laid before the altar of the Holy Cross situated in the middle. As best he could, with head, eyes, and hands stretched toward heaven, he prayed at length. Very many were present from both clergy and people, at once wondering and pierced with compunction by the sweetness of his prayers and the devotion of his supplication. Truly, at every time, and especially then in his last moments, that Davidic saying fittingly applied to him:

> “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice.” (Ps. 140)

When his prayer had been completed with its sweet fragrance and religious example, he was carried into the chamber adjoining the chapel. The aforementioned abbot was kept by him for consolation. During two successive nights, whenever he took a little sleep, he was instructed by lofty visions that this illness would undoubtedly cause the bishop to depart from the body.

## CHAPTER XXX. Visions of Abbot Elias concerning the death of the holy man.

One such vision was as follows. At once, in the morning hour, he told it in this way to the blessed man, who desired release from his flesh: [Col. 0419C]

“I saw myself entering the chapel of Blessed Peter, and behold, it was filled as though with a great and solemn assembly. Splendid choirs of clerics and holy women stood there, apparently ready to go out and meet some great personage, so that he might be honorably received by them. Such an honor is the custom of the Church in welcoming sacred and illustrious persons in due time.

“I did not know who that person was to be; nevertheless, my dreaming mind perceived that some great person of exceptional dignity was to be received. Though trembling, I remained motionless in my place. Then I summoned the one who seemed first among them and asked who was to be received by them.

“He answered: ‘We have come to receive Herebert the archbishop, beloved by God and by all the saints.’

“Astonished beyond measure at the festal splendor of so great an encounter, I immediately heard him add: ‘If you knew in what manner, or by whom, he is afterward to be received, you would not marvel at our procession, which in reality is far inferior.’”

When the man who had seen this vision recounted it immediately at dawn to the blessed man, he truly gladdened with this good news the holy soul that desired “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1). For it promised that a swift fulfillment of his longing expectation was near and confirmed the foreknowledge of his departure already mentioned. [Col. 0420A]

Before this vision, the same venerable man Elias had also seen something else that undoubtedly pertained to the signification of the same event. He had dreamed that the bishop himself, adorned in sacred and festal vestments, was proceeding as though to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, but alone and unaccompanied, while the clergy stood waiting in silence. The bishop, as though about to leave on a journey to Rome, asked for a blessing; then, as it seemed, he withdrew alone and was nowhere found.

Although Elias reported these things sorrowfully, they had an unmistakable meaning, and the blessed man received them with abundant joy. Long since foreknowing his own end, he was encouraged by these present signs, so that he might say: “Break my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115). Greater matters, by which the departure or merits of this blessed man were more fully and particularly signified, have been reserved for another place. Now let the narrative continue its begun account of his death.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How the holy man consoled his weeping brother.

Since the Lord was now undoubtedly knocking through the suffering of his present illness, this faithful servant hastened to open to him, his loins long since girded and his lamps brightly burning. All that remained was distributed to the poor, so that when he departed for the eternal dwellings, he himself, now poor, might be received in grateful return.

His brother, Count Gezemannus by name, sat at the head of the bed [Col. 0420C], shedding deep tears and continuing most bitter groans, like a shipwrecked man who looked around upon a storm on the great sea while his rudder was broken and he was in peril.

The most compassionate man, deeply sympathizing with him, said: “Why, my brother, do you afflict yourself with such miserable lamentation? Spare your tears and groans, I pray, because God will not lack counsel and consolation for those who hope in him. Cast your care upon him. Since the time of living is short for all in this world and we must depart, prepare yourself meanwhile and have mercy upon your own soul, that you may be deemed worthy of the age to come.

“This is the most necessary and best manner of preparation for you: as far as you are able, share your possessions with the poor and make friends for yourself, so that, when you fail, as our Lord says, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 10).

To these and similar saving admonitions, the brother replied: “My lord, with God’s inspiration I shall endeavor to do these things willingly; but your departure from this life means the orphanhood of your brother and the inconsolable widowhood of my soul. Moreover, you know that the imperial majesty has always been hostile to all your relatives; and while you still lived, our position in this present life was dangerous because of him. But now our refuge, our wall and bulwark, falls when you depart this life—you whose strength and grace, and whose great merits publicly known before God and men, protected us.”

To this the man of God, instructed beforehand by the prophetic Spirit, answered: “Strive to make the immortal King favorable to yourself by the means I have already described. But as for this man, the common necessity will bring about his end, so that he too shall enter the way of all flesh. For know that after my death he will not complete the course of three years.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. How at his end he showed himself mindful of the poor.

After this, as the illness grew worse and his death was no longer uncertain, spiritual funeral rites were begun at his command by the brethren with the singing of psalms. He too, as far as his panting breast allowed, stretched forth the harp, singing with them and in some manner saying:

> “I shall enter the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and confession.” (Ps. 41)

Meanwhile he saw near him, among the throng of mourners, the provider for the poor to whom he had committed their care.

“And what are my brothers doing now?” he asked. “Does anything fail in their provision?”

He meant the poor; for in humility of conscience he was accustomed to consider them his brothers, indeed also his lords and patrons before God. [Col. 0421B]

When the man answered that he had spent everything assigned to him and that nothing now remained, Herebert immediately summoned the provost of the Church and the advocate of the city, addressing them thus:

“You have heard, beloved ones—or rather, you ought attentively to hear—Scripture saying: ‘He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord’ (Prov. 19), and, ‘As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving resists sins’ (Ecclus. 3). If I have offered you any good example in accordance with these words, if I have sown anything among the poor, the recompense now laid up will be repaid, and the harvest that I have acquired is now to be received, as it is likewise written: ‘He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings’ (2 Cor. 9).

“For I shall no longer be here with you, where seed is sown. I must depart, and the hour is now at hand when I shall receive there, where the harvest is gathered, what is proper to my body, according to what I have done. Therefore, as a dying father drawing his final breath addresses his most beloved sons, I charge you with this last testament: be mindful of the poor, and afford this consolation to my soul, that until a successor bishop is appointed, the relief I have established for the poor may not fail through your supporting care.”

On hearing this, they were greatly pierced with compunction and promised most willingly to do it. They mourned all the more for his departure because, looking to what he had done in the past, they saw how fitting were his last words: what manner of man he was, how he had lived, with what constant zeal he had stored up mercy for himself, and how wisely he had provided for the necessity and end of the approaching hour, in which all praise is sung.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. He foretells who will succeed him, and dies.

Because he had mentioned a successor, they were stirred to still deeper lamentation. Like orphans now deserted, they asked and inquired who would receive as their mother the Church left widowed by so great a bishop.

“That man,” they said, “is venerable in life; and that other one is at least somewhat suitable,” and thus, weighing the qualities of various persons, they exchanged their anxious thoughts with longing.

But he, as was said above, instructed beforehand by the prophetic Spirit, said: “Neither that man nor this one whom you think of; but you shall have Pilgrim as bishop, and he shall administer the office of bishop in this Church for a short time.”

Having said these things, released from the flesh, he ascended from the distress of this present life to the eternal consolation of his everlasting homeland, receiving the fruit of perpetual joy. He died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, and was buried in the fortress of Deutz, in the chapel of the Holy Mother of God which he himself had founded. There afterward he shone through many miracles, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When his holy body had been buried there, the man who had been steward of the holy bishop on that estate—the estate in which, as stated above, the chapel had been built through the aforementioned revelation—then remembered and, marveling at divine providence, said: [Col. 0422B]

“This place, in which this holy body has been buried, was always a grassy mound, ever clean and pleasant, continually delightful to every eye.”

This surely adds to the praises of the most blessed man: by God’s command the appearance of the place had thus prepared itself for his future funeral and for the preservation of his relics, so that the green bosom of the earth in which the possessor of everlasting greenness was to rest might always remain green—he for whom was laid up an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.

Therefore with the Apostle let us say to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to God alone, [Col. 0422C] honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen. (1 Tim. 2)

## CHAPTER XXXIV. A vision granted to Bishop Eppo after the death of the holy man.

At the same time the notable man Eppo, bishop of Bamberg, flourished in distinguished character and considerable virtues. Though so far away, on the very night when the man of God Heribert, after completing the warfare of this life, received, as has been said, the heavenly reward, he saw the following vision. He seemed to enter a vast and splendid capitol; and behold, there sat there an innumerable assembly of venerable persons—bishops, abbots, kings and emperors, and illustrious men of every rank—each clothed according to his own order [Col. 0422D]. All were beautiful and reverend, as though gathered to conduct a general council.

Moreover, in the middle of those seated there appeared an episcopal chair, conspicuously placed, though not yet occupied; nevertheless, it had been prepared for someone to sit in it. When, therefore, as he himself related, he had looked into a place of such majesty and an assembly of such venerable multitudes, he stood overcome alike by amazement and fear, and did not dare to enter. At daybreak he hastened to report this vision to Emperor Henry, who was then staying there and observing Lent.

He said: “As I stood thus stupefied, behold, one of that holy senate and, as it were, that great heaven of patricians [Col. 0423A], rose and came out to me, standing before the doors. I had known him formerly. Taking me by the hand, he led me in and signaled that I should sit upon the vacant seat just mentioned. But I, afraid, refused to do so. For I knew that this chair had been placed not for me but for another man, whom I did not then know, one of greater reverence and more ample dignity.

“Without delay, the one who seemed to hold primacy in that same assembly ordered two venerable bishops from among those seated there to go outside, bring in the first person they found standing and ready, and honorably place him in the central seat, since it had been prepared for his sitting. They did as they had been commanded. And behold, the man whom they brought was Lord Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne, adorned in sacred vestments as on a feast day for the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass [Col. 0423B]. As they had been commanded, they made him sit in that central chair.

“One element of his adornment, however—namely, his girdle—seemed to be missing. When those great princes sitting there saw him and noticed that he lacked a girdle, they were stirred by vehement astonishment and asked who had dared diminish the adornment of so great a bishop. While he himself said nothing, one of the foremost spoke first and said that it was Emperor Henry.”

As has been said, the venerable bishop reported these things to the emperor in the morning. And, being certain of the vision’s truth, he affirmed that Saint Heribert of the Lord had already been separated from earthly things and transferred to the immortal senate of the heavenly court. Nor did his confidence deceive him. For after a few days a messenger came and announced to the emperor, who was there observing the holy Lent as already mentioned, the death of the Archbishop of Cologne. When he was carefully asked when the archbishop had died and whether he had departed from the body by night or by day, and answered according to the facts, both the emperor and the bishop who had seen the vision marveled that the Lord had deigned to reveal such things to persons so far away. For it was established that the saint of the Lord had departed on the very night on which the bishop had seen the vision.

But even before the aforesaid messenger arrived, the emperor, not disbelieving the vision, had answered the bishop as he told it: “If that holy and venerable man lacked his girdle because of me, a robber, then, with the Lord’s help and through my own efforts, this robbery shall be restored to him” [Col. 0423D]. He also recalled their last conversation, in which the emperor had made satisfaction before him for his offense and had heard from him that they would not see one another’s faces again. Nor did it escape him, a prudent interpreter in this matter, that saying the great man had been stripped of his girdle meant that he himself had not honored him worthily according to his merits.

Accordingly, extending the imperial hand more generously, he distributed gifts to the churches of Christ and to the poor; and he ordered the departure of the blessed bishop to be commemorated with the sacred solemnities of Masses, psalms, and prayers—the bishop whose girdle he himself had taken away, that is, whom while living he had honored far less than was fitting. Truly, he acted as a wise man; for assuredly he could restore this robbery in no better way [Col. 0424A] than by producing in himself fruits worthy of repentance.

It may therefore be supposed that such a vision was granted not only for the honor of the blessed bishop, but also for the improvement of the same emperor. By the satisfaction mentioned above, he had deserved that, just as the person himself did not accuse him, so neither should a surviving trace of the case accuse him. For in the vision, when the holy council asked who had diminished the saint’s adornment, it must be carefully noted that the blessed bishop himself did not answer, nor did he accuse the emperor, because while living, mindful of the evangelical command, he had forgiven him everything from his heart (Matt. XVIII). Thus this vision nobly helped ensure that even the slight remaining trace of the matter would not accuse him [Col. 0424B], stirring his soul to works of mercy.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Of miracles at his tomb, and a certain wondrous vision.

Meanwhile, the tomb of the blessed man appeared, as it was, to be a place of refuge for those possessing faith and fleeing in whatever need to the protection of the God of heaven; and, like a stream of paradise, the grace of healings flowed thence abundantly. The sick were healed, the blind enlightened, the lame raised up, and demons driven out of possessed bodies.

One event among the rest occurred within the thirty-day period following his burial, which, because of its greatness, ought not to be passed over, but rather especially recounted. The event was exceedingly marvelous [Col. 0424C], and would almost be unbelievable, if the holy and canonical Scriptures did not establish that angels—who are certainly spirits and not clothed in flesh—have sometimes been seen and heard by human bodily senses. Indeed, it happened that the spirit of this blessed man, now freed from the flesh, visibly appeared to a living man and spoke with him. The truth which subsequently followed the words spoken testifies that what was shown was not a phantom but true and divine.

The event occurred in this way. The venerable Volpert, first father of the monastery founded by that holy bishop, was, by the recent death of so great a bishop, stirred even more strongly to constant prayers, especially vigils by night. He was the father of many monks, since, because of his outstanding manner of life, learning, and abundance of love, not only the care and oversight of the aforesaid monastery, but also that of the monasteries of Saint Pantaleon and Saint Vitus, had been entrusted to him [Col. 0424D]. Throughout his life he had made it almost his unceasing practice to anticipate the morning hymns and, in solitary vigils, chant Davidic psalms. His grief at the death of so great a father had, as stated, made this holy fervor greater.

One night, therefore, while he was applying himself more ardently to this very work and offering the incense of holy prayer in a great fire of love, truly the smoke of his spices rose higher and reached heaven before the eyes of the Lord. For while he continued at prayer [Col. 0425A], the divine regard came upon him, and the place trembled, in accordance with what is written in the psalm—without prejudice to its higher meaning: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. CIII).

He stood near the tomb of the blessed bishop, and he who had loved him while living clung ardently, in mind and body, to him now buried. When, then, the place shook so violently that the whole fabric of the monastery seemed to be shaken to its foundations, he shuddered as a mortal man, but, having no slight faith, continued the prayer he had begun, holding the horn of the altar. Again, from the eastern side, the wall of the church shook with a great sound, and everything around seemed to move. Then behold, the tomb of the blessed man was opened, and the saint of God himself seemed to come forth [Col. 0425B]. Standing near the man just mentioned and lightly touching him, he asked what he was doing.

This would appear entirely incredible, as stated above, if ecclesiastical writings did not contain examples of the spirits of the dead, by God’s will, being visibly seen in bodily form; and if angels also had not been received as guests by persons pleasing to God (Gen. XVIII, XIX). Daniel, too, troubled by an angelic vision, was strengthened by him who had appeared to him (Dan. X). When the blessed bishop began to speak to this man, first touching his side with the episcopal staff with which he had been buried, he recovered his strength and was able to answer the questions put to him. For the vision and the aforesaid crash had so terrified him that he was unable to stand; indeed, he had scarcely strength enough even to sit [Col. 0425C].

When, therefore, he had briefly answered the question what he was doing, the one who had appeared immediately added these words:

“Brother, diligently and watchfully persevere in prayers; and, entreating salvation for your living and dead parents and kinsfolk, remember me also more abundantly. For know—and give faith to me who speak the truth—that on the thirtieth day of my death, now approaching, you shall dine with me.”

Hearing this, Volpert sat down in the same place almost lifeless. At length, gradually drawing breath, he recovered himself; leaning on his staff, he rose, and, trembling in body and mind, barely reached his bed. In the morning, when he came out as usual to the assembly of brethren, he delivered an edifying address, sufficiently eloquent and adorned with spiritual beauty. Among other things he especially urged that which is the excellent ornament of monks: that they should keep their mouths in silence, because, as the prophet testifies, “Silence is the cultivation of righteousness” (Isa. XXXII) [Col. 0425D]. For the time being, however, he kept secret the vision that he had seen.

After the assembly had been dismissed, he called aside only the elders and those who seemed more spiritual, and recounted in order everything that he had seen and heard. But they did not understand the matter as it was, and valued it far less than they should. Speaking according to their own judgment, they told him it was nothing other than a common human experience: he continually turned over in the thought of his heart the one whom he had loved in life; and dreams of this kind followed upon waking thoughts and the concern of love which he bore toward him [Col. 0426A].

But although he heard these things, he nevertheless knew what and how he had seen, and trusted his own conscience more than the ignorant conjectures of others. What more need be said? The thirtieth day after the blessed man’s death was approaching, and the aforesaid father of the monastery prepared abundant provisions for the poor for that day. To make these preparations, he had to go to a village belonging either to himself or to the church, about ten miles from the monastery, where he hastened personally to order what was necessary for the coming day.

After doing this, he boarded a boat and swiftly returned by the channel of the Rhine to the monastery. By the sixth hour his companions urged him to take supper, since this was pleasant to them according to custom and the hour was sufficiently appropriate [Col. 0426B]. He did not refuse; indeed, yielding in charity to the young men who served him, he first performed the work of God and began to sing the office of the sixth hour, as customary, with two brethren attending him. When they came to the reading which we call the chapter, it was this: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him. For in that he died …” (Rom. VI), etc. As they responded, “Thanks be to God,” he immediately breathed out his spirit.

When the brethren, associates, and companions present saw this, they were deeply astonished and seized by sudden shock. After pausing for a little, they at once raised voices of wailing. A little before they had been happy, but now they were sad, seeing their harp turned into mourning and their organ into the voice of those who weep [Col. 0426C]. One man went out and hastened overland to the monastery to report the event to the brethren.

At the hour when this messenger arrived, the brethren had sat down to supper, happily expecting their father’s arrival and the spiritual rejoicing of the following day, the thirtieth day of the blessed bishop. When news of this kind became known to those seated together, all alike groaned heavily, shaken in mind and almost all driven from their seats, with gestures so mournful and a procession so tearful that no abundance of words could adequately express it. For upon the wound still fresh—that is, the grief caused by the blessed bishop’s death—another wound had been added [Col. 0426D]. The deaths of fathers so near together and so continuous touched the hearts of their sons profoundly.

Yet that venerable father, who had now departed in this way, had indeed gone happily when called to the banquet of eternal life and the supper of immortality. By his death he confirmed both his vision and the true oracle of him who had said: “On the thirtieth day of my death you shall dine with me.”

When the body of the dead man had been brought back, it was laid near the tomb of his prophet, namely the holy bishop, with the rites of burial. Then, during the funeral vigils, a certain poor man, crippled from the cradle, whom the same holy bishop, while still living, had supported with a father’s care, sadly crawled between the saint’s tomb and this dead man’s bier. Lying between the two dead men, the patrons of his poor life, he mourned all night that he had survived them [Col. 0427A].

Those who lived before God saw him; and with the same mercy by which, while alive in the flesh, they had provided him sustenance for life, they now, being dead, wrought a miraculous healing of his entire body. At the dawn of light, while the brethren were performing the morning hymns, the man who had lain crippled suddenly cried out loudly, as though help had come to him—struck, that is, by an invisible power—and his sinews were loosened and he was stretched out full length. Hearing his cry, some of the elder brethren ran to him and saw him lying stretched out, while a stream of foul blood ran across the pavement [Col. 0428A]. Water was immediately brought; he was refreshed and, after a little while, rose up whole and remained sound.

This work of power ought rightly to be ascribed to the merits of both men. Moreover, within the course of a few days after the blessed bishop’s death, about forty-five men and women, freed from various afflictions at his glorious tomb, praised the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives eternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0427]

# THE PASSION OF BLESSED ELIPHIUS, MARTYR.

## RUPERT’S PROLOGUE. TO ALBAN, THE VENERABLE ABBOT OF SAINT MARTIN.

[Col. 0427B] The first man, who long before and in the night-time wrote the martyrdom of the precious martyr Eliphius, laid the foundation; but you, dearest brethren—you, Father Alban, together with your spiritual sons—compel my insignificance to build upon it. For a long time I resisted your charity with excuses, and the chief ground of my excuse was this: that I could not lay any foundation other than the one already laid (I Cor. III).

For I found no other material to be found concerning the memory of this martyr and your patron, whose precious bodily treasure you rejoice to possess deposited among you, except that writing which you, no less than we, consider neither sufficiently pleasing nor sufficiently suitable [Col. 0427C], because of its excessive simplicity of style. It not only fails to adorn the event with its proper splendor, but even somewhat obscures it, as if with a kind of smoke.

Therefore I refused, judging what your charity demanded to be exceedingly difficult and almost impossible; as if an architect were told: “Upon this narrow and slight foundation, build us a broad and spacious, firm and splendid structure.” But at last this saying came to me and entered my resistant mind: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Matt. IX). And likewise the saying of the Holy Spirit in the psalm: “Open your mouth”—or, “Open wide your mouth”—“and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX).

Conquered, therefore, by charity, by which it is surely devout and honorable to be conquered, I now open my mouth, to be filled through your prayers by him who commanded it to be opened, so that I may build more religiously gold, silver, and precious stones [Col. 0428C] upon this foundation. Thus may the composition, or fitting arrangement, of sentences—as though crowning them—vie with the beauty of the material, rather than being poor and deficient in eloquence, and may it suit the dignity of the events.

## THE PASSION OF BLESSED ELIPHIUS BEGINS.

[Col. 0427]

[Col. 0427C] In the time when the impious apostate Julian disturbed the majesty of the Roman Empire, Eliphius, a man glorious in worldly rank and most distinguished in Christian faith, flourished in the city of Toul, a city of Gaul. The natives of that place were anciently called the Leuci, and the city itself Leucha.

This holy man had a most holy brother and three virgin sisters, all memorable citizens of the heavenly city Jerusalem, whose names are written in the book of eternal life. His brother Eucharius, exercising the honor of episcopal grace, happily attained also the palm of martyrdom, and his body was buried in the fortress called at Liverdun. His first sister was Menna, the second Libaria, and the third Susanna. As they were of one faith, so they were all of one and the same profession, namely the monastic profession.

Concerning the first, the holy virgin Menna, antiquity has not recorded in writing whether she ended her present life by the palm of martyrdom; only that, remaining in virginity, she died and was buried in the place called Portes [Col. 0428D]. The second, Libaria, and the third, Susanna, fulfilled their manner of life by the holier glory of martyrdom: Libaria near the city called Grand, and Susanna was buried in Champagne.

Having said this concerning the kinsfolk according to the flesh and fellow-heirs according to faith of this holy man, we must speak of the time already mentioned, which was so grievous that no one should wonder that it could disturb those regions of Gaul as well.

The aforesaid Julian, at the beginning of his reign, spared Christians and seemed rather merciful. For he knew that the earlier persecutions had done nothing to increase paganism; rather, Christians had increased through them and, dying for the true doctrine, had become glorious. He had been a domestic enemy, a pretended Christian. Fearing Constantius, who in terror of tyranny killed even relatives by blood, he had had his hair cut, feigned the monastic life, joined the choir as a reader, and read the divine books in church while the people listened [Col. 0429A].

Knowing this, and envying the glory of Christians, he abstained from tortures, judging it necessary to persuade the people toward the worship of paganism by discourse and exhortation rather than force; he even believed that he would thereby show himself merciful. For he thought paganism would be strengthened more effectively if he showed himself patient and mild toward the Christian people. Yet beneath this pretence of philosophical mildness, the praise of which he eagerly desired, the cruelty of the impious man could not long contain itself.

He repeatedly took away money and sacred ornaments; churches founded under Constantine and Constantius were destroyed; and money previously granted for buildings was demanded back. On this pretext priests, clergy, and the Christian people were cruelly harassed. Seeking out all the possessions and monies of the churches with beatings, he ordered them brought into public account. Then, writing also to the priests of the temples and governors of provinces, he made clear how much zeal he had for paganism and how much hatred for Christianity [Col. 0429B].

The pagans, therefore, having acquired liberty for their madness, exacted vengeance upon Christians, complaining against them for injuries to idols and temples, which had been destroyed in the times of Constantius and Constantine. Thus innumerable acts were committed everywhere, on land and sea, by the impious against the devout, at that time when the emperor, openly hateful to God, enacted laws against piety, supported by the favor of priests and governors, and especially of his uncle Julian, devoted to paganism and intensely hateful toward Christians [Col. 0429C].

A storm arose under a wind so strong and so adverse, roaring, as already stated, against Christians in Gaul as throughout the world. The little ship of the holy Church appeared, as though tossed by waves in mid-sea, to be deprived of divine aid. Julian, the uncle and prefect of the apostate Julian already mentioned, is said to have insulted it by urinating shamelessly against the sacred altar and declaring that the Christian religion had been deserted by divine care [Col. 0429D].

But the Lord Jesus was truly present, walking invisibly upon the waters; and Peter too, in his accustomed manner, walked upon the waters in order to come to Jesus, while the faith of the holy Church was crowned by the victories of martyrs. Among these, Saint Eliphius shone victoriously with the Germans already mentioned. Indeed, unless the Lord Jesus had shortened the days of this tyrant, he would have wished to fulfill his threat that he would not allow the Galileans even to retain their heads—for this was the name he customarily gave the worshipers of our Savior in mockery. But already, for the sake of the elect, the Lord shortened the days.

Thus it occurred as Saint Athanasius said when he was being compelled by Julian to flee. Seeing about him the Christian people weeping, he said: “Take courage, children; it is a cloud, and it will soon pass away” [Col. 0430A].

In so great a blast of spirit and amid such waves, Saint Eliphius, the true worshiper of Christ, was seized. First the faithless Jews, joined with the pagans, captured him and confined him in the same prison with many others—namely, thirty-three Christian men imprisoned for the name of our Savior Jesus Christ.

By divine providence, however, the prison was opened at night. Saint Eliphius, together with those thirty-three Christians already mentioned, came out of prison and entered Leucha, that is, the city of Toul. There he buried his mother according to the flesh, who had died, rendering her the final honor with the affection that was due [Col. 0430B]. There too, like a man who in other matters was not a deaf hearer of the law saying, “Honor your father and mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. XX), he fulfilled this service of due filial devotion.

Then the athlete of Christ was again sought, not only by Jews and pagan soldiers, but also by the highest and principal men themselves, so that he might either consent to impiety or, refusing consent, undergo death.

It is not without reason asked by what occasion the Jews at that time devoted themselves more vehemently and aggressively—or could devote themselves—to actions of this sort, so that they are recorded as having been almost more prompt and zealous than the cruel pagans themselves against this martyr of Christ and many others [Col. 0430C]. The answer is that the impious Julian raised up those impious men, made their pride swell, put weapons into their hands, and wished them to become strong and confident, because he knew that they were especially the fiercest enemies of the name of Christ.

Church history relates:

“Julian also armed the Jews against the Christians. Summoning them first, he asked why, although the Law commanded them to sacrifice, they did not use sacrificial offerings. When they answered that they had been permitted to offer sacrifice in one place only, the emperor hateful to God immediately ordered the destroyed Temple to be rebuilt. Miserable man, he believed he could overthrow the word of the Lord, whereas by this he showed its truth even more clearly.

“The Jews gladly received these words and sent orders to Jews throughout the whole world; and Jews gathered from every direction, cheerfully contributing money for the building. The emperor himself provided very much, not out of generosity, but in opposition to the truth; and he likewise sent a governor, a most worthy executor of his impious commands [Col. 0430D]. It is said that they had silver mattocks, baskets, and shovels for clearing the site. When they had begun the work under the established agreement, a vast multitude worked by day, while at night earth spontaneously rose from the valley. After even the remnants of the former foundation had been removed, they prepared everything anew.

“Having gathered many thousands of measures of gypsum and lime, a great force of winds suddenly broke forth, and storms and tempests suddenly arose and scattered everything that had been collected. While they still raged and were not corrected by divine forbearance, a great earthquake first occurred, and everyone not initiated into the divine mysteries was violently crushed. Since they were not frightened even by this judgment, fire came forth from the foundations they were digging, burning many of the diggers and dismembering others. Moreover, when many were sleeping by night in a nearby portico, the portico itself suddenly fell with its roof and crushed the sleepers [Col. 0431A].

“On another day a shining sign of the cross appeared in the sky; moreover, the garments of the Jews were marked with the sign of the cross—not in a shining color, however, but in black. Seeing these things and trembling at the divine scourges, those rebels against God returned to their own homes, confessing that there is a God, who is proved to have been hung upon the wood by their ancestors.”

Since these things were so, when impious persons were so pleasing to that most impious emperor, consider what a spirit of wickedness they must have breathed in for themselves, and by what means, wherever they were, they pursued their seemingly natural hatred of Christians, joined with pagan persecutors, flattering rulers, and promulgating edicts as though they were doing good.

Therefore Saint Eliphius, a man of divine power as already stated, having come out of prison and completed his mother’s funeral rites according to custom, was again sought by pagan soldiers as well as Jews. Since he did not wish to hide, because he did not flee martyrdom, he was quickly found.

For he returned and entered the city of Grand, where Julian is remembered as being at that time [Col. 0431C]. Remaining there two days, he bestowed many benefits upon not a few sick persons. Crossing the river called the Vair, he encountered impious agents worshiping the shrines of demons on its bank; Jews, it is related, were also present there in the same sacrilege.

Some consider this assertion trivial and excessively simplistic, because in our own times nothing of this kind is found among Jewish sacrileges. For Jews do not now sacrifice to idols, but vainly boast that they worship one sole Creator God. Consequently, learned readers might wish the writer had said or written otherwise than he did. For after saying, “He encountered Jews worshiping shrines of demons on the bank,” he adds: “It was the Sabbath, the Jews’ festival day [Col. 0431D]. Behold what the wicked Jews do on their Sabbaths. They despise Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, and worship demons to their own ruin. For as the deserts of their faithlessness demanded, they rejected the oracles of the prophets and the proclamations of the apostles, but willingly lent their ears to demons.”

But I think that this statement could by no means be trivial; rather, it is supported by solid truth. For the situation at that time was not as it is now. Why do Jews today not worship the images of the nations? Surely because they do not exist. So long as they existed, so long as these works of human hands were made, the Jews were always prone to worship them, as their own books testify.

But now, after the Lord, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “riding upon a swift cloud,” entered the Egypt of this world, and the images of Egypt were shaken before his face and perished (Isa. XIX), despite the vain desire of Egyptians to retain them—persons such as this Julian, who was a most notorious and truly Egyptian man—now, I say, because they do not exist, Jews do not worship the images of the nations [Col. 0432A]. And that one thing which remains, which overthrew those images, and which is wholly unrelated to images of the nations, they therefore do not worship because they hate the truth: namely, the reality prefigured mystically by the bronze serpent which Moses raised in the wilderness, raised up before our eyes and theirs.

Therefore it is no praise of Judea or the Synagogue that the prophet Hosea said to her: “You shall wait for me many days, and you shall not commit fornication, nor belong to a man” (Hos. III). For her not committing fornication with idols comes not from the strength of her own continence, but from the disappearance of idolatry, which after Christ’s coming neither pagan rulers could preserve nor this apostate could restore [Col. 0432B].

Accordingly, when the blessed man Eliphius found both groups—the pagans and the Jews—in the same sacrilege, he proclaimed to them the word of truth: that there was nothing in the phantasm of demons but ruin; that they should instead believe in and worship the living and true God, Creator of visible and invisible things, and his Son Jesus Christ, together with the Holy Spirit, as one God, so that they might find forgiveness of sins and eternal rest for their souls.

By his exhortation, with the grace of the Lord cooperating, about six hundred and twenty men, apart from women, are said to have believed and received the baptism of salvation [Col. 0432C].
