These things were reported to the most impious Julian, who was then, as stated, staying in the same Gallic city of Grand.

It is uncertain, however, whether in those days he was only Caesar or already emperor. For since he died in the third year of his reign, the seventh from the time when Constantius had made him Caesar, and in the thirty-first year of his life, the histories do not establish whether at any point during his imperial reign he went into Gaul. But there is no doubt that he came into Gaul when he was Caesar. For Emperor Constantius, as church history relates, appointed him Caesar and sent him to Gaul against the barbarians. These barbarians, whose assistance Constantius had sought against the tyrant Magnentius, having been of no use against the tyrant, were ravaging Roman cities [Col. 0432D].

Whatever the time may have been—whether he came to Gaul on repeated occasions, though that he came there at some time is beyond doubt—leaving this matter undecided, let us continue with the rest.

Upon receiving this report, the tyrant forgot his hypocrisy—that is, his pretence of philosophical endurance, by which he strove to show himself merciful. For he grew angry, he who wished to be called by the impious gentle and far removed from wrath, and who delighted excessively in this reputation. I believe the glorious man’s freedom was so great, and the fervour of good zeal in him so vehement, that the weight of true virtue, speaking words worthy of truth through this man’s mouth—in which Christ himself undoubtedly spoke—surpassed the strength of the pretence, or of the pretender. [Col. 0433A] Nor did he betray his reputation for patience in this case alone, but also in several others: driven into fury, he ordered their heads to be cut off. Although he at times forbade the blood of some to be shed, led by envy lest they should become glorious by dying, he did not permit those whom he found stronger and resisting him to his face to live in the cities.

It is remarkable that, at about the same time, he allowed blessed Martin, a new recruit wishing to serve as Christ’s soldier and saying to him, “Until now, Caesar, I have served as a soldier under you; allow me now to serve as a soldier for God,” to live. He indeed raged, but did not kill him. Yet this man he could neither endure nor defer from making a martyr of Christ, though he envied martyrs, by any fabrication of patience. Therefore, as I have said, I believe that the praiseworthy man had done or said something with great zeal of the sort for which that vain man was accustomed to kill Christians—as guilty of treason, not simply on account of the cause or profession of Christianity as such; namely, either for destroying temples or for some word that might seem insulting to imperial honour.

For example, when near the city of Daphne two young men, one named Viventius and the other Maximinus, distinguished in military service, groaned as they saw Julian’s abomination—for he had polluted springs and cities with sacrifices, and defiled everything offered for sale in public with criminal sprinkling, so that those eating and drinking might be polluted—they used the words of the three radiant youths in Babylon, [Col. 0433C] saying: “For you have delivered us to an unjust king, who has departed from you beyond all the nations that are on earth.” Hearing this, he who was called gentle and a philosopher by men like himself immediately unveiled the face of his impiety, ordering the bitterest blows to be inflicted upon them. He also deprived them of sight—or rather, which is truer in the misery of that age, set them free and sent them onward to everlasting crowns. Many also among the nobles and those radiant in rank, using such boldness, were crowned with equal crowns. For he pretended that he was, as it were, avenging the cause of an injury to imperial dignity, and ordered this to be publicized, envying the champions of truth both the title of martyr [271] and its honour.

Arthemius also, [Col. 0433D] who had been commander of Egypt in the time of Constantius and who in that emperor’s reign had shattered many idols, he not only stripped of possessions but also punished by decapitation. Let these examples be given to show the kinds of causes for which he was not unaccustomed to kill saints, though, as has been said, the impious called him gentle and remote from anger. The simple account of the martyrdom testifies that he had both causes for killing this most holy man as well. For it relates that, among other things, his accuser said: “Consider, Caesar, that he prophesies not prosperity but adversity for you and your offspring, and boldly rebels against your power without any fear of you.” It also represents Julian himself as speaking thus against this martyr of Christ: “Eliphius, why have you destroyed the gods and brought them to nothing by wicked incantations? Unless you obey my command and restore and worship the gods that you shattered into fragments, my sword shall divide your head into fragments.” Hence it is evident that he had both the cause for which the above-mentioned young men, Viventius and Maximinus, and others like them were punished, and the cause for which the commander Arthemius and many others were slain by the tyrant: namely, because the outstanding man did not fear publicly and freely to oppose his impiety among the people, and because he overthrew and shattered temples or idols which Julian both worshipped and commanded to be worshipped.

Therefore, when he would not yield to Julian, who compelled him to restore the images he had shattered, saying that it was most just to die gloriously for faith in our Lord Jesus [Col. 0434B] Christ, so that he might deserve to rejoice with him in eternal blessedness, the tyrant, now unable to contain his beastly spirit within the cage of pretence—although he envied Christians such a hope, namely the glory of martyrdom—ordered him to undergo capital sentence: “Bend your knees to the ground,” he said, “stretch out your neck, and receive the deadly blow of the flashing sword, as I foretold you.”

Then Christ’s martyr asked that a brief respite be granted him to offer prayer to God. When this was granted, he prostrated himself upon the ground and, raising his voice, prayed, saying:

“Lord God almighty, who created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and placed in paradise the human being made in your image and likeness; who, when that human being had fallen at the devil’s urging, restored him through the incarnation [Col. 0434C] and passion of your Only-begotten Son; and who sent your saints and chosen ones not to the joys of this world but to labours and tribulations: hear the supplicating prayer of your servant. Because I fear you alone and love you with the whole eagerness of my heart, and now desire, for your name, to undergo not only every bodily torment but death itself, command that my soul be received by the hands of angels into your heavenly paradise, with the crown of martyrdom. But to those by whom I am to be killed—whoever they are that act in ignorance and error—grant forgiveness of all sins and a share with your saints in your kingdom: you who live and reign with your Only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, one true God, for ages of ages.”

When the faithful present had answered, “Amen,” he rose from prayer and, standing in the midst of the crowd, said to [Col. 0434D] Caesar: “I ask that, when you kill me, you grant my body a place for burial.” He replied: “I grant whichever place you choose.” Raising his eyes, therefore, Christ’s martyr looked around and saw a high mountain at a distance. Turning toward Julian, he said: “Behold, Caesar, do you see that mountain? There, by Christ’s will, I shall have my burial.”

Meanwhile, while he still addressed some words suited to the occasion and time to the crowd of faithful present, the tyrant waited as though patiently—indeed, with the devil who worked through him panting to devour the soul rather than to kill the body. Finally, when that most faithful witness of Christ was saying, or might truly have said with the Apostle, “I desire to depart and to be with [Col. 0435A] Christ, for it is far better” (Phil. 1), and likewise, “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith; a crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4), Julian cunningly turned to flattery:

“Receive offices; receive honours; receive gold and silver; possess every good that is precious to us; and be our friend, in the same knowledge and in the same mind.”

The holy man, mindful of that showing in which the tempter, the devil, displayed to our Lord Jesus Christ the kingdoms of the world and their glory and said, “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4), said to him: “Caesar, you have been deceived by the devil and hasten to deceive Christian seekers of truth. ‘May your money,’ and whatever you promise, ‘be with you unto destruction’ (Acts [Col. 0435B] 8). For you promise earthly things in order to take away heavenly things; you promise transient life in order to withdraw eternal life; and, finally, you undoubtedly urge fleeting joys in order to remove those which are eternal.”

Then, bursting into a cry of exultation and confession against pagan, Jewish, and heretical impiety—which impiety was then troubling the Catholic Church like Cerberus, the infernal dog with three heads—he cried out and said:

“I believe in the true God and worship him: one in substance, three in persons; Creator and governor of the whole world, having neither beginning nor end, whose incorruptible kingdom remains for ever. I believe in the only-begotten Son of God the almighty Father, consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with the Father; conceived from Mary through the working of the Holy Spirit; true man, born of her without violation of virginity; crucified under Pontius Pilate; raised from the dead on the third day; received into heaven; and on the day of judgment to judge the living and the dead and render to each according to his works.”

Meanwhile tears flowed from his eyes from the beginning of the prayer which, as has been said, he poured out during the respite granted him. This seemed a weakness to those who did not know what is said in the psalm: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50); and elsewhere: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114). And the Apostle says of the very head of the blessed mourners—who are blessed precisely because they mourn [Col. 0435D] (Matt. 5): “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and many tears to him who was able to save him, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

Many of those present did not know these things, especially that tyrant, whose heart was hardened like Pharaoh’s heart; and therefore Christ’s martyr appeared weak and wavering to him. [Col. 0436A] Hence the same ineffectual craftsman of wickedness tried to entangle him with his promises, as has already been said. But when, amid the very tears, this witness of the Lord raised such a cry of exultation and confession, then Julian, hateful to God—or rather the wicked spirit dwelling in his heart—could endure no longer. Ordering his head to be cut off without delay, he said mockingly: “I shall see whether your Christ delivers you and makes you rise and walk upon your feet.”

For he mocked him because, as said above, after requesting and receiving the choice of a burial-place [272], he had said to him: “Behold, Caesar, do you see that mountain, in which, with Christ showing the way, I shall have a tomb.” Thus the wicked spirit, having determined in Julian’s heart that no tomb would be made for him otherwise than if he walked on his own feet to the distant mountain which he had chosen, uttered this mockery. But the Lord Jesus deigned, on the contrary, to make his glory manifest, so that his enemy—the false emperor of the impious and true satellite of the devil—might see and be confounded, and the fire of envy might devour him ever more fiercely.

For the martyr’s body rose by Christ’s power and, embracing its own head in both hands, carried it for one mile, with angels surely accompanying it and praising Christ. Thus it reached that mountain without any hindrance; then it ascended the mountain itself, and there, finding a white stone lying flat, it sat upon it. Immediately the stone’s hardness courteously yielded to the pious martyr. Like soft wax, opening a hollow lap to the one sitting upon it, it provided a concave seat memorable for succeeding ages. Hence even to this day that mountain is called the Mount of Saint Eliphius. It lies midway between Frumentosa and Grand, six miles from each, with the city of Toul to the north and Grand to the south. [Col. 0436C]

Meanwhile very many sick persons, afflicted with various diseases, venerating the passion of the glorious martyr and praising Christ’s name in it, were restored to health through his merits. Seeing these things, the pious rejoiced; the impious burned with malign envy. A conflict arose between the two parties. The faithful, aided by the merits of the magnificent martyr and with Christ granting it, defeated the unbelievers, gained a glorious victory, and threw the bodies of the slain pagans into the nearby river. The blessed martyr was martyred in a pleasant meadow situated on the bank of the above-mentioned little river, named Vera, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November [16 October]. Over his most sacred body the faithful built an oratory, where many benefits of miraculous powers are bestowed upon those who ask faithfully.

[Col. 0437]

**One Book of the Reverend Lord Dom Rupert, Abbot of Tuit, On the Will of God.**

273. **Preface**

[Col. 0437A]

Desiring to confess and proclaim the omnipotence and also the benevolence of God almighty, who must be named with the highest and utmost reverence, we ask from above for the good gift and perfect gift from the Father of lights himself (James 1): namely, the single eye best suited for this purpose, having no portion of darkness (Luke 11). For the Light itself, the very illumination of our eyes, says: “If your eye is single, having no portion of darkness, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6). For what did he intend by the single eye except a right and devout intention? It enables us, by approaching the Lord, to be enlightened; by entering the house, to see the light; and not to be dim-sighted before the lamp [Col. 0437B] of truth, standing upon the great lampstand of its dignity.

Therefore, that the whole body of our work or discourse may be full of light, with no such portion of darkness—with which the light of truth has no fellowship—far be from us an evil eye. That is, let us entertain no suspicion about the good God that the devil or our father Adam sinned by his will. Rather, as it is written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1), so that we may deserve to experience what follows: “For he is found by those who do not test him, but appears to those who have faith in him” (ibid.).

## Chapter I. That this division is impious and inept: one will of evil approves, another permits.

[Col. 0437C] This is why we now begin to speak these things to you, O masters famous in our time—William, bishop of Châlons, and Anselm, light of Laon—because one of our own admits that he learned from your schools to say: “God wills evil to occur, and Adam’s transgression was by God’s will.” He relies not on authorities from Scripture but on the greatness of your name, and with lengthy argument maintains that you handed down the following division: “Of the will of evil, one kind approves and another permits.”

We should have wished first to ask you, if an opportunity or occasion for speaking to one another face to face were afforded, whether it can be true that you, called masters of the arts, are said to have made so clumsy a division. For what follows? If “will of evil” is a genus, and its differentiating species are one that approves and another that permits, will this will which he calls permitting be good or evil? If evil, how is it opposed to the will approving evil? If good, how is it a species of the will of evil? We therefore do not believe the man who says that you were the authors of this division, which both accuses God and does not preserve the consistency of logical method.

## Chapter II. That God’s permission is the same thing which Paul calls God’s goodness, patience, and long-suffering; likewise, what it means that “God gave them over to the desires of their heart,” and similar expressions.

We ask what God’s permission is, and from the authority of Scripture quickly find that it is God’s patience. For the Apostle says: “God, wishing [Col. 0438B] to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9). And in the prophet God says: “I have been silent; I have always kept silence; I have been patient; like a woman in labour I shall speak” (Isa. 42). Therefore we confidently say that God never permitted evil to occur by willing it, but was patient by enduring evil persons.

This endurance or patience certainly cannot rightly be called a difference or species of a will of evil, 274 but rather God’s goodness or kindness. For the same Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?” (ibid.). By saying “goodness, patience, and long-suffering,” he expressed the same thing by three names—indeed by four, adding: “Do you not know that the kindness of God” (ibid.)? We say that this is God’s patience. If one asks what God’s patience is, we say that it is his long-suffering. And in saying this knowingly, we mean that God is not patient passively. For he is called patient because he is long-suffering: that is, because he does not immediately punish the sinner. If one asks what God’s long-suffering is, it is his goodness. Indeed, while not immediately punishing, he in some sense permits evil to occur; yet that permission cannot be ascribed to an evil will or a will of evil, as it is placed under that term as a genus in the division mentioned above. On the contrary, it is God’s goodness. For, as has been said, the one and same thing must be understood as signified by all these names—goodness, patience, long-suffering, and kindness—which leads the sinner to repentance.

What then does the same Apostle mean when he says of some people: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness; he gave them over to dishonourable passions; he gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. 1)? Clearly it means what God himself says in the psalm: “And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. 80). For both the reasoning of truth and the sacred authority of the Fathers and doctors of the Church most soundly maintain that “God gave them over” is the same as saying “God abandoned them”: namely, because of the inward sin of pride, which God does not will, he allowed them outwardly to do, according to the desires of their heart, the evil of uncleanness—which likewise God, being good, does not will them to do; yet, being just, he does not deliver them from it.

## Chapter III. That God permits evil unwillingly, but not under compulsion.

[Col. 0439B]

But people say to us: “Since, as you yourselves acknowledge, God permits evil to occur, we ask whether he permits it willingly or unwillingly. If he permits it unwillingly, he permits it against his will; if against his will, under compulsion; if under compulsion, he is not omnipotent.”

To this we say: Has such a person understood what he himself has said, while he is confident that he has driven us into this difficulty? For he has said: “If he permits unwillingly, he permits against his will, under compulsion.” Let him therefore be shown to himself, so that when he says “willingly,” he may see what must be supplied: “to permit,” or “for evil to occur.” For if we say that God permits unwillingly, it certainly follows [Col. 0439C] that he permits against his will. But if, as is more to the point, we say that he does not will evil to occur yet permits it to occur, it does not follow that he permits against his will or under compulsion. Rather, because of the aforesaid riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, he permits it on account of his kindness, by which he leads the evildoer to repentance, although he meanwhile knows that, according to his hardness and impenitent heart, the latter stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment (Rom. 9).

## Chapter IV. That, when God hardens someone, he does not will evil, but wills that the person be punished according to his justice.

A person still says: “If God does not will evil to occur, how is he said to harden someone?” For the same Apostle says: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9). First we ask here what “to harden” means, so that we may then answer this person, who is called “a human being” because of the very presumption by which he dares to answer God.

What, then, is meant by “God hardens whom he wills,” except that he does not soften whom he does not will to soften? For in one man, namely Adam, we all deserved hardness, in whom we all sinned. From that point God owes no one anything but punishment, but judgment—the judgment by which, condemned in Adam, that is, judged, we all were before we were born. God has mercy by gratuitous mercy upon whom he wills, so that the person may be softened through the spirit of repentance and, confessing with tears that he is a sinner, strive to be justified by faith in the other man, Jesus [Col. 0440A] Christ. Whom he wills, he leaves in that hardness, in that wrath which his father stored up for him.

Thus, when two eunuchs sinned against Pharaoh, his cupbearer and his baker, he owed neither of them anything except a sentence of condemnation. Yet he granted favour to one and exacted punishment from the other, and no one reproves him, since he mercifully granted life and the former rank to one to whom he owed nothing, and justly inflicted punishment upon the one to whom it was due. How, then, can anyone reproach God for that whose equivalent no one could justly reproach in a human being?

## Chapter V. Certain scruples of the curious, who argue that God wills evil.

Let what has been said thus far suffice concerning that argumentation, as inept as it is useless. Yet for our own instruction we must proceed further, to matters which seem to raise difficulties for such curious persons. They say: “If God does not will, or did not will, evil to occur, why did he not create a creature incapable of turning—that is, one unable to turn aside or decline from good to evil? Did he not will it, or was he unable? If he did not will it, how did he not will evil to occur? If he was unable, how do we say or proclaim that he is omnipotent?

“Furthermore, why did he give the first human being a command, if he did not will the evil of transgression—which he could foresee—to occur? If he did not will that this evil be committed by the human being, or if he willed the human being to be saved, why did he not permit him to remain free, but bound him by a command, knowing that he would transgress and intending to condemn the transgressor? Finally, why,” they ask, “does he allow people to be born for whom it would have been better never to have been born, since they are not predestined for life?”

To these seedbeds of the aforementioned suspicion, the matter requires that we give some answer, yet not forgetting the Apostle’s most forceful cry: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). For he speaks of God’s will against whoever it may be that rashly snatched a word from his mouth in order perversely to say what the Apostle had rightly said: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9). And immediately: “Why is fault still found? For who resists [Col. 0440D] his will?” (ibid.). Therefore we shall not attempt to comprehend God’s incomprehensible judgments or investigate his unsearchable ways; but, if he deigns to assist us by the Spirit of that same God—of whom the same Apostle says, “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2)—we shall provide some small relief for our poverty.

## Chapter VI. That it is not characteristic of a sound mind to raise questions of this sort about God’s will; illustrated by the likeness of the potter and the vessel.

But here it must first be said that it is not characteristic of a sound and well-ordered mind to raise and agitate questions of this kind. For this is to wish, or to have wished, to give God advice, and as if demanding a debt from a hired workman, to exact from him the manner of his work. Yet the same Apostle says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and shall be repaid by him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11).

This is surely a right and just defence, lest a crude little man born today should wish to teach the Ancient of Days, venerable and mature of head, how he ought to have worked—he who began to work when none of us could have been present to show him the rule of the work or to guide or draw back the worker’s fingers in any direction. Therefore he says: “Who has been his counsellor?”—the implied answer is, no one, except his own Spirit, of whom that other prophet says: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor and shown him?” (Isa. 40), and so forth.

It is, I say, a just and lawful defence, lest the work demand from its maker the manner of its own making—that is, lest a human being demand from God recompense in the quality or quantity of dignity, though he gave God nothing in order to come into being or be formed by him. Therefore he says: “Who has first given to him, and shall be repaid by him?” It is as if the thing fashioned should say to the one who fashioned it: “Why did you make me thus?” If it could say this, the potter would rightly answer: “Did I even owe you this—that I made you thus? What had you first given me, O clay, that I should make you for this or that honour according to your preference? However much I may have made you a vessel for dishonour, you have the gratuitous favour that I even expended labour so that you might be something more than you were: for you were shapeless clay, and now you are a vessel, of whatever sort, that has been shaped.”

And what were we but shapeless clay in the hand of him to whom we truthfully say with the prophet: “You are our potter, and we are clay” (Isa. 64)? For God formed the first human being from the mud of the earth; and after him, or from him, whoever was formed, we were clay: the mud of flesh—that is, a liquid mass—received through propagation. What did this potter take away from such clay, except that he gave form to what was shapeless? Was Adam not of greater worth, even clothed in a garment of skins, than that clay or mud from which he was made—the more abject part, certainly, of inanimate earth? Was Esau, a human farmer and a man skilled in hunting, though hairy and rough, not of greater worth or quality in substance than the mud received through propagation from Isaac, from which this potter formed him and his brother Jacob? But now let us return to the matters raised.

## Chapter VII. That God made no creature exempt from passions and vices because such a nature would be the nature of God himself.

The first of the questions which we said above were being asked is this: If God did not will evil to occur, why did he not make his creature incapable of turning—that is, incapable of declining from good to evil? Was it because he could not, or because he would not? And if he could not, how is he omnipotent?

To this we say: Clearly all things proclaim God to be omnipotent—heaven, earth, sea, and all things that he made in them. But does it consequently follow that one may demand of him why he did not create, [Col. 0442A] or why he ought to have created, a nature incapable of turning or changing—that is, receptive of no passion or vice? Or, if such a nature could not be created, does it therefore follow that God should not be proclaimed omnipotent? Certainly not. For an unchangeable nature is above all things, beyond all things, outside all things; and this is the nature of God alone, who certainly was not made or created.

Indeed, it is sacrilege to affirm of the divinity of the Trinity alone that it is changeable, as Arius did when he said: “The Son of God is changeable and mutable, like all rational beings.” Therefore nothing of that kind could be created by the uncreated God; and yet he is truly omnipotent, because he could do all things and made all things. For there is nothing that he did not make.

## Chapter VIII. He teaches, by an analogy, that something unchangeable could be begotten by God, but not created by him.

[Col. 0442B]

That one thing which is above all things, beyond all things, outside all things—the Omnipotent, as has been said—he made not potentially or voluntarily, but naturally begot. Let us take proof of what we say from the familiar image of God, namely the human being. Behold: a human being can both generate naturally and work voluntarily. What he generates cannot be other than what he himself is; what he makes can in no way be what he himself is. A human being generates nothing but a human being; he makes, for example, a house in which to dwell, or an attractive garment to wear. None of these is himself; yet he is praised if he has made them skilfully or conveniently, as befits him.

So, indeed, God begot that which is himself—God from God, impassible from impassible, immutable from immutable, incapable of turning from incapable of turning. But he made his garment, namely his Church; or that of which it is written in the psalm, “Clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103)—namely the angelic creature, when he said, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1)—and this fabric of the world, in which he made the human being in his image and likeness (ibid.). None of all these either ought or could be the very same thing as he who made them, or equal to him whom the same Maker begot, just as a building or a painting can in no way be the same as the builder or painter, or as what that person has begotten from his own flesh.

But it is worthy of praise, and ought to suffice our inquiry, that the omnipotent Maker was able to make such a creature as could be capable of that same Maker, and could attain through effort, assisted by grace, to the divinity which it does not possess by nature. Therefore angel and human being necessarily had to be mutable or capable of turning, as created from nothing; indeed, that from which they were created was created from nothing. Each was created pure and innocent, in such a way that from innocence itself each could either advance to the highest things or fall away to the lowest. For the Apostle too bears witness that the holy angels have advanced—indeed still advance—when he writes to the Ephesians: “That through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in [Col. 0443A] the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

## Chapter IX. That God willed to make a creature equal to himself, and did so by uniting in the one Christ the diverse substances of his begetting.

It may perhaps seem harsh to someone that we say God almighty could not create a creature equal to himself or to his nature. But it would rightly be judged harsher and more intolerable if we said—far be it!—that he did not will to do so. For in saying this we would proclaim him less good and, what is wicked even to utter, render him suspect of envy.

Therefore let us say faithfully; let us say confidently: God, who is truly good, willed to make a creature equal to himself; and, according to what is written of him, “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113), he did not cease until, in whatever way and by whatever art of his wisdom, he made the very thing which he willed. And how did he make it? He joined the diverse substances or natures of his begetting in one person; and, preserving the truth of both natures, in order to make man God, he made God man when he willed his Word to be incarnate. He did this because he is good, because he is benevolent.

## Chapter X. That it is an argument for omnipotence that God assumed human nature, which nothing apart from him could have assumed.

[Col. 0443C]

Indeed, if it pleases us, let us say that the Omnipotent did this because the Omnipotent could so regard lowly things and so descend. For none other of those who were—or are—in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could have done this. If you think of the angelic creature, we confidently say that no angel could assume human nature, or clothe itself with a human soul. For the angelic spirit is not in the least more subtle than the human soul; therefore neither is graspable by the other, that is, neither angelic spirit by human spirit nor human spirit by angelic spirit, and neither is capable of the other.

Finally, God alone—the uncreated, uncircumscribed Spirit—while himself capable of none, is apprehensible by every rational spirit, angelic or human. [Col. 0443D] Accordingly, when someone is said to be filled with a devilish spirit, it must not be supposed that the substance of a devilish spirit has entered the substance of a human soul. Rather, it has crept into the hidden cavities of the body and strikes the soul, caught in its own seat, with infernal scourges, infects it with poisons, and inflames it with fires. How then could an angel assume human nature, or put on a human soul, to which it is not more subtle?

Thus the Omnipotent did this as well. This work is truly divine and is a sufficient proof that the Word of God possesses true divinity: a work no less of mercy than of power. For God willed, and God alone could, to assume our nature; the Creator willed, and the Creator alone could, to join a creature to himself in one person.

## Chapter XI. That the creature which could not sin was a proof of God’s omnipotence. Likewise, how God almighty cannot do evil.

[Col. 0444A]

Accordingly, since it could be made by the good and omnipotent Creator, there was made—not so much by creation as by assumption—a creature such that it would not merely refuse to sin, but could not sin. Thus says that same new creature, the Son of Man, and the same ancient Creator, the immutable Son of God: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5). Likewise: “I can do nothing of myself” (ibid.). For what is it for anyone to do anything of himself, except to do evil? [Col. 0444B] Therefore, he says, “I cannot do anything of myself”: that is, apart from God, separately, apart from the truth, by myself, my will divided from the will of God the Father—as the renegade angel, or as the first transgressing human being, could do and did; for each was a creature, and consequently a made thing capable of turning, and therefore mutable.

For whether angel or human, so long as one admits any accidental quality after turning away from the essential Good, so long one acts of oneself—for example, when one calls evil good and good evil (Isa. 5), when one judges unjustly, condemning the just and justifying the wicked. Whence does one do these things, or others like them, except of oneself, when in the essence of things it is otherwise? A human being, if very just, can do such things but does not wish to do them; but if only slightly just, or only now first disposed toward justice and not yet clothed in the habit of that justice—slightly just, I say, if one does not dare to do them. [Col. 0444C] God, however, just as he is subject to no vice and to no accidental qualities whatever, so too, being supremely just, cannot do anything of this kind at all. When we say that he cannot do evil, by that very statement we proclaim his true omnipotence—as though we said, “There is nothing that he cannot do.” For a certain writer, in philosophy not vain but true, says: “No one in possession of reason can doubt that God is omnipotent.” And immediately: “But he who is omnipotent has nothing that he cannot do.” Having granted these two propositions, he at once infers: “Can God, then, do evil?” “By no means,” [Col. 0444D] he says. And he concludes thus: “Therefore evil is nothing, since he who can do everything cannot do it.”

## CHAPTER XII. The angels’ inability to sin is not theirs by nature, but was received by grace. Further, why God did not establish them firmly when he did so, or at least before evil occurred.

The holy angels indeed were made firm; and because, when the evil angel did something of himself—that is, did evil—they preferred to cling to God, their own beginning, they received this as their reward: that thereafter they could not do evil, because, when they were able to do it, they would not. Yet this is not through the power of their own nature, but through the rewarding [Col. 0445A] grace of the divine will. Therefore, even if it is correctly said that they can no longer do anything of themselves, it is nevertheless not true to add that they do whatever they see the Father doing (John 5). Yet they were formed.

Perhaps, then, someone says: If God did not will evil to occur, why did he not do beforehand what he was later going to do? Why did he not prevent evil from occurring, by establishing all firmly with the same power with which, after evil occurred, he made firm those whom he willed? Or at least, when he created them, why did he delay making them firm and not establish them at the very moment at which he created them?

We answer this: certainly because it was, and is, one thing to be created and another for a creature to be established in a good state. For every creature could indeed be created from nothing, and every thing made could be formed; but no rational nature—that is, angelic or human [Col. 0445B] nature—could be established from nothing. For “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). For it is one thing for a stone to exist and to have holes prepared, and another to be bound with gold; so it is one thing for rational creatures to be formed, and another for them to be established by the Word of the Lord and the Spirit of his mouth, so that they may be heavens, that is, the dwelling places of God.

Certainly, rational creatures being created was like precious stones being prepared with their holes; but those same creatures being established was like stones receiving into their holes the gold by which they would be bound. Yet the gold of divinity, the gold of the Word of the Lord, the gold of the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, is accustomed to insert itself only into a willing creature. Some did not wish to receive that gold, scorning it as a woman might scorn her lover. [Col. 0445C] How, then, ought God to have forestalled evil so that it would not occur, when the first evil was precisely the refusal to receive the bond of the Word, the bond of love, by which every firm creature has been made firm, and without which no creature at all can be made firm or stable?

## CHAPTER XIII. He refutes the impiety of the flesh, which argues that God established a law for Adam because he wished him to become a transgressor.

No history reports what command, or what kind of command, was laid upon the angels; but upon the first human beings this was laid: “From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, [Col. 0445D] you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Concerning this which we were discussing above, the question is asked—and asked most improperly—why God commanded this, why he imposed the precept, if he did not wish the evil of transgression, which he could foresee, to occur.

Here we seek not now what we should say, but how we should say it, because the matter itself with which we are dealing is truly greater than our whole discourse can bear. First, we cannot sufficiently marvel at the deep darkness of human wisdom, which, in searching and investigating the reasons for that command, has deserved to find or attain no other than this: to say that God wished the human being to become a transgressor. Do not those who say this seem to think that God gratuitously placed a stumbling-block in the path of his creature and offered an opportunity to the malignant devil, wishing that the human being should [Col. 0446A] be caught, wishing there to be something by which the human being might be deceived? A bad opinion, a perverse suspicion.

But perhaps they seem to themselves to honor the wise God in this very thing, and to have adequately excused him, by attaching this kind of reason: that he wished this evil to occur in order to use it for good; that he wished iniquity to abound so that grace might superabound (Rom. 5). This is an exceedingly perverse excuse for God, a perverse and unworthy flattery concerning God’s wisdom. Do they not seem to you to assert that God said: “Let the devil, and Adam and Eve, do evil; let them do evil, so that good things may come”? For what then? If the condemnation of those who said that the Apostle of God taught, “Let us do evil so that good things may come,” is just (Rom. 3), how much more just is the condemnation of those who say that God himself said, “Let evils happen so that [Col. 0446B] good things may come”? Let us therefore seek in that command a better intention of God: a holier will, worthy of God.

## CHAPTER XIV. God gave the human being a command so that his goodness might make that person blessed and truly living.

Why did God give the human being a command? Truly because of his goodness. For what purpose was that goodness directed? Toward the goodness of his love, directed to making the human being blessed and alive forever. “Then,” you say, “could this not occur without the giving of a command?” Certainly not, as Scripture testifies when Moses says in Deuteronomy: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word [Col. 0446C] that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8). Understand that this was likewise said to the first human being: A human being does not live by every tree of paradise, but by the command of God. For the Son of God himself says in his Gospel: “And I know that his command is eternal life” (John 12). And truly so. For what is God’s command except God’s Word? And what other life is there for a rational creature than the Word of God, without whom not even the creature’s substance could have been made?

What we have said, therefore, we say again: just as through his goodness God both made the human being and placed him in paradise, so likewise through his goodness God gave the human being a command, so that the human being might live eternally, in body and soul, and be eternally blessed. For in order that the person might live blessedly in the body, God placed him in such a place; in order that the person might live blessedly in soul, [Col. 0446D] he gave that person his command.

## CHAPTER XV. Those who think the command not to eat the fruit was slight are mistaken; this is shown by comparison with the sun.

But someone says: What sort of command, or how great a command, was that, that we should rightly say, in regard to it, that God’s command was eternal life? Or how was it fitting for Majesty to place human life and death in so slight a matter: that if a person did not bite one fruit, that person would live in body and soul, but if he bit it, he would incur the death of both—that is, of body and soul? This thought has gnawed at the souls of no few people, leading them to think that God’s command was superfluous and had [Col. 0447A] no useful purpose except that God willed it. Just as one fruit of any tree is a small thing, so they judge that command of God to be slight. But because it seems small, is it therefore truly small? Or rather, do we have feeble faculties of understanding?

Thus this sun appears small in heaven, and yet is not truly small; rather, we have eyes too small to look up at it. For its sphere, measured by wise persons with plausible reasoning, is found to be many times greater than the globe of the earth. Let us therefore measure that command of God by reason rather than by the bodily senses, and it will certainly become clear that what was thought small is great.

## CHAPTER XVI. Faith, hope, and love, in which eternal life consists, were required in that first command.

[Col. 0447B] Great indeed is the word by which these three things are jointly required of the human being: faith, hope, and love; possession of them is undoubtedly eternal life. For this is such a word: “From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Indeed, that great generosity of the Creator, by which, without any preceding merits, he placed the human being in paradise and said, “From every tree of paradise eat,” required from that person the debt of great love. But when he said, “From that particular tree do not eat,” he established hope for a great reward: namely, that God would give no small reward for observing the command, since he had already given so much freely. Finally, when he said: “On whatever [Col. 0447C] day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” he required faith: that God should be believed as one speaking truth, and the Word of God should be believed as truth.

Therefore it was a great word, worthy of hearing, by which the same three things were sought from our first parents: love, hope, and faith. These too are now required of us in reverse order, concerning which the Apostle says: “But now faith, hope, love remain—these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Cor. 13). What beyond these does all divinely inspired Scripture set forth? In both extensive Scripture and the brief command, one and the same way, truth, and life are proclaimed; when these three—faith, hope, and love—receive it, then at last the creature lives blessedly.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 0447D] The command concerning the fruit of paradise was sufficiently great, since at that time no other command needed to be established; and by this command, whatever its kind, Adam’s faithfulness or iniquity could be tested.

But, as has already been said, people of small understanding judge it to be small because the fruit of the tree from which they were forbidden was a small matter. Therefore, it may seem that one should consider not what someone does, but the magnitude of the object involved—so that one is not called greatly unfaithful unless one has been unfaithful in a great matter. But both divine and human judgment oppose this. For the Lord says: “Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in greater things; and whoever is unjust in a small thing is unjust also in a greater” (Luke 16). And a certain pagan says:

> For when from a thousand bushels of beans you steal one,  
> The loss, not the crime, is by this reckoning lighter for me.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.16.55–56

[Col. 0448A] Therefore the deed cannot be thought slight merely because that fruit was a small thing. What more important matter could we have wished God, at that time, to make the subject of his law? Should he have said, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20)? There was no one who could be killed. Should he have said, “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.)? There was no woman besides the one whom he had made for him. Should he have said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (ibid.)? There was no neighbor of his own kind. Let us not, then, wonder that the matter for faith was sought in a moment involving a small thing, in the insignificant fruit of a tree.

## CHAPTER XVIII. This tree was especially forbidden because, being beautiful, it would more easily ensnare the human being once that person had already begun to neglect God.

[Col. 0448B] Why was the test of faith sought in that tree rather than another? Clearly because it was beautiful, as is written below: “The woman therefore saw that the tree was good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance” (Gen. 3). This must be carefully noted, because our aim is that no one should suspect God of having given the command with a will or expectation of transgression.

The human being had already swelled inwardly, inflated by diabolical pride. For unless the person had first swelled inwardly, when tempted outwardly he would not have yielded so easily. The lust of the eyes immediately followed the inward swelling of the mind. The rational human being began willingly to look upon and admire something other than God. [Col. 0448C] Therefore the bridle of the command was imposed to restrain growing desire. The devil, the tempter, approached from outside through the serpent; and when the bridle of the command had been broken, they violated the desired tree. Hence at once penal desire was increased. For just as, before they had inwardly swelled in mind through disdaining God, they desired the beautiful and delightful tree, so, before they bit the forbidden thing, they burned with desire for themselves in the manner of beasts.

Indeed, they could have begotten only children of blessing without any itch of lust, and there would have been no shame of the flesh, had pride not first raised the spirit in contempt of the Creator. But because the human being, though in honor, did not understand, he was therefore compared with senseless beasts [Col. 0448D] and made like them (Ps. 48). All this occurred not because God willed it, but because God permitted it; not by God’s will, but by the law of natures. For this is the natural law of Creator and creature: wherever a creature turns itself away from love of the higher Creator, by that same turning it falls and plunges into desire for lower things; and the shame of the flesh is as great as the spirit has turned away from seeking the glory and honor of God.

## CHAPTER XIX. They are slanderers of God for whom God’s good will is not proved by the fact that he always forbids evil.

[Col. 0449A] This does not suffice for the contentious: when, desiring to prove that God never willed or wills evil to occur, we take our argument from the contrary—namely, from the fact that he always prohibited and prohibits evil from occurring. A simple eye readily sees how great a slander against God this is. For no one but a double-minded or deceitful person both prohibits one and the same thing at the same moment and wills it to occur; such a person is rightly said to be opposed to himself.

And what do they say? “God did prohibit the human being before the act of sin; but in the very act he did not prohibit it.” What do we suppose these people think God ought to have done at the very moment when he saw the woman see the tree as good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance, and take from it in order to eat? Surely they think that he ought to have cried out and said something such as he later said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good [Col. 0449B] and evil. Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, 279 and eat and live forever,” etc. (Gen. 3).

In the same way God could indeed have said: “Behold, the woman has been persuaded by the serpent, and through the woman the man will undoubtedly be persuaded. Now therefore guard the way to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, lest they put forth their hands, take of its fruit, eat, and die by death.” But it must be understood that, according to the order of justice, he ought not to have spoken or acted about that tree as he spoke or acted about this one. With his help, we have ready at hand the reason why we think this.

## CHAPTER XX. The human being had to be excluded from the tree of life on a different ground than from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because death resulted from the latter on one ground, while life was to be expected from the former on another.

[Col. 0449C] God ought not, therefore, to have prohibited the human being from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the same manner in which he prohibited him from the tree of life, because that tree did not possess in itself the effect of life in the same way. For God himself naturally gave this tree the property that, if a person ate from it, he would live forever. But God did not naturally give that other tree the property that, if a person ate from it, he would die forever; rather, human guilt brought it about.

For had he eaten without being forbidden, he would have died neither in body nor in soul because of it. But because, forbidden and disobedient, he ate, on that same day he died by death: not with the death of the body [Col. 0449D] through a natural power of the tree, but with the death of the soul through the guilt of disobedience. Conversely, if perhaps he had put forth his hand and taken from the tree of life, he would have lived forever—not with the life of the soul, which he had lost through guilt, but with bodily life through the natural power of such a tree.

Thus, dead in soul and yet destined to live forever in body, he would have possessed a miserable eternity and eternal misery, and would have been beyond recovery, as demons are. Therefore God prohibited the human being from each tree as was proper: differently from this one, differently from that—by a command from that one, by a flaming sword from this one. For in that tree the human being had been the author for himself of an evil death; but in this tree the nature of the tree, which God had made, would have been an occasion to the human being of an evil eternity. If he did not restrain himself from that tree when he heard, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” how much less would he have restrained himself from this one merely because of a command, if he knew that by tasting it he would attain the eternity of bodily life? [Col. 0450A]

## CHAPTER XXI. As God willed obedience, so he also brought it to completion in Christ, crucified and dying for us.

At last an opponent may say: “Granted that God did not will the evil of transgression to occur, but willed the human being to live by God’s Word, and therefore gave him the command, because his command is eternal life” (John 12). But does not Scripture say: “Our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113)? How, then, did he not bring it about that the human being should be obedient, if he willed him to be [Col. 0450B] obedient?

As though God had failed to do what he willed! Does not the human being today live through God’s command, through God’s Word? What if, at that time, the first human being did not consent to God, who willed his life and salvation? Did his rebellion render God’s good will void? Far from it. The good God took up the rod of discipline, thus having mercy upon us as a father has mercy upon his children. What rod, or whose discipline, did he take up? Surely the sentence by which he struck our proud flesh, so that we might all die and, being dust, return to dust.

This greatly helps to humble us, that we may bend our clay necks beneath the yoke of God’s command and not arrogate to ourselves that we are like gods—although even so certain wretched princes of our race imagined themselves to be gods. [Col. 0450C] Having begun thus, God did not cease until he completed the purpose for which he gave the human being a command. For he powerfully made faith, hope, and love blossom anew from that trunk. The first man indeed proved maimed for God’s work and, contrary to God’s work or command, through desire stretched out unrestrained hands; but from his stock was found a man according to God’s heart, who, by an obedience penal to himself, stretched hands restrained from every desire upon the wood of the cross. Having trampled sin beneath his feet, he set before many thousands who would follow him examples of life to be read.

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 0450D] God accomplished what he willed not through another, but through himself.

Therefore, even though the created thing turned aside into what our God did not will, he himself “did whatever he willed” (Ps. 113). This must be understood clearly, because it is not the same as saying: “Everything that our God willed, his creature did.” It is most apt for the present argument that, when we say, “Our God did whatever he willed,” we understand: he himself did it through himself. Everything, I say, that he willed his rational creature to do, he did himself. For unless he himself had done it through himself, all that he willed would not have been done by another or through another.

[Col. 0451A] For the will of our God is so great, so good, so well pleasing, and so perfect that no one but he alone could attain to accomplishing all that he willed. We do indeed read of some who had testimony that they did what God willed—for example, David, of whom he himself said: “I have found a man according to my heart, David son of Jesse, who shall do all my wills” (Acts 13). But even he did not do everything that our God willed; indeed, he did some things that God did not will. And what shall we say of the angels? “Behold,” says someone, “the heavens are not clean in his sight; how much more the abominable and useless human being, who drinks iniquity like water?” (Job 15). Therefore it was not another acting for him, but our God himself, who did all that he willed.

Let this saying, then—“He did whatever he willed”—be a great and true proclamation both of the power and of the goodness [Col. 0451B] of our God: of his goodness, because he willed only good things and all good things; of his power, because he did all the things that he willed. By contrast, each of us sometimes desires small and few good things, and is unable to do them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. If God had willed evil to occur, so that he might correct it for his own glory, then his suffering in assumed flesh would not have been gratuitous but owed.

Far be such a leaven, as it is thought, from us, lest, when the Holy Spirit sings to us in David, saying, “Our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113), we should say: “Then he willed, or wills, evil to occur.” For it would then be permissible to infer: “Therefore he caused evil to occur; therefore he caused the human being [Col. 0451C] to transgress.”

That swollen defender of himself, that accuser of God, did not dare to say this so openly and boldly, but touched upon it indirectly: “The woman,” he said, “whom you gave me as companion, gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3); yet he was expelled from paradise. But if it is said with such moderation that God willed that evil to occur in order to use it for good, in order that there might be a reason why he should assume human nature and restore the lost human being above the dignity of first origin, and thereby make his power known and display the riches of his glory, we who have recognized God’s grace are offended more and more.

For on this reckoning grace is no longer grace. God became human and suffered for human beings not freely but as a debt, if he himself willed the evil to occur which he might correct for the manifestation of his glory. God did not act thus; rather, he redeemed, by his own will, the human being who had become a transgressor against God’s will. By the debt of justice he consigned all, in one, to death; again, in one, by the grace of mercy he gave life to all.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Just as God is not unjust in destroying the substance of a creature already corrupted, so neither was he unjust in condemning the foreknown wickedness of a future human being.

The last of the questions that we said above were asked is this: why God, foreknowing all things, allowed those to be made or born for whom it would have been better had they not been made or born, since they were not predestined for life. For simply speaking, it is better not to exist than [Col. 0452A] to exist badly. “Why,” they ask, “did the good and merciful Creator make those whom he foreknew would perish?”

A remarkable and importunate—indeed violent—question, and so inept that there is no reason in its meaning. For what could be foreknown except what was going to occur? But how would that which had been foreknown to be going to occur in this or that way not occur? It would be closer to reason if it were said thus: “Why does God permit the substance of evil spirits or impious humans to continue to exist, since it exists badly, rather than cause it utterly to perish, as the spirit of a beast perishes and ceases to exist?”

For one might answer that it is just for one always to be in punishment who, because of his own guilt, lacks the condition of being always in glory. Is God’s justice, then, younger than his foreknowledge? Therefore, just as it is not unjust that he does not now [Col. 0452B] utterly destroy the substance of the corrupted creature, so it was not unjust that he condemned its foreknown wickedness and nevertheless did not omit to create a good nature. But because nothing suffices the contentious questioner, let us now say to him with the Apostle: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” etc. (Rom. 9).

## CHAPTER XXV. The prophet’s words, “I, the Lord, make peace and create evil,” concern not the evil of sin, but the evil of affliction; these are distinguished as doing and suffering are distinguished from one another.

Finally, the place requires us to say that there is a certain evil, though not of the same kind, which God not only wills to occur but himself does, as [Col. 0452C] he says in the prophet: “I, the Lord, make peace and create evil” (Isa. 45). Likewise another prophet says: “Will there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3). These and similar passages seem to support the sense mentioned above, against which our present discourse is directed. But both reason itself agrees that they must be understood differently, and the authority of the orthodox Fathers hands this down.

Let us therefore say: the evil which the Lord creates or does is affliction owed to the evil which the Lord neither made nor willed to occur. This is indeed called evil, but it is not evil; rather, it is good. For it is just vengeance, vindicating justice. It is called evil according to the perception of the sufferer; it is good—that is, good justice—according to the reason of the one who inflicts it. [Col. 0452D] Indeed, by the authority of Scripture it is called not only evil but also wickedness. For it is written in Jonah: “And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and he had mercy concerning the wickedness which he had said he would do to them, and did not do it” (Jonah 3).

This evil—that is, the evil of affliction—and the evil of which we spoke above—that is, the evil of sin—are not of the same kind; they differ as greatly as the two most general categories, doing and suffering. The creature does the evil of sin, but suffers the evil of affliction; conversely, the Creator does the evil of affliction, but suffers—though impassibly—the occurrence of the evil of sin. To the evil of sin belong all things that cooperate toward the death of the soul, which God did not make; [Col. 0453A] to the evil of affliction belong all things that cooperate toward bodily death, by which, after sin, God mercifully willed the human being to die.

What these things are, he himself says, distinguishing them into four parts in Ezekiel: “Even if I send my four very evil judgments—sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—upon Jerusalem, to destroy from it human being and beast, yet there shall remain in it a saving remnant, bringing out sons and daughters” (Ezek. 14). Concerning such things Jeremiah also, when the Lord had sent them and the city had been handed over to the Babylonians, spoke against one who might think it happened by chance and not by God’s ordering or command: “Who is he who said that it should happen, when the Lord did not command? From the mouth of the Most High do not both good things and evils proceed?” (Lam. 3). And immediately, against one who would blame God [Col. 0453B] because evils had gone forth from his mouth: “Why has a living human being murmured—a man because of his sins?”

## CHAPTER XXVI. Those through whom the evil occurs which the Lord creates are not excusable, because the Lord neither willed nor made them evil; rather, when they were evil, he used them as a rod of discipline.

What then? Are those through whom these evils occur, which the Lord declares that he creates or does, excusable? By no means. Kings or powerful persons do not become evil because God wishes to use their power for the correction of sinners; [Col. 0453C] rather, because they are evil and reprobate, they are permitted, where such a cause requires, to become kings or powerful persons. Hence he says to Pharaoh, as the Apostle also recalls: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Rom. 9).

It is as though he said: “I did not make you evil, nor did I will you to become evil; but since you were evil, I raised you up as king at such a time, so that I might use your hardness as a rod for striking my son, that he might remember me, and that from the breaking of your hardness all the earth might learn my power, which it is expedient to know.” The same must be thought about Annas and Caiaphas. For it was not because the Lord wished to use their evil so beneficially that he therefore willed or caused them to be evil; but because they were evil—princes of Sodom and a people of Gomorrah, as the prophet says—they were therefore brought to that day; [Col. 0454A] therefore that hour and the power of darkness were given to them.

It is indeed written: “He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart” (John 12)—and therefore, says the Evangelist, the Jews could not believe (ibid.). But another Scripture likewise says: “Their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 3). Therefore the statement, “God blinded them,” is the same as saying: “He permitted them to be blinded by their own wickedness.”

Moreover, because according to the Hebrew it is written thus: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes” (Isa. 6), and this was said at the beginning of the vision; while at the end of the same vision he says: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8), and the prophet answers: “And I shall wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I shall await him” (ibid.)—without doubt the same must be understood in that blinding as in the confession of our Lord, in which he says: “Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

But the Evangelist’s statement, “Therefore they could not believe because Isaiah said these things” (John 12), is the same as saying: “Therefore they could not believe because they themselves were those of whom this had been prophesied, and it was impossible for the prophetic Spirit to be mistaken in considering them.”

## PERORATION

As we pursue more carefully the causes of the question, like the roots of a useless tree, we dig around many things [Col. 0454C] and perhaps seem to have indulged in much speaking—at least to one for whom the cause that we have undertaken to treat seemed small. But can it seem small to you who love God and know the goodness of God, for whom we have written these things? Certainly not. For you know that holy Scripture is more ensnaring to no understanding than to this one by which God is thought to will or to have willed evil to occur—especially that evil through which we all died in Adam, that is, were constituted sinners. It is for you, then, at least by some interpretation, to demolish the opposing argument, which is drawn as though from the judgment of the matter itself—that is, from your authority—to disparage our innocent Creator God, who is good and wills good things alone.

[Col. 0453]

# One Book of the Reverend Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, On the Omnipotence of God.

## 282. PROLOGUE

[Col. 0453C]

When the Psalmist had said: “I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 38), he immediately added: “And my sorrow was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire will blaze forth” (Ps. 38).

It is as though he said: Because speaking sometimes harms more than it profits, I became mute and resolved to keep silence even from good things; yet, through that very silence, my sorrow was renewed, since, plainly, as formerly I sinned by speaking too much, so now I sinned by being too silent. Thus, as fire is stirred the more intensely as it burns, so too my heart grew hot; for that sorrow sprang from love, and from the fire of love my meditation blazed forth.

I feel that something very like this has happened to me, O our teachers and good hearers of God, S. and A., who, together with my abbot II., were present before the distinguished man of your Church, at once archdeacon and dean II., as judges of the cause of God and of ourselves, and who grieved over the injury I suffered for the truth. For I had spoken with my tongue, writing a little book on the will of God because of the rashness of certain persons who say that God wills evil to occur, and that Adam’s transgression was according to God’s will. This controversy stirred up excessive tumults against me, as though they were defending God’s omnipotence. For they say: If evil occurs without God willing it, and nevertheless evil has occurred and occurs, it follows that he is not omnipotent. For how is he omnipotent if he cannot prevent from occurring the evil which he does not will to occur?

While they said such things and raged against me, I was silent for a little while, was humbled, and kept silence even from good things, as Jeremiah also says: “I will not remember him, nor will I speak any more in his name” (Jer. 20). Yet he too immediately added: “And it became in my heart as a raging fire, shut up in my bones; and I was worn out, unable to bear it” (ibid.). This is plainly the same meaning as that expressed in the previously cited verse of the Psalm: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire will blaze forth.”

Therefore I have spoken, and shall still speak with my tongue—not now only, as in that little book, concerning the will of God, but concerning both the will and the omnipotence of God. As for their further assertion that I am now doing, and long ago did, this thing through corrupted arrogance and stirred by a spirit of pride, I commit the whole matter to God, who knows the secrets of hearts better, as it is written: “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (3 Kings 8). Let me say only this: let them remember that in this matter they too can be mistaken, as Eliab, David’s elder brother, was mistaken when, angry with him, he said: “Why have you come, and why have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart: you came down in order to see the battle” (1 Kings 17).

## Chapter I. That God’s omnipotence has two ways, mercy and truth, and likewise two hands, right and left, by which it advances toward the glory of God.

God’s omnipotence proceeds not by one way only but by two; it works not with one hand only but with two, striving from both sides toward one end—namely, toward the glory of God himself. His ways are mercy and truth, as it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Here, undoubtedly, when “truth” is mentioned, one must understand “in judgment,” so that “truth” in that place means a true judgment, according to the saying: “As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is true” (John 5). Therefore we sometimes read “mercy and truth,” and at other times “mercy and judgment.”

Moreover, one of his hands is called the right and the other the left, as in the passage: “He shall set the sheep indeed on his right hand, but the goats on his left” (Matt. 25). Here likewise the hearer understands the same ways, or rather the ends or consummations of those ways; for there these two, mercy and judgment, will be brought to completion for the glory, as has already been said, of that same omnipotent God.

## Chapter II. That, when it is asserted that God does not will evil, the impious argue that he is not omnipotent; and that this is why he also discusses omnipotence.

The question now arises why the Lord’s ways are not one but two. Who asks this? Rather, who compels us to ask it? Surely the one who now, with novel rashness or rash novelty, teaches that God wills evil to occur, and that the first human being fell by God’s will. He maintains that this is sufficient proof: God did not avert that evil from happening, though, since he is omnipotent, he could have done so.

We said a few things on this subject in the earlier little book, but the dispute has not been softened. Therefore we are compelled more and more to have recourse to the protection of Scripture and of every kind of reason, so that, while proclaiming God omnipotent, we may nevertheless demonstrate that evil or sin occurs or has occurred without his will.

God, I say, is omnipotent, although it could not come about that, with mercy running through all things, no angel or human being should remain concerning whom, or against whom, judgment would be exercised. And, in treating of God’s will, we have laboured especially to establish firmly in our hearts that through it or from it no evil has ever proceeded by which his creature might perish.

Accordingly, the matter now seems to require an inquiry into what evil is, or what was the beginning of an evil will: that is, whence it came about that a good creature should will evil, since it did not occur through God’s will. The diligent reader may find this most acutely investigated by the holy Fathers, especially by the eminent Father and teacher Augustine. For he says:

## Chapter III. That the beginning and cause of an evil will in a good creature was nothing.

[Col. 0456D]

“When the cause of the misery of evil angels is sought, the fitting answer is that they turned away from him who exists in the highest degree and turned toward themselves, who do not exist in the highest degree. And what is this defect called except pride? ‘For pride is the beginning of every sin’” (Ecclus. 3).

“They therefore refused to keep their strength for him” (Ps. 48), “and, though they would be more by cleaving to him who exists supremely, they preferred themselves to him and chose that which is less. This was the first falling away, the first deficiency, and the first beginning of that nature which was so created that it did not exist supremely, yet could enjoy him who exists supremely in order to possess blessedness. When turned away from him, it would not indeed be nothing, but it would be less, and for that reason would become miserable. If, moreover, one asks for the efficient cause of this evil will, none is found.”

[Note: [Col. 0457D] St Augustine, *The City of God*, book XII, chapter 6.]

And after some intervening material:

“Those who wish to know what thing made an evil will proper to a human being, if they look carefully, find nothing. For if we say that he himself made it, what was he before the evil will except a good nature, whose author is God, who is immutable good? Therefore, anyone who says that the person who consented to a tempter and persuader, whereas another did not consent, to make unlawful use of a beautiful body—which was equally present to the sight of both, while before that sight and temptation both were alike in mind and body—made an evil will for himself, although he was certainly good before the evil will: let him ask why he made it, whether because he is a nature or because he was made from nothing. He will find that an evil will begins to exist not from the fact that he is a nature, but from the fact that the nature was made from nothing.”

[Note: [Col. 0458D] St Augustine, ibid., *Patrology*, vol. XLI.]

## Chapter IV. That this is true knowledge of confession: to recognize that evil is from nothing and tends toward nothing.

By saying this, he opened a very broad path to understanding, so that a person may know himself and, with a contrite heart, submit himself as creature to the Creator, remembering his own origin. For he defends and justifies, as is fitting, the will of God: namely, because the creature’s evil will arose not from God’s will but from nothing—that is, from the fact that it was made from nothing.

Nothing of our miseries will remain hidden or unknown to us if we rightly attend to what he said; nor will our knowledge of true confession be uncertain, so that we may accuse ourselves not only truthfully but knowingly in all our sins and calamities, saying whenever we sin: “Behold, this is from nothing—that is, from the fact that we were made from nothing.” Do we contract this or that from the will of God, rather than from our own most faulty will—we who were made from nothing and tend toward nothing, although we can no longer be nothing?

For someone elegantly said of such things:

> And they tend toward nothing, yet cannot be nothing.

The command of the Almighty indeed perpetuates the creature’s substance, concerning whom it is written: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32). Yet the creature tends or returns toward nothing for the worse by going too far away from the Word through whom it was made—especially by knowingly standing against the word of truth and speaking a lie. For, by speaking what is not, it itself becomes nothing and is nothing.

## Chapter V. That a creature of evil will tends toward nothing in two ways: first through the error of ignorance, and secondly through the lie of malice.

For in two ways the creature of evil will, which was made from nothing, again tends toward nothing. One way is by striving after that which neither is nor appears to be; the other is by desiring that which indeed appears to be, but is not. To turn away from God, who alone truly is, in the first way is diabolical; to wander from him in the second way is human.

For the devil sins with respect to that which neither is nor appears to be. He knowingly speaks a lie, not by wandering through ignorance but by fabricating through malice. Therefore Truth speaks of him thus: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8).
