But a human being sins with respect to that which appears to be and is not: either by speaking in error what is not so, or by loving what is not truly real because it is transitory; not yet overthrown through malice, but wandering through ignorance, or drawn away and enticed by desire (Jas. 1). Therefore he is not yet called a liar, but is reproved for vanity, as it is written: “Youth and pleasure are vanity” (Eccl. 11). “Nevertheless every living human being is altogether vanity.” Again: “Nevertheless man passes away in an image, and indeed is troubled in vain. He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38).

But when a human being too, knowing the truth, resists the truth and stubbornly speaks a lie, he is then rightly called not a human being but a devil, or a son of the devil, because the devil’s sin is his sin. Therefore, like the devil, he is given over to an unrepentant heart, so that he may deserve no forgiveness. For this is to speak a word against the Holy Spirit, concerning which sin the Lord says: “It shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

These are those whom, as the Apostle says, God “gave over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting” (Rom. 1). Certainly not because he willed them to do so many or such great unfitting things, but because he no longer cared at all what they did, since he was angry, as it is written: “According to the multitude of his anger, he will not seek” (Ps. 9). God’s will concerning them—indeed, his judgment upon them—lies only in this: that they may never bend toward the humility of repentance, as it was said of certain persons: “And they did not listen to the voice of their father, because God willed to kill them” (1 Kings 2).

Thus in two ways, one evil and the other most evil, the creature tends toward nothing by its own will, being changeable in this manner from no other source than that it was itself made from nothing.

## Chapter VI. That good will is not naturally present in a human being or angel, but is given by God’s gift and grace.

Since, therefore, all things were made from nothing, and nothing itself, as an efficient cause, is the cause of evil will in a rational creature, whence does good will come to some, making them angels or human beings of good will?

For we are no longer asking what many customarily ask—namely, whence evil will came to a good creature—because it is evident that, from the fact that it was made from nothing, the apostasy of evil will arose or has arisen, by which it again perversely tends toward nothing. Whence, then, does it have the good will by which it tends not toward the nothing from which it was made, but toward God by whom it was made, or toward the Word of God through whom it was made? Whence, unless from the goodness or grace of God?

For the Apostle says of this same grace: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, for good will” (Phil. 2). A rational creature does not naturally have the will for God, or the desire for God’s Word, in the way that the body of a living creature naturally and spontaneously seeks the earth, hastening by natural appetite to live from that from which it was made. It needs assisting grace, because it was not taken from God as a body is from the earth, nor was it made from God or from God the Word, but was created by God and through God’s Word.

Therefore, only through assisting grace and only by the Creator’s gift could the creature possess good will or love the Creator. He gave this gift of good will to some; and we know that he gave it so greatly and so powerfully to some angels and human beings that certain angels deserved to be called seraphim—that is, “burning ones” or “those who set aflame”—while certain human beings, likewise still placed on earth and living in the flesh, burn so intensely that charity cannot be extinguished in them by many waters of temptation or many floods of tribulation.

## Chapter VII. That God gave good will not to all creatures, not because he himself did not will or could not do so, but because they did not receive it.

We have now reached the summit of the question. For it is asked: if a creature’s good will is the Creator’s gift, why did he who created all not give it to all? Why did he leave any angel or human being in an evil will? Did he not will, or was he unable, to work good will in all?

If we say that, though able, he did not will it, there will seem to be a deficiency of good will in God; nor shall we judge true what the Apostle says: “Who wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2). The aforementioned Father Augustine says rather:

“If the good angels themselves made good will in themselves, did they make it by some will or by no will? If by no will, certainly they did not make it. If by some will, was it good or evil? If evil, how could an evil will be the maker of a good will? If good, then they already had it. And who had made this, except he who created them with good will—that is, with the chaste love by which they cleave to him—at the same time both establishing their nature and bestowing grace? Therefore one must believe that the holy angels have never existed without good will, that is, without God’s love. But those who, though created good, nevertheless became evil by their own evil will—a will which their good nature did not make, except when it voluntarily fell away from the good—so that the cause of evil is not good but a falling away from the good: either they received a lesser grace of divine love than those who persevered in it; or, if both were created equally good, then, when these fell by an evil will, the others were more greatly aided and attained that same fullness of blessedness by which they became altogether certain that they would never fall away from it.”

[Note: [Col. 0459D] St Augustine, *The City of God*, book XII, chapter 9, *Patrology*, vol. XLI.]

After saying that God made in them the good will by which they might cleave to their Creator, establishing their nature and bestowing grace at the same time, and so forth, Augustine did not say of the reprobate angels that God did not will to work good will in them. Rather, he said that they did not receive it and fell by an evil will.

Therefore neither ought nor wish we to say that he did not will it; indeed, we utterly abhor, and do not allow ourselves to hear, the assertion that he himself willed them to have an evil will. But if, on the other hand, we say that he could not, we shall seem to derogate from the Omnipotent, unless we are supported by reason and by the unquestionable authority of Scripture, showing that there are circumstances and times in which it cannot happen that the Omnipotent works with the hand of mercy, and in which he must consequently exercise the other hand, the hand of judgment.

## Chapter VIII. That God must work with the other hand, the hand of judgment, where there is the evil heart of unbelief.

Where, then, or when, can it not happen that he works with the hand of mercy? Clearly where there is an evil heart of unbelief: when the heart is hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. This is the worst kind of evil will among those mentioned above.

For the Evangelist writes: “And he could do no mighty work there, except that he cured a few sick persons by laying his hands upon them. And he wondered because of their unbelief” (Mark 6). He had previously said of them: “And many, hearing him, were astonished at his teaching, saying: ‘Whence has this man all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him?’ And such mighty works as are accomplished by his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon? Are not his sisters also here with us?” And they were scandalized at him (Mark 3).

Where, therefore, there is an evil heart of unbelief, when unbelief is caused not by the error of ignorance but by the envy of an evil and proud heart, then there it cannot happen that this hand of the Lord—the hand of God’s clemency—performs any mighty work that is true and sweet, by which sinners dead in the death of the soul rise again.

Accordingly the teacher already mentioned says: “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity” (Ps. 58). “There is a certain iniquity which, when a person commits it, makes it impossible for God to have mercy on him. Perhaps you ask what it is. It is the defence of sins. When anyone defends his own sins, he commits a great iniquity. He defends what God hates. And see how perversely, how unjustly: if he has done any good, he wishes it to be imputed to himself; if any evil, to God. For in this way people defend sins in God’s name—which is worse. What is this? No one dares say: ‘Adultery is good; murder is good; fraud is good; perjury is good.’ No human being at all. Indeed, you do not find a soul so perverse, so alien to the fellowship of humankind and the common participation in Adam’s blood, as to think adultery good, or, as I have said, fraud, robbery, or perjury. But how do they defend these things? ‘If God had willed it, I would not have done it.’ Thus you defend your sin in such a way as to accuse God. The guilty person is excused in order that the judge may be blamed. God certainly will not have mercy on those who commit such an iniquity.”

The evil of unbelief just described was in Adam, because, swelling with pride from a desire for divinity, he obeyed the voice of his wife more than the voice of God; and she believed the serpent saying, “You shall not die at all” (Gen. 3), more than God, who said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Therefore God could not perform a mighty work in him, as John Chrysostom too—golden of mouth, in accordance with his epithet—did not hesitate to say in his sermon *On the Fall of the First Human Being*: “He who considers pardon accuses the cause of the despised law. He rebukes the fault so that he may grant pardon, so that those whom he could not form by instruction he may cleanse by confession.”

Likewise, in those proud persons of whom it is written, “There were giants upon the earth in those days” (Gen. 6), there was an evil heart of unbelief. Thus the Apostle Peter says: “They had formerly been unbelieving, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built” (1 Pet. 3). Scripture forcefully expresses in its narrative that they resisted God’s will greatly, and that God did not at all will the evil that they committed, when it says: “And God, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was intent upon evil at all times, repented that he had made human beings upon the earth” (Gen. 6). And, looking ahead: “And, touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, he said: ‘I will destroy the human being’” (ibid.), and so forth.

## Chapter IX. That the objection of some—that no one can resist God’s will—is defective; for one must add: “and have peace.”

But you say: Is it not written, “And there is none who can resist your will?” (Rom. 9). Truly, I say, but one must understand: “and have peace.” For blessed Job says: “Who has resisted him and had peace?” (Job 9).

Discussing this, blessed Gregory says:

[Note: [Col. 0461D] St Gregory, *Morals*, book IX, on Job 9:4, *Patrology*, vol. LXXV.]

“He who wonderfully creates all things himself orders them so that the things created may accord with himself. Therefore, where the Creator is resisted, the agreement of peace is broken, because things cannot remain ordered when they lose the arrangement of heavenly governance. Those things which, subject to God, would have remained in tranquillity, when left to themselves throw themselves into confusion; for they find no peace in themselves when they oppose, in the Author, that which comes down from above. Thus that highest angelic spirit, which could have remained in the summit if subject to God, suffers its own rejection because it wanders outward through the restlessness of its nature. Thus the first parent of the human race, because he resisted his Author’s command, immediately experienced the disgrace of the flesh. And because he refused to be subject to his Creator through obedience, cast down beneath himself, he immediately lost peace.”

## Chapter X. That unbelievers do indeed resist God’s will, but do not conquer it; rather, they themselves are conquered.

Blessed Augustine also, in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, says:

“God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth, yet not in such a way as to take away their free choice, by using which well or badly they may be judged most justly. When this happens, certain unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel; yet they do not thereby conquer that will. Rather, they defraud themselves of the great and highest good and entangle themselves in penal evils, destined in punishments to experience the power of him whose mercy in gifts they despised. Thus God’s will is always unconquered. It would be conquered if he did not find what to do with those who despised him, or if they could in some way escape what he has decreed concerning such persons.

“For example, someone who says, ‘I will that the people who are my servants work in the vineyard and, after their labour, feast while resting; but whoever among them does not will this shall always grind in the mill-house’—anyone who scorns this appears indeed to act against his master’s will. But he conquers that will only if, scorning the mill-house as well, he escapes it—which can in no way occur under God’s power.”

Therefore, when we read or hear, “And there is none who can resist your will,” one must understand: “and have peace.”

## Chapter XI. That God has two ways and hands, mercy and judgment, as he demonstrates through the law concerning the conquest of a city, which he himself gave.

Therefore, as stated above, God’s omnipotence proceeds neither by one way alone nor weighs out its actions with one hand only, but with two—the hands of mercy and judgment—according to this law: that he first strives to work with the hand of mercy; and where, because pride stands against it, he cannot perform any mighty work with that hand, only then does he stretch forth the other hand, the hand of judgment, and break like potter’s vessels those whom he could not soften.

For this reason he gave such a law to humankind, undoubtedly for imitation of himself: “When you approach to conquer a city, you shall first offer it peace. If it receives this and opens its gates to you, all the people who are in it shall be saved and shall serve you under tribute. But if they are unwilling to make a treaty and begin war against you, you shall besiege it. And when the Lord your God delivers it into your hand, you shall strike with the edge of the sword every male in it, except the women and children, the beasts, and the other things that are in the city” (Deut. 20).

This, I say, he commanded to be done in imitation of himself. For God himself first acted thus toward the human being whom he had made and whom, by blessing and saying, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 3), he had ordained to be the father of a great and glorious multitude of saints. He approached to conquer him healthfully and subject him to his word and command, so that he might not become proud and fall into the judgment of the devil, but might live humble and obedient.

But he was unwilling to make a treaty with God; instead he began war against him. Therefore God besieged him and struck with the edge of the sword—that is, with the sentence of death—the whole human race that came from him. Yet in the final day of the great judgment God was to conquer again the whole city of this world, together with its prince the devil and his angels.

Therefore he again first approached to offer peace, sending his Son into this world through the mystery of the Incarnation, so that through the cross he might kill the enmities in himself. Asking in his gracious mercy that his peace be received, he sent throughout the world to all nations an embassy of his peace. Hence the Apostle says: “For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their offences to them; and he has placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We entreat you for Christ: be reconciled to God. Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. And, as helpers, we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 5–6).

## Chapter XII. That it is God’s will that all receive peace and be saved; but the stiff-necked do not approach, indeed reject God’s mercy once known.

That law of God therefore says: “If it receives peace and opens its gates to you, all the people who are in it shall be saved and shall serve you under tribute” (Deut. 20). That all the people may be saved if they receive peace is the will of God who, as the Apostle mentioned above says, “wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2), provided that they too are willing to receive his peace or salvation.

Thus, on this saying of the Apostle, blessed Ambrose says:

[Note: [Col. 0463D] St Ambrose, *Commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy*, chapter II, verse 4, *Patrology*, vol. XVII.]

“God wills all human beings to be saved, but if they approach him. He does not will to save them unwillingly; rather, he wills them to be saved if they themselves also will it. For he who gave the law to human beings excepted no one from salvation. Does not a physician set himself forth publicly in order to show that he wishes to heal all, provided that he is sought by the sick? But this medicine is not bodily but spiritual, and it benefits neither the doubtful nor the envious. For faith gives salvation; unless the mind receives it with its whole will, it not only profits nothing but also harms. Grace indeed has this power: it pours divine healing into those devoted to it, but gives disease to those not devoted to it, through which the whole person perishes.”

Therefore God does not will evil to occur, but rather wills all human beings to be saved from evil. If you ask further, saying, “Why does he not do what he wills?”, we say that in the case of no human being does he cease to employ the instrument of this will of his, insofar as he sees it expedient for each.

For how, or through what, does one come to salvation except through the knowledge of truth? For Truth itself says in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Therefore, after saying, “Who wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2), the same Apostle immediately added, as though you had asked the means or approach by which salvation is attained: “and to come to the knowledge of truth” (ibid.).

But you say: “He does not give all people the capacity to know the truth. For he did not make all human beings know him as the true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. He hid that truth from many. How, then, does he will or did he will them to be saved?”

We answer: He hid it from many by sparing them—namely, lest truth once known should become for them a cause of graver judgment. For it is better not to know the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. Such were, or were beginning to be, those to whom he said, after they had come out of Egypt by a mighty hand, through which they had already begun to possess knowledge of truth: “For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people, lest perhaps I destroy you on the way” (Exod. 35).

For those with whom God does not go up do not remain unharmed; but those with whom God goes up—that is, to whom he gives knowledge of truth—and whose knowledge is despised and rejected through stiff-necked rebellion, are destroyed much more severely.

## Chapter XIII. That it would have been better not to have known the truth than to hold the truth once known in unrighteousness.

Human rashness might seem somehow able to excuse itself if there were not many well-known examples. For God gave some persons knowledge of truth—not only Jews, I say, but also Gentiles, and especially philosophers among the Gentiles—and that very knowledge became an occasion of graver wrath for them.

For they are those of whom the Apostle already mentioned says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings, who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest among them. For God revealed it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are discerned through the things that have been made; likewise his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse, because, though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1), and so forth.

Would it not have been better not to know God than, knowing him, not to glorify him as God or give thanks? But if anyone still dares to say, “I would not have been such a person; had I known God, I would have glorified him as God and given thanks,” let that person return to his conscience and see whether he has kept the small measure of knowledge of truth which he had, and lived according to it.

For there is no one who has not known at least the truth of the natural law expressed in the saying: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4). The Lord himself says: “Whoever is unfaithful in a little thing is also unjust in a greater” (Luke 16). Therefore, whoever has observed this truth and yet has been abandoned may complain that knowledge of the true God was denied him and may say: “For if I had known, I would have glorified him or given thanks.” But if he did not observe it, his mouth is stopped, so that he may not charge God with not revealing to him the knowledge of truth by which he might be saved. And in this way too is fulfilled what is written: “And you shall prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50).

For it cannot be refuted that it is said most truly of God that “he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2).

## Chapter XIV. That the Lord did not make truth known to certain persons, not because he did not will them to repent, but because he foreknew that they would not practise true repentance.

But perhaps you say: “I have clear testimony from the Gospel that God does not will all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth; indeed, that he did not will, or does not will, to make the truth known to some, lest they be able to be saved.” For there, namely in the Gospel, it is written: “Then Jesus began to reproach the cities in which very many of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented: Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, [Col. 0465B] Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth” (Matt. 11). And shortly afterward: “For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps they would have remained until this day” (ibid.). How then is it true that he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth, when he neglected those whom he knew could have been saved through repentance, and was unwilling to make the truth known to them by any mighty works?

We answer briefly that God’s concern is not for repentance of every sort such as would require him, for its sake, to perform his mighty works and signs. For repentances differ according to the intentions of those who repent. It is one thing to seek eternal salvation by repentance, and another to seek by repentance a transitory [Col. 0465C] safety or happiness. The Ninevites too sought transitory safety by repenting, since, when Jonah preached, they had heard only of the danger threatening them; but they had no concern at all for eternal salvation. Thus preaching was indeed delivered to them as a figure of evangelical preaching, together with the sign of the Lord’s Passion; and Nineveh also bore the type of the whole world. Yet, once safety had been restored to them after repentance, they quickly returned to the same crimes, or even worse ones; consequently, when the Chaldeans devastated them, they were overthrown, in accordance with the same prophecy of Jonah, as we read in the Book of Tobit, where he himself says: “The destruction of Nineveh is near; for the word of the Lord does not fail. And now, my children, listen to me: do not remain here; but on whatever day you bury your mother [Col. 0465D] beside me in one tomb, direct your steps from that time onward so that you depart from here. For I see that its iniquity will bring about its end” (Tob. 14).

Such, certainly, would have been the repentance of the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Sodomites if the calamities threatening them had been foretold with the testimony of so many signs and mighty works. But such a manner or intention of repentance would not have been worthy enough for signs or mighty works to have been performed in order to compel it. Therefore, it was not because God was unwilling that human beings be saved, but because he knew that their repentance would not be worthy or sufficiently fruitful, that the manifestation of mighty works among them was lacking. The Jews, moreover, are declared harder in comparison with them, and therefore liable to a more intolerable judgment, when he says: “It will be more tolerable for them on the day of judgment than for you” (Matt. 11), because [Col. 0466A] although the Lord threatened them not merely with the temporal destruction that they were to suffer at the hands of the Romans, but also with the hell of unquenchable fire, unless they repented—and promised the kingdom of heaven if they did repent—they nevertheless could by no means be brought to believe or to repent. Hence, severely censuring them, he had first said: “To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, crying to their companions: ‘We played for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn’” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV. From the example of Joshua: God remains almighty even if not all accept the peace offered by him, provided that he conquers and strikes all.

Accordingly, grave indeed is the judgment of those to whom it was not made known; but most grave is that of those to whom God made himself known and revealed his truth, though he knew that they would not glorify him or give thanks. Or, to pursue the tropological parallel drawn above from the Law: it is grave indeed not to have heard the embassies of peace from him who is to come on the day of judgment to conquer almightily the city of this world, made God’s enemy from the time Adam sinned; but it is most grave to have heard and despised them. Almightily, I say. For because the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Hivites did not accept peace from the children of Israel—as it is written: “Joshua fought against these kings for a long time; there was [Col. 0466C] no city that surrendered itself to the children of Israel, except the Hivite who dwelt in Gibeon; he took them all in war” (Josh. 9)—was Joshua therefore not strong, not powerful? On the contrary: he was strong and powerful precisely because he took them all in war; he struck them all with the edge of the sword.

Likewise, God—or his Word, that is, his Son Christ—is not non-almighty because, in offering peace, he laboured crying out and his throat became hoarse (Ps. 68), yet not all accepted his peace. Rather, he is thereby the almighty and most strong God of spirits: because against all despisers of peace and mercy his wrath will then rage mightily in judgment; and, as was said through the prophet: “Before the face of his indignation no one shall stand, and no one shall resist the wrath of his fury; there the mighty man shall be troubled, and human beings shall be troubled, and they shall walk as blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord; and their blood shall be poured out like smoke, and their bodies like dung” (Zeph. 1).

## CHAPTER XVI. Scripture chiefly proclaims God’s omnipotence in his punishment of sinners and casting down of the proud.

For omnipotence proceeds, as has already been said above, or is carried out by two hands—mercy and judgment: here raising up the humble, there casting down the proud and rebellious. Yet Scripture customarily proclaims it more particularly in this: that sinners are punished by his judgment and the proud cast down by his arm. We first find this name [Col. 0467A] where the Lord appeared to Abraham, when he had begun to be ninety-nine years old, and said to him: “I am the Lord Almighty; walk before me and be perfect” (Gen. 18). He did not show him by an act what he could do according to this name—how strong, how terrible he was, how greatly he could rule over all creatures or natures—except by giving him a son from Sarah, long barren and elderly.

For this reason, afterward speaking to Moses and intending immediately to perform the miracles of his omnipotence against Pharaoh and his servants, he says: “I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 6). When he says this, it is to be understood: “as I shall now make it known to you, in that I shall lead [Col. 0467B] you out of the prison-house of the Egyptians, rescue you from slavery, redeem you with an uplifted arm and great judgments, and bring you into the land over which I raised my hand, to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

For this reason the same Wisdom says: “While a peaceful silence held all things, and night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty word leaped down from heaven, from the royal thrones, a stern warrior, into the midst of the land of destruction; a sharp sword, bearing your unfeigned command, and standing, it filled all things with death” (Wis. 18). Therefore the name of the Almighty is especially proclaimed in the casting down of the proud; all his activity in that dreadful judgment will be most fully revealed, when that king of all the children of pride (Job 41), together with all his followers, will be confined by his hand [Col. 0467C] and cast down before the sight of all (Job 40).

## CHAPTER XVII. The hand of mercy is equally—indeed, more—wonderful than the hand of judgment, if one considers more deeply.

Yet if we consider the works of mercy more carefully, his name is no less wonderful, so that we acknowledge him as almighty and our mouth is filled with his praise. For no power and no deceit can resist his will and, by resisting, overcome it—whether in the past, present, or future—so as to prevent him from having from the human race as many elect as he purposed before all ages to have, those very persons whom he chose and whose names he wrote in his book before the foundation [Col. 0467D] of the world.

Many things have arisen to oppose this purpose of his since our nature sinned in Paradise in one man, or through one man. That man, as Father Augustine says, was so made upright that he could remain in that uprightness only with divine assistance, while by his own choice he could become perverse. Whichever of these he chose, God’s will would be accomplished, either by him or at least concerning him. Accordingly, because he preferred to do his own will rather than God’s, God’s will was accomplished concerning him: from the same mass of perdition which flowed from his stock, God makes one vessel for honour and another for dishonour—one for honour through mercy, the other for dishonour through judgment—so that no one may boast in a human being, and therefore not in himself.

Many things, I say, arose to oppose God’s purpose, [Col. 0468A] but they did not prevail, because they did not diminish by even one the least number of the elect. Indeed, it would have been a great work of omnipotence to make so many vessels of honour from an uncorrupted mass, such as Adam’s had been before transgression; but it is the greatest work to make, from a corrupted, condemned, sinful mass—from which, by right, only vessels of dishonour and vessels of wrath would be made—as many vessels of glory and vessels of mercy as he willed or purposed.

Therefore the almighty hand of mercy is no less wonderful than that other hand, the hand of judgment. Indeed, this hand is more wonderful and venerable, because it acted so powerfully in the guise of weakness that Mercy itself deigned to assume a human body, to experience the injuries belonging to every misery and condemned condition, to be afflicted with spitting and scourges, insults and pains, [Col. 0468B] and to be fastened to the gibbet of the cross. Proclaiming him almighty in both respects, we say with blessed Job: “He alone is, and no one can turn aside his thoughts; and whatever his soul willed, that he did” (Job 23).

Of this will, blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0467D] St Gregory, *Morals*, book XVI, on Job 23:13, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXV.], not even those things oppose it which seem to happen against his will, because he sometimes permits even what he does not command to happen, so that through it what he commands may be fulfilled more certainly. The will of the apostate angel is indeed perverse; nevertheless it is wonderfully ordered by God, so that even that angel’s snares serve the benefit of the good, whom they purify while tempting them. Thus, whatever his soul willed, that he did, so that even from that which seemed to resist his will he might fulfil his will.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The daily birth of the wicked through the vice of parents does not mean that God wills evil.

[Col. 0468C]

But perhaps an objection is raised concerning the very vessels of wrath or dishonour: that God wills them to come into being, so that, since we cannot deny that even those persons who do not belong to salvation are born by God’s will, it may consequently be inferred: therefore God wills evil to occur. Here we first ask whether it is evil or good that nature has been so constituted that from a small, formless, confused seed a human being is formed and born, whatever manner of life he will later pursue, yet as a rational creature. I do not think anyone is so foolish as to dare say that this is evil. On the contrary, it cannot be denied to be good.

Rather, it must be said that this is evil: that, on account of the sin [Col. 0468D] of pride in the first root, the human race has been so corrupted that, like beasts, a human being rushes into lust not so much in hope and love of children as in order to satisfy bodily pleasure; so intoxicated by the poison of luxury that, even if he is a believer, in the very act of pleasure he either scarcely remembers, or utterly forgets, to seek the whole faith and honour of God in the procreation of children. That truly is evil; and from it corrupt offspring multiply beyond the number, God—as a certain student of Christian philosophy says—not counting those whom nature, according to its own manner, had produced. For unless this punishment had followed the preceding sin of pride, none of those called vessels of wrath [Col. 0469A] would be born; rather, only vessels of mercy would be born, according to the blessing given over male and female.

## CHAPTER XIX. He is judged simple and unlearned who does not assent to the opponents’ impious subtlety.

Whatever we say, we are reported as having said nothing relevant; indeed, we are judged simple and unlearned, incapable of grasping the subtlety of the proposition by which, as they say, it is most truly stated and most firmly to be maintained that God wills evil. They deny that they assert in God a will for evil, yet they do not cease to affirm that God wills evil to occur. They profess sound beliefs, yet do not cease to utter a perverse assertion. And because we do not grant this, they maintain, as has been said, that we are simple and rustic, incapable of grasping the force and marrow of their arguments.

Nor is this surprising. For the simple doctrine—or learned simplicity—of the faithful has often been mocked in this way. “But see,” says someone, “that we understand your subtleties and your secrets, which you discuss in rooms and corners and which the people standing outside do not deserve to hear; let us bring them into public.” This is what you mean when, bringing your hand to your ear and snapping your fingers, you say mockingly: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” and “The king brought me into his chamber” (Cant. 3). Therefore it is no wonder; nor do we boast against you of skill in speech, mindful that Christ’s Apostle said: “I did not come to announce to you the testimony of Christ in loftiness of speech or wisdom. [Col. 0469C] For I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). Yet we understand that this is not so much subtlety as dullness.

## CHAPTER XX. Those who maintain that God wills evil wrongly defend themselves under Augustine’s patronage.

It is said that the entire support for the proposition that God wills evil rests upon that passage in which Blessed Augustine, speaking extensively about God’s omnipotence and devoutly attentive to it, says [Note: [Col. 0469D] St Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapters 95–96, *Patrologia*, vol. XL.]:

> Therefore nothing happens unless Almighty God wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself. Nor should it be doubted that God acts well even in permitting whatever happens wrongly to happen. For he permits this only by a just judgment. And every judgment that is just is certainly good. Therefore, although evil things, insofar as they are evil, are not good, nevertheless it is good that there should be not only good things but also evil ones. For unless it were good that evils should exist, the almighty Good would by no means permit them; and undoubtedly, as it is easy for him to do what he wills, so it is easy for him not to permit what he does not will to exist. Unless we believe this, the very beginning of our Confession, by which we profess faith in God the Father Almighty, is endangered.

And, after some intervening matter:

> Therefore the “great works of the Lord are sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110), so that in a wonderful and ineffable manner nothing occurs outside his will, even that which occurs against his will; for it would not occur unless he permitted it. And he permits it not unwillingly but willingly. Nor would the good God permit evil to occur unless, being almighty, he were able to make good even from evil. [Note: [Col. 0470D] St Augustine, *ibid.*, chapter 100.]

Those who assert that God wills evil are said to have derived all the support for their view from these sayings of Blessed Augustine, affirming that they received it from great and celebrated masters whom we cannot hear or consult. But now, examining the matter carefully, we are pleased first to observe this: just as nowhere else, so neither here is heard the very dreadful assertion which we detest, “God wills evil.” If Augustine had said this, he would deserve to rebuke himself more justly than where, reconsidering and rebuking himself over one very small expression, he says: “The offence to religious ears should have been avoided here.” Rather, he proclaims the contrary: that God wills good to occur, saying, “For he permits this only by a just judgment; and every judgment that is just is certainly good.”

Let us therefore examine these very words carefully, with the light of grace and truth brought to bear; and let us strive, together with ourselves, to defend the dignity of so great a teacher from that assertion which does not tend to God’s honour.

## CHAPTER XXI. It is falsely attributed to Augustine that God wills evil to occur, unless “by permitting” is added; only then is the statement complete: God wills, by permitting, that evil occur.

“Therefore,” he says, “nothing happens unless Almighty God wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” This statement is correctly understood only when it is first taken as complete, because after saying, “Nothing happens unless Almighty God wills it to happen,” he immediately added: “either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” For it would not be true if he had stated absolutely: “Nothing happens unless Almighty God wills it to happen,” especially throughout the present state of life, in which God’s will is perfectly fulfilled by none of the living. That peace belongs to the age to come, when nothing will resist God’s will.

For example, it is God’s will that a human being be without sin; and for this end, as the Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word, that he might present to himself a glorious Church [Col. 0470D] without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind” (Eph. 5). Hence the same Father says, in the first book of his *Retractations* against the Pelagians: “This is the washing of water in the word by which the Church is cleansed. But since, as long as she is here, the whole Church says, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matt. 6), she is not here without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. Yet by what she receives here, she is brought to that glory and perfection which is not here.”

Therefore it was not enough to say, “Nothing happens unless Almighty God wills it to happen,” unless he had added, “either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” Here there is great force in what he says, “by permitting it to happen”: namely, when evils are under discussion—evils which God certainly hates—it is not permissible to join the word “wills” with the infinitive “to occur,” especially when, after inserting the other verb, “permits,” he immediately says: “Nor should it be doubted that God acts well even in permitting whatever happens wrongly to happen.” And immediately: “For these things occur only by a just judgment.”

You whose sound ears receive these words from us, consider how greatly, in this matter, these two small words, “wills” and “permits,” differ. In the former, when it is said “he wills it to happen,” injury is rashly and irreverently done to God’s goodness so damnably that, as we have mentioned above, the same Blessed Augustine says that God cannot possibly have mercy upon those who commit such wickedness—that is, those who defend their evils by such speech. For when he says in the first book of the *Soliloquies*: “God, who never does evil, yet causes it to exist lest the worst occur,” he plainly means adversity, which God causes to exist in order that the worst evil—namely, the evil of sin, which he never made or willed to occur—may be prevented. I recall that I spoke more fully of this in the preceding book.

But in the latter expression, when it is said “he permits it to occur,” and “he permits it not unwillingly but willingly,” there is honour to God’s judgment and praise of his omnipotence. For he permits what he does not will to occur, but he willingly wills to permit; this is clear to anyone who knows or reflects that the almighty Creator could remove every capacity for evil from a creature willing to do evil, as he will do in his own time, namely on the day of judgment. But the reason why he presently wills to permit it is that, while he overlooks and does not immediately punish, the sinner may either turn or become inexcusable, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2).

Nor meanwhile is God’s patience, waiting, or permission without fruit, because he brings good even from evils, as the often-cited teacher says at the end of the same statement: “Nor would the good God permit evil to occur unless, being almighty, he were able to make good even from evil.” Hence I wonder that this passage should be used to say that God wills evil, when more truthfully and reverently, in accordance with its meaning, one could—or should—say that he wills to make good from evil, or that he can use evil for good. [Col. 0471D] For the passage must be understood in such a way that so great a teacher does not appear contrary to himself when he says in his letter to Honoratus: “All are comforted, built up, and exhorted to pray to the Lord, who can turn away all things that are feared, prepared for either outcome: so that, if this cup cannot pass from them, the will of him who cannot will anything evil may be done.”

## CHAPTER XXII. Augustine’s example teaches that one who rightly rebukes error should not be reproved for the source from which he acquired learning.

From the same passage they have nevertheless very violently extracted the claim that, by making a division, they should say that one kind of will approves and another permits. But the question was not simply God’s willing, but the combined phrase “to will evil”: whether this could suitably be asserted of God. For the controversy arose because it was said that God wills evil to occur. Thus, by saying that one kind of will approves and another permits, they did not make—nor was it relevant to our purpose that they should make—a primary division of will; rather, they made a subdivision of the will of evil. Therefore I said in that book:

> What then? If the will of evil is a genus, and its dividing differences are one kind approving and another permitting, will this permitting will of which he speaks be good or evil? If evil, how is it opposed to the will approving evil? If good, how is it a species of the will of evil? We therefore do not believe the person who says that you were the authors of this division, which both accuses God and fails to preserve the coherence of the art.

When the disciples of the masters to whom we wrote these things reread them, they at once raised an immense cloud of agitation among crowds of hearers wholly ignorant of the matter up to that point. They made great odium against me, a monk, on the ground that in a matter so great and divine I had improperly employed the snares of dialectical art, though ignorant of that art, since I had been enclosed from childhood in monastic silence and had never heard masters.

As though monasteries altogether lack people possessing knowledge, or as though authority, right, and the rule of speech lay with human beings alone [Note: [Col. 0471D] Horace, *Ars Poetica*, verse 72.], and some persons could so take away the key of knowledge that you could accomplish nothing without them—concerning whom it is written: “He who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3).

Will even Father Augustine therefore be despised or refuted? He says of himself to the Lord in the book of his *Confessions*, as truthfully as humbly:

> And what advantage was it to me that, when I was nearly twenty years old, certain Aristotelian works called the Ten Categories came into my hands? When my master, a rhetorician at Carthage, mentioned their names with swollen cheeks and rolling pronunciation, and when others thought learned gazed eagerly upon them as upon something great and divine, I read them alone and understood them. When I compared them with those who said that they had scarcely understood them even from most learned teachers who not only spoke about them but drew many diagrams in the dust, they could tell me nothing other than what I had learned by reading alone to myself.

And afterward:

> And what advantage was it to me that I, then the most wretched slave of evil desires, read and understood by myself all the books of the arts called liberal that I could read, and rejoiced in them, while not knowing whence came whatever was true and certain in them?

Nor have I mentioned the great and supremely illustrious intellect of that venerable man, a lamp of God, in order to dare make such a confession about myself. Rather, it should be known from this great example that the argument is not merely weak but defective which holds that anyone’s speech ought to be rejected because he did not, like celebrated merchants, change climates to purchase pearls of knowledge or sail across the sea. For, wherever it comes from and wherever it goes, “the Spirit,” says the Lord, “breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice” (John 4). Did he say, “If you do not know, you must inquire where it comes from”? Certainly not. Rather, he says, “You hear its voice,” wishing the hearer to be content that whatever he hears from the Spirit is true, wherever it comes from.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The opponents, attempting to defend the division they had made concerning the will of evil by saying that some contraries are mediate and some immediate, fall into a still more absurd error.

I cannot sufficiently describe the great and injurious violence with which they wished to make mine the aforementioned division, which was theirs, because they finally recognized that it was foolish. For they would desire nothing more eagerly than that it be impressed upon all minds that in this controversy I was led not by love of truth and God’s honour, but by service to utterly vain display; and that—most shamefully—while I boasted of expertise, I showed my ignorance.

Accordingly, as though there were or had been no other issue, they mocked me, sometimes in my absence and sometimes in my presence, saying that I had come late to the study of dialectical art because I did not know that some contraries are mediate and some immediate. To this I say: if a division is or becomes defective, who is to blame: the one who made it, or the one who from the opposing side criticized what had been made?

I confess to my Lord, to you as to all who deem it worthy to read or hear these things, that I have neither adopted the profession nor made a display of this art. Even if I knew it, I would never deign to summon it except under compulsion, or unless it spontaneously presented itself—as it does among the wise, the voluntary companion of its mistress, divine wisdom—to assist and aid God’s holy and simple truth when necessary battle is waged against subtle falsehood. For I judge the simple words of shepherds and fishermen, with whom God spoke, stronger than the arguments of philosophers or wise men whom God gave over to a reprobate mind.

But even if we do not know this art, we have at least heard of its reputation; what difference does it make in this matter whether those things by which, according to them, “to will evil” is divided are mediate or immediate? For grant that, as they say, the will of evil, or willing evil, is one kind approving and another disapproving, since these are contraries, and that they name another permitting as occupying the middle position. Does not “willing evil,” or the will of evil, according to them, apply equally—as, for example, “even number” applies to evenly even number and its contrary, evenly odd number, and their middle, oddly even number—to the approving kind, its contrary the disapproving kind, and their middle, the permitting kind?

And what is more opposed to willing than disapproval? Just as, for example, peace is opposed to enmity and war to friendship, so disapproval is opposed to willing. It is established, moreover, not only by the authority of all divine Scripture but also by the freely assenting nature of the rational creature itself, that God hates and disapproves evil. [Col. 0474A] How then can disapproval be a species or difference of willing? How, I ask, can God both will and disapprove evil? Contradictories cannot coexist concerning the same thing. Thus, while they demand mediates, see how much more they run into absurdities.

## CHAPTER XXIV. God so little wills evil to occur that he does not even permit it in every way. He permits it not by granting it, but by not opposing evil effects.

Again, since among those whose profession is dialectic, acting and being acted upon are two most general genera, why do they take what was said—“either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself”—as though these were distinctions or modes of willing? For to permit and to suffer are nearly equivalent in meaning, unless perhaps God is more properly said to permit or allow something in what belongs to him rather than to suffer it, because he suffers nothing in himself, being impassible. For when he is called “patient” in sacred Scripture, this is fittingly expressed there by the other term “long-suffering.”

Therefore, willing is rather a mode of permitting or doing, so that the sense is: Almighty God does nothing or permits nothing except willingly. Thus, when Blessed Augustine says that the good God permits evil to occur, the question should be: how does he permit or allow it? For permitting is one thing by granting, another by not opposing the effects of an evil will. In which of these ways, then, does God permit evil to occur? By granting it, or by not opposing evil effects?

Certainly not by granting it, for he always forbids evil to occur, both by written law and by natural law. Even if you do not know the written law, wherever you turn to commit evil, the conscience received from him gives back to you—indeed, brings forth against you—the testimony of natural law: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” Therefore God does not permit evil to occur by granting it; he permits it in the other manner, namely, by not opposing the effects of an evil will—for example, by not withdrawing or paralysing the hand that wishes to steal, murder, or stretch itself toward the forbidden tree.

Yet not even in this way does he always permit evil to occur. For the time will come when he will utterly remove every will for evil from the elect and every capacity for evil from the reprobate. Yet even the sins of the elect sometimes deserve that the reprobate be permitted, at least temporarily, to rage against them. Therefore God not only does not will evil to occur; he does not permit it in every respect. He does not will evil to occur in any manner; yet he permits it in some manner for a time, and in another manner does not permit it. He does not permit it because he forbids it; he permits it because he gave free will. If you ask why he permits it even thus: “Did God,” says Blessed Augustine, speaking of the fall of the first human being, “make a stone statue, rather than a rational creature which ought to be governed by command?” Therefore, as the same Father says—and as we recalled above—because he preferred to do his own will rather than God’s, God’s will was accomplished concerning him, and so forth, as above.

## CHAPTER XXV. As the evangelical father of the household let his son go but did not will him to perish, so God permitted sin to occur but did not will it.

[Col. 0475A]

What shall we say to this, concerning ourselves or our gentile forefathers, whom God permitted to do evil? Did that evangelical father of the household, who had two sons and divided his property to the younger at his request, will evil to occur by doing so and by allowing his son to depart? Did he will him to be luxurious, to squander his substance with prostitutes, and finally to feed pigs, because he let him go? Who in his right mind would say this?

He willingly permitted him to go; he willingly divided the property: indeed, had he preferred, he could have bound the deserter in prison and iron fetters. But he did not will the evil to occur—the evil of desertion, by which the son’s heart would be alienated from the father’s devout authority; nor that, released to himself, he should live luxuriously with prostitutes and feed pigs, becoming an ignoble man from a noble one.

The father’s own going out to meet the returning son is witness; the entire gesture and manner of falling upon his neck and kissing him is witness; the whole melodious festivity of consolation at the banquet is witness, I say, that the son had never died or been lost with the will of such a father. For the consolation would be vain if true grief had not preceded it. But the grief would not have been genuine or sincere if that which caused it—the son’s loss and death—had occurred only by the father’s will.

Therefore, that the son was allowed to go happened only by the father’s will; but that he asked to be released, and that he consumed his substance by living luxuriously with prostitutes, happened not with the father willing but grieving. This comparison is familiar and celebrated: that father is God, while the two sons are the Jewish people and the gentile people respectively. Therefore, that the gentile people wished to be content with its own portion—that is, natural intelligence—without the grace of God the Father, and, expending even this upon vanities of vanities and philosophizing about creatures, squandered its substance as it were with prostitutes, and at last fed pigs by “changing its glory into the likeness of an image of corruptible human being, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents” (Rom. 1): this was certainly evil, which God did not will to occur.

But that it was free to commit these evils—for example, because wrath did not come upon it to destroy human beings, as happened at the time of the flood—was God’s just and good permission, awaiting the time for the repentance of the gentiles.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why he replied late to the foregoing: at first he did not know that his opponents had derived their opinion from Augustine; it is to be rejected as water from a clear spring polluted by the filth of baths.

We have dwelt at some length on these sayings of blessed Augustine because we learned that the assertion that God is said to will evils had been taken from them. It would indeed have been fitting to discuss or answer these points at the beginning of our discourse; but we had not yet learned [Col. 0476A] that they had drawn this conclusion from there, or thought that it could be confirmed from there. We wondered whence our opponents obtained a defence for their cause, since they could produce no authority from the Scriptures. It was as though we saw the great mast of a warship, with a small emblem like a victory-sign mounted upon it, being hauled by ropes, while we did not see those hauling it—until, behold, reliable messengers informed us that there really were certain masters of eloquence in France who were doing this, and were deriving almost all their force from the cited passage of blessed Augustine.

Yet Anselm of Laon—that man whose faith and learning have hitherto borne fruit in Christ’s Church with a wholesome fragrance above those of others—does not, as we have truly learned, support them by his authority. May the light of truth preserve forever [Col. 0476B] the prudent learning of this illustrious man, lest through any rash utterance in matters of this kind he inflict some stain upon his own glory; and if at any time he deigns to answer the preceding little book, as he promised he would, may he come to us as a white dove beside waters full to overflowing, by the undefiled waters of the Scriptures.

At last let your reverence know, O prudent men, that we shrink from reading or accepting that passage in the sense in which they hand it down, just as we refuse to drink water, though brought from a pure and clear spring, after it has been polluted by the filth of baths. For where the good discourse of so great and so ecclesiastical a teacher is compelled to serve human opinion and the glitter of popular glory, it is polluted by human impurities like water from a pure spring consigned to baths. Now, since enough has been said about this, let us complete the discourse [Col. 0476C] begun to you.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That with God no word is impossible; that is, whatever He Himself has spoken in the Scriptures—not whatever some impious buffoon may utter against the justice of God.

Above we spoke of God’s will and omnipotence because of those who say that we detract from the Almighty when we say that He never wills, or has willed, evil to occur, although evil does occur or has occurred. We have said some things, as the Lord granted; and though much more might be said, we wish to say a few things and to use brevity.

Tell us, then, you who so zealously uphold omnipotence that, so far as lies in you, you diminish the praise of goodness and mercy: what, or how much, do you understand by the name Almighty? Surely, that He can do [Col. 0476D] everything, that there is nothing He cannot do. And together with you we believe and confess that this is so. But what are, or where are, those “all things,” beyond which nothing need be sought? Unless we also discern this, every argument that offers service to almighty God is of little value.

Let us therefore attend, if we have the pointing finger—that is, the Spirit of truth. Let us attend, I say, to the whole breadth of Holy Scripture, from the beginning of Genesis to the end of the Gospel, and to that corner in which Paul, the youngest of all the apostles, stands with his Epistles; and let us say that the hand of the Lord could, can, and will be able to do all these things. Looking upon these, let us confess, as intelligently as faithfully, that He is almighty [Col. 0477A].

But whatever can be imagined or fabricated by argument outside this Holy Scripture, being devoid of reason, has absolutely no bearing upon the praise or confession of God’s omnipotence. Did not the holy angel make this distinction when speaking to Mary? After announcing the conception of that Virgin and declaring the conception of her who was called barren, and that she was now in her sixth month, he added this reason: “For no word shall be impossible with God” (Luke 1). What is “every word” except whatever, or all things whatsoever, God has spoken through the mouth of His holy prophets from of old? (cf. Luke 1).

For we do not take “word” so lightly that, for example, if someone says facetiously: “Although God is almighty, nevertheless He cannot bring it about that three and four are not seven,” we should count this a “word.” Rather, as we have already said, a word is whatever Holy and divinely inspired Scripture contains, except those things which are sometimes reported there as uttered by another spirit.

For example, in Daniel:

> [Note: [Col. 0477C] St Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel*, chapter 4, §32, *Patrologia*, vol. XXV.]

Nebuchadnezzar, praising the Almighty, says: “For according to His will He acts both in heaven and on earth, and there is none who can resist His hand and say, ‘Why have You done this?’” (Dan. 4).

Jerome says: “He says this as a man of the world. For God does not do whatever He wills; rather, He wills whatever is good. Nebuchadnezzar spoke thus so that, while proclaiming God’s power, he seems to accuse His justice, because he himself had undeservedly suffered punishments.”

We therefore confess that none of all the words which God speaks in the Holy Scriptures—whatever He promises or threatens—has been or is impossible with the Lord [Col. 0477C]. Their sum is contained in the Creed, concerning which, without doubting, we truthfully confess that we believe in God the Father Almighty.

Accordingly [Col. 0478A], whatever can be devised outside the rule of the Holy Scriptures, no one can rightly demand from a Catholic person, as a confession of the power of the Almighty over all things. For example, Scripture does not state that God will crown a virgin after her fall. Thus, when someone says—as Jerome, the aforementioned man of known and steadfast faith, says—“Although God can do all things, He cannot restore virginity after its loss; He can indeed free the corrupted woman from punishment, but He cannot crown her,” he does not detract at all from omnipotence, but commends inflexible justice.

Likewise, if he says that although God can do all things, He cannot restore an angelic creature corrupted by lying, nor anyone who follows the devil, the father of lies, by speaking a word against the Holy Spirit—that is, by knowingly defending falsehood against truth—nor give such a person the crown of truth, he does not detract from the Almighty but proclaims justice and truth. If you ask whether He can at least free such a person from punishment, let Him Himself answer you. For after He had said, “Those who have done good shall go forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment,” lest anyone flatter himself concerning God’s goodness, saying, “How will One so good endure to see such great and such lasting punishments of the wretched?” He immediately added: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge; and my judgment is true.”

Therefore let us not flatter the Almighty by saying that the devil, or any angelic or human creature, was corrupted and made evil by His will. Rather, with His help let us labour [Col. 0478C], so far as we are able, not to fall into that judgment of the devil from which He cannot deliver us—He who, though Almighty God, can neither do nor will anything outside the truth of the Scriptures.

[Col. 0477]

# OF LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON CERTAIN CHAPTERS OF THE RULE OF THE HOLY ABBOT BENEDICT

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0477D] 293 You ask of me a small matter indeed, yet, as it seems to you, a useful one; and you urgently demand it, O Chuno Philochristus, lover of truth: namely, that, God granting, I should endeavour to set forth such suitable reasons as I can concerning certain chapters of the Rule of blessed Benedict, especially those about which certain servants of God—religious men of our, that is, monastic profession—have raised questions not to be despised [Col. 0478D].

Long ago, before anyone troubled us with questions of this kind, we had discussed the Rule of that most holy Father just mentioned: that the Holy Spirit, with whom he was filled, had truly ordered it through his mind and spoken it through his mouth; and that it had altogether been built upon the foundation of divine ordinance, the foundation of evangelical authority, upon which, evidently, such a builder or writer fixed the open eyes of his mind as he wrote.

The first matter of which we spoke was the order of the vigils of Sunday night, which are arranged with the number twelve of psalms, readings, and responsories, and are so concluded that the entrance of the priest—greeting, as it were suddenly, the assembled Church—and the reading of the holy Gospel make their ending very joyful and serene [Col. 0479A]. There I gave, as best I could, the reasons for this order. Delighted with them, you began to demand that I commit to writing, as matters usefully to be known, what had been said or was still to be said. At first you pressed less insistently; now more earnestly; and for almost the whole present year you have allowed me no rest, though I resisted.

Therefore, if I offend anyone by writing these things, whoever he may be, let him impute the whole matter to you, whether his offence is just or unjust. For He in whose sight we are, and in whose ears are our words, knows that I did not grant you this assent without some fear, because of what He once said to men wiser than ourselves: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job” (Job 42). For that invisible hearer must be feared, lest perhaps not all that we say pleases Him.

Likewise, if anyone receives any consolation from this, if anyone, as you desire, is usefully strengthened in his humility and simplicity from our words, let it all nevertheless be yours with God [Col. 0479C]. For if you do not permit the other things which I have written, whether voluntarily or at another’s request, to be mine and laid to my charge, how much less this work, to which you have almost driven me by force? Since, as you are accustomed to say, I am a little man with a sluggish belly, and nearly like any Epicurean, you declare that you do not deign to impute the things I have written thus far to me any more than to an ass. And rightly so, I confess. For when Balaam’s she-ass spoke and rebuked her rider, the prophet (Num. 22), who ever attributed this to the she-ass rather than to God alone, who made both the ass and the prophet?

I will therefore do, as I can, what you wish. Yet first bear with me while I say whatever my mind suggests. For if I bear with you, who so often weary me as though under compulsory public service, why should you not bear with me while I hasten first to speak of other things which [because] present themselves together through the occasion of the matters you have put before me to write about?

You have now called me down, as it were, from the height of a lofty mountain; for, intending to write about the glory and honour of the Son of Man, and having entered the Gospel according to Matthew with this intention, I was there in mind and almost continual thought—I stood upon that mountain where He sat down, opened His mouth, and taught His disciples with His most beautiful discourse (Matt. 5). You have called me away from there before the discourse was finished. Since, then, you have unwillingly led me down from that height into this valley—that is, to write these things, in which there is some [Col. 0480A] controversy—I shall first speak, not yet of this matter, as I have said, but of whatever my mind suggests. What is it?

“An impoverished man has spoken,” says Wisdom, “and they say: ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they will overthrow him” (Ecclus. 13). This my mind suggests to me; for this saying also concerns me. For I have spoken, and because I have spoken, they have said: “Who is this?” You know what I have said and gladly embrace my utterances; nevertheless, I shall speak of this too later. For now it is better to say whence, or in whose judgment, I have been regarded as poor.

I was considered poor in their estimation because from my boyhood I have been content, or confined, as a monk within the cloisters of a monastery, and have not travelled over sea and land like those wealthy merchants in whose estimation I am poor. Each of them perhaps presumes that the parable fits him which the Lord speaks: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls” (Matt. 13), and so forth. For they went into distant lands; they travelled among celebrated teachers; and after many pearls that seemed good—the pearls of poets and philosophers—they found the one truly good and truly precious pearl, the pearl of Holy and divine Scripture. They purchased it at the high price of wakefulness and diligence; and may they have found it perfectly and possess it forever!

I did not do this; but, like simple Jacob, I stayed at home with my mother Rebecca (Gen. 25). Hence, in their judgment [Col. 0480C], I am poor and contemptible, and they said: “Who is this? He writes and speaks, speaks and writes—he who was never worthy even to see our masters and teachers.” I am also poor for this reason: I could scarcely obtain or acquire even sheets of paper upon which to write.

But I saw the Wisdom of God; I saw, in some manner, the incarnate Word, Christ the Son of God—wholly golden, wholly as though having a body formed of the finest gold—and from that very body living waters flowed into me with force, through many channels projecting everywhere from His body. Was not Wisdom consoling the poor man in such an appearance and speaking what belongs to itself?

“I,” says that same Wisdom, “love those who love me, and those who keep watch for me in the morning shall find me. With me are riches and glory, splendid wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce than chosen silver, that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries” (Prov. 8).

Again: “I, Wisdom, have poured out rivers; I, like a channel of immense water from a river. I went forth like the river Dorix, and like an aqueduct from Paradise. I said: ‘I shall water my garden of plants and make the fruit of my offspring drink.’ And behold, my channel became abundant for me, and my river approached the sea, for I illumine doctrine like the dawn for all and will declare it even into the distance” (Ecclus. 24).

Was not that vision, I say, speaking to me according to the sense of such words? And if I did not immediately understand [Col. 0481A] what was signified, yet its interpretation is now trustworthy, because its effect immediately followed and continues to this day. And if this perhaps appears ridiculous or childish to anyone else, it ought at least to seem pleasing and venerable to you; for through you it began then to happen that, when I wished to write and by writing to pour back out the living waters flowing into me from that golden image, money did not fail me and parchment did not run short. Thus I can say that Christ, the Wisdom of God, truly, according to that golden vision, is rich and has enough gold and silver.

May it happen to me according to that sign, which also gave a kiss with a firm mouth—a mouth, as has been said, of gold: namely, that knowledge of His secrets, owed only to friends, may not be lacking to me; and that I may experience ever more fully in practice that the ever-flowing streams of Christ’s living spring are better than the baths or cisterns of men.

How did they say concerning this poor man who spoke, “Who is this?” How were they amazed? How were they jealous? Surely as it is written. For sometimes it is permissible, on account of a certain likeness, to compare the least with the greatest. “They embittered him, quarrelled with him, and those who bore arrows envied him.” But again it is written of him, and of every other like him: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm” (Ps. 80).

May God, the hearer of all, who knows that I endured their curses and resisted them to their face for this reason—lest they bring in again the heresy of Florinus by saying and stubbornly affirming that God wills evil to occur, and that that evil, that sin through which death entered this world by the devil’s envy (Wis. 2), occurred by God’s will—see me in the hidden place of the storm [Col. 0481C].

For, as I suppose, you know that there were two contrary heresies: the Colitian and the Florian. The Colitians, named after a certain Colitus, said that God makes no evil whatsoever, contrary to what is written: “I am the Lord making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45). Here is to be understood not the evil contrary to virtue, but the evil of affliction, which must sometimes occur for the chastisement of evils—that is, of sins—for example famine, sword, pestilence, and harmful beasts, which the Lord Himself in Ezekiel calls His four most grievous judgments (Ezek. 14).

The Florians, named after Florianus, on the contrary said that God created evils, including those contrary to virtue, plainly against what is written: “God saw all things which He had made, and behold, they were very good” (Gen. 1). This was that heresy which blessed Jerome anathematized:

> [Note: [Col. 0481D] St Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book XIII, chapter 45, verse 7, *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV.]

Having expounded in its sound sense the phrase in Isaiah, “Making peace and creating evil,” that is, war (Isa. 45)—for just as darkness is opposed to light, so war is opposed to peace—he immediately says: “Let the heresy, therefore, which thinks God the creator of evils, be confounded; for here evil is not set in opposition to good, but stands for affliction and war, according to what is written in the Gospel: ‘Sufficient for the day is its own evil’” (Matt. 6).

It was reported that great masters and celebrated teachers, illustrious lights of all France, to whose lectures crowds of pupils hastened from almost every province, had advanced and steadfastly defended that opinion concerning God’s will. Consequently, whatever I said was not only unheard, but was even despised as foolish. Thus the opponents were, or seemed to themselves to be, secure in what they considered the unanswerable authority of those men, as though an angel from heaven had spoken to them—though such an angel ought not to be heard in matters of this kind, or if he should contradict the Scriptures of truth in any other way.

Indeed, the wiser among them were somewhat tolerable in their opposition. But what shall I say to you of the unlearned rabble of the schools, who favoured the opponents—as clerics against a monk, as masters against an unlearned man? What reproach from such people was directed at me! Truly I learned by experience to feel in myself more deeply that which holy Church says through the mouth of blessed Job:

> “But now younger men mock me, whose fathers I would not have deigned to place with the dogs of my flock; whose strength of hands was worth nothing to me, and whom they thought unworthy even of life—sterile through want and hunger—who gnawed in solitude, wasted by calamity and misery, and ate herbs and the bark of trees; juniper roots were their food. Snatching these things from the valleys, whenever they found anything, they ran to it with shouting. Now [Col. 0482C] I have become their song and their proverb. They abhor me, flee far from me, and do not hesitate to spit in my face” (Job 30).

But I despised all their song and all their contempt with a hard brow, 295 so that I can now, remembering that affair or time, marvel and rejoice that this prophetic saying too befell me: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like a diamond and like flint I have made your face” (Ezek. 3).

I went into France chiefly to engage those masters in the battle of disputation. Their authority over me and against me was so great that whenever I recall that time, I must also recall that most true saying of Wisdom: “A rich man has spoken and all were silent, and they will carry his word up to the clouds; an impoverished man has spoken, and they say: ‘Who is this?’” (Ecclus. 13). For one of those men was both master and bishop; the other was more famous than any bishop, though he himself was not a bishop.

Now the spectacle of that recollection seems marvellous to me: how I alone, a young man riding on a lowly little ass and accompanied by only one boy, set out to distant foreign cities for conflict against men of whom I knew that eloquence, intellectual ability, and great dignity both of office and teaching were present—and that there would not fail to gather, as in fact happened, a company of masters and disciples like a not insignificant army, to hear me and to refute me [Col. 0483A].

But this seems still more marvellous: when I entered the city, the first and chief of the aforementioned masters, drawing his last breath, ended his life immediately after my arrival. The other, with whom I had a bitter conflict, I do not know whether he survived a full year. From then on, because many religious and learned men disapproved of that opinion—and had disapproved of it, though with excessive silence, while those men were still living—the wind of that dispute ceased. But those against whom I first contended long retained the old hatred they had conceived toward me, so that they might truly say: “They hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him” (Gen. 37).

How they sought revenge, and by what retaliation they wished to console themselves against me, I shall say later.
