Now it seems proper first to show from which passages of Scripture they sought to prove their opinion concerning God’s will, and at the same time to show that they did not understand those passages perfectly.

There are four passages. The first is the Apostle’s: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity. God gave them over to dishonourable passions. God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things unfitting” (Rom. 1). The second is from the Apocalypse: “Let him who harms, harm still; and let him who is filthy, be filthy still” (Rev. 22). The third is the saying of Moses: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 13). The fourth: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close [Col. 0483C] their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

To the first passage I replied: God gives no one over to such passions unless that person has first given himself over. For the same Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Having despaired, they gave themselves over to impurity, to the practice of every uncleanness, in greed” (Eph. 4). And to the Romans, before saying why God gave them over, he set forth that they had given themselves over in these words: “They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed creatures, and serpents” (Rom. 1).

What, then, does “gave them over” mean, except as though it were said, “He did not deliver them”? It is easy to learn from another Scripture the reason why He gave them over—that is, did not deliver them. Let us seek that Scripture, to which we think the Apostle especially looked when, having made a just denunciation against the Greek—that is, the Gentile—and three times said, “Therefore God gave them over,” he then turned to the Jew, from whose pride—lest I say righteousness—the whole controversy had arisen. Thus he says: “Therefore you are without excuse, O every man who judges; for in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2).

And indeed almost all Scripture, of the Law and the Prophets, as well as the historical books [Greek: *epistatikōn*] and Kings, plainly testifies that the Jew committed the same crimes which the Gentile or Greek is known to have committed. Nevertheless, we think the Apostle looked most especially to the prophet Hosea when he said these things. For Hosea, judicially arraigning the fornicating Jew, both for spiritual and carnal fornication—or rather, not so much Hosea as the Lord who speaks in him—begins thus: “There is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed; blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4). He likewise three times gives that Jew over by the same surrender by which, as has been said, the Apostle declared the Gentile given over three times, and he gives the reason for the surrender three times.

First he says: “Yet let no one judge, and let no man be reproved” (Hos. 4). For what is it to say this except to give over—that is, to abandon? And immediately he gives the reason: “For your people are like those who contradict the priest” (ibid.). To this one must supply: and therefore they ought to obtain no mercy. For the Law decrees that the proud man who refuses to obey the priest’s command shall die, and that this evil shall be removed from Israel, so that all who hear may fear.

Of such people blessed Job says: “They themselves were rebels against the light,” and so forth, down to: “May mercy itself forget him; God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride” (Job 24).

Second, he says: “Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication, and your brides shall be adulteresses. I shall not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery, because they themselves consorted with harlots and sacrificed with the effeminate” (Hos. 4)—namely, in that practice contrary to nature. The Apostle likewise describes this crime in the second instance of surrender when he says: “For their women changed the natural use” (Rom. 1), and so forth. What is “not to visit” except to give over—that is, to abandon?

In the third instance he says: “Ephraim is a partner of idols; leave him alone” (Hos. 4). For what is it to say “leave him” except to give over—that is, to abandon? And he immediately gives these reasons: “A spirit has bound him in its wings” (ibid.); that is, he sins not through ignorance but through a spirit of pride, and therefore cannot be loosed or corrected. Again: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me. They will not give their thoughts within themselves, and they have not known the Lord” (Hos. 5); that is, they did not approve to hold Him in knowledge, as the Apostle said of the Gentile.

This reason alone sufficiently vindicates God: He does not give someone over or leave him because He wills evil to occur, since, after first saying “Leave him” (Hos. 4), He adds, “For I know that they will not give their thoughts so as to return to the Lord.”

When asked about the second passage, “Let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Rev. 22), I spoke thus: What is it to be in filth except to take pleasure in one’s filth and defend that very filth? For there is another judgment concerning the person who wishes to be made filthy through ignorance, and the person who falls into filth, or has been in filth, through weakness, than this judgment, “Let him be filthy still.”

For example, God says to Abimelech: “Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” But Abimelech had not touched her. And he said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? I did this in simplicity of heart and purity 296 of my hands.” God said to him: “I too know that you acted with a simple heart, and therefore I kept you from sinning against me and did not permit you to touch her” (Gen. 20).

And the Apostle says of himself: “But I received mercy because I acted in ignorance” (1 Tim. 1). Someone asks: Why does He not similarly prevent all who are ignorant, so that they may not sin? Clearly, because He knows all persons, and knows that not all, even if forewarned, would beware of evils—as Cain did not beware, although He Himself warned him (Gen. 4). It is better for them not to know the truth than, having known it, not to keep it.

But it happens to the person who falls into filth through weakness—whose person the Apostle assumes in himself when he says, “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7)—as Wisdom says: “You have mercy on all, O Lord, and hate none of the things which You have made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance” (Wis. 11). Such a person is not here forewarned for caution but awaited for repentance.

But if through pride he defends the very filth in which he is, God no longer concerns Himself with what he does; and, by the judgment of One who abandons, it is said, “Let him be filthy still,” just as it is written in the Psalm: “According to the multitude of his anger, He will not seek him” (Ps. 9); that is, He will not rebuke him for this, because of the multitude of His wrath.

[Col. 0485C] To the third passage, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 13), he replied briefly thus: Was Pharaoh not sufficiently hard before God said, “I will harden”? Was it not great hardness when he said, “Come, let us oppress this people wisely, lest they multiply” (Exod. 1); when he said to the midwives, “When you act as midwives for the Hebrew women and the time of delivery comes, if it is a male, kill him; if female, keep her alive” (ibid.); and again to all his people, “Cast into the river whatever male child is born; preserve whatever is female” (ibid.)? And when the Egyptians hated the children of Israel, afflicted them with mockery, and brought their life to bitterness through harsh labours of clay and brick, and every service by which they were oppressed in the works of the land? (ibid.)

What, then, does it mean to say, “I will harden,” except as though it were said: “Since he is hard, and hates and envies with a hard heart, by performing signs and showing my care for the children of Israel, I shall not only fail to soften that most wicked heart; rather, the opposite will happen to him, so that he who is hard will become harder still”? For it is not soundly understood otherwise, nor was it otherwise understood by the holy Fathers, concerning that saying in the Psalm: “He turned their heart so that they hated His people” (Ps. 104), except thus: by doing good to His people and multiplying them, He made a torment for those who envied them, so that they were hardened more and more by the benefits made evident—just as clay [Col. 0486A] becomes harder the more it is baked by the burning sun:

> “Not even the envy of the Sicilian tyrant  
> found a greater torment,”

says a certain author (Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.58), although what a human tyrant envies in another human tyrant is far different from what an earthly man envies in God and the King of heaven. This Pharaoh, an image of the devil, did the latter.

Did he then first become envious, impious, and hard-hearted when, at the first word of one saying, “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness,” he answered: “Who is the Lord, that I should hear His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 9)? Rather, even before he became king he was hard and impious. Therefore God the judge raised him to the kingdom, so that he might be a notable person in whom He might show by a notable example how He would judge the impious and envious.

This is what He Himself said, and what the Apostle also recalls: “For this purpose I have established you, that I may show my power in you and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (ibid.). Accordingly, the Apostle’s saying, “Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills” (Rom. 9), has a straightforward sense if, as most teachers wish, and especially Origen, you understand it as spoken in the person of the objector.

For where Isaiah says, “Why have You made us wander, O Lord, from Your ways? You have hardened our heart lest we fear You” (Isa. 63), blessed Jerome says thus: “Although the Epistle which Paul writes to the Corinthians is written to the people of one city, because of the diversity of its inhabitants—that is, saints and sinners—he now praises them, now rebukes them; now teaches, now reproves. He summons them to continence, does not reject marriage, recalls them from idolatry, instructs them concerning the resurrection, and extends a hand to second marriage lest it provide an occasion for fornication. We have said this so that we may understand the present passage too, which is composed wholly from the prayer of a people beseeching God, as belonging either to the righteous or to sinners, and as now praising the Lord, now raising a question with the Lord, and attributing their own fault to God.”

In the fourth chapter, where it stood: “Make the heart of this people blind, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, [Col. 0486D] understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them” (Isa. VI), there seemed to be force enough for my adversaries to shut my mouth even by this passage. But I, having scarcely prepared anything beforehand, immediately answered thus: The beginning of a vision is better understood from its end. For in that same vision which the prophet begins to recount in this way—“In the year in which King Uzziah died,” where he sees “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” (ibid.), and so forth—the house is said to have been filled with smoke; and what this signifies is intimated by the words that follow, “Make the heart of this people blind.” But near the end of the vision the Lord himself says: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. VIII). Is it an evil thing that the Jews should thus be blinded, or should have been blinded, so as not to understand, not to hear, not to receive the evangelical faith? On the contrary, it is very good for all the Gentiles; for if the Jews had believed, and their place and temple had remained standing, it would have been a great stumbling-block to the Gentiles, nor would their reception of the Gospel have profited the Jews themselves.

Let us draw our argument from those few who did believe. For they said to Peter: “Why did you go in to men who have the foreskin, and eat with them?” (Acts XI). Having heard his explanation, they were indeed silent at that time; but afterwards they stirred up great dissension against the apostles, teaching the brethren: “Unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved” (Acts XII). This happened at Antioch; and when, because of the same serious dissension, Paul and Barnabas and certain others had gone up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, and the Church had assembled, “some who had believed from the sect [Col. 0487B] of the Pharisees rose up, saying that they must be circumcised and commanded to keep the whole law of Moses” (Acts XV). A great dispute over this matter arose, and was with difficulty quieted through Peter and James (ibid.). If those few had already caused so great a scandal, and had already, so far as lay in their power, mingled Christ’s Gospel with carnal ceremonies, what do you think would have happened if the entire nation had believed and the place and temple had remained standing? Certainly their having believed would have profited neither them nor the Gentiles: for, since they hated the salvation of the Gentiles, the latter would not have been allowed to believe; and if they did believe and were compelled by the Jews to be circumcised, Christ would have profited them nothing.

Accordingly, blessed Jerome, on this chapter, expressed himself briefly as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 0487D] St Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book III, on chapter VI, 10, *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV.]

“If they should see and be converted, and understand and be healed, the whole world will not receive healing. Likewise, universally concerning all those for whom the just God closes, or does not open, the eyes of understanding, it must be known that it is better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. For if they would have kept the truth once known, God, undoubtedly foreknowing this, would have been their guide and the author of their coming to know that same truth.”

Here there comes to mind what the Lord himself said in reproaching certain cities: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. XI). And elsewhere he says: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps they would have remained until this day” (ibid.). Yet he did not perform mighty works in those cities—in Sodom, Tyre, and Sidon. For he was speaking of those cities. What then? Did he at least will evil for those cities—the perdition of those people—that they should not be saved, but should perish?

Blessed Father Augustine, in the *Enchiridion* which he wrote to Laurentius, seems to labour greatly in this chapter, as though between flight and battle: he flees from agreeing that any such evil has ever been, or is, brought about by God’s will; yet he contends that God did not will them to be saved, and rightly did not will it. Whoever attentively considers his words perceives the labour of his intention. For, treating it as utterly certain that God did not will them to be saved, and unable to excuse God on this point, he speaks, as though dashed against an obstacle, more weakly than he himself wishes—as you can plainly observe by reading him. “Therefore,” he says, “nothing happens unless almighty God wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself. Nor should it be doubted that God does good even in permitting whatever things are done badly.”

I knew what that man of holy and devout will intended, striving with all heart and mind toward the honour of divine justice and divine goodness. But my adversaries, rejoicing as though they had the statement of so great a doctor for their patron, would not allow me to do so; they quoted, “Therefore nothing happens unless almighty God wills it to happen,” and would not endure my examination of the words that followed: “either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” Therefore, after struggling, I too at last boldly said that, although that most holy doctor had retracted many things in his writings, this too was worthy of retraction.

And I venture further: having a good will, I do not hesitate to cry out to so great a Father, since I read that Jethro, priest of Midian, gave counsel to holy Moses, who was certainly better, holier, and wiser: “What is this that you are doing among the people? You are not doing a good thing. You will be worn out by foolish labour, both you and this people who are with you. The task is beyond your strength. But hear my words and counsels, and the Lord will be with you” (Exod. XVIII), and so forth. Therefore, that I might not fear my adversaries, I dared and did not fear, because the matter required me to answer back to so great a Father and in some fashion say to him: “What is this that you are doing? Why, wishing as it were to help God, do you exhaust yourself in prolonged labour? There is a shorter road to what you seek.

“Consider, indeed, that he did not say: ‘If the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, and in Sodom, the Sodomites would have been saved, the Tyrians and Sidonians would have been saved’; but only this: ‘They would long ago have done penance in ashes and sackcloth; perhaps they would have remained until this day.’ Are doing penance and being saved equal or equivalent things? Do the statements ‘the cities of the Sodomites would have remained until this day’ and ‘the Sodomite people would have been saved’ have the same meaning? Certainly not. For not all persons who did penance sought salvation, nor are all persons whose cities remain until this day saved.

“For example, the wicked king of Israel, Ahab, did penance, but not for the world to come—rather, for the present age. This distinction must be carefully observed, because before God it makes a great difference whether one does penance for the world to come or for the present age. If Ahab had fasted and slept in sackcloth, walking with bowed head, for the life of the age to come, he would by no means have persisted in the worship of calves and the service of Baal. Likewise, if the Ninevites had done penance for faith or for the life of the age to come, they would by no means, once they had regained confidence because the present vengeance did not come quickly, have returned to their former sins. Since they did so, they were overthrown by the Chaldeans.

“Therefore, when the Lord says that if mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon and in Sodom, and so forth, it does not follow that he did not wish them to be saved. Rather, it follows that he did not concern himself with their repentance, because it would not have been able or sufficient to obtain the fruit of true—that is, eternal—salvation. ‘Do penance,’ says the Lord himself, attaching this reason: ‘for the kingdom of heaven will draw near’ (Matt. III). This is the sole reason for which he deigns to preach repentance and perform mighty works: that people may be invited to believe.

“Hence it should be carefully noted that, just as he did not order the kingdom of heaven to be preached to the Ninevites, since they would not care for it, so neither did he order repentance to be preached to them; but only their coming overthrow. Yet his intention was that, when they did penance—as God foresaw they would—Israel might be shown, by comparison with the Gentiles, to be exceedingly unjust and unworthy of mercy because it was unrepentant; and that the Lord might prove true what he was accustomed to say to any of the prophets in words such as these: ‘For you are not being sent to a people of deep speech and difficult tongue, nor to many peoples of deep speech and an unknown tongue, whose words you could not hear. And if I sent you to them, they would hear you; but the house of Israel will not hear you, because they will not hear me’ (Ezek. III).

“What then was the Lord’s purpose in saying such things about Tyre and Sidon and Sodom, while reproaching the Jewish cities? Surely it was that we might know it to be just that, as he himself says, the land of the Sodomites should fare more leniently on the day of judgment than the Jews. For the Sodomites would at least have done penance in order to avoid evils soon to come upon them, if these had been foretold to them with mighty works bearing witness; whereas the Jews did not do penance either from fear of Gehenna, though it was, as it were, to come in a distant future, or from fear of temporal ruin soon to arrive—rebellious and unbelieving in every respect.”

I have stated, as briefly as I could, the causes that became seeds of hatred against this poor man: so that when he spoke they would say, “Who is this?” eagerly scrutinizing him, that if he stumbled in anything he said, they might overthrow him. It must now be said what I spoke, and how certain of them, wishing me to have offended, attempted to overthrow me, in revenge or retaliation for the rebuke in which, against them, I persevered steadfastly and without failure according to what has thus far been said.

First I spoke the little work *On the Divine Offices, or Sacraments throughout the Course of the Year*, divided into twelve books; and I compressed a very extensive subject, as you yourself confess, into a work briefer than it ought to have been. Then I wrote fourteen books on the Gospel according to John. After this, forty-two books on the Holy Trinity and its works. Then twelve books on the Apocalypse of John. Then thirty-one books on the twelve prophets. Then twelve books *On the Victory of the Word of God*. And now, most recently, at your request I began the work most dear to you, as you yourself confess, *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man according to the Gospel of Matthew*; I was wholly engaged in it when you interrupted me.

These things the poor man has spoken, not on his own authority, but on that of him of whom it is written: “The lion roars: who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?” (Amos III). What offence, then, did they find in all this sort of speech by the poor man? Or rather, how did they seek in order to find it, and fail while seeking? That well-worn Virgilian saying is familiar to nearly everyone:

> “. . . And from one accusation  
> Learn all the rest.”  
> (*Aeneid*, II.65–66)

If you please, I shall tell you of one man; from one, learn them all.

That one man, whom you know—a man of good conduct but recent conversion, of great name but doubtful reputation, already a prelate and preacher but scarcely ever a subject or hearer—asked me familiarly, as though for the sake of study, to lend him something from my little works. I lent him the above-mentioned work *On the Divine Offices*. He received it, went away, read as much and as long as he wished, and after many days returned the book without saying or asking anything to me, whether good or bad.

Then, after several days, I hear it, and many report it to me; learned brethren are even sent to me from other cities to ask and inquire whether a report widely spread concerning me were true: namely, that I had said and written that the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary. I shuddered, I confess; and, fortified by the shield of my conscience, I diligently sought who could be the author of this rumour. Why say more? After a long search, through certain of our fellow brethren it was at last established for me that the author of this accusation—or rather, false accusation—was the man of whom I spoke; and that, from reading the book I had lent him, he had wickedly hunted out this claim from words of this kind in the office for the Fourth Sunday of the Lord’s Advent:

> “For who can investigate how the Word is embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the womb of his mother, how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived? How—or what—did he bring forth before this Word?”

How, then, did he think the poor man had offended? How did he wish to overthrow him? He proclaimed the book heretical and fit to be burned in flames—and did so among unlearned people, many of them wholly ignorant even of letters, who followed and listened to him. And such people, as is their way, display in divine and profound matters an almost greater boldness than the learned; they were excessively hostile to the book, demanding it and hastening to seize it for burning.

What should one condemn more in this: ignorance or envy? For unless he had been ignorant, and less learned than he himself thought, he would surely have known whose words they were that he was so irreverently calumniating. If he had not been envious—or rather, if he had not been desirous of petty glory—he would first have discussed with me the words which he thought mine or first uttered by me. For what? Are these not the words of blessed Pope Gregory in his homily on that Gospel reading: “The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him, ‘Who are you?’” (John I)?

But perhaps I am guilty or liable. For it is written: “If anyone opens or digs a cistern and does not cover it, and an ox or ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals; but what is dead shall be his” (Exod. XXI). I opened and dug the cistern, because I inserted into my writings a profound statement. Yet I did not cover that cistern, because I did not place the authority of the name above it, so that everyone might see whose statement it was. If I had said: “For, as blessed Pope Gregory says, it cannot at all be investigated how the Word is embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the womb of his mother,” then the cistern would certainly have been covered, secured by the authority of the name—that is, by the author’s name—and the one who fell would not have fallen into the cistern: the man who came close to blasphemy.

For whom did he proclaim heretical if not blessed Gregory? What did he almost deny, except that the Word of God—God the Word—is Spirit? Yet he did not deny it altogether; but because he had less love than he ought, and bore some hidden hatred against me, by which the eye of the heart is accustomed to be darkened, he neither saw nor reflected that God is Spirit: the one God—Father, Word, and Holy Spirit—is one Spirit. Spirit, I say, is not body. Yet only the third person is called and is the Holy Spirit, by a compound name, because the Father is spirit, the Son is spirit, the Father is holy, and the Son is holy.

And if you consider it rightly, this third person, namely the Holy Spirit, began to be proclaimed as Holy Spirit from the time when he was given for the sanctification of the human race, when he began to be given to human beings for the remission of sins. Finally, before the grace of the Gospel, before the incarnation of the Son of God, he was called or written of as the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Lord; and, apart from one place in the prophet David, saying, “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L), you will scarcely or almost nowhere find him designated by this name before the angel said to Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke I), and, concerning John at about the same time, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (ibid.).

Was it said in our statement—or rather, in blessed Gregory’s statement—“how the Holy Spirit is animated within the womb of his mother”? No; but, “how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the womb of his mother.” Therefore, as I have said, I am guilty or liable; and for that fall which occurred I render what compensation I can—namely, this present silver coin of reasoning—so that the fall of one person may be compensated by the standing firm of another. Perhaps, on reading this reasoning, the latter will stand more securely, as he advances somewhat by reflecting and understanding more vigilantly that this person whose name is Holy Spirit is not the only one: the Father and the Son, and the love of them both, the Holy Spirit, are one God, the holy Trinity—one substance, one Spirit.

What fell is not dead, because, as I heard, the man of whom we speak, when corrected and shown the authority of so great a doctor, quickly recovered his senses, though embarrassed. Had he not done so, it would have been, and ought to have been, as the previously mentioned legal statement says: “But what is dead shall be his.” For I would rightly have brought him to judgment as my own property, asking the Church—as I had already begun to do—to pronounce a just sentence upon him as an accuser, because he did not wish to correct me if I had erred; but, himself in error, he hastened secretly to defame one walking rightly and unsuspecting of him, forgetful of the saying of Ecclesiastes: “If a serpent bites in silence, he who secretly detracts is no better” (Eccles. IX).

For this was to bite in silence; this was secretly to detract: passing me by, he carried the book about, pressed the chapter upon simpler people, and whispered to each one, as though groaning with them, that I had ignorantly and foolishly said and written that the Holy Spirit had been incarnate of the Virgin Mary; that I therefore appeared a heretic; and that the world would perish because such things were being written. In my judgment, he would not have acted thus unless some hidden hatred lay beneath it.

Yet I do not know how I had offended him, except that I was not wholly pleased with, or did not consider sufficiently prudent, this: that, being young and only recently converted from secular life, he had suddenly sought the priesthood and taken up the public office of preaching, asserting, as was reported, that with apostolic authority he had undertaken eleven bishoprics to be treated by the remedy of preaching. I confess that it still seems to me, and to many wiser persons, that this order, which suits everyone well, would have suited his age and former way of life especially well: that he should have endeavoured to be not a prelate before a subject, but a subject before a prelate.

I told you, “From one, learn them all”; for in truth almost all my adversaries acted similarly. Some of them pored over my writings with greater zeal and scrutinized them more insistently, desiring to find something they might cast against me, something pertaining to the contagion of any heretical stain, in revenge for the above-mentioned reproach which, they thought, had been inflicted upon them by me in that controversy concerning God’s will. At last they imagined that by their scrutiny they had found something; and for a while they began to rejoice as enemies because I had said that angels were created from darkness. “This,” they say, “is plainly heresy.”

But I answered them: “Heresy is to contradict holy and canonical Scripture: to affirm something which it denies, or to deny something which it affirms. What Scripture contradicts this, or to what Scripture is it contrary?” Since they failed in this and could find no authority for the contradiction, I said: “Your objection, then, is plainly calumny—especially since the question concerns not the Creator but a creature, and none of you can contradict it with authority. You merely wish the name ‘darkness’ to seem dreadful to simple people, unwilling to distinguish good darkness from evil darkness.

“For there is good darkness, of which the Psalmist says: ‘You set darkness, and night came to be’ (Ps. CXXX), certainly speaking to God, who saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good (Gen. I). God himself also says: ‘I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness’ (Isa. XLV). How or when did he form light, or what darkness did he create? Certainly, in the beginning, when heaven and earth had been created, darkness was upon the face of the deep, and God said, ‘Let light be’ (Gen. I). Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: ‘For God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus’ (II Cor. IV).

“That darkness upon the face of the deep was dense and moist air, not yet illuminated by sun, moon, and stars. For where light is not, darkness must necessarily be. Blessed Augustine, however, wishes that light to be understood as the angels, whom God commanded to shine out of darkness according both to Genesis and to the Apostle just quoted. For he says in the eleventh book of *The City of God*:

> ‘Where the sacred writings speak of the constitution of the world, it is not stated plainly whether the angels were created, or in what order. But if they are not omitted, they are signified either by the name of heaven, where it is said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I), or rather by this light of which I speak.’

“And afterwards:

> ‘For when God said, “Let light be, and light was made” (ibid.), if the creation of angels is rightly understood in this light, they were surely made participants in eternal light, which is the unchangeable wisdom of God himself, through whom all things were made, and whom we call the only-begotten Son of God; so that, illuminated by the light by which they were also created, they might become light and be called day through participation in the unchangeable light and day, which is the Word of God, through whom both they themselves and all things were made’ (John I).

He plainly shows what he means. But we must know why, speaking doubtfully and almost like one fleeing, he said, “if the creation of angels is rightly understood in this light,” and similar things, which it would take far too long to write out here. For before him other holy men also, and eminent writers, had written on the work of the six days and on that light; and the view seemed weak, uncertain, and insufficiently probable to him—namely, that before the creation of the sun, which was created on the fourth day, there was bodily light and night was distinguished from that same light three times.

To the matters already said I wish to add what the same Father says in the twenty-first book of the same work, *The City of God*, when discussing what sort of punishment the devil’s punishment will be. Among other things he says:

> “Here it arises to ask whether the fire will not be incorporeal, like the pain of the mind, but bodily and harmful to the touch, so that bodies may be tormented by it. How then will there also be punishment for evil spirits, since the same fire will be assigned as punishment for human beings and demons, as the Lord Christ says: ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. XXV), unless demons also have certain bodies of their own, as learned men have thought, from this dense and moist air, whose motion is felt when the wind blows? If that kind of element could suffer nothing from fire, it would not burn those heated in baths. For in order to burn, it is itself first burned, and does what it suffers. But if anyone maintains that demons have no bodies, this matter should not be pursued by laborious inquiry or contested by contentious argument.”

He ends here by saying, “This matter should not be pursued or contested by contentious argument.” Let them therefore choose which they wish. If they approve the view of so great a doctor, blessed Augustine—that when God said, “Let light be, and light was made,” then the angels were created, who are called and are light by participation in the unchangeable light which is the Word of God—let them also hear the Apostle saying that God commanded that light to shine out of darkness. But if they will not grant or hear that the angels are that light, let them say when or from what the angels were created.

And if they say that angels were omitted in that Scripture, the same doctor says: “I do not think they were omitted here, because it is written that God rested on the seventh day from all the works which he had made” (Gen. II), when the book began thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” so that he appears to have made nothing before heaven and earth. Then he says: “Since all things which are said to have been completed through six days were arranged by creation, how could angels be omitted as though they were not among God’s works, from which he rested on the seventh day? Yet that angels are a work of God, holy Scripture testifies elsewhere in the clearest voice. For in the hymn of the three men in the furnace of fire, after it had been said: ‘Bless, all works of the Lord, the Lord’ (Ps. CII), angels too are named in the enumeration of those same works. And the psalm is sung: ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels,’ and so forth, up to: ‘For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created’” (Ps. CXLVIII).

Here too it is most plainly said by divine authority that angels were made by God, when, after they have been mentioned among the other heavenly things, the statement “He spoke, and they were made” is applied to all. Let them choose, I say, which they wish. For I do not fear their voices, provided they cannot show that in any statement I am contrary to the words of holy canonical Scripture.

I shall add this as well: whenever holy doctors—who are certainly united in the faith—differ in some opinion, I shall more willingly and confidently, as a disciple to a master, lend my ear to the one whose opinion I hear more strongly or better supported by the testimonies of canonical Scripture. For example, this same blessed Augustine, commenting on the Gospel according to John where it is written, “And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot” (John XIII), says among other things:

> “But Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, as some careless readers suppose. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed to all of them the sacrament of his body and blood, at which Judas himself was present, as Saint Luke narrates most plainly.”

But blessed Hilary of Poitiers, in his commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, says:

> [Note: [Col. 0493D] St Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 30, 2, *Patrologia*, vol. IX, Migne edition.]

> “After this Judas the traitor is identified, without whom the Passover is completed, the cup having been received and the bread broken. For he was not worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments. For it is understood that he departed immediately from here because he is shown returning with the crowds. Nor indeed could he drink with God who was not to drink in the kingdom, when he promised that all who drank this fruit of the vine would afterwards drink it with him.”

If it should become necessary to ask whether Judas was still with the disciples at that hour, or had already gone out by that departure which John specifies when he says, “When therefore he had received the morsel, he went out immediately” (John XIII), which of these is to be heard or followed more? Certainly the one whom reasoning drawn from the text of the Gospel narrative supports more.

Blessed Augustine’s reasoning is this: Luke narrated it in such a way that, after first mentioning that typical supper, he wrote, “And when the hour had come, he reclined at table, and the twelve apostles with him; and he said to them, ‘I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you’” (Luke XXII), and so forth. Before writing the Lord’s words, “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (ibid.), he first wrote: “And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, ‘This is my body,’” and so forth. This is blessed Augustine’s reasoning. Therefore, if the Lord spoke these words concerning Judas—“Behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table”—after he had delivered to them the sacrament of his body and blood, it follows that Judas too was present at that sacrament with the other apostles.

But according to the other evangelists, Matthew and Mark, the Lord spoke these words concerning Judas not after but before he delivered the sacrament of his body and blood: “Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me,” and so forth, up to, “You have said it” (Matt. XVI; Mark XIV). Only then does there follow, “While they were eating, Jesus took bread” (ibid.), and so forth. This is blessed Hilary’s reasoning.

If, therefore, it is necessary or desirable to know whose reasoning is stronger, one must first see how Luke does not differ from the other evangelists Matthew and Mark in this narrative, since blessed Augustine did not seek their agreement here, appearing to follow Luke’s narrative. The answer already meets those who ask how Luke does not disagree with the others. For after Luke had said, “And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, ‘This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me,’ likewise also the cup,” he specifies this by saying, “after he had supped” (Luke XXII).

Certainly, if it was after he had supped, then it was also after the words, “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (ibid.), because, as already said, according to the other evangelists he spoke these words not after he had supped but while he was supping; and from that very supper he gave Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas, as John reports, immediately went out (John XIII).

Why do I say this? That you may reflect why I was almost condemned in my absence, so that every liberty of writing might be taken from me, and how blessed Hilary, as though sent from heaven by God on my behalf, came to meet you and put before your hands his book and before your eyes his opinion—an opinion you were not seeking and did not even know existed anywhere. I was still almost unknown to you, having been seen only once and having spoken only a few words with you, when this happened, while my adversaries, without my knowledge and while I was far away, were stirring up great envy against me.

For I had had a very troublesome contest concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood with a scholar of great name and reputation, though a monk. Among other means by which he tried to diminish the majesty of so great a sacrament, he objected to me that the Lord had given that sacrament to Judas his betrayer as well as to the other apostles. By this he plainly intended to argue that the Lord would never have given it to Judas if it were the true substance of his body and blood. And he had ready to hand the authority of blessed Augustine to establish that it had been given to Judas the traitor together with the others.

Necessity in this matter compelled me to say that blessed Augustine’s writing is not in the canon and that he is not to be trusted in every respect as the canonical books are. Did I suppose this was new or unknown to my adversaries—especially men of renown, who boasted not a little of their learning, above all in comparison with me, whom they considered an unlearned young man? Yet on this account they began to defame me as a heretic because I had said that blessed Augustine is not in the canon.

You know where, when, and how blessed Hilary, of whom I have just spoken, came to you and defended me in such a way that without him I could not have been judged a heretic. This was a miracle to me which no forgetfulness will ever erase from my heart; and as long as I am, so long shall I be grateful to him through Christ’s grace, both in this present age and in the age to come.

I also rejoice somewhat in the steadfastness of my mind in the Lord, because, although I knew of no holy doctor who would be my patron in this opinion—for I knew no more than you that blessed Hilary had written anything on this subject—I nevertheless exercised a good zeal according to what I had conceived from the Gospel, knowing that it is written: “All things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. VIII). Thus it happened to me according to what the wise Jesus son of Sirach said: “The mercy of God is beautiful in the time of tribulation, like a rain-cloud in time of drought” (Ecclus. XI).

For when tribulation threatened my homeland—who indeed did not hear of that tribulation?—when, I say, the severe tribulation of my homeland was now close at hand, while I was delaying to depart and return to you, who strongly invited me, the angel of the Lord undoubtedly took hold of my hand and led me out through the gate of obedience. For Frederick, of holy memory, having been elected bishop—whose cause God, who is conscious of and witness to it, defended and made illustrious by so many and such frequent miracles—brought me here with him to the metropolitan see of Cologne, together with the witnesses of his election. From that time I have obediently allowed myself to be detained here; and because I did not experience the tribulation that followed, but rather found the sweet refreshment of consolation, I have said, and say again, as one who has experienced it: “The mercy of God is beautiful in the time of tribulation, like a rain-cloud in time of drought.”

Let adversaries, then, even now cease saying of this poor man who has spoken: “Who is he, and what need is there for him to speak, when the holy doctors of old have spoken sufficiently?” But if they do not yet cease, I shall dare still to speak, and to say that saying of Isaiah: “Because, after all—or beneath all—the ends of the earth,” that is, the humble who remembered the name of the Lord and spoke in the Lord’s name, perhaps this poor man also is included: “Lord, in distress they sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your instruction was with them. As a woman with child, when she draws near to childbirth, cries out in pain in her pangs, so have we become before your face, O Lord. We conceived, and as it were travailed and gave birth” (Isa. 26).

Who, I ask, is wise enough to say to a woman who has conceived and is near childbirth: “Why do you cry out? Why do you not keep silent? Why do you not impose silence upon your mouth?” Perhaps someone will say to me: “Are you such a one? When or how did you conceive? How do you know that you conceived before the face of the Lord, so that you spoke as one in travail in what you wrote?” But to this I say: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine; woe is me!” (Isa. 24). Nevertheless, let them cease, because Isaiah likewise says: “Woe to him who says to a father, ‘What are you begetting?’ and to a woman, ‘What are you bringing forth?’” (Isa. 45). For he disparages the father who envies the pregnant woman; he disparages the begetter who envies the woman in labour. The Father of mercies and God of all consolation begets mercy and consoles the widowed soul by his word, and you say, “What are you begetting?” The word conceived in the mind seeks a voice, and you say, “Woman, what are you bringing forth?”

Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, was vindicated by fitting proofs, saying: “I have conceived by the man to whom these things belong. Recognize whose ring, bracelet, and staff these are” (Gen. 38). You too, if you wish, recognize whether or not there is in my writings the ring of faith, the staff of hope, and the bracelet of charity; and hear my soul saying, “I have conceived by the man to whom these things belong.” For I also recall something perceptibly done within me, so that I may say without hesitation that this gift—or endowment—is “from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0497]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0497C]

By now, my friend, I suppose you are weary with boredom, and my narrative is like a burden to you on the road while your mind hastens toward something else, while you eagerly await what you asked for. Yet let love retain its judgment in these matters also: namely, that I ought not to have maintained perpetual silence about such things. For how, by keeping silent about matters of this kind, could I observe the counsel of the Wise Man: “Do not show partiality against your own face, nor speak falsehood against your own soul” (Ecclus. 4)? Therefore, if you do not disdain these things or regard them as a burden, you will receive without ingratitude what follows and what you requested.

The first of the matters from the Rule of Saint Benedict about which I undertook to answer you is the order of the night vigils of the Lord’s Day. “At every season,” says the same holy Father (ch. 11), “whether summer or winter, it is to be observed alike on the Lord’s Day.” Here it must be said—as no Christian is ignorant, or ought to be ignorant—that the Lord rose at midnight on Sunday, having lain enclosed in the tomb for thirty-three hours. They are reckoned thus: at the ninth hour he gave up his spirit and was buried, while three hours of that same day remained. The following night and the following day—night, I say, and day—make twenty-four hours; adding the three already mentioned makes twenty-seven; add midnight, that is, six hours, and the total is thirty-three hours.

Thus he rested in the tomb for three days, though not whole days; and he rose at midnight. Accordingly, we rise at midnight to give praise to the holy Trinity, to whom Christ’s true humanity made satisfaction for humankind by such an ending. Thus the whole first day of the week, with the night or evening “which dawns toward the first day of the week,” deserved to be called the Lord’s Day.

Consider this still more fully. He lived in seclusion for thirty years, a number in which three is multiplied by ten; he suffered in the third year of his preaching; he lay lifeless for thirty-three hours, as has been said; and he rose on the third day. Add also this further beautiful point: he was brought to completion by three sufferings—scourged with whips, fastened to the cross, pierced by a spear; himself the third among two thieves, exchanged for the thief Barabbas. Rightly, therefore, the appeased Trinity immediately began to show its face to the human race, after bringing out of the region of darkness all who had departed this life with faith in him who was to come; and it willed that we who remained should be preached to, so that we might be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER II

After the verse has first been said, “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me,” “the third thing to be said,” blessed Benedict states (ch. 9), is: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.” Why this, unless because the Lord himself, the Son of Man—in whose person, as risen, we undoubtedly say this—then began, with lips and mouth opened, to declare the praise of the holy Trinity? This is clear from the psalm, where he says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). Having answered, “I shall arise early,” he immediately added: “I shall give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations” (Ps. 56).

For he had been mute, had stood before the governor with his mouth closed and his lips unopened, so that the governor marvelled greatly, according to the saying: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a mute man not opening his mouth” (Ps. 37); and likewise: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). “There is a time to be silent and a time to speak” (Eccles. 3). The time of silence came to an end, and the time of speaking began, with the response already mentioned which he made to the Father: “I shall arise early.”

Therefore, as we rise at midnight and wish to remain wakeful in contemplation of that hour, the Holy Spirit—of whom the same Father was full—says that the third psalm and the *Gloria* are to follow. For that psalm is the voice of Christ himself rising again; if you rightly consider it, you will certainly perceive that it is highly pertinent. First, it sets down the evil case of his adversaries, then his own good and glorious case, and finally judgment and mercy: judgment upon his adversaries, mercy upon the believing people.

The evil case of his adversaries is this: “Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me. Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God’” (Ps. 3). His own good and glorious case is this: “But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (ibid.). Again: “I lay down and slept, and rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (ibid.). Then the judgment upon his adversaries is this, with a terrible trumpet as though a trumpet of war: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me. Arise, O Lord; save me, my God, because you have struck all who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners” (ibid.).

Who has not heard of the striking down of the Jews who opposed him—the striking of their bodies, to say nothing now of the striking of their souls—and of the breaking of the teeth of which it is elsewhere said: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56)? Who has not heard of it? Who is ignorant of the overthrow or destruction of that nation and its rulers? But upon believers the mercy is this: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3).

## CHAPTER III

“After this,” he says, comes Psalm 94, which is indeed very fitting to the subject and the time, especially from the verse, “Today, if you hear his voice,” to the end, “they shall enter into my rest.” For that day which the Holy Spirit there defines, as the Apostle also recalls when he says: “Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again defines a certain day, ‘Today,’ saying in David, after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’” (Heb. 4)—that day, I say, began or dawned from the hour at which Christ rose. For that day is the resurrection.

Knowing this, the holy evangelist said: “And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, the sun having already risen” (Mark 16). For if you wish to understand “very early” and “the sun having already risen” in the ordinary sense and without mystery, how do they agree with one another rather than conflict: “very early,” and “the sun having already risen”? This day, therefore, is the resurrection; it is the eighth day, which has no end—the eighth day long desired and prefigured by the prophets and holy Fathers, as is testified by certain psalms inscribed “for the eighth,” and by David’s singers who sang “for the eighth,” as is written in Chronicles: “Some made secret music on harps; others played on lyres for the eighth; others sounded trumpets before the ark of the Lord” (1 Chron. 15). In that return of the ark, this very resurrection of the Lord was prefigured.

It is called the eighth day, of course, after those seven days which Holy Scripture distinguishes at the beginning of itself, saying: “And evening and morning came: one day”; “and evening and morning came: the second day”; “and evening and morning came: the third day”; “and evening and morning came: the fourth day”; “and evening and morning came: the fifth day”; “and evening and morning came: the sixth day” (Gen. 1). But concerning the seventh day it did not say, “And evening and morning came: the seventh day,” because that day on which God rests is not made, but is his very Word and Wisdom.

The other six days were made; and, as blessed Augustine holds in Book XI of *The City of God*, they are six kinds of works through which we know God in the mind, just as by the days of this sun we are illuminated to see something bodily. Therefore at the beginning it was not said, nor ought it to have been said, “And evening and morning came: the first day”; but it was said, “one day,” because neither an angelic nor any other creature is the first day. Rather, the day in which God rests is seventh in the order or numbering of Scripture, but first by nature.

Thus the Lord’s resurrection is itself the eighth day; and this eighth is the same as the first, because he through whom God made all things, in whom he rests, and he who rose from the dead, are one God—true and eternal—one and the same God and man, Jesus Christ. Every human being will rise not in another kind or nature than that in which he is a creature, although in another glory.

## CHAPTER IV

Although we are hastening to other matters and must avoid wearying the reader with excessive speech, nevertheless, in order to stir devotion during the vigils of the night of the Lord’s Nativity, I wish to say something briefly about the mystery of that same night or day, according to what we can understand from the evangelist’s words: “On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the week” (Matt. 28).

The solemnity of this evening or night and the following day ought to be most pleasing to us, as a beholding—or occasion for beholding—the face of the day already mentioned, of Jesus Christ as God [variant: “of God”] and man. For because the holy Church joins the Sabbath with the following morning, that is, with the first day of the week, in a single feast of Jesus Christ, we fittingly recall through meditation that, in accordance with this likeness, God’s Sabbath—that is, the Word or Wisdom of God—comes together in one person with the true humanity of that same Word.

And this humanity of his—humanity glorified with the glory of resurrection—is, for God the Father, the first day of the week: that is, the chief cause or material of rest and delight; for, as it is written, “The Lord will indeed rejoice in his works” (Ps. 103). For among the other works which he deigned to perform, God never made anything like this. They were indeed very good, but nothing such as humanity joined to the Word in unity of person.

Take the likeness from the harp, because the Father said of this humanity: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). In ancient times harps were made with eight strings. The eighth string, however, is the same as the first, except that it sounds at a higher pitch—a sound which the discipline of music calls *diapason* [the octave]. Thus, just as in this harmony called *diapason* no string or note except the eighth is the same as the first, so in the whole creation, completed in six days, there is nothing joined, or that ought to be joined, to that day which, as has already been said, is first by nature but seventh in number—to that Word or Wisdom of God—as is this one man, God and Saviour of human beings, God and ruler of angels.

All the strings indeed sound well, for all the works of the six days are very good; but this string is both one with the first and another: one according to person, another according to substance. It is also most beautiful to consider that the Sabbath, or rest, of the Lord has no evening in Genesis but does have one in the Gospel, where the divine evangelist says: “On the evening of the Sabbath” (Matt. 28). So that you may not suppose this evening to precede it, as each evening precedes its respective day in Genesis, he specifies it by saying, “which dawns toward the first day of the week” (ibid.).

Finally, the Word that was in the beginning with God never had any evening in itself; indeed, it itself is and was before all things. Yet according to the humanity it assumed, it has both evening and morning: one day, as has been said. The other days had their evening in this: “Whatever was made, in him was life” (John 1); and in him all things lay hidden, among them that humanity of his of which we are speaking, predestined to be glorified by the glory, or morning, of resurrection.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, invited by the words of the Psalm already mentioned, Psalm 84, as we assemble and stand for the glory of the present day—the day which dawned from the Lord’s resurrection and will have no end—we ought to declare to ourselves the testimony of faith: that we are orthodox; that our choir or assembly is not a conventicle of an Arian or any other heretical party; but rather that it is an assembly and solemnity of catholic peace, in the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity.

How? “Then,” says blessed Benedict, “let the Ambrosian follow.” By “Ambrosian” he means the hymn, the practice of singing which Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, introduced into the western provinces during the Arian persecution. For when the empress Justina, favouring Arian impiety, insisted with stubborn fury that the catholic bishop be carried off into exile, the catholic people, gathered in the church, kept watch almost through entire nights to guard their shepherd. At that time antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan; and the devotion of that celebration remains to the present day not only in that Church but also throughout nearly all the western provinces.

At Constantinople, during the same period, hymns sounding forth the faith of the holy Trinity were likewise established by Bishop John against the madness of the Arians. For the Arians held assemblies outside the city; but on Saturday and Sunday they gathered inside the gates and in the porticoes, chanting hymns and antiphons composed according to Arian doctrine. They did this through much of the night and, at daybreak, went out through the city’s midst with these same antiphons, passed through the gate, and hurried to their church. Since they repeatedly persisted in doing this, as though to reproach the orthodox—for they also often sang, “Where are those who say [that] one [is] by triple power?”—John, fearing that the simple might be drawn in by such songs, organized his people also to occupy themselves with nocturnal hymns, so that the Arians’ activity might be obscured and the profession of the faithful strengthened.

When the clearer hymns of the *Homoousians* appeared by night—he had also made silver crosses, carried with silver candles, while the empress Eudoxia supplied the expense for these—the Arians, provoked by jealousy, rose up even to murder, and some people from each party were killed. Moved by this, the emperor prohibited the Arians from publicly chanting hymns.

But much earlier at Antioch in Syria, Ignatius, third bishop after the apostle Peter, who is said also to have lived with the apostles themselves, is reported to have seen a vision of angels, namely how they sang hymns to the holy Trinity by antiphons; and he is shown to have handed down the pattern of that vision to the Church of Antioch. Therefore, at the beginning of the night vigils after Psalm 84, blessed Benedict says, let the Ambrosian follow—that is, the hymn, a testimony of catholic faith—because the use of such singing was begun by the orthodox against the impiety of heretics, especially Arians sinning against the blessed Trinity.

## CHAPTER VI

“Then,” he says, “after six psalms and a verse have been sung, with all seated in proper order in the stalls, let four readings be read from the book with their responsories,” and so forth. Psalms, readings, responsories, and canticles from the prophets are Scriptures of which he said: “These are they which bear witness concerning me” (John 5), and: “All things written concerning me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

From what else is the whole order of these vigils constructed than the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and lastly Gospel readings? On summer Sunday nights, you may perhaps think or say that the readings and responsories are not from the Law or Prophets because they are taken from the Books of Kings. But that Scripture too is rightly called prophetic, because, as blessed Jerome says, the first and second Books of Kings are called Samuel; and in the deeds narrated in the books of Kings no less than in the sayings of the prophets, many prophetic mysteries of Christ are contained.

Who does not recognize that Solomon’s three books—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—are directed toward the mystery of Christ’s grace or glory? The Scripture of Maccabees is wholly military in subject, but is companionably and amicably joined to prophetic truth, because the laborious Maccabean warriors greatly assisted in preserving the nation from which, in accordance with the promises to the fathers, Christ was to be born, so that the prophecies might be fulfilled. I have explained this more fully in the work I wrote for you, *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

Therefore, although the books of Maccabees, Judith, Tobit, and those called the Hagiographa are each read in these Sunday-night vigils at their appointed times, we ought nonetheless rightly to attend, throughout the whole order of these vigils, to what Christ himself truly said: “All things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.” Thus, through the use of psalms, readings, and responsories, by which the Lord’s school is not only instructed but also naturally and beneficially delighted in such a matter through the sweet power and powerful sweetness of music, we may know that it was so written and therefore rejoice that this proclamation, by which Christ is preached as risen from the dead, is not a new or human invention.

## CHAPTER VII

Why, or with what intention, does he so diligently insist, saying that “this order of vigils is to be observed alike on the Lord’s Day at every season, whether summer or winter,” unless perhaps—far be it!—if they rise later, something must be shortened from the readings or responsories? Why does he never wish us to fall below the number twelve in the psalms, readings, and responsories of the Sunday-night vigils? Clearly, so that, whether we are more or fewer in any place, when we rise at midnight to give praise, we may represent in ourselves the number of the apostles, whose joy was renewed from that midnight and whose sorrow began shortly to be changed into joy.

For the completion of the vigils, fashioned by the Holy Spirit’s true direction according to this most beautiful pattern, signifies this to one who understands: while the choir resounds with that joyful hymn and sings it alternately, “We praise you, O God,” before that hymn is finished, the priest enters clothed in sacred vestments, preceded by the light of candles and the fragrance of holy incense. Whether he is the abbot himself or any other priest, he bears the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, who on the very day on which he rose stood in the midst of the apostles already mentioned and said to them: “Peace be with you” (John 20).

He enters while the choir, as has been said, resounds with the glorious hymn, although a hymn is properly understood to be praise composed in meter. Yet because *hymnus* is Greek and means “praise” in Latin, and because this praise, “We praise you, O God,” which we then joyfully sing in alternation, is not insignificant among all God’s praises, the venerable Father rightly called it a hymn.

He enters, I say, while the choirs alternate this praise, because when the Lord Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples, as already noted, they, astonished at him through the overwhelming flood of joy, were speaking of him, as the evangelist Luke recounts more clearly: “Rising in that same hour, the two disciples returned from the village to which they had gone, named Emmaus, to Jerusalem; and they found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying, ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’ And they themselves recounted the things that had happened on the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread. But while they were speaking these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them, ‘Peace be with you’” (Luke 24).

Therefore, as we resound with praise in alternation, the priest enters in the manner already described, greets the assembly, saying, “The Lord be with you,” and reads the Gospel lesson while all stand in fear and trembling. For the Lord, as has been said, standing in the midst of the disciples, said to them, “Peace be with you,” and then entrusted to them the good news concerning us Gentiles, saying among other things, while they still did not believe and marvelled for joy: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations” (Luke 24).

The other evangelist, John, puts it thus: “Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20). They all rejoiced, and without doubt uttered voices of joy and cried out, especially that Thomas who touched him and cried: “My Lord and my God!” (ibid.). Therefore, is it not most beautifully and most holily done that, after the Gospel lesson has been read, all respond, “Amen,” and together, following the abbot’s or priest’s lead, take up this hymn by command of so great a Father: “Praise befits you; hymn befits you”? “And thus,” he says, “let the night vigils end”: namely, in contemplation and signification of the great joy, the joy of which he said: “I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

## CHAPTER VIII

Nor should we allow this also to seem without reason: that these vigils are divided in this manner into three sections. “After six psalms and a verse have been sung,” he says, “let four readings with their responsories be read; after these readings let another six psalms follow in order. And again let another four readings with their responsories be read. Then three canticles with an antiphon; then, after the verse has been said and the blessing given, let another four readings be read from the New Testament, in the order stated above.”

It should not, I say, seem without purpose that the number twelve of the readings is thus divided into three sections. It is so because there are three watches of the night, and in the fourth day breathes forth and the shadows decline; for in the fourth watch he once came to them, namely his disciples, as the evangelists recount thus: “After dismissing them, he went up the mountain alone to pray. When evening came, the boat was in the midst of the sea, while he was alone on land. And seeing them labouring at the oars—for the wind was contrary to them—he came to them in the fourth watch of the night, walking upon the sea. And when he had said, ‘Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid,’ Peter answered and said: ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters’” (Matt. 14), and so forth.

For that storm, calmed in this way, prefigured the Lord’s passion, by which the apostles were to be troubled, Peter was to deny him, and all were to flee, leaving the Lord alone. But he, after completing prayer—that is, after undergoing the passion and the death of three days, which was surely a prayer for the salvation of the whole world—began to return to them in order to change the storm of their sorrow into the calm of joy.

This began, certainly, in the fourth watch of the night, that is, when day was already breathing forth, when the angel sat at the Lord’s tomb and spoke to the women. In regard to that glorious event, we sing the morning praises, of which more will be said later. Therefore, so that we may know how to render all the night watches due to our Creator and Saviour, so far as human weakness allows, we rightly and beautifully divide the often-mentioned threefold number according to the four watches of the night, and then keep watch in the morning praises.

## CHAPTER IX

Since these things are so, it is surely not without reason that the blessed Father wished this third nocturn to differ from the others (ch. 11): “Let not psalms but three canticles from the prophets be sung, and let another four readings from the New Testament be read.” Whatever the sources of the preceding two sets of four readings may be, he wills these readings of the third nocturn to be from the New Testament, so that, as an upper millstone is added to a lower one and by its swift revolution makes God’s grain that has been ground produce ever more firmly in our minds the meaning of the Lord’s mystery.

Why is this? Because the whole night is holy and festive; yet the cause of its holy festivity, or festive holiness, shone forth at the beginning of the third watch—which is midnight—because then the Saviour rose. The order of the third nocturn, as has been said, looks toward that third watch. Thus, after the beautiful prophetic canticles come four readings from the New Testament, readings from the holy Gospel, so that we may contemplate the joy of both the sower and the reaper, as the Lord himself said in one place: “He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. For in this the saying is true: one is the sower and another the reaper. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour. Others laboured, and you entered into their labours” (John 4).

Those who laboured, those who sowed this great mystery of the Lord’s passion and resurrection, were the prophets. For example, Isaiah, who said in wonder: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63), and so forth; Hosea, who said: “Come, and let us return to the Lord; for he has begun and will heal us; he will strike and cure us; he will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his presence” (Hos. 6); and Zephaniah, who said: “Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, until the day of my resurrection in the future” (Zeph. 3), and so forth.

These and the other prophets undoubtedly laboured and sowed, because they foretold with labour and fear that the Word of God would become flesh, as one of them says: “Shall priest and prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord? Prophecy and destruction have become terror and a snare to us” (Lam. 2, 3). But now, since Christ has risen, both he who sowed and he who reaps rejoice together, namely both prophets and apostles. To contemplate this in the conjunction of canticles from the prophets and readings from the holy Gospel is doubtless sweet and is the fruit of our solemnity.

## CHAPTER X

In the fourth watch of the night, when, as was noted above, he came to them walking upon the sea, the angel sat at the tomb, proclaiming that he had risen from the dead; this undoubtedly signified that he had overcome the storms of hell and the abyss of death. This is the morning watch, this the morning guard, of which we also read in Exodus: “And now the morning watch had come; and behold, the Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, destroyed their army, and overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were carried into the deep” (Exod. 14). And in the psalm we sing: “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord” (Ps. 129).

This watch is very bright and very suitable for meditation and holy contemplation, aided by the body’s sobriety in supporting the mind’s endeavour. Hence the Psalmist also says: “If I remembered you upon my bed, in the morning watches I shall meditate upon you, because you have been my helper” (Ps. 66).

## CHAPTER XI

Therefore, at Matins on the Lord’s Day, blessed Benedict says (ch. 12), “First let Psalm 66 be said straight through without an antiphon. After it, let Psalm 50 be said with Alleluia. After it, let Psalms 117 and 62 be said. Then the blessings and praises.”

Psalm 66 is this: “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us” (Ps. 66). Now concerning the angel who sat at the Lord’s tomb in that watch, the fourth or morning watch, the holy Gospel says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his garment like snow” (Matt. 28). Thus does not this psalm, when we say it first, aptly send us to contemplate that angelic countenance by these words: “May he make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us” (Ps. 66)?

Finally, the lightning-like appearance of the angel signified the fulfilment of what the prophetic spirit had requested and foreknown as future, saying: “May he make his face shine upon us,” and adding, “that we may know your way upon earth, your salvation among all nations” (ibid.). His garment, which was like snow—or the white robe in which the young man seated on the right was clothed, as another evangelist says (Mark 16)—undoubtedly signified the joy of the nations and the judgment by which the sheep will be placed on the right at the day of the universal resurrection. By this appearance he undoubtedly corresponded to the verse of the psalm already quoted: “Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth.”

What more need be said? God, our God—the Father and the Son—has indeed blessed us; God the Holy Spirit has blessed us, because we have been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, where Christ suffered and died and rose from the dead, and where we receive varieties of graces. Hence the Apostle says: “He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places” (Eph. 1). Yet it is profitable for us that he should bless still further: that the number of believers may increase, that by his daily blessing he may increase faith, increase hope, increase charity in us, and that all the ends of the earth may fear him more and more—with a wholesome and beneficial fear, not like the guards who were terrified by fear of that angel, but like the women who, though afraid and lowering their faces to the ground, deserved to be strengthened by him when he said: “Do not be afraid, you” (Luke 24).

## CHAPTER XII
Psalm Fifty: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy,” and Psalm One Hundred and Seventeenth: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever,” look toward those subjects which we ought especially to meditate upon at that time, according to what we immediately sing in Psalm Sixty-Six: “If I have remembered thee upon my bed, in the mornings I will meditate on thee, because thou hast been my helper.” [Col. 0507D] What are those subjects? Assuredly, the first resurrection and the second resurrection. The first resurrection is the resurrection of souls; the second resurrection is the resurrection of bodies. Christ, by dying once, acquired both for us; hence, giving thanks, we say that by dying he destroyed our death and by rising again restored our life.

The Psalm Fifty which we immediately sing looks toward, and causes us to look toward, that first resurrection.
