For what else is the first resurrection—the resurrection of the inner person—but justification from sins, by which we have indeed risen, all of us who believe in Christ? “For all we who have been baptized,” says the Apostle, “into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

What else, I ask, did that true penitent and holy prophet both ask for and prophesy when, in this Psalm, after first saying among other things, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me,” he then said: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow”; and shortly thereafter: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inward parts”? This, indeed—all of it—is the first resurrection: the blood and water which flowed from his side, and the Holy Spirit whom he gave us for the remission of sins, saying to his Apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX). [Col. 0508B] He both asked for this and prophesied that it would come to pass; but we, singing the same Psalm, proclaim it accomplished.

Further, the Psalm One Hundred and Seventeenth, which we recite after Psalm Fifty—“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good”—is a song of the resurrection of the flesh, in which alone Christ rose; for he died only by the death of the flesh. It will be for us the second resurrection on the last day. For what else is it to say in this Psalm, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,” except: Christ, whom they cast outside the city and crucified, has risen from the dead, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him? [Col. 0508C]

Likewise, what is the day which he names and indicates thus: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it,” except the resurrection of the dead in Christ and through Christ, most clearly brought forth? Finally, the Lord made such a day—made it, I say, not merely as one work among others, but as the greatest and foremost of all his works. For what is comparable to the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus? He is truly the day, because he is resurrection and life; and he was indeed made according to his humanity. Therefore, this is the day which the Lord has made.

## CHAPTER XIII

Why, then, does he command that both the canticles already mentioned, these morning Psalms, and the other hours on the Lord’s Day be said with alleluia? (Chapter 8.) [Col. 0508D] Clearly because *alleluia*, which means “Praise the Lord,” is the distinctive song of the resurrection: the proper praise of a work completed, to be sung confidently at the end.

Accordingly, in the Apocalypse, after judgment has been executed upon the great harlot Babylon—that is, upon this unhappy age—then at last, he says: “I heard as it were the voice of many trumpets in heaven, saying: Alleluia. And again they said: Alleluia. And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshipped him who sits upon the throne, saying: Amen, alleluia. And I heard as it were the sound of a trumpet, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of great thunders, saying: Alleluia” (Apoc. XIX).

What, therefore, is to be sung happily then, and fully, by all the children of God—the children of the resurrection—we rightly anticipate and taste beforehand on the day on which the giver himself and author of that resurrection rose. How, or under what arrangement?

“From holy Easter,” he says, “until Pentecost, alleluia is to be said without interruption, both in the Psalms and in the responsories. But from Pentecost until the beginning of Lent, it is to be said at Night Office every night only with the last six Psalms. On every Sunday outside Lent, however, the morning canticles, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None are to be said with alleluia. Vespers, however, are now with an antiphon. Responsories are never to be said with alleluia, except from Easter until Pentecost” (Chapter 2).

Although this text is clear and free from difficulty in other respects, it has produced disagreement and difficulty between us and those religious and very diligent investigators of the Rule of blessed Benedict, because of whom, as I said in the Prologue, we have disputes among ourselves concerning certain chapters of the same Rule. For because he said, “until the beginning of Lent,” or, “on every Sunday outside Lent, alleluia is to be said at the Hours,” they do not observe what the Roman Church has decreed and what the universal Church, apart from them, observes. [Col. 0509B] Namely, that alleluia is omitted from Septuagesima; but they continue to say alleluia until Monday—or until that Sunday—which is called Quadragesima, on the same principle by which the preceding Sundays are called Quinquagesima, Sexagesima, and Septuagesima. They wish the beginning of Lent to mean nothing other than the said Sunday, or the Monday following it.

But it seems to me altogether sounder and more reasonable to understand the beginning of Lent as Septuagesima, than to depart from the holy and truly mystical custom of the universal Church because of such a phrase. For the seven Sundays are not without, or with only slight, mystery. On the first, the Church cries: “The groans of death surrounded me” (Ps. XVII); on the seventh she sings: “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (Isa. LXVI). Then, after the spectacle of the holy Passion has intervened, the eighth Sunday arrives, on which the life and resurrection of all says to his Father: “I have risen, and am still with thee.” Until that eighth day, no weekday or Sunday admits alleluia; rather, in place of this song the tract has been appointed—a song, indeed, mournful and laborious.

In the book which I wrote *On the Sacraments, or Divine Offices*, I set forth the reasons for this observance. I have long since learned that many read them gladly; and their height or depth is so great and of such a kind that they cannot briefly be repeated here, especially because brevity must be pursued and the reader’s weariness avoided.

## CHAPTER XIV

Perhaps someone will say that, at the time when blessed Benedict wrote this Rule, the times, stations, and sacred offices of the entire year had not yet been arranged in this manner in the Roman Church. We do not deny it. For blessed Pope Gregory, undoubtedly younger in time than blessed Benedict himself, was chiefly responsible for arranging these times and ordering the stations of the Roman Church. He was most illustrious and most beloved of God among holy and distinguished Fathers—one of whom you may rightly say that they ordered the times of Christ with a good fragrance until life’s consummation. [Col. 0510A]

For they perceived the most sweet fragrance, the fragrance of the true sacrifice—that is, of Christ’s most holy Passion—and discerned in mind how it belonged to all the ages of the world. Therefore they brought those same seven ages, as they were able, to the reverent celebration of the solemn rites of so great a funeral; by the seven Sundays already mentioned they intended those ages to be understood. With these Sundays going before, and then the funeral, as it were, of the Lord proceeding—which we celebrate for nearly fifteen days—then at last follows the eighth Sunday, on which, in faith and in the confession of the Lord’s resurrection, we rightly celebrate with alleluia, with such rejoicing as we can, the future universal resurrection. *Alleluia* very briefly signifies every song of the life and immortality for which we wait.

They removed alleluia from the other Sundays because they look not toward joy but toward mourning, although, according to another consideration, every first day of the week is illumined by the joy of the Lord’s resurrection.

For the first Sunday looks toward that first sorrow of the age which the human race received from its first parents, and which Cain began to increase when he killed his brother Abel, hastening to offer the first fruits of death and murder. The second looks toward that increase of miseries by which the flooding deluge exacted vengeance from the corrupted earth upon all flesh. The third looks toward the time when Abraham’s race—to which the promise of the blessed seed, that is Christ, had been made—greatly provoked by many sins him who had promised; the first of these sins was the sale of Joseph, because of which that people served as captives in Egypt. [Col. 0510C]

The fourth looks toward the fact that, in the fourth age, the same people, by withdrawing from the house of David—to whom, after Abraham, the promise had been made—almost, so far as it lay in their power, rendered that same promise void: by worshipping the golden calves made by Jeroboam; by serving Baal, whom Jezebel introduced; and by killing the prophets of the Lord. The fifth looks toward the fact that at last the two remaining tribes were led captive to Babylon because of the same flood of idolatry and the much innocent blood which they shed.

The sixth and seventh Sundays look toward the sixth and seventh ages of the world. In one of them, namely the sixth age, we are still in the body, absent from the Lord (II Cor. V), and live in toil and affliction (II Cor. XI). In the other, namely the seventh, the souls of the elect indeed rest, but do not yet possess that perfection of joy which they shall receive in the resurrection.

What then? Is the Holy Spirit—by whom blessed Benedict, being full of him, and the apostolic Fathers, undoubtedly inspired, arranged the times, as has been said, and better than we can express or understand—changeable or of a different intention, so that, breathing through the pipes of his music, he made this discord in one matter only: the times at which alleluia ought to be said? Truly it is far sounder, and more conducive to the preservation of peace and charity, to understand the beginning of Lent as Septuagesima, as stated above, than to represent blessed Benedict as dissenting from the Roman Church by a divergent usage. [Col. 0511A] Let us not be such heedless flatterers of any saint that, as though by his authority, we dissent from others—especially since the often-mentioned Father himself granted even to superiors the liberty of ordering things differently from his own ordering. For example, he says: “If perhaps this distribution of the Psalms displeases anyone, let him arrange it otherwise, if he judges it better.”

## CHAPTER XV

The following point also pertains not irrelevantly to the question: although blessed Benedict gave commands and carefully arranged all the rest of the Work of God—namely Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, equally with the Night Vigils and Matins—he was silent concerning the Mass and the entire office of the altar, and established nothing to be done in this respect by the authority of his Rule. [Col. 0511B; 0512A]

As for the seven canonical Hours, which the Prophet also foresaw when he said, “Seven times in the day have I given praise to thee” (Ps. CXVIII), and the reasons they possess—why we ought to offer solemn praises to our Creator at the first hour rather than the second; at the third rather than the fourth and fifth; and at the sixth and ninth rather than the seventh and eighth—I have discussed this, to the extent of my ability, in another work, namely the above-mentioned book which I wrote *On the Divine Offices*. I therefore pass it over now in pursuit of brevity, particularly because I have so far found almost nothing different among those whose practice, differing from ours in many respects, compelled me to say or write these things.

# BOOK THREE: ON THE OFFICE OF THE ALTAR

[Col. 0511]

## CHAPTER I

“If thou knowest not thyself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow the tracks of the flocks, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents” (Cant. I).

I recall this passage because I have undertaken to speak about the ministry of the altar and why blessed Benedict laid down no rule concerning it in his Rule. The reason is that today some souls, through ignorance of themselves, neglect that inward beauty by reason of which they deserved to be admitted to the office of the sacred altar. [Col. 0511C] Since they are monks, and blessed Benedict ordained manual labour for monks, they almost forget that they are priests. This is especially so because the same Father, as has been said, did not prescribe in his Rule how, or with what zeal, monks ought to frequent the office of the sacred altar.

Their intention—by which, intent upon manual labour, they are said to have little or almost no concern for the daily celebration of Masses—ought to be left to silence on our part, unless they disturbed many of the simpler brethren in our monasteries, as we have learned from many experiences. You yourself know these experiences better, having received them as guests more than once and having received no good return for such hospitality. Yet, when they were exposed—for they do this secretly—and asked forgiveness, you sometimes pardoned them for thus violating the laws of holy hospitality. [Col. 0511D]

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, whoever you are, O soul, troubled by those who say, “You cannot be saved here, because you do not live by the labour of your hands according to the Rule or commands of blessed Benedict,” consider that this concerning the canticles has been said by me for your sake: “If thou knowest not thyself, O fairest among women,” and so forth, as above.

For you are beautiful although black, so that you may rightly say, or be able to say: “I am black but beautiful” (ibid.). And indeed the Church as a whole speaks this truly amid her persecutions and afflictions. But it especially befits you to say this, since beneath the blackness of the monastic habit or profession you possess the beauty and loveliness of the holy priesthood. Many are ignorant of you and wish to remain so; but you yourself ought not to be ignorant of yourself.

How, or in what respect, are many ignorant of you, or wish to be ignorant? Assuredly in that they consider only that you are dark, and refuse to consider that “the sun has darkened me” (ibid.). We must now approach more directly the point toward which we are aiming. [Col. 0512B–C]

## CHAPTER III

There are two orders among those who seek the Lord in the one life, namely the contemplative life. One is the order of the righteous; the other, the order of penitents. By “righteous” I mean not those who are righteous in their own judgment, but those who are righteous in the judgment of the Church, and thus deserve to exercise sacred orders; for they have not been accused of any crime, although they are not, and cannot be, without sin.

Those especially are called, or are, penitents who, repenting of past crimes, undertake a public mourning in their monastic profession. Of these two orders the following words in the Song of Songs are also beautifully understood: “Thy hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. Thy teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Cant. IV).

For the present, the flock of shorn animals—that is, sheep—represents the order of the righteous: those who, being without accusation of crime, pass beneath the bishop’s pastoral staff and receive the sacred orders of the altar. The flock of goats, however, represents the order of sinners: those who were formerly entangled in crimes and therefore, submitting themselves beneath the abbot’s pastoral staff, have undertaken penitential mourning. [Col. 0512D]

But, I say, what if one and the same person is both righteous and penitent: possessing a reputation or conscience free from crime and nevertheless entering upon a penitential profession, that is, the monastic profession? Is not such a soul both black and beautiful? “Do not look upon me,” she says, “because I am dark, because the sun has darkened me” (Cant. I). That is to say: Do not prejudge me as if I were dead and ought not to speak, as though it were unlawful for me to open my mouth in the midst of the Church because of the penitential habit. For the very fact that I go about in a mournful habit is produced not by the guilt of adultery but by the righteous sorrow and devout love caused by my bridegroom’s being taken away from me. [Col. 0513A]

## CHAPTER IV

Again, when I wished to proceed by a clearer path, I have returned to mystical utterances; and I fear that the saying of the Wise Man may apply to me: “A parable from the mouth of a fool shall be rejected, for he does not speak it at its proper time.” [Col. 0513B]

What is at issue? This discussion enters between parties holding differing views and ventures to decide which party has the firmer foundation of reason: the one which prefers manual labour according to the ordering of blessed Benedict’s Rule and maintains that living by the labour of one’s hands is apostolic perfection; or the other which asserts that serving the altar and living from the altar is better.

Therefore, so that what may be inferred from this may be more certain, we must first carefully consider whether the Rule’s ordering of manual labour was commanded for its own sake, as necessary to salvation, or allowed for some other purpose, as bringing assistance to necessity. For not everything that appears to be commanded has been commanded or given for its own sake as necessary to salvation, but for another purpose.

For example, the carnal sacrifices of the ancient Law were not commanded for their own sake, but allowed for another reason: because that people, newly departed from Egypt, could not be weaned from sacrifices of this kind, which the other nations offered to idols. Therefore God allowed these things and permitted them to be offered to himself by the people whom he was taking as his own peculiar people, in fulfilment of the promises to the fathers. Thus they were not so much commanded as permitted.

Hence God himself speaks in Jeremiah: “Add your burnt offerings to your victims, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak to your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and victims” (Jer. VII). And in Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fatlings, and I have not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. Who has required these things from your hands?” (Isa. I). And in David: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XL).

Since, therefore, not everything that seems to be commanded is a command of righteousness without which a human being cannot live, we must inquire concerning this matter also—namely manual labour—whether it is commanded for its own sake or allowed for some other purpose. [Col. 0513C–D]

## CHAPTER V

Concerning that manual labour by which sustenance is chiefly acquired—ploughing, sowing, reaping, and cutting down woods—it is clear that this is not blessed Benedict’s command, but merely a permission, or a counsel of forbearance. For in one place he says as follows (Chapter 41):

“From Pentecost and throughout the summer, if the monks do not have agricultural labours, or if excessive heat does not trouble them, they are to fast on Wednesday and Friday until None; on the remaining days they are to take their meal at Sext. But if they have agricultural work, or if the heat of summer is excessive, the meal at Sext is to be continued; and provision for this shall be left to the abbot.”

Certainly, when he says, “if they have agricultural labours,” or “if they have agricultural work,” it is easy and clear to discern that he did not impose upon monks the necessity of a command concerning work of that kind. Indeed, he did not wish them to be under the necessity of this occupation. For elsewhere he says (Chapter 66):

“If possible, the monastery should be so constructed that all necessities—that is, water, a mill, a bakehouse, a garden, and various crafts—may be exercised within the monastery, so that there may be no need for the monks to wander outside; for this is in no way advantageous to their souls.” [Col. 0514A–B]

It is manifest that one who says this does not wish monks to be occupied in those manual works which cannot be performed except outside, but permits this to be done only out of necessity. Finally, elsewhere he says (Chapter 8): “But if the necessity of the place or poverty compels them to be occupied personally in gathering the harvest, they should not be saddened, for then they are truly monks when they live by the labour of their hands, as did our Fathers and the Apostles.” By “the Apostles” he means only Paul and Barnabas. For no other Apostles are recorded as having performed manual labour after the coming of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, Peter the Apostle said: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI). [Col. 0514C]

## CHAPTER VI

And where the necessity of the place or poverty requires it, he rightly wishes us to be comforted by the example of those Apostles, Paul and Barnabas. But where no necessity compels, he himself does not wish us to wander outside, because, as he himself says, this is in no way advantageous to our souls. Nor do the Apostles just mentioned wish us to be ignorant of our right, since we are ministers of the altar.

“Do we not have the right,” Paul says, “to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take about with us a woman as a sister, as also the other Apostles, and the Lord’s brother, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas lack the right to refrain from working? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat of the things of the sanctuary? Those who serve the altar share in the altar. So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (I Cor. IX). [Col. 0514D]

By these and other such words of the same Apostle we are instructed to know both what he did rightly in other Churches and what he endured at Corinth out of necessity because of their avarice. “I despoiled other Churches,” he says, “taking wages for your service. And when I was with you and in need, I was burdensome to no one; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked” (II Cor. VIII), and so forth. [Col. 0515A]

## CHAPTER VII

From the sayings of blessed Benedict already mentioned, I think it can clearly be discerned that he wished manual labour to be an assistance for monks’ poverty where necessary resources are lacking. The examples of saints further support this very point.

I pass over many others—blessed Gregory and other holy Fathers—who provided or accepted for their monasteries so many and such great estates that monks had no need to procure their sustenance by the labour of their hands; nor are they charged with having acted contrary to blessed Benedict’s institution. Let us look at the one whom he himself nourished and taught through the cooperation of the grace of the Holy Spirit: the most blessed Maurus, whom, when asked to establish in France a monastic community according to the discipline of his holiness, he sent forth.

Did he not know, or had he not read, or did he not wish to observe, the Rule of his most beloved Father? Yet, received by kings and princes, he accepted abundant estates from their hands, whose revenues could support one hundred and forty brethren. He fixed the community at this number, as the book of his Life testifies, because the estates which he had received could support so many, but no more, servants of God there.

Therefore this ought not to be doubtful for us, given the testimony of so great a disciple: blessed Benedict, his master and Father of monks, did not prescribe an order of manual labour for monks in such a way that he wished the leisure of holy contemplation to be disturbed. [Col. 0515B–C] The generosity of wealthy believers makes room for that leisure. Of them it is mystically said in the Psalm: “The trees of the field shall be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted. There the sparrows shall make their nests” (Ps. CIII).

We are, or ought to be, those sparrows: little in our own eyes, yet flying aloft on the small wing of contemplation. For sparrows of this kind God has prepared the trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon—that is, the wealthy of the world—so that all of us who pursue a spiritual purpose may rest in their resources. [Col. 0515C]

## CHAPTER VIII

It is good indeed for monks to avoid idleness by working with their hands, since idleness is the enemy of the soul. But it is best both to avoid idleness and nevertheless, with the word of God, to keep sabbath in holy leisure.

“Martha, Martha,” says the Lord, “thou art anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary” (Luke X). What is that one necessary thing? Certainly, to sit beside the feet of the Lord and hear the words of his mouth. But where are his feet, except in the sacrament of his altar? For there are the traces of his Passion, the traces of his resurrection and ascension. Therefore, to serve the sacrament of the altar, and for that reason to be free from all occupations so that you may have leisure to meditate on the sacraments of our salvation which he has wrought in the midst of the earth (Ps. LXXIII)—this is to sit at the Lord’s feet and hear the words of his mouth. [Col. 0515D]

But you say: “You admit many laymen who know nothing of this sitting or hearing, who are untrained and inexperienced. Are they not idle among you?” To this I reply: When Israel was fighting Amalek, Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the summit of the hill (Exod. XVII). Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed. Moses’ hands were heavy. Therefore, taking a stone, they put it beneath him and he sat upon it, while Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on either side. And it came to pass that his hands did not grow weary until sunset (ibid.).

Shall we say that Aaron and Hur were idle there? Certainly not. For though they did not pray, they nevertheless performed their work so that the hands of the one praying might not grow weary. Thus, preserving the more sacred sense, monks who are unlettered and consequently fit neither for priestly nor Levitical offices are not altogether idle when they give such daily assistance as they can and know how to give to priests and Levites in the divine offices. Afterwards they practise the crafts they know, but only within the enclosure of the monastery, as the above-mentioned statement shows that blessed Benedict intended. [Col. 0516A–B]

## CHAPTER IX

“If this is so,” you ask, “why did blessed Benedict give no commands to monks concerning the observance of this holy manner of life and holy dignity? Why did he pass over this best part?”

As though he had set down, or undertaken to set down, every observance of righteousness in his Rule. He himself says: “We have written this Rule so that, by observing it in monasteries, we may show that we possess at least some honesty of conduct or a beginning of good life. But for the one who hastens to the perfection of life, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the height of perfection.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever, therefore, hastens to the heavenly homeland, fulfil with Christ’s help this least Rule of beginners which has been written down; and then, under the Lord’s protection, you will at last attain greater things.” [Col. 0516C]

This was said not only humbly but also truly. Among all the greater things attained through this beginning of the religious life, the highest is the dignity of sacred orders. No one is prepared for their most holy exercise in a better way than by living under monastic discipline, so that he may be judged worthy of the same orders.

Hence he says: “If any abbot asks that a priest or deacon be ordained for him, let him choose from among his own men one who is worthy to exercise the priesthood. But once ordained, let him beware of self-exaltation or pride,” and so forth. [Col. 0516D]

This is a most proper and well-ordered progression: first, one should become accustomed to a holy and celibate life under the yoke of obedience; then at last one should receive the crown of that obedience, namely the priestly stole. When it is placed upon his neck, it certainly signifies the Lord’s sweet yoke; and whenever a deacon receives it upon his shoulder, it signifies his light burden. This, I say, is a most orderly progression; and no small fruit of monastic profession is becoming a worthy cleric—that is, being worthily promoted to the diaconate or priesthood.

Hence blessed Jerome says in his letter to Nepotian, *On the Life of Clerics and Monks*: “I know indeed that from your uncle, blessed Heliodorus, now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned holy things and continue to learn them daily; and that you hold his rule as an example of virtues. But receive also our writings, such as they are, and join this little book to his little book, so that when he has instructed the monk, this one may teach him to be a perfect cleric.”

Likewise, to the monk Rusticus: “If you wish to be a monk, and not merely to appear one, take care not of an estate, which you renounced when you began to be a monk.” And after some further remarks: “I say this also so that, if the desire for clerical office tempts you, you may learn what you can teach and may offer God a rational sacrifice; lest you be a soldier before being a recruit, or a master before being a disciple.”

See, then, that there is some distinction among monks: some are simply monks, while others are monks and clerics together. In those who are simply monks is considered that beginning which blessed Benedict declares his Rule to be; but in those who are both monks and clerics is apostolic perfection. By perfection I mean perfection of office, not of merit. [Col. 0517A–B]

It is also not far from the truth that those who are clerics without monastic profession are nearer to the apostolic rank than those who are monks without clerical office—that is, without the ministry of the altar. Hence the aforementioned blessed Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus, then a monk and later a bishop, says: “Not to wish to be perfect is to sin. But driven from this rank, will you appeal to clerics? Shall I dare say anything concerning those who certainly dwell in their cities? Far be it from me to say anything unfavourable about those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, make Christ’s body with their sacred mouth; through whom we too are Christians; who, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in a sense judge before the day of judgment; who preserve the Lord’s bride in sober chastity. But the case of monks is one thing, that of clerics another. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; but for me, as for an unfruitful tree, the axe is laid to the root.”

He spoke this last sentence in the person of a cleric, although he too was a cleric, being a presbyter. Conversely, although he was a monk, he said elsewhere, among other things, in the person of a cleric: “But if I am the Lord’s portion and the lot of his inheritance, I receive no portion among the other tribes; but, like a Levite and priest, I live from tithes, and, serving the altar, am sustained by the altar’s offering. Having food and clothing, I shall be content with these, and naked I shall follow the naked cross.” [Col. 0517C–D]

## CHAPTER X
Therefore, because Blessed Benedict said almost nothing about the celebration of Masses, you who have been troubled or induced by workers of that sort, who place nearly all their hope in manual labour, must not, I say, on that account neglect your crown or diadem—namely, the holy office of the sacred altar. Nor should you ever, except under the greatest necessity, become so occupied in gathering crops or felling trees that, for any such reason, you approach less frequently or more negligently that unique and incomparable banquet in this life—the banquet of the charity of Christ, his Father God, and the Holy Spirit together. [Col. 0518A]

Consider the will of him who says: “Take and eat: this is my body; do this in remembrance of me. This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you receive it, in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). For he who says these things, as the Apostle took care to express, speaks as one “meek and humble in heart.” It is evident what he desires; and the attentive hearer perceives that he wishes to please us and to delight our heart, so that we may make a diligent and frequent remembrance of him. Under heaven there is no other commemoration like this; and this is not from the necessity of a command, but from the voluntary resolve of love. For then it is done worthily, when such a commemoration of him is made solely from love and affection for him. And what other work, done or to be done by a human being, could the inspector of a loving soul more gladly say of: “She has performed a good work upon me” (Mark 14)?

In this work he is shown to us “in another form.” We read in the Gospel that, on the day of his resurrection, he was shown in another form to two of his disciples as they walked on their way to a village (Luke 24). This present life is our road. In it, when we speak of him, when we celebrate the sacrament of his passion at the holy altar, we undoubtedly behold him there in another form, because the holy sacrifice of bread and wine is Christ himself. Then it will come to pass that, wondering at this our blessedness—because we do not yet know it fully—we shall say: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus, while he spoke [Col. 0518B] on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid.).

“And how will he not also, together with him, give us all things?” (Rom. 8). And, to speak in the same manner, how did he not also, together with so great an office, or in return for so great a service or ministry, give us tithes and all things belonging to the altar? Yet we must fear and consider carefully lest we be dutiful priests and frequent ministers merely for the sake of such payment. For above all, the crowd of hirelings of this sort has made the rank of presbyter contemptible among the people; and to such persons the saying of the Lord applies and strikes them with severe rebuke: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” (John 6).

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0518D]

The same author quoted above says: “Let bishops and presbyters have as their example the apostles and apostolic men, whose honour they possess and whose merit they should strive to possess. But let us have as leaders of our profession Paul, Antony, Julian, Hilarion, and Macarius.”

Here someone now says—for I have heard someone saying it—“What are so many priests doing in monasteries?” Yet this same man held the rank of priesthood or presbyterate. But because he was a vehement champion of manual labour, and could not overcome by reason one who maintained that a monk possessing holy orders and serving the altar ought to live from the things belonging to the altar, he went so far as to say that it was superfluous for monasteries to have so many priests.

His importunity against us seems to find support in this: that Paul and Antony were saints and pleased God, although they were not priests. What then? Is the priesthood for that reason less worthy or less reverent, because such great Fathers chose to be without it? Far from it! Otherwise Zacchaeus, to whom the Lord said, “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must remain in your house,” and who came down quickly and received him joyfully (Luke 19), would seem to have attained less than the centurion, to whom the same Lord said, “I will come and heal your servant,” and who answered, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8).

It is not ours to judge concerning these matters. Nevertheless, I consider him more blessed, in the likeness of Zacchaeus who was commanded to come down and received the Lord, who approaches through obedience and receives holy orders not impelled by ambition but called by lawful command, than him who always says, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof,” and persistently declines to receive so great a gift of such great grace. But do we read that those Fathers were ever commanded and refused? Indeed, if they had been commanded and had refused, they would not have been very great or very holy.

When most blessed Ephrem came to Saint Basil, Basil said: “Welcome, welcome, O father of the sons of Jeremiah, who have multiplied the disciples of Christ in it, and have ruined demons through Christ.” Then he said: “Why, lord Ephrem, do you not receive ordination to the presbyterate? For it befits you.” Saint Ephrem answered him through an interpreter: “Because I am a sinner.” Basil replied: “Would that I had your sins!” And, rejoicing spiritually for three days, the holy priest ordained the interpreter a deacon and Ephrem himself a presbyter, and dismissed them in peace. [Col. 0519C]

Would none of the other Fathers of this sort likewise have obeyed, if he had similarly been commanded—provided only that he did not lack the learning necessary for such an office? For many holy Fathers lacked such learning, as did that simple Paul, who is recorded to have asked whether the prophets existed before Christ, or Christ before the prophets. In those times the state of the Church was not such as it is now, nor was there need for so many priests. For then, while the persecution of pagans and heretics raged, Christians fled and hid in deserts, just as formerly, while Jezebel and Ahab and other idolatrous kings persecuted them, the sons of the prophets lived in wildernesses and in fields.

Hence the same writer quoted above, writing to a monk, after saying, “But let us have as leaders of our profession Paul, Antony, Julian, Hilarion, and Macarius,” added these words: “And, to return to the authority of Scripture: our leader is Elijah; our Elisha; our guides are the sons of the prophets, who lived in fields and solitude and made themselves shelters beside the streams of the Jordan.” As those men, so also these suffered persecution under impious kings, under pagan and heretical rulers: “they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11).

But now the state of the Church is different. The kings and rulers of those same kingdoms and principalities who then persecuted them and compelled them to flee and wander have now filled cities and villages with churches and monasteries, and have enriched them from their own revenues. [Col. 0520A] And that was fulfilled which the Beloved, Christ, once promised to the beloved, the Church, in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come: you shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the height of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4).

## CHAPTER XII

What then do you mean by saying to me, “Why are there so many priests in monasteries?” Indeed, there are many monasteries formerly well ordered which are now so stripped, together with their other resources, even of their number of priests that you might more properly say: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” (Matt. 9). So many Christians live round about; so many have given their alms and commended themselves to the priests’ prayers; so many congregations of faithful Christians are everywhere, whose faith is known to God, for whom we offer, or who themselves offer, the sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and well-being; so many likewise have preceded us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few.”

Has God’s work become shortened, so that it is insufficient to keep a labourer occupied and prevent his idleness? On the contrary, in well-ordered monasteries even summer days scarcely suffice to complete the course of the rule, especially if the community is larger or more numerous. And if they sometimes undertake some manual task, going out together to work, then, because of the brief time expended, I would call it not so much work as an appearance of work: almost the whole daily exercise of spiritual work becomes tasteless, impeded, and deprived of some portion of itself. Thus, whenever a zealous worker in divine praise sees such a thing, he must recall the saying mentioned above: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6). [Col. 0520C]

## CHAPTER XIII

Let what we have said thus far concerning manual labour be understood as spoken not in disapproval or contempt of your voluntary poverty, but in defence of the right of all who serve the altar; nor as excusing idleness, which is the enemy of the soul, but as approving only the better occupation of God’s work and that labour which can be carried on within the enclosure of the monastery. For, as Blessed Benedict himself says, and as was stated above, the need to wander abroad is altogether harmful to monks’ souls.

Now I ask one thing of you, indeed something quite remarkable; and, if you deign to hear me, I gladly urge it upon you: do not glory in the cheapness of your clothing. For it is remarkable to glory in cheapness and to make humility itself a matter for pride. Do I say this on my own authority? Blessed Jerome says to Nepotian: “Avoid dark garments no less than white finery; and dirt must equally be avoided, because the one smells of luxury, the other of glory.” The latter, that is, filthy clothing, he says, smells of glory.

Some pagan philosophers too could glory in this fashion, striving, namely, to be unlike others and, as Seneca says in writing to his nephew Lucilius, pursuing ambition by a perverse path. “I warn you,” he says, “not to do, after the manner of those who desire not to make progress but to be noticed, anything conspicuous in your dress or manner of life. Avoid harsh apparel, uncut hair, a too-neglected beard, and whatever else pursues ambition by a perverse path. The very name of philosophy, even if handled modestly, is sufficiently invidious. What if we should begin to oppose ourselves in body to human custom? Let everything within be different; let our face conform to the people. Let the toga neither shine nor be dirty. Let us seek a life better than that of the crowd, not a contrary one. Otherwise we drive away and turn aside from us those whom we wish to correct. We also bring it about that our people are unwilling to imitate anything, while they fear that everything must be imitated. This is philosophy’s first promise: common sense, humanity, and fellowship. Difference will separate us from that profession. Let us see whether the things by which we seek to gain admiration are ridiculous and hateful.”

You see, therefore, how excessive difference, because it smells of empty vainglory, has been judged offensive not only to ecclesiastical but even to philosophical nostrils. But you say: Blessed Benedict commands (ch. 55) that monks should not complain about the colour or coarseness of their clothes, but should have such garments as can be found in the province where they live, or as can be bought more cheaply. This is true. Yet the same Father directs that the tunics and cowls of those sent on a journey should be moderately better than those which they are accustomed to have. Therefore, even in Blessed Benedict’s judgment, we must avoid that which is especially displeasing in human eyes and not very pleasing to God—or rather, which may displease him because of vanity.

For what reason, what usefulness, what grace or truth is there in seeking in clothes a colour other than that which they found? For black was, as it is now, the customary colour of clothing in monasteries, for both sexes, monks and nuns alike. But they began to use a whitish, dubious, and uncertain colour, the causes for which we do not know. Perhaps if we had worn white clothing, they would now wear black. And indeed their difference would then be more excusable, because among all colours black is the darkest and white the brightest, while the other colours are intermediate between these opposites.

Both sexes of the monastic profession most especially avoid this black colour, the use of which we found and retain. For what purpose this serves we do not know, unless this spectacle signifies that the unity of which we sing in the psalm has been somewhat injured: “God, who makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house” (Ps. 67). If this is so, it is some consolation to us, however slight, that it is not we who have turned away from them, but they who have turned away from us, or gone out from us, in this manner. [Col. 0522A]

## CHAPTER XIV

Nevertheless, we must attribute it to our sins that some of the little ones have often been scandalized by our manner of life. Who are these little ones? Surely the inexperienced, especially those who, newly coming from secular life to the monastic profession, think—or wish to think—of monks as though they were not human beings. They ought rather to know that no profession or manner of life more than this is that furnace of which Wisdom says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the furnace of temptation tests those fit for receiving it” (Ecclus. 27). And again: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2).

When, therefore, they see any vessels crack in such a furnace, or what was thought to be gold or silver fall into the nature or vice of lead; when monks sometimes contend over which of them is greater; or, worse still, when some device exposes among them a thief of the Lord’s moneybags; when, I say, they see them quarrelling anywhere over the slightest matter and one swelling against another, they are scandalized—as though every crack were the fault not of the vessel but of the furnace, or as though the furnace had made lead from silver rather than shown what that which was thought to be silver really was. And they wish to live where only good people are, which is nowhere but in heaven, just as in truth only evil people are nowhere but in hell.

“Woe indeed to him through whom scandal comes”; yet for the little ones who are scandalized, the scandal itself is very dangerous. Thinking that they are advancing, they fall away, making void the first faith which they promised in their monasteries and persuading others to do likewise—as we have learned by experience. Therefore, at the beginning of this little book, I addressed you, to whom such counsel is given and who have not yet been persuaded, thus: “If you do not know yourself,” etc. [Col. 0522C]

## CHAPTER XV

Although they are of holy manner of life, remember that they can sometimes err. For they are human beings, and error more quickly steals into those who possess the greatest zeal for holiness without knowledge or the spirit of discernment. What if they were even prophets, foretelling future things by a prophetic spirit? Would they therefore be heard where they urged a manifest transgression? Certainly not. Rather, they must be discerned cautiously, because of what the Apostle says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11).

The prophet who came from Judah by the Lord’s command and foretold what Josiah would do at the altar of Bethel—how, and through what kind of man, was he deceived? Surely through a prophet who said to him: “Come home with me, that you may eat bread” (3 Kings 13). When he replied, “The Lord spoke to me by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘You shall not eat bread or drink water there, nor return by the way by which you went,’” the other said: “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘Bring him back with you into your house, that he may eat bread and drink water.’” He deceived him and brought him back with him. So he ate bread in his house and drank water.

And as they sat at table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet who had brought him back, and he cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah: “Thus says the Lord: Because you have been disobedient to the word of the Lord, and have returned and eaten and drunk in the place where he commanded you neither to eat nor drink, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (3 Kings 13). And so it happened: for a lion found him on the road and killed him (ibid.). It is remarkable that the word of the Lord came to such a man, unless this example had to be established for us who come after, so that we should not easily yield to human beings, however holy and religious, in dangerous matters.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0523B]

But apart from colour, there are still other things in our clothing which they reject—namely garments of sheepskins which we have because of the cold. They argue that, where Blessed Benedict speaks of the brothers’ clothing and footwear (ch. 22), he does not mention clothing of this kind. “For it is enough,” he says, “for a monk to have two tunics and two cowls, because of the nights and for washing these garments. Whatever is beyond this is superfluous and should be cut off.”

But he believed that these were sufficient not in every place, but in temperate places. For he began thus: “Let clothing be given to the brothers according to the nature of the places where they live or the temperature of the air, because more is needed in cold regions and less in warm ones. This consideration belongs to the abbot. Yet we believe that, in temperate places, one cowl and one tunic for each monk are sufficient: a shaggy cowl in winter, and a plain and worn one in summer.”

By “temperate places” he meant those neither in the torrid zone nor very near the northern pole—the kind of places in which he himself lived. Yet in the present year, on the day of Christ’s Nativity, when an extremely severe cold destroyed nearly all our vineyards in these regions—a disaster over which this whole province now laments—I was at Rome, where there were hail, thunder, and a very violent storm. So different is that air from ours, though it must nevertheless be reckoned among the places he calls temperate.

Certain persons wish to adhere to the letter in their own way, but they cannot. For two cowls and two tunics do not suffice for the change which he mentions, “because of the nights and for washing these garments.” Indeed, when the severity of the cold requires it, all are put on at once, and perhaps more besides. Why do they not at least agree with the authority of Scripture that those garments which are made of skins may rightly also be called tunics? For it is written: “God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them” (Gen. 3). What does “tunics of skins” mean except tunics made from skins?

But if they will not admit this, so as to say or concede that Blessed Benedict ever had such tunics in mind when he said that two cowls and two tunics were sufficient for a monk, let them tell us whether Blessed Benedict himself possessed any garment of skin. For the book of the Acts of his Life says (Dialogues, VI, VIII): “At the same time shepherds found him hiding in a cave. Seeing him clothed in skins among the bushes, they thought that he was some beast.” He was clothed in skins: what is that except a garment of skin?

Again, when his disciple Maurus ran over the water and, holding the boy Placid by the hair, returned swiftly over the water, Blessed Benedict attributed this to Maurus’s obedience, while Maurus, on the contrary, declared that it had been done by Benedict’s command alone. In this friendly contest of mutual humility, the boy who had been rescued came forward as arbiter. “For,” he said, “when I was being drawn from the water, I saw the abbot’s *melotes* over my head, and I saw him himself drawing me from the waters.” Therefore he had a *melotes*, a garment certainly made from skins.

For *melotes* was a garment of goatskin, which Egyptian monks also used, as Postumianus relates; it was called *melotes* because it was black. For what we call black, the Greeks call *melan*. What then do you think? The clothing for which they censure us—the garment or tunic of skin—Scripture, our witness, declares that God himself made for human beings. Blessed Benedict himself was not without such a garment, nor were monks and Egyptian Fathers older than he, nor prophets or sons of the prophets, whom Blessed Jerome maintains were monks of the Old Testament. For they too, as the Apostle says, “wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins” (Heb. 11).

You therefore say to me: “If it was customary for the older monks and for Blessed Benedict himself to wear a garment of skin, why did he issue no command concerning it?” Clearly because he judged that only those garments without which a monk’s outward habit is incomplete belonged to his regulation; the rest he left to the abbot’s consideration, as appears from the preceding words. [Col. 0524C]

## CHAPTER XVII

I come to that offensive expression (*cacenphaton*) which they make against us concerning breeches. Since the same Father says, “Those who are sent on a journey are to receive breeches from the clothing store, and on their return restore them there washed,” they wish it to mean that, in the province where he lived, the use of breeches existed before his time, and that he began to deprive monks of the customary garment worn by the people, allowing it only for decency’s sake, so that those sent on a journey or travelling on horseback might use trousers lest their nakedness be exposed.

This interpretation is almost contrary to the writer’s own intention. For he wished not to take breeches away from those who had them, but, so far as he could, to provide them to those who lacked them. We are the ones who have them, since we live in provinces where breeches are worn. The Scots and Britons are those who lack them, and scarcely less so the people among whom the Father himself lived. For even today traces remain of that by no means decent custom, as we ourselves saw when, lodging in those places, we sat by the coals among men with their legs spread apart.

Certainly the holy Father, who desired both the beauty of virtues and a religious propriety of manners and dress, needed to lay down a command about this for monks according to the character of the place. There was no need for that command in our case. For even if we were not monks, according to the character of the place—that is, of the provinces in which we live—we would walk about wearing breeches both outdoors and indoors.

Reason also proves this: what is decent to do at one time is more decent to do more often and always. Or, as Blessed Jerome says against Vigilantius: “What is good to have done once cannot be evil if it is done more frequently.” Whether we are outside or inside, awake or asleep, modest chastity especially desires that garment; and most especially because we are priests and ministers of the altar and minister daily to the sacraments, we ought not to be without this garment on any day. For the Lord said to Moses: “You shall make linen breeches, to cover the flesh of their shame; and Aaron and his sons shall wear them when they enter the tabernacle of testimony, or when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest, being guilty of iniquity, they die” (Exod. 28).

But what need is there of many words? “This consideration belongs to the abbot,” says the same Father, having first stated: “Let clothing be given to the brothers according to the nature of the places where they live or the temperature of the air.” What the temperature of the air is needs no explanation; and if you ask what the nature of places is, that too is well known, because the whole population of these places wears breeches. Formerly one part of the threefold division of Gaul was called “breeched Gaul”; now the threefold division of Gaul, Germany, and the other provinces of this climate wear breeches.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0525]

Concerning the contention of monks who say: “I belong to Augustine,” “I belong to Benedict,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER I

Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle says: “It has been reported to me concerning you, brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you. Now this I say: that every one of you says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul; I to Apollos; I to Cephas; I to Christ’” (1 Cor. 1). But he had previously said: “I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you” (ibid.). And after a few things he says: “I have transferred these things to myself and Apollos for your sakes, that in us you may learn not to be puffed up, one against another, on behalf of one person” (1 Cor. 4). Then: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who committed this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore, to contend in this way, to say in this way, “I indeed belong to Paul; I to Apollos; I to Cephas,” is schism; it is a tearing apart of minds. The prudent person understands how great an evil this is. Likewise, how severely saints bear flatteries of this kind directed toward themselves can be seen from the fact that the same Apostle reacts so harshly against those who were zealously attached to him, as it were, on account of the greatness of his teaching or wisdom. He casts in their faces the filth of the fornication which was among them, saying: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who committed this deed might be removed from your midst.”

Is not what we now hear and see almost like this? For there are contentions among us. I mean this: each of us says, “I indeed belong to Augustine; I to Benedict; I to this Rule or that Rule; I to Christ”—the last confession being, of course, true and good when made without contention. Is not having such contentions the making of schisms? For no one contends without puffing himself up, nor is one puffed up against another only slightly on behalf of someone else, when a man who professes that he belongs to Augustine says against one who professes that he belongs to Benedict: “Augustine is a bishop; Benedict is a monk; and undoubtedly a bishop is greater than a monk. Is not my order therefore higher than yours?”

Such contention has grown through days and times, and has advanced so far that men not only say it is unlawful for a cleric to become a monk, but even dare to say that it is lawful and perfect for one who has been a monk to become a cleric. These and similar matters, which are instruments of contention, must not be handled without the holy spirit of piety, because of the Apostle’s saying mentioned above: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who committed this deed might be removed from your midst.” For something of such a kind may have been or may yet occur among us. If we look to this, we may perceive—being struck, as it were—that one should not be puffed up against another because of the height of one’s profession or the differing merits of our Fathers. [Col. 0526C]

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, with the spirit of piety preceding and cooperating, so that we may be free from such puffing up, I shall try to say something on this subject, and first concerning the pastoral staffs of abbots and bishops: whose authority each staff or crozier is, and how ancient that authority is.

For among the contentions already mentioned, this too has become a matter of dispute: whether reasonably, or without the support of reason, the man who says, “I belong to Augustine,” wishes to be invested with a pastoral staff and to be called an abbot in the Church. In the regions of upper France this has now especially begun to be done; and many of us wonder whence the rationale or authority for it has been taken.

On this matter Frederick, the venerable archbishop of Cologne, not many days ago sent a letter to Adelbero, bishop of Liège, of which this is a copy:

> Just as we younger men ought to maintain and carry forward the ancient institutions of the holy Fathers which we find, upon the foundation of the divine ordinance, to have been rationally ordered, so we neither readily admit nor rashly hasten to introduce anywhere novel practices—especially those which display no foundation of reason from the authority of Scriptures or the examples of the Fathers. For it is written: “Do not pass beyond the ancient boundaries which your fathers set” (Prov. 22).
>
> We were born to find these boundaries in the Church of God: clerics, precisely because they are clerics—that is, because they possess holy orders from the bishop’s hand and belong to the ministry of the altar—are subject to the staff of the bishop alone. Those, however, who have undertaken a penitential life in the monastic habit and are simply monks are subject to the staff of the abbot alone. But those who, being monks, have received clerical orders, or who, being clerics, have professed the monastic life, are rightly subject to both staffs, namely those of bishop and abbot alike. Nor is a judgment concerning a monk who is a presbyter to be determined by the abbot alone unless the bishop is called in as witness, according to the sound and lawful institution of Blessed Benedict himself.
>
> Having considered these things, we have not yet presumed to approve or receive this new custom: that prelates of clerics, even regular clerics, should be invested with the pastoral staff and use it as abbots of monks do. For Blessed Father Augustine, whose Rule they profess, is nowhere recorded to have been called an abbot. At the time when he entered upon that manner of life, he was not yet a bishop, just as he was not an abbot, but only a novice presbyter, having recently been converted to the Catholic faith. If, therefore, no reason is at hand to support this institution which, as we have heard, is already beginning to come into use, it is good that you should exercise restraint in this matter, according to the saying: “Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Tim. 5).

Accordingly, the subject requires us to say something about the right or just custom by which the Fathers of monks are called abbots and use the pastoral staff after bishops.

## CHAPTER III

First, it should be known that the staff or crozier, as an instrument used by bishops, took its beginning from Aaron; but as an insignia bestowed also upon Fathers of monks, it took its beginning from Elisha. For Aaron was, under God’s law, prince or first of the priests; while Elisha was the spiritual father of monks, that is, of the sons of the prophets. For the people called sons of the prophets were already monks at that time.

Thus Blessed Jerome writes to the monk Rusticus: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read were monks in the Old Testament, built themselves little huts beside the streams of the Jordan, and, leaving crowds and cities, lived on gruel and wild herbs.” Likewise, writing to Paulinus: “Our leader is Elijah; our Elisha; our guides are the sons of the prophets, who lived in fields and solitude and made themselves shelters beside the streams of the Jordan.” Among these also are the sons of Rechab, who drank neither wine nor strong drink, who lived in tents, who are praised by the voice of God through Jeremiah (Jer. 25), and to whom a man standing before the Lord is promised.

Likewise, as to the clerics of the Old Testament, no one doubts that all were priests and Levites, and belonged solely to the tribe of Levi. Their leader, as already said, and first and supreme high priest was Aaron. From this they were called *clerici*, either because they belonged to the Lord’s lot, or because the Lord himself was their lot: for Greek *klēros* (κλῆρος) is called *sors*, “lot,” in Latin. The tribe of Levi received no portion in the distribution of the promised land as the other tribes did; instead, the Lord, or the Lord’s sanctuary, was its portion, so that they might live from the tithes and lawful offerings of the entire people of both orders, namely clerical and monastic.

Divine authority consecrated the staff or crozier, the insignia of pastoral care, for all Fathers in those two first persons already mentioned, Aaron and Elisha.

## CHAPTER IV
The first rod of Aaron was the rod of Moses. “What is that,” says the Lord to Moses, “which you hold in your hand?” [Col. 0528B] He answered, “A rod” (Exod. IV). He said, “Throw it upon the ground.” He threw it down, and it was changed into a serpent (ibid.), and so forth. And afterwards: “Aaron shall speak for you to the people, and shall be your mouth; but you shall be to him in those things which pertain to God. Take also this rod in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs” (ibid.). And after a little: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. And when Pharaoh says to you, ‘Show signs,’ you shall say to Aaron: ‘Take your rod and throw it down before Pharaoh, and let it become a serpent’” (Exod. VII). “Take your rod,” he says. Therefore Moses’ rod was Aaron’s rod: it was changed into a serpent once and again—once in Moses’ hand, and again when Aaron cast it down from his hand—and with it the other signs were performed. The last two of these were most beautiful and most holy [Col. 0528C]: in the dispute of Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and the other leaders contending for the priesthood, it was found to have budded; from swelling buds flowers burst forth, which, as their leaves spread, took shape as almonds (Num. XVII); and afterwards, taken from before the Lord to the waters of contradiction, its striking brought water from the rock.

Scripture does not explicitly state what workmanship that rod had; but from its pastoral use—for Moses tended with it the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro, priest of Midian (Exod. III)—it is clear that it was curved, to catch the feet of the cattle. Hence such a rod is called a *pedum*, a shepherd’s crook. Do you suppose that Moses’ rod was as finely wrought as every rod now is in the hand of any bishop? [Col. 0528D] I do not doubt that the adopted son of Pharaoh’s daughter—though then an exile, yet the son-in-law of a wealthy priest—wished, or was able, to carry a handsome rather than a shapeless rod. For tending a flock was not then the occupation of poverty for men whose chief wealth consisted in flocks. Hence even today a diversity of possessions is generally called *pecunia*, as though from *pecudia*, livestock, because nearly all the wealth of the ancients lay in cattle.

Nevertheless, it is superfluous to inquire into the beauty of that rod or staff, provided it is agreed that, for the reason just stated, it was a curved rod. Some authority might be adduced concerning its beauty, showing that not Moses alone, great as he was, but shepherds far inferior to him gladly carried handsome rods in the same employment [Col. 0529A]. For in Virgil a shepherd speaking to a shepherd says:

> But take this crook, which, though he often begged for it,  
> Antigenes did not receive from me  
> (and then he was worthy to be loved),  
> Fair Menalcas, handsome with matching knots and bronze.

VIRGIL, *Eclogue* V, vv. 88–90.

I have said this so that it may not all be charged to the craftsman’s fancy that our bishops began to carry such handsome staves, adorned with shining—that is, ivory—knobs, and with bronze, indeed gold or silver, inlay; for perhaps Moses’ rod was more beautiful still.

## CHAPTER V

The second rod, or rod of the second order—namely Elisha’s rod—though certainly not so illustrious, was nevertheless [Col. 0529B] consecrated by the same divine authority. “Gird up your loins,” Elisha says to Gehazi, “take my staff in your hand, and go. If a man meets you, do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him; and place my staff upon the face of the child” (IV Kings IV).

Finally, that which was mystically signified by the fact that Aaron’s rod indeed afflicted Pharaoh and the Egyptians with so many signs, yet did not compel them to release the children of Israel except through the sacrifice of the lamb, was likewise signified by Elisha’s sending his staff ahead and ordering it laid upon the face of the child who lay dead. Gehazi did so, but the child did not revive until Elisha himself came, went up, and lay upon him; he put his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon [Col. 0529C] his eyes, his hands upon his hands, and bent himself over him (ibid.).

What is that mystery? Surely it is “the great mystery of godliness, which was preached to the nations and believed in the world,” as the Apostle says (I Tim. III): because “what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII), and so forth. As Aaron’s rod was weakened and did not accomplish, by the ten plagues, that Pharaoh should release the people unless the lamb was sacrificed, so the Law was weakened and did not accomplish, by the ten commandments, that the prince of this world should be cast out unless Christ suffered. And likewise, as Elisha’s staff was weakened and did not make [Col. 0529D] the child rise unless Elisha lay upon him or bent himself over him, so that same Law was weakened and did not make the human race return to eternal life unless Christ took upon himself our temporal death.

Therefore both, as has been said—the rod of Aaron the priest and the rod or staff of Elisha the prophet—were consecrated by the same divine authority. For the finger of God was surely with Aaron’s rod; and in Elisha when he sent his staff, the same Spirit of God, the worker of mysteries, was certainly present.

## CHAPTER VI

These are the two ecclesiastical orders: one, the order of clerics; the other, that of monks. Of them holy Church is spoken of once and again in the Song of Songs:

> Your hair is like flocks of goats  
> that have ascended from Mount Gilead.  
> Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep  
> that have ascended from the washing.  
> All bear twins,  
> and none among them is barren.  
> (Cant. IV)

By the hair resembling flocks of goats [Col. 0530A] are rightly understood the companies of monks, who in their own judgment are sinners, and therefore, displeased with themselves, have hastened to ascend from Mount Gilead—that is, to take up their cross and follow Christ—professing by their very habit that they are crucified to the world and bearing a voluntary martyrdom, that is, a testimony; for this is what the name Gilead signifies. It is interpreted “heap of testimony,” and signifies all who have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts (Gal. V), but especially those who profess this very thing by the habit which ecclesiastical authority established in a certain [Col. 0530B] likeness of captive blackness—a form of dress of which more must be said below.

What does hair do upon a woman’s head except provide adornment? Yet it does not even adorn unless it is bound and veiled; rather, it causes disgrace. In accordance with this likeness, monks are superfluous in their own judgment; but they have hope in this: if bound by regular discipline and hidden within, they continually direct their thoughts toward the Lord, in the manner of goats ever seeking higher pastures as penitents [variant: *petentium*, “seeking”].

By teeth resembling flocks of shorn sheep are likewise rightly understood the ordered ranks of clerics. In our judgment, or in the estimation of all men—indeed by the will of the Scriptures and sacred canons—they are simple as sheep, that is, without fault; and therefore, by pleasing God and men [Col. 0530C], they have resolved to ascend from the washing, that is, perhaps to become the Lord’s lot. The very office of the sacred altar which they perform requires them, stripped of other possessions, to live from the altar, ever ready to kill those who live wickedly and, by incorporating them into the Church, in a manner to eat them; according to the saying: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X). For as speech is formed through the tongue only with teeth, so public preaching ought not to be administered by anyone through learning, however great it may be, except with clerical office.

## CHAPTER VII

Here a scarlet cord is necessary, of which there immediately follows: “Your lips are like a scarlet cord, and your speech is sweet” (Cant. IV). What are those lips like a scarlet cord except lips uttering the sweet and friendly word of peace and charity [Col. 0530D]? For example: “Now I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you; but be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge” (I Cor. I).

Such a scarlet cord is necessary, I say: that is, brotherly love. For it is the bond of peace by which we too must be bound and held together, so that there may be no schisms among us, but that we may all say the same thing. What is this “same thing”? Surely not what I may happen to wish, or what you wish, but what the holy catholic Church has long since received and approved. For it is written, and I have already mentioned it above: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers set.” [Col. 0531A]

Tell me: do you acknowledge that the Rule of blessed Benedict belongs to the boundaries established by your Fathers? Blessed Gregory, the first among the most renowned of your Fathers—or of our Fathers—is the shining lamp of the apostolic see; and, by the merit of his outstanding teaching, the silver column and golden couch of the holy universal Church, upon which Wisdom itself undoubtedly reclined. He said and wrote that blessed Benedict was filled with the spirit of all the righteous, and he himself first praised the Rule composed by Benedict as distinguished in discretion and eloquent in expression; and after him all apostolic Fathers, all Christians, all Catholics did so. Therefore this Rule is protected by the law of ancient boundaries, so that it may never be transgressed by any newly introduced tradition. But you wish to introduce its transgression into [Col. 0531B] the Church.

For blessed Benedict himself says in the Rule: “If anyone of the order of priests asks to be received into the monastery” (ch. 60), and so forth. “Of the order of priests,” without doubt—that is, bishops. For he says: “Nevertheless, let him be permitted to stand after the abbot and to give blessings or celebrate Masses, if the abbot commands him.” Again: “If perhaps there is an ordination or some other occasion in the monastery, let him take the place which he held when he entered the monastery, not that which was granted him out of reverence for the priesthood.” And immediately concerning the other ranks: “But if any cleric,” he says, “desires from the same desire to join the monastery, let him be placed in a middle rank; provided that he promises observance of the Rule and his own stability.”

Against this you say: “It is not lawful for a cleric to become a monk.” See, then [Col. 0531C], whether this is not to transgress the ancient boundaries set by the Fathers—and not merely to transgress them in some fashion, but indeed to contradict the Holy Spirit. For Benedict was full of the spirit of all the saints. But you say still more: not only is it unlawful for a cleric to become a monk, but it is lawful for a monk to become a cleric. You think you have the authority of blessed Jerome as patron of this teaching, since, writing among other things to Nepotian, a monk, he says:

> I know indeed that from your uncle, blessed Heliodorus, now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned holy things and learn them daily, and that you have his rule of virtues as your model. But receive also our writings, such as they are, and join this little book to his little book, so that, as he has instructed you as a monk, this may teach you to be [Col. 0531D] a perfect cleric.

Again, to Rusticus the monk: “I say this so that, even if the desire for clerical office tickles you, you may learn what you can teach, and offer Christ a rational sacrifice; lest you be a soldier before being a recruit, or a master before being a disciple.”

Therefore, you say, it must be granted that it is lawful for a monk to become a cleric. But how, I ask, can or should one who is a monk become a cleric? Surely not by becoming an apostate and a transgressor of his habit or order, assuming the habit and yet the clerical profession which the common people alone know, and which you learned at the crossroads? A splendid doctor and defender of blessed Jerome in such matters! For what is it for a monk to become a cleric except for a monk to be ordained priest or deacon?

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0532A]

I do not inveigh against you, O clerics, the glory and defense of the Christian people; but I address the man whom I have heard, and whom I have found, excessively to disdain and oppose the monastic order or habit. Tell me, I ask: for a monk to be “tickled by the desire for clerical office,” as blessed Jerome says—what is that except to wish to perform the sacred orders of the altar, out of love and delight in divine service, in that singular service which is to make the body and blood of the Lord and to preach the word of God in the Church? For what do you suppose clerical office is except the sacred ministry of the sanctuary or altar?

But you attend only to the outward skin, by which the common crowd, with what they call bovine eyes, distinguishes a cleric from a monk. Otherwise, if you attend to outward attire where you ought to attend to it, when or where we perform the office of a cleric [Col. 0532B], what distinction is there between us? The bishop has vested me and you alike with the same insignia. Do you think clerical and monastic life are opposites and cannot coexist in the same person? Rather, your mind stands opposed to the monk, and for that reason you regard those things as opposites. But they are companionable and friendly, and one is adorned by the other, as blessed Jerome says: “We blush at absurdities among monks and clerics, whose priesthood is adorned by their purpose of life, and whose purpose of life is adorned by their priesthood.”

“If any abbot,” says blessed Benedict (ch. 62), “asks that a priest or deacon be ordained for him, let him choose from among his own men one worthy to perform the priesthood. But once ordained, let him know that he is all the more subject to regular discipline; let him not, on account of his priesthood, forget obedience to the Rule and [Col. 0532C] discipline, but advance more and more in the Lord, always retaining the place which he held when he entered the monastery, apart from the office of the altar.”

It is therefore clear to you as well, though unwillingly, how you ought to understand the intention of the writer, namely blessed Jerome, from whose writing you wished to argue that a monk might lawfully be promoted into your clerical state, or habit, as into a higher rank.

## CHAPTER IX
