I scarcely know how or from what source this occasion for boasting against the monastic order has come to you—or to others too, though not so fiercely envious. It is indeed something new. Life is conducted more strictly now than formerly; but remember what the Apostle said: “Though I distribute all my possessions to feed the [Col. 0532D] poor, and though I give my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.” True charity, always walking with humility as its companion, preserves unity.

You have indeed increased the strictness of the Rule of blessed Augustine; but consider for a moment. Tell me: do you think it superfluous or idle to observe the monastic habit and solemn consecration as they were handed down by the holy Fathers and received by the Church, or not? The holy Fathers—indeed, he who worked in the holy Fathers—willed that such a habit or garment should be held as a sign of mortification, as a likeness of the Lord’s cross; so that, in his own consecration, the monk in a manner dies and is buried [Col. 0533A] with Christ anew. Thus, for three days, with his head covered, he bears the witness of mortification or of the penance undertaken, becoming a spectacle to angels and men; then, on the third day, his head is uncovered by the abbot, who gives him the kiss of peace in likeness of the Lord’s resurrection, who, appearing alive again to his disciples after their three days of sorrow, said to them: “Peace be with you” (John XX).

Far be it from anyone who lives under God and desires to be nourished by the sweetness of a mother’s grace to regard such an institution as worthless or to wish to abandon it. For it is a great refuge of piety to which anyone may flee who, overwhelmed by sins, has lost the first grace of holy baptism and may recover the first robe. Whoever, consecrated by this rite, bears in his habit the sign of mortification or of the Lord’s [Col. 0533B] cross, even if he does not receive the sacred orders of the altar, is equal to a cleric without this form of dress who performs the orders of the sacred altar. This is attested by canonical authority, which commands that a monk who is not a cleric and a cleric who is not a monk, if guilty of the same crime, be punished by the same measure of penance.

## CHAPTER X

Mark this point which I make: by what right do abbots—that is, fathers of monks—carry the pastoral staff after bishops? Is it because they are priests or presbyters, or because they are monks and leaders of monks? This question has remained almost unknown and insufficiently considered because, as the beauty of the house of God has increased, nowadays scarcely any [Col. 0533C] abbot is ordained unless he has first been ordained a priest. Formerly it was not so. There were many abbots who did not possess sacred orders.

For example, Equitius the abbot, whose life and deeds blessed Pope Gregory recounts in the first book of the *Dialogues*, presided over both men and women by a certain privilege of grace, which he said he had himself received from heaven through an angel; yet he did not possess sacred orders. Hence someone who questioned him familiarly said:

> You have no sacred order, and have not received from the Roman bishop under whom you live permission to preach. How do you dare to preach?

Compelled by this questioning, he said: “I too consider within myself the things you say to me. But one night a beautiful young man stood by me in a vision and placed upon my tongue [Col. 0533D] a medicinal instrument for bloodletting, saying: ‘Behold, I have placed my words in your mouth. Go out to preach.’ And from that day onward, even when I wish to do so, I cannot be silent about God.”

For the same reason, when clerics proceeded against him, he was at one time summoned before the apostolic see—not because he was an abbot, as he indeed was, for, trusting in the power of almighty God, he presided equally over women and men, so free from temptation as though he had no sex in his body; but because he preached, without possessing sacred orders, as has been said. For both reason and authority maintain that a monk who does not possess sacred orders, however learned, ought not presume to preach. Equitius indeed was protected by divine miracles; [Col. 0534A] yet miracles, as has been said before our time, are not to be drawn into precedent. Nevertheless, care is taken that no one should dare to seize such an office of preaching. “For how shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. X). But to be sent is to be ordained.

Examples from others might be brought forward to show that fathers of monks, that is abbots, used to be ordained without the office of the altar; but I preferred this example, whose reason is clearer from what happened.

## CHAPTER XI

If, therefore, the monastic habit and the consecration of monastic profession have such power that one who, apart from this grace, is otherwise a layman can lawfully administer the care of souls, why is it so [Col. 0534B] contemptible to you? And if you seek authority even on this point—whether the dignity of this habit, so different from your own clothing and that of everyone else, is built upon the foundation of Scripture, and whether consequently such a form of dress ought to carry great weight in ecclesiastical arguments—behold, in the same Elisha already mentioned above, you have authority for consecration and monastic dress as well as for the staff mentioned earlier.

“Go,” the Lord says to Elijah, “return by your way through the desert to Damascus. When you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael over Syria, and you shall anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat, who is of Abel-meholah, you shall anoint prophet in your place” (III Kings XIX). And afterwards: “When Elijah came to Elisha, he cast his mantle over [Col. 0534C] him” (ibid.).

“A mantle,” says Isidore, “is that with which the shoulders of ministers are covered, so that while ministering they may move about unencumbered. It is called *pallium* either from *pellis*, ‘skin,’ because the ancients first used an outer garment of skins, as though *pelleum*; or derivatively from *palla*.”

Whatever workmanship that mantle had, having been handed down in this way to the prophets by divine authority for their consecration, and transmitted by them to posterity, and however unchanged it was preserved by those Jews called Hasidaeans or Essenes—of whose nearly monastic life Josephus writes in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities*—it was then truly sacred. And now, because it has been perfected into the likeness of the Lord’s cross, this garment, the insignia of a withdrawn manner of life [Col. 0534D], is most sacred.

I have said this so that you may not think contemptible either our solemn consecration to this sacred profession or our distinction from the clergy by such clothing, although many of us, as was mentioned above, are clerics because we possess sacred orders.

## CHAPTER XII

Was it not divinely provided in that beginning as well? Elijah was both priest and monk—or, as blessed Jerome calls him, the first monk of the anchorites. Elisha, however, was not a priest but only a monk, the first father of cenobitic monks. Under him, monks were then called sons of the prophets; afterwards, under other names, Hasidaeans or Essenes; under the Apostles, disciples; and then [Col. 0535A], in Egypt under the evangelist Mark, who was the first to bring there the manner of life handed down under the Apostles, they were called monks by the Greek term.

Add to those two the blessed high priest of the Lord, Jehoiada of Jerusalem, who was the third and last to put his hand to the expulsion of Baal, whose worship the most impious Jezebel had introduced; and behold, you have three men: Jehoiada, priest and not prophet; Elisha, prophet and not priest; Elijah, both prophet and priest.

That Elijah was a priest is evident even from the fact that he offered sacrifice or a burnt offering, and, in offering it, contended with and defeated Baal and his priests: “Hear me, O Lord, hear me, that this people may learn that you are the Lord God, and that you have turned their heart again [Col. 0535B]” (III Kings XVIII)—understand, after you first turned their heart when, through Moses and Aaron, you led them out of Egypt. Read the rest as written in the book of Kings: how Elisha, by anointing Jehu, utterly destroyed from Israel—that is, from the ten tribes—the statue of Baal and burned it, likewise destroyed Baal’s temple and made it into latrines, thus blotting Baal out from Israel; and then how Jehoiada the high priest removed that same Baal from Judah, after the murder of Jezebel’s most impious daughter Athaliah.

He who reads rightly and understands does not lightly esteem those three distinctions among the men of God which I have stated. Through them, while they kept and restrained the people in the worship of the one true God, a way was prepared for the coming salvation, so that the word of promise, first made to Abraham and afterwards to David, might be fulfilled. [Col. 0535C]

From then until now this sacred practice has endured in the Church. For whenever any priest and monk, such as the jewel of priests, Saint Martin, or the bishop of the Roman see, blessed Pope Gregory, clothes any monk in the habit and blesses him, or even ordains him to preside as abbot and bear the care of souls, Elijah, in accordance with the Lord’s command, plainly anoints Elisha and places his own mantle upon him [Col. 0535D]: that is, he gives him his own—his own, I say, meaning the same monastic habit which he himself wears. For if the bishop does not have such a habit, and not the same habit as Elijah—just as Jehoiada the high priest at that time was neither of Elijah’s way of life nor of the same habit—he does not give such a mantle, because it is not his own; but he anoints him, that is, blesses him as abbot.

## CHAPTER XIII

Why, then, do you despise a sacred custom established and founded by divine tradition? “Though I have all virtues and charity”—for the Apostle says, “Though I do this or that, and possess this or that, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII).

I remember a saying which I heard from you, and I hesitate to judge what sort of saying it was or from what spirit it proceeded. You said: “After the Babylonian kingdom had grown immensely, it ceased to grow, and another kingdom arose and grew over it, namely that of the Persians and Medes; and afterwards another over this, namely the Macedonian kingdom.” Having proposed this as a comparison [Col. 0536A], you added that it would be so in the future—and ought already to be happening—that the greatness or eminence of those who have hitherto flourished in monastic life, especially the Cluniacs, of whom I do not know whether you have ever spoken a kindly word, should be brought down and greatly diminished, and that another beginning should arise among the humble.

What sort of likeness or comparison is this? Those four bestial kingdoms were without God; but monastic life, or every ecclesiastical religious order, is in no way like those beasts—rather, it is their opposite—since it pertains to the ministry rendered to the Ancient of Days and to the Son of Man, to whom he gave authority and his kingdom, who judged those beasts and, after taking away their power, delivered their bodies to fire. You did not rightly [Col. 0536B] wish to compare opposites with opposites.

You would have spoken more beautifully and more lovingly had you said that, as the moon, once it has grown full, immediately begins to wane and almost disappears, but when it is thought to have vanished rises and grows again; or as Arcturus continually turns yet never sets or sinks; so holy Church, and especially the spiritual order established by the Holy Spirit, sometimes declines in one place but flourishes again, and almost always turns through diverse customs according to the manners of peoples and nations, yet will never be scattered or destroyed.

The Church of God will not listen to you in this matter, so as to judge it lawful for one who was a monk to become a cleric in any way other than this: by receiving sacred orders of the altar, as was said above [Col. 0536C].

If you wish to derive authority from the austerity of life which you have newly undertaken, a layman may do the same against a cleric if he wishes to be more abstinent. But it is written: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good” (Ecclus. XLII). For to the woman—that is, to the arrogant person—an occasion for doing good sometimes comes from her intention, and that very good deed becomes matter for pride. But into the man—that is, the obedient person, who obeys the rule set before him—something wrongful sometimes creeps by temptation through complacency; and that very wrongdoing or weakness becomes for him an occasion of virtue. Thus the Lord himself says to the Apostle: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII).

Some years ago [Col. 0536D] I was conversing with Lord John, bishop of Ferns, a religious and venerable man, concerning a certain monk who had formerly been a cleric under the Rule of blessed Augustine. I said that it had always been lawful, and would always be lawful, for a cleric to become a monk, with the authority of the canons and the Rule of blessed Benedict, supported by every rational consideration—considerations which I then had leisure and inclination to explain at length. We had not yet heard, nor had it until then been customary, that clerics of that profession should continually abstain from eating flesh; and in many other respects their observance was more relaxed than it is now.

I therefore mentioned Noah’s ark, in which Scripture, carefully specifying its measurements, testifies that each level was the higher the narrower it was, and conversely the lower the broader it was (Gen. VI). I said that the house of God, which is the Church, is ordered in this manner, and that the professions of clerics and monks are rightly distinguished so that each is higher insofar as it is stricter, and conversely lower insofar as it is more relaxed [Col. 0537A]. The bishop just mentioned belonged to that profession and Rule then, and had done so before becoming bishop; consequently, he was more reluctant to grant the arguments I advanced.

To what end is this said? To indicate the cause of the holy contention by which certain novices of that same profession now boast, reversing the case, that they occupy the higher place in the ark mentioned above because they have voluntarily rejected not only the eating of flesh but even the use of fat. But this neither increases their height of merit in the Church [Col. 0537B] nor diminishes that of the others. For the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to blessed Peter. The Church, moreover, having such authority, by a general synod permitted monks—because they did not have an abundance of oil—not flesh, but fat akin to flesh. “Let him who is weak eat only vegetables,” says the Apostle (Rom. XIV). Indeed, one is permitted, if he wishes, to abstain from flesh even at Christmas, if he has such weakness as to think that the kingdom of God is food and drink (ibid.).

However much more abstinent than a monk you may be, you will not be Badoch or Abiathar, or certainly [Col. 0538A] the aforementioned priest Jehoiada; nor will you be the same as Elijah, priest and anchorite. And Elisha, however much more abundant a spirit he possessed than Elijah, will not be the same as Elijah. Each is blessed in his own order. Elisha obtained what he asked: “I pray, my lord, let your spirit become double in me” (IV Kings II); for he performed twice as many signs as Elijah. Yet there are divisions of graces; nor does one who is more richly endowed in one grace surpass another in all things, as Elisha did in this grace, namely the working of miracles. Similarly, one who is simply a monk may precede in some grace one who is both monk and priest; and one who is simply a priest may precede one who is both priest and monk. Yet he will not equal the man who excels by the grace of both orders [Col. 0538B].

What, then, is the end? For unwillingly I have been detained so long in this valley of dispute; I hasten to return to the peaceful words of the Lord seated on the mountain, which I had first begun to hear. If this discourse of mine has wounded you, whoever you are, regard me as having fled, like an axe slipping from its handle while we were perhaps carelessly cutting wood, to one of the cities of refuge; and cease to pursue me (Deut. XIX).

**THE END**

Mystery of the abbot’s staff:

> Gather the wandering, support the sick, spur the slow.  
> [Col. 0537]

# DISPUTATION OF MONK AND CLERIC, ON WHETHER A MONK MAY LAWFULLY PREACH, COMPOSED BY LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ

[Col. 0537C] **MONK.** You act unjustly, resisting me to my face and shutting my mouth, so that I do not dare open it in the midst of the Church and proclaim the word of God. Tell me at last: by what authority do you think yourself able to stop my mouth?

**CLERIC.** I shall tell you, and show by reason of justice that I do not act unjustly. First, because, in professing yourself a monk, you confess that you are dead. For he is not a monk who is not dead to the world; but how can a man be dead [Col. 0537D] if his voice is heard outside? Therefore he is not a monk who is shown, by the very outcry of his preaching, to live to the world.

**MONK.** You have struck me forcefully and cleverly, as it seems to you. But now I turn against you this very weapon which you have hurled at me. For I say: you too are dead. Indeed, the Apostle says both to you and to me: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). Do you suppose that this is said only to monks? Were all the Colossians, and the others to whom it was written, monks? Or does he say this of the mortification of monastic profession, rather than of the mortification of baptism? For in the Epistle to the Romans he says: “All of us who have been baptized [Col. 0538C] into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death; we have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI), and so forth. Either, then, being dead in this manner yourself, be silent about the word of life; or, dead with the dead alongside me, allow me to mortify those who still live to the world.

**CLERIC.** I shall not do so. I shall never concede that this is lawful for you. The sacred canons forbid it; authoritative writers deny it. For Pope Pius decrees that a monk, whatever his learning, must not dare to preach. And Jerome says that a monk does not have the office of teaching, but of mourning.

**MONK.** Cleric, you read Scripture with your mouth open but your eyes shut. For if Jerome’s statements are taken as you understand them, it follows that you make Jerome himself greatly inconsistent with himself, and Pope Pius contrary to his own judgment, when he says that a monk, whatever his learning, must not dare to preach [Col. 0538D]. For the apostolic see admitted blessed Gregory, resplendent in monastic habit, and very many other men of this order, to the office of the apostolic eminence, and does not cease to do so even today. And Jerome, who says, “A monk does not have the office of teaching, but of mourning,” is a monk [Col. 0539A] while he says this in the very office of teaching; and by teaching throughout his life, and by writing enduring doctrine, he deserves to be numbered among the greatest teachers.

Did you not know that Jerome, whose judgment you claim as patron, was a monk? I therefore do not wonder that you chatter so foolishly against monks, when you are so unversed in sacred literature that, upon hearing that Jerome and Gregory and the other stars of the heavenly palace were monks, you stand astonished.

**CLERIC.** How, then, is either of them not inconsistent with himself, when he himself does what he says lies outside the monk’s office? Tell me how I read Scripture with closed eyes. What else have you found in statements so plain by which you may correct my understanding [Col. 0539B], provided that in your presumption you do not do violence to Scripture?

**MONK.** I shall do so, if first you answer me briefly concerning what I ask.

**CLERIC.** Ask as you please.

**MONK.** You who are a defender of clerics and such a vehement assailant of monks, who glory in clerical office and, upheld and exalted by this profession above the monk: do you know why you yourself are called a cleric, and what clerical office is?

**CLERIC.** Are you asking for the etymology of the name *cleric*?

**MONK.** That is indeed easy to explain. A cleric is so called because he is chosen by lot. But I want more. I ask you about the thing itself signified by this name, *clerical office* [*clericatus*]. Why do you hesitate? Either speak, or, if you are the lesser, listen.

**CLERIC.** I am listening.

**MONK.** The clerical office is not learning in letters,[^c0052-321] nor your tonsure or dress, but the ministry of the altar. It is reckoned by this name because, when in the old Law the Lord divided the land among the tribes of Israel by lot, “with the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. 77 [78]), the tribe of Levi, which was to minister in the sanctuary, received as its lot none other than the Lord himself—that is, the altar of the Lord—so that one serving the altar might live from the altar. Therefore all who serve the altar are clerics, and *clericatus* signifies nothing other than the ministry of the altar.

**CLERIC.** I accept this.

[Col. 0539D]

**MONK.** Therefore you must concede that you are called, or are, a cleric for no other reason than that you perform the orders of the altar.

**CLERIC.** I concede it.

**MONK.** Yet I too perform the same orders. Indeed, under the authority of my Rule I have exercised the priesthood. And perhaps while you are still merely reciting the Gospel, I am already celebrating Masses.

**CLERIC.** I cannot deny it.

**MONK.** Therefore I too am a cleric.

**CLERIC.** I echo: “No—you are not a monk” (perhaps: “Therefore you are not a monk”).

**MONK.** On the contrary, I am nevertheless a monk. But these things seem opposed to you—monasticism and the clerical office—as though they could not coexist. Your eye, which does not regard monks fairly, dreams this. They are indeed distinct, and each can exist without the other: in you, or in such a man, the clerical office exists without monasticism; likewise, in any lay convert, monasticism may exist without the clerical office. I do not deny that, by the authority of the canons, you are equal to such a person: if a monk without any grades of orders falls into sin, the canons prescribe him the same manner of penance as a cleric of Levitical order.

But I, who exercise the honor of priestly and Levitical order together with the splendor of the monastic order, do not allow you to appear my equal in any way. For, as someone has most truly said: “Mary was a virgin, and John was a virgin. Yet Mary possesses the greater fullness, because John was only a virgin; Mary, however, was both mother and virgin.” Thus, certainly, there is a greater fullness in me than in you [Col. 0540B]. For you are only a cleric; I am both monk and cleric. These, I say, as I began to say, are distinct but not contrary, since both are present in the same person. You now understand what has been established: I, who am a monk, am also a cleric, because I perform the orders of the sacred altar.

**CLERIC.** I cannot deny it.

**MONK.** Yet from the fact that you are a cleric, you claim for yourself authority to preach.

**CLERIC.** And rightly so.

**MONK.** Then you cannot take away from me this same right to preach without injustice.

**CLERIC.** I should like to do so; but since I am caught in this conclusion, I can accomplish nothing unless I break the bond of the argument.

**MONK.** For the present, our purpose must be carried through.

**CLERIC.** What purpose?

**MONK.** The purpose for which these matters have been established.

**CLERIC.** What is that?

**MONK.** Namely, that it may appear how Jerome, although a teacher and a monk, is not inconsistent with himself when he says that a monk has not the office of teaching but of mourning, and so forth.

**CLERIC.** Proceed; argue as you please.

**MONK.** First, it must be known that these words were said against the blasphemies of Vigilantius, in defense of those who, leaving the world and giving all their possessions to the poor, embraced the solitary life. A little earlier Jerome says of them: “Monks are not to be deterred from their pursuit by your viperous tongues and most savage bites, by which you argue and say: ‘If all shut themselves up and live in solitude, who will celebrate the churches? Who will win secular people?’” And a little afterward: “A monk has not the office of a teacher, but of one who mourns.” These words were said concerning the life of monks alone.

But in writing to Nepotianus, he writes concerning the life of monks and clerics—that is, of those who are at once monks and clerics.

**CLERIC.** Ah! You perversely interpret that title according to your own sense.

**MONK.** Who is perverse—am I?

[Col. 0541A]

**CLERIC.** It should not be understood in that way.

**MONK.** How, then? Do you suppose that he proposes here to write a rule for monks and there a rule for clerics? Read what follows with wakeful eyes, and you will find it as I have said. For Nepotianus himself, to whom or for whose sake he writes, is one and the same person, both monk and cleric. For after some remarks Jerome says to him:

> “I know that from your uncle, blessed Heliodorus, who is now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned what is holy and daily continue to learn it, and that you possess in his manner of life an example of virtues. Yet receive also such counsels as mine may be; join this little book to his little book, so that, when he has instructed you as a monk, this may teach you to be a perfect cleric.”

Thus, beginning with this one Nepotianus, he instructs those who belong to both orders, the clerical and the monastic, concerning how they ought to conduct themselves. For example, when, as he says shortly afterward, because of the duty of the clerical office, a widow or a virgin is visited. Therefore that letter is entitled *On the Life of Clerics or Monks*: of these, as he himself says in the same letter, “the priesthood is adorned by their religious purpose, and their religious purpose by the priesthood.”

But the words of the letter which he wrote to Heliodorus apply to one who is only a monk—and who thereby loses even that standing.

**CLERIC.** From where do you infer this?

**MONK.** From the words of the letter itself. When Jerome rebuked Heliodorus because, on account of affection for relatives and expectation of an inheritance, he remained amid the crowd, and said to him, “What are you doing in the crowd, you who are alone?” he adds after some remarks:

> “If the pious entreaties of the brethren summon you to the order of clerics [Col. 0541C], I shall rejoice at your ascent, but fear for your fall.”

And when he says in the same place, “I am not permitted to sit before a presbyter,” he does not speak in his own person, since he himself was a presbyter, but in the person of the one to whom he writes. That man, being only a monk, had not yet deserved to attain that order of clerics who, as Jerome says in the same place, succeeding to the apostolic rank, “by their sacred mouth make the body of Christ.”

Likewise, the letter to Paulinus indicates that Paulinus himself is only a monk, and therefore has no business in cities. Jerome says to him:

> “If you wish to hold the office of a presbyter, if the work or perhaps the honor of the episcopate attracts you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others gain for your own soul.”

Thus Jerome is not inconsistent with himself, because he grants the authority to teach not only to himself but also to all those whose priesthood is adorned by their religious purpose and whose religious purpose is adorned by priesthood. Nor does the Apostolic See act contrary to his opinion when, while forbidding monks to preach, it nevertheless admits monks to the office of the apostolic eminence. When you open your mouth to speak, please first open your eyes to read.

**CLERIC.** Are you speaking angrily?

**MONK.** Rather, “I have been zealous for the house of the Lord.” You, rather, are angry because you have been defeated; and because you fail in arguments, you break out into insults. But please [Col. 0542B], wait a little. There is still one thing which I will not allow you to remain ignorant of.

**CLERIC.** What is it?

**MONK.** Why the authority of the Apostolic See, or Jerome’s aforesaid statement, excludes those monks who lack clerical office from the ministry of preaching.

**CLERIC.** Go on; speak as much as you wish, since you have begun to advance remarkable and unexpected things.

**MONK.** Remarkable indeed, and great. Yet whoever finds these things remarkable or great is neither great nor remarkable, since he testifies against himself that he has made little progress in the Scriptures.

**CLERIC.** At last say whatever that thing is.[^c0052-322]

**MONK.** The Apostle, speaking of preachers, says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10). A preacher, therefore, must not presume the office of preaching on his own authority. Rather, as Christ says: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 20). The Father sends Christ; Christ sends the apostles; the apostles, archbishops; archbishops, bishops; bishops, presbyters—namely, when they ordain them. A monk is exempt from this sending so long as he has not yet received sacred orders. How, then, shall he preach?

[Col. 0541]

## On the Same Matter: Letter to Everard, Abbot of Brunwiller

> **Note:** [Col. 0541D] Everard, called the seventh abbot of the monastery of Brunwiller, was a man of exceedingly conscientious character. Since he had several churches to govern, he was troubled in conscience by the fact that the etymology of *monk* conveys the meaning “single” or “solitary,” and he feared to place his brethren over churches. [Col. 0542D] He therefore consulted the learned and renowned venerable lord Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz, about this matter; Rupert sent him the following written reply. — From the *History of the Venerable Abbots of the Monastery of St Nicholas at Brunwiller*.

[Col. 0541]

[Col. 0541D]

**To EVERARD, by God’s grace venerable and religious abbot of the monastery of Brunwiller, Brother RUPERT: greeting and every joy in the consolation of the Holy Spirit.**

[Col. 0542D]

The complaint of certain clerics which you mention, reverend Father, is genuine and of long standing: why should a monk, since he is dead to the world, dare to undertake the office of preaching, baptizing, distributing communion [Col. 0543A], and absolving penitents? They also occasionally produce examples or decrees from the writings of the venerable Fathers, by which they seek to prove that a monk cannot lawfully do these things. For example, blessed Jerome says: “A monk has not the office of teaching, but of mourning,” and other statements of that sort.

There is no need to draw out at length the rope of controversy over these matters. Rather, we grant to those who say this that the office of teaching or preaching is permitted only to a cleric. Yet Jerome himself, though a monk, exercises the office of a teacher not only by speaking but also by writing. We therefore ask them how he is not inconsistent with himself. If they cannot say, we further ask them what the clerical office is. If they think correctly, they will say that *clericatus* is nothing other than the ministry of the altar, according to the interpretation of the names.

For in Greek *klēros* means “lot” in Latin; hence *clericatus*, that is, “allotment,” and *clericus*, that is, “one allotted,” because he belongs to the Lord’s lot, or because the Lord’s altar is his lot. For, as the Apostle says, those who serve the altar live from the altar (1 Cor. 9). Jerome belonged to this same allotment, for he was a priest. Therefore he was not merely a monk but also a cleric. Accordingly, he is not inconsistent with himself when he says that a monk has the office not of teaching but of mourning, and yet himself teaches. For he says this of a monk who is only a monk and is not also a cleric or priest. If a monk has been made a cleric, he ought to teach.

Hence the same Jerome says to Salvina:

> “Why do we write to one whom we do not know? Surely because, by reason of the office of priesthood, we love all Christians as sons [Col. 0544A], and their progress is our glory.”

The same must be understood of the decree of Pope Pius which forbids a monk, however learned he may be, to preach. For it intends this concerning one who is only a monk and does not hold the ministry of the altar. “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” But one who has not been ordained cleric or priest has not been sent to preach. Therefore a monk who does not have the ministry of the altar ought not to preach.

Let each of us, therefore, acknowledge his own dignity with humility against persons of this sort, and say: “Why do you not allow me to open my mouth in the midst of the Church? I am greater than you by a twofold fullness. For you are only a cleric, whereas I am both cleric and monk. Mary was a virgin, and John was a virgin; yet there is a greater fullness in Mary. For John was only a virgin, whereas Mary was both virgin and mother. So you are only a cleric, but I am both monk and cleric.”

But you say to me, “I am dead to the world.” Answer me, please: do you then live to the world? Therefore you are dead to God. Consider more carefully that not all the Corinthians [variant: Colossians] were monks when the Apostle said to them: “For you are dead” (Col. 3). But all Christians are dead in accordance with that saying, because they have been baptized into the death of Christ Jesus.

To say more now about this matter, venerable Father, another task prevents us, especially because we formerly composed a small work specifically on this very subject, which we do not now have at hand to send to your charity. Fare well in the Lord Jesus, maker of all creatures [Col. 0544C].

## On the Violation of Virginity

[Col. 0543]

### Question Concerning the Violation of Virginity, and Whether a Defiled Woman May Be Consecrated

[Col. 0543C]

To Lord Rupert, abbot of Deutz, distinguished by every wisdom of character and learning: I, hungering for knowledge, desire to be crowned among the sixty queens of the true Solomon on the day of joy and gladness. I write to you, O venerable among abbots, to be known more by heart than by face [Col. 0543D], and I shall be more a burden than a service to you. This I presume not from rashness or arrogance, but from confidence in the prudence and goodness of your charity.

I judged that I, N. N., would burden your fatherhood if I were to seek from you in charity those things which you generously bestow upon others unsolicited. It seems right that my littleness, when it does not know something in the sacred Scriptures, should question your so learned wisdom, whose power of reasoning I have come partly to know from great and deservedly praised works.

I therefore beg you through the Son of the Virgin to deign to write back to us whether one loses the palm of virginity—man or woman—who, by his or her own hands or those of another, or by any other means apart from natural intercourse, has drawn forth semen. [Col. 0544C] Or whether one defiled while under a vow of virginity ought, or can, be consecrated.

These, venerable Father, are the questions concerning the salvation of the soul and counsel which I desire to have resolved for me by your charity. In this you will benefit not only me but also many of both sexes [Col. 0544D] who urgently request these matters with me. And if there are points which create doubt about these questions, may your diligence carefully unravel them—points which I thought should be passed over both for brevity’s sake and because I question one who is eloquent and knows how to notice them more easily than I do.

I also ask, if it please your charity, that you would be willing to send us your *Apologetic* works, which you wrote to distinguished men. For when we came to that passage in Matthew, “Thy will be done, as …” (Matt. 6), we found the opinion of your slanderer, which my teacher wholly rejects with full freedom, and he has, as they say, entered upon your ground with both feet.

Yet although both of us had read those same books of yours while you were still at Liège [Col. 0545A]—for we had come there from Stavelot because of you and your works—we could not easily retain their whole argument. But this we remember: by subtle reasoning and reasonable subtlety you proved victorious that no diversity or duplicity can occur in the will of God [Col. 0546A].

If I obtain from you these things—small indeed to you but great to me—you may perhaps encourage me to inquire into matters concerning which your excellence may fittingly respond, and in which my own weakness and that of those like me may make progress. Farewell.

[Col. 0545]

# Book of R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, on the Violation of Virginity and Whether a Defiled Woman May Be Consecrated

## Prologue to the Treatise: In Which a Brief Question Proposed Concerning Virginity Is Said to Be Like a Mustard Seed

[Col. 0545B]

When I had received your letter, dearest brother in Christ, W., I immediately prepared to give a short answer to your question. But when I began to pour forth words, many things presented themselves to be said to the scribe receiving them by his pen, things bearing on the same meaning and seeming able to bring some benefit to readers in this matter. Therefore, as I received what came to mind and committed it to the pen, the discourse suddenly became longer than I had intended. Yet it was not a body divided, as it were, into its limbs, but rather a confused mass, since it was marked off by no chapters.

I confess that I then remembered that parabolic saying of the Lord: [Col. 0545C]

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the least of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches” (Matt. 13).

I remembered this saying, or parable, not without reason, because your question pertains to the kingdom of heaven. For you asked concerning the palm of virginity: whether it falls from a man or woman because of certain defilements, because of some rubbing and emission of semen, even though the act of sexual union or intercourse has not been performed—as must be plainly stated, since the matter itself demands it. For these are your words:

> “I beg you through the Son of the Virgin to deign to write back to us whether one loses the palm of virginity—man or woman—who [Col. 0545D], by his or her own hands or those of another, or in any other way apart from natural intercourse, has drawn forth semen.”

This matter, as I have said, indeed pertains to the kingdom of heaven, because the question concerns holy virginity, which above all grades of merits possesses the kingdom of heaven. Yet the matter seemed to me small and full of shame, and therefore it was worth no more to me than a grain of mustard seed. I began, then, to answer more slowly and carelessly.

But just as the mustard seed, “when it has grown, is greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches,” so I now say of this matter: if it is treated by one who is truly wise, the result will be “a faithful saying and worthy of acceptance” (1 Tim. 4), useful not only to you but also to many of both sexes who, as you report, urgently request this with you.

But I am not wise, as you suppose, such that these matters should be treated by me. Rather, what the wise man says in humility in Solomon, I can say truthfully of myself in fact: “I am the most foolish of men, and human wisdom is not with me. I have not learned prudence, nor have I known the knowledge of the holy ones” (Prov. 30). Nevertheless, because you adjured me, saying, “I beg you through the Son of the Virgin to deign to write back to us,” I did not dare to remain wholly silent. I too beseech the same Son of the Virgin, the flower of virginity, and the Spirit of the Lord who rests upon this flower, that he may suggest to me a true and cautious word and understanding, both in this matter and in the rest.

## Chapter I. There Are Many Kinds of Defilement Apart from Natural Intercourse; Once They Are Committed, the Palm of Virginity Is Undoubtedly Lost

Since there are many kinds of defilement by which human frailty may be contaminated or soiled, you seem to doubt whether one who falls into any of them apart from natural intercourse loses the palm of virginity. For you asked whether one loses the palm of virginity, man or woman, who by his or her own hands or those of another, or [Col. 0546D] by any other means apart from natural intercourse, draws forth semen.

But tell me: have you forgotten, or do you also doubt, that kind of fornication which the Apostle mentions, saying:

> “For their women exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature; and likewise the men also, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their desires toward one another, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the recompense due for their error” (Rom. 1).

Do you, I say, also doubt whether the palm of virginity is lost through this kind of fornication? Indeed, not only is the palm of virginity lost, but the dignity of human nature itself is destroyed, and eternal death is acquired. For “those who do such things are worthy of death,” says the same Apostle (ibid.). And in the Law the Lord himself says: “Whoever lies with a male in female intercourse shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 20).

There is also another kind of fornication, concerning which the same Lord is judge and avenger: “Whoever has intercourse with an animal,” he says, “shall surely be put to death” (Exod. 22). And again: “A woman who submits herself to any animal shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 18).

It seems to me excessive to mention these matters, had you not said, “or by any other means apart from natural intercourse” [Col. 0547B]. Nevertheless, I judge that in framing your question you thought only of those men and women whom “no temptation has overtaken except what is human” (1 Cor. 10): that is, those for whom their nature is at times troublesome through their desires, yet who are not drawn into things contrary to nature.

## Chapter II. On the Psalmist’s Saying, “All the Ways of the Lord Are Mercy and Truth”; and How, If Judged Without Mercy, Even Adultery May Be Committed by the Look of Desire Alone

In answering your question about such persons to the best of my ability, I first say to you with the Psalmist: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24 [25]). If judgment is rendered with mercy removed, how few men or women are there in whose hands the palm of virginity remains? For who shall glory that he has a chaste heart?

But, as has already been said, there is not only one way of the Lord; all his ways are at once mercy and truth. Those against whom he proceeds by truth alone are those who are unworthy of mercy; of such persons the Apostle says: “We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. 2). Likewise: “Judgment without mercy is for one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2).

God’s mercy, however, never occurs without truth; rather, the two are always companions in human salvation, as the same Psalmist says: “Mercy and truth have met together” (Ps. 84 [85]). Immediately he adds the same realities under other names: [Col. 0547D] “Righteousness and peace have kissed” (ibid.). For righteousness is truth, and peace is mercy.

And because that chapter concerns the coming of the Savior, who came to us blessed in the abundance of mercy, it is fitting to say that the very fact that God the Father “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8), he did so in mercy, in such a way that the truth of judgment was not absent from so great a work of mercy. For before God, by his prevenient grace, delivered up his own or only-begotten Son for humankind, Abraham—being tested and obedient—stretched out his hand and took the sword to sacrifice his son. But the Apostle meets this with the words: “Who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11). Truly, no one; because Abraham’s act, in first offering his son to God, was itself done by God’s giving and inspiration.

The same must be thought concerning God’s other benefits bestowed upon us—for example, when he forgives our sins. Mercy is not without the fellowship of truth, because he forgives only the penitent. But now we must come closer to the matter itself. If the question is asked according to truth without the justice of judgment—which is one of the Lord’s ways—it is plainly evident that whoever, man or woman, draws forth semen by his or her own touch or another’s loses the palm of virginity, although the seal of that virginity is not lost.

This is so true that adultery may be committed even without bodily violation. For the Lord himself says: “But I say to you, that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Who, conversely, can rightly deny the statement: “Every woman who looks at a man in order to desire him has already committed fornication with him in her heart”?

This truth is manifest, and the judgment is evidently just, because everyone is rightly judged according to his own senses and wills, and is held guilty of the sin which he wishes to commit. According to the same truth it was said: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3); and likewise: “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5; cited as John 5). This was not said of slight anger, such as may be compared to a speck, lightly clouding the eye of the mind through the stirring of hot blood; but of beam-like anger, such as Cain’s anger when he was angry and his face fell (Gen. 4), so that he plotted murder—indeed, fratricide.

But let the discourse return to the proposed subject, namely virginity. For its destruction is sufficiently brought about by will alone, when that will is made manifest by touch, defilement, or voluntary emission of semen, if, as has been said, we judge according to truth or justice without mercy.

## Chapter III. If We Are Met by Mercy, Virginity Is Judged Preserved So Long as Bodily Integrity Remains; and How the Law Supports This

But if the question is considered according to mercy, it is mercy through which the palm of virginity is reserved in such falls. Although they are grave and shameful, they nevertheless do not reach the point at which bodily integrity is broken—that is, at which the genital enclosure, where nature has placed the seal of virginity, is violated.

I do not deny, dearest brother, that there are, or have been, certain severe judges who thought that bodily enclosure was to be considered of little account in bodies lacking chastity of mind. Yet the authority of the sacred Law supports it, as follows:

> “If a man takes a wife and afterward hates her, and seeks occasions on which to dismiss her by casting a disgraceful accusation upon her, saying, ‘I took this wife and went in to her, and I did not find her a virgin,’ her father and mother shall take and bring the signs of her virginity to the elders of the city who are at the gate. And the father shall say: ‘I gave my daughter to this man as wife, and because he hates her he casts a disgraceful accusation upon her, saying: “I did not find your daughter a virgin.” But behold, these are the signs of my daughter’s virginity.’ They shall spread the garment before the elders of the city. The elders of that city shall seize the man and beat him; moreover they shall condemn him to one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl’s father, because he has cast a disgraceful accusation upon a virgin of Israel. And she shall be his wife, and he may not dismiss her all the days of his life” (Deut. 22).

This passage is obscure to chaste sensibilities, though I have set it down as appropriate testimony. For what chaste mind can patiently endure even to think how bloody traces of ruptured virginity are preserved on a cloth? Yet in this place too may the Wisdom of God console us, crying concerning such scriptural writing: “For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclus. 24); and then: “Those who elucidate me shall have eternal life” (ibid.).

With God’s help, insofar as I could, I have done this in those little works which your benevolence, in highly valuing their argument, testifies contain wisdom received by me from God—would that this were true! You will find there how I attempted to elucidate this chapter, what mystery of the Spirit, and what brightness I drew forth from the dark cavern of this letter; there I also treated certain other matters from the book of Deuteronomy.

For the present question, this alone matters: know that although severe judges consider that enclosure of little account unless chastity of mind is maintained, nevertheless, so long as the body is so constituted that, when a man approaches, such signs can be drawn forth from it by the force of intercourse, she is a virgin. For you have here: “Behold, these are the signs of my daughter’s virginity”; and “the elders of that city shall seize the man and beat him, moreover condemning him to one hundred shekels of silver because he cast a disgraceful accusation upon a virgin of Israel.”

## Chapter IV. Virginity, Though Defiled by Some Touch While Bodily Integrity Remains, Even to the Emission of Semen, May Be Like the Girl of Whom the Lord Said: “She Is Not Dead, but Sleeps”

But any woman of this kind, whose flesh, though in some measure defiled, has nevertheless not been ruptured or opened, may have looked upon a man in order to desire him, just as a man may have looked upon a woman in order to desire her. She has therefore lost the palm of virginity if, as has been said, judgment is made without mercy according to God’s truth [Col. 0549D].

But if, as has likewise been said, mercy is sought, mercy knows and is able to excuse such danger or death of virginity, and to declare against the malicious spirits who mock that virginity has not died there, according to that mystical example in the Gospel:

> “When Jesus came into the house of the ruler and saw the flute-players and the tumultuous crowd, he said: ‘Depart, for the girl is not dead, but sleeps.’ And they mocked him” (Matt. 9).

Certainly he did not say this concerning that young man who was being carried out dead through the gate of the city, nor concerning Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb. He said it only concerning the girl who lay dead in the house: “The girl is not dead, but sleeps.”

Thus, where virginity has been corrupted by the act of sexual union, and where the act of union itself has become habitual, the righteous judge God by no means says that virginity is not dead. He says this only where the flesh has been corrupted in mind alone while still remaining bodily intact. If Jesus is truly invoked through penitence, he can say: “Virginity is not dead,” although both may have been defiled.

It is one thing for a garment to be rotten and torn because of its rottenness; it is another thing for it to be disfigured by some stain but nevertheless whole. Yet how great loss or injury does this stain bring? Certainly very great, unless it is cleansed by the great lamentation of penitence. For who does not know that eternal life, the country or region of the living, the kingdom of heaven, is one temple—a holy temple and holy of holies—into which nothing defiled ought to be admitted?

Therefore virginity defiled in whatever way, while the flesh remains intact, should labor through repentance to cleanse every stain of defilement, and should have with it bright works of charity, mindful of the Scripture saying: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9).

## Chapter V. Humility Is Especially Necessary for One Who Desires the Palm of Virginity

Meanwhile, lest virginity be not only struck by the judgment from above but even, when the door of the heavenly wedding has been shut, be found outside like a foolish virgin, it should lay hold, along with the lamp of conscience and the oil of charity, of that supreme defense: humility [Col. 0550C]. That is, it should in some manner not look to the palm which you named, but should sigh only for pardon from the mercy of God.

What I say, I myself scarcely understand; nor do I think anyone can understand it except one whom the teaching of the Spirit of loving-kindness has imbued. The knowledge of true humility is a subtle discipline. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ declares that no other person is the teacher or example of this discipline but himself: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). He immediately adds: “And you shall find rest for your souls” (ibid.).

Therefore, dearest brother, many souls do not find rest because they have not yet learned to be meek and humble of heart. Therefore virginity, in many bodies worn down by frequent storms, is endangered because it has not borne upon itself the sweet burden of holy humility. Sometimes too, as lightning strikes the highest mountains, so by heavenly judgment virginity is entirely betrayed through the consummation of corruption, because it is exalted in its own eyes and despises the other states of mortal life as lower.

But whoever, man or woman, has learned to be meek and humble of heart finds rest for the soul, because there are many temptations which cannot even find one hidden in the deep valley of humility. “There rests the weighty people, among whom I shall praise you” (Ps. 34 [35]), says Christ himself, who handed down this discipline when he said, “Learn from me.” Apart from him, there has not been and is not anyone who could teach a human being such knowledge, so that the person might know how to be meek and humble of heart.

Truly, one who has learned this—even if in this life he does not yet find complete rest for the soul by living free from all temptations—nevertheless has such labor greatly eased. Hence the Psalmist, pronouncing him blessed, says: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law, that you may give him relief from evil days” (Ps. 93 [94]).

## Chapter VI. On the Humility of the Blessed Virgin Mary: How It Was the Cause of Her Vow of Virginity

[^c0052-321]: The printed note marker is present without corresponding note content in the supplied text.

[^c0052-322]: The printed note marker is present without corresponding note content in the supplied text.

Our Lady Saint Mary was wonderfully instructed in such learning. For before all mortals—indeed, before every creature, angelic as well as human—she was meek and humble of heart, as she herself testifies, magnifying the Lord and rejoicing in him, and saying: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1). In this brief but deeply resonant utterance she revealed to us the great treasure of her conscience. Truly, if we have ears to hear, we can in some measure perceive what reason she had for making a vow of virginity, for which she had no example.

For if anyone should say that she chose virginity because marriage and the bearing of children appeared to her a lowly condition and a contemptible life, this is altogether contrary to the truth of the profession already cited: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” Of many persons devoted to virginity, there should be no doubt that their keeping of virginity pleased them because they despised the sacrament of marriage which God joined together. It must be thought that some possess such humility that, although the Apostle says of such persons, “of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews 11), they, on the contrary, deem themselves unworthy of the world. For although they share the same purpose as those of whom the world was not worthy, nevertheless each man or woman, in a marvellous manner, contends and judges in the silent conscience concerning his or her own person, deeming himself or herself unworthy of the world.

What else should we think of that most blessed Virgin, who said—and said truly—“He has regarded the humility of his handmaid”? I confess to you, dearest brother, that both I and some whom I have known, who have affection and admiration for that Blessed Virgin, hold this opinion: that she judged there to be no man’s body in the world whose companionship [Col. 0551D] or marriage she could consider herself worthy to share. At the very least, it is certain that incomparable—and, after the humility of God, greatest—was and is the humility of that handmaid of the Lord, in which so admirable a virginity could rest and not be exalted.

I have not said this without purpose in relation to the present subject, because it is fitting for those men or women who have undertaken the purpose of imitating her virginity first to strive to imitate the example of that same true humility, if they desire to inherit the fruit of her womb, who is God himself and the Son of God: the Word born from the heart of the Father, the Word made flesh from the womb of so great a Virgin. For they cannot otherwise escape perfectly the defilements of the flesh, through which the palm of virginity is lost, except by following the humility [Col. 0552A] which the Lord regarded in her, and by meditating upon the faith of the Word which the heart of God the Father uttered into her mind and into her womb (Psalm 44).

## CHAPTER VII. That where virginity lacks humility, an example was present [as printed: *inerat*] in Dinah, whom a corrupter violated while she wandered.

Therefore the palm of virginity comes from humility, which conquers all things. But the fruit of this palm is the Word of the Father—whence what has been said, and still must be said. May it be of use to one willing to read it for avoiding the contaminations concerning which you questioned me in the school of the Word.

A faithful and prudent virgin must always devote herself to this Word; for without the Word of God virginity is empty and is vainly so called, just as a lame man vainly possesses handsome calves. “The soul of the idle is always in desires” (Proverbs 21). And how shall such a soul, extending itself outward and unable to bear sitting quietly at the Lord’s feet in the hearing of God’s Word, endure? How shall its virginity live, or be safe and unharmed? For an opportunity is given to the crafty tempter, whom virginity bereft of God’s Word will not be able to escape by its own strength. It is like Dinah, daughter of Jacob, who went out to see the daughters of the land and was forcibly violated by the corrupter Shechem, son of Hamor.

“Shechem” means “shouldered,” Hamor “ass,” and Dinah is interpreted “cause.” Therefore some proud son of folly is Shechem, the son of Hamor; and every soul which, because of its own wandering, is itself the cause of its corruption, is Dinah. For if she had remained within, where the angel found the Virgin and exemplar of virgins, blessed Mary, [Col. 0552C] she would not be corrupted by the evil examples of the proud and foolish. Therefore, lest virginity encounter the mire of the streets and the filth of asses, such as are understood by the name Hamor, let it remain within; and, lest it be barren and vain, let it receive something of the fruit of the virginal womb of blessed Mary by governing or by hearing.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the bridal song, and that the good Word uttered by the Father’s heart is the proper inheritance of holy virginity.

You know, brother, how often, on account of some person who has passed along an undefiled path through the defilements of the flesh, holy virginity is celebrated in the Church; with what dignity, with what beauty, that most lovely bridal song resounds in varied tones from the clear voices of singers [Col. 0552D], rejoicing with holy virginity and with its flower, Christ the Son of God.

There the person of the Father is not absent. In order that he may strengthen ever more firmly, through growing desire, the souls of virgins still living in the flesh in the love of their virginal purpose, he tells how well and how wonderfully he has wrought in holy virginity. For he says: “My heart has uttered a good Word; I speak my works to the king; my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Psalm 44).

When some lesser or greater choral musician (*choraula*) has sung these words—or indeed when the entire choir together suddenly resounds in the person of God the Father—another precentor, either alone or followed by others, says to the king and to the virginity of which he himself is the Son: “Grace is poured out upon your lips” [Col. 0553A] (Psalm 44), and so forth. Why is this done, except that the virginal soul may be set ever more ablaze with heavenly desire to maintain its purpose?

Finally, this is evident also from the fact that a chant suddenly sounds in the person of the Father, as though he were inclining himself to the ear of the faithful soul, whom he wishes to remain his daughter-in-law, and giving fatherly counsel, saying: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (ibid.), and so forth.

When all these splendid utterances of such a song are set forth in commemoration of any person who has clung to the Word of God in a virginal purpose, and thereby conquered the world, this is undoubtedly done and intended: that virginity still living in the flesh may deserve to become a participant in that same [Col. 0553B] Word whom Blessed Mary conceived wholly and bore, and may receive something from him by which it may be safe. It is as though someone were reminded of an inheritance or a possession belonging especially to him, lest he neglect what is rightfully his. For truly the Word of the Lord is the proper inheritance of holy virginity; and it befits that soul in which virginal grace flourishes especially to dwell upon this good and to know the Word of the Lord more clearly.

The clearest judgment in this matter is the brilliance of John the Evangelist, the apostle beloved by the Lord, who throughout the whole texture of his discourse sufficiently shows with how open eyes, like an eagle, he beheld the rays of the eternal sun.

## CHAPTER IX [Col. 0553C]. How not John alone, but also the ancient saints to whom the Word of the Lord came, are rightly called and are virgins.

But if someone objects that the holy ancient writers of the Old Testament—Moses and David, and likewise the other patriarchs and prophets—to whom without doubt the Word of the Lord came, and whose entire Scripture is canonical because they did not learn from man but the Holy Spirit spoke through them, were not virgins in body: that is another matter.

For all those were truly virgins according to that time; that is, they were virgins in the manner in which the Word of God required them to be. This must be observed carefully and with subtle discernment: the Word of God dealt reasonably with human beings, so as not to require bodily virginity from anyone before [Col. 0553D] he himself became flesh and showed forth the integrity of the flesh most worthy of himself. When he came to the incarnation and by his incarnation in some measure honoured sex, being himself a man born of woman, then at last the Holy Spirit judged—and inspired the minds of many—that it was fitting that the sons or daughters of such a Bridegroom should preserve, together with virginity of mind, virginity also of body.

Before that, the Word of the Lord itself required wholly this: that its ministers should be virgins in virginity of mind. And thus all who wrote the holy canonical Scripture were truly virgins, because “they were not defiled with women” (Revelation 14)—that is, with idols or carved images of neighbouring peoples, into which the children of Israel very often fell, especially through desire for women. [Col. 0534A]

Since this is certain of all, doubt remains concerning Solomon alone, whose soul was deprived of its virginity through women, so that he committed fornication against the Lord God and served idols. He wrote excellently many great and profound mysteries of the Word of the Lord, but it is uncertain whether he wrote before or after the already mentioned loss of his soul’s virginity. Some maintain that, after his fall and subsequent repentance, he wrote everything—that is, his three books. But since this has no authority from the canonical Scriptures, it is rejected as readily as it is asserted.

For although in Ecclesiastes he is said to have declared, “At last, having turned back, I did penance,” as Blessed Jerome testifies in his commentary on Ezekiel, it does not necessarily follow that he wrote the aforementioned books after his repentance. Nor is the very wording, “At last, having turned back, I did penance,” found in the translation of the same Blessed Jerome. Hence it may be understood that he dictated that commentary on Ezekiel before translating the books of Solomon himself.

Thus, as has been said, doubt concerns Solomon alone: whether, while his soul was still virgin, he became a minister of the Word of the Lord by writing. For concerning all the rest it ought to be certain that their souls never committed fornication against the true God in order to follow a foreign god; and in this way they remained virgins. This was truly great amid so many fornications of those times, amid so many abominations and idolatries, not only of foreign nations but also—what was more dangerous—of carnal Israelites. [Col. 0554C] Let these remarks suffice concerning the authorities of the holy Old Scripture.

## CHAPTER X. On the writers of the New Testament: how all were virgins; and on the apostle Peter, who had previously been married.

Concerning those who wrote the New Testament, this is certain: all remained virgins in mind, as did those earlier writers; in body some were virgins, while all remained entirely continent after receiving knowledge of the Word incarnate from the Virgin.

They remained virgins in mind, I say, because they never allowed in themselves the defect of any heresy. In body, some were virgins; others, as has been said, were wholly continent, because those who had already known wives left them altogether, and those who had not known wives did not afterwards seek them. Since through the mouths of all of them the Holy Spirit uttered luminous and lofty testimonies to the Word of God, it is plain that more luminous and loftier are the things he spoke through those who remained virgins in mind and body. Of these, the aforementioned John is the best-known.

Paul also, the chosen vessel, almost gives us to understand concerning himself that he lived in virginal flesh. For when he was giving counsel concerning virgins, among other things relevant to this counsel, he said: “I would, however, that all men were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7).

Perhaps someone is silently troubled by a grave scruple when so much is preached concerning bodily virginity—especially on account of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who was certainly married before he followed our Lord when he called him. What then? Is his crown less than that of any of the apostles, when he himself is their prince? Does he possess a less illustrious palm? I do not think devout and religious ears can patiently endure the assertion that, because of that marriage, he is less crowned in heaven than the virgin John; for indeed it is not so. The grace of God is not bound by such a law that, especially in such a person, he could not crown a virginal soul equally with the virginity of body and soul which he crowned in John.

## CHAPTER XI. Again on the same subject, and on the statement previously cited that a virgin cannot be crowned after a fall.

But here we encounter what the blessed and illustrious man Jerome, instructing a holy virgin toward caution, says among other things:

> I shall speak boldly: although God can do all things, he cannot crown a virgin after her fall. He does indeed wish to free her from punishment, but he cannot crown one who has been defiled.

If anyone is unsettled by this, let him know that this was said—or could have been said—not of virgins entering into the union or honourable marriage-bed of lawful marriage, which, as the Apostle says, is undefiled; but of virgins falling into fornication through unlawful desire. Such persons are rightly said to have fallen.

Therefore one must carefully distinguish in what sense he spoke. He did not say, “God cannot raise or crown a virgin after the union of lawful marriage”; rather, he said, “He cannot raise a virgin after a fall; he cannot crown one who has been defiled.” What wise person would say of a woman who is or has been lawfully married that she has suffered a fall or has been defiled—especially when she made no unlawful vow of virginity for which she could be accused as guilty of breach of faith?

There, where the crime of fornication is proved, fall and defilement are rightly proclaimed. For truly, concerning those lawfully married, just as it is rightly said, “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matthew 19), so likewise it must rightly be said: those whom God or God’s law has joined have neither fallen nor been defiled; rather, theirs is honourable marriage and an undefiled bed (Hebrews 13).

Thus anyone with reason readily at hand understands that the aforementioned statement—“God cannot raise a virgin after a fall; he cannot crown one who has been defiled”—was firmly said, or could be said, for this reason: God cannot be unjust. To free from punishment belongs to mercy; not to crown one who has been defiled belongs to justice. But no justice opposes God’s crowning holy continence after marital union, since no divine or human law condemns persons lawfully married.

Therefore, when crowned virginity is proclaimed in Blessed John or in any others, let no suspicion trouble anyone concerning Blessed Peter or similar persons, as though the just and omnipotent God ought not or could not crown them likewise. Otherwise, if virginity is crowned nowhere except where the flesh remains intact, the Apostle spoke in vain not only to those with intact bodies but to the whole Church: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

## CHAPTER XII. That in the virginity of the female sex divinity wrought more and more wondrously.

Virginity is indeed beautiful and precious in both sexes; nevertheless, in the female sex it is more beautiful and more precious. For in the virginity of the female sex the omnipotence of divinity wrought more abundantly [Col. 0556B] and more wonderfully, according to the above-mentioned song of the bridal chamber, where the person of the Father thus chants: “My heart has uttered a good Word; I speak my works to the king; my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Psalm 44).

I dwell on this gladly, and I seem to add something beyond measure to your question. My purpose is that holy virginity may in some degree know its own nobility and may not bring to shame, by the contrivances about which you asked me, the grace of its palm.

Therefore, when we meditate upon the work signified by the verses cited, first, just as we understand the good Word of God the Father to be the Son, so by his tongue we recognize the Holy Spirit. For he himself, appearing above the apostles of Christ in tongues of fire, makes us understand that he is that tongue of which the person of the Father says, “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.” He is both one tongue and many tongues, because he is both one Spirit and the seven Spirits [Col. 0556C] of God: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

It was a great and splendid work that God the Father, through such a tongue of his, as through the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, swiftly placed his Word in the minds of the apostles, so that men who had until then been unlettered and ignorant suddenly became wise and understanding, learned in law and strong, knowing and devout, founded upon the beginning of wisdom, which is the fear of the Lord.

That was indeed a great work in virginal souls of the male sex; but he did something much greater, more splendid, and more wonderful in a virginal soul and a virginal womb of the female sex, when the Holy Spirit came upon blessed Mary and, through the operation of that Holy Spirit, the wondrous Virgin conceived in mind and womb the whole substance of the good Word.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the incarnation of the Word of God, by which God honoured the virginity of the female sex, according to the aforesaid song.

The praiseworthy Father rightly rejoices and glories in that wonderful work, saying: “My heart has uttered a good Word; I speak my works to the king; my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Psalm 44).

This may rightly be understood by comparison with some good and wise man who might say: “I did not wish my wisdom to remain hidden; but, having taken a well-prepared and finely polished skin of sheep or calf, and using a pen, I carefully wrote down the understanding or knowledge which I had kept in my silent heart, so that any others who were teachable and well-disposed might see and read it—persons whom the desirable treasure resting in the mouth of a wise man can benefit.”

According to this comparison, the heading of the psalm is understood to say that God the Father acted thus. For, being omnipotent, he formed the human nature—that is, the human body and rational soul—in the womb of the most holy Virgin with omnipotent power, and polished it perfectly. That is, he caused it to be conceived so that this little skin of our nature had nothing rough or hairy from the antiquity of original sin.

Then, using his tongue—that is, his Spirit, the wondrous craftsman—as the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, he wholly inscribed in that creature, namely in the rational soul, his entire Word, the good Word, his wisdom, wisdom coeternal with himself, [Col. 0557B] so swiftly, fully, and truly that nothing was lacking to it from all that treasure which rested, and still rests, in the heart of that wise Father.

For although it was introduced into that creature, nevertheless the whole Word remained and continues in the Father’s heart, far more surely and steadfastly than your verse remains in your heart after you have written it upon wax or parchment. This inscription was that utterance of God which he had introduced beforehand: “I speak my works to the king.” To what king, indeed, except to the assumed man? For this was accomplished there in our nature: the person of God the Father performs no work of which that assumed man does not know, to whom he thus spoke his works.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the saying: “And let him who is filthy be filthy still.”

[Col. 0545B]

I have said these things for the glory of holy virginity in the female sex, so that that sex may know how greatly divinity honoured its virginity in so wonderful a work. And let both sexes, knowing this nobility of their purpose, reject the baseness of such defilements, on account of which this discourse was begun; and let them not despise fear, because it is said: “And let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22). Again: “He who despises small things shall fall little by little” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

Whether a person has admitted greater or lesser defilements, contempt is exceedingly destructive to every soul. For it must be understood that it is one thing to sin through ignorance, another through weakness, another through pride—that is, through contempt.

If a person sins through ignorance, and is such that, once the truth of the matter is known, he abandons the sin itself, God quickly comes to the aid of that ignorance, whether through a vision or through Scripture, as we have in the case of Abimelech: “Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” And he said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation?” And God said to him: “I too know that you did this with a simple heart, and therefore I kept you from sinning against me, and I did not permit you to touch her” (Genesis 20).

But if a person sins through weakness, so that he can say: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind [Col. 0558A] and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7), then merciful God overlooks it while waiting for repentance, as we have from the book of Wisdom: “You have mercy upon all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking the sins of men for the sake of repentance” (Wisdom 11).

But if he sins with pride and contempt, it is deservedly said of him: “Let him who is filthy be filthy still.” And in the Psalm: “The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek” (Psalm 10)—that is, he will not correct him in mercy because he is greatly angered. And of such persons the Apostle said: “Therefore God handed them over to passions of dishonour” (Romans 1); that is, he abandoned them and did not free them from passions of dishonour, from which he deigns to free us, his humble servants, whether we are in ignorance or in weakness. [Col. 0558B]

## CHAPTER XV. Whether, or how, she who has been defiled while in a holy purpose ought or can be consecrated.

You wrote me another question: whether she who has been defiled while committed to virginity ought or can be consecrated. I answer you concerning this that it is plainly adultery when one who has already made a vow or undertaken a purpose to be Christ’s bride is defiled. Nevertheless, in Jeremiah we read the Lord saying:

> It is commonly said: If a man sends away his wife, and she departs from him and takes another husband, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have committed fornication with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you.

Since the Lord says this, I do not dare to say that she who has departed from her bridegroom Christ in the manner just described ought not or cannot be consecrated.

Yet the order of consecration differs somewhat. She who has preserved the seal of virginity, when she receives the sacred veil, stands with uncovered head and unveiled face to behold the glory of the Lord; she receives the ring as a sign of her first fidelity and publicly says: “My Lord Jesus Christ has betrothed me with his ring and adorned me as a bride with a crown.” Again: “He placed a sign upon my face, that I may admit no lover except him.”
