These insignia are not performed for one who, after living in the world [Col. 0558D] and knowing a man, comes to conversion and receives the sacred veil. Rather, with her head covered and without a ring, she puts on the sacred veil, receiving the grace of the secular order—that is, the order of widows. She who has been defiled in a holy purpose gains no small benefit if, returning to her husband Christ, she is received in this manner.

## CHAPTER XVI. Again on the same matter, and on the distinction concerning hidden crimes in the male sex according to the canons.

Yet if no one knows of her defilement except him to whom perhaps she has offered a secret and voluntary confession, I confess to you that I do not dare determine that she ought not or cannot be consecrated with the full consecration.

For in the male sex the decrees of the saints reserve a great place not only for pardon but also for grace, where sin has not been committed in such a way that the public knows it and the person is considered infamous. For example, if adultery has been perpetrated, publicly reported, or established by witnesses in a court of law, such a person ought not to serve in sacred orders, lest he cause scandal to the people and render the sacred ministry contemptible.

But if no one knows this except God and the person to whom it is revealed by secret and voluntary confession, it has been cautiously and mercifully allowed that after repentance—still secret—that person may nevertheless be admitted to the sacred mysteries. This accords with the example of David, who, doing penance, not only hopes for pardon but presumes that the grace of prophetic teaching which he had possessed will be restored, saying: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the impious shall be converted to you” (Psalm 50).

Knowing that you have read, or can read, this distinction in the decrees of the Fathers, and especially those of the great Leo, I have set down only its sense briefly. My intention is to suggest that an equal measure of mercy or grace may come also upon the weaker sex, where she can say of her fall, known to God alone and not making her infamous: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” (ibid.). Yet I dare determine nothing, lest I be called contrary to blessed Jerome, who, as I recalled above, says so firmly that a virgin cannot be raised after a fall or crowned when defiled.

## CHAPTER XVII. On her who has been defiled by force, and how the authority of the sacred law defends her.

But again, reason perceives and sacred law decrees [Col. 0560A] that a girl who has been defiled by force ought to suffer nothing. For thus it is written in the book of Deuteronomy:

> If a man finds in the field a betrothed girl and, seizing her, lies with her, he alone shall die; the girl shall suffer nothing and is not guilty of death. For as a robber rises against his brother and kills his life, so the girl also suffered. She was alone in the field, she cried out, and no one was present to rescue her.  
> (Deuteronomy 22)

Likewise, a faithful virgin says in her suffering and confession of Christ: “The body is never defiled except by the consent of the mind. For if you cause me to be violated against my will, chastity will be doubled for me unto a crown. For chastity suffers a violator as it suffers a serpent, a robber, a barbarian.”

Therefore, at least in such a case—that is, of one who has suffered violence and has been defiled—it must be granted that she can be crowned, and consequently that she may be consecrated as though undefiled. Although blessed Jerome made no exception or qualification regarding the preceding case—that is, a secret fall which caused no scandal in God’s Church and made the person not infamous—let the wise judge.

It seems to me an inequality of mercy if the inferior female sex is not treated with the same condescension as the stronger, that is, the male sex: namely, if a cleric who has fallen secretly may, by concession of the canons, even be admitted to the priesthood, while a girl who has secretly fallen may not be admitted to the consecration customary to her purpose.

[Col. 0559]

# THE RING, OR DIALOGUE BETWEEN A CHRISTIAN AND A JEW, OF RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ.

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

I had long known, most reverend father and venerable abbot, what you now say; I knew it, and felt it with a wounded heart to be so, as you have at last observed: that what I have written [Note: [Col. 0559] See the *Apology for Rupert*.] or write is not without the Spirit of God, and that all the objections made against our books by men of ill will have sprung from the root of bitterness.

But how could I know this except from the glorious testimony of conscience? “For,” says the Apostle, “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1). Since, then, I knew this—and could even, by certain indications, refer it to the glory of God, showing where, when, and how I received the visitation of the Spirit, who breathes where he wills and distributes to each as he wills—ought I to yield to that envy of the devil, as you call it, and to the bitterness of men of ill will? Was it fitting for me to cease from praise or from the ministry of the divine Word, and to hold in silence within myself the little grace bestowed from above?

Certainly, even if I wished it, I could by no means be silent. To say nothing meanwhile of friendly persons of good will—of whom I now have no fewer, including yourself, who urge me toward the work long desired—to say nothing, I say, of people who do not allow me to sleep, God himself, the Word of God, does not permit the door of my mouth to be closed against him. In certain ways he exercises over me the right of his teaching office, so that, even if I wished, I could not be silent concerning him.

I do not dare call myself unhappy even in this respect, because through certain experiences I have learned in some measure what that force is beneath which blessed and holy persons are overcome. One of the greatest of these, Jeremiah, after first saying: “The word of the Lord became to me reproach and derision all day long; and I said: I will not remember him, nor speak in his name” (Jeremiah 20), immediately adds: “And it became in my heart as a burning fire” (ibid.).

The Psalmist likewise, in the same sense, after saying, “I set a guard upon my mouth while the sinner stood against me; I became mute and was humbled, and kept silence even from good things” (Psalm 38), immediately indicates his distress in these words: “And my sorrow was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze” (ibid.). And immediately: “I spoke,” he says, “with my tongue” (ibid.)—understood: “I, who had resolved to be silent.”

Truly, I have learned the sense of these words better by experience than I could have learned it by reading; and for this reason I too have spoken until now, and shall speak with my tongue, with a brow hitherto unyielding and a hard face like adamant. But leaving aside these things, which perhaps seem to breathe excessive confidence—although humble confidence, moderated by humility, is more useful—I shall now enter upon the matter, the work which you have long awaited and long urgently demanded.

Since you ask it, I must construct a certain single combat of Christian against Jew, so that the whole duel may proceed in dialogue: the Christian inviting the Jew to evangelical faith, and the Jew, as far as he can, striking back against the Christian from the letter of the Law and from his own understanding. For you think, and perhaps not without reason, that this disputation, even if it is not necessary for veterans, may at least benefit our recruits, when they find here assembled from the multitude of the Law and Prophets, and indeed from all the holy Scriptures, certain materials by which, armed as with weapons, they may confidently overthrow the Jewish understanding that exalts itself against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10).

I shall undertake this, as you wish and urgently require, insofar as God grants and as it proves possible while my mind is occupied with other matters. And, just as by every means I shall be able faithfully to arm the Christian, so I shall carefully see to it that the Jew is equipped with every objection. This spectacle is fitting for faithful boys; perhaps it is not necessary for old men, nor have they leisure or pleasure to attend or direct their minds to such a contest, since in their minds the foundation of Christian faith has been well founded upon the rock and stands firm.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0561]

[Col. 0561A] **CHRISTIAN.** I, baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, have washed away in myself the stain of original sin, the guilt of the disobedience of the first man. And in place of the food of the forbidden tree which that first man ate, I have received, by God’s gift, the body and blood of Christ from the tree of the cross; and by eating and drinking I attain the grace and glory of adoption as a son of God.

**JEW.** I, circumcised with the circumcision which God—the God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob—delivered by his authority, am the firstborn son, as God himself says to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Let my son go, that he may serve me; and you refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your firstborn son” (Exodus 4).

[Col. 0561B] **CHRISTIAN.** I know, and shall tell you, the reason or benefit for which I ought to have been baptized, or was necessarily baptized. You first tell the reason or benefit, if you know it, for which you were circumcised. For I am prepared to show you that the wound of circumcision cannot at this time make you a son. Now recite the very ordinance of God, the ordinance concerning circumcision.

**JEW.** God said to Abraham my father: “And you therefore shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is the covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you. An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you; every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought, shall be circumcised, including anyone who is not of your stock. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall have that soul cut off from his people, because he has made my covenant void” (Genesis 17).

CHRIST. I have long since read and reread this tradition; I have revered it and shall never cease to revere it, because it was a tradition of God. But both you and I must consider the intention of Him who gave it, according to this saying: when He had said, “You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin,” He added and said, “That it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” First I ask you what a covenant is, and what is called a sign of a covenant. Tell me, then: what is a covenant?

[Col. 0562B] JEW. A covenant is an agreement of friendship, a union of hearts loving one another mutually.

CHRIST. You have answered rightly. God, the Creator, entered into covenant with His creature; God was united to the man Abraham through friendship, and He willed circumcision of the flesh to be the sign of that mutual covenant. Tell me, then, what or what kind of covenant that was, as a sign of which God, entering covenant with His human friend, gave circumcision. For thus it is written: God so loved that circumcision should be a sign of the covenant.

JEW. What else, except that our father Abraham was a good man, a holy man, and by living holily pleased God?

CHRIST. I do not want you to answer me from your own heart; rather answer me from what is drawn from Sacred Scripture itself. It is indeed true that Abraham was a good man [Col. 0563A]; but I seek a definite passage in Scripture’s own words, by which we may receive unquestionable testimony of his goodness or holiness. Why do you stand still? Why are you silent and hesitant? I will tell you: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV; Rom. IV; Gal. III). This was neither said nor written of any work of his—that it was reckoned to him as righteousness—except this alone: that he believed.

JEW. It must be conceded; for it is plainly so.

CHRIST. “On that day,” Scripture says, “the Lord made a covenant with Abraham” (Gen. XV); and then, not fewer than fourteen years later, the Lord appeared to him and said what you have already recalled: “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise [Col. 0563B] the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” Therefore the covenant is one thing and the sign of the covenant another, because the covenant is the reward of faith. For through faith Abraham was justified before God, and God entered into covenant with Abraham; but circumcision is the sign of the covenant, commanded after so many years. Therefore, when God says, “My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant,” do not understand Him as saying, “You shall circumcise your flesh for ever.” The covenant is indeed everlasting, but circumcision cannot be practised for ever, since not even the succession of those circumcising is everlasting.

JEW. Yet it is necessary for eternal salvation, because He says: “The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall have that soul cut off from his people, [Col. 0563C] because he has made my covenant void.”

CHRIST. It was necessary as long as it had to be practised.

JEW. Was it established for a time, or commanded to be observed for a time? Or is God, who commanded it to be observed, changeable? What then do you mean when you say, “As long as it had to be practised”?

CHRIST. Recall what has already been settled between us: namely, that circumcision is not the covenant or compact, but the sign of the compact or covenant; and that father Abraham was justified through faith before circumcision, and was made God’s friend.

JEW. I do recall it; but nevertheless it is established that circumcision was given without any determination of time [Col. 0563D] by the eternal and unchangeable God.

CHRIST. Therefore circumcision is “a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV). But now I ask you about the substance of that faith itself: in what did Abraham have faith? What did he believe? What matter was set before him in which he was found faithful? Why do you again stand still? Why do you hesitate? I shall tell you: the promise of the Seed in whom all nations would be blessed was the first and final article of his faith. For when God first spoke to him: “Go out,” He said, “from your country and from your kindred,” and so forth, ending with, “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XII), Abraham already believed then; for he went out as the Lord commanded him. But after the labours of pilgrimage and waiting, when the Lord appeared to him a fourth time [Col. 0564A] and said, “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you are able; so shall your seed be” (Gen. XV), only then does Scripture say: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (ibid.).

JEW. What was that Seed? Or what do you wish me to understand by what you recount: “And in you,” or, as it is said elsewhere, “And in your seed,” “all nations,” or “families of the earth,” shall be blessed?

CHRIST. Ask your father, and he will tell you—your father Jacob, whose father he is in the flesh, in which you glory: “He who is to be sent shall come, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). What he calls “the expectation of the nations,” understand here as “the blessing of the nations”; and understand this blessing to be remission of sins, because sin is a curse, through which [Col. 0564B] death entered this world (Rom. V). Therefore that Seed of Abraham is the Messiah, whom your fathers awaited; and in this Seed Abraham believed, and his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness. For the merit of this righteousness and faith God made a covenant with him, and God willed circumcision to be the sign of that covenant.

JEW. If circumcision, as you say, is a sign of the covenant or of faith, why was it placed in a part of the body which is not visible? For a sign, or that which is set as a sign, ought to be put where it can be seen. Why then was the sign not placed rather on the face, or the ear, or in some visible part of the body?

CHRIST. Nothing is unseen by God; rather, all things are naked and laid open before His eyes (Heb. IV). It was therefore better and [Col. 0564C] more reasonable that, since faith concerned the Seed who was to come, the sign of faith should be placed in that part of the body through which seed is naturally transmitted. So Noah also, who was likewise justified through faith—for he believed God when He said, “Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood” (Gen. VI), and so forth, while nearly all the rest remained unbelieving—received a fitting sign according to the character of his faith. Therefore Scripture says of him that he was righteous and perfect, walking with God (ibid.). For because he unquestionably believed God saying, “Behold, I will bring floodwaters upon the earth,” and again, “I will rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights” (Gen. VII), and made the ark as the Lord commanded, he received a sign [Col. 0564D] not anywhere whatever, but in the clouds of heaven, from which rain comes down, as he had believed. For God says: “Behold, I establish my covenant with you, and this is the sign of the covenant between me and you: I shall place my bow in the clouds of heaven” (Gen. IX).

JEW. What need was there, as you say, for circumcision to be given as a sign of the covenant?

CHRIST. Why do you ask this? Ask at the same time what need there was, or what benefit it served, for the rainbow—the sign of the covenant—to be placed in the clouds of heaven. But if you ask this, not I but God Himself will answer: “I shall see it,” He says, “and remember the everlasting covenant, so that there may no longer be waters of a flood to destroy all flesh” (ibid.).

JEW. Is God, then, forgetful, so that He needs to be reminded by a memorial sign?

[Col. 0565A] CHRIST. He is not forgetful; but He is rightly said to remember when He causes us to remember.

JEW. I agree; for He also said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXII), though He had known this beforehand, just as He knows all things.

CHRIST. Therefore, if you ask why circumcision was given as a sign of the covenant, He Himself will answer you—if not in the same words, yet in the same sense: “I shall see the sign and remember my covenant, which because of faith I made with Abraham, because he believed in the Seed whom I promised. I shall remember,” I say, “and I shall cause Abraham’s descendants to remember, so that they may be certain that I shall not cease to be faithful and true until I fulfil the word of promise.”

JEW. What is the point of all this? Where are you tending, or where do you wish [Col. 0565B] to lead me?

CHRIST. Did I not previously propose to demonstrate to you that the wound of circumcision cannot at this time make you that son of whom God said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son; let my son go, that he may sacrifice to me” (Exod. IV)? Wait a little; we shall soon come to that. I further tell you that God, who cannot lie, was not content merely to give circumcision as the sign of His promise and covenant, but added an oath to His promise in these words: “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son, I will bless you, and in your Seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). For the faithful God desired that people should be certain [Col. 0565C] of the immovability of His purpose, and therefore, together with the aforesaid sign of the covenant, He also introduced an oath, swearing by Himself because He had no greater by whom to swear (Heb. VI). Behold, He has fulfilled what He promised; He has not forgotten what He swore: God is justified in His words, as David prays (Ps. L), and faithful in all His words, as the same man says (Ps. CXLIV), because from Abraham’s Seed the Messiah, who is called Christ, was born, and in this Seed all nations have long since been blessed.

JEW. How many do not seek this blessing; how many throughout the world despise him whom you call Christ! How then do you say that he is that Seed in whom, as was promised [Col. 0565D] to Abraham, all nations or families of the earth shall be blessed?

CHRIST. Was this promised to Abraham: that all human beings would be blessed in his Seed? Certainly not; rather, all nations, all families—that is, whoever and whatever sort of persons from all nations and families believe—so that in this blessing there is neither, nor is there a distinction between, male and female, Gentile and Jew, circumcision and foreskin, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free. Formerly, before this Seed came, this blessing—or rather, the promise of the blessing—was confined within Judaea alone, and while those prophetic utterances were heard, it was not preached to the other nations.

JEW. On the contrary, it was preached to other nations as well, and we [Col. 0566A] have this plainly in the prophets. It was proclaimed to Assyria; prophesied to the Babylonians; announced to Moab; cried out to Egypt; spoken to Media and likewise to Edom. Arabia was not left unmentioned; commands were given to harlot Tyre; and through the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel things to come were announced to the other nations.

CHRIST. Certainly we know that many nations were told of their own evils: Assyria had its own woe, Babylon its own burden, Egypt its own burden, and so with the other nations, too many to enumerate. But that was not the preaching to the nations of the blessing of Abraham’s Seed. It was one thing for a prophet, sitting in a corner of the Jewish house, to write in the letters of the one Hebrew language what would happen to whatever nations; it was another for the apostles to go to the nations and, in all languages, preach [Col. 0566B] repentance and remission of sins in the name of Abraham’s Seed.

JEW. But the prophet Jonah went to the nations: he was sent to Nineveh, the capital city of the Assyrians, and preached.

CHRIST. What, I ask, did he preach? Did he preach the blessing? Did he preach the kingdom of God? Certainly not. He preached only this: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. III). He neither preached, nor was sent to preach, that the nations should turn to the Lord; for the time for the conversion of the nations had not yet come. Rather, this was done so that the Assyrians, to whom Israel was to be delivered into captivity, might be proved more righteous than Israel: those same Assyrians believed the preaching of their imminent destruction, [Col. 0566C] while Israel remained unbelieving, though the same captivity had long been foretold to Israel by many prophets, with many miracles accompanying the prophecies—especially those God wrought through Elijah and Elisha. Why do you now stand silent? As I see, you have nothing to say in reply by which you can weaken the truth of the plain fact that we affirm: the Seed of Abraham, whom the faithful God promised and promised again with an oath, has come for the blessing of all nations.

JEW. Everything you say is mine; you have taken it from my books. What have you to do with these things? What have my Scriptures to do with you?

CHRIST. “Am I not, or ought I not to be, well deceitful?” Jacob said to his firstborn son Esau, “and he took your blessing” (Gen. XXVII). Clearly, just as Rebekah the mother adorned me, a Christian, with Esau’s very good garments—which you, Jew, say are yours. But let us now come to the point, since I proposed to demonstrate to you that your circumcision is of no benefit at this time, and that it ought to have ceased after the coming of Abraham’s Seed.

JEW. I have no leisure to give further hearing to such discourse; I am occupied with other business. I shall return to hear and answer when it is convenient.

CHRIST. O Jew, how often have you escaped by such pretexts and failed to keep the day appointed between us? You flee and cannot endure the arguments of truth, your eyes being dazzled by its light. Thus formerly [Col. 0567A] your fathers fled, unable to bear the brightness of Moses’ face unless it were veiled. But stay now, I beg you, for I love truth and seek your salvation as well. I do not reproach you for not being wise, in accordance with what one of your prophets said: “Therefore my people has been led captive because it had no knowledge” (Isa. V). And another said: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I shall reject you, that you may not exercise the priesthood for me” (Hos. VI). And there are many other similar sayings. But I wish to impress this upon you: do not think yourself so knowing that you are unwilling to learn further; do not, I say, become so wise in your own estimation that, upon hearing truth, you contradict truth.

JEW. Say the rest; continue as long as you wish.

CHRIST. Certainly, if you remember properly, and as you have recited the utterances of Scripture up to this point weigh their meaning carefully, [Col. 0567B] you see this: the sign of the covenant, the seal of faith, circumcision of the flesh, which father Abraham received at God’s command, was a certain figure or outward form of confession, bearing witness to believing people of hope and expectation, so that believers might hope for and await the coming of the blessed Seed of Abraham, namely Christ. Having this testimony, they were bound, by righteous mercy and merciful righteousness, to be perfectly justified at His coming. It was also a reminder to God Himself, who had promised: that He might see that sign, remember His covenant, and send the Seed which He promised and swore to send. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—then circumcision undoubtedly ought wholly to have ceased after the coming of that Seed. For to be circumcised is to say: “Send him whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV); send him, because you have not yet sent him. For we do not receive him whom you say you have sent. And this is to deny Him who has already come, blessed in the name of the Lord. Therefore it is truly and rightly said to me—whom you were trying to persuade to be circumcised, saying at the very beginning of evangelical preaching to Gentile hearers of the Gospel, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts XV)—it is rightly and truly said to me: “If you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing” (Gal. V).

JEW. Even if you wish circumcision not to be advantageous to you, circumcision benefits me, just as my fathers were circumcised on the eighth day—my father Isaac, my father Jacob.

[Col. 0567D] CHRIST. Why did you not say rather, “Just as Ishmael was circumcised, just as Esau was circumcised”? Indeed, as far as the circumcision of unbelieving Ishmael and Esau differs from the circumcision of Isaac and Jacob, so far does your circumcision differ from the circumcision of every believer before the coming of this blessed Seed. Tell me now, if you know: what more was there in Isaac’s circumcision than in Ishmael’s, or in Jacob’s than in Esau’s? All received one and the same wound of circumcision in their flesh. Ishmael and Isaac were two sons of one father, namely Abraham; Jacob and Esau were two sons according to the flesh of one father, Isaac; and they were circumcised on the same day.

JEW. Say what you proposed: what difference there was between their circumcisions.

[Col. 0568A] CHRIST. I shall say it briefly. Since there are two things—the covenant and the sign of the covenant—as has hitherto been most clearly demonstrated, Isaac and Jacob, like their father Abraham, received both the covenant in the mind and the sign of the covenant, namely circumcision in the flesh. But Ishmael and Esau suffered the sign—the circumcision—without the treasure of faith, without the agreement of the covenant, and, like empty vessels, were sealed with a superfluous seal. Therefore their blessing was wholly in the flesh and in bodily things. God said to Abraham: “Concerning Ishmael also I have heard you: behold, I shall bless him and increase him and multiply him exceedingly” (Gen. XVII). Isaac said to Esau: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be” (Gen. XXVII). But Isaac’s blessing and Jacob’s blessing lie in spiritual and everlasting goods. God likewise said to Abraham: “But I shall establish my covenant with Isaac” (Gen. XVII); Isaac said to Jacob: “Let peoples serve you, and tribes worship you” (Gen. XXVII). This was said on account of Christ, in whom we unquestionably worship Jacob’s flesh; although temporal blessing also—the abundance of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth—was not lacking to these men. O Jew, God regards your circumcision, you who are circumcised today, as He regarded that of Ishmael and Esau. For just as they did, so you receive without faith and without a covenant the sign of faith, the seal which was once of the covenant: namely, the empty wound of circumcision.

JEW. As far as lies in your power, you disgrace our nation [Col. 0568C] and endeavour to erase the memory of our race, so that, remaining uncircumcised, we may differ in nothing from the other nations, and thus the name Israel may be blotted out.

CHRIST. I do not disgrace your nation, but desire you to attain true glory: that you may glory not in flesh but in faith in Abraham’s Seed. For one nation, a great nation, was promised to Abraham according to faith in his Seed, God saying, “I shall make you into a great nation” (Gen. XII), and adding, “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (ibid.). What then seems better to you: to die in faith within a nation—your little nation, captive and scattered—or through faith to be in that one nation, Abraham’s great nation, the radiant nation inscribed in heaven, according to the saying, “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you are able; so shall [Col. 0568D] your seed be” (Gen. XV)? There is Abraham’s Seed, like the moon; there are all the saints and elect, like stars: an innumerable multitude numbered by God alone. Do as you wish. For, giving the reason concerning your circumcision according to my proposal, I say that it is useless, as I said at the beginning; because I, baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, have, in faith in Abraham’s Seed, put off the sin of the first father, old Adam, and obtained the glory of adoption as sons of God, sons of Abraham.

JEW. If through your baptism you have put off the sin of the first parent Adam, why do you die? Is not death the punishment of sin? If, then, that sin has been remitted to you and not to me, why do you die just as I do, [Col. 0569A] when death itself is the punishment of sin and sin was the efficient cause of death?

CHRIST. I live; and by the grace of baptism I have been liberated from the death which entered through sin and together with sin.

JEW. You die daily. Daily, Christian, since you are dust, you return to dust no less and no more slowly than the Jew.

CHRIST. You have a veil over your eyes, and therefore you see only one death, only the death of the body. Let your eyes be unveiled, so that you may see that there are two deaths: one of the soul, by which the soul is separated from God; the other of the flesh, by which the soul leaves the flesh. Sin brought about the death of the soul on the very day on which man ate the forbidden thing, according to the truth of God saying [Col. 0569B]: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II). God mercifully imposed the death of the flesh not on the very day he ate, but in his nine hundred and thirtieth year. Abel may have died earlier, and others may have died or been slain throughout so many years; but the man who ate did not die the death of the flesh on that same day, but after so many years. The chief difference between the two deaths is this: the death of the soul was brought upon him by the devil through sin; the death of the flesh was added by God through His most provident mercy.

JEW. How through mercy? Was it not rather wrath and indignation, not mercy, when, lest man perhaps stretch out his hand, take from the tree of life, eat, and live for ever, [Col. 0569C] He expelled him from the paradise of delight? (Gen. III).

CHRIST. Truly it was not wrath but great mercy, already wisely watching over us. For He saw that it would be exceedingly harmful for man to live for ever in the body while dead in soul; he would remain irrecoverable, like the demons, and possessed of ungovernable pride. Even now he is scarcely subdued by the spirit of humility, although he dies daily. Thus the grace of the Deliverer has already liberated me through baptism from the death of the soul; but He has delayed taking away the death of the body, which cooperates greatly with all the miseries of this life, so that, with head bowed and neck bent, [Col. 0569D] all those predestined to eternal life may more quickly be led to seek grace and avert the Judge’s wrath. That is, those whose cause for being born was not sin—which, once committed and strengthened by self-defence, led God to say to the woman, “I shall multiply your pains and your conceptions” (Gen. III)—but blessing, by which, before Adam and Eve sinned, He blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I), and so forth.

JEW. Without your baptism, my father Abraham was saved from that death which you call death of the soul. For, as you yourself do not deny, he was righteous and holy, and on account of the merit of his righteousness God made him His friend in an everlasting covenant.

CHRIST. When do you think Abraham was saved and entered paradise?

JEW. Do you dare to oppose even this and [Col. 0570A] say that Abraham himself, our father, did not enter the kingdom of God, as you are accustomed to assert that absolutely no one entered before the coming of your Christ?

CHRIST. I wish nowhere to oppose Holy Scripture; and again, without its authority, I permit neither your opinion nor anyone else’s to be accepted—especially in so great and difficult a matter of knowing truth. Tell me, therefore, on the authority of Scripture when either father Abraham himself or any other of the saints of old entered paradise or the kingdom of God. For of Abraham, our excellent and most holy father, we read only this at his end: that he failed and died in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days, and was gathered to his people; and his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him [Col. 0570B] (Gen. XXV). But if you wish “to be gathered to his people” to mean the same as entering the kingdom of God or paradise, this is strongly contradicted by father Jacob, who mourned for his son Joseph, whom he thought dead, and would not listen to his consoling sons: “I shall go down,” he said, “mourning to my son in hell” (Gen. XXXVII). Likewise: “If any misfortune should happen to my son Benjamin,” he said, “in the land to which you are going, you will bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to the lower world” (Gen. XLII). Therefore it is not I, but the authority of Scripture, that opposes you, lest you say or suppose that the place where Abraham was gathered to his people was already heaven or paradise. Moreover, nowhere in the whole course of Abraham’s life do you find that God promised him anything other than the Seed in whom the world would be blessed—that is, [Col. 0570C] saved—and the land of Canaan, where Abraham’s children were to dwell until that same promise was fulfilled.

JEW. Did Abraham, then, and the other holy fathers descend into hell, and was that what it meant for them to be gathered to their people?

CHRIST. They certainly descended into hell; yet not into the lower hell, where the impious are buried, of which the Psalmist speaks when he says, “You delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. LXXXV), but into a place or region lower not only than heaven or paradise but also than the dwelling-place of this world. There they were not only free from the punishments of the impious, but were also frequently visited by and enjoyed converse with holy angels. For our Lord also—[Col. 0570D] whom I wish you had long ago recognized—said of a certain poor man: “It came to pass that he died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke XVI); and He added concerning the rich man: “He too died and was buried in hell” (ibid.).

JEW. What, then, did they lack, if they were not deprived of the fellowship of holy angels? Or what could be closed to them of God’s kingdom if they were not separated from the citizens of that same kingdom of God?

CHRIST. I can show you by an analogy from the holy ecclesiastical and catholic order of my own religion. If you do not accept it, any faithful persons, small or great, who wish to attend to this discussion will gladly receive it and truly recognize it. And [Col. 0571A] then I shall show it again by an analogy from what you call your law of Moses. To her catechumens Mother Church shows maternal sweetness in all things, speaking with friendly intimacy and kindly fellowship and living with them. Every believer sets before them, insofar as he can, the milk of doctrine or even the solid food of the Scriptures. And although in these and other such ministries the ecclesiastical order makes itself common to them, nevertheless it does not admit them to the altar itself and the particular rite of the holy sacrifice until the sacrament of holy baptism has been completed in them, by which the stain of original sin is utterly cleansed away. But perhaps you care little for this analogy; therefore I shall give another, as I proposed. The law of Moses excludes a menstruating woman from entrance into the temple or altar [Col. 0571B] until, after the lawful days have passed, she comes to the temple with sacrifices of purification. According to the first analogy, Abraham and all the saints of old were like catechumens; and, because they had not yet been washed, they were not admitted to the heavenly sanctuary or altar, where true and everlasting communion consists in the present sweetness itself—the sweet presence of the vision of God. But let me show you the same thing according to the other analogy I have presented from Moses’ law concerning the menstruating woman. Remember first that Isaiah, one of those most famous saints, said: “We have all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV). And the prophet Zechariah said: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing [Col. 0571C] of the sinner and of the menstruating woman” (Zech. XIII). Therefore, according to this analogy, since the righteousness of the law was like a menstruating cloth until the open fountain of the house of David should come into being, it must be granted that, just as a menstruating woman under the law was barred from the sacred thresholds until, after the days of purification had passed or been completed, she came with the lawful offerings, so it was just that all saints or righteous persons—whose righteousness was certainly imperfect—should keep watch outside the sanctuary of heaven and of the vision of God, until He came who would wash the menstruating woman, who, as the Psalmist says, being the lawgiver, would give blessing (Ps. LXXXIII).

JEW. And who is He?

CHRIST. He, indeed, to whom the prophet Zechariah said: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth [Col. 0571D] your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. IX).

JEW. And who is He?

CHRIST. Certainly He who, coming to Jerusalem to shed the blood of His covenant, sat upon an ass, or upon the colt of an ass: truly one who despised the vanity of the world, truly meek and humble in heart. For the same prophet had promised: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a saviour, himself poor, riding upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass; and he shall speak peace to the nations” (ibid.). And now, turning to Him, he says: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

JEW. Did your Christ, then, bring our father [Col. 0572A] Abraham himself out of the pit? Where, when, and how did He do this?

CHRIST. When my Christ had already died. One of the soldiers opened His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out (John XIX). In that blood of His covenant, in that water joined with His blood, He sent forth Abraham and all His prisoners from the pit in which there was no water. And it came to pass, as the aforesaid prophet Zechariah foretold: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman” (Zech. XIII). This was their hope, as their Scriptures testify. For example, David says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). And through Ezekiel the Lord Himself speaks: “And the nations shall know that I am the Lord, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes. For I shall take you from the nations, gather you from all lands, bring you into your own land, and pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. XXXVI), and so forth. [Col. 0572B] Behold, you have both on prophetic authority: the clean water for cleansing, and the blood of the covenant for sending prisoners forth from the pit in which there is no water. Many other things besides these could be said to demonstrate that the sacrament of baptism flowing from Christ’s side—the sacrament of the blood by which we are redeemed, the sacrament of the water by which we are washed—was not a new design for all who have faith in the blessed Seed of Abraham, namely Christ; rather, before it came to pass, it was in the ancient purpose of God our Creator and Saviour.

[Col. 0572C] JEW. Did the blood you speak of descend into hell? Or did that water flow into that pit—I know not which—in which there was no water? Was there such a flood or abundance of that water and blood that it could pour over and wash that entire people to whom father Abraham was gathered, to whom Isaac was added, and to whom Jacob was added? Already in Moses’ day their multitude was so great that they could be called “peoples” in the plural, as the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Hor: “Let Aaron go to his peoples” (Num. XX). How great, do you think, was the multitude of that people, or of those peoples, later in David’s time, when he slept with his fathers? You recalled that he said—and believe that he said concerning your baptism—“You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, [Col. 0572D] and I shall be made whiter than snow.” And further, when that Jesus, your Christ, was crucified and pierced with a spear, and when, already dead, He poured blood, as you say, and water from His side: how great was the multitude of that people, and how great was the stream of that blood and water, that its flood could suffice to wash all that multitude?

CHRIST. I do not want you to attend in that blood and water only to what was visible, as you wish, but to the cause of that outpouring and to the invisible power which the world cried out that it could not endure. For the whole earth shook, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0573A] arose—not immediately, nor before Him, but with Him (Matt. XXVII). Certainly the power of that blood, by the same blow with which it shook the earth, also disturbed hell; its cause cleansed that entire people, in accordance with the truth of the prophetic Spirit, who said of Him through Isaiah: “If He shall make His soul an offering for sin, He shall see long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in His hand. Because His soul has laboured, He shall see and be satisfied. By His knowledge the righteous one himself shall justify many of my servants, and He himself shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I shall allot Him many, and He shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because He delivered His soul unto death and was numbered with transgressors” (Isa. LIII).

JEW. If it is as you say, why is it necessary that you yourself [Col. 0573B] should now be baptized? For if, according to your assertion, He then washed by His blood and water all who believed in Him, what reason is there for you to be washed again? Only believe and do not be baptized.

CHRIST. Before I was born, I could not be reborn; before I existed, I could not be washed. Nor can anyone be effectively washed unless he first believes. Those who already were, or had been, believers in Him at that time He undoubtedly washed, as has already been said. From those very many people, numberable by God alone, the one Church was then born anew from the side of Christ sleeping in the sleep of death, according to the analogy of the woman who was formed from the side of the man sleeping in the sleep of slumber. But for me, wishing to be incorporated into that same Church, [Col. 0573C] the sacrament of that same regeneration has been set at her doors by the ordinance of Him who said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

JUD. You speak as you please; in accordance with your own intention you lead, bring back, and draw the words of the Scriptures wherever you wish. But reason supplies me with grounds for standing immovably firm in holding that the Jesus whom my fathers crucified is not the Messiah—that is, the Christ—whom my fathers expected. For if he is that one, where are the blessings of Jerusalem and the prosperity of Zion? Where are Jacob’s exultation and Israel’s joy, promised in such great prophetic utterances, which ought to abound at his coming? Indeed, after this Jesus came, not only did that not happen which, for example, I shall now recall from the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Jerusalem shall dwell secure, and this shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all the nations that fought against Jerusalem; and the riches of all the nations round about shall be gathered together—gold and silver and very many garments” (Zech. XIV). But Jerusalem itself is recorded never to have been so struck, deprived also of its own gold, silver, and garments, and overthrown, as it is now, from the time when there was that one whom you call Christ, king of Zion, king of Jerusalem. Would the prophet, then, say of this man what you previously recalled: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a Saviour” (Zech. IX)?

[Col. 0574A] CHRISTIAN. O Jew, see lest that which is written in the Psalm has come upon you: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling-block; let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see” (Ps. LXVIII); and elsewhere: “He rains snares upon sinners” (Ps. X). For I tell you that for your sinful people their own table, the sacred Scripture, is full of snares—especially because of their excessive greed and insatiable avarice, through which your fathers killed Christ, the Lord, King of Jerusalem or Zion: a poor king. For, when the prophet in the passage already cited had said, “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion,” etc., he added: “He is poor, and riding upon an ass” (Zech. IX). Unless you take heed and lay aside greed, the Scripture which is your table has ensnared you by promising [Col. 0574B] gold, by promising silver, and Jerusalem’s security. Now tell me: when you read “Zion” and hear “Jerusalem,” do you understand stones or people?

JEW. I understand the people who then held the citadel of Zion—my race, which then lived in Jerusalem.

CHRISTIAN. I grant it; and you may rightly call “Jerusalem” also the people of the other cities, of which Jerusalem was the head, who came from every quarter on feast days to worship in Jerusalem. But tell me: when those people who inhabited Jerusalem, and who came to worship at Jerusalem, died and were gathered or added to their people—as was mentioned above concerning the fathers—did they cease to be called Jerusalem? Did they cease to be Zion? Rather, was not that people to which each was gathered at death rightly reckoned before God under the name by which they were called while alive—namely, Zion and Jerusalem—together with their king David, who captured the citadel of Zion, whose city was Jerusalem? I say nothing now of the mystical interpretation of the names; according to ordinary human usage, I am now speaking with you about the name Jerusalem. A certain distinguished secular author says:

> For just as the Hyperborean icy Wain [lies] beneath the Bear,  
> Or the region where the axis, closed in by clouds and rushing vapours,  
> Suffers neither nights nor unequal-growing suns—  
> If fortune so ordain, the supreme power of the world will follow us,  
> And the Tarpeian empire, companion to its burnt seat,  
> While Camillus dwells at Veii amid Gallic torches—  
> [Col. 0574D] There was Rome; the Senate never lost its authority.  
> Though the site was changed, Caesar possesses its grieving houses,  
> Its empty homes and silent laws,  
> And its law-courts shut by sorrowful justice …  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, V.23–32).

The Roman Senate, with the consuls and Pompey as leader, was then in Epirus, a Greek city, fleeing Caesar. If, therefore, it could truly and elegantly be said that that assembly was Rome rather than the buildings where it had been left behind, and if such language does not depart from ordinary human speech, how much more rightly should that people be called Jerusalem or Zion—to which individuals, as has been said, were gathered in dying from Jerusalem and its cities, worshippers of God—rather than that small portion itself, one generation, which lived in its own time within the buildings of Jerusalem or Zion!

[Col. 0575A] Therefore, when you read, “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem,” do not look only at the generation which lived in the buildings of Jerusalem at that time, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Do not argue from this that Jesus of Nazareth is not king of Zion or Jerusalem because that generation did not receive him. Nor say that Zion did not rejoice or Jerusalem shout at the coming of this Christ of mine merely because, after his passion, every evil came upon that generation. Look upon all the generations of thousands of years which, departing this life, had been gathered into one people; look upon that whole people, or multitude of peoples—truly Zion, truly Jerusalem—and you will recognize how effectually and how far from vainly it was said: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem,” and many similar things.

JEW. What you have now brought forward against me from the Psalm—“Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling-block; let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see”—and that passage from Isaiah—“Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them” (Isa. VI)—I have often heard thrown at me; and many of your people have cited these things mockingly. Is God such as you suppose him to be: one who wishes someone to be deceived and led into error?

[Col. 0575C] 338 CHRISTIAN. Does not Jeremiah say, “You have deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived; you were stronger than I and prevailed” (Jer. XX)? Does he not say, speaking against King Ahab to the spirit of falsehood, “You shall deceive him and prevail; go forth and do so” (III Kings XXII)? Nevertheless, listen to me: there is not just one kind of deception. There is a deception by which a person is led from good to evil. God knows no such deception. Conversely, there is a deception from evil to good; and by this deception God has deceived you and your race, in willing the sacred Scripture to be such that, in reading it, your eyes should be darkened. For if he had not enclosed its mysteries under figures and riddles, if he had expressed them in plain words, would your fathers—especially rebellious [Col. 0575D] and unbelieving men, as Moses himself said—have endured it? Assuredly, they would have acted as King Jehoiakim did, who cut up Jeremiah’s scroll and threw it into the fire until it was consumed by fire (Jer. XXXVI); and as you report that Isaiah was sawn asunder by Manasseh on this occasion, because he said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI), whereas God himself had said to Moses, “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). Thus they would have burned all the Scriptures and killed all the prophets—and done so much more madly—unless the Scriptures had been closed and sealed to them; if the prophets had plainly proclaimed everything that was to happen and had to be done concerning Christ—for example, how and in what order he was to be exalted upon that high and exalted throne of which Isaiah said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high [Col. 0576A] and exalted throne.” Therefore they seemed to close up the message and seal the book, to bind up the testimony and seal the law; and they did this while prophesying in great fear and at peril of their lives, as one of them, Jeremiah, did when he said: “If priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord” (Lam. II)—“terror,” he says, “and snare have become our prophecy, and destruction” (Lam. III). Good, then, was the deception by which it came about that the Scriptures, not being held in intense hatred, were not destroyed along with those who wrote them, but were preserved for the benefit of coming ages.

JEW. What sort of good is it, as you say, that my eyes should be darkened and my table made a stumbling-block to me; that God should take precautions and say, “lest perhaps he turn and I heal him” (Isa. VI)? For this is as though a curse were pronounced upon a deaf person and an obstacle placed before a blind person. See, then, that while you wish vehemently to accuse me, you excuse me. What fault is there in me if I am darkened or blinded, when I wish to see, and even think that I have eyes for seeing, ears for hearing, and a heart for understanding?

CHRISTIAN. No one is ensnared or caused to stumble here except willingly; no one’s eyes are darkened or blinded except those of one willing to be darkened.

JEW. And who is willing to be blinded, willing to be ensnared, willing not to see with the eyes, hear with the ears, or understand with the heart?

CHRISTIAN. The one who wishes that Christ—whom he fed with gall [Col. 0576C] and gave vinegar to drink (as I myself said in the preceding verse of that same Psalm, which is written wholly in his person: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” [Ps. LXVIII]; and before this: “Zeal for your house,” he says, “has consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me” [ibid.])—the one, I say, who wishes this Jesus Christ absolutely not to be Christ, and desires to obtain support from the Scriptures by which he may appear to deny him rationally: he is the one who desires his eyes to be darkened, who knowingly and deliberately strives to put his feet into the snare (ibid.). He is therefore justly granted this and abandoned to the desires of his heart, when it is said: “Let their table before them become a snare,” etc.

[Col. 0576D] JEW. What sense is there in saying that God said, “lest perhaps he turn and I heal him,” which you maintain was said against me?

CHRISTIAN. What sense is there in God’s saying: “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart so that he will not let my people go; I shall harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they pursue those passing through the Red Sea” (Exod. VII, VIII, IX, X, XI)?

JEW. Do you therefore wish me to be regarded as Pharaoh, as an Egyptian?

CHRISTIAN. Certainly as an Egyptian, just as a Canaanite, according to the true prophecy spoken through Ezekiel to your earthly, bloodstained Jerusalem: “Jerusalem, your root and your birth are from the land of Canaan; your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI). Its meaning is this: because you, though born from Abraham’s flesh, are not from Abraham’s faith, you are to me as Canaan, as an Amorite, and as a Hittite. Therefore also as an Egyptian, because, just as the Amorite and Hittite, so Mizraim, from whom the Egyptians are descended, sprang not from Shem but from Ham. Hence the Psalm: “He struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first fruits of all their labour in the tents of Ham” (Ps. LXXVII). If, therefore, you rightly understand how God hardened the Egyptian so that he would not let the people go, then likewise you rightly understand how it was said: “Blind the heart of this people; make their ears heavy; and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.”

JEW. You tell how God hardened the hearts of the Egyptians, so that you may then tell, correspondingly or similarly, how he blinded my heart.

CHRISTIAN. Would that you ask in such a manner as to desire to hear, and are not the person of whom it is written in the Psalm: “He did not wish to understand, so as to act well” (Ps. XXXV). God hardened the Egyptians’ hearts by lavishly bestowing his most splendid benefits upon those whom the Egyptians envied. For this is the nature and distinctive property of this disease, envy: whoever greatly envies someone suffers great torment from that person’s prosperity. The Egyptians hated and envied the children of Israel; you hate the salvation of the nations and envy us. This, moreover, is the devil’s sin, through which death entered into this world (Wis. II). Therefore, just as the efficient cause of the Egyptians’ hardness was their own envy, because they envied the children of Israel, so the efficient cause of your people’s blindness is its own envy, because it hates the salvation of the nations. Accordingly, just as you understand—and ought to understand—that the Lord hardened the Egyptians’ hearts until they perished while pursuing the children of Israel fleeing through the Red Sea, so understand this: that your people was blinded until it was destroyed while persecuting those who believed in Christ and fled through the sacrament of baptism, according to these words that follow in the same prophecy. The prophet said: “How long, Lord?” (Isa. VI), and the answer was: “Until the cities are desolated without inhabitant, and the houses without a human being, and the land is left deserted, and the Lord removes people far away” (ibid.). This is as though he said: “Those Jews who remain shall be led captive among all nations.” Those two evils occurred there: namely, blindness of heart and dispersal in captivity. The prophetic pronouncement at the passage cited continues, saying: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back [339] always” (Ps. LXVIII); and both are beneficial to Christ’s Gospel. For if you saw—that is, if you believed in Christ—you would have mixed baptism and circumcision, as those few from your people who were converted and healed, that is, baptized, at the beginning of Christianity wished to do; they stirred up disturbances against the preachers of the Gospel. And, if you sat upright-backed in your cities rather than being bent, you would wish preaching to be carried on according to your own judgement and would permit no gentile to be admitted unless circumcised. In that way Christ would belong neither to me nor to you, and the Gospel would profit neither me nor you.

JEW. You mock my misfortunes, not recalling that it is written: “When the Lord restores the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel rejoice” (Ps. XIII).

CHRISTIAN. I do not mock, but, as brother to brother, I bring you words of truth, repaying you good for evil. For you hate my salvation, whereas I desire yours. Do you know that parable of my Lord? “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me” (Luke XV), etc. You and I are those two sons: one God created us; one Adam begot us both. Behold, you stand outside in anger and indignation because my Father received me safe and sound, and you do not wish to enter and feast with us. But I go out to you and ask you to come in, showing you the first robe which the Father gave me in the washing, together with the ring of faith and the shoes of knowledge of the truth. Receive this ring with me; admit this faithful saying, which, because it concerns faith, I have chosen to call a ring. Be clothed with this robe and shod with these shoes together with me.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0577]

[Col. 0577D] CHRISTIAN. Almighty God, being himself faithful in all his words (Ps. CXLIV), demands faith from man before all else; and without faith it is impossible to please him (Heb. XI). He sought this in the first man and did not find it, for that man believed the serpent rather than God. He sought it in Noah and found it; he sought it in Abraham and found it; he sought it in the Virgin Mary and found it—giving none of these any sign beforehand, so that they might believe him when he promised something new and unheard of. Delighted, therefore, at finding faith, God, as though upon finding a great treasure, placed his seal upon it and entered into an indissoluble covenant with humankind: with Noah, namely, he set his bow in the clouds of heaven, that upon seeing this sign he might remember his covenant, so that there should no longer be waters of a flood; with Abraham, however, the sign of circumcision, that he might remember his promise—namely, the seed which he promised, and again promised with an oath, to give him. The third sign of faith—that faith, namely, which, as has been said, he found in the Virgin Mary, who believed that she would bear Christ the Son of God without a man, and in the whole Church which faithfully believes that the Virgin bore him—the third sign of faith, I say, is the seal [Col. 0579A] of that same cross of Christ, Son of God, together with the sacrament of baptism, so that he may see and remember his covenant and not strike us on the day of judgement, as once in Egypt: “I shall see the blood,” he says, “and pass over you; and there shall not be in you a destroying plague when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. XII). If the preceding little book has not satisfied you concerning this faith, bring forward whatever you think to the contrary.

JEW. You look at only one side, and if you discuss Abraham’s faith, you do so as though forgetting Moses’ law, God’s law. You do not recall the signs and wonders which God performed in the land of Egypt in order to give us the law on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after departure from Egypt, with such great indications of God’s own presence. For thunders were heard, lightning flashed, [Col. 0579B] and all the people heard voices and the sound of the trumpet; they saw flames and the smoking mountain (Exod. XX). You have made no mention of the covenant which he then made with us, as Scripture says in the same place: “Moses took half of the blood and put it into bowls, but poured the remaining portion upon the altar. Taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people; then he sprinkled the people with the blood he had taken and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words” (Exod. XXIV). Now tell me: if Abraham was justified by faith with a sufficient justification, and if that covenant which God made with him because of faith sufficiently established his righteousness, what further need was there for the justification of the law, the sprinkling of the blood of the covenant, or the covenant of sacrificial blood, and every rite of ceremonies or sacrifices handed down to us for cleansing each transgression? What purpose had the entire worship of the tabernacle of the covenant?

CHRISTIAN. I shall ask you one question; if you answer it for me, I shall tell you the purpose of all those things, and why the law was given. Why did Abraham, the father of our faith, go in to Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian maidservant, ten years after he began to dwell in the land of Canaan, after the Lord had made a covenant with him, after Scripture had said: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV)?

JEW. Because Abraham’s wife Sarai had borne no children, Scripture says, but had an Egyptian maidservant [Col. 0579D] named Hagar. She said to her husband: “Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I may not bear children; go in to my maidservant, that perhaps I may receive children from her” (Gen. XVI). He yielded to her entreaty, went in to the maidservant, and begot Ishmael by her (ibid.).

CHRISTIAN. It is as you have said; but at the same time you must remember what God said through the prophet: “I multiplied visions, and was likened through the hand of the prophets” (Hos. XII).

JEW. I remember the prophet in whom these words are spoken—and Hosea himself.

CHRISTIAN. And that father Abraham was a prophet, and the first of the prophets. For he is the first of those to whom the word of the Lord came, as it is written: “You have not given me seed, and behold, [Col. 0580A] my household servant shall be my heir.” And immediately the word of the Lord came to him: “This one shall not be your heir” (Gen. XV), etc. God also spoke on his account to Abimelech: “Now therefore return the man’s wife, for he is a prophet and will pray for you” (Gen. XX). And in the Psalm, concerning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, it is written: “He permitted no one to harm them, and rebuked kings on their behalf: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets” (Ps. CIV). Therefore I now say: if God was likened through the hand of the prophets—which he cannot be denied to have said by a prophetic mouth—how much more was he likened through the hands of these men, who were both prophets and fathers and chiefs of the prophets? Therefore, although you hate our allegories and are accustomed to despise them, allow yourself to hear how God was likened in the hand of Abraham, according to that event which God set forth.

JEW. Proceed where you wish; bring to completion what you intend; give the likeness of God in the hand of my father the prophet which you promise.

CHRISTIAN. In Abraham God, the Father of us all, was represented; in Sarah, faith; and in Hagar, the law of Moses. In Sarah’s barrenness, faith’s barrenness was represented. For just as that free woman, that mistress, was barren for a long time, so faith—which alone is the true freedom and nobility of the human race—was almost barren after it was joined to God, our Father and Creator; after, on account of it, God deigned to make a covenant with humankind and to unite himself to the human soul in a conjugal covenant, a marital union. For how many sons of faith, sons of promise, besides Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph [Col. 0580C] can you show? Certainly, even if there were some more—leaving aside for the moment the multitude of Ishmael’s line and Esau’s line; I speak of the line of the patriarch Jacob—even if, I say, there were some more sons of faith besides those whom Scripture names, they were nevertheless so few compared with the multitude of sons of the flesh that you may truly say faith was barren while flesh was fruitful.

JEW. Distinguish more clearly for me whom you call sons of faith and whom sons of flesh. What is the distinction or difference between sons of flesh and sons of faith? In what respect, or according to what criterion, do you distinguish the two generations?

CHRISTIAN. Two things were promised to Father Abraham. One was: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII); the other: “To your seed I shall give this land” (Gen. XII), the land of Canaan. All those born from Abraham who awaited the promise of the blessed seed, according to faith, looking upon the promises from afar, greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth (Heb. XI), were sons of faith. But those who awaited only the promise of the land of Canaan, and cried to the Lord only for that reason when they were afflicted in Egypt, were sons of flesh. Now, I ask you, from the time when the envious brothers, faithless toward their own father, sold Joseph until Moses himself, how many were there who said, or even knew how to say, what Moses said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. IV)? Therefore faith was barren; but flesh had already become fruitful, bearing children into slavery not to God but to Egyptian people—indeed, serving also the gods of Egypt. God himself recalls this through the prophets, especially Ezekiel. Thus the faith of the fathers, who, though dead to the world, nevertheless lived and live to God, was joined to God; but it did not bear children, following the likeness of Sarah, who, though a lawful wife and a free wife, was barren and bore no children. Yet faith itself deserved, and demanded from God, that at least the law should intervene, so that by binding that multitude to the worship of God it might bear children into the service of faith, after this likeness: Sarah says, “Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I may not bear; go in to my maidservant, that at least I may receive children from her.” Abraham yielded to her entreaty, went in to the maidservant, and begot Ishmael. God the most high Father yielded to the secret ears of the faith of the fathers as it pleaded with him; admitting the ceremonial law, he begot through it a people fitted not so much for freedom as for slavery—that is, one worshipping and knowing God the Father, or its Creator, not so much in love as in fear. For I want you to know this: God did not command that law, but admitted it; he did not will it, but permitted it.

JEW. What is this that you say? God did not will the law? God did not command the law? Did he not write the tablets with his own finger and say to Moses: “These are my commandments, these are my judgements; thus and thus you shall command the children of Israel; thus and thus you shall make the burnt offering and the sin offering”?

[Col. 0581C] CHRISTIAN. You must hear and understand Moses in such a way that you also hear and understand the Psalms and the prophets. In the Psalm God himself speaks: “I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices,” and so forth, down to: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX). And in Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? says the Lord. I am full; I have not desired the burnt offering of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my presence, who required these things at your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not bring a useless sacrifice any longer. Incense is an abomination to me; the new moon, Sabbath, and other festivals [Col. 0581D] I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous; my soul hates your new moons and your solemnities” (Isa. I).

JEW. Those things were said because of Jeroboam, because of the calves which Jeroboam made and which Israel worshipped. Therefore God said that he did not desire burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, and so forth, because they sacrificed to calves.

CHRISTIAN. The calves were not worshipped in Judah, nor were sacrifices made to those calves in Jerusalem, but in Samaria—that is, among the ten tribes. But this prophetic reading bears this title: “The vision of Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” (ibid.). Therefore he was not speaking in the present about Samaria because of those calves, but prophesying about Jews and Jerusalem in the future because of righteous blood. For after saying the words already quoted as far as “and when you multiply prayer, I shall not hear,” he immediately adds this reason: “For your hands are full of blood” (ibid.). Before Christ’s blood, he did not will these things, although he permitted them, nor did he demand them, as it is also written in the Psalm: “You did not demand burnt offering and sin offering” (Ps. XXXIX). But from that time onward he not only does not will or demand them, but also says: “My soul hates them; they have become burdensome to me” (ibid.). A further great and evident testimony in Jeremiah that he never willed, sought, or demanded them is this: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the flesh. For I did not speak with your fathers or command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but I commanded them this word, saying: Hear my voice, and I shall be your God and you shall be my people; and walk in every way which I command, that it may go well with you” (Jer. VII).

JEW. What distinction do you make between the word concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices, and the voice or word which God commanded us—or, indeed, the way which he ordered us to walk in, that it might go well with us?

CHRISTIAN. I do not make it; I find it already made, a great distinction. Warned by the words quoted above, I looked more carefully at the text of the law itself and found it there, so that I can show you the meaning as well. Behold, you have the voice of the Lord, or the way which he commanded and ordered, in Exodus before the guilt of the molten calf which they made and worshipped: “You shall have no strange gods before me,” etc., down to, “Keep all that I have said to you; and you shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth” (Exod. XX–XXIII). These are the commandments and judgements of which the Lord himself says that a person who does them shall live by them. But afterwards, when Moses delayed on the mountain with the Lord, the Lord, speaking to Moses, laid upon them the very heavy yoke of the ceremonial law because of the guilt, as has been said, of the calf which they made. Hence the Lord himself speaks through Ezekiel: “Therefore I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgements, which a person shall do and live by them” (Ezek. XX). And shortly afterward: “Again I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the lands, because they had not performed my judgements, had rejected my commandments, had violated my Sabbaths, and their eyes had followed the idols of their fathers. Therefore I also gave them commandments not good, and judgements by which they should not live; and I defiled them in their gifts, when they offered everything that opens the womb, because of their transgressions” (ibid.). Consider the commandments and judgements he gave first: they are very good, their sum being, “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV), or, “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII). Then consider the commandments he gave afterward: they were not indeed evil, but were not good, because they could neither be borne nor possessed in themselves the life of a human being. For how could one live by or because of the blood of brute animals; by observing clean or unclean animals; human leprosy and non-leprosy; garments and houses; and the other such matters written especially in Leviticus?

JEW. Before the guilt of the calf of which you speak, Moses himself offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. For it is written in the same place: “Moses wrote all the words of the Lord; and rising early in the morning, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent young men from the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed twelve calves as peace offerings to the Lord” (Exod. XXIV).

CHRISTIAN. Even if you have read that this was done, have you read that God commanded it? You might also object that Noah, long before Moses, after leaving the ark, built an altar to the Lord and, taking from every clean animal and bird, offered burnt offerings upon the altar; and the Lord was pleased by the sweet savour (Gen. VIII). If you had objected this to me, I would have added something else: that Melchizedek, king of Salem, who is not implausibly thought to have been Shem, son of that same Noah, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, offered bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High—and blessed him (Gen. XIV). Behold another sacrifice, long before Moses; neither was commanded, both were voluntary. I do not fail to know which of these was more pleasing to the Most High, nor may you fail to know, since Scripture says of one whom you would wish to ignore: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). But another time will be more suitable for that matter. For now it is preferable to say why God first permitted sacrifice of the flesh and blood of brute animals, and himself, as lawgiver, instituted its rite by command. Clearly, because the carnal people could not be drawn away from such sacrifices; and, had they not been permitted to sacrifice such things to God, they would more readily have offered them to idols. The proof was already at hand: when the calf had been fashioned, they rose early in the morning, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play (Exod. XXXII). Therefore, because both the faith of the fathers, as has been said above, intervened, and it was necessary at that time that the growing multitude of sons of flesh should be bound to God’s worship through the severity of the law, God yielded and ordered the law of God and the rite of sacrifices by his command in such a way that, in those nonessential things, there was the shadow or figure of a necessary reality and truth.

JEW. Do not argue with me concerning figures or shadows, but concerning the words of Scripture themselves and their plain senses, simply, clearly, and in an intelligible manner of speech. What have I to do with things which Scripture itself has not handed down, nor commanded me to investigate?

CHRISTIAN. Did I not tell you above—and you ought to know—that prophetic saying: “I multiplied visions, and through the hand of the prophets I was made like [them]” (Hos. XII)? Did not the same Lord say also to Moses himself, the greatest prophet, after whom, Scripture says, “there did not arise a prophet in Israel like him, whom the Lord knew face to face” (Deut.
