XXXIV), when he commanded the tabernacle to be made: “See and make according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV)? What sort of pattern do you suppose was shown him?

JEW. What should I suppose, except what Scripture itself says: that God had made a tabernacle and showed it to Moses, so that he might make one like it?

[Col. 0584B] CHRISTIAN. If it had been so, would it not have been easier to give Moses that very tabernacle, as he gave him the tablets, than to make another with so much labour and expense? Rather, there was certainly a spiritual and heavenly sanctuary in God’s purpose, to be revealed in the fullness of time; and because the time for it had not yet come, he willed that its image should go beforehand in those holy things made by human hands. Thus it occurred according to the likeness already described of the free woman and the maidservant: at the free woman’s request, because she was barren, the lawful husband of the free woman went in to the maidservant—that is, because of the merit of the fathers’ faith, since that faith bore fruit in very few people, God admitted the law, so that the free woman might at least receive from the maidservant children who would be saved.

JEW. According to your view, why was it necessary that faith should be barren and that the law should enter because of its barrenness? Could not God have made faith bear children already then, so that, in your view, legislation would not have been needed?

CHRIST. Do you ask this—why that seed promised to Abraham, in which all nations were to be blessed through faith, did not then come? I tell you: it ought not then to have come because God was angry. For you have this: when Moses, yearning for that seed, said, “I beseech you, Lord, send him whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV), it is immediately added: “The Lord, angry with Moses, said: Aaron your brother the Levite—I know that he is eloquent” (ibid.), etc. For this is the meaning: because the Lord was angry, he gave no answer concerning what Moses entreated, but proceeded with the other matters he had begun.

JUD. For what reason was God angry at that time?

CHRIST. Surely because of the sins of the house, or rather the same race, of Abraham, to whom God had promised the oft-mentioned blessing—namely, because of the sacrilege of Jacob’s sons, who sold their brother Joseph.

JUD. Had Moses sold him? How then could it be said, “The Lord was angry with Moses,” on account of that matter?

CHRIST. Moses spoke thus of himself, “The Lord was angry with Moses,” because he alone, or nearly alone, knowingly held the promise of that expectation. [Col. 0585A] Was that cause insignificant—the sale of such a brother, the iron of whose sale had so long wounded the soul of that holy father? That evil had been foreshown to Abraham himself, the father, when the Lord made a covenant with him, in that vision. For after it had been said to him, “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall reduce you to servitude,” etc., down to “but in the fourth generation they shall return here” (Gen. XV), this was immediately added: “When, therefore, the sun had set, a dark gloom came to be; and behold, a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire passed between those divisions” (ibid.). That smoking furnace with its dark gloom foreshadowed the smoky, dark furnace of envy, by which Jacob’s sons, scorched, consumed, and darkened, sold their excellent brother; and that bright lamp of fire foretold the miracles by which they were to be delivered from Egyptian slavery, to which they had been handed over until the fourth generation because of that sin. But Joseph, sold as a slave, served for fourteen years. For when he was sold, he was sixteen years old; but when he was brought out of prison and stood before Pharaoh, he was thirty. Therefore, by a just judgment, it was fitting that the seed of blessing promised to Abraham should be deferred for fourteen generations on account of that sin, and that a generation should be counted for each individual year, just as elsewhere a year was reckoned for a day for that generation which came out of Egypt. “According to the number of the forty days,” says the Lord, “in which you surveyed the land, [Col. 0585C] a year shall be reckoned for a day; and for forty years you shall bear your iniquities” (Num. XIV).

JUD. Did that seed which you mean—your Christ, whom you say is the seed promised by God to Abraham—come immediately after fourteen generations? Far more generations passed from Abraham to the days of Herod, during whose reign the one whom you call Christ was born.

CHRIST. Wait a little, while I tell you what you yourself cannot deny to be true. Fourteen generations from Abraham, to whom that smoking furnace was shown beforehand, ended in David. Yet he sinned no less, by taking Uriah’s wife and killing Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites’ sons. Therefore, [Col. 0585D] says the Lord, “The sword shall never depart from your house” (II Kings XII). Justice therefore required that God should defer his Christ by no fewer than fourteen generations. Once these had elapsed, it was nevertheless just that he should defer him for another fourteen generations; and not only that Christ should be deferred, but that the people also should be led into captivity, especially because of Manasseh’s sins. For they had filled Jerusalem to the brim with innocent blood.

JUD. Which prophet stated these reasons? Or in what Scripture have you read that these delays occurred, or ought to have occurred, in this manner?

CHRIST. The divine Evangelist, not without that Spirit in whom the prophets spoke, after setting out in order [Col. 0586A] the generations from Abraham to Christ, immediately distinguished them thus: “Therefore all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matt. I). By saying this, he directs the attentive hearer to seek in the Scriptures the reasons for the delays; and behold, the reasons are plain.

JUD. I pay no attention to your Gospels. But I know this: when the one whom you call Christ was born, iniquity was more abundant than it had ever been before—unless perhaps you also wish to maintain that David’s sin was greater than all the beastly cruelty of Herod.

[Col. 0586B] CHRIST. Herod’s impiety, and all the blood he shed, ought not to be imputed to the generations of the Jewish race. For he was not a Jew but a foreigner, born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother. Hence you must also grant this: that the time had come for him who was to be sent to be sent, since in him the sceptre had been taken away from Judah. For the patriarch Jacob had said in blessing Judah: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX). But let us now return to the exposition of the comparison we began. For if you wish—if your heart does not lack goodwill—it may be enough for you no longer to ask why God allowed faith to remain barren so long and meanwhile admitted the Law, according to the likeness [Col. 0586C] of Sarah’s barrenness, on account of which father Abraham went in to the handmaid at his mistress’s request. For this is rather to be wondered at, to the glory of the faithful God: that in the end he did what he had promised, though offended by so many and such great evils committed by those whose fathers received his promise.

JUD. Enough has now been said concerning that comparison. What more have you to say from it?

CHRIST. I know that for a long time now you have scarcely endured to listen, and I fear that, while I desire to lift for you the veil from Moses’ face so that you may see its brightness, you may flee as your fathers fled, 343 when they saw his splendid face still unveiled and feared to draw near. I wish to unfold the whole comparison for you, as far as this: “Cast out the handmaid and her son; for the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI). That handmaid, when she saw that she had conceived, despised her mistress; and after the Law entered in, it gave the carnal multitude an occasion to despise and almost consign to oblivion the righteousness of faith, supposing that it could be justified by works of the Law. Thus, when I asked you above by what Abraham was justified, you did not know what to say. So completely, because of the handmaid—the Law—you had neglected faith, the mistress, that you would not even have remembered that it had ever existed, unless I had confronted you with the incontrovertible and true statement: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV). Then it follows: “Behold,” Abraham says, “the handmaid is in your hand; [Col. 0587A] use her as you please. Therefore Sarai afflicted her, and she fled” (Gen. XVI). Whatever upright judges of Israel and faithful kings did in restraining the people from unlawful acts was an affliction to that handmaid; therefore she fled. The beginning of her flight was when, in the wilderness after the departure from Egypt, the people made themselves a calf and worshipped that carved image, rejoicing that in its worship they might be free to eat and drink and afterward play. The completion of the same flight was when the ten tribes, torn away from David’s house, likewise made themselves two calves. But behold the angel of the Lord: “Hagar,” he says, “handmaid of Sarai, where have you come from? Or where are you going?” She answered, “I flee from the face of Sarai, my mistress.” And the angel of the Lord said to her, “Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand” (ibid.). Did not the word [Col. 0587B] of the Lord through the prophets likewise recall—and never cease to recall through the prophets—the fugitive people from the worship of calves, Baal, and the other demons, to the worship of their God? At last it scarcely brought about the return of the tribe of Judah to the worship of its God. For the ten tribes, separated by Jeroboam from David’s house, never abandoned the worship of the calves which Jeroboam made; because of this they were carried away to Assyria into an irreversible captivity. Hence the Lord himself said through Hosea: “For I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy on the house of Judah” (Hos. II). Certainly, when the tribe of Judah repented and, returning from Babylonian captivity, rebuilt the temple and the city, then the handmaid returned to her mistress and was humbled under her hand. At last the free woman bore [Col. 0587C] Isaac: that is, the most noble and chief faith, from the womb of the Virgin Mary, brought forth Jesus Christ, conceived by the Holy Spirit. When this occurred, Sarah saw the handmaid’s son playing with her son Isaac and said to Abraham: “Cast out this handmaid and her son; for the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” But, surely, most free faith saw carnal Judaism playing—that is, mocking, indeed persecuting—Christ and Christ’s apostles; and behold, the Jewish people, chosen with its Law according to the flesh alone, was cast out, so that it might not be heir in the kingdom of God; it was also expelled from the place of its earthly possession, so that it might not be at leisure to play—that is, to persecute the freedom of faith.

JUD. If it is as you say, I have great cause to hate your Christ. For, according to the contrived [Col. 0587D] comparison which you have introduced, his coming is the cause for me of every evil—the cause of ruin, captivity, dispersion, and an exceedingly long captivity. Before he came, I was God’s people; now, in your view, I am neither a people nor God’s. Therefore his coming has dealt very badly with me.

CHRIST. That is false. You did not cease to be a people because of his coming; rather, because of his coming you remained a people longer. For the sake of his birth—for there to be a source from which, when he was born, the promise might be fulfilled—you were preserved; the tribe of Judah was preserved, when the ten tribes were condemned to perpetual captivity; and your city Jerusalem was rebuilt, from which so great a salvation had to come, according to the saying: “For from Zion shall go forth the Law, [Col. 0588A] and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II). For had that earthly Jerusalem of yours sinned less than Samaria? Indeed, through the prophet it is charged with having sinned more, when the Lord says to Jerusalem herself: “As I live, Sodom your sister did not do as you did; nor did Samaria commit half your sins; but you surpassed them in your crimes and justified your sisters by all the abominations which you committed” (Ezek. XVI). Lay aside, then, the greatness of that hatred and anger of which the Psalmist speaks in Christ’s person: “And, speaking in earthly wrath, they devised deceit” (Ps. XXXIV, v. 20); for you did not lose your land because of his coming. Rather, because of him—so that, at his birth, the truth of God, who had promised Abraham and sworn to faithful David, might be fulfilled—you possessed it longer than the ten tribes, who were not more unjust but rather more just than you, possessed Samaria.

JUD. Above you said that the commandments and judgments given before the guilt of the calf were commandments and judgments of righteousness, and that God said of them through the prophet: “I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live by them” (Ezek. XX). Was not the command concerning Sabbath observance among those first commandments of righteousness? For God said: “Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day. For six days you shall work and do all your works; but on the seventh day, the Sabbath of the Lord your God, you shall do no work—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your beast, and the stranger who is within [Col. 0588C] your gates. For in six days God made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; and God rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it” (Exod. XX). Why, then, do you not keep the Sabbath? Why do you despise this commandment, one of the ten commandments written upon stone tablets by the finger of God?

CHRIST. Because I do not keep Sabbath with you, do I transgress the commandment and have no Sabbath? On the contrary, if I kept Sabbath with you, I would incur God’s hatred. For God said in Isaiah—and I already reminded you of this far above—“Your new moons, Sabbaths, and other festivals, your calends and your solemnities, my soul has hated. They have become burdensome to me” (Isa. I). I have therefore departed [Col. 0588D] from your Sabbath and have taken for myself a better Sabbath observance: I keep holy the first day of the Sabbath, the day on which my Christ rose, and with whose blood you stained your Sabbath and made it hateful to God. For it was the preparation day of your Passover, and that great Sabbath day was at hand when your fathers completed that sacrilege.

JUD. God sanctified not the first day of the Sabbath but the Sabbath itself; he blessed not the first day, but the seventh. He blessed it because on it he rested.

CHRIST. What do you understand by the designation of that seventh day? Do you suppose it to mean only the interval from sunrise to sunset? If you refuse to understand anything further, I tell you that that day was not the seventh but the fourth from the day on which God made this visible sun. [Col. 0589A] I ask you further: how, or by what operation, did God make all those things in six days?

344 JUD. By saying, “Let it be” (Gen. I); and, as the Psalmist also says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII).

CHRIST. It is as you say. By speaking he made; by speaking he worked; and on the seventh day he rested from his works.

JUD. He did indeed rest; and therefore he blessed and sanctified the seventh day.

CHRIST. Why do you speak on the Sabbath day? For if God made all things by speaking and on the seventh day rested from that manner of his operation, why do you who keep Sabbath for that reason say anything on the Sabbath day? I ask you something else: since you understand that day as extending from sunrise to sunset, did God rest for so short a time? Is his rest the rest of one such day? But I tell you that he still rests and was resting when he said in David: “They did not know my ways; therefore I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. LXIV).

JUD. You weary me, and you nearly make me not know even what I do know. For what else should I know except what the plain face of the letter manifestly tells me? “For six days,” it says, “you shall work; but on the seventh day you shall do no work, because in six days God made heaven and earth and sea and all that is in them” (Exod. XX).

CHRIST. O Jew, God’s kindness nursed your infancy. He did both: he hid within the secret things of his wisdom, which you could not have understood; and [Col. 0589C] on the surface of the letter he nursed you, so that you might know not to close your heart to your workers and not to deny rest to those wearied in your service. Finally, in Deuteronomy he plainly declares this purpose. For after speaking of Sabbath observance, he said: “You shall do no work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your ox, your ass, every beast of yours, and the stranger within your gates” (Deut. V); he immediately added: “So that your male servant and female servant may rest as you do. Remember that you too served in Egypt, and that the Lord your God brought you out of there with a strong hand and an outstretched arm; therefore he commanded you to observe the Sabbath day” (ibid.). For this purpose the first day of the Sabbath does the same as the Sabbath day itself: my servant and [Col. 0589D] my female servant, my ox and my ass, rest one day out of seven. But I would have you understand better what it is to sanctify the Sabbath day according to the Lord’s rest; and concerning this I shall say something which, even if you do not accept it, the disciples of faith will gladly accept—those whose God has opened their hearts to understand the things of the Spirit, so that, with the veil removed, they delight to behold Moses’ face. Some of our elders understood the first six days to be the six kinds of creature of which the world consists, which God made in his wisdom, as the Psalmist says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII); but wisdom itself to be the seventh day, in which God truly rests. This day, indeed, is seventh in number but first in nature. [Col. 0590A] Therefore it should be noted that when Scripture had said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I), by which light we understand the angelic creation, it did not say, “And evening and morning came to be, the first day,” but, “And evening and morning came to be, one day” (ibid.). For he who, as has been said, is placed seventh in number is first by nature, and is rightly placed seventh though he is first; because all things that were made pass away and change, while that day remains eternal and will never have evening. This is he who speaks against you in his Gospel: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘He blasphemes,’ because he said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John X). For since Scripture had said, [Col. 0590B] “And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it,” it accords well with his saying, “him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world”—that is, God made man, the incarnate Word. Allow me, then, to continue, since you have objected to me the sanctification of the Sabbath; for this word concerning sanctification is splendidly set forth both in Exodus and in Deuteronomy. In Exodus he says, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX); in Deuteronomy, “Observe the Sabbath day, that you may sanctify it” (Deut. V). What, I ask, is it to sanctify the Sabbath day except to devote oneself to the word of God in the festivity of holy leisure and, setting aside all things belonging to care for the flesh, to seek the kingdom of God by every means? Whoever has not acted thus, has he sanctified the Sabbath day? The prophet says: “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath, from doing your own will on my holy day, you shall call the Sabbath delightful and the holy day of the Lord glorious” (Isa. LVIII). Whoever thus begins to keep Sabbath is perfected while he lives; when he passes from the present age, he enters the Lord’s rest and rests from his works, just as God also rested from his works.

JUD. You observe neither the Sabbath nor the day which you call the Lord’s Day. For you conduct business, travel, and occupy yourself with all manner of affairs; moreover, you make carved images and venerate them, against another commandment of the Decalogue, which says: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or on earth below, or of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. I am the Lord [Col. 0590D] your God, mighty and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. XX).

CHRIST. If on the Lord’s Sabbath—which is to be at leisure and to see that the Lord himself is God (Ps. XLV)—I allow anything that impedes me from that leisure and holy study, I confess that I sin. Yet know that the same rationale laid down for you does not apply to me, nor am I bound to servitude in every respect as you are. For in connection with your observance of the Sabbath it was truly said to you, because of the rest of your male and female servants: “Remember that you too served in Egypt, and [Col. 0591A] that the Lord your God brought you out of there with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore he commanded you to observe the Sabbath day” (Deut. V). I did not serve in Egypt, but I eat my own bread; and in me is fulfilled what was said through Isaiah: “Seven women shall seize one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and clothe ourselves in our own garments; only let your name be called upon us—take away our reproach’” (Isa. IV). The same prophet had first said: “Because the daughters of Zion have been exalted and have walked with outstretched neck,” etc., down to, “Your most handsome men shall fall by the sword, and your strong men in battle; her gates shall mourn and lament, and she, desolate, shall sit upon the ground” (Isa. III). Having said these things beforehand, he immediately added what I have just quoted: “Seven women shall seize one man.” You were that earthly Zion, an exalted woman walking with outstretched neck, since you could never say, “I shall eat my own bread and clothe myself in my own garments; only let your name be called upon me.” For you had no bread and no garment; indeed, you served as a stranger in Egypt. Yet so that the Lord’s name might be called upon you, he gave you another’s bread and garment, as it is written: “And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. CIV). But the seven women who said, “We shall eat our own bread and clothe ourselves in our own garments,” are all my Churches—that is, those of the Christian name—[Col. 0591C] which, because of the invocation of the Lord’s name, because of the faith they received from that one man, whose you too ought to have been, sought or received no regions or labours of others, but, remaining in the regions which they had possessed from ancient times, keep the Lord’s ordinances and seek his law. Therefore God himself, while giving you the law of the land, says in that same law: “For the land is mine; but you are my tenants” (Lev. XXV).

JUD. Was that land alone—the land of Canaan which he gave us—the Lord’s land? Is not all the earth also the Lord’s? “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it; for he founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers” (Ps. XXIII).

[Col. 0591D] CHRIST. Certainly all the earth and its fullness belongs to the Lord, and after the flood he gave it to the children of men, the children of Noah, saying: “But you, increase and multiply, spread over the earth and fill it” (Gen. IX). But consider what was done and said afterward. The descendants of Ham, Noah’s sons—especially the Canaanites, whose father was Canaan, whom Noah, offended in the person of his father, cursed, saying, “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (ibid.)—lost the land which they had received because of their crimes. Indeed, the land itself vomited them out, as the Lord himself says after enumerating those crimes: “Do not defile yourselves in all these things, by which all the nations whom I cast out [Col. 0592A] before you have been defiled, and by which the land has been polluted; whose crimes I will visit, so that it may vomit out its inhabitants” (Lev. XVIII). Take care, therefore, lest it likewise vomit you out when you have done the same things, as it vomited out the nation that was before you. Thus the Lord rightly called his own the land which, by a just judgment, he chose to take from its possessors and keep for himself, so that he might have in it a memorial of his name, his holy tabernacles, and the temple in which his name ought to be invoked.

JUD. He gave that land to my father, to my father Abraham and his seed; and I am that seed, by the same right by which, as you have just recalled, he gave the earth to Noah’s sons. How, then, could he call that land his own rather than the other lands which he gave to other people?

[Col. 0592B] CHRIST. He gave it indeed, because he promised to give it; but that land was not the whole promise, but a kind of addition, so that those seeking the kingdom of God, toward which the promise undoubtedly tended, might not lack the necessary provision required for the course of this present life. Although he had promised that he would give them that land, your fathers, Jacob’s sons, made themselves unworthy to dwell in it by selling their brother Joseph into slavery. Moreover, God foresaw that, on entering that land, they would defile it more than the nations had defiled it; and therefore he chose to give it only under conditions, saying among other things: “For the land is mine; but you are my tenants.” Therefore I, as I have already said, if on the Lord’s Sabbath—which is to be at leisure and see that the Lord is God (Ps. XLV)—I allow anything that hinders me from that leisure and holy study, I confess that I sin. Yet know that the rationale laid down for you is not also laid down for me, nor am I bound to servitude in every respect as you were. I am not required to make my land keep Sabbath in the seventh year, because I did not receive my land from, or for the sake of, the Gospel in which I believed. I have obtained only spiritual goods through the Gospel, and therefore my Sabbath must be spiritual. Your Sabbath was and is a Sabbath of servitude and flesh; my Sabbath is a Sabbath of liberty and faith. To speak more plainly, your Sabbath was one day, and was hidden from you because you could not bear its brightness unless it were covered by the veil [Col. 0592D] over Moses’ face. But my Sabbath consists of two days: it is the one and the same God and man, Christ Jesus, the first and the eighth day—first because he is God; eighth because, having become man, he is made radiant by the glory of his resurrection. I told you above that the seventh day, which God blessed and in which he rested, though numbered seventh, is itself first by nature and eighth by grace, because by grace he became man for our sake; and, passing from your seventh day, a transitory and shadowy day, he brought me across to the eighth, so that the eighth day, which is also the first, may belong to me, and so that in one person I may celebrate both with a bright festival: namely, because in him all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created; and because he is the beginning, the firstborn from [Col. 0593A] the dead, and through him it pleased God to reconcile all things, whether on earth or in heaven (Col. I).

JUD. If he was first by nature, why was it necessary that he be placed seventh in number? Could it not have been said or written: “On the first day God rested, and on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh he made your works”?

CHRIST. For you, or for those on whose account Scripture was composed, the day of rest was rightly placed after the days of works, although God rested in it both before he worked and rests after he worked. For we are not called from rest to work; rather, after our works, when we have worked well and made good use of God’s creatures, we enter into rest. For we shall rise in a twofold manner—both in soul and in body—whoever faithfully and lovingly believe, according to the reasons stated above, that Jesus Christ is the first and the eighth day. This is my answer to you concerning the Sabbath. Now, concerning the commandment of which you accused me—that I am also a transgressor of the other commandment of the Decalogue which says, “You shall not make carved images for yourself; you shall not worship or serve them” (Exod. XX)—I would likewise answer what is true. But first I must complete what I began above concerning the sacrifice of flesh and blood, which was ordained in the Law through Moses, and concerning the sacrifice of bread and wine, concerning which the Lord swore to Christ according to the order of Melchizedek. I shall persist in doing this; but, that I may make you well disposed to listen, I wish to persuade you to lay aside the contempt of mind by which you are accustomed to despise the Gentile nations, imagining yourself alone to be a noble people, or the noblest of all peoples.

JUD. I rightly think so, because I, a Jew—or the Jewish people—am not like other human beings, like the other nations. Do you yourself think otherwise, or do you wish to advance an opinion contrary to the nobility of our race?

[Col. 0594A] CHRIST. I do not wish to advance an opinion contrary to truth. But if you wish to boast of nobility according to the flesh, I can truly show you that you have no ground for boasting. And 346 to do so briefly, tell me now in what persons the nobility of your race has been most conspicuous.

JUD. In our kings, especially David; in Jerusalem, the city of God; in the Temple; and in all the glory of the priestly and Levitical order.

CHRIST. First, concerning the entire royal tribe, the tribe of Judah, which was most noble: I tell you that, if you had attended to what is true, you would never have said against my Lord, “We were not born of fornication” (John VIII). For Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, committed fornication with that same father-in-law and conceived Perez and Zerah, from whom the whole tribe of Judah was propagated. Levi also, from whom came all the priestly and Levitical families, was born from Leah, who was introduced to Jacob by deception when he had served for Rachel. And, if you consider rightly, Joseph and Benjamin alone were begotten by the lawful wife. Hence father Jacob himself said to his ten sons: “You know that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said, ‘A beast devoured him,’ and he has not appeared until now. If you take this Benjamin also and anything should happen to him on the way, you will bring my grey hairs down to the grave in sorrow” (Gen. XLIV). In saying this he intended Rachel alone to be understood as his lawful wife; and indeed it was so, since six sons were born of Leah, introduced as she was by deception, and four from the handmaids; [Col. 0594C] and, as already stated, he served only for Rachel, to whom he had been betrothed. What shall I say of father Abraham? By race he was a Chaldean, like other human beings. In saying these things, I by no means wish your nation, or the succession of the Israelite race, to be regarded as ignoble; for it is agreed that it was very noble. But my purpose is that you may know that its nobility was not according to the flesh, but according to faith.

## Book Three

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593C] CHRIST. In the brief preceding portion of our disputation, I think it was sufficiently demonstrated that the carnal sacrifices of the Law were not commanded but permitted; not demanded, but voluntarily brought by human beings. Therefore, so that you may no longer doubt, recall who was the first offerer of a sacrifice of this kind, and see whether, according to the testimony of Scripture, he offered it by command or not.

JUD. Abel was the first offerer, as it is written: “Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a tiller of the ground. After many days it happened that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth; Abel likewise offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat” (Gen. IV). Indeed, I read that neither of them was commanded to offer; nevertheless, the sacrifice from the firstborn of the sheep pleased the Lord before the offering from the fruits of the earth, of whatever sort [Col. 0594D] they were. For it follows: “But to Cain and his gifts he did not look” (ibid.).

CHRIST. Certainly, the Lord’s not looking upon Cain’s gifts from the fruits of the earth was Cain’s own fault: he offered well indeed, but divided badly, keeping his heart for himself in unbelief while offering his possession to the Lord. Abel, however, offered himself, or his heart, to the Lord through faith, and his possession through love. For you observe that to offer the fruits of the earth in faith—especially offerings of bread and wine—is no less praiseworthy and pleasing to God, since even at that early time someone made such an offering, though Scripture nowhere records it before the flood. This is especially clear because, soon after the flood, Scripture commemorates a certain man so notably for such an offering that it says: [Col. 0595A] “But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was priest of the Most High—blessed him,” namely Abraham (Gen. XIV). And the priest of this sacrifice blessed the one who had received blessings in the promise. I say, therefore, that the sacrifice of bread and wine has always pleased, and ought always to have pleased, more than the sacrifice of any brute beast; Scripture itself testifies by preferring it in this way: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). Nevertheless, you must know and acknowledge that neither sacrifice was yet commanded at that time; rather, both were accepted by one and the same God according to the merit of the faith of those who offered voluntarily—for example, the faith of Noah and the faith of Melchizedek.

JUD. If it was not commanded, from where did they get the idea to offer? What cause suggested to human beings that they should offer something to the Creator who possesses all things, if he himself had not first commanded it?

CHRIST. The cause of sacrifice or of an offering that ought to be offered to the Lord as a sacrifice was sin. For unless sin had occurred, no sacrifice and no gift of redemption would have been needed by us. Sin itself, however, was committed through eating; through food it seized the human being in disobedience—the human being excessively desirous of the likeness of God—and delivered him over to death. For that food, the fruit of the forbidden tree, was indeed a small thing and in itself of no importance before the Lord; but the intention of the eater was exceedingly [Col. 0595C] great and exceedingly dreadful, according to those words of the serpent: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III). Was this not the sin of the Devil, who first in heaven desired the likeness of God? Therefore, because sin was committed by seizing what was forbidden and eating it, the principle of justice required that a sacrifice be offered to God which should be of such great worth that, by eating it, satisfaction might be made and reparation rendered for the seizure of that food which man had eaten with such an intention. But where, or from where, could man receive or find such a thing?

Therefore God did not wish, nor ought he, to command man anything concerning a sacrifice, because he knew that man possessed nothing by which his sin could be redeemed. But the faithful man—such as Abel was, [Col. 0595D] such as Noah was, such as Melchizedek was, such as Moses was—eager to recover the grace of his Creator, came willingly, sacrificed voluntarily, and offered voluntary gifts, such as or as great as he could obtain from his labours: one from his flocks, in tending which he had laboured; another from the fruits of the earth, which are acquired with greater labour, namely those fruits of the earth of which bread and wine are chief and come only with the greatest labour. For the Lord says: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; and when you have worked the earth, it shall not yield its fruits to you, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (ibid.). The Lord saw those who offered willingly, and deigned to look upon their gifts, though he had need of none of them, according to the Psalmist: “I said to the Lord,” he says, “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV).

[Col. 0596A] He saw them and accepted them according to the merit of the faith of the offerers; and he so honoured the things offered and accepted that in those things which they had prepared to offer or sacrifice he placed sacraments of that single sacrifice which he alone could give, by which alone man could be redeemed from sins or death. This is what we say and know; but you do not wish to know or hear what was the reason underlying the animal sacrifices which were voluntarily offered, as has already been said, on account of which God commanded their rites to be performed thus and thus: certain things wholly burnt, blood poured out or sprinkled in such and such a manner, all the fat consumed by fire, and the rest handled with the most careful ritual. He commanded all to be done as a mystery of the sacrifice to come, [Col. 0596B] under holy and mystical figures, according to what he himself said to Moses in one place, as was recalled much earlier above: “See, and make according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV).

Moreover, in the sacrifice of bread and wine—which you yourself know, and which has already been mentioned above—Melchizedek is read to have been the first to bring it forth; through himself he set forth the cause and power of that same true sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Rupert, book III, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 22; see *Apology for Rupert*.] Its cause, because it has now come; its power, because this sacrifice effects forgiveness of sins, not now in hope but in actuality, for one who receives it faithfully—something impossible for those carnal sacrifices.

JUD. You say that he set forth its cause and power. Who, I ask, set them forth?

[Col. 0596C] CHRIST. Clearly, he of whom that which I mentioned above was spoken: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

JUD. But who is he? I know where you are tending, namely toward Jesus Christ, whom my fathers crucified. But where was he shown to be a priest? Where was he consecrated, or where did he offer sacrifice?

CHRIST. He was nowhere a priest in the order of Aaron, nor ought he to have been, since that alone is the order of priesthood to which you attend; rather, he was in the order, or according to the order, of Melchizedek. Why do you again stand there stupidly? Why do you hesitate? O Jew, whatever the Scriptures say is either true or not true; but who would dare say that they are not true? But if they are true—indeed, because they are true—[Col. 0596D] seek someone in whom the truth of the Scriptures has been fulfilled; and you will find no one except this one Jesus Christ.

I do not now send you far, nor through the many and exceedingly broad expanses of Scripture. Search this one short psalm from which this verse comes: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent”; and you will find the person of the priest, the order of priesthood, the power of the order, the glory and honour of the priest who preceded in his power, the loftiness of his session, and almost everything great and victorious that I have learned through the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, son of David and Lord of David.

I tell you that he suffered and died, and for this reason God exalted him by the exaltation of his ascension into heaven, in the sight of many. What [Col. 0597A] else did that same psalm say in its final verse: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head”? I tell you that he now sits at the right hand of God: according to the flesh, the Son of David; according to divinity, David’s Lord. What else was in the first verse of the same psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand”?

I tell you that his kingdom and priesthood, beginning from Jerusalem, extend themselves to the nations; and that among his enemies—namely Jew and Gentile—his name has grown, and he is preached as Lord of all. And therefore the Jews were led captive among the nations that believe in him, because they are his enemies and refused to become friends through faith. What else does the following verse of the same psalm say: “The Lord shall send forth from Zion the rod of your power: rule in the midst of your enemies” [Col. 0597B]?

I tell you that before he appeared visibly as a human being, before heaven and earth, before every visible or invisible creature, he was God with God, born from the Father’s heart, coeternal and consubstantial with him. Therefore he rightly declared himself to be the Beginning, just as the Father is Beginning. What else does this psalm say in the following verse: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”?

I tell you that he is judge of the living and the dead, and that on the day of judgment he will judge all the ungodly, both nations and kings of nations, but will glorify the righteous and humble. What else is said to him or concerning him in the two following verses: “The Lord at your right hand has broken kings in the day of his wrath. He shall judge among the nations; [Col. 0597C] he shall fill up ruins; he shall shatter heads in the land of many”?

JUD. You are accustomed to handle the Scriptures according to your own interpretation and, as I have already said, to lead and bring them back into whatever direction you wish.

CHRIST. I do not entangle the Scriptures according to my own interpretation; rather, I desire to show you that, as Ezekiel saw and wrote, “there is a wheel within a wheel” (Ezek. I): that is, the evangelical Scripture, which you do not accept, stands founded upon the manifest authority of the old Scripture, legal and prophetic. I know that you are troubled by this and recoil from what is pressed upon you to see; for the prophet already mentioned neither kept silence about nor was ignorant of this also. “There was stature in the wheels,” he says, “and height, and a terrible appearance” (ibid.).

Now I return to [Col. 0597D] what you asked by way of objection. For you said: “Where was he whom my fathers crucified shown to be a priest? Where was he consecrated a priest? Where did he offer sacrifice?” But I say—and have told you—that he was nowhere a priest in the order of Aaron, nor ought he to have been; but he was in the order, or according to the order, of Melchizedek. Unless he had done this, unless he had passed over to that order, how could the oath of the Lord, who cannot lie, have stood? For the Lord said with an oath: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” If your heart were not excessively hard and perverse, then at least because [Col. 0598A] the Lord swore, you would perceive and agree that all things had to be done as Jesus Christ did them.

For on the night in which he was betrayed, he took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: “This cup is the new testament in my blood. Do this in remembrance of me as often as you drink” (I Cor. XI). There he exercised priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, making, after the eating of the lamb, the sacrifice of bread and wine. There the desire of all the saints was fulfilled, who, not possessing a sacrifice sufficient to expiate sin, prepared to sacrifice what they could. Of them Jacob also says in his blessings of [Col. 0598B] Joseph: “The blessings of your father,” he says, “have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the Desire of the eternal hills should come” (Gen. XLIX). [Note: [Col. 0597D] Rupert, book III, *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 23. See *Apology for Rupert*.]

By doing or receiving this, we are healed with a fitting antidote, while the order of justice is preserved: since the first human beings believed what they did not see—namely, that in that apple, according to the serpent’s saying, there was an effective power of divinity or divine likeness—and died by eating it, let us, on the contrary, believe what we do not see with bodily eyes: namely, that in the sacrifice of bread and wine, according to the saying of the Son of God, there is the reality of his flesh and blood, so that by eating we may live, obtaining through this forgiveness of sins.

JUD. Perhaps you will say the same thing to me concerning that sacrifice [Col. 0598C] of bread and wine that you said to me concerning Baptism: namely, that its power descended to hell and that all who were there were refreshed by the same food and drink.

CHRIST. [Note: [Col. 0598D] Rupert, book II on Exodus, ch. 6; book III, *On Wisdom*, ch. 2; book X on Matthew and John.] Certainly I say this: that for this reason my Lord Jesus Christ, according to that whereby he is God, the Word of God, is called—and truly is—the bread of angels, refreshed and fed by his visitation the whole multitude of faithful souls; and according to the body, received into that same belly of the earth in which their bodies had been buried, he became for them the food of the earth, that they might rise to eternal life. As a pledge or testimony of this matter, even now many bodies of saints have risen with him.

What, in that form in which he hung upon the cross [Col. 0598D] and was buried, he then bestowed on those who had gone before, the same Christ bestows upon us who remain in these forms of bread and wine, while, washed by the sacrament of blood and water—which both then flowed from his side—and now dead and cleansed from sins (of which original sin was their greatest reproach), we eat and drink, as I have said, against that food of the first transgression, that we may be children of God.

JUD. If you wished, you would speak something better concerning the holy law of God, the law of Moses, and the sacred order of every sacrifice. You speak altogether as though forgiveness of sin were in your sacrifice alone, and not in the sacrifices of the law. Does not the Lord say in the law: “The priest shall pray for [Col. 0599A] him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him” (Lev. IV)? Or is this said only once? Clearly, forgiveness established by law is also proposed in the offering for every soul—whether one has forgotten an oath or transgressed the ceremonies through ignorance—and in other such cases, with the words: “The priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him.” Either you do not remember these things, or, though you did remember, you dissembled, in order to exalt the order of your sacrifice above measure and to abase my order.

Likewise, when you have said much above concerning the covenant which the Lord made with Abraham my father because of faith alone, as you say, you have been exceedingly negligent in speaking of the covenant or treaty which he made on Mount Sinai concerning the words of the law.

[Col. 0599B] CHRIST. What could I say concerning that covenant except that it was made void? Is this not what the prophets say—indeed, what the Lord speaks in the prophets? For example, Jeremiah says: “Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—the covenant which they made void, and I ruled over them, says the Lord—but this shall be the covenant which I shall make with the house of Israel” (Jer. XXXI), and so forth.

But the covenant of faith, which he made with Abraham, concerning which also, as he had sworn to Abraham, he swore again to David, could not be made void. Thus the same Lord said in the same Jeremiah: “If my covenant with day and my covenant [Col. 0599C] with night can be made void, so that day may not be in its appointed time, then my covenant with David my servant may also be made void, so that there may not be from him a son to reign upon his throne” (ibid. XXXIII). Again: “If I have not established my covenant between day and night, and the laws of heaven and earth, then indeed I shall reject the seed of Jacob and David my servant, so as not to take from his seed rulers of the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (ibid.). That covenant of which you complain was not so firm, or established so firmly, that it could not be dissolved without injury to the justice and truth of God.

JUD. How could the covenant of the law be dissolved, with the truth of God preserved, more than that covenant which, as you say, was the covenant of faith, made with Abraham and David?

[Col. 0599D] CHRIST. If you wish, you can quickly understand the reason. Is not that book of the covenant of which you read thus: “Moses, taking the book of the covenant, read it while the people heard,” and so forth, down to: “This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words” (Exod. XXVI)—is not that whole book, I say, written under a condition? For the Lord began those words, which he commanded to be written in that book, thus: “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I bore you upon eagles’ wings and took you to myself. If therefore you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my peculiar possession above all peoples” (Exod. XIX), and so forth.

Did he speak in the same conditional manner in the promise or promise anew to [Col. 0600A] Abraham and David? Not at all; rather, he said to Abraham without an intervening condition: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And elsewhere: “Look up to heaven,” he says, “and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be” (Gen. XV). But to David: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your seat” (Ps. CXXXI). And elsewhere: “When your days are completed and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom for ever” (II Kings VII).

Since promises of this kind were uttered without condition, they could not be made void while the truth of God remained intact. But those promises of the law, since they were uttered conditionally—“if you hear my voice,” “if you keep my covenant,” and so forth—were made void without the truth of God being weakened; and they began to be made void already at the guilt incurred through the calf. In order that you may weigh more and more properly that this is so, [Col. 0600B] tell me: when, angered because of that calf, did he say that he would destroy them? By saying what did Moses, standing in the breach before him, restrain him? Recall the very words of the man who held back God as he said: “Let me go, that my fury may be angry” (Exod. XXXII).

JUD. The words of the one praying to the Lord are quite readily at hand: “Remember,” he says, “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I shall multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and all this land of which I have spoken I shall give to your seed’” (ibid.).

[Col. 0600C] CHRIST. Why did he not say: “Remember the covenant which you very recently made with us, of which I, your mediator, said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words’”? Clearly because, through such a reminder, it would have had no force, since the conditions of that covenant had already been violated on the people’s side. He was strong in the former case and could hold God fast because, as has already been said, God promised and swore to Abraham without condition.

David too used this same strength when, anxious lest he be considered unworthy, because of the sin he had committed against Uriah the Hittite, of the promise by which God had promised and sworn to him that an everlasting king should be born from his seed, he said: “Have mercy on me, O God, that you may be justified in [Col. 0600D] your words” (Ps. L).

JUD. You have said more than enough concerning the difference between covenant and covenant, promise and promise, and have displayed your very great learning. But I had first and chiefly proposed this: that in my order, in the sacred rite of legal sacrifices, forgiveness of sins is plainly given and proclaimed; and I showed Scripture speaking from the Lord’s mouth: “Whoever has sinned in this or that way shall offer this or that, and the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him.” Therefore you wrongly ascribe forgiveness of sins to your priesthood alone, which you say is according to the order of Melchizedek.

CHRIST. I am ready to answer you concerning this too, nor had I forgotten it; but since you had proposed two matters, I could not answer both at once. I know certainly that the Lord said—and what he said must be true—“the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him.” But must every forgiveness, wherever it is named, be understood as sufficient and perfect? It strongly conflicts with this that, after the Lord had forgiven the sin of the people and had been appeased so as not to do the evil that he had spoken, he later said: “But I shall visit this sin of theirs in the day of vengeance” (Exod. XXIII). And it is evident that the forgiveness of which it is said, “the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him,” is the better forgiveness.

Nevertheless, it does not attain to the measure or equality of this forgiveness which is given in the sacrifice of bread and wine, the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. For it is one thing, in forgiveness, to have punishment merely remitted; another not only to have punishment remitted, but also [Col. 0601B] to receive glory. There are therefore three modes of forgiveness. There is a slight forgiveness, by which sin is so forgiven that, for the present, temporal evil is not inflicted—a matter about which many are concerned, as Ahab and the Ninevites were. And there is the greatest forgiveness, by which sin is so forgiven that the sinner not only escapes punishment but also attains eternal glory.

Between these was the forgiveness by which sin was forgiven in the law: so that because of it the soul would not be punished in hell, possessing the glory of eternal life not yet in actuality but in hope, which was to be given or fulfilled only in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ. Concerning that hope of the saints awaiting in hell, the earlier little book dealt more extensively with testimonies from the Scriptures.

[Col. 0601C] JUD. You linger where you please, and, importunately, repeat and rework what you declaimed long ago; and the matter in which I had caught you, you have either forgotten or evade by dissembling. For I say that you have not abandoned the worship of idolatry, but changed it; and, contrary to the command of the sacred law which says: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or in earth beneath, or of those things which are in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore or worship them” (Exod. XX), you make carved images and worship them.

CHRIST. I make and adore the likeness of the humility of God Most High, who, though he is man, is himself the Most High, as the psalm testifies when it says: “A man was born in her; the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). [Col. 0601D] And in doing this I flee far from the judgment of the devil, in which he made man guilty together with himself, having himself first sinned in saying: “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV); and, promising man the same likeness of God, he said to Eve: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III). For by this I signify clearly enough that I dissent greatly and have departed in mind far from that sacrilegious presumption, since I adore the humility of him hanging upon the cross, whose majesty reigning in heaven that king of the children of pride despised.

JUD. “The idols of the nations,” says the Psalmist, “are silver and gold, the works of human hands; they have a mouth and do not speak,” and the rest down to, “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII). [Col. 0602A] And he speaks in Isaiah, saying: “Is there a God apart from me, and a maker whom I do not know? All makers of an idol are nothing. Who has formed a god and cast a carved image useful for nothing?” and so forth, down to, “A foolish heart has adored this, and he has not delivered his soul, nor says: ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand’” (Isa. XLIV).

CHRIST. And afterward the same God says through the same prophet: “Behold, I shall lift up my hand to the nations, and shall raise up my sign to the peoples. With face bowed down to the earth they shall adore you, and they shall lick the dust of your feet” (Isa. XLIX). Between these things, which were spoken by one and the same Lord, maintain the middle position thus: that you rightly detest the idols of the nations, yet ought to adore some sign, since he says, “I shall raise up my sign”; and, turned toward it, [Col. 0602B] he says, “With face bowed down to the earth they shall adore you.”

JUD. Show that middle position. Explain to me, if you can, the way in which it can ever be permitted for a human being, made in the image of God, to adore some image, some work of hands.

CHRIST. First I tell you this: the object for which you accuse me is not one of the idols of the nations. For the nations, so long as they are or were nations—that is, Gentiles—do not and did not adore such an image. And the difference between them is clear to me: all the idols of the nations are lies, but this image is a sign not of falsehood but of supreme truth. Therefore one who makes and adores the idols of the nations makes a lie and adores a lie.

[Col. 0602C] JUD. Without any distinction, without any exception, God who does not change said: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or in earth beneath, or of those things which are in the waters under the earth” (Exod. XX).

CHRIST. And afterward he himself said to Moses: “You shall make two golden cherubim, wrought in relief, on either side of the oracle. Let one cherub be on one side of the oracle and the other on the other side. Let them join both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle; and let them look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” (Exod. XXV). And it is written in the book of Numbers: “Make,” says the Lord, “a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. Whoever has been struck and looks upon it shall live.” Therefore Moses made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and when those who had been struck looked at it, they were healed [Col. 0602D] (Num. XXI).

JUD. Even if God commanded those things to be made, still he did not command—indeed, he forbade—anything of that kind to be adored or worshipped.

CHRIST. Certainly he did not command or wish them to be worshipped. Indeed, lest youthful minds inclined toward idolatry, captivated by the beauty of the forms or of the metal, should worship them, he wished them to be hidden and forbade them to be seen uncovered. “When Aaron and his sons have wrapped the sanctuary and all its vessels for the moving of the camp,” he says, “then the sons of Kohath shall enter to carry the wrapped things, and they shall not touch the vessels of the sanctuary, lest they die” (Num. IV). Again: “Aaron and his sons shall enter, and shall arrange the burdens of each and assign what each should carry. Let no others, through curiosity, see the things in the sanctuary before they are wrapped, lest perhaps they die” (ibid.).

JUD. What grounds have you for saying that if those cherubim had been exposed to view they would have been worshipped, and those who saw them would therefore die; and that this is why God said, “Let no others see them out of curiosity, otherwise they shall die”?

CHRIST. Scripture recounts concerning King Hezekiah that he broke up the bronze serpent which Moses had made, because until that time the children of Israel burned incense to it (IV Kings XVIII). If, then, they were able to worship the bronze likeness of a serpent, how much more, or more quickly, would they have worshipped the golden likenesses of the holy Cherubim?

Therefore the Lord forbade this when he said: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image nor any likeness [Col. 0603B] which is in heaven above, or in earth beneath, or of those things which are in the waters under the earth” (Exod. XX), lest the making of them be followed by their worship. Hence he added: “You shall not adore or worship them.” And rightly so, because there was nothing in heaven or in the waters whose likeness ought by right to be adored or worshipped, except God, whose uncircumscribed substance was invisible and whose likeness they had seen none, which an artisan could imitate. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: “You saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you in Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest perhaps, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness or image of male or female” (Deut. IV), and so forth.

Thus that commandment of the law works not against me but for me, namely against the Anthropomorphites, against whom Christianity at one time had to contend, so that those who said that man was made in God’s image according to the fashion of his body might be manifestly convicted of error. [Col. 0603C] As has already been said, it does not work against me because at that time God had not been seen, nor was he seen on earth conversing with human beings; but now he has been seen on earth and has conversed with human beings in that form (Baruch III), which Christ—God and man, and the same crucified one—knows best. Accordingly, I make his likeness and adore it with a hope, not vain, of healing and salvation in the faith, or through the faith, of him who hung for me upon the cross in this likeness.

For if those struck were healed by looking upon the bronze serpent set up as a sign—not upon a living serpent but upon the inanimate likeness of a serpent—then how much more should I, looking upon this sign, concerning which, as I have already recalled, the Lord says: “Behold, I shall lift up my hand to the nations and shall raise up my sign to the peoples” (Isa. XLIX), how much more, I say, should I, looking upon and with face bowed to the earth adoring this sign, and licking the dust of his feet, be healed from the bites or strokes of serpents [Col. 0603D] (ibid.), that is, from vices and sins, which are the strokes of evil spirits?

JUD. Then is that sign which you adore a sign of God, rather than of a dead man? For God said to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII); but this one was seen by human beings, seized, and killed.

[Col. 0604A] CHRIST. God is invisible; and in order to be seen he became man. The reason is not unknown to those who rightly recall that it is written first in Exodus and then in Deuteronomy: “Terrified and shaken with fear, they stood at a distance, saying to Moses: ‘Speak to us and we shall listen. Let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die’” (Exod. XX), and so forth. Mindful of this, the Lord himself said to Moses: “I have heard the voice of the words of this people which they have spoken to you; all that they have said is good” (Deut. V).

And Moses himself said to the people: “The Lord your God shall raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him, as you asked from the Lord your God at Horeb when the assembly was gathered, and said: ‘I shall hear no more the voice of the Lord my God, and I shall see this great [Col. 0604B] fire no more, lest I die.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘All that they have said is good. I shall raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and shall put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever refuses to heed his words which he shall speak in my name, I shall be the avenger’” (Deut. XXVIII).

These things and the rest, which would take too long to recount here, make plain to everyone who has eyes to see and ears to hear that God became man because the vision of his substance could not be seen by human beings, namely because of the ancient enmities, whose wall stood between God and humanity because of the sin of the first man. Hence comes that which you do not yet wish to read or understand: “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom [Col. 0604C] of the Father, has declared him” (John I); that is, having dissolved the wall of enmity, he showed human beings the vision of God. This is that prophet concerning whom Moses, as has been said, declared: “The Lord your God shall raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me,” and so forth.

JUD. Behold, then, two gods: God the Father and God the only-begotten Son. But it is written in the law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). And elsewhere: “I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God” (Isa. XLV).

CHRIST. Did the only-begotten Son say this of himself, or did any one of all those who maintain his cause say of him, that he is a Lord God apart from God? Is it to say that God is outside God, or apart from God, when one says, as I just recalled, “the only-begotten Son, who is [Col. 0604D] in the bosom of the Father”? “I,” he says, “am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV). Therefore there are not two Gods, because the Son, who is God, is not outside God the Father; rather, the only-begotten Son is in the bosom of the Father.

JUD. Whatever sort of Christ you make or wish your Christ to be, I tell you that what you adore is neither God nor man.

CHRIST. But the image represents both. I have already told you above that I do not adore the idols of the nations; rather, I adore a sign of truth, which truth the nations, so long as they were nations, did not know.

JUD. Yet you adore an idol, a work of human hands. For Scripture says: “Let those who make them become like them” (Ps. CXIII).

[Col. 0605A] CHRIST. Like them in what—body or soul? If you mean in body, this has never happened, that the body of a man making idols should become like them. But if in soul, you must say it thus: “Let those who make the images become like those whose images they are.” And so let it be, because in truth men are like those whose idols they make and in whose idols they trust. For example, when your fathers were initiated into Baal-peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead (Ps. CV), they became like that same Baal-peor, namely the most shameful Priapus, by committing fornication with Midianite women according to the example of Priapus, who, it is agreed, was exceedingly licentious.

So also concerning the other monsters of the nations, if you understand “let those who make them become like them” according to the soul, you understand rightly: namely, that those who make their idols and those who trust in them are condemned with Jupiter and Mercury, with Juno and Venus, to a like condemnation [Col. 0605B] (Ps. CXIII). What follows for me, then, except that, by making an image of Jesus Christ, Son of God, crucified for me, and adoring this sign of his holy humility, I become like him and become myself a son of God, namely through the grace of adoption?

What do you now say in reply? As I see—or rather, as I have long known with complete certainty—you fail in every respect and flee with your whole mind, though you cannot escape; and there is fulfilled in you what Moses, in whom you trust, pronounced among the other curses of the law and commanded to be pronounced in a loud voice: “May God deliver you falling before your enemies. You shall go out against them by one way and flee by seven” (Deut. XXVIII).

This has been fulfilled in you in two ways, that is, both bodily and spiritually. Bodily, indeed, because you fell before your enemies, namely before the Roman soldiers: because, having dared to go out against them by one way, through confidence in one fortified city, you fled from them by seven ways—that is, you who survived the sword were scattered through every land. Spiritually, however, because, boasting in one thing, namely the flesh of Abraham, before all people seeking truth—people to whom you have made yourself hateful—you fall daily; and while you put excessive confidence in this alone, as has been said, namely that you too are Abraham according to the flesh, and go out against me, you turn your back, convicted by seven ways, that is, by all the Scriptures of truth, [Col. 0605D] preferring to flee truth rather than believe truth.

JUD. Then are you my enemy, and do I fall before you as before an enemy? Where is what you said, that you sought my salvation, when you declare that you act as an enemy?

CHRIST. It is written in the Psalm: “With perfect hatred I hated them” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Perfect hatred is where not human beings but human errors are hated, especially when the error is joined by a defense of the error. Tell me now for what reason the Lord delivered you, as I have said, to fall before your enemies, and caused all the curses which Moses wrote to come upon you and overtake you.

[Col. 0606A] JUD. Because I did not listen to the voice of the Lord my God, to keep and do all his commandments and ceremonies which he himself commanded me.

CHRIST. Truly, you did not listen; truly, you did not keep them. This—and no more—has been your customary answer to me. But I seek from you a definite point, that you may confess wherein you did not listen and wherein you did not keep them. For God never delivered your fathers into the hands of enemies without first indicating and making apparent the cause. For example: when the children of Israel took wives from among the daughters of the Canaanites and gave their own daughters to the sons of those people, and did evil in the sight of the Lord by serving their gods, the Baals and the Astartes, the Lord was angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia. This evil—namely, prostituting themselves to foreign gods and worshipping them—Scripture always sets forth before it recounts the Lord’s wrath in delivering Israel to its enemies.

But when was Israel delivered as it has now been delivered? When was Israel captive and scattered in this fashion, and for so long? Therefore, if, when it was more lightly handed over while still dwelling in its own land, though serving its enemies, the fault or cause was specifically stated—and ought to have been stated—how much more does your present captivity and dispersion, surpassing in its magnitude all the former calamities of your race, have a cause which you ought specifically to know and confess? Indeed, you are not ignorant of it, but pretend ignorance, wishing to say nothing but, “Because of my sins.” But I shall tell you—or rather, I shall show you that Moses and the prophets foretold it.

For where Moses set down all the curses which have now come upon you, he added this cause: “Your life shall hang, as it were, before you; you shall fear by night and by day, and shall not believe your life” (Deut. 28). Daniel states it more plainly: “After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain” (Dan. 9). This is the cause; and immediately he added what you now suffer: “And the people who shall deny him shall not be his people. And the people with their coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; its end shall be desolation; and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed, sacrifice and offering shall fail, and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation; and desolation shall continue unto consummation and the end” (ibid.).

Confess, therefore, that because of the sin of denying Christ—whom you denied before Pilate and killed—the Roman people, with their leader, namely Vespasian or his son Titus, destroyed the city of Jerusalem and the sanctuary; that the decreed desolation continues; and that you are not his people, whom you denied. Than this evil of yours—namely, not being his people—nothing is worse. He did not say, “The people who will kill him shall not be his people,” but “the people who will deny him.” That you killed him would not harm you, unless you denied him obstinately.

Behold: as Moses said, as I have already recalled, your life hangs, as it were, before you, and you do not believe your life. Long ago one life truly hung—not all day, but from the sixth hour until the ninth hour (Matt. 27); but now it hangs, as it were, wherever you are scattered, as the same Moses had previously foretold: “The Lord shall scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth unto its bounds” (Deut. 28). For Christ, who truly hung, is that life which hangs, as it were, before you, because the likeness of him who hung is openly worshipped, while you look on, in so many places of his dominion. It hangs, as it were, and shall hang, as it were, as he himself foretold: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3). And this likeness shall hang before you, though you refuse to see it; and, turned to fury and not knowing what you say—for it is irrelevant—you cry out against me, cry out against this exalted sign of the Lord: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands” (Ps. 113).

JUD. Do you, then, worship only that image of your crucified one, whom you call your God and seek to persuade me is the Messiah, that is, Christ? You also make innumerable other images for yourself, both male and female, and your temples are full of images of those who are not gods.

CHRIST. I have already told you that Moses too made cherubim, and that Solomon enlarged such images in the temple which he built, as it is written: “He made in the inner sanctuary two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high. One wing of one cherub was five cubits, and the other wing five cubits—that is, ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. The second cherub also was ten cubits high, of equal measure. The workmanship of the two cherubim was one: one cherub was ten cubits high, and likewise the second cherub. He placed the cherubim in the midst of the inner temple; the cherubim stretched out their wings, and one wing touched the wall, while a wing of the second cherub touched the other wall; their other wings met one another in the middle of the temple. He overlaid the cherubim with gold, and carved all the walls of the temple round about with various carvings and work made by the lathe. He made upon them cherubim, palms, and diverse figures, as though projecting from and emerging out of the wall” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 6), etc.

After that time many memorable things—and many more, or greater things than before—were accomplished through the ministry of holy angels; and many innumerable palms and cedars have grown high among us, such as those of which the psalmist says: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm-tree; he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon. Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God; they shall still multiply in a fruitful old age” (Ps. 91).

Therefore I commendably carve all the walls of churches with varied engraving and turned work; and I multiply not only cherubim and palms, but also diverse representations, presenting to my remembrance the memorable deeds of the saints: the faith of the patriarchs, the truth of the prophets, the glory of kings, the blessedness of apostles, and the victories of martyrs. Among all these sacred images, the cross to be worshipped, together with the image of my Saviour, shines pre-eminent. I wonder that you could have killed him by no manner of death such that an image of that death might have been set before the sight of the whole world in so great and evident a display. If you had hurled him down from the brow of the mountain, as you wished to do; if you had stoned him, as once and again you wished to stone him; if you had struck him with the sword, as the accursed Herod wished to slaughter him when he was an infant: in none of these cases could an image of his death have been proposed so conspicuously for the world to behold.

But now let us end the dispute. Come with me inside into the house of the Father who received me, and, celebrating a feast for my return, ordered the fatted calf to be killed; and said, “Let us eat and make merry, because this my son was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15). Come inside, that we may feast together; believe, that you may be saved with me.

JUD. Is this what you wish to persuade me—to eat with you and also eat pork and the other unclean things forbidden by the Law?

CHRIST. It matters very little to me to speak with you about this, because, as I have said elsewhere, commandments of this kind are “not good commandments,” and were given especially because of the guilt of the calf. For God himself, in Ezekiel, after first saying, “They provoked me, did not walk in my commandments,” and so forth, down to, “their eyes were after the idols of their fathers” (Ezek. 20), adds: “Therefore I too gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they should not live” (ibid.). To me every creature is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4). For after the flood God said to Noah and his sons: “All the fishes of the sea are delivered into your hand; and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. As green herbs I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood” (Gen. 9).
