JUD. Therefore, if God says, without distinction, “All the fishes of the sea are delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; as green herbs I have given you all things,” why do you not also eat flesh? Why do you not swallow a frog or a toad?

CHRIST. I cannot persuade my heart to it; my sense recoils; reason does not assent to such excess. But why should I spend longer with you over such matters? For my Lord says, “What enters the mouth does not defile a person, but what proceeds from it, that defiles a person. What enters the mouth goes into the belly; but the things which proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile a person. For evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies proceed from the heart. These are the things that defile a person” (Matt. 15).

Accordingly, my fathers most rightly said and wrote to me: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication; and that you do not do to others what you would not have done to yourselves. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well” (Acts 15).

JUD. Who are these fathers of yours?

CHRIST. The apostles of Jesus Christ, who begot me through the Gospel—the begetting of faith, the generation of the Word of God—so that I might believe and know that the promise which the faithful God promised and swore to your fathers had been fulfilled.

JUD. I pay little attention to those fathers of yours, nor do I care for what they said or wrote. I am a disciple of Moses, and I know that God spoke to Moses; but I do not know where your apostles are from.

CHRIST. How do you know that God spoke to Moses? How do you know that God spoke to the prophets?

JUD. Scripture has declared this to me, and trustworthy testimony has been furnished through signs, wonders, and miracles.

CHRIST. Scripture has likewise declared to me concerning my fathers, the apostles, that God spoke to them, “the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16). But I shall say to you one further thing, which you have not yet properly considered. I know—and you ought to know—that God spoke to Moses and to the prophets because what they were instructed or taught in was not according to man: they neither received the word from a human being nor learned it from one. Though most of them were unlearned—indeed shepherds, as Amos plucking sycamore fruit and David tending his father’s sheep—they were invisibly taught through the revelation of the Spirit of God, made wise; and the fulfilment of events followed their word of wisdom. For this reason they were received, and ought to have been received, at so lofty a height of authority that not to hear them was, or is, not to hear God, as God himself said to one of them: “The house of Israel will not hear you, because they will not hear me” (Ezek. 3).

Now behold: my fathers, the apostles, neither received nor learned from a human being nor through one. Though they were unlettered and unlearned men, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and suddenly they were made wise and knowledgeable and able to speak in every language; and the fulfilment of events followed—and follows—their word of wisdom. For example, while your city, earthly Jerusalem, still stood in its glory, they wrote and said that its destruction would soon come, as they had heard from the Master of Truth: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near. But woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days; for there shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath upon this people. They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21). For not only did the Master foretell this, but the disciples wrote it before it happened, so that what was said or written by them came to pass. And at least this portion of the truth you cannot hide: you have been led captive, not to one place, but to all nations, surviving the swords of the Romans.

Therefore, since both my fathers, the apostles, and Moses and the prophets, did not learn from a human being nor through one, but were suddenly taught by the Holy Spirit, they are rightly fathers to me upon the same summit of canonical authority. And because you refuse to hear them, I say truly that you refuse to hear God. Behold, I shall have two millstones with which to grind the wheat of God’s word and make life-giving bread. But you, who profess to hear Moses and the prophets, though you do not truly hear them, and who neither hear nor profess willingness to hear the apostles—you have only one stone, the lower one, lying idle; hence you make no flour. That is, you find no secure authority in the Scriptures which you think you possess.

I tell you now, as I said: do not remain outside, nor envy the robe, the sandals, and the ring—the seal of faith—which the Father gave me as his repentant son; rather come inside and share in the joy and the feast. But if you do not, I shall wait and endure your indignation until the Father himself goes out and entreats you (Luke 15). Meanwhile I shall say to the glory of that same Father: “My ring is mine, my ring is mine.”

## On the Truly Apostolic Life

[Col. 0609]

**The Five Books of Dialogues on the Truly Apostolic Life, by, as it appears, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz.**

(Edited by Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, col. 969, from a manuscript codex of Graffschat Monastery, whose script appears to be about six hundred years old.)

### Preliminary Observation

These five books of dialogues, *On the Truly Apostolic Life*, seem to have been written for no other reason than that their author might demonstrate that monks are fit to undertake every office of the Church, and that regular canons inflict the gravest injustice upon them. The regular canons, scarcely having arisen in the eleventh century, immediately declared war on the monks, believing and everywhere loudly proclaiming that monks, as incapable of preaching the divine word, administering the sacraments, and pastoral care of parishes, should be shut up within the narrow confines of their cells. Yet hitherto monks had converted almost countless peoples, whole nations, and no few kingdoms to faith in Christ through their preaching; they had administered not merely certain parishes but almost the entire dioceses of the whole world, and had occupied the apostolic see itself more than once, and not without fruit. For, without any fault of empty boasting, we may maintain that churches have scarcely ever flourished more than when they had monks as bishops.

The author of these *Dialogues* intentionally concealed his own name, attributing whatever good he set forth in them entirely to God, from whom comes every good thing. He wished that the book itself might be read mute in its own praise, provided that it speak the praise of God and the Church. Nevertheless, we may assert with no slight probability that they were written by Rupert, abbot of Deutz near Cologne. Graffschat Monastery, from a codex written at that period we copied them, lies in the diocese of Cologne; and we later found a similar exemplar in Rupert’s own monastery at Deutz, almost the only surviving one there among all the works of so great a man.

Moreover, the author concludes his third book in these words: “The approaching feast of Saint Nicholas compels us to attend to it, and therefore compels us to divide off a fourth book, in which we may be aided by his prayer.” Saint Nicholas, moreover, is patron of the nearby Brunvilar Monastery at Deutz, with which Rupert doubtless had close association. Finally, it is certain that Rupert composed some work on this subject, as we learn from Anselm of Havelberg’s letter to the abbot of Huysburg. On the occasion of a certain Peter, a regular canon, who had transferred to the monks for the sake of greater perfection, Anselm had published a treatise on the same subject. Wishing to refute it, he speaks of Rupert with great contempt:

> “Furthermore, you append the teaching of some Robert or other, whose authority, because it is unknown in the Church, is as easily despised as it is approved. Perhaps he is thought great among you, not because he wrote anything great, but because he happened to be abbot of monks. I confess, indeed, that I read some of his writings with frivolous curiosity; I even saw and knew him. But I found true of him the Greek proverb admirably spoken: ‘A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.’”

Such are the pleasantries with which this bishop entertains that outstanding man, whose writings and holiness the Church has hitherto venerated. But those who defend a just cause seek victory not in abuse or insults, but in the strongest arguments.

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0611A]

When certain brethren observed everywhere how the holiest things were being trampled under foot and the stones of the sanctuary scattered at the head of every street, their hearts raged with that zeal which made the inward parts of Mattathias tremble. They earnestly urged me also to take up my own staff, so that, if I could not overthrow, I might at least wound the devil, who daily reproaches Israel.

When I told them that I was still, as it were, unarmed and powerless, and not equal to the task, they attempted to convince me by this comparison: “How,” they said, “has divine and human law established that every traveler who sees a wolf attacking a flock must reveal it by whatever voice he can, lest, if he delays to report it, he be held guilty of the sheep carried off? Even the little ones, together with the greater, ought to seize clubs or whatever weapons of defence they have when they see fiercer warfare rising against them. Those who do not wish to overthrow the common enemy must spare no sort of weapon. Thus David, though small in stature, overthrew Goliath with sling and stone, when he reproached all Israel to their face.”

Conquered, then, both by their reasoning and by their request, I chose with my own pen to expose to the children of God Satan, who wishes to scatter them while remaining hidden among them without being recognized. Therefore, whoever you are who truly are children of God, or truly desire to be counted as Israel, observe that I direct the following little work on your behalf and to you. It is clear that I write not against you, but against him who is king over all the children of pride. For although he said that he had gone around and walked through the earth, he nevertheless said that he had stood before God with the children of God—namely, so that they, conceiving by his spirit, might bear children of pride, while he begrudged them their being children of God.

For when there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not human and carnal, though spiritual brethren must plainly be children of God and peacemakers? For this controversy is old between monks and clerics: which of them are worthier to handle the mysteries of the Church? It has gone so far that, while they contend with one another for apostolic dignity, they walk empty of apostolic charity. Indeed, since monks and clerics are, as it were, the two eyes of the whole people’s body, if these are shown blind through the spirit of pride, in what great darkness is the people enveloped? For “if your eye is dark, your whole body will be dark” (Luke 11:34). If, in one head, two eyes refused to see together, would it not be just that both be plucked out of the head?

Therefore, having seen these eyes gravely sick with the phlegm of pride, each setting itself above the other, and having often been present in this warfare, I have endeavoured, as some sort of physician, to describe their disease and offer them this little work as a kind of eye-salve: both that, when contention is destroyed, they too may walk in love; and that the grounds may become clearer to all as to who are worthier in apostolic dignity.

As for having equated the life and rule of monks, with such authority, to the Gospel and to the dignity of the apostles, I call to witness the coming judgment and Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, that I have done this not from partiality toward persons but because I was instructed by truth and by a vision of this kind. For one night, when I was troubled in anxious thought over this very question, I was suddenly overcome by sleep and seemed to myself to be celebrating Mass. And behold, I saw at the right side of the altar three men of wondrous authority, standing beside one another with serene faces. As I stood astonished and did not know who they were, suddenly a voice sounded, making known to me that two were apostles, Bartholomew and Thomas, and that the third was Saint Benedict the monk.

Then I looked again to the left side of the altar, and behold, a certain cleric, indeed in incomparable dress but with a terrible face, approached me. When he hurried forward as though to inflict something upon me, he was restrained by the three who stood at the right, so that he might not burden me in any way. When Mass was finished, the three departed alike with serene countenances. Thus I understood that I ought to describe monastic and apostolic life as possessing equal dignity, since blessed Benedict had deigned to show himself in the vision as equal to the apostles, expressing in this vision what I saw to be the question of the whole book. Yet whether this vision should be understood otherwise, I leave to the reader’s judgment.

I have withheld my name because, if I have said anything useful, I give glory for it not to my own name but to his, so that the book may be read mute in my praise, provided that it speaks the praise of God and the Church. Therefore, in place of my name, let this work be called a *Dialogue on What the Truly Apostolic Life Is*, for this is the sum of the entire book. I composed the following little work in dialogue because, since this question plainly lay between monks and clerics as between two parties, I wished to choose someone to ask questions, so that, while he would spare nothing in questioning, everything made clear in answer might be pure. I also wished to support by authority that which I could prove by reason. I ask, moreover, that this prologue, with the chapters, be prefixed to the work itself as I have arranged it.

## The Chapters of Book One Begin

[Col. 0613B]

I. On the disciple’s reasonable urging of the master in defence of the Church.  
II. On the fact that the central question, on which the entire book depends and is written, is set forth in four ways.  
III. That the three orders of the Church, while contending among themselves, grievously wound the fourth through error.  
IV. That, just as many questions may seem to be raised under one objection, so many may be cut off under one answer.  
V. On the argument by which it is proved that those judged more perfect ought to be left to God’s judgment.  
VI. That, if this argument is granted, an absurd consequence follows.  
VII. By what argumentative structure the objection of the monks is strengthened.  
VIII. What the monks object to the regular canons.  
IX. That regular canons and monks make the same objection to those called clerics.  
X. That monks and those called clerics agree neither in their manner of life nor in their objection to others.  
XI. That all are answered by the testimony of the apostle; this is also called the preliminary exercise.  
XII. By what argument it is found that no one is taught except by Truth itself.  
XIII. How it is established that authority has been found to agree with reason.  
XIV. That those who seem unjustly strengthened by both reason and authority ought to be refuted by reason and authority.  
XV. How authority testifies that expelling vices is more difficult than acquiring virtues.  
XVI. That authority establishes that those who oppose by reason alone are sometimes to be convicted, and that conclusions are sometimes to be drawn from authority that has been adduced.  
XVII. That one who must bring the discordant back to peace ought so to rebuke some that he seems to defend others, and conversely; but now to correct all or bring all back to peace.  
XVIII. That, where discourse is for truth, it is easier [read: better] for scandal to arise than for truth to be abandoned.

## Book One Begins: On What the Truly Apostolic Life Is

[Col. 0613D]

### Chapter I

**DISCIPLE.** Beloved master, do not permit the holy Church to be disturbed any longer by the calumny of certain persons, since you are able to defend her both by the truth of reason and by the authority of Scripture.

**MASTER.** What do you command to be done?

**D.** Permit me to question you in the words of certain objections, so that you in turn may be able, by the bridle of reason and authority, to restrain the mouths of those who speak wickedly.

**M.** The Church is believed to be built upon a firm rock. Will she then, who has Christ as her foundation, need the support of such a little man as I? Who props up an immovable mountain with a straw, or filters a most lucid fountain with muddy water? Who illumines the brightest radiance of the sun with bleary eyes, or touches with a filthy hand one clothed in the whitest robes?

**D.** Come now: even if, as you say, the Church needs no defence from anyone, at least grant that one who asks questions needs an oracle from one who answers.

**M.** Come then: overcome already, I grant that you should state briefly the things which seem to you to be objected.

**D.** Since it is evident that I am labouring to bring forth certain great and useful things through my questioning, I ought not hastily pass over what I think. Thus I cannot state them so briefly, lest afterward I be compelled to repent of speech that was too hasty.

**M.** I do not know what anxiety of yours makes me anxious.

**D.** I have need of it.

**M.** Need of what, at last?

**D.** With your permission, that, after the first and principal question, I may be allowed to submit to your examination every question which seems to arise from it, as it occurs.

**M.** You ought by no means to ask this from a human being, but from the examination of reason. Therefore, if something moves you, set it forth at last.

### Chapters II–III

**D.** The Church seems divided into four members, three of which, while holding contrary opinions among themselves, leave the fourth—which follows the three—in grave error.

**M.** I hear only words; I therefore need their meaning.

**D.** For example, there are monks under a rule; there are also regular canons; there are those called clerics; and there are laypeople. Since monks, regular canons, and clerics each claim for themselves the dignity of apostolic perfection, you surely see how gravely they scandalize the laity. For while each of these strives to claim apostolic dignity as though it were his own particular possession, he thereby undeniably deprives the rest of it. It follows that, if monks alone possess the apostolic life, then regular canons and clerics are all strangers to it. Likewise, if regular canons possess it, clerics and monks are excluded. But if clerics possess it, monks and regular canons are excluded. Thus it comes about that, as though its head were blinded, the whole people, like a blind body, seems to grope in darkness; and those wishing to renounce this world do not know to which group they ought to attach themselves.

### Chapter IV

**M.** Very cleverly, under the pretext of one question, you are shown to raise innumerable questions, so that, while I am obliged to resolve this one for you, I am almost compelled as a debt to explain to you what concerns nearly the whole Church. Therefore, I think it is judged fitting that the same measure be measured back to you.

**D.** What measure, I ask?

**M.** What measure, except that, just as you seem craftily to thrust many questions upon me under one question, so I too may seem craftily to cut off many questions for you with one answer?

### Chapter V

**D.** Please do not be angry, lest you seem to return evil for evil.

**M.** Then say, concerning all things: is God’s judgment or a human being’s to be preferred?

**D.** Whoever does not say God’s judgment, I consider foolish.

**M.** Therefore those whom God judges dearer to himself are surely more perfect in the whole Church; they are nearer to apostolic perfection itself. It must therefore be left to God’s judgment which persons are to be considered more perfect, preferred to all others in apostolic dignity.

**D.** This is a very short shortcut over a long journey.

**M.** Therefore the whole matter is settled.

### Chapter VI

**D.** See, then, whether this very short shortcut is followed by an excessively confused silence.

**M.** You must complete what you seem to say.

**D.** If it is evident that the Church has rightly taught preachers and has justly learned from them, then it is certain that you have reached a conclusion which is according to reason in one respect but not according to the edification which is expedient.

**M.** What you say does not yet seem coherent.

**D.** Moses plainly related that God created heaven and earth and everything in them; yet, among all these matters, God’s judgment is to be preferred to Moses’ judgment. Therefore, if Moses ought to have reserved all that he said for God’s judgment merely because that judgment is preferred to his own, it follows that Moses either lied or erred in everything he said.

**M.** You go too far.

**D.** By similar reasoning all the preachers of the Church are shown to err if they ought to have committed the things they preached solely to God’s judgment. But it follows: if preaching is removed, faith is not received; if faith is not received, the Church’s foundation is overturned. Therefore, if the Church is destroyed, paganism is introduced; all councils must be annulled, the volumes of all books shut up, and at last every lip must be mute.

**M.** How then am I compelled to answer you by reason? Go on confidently, therefore, and pursue your question.

### Chapter VII

**D.** The objection of the monks is strengthened by the following structure of arguments. When Christ spoke of apostolic perfection, he addressed these words to a certain young man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Therefore, they say, because we are plainly fulfilling this command, we are proved to possess this perfection.

**M.** They would not say this altogether absurdly, if they did not presume it of themselves.

### Chapter VIII

**D.** Furthermore, they say that regular canons do not possess so great a perfection, since it is evident that many things forbidden to monks are allowed to them. The more anyone labours, moreover, the greater reward he will receive for his labour; for each shall receive his own reward according to his labour. They seem to say many things in this fashion, which, if you please, may be reserved for objection later.

**M.** It pleases me. Therefore proceed to the rest.

**D.** “We regular canons,” they say, “are made like the apostles themselves, since, being placed in their position, we imitate their conduct and life. For just as it was said to the apostles, ‘You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do people light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house’ (Matt. 5:14–15), so we hold that this is said to us, whose life, habit, and conduct we possess. Therefore, if we are the light of the world, a city which cannot be hidden set upon a mountain, and a lamp placed upon a lampstand, we must preach to all in the household of the Church and fulfil the work of evangelists and apostles.”

**M.** Sufficiently imperious.

**D.** Moreover, the monks say that, since they are known to live the life of penitents, they ought to conceal themselves in the cloister as though beneath a bushel. For they are dead, and their life is hidden with Christ in God. Therefore, when Christ appears, their life too will appear with him in glory. As they are dead here and alive there, so they ought to appear there and lie hidden only here. Therefore they ought neither to preach nor to baptize. Their habit also testifies to this: just as they are contemptible in both clothing and tonsure, so in this life they are not esteemed by this world.

**M.** I think that this insult turns to their glory.

### Chapter IX

**D.** Those called clerics seem to make all these objections to monks together with regular canons. Yet clerics claim for themselves what regular canons think of themselves. Likewise monks and regular canons jointly agree against clerics, judging them, because of their worldly way of life, unworthy even of the name of cleric. Therefore they do not share in the sacraments with them, saying with Gregory: “When their life is despised, it remains that their preaching should be condemned.”

**M.** These would seem to have reason, if they did not glory in themselves.

### Chapter X

**D.** Moreover, monks and those called clerics seem as far apart from one another in profession of life and manner of conduct as they fail to agree either in assigning dignity to themselves or in rejecting others.

**M.** You pursue everything very diligently, for you seem to omit nothing.

**D.** Even if I seem through carelessness to neglect something, I made an agreement with you, as you know, that you may correct me.

**M.** To give you first a kind of preliminary exercise, all may be answered by this one testimony of Paul: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord; for not the one who commends himself is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Cor. 17:8 [probably 2 Cor. 10:18]); and, “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Rom. 12:16); and, “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Therefore all who glory in their own profession are proved to be destroyers of their own profession. Thus, while each strives to stand at the summit of the Church’s dignity, all are excluded outside from every dignity in it. For it is fitting that the body should cast outside itself those members for whom it is not enough to retain their own places.

**D.** The discourse is now almost beginning to move forward.

**M.** Yet what do you wish to learn concerning all these matters?

### Chapter XI

**D.** Indeed, the truth of reason.

**M.** From Truth itself, or from anyone else?

**D.** Provided that I might learn it, I confess that I would wish to learn from anyone else.

**M.** Therefore you evidently wish to learn truth from a beast.

**D.** Who, if sane, would say that?

**M.** You yourself are shown to say precisely this.

**D.** Do you then seem angry?

**M.** For you confessed that you wished to learn truth from anyone other than reason itself; but anything whatsoever other than the truth of reason itself is a beast. Therefore, if you wish to learn truth from anyone else, you must learn truth from a beast.

D. Though confused, I confess that I ought to learn the truth of reason only from Truth itself.

M. It is therefore established that Truth teaches all of us concerning itself.

D. It is plain that you prove this reasonably; but it is also plain that I now despair of finding it.

M. May God defend you from that calumny.

D. What then? If it is established that Truth teaches everyone concerning itself, it follows also that we ought to question it alone concerning every truth. How, then, should I presume to do this, or who ought to presume this of himself?

[Col. 0618B] [CHAP. XII.] M. You must therefore recall the words of Truth, if authority anywhere is found to agree with reason.

D. O how wonderfully you have reminded me! For I recall that Truth itself said: “Do not be called masters, for one is your master, Christ” (Matt. XXIII, 10). “One” is used there as though “alone” were said. But Christ is Truth; therefore Christ alone is understood, without doubt, to be the master, and Truth alone. Thus, just as the one—that is, unique—master is proved to teach all who are taught, so it is concluded by the clearest reasoning that Truth alone teaches all.

[CHAP. XIII.] M. At last you have properly awakened, showing very beautifully that authority agrees with reason. [Col. 0618C] Therefore, if it pleases you, henceforth we must observe this method throughout: whenever I endeavor by reason to refute or establish anything I say, you likewise must make the authority of Scripture accord with reason.

[CHAP. XIV.] D. Very well indeed. For since the professions of the several parties seem to be strengthened partly by the truth of reason and partly by the authority of the Gospel, it follows that they ought to be refuted or established by that same truth of reason and authority of the Gospel.

M. So that, like Goliath, those who boast may seem to fall by their own sword; or, like David, the humble may be proved to defend themselves with sling and stone.

D. We are composing this well. For I seem to recall the authority of Truth [Col. 0618D] by which I may be raised from that despair of mine: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst,” says the Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. XVIII, 20). But Christ says: “I am Truth” (John XIV, 6). Therefore, if Christ is not doubted to dwell in the midst of those gathered in his name, we testify without doubt that we have Truth in our midst.

M. Why then do we hesitate to question Truth itself, if it deigns to place itself in our midst?

D. O wretched, wretched soul, deprived of so great a glory—she through whom the Father made even the ages; she who, being the radiance and image of her Father, and upholding all things by the word of her power (Heb. I, 3), and a word sharper than every two-edged sword, [Col. 0619A] reaching even to the dividing of the soul (Heb. IV, 12), reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly (Wis. VIII, 1), deigns to dwell in a prison, in the midst of the wretched people placed in this exile, she who in heaven is proved to preside over all the choirs of angels.

M. The order of reasoning seems to require that we answer the objections of the several parties: first, that the perversely spoken words of those who boast and are proud should be demolished, like old buildings; and afterward, that the statements of the humble, who place their hope not in themselves but in God, should be built up, as upon a new structure.

[CHAP. XV.] D. Authority also attests this, when God spoke to Jeremiah: “Behold,” he says, “I have sent you to uproot and destroy, to overthrow and scatter, and [Col. 0619B] to plant and build” (Jer. I, 10). He named four acts in the destruction of vices, but joined two in the building of virtues. Therefore, just as it is prior and more arduous to destroy what is vicious, so it is later and easier to build what is virtuous.

M. Therefore I ought, with greater labor, to destroy Adam, the old man, with his deeds, so that I may be able to raise up the new man, who was created according to God.

D. May God do and add this: that the one may be utterly destroyed here and in us, and that the one from above may be raised up in us.

[CHAP. XVI.] M. Remember this also: that by a rational order I must sometimes proceed by reason alone, and sometimes, from an authority introduced into the discussion, conclude what is necessary.

D. This too is very reasonable. For we read that the Lord did both. When the Jews themselves answered that Christ was nothing other than the son of David, he introduced David’s own authority into the discussion—“The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. CIX, 1), etc.—and concluded that Christ, which they denied, was David’s Lord; and thus he inferred by reason that he was true God: “If David then calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?” (Matt. XXII, 45). Again, when they accused him of having restored a man to health on the Sabbath, he proved by reason alone that it was lawful for him to do so, saying: “Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, does not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath day?” (Luke XIV, 5). As though he said: [Col. 0619D] If it is lawful for you on the Sabbath to draw an ass from a pit, it is much more lawful for me to heal a man.

[CHAP. XVII.] 359 M. Grant me this also: that, while I seem now to accuse the professions of the several parties of presumption, now to recall them to the peace of concord by discourse, I may sometimes seem so to accuse some that I seem thereupon to defend others; and again so to defend some that I seem to correct others; while at other times I am prepared to correct all for presumption, or to defend them according to their profession.

D. Authority likewise establishes that you ought to do this, since the Apostle Paul seems to do the same in the same matter. Speaking against Jews and Greeks, he seems to restrain the Jews, who gloried in the Law against the Gentiles, in such a way as to attribute the fulfillment of the Law to the Gentiles, saying: “If the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the Law, shall not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision?” (Rom. II, 26). At other times he seems so to accuse the Gentiles, who excuse themselves against the Jews on grounds of ignorance, [Col. 0620B] that he seems to attribute much more to the Jews, saying: “What advantage then has the Jew, or what profit is there in circumcision? Much in every way” (Rom. III, 1). Again, he rebukes all alike: “For we have charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin” (ibid.); and again he recalls all to the peace of concord, saying: “Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace with God” (Rom. V, 1), etc.

M. You seem to assist me greatly indeed.

D. Not I, but may Truth itself deign to teach us here and everywhere.

M. So be it, so be it. Therefore those who desire this truth wish to warn beforehand that no one ought, as though because of the superfluity of an abundant discourse, to find fault when they see me range in speech through nearly the whole Church, since I am compelled to discuss all the professions into which the whole Church is known to divide itself.

[Col. 0620C] [CHAP. XVIII.] D. Authority establishes that it is easier [perhaps better] for scandal to arise than for truth to be abandoned; and again, insofar as we can without loss to truth, we ought to avoid scandal to our neighbors. For when the Lord testified that not everything entering into them, but what proceeds from the mouth, defiles a person (Matt. XIV, 11), he preferred that the Pharisees should be scandalized rather than that truth should go unattested, saying to his disciples: “Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (ibid., 14). Again, lest they should be scandalized, he commanded that a stater be given as the tax for himself and Peter to Caesar (Matt. XVII, 26). By the Lord’s example, therefore, if your discourse is for truth, you ought first to leave all in scandal rather than, by silence, to abandon truth. Therefore Truth is Christ; whoever denies truth, then, denies what but Christ?

M. You see, therefore, how seriously we sin whenever, knowing Truth, we deny Truth itself. Therefore, that we may hear truth, let us proceed together to its counsel.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 0619]

[Col. 0619D] I. That monks ought not to ascribe to themselves alone what is known to be possessed by many. [Col. 0620D] II. That, if they confess that they have attained the dignity of the apostles, they are proved by no means to have been their imitators. [Col. 0621A] III. How those who accuse themselves are justified. IV. That, just as humility is the way by which one goes to God himself, so pride is the way by which one goes to the devil himself. V. That every human being is proved imperfect if judged strictly. VI. That, if abstinence is granted to be good or evil in itself, an absurdity follows. VII. How fasting is proved to be neither good nor evil, but intermediate. VIII. Objection: why it is proposed for our imitation if it is proved neither good nor evil in itself. IX. That it is not sayings and deeds, but the disposition, that is proposed for imitation. X. That the kingdom of heaven is given more on account of the pursuits of a good [Col. 0621B] disposition than on account of fasts themselves. XI. That those who could fall away were never monks. [Col. 0622A] XII. That regular canons are shown never to be destined to judge with the Lord, since they wish to exalt themselves above monks. XIII. That, if they say they have the dress of the apostles, they ought all to clothe themselves in a white *colobium*, and to become so ragged as to be shameful to look upon. XIV. That whoever wishes to presume upon dress cannot escape this charge. XV. That those unwilling to be younger and humbler are convicted of not having a holy life and holy morals. XVI. That it is not performing miracles, baptizing, or preaching that makes an apostle, but possessing virtues and humbling oneself. [Col. 0622B] XVII. That manifold absurdities follow if apostolic life is understood to consist in these three things.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621B] [CHAP. I.] D. “If, then,” say the monks, “Christ says, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’” (Matt. XIX, 21), “and it is manifest that we fulfill this, we are proved to possess this perfection.”

M. If it is established that many saints, in every perfection, gave all their goods to the poor and followed Christ, then monks ought not to boast uniquely in their profession of this perfection, which many in every profession are certainly known to share with them.

D. Such persons indeed have existed in every profession, so that it would be wicked for anyone to doubt it; nor is there any need to name those who are known to abound.

M. Therefore monks ought not to ascribe to themselves alone what is known to be possessed by many.

D. “But if,” they say, “we possess this not alone but together with others, it is nevertheless certain that we possess it.”

[CHAP. II.] M. Reason requires that those who say they possess apostolic perfection should be compelled to imitate the apostles themselves. But it is certain that the apostles themselves by no means ascribed to themselves the perfection of their apostolate.

D. This is established. For the Apostle Paul says of this perfection: “I do not reckon myself to have attained it” (Phil. III, 13); but, that he might afterward attain it, he says that he strained forward. And of all the apostles he says that they share this judgment: “Therefore, as many of us as are perfect, let us think this way” (Phil. III, 15).

M. You see, then, what follows. If monks follow the apostles, they do not reckon that they have attained this; or, if contrary to the apostles they say that they have attained it—which the apostles manifestly did not dare to confess of themselves—it follows that they [Col. 0622B] were by no means imitators of the apostles, and therefore not attainors of their dignity.

D. It is wicked for anyone to resist what is concluded by unassailable reasoning. For I see that the Apostle’s saying can also be fulfilled thus: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).—“Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 12).

[Col. 0622C] [CHAP. III.] M. You see, therefore: if they are righteous, they ought to be accused; if they wish to be exalted, they ought to be humbled. But if they are exalted because they are humbled, and are justified because they accuse themselves, it plainly follows that the nearer they think themselves to this righteousness, the farther they become from it.

D. What supreme Justice itself commands us seems contrary to this: “Draw near to me,” says Justice, “and I will draw near to you.” And again: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). That by which a human being is enlightened is proved to be light; but God himself is light, as it is said: “That was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9). Therefore we are commanded to approach the light so that we may be enlightened; that is, to approach God, so that, if I may put it thus, we may be deified. But who is deified except one who is justified? And whoever is justified seems to approach righteousness. It is therefore contrary for us to approach in order to be justified, and to withdraw in order to be justified. Hence it seems to follow: if we are justified because we approach righteousness, then we are not justified because we withdraw from it.

M. You have raised, I confess, a point that seems to trouble me also. Since this contradiction arises from the words, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted,” we must carefully examine what sound meaning is to be found in these words.

D. O how I desire this from you!

[Col. 0623A] M. What, then, is understood in this saying, “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted”? For a person to humble himself is for a person to have humility; and for a person to have humility is for a person to know himself. But a human being is a sinner; therefore, for a person to know himself is to know himself as a sinner—that is, to understand concerning himself what is true. Whoever understands what is true concerning himself acts justly; but no one can act justly unless righteousness brings this about. Yet righteousness cannot bring about anything justly unless the one who acts justly approaches righteousness itself. Therefore, whoever humbles himself is one who approaches righteousness; and righteousness is proved to approach the one who approaches righteousness. Further, the one to whom righteousness is proved to draw near as he draws near is one justified by righteousness. Therefore it is concluded that approaching God and being enlightened, a human being’s approaching God and God’s approaching us, are the same as being humbled and exalted—that is, being justified.

D. If, therefore, to be humbled is the same as to be justified, and whoever is justified is exalted, then if the Lord forbids a person to be exalted, he forbids that person to be justified—to become righteous. Therefore, if God forbids a person to be justified, he forbids a person to become righteous. But one who forbids a person to become righteous is proved unjust. Is God, then, unjust, who forbids a person to become righteous?

M. It would become you sometimes to pass something over and not burden me so heavily.

[Col. 0623C] D. If, not seeing truth, I pretended that I saw it, I should defraud myself of Truth itself. But no one ought to defraud himself of truth; therefore neither should I conceal it.

M. From what source do you think this contrariety of arguments arises?

D. From your having proved that being exalted is the same as being justified.

M. With open eyes you see why: if such contrary conclusions follow because those things are understood as the same, then, if these two—that is, being exalted and being justified—are understood as opposites, no impossibilities follow from this.

D. I now seem to see.

M. You must say this as well.

[Col. 0623D] D. Namely, that where it is said, “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted,” “shall be exalted” should be understood as though it said “shall be justified.” You have excellently proved that the person known to be humbled is justified. But where it is said, “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled,” “to be exalted” should be taken as though it said, “whoever is proud.”

M. Therefore, just as humility and pride are opposites, so he who commands a person to humble himself in order that he may be exalted—that is, justified—and who forbids a person to exalt himself in order that he may not be humbled, seems to command nothing other than that humility be set before one person and pride be removed from another. The whole of this is to make a person righteous. Therefore God is not unjust, who is proved to command or forbid this.

[Col. 0624A] D. I do not regret having raised this question, since it has been resolved to my great advantage.

M. Say, then, in what way?

D. I now see that, just as nothing is more detestable than pride, so nothing is more beneficial than humility.

M. Although we have lingered over this longer than I wished, nevertheless, that I may usefully move you by it: humility is the way by which one goes to God himself.

[CHAP. IV.] D. Pride, then, is the way by which one goes to the devil himself.

M. Indeed, it is that which made him the devil himself.

D. You shudder; I shudder. For before pride he is known to have been a most splendid angel.

M. Therefore it came about, when he became proud, that he became a most unclean devil. Therefore, as I think, even if monks were known to be holier than all human beings, you see that they ought, for that very reason, to be humbler. But humility is always proved to think humbly of itself; therefore monks ought to presume nothing concerning their own holiness.

D. It is good that they should attend carefully to your admonition. For I see that they defend their cause only by humility.

[CAP. V.] M. Everyone who begins a good work does not know whether he can bring it to a good completion, since every person is known to be ignorant even of his own life. The completion of a good work is its perfection. Therefore all are established to be imperfect who do not know that they can bring the perfection of a good work to completion. But if a person lived forever, he would certainly always have to do good. Therefore, if strict justice exacts from him what he ought always to do, every person, when he dies, is left imperfect.

D. This seems capable of being challenged, except that authority itself is known to attest it: “When,” says the Lord, “you have done all that you ought to do, say: ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke XVII, 10).

M. But if, after accomplishing all that we ought to do, we must call ourselves useless servants, and useless servants are imperfect, then every human being is concluded to be imperfect. Therefore, if this seems sufficient to you for the present, let the discussion proceed to what remains.

361 D. Further, the regular canons add that they do not possess such great perfection, since it is manifest that many things which are not permitted to monks are permitted to them. But the more anyone labors, the greater the reward he will receive for his labor. For each shall receive his own reward according to his labor.

M. Is it good to abstain?

D. Good.

[CHAP. VI.] D. Are not good and evil opposites?

M. Opposites.

D. But we are commanded always to do what is good, and always forbidden to do what is evil. Therefore, if abstaining is good, we are commanded always to do it. It follows, then, that if we are commanded always to abstain, we are always forbidden to eat. But what we are always forbidden to do we ought never [Col. 0625A] to undertake. Therefore we ought never to eat.

M. You seem to me to be doing me an injustice. For it is established that I answered truly when you questioned me; and falsehood does not follow from anything conceded to be true. Therefore, if I am known to have conceded something true, you ought not to have concluded something false from what is true.

D. Come now: concede it to me, or, if you can, contradict it; or, if you cannot, answer again from the beginning.

M. I cannot contradict your reasoning; yet you see that what I conceded is true. Therefore, that I may escape your objection, I concede that abstaining is evil.

D. But we are forbidden to do everything that is evil; therefore abstaining is evil. What we are forbidden to do, however, we ought never to undertake. Therefore [Col. 0625B] we ought never to abstain.

M. I am hemmed in on every side. For I see that I have fallen into that inextricable labyrinth of which they speak, or into that house of Daedalus, from which whoever enters cannot find an exit. For if I concede that abstaining is good, you conclude that we must sometimes eat; but if I concede that it is evil, you conclude that we must sometimes abstain. Yet what is more contrary than that a person should never eat and never abstain—that is, should always eat?

D. If you wished to accept by authority alone all that is said, you could, like the simple, believe briefly; but you would not understand with certainty whether things are so or not. But if you wish by reason to investigate whether all things are so and cannot be otherwise, you must endure the long circuits of reasoning. For as reason precedes all things, so it is sufficient by itself alone. But because it belongs to very few to understand reason, and yet all human beings, being rational, ought to attain reason, authority must condescend to the little ones, so that, while they accept it, the little ones may ascend with the greater to reason.

M. Let it go and make its circuit; I endure it willingly, I confess, provided that it brings us back to itself. But because I have not dared to answer that abstaining is either good or evil, I shall say, then, that it is neither.

[CHAP. VII.] D. What does it mean to be neither?

M. That it seems, for the present, to be intermediate.

D. But every intermediate thing stands in relation to a first and an extreme. Therefore abstaining is neither evil in itself nor good in itself. For it has been proved to be intermediate between good and evil. Therefore it will be judged according to the intention of those who use it: so that, if good persons use it, it is judged good; but if evil persons use it, it is judged evil.

M. Now that the darkness of ignorance has been driven away, I seem to be in the light.

D. But when monks say that they are better than regular canons because things permitted to the latter are, as they say, not permitted to themselves, they plainly indicate that they abstain from many foods more than the canons do.

M. Thus those who are more abstinent from foods are thought holier.

D. But abstaining has been proved to be neither evil nor good in itself. Therefore, if they are better because they are said to abstain more, they are concluded to be better on account of what is neither good nor evil. But to be better is to be more good; and to be more good through what is not good in itself is, as contrary to every good thing, likewise false. Therefore it is false that monks are better because they are said to abstain more.

M. Because I hear you drawing unheard-of conclusions, I ought to raise every objection I can.

D. State it well.

[CHAP. VIII.] M. It is just that each should receive a reward according to his own labor. Therefore whoever labors more will receive a greater reward. But those who are proved to abstain more are judged to labor more. [Col. 0626B] Therefore those who abstain more must necessarily receive a greater reward. Further, those who are richer in reward are certainly better. Therefore your conclusion, that they are not better because they abstain more, is false.

D. You are very troublesome.

M. But be kindly disposed.

D. Have you seen some hypocrite abstaining rigorously, and some saint partaking of every food with thanksgiving?

M. Even if I confessed that I had not seen it, it would nevertheless be established that both have existed according to the Savior’s saying: “When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites” (Matt. VI, 16). And again it is said of the holy apostles that “the sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. IX, 15).

D. Therefore, if those who abstain more are better, and a hypocrite does what some saint does not, then a hypocrite is better than some saint, and the Pharisees and disciples of John, who abstained, are better than the apostles, who ate. But the apostles were holy and the Pharisees wicked; therefore the wicked are better than the holy.

M. Since it is wicked for me any longer to reject manifest truth, you must at least resolve what for the moment seems contrary to it. For, to pass over many saints who seem to have received the kingdoms of heaven on account of fasts, why are Moses and Elijah praised for having fasted forty days: the former receiving the Law by fasting, the latter deserving by fasting to pass into heaven in a fiery chariot? Why is Christ himself, after baptism, proposed to us for imitation as having fasted forty days and forty nights, if fasting is by no means said to be good in itself?

[CHAP. IX.] D. If it were established that you had carefully understood what has been said, you certainly ought not to have raised these objections; for all these matters are known to be resolved by what has been proved above.

362 M. There is a great difference between one who sees and one who has bleary eyes, if you think that all things are clear to me in my bleary sight because you are known to see clearly.

D. Do you think the same words are the same words? They are not the same: “I am not a murderer,” “I am not a murderer”; and is the same fasting the same fasting?

M. I must confess that both are the same.

D. Let a holy person and a murderer, then, utter these same words. Do you think they are the same if the murderer says, “I am not a murderer,” and the righteous person says, “I am not a murderer”?

M. I should never say this; rather, the one is false and the other true. For the murderer lies, while the holy person speaks truth.

D. Why, then, does it happen that, although it was established above that the same words are the same words, now what is said by a righteous person and by a murderer is judged false and true?

[Col. 0627B] M. Because, indeed, everything said is understood not according to the sound of the words, but according to the intention of those speaking.

D. Therefore in all that is said, it is not the sound but the intention of the speakers that is set before us for imitation; for example, if someone says something with a good intention, it is praiseworthy and should be imitated by us. Likewise, if someone says something with an evil intention, it is blameworthy and should not be imitated by us. But words are known to be the same unless they are spoken with either a good or an evil intention. It follows, therefore, that in all that is said nothing but the intention is blamed or praised. See, then, what follows concerning fasting.

M. There is no need to labor so much over that, though you leave it for me to discover.

D. You seem to me to see why I asked whether the same fasting was the same fasting.

M. Because, I suppose, although the same fasting is the same fasting, it is judged evil because a hypocrite does it with an evil intention, namely for vain glory; or good because a good person does it with a good intention, namely for eternal glory. Thus it is not fasting alone that should be considered, but either the evil intention is set before us as blameworthy or the good intention as praiseworthy.

[CHAP. X.] D. Therefore, if, as has been proved, in all things said or accomplished in deed, not merely the words or deeds themselves but the intention is blamed or praised; and whatever is blamed [Col. 0627D] ought not to be imitated by us, while whatever is praised ought to be imitated; then, when Christ, Moses, and Elijah are praised to us while fasting, not their fasting alone but their good intention is proposed for our imitation. You see, therefore, that when many saints are reported to have fasted, Scripture commends to us not the fact that they fasted, but how—that is, with what intention—they did it. It follows, then, that they received the kingdoms of heaven not on account of fasts, but on account of the pursuit of a good intention.

M. The Lord is known to have thought the same even about that fasting which you proved not to be good in itself. For when some thought this sufficient, the Lord deigns to rebuke them. For they said: “We have fasted, and you have not looked upon us; we have humbled our souls, and you have not known it” (Isa. LVIII, 3). But the Lord said that he had not heard their prayers: “Behold,” he says, “on the days of your fasting your own will is found, and you exact all your debts; behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and strike wickedly with the fist” (ibid., 4). Thus there, because they are proved to have fasted with an evil intention, they are rebuked by the Lord. And again, he deigns to teach how fasting is reckoned good because it is done with a good intention, adding: “Do not fast as you do this day, to make your cry heard on high. Is this the fast that I have chosen: for a person to afflict his soul for a day? To bend his head like a circle, and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath himself? Would you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord? Rather, this,” he says, “is the fast I have chosen: to loose the bonds of wickedness” [Col. 0628B] (ibid. IV, 6), and similar things. And unless fasting were proved intermediate, the Apostle would never say: “Let not the one who eats despise the one who does not eat, nor the one who does not eat despise the one who eats” (Rom. XIV, 3). Moreover, not only concerning fasting but concerning all things done for vain glory, the Lord shows that we obtain no reward for our labors: “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 16).

D. Therefore, if this seems sufficient to you for the moment, let our reasoning endeavor to run on to what remains.

D. “We regular canons,” they say, “are likened to the apostles themselves, since, placed in their position, we imitate their morals and life. For just as it was said to the apostles, ‘You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house’” (Matt. V, 14–15), “so we maintain that this was said to us, whose life, dress, and morals we possess. Therefore, if we are the light of the world and a city that cannot be hidden, set upon a mountain, and a lamp placed upon a lampstand, we ought to preach to all who are in the house of the Church and to fulfill the work of evangelists and apostles.”

M. These are known to be ignorant of the way of truth.

D. But the way of truth, as has been proved above, is humility, by which one goes to God.

M. It is manifest, then, that they wander in the darkness of ignorance without the way. Finally, whatever has been said above against the presumption of monks can also be said [Col. 0628D] against the boasting of canons. It has been proved that the holier anyone wishes to be, the humbler, lower, and more distant from God in his own confession he ought to be. I believe that this whole point, as it is not hidden from you by the foregoing reasoning, you can see everywhere also in the holy authority of Scripture.

D. Since I recall that above you said those who seem strengthened against authority and from authority itself ought to be refuted by authority, you must now rest from reasoning and prove, from authority introduced into the discussion, that they have spoken well or ill.

M. Did I not tell you that I had done this entirely, and that you had understood it entirely?

D. Do not be burdened; for their argument seems forceful. Therefore it must be forcefully and powerfully refuted; or, if you cannot do this, let them have the palm.

M. Do you not yet understand that the apostles had the same case, and that they are known to have contended about precedence?

D. I know. For it is written thus: “A contention arose among the disciples of Jesus as to which of them seemed to be greater.”

M. Do you also read there how this error of theirs was suppressed, and what was proposed to them if they wished to be greater and more perfect?

D. It is established that the Lord proposed this: those among them who wished to be greater should become younger, and those who were leaders should become like servants. For Christ proved himself to be the greatest of all, 363 yet said that he was in their midst as a younger servant.

M. Why, then, are you silent concerning what he told them about the ordering of the kingdom? He said not only that he would appoint for them a kingdom, as his Father had appointed one for him; he also said that they would sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

M. You see that they can possess the privilege of sitting upon twelve thrones and judging the twelve tribes of Israel only if they are willing to remain in the purpose in which they were commanded to become younger, serving ministers.

D. It is manifest that no one can attain this unless he wishes to remain under this command.

[Col. 0629C] M. But these men say that they are placed in the apostles’ place, and so presume that what was said to them was said also to themselves. Yet they do not wish to be younger servants, as was commanded to the apostles; therefore they shall not be greater leaders.

D. So it follows.

M. Wait for the moment. Do you doubt that monks are Christ’s disciples?

D. I should never doubt this, although I have seen some of them fall away.

[CHAP. XI.] M. Those who are known to fall away were never monks, because it is impossible that even one of the elect should perish; therefore this must not happen to true monks.

[Col. 0629D] D. According to the definition of their name, I grant that true monks do not fall away, just as neither do the eleven who are known to have been Christ’s true apostles. But if anyone seems to do this, like Judas, he was never an apostle, though he seemed to be one; likewise, that person was never a monk.

M. You understand well. For if he had been an apostle, Christ would never have said of him: “One of you is a devil” (John VI, 71). Therefore monks are established to be Christ’s disciples. But those who wish to be greater leaders than Christ’s disciples ought to become younger servants. Further, those who become younger servants than Christ’s disciples ought, beyond doubt, to become—as those seated upon the twelve thrones—judges with the Lord over the twelve tribes of Israel. [CHAP. [Col. 0630A] XII.] Therefore, if these men wish to be greater than monks, who are known to be Christ’s disciples, and if this is impossible unless they are proved younger servants than all Christ’s disciples, yet they refuse to do this while they attempt to exalt themselves above monks, it follows that they shall never sit upon the twelve thrones nor judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

D. Truly, it is now established that you conclude this plainly.

M. You ought still to wait.

D. I wait; set forth what you wish.

M. No apostolic dignity is greater than this judicial power; but this has been promised not only to the apostles but to all who renounce the world. Therefore, if these men, as has been proved, are excluded from this dignity, you plainly see that they are excluded not only from this higher dignity but from every glory of those who renounce the world. It follows, then, that those who strive to attain a greater dignity are found in no glory at all.

D. It would be better for them to confess themselves younger, so that they might be raised to this greater glory.

M. Can you, from their own words, clearly discern in what respect they seem to themselves most like the apostles?

[CHAP. XIII.] D. Very easily: because they say that they possess the apostles’ life, dress, and morals.

M. I would prefer that someone else answered you concerning all these matters, since I can satisfy you only with certain rather laughable conclusions; and therefore it is better for you to consider these things within yourself.

D. I could indeed infer much from this; but it is one thing to infer, another firmly to hold what is true. Therefore you ought not excuse yourself from investigating anything true that you can discover.

M. Who can know with certainty what dress the apostles used, when almost all this has been concealed from us?

D. You are not excused for that reason; for Simon and Judas are recorded to have worn clothing so ragged that it was shameful to hear or see them.

M. If this is established only concerning those two, what shall be said of the others?

D. Indeed, if the devil’s testimony is believed, St. Bartholomew is recorded to have used a white *colobium*, purple-striped clothing, and to have been clad in a white mantle which had a purple gem at each corner; and although he wore it for twenty-six years, it is nevertheless recorded never to have grown old. John the Evangelist and Apostle too is said to have used linen, and Thomas and James white *colobia*.

M. Do you see, then, what follows from this?

D. Not at all.

M. Certainly regular canons, if they say that they have the apostles’ dress, ought all to clothe themselves, following Bartholomew, John, Thomas, and James, in a white *colobium*, a white purple-decorated, gem-studded mantle, and linen; and again, following Simon and Judas, they ought to become so ragged as to be shameful to behold or hear.

D. Each alternative is as highly unbecoming as it is utterly unsuitable. They differ greatly from both: for they are neither disgraceful in dress like Simon and Judas, nor clothed in *colobia* like Bartholomew, John the Apostle, Thomas, and James, but stand between the two, wearing hoods and surplices.

M. Let them therefore cease testifying that they resemble those apostles in dress.

D. What if canons raise this same objection against monks?

M. Then they too, if they took pride in their dress, would by no means escape this charge.

D. Yet is some holiness to be attributed to place and dress?

[CHAP. XIV.] M. Nothing else, except that these things must be used with discrimination. Judas betrayed Christ beneath the apostles’ dress, while Sebastian underwent martyrdom beneath a military cloak. Again, the devil held apostolic rank in heaven, and Job, sitting upon a dungheap, praised the Lord.

[CHAP. XV.] D. Come now: let us speak not of their dress but of their morals and life. Canons claim to imitate the apostles; why they do so, and what sort of claim this is, you ought to examine.

M. Since these questions have been resolved above, by raising them again you seem either excessively superfluous or troublesome. Was it not proved among all the apostles and disciples of Christ that whoever wished to be greater and more worthy had to be younger and humbler? And what is it to be younger and humbler except to possess a most holy life and most holy morals? But these men do not wish to be younger and humbler. They are therefore convicted of not possessing a holy life and holy morals; and if they are proved not to possess these, how do they imitate the humble apostles? Which of the apostles said, “I am greater than the others”? Do you not see Paul—who, as is certain, was caught up into the third heaven—saying: “Last of all he was seen by me also, as by one untimely born; for I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:8)? Did he not utter such an oracle concerning all the apostles when he called them, all alike, as it were the world’s refuse and a spectacle to the world? Which of them did not call himself a sinner, younger, inferior to the rest? Which did not flee the tongue of flatterers as a deadly poison? Which of them, though able to be worshipped as God with lamps and candles, preferred to be rejected amid every reproach and disgrace? Which of them did not strive with all his might to abase himself, as though this alone were ascent?

[CHAP. XVI.] But if regular canons point to that life and conduct of the apostles by which they are known to have shone through innumerable miracles, and to have converted almost the entire world as they travelled everywhere baptizing and preaching; and if, because they testify that they do all these things, they call themselves imitators of the apostles—then they must show by what miracles they have shone, what regions of the world they have travelled through and converted by baptizing and preaching, or to what parts of the world the apostles, already sent by the Lord, were directed for conversion or had converted. If they cannot show any of this concerning themselves, then let them cease to understand the life of the apostles as consisting in baptism alone, preaching alone, and miracles. For preaching, baptizing, and working miracles do not make an apostle; rather, it is the possession of virtues and, as was enjoined upon them, humbling oneself before others.

For if apostolic life and apostleship consist only in baptizing, preaching, and working miracles, two utterly absurd conclusions follow: either all who did such things possessed apostolic life and were apostles, or those who did not do such things never possessed apostolic life and were not apostles. Yet evil men, just as they performed many miracles, also baptized and preached. It follows, therefore, that evil men possessed apostolic life and were themselves apostles.

[CHAP. XVII.] Again, many most perfect and apostolic men, just as they never cared to work miracles, neither baptized nor preached; and it follows concerning all of them that they possessed neither apostolic life nor apostolic character. Since these conclusions are contradictory, they are proved false. Therefore apostolic life does not consist in these things alone. Moreover, what could be said more absurdly than that, in this age when miracles are not performed, the whole Church should be deprived of apostolic dignity? Finally, not so much a strange as a contrary conclusion would follow: that no canon and no monk would seem to possess apostolic life unless he worked miracles, preached, and baptized; while any utterly unclean cleric, known to do both—baptize and preach—would be proved to possess apostolic life.

D. The whole argument is exceedingly, exceedingly reasonable. Oh, if only I might always see you so stirred! Shining by miracles, baptizing, and preaching must, together with fasting, place, and dress, be counted as matters of indifference. For all that you have proved stands clearly upon manifest authority. Nowhere is the Lord recorded as saying, “Learn from me to shine by miracles, to baptize, to preach”; rather, he says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). For when certain persons did these things and gloried as though they sufficed for salvation, the Lord is reported to have answered that they ought not to glory in them: “Do not rejoice,” he says, “that demons are subject to you, but that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). And to those who trust in miracles he will say at the end: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

Paul also, in whom Christ himself spoke, bears the same witness concerning baptism and preaching. For when some wished to place more confidence than was proper in preaching and baptism, he proved from that fact alone that they wished to divide Christ, setting it forth thus: “What I mean is that each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided?” (1 Cor. 1:12). It is as though he said: If baptism is divided among however many administer it, while in every baptism one Christ is received through faith, then the one Christ is divided among however many baptize. He even gives thanks to God that he baptized none of them except Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas; besides these, he does not know whether he baptized anyone, lest anyone should boast in his name. For he did not say that Christ sent him to baptize, but to evangelize.

What, then, could be more foolish than that Paul would not be a complete apostle if he omitted one of these three things, although he said it had been imposed upon him? Yet all this would follow if apostolic life and apostleship consisted only in those three things. At length he speaks thus of himself as planting and Apollos as watering—that is, preaching and baptizing: “Neither he who plants,” that is, preaches, “nor he who waters,” that is, baptizes, “is anything” (1 Cor. 3:7). Therefore your argument is proved wholly true.

M. As you see, night is coming upon us and compels us to rest. Therefore, if these matters now seem sufficiently treated to you, let what remains be reserved for the following day.

## Chapters of the Third Book Begin

[Col. 0633]

I. That, if what is alleged against monks is true, an unsuitable conclusion follows concerning all saints. II. That if monks are rightly blamed for the life of penitents, all saints are proved guilty of the same fault. III. Likewise, that it follows that Christ alone ascended to heaven and alone remained there without saints. IV. That, because these unsuitable conclusions are proved false, monks are permitted to do these things. V. What authority monks possess concerning the life of orthodox believers. VI. That, because monks are said to be dead in Christ, they are permitted to undertake spiritual matters. VII. That every monk who is ordained priest is permitted to preach and baptize. VIII. That if this is not permitted to an ordained monk, he is called not a full priest but a half-priest. IX. That, if monks are faulted for mean dress, all saints who used it are to be regarded as nothing. X. Objection: that regular canons are not the same as those called clerics. XI. Resolution: that all clerics are called regular. XII. That, just as those living without Christianity are not Christians, so those living without the rule of canons are not clerics. XIII. That, just as those doing irregular things are to be called irregular, so those doing non-clerical things are not to be considered clerics. XIV. That this must be so according to the Gospel and the canons. XV. That only those who are known to live according to the apostles’ rule ought to have the power of binding and loosing.

## The Third Book Begins

[Col. 0633]

D. 365 [CHAP. I.] As the onset of night compelled us to rest, so the dawning day urges us to rise. Therefore you ought carefully to examine what is alleged against monks.

M. Provided that God deign to help me, I am ready to do so. You should therefore first state what is alleged.

D. The regular canons say: Since monks are known to live the life of penitents, they ought to hide themselves in the cloister as beneath a bushel; for they are dead, and their life is hidden with Christ in God. Therefore, when Christ appears, then their life too will appear with him in glory (Col. 3:3–4). As they are dead here and alive there, so they are to appear there but ought to remain hidden here. Therefore they ought neither to preach nor to baptize. Their dress also bears witness to this: as they are contemptible both in clothing and tonsure, so they are not worthy of approval in this world. Those who are called clerics, since they think that they live the life of regular canons, appear to make these same objections against monks together with the canons themselves.

M. They ought to have raised these charges not against monks alone, but against all patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—indeed, against all saints—since all are known to have lived the life of penitents.

D. If this is the sense, no one is exempt from this reproach; for it is written: “God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy upon all” (Rom. 11:32); and “all have sinned and need the grace of God” (Rom. 3:23). The apostles themselves say of themselves: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

M. Everyone said to be shut up under sin must, if saved, have repented of sin. To repent of sin is to live the life of penitents. Therefore, if all saints are known to live the life of penitents, all saints ought to hide themselves beneath a bushel. No one, then, ought to have preached, baptized, or performed any miracles.

D. Nothing could be said more false than this.

M. Nothing, therefore, could be more falsely alleged against monks.

D. They say that “living the life of penitents” is not understood in this way, but only of those known to do so because of criminal sins.

M. [CHAP. II.] It follows, then, that Peter and Matthew ought to have hidden themselves beneath a bushel and performed no miracles.

D. So it seems, for Peter denied the Lord three times.

M. No wise person ever denied that this was a criminal sin, apart from perhaps the many sins he had previously committed in life.

D. But God looked upon Peter, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

M. Because he began to weep bitterly over his denial of God, he repented of a criminal sin. Therefore Peter is concluded to have lived the life of penitents. You see, then, that what we first concluded must follow from this.

D. I see it. For if Matthew calls himself a public sinner, seated openly at the tax-office, it is clear that you have rightly concluded this of both.

M. Indeed, I can show many utterly absurd consequences from it.

D. Since I see this is necessary, do not be reluctant to do so.

M. Either they are said to live the life of penitents in such a manner that we must understand this of all sins, or in such a manner that they appear to repent only of criminal sins.

D. I beg you carefully to examine what follows from either position.

M. For if they ought to remain hidden and neither baptize nor preach because they are said to repent of all sins, it follows that no apostle, no saint, indeed no ecclesiastic whatsoever ought to have done these things. It further follows that none of the saints received the kingdoms of heaven, if they are proved to have done this disobediently and against God; and that the whole Church was always in error.

[CHAP. III.] From this—an astonishing thing!—it follows that Christ alone ascended into heaven and sat there alone, on an empty seat, without all the saints.

D. O a thing not so astonishing as detestable!

M. But if they are said to live the life of penitents in such a manner that they must do so only because of criminal sins, and must therefore neither preach nor baptize but always remain hidden, it follows not only that Peter, Matthew, and innumerable saints who are known to have sinned grievously ought never to have attained any dignity, but also that no one could be a monk unless he were known to have committed criminal sins.

D. May God, through his grace, protect the Church from this.

M. It is therefore concluded to be false that monks ought to remain hidden because they are said to live the life of penitents.

[CHAP. IV.] D. The argument, as the saying goes, proceeds very reasonably. Authority also concedes that this is so. For if monks had not been permitted to do these things, the Church would not have been so strong; for monks are said to have converted nearly half the inhabited world, and that this is so is proved by the authority of all writings.
