For, to pass over the innumerable men of monastic life, incomparable in holiness, who preceded the time of most blessed Martin—who performed innumerable signs and left to the entire world examples of holiness to be imitated—among whom all Egypt’s hope was in the great Antony, who shone in faith, while all Syria hung upon Hilarion, whose holiness demons everywhere bore witness to, and who, as blessed Jerome writes of him, could nowhere remain hidden because of his miracles, as people streamed to him in rivalry from the whole world: all these, imitating Elijah and John the Baptist in the wildernesses, although they wandered about and avoided working miracles, nevertheless drew innumerable peoples by their holiness; and though they wished to remain hidden, they could by no means do so. The monks themselves preached and worked miracles.

But, I say, passing over all of them, what shall I say of most blessed Martin? Who can recount his miracles? Who can attain the heights of his holiness? In the name of the Trinity he deserved, equal to the apostles, gloriously to raise three dead persons; so that in his time heaven was upheld by Martin the monk alone, the whole Church was illuminated, and he appeared almost the sole apostle before all bishops, while the threefold division of all Gaul rejoiced that it would be converted through him. Even now, who does not exalt Martin to heaven? What mind does not tremble at Martin’s holiness? Which tyrant, on hearing Martin’s name, does not, as though struck by some thunderbolt from heaven, lay aside his ferocity, if only briefly? Yet this monk preached, baptized, and fulfilled the work of evangelist and apostle.

What shall be said of most blessed Gregory, who, as the sweetest instrument of the Holy Spirit, by working many miracles, preaching, and baptizing, both adorned the universal Church by holiness and illuminated it by the teaching of his preaching? Finally, what shall be said of most blessed Benedict, founder of monks, who, just as Gregory himself describes him as filled with the spirit of all the righteous, is such that no one is permitted fully to unfold his holiness and miracles? Yet this monk, as the same Gregory testifies, is shown to have preached the word of life to all who flocked to him. It would take long to set forth individually how many monks became bishops, preached, and converted how many parts of the world by their preaching. But perhaps, for the moment, you judge it better that I be silent.

[CHAP. V.] M. I would not have us linger so long over these matters, but examine the character of the objection.

D. It lies before us: since they are dead and hidden in Christ, when Christ appears they ought to appear; here they ought only to remain hidden, and, as they are contemptible in dress, so they are not approved in this world.

M. Is it glorious for monks to hide their life with Christ and rise again with Christ?

D. It is certain that all saints ought to do this.

M. Therefore all saints ought to remain hidden.

D. It follows so.

M. If, therefore, all saints ought to remain hidden, none ought to have worked miracles, baptized, or preached; and the same absurdities follow that were concluded above.

D. These things seem sufficiently said, since they were proved above.

M. Tell me, then: are those said to be dead in Christ permitted to live in spiritual things or in carnal things?

[CHAP. VI.] D. Whoever says that they live in carnal things wishes them freely to sin; but since this is impossible, they must live in spiritual things.

M. Are baptizing, preaching, and working miracles carnal works or spiritual works?

D. Whoever calls them carnal wishes the saints to be brute animals. Since this is contrary to reason, they are therefore spiritual works.

[CHAP. VII.] M. Therefore, if all who are said to be dead in Christ are permitted to live in spiritual things, while baptizing, preaching, and even working miracles are spiritual works, monks, if they are said to be dead in Christ, are by no means prohibited from spiritual acts—that is, baptizing and preaching. Again, whenever certain men are ordained priests, are they not thereby made capable of the priestly ministry?

[CHAP. VIII.] D. Unless they are permitted to do everything belonging to priests, they are proved to be unordained. But those who are ordained cannot be proved unordained.

M. Therefore all ordained priests are shown to be capable of their priestly office. But the complete office of priestly ministry is to baptize, preach, perform like acts, and chant masses. If this is not permitted to monks who are ordained, then they are called not full priests but half-priests.

D. O, this is not so much a reproach as ridiculous!

M. But because it is impossible for those who are ordained not to be ordained, and because every power of his office is granted to one who is ordained, it follows that every monk who is a priest ought to preach and baptize.

D. Whoever does not accept this conclusion is proved very foolish.

[CHAP. IX.] M. Further: because they are called unacceptable to this world on account of their contemptible dress, this means that if the world recognized in them something belonging to itself, the world would love in them what was its own.

D. This is wonderfully explained; and therefore the following applies to them: “Because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

M. If they are hated by the world, therefore they are chosen by God. Those chosen by God are permitted to do the things of God. But preaching, baptizing, and performing similar acts are works of God. Therefore monks are proved obliged to do all these things.

D. Yet men judge that those known to wear such mean clothing ought not to enjoy honour in the Church.

M. Then John the Baptist, greater among those born of women, ought to have been excluded from every ecclesiastical dignity—he who is known to have been clothed in camel hair and girded with a leather belt—as should Simon and Judas, other apostles, Martin the bishop, and finally thousands of saints recorded to have worn garments of the utmost poverty. Therefore, if monks are blamed for their extreme poverty of dress, all these should be excluded from ecclesiastical honour.

D. Not at all: all who wear rough clothing seem rather to be praised by the Lord along with John the Baptist.

M. Then those who wear soft clothing ought to be blamed. Those who wear soft clothing ought, then, to be in the houses of earthly kings; while those who wear rough clothing are in the court of the heavenly kingdoms.

D. But this seems contrary to what was established above: that dress possesses no holiness.

M. Did I not tell you that you are either excessively superfluous or excessively troublesome? For you seem to me to have forgotten that judgment according to which dress, like every mean thing, must be referred to a rightly disposed mind.

D. Forgive, I ask you, both my foolishness and my own modest shame.

M. But take care that you do not again demand proof of matters already proved above.

D. What then of those called clerics, who, claiming to live the life of regular canons, appear along with them to make these objections against monks?

M. If they appear to live the same life as those men, they should likewise appear everywhere to adopt their judgment. So, if the remaining matters trouble you and seem fitting, state them.

D. You seem to me either to evade the matter or not to examine correctly what you say.

M. You must then show in what respects I appear to do this.

[CHAP. X.] D. Because you say that those called clerics are the same as regular canons.

M. Must I then tell you something other than what I understand to be true?

D. As what is heard is astonishing, so are the consequences that follow from it.

M. Let it be as you please.

[CHAP. XI.] D. Who, looking at the life of clerics, would call it that of regular canons? As far as heaven is from earth, and the synagogue of the Jews from the Church of Christians, so far is the life of clerics from that of regular canons. The former, scattered throughout the world, enjoy the delights of possessions; the latter, gathered in the cloister, are bound by the disciplines of a rule. The former possess everything privately; the latter, everything in common. The former wander everywhere without any shepherd; the latter are gathered together under one master. The greater part of the former are joined to wives; the latter are wholly separated from them. The former wear grey garments, marten-fur or sable-fur; the latter wear woollen, linen, or lambskin garments. The former hunt hares or whatever beasts are permitted; the latter search books or whatever teachings of the saints. The former possess as much of the world as they please; the latter renounce the whole world. In the former, everything contrary to religion and irreligious is censured; in the latter, the opposite and religious is proved.

M. Have you heard men called by one designation who are known to serve Christ and the devil?

D. Alas, yes! Human affairs are so ordered that good things are called vain, while evil things are called such as are not proved to be evil.

M. But good things are good and evil things evil; things are not changed merely because they are called by another name.

D. What you are known to say seems fitting in their case.

M. Why then are you surprised if they are called by the name of clerics although they are proved not to be such?

D. I am not surprised. For if every person were what he was called, Judas would still be considered an apostle.

M. Are not clerics those who ought both to teach and to govern the people?

D. This is evident.

M. Then is it fitting that those who bind others under a rule should themselves be without rule, so that teachers of the rule are irregular? Ought any Christian to live without the rule of the Church?

[CHAP. XII.] D. Just as those who live without Christianity are not Christians, so those who live without a rule are not clerics. And since Christ and the apostles gave a rule to all Christians, just as clerics occupied their places, so they handed down to clerics for observance the rule which they themselves kept.

M. Therefore, if they are called regular from a rule, and all clerics who compel the people to be taught under that very rule ought much more themselves to fulfill the rule, all clerics ought to be regular.

D. Whoever does not grant that this must be so wishes clerics not to be clerics.

M. Now *canon* is Greek and *regula* Latin; whence *canonici* in Greek and *regulares* in Latin. Therefore, when “regular canons” is said, it is no different from saying “regular regulars.”

D. Nothing appears capable of objection here.

M. But those convicted of doing everything contrary to their own rule are not said to live under their rule. You said above that clerics enjoy luxuries, possess private property, wander everywhere, are joined to wives, wear marten and sable garments, hunt, possess the world, and are censured for many other contrary and irreligious practices. But all these are irregular, because they are contrary to the rule of clerics.

[CHAP. XIII.] Therefore, just as those who do all irregular things are to be called irregular, so those who do things contrary to clerics and, so to speak, non-clerical things, are not to be considered clerics. Rightly, therefore, do monks and true regulars reject these men and refuse to participate with them in the sacraments; for since they are manifestly proved not to be clerics, it is fitting and just that they should be despised not only by monks and true regulars but by all Christians. And if you wish to examine the holy Gospel and sacred canons—that is, their rules—you will be able to prove this most clearly.

[CHAP. XIV.] D. Clearly so. For it is said of them: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you” (Matt. 18:9). It is better, therefore, for a one-eyed people to enter life without a blind eye than for blind clerics to lead a blind people and both to fall into a pit. Again: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savour, it is good for nothing any longer except to be cast out and trodden under foot by all” (Matt. 5:13). It is better, therefore, to cast out a cleric of reprobate life as salt that has become foolish, than to leave the whole people—seasoned by foolish salt yet without salt—stinking in the stench of sin.

The sacred canons too plainly bear witness to this, commanding all the faithful to abhor such men. For Pope Clement says in his letter to James:

> “Ministers of the altar—priest, deacon, or subdeacon—are to be chosen for the Lord’s offices only if they have left their wives before ordination. But if after ordination it happens that a minister enters his wife’s own bedchamber, let him be neither bearer of the sanctuary nor of the sacrifice; let him not touch the altar, nor receive an offering of holocaust together with those who offer it, nor approach to a portion of the Lord’s body. Let him hand water to the priests for washing their hands, close the doors from outside, and perform lesser offices. These things, therefore, brother James, I heard from the mouth of holy Peter as he commanded them. If anyone does not observe these commands in their entirety, let him be anathema until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And again, Alexander the pope is proved to command in these words that all ought to live the life of regular canons, as you proved above:

> “We command by precept that no one hear the mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to keep a concubine or a woman secretly introduced. Therefore the holy synod, establishing this from its beginning under excommunication, says: Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the decree concerning clerical chastity made by our predecessors of blessed memory, the most holy Popes Leo or Nicholas, has openly taken a concubine or has not put away one whom he has taken, we command and altogether prohibit, by the authority of almighty God and of Peter and Paul, that he sing no mass, read neither Gospel nor Epistle, remain in the presbytery for divine offices with those obedient to the aforesaid decree, or receive a share from the Church. And we decree by command that those of the aforesaid orders who obey those same our predecessors and preserve chastity should, at the churches to which they were ordained, eat and sleep together, as religious clerics ought, and hold in common whatever is due from the churches. Entreating them, we exhort them to strive to attain the apostolic—that is, common—life, so that they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland with those enriched by the hundredfold fruit and attain perfection with them. Thereafter let the first-fruits and offerings of the living and dead be faithfully rendered by laypeople to the churches of God, to be at the bishops’ disposal. Those who retain them are to be separated from communion with the holy Church. Let no cleric or priest acquire a church through laymen, neither freely nor for a price; let no cleric hold two churches; let no one be ordained or promoted to any ecclesiastical office through the Simoniac heresy; nor let anyone be expelled from churches. Let no one assume the monastic habit in the hope or on the promise of becoming abbot. Let no layman be suddenly promoted to any ecclesiastical rank unless, after changing his secular habit, he has been proved in divine conduct among clerics.”

Therefore faithfully observe these and other decrees of the holy Fathers with Christian reverence, if you wish to enjoy the peace, communion, blessing, and absolution of the holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See. Yet I ask: why do they testify that they possess the power of binding and loosing, whatever their manner of life may seem to be?

[CHAP. XV.] M. Have not you by authority, and I by reason, shown that those who are not proved to live ecclesiastically ought not to have the power of binding and loosing? No one except the Church possesses this power. But the Church—that is, clerics [the text perhaps reads *clerici* for *Ecclesia*]—ought to live ecclesiastically, according to rule, in common. Therefore all who are proved to live with the morals condemned by the Church ought beyond doubt no longer to possess this power; for God is denied more by wicked deeds than by evil words. Hence it follows: although someone may confess God in words, he is nevertheless convicted of denying God by wicked deeds. Those known to deny God by living wickedly certainly deprive themselves of this power, since only the Church can loose and bind, and the Church ought never to deny God. This, unless I am mistaken, may be shown from authority.

D. Paul bears witness to this, saying: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:10). Again, blessed Augustine says concerning the power of binding and loosing:

> “Those alone possess the power of binding and loosing who, placed in this flesh, like the holy apostles, uphold together their example, life, and teaching, and have all things in common according to the apostolic rule.”

Likewise:

> “Just as he who bought Joseph was a eunuch, so he who buys grace does not possess living seed, having dried genitals. Likewise the fire of sacrifice, which had lived beneath water through the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity, was extinguished when Jason sold the priesthood to Antiochus; this signifies truly that the fire of the Holy Spirit is not permitted in simoniacal sacraments.”

From this, as I attempt to discern something by reason, the true light is proved to resolve the entire question.

M. Strive, I ask you, to demonstrate this same point.

D. For if, as has been shown above from reason and authority, those alone possess the power of binding and loosing who, like the holy apostles, maintain their teaching and have all things in common according to the apostolic rule, then if either canons or monks are proved better than others to possess the apostles’ teaching and all things in common according to the apostolic rule, it follows that they, before others, more truly and worthily may not only bind and loose but administer all spiritual things. Therefore I urge you now to continue successfully and show who in the Church possess the apostles’ life more worthily.

M. I thought that I ought now to rest from these matters, but you compel me to speak of things beyond me. For I cannot suitably demonstrate what you urge unless I ascend to the apostles themselves and behold with clear sight how they established the whole Church; and then how the Church itself came down to us, as it were derived from the truest root of its first institution, or also gradually strayed and deviated from that perfection.

D. You have not yet fulfilled the obligation of your promise, nor completely untied the knot of the whole question. Even if you seem able to accomplish this difficult task, you will by no means be able to demonstrate it. For you plainly said this: “First I must destroy the old Adam, so that I may be able to raise up the new man, who has been created according to God” [Col. 0642C]. Therefore, since you have destroyed the proud, you are compelled to raise up the humble; since you have scourged undisciplined unrest, to nourish a peaceful household. And you know that, if Saul had not been raised up after being cast down, the Church would have been deprived of a great apostle.

M. As you see, the sunset brings the day to an end; therefore the third book may properly be concluded.

## THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE FOURTH BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641C] I. Why, for the complete resolution of the whole question, he ascends as far as the founding of the primitive Church by the apostles. II. That, as all the apostles possessed one doctrine, so they established the whole Church in one perfection. III. Concerning the Egyptians and Alexandrians, first instituted by Mark the Evangelist in the same manner as those who believed in Jerusalem. IV. That the whole Church took its beginning from monastic life. V. From what source nuns who are veiled with the sacred veil seem to derive their authority. VI. That those who believed under the apostles possessed the practices of the most perfect monks. VII. Why the whole Church did not persevere in its first perfection; in what respects it departed from that perfection; and in what respects it endured in it. [Col. 0642C] VIII. Why they were called monks, or why cenobitic communities were first established. IX. How the anchoritic life sprang from monastic life. X. That, just as monastic life remained under the honour of the Gospel, [Col. 0642D] so those who departed from it remained under the terror of the Law. XI. That all the apostles were truly monks. XII. By what reasoning and authority this is proved alike. XIII. That no absurdity would follow if every perfect person were regarded as a monk. XIV. On the difference between clerics and monks according to their rule. XV. By what necessity we are compelled to say that the rule of canons is inferior to the rule of monks. XVI. Why Saint Augustine wished to compose a rule for canons, when he knew that the monks’ rule had existed earlier and was more perfect.

## THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643A] 369  
### CHAPTER I

D. As I see, the coming morning brings pleasant rest to an end. You must therefore rise and attend to the matters proposed.

M. Since, for the complete resolution of the whole question, I am compelled to ascend as far as the founding of the primitive Church by the apostles, it is fitting to introduce their incontrovertible orthodox authority, which no one would dare contradict, and which is known to instruct us more truly and more perfectly from that very source.

D. I confess that this greatly pleases me, provided that you also deign to set forth their words; so that, just as trust is placed not in your authority but in that of the Church, so what is said may be strengthened by the words of the Church itself.

M. I shall do what is necessary, avoiding superfluities as far as I can.

[Col. 0643B]

D. May the grace of the Holy Spirit then be with you!

M. After the coming of the hope of that same Holy Spirit, all servile fear having been driven far away, all the apostles burst forth from their upper room. Some first openly preached the word of God in Jerusalem; then they dispersed throughout the whole world. But with what great perfection that multitude which first believed at Jerusalem was instituted by the apostles is declared by the most manifest testimony of Luke the Evangelist in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “The multitude of believers,” he says, “was of one heart and one soul; nor did any one of them say that anything which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. Neither was any needy person among them; for as many as owned lands or houses sold them, brought the prices of what they sold [Col. 0643C], and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4:32).

### CHAPTER II

D. No one seems to doubt concerning the multitude gathered at Jerusalem and the greatness of the perfection with which it began—provided we show that, in other parts of the world, the other apostles began the Church in the same perfection.

M. Hold most firmly that, just as all the apostles possessed one doctrine, so they established the whole Church in one perfection. Far be it that, while the multitude had one heart and one soul, the apostles, its teachers, should have instituted different churches in different customs!

[Col. 0643D]

D. Yet I would like to hear by what authority you would prove this.

### CHAPTER III

M. As ecclesiastical history testifies, Peter, preaching at Rome, made the Church equal in the same perfection as that at Jerusalem. Afterwards he first sent Mark the Evangelist, his disciple, with the Gospel which he had written, into all Egypt by his authority. Mark preached the Gospel in Egypt. Afterwards he came to Alexandria, and there first shaped the Church, as the apostles had done at Jerusalem and Peter, his teacher, at Rome.

In that same ecclesiastical history a certain man named Philo is introduced [Col. 0644A], relating matters concerning the whole Alexandrian Church established under Mark the Evangelist. A most truthful writer, he saw Peter himself at Rome and unquestionably committed to writing for the whole Church what he had learned from Peter and Mark. So great, it is related, was the multitude of believing men and women gathered at the first arrival of Mark the Evangelist, following examples of his sobriety and continence, that the manner of life of those who had believed through him, their life of complete abstinence, and their frugal and sober meals, were committed to literary remembrance.

Describing all these things in the little work which he entitled *On the Contemplative Life, or the Suppliants*, this same Philo added absolutely nothing of his own or from outside sources. He says, then, first of all, that those who believed under the apostles renounced all their possessions [Col. 0644B] and handed over their goods to the brethren; next, that they cast away all life’s cares far from themselves and, leaving the city, lived in gardens or in little plots of land, fleeing associations of unequal purpose and shared dwellings with persons of unlike life, knowing that all these things obstruct those who wish to walk the narrow way.

You see, therefore, that the Church here in Alexandria and Egypt began in the one perfection and one practice in which that first Church gathered under the apostles at Jerusalem, and that initiated under Peter at Rome.

### CHAPTER IV

D. It is clear that he relates of the Egyptians and Alexandrians the very things he relates of those who first believed at Jerusalem. For, as it appears, both the order of the words themselves and the very perfection of those who renounced all things show that [Col. 0644C] the Church began from the life of monks.

M. If you wish to consult all the testimonies of Scripture, they seem to say nothing other than that the Church began from monastic life, as the following words show:

> “In many parts,” says Philo, “of the inhabited world there is this class of people who follow the apostles. … It was certainly fitting,” he says, “that all Greece and all the barbarian world should share in this good. In Egypt, however, their numbers are greater in every district, especially in Alexandria. For the best persons from every place hasten there like settlers to the rich soil of a native land. … In every place,” he says, “there is a consecrated house of prayer, called a *semnion* or a *monasterium*, which is translated ‘an assembly of honourable persons.’” [Col. 0644D]

> “There,” he says, “they celebrate the mysteries of an honourable life, reserving within it nothing except books of the Law, volumes of the Prophets, hymns, and writings like these, by which they are trained in perfect discipline. From sunrise,” he says, “until evening they devote themselves to these pursuits. … They also,” he says, “have certain discussions and interpretations of ancient men who were their founders, who left them monuments setting forth a norm of understanding and perfect life. They follow their institutions and custom alike, as those of guides and founders of their own journey.” [Col. 0645A]

Without doubt, their guides and founders are called apostles, whose institutions and customs they follow alike.

> “Again,” he says, “they not only understand more subtly the hymns of old, but themselves make new ones to God, modulating them in every sort of metre and melody with a composition more honourable and sweet.”

D. All these things, as they are more commonly read of, seem to be done by monks, and thus seem especially suited to them.

M. See further that this is attributed to them more particularly; for he continues:

> “They establish continence first in the soul, as a kind of foundation, and then build the remaining virtues upon it. None of them takes food or drink before sunset, associating the time of light with philosophical studies and the care of the body with night. Some come to share food only after three days, urged on by a more ravenous hunger for study. Others are so inflamed by the reading of sacred volumes that they grant the body food—not desired so much as necessary—only on the sixth day, not on the fourth or fifth. No one tastes wine, nor any kind of flesh; their drink is only water, and their food bread with salt and hyssop.” [Col. 0645B]

D. It is plain that monastic life arose from the authority of these persons.

### CHAPTER V

M. “Further,” he says, “the men live separately by themselves, and the women separately by themselves; among the latter are aged virgins, preserving their integrity not [Col. 0645C] from necessity but from devotion, consecrated not only in spirit but also in body. They deem it unworthy to enslave to lust a vessel prepared for receiving wisdom, or to bear mortal offspring, when they seek the most holy and immortal union with the divine Word, from which a posterity may be left that is in no way subject to the corruptibility of mortality.”

D. From this, nuns who are veiled with the sacred veil seem to derive their authority.

### CHAPTER VI

M. Do you still wish to know from what great perfection the whole Church was instituted by the apostles? Consider what the same man adds:

> “The whole Law,” he says, “seems to these men like a living creature: it has a body, namely the letter itself and the things observed according to the letter; but they contemplate its soul, the spiritual and invisible meaning hidden in the letter, as they have been taught by the apostles.” [Col. 0645D]

D. These men are shown to have transcended the whole Law and to have lived perfectly and truly under the Gospel.

M. Do these not seem to you to have possessed the practices of the most perfect monks—practices which monks after them have scarcely been able to preserve to the present day as handed down by these men? What is known to have been done concerning the Church at Jerusalem and by Peter at Rome, in Galatia, Bithynia, and Cappadocia, and by Mark in Egypt and Alexandria—this Thomas did in Parthia, Matthew in Ethiopia, Bartholomew in nearer India, Andrew in Achaia, John in Asia, Simon and Jude in Persia, both Jameses in Judaea, Philip in Scythia, and Matthias in [Col. 0646A] Samaria. And what shall be said of Paul, by whom everything from Jerusalem to the Illyrian Sea was filled with the Gospel?

### CHAPTER VII

D. Since, therefore, you seem sufficiently to have proved in what perfection and under what institution the whole Church was first established under all the apostles, it remains for you also to say for what reason, and through what impediment, it was not permitted to remain in this perfection; in what respects it departed from this perfection; and in what respects it is shown to have persevered in the perfection once begun.

M. Although I could do this quickly in my own words, I prefer to bring forward an authority that no one can contradict. For in the Twenty-Four Conferences of the most holy Fathers—men who, while still on earth, are judged by all the wise not merely to have led an apostolic life, but even an angelic one—and in the institutions of all apostolic perfection, all these matters are expounded more clearly than light:

> “Therefore,” says the aforementioned book of the *Conferences*, “the discipline of cenobites—that is, of the most perfect monks—took its beginning from the time of apostolic preaching. For such was that entire multitude of believers at Jerusalem which is described in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul’ [Col. 0646B] (Acts 4:32), and the other things subsequently set down there in the Acts of the Apostles. … Such,” he says, “was the whole Church at that time, as it is now difficult to find even very few in cenobitic communities.

> “But when, after the departure of the apostles, the multitude of believers began to grow lukewarm—especially those who flocked to faith in Christ from alien and diverse nations—the apostles required of them, on account of the first rudiments of faith and their ingrained habit of paganism, nothing more than that they abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood. This liberty, granted to the Gentiles because of the weakness of their first faith, gradually began to contaminate even that perfection of the Church which existed at Jerusalem. As the number both of natives and of newcomers increased daily, the fervour of that first faith grew cold. Not only those who had flocked to faith in Christ, but even those who were leaders of the Church, were loosened from that strictness. For some, imagining that what they saw permitted to the Gentiles because of weakness was also lawful for themselves [Col. 0646C], believed that they suffered no loss if they followed faith in Christ and its confession together with their property and possessions.

> “But those in whom apostolic fervour remained, mindful of that former perfection, withdrew from their cities and from the association of those who believed that the negligence of a more relaxed life was lawful both to themselves and to the Church of God. They began to live together in suburban and more secluded places, privately and particularly practising what they remembered had been generally established by the apostles for the whole body of the Church. Thus grew up the discipline, as we have called it, of disciples who had separated themselves from the contagion of those others. As time went on, separated from the crowds of believers because they abstained from marriage and withdrew themselves from the society of their parents and from the intercourse of the world itself, they were called monks, or *monaziantes*, from the strictness of a singular and solitary life.” [Col. 0647A]

### CHAPTER VIII

Consequently, from their life in common fellowship they were called cenobites, and their cells and lodging places were called cenobies. This, then, was the sole and most ancient kind of monks, which was first not only in time but also in grace. For many years it endured inviolate down to the age of Abbot Paul or Anthony; and even now we see its traces remain in strict cenobitic communities.

### CHAPTER IX

> “From this number of the perfect,” he says, “and, so to speak, from this most fruitful root of the saints, flowers and fruits of holy anchorites were afterwards brought forth [Col. 0647B]. We know that the leaders of this profession were those whom we mentioned a little before, namely Saint Paul and Anthony. They sought the hidden places of solitude not, as some do, from faintheartedness or the sickness of impatience, but from the desire for a more exalted perfection and divine contemplation—although the former is said to have penetrated the desert on grounds of necessity, while in the time of persecution he fled the plots of his kinsfolk.”

Thus another kind of perfection arose from the discipline we have described. Its followers are rightly called anchorites, that is, “withdrawers,” because, not content with that victory by which they had trampled underfoot the hidden snares of the devil among men, they desired to engage demons in open contest and manifest battle. They did not fear to penetrate the vast retreats of the desert, in imitation, that is, of John the Baptist, who remained in the desert throughout his life; also of Elijah and Elisha; and of those whom the Apostle thus recalls:

> “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, distressed, afflicted, wandering; of whom the world was not worthy; wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the ground” (Hebrews 11:37). [Col. 0647C]

### CHAPTER X

D. As reason and authority declare, under the apostles the whole Church took its beginning from monks in apostolic perfection; so thereafter among them remained the privilege of all perfection. And just as the shadow of the Law remained with the Synagogue while the true light remained with the Church, so all who separated themselves from this perfection remained under the terror of the Law; only monastic life—which is the perfect and primitive Church, and therefore apostolic—remained under the honour of the Gospel.

M. Have you considered, in the authority just quoted, the definition of the term *monk*, and why those who separated themselves from the contagion of others were called monks?

D. It is plain, as is said there, that they renounced the whole world, like the apostles who founded them; and, separated from relaxations, crowds, the society of parents, and the contagion of the whole world, they were named monks or *monaziantes*—that is, single or solitary persons—from the sanctity of a singular life. [Col. 0647D]

M. By what exemplar were they thus formed?

[Col. 0648A]

### CHAPTER XI

D. Did I not tell you: by the apostles, their founders?

M. If, then, everything which gives form to something else must necessarily possess in itself the form received by what is formed from it; and if monks, insofar as they are monks, receive their form from the apostles themselves: therefore all the apostles were true monks.

D. This is nowhere read, yet it follows from what has been said.

### CHAPTER XII

M. Is it not read that the apostles renounced the whole world, separated themselves from every marriage, denied themselves, followed Christ, and were obedient to Christ even unto death?

D. This is read everywhere plainly.

M. But to observe all these things is to be a monk [Col. 0648B]. Therefore it is read that the apostles were monks.

D. What I say is that they were not called by this term, *monk*.

M. Is not *monk* in Greek called in Latin *singularis* or *solitarius*, “single” or “solitary”?

D. Who denies it?

M. But the apostles were singular in holiness, and, though they lived under such a roof, solitary in mind. Since the books everywhere say this in Latin, they therefore say in Greek that they were monks.

Further: one must not be concerned with the name by which someone is called, when it is proved that he possesses what the name signifies. Otherwise great contradiction would follow in many matters. For if each person were at once what he was called, as you said above, Judas would still be regarded as an apostle; and conversely, as soon as anyone were called holy, he would immediately be shown perfected in virtue. Thus an utterly absurd and contrary result would follow: no one would need to labour to acquire virtues, but would merely call himself by the name of virtues. Thus what would be called holier in names would itself be worshipped as God.

[Col. 0648C]

D. I truly confess that I am compelled to desist from these objections.

M. Were not the apostles righteous, chaste, holy, gentle, prudent, wise, strong, discerning, patient, obedient, and charitable?

D. Whoever denies this has no faith.

M. But they taught people to be righteous, chaste, holy, gentle, prudent, wise, strong, discerning, patient, obedient, and charitable. Did they, then, by teaching people to possess these virtues, empty themselves of these virtues by their teaching?

D. Who, even if of the maddest mind, would say this of those whom he believed to be apostles?

M. Those who are unwilling to grant that the apostles were monks seem to do this.

D. To tell the truth, I shall never be compelled to say it.

372 M. Therefore, just as the apostles, teaching others to be holy, charitable, and so forth, themselves were what they taught, so, teaching monks to live, they themselves were truly monks. Finally, leaving aside others, does not Paul seem to you to have been a true monk, when he is known to have said:

> “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom [Col. 0649A] the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14)?

Were not all true monks, since this was suitable to all:

> “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8)?

What else does Paul seem to you to have meant when he said,

> “I desire every person to be as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7:7),

if not a true monk? For he did not desire every person to be an apostle, especially since he says elsewhere:

> “Are all apostles?” (1 Corinthians 13:19);  
> “If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be?” (ibid., v. 17).

### CHAPTER XIII

By renouncing this world, he separated himself from marriage and from the contagion of the whole world; content with food and clothing, he denied himself and followed Christ. This is to be a monk. Therefore, since he wished every person to be as he himself was, he wished every person [Col. 0649B] to be a monk.

D. But if every person were a monk, the world would quickly perish: for if no one begot, no one would be begotten. Thus it would follow that the world ended even in Paul’s time, or not long after him. What then would be said of those saints who came after him until the end of the age?

M. It is established that the number of the elect is certain and determined; and the world is shown to continue for no other reason than that this number of the elect may gradually be gathered from it. It therefore seems to follow that, if in Paul’s time every perfect person had been a monk, the number of the elect would quickly have been hastened at one time, whereas afterwards it appears to have been gathered gradually.

D. Nevertheless, regular canons seem to possess in the same way the privilege of apostolic dignity which true monks have been shown to possess from the time of apostolic preaching down to our own time. [Col. 0649C]

### CHAPTER XIV

For they renounce the whole world, deny themselves to themselves, separate themselves from marriage and the contagion of the world, content with food and clothing, and promise obedience to their superiors unto death. Since this is the life of monks, the life of regular canons seems not to differ from it.

M. Since I see that nothing is enough for you, I must deal with you at greater length. Tell me, then: who made their rule?

### CHAPTER XV

D. Above all others, Saint Augustine.

M. Tell me also: were not all monks in the time of blessed Augustine, just as they were holier, so also more renowned throughout the whole Church than they are now?

D. Augustine himself many times called monastic life truly apostolic, saying that it could neither be admired enough nor praised in words as it deserved.

M. But just as that life is proved by his own testimony to be truly apostolic, so the institutions of the apostles existed in it from the time of the apostles themselves. For just as the apostles established that life, so either they themselves or men equal to the apostles handed down its institutions.

[Col. 0649D]

D. No one is permitted to contradict what you seem to say.

[Col. 0650A]

### CHAPTER XVI

M. If, then, by his testimony this life is truly apostolic, and if within it the institutions of the apostles existed before his time, why did Saint Augustine establish a rule for canons, giving institutions altogether different from those which he knew had been handed down before his time by the apostles or their followers to this life? Or, if he wished the canons’ rule to be the same as the monks’ rule, why was he not content, just as with apostolic life, so also with the apostolic rule, and equally with the discipline and institutions of monks?

D. Here I see that I fail; you ought therefore to untie the knot.

M. Either, then, Saint Augustine wished the rule of canons to be equally apostolic with that of monks, or superior and holier, [Col. 0650B] or inferior and less holy.

D. As it seems, equally apostolic.

M. If he wished it to be the same, he is found not merely superfluous but even contrary: superfluous, if he understood it to be the same and nevertheless composed another; contrary, if he understood the institutions of the same rule to be the same and nevertheless gave much more relaxed and therefore different observances. For who does not see that eating meat on three weekdays apart from feasts, using soft and very white linen, and performing the divine office much more briefly and lightly, differ from and are much more relaxed than the practices of those who abstain from meat, wear coarse woollens and garments most contemptible in the eyes of this world, and are more occupied with psalms and divine exercises?

Moreover, he will be judged to have injured the apostles and apostolic men, whose rule he is shown to have changed into something more relaxed. He also seems to deprive of great reward those who, by observing the greater institutions of the monks’ rule, would be known to expect a greater reward. [Col. 0650C]

D. Everything seems false and contrary to Saint Augustine.

M. Augustine, therefore, did not understand the rule of canons to be the same as that of monks.

D. Very well: suppose he understood the rule of canons to be much higher and holier than that of monks.

M. If, then, he wished it to be much superior and holier, he was contrary to himself in giving one much lighter [Col. 0650D] and more relaxed. It follows that the lighter and more relaxed rule of canons is considered much higher than the higher and holier rule of the apostles and monks. From this a strange and contrary conclusion is drawn: the more relaxed a person’s way of life, the higher and holier he is shown to be. Thus the rule of canons is no longer apostolic, but composed above the apostles and apostolic men.

D. Therefore it is contrary to all the apostles.

M. Augustine, then, did not wish it to be superior or holier.

D. As it seems, we are compelled by necessity to say that the rule of canons is inferior and less holy than the rule of monks. 373 It is therefore rightly asked what cause compelled Saint Augustine to compose this rule, not so perfect [Col. 0651A], when he knew that before his time the more perfect—and indeed apostolic—rule of monks existed.

M. If Adam and his descendants had wished to keep the natural law given to him by the Creator, it would by no means have seemed necessary for God later to give the Law together with the Prophets. Hence, if they had wished to observe the Law and the Prophets spiritually, there would have been no need for the Gospel to be written. For this is to be “a wheel within a wheel”: the Gospel within the Prophet. It follows that, if the Gospels were diligently observed by all, neither canons nor any rules whatever would be imposed. For whoever wished in every respect to live righteously and perfectly as the Gospel commands would have no need, just as the apostles themselves had no need, to live under another law or rule.

For this reason, just as the Son of God, seeking humankind, willed to humble himself to it, so all Holy Scripture had to condescend to humankind in order to draw humanity back to him: so that one who was a transgressor of the natural law might be admonished by the written Law and the Prophets. Further, if that person transgressed these, he might be drawn back by the written Gospel; and again, if he attended to the Gospel with insufficient care, he might submit himself to canons or to whatever rules. It is therefore beyond doubt that, if clerics in Augustine’s time had wished to live rightly under the Gospel or to submit themselves to other more perfect rules, it would have been superfluous and even dangerous to write another rule for them. And just as Scripture from the beginning has been shown to have condescended with humankind, so Augustine had to compose his rule by condescending to those who then existed [Col. 0651C]: namely, because he saw that they neither lived strictly under the [Col. 0652A] Gospel as the apostles themselves did, nor submitted themselves, like their followers, to some stricter rule of the saints, he had to condescend and make such a rule for them, so that those unable to ascend higher might live in this common rule.

D. You have plainly made this distinction rightly. Thus I now see clearly that even blessed Benedict condescended in some respect to monks, since he is shown to have granted them permission to drink wine. For he says that he had read that wine was altogether unsuitable for monks. Since in his own time, as he testifies, this could not be persuaded to monks, anyone may see that he condescended to them in the matter of wine. Similarly, if blessed Augustine could have persuaded all clerics to abstain from what he allowed them, who does not see that he would gladly have wished to do so?

M. Therefore clerics are always shown to be weaker than those to whom blessed Benedict is judged not to have condescended so far from evangelical perfection as other masters of stricter rule. Nevertheless, we must confess that Saint Augustine showed the highest discernment in this rule.

[Col. 0652B]

D. No one who desires and is able to examine his books with a very clear eye can fail to know this. Since you say that the rule of monks derived from the rule of the apostles as from a fountain, it is most necessary for you to show that the monastic rule agrees in every respect with the apostolic rule.

M. The approaching feast of Saint Nicholas compels us to devote ourselves to it. We are therefore compelled to divide the fourth book, and may be aided in this by his prayer.

## THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE FIFTH BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651C] I. Who and how incomparable were the men who composed the monks’ rule. II. What agreement there is between the rule of blessed Benedict and evangelical perfection. III. Where in the Gospel the ladder which Jacob saw in sleep is raised. IV. That the same ladder which Jacob saw in sleep, and which Christ raised in the Gospel, is raised in the Rule. V. Why it is said to have eight steps in the Gospel, whereas in the Rule it is divided into twelve. VI. That the first step named in the Gospel is divided into three in the Rule. VII. That the second step set down in the Gospel is understood as the fourth in the Rule. VIII. That the third step found in the Gospel is shown to be the fifth in the Rule. IX. That the fourth step set forth in the Gospel is subdivided into the sixth and seventh in the Rule. X. That the fifth step marked in the Gospel is the eighth in the Rule. XI. That the sixth on the evangelical ladder is divided into three—the ninth, tenth, and eleventh—in the Rule. XII. That the seventh shown in the Gospel [Col. 0652C] is the twelfth in the Rule. XIII. That the first and eighth steps in the Gospel are the same step. XIV. Why the ladder of humility is divided into twelve steps in the Rule, and why no other virtue is adopted for this purpose. XV. How, if both rules are considered, monks are rightly preferred to canons. XVI. What privilege of their dignity monks possess that canons do not possess. XVII. That canons should not be forbidden, if they wish to become monks. [Col. 0652D] XVIII. On the privilege which some claim to possess: that canons ought not to make themselves monks. XIX. What absurdity follows if this privilege is accepted generally. XX. That the example of most blessed Martin is brought forward, and should be regarded as more certain than any argument. XXI. That it is neither fitting nor necessary for canons to preside over nuns who observe the rule of blessed Benedict. XXII. On the clothing of monks, derived from the clothing of the apostles. XXIII. On correction arising from a faulty division.

## THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653A]

### CHAPTER I

D. The feast having been completed, we remain under the same necessity. You must therefore discharge what you know I claim from you as a debt.

M. Several men composed rules for monks, men of incomparable holiness. Of these, blessed Pachomius handed down to monks a Rule dictated to him by an angel from heaven—not, indeed, as a human work, but as a divine oracle. Blessed Basil, who by God’s testimony was a pillar raised to heaven, who spoke with fiery tongues, handed down a rule to all the monks in Cappadocia. After them, most holy Benedict, who, as it is said, full of the spirit of all the righteous, penetrated the secrets of divinity itself, set forth a rule for monks. It is enough for you to choose one of these, through which I may attempt to show what you urge.

[Col. 0653B]

D. Although the first handed down a rule dictated from heaven, and the second issued his in fiery tongues, you should take up the Rule of most blessed Father Benedict, father of Latin monks. From it you must show the fullest agreement with evangelical perfection.

### CHAPTER II

M. I believe no rule of the apostles is understood to be worthier than the four Gospels themselves. For just as they are the doctrine of all doctrines, so they are the rule of all rules. Therefore, if it pleases you, select whatever commands are loftier and more perfect in them, spoken to the apostles alone and appropriate to the matter, so that the Rule of most blessed Benedict may, if possible, be compared with them.

[Col. 0653C] 374

D. Very well indeed. For I now see that in the one Gospel of Matthew all the loftier things can be shown together in one place. This is where the Lord, leaving the crowd on the plain, went up onto the mountain and taught the apostles alone, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), and so forth. And because he was teaching the apostles alone, he went up the mountain, indicating that he was teaching the apostles commands so lofty that the crowd which he left behind could not ascend to them.

M. Therefore, just as he wished to lead the apostles with himself higher than the others onto the mountain, so by what he taught there he wished them, more perfectly and more highly than others, to ascend higher into heaven. There he deigned to raise the most lofty ladder of the eight beatitudes—that is, of eight steps—up to heaven itself, a ladder which none but the most perfect despisers of the world, in these beatitudes and like the apostles themselves, could climb.

[Col. 0653D]

### CHAPTER III

D. It seems that here was raised that ladder which Jacob saw in dreams, whose summit touched the heavens and on which he saw angels ascending and descending; concerning that place he also added how terrible it was.

[CAP. IV.] M. Therefore contemplate and weigh carefully that the most blessed Benedict testifies that in his Rule he raises the same ladder which Jacob saw in sleep and which Jesus raised for his disciples on the mountain, so that monks may be proved, by ascending it, to attain that same height of heaven to which Christ wished his disciples to ascend by the ladder which he himself raised on the mountain.

D. O grace of God, with highest glory!

M. For concerning this ladder he spoke thus in the Rule (ch. 7): “Therefore, brothers, if we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility and swiftly arrive at that heavenly exaltation to which one ascends through the humility of this present life, then, as our deeds ascend, that ladder must be raised which appeared to Jacob in sleep, by which angels descending and ascending were shown to him. Without doubt, we understand that descent and ascent as nothing other than descending by exaltation and ascending by humility,” etc.

[Col. 0654B] [CAP. V.] D. O truly most holy man, who penetrated the secrets of divinity itself, when he testifies that Jacob, in his vision, saw no ladder other than that which he himself is shown to have raised in his Rule. But why is this ladder taught to have eight steps—that is, eight beatitudes—when raised by Christ on the mountain, whereas in the Rule it is said to have twelve steps? Why is it said here to have twelve and there eight steps, or how can that which is understood to have twelve steps be the same as that which has eight?

M. First, there were twelve apostles for whom the Lord set forth the evangelical ladder on the mountain. Therefore, so that blessed Benedict might indicate that he was instituting no life other than that of the twelve apostles, he wished to distinguish the evangelical ladder in his Rule by twelve steps. Those twelve steps are doubtless understood to be the same as those said there to be eight.

[CAP. VI.] D. Now, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3), is called there the first step.

M. In the Rule it is placed third, with two beneath it, through which one ascends to that third step.

D. This is not yet understood.

M. The third degree of humility is said to be when someone, made obedient to the abbot for the love of God, becomes obedient even unto death. No one can do this unless he wishes to lose his life in this world; and such a person can without doubt be called poor in spirit. You see, then, that the one whom the Lord began as first in the Gospel is third in the Rule.

Moreover, no one who has become obedient even unto death can deny himself unless he must first renounce these two things: first, impoverish himself of worldly substance; and then, not loving his own will, cut away from himself the desires of the flesh. Blessed Benedict is therefore said to have placed two steps beforehand, through which, as I said, one ascends to the third. For he placed the first degree, concerning the fear of God, at the bottom of this ladder; because, since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:9), the twelve degrees had to begin in the fear of God, and plainly reach their completion [Col. 0655A] in the fullness of his wisdom. Since we cannot serve God and mammon, fear lest we lose God has cast away the mammon of iniquity, so that afterward we may serve God. He then placed second the degree concerning the cutting off of desire, because one who, having cast away mammon, is known to serve God ought to cut off from himself the desires of the flesh. Thus he fittingly ascends to the third: becoming obedient even unto death—that is, losing his life—and such a one can without doubt be called poor in spirit.

[CAP. VII.] D. But the second is placed in the Gospel when it says, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4).

M. This is undoubtedly understood as the fourth in the Rule. For to say, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth,” has the same force as to say, “Blessed are the patient, for they shall possess their own soul,” which, while in this world they endure every adversity for Christ without avenging themselves, they seem almost to lose. For he who said, “Whoever loses his life in this world shall possess it in eternal life” (Luke 9:24), himself said, “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Therefore, if “Blessed are the meek” means the same as “the patient,” blessed Benedict teaches that the patient belong to the fourth degree. That is (ch. 7): those who fulfill the Lord’s command even amid adversities and injuries through patience; who, when struck on the cheek, offer the other; who leave also their cloak to one who takes their tunic; who, compelled to go one mile, go two; who, with the Apostle Paul, endure false brethren and persecution; and [Col. 0655C] who bless those who curse them. Thus the same degree is understood in the Rule which is placed second in the Gospel, after the first.

[CAP. VIII.] D. But the third follows in the Gospel, when it adds: “Blessed are those who now mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

M. This is the same as the fifth placed in the Rule, which blessed Benedict frames thus: “If,” he says, “a monk does not conceal from his abbot, by humble confession, all evil thoughts that come into his heart, or evil deeds secretly committed by him.” Therefore, if to make humble confession even concerning thoughts is to mourn for them here, these are the people who shall afterward be comforted. Thus the fifth in the Rule and the third in the Gospel are concluded to be one.

[Col. 0655D] [CAP. IX.] D. But the fourth is framed thus in the Gospel, when it introduces, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

M. In the Rule this is divided into the sixth and seventh for the following reason. One who is said to hunger and thirst for righteousness is proved to be exceedingly righteous; and one said to be exceedingly righteous ought exceedingly to accuse himself, as it is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17); and, “The greater you are in all things, humble yourself” (Ecclus. 3:20). Now an exceedingly righteous person ought to accuse himself in two ways: namely, by being content with every abasement or extremity, which is to ascend the sixth degree [Col. 0656A] of humility in the Rule; and again, by declaring with his own tongue, as an example to all, that he is humbler and more worthless than all others, which is to complete the seventh degree of humility in the Rule. Since one who hungers and thirsts for righteousness ought to do both these things (Matt. 5:6), the fourth degree of the evangelical ladder is divided into the sixth and seventh degrees of the Rule.

[CAP. X.] D. But the fifth is noted thus in the Gospel, when the Lord adds: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

M. This is said to be the eighth degree of humility in the Rule (ch. 7): “If a monk does nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge.” For who does not see that these are very merciful? Although, as righteous persons, they are known to be held under no law, nevertheless, so that by accommodating themselves to others they may show mercy, they ought to be restrained under the common Rule of the monastery alone: namely, that they may become all things to all, in order to gain all. Since this is what the merciful ought to do, you see that the fifth of the Gospel and the eighth of the Rule are one and the same.

[CAP. XI.] D. Now the sixth degree in the evangelical ladder is framed when it introduces: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

M. This is consequently divided into three in the Rule, being stated as the ninth, tenth, and eleventh, so that one may deserve to see God and may not appear to cloud purity of heart even by an idle word. He ought not to open his tongue, closed in silence, except when questioned; hence he ought not to be quick to laugh, but, when he speaks, to speak gently and without laughter, humbly and with gravity, using few and sensible words. Since the pure in heart ought to accomplish all this, you see that the sixth in the Gospel is divided into three in the Rule.

[CAP. XII.] D. But the seventh is shown as a step for us to ascend in the Gospel, when above the rest is placed: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

M. This is set above the others as the twelfth in the Rule (ch. 7): “If a monk indicates humility to those who see him, not only in his heart but also in his very body always”—that is, at the Work of God, in the oratory, in the monastery, in [Col. 0656D] the garden, on the road, in the field, or wherever he may be, sitting, walking, or standing—“let his head always be bowed and his eyes fixed upon the ground,” etc.

Who, moreover, does not see that such a person is exceedingly peaceable, whose body is rendered so gentle that, just as it commits nothing contrary to his spirit in any place, so it presents no offense displeasing even to the eyes of any neighbor who sees him? For he is not proved to be peaceable whose body still resists the spirit and does not enjoy steadfast peace, whose body still displays something unbecoming to a neighbor. This is what the Lord says: that two agree upon earth—namely, that body and spirit disagree in no good thing. This is what it means if a monk indicates humility to those who see him not only in heart but also in his very body always—that is, at the Work of God, in the oratory, in the monastery, in [Col. 0657A] the garden, on the road, in the field, or wherever he may be, sitting, walking, or standing, let his head always be bowed and his eyes fixed upon the ground. This is, according to Ezekiel, for the heavenly creature, full of eyes, to look round everywhere before and behind itself (Ezek. 1:18). Hence you must call truly peaceable the man who, standing on the twelfth degree of the Rule, is proved to stand on the seventh of the evangelical ladder.

D. It seems most marvelous if greater perfection is possessed in this life, since for one known to ascend the degrees in so great a consummation of virtues nothing remains except that he ought to receive from the just Judge the supreme crown of the highest contest.

[CAP. XIII.] M. From this you may recognize that the eighth degree [Col. 0657B] of the evangelical ladder, in which those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake are called blessed (Matt. 5:10), ought to be understood as nothing other than preserving the righteousness completed in the seven degrees. And because they defend it against persecution, lest they allow themselves to lose the righteousness acquired by such labor in the seven degrees, they are called blessed.

D. Perhaps this is why in the eighth no reward other than the kingdom of heaven is promised—the reward proposed in the first.

M. You understand rightly. For just as all time revolves through seven days, while in the Lord’s Day the beginning and end of the entire week are brought together, so the whole consummation of virtues is completed in these seven degrees. [Col. 0657C] In the eighth, however, the beginning and end are repeated.

D. Thus it is plainly proved that blessed Benedict, in the ascent of this ladder, seems to lead monks to the same summit of glory to which Christ led the twelve apostles by the evangelical ladder.

M. No one is allowed to doubt it, since the degree of perfection involved in standing at the summit of this ladder is shown in these words (ibid.): “Therefore,” he says, “when all these degrees of humility have been ascended, the monk will soon arrive at that love of God which, being perfect, ‘casts out fear’ (1 John 4:18); through it, all that he formerly observed not without dread, he will begin to keep without any labor, as though naturally, by habit—not now from fear of hell, but from love of Christ [Col. 0657D] and from good habit itself and delight in virtues, which God will deign to manifest by the Holy Spirit in his worker, now cleansed of vices and sins.”

For if, as you see, the monk is brought to the perfect love of God which casts out fear, and God himself is love, and the person who abides in love is, by John’s testimony, said to be in God, then it is plainly concluded that the perfect monk is in God and God in him. Hence no one is permitted to doubt that the perfect monk ought to inherit the kingdom of God as that of his Father.

[CAP. XIV.] D. Why, I ask, is humility alone divided into twelve degrees, while no other virtue is chosen for this as though less suited?

[Col. 0658A] M. Was it not established above between us that humility is that by which one goes to God himself, just as pride is that by which one goes to the devil himself?

D. I have not forgotten what I am reminded of.

M. But you know that pride was a downward-sloping ladder by which the first man is proved to have descended from God to the devil. Therefore, if we wish to ascend from the devil to God, we must raise a ladder of humility. Humility alone, because it is proved safe, has chosen to ascend from the devil to God. Blessed Benedict therefore chose to distinguish humility alone into twelve degrees, so that this alone might appear to ascend, since it alone can safely do this. I therefore ask that all monks be admonished to strive above all things earnestly to attain it. For although in the ascent of this [Col. 0658B] ladder a multitude of virtues is displayed, yet while each of them seems to ascend there with faltering steps, humility alone is given a safe way all the way to heaven. Nor does any other ascend unless this guide takes it by the hand.

D. In the same way, then, they must be admonished to strive above all to avoid pride, which is written to be the beginning of every sin, just as it alone suffices for the precipice of this ladder. Nor is anyone cast down from it unless he is dragged downward by its hand. For first he slips with the foot of pride, then he is dragged downward by its hand. “There all those who work iniquity have fallen.”

M. You see, then, that pride is called the foot and hand of sin; and since foot and hand seem to be the end and beginning of the whole body, what a dreadful monster pride is shown to be: the beginning and end of every sin, into which everyone who falls is first shown to have slipped. Hence, because humility is proved to be its opposite, rightly everyone who ascends the ladder of virtues is joined with it in the first degree and, standing at the summit, is completed in it.

[CAP. XV.] D. Truly we must acknowledge that the rule of canons is placed on a lower degree, since it is evident that the Rule of the most blessed Benedict is measured by so lofty a cubit of virtues.

M. Further: let two persons, still free from the yoke of either rule, be chosen, to whom both rules are read from the beginning. One, however, is not yet so disposed that he can be content with every abasement and extremity, nor can confess from the heart that he is to be regarded as humbler and more worthless than all; nor does he presume, with a feeble spirit, to enter upon so lofty a course of degrees, by which the Rule of the most blessed Benedict is shown to lead its followers with the strongest spirit. Let him choose the Rule of Saint Augustine, which seems more accommodating to the weak. For it does not appear to demand from its followers such lowly and extreme things in bodily use, nor such arduous precepts of virtue.

But let the other, possessing a stronger resolution of mind, prefer for love of Christ to choose the Rule of blessed Benedict, professing things lower and more extreme in bodily use and likewise higher precepts of virtue. Which of them, I ask, do you judge will be stronger and holier, and therefore dearer to God?

[Col. 0659A] D. The one who, with a stronger resolution of mind, for love of Christ prefers to choose every lower and more extreme thing and the higher precepts of virtue—I judge that he is stronger, better, holier, and dearer to God.

M. Therefore, if only the two rules and their professed adherents are considered, all who profess the Rule of blessed Benedict are judged, in comparison with those who profess the Rule of blessed Augustine, to be stronger, better, holier, and thus dearer to God.

D. I have nothing to object to this.

M. Therefore every monk, if he observes his rule, is rightly to be preferred to a canon. For unless the monk’s vocation were judged most lofty, one who wishes to profess the rule would never be commanded to be tested beforehand for a full year, when it is evident that nothing of the kind exists in the Rule of Saint [Col. 0659B] Augustine.

[CAP. XVI.] D. Do monks have another privilege of their dignity which canons do not have?

M. A great one, and very different from theirs. For, as is read in the Rule, after a full year he is received after proving his patience; and, when a most solemn office has been performed and he professes the Rule, he becomes a monk. Everywhere his head is covered, as though a tomb had been placed over him; for three days he is buried with Christ, and on the third day he rises with Christ, when his head is uncovered from the cowl as though the tomb had been opened.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] On this rite, see, if you wish, what we have said in the commentary on the Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 58 (Patrologia, vol. LXVI, col. 803).]

At that time Mass is also celebrated over him, and the abbot, giving him Christ’s peace, kisses him and addresses him as Christ risen: “Peace be with you; it is I. I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.” Hence, if he perseveres, he is proved to be a true disciple of [Col. 0659C] Christ.

D. What then if one of the canons wishes to ascend to this privilege of holiness? Will he be judged bound to do so?

[CAP. XVII.] M. Without doubt he will be judged bound to do so, provided that he wishes humbly to seek permission for this from his superior; nor is it good for the latter rashly to oppose him if he so wishes. For many holy bishops made themselves monks even after their episcopacy; this is judged more worthy of praise and is censured by no one except the most foolish person.

For even in our own memory blessed William, bishop of Châlons, although he was a perfect regular canon and approved in everyone’s judgment, and although he had thrice tried to escape it, was at last made bishop against his will. No one who knows this is permitted to doubt how holily he lived in that office.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] This is that most celebrated William of Champeaux, an eminent teacher, who, having assumed the habit of regular canons, gave rise to the distinguished monastery of St. Victor at Paris. Taken from there in 1113, he was made bishop of Châlons; he is said to have died in 1121, on 25 January, as is recorded in the Chronicle of Morigny, and was buried at Clairvaux, perhaps having assumed the monastic habit at the end of his life.]

[Col. 0659D] This holy regular canon and bishop, whose eye was, as it were, so clear that nothing in all divine Scripture escaped him, testified that the Rule of Saint Augustine did not suffice for perfection; he wished, and did in fact arrange, to become a monk. Such a man certainly would never have done this had he known it to be unlawful.

[CAP. XVIII.] D. Everyone who had occasion to see or hear him testifies how perfect and learned he was. [Col. 0660A] Why, then, do certain people say that they have a privilege from the Apostolic See by which no one may ascend from canonical life to monastic life, when it is established by such authority and reason that this life excels the other?

M. To one contemplating all the volumes of holy Scripture, nothing seems to occur by which it could be proved unlawful, since both holy Scripture and the examples of saints testify that it was done so often. For Saint Augustine himself, whose Rule they possess, seems in *On the Trinity of God*, when speaking of the contemplative life, to interpret this passage of the Apostle—“A man ought not to pray with his head veiled” (1 Cor. 11:7)—to mean that a man is commanded not to veil his head lest, when he wishes to ascend higher in the contemplative life, he be prevented by someone.

For “man” there is understood as the rational faculty of the mind, which is the best part of a human being. Since it was made in the image of God so that it should continually ascend in contemplation of him, it is commanded not to have a veil over itself. Therefore, whoever prevents a person from ascending higher in the contemplative life both wishes, contrary to the Apostle, to place a veil over the man’s head and, contrary to God, prevents a person from loving his Creator. This, according to the Gospel, is to choose Mary’s better part (Luke 10:42), which Christ appears to set before those who love him as the one thing necessary.

For when Martha wished, by a tearful complaint, to hinder Mary from the part she had chosen, Christ did not at all command Mary to assist Martha; rather, praising her, he allowed her to sit at his feet. Hence one must by no means believe that this was universally forbidden by any Apostolic authority, unless perhaps in some cloister, when someone was striving to do this rashly and improperly. Granting the privilege you mention, it was necessarily restricted so that such scandal might not arise. Therefore it is by no means forbidden universally, although some persons may have received some privilege, as was then necessary, to avoid the importunity of certain people.

Otherwise, if all were barred by this privilege, not only the aforementioned blessed Bishop William, who later did this, would not be held in the communion of the Church, but also many who later did it would have died outside the communion of the Church. Since all these consequences would be contrary to the Church, let certain persons be content with their private privilege.

[CAP. XIX.] D. Again, how could the most blessed Benedict himself command in his Rule that the abbot esteem priests—that is, bishops—as well as the other clergy, if he, who beheld the whole world gathered under one ray of the sun, judged that this was unlawful before God?

M. If a monk becomes a canon, what do you think he does?

D. In my view, as in everyone’s, he apostasizes.

M. But to apostasize is to descend downward from God.

[Col. 0661A] D. I must grant this.

M. Therefore, if to apostasize is to descend downward from God, and one who becomes a canon from being a monk seems to do this, then one who becomes a monk from being a canon is proved to ascend upward to God.

D. No one can contradict this.

M. But a person is proved permitted to ascend upward to God.

D. Who can deny it?

[CAP. XX.] M. A canon is therefore permitted to become a monk. From this consider how far canonical life is judged to differ from monastic life: descending from the latter into the former appears to be apostasy, while ascending from the former into the latter is proved to be an ascent upward to God.

Finally, let us bring forward one example, that of the most blessed Martin, by which this assertion may be held more certain than by any argument. For, as is read in his Life, he built for himself a cell woven from wood, set apart; and just as it was separately built, so he lived separately in it with that most noble company of his monastic disciples. The canons, however, who, so to speak, were most regular under Martin, lived in the monastery—that is, in the episcopal seat—by his command.

Thus, if monastic life were not held worthier than canonical life, it would certainly not have seemed worthier to Martin to live separately with the monks. For, since both groups had been entrusted to him equally by the Lord as sheep, the nature of his episcopal office seemed to require that he should live as bishop in the episcopal seat. But he preferred to dwell with those who belonged to the worthier and holier life. Martin therefore left an example: whoever wished to live more holily ought to take refuge in monastic life.

[Col. 0661C] D. Even if there were no argument, this one example of the most blessed Martin would suffice to establish that the life in which Martin deigned to dwell was held worthier than the others. I therefore wonder whether it seems just for any canon to be placed as superior over persons following a worthier life, as I hear that certain regular canons preside over nuns. This seems to me unsuitable and unnecessary.

[CAP. XXI.] M. If nuns are proved to live under the discipline of the holier Rule of blessed Benedict, then, as you say, it is unsuitable and unnecessary that masters of an inferior Rule should be set over them—especially when persons more numerous and holier, following the same Rule, can be found and are judged worthier to govern them. For it is shameful and dangerous for a shepherd to teach things which he himself has no wish at all to maintain in his own life. Finally, does he form them according to his own Rule, or according to their Rule of Saint Benedict?

D. What else would it seem except according to the Rule which they observe?

M.
