If he forms them according to his own Rule, when he has professed another, he incurs that evangelical danger in which it is said: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). Hence a remarkable consequence must follow: [Col. 0662A] he is compelled to observe both Rules—one, of which he is professed adherent; the other, of which he is master and which he appears to teach. For whoever wishes to teach another is himself compelled to fulfill the same thing.

But if he wishes to form them according to the Rule which he professes, he plainly compels them to depart from their own: since they are taught one Rule and profess another, neither seems to be fulfilled. Further, if he wishes to teach them both, he seems to incur the same danger, equally unsuitable.

[CAP. XXII.] D. You seem reasonably to oppose this. For the canons, too, are known to forbid it. I ask you, then, to show by what authority monks are proved to have such a garment.

M. Just as they are proved to have the privilege of the life of the apostles, so the origin of their garment was taken from the apostles’ clothing. For the apostles wore the *colobium*, in which they imitated Christ’s use of a seamless tunic. Moreover, because Christ used this tunic, each apostle wore only one tunic. From necessity the same *colobium* was called a *cuculla* [cowl], without sleeves, so that no one might seem to possess anything superfluous. Thus the monks’ cowl rightly imitates the apostles’ *colobium*.

Moreover, with sleeves added and the cowl removed, the same *colobium* was changed into a dalmatic, so that it is an honor for ministers to use the dalmatic as the garment of the apostles. Therefore, with the cowl removed and sleeves added, monks also use the tunic as though it were a dalmatic.

A spiritual interpretation of this garment is read in Saint Boniface: since monks are known to have the life of angels, the six wings of the seraphim are represented in this garment. In the hood, two wings signify, as it were, faith [Col. 0662C] and hope, by which the five senses of the head are governed. In the two sleeves are two wings of love of God and neighbor, by which they are raised to heaven. In the two parts of the cowl, before and behind, by which their bodies are covered, are expressed fear and penitence, by which they cover themselves before the eyes of God. The lowly garment, signifying contempt of the world and seeming to extend down to their feet, signifies their perseverance in their vocation to the end. The broad monastic tonsure is taken from Christ’s crown of thorns, so that, as they ought to share with him the dominion of the kingdom, so they may bear with Christ the reproach of the cross.

D. O how delightful, and what a grace-filled joy, to wear under this hope the broad crown and lowly garment!

M. These points having thus been completed, turn your eyes back to that first definition of the Church. When you divided it into four members, you were troubled because, through the disagreement of the three among themselves, the fourth was left in great error. You indicated that this fourth was the people, who, if they wished to renounce this world, would not know to what body they should attach themselves.

[CAP. XXIII.] D. I see both points: that I divided the Church into four members with far too little care, since you have evidently placed two members under one, proving that all clergy ought to be regular; and that counsel is given to the people who wish to renounce this world—namely, whether they ought to attach themselves to clergy or to monks.

[Col. 0663A] M. Can you at last give sound advice to everyone, without seeming to prejudice anyone?

D. Although I could easily do so from what has been established, nevertheless, lest I seem a disciple to prejudice you as my teacher, I prefer that you put the finishing touch to this matter by giving the counsel.

M. Since, therefore, it is certain that Jesus cries out so often in the Gospel that no one can be his perfect disciple unless he wishes to renounce all that he possesses and, following him, bear the cross; and since it has been established by reason and authority that monks who strive to fulfill their vocation, like the apostles themselves, are worthier and more perfect: you may give sound counsel to all who wish to renounce this world and attain perfection as true disciples of Christ, that they ought to attach themselves to monastic life.

For “the glory of the sun is one, and the glory of the moon another; and star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 12). Thus the glory of a monk is one thing, that of a canon another, and that of a layman another. Therefore, one who lives as a good layman does well; better is the canon; best of all is the monk.

[Col. 0663]

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Robert, the writer of this letter, seems to me to be none other than Rupert, abbot of Deutz, who pursued the same argument elsewhere as well (in the work entitled *The Debate of a Monk and a Cleric*, above [Col. 0664D]).]

## LETTER OF ABBOT ROBERT TO LIEZELIN, A CANON, ON THE GROUNDS BY WHICH THE ORDER OF MONKS EXCELS THE ORDER OF CLERICS

(Edited by Dom Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 285, from the manuscript of Mont-Royal.)

[Col. 0663B] ROBERT, least among monks, to LIEZELIN, a canon by profession and merit, most beloved brother in flesh and spirit: may you rejoice in the certainty of hope in these words spoken to us, “For we shall go into the house of the Lord.”

If now, dearest brother, your feet stand in the courts of Jerusalem; if, I say, as I believe, hope, and trust, your thoughts stand firmly fixed in the expanse of the heavenly Jerusalem, so that you can say, “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), I rejoice and give thanks. I pray also that, while that Jerusalem is being built as a city from living and chosen stones, I too may deserve not to be a rejected stone, but that in it there may be participation with you *in idipsum*—that is, in stable, unchangeable, everlasting being.

For that sword which the Lord came to cast upon earth, to divide a man from his father, a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law, has not separated you from me. Rather, by the grace of God, in the same will and the same purpose we say: “Let us run, let us run, for we shall go into the house of the Lord.” For neither of us strives to call the other back or delay him from that Jerusalem, to which the tribes ascend, the tribes of the Lord—namely, those having the whole testimony of Israel, that is, bearing witness by faith and deed that they are Israel and worthy to see God.

Indeed, I rejoice, and for this reason bear your bodily absence more lightly, because I know that you, enrolled in the noble tribe of regularly living canons, are making your way to enter the house of the Lord, to give thanks to the name of the Lord. I would even wish that, if you grant that there is a higher order, you might ascend to it also by the degree of advanced humility. I would wish it, I say; but now I do not dare either to wish it or exhort you to it. I shall first state why, after earnestly asking you to receive my words—once reason has been admitted and hostility set aside—so that uninjured charity may preserve untouched brotherhood.

In certain letters of yours which you sent to one of our brethren, in which you complained of Arnulf’s apostasy, you said that your order is greater than the order of monks, and that certain monks also attest this. Whether, as you said, some monks have attested it, I care little. For even if there are some monks who, loving the world, neither know nor love their own order—like wandering or falling stars—the moon, remaining fixed in its order, that is, holy Church, says: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, that I may know what is lacking to me” (Ps. 38:5)—understand: what is lacking for me to reach that end, namely perfection.

Those who are of this sort, supported by the authority of divine Scripture and the holy canons, oppose your assertions for three reasons.

The order of monks is higher than your order because no degree of your order is lacking to the monastic order. For, together with the ecclesiastical orders which both we and you exercise, the monk also has a consecration proper to himself, which, by the authority of the holy Fathers and sacred canons, is a second baptism and is conformed to the Lord’s death of three days.

Since, therefore, we have more than once heard certain of your party say, “We are first; we proceed according to the order of Saint Peter,” in the manner of those who said, “I indeed am of Paul; I, however, of Apollos; and I of Cephas” (1 Cor. 1:12), we also add—and shall prove it reasonably—“But we are of Christ.” In this matter, we dare—speaking in folly, as the less wise say—to say that we are more.

Yet every charge of folly is removed when the case is proved: for the question concerns not the merits of private life, but public order; not what sort of persons you or I may be in this or that order, but which order, when legitimately observed, crowns or rewards more richly its worker who has labored more greatly.

I say, then: is not the stricter order also the higher? Let us consider the construction of Noah’s ark, which at its lower level was three hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide [Col. 0665B], and, rising to thirty cubits in height, narrows to a single cubit. It plainly bears the figure of the human body, whose height is tenfold and whose breadth sixfold; and thus it prefigures Christ’s body, which likewise received a window in its side—that is, the wound from the soldier’s lance. That ark therefore prefigures the whole Church, which is Christ’s body, and which has chambers because of the distinction among the various orders within the Church. In its lower parts the ark contains animals and four-footed beasts, and in its upper parts human beings; for the Church likewise has, below, the life of those who are carnal, and above, the life of those who are spiritual.

Let us consider, I say, the construction of the ark, which begins with great breadth and, gradually narrowed [Col. 0665C], ends in a single cubit. There, certainly, whatever is narrower is also higher, without any contradiction. Thus indeed in the holy Church: the stricter any order is, the higher it also is. The monastic order, therefore, is stricter than your order, because monks neither eat meat, nor wear linen garments, nor enjoy the soft comfort of bedding; they are more wearied by appointed vigils; and, having embraced a stricter discipline, they vigorously forestall the Lord’s wrath. More readily they have placed their blood under the power of their father’s rod, so that the father may strike his son with the rod as much as he wishes, provided he delivers his soul from death; and in many other ways they are, according to rule, more strictly constrained for Christ’s name than you are. Therefore, according to the similarity set forth above [Col. 0665D], since the monastic order is far stricter than yours, it is also higher. And because, as blessed Job says, “Wisdom is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28:13), this order approaches wisdom all the more closely inasmuch as life in it is less pleasant than in your order.

I shall now come to the second reason. Tell me: are you merely clerics, or canons? That is, you belong to the Lord’s portion, to the portion and ministry of the altar—that is, priests, deacons, and subdeacons. Are not we also adorned with these offices? Certainly we are, and this is a very great part of our crown; its remaining part, however, is the monastic order itself. Thus, formed from both, it is complete and rightly ought to be marked with the same hands and fingers [Col. 0666A] by which the crown of virginity is impressed. It surpasses both orders when they shine only with simple clerical status by as much as the hundredfold fruit exceeds the sixtyfold.

But among us, those monks who have been converted from lay status and have not been advanced by any grade of clerical office to the ministry of the altar, we admit are not superior to a canon; rather, by the authority of the sacred canons, they are equals. For the canons subject a fall committed by such monks to the same judgment or penance to which they decree that a fall by canon-deacons is liable. Pope Pius therefore forbids such men to preach, however great their learning may be, because, not having been ordained by bishops, they are as though not sent by the apostles and do not have the power of binding and loosing—unless they are priests sent by the high priests as by the apostles, that is, [Col. 0666B] ordained.

Accordingly, your order imitates cherubim alone—that is, the fullness of knowledge—because it is the duty of your office to teach the people. But our order, all of us who shine in monastic habit together with the office of the altar, imitates both cherubim and seraphim: cherubim in the office or knowledge of preaching and teaching; seraphim, however—which is interpreted “burning” or “kindling”—in that it consumes former sins as though by a fiery coal.

And lest anyone think that a monk, cleric or layman alike, has too little of the imitation of seraphim, Pope Boniface describes the monk’s habit itself thus, after some preliminary remarks:

> “Monastic priests and canons who proclaim God’s commandments are called angels; but each angelic order, the more closely it contemplates God, is established in proportionately higher dignity [Col. 0666C]. For do not monks, like seraphim, stand veiled with six wings? Two are demonstrated by true assertions in the hood by which the head is covered. What is extended over the arms, we say, are two wings; and that by which the body is covered, two wings. Thus the number of six wings is most certainly made up.”

Therefore we surpass you by a double proportion; and, as someone has said, “Mary is a virgin and John is a virgin, but the greater proportion is in Mary, because she is both mother and virgin.” So we too say: Robert is a cleric and Liezelin is a cleric, but the greater proportion is in Robert, because he is both priest and monk.

But someone says: “Were the apostles monks?” To this I say: by no means. For at that time our Noah—that is, Rest, namely Christ the Lord, who caused us to rest from everlasting labors—was first making the ark for himself with these men, as it were hired craftsmen [Col. 0666D]; and the craftsmen had no leisure, since the chambers had not yet been arranged in which they might be placed upon the couches of monastic contemplation.

How much more beautiful monastic contemplation is than apostolic activity is witnessed by blessed Gregory. Compelled, though a monk, to leave the cloister and undertake the apostolate, he laments in his letters that he has suffered grave loss; and he forbids people to call him Naomi, that is, “beautiful,” but says, “Call me Mara” (Ruth 1:20). Likewise he laments that, though he had loved Rachel, Leah had been substituted for her. By Rachel he undoubtedly signifies monastic contemplation, and by Leah apostolic action.

Nor are we ignorant of the height of apostolic rank [Col. 0667A]. But, as Daniel says, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4). Nor do those depart from the apostolic standard who adorn with gold and precious stones the house built by those wise architects, unless someone is so mad as to suppose that persons coming down from apostolic grades into the monastic profession are going backward, when such persons lose none of what they possessed and add what they did not possess.

We do not despise blessed Augustine the bishop, but we confidently place before him Martin, bishop and monk; and Gregory, pope and monk, still more so. And you, dearest brother, I do not think little of as a priest; but I confidently place myself before you as priest and monk. The matter is not the merits of one’s private life, but the public order and public profession, whose consecration Pope Gregory commends when he says: “A bishop ought to celebrate Mass at the ordination of a presbyter, and an abbot at the consecration of a monk,” and so forth, as far as the Three Hundred and Eighteen Fathers [Col. 0667B].

You should know, most loving brother, that I have said these things with a calm and brotherly spirit. For I know the gentleness and modesty of your mind, and I trust in the Lord that from day to day you advance further in the steps of piety. But there are, have been, and will be persons whom evil jealousy raises up against monks, and whom the sacred canons strongly rebuke. I have not inserted their judgments here, to avoid making this letter too long. Yet perhaps such people know neither the sacred canons nor themselves, so little do they understand what they say or what they affirm concerning [Col. 0667C] (1 Tim. 1:7). They think that the most ancient order of monks began with blessed Benedict; and they fail to see that blessed Martin and Jerome, that lamp of the Eastern Churches, either lived as monks or existed before Saint Benedict, as did innumerable Fathers through whom the whole world flourished before blessed Benedict.

For this purpose was in the hearts of the saints by the Spirit before it was permitted for congregations, whether of monks or clerics, to exist in the Church: while the ungodly persecuted, they went out and dwelt in deserts, imitating John the Baptist or Elijah, until, as impiety gradually declined and religion increased, it became lawful for Churches to be crowned with the diadem of this order. Thus this order then began to be sent forth to the people in apostolic or episcopal office, all the more worthily because, with lips truly cleansed, after the example of Isaiah, by the coal from the fire of the altar, they were worthy to preach the Gospel; for they had been baptized anew with the Holy Spirit and with fire in the burning ardor of their holy profession, by which we imitate the seraphim.

But [Col. 0668A] let it be granted that we follow blessed Benedict: he wrote our Rule. Yet he discreetly softened, with the oil of piety—that is, with the mercy of the Holy Spirit dwelling in him—the Rule of our father Basil and the institutions of the ancient Fathers, which were too rigid for our weakness. Nevertheless, whether blessed Benedict was the founder or the illustrious expounder of this order, who but a senseless person would wish, or be able, to disparage the institutions of so great a man, when blessed Gregory thunders from the city of Rome—indeed, from the height of heaven—that Benedict, the man of God, was filled with the spirit of all the righteous? He who was full of the spirit of all the righteous—was he not also full of the spirit of Peter? Who is proved to imitate Peter better than he who was filled with the spirit of Peter and of all the righteous?

But for those ignorant of these matters, at least this authority ought to have sufficed [Col. 0668B]: that it was lawful, and always will be lawful, for a canon to become a monk. This has been done by innumerable holy men, and by many in whom the Holy Spirit, working prodigies and great signs, certainly could not have erred. And a monk who was formerly a layman may become a cleric by receiving sacred orders, yet without withdrawing from his monastic profession or habit.

For this universal order, like the most capacious bosom of divine mercy, embraces every rank and every sex; it adorns holy priests more splendidly; it reconciles sinners more safely; it marries sacred virgins—that is, nuns—to Christ more splendidly; it receives sinful women into the asylum of mercy in order to rescue them. Who could count how many Ninevites this order has rescued and rescues at the preaching of our Jonah, namely Christ, fleeing the future overthrow of Nineveh—that is, the destruction of the world? The world is full of such Ninevites weeping in sackcloth and ashes: men and women; oxen and cattle—that is, those who formerly lived like animals and did not perceive the things of God; children and calves—that is, those who had been foolish and wanton. They taste nothing, but cry out mightily for three days lest they perish like Sodom: namely, during the three days of their consecration, with covered heads, imitating the Lord’s three-day death. What they had unknowingly signified in baptism by triple immersion, they now knowingly and with instruction repeat in this form.

Therefore, dearest brother, all ought rather to be persuaded, laying aside such [Col. 0668D] jealousy, that each of us in his own order should pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem, and say: “May peace be in the lesser orders, as in your strength; and in the greater, as in your towers.” Farewell.

[CHRONICLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE OF LIÈGE.]

[Col. 0669]

RUPERT’S *CHRONICLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE OF LIÈGE.*

(Edited by W. Wattenbach, Ph.D., in PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 261.)

[NOTICE.]

Rupert [Note: [Col. 0669A] This is the usual spelling; Reiner calls him Robert; a manuscript cited by B. Pez, *Thesaurus* I, p. XXXIX, calls him Ruodpert.]—abbot of Saint Heribert of Deutz, who at the beginning of the twelfth century enriched sacred learning by a great mass of writings—came from the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège, where he had been trained under Abbot Berengar. Since he had been educated there from childhood, as Reiner relates in his *Life* [Note: [Col. 0669A] Book I, *On the Deeds of the Abbots*, or *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*, edited in Pez, *Thesaurus* IV, 3, 20. This book gave rise to the wholly false opinion that Reiner had published the *History of Saint Lawrence*.], “in one little book he set forth the condition of our Church: namely, by whom it was built, and what good things or what evil things it had received from the hand of the Lord, from Evraclus, bishop of the people of Liège, down to Obert.”

Afterward, when he had become a priest, he wrote very much. Recommended by Berengar to Cuno, abbot of Sigeberg, he was finally placed over the monastery of Deutz by Archbishop Frederick [Note: [Col. 0669A] Ralph, *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond*, book XI.], where he died on 4 March 1135 [Note: [Col. 0669A] According to the epitaph preserved in the manuscript of Saint Lawrence; another manuscript says that he died in 1127. See (Martène and Durand), *Voyage littéraire*, p. 187. Adrian, in Martène and Durand, *Collectio* IV, 1083, reports that he became abbot about 1113 and died in 1128. In 1128 he subscribed a charter of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, in Chapeavill. II, p. 8. He himself records the reasons for changing his place in the letter prefixed to his books *On the Trinity*, written to Abbot Cuno in 1117: “Accordingly, I believe it came about through God’s providence . . . that I should come to the knowledge of your charity and faith, and that afterward my father, Berengar, abbot of Saint Lawrence on the Public Hill of Liège, a man venerable in life and memorable in wisdom, when about to depart from this world, should entrust me to your faith as a ward to a guardian. For only the man who has now succeeded him, the faithful and prudent Heribrand—who himself had been the learned master of my childhood—could not protect me so far as that point to which, as you know, hostility toward my name had reached.” Heribrand held office 1115–1130.].

These details concerning the man’s life are sufficient. We do not deal here with his theological works; for the *Life of Heribert*, which he wrote more elegantly after Lantbert, see *Monumenta SS.* IV, 740. But whereas very many manuscripts and not a few editions of those works are found, only traces of the history of Saint Lawrence remained in a later history of that place, written at the end of the fifteenth century by Adrian of Vieux-Bosco, monk of Saint Lawrence. This was published by the two men who had rendered such distinguished service to letters, Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, in *Collectio amplissima* IV, 1034–1164.

The manuscript which they used has perished and is not adequately described in their preface. For they speak of a manuscript of the twelfth century; they say nothing of a continuation; and the older manuscript itself seems defective at its end. Yet Adrian proceeds immediately, and even adds certain notes to the earlier portions already. Therefore Adrian either copied that manuscript or prefixed the ancient exemplar itself to his own volume; I believe the latter more likely.

It contained a work by someone concerning the deeds of the bishops of Liège, divided into five books. The first three books had been erased and had yielded their place to Bernard’s work on the *Song of Songs*. Adrian himself observed in chapter 4 that the matters there narrated concerning the foundation of the monastery of Saint Lawrence had been taken word for word from Rupert’s writings, though some things were abbreviated. But the further material we find there concerning the deeds of the bishops can neither everywhere be separated from Rupert’s work nor lacks value. I have therefore preserved it here, except only what the author copied from Sigebert, repeatedly adding that all these things were done either in the time, or by the counsel and aid, of the bishops of Liège.

I have accordingly indicated these matters only briefly in notes. But the more expansive narratives that report popular tradition I judged worth preserving, whether Rupert or some other person wrote them, since here we have the earliest traces of tales later handed down in a fully developed form, so to speak, by John of Outremeuse. This part of the work ends at chapter 36. Adrian continues and observes on p. 1078 that the foregoing was “for the greater part excerpted” from Rupert’s book.

What Adrian added further is readily recognized. It was taken from Reiner’s *Life of Reginard* and *Book on the Deeds of the Abbots*; from Aegidius of the Golden Valley; from Ralph’s *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond*; and from the charter-book of Saint Lawrence. Omitting these items, I have attempted to restore Rupert’s work, and I do not think that much has been lost to us. We possess a history of the foundation mingled with legends and, after a short account of the monastery’s vicissitudes, a fairly accurate narrative of the persecutions endured through Wolbodon and Obert, down to the restoration of Abbot Berengar in 1095.

In the earlier part he used Anselm’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* and Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, yet in such a way as to alter much in wording and some things in substance. He also had the *Life of Saint Lambert* by Godescalc [Note: [Col. 0670A] Chapter 5.] and the account of Louis the Elder concerning the arrival of Saint Lawrence’s relics [Note: [Col. 0670A] Chapter 35.]; of the latter events he himself was a witness. Still in the same century, the author of the Chronicle of Saint Hubert used Rupert’s work; then, in the thirteenth century, Reiner used it in writing the Lives of Evraclus [Note: [Col. 0670A] Pez, *Thesaurus* IV, 3, 155.], Wolbodon [Note: [Col. 0670A] *Acta SS.* May II, 857; Mabillon, *Acta SS.*, century VI, 1, 176.], and Reginard [Note: [Col. 0670A] Pez, *Thesaurus* IV, 3, 167.]; and Aegidius, monk of the Golden Valley, in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* published by Chapeavillius [Note: [Col. 0670A] Here, however, he used Reiner’s works more; and in the *Deeds of Obert* he used neither our work nor the Chronicle of Saint Hubert much, because, eager for the bishops’ praise, he omitted matters that he found alleged against them by their opponents.].

Both he and perhaps [Col. 0671] Reiner seem to have used our manuscript, since they also received material that must be regarded as interpolated, unless we wish to attribute everything to Rupert. That Reiner used our text, rather than copied from an interpolator, is indicated both by the character of the style and by chapters 17 and 24, which in his work are combined with Anselm’s words. In writing the text I have restored the usage of the age, which the editors had effaced; I have added the division into chapters.

## CHRONICLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671A] **379 1. (ANSELM, ch. 24).** When Baldrick, the first bishop of that name, died (959), Evraclus, provost of the place called Bonn, was raised to the episcopal see. Since in this city of Liège he acquired so great a memorial for himself, I have not wished to pass over in silence what I found written elsewhere concerning him. He was so thoroughly educated in every branch of school learning that no equal to him could possibly be found in his time. Hence he is said to have been so dear to Emperor Otto and Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, that they undertook no business of greater importance unless he was present and their plans were supported by his counsel. He devoted the whole church of Liège—indeed, the entire province, hitherto distinguished by no learning—to study; he established schools, gathered learned clerics from every direction [Col. 0671B], appointed them teachers, and generously supported them at his own expense. He himself also frequently attended them and read the divine page most eloquently to the more advanced [380] pupils. And whenever public business took him farther away, he was not without companions with whom he could discuss the Scriptures during the journey.

**2. (ANSELM, ch. 24.)** At one time, therefore, summoned by the emperor on affairs of the realm, he came to Calabria. While he was there, in the middle of the day, at noon, an eclipse of the sun suddenly occurred; and while all were astonished and, in extreme terror, fell to the ground, fear and trembling came upon everyone (22 December 968). But the bishop alone among them all stood unafraid, since he knew that this had happened through the natural full moon being placed beneath the sun. [Col. 0671C] He approached his men, ordered them to rise, explained what it was, and suddenly the face of the sky returned, as before, to complete brightness.

[Note: [Col. 0671] What followed here was taken from Sigebert, and I judged it should be removed. The person of Evraclus is inserted everywhere, in this manner: “Yet he predicted that some misfortune would soon happen to the king and his men; and this occurred. For a certain man,” etc. Sigebert, year 969—“would tear apart. But by the counsel of this bishop the emperor”—“the king, calmed by the counsel of our bishop”—“might deserve.” Year 964. “That Theoderic”—“island.” Another misfortune also happened to the emperor, in accordance with what Bishop Evraclus had foretold to his men concerning the eclipse of the sun. For while the king himself [took] a part, etc. Sigebert, 969—“for vindication, having received counsel from the aforesaid Bishop Evraclus, the emperor”—“rise up.” Sigebert, 971: “But he, fearing”—“advised his firstborn John”—“commanded.” I have recalled these extraneous matters in order that it may be plain to all how great was this man’s ability, whom the emperor thus held in such high regard in all his counsels. Further, it will have to be related in its proper place how great an error the holy Church was in during his days, though under his care it did no harm at all to his diocese. The event occurred as follows. Sigebert, 963: “Having assembled”—“is irregularly ordained.” Now let us return to the preceding matters.]  

**3.** We shall pass over the many things that might be told concerning the humility and patience of Bishop [Col. 0672A] Evraclus, since he never returned evil for evil or curse for curse to anyone. Although many envied and maligned his holiness—for nothing lacks envy except misery—he never acted in such a way because of an injury received. For once, when citizens of Liège treated him with much insult, forcibly broke into his storeroom, and poured out all his wine, though he could have avenged the grave wrong with the aid of many men, he preferred to forgive them rather than avenge his injury.

**4.** Because [Note: [Col. 0671] In the manuscript Adrian of Vieux-Bosco placed this observation in the margin: “Here begins the account of the foundation of this monastery. Note, however, that everything found here concerning the foundation of this monastery is taken word for word from the writings of Lord Robert; nevertheless, the author abbreviated some of his statements.” Thus Adrian possessed Rupert’s work, now no longer found, and its abridgment. How otherwise could he have made that judgment? I wish he had told us the name of Rupert’s abridger. MART.] in this place [Note: [Col. 0671C] On the Public Hill, to which Evraclus transferred the bishop’s residence, as a diploma in Martène and Durand, *Coll. ampl.* VII, 55 testifies. Though I doubt that the preceding passages were taken from Rupert’s work.] our church, the church of blessed Lawrence the martyr—under whose faithful patronage I, the unworthy man who published this little work, live—began to be built, I judge it useful to write [Col. 0672B] by whose agency this church of Saint Lawrence was constructed [381–382] and has stood to this day, and what good things from the Lord’s hand or what evil things it has received in the winepresses by which God’s Church is always pressed throughout the world.

We ask all who serve God in this place, or shall serve him, to be most watchful against the snares of the enemy. For that great red dragon which, in John’s Apocalypse, because it could not devour the woman who gave birth and her male child, began war with the rest of her seed—for perhaps, because the glorious martyr crushed its head much more powerfully on the day of his contest, it has begun and will always begin war against us, who especially serve him in this place [Col. 0672C]. For from the earliest foundations it long and greatly hindered this place from being built, and when built it always assailed it with great wrath. But by God’s grace and the merits of blessed Lawrence the martyr, whatever stream it may send from its mouth, though only a little [Col. 0673A], the earth will swallow it up, and the woman—that is, the Church—whom it pursues will not be swept away by the stream from its mouth.

**VICTORINUS.** I wish you would explain more plainly and at greater length what is meant by the statement: “The earth helped the woman; the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the stream which the dragon sent out of its mouth” (Rev. 12:16).

**JOHN.** Certainly when the most beautiful Council of Nicaea was called by the zeal of the Christian emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0673] “And” appears to be a deletion.], who ordered bishops and their companions to come to the synod on public asses, mules, and wagon-horses—then, I say, the earth helped the woman, because from nearly the whole earth, from the whole world, eminent men from every people came together [Note: [Col. 0673] Either *conveniebant*, “were coming together,” should be read, or a verb must be supplied; but several things here appear corrupt.]: religious men, renowned men [Col. 0673B], men skilled in disputation and practiced in every art of eloquence, to defend the Church of catholic truth. In that Church, from the face of the serpent—that is, in such a way that she need not fear the serpent—for a time, times, and half a time, that is, three and a half years, during which the Antichrist will harass the world by his persecution. Therefore this period rightly signifies the time during which the Church suffers persecution because it lives devoutly in Christ.

**VICTORINUS.** Now we must return to what you had left aside, since my question has plainly been answered.

**5. JOHN.** After [Note: [Col. 0673D] Chapters 5 and 6 were copied by Aegidius of the Golden Valley in Chapeavill. I, p. 198; Reiner excerpted them in the *Life of Evraclus*, ch. 6.] the aforesaid Bishop Evraclus had built and richly endowed monasteries of Saint Paul and Saint Martin in this city, [Col. 0673C] now an aged man who had earned his rest and was near the end of his life, he flourished anew in order to bring his devotion to blessed Lawrence, or rather, through Lawrence, to God, to whom Lawrence was offered as a pure sacrifice in an odor of sweetness. Therefore, as a worshiper of the Trinity, he laid in this place the foundations of a third monastery in Lawrence’s honor.

The place itself had been infamous, polluted by the hanging of thieves and the slaughter of wicked men. But perhaps it was all the more suitable for this work to so wise a man because it seemed more like that Calvary on which our Lord, the Holy of Holies, was crucified. Antiquity, not without authority, also reports that this was the place where the murderers of Saint Lambert, when returning after committing their crime, divided between themselves their most fitting spoils: namely, by inflicting death upon one another with mutual wounds, and with frenzy offering up both their souls and bodies, owed to the devil whom they had served [Col. 0673D] [Note: [Col. 0673D] See Godescalc, *Life of Lambert*, ch. 13.].

But who but an unwise person [Note: [Col. 0673] Aegidius rightly has *non sapiens*, “not wise.”], considering the site and the opportunity offered, would dread such things [Col. 0674A], when the Lord Jesus, as has already been said, himself both the true Temple and the God of the Temple, hung on the shameful place of Calvary [Note: [Col. 0673] Aegidius has *ita* for *pependeret*, “might hang.”]; and when all of us, once vessels of wrath, have been plundered from the strong man armed by Christ the stronger and made temples of God? Therefore, since according to the law of war the victor may take from the conquered whatever pleases him, here too, where sin abounded so that grace might abound still more, the Church of God was founded and the victor’s standards were planted.

When the work had thus been begun, as soon as the walls had risen a little above the foundation, the memorable bishop, like a bridegroom eager for his promised marriage who betroths a maiden long before she is marriageable, enriched the infant little church with certain estates that we still possess, as with its first dowry. He had not yet dedicated the greater altar, which was Saint Lawrence’s; but meanwhile, beside it [Col. 0674B], he dedicated a lesser one in honor of blessed Sixtus, pope and martyr [Note: [Col. 0673D] On the third day before the Nones of September [3 September]. MART.]. Not long afterward, alas, sorrow covered the joy of this betrothal through the death of the venerable bishop, when the Lord of the vineyard called his laborer to receive the penny of eternal life (27 October 971).

**6.** The church was therefore left unfinished, endowed indeed only slenderly, but, as has been said, unfinished, unadorned, and without the consolation of any children. When the man of God Evraclus, as his bodily sickness grew worse, recognized that his end was near, he ordered a tomb to be made for him in the church of Saint Paul the Apostle. But on the day [Note: [Col. 0673] Aegidius perhaps has *eo die*, “on that day.”] on which he was to die, blessed Paul appeared to him in a vision and declared that it was not his will for anyone, however just and holy, [Col. 0674C] to lie in his church [Note: [Col. 0674D] “The apostle’s command,” says Fisen, book VI of the *History of Liège*, no. 39, “has been observed to this day. There is no tomb in the whole church. The canons are buried in the earth, either in the adjoining sacred porticoes or in the chapels situated on either side of the church.” MART.]. He should therefore order the tomb closed, and Paul himself would open for him the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

After seeing this, he ordered his friends to be called and revealed to them what had been shown him. With their agreement, he ordered himself to be buried in the church of Saint Martin. This was done, to the praise and glory of Christ Jesus. Amen.

**7.** After his death, Nothger, a man of holy memory, succeeded to the episcopate. At the head of this city, as can still be seen, he splendidly fashioned a diadem: that is, he rebuilt from the foundation the church of Saint Lambert together with the episcopal residence; he encircled the city with a wall; and on the island he most devoutly constructed the house of Saint John the Evangelist and Beloved of the Lord, and also that of [Col. 0674D] the Holy Cross. O blessed commonwealth, if modern bishops, in proportion to the money that flows in upon them, showed zeal for such things! But they, according to that saying of the wise man, “Pass on, stranger, and adorn the table” (Ecclus. 29:33), now, while they live, adorn the table because they enlarge the praise of the altar; afterward, however, there will be silence about their life and death, as though concerning a traveler’s passing.

**8.** The venerable priest Nothger took care [Note: [Col. 0675D] Compare Anselm, ch. 25; but here we already have the beginnings of legends that were increasingly embellished as time went on. You will find more already in Aegidius, p. 201. Polain recounts later inventions from John of Outremeuse, *History of the Former Country of Liège*, 1844, 8, 1, 133.] not only for the present, so that peace might exist only in his own days; he was also greatly concerned for the future, lest something grow up under him that would afterward become a snare for them.

Now Caput Mundi, a notable fortress—so named because before Charlemagne the royal seat, which he transferred to Aachen, had been there—he foresaw would harm not merely the present generation but future ones. He captured and destroyed it with extraordinary cunning and exertion. The relics of the saints, which were in three churches built upon the very summit of the hill, he transferred to monasteries recently constructed by him [Col. 0675B]. What great benefit this brought to our city is felt by those now living and will be felt by those to come, since soldiers and robbers used to break forth from that castle, which lay too near Liège, and throw everything into confusion by slaughter and plunder.

[Note: [Col. 0675] I have removed as extraneous what followed here, namely: “By what skill he accomplished it, and how disturbed the commonwealth was, I shall relate. Emperor Otto,” etc. Sigebert, 981–983, 992: “Meanwhile at Reims”—“flourishes.” Year 1001: “Otto”—“1003: does.” “Troubled by so great and such a necessity of the commonwealth, which had been so disturbed, the man of God Nothger began to be anxious lest any evil might arise from the aforesaid fortress, and how he might capture it or bring it under his control.”]

Yet it was so strong and inaccessible that he had no hope of taking it; all human [Note: [Col. 0675] It seems that every aid of prudence or cunning has dropped out.] assistance was altogether unavailable unless help came [from elsewhere]. He therefore summoned the archdeacons and certain persons in whom he had the greatest confidence, disclosed his plan, asked them to follow him armed beneath their cloaks, and urged them to be ready and of stout heart.

It was Thursday before the Lord’s Passover, when penitents are received and the sacred chrism is blessed. The bishop therefore directed those in the aforesaid castle to open it to him, because he wished to celebrate there that day the sacred office of the day [Col. 0675C]. Suspecting nothing on such a day and on such an occasion, they opened the gates and kindly received the pontiff and his company. Once inside, they threw off the cloaks beneath which they had been concealed, drove out and expelled everyone they found there. Thus the bishop, having gained possession of the castle he had so long and ardently desired, destroyed all its fortifications; and from that day onward it could not serve the enemy as either refuge or stronghold.

9. I shall relate also another deed which he performed, by which he provided greatly for his city—indeed, for all of us.

[Note: Whether these matters are by Rupert or another author, they are related, though in expanded form, in Anselm, ch. 26. The narrative was later embellished still further; see Polain, loc. cit.; Mone, *Anzeiger* (1836), p. 314.]

There was in the middle of the city a high and elevated place

[Note: “[having a strong tower]” was added by Adrian of Veteribusco. MART.]

which nature had at that time so fortified that it seemed inaccessible from either side. A certain man, noble and powerful in resources but of wicked and perverse disposition, passed by it and coveted it, because he believed that he would become lord of the city if he gained possession of it and established a fortification upon it. Why say more? Having obtained it from the king by crafty cunning, he approached the bishop and requested that he too should not oppose the place’s having been granted to him by the emperor, saying that he would be the defender of the city and its churches if he established some fortification there.

The bishop, being a man of higher intelligence and prudence, understood the schemes which the other was devising; but, as a good watchman vigilant in the night, he was concerned about the means by which to counter him. He feared danger on either side: if he allowed it to be done, he foresaw the ruin of the entire city; if he opposed what had been granted to the man by the emperor, he feared the offense of so powerful a man, who would harm its external goods. Having therefore taken prudent counsel, he delayed as though occupied, and fixed a more distant day on which he would grant the request. The barbarian withdrew as though already secure.

But the bishop summoned the archdeacon and provost of the greater church, named Robert, explained the matter as he had heard it, and warned and exhorted him to lay the foundations of a church as if without his knowledge, promising himself to supply every necessary thing. Robert willingly and promptly obeyed, for he too had already conceived in his mind the desire to offer something to God, by which, with the righteous, he might deserve to be remembered eternally as a righteous man. He laid the foundations, built the church, and set up an altar in honor of the holy and most victorious Cross.

[Note: Robert was buried there, in the nave of that church, on 10 March; and Fisen, VII.6, observes from the church archive that he was a chorepiscopus. MART.]

Meanwhile, when the day granted him by the bishop arrived, the barbarian returned and recognized that he had been deceived. Gnashing like a beast, he hurled a thousand insults at the holy pontiff. The bishop, however, as though unaware why he was being thus abused, wholly concealed the matter and most patiently asked why he was being subjected to so many insults by him. Inflamed with excessive anger, the other said: “It is manifest that you are of that most wretched race of Alemanni, who have always been faithless and fickle in mind: you cannot depart from your kind. Why, in my absence, did you cause the place granted to me not only by you but also by the king to be built upon? I shall avenge my injury by destruction.”

[Note: Compare Sallust, *Catiline* 31.]

The bishop, asking as though ignorant by whom this had been done, ordered the provost to be summoned. In order to mitigate the madness of the raging barbarian, he sternly rebuked him and harshly demanded before the latter why he had dared do this and by whose order he had undertaken it. Robert, wholly unmoved, replied humbly that he had done it not out of presumption but devotion; that he did not know what had been promised to the man; that a work had been begun in veneration of the holy Cross; and that it lay in that man’s power if it must be destroyed.

The bishop said to him: “If you had built anything else in that place, you should know for certain that it must be destroyed, and that faith must be kept with our duke; for I would rather lose success than lack faith. But since it is not prudent to offend our Redeemer in his Cross, which he sanctified by his precious blood, complete what you have begun.”

Thus the prince’s savage anger was appeased; and the church, as it had been begun, was built and completed, and endowed with many possessions. (ANS., ch. 27.) Another church also was built by the counsel and assistance of his provost Nithard, dedicated under the title of Saint Dionysius the martyr.

[Note: 12 March. MART.]

In it he first installed twenty canons, and later added ten more.

[Note: Once again I have removed the scraps taken from Sigebert, although they are found interpolated in the same fashion in Aegidius, p. 206: 989: “In his time, a drought … occurred. It is also reported that through his prayers the grain supply … entirely.” Bishop Nothger, however, having proclaimed a common fast, repelled the impending danger. 1000: “The lands … feet.” These dangers were annihilated by the prayers of the man of God. 998: “At that time … does.” This custom Bishop Nothger of Christ also transferred to his own diocese and ordained that it should be solemnly observed. 1006: “Moreover, the castle of Valenciennes … Normans.” But because that same king had returned ineffectually from the siege, he summoned the aforesaid Bishop Nothger to his aid and gave [it] over against [them].]

10. Although Nothger had done such great things, he regarded this place rather negligently, as though it were another’s foundation. Yet, when its walls had merely been completed and leveled, he covered its nakedness, exposed to the eyes of all, with a roof.

[Note: Reiner copied this in the *Life of Evraclus*, ch. 6.]

After this he received, together with his companions, a certain Leo, bishop and one of the noblest Greeks, who came to him as a refugee. Leo had been expelled by the Greeks in the Calabrian war which Emperor Otto II waged against them, because they alleged that he had betrayed Calabria to the Romans. Since necessity had turned his compelled exile into a voluntary holy pilgrimage, so that he might attain that true land of promise for which our fathers awaited, Nothger established him and his companions here to remain in a holy place and under a holy rule, living from the church. By living holily he persevered here to the end; and at last, departing to the Lord, he rests in body at this same place of his sojourn, before the altar of Saint Gereon.

[Note: The following epitaph is seen carved upon his tombstone: “Here lies Leo, a Greek bishop who was an exile. In the year 1000.” MART.]

Thus the venerable man Nothger presided over the church of Liège for thirty-six years; at length he died in a good old age and departed, and rests buried in the church of Saint John, beloved of Jesus, to whom he had devoted himself wholly in body and soul (10 April 1008).

11. (ANS., ch. 31.) After his death, Bishop Lord Balderic succeeded him, a man of most noble birth and outstanding in every moral virtue. To summarize all his good works briefly: there was no basilica in his bishopric which he did not assist by some benefit, whether through generous grants of churches or of possessions. He gave to blessed Lambert the allodial estate of Pandnard, his own property, together with one church, from which twenty-four poor people are supported daily by an allowance.

At that time Gerard, bishop of the church of Cambrai, together with his brother Godfrey, built the monastery of Florennes, liberally endowed it with lands and possessions, and entrusted it to Saint Mary and Saint Lambert. Bishop Balderic added two churches to that monastery, so that those serving God there might seem to lack nothing. Together with Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, he dedicated by the due rite of consecration the aforesaid church of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, recently built by his predecessor Nothger. He also consecrated, with the aforesaid archbishop, the church of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle in the suburb, built by a venerable man of life, Godescalc, provost of the greater church; and he performed many other useful works.

[Note: There followed material from Sigebert under 1013: “The castle in the town … kills.” 1015: “Godfrey … gave.” 1010: “The Hungarian people … through the prayers of this bishop and other holy men who flourished in merits at that time, and through Gisle … entrusted.”]

12. [Note: P. *ut praediximus* (“as we have said”), in the same manuscript.]

At that time there flourished the most noble Count Hezelo, who was also called Henry

[Note: Rather, Herman. What follows has the flavor of fable; for, when his son and daughter had died in infancy, he handed Brabant over with his other daughter to Reginar of Mons. Sigebert, *Continuation of Affligem*, under 1005. The *Life of Abbot Richard*, ch. 10, adds a son Gregory, archdeacon of Liège; Hugh of Flavigny adds Godfrey and a daughter Odilia. He dedicated a monastery to Saint Lawrence near Ename, *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, II.45, and an oratory in the monastery of Saint Vedast; *Life of Richard*, ch. 9.]

brother of Duke Gozelo, a man renowned for counsel and wisdom, and—what we should proclaim and remember with especial piety—singularly and uniquely devoted to blessed Lawrence. On what occasion this happened, and by what necessity he entrusted himself and his possessions to blessed Lawrence, I shall not improperly add to this work.

He had two little children of remarkable beauty and grace, whom he loved most tenderly as heirs to a great inheritance and estate. It happened, then, on the most holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, that the count, together with his very devout wife, went early to church, heard the divine office according to custom, and received communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord.

The children rose in the morning and received bread from a household servant, intending to eat. Entering the kitchen and finding no one there—for by chance the cook had gone out—they took the meat which was roasting over the fire, arranged around spits, and which had been prepared as food for their master when he returned; and they ate it. Meanwhile, quarrelling in childish fashion and growing angry with one another, they pierced each other to the heart with the sharp spits; and, alas and woe, they fell dead.

The chief cook returned, found the children lying dead, was horrified, cried out, and collapsed half alive; only with difficulty did he finally recover his senses. He did not know what the wretch should do. Yet, wishing to conceal the matter lest the parents of the dead should suddenly despair at such news and disaster, he hid the little ones who had been carried away and entirely concealed what had occurred.

When the offices had been completed, the count returned with his wife from church and sat down to eat. The countess, as was her custom, ordered the little children to be brought before her. The man who had hidden them answered that they had gone some distance away to play with other children. She believed him and ate; but while eating, inwardly touched by a certain natural and foreboding anguish of heart, she ordered the little ones to be fetched at once, saying that she would not eat until they had come.

The man who wished to disguise and conceal the affair, not knowing what to do, disclosed and showed the matter to the count. Immediately the count rose from the table after it had been cleared, wept over the children, and made blessed Lawrence heir of his possessions. His devotion accomplished this; his counsel is the work of others; gratitude is due to his soul. For, like Nehemiah, that most ardent lover of the Lord’s temple, he interceded with several bishops of this city, one after another, for this place, and did not cease until his own eyes saw his desire fulfilled.

13. First, repeatedly seeking out Lord Balderic in frequent and familiar conversation, he persuaded him now by compassion for the place, now by extolling the merits of blessed Lawrence, to extend the hand of his generosity to this solitude. At length he prevailed. The bishop made the place glad by his coming, approached the altar, made vows, offered estates with churches, and turned his mind to establishing the church in its entirety.

But behold, a certain John, a Lombard by nation, a bishop by rank, and an outstanding painter by art,

[Note: Compare the *Life of Balderic*, ch. 20.]

sent by God, as we believe—because the time for having mercy on this place had not yet come, while merciful Jesus had already resolved to honor his brother blessed James, already decreeing for him a church in which he might be served by his faithful with familiar devotion—approached the bishop in devoted familiarity and thus turned his mind from this decision. For he said that the bishop was not acting wisely enough, because he was building a memorial not his own: the foundation upon which he proposed to build was not his but another’s. And because his predecessor Nothger had established the memorial of Saint John, beloved of the Lord, he himself should now add a church of James, the Lord’s brother, so that their patronages might be joined in proximity as in merits.

When the bishop hesitated because he had already pledged himself to this little place, and wondered how he could take away what he had once given, John added that nothing prevented it: for in this way he would wrong neither God nor men. Not men, indeed, because the place itself had no human guardian to protest on its behalf; and not God, because he had made his vow to Him and would nevertheless fulfill his vows to Him wherever he might be.

Why say more? At last the bishop approved the counsel, withdrew himself and his resources from this place, and founded on the island a monastery of Saint James, the Lord’s brother, who is also called James the Less. There he established an abbot

[Note: Olbert of Gembloux.]

and monks, and a rule of holy religious life, as is still seen to this day; and there he subsequently rests in body.

[Note: In the crypt which he had dedicated in honor of Saint Andrew. His marble tomb may today be seen in the middle of the choir, erected by Abbot Aegidius Lambrecht, of pious memory. MART.]

He was made a participant in the blessings which Joseph, the increasing son, merited there—a son upon whom alone Jacob, though he had twelve sons, poured out his own lineage, that is, the beauty of his own or his father’s likeness.

**SPECIOSUS.** In whom?

**JOHN.** In him, etc.

(The longer dialogue, as having no bearing on the matter, I have omitted.)

14. (ANS., ch. 32.) When, as we have said, Bishop Balderic died (29 July 1018), Wolbodo, a man distinguished by piety and provost of Saint Martin’s at Utrecht, succeeded to the bishopric and fulfilled it by his character. I do not see how I could adequately attain, in words, what is owed him by us. The return of words is meager when his benefactions are to be enumerated. For he is our father and guardian; he is the precious stone of this church of Saint Lawrence; he is the pillar and wall of this house. Nor can there be doubt that this may be said of this house: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains,” since it deserved to be founded upon the venerable body of this holy bishop. But what follows will make these things understood. Let us now continue the sequence.

15. (Ibid., ch. 33.) Emperor Henry loved him with remarkable affection while he was still provost, took him with him, bound him more closely to himself, and retained him in his palace.

[Note: Reiner expanded this in the *Life of Wolbodo*, ch. 5.]

But, as we have said, when the church of Liège had been bereft of its shepherd, the canons came together before the emperor—for at that time a bishop was made not by election but by royal gift—announcing the death of their pontiff and asking for another. Then the emperor gave them the aforesaid Wolbodo, although he resisted long and earnestly, wept most bitterly, and cried out that he was unworthy. The emperor kindly urged them to honor him as a father and to strive to be loved by the man whose favor, they knew, he held at great value with himself. Delighted and greatly rejoicing in so great a bishop—for they were not ignorant of his holiness—they returned to Liège with immense joy. The whole city applauded those who came: the bishop for his holiness, the clergy for their good embassy.

16. (Ibid.) This man of God, Wolbodo, was of such height and bodily stature that, amid the crowd of people devoutly gathered around him, everyone could tell who he was, and he stood out above all others by the height of his shoulders.

[Note: Ibid., ch. 6.]

Yet although he practiced much abstinence according to custom, his countenance nevertheless shone ruddy; indeed, as it is written, “The light of his face, not falling to the ground, shone all the more” (Job 29:24), and he appeared all the more comely. He might be compared with the holy youths to whom that royal food produced loathing. For when more sumptuous foods, as befitted so great a pontiff, were set before him daily, he ordered the poor to be admitted and, serving them most attentively, offered them the delicacies laid out, while he himself was content with bread and water.

He was very compassionate and bore such tender feelings toward the afflicted that, when he had nothing else, he would often give tapestries or other furnishings of the church to the poor, until they were redeemed by his chamberlain. He was likewise so patient in vigils and cold that, while the others slept, he often spent the night in church barefoot. And just as we read of Saint James the Less

[Note: Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, II.23.]

that through many genuflections his sinews had become hardened like those of camels, so his feet had become calloused through frequent bareness and the practice of hardship.

[Note: A word preserved from Anselm’s text; perhaps *solebat* (“he was accustomed”) should be read, with Reiner, in place of *solet* (“he is accustomed”).]

For one of his intimates was accustomed to testify that, while washing his feet, he had seen them scorched by the cold and icy severity of the roads, although Wolbodo had long concealed this with every effort, avoiding the unstable breath of human favor after the example of the Lord. I shall recount one further example of this saint, a great proof of his constancy.

17. (ANS., ch. 34.) The aforesaid Emperor Henry, placing undue trust in certain familiar associates, had become somewhat suspicious of him and was estranged from him by a false suspicion of mind.

[Note: From this chapter and Anselm’s ch. 34, Reiner composed ch. 8 of the *Life of Wolbodo*.]

The bishop wished to appease him, at least by gifts, just as Jacob appeased his brother Esau, and came to his court intending to offer him some money. The emperor was informed that he had arrived with great gifts. A day was appointed upon which he was to present himself before him. But that night he distributed everything among the poor who came to him, wisely choosing thereby to gain the favor of the heavenly King rather than to win human favor; for, as the Psalmist says, “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Psalm 117:9).

The next day he entered before the emperor, now secure and without a gift, though before he had been afraid to enter with gifts. He was asked where was what he had brought. “The envoys of our King and Emperor, God, came upon me,” he said, “and through them I sent everything to him. For I did not hesitate to prefer him to you, nor do I suppose that you would judge yourself to be preferred to him. For you are in his hand, and every kingdom of the world; and he will give it to whomever he wishes.”

The emperor, quickly recalled to reason, restored his favor to him, calling Wolbodo truly holy and himself a sinner and guilty man. He declared that the man who had thus honored the Most High God, disregarding imperial majesty, ought to be honored; that the man who showed himself friend and intimate of God’s kingdom would be of very great power in his own kingdom. Thus human rule is strongest when it counts for less for the sake of God’s kingdom, when it is held cheap in comparison with that kingdom.

“And I earnestly ask,” he said, “that religious concern not abandon this most humane undertaking; for by such nourishment above all my kingdom will be made secure. Not that I fear that your diligence will grow slack under such praise; rather, I hope that your goodwill, if anything can be added to what is full, will prove yet more generous. For it is characteristic of good people to increase good endeavors when they perceive that the favor shown them does not perish.”

Thus the man of God appeased royal magnificence and did not lose the grace of almighty God.

18. Count Arnulf of Ghent, fighting against the Frisians, was defeated and sought safety in flight; but he was overtaken by them and killed, and his attempt was in vain.

[Note: That is, of Ghent. These matters have been enlarged from Sigebert under 1018 and 1019. Reiner copied them in ch. 11, and Aegidius, p. 247.]

His son Theodoric, undertaking to avenge his death, devastated almost all Frisia with fire, sword, and every device of harm (1018). To defeat him, Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia, was sent by the emperor. When battle had been joined, a voice was suddenly heard by all, though no one knew whence: “Flee, flee; seize, seize!” As all at once fled like locusts and many of the enemy were killed here and there, Duke Godfrey himself was captured by the enemy.

For his release the venerable Bishop Wolbodo was sent, because Godfrey was known and dear to him. Like “the rush of a river that makes glad the city of God,” he poured forth words of peace and concord from a good conscience and unfeigned faith, and, as though he possessed some heavenly power, he was wholly revered by all. Why say more? He obtained pardon from the emperor for the raiders, recovered the duke unharmed, and, once all was pacified, the assaults of war ceased (1019).

19. Pope Benedict of Rome, invited by the emperor for certain affairs of the kingdom and Church, came into Gaul. Many bishops came together from every quarter for a synod, and many useful and honorable decrees were enacted there, all of which were supported by the approval of our Wolbodo. For although the emperor was sustained by the great authority and learning of his archbishops, nothing was firm, nothing stable, unless it had been strengthened by Wolbodo’s counsel and holiness. He was pleasing to all, no less to those who had come with the most holy pope than to those who were with the aforesaid king; for he was skilled not only in royal institutions but also perfected in ecclesiastical discipline.

[Note: Compare Aegidius, p. 250.]

He ordained that, on holy Easter Day, on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, and on the day of Pentecost, clerics from every church should assemble at the greater church in solemn procession and sing sweet chants from those solemnities in the middle of the church. Moreover, he adorned the church with many useful practices and honorable customs. For he established that clerics should go in white linen on Sundays and holy days, which is known to be a sign of innocence; but in Advent and from Septuagesima until Easter he instructed them to clothe themselves in black copes, like penitents.

[Note: Reiner ascribes this to Evraclus in his *Life*, ch. 5.]

20. The aforesaid king had inflicted many injuries upon Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, because Heribert had handed over the lance, crown, and other regalia only by judgment of the nobles.

[Note: Compare Sigebert under 1021. But neither there nor in Rupert’s *Life of Heribert* is there any mention of Wolbodo. Reiner, ch. 9, and Aegidius, p. 251, followed our account.]

For a long time there were great hostilities between them; for a long time the entire Church was scandalized, severely afflicted, and shaken by this matter. The man of God Wolbodo was greatly distressed, both because he was most intimate with the king and loved his welfare and honor, and because the archbishop whom the king had offended was his own lord, a holy man who shone also in manifest virtues.

He therefore privately advised the emperor not to prolong his anger further against the Lord’s saint. It was just and pleasing to God, he said, that the man who had injured him without cause should himself first seek his favor with satisfaction. The emperor should remember the Lord’s saying: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2:8). It would be better for him to go beforehand before the face of the Lord, who would severely avenge injuries done to his servants.

Moved by this speech, the emperor came to Cologne and, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, made satisfaction before all to the archbishop (1020). Thus the faction of wicked men, which had grown up on this occasion and was oppressing the Church, was dissolved.

21. (ANS., ch. 34.) Meanwhile the priest of the Lord was afflicted, long before the day of his death, with a most severe illness of the stomach, so that, if he had perhaps incurred any sins, the prolonged illness might heal them; for “the Lord chastens every son whom he receives.”

When, at the Paschal solemnity, he had celebrated the sacraments of the Mass according to custom, he felt himself so overcome by weakness that he did not doubt his end was close at hand (2 April 1021, ch. 35). The matter could no longer be hidden and uncertain, because he felt the failure of his whole body. Therefore he ordered straw and coarse haircloth to be prepared for him. Sprinkling these with ashes, the truly blessed old man laid himself down upon them; and behold, he saw the devil standing behind him.

“Why do you stand here,” he said, “O enemy of truth? Depart, depart, bloody beast! The Lord is my helper; therefore I have not been confounded. There is no danger for those who hope in him. Believe me: you will not prevail against me; you will find nothing deadly in me. For although I have sinned, I have anticipated the face of the Lord in confession. He will receive me; against you he is my guardian and most mighty warrior.”

As he said this, the enemy departed.

22. But as Wolbodo lay sick in this manner, blessed Lawrence appeared to him and spoke familiarly: “On Thursday you will be with me.”

[Note: Compare Reiner, ch. 12, who used our account.]

O thrice and four times blessed lily, which deserved to be planted with such a rose in the garden of the saints! It is not itself a rose, because it is not reddened with the blood of martyrdom; but through the nearness of the rose it is more pleasing in its confession and beauty.

Having received the grace of so great a promise, he joyfully announced it to the clergy and leading men of the church. They rejoiced with him and at the same time mourned, because it was fitting to rejoice and fitting to weep over the departure of so great a man. He himself prepared his soul in longing for that day.

As he lay for a long time in ashes and haircloth, tormented by grievous pain, he summoned John, the archdeacon and later provost, and said: “My dearest son, do not keep anyone from entering here; let all enter, that they may see wretched Wolbodo, see one who will soon be worm and ashes. Let the flock look upon its shepherd; let it remember that final hour in which it shall see its pontiff failing in his last struggle. At least let my punishment be its remembrance of the last day. Example accomplishes this; speech itself does not. It is greater to teach by example than by voice.”

23. Meanwhile he summoned Poppo, abbot of Saint Remaclus, and entrusted to him the care of governing this monastery.

[Note: Reiner copied this in chs. 12–13.]

But when the desired Thursday came, the fulfillment of his desire did not gladden one who awaited dissolution and to be with Christ. Looking sadly into his own heart, he discovered fault in himself: namely, that he had too joyfully revealed a vision of such condescension to worthy and unworthy persons alike. He summoned Wieland, his intimate and devout cleric, and bound him by the authority of the divine name:

“I see,” he said, “what the justice of the times, what the goodness of our cause, what your care, if I am so dear to your heart, can accomplish. For I have lost my crown unless gracious Jesus has mercy on me. He was to come on Thursday, and he did not come, because I believe that I provoked him by carelessly disclosing his vision to everyone. Therefore make me suffer blows for what I have done wrong, so that I may deserve pardon for this sin.”

Saying this, and being bound by the cleric, the pious penitent subjected his body, weakened by illness, to lashes.

Then on Thursday of the following week the gracious Lord Jesus came. As Wolbodo lay in his final agony, he ordered an image of him to be brought to him; he received it devoutly, clasped it for a long time in the kisses of his mouth, moistened it with tears, and wiped it with his hair, following the pious example of that sinful woman of whom the Lord said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, what she has done shall be told in memory of her” (Matthew 26:13).

And while he was wholly intent upon these things, as the Lord called him amid those sweetest kisses, he did not merely yield up but thrust forth that noble spirit, which despised all power (21 April 1021). Thus his holy soul was received into the joy of its Lord, and his holy body, worthy of all veneration, was honorably buried in this church of Saint Lawrence.

Abbot Poppo would have faithfully carried out the care committed to him for this little church; but Satan, who, as has been said, always stood opposed to this place, found how and through whom he might oppose it.

24. For when Durandus became bishop, he did not follow his predecessor or the others who had planted vineyards—that is, churches—through their devotion; rather, on the contrary, he took the things which his holy predecessor Wolbodo had offered to blessed Lawrence, gave some of them to soldiers, and retained some for the table of the bishopric.

[Note: From this chapter and Anselm’s ch. 36, Reiner composed ch. 16.]

Because no persons had yet been appointed to serve God in this place as soldiers, he considered it a small matter to take, without anyone opposing him, what had been prepared before the service began. He did not remember the mercies of the Lord, who had raised him from the poor nest in which he had been born and reared, all the way to the highest ranks of nobles, so that He made him lord and bishop of his own lords.

I say that he did not remember the kindness shown to him by the venerable Bishop Wolbodo. When the emperor sought a cleric learned in letters, Wolbodo had passed over others and commended this poor man, asking the emperor also to set his eyes upon him. The emperor had considered the bishop’s recommendation worthy of such favor that he made him bishop of this city and, as has been said, lord of his own lords. Therefore a terrible vision appeared to him once and again because of this.

25. The vision was of this kind: he saw the same venerable bishop standing against him and looking at him with a stern countenance, demanding back the alms which he had himself taken away, though it had been offered by Durandus to God and to His martyr.

[Note: Reiner, *Life of Wolbodo*, ch. 17.]

When Durandus disclosed this, somewhat troubled, to his associates, they said—especially those to whom he had distributed the plunder—that he ought not to heed dreams. They said that he was a wise man; that many cares give rise to dreams; and that he saw such things in sleep because while awake he pondered similar matters. By these and similar words the tongue of flatterers easily licked every fear out of his heart.

But behold: appearing a third time, the holy and more powerful bishop Wolbodo came with the rod of wrath, a harsh messenger sent against him. Threatening terribly, he said that Durandus could not live much longer: the axe was already laid to the roots of the tree, because he had refused to turn evil fruit into good. Amid such words he struck him down most grievously, and immediately an illness foretelling death seized him.

Waking, he caused his household to be disturbed by his cry. He summoned the archdeacons and the leading men of the city, and, recounting what he had seen, said: “Behold, I am dying. Cast me upon the mercy of my lord Saint Wolbodo. Bury me opposite him, outside the church of blessed Lawrence, beyond the wall.”

And he gave to Saint Lawrence the estate at Wasegga, which he had recently bought from Robert the archdeacon, and promised the sole remaining sum, four marks of gold—from which an excellent chalice was later made. He promised that, if time were granted him, he would restore in full all that he had taken. But he died before he was granted that time, and was buried there outside the church as he had requested (January 1025). There he lay exposed and without a roof until the new church was founded; then, when the building had been enlarged, he was enclosed by its wall and admitted beneath its roof. Abbot Stephen, in reverence for the bishopric, placed over him the tomb which is still seen today.

### 26

This is Abbot Stephen, the early-rising and first worker in this vineyard which God willed to be planted here [Col. 0686B]. For thirty-three years and two months—namely, a long day, because of his hope for the denarius—he completed his labor in this work. Yet even before he had been called to this task, indeed before he had undertaken the holy purpose of monastic life, he did not pursue idleness abroad; wherever he was, he always labored in the Lord’s vineyard.

For, while he was a canon of Saint-Denis, he pleased holy Bishop Wolbodo, still living, at their very first meeting. When Wolbodo had carefully asked his brethren concerning Stephen’s character and had learned praiseworthy things, Stephen became his familiar companion and was dearer to him than the rest. This happened on the day when Wolbodo, after dedicating the church of the aforesaid martyr, also gladdened the brethren with a meal; Stephen served as cellarer.

He was therefore invited—God so disposing, as we believe—that he who had once pleased Wolbodo while the latter lived might remain forever in the fellowship of him now dead. But at the beginning he had the pains of a woman in labor, because the bishop [Note: [Col. 0686D] Reginard. Reiner used what follows in the *Life of Reginard*, chapter 3.] utterly neglected the place and because Stephen, together with those who had come with him, namely six brethren, lacked necessities.

Therefore, when the humble servant of Christ saw himself as an exile and destitute man, and for the sake of this place wept and prayed throughout the nights around the tomb of the holy bishop, one night, after abundant tears, as he sat with his head bowed into his hands and fell asleep for a little while, divine grace consoled him there in the following manner.

He saw standing beside him a handsome and radiant young man, who declared that he had been sent by the pious Father Wolbodo. Consoling him, he said:

“You indeed now have sorrow [Col. 0686D], but soon this sorrow of yours will be turned into joy. For Saint Lawrence and Saint Wolbodo have jointly undertaken this place before God, and its foundations are upon those holy mountains. And so long as seekers of God’s kingdom are here, all things necessary for the body shall be added to them. And this shall be a sign to you. Soon the bishop, by the Spirit of God’s breathing, will turn his mind to this place; escaping from the great danger in which he now is, he will here fix the anchor of his hope.
