Behold: that brother whom today you are sending [Col. 0687A] to borrow something for the purchase of clothing, when he arrives at the market where wares are sold, will find a man prepared by Saint Wolbodo, who will freely give him as much as is needed.”

On receiving these words, Stephen awoke and immediately ordered that Brother Renuard, whom he had instructed to go to the market at Visé and who had already gone out and was already on his way, be called back at once. The vision was explained; and, while all rejoiced, he ordered the same brother to depart. From its outcome he learned with firmer confidence what he ought to hope concerning the other promises of the oracle.

For when the brother stood in the market and was asked by a man unknown to him what he sought, he replied that he had been sent by Saint Wolbodo to bring the brethren some clothing and that he had no money. The man most cheerfully gave him sixty solidi of approved coinage, which he received in great joy.

### 27

[Col. 0687B] Meanwhile, a certain caretaker of our church, a poor and lowly man, but perhaps great in merits before God, reported that through nightly visions he heard and saw certain marvelous things. Going through the city on feast days with rustic simplicity and with a certain freedom belonging to true poor people, he openly proclaimed before all that Saint Lawrence and Saint Wolbodo had a common dwelling on Public Mount; that throughout the nights they measured their habitation; and that, because it seemed too small to them, they had agreed that the old building ought to be demolished and a new one erected.

Showing its dimensions to many, he said: “Thus far in length, so far in breadth, and so much in height they themselves stretched their lines.” Everyone considered him foolish and close to madness until the event proved all his words to be true.

[Note: [Col. 0687] Here ends the fourth book. The fifth begins. These words in the manuscript are foreign to Rupert’s work.]

### 28

[Col. 0687C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1025, Reginard became bishop after Durand.

He [Note: [Col. 0687D] Reiner relates the same in chapters 1–2.] did not enter through the door—we must, for God’s glory, openly proclaim the sin of one who repents, as David’s adultery and homicide, Peter’s denial, and Mary’s seven demons. He, I say, did not enter through the door, but climbed into the sheepfold by another way. For, having been designated for the bishopric of Verdun, he instead coveted the church of Liège, which was vacant at the same time after the death of Bishop Durand. Approaching Conrad, then emperor, he obtained with money what he desired.

When he had acquired this bishopric, Abbot Poppo released himself from the care of this place, which he had received from holy Father Wolbodo, since he had already begun to despair of it, and restored it into the hand of the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0687D]. Then Count Hezelo earnestly urged the bishop to appoint an abbot over the place, saying that at Verdun, at Saint-Viton [Note: [Col. 0687D] At Saint-Viton; cf. *Life of Abbot Richard*, chapter 12.], he knew a monk of proven life, named Stephen, formerly a canon of this city. The bishop promised that, if Stephen could be brought, he would do so [Col. 0688A]. Upon hearing this, the same count quickly took pains to have him present.

### 29

(SIGEBERT, 1034.) At this time, after the death of Frederick, duke of the Mosellans, because he had no male sons to whom the duchy belonged, Duke Gozelo, having obtained from the emperor the duchy of the Mosellans as well, ruled more nobly in Lotharingia.

(SIGEBERT, 1035.) Since the Burgundians [Note: [Col. 0688D] Reiner, chapter 8.] did not cease from their customary insolence against their king, King Rudolph handed over the kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Conrad. The kings of his line had held it from the time of Emperor Arnulf for more than 130 years; thus Burgundy was again reduced to a province.

(SIGEBERT, 1036.) Odo of Champagne, demanding from Emperor Conrad, his nephew, the kingdom of his uncle King Rudolph, requested that he be allowed to rule Burgundy under him [Col. 0688B]. When the king refused him, Odo made war against him, invaded Lotharingia, attacked castles, besieged the city of the Leuci, called Toul, and restrained his fury in no respect.

(SIGEBERT, 1048.) At that time the bishop of that same city was Lord Bruno, who later became pope of the Roman Church and was called Leo IX. He was of such holiness that, as he was traveling to Rome to assume the apostolic see, he heard angels singing: “Thus says the Lord: I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction.”

(SIGEBERT, 1037.) When he, now pope, encountered a poor leper before the doors, he carefully tended him and placed him in his own bed. When the door was opened and he could not find him, he marvelled that he had received Christ in the poor man [Col. 0688C].

This Bruno, therefore, as we have said, while his city was besieged by that tyrant, prayed more earnestly to God that He would send him the help of His mercy as quickly as possible. Odo nevertheless continued his violence and besieged and captured the castle of Bar.

Troubled by so critical a danger, Duke Gozelo came to Liège and urgently begged and entreated Lord Bishop Reginard to help not only him, but all Lotharingia—indeed, the whole empire. For, he said, should the aforesaid Odo prevail, the empire would be marked with everlasting disgrace. All the French and all Burgundy had conspired with him and were devising nothing but an invasion of the Roman realm.

“Your diligence, tested by experience,” he said, “promises us release from this anxiety. Do not delay; if you come, I have sufficient aid. But I hesitate to yield to the words of your praise, lest I seem too close to one who flatters; although the contest of a familiar duty is sweet. When resources fail, there is no point in indulging words. The matter itself sufficiently stirs your experience.”

After consulting his men, the bishop promised his help. Gozelo was to go ahead, lest Reginard’s absence increase the enemies’ boldness and his own men’s fear and inaction; Reginard would follow quickly when his army was ready [Col. 0688D–0689A].

Delighted by these promises, Gozelo departed swiftly. He knew the bishop’s great strength in such matters, his wisdom—so valuable in the art of war—and the multitude of noble soldiers under his command. He greatly cheered his own men, whom he had left in deep grief and the varied turmoil of anxieties. Yet he did not dare engage the enemy until the bishop came and heartened the army by his presence.

As soon as Reginard arrived, the forces were divided for battle into squadrons and wedges of soldiers, and trumpets sounded on every side. The battle began, and for a long time the uncertain hazard of war consumed the army (15 November 1037). The multitude accompanying the enemy promised them victory; innocence alone protected these men [Col. 0689B]. Pride had armed the former; justice, the latter.

Odo, leader of the enemy, after his left wing had been driven back, turned his soldiers about and directed the entire business of war against the bishop, whose troops he saw and felt were pressing him more than all others. The bishop invoked God’s help in the present danger. With fatherly exhortation he stirred the minds of the noble young men; he urged the old men to remember their former valor and not let their final courage falter. He recalled the noble deeds which one had long ago displayed, and addressing another by name begged him to strike the enemy bravely.

Duke Gozelo rallied his men whom he had recalled from wandering, restored the legions for a renewed assault, and stood firm beside the bishop as he fought bravely. Again sword met sword in a death-dealing storm; “every image of death moved about” (*Aeneid* II.369) [Col. 0689C]. The bishop drove back those attacking from the flank and sent forward chosen reserve legions.

Count Albert of Namur, who was with the bishop, rushed into the densest mass of enemies through excessive zeal to crush the foe. From every direction he was overwhelmed with missiles; but, believing retreat shameful, he did not perish unavenged, having inflicted great losses upon the enemy.

Courage grew amid adversity. For the bishop and the duke, seeing that the count had been killed, rushed upon the enemy with full rein, slew Odo together with all his nobler men, and pierced the rest wherever they scattered. Thereafter the French did not again invade the borders of the Lotharingians. The city of Toul, worn down by a long siege and about to surrender unless divine mercy had intervened, was freed. Bishop Bruno, who was shut up under siege there, gave thanks to God [Col. 0689D] that he had been heard when the raiders were subdued.

Bishop Reginard, having gained a complete victory and been magnificently glorified by all, returned to Liège. For all of his men who had fallen in the campaign, he offered God a sacrifice of praise. Great joy arose for Emperor Conrad and all the leading men of the court. Lord Reginard was praised by all, since he had crushed so great an enemy of the empire and, as it were, removed reproach from Israel.

### 30

[Col. 0690A] Meanwhile, Bishop Reginard had begun to experience through divine action what the Lord says through the prophet: “You shall go even to Babylon, and there you shall be delivered” (Micah 4:10). For he had come to Babylon, that is, to the confusion of a great sin; and there, looked upon by Him who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble—at whose glance Peter wept bitterly—he himself trembled and wept, terrified by the greatness of his danger.

Therefore, in order to be delivered, he began earnestly to seek God with his hands. Feeling that he was bound in his hands, and that unless the knots of the bonds were uncovered he would deserve release [Note: [Col. 0689D] A second negation seems to be lacking.], he went to Rome, to the feet of the prince of the apostles, humbly to disclose to one who had power to loose the iron by which he was bound. Although in mind he had already, following the example of the king of Nineveh, descended from his throne, he nevertheless went [Col. 0690B] with so great a pomp of nobles that it seemed less a pilgrimage than an army. Some traveled with him for honor, others out of devotion to him. He was indeed the more truly penitent because he was less ashamed before a multitude of acquaintances of what he intended to do.

Entering Rome and the church of the prince of the apostles with these men, as soon as he saw Pope Benedict [Note: [Col. 0690D] The ninth; but Reiner calls him John.], he fell with a great groan at his feet before the church and his companions. All were moved; his own men especially were astonished by the spectacle. Tears forestalled speech, and sobbing interrupted the voice of one lamenting rather than speaking.

Thus, like Lazarus shaken at the great voice of the Lord, when the pope questioned him and awaited the cause, he came wholly out, as it were, from the tomb [Col. 0690C]. He confessed the nature of his death and of the bond by which he was fettered: namely, that he had obtained through money the bishopric which he had not deserved through grace. He said that he wished to relinquish what had been so wrongly acquired; he did not doubt that he ought to cut off and cast away his right hand, because it caused him to stumble. For it was better, he said, to enter life deprived of one hand than, powerful with two hands, to suffer powerfully the torments of the hell of fire.

Accordingly, in accordance with his own judgment, and with the pope likewise declaring that this was more fitting, he laid the pastoral staff upon the altar of Saint Peter. Released by the apostolic blessing, he was ordered to depart as a private person. While those with him mourned, he rejoiced as one freed from bonds, snatched from hell [Col. 0690D], and raised from the dead.

### 31

Meanwhile the pope reflected that Reginard should be treated more mercifully. Reginard had not been captured by the pope’s own sword and bow, but had voluntarily revealed his sin. For the risen Lord also recalled Peter by name from apostle to apostleship because he had voluntarily wept.

On the third day, the pope sent for the former bishop of Liège and said to him:

“Since until now you have sat in the temple of God as a trader [Col. 0691A], and, recognizing this, have yourself overthrown your own throne without waiting for the Lord’s scourge, now, in Christ’s name and by the authority of the Apostle Peter, receive the care and governance of the holy church. Remaining in it, bear fruits worthy of repentance. According to your means feed the poor and relieve those failing in need. And, if you are able, build the church of some saint, so that, when you fail, it may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

Having experienced in himself how good it is to anticipate the Lord’s face in confession, he returned to his own country strengthened by the Lord’s blessing. Thus he returned bearing in himself a likeness to David: just as David, after fleeing from the face of his son Absalom, was restored to his kingdom, so Reginard, after fleeing from the face of sin, that evil son [Col. 0691B], deserved to return again to the kingdom of the Church.

### 32

As he returned [Note: [Col. 0691D] Reiner, chapter 5.] and was descending by Public Mount, and already saw the small asylum situated there, Count Hezelo, knowing something of his secret, approached his side and said: “Behold, lord, Saint Lawrence, who, if you deserve it from him, will powerfully help you before Christ.”

At these words the place itself and the name of the holy martyr entered his mind in a wonderful manner. Therefore, after he entered the city, was received with due honor, and had settled in peace, one day at early dawn he went up to pray, visited the place, consoled the humble and very poor Abbot Stephen, and promised everything corresponding to the vision written above [Col. 0691C].

Since winter was already approaching—for it was the second day of November—he then postponed carrying out the plan he had conceived. But when winter was nearly over and the mildness of spring approached, behold, suddenly, at early dawn on the third day of February, the bishop’s officials came up. Going up, they began with the greatest eagerness, great joy, and shouting to tear apart the roof of the church and overthrow its wall. Thus the matter had been deliberated in the bishop’s house only on the previous evening, so that the sudden crash served as the announcement to Abbot Stephen, who was still asleep.

Once the old building had been demolished, the site on which it stood was divided through the middle after foundations had been laid. The foundations of the new church extended from its middle outward toward the west [Col. 0691D]. The remaining eastern part, yielding for the dwelling-place of holy Bishop Wolbodo, received the foundations of a crypt in honor of the Blessed Ever-Virgin Mary.

The bishop’s helpers in this work—indeed, God’s helpers—were Abbot Olbert of Saint James and of Saint Peter of Gembloux [Col. 0692A], a man wholly formed from wisdom and virtues; Huneco, the bishop’s brother; and Meinerus [Note: [Col. 0691] Thus for “Memmerus” in Reiner, in the cited place, and in Reginard’s privilege in Martène and Durand, IV, 1169.], then judge of the city.

### 33

Nor should the following occurrence be passed over [Note: [Col. 0691D] Reiner, chapter 5.]. A certain small tree, commonly called a *salandra* [Note: [Col. 0691D] Reiner writes *salangra*. Aegidius, *salanga*; Stavelot, *sambucus* [elder]; Papebroch, in the *Life of Saint Wolbodo*, thinks it was *salvia* [sage]. MART.], had been left outside the circuit of the foundations. The above-mentioned visionary declared that it would certainly be enclosed within the entire length of the church. The walls had already risen considerably, yet he confidently continued to assert that this would happen. Nor did this confidence disappoint him.

For the bishop’s aforesaid brother came, inspected the work, and began to criticize it, declaring that he greatly disliked the measurements of its length and that his lord could complete much better what he had begun [Col. 0692B]. Saying this, he forcefully and confidently ordered the workmen to extend the walls forty feet in length, asserting that, if the bishop did not approve, he himself would supply the cost of the addition from his own resources. Thus the small tree of which we spoke was enclosed; and the poor man, smiling at those who had mocked him, taunted them as though victorious.

### 34

Thus, although hostile men, like certain Samaritans, had long and greatly impeded this work, it was at last permitted to be done by the Lord’s command and was completed more quickly than anyone had thought possible [Note: [Col. 0692D] Thus Reginard himself speaks in the privileges in Martène and Durand, IV, 1165.].

Then, apostolic authorization having been sought, and John, bishop of Porto, and Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, having come, the church was dedicated in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1034, the second indiction, and the tenth year of Reginard’s episcopate [Col. 0692C], with the greatest joy and honor [Note: [Col. 0691] What followed, from Sigebert under the year 1025—“The aforesaid John, bishop of Porto, when later made pope of Rome, appeared to his brother Stephen, the pope of the same city”—is absent even from Reiner and conflicts with chronological calculation.] (3 November 1031).

### 35

It was sufficiently established that the merits of the holy martyr Lawrence thereafter came to the aid of the whole city [Note: [Col. 0692D] Reiner, *Life of Reginard*, chapter 6]. For in earlier years, while the old basilica stood here neglected, the night of blessed Lawrence’s passion was always expected with terror. The aerial spirits, whom he had conquered, endeavored through the horror of a storm to darken the joy of his victory. For the air thickened into a black cloud, winds battled, rain poured forth, thunder crashed, and frequent darts of fire flashed, so that it was plainly understood that the elements themselves were being afflicted by evil spirits because of their hatred for him [Col. 0692D].

But when due honor began to be offered here to the conqueror of the ancient serpent, all that tempest and opposing spirit fell silent at the Lord’s rebuke. Hence a custom arose in this city: whenever excessive injury from rain or drought, or any other affliction, threatened, clergy and people assembled with litanies to seek the aid of blessed Lawrence [Col. 0693A].

Although he often gave aid, he especially obtained for the earth the joyful brightness of God’s countenance on the day when Godefrid, canon of Saint Lambert, brought the relics of the same holy martyr from the city of Rome, as is written among us [Note: [Col. 0693D] By Louis, author; edited by B. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV.3.3. It occurred 3 June 1056.]. For throughout a whole month the sun had given no benefit of warmth to the growing crops, and excessive rains had almost destroyed every hope of the entire year, both in the fields and in the vineyards. Those seeking mercy from the Lord were not heard, for He had placed a cloud before Himself lest prayer should pass through.

But on that day, after the clergy and people assembled in this church and celebrated Masses for fair weather, as soon as the cry “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) was raised, the clouds were torn apart at that same instant [Col. 0693B], the clear sun shone forth, and thereafter restored the earth with long-lasting and sufficient warmth.

### 36

In this way, as angels rejoice over one sinner doing penance, this place also became a participant in their joy. But he, namely Bishop Reginard, after consoling the place and making its wilderness like delights, wished still to increase its joy and exultation, but was overtaken for us by death far too soon.

Therefore, in dying, he desired and deserved to have burial in that place, where day and night, whenever we enter to entreat the Lord’s face, he continually presents himself to our sight, so that we may remember him. The almsgiving of the great bridge [Note: [Col. 0693D] Reiner, *Life of Reginard*, chapter 8, has the same.] which he constructed over the Meuse at great expense also prays to the Lord for him; so do the 1,200 poor people whom he fed in the time of the great famine: 300 at Liège, 300 at Huy, 300 at Dinant, and 300 at Fosses. He also hired for wages on public works those whom modesty prevented from begging [Note: [Col. 0693] Thus far Rupert’s abridger, writing five hundred years ago. What follows Adrian of Veteribusco collected and copied from Reiner and other ancient writers, as he himself testifies below under the year of Christ 1218. I have removed the following material concerning Reginard’s anniversary, later than Rupert, as well as the enumeration of the church treasury and Reginard’s offerings, which is foreign to Rupert’s style. Chapeaville also published the same from an old manuscript of Saint Lawrence, I, 274.].

### 37

Thus, in the fourteenth year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0693D] Reiner more correctly gives the thirteenth; see Anselm’s *Deeds*, chapter 37, no. 69.], he was withdrawn from the light of temporal life. Under the guidance of blessed Lawrence, ascending from the valley of tears, he entered into the joy of his Lord in the year 1036 of Christ’s incarnation, on the Nones of December (5 December 1057) [392]. His body was honorably laid to rest with the greatest veneration before the high altar in this church which he had built. The following epitaph was carved over his tomb:

> This house bears witness to him; this is all his equipment;  
> Nor was his episcopal dignity less than this witness.  
> Here he is taken up, his lot fulfilled, on the Nones of December.  
> His entrance was equal to his departure, and equal was his return.

[Col. 0694A] In the year of the Lord 1036, Lord Reginard, venerable bishop of Liège, died.

[Note: [Col. 0693] I have removed Everlin’s epitaph, taken from Reiner, chapter 9.]

### 38

After the death of Lord Reginard [Note: [Col. 0694D] See Reiner, chapter 9.], Lord Abbot Stephen, a man distinguished by learning but more distinguished by conduct, showed himself a worthy householder. Like an orphan without a father, abandoned to God alone, sustained by God, he completed the buildings and workshops of the cloister. Cutting down the forests all around, which had endangered every traveler because of ambushes by robbers, he planted vineyards, cultivated newly cleared land, acquired estates, and built structures. With all his strength, insofar as he could do so without damage to spiritual things, he labored at these tasks.

Yet, through Satan’s agency, he endured many adversities of this world. Like a sweet grape from the vineyard of Soreth—that is, “chosen” or “best”—he was frequently pressed in the winepress of tribulations [Col. 0694B]. For Nithard, nephew through a sister of Lord Reginard, keeper of Saint Lambert’s, who succeeded his uncle in the episcopate, retained and usurped all the furnishings, much gold and silver, which Reginard had stored up for Saint Lawrence so that they might be spent in acquiring estates for this church for Reginard’s soul. Nithard did not remember how many good things his pious guardian had done for him.

### 39

After Nithard’s death (August 1041), his successor Bishop Wazo greatly afflicted Lord Abbot Stephen. He wished to infringe certain rights of the surrounding land, which venerable Reginard had assigned to this church free from every exaction.

[Here Wazo was brother of Wenson, abbot of Florennes. [Col. 0694C] “Here first,” etc. I have suppressed Adrian’s excerpts from Anselm.]

### 40

Theoduin succeeded Wazo (1048), the placid star of the church of Liège. With great devotion and equally great exertion, he built at Huy the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0694D] See Reiner, chapter 9; Aegidius III.1.].

[“In which he was also buried,” etc. I have omitted excerpts from Aegidius, chapters 5, 7, 8, and 9.]

But in the thirteenth year of his episcopate (12 January 1060), Lord Abbot Stephen—the first father of all the monks of this church, who served Christ the good ruler faithfully even into old age and decrepitude—was at last, old and full of days, called away from the labors of this life. He passed to the crown corresponding to his name, which is interpreted “crowned” or “standard,” and received the robe of eternal peace and rest [Col. 0694D], after presiding over this church for thirty-three years and two months.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] On the twelfth of January, in the sixty-ninth year of his life; concerning him the necrology has the following: “IV [thus the edition]. On the Ides of January, Lord Stephen, God leading, passed to the crown of his name. He was the first to preside over this Church for thirty-three years, two months, and eleven days. In the year 1656, on the day of the elevation of Saint Wolbodo, his body was found whole and incorrupt, clothed even in an unimpaired monastic habit, his head still venerable with gray hair.” It is pleasing to append his epitaph from the papers of R. P. Caelestinus Lombard:

> You are laid in this tomb, undergoing the law of death,  
> Stephen, first Father; now the pious mother,  
> The heavenly Jerusalem, where true peace and rest are, holds you.  
> For you lived well and cared well for the flocks;  
> Now you receive your rewards and flourish again in everlasting life,  
> That we may be joined to you and, through your prayers, be made worthy.  
> What this stone presses down shall rise when Christ comes.

“He presided 33 years, 2 months, 11 days; he departed in the year of the Lord 1058, on II Ides of January. May he rest in peace. Amen.” MART. But the thirteenth year of Theoduin, in January [Col. 0696D], falls in 1061, or, if we calculate less precisely, in 1060. We find the same year if we count from the foundation of the monastery, which the Annals of Laubach and Liège place in the year 1026. The second day before the Ides of January is also entered in the Stavelot manuscript missal.]

He was buried in the crypt [393], before [Col. 0695A] the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the feet of Bishop Saint Wolbodo, with whom, because of his religious devotion and honorable conduct, he had enjoyed much favor and intimacy.

[Note: [Col. 0695] I consider the final words interpolated from the *Life of Reginard*.]

### 41

Our second abbot, Lambert, succeeded. He too prospered in his time, a man of many kinds of usefulness. He wrote the life and miracles of Heribert, archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0696D] Edited in *Monumenta SS.* IV, 739. Cf. Reiner, *On Distinguished Writers*, I.1.], composed certain musical works concerning him, and possessed a notable talent for writing verse.

But, if small things may be compared with great (cf. Virgil, *Georgics* IV.176), the golden age of the holy order which had existed before him under Lord Abbot Stephen degenerated under him into a silver age. He presided for about ten years and was buried at the right hand of Lord Abbot Stephen (1070).

### 42

[Col. 0695B] As the third shepherd after Lord Abbot Stephen, we received Everard [Note: [Col. 0696D] Cf. Reiner, book, chapter 4.], a monk of the church of Florennes, chosen because of his experience in external affairs. He benefited this church little, since he did not survive even one full year. On the same day on which his predecessor died, though after the year had come round, he too died (1071). Because he was devoted more to external than internal things, under him the state of holy religion degenerated, as it were, into an age of bronze.

He was buried in the crypt, namely at the left hand of Lord Abbot Stephen. After him Wolbodo succeeded, more comparable to iron because of hardness than because of strength [Note: [Col. 0695] I have removed here excerpts from the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond* concerning Adalard II.].

### 43

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1071 [Col. 0695C], Wolbodo assumed the pastoral governance of our church. We judge that he was indeed a prince, but that the Lord did not know him; that is, because of the sins of those dwelling in this place, the Lord permitted him to preside. For he trusted excessively in his glory and nobility because he was a near kinsman and relative of the venerable bishops Saint Wolbodo and Reginard, calling the former his father’s paternal uncle and the latter his mother’s maternal uncle [Note: [Col. 0696D] Aegidius III.11 has the same words. For the rest he used the *Chronicle of Saint-Hubert*, chapters 28–29. Cf. his Preface.].

Exalting himself excessively on this account, he lived very differently from what befitted the monastic profession [Col. 0696A]. In all his bearing he conducted himself more as a prince than as an abbot. Therefore, while those saints were being trampled upon and the goods of the church plundered, it happened that Lord Theoduin departed this life in the year of the Lord 1075 (23 June).

After his death, disagreement arose among the powerful concerning the conduct of the election. Although many wished to become bishop, it befell none of them to become bishop. The people of Liège nevertheless instructed Theoderic, abbot of Saint-Hubert, to report to Emperor Henry, called “the Peaceful,” the election by which they had chosen him [Note: [Col. 0696D] Because of the peace which he made in 1071, six days before the Kalends of April; see Aegidius, chapter 12. But I judge that these words were interpolated later.]. The emperor confirmed the election.

44. Henry, therefore, was consecrated the fifty-fourth bishop of Liège, or Tongeren, by Anno, archbishop of Cologne, who had built the monastery of Siegburg. [Note: [Col. 0696D] Aegidius 34 says the same; whence these statements appear to have been inserted here by Adrian. The Chronicle of St. Hubert, chs. 29 and 36, borrowed part of what follows from this source and recounted it more briefly; other details it added itself.] He was also adjured by him, under witness of the blessing conferred upon him, to use his own words: “By the blessing of your father Anno, I implore you: destroy the pride and insolence of Wolbodo, abbot of St. Lawrence.”

Bishop Henry, however, rebuked Wolbodo himself in a spirit of gentleness; through the intervention of nobles to whom Wolbodo was related, and especially of William, bishop of Maastricht, he deferred action for a time and awaited his amendment. But when the bishop made no progress in this way, and Wolbodo, through pride and indignation, declined to worse conduct, he appointed a day for his public examination (October). The church having been assembled, together with the abbots belonging to this diocese, Wolbodo was ordered, by their counsel and judgment, to undergo exile at Verdun in the monastery of St. Airy. [Col. 0696C]

At first he assented to the judgment of the wise; but, after speaking with his associates, he evaded by public contradiction the execution of what he had previously promised. When the bishop demanded [Note: [Col. 0695] I supplied from the Chronicle of St. Hubert a word omitted in the earlier edition.] that sentence be given upon this disobedience, the whole assembly decreed that he should abide by his own judgment [Note: [Col. 0695] That is, the judgment.] and dispose freely, at his pleasure, of the abbey whose abbot, convicted of crimes, refused to obey him for correction.

Without delay Wolbodo went to Emperor Henry, by whose violence he attempted to defend himself against the bishop. Yet not even the king’s entreaties could induce the bishop to restore him. The bishop declared that he would rather relinquish the episcopate for a time than endure such insolence without fitting satisfaction. Wolbodo therefore went to Rome, seeking refuge at the apostolic see. The pope sent letters to the bishop directing him either to restore Wolbodo or to determine his deposition in the lawful order of judgment.

Having received these commands, the bishop set a day for a general synod (A.D. 1076), so that Wolbodo, wherever he might be, should come and be canonically heard if he had any just complaint. But he did not appear, although, at the bishop’s command, an exceedingly large gathering of abbots, archdeacons, clerics, and laymen had assembled from the whole diocese. The bishop therefore asked the holy assembly, for Christ’s sake and according to Christ, to give him sound counsel. Then the entire assembly deprived Wolbodo of office and advised the bishop to appoint in his place another who was worthy.

The bishop then asked the holy man Theoderic, abbot of St. Hubert, to give to God and to himself a monk from his flock suitable for this task. Theoderic presented to the bishop, to be ordained abbot, the prior of his monastery, named Berengar, a man most proven in religious life. It must not be passed over concerning him that, though he had been poor, the Lord had raised him from the dust; and, what is more worthy of proclamation, having deposed the mighty man from his seat, He exalted the humble in his place.

Thus the Lord then visited His sheep after their long dispersion, when this abbot and shepherd was ordained and undertook their care (17 September). [Col. 0697C] His life matched his name; he was a man mighty in deed and word; God was with him, and he prospered in every undertaking and every counsel. The Lord blessed this house through him and multiplied all the Church’s substance, both in tithes and in lands. Helpers of God, who had renounced the world, also increased around him, seeing that the grace of God was in him. [Then the venerable Robert became a monk.]

Meanwhile, he was sometimes repaid evil for good: some cast against him the reproach addressed to the Savior, “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” and said, “He has supplanted a nobleman in his honor.” Moreover, when King Henry was celebrating Easter at Liège, [Note: [Col. 0697D] In 1080, or 1079, since Berengar thereafter governed prosperously for twelve years.] Wolbodo returned after travelling through Poland and England. On the holy day of Easter itself, during the solemnities of the Masses, he fell prostrate before the king, making complaint and invoking royal authority.

The bishop, avoiding the odium of his action, did not refuse to return with him to judgment, [Col. 0698A] and set him a day on which he should appear to be heard in all his complaints. When Lord Abbot Berengar heard this, he appeared on the appointed day; and because Wolbodo, as was his custom, did not appear, Berengar rose into the midst of the whole gathering. Having set out his case as well as he knew how, he laid aside the pastoral staff and sat, as a private person, under his abbot among those of private rank.

Then all who had assembled renewed their judgment against Wolbodo, adding that he was worthy of no prelate’s office either in this church or in any other within the diocese. But Berengar was entreated by all; and, compelled by the bishop’s authority and reasoning, he took upon his subjected shoulders the burden of the ark of the Lord. He thereafter governed prosperously for twelve years. Wolbodo, however, withdrew with the king and remained with him until Lord Henry’s death. [Col. 0698B]

This bishop gave St. Lawrence the church of Aioncourt and half the estate with all its appurtenances, [Note: [Col. 0697D] Compare the History of St. Peter of Eyncourt, by Adrian of Veteribus, in Martène and Durand, *Collection* IV, 1183, where the charter of donation has been preserved; and these words from the “martyrology of the monastery of St. Lawrence”: “On the second day before the Kalends of June, commemoration of Lord Henry, called the Peaceful, bishop of Liège, who gave—his [possessions], as above.” Nevertheless, I doubt that this passage came from Robert.] and the tithes of the vineyards at Frangeis. [Note: [Col. 0697] I have removed what Adrian inserted here, taken from the cartulary of St. Lawrence, then excerpted from the *Deeds of the Abbots of St. Trond* and from Aegidius concerning Bishop Henry.]

45. At that time there was in the church of Liège a certain canon named Obert, provost of Holy Cross. [Note: [Col. 0698D] From this point compare the Chronicle of St. Hubert, ch. 66 ff.; but it does not appear that its author there used our author.] Having obtained permission to go to Rome, he found the king in Italy and joined him in his court with the other chaplains. There he became an intimate of our Wolbodo; recommended to King Henry both by Wolbodo and by the others, he attained such favor with the king that the latter, when informed of Bishop Henry’s death (A.D. 1091), sent him back to Liège, bestowing on him the gift of the bishopric. [Col. 0698C] But Obert gave his pledge before the king that, on the third day after his entrance, he would expel the venerable Lord Berengar and restore Wolbodo in this church.

Wolbodo therefore, rejoicing, borrowed a large sum from the merchants of that region, which he would repay out of this church. Of it the king received three hundred marks, and Obert received no small share. News of this deed accordingly reached Liège: Wolbodo was coming, bringing much wealth with him. As soon as this report reached the monks’ ears, those in whom the light of prudence dwelt mourned. Others, light of heart, rejoiced out of desire for novelties; and some, to whom discipline had been burdensome, rejoiced from hatred of their present father. In short, the entire city was filled with talk of Wolbodo’s noble birth and riches. Yet he, most needy of all men, had borrowed money which he intended to pay out of the flesh and bones of the monks.

46. Obert accordingly came to Liège with Wolbodo on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0699A] (24 December), but attempted no action before he had been confirmed by episcopal consecration in his see. He was therefore ordained at Cologne on the eve of the Purification of Blessed Mary (1 February 1092); and there the decision was confirmed that the king’s command must be carried out.

When he had returned, he summoned Lord Berengar before all the clergy, people, and almost all the princes. Not by his own judgment, but, as it were, by the king’s judgment, and unwillingly, he declared that Berengar must depart. Yet in that great assembly, although Berengar had many enemies, there was no one bold enough ever to launch even a single attack of speech against him in order to wrest the pastoral staff from him.

But that venerable man, having explained as well as he knew how the diligence he had exercised in pastoral care, passed before them and went through their midst. [Col. 0699B] Nearly all alike, clerics and laymen, denounced this overturning of judgment; and, escorting him with honor, they gave him horses to carry the brothers who had chosen rather to be exiles with their father than to live under a hireling or hear the voice of strangers.

47. Thus the venerable man of God, so necessary to this church, having been expelled, came with his brothers to Theoderic, abbot of St. Hubert. Theoderic received and consoled him kindly, and gave him a priory near the city of Reims [Note: [Col. 0699D] Eberneicourt.], where this great exile remained for three and a half years, highly esteemed by all who knew him and devoted to God.

The shepherd having thus been struck, that unhappy hireling was received with ill-omened songs, [Col. 0699C] the monks chanting the responsory: “God of my lord Abraham, direct my way,” etc. O unhappy day, followed by such great darkness! On the following day there was also received that Lupo of Hesbaye, who had made the church of St. Trond a den of thieves. O truly unhappy times! For armed poverty at once revealed itself when Wolbodo arrived, his debts driving him as fierce hunger enrages a wild beast.

At first he pressed heavily as a harsh exacter upon the poor household of the church, making prey of their resources now by entreaty, now by the hard law of an agreement. Then he gradually pledged the church’s estates and tithes: some he sold and alienated forever; some he emancipated upon condition of an annual payment; others he granted as benefices to outsiders and their heirs. [Col. 0699D] Seeing this, the monks began to curse one another amid quarrels, declaring that Abbot Berengar had foretold all these things; remembering his benefits, they accused their own ingratitude.

The princes of the region, together with Duke Godfrey, also exerted pressure, and had scarcely prevailed upon Obert to summon Lord Berengar back and rescue this house from the hand of so great a robber. But the bishop, having summoned Wolbodo, reproved him publicly for his conduct. Wolbodo, however, taken unawares, obtained a respite only until the next day. He spoke with the senior monks who favored his party and, armed with their defense and with whatever fabricated justification he could devise, returned so that he who was doing harm might continue to do harm. For they themselves trembled with fear where there was no fear: namely, lest, if Lord Abbot Berengar returned, he should turn so great an evil upon them because they had in some fashion caused the disturbance. Therefore, when the powerful were provoked, contempt for the monastery increased, and the monks became contemptible in the eyes of all who feared the Lord. [Col. 0700A]

48. Lord Berengar and those with him, however, were praised and commended by all; all who had spoken against him came to him. Even Gerard, bishop of Maastricht, [Note: [Col. 0700D] Conrad was then bishop of Maastricht.] seeking his favor, honored him with worthy gifts and promised his assistance in raising up this church, as he afterwards did. But although Berengar was beloved by everyone else, he became hateful to Obert alone, because Obert blamed him for the fact that his own famous name was everywhere covered with disgrace.

Meanwhile, by God’s will, affliction gave understanding to hearing; and although with differing intentions, all the monks began together to burn against Wolbodo with the single fire of discord. The whole city heard the crackling of the conflagration, and the bishop himself hastened to extinguish it. This was attempted once, twice, and three times in vain. For the monks began to denounce Wolbodo as a simoniac, reproaching him because, having formerly been deposed, he had now through money been introduced to tyrannize over the goods of the Church. [Col. 0700C]

Then the bishop, who had foolishly betrayed himself by acknowledging that he had possessed a share of that money, rose wholly against the monks. Seeing this, the monks established common supplications by common agreement. Every night they prostrated themselves in the crypt before the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary and at the tomb of the holy bishop Wolbodo. It was made known by heavenly revelations that this was accepted. For someone saw a ship, storm-tossed at sea with monks aboard, brought to shore by Blessed Mary; and he saw the holy bishop Wolbodo offer a sacrifice of praise at the altar of St. Lawrence, while Wolbodo’s pastoral staff, in his hand, burst apart into countless fragments. [Col. 0700D]

49. Bishop Obert, hostile to the monks because they had mentioned simony, on the Wednesday of Passion Week (21 March 1095), could not bend them by any authority or cries to submit to Wolbodo. They had severed themselves from his communion and, encouraging one another, had vowed steadfastness with hearts mutually strengthened. Obert did not even restrain his hands: he violently delivered some of the priors to laymen to be carried away. Since he could not overcome them by these violences, he handed them over to Stephen, abbot of St. James, to be held in exile with him. [Col. 0701A]

Those who remained were scattered at the head of every street. At last they boarded a ship, and some of them reached the bishop of Maastricht. Soon afterwards the bishop ordered them all to leave his territories, because they were disobedient to him. Boarding a ship, they made a long voyage to Abbot Berengar. He kindly received them with the kiss of peace and consoled them. Thus this church remained desolate for three months, its children scattered. [Note: [Col. 0701B] Until 9 August, when Berengar had been an exile for three and a half years. These facts agree well with one another; and in 1096 Berengar, having returned, issued a writing concerning the relics of St. Lawrence deposited in the altar, which Adrian appended here. Therefore Urban II’s letter to Berengar in exile, in Martène, *Collection* I, 553, was given from the Council of Piacenza rather than Clermont. Concerning the siege of Clermont, situated on the Meuse, see the Chronicle of St. Hubert, ch. 78, and Aegidius, ch. 19: “Likewise he acquired at great cost for Blessed Lambert the castle of Clermont.”]

50. At last the Lord stirred up the spirit of Duke Godfrey [of Bouillon] and of the princes of that region, so that they might reasonably exert a certain pressure upon Bishop Obert. For when he requested their help in besieging the castle of Clermont, they answered that it was unsafe to put either their own souls or those of their men in danger for him; and that they feared those dying for him might be damned, since, with their consent, he had destroyed churches and driven God’s servants from their homes. [Col. 0701B]

Then Obert suddenly deposed Wolbodo, whom he had summoned to himself, and kept him in custody. He hoped that he might cunningly repel Abbot Berengar, whom he nevertheless summoned back with his brothers. When recalled, Berengar sent all his brothers ahead of him; and he preserved them, though dispersed, with such vigilance and industry that he lost none of them.

Thus all the brothers who had departed from this place with or after him returned again together on one day, the vigil of Blessed Lawrence, our glorious patron (9 August). [Col. 0702A] Accordingly, beginning with First Vespers of the solemnity of that martyr, they resumed the divine office which had long been interrupted.

Lord Abbot Berengar then came after the brothers and presented himself to the bishop before clergy and people. Though ordered to return to his place, he did not consent until he had required all Wolbodo’s grants to be declared void. This was immediately done, to the great benefit of this church. What had been given away without payment, it recovered without payment, although not without the hatred of many. What had been sold for a price, it redeemed with money sought from every side, through great labor. Berengar subjected himself to the most sweet yoke of Christ and kept his sons with him upon the paths of that narrow way which leads to life, restraining them by both examples and teaching. [Col. 0702B] Under him no opportunity existed for anyone to wander or to stray from the path of holy religion.

For this reason the Lord touched the hearts of many who feared Him, so that they generously extended helping hands to Berengar in redeeming the properties which Wolbodo had disposed of or sold for money. Thus, in a short time, with God’s help, the diligent care of the shepherd restored whatever Wolbodo had wickedly done.

[Col. 0701]

## Letter of the Canon Mengoz to Rupert

He returns Rupert’s books to him, praising them highly.

(Martène, *Anecdota* I, 290.)

[Col. 0701C] To Lord and friend ROBERT, venerable abbot of Deutz, MENGOZ, canon of St. Martin’s, greeting in the Lord.

I have returned your books by the present messenger, as you instructed. Having read them through and reconsidered them several times, I gave thanks to the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift. By His Spirit, an enlightened heart has been able to meditate upon such matters in the sacred Scriptures and to portray the graces of a living style for the instruction both of posterity and of those now living.

For although the same matters may appear to have been treated by others, they are not treated in this or in so fitting a manner, nor with such directness. Since all things are most appropriately referred to the end of the undertaking and purpose assumed, they thereby appear new and wonderful. This is so in the book *On the Victory of the Word of God*, in which the victory of the Word, from the beginning of the world to its consummation, is set forth so magnificently in individual cases and in all things [Col. 0702C] that, although elsewhere I have known the same matters separately and scattered about, here I seem to have been admitted, as it were, to the spectacle of a new contest—an astonished spectator and amazed admirer because of the most fitting arrangement of the subject undertaken.

In the books of yours that I have read so far, I neither wish nor justly can find any fault at all. I find in them so many good things that slight blemishes would not disfigure so beautiful a body. Yet some object that you say angels were made from air; and that the first angel, father of pride and falsehood, was long swollen in mind against God and persuaded the apostate spirits who followed him of the same thing, until at last he was cast by God the Father, through the victory of the Word of God, out of the kingdom of heaven and driven by the Spirit of God from the fellowship of the holy angels. [Col. 0703A]

I refrain from setting forth their reasons and arguments, because when creatures are under discussion, a faithful mind is not disturbed by differing, and sometimes contrary, opinions. Blessed be God that, so far as I have read and been able to understand, you have never departed from the faith by which the righteous person lives. A creature cannot, either for another creature or for itself, so far as it is a creature, be salvation; but God is the salvation and life of all.

It is therefore pernicious to define contrary things about God, [Col. 0704A] or things which are not; but to be ignorant of something concerning creatures, or to hold diverse opinions, is not dangerous. My father, I think so highly of your writings that I wish you may live long, study long, and write long, because your life, your study, and your writing produce great benefit for people now living and for those to come. When it is convenient for you, send me the rest of your little works. Farewell.

## On the Life and Writings of Rupert of Deutz

[Col. 0703]

# Chronological-Historical Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Rupert

*Literary History of France, by Benedictine Religious of the Congregation of Saint-Maur*, vol. XI, p. 422.

### § I. History of His Life

[Col. 0703B]

We do not know Rupert’s native country. [Note: [Col. 0703C] He is consistently called Robert in the Chronicle of St. Trond, which speaks of him with praise. Other writers also call him Robert. This name is the same as Rupert (*Spicilegium*, vol. VII, p. 485).] Although Mathias Agricius Witlichius made some investigations on this subject, he was unable to discover it. Trithemius and Cochlaeus believed that he was German. The education he received from childhood in the monastery of St. Lawrence near Liège persuaded Dom Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0703D] *Annals*, book LXVIII, no. 44, p. 301.] that he was from that city or its territory.

Whatever Rupert’s birthplace may have been, in his very earliest youth he was offered to God in the Benedictine monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège. There he was brought up under Berengar, its abbot, as his master in monastic discipline, and under Heribrand, who later succeeded Berengar, as his master in letters. Since Rupert had by nature little quickness of mind or aptitude for learning, he initially made little progress. But having had recourse to the Mother of uncreated Wisdom, he obtained from her such great facility that no one of his age surpassed him. [Col. 0703C; Note: [Col. 0704C] *Annals*, ibid.; *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 1087, new edition; Martène, *Literary Voyage*, p. 190; Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, p. 520.]

He then applied himself to study with great success. In order to develop a style, he sometimes turned prose into verse and sometimes verse into prose; and he succeeded in forming one better—or less bad—than that of most writers of that century. When he reached a more advanced age, he devoted himself wholly to theological study. Yet he never lost sight of the obligations of his state; rather, he became still more punctual in attending the divine offices and fulfilling all the duties of religious life, far from treating study as a legitimate reason to excuse himself from them. [Note: [Col. 0704C] Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, pt. 3, p. 25.] His ardor for reading the sacred books was so great that it prevented him from resting. From the motion of his lips one could see that, even during sleep, he recalled what he had read from them during the day.

When he had become accomplished in learning and piety, his abbot Berengar wished to have him raised to the priesthood. [Col. 0704B] Rupert’s humility at first prevented this. [Note: [Col. 0704C] Rupert, book 12 on Matthew.] Judging himself unworthy, he gave various reasons to excuse himself from obedience, until, having learned God’s will through a vision, he declared to Berengar—without revealing the cause of his change—that he would no longer resist him and was ready to submit to the yoke Berengar wished to impose. The abbot congratulated him and had him receive priestly ordination.

Dom Mabillon believes that Rupert did not receive it until after the death of the antipope Guibert, which occurred in September 1100, because, besides regarding himself as unworthy, he avoided schismatic bishops and did not wish to receive ordination from their hands.

The sacred character became for Rupert an abundant source of illumination, as he himself testifies. From that time he applied himself to composing works, beginning with his twelve books *On the Divine Offices*. He was working on the eighth in the year 1111, as may be seen from the dedicatory epistle to Cunon, who later became bishop of Regensburg. [Col. 0704C]

Our author’s productions were not exempt from contradiction and criticism. [Note: [Col. 0704C] Rupert, letter to Cunon; Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 562.] “Why,” some said, “so many writings? The works of the holy Fathers are sufficient for us. We cannot even read all that they wrote, much less what these unknown and unauthorized persons write out of their own heads.” Besides these general complaints, which concerned other writers of the century no less than Rupert, particular charges were brought against him. He even had serious disputes with two of the most celebrated men of that time, of which we shall have occasion to speak.

Abbot Berengar, who had a tender affection for Rupert, saw himself near death and feared that Heribrand, his successor, would lack sufficient firmness to defend Rupert from the attacks of his envious opponents. [Note: [Col. 0704D] *Annals*, ibid., vol. V, p. 588.] He therefore commended him to Cunon or Conon, [Col. 0705A] abbot of Siegburg in the diocese of Cologne.

This abbot not only granted protection to Rupert, who, after Berengar’s death in 1113, withdrew to Siegburg; he also procured for him the protection of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and William, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Holy See. These three protectors, considering Rupert’s piety and learning, did not merely honor him with friendship and protect him from the envious persons who still pursued him; they encouraged and even urged him to write, which he did.

He answered his adversaries’ complaints, composed a treatise *On the Will of God*, and wrote other highly important works, of which we shall give an account below. It is enough here to say that the jealousy of certain disciples of Anselm of Laon and William of Champeaux provided the occasion for some of his writings and was properly the origin of their disputes. Excessively zealous supporters of their masters’ reputation, and too humanly attached to them—as happens only too often, and often causes division, as was seen even in the time of the Apostles—they thought it very wrong that a monk who had never left his cloister should dare to think differently from them and take the liberty of attacking the opinion of famous masters. [Col. 0705B] Those masters drew to their schools the most learned men not merely from the extremities of a vast kingdom but even from foreign lands.

Hence came complaints against Rupert, both from the disciples and from the masters themselves, who did not see without pain that their opinion was being contested. Self-love is never wholly extinguished, even in good people. The splendor of outward virtues and the noise of applause often prevent one from noticing it, or from seeing and hearing what occurs in the heart.

Anselm, however pious he may have been, was deeply offended by Rupert because of the treatise *On the Will of God*. He wrote to Heribrand to complain, [Note: [Col. 0705D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXII, nos. 133–134, vol. V, p. 624.] regarding him as Rupert’s abbot, although Rupert was living at St. Lawrence in Liège. When Heribrand received Anselm’s letter, he summoned Rupert to Liège to account for his conduct. This monk set out his views before the dean of the church of Liège and other learned persons, who approved them. Afterwards he composed a new work, *On the Omnipotence of God*, against William of Champeaux and Anselm. [Col. 0705C]

Not content with refuting his adversaries in writing, he also wished to refute them orally in a formal disputation. Having made his decision, he left his monastery, mounted on a donkey—*vili asello residens*, “seated on a humble little ass”—and set out, though still young—*juvenculus*, “a young man”—for a foreign country, to contend with famous masters. They possessed intelligence and eloquence and were held in high esteem [Col. 0705D] for their dignities and offices. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXIII, no. 39, vol. VI, p. 19; Rupert, book I, *Commentary on the Rule of St. Benedict*.]

This resolution was all the bolder in its author because he knew that he must also expect to encounter a large assembly—indeed, as it were, an army of masters and disciples—gathered to hear him and to combat him. Rupert himself later expressed amazement when he remembered this undertaking:

> “It is now a wonder even to myself, this spectacle of my memory: how I alone, seated on a humble little ass, a young man attended by only one boy, set out so far for foreign cities to engage in conflicts against such men. I knew that they possessed eloquence and intellect and great dignity both of office and of teaching; nor would there be lacking—as indeed happened—a gathering of masters and disciples alike, like a not inconsiderable army, assembled to hear me and to refute me.” [Col. 0706A]

Hardly had he arrived at Laon when Anselm, the more famous of the two adversaries whom he had refuted in writing, breathed his last. Seeing Anselm dead, Rupert continued his journey and went to Châlons-sur-Marne to seek the other adversary, William of Champeaux, in order to contend with him. He had a very sharp dispute with William: *cum quo acerbum habui conflictum*, “with whom I had a bitter conflict.”

Dom Mabillon places this event in 1118, but it must necessarily have preceded that year, since Anselm died on 15 July 1117, just as Rupert was entering Laon with the intention of disputing with him. It should be observed that Rupert was not as young when he came into France as the term *juvenculus* might suggest. We have seen that he received priestly ordination about the year 1100; consequently, in 1117 he was no longer a young man. He used this expression because the adversaries whom he went to confront were both much older than he; compared with them, he was in some sense a young man. [Col. 0706B]

The deaths of Anselm and William of Champeaux ended this quarrel, but their disciples did not so quickly forgive Rupert. He still had other adversaries, as may be seen from what he wrote on the Rule of St. Benedict. When discussing his works, we shall see what accusations were brought against him and what was criticized in his writings.

In the year 1119 Rupert left, in obedience, the monastery of Saint-Laurence at Liège in order to return to that of Siegburg, whither Abbot Cuno, his protector, urged him to come back. The church of Liège was then rent by a schism which arose after the death of Otbert [Note: [Col. 0706D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXIII, no. 86, vol. VI, p. 42. Rupert, book I, *On the Rule of St Benedict*.]. Frederick, canonically elected to succeed this prelate, came to [Col. 0706C] Cologne with witnesses to his election and brought Rupert with him. Rupert was retained in that region—that is, not in Cologne itself, but in the abbey of Siegburg, which lies within that diocese. It was then that Rupert became more closely acquainted with Frederick, who was archbishop there. Abbot Cuno, who had mediated this connection, induced Rupert to compose his Commentary on the Apocalypse, which he dedicated to the archbishop.

John Cochlaeus esteemed it so highly that, in a letter to Henry, abbot of Thuin, he did not hesitate to say that it surpassed all works written on this part of Scripture. During his stay at Siegburg, Rupert composed or began several other works before being elected abbot of Thuin. In 1120, and not earlier, he succeeded Macward, who, while at Siegburg—whence he had been taken to occupy the abbatial seat at Thuin—had persuaded Rupert to recast in a better style the Life of St Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.

[Col. 0706D] We shall not dwell further upon Rupert himself, since his writings will give us occasion to discuss him more fully. This learned and pious abbot governed his abbey of Thuin very wisely for fifteen years, and most holily ended his life on 4 March 1135: *vitam sanctissime finivit*, “he ended his life most holily.” At his death he left so great an impression of virtue that no one doubts his sanctity, although he is not honoured with a solemn cult. Bucelin calls him a saint and an outstanding doctor of the Roman Church.

Rupert was buried in the cloister of the abbey of Thuin, where, according to Dom Martène, he died in the odour of sanctity in 1127 [Note: [Col. 0706D] *Bollandists*, under 4 March.]. Martène adds that the place where he rests is now unknown [Col. 0707A] [Note: [Col. 0707D] Molanus, *Natalia Sanctorum Belgii*, 3 March; Bucelin, *Menologium Benedictinum*, 3 March; Martène, *Voyage littéraire*, p. 263.].

Two manuscripts of the abbey at Liège, written in a hand about three hundred years old, state that he died in 1127. This agrees neither with the historians and bibliographers, all or almost all of whom place Rupert’s death in 1135, nor with his epitaph, which Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0707D] Ibid., p. 187.] saw at Liège and was told had been taken from the monastery of Thuin. It reads:

> In the year of the Lord 1135, on the fourth day before the Nones of March [4 March], died the venerable Father and lord Rupert, abbot of this monastery, a man most learned and most devout, as is most plainly evident from the books which he published.

Although, as Dom Martène says, this epitaph is in a recent hand [Note: [Col. 0707D] The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 734, maintain against Dom Mabillon that Rupert was made abbot not in 1120 but in 1117. If that were so, he would have held the abbatial seat for about eighteen years, having died, as they themselves acknowledge, in 1135. Yet the same authors allow him only fifteen years of government.], its authority concerning the year of Rupert’s death, joined to that of nearly all historians who place it in 1135, nevertheless seems preferable to that of the two Liège manuscripts, which, by Martène’s own admission, are no more than three hundred years old.

## § II.—His genuine writings

[Col. 0707B]

In the account we propose to give of Abbot Rupert’s works, we shall follow not the chronological order in which he composed them, but the order they hold in the last edition, published at Paris in 1638. Yet while following that order, we shall take care to establish the date of each work.

The first is his work *On the Trinity and Its Works* (*De Trinitate et ejus operibus*), which the author dedicated to Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, in a letter dated 1117. In it he praises the abbot’s love of learning and zeal for monastic discipline. Having expressed his gratitude for Cuno’s protection against his persecutors, he sets out the plan of his work. He divides it into three parts, concerning everything done from the beginning of the world and everything to be done until its end.

The first part [Col. 0707C] covers the origin of the world until the fall of the first man; the second, from that first man’s fall until the incarnation of the second man, Jesus Christ, Son of God; and the third, from the incarnation until the consummation of the ages—that is, until the general resurrection of the dead, at which point the work concludes. The first period belongs to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit. He calls what was done in the first period the proper work of the Father; what was done in the second, the proper work of the Son; and what was done and was to be done in the third, the proper work of the Holy Spirit. The first part—the proper work of the Father—contains three books; the second, thirty; and the third, nine: forty-two books in all.

Such is the plan and division of Rupert’s work *On the Trinity and Its Works*, as [Col. 0707D] he himself explains it both in his letter to Cuno and in the prologue following it. He observes that although the Trinity, being one God, is inseparable and works indivisibly, nevertheless, because each person has a proper characteristic, one must consider in the perfection of this world the particular operation of each person. The Father’s proper work is creation; the Son’s is redemption; and the Holy Spirit’s is the renewal of the creature.

This is not to say that each person does not cooperate in what another does. When the Father makes all things through the Word, the Holy Spirit cooperates; when the Son—that is, the Father’s Word—comes into the world to save the human race, the Father and the Holy Spirit cooperate. Yet the Word alone, as a person, is incarnate.

Rupert did not write his work against Arians, Socinians, and other declared enemies of the Trinity in order to defend this mystery. Nevertheless, he regards his treatise as a testimony rendered to truth, because all who bear testimony to truth must certainly be crowned by Truth itself: *Testimonium veritati quicunque perhibent, certissime ab ipsa sunt veritate coronandi*—“All who bear testimony to truth must most certainly be crowned by that Truth itself.” He hopes that Truth will receive him among her servants. Although he has not sealed with his blood the testimony he bears to her, he bears it nevertheless in speech and writing. He wishes the same lot for the man who enabled him to continue his work and to put the final [Col. 0708B] hand to it, a task that occupied him for three years.

Rupert had begun it before knowing the abbot of Siegburg [Note: [Col. 0708D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXIII, no. 9.]: *quod ante cognitum incoeperam*, “which I had begun before I knew him.” He had also begun it during the lifetime of Abbot Berengar, who had commended the work to him before his death in 1113. But Rupert had been obliged to interrupt it in order to work on other, more urgent writings, so that he completed it only in 1117.

In the prologue following the letter, he seeks the reason why God did not clearly reveal through Moses the truths disclosed to us through Jesus Christ. He answers that, since the children of Israel could not bear so great a light, those truths had to be presented to them under the coarse text of the letter, which concealed their brilliance. He then repeats what he has already said about the plan of his work and explains why he divided the works of the Trinity, which are in themselves inseparable. [Col. 0708C] Finally, having invoked God’s assistance in an entirely allegorical prayer, he begins the subject.

The first three chapters of Genesis [Note: [Col. 0708D] First part of the writing on the Trinity: the proper work of the Father.], which contain the history of the creation of the world, furnish the matter of the first part of the work on the Trinity and its works. This first part, as already said, concerns the proper work of the Father and is divided into three books: the first has fifty-seven chapters, the second forty, and the third thirty-six.

Rupert comments on this portion of Scripture according to the taste prevailing in that century: that is, as M. Dupin observes [Note: [Col. 0708D] Dupin, *Bibliothèque*, twelfth century, § 2, part, p. 720.], in much the same manner as theology was treated through the principles of dialectic, “adding various subtle questions concerning dogmas and introducing a quantity of commonplaces.” Such was the method of that period. It is approximately the method Rupert followed in his Commentaries on Genesis and [Col. 0708D] in most of those he made on a large portion of the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments.

The work of which we speak is a mixture of literal meaning, mystical meaning, and both dogmatic and philosophical questions; all is treated rather concisely. The author seems to have read ecclesiastical and pagan authors, commentators on Scripture, philosophers, physicians, and even poets. Among the latter he especially esteems Virgil, whom he calls the most excellent author of paganism. He uses expressions [Col. 0709A] from that poet and several others—Horace, Ovid, Lucan, and so forth—without citing them.

Rupert also possessed some knowledge of natural philosophy and even astronomy, as may be seen in what he says about the revolution of the stars, their position, their distance, the situation of the earth, and so on. Yet it is difficult to decide whether what he says rests upon knowledge he himself possessed, or whether he merely copied and adopted what he found in authors older than himself.

He is also seen very frequently citing and interpreting Hebrew and Greek terms (book I, chapter 3), which might lead one to believe that these two languages were not unknown to him. But there is reason to doubt this, when one knows that he appropriates passages from the Fathers, especially St Jerome, without identifying the source from which he drew them (book III, chapter 24). Nevertheless, as regards Greek, it seems certain that he had been taught it, since it is scarcely possible that a writer ignorant of it could speak of it as he does in various places, especially in the thirteenth chapter of the third book on Kings. Be that as it may, one cannot deny that he possessed learning unusually broad and uncommon for his age. He had read Scripture thoroughly and mastered it so completely that, whatever subject he treated, he assembled all texts bearing upon it.

After these general observations, let us enter into some detail. Speaking of the creation of the world (chapter 1), our author rejects the ideas and forms admitted by the wise men of the age—that is, by philosophers. “What model,” he asks, “did the Trinity possess in creating heaven, earth, and their adornments?” The Trinity had no other model than itself, since nothing existed besides God: *profecto cum praeter Deum nihil existeret, sola sibi ut haec tria faceret, exemplar fuit Trinitas*—“Certainly, since nothing existed apart from God, the Trinity alone was its own model for making these three things.”

In the second chapter, he says that the first book of Moses is rightly called Genesis, because along with the generations of heaven and [Col. 0709C] earth it speaks of the twofold generation of Jesus Christ, Son of God, who is God and man together. He interprets Genesis’s first words, *in principio* (“in the beginning”), as referring to the Son of God, and regards them as, in a sense, a name which the Son of God adopted for himself. In this connection he cites the Saviour’s answer to the Jews who asked him who he was: *Principium, qui et loquor vobis*—“The Beginning, the one who speaks to you also.”

God created heaven and earth in this Beginning, because all things were made through him. He is Son because he is born of God; he is Beginning because he is shown to be the first and efficient cause of all creatures: *Principium vero quia creaturarum omnium prima et efficiens causa esse probatur*. Thus Rupert understands the words *in principio creavit Deus coelum et terram* as meaning: “God created through his Son all things visible and invisible.”

What is said in the same place—that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters—must be understood of the Father’s substantial love, proceeding from the Father and the Son and consubstantial with both. Thus, from the beginning of this book, he says (chapter 9), the presence of the Trinity, which creates all things, manifests itself conspicuously.

He approves and follows the opinion of those who believed that, when God said, “Let light be made,” the light made was the angelic nature. Angels, compared with human beings, are spirits (chapter 11); but he maintains that, compared with God, they are corporeal and have bodies formed of that coarse, moist air whose effect is felt when it is stirred by the wind [Note: [Col. 0709D] “Angels, although they are called and are spirits in comparison with us, are nevertheless corporeal in comparison with God. For, as learned and great men also affirm, they have bodies of this coarse and moist air, etc. … Therefore, since it is clear that angels, although their bodies are subtle, nevertheless possess them from their very origin, this is also evident from the fact that they are located in place and, when they wish, appear to human beings.”]. This opinion, he says, is not peculiar to Rupert; it is held by several learned and great men.

Yet, although supported by great men and even by some Fathers, it does not accord best with Scripture, which elsewhere teaches that angels are pure spirits. The separation God made between light and darkness signifies, according to our author (chapter 13), the terrible judgment God executed upon the devil and the rebellious angels, separating them from the good angels. This is what the words “he separated the light from the darkness” signify.

That separation is irrevocable: those who fell cannot rise again, and those who persevered while they were able to fall [Col. 0710B] can no longer sin. All had been created in innocence and could progress in goodness; but, being creatures drawn from nothing, they were also capable of evil. Our author raises various questions on this subject (chapters 14–15), asking why a good and merciful God brought into being creatures whom he foresaw would perish. He calls this an importunate question; indeed, it seems to him so foolish that he sees no reason for proposing it: *sic inepta ut in sensu ejus nulla sit ratio*, “so foolish that there is no rational ground in the thought itself.”

He nevertheless answers it; and, after his answer, he adds, to silence anyone wishing to dispute, the Apostle’s words: “O man, who are you to contend with God? Has not the potter power from the same lump of clay to make one vessel for honourable use and another for base and shameful use?”

After speaking in his first book [Col. 0710C] of the creation of heaven, earth, and all their adornments, Rupert proceeds to the creation of man, whom God deigned to create in his image and likeness (book II, chapters 1–4). The expressions used by Scripture in recounting the creation of man enhance man’s dignity and excellence. God did not say, “Let man be made in our image and likeness,” as he had said, “Let light be made.” Rather, the three persons of the Trinity seem to take counsel and exhort one another, saying, “Let us make man”: *Tres personae quasi mutuo se cohortantur dicendo faciamus*.

The words “Let us make man in our image and likeness” must be understood only of those whom God predestined to life [Note: [Col. 0709D] *Ista dictio faciamus hominem, etc., solos eos amplectitur, quos praedestinavit ad vitam*: “This expression, ‘Let us make man,’ etc., embraces only those whom he predestined to life.”], and not of the reprobate. For, he says again (chapter 5), only the elect are created in God’s image and likeness: *Ad imaginem autem simul et similitudinem Dei soli electi facti, imo et perfecti sunt*—“Only the elect have been made, indeed perfected, in both the image and likeness of God.”

The blessing God bestowed [Col. 0710D] on Adam and Eve after creating them relates especially to the elect (chapter 8). The grace of that blessing represents the purpose of God which St Paul has in view when, after saying, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God,” he immediately adds: “to those who are called according to his purpose to be saints” (Rom. 8:28).

[Note: [Col. 0710D] “The grace of this blessing surely echoes that purpose of God which the Apostle has in view when, having said, ‘We know that all things work together for good to those who love God,’ he immediately added: ‘to those who are called according to the purpose, saints.’ Since that purpose could in no way be turned aside by the intervention of evils, he then proceeds in a beautiful progression and adds below this order: ‘For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son … those whom he predestined, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified’ [Col. 0711D]. This blessing, I say, commends that purpose of God, which, holding before its eyes those belonging only to grace, foreknown and predestined before the ages, blessed them then in those first roots of our race, male and female [Col. 0712D], and will finally glorify them, called and justified, in the fullness of time, etc.”]

By blessing [Col. 0711A] our first parents, God blessed in their first origin those whom he alone had foreseen and predestined before all ages (chapter 7), those whom he had in view—*praedestinatos prae oculis habens*, “having the predestined before his eyes”—and to whom, in the fullness of time, after calling and justifying them, he would one day say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

But what God said to our first parents in blessing them—*replete terram et subjicite eam vobis*, “Fill the earth and subject it to yourselves”—applies to both the elect and the reprobate (chapter 9). Both fill the earth, but there is a great difference concerning the phrase, “subject it to yourselves.” The elect alone, to whom belongs the land of the living, subject to themselves, by the freedom of their spirits, the earth inhabited by their bodies, because, preferring God to all things, they generously despise everything earthly. The reprobate also in some way subject the earth to themselves, cultivating it and mastering it [Col. 0711B] by force of arms; but this subjection does not come from God’s blessing.

He rejects the opinion of those who maintained that humankind would not have begotten children if it had persevered in innocence—as though, he says, sin had been necessary in order that humanity might be able to beget, and as though God could not have made a nature that generated without sin’s assistance.
