Yet, he adds, no lengthy disquisition is necessary to prove the contrary, since God said to them: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” Had man not sinned, he would have begotten only elect persons, who would have been the fruit of the blessing received at the moment of his creation.

Speaking of angels (chapter 15), he says that only after the fall of the rebellious angels were the good angels divided into nine different choirs or orders: Angels, Archangels, Thrones, Dominations, Principalities, Powers, Virtues, Cherubim, and Seraphim. These various orders, into which they were established according to the degree of their merit, are their reward, assured to them forever.

He discusses at length (chapters 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19) the seventh day: how it differs from the other days; why God blessed and sanctified it; and what the rest of that day is. Returning to man, whom God formed from the dust of the earth, he cites (chapter 20) various passages from Isaiah and Jeremiah in which these holy prophets, acknowledging their origin, say to God: “You are our Father; we are but clay” (Isa. 64:8). He then cites St Paul’s words—calling him *ille juris-peritus coelestis Paulus*, “that heavenly expert in the law, Paul”—“Does a vessel of clay say to the one who made it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Rom. 9:20–21).

Therefore, our author continues, when we read that God formed man from the dust of [Col. 0711D] the earth, we should not ask why he formed him thus. Rather, each person should fear for himself lest the vessel God made should break in his hands and he make another as he sees fit. We may, however, humbly inquire and marvel how God, who could have repaired the loss of angels with new angels, created as many as had fallen, and placed them in heaven so that the entire race and nobility of the heavenly homeland might be of one nature, chose instead to create human beings—of a different nature and condition—to replace the angels. We may ask why he did not create them all together, [Col. 0712A] or several of them, but only one, from whom all the others were to derive their origin. God willed it thus; his wisdom prescribed it (chapter 21).

He breathed upon man’s face a breath of life. This breath of life is the human spirit, or rational soul, distinguishing man from animals. This soul is not transmitted by generation; on this point there is no diversity of opinion among Catholics: *Animas non ex traduce fluere omnium orthodoxorum una est sententia*—“That souls do not proceed by propagation is the unanimous opinion of all orthodox believers.”

We shall not speak of what our author says concerning the earthly paradise—its location; the fountain watering it and dividing into four great rivers; the tree of life and of the knowledge of good and evil, so called, he maintains, by irony; God’s prohibition against Adam’s eating the fruit of that tree; the help God gave Adam by forming Eve from one of his ribs; or the close and indissoluble union established between man and woman (chapters 23–30, etc.). [Col. 0712B] But we cannot refrain from reporting the judicious reflections he makes (chapter 40) upon the statement in Genesis that Adam and his wife were naked and were not ashamed.

“It was not dishonour but honour,” he says, “for them to be naked”: *non erat hoc ignominiae, sed honoris quod nudi erant*. “It was not from shamelessness but from security that they did not blush at their nakedness”: *Non erat insipientiae, sed securitatis quod nuditatem suam non erubescebant*.

For could they have received this feeling of shame from their Creator? Could God’s work contain anything indecent or dishonourable of which it ought to be ashamed? Does this shame arise from nature? Does it not arise from concupiscence? Shame, which causes torment, has now become almost like a natural condition; but it does not come from humankind’s original state. It originates in sin.

Why are we ashamed of our [Col. 0712C] nakedness? Because we feel our weakness and the rebellion of the flesh against us. Conscience was then pure; there was no concupiscence of the eyes leading to evil. For the concupiscence of the flesh is the penalty of sin and the punishment of the prior pride of the spirit. Scripture says that God created man upright and righteous (Eccles. 7:30). This testimony is true, Rupert adds, because a most righteous God created man only in uprightness and righteousness.

Human uprightness and righteousness consisted in the spirit’s being superior to and ruling the flesh, while the flesh was subject and obedient to the spirit. The rational spirit of man stood between God and the flesh in order to command the flesh. Since it disturbed and inverted this order by disobeying God, the spirit, formerly superior to the flesh, was justly subjected to the flesh for its disobedience to God, to whom it ought to have been subject.

This is the source of the shame of the face, which springs from the secret of conscience, appears outwardly, and compels one to hide beneath clothing the cause of one’s shame—the penalty of disobedience. This infirmity, or rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, did not then exist. Thus man and woman were naked and were not ashamed, because there was nothing in them to cause shame: *Bene igitur nudus erat uterque et non erubescebant, quia, quod erubescerent, non habebant*—“Rightly, then, each was naked and they were not ashamed, because they had nothing of which to be ashamed.”

This passage, in which the Church’s doctrine concerning the state of our first parents and concupiscence is so firmly established—a doctrine [Col. 0713A] St Augustine defended so vigorously against the Pelagians—seemed to us so important that we believed it necessary to report it in full.

In the third book of the Commentary on Genesis (chapter unspecified), our author speaks of humanity’s temptation, fall, and the judgment God pronounced against it to punish its disobedience. One must not believe that the temptation or sin of man began with Eve’s conversation with the serpent. The external temptation had been preceded by an internal one: the devil had already attacked the human heart by inspiring pride and contempt for God’s commandment. If man had not first been inwardly swollen with pride, he would not have yielded so readily to the external temptation: *Nisi enim intus per superbiam prius tumuisset, foris tentatus tam facile non cederet*—“For unless he had first swelled inwardly through pride, when tempted outwardly he would not have yielded so easily.”

The devil therefore attacked man directly within, and outwardly through the serpent’s agency. This animal [Col. 0713B] was not in the earthly paradise, according to Rupert (chapter 2). Consequently, he maintains that the woman, walking in that garden of delights and perhaps observing what was occurring beyond it, gave the devil an occasion to tempt her under the form of a serpent that had approached that delightful land.

The sentence God pronounced against Eve is more severe than that against Adam because, Rupert says (chapter 21), her sin is three times greater: *quia peccati quantitas in muliere triplo major quam in viro*, “because the measure of sin in the woman is threefold greater than in the man.” He interprets the words: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, between her seed and yours.”

“God,” he says (chapter 19), “promises a great work of his grace: *Profecto magnum gratiae suae opus promittit*. He promises that the woman, who was overcome by the devil’s craft, will one day triumph over the devil by open force. But it is not the woman herself who is to wage this war; it is her seed that will wage and continue it until it gains a complete victory. [Col. 0713C] This is why, after saying, ‘I will put enmity between you and the woman,’ he adds, ‘between your seed and hers’ (Gen. 3:15).

“For of what seed is this said, if not of one alone, Jesus Christ? He alone is the seed of the woman without being the seed of the man. He it is who fought against the ancient serpent and crushed it by the strength of his arm. Which of all of us, born from the union of man and woman, can boast of possessing complete enmity against this seducer? Are we not rather all enemies of God unless reconciled through the one who is solely the woman’s seed? By the effect of his grace we are God’s friends and children; but of ourselves and through our first parents we have been only companions in his rebellion … It is therefore certain that these words contain the promise of him who is the woman’s seed—that is, Jesus Christ—[Col. 0713D] because the sex which was deceived crushed the deceiver’s head, when the blessed Virgin brought forth without sin that new and heavenly man who destroyed sin.”

Moreover, our author says, there is between the woman and her seed, and the species of animal by which she was deceived, an affinity arising less from reason than from natural feeling. The woman always has the power to crush its head, so that if she touches a serpent’s head with the sole of her bare foot, even lightly, she immediately kills it—something neither levers, nor hammers, nor a sword could do so promptly. Rupert says he learned what he relates from the faithful report of persons who had examined the matter with great care. Likewise, a serpent, however small, kills a woman if it bites the sole of her foot. The reader may think what he wishes of this alleged discovery.

[Col. 0714A] To punish man’s pride, God (chapter 24) condemned him to die and to return to the dust from which he had drawn him. Before this sentence, man was already dead with the death of sin, which separates the soul from God; but he did not feel the bitterness of that death, just as we ourselves do not now feel it.

Given over to our passions, deprived of eternal goods, and even on the point of being stripped of temporal goods, we are insensitive enough to live in joy and amusements while seeing so many people die before our eyes every day. What would it be like if we were never to die? How insensitive would we be to the death of the soul and to the Last Judgment to take place at the end of the ages, if, though due to die tomorrow, we give ourselves over to pride today?

Thus God, who is wholly good, rightly condemned man to death in order to make him feel how disastrous the death of the soul is, and to prevent him from living securely and [Col. 0714B] immersed in pleasures until the day of judgment. He did so in order at least to awaken some by fear of an evil that may befall them at any moment. The sentence of death God pronounced upon corrupted man must therefore not be regarded as an effect of his angered justice, but as one of merciful grace (chapter 25): *Igitur non iratae justitiae, sed miserantis est gratiae, quod vitiatum hominem Deus mortalem esse voluit*—“Therefore, that God willed corrupted man to be mortal belongs not to wrathful justice but to merciful grace.”

Even a pagan philosopher, Plotinus, recognized that God gave human beings mortal bodies out of mercy: *tunc pater misericors mortalia illis condebat corpora*—“then the merciful Father fashioned mortal bodies for them.” To keep man humble, he willed the hour and day of death to be uncertain, so that man might always be attentive and on guard, being ignorant of the time when that which he knows must certainly come will arrive, and might live as one who must every day be judged and render an account of his conduct.

[Col. 0714C] In Rupert’s time, some doubted whether Adam had obtained mercy through Jesus Christ, because Scripture does not tell us that he did penance (ch. 31). It is indeed said in the Book of Wisdom that Wisdom preserved him whom God first formed to be the father of the world, when he alone had been created; and that she also drew him out of his sin (Wis. 10:1–2). But this book, our author replies, is not in the canon, and what is cited is drawn from no canonical book. Thus one is at least as free to reject as to admit the words *eduxit illum a delicto suo*—“she drew him out of his sin”—because it is not shown when Adam acknowledged his sin or when he did penance. Therefore, since no good works are seen in the first Adam, and the new Adam is set in opposition to him—for as all die in Adam, so all shall live again in Jesus Christ [Col. 0714D] (1 Cor. 15:22)—many freely deny that he is saved, and no one has defended this sufficiently firmly: *Salvatio ejus et a multis libere negatur, et a nullo satis firmiter defenditur* (“His salvation is freely denied by many, and sufficiently firmly defended by no one”).

Rupert does not seem absolutely to take a side in this controversy, but merely to report the differing opinions. He even observes, lest anyone decide rashly—*ne quis temere definiat*—that ecclesiastical history teaches that the first to maintain that Adam was not saved were the Encratites, heretics whose leader was Tatian. With regard to the passage in the Book of Wisdom favoring Adam’s salvation, it is no longer permissible to take the liberty which was taken in Rupert’s time, of receiving or rejecting it as one judged fit. The Council of Trent removed all doubt on this point by placing this book among those inspired by the Holy Spirit. It is true that in antiquity it [Col. 0715A] was not included in the canon of the Jews; nevertheless, it remains certain that the greater part of the Greek and Latin Fathers always regarded it as a canonical book, and several even believed Solomon to be its author.

Saint Augustine in particular, in refuting the priests of Marseilles, proves to them in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, by tradition and by the constant practice of reading the Book of Wisdom in the public assemblies of the faithful, the veneration and respect that the Church has always had for this divine book.

This holy doctor, replying in his Letter 164 (ch. 3, vol. II, p. 575) to several questions proposed to him by a bishop named Evodius, says that almost the whole Church agrees:

> [Note: [Col. 0715D] *De illo quidem primo homine patre generis humani, quod eum inde solverit, Ecclesia fere tota consentit.* — “Concerning that first man, the father of the human race, that He delivered him from there, almost the whole Church agrees.”]

The first man, the father of humankind, was among those whom Jesus Christ delivered when “he went and preached to the spirits held in prison” (1 Pet. 3:19). This, Saint Augustine adds [Col. 0715B], must not be imagined to be something the Church believes vainly, even if it were not supported by the express authority of Holy Scripture. On this point he cites the words of the Book of Wisdom which establish the Church’s view concerning the salvation of our first parents. “With very good reason,” Saint Augustine says elsewhere,

> [Note: [Col. 0715D] *De pecc. mer.*, bk. II, ch. 34 — *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 34.]

we believe that the first two human beings, after their sin, lived a holy life amid the labors and miseries that overwhelmed them, and were delivered from eternal punishments by the power of the blood of Jesus Christ.

When God had expelled man from the earthly Paradise (ch. 32), he placed cherubim at its entrance, flashing a fiery sword to guard the way to the tree of life. Rupert makes various reflections upon this fiery sword and takes occasion to speak of the fire which must purify human beings from their sins before they enter heaven:

> [Note: [Col. 0716D] *Quique nostrum pro diversitate peccatorum, alii citius, alii tardius purgati, paradisi felicitatem ingredientur.* — “And each one of us, purified more quickly or more slowly according to the diversity of sins, will enter the blessedness of Paradise.”]

But these cherubim and this fiery sword, set at the entrance to the [Col. 0715C] garden, signify especially how difficult it is for the children of blessing, born in this exile, to return to the place to which God’s grace recalls them.

After speaking in the first part of the treatise *On the Trinity* (ch. 34) of the works proper to the Father—the creation of man, his fall, and the decree of his condemnation—our author proposes in the second part to speak of the works proper to the Son. In the first part, he says, he has done no more than creep; but in this one he will place before his readers objects more pleasing and consoling.

There will be seen how the Word, through whom all things were made, made himself known little by little, throughout six different ages, to man expelled from Paradise and held captive: drawing near to his creature until he took flesh like ours, which he offered in sacrifice to his Father for the salvation of the world. Through this sacrifice he entered into [Col. 0715D] his rest, and brought into it the man whom he redeemed. Rupert thus divides the six ages during which the Word manifested himself to human beings through differing increases of grace.

The first age (ch. 36) extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth from the Babylonian captivity to the Incarnation, which constitutes the sixth age. In the first, Jesus Christ appears only in figure; in the second, he shows himself by actions and discourses familiar to human beings, with whom he is willing to make covenants; in the third, [Col. 0716A] the birth is promised of him in whom we are to be blessed; in the fourth, he is King; in the fifth, it is announced that he will be Priest; finally, in the sixth, he himself comes by becoming incarnate.

These six ages correspond to the six days mentioned above, but with this difference: during the six days new natures were created, whereas during the six ages it is a matter of restoring the human nature that was corrupted. Thus the works of the six days belong to the person of the Father, while these properly belong to the person of the Son. And, since the Son is in all things like the Father, Rupert proposes to demonstrate that the spirit of fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom shines forth in the works of the Son just as in those of the Father—that is, in the six ages as in the six days. These are the characteristics he assigns to each age.

Such is the plan of the second part of the treatise [Col. 0716B] *On the Trinity*, which contains thirty books: six commentaries on the remainder of Genesis, and the others on a large part of Scripture—namely, four on Exodus; two on Leviticus; two on Numbers; two on Deuteronomy; one on Joshua; one on Judges; five on both the books of Kings and the Psalms; two on Isaiah; one on Jeremiah and Lamentations; two on Ezekiel; one on Daniel, to which he has joined the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi; and one on the four Evangelists.

The reader does not expect us to provide continuous extracts or analyses of all these commentaries; that would carry us too far. We have dwelt sufficiently on the first three books of commentary on Genesis to make the author’s character known. The same tendency prevails in those which follow. We shall therefore content ourselves, in passing through them, with collecting some of the [Col. 0716C] passages that appear to us most useful and noteworthy.

In the first chapter of the fourth book on Genesis (ch. 1), Rupert makes a rather ingenious comparison between the patriarchs and righteous persons who died before the coming of the Messiah without receiving the promised reward, and catechumens under the new law. However perfect and enlightened the faith of catechumens may be, they do not partake in the holy mysteries until they have received baptism. Thus the patriarchs and ancient righteous persons were not to be admitted into heaven until Jesus Christ had expiated the stain of the first transgression. We must therefore consider all the saints and elect, the whole body of the Church that preceded Christ’s Passion, as one catechumen.

In the second chapter, he calls Abel the first witness of the Son of God, who offered the firstborn of his flock [Col. 0716D] through faith in the Passion of God’s only-begotten Son. All that Abel did and suffered (chs. 4–5) is a figure of Jesus Christ, who, at the Last Supper, having offered himself with his own hands, was handed over by his disciple, seized and crucified by the Jewish people, which was his brother according to the flesh. The curse that God pronounced upon Cain in punishment for murdering his brother, when he said to him (Gen. 4:14), “You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer upon the earth,” is a figure of what happened to the Jews (ch. 6), and of what the whole world now sees fulfilled in the people who killed Jesus Christ.

Rupert believes (ch. 16) that among those who perished in the waters of the Flood there were some whose sin was wiped away. On the occasion of the year of the Flood, he shows [Col. 0717A] (ch. 25) that years were not then shorter, as some have imagined, but had the same duration as today—“clearer than daylight,” *luce clarius*, he says. The sacrifice Noah offered to God after leaving the ark (ch. 27) was a figure of the new sacrifice by which Jesus Christ offered himself as a holocaust to God his Father, a sacrifice which he does not cease to offer him both in his own person and through the hands of his priests. The covenant God made with Noah (ch. 36) was a figure of that of Jesus Christ, who by his death on the cross reconciles us to his Father, washes us from our sins by his blood, and pours upon us the Holy Spirit of his charity. Nor should we omit our author’s judicious reflection (ch. 42) on the multiplication and confusion of languages, by which God confounded human pride and scattered their vain undertaking, introducing division among the children of Babylon.

[Col. 0717B] “When God said, ‘Come, then, and let us go down there, and so confound their language that they may no longer understand one another’ (Gen. 11:7), he was one day to give, through the ministry of Moses his servant, Holy Scripture, in which is found the knowledge of one God, which alone leads to heaven. Now human beings then had only one language, namely that still called Hebrew. Therefore, so that these pearls, when they are given, may not be trampled underfoot by these swine, he says: ‘Come, and let us confound their language.’ God alone could thus punish human beings, using to scatter them the very thing through which they are most divided.

“When he says in the plural, ‘Come, let us go down, let us confound,’ he does not summon multitudes of angels to his aid; rather, these words signify that the whole Trinity, in one God, is present to punish human pride. This is seen still more clearly in what happened when [Col. 0717C] these same languages were recalled and multiplied in the mouths of the apostles. The Trinity showed itself to humankind on that day when the humble were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is the true structure of the most high tower through which man rises from earth to heaven in order to be reunited with God.”

This reflection shows how the multiplication of languages, which served to punish human pride and divide humankind, serves in the mouths of the apostles to draw them to faith, humility, and unity in the body of Jesus Christ, and to make of all nations a holy people having but one heart and one soul.

The fifth book on Genesis begins with the calling of Abraham, the father of the faithful. This is the third age of the world according to our author’s division, and he gives it the title of the age of knowledge because God gave “to human beings in this age the knowledge of the great salvation and of the promise through his [Col. 0717D] word and through the written law.” Before entering upon his subject, he invokes the spirit of knowledge in order to uncover a treasury of testimonies concerning Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

Abraham (ch. 4) is the first to whom God revealed the mystery of the Incarnation, in saying to him: “All peoples of the earth shall be blessed in you” (Gen. 22:18). For this blessing is none other than that by which the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out upon all nations through Abraham’s seed—that is, through Jesus Christ. Circumcision (ch. 33) was the sign of the covenant that God made with Abraham. Not to bear this sign would have been to renounce Abraham’s seed. Now without faith in this seed, which is Jesus Christ, it was impossible to be saved: *Sine fide seminis tui, quod est Christus, salvari impossibile est*—“Without faith in your seed, which is Christ, salvation is impossible.”

Why then, someone will say, if the holy Fathers were justified by faith in Jesus Christ in receiving circumcision, did they not enter the kingdom of [Col. 0718A] heaven? Our author answers this question by the comparison already reported: just as catechumens are not admitted to the participation of our holy mysteries, although they believe in Jesus Christ and confess him with their mouths, unless they are regenerated through baptism; so ancient righteous persons were not to be admitted to eternal glory before Jesus Christ had shed his blood to purify them.

In the tenth chapter of the sixth book, Rupert makes this judicious observation concerning the passage which says that the angels urgently pressed Lot to leave Sodom and, as he continued to delay, took him by the hand, together with his wife and two daughters, and led them out (Gen. 19:16). Although Lot was righteous in comparison with Sodom’s inhabitants, he was an imperfect righteous man, without as great a faith as Abraham’s. He was attached to a country so beautiful and delightful; and, as though he had not properly understood what the angels told him about the danger threatening him, love of riches made him turn his eyes away from the light.

This often happens to someone who knows heavenly goods, to whom God’s wrath has been revealed by the Gospel, and who is instructed in spiritual things, yet, carried away by the love of the world, conceals from himself the threats of the Last Judgment which he knows, in order to follow the attraction of his own concupiscence. If, while he delays making use of his enlightenment, God takes him by the hand before he falls into sin and draws him out of the city—that is, delivers him from temptation—then, returning to himself, he says to God: “Lord, your servant has found grace before you; you have shown forth your mercy toward me by delivering my soul.” Indeed, when God comes to the aid of one who wishes to lose himself and is on the point of committing a sin, and checks his will at the very moment when it gives itself over to folly, he truly takes him by the hand and draws him out of Sodom. The one [Col. 0718C] thus delivered, feeling that this deliverance has come by grace, is inwardly ashamed that for a moment he entertained an evil will, and gives thanks to the Lord for having shown his mercy toward him.

What Rupert says (*ibid.*, ch. 28) on the trial to which God subjected Abraham’s faith and obedience, in commanding him to sacrifice Isaac, is no less edifying or instructive. God, who had already often tested this holy man, wished to reveal to us, his children, the treasury of faith and fear of the Lord which was in him, in order to make it a model for us. He tested him and commanded him to take his son and sacrifice him. The words accompanying God’s command are, as our author observes, especially fitted to pierce Abraham’s heart by dwelling upon everything that could move and afflict him. These are the words of the one testing: *Verba tentantis haec sunt*.

“Take [Col. 0718D] Isaac, your only son.” He calls him his only son; and he adds, “whom you love”—*addit: quem diligis*. He calls him by his name Isaac, in order to touch his father’s heart more keenly at the very moment of so great a trial: *Ne parum praesentes adessent patris affectus sui in ipso articulo tantae hujus tentationis*—“lest the father’s own feelings should be insufficiently present at the very point of this great trial.”

But Abraham (chs. 29–31), having the fear of God before his eyes, does not hesitate; he at once prepares to carry out the command he has received. Rupert then sets Isaac alongside Jesus Christ, of whom Isaac was the figure; and adds (ch. 32) that the Church today continually offers to God the Father the Son of God, who is immortal and impassible. He says that the sacrifice offered in the Church is rightly compared with that of the pious and faithful patriarch, because, just as Abraham did not shed his son’s blood, so today Christ’s blood is no longer shed; rather, this Son, living and whole, is presented [Col. 0719A] by the hands of ministers and received in the mouths of believers.

Rupert, wishing in this chapter to explain how what appears to be bread in the Eucharist is Christ himself—*quomodo, inquis, panis qui videtur est Christus*, “how, you ask, the bread which is seen is Christ”—uses a comparison liable to be understood in an improper sense. But a fair-minded reader knows that comparisons must not be pressed strictly.

Moreover, his purpose, as he says, is not to treat this subject, but only to show that just as Isaac was offered without being put to death, so Jesus is offered as a sacrifice impassibly: *Hoc solum ad praesentem causam pertinet, quod sicut Isaac ille immolatus et non tamen occisus est, sic et Christus immolatur quidem, sed impassibiliter sacrificatur et immortaliter*—“This alone pertains to the present matter: just as that Isaac was offered yet not slain, so Christ indeed is offered, but is sacrificed impassibly and immortally.”

Up to this point it may have been observed—and it may again be observed in what remains to be said concerning Rupert’s commentaries on Genesis and on the other books of Scripture—that this commentator [Col. 0719B] sees everywhere only Jesus Christ and the Church. Saint Augustine, several centuries before him, gave us this fine rule for understanding Scripture: not only the words, but also the lives, marriages, children, and actions of those saints who preceded Christ’s birth, were prophecies of what we see occurring in the present time, when the Church is formed from the Gentiles (*Augustine, On Instructing Beginners in Faith*, no. 33). Rupert seems to keep this rule so constantly before his eyes that, throughout the course of the patriarchs’ lives and actions, and in all the events he recounts, he sees only Jesus Christ, his Passion, his mysteries, the formation of the Church, the trials to which it is exposed, the rejection of the Jews, their recall at the end of the ages, what he has done for his elect, the mysteries of grace which delivers them—*gratiae liberatricis mysteria*—and so forth.

In Jacob, serving Laban in order to marry Rachel, he sees Jesus Christ who, possessing the form and nature [Col. 0719C] of God, [lacuna] emptied himself by taking the form and nature of a servant (Phil. 2:6), did penance for the sins of the world, and finally died upon a cross to expiate them (book VII, ch. 29). In Leah, whom Laban brought into Jacob’s chamber in place of Rachel, whom he had promised Jacob and for whom Jacob had served seven years, he sees the Church formed from all the nations of the world that neither knew nor invoked the Lord’s name, substituted for the Synagogue, for whose sake alone Jesus Christ seemed to have come into the world, as he testified when he said to the Canaanite woman: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

In the female slaves whom Laban gave to each of his daughters (*ibid.*, ch. 30), and by whom Jacob was to have children, he sees what happens in the Church, where some submit to the Gospel through love, others through fear, and others from motives other than Jesus Christ. Some, having a pure and complete faith, beget spiritual children for Jesus Christ; but others, possessing only the appearance of piety, preach and baptize outside the Church. Their sects are like concubines whose children shall have no share in their father’s inheritance unless they return to the bosom of the Catholic Church, their mother.

In the joy shown by Jacob’s wives when they bring children into the world (ch. 34), he sees a model for Christian souls, which ought to have the same desire to beget spiritual children for Jesus Christ. In Laban, pursuing Jacob when he leaves Mesopotamia with his wives and children to return to his homeland (ch. 46), he shows us how the world pursues even those who abandon it without wishing to possess anything, using not only seduction but violence as well to force them to follow its deadly examples. On the other hand, [Col. 0720A] in Rachel stealing Laban’s idols, he considers those who, after leaving the world, give themselves to avarice, which is idolatry, even so far as to use ecclesiastical ministry to deceive and to put a money-price upon God’s spiritual gifts.

In Pharaoh’s conduct toward two equally guilty officials (book VIII, ch. 37), punishing one and pardoning the other, he makes us consider God’s conduct toward human beings. The chief cupbearer and the chief baker of the king of Egypt had both offended their master and deserved death. But the prince, using indulgence toward one, restored him to his former position; while treating the other according to the rigor of justice, he had him fastened to a cross.

Rupert therefore asks those who wish to probe God’s judgments, and find fault with his saying to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I please” (Exod. 33:19)—he asks, I say, those who criticize God’s judgments—whether they wish to blame Pharaoh for pardoning one of these two officials and granting favor to the one to whom he was pleased to grant it. For he could have punished both; he could also have pardoned both: *Communem ergo iram, vel communem utrique poterat exhibere clementiam*—“Therefore he could have displayed a common wrath, or a common clemency to both alike.” But he wished neither to pardon both nor to punish both; he kept the mean by punishing one and pardoning the other. Is there anyone able to blame this prince’s conduct? Reason does not permit it. For if clemency honors a king, royal majesty loves justice; and when all are punished, severity degenerates into cruelty and stains the throne, whereas when all are pardoned, royal majesty falls into contempt, since there is no fear of discipline.

Now who does not know that the whole world, or the whole mass of the human race, is in God’s hands as two criminals are in the hands of a king or judge? Since Adam, our first father, sinned, we have all become guilty of his transgression; we are all prisoners because of him; but one is taken and another left.

[lacuna] “O man, who are you to contend with God?” (Rom. 9:20), you who cannot answer Pharaoh! Since all are guilty, does not God have the power, like Pharaoh, to pardon one and punish the other? More than this: since the human being whom God by his grace created for the glory of his image and likeness became clay through his own fault, does not the potter have authority to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honorable uses and another for vile and shameful uses (*ibid.*, v. 21)? [lacuna] The potter takes nothing from clay by making a vessel for shameful uses, since clay is itself vile; but he gives it much when he makes it a vessel for honorable uses.

“Lord,” says the prophet, “you [Col. 0720D] are our Father, and we are but clay; it is you who formed us, and we are all the work of your hands” (Isa. 64:8). We are all only clay, not merely because we were formed from dust, but because, whereas we ought to have shone like silver and gold through the likeness of our Creator, we have all fallen back into dust and become mortal through the sin of our first father. Thus every mouth must be stopped. For God takes nothing from those who, by his permission, have become vessels for shameful uses, because it is through their own fault that they have become clay. But it is an effect of his wholly gratuitous grace when he chooses some among them to make them vessels for honorable uses.

“Joseph in prison, between these two officials—one restored to his former state and the other put to death—is a figure of Jesus Christ fastened to the cross [Col. 0721A] between two thieves, one of whom dies in his sin while the other enters Paradise” (ch. 38).

Joseph’s brothers (book IX, ch. 1) intended by the unjust treatment they inflicted on him to prevent the fulfillment of his dreams; yet by that very means they brought about their fulfillment. So the devil, whose will is always opposed to God’s, works only toward the execution of God’s designs. “He is an everlasting slave,” our author says (ch. 4), “who serves as successfully as if he were faithful, who cooperates and benefits the good as though he wished to assist the Spirit of the Lord”: *Voluntate quidem adversatur [lacuna] actu autem servus est sempiternus, et sic servit tanquam sit fidelis; ita cooperatur et bonis proficit tanquam adjuvare velit spiritum Domini, etc.*—“In will indeed he opposes; [lacuna] but in deed he is an everlasting slave, and so serves as though he were faithful; thus he cooperates and benefits the good as though he wished to help the Spirit of the Lord, and so forth.”

When famine compelled Joseph’s brothers to go to Egypt for grain, he first had them arrested and put in prison for three days. This made them acknowledge their fault, saying: “It is just that we suffer all this, because [Col. 0721B] we sinned against our brother” (Gen. 42:21).

Rupert proposes this conduct as a model for Christian rulers who have Jews in their realm. He does not wish Christians to put them to death; but he is of the opinion that, following Joseph’s example, who by a pious punishment—*pia tortura*—drew from his brothers an admission of their crime, some severity should be used to bring them to repentance, for example a substantial tax. He acknowledges that those who chose to believe in Jesus Christ to avoid such treatment would not be good Christians; but, he says, their children would receive baptism more faithfully. Thus by this means either the fathers or the children would be gained.

But would such conduct accord with the spirit of the Gospel? Is this how Christianity was established? Jesus Christ, Prince of Peace, inspires in his disciples only gentleness and humility. Faith ought to be preached by gentleness, not by severity; by instruction, [Col. 0721C] not by persecution. This is why Saint Augustine formerly said (Letter 100, p. 270), in a letter to Donatus, proconsul of Africa, charged with enforcing the imperial laws against the Circumcellions, who inflicted unheard-of cruelties upon Catholics, that “however great the evil which one wishes to make people abandon, and however great the good which one wishes to make them embrace, it is a labor more burdensome than useful to compel rather than instruct them”: *onerosior est quippe quam utilior diligentia, quamvis ut magnum deseratur malum, et magnum teneatur bonum, cogi tantum homines, non doceri*—“For the effort is more burdensome than useful, even though the evil to be abandoned be great and the good to be held fast be great, when people are merely compelled and not taught.”

When Jacob (ch. 17) had the consolation of seeing Joseph again, he spoke these touching words to him: “I shall die content, since I have seen you and leave you surviving me” (Gen. 46:30). Each of us should make such tender words his own and say to the Son of God, our Lord, who is truly the [Col. 0721D] Savior of the world: “I shall die content, since I have seen you [lacuna].” Christian, when you are near death, and even while you enjoy life, since you must die, say to the only-begotten Son of God, your Savior: “I shall die content, since I have seen you,” and so forth.

Jacob’s request to Joseph (ch. 21) that after his death he should carry his body away to bury it in his fathers’ tomb, and the oath he requires of him on this subject, give our author occasion to ask why this holy patriarch, this citizen of heaven, for whom the whole earth was an exile during his life, took such care to ensure the place where his body would be reduced to dust. It was, he says, because this was the land God had promised him; and every gift of God, whether great or small, ought to be precious in the eyes of the wise.

Therefore, he adds, if Jacob, ready to die, showed such respect and gratitude for the promises made to him that he wished his body to be carried there after death as though to take possession of it—*ut saltem mortuo corpore illam tenere cuperet*, “so that at least with his dead body he might desire to hold it”—how much more ought those who entered into possession of that land to have applied themselves to live in such a way that, by their ingratitude, they would not compel God to deprive them of the gift he had given them? Jacob thus gave after his death an example to the living, teaching them to live in hope of the heavenly homeland and, in its pledge, to love the repose of the eternal inheritance: *Exemplum enim vivis mortuus dedit, ut in spe patriae coelestis pignus amarent requiem aeternae haereditatis*—“For, though dead, he gave an example to the living, that in the hope of their heavenly homeland they might love, in its pledge, the rest of the eternal inheritance.”

The nine books of commentary on Genesis are followed by four others on Exodus, in which the author continues to interpret Scripture as he began. That is, he passes rapidly over the literal sense and applies all his strength, as he says, to discovering there the hidden mysteries of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0722B] Son of God. For, first, there is scarcely anyone who does not know that the new king who did not know Joseph was a figure of the devil; that the Paschal lamb was a figure of Jesus, Son of God; Egypt, of this world; and the passage of the Israelites through the Red Sea, of the baptism of Jesus Christ. To treat these matters more methodically, the author goes further back and inquires into the meaning of the children of Israel’s entrance into the land of Egypt, so that we may know that their entrance into that land, just as their departure from it, were both figures of all those who, regarding themselves as strangers in this world, sigh after the heavenly homeland for which they wait.

The first step on your path of justice and salvation, O Israel (Book I, ch. 2)—that blessed nation, that people whom God chose as his inheritance—is to know and confess that it was through its own fault that it was relegated [Col. 0722C] to the exile of this world, far from God and from the land of the living; and that grace alone can draw it out of this corrupt age and bring it into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son. Israel would not have come to the knowledge of this truth unless God had made it understood through the likeness of some outward event. This is why that particular people, Israel—that carnal people—entered Egypt; yet in such a way that it entered there through its own fault and departed only through the grace of God, who delivered it from Pharaoh’s hands.

This new king wished to destroy Jacob’s posterity, and urged his subjects to do so, saying (Exod. 1:9–10): “The children of Israel have become more powerful than we. Let us oppress them prudently, lest they increase still further and, if war should arise against us, join [Col. 0722D] our enemies and, after defeating us, depart from the country” (ch. 4).

Rupert (ibid.), considering the king who speaks thus to be a figure of the devil and prince of darkness, who is king of all the children of pride, answers him in the name of the elect:

> “However great the jealousy that makes you speak in this way, you have spoken truly, Satan; and all the Egyptians, your satellites, have spoken without falsehood. We have multiplied and form a people stronger than yours. And should war arise against you—indeed, this war arose long ago—Jesus Christ, the Son of God, declared it against you when he raised against you the standard of his cross. We join your enemies, that is, the holy and blessed angels who put you to flight; and, after overcoming you, we shall leave this land, because heaven awaits us.”

The multiplication of the children of Israel amid the labours with which the Egyptians burdened them represents the progress of the elect in the war waged against them by the devil (ch. 5). Our author maintains that the Egyptian midwives did not lie in the answer which they gave to the king. He cannot, he says (ch. 7), cast the darkness of falsehood upon so conspicuous an act of charity: *Nullas igitur quasi mendacii tenebras ascribam lucido charitatis operi*—“Therefore I shall ascribe no shadows, as it were, of falsehood to the bright work of charity”—by which they deceived an impious man and preserved the lives of so many people, since God judged the act worthy of praise and reward.

These reasons are not very sound. However impious Pharaoh may have been, a lie did not cease to be a lie because it was used to deceive him and save innocents.

Nor does Rupert’s further statement—that God judged the midwives’ action worthy of praise and reward—prove that they did not lie.

Two things must be distinguished in their conduct: [Col. 0723B] what they did from fear of God and what they did from fear of the king of Egypt. They feared God and refused to lend their assistance to that prince’s cruelty: this is what was worthy of praise and reward, and what God rewarded, as Scripture says: *Et quia timuerunt obstetrices Deum, aedificavit eis domos* (Exod. 1:21), “And because the midwives feared God, he built houses for them.” But the answer which they gave the king in order to escape danger contained a lie that cannot be excused from sin, although the circumstances lessen their fault. It should nevertheless be observed that Rupert does not claim to excuse lying from sin; he merely wishes—though on very weak grounds—to hold that the midwives did not lie.

Moses’ resistance when God commanded him to go to Pharaoh gives our commentator occasion to propose a very wise maxim to those whom the Holy Spirit calls to go [Col. 0723C] and fight Pharaoh—that is, the devil—in some office of the ministry for the salvation of souls. Moses’ example in refusing is very beautiful and worthy of imitation. Isaiah’s example, in offering himself and answering the Lord, “Here am I; send me,” *Ecce ego, mitte me* (Isa. 6:8), requires caution. Obstinacy and presumption must be avoided.

We must (ch. 13), following the Israelites’ example, despoil the Egyptians, by making the arts and sciences which the world employs to adorn falsehood serve for the defence and adornment of truth and religion (ch. 15). As the Israelites in Egypt were a figure of the elect upon earth (ch. 16), so the wonders performed by Moses, by which they were to recognize the time when God visited them, had to be figures of better wonders, by which they were to recognize the time of their redemption through Jesus Christ. The ten plagues with which God struck Egypt were, according to [Col. 0723D] our author’s interpretation (chs. 28–29), figures of the Ten Commandments. These ten plagues could indeed torment Pharaoh and overwhelm Egypt, but could not overcome their resistance. Only after the immolation of the Paschal lamb and the death of the firstborn did they allow the Israelites to depart. Thus the Ten Commandments, all contained in love of God and neighbour, could indeed afflict the devil, figured by Pharaoh, and disturb the reign of death, but could not destroy it; for the law brought no one to perfect righteousness (Heb. 7:19). Finally, Jesus Christ, Son of God, the true Lamb, came into this world to be sacrificed; and by the shedding of his blood, offering a sacrifice of righteousness, he accomplished [Col. 0724A] what human righteousness had been unable to accomplish, however zealous men might have been in observing the commandments of the law: “For what the law was unable to do, because the flesh rendered it weak and powerless, God did, by sending his own Son clothed in flesh like sinful flesh; and he condemned sin in the flesh of Jesus Christ because of sin committed against him, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom. 8:3).

Speaking of the wonders Moses performed before Pharaoh (ch. 30; Exod. 7 ff.), Rupert appears convinced that no real transformation occurred in what the magicians did. He believes that their rods remained what they had been, *illae enim virgae erant quod fuerant*—“for those rods were what they had been”—but that, through enchantments and certain secret arts, they bewitched people’s eyes, so that their rods appeared to be serpents: *Fascinaverunt magi oculos hominum, ut virgae viderentur eis speciem habere draconum*—“The magicians bewitched men’s eyes, so that the rods appeared to them to have the form of dragons.” He says the same concerning the frogs made by [Col. 0724B] the magicians (ch. 33), and the water which they changed into blood: *Praestigiatores ranas falsissimas et sanguinem fallacem fascinatis oculis ostenderunt*—“The tricksters displayed utterly false frogs and deceptive blood to bewitched eyes.”

The immolation of the Paschal lamb, followed by the death of Egypt’s firstborn, was a figure of the Passion of Jesus Christ, by which original sin and all the sins of the world were erased (ch. 40). This great work of the Lamb of God, holy and spotless, is the subject of the second book of Rupert’s Commentary on Exodus. The true Lamb wished to be sacrificed at the very time which he had prescribed for the immolation of the lamb that was only a figure (ch. 6). On the fourteenth day at evening, after eating with his disciples the lamb of the old Passover, Jesus Christ, the Lamb of the new sacrifice, [lacuna] offered himself to God his Father with his own hands, taking bread and wine and, by a wondrous and ineffable power of sanctification, changing them into the sacrament of his body and blood.

> [Note: [Col. 0723D] *Ipse novi sacrificii Agnus . . . propriis manibus Deo Patri semetipsum immolavit, accipiens panem et vinum, et mira atque ineffabili sanctificationis* [Col. 0724D] *potentia, transferens haec in corporis et sanguinis sui sacramentum.*  
> “The Lamb himself of the new sacrifice [lacuna] with his own hands sacrificed himself to God the Father, taking bread and wine and, by the wondrous and ineffable power of sanctification, changing these into the sacrament of his body and blood.”]

[Col. 0724C] Rupert repeats the same point in the same chapter and says that the high priest offered with his hands his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine: *manibus suis . . . corpus et sanguinem suum sub specie panis, ipse summus Pontifex obtulit*—“with his own hands, the high priest himself offered his body and blood under the appearance of bread.” These clear expressions, which set forth plainly and precisely the Church’s faith concerning the mystery of the Eucharist, teach us Rupert’s true views on this mystery. He must be judged by them, and not by a few obscure terms or comparisons which, considered by themselves, might admit an unsound sense. Such is the comparison he makes in the tenth chapter of this same book between the hypostatic union of Christ’s two natures in the unity of his person, and the union of Christ, God and man, in the Eucharist. It is evident that his sole purpose is to establish the real presence and [Col. 0724D] prove that Jesus Christ is truly in this sacrament, although the appearances of bread and wine seem unchanged to our senses; just as he was God and man together, although outwardly he appeared to be merely a man (Book II, ch. 10).

When he says that the Holy Spirit does not destroy the substance of bread and wine—words which gave some undiscerning and unfair writers occasion to accuse him of error—he meant nothing else than that the Holy Spirit does not destroy bread and wine with respect to their appearances and to what is manifest to the senses. Rupert says so expressly; it is astonishing that his accusers did not attend to it: *substantiam panis et vini SECUNDUM EXTERIOREM SPECIEM, quinque* [Col. 0725A] *sensibus subactam, non mutat aut destruit*—“he does not alter or destroy the substance of bread and wine ACCORDING TO ITS EXTERNAL APPEARANCE, apprehended by the five senses.” Thus bread and wine are truly changed into the body and blood of Jesus Christ, as he says in a hundred places; but they are neither destroyed nor changed with respect to the appearances remaining after the change of the substance of bread and wine. In short, bread and wine are truly changed into body and blood, but without acquiring the taste of flesh or the horror of blood: *panis et vinum fit corpus et sanguis Christi, non mutatum in carnis saporem, sive in sanguinis horrorem*—“bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, not changed into the taste of flesh or the horror of blood.” It would be easy to cite here a multitude of passages from this author’s various writings, in which he teaches that the substance of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Jesus Christ. Some have already been seen; we shall therefore content ourselves with adding one from the seventh chapter of the following book: *substantia panis et vini in veritatem nobis convertitur corporis ejus et sanguinis*—“the substance of bread and wine is changed for us into the reality of his body and blood.”

What, then, does Rupert mean [Col. 0725B] when, speaking of the change effected in the Eucharist, he states that the Holy Spirit does not destroy the substance of bread and wine because he does not destroy the nature and substance of things? He means that the Holy Spirit does not destroy substance in such a way that it falls back into nothingness and nothing remains of it; for, through the change which the Holy Spirit effects, the substance of the thing changed, while ceasing to be what it was, becomes better. Thus bread and wine are not destroyed in such a manner that they fall back into nothingness and absolutely nothing remains; rather, they cease to be bread and wine in order to become the body and blood of Jesus, with nothing of the bread and wine remaining except the species or appearances—that is, colour and flavour. This is the sense in which Rupert teaches that the Holy Spirit does not destroy the substance of things by his operation. We shall have further occasions to speak of his view concerning the Eucharist and to show its [Col. 0725C] perfect conformity with the faith of the Church.

Saint Paul (1 Cor. 10) did not wish us to be ignorant that everything which happened formerly to the Israelites was, for Christians, a figure intended for their instruction. To enter into the Apostle’s meaning, Rupert, having shown in the second book on Exodus that the Paschal lamb was a figure of the Eucharist, the Israelites’ passage through the Red Sea a figure of baptism, and so forth, proposes (Book III, ch. 1) to speak of their murmurings in the wilderness, their idolatry, and the punishments with which God chastised them, in order, he says, that we may profit from these examples to correct ourselves. But his principal purpose is to seek, in figures of temporal things and according to the Apostle’s spirit, the mysteries of Jesus Christ, Son of God. Explaining the words (ch. 10), “all were baptized [lacuna] all ate of the same spiritual food,” and so forth, he shows that the Jews possessed only figures, while Christians possess the reality and the things themselves. “Moses has not given you the bread of heaven,” says Jesus Christ, “but my Father gives you the true bread of heaven” (John 6:32). The spiritual food which the Jews ate in the wilderness was not the same as that received by Christians. Reason does not permit one to say that figure and reality are the same thing: *Nec enim ratio patitur ut figura et res idem sint*—“For reason does not allow figure and reality to be identical.”

The Israelites were commanded to leave the camp daily in order to gather manna. Thus (ch. 11), we must go out by abandoning our former life and leading a new one.

> “For we must not gather this manna, nor eat the Lord’s bread, until we have put off the old man. If we wish [Col. 0726A] to eat it worthily, we must renounce every curiosity of the senses and not imagine that by sight, taste, smell, or touch we can judge whether what we receive is truly the body of Jesus Christ and his true flesh. The colour, odour, and flavour remaining, there remains what suffices for Christian faith and piety [lacuna] Let each gather what suffices for him: that is, let him believe that the Lord’s words are spirit and life, and that through these words bread and wine are changed into the true substance of the living body and blood of Jesus Christ, although the external appearance is not changed.”

*Credat verba Domini spiritum esse et vitam, et per ea panem et vinum, exteriori specie non mutata, transferri in veram viventis corporis et sanguinis Christi substantiam, etc.*—“Let him believe that the Lord’s words are spirit and life, and that by them bread and wine, though their outward appearance is unchanged, are changed into the true substance of Christ’s living body and blood, etc.”

The Jews once said while murmuring (ch. 15): “How can he give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:53). This murmur continues today, both among the Jews [Col. 0726B] and among heretics. When we tell them, “It is the flesh of Jesus Christ,” they never cease saying: “How is this? How is this?” *Quomodo est, quomodo est?* In Rupert’s time (ch. 17), very small breads were used, and, as today, only a small quantity of wine was taken for consecration; because, as regards the power of this spiritual food, the body of Jesus Christ, one does not receive the spiritual grace of the life-giving Spirit according to the quantity of visible species. That is, one receives as much under the smallest particle as if one received everything offered.

> [Note: [Col. 0725D] *Sic quisque nostrum, non pro quantitate particulae vivifici panis, quae frangitur illi, quam ore sumit, aut dentibus premit, gratiam vel vitam accipit,* [Col. 0726D] *sed tantum illi valet ad consecutionem justitiae exiquum quid percipisse, quantum valeret, si totum quod oblatum est, proprio solus perciperet ore.*  
> “Thus each of us receives grace or life not in proportion to the quantity of the particle of life-giving bread which is broken for him, which he takes with his mouth or presses with his teeth; rather, receiving a very small amount benefits him for attaining righteousness as much as it would benefit him if he alone received with his own mouth the whole of what has been offered.”]

In the fourth book on Exodus, Rupert speaks of the tabernacle which Moses made by God’s command, according to the pattern shown him; of the gifts offered to build it; of the ark of the covenant; the mercy-seat; and so forth. Before Moses made all these earthly things, God spoke to him and thereby gave him knowledge of the heavenly things that were to [Col. 0726C] serve as his model. He made known to him the great mysteries of the Incarnation which were to be fulfilled in the course of the ages.

> “He did not conceal from this lawgiver, with whom he spoke as with a friend, that the Word would become flesh; that Jesus Christ, God and man, would redeem men from their sins; and that he would place in the tabernacle—that is, in the Church—a table upon which his body and blood would be offered” (ch. 2).

Moses saw all these spiritual or heavenly things before giving earthly and carnal ones to the people. The latter are only the first shadow and figure.

The tabernacle was a figure of the Church (ch. 15). In this Church is found the Lord’s table, on which a double nourishment is served, prepared to sustain men in the conflicts of this life. There is set forth the bread of Holy Scripture, which nourishes the soul with the [Col. 0726D] word of God; and the bread of Christ’s body and the cup of his blood, which the Christian receives as a means of attaining eternal life.

Moses’ conduct toward God’s people (ch. 27), mingling gentleness with severity, is a perfect model for the conduct pastors must maintain toward those subject to them. As they must have gentleness, so they must also possess a godly severity in order to maintain order and punish crime: *pie saeviens disciplina*, “a discipline raging piously.” Moses’ tenderness toward the Israelites appears in the prayer he made to the Lord, by which he disarmed wrath ready to fall upon an idolatrous people who had made themselves a golden calf to worship. On the other hand, his severity was displayed in the order he gave the tribe of Levi: each was to take his sword, pass back and forth [Col. 0727A] through the camp from gate to gate, and kill his brothers, friends, and nearest relatives. All who are entrusted with the care of souls (ch. 28) will learn from this example what must be done in governing them—or rather, in benefiting them. They will learn how to disarm God’s wrath through prayers issuing from a heart full of pure and ardent love, while nevertheless punishing crime. Our author observes that Scripture recounts in great detail what Moses did on this occasion in order to encourage pastors by his example, not to affect wearing on their garments wider parchment bands than others and longer fringes, but attentively to watch over the souls entrusted to them, lest they be found stripped of God’s grace and naked amid their visible and invisible enemies; to cover them with their merits and defend them by their prayers.

[Col. 0727B] Rupert concludes his Commentary on Exodus with a very judicious reflection upon Scripture’s statement that God filled Bezalel and Oholiab with his Spirit and gave them wisdom, understanding, and skill to work in every kind of gold, silver, bronze, and other work for which he had chosen them.

> “Who, then,” he says (ch. 44), “can doubt that these arts and others like them are gifts of God? Therefore, wherever useful and lawful arts are found in any person, they ought to be cherished; and skilled workers should be exhorted to exercise them and make them fruitful as God’s talent, which does not come from themselves but from the Creator who entrusted it to them and will call them to account for it.”

The Commentary on Leviticus, divided into two books, has the same character as the preceding works, except that it is somewhat more moral. The sacrifices of the old law (Book I, ch. 1), whose ceremonies Moses [Col. 0727C] prescribes in Leviticus, were not instituted as necessary means for attaining salvation: *Non tanquam perficiendae salutis instrumenta necessaria*—“not as instruments necessary for the accomplishment of salvation”—but merely to avoid obstacles and prevent the Israelites from offering victims to idols. In the sixteenth chapter of the first book, our commentator, giving a mystical meaning to the ceremonies of the sacrifice offered by the high priest when he had sinned and caused the people to sin, teaches in the most precise manner the real presence of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist: *Nomine, re, atque effectu, caro vera est atque sanguis verus*—“in name, reality, and effect, it is true flesh and true blood.” These expressions establish the Church’s faith concerning this mystery so clearly that it is surprising anyone could have cast suspicion upon the author’s faith.

In the eighteenth chapter, speaking of sins committed after baptism, he says that we no longer have for obtaining their remission the same remedy [Col. 0727D] and the same abundance of grace which we received in baptism. Therefore, if, after being purified by baptism, we have the misfortune to sin, we must produce worthy fruits of repentance.

Only by sacrificing oneself through the mortification of actual repentance, *per actualis poenitentiae mortificationem mactabit semetipsum*—“through the mortification of actual repentance he will sacrifice himself”—only by punishing oneself, can one obtain forgiveness and be saved: *Si salvari cupit, poenitendo puniet semetipsum*—“If he desires to be saved, he will punish himself by repenting.” [Col. 0728A] Rupert observes, and even repeats twice, that with respect to forgiveness of sins committed after baptism, we do not have the same security and certainty as we have concerning those of which we were guilty before receiving it.

> [Note: [Col. 0727D] *Etenim comparatione securitatis quam in baptismo accepimus, valde scrupulosa est redemptio, si iterum peccaverimus.*  
> “For, compared with the security which we received in baptism, redemption is very fraught with anxiety if we sin again.”]

In the twenty-fourth chapter, he calls baptism and the Eucharist the greatest sacraments of the Church, instituted by Jesus Christ: *Sacramenta Christi Filii Dei, quorum baptismus et eucharistia vel maxima sunt, quae ab ipso Domino nostro sunt instituta*—“the sacraments of Christ the Son of God, among which baptism and the Eucharist are indeed the greatest, which were instituted by our Lord himself.” He then adds that, for those of the second rank, *secundaria vero*, the apostles or apostolic men subsequently established their ceremonies. It must not be inferred that Rupert recognized only two sacraments instituted by Jesus Christ, but only that he regarded baptism and the Eucharist as the most important among those he instituted, as he himself makes clear: *Quorum baptismus et eucharistia vel* [Col. 0728B] *maxima sunt*—“among which baptism and the Eucharist are indeed the greatest.” What he calls the sacraments of the second rank, *secundaria vero*, is nothing other than the ceremonies and manner of administering them, subsequently regulated by apostles or apostolic men. It is sinful to administer holy things with a distracted heart and wandering eyes, and especially, through negligence, to allow to escape—something greatly to be feared, *quod valde pavendum est*—the most precious substance of the Lord’s body and blood. He wishes one who has committed such a fault to expiate it by his own prayers, by the prayers of his brothers, and by making suitable satisfaction.

In several passages in both the first and second books of the Commentary on Leviticus, the author speaks of confession. He wishes (Book I, ch. 38) that the sinner carefully examine his actions and thoughts in God’s presence; judge himself; and, after resolving to amend himself, [Col. 0728C] confess to the priest. Contrition and change of life are necessary; otherwise there is no salvation for the sinner who, confessing without a sincere will to amend his life, would make a profession of crime rather than confess it.

> [Note: [Col. 0727D] *Cum hoc propositum habuerit, quod de caetero emendare velit, tunc demum confessionem puram offerat sacerdoti . . . . . nec enim confessio, non sequente contritione et correctione, salvare poterit;* [Col. 0728D] *magisque dicenda est peccandi professio, quam peccati confessio. Lib. II, in Lev., cap. 38.*  
> “When he has formed the purpose of wishing henceforth to amend himself, only then should he offer pure confession to the priest [lacuna] for confession without accompanying contrition and amendment cannot save; it ought rather to be called a profession of sinning than a confession of sin. Book II, on Leviticus, chapter 38.”]

The priest must neither flatter nor deceive the penitent, like those bad physicians who neglect to cut away dead flesh; rather, he must carry the blade to the bottom of the wound, urging the penitent to groan and bear worthy fruits of repentance. Great reserve must be exercised in the remission of sins; for, he says (Book II, ch. 42), most people forgive with great ease the injury done to God, yet are very reluctant to forgive an injury done to themselves. There are faults which, if not expiated in this life by sufficiently worthy fruits of repentance, will be expiated in the next by the flames of purgatory.

> [Note: [Col. 0728D] *Talium culpae, etsi in praesenti saeculo non satis dignis poenitentiae fructibus redemptae fuerint, saltem in futuro venia non carebunt, sic tamen quasi per ignem purgatorium.*  
> “The faults of such persons, although in the present age they have not been redeemed by sufficiently worthy fruits of repentance, will nevertheless not lack pardon in the future, though as if through purgatorial fire.”]

Rupert here testifies that he does not know what Origen meant when he asserted that the Church admits persons to [Col. 0728D] penance only once: *Origenes . . . nescio quid volens, semel tantum, inquit, in Ecclesia est poenitentiae locus*—“Origen [lacuna], meaning I know not what, says: ‘In the Church there is a place for repentance only once.’” A somewhat fuller knowledge of the ancient Church’s discipline concerning public penance, which was granted only once, would have enabled him to understand Origen’s thought.

The person who hears confession (Book II, ch. 43) must be instructed in God’s law, and above all must possess great discretion, so as to know with what weight, measure, and moderation he [Col. 0729A] should deal with penitents, imposing upon each penances proportionate to their sins and strength. Confession must be exact and sincere: *pura ac sincera confessione aperire*, “to disclose by pure and sincere confession.” The sinner must declare the number of sins: *rarius an crebrius peccatum sit iteratum*, “whether the sin has been repeated more rarely or more frequently”; and must perform a more or less rigorous penance in proportion to the sins committed. For one who has fallen only once ought not to be punished like one guilty of many sins.

The Commentary on Numbers is divided into two books composed in the same manner as the preceding ones. The author, who until this point had found only pleasure in his labour, declares that this sacred book strikes him with fear and causes him the same bitterness which the book of which Saint John speaks in the Apocalypse once caused that apostle (Rev. 10:10). The reason for his fear is that more than [Col. 0729B] 600,000 Israelites, whose census the Book of Numbers contains, perished in the wilderness and did not enter the promised land. Now, according to Saint Paul’s testimony, all the things that happened to the Israelites were figures for us, and were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). They were figures for us in this respect: just as the Israelites who were numbered did not enter the promised land, so too, although all Christians are numbered by the profession they make of religion, and have enrolled their names by receiving baptism, not all run in such a manner as happily to reach the end of the course. Let us therefore, Rupert says, rejoice in our calling; but let the uncertainty whether we shall arrive, and the fear of failing to win the crown, cause bitterness in our hearts.

[Col. 0729C] In this commentary we observe new proofs of the purity of the author’s views concerning the real presence of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. After giving, in the second chapter of the first book, mystical interpretations of the names of the chiefs of each tribe, he adds that these chiefs represented us, “who eat the same spiritual food and drink the same spiritual drink from the rock, which is no longer now Christ in figure, but in reality”: *quae non jam in figura, sed in veritate Christus est.*

In the fourth chapter of the same book, he says that the Levites, who were not numbered, are those who perform the offices of the holy ministry in the Church. This is why the canons forbid them to involve themselves in secular affairs and prohibit commerce, hunting, and war. He complains that in his time most persons entered the ecclesiastical state of their own accord and gloried excessively in their position, despising laypeople. [Col. 0729D] The priesthood needs the aid of princes (ch. 5). When the two powers are well united, nothing is safer; conversely, when they disagree with one another, nothing can be more harmful to the Christian order in this world.

> [Note: [Col. 0729D] *Cum sibi conveniunt, nihil tutius; cum autem adversus invicem dissentiunt, nihil statui Christianitatis in hoc mundo, potest esse perniciosius.*  
> “When they agree with one another, nothing is safer; but when they disagree against each other, nothing can be more destructive to the condition of Christianity in this world.”]

The two books on Numbers are followed by two others on Deuteronomy. This book of Holy Scripture, which is a brief and clear interpretation of the Law, brings again before the reader almost all the preceding events. Everywhere one sees the charitable care of the meekest of all men, in leading to God the people whose guidance had been entrusted to him. This part of Scripture contains many things able to inspire in readers love of [Col. 0730A] God through the recollection of his benefits which it recalls; it contains a still greater number which the author of the Commentary says are too lofty for him and beyond his reach. Yet, because he has already treated these matters elsewhere, each in its proper place, he confines himself here to what is essential: that is, what concerns the promise of Jesus Christ, Son of God, and his coming. Such is Rupert’s plan in his Commentary on Deuteronomy.

In the sixth chapter of the first book, he criticizes these words of the Septuagint version: *Maledictus omnis qui pendet in ligno* (Deut. 21:23), “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” He maintains that this is not the meaning of the Hebrew, which at this point, as at many others, was often mistranslated by the Septuagint translators, who were interpreters and not prophets perfectly filled with the Spirit of God. Since Saint Paul cited this scriptural text according to the Septuagint version, which creates a presumption in its [Col. 0730B] favour, he replies that Saint Paul, writing for Greeks among whom this version—published as early as the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus—was held in high esteem, used it rather than cite another version which, though more correct, might have offended those to whom he wrote.

In the ninth chapter of the same book, he teaches that one may use profitably whatever is good in heretics’ works. He cites in this connection the example of Theophilus of Alexandria, who read Origen’s writings, although he had made the reading of them a crime in Saint Chrysostom and included it among the principal accusations upon which he condemned the patriarch of Constantinople. Rupert could have cited in his favour examples of greater authority than that of a prelate who became more famous in history for his ambition, intrigues, and cruel persecution of Saint Chrysostom than for the qualities and virtues required by the episcopate.

[Col. 0730C] In the thirty-first chapter, he reconciles two scriptural texts that appear to contain a contradiction. Exodus 34:7 says that God repays fathers’ iniquity upon their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generation; yet Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting fathers to death for their children or children to death for their fathers. Our commentator reconciles this by saying that God punishes the fathers’ iniquity in children who imitate their transgressing fathers, and does not punish it in those who do not imitate them. He then adds that there is a great and ancient question concerning children who, guilty of no actual sin, are damned for the sole iniquity of their fathers—that is, original sin. The solution he finds for this question is to say to God: “Your judgments are a great deep”: *Judicia tua abyssus multa* (Ps. 35 [Vulgate]).

[Col. 0730D] Rupert teaches, as we have seen elsewhere, that the Church needs the assistance of secular power; but he is very far from believing that it may employ the sword to compel the acceptance of the Gospel. He recognizes no other means of commending it than the gentleness of preaching joined to the cogency of arguments. To use force and violence in order to compel someone, against his will, to embrace the Christian religion is, he says [Note: [Col. 0729D] “To wish to build an altar to the Lord out of stones which iron [Col. 0730D] has touched is to impose the Christian law by compulsion or some violence upon unwilling hearers. But the sacred law forbids this.” Book II, Commentary on Deuteronomy, ch. 4.], what the sacred law forbids: *Sed hoc vetat sacra lex*—“But the sacred law forbids this.” He concludes his commentary on Deuteronomy by asking God’s forgiveness for any faults he may have committed, and proceeds to the book of Joshua.

In commenting on this book, which he does in twenty-two chapters, [Col. 0731A] he continues to deal with the Passion and mysteries of Jesus Christ, with this difference: he is less expansive than in the preceding works, contenting himself with selecting certain passages that seem better suited to his purpose and to be more vivid and illustrious figures of the Sun of righteousness. Joshua’s triumphant entry into the promised land, and his bringing the Israelites into it after many battles and victories—what Moses had been unable to do—represents Jesus Christ, our leader, the Saviour of the world, who has brought us into the land of the living, having himself first entered it after his resurrection.

At the conclusion of his work on Joshua, the author announces (ch. 22) that he is moving on to the book of Judges; and that, touching only lightly upon the surface of a sufficiently well-known history, he will seek out the adorable mystery in which the Word of the Lord discloses itself according to subject and time. In fact, he confines himself to giving mystical meanings to several of the principal events [Col. 0731B] that he has selected from this book because they more particularly figure certain circumstances of the life of Jesus Christ and of the preaching of the Gospel. In the fifth chapter one may observe the author’s care in following the original text of Scripture. He repeatedly stresses the difference between the Hebrew text and the Septuagint and Vulgate versions, and adheres to the former.

The Commentary on the Books of Kings is divided into three books. Here, according to the plan the author has formed, begins the fourth age, characterized by the spirit of fortitude (Book I, ch. 1). This age displays before our eyes the splendid spectacle of the great deeds of kings and the heavenly utterances of the prophets who prophesied during their reigns and announced the coming of the Messiah more clearly than it had hitherto been announced. Earlier promises of this Messiah proclaimed him only as a man; but in the fourth age [Col. 0731C] he is promised as a king whose reign must be eternal. Rupert therefore proposes, in his Commentary on the Books of Kings and in those that follow it down to Jeremiah, to show that the prophecies concerning the Messiah unfold, throughout the period which he calls the fourth age, more clearly and brilliantly through the heroic deeds of kings and the teachings of prophets than they had in the preceding ages.

In this work Rupert frequently cites Jewish commentaries. He believes (Book II, ch. 20) that the books mentioned in Scripture under the titles *Book of the Just* and *Book of the Wars of the Lord* are not writings that ever existed; and he says that the latter is nothing other than the whole of Scripture.
