Notwithstanding the words of Ecclesiasticus, which he himself cites (Book II, ch. 17), saying that Samuel prophesied after his death, he maintains that the holy prophet [Col. 0731D] did not truly appear to Saul, but that it was an appearance of the evil spirit under Samuel’s likeness [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Although we read in Ecclesiasticus that Samuel too prophesied after death, it must be believed that not so much Samuel [Col. 0732D] as an evil spirit appeared in the phantom of Samuel.”]. Several Fathers before Rupert, and some commentators, explained this event in this manner. But it must be acknowledged that the more general view, and the one more consonant with Scripture and therefore safer, regarding the nature of this apparition, is that it was real: it was not an empty phantom that appeared, but Samuel himself, who, as Ecclesiasticus says, after he had fallen asleep in the tomb spoke to the king and foretold the end of his life; and, rising from the earth, raised his voice to prophesy the ruin of the people and the punishment due to their impiety (Ecclus. 46:23).

In the seventeenth chapter of the third book, Rupert extols Solomon’s wisdom in a manner [Col. 0732A] that may seem excessive; for he maintains that Solomon was wiser than Abraham and Moses, who preceded him, and than Daniel, who came after him. But he states nothing definite concerning Solomon’s penitence, contenting himself with saying (Book III, ch. 32) that learned persons are divided on the matter. What is certain, he says, is that Solomon’s example ought to teach the wise not to presume upon their condition during this life, since a king who surpassed in wisdom all who came before and all who would follow him suffered such a lamentable fall.

The two following books belong with the three preceding ones. Thus the first, which is a commentary on the Psalms, counts as the fourth book on Kings, and the other as the fifth.

At the head of this Commentary on the Psalms, or fourth book on Kings, is a prologue divided into four chapters. There the author says (ch. 1) that, after unfolding the glory of Jesus Christ [Col. 0732B] in the illustrious deeds of the kings of the fourth age, he will seek new testimonies to the Messiah in the utterances of the prophets. David is the first, or the foremost, of all—*primus vel praecipuus*—because he is the first to have spoken clearly of the kingdom of God, the punishments of hell, and the Last Judgment. Neither Moses, Joshua, nor Samuel had spoken of these things before him—not because they were ignorant of them, but because carnal and coarse people would not have received them. God willed that these truths should be proclaimed through David’s mouth (ch. 3), because his divine word is so foreign to the corrupted world that men would not have listened to it unless they had heard it through the channel of so great and powerful a prince as David was. The author next sets out (ch. 4) the plan that he proposes to follow in his exposition of the Psalms. The division of these holy songs into three groups of fifty signifies faith, [Col. 0732C] hope, and charity; for, as man was lost by losing charity, hope, and finally faith, he can rise again only by retracing his steps in a different order: first by faith, then by hope, and finally by charity. The first fifty psalms contain what must be believed concerning Jesus Christ. In the next fifty we find the grounds of our hope; and in the final fifty, the means of advancing and being perfected in the love of God. This commentary is a mystical and very concise exposition of these holy songs. The author selects only certain verses which seem to him to relate most closely to his plan concerning Jesus Christ, his mysteries, and his Church, which he presents as the objects of faith, hope, and charity.

Following the Commentary on the Psalms, the author offers a specimen of what he might have done in the same manner with the three books of Solomon—the [Col. 0732D] Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs. The first, he says, calls us to faith; the second, to hope; and the third, to charity. But fear of interrupting the course of his work prevents him from entering so profound an abyss, and he resumes his exposition of Kings—that is, of the Third and Fourth Books—of which, however, he explains only a very small part. This exposition, which forms the fifth book of the commentaries on Kings, is divided into thirty-eight chapters. In the thirtieth, he shows that the answer given by the prophet Elisha to Naaman (4 Kings 5), who had begged him to pray to the Lord to forgive him if, when the king his master entered the temple of Rimmon to worship while leaning on his hand, he himself bowed as the king bowed—he shows, I say, that Elisha’s response, “Go in peace,” has nothing contrary to what St Paul says (1 Cor. 8) against those who found themselves at tables where food sacrificed to idols was served. “The prophet,” he says, “reassured by his answer a man of good will . . . . . . He does not permit him to worship Rimmon in the temple of Rimmon, but to worship God, who, being everywhere, could be worshipped even in the temple of Rimmon.” After reconciling several other texts, Rupert makes a very sound observation upon the words and example of the Apostle, which, he says, teach us to distinguish the circumstances in which we ought patiently to endure communion or association with the wicked, and those in which we ought prudently to avoid them. Those who lack this wise discernment often cause scandal and sustain divisions in the Church, because, although they have zeal for God, that zeal is not according to knowledge.

The miracle God performed on behalf of Elisha, in order to [Col. 0733B] deliver him from the hands of the Syrians whom the king had sent to seize him, and what the holy prophet said to reassure the frightened Gehazi, give the author occasion (ch. 33) to observe what God invisibly does at all times for his faithful servants against the enemies of their salvation, and for the Church against those who attack doctrine: “Do not fear,” Elisha says, “for there are many more with us than with them . . . . The Lord opened the eyes of that servant, and he saw around Elisha a multitude of horses and chariots of fire” (4 Kings 6:16–17). “Let us likewise say,” says Rupert, “when we are surrounded by the enemies of Jesus Christ, whether visible or invisible; let us say in faith, in firm hope, and while approaching God through charity: ‘Do not fear, my soul; do not fear, Church: there are many more with us than with them.’ For if it is a matter of an invisible struggle against evil spirits, the Lord [Col. 0733C] is with us; the host of angels is with us; the Holy Spirit is with us, to fight and to make us victorious in this spiritual contest. If it is a matter of fighting the visible enemies of the Church in the persons of heretics, the Lord is likewise with us; the choir of apostles is with us; the multitude of patriarchs and prophets is with us. The army of martyrs is with us; the Holy Spirit, together with all Holy Scripture, is with us.”

Rupert concludes his exposition of Kings at the fifteenth chapter of the fourth book, that is, with the reign of Uzziah, under whom Isaiah began to prophesy. Christian piety, he says after St Jerome, has always regarded this prophet as an evangelist rather than a prophet. For he recounts the mysteries of Jesus Christ and of the Church so clearly that he resembles more a historian reporting past events than a prophet [Col. 0733D] announcing future things. The Commentary on Isaiah is divided into two books, in which the author, setting aside what is historical and moral, confines himself to seeking proofs of faith in Jesus Christ, according to the plan he has proposed for this work. He does not even oblige himself to gather exactly everything that relates to his design; hence, at the conclusion (Book II, ch. 30), he declares that he has omitted several passages with a very evident relation to faith and the calling of the Gentiles. Indeed, it may be said that he omitted a great many passages much better suited to his purpose than those he chose, so that it appears he [Col. 0734A] intended to leave aside those that are so clear and evident that it is impossible not to recognize Jesus Christ and his Church in them.

What Rupert did with Isaiah, he did with the other three major prophets. His Commentary on Jeremiah is contained in a single book of eighty-nine chapters. This prophecy marks the beginning of the fifth age—or, in the author’s language, its dawn. In the first age (ch. 1), before the Flood, man, like a little child, is left to himself without hearing the word of God. In the second age, like a child beginning to walk and speak, he receives the first elements of instruction in the covenant God makes with Noah. In the third age, man, being as it were in adolescence, receives in Abraham the promise of a blessed offspring, and in Moses the instruction of the law. In the fourth age, like a fully formed young man, he receives the promise of the kingdom of Jesus Christ. In the fifth age, which is [Col. 0734B] like mature adulthood, he receives the promise of the priesthood of Jesus Christ. It is in this capacity that the Messiah is represented by events and prophecies. It is true that in the preceding age Jesus Christ is already proclaimed as an eternal priest according to the order of Melchizedek; but in this age the cause and effects of his priesthood are represented more clearly, and the time of his coming is fixed more definitely. This priest, who was to deliver men from their sins, is true God, because only God can deliver from sins. The plan is very fine. One might wish that the author had been equally successful in its execution. But this cannot be said. We find only a few passages treated fairly well.

The reflections he makes (ch. 10) on what occurred at the potter’s house, where the Lord sent Jeremiah in order to make him hear his word (Jer. 18), [Col. 0734C] are . . . . . of a kind to inspire Christian humility. Jeremiah, having gone to the potter’s house, found him working at his wheel. At that moment the vessel he was making from the clay in his hand was spoiled, and immediately he remade it into another vessel, giving it whatever form he pleased. Then the Lord addressed his prophet, saying: “House of Israel, shall I not be able to do to you what the potter does with his clay? For you are in my hand what clay is in the potter’s hand” (Jer. 18:6). “Here,” says Rupert, “is a great lesson for us, teaching us to remain reverent and silent and to restrain our tongues [Note: [Col. 0733D] ‘A great lesson in reverence; a great and fitting instrument of silence and restraint of the tongue. God is our potter, and we are clay. We, I say, all alike—Jews as well as Greeks—are one [Col. 0734D] mass, one clay. Therefore let us not boldly examine God’s judgments, nor criticize our potter’s fingers. The Apostle, the vessel of election, exhorts us to this with vehement rebuke, etc.’]. God is the potter who forms us, and we are the clay. Yes, we are, Jews and Gentiles alike, one mass, one clay. Let us not therefore dare to probe God’s judgments or find fault with the work of our Creator. The Apostle (Rom. 9), that vessel of election, uses this example to instruct us forcefully, [Col. 0734D] and directs us to consider with the prophet the power of God.” After citing the words of St Paul, he continues: “To speak thus, the Apostle had to descend humbly in spirit into the potter’s house and see that the whole house of Israel was clay, like every other nation; and that God, the potter who forms them all, drew Abraham out of the clay of Chaldea—not because he owed him anything, but by grace alone—and that, from the same mass of clay of Abraham’s descendants, he made, as he willed, vessels of mercy, vessels of honour and grace. What [Col. 0735A] did he owe Abraham more than to the whole mass of clay descended from Adam?”

Of the eighty-nine chapters on Jeremiah, the author devotes only eleven to the explanation of the prophecies; the rest concern the Lamentations. He applies everything the holy prophet says about Nebuchadnezzar’s capture of Jerusalem to the siege and capture of the same city by the Romans.

The Commentary on Ezekiel is divided into two books. The Fathers, especially St Jerome and St Gregory, observed that this prophet is obscure and difficult to understand, particularly the vision of the mysterious living creatures and that of the structure of the temple and the city of Jerusalem. Rupert dwells especially on these visions; for, although they have been explained in various senses and at great length by many authors, nevertheless in a subject so elevated and obscure there always remains, he says, something to say after others and to clarify. His entire aim, as he says (Book II, ch. 1), in explaining [Col. 0735B] the vision of the living creatures is to discover in it the glory of the Holy Trinity, faith in Jesus Christ, and the glory of his kingdom. Following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers who explained this part of Scripture before him, he also makes his investigations (ch. 18), and congratulates himself on having found that this holy prophet, directed by the Holy Spirit, did not omit the childbirth of a virgin.

The Commentary on Daniel is contained in a single book, although the author adds Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who are the last three among the twelve minor prophets. The brevity he had prescribed for himself did not permit him to give explanations of the others. In the nineteenth chapter of this commentary one may note the author’s assertion that the Son of God would not have become incarnate if Adam had not sinned.

Finally, Rupert concludes the second part of his work on the Trinity with the Commentary on the Four Evangelists, which he contains in a single book. Until now [Col. 0735C] Jesus Christ had instructed men through the prophets whom he had sent to them; but now he himself is to speak to them. His birth (ch. 1) marks the sixth age, corresponding to the sixth day of the world’s creation. Our commentator is chiefly concerned to show that Jesus Christ is the one true King, yet King of an eternal kingdom. He is very brief in his commentary on this most precious part of Holy Scripture and explains only a few passages of the holy Gospel—apparently those which seemed to him most suited to his purpose: namely, to establish the spiritual kingship of Jesus Christ, by which, from being slaves through the birth we drew from a father enslaved to sin, he restored us to liberty and our ancient nobility by becoming incarnate for us.

The third part of the work on the Trinity, in which the author treats the works proper to the Holy Spirit, is divided into nine books. In the first he shows [Col. 0735D] (ch. 1) that, God having turned his face away from the children of Adam because of the father’s transgression, all died in soul and body, and that this double death is sin’s punishment. But we must also believe and remember, with every kind of thanksgiving, that God, because of the righteousness of one man, Jesus Christ, sent his Spirit, who has created us anew and renewed the face of the earth. “We must,” he says, “recognize in the gift of this twofold grace the glory of a twofold life. For, at the moment when a man believes in Jesus Christ and receives the sacrament of baptism, God sends his Holy Spirit and he is created, so that, the old age of sin having been destroyed, he [Col. 0736A] becomes a new creature with respect to the soul. Moreover, the face of the earth will be renewed; that is, the earthly body which has grown old and died because of sin will be renewed on the last day, which will be the day of resurrection.”

This twofold renewal of soul and body, or this twofold resurrection of the dead, is the subject Rupert proposes here to examine and discuss, to the glory of the Holy Spirit, who gives life to our souls and will restore it to our bodies.

The true way of considering this grace (ch. 2) is first to know Jesus Christ made man, the author and dispenser of grace, the mediator between God and men. Following this idea, the author undertakes in this book to show that the greatest, most excellent—in a word, most perfect—work of the Holy Spirit is the formation of Jesus Christ as man. By this means God has delivered us from the captivity to which we had been reduced; he has poured out upon us his [Col. 0736B] graces; and one day he will fill us with glory. He also proves that the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, distinct from the Father and the Son though of the same nature; that he proceeds from the Father and the Son; and that he is coeternal and consubstantial with them, truly God (chs. 3–6). He discusses (ch. 20) the appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and gives the reason why he chose this form rather than another. He compares the old man and the new, showing the difference between them by citing (ch. 24) what Holy Scripture says of them: “It is a certain thing, which no one can doubt, that all the saints of former ages, from the beginning of the world, were purified from their sins in the Holy Spirit, in the water, and in the blood that flowed from Christ’s side.” This leads him to say later (ch. 27) that “all the saints, up to St John, died before they had received remission of sins, because, after [Col. 0736C] awaiting it for a long time, they finally received it only in the Passion of Jesus Christ. They were formed in faith, mighty in miracles, and possessed the gift of prophecy; nevertheless they were all held” in hell on account of original sin [Note: [Col. 0735D] “For all up to John . . . . died before they received remission of sins. For they finally received, in Christ’s Passion alone, the remission long awaited. They were strong in faith, mighty in miracles, [Col. 0736D] endowed with prophetic grace; and yet all were held in the lower regions because of original sin.”]. One who speaks in this manner did not attribute to circumcision the power to remit original sin. According to Rupert (ch. 28), the division of the gifts of the Holy Spirit derives from his proceeding from the Father, while the grace of the remission of sins derives from his proceeding from the Son.

At the end of this first book on the works of the Holy Spirit, he sets out the plan of the others (ch. 31), in which he proposes to treat the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus these seven gifts constitute the matter of the third part of the Treatise on the Trinity and its Works, just as the seven days of creation, which are the works of the Father, formed the matter of the first part; and the seven ages of the world, which are [Col. 0736D] the works of the Son, formed that of the second.

The spirit of wisdom provides the subject of two books, the second and third. In the first of these, or second book overall, he shows that Christ as man received the fullness of wisdom; that the wisdom of this world is opposed to the wisdom which comes from the Holy Spirit; and that the one overturns order while the other establishes it. Rupert explains in this book (ch. 2) certain passages of Job, who, by his patience in suffering, was a figure of that of Jesus Christ. This gives him occasion to speak (chs. 3, 4, etc.) of that holy man—especially pleasing to him because he regretted not having yet mentioned Job in speaking of the patriarchs, prophets, [Col. 0737A] and kings who were figures and living images of Jesus Christ. Job, in cursing the day of his birth, curses the sin of the first man. The author indicates (ch. 7) that he has drawn part of what he says from St Gregory’s explanations. He follows this holy pope’s opinion concerning the sinful woman (ch. 27), whom he identifies with Mary Magdalene and with Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Having observed (ch. 28) that Mary, whom he claims is the sinful woman, had the advantage of seeing Jesus Christ after his resurrection before all the apostles, and that St Peter, who had denied him, likewise had this advantage over St John, the beloved disciple, he adds that the spirit of wisdom intended thereby to inspire confidence in sinners, strengthen the weak, and give them weapons with which to do violence to heaven. Yet its wisdom shines still more brightly in having allowed those upon whom it wished to confer such great favours, and whom it had predestined before all ages, to fall into [Col. 0737B] such great abysses of crimes. What fruit, what benefit, ought we not to draw from this?

Rupert here explains what he had said elsewhere: although all the apostles received jointly the power to bind and loose sinners, St Peter was nevertheless favoured with a particular privilege because he was the first to confess the divinity of Jesus Christ. This particular privilege granted to St Peter consists in the fact that St Peter was destined to be prince of the apostles—*princeps quippe apostolorum destinatus fuerat*—and was specially to receive, or had already received, the great power that Jesus Christ gave him when he said: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah . . . . . and I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16), etc. Rupert also reports what Jesus Christ said after his resurrection to the same apostle: “Simon, do you love me more than these? Feed my lambs; [Col. 0737C] feed my sheep” (John 21). He then continues: “Christian emperors and princes of the Church, founded upon the authority of this evangelical truth—*tali et tanta praeeunte evangelicae veritatis auctoritate*—established long afterwards, by an immutable law, that just as all governors and judges obey the emperor, so all prelates of the other Churches should be subject to Peter and to the Roman Pontiff because of the excellence of his dignity.” This is a great honour and a great elevation—*magnus honor, magna celsitudo*. Cyprians, Basils, and the other Fathers, especially in the first centuries of the Church, did not have such an idea of St Peter’s particular privilege; nor did even the holiest popes, such as St Gregory the Great, possess it . . . . . [“Humility kept the claim silent; but all, whether popes or bishops, no less recognized the supremacy in the person of St Peter’s successors [Col. 0737D].”—Editor P.]

Let us therefore acknowledge the genuine prerogatives of St Peter, which passed to his successors; let us acknowledge his primacy by divine right. But let us beware of degrading his colleagues and brothers in the episcopate; let us beware of believing that they owe him the same submission and obedience which governors and judges owe emperors and kings. Rupert seems to soften somewhat what he has asserted by adding that he who conferred so high a dignity upon St Peter gave him this warning: “Let him who is greatest among you become as the least, and he who governs as one who serves.” The author’s aim in this chapter is to show that God permitted St Peter’s enormous fall only to keep him humble at the high degree [Col. 0738A] of elevation in which he intended to place him, and to furnish, in his person, all those raised above others with a striking example teaching them to be humble and to bear with kindness and compassion the weaknesses of those under their care.

In the third book (ch. 1), which is the second concerning the spirit of wisdom, Rupert treats the two great sacraments by which we are renewed according to the pattern of the new man and which the same spirit of wisdom causes to flow upon us from the fountain of Christ’s Passion. These two great sacraments are baptism and the Eucharist, both so necessary to salvation that the kingdom of heaven is closed to anyone who does not receive them. This third book is a kind of abbreviated treatise on these two sacraments. He shows in it (ch. 3) the necessity of Christ’s baptism and how it differs from that of St John; then explains what St John means by the three that bear witness [Col. 0738B] on earth—the spirit, the water, and the blood (1 John 5). He derives proof of the divinity of Jesus Christ, his incarnation, the necessity of baptism, and its effects from what the same apostle adds: that there are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit.

To these six witnesses he adds (ch. 18) a seventh: the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus. It is impossible to speak more clearly and more orthodoxly concerning the real presence of Jesus Christ in this august sacrament than Rupert does in chapters 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24. If anyone, after reading these chapters, still had doubts concerning the purity of Rupert’s faith, one may say with Dom Gerberon [Note: [Col. 0737D] Gerberon, *Apology for Rupert*, p. 233.], “for such a man the earth is surely shaking and the sun is darkened”: *Si Ruperti fides vel dubia vel obscura cui videtur, ipsi sane terra nutat et sol tenebras habet*—“If Rupert’s faith seems doubtful or obscure to anyone, then surely the earth itself shakes beneath him and the sun is in darkness.”

[Col. 0738C] Not content with having established the faith of the Church concerning the real presence in chapter 21 and in the other chapters we have cited, he defends it (ch. 22) against those who, misusing a text of Saint Augustine, attacked it; and he shows that they had misunderstood the meaning of that holy doctor’s words: “They believed,” he says, “that Saint Augustine had asserted that it is not the body or blood of Jesus Christ which the unworthy receive; and that consequently, in the judgment of this great doctor, what we visibly receive at the Lord’s table is not the body and blood of Jesus Christ, but only the figure of his body and blood. He neither said nor thought this: *hoc ille non dixit*—‘he did not say this.’ He is not accustomed to contradict Jesus Christ. Now Christ, speaking in his own person, said: This is my body, this is my blood; and, speaking through his Apostle, … he said: Whoever shall eat unworthily the bread of the Lord and drink unworthily the chalice [Col. 0738D] of the Lord shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, … for he who eats and drinks it unworthily eats and drinks his condemnation. He does not say: He who eats and drinks it unworthily eats ordinary, common bread and drinks wine such as it was before consecration; rather, he is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord; he drinks and eats his own condemnation, not discerning the body of the Lord.”

Rupert then explains the meaning of Saint Augustine’s words, distinguishing with him the sacrament from the effect of the sacrament. He who approaches it unworthily, he says, does not partake of Christ’s sufferings; he does not receive with the mouth of the soul what he receives with that of the body, and in this very respect he is unworthy of it. This visible sacrament, therefore, is the body and blood of Jesus Christ which he receives; for his [Col. 0739A] unworthiness does not nullify the dignity of such a consecration. But he does not receive the effect of the sacrament, because he does not consider Christ’s Passion with a heart and faith working through charity. Therefore he does not receive the effect of this same sacrament in such a way that Christ’s body is delivered up and his blood shed for him, to obtain eternal life and rise again on the day of judgment. Rather, what he receives produces in him the wholly contrary effect: he makes himself guilty of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, and eats and drinks his condemnation. How could an author who speaks in this manner, and combats so vigorously the error of those who maintain that Christ’s body and blood are present in the Eucharist only figuratively—how, I say, could such an author have been accused by Bellarmine and others of holding views contrary to the Church’s faith concerning the real presence?

Each person ought to examine himself, as the Apostle says, [Col. 0739B] in order to eat this bread and drink this chalice; for so great a sacrament should not be given to those unworthy of it (ch. 23). When we speak in this way, most people are troubled: some because their conscience reproaches them with faults; others because Christian humility makes them believe themselves unworthy of so great a mystery. Yet there is a great difference between considering oneself unworthy and being judged such by others. Whoever considers the greatness of this sacrament is right to think himself unworthy of it, and it is praiseworthy to have this feeling; for who can boast of having a pure heart? (ch. 24). It is of such persons that the Apostle says: If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged.

Jesus Christ said: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16); he also said: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). This shows the effects and necessity of the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist. [Col. 0739C] They were instituted to erase the twofold sin committed by our first father in violating God’s commandment. A double evil required a double remedy: pride was to be healed by humility, and the vice of gluttony by the antidote of better food (ch. 26).

> [Note: Col. 0739D] “If you ask why … both sacraments are necessary for a human being’s salvation, … it is plainly because sin was committed by man in a twofold manner. One sin was indeed that of pride; the other was that of gluttony. … Therefore, because the sin was doubled, the sacrament too was rightly doubled.” [Col. 0740D]

The first resurrection is to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and then to eat the body and drink the blood of the Lord. But since, in being reborn through baptism into Jesus, we are delivered from the guilt of our first father, why, someone may perhaps ask, do we still bear the penalty of his sin? Why do we die? Why do we not pass from this life to a better one without undergoing the penalty of death? It is because God, by an effect not only of his justice but also of his mercy, in remitting Adam’s sin to the recipient of baptism, does not exempt him from the penalty of death to which he condemned [Col. 0739D] the first sinner and all his posterity. By wise providence God imposed upon man a punishment so fitted to humble his pride. It is even an effect of his mercy; for if God had allowed us to be immortal after sin, we would be like demons, because we would have a miserable eternity, or an eternal misery.

> [Note: Col. 0740D] “For if, after sin, we had been permitted to live the life of the body and to be immortal, we would be like demons, because, no less than they, we would have a miserable eternity, or eternal misery.”

In the fourth book of the third part (ch. 1), Rupert treats of the spirit of understanding. Who, he asks, received this spirit, and to whom did God give understanding of the Scriptures? Not orators but sinners; not the scribes [Col. 0740A] and Pharisees, but simple and unlearned people. He then speaks of the admirable change wrought by the Holy Spirit in the Apostles on the day of Pentecost. To convey an idea of the abundance of light they received that day (ch. 4 ff.), of the understanding of Scripture and knowledge of all truth which they acquired, he recounts Saint Peter’s explanation of the prophet Joel’s words in the first instruction he gave the people immediately after the descent of the Holy Spirit. Entering into greater detail, he shows by the example of those Apostles who wrote—Saint John, Saint Matthew, Saint James, and Saint Jude—what abundance of grace and illumination they received for understanding the Holy Scriptures.

As for Saint Paul (ch. 18), that vessel of election, it is true that he was not an unlearned man, since he had been instructed by Gamaliel, as he himself tells us (Acts 22:3); yet it was through a special revelation of Jesus Christ, and not [Col. 0740B] through the ministry of any human being, that he received understanding of the spiritual sense of the Law and of Christ’s Gospel. Although he was not among the Apostles when, by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they received the grace of apostleship and understanding of the Scriptures, this same grace was bestowed upon him in abundance (ch. 20 ff.). Our author demonstrates this by selecting, among his letters, that addressed to the Romans, in order to uncover the treasures of wisdom and knowledge which the Holy Spirit placed in this vessel of election.

We shall not enlarge upon what Rupert says of this admirable epistle, but we cannot refrain from recalling a judicious observation he makes in the eighth chapter of this same book concerning the certainty we must have regarding everything said by the sacred writers: “Since these writers were instructed,” he says, “not by men but by the Holy Spirit, by the spirit of understanding, which wonderfully revealed to them the treasure [Col. 0740C] of the Scriptures, we receive and hear their words as proceeding from the mouth of God, and regard it as a crime to doubt any of the things written by those to whom this sacred fire gave an understanding heart and a learned tongue.”

What Rupert says here he extends not only to all the Apostles who wrote, but also to the patriarchs and prophets to whom God’s word was addressed without the mediation of any human being. “As for all other writers who are not of this number and were not, like them, directly instructed by the Holy Spirit, he declares that he believes what they say only insofar as they support their assertions by the authority of the former writers, or by some sound reason; not merely because they said it or held such an opinion.” He repeats at the close what he had already said: that he regards it as a crime to doubt the least thing written by [Col. 0740D] the sacred writers:

> “Therefore we believe in every respect these writings of the peoples, the writings of rulers—that is, of prophets and Apostles—so that we judge it wicked and alien to faith in Christ to doubt anything concerning them.”

He counts five Apostles who wrote: Saint Peter, Saint John, Saint James, Saint Matthew, and Saint Jude; to these he adds Saint Mark and Saint Luke.

The spirit of counsel is the subject of the fifth book, whose plan the author set out in these words at the end of the first book of the third part of the work on the Trinity: “We must glorify the Holy Spirit of counsel in the blindness which befell Israel until the fullness of the nations should [Col. 0741A] enter, and in the destruction of the temple of the old worship, which was overthrown so that it might not impede the rapid advance of the Gospel.” Rupert carries out this plan in his reflections on the judgments of God, whose designs over the children of men are terrible. This appears very strikingly in the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles (Book V, ch. 1).

Our author (ch. 3) distinguishes two kinds of counsel: one which God deigns to employ for his glory on behalf of human beings; the other which human beings employ for God’s glory and for their own salvation. He gives as an example of the first kind what God did in abolishing circumcision, the Law of Moses with all its ceremonies, and other things which he had established and been pleased to approve for a time. The example of the second kind of counsel is taken from what is done by persons who, not content with abstaining from unlawful things, renounce even things that are permitted. Such are Christian virgins who live according to the counsel Saint Paul gives them. Such are those who, aspiring to perfection, sell all their possessions and give them to the poor in order to follow Jesus Christ.

Having thus distinguished (ch. 4) the two sorts of counsel, Rupert, turning to the first, speaks of the terrible judgment God exercised in rejecting a people dear to him in order to substitute the Gentiles; in enclosing all people in unbelief in order afterwards to pour out his mercy upon all (ch. 5). What do these words mean: “God willed that all should be enclosed in unbelief, in order to show mercy to all” (Rom. 11:31), unless it be that God ordered matters so that no one might be saved except through mercy, and that by this means all might be delivered from the malign sword of pride? This suited our wretched condition, so that every occasion for pride might be taken away, because the angel fell through [Col. 0741C] pride, and after the angel’s fall, man, created in God’s image, likewise fell through pride. Therefore, wishing to remove from man every occasion of glorying, God rejected even the people that gloried in being Abraham’s race.

> [Note: Col. 0741D] “What does it mean that God enclosed all in unbelief in order to have mercy on all, except that God provided that no one should be saved otherwise than through mercy, [Col. 0742D] and that thus all might be delivered from the malign sword of pride? For this was expedient for our wretched condition, that every occasion of pride might be taken from us, etc.”

From this one sees that God’s purpose in all his dealings with human beings is to deprive them of every pretext for proud self-exaltation, so that the earthen vessel may not presume to say to the potter: Why have you made me thus?

When the fullness of the Gentiles entered by receiving the Gospel, the Holy Spirit relieved them of the heavy yoke of the ceremonies of the Law of Moses (ch. 6, 7, etc.); and indeed it was fitting that circumcision and the whole apparatus of these ceremonies should cease when the grace of the Gospel appeared. God himself testifies through his prophets that he did not require the Jews to offer sacrifices to him (ch. 11). It was likewise by a consequence of God’s designs (ch. 15) that the city of [Col. 0741D] Jerusalem with its temple was reduced to ashes, and the inhabitants of that unfortunate city were put to the sword or perished from hunger during the siege, except for a small number who, escaping misery, fire, or sword, were scattered and carried captive into different parts of the world. There, unwillingly, by their captivity and dispersion, they bore the most conspicuous testimony to the truth of the Gospel.

Having thus explained what he means by saying that God deigns to use counsel for his glory on behalf of human beings, Rupert also explains how human beings employ, or ought to employ, counsel for God, for his glory, and for their own salvation. To employ counsel, he says, is not to be content [Col. 0742A] with doing what is commanded, but to go beyond it and do something more than is ordered, in order to merit one’s master’s favor and a greater reward. He then applies his rule to the Ten Commandments and shows with what spirit of counsel they should be observed in order to please God and render oneself worthy of reward.

In the sixth book (ch. 1), Rupert treats of the spirit of fortitude. He considers this spirit first in Jesus Christ, then in the Apostles and apostolic men who preached the Gospel, and in the martyrs who shed their blood in its defense. What a change did not the spirit of fortitude make in Saint Peter and Saint Paul? Who could recount all the marvels it worked through the Apostle of the nations? He portrays (ch. 9) these two Apostles as two brothers united by the spiritual bonds of holy union, sent to Rome against the two brothers who founded that city, one of whom had [Col. 0742B] dipped his hands in the other’s blood. They were sent to preach Jesus Christ there, establish the foundation of concord upon the ruins of discord, and shed their blood to found a new city which, through the solidity of apostolic faith, deserved to be called the seat of justice and the house of faith; whereas it had formerly been the throne of pride, the abyss of avarice, and a gulf of blood and murder. It was under the cruel and infamous Nero that Saint Peter and Saint Paul preached the faith at Rome and sealed it with their blood (ch. 10).

The same spirit of fortitude shone forth in the other Apostles who carried the standard of the cross throughout the world, triumphed over the devil, and shed their blood to establish Christ’s Church (ch. 11–12). Although Saint John did not shed his own blood and died in peace after surviving all the Apostles, he nevertheless drank the Lord’s chalice. Next come the struggles of the martyrs, of whom Saint Stephen is first, while Saint Lawrence holds a distinguished place among them. Rupert dwells at length upon both. He had a particular reason for doing so in the case of Saint Lawrence, the titular saint of his monastery.

The martyrs, who had received the spirit of fortitude in order to fight and defend the faith by the shedding of their blood, were succeeded in Christ’s Church by doctors filled with the spirit of knowledge in order to defend it with their pens. It is of this spirit that Rupert speaks in his seventh book (ch. 1). The devil, who had initially attacked the Church through the open persecution waged against it by Nero and the other emperors, saw himself, despite his efforts, expelled from his temples and even pagan princes embracing the faith. He then attacked it as a dragon: that is, by employing cunning and artifice and raising up heretics who, under the name of Christians, deceived the faithful and caused them to fall into error. Thus, after the spirit of [Col. 0742D] fortitude, the spirit of knowledge became necessary to the Church for the defense of the faith amid the dangers in which it found itself.

Rupert examines (ch. 2) the difference between knowledge and wisdom, and what vain knowledge and useful knowledge are. Saint Paul did not condemn the latter (ch. 3–4), “nor the schools of grammarians, dialecticians, rhetoricians, arithmeticians, geometers, musicians, and astronomers. But he reproves them because in these arts they did not seek the fruit for which God gave them to humankind: namely, to rise to their author and glorify him.” Some are wrong to be prejudiced against knowledge because Saint Paul said, “knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1), as though these two things were [Col. 0743A] opposed to each other and could not coexist.

Not only (ch. 9) the gift of prophecy but every lawful kind of knowledge is God’s gift: *Prophetica et omnis licita scientia donum ipsius est*—“Prophetic knowledge and all lawful knowledge are his gift.” Yet he customarily fills more abundantly with his gifts those who make good use of them. Therefore he willed that those whom he destined to defend the faith, and whose tongues he deigned to use in combating heretics and spreading instruction in the Church, should be educated in the liberal arts. He willed that they should not only read and understand others’ writings, but also compose writings themselves whose reading would benefit the faithful. Thus the seven liberal arts, leaving profane and licentious schools, entered as handmaids into the service of wisdom, to be employed, according to God’s commands, in useful works (ch. 10).

But why do we say that the arts entered this school, since they were already there, and since those who have read and examined the Holy Scriptures agree that they are found in them? Our author proves this (ch. 11), showing in detail that it is in Holy Scripture that the first use of the liberal arts is discovered; and therefore the Greeks are wrong to claim their invention, since Scripture, which speaks of them, surpasses all other books not only in its divine authority and its usefulness, because it leads to supreme happiness, but also in antiquity. Rupert examines each liberal art in turn—grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy—and in as many chapters shows the use made of them in Scripture, where they possess a beauty and brilliance which they can have in no other writer. “We believe,” he says (ch. 12), “and certainly are not mistaken, that there is no work by any secular writer which, [Col. 0743C] when compared with the narratives of Holy Scripture, does not appear feeble, diffuse, and obscure.”

To fulfill his plan properly, Rupert should, after speaking of the holy books, have spoken at suitable length of the writings of the holy Fathers and shown the use they made of arts and sciences. But he contents himself with saying only a word concerning Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine. He gives the latter high praise, saying (ch. 19) that the Holy Spirit visibly wrought wonderful things in him for God’s glory, for the defense of the Church and Catholic faith, and to protect it from the enemy’s insult. “This Augustine,” he adds, “is the pillar and foundation of truth—*iste est Augustinus columna et firmamentum veritatis*—the pillar of cloud in which God’s wisdom placed its throne, and from whose mouth there continually flows a saving rain, or rather a rushing torrent against heretics.”

He observes that God permitted Augustine in his youth to be given over to Manichaean errors, but that even while he was in error the Holy Spirit, without his knowing it, placed within him a great gift of knowledge, which he would one day employ for the Church’s good. After relating what Saint Augustine says in his *Confessions* concerning the abilities God gave him for learning, he continues and concludes his eulogy: “In this we must praise the spirit of knowledge, which thus prepared this great man and used him to fight heretics throughout his life, not only by the living voice but also by so great a number of writings that one human lifetime would not suffice to read them.”

The spirit of piety is the subject of the eighth book, which properly consists only of a long paraphrase of the parable of the prodigal son, from which Rupert takes occasion to commend God’s goodness toward penitent sinners. The murmur of the elder brother, [Col. 0744A] angered at the welcome his father gave his brother after he had squandered all his property, returns our author to the subject of the Jews’ conversion, in accordance with the plan he had formed (Book I, ch. 31): “We must praise the spirit of piety in that, when the fullness of the nations has entered, then the veil will be removed and the remnant of Israel will be converted.”

He maintains (ch. 19) that the Jews’ return will occur only after they have recognized Antichrist as the Messiah and are disabused when they see him destroyed. This is an idea peculiar to him and a result of his taste for allegory. In reading this book one notices that the author knew the ancient canons of the Church concerning penance. According to these canons, clerics who had fallen into certain crimes were excluded forever from the holy ministry and reduced to lay communion. He understands this only of those who did not acknowledge their crimes and were convicted of them by some means other than their [Col. 0744B] own confession (ch. 7). As for those who confessed them and did penance, they were restored. It even appears that, according to the discipline of that age, both alike were restored to their ministry when they had performed suitable penance.

One sees (ch. 21) that the ancient discipline of the Church concerning penance had been greatly weakened, and that sins which formerly were expiated only by seven or twelve years of penance were remitted by penances of one year, or even forty days, and sometimes three days, following Nineveh’s example. The sinner (ch. 22) must be raised again in order to be admitted to participation in our holy mysteries: *nisi enim qui mortuus fuerat revixerit, non licet eum invitari vel admitti … ad participationem corporis et sanguinis Domini*—“for unless the one who was dead has come to life again, it is not permitted to invite or admit him … to participation in the body and blood of the Lord.” But how is one to know whether he has come to life again? By the confession and penance he has performed: *Nimirum vox confessionis … Quia confusus est et dignam poenitentiam* [Col. 0744C] *obtulit*—“Assuredly, [it is] the voice of confession … because he has been put to shame and has offered worthy penance.”

Finally, Rupert treats of the spirit of fear in the ninth book, which is the last of the third part and of the entire work on the Trinity. The end of all the truths (ch. 1) which Scripture sets before us for belief and confession is the universal judgment, which is the greatest and principal foundation of the fear of the Lord. Indeed, it must be a great cause of fear, and of intense fear, for all human beings. This final day of the world bears a particular relation to the first day of its creation. Just as God on that first day separated light from darkness—which our author understands as the separation of good from evil angels (ch. 2)—so on the last day he will judge human beings and separate the good from the evil by an irrevocable sentence.

Rupert speaks very precisely and as an able theologian concerning fear (ch. 4). What he says on [Col. 0744D] this subject deserves particular attention. He distinguishes two good kinds of fear according to the differing character of those who fear God: one is that of slaves, who fear punishment, and he calls it servile; the other is that of children, who fear losing grace, and he calls it honorable or free fear. To distinguish these two fears more clearly, he adds: “Servile fear, accompanied by pain, is the fear of beginners—that is, of those who begin to turn to God and call to mind the pains of hell, and who, by the remembrance of these pains, endeavor to resist sin. This is not yet wisdom, but only the beginning of wisdom; it is not the fear of the Lord, but fear of death; it is not truly holy fear, but only fear, or fear [Col. 0745A] accompanied by pain and disturbance. But the fear of children is the fear of the perfect, or of those tending toward perfection: namely, those who, considering the great graces they have received, are themselves moved to fear losing them. This fear differs greatly from the other and in many ways, above all in this: perfect charity casts out this servile fear which is accompanied by pain, whereas filial fear always remains. They have this in common: each wounds the soul and, as it were, draws blood from it through the tears shed by the eyes. Yet the cause is quite different. In servile fear, it is the grief of a troubled soul afraid of hell; in filial fear, it is the desire of an exiled soul which sighs after its homeland.”

These two kinds of fear are both good. But there are two others which are bad [Col. 0745B] (ch. 5). This makes four kinds of fear of which the soul is capable. The first of these bad fears is a certain passion or disturbance of the soul which proceeds neither from faith nor from the Spirit of God, and which even pagan philosophers condemn. This fear is bad because it disturbs the soul over things for which it ought not to be disturbed, such as the loss of worldly riches or adversities by which it is threatened.

There is another bad fear which comes from faith but not from the Spirit of God, through which the soul is troubled but does not amend itself. “This fear is bad, although it comes from faith and not from the Spirit of God, because it does not come from a faith which works through charity, but from an idle faith, and therefore a dead one.”

> [Note: Col. 0745D] *Est ergo timor malus ex fide quidem, sed non ex Spiritu Dei, quia non ex fide per dilectionem operatur, sed ex fide otiosa et ideo mortua.* “Therefore this fear is bad: it comes indeed from faith, but not from the Spirit of God, because it does not work from faith through love, but from an idle and therefore dead faith.”

This is the fear of all demons. It is also the fear, not of all wicked persons, but of many. It was the fear of Felix, governor of [Col. 0745C] Judaea, who was terrified while hearing Saint Paul speak of justice, charity, and the last judgment, but did not amend himself (Acts 24:25).

After speaking of the two kinds of fear he calls bad—which must be understood in relation to the dispositions of those in whom they are found—Rupert returns to the two kinds of good fear: one the fear of slaves, the other that of children; one of beginners, the other of the perfect. The first, or the fear of slaves, is a passion and disturbance of the soul which comes from faith and the Spirit of God. Though imperfect, this fear is good and produces a very good effect by introducing division into a person through the conflict it causes between spirit and flesh.

The terrible judgment of God, which Scripture announces as to be held on the last day, is quite capable of inspiring fear in anyone willing to reflect upon it and consider that after this [Col. 0745D] life no time remains to the sinner and ungodly person for doing penance. Our author gives a fairly vivid picture of that dreadful day and its consequences: the resurrection which shall take place in a moment at the trumpet’s sound; the irrevocable sentence to be pronounced; the deeds for which human beings will be judged; the reward the righteous will receive; and the eternal punishments and fire to which the wicked, together with the devil and rebellious angels, will be condemned.

It may be said of this work that its plan is fine, but that it is not carried out as successfully as it might have been had the author been more methodical, less given over to his taste for allegory, and more concerned, by employing his learning and erudition—which were considerable for the age in which [Col. 0746A] he lived—to treat questions soundly rather than multiply them needlessly. Wishing to speak of an infinity of matters and of all the truths of religion, he has almost merely indicated them without supporting them by solid proofs, and he often loses sight of his subject. It is true that he speaks to believers convinced of the truths he places before them and entertaining no doubt of them. He was not then dealing with pretended philosophers such as those we see today, whose foolish hearts are full of darkness; who, calling the most certain truths into question, devote themselves to reasoning as vain as it is impious against a religion which has always triumphed, and always shall triumph, over error and falsehood.

Whatever its quality, this work must have cost its author much labor; it shows that he had not only read and meditated much upon Holy Scripture, but was also very well versed in reading the Fathers, ecclesiastical writers, and even [Col. 0746B] secular authors, especially poets.

**2.** The second work of Rupert, according to the order of the latest edition which we follow, is his *Commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets*. Addressing it to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, who had urged him to undertake this work, the author declares that in the books of the prophets, as in the other books of Holy Scripture, he sought only Jesus Christ, “whose truth,” he says, “possessed their hearts, filled their mouths, and guided their pens, so that they had no other intention than to honor and glorify him.”

The Commentary on Hosea, the first of the twelve minor prophets, is preceded by a preface in which our author explains why these sacred writers wrote obscurely, and why the Jews placed their writings among the sacred books although they had persecuted their authors during their lifetime. To the first [Col. 0746C] question he replies that the prophets acted thus from prudence, and to avoid the ill-treatment of a nation which, as it persecuted Isaiah and Jeremiah, would have persecuted them had they announced plainly and without figure that the Jews would one day crucify the Messiah sent to them and that the Temple would be destroyed. To the second question he replies that, since the prophets foretold events, some of which were not to be fulfilled until after a long succession of centuries while others were to be fulfilled soon after the prophecy, the fulfilment of those events predicted as imminent led the Jews to judge that those who had announced them had prophesied through the Spirit of God; and that fulfilment became for them proof of the truth of the things they had foretold for more distant times. Thus they placed their writings in the canon of inspired books.

[Col. 0746D] The Commentary on Hosea is divided into six books. In it the commentator employs the light he drew from Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine for understanding this difficult and obscure prophet. His commentaries on the other minor prophets consist of one book on Joel, preceded by a prologue; four on Amos, with a prologue; one on Obadiah, with a prologue; two on Jonah, with a prologue; three on Micah, and a prologue.

After commenting on these six minor prophets, Rupert’s zeal slackened because of the difficulty he encountered in continuing his work; and, believing that there was presumption in his undertaking, he interrupted it. During this interval Cunon, abbot of Siegburg, believing Rupert had completed his commentaries, persuaded him to undertake [Col. 0747A] another work under the title *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Once this work was finished, Rupert resumed the one he had interrupted and continued his explanations of the other six minor prophets at the urging of Ekkenbert, abbot of Corbie, or Corvey, in Saxony. He addresses them to Ekkenbert in a preface placed at their head. These explanations comprise several books: three on the prophecy of Nahum; three on that of Habakkuk, with a preface; two on Zephaniah, with a prologue; one on Haggai, with a prologue; five on Zechariah, with a prologue; and one on Malachi, with a prologue.

We shall not dwell upon these explanations, which are in the same manner as those already discussed. Jesus Christ and his Church are what Rupert seeks everywhere; and indeed they are what must be sought in Holy Scripture. But he does not do so with sufficient order and method. Consequently, in general his explanations of the various sacred books are less continuous commentaries, suited to clarifying and [Col. 0747B] imparting the meaning of the text, than a collection of excellent thoughts and pious, edifying reflections upon the sacred text, which gives him occasion to speak of Jesus Christ and his mysteries, his Church, his elect, and the truths of Christianity. The literal sense of Scripture is too much neglected; the mystical and moral senses are those to which the author applies himself, though otherwise he displays learning and erudition uncommon for his age.

His commentaries on the minor prophets seemed to M. Dupin “more continuous [Note: [Col. 0747D] Twelfth century, p. 721.], and more in the form of commentaries than those on Genesis and other books in which he treats of the Trinity and its works; they depart less from the manner of the ancients, although they are extremely mystical and full of excessively subtle reflections and observations which do not possess all possible correctness.”

Rupert himself supplied three catalogues of his works. In the first he counts only [Col. 0747C] thirty books of commentaries on the minor prophets; in the other two he counts thirty-two. But there is a copyist’s error, as Dom Gerberon observes [Note: [Col. 0747D] *Apology for Rupert*, p. 52.], for thirty-two are found in every edition.

### 3. Commentary on the Song of Songs, on the Incarnation of the Lord

The Commentary on the Song of Songs, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, is divided into seven books and preceded by a prologue, in which the author informs us of the motives that led him to undertake this work. Some years previously he had intended to compose a work on the Incarnation, on the occasion of a vision in which he felt, as it were, the breath of a gentle wind enter his ears with inexpressible swiftness and deposit there these two verses:

> A woman conceived God in her mind, Christ in her body;  
> Whole and undefiled, she brought him forth, with no man acting.

Rupert had abandoned his intention when the [Col. 0747D] urgings of Cunon, abbot of Siegburg, who often pressed him to write, led him to take up the pen to carry it out, recalling his vision. The Song of Songs serves him as the basis for treating of the Incarnation. Every song in Scripture is an act of thanksgiving to thank God for some benefit received. Such is Moses’ song after the crossing of the Red Sea. Solomon’s song is the most excellent of all, having as its subject the incarnation of the Son of God, the greatest benefit humankind has ever received from [Col. 0748A] God and the greatest mark of his love. This is why it is called not simply a song, but the *Song of Songs*: because the benefit for which God is thanked in it is the benefit of benefits: “The Song of Songs is therefore rightly so called, because what is sung in it is the benefit of all God’s benefits.”

It is difficult to determine when Rupert composed this work. All that can be said, from the information provided by Dom Gerberon [Note: [Col. 0747D] *Ibid.*, p. 21 ff.], is that he composed it after his treatise on the Trinity and before he put the finishing touch to his work on Saint Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. Rupert’s apologist establishes both points by fairly solid reasons.

This work is a continuous commentary on the text of the Song, which the commentator applies almost entirely to the Blessed Virgin. He extols the excellence of her virtues and the prerogatives she received from God as mother of Jesus Christ, God and man. [Col. 0748B] This is the sense in which he explains this book *On the Incarnation*, which in his plan ought to have been its principal subject, but in the execution is merely secondary. As in his other commentaries, he ranges at length over numerous commonplaces: the mysteries of Jesus Christ, the sin of our first parents, the promises made to Abraham, the persecutions stirred up by the devil against the Synagogue and the Church, and so forth. The seventh and final book, in which he explains the last chapter of the Song, is wholly concerned with the Church of Jesus Christ, especially with its birth and beginnings.

Although Rupert extols, as we have said, the excellence of the Blessed Virgin’s virtues and her prerogatives above all other creatures, he nevertheless does not grant her the prerogative of being able to say that she was conceived without sin:

> “You could truly say,” he says in Book I, addressing the Blessed Virgin, “I was conceived in iniquity, [Col. 0748C] and my mother conceived me in sin; for, being of the mass corrupted in Adam, you were not free from the hereditary stain of original sin. But neither this sin nor any other could stand before the love of God with which you were filled; before this fire all straw was consumed, so that the dwelling-place in which God was to dwell for the full nine months might become wholly holy, and that the material from which the wisdom of God was to build for itself an eternal dwelling might be altogether pure.”

[Note: [Col. 0747D] “For since you were of the mass that was corrupted in Adam, you were not without the hereditary stain of original sin; but before the face of this love neither that sin nor any other could stand. Before the face of this [Col. 0748D] fire all straw perished, so that the dwelling in which God would dwell for the whole nine months might become wholly holy; the material altogether clean from which the holy wisdom of God would build an eternal house for itself.”]

### 4. Commentary on Job

The Commentary on Job is divided into forty-two chapters. In the prologue placed at its head, the author, adopting Saint Jerome’s view, says that some were mistaken in asserting that Job was descended from Esau and in claiming that he was descended from Nahor, whose eldest son was named Uz and gave his name to the country inhabited by Job.

The last editor of Rupert’s works boasts [Col. 0748D] of being the first to publish this work. Nevertheless, Lipen records three different editions at Cologne, in 1533, 1566, and 1602 [Note: [Col. 0748D] Lipen, *Theological Bibliography*, vol. II, p. 111.]. But Lipen is certainly mistaken regarding the edition of 1602, in which the Commentary on Job is not found. It may also be absent from the editions of 1533 and 1566.

Dom Gerberon [Note: [Col. 0748D] Gerberon, *Apology for Rupert*, p. 7.] places this work among the earliest productions of our abbot and believes it is the work mentioned in his dedicatory epistle to Cunon at the head of the first book on the Rule of [Col. 0749A] Saint Benedict. He says in that epistle that he made a short commentary on Job, an abridgment of the fertile abundance both of Saint Gregory’s meanings and of his expressions. Although this commentary is divided in printed editions into forty-two chapters, like the book of Job, rather than into ten books, as Rupert says, it is evident that it is the same work; and the present difference in division derives from copyists who imagined that a division into forty-two chapters would be more convenient than the division into ten books made by Rupert. This is Dom Gerberon’s observation, and in support of it he further notes that both in the catalogues made by Rupert himself of his works and in the printed editions only one Commentary on Job is mentioned.

A further confirmation that the commentary divided into forty-two chapters is the same as that which Rupert divided into ten [Col. 0749B] books is that the forty-two-chapter work corresponds perfectly to Rupert’s own description of his work as an abridgment of the fertile abundance of Saint Gregory’s meanings and expressions. Indeed, if one takes the trouble to compare the Commentary on Job in forty-two chapters with Saint Gregory’s *Moralia* on the same book, one will see that it is properly only an abridgment, and that the author contributed very little of his own. This is so evident that, having noticed it, the editor believed he could omit the fourteenth chapter, referring readers to Saint Gregory’s work. The commentary in question is historical, allegorical, and moral. Dom Gerberon believes that it was composed after the books on the Divine Office.

### 5. Commentary on Ecclesiastes

The Commentary on Ecclesiastes, divided into five books, concludes the first volume of the edition of 1638. In Dom Gerberon’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0749D] Gerberon, *Apology for Rupert*, p. 40.], it is one of the last productions of Rupert’s pen. He composed it in old age and addressed it to a monk named Gregory, with whom he was bound in very close friendship. Gregory himself had urged Rupert to this task and asked him to make the commentary according to “our translation,” that is, “the Hebrew truth” (*secundum nostram translationem, scilicet Hebraicam veritatem*). That is to say, Gregory asked Rupert to follow the translation made from Hebrew, because the commentary Saint Jerome had made by following the Septuagint version seemed mutilated and very imperfect.

To comply with his friend’s wishes, Rupert read and reread the commentary Saint Jerome made on Ecclesiastes following the Septuagint version, in order to determine whether that version was as imperfect as Gregory claimed. Through this examination Rupert became convinced of the truth of what his friend had said concerning the imperfection of the Septuagint version, and composed his commentary on Ecclesiastes in conformity with Gregory’s request. Dom [Col. 0749D] Gerberon [Note: [Col. 0750D] *Ibid.*, p. 138.] concludes from this that Rupert knew Hebrew and Greek very well, since he composed commentaries on Ecclesiastes following the Hebrew truth and recognized the deficiencies of Saint Jerome’s work, who, while working on the same book of Scripture, had followed the Septuagint version.

However plausible this reasoning may appear, it is difficult to persuade oneself that Rupert possessed enough knowledge of Hebrew to translate a book of Holy Scripture from the Hebrew original. The words *secundum nostram translationem, scilicet Hebraicam veritatem* do not expressly indicate that Gregory urged Rupert to work from the original itself. They can quite readily be explained in another and more natural sense: Gregory asked Rupert to follow a translation made from Hebrew which was [Col. 0750A] preserved in his monastery and which he therefore called “our translation.”

We grant here, as we have already done elsewhere, that many passages, particularly in the earlier works of which we have spoken, give reason to believe that Hebrew was not unknown to Rupert. Yet, besides the fact that it is quite likely that even in those passages he speaks only after Saint Jerome, he is sometimes seen to be perplexed by texts that would have posed no difficulty to him had he possessed any knowledge of Hebrew. All things considered, this does not permit us to believe that he was sufficiently skilled in that language to compose a commentary on the original text of Ecclesiastes.

At the head of the first book of this commentary, which is divided into five, the author provides a fairly accurate conception of Ecclesiastes, which greatly surpasses all the writings of the most celebrated philosophers of antiquity, such as Plato, Pythagoras, Socrates, [Col. 0750B] and Aristotle. Each of the other four books is preceded by a short preface addressed to Gregory. Although Rupert assures us that he did not wish to employ an elevated style and indeed neglected it, this is nevertheless one of his works in which he most displays the knowledge he had of authors of good Latin, particularly poets, including Virgil and Horace. He always shows a preference for the former of these two poets. He places him not merely above the poets, but does not believe him inferior to the philosophers. He cites several other good authors—Terence, Cicero, and so forth. It is apparent that he had read Plato, Aristotle, and other ancient philosophers. He uses the Fathers, Saint Augustine and others, but ordinarily without citing them. All this proves the breadth of his learning and knowledge.

Of all Rupert’s commentaries, this is the most continuous, the most literal, and the one in which he least indulges [Col. 0750C] in allegory, though it is not wholly free of it. It is full of fine moral observations. Speaking in Book IV of the preachers of his own time, he describes them in a way that does little credit to them or to the taste of the age: “The most ignorant, provided they were shameless and possessed great fluency of tongue, never failed to gain the people’s favor, while the most learned languished in poverty and misery.” Speaking of children who die without receiving baptism, he expressly says in Book I that they are “held in the fire of hell” (*infernali igne detinentur*).

### 6. On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man

The work *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man* was composed at the solicitation of Cunon, to whom it is dedicated. Rupert had resisted for some time for various reasons, among which he does not forget the malice of his envious detractors, who read his writings only in order to lay snares for him. But he set aside all the reasons that could have dissuaded him [Col. 0750D] from writing, in order to carry out Cunon’s desire. The title of bishop of Regensburg which Rupert gives Cunon in the prologue approximately establishes the time of composition. For Cunon, to whom the work is dedicated as bishop of Regensburg, did not ascend that see until 1126; therefore the work in question cannot have been presented to him before that date.

Since the author’s aim was to establish the glory and greatness of the Son of Man—that is, of Jesus Christ, God and man—he chooses the Gospel of Saint Matthew as his matter and foundation. He offers a continuous commentary on this Gospel down to the thirtieth verse of chapter twelve. He uses nine books to comment on these twelve chapters. Then he suddenly passes to the Savior’s Passion, whose history the holy Evangelist relates in chapters XXVI and XXVII.

In the plan of this work, [Col. 0751A] more than in any other by the same author, his dominant taste for allegory appears. The vision of the prophet Ezekiel at the river Chebar forms its design, and the four living creatures seen by the holy prophet provide its division. For it is nothing but a perpetual allegory of the four creatures, each of which had four faces. These four faces, according to Rupert’s allegory, are the four great mysteries of Jesus Christ: his Incarnation or Birth, his Passion, his Resurrection, and his Ascension. Such is the plan of this work, divided into thirteen books, nine of which are devoted to explaining the first face, that of the man. There he proves that Jesus Christ is the true Messiah, the object of the expectation of the righteous of old. He shows this through the circumstances of his birth and baptism, through his miracles, doctrine, entire conduct, the power he communicated to his apostles to work miracles, and so forth. But this is submerged in so many extraneous reflections and [Col. 0751B] allegories that the principal object is lost from view.

The second face, that of the calf, represents the Passion of Jesus Christ and provides the subject of Books X, XI, and XIII. He speaks very briefly of the other two faces, those of the lion and eagle, at the end of the final book. Book XII is merely a digression on certain visions which were overly familiar to him and on some incidents from his life.

This work, as we have already said, is overloaded with allegories, in accordance with the author’s taste. He himself admits in Book VI that allegory pleases him more than the literal sense. It is full of theological questions foreign to its subject and treated superficially, so that one sometimes has difficulty grasping his thought; nevertheless, excellent material and great variety are found in it.

In the first book, he puts forward this question: why, since the three persons of the Trinity are all spirit and equally holy, is only the third person called the Holy Spirit, as though this were an attribute proper to him? He replies in Book I that it is because “the whole operation of the Holy Spirit concerns the sanctification of the creature. Great attention must,” he says, “be paid to this distinction of operations. Everything that was made, God made through the Son. Everything holy, he sanctified through the Holy Spirit. For what is his Spirit but his love? And how could, or can, any rational creature ever be sanctified otherwise than by loving its Creator? *Quomodo creatura quaecunque rationalis aliter nisi amando creatorem, potuit unquam, vel poterit sanctificari?*”

Thus the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy; nevertheless, the third person of the Trinity alone is rightly called the Holy Spirit, whose proper operation is the sanctification [Col. 0751D] of the creature, without whom neither angel nor human being is holy; without whom the angel is only a demon, and the human being only an Antichrist or a member of the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] “Therefore, although both the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, this person alone ought rightly to be called the Holy Spirit. His proper operation is the sanctification of the creature; without him neither angel nor human being is holy. The angel who does not possess him is a devil; the human being who does not possess him is an Antichrist, [Col. 0752D] a member of the devil.”]

At the beginning of the third book, our author launches an attack on those who criticized his works: “Mock as much as you please, you who read my works only to find material for criticism; add, if you wish, ‘How can this man be learned, having never studied?’ But by sharing in the reproach addressed to him, we shall share in his glory.” Therefore, despising the blows of envy, he continues the work he has begun.

Speaking of Christ’s baptism, he says that although Christ was the Holy of Holies, unstained by any sin, yet, because he had taken a body like ours, he wished in being baptized by Saint John to provide us with an example of humility and a remedy for curing the pride which had caused the fall of the first man. He chose the waters of the Jordan because the Israelites crossed that river to enter the promised land. The priests who remained in the midst of the river while the people crossed were a figure of Jesus Christ, the first High Priest of the new covenant, and of Saint John, the last of the old covenant, the end of the Law and the Prophets. Christ’s priesthood is infinitely above that of Aaron, which was only a very feeble figure of it.

Our author speaks at length of Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness and compares [Col. 0752B] it with that of the first man in the earthly paradise; what he says on this point is very judicious. He teaches that before the Messiah’s coming it was permitted, and even praiseworthy, for kings, priests, prophets, and patriarchs to fight for religion using the sword, as appears in the example of David and the Maccabees, who fought bravely against nations seeking to destroy them and to prevent the promise of the Messiah. But after its fulfilment, after the birth of the Prince of Peace, it is no longer permitted to employ material weapons. One must use those represented by the trumpets and the lamps in earthen jars, with which Gideon triumphed over the Midianites. The lamps figured the gifts of heavenly graces, and the trumpets the preaching of the Gospel; these alone are now lawful weapons.

On the calling of the apostles, Rupert [Col. 0752C] asks why Jesus Christ chose poor men rather than rich ones; or rather, why, having known them in his foreknowledge and predestined them before the very creation of the world to be conformed to the image of his Son, and having purposed to justify them and fill them with glory, he wished them to be born poor in the goods of this world. This was for their instruction, he says, because awareness of one’s poverty is for the creature a great means and a most effective lesson for keeping it in its proper condition and making it know the order of things and what it is in relation to God.

What is this order? It is that proclaimed by Saint Paul when he cries: “O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and incomprehensible his ways! For who has known the designs of God, or entered into the secret of his counsels? Who has first given him anything, to claim a recompense? Everything is from him, everything is through [Col. 0752D] him, and everything is in him” (Rom. 11:33–35).

“This,” our author continues [Note: [Col. 0752D] “This is the lawful order, the necessary order: that the creature be subject to its Creator, knowing and confessing that from him, through him, and in him are all the good things possessed either by the blessed human being or by the holy angel.”], “is the lawful order, the necessary order: that the creature be subject to its Creator, knowing and confessing that from him, through him, and in him are all the good things possessed either by the blessed human being or by the holy angel. The memory of the poverty in which the apostles were born—without learning as well as without possessions—was highly suited to making known, or recalling the knowledge of, so salutary a truth. Finally, the more abundantly the apostles were to be filled with the gifts of [Col. 0753A] heaven, the more they needed to be firmly grounded in humility in order to bear their weight.”

Our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount is the subject of Books IV, V, and VI, and part of Book VII. In explaining this sermon, the author extols the excellence of the new covenant over the old: Jesus Christ, the legislator of the new covenant, not only gave a perfect example of everything he commanded, but also joined to the letter the spirit of love and charity in order to bring about the fulfilment of the commandment.
