Since the old covenant, in Book V, possessed neither the one nor the other, it was impossible for it to bring the Jew to perfection as the Christian reaches it, having before his eyes Christ’s example and the Gospel accompanied by the spirit of love.

The pagan philosophers knew neither temperance nor the other virtues. They used their names, but were ignorant of their nature or dignity, and lacked their foundation. “Love is the foundation and root of all good works” (*ibid.*); without love, the beauty of good works is hypocrisy.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] “If, then, the root of love is fixed in the heart, almsgiving is good, prayer is good, fasting is good and useful … Yet these same things can be produced outwardly without the root of love, but with such a result that all the beauty of their fruits is hypocrisy.”]

Thus, one who gives alms, prays, and fasts without love in the heart is a hypocrite.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] “To put it more closely: that person is a hypocrite who gives alms, prays, and fasts, but, lacking inwardly the gold of love, walks in a double manner: his inner chambers are foul, while his surface is golden.”]

In the same book, after a kind of dissertation on the meaning of the words, “But when you pray, do not affect many words” (Matt. 6:7), Rupert defends the long prayers of ecclesiastics and monks. He also justifies the use of music in churches, considering it a means suitable for sustaining attention and drawing the grace of the Holy Spirit into the heart. He does not doubt that many have experienced beneficial effects from singing. As for himself, he acknowledges that it moves him deeply. Our author explains the Lord’s Prayer very soundly, and in what sense we ask God that his name be hallowed, his kingdom come, and his will be done, although his name is always holy, his kingdom has already come, and his will never fails to take effect: “For who reigns and does not have his will done?” (*Quis enim regnat et non fit ejus voluntas?*)

Speaking of fasting in Book VI, Rupert observes that Moses is the first man of whom we read that he fasted: “Moses is read to have been the first of all to fast” (*Primus omnium jejunasse legitur Moyses*). He then treats of the qualities fasting must possess in order to be pleasing to God.

At the beginning of Book VII, he tells his friend Cunon, with a kind of apprehension, that he has experienced, though feebly, the manner in which God communicates himself to holy souls. Necessity obliges him to make this declaration because some people were scandalized that he treated the mysteries of Scripture, attributing it to presumption and vanity, and insulted him by saying: What need is there to write on matters that so many [Col. 0753D] Fathers, who lived long [Col. 0754A] before us, have sufficiently treated?

After making this admission to Cunon, who strongly urged him to compose works, he adds that even if he wished to remain silent and cease writing, it would not be possible for him. He approves what one of Job’s friends says: “Who can hold back a conceived word?” (*Conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit?* Job 4:2), provided it is done with wisdom and discernment. To be unable to restrain one’s words when they are evil or useless is a vice and folly. To be unable to restrain necessary or useful discourse is glorious.

“But in any event,” our author continues, “however those who live with us may judge us, those who come after us will judge more kindly. For as long as we live,” he says after Saint Jerome, “and are enclosed in this mortal body, the zeal our friends show us seems beneficial and the insults of our envious detractors harmful. But [Col. 0754B] when all alike have returned to the bosom of the earth—both the writers and those who judge their writings—when pale death has carried away both parties and another generation has succeeded them, then things will be judged without regard to great names and dignities, but only by intellects. The reader then cares very little whose work he reads, whether it is by a bishop or a layman; an emperor and lord, or a soldier and slave; a man clothed in purple and silk, or covered in rags. Difference of fortune among authors will not be the reader’s rule of judgment; rather, each will be judged according to his merit.”

[Note: [Col. 0753D] “Nevertheless, however those present may wish to judge us, those to come will judge more kindly. For while we live, says the illustrious man Jerome, and are contained in a fragile vessel, the efforts of friends seem to benefit us and the reproaches of rivals to harm us. But after earth has returned to its own earth, and pale death has removed both us who write and those who judge us, and another generation has come, [Col. 0754D] with the first leaves falling and the green forest growing up again, then intellects alone are judged, without the dignity of names. Nor does the person who is about to read consider whose or what sort of work he is about to read: whether its author is a bishop or a layman; emperor and lord, soldier and slave; whether he lies in purple or silk or in the meanest cloth. He will be judged not by diversity of worldly goods, but by the merit of his works.”]

Our author next enters upon his subject and treats various points of morals. He shows that the command to love one’s neighbour as oneself, to do to others only what we would willingly have done to ourselves, extends to our enemies; that this law, which appears so burdensome to flesh and blood, is so only for the proud who walk in the broad way, and not for the humble who walk in the narrow way. He shows the difference between the miracles of Jesus Christ and those of Moses, consisting chiefly in this: according to Isaiah’s prophecy, the miracles of the Son of God had no purpose but to benefit human beings, healing bodily diseases in order thereafter to bring about the healing of souls. The Saviour nevertheless performed miracles of the kind performed by Moses, but he did so with sovereign authority, whereas Moses performed them only by virtue of the power he had received from God. Jesus Christ commanded the winds and the sea as their master, and they obeyed him. The storm which he stilled by his command was a figure of the persecutions endured by the Church at the hands of the gentiles and pagan emperors.

> [Note: Col. 0754D] This too was to happen in the Church: the violence of open persecution, through great rulers among the nations, would thunder forth like a storm raised upon the sea by great movements of the winds, and would violently batter the little vessel of the Church itself, as though Jesus were asleep, almost to the peril of its life and safety. What, then, is Jesus’ sleeping in the vessel, except the withdrawal from the Church of the aid of assisting grace? And when this happens, it happens indeed so that those who are approved may become manifest; that those who might have been deceived by prosperity may be instructed; that those who were in sins may be cleansed; and that many martyrs may be crowned. Therefore the Lord Jesus sleeps, or has slept, as it were in the vessel, and a great movement arises on the sea so that the vessel is covered by the waves, whenever, by a most orderly arrangement, he delays and for a time withdraws the necessary aids, while the restless devil, the mover of the winds of this age—such a wind as Nero surely was, or deadly Decius, or indeed Diocletian or Maximinus—stirs up persecutions and, through their laws and edicts, agitates the sea, that is, the multitudes of the nations, with deaths or oppressions of the saints. Alas! How often, when such a movement arose, was the vessel covered by the waves? Yet this awakening ought always to have been, and ought to be, gentle and sweet rather than troublesome: that is, with faith and without despair, with perseverance and without impatience.]

The sleep of Jesus Christ in the vessel while it was beaten by the storm figured what occurs in the Church when the Saviour withdraws from her the assistance of his grace: thereby those among the faithful who are firmly devoted to God may be discovered; those who might be corrupted by prosperity may be instructed through adversity; those who have sinned may be purified; and finally many may receive the crown of martyrdom. Thus Jesus Christ is, or has been, as though asleep in the vessel whenever he delayed to aid the Church, while the devil stirred up persecutions such as those of Nero, Decius, Diocletian, and Maximinus; whenever the saints were put to death or oppressed, and the nations rose against them under the edicts and laws of rulers hostile to the Christian name. Then the disciples approach the Saviour to awaken him and implore his help. This must always be done gently, with faith, without losing hope, and with a perseverance unmingled with impatience. Otherwise the Lord says to those who awaken him: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” (Matt. VII), as though he said: “The Lord will not leave the race of the righteous under the rod of sinners” (Ps. CXXIV). That is, he will not permit persecution to last long. The persecutors who exercised their power against the righteous, predestined to eternal life by the gratuitous choice of mercy, did not endure long. *Nunquid diu duraverunt?*—“Did they endure long?” Even when for a time they appeared to prevail against them, did this not work for the good of the righteous, or of those who love God? Therefore do not be afraid or timid, but possess your souls in patience, because the rod of sinners will not endure long enough to force the righteous, as though deprived of all help, to stretch out their hands toward iniquity. On the contrary, it will soon be broken and cast into the fire, to be reduced to ashes.

While Rupert was engaged upon the work of which we are giving an account, the bishop of Cologne, under whose protection Cunon had placed him in a time of persecution, asked him to work on the Books of Kings. Unable to refuse so venerable a prelate, yet also finding it difficult to interrupt the work he had begun, our author found himself compelled to give half his heart to the one and half to the other: *Igitur necessitate compulsus, dimidium cordis mei uni, et dimidium cordis mei alteri praebui*—“Therefore, compelled by necessity, I gave half my heart to the one and half my heart to the other.” Thus he worked on the Kings without entirely suspending the work *On the Glory of the Son of God*.

This glory shines forth in the calling of Saint Matthew, whom Jesus Christ saw, and saw so efficaciously—*vidit et tam efficaciter vidit*—that is, with that inward gaze by which he knows and predestines the elect before all ages. This is that admirable gaze; this is that grace of which the Vessel of Election speaks in wonder: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII.29). He foresaw and predestined them before all ages, but called each in his own time. Thus he called Saint Matthew, who followed him joyfully.

In the sending of the apostles Rupert observes and admires a sovereign master of nature, who sends twelve men to preach in the world, giving them power to cast out demons and heal diseases. Never had a man clothed with such power appeared upon earth. Jesus Christ did not ordain his apostles when he chose them and sent them to preach; they were ordained only when that great High Priest of the new covenant fulfilled the priestly office and entered the sanctuary by shedding his blood. Then he consecrated them; then, rising from the dead, he gave them full and complete power, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; the sins are remitted to those to whom you remit them” (John XX). This power of remitting sins, the greatest received by the apostles, was given them only after the resurrection. They had received the power to cast out demons, heal diseases, and raise the dead, but not to remit sins.

[Col. 0756B] In sending the apostles, Jesus Christ forbade them to have either gold or silver …, or a staff (Matt. X.10). In another evangelist it is stated that he commanded them to carry nothing except a staff (Mark VI.8). To resolve this difficulty, Rupert distinguishes two kinds of staff: “one belonging to the kings of the nations, the other to the disciples of Jesus Christ. The staff of the kings of the nations is a staff of domination; the staff of the disciples of Jesus Christ is a staff of charity, a staff of pastoral office, watchfully attentive to the care of souls: *Virga discipulorum Christi, virga delectionis, virga pastoralis officii super curam animarum sollicite vigilantis.* The staff of domination was not given to the ministers of the Gospel of peace. It is this domination which Jesus Christ forbids them here, when he says: ‘Carry neither … staff.’ He forbids it still more explicitly in these other words: ‘The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them take the title of benefactors. But you are not to do so’” (Luke XXII.25). “That is the staff, or domination, which Jesus Christ forbids his disciples.”

Saint Peter, instructed in this truth, forbids pastors to lord it over the Lord’s inheritance: *hoc sciens apostolus Petrus dicit, neque dominantes in clero*—“knowing this, the apostle Peter says, ‘not lording it over the clergy’” (1 Pet. V.3). Similarly Saint Paul declares to the Corinthians that he is far from lording it over their faith: *non quia dominamur fidei vestrae*—“not because we lord it over your faith” (1 Cor. IV).

Paraphrasing the instructions Jesus Christ gives his disciples, our author explains in Book VIII the words: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X). He first warns that one must not so presume upon the spirit of fortitude as to forget the Saviour’s counsel to flee; then he adds: “How do you know that you possess the spirit of fortitude? How indeed do you know whether you are worthy of love or of hatred? Therefore do not rashly cast yourselves into the furnace of temptation; but rather, fearing that you may be unworthy of martyrdom, leave the city in which you are persecuted and flee to another. For this depends not on him who wills, nor on him who runs, but on God who shows mercy. Unless, therefore, one truly experiences the spirit of fortitude within oneself, and the Holy Spirit has in some manner revealed it, it is safer to flee in a spirit of humility and in the spirit of the fear of the Lord. *Tutius est ut fugias in spiritu humilitatis, in spiritu timoris Domini, quia Petrum quoque apostolorum principem, cum sibi videretur fortis, ancilla ostiaria terruit*—‘It is safer for you to flee in a spirit of humility, in the spirit of the fear of the Lord, because even Peter, the chief of the apostles, when he seemed strong to himself, was frightened by a maidservant at the door.’”

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). Here, Rupert says in Book VIII, someone may rightly say: “Give, Lord, what you command, and command what you will. Behold, you command us not to fear those who kill the body; and reason agrees that he should rather be feared who can destroy both body and soul. But what flesh does not fear being killed? Peter, first of the apostles, was afraid; and, fearing to die, he denied Life. Why was this, except because you had not yet given him not to fear? But after you gave it to him, he was able to do what you commanded. Therefore be our strength, and do in us what you will us to do.”

> [Note: Col. 0757D] Here someone may rightly say: “Give, Lord, what you command, and command what you will. Behold, you command that we not fear those who kill the body, and reason agrees that he should rather be feared who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna. But what flesh does not fear being killed? Peter, first of the apostles, was afraid, and fearing death denied Life. Why was this, except because you had not yet given him not to fear? But once you gave it to him, he was able to do what you commanded. Therefore be our strength, and do in us what you will us to do.”

Up to this point our author had executed only one part of his design, though he had gone beyond the limits he had set himself. Therefore, retracing his steps in Book X, he resumes his subject. Having spoken of the face of the man in the first nine books, he speaks in the tenth of that of the calf, passing from the twelfth chapter of Saint Matthew to the twenty-sixth. The murmuring of the apostles at the costly perfume poured upon the Saviour’s head gives him occasion to make a digression upon those who murmur against the writings of others. He sets himself forth as an example, having experienced opposition to his own works: *nos ipsi nostris diebus nostris pro opusculis nonnihil experti sumus*—“we ourselves in our own days have experienced something on account of our little works.”

He observes in this book that the different order followed by the evangelists in narrating what occurred at the Last Supper gave rise to differing opinions among the Fathers concerning Judas. Some maintained that he received the body of Our Lord together with the other apostles; others claimed that he did not receive it and had already gone out. Saint Augustine, following Saint Luke’s narrative, held the former opinion; Saint Hilary, adhering to Saint Matthew’s, held the contrary view. Which opinion, one asks, should be preferred? Rupert answers that one should follow the opinion most in agreement with the text of the Gospel. He acknowledges that most people, indeed almost all, follow and embrace Saint Augustine’s view rather than Saint Hilary’s, whose differing view was known to very few.

> [Note: Cols. 0757D–0758D] I am not unaware that most people, indeed almost all, follow and embrace the opinion of blessed Augustine more readily than that of blessed Hilary, although until now very few had known that he thought or wrote otherwise.

“For they say that many unworthy persons now receive the same sacrament and, in receiving it, eat and drink judgment upon themselves. They say also, and very truly, that this sacrament ought not to be denied to anyone except one who has confessed to a crime or has been convicted of one; and although they can establish this by another reason—indeed, by many reasons—they rely principally on the fact that the Lord did not deny communion in the same sacrament to Judas the betrayer, any more than to the other apostles.”

> [Note: Col. 0758D] They say also—and this is likewise true—that this sacrament ought to be denied to no one except one who has confessed to, or been convicted of, a crime; and although it may be demonstrated by another reason, indeed by many reasons, they rely especially on this reason: that the Lord did not deny communion in the same sacrament to Judas the betrayer, just as he did not deny it to the other apostles, though Judas had not yet confessed or been convicted.

Rupert then examines whether Judas had confessed his crime and whether he had been convicted of it. Having shown from all that occurred and from the Lord’s words, *tu dixisti*—“you have said it”—that his crime was notorious, he concludes: “I have said this in order to show that, if we follow the foregoing opinion of Saint Hilary, we must nevertheless know for certain that holy communion is not to be denied to anyone unless he has confessed to, or been convicted of, a crime: *Haec idcirco dixerim, ut si sententiam beati Hilarii supra scriptam sequamur, nihilominus constare sciamus, quod sacra communio nemini deneganda sit, nisi de crimine confessus sit aut convictus.*”

In this tenth book we find the strongest proofs of the purity of the author’s faith concerning Christ’s presence in the Eucharist. He cites the Apostle’s words to the Hebrews: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for and a sure proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI.1); then continues: “It was necessary, therefore, that the things remain hidden in order that this faith, which is their substance, might have place; the things, I say—that is, it was necessary that the flesh and blood should not appear, not only lest they revolt the senses of those who eat his flesh and drink his blood, since they naturally shrink from eating human flesh and drinking human blood, but also in order to make room for faith, which is the substance of things hoped for and a sure proof of things not seen.”

In the twelfth book Rupert recounts, with much modesty, several circumstances of his life, particularly various visions he had seen. He declares that he does so with great reluctance and out of reverence for the holy name of the Trinity, which Cunon, bishop of Regensburg, had invoked in order to persuade him to write them. It was after one of these visions that he consented to receive the priesthood, which he had until then refused. From that time he received such illumination, such facility in writing, and such great ardour that he was no longer free to stop. Here he recalls what he had suffered at the hands of certain persons who, excessively prejudiced in favour of their teachers, rose against him because he departed from their opinions in order to follow better ones, more consonant with Scripture. As for himself, although he too had had teachers, had attended the schools, and had devoted himself with great care to the arts, he declares that the lessons he received from above had benefited him more than ten such fathers and teachers.

He makes a lengthy digression concerning Cunon, his protector, through whom he experienced, in accordance with Jesus Christ’s promise (Mark X), that those who leave everything to follow him receive a hundredfold in this life, even amid persecutions. All the remainder of this book is devoted to the praise and history of the life and virtues of this prelate, who had been made bishop of Regensburg after having been a monk of Siegburg.

In the thirteenth and final book he treats briefly of the face of the lion, a figure of Christ’s resurrection, and of the figure of the eagle, a figure of his ascension. In this book he mentions a poem he had composed in honour of the Holy Spirit. It is in iambic verse and is found at the end of the commentary on Saint Matthew.

[Col. 0759A] **7. On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit.** At the head of this work is an epistle by which the author offers it to the pope. This pope can only be Honorius II, who occupied the Roman see from 1124 to 1130, or Innocent II, who succeeded him in 1130 and died in 1143. We do not know in what year it was composed; but it is certain that it was after 1126, since Cunon then occupied, as appears from the prologue following the letter, the see of Regensburg, to which he was not appointed until 1126.

Rupert had previously composed a dialogue between a Christian and a Jew under the title *Annulus* (“The Ring”). Cunon, at whose request he had composed it, saw it and was greatly pleased with it; he pressed the author to continue working on the same subject and to combat: first, the perfidy of the Jews, proving the mystery of the Trinity from the Law and the Prophets—that is, from texts drawn from Scriptures which the Jews themselves receive as canonical; second, to show why and how it was more fitting that the second person of the Trinity, the Son, should become incarnate than that the Father or the Holy Spirit should do so; and finally, to demonstrate that the time at which the prophets foretold the Messiah’s coming is the time in which Jesus Christ was born.

Such is the plan of the work *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. If attention is paid to its title, the author has not badly fulfilled the first part, having carefully gathered from Scripture everything he believed suited to magnify the glory of this mystery. As for the second part, the procession of the Holy Spirit, he dwells upon it very little, although he speaks at sufficient length concerning the gifts and divinity of the Holy Spirit. This accords with his plan, which is to prove to the Jews that there are three persons in God. Thus M. Dupin (*Dupin, Twelfth Century*, pt. II, p. 720) has given a rather inaccurate account of the writing under discussion when he says that it contains an explanation of several Scriptural passages bearing upon the questions treated by the author concerning the three divine persons, and especially concerning the Holy Spirit. According to the plan explained in his prologue, Rupert was also to show that it was more fitting for the Son to be incarnate than for any other person of the Trinity, and that the time of Christ’s appearance agrees perfectly with Jacob’s prophecy concerning the time of the Messiah’s arrival. But these two points are rather poorly executed, for he scarcely speaks of them.

Our author (Book I, ch. 1) compares the mystery of the Trinity to a treasure of inestimable value hidden in a field. This field is the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament. “It is rightly called a field,” he says (ch. 2), “because it is a public thing, a thing set openly before view and offered to all human beings, indeed to all peoples who desire to read or hear it. … The Scriptures are offered to all peoples who can read them. … Even the simple are not excluded from this reading, because although they do not quickly perceive the mysteries enclosed in them, they nevertheless readily grasp their literal and also their moral sense.”

> [Note: Cols. 0759D–0760D] This field … is the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament. And it is rightly called a field, because it is indeed a public thing, a thing set openly before view and offered to all human beings, indeed to all peoples who desire to read or hear it. Hence comes that true saying in the Psalm: “The Lord will recount in the writings of the peoples” (Ps. LXXXVI). For what does he mean by saying “in the writings of the peoples,” except as if he said: “in the writings that are set before the peoples, or that can be read by all peoples”? … The sacred Scriptures … do not exclude the simple from their reading; for although they do not quickly perceive the mysteries, they at least easily grasp with their understanding the literal sense and the moral sense as well.

The mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation of Jesus Christ are a treasure hidden in the Scriptures; but it is hidden only from those unworthy to discover it. It can be found not in only one part of this scriptural field, but everywhere, throughout its entire extent (chs. 4–5). In the first word of Scripture one discovers the second person of the Trinity, the Son, under the veil of the name “beginning”—*sub velamine nominis principii*. The reason why the Son of God, or the Word, should fittingly be called “beginning” is that through him all things were made; not only were all things made through him, but they were also made for him (ch. 6). Rupert dwells at length on the term “beginning,” which properly belongs to the Son of God and which Jesus Christ applied to himself in Saint John’s Gospel: *principium, qui et loquor vobis*—“the Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John VIII).

He then comes to the procession of the Holy Spirit, but speaks less of his eternal procession, by which he proceeds from all eternity from the Father and the Son, than of his outward operations. He reduces these to three: the creation of the world, in which the Spirit co-operated with the Son; spiritual gifts; and the remission of sins (ch. 11). In the seventeenth chapter he attacks the Greeks, who maintain that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son. In several places, especially in the second book (Book II, chs. 2, 3, 4, etc.), he maintains that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, citing to prove this truth the Scriptural texts customarily used by theologians. He combats vigorously the heretics who denied the divinity of the Son and that of the Holy Spirit. In the eighteenth chapter of the same book (ch. 18), the author relates two visions to prove that the Holy Spirit still communicated himself sensibly in his own time.

The Holy Spirit communicates himself to human beings in two ways: by his various gifts and by the remission of their sins (Book III, ch. 8). But he communicates himself to angels only by the gift of graces, not by the remission of sins. There is no forgiveness for the rebellious angels because they sinned not through ignorance or weakness, but through pride.

[Col. 0760C] Rupert maintains (ch. 10) that the angels did not sin immediately after their creation, but that some interval elapsed between their creation and their fall. He refutes the opinion of those who believed that, had the angels persevered, humankind would not have been created. If this is granted, he says, one must take care not to be so simple as to believe that God had no purpose of creating humankind before the angels’ fall, and that the thought occurred to him only afterward, in order to repair through the creation of humankind the ruin of the angels. He considers it more probable (ch. 21) that angels and human beings were created for Jesus Christ than that human beings were created to fill the number of angels who had fallen.

Having spoken of the angels in the fourth book, he treats in the fifth (ch. 1) of the human creature, to the praise of the Trinity and in honour of the Holy Spirit, who has splendidly poured out his gifts upon this creature (ch. 9). He considers it irony when God—that is, the Trinity—says to Adam after his fall: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. III). But this irony was followed by a wonderful effect: the second person of the Trinity became man, so that a great number of Adam’s children might become like one of the Trinity—that is, might be made by grace sons of God, brothers and co-heirs of the only Son, who is one of the Trinity (ch. 10).

But great preparations were necessary for the fulfilment of so admirable and ineffable a mystery. Faith and humility are this great preparation, repairing Adam’s crime: Adam believed the devil rather than God’s word, and in pride wished to become like God. Faith, which is the preparation for this great mystery, is a gift of the Holy Spirit. The patriarchs received it together with the gift of prophecy. But they were few in number, and Scripture expressly names only two or three before the Flood (ch. 12).

Although they were then called children of God because of their faith and the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, these gifts were only preparations for the regeneration of God’s children. By a particular favour bestowed upon us, God willed that they should receive the fulfilment of their blessedness only together with us (Heb. XI.40). For it is through the blood of Jesus Christ alone that both those ancient patriarchs and we received the Holy Spirit in that grace which is remission of sins: *Nam per sanguinem hujus solius, tam illi quam nos Spiritum sanctum in ista gratia, quae est remissio peccatorum, accepimus*—“For through the blood of this one alone, both they and we have received the Holy Spirit in that grace which is the remission of sins.”

Our author makes this distinction between the ancients and the moderns—that is, between the righteous before the Incarnation and Christians: the former received the various spiritual gifts of the Holy Spirit before the remission of sins, whereas the moderns, that is, those regenerated by baptism, receive remission of sins before spiritual gifts. Cornelius alone was an exception, receiving the gifts of the Holy Spirit before being baptized. Rupert therefore applies to the former Job’s words, *Concepti non viderunt lucem*—“Those conceived did not see the light” (Job III), because before the Messiah’s death they did not receive the reward of their faith: *quia non pervenerunt ad jam dictae remunerationis diem*—“because they had not reached the day of the reward just mentioned.” This shows in what sense Rupert must be understood when he says in various places in his works that before Christ’s passion the grace of the Holy Spirit, which consists in remission of sins, was not received.

The faith of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is not inferior to that of Moses (Book V, ch. 3), although they performed no miracles like that lawgiver of God’s people. On the contrary, Rupert says (ch. 7), their great faith ought to seem all the more radiant because it did not need such outward signs to strengthen and increase it. All the ancient patriarchs had but one desire, a groaning desire, whose object was Christ’s birth and the Saviour’s coming: *Omnium quippe desiderium erat unum, desiderium gemituosum, nasci Christum, venire Salvatorem*—“For the desire of all was one: a groaning desire that Christ be born, that the Saviour come.”

By the effect of this desire Moses said to God: “Either forgive them this fault, or blot me out from the book which you have written.” For if God had destroyed the people from whom the Messiah was to be born, Moses would thereby have been blotted out of the book of life, since no one could be saved unless Jesus Christ had come into the world. Such is Rupert’s explanation of Moses’ prayer to God that he might forgive his people. Before giving it, he complains that even among Christians there are still many weak persons and little children who do not know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ with that knowledge which belongs to the perfect: *Parvuli enim sunt hodieque quam plurimi, quia nondum cognoverunt illa cognitione quae perfectorum est, gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi*—“For even today very many are little children because they have not yet known the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ with that knowledge which belongs to the perfect.”

David speaks more clearly of the Trinity than Moses did. In Psalms II and LXXXVIII he expresses the relative names Father and Son, and even the two natures of the only Son of God. He was the first to name the Holy Spirit, saying: *Spiritum sanctum tuum ne auferas a me*—“Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). Before that, he was called the Spirit of God or the Spirit of the Lord. The distinction of the three persons is expressly marked in the Psalms of the holy prophet-king. Our author observes (chs. 7–8) that the first Scriptural texts employed by the apostles concerning Jesus Christ, after the Spirit of truth had given them understanding of them, and even before Pentecost, were drawn from David’s Psalms. He explains what the Spirit of truth announces concerning Jesus Christ in Psalms I, II, III, IV, and so forth.

Three things concur in making humankind the image of God: faith, hope, and charity (chs. 10, 11, 12, 13, etc., 19). In accordance with this, Solomon composed three books: the Parables, or Proverbs, to instruct in faith; Ecclesiastes to strengthen hope; and the Song of Songs to increase charity. This is the aim of all Scripture, but especially of Solomon’s three books. Our author, having intended to finish his work here, thought that he ought to dwell longer upon these three books, lest he give occasion for complaint and have applied to him what a poet says:

> Mountains will labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, v. 139.)

He therefore continues to speak of faith, hope, and charity (Book VII, ch. 1); but the joy he feels at having discovered this treasure in Solomon’s three books is tempered by the dread inspired by the terrible fall of that so wise prince.

The opinion of some, who believe that Solomon rose again and did penance, provides some consolation, but does not prevent trembling at seeing such a pillar fall. What then can we say? Nothing other than what the Apostle says: “How incomprehensible are God’s judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI).

Resuming his subject, Rupert proves (ch. 2) from the words of Wisdom that Jesus Christ is coeternal with the Father. He applies to the Church all that is said of the strong woman in the last chapter of Proverbs. But how can generations over so many centuries, so great a multitude of persons or souls, be called one woman, one Church formed of all of them, having God as her husband? What cause produces such an effect, if not faith? He speaks (chs. 5, 9) of faith’s dignity and admirable power, and then turns to hope. On hope the Wise Man gives lessons by making rational man understand what he ought to hope for and what things do not deserve to be objects of his hope. That is why he begins thus (ch. 11): “Vanity of vanities.” Yet in giving the name of vanity to all creatures, he has less in view the creature itself than the use of the creature, or disordered love for it: *Non tam ipsa creatura quam creaturae usus, vel amor immoderatus, vanitatis arguitur*—“It is not so much the creature itself as the creature’s use, or immoderate love, that is charged with vanity.”

These two things, namely faith and hope, operate through a third, namely charity (ch. 13, 16). By these three means man, who had been created in the image and likeness of God and had lost that likeness through sin, recovers it. But since it is through faith, hope, and charity that the image of the Trinity is restored in the human soul (ch. 17), why does St Paul establish an inequality among these virtues, saying that charity is the greatest of the three? (1 Cor. XIII.) For there is no inequality in the Trinity: none of the three persons has anything above another, all three being perfectly equal in all things. Rupert answers that “true faith is never without charity, nor true charity without hope”; and that, just as the one God is indivisible in three persons, so these three virtues are one [Col. 0763A] in three:

> [Note: [Col. 0763D] “To this I reply: true faith is never without charity, and true charity is never without hope. As the one and triune God—the Father and [Col. 0764D] the Son and the Holy Spirit—is indivisible, so the one and triune virtue, faith, hope, and charity, which is brought about in the souls of human beings in relation to the Trinity, is indivisible.”]

As for St Paul, when he speaks of faith, he includes in it hope and charity, which are inseparable: “Finally, in his own sense he proclaims faith, so that, when he says . . . ‘Faith is reckoned for righteousness’ [Rom. IV], he simultaneously comprehends faith, hope, and charity, because these are truly inseparable,” etc.

Our author does not mean, in speaking thus, that these virtues are so inseparable that charity cannot be lost without faith also being lost; that would be an error. Moreover, it must be observed that he speaks of justifying faith, which is inseparable from charity—that is, which cannot justify unless it is joined with charity. He ends his seventh book (ch. 18) with a prayer addressed to the Trinity, asking for an increase of faith, hope, and charity, which, he says, are our riches, our treasure, our life, our wisdom, our glory, our strength, etc.

The eighth book contains nothing noteworthy. The author does not even speak there of Solomon’s three books, which had led him to give his work [Col. 0763B] a greater extent than he had initially intended. But he returns to them in the ninth book (ch. 1). The words of the ninth chapter of Proverbs are its subject (ch. 2, 3): “Wisdom has built herself a house, and has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. IX). This house, or temple, is the body of Jesus Christ. The seven pillars are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

**8. Commentary on the Gospel of St John.** In the first edition of Rupert’s works, published by the celebrated Cochlaeus and printed at Cologne in 1526, in two folio volumes by Franz Birckman, there is a dedicatory epistle missing from the editions of 1533, 1577, 1602, and even the last edition of 1638. The suppression of this epistle, addressed to Cuno, was an all the more inexcusable negligence on the part of those who supervised these editions because they had no research to undertake in order to find it: it lay before their eyes in Cochlaeus’s edition. The importance of the omitted piece [Col. 0763C] makes the editors still more culpable. I say its importance, for this dedicatory epistle alone would suffice to vindicate Rupert against the suspicions and unjust accusations raised against the purity of his faith concerning the Eucharist. For, far from teaching anything contrary to the Church’s belief concerning this mystery, we learn from this epistle that some of those attacking Rupert’s works were disciples of Berengar, whose errors our author opposed. Concealing their true purpose, these censors accused Rupert of vanity and presumption because he wrote commentaries on Scripture and on St John, and worked upon matters already treated by St Augustine. Most, I say, of those who spoke thus were infected with Berengar’s errors. Following their master, they maintained that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is merely a sign [Col. 0763D] of a sacred thing; they even claimed that this had been St Augustine’s view. This, Rupert says, is wholly false.

“For my part,” he adds, “I combat this opinion, and maintain that it is the true body of Jesus Christ which was given up for us, and his true blood which was shed for us, as the Church believes. This,” Rupert continues, “is what caused them to say that by holding views opposed to Augustine’s I derogated from his authority and reputation—views which Berengar habitually cited in support of his errors by assigning a wrong meaning to Augustine’s words.” But no one now dares either openly to profess or defend that opinion, since the whole Church [Col. 0764A] affirms that it is the true body and the true blood of Jesus Christ.”

Our commentator was further accused because, contrary to St Augustine’s view and in conformity with that of St Hilary, he had doubted whether Judas received the body of Our Lord as the other apostles did. “This, Father,” he says to Cuno, “is what makes me so monstrous in their eyes. They say that I am so arrogant, so extraordinarily haughty, that I cannot allow any reputable clerk to live in peace”—at that time this term meant a learned person, of whatever profession, secular or ecclesiastical—“and that I accuse every one of them without exception of heresy. What then am I to do? One does all in his power to take from me the reality of the Lord’s blood; another accuses me of mortal hatred for the writings of our doctors, because I do not make them equal to the writings of the prophets and apostles. Another taught that God is the author of evil; this same man, and several others, maintained that Jesus Christ [Col. 0764B] as man, who clothed himself in our nature in unity of person with the Word of God, was not equal to God.”

The author adds that he has sufficiently justified himself in the apologetic books addressed to pious and learned ecclesiastics, who know, as Cuno does, that he has taught nothing but what is true. It is true that he believed he ought to oppose his censors, and he prefers their wholly gratuitous hatred to their friendship. “Let them attack me,” he says, “and blacken me without cause: truth will triumph in the end. It is truth that will pronounce judgment; I submit to its decision.”

After all this, Rupert explains to Cuno his views on the Eucharist as follows. “The body and blood of Jesus Christ agree in three modes of being and differ in the fourth. They agree in name, reality, and effect, and differ in appearances. They agree, I say, in name, because the supreme Pontiff of [Col. 0764C] heaven, being Truth itself and not accustomed to give empty names to things, spoke with such force: he did not merely say, ‘Let this be called my body; let this be called my blood’; but he said, ‘This is my body; this is my blood’ (Matt. XXVI). They agree in reality, because certainly he is the Holy of Holies under this form as truly as under that in which he was given up and pierced with a lance. They also agree in effects, because, just as he wrought the remission of sins under that form in which he was nailed to the cross, for all who had awaited him from the origin of the world with faith, or with the sacraments of the Law joined to faith—from righteous Abel to the good thief—so he truly works, under the appearances of bread and wine, the remission of sins for all who have had or have the same faith, since he left the world to ascend into heaven. Fourth, he differs under the forms—that is, under [Col. 0764D] the species or appearances—which is greatly advantageous, lest the colour or taste of blood should inspire horror in those receiving it; but also in order to remedy, by an appropriate and suitable antidote, the excessive credulity of our first parents. For they believed the devil’s deceitful words concerning a thing they did not see, believing that the tree of the forbidden fruit contained within itself a power able to make them like God; by eating that fruit they died. Let us, on the contrary,” he says, “believe God our Saviour, who is true and sincere, concerning a thing we do not see: namely, that bread and wine are changed into the true substance of his [Col. 0765A] body and blood. Let us eat and drink of them, that we may live eternally.”

Cuno was not yet a bishop when Rupert addressed this work to him, for he gives him no title other than that of abbot. It was therefore composed before 1126. It even appears certain that this work is earlier than 1117, and was published by Rupert before he put the finishing hand to his treatises on the Trinity. This is established both by the catalogue of his works which the author himself gives in the first book of his Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict and in his epistle to Cuno prefixed to the books on the Divine Offices, and by Reyner, monk of St Lawrence at Liège, in his treatise on the illustrious men of that monastery.

In a prologue prefixed to the Commentary, Rupert thus relates the reason why St John wrote his Gospel. “This beloved disciple, [Col. 0765B] having been sent into exile by Domitian, the second persecutor of the Church, wolves—that is, the heretics Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and other antichrists—took advantage of the shepherd’s absence, entered the sheepfold, and defiled the purity of faith with evil doctrine, teaching that Jesus Christ did not exist before Mary. Then nearly all the bishops of Asia urged St John to write in defence of the faith. Yielding to their desires, the holy apostle ordered a fast, prayed to the Lord, and, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, wrote his Gospel. By the radiance of truth it soon dispersed the darkness with which the heretics had sought to obscure the faith.”

This Commentary on St John, divided into fourteen books, is one of the works upon which the author laboured with greatest care, one of his best written works, and one from which most profit may be drawn. He follows the text verse by verse and explains it literally, but often also in an allegorical sense, in accordance with his prevailing inclination. [Col. 0765C] It is filled with excellent material, mostly drawn from the Fathers, though they are seldom cited. Following the spirit of the age, in which scholasticism was beginning to advance, the author treats a quantity of questions, but too superficially. The first seven books form a kind of course in theology. Rupert’s chief aim is to establish the divinity of Jesus Christ and to show that he is truly Son of God and truly man. He discovers this truth in every verse of the Gospel he comments upon, and joins to it passages from the Old Testament, identifying with considerable accuracy those which relate to certain circumstances of Jesus Christ’s life. One could wish that Rupert had known how to confine himself and had not embraced so many subjects. For, wishing to interpret a great part of both Scripture and Catholic doctrine, he heaps passage upon passage and runs through everything he treats so quickly that he ordinarily [Col. 0765D] does no more than indicate what he seeks to establish.

**(Book III.)** Just as sailors, having embarked and wished one another a fortunate voyage, always keep their eyes fixed on the fixed stars and avoid the wandering ones, lest they suffer shipwreck or be cast upon unknown lands, so our author, undertaking to explain the profound mysteries contained in the Gospel of St John, takes as his compass and invokes the Spirit of whom the Psalmist speaks thus: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (Ps. CXLII).

The holy doctors whose faith was always sound and who never fell into any error are likewise, for our interpreter, like shining stars, *lucida sidera*, upon which he fixes his eyes, so as not to go astray and in order to walk in their footsteps. But as for heretics, whom he calls pirates and wandering stars, [Col. 0766A] he will flee them with all his might. He regards the Gospel of St John as that book of all Scripture in which it is dangerous to be mistaken, because the holy Evangelist speaks in it of the most sublime truths of religion.

Rupert followed exactly the rule he had laid down in his Commentary; for all the doctrines of religion which he discusses there are explained in a very orthodox and very clear manner, though very briefly.

**(Book VI.)** Since the author’s faith was especially attacked on the article of the Eucharist, in the sixth and seventh books he deliberately explains himself concerning this mystery with a clarity and precision capable of silencing his enemies forever. He establishes the real presence of Jesus in the clearest manner and combats the false reasoning of those who maintained that Jesus Christ is present in the Eucharist only figuratively, supporting themselves [Col. 0766B] with the Apostle’s words concerning the Israelites in the wilderness: “They all ate the same spiritual food; they all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank water from the spiritual rock which followed them, and that rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). Rupert first sets against the “detestable presumption,” *detestabilem praesumptionem*, of those who abused the Apostle’s words to defend their errors the authority of Truth itself, which says to the Jews: “Moses did not give you the true bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John VI). He then explains St Paul’s text and shows that, in saying that the Israelites ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, the Apostle neither alludes to nor compares it with Christ’s words, “This is my body; this is my blood.” His purpose is to make the faithful understand that they must not consider themselves perfect merely because they have received the sacraments of the Christian faith.

“For all these things,” he says—that is, everything which happened to the Israelites—“were only figures of what happens to us, so that we may know from the experience of former times that, although we have all been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; although we all eat the body of Jesus Christ and drink his blood, we nevertheless must not believe that we shall all equally please God, whatever life we live and whatever our actions may be. For just as not all the Israelites were brought into the promised land or were pleasing to God, although he had performed the same miracles for all, so God will not bring us into his kingdom if we surrender ourselves to evil desires, as some of them did; if we fall into fornication, as some of them fell; if we tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him; [Col. 0766D] if we murmur, as some of them murmured. Thus, in saying that the Israelites ate one and the same spiritual food, the Apostle does not mean that it was the same life-giving food and drink which we receive in remembrance of Our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Still further pressing the defenders of the error he combats, Rupert tells them that if they wish to take these words in a spiritual sense, the Apostle stops them, however greatly they may strive, by saying: “All these things were figures” (1 Cor. X). “For,” he says, “if everything was a figure, the food they ate and the drink they drank were therefore only figures. Consequently, the manna was no more the true bread, and the drink which the Israelites drank was no more the life-giving drink—which we believe and confess truly to be the blood of Jesus Christ—than the inanimate and insensible rock which Moses struck with his rod [Col. 0767A] was Jesus Christ. For everything was a figure for them, as we have already said. Now a figure never equals the thing of which it is the figure, just as a shadow is not the substance of a body.—That is true, they say; likewise the bread which we consecrate on the altar is the figure of the living bread which came down from heaven, and not the living bread itself.—On what authority,” Rupert replies, “do you base such language before Christian ears? When the living bread itself said of the bread which it held in its hands, ‘This is my body,’ did he say anything comparable to what St Paul says when, after saying, ‘The rock was Christ,’ he adds, ‘Now all these things were figures for them’? If Jesus Christ, or the Evangelist, or some apostle had spoken thus, you would not be blameworthy. But if someone says that this expression is figurative in the sense I explain: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall have [Col. 0767B] no life in yourselves’ (John VI), he proves nothing against us, because this figurative expression does not destroy the truth of the thing, just as the parabolic expressions in the parable of the sower do not destroy the reality of the person who truly sows. For what is a figurative expression? It is when one thing is said and another must be understood. Therefore, if the expression of which we speak is figurative—for the Jews understood it otherwise than Jesus Christ intended—this figure does not destroy the truth of the thing. Rather, the figure itself is destroyed while the thing remains, since it is stated quite plainly of bread and wine: ‘This is my body; this is my blood.’ By this the Jews’ understanding is destroyed. For it is clearer than daylight that one must not eat the body of Jesus Christ in the sense in which they understood it. They believed that Jesus Christ wished his flesh to be cut into pieces and eaten, [Col. 0767C] as one cuts up and eats the flesh of a lamb. Thus the figure is destroyed, while the sense in conformity with the text remains: namely, that bread by divine power is changed into the true substance of his body: *scilicet quod panis in veram substantiam corporis ejus divina virtute convertatur*.”

After proving the possibility of this change by arguments more philosophical than theological, Rupert continues to press those who attacked this mystery. “Truth says, ‘This is my body,’ and adds, ‘which shall be given up for you’; and do you say that it is not the same body? Now if it is not the same body, if it is not the same living bread which came down from heaven, then it is not the body given up for us. But everyone has long known what obstructs your altogether carnal and animal understanding, and consequently makes it incapable of comprehending the things of God. It is because bread and wine retain the same [Col. 0767D] outward form that you cannot, or will not, understand that they are truly the body and blood of Jesus Christ. It follows that if a white bishop had baptized you, though you were a Moor, you would not believe that through baptism you had become before God what he who baptized you is—that is, that you had become a son of God from a son of the devil—because your black hair and Ethiopian skin retained their colour and did not become white like the person from whom you received baptism. But if you shrink from admitting this, lest you be considered worse than an unbeliever, and prefer to acknowledge that, although there is no outward change in you, you have passed from one body—namely, that of the devil, the mass of all the reprobate—to another body, that of Jesus Christ, namely the Church, then believe also that this visible bread [Col. 0768A] and wine, although there is no outward change, are nevertheless changed into another food, the food of angels.”

After this, our controversialist proposes to himself the objections of those “great and sublime teachers of children,” who have more taste for Plato’s Academy than for the Lord’s life-giving table. Thus he calls the supporters of the error he attacks, who, as he says, deployed all their strength against the truth of the body and blood of Jesus Christ. He returns again to the objection drawn from the words of St Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. X), “They all ate the same spiritual food,” etc., and shows that St Paul did not mean that the Israelites ate the same spiritual food which Christians eat in receiving the Eucharist. To maintain that St Paul said that the Israelites ate, under those shadows, the same food which we now eat under the law of grace; that manna and the bread of Jesus Christ’s table differ only in signs; is to maintain that this bread is no more the body of Jesus Christ than manna was, and has no more power or efficacy. It would follow that the sacrifices of lambs and rams were holier than the new sacrifice of bread and wine, and that the loaves offered in the old Law greatly surpassed the bread placed and consecrated on Jesus Christ’s table.

Our author cites a collection of Sentences concerning the body and blood of Jesus Christ, which gives preference to St Ambrose’s words:

> “It is therefore certain that a virgin gave birth contrary to the order of nature, and that this bread which we have consecrated came forth from the virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when Jesus Christ was born of a virgin contrary to the order of nature? It is the true flesh of Jesus Christ which was crucified [Col. 0768C] and which was buried; therefore it is the true sacrament of his flesh. Just as Our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God, not by grace as human beings are, but as Son from the substance of the Father, so it is his true flesh that we receive, as he himself said.”

After these arguments and texts from St Ambrose, Rupert concludes that if an angel descended from heaven and announced the contrary, assigning to the Apostle’s words—“They were all under the cloud . . . they were all baptized . . . they all ate the same spiritual food” (ibid.)—a meaning by which he attributed to those shadows the same power and efficacy as the sacraments which now operate, in the day of salvation, through faith in Jesus Christ, then, he says, we ought not to regard such an angel as an angel of light or as a faithful interpreter of the text of Christ’s Apostle.

[Col. 0768D] Since Jesus Christ said, “This is my body; this is my blood,” if we add to his words by saying that he spoke figuratively, we incur the curse with which St John threatens those who add or take away anything from what he wrote. We therefore must add nothing to or take nothing away from what proceeded from the mouth of the incarnate Word; and we confess, not through fear of the plagues threatened against those who add to or take away from the word of God, but through love of truth, that this bodily bread and this wine become the body and blood of Jesus Christ as soon as the Church has pronounced the words of consecration.

Rupert raises an objection and asks (Book VI): What, then, did the ancient saints, prophets, patriarchs, and all the elect eat in order to possess eternal life, if they did not formerly eat the living bread come down from heaven which the Father now gives, without which we cannot have [Col. 0769A] eternal life? Were not all guilty of the same sin, both before and since the Incarnation? Did not the sin of both require expiation by the same remedy? Our author answers that everyone knows that all the saints from the world’s beginning awaited the Redeemer of the human race, and that, unless this Lamb had come to blot out sins, they could not enter into possession of paradise. He instituted the sacraments of baptism and of his body and blood, necessary for our salvation. The ancients were justified by the power of the Passion of Jesus Christ which they awaited; and through it he became the food of the dead and the living, upon which both were to feed, each in the manner appropriate to them: “He willed to hang upon the wood of the cross and, through the passion of death, to become at once the food of the dead and of the living, so that both dead and living might each eat him in his own manner.” The souls of the saints ate him in the same way as the angels [Col. 0769B] eat him: “The souls of the saints ate him, namely in the same manner in which the angels too eat him.” Thus ancient and new saints alike were all healed by the same remedy. At the moment of the Lord’s death, all were purified by the blood and water which flowed from his side.

In his response (Book VI) to another objection, our author too lightly abandons a passage of St Augustine, which the enemies of Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist abused in support of their error. This passage is one in which the holy doctor, distinguishing between the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, says that the latter is the unity of Christ’s body, and that the Lord’s bread is the sacrament of that reality. Rupert says of this that he is not so excessive a flatterer of St Augustine as to agree with those who used this distinction to defend their opinion. “For [Col. 0769C] the Church,” he says, “is indeed the body of Jesus Christ, but it is not the body which was given up for us. And if the bread of the Lord’s table is merely the representation of that sacred reality—that is, of the unity of the Church—it is not the body which was given up for us. Let them draw from this whatever comparisons they judge suitable; let them say that, just as the bread of the Lord’s table is made of many grains of wheat and the wine of Christ’s chalice of many clusters of grapes, so there is one Church composed of many persons. Let them make such comparisons, or others like them, which have their usefulness, provided the foundation laid by him who said of bread and wine, ‘This is my body which shall be given up for you; this is my blood which shall be shed for you,’ is preserved.”

What Rupert says here is very sound, and at the same time very much in conformity with St Augustine’s doctrine. He could therefore have contented himself with showing the adversaries of the reality that they abused this holy doctor’s words, whose doctrine is wholly opposed to their error, without abandoning a distinction which does not attack the foundation laid by Jesus Christ and rests upon such respectable authority. Moreover, Rupert, who in various places shows great respect for St Augustine, himself acknowledges here that comparisons and similes, such as that involved in St Augustine’s distinction, are useful when the foundation is preserved; and the holy doctor’s text most certainly does no injury to that foundation.

Our author here refutes a false interpretation which some gave to Christ’s words: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” These interpreters, claiming that abiding in the unity of faith was eating the body of Jesus Christ and drinking his blood, [Col. 0770A] did not regard the bodily eating of Christ’s body as necessary to salvation. Rupert replies that if everyone thought so, Christ’s gift would become useless and no one would eat his body or drink his blood, in contempt of the command he gave before his Passion. “Let such a view perish from every Christian heart,” our author exclaims: *Pereat igitur a corde christiano hic sensus.*

“This is not what Jesus Christ taught; rather, he said: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood in the manner in which I shall give it, believing in his heart unto righteousness and eating and drinking it with his mouth—that man abides in me and I in him,’ so that they are no longer but one flesh. For eating and drinking is the cause which makes him abide in me and me in him. It may happen that someone eats it unworthily; but no one ought to eat it unless he is worthy. For bread once consecrated never afterwards loses the power of consecration [Col. 0770B] or ceases to be Christ’s flesh”: *Panis namque consecratus nunquam postea virtutem consecrationis amittit, aut Christi caro esse desinit.* But it benefits nothing the person who receives it unworthily, whose faith, being without works, is dead.

Further on, Rupert explains at greater length and refutes the objection strongly urged by many followers of Berengar, who claimed it was St Augustine’s teaching: namely, that eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood is abiding in the unity of faith. Rupert does not hesitate to admit this, provided no injury is done to the truth of Christ’s words: “This is my body; this is my blood.” But, he says (ibid.), we do not receive this explanation as the principal rule or ordinance for eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood, since he himself gave, from his own mouth, such an exact [Col. 0770C] definition of it when it pleased him, to those he wished and judged worthy. . . . Supreme Wisdom, wishing to declare in what manner it gave us its flesh to eat, said, “This is my body,” and added, “which shall be given up for you”; and, prescribing the whole manner of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, said, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Thus, putting away every cloud of figures and similes, we most firmly believe that we eat not some body whatsoever, not Christ’s body which is the Church, but that body of the Lord which was given up for us; and that we drink that blood which was shed for us.” *Proinde cunctis figurarum vel similitudinem nebulis amotis, non corpus quodlibet, non corpus Christi quod est Ecclesia; sed illud corpus Domini, quod pro nobis traditum est, nos manducare, et illum sanguinem qui pro nobis fusus est in remissionem peccatorum, nos bibere indubitanter credimus*, etc.

One would have to copy the greater part of this book if one wished to extract everything the author says in favour of the real presence, whether to establish the truth of this mystery or to combat those who attacked it.

The following book, the seventh, supplies us with no fewer proofs. In it the author continues to defend the faith of the Church and refutes the objections of the enemies of reality. Since they insisted greatly on these words, “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no avail” (John 6), Rupert deprives them of this support by showing that they do not favor their errors. “This text,” he says, “in no way destroys or weakens the preceding one, where it is said: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,’ etc. Rather, it corrects the carnal understanding of those who misunderstood it, without in any way impairing the truth of the eating of his flesh; it merely adds that, in eating [Col. 0771A] the flesh, one must unite with it the spirit of that same flesh.”

We shall not dwell further here on this subject; concerning the other matters treated by Rupert, we shall be content to report a few features, since it is not possible to analyze everything. Fear of being too lengthy causes us to omit an infinity of fine passages, which might be as instructive as they are agreeable to the reader.

Explaining these words of Saint John (John 6), “Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was that would betray him,” he says: “He knew this not from some event, by chance, or by conjecture, but as God and from the beginning—that is, from all eternity. For before the creation of the world, he foresaw and predestined those who were to be called to be holy and pure in his presence. And he said to them” (ibid.): “This is why I told you that no one can come to [Col. 0771B] me unless it is granted him by my Father. . . . For if the Father had drawn them; if it had been granted them by the Father to come to the Son—that is, if, by a divine power, he had persuaded them to become his disciples by inspiring in them a willing disposition—they would have believed; and, believing and tasting that sweetness by which all the elect are drawn, they themselves would have been drawn more and more.”

> [Note: [Col. 0771D] “For if the Father had drawn them; if it had been granted them by the Father to come to the Son—that is, if, by a divinely inspired good will, he had persuaded them to become his disciples [Col. 0772D]—then, believing and through belief tasting that sweetness by which all the elect are drawn, they too would have been drawn more and more. . . . .”]

“It belongs to man to cry out and make a sound outwardly in the ear; but it belongs to God alone, by his invisible hand, to seize the heart of the hearer and draw it to Christ.” *Hominis namque est clamare et strepitum extrinsecus ad aurem facere, Dei autem solius manu invisibili cor audientis apprehendere et ad Christum attrahere.*

In this seventh book Rupert discusses several questions concerning Judas, and concludes by saying that he was never anything but a son of perdition, and thus did not become evil after having been good before his [Col. 0771C] election. Rather, though evil, he was chosen for a necessary work by him who knows how to use the wicked to execute his purposes and who knew what Judas was when he chose him. He discusses at length in order to prove that the apostles were not made priests and bishops when Jesus Christ sent them to preach and gave them the power to work miracles, and that this occurred only after the Passion. The reason he gives is that, before being consecrated, it was necessary that they be redeemed by the death of Jesus Christ; that the Savior be glorified; and that this supreme High Priest be clothed in the vestments of his priesthood in order to communicate it to them and establish them as his vicars.

Speaking in the ninth book of the miracle of the man born blind, he observes that this man, full of gratitude and enlightened both in mind and body, preferred to expose himself to the shafts of envy rather than fail in his duty to God by keeping silent [Col. 0771D] about the wonder he had worked upon him. Thus he was the first to have the glory of being attacked and suffering persecution for Jesus Christ: *Primus omnium pro Christo quaestionibus pulsatus et persecutionem passus est*—“He was the first of all to be assailed by examinations for Christ and to suffer persecution.”

In the tenth book, he points out the striking works of Jesus Christ which left the Jews without excuse for not believing: the power he exercises in raising souls dead through sin and in bringing already corrupted bodies out of the tomb. He finds the example of this twofold resurrection in a single house—that is, at Bethany, at the very gate of Jerusalem. Mary, Lazarus’s sister, whom our author wrongly identifies with the sinful woman, provides [Col. 0772A] him with an example of the resurrection of the soul, and Lazarus with that of the body. In the same place he gives very wise counsel to those entrusted with the dreadful ministry of the keys, warning them to be on guard—*cavendum*—lest they loose those who are dead and bind those who are alive. He impresses upon them the danger of following their own caprice in the exercise of their office, binding according to their own pleasure, *pro arbitrio vel animo suo*, the one who is alive and loosing the one who is dead; thus condemning the just and justifying the wicked.

*(Book X, about the middle.)* The advice Caiaphas gave the Jews when he said (John 11), “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish,” contained a great truth of which this high priest had no knowledge. The Evangelist, admiring this truth, says that Caiaphas did not say this of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus [Col. 0772B] was to die for the nation, and not only for the nation but also to gather into one body the children of God who were scattered abroad. . . . “What does ‘he did not say this of himself’ mean,” Rupert adds, “except that he did not himself devise what he then said? Before Caiaphas existed, before the prophets and patriarchs, it had been determined in God’s purposes that Jesus Christ should die for the nation. Thus Caiaphas did not say this of himself. But why is it said, ‘Being high priest that year, he prophesied’?” Rupert replies by comparing Caiaphas to a sounding cymbal, because this pontiff understood the force of what he said no more than a cymbal feels the sound it makes: *quia videlicet virtutem loquelae suae non magis advertit, quam tinnitum suum cymbalum sentit.*

“He did not understand what we understand when we hear these words: namely, that it was expedient that one single man—the Holy of Holies, [Col. 0772C] the only righteous one, Jesus Christ—should die for Abraham’s nation, and not only for Abraham’s nation, but for all the predestined from the creation of the world, for the children of God taken from the mass of humankind, in order to gather them from the four corners of the earth, where they are scattered, up to the last of the elect. Caiaphas had only a falsehood in mind: that it was fitting for Jesus Christ to die lest the Romans destroy the Jewish nation if he bore the name of king. But he did not understand the force of what he said, nor did he say it of himself. Rather, the hand of God, guiding the senseless heart—or rather, the tongue—of this pontiff, made him utter an oracle in a clear and intelligible manner, though he himself did not understand it. Therefore, since he did not say it of himself and yet spoke the truth, the holy Evangelist and the whole Church have taken these words from the mouth of an evil prophet and an [Col. 0772D] unworthy pontiff.”

*(Ibid.)* On the occasion of Judas’s murmur, complaining that, instead of pouring a precious perfume upon the Savior’s head, it had not been sold and the money given to the poor; and of Saint John’s statement that Judas spoke thus not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief who kept the purse: our author asks why Our Lord, who knew all things, chose such a person and even made him steward of the other apostles. Rupert answers this question with another. Why, he asks, does Our Lord permit there to be many prelates in his Church who resemble this apostle? For one who steals what belongs to the Church is comparable [Col. 0773A] to Judas. Now how many are there who steal the property of the Church by abusing the ministry with which God has permitted them to be invested? How many, by failing to give the poor goods that belong to them, commit theft—not simple theft, but even sacrilege? If secular courts make a great distinction between ordinary theft committed against a private person and embezzlement, which is theft committed against the commonwealth; if the latter theft is punished more severely than the former, how much more severely should one be punished who, adding sacrilege to theft, dares to take away the very property of the Church? Since, then, there are today many like Judas, if we are asked how they could have attained ecclesiastical ministry, we can make no other reply than that God permits many things which he does not approve.”

Rupert adds that it is unknown whether Jesus Christ himself chose Judas to entrust him with the purse or whether, as seems more likely to him, [Col. 0773B] Judas thrust himself forward: “as most people,” he says, “now thrust themselves into ecclesiastical ministries with such importunity that, if they were not admitted, they would perhaps cause souls graver scandals through fostering division than, if they are admitted, they inflict losses upon ecclesiastical goods.”

> [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Just as most people now thrust themselves into ecclesiastical ministries with such importunity that, unless they are admitted, they almost bring souls graver scandals through discord than, if they are admitted, they bring losses upon ecclesiastical property.”]

On these words of Saint John and Isaiah (John 12; Isaiah 6), “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I heal them,’” our author observes, “that people have never ceased to dispute about God’s foreknowledge and predestination; indeed, there are sinners who dare excuse themselves by saying that, if they are not good, it is because God foresaw that they [Col. 0773C] would be evil and did not predestine them. Thus excusing themselves and accusing God, they rely upon these texts to defend their madness. If God’s predestination and foreknowledge did not do violence to human wills, the Evangelist would not speak in this manner.” Rupert, although able to refute this objection, contents himself with answering these presumptuous persons with Saint Paul: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Can the clay vessel say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Romans 9).

In the eleventh book Rupert makes a very judicious observation on these words of Our Lord (John 15): “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch of the vine cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains attached to the vine-stock, so neither can you unless you remain in me.” According to our author’s observation, these words are directed against the extreme defenders of free will [Col. 0773D] and against schismatics. Jesus Christ our Lord, the head of the Church, teaches the former, who presume upon their own power, how dreadful their destitution is; and he commends and defends against the latter [Col. 0774A] the unity of the Church, which is his body.

> [Note: [Col. 0773D] “How terrible is the destitution which Christ the Lord, its head, declares to all those who presume upon human power; how truly he commends and defends the unity of the body which is the Church! For what is the case? Do the excessive defenders of free will seem to themselves not to need the helping and pitying grace of God, as though, by willing and running, they could by their own swiftness grasp the fruit of eternal life? But he says: ‘As the branch cannot,’ etc. Therefore, presumptuous and proud evil branches, you rightly deserve to be removed by the farmer’s dreadful hand, unless you confess that all beauty and all the loveliness of fruits proceed not from yourselves but from the vine’s innermost root. Likewise, you too, O schismatics, etc.” [Col. 0774D]]

In the fourteenth book Rupert does not show great esteem for the Septuagint version. He maintains that they did not correctly apprehend the meaning of the original text; and that, being not prophets but interpreters, they often failed to translate exactly.

> [Note: [Col. 0774D] “For the letter of Hebrew truth is not as the Seventy translated it, since they did not possess the mind of God perfectly. For they were not prophets, but interpreters; whence they translated this, as also many other things, not quite accurately: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’ whereas in Hebrew it reads: ‘Cursed by God is he who hangs on a tree.’”]

Since the Apostle cited, according to the Septuagint version, the text which Rupert says was mistranslated, he anticipates this objection and answers it by saying that Saint Paul acted thus because he preached the Gospel to Greeks, among whom that version had been held in great honor since the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, and who would have been offended had he told them that it was inaccurate.
