Thus Paul preferred to follow that version, which moreover presents an edifying meaning, rather than offend them by correcting it.

9. The Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John is followed by another Commentary on the Apocalypse. Rupert addresses it to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, [Col. 0774B] who, like Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, had urged him to undertake this work. He does so by a dedicatory epistle in which he praises this prelate and extols the excellence of the book which he proposes to comment upon. It is saying little, and does not sufficiently praise this book, merely to affirm that it contains as many mysteries as words: *tot habet sacramenta quot verba*—“it has as many mysteries as words.” Answering complaints that he had undertaken to interpret a book upon which persons more enlightened and more pious than himself had labored, our author says that Scripture is a spacious field, common to all confessors of Jesus Christ, and that one cannot without injustice prevent anyone from explaining it, provided that the writer sets down nothing contrary to the faith. We have already often seen him respond to similar complaints in most of the prologues prefixed to his different works. It appears from this work’s dedicatory epistle that he composed it [Col. 0774C] before Cuno’s episcopate, since he gives him only the title of abbot, and after his Commentary on the Gospel according to Saint John—that is, between 1117 and 1126.

In it the author follows the sacred text and explains it verse by verse. But instead of seeking predictions concerning the future, he finds in Saint John only figures of the past and of what has happened since the beginning of the world, especially since Abraham’s time, and still more from Moses to Jesus Christ. He sees there only allusions to events concerning the Church, whether under the old or the new covenant. He seeks only the anagogical and mystical senses, mingling in some moral observations. His principal aim is to show that the seven visions by which Saint John represents the present and future state of the Church must all be referred to the seven spirits before the throne of God. This, properly speaking, is the whole aim and plan of his work, [Col. 0774D] well conceived in itself, but not as happily executed, though it cost the author much labor and reading. One sees that he had read, or at least consulted, commentaries [Col. 0775A] written on the Apocalypse, especially that of Saint Jerome. Yet the esteem he has for the work of those who preceded him, and the approval he grants to their views, do not prevent him from seeking in Scripture’s majesty senses other than those they had found there.

It would be difficult to provide a continuous analysis of this commentary according to the author’s plan, because he himself departs from it so often and loses sight of it so completely that he seems to have forgotten it; consequently, in trying to follow it one would lose oneself amid the commonplaces with which it is full. This is not to say that it does not contain many excellent things which are instructive and edifying; but they are neither arranged nor even suited to the plan the commentator proposed. The author, who is very exact in doctrine throughout all his writings, is equally exact in this work. This may be seen from what he says, though in few words, concerning faith without works, fear, grace and predestination, [Col. 0775B] and the real presence of Jesus Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist. And however diffuse he may otherwise be through the abundance of his thoughts and the multitude of subjects he embraces, he has the talent of setting forth what he says very succinctly, even with great nobility and force of expression.

To give an example which first presents itself, in explaining the words of Revelation 1:6, “He has made us kings and priests to God his Father,” he says (Book I): “What goodness! He redeemed us by his precious blood, not to make us slaves but to make us kings and priests. He alone was king and priest; and from slaves of sin that we were, he makes us ourselves kings and priests. There is no distinction between nation and nation, between tribe and tribe, because he has begotten us not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. And although all are not called to discharge the offices of the priesthood by consecrating the body of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0775C] nevertheless we are all priests in order to offer ourselves to God; and the sacrifice will never cease, because after this life we shall offer him eternally the sacrifice of praise.”

The two witnesses of Jesus Christ mentioned in the Apocalypse are, according to our author, Enoch and Elijah, who will be put to death by the beast when they have completed their testimony. The beast is the Antichrist, who will wage war against the two witnesses—that is, the kind of war which falsehood wages against truth. Rupert observes that defenders of truth do not wield the material sword in its defense. After citing these words of the Apocalypse (Book VIII, on Revelation 13): “He was given power . . . to put to death all who would not worship the image of the beast,” he continues: “Jesus Christ did not do this; neither prophets nor apostles taught it; and princes who embraced Christianity did not receive [Col. 0775D] authority to kill and shed blood in order to compel the worship of Jesus Christ. For the true God desires not compelled service but voluntary service.” *Verus namque Deus, non coacta, sed spontanea vult servitia.* “And by this above all, those possessing sound judgment and reason will clearly see that he is the Antichrist, and is not the true Christ but is opposed to him, as his name indicates. He who shed his own blood is Christ; by contrast, he who shed another’s blood is Antichrist.” *Hic est Christus qui sanguinem suum fudit. Hic est antichristus qui sanguinem fudit alienum.*

The celebrated Cochlaeus, who generally held all Rupert’s works on Holy Scripture in high esteem, did not hesitate to say of his Commentary on the Apocalypse that it far surpassed every other commentary: *In Apocalypsim omnes omnium commentarios longe superavit*—“On the Apocalypse he far surpassed all commentaries of everyone.”

1. On the Victory of the Word of God. *De victoria [Col. 0776A] Verbi Dei.* In the preface the author tells us what led him to compose this work. Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, having come to the monastery where Rupert lived, the two friends were one day conversing about the greatness of Holy Scripture, which was the ordinary subject of their discussions. They spoke of the vision of the prophet Daniel, who had seen four savage beasts, figures of four great monarchies. The reason these monarchies had been represented by cruel and bloodthirsty beasts was that the monarchies themselves had been extremely cruel, filled the earth with blood and slaughter, and persecuted the saints of God Most High. By contrast, since the kingdom of God is the kingdom of peace, the kingdom of charity, the empire of piety, and the dominion of truth, justice, and gentleness, it was to be announced under different figures, as may be seen in the same prophet.

Such was the subject of Cuno’s and Rupert’s conversation when the former [Col. 0776B] interrupted it and turned it to the Maccabees, expressing a desire that Rupert should make known to him why we celebrate their military exploits by reading and chanting in the Church their battles and victories, just as we celebrate the invincible patience of the martyrs. Rupert satisfied him and replied that the Maccabees had rendered a signal service to the world by opposing the efforts of the devil, who wished through the agency of Antiochus to destroy the nation of the saints, from which the Messiah was to be born, and thereby make void the promise God had made to Abraham. Thus the Maccabees triumphed over the devil’s efforts; they saved the root from which so excellent a fruit sprang, namely the Messiah; and they vindicated the truth of God’s promises. This is why the name of the Maccabees, who did such great things, is celebrated in the Church. The same must be said of Esther and Mordecai.

Cuno, charmed by his friend’s answer, immediately said to him: [Col. 0776C] “Compose for me a work on the victory of the Word of God.” He repeated this several times, and afterward pressed Rupert so insistently that at last, because of the great affection he had for him, Rupert yielded despite the difficulty of the undertaking.

This work is cited in *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, Book III, chapter 21, and Book VII, chapter 14. It is also cited in *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, Book XII. It is consequently earlier than both. Finally, it is cited in the prologue prefixed to the final six books of Rupert’s Commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets. Thus it was composed in the interval between the composition of the commentary on the first six Minor Prophets and that on the final six, and before Cuno’s episcopate.

It is divided into thirteen books, and each book into several chapters. The author begins by giving an [Col. 0776D] account of the subject he undertakes to treat. “By the Victory of the Word of God,” he says, “we mean the effect and completed work of God’s purpose, which neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither violence nor height nor depth, nor any creature has been able to prevent God from doing, nor will prevent him from doing, what he has determined.”

In order to make the greatness and importance of the Word’s victory more admirable, he identifies the enemy against whom it had to fight and who wished to thwart God’s purposes (chapter 1). This is the great dragon with seven heads and ten horns, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan. This is the enemy of the Word of God, who, despite all his efforts, could not prevent the execution of the decrees of the Almighty. He then speaks (chapter 2) of the Word of God, who is God himself, consubstantial with the Father. He is known through all creatures, all of which were created by him; but he is known more perfectly through himself.

Humanity (chapter 3) is the occasion of the struggle, lasting from the beginning of the world and ending only with it, between the Word of God and the devil. This ancient serpent has always made every effort to prevent the fulfilment of the purposes of God’s mercy toward humankind, and has been the irreconcilable enemy of the Word of God. Since humanity was created in the image and likeness of God, the devil wished to rob it of this perfection by making it like himself—proud and disobedient.

To carry out this plan, our author surveys the sacred books and extracts all the passages, facts, and events in which one sees the efforts the devil made to halt the effects of God’s grace and goodness toward humanity. “All Scripture,” he says (Book II, chapter 18), “is the book of the wars of the [Col. 0777B] Lord of which Moses speaks. He wrote a considerable portion of it, namely the Pentateuch; and, being a prophet, he knew through the spirit of prophecy that the other books, of both the Old and New Testament, would be written. Who can doubt that Holy Scripture is rightly called the book of the wars of the Lord? For what else does it contain but the war and battles of the Word of God for the destruction of sin and death? This struggle began when God said to the serpent: ‘I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and hers; she shall crush your head, and you will seek to bite her heel’” (Genesis 3).

“From there,” our author says, “let us contemplate, as from the summit of a high mountain, the valor of the Word of God, descending as into a broad and spacious plain against the malice or falsehood of the devil, that ancient serpent. Let us consider how he fought it, conquered it, and triumphed over it; finally, after accomplishing the purpose he set himself when he blessed our first parents from the beginning of the world, he says: ‘Come, you blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world’” (Matthew 25).

Cain is the first of the serpent’s race, and Abel the first of the woman’s race (chapter 19). The latter’s death was a figure of the victory of the Word of God. Cain is the head of all the reprobate, and Abel of the elect. The race of the righteous, extinguished according to the flesh through Abel’s murder (chapters 22–23), was restored by the birth of Seth and then of Enos. The devil again corrupted the race of the righteous through the alliance they contracted with foreign women—that is, women of Cain’s race. Corruption became so great that God wished to exterminate all humanity (chapter 30), and there was only one righteous person who found grace before the Lord, namely Noah: *solus Noe justus atque perfectus*—“Noah alone was righteous and perfect.” Noah, [Col. 0777D] together with his children, was preserved from the waters of the Flood (chapter 32), after which he received the same blessing God had given to our first parents when, after creating them, he said: “Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1). God thus sufficiently disclosed his purpose concerning the elect and predestined who were to be born, multiply, and grow in merit until the end of the ages. In the person of Noah and his children, the Word of God thus formed for himself notable persons to carry out his purposes. The race of Shem was specially chosen (Book III, chapter 1). It received the adoption as children of God, his glory, his covenant, his law, his worship, and his promises, which were made to Abraham, a descendant of Shem.

It is not possible to follow Rupert in all that he says on the subject he undertook to treat. We shall say only that, setting aside the allegories and mystical senses which ordinarily attract [Col. 0778A] his principal attention, he writes in the form of history of the wars of the Word of God against the devil, applying to his plan the principal events reported in the sacred books. He describes historically the efforts of the ancient serpent, or dragon, to devour the woman who was to give birth to the male child mentioned in the Apocalypse. He shows the ill will of the angel of darkness toward humankind and toward God himself, whose promises he sought to annihilate through the oppressions, persecutions, and wars he stirred up against the Israelites in order utterly to destroy that nation, from which he knew the Messiah was to be born.

The maltreatment inflicted upon this people by the Egyptians and the other neighboring nations; the schism and division of the two kingdoms of Judah and Israel; the nation’s own iniquities, especially idolatry; the wars waged against it by the four great monarchies, especially by Antiochus: all these were means successively employed by the dragon [Col. 0778B] to halt the effect of God’s promises. But the Word of God rendered all his efforts vain, and the woman who was to bring forth the male child was preserved from the dragon pursuing her. Her cries—that is, the prayers of the Church—were heard. The promised Messiah came at the appointed time; he fulfilled his ministry, conquered the devil by his death, formed his Church, and triumphed over all his enemies. His apostles and disciples preached his doctrine throughout the world and established the Church despite all the Roman power which the devil had armed to oppose its establishment. The devil himself, driven from his temples and also from human hearts, was compelled to yield to the true God who had disarmed him.

Nevertheless, this ancient serpent employed another means more dangerous than the preceding ones: the way of seduction, through heresies that he raised up in the Church [Col. 0778C] in order to corrupt the faith and destroy the faithful. But his purposes again failed. Whatever efforts he made, neither through pagans nor Jews nor heretics could he prevent the fulfilment of the promises made to Abraham, in whose seed all nations were blessed. The Word of God overturned every obstacle opposed to his merciful purposes. Finally, he has always been and always will be victorious until the end of the world, when he will destroy the Antichrist by the breath of his mouth. Then death will be destroyed; and the destruction of death will be the consummation of the victory of the Word of God and the fulfilment of God’s purpose concerning the elect, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the creation of the world.”

Our author maintains (Book XIII, chapter 1) that, as the Word of God is God and man, the Antichrist will be devil and man: *Unus exsurrexit qui Deus et homo est, et alius, qui diabolus [Col. 0778D] et homo erit, venturus est*—“One has arisen who is God and man, and another is to come who will be devil and man.”

Such, in general, is the plan of the work *On the Victory of the Word of God*, one of our author’s most continuous and methodical works, and one in which he departs less from his subject. He displays much elevation in this writing, and one sees in it great and noble ideas concerning religion, the study of which was his sweetest occupation. Although, when citing Scriptural texts, he follows explanations given before him by the Fathers and doctors, he does so in a manner and style possessing the charm of novelty. He often recalls the mystery of the woman who is to bring forth a male child, and of the seven-headed dragon always ready to devour it as soon as it is born; but he does so because this chiefly constitutes the aim of his work.

The first chapter of Book IX is a short preface in which he displays great piety and humility [Col. 0779A]. In the second chapter we learn that Cunon had asked him to include in his work an explanation of the letter from the Jews of Jerusalem to their brethren in Egypt. This he does from the fourth through the twenty-third chapter. It may be observed that, although he often cites the Book of Revelation, he says nothing there of his commentary upon that book—a sign that he had not yet composed it.

Rupert disputes (Book I, ch. 21) the opinion of those who maintain that the rebellious angel fell immediately after his creation. He relies on these words of Ezekiel (Ezek. 28): “You walked perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you,” applying to the angel all that the holy prophet says of the king of Tyre. Nevertheless, he teaches that angels in general were not created absolutely perfect, and that, after the fall of the wicked, they grew in perfection. He answers (ibid., ch. 24) [Col. 0779B] the question someone might ask concerning the rebellious angel—why God created him, knowing that he would fall—and ends his reply with these words of the Apostle (Rom. 9): “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” etc. He acknowledges (ch. 30) that the good angels were anticipated by God’s grace and mercy, which prevented their fall: “They recognized in themselves the grace and mercy of their Creator, by which they knew that they too had been forestalled, lest they should fall.” Finally, he counts their perseverance among the victories of the Word of God.

## XI. Treatise on the Divine Offices throughout the Year

The author addresses it to Cunon in a dedicatory epistle, telling him that this writing is the first fruit of his pen: “I now offer the first fruits of the produce of the land which the Lord has given me.” He repeats this several times. Thus there can be no doubt that this was the first of all Rupert’s works: “For these are the first fruits of all my works.” Nevertheless, he did not publish it—or at least did not dedicate it to Cunon—until 1126 or the following year; for Cunon was then bishop of Regensburg: “But now … bishop of the Church of Regensburg.” Rupert had already dedicated several works to Cunon, and some to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne. Yet this work on the divine offices, the first of all, composed as early as 1111, he had left, together with several others, without any dedication, “without the distinction of any title.” He gives as his reason that he was then unknown to any bishop to whom he might address himself, as prescribed by the Law, in offering the first fruits to the Lord; and that, besides, caring little for the protection of prelates, he had kept his productions in his study until Cunon made Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, known to him. But Cunon himself having been placed on the see of Regensburg, Rupert offers him, to present them to the Lord, not only the twelve books on the divine [Col. 0779D] offices, which are the first fruits of his works, but also all the other writings he had composed, and which he here enumerates. These are the works already noticed, though he assigns them a different order from that given them when published. After the treatise on the divine offices, he places first the commentary on Job, which, he says, is an abridgment of what St Gregory wrote on that book; then the treatise on St John, the forty-two books on the works of the Trinity, and so forth.

In recent centuries a dispute arose concerning the author of the *Treatise on the Divine Offices*, occasioned by the famous English heresiarch Wyclif. This impostor, wishing to bolster his error on the Eucharist by the authority of some Catholic doctor, cited a work on the divine offices divided into twelve books, sometimes under the name of St Isidore, sometimes under that of St Fulgentius, St Ambrose, or others [Col. 0780A], alleging that they taught the same doctrine as himself. Catholic writers differed concerning the author of this work, some attributing it to one writer and some to another. It was soon established that it was neither by St Isidore, St Fulgentius, nor St Ambrose. Yet some, such as Thomas Walden, Domingo de Soto, Alain, the doctors of Oxford, and Vasquez, attributed it to a certain bishop named Walram; others to Rupert. Bellarmine adopted the latter opinion. But in restoring to Rupert what was his, he did him greater injury than if he had taken it away, by unjustly accusing him of having genuinely taught the doctrine attributed to him by Wyclif. These two critical questions—first, whether Rupert was the author of the *Treatise on the Divine Offices*; second, whether its author taught the error of impanation in the Eucharist—were so fully clarified by Dom Gerberon that nothing further remains to be desired. This wise and judicious critic demonstrated [Col. 0780B] by unanswerable arguments that the book was by Rupert, abbot of Tuit, and vindicated the author against the unjust charge brought against him by showing, in the clearest manner, the soundness of his views on the real presence of Jesus Christ, in an apology which ended the dispute.

It is surprising that there should have been writers so lacking in critical discernment as to rob Rupert of a work which he himself declares to be the first production of his pen, and of which all those who composed catalogues of ecclesiastical writers recognize him as the true author, to say nothing of a multitude of other writers. The continuator of Henry of Ghent, Trithemius in his book on ecclesiastical writers, Bellarmine, Theophilus Raynaud, Sixtus of Siena, and others unanimously attribute the work *On the Divine Offices* to Rupert. The author of this writing expressly declares (Book II, ch. 20; Book VIII, ch. 4) that he is a monk: “The subject requires that we should not pass over anything proper to our order, that is, to monks.” [Col. 0780C] Yet those who wish to take it from Rupert, who was a monk, attribute it to a bishop.

As to the second point, concerning the doctrine of the author of the treatise on the divine offices with respect to the Eucharist, nothing is less well founded than the accusation brought against him by Vasquez, Bellarmine, and others. His doctrine is pure and sound, as conformable to the Church’s faith concerning this adorable mystery as it is opposed to that of the heresiarch who wished to support himself by this writer’s authority. The celebrated Cochlaeus, that zealous defender of the Catholic faith, who was, as it were, the Church’s advocate for more than forty years, ceasing to combat and write against Lutheran errors only when he ceased to live, was so convinced that Rupert’s *Treatise on the Divine Offices* contained only orthodox doctrine that he himself published it at Cologne. This appears from [Col. 0780D] his letter of 1526 to Henry, abbot of Tuit. Would this zealous defender of the Church’s faith concerning the mystery of the Eucharist have had so little discernment as to publish a work contrary to it? Would this irreconcilable adversary of the Lutherans, who throughout his life kept his pen in hand against them, have given the public a work which would have made them triumph?

Who, then, will not be astonished that Bellarmine should have without scruple surrendered to the heretics of recent times an author as considerable and worthy of respect as the author of the *Treatise on the Divine Offices*, whom he himself admitted to be Rupert, abbot of Tuit? This theologian, otherwise a skilful controversialist, must have made very little use of his discernment and read Rupert’s writings with great negligence, to accuse him of teaching an error “which consists,” he says, “in his believing that in the Eucharist bread is not changed into the body of [Col. 0781A] Christ, but that the Word is united to bread, as he was united to humanity in becoming incarnate.” Bellarmine [Note: [Col. 0781D] *De Script. eccles.*, “On Rupert.”] maintains that this is clear from what Rupert teaches in his sixth book on St John. On the contrary, it is clear—and clearer than daylight, we say boldly—from the very book on St John which Bellarmine cites as proof of his assertion, that Rupert, far from teaching the error of which he is accused, firmly establishes the Church’s belief. We ask our readers, in order to be convinced of this, to look at the passages from Rupert’s commentary on St John which we have extracted, and which were also published by Cochlaeus. Those extracts, together with those which we have given on the same matter while reporting on Rupert’s different works, are enough to justify him and might spare us from entering into greater detail. Nevertheless, we shall add here several passages drawn from the very *Treatise on the Divine Offices*, which occasioned the accusation [Col. 0781B] that this author taught: first, that Jesus Christ is present in the Eucharist only figuratively; secondly, that his body and blood are received there only by faith; thirdly, that bread and wine remain in the Eucharist; fourthly, that the Word is hypostatically united to bread and wine as he was united to humanity.

To overthrow the unjust accusations brought against Rupert, it is enough, we repeat, to look at the *Treatise on the Divine Offices* itself, which gave occasion for accusing him. “At evening,” he says in the sixth chapter of the first book, “our Lord, taking bread and wine, and setting forth the reality of his body and blood, borne in his own hands, left humility and charity by testament to his heirs.” In the seventeenth chapter of the same book, speaking of the mystery of the altar and distinguishing reality from what is merely its sign, he expresses himself thus: “What in the Old Testament was promised, prefigured, signified, and greeted from afar, has in the New been given, revealed, and openly made known; it is here presented as actually present—not in shadow but in reality, not in figure but in the thing itself … when Jesus Christ was borne in his own hands and said, holding bread and wine: ‘This is my body; this is my blood.’” [Note: [Col. 0781D] “What in the Old Testament was promised, prefigured, and greeted from afar, but in the New given, revealed, and openly made known, is here exhibited as actually present, not in shadow but in reality, not in figure but in the thing itself … when he was borne in his own hands, holding bread and wine and saying: ‘This is my body; this is my blood.’” [Col. 0782D]]

Our author repeats the same thing in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth book, where he explains the words, “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord,” taken from Psalm 33, bearing this title: “Of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, who sent him away.” According to our author, David on this occasion was a figure of Jesus Christ, “who changed his countenance before the Jews—that is, the manner of sacrifice—when, after sacrificing the paschal lamb of the old covenant, taking bread and wine, he was borne in his own hands, saying, ‘This is my body; this is my blood,’ etc.” [Note: [Col. 0782D] “After the lamb of the old Passover had already been sacrificed, taking bread and wine, he was borne in his own hands, saying: ‘This is my body; this is my blood,’ etc.”] How was Jesus Christ borne in his own hands—*portatus propriis* [Col. 0781D] *manibus*—unless when, having taken bread and wine, he changed the bread into his body and the wine into his blood, as Rupert says in so many places, by the power of the words which he pronounced: “This is my body; this is my blood”?

Such are the views of the author of the treatise on the divine offices, whom people accuse of error concerning the Eucharist. He teaches that Jesus Christ is really and truly present—*praesentialiter, in veritate, in re*, “actually present, in reality, in the thing itself”—in this sacrament. With the faithful, he adores the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ, who, as St Augustine said before him [Note: [Col. 0782D] Homilies 1 and 22 on Psalm 33], [Col. 0782A] was borne in his own hands when he said to his disciples, “This is my body; this is my blood.” Who will not be astonished that such an author should have been accused of teaching that Jesus Christ is present only figuratively in the august sacrament of our altars? Rupert’s accusers must either never have read his writings or have read them with very little attention and with strong prejudices, in order to attribute to him errors which he refutes and to make him attack truths which he defends in the very work in which he is accused of overthrowing them.

If further proofs are required, we are able to supply them from the same book, and they are no less decisive.

In chapter 2 of the second book, he expressly says that bread and wine are changed into the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ: “Bread and wine are transformed into the true body and blood.” If bread and wine are changed, as Rupert says, there is therefore neither bread nor wine in the Eucharist; thus there is no longer impanation, nor any hypostatic union of the Word with bread and wine. In the same chapter our author combats the unbelief of those who, lacking the eyes of faith, see nothing but bread and wine in the Eucharist and, when told that it is the body and blood of Jesus Christ, murmur: “How can this be?”—*Quomodo est?* He represses their murmuring by teaching them [Col. 0782B] “that, as soon as the priest has pronounced the words over the bread and wine, the Word of God receives from the altar the bread and wine, which are changed into his body and blood by the same virtue, the same power, and the same grace by which, as he willed, he clothed himself with our flesh in the Virgin’s womb. … It is the same body which Jesus Christ took in the Virgin’s womb, which was fastened to the cross, and which is offered daily on the altar, where he renews the Lord’s passion.”

In this chapter Rupert uses the phrase *sursum est in carne, hic in pane*—“above he is in flesh, here in bread”—which led Bellarmine to believe that he admitted bread in the Eucharist. But this is mere quibbling, which would apply equally to St Paul’s words, “the bread which we break,” and to the words of Jesus Christ himself, “whoever eats this bread.” The term *panis*, “bread,” used by Rupert means nothing other than the appearances or species of bread and has nothing in common with the error of Wyclif and Luther. The body of Jesus Christ is the same in heaven and on our altars, with this difference: in heaven it is *in carne*, “in flesh,” whereas on the altar it is hidden under the appearances of bread, *in pane*, “in bread.” This is all our author intended to say. Had Bellarmine used his discernment, he would not have seized upon a few terms—which natural fairness required him to interpret favourably—to accuse of error a most Catholic writer who, in a hundred passages of his works, teaches in the clearest way the truth opposite to the errors of which he unjustly accuses him [Col. 0782C].

[Col. 0782D] It is unnecessary for us to dwell longer on this subject. What we have said so far, together with what Dom Gerberon wrote in Rupert’s defence, dispenses us from doing so. Everything that the adversaries of this abbot—especially Bellarmine, Vasquez, and Gregory of Valencia—have alleged against him has been so solidly refuted, and the purity of his faith so clearly demonstrated by this apologist, that no sensible person can refuse to recognize the innocence of the accused and the injustice of his accusers.

[Col. 0783A] Having vindicated the author of the treatise on the divine offices from the affront offered him by some unfair writers, who made his faith suspect concerning the mystery of the Eucharist, it remains for us to describe the work, which is divided into twelve books.

The dedicatory epistle already mentioned is followed by a prologue. The author first says that the divine offices celebrated by the Church throughout the year require an attentive hearer and a master skilled in Scripture to explain them. He then shows the advantage of being instructed in the reasons and motives which led the saints to establish offices and ceremonies in honour of Christ. These saints, not content with preaching orally and in writing the mysteries of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension—which they knew perfectly—also wished to recall these mysteries to the faithful through [Col. 0783B] offices and ceremonies. To celebrate them without knowing the reasons for their institution is like speaking a language whose interpretation one does not know. Now, St Paul says (1 Cor. 14), one who speaks in a tongue should ask for the gift of interpretation. Rupert adds, however, that those who attend the Church’s offices and ceremonies in faith and piety, without possessing this knowledge, nevertheless derive benefit from them. The author concludes by imploring the aid of the Holy Spirit, whose illumination he needs to carry out his design. He asks persons who have read the same subjects treated by writers older than himself not to despise his work because it is new, since he does not claim to lessen the merit of those who preceded him, such as Amalarius and others.

In the first book (ch. 1), he treats the seven canonical hours and says that no one can omit them without ingratitude. They are like a tribute [Col. 0783C] of praise and thanksgiving which we owe to our Saviour for the signal benefits we have received from him. Nothing could be more edifying, instructive, or better suited to nourish piety than what Rupert says concerning each canonical hour. He observes (ch. 16) that bells, whose sound calls the faithful to celebrate the divine offices, succeeded the trumpets formerly used at God’s command to assemble the people. He then turns to the minister of the altar and describes all the vestments with which he is clothed to offer the sacrifice. In treating of the pallium (ch. 27), which the pope sends to archbishops, he speaks of several of the most ancient sees of Gaul and gives the Church of Reims precedence over all the rest: “Among the other archprelates of Gaul, Reims rightly holds preeminence by its authority.” The reason he gives is that this church, already a metropolitan see, had the advantage of having as its pastor the great St Remigius, who converted the king and nation of the Franks to the Catholic faith. He gives the Church of Trier St Maternus as its first bishop, whom he says was sent by St Peter; to Mainz, St Crescens, whom he maintains was a disciple of St Paul and who also founded the Church of Cologne; hence the latter has the primacy [Col. 0783D].

After speaking of the minister’s vestments, he treats of the sacred ministry and explains every part of the sacrifice of our altars, beginning with the Introit and continuing to the end.

In chapter 8 of the second book, on the matter of the sacrifice, there occur the strongest expressions concerning the real presence of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist and proving the soundness of his views on this mystery. We should note, however, that a writer of the author’s own century was struck by what he says in the same chapter: that the life of Jesus Christ [Col. 0784A] in the sacrifice is a spiritual life without animal life: “But this life of his is spiritual in the body of the sacrifice, without his animal life, just as the light of the sun is represented to us in the body of the moon without its heat.” This writer was William of Saint-Thierry [Note: [Col. 0783D] *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. IV; *Annales*, vol. V], and not, as some have falsely claimed, St Anselm, who, having died in 1109, could not have found fault with a work composed in 1111. William wrote Rupert a very courteous letter in which, after telling him of the satisfaction he had received from reading his work *On the Divine Offices*, he adds that, since truth and charity should banish flattery, he thought he had seen a blemish in his fine work which might provide those who like to criticize the writings of others with occasion to attack it.

William found ambiguity in what Rupert called “the body of the sacrifice.” This body is the one that died, rose again, and sits at the Father’s right hand; in short, it is the body of Jesus Christ [Col. 0784B] which possesses motion, sensation, and so forth. Rupert taught nothing contrary to William’s belief, since he repeatedly says that the body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist is the same body which the Word formed for himself in the Virgin’s womb, which was fastened to the cross, which rose again, and so on. But he meant—and this is what most theologians teach—that Jesus Christ in the Eucharist performs no function of the external senses and exists there as in a state of death. “For,” he says, “there is animal life and there is spiritual life. Animal life consists in the five senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. This animal life is carnal; it is flesh. But the Lord says that the flesh profits nothing. … Therefore, if animal life, because it is flesh, were present in the Lord’s body, it would profit us nothing.” He in no way doubts that the body of Jesus Christ is alive in the Eucharist; but it is not alive in a manner perceptible to us, and it is not fitting that God should feed our curiosity with unnecessary miracles: “for it does not belong to his wisdom to feed our curiosity with miracles that are not necessary.” Let us add that William, far from accusing Rupert of any error concerning the august mystery of our altars, does not even maintain that the expression displeasing to him is blameworthy. Having stated his difficulties, he leaves it to Rupert’s judgment whether what troubled him needs correction [Col. 0784C].

In chapter 21 of the second book, Rupert relates what he holds each pope prescribed for the celebration of the sacred mysteries, which in the earliest times were not celebrated with as much splendour and ceremony as they have been since. In chapter 22, he defends the use of unleavened bread in the Latin Church. There he highly extols the Roman Church and treats the Greek Church rather harshly, especially the see of Constantinople, whose arrogance, he says, gave birth to many heresies: “The arrogance of the see of Constantinople, mother of many heresies.”

[Col. 0784D] We shall not follow our author through all the details into which he enters concerning the various offices celebrated throughout the year. This would carry us too far without bringing the reader much advantage, since he does not go back to the ancient origins of usages and practices; instead of seeking natural reasons for their institution, he gives only mystical explanations or makes pious reflections. He also introduces many questions which might be better placed elsewhere. From the immense detail he provides concerning the celebration of divine offices and the usages of the Church, one sees that what was practised in his time is, with few exceptions, what is practised today. Du Verdier, in his *Bibliothèque*, mentions a French translation of this work, made by Jean Bouillon, priest, native of Sens, curé [Col. 0785A] of Jaune-lès-Bray-sur-Seine, published at Paris in 1572 by Claude Tremy.

Sanderus [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum Belgii*, Part I, p. 42] mentions a work on the divine offices by one Master Robert—*magistri Roberti*—which differs from Rupert’s. This is apparent from the words of its prologue: “I remember that, concerning the ecclesiastical offices, certain small matters,” etc.; whereas Rupert begins: “Those things which, through the circle of the year,” etc.

## XII. On the Fire of the City of Tuit, which Occurred on 25 August 1128

A few days afterwards Rupert composed this small work, divided into twenty-three chapters. In it he addresses the religious of his monastery, exhorting them to submission to God’s commands and to gratitude for having been miraculously preserved from the flames. It appears to be a discourse delivered in the presence of his monks, to whom he gives substantial and moving instruction upon this sad event. It contains no detailed account of the accident which supplied its subject; such an account would have been unnecessary, since he was speaking to persons who, like himself, had witnessed it. Yet it contains profound religious feeling and great zeal for the maintenance of monastic regularity. In a word, the piece is highly edifying because of the piety that pervades it and gives a very favourable idea of its author.

He relates (ch. 5) a miraculous event which alone proves how fully persuaded he was of the real presence of the body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. Fire having seized the parish church of the place, the parish priest, named Stephen, had forgotten to remove the Blessed Sacrament, although he had taken the precaution of removing several other things. This caused him deep grief. Passing through the flames and the burning wreckage of the roof, he went to the place where stood a wooden pyx containing the body of Our Lord and found it safe and intact, although the flame had consumed everything around it—namely, another box full of unconsecrated hosts [Col. 0785C], the cruets, a censer, and so forth—which were in a vaulted cupboard beside the altar. Overjoyed, the parish priest brought the box to Rupert, whose joy was no less than his own. The following day, a Sunday, the pious abbot had the body of Our Lord, in the box preserved from the flames, carried in procession in thanksgiving. To preserve the memory of this miracle, he had the box placed upon the altar with a corporal which, in the same fire, had been the instrument of another miracle: thrown into the flames, it had been driven by them, without damage, as far as that part of the town which the fire spared. Above the box he placed this inscription: “This body of the Lord conquered the flames in the pyx” (*hoc corpus Domini flammas in pixide vicit*) (ch. 6).

Rupert does not conceal (ch. 19) his anxiety that, if the fire reached his monastery, he might lose what was in this world his sweetest consolation [Col. 0785D]—that is, his works, especially those which had not yet left his hands. Among these was the work *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which he had composed very recently: “Alas, how I feared that my work might burn—the work which is my greatest consolation in this life, namely, the work of the books which I have laboured over,” etc.

## XIII. *De meditatione mortis*: On Meditation upon Death

This work consists of two books, the first containing nineteen chapters and the second nine. It is a continuation, as it were, of the preceding work, having been composed on the occasion of the fire at Tuit.

Although it is useful for a person to remember that he must die (ch. 2), since this thought inspires anxiety and fear regarding the account he must render after death, nevertheless [Col. 0786A] this alone does not constitute meditation upon death, which makes the wise person’s life perfect. “It consists in firmly believing that, since man is dead in soul through sin, it benefits him that God should cause his body to die and that he should not live forever; for from the very bosom of death he draws a treasure of life and salvation through Jesus Christ, who willed to submit himself to death as we do.” All the afflictions of this life, and death—the greatest of them all—are consequences of the state into which humanity fell through sin. A person ought to regard them as instruments of life and salvation which God puts in his hands, that he may make good use of them with the aid of grace. This is what Rupert proposes to treat in his work on meditation upon death. The execution of this plan, very fine in itself, is not among the most brilliant. Yet it contains very sound and solid reflections and felicitous comparisons. Such is the comparison he makes between the death of the body and the death of the soul (ch. 9). Just as a body separated from the spirit which gives it life is nothing but a corpse that decays and is reduced to ashes, so, when the soul is separated by sin from God its Creator, the human being is dead, like a corpse and a sepulchre full of corruption.

The wise person (ch. 9) always remembers this death, whose memory is bitter to him, by which the sinful soul, abandoned by the Spirit of the living God, becomes the sepulchre of a dead person—that is, of the devil. But when he sees the image of this death in that of someone dear to him, he remembers this great death more powerfully, because he considers, on the one hand, the loss of a friend whose companionship was his consolation and, on the other, reflects upon the state of that friend’s soul, and doubtless upon his own as well, in accordance with the saying of the wise man: “Have pity on your soul.” For can anyone know whether he is worthy [Col. 0786C] of love or hatred—that is, worthy of life, which is God, or worthy of death? The death of the soul precedes that of the body; for when we are born, we are dead in soul through the sin of our first parents. The death of the soul comes from the devil, and bodily death is a just punishment which God’s wise providence imposed upon humanity. For if, after sin, God had allowed us to be immortal, we would have resembled the demons, since we would have had, like them, a wretched eternity, or eternal wretchedness (Book II, ch. 9) [Note: [Col. 0785D] Baillet, 16 March; Molanus, 16 March].

## XIV. Life of St Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne

[Note: [Col. 0786D] *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. III.]

It is divided into thirty-five chapters and begins with a dedicatory epistle addressed to Macward, then abbot of St Heribert’s, to which monastery he had been transferred from the monastery of Siegburg in order to restore regular discipline there. At Macward’s request, Rupert undertook this work and revised the style of the Life of the holy prelate written by Lambert, abbot of St Lawrence [Col. 0786D] at Liège. Dom Rivet discussed the latter’s work in the eighth volume of the *Histoire littéraire de France*, p. 7 and following. But Rupert was not content merely to revise Lambert’s style: he expanded the material, so that the Life of St Heribert which he gave us is twice as long as the work on which he laboured. Both are found in Bollandus’s great collection, under 16 March.

XV. Martyrdom of Saint Eliphius. *Passio beati Eliphii* [Note: [Col. 0786D] Surius, 16 October; Baillet, 16 October; Tillemont, I.] The author of this short work tells us, in the prologue prefixed to it, that Alban, abbot of Saint-Martin, and his monks, dissatisfied with an old Life of the holy martyr because of its simplicity and obscurity of style, had asked him to revise it and to add moral reflections. Overcome by [Col. 0787A] their entreaties, he undertook to satisfy them and revised the old Life of Saint Eliphius. This new Life was published by Surius. M. Baillet derived from it the greater part of what he says concerning the holy martyr in the Life he composed of him. These various writers may be consulted. We shall observe only here that Rupert gives a fairly accurate idea of Julian the Apostate’s conduct toward Christians. But the speeches which he puts into the mouth of this apostate, as well as those which he makes Saint Eliphius deliver at the moment of his execution, and certain other circumstances of his martyrdom, do not appear to us very credible.

XVI. On the Will of God. *De voluntate Dei.* The work is divided into twenty-six chapters, preceded by a preface which is a prayer in which the author asks God for the light necessary to treat properly the subject on which he undertakes to write, so that he may say nothing except what accords with truth.

[Col. 0787B] In it Rupert attacks two celebrated men of his time: William of Champeaux, then bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne, and Anselm of Laon. Since William was not placed in the see of Châlons until 1113, Rupert cannot have composed his work *On the Will of God* before that date. The following was its occasion. One of the disciples of these two famous masters, who was in Rupert’s monastery, declared that he had learned from them that God wills evil to occur, and that He willed Adam’s sin. [Note: [Col. 0787D] “One of our own admits that he received this teaching from your schools, so as to say that God wills evil to be done, and that Adam’s transgression was according to God’s will. He relies not upon the authorities of Scripture but upon the greatness of your name, and, with prolonged contention, maintains the division handed down to him: the will with regard to evil, he says, is of two kinds, one approving and the other permitting.”]

This pupil of William and Anselm maintained this proposition (ch. 1), not by the authority of Scripture but by relying on the great name of his masters; and he admitted a twofold will with regard to evil, one that approves it and another that permits it. Rupert addresses William and Anselm and tells them that, had he been able to confer with them, he would have asked whether it could truly be the case that masters of the arts, *magistri artium*, had taught what was attributed to them by admitting so frivolous a division as that of two wills concerning evil, one approving it and the other permitting it. He then presses them with this reasoning:

“What then? If the will of evil is the genus, and the differentiating species contained under this genus are one approving and another permitting, will this which he calls the permitting will be good or evil? If evil, how is it opposed to that which approves evil? If good, how can it be a species of the will of evil?” [Note: [Col. 0788D] *Quid enim? Si voluntas mali genus est, et generis hujus divisivae differentiae sunt, alia approbans et alia permittens, haec quam dicit voluntatem permittentem, bona erit an mala? Si mala, quomodo approbanti malum opposita? Si bona, quomodo species voluntatis mali?*]

He next maintains and proves (ch. 2), on the authority of Scripture, that God’s permission is nothing other than His patience, goodness, and long-suffering. It is true that, by delaying the punishment of sinners, God in some sense permits evil to happen; but this permission (chs. 3–4) cannot be attributed to an evil will, or to a will for evil. On the contrary, [Col. 0787D] it is God’s goodness, inviting the sinner to repentance. He shows (ch. 3) that God does not will evil, although He permits it; and he explains how one must understand Scripture’s statement that God hardens Pharaoh. All men, he says (ch. 4), sinned in Adam; all deserved death and were worthy only of eternal punishments. By an act of wholly gratuitous mercy God pardoned some, while by an act of justice He punished others. He touched the former in order to lead them to repentance; He hardened the latter by not softening [Col. 0788A] their hearts. Thus, of two officers equally guilty, Pharaoh punishes one and pardons the other. No one blames what that prince did; how, then, does anyone dare find fault with God’s conduct toward mankind?

Having refuted (ch. 5) his opponents’ opinion, Rupert does not stop there, but undertakes to answer several difficulties which they raised. If God, they said, neither wills nor willed evil, why did He not create human nature so that it could not change and pass from good to evil? Why did He give man a commandment if He did not will him to violate it, since He knew by His foreknowledge that he would violate it? Why does He allow the birth of those for whom it would have been more advantageous never to have been born, since they are not predestined to eternal life? Rupert proposes to clarify these difficulties, but without losing sight of what the Apostle says concerning the depth of God’s judgments, and without seeking to comprehend them: [Col. 0788B] “Yet not forgetful of the Apostle’s most forceful exclamation, by which he says, ‘O the depth!’ etc.” (*Rom.* IX). Our author first remarks (ch. 6) that it is unbecoming for a virtuous and sensible man to debate such questions: it amounts to offering counsel to God and finding fault with His works. He then answers them in a manner showing that, on grace and predestination, he follows what Saint Paul, Saint Augustine, and the Fathers taught. He does not cite them, but one readily perceives that he had read them and was their disciple.

XVII. On the Omnipotence of God. *De omnipotentia Dei*: one book, divided into twenty-seven chapters, with a prologue in which he explains the silence he had kept for some time in response to his opponents’ complaints against his work *On the Will of God*, and the reasons that lead him to take up the pen again. This book *On the Omnipotence of God* is [Col. 0788C] a continuation and, as it were, an apology or defense of the preceding work. In the first, as we have said, he had combated the view of certain theologians who maintained that God wills evil and willed Adam’s fall. Those whom he had refuted rose up against his work; and, claiming to defend God’s omnipotence as though he had attacked it, they strongly urged this argument: if, though God does not will evil to be done, evil nevertheless occurs, it follows that God is not omnipotent. For how is He omnipotent if He cannot prevent the occurrence of evil which He does not will to occur?

After keeping silence for some time, Rupert took up the pen again with fresh zeal, to combat his opponents’ opinion and answer their difficulties. His whole purpose in this work is therefore to show that moral evil—that is, sin—does not happen by God’s will, and [Col. 0788D] that this in no way detracts from His omnipotence. To prove what he asserts (ch. 3), he uses the authority of Scripture and of the Fathers, especially Saint Augustine: “this [is taught] by the holy Fathers, and especially by the eminent father and doctor Augustine,” etc. The author lays down the true principles concerning the cause of good and evil, and of good and evil will. Sin or evil (chs. 3–6) comes from the creature, while good comes from God. The creature, drawn from nothing, tends of itself toward nothing and falls back into it. It turns away from God, who is supreme being, [Col. 0789A] turns toward itself, and thus tends toward nothing. This is the source of evil, of evil will, and of sin. In short, evil will comes from the fact that the creature is drawn from nothing; good will, which bears it toward God who created it, or toward the Word through whom it was created, comes from grace. “Whence, then, does it have good will … unless from gift or from grace?”

There are nevertheless some passages in this work that seem less exact; but they must be explained by those in which the author speaks in accordance with the principles he had drawn from Scripture and the Fathers. This is a rule of natural fairness which one cannot dispense with observing, especially in the case of a writer who, in most of his works and with such clarity, establishes the truths taught by the Church concerning grace and predestination.

The disciples of the famous masters whom Rupert had attacked in his work *On the Will of [Col. 0789B] God*, and whom he was still attacking in this one, made much noise against him and treated him contemptuously. They reproached him with wishing to employ dialectic although he was ignorant of the art, having never attended the schools—as if, he says, no one in monasteries possessed learning: “As though monasteries were altogether devoid of persons possessing knowledge.” He cites (ch. 22) the example of Saint Augustine, who learned without the assistance of any teacher things regarded as very difficult; not because he wishes to compare himself with that great mind, but to show that one need not change country and cross the seas in order to acquire learning. The Spirit of God blows where He wills. Our author admits (ch. 23) that, with regard to the art of dialectic, he has never made a display of it; and that even if he were skilled in it, he would not employ it unless compelled to do so when simple truth must defend itself in the conflicts [Col. 0789C] it is obliged to sustain against falsehood.

Rupert certainly composed this work before 1117, since in it (ch. 26) he expressly speaks of Anselm as still living. He praises him, places him above all the masters then in France, and states that he had learned that Anselm did not approve the doctrine which he combats. [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Yet Anselm of Laon, whose faith and learning have hitherto borne fruit in Christ’s Church with a good fragrance beyond those of others, does not support them by his authority. May the light of truth preserve forever the prudent learning of that illustrious man, lest by rash speech in matters of this kind he should inflict any stain upon his glory; and if at any time he deigns to answer the preceding book, as he promised to do, may a white dove come to us.”] He further tells us that Anselm had promised to reply to his preceding work—that is, *On the Will of God*. It is certain from the prologue to the book *On the Omnipotence of God* that its author composed it during the time of Héribrand, abbot of Saint-Laurent at Liège, successor of Bérenger.

XVIII. On Certain Chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict. This work, composed by Rupert at Cunon’s request, is divided into four books. In the first, after relating what led Cunon to urge him to write on this subject—something [Col. 0789D] he did only after a year of entreaty—he makes his defense against his opponents’ reproaches and accusations. He begins by applying to himself these words of Scripture: “When a poor man speaks, people say, ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they overthrow him completely” (*Ecclus.* XIII). He is treated in this way because he embraced the religious life while very young and did not travel through the world or cross the seas to hear famous masters. “This,” he says, “is what makes me contemptible in their eyes, and makes them say: ‘Who is this? For he composes and speaks; he speaks and writes, though he has never seen our masters and doctors.’ I am indeed [Col. 0790A] very poor,” he says, “for I have scarcely been able to obtain paper on which to write.”

He then recounts what he had to endure from those who maintained that God wills evil, and what he did to prevent them from reviving the heresy of Florinus. This heresy consisted in making God the author of moral evil, that is, sin. The Colitians, on the contrary, embracing the other extreme, taught through an opposite error that God does not produce physical evil, contrary to Scripture, which says: “I am the Lord making peace and creating evil”: *Ego Dominus faciens pacem et creans malum* (*Isa.* XLV). This, our author judiciously adds, must be understood not of evil contrary to virtue, but of evil as affliction: *non malum quod est virtuti contrarium, sed malum afflictionis*. This physical evil is famine, war, and the other scourges which God sends, according to the testimony of the prophets, to punish human sins.

After [Col. 0790B] citing with praise the authority of Saint Jerome, who, in explaining Isaiah’s words *faciens pacem et creans malum*, equally avoids the two opposing errors of the Florinians and the Colitians, he continues:

“It was reported that celebrated masters, the brightest lights of all France, who drew a great number of disciples from every province to their schools, had advanced this proposition concerning God’s will and maintained it steadfastly. Accordingly,” he adds, “whatever I might say, not only was I not heard, but I was despised as a fool. My opponents, supported by the authority of their masters, stubbornly maintained this opinion as if they had received it from an angel descending from heaven—whom, nevertheless,” he says, “one ought not to heed any more than in any other matter contrary to the truth of Scripture.”

Rupert complains particularly of an ignorant young man, the refuse of the schools, who, having taken [Col. 0790C] his opponents’ side, as though to favor clerics against a monk, overwhelmed him with reproaches and insults, while the more able men treated him with consideration and restraint. These reproaches made him feel in himself what the Church says through Job: “Now I am a laughing-stock to men younger than I, whose fathers I would not have wished to set with the dogs that guarded my flocks” (*Job* XXX). But he despised all his opponents’ reproaches, and, like Ezekiel, presented them with a diamond-hard forehead, stronger than stone, and a countenance firmer than theirs.

In a kind of dissertation that follows, Rupert discusses four texts of Scripture upon which his opponents relied to defend their opinion. He maintains that Saint Augustine was perplexed when attempting, in his *Enchiridion* addressed to Laurence, to explain these words of Jesus Christ: [Col. 0790D] “If these miracles had been done in the cities of Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (*Matt.* XI). What Rupert says on this subject appears to us neither sound nor sufficiently respectful toward Saint Augustine, although, in departing from his view, he compares himself to Jethro, who gave very wise advice to Moses, who was holier and wiser than that priest of Midian.

Our author then enumerates the works from which his opponents had sought material for their accusations against him. One among them, to whom he had lent his *Treatise on the Divine Offices*, made a charge of the following words found in [Col. 0791A] chapter eleven of the third book, where he speaks of the office of the Fourth Sunday of Advent:

“For who can investigate how the Word takes bodily form; how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the mother’s womb; how He who has no beginning both exists and is conceived?”

The censor, failing to grasp the sense of this text—which was taken from Saint Gregory the Great’s exposition of Saint John’s words, “The Jews sent priests from Jerusalem” (*John* I), etc., though Gregory was not cited—and in which the matter concerns only the Word, who is Spirit, and not at all the third Person of the Trinity, claimed that Rupert taught that the Holy Spirit was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb. He vehemently declaimed against the work, saying that it was heretical and deserved the fire; this he did amid a crowd of ignorant people who were already demanding the writing in order to do it justice by consigning it to the flames.

Rupert does not name this censor, but the portrait he gives sufficiently reveals him. “He is a man,” he says, “of ordered life, but newly [Col. 0791B] converted; of great name, but suspicious reputation; already a prelate and preacher, but scarcely ever previously subject or a disciple.” These words plainly designate Saint Norbert. Rupert attributes Norbert’s conduct toward him—publicly declaiming against him [Note: [Col. 0791D] Mabillon, *Annals*, bk. LXXIII, no. 40, vol. VI.] instead of charitably warning him—to a secret hatred, because Rupert had declared his disapproval of a young man, newly converted, passing so quickly from secular life to the exercise of priestly functions and the ministry of public preaching; he had said that it was suitable neither to Norbert’s age nor to his former life for him to become a prelate before having been subject to another. Whatever may be said of Rupert’s claim, and although Saint Norbert erred in misunderstanding this author’s words, which were those of Saint Gregory the Great, we are persuaded that Saint Norbert acted on this occasion out of religious zeal, not secret hatred.

[Col. 0791C] Our author defends himself very well against the charge of heresy brought by his opponents because he had asserted that angels were created from darkness. “Heresy,” he says, “consists in contradicting holy and canonical Scripture: affirming something which it denies, or denying something which it affirms”: *Haeresis est contradicere sanctae et canonicae Scripturae, affirmare aliquid quod ab illa negatum est, negare aliquid quod ab illa affirmatum est.* Having given this definition of heresy, he challenges his opponents to show that what he has said concerning angels is in any respect contrary to what Scripture says about them. The Fathers held different opinions on this matter, as he shows, and he reports at considerable length what Saint Augustine wrote on it in the eleventh book of *The City of God*. Now, when the Fathers, always agreed in matters concerning the faith, are divided in differing opinions on other points, Rupert considers himself free to embrace the opinion that seems to him [Col. 0791D] most in agreement with scriptural texts. This is what he did in preferring Saint Hilary’s opinion to Saint Augustine’s concerning Judas. The former Father believed that Our Lord did not give the Eucharist to that treacherous disciple; the latter, on the contrary, teaches that he received it.

Among Rupert’s opponents was one whom he describes as, although a monk, a scholastic of great name and reputation, with whom he had an unhappy dispute concerning the body and blood of Jesus Christ. This scholastic, who, according to Rupert, sought to diminish the majesty of this mystery, maintained, on Saint Augustine’s authority, that Jesus Christ gave this sacrament to Judas, who was to betray Him, as well as to the [Col. 0792A] other Apostles. “By this,” Rupert says, “he wished to imply that He would not have given it to him if it had been the substance of His body and blood.” Rupert thought he could dispose of the objection from Saint Augustine’s authority by replying that the writings of that holy doctor did not rank among the canonical books and did not possess an authority requiring the same reverence as is rendered to those books. But this answer was badly received, and it was held against him as though he had advanced a heresy. This shows how far reverence for that holy doctor extended at that time.

Later Rupert discovered that Saint Hilary had taught the same thing as himself: namely, that Jesus Christ had not given the Eucharist to Judas; this greatly consoled him. As for the highly reputed scholastic of whom he speaks, we believe with Dom Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0791D] *Annals*, bk. LXXIII, no. 41, vol. VI.] that he was Sigefroid, who was made abbot of Saint-Vincent in the same city after being prior of Saint-Nicolas-au-Bois near Laon. What Rupert says of [Col. 0792B] him—that he sought to diminish the majesty of the mystery of the Eucharist—seems to us an unfounded suspicion and an unjust accusation. We possess a work by Guibert of Nogent [Note: [Col. 0792D] *Literary History*, vol. V.], addressed to Sigefroid under this title: *Letter on the Piece of Bread Given to Judas and on the Truth of Christ’s Body*. We have spoken elsewhere of this work, from which it appears that the prior of Saint-Nicolas—that is, Sigefroid—had proposed certain difficulties concerning the Eucharist to the abbot of Nogent, so that he might learn how they ought to be resolved, but not with the intention of disputing this mystery.

At the end of the first book, Rupert lets his opponents know that, whatever they may say or do against him, they will not succeed in preventing him from writing.

The second book is solely a wholly mystical explanation of chapters 9, 11, and 12 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, in which that saint regulates the night office for Sundays. What Saint Benedict calls in the ninth chapter the *Ambrosianum* signifies, according to Rupert, the hymn of Matins said after the invitatory. It was given this name because Saint Ambrose introduced its use into the Western Church.

The third book is entitled *On the Service of the Altar*, *De altaris officio*. The author gave it this title because, since Saint Benedict prescribed nothing on this subject in his Rule, while strongly commending manual labor, some maintained that monks ought not enter the clerical state and that, in order to live in accordance with their Rule, they had to live by the labor of their hands. Rupert therefore shows (ch. 62) that monks may enter holy orders; that the state of penitence which they have voluntarily embraced ought not exclude them, unless they are otherwise excluded by the rules of [Col. 0792D] the Church; and finally that this is entirely consistent with their Rule, in which Saint Benedict directs that an abbot who wishes to have one of his monks ordained priest or deacon should choose one worthy to fulfill the office: “If any abbot requests that a priest or deacon be ordained for him, let him choose from among his own one worthy to perform priestly service.”

As for the manual labor prescribed by the Rule, our author wishes it first to be observed that not everything commanded by a law is commanded for its own sake as necessary to salvation; often the legislator has another object: “For not all things that appear to be commanded have been enjoined or given for their own sake, as necessary for salvation, but for another purpose.” This granted, Rupert sets about proving, from several texts of Saint Benedict’s Rule, that, in prescribing [Col. 0793A] manual labor for monks, that holy legislator did not command it as something in itself necessary to their salvation, but only to supply their needs—“a relief for poverty where necessary things are lacking”—and to avoid idleness. To the texts drawn from the Rule he adds examples, particularly that of Saint Maurus, who, having come to France, received from the generosity of the king and princes lands and revenues to support a great number of monks. Would this disciple of Saint Benedict, educated by the legislator himself, who had read the Rule and knew its spirit, have departed from it in a matter so essential? Would he have accepted possessions to maintain monks who could be saved only by living from the labor of their hands?

In maintaining his opinion, Rupert is far from blaming poverty or from favoring or excusing idleness. But he believes that the service of God, being an occupation for which one is not [Col. 0793B] obliged to leave the precincts of the monastery, is also the most advantageous and even the most in keeping with Saint Benedict’s spirit.

Having remained on the defensive, Rupert next becomes the aggressor. He complains that those whom he answers in this work chose, without any reasonable motive, to distinguish themselves by the color of their clothing, adopting a color different from that which they had found. For all persons of either sex who profess the religious life are dressed in black; “and we do not know,” he says, “why they adopted white.” Perhaps, he adds, if we had worn white garments, they would now wear black: “Perhaps, if we had used white clothing, they would now be wearing black.”

Here our author says several very sensible things about dress, in which one must avoid a singularity that, without pleasing God, offends men. Regarding the scandal that may be taken from the conduct of certain monks, he says that it is only in heaven that the good are found wholly unmixed; however holy the religious profession may be, one must remember that those who have embraced it are human beings and consequently capable of faults.

The fourth book bears the title: *On the Contention of Monks Who Say: “I Belong to Augustine; I Belong to Benedict.”* In it Rupert blames and condemns, as contrary to charity and humility, the disputes between clerics and monks, some of whom said, “I belong to Augustine,” while others said, “I belong to Benedict.” “To have such disputes,” he says, “is to make a schism. For one does not dispute in this manner without pride; one is not a little swollen with vanity when, adhering to one rather than the other, the man who professes himself Augustine’s says to the one who professes himself Benedict’s: Augustine is a bishop, Benedict a monk; now a bishop is unquestionably greater than a monk; therefore my order [Col. 0793D] is above yours. These disputes grew so heated that people came even to say that a cleric may not become a monk, whereas a monk may be drawn from his cloister to be made a cleric, and that this is more perfect.”

Our author rises vigorously against these disputes. He seeks to inspire both parties with a spirit of unity and charity and exhorts them to rid themselves of these ideas of preeminence, which have no source except vanity. He proves from Saint Benedict’s Rule, received in the Church and praised by Saint Gregory the Great, of whom he gives high praise, that it is permissible for a cleric or priest to become a monk. He explains various passages of Saint Jerome and shows that, if a monk may become a cleric, this is not by leaving his state to embrace another, but by receiving the order of priesthood or the diaconate.

He asks a regular canon, who had an extreme aversion to [Col. 0794A] monks and seemed to locate clerical status in outward dress, whether he believes clerical status and the monastic state so opposed that they cannot coexist in the same person. “It is your own mind,” he says, “that represents them to you in that way because of your aversion to monks. But, far from being opposed, they are companionable and friendly; each adorns the other, as blessed Jerome says. Do you suppose that clerical status and monastic status are opposites and cannot both exist at once in the same person? Rather, your mind stands opposed to the monk, and therefore you regard them as opposites; but they are allied and friendly, and one is adorned by the other, as blessed Jerome says.”

This work shows that there was another subject of dispute: namely, whether a regular canon—that is, one who says that he belongs to Augustine—has the right to be invested with the pastoral staff and to bear the name of abbot: “Whether reasonably, or without the support of reason, one who says, ‘I belong to Augustine,’ wishes to be invested with the pastoral staff and called abbot in the Church.” [Col. 0794B] This custom had begun to be introduced in several parts of France, and many people were astonished by it, seeing neither on what ground nor by what authority it was done. Rupert reports a letter from Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, to Adalbert, bishop of Liège, in which he disapproves this new custom, *novam consuetudinem*, and does not wish the superiors of clerics, though regular clerics, to be invested with the pastoral staff like abbots of monks. For, he says, nowhere do we read that Saint Augustine, whose Rule they profess to follow, was called an abbot.

Rupert next seeks the origin of the pastoral staff, or crozier. He derives that of bishops from Aaron’s rod—or rather Moses’—and that of abbots from Elisha’s staff. He maintains that the staffs of the ancients who pastured flocks, such as Moses, adopted son of Pharaoh’s daughter and son-in-law of the priest of Midian, were magnificent and richly adorned.

Rupert declares that he does not know what occasion gave rise to the present dispute or prompted the regular canon whom he combats to glory thus and exalt himself against the monastic state. He places before his eyes what Saint Paul says concerning charity, and adds that true charity, always proceeding with humility as its companion, preserves unity: “True charity, always walking with humility as its companion, preserves unity.” He reproaches him for having said in his presence, speaking of monks—of whom he never spoke well, especially the religious of Cluny—that the monastic state would meet the fate which had come upon the Babylonian kingdom: after rising to the highest degree of glory, it had fallen. Thus the monastic order, after having been greatly exalted, would fall and make place [Col. 0794D] for other, little-regarded bodies which were only then arising: *atque humilibus suborientibus fieret aliud principium.* (It appears from this admission that the regular canons did not then claim to be very ancient.)

Rupert replies that he could make a more just and less odious comparison by saying that, just as the moon, when it has reached its highest degree of light, immediately begins to wane and seems almost annihilated, yet then is reborn and increases anew, so too “the holy Church, and above all the spiritual order which the Holy Spirit has established, sometimes indeed declines in some place, but afterward makes fresh progress [lacuna]; yet it shall never be scattered or destroyed.”

Our author ends this work with the following verse, [Col. 0795A] which contains a mystical explanation of the abbot’s crozier:

> Gather in, support, spur on, [the] wandering, sickly, and sluggish.

XIX. Disputation between a monk and a cleric; by Rupert, abbot of Deutz, a work in which he shows that a monk may lawfully preach. It is the same work as that found among the manuscripts of the Abbey of Weissenau, under these two differing titles: *Ruperti conflictus cum Norberto* [Rupert’s conflict with Norbert]; *Conflictus Roberti Coloniensis Abbatis cum Norberto* [Conflict of Robert, Abbot of Cologne, with Norbert] (HUGO I, part II). The Annalist of Prémontré, who informed us of these manuscripts, has spared us the perplexity into which we might have fallen concerning this work by reporting its opening words: *Inique agis resistens in faciem meam*—“You act unjustly in opposing me to my face.” For these words remove every difficulty, informing us that this work differs only in title from the one of which we have spoken: *Altercatio monachi et clerici*, etc. [Disputation of a Monk and a Cleric, etc.].

It is a short dialogue in which [Col. 0795B] the author introduces a monk who complains that the cleric is silencing him by refusing to permit him to proclaim the word of God in church. The cleric replies that, because a monk has died to the world by his profession, he ought neither to speak nor to make his voice heard through preaching.
