The monk turns this argument against the cleric, telling him that he too is equally dead: that what Saint Paul says—“You are dead, and your life is hidden in Jesus Christ”—is addressed to clerics as well as monks, indeed to all Christians. The cleric then objects to the monk with the authority of Saint Jerome, who says that a monk’s occupation should be mourning rather than teaching: *Monachus non doctoris habet officium, sed plangentis*—“A monk has not the office of a teacher, but of one who mourns.”

The monk grants that a mere monk may not teach, but maintains that he may do so when he has been honoured with the priesthood, because he is then both cleric and monk; and by his ordination he has received the commission to proclaim the [Col. 0795C] word of God to the people. Saint Jerome himself is strong evidence that a monk may teach, since throughout his life he taught and wrote, and thereby deserved to be numbered among the eminent doctors. Clerical status consists neither in learning, nor tonsure, nor dress, but in exercising the ministry of the altar. Therefore, a monk who has received ordination, since he may exercise this ministry, may preach; nor can anyone lawfully contest this right: *Mihi ergo*, he says, *hoc ipsum praedicandi jus detrahere non potes absque injuria*—“Therefore you cannot deprive me of this very right of preaching without injustice.” We agree with Dom Gerberon that this work is the same as that which Reyner includes in his catalogue of Rupert’s writings under this title: *De monacho clericus factus, egressus est monasterium, et suum errorem allegationibus defensabat improbis*—“Concerning a monk who, having become a cleric, left the monastery and defended his error by shameless arguments.”

XX. Letter of Rupert to Everhard, abbot of Brunwyller. This abbot, who possessed much piety and a [Col. 0795D] very scrupulous conscience, hesitated to entrust to his monks the administration of the many churches dependent upon his monastery. He consulted Rupert on this subject, asking whether this was compatible with the profession of a solitary. The abbot of Deutz replied that this was the subject of an old and prolonged controversy between clerics and monks. The former maintained that, since a monk has died to the world, he cannot exercise the ministry consisting in preaching, baptizing, administering communion, and absolving penitents. This letter is properly only an abridgment of the preceding dialogue, to which Rupert refers his correspondent.

XXI. *De laesione virginitatis, et an possit consecrari corrupta*—“On the Violation of Virginity, and Whether One Who Has Been Defiled May Be Consecrated.” This work is divided into seventeen chapters, preceded by a Prologue. In it Rupert answers the consultation of a monk of Stavelot, whose letter is printed at its head. It appears from this letter that our abbot enjoyed a high reputation for learning and [Col. 0796A] piety, and that great confidence was placed in him. As for his response, it does not seem very clear or precise on the first part of the case proposed. On the second, he expressly declares that he wishes to decide nothing, lest he appear to depart from Saint Jerome’s opinion that *virginem non posse suscitari post ruinam, vel coronari corruptam*—“a virgin cannot be restored after her fall, nor one who has been defiled crowned.” Nevertheless, he thinks that if violence was done to her and she gave no consent whatsoever, she may be consecrated, although Saint Jerome seems to admit no exception.

These are all Rupert’s works contained in the latest edition, which, although fuller than all those preceding it, nevertheless does not contain them all. Since, in giving an account of Rupert’s writings, we have followed not the chronological order in which the author composed them, but the order in which the latest editor published them, we shall now place them before the reader according to their chronological rank; and we shall add those which have [Col. 0796B] not yet appeared, following the catalogue drawn up by Rupert’s apologist.

## Catalogue of the Works of Abbot Rupert, Printed and Unprinted, in Chronological Order

### I. His writings before he became a priest

1. A hymn in Sapphic verse in praise of the Holy Spirit: *Flamine magno*, etc. He quotes it in full in the twelfth book on Saint Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man* (Pez, *Anecdota*, IV, p. 25).

2. Another hymn in iambic verse on the same subject. It occurs at the end of the thirteenth book on Saint Matthew.

3. A book of various sayings of Scripture: *De diversis Scripturarum sententiis*—“On Various Scriptural Sayings.” Dom Gerberon (*Apologia*, part I) thinks that this lost work was merely a collection of biblical texts, because Rupert did not apply himself to interpreting the sacred books [Col. 0796C] until after receiving the priesthood.

4. A poem in heroic verse on the Incarnation of Our Lord.

5. *On the State of the Monastery of Saint Lawrence near Liège*, from Eraclius, bishop of that city, down to Otbert, in five books.

6. A short work in Sapphic verse on the same subject.

7. Life of Saint Augustine.

8. Life of Saint Odilia. Dom Mabillon (*MAB.*, *Acta*, IV), in his preliminary observations on the Life of Saint Odilia, virgin and abbess of Hohenbourg in Alsace, observes that Reyner, monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège, in his treatise on the illustrious men of his monastery, attributes to Rupert a Life of Saint Odilia the Virgin. But he could discover neither which Odilia this was nor what had become of the work. He nevertheless believes that the Saint Odilia whose life Rupert wrote was one of the virgins who suffered martyrdom at Cologne, from which the monastery of Deutz [Col. 0796D] is not far distant.

None of these writings, known to us only through Reyner, has come down to us, except for part of the work *On the State of the Monastery of Saint Lawrence*.

### II. His writings after he became a priest

1. A chant on Saint Theobald, martyr, and Goar and Severus, confessors.

2. Twelve books *On the Divine Offices*, composed in 1111; but the dedicatory epistle to Cunon, bishop of Regensburg, was written no earlier than 1126. This work, which Rupert himself calls the firstfruits of the land which the Lord had given him, ought to have occupied the first place in the edition of his works. Dom Bernard Pez says (*Anecdota*, introductory dissertation, vol. I, p. 39) that he found among the manuscripts of Saint Emmeram’s Abbey at Regensburg Rupert’s *Treatise on the Divine Offices*. He even believes it to be the original which the author [Col. 0797A] sent to Cunon, because on the first page of this folio manuscript Bishop Cunon appears painted, with Rupert at his right and Stephen at his left, and is crowned with these two verses:

> Here, from the fruits of the divine offices,  
> he gives the bishop the bright gift of the firstfruits.

3. Commentary on Job, ten books divided into forty-two chapters. We find no precise date for this work in Rupert’s writings.

4. *On the Will of God.*

5. *On the Omnipotence of God.* These two works were written after 1113 and before 1120.

6. Commentaries on the Gospel of Saint John, fourteen books. Rupert composed this work after the preceding two and before completing the one that follows; consequently, before 1117.

7. *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works.* This work, begun about 1114, was not completed by the author until 1117, because he was diverted from his labour [Col. 0797B] by other occupations, especially by the dispute concerning the will of God which he had with Anselm of Laon and William of Champeaux.

8. *On the Apocalypse*, twelve books, dedicated to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.

9. *On the Song of Songs*, seven books. Dom Gerberon admits that he could not determine with certainty when Rupert worked on this book, and that he relies only on conjectures in assigning it the position it holds in his catalogue.

10. *On the First Six Minor Prophets*, seventeen books.

11. *On the Victory of the Word of God*, thirteen books.

12. *On the Last Six Minor Prophets*, seventeen books.

### III. Rupert’s works after he became abbot

1. *On Saint Matthew, On the Glory of the Son of Man*, thirteen books.

2. *On the Books of Kings, On the Glorious King David*, fifteen books addressed to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.

[Col. 0797C]

3. *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*, four books.

4. Dialogue of a Christian and a Jew, three books. When Dom Gerberon was working on his Apology for Rupert, he did not then know that this dialogue, of which he knew Rupert to be the author, was preserved in manuscript in the library of Liessies. But Dom Gerberon himself later discovered it and published it at the end of the works of Saint Anselm, under this title: *Annulus seu dialogus Christiani et Judaei de fidei sacramentis, auctore Ruperto abbate Tuitiensi*—“The Ring, or Dialogue of a Christian and a Jew on the Mysteries of Faith, by Rupert, Abbot of Deutz.” It is dedicated to an abbot whose name in the prologue is indicated only by the initial letter R. The work is divided into three books. The author makes use of his extensive knowledge of Scripture, drawing from it what he places in the Jew’s mouth in defence of his case, and in the Christian’s mouth to demonstrate that the old law no longer applies; that the new law has replaced it; that this new covenant [Col. 0797D] was announced to Abraham even before he received circumcision; that circumcision was only the seal of the promise made to Abraham and of the righteousness he had through faith before being circumcised; that Abraham, though justified by faith, was neither delivered nor admitted into heaven except through Jesus Christ; that Jesus Christ is the Messiah, or the seed promised to Abraham; that circumcision, the ceremonies, and the sacrifices of the Mosaic law are abolished; and that a new law has succeeded the old, and the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek that of Aaron, etc.

[Col. 0798A]

5. *On the Glorification of the Trinity* and *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, nine books, with a letter addressed to the Pope.

6. *On the Burning of the City of Deutz.*

7. *Meditations on Death*, two books.

8. *On Ecclesiastes*, five books.

9. Life of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.

10. Martyrdom of Saint Eliphius.

11. Disputation of a cleric and a monk.

12. Rupert’s response to a letter of Everhard, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Brunwylers.

13. *Against Certain Religious*, etc. Dom Gerberon, who assigns this work to Rupert, does not tell us whether he saw it in print or manuscript. We do not find it among the printed works.

By means of this catalogue of Rupert’s works, one may correct, revise, and supplement what is lacking in those given by the bibliographers, none of whom is exact either with respect to the number of our abbot’s productions or to the order [Col. 0798B] in which they are arranged.

> **Note: [Col. 0797D]** Of all bibliographers, the one who supplied the most exact list of Rupert’s writings was Jean-François Foppens, canon and grand penitentiary of Mechelen, in his *Belgian Library* (vol. II). But this writer, highly partisan and filled with prejudices against the best authors, adopts the unjust accusations brought by Cardinal Bellarmine against the abbot [Col. 0798D] of Deutz. Was it owing to these prejudices that he omitted from his catalogue the short works on the Will and the Omnipotence of God? This omission is inexcusable in a bibliographer who had before his eyes the 1638 edition of Rupert’s works, in which these short works occur, along with others which he also omitted.

But although this catalogue is fuller and more exact than any of those given by Reyner in his treatise on the illustrious men of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège, by Bellarmine, Sixtus of Siena, the Magdeburg Centuriators, Possevino, and others, it does not contain all Rupert’s writings. Since Dom Gerberon, who supplied us with this list of Rupert’s works, further discoveries have been made, which we shall now report.

1. *De vita vere apostolica dialogorum libri quinque*—“Five Books of Dialogues on the Truly Apostolic Life.” These five books of Dialogues on the truly apostolic life were published by Dom Martenne (*Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, p. 96) and Dom Durand as being, in their view, by Rupert: *auctore, ut videtur, Ruperto*—“Rupert appearing to be the author.” The editors’ conjectures rest upon the following grounds:

1. The monastery of Grafschaft, where they found the work in a manuscript approximately [Col. 0798C] six hundred years old, lies in the diocese of Cologne; and they subsequently saw a similar manuscript of the same work in Deutz Abbey, where almost the sole surviving work among all Rupert’s writings was preserved.

2. The author of these dialogues was a neighbour of Saint Nicholas’s Abbey at Brunwylers near Deutz, with which Rupert was closely connected.

3. Rupert wrote on this subject, as appears from Anselm of Havelberg’s letter to the abbot of Usperg, who had himself composed a work on the subject on the occasion of a regular canon who, desiring a more perfect life, had embraced monastic life.

If these conjectures are not conclusive, they at least suffice to place this work among Rupert’s doubtful writings.

The author’s purpose, as the editors observe, is to show that monks are capable of fulfilling all the functions of the Church, and that [Col. 0798D] the regular canons—who had scarcely come into existence in the eleventh century—wrongly declared war upon them by maintaining that the administration of the sacraments and the governance of parishes were forbidden to monks, who ought to be confined to their cloisters. Yet by their preaching monks had until then converted exceedingly numerous peoples and entire nations, governed not merely a few parishes but even most dioceses, and often honourably filled the See of Saint Peter.

It appears from the prologue prefixed to the work [Col. 0799A] that this question was then debated with great heat on both sides. The author condemns these disputes and states that he took up his pen only to make the children of God recognize Satan, who is among them without their knowing it. “Since there are among you jealousies and disputes,” he tells them with Saint Paul, “is it not evident that you are carnal? For it is certain that the children of God, as spiritual brothers, are peaceable. There is an old controversy between monks and clerics as to who are more worthy to exercise the ecclesiastical ministry; and while they thus dispute over apostolic dignity, they lack apostolic charity. Since monks and clerics are, in relation to all the people, like the eyes of the body, if they are blinded by the spirit of pride, by what darkness will that body not be enveloped?”

Our author, often witness of these disputes, “seeing,” as he says, “these two eyes sick with the pride which led them to prefer [Col. 0799B] themselves one to the other, has sought, like a physician, to expose this sickness and has composed this work, which he presents to them as a remedy for healing it.” Thus, his aim is to end disputes, lead both parties to love one another mutually, and show, through clear and evident proofs, who are more worthy to exercise the ecclesiastical ministry.

The dialogue is between master and disciple. The latter asks questions and the former answers. Yet the disciple often appears as skilful as the master, and even gives him lessons. The author does not display much critical judgment, and his reasoning often lacks soundness. But justice must be done him: in defending his cause he treats his opponents with every consideration and moderation one could wish. He speaks nobly of religion and lays down very fine principles. He wishes that “following the example of Jesus Christ, when truth is at stake, one should sooner allow the whole world to take offence than abandon it through silence. Since Jesus Christ is the truth, to renounce truth is to renounce him.”

*Exemplo ergo Domini, si tibi sermo pro veritate est, debes prius in scandalo relinquere, quam tacendo veritatem deserere. Veritas autem Christus est. Qui ergo veritatem, quid nisi Christum abnegat?*

“Therefore, following the Lord’s example, if your discourse concerns truth, you ought rather to leave people in offence than abandon truth by keeping silent. But truth is Christ. Therefore whoever renounces truth—what does he renounce but Christ?”

He teaches that fasting in itself and the austerities practised by monks do not make their practitioners better, but rather inward dispositions do; for hypocrites are seen to undertake great abstinences, while saints eat every kind of food with thanksgiving. He takes great care to inspire humility in monks and regular canons. He removes from both the pride of personal merit and unites them in Jesus Christ through the bond of grace and the spirit of humility. He recalls to them the apostles’ dispute over precedence [Col. 0799D] and Our Lord’s instruction on this matter. By the example of Saint Sebastian, who suffered martyrdom under a soldier’s dress, and Judas, who under that of an apostle betrayed Our Lord, he shows that no one ought to glory in the habit he wears.

He teaches that priests receive through ordination the power to exercise the ministry, which consists in baptizing, preaching, celebrating Mass, and so forth. He adds that if monks elevated to the priesthood did not have authority to discharge these same functions, they would be merely half-priests:

*Ergo compotes sui sacerdotalis officii probantur, quicunque presbyteri ordinantur. Est autem plenum officium sacerdotalis ministerii, baptizare, praedicare et his similia, et missas canere. Si igitur hoc non licet monachis qui ordinantur, ergo non pleni presbyteri, sed semipresbyteri . . . . . Quia autem est impossibile non ordinari qui ordinantur, huic autem qui ordinatur, [Col. 0800A] omnis potestas sui officii conceditur, ergo omnis monachus presbyter, praedicare, baptizare debere concluditur.*

“Therefore all who are ordained priests are shown to be possessed of their priestly office. Now the full office of priestly ministry is to baptize, preach, perform similar acts, and sing Masses. If, then, this is not lawful for monks who are ordained, they are not full priests but half-priests. … Since it is impossible that those who are ordained should not be ordained, and since to the person ordained every power of his office is granted, it follows that every monk who is a priest ought to preach and baptize.”

Although the author combats the claims of the regular canons, he speaks of them with great esteem. He makes a comparison, highly honourable to them, between their life and that of the clerics of his own age, saying that the life of clerics is as far removed from that of regular canons as heaven is from earth, and that there is as great a difference between them as between the Jewish Synagogue and the Christian Church.

2. *Epistola Roberti abbatis, qua ratione monachorum ordo praecellit ordinem clericorum, ad Liezelinum Canonicum*—“Letter of Abbot Robert to Canon Liezelin, on the Grounds upon Which the Monastic Order Excels the Order of Clerics.” Robert, author of this letter, is none other, according to Dom Martenne (*Thesaurus anecdotorum*, I, p. 285) and Dom Durand, who published it, than Rupert, abbot of Deutz. He treats in it the same subject as in the preceding work. This letter is followed by another addressed to Rupert by a canon named [Col. 0800B] Mengoz, who, in returning several of his works, gives them high praise. He speaks particularly of the books *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Thus Mengoz’s letter to Rupert was not written about the year 1100, because that work had not yet been composed at that time. Robert’s, or Rupert’s, letter to Liezelin, which the editor likewise supposes to have been written around that time, that is, around 1100, must be later than that date.

3. Rupert is the author of a history of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège, which Dom Gerberon believed no longer existed. But Dom Martenne (*Amplissima Collectio*, IV, p. 31) and Dom Durand inform us that some remnants of it still survive in the monastery of Saint Lawrence. On examining the manuscripts of that abbey, they discovered that someone with little appreciation for the value of such monuments, wishing to save paper, had scraped away the manuscript containing Rupert’s work in order to substitute an abridgment [Col. 0800C] of Saint Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs. Thus, of five books scarcely two remain: the fourth and fifth. In this twelfth-century manuscript, Dom Martenne says, evidence of this outrage can still be seen in the traces of the erased letters. Dom Martenne adds that the history of Saint Lawrence’s monastery at Liège which he publishes contains an abridgment of Rupert’s work, and that what it says concerning the foundation of this abbey is taken word for word from Rupert’s writings, which still survived in the time of Adrien du Bois, monk of Saint Lawrence and one of the history’s continuators. This history is all the more valuable and interesting because it was successively continued by different writers, who from century to century recorded matters of which they had themselves been eyewitnesses.

We might also have spoken of certain writings found in Flemish manuscripts [Col. 0800D] under the name Robert, which probably belong to Rupert; but since we have not seen them, we prefer silence to risking conjectures.

Among the manuscripts in the Vatican Library, Dom Bernard de Montfaucon cites one containing a work under this title: *Ruperti abbatis Stimulus charitatis in Jesum Christum. Ejusdem libri De divinis officiis in compendium redacti*—“The Spur of Love toward Jesus Christ, by Abbot Rupert. Abridged books by the same author, On the Divine Offices” (*Bibliotheca*, vol. I).

## § III.—Writings Falsely Attributed to Rupert

The theologians of Louvain (*Appendix*, vol. IX), in their edition of Saint Augustine, attributed to Rupert a treatise *On Antichrist*, which belongs neither to him nor to Saint Augustine, Alcuin, or Rabanus Maurus, but to Adso, abbot of Montier-en-Der, as Dom Rivet proved in the sixth volume of the *Literary History*. In the 1712 edition of Moréri’s Dictionary, it is said that Rupert’s principal theological work [Col. 0801A] is his treatise *On the Sacraments*. This author cannot have ever seen Rupert’s writings, for this alleged treatise *On the Sacraments* occurs in none of the editions of this abbot’s works. The catalogue we have given is sufficient to acquaint the reader with the other works falsely attributed to the abbot of Deutz, and spares us a more extended discussion of them.

The extracts we have made and the details into which we have entered in giving an account of his works likewise spare us from setting forth his doctrine and opinions or defending them.

We shall add only that no writer of this century displays as much learning as Rupert. In his works he cites not only the Fathers and ecclesiastical writers, in whom he appears to have been very well versed, but also secular authors, Greek and Roman alike—philosophers and historians as well as poets. The [Col. 0801B] library of his monastery must have been very rich. It may be noted that he cites Trogus Pompeius several times in his work *On the Victory of the Word of God*, without ever mentioning Justin, that historian’s epitomizer. Could it be that in his time this history still existed complete? As for his knowledge of Scripture, we need not speak of it: his works on almost all the sacred books sufficiently show how much he had studied them. Through the profound meditation he had devoted to them, these oracles of the Holy Spirit were so familiar to him that, besides citing them continually, he often employs their words without citation.

## § IV.—Various Editions of His Works

Although Cardinal Bellarmine (*Script. eccl.*, p. 302), as inaccurate in the enumeration of Rupert’s [Col. 0801C] writings as he was unfair in his judgment of them, asserted that they remained for about four hundred years in obscurity and neglect, it is certain that they were always highly esteemed, both in the author’s lifetime and after his death, and that a great number of editions were produced, several of which had already appeared when Bellarmine wrote in this manner.

Cochlaeus, the celebrated defender of the Church’s faith concerning the mystery of the Eucharist against the new heresies, was the first to publish Rupert’s works from various manuscripts in German libraries, in 1526. In a dedicatory epistle to Henry, abbot of Deutz, who had supplied him with manuscripts, Cochlaeus calls Rupert the ornament of Germany. He styles him a truly solid doctor, an illustrious scholastic, who may justly be compared with the ancients, Greek as well as Latin, in his exposition of Scripture. He does not hesitate to say that no one wrote more accurately or more [Col. 0801D] clearly on the Gospel of Saint John and the Apocalypse; that Rupert examines every word, explains and supports everything he says by passages from Scripture; that one finds in him very fine passages from Saint Chrysostom, Saint Cyril, and Saint Augustine; and that he does not limit himself to making his reader better informed and more enlightened in order to make him a doctor, but seeks to form him for a pure and holy life, to inflame him with the love of God, and inspire in him piety, humility, submission to the Church, and respect for superiors. Such was Cochlaeus’s judgment of Rupert’s writings. As can be seen, he was far from considering them infected with the errors of Wycliffe, Luther, and Calvin concerning the Eucharist. He therefore hastened to make them public, and by his efforts they first appeared at Cologne, from François Birckman and his brother Arnould, in 1526, 1527, and 1528. Father Lelong cites an edition of all Rupert’s works printed at [Col. 0802A] Cologne in 1540, in two folio volumes, by Arnould Birckman.

In 1577 the heirs of Arnould Birckman collected all they could of Rupert’s writings, carefully revised them, and published them in three folio volumes. This Cologne edition includes several writings which had not yet appeared: the Life of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne; the book *On the Burning of Deutz*; and the two books *On Meditation upon Death*.

Arnould Mylius, having acquired Birckman’s printing house, published a new edition at Cologne in 1602, in two folio volumes, in which he gave Rupert’s works a better order. He added the acts of Saint Eliphius’s martyrdom, a very full subject index, and another index of texts drawn by the author from Holy Scripture. The editor, Arnould Mylius, addresses this edition to Dom Gerard Foeller, abbot of Deutz, in a very fine letter in which he dwells particularly [Col. 0802B] on the authority of the Fathers and shows that the Church has always sought and found in their writings weapons for defending her doctrine and confuting heretics.

Herman Mylius, printer at Mainz, put the works of the abbot of Deutz through the press again and added several that were not in the preceding editions: the two short works *On the Will* and *On the Omnipotence of God*, recently printed at Nuremberg; the four books *On Certain Chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict*; the commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the Book of Job; *De laesione virginitatis*; the Disputation of the Cleric and Monk; and the Letter to the Abbot of Brunwyler. This edition appeared in two volumes in 1631.

Charles Chastelain, seeing that Rupert’s works were much sought after and that it was difficult to obtain them from Germany because [Col. 0802C] of the war, conceived the idea of producing a new edition. He carried this out in 1638. It is dedicated to the Fathers of the Congregations of Cluny and Saint-Maur, whose superior general, Gregory Tarrisse, supplied the editor with a copy of the Mainz edition of Rupert’s works, upon which the Paris edition was made.

Doctor Grancolas, in his abbreviated critique of the works of ecclesiastical authors (vol. II), after listing the following editions of Rupert’s works—Cologne, 1533, 1566, 1577, 1598, and 1602—adds: “And the most correct was produced at Paris in two volumes in 1638, through the care of Dom Gerberon, then a Benedictine.” Dom Gerberon was born in 1628: how could he have produced an edition of Rupert’s works in 1638? This remark offers no high opinion of the learning and ability of a man who sets himself up as a critic of the works of ecclesiastical authors. [Col. 0802D] Although the same critic assures us that the Paris edition of Rupert’s works is the most correct, we may boldly say that it swarms with errors, even very gross ones. One scarcely finds two consecutive sentences whose punctuation is accurate and in which some word has not been corrupted.

Besides the general editions of Rupert’s works—if indeed they may be given that title, since none contains them all—there are a great many individual editions, most of his works having been printed separately in various places: Cologne, Antwerp, Louvain, Mainz, Paris, and elsewhere. All these editions are so defective that one could well wish someone would undertake a good one (*Journal des savants*, September 1751, pp. 628–629). A Venetian printer, Michel Pleunich, formed this design some years ago and published a prospectus addressed to theologians, informing them of his resolution to print a collected edition of Rupert’s works and promising writings that had not yet [Col. 0803A] appeared up to that time. We do not know whether this printer is working to carry out his plan.

> **Note: [Col. 0797D]** This edition appeared at Venice in 1749. EDITOR.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1134

# HERMANN, A CHRISTIAN FORMERLY JEWISH

[Col. 0803]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae latinitatis*, book VIII, p. 238)

Hermann of Cologne, formerly called Judah, an Israelite by birth and of the tribe of Levi, a Christian converted from Judaism, was moved by the conversations of Rupert, abbot of Deutz from the year 1124, of Eckbert, bishop of Münster from the year 1127, and of other clerics; having also brought his brother over to the Christians, he became a canon of Cappenberg of the Premonstratensian Order in Westphalia. He wrote a short work on his conversion, addressed to Henry, whom he calls now his son, now his dearest brother. From the manuscript of the Pauline Library at Leipzig, in which it was joined to Jerome’s Commentaries on Isaiah, the late Johann Benedict Carpzov published it at the end of Raymond Martini’s *Pugio fidei*, illustrated by the observations of Joseph de Voisin. Leipzig, 1687, folio.

[Col. 0803]

# SHORT WORK OF HERMANN THE JEW ON HIS CONVERSION

(Edited from the manuscript of the Pauline Library of the University of Leipzig by Carpzov at the end of Raymond Martini’s *Pugio fidei*, Leipzig, 1687, folio.)

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

Johann Benedict Carpzov, D., sends greetings and best wishes to the most reverend and illustrious Theophilus Spizel of Augsburg, most vigilant pastor of the orthodox Church of Saint James in his native city, most celebrated theologian and polymath, honoured friend, fellow-countryman, and brother in Christ.

When, having long conceived the plan of publishing Raymond’s *Pugio*, I finally set my hand to it last year as it was drawing to its close, it occurred to me, excellent Spizel, that the theologian of blessed memory Martin Geier, my kinsman, six years before it was first printed at Paris, had noted in his inaugural dissertation—proposed for discussion from Isaiah’s prophecy concerning the Messiah’s death, burial, and resurrection—that a copy of it was preserved in the Pauline Library of our Academy, which at that time could only have been a manuscript. I therefore proceeded to search and inspect the parchments; but although our most deserving librarian in literary matters, Joachim Feller, my most honoured colleague, examined them all with the greatest diligence, and though they had also been listed in a separate catalogue published for public use, he nevertheless found Raymond nowhere. Thus, unless perhaps that most blessed man’s memory deceived him, I can readily believe that the library was deprived of this treasure, being before these times without catalogue, order, and more vigilant care.

Meanwhile, while I sought Raymond in vain, the most diligent librarian recommended to me, under this title, Jerome’s Commentaries on Isaiah written on parchment: they also contain a little work by a certain proselyte concerning his conversion from Judaism to Christ, written in an elegant script indeed, but by an ancient hand. He sent the codex itself, certainly a most precious one, to my house so that I might examine it a little more carefully.

I did not remember that this Hermann—for that name appears subscribed to the author—was mentioned anywhere among writers, even among those who discuss in particular converts from Judaism to the Christian religion; much less had I ever seen the little work printed. This was likewise denied both by friends present and by others consulted by letter. I therefore thought that I should not be wasting all my labour if I freed it after so many years bound in chains, so that it might accompany Raymond, now appearing at Leipzig, in the capacity of an attendant—even though it precedes him in age by a century and a half, and is therefore worthy of recommendation at least on account of its antiquity, if for no other reason.

For Hermann himself thus reveals his date [Col. 0805], when he recounts that in the thirteenth year of his age he saw in a dream Emperor Henry, predecessor of Lothair, still holding the reins of empire at that time. That Emperor Henry, the fifth of this name, died in the year of Christ 1125. Moreover, he praises Robert, abbot of the monastery of Tuitiensis, as “a man,” he says, “subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and most learned in both sacred and secular letters,” with whom he disputed concerning religion. The facts themselves show that this is none other than that Rupert renowned for his commentaries on Genesis, the book of Job, the Song of Songs, the Minor Prophets, the Gospels of Matthew and John, and the Apocalypse, as well as for many other outstanding monuments of his genius; he died two years before Emperor Lothair, in the year of recovered salvation 1135.

Hermann was therefore a contemporary of the mellifluous Doctor Bernard, later enrolled among the saints, abbot of Clairvaux. In this little work he gives us further information, besides the history of his conversion, concerning certain not unimportant matters of that age, indeed also concerning some points of doctrine. Thus I have not yet reason to regret the labour expended here. Yet almost every inconvenience was spared me by one of the more distinguished of my hearers, Master Christian Feustel, a young man commendable to all good persons for talent and industry. Having come to us trained in these studies under the instruction of the most illustrious Christian Daumius, he produced the whole little work, transferred from parchment to paper, more quickly than one would have expected; and thus made it possible for it to be added to the *Pugio* with almost no labour on my part.

Since this should not be concealed, so I fear, dearest Spizel, that you may take it ill that I place your most celebrated name at the head of these sheets, as though about to dedicate a book which I did not myself write and whose publication has cost me few vigils. Yet I have not forgotten the honour with which, twenty-seven years ago, you favoured me, when you wished to dedicate to me alone your excellent treatise on Chinese learning—one that smelled no less of the lamp than of bitten fingernails—which you were publishing at Leiden, and which had been received with the applause of learned men.

From that time onward I have always thought of some memorial of reciprocal affection. But since until now I have not been able to offer an equivalent, I thought this professorial tablet of our mutual regard would come before more people if it were prefixed to Raymond’s celebrated book—which I too owe to your generosity, having once received it at Paris at your expense—together with this little work rescued from neglect and decay, the kind of antiquity of which I know you to be both a lover and an investigator, than if I offered the particular fruit of a barren little field.

In any case, we reproduce Hermann faithfully as we received him portrayed in the parchment, adding only corrections and conjectures in brackets. Anyone will observe that the summaries prefixed to each narrative are the author’s own.

Farewell.

Written at Leipzig, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the year of restored salvation 1687.

## HERMANN’S LETTER

[Col. 0805]

To his dearest son Henry, Hermann, by God’s grace what he is, sincere affection in Christ.

Many religious men and women are accustomed to ask me how I was converted from Judaism to Christ’s grace, and what temptations of the malignant enemy I endured at the very beginnings of my conversion. Thus recently, while you were present, I was compelled by the devout request of certain women of holy life to recount its entire course. For I was not converted with that ease with which we often see many unbelievers—whether Jews or pagans—converted to the catholic faith by a sudden and unexpected change, so that those whom yesterday we grieved over as faithless, today we rejoice to see become believers and our fellow-heirs in Christ’s grace.

My conversion, however, was finally brought about only through the ever-recurring storms of very grievous temptations at its beginning, many snares set against it by the ancient enemy, prolonged wavering, and the greatest labours. For this reason it is so much the more pleasing to devout ears to hear, as it proved more wonderful through the very difficulty of its accomplishment. Therefore, kindled by the devotion of many, and especially encouraged by your pious exhortation, dearest brother, I judged it worthy to commit this to writing, and thereby faithfully to proclaim to believers both of the future and of the present age, to the everlasting praise and glory of him who called me from darkness into his marvellous light, his inestimable grace.

Here ends the letter.

## IN THE NAME OF THE LORD BEGINS THE LITTLE WORK OF THE BROTHER OF BLESSED MEMORY, HERMANN, ONCE A JEW, CONCERNING HIS CONVERSION

[Col. 0805]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the vision he saw while still a boy

[Col. 0805A]

Therefore I, Hermann, a sinner and unworthy priest, once called a Jew, an Israelite by race, of the tribe [Col. 0806A] of Levi, born of David my father and Sephora my mother in the metropolitan city of Cologne, while I was still held entangled in the bonds of Jewish unbelief, God foreshowed to me by the most delightful omen of such a vision the benefits of his grace that were to come to me.

In the thirteenth year of my life I saw in a dream that the Roman Emperor Henry—who, predecessor of the glorious King Lothair, was reigning at that time—had a certain exceedingly powerful prince. When that prince died suddenly, the emperor himself possessed all his property. Then this same king, as it seemed, came to me and offered me a horse of snowy whiteness and marvellous size, and a belt woven from gold with the utmost workmanship, with a silk purse hanging from it, in which seven very weighty coins were enclosed.

When he had handed all these things over to me, he said: “Know that my dukes and princes are greatly indignant at the benefit I have bestowed upon you; nevertheless, I shall add things far greater than these for you, and shall give you the entire inheritance of this deceased prince, to possess by perpetual right.”

Then I returned the thanks due for royal generosity, girded myself with that noble belt, mounted the horse, joined the king at his side, and accompanied him as far as his palace. There, while he dined splendidly with his friends, I reclined next to him as though his dearest friend and ate with him, from the same dish, a vegetable preparation made from many kinds of herbs and roots.

Awakening in the delight of this vision, though I was a boy, I did not in childish frivolity judge those extraordinary things I had seen to be empty. Rather, thinking that some great thing was foreshown to me by their omen, I went [Col. 0807A] to a kinsman of mine, Isaac by name, then a man of great authority among the Jews. Having related the dream to him in order, I asked him to interpret it for me according to his understanding.

He, minded only toward the things of the flesh, offered me a conjecture based upon fleshly prosperity. By the great and white horse, he said, was signified that I should obtain a noble and beautiful wife; by the coins enclosed in the purse, that I should possess many riches; and by the feast celebrated with the emperor, that I should become highly honoured among the Jews.

But much later divine grace more clearly fulfilled this vision in me through spiritual gifts, as the subsequent interpretation of the same vision showed and the outcome itself proved. Now I shall set forth in sequence how the occasion of my conversion first arose.

## CHAPTER II. By what first occasion he attached himself to Christians, and how much he profited from their fellowship

[Col. 0807D]

Seven years after this, I came to Mainz to conduct business in various mercantile transactions. For all Jews engage in trade. At that time the glorious King Lothair was there, having with him the venerable Eckebert, bishop of the Church of Münster, a man who shared fully in all his counsels.

Since the king detained him there, occupied with affairs of the realm, beyond the time he had intended to remain, and since the money in his purse had been exhausted, necessity compelled him to borrow silver from me. Yet I took from him no pledge such as Jewish custom required, counting the faith [Col. 0808A] of so great a man a precious security.

When my parents and friends learned this, they rebuked me in a rather harsh attack, saying that I was far too careless to presume to lend money to anyone without security, especially to a man often distracted by numerous engagements; according to the well-known Jewish practice, I should even have demanded a pledge worth twice as much. Their advice, therefore, was that I should go to the bishop mentioned and remain attached to him until I received the whole debt from him.

Fearing, however, lest—as in fact happened—by living among Christians I might, under their influence, be turned away from zealous devotion to ancestral tradition, they hired an elderly Jew named Baruch for payment and entrusted me to his watchful care as tutor.

Complying, therefore, with the counsel of my parents and friends, I went to Münster, the city which is the seat of that bishopric. There I found the bishop and demanded the debt, saying that I did not dare return to my parents until I had received it. Since for the moment he had nothing with which to repay me, he kept me with him for nearly twenty weeks.

During this time, when that good shepherd often, as was his custom, supplied the pasture of God’s word to the sheep entrusted to him, I, enticed by the curiosity natural to a young man, joined the flock of those sheep—by rash presumption indeed, since because of the foulness of my error I was still more worthy to be reckoned among the goats than among the sheep.

There I heard a scribe learned [the manuscript: “unlearned”] in the kingdom of heaven bringing forth from his treasure things new and old: referring the Old Testament [Col. 0808C] to the New, and demonstrating the New from the Old by a sufficiently fitting argument. He taught that certain legal commandments, such as “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not bear false witness,” and “Honour your father and mother” (Exod. 20), must be observed according to the surface of the letter alone. Others, however, such as “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22), and “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23), he declared superfluous insofar as the letter is concerned, but transferred to allegorical meanings by an exceedingly beautiful rationale.

In making this distinction he used the following comparison: Jews, like brute beasts, are content in such matters with the letter alone, as with straw; Christians, using reason as human beings do, are nourished by spiritual understanding, like the sweetest marrow of the straw. I listened to the bishop’s public exposition of these and similar matters all the more eagerly and delightfully because I retained in memory much that he recalled from the histories of the Old Testament, having often read it in Hebrew codices.

Knowing also that the Law counts animals that do not chew the cud among the unclean (Lev. 11), I sent into the stomach of memory to be repeatedly chewed over whatever from his preaching I had heard and liked. Christians, seeing with great astonishment that I was listening very attentively to what was said, asked whether the bishop’s sermon pleased me. I replied that some parts pleased me less, and some more.

Rejoicing at my curiosity and at the same time pitying my error with devout affection, they most earnestly exhorted me to join catholic unity, affirming that their Jesus was most merciful and rejected no one who came to him, according to his own testimony in the Gospel: “The one who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6).

To commend the abundance of this grace, they also set before me the example of his apostle Paul, in whose honour a smaller basilica had been built and dedicated in that city. They said that he had first been a Pharisee and such a zealot for the Law that, with authority from the chief priests, he persecuted Christ’s believers with insatiable cruelty; but in the midst of that criminal undertaking he was struck down to the earth by a blow of heavenly light and received from Christ above a prohibition against his violence. By God’s mercy he was wonderfully transformed from Saul into Paul, from a wolf into a sheep, and from a persecutor into a preacher (Acts 9).

By these and similar words, as by certain incantations, so to speak, Christians soothed me and greatly encouraged me to renounce [what is unspecified in the text]. As time went on, their frequent conversations made me more eager to investigate the ecclesiastical mysteries carefully. I entered the basilica, not yet so much devoutly as curiously, though I had previously dreaded it as though it were some pagan shrine.

Inspecting everything there more closely, among the artistic variety of carvings and paintings I saw a certain monstrous idol. For I beheld one and the same man humbled and exalted, despised and raised aloft, dishonoured and glorious: wonderfully hanging below upon a cross, while above, by the falsehood of the painting, a most beautiful man sat, as though made divine. I confess that I was astonished, suspecting such representations to be images of the kind which paganism, in its manifold error, was accustomed to dedicate to itself. Indeed, my former Pharisaic teaching had persuaded me that this was truly the case.

But that tutor of mine, whom I have mentioned above, cleverly observing what I was doing, discovered that I frequented Christian gatherings so often and lingered at the thresholds of churches. He harshly rebuked me as one entrusted to his guardianship, protesting that he would report all the follies of my unlawful curiosity to my parents.

Yet I, deaf to his threats and rebukes, devoted myself daily to so great a curiosity, all the more because, living under the bishop’s care, I was entirely free from every business concern. I also often entered the schools of the clergy and received books from them. Carefully considering the properties of the individual letters and shrewdly investigating their names, I suddenly began, to the great amazement of those listening, to join letters into syllables and syllables into words, with no one teaching me. Thus in a short time I acquired the ability to read the Scriptures. And lest this perhaps seem incredible to anyone, let it be ascribed not to me but to God, to whom nothing is impossible.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning his dispute with Robert, abbot of Tuitiensis

At that time there was staying there Robert by name, abbot of the monastery of Tuitiensis, [Col. 0810A] a man subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and most learned in both sacred and secular letters. When I saw him, I invited him to the contest of a disputation.

According to the apostle, ready to give an answer to everyone who asked him concerning the faith and hope in Christ, he seized the opportunity of place and time and promised, with God’s help, to satisfy me concerning every matter that I wished to raise, both by reason and by the authority of the Scriptures.

Then I began to speak to him as follows:

“You Christians commit a great injustice against the Jews, when you curse, abhor, and spit upon them as though they were dead dogs. Yet you read that from ancient times God chose them out of all the nations of the world as his special people, whom alone he deemed worthy of knowledge of his holy name; and that to them alone he deigned not only to command the most perfect rule of his righteousness, by observing which they might live and become holy as he himself is holy, but even to inscribe it with his own hand upon tablets of stone. To them alone, I say. For this Scripture, daily chewed over by your own mouths, testifies: ‘He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel’ (Ps. 147).

“But you, blinded by excessive envy of divine favour toward us, regard as hateful above all mortals those whom you acknowledge, when reading, to be more honoured and beloved by God than all other human beings. Yet let it be so. We bear patiently and calmly the reproaches and mockery of human beings, provided that we faithfully persevere in the law of God and its ceremonies. ‘It is better to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of our God’ (Dan. 13). What indeed is more to be feared: to endure God’s wrath and be spat upon by men, or to be cursed by God?

“For it is written in the divine Law: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in this book’ (Deut. 27). In these words, certainly, the righteousness which is ours from the Law is defended against all your clamours by invincible authority; and your arrogance is likewise plainly convicted—the arrogance by which you vainly boast in observing the Law and wickedly disparage us who observe it simply, as we received it from our fathers.

“For when it is universally said, ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in this book,’ nothing is distinguished or excepted. Yet you, not doers of the Law, as you claim, but plainly its judges, correct it, ridiculous as it is to say, according to your own will. Some things you accept, but the rest you either reject as superstitious or corrupt into mystical meanings and into modes of understanding different from what is said, by foolish and old-womanish fictions, as each pleases.

“It is plainly foolish madness and wholly laughable presumption for human beings to wish to correct what God established and commanded human beings to observe under a dreadful curse. You Christians are certainly liable to that curse, since, while you presume to be judges of the Law, you are proved to be its transgressors.

“For, to bring forward only one example out of many for the moment, why do you, who exalt yourselves over your observance of the Law, oppose it by manifest impiety in idolatry? For behold: in your shrines, as I have seen with my own eyes, you set before yourselves for worship large images fashioned by the painter’s and sculptor’s arts. And would that you worshipped the likeness of something else, rather than of the crucified man, to add to the measure of your destruction.

“For, since according to the decree of the Law, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’ (Deut. 21), how much more cursed are you who worship one hanging upon a tree? Again, if, as another Scripture testifies, ‘Cursed is everyone who trusts in a human being and makes flesh his arm’ (Jer. 17), under how much heavier a sentence of curse do you lie, who even place your hope in one crucified?

“Since you not only do not conceal the madness of this superstition of yours, but, what is a greater crime, even glory in it and proclaim your sin like Sodom, choose now whichever of two alternatives pleases you: either produce for me some authority for this abominable worship of yours, if perhaps you know one; or else, if you cannot—which follows, indeed plainly you cannot—confess in shame that this error is damnable and contrary to the sacred Law.”

## CHAPTER IV. Response

To this Robert replied:

“In all that you appear to have raised against me, however suitably, I am not at all alarmed. For we have an abundance of authorities from your own books for the defence and confirmation of the truth of our religion. Fortified by them as by an impregnable shield, we can surely confront and withstand the darts of your objections without fear.

“Therefore the very idolatry of ours which you allege, now, if you are willing patiently to hear and attend, I shall show you by clear reasoning to be full of piety and religion and conspicuous in the light of all truth.

“We abhor and utterly detest in every way the charge of idolatry which you attempt to lay upon us, and faithfully embrace the worship of the one true God. Nor, as you slanderously assert, do we worship as a deity the image of the crucified one or of anything whatsoever. Rather, by the form of the cross we devoutly represent for ourselves the passion of Christ, who, in order to free us from the curse of the Law, himself became a curse for us upon the cross.

“Thus, while we outwardly picture his death through the likeness of the cross, we may also inwardly be kindled toward love of him; and while we unceasingly contemplate that he, wholly free from every sin, underwent so ignominious a death for us, we may always consider in devout thought how much we, entangled in many and great sins, ought to endure for love of him.

“This is the general rationale of the images you see among us. More particularly, images were devised because of the simple and unlearned, so that those who cannot learn by reading in books the passion of their Redeemer may be able to behold, with the cross displaying it, the very price of their redemption. What codices are for us, images represent for the uneducated populace.

“But lest this observance of our religion seem to rest on human reasoning alone, it is also supported by the authority of the Old Testament. For ancient history recounts something very similar to us.

“Once the children of Israel had been brought into the promised land, the children of Reuben, the children of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, returning to the land allotted to them, built an altar of immeasurable size when they came to the mounds of the Jordan. But the Lord had commanded in the Law that all the children of Israel should have one altar in common, in the place which he himself had chosen for invoking the power of his majesty, in order to celebrate the rite of sacrifices. At that time this place was held in highest renown at Shiloh (Deut. 12; Judg. 20).

“When this deed of the Reubenites and Gadites became known to the children of Israel, they were greatly angered against them as transgressors of the Law and took up arms to punish in them the audacity of so monstrous an offence. Yet, using prudent counsel, they restrained their hands for the time from shedding their brothers’ blood, until, after sending delegates from the individual tribes [manuscript: *tribubus*] to them, they might learn through their investigation the occasion of so bold a deed.

“When the delegates came, they rebuked them for presuming, contrary to the Law’s prohibition, to build an altar for the scandal and ruin of all Israel. They received this answer from them:

“‘The Mighty God, the Lord, he himself knows: if this altar was built with the intent of transgression, may he not preserve us but punish us at once. And if we did it with the purpose of placing upon it burnt offerings, sacrifices, and peace offerings, let him himself require an account and judge. Rather, we did it from this thought and plan: that we might say, “Tomorrow your children will say to our children: ‘What have you to do with the God of Israel? The Lord has set the Jordan River as a boundary between us and you, O children of Reuben and children of Gad; therefore you have no share in the Lord.’” And by this occasion your children would turn our children away from the fear of the Lord. Therefore we thought it better and said: “Let us build an altar for ourselves, not for burnt offerings nor for offering sacrifices, but as a testimony between us and you, and between our offspring and your descendants, that we may serve the Lord”’ (Josh. 22).

“Therefore, just as they built an altar not to sacrifice victims and burnt offerings upon it, but to show by such a testimony that they and their posterity belonged to the lot of God’s people, so we also, by similar reasoning, hold Christ’s cross in great reverence because of him who hung upon it. Yet we do not render to it worship belonging to divinity. Rather, as the altar was made a testimony for them, so the cross is made a testimony for us, in order that, while we consider that the price of our redemption hung upon it, we may rejoice that through it we belong to the fellowship of the saints and the eternal inheritance of the heavenly Jerusalem.”

Thus Robert repelled all my objections, both by most beautiful arguments and by very strong authorities of Scripture, driving them away like the darkness of a gloomy night with the brightest rays of his answers [manuscript: “of his answerings”]. But wretched I, like the deaf asp that stops its ears, did not receive with the ears of my heart the words of his most sweet incantation. Nor could I behold with the eyes of the mind, over which the mist of Jewish blindness had spread, the light of truth [the manuscript reads: “I could behold”].

But since it is far too lengthy to recount the entire course of this disputation between us, it will suffice to have touched here upon some parts of it. Let us now carry on the undertaking of the historical account we have begun.

## CHAPTER V. That the charity and faith of a certain man greatly encouraged him toward faith in Christ

At this point I recall an incident which I consider worthy of inserting here: first, because by its sweetness it afforded me a great inducement to conversion; and secondly, because it can offer readers a brilliant and imitable example of perfect charity and unfeigned faith.

The aforementioned bishop Eckebert had a steward of his household, named Richmar, a man who, as I had sufficiently proved, was very devout in all his conduct. One day, while the bishop was at table, he sent to him through his own server, as is customary for lords, half a loaf and a portion of roasted *esox*—that is, pike. But he, being a man most full of the affection of piety, set before me with the greatest cheerfulness and charity what had been sent to him, for I was sitting beside him; he himself remained content, according to his customary religious practice, with bread and water alone.

I was not merely pleased by this, but greatly astonished that a man whom I had considered altogether lawless and without God could possess such power of charity, especially toward me. As an enemy of his sect, he could in the same way have detested me rather than loved me, according to the just judgment of the ancient Law, which says: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5; Lev. 18).

But as a true disciple of the evangelical Law, which says, “Love your enemies” (ibid.), and the rest, he knew that he must do good not only to those of his own household of faith, but to all people (Gal. 6). Accordingly, he bestowed upon me, though unworthy, the diligent benefits of his affection and continually strove, by exhorting and entreating me in gentle conversations, to tear me from ancestral error and gain me for Christ.

For he knew, as the apostle James says, that “the one who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way shall save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5). But when he saw that he could not soften the adamantine hardness of my heart by these arts of piety, considering of me what the apostle testifies in one place—namely, “the Jews seek signs” (Matt. 16)—he most resolutely proposed this condition to me: if, carrying red-hot iron in his bare hand, as is customarily done, as proof of his faith, he felt no burning, then I, having wiped away from my heart all the darkness of unbelief, would faithfully undergo the remedy of holy baptism.

But if his hand received a mark of burning, it would again be for me to decide what I wished to do and choose; he himself would offer no further persuasion in this matter.

When I accepted this most resolute proposal of his with a glad heart, he became most joyful, already as if assured of my conversion. Hastening to seek the bishop, he begged him to deign to have the iron exorcised [manuscript: *exorcizare*, “to exorcise”] for the performance of this spectacle of faith.

But because the time for pity upon me had not yet come, he obtained no fulfilment of his pious request, contrary to his hope. For though the bishop marvelled at and praised the great steadfastness of his faith, he nevertheless judged, in the higher balance of his discernment, that this request was not so much devout as disorderly. He corrected him with a gentle response:

“You indeed have zeal for God in this matter, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10). “God must by no means be tested by examinations of this kind, but rather entreated, that he who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2) “may, when and how he wills, by his most merciful goodness loosen the knots of unbelief and deign to make the disciple of error into a disciple of truth.

“Moreover, for the sake of this matter you must neither ask nor eagerly desire some sign from God. It is certainly most easy for his omnipotence, without any miracle, by the sole hidden visitation of his grace, to convert whomever he wishes. And a sign visibly displayed outwardly is useless if he himself does not work invisibly in the human heart through grace.

“For we read that many have been converted without signs, while countless others have remained unbelievers even after miracles were seen. You must further understand that faith persuaded by miracles has either no merit for you or very little merit; but the faith which is received without any inducement of miracles, in simple devotion and devout simplicity, is of the highest merit and greatest praise before God.

“The author of faith himself, our Lord, bears witness to this. In his Gospel he rebukes the royal official for unbelief: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe’ (John 4). Yet he so exalted the faith of the centurion—who believed before he saw a sign, indeed by which rather he deserved to receive a sign—with praise, that he said he had not found such faith even in Israel (Luke 7).

“Likewise, after his resurrection, he indirectly recalled Thomas’s unbelief, since Thomas could not believe unless he had touched the scars of his wounds. ‘You have seen me,’ he says, ‘and you believe’; and by adding, ‘Blessed are those who have not seen,’ and so forth (John 20), he commended the faith of those whom he foresaw would believe in him through hearing preaching alone.”

Thus that outstanding teacher dissolved the agreement of our compact—upon whose fulfilment we both hung with equal eagerness—not by forbidding it through episcopal authority, but by dissuading us through the manifest truth of his arguments.

Therefore, so that those who read this little work with pious intention may obtain from its reading a fruit of no small usefulness, let them imitate in the bishop the outstanding example of great discernment; and in his steward, the admirable example of faith and perfect charity. And just as he did not curse me as faithless and unworthy of Christian fellowship, but rather showed me the zeal of his charity and pity as though I were a Christian [sic], so also let them not spit upon or abhor people of Jewish or any other error, as some are accustomed to do. Instead, as true Christians—that is, imitators of Christ praying for those who crucified him—let them graciously open to such persons the bosom of brotherly charity.

For since, as the Saviour says, “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4), and since his apostle Paul also testifies that “through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Rom. 11), it is entirely fitting and pleasing to God that Christians, insofar as they can, should labour for the salvation of those from whom they themselves deserved to receive Jesus Christ, the author of eternal salvation.

If they are commanded to extend their love even to those from whom they suffer evil, how much more ought they to extend it to those through whom the universal good came? Let them strengthen their charity toward them, insofar as they are able, by sharing in their needs and by becoming to them an entire pattern of piety, so that they may gain by example those whom they cannot gain by word. For truly, as someone has said, each person is taught better by example than by speech.

Let them also pour out diligent and simple prayers for them to the Father of mercies, in case, as the Apostle says, God may give them repentance to know the truth, and they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will (2 Tim. 2).

But having said these things in a digression, not vainly, I hope, nor uselessly, let us now return to carry out in sequence that which we began.

### Chapter VI. How, on coming with Bishop Eckbert to the monastery of Kappenberg, he was pierced with compunction at the sight of the brothers’ way of life.

While I was still attached to that venerable bishop in expectation of receiving what was owed to me, and was frequently travelling with him as he visited various places in his bishopric, [Col. 0815C] it happened on one occasion that I came with him to the monastery of Kappenberg. This place, situated on a mountain summit, had once been famous for a castle renowned throughout all Westphalia. Its counts, of magnificent and royal nobility, Godfrey and Otto, brothers, still flourishing in the rosy flower of early youth and abounding in riches and the pleasures of all worldly splendour, were inflamed with the fire of divine love. With eager devotion for Christ they had abandoned whatever delights they possessed, or could have possessed, in this world; and joyfully offering the castle itself, with ample estates from their patrimony, to God in the simplicity of their hearts, they converted it into a monastery for clerics observing the rule of blessed Augustine. [Col. 0815D]

Knowing, moreover, that it belongs to the perfect not only to leave their possessions but even themselves (Matt. 16:19), these most fervent imitators of evangelical perfection denied themselves together with all that was theirs. Having assumed the habit of that same perfection, they most meekly submitted their necks to the yoke of some rule, striving to surpass all the brethren in the humility of complete self-abasement, just as they had formerly surpassed them in secular rank.

Coming there, as I had begun to say, I saw spiritually fulfilled in this fellowship of Christ’s faithful, gathered from men [*hominibus*] of every condition and diverse nation, Isaiah’s prophecy concerning the times of Christ—a prophecy which, for the defence of my error, I had supposed was to be fulfilled bodily at Christ’s coming: “The calf,” he says, “and the lion and the sheep shall feed together, and a little child shall lead them” (Isa. 11). Through this prophecy the Jews defend their unbelief: because they do not see fulfilled in a bodily sense what was foretold, they distrust that he has yet come whose advent had been predicted. But when wise and unlearned, strong and weak, noble and ignoble alike were nourished there by the food of the divine word, what else was it but that calf, lion, and sheep were feeding together? And a little child led them, namely because a spiritual father—little indeed in malice, but perfect in understanding—governed them in Christ’s place. [Col. 0816A]

Seeing, then, the religious life of these counts and monks—the, as I felt it, shameful baldness of shaving or tonsure, the manifold lowliness of their dress, the mortification of their flesh, the continuance of prayers and vigils—I, wretched and pitiable as I was, considered them so much the more unhappy because I supposed that they endured this labour in vain hope and without the fruit of reward. For just as, for example, if I saw a man running swiftly through trackless places by an unknown road, I would judge him more miserable in proportion as I saw him, by the very swiftness of his course, further removed from the road; so also I pitied rather than detested these men, as more miserable than all others: though running resolutely through various exercises of labour, they were, as I thought, running without the royal road of legal observances. For they afflicted themselves in this life with fruitless labour and, after this life, would find before God the Judge not only no consolation for their former affliction, but would most certainly receive from him the sentence of eternal damnation, as unbelievers and faithless men. [Col. 0816B–C]

Thus I, truly miserable, inwardly pitying them as miserable men out of human feeling, and drawing deep sighs from the depths of my heart, began to argue within myself about them in such terms, as though against God:

“What, O Lord, is this abyss of your judgments, so great and so unfathomable, that you reject from your commandments these most learned servants of yours, who seek you with their whole heart? Why do you conceal from them, while they wander, the way of your truth by which, walking, they can be saved? They have despised all the pleasures of the world; they have chosen you alone to be followed, you alone to be loved; and they have cast all their care upon you in confidence. For love of you they continually endure the martyrdoms of such great labours, even heavier than death itself.

“It is not like you—who judge the world in equity, whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. 24)—it is not like you, I say, to turn away those who serve you, to abhor those who love you, to hide yourself from those who seek you and desire to know you. For yours is that voice which says: ‘I love those who love me’ (Prov. 8), and so forth. You also promised through the mouth of the prophet that utterance full of mercy: ‘I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. 23). [Col. 0816D]

“You who show that you desire the life of sinners, and invite them to conversion so that they may live—it is altogether fitting, and consonant with your goodness, whose mercy is without number, that you too should turn in your most kindly compassion toward these brethren, who have now turned to you by a distinct repentance. For elsewhere you deigned to promise through the prophet: ‘Turn to me, and I will turn to you’ (Zech. 1). In accordance with the voice of this promise, you formerly accepted the three-day repentance of the Ninevites and mercifully averted, by sparing them, the sword of your vengeance already threatening them (Jonah 3), thereby showing in such an example with fatherly tenderness how patiently you desire the repentance and salvation of sinners. For you, Lord, are gracious and gentle, and of great mercy to all who call upon you (Ps. 85). And if to all, how much more to these your servants, who perform repentance not for three days, as those Ninevites once did, but continually, and who, for love of you, despise not only the world and the things in it, but also—and this is far harder—even themselves, in all humility and lowliness.” [Col. 0817A–B]

While I pondered these things with groaning and in some sense, if it may be said, contended with God in judgment on behalf of these cloistered men, a great scruple arose in my heart from the contrary and mutually divergent laws of Jews and Christians. For, since I saw that it suited God most fittingly—God whose nature is goodness and whose judgment is mercy—to show the way of truth to his servants, who, according to the Psalmist’s words, “are put to death all day long” for his sake (Ps. 43), I began to waver inwardly and to think that perhaps, while the Jews were in error, Christians ran in the way of God’s commandments. For, I said, if the observance of the legal rites still pleased him, he would not have so deprived the Jews, their observers, of the aid of his grace that he scattered them, stripped of all goods and country, far and wide among all nations of the earth. Conversely, if he abhorred the sect of the Christian religion, he would not permit them to be so extended and strengthened throughout the world. [Col. 0817B–C]

Placed, then, in this twofold uncertainty, I did not know where to turn or to which way I should chiefly entrust myself, because I was wholly ignorant what their respective outcome would be. While thus hesitating and enduring in my heart the greatest conflicts of thoughts at variance with one another, I remembered what I had formerly heard from Christians, both clerics and laypeople, about the conversion of blessed Paul: how, by the wonderful mercy of God, he had been called to the Catholic faith and made a preacher and champion of the Church which he had formerly persecuted with tyrannical cruelty (Acts 9). Immediately turning my whole mind toward God, I tearfully begged him that, if he was indeed the author of the Christian religion, he would reveal this to me either through hidden inspiration, or through a vision in a dream, or at least—what I thought most effective—through some visible sign. And I prayed that he who drew the Apostle Paul into the fold of his Church [“to the fold of his Church”], though Paul had proudly kicked against his goad, would also bring me there, as I most humbly obeyed his prayers. [Col. 0817D]

But God, the merciful hearer of a just petition, delayed this desire of mine for a long time, yet did not take it away; later he deigned not only to fulfil it, but also to heap upon it ampler gifts of his grace, as the outcome of events proved. [Col. 0818A]

### Chapter VII. How, when he returned to his parents, the Jew appointed as his guardian accused him.

After this, when the Paschal feast arrived and what was owed to me had been restored by the bishop, I returned with that Jewish adversary of mine to the metropolitan city of Cologne, where I lived. As he had long threatened to do, he greatly weakened the affection of my parents and friends toward me by his accusations, asserting that I had attached myself to Christians with such unlawful assiduity and familiarity that I could now have been thought not a Jew but a Christian, unless, under a pretence of piety, I had lied about my ancestral religion by outward appearance alone. [Col. 0818B]

But the Lord, the God of vengeance (Ps. 93), soon rendered him a fitting retribution for this malicious accusation; for, according to the prophet’s utterance, he crushed him with a double destruction (Jer. 17). At once seized with the severe pain of fevers, he died within fifteen days and passed unhappily from temporal punishments to the eternal torments of Gehenna. Thus the just Judge displayed mercy and truth in one and the same event: truth, by repaying him the punishments due to his deserts; mercy, by freeing me from his snares and accusations.

### Chapter VIII. How he afflicted himself with a three-day fast for his enlightenment.

[Col. 0818C]

I, however, trusting all the more in God’s mercy because I had experienced it in the vengeance inflicted on my accuser, began again, as before, to implore him with frequent prayers that he might deign to reveal to me the way of truth through a nocturnal vision, just as he had once revealed the mysteries of dreams to holy Daniel (Dan. 7). Following the example of that same Daniel, in order to obtain this most ardent desire of mine, I vowed to God a three-day fast (Dan. 9).

Knowing, however, that Jews and Christians did not observe the same rule of fasting—for Christians, eating at the ninth hour on fast days, abstain from meat, whereas Jews continue until evening and consume meat and whatever else it is lawful for them to eat—I did not know which of these was more pleasing to God, and therefore resolved to observe both without distinction. Accordingly, in accordance with the Christian rite, I abstained from meat; and according to Jewish custom, prolonging the fast until evening, I remained content with a little bread and water. [Col. 0818D]

Because of the excessive intensity of my desire, I also gave myself to sleep earlier than usual, hoping that divine consolation would come to me in the manner for which I had asked. But in vain. Indeed, because my sins required it, that night passed without effect. Though I grieved deeply, I nevertheless did not break out into impatience. Rather, as my desire grew through this very delay, I judged the moderation of the preceding day unworthy of obtaining so great a thing, and decided to taste nothing at all that day. Going to bed early as before, I awaited with unutterable desire the aid of the divine visitation. But that night likewise passed fruitlessly, taking its own darkness away with it but leaving me, unhappy as I was, wrapped in the dreadful gloom of unbelief. [Col. 0819A]

Yet even so I did not despair of God’s consolation, but began again to pour forth tearful prayers before the eyes of his mercy, that he might deign to make me, held in such eager expectation, attain my vow. But, exhausted by excessive hunger—for it was the summer season—and now failing throughout my body, I could not defer my vow of abstinence until evening; unbearable bodily weakness compelled me to take a little water around midday.

Thus the third night approached, upon which the final expectation of my visitation depended. Yet it too passed without result. When I awoke in the morning and saw the dark night illuminated by the glowing sun, I groaned heavily and grieved beyond what can be said or believed, because by such an image I had not deserved to be illumined by the golden Sun of righteousness. [Col. 0819B]

The Jews, seeing me mortified by abstinence so unusual for me, suspected that I had committed some criminal offence among Christians; the accusation of the aforementioned Jew also supplied them with material for this suspicion of religious devotion. When I learned of their suspicion, it became the cause of another disturbance, and so the heap of sorrow in my heart increased. For I, who had always lived acceptably and without reproach among the Jews, could not bear this disgrace among them without shame.
