Nevertheless, considering that the merciful God, when he intends to give great things to human beings, is accustomed first to test their perseverance in prayer and to exercise their patience through delay, I recovered firmness of mind amid this faint-heartedness. Once more I began, to achieve the fulfilment of my desire, unceasingly to knock at the door [*ostium*] of divine goodness with tears and prayers, saying to him with the Prophet: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth, and teach me” (Ps. 24). [Col. 0819C]

### Chapter IX. How he devoted himself to disputation with clerics in order to investigate the Catholic truth.

As I again considered by what studies I might attain knowledge of the truth, it seemed good to seek out ecclesiastical men highly skilled in the Old Testament and to hold a discussion with them concerning the mutually opposed religions of Christians and Jews. If they could show me from the clear testimonies of the Law and Prophets the authority of their sect, and plausibly affirm that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom lay open to this sect alone, then I would yield to reason, consult for my salvation, set aside the ancestral tradition which I emulated, and gladly embrace the truth approved for me. [Col. 0819D]

Accordingly, I did not cease continually, in season and out of season, to present myself to the religious teachers of the Church, especially, as I have said, those practised in the Old Testament, and to press them with my questions. Seeing that I did this not in the contentious spirit of seeking contention, but from a desire to know the truth, they desired to separate me by their disputations and admonitions from the synagogue of Satan and laboured to incorporate me into the bosom of the holy Church.

Although they offered me many testimonies concerning Christ from the Law and the Prophets, I clung most obstinately to the letter alone. I maintained either that these things had not been foretold about Christ, or, if I could not deny them, I distorted them by some perverse interpretation; or certainly, if manifest reasoning so hemmed me in that I could do neither, I cleverly evaded them and led them by verbal detours to another question for them to resolve. [Col. 0820A]

For, because my people considered me a scribe learned in the Law, I was ashamed to be defeated or confuted by Christian assertions which they despise as old wives’ tales. Wretched man that I was, I did not consider that the humiliation by which I was put to shame over my own error pleased God and would bring me not disgrace but rather glory. Thus, through a desire for empty glory, as by a kind of bolt, I myself barred the entrance of truth to myself, lest I should be able to believe, in accordance with what the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel: “How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?” (John 5).

Yet although, while disputing with the clerics, I appeared verbally to oppose their assertions, whatever they proved to me by clear reasoning and manifest authority I received with a rejoicing heart. And the most beautiful allegories which they drew forth [*producebant*] from the Old Testament I stored away most diligently in the treasury of my breast. [Col. 0820B–C]

### Chapter X. How, against his will and intention, he was compelled to take a wife, and through love for her was bound in his former error.

But the devil, author of envy, who still held me entangled in the bonds of unbelief, saw me hurrying daily to church and eagerly hearing the word of God, by which I might arm myself against all the snares of his tyranny. Wasting away with fierce envy at these advances of mine, he attacked me with the weapons of his ancient deceit.

For he who gave the first parent the taste of death through a woman (Gen. 3), and who reserved for the most holy Job, out of all his possessions, his wife alone—not for consolation, but for his overthrow (Job 2)—joined a woman to me in marriage for my ruin. [Col. 0820C–D]

A Jew named Alexander, whose virgin daughter I had betrothed, came to me and began urgently to press me, by admonition, exhortation, and entreaty, to set a day for the wedding. But I was still uncertain whether I should remain in Judaism or turn toward Christianity; and prudently reflecting that, once bound to a wife, I would have to care more for domestic affairs than devote myself, as I used to do, to daily disputations, I thought that meanwhile I should defer the wedding on any suitable pretext I could find, until, by God’s mercy, I might deserve to know through some certain indication what I ought chiefly to do for the remedy of my soul.

After deliberating within myself, I replied that I gratefully received his counsel, as proceeding from affection, but that for the present I could not comply with it, since I had first resolved to go to France for the sake of study. [Col. 0821A]

When he repeatedly tried to bend my mind to assent to his purpose and saw that he made no progress at all, he turned, after prayers and blandishments, to threats and terrors, like a scorpion striking with its tail. Having convened a council of the Jews, he alleged that I had been so corrupted by the pernicious conversations of Christians that I could not be brought to consent to marriage either by the pious advice of parents or friends, or even, what was more serious, by legal authority.

Questioned by the Jews as to whether these things were so, I replied that I was not refusing marriage altogether, but only wished for the present to defer it by way of arrangement, putting forward to them the same reason for this delay as I had given my father-in-law. When they heard that I wished to go to France, and suspected that I offered this pretext not simply—as indeed I did not—they all unanimously set themselves against me. In brazen words they cried out that this was a sign of apostasy, and that I was moved to this plan of study, as I said, not by study but rather by a desire to embrace Christian superstition. [Col. 0821B]

And why say more? Once they had learned at last the steadfastness of my mind in its purpose, they proposed that I choose one of two alternatives: either, putting aside every excuse, I must consent to marriage according to the ordinances of the Law, or, if anything else pleased me, I must be outside their synagogue. Lest anyone perhaps suppose this a light matter among them, let him know that being made outside the synagogue among Jews is the equivalent of being expelled from the Church through excommunication among Christians.

But, as Scripture says, “Where there is no hedge, the possession shall be plundered” (Ecclus. 36), I, unhappy man, since I was not surrounded as I ought to have been by divine protection because of my unbelief, lost, as the devil plundered it, the little possession of all my former devotion to seeking the way of truth. At the Jews’ first threat I was wholly frozen with immense fear, as though once excluded from their synagogue no way whatsoever of remedy would thereafter lie open to me. [Col. 0821C]

And even if there were some entrance to salvation outside the synagogue, yet because I neither knew it nor, as I had found, could arrive at a complete discovery of it by any efforts, I judged it safer to persevere to the end in the tradition which I had, as it were, sucked from their maternal breasts, rather than rashly to aspire to some new religion not persuaded to me by any evidence of signs or arguments—especially since, even if I erred through an unavoidable ignorance, I might easily obtain indulgence from a merciful Judge.

So completely did I become vain in this most senseless thought, and so darkened was my foolish heart, that, putting aside every former intention and neglecting the most ardent desire with which I had earlier burned in the search for truth, I gave complete joy to the devil raging against me; delivering myself entirely to perdition, I made, as the Lord reproaches certain persons through the prophet, “a covenant with death and a pact of vain security with hell” (Isa. 28). [Col. 0821D–0822A]

For, without any reservation, yielding altogether to the will of the Jews, I appointed them a day on which the bridal chamber should be set up. Such exultation and such universal rejoicing toward me followed my betrothal that the common favour of all drew me more toward their assent than their terror had previously compelled me.

When the day of the wedding feast came, many gathered there, not only Jews but also Christians familiar to me. The former came to rejoice in my false happiness; the latter, grieving in Christian affection at my fatal condition, prayed that the light of mercy spoken of above might be granted to me. They said:

“How, wretched Judas, have you fallen so soon and so easily from a good purpose into so great an abyss of perdition? How, after putting your hand to the plough, did you look back so quickly? We always gave you counsels of salvation, hoping that you would at some time consent to them and believe in Christ, the author of our salvation. And behold, contrary to our hope, you chose rather to follow your own desires, and, despaired of salvation, have wholly given yourself over to perdition. Alas, unhappy man: you have deceived us, and have yourself been miserably deceived. [Col. 0822A–B]

“Would that you were wise and understood, and foresaw the last things, so that you might know what punishments await you, what fires of burning Gehenna will receive you if you remain in this superstition. Therefore let the saving counsel of our charity now please you; and while the way of repentance is still open to you, with every effort care for your salvation, lest, if you refuse to do this while you can, you begin too late to wish it when you cannot.

“But if you embrace the faith of Christ with your whole heart and are reborn through his saving washing, you will obtain from him full pardon for your errors and perfect knowledge of the whole truth which you began to investigate. For although, as he himself says, he casts out none who come to him, he nevertheless bestows his grace more abundantly on those who return to him through faith—those alone whom, he declares, he was sent by God the Father to recall from their error: ‘I was not sent,’ he says, ‘except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (Matt. 15). Therefore he who came first to seek you will surely make himself easy for you to find, if you seek him with right faith and a pure heart.” [Col. 0822C–D]

With the ploughshare of this Christian exhortation they strove to tear apart the adamantine hardness of my heart and soften it to the grace of compunction. But I did not hear their most wholesome warnings, like a deaf man, because I did not possess the ears which the Lord required in his Gospel when he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13): that is, the ears of the heart, the ears of understanding. And because I lacked spiritual hearing, I despised what I had received through the bodily ear alone. Thus was fulfilled in me what is written: “When a sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18).

But as soon as I experienced the corruption of the flesh, slippery pleasure and affection for the wife joined to me so blinded my mind that I could not even feel the most serious sickness of my soul—a thing which is usually a sign of utter despair. Since I no longer overcame, as before, any assaults of temptation, being feebly subject and wholly defeated by them, I thought myself blessed in this false peace of vices. I began to lie with supreme pleasure of the flesh in that place into which I had formerly feared to cast myself. [Col. 0823A]

And as the Apostle says concerning married persons: “He who has a wife is concerned with the things of this world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided” (1 Cor. 7), I began to be carried away amid the various cares of the world and no longer to seek anything of God; rather, I delighted only to devote myself to those things by which I might please the eyes of my bride. [Col. 0823B]

### Chapter XI. How, after being bound to a wife, his devotion to truth was kindled anew.

But after three months had passed from the time when I began to suffer from this lethargic sickness of my soul, by God’s mercy I returned to my heart and, as though awakening from a heavy sleep of former ignorance, began to reflect upon the cause of my fall through negligence and the depth of the miserable abyss of pleasure into which I had come.

And when, as it is written, “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1), I began to be pierced by grievous pain in contemplating this misery of mine. I struck my breast with my fist and, amid frequent sighs, poured forth abundant tears, declaring myself wretched and unhappy because for a small pleasure of the flesh I had hurled myself into so great an abyss of perdition. [Col. 0823B–C]

Therefore, through the grace of this compunction, recovering a little confidence in the abundant mercy of God, I began to cut away superfluous worldly cares from my mind, to restrain the desires of the flesh with the bridle of continence, and, just as I had presented my members as weapons of iniquity to sin, so I strove in every respect to present those same members as weapons of righteousness to God.

Still retaining my former uncertainty concerning the mutually opposed faiths of Jews and Christians, and knowing that without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11), and that “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14), I began once more to strive, if somehow by God’s favour I might drive from my heart the darkness of this uncertainty and find the light of true faith. [Col. 0823C–D]

Accordingly, as before, I diligently sought out the most learned teachers of the Church and required of them an account of their faith and religion. When they gave me this most abundantly from many testimonies of Scripture and diverse figures of the Old Testament, I wished in a disordered sequence to anticipate faith by understanding. Thus I was wholly unable to attain that understanding which is acquired by the merit of faith, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7).

One day it happened that I entered into a disputational contest with a certain named master. Though our discussion had been prolonged, none of the points he plausibly advanced could draw assent from me. One of the clerics seated beside him, seeing the obstinate hardness of my heart, said: “Why, master, why do you strive in vain? Why pour words into the wind? Why entrust seeds to sand? You know indeed, as the Apostle testifies, that even to this day, when Moses is read to the Jews, a veil lies upon their heart” (2 Cor. 3). [Col. 0824A]

Hearing this, and understanding very well, as one trained in the Old Testament, from where the occasion for this saying had been taken, I was greatly terrified. I considered whether perhaps, just as the children of Israel of old could not look upon Moses’ face, made radiant on the mountain, except through a veil (Exod. 34), so I could not attain with the clear sight of my mind to the mystical understanding of the Mosaic Law except through the intervening shadows of certain bodily figures.

Again I began in anxious agitation, not knowing what I should do or how I could remove this veil from my heart so that, with the eye of my mind unveiled, I might behold the clear light of truth. Therefore I fled to the Father of lights with a contrite and humbled heart, and laid tearful prayers before the sight of his goodness, crying out with the Psalmist: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your Law. Give me understanding, and I shall search your Law, that I may keep it with my whole heart” (Ps. 118). [Col. 0824B]

And, because Christian teachers had made known to me the great power of the sacred cross, I frequently marked my heart with the sign of that cross, hoping that its help would be most effective in removing from me this veil of unbelief. But what did that most savage enemy, skilled in a thousand arts, do when he saw me—whom he still held captive under the dominion of his tyranny through the snares of unbelief—arming myself with such a defence against him? When would he permit his own slave, whom he held by the laws he considered just, to depart free, he who does not cease, by impious and unlawful cruelty, to persecute and enslave even the servants of his Lord, all the faithful?

Therefore, so that he might more easily deceive me while I was less guarded, he transformed himself into an angel of light: he set out to attack me not now openly, but by subtle fraud. He began to bring back to my memory the commandments of the Law, among which the Jews had also received this precept (Exod. 34): that in no respect should they imitate the unclean and God-abominable rites of the nations, lest those whom God had chosen from all nations as a people of his own possession (Deut. 7) should be seen to share in, or resemble, those superstitions in any respect. [Col. 0824C–D]

This most cunning enemy must be thought to have done this in order to draw my intention more easily away from its purpose, by showing me thereby to be a transgressor of the Law. And so it happened. At the devil’s prompting, my conscience began severely to accuse me concerning this act as a transgressor of the divine Law; and, in order to obtain pardon for what I thought such an enormous offence, I chastised myself with a prescribed penance of tears and fasting.

But afterwards, returning from this madness to my senses and finding that this penance was not an act of appeasement but rather of offence, I began again to lament the error of my ignorance and, with the same urgency as before, to fortify my heart inwardly with the sign of the cross. But alas, I deserved to feel none of its remedy, for I had not yet known myself redeemed by its life-giving price from the curse of the Law. [Col. 0825A]

And what was I to do? Every hope of counsel and aid had fled from my mind. Again tears flowed in streams; again heavy groans began to burst forth from the depths of my breast. And I said against myself: “Alas, wretched me, what shall I do? Where shall I flee? What hope of salvation can remain for me, when I am neither fully a Jew nor a Christian? If the final day of my life, coming suddenly like a thief (2 Pet. 3), should seize me in this condition, where shall I go? Surely I shall perish.”

The bitterness of my heart was so great that, even while my tongue was silent, my very face more clearly showed it by the evidence of its emaciation and wretched appearance. For all who knew that I had been born of high rank and was powerful both in knowledge of the Law and in material resources were all the more astonished to see me suddenly, contrary to my usual condition, consumed by such emaciation, because they had never seen me afflicted by the troubles of any misfortunes whatsoever. [Col. 0825B]

### Chapter XII. How he was enlightened through the prayers of religious women.

I, however, fled with complete confidence to God, who alone beholds toil and suffering, as to a tower of strength. Pouring out my prayer before Him, I declared before Him the tribulation of my heart, tearfully begging that, [Col. 0825C] according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, His consolations might gladden my soul, and that He might deign to extend the right hand of His majesty to draw me out of darkness and the shadow of death, seeing that through my own weakness I had failed everywhere. What I faithfully sought from Him, therefore, I deserved to obtain effectively.

For through His inward inspiration I began prudently to consider that, just as a servile person who has lost his master’s favor cannot return to it except through the intercession for him of that same master’s friends, so neither could I merit Christ’s grace unless supported by the intercessions of the holy Church. As I considered to whose prayers, as being of greater merit before God, I should especially commend myself, I remembered two sisters who, near the monastery of Blessed Maurice beside the city of Cologne, lived enclosed for God and together led a celibate life. One was called Berta, the other Glizmut; their holy way of life had spread the sweetest fragrance of good repute throughout the neighborhood of that city.

Hoping that their patronage could greatly aid me before God, I hurried to them and, with many tears, disclosed how severely I was pressed by the stings of temptations. I humbly begged them to deign to direct their prayers to God for my illumination. Being full of every feeling of mercy and compassion, they poured out abundant tears over my great miseries and vowed that they would unweariedly offer supplications to God for me [Col. 0826A] until I should deserve to receive the desired consolation of heavenly grace.

O how true is that saying of the apostle James: “The persistent prayer of a righteous person avails much” (James 5)! For not long afterward, through their merits and prayers, such brightness of Christian faith suddenly shone upon my heart that it utterly drove away the darkness of all my former uncertainty and ignorance. It was, surely, a fitting exchange: through a woman came the fall, and through women’s prayers came my lifting up.

Therefore, O devout and holy women, whoever read or hear these things read, take in these blessed women a splendid example worthy of imitation in prayer. Know that the more tranquil your prayers are, the more sincere they are, and the more effective [Col. 0826B] before God in obtaining whatever you seek. For behold: I, whom neither an explanation of the faith given me by many people nor the disputation of great clerics could convert to Christ’s faith, was drawn by the devout prayer of simple women.

## CHAPTER XIII. How he advanced in the faith

Having therefore found through God’s grace the one precious pearl of the Catholic faith, I began, following the example of that Gospel merchant (Matthew 13), to despise all temporal things for love of it, so that I might deserve to be enriched by its most delightful and health-giving possession. Freeing myself, as far as I could, from every care, I became so impatient of delay that I could scarcely take food at home. With great devotion I began to frequent the holy basilicas and to apply gladly both the hearing of my heart and that of my body to listening to God’s word.

Yet I did this secretly, because, still weak and tender in faith, I feared persecution by the Jews, like that Nicodemus who came to Jesus by night (John 3). Thus, hearing with Nicodemus the Lord’s terrible declaration in His Gospel—“Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (ibid.)—I began to desire this washing of rebirth all the more ardently, because, according to this saying of the Lord, it was clear that without its remedy I could not enter the heavenly kingdom [the text prints “could enter”].

## CHAPTER XIV. How he drew his brother away from Judaism, and how the Jews conspired against him

[Col. 0826D] Knowing that the Lord had commanded the children of Israel, when they went out of Egypt, not to depart empty-handed but to despoil Egypt as they left it (Exodus 11), I too, taught by such an example, did not wish to depart empty from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of Jewish unbelief. Rather, I wished to bring away from it some rational spoil of gold and silver, or of any precious garment, which might not only adorn but itself become the temple of the supreme King, according to the saying of the apostle Paul: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

I had at Mainz a brother by my father, not by my mother, seven years old; with the most ardent desire I wished that through the washing of rebirth he might become a co-heir with me of divine grace, so that, though we had not had one mother through carnal birth, we might together have one mother, the Church, through spiritual rebirth. But when the Jews saw that I never attended their synagogue, as was customary—whose communion, as can be learned from what precedes, I had formerly so greatly feared to lose—they perceived that there was no slight cause for so unexpected a change. They therefore laid snares for me and began to investigate all my ways and actions more closely.

When they found that each day I did scarcely anything other than devote myself to ecclesiastical instruction, they all burned with such zeal against me that, if any opportunity to commit the crime had presented itself, they would not have feared to stone me with their own hands. But blinded in the darkness of their perfidy and malice, they strove, to increase their own condemnation, to involve others in the parricidal crime which they could not perpetrate themselves; and, unable to accomplish their wickedness, they rushed headlong into guilt of intention alone.

For when they learned that I intended to go to Mainz, they assembled against me and devised, as it is written (Psalm 2; Matthew 26), plans which they could not establish. They secretly sent letters written in Hebrew to the Jews of Mainz through a certain Volcquin, chaplain of Queen Richza. Their substance was that they should seize me as a traitor and apostate and punish me with an appropriate penalty according to the strict judgment of the Law. But, as the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Romans 8). He, therefore, who scatters the counsels [Col. 0827C] of the nations and rejects the designs of princes (Job 5; Psalm 32), by His will scattered their design; He powerfully freed me not merely from their snare, but mercifully brought to fulfillment the pious desire that I had conceived of gaining my brother.

## CHAPTER XV. How he wonderfully discovered the letters written against him by the Jews

By God’s providence, I happened to join that same cleric on the road as he was going to Mainz on the business of his mission. Neither of us knew what business the other had; as we travelled, we conversed about various matters. Unaware that they were my kinsmen, he began to name certain of my relatives residing at Mainz, saying that he was carrying them some secret message. When I heard this, although I still knew absolutely nothing of the Jews’ plots against me, I nevertheless began to suspect in his mission precisely what was in fact the case: namely, that the Jews were plotting great harm against me through it.

Addressing the cleric about this, I said that he was carrying letters of the Jews at the greatest peril to his soul. Since he had been asked to conceal the matter, he denied that he carried any letters. But I gave no credence to his denial; I firmly asserted that matters stood as I had said, adding that a heavy burden of divine vengeance threatened him if, against my advice, he presumed to deliver the letters he had received to the Jews of Mainz, because a seed of great evil lay hidden in them. At last, after much urgent entreaty and threatening, I wrung from him a confession of the truth.

He confessed that everything was as I had said and asked me to disclose to him the matter contained in the letters. Then I—something wonderful to relate, but, with God as my witness, utterly true—explained to him from the conjecture of my heart alone both their meaning and substance as though I had either read them or learned them through someone’s disclosure. This was certainly not accidental but was accomplished by God’s prompting and providence, who intended to rescue me from the most malicious expectation of the Jewish people and bring the holy undertaking in which I was engaged to a glorious conclusion.

Receiving the letters themselves when he produced them for me, I opened and read them. I found written in them, just as I had conjectured, the Jews’ most malicious accusation against me. With the greatest exultation, giving thanks to God for my deliverance, I burned those deadly characters in the fire.

## CHAPTER XVI. How, on coming to Worms, he boldly preached Christ in the synagogue of the Jews

Then, singing with the Psalmist in inexpressible joy, “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Psalm 123), I began to burn so strongly in the love of Catholic faith and religion that, casting out through charity all fear arising from my faint-heartedness (1 John 4), I dared not only to believe unto righteousness and confess with my mouth unto salvation that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1; Romans 10), but also to preach this steadfastly and freely to His enemies, the Jews.

For when I came to Worms, where I had a full brother named Samuel, I entered the synagogue of the Jews on the day on which they customarily assembled, and I heard them reading their Gamaliel’s superstitious commentaries upon the Old Testament. At once, inflamed with divine fervor and with great confidence and eloquence, I entered into a prophetic disputation with them. There I fittingly demonstrated what faith I held and how much I had profited from many disputations with Christians concerning orthodox faith. Against the foolish and old-womanish fables which that same Gamaliel had compiled [the text may read *conflixerit*] from the Scriptures for them, I poured forth the honeyed sweetness of spiritual allegories, stopping their mouths with many strong authorities from the divine utterances—the mouths which, by blaspheming Christ and disparaging His holy Church, blind pride and proud blindness presume to set [Col. 0828D] against heaven.

How great, then, do you think was the astonishment that seized all the Jews present when they saw me as the strongest assailant of their ancestral traditions, of which, as a Jew of Jews, they had expected me to be the most faithful defender? Taking up also a singular contest of disputation against the archisynagogue, named David, and against my aforesaid brother, I long turned over before them the pages of the Law and the Prophets. From their most ample testimonies I defended and demonstrated the Christian faith, shutting off every avenue of calumny against Christ and His holy Church.

When they saw me favoring Christians with such obstinate zeal, they began to call me a “half-Christian,” throwing this name in my face as though I had been badly deceived by Christians’ crafty persuasions. At last they asked whether my mind and tongue agreed in everything I had brought forward against them in defense of the Christian faith. Fearing that, if I confessed the naked truth to them, I might in some degree be hindered by their plots from rescuing my brother, I so moderated my reply that I neither denied being a Christian nor openly proclaimed it:

> “Since I have often disputed with Christians and have learned for the most part their subtle arguments against the Jews, I wished to assume their person in myself, so that, instructed by this preliminary exercise in my assertions, you might be found more cautious against them at a moment of necessity.”

They gratefully accepted this answer.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, upon reaching Mainz, he secretly led away his brother

After this I came to Mainz. I secretly snatched the child from his mother and wished, for fear of the Jews, to lead him secretly outside the city, where I had ordered a servant with horses to wait for us at a certain place. But the most savage enemy of human salvation, understanding that this theft had been carried out not by his prompting but by divine inspiration, and that it belonged not to his lot but to God’s, attempted to hinder it by the crafty art of his malice.

Though I knew the passages through that city very well, my eyes were, wonderful to relate, so blinded by diabolical illusion [Col. 0829C] that from the first hour of the day until the sixth I wandered through all the streets of the city and could not find its exit. The child was tired and weeping from exhaustion. Moved with pity for him, I put him upon my shoulders to carry him; many Christians who saw this mocked me as a fool.

Placed in great shame of countenance and incredible anguish of heart, I humbly implored the divine help—the one refuge open to me—and secretly impressed upon my forehead the sign of the holy cross. A marvelous thing! I had repeatedly gone around and around the city gate and had been utterly unable to find it; but as soon as I armed myself with the sign of the cross, the diabolical illusion that had blinded me was annulled. I saw and recognized it joyfully, went out, and found the servant waiting for us with the horses where I had commanded.

After we had gone a little way from the city, Jews from Cologne arrived by boat and disclosed to the Jews of that city whatever they had learned concerning me as hostile to their religion: namely, that at Cologne I had hidden books together with money among Christians because I had resolved obstinately to transfer to their sect. When she heard this, the boy’s mother was deeply disturbed and terrified, and had a most diligent search made for me everywhere. But when I was not found, she became, through excess of grief, as though insane. With most bitter wailing she ran to the leading men of the city, tearfully proclaiming that her son had been secretly taken from her. They immediately sent messengers to seize me.

But just as they could not resist God’s ordinance (Romans 13), so neither could they seize me while I served that ordinance. Thus, fleeing with the boy and continuing upon the journey I had begun, I reached at evening the monastery called Welanheim. When the brothers learned the pious desire of my heart, they received me with great joy and charity. Yet while we were still eating, behold: the messenger appointed to search for us stood before the gate and asked the porter whether a Jew leading a boy had entered there. The porter, being a simple man and suspecting no plot in anyone, simply revealed the truth to him.

Therefore, lest those brothers suffer any trouble on my account, I commended the boy to them, so that he might be instructed by them in the sacred writings. Then I secretly fled from there and came to the monastery called Revengresburch. There I was received with great rejoicing by the brothers, kept, and catechized on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October].

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the vision that he saw before baptism

When nearly three weeks had passed after I became a catechumen, on the Wednesday before the Sunday on which I was to be baptized, I saw a dream as sweet in its telling as it was in its vision. I saw heaven opened toward the east; the imaginary structure that appeared to me in the vision was throughout adorned with the purest gold. There I saw the Lord Jesus seated most powerfully and honorably upon a lofty throne in paternal majesty, holding, in place of a scepter, the triumphant sign of His cross upon His right shoulder. Standing near Him, as it seemed to me, together with His most excellent friends, I was inexpressibly delighted by the ineffable sweetness of His contemplation.

Then behold: two sons of my aunt, one called Nathan and the other Isaac, passed swiftly behind my back. Their passing itself plainly made those who observed understand that this blessedness was shown to them not for consolation but for punishment, so that they might be inwardly tormented precisely because they did not deserve to enjoy the glory of the saints which they beheld.

Turning to them, I addressed them thus:

> “O wretched and unhappy men, does not this sign of the cross which you see upon Christ’s shoulder now recall to your minds that prophecy of Isaiah: ‘His dominion is upon His shoulder’ [Isaiah 9]? You once scorned, at my exhortation, to believe this prophecy concerning Christ; yet behold, to your everlasting confusion, you see it fulfilled.”

Overwhelmed by excessive terror, they scarcely answered me in a few words, in a low and subdued voice:

> “What you recall is indeed true, O nephew; but alas, it has been proved to us too late, now that the saving opportunity for repentance has been lost and we have been assigned to eternal Gehenna without hope of attaining salvation.”

They had scarcely finished speaking when they vanished from sight, and the Scripture was fulfilled in them which says: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26).

When I awoke and remembered how often I had formerly striven, by prayers, tears, and frequent fasting, to obtain from heaven such a vision for my illumination, I began to abound in spiritual joy over what I had seen and to render due thanks to God for so sweet a vision, by which I had deserved to be strengthened in His faith.

## CHAPTER XIX. How he was baptized, and what devices of the devil he endured in that baptism

The Sunday came on which I was to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new through the washing of rebirth. All the clergy of the city of Cologne therefore gathered with festive rejoicing in the basilica of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where a font had been prepared for celebrating the saving mystery. When it had been consecrated about the third hour and made fruitful for souls to be reborn by the invocation of the Holy Spirit, I confessed with my whole heart faith in the holy Trinity and entered it with great devotion and contrition of heart.

But alas—grievous to tell—even at the moment of baptism hostile deceit did not cease its assault upon me. For just as, according to the Evangelist, the boy about to be delivered from a demon by the Lord’s compassion was more violently thrown down at the very moment when the wicked spirit was compelled to leave him (Luke 9), so the ancient enemy made more severe assaults upon me when he saw that, through the saving sacrament of divine institution, I was being snatched away from his tyranny.

For although I had been instructed sufficiently for my capacity in the other matters belonging to orthodox faith, I had not been taught—through the negligence of the ministers, or rather through the deceit of the enemy lying in wait for me—that baptism was to be administered by a threefold immersion in the name of the holy Trinity. Entering, therefore, the waters of the life-giving font and being immersed once in it facing east, I believed that this one immersion had sufficed for the renewal of my former oldness. But the clerics standing around the baptistery cried that I ought to be immersed more often.

Since I had just emerged from the font, I could not distinctly hear their voices or clearly see the gestures they made to me, since water was streaming from my hairy head in every direction. I wiped the water from my face with my hands and heard what they wanted; but constrained by the great cold of the font, I was at first unwilling to obey them. Nevertheless, softened by the gentle admonition of my baptizer, I did what had to be done for salvation.

Thinking that I had satisfied the divine mysteries by this second dipping, I began to wish to leave the font, for I had almost entirely become numb from its excessive cold. But the clergy again shouted loudly that, for completion of the sacrament, I must humbly submit myself to the saving waters facing south. Deceived, therefore, by diabolical fraud, I suspected that they were making sport of me. Hence, just as Naaman the Syrian had once indignantly begun to depart after receiving from the prophet Elisha the command to wash seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5), so I too, in like madness, inflamed with great fury of mind and wholly impatient of delay, wished to leap out of the baptistery.

But thanks be to God: though the enemy raised himself up, he did not prevail against me. For, just as that same Naaman, softened by the admonition of his companions, obeyed the saving counsel of the prophet (ibid.), so the gentle exhortation of the religious clerics who were present drove from my mind the infection of the evil suspicion I had conceived and strengthened my faint-heartedness in faith.

Thus, that new things may in every respect be compared with old, Naaman, washed seven times in the waters of the Jordan, was visibly cured of bodily leprosy (ibid.); I, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism, was invisibly cleansed of the leprosy of my soul. His flesh, cleansed of the filth of elephantiasis, received the purity of a child; the virgin mother Church, stripping me through the washing of rebirth of the skin of oldness, brought me forth into a new infancy. In that washing, I changed both the order of my former life and the particularity of my name: I who had previously been called Judas received the name Hermann.

What praises did not the clergy—and indeed the whole body of the faithful—raise for this glorious change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76), this carrying back of the lost sheep upon the shoulder of the good Shepherd to the fold of the holy Church (Luke 15)? With what common joys did they celebrate it! Nor without reason. For how could the Christian people fail to rejoice over the repentance of a converted sinner, when even the host of angels, as the Lord Himself testifies, rejoices more over him than over ninety-nine righteous persons (ibid.)? But the Jews, having zeal indeed for the Law, though not according to knowledge (Romans 10), mourned me most bitterly and inconsolably as a faithless and lost man.

## CHAPTER XX. How, after baptism, he renounced the world and devoted himself to divine service under the canonical rule

[Col. 0832C] Therefore, after the unclean spirit had been driven from the house of my heart through the washing of rebirth, I feared—and feared exceedingly—that, returning and finding that same house, though cleansed by the saving washing and adorned with Christ’s sacraments, nevertheless vacant of the exercise of spiritual discipline, he would enter in order to occupy it more grievously than before with sevenfold pestilence, and thus my last state would become worse than the first (Matthew 12). I therefore labored with watchful care to ensure that, made secure against the malignant invader, it might become a worthy dwelling for the gracious Christ.

Hearing, therefore, the Gospel commandment, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Mark 10), and also, “Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), I began cheerfully to despise, in hope and desire of eternal things, all that I seemed to possess temporally. Thus, freed from the burdensome load of the world, I might walk with unencumbered and free foot along the narrow way that leads to life.

Learning also, as the Psalmist says, that it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity (Psalm 132), I escaped to the renowned monastery of Capenberg, of which I have spoken above—a place of all religious observance—as to a harbor of salvation from the shipwreck of this world’s sea, there to wrestle naked with the naked enemy. There I changed my life together with my clothing, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, awaiting the end of this present life and the promise of the life to come.

Moreover, applying continual effort to learning Latin, I made such progress within five years, God helping me, that the charity of the brothers judged me fit to receive sacred orders and kindly drew me toward them. Yet I humbly submitted, as was right, protesting that I was unworthy and insufficiently suited for this; and I resisted modestly, as far as I dared and as was fitting. But God, who always gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5), seeing that I had chosen the lowest place among His guests, deigned to say to me: “Friend, come up higher” (Luke 14). Rejoicing at His call, not in fear but with trembling, as it is written (Psalm 2), I ascended step by step through the canonical orders until I came to the dignity of priestly excellence.

Then I first understood what the dream seen before my conversion, inserted at the beginning of this little work, had foretold would happen to me; and I shall now explain its interpretation, as I promised above.

## CHAPTER XXI. How he understood and interpreted the dream first seen in his childhood concerning Christ’s future grace in him

The interpretation of the vision, then, is this. The earthly emperor who appeared to me signifies the heavenly King, of whom the Psalmist says: “The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (Psalm 23). This King had a certain great prince: namely, that angel whom, at the beginning of His creation, He made nobler than all angelic spirits and set over all the other orders of angels. He truly died when, raising himself proudly against God (Isaiah 14), he was stripped of the glory of his dignity and from an archangel became the devil.

This King of kings deigned to visit me by His grace and offered me a white horse when He granted me the grace of holy baptism, by which I might be made whiter than snow. He also gave me a belt, by which He granted me the strength to extinguish the unstable desires of the flesh. In the seven denarii of weighty coinage are rightly understood the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit; when they fill anyone, they adorn that person with gravity of character. Once a person has begun, through these gifts of the Holy Spirit, to shine in purity of life like refined silver, that person also begins to ring sweetly to others concerning God’s love and eternal life; this is well signified by the sound of silver.

That these seven denarii were enclosed in a purse so as not to be easily lost signifies, I hope, that the charisms of the Holy Spirit mercifully granted to me will not abandon me [the text prints *derelinctura* for *derelictura*], but will remain with me to the end, enabling me to overcome all the troubles of temptations and to merit the heavenly kingdom.

The princes, however, were angered by my so happy a success. This signifies that the evil spirits—whom the Apostle calls the rulers of the world (Ephesians 6)—or the Jews, who claimed precedence among the other nations on account of the Law received from God, begrudged me Christ’s grace, of which they themselves were unworthy. But girded with that shining belt, that is, with the strength of continence, I mounted the royal horse. This means that the grace of baptism was not empty in me; rather, as the use of the horse indicates, with God’s help I always labored to cultivate it by spiritual exercise and direct it to good use.

I also followed Christ the King by despising the world and what is in the world, denying not only all my possessions but even myself for His love, doing what He Himself testifies concerning Himself: “I came not,” He says, “to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6). And I fittingly accompanied the King upon a white horse, because no one can be fit to follow Christ’s footsteps unless that person has received the grace of baptism which, as we have said, is symbolized by the white horse.

The palace into which I followed Him, I judge, signifies the place of my conversion. For in an assembly of clerics there, or in the monasteries of any religious living under rule throughout the world, what else is indicated but certain palaces of the supreme King? In these, through chastity of life and religious conduct, Christ is believed by grace to dwell in a certain domestic and familiar manner, as a king in his palace.

I approached to feast at the King’s table when, though unworthy, I undertook the most holy ministry of the altar. To sit at the table means humbly to approach Christ’s altar. But what kind of banquet belongs to this heavenly table, what sweet delights it possesses, cannot worthily be explained in words; only those know it who have deserved to experience it through God’s grace.

What a banquet it is for the faithful soul to approach the venerable table of the altar with whole faith, true humility and contrition of heart, and sincere devotion of mind; to be fed there with the flesh of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ, and made drunk by the cup of His most holy blood—no one, as I have said, understands this except one who has experienced it.

The vegetables which I seemed to eat at the royal table, moreover, I judge signify Christ’s Gospel. For just as those vegetables were made from various kinds of herbs, so Christ’s Gospel consists of various precepts relating to eternal life. Thus, to eat vegetables at the royal banquet is for a priest standing at the Lord’s altar to ponder diligently and subtly the precepts of the holy Gospel, as though chewing them in the mouth of the heart: considering how humble, devout, pure in chastity, and fervent in charity one must be who wishes to celebrate worthily and acceptably to God the mystery of so great a sacrament.

Christ the King also feasts with us, because He is fed by the sweetness of our spiritual progress. He Himself testifies in the Apocalypse that He finds sweet refreshment in a devout heart devoted to divine service: “Behold,” He says, “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

Nor do I think it without significance that I seemed to eat from the same dish as the King. The one dish signifies the unity of the Catholic faith. Thus whoever, with Christ’s cooperating grace, keeps the precepts of the holy Gospel in the unity of Catholic faith eats vegetables with Christ from one dish.

In this unity I now stand through God’s grace, as was shown beforehand in the portent of that once most blessed vision granted to me; and I serve Him, as it is written (Psalm 2), with fear and rejoice with trembling. I rejoice with trembling, I say, because I ought to rejoice in the grace by which I am now faithful; yet there remains cause for fear in the deepest and unsearchable abyss of His judgments, because I do not know whether I am worthy of love or hatred (Ecclesiastes 9). For what mortal, however righteous or holy, would not fear that terrible judgment of our Savior: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20)?

Yet I trust in the Lord Jesus that He who began a good work in me will bring it to completion unto the end. Indeed, the greatness of His previous benefits gives me the greatest hope of future things. For behold, the merciful and compassionate Lord raised the poor from the dung heap and set him among the princes of His people (Psalm 112), when He mercifully rescued me from the most foul superstition [Col. 0836A] and most abominable sect of Judaism. He deigned, piously and mercifully, not only to join me to His faithful through the unity of Catholic faith, but also to add me, through the grace of priestly dignity, to the glorious companions at His table.

Who, O Lord, can weigh the inward compassion of Your mercy toward me, unworthy as I am? Who can worthily estimate such immeasurable riches of Your goodness? I hope, Lord, and, confidently relying upon such great kindness, I believe that Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life. You have deigned already to bestow upon me such great pledges of grace; for these, as is fitting, I do not cease to offer praise and sacrifices of rejoicing to You, my most gracious illuminator.

And you also, whoever read or hear these things, rejoice and congratulate me, because I was dead and have come to life; I was lost and have been found. Therefore magnify the Lord with me, who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1135

## UDASCALCUS, MONK, TO SAINT ULRIC OF AUGSBURG

[Col. 0835]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, VI, 288)

Udascalcus, born into the honourable family of the noblemen of Maisack, a monk of St Ulrich’s at Augsburg, the inseparable companion of Abbot Egino, a religious man and outstandingly learned, a poet by no means to be despised, an eminent musician and composer, and indeed the most celebrated theologian of his age, was chosen abbot in the year of the Lord 1126. He governed prudently and faithfully for twenty-five years. He wrote a book *On Music*, histories of many saints—above all, of St Afra, St Udalric, St Maurice, and St Mary Magdalene—in verses of various kinds. Many of his epigrams, inscribed here and there upon walls, still survive; they display very clearly and splendidly both his extraordinarily fertile talent and his far-from-ordinary learning. He died in the year of the Lord 1151.

These details are given by Caspar Bruschius in his *Chronology of the Monasteries of Germany*, p. 497; compare Sigismund’s Pistorian *Chronicle of Augsburg*, vol. III, p. 605. His *Narrative concerning the Controversies between Hermann, Bishop of Augsburg, and Egino, Abbot of St Udalric*, survives today, edited by Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. III, part II, p. 1. A single epigram of his on Egino, his predecessor, appears in Bruschius, p. 496. Mabillon, in the fifth Benedictine century, p. 415, says that some considered him the author of the *Life of St Udalric, Bishop of Augsburg*, published by Velser, Mabillon himself, and in the *Acts of the Saints*. But since that author states in two places that he had seen Udalric, whereas our writer lived two centuries later, he could not have written it. Sigismund, on the contrary, in the place cited, teaches that Udalric’s life in verse was composed by Udalscalcus; for it begins with these words: “We venerate the illustrious [saints] with devotion,” etc. Add John Pinius, in the preliminary commentary on the *Life of St Udalric*, in *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II for June, p. 95; and Oudin, vol. II, p. 1013.

[Col. 0837]

# UDALSCALCUS’S NARRATIVE OF THE CONTROVERSIES BETWEEN HERMANN AND EGINO

(Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, ed. Basnage, vol. III, part II, p. 3.)

## JACQUES BASNAGE TO THE READER

Canisius wrote the following concerning Udalscalcus in the preface to his second volume:

> “I obtained Udalscalcus from manuscript codices of the monastery of St Udalric and Afra at Augsburg; but Bruschius, in his work *On Monasteries*, explains who Udalscalcus, Hermann, and Egino were.”

### I. On Egino

Since Bruschius’s book is not at hand, and undoubtedly very many persons lack it, we have thought it proper to extract a few points here. That controversy between Abbot Egino and Bishop Hermann first arose over investitures. Hermann had held the episcopal see for a long time, and the abbot, bound to him in closest friendship, had adhered to him; but controversies suddenly arose between them. The bishop was regarded by the abbot as though excommunicated; the abbot repeatedly charged him with crimes, both before the pope and before Arnold of Mainz. From this the schism arose.

The abbot sought safety in flight. The monks deserted him and denounced him as a disturber; for this reason he was compelled to write them an apologetic letter in reply. But while travelling through Italy, he died on the journey.

### II. On Udalscalcus

This Udalscalcus was a monk of Augsburg and afterwards abbot. He was Egino’s companion on his travels and was present when the unfortunate abbot departed this life. Thus Egino says of him:

> “Since the ship could not contain, because of the multitude of people, Brother Udalscalcus, the companion of our labour,” etc.

Udalscalcus himself, describing his patron’s death, writes:

> “I too arrived at Pisa, hoping for an end to my labour and grief, when I should find my lord and father; but sorrow upon sorrow was added to me, since he had already been brought to the point of death.”

Udalscalcus was therefore a most vehement defender of his abbot, so devoted to his patron’s cause that he did not shrink from comparing Emperor Henry with Nero. Indeed, he sharply rebukes the pope himself because he did not rage against Hermann at his own pleasure. When he had quoted letters of Paschal II, he cries:

> “O Roman prudence—how greatly, may I say it to thy credit, hast thou fallen asleep through negligence!”

Vossius attributes to this Udalscalcus the Lives of Mary Magdalene, Afra, and Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, and not without reason. For the Augsburg Chronicle makes clear that Udalscalcus wrote the entire legend of St Afra, both her conversion and her passion, and likewise that of the gracious confessor Udalric, beginning:

> “We venerate the illustrious [saints] with devotion,” etc.

For, at the request of the bishop of Constance, he had bound it in metre. Concerning blessed Mary Magdalene, whom he revered with singular devotion, the same Chronicle reports (*book* II, chapter 2):

> “He composed a special chant upon the words of St Gregory.”

Nor are these Udalscalcus’s only works. The people of Augsburg call him the special glory of the musical order and most learned. In tragic verse he described the burials of the abbots, and in elegiac verse those of the brethren near the entrance of the dormitory, imitating Prudentius. He was therefore not merely a historian, but also a poet, often singing in heroic verse; he was likewise most skilled in music. After Egino’s death, Udalscalcus returned from Italy and was made abbot of Augsburg in Egino’s place.

### III. On the Time When He Wrote

There can scarcely be any doubt about the time when he wrote the *Narrative*: it was composed under Callixtus II. First, he relates that Hermann was condemned by Paschal, Gelasius, and Pope Callixtus II, who was still alive and holy. Callixtus was therefore still living when Udalscalcus committed this controversy to writing.

Second, he indicates the year even more clearly. He states that Egino was elected abbot in the year of Christ 1109; that lawsuits had been conducted against Hermann for ten years from the time of Egino’s election; and that Hermann himself had been promoted to the episcopate by Henry IV in 1094. Egino died in 1119, while those controversies were still continuing. There is therefore no doubt that Udalscalcus committed them to memory in 1120, or at least before Hermann’s death, which occurred in 1124, when Walter the Count Palatine of Tübingen succeeded him.

Udalscalcus’s *Narrative* is brief, though in it he digresses to recount certain miracles. More particularly to be noted is that he inserted into his narrative various letters of Pope Paschal, Arnold of Mainz, and Abbot Egino, whose side he defended. For whatever Hermann or the monks, after Egino’s flight, produced in their own defence, he omitted.

# PREFACE TO WHAT FOLLOWS

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837A] Udalscalcus, their servant—would that he be not useless—to the communities of St Udalric and St Afra, scattered for Christ under the venerable Abbot Egino: may they be granted the prize of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0838A] Enlightened by the grace of the Sun of righteousness (Mal. IV [printed “XLII”]), you have renounced the blindness of a depraved and perverse nation; and therefore, afflicted in persecution for righteousness’ sake (Phil. II), you have deserved, by evangelical testimony, [Col. 0839A] to be blessed (Matt. V). For you have preferred your spiritual father to flesh and blood; you refused to touch what was unclean, since, following his teaching, you did not receive the aforesaid bishop of Augsburg in his prohibited sacraments.

Therefore, as a reward, as it were, for your holiness, it is granted that, if any among you were ordained by him, they shall on that account be subject to no severity of the canons; rather, it shall remain within the authority of that same father of yours to absolve you from such contagion by apostolic authority—especially those who, after the suspension of the pontifical office had been imposed upon him, received any consecration from him.

But so that this same Father may be honoured [Col. 0840A] and loved more and more, let it be set down in writing how he was established abbot: both to guard against the falsehood of barkers and to preserve the truth of this matter. Then let it be shown how the said bishop was invested, so that it may be taught that everything received in or under him by the Church must be ascribed wholly to grace. Nor should it be withheld from memory, to the praise of God, with how many benefits of miracles your place was made manifest under such an abbot. Finally, since the tyranny of the wicked prevailed, let it not be concealed by the pen how, at the Church’s command, you left that place; so that posterity may be stirred to emulate so great a zeal for righteousness.

# NARRATIVE OF THE CONTROVERSIES BETWEEN HERMANN AND EGINO

[Col. 0839]

## I

[Col. 0839B]

### Abbot Egino; Emperor Henry plays Nero

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109, at the Augsburg monastery founded in honour of St Udalric and St Afra—

> [Note: [Col. 0839D] The church of those same saints was built by Abbot Henry III; Udalscalcus succeeded him in the government of the monastery in 1184, as the Augsburg Chronicle reports, book I, chapter 1, p. 790. BASNAGE.]

—Lord Abbot Egino was enthroned. As a boy, he had been offered to God by his parents in that same place, to be trained in the regular discipline under Diemar, the venerable abbot of the monastery. As time advanced, he was thoroughly instructed in sacred letters. Having passed from the bloom of childhood to the maturity of youth, he showed a zeal for a more honourable life.

But because, at that time, the schism whose head was King Henry and whose cause was Wibert flourished there, he wisely changed his dwelling-place—especially since he had long before been bereft of that most holy father and did not wish to be subject to another who stood in the same schism. Accordingly he came to the cell of St Blasius, situated in the Black Forest, where all received him kindly. There the prudent novice remained until he was taken into the service of Gebehard, bishop of Constance of good memory, who had already been expelled from his see.

For the aforesaid tyrant burned with such furious persecution against the Catholic Church that one might have feared Nero himself, working the mystery of iniquity, had emerged from hell—except that Nero, after killing Peter, had not imposed upon the apostolic see a heresiarch as this man imposed Wibert, and, after driving out all Catholic bishops, had subjected their sees to intruders (2 Thess. II).

This Father was so necessary and so welcome to that reverend bishop that he often performed an embassy for him to the lord pope, sometimes laying aside his monastic habit in obedience, so that the enemy might be deceived by his simulated appearance as a layman. Why say more? He remained his inseparable companion in all labour and distress until peace was restored to the Church and the bishop recovered his own see.

At the same time the aforesaid Augsburg monastery lacked a father; and Lord Egino, now a veteran soldier, had received the quiet of the monastery as though it were his reward. The brethren of Augsburg sent messengers there, recalled their fellow-brother, and with one accord elected him as their abbot. He would have refused and wholly renounced the honour, regarding it as a burden, had he not consented to accept it at the command of the bishop mentioned above and at the persuasion of many spiritual and Catholic persons—especially since the bishop of Augsburg, from whom he was to receive investiture, had by then received the Church’s communion and had moreover made an abjuration of every heresy in the presence of a legate of the Apostolic See.

For none of those who had agreed with the heresy of Wibert [Col. 0840C] and Henry was received by the Apostolic See unless he had first abjured that same plague together with its leaders and publicly professed the Catholic Church.

At this point it seems not wholly to be passed over that certain subverters of truth, reasoning as it were, slanderously say that no vacant see was available to this Father, because they admit that three had held office there when he arrived. O lying tongue, O deceitful lips! They have set their mouth against heaven, so that their tongue may pass over the earth (Ps. LXXII [73]).

“They say three sat there.” If there were three, either all of them, or two of them, were intruders. If all, none of them was abbot; but if two, then this Father was not set over three, but over one. Therefore, whether the one alternative or the other is true, what they say is false.

Yet, so that the truth of this matter may be clear to the faithful and they may not stumble, let us pass by with stopped ears the Scyllaean dogs and attend to what follows.

## II

### Hartmann, Abbot of Augsburg; Egino is elected abbot

[Col. 0841A] After the death of the abbot of that Augsburg house, named Sigahard, Lord Hartmann, abbot of Göttweig, was placed over the same monastery. Since the Church considered it intolerable that such a person should have received the title of governance from a schismatic bishop, he corrected upon his return what he had done incautiously.

Then, not long afterwards, a certain Beringarius, professed of Fulda but unknown to the Augsburgers, undertook the governance of the place as a service rendered to his brother. Although he was unlearned, he nevertheless understood that he had come there contrary to the statutes of the canons, since he had not been elected by the brethren and was, moreover, unknown to them. Understanding this, he too corrected matters by departing.

Yet all these things occurred in the schism and through a schismatic bishop. At length, when the general dispensation of absolution had been spread through the broad extent of the German kingdom by legates of the Apostolic See, namely Richard, bishop of Albano, and Gebehard, bishop of Constance, even the bishop of Augsburg was not excluded from reconciliation. As has been said, he was reconciled through abjuration of heresy and profession of the one Church.

Nevertheless, because the time for showing mercy (Ps. CI [102]) had not yet come, another religious man, the abbot of a different place, namely Weingarten, came and was again set over this Augsburg house. The more prudent he was in seeking things too high for himself (Ecclus. III), the more swiftly he fell; but, when his own brethren demanded the same thing, he rose again by returning to his own house.

At last, when ecclesiastical affairs had been tranquilly arranged as stated, Father Egino—no novice, no stranger, not occupied with another fold, but professed in that house from infancy—was elected abbot with no one presiding; and, having been canonically elected, he was ordained.

Over what, or over whom, was he set? The Church deposed the man placed in office during the schism; the foreigner abandoned sheep that were not his own; the forsaken flock received its own shepherd. Thus indeed, with three abbots established—or rather displaced—this Father is said to have been set over them as the fourth.

But, to conclude briefly against the barkers: either let this man be established and those others deposed, or let those three be approved and this man rejected. Of these two alternatives, we leave them, who trouble themselves little, one to prove as probable—indeed necessary—and the other for them, always labouring, to prove. Nor can the pen yet be withdrawn, since there comes to mind how the enemy is pierced by his own sword.

## III

[Col. 0841D]

### Hartmann abdicates

There was a reason why the aforesaid abbot of Göttweig came to Augsburg and was present at this investiture of our Father. Then one could have seen a great spectacle: how the abbot, like a stronger master of the contest, overcame our elect before the eyes of those awaiting the outcome. Such is the character of a popular gathering: it delights in lawsuits and seditions, applauding one party here and mocking another there.

But because no contest took place, the hope of those who desired it was disappointed: no one conquered and no one fell. For the abbot publicly renounced the care and title of this office—something he had not previously done—releasing the brethren from their vow of obedience and the household also from the oath by which it was bound to him.

Yet a mighty cry of the people, praising God for these events, arose, so that by such an acclamation the adulterating suspicion of an ambusher might be removed. You see still, O rival, that the first and greatest of those three abbots has given us his right hand. You will see that the last, though not the least (Gal. XXI), did the same afterwards—unless, in contradiction to yourself, you confess with us that neither of them was necessary.

For one who usurps authority outside the law does no harm by yielding place to the person to whom it is legally due; but by ceasing from what is unlawful he provides, not for that person’s welfare, but only for his own. For the Lord executes judgement for those who suffer wrong, not for those who inflict it (Ps. CXLV [146]).

Thus enthroned, this Father, like another Jeremiah (Jer. I), began with all his effort to uproot the thorns of vices that had grown there beyond measure, and, by summoning religious men of every kind, strove to cultivate the shoots of virtues. Consequently, a place long despised and contemptible because of the depravity of its inhabitants came, through the fragrance of his good way of life, to be esteemed and honoured. In a short time the number of those faithfully serving God increased, and it was enriched more abundantly with estates and with the treasures of the Church. The saints whose patronage was venerated there were also made illustrious with a greater glory of signs and miracles. Of these, omitting many, let a few be recorded that seem to belong more especially to the consolation of this same Father of ours.

## IV

### The demoniac Bruno is healed

A certain man converted from lay life, called Bruno, was made a monk by him [Col. 0842C] and remained healthy and sound for some time. I believe that, when the fervour of his novitiate had grown lukewarm, the demonic force which had withdrawn for a time returned, now increased sevenfold. He was grievously seized by frenzy and, as is usual with this kind [of affliction], could scarcely be held when captured even by many persons (Matt. XII).

While we wondered and stood amazed at this, Lord Abbot himself also hurried up. The poor man ground his teeth; a harder piece of wood was put in place, lest he wear away his tongue by chewing it, and he made a gurgling sound. You could see his chest swell into a mound, where it was less tightly confined; his face turn pale; his whole body tremble; and him wish to seize and tear apart every adjacent object along with himself.

But when he received the blessing of our Father, he gradually sat up, as though awakened from a heavy sleep, and so recovered that the demoniac affliction never returned.

## V–IV

### Epileptics healed at St Afra

Two other brethren of the same monastery, one named Adalgoz and the other Hecil, were seized by the same epilepsy at different times, though not in different ways. When certain holy words were chanted over them by the Father himself, in our presence they were healed at once.

At one time crowds were streaming from all directions to the feast of our patron St Udalric. A certain man, so contracted for nine and a half years that the soles of his feet seemed as though born into his buttocks, arrived riding on a little ass. The rider’s toes could even be seen impressed on the ass’s back, so that the degree to which bodily deformity had prevailed over human nature might be inferred from the wound inflicted contrary to nature upon the animal.

While we were celebrating the solemnities of Mass at the altar of St Udalric, he crawled on hands and knees to the tomb of blessed Afra. There, with some hope of health, as he himself later related, he poured out prayer. Meanwhile he conceived the desire to stretch out limbs that had long been contracted, especially because they had begun to hurt more severely than usual. Straining with all his strength, he could scarcely withdraw the soles a little from the cavities of his flesh. His sinews gradually stretched out, and they could be heard cracking, as though very dry brushwood were being broken.

Then, as he cried out loudly because of the excessive pain, the crowd rushed in, raised him up, and carried him to the tomb of St Udalric. There, after he had lain for a long time without voice or movement, his chest suddenly began to swell so greatly that all the body’s inner parts were feared to be on the point of bursting forth. Accordingly, while all present awaited the departure of his soul, the often-mentioned Father of the monastery put a leaf of sage beneath the mute man’s tongue and asked how he was.

“Very well, lord, very well,” he said, “if only you will take care of me.”

Thereupon the Father took him in as his own. Before seven days had elapsed, when clergy and people assembled, this man—so long a worm and no man—carried a cross through the middle of the city. As all glorified God with great rejoicing because he had been restored to complete health, he demonstrated his joy by leaping.

## VII

### A lame girl walks

A girl of seven years, lame from her mother’s womb, was brought with her parents to the same place. Although we had learned from trustworthy persons of many other wonders, extraordinary for her age, we took care to record only what we saw.

As stated, she was weak and frail of body, yet she ate especially austere food, counting it a great delicacy whenever she was refreshed by eggs or milk. The name of Jesus was constantly on her lips, and her face shone with a countenance more angelic than human. Beyond all desire, she delighted daily in receiving the Lord’s sacrament. With what reverence and compunction of tears she approached it! She frequently judged the conscience of those who looked upon her. She assessed persons according to the merit of their lives: she gladly looked at some, but turned her gaze away from others, as though repelled by wickedness.

When we asked why she did this and set before her the example of the Lord eating with publicans and sinners (Matt. IX), she said:

> “I call God himself to witness that I do this not out of contempt, but out of fear; this stream of my sweat also proves it. For, to mention one instance among many, when she saw two clerics approaching, she addressed one and abhorred the other.”

Those around her begged her to look upon the other as well.

“See,” she said, “I yield to your entreaty; but, I beg you, spare me this affliction of mine.”

For her face grew pale, and sweat ran over her whole little body. We, moved as though to penitence, were sad in compassion for her pain, yet rejoiced at the confirmation of a doubtful matter. More diligently inquiring into the conduct of the clerics, we learned truthfully that the man whom the girl detested had been a monk but, having cast aside the better habit, had put on the dress of a cleric.

But lest anyone object that she had known them beforehand, and that consequently there was nothing miraculous in her assessment of the two, she disclosed, apart from the true signs already shown which could lend credence to her words, many more hidden sins. We sometimes proved through those who confessed that these had indeed been revealed to her.

While she continued almost night and day in the church with persistent prayer, one evening she crawled around the shrine of blessed Udalric as far as the altar. When, kneeling, she touched its pall, the place where she clung suddenly moved, so that the girl slipped more violently. Those standing by hurried to raise her and, according to custom, settled the lame girl into a sitting position.

Then she said, “Set me upon my feet, for the Lord has directed my steps” (Ps. XXXIX [40]).

They did this, not without amazement, and still held her lest she fall. But she left them all and walked forward, at first unsteadily using feet as though they belonged to another; but soon all her natural powers were restored.

Without delay she was swept into the crowds; and, as human curiosity is, the household which received this gift became more cheerful. Feasting was accompanied by wantonness; empty talk was poured into the innocent girl’s ears; her childhood was drawn toward frivolity; grace was diminished by the appearance of good. Yet, by God’s mercy, she was seized with very sharp pain and, after her little body had been worn down by prolonged chastisement, was delivered from this present wicked world in the confession of the Lord.

## VIII–XI

[Col. 0844C]

### A blind woman sees

A certain woman, a well-known citizen of Augsburg, was covered by the cloud of blindness and deprived of sight for more than eight years. One day, while she was prostrate in her usual humble supplication at the tomb of blessed Udalric, she suddenly filled the entire basilica with cries, summoning all to rejoice at the grace of light restored to her. The report called together the whole city to praise the Lord’s mercy for so manifest a miracle.

The same Father whom our pen serves testifies that he saw a certain mute man sit beside the mausoleum of the often-mentioned St Udalric; suddenly the bonds of his tongue were loosed and his power of speech restored, as was shown by blood flowing from his mouth.

What should I say about the possessed? We saw them there delivered almost as often as they were afflicted. For it happened that, when a certain woman had been healed through the merits of blessed Afra and was carrying a cross, according to custom, before the crowd gathered through the middle of the city, she encountered another possessed woman who had been delivered in the church of the holy Mother of God, accompanied by a crowd joined to her. Thus, with the two standards of Jesus, ever victorious, united, the people of God returned home exulting on both sides with praises in a double triumph.

At the dedication of this our church, while the aforesaid Father was once speaking the word of life to the people, a certain man possessed by a demon began to make a great outcry, so that the crowd was occupied more in restraining him than in hearing the word. Then suddenly the enemy of humankind said:

> “Why are you so eagerly quieting me, when in a little while you will see how useful a business I shall be engaged upon?”

As we heard this and, as far as we could, turned everyone away from one who had been a liar from the beginning (John VIII), behold: we saw a bloodstained soldier running through the midst of the people as though fleeing from battle, announcing with a terrible cry that the city had been captured by enemies. All raised a mournful cry; no one waited for the fugitives; they despaired that the house of God could serve as an asylum. Even the unarmed populace went out; weapons were seized from the suburbs; people hurried to the place of conflict; each rushed against the other, yet found no enemy to strike.

At last, returning to themselves, they recognized Satan’s wiles. They searched for the lying soldier but could not find him, since the phantom’s assumed form had vanished. Although it is unknown through whose sin this illusion occurred, nevertheless whenever we gather to hear the divine word, this event exhorts us all not to direct our attention elsewhere.

## XII

### A thief is detected through a vision

A certain priest named Luipold, sacristan of the same church, died, already worn out by old age. At his burial, another priest from nearby seemed in sleep to see the dead man vomiting forth a chain five cubits long.
