When he reported the vision, it was decided that all the dead man’s belongings should be searched, lest something belonging to the Church might perhaps be hidden there.

The house was accordingly pulled apart, and a belt of the finest purple cloth was found. Measured in accordance with the indication of the dream, it proved to be as long as the chain in the vision. It was immediately recognized by the brethren and placed in the vestry.

## XIII

### A woman vanishes

A poor woman stole two silver chalices with patens; but, unable to leave the church doors, she was exposed as guilty of sacrilege. The wretched woman was seized and, after the stolen goods had been restored, was led away for punishment. Yet she who, burdened by the crime, though it had been hidden, could not escape, escaped the hands of the torturers after being relieved of her burden, God sparing her.

For when all ran to that cruel spectacle, they looked for the woman who was to be punished; but although long sought, she could not be found.

## XIV

### Various relics

I say that our saints were made illustrious by greater glory of signs and miracles, and under this our Father were venerated with greater zeal. [Col. 0845D] To say nothing of Cologne . . . .

> [Note: [Col. 0845D] Note here that the eleven thousand virgins are celebrated. BASNAGE.]

—of [relics] from the eleven thousand virgins, likewise of the martyr Albinus, of the holy Mauri, and of many relics of saints which he acquired from every quarter—when these had been brought to Augsburg, saints hitherto hidden there were at last discovered to have arisen, as if citizens well known to them: namely Dionysius, the first bishop of that city—

> [Note: [Col. 0845D] Zosimus was the brother of Hilaria, Afra’s mother; when he was baptized, his name was changed and he was called Dionysius. [Col. 0846D] How many fables are told about them! Dionysius and Afra never came to Augsburg. BASNAGE.]

—and Quiriacus with his twenty-four fellow martyrs.

Passing over these, as it were, new discoveries, he decreed that the discovery of blessed Afra, almost obliterated by ancient forgetfulness, should be solemnly celebrated. He likewise decreed that the feast of the aforesaid twenty-four martyrs, who suffered together with St Hilaria, should be venerated on one day. Nor was he frustrated in such zeal, since he was rewarded with a most precious treasure: the head of that martyr Hilaria, discovered in those days.

## XV

### The abbot’s disputes with the bishop

But the adversary of all goodness, like [that in the case of] Job (chapter I), thought that this Father did not worship God for nothing, since he was surrounded by prosperous circumstances and honours. Considering it of no account to deprive him of outward possessions, he desired, as it were, to scourge his flesh and bones. He planned to drive him and his brethren from the place itself—brethren attached to him as flesh to bones through unity of heart and soul—while some of them, having withdrawn their steps far from him in life, had been consumed as in a banquet of pleasure by fire.

Therefore the man who held the name of shepherd over the fold of the same city stirred opposition against him, so that he who ought to have defended the flock from the bites of wolves—not fleeing as a hireling, but himself becoming a wolf—seized, tore, and scattered the sheep.

For the cause of this persecution, the episcopal office was prohibited to the bishop himself by the Apostolic See; and our abbot refused to participate in so great a presumption while he abused that office. But, so that the end of this affair may follow more clearly, let its beginning also be set forth more carefully by the pen.

## XVI

### Election of the bishop of Augsburg

While Pope Urban of blessed memory presided at Rome, the see of the Augsburg Church was vacant. The aforesaid tyrant, Emperor Henry, was then staying at Verona, unable to enter Lombardy because Lady Matilda prevented him, nor to leave Italy because German princes opposed him.

> [Note: [Col. 0846D] “Domina,” or “domna”: “lady.”]

A certain count, named Udalric, an adherent of his tyranny, saw him pressed by great difficulties on every side. Having borrowed five hundred talents from the people of Verona in order to give the bishopric of Augsburg to his brother, he offered himself to him. In addition, he promised to accompany him into the German territories, and he fulfilled this promise.

By this arrangement the count’s one-eyed brother was brought forward. He was not invested by the excommunicated lay hand until he had been bound by oath to pay the aforesaid weight of silver to the Veronese. Thus the count, escorted by a great force of soldiers, brought his brother—whom I will not call elected, but not even known by sight—to the Augsburgers.

Compelled, however, by fear of the armed force, Augsburg received him as bishop; but, when he was more closely inspected in order that he might be known, the city gradually marvelled that it had received a blind man. The people jointly lamented that the Prophet’s curse had been fulfilled in him:

> “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back continually” (Ps. LXVIII [69]).

For the man whom they had received as an eye to look out for their welfare (Rom. II), they quickly recognized as born with both outward and inward blindness, through the bending of his back—that is, through his own strength. For if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit (Matt. XV).

Such an elected man was promoted to the rank of priest contrary to the statutes of the canons, and was thereafter to undergo the ordination of the pontificate in an access not unfitting for him. He was ordained by the bishop of Aquileia, who is improperly called patriarch, under the pallium of Wibert the heresiarch, after two oaths had been given beforehand.

For when the man to be ordained declared that he had received permission for such a consecration from his master, the archbishop of Mainz, he was not believed on mere words by the ordainer, although the latter had been excommunicated by two apostolic men, namely Urban and Gregory. Therefore a ministerial from the foremost household of Blessed Mary was sought who might prove this by oath.

When none was found, a certain dependant of the same household, named Bero, was dressed in the finest clothes. First, he falsely swore that he was a ministerial knight, because he was a man of large stature; second, he was compelled to deceive by swearing that his lord possessed the archbishop’s permission to receive consecration. He himself later reported this to us after his conversion.

## XVII

### The bishop despoils the Church of Augsburg

The course of events thus begun in this detestable manner was visited by a corresponding omen. For the new pontiff entered the Holy of Holies, not to appease God but to provoke him. When the office of Mass had apparently been performed for this purpose, the deacon, intending to exhort the people to bow themselves for the bishop’s blessing, used this proclamation—not, as was thought, because his mind was deranged:

> “Bow your heads to God.”

Everyone suggested the customary exhortation for the pontifical blessing; but the levite repeated again and again that the people should bow their heads to God.

> “He persisted in saying such things, and remained fixed [in that resolve].”
>
> VIRGIL, *Aeneid* II.649.

The deacon, questioned afterward by members of the household whether he had done this deliberately, testified that he had proclaimed “God” not voluntarily but as though in ecstasy. At length the bishop, established by falsehood, returned to Augsburg, now to oppress clergy and people with unrestrained tyranny. For he plundered rich and poor; through him the church of the holy Mother of God was stripped of an immeasurable treasure; the estates and offerings of the canons were assigned as benefices to laymen; the canonical hours and Mass were not celebrated, while, in place of God’s praises, complaints over lack of food were frequent. In those days the aforesaid legate of the Roman See, Richard, bishop of Albano, having been sent into the German regions, arrived at Mainz. There, after he had deprived Emperor Henry at Ingelheim of the royal insignia—having, that is, cut off the head of heresy—and had restored communion to all, the several members of the Church were reconciled into one. This bishop, I say, this same bishop, was not excepted in the general absolution, but, after abjuring the heresy of Wibert, was received among the rest before his own case had yet been examined. When the legate also came to Augsburg, the complaints of clergy and people were laid before him: namely, that the said bishop had invaded that see without canonical election or consecration. The matter, once heard, was investigated more carefully. It was asked whether any canon would withdraw himself from this accusation; all, saying one thing and thinking the same, subscribed by name. It was deferred that everything should be concluded in the presence of the lord apostolic. A synod was assembled at Warstein; representatives of the Church of Augsburg attended with their bishop. The legate reported what he had heard and how he had deferred what he heard; the proper accusation was repeated. No excuse was offered; all readily agreed that such a bishop ought to be deposed. And this would have been done, had not Gebehard of Constance persuaded the Church of Augsburg that it should be done. For at that time the lord pope had intended to visit the German kingdom, which, to the ruin of many, he was unable to accomplish. Nevertheless, suspended from episcopal office, the half-bishop returned. A deadline was appointed for finishing the affair. Augsburg waited sorrowfully for its liberation; but, disappointed in its hope of the apostolic’s coming, the same bishop, within the appointed term, approached the apostolic concerning the restoration of his prohibited office, and received from him letters containing the following.

## XVIII.

### Letter of Paschal

> “PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons and other parishioners of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Our brother Herimann, bishop of your city, came to us uninvited, asking that his case be brought to a more definite conclusion, etc. See Paschal II, under the year 1118 . . . . For we wish that both he and the Church under him may, until the appointed time, enjoy peace and tranquillity, by the Lord’s gift. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December.”

## XIX.

### Another Letter of Paschal

He had scarcely carried these letters to Venice when, having taken counsel, he compelled all who knew of them to swear that they would not reveal them for the space of a year; and so, fabricating lies at will, he returned home. Then, devising an even graver wickedness, he bribed one of his accusers, who seemed more eminent than the others, and secretly sent through him letters to the apostolic, as though from the people of Augsburg. This messenger of falsehood was graciously received; while he was heard, the pope fiercely expressed great indignation against the bishop, who was discovered by all to speak with a double heart. Yet, at the entreaties for him of the bishop of Chur and Abbot Gotwig, he was allowed to depart, bearing letters presented as though in answer from the Augsburgers, to report truths together with falsehoods. The true letters were as follows:

> “PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the clergy of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “After the accusation which you made against your bishop, we received the letters of your charity. Since in them you signified to us that you have peace and concord with the same bishop, we rejoiced, if it shall be established that this concord was freely made. Nevertheless, we await the appointed term, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may carry out whatever equity shall prescribe. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of February.”

## XX.

### Hermann Recognized as Bishop of Augsburg. Hermann an Adulterer

When these letters had been read secretly to the bishop, he raged against the messenger. He complained that the messages sent back to him did not correspond fairly to the price; with the father of lies again prompting him, he threatened that such adverse matters should not be disclosed, but favourable things fabricated. He came out in public; the ears of those waiting were raised.

> Mountains are in labour; a ridiculous mouse will be born.  
> —Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 139.

The bishop was falsely greeted with an apostolic blessing, and the people were made participants in the same favour. Not much time passed before a cardinal named Divitius, sent by the pope, entered the German lands. After his return to Rome, the bishop—supposedly restored through the cardinal, yet under no testimony whatever—misused the pontifical office. Now employing the more useful counsel of Achitophel (2 Samuel 15, 16, 17), he admitted into his more secret fellowship any more powerful members of clergy or laity, so that, inferior persons being stifled, no one might be a betrayer of falsehood or a herald of truth. Thus the pontiff was scarcely proclaimed a second Melchizedek; all things previously said or done having been consigned to oblivion, he was everywhere received as legitimate.

In the dark course of this interval of silence and night, Father Egino, herald of the true light, was recalled to Augsburg, as stated above, and raised to the honour of abbot. He too was received as a friend, as one holding precedence among the foremost. Before long he wondered at such a bishop, remembering his own father, namely the bishop of Constance. Gradually he withdrew himself from the bishop’s familiarity, though not from unity of communion, because he had not yet learned anything certain concerning the enormity of so great a presumption. But God, unwilling that so great a man should longer be deceived by such fabrications, revealed in this manner how blood touches blood.

The said bishop, now caught more frequently in the foulness of fornication, was reported to have committed adultery in the Church after intercourse with nuns and other prostitutes. The husband of that wife, being conspicuous for courage and worth, could easily have roused the whole city to kill the adulterer. But preferring that judgment be rendered for him by the spiritual rather than the material sword, he appealed to the Apostolic See to lodge a complaint concerning the crime. The Church of Augsburg, awakened by so great a wickedness as from a most grievous sleep of error, sent letters to the same see, asking what it ought to decide concerning such a bishop. It was instructed by the following writing.

## XXI.

### Letter of Paschal

> “P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, clergy of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing, etc. See Paschal II, under the year 1118 . . . We commend to your brotherhood the bearer of this letter from the Apostolic See, who seeks assistance, so that in the complaint which he brings against that bishop you may uphold his justice. Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.”

## XXII.

### Letter of Paschal to the Bishop of Mainz

The complaints having also been laid before the bishop of Mainz, an examination was enjoined upon him by these letters.

> “P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ARNOLD, venerable brother, archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing, etc. See Paschal II, under the year 1118 . . . Whatever, indeed, you shall establish justly and reasonably, with God as author, we shall hold as ratified.”

## XXIII.

### Letter of Arnold of Mainz

Having received this command, the archbishop invited the prelates of Augsburg by this directive:

> “ARNOLD, by the mercy of God propitiously granted, devoted servant in Christ of the flock of Mainz, to the reverend abbot together with the dearest sons, brothers and lords, of the Church of Augsburg: counsel of paternal affection in the spirit of divine consolation.
>
> “Dearest brothers, we inform your charity that we have recently received letters from the Apostolic See, in which examination of your bishop is enjoined upon us. It has pleased us to undertake this with the utmost diligence, by the counsel of our Church and brethren, preserving canonical procedure, lest the case be lost to the plaintiff, or the supreme pontiff have reason to complain of our negligence. Since we possess the whole complaint, known to you, sent on to us by the aforesaid see and to be reconsidered in its proper place and time, we send you copies of those sealed letters of the lord pope. Admonished by their authority, send to us, at the time of the court at Würzburg, either the lord abbot or any suitable prelates among you; then we shall make known to you more fully through your representatives whatever the Spirit shall meanwhile suggest to us and to our Church and brethren. Farewell.”

## XXIV.

### Concerning Hermann. Cases to Be Judged by the Pontiff

But because at this same time the bishop was lingering in Lombardy on the royal expedition, under a cloud of infamy, our abbot sent to him at Augsburg one of his brethren, named Retpoton, carrying apostolic letters, urgently advising him to approach the pope in order to seek restoration to office and purge himself of the sacrilege alleged against him. But the bishop, rejecting the sounder counsel, armed himself, as one conscious of guilt, with his habitual defence of falsehood. For letters were fabricated as though from the Church of Augsburg and sent to the apostolic through the canon Conrad and the said brother Ratpoton. Their deceit is exposed by the following reply.

## XXV.

### Letter of Paschal

> “P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, D., dean, and the other canons of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “It has long been since our brother Hermann, your bishop, was accused before us on three counts, etc. See Paschal, under the year 1118 . . . . If your bishop has made amends concerning ecclesiastical property and correction of his perverse conduct, and if he has cleared himself of the other charges brought against him by the hand of three bishops or five priests, let him obtain restoration of the office prohibited to him. Given at Benevento, on the Kalends of April.”

## XXVI.

### Crimes Imputed to Hermann. The Pontiff Slumbers

It seems necessary to dwell briefly upon these letters, since they contain a full knowledge of the foregoing matters. First, indeed, the first point is set forth: how this man—would that he were a hireling—entered not through the door (John 10), but by another way; having entered to slaughter and destroy, he was execrated instead of consecrated. Then follow the consequences: namely, a perverse life together with rapine. A term, they say, was appointed, to which each party was summoned. The accused party concealed under oath, as stated above, the letters indicating the term, so that the other, ignorant of the place of justice, might fall silent. Therefore neither party appeared. And this is what is said: that the bishop would have been free unless they met at that appointed term. Yet this is determined by irrefragable confirmation, as they say Conrad asserts.

O Roman prudence, how deeply you have fallen asleep! I might, for your sake, call it negligence, lest perhaps I should have to say that, like good Homer, you sometimes nod. Why, “as he asserts,” and not “as you assert”? Although you know the rest by heart, you define the number of counts; you do not pass over the suspension from office; you restate the deadline by which all things were to be examined and concluded; yet you do not know the condition of release, and so exhort us too not to know it? But when they say, “because of the difficulties of the journeys and the infirmity of the person,” etc., an evident falsehood is inferred from this. For there were difficulties of travel and infirmity of person when, as we learned later, he was perfectly healthy but unwilling to appear. For when we asked that same canon why he fabricated such things, he made this apologetic reply: “I spoke the truth when I regarded one blind from birth as infirm.”

Moreover, lest anyone wonder that a matter committed to the archbishop was entrusted by the apostolic to another for examination, let him know that this canon, author of this very alteration, was the brother of the bishop of Chur; and therefore Mainz was detested at Augsburg as an enemy of the king, while he maintained that his own brother would not refuse to undertake the case there. Yet the latter too is more cautiously instructed: namely, “if the bishop has made amends concerning ecclesiastical property and the correction of his perverse conduct,” as the false letters testified, etc.

This bishop, I say, came to Augsburg, induced by many promises. Clergy and people objected that the bishop’s purgation should by no means be accepted unless a real, and not feigned, amendment had been made. Four persons of ill repute were chosen; a fifth was bound to the penalty of swearing, while more than five hundred were convicted of false oaths. Thus purged, the bishop asked the bishop whether pontifical office was now lawful for him. The latter did not consent, but advised him to appeal to the apostolic for its restoration; and they departed. Then the said bishop again set out for Italy in the company of the royal expedition, entered for the third time with an armed hand into the house of blessed Peter, and did not fear to communicate with the excommunicated. The archbishop did not delay to report this otherwise to the Augsburgers.

## XXVII.

### Letter of Arnold

ARNOLD, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Mainz, to Lord E. [Egino], abbot of the Augsburg monastery, together with the other faithful members of the Catholic Church: may you grow into the body of Christ in the Spirit of unity.

Long ago a cry ascended to heaven (Exodus 2) concerning him who is called your bishop; and, as you know, we received from the Apostolic See itself the account of the complaint and the command to examine him. But because charity never fails (1 Corinthians 13), and loves even those who hate it, we would, beyond what was required, if possible, call back one who flees, and apply great remedies to great wounds, if your sick man recognized himself and did not reject even the physician who calls him.

Now, therefore, this case summons you in a certain manner. Whichever way it falls, it seems advisable that, in accordance with our admonition, you meet him in person and urge him to come to his senses, to take thought for his salvation at least now, to abandon the contagion of excommunication, and not go beyond the end by continual transgression. You know, and he himself knows, under what dreadful threat of punishment he has long been suspended from office by the vicar of blessed Peter himself; yet he has not considered how he has also defiled himself by excommunication, nor has he sought from it any way of salvation.

Therefore, as we do what belongs to us, so do you what belongs to you. By ecclesiastical correction tell him that the way of salvation will be nearer to him if he humbles himself and seeks pardon than if he awaits a synodal hearing, where the judge ought not to be bent toward either side. But if he gives no heed to the words of your brotherhood and to these our warnings, we meanwhile withdraw from him, in addition to the office already forbidden, the obedience of clergy and people, because we judge him incorrigible and disobedient.

## XXVIII.

### Egino Goes into Exile

When the abbot received these letters and they were read to the entire Church, the bishop returned, not doubting that he would be received as a Catholic. He therefore entered our church as usual; no one came to meet him. For the abbot had refused the interdict and had directed his own people to beware of it. The reason for this contempt was asked; all the facts were reported. Then indeed you would have seen nothing human in the man; from his raging and rushing about you would have thought him a beast. The abbot was assailed with blasphemies and threats, and proscribed as a public enemy of the realm.

Yet because the citizens of the city would not endure the expulsion of so great a man, a crowd of relatives and friends gathered armed; and even so the most wickedly conceived purpose could not be effected. Meanwhile the archbishop sent him another letter in this form.

## XXIX.

### Hermann Excommunicated by Arnold

To the sons and brothers of the holy Church of Augsburg, together with E. [Egino], abbot of Saint Ulrich: ARNOLD, unworthy minister of the see of Mainz, fraternal love with prayer.

What was recently announced to you by apostolic authority from the lord bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Roman See, we too announce to you. But because you disregarded this, neither you nor he whom you call your bishop attended the holy council. Know that he, since he has long been suspended by the lord pope from episcopal and priestly office, is deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord until he makes satisfaction. You, however, are for the present spared through our intercession, but will undergo the same punishment unless you cause the abbots and prelates of your Church to attend the holy council to be held at Fritzlar on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. This we command both by apostolic authority and our own, as we have received it in the mandate.

Furthermore, we notify your brotherhood that we have confirmed, concerning the complaint of your Adalbert, the same measures which we learned the Apostolic See had taken. For we have excommunicated the adulterer, the adulteress, and all who consent. Your said bishop is not excepted in this condemnation, since, by failing to do justice to one suffering wrong, he is shown to have given consent to the crime.

## XXX.

### The People Refuse Confirmation from Hermann

When these things had again been proclaimed by our Father, and all were now inclined by fear of the king toward the bishop’s crime, the whole weight of the struggle rested upon the head of the abbot alone. Holy Saturday of Pentecost arrived. On that day he went not far from the monastery in order to baptize the daughter of a certain count. The bishop, however, wishing to discover whether we would receive his chrism, sought out the same monastery. The office of baptism was being performed by the prior of the place, named Markward. When matters came to this point, at the bishop’s command our chrism, received from a Catholic minister, was taken away from the priest, and his own was offered to the baptizer. Then the latter, as though afraid to touch something alien, looked for the familiar vessel of the sacrament.

“This,” said the bearer of the execrated liquid, “you must receive; you shall have no other.”

The baptizer publicly declared that he did not wish to be defiled by the sacrament of a heretic. The bishop sprang up and shouted more loudly. There was an uproar among the people; the clergy ran about; divine and human things were thrown into confusion. What was the disciple of Christ’s forerunner to do? He awaited only the executioner’s sword: unless, as Herod killed John in prison (Matthew 14), the enemy of the Church should slaughter this man beside the altar; yet each would fall for the truth. For the prelate raged with such fury that the delay of sacrilege might rightly be imputed, not to himself who commanded, but to the people who did not obey.

At length the solemnities of Mass were begun; the priest went forward to the altar, truly to offer a sacrifice worthy of God—himself almost the victim. The mouths of those chanting above were stopped by blasphemies; they were driven violently from the church; divine offices were thereafter forbidden to the brethren. Satisfied with this triumph, the despised pontiff entered the cloister, and a table was set for his meal. When all had eaten, they went out. The Father of the monastery returned, and the sequence of events was recounted. The evening synaxis was solemnly performed with the abbot presiding, and the same Father urged all the more persistence in divine service because this was believed to be done in defiance of Satan.

He himself no longer went out publicly, for fear of death met him on every side. The bold obstinacy of the wicked was sought out; abundant money and other benefices were promised for the abbot’s death. The bishop declared that this was done not as sacrilege but by a just judgment. Nevertheless, a procession being arranged, they entered the church of the holy Mother of God. When the people of the whole city had gathered there, the letters set out above were read at the abbot’s command and interpreted also for the laity.

“This,” said the Father, “is the cause for which, as you know, I suffer such adversities. Behold, I am driven out from before you with the children whom God has given me; let the conscience of all of you be witness to these things.”

When this was done, the litany began. A sword threatening their necks, they passed through without injury under God’s protection.

## XXXI.

### New Disturbances over the Election of an Abbot

The tenth year of this Father’s ordination was now approaching, and, as it were, the tithe of good fruits was offered to God when the Father with his sons was deprived of his home for righteousness’ sake. For the same monastery having been filled with a hostile force, and no brother being found unwilling to follow his Father, peace was gained through flight and departure was prepared for the new travellers.

Nor was there lacking an omen of divine vengeance, by which the proud might be terrified and the humble consoled. The precinct of the monastery was shaken by a most violent earthquake. The church, rocking with the ground and with its bells striking here and there, threatened collapse. The tomb of blessed Afra seemed to open as its metal fastening gave way; by this sign the Lady’s retinue was promised dispersal among her servants. After more earnest thanksgivings had been offered to God, who is wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67), the band set out on foot over the foreign sea of the world. On either side, the wet faces of those who wept were concealed by faces fixed upon the earth. The Lech was crossed, and the nearby monastery of Saint Peter was reached. There was a great gathering of those who came to meet them. When the praises of God with which they were received and the consolations of the most sacred reading were concluded, the sheepfold of a double flock was united under our shepherd.

We had scarcely remained there seven days when Augsburg, unable to bear the destruction of its chief place, approached the bishop as another Aegeas; we were asked to return together and urgently required to be restored. A Good Friday was mimicked in every respect: the altars were stripped, the bells were not rung, and the divine offices were mourned in silence. More suitable persons were therefore selected and sent to procure our return; by letter they promised that whatever violence we had suffered from the opposing party would not be repeated. After taking counsel with Catholic men, we returned. Clergy and people rushed out to meet us and received us with praises.

But while Satan sought to sift us like wheat (Luke 22), Christ interceded for Peter’s faith: false brethren were distinguished among us, while the true were not overthrown. Therefore we entered upon a new conflict. We were seduced by the flattery of a pestilent persuasion: namely, that, renouncing our Father, we should elect another, since we could not retain him, as being the prelate’s enemy. The abbot was quickly expelled with those subjects who remained there; the place was made available for perpetrating the crime.

Yet even thus, when their conceived grief had been brought to the birth of iniquity (Psalm 7), they devised this means to remove the abbot from their midst. A crowd of wicked men was assembled; the abbot was promised a place where he could defend justice; he was told that nothing remained except his appearance in person. More gladly the Father hurried to the city, prepared to conclude whatever he had proposed. But he who revealed through his angel to Joseph that he should go down into Egypt with Jesus, avoiding Herod’s persecution (Matthew 2), likewise deigned to take precautions so that this innocent Father’s blood might not be shed. For he had covered the greater part of the journey; and behold, he encountered a messenger carrying letters from his brethren, which indicated that ambushes had been prepared for him both within and outside the city. The abbot turned back and was delivered from the bloody disputation of his tormentors.

## XXXII.

### Letter of Egino

Meanwhile the king, now excommunicated for the second time, came into the German kingdom from Italy and entered Augsburg with two bishops condemned by the same excommunication. Since he was received with particular care by the aforesaid brethren, the good shepherd, grieving that the flock entrusted to him had been rashly polluted by this contagion of participation, sent them the following command:

> “The discernment of your brotherhood knows how, grieving for our mother, holy Church, we fled those persecuting her in body and spirit; it knows by what promises of peace and truth we were recalled, and yet did not obtain these things from those who promised them. For the world can promise peace, but cannot give it (John 14). But I, seeking that peace which Christ gave to his disciples, again withdrew with Jesus from Herodian persecution in the night of tribulation (Matthew 2), having first informed you that you ought to do the same.
>
> “On the contrary, forgetting fear of the Lord and paternal love, you, the flock of my littleness—you, I say, my sons whom I begot in Christ (1 Corinthians 4)—have followed in all things that Gunther, a stranger and enemy of our profession. Since I, who seek to defend the justice of my office in the sight of the whole Church, have been violently expelled, barefoot lamentation would have suited you better than royal rejoicing without a head. This could have been an honourable occasion for you; this could have been advanced as brotherly compassion for my expulsion.
>
> “To this is added the fact that you have received into communion, by following and embracing him in every way, that other Judas, my betrayer Ratpoton, whom, when my spirit and body were gathered with you, I delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5). You did not resist those communicating with him; and thus nearly all of you have been defiled by such contagion. In all these things, because you obeyed the bishop’s commands, alas, you violated the vow of obedience which each of you promised me by name before God and his saints.
>
> “What more shall I do to you? Through that said ravager Ratpoton, you stripped the lord prior, your master, who was fleeing after me and following me—an act shameful even to speak of. And if not all of you consented to this, as I believe, you nevertheless did not burn with fitting vengeance against those who did it. What shall I say? ‘The anathema is in your midst, O Israel; you cannot stand against your enemies’ (Joshua 7). Our elder, Lord Engilbold, did not rise among you as a leader like Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2). Let him see what he has done.
>
> “Nevertheless, because he and a very few others, after all these things, have sent me the services of their obedience, what I said when present I command also when absent. For I told you that you ought not change your place so long as you could keep yourselves from communion with that bishop. Since you have transgressed, let whoever wishes now at least to belong to the Lord not delay to follow me. For I await you not far from you; if I am found worthy to receive any of you, I give thanks. Meanwhile, know that this Henry, grown old in evil days, is deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord.”

## XXXIII.

### Flight of the Monks

When this was heard, some groaned deeply, while others mocked. But a priest named Eberhard, together with a youth of good character named Odalric, left the monastery and had scarcely crossed the streams and marshes of the Lech when horsemen sent by the said Ratpoton pursued the weary pedestrians. Unarmed, they were seized by armed men; stripped, they were threatened like sheep. Having somehow escaped the danger of the torrent, they were forced to enter [the reading is incomplete or uncertain]; barefoot, they were brought back through the middle of the streets as a spectacle for the populace. Some more merciful persons obtained for them the return of their plunder; but from Ratpoton they received this as their reward: permission to take away, if they could, anything from such fugitives.

Released, they again took the same road. Though their limbs failed, their spirits did not fail in following the command of their Father. O miserable spectacle of affairs! In the midst of a wide field, now exhausted, they fell down; cold dissolved their drenched limbs; the comfort of day was taken away and the terror of night descended. At last, when the stronger man had recovered a little breath, they wandered through byways; their sight being dim, they felt about to see whether any human habitation might appear. A village was unexpectedly encountered; they knocked at the door of a neighbouring house and were asked who was there at such an unseasonable hour of night. They humbly begged that it might be opened to poor men for God’s sake. Though only slowly, they were admitted; a fire was lit, and it was seen that he was truly poor.

They pleaded for the companion left on the road; their request was granted. The priest was placed on a cart and, like the man aided by the Samaritan, was brought to an inn (Luke 10). When their limbs had been warmed, food was set before the hungry men. Matins were performed, and they set out for the place agreed upon for them. Other brethren too put aside the monastic habit and joined merchants; others escaped by night and followed our Father. Yet some of them, with a deceitful intention, sent assurances of obedience to their abbot, while approaching him neither in bodily steps nor in heart. The following letter was sent in reply.

## XXXIV.

### Letter of Egino

> “EGINO, by God’s grace what he is, to the brethren: ‘to those who love God all things work together for good’ (Romans 8).
>
> “I have now received several times letters affirming the fidelity of your obedience; but that this same faith is not universal among you is testified by your partial dissent—indeed, contention. The Church does not possess the factions of those who disagree (1 Corinthians 11). Therefore those are proved then to be outside the Church who are concluded to have made void the faith which is in Christ (1 Timothy 5). Thus I would rather that you had not directed to me, as though jointly, the blessing of obedience, but that, divided from us in heart and pen, you had written separately.
>
> “The names of those who did not fear to disparage the message recently sent to you by me ought not to remain hidden, to the shame of the children of iniquity. But I ask: let them say what offended them there. I think the royal admonition disturbed the sons of the kingdom. I shall repeat that same admonition for their confusion—or, what I would prefer, for their correction (Matthew 8):
>
> “‘Since I, who seek to defend the justice of my office in the sight of the whole Church, have been violently expelled, barefoot lamentation would have suited you better than royal rejoicing without a head.’ Without a head, I say—that is, without an abbot, without a prior; again and again I say, without a head. ‘But Abbot Gunther,’ they say, ‘was merely standing by.’ What is this place of defence? How was he standing by? As head, or as tail? He himself does not concede that he stood as tail, and you do not concede that he stood as head. That he was neither of the two is proved both by his usurpation and by your ineffectual resistance.
>
> “‘Since I have been violently expelled.’ Do not those men seem to do violence to reason who, by such words, acknowledge that I inflicted wrong upon the king? If one of two points is conceded, is the other not conceded? Or when music is excluded in mourning, is it not admitted in joy? In this manner, since I was taken away from the sons of the bridegroom, whatever kind of bridegroom I may have been to them, barefoot lamentation would have suited you better than royal rejoicing without a head.
>
> “Why do the literate not heed the letter itself (Ecclesiasticus 22)? Is not to walk barefoot to move a judge to mercy? Thus those rather offended the king who met him with feigned joy and thereby with a double heart. This, I say, could have been for you an honourable occasion—not, as they suppose, for failing to honour the king, but for refraining from rejoicing; this could have been advanced as brotherly compassion for my expulsion. If we explain these words, we make a game for children, though they openly confound those who offend in the foregoing matters.
>
> “Moreover, as you have begun, do not offer a sacrifice of shouting (Psalm 26), namely by abstaining from the office of Mass and performing the canonical hours in silence, though diligently.”

At the end he concluded his admonitions and commands with the following sentence.

## XXXV.

> “EGINO, by God’s grace what he is, to those chosen in Christ, for whose sake I endure all things: that you may think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ (Romans 15).
>
> “Since I have informed your brotherhood, both absent and present, of all that had to be said concerning the dangers now pressing upon us, it remains that we, obedient to Christ, gather ourselves from the face of iniquity into the bosom of mother Church; but that we cut off, by the sentence of just censure, those who apostatize from God and thereby from our obedience, because they trouble the children of God.
>
> “Therefore we command in the word of the Lord that whoever among you recognize themselves as children of the Church shall no longer remain in a place polluted by disobedience, lest they perish when hell swallows them with Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16). But to those who have determined to persist in the obstinacy they have begun against us, we interdict that same place by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 15), lest through them the name of God be blasphemed any longer among the Gentiles (Romans 2).
>
> “For, in a strange way, they strive to make obedience local and conditional, asserting that monks must observe it only within the enclosure of the four walls of the cloister, and only when the bishop is not angry with the abbot. Because they follow the licence of the Sarabaites, they are excluded from the most steadfast order of cenobites. But, to make an end with words of many kinds, we summon to the place appointed by our messenger all bound to us in Christ by the vow of holy obedience; and those who turn back and flee the fellowship of our brotherhood we sever from the unity of the body of the Church by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6).”

## XXXVI.

### Egino Defends Himself

When the Augsburgers accused the abbot of all these things and cried out that he was the destroyer of their place, the same Father defended himself in the following writing:

> “To all the sons of the holy Church of Augsburg, EGINO, by God’s grace, what he is.”

«I know, your blessedness, how I have conducted myself among you up to this point; how I was driven away by force; and how I returned when summoned. I trusted the promises of that summons, especially because they overflowed with Catholic utterances: that I might be permitted to speak among you whatever was just, whatever canonical, whatever necessary alike to your salvation and mine; indeed, that your counsel and aid would not be withheld from me when I spoke. Since then I have said nothing contrary to this, nothing novel, nothing doubtful, for which I ought to be expelled—neither having confessed nor been convicted. I have now departed as an exile: why do you further permit a fugitive to be pursued? My brothers follow me at the call of holy obedience; men of your number, armed against the unarmed, pursue them, maltreat them, and despoil them. O the prudence, O the courage of the people of Augsburg, reduced to such a point that they fear to resist one man trampling upon their sacred rights and do not blush to submit to him. For among you obedience is rendered to the command of that apostate Ratpoto, persecutor of monks: a man who has no standing before God has such power among you that, after he has succeeded in expelling us with his deceitful tongue, he is also able to pursue us with the sword. At last, I beg you, return to your hearts; for if you are touched inwardly, you will see that I have spoken nothing among you but truth, and therefore you will cease persecuting me.»  
[Note: Col. 0857D: “. . . . . I now have no hope whatever that this gap can be repaired, since, so far as I know, no other copy exists. Certain extraneous matter had been inserted at Col. 0858D by another hand later, apparently so that the page should not stand empty. CAN.”] [lacuna]

XXXVII.

Eginon’s Apology.—“To the revered fatherhood and beloved brotherhood—every faithful person of either sex in Christ—EGINO, whose sojourn upon earth has been prolonged (Psalm 119), wishes association with the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

“Since God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God and God in that person (1 John 4), everyone who remains in God—or rather, in whom God remains—is undoubtedly filled with the spirit of love. From the fountain of love flows the stream of compassion. Therefore, overflowing with this wholesome spring, I have thought it necessary briefly to set forth the misfortunes I have suffered, first stating the cause which provoked so many adversities, so that the virtue of compassion may increase through the cause of justice and truth. Although a sinner unworthy of the office of government (1 Corinthians 18), as many of you know, I was serving as abbot of the monastery of Augsburg. How great things God accomplished there in our time—not, I say, through our merits—namely, how he gathered religious men there, and how greatly that same place quickly increased both in virtues and in outward resources, could not remain unknown not only to those nearby and adjoining, but even to those at a distance.

“But because, according to the excellent preacher, heresies must occur, so that those who have been tested may become manifest; and because Satan sought to sift us like wheat (Luke 22), we experienced as a cruel persecutor the bishop of Augsburg, whom we had hoped would be our defender and champion, as though he were the shepherd of the Lord’s flock. Since he had been forbidden by Pope Paschal of blessed memory, because of his long-standing disobedience, from every pontifical function, and condemned by his successor Gelasius II, and likewise by Pope Callixtus II, still living and holy, without hope of recovering that office, we received this command from the Apostolic See: to avoid such a man as something deadly (1 Corinthians 15). Yet, being less than perfect, we did not immediately find strength to carry this out. With Peter, that is, we still feared at the voice of the maidservant of the flesh (John 18); and, acquiescing in things so wicked—or rather, in human wisdom—instead of obeying divine and apostolic commands, we dissembled.

“Finally, when he was attacking in every manner against right and justice, even to the point of rejecting the Catholic pope, receiving Burdinus, ordering Burdinus’s name to be recited in the blessing of the Paschal candle, and polluting the people subject to him with the greeting of so great a heresiarch’s letters, he compelled us too to be contaminated with him in all these matters. At last, so that the bow of the mighty might be overcome (1 Samuel 2), we, hitherto weak, were girded with divine strength and stepped forward. With the apostles, though far their inferiors, we declared: ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5). At this utterance the bishop was stirred to a fury no less than that of the Scribes and Pharisees; immediately he threatened chains, prison, and exile, and never ceased until I and my brothers, who with the Twelve followed Christ (John 6), while others turned back, were driven from the peace of the monastery. Yet this bishop was not satisfied, after innumerable insults and injuries, even with our expulsion, unless his persecution followed us, so far as he was able, to every region of the earth.

“Accordingly, when I approached our archbishop, and likewise a great gathering of Catholic bishops, abbots, and princes, they were all amazed and lamented together at the enormity of the crime laid before them. Therefore, after taking counsel with the wiser men, I was directed to the Roman See, both for our particular necessity and for the common good of the Church. When I undertook that journey, most perilous because of the enemy’s ambushes, I somehow reached Piacenza, taking byways rather than the royal road. There my servant, whom I had raised from childhood, fled by night with all our belongings except the riding horses. I, who had often despaired of completing the journey when I possessed little, now, possessing nothing, put my confidence in the mercy of him who created all things from nothing.

“Why say more? We passed through mountain precipices, through a vast wilderness, through a land of hunger and thirst where no human footprint was found. Yet, as if in reward for such toil, we found the lord Apostolic in the coastal region, namely at the city of Roselle; and he received us, cheerful as he is in countenance. We were brought with him to Rome, to recount, in his own words, the Church’s triumph in our land. For what a concourse there was in that city! What an array of every sex and age! How delightful was the escort of the Roman soldiery, coming out more than three days’ journey to meet him! Caesar, if he had survived, would have looked on in resentment; perhaps Cicero would have been drawn there, when he saw that the trophies of all consuls and emperors were surpassed by the banner of the Cross.

“As the supreme pontiff approached the City, he was welcomed with the praises of boys and infants coming out with branches from every sort of tree. Lest anyone should crush or drive them away, he blessed them with Jesus, saying: ‘Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 19). Then, crowned—as though you would believe the Church possessed a royal priesthood—he was led through the center of the city, its streets everywhere adorned with gold, most precious gems, and cloths. Nor were there lacking, amid the harmonies of Greeks and Latins, the confused applause of Jews, so that the blind people, even unwillingly, might confess that for which they are more severely punished.

“It was scarcely the tenth hour, on the third day before the Nones of June, when the thronging processions, prolonged from morning, began to thin. The same universal Father, received from the Lateran seat into the palace, was conducted there, as is customary, by the legal chant of the judges. From then until the Kalends of July I continually enjoyed the presence of that man of such holiness, with an eagerness that knew no weariness, because desire was always kindled to greater intensity. For a cheerful countenance under the weight of words; discretion in fasts and vigils; and, apart from what lies hidden within (Song of Songs 4), a marvelous effect plainly visible to all who looked upon that Father—the working of one and the same Spirit—all these things were manifest. All praise falls short, since this man, truly apostolic, was proved still more exalted by virtues and signs of miracles. Since all France, Lombardy, Tuscany, and Apulia proclaim these things, let the narrowness of this little sheet pass them over.

“Having received communion in the Lord’s sacrament from his holy hands and, amid frequent kisses, his most abundant blessing, I set out upon my return journey. Intending to cross the sea by ship, I entered the city of Ostia with the bishop of Acqui. Since the ship could not hold Brother Udalscalc, my companion in our labors, because of the multitude of people, he boarded another ship, which was nevertheless to travel with ours. But when the sea was suddenly disturbed, the ships were so scattered that for fourteen days we could neither speak with nor see one another. I began to grieve beyond measure for my lost brother, to grow ill through grief, and was scarcely able to be carried to Pisa. How my brother found me there, and what afterward became of me, let him faithfully relate, and let him commend my soul to your prayers.”

XXXVIII.

Eginon’s Death.—Alas for me! Beloved Father, what shall I do? You leave your son orphaned and fatherless in exile, while you go on to the homeland and to the Lord. I shall set down very few words, because then I rejoiced more in grief than I spoke with my mouth. Therefore, on the fourteenth day, as has been said, after innumerable perils of sea, hunger, and thirst, I too reached Pisa, hoping for the end of my labor and sorrow when I found my lord and Father. But sorrow upon sorrow was heaped upon me, since he was already at the point of death, and no hope of consolation could be found.

Then with what sighs the Father embraced his son, with what tears the son bathed his Father! His death, precious in the sight of the Lord (Psalm 112), bears witness: having received me, who had perished, he immediately prayed that he might be delivered from the present wicked world. Taking leave through me of his brothers and friends, exhorting them to remain in the Church’s obedience unto death, and as if wearied by present things, he was already carried away to those that are to come. For until his last breath no sound issued from his mouth except the voice of psalmody. The psalm he repeatedly recited was: ‘Praise the Lord, O servants; praise the name of the Lord’ (Psalm 115). Its final verse accompanied his departing spirit, foreshadowing by those words the desired ‘Well done’ which he would shortly hear: ‘You who have been faithful in a few things have been set over many’ (Luke 16). Those whom he begot in Christ through the Gospel (1 Corinthians 4), he joyfully receives, as a mother receives her children, worthily into the house of the Lord unto glory.

Thus, with the most devout congregation of the Camaldolese Order standing by, after an inward confession of his sins, after the anointing with most holy oil, strengthened by the Lord’s sacraments, on the Ides of July he exchanged the death of this present age for eternal life. He was buried in the monastery of Blessed Michael, beside the incomparable riches of the Pisans, in the excellent mausoleum of the archbishops, where darkness is unknown, being continually banished by sun or lamp-oil. Therefore let none of the simpler sort be scandalized by events of this kind, apparently accidental and adverse from the human point of view. For Abraham the patriarch was divinely commanded to leave the land of his birth (Genesis 12); Moses and Aaron died outside the promised land (Deuteronomy 34); and the apostles were scattered through all the ends of the earth (Deuteronomy 32), so that by words and examples we too may be taught that our homeland is not on earth but in heaven (Psalm 38).

[Col. 0861]

UDALSCALC’S POEM ON THE JOURNEY AND DEATH OF EGINO, ABBOT OF ST UDALRIC AT AUGSBURG

[Col. 0861C]

Here is the Father’s setting, as he tends  
Toward the rising of the true Sun, and the haven  
That knows no season of decline.

For so distinguished a crown, child,  
You must rejoice with a good mind,  
Yet with the same mind you must also grieve.

For you remain as one bereft  
Of your spiritual father;  
And that from which he is blessed is counted for you as a cause of evil.

Yet there is a pious hope, through which this grief is eased—  
That excellent reality by which every righteous person is blessed:  
There the fatherly bosom restores the father to his child.

Therefore may that heavenly Father join us there.

O pen of one lamenting, why do you wander through divers paths?  
As the grief is one, so employ one voice.

Let an end be given to this utterance of words;  
The Father’s end admonishes us to keep the end in view.  
For though the mind is constrained by varied coverings,

[Col. 0861D]

Yet it often speaks what it is always meditating.

Let this most pitiable event be told under the honor of God,  
So that from it may be seen how great his mercy is.  
For he is shown generous in aid to the wretched:

The son goes into exile with the Father; their only servant accompanies them.

[Col. 0862C]

He was in the guise of a servant, so that [*udas toleratur*: materially uncertain].

For in no respect do they differ in service; the servant resembles his lords.

Now, far from their homeland, the road through the wilderness lies before them.  
There a place is prepared in the thief’s heart for fraud.  
Night arrives; he is made darker still by deceit.  
For he departed after stealing all the goods by which that journey was supported.  
Fortune threatens death.

But the almighty Father aids the despoiled,  
Giving hope that the journey may be completed; nor is there doubt,  
For firm hope proves a great gift to the wretched.

Why delay? The wilderness is entered and at last traversed.  
Yet for eight suns he wanders there in sweat,  
While an obstinate thief and a difficult road must be endured.

Behold the honor of their toil: the holy Pope is staying nearby.

[Col. 0862D]

Then you would have judged men to be winged, so swiftly do they hasten.  
They can scarcely wait until they reach him.  
When found, he receives them kindly, loves them, and honors them.

There is room for this Father’s arrival to be recounted—  
For the manner in which he is established in the chair by Roman law.

[Col. 0863A]

Every age is present, where both sexes gather.  
The voices of clergy and people sing joyfully.  
The road along which he passes is made splendid with every adornment.

Such a triumphal procession is denied you, Caesar;  
At your coming, the glory of the fathers together with the law is put to flight.  
At this man’s arrival the law of justice is renewed.

You wage war with your father-in-law; civil evil prevails.  
Through you there is no peace, while Cato dies of thirst.  
But under this pious Father nation is reconciled to nation,  
And the Church’s condition and rightful authority are restored to their own.

[Col. 0864A]

God performs very many signs upon the sick:  
Through his merit every fever is relieved.  
Since Tuscan, Ligurian, and Apulian attest this,  
Let the present poem pass over more extensive matter.

But let us return to those whom this composition serves.  
They made for the sea in order to avoid the enemy on the road.  
When the ship puts out, the engulfing wave rises.  
The Father is separated from his son by a pitiable fate.  
Who, unless he has suffered it, can reflect upon such a condition of affairs?

[Note: Col. 0863A: “Certain matters appear to be lacking; for here too some extraneous matter was added in the manuscript by another hand, apparently so that the page should not stand empty.”] [lacuna]

[Col. 0863]

THE LIFE OF CHOUNRAD, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE, BY UDALSCALC.

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 429.)

NOTICE

When Udalric I, bishop of Constance, petitioned Pope Callixtus II that his predecessor Chounrad be enrolled among the saints, he received the answer that this could not be done unless Chounrad’s Life were read and approved before the pope in a general council. He therefore employed Udalscalc, a monk of Saints Ulric and Afra at Augsburg, to write the Life. [Note: Col. 0863A: “See below, *History of the Translation of St Chounrad*.”] Udalscalc faithfully accompanied Abbot Eginon, who had been expelled from Augsburg by Bishop Hermann, a supporter of Emperor Henry V’s party; while he was then living in exile as Udalric’s guest [Note: Col. 0863A: “Compare Udalscalc’s book *On the Controversies between Bishop Hermann and Abbot Eginon*, in Canisius’s *Thesaurus*, 2nd ed., vol. III, pt. II, p. 1 ff.; and Sigismund’s *Ecclesiastical Augsburg Chronicle*, bk. II, ch. 2, in Pistorius’s *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 675.”], he fulfilled the task imposed upon him. Relying upon old notes and ancient reports furnished him by Udalric, he compiled the book. [Note: Col. 0863A: “See the Preface.”] When it had been presented to the pope through him and Henry, the papal vicedominus, Callixtus II replied by decree of the council that, if the miracles said to have been worked by God through Chounrad were found true, his memory should henceforth be maintained in writings and readings.

After receiving this favorable reply, the envoys set out homeward, but were captured on the way and imprisoned for some time. There Udalscalc, at the request of his fellow-captives, “sweetly composed” the history of Chounrad. Not long afterward, when released, he brought it, together with Callixtus’s letters, to Bishop Udalric. Once these had been brought, Chounrad’s body was elevated on 26 November 1123. [Note: Col. 0863A: “See *History of the Translation*.”]

The book, composed by Udalscalc nearly one hundred and fifty years after Chounrad’s death and rather meager in content, is now published from the assistance of:

1. A codex of the monastery of Holy Cross in Austria, which I examined in 1821, and which Mr Francis Goldhann of Vienna recently transcribed for our use. It is a parchment manuscript in large folio, of the twelfth century. It contains substantially the same text.

2. The *Chronicle of the Bishopric of Constance* by Jacob Manlius, into which it was incorporated. [Note: Col. 0864A: Pistorii, *Scriptores*, III, 711–717.] From this it was possible to correct several passages and supply one chapter.

3. Concerning the manuscript bearing Udalscalc’s name, which Leibniz mentions among the Vienna books [Note: Col. 0864A: *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, II, Preface, p. 2.], I have discovered nothing. Certainly the manuscript which I myself noted in our *Annals*, following library catalogues [Note: Col. 0864A: II, p. 498 (in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical History*, 111)], does not contain this Life, as our Chimelius, when asked, reported to me. [Note: Col. 0864A: Bethmann saw a copy of the manuscript once found in the monastery of Bodeken among the papers of the Bollandist associates at Brussels, in Royal Manuscript 8953.]

PROLOGUE

[Col. 0865]

[Col. 0865A] To the most holy lord Pope Callixtus, Udalric, servant of the Church of Constance, together with the whole fold of the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, offers the due vows of obedience and service, together with earnest prayer.

[Note: Col. 0865: “D. and venerable” in witness 2.]

We magnify with more fervent thanksgiving the mercy of divine regard, which, under the helm of your fatherhood, consoles our days with many blessings. We rejoice in the peaceful state of affairs and in the new splendor of saints by which diverse churches are illumined. For just as the radiance of the true Sun has penetrated many regions of the world, as it were with so many rays, through the merits of his elect, so, turning also toward our western region, it has flooded all Alamannia in our time with no lesser light through the miracle-signs of Chounrad, bishop of Constance, of happy memory.

Having long and repeatedly appealed by letter to the presence of the Apostolic See for his glory to be canonized, as is the custom of churches, I received this answer as an unalterable judgment: that his Life must be read and approved in a general council, and that suitable witnesses of the signs which are wrought or have been wrought through him must be produced there as well. Thus universal reverence among the faithful may arise from such great benefits of heavenly gifts, and particular envy—which spares not even the dead—may be shut out, when the magicians of Pharaoh are overcome by the finger of God.

Therefore I have taken pains to compile the following little work from the notes of the fathers, containing this man’s most worthy manner of life before God rather than miracles, which are sometimes common to the reprobate and the saints; and I send it to your sublimity for examination. I would rather expose my simpler style to embarrassment than allow a city that ought to be set upon a mountain to lie any longer hidden in the valley of torpor and oblivion. Finally, from innumerable signs by which many nations rejoice at his memory on credible testimony, I have added only a few, lest, just as they give joy to those who see them, so by their abundance they produce weariness in those who hear them.

[Note: Col. 0865 apparatus: “and service” absent in witness 2; “prayers” in 2; “Divine mercy” in 2; “to be consoled” in 2; “let us magnify” in 2; “other” in 2; “regions” in 2; “is absent” in 2; “and” in 2; “be observed” in 2; “their trouble may be overcome” in 2; “before God” in 2; “may generate weariness of themselves” in 2.]

THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0865]

[Col. 0865B] 1. Thus blessed Chounrad, sprung from a noble Alamannic stock, as a shoot bursting forth in paradise more richly adorns a flower, adorned the illustrious line of his birth. The higher birth of the flesh produced him distinguished, but the nobility of the spirit made him more distinguished and more excellent; so that from his very tender years he was wholly transformed into this latter nobility. Heavenly grace accompanied his beginnings with the first principles of virtues; and, in proportion to his age, no small indication of what he was to become was already formed in him.

At last his parents entrusted him to the brethren of the Church of Constance to be instructed in letters. Received into their fellowship by the lot of him whose is our election, he was initiated into Levitical service at the watches of the tabernacle which God has pitched. Nor was the anointing of the Spirit lacking to the heart of its foster-child; it did not allow the labor of the person teaching outwardly to be fruitless, while he more eagerly stored up the seeds of every liberal discipline, which were at times to produce manifold fruit.

[Note: Col. 0865 apparatus: “of paradise” in 2; “noble” in 2; omitted in 2; “more tender” in 1?; “piety” in 1; “was formed” in 2; “minister” in 2; “discipline,” witness 1, with the word *doctrina* deleted.]

2. Having passed through the unstable stage of that age in these studies, he strengthened his mind by progress in firmer understanding and conduct, so greatly that he moderated the heat of corruptible nature by divine fear, and thereby established in his breast a seat for wisdom. For, as if seated upon a higher throne of gravity of character, he wondered, looking back, that he had escaped the precipice of youth with unguarded step. Yet, not presuming upon the innocence preserved up to then, he regulated his life with the observance of stricter frugality.

[Note: Col. 0865 apparatus: “and” in 2; “now” in 2; omitted in 1; “having regulated” in 1?]

3. At the same time the venerable bishop Nothingus governed the Church of Constance (920–934). When he discovered this man’s commendable and honorable conduct, he took him into the work of his ministry, so that, like Joshua, he might be trained to be placed over the people of God, and might someday obtain spiritual leadership as successor to the bishop himself, as to Moses. Diligently attending to public and private affairs of ecclesiastical care, more mature in counsel and more ready in speech, through the grace of him from whose fullness we have all received, he was heard by all with increasingly watchful admiration. In individual cases and with individual persons, he seemed to be the same man to himself but different to others according to the nature of the situation.

Toward the needy and poor, understanding their want to be that from which others’ wealth had removed him, he desired to experience compassion; counting himself more wretched and inferior if he did not, according to his ability, assist everyone. To all the oppressed who then approached the bishop for relief, he proved approachable, an advocate not bought for money, and finally a helper in their necessities. But because a man of such virtue ought to be tested by a worthier exercise, the brethren elected him provost, and thereby provision was made for the common utility of affairs. For in proportion to the honor of the rank he had attained, what he had hitherto done willingly he thereafter did for the good of all through liberality of resources. Above all, he was ignorant of the blindness of ambition, which avarice certainly engenders; but the greater he was, the more he pursued humility, and the more generously he embraced the kindness of love. He was no less held by all to be honorable and lovable, both because of reverence for his office and because of paternal affection. They truly judged that age blessed, in which a man of such example had been divinely given to the world.

[Note: Col. 0867 apparatus: “diverse,” witness 1, where *aliis* is absent; “understanding their poverty” in 2; “we deem ourselves more wretched” absent in 1; “of himself” (*sui*) in 1?; “revelation” in 1?; “a helper in opportunities” in 2; “attained” in 2; witness 1: *voluntate*—*liberalitatem*; “blindnesses” in 2; “the more” in 2; “while” in 2; “wisdom and prudence” in 2; “especially” in 2; omitted in 2; “more brightly the sons consecrated to God” in 2; “watchful” in 2.]

4. Meanwhile, the aforesaid bishop Notingus paid the debt of human nature and died; his body was buried by the holy and venerable Udalric, bishop of Augsburg. This father of admirable life, being guided, in the choice of a bishop for the widowed church, by a heavenly oracle, proclaimed a three-day fast to all clergy and people, declaring that the greater counsels of divine matters must be sought with greater devotion from the Spirit of counsel.

When, on the appointed day, there was a great gathering of both sexes and every age, all eagerly awaited whom the God-filled Father Udalric would first designate as a shepherd worthy of the Lord’s flock. Instructed by the Spirit, he exhorted Chounrad to undertake this good work, not merely as blameless, but perfect in every quality by which the Apostle describes a bishop. Without delay, this cry was on everyone’s lips: “According to the general wish, God has given us a bishop!” Thus Constance raised her Chounrad to the episcopal chair, though he resisted and cried that he was unworthy, and lifted her chosen one up to heaven with praises.

The clergy rejoiced that they had merited such a pontiff, able to govern them by wisdom and foresight: the one particularly concerns that order, and the other is especially needed by it. For although the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light, their eye is greatly darkened with respect to that wisdom which is from above; its rays illuminate those consecrated to God more brightly as their own. Their purer sight must also be guarded by the diligent care of one who presides, lest it be disturbed by some cloud of the dark age. For purple cannot endure rain—the purple with which the golden altar of the tabernacle of the covenant is wrapped—whereas a storm of wind and rain is harmlessly received by coverings of haircloth.

[Note: Col. 0867 apparatus: “bishop” in 2; “grace” in 1?; *Hec* (“these things”) in 1?; “greater” in 2; “then” in 2; omitted in 2; “cleric” in 1?; “therefore” in 2; “prelate” in 2; “and wisdom” in 2; “especially” in 2; omitted in 2; “more brightly the sons consecrated to God” in 2; “watchful” in 2; “which” in 1.]

5. But to return the pen to the new bishop: the people rejoice in so exceptional a shepherd, by whose voice they are continually invited to the most abundant pastures of heavenly blessedness, and whose life in no way differs from sound teaching. For human beings of unlearned disposition are so constituted that, if a preacher does not act in accordance with the doctrine he teaches, they do not even suspect that what he says is true. But this teacher of truth, this doer of justice, was celebrated in popular praise by the commendation of his deeds, and thereby won no few souls for God.

The poor confess that they have truly found a father in him. Their misery was cooled as in a furnace during his days; their nakedness and hunger were continually relieved by the generosity of this hospitable man. He also built them a house in the city itself, in which he established that twelve poor persons, besides others arriving at every hour, should continually be fed at the holy number of the Church’s princes. Finally, nobles and powerful persons of the world themselves learned from his example to humble themselves beneath the mighty hand of God. There was now no condition of mortals, of either sex, that was not instructed by his example or teaching, or refreshed by his beneficence.

[Note: Col. 0867 apparatus: witness 2 reads: “as a little child returns to its mother’s bosom, the people rejoice in the service of the new bishop”; “invited to the pastures of eternal life” in 2; “his deeds do not differ from salutary teaching” in 2; omitted in 2; “true things . . . which” in 2; “truthful teacher” in 2; “speaker” in 2; “was winning” in 2; “received” in 2; “where the sacred number of the Church’s leaders…” in 1; “besides arrivals” in 2; *Dei* in 2; “example or” absent in 2; “or” in 2.]

6. Moreover, he enriched the principal church of the Mother of God with a double treasure: abundant relics of saints gathered from every quarter, and brilliant works of metal in gold and precious gems. He also constructed three basilicas, one outside the city wall and two within, and endowed them with abundant estates. In the one founded in honor of Blessed Maurice, he adorned all around with marvelous goldsmith’s work a representation of the Lord’s tomb, modeled on the Jerusalem tomb; there also he established twelve clerics with assigned stipends.

He increased the number of brethren in the greater church and granted them from his own resources a spacious and notable allod, lest, if those serving as soldiers for God should suffer too grievously from lack of food or clothing, the poison of serpents should creep into them—as into those murmuring in the wilderness—a poison driven away only by contemplation of the Lord’s Passion. Although he knew that those who fear God lack nothing, since they either abound in goods or in the patience alone by which they overcome scarcity, he nevertheless took every possible precaution lest even the least of Jesus’ little ones should stumble through scandal or want. For, full of eyes before and behind, he provided for present and future things alike; and there was no pursuit of ecclesiastical tradition or religion from which the greatness of labor could frighten his soul, fervent in God.

[Note: Col. 0867–0869 apparatus: “namely” in 2; “from every side” in 2; “and endowed them with abundant dowry” in 2; *illa* (“those”) in 2; “that” in 2; omitted in 2; witness 2: “a splendid memorial of the Lord’s tomb, fashioned from precious work”; “serpentine” in 2; omitted in 2; “or” in 1; “or” in 1; “you add” in 1?; “fervent” uncertain; witness 2: “his promise and eyes contemplated.”]

7. Three times he risked the dangers of the sea, so that he might as often see Jerusalem, though earthly. He did not consider it a small thing to behold with the eyes of the flesh the land of promise, where, passing beyond the figures of the patriarchs and the utterances of the prophets, he might contemplate with the eyes of faith God made man, who opened the seven seals of assumed humanity which they had foretold.

[Note: Col. 0869 apparatus: “the promise and behold with the eyes” in 2; “and man” in 2; “his own” in 2.]

8. He enjoyed the friendship of the aforementioned Father Udalric, as David did that of Samuel, and it was exercised through frequent mutual visits. Nor was this unfitting; for this bishop was chosen by a bishop in the same Spirit in which there a king was anointed by a prophet. In the territory of Constance is a castle called Laufen from the character of its site. [Note: Col. 0869D: “Laufen below Schaffhausen.”] While the two were staying there together, they watched one day the vast waters of the Rhine, plunging there as though into an abyss and boiling up again in a terrifying spectacle. They saw two birds circling in unceasing flight around rocks projecting from the middle of the river. As the waters’ swirling force repeatedly increased, the birds began again and again to be hurled into the torrent; then they emerged once more, presenting a pitiable sight to those watching.

The gaze of the saints was not long frustrated by this unexplained occurrence. Through the Spirit they were taught that souls not yet fully purified were being tormented in that manner under the appearance of birds. They therefore hastened to the most renowned aid of the heavenly table; and Udalric, as the first guest, was obliged to approach first, to offer the sacrifice of life. When this had been divinely received, only one little bird appeared. Then the master of the house, Chounrad, offered the victim of salvation, and the other soul too was freed in a like manner of release.

[Note: Col. 0869 apparatus: “deservedly” in 2; “indeed” in 2; witness 2: “this bishop is chosen by a bishop in the same Spirit in which there a king is anointed by a prophet”; “exit” in 1; “Lauffen” in 2; omitted in 2; “terrible” in 2; “projecting from the river and circling in unceasing flight” in 2; witness 2: “when the whirlpool of waters arose, they were sometimes hurled into it”; “the unusual sight did not long frustrate the holy men” in 2; “not yet almost fully purified” in 1; “not yet wholly purified” in 2; “the senior Udalric” in 2; “received” in 2; “Chounrad added” in 2; “offered” in 2.]

9. Furthermore, that the spirit of prophecy was not lacking to most blessed Chounrad may be inferred from what follows. On one occasion he went out of the house in which he was staying, intending to take counsel with a few persons concerning some business which had to be settled. Gebehard, a man of excellent disposition and the third bishop after him, sat down on Chounrad’s seat, left in the middle, not in earnest. When the Father returned, Gebehard was found sitting there and heard these words, not without embarrassment:

“Gebehard, you have seized my seat too soon; before the time, you have invaded the bishop’s place. The one who will succeed me is he who will sit before you in this chair.”

How true this was, the event proved. When the man of God, blessed Chounrad, had been taken from present things, a certain Gamenold was received upon the vacant throne. When he too died before the completion of five years, Constance obtained the said Gebehard as its shepherd—truly heir in all respects to the sanctity and character of his predecessor Chounrad.

[Note: Col. 0869 apparatus: “prophecy” in 1; “which then perhaps had to be settled” uncertain; “sat” in 2; “from” in 2; “blessed Chounrad” absent in 2; “Gemenold” in 1.]

10.
