The constraints of an epistle do not at all permit us to recount any of his virtues, especially since they are believed to have been so great that the subject itself seems impatient of brevity in his praise. At last, as my pen hastens toward the passing of Father Conrad, let one deed be set down from among the many works that could be related in honour of God and of His bishop—one judged not unworthy of narration both for imitation and for admiration. For the day of Paschal rejoicing arrived, on which this man offered to God the Father, amid the celebration of the Masses, the Lamb by whose blood both the lintel of our intention and the doorposts of body and soul are cleansed. Having therefore received the sacrament of the Lord’s body, he came to partake also of His blood. As customary, the chalice was covered by the paten; a spider was seen to have fallen into the liquid of life. The creature of death threatened destruction to the outward man; but meanwhile he was quickened by the cup of immortality. What did the minister of the heavenly banquet do? Armed with the utmost faith, he considered nothing in this matter mortal, nothing deadly; more eagerly he consumed both what belonged to the sacrament and what belonged to destruction, not forgetting that the venom of the ancient serpent had been nullified by the antidote of the Lord’s Passion. You might have seen the fellow-ministers of this ministry turn pale and indicate to those standing around the danger of death which, as they supposed, threatened the bishop. All alike were grieved and afraid; the day of rejoicing was changed into mourning. Yet, after the distribution of Communion had been completed, beyond everyone’s expectation he approached the table to refresh limbs worn down by fasting, but sat for some time without tasting food. More privately, he was asked what he was about to do. “I am waiting,” he said, “for a guest who is coming shortly.” Then, resting his head upon the table, he offered his open mouth to receive the spider’s deadly threat; yet the spider could neither die within the man of God nor bring death upon him. How great then was the rejoicing of the guests, how great the admiration aroused by the man’s steadfastness—the reader should rather conceive it in his mind than demand that it be expressed in words.

11. Moreover, blessed Conrad, full of days, completed his course and kept the faith, and thereafter was to receive the crown of righteousness laid up for him by the Lord, the righteous Judge. He passed from the darkness of this exile on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 976, and in the forty-second year of his episcopate: having, that is, happily traversed the most vast wilderness of the world in the progress of virtues, as though under this number of encampments. When his spirit had therefore been taken up to the heavenly homeland, his holy body was buried with every reverence before the church of Saint Maurice the martyr, which he himself built and in which, as we have already said, he adorned the Lord’s Sepulchre with wonderful workmanship.

12. The notable miracles of the blessed bishop Conrad, which we believe to have been innumerable even in this life, are little known in our own times through the negligence of writers. Accordingly, we have omitted to commit to writing for posterity those things which we learned on less credible testimony; especially since his merits do not need the testimony of antiquity, being continually manifested by new instances of every sort of healing at his tomb.

13. For, to mention certain of these things, we saw there two persons blind from birth enlightened at different times; and the promises of Truth were fulfilled: “He who believes in me will himself also do the works that I do” (Job 14:12). For Christ gave sight to a man blind from birth; the Pharisees, slandering him, said that this could not be done under Moses, but Conrad can do it through Jesus Christ and will be able to do so.

14. It is reported that a certain man, deprived of the use of both feet for four years, spent six months going about near the memorial of this man, supported by crutches, and continued night and day in frequent prayers to obtain health. There, while on one day he was leaning upon his wooden supports and attending more earnestly than usual to his customary prayer, sudden darkness dulled his sight, his hands grew numb, his strength failed, and, the crutches slipping away, the man fell. Those standing near ran up, eager to raise the fallen man; and, as he remained without voice or movement, they believed him dead. Yet, intending to perform his funeral rites, they lifted the body; and behold, they saw the half-dead man slowly open his eyes and, more joyfully, saw him stretch out legs that had until then been bent. Thus the man was wholly restored in an instant, increasing both praise to God and faith among mortals.

15. Although signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers, believers too are sometimes stirred by the grace of healings, that they may grow in faith and advance in hope of eternity and in the fervour of charity. A certain boy, weakened by a long bodily affliction, crawled on hands and feet, unlike a human being walking. Touched by the report of the blessed man’s benefits, he earnestly begged his father to take him to Constance. His father, rejoicing in his son’s faith, agreed to the request. He was accordingly carried by a small boat to the desired place, received in the hold of the vessel, and laid down before the bishop’s tomb like an immovable object. There, after an offering had been made, he was brought out so that those present might pity his wretched condition. You might have seen the man crawl like a quadruped; and, because he was hindered from entering the sanctuary by the threshold or the edging of the steps, he was forced to stretch out his twisted knees. Climbing with such effort, he reached the altar of the Mother of God. There, intending to offer a small gift, he first began to cling to it and then to reach upward with his hands, until he completed his vows. Thus in this manner the creature that had remained prone stood upright, and the father received back an intact son from one who had been a misshapen man. One might think that the Mother of the Lord had granted this, if the simpler faith of the healed man accorded with that healing. But that Conrad could accomplish it through her and with her, no one doubts; and therefore what one in need obtained by hope, and the other by actual deed, is not inappropriately ascribed to both.

16. We saw a woman whose buttocks had been drawn up toward the soles of her feet, so that she crawled about the tomb of the often-mentioned father, and who for several days begged his aid with all her strength. When her former manner of walking had been restored, she was for many years there a testimony to the cure she had received.

17. Another woman, worn down by a ten-year illness, came to the point that pus from ulcers broke out dangerously both from her left side and from her neck. At last that dreadful discharge dried up somewhat, but her arm and hand on that side remained wasted away. Finally, she repeatedly saw in dreams that she was standing at the memorial of the blessed man and departing thence healed. On waking, she was sorrowful indeed at this imaginary healing, but was comforted by a certain more hidden hope. In that hope, when she entered the city with companions and others whom the festival of that time had drawn there, and her companions hurried toward the church, shame at her nakedness kept her alone at the lodging. O wonderful, O astounding judgments of the Creator! Many indeed are ignorant and abound in riches, are naked of righteousness, and walk clothed in gems and purple; but this poor woman, afflicted by the harshest torments, hid herself more modestly with naked Adam—except that he mourned his expulsion from paradise, while she mourned her exclusion from the church; yet both were subject to death and therefore to the confusion of shame. Thus this little woman, kept from public view by poverty, was doubly miserable, tortured both by the pain of frustrated hope and by that of destitution; and with copious streams of tears she moved several persons who knew her to compassionate pity. Garments were therefore contributed by popular generosity, and she was clothed and led amid a great crowd to him who had hitherto appeared to her in visions. Resting her withered hand upon his sarcophagus, she offered, with full faith, a sacrifice of her misery. Nor was her supplication long delayed: her hand, together with her arm, was granted life again and withdrew with movement.

18. Likewise, a girl accompanied the countless crowd flocking to this place; her fingers were twisted into the palm, and she had suffered from her mother’s womb. When she was immediately healed, whether from playfulness or simplicity, she left while concealing the fact. At once she was seized by her former disability; maimed, she was in danger through excessive bewilderment. Yet she returned more quickly, confessed what she had concealed, and, to the amazement of all, received again the health she had lost.

19. A certain Frenchman from Poitou, lame for twelve years, came to the city of Constance as an aged traveller. As is usual, he was not supported in place of one foot by a wooden peg; rather, he was borne on three supports, with crutches chafing his armpits. For his shin and foot had withered and been reduced almost to the thinness of a reed; all the harmful fluid had gathered in his knee, and therefore the knee had swollen to enormous size. He remained in the city for six months and, seeing such great benefits of healing, was encouraged to hope for recovered health. He frequented the church and humbly prayed that the holy father might have mercy upon him, one who had long endured pain and who had come from far away. Meanwhile the most holy night of Pentecost arrived, during which he devoutly kept vigil near the tomb. The time came for the Matins vigil, and limbs long since dead began to be tortured by a new agony, so that he was afflicted more by the sudden pain than by loss of his ability to walk. Soon he lost consciousness, and even speech was taken from him. The hour for singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—was at hand, and the man recovered his strength together with his natural gait. Therefore God was celebrated with suppliant praise, while the Paraclete Spirit consoled all alike by His own feast and by the man’s deliverance.

20. A certain boy enrolled among the clergy, but disabled by premature paralysis, was brought by his parents to this patron. Because they were of no low birth, many persons gathered, sympathizing with the affliction both of the boy and of his parents. Surrounded therefore by no small crowd, they placed their disabled child before the memorial of the man of God and cast themselves supplicatingly upon the ground for him. What more need I delay? Their faith was regarded from on high; the sick boy was raised by Conrad’s merits; the supreme bishop was honoured in the minister of the more perfect tabernacle; and God, wonderful in His saints, was proclaimed.

21. In a certain monastery of nuns, two virgins suffered from different painful illnesses. One, unable to retain food because of continual vomiting for eight months, was despaired of; the other, prostrated by most severe paralysis, was in danger. Having learned of the renowned virtues of this father, they were drawn by devout hope from the very bolts of the cloister; but shame at their illness and physical weakness kept them from public view. They therefore waited for night to satisfy this uncertainty; placed in a boat, they reached the city in the first watch—for they did not live far away. Admitted and placed as if before the bishop’s very feet, they prostrated themselves in fullest faith; those keeping vigil poured forth prayers with tears for the long-hoped-for healing. In that same place there is still preserved, with due veneration, a wooden cup of the aforementioned man. When they had eagerly tasted a little water from it, a certain heavenly power accompanied the liquid and wrought a perfect cure in them. Voices of praise rose on every side toward heaven; for the virgins, whom the clergy and people of the city had accompanied with rejoicing, were received unharmed by their sisters.

22. We also saw another paralysed from infancy and healed there when already of mature age. Forgetful of the grace she had received, she wandered about too boldly; and, having lost her virginity, she became pregnant by a certain professed cleric. She therefore conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity, because she immediately put on again the disgrace of her former disability. The wretched woman was compelled to repentance, revisited the mercy of Father Conrad, and again obtained, through him, pardon together with healing. Yet afterward she was by no means wholly restored, so that her weakened limbs might lament the lost integrity of her violated mind.

23. Now this eminent man, drawn by fame, is frequented not only at the place where he rests by those who are ill, but his aid is also invoked and entreated in every distress throughout all lands. Thus a certain young man, wishing one evening to cross the river Thuria at some uncultivated ford, suddenly became entangled in its muddy bottom and in roots of trees heaped together by the water. A stronger current drove him onward; and, because he found no place to resist or turn aside while caught fast, he spread both feet apart in order to swim. His hands struck through the water, but, with his feet immovable, the force of the water and the brushwood submerged his head. Those guarding on the bank the clothes which he had laid aside while naked were overcome with alarm and summoned the young man’s parents with loud cries. The grievous event was reported in broken speech and sobs by his two sisters—for they had accompanied their drowned brother. The place of danger was shown; people ran about and searched, but did not find him. The entire village, struck by the lamentations of those crying aloud, rushed together; and because the missing man did not appear, they worked with nets, if only to recover his body for burial. The darkness of night was now approaching, bringing an end to the search and taking away hope of finding him. Therefore, by the common prayer of all, the man was entrusted in a special manner to the patronage of blessed Conrad, whether in the body or outside the body; and thus they returned to their sorrowful homes.

When a third part of the first night-watch had passed, behold: a heavier wave, as though angered at a barrier, gathered itself into a whirlpool near the opposite bank, and, breaking forth in this winding rush, carried him across to the shore opposite through the waters. Made of earth, he marvelled at dry land as though it were foreign to him; nor did he regard the water, contrary to nature as it seemed—for it had not been able to extinguish him—as hostile, since both elements serve the Creator alike, whether for life or for death. Moreover, pondering the reversal of things and wondering why he suffered this darkness when he had entered the waters in broad daylight, he judged a very long delay of destruction, with the order reversed, to have been very brief; for conversely everything pleasant seems short and everything dangerous long. At last, coming back to himself, he returned home, not yet mindful of his nakedness. But once recognized as their son, he was received in his parents’ astonished embraces. The next day dawned, and, like one risen from the lower world, he was surrounded by a rushing crowd as a messenger from another age, questioned about what had happened to him and how he had escaped. Thus every other explanation of his deliverance, after no slight inquiry, remained unknown, except that which was proved most true by the unanimous faith of all: namely, that he had been delivered by the merits of him to whose special protection he had been entrusted when deprived of human help.

Editorial and textual notes on §§10–23: §10: Witness 1 lacks chapter 10; witness 2 reads *laetitia* (“rejoicing”) for *laetitiae*; the reading *celebrationem* (“celebration”) is queried. §11: Witness 2 lacks “blessed Conrad”; it reads, in abbreviated form, that he “received from God … the crown of righteousness laid up for him,” followed by “He passed [away]”; it also lacks “of his [episcopate]” and reads *scilicet* (“namely”) for *videlicet*. Witness 2 reads *excursa* (“traversed”) for *transcursa*, and lacks the words from “When his spirit” through “adorned.” §12: Witness 2 reads: “whose signs or miracles, by which we believe that he shone more abundantly in this life”; it reads *relatione* (“report”) for *attestatione* (“testimony”), *noluimus* (“we did not wish”) for *omisimus* (“we omitted”), lacks “his,” and reads *ejus* (“his”) for *illius* (“that man’s”). §13: Witness 2 lacks “Conrad”; its reading is “through Jesus Christ,” whereas the text has “through Jesus”; note 119 likewise gives *Christum* (“Christ”) in witness 2. §14: Witness 2 reads *ubi* (“where”) for *ibi* (“there”); witness 1 reads *solito innixus* (“leaning as usual”; remaining abbreviated words uncertain); witness 2 reads *occurrunt* (“they run up”) for *accurrunt* (“they ran up”), and *sed* (“but”) for *et* (“and”). §15: Witness 2 reads *enim* (“for”) for *autem* (“however”), and *non tamen* (“not, however”) for *nonnumquam* (“sometimes”); it reads *ac* (“and”) for *et*, *attractus* (“drawn”) for *attactus* (“touched”), and *supplicat enixius* (“he begs most earnestly”) for *supplicavit innixius* (“he earnestly begged”). Witness 2 reads *unde* (“whence”) for *inde* (“thereupon”); witness 1 reads *sanitati* (“with the healing”) for *sanati* (“of the healed man”) and *commodaret* (“would grant/favour”) for *concordaret* (“would accord”). Witness 2 reads *ac per* (“and through”) for *at pro* (“but for”). §16: Witness 2 reads *mulierem quandam* (“a certain woman”). §17: Witness 1 reads *exsicatur* and witness 2 *siccatur* (“dries up”) for *exsiccatur*; witness 2 reads *reman et* (“remains”) for *manet* (“remains”), though not all its readings have been reported. It reads *sociisque* (“and with companions”) for *sociis* (“with companions”), *cum* (“when/although”) for *enim* (“for”), and *dirissimis* (“most dreadful”) for *durissimis* (“harshest”). Witness 1 perhaps reads *quidem*; it reads *gemina* (“twofold”) for *gemino* (“twofold”), and witnesses 1 and 2 read *ita* (“thus”) for *vehementia* (“generosity”). Witness 1 reads *dexteram fulciente manu* (“supporting [herself] with her right hand”) for *aridam dextera fulciente … manum* (“supporting her withered hand with her right hand”). §18: Witness 1 perhaps reads *uoluam*, apparently for *volam* (“palm”). §19: Witness 2 reads *claudus Constantia* (“lame [at] Constance”) for *claudus … Constantiam*; it lacks the passage from “but” through “was borne.” It reads *salutis* (“salvation/health”) for *sanitatis* (“health”). Its reported variant spans read *multum habentis* (“having [pain] for a long time”) and *venientis* (“coming”); witness 1 perhaps reads *amittit* (“loses”) for *amittitur* (“is lost”). Witness 2 lacks “to God.” §20: Witness 2 reads *geniti* (“the child/offspring”) for *genitorum* (“the parents”), and *amorer* (“shall I delay?”) for *amplius morer* (“need I delay further?”). §21: Witness 1 reads *duo* (“two,” masculine) for *duae* (“two,” feminine). Witness 2 reads, across the paired clauses, *desperatur … periclitatur* (“is despaired of … is in danger”); it also reads *coram positi, vera fide* (“placed before [him], in true faith”) for *velut coram vestigiis positae, fide plenissima* (“placed as if before his feet, in fullest faith”). §22: Witness 1 reads *petite* (an uncertain form) for *potitae* (“having obtained”); it perhaps reads *precum* (“of prayers”) for *per eum* (“through him”), and *implorent* (“may implore”) for *deplorent* (“may lament”). §23: Witness 2 reads *impretatur* (“is entreated”) for *imprecatur* (“is invoked”); witness 1 reads *unde* (“whence/by which”) for *unda* (“water”), while witness 2 lacks “with both feet.” Witness 1 reads *quis* (“who”) for *quas* (“which”), and *hec* (“these”) for *hae* (“these [women]”). Witness 1 reads *aqua se collegit* (“the water gathered itself”) for *animal collegit* (“gathered the living being”); it lacks *aridam* (“dry [land]”). Witness 2 reads *genitoribus stupentibus excipitur* (“he is received by his astonished parents”) for the text’s “he is received in the embraces of his parents”; and *exundanti* (“overflowing”) for *concordanti* (“agreeing, unanimous”).

ANNO DOMINI 1134

MUNIO, BISHOP OF MONDOÑEDO; HUGH, BISHOP OF PORTO IN GALICIA; AND GERARD, PRIEST

[Col. 0875]

NOTICE

(Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, vol. II, p. 19)

[Col. 0875B] Among the distinguished monuments of our ancient national history, the *History of the Church of Compostela* has always occupied a particularly eminent place. Its authors were Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo, and Hugh, bishop of the see of Porto in Galicia, together with the priest Gerard. Munio—otherwise Martin (a name identical in meaning with Nunnus or Nonnius, commonly among us Nuno, as the defenders of our national origins observe [Note: (1) Mariana, book XVI, chapter 6; Colmenares, *History of Segovia*, p. 282])—was made bishop of Mondoñedo from being treasurer of the Church of Compostela. He is said to have been chaplain and secretary to King Alfonso VII, surnamed the Emperor, on the evidence of an instrument to which he subscribed thus: “Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo and royal chaplain, recorded [this].” This was in the year 1126 [Note: (2) Aegidius González Dávila, *Theatre of the Church of Mondoñedo*, p. 421.]. He also took part in the royal expedition against the Saracens undertaken about 1130. Prudentius Sandoval observed in his *History of King Alfonso VII* that Munio was among the bishops who participated, as was customary [Note: (3) Fol. 146, p. 2], though under the title “bishop of Vallobricense,” which Sandoval says is the same as bishop of Mondoñedo. For the place where the city was built was indeed Vallibriense [Note: (4) Dávila, in the place just cited, pp. 407 and 412; Yepes, *History of the Order of Saint Benedict*, cent. 1], now called Valdeabria. No one here calls him Munio Alphonsius [Note: (5) Pellizer, in the *Memorial de los Saavedras*; Aegidius González, *Theatre of the Church of Compostela*, chapter 9, p. 44; Zurita, book I, chapter 39].

Hugh, likewise bishop of Porto, was French by nationality, it is believed, both from his own name and from that of a certain William, who, during the days when Hugh held this see, subscribed to a document as the bishop’s brother. Rodrigo da Cunha informs us about him in his history of the bishops of Porto. For the ancient town of Portucale, mentioned by Hydatius [Note: (6) In the *Chronicle*, under the reign of Marcian] and in Dulcidius’s poem concerning the bishops of his own time, is the same as the Portuguese Portus or Porto, over which the aforesaid Hugh presided. This is also that Hugh of Porto whom the fabricators of this century, some years ago, invented as author of a letter written to Maurice, archbishop of Braga [Note: (7) See Bivarius, in the commentary on Dexter’s *Chronicle*, among the encomia, p. 9], so that they might retail as certain, concerning the preaching of the Apostle James and the vicariate of Peter of Rates throughout Spain, whatever had come into their heads.

Gerard, himself also a Frenchman, canon of the Church of Compostela and parish priest of the sacred church of Saint Anastasia, supplied the completion of the work. He was a familiar of Diego Gelmírez, archbishop of Compostela, that greatest man of his age. In the prologue to the part which he undertook to write, addressed to Bishop Diego himself—at whose command and under whose auspices the whole work was truly begun and completed—Gerard did not wish posterity to remain ignorant to which authors it ought to attribute the work. “Obeying the exhortation of your holiness,” he says, “most reverend Father Diego the Second, bishop of Saint James, we have endeavoured to compose in part the sequence of the preceding book. For the earlier portions of that book were written by Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo, and Hugh, bishop of Portugal, men prudent and venerable indeed.”

[Note: (8) Since this Diego Gelmírez was the first bishop of Compostela, the author therefore calls him “the Second,” because shortly before this time another Diego, surnamed Peláez, had presided over the Church of Iria, for which Compostela was substituted. Diego, first of that name and surnamed Peláez, presided over the Church of Iria from 1070 to 1088. In that year, as is stated in the *Historia Compostellana* (book I, chapter 2, at the end), he was seized by Lord King Alfonso [VI] of Castile, on account of his deserts, and remained in chains for fifteen years. For the rest of his deeds see the *Historia Compostellana*, edited by the distinguished Flórez, vol. XX, and, more systematically, the same author, vol. XIX, beginning at p. 201.]

[Note: (9) He styled himself bishop “of James,” not “of Compostela,” in the same manner in a dedication at the monastery of Cluny: Dalmatius, predecessor of this Diego. See Aegidius González, *Theatre of the Church of Compostela*, p. 42.]

The quoted words of Gerard were copied from a manuscript codex of this history by the aforementioned Rodrigo da Cunha. João Vaseu also reported the same words, from another copy in the College of Saint Saviour of Oviedo at Salamanca, concerning these three authors [Note: (10) In the *Chronicle of Spain*, chapter 4, no. 10]. Prudentius Sandoval, however, did not know them, when he conjectured that Alonus—he should have said Alon—“the grammarian,” whom he says is mentioned in the work, was its author [Note: (11) In the *History of Alfonso VI*, fol. 105]. We know that another copy of the work is preserved in the library of the Church of Toledo. It contains, as Vaseu says, the beginnings, fortunes, and growth of the Church of Compostela; and he says that he found in it very many things worthy of notice, which he intended to place in their proper locations. See concerning it Morales, book IX, chapter 7 [Note: (12) Fol. 232, p. 2, and fol. 241, p. 1]; Sandoval, in the *History of King Alfonso VII* [Note: (13) Fols. 136 and 144]; and Ramírez, on the pseudo-chronicle of Liutprand [Note: (14) P. 453, Antwerp edition]. The last teaches that it consists of three parts, of which the first was by the two bishops and the second and third by Gerard.

Are these perhaps the same as the Compostelan Annals which Morales uses more than once [Note: (15) Book IX, chapter 7, fol. 241; and book XV, chapter 19, at the end]? I scarcely think so. For he elsewhere cites in precisely the same words the Annals of the Church of Compostela which are read at the beginning of its book of privileges—the *Tumbos*, as they call them. We believe that he means certain shorter annals, called “Compostelan” because they had been found by him in a book of that church [Note: (16) The *Shorter Compostelan Annals* were, I believe, first published by the Benedictine monk Francisco Berganza, vol. II of *Antiquities of Spain*, Madrid, 1721, from a recent copy belonging to the Benedictine monastery of Saint Martin at Madrid; soon afterward by the distinguished Flórez, vol. XXIII, beginning at p. 317, from the Compostelan manuscript commonly called the *Tumbo Negro*], rather than the *History of the Church of Compostela*, which Morales was accustomed to call by its proper name. He seems rather to mean this history when, in book XVII, chapter 20, he refers to the earlier history of the archbishops of Compostela.

We have also read that a certain handwritten history of the Church of Iria in the vernacular circulated [Note: (17) Sandoval, *Observations on the Bishops*, p. 219; Pellizer, on the *Chronicle of Dulcidius*, fol. 30; Tamayo, *Spanish Martyrology*, March, pp. 38–39]. But it has nothing to do with the History of Compostela of which we speak, although it sets forth the Irian origins from which Compostela was derived. This ancient and most precious historical monument is still almost hidden, having formerly been seen by few; nevertheless, those few say that they extracted from it for their own collections whatever was most worthy of observation and remembrance—namely Vaseu, Morales, Sandoval, Juan Tamayo, and others. We said “almost hidden,” because Don José Pellizer, royal historian, informed us that this history had already been printed in a petitionary booklet, or *memorial*, as we call it, prepared for the litigation concerning the Vow of Saint James—that is, payment to the Church of Saint James at Compostela of the portion said formerly to have been promised throughout all Spain by vow [Note: (18) In the work entitled *Trophy of the Truth of History*, fol. 34]. He added that he possessed a copy written in the hand of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo himself.

But our friend was mistaken if, speaking of the *Historia Compostellana* under discussion, he asserted that it had been printed in the aforementioned memorial, rather than the *History of the Church of Iria*, which the author of the memorial published. Nor should it be omitted that this *Historia Compostellana* was once in the Olivares Library, now, we believe, in the gardens of the Marquis del Carpio at Madrid. Yet the manuscript catalogue which we possess misnames it as follows: “Chronicle of Spain by Archbishop Don Gil Almeírez,” with this marginal note: “It is at Salamanca in the College of Saint Saviour.” [Note: (19) In the catalogues of the library of the Count-Duke of Olivares, compiled in 1625 by Brother Lucas de Alaejos, a monk of El Escorial, and written in his own hand—we possess the autograph copies—in two folio volumes under the letters C. M. S., the first volume, p. 170, reads: “Chronicle of Aegidius Ramírez, archbishop of Compostela, folio C. 4.” A little below, at p. 171: “History of Compostela, author unknown: from the year 1327, an old note in folio, C. 2”; but in both places there is absent: “It is at Salamanca,” etc. Likewise, in the same volume, in the index of subjects under “Spain,” p. 143: “Chronicle of James Gil Ramírez” [for Gelmiride or Gelmírez], “archbishop of Santiago: concerning things which happened in ancient times. At the end it contains the wars of the archbishop of Urgel” [for Berenguer], manuscript folio, Latin C. 4. The same *History of Compostela* of Diego Gelmírez—or Gelmírez, as Spaniards pronounce patronymic surnames—written by the triumvirs Munio, Hugh, and Gerard, still exists at Salamanca in the library of the College of Saint Saviour of Oviedo. We handled it often up to the year 1746 and copied a considerable part of it.]

“At the end are the wars of Don Fray Berenguel. [Col. 0878C] It belongs to the archive of the Church of Santiago.”

HISTORY OF COMPOSTELA, OR OF THE DEEDS OF LORD DIEGO GELMÍREZ, FIRST ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA, in which many matters previously unknown concerning supreme pontiffs, cardinals, bishops, councils, kings, and illustrious men—especially from the year 1100 to 1139—are committed to memory; EDITED BY THE REVEREND FATHER, MASTER AND DOCTOR, BROTHER HENRIQUE FLÓREZ, OF THE ORDER OF THE HERMIT FRIARS OF SAINT FATHER AUGUSTINE. (*España Sagrada*, vol. XX. Madrid, 1791.)

[Col. 0879]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE CONCERNING THE HISTORY OF COMPOSTELA AND ITS AUTHORS

[Col. 0879A] 1. One cannot recall without sorrow so many and such illustrious ancient Spanish men who, having written works worthy to be preserved in cedar, have not to this day found a benevolent patron to bring them to light. One of these is the *Historia Compostellana*. Passing through the hands of some persons, they contented themselves with making known that they possessed it; and after six hundred years it still remains closely shut away in archives. Those whose office it might have been to render this service to the public perhaps have not done so because of some private consideration. But anyone who treats of the bishops of Compostela, including the last bishop, who was the first archbishop of Santiago, if he is to offer proofs for the deeds he recounts—as he must, if he wishes to establish their authority—cannot avoid putting the *Historia Compostellana* first; for it alone is like the text for what is related concerning the bishops of Santiago. This makes publication of the work indispensable; and since it is now appearing publicly for the first time, it is fitting to give an account of its importance, its authors, the time, and the purpose for which they wrote it. For, having never appeared before the public, it has not been possible to form an exact idea of it, and some ill-founded statements have been made.

Utility of the *Historia Compostellana*

2. Any document from the ancient centuries, written by one who was present at the events, possesses such importance for scholars that its absence cannot be made good by the learned men of later times. What I write today from ancient documents may be done by others, present or future, with better method and greater success; but no one, nor all persons alive, can recount the past, which, when it leaves no traces, requires a spirit such as that of those who prophesy the future. We should know nothing of what occurred in the world before and after the Flood, had God not revealed it to Moses and had his writings not endured. The beginnings of churches for which we have no ancient documents are wholly unknown. The same would happen with a thousand items of information concerning the holy Church of Santiago, if not for the *Historia Compostellana*. One of the greatest men deserving applause in ecclesiastical history—its first archbishop—would lie buried in oblivion if not for this work; and even with it, there is no knowledge of his famous deeds, because it has not until now come into public light.

3. The excellence of the Church of the Apostle James, our patron and captain-general, is involved here as nowhere else. It deserves that the world should see its greatness in an original portrait: the manner in which it obtained the pallium; the metropolitan status with which it was honoured; the apostolic legateship of its first archbishop; and finally such a mass of exploits in that great man, Lord Don Diego Gelmírez, as ought to immortalize him among heroes. Besides these benefits proper to the Church of the Apostle, there are others of general concern, especially for the holy apostolic Roman See, through many pontifical letters hitherto unknown to the public; particular events concerning popes and antipopes, of which either there was no knowledge or whose original proof is found here. There are various letters, journeys, and occurrences involving cardinals, the patriarch of Jerusalem, Cluniac abbots, and princes of France, which will be found nowhere else. Concerning Spanish prelates, archbishops, abbots, and other ecclesiastical men, there are particular facts which even their own churches would not know if this work were lacking—as is the case with Toledo, Ávila, Salamanca, Saragossa, and especially Granada. Here there is, in book I, chapter 113, confirmation not previously known of the continuance of a bishop at Granada in 1116. In vain will various councils be sought outside this work, for they have left no trace elsewhere. The same I say concerning the kings and lords of Spain from King Don Alfonso VI throughout the reign of his daughter Doña Urraca and that of Emperor Don Alfonso, in whose times this work was being written. Consequently, from the year 1100 onward it is an original and contemporary source which would have been of great use to Baronius or Pagi had it not remained hidden; they would have avoided errors made on various points—for example, concerning the date of Santiago’s metropolitan status and the suffragan sees belonging to it. This arose from the work’s not having been published, and confirms its utility—or, rather, the necessity of its publication.

Its authors, time, and motive.

4. A work is also commended by the circumstances of its author: by his truthfulness, judgment, diligence, and the documents he employs. The *Historia Compostelana* had not one writer but three: two at the beginning, united as though one, and another in the middle and at the end. The idea arose with the last bishop of Santiago and archbishop, Lord Don Diego Gelmírez. Wishing to perpetuate the memories of his ancestors, and of the many things he had done and intended to do for the exaltation of his Church, he entrusted the work to two of his most learned and intimate canons [Col. 0881B]. One was called Don Munio (or Nuño) Alfonso, treasurer of the Holy Church; the other Don Hugo, an archdeacon and a Frenchman by birth. Both were esteemed by the prelate, who entrusted his greatest secrets to them and made use of their counsel and diligence in the most arduous matters.

To these men, thoroughly informed of affairs from within, he entrusted the work. He employed two so that it might be done with greater accuracy and promptness, for it is clear that each wrote what had occurred through his own participation. This may be seen in the translation of the relics from Portugal to Santiago, written by Archdeacon Don Hugo, who accompanied the bishop on that journey, as he states here in Book I, chapter 15. Don Nuño wrote other matters, as Book I, chapter 10 proves, where he says, “I myself, Munio Adefonsiades, etc.”; and in chapter 16, no. 3, “Myself, Munio, etc.” Accordingly, the work is recommended by the quality of its authors, who wrote of matters at which they themselves had been present.

[Col. 0881C] 5. This requires us to distinguish between what the work relates concerning the ancient prelates of the Church of Iria and what pertains to Don Diego Gelmírez. The force of authority which we attribute to this work rests upon the latter, since there we have precise reports of matters seen by capable and truthful persons. The rest does not possess equal authority, since it depended upon reports, which are apt to become distorted in the course of time. Thus, in events remote from the eleventh century there is room to suspect the admixture of imprecise information. But once Lord Gelmírez begins to be mentioned, there is no prudent basis for doubt, since these are matters seen and related by the prelate himself, or witnessed by the very writer.

To the ancient material we grant the prerogative of giving it precedence whenever nothing contrary is discovered, because the circumstance of its having been written within the very Church ought to prevail when there is no other contemporary document [Col. 0881D]. If there is one, judgment must be formed from the totality of the circumstances.

6. This is as regards the authority of the work, which is better understood by specifying the date—a subject upon which some have spoken ill-informedly. There is no doubt that it was written after the year 1100, when the man who ordered this work to be written began to be bishop, and after 1102, when the translation of the relics took place, written by Don Hugo, as is related here. This is the only thing known to have been written by Don Hugo. The remainder belongs to Don Nuño—not without the agreement and approval of his companion—for, besides the cited words, “I myself,” “myself,” we see the affairs of his time continued in the singular, in the author’s own words: “I shall undertake,” etc. This appears to be Don Nuño, since he disclosed his name more fully; although all proceeded under the responsibility of both, for the continuator attributes to each of them what they wrote (Prologue to Book II).

[Col. 0882A] We make the distinction mentioned only because they themselves declared it in their work. Thus, whoever wishes to cite the name of the author may cite both as though they were one: Don Hugo for the translation of the saints from Portugal; Don Nuño for the rest. This concerns what belongs to their pen; but there is greater difficulty in determining how far they wrote, since they did not mark this distinction. Consequently, some wrongly cite Don Nuño for what belongs to Girard, and conversely, because they have not been informed what belongs to each.

On this point I say that Don Nuño and Don Hugo carried the work forward until 1112, when both were elected bishops at the same time: Don Nuño of Mondoñedo and Don Hugo of Porto, as chapter 81 states. It is therefore astonishing how carelessly Ferreras, in volume XVI, page 7 of the Appendix, said that the *Historia Compostelana* was written by Don Munio, who was bishop of Lugo, and Don Bernardo, [Col. 0882B] prebendary of that Holy Church—things which he could only have dreamed, not read either here or in authors who have written about the Compostelana. There he gives it to be understood that he wished to publish it; but, he says, because the work is so extensive, means are needed for it to be brought to light by itself alone. And although certain overtures have been made to the prelates of that Holy Church, occupied with greater concerns, their attention has not been obtained.

Pellicer, in his *Dulcidio*, committed another error no less great, saying at folio 30b that the *Historia Compostelana* was written by Don Diego, bishop of Orense, and Don Gerardo, canon of Santiago. In this he confused the authors of the two works, the *History* and the *Chronicon*: he assigned the latter to Don Nuño and Don Hugo, who are authors of the beginning of the Compostelana, and not of the *Chronicon*; and he assigned the *History* to one who had no part in it, Don Diego, bishop of Orense.

7. Once Don Nuño and Don Hugo had been selected as bishops, it became necessary to choose another pen [Col. 0882C], because, their respective churches needing the presence of their shepherds, they could not continue what they had begun. Accordingly, the bishop of Santiago entrusted the work to another canon in whom he had confidence, called Girard or Giraldo, identified as French by Don Nicolás Antonio, among others. I do not know whether he wished to declare his homeland when, recounting a tumult in the city, he says in chapter 109, no. 4, that he would have preferred then to be at Beauvais, a city of Belgic Gaul in the Île-de-France—but not without the prelate: *Mallem esse Belvaci, eo tamen non absente* (“I would rather be at Beauvais, provided that he were not absent”).

That he was a canon of Santiago he himself says in Book II, chapter 6: *Ego Girardus Ecclesiae B. Jacobi canonicus, qui prioribus negotiis interfui, et hujus paginae seriem contexui* (“I, Girard, canon of the Church of Blessed James, who took part in the earlier affairs and wove together the sequence of this account”). He completed the work, continuing it from the point at which the first writers left it. This corresponds to chapter 83 of Book I, where the election and consecration of the first writers end. That material seems to belong to the same pen as what precedes it, because when, in chapter 81, they speak of the election of the two, they say of the bishop of Santiago, *de quo superius tractavimus* (“of whom we have treated above”). Those who wrote the preceding material were Don Nuño and Don Hugo, not Girard, who had no need to take up the pen until those who had gone to govern their churches laid it down in 1113.

From that point Girard began, for he says in the prologue to Book II: *Praecedentis libri seriem ex parte contexere studuimus: ejusdem namque libri praecedentia Munio Minduniensis, et Hugo Portugalensis episcopi, viri scilicet prudentes ac reverendi scripserant* (“We have endeavoured to weave together part of the sequence of the preceding book; for the earlier portions of that book had been written by Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo, and Hugo, bishop of Porto, men indeed prudent and venerable”). If Girard wrote part of Book I, as he here affirms, we must attribute to him what occurs after the first writers of the work were consecrated bishops, that is, from chapter 83 of Book I. Thus Girard began to treat what happened from 1113 until the end, which was the year 1139.

8. The others spoke of the ancient prelates of [Col. 0883A] Iria and of the first events concerning Don Diego Gelmírez, but with the noteworthy difference that they reduced what occurred over eleven centuries preceding Don Diego Gelmírez to about six leaves, while giving all the remainder of the work to the life of this prelate. The other bishops were mentioned merely by way of connection, in order to introduce their hero, for whom alone they cared and who was the entire reason for writing, as the work’s title proves: *Incipit primus liber Registri venerabilis Compostellanae Ecclesiae pontificis Didaci secundi* (“Here begins the first book of the Register of Diego the Second, venerable pontiff of the Church of Compostela”). The prelate himself ordered this title, *Register*, to be given, as the authors say in the prologues to Books I and III.

There is another difference. The first writers proposed only two books: one concerning the time during which he was bishop, and another from the beginning of his archbishopric. But, seeing that the second part was becoming very large, he divided it into two books, as Girard declares in the prologue to the third: *Divisit Registrum illud in tres libros, quorum primus episcopatus [Col. 0883B] liber: alii duo archiepiscopatus non irrationabiliter intitulantur* (“He divided that Register into three books, of which the first is entitled the book of the episcopate, and the other two, not without reason, books of the archiepiscopate”).

This is why Vasaeus and others count only two books in this work: they recognized no more than the first prologue, where it is divided into two, one concerning the episcopate and the other concerning the archiepiscopate. Yet the work itself shows three books, and Girard affirms in the prologue to the third that this division was made by the archbishop.

9. From this difference of authors arose the diversity that the most diligent reader may observe in this work, not only in style but also in certain matters—for example, the manner in which the first writers speak of the daughter of Don Alfonso VI, Doña Urraca, more honorifically than the last writer. For when the former wrote, the infanta had not yet displayed the inconstancy and frivolity with which she afterwards conducted herself.

10. It will also be understood from what has been said that this work was not written by two bishops, as some [Col. 0883C] report, still less by three, as Ambrosio de Morales said; for none was a bishop when he wrote. The first two afterwards assumed the mitre; but we do not know that the continuator ever attained it. Indeed, it is credible that he died before the archbishop, since he did not write of the prelate’s death.

11. From the principal purpose of writing this work—to perpetuate the many and great deeds of Lord Gelmírez, as both its title and text prove—several conclusions follow against those who construct negative arguments from the silence of the Compostelana. What does not belong to the purpose of the writing ought not to be found there; or at least we should not be surprised if it is absent. Such is what concerns the life and preaching of the Apostle James, of which there is no treatment there. The authors did not intend to write of the Apostle’s affairs or of other particulars of his Church; they concerned themselves solely with relating the principal actions of the hero whom they intended to perpetuate.

For this reason they noted something of events in their own day without mentioning their origin, as happens, for example, in the privilege concerning the Vows. There they offer the pontifical confirmation commanding that they be paid, without relating the privilege itself, because that did not belong to the period of their subject; only the command to preserve the ancient custom did. We have already said that they did not concern themselves with the privileges of ancient prelates, but with those obtained by Lord Gelmírez. Therefore one should not look for what is irrelevant; rather, one should recognize from this the harm caused by the failure to publish this work. Only one who has not seen it can give any force to negative arguments, believing that, if such and such an honourable thing had existed in antiquity, those who wrote the history of the Church itself would not have failed to recount it. But one who sees that it is ordered around and confined to the first archbishop will recognize that those arguments arose from ignorance, and will add the argument which I make in order to persuade [Col. 0884A] the world of the usefulness of seeing it: through it, objections arising from not having seen it are dispelled.

12. I have some suspicion that people have been deterred from printing it because the text appears so disordered that, without serious labour and comparison of different copies, it is impossible to understand its meaning. At least this is so in the exemplars I have seen. Whoever sees it running smoothly will believe that it would be enough to make a copy; but only one who examines them will understand the exceedingly troublesome labour required to ascertain the meaning of what is printed—obtaining it not through new invention, but by study: now of what the context of the Latin phrase demands, now with the assistance of another copy—so that everything may belong to the ancient authors and nothing to the editor.

The greatest concern is that this work may have remained unpublished because of passages that do not seem favourable to Galicia: for example, whether among the Galicians of that period interest prevailed over truth; whether [Col. 0884B] they looked more to their own advantage than to justice; and certain popular tumults against the bishop and against Queen Doña Urraca. But none of these things should prevail against the work’s many benefits, in which the actions of distinguished Galicians are more praiseworthy than those of the populace are blameworthy; the lesser ought not to outweigh the greater.

Every nation or province commonly has its nickname, introduced in jest or in earnest through rivalry with a neighbouring people. But sensible persons distinguish what is general from what is particular, and recognize that not all Israelites are good, nor all people of the land of Uz evil. Nation, land, and sky are not fate. Galicia is the native soil of families foremost in the nobility of Spain; even kings chose it for the upbringing of their children. In every province the conduct of the noble differs from that of the commoner. Whoever wishes to stigmatize it directs his attack at what is lowest; the principal part therefore remains untouched. Without leaving this [Col. 0884C] work, one will see in both classes more glories than disgraces for Galicia.

Moreover, the circumstances of who speaks and when must be considered. The speaker is a Frenchman, raised in another country and unaccustomed to the temper of our people. Though he wrote in Galicia, that did not compel him to restrain himself, since he was speaking in favour of one who was, as it were, viceroy of the province. The time was one of tumult, when men heed neither laws nor what is right, but solely the cause to which they are committed; in such a time the noblest and most powerful often violate justice more greatly, so that the law of their passion may prevail. It was also a time when arms were in the cities and in the hands of great lords, and therefore they looked to their own interests more than to the common good.

Even when the author appears most heated, he warns that all this is to be understood without prejudice to the honourable men of Galicia: *Sed haec velim dixisse pace proborum Gallaeciae* (“But I would wish to have said these things with the good men of Galicia unharmed”), as he states in chapter 108, no. 3. I forgive the author whatever he may wish to say about the Galicians because of the good things he publishes about others, and especially about the principal hero, who was a Galician. That man, who knew how to honour a nation, is enough to vindicate and bring credit upon a province.

[Col. 0884D] 13. In this connection, the purpose of the work itself must be kept in mind: to relate the deeds of the prelate, who was then alive. In order to exalt one man, it is very usual, and almost unavoidable, to cast the opposite party in an unfavourable light or to give its blemishes a vividness which they would not possess apart from the contrast. Seeing, therefore, in the bishop such zeal for the good of his country, such solicitude to exalt the Church, and that he was not without rivals—as others of that and greater rank have not been without them—it was almost inevitable that, as ingratitude contended with beneficence, the pen of one heated by comparison should cast off some sparks that blackened the ungrateful.

Yet all this was without prejudice to the rest—*pace proborum* (“with the honourable men unharmed”)—as [Col. 0885A] the author says. Thus the province remains like all the others, superior to them in having produced this hero, and the Church of Compostela retains its right that its general importance should not suffer from one or another individual occurrence.

## Copies of the *Historia Compostelana* and of the *Chronicon Iriense*

14. The high esteem in which learned persons held this work led to the making of several copies. Those which I have seen append, at the end, a portion of Iriense history, which Berganza published in his *Ferreras Convencido* under the title *Chronicon Iriense*, beginning: *Cum Vandali, Silingi, et Ugni* (“When the Vandals, Silings, and Huns…”). This is not part of the work; but those who saw it at the end and did not read the preceding material believed that everything was the *Historia Compostelana*, as happened to Don Nicolás Antonio in chapter 22 of Book VI of his *Bibliotheca*, nos. 500 and following. Yet he has an excuse [Col. 0885B], because he immediately acknowledges that he did not possess that *History*, and he followed what Pellicer wrote in his observations on *Dulcidio*, page 30, where he attributes the *Chronicon Iriense* to Don Nuño, bishop of Mondoñedo, and Don Hugo, bishop of Porto.

This might be admissible if the *Chronicon* were considered part of the *Historia Compostelana*. But Pellicer distinguished them, assigning different authors to the latter—Don Diego, bishop of Orense, which, as we have said, is false, and Don Gerardo, canon of Santiago—in the year 1112. Don Nicolás, in the cited place, did not distinguish the two things, for he said, “the Compostelan history or chronicle,” adding that it was written around the year 1000, during the reign of Don Bermudo II, by the two aforementioned bishops, Don Nuño and Don Hugo.

None of this was so. The bishops did not write the *Chronicon*, nor were they living in the year 1000, but a hundred years later, as Don Nicolás himself recognized in the next volume when speaking of the Compostelana. The *Chronicon* ends with Don Bermudo II, and this made men believe that it was written at that time. But it is not of that period; it is much later, when accounts of that age were already being distorted. For it states that Don Pelayo, bishop of Lugo, succeeded St Rosendo and Sisnando II—something incompatible with a contemporary writer, since Don Pelayo, bishop of Lugo, did not transfer to Santiago. It adds that Bermudo deposed him while his competitor Don Ramiro was still living, which is false, as was said there. It likewise confused King Don Sancho Ordóñez of Galicia with Don Sancho the Fat of León, which is not compatible with a writer of the same century. Nor is what it affirms concerning Don Bermudo, with whom it ends, true: it says that he entered the kingdom through a multitude of troops supplied by the Moorish king; but this was not so. Rather, he entered upon the death of Don Ramiro, when he no longer had a competitor.

It appears, therefore, that much is lacking there, if the author of the *Chronicon* wrote down to his own time. Judging from the scant accuracy of its ancient information, and from the childish manner in which it plays upon the name *Compositum tellus* (“composite land”) for Compostela and upon *Ilia* as the daughter of the Trojan prince, it seems to belong to a century in which fables had already gained acceptance.

15. It is certain that this fragment is not part of Diego Gelmírez’s Compostelana, but was written by someone as a continuation of that work, which was left unfinished; and if the original had blank leaves, the person who added it made use of them. Others, seeing it written after the Compostelana and not noticing the complete disconnection of the subjects, believed it all to be one work. I have not seen the original, nor do I know that it survives. But it is more likely that this *Chronicon* was written at the end of some transcript of the Compostelana and incorporated there because it spoke of the bishops of Compostela. In the same way, at the beginning of some copies they inserted other chronicles of the Suebi, Goths, and kings of León, with a catalogue of the archbishops of Santiago, which [Col. 0886A] in the copy used by Ambrosio de Morales extended to the year 1465.

They likewise incorporated at the beginning the history of Archbishop Don Fray Berenguer, from 1317 and following, which other copies place at the end, as happened in the copy of the Count of Olivares cited by Don Nicolás Antonio in Book VII, chapter 4, no. 69. Morales’s copy and mine begin at folio 1 with this Don Fray Berenguer. These are clear proofs that all this depended upon the copyists, who inserted and placed the pieces as they wished. None of it was the work of those who wrote the Compostelana: not the piece on Don Fray Berenguer, which is two centuries distant from that period; not the *Chronicon*, which expressly mentions St Isidore in that very passage; nor the chronicle of the Visigoths, which begins with Wamba and reaches King Don García. For this was written in Asturias: *In hac regione Asturiensium* (“In this region of the Asturians”), as it says when speaking of Don Pelayo. A work of canons of Santiago would not have said “in this region of Asturias,” nor would men of the twelfth century have been content [Col. 0886B] to write only as far as Don García at the beginning of the tenth century.

Nor is the piece which ends with the death of Queen Doña Urraca and her son Don Alfonso theirs, for it speaks of the Queen’s death in a manner very different from the author of the Compostelana. It ends there because the first archbishop of Santiago began then, and its purpose was to provide a catalogue of archbishops. It therefore mentioned no more kings than were necessary to introduce the first metropolitan and continue its catalogue of archbishops. This begins with Don Diego Gelmírez, and the vellum codex which I now possess in my study includes only the ten prelates who had existed up to the date of writing; afterwards others added more. In the fourteenth century they bound the book together, inserting at its beginning the *Life of Archbishop Don Fray Berenguer*, for when the Catalogue names him it says: *Cujus vitam inclytam . . . in primo folio libri hujus reperies* (“Whose illustrious life … you will find on the first folio of this book”). This was also written after that life had been placed at the beginning of the codex, since it says *in primo folio* (“on the first folio”). Therefore the historical material preceding the Catalogue belongs to the same author, and all of it is much later than the writers of the Compostelana.

[Col. 0886C] 16. It follows that none of these pieces belongs to the authors Don Nuño and Don Girard, still less the *Chronicon Iriense*, in which there are matters opposed to the Compostelana. This is apparent in the bishops of Iria, where the *Chronicon* gives Felix the sixth place, though he is unknown in the principal work of those who say that they possess only the names and succession of the bishops. The author of the *Chronicon* seems to have undertaken to comment upon that clause, adding the kings in whose reigns they flourished and the councils at which they were present. He also inserts the endowment of King Miro, which is not mentioned in the Compostelana.

The revelation of the body of James is in the *Chronicon* without an account of the manner in which it occurred. That account is read in the Compostelana. In place of what it omitted, the *Chronicon* adds an assembly of wise men to name [Col. 0886D] the place of the discovery; and there it strings together the conceits of *Compositum tellus*, *Illia*, etc., of which there is no trace in the Compostelana. Nor did these authors, who briefly related the bishops of Iria and Compostela down to Don Diego Gelmírez, need to write another *Chronicon* on the same subject when theirs dealt precisely with the period from 1100 onwards; for their purpose it was enough to give a brief account of the bishops who had preceded in that see. This they did; but for that purpose it was unnecessary to compose a separate *Chronicon*.

## On the Present Edition

17. Among the various copies of the *Historia Compostelana* which I have seen, only three have served me in preparing this edition. One was used by Ambrosio de Morales, as several marginal notes in his hand show; he used them to find quickly what was contained in the text. It is [Col. 0887A] a paper copy made by a scribe who did not know Latin. Thus it is extremely common to read *noluit* (“he did not wish”) where the sense requires *voluit* (“he wished”), and the reverse, together with a thousand other individual errors of this kind. It is now kept in the Royal Library of Madrid.

The second manuscript belonged to the library of the Most Excellent Count of Villaumbrosa, President of Castile. The copy was made from another which the Most Illustrious Don Diego de Covarrubias, bishop of Segovia, had ordered to be made from the copy held in the archive of the Holy Church of Santiago. He placed it in his major college of St Saviour, called Oviedo, in the University of Salamanca. From that exemplar the transcript was made in 1672 for the Count of Villaumbrosa, Don Pedro Núñez de Guzmán. It is now in Madrid along with a great many other manuscripts, and I have had it in my study for collation.

The third is a vellum codex which I learned was in the library of the Most Illustrious Major College of Salamanca called that of the Archbishop. Someone told me that it was original. Having experienced [Col. 0887B] the scant fidelity of copies, I secured, through the patronage of the Most Illustrious Don Francisco Cepeda, of the Council and Chamber of Castile, permission to see it for the purpose of collation. It is a beautiful codex, with some well-illuminated golden letters, in accordance with the usage of the thirteenth century, in which it was written, as the character of the script shows. At the end it has a note from the year 1347 which does not belong to the work; but since it is in a more modern hand, it proves that the principal work had already been written in the preceding century.

More importantly, the catalogue of archbishops written at the beginning of the codex, after the small *Chronicon*, ends with Don Bernardo II, the tenth archbishop, who was alive in 1226. Although the catalogue of archbishops continues, it is in a different ink and hand. This proves that the codex was written while Don Bernardo II was alive, around 1230. It is in the handsome script used at that time, now called monastic because it survives, with little difference, in the choir books of our [Col. 0887C] monasteries. But the scribe did not know Latin, a fact which, together with extremely frequent abbreviations, much joining of letters, and defective orthography, often delays the reader.

18. Nevertheless, this is the copy which has been most useful to me for discovering the sense of certain clauses imperceptible in the other manuscripts. Being ancient, it preserves the strokes customarily placed over certain letters in abbreviated words. By their help I have been able to discover the sense of some clauses imperceptible in the other copies, supplying from one what is missing in another, since none is perfect.

All this has entailed no small trouble: both through the time consumed in collations, and through the vexation and delay caused by the scribes’ ignorance of Latin; likewise through lack of punctuation, which often alters the meaning, and disorder in orthography—partly characteristic of the ancient period, partly resulting from the copyists themselves, who accommodated their writing to common usage rather than to the propriety of Latin. Thus, for example: *magestas* for *majestas*, *Osmensis* and *Osomensis* for *Oxomensis*, and *Gallicia* for *Gallaecia*. In these and similar matters they were not consistent, and therefore we do not retain their manner of writing.

Worst of all is the extreme difficulty of determining the sense, which sometimes remains imperceptible; and where it does not, it has been ascertained by repeated examination. Here it is of no use to study the particular habits of the scribe, because he is not consistent. He is only constant in placing aspiration where it does not belong, as in *hodiosa*, *honerata*, *huberiora*, etc. We do not adopt this practice, nor the use of *quatinus* for *quatenus*, *puplico* for *publico*, or *Ilia* for *Iria*, for where one copyist uses the first form another uses the second, and the same copyist uses them indiscriminately.

The same occurs with *Salamanticense* and *Salmanticenses*, *Emeritanae* and *Emeretanae*, *baselica* and *basilica*, *paleum* and *pallium*, *previlegium* [Col. 0888A] and *privilegium*, *langore* and *languore*, *jocunditas* and *jucunditas*. Although *jocundatio* is found in Late Latin, *jucunditas* does not deserve the *o*. We retain the spelling *reverentissime* and *benivole*, because, although not consistent here, they are found in other ancient documents. The same is true of some of the forms mentioned above; but seeing that they are not used consistently, we content ourselves with this warning and use them occasionally, so that beginners may not be surprised when they encounter them in certain manuscripts—for example, *temptet*.

The terms *Galliciani* and *Gallaecos* are read here indiscriminately. It should be noted that the inhabitants of the town of Nájera are called *Nazarenos*, because they called the town *Nazara*, as may be seen in the privilege of King Alfonso VIII in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 1433. But because *Nazarenos* is not recognized today, we substitute *Najareni*, noting this at the first occurrence in the text, Book I, chapter 73; and because that name is no longer known, we use *Najareni*.

[Col. 0888B] 19. The vellum codex begins, as it is bound, with the *Life of Archbishop Don Fray Berenguer of Landorra*, but in a more modern script and hand. This is followed by the *Chronicon*, beginning *In aera CCCC* (“In the era 400”) and ending with Don Alfonso VII, together with the names of the first ten archbishops of Santiago. From that point the codex continues in a single hand. Between the *Chronicon* and the *Historia Compostelana* is a blank leaf, and immediately thereafter the work begins without any title, each page divided into two columns. In the first is written: *Didacus Dei gra[tia] Compostellanae sedis archiepiscopus jussit hunc librum fieri, etc.* (“Diego, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, ordered this book to be made, etc.”), as may be seen here at the beginning of the work.

This occupies half a column; the other half is a gold illumination with an architectural structure of two arches. Beneath one stands the bishop with his mitre and staff; beneath the other, an angel holding a censer. In the middle, where the arches meet, hangs a lamp. [Col. 0888C] Below are three chests, one larger than another: the central one is covered, while the other two have no lids, as the engraving at the beginning shows. This is undoubtedly a representation of the manner in which the Apostle’s underground vault actually existed, for the canons who authored this book would have seen it well before the prelate closed off communication between the lower part of the church and the vault containing the body.

20. This codex does not contain the *Chronicon* of St Isidore, with the continuation found in the other codices and including Don Ordoño I. Therefore we do not include it here either, since it is not part of the work; nor do we include the *Life of Fray Berenguer*, because it belongs to its own period. We publish the *Chronicon* followed by the catalogue of archbishops, but not at the beginning of the work, where it does not belong; rather, at the end, as the order of those who succeeded the first archbishop requires, for the work concerns him alone.

21. None of these manuscripts has chapters, and since without them texts cannot be cited in such a way that they may be readily found, it was necessary to add them. The authors were very liberal with headings, sometimes multiplying them unnecessarily for a single matter. Therefore we do not add a chapter number to every heading, since it concerns the same subject. This occurs in chapter 32, where on one and the same leaf they placed ten headings: *Item de eodem* (“Likewise, concerning the same matter”); *Item* (“Likewise”); *Item*. We suppress these here, since for citations the numbers which we have added in the margin to each are sufficient.

22. We have added another matter, no less important and timely: for just as citations cannot be made use of without chapters, so readers cannot know the time under discussion without chronology. Here labour has contended with usefulness: for the authors were not fond of chronology, as the scant use they made of years shows. The copies are not always faithful in their numbers; and if on one side the times begin to be put in order, on the other they emerge disordered. [Col. 0889A] This has cost me no little time; and the patience and perseverance required not to abandon the undertaking were even greater. But at last, persisting through lengthy comparisons, the numbers of the year being discussed have been placed in the upper margins of the pages. The authors intermingle among them events of other years, because they concern the same subject; and for this purpose they set forth the origin or confirmation of a matter concluded or begun outside the year of which they are treating, as they sometimes expressly state, while in other cases the subjects themselves make it clear. These incidental years are not marked in the margin, lest the chronological order be disturbed—as would happen if, after dealing with the year 1104, that of 1102 were inserted—but readers are warned of them in the text, and sometimes at the foot of the page. Thus the work, in which it was impossible to find a citation or ascertain the time of events without the readers’ prolonged reflection, is made accessible to all in both respects without difficulty; and errors are avoided [Col. 0889B] which some authors committed when they published fragments of the *Compostelana* under years wholly contrary to its chronology, trusting bad copies whose defects they could not discover without much examination and extended comparison of the subject matter. For example, the Council of Palencia was placed by Cardinal Aguirre in the year 1114, and by Pulgar in [Col. 0890A] 1118, whereas a careful examination of the History itself establishes that it was in the year 1113. The author—Canon Girard, not Don Nuño—is undoubtedly treating of that year, as is demonstrated by what precedes and follows that council, placed here in chapter 92 of Book I with the year 1113 in the margin. By this means the difficulties and risks which otherwise were virtually inevitable disappear.

Mariana, when recounting certain events of the reign of Doña Urraca, omitted the years, admitting the difficulty; other years which he specified proved erroneous—as happened to Zurita and Sandoval, because they did not carefully compare and examine the material. I excuse them all, for even though I had handled the *Compostelana* several times, I could not determine these matters through the bulk of a folio volume—the form of the manuscript copies—so extremely sparing in indications of time, whose obscurity and the protracted trouble required to clarify so many years made me withdraw my hand on several occasions. Finally, having resolved to publish [Col. 0890B] the work, I determined to spare no labour, however arduous, until I had discovered the years, for the relief and convenience of all who might wish to use it. It may be that not everything will please everyone; but the lesser defects should be pardoned me for the greater achievement, and perhaps this very labour may have obscured my keenest desire to be correct.

[Col. 0889]

# HISTORY OF COMPOSTELLA

[Col. 0889]

## BEGINNING OF THE WHOLE WORK, WITH THE FOLLOWING WARNING AND THREAT

Diego, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Compostela, ordered this book to be made and deposited in the treasury of Saint James. If anyone wishes to read it, let him read and learn how many honours, inheritances, ornaments, and dignities that Archbishop acquired for his Church; and how many persecutions and perils he endured from tyrannical powers in defence of his Church. After reading and learning all this, let him replace it in its proper place, and let it always remain there; and let no one remove it thence or take it away through fraud or envy. But if anyone does so, or removes it through ignorance, or destroys it by any deceit, then by the authority of Almighty God, of the Blessed Virgin Mary, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, of the most blessed James, of all the saints of God, and by our authority, let him be cursed and excommunicated; and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, and with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive, let him be eternally condemned in hell. Amen, amen. And whoever preserves and guards it well, let him be blessed and sanctified for ever and ever by God the Almighty Father and by Saint James the Apostle, His disciple. Amen.

## IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY AND UNDIVIDED TRINITY BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE REGISTER OF DIEGO THE SECOND, VENERABLE PONTIFF OF THE CHURCH OF COMPOSTELLA

[Col. 0889]

## PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0889C]

The Fathers of old, concerned for the instruction and education of posterity, were accustomed to commit to writing the deeds of kings and dukes, and likewise the virtues and achievements of illustrious men, lest, erased by long antiquity or extended intervals of time, they should sink into the pit of oblivion. They therefore judged that such things ought by no means to be consigned to forgetfulness, but rather should be entrusted through the record of writing to a living and enduring memory, so that later generations, frequently reading them, might mark in those histories the character and praises of the wise and those who lived well; and, kindled to virtue by remembrance of deeds accomplished, might earnestly endeavour to imitate worthy and industrious men in worth and industry and to follow in their footsteps. Conversely, they might wholly avoid the vices and evil [Col. 0891A] customs of fools and those who lead perverse lives. For in writings the minds of hearers are instructed by teaching concerning life and by discipline of conduct, and are stirred up [perhaps *suscitantur*, “are roused”] to zeal for good works; because writings were composed by discerning and wise teachers for uprooting evil habits and building up good ones, as the outstanding preacher attests in the Epistle to the Romans: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction,” etc. (Rom. 15:2).

Accordingly, the reverend Bishop Diego the Second of the see of Compostela, following the custom of the ancient Fathers in compiling this register, ordered the deeds of his predecessors to be written down and recalled to memory from the beginning of this apostolic see. Some of these deeds he had himself seen with his own eyes; others he had truthfully learned through frequent report from authoritative persons and men. He did so that whatever a diligent reader found praiseworthy and worthy of imitation in them, he might praise and earnestly strive to imitate; and conversely, if he observed anything blameworthy and reprehensible in them, he might not cease to blame and reprove it for the correction and amendment of others. For as one who punishes evil men insofar as they are evil is a minister of God, so one who with devout intention rebukes those who deserve rebuke is a minister of God. Thus the Apostle, writing to his disciple, exhorts him to rebuke the rebuke-worthy in these words: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Tim. 4:2).

He also took care that his own deeds should be recorded in this register together with the deeds of his predecessors, so that his successors, reading them, might learn how greatly he had laboured for [Col. 0891C] the exaltation, benefit, and honour of his Church; and how many persecutions and perils he had endured from tyrannical powers in its defence. Having learned these things, they should follow his examples and labour manfully for the benefit, honour, and defence of their Church, setting themselves as a wall for the house of Israel, lest they be proved to be hirelings rather than good shepherds; and so that from the Shepherd of shepherds they may earn the reward of a good shepherd for their pastoral care.

For the aforesaid reason, therefore, he ordered this register to be made in two volumes [Note: [Col. 0891D] (20) A third book was later added by the third writer of this work.], one entitled *On the Episcopate*, the other *On the Archbishopric*. In the book *On the Episcopate* are contained his successes and adversities, the honours and inheritances which he acquired for his Church, and many other matters, each of which the diligent reader will fully learn by reading this book. He also acquired many things and brought them under the power and lordship of his Church: namely honours, villages, inheritances, possessions, palaces, houses, church ornaments, and pontifical vestments. These are not written in the sequence of this book, either because he consigned them to oblivion or because they were passed over amid the emergence of greater concerns. The book *On the Archbishopric* contains how, through supreme labour and manifold expenses, divine grace going before him and Saint James assisting, he transferred the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida to the Church of Compostela. [Col. 0892A] That same book contains many other matters, which we have judged wholly unnecessary to enumerate one by one in this prologue, in order to avoid wearisome prolixity. If anyone applies himself to read this book, which is adorned with scarcely any polish of eloquence, we earnestly beg him to approve and retain what he finds in it worthy of approval and retention, and to correct and amend what needs correction and amendment. Let him not gnaw away at the writing and its author with the venomous bites of envy; rather, keeping before his mind that philosophical maxim that nothing perfect can be found in human actions, let him grant pardon to human capacity. But Thou, O Lord, etc.
