## CHAPTER I. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the translation of Saint James, brother of John the Apostle and Evangelist

[Col. 0892B]

As we have learned from Gospel truth, when our Lord and Redeemer, on the fortieth day after His resurrection, was about to ascend into heaven, He commanded His disciples to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world and to baptize the nations converted to the true faith in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, saying: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature,” etc. (Mark 16:15). Accordingly, while the other Apostles, by the Lord’s command, travelled to various provinces and cities in zeal for Gospel preaching, Saint James, [Col. 0892C] brother of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, preached the word of God in Spain and at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0892D] (21) Thus some codices; others read: “He remained at Jerusalem, intending to preach the word of God; and there,” etc.]. There he was beheaded by Herod for confessing Christ and affirming the Catholic faith, and became the first of all the Apostles to undergo martyrdom. Hence Saint Luke the Evangelist says in the Acts of the Apostles: “King Herod laid hands upon certain persons of the Church to afflict them; and he killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Acts 12:1).

The Jews, led by ill will and envy, would neither bury the venerable body of this most blessed Apostle nor allow it to be buried by the Christians then living in Jerusalem. Rather, as Pope Leo affirms in the letter which he sent to the Spaniards concerning James’s passion and the translation of his body into Spain [Col. 0892D]: “They cast forth the whole body with the head outside the city, exposing it to be devoured and consumed by dogs, birds, and wild beasts.” But his disciples, having been warned by him while he was living to carry his body to the Spanish land for burial, seized the whole body with its head by night, Pope Leo bearing witness, and quickly reached the shore of the sea. While they were concerned there about a vessel in which they might cross into Spain, they found on the seashore a ship divinely prepared for them. Giving thanks to God with one accord, they placed the most sacred body aboard, gladly embarked, and, under the guiding hand of the Lord, avoiding Scylla [Col. 0893A] and Charybdis and the dangerous shoals, first reached the port of Iria by a prosperous voyage. Then, carrying the venerable body to the place then called *Liberum donum* (“Free Gift”), but now called Compostela, they buried it there under marble arches according to the rite of the Church.

2. In ancient times Christian religion had flourished in that place among those who cultivated the Catholic faith. But when persecution arose and the proud tyranny of the pagans trampled down the dignity of the Christian name, almost the whole practice of Christian religion had already long vanished from there. Thus throughout the time of the Saracens, and for a long time even after the restoration of the faithful, the Apostle’s venerable tomb, unvisited by any Christian, remained for a very long time covered by the density of brushwood and forest. It was revealed and known to no one until the time of Theodemir, Bishop of Iria. But when it pleased Almighty God mercifully to visit His afflicted Church and turn its adversity into the tranquillity of prosperity, He immediately changed the time by His mighty command: He transferred the kingdom of Spain, and, the heathen superstition having been trampled down and wholly abolished throughout the Spanish region, He restored there the name and faith of His Christ.

3. Before that expulsion, Miro, king of good memory, receiving the sceptres of the kingdom by divine disposition, first established episcopal sees throughout the provinces of Spain, divine grace inspiring him, according to the rule of the Roman Church; and, choosing Andrew as bishop, he first elevated him to the chair of Iria. We read that the following persons succeeded him in order—as is written below—although we have no information whatsoever about them beyond their names: Dominic, Samuel, Gotomar, Vincibilis, Ildulf, Selva, Theodesind, Bemila, Romanus, Augustine, Honoratus, Quendulf, and another Quendulf.

## CHAPTER II. On the revelation of the body of Saint James, brother of John the Apostle and Evangelist

Theodemir is said to have succeeded the bishops mentioned above, being raised to that same see by divine ordering grace. In his time the omnipotence of the divine majesty deigned to visit and enlighten the Western Church through the revelation of the tomb of so great an Apostle. The following page explains how it was revealed to him. Certain men of distinction and great authority reported to the aforesaid bishop that they had often seen lights burning at night in the grove which, through long antiquity, had grown over Saint James’s tomb, and that angels had repeatedly appeared to them there. On hearing this, he himself went to the place where they declared that they had seen such things, and without doubt saw with his own eyes the lights burning there. Inspired therefore by divine grace, he promptly approached the little grove and, after a more careful examination, found among the woods and thickets a small structure containing within itself a marble tomb [Note: [Col. 0893D] (22) In the copy used by Ambrosio de Morales, he wrote in the margin: “This marble tomb is doubtless those marble chests repeatedly mentioned under this very name in royal privileges. And they are indeed often read in a most corrupt form.” But perhaps he would have observed this more suitably at the end of no. 2 of the preceding chapter, where it is said that the body was buried “under marble arches.”]. Upon finding it, he gave thanks to God and immediately sought the presence of Alfonso the Chaste, king, then reigning in Spain. He truthfully informed him of what he had heard and seen with his own eyes. The king, filled with joy at such news, swiftly came into those parts; and, restoring a church in honour of so great an Apostle, he transferred the episcopal see of Iria to this place called Compostela, with the authority of many bishops, servants of God, and noble [Col. 0894B] men, and by royal privilege. We have heard many report that this happened in the time of Charlemagne.

Bishop Theodemir, moreover, raised the eyes of his mind to contemplation of the heavenly country with all the more confidence because he more frequently saw Saint James shine forth in miracles and powers after the basilica had been built for him. Thus, endowed with hope of heavenly things, after some interval of time he peacefully yielded up his life when his final lot intervened.

2. Adaulf, succeeding him, fed the flock entrusted to him with the nourishment of the divine word, according to his ability and with watchful care. A second Adaulf, taking up the government of the pontifical order, was so inflamed with desire for the inward vision that, through envy, certain enemies accused him before the king then ruling Spain of the Sodomitic vice. The king, hearing of the commission of so great a crime and stirred by violent anger, ordered him, according to his most impious judgment, to be exposed before the whole assembly to an untamed and most ferocious bull [Note: [Col. 0894D] (23) We have shown in the preceding volume, in the Life of Adaulf II, that this is an invention.], on the condition that he who was alleged to be guilty of so grave a charge should be utterly torn to pieces by the attack of the impatient bull. But He who by hidden judgment weighs the state of justice in an equal balance, not permitting the ray of truth to be obscured by the shadow of falsehood, so calmed the ferocity of the raging bull that, although it was urged on by dogs, it could inflict no harm upon that religious man.

We believe that this happened because, though he had already been condemned in human eyes, trusting nevertheless in divine mercy, before he came to the judgment of such cruelty he celebrated the office of the holy Mass. Clothed in the pontifical mitre [Note: [Col. 0894D] (24) Another codex has *chasuble* instead of *mitre*.], like an unconquerable athlete of God proceeding to martyrdom, he arrived at the place of spectacle, to be protected by divine compassion. For the bull, most violently enraged by the hunters’ trumpets and dogs, when it saw him, became tame though formerly untamed, and of its own accord yielded its horns into his hands; [Col. 0895A] and so the servant of God escaped unharmed. When the king and all who were with him saw the miracles of such power, they fell at his feet and with open cries confessed that they were guilty of the false testimony by which they had wickedly sought to condemn him. But he, following the Apostle in returning good for evil, mercifully forgave them. That same hour, relinquishing the dignity of his episcopate, he entered Asturias, there to put aside the transitory things of this fleeting life and serve God alone. Leaving others an example of holy conduct, he paid the debt of nature in the Era 904.

The chasuble in which he celebrated Mass on the day of the aforesaid ordeal was endowed by God with such power that if anyone, about to administer a sacrament, put it on and happened to be perjured, he could by no means take it off.

3. Sisnand, bishop of this Church, who by divine providence succeeded Adaulf of holy memory, laboured so hard in the work of holy preaching that, despising the concerns of worldly affairs, he devoted himself with all his heart’s affection to heavenly contemplation. Recalling also the holy life of his predecessor Adaulf, he entered Asturias in the supreme desire of brotherly love, carried his body after death to Compostela, and buried it with the greatest reverence. Moreover, with the counsel and obedience of the most holy Emperor Alfonso and Queen Ximena, he enlarged the church of this most reverend Apostle and, once enlarged, consecrated it with many bishops. He also founded the monastery called *Ante altaria* (“Before the Altars”), and Pinario, where the monastery of Saint Martin was built in honour of God. He founded Lovio as well, where the relics of Saint Felix are kept.

Further, bringing before his mind’s eye the saying of blessed Job, “I was a foot to the lame and an eye to the blind” (Job 29:15), he caused places to be established near the tower of the principal entrance to this church for lame and blind persons and all the infirm, with the intention that their poverty should be supported from his alms and from the offerings of the faithful. The aforesaid monasteries—namely *Ante altaria* and Pinario—this venerable bishop built from Saint James’s own resources with the following intention: if any of the senior members of this Church should desire, under the Rule of Saint Benedict, to wash away the stains of their sins with the tears of divine compunction, he might become a monk in either of them as in a familiar and private dwelling. Lovio was likewise founded by that bishop for the same purpose: that if anyone of the household of that Church became infirm, he might retire there as one discharged from service, as it were, for rest.

We shall truthfully relate the origin of that household as we have learned it in fact. For the aforesaid Bishop Sisnand, remembering the utterly wicked betrayal and accusation of his maternal uncle, the religious Bishop Adaulf, handed over by royal authority and enduring decree to the servile condition of performing the offices of this Church all those whom he could find from the kindred and descent [Col. 0896A] of the persons who had betrayed him. This was on the condition that some of them should be cooks and others liable for every sort of service, and that they and their descendants should remain so forever. Afterwards, when some time had elapsed, that Catholic bishop ended his life in peace in the Era 958.

4. Gundesind, son of Count Aloit, succeeding him in whatever manner, devoted himself with more ardent zeal to worldly than to heavenly things. Near the end of his life, living, as he had begun, still less religiously, he is said to have been torn more violently from the dwelling of the flesh. His mother, deeply consumed by grief over this, prayed day and night more earnestly to the mercy of heavenly compassion for the remedy of his soul. She distributed all that she possessed to the poor and remained for a long time in vigils and prayers before the altar of Saint James, believing that he had undergone torments of various kinds, that through the immeasurable mercy of Almighty God and the intercession of most holy James he might attain the fellowship of the heavenly citizens.

Meanwhile, pouring out her thirsting mind in most anxious attention toward contemplation of the heavenly country, she at last knocked upon the door of divine mercy in this way: if her prayers, poured out before the sight of the heavenly Majesty, had been accepted, she might learn through some holy revelation what was the condition of her son. Thus, one night, warmed by the affections of charity, while she spent the night in the church of this most sacred Apostle, around midnight she gave eyes already nearly weighed down by continual vigil a momentary sleep. While she slept, she seemed to see the books which she customarily placed in the library for the service of the Church set on fire by a most holy man; and, awakening at their burning, she rose. When, amazed, she lay down again, she heard a voice say to her: “Know that your son was admitted this night into the company of the elect.”

5. After him Ermegild was elected bishop. After his election, given over to the evil desires of this present exile, he submitted the neck of his mind to the dominion of iniquity as long as he lived. A little before the day of his death, however, being violently angered, he ordered a widow’s only cow—the milk of which fed herself and her children—to be taken away. The next day, while he sat at table with his soldiers, his steward served among the other dishes, on a silver platter, one of that cow’s entrails, called in the Galician tongue *duplicia*. Already swollen with the variety of foods and drenched in the liquid of nectar, when with the first bite he sought to eat the *duplicia* set before him, he burst in the middle of his belly before those present. After he was buried, we heard from many persons that his tomb had been burned; and we ourselves saw with our own eyes signs of that burning [Note: [Col. 0895D] (25) In the preceding volume, in his Life, we have shown that a somewhat more lenient judgment should be made regarding the affairs of this bishop.].

[Col. 0897A] 6. King Sancho ordered Sisnand, son of Count Menendo and nephew of the aforesaid Bishop Gundesind, who succeeded to him by a certain chance of power, to be confined in dark prisons. In his place he appointed Reodesind [Note: [Col. 0897D] (26) Understand Saint Rudesind.], a religious monk of Celanova. Upon the death of King Sancho, Sisnand was promptly released from his bonds. On Christmas Day he entered Compostela with armed force, drew his sword, and threatened to behead Bishop Reodesind [Note: [Col. 0897D] (27) See what we have written concerning the posthumous reputation of Sisnand II in his Life.]. Reodesind, that most holy man, standing undaunted in the love of divine strength, pronounced this curse upon Bishop Sisnand: “Sisnand, you who threaten me with the deadly sword, shall yourself be violently pierced by the deadly sword.”

While Sisnand continued in the episcopal chair by the power of tyranny, Reodesind fled the tumult of this present exile and, by the Lord’s mercy, reached the monastery of Celanova as though a harbour of tranquillity. There he died in Era 1015. When the Northmen, coming from the port called Juncaria and making for Iria, were plundering these regions, Sisnand left the city and, surrounded by the strength of his army, pursued them on Mid-Lent Sunday as far as the estate called Fornellos. There, beginning a most fierce battle against them, he was struck by the arrow of Saint Reodesind’s curse and was killed when chance intervened, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, Era 1006. [Note: [Col. 0897D] (28) The parchment codex has Era 1006. Others wrongly have 1016.]

7. Pelagius, son of Count Rodrigo Velázquez, took up after Sisnand the dignity of this episcopate by secular power. He neither exercised care for the honour he had assumed nor humbled himself, as he ought, before his Creator in the valley of this pilgrimage through lamentation born of heavenly desires. Therefore, since divine providence was unwilling for the Church to be unjustly occupied by him any longer, he was expelled by King Bermudo [Note: [Col. 0898D] (29) The matters we wrote concerning Pelagius in the preceding volume should likewise be consulted.].

8. In his place Peter of Mosonzo, namely abbot of *Ante altaria*, was appointed through the grace of divine providence. Terrified by fear of the strict judgment, he began most bitterly to chastise the stains of his filthiness through the laments of penitence and to raise himself into lofty contemplation of God. Moved by this man’s holiness and religion, and by the love of heavenly fear, King Bermudo ordered that everything the Church [Col. 0897D] of Saint James had lost in the times of all the bishops should be wholly restored to this most reverend man.

Meanwhile Rodrigo Velázquez, father of the aforesaid bishop, together with the other leading men of this land, brought the Saracens with their leader Almanzor into these parts. Arriving at Compostela, they utterly destroyed the greater part of the walls of the church of Saint James, except for its most holy altar. Saint James, therefore, wishing that they should not escape unpunished from his church, which they had crushed beneath the foot of such great arrogance, struck them with so severe a disease of dysentery that, when a great many of them had died, very few returned home. When their leader Almanzor, reflecting inwardly, saw his people struck so severely by the peril of such vengeance, he is said to have asked his guides who was the man whose court had almost been destroyed by their assault. Learning from their answer that James, one of the disciples of the Son of the Virgin Mary—whose name among them, “behold, is called Mary”—was most certainly buried there, and repenting of such audacity, he stubbornly took flight. While fleeing, he was struck by sudden illness and died at Medina Celim, where he was buried; and he unhappily commended his soul to the bosom of Muhammad.

The king, aroused by the spur of heavenly love, came to this city with earnest purpose and, with the assistance of God, restored with Bishop Peter the church of this Apostle, which he found ruined. After the restored church had been consecrated, Bishop Peter fell asleep in the Lord.

9. Thereupon Pelagius Díaz, supported by temporal power, usurped after him the dignity of pastoral care. Because, under the cover of so great a prelacy, he swelled with the vice of pride, he was disgracefully cast down by the princes of the land through divine judgment. His brother Vimara Díaz succeeded him; because under the pretext of religion he strove to serve not God but his own glory, he was drowned in the river Miño, whether by accident or by treachery. [Col. 0898C] Instruarius, taking up the pontifical office after him, so trampled underfoot the teaching of holy life by evil conduct that, as his merits required, he was placed in bonds by King Bermudo and paid the debt of nature in the Era [Note: [Col. 0898D] (30) There is no blank space here; but the author undoubtedly intended to state the year of the Era.].

10. Gresconius, born of a most noble family, shone with the brightness of such nobility that, through the prudent valour of his soldiery, he utterly exterminated the Northmen who had invaded this land. He constructed buildings of walls and towers to fortify the city of Compostela. When, after completing the church of Saint Mary which he himself, God assisting, had made, the end of his life was already approaching, he arrived at the castle of Honesti, which he had built for the defence of Christendom; there he was overtaken by the onset of dreaded death in Era 1106.

11. Gudesteus, his nephew, was raised to the summit of the episcopate after him. Because he wished, according to the strictness of his predecessor, to advance the dignities and honours of this apostolic church to a condition of rectitude, many violent conflicts of dissension arose between him and his uncle Count Froila. As they were accustomed to be at one time reconciled and at another at variance, one day, after peace between them had been confirmed by an oath of faith, Count Froila sent his messengers deceitfully to Iria, [Col. 0899A] where the lord bishop was observing the sacred days of the forty-day fast, ostensibly to speak with him. Received kindly by him, they sat at his table to take food and, as though they were members of his household, lay down to sleep in the same chamber with him. While the bishop slept, they arose in the night, went out through the doors with silent steps, came to the grove where that most impious Froila, mentioned above, lay hidden with his army, and then emerged thence gradually and stealthily with him. Rushing in through the door of the chamber where he lay asleep, they tore him to pieces with impious cruelty in Era 1107 [Note: [Col. 0899D] (31) See below, Book II, chapter 55.].

12. Thereafter Diego Peláez was elevated to the same see by King Sancho. In his time the Toledo rite was abolished among the Spaniards and the Roman rite received. This Diego flourished for a long time in this present life in nobility and high birth. Yet he was so entangled in outward concerns that he did not, as he should, subject his inward intention to the rule of the ecclesiastical habit. Therefore, as his merits required, he was captured by King Alfonso and remained in chains for fifteen years [Note: [Col. 0899D] (32) See Book II, chapters 2 and 55.].

## CHAPTER III. The promotion of Peter, monk of the monastery of Cardeña, to Bishop of Compostela
1. Meanwhile, King Alfonso, a Catholic man, having perceived in his inmost reflection that the Church of the most blessed Apostle, placed in danger of widowhood, could in no way remain unharmed unless fortified by pastoral oversight, strove to raise another to the pontifical chair of the church of St. James. Accordingly, while Richard, cardinal and legate of the holy Roman Church, was holding a council at Saint Mary of Fusellos, King Alfonso himself was present and ordered the aforesaid bishop, whom he had long caused to be committed to chains, to come to the council as though released, though still under guard: namely, so that he might depose him from pontifical rank. Then the aforesaid bishop, through fear of the king and hope of release, submitted to the adverse judgment of the Roman cardinal; and before the whole council, declaring himself unworthy of the episcopate, he returned the ring and pastoral staff to the cardinal. The cardinal, however, granted permission for another—namely Peter, abbot of Cardeña—to be enthroned in the pontifical chair of the Church of St. James. After this the same bishop, although burdened by the judgment against him, was nevertheless again committed to the king’s custody.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] (33) The commonly published Council of Fusellos was convened in the year 1088 [Col. 0900D].]

[Note: [Col. 0900D] (34) Today, Cardeña.]

Therefore, when these matters were afterward discussed at Rome, the aforesaid Richard, cardinal and legate of the holy Roman Church, was pierced by the dart of disgrace and ignominy. Pope Urban and the holy Roman Church severely rebuked and censured him, because he had burdened the aforesaid bishop of Compostela, who had been committed to custody, with an adverse judgment and had unjustly deposed him. Accordingly, he too was deprived of the legation in which he had presumed to do such things. King Alfonso, however, by the common counsel of the wise men of Spain, placed over this apostolic Church a certain Peter, abbot of the monastery of Cardeña. After governing the flock entrusted to him, he remained two years in the episcopate; but because he had been advanced to the height of so great an honour without the consent of our mother, the holy Roman Church, he was justly and canonically deposed at a council held at León by Cardinal Ranier, who afterward became pope in the city of Rome and took the name Paschal.

### On the stewardship which followed during his absence

For a certain parishioner of the Church of St. James, Peter Vimara by name, a layman and royal steward, received from the hand of the most holy King Alfonso the entire estate and jurisdiction which the bishop had held [Col. 0900B], and returned to his own place. There he continually exercised such cruelty in plundering poor and rich alike that, devastating and destroying everything in the manner of an enemy, he laid all waste. Since he presumed that he would relentlessly melt down and seize everything, he most wickedly sought the favour of certain persons and consented to allow the land called in our language Montanos, a certain castle of Saint George, and a certain part of that parish called Cordarium, to be wholly taken away from our patron, St. James.

After that man’s deposition, and after the most venerable Count Raymond had taken in marriage the most august daughter of the Catholic King Alfonso, Arias Díaz was made *majorinus*—chief royal officer—of this land. Being cruel and inflamed with the most ardent greed, he greedily seized and destroyed with thirsty mind whatever he could extort and plunder. Thus both powerful and powerless, crushed under the most intolerable burden of such affliction, remained in the sharpest distress until his death. The canons of this Church, who ought to have been stewards of ecclesiastical dignity, then fell into such want that, bound by the chains of poverty, they lacked by every means even food for bodily sustenance within the canonical house itself. What is especially shameful and grievously lamentable: clad in the cheapest and various garments, as though strangers to the whole discipline of ecclesiastical custom, they sang God’s praises disorderly in choir [Col. 0900D].

### The author’s words

Obeying with willing and devoted mind the commands of Lord Diego, second bishop of the see of Compostela, I have thus far committed to writing, as truthfully as I could, the deeds of his predecessors. Now, with divine grace going before me, I shall undertake to describe and recall for the memory of posterity the successes which this reverend bishop enjoyed in this office; the adversities which he manfully endured in it; and those things which, with the Lord’s aid, he wisely and judiciously accomplished for the honour of God and the benefit of his Church.

Our help is in the name of the Lord.

Who made heaven and earth. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV. On the elevation of Diego Gelmírez

Count Lord Raymond, a capable and prudent man, grieving for the Church of Compostela, which, as we have explained above, had not been ordered according to the institutions of the canons, addressed certain elders and the people of this Church, not without consulting four bishops—Peter of Lugo, Gonzalo of Mondoñedo, Auderic of Tui, and Peter of Ourense—out of inward compassion, saying:

> “Go, and take counsel for yourselves: whomever you wish to ask from me, you may, by God’s mercy, now have as protector and defender.”

Hearing this, they took counsel apart. Then all the leading men of Galicia came together before Lord Raymond and, standing in his presence, unanimously asked him with the utmost entreaties for a certain cleric, Diego Gelmírez by name, an honourable man of great prudence. They recalled that his father had governed Iria and the neighbouring district—namely, the country between the two rivers Ulla and Tambre—with remarkable discernment, the greatest firmness of administration, and for many years.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] (35) His father was called Gelmírez. See Book II, chapter 2.]

Yielding from his very heart to their request, the venerable count set Lord Diego, canon of the Church of St. James, over the whole land and estate of the most reverend Apostle James. He had honourably retained Diego in his court as his chancellor and secretary, by the hand and permission of all the canons.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] (36) The term *secretarius*, denoting the office and dignity of the official who dealt with confidential matters at court, was already in use at that time [Col. 0902D].]

Supported by the light of an unconquerable purpose and aided by the prudent counsel of noble men, he began to restore what had been destroyed, preserve what had been restored, and, by much labour, bring what had been preserved almost to a condition of proper order.

## CHAPTER V. On Dalmatius, monk of Cluny, promoted bishop of Compostela

Moreover, after the passage of one year, the venerable King Alfonso, his son-in-law Lord Raymond, and his wife, the most noble Lady Urraca, by the counsel of the clergy and people of St. James and with the authority of the holy Roman Church, made bishop of the Church of Compostela, with God’s help, a monk of the Cluniac observance named Dalmatius: a chaste and religious man, with the blessing and permission of his abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] (37) Almost always this name, and others, is indicated only by its initial letter.]

Finding the see like an uncultivated vineyard, he devoted himself with most ardent love to the advantage of the holy Church, according to the model of holy teaching that he knew. For when Pope Urban, the most provident bishop of the holy Roman Church, was holding a council at Clermont, this religious Dalmatius appeared before the pope at that council with certain bishops of the same province, who, joined to him by brotherly love, adhered to his holiness. There, greatly honoured by all, he obtained from the pope by the most earnest prayers this privilege, set down in the following text, which none of his predecessors had been able to obtain; he secured it together with the following letters concerning the confraternity of this Church.

### Liberty of the Church of Compostela

“Urban, bishop,” etc.

“Of the ancient synodal …,” etc. See Urban II under the year 1099, *Patrologia*, vol. 151, col. 440, no. 000.

## CHAPTER VI. The death of Bishop Dalmatius, and the second elevation of Diego Gelmírez

Returning adorned with so great a gift, he adorned the Church of Compostela with the strength of liberty. But because no one endures whom death seeks to overthrow, eight days suffice for grief to consume us. Therefore the clergy, who believed that after so many dangers and tribulations they had reached a haven of peace, saw themselves tossed hither and thither amid such storms, as a ship is often driven from shore into the midst of the sea when a tempest arises.

Yet the mercy of almighty God, which according to the ordering of its providence extends to shipwrecked men, when their vessel is broken, the hand of perfect consolation, divinely moved our Catholic ruler, King Alfonso, and his most pious son-in-law Count Raymond with his wife Lady Urraca, mercifully to draw them back from such continual assaults to a harbour of tranquility. How this occurred is set forth in proper order.

The clergy and people of the Church of St. James, not forgetful of all the benefits which Lord Diego Gelmírez had first conferred upon them, laboured to knock with such urgent petition at the door of mercy of the aforesaid princes that they obtained the same Lord Diego from their favour as governor and lord.

## CHAPTER VII. The removal of the first Diego from the episcopate

The aforesaid Bishop Diego Peláez, now released from the king’s custody, heard that the most holy Bishop Dalmatius had paid nature’s debt and that another held the whole estate and jurisdiction—not with pontifical dignity, but with viceregal authority for the time being. He hastened to Rome and there complained with insistent cries that he had unjustly lost pontifical dignity and had suffered violence.

Thus it came about that after Lord Dalmatius’s death, this Church, placed amid diverse straits, remained for four years with the matter unresolved. During those four continuous years Lord Diego Gelmírez, as vicar, governed the whole estate and jurisdiction of this Church by the common counsel and consent of good men.

At last, divine mercy inspiring and providence persuading toward the common good, the most excellent King Alfonso, wishing to settle the case of the aforesaid dispute, which had been pursued through so long a delay, sent his envoys to Rome with clerics of this Church to lay out and argue his case against the same Diego Peláez, who was still unjustly bringing accusations against him. They arrived at Rome with pious intention and found Pope Urban, of blessed memory, to whom they had been sent, dead, and Paschal already substituted in his office on 15 August 1099. Before gaining the papacy, Paschal had been called Ranier and had already served as legate in Spain; he knew with complete certainty the whole of this dispute and the calamity of the Church of St. James.

Therefore the most reverend Paschal, bishop of the holy Roman Church, listened most attentively with the open ear of his heart to their arguments and objections, carefully discerned the substance of so great a disturbance, and, justice declaring it, judged Diego Peláez unworthy of the presidency of so great a dignity. Thus this Church, which for fifteen years had remained almost sickly in the aforesaid miseries, was mercifully liberated by the Lord. The same pope sent the following letters to our venerable king and to the clergy and people of St. James.

### To the king, concerning the liberation of the Church of Compostela

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“Your petition …,” etc. See Paschal under the year 1118, *Patrologia*, vol. 163, no. 4.

### To the clergy and people of the Church of Compostela, on the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“Since for so long …,” etc. See above, no. 5.

## CHAPTER VIII. Postponement of the election

Although these commanding letters permitted us to hold the long-desired election, we deferred it in every way until the return of our provost, Lord Diego Gelmírez, who had visited the threshold of St. Peter for prayer and there was promoted to the order of subdeacon. Since we knew his life and character, and after seeing the following letters of the lord pope, we elected him bishop—though unwilling and resisting—with the leading men of all Galicia, and with the assent of King Alfonso and Count Raymond, who were present with us and approved [Col. 0903D].

### The ordination at Rome of the aforesaid Lord Diego as subdeacon

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“Diego of your Church …,” etc. See above, no. 11.

## CHAPTER IX. His election and consecration

With the Lord’s assent, the aforesaid Diego was elected bishop on the coming Kalends of July, in the year 1138 of the Spanish Era (A.D. 1100), and was consecrated bishop on the coming Easter, eleven days before the Kalends of May. Great joy therefore arose in our Church.

[Note: [Col. 0903] (38) See below, Book II, chapter 2, on the bishops who were present at his election.]

After his election he went with many persons of this Church to Toledo, where King Alfonso was. There he was received by the archbishop of Toledo with a great procession. Returning thence, greatly honoured by royal favour, he recovered with the king’s vicar, God helping, a certain portion of the properties and rights which the Church of St. James had unjustly lost in the times of its predecessors (A.D. 1101). Since we knew that this elect was to be consecrated at Rome according to the privilege of his predecessor Lord Dalmatius, we grieved deeply, with unbroken sighs, lest he should perhaps be captured through the deceitful plots of his enemies on his journey there or back.

For Diego Peláez, the former bishop, and his relatives were staying with Lord Peter, king of the Aragonese, through whose kingdom the elect had to pass. Therefore the glorious King Alfonso and the Church of St. James by no means allowed him to go to Rome for consecration, fearing for him the danger of capture by the enemies just mentioned. Accordingly, having requested letters of entreaty from our lord King Alfonso, we sent two of our canons with them to the pope, that he might permit the elect to be consecrated among us. They received these letters, but Lord Hugh was weighed down by illness, while the other, Vincent, went the way of all flesh.

### On the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“To the destruction of the Church of Compostela …,” etc. See above, no. 25.

### Likewise on the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“May your brotherhood know …,” etc. See above, no. 41.

### Likewise on the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“As concerning your …,” etc. See above, no. 26.

## CHAPTER X. Likewise on the same matter

And because one envoy had already died and the other was oppressed by the full weight of sickness, we were utterly unable to obtain the foregoing letters, by whose authority our elect was to be consecrated. Therefore I myself, Munio Alfonso, and another Munio Gelmírez, brother of the same bishop, were sent to Rome by the canons of this Church with repeated letters from our most holy emperor. We went diligently and, by divine mercy intervening, brought back with the utmost labour these letters, copied in a fuller collection.

### Likewise on the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“To the destitution of your Church …,” etc. See above, no. 42.

### Likewise on the same matter

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“In the past autumn …,” etc. See above, no. 43.

## CHAPTER XI. Confirmation of liberty

After his consecration, this bishop, in accordance with the prophet Ezekiel, brought back what he knew had been driven away from the flock entrusted to him; what he found broken, he bound up as best he could; and he laboured with provident diligence to raise the Church to the height of most worthy liberty.

In the first year of his pontificate, before I was made treasurer, he carefully sent me and a certain Geoffrey, archdeacon, to Rome, so that the most holy Pope Paschal, successor to Urban, the Roman bishop of holy memory, might confirm with the strength of his authority the privilege of liberty which his predecessor Dalmatius had obtained from Urban for the Church; and that in confirming it, he might provide certain benefits useful to our Church. While we were there in a time of peace, aided by the assistance of the cardinals, we caused the privilege of so great a liberty to be copied from its exemplar, had it more firmly confirmed, and brought back with it the following letters.

## CHAPTER XII. Confirmation of the diocese, liberty, and vows of Compostela

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“The order of justice and reason …,” etc. See above, no. 56.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the cardinals

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“The Church which you are to govern …,” etc. See under Paschal.

## CHAPTER XIV. For obtaining liberty for the parishes of the see of Compostela

Again inflamed by love for St. James and stirred by the fragrance of this earlier success, he sent two of our canons, Hugh and Diego, to Rome for the honour and reverence of his Church. Receiving from them on their return the letters subscribed below, he left them to his successors.

### Liberty of the Church of Compostela

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“As unjust …,” etc. See above, no. 93.

## CHAPTER XV. When he visited Portugal

Therefore, lest he should in any way, so far as human capacity allowed, depart from the saying, “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly,” he laboured most vigilantly in everything he could, lest, through an insidious attachment to this present life, his mind should be buried beneath a mound of earthly thought. Accordingly, when inflamed by divine grace he entered the regions of Portugal, he accomplished with the Lord’s help whatever is read in what follows.

### Translation to Compostela of St Fructuosus, Silvester, Cucufas, and Susanna, virgin and martyr

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102, the venerable Father Diego II, by divine grace bishop of the Church of St. James of the see of Compostela, resolved in the second year of his episcopate to visit, as was right, the churches, cells, and estates in the Portuguese district which were known to belong by right to the Church of Compostela. For it belongs to a good shepherd to provide both for the external goods and the inward affairs of his Church; and if he finds in them any loss or disorder, to restore and set it in order by his oversight.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] (39) He placed above a bull dated 1103, because it followed another obtained in 1102, as appears from his words in the preceding chapter: “Stirred by the fragrance of this earlier success [of the year 1102],” etc. Now the narrative returns to the bishop’s deeds in that same year, 1102.]

He therefore took with him some of the leading persons of his Church and set his course toward Portugal. As they approached the city called Braga, he sent ahead his messenger to announce his arrival to the archbishop of that city. The archbishop, named Gerald, a prudent and religious man, heard that the bishop of St. James was coming to his city. Filled with great joy, he gathered all his clergy, went out to meet him with the citizens and the other ornaments of his church, received the bishop of Compostela into procession with great veneration, and, while the clergy sang, led him by the right hand into his church. He earnestly obtained from him permission to celebrate Mass there that day.

After Mass, the archbishop honourably escorted the bishop to the table for refreshment; after the meal he escorted him also to his own private chamber, offered him his own lodging, and himself went to stay in another residence. Thus the bishop of St. James spent that day with the archbishop of Braga. On the following day, after greeting and blessing the brethren of that Church, the aforesaid bishop, accompanied by the archbishop, went to the church of St Victor, of which one half is said to belong to the jurisdiction of the city of Braga; and he was received as lord into its royal palaces.

Meanwhile, as he went around and visited his churches and celebrated the solemnities of Mass in them, he saw the bodies of many saints, half-buried in those places and deprived of due honour. He groaned with pious feeling, and pondered devoutly in his heart, with zeal for piety, that which he afterward fulfilled with divine assistance. For with fervent zeal he considered how he might remove precious pearls from unsuitable places and bring them to the city of Compostela.

He therefore summoned his familiar clerics and trusted counsellors, disclosed what and how he wished to act, and said:

> “Dearest brothers, you know that we have come to these regions so that, if anything in these churches or estates had been destroyed or disordered, our presence might restore and set it in order, and might change what had been ill placed into a better condition. Now your diligence does not fail to see what unsuitable things are found in them. For you observe that very many bodies of saints lie scattered through them, honoured by no cult, naked and exposed to public view; and you know that they lack the veneration due to them. If, therefore, your wisdom counsels us to do so, we shall take care to remedy this and shall endeavour to transfer to the see of Compostela certain bodies of precious saints to whom no cult is here paid. Yet this must be done secretly, lest perhaps the undisciplined people of this land, despoiled of so great a treasure, raise a sudden uprising against us, and we grieve that we have attempted in vain what we dare to undertake.”

When his clerics approved this counsel, affirming that a counsel born of divine inspiration ought not to be deferred, the venerable bishop, filled with the greatest joy of mind, answered:

> “May the Lord Jesus Christ, in whose mercy we trust, in his goodness fulfil what we desire and deign to bring the devotion of our purpose to a good end.”

Then, entering the church of St Victor and celebrating Mass there, he ordered digging at the right side of the high altar. Immediately beneath the ground a marble chest, wonderfully and delicately fashioned, was found. When they opened it in the bishop’s presence, they found two silver caskets within. The aforesaid bishop received them with great fear and, glorifying the Lord’s name with psalms and prayers, opened them. In one he showed relics of our Lord and Saviour; in the other, relics of very many saints. He then entrusted them, closed and firmly sealed, to his faithful clerics to guard.

On another day he went to the church of Blessed Susanna, virgin and martyr, which is not far from the church of St Victor, and celebrated Mass there with the greatest devotion. After Mass, still vested in his sacred garments, he approached with trembling mind the tombs of the martyrs Cucufas and Silvester, who rested in the same church. He secretly removed their glorious bodies, wrapped in clean linen, from unsuitable sarcophagi, caused them to be carried with great reverence by suitable and faithful ministers to his chamber, without the knowledge of others, and had them faithfully guarded. When he came likewise to the tomb of St Susanna the virgin, he took her venerable body with weeping, tears, and sighs, and entrusted it to be secretly guarded with the others.

Moreover, the man of God, recognizing that divine mercy had granted him the task of honouring the bodies of saints, determined similarly to transfer and place more fittingly the glorious bodily remains of Blessed Fructuosus, confessor and bishop. Two days later they came to the church of Blessed Fructuosus, where he solemnly celebrated Mass. When Mass was finished, vested in sacred garments, he approached Fructuosus’s tomb. But because St Fructuosus was defender and patron of that region, the bishop removed him in greater fear and silence from his own church, which Fructuosus himself had built while still living in the flesh. This he did by a pious theft; and having removed him, he entrusted him to his faithful guardians for safekeeping.

Although no one knew of this deed except those privy to the plan, the bishop could by no means sleep securely on the following night, for he feared to lose what he rejoiced to possess. But when day came and he learned that what he had done had not been disclosed, he joyfully and gladly carried his hidden treasure away, hastening back as though beginning a flight to a village of St. James called Corneliana.

At Corneliana, the rumour of the people struck the bishop’s ears: it was reported that the bishop of St. James was committing an unworthy crime, attempting to transfer to his own city saints carried away from Portuguese land—the defenders and patrons, that is, of their native country. Hearing this, the man of highest prudence and exceptional piety feared that, by some occasion or violence, he might lose the precious burden. He entrusted the saints’ bodies to a faithful archdeacon and instructed him in prudent words how to convey them by hidden paths to the city of Tui.

While the bishop remained at Corneliana, the archdeacon, travelling as he had commanded, successfully reached the River Minho, which flows beside Tui. For three days the river had been so violently disturbed by harsh storms that no boats could cross it. But after the saints’ bodies had been placed on the riverbank, the river seemed to perceive their reverence. The violence of the heavy wind was removed, the turbulence of the air disappeared, and the river is said to have afforded, for conveying the saints across, as great an opportunity for crossing as its level water could provide. Its waves having been calmed, it bore such great tranquility that not even a small ripple stirred it.

Having brought the saints across by the river’s calm, they placed them in the monastery of St Bartholomew, situated in the suburb of the city of Tui. Leaving with them a certain deacon, a canon of St James the Apostle, for faithful custody, the archdeacon returned to the bishop at Corneliana and reported to him everything that had happened on the journey and where he had left God’s saints. Then, by the bishop’s command, the deacon whom we said had been appointed guardian reverently brought the aforesaid saints to the church of St Peter of Cella, which Blessed Fructuosus had built. There, while awaiting the bishop for ten days, he rendered them due veneration.

When the bishop heard that the saints had now crossed the River Minho and had been placed in a safe place—for this river separates Portuguese territory from Galicia—he prepared everything that needed to be prepared and hastened to the monastery where the saints had been placed. Taking them from there, he began to return, now openly, through the villages of St James, with great reverence and joy, to the city of Compostela.

When he reached the village called Gosgildum, he sent messengers ahead to the clergy and people of Compostela, to announce the saints’ arrival and, by the bishop’s command, instruct them how they ought to receive them. The clergy and people of Compostela, hearing that divine mercy had permitted the bodies of saints to be transferred from Braga to the city of Compostela, rejoiced greatly. They understood that through the saints’ merits and intercession, as well as through the most merciful patronage of St James the Apostle, by the presence of whose most holy body the city of Compostela is made illustrious, they would be freed from every plague and from the weakness of diseases.

Therefore the clergy, going out barefoot to meet them, followed by all the people of the city, made a religious procession as far as the place called Humiliatorium. When the bishop arrived there and ordered both himself and those with him to remove their shoes, the clerics, clothed in sacred vestments and barefoot according to his arrangement, received the glorious bodies of the saints. With the crowds following behind them, and with the bishop leading, they carried them into their city with hymns, songs, and pious devotion, and placed them in the church of St James the Apostle of the see of Compostela.

The body of St Fructuosus, confessor and bishop, was placed at the altar of the Holy Saviour in the principal crypt of that church. Yet after four years had passed, the aforesaid bishop and his clerics judged it better to make a proper dwelling for Blessed Fructuosus, whom they had taken from his own abode. Accordingly, in his honour an altar was built and dedicated, and the same bishop consecrated it in the left side of the same church, in the crypt between the gate leading into the cloister and the altar of St James. There the body of Blessed Fructuosus was placed and interred, and there it rests, as in its proper seat, glorious in miracles unto everlasting day.

The altar of St John the Apostle and Evangelist received the holy martyr Cucufas; and the body of St Silvester the martyr was interred at the altar of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul in the body of the same church. Blessed Susanna, virgin and martyr, rests honourably placed in the church known to have been founded in honour of the Holy Sepulchre and All Saints, in a place formerly called *Uterium puldrorum*.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] (40) Henschenius printed *ante altare Sepulcrorum* (“before the altar of the Sepulchres”). But *Auterium pullorum* should better be retained, which in Spanish may be called *Otero de Potros* (“Hill of Foals”); for fairs for young horses are held there. See the remarks in the preceding volume under this year. Below, chapter 116, *pullorum*, not *puldrorum*, is written [Col. 0910D].]

I, Hugh, canon and archdeacon of the same see of Compostela, who was privy to the aforesaid secret and was personally present as a most faithful adviser and diligent collaborator, devoted in mind, in the discovery of so great and precious a treasure and in the administration of what was discovered, have diligently written the prosperity of the aforesaid event, lest it should sleep in the darkness of forgetfulness, and have faithfully handed its memory down to posterity.

The translated bodies of the saints, therefore, as stated above, were placed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVI. When he went to Rome for the pallium

Furthermore, not long afterward, the same venerable bishop, bearing infinite concern for the ministry and dignity of the holy Church, visited with most humble affection the presence of our Catholic emperor, Lord King Alfonso, accompanied by the most noble persons of this Church. Whatever beneficial measure suitable for his Church he remembered having laid up in the treasury of his heart, he set forth before the king’s discerning ears. As they spoke together of various matters, they quietly arranged that the bishop himself, strengthened by confidence in divine mercy, should go to Rome with certain of his canons in order to obtain a certain dignity; and that, lest he suffer any harm brought upon him by the king’s enemies, he should travel by secret detours.

The aforesaid bishop displayed such prudence in carrying out these matters that he departed from none of the things arranged there with our most holy king, and allowed the eminence of his dignity to be lowered in no way except through the intervention of holy humility. Before he left the region of Campania—the district inhabited by the ancient Vaccaei, which is still called in the native tongue *tierra de Campos*—Bishop G. of Burgos received him most honourably with a great procession and did not cease to serve him most generously, as far as he was able, throughout the parishes of his episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0910D] (41) By “Campania” he means the district inhabited by the ancient Vaccaei, still called in its native speech *tierra de Campos*.]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] (42) The bishop of Burgos at that time was named García.]

After he had crossed the Pyrenees, surrounded by many suitable persons, both clerics and knights, and had entered the regions of Gascony to the honour and safety of our Church, he was so affectionately honoured by the leading men of those lands and by others that, even if the description of my incompetence were not as dull as you see, it could in no way adequately convey it.

### On honours and processions

As flying fame spread these things everywhere through those regions, the most noble archbishop of Auch came out to meet him on the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary. This feast is annually celebrated by the inhabitants of those parts with a more particular devotion than other feasts. He received the bishop honourably with the greatest procession. There too, on that same day, although exhausted by travel, Diego was compelled by the many prayers of the archbishop and all the canons to celebrate the principal Mass. According as the grace of the Holy Spirit gave him strength, he nourished with the food of holy preaching the multitude of people who had gathered from various places for the feast. Therefore, joined to the archbishop and nearly all the worthy men present by an indissoluble bond of affection, he left the city after the third day with still greater veneration.

### Likewise on the same matter
Thence, lingering for some time through the territories and estates of blessed James, he entered Toulouse with the highest honour. And when, by God’s providence, he learned there that certain enemies of the aforesaid emperor, Lord A., had laid snares for him, he sent ahead to Rome myself, Munio, and the archdeacon of this Church, named Geoffrey. He himself, proceeding by byways with his other clerics—namely Archdeacon Oduarius, Hugh the cardinal-chaplain, Peter Anajade, Peter Pelagiade, and many others—and with his knights, reached, with the Lord’s help, the monastery of Saint Peter of Moissac, as though a harbour of tranquillity. There, having been worthily and laudably received with the rite of a sacred procession, he set out with certain prelates of that same monastery to visit the city of Cahors. Its bishop, indeed, troubled by news already brought to him of his arrival, hastened with prudent diligence to prepare whatever was fitting for a man of such consequence, and joyfully received him as he approached with due reverence.

## Again concerning the same man

Leaving there, he came to the monastery of Saint Peter of Uzerche, where he was received no less honourably by the religious monks and the abbot who were there. Thus, as we have explained above, honoured everywhere by all, he faithfully came to Limoges, where the body of Saint Martial is truly known to be. There he was honoured with such reverence that, even if it may be fully conceived in the human heart, it can be expressed only inadequately by the mouth. Yet if, in accordance with what actually occurred, we carefully weigh each of the subsequent acts of service later rendered to Salvinus, bishop of Compostela, at Saint Leonard’s and Saint Valeria’s, we see beyond doubt that those things mentioned above were lesser.

## The same concerning the same man

When the aforesaid bishop, distinguished by so many and such great sacred honours, came to Cluny—the head, that is, of all monastic religion—he was received more intimately and especially amid processions of various orders, by the blessedness of that most holy congregation which we believe truly to be there by divine appointment. For just as we know that Cluny surpasses nearly all monasteries in the quality of its holy observance and in the number and splendour of its dignity, so we recognize that its charity toward all who come is overflowing and most ready.

Therefore that venerable bishop was so bound to the most holy abbot and his holy congregation by a kind of privilege of love that, seeking counsel from the lord abbot concerning the reason for undertaking so great a journey, he poured the matter into his ears. Struck by the hearing of so grave a business, the abbot began to turn over within the recess of his mind, as though repeatedly pondering the remarkable things he had heard; and, in reflecting, he disclosed to him the following matters, which had been hidden from the bishop of Compostela:

“When Lord Urban, most beloved in Christ—who had first been a monk of Cluny and afterward became pope of the holy Roman Church—held a council at Clermont, our son Lord Dalmachius, as your charity knows, the religious bishop of the Church of blessed James, came from the city of Compostela and attended that council. There, together with many religious bishops, he earnestly entreated the lord pope for the dignity of the pallium, to name the matter more explicitly. Yet, although both were associates of our congregation, he obtained nothing from his favour and suffered a refusal.

“Another impediment also threatens which I have known for a long time to have greatly harmed your Church, most reverend brother. For at a certain time, when one of the cardinals of the Roman Church entered Galicia as legate, he sent messengers ahead to the bishop of Compostela, that he might render the obedience due to him as his subject and receive him reverently with the rite of a sacred procession. Hearing these words which he was to receive with a deaf ear, and taking them ill, he is said to have answered them, not with religious courtesy, thus: ‘Go,’ he said, ‘to the cardinals of this Church, and let them show to the cardinals of the Roman Church as much obedience and honour as the Roman cardinals, in return, are afterward to show at Rome.’

> **Note:** [Col. 0911D] (43) Another manuscript reads *exhibitum est* (“has been shown”), and shortly above has *prius a Rom. cardinalib.* (“previously by the Roman cardinals”). From this it seems preferable to read: “as much as has previously been shown to them by the Roman cardinals in return at Rome,” that is, the past being compensated by the present, rather than present service being performed for the future—something not within the power of the person rendering obedience. So also below, book II, chapter 1.

“Therefore, when the Roman Church, which is the head and model of all Churches, heard this, it decreed by common resolution that the Church of Compostela should no longer be raised up with its consent. I greatly fear, dearest son, that these matters stated above will oppose your petition. These things continually trouble my mind; and I would wish them to be entirely removed from the stubborn memory of the cardinals of the Roman Church through the merits and intercessions of Peter, prince of the apostles, and blessed James. But you, supported by the shelter of the patronage of blessed James, do not refuse to visit your mother, the holy Roman Church, as you have now begun to do; and lest perhaps the lord pope should decline to grant your petition, attempt to obtain the aforesaid dignity, not through yourself, but through your clerics.”

Giving credence to these words, the aforesaid bishop, moved by their prayers, celebrated the principal Mass in their community on the feast of Saint Michael. This most reverend minister of the Church of Compostela also, instructed by the piety of fear and living amid ecclesiastical affairs in the form of holy humility, restrained by the spiritual governance of his mind whatever carnal thing he perceived in himself to need correction. With the sincere discernment of reason he diligently sought the repose of eternal peace; and, in seeking that repose, he divinely obtained from the lord abbot the favour that, after his death, an anniversary observance and a trental should be held there for him in perpetuity.

## CHAPTER XVII. Again concerning the same man

Then, strengthened by the blessings of the holy congregation, he reached, with the Lord’s help, through the cells and estates of Cluniac obediences as far as the valleys of Maurienne. There Count Humbert also received him honourably and conducted him with the greatest reverence as far as the city of Susa.

> **Note:** [Col. 0913D] (44) Another reading: *Seusia*. I read *Setia*, a city in papal territory.

There, because of fear of the German emperor, who at that time had laid ambushes for those going to the lord pope, he put on military dress and made his way to Rome through various hardships. When he entered the sacred palace, the lord pope received him with such deep-hearted affection—for no bishop of this Church had voluntarily been at Rome—that, if we consider more carefully, we judge that he received very few in this way. And, lest we weary ourselves by recounting every detail, let us, setting aside all digression, come to those things which we obtained there by continual prayers over the space of ten days.

Accordingly, the venerable bishop, not forgetting any of the matters which the lord abbot of Cluny had made known to him, sought the dignity of the pallium from the lord pope through his clerics, with the intervention of all the cardinals; nor did he labour fruitlessly to obtain the pope’s assent to his petition. At last, with heavenly grace cooperating, he devoutly received in the church of Saint Lawrence, from the altar, according to Roman custom, the pallium which he had greatly desired, trusting in God’s mercy; and by the following privilege he granted it to the Church of Saint James in perpetuity.

## Grant of the pallium

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“The body of the apostle James,” etc. See above, no. 121.

## Obedience promised to Pope P.

The aforesaid bishop promised Pope P. the following obedience:

“From this hour onward I shall be faithful to Saint Peter, to the holy apostolic Roman Church, and to Lord Pope P. and his successors canonically elected. I shall not be party, in counsel or deed, to their losing life or limb, or being seized by an evil seizure. Any counsel which they shall entrust to me personally, by letter, or by messenger, I shall knowingly disclose to no one to their harm. I shall be an assistant in retaining the Roman papacy and the regalia of Saint Peter, saving my own order, against all persons. When summoned to a synod, I shall come unless prevented by necessity. I shall honourably receive a legate of the Apostolic See whom I know with certainty to be its legate. Every three years I shall visit the thresholds of the apostles, either personally or through my messenger, unless released by their permission. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the restoration of the altar of blessed James and of the others

Among the dignities with which the aforesaid bishop hastened, with untiring solicitude, to adorn his Church, we have taken care to preserve from the destruction of oblivion whatever his restoring hand accomplished at the altar of that Church, lest in future it be obscured by the cloud of ignorance. But lest, by recounting everything, we wander too far by indirect paths, let us direct our intention along a straight track, so that we may commit to the memory of posterity, as far as our ability permits, those things which we have seen with our own eyes.

The altar of Saint James, however small it may have been, may more truly be judged from the size of its little altar itself, lest we be deemed to speak too little truth. As religious devotion to the Christian profession increased in knowledge of the faith, the ancient memory of our forefathers has clearly informed us, both through the report of trustworthy words and through reliable documentary evidence, that another little altar, somewhat larger, was placed upon it by worshippers of the holy faith.

But the aforesaid bishop, intensely concerned to increase the splendour of his Church, reflected with pious consideration that the little altar, now enlarged for the second time, was not at all worthy of so great an apostle and that the apostolic altar ought to be enlarged. Therefore, strengthened by the prudent counsel of religious men, he announced to the chapter of canons, who strongly opposed him in this matter, that he would demolish the structure built from the columns of the apostle in the likeness of a lower mausoleum, within which we know the most sacred relics of the apostle to be enclosed without any doubt. For with many arguments they maintained that a work built by the hands of such great men, although rough and ugly, ought by no means to be destroyed, lest they themselves or their lord, struck by the thunderbolt of heaven’s vengeance, should immediately suffer the perils of such audacity.

But he, like a valiant soldier armed with the impenetrable shield of his good judgment, perceived that they directed the eye of their discernment more to outward things than inward; trampling down their fear, he demolished the aforesaid structure to the ground with the foot of good intention. The altar, which had formerly been of modest size, he now enlarged for the third time, fitting marble stone over it on every side, as was proper. Around its excellent and very fine dimensions, without delay, he marvellously began and still more marvellously completed a silver frontal. He also had the pavement and the steps by which one ascends to the altar rebuilt in level work and adorned with every ornament.

> **Note:** [Col. 0913D] (45) This work was completed in the fifth year of his episcopate, namely 1105, as the verses engraved on the same sculpted silver plaque—now called the *Frontale*—testify. See the preceding volume.

His own sight revealed to human investigation also the ciborium, made by his order in a fitting variety of workmanship, in gold and silver, for the honour of the apostolic altar.

> **Note:** [Col. 0914D] (46) Elsewhere *ciborium*: namely, a covering and canopy of the altar, supported upon columns.

For when the altar had been constructed in the way already mentioned, it lay open on every side to human eyes; no hidden place remained in which the faithful might fulfil the vow of private prayer. Yet it was fitting and necessary for holy meditation that minds shining with the splendour of inward contemplation should cleanse in a secret place the stains of their conscience with a poured-out stream of tears, and, refreshed by the helps of holy prayer as by banquets of heavenly nourishment, return relieved of the poisonous burden of vices. Therefore the bishop began to apply himself to thought within the lodging of his mind and to strive with unwearied eagerness to make a confession at the altar. What size and character of confession he built between the two columns of the altar which support the ciborium is apparent when it offers a fortunate entrance to those who enter.

## CHAPTER XIX. Consecration of the altars; offerings granted to the hospital; and the church of the Holy Sepulchre

In that same work he caused all the surrounding altars, fittingly arranged by appropriate craftsmanship—those of Saint Mary Magdalene, the Saviour, Saint Peter, Saint Andrew, Saint Fructuosus, Saint John the Baptist, and, in the left wing, the altar of Saint John the Apostle and of the Holy Cross—to shine more splendidly with the ornament of divine nobility after he had anointed them with the sacred unction of chrism. Since his mind was fixed unchangeably upon contemplation of the heavenly homeland and he always burned with reciprocal charity, when asked by the prayers of Peter, bishop of Pamplona, he yielded to him, granting with great reverence the altar of the holy see for consecration.

After the consecration of all the altars, and the dedication of the altar of Saint Michael in the upper part, since we wish to proceed beyond the city, we must insert here, though not in their proper place, some matters which we have omitted: namely, concerning the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene and that of the Holy Cross, mentioned above. He granted to the hospital of pilgrims and the infirm one half of all alms offerings placed there by the faithful. This share he had indeed purchased at his own expense before obtaining episcopal consecration, and had enlarged more generously from his own resources.

Having noted these matters above, since he knew that the monastery of Piniario had been built, as already stated, through the enterprise of his predecessor, Bishop Sisnand of good memory, he diligently enlarged, together with Leovegild, minister of that church, the church of Saint Martin, almost destroyed already, for the use of monastic religious life; and, having enlarged it, he more diligently consecrated it. In the suburb of the same city he built the church of the Holy Sepulchre, made more splendid by the venerable body of Saint Susanna, which he had brought there from the city of Braga. When the solemnity of Paschal joy had been completed, he established by firm ordinance that a procession should be held to it annually on the following day, so that, when Mass had been solemnly celebrated there by the clergy and all the people of Compostela, each might cheerfully return home.

## CHAPTER XX. The church built and consecrated on Mount Joy; the episcopal palace; and the order and number of the canons

Finally, through the great diligence of the aforesaid prelate—whose purpose from almost his earliest cradle had always been both to build up what had been destroyed and to preserve what he built in such a condition that it should not collapse again—he consecrated, according to ecclesiastical custom, on the other side of the city, on Mount Joy, the church of the holy and venerable Cross, built in plain workmanship at his command. He ordained that at the completion of each year, on the Greater Litany, namely on the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist, whose sacred relics we venerate and honour in that place, both clergy and people should go there in procession, after the model of the Roman curia; and, after Mass had been solemnly celebrated by the bishop of the Apostolic See, all, refreshed with the food of eternal life, should return directly and in order to their homes in the same order in which they had first gone.

Moreover, after he ascended to the height of the episcopate, he found that the Church which, by God’s disposing grace, he had undertaken to govern had for a long time been deprived of the protection of its own shepherd. He could find there not merely no suitable and honourable dwelling for a bishop, but not even clerics, except crude men almost wholly undisciplined in ecclesiastical observance. Therefore, deeply moved within his heart, and having wisely adopted a sound plan, he began within the walls of the same city, beside the newly begun work of blessed James, a three-chambered throne with a tower, by his remarkable skill; and, with no slackening of speed, he brought it more fittingly to completion.

Then he laid out houses all around in a marvellous arrangement; there, vested with the pontifical mitre, he consecrated with the highest reverence a church marvellously built and still more marvellously painted. Because he administered external matters with fitting moderation and foresaw internal matters with a still keener intelligence of mind, preferring greater things to lesser, his overflowing generosity made for the canons a remarkable and suitable refectory. After its model, as we often heard from his own mouth, he promised that, if bodily illness did not overtake him, he would complete in the square of the palace a cloister furnished with such buildings and appendages.

Furthermore, he gathered not only the clerics who had abandoned their own Church because, from the Church’s revenues, they could scarcely obtain food until the middle of the year, but also others from various regions. Having hired a master of eloquence and of that discipline which more fully furnishes the faculty of discernment, he entrusted us to his authority, that he might draw us away from the rudiments of childhood. Finally, by the brilliance of his intelligence, he so wisely organized ecclesiastical matters that, in accordance with the numerical company of the Lord’s disciples, he selected seventy-two canons, for whom sufficient food should not fail throughout the yearly cycle. He was bound to them with all his strength both by harmony of charity and by the favour of excessive affection, as befits a good shepherd.

But because the cunning of the ancient enemy never ceases to stain with the gall of its envy those whom it sees so closely joined, the bishop recalled the events of the Old Testament concerning two brothers, one of whom, Cain, committed fratricide. He recalled also that, at the beginning of the New Law, one of the twelve disciples was a traitor. Because all these things deeply troubled the bishop’s mind, he sought counsel from the leading persons of his Church as to how that root of treachery, which had sprung up long ago, might be uprooted, lest it kill those then present with the poison of its deadly persuasion. By their counsel, so that the aforesaid things might not happen, he received from each canon an oath of obedient subjection in accordance with the ensuing form.

## On the oath of the canons

In the year 1120, on the Kalends of May, in the second year of his episcopate, the canons of the Church of blessed James the Apostle made this oath to their bishop, Lord Diego II. Their names appear written and individually noted below.

> **Note:** [Col. 0917D] (47) If this oath was made in the second year of his pontificate, it must without doubt have been in 1102, and in no way should 1120 be read. It is reported around the year 1105 because the text treats of the concord of the canons and their common food and dwelling.

## Oath

“I, N., swear to you, Lord Diego, present bishop, by God the almighty Father, that from this present day onward I shall always be obedient and faithful to you in all things. I shall defend and exalt your life, your limbs, and every honour which you now possess or shall possess, without any deceit or evil intent, according to my power and understanding, on all the days of my life. So may God help me and these holy Gospels!”

## Their names

Abbot Gundensindus; Munio Gelmírez; Pelagius Gunsal; Geoffrey, archdeacon; Hugh, chaplain; Oduarius, archdeacon; Pelagius Did.; John, archdeacon; Peter Astuariz; Munio Adef.; Pelagius Muniz; Diego Rud.; Martin Pel.; Munio Mr.; Alfonso Atinez; Arias Muniz; Peter Pel.; Cyprian Pel.; Peter Didaci; Alfonso Did.; Peter Gundesindiz; Bernard Gutierre, priest; Michael Gunsal; Peter Did.; John Rud.; likewise Peter Did.; Pelagius Mun.; Munio Sisnandici; Arias, archdeacon; Diego Bod.; Peter the Judge; Diego Rud.; Pelagius Anajaz; Vimara, abbot; John Guimiriz; Michael Janardiz; Diego Pel.; Aloitus Bned.; Fagildus P.; Pelagius Tanaoiz; Oduarius, priest; Gundensindus, priest; Adrian Rud.; Diego Jul.; Peter Al.; Ruderic; Brother Aloitus John; Martin Beraldus; Pelagius Manso; Peter Cresc.; Pelagius Gelmi; Peter Anaide; Peter Mr.; Martinez Cidiz; Romanus Romaz; Vimara Astrariz; Riquila, cleric; Alfonso Pel.; Peter the Abbot; Guntadiz; Martin Pel.; Peter Cresc.; Erus; Peter Eliae; Adulfus; Gerald, archbishop of Braga; Pelagius John; Arias Gunsalu; Peter Fulco; Arias Did.; D. A., bishop of Ourense; bishop of Tui.

> **Note:** [Col. 0918D] (48) The bishop of Tui was called Audericus, while the bishop of Ourense was named Didatus.

## On their order

After they had thus been arranged by ranks, although all of us resisted like brute animals not yet weighed down by any yoke’s harshness, he permitted no one either to enter the choir or to ascend from the altar steps to the altar unless clothed in surplices. Why say more? By softening the harsh hearts of the clerics with the ploughshare of discipline, he brought it about that even those who, rushing headlong into every action, had never been restrained by any curb of moderation and who thus—horrible to say—broke out into mutual slaughter, were not only united in the harmony of charity but now abounded in every moral decency.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the building of the church at Conxo

Ever intent upon these and other similar labours, he founded the church of the holy and undefiled Virgin Mary at Conxo, with houses arranged around it, situated not far from the city. With what great or what kind of intensity of purpose he established it cannot be perfectly told by mortals except at the judgment of the future blessedness. For he saw that the religious women throughout all Galicia lived without regular discipline—for within the whole extent of so great a kingdom there was no monastery of religious women. His mind, therefore, kindled with the warmth of fraternal charity, could not find a site better suited for accomplishing this purpose: both because, through the continual sight of and conversation with the bishop of the Apostolic See, they might more frequently be instructed concerning the continence of their own life, and because, owing to the close proximity of the place, necessities might be supplied to them more abundantly and conveniently.

Moved, then, by divine love and desiring with all the intention of his mind to build that place, he caused not only an orchard and cherry-grove to be planted around it—though not even part of a tree was there—but also every kind of fruit-bearing tree found suitable in those regions.
