And in the river which runs through the bounds of the church, as we often heard, he ordered fishponds to be made, so that when fish could not otherwise be obtained, the religious women who dwelt there might receive their support from them.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the restoration of churches at Padrón, Iria, Santa Cruz, Santa Eulalia, Santa Leocritia, Nevaro; and on the cultivation of the estate called Godegild

I also judge that this must by no means be passed over in silence: while he continued in the eminence of pastoral care, visiting estates and churches in his diocese with holy visitation like a good shepherd, he could find nowhere in all his bishopric, wherever he frequently came, places suitable for the performance of divine offices, because they were excessively darkened by age. Therefore, with a certain priest Pelagius of good memory, he built the little church of Saint James at Padrón from the very ground of the church up to the highest peak of its roof. And, just as he restored the altar of Saint Eulalia at Iria, so in the district of Pistoia he built the churches which we bring below from the darkness of ignorance into the common knowledge of light: Saint Cross, Saint Eulalia, Saint Leocritia, and Saint Mary of Nevaro. Finding them demolished to the ground or like mere huts, he is known to have founded them through tireless exertion, after fitting buildings had been constructed around them; and he honourably consecrated them all, attended by the college of his canons.

Near the estate of Saint James at Paratella, he freed the church of Saint Michael of Bojón by a just act of liberation from the power of certain knights who held it as though it were their own. Since at that place there was no suitable lodging near the estate for receiving the bishop, he built palaces and fitting houses around it. In the district of Salnés he wholly removed from lay possession the royal estate called Godegild, desolate and abandoned through lack of cultivators and severely overgrown with dense thickets, and quickly introduced his own cultivators to farm it. Near that estate, he freed the church of Saint Mary of Lua, by a just act of liberation under the judgment of the laws, from the thirsty greed of knights before the presence of the most pious Count Raymond; after he had consecrated it in accordance with his right, he restored it to the jurisdiction of his Church.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the liberty of the citizens of Compostela

While the aforesaid Count Raymond, who excelled among western peoples both in brilliance of intellect and nobility of birth, held the kingdom of Galicia, we know that a great dispute arose between the citizens of Compostela and the noble lords of the land. For the nobles, whenever citizens pursued commerce outside the city through their estates, took from them by force tolls, transport animals, and all that they carried, without any demand of justice or any lawful reason.

When the matter had been rationally considered by both sides, that same Count R., a man of the highest prudence and wisdom, wishing to put an end to it, issued the following edict in the presence of a considerable crowd of knights and noblemen: no citizen should ever be distrained upon, except solely for his own cause, after justice had first been sought and denied by the bishop of the Apostolic See. If anyone, swollen with pride and fattened with arrogant haughtiness, should attempt in any respect to violate this edict, strengthened by his authority, he should repay with double compensation the things upon which he had distrained; and for the rashness of this presumption he should pay sixty solidi. The count confirmed this by a definite written declaration.

After this judgment had been given, his most illustrious father-in-law, King Alfonso, having zealously visited the thresholds of blessed James for prayer, was urgently petitioned by the citizens to confirm this judgment. Assenting to their most just request, he left to his successors a written record of his decision and bound with perpetual anathema anyone who should fail to observe it.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the toll of Saint Pelagius of Luto

When the aforesaid count was afflicted at the city of Zamora both by dysentery and by the sickness of an acute fever, the aforesaid bishop vehemently reproved him in a strong address regarding the due owed at Saint Pelagius of Luto, commonly called the *portaticum* [market or transit toll]. For everyone who either conducted business in that place or passed through it wept continually, not only because of the loss of money but also because of the great humiliation of his body, being frequently stripped naked of his clothing.

The bishop, compassionately recalling their sufferings, knew that the count was then suffering a lack of revenue—for the count had promised much to his military household but lacked the means to pay it. He therefore wished to grant him, from the resources of his own Church, an equivalent payment of the revenue customarily given to the Church from that castle. But because the count knew that the bishop was persistently urging him for the salvation of his soul, he completely abolished this due by a firm written instrument among the other gifts of his alms, with the counsel of his wife; and he forbade his descendants by every means to reclaim it.

## CHAPTER XXV. On houses acquired at Compostela, and on Pilonio and Branderitio

Furthermore, we have learned that the most holy Geloyra, sister of the most holy King Alfonso, when brought low by her final lot, bestowed upon the Church of blessed James the entire estate of the money-changer Anaemaris. We have likewise ascertained that this Geloyra gave one half of the monasteries of Pilonio and Branderitio, with their dependencies. Her sister Urraca, the prudent and noble daughter of King Ferdinand, considering her worthy footsteps with deep reflection, likewise granted, before her spirit escaped the prison of the flesh, a certain plot in the urban city of Compostela near the market, by splendid documentary attestation.

In acquiring the other half of the aforesaid monasteries, Pilonio and Branderitio, with all things belonging to their lordship by ancient right, our Church laboured so greatly that at last King Alfonso—a man of highest prudence and piety—together with Urraca, who was joined to him by the closest degree of kinship, namely his sister born of the same womb, bestowed it, confirmed with the firm strength of stability by a reliable written instrument, upon the clerics of the Church of James.

## On the investigation of the boundaries of Pilonio

After these things had been obtained and carefully received by the bishop, a certain raven, namely Alfonso Ramírez, learned that the bishop was coming to his church of Saint Eulalia of Losón, which belonged—and was said to belong—to Pilonio. Infected with the gall of his evil intention, he went to Luzus Arias, steward of the land, and through him presented himself to the count and his wife, seeking to subject that church, together with things that were not his by right, to their lordship.

When the bishop learned of this, he discussed the aforesaid matter with the Infanta for so long, now with gentle words and now with harsh reproaches, until her husband, after the questions concerning these matters had been examined and established by a true investigation, subjected both Alfonso himself and his inheritance to the bishop’s lordship, because they had learned that these belonged to the Church of blessed James.

After receiving Pilonio, and carefully investigating its jurisdiction, he then learned that the entire lordship from Viniola to Carrium and from Carrium to the harbour of Mouri—of which he found himself to possess one half in name only—belonged by true right to the jurisdiction of his Church. Having learned this, he quickly approached the count’s presence and brought before him a complaint regarding these boundaries. By the count’s judgment and fixed decision he rejoiced to have obtained the other half from Viniola to Carrium. Because the other half from Carrium to the harbour of Mouri remained to be determined under the decision of judges, reason requires that it be settled at a suitable time.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the settlement of the dioceses of Osma and Burgos, and on the illness of Count Raymond

After some time had passed, the lord pope sent letters of command to him as to his beloved and especially close son, directing him, with the bishops of the provincial sees—namely Peter of León, Pelagius of Asturias, and others whom we omit to avoid prolixity—to determine by the surest investigation the dispute over the boundaries of their common parish which existed between the clergy of the Churches of Osma and Burgos. After making the determination, they were to inform the lord pope by their letters on all these matters.

Obeying this command without delay, as a man of great authority and humility, he set out with all speed to investigate the boundaries. When his arrival became known in the region of Campania, the most illustrious Count R.—whom nature and excellence of character had notably adorned among western peoples—was being held by the languor of a severe illness at the estate of Grajal, situated beside Saint Facundus. Aware of the aforesaid bishop’s well-known mercy, the count sent messengers to him, as to a desirable refuge for the salvation of his soul, asking that he might deign to come to him.

When he had reached the count’s presence in hurried haste, the venerable bishop was received with such reverence that we pass it over in silence, lest we remain too long and tediously upon its description. For after the count had washed away the stains of his sins with fitting tears of repentance, and had committed both himself and all things under his power to the bishop’s will, he desired to give to the Church of Saint James, by a most trustworthy written attestation, the monastery of Plantata, with its dependencies, on the bank of the river Miño.

> **Note:** [Col. 0921D] (50) Plantata is today Chantada.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the testament of Saint Mamet and the death of the same count
But since our Church was being assailed by frequent attacks from its stewards not only in its head but also in its members, both inwardly and outwardly, he repeatedly appealed to the ears of the aforesaid prince with the sweet converse born of inward piety, and at length persuaded him that, just as, by the counsel of the lady Infanta U., his wife, he had by testament removed the yoke of due servitude, with unshaken permanence, from persons born in servile condition who belonged both to the royal estates and to the county and dwelt in the city of St. James [Col. 0922B], so he should compel me, Peter, then not yet a chaplain, to draw up a charter concerning St. Mametus with all its appurtenances. Before the presence of his father-in-law, the catholic lord King Alfonso, who had come to see him in his illness because he loved him with the privilege of special affection, he confirmed it by his authority.

When these things had thus been accomplished, now warning his wife of the terror of a sulphurous storm, now promising her the joys of future blessedness, after he had persuaded her that she should convey by testamentary grant to the apostolic Church all the churches and inheritances—except the inheritance of Superatus and one court in the city, between the rivers Ulla and Tambre—as indeed she did convey them [Col. 0922C], his holy soul, paying nature’s due, was torn away from its dwelling in the flesh. Therefore, by the common counsel of the clergy, he sent two of his clerics, together with Peter, bishop of León, and other companions, to investigate the aforesaid boundaries. He himself, returning home, dutifully performed with devoted piety the offices owed by humanity at that man’s funeral and precious burial in the church of Blessed James.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the borough of Tabulado and the coinage of St. James, granted by the king; and concerning the dispute over John the Lombard and his brother

Finally, the aforesaid emperor, Lord Alfonso, considering in his heart [Col. 0922D] the diligence of so great a shepherd, ever intent upon the work of that Church, and desiring from the abundant fruitfulness of his own resources to relieve the work’s poverty, granted the borough of Tabulado on the border of the valley of Carcer, and the coinage of St. James, wholly free in every respect, on this legal condition: that, once the structure of that work had first been completed, it should thereafter remain forever for the expenses of the clerics serving there and for the Church’s uses necessary to its needs, without any claim by any of his descendants.

> **Note:** [Col. 0922D] (51) Tabulado is today Trabadelo.

Therefore, when the coinage had been received entirely free, as you have heard above with the open ear of the heart, the same bishop, with the utmost diligence, appointed Tandulf, a man of greater ingenuity, over all his moneyers [Col. 0923A], taking great precaution; he entrusted to Tandulf’s guardianship the complete administration of the coinage, lest it should be counterfeited.

By the secret command of the often-mentioned pontiff, Tandulf brought a complaint, in the discerning ears of the most pious King Alfonso, against two citizens of his: John the Lombard and his brother Geoffrey. One of them, John—keeper of the king’s daughter—had been taken into the queen’s protection by her command and at the bishop’s earnest request; the other had been received by Count Peter from the same pontiff for a like reason. Protected by their authority, the bishop was then unable to obtain justice against them.

When this complaint had been heard, the king commanded that the bishop be summoned before him with great reverence, and demanded from him without delay justice concerning these citizens [Col. 0923B]. Since these matters had been done at León, where Count Peter and the queen were then present, the bishop summoned them to determine before the king the cases concerning those men, together with his moneyer. Count Peter was accordingly sent to argue the cases carefully on behalf of himself and the queen. When the complaint of both parties had already been debated for a long time in the presence of the nobles then attending, the king forever took away from both his daughter and the count all lordship over the citizens, declaring that the lordship of the church of Blessed James had been granted by his grandfathers and great-grandfathers on this legal condition: that no person and no jurisdiction should have authority in the city. He handed them over to the pontiff to be judged as his own men.

Moreover [Col. 0923C], with every manner of curse he forbade all his future descendants that anyone descended, or to descend, from his stock should by any rash audacity wish to violate this judgment. If anyone presumed to do so, he should swiftly incur the sentence of his curse, become an exile from his paternal stock, and lie subject to the vengeance of the just divine dispensation.

### Concerning the chirograph of the coinage

At the same time the same bishop left two of his clerics at Burgos with the king—namely Didacus the Briton and his brother Munio—to obtain the chirograph of the coinage which was to be made.

> **Note:** [Col. 0923D] (52) *Cyrographum* is the same as *chirographum*.

Since they could by no means obtain this deed, because the king asserted that he would offer it upon the altar of the Apostle [Col. 0923D], they returned home with all speed.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the death of the king’s son Sancho, and the chirograph of the coinage obtained

After nearly three years had passed,

> **Note:** [Col. 0923D] (53) The aforesaid grant of the coinage appears to have been made about the year 1105, if an interval of three years intervened. But since the document was confirmed after the death of the boy Sancho, the author has not inappropriately reserved its mention for this place. That royal boy died in the year 1108.

in the region where the heat of the sun makes men resemble Ethiopians, they attacked more fiercely than usual the fortresses and towns subject to Toledo. Having killed the men who opposed their force, and being protected by the strength of their soldiers so that they feared no enemy missiles, they pitched their tents there as though established in complete security [Col. 0924A].

When this was reported to the king’s son, Sancho—who, by his father’s command, had been entrusted with the lordship of Toledo—he gathered the nobility of the counts and, attended by the valor and soldiery of noble men, hastened forth to drive away the enemies who were destroying his country. As he struck them down with continual blows and harsh attacks, he met, lamentably to tell, with the opposite of what he wished: he himself, with all his nobility, fell unhappily beneath the missiles of the Moors.

When news was received of his destruction and of the slaughter of the noblemen, the bishop’s prudence gathered a multitude of his soldiers; and, together with the king’s daughter Urraca, he came, as eagerly desired, to the places which the Moors had invaded. Once the host of enemies had been put to flight, a severe illness immediately followed him [Col. 0924B]. But since almighty God was unwilling that the Church of St. James should be deprived of the presence of so great a shepherd, so that those requiring correction might be corrected through the vigilant care of pastoral office, He restored him to his former health; and he entered as swiftly as possible the city of Segovia, which rejoiced in the king’s presence.

There, when the dawn was rising, as he addressed the king concerning both ecclesiastical causes and secular business, as befits a good ruler of the Church, he urgently requested among other things the document concerning the grant of the coinage which the king had already ordered to be made. When, despite his persistence, he received no response, and on the following day the bishop repeated the request, he is said to have received this answer:

> “First,” he said, “I shall go to see the walls of Toledo; and then, in the garb of a pilgrim, I shall gladly take up the pilgrim’s bag, and, travelling by the direct road, shall take care to visit the long-desired thresholds of Blessed James, my patron and protector. When, with God’s help, I arrive at those places, you shall obtain, through my making the offering, the chirograph which your charity urgently requests.”

The bishop said: “Lest, when the moment of death steals upon you, you be unable to attain the full expression of your devotional desire, while it is possible for your discernment to grant it—since what you do while living will not be undone by your descendants, who desire more to acquire than to bestow holy gifts upon churches—you ought to confer the generosity of your gift. For almighty God, who is the true inspector of our hearts and thoughts [Col. 0924D], does not look at the places or the gifts of those who offer, but beholds from on high what gifts are given and with what intention; and for such persons He keeps without end the rewards of eternal blessedness.”

When by these and similar words the king’s mind had been warmed: “Go,” he said, “and today we shall provide you with all that is necessary; tomorrow we shall answer concerning all these matters according to what God grants us.”

Accordingly, in the morning, when the king and queen were seated in the dwelling of their secretary, the bishop was honorably received by them and learned from the king’s report what his mind had considered throughout the whole night. The king summoned the keeper of his treasury, had his chests opened, and ordered the aforesaid document to be brought to him [Col. 0925A]. Receiving it, he bent his knees to the ground, moistened his cheeks with a stream of tears, kissed the pontiff’s feet, and granted it to him with great reverence.

## CHAPTER XXX. That he built the borough of Cacabelos, etc.

We recall to your knowledge how greatly the same bishop labored with vigilant activity upon the French road, lest knowledge of these things should lie hidden from future generations, darkened by the shadows of ignorance. For he built the borough of Cacabelos, which he found razed to the ground; and, after houses had been built there, he consecrated the church with great honor.

Finally, as he frequently visited the regions of Campania in order to obtain honors for his Church, and very often passed through Astorga and León, he found no place to rest in the properties of Blessed James themselves [Col. 0925B], for they appeared ruined and utterly uncultivated for human use. Holding within the dwelling of his mind, as it were, a veil of sorrow, yet showing no trace of it outwardly, he considered in every way how he might bring them to the height of perfection.

After no long interval of time, he assigned from his own resources a rent and everything necessary to one of his stewards. Anyone wishing to know by what skill that steward made them spacious may learn it more fully from their completed condition, lest we appear to say less than the truth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the gifts of counts

[Col. 0925C]

Since, therefore, we have thus far briefly described what we have said about kings and the gifts of kings’ sons, the course of our work requires us, laying aside all delay, to return to the gifts of counts.

For Count Sancho, administering with the highest moderation the rights properly belonging to a count, just as he assigned by testament the estate of Mauri at Aviancos, so also, as we have heard with no deaf ear, he gave a church in that same place. Desiring to follow him with complete devotion of heart, Count Peter—whose wife’s mind did not differ from his own will—left to our Church, to possess forever, as he had left a plot of land in the city near the mint, so also, after the dissolution of his body, the church of St. Tirso at Nemitos [Col. 0925D], the estate of St. James at Avecundo with persons bound to due servitude, and the estate of Pausata.

His sister Munima frequently considered in her mind’s eye his sincere devotion. Since she had already caused her nephew Froila, son of the aforesaid count, to give to Blessed James the estate of Eruedino at Nemitos with its slaves, she judged that she herself could be no less generous. Thus, imitating her nephew, she granted forever to the clerics of the Church, in the territory of Salinas, the estates of Romariz and Octario.

Likewise, in Lemos we declare without hesitation, because we know it, that Countess Geloyra gave a portion of the monastery of St. Verissimus with all its benefices and dues.

### Concerning the gifts of knights

[Col. 0926A]

Having dealt with the gifts of counts, and having examined them carefully according to our measure, we who descend step by step to the lower ranks of knights ought not to omit their gifts, though lesser ones. For by these even those of lesser means are suitably stirred to the exercise of good works, while the powerful are wholly kindled to accomplish loftier things.

Lucius Ariades, severely afflicted with the grievous distress of fever, had learned that his wife Majora, placed at the final point of her end, had bestowed half of the estate lying beside the bridge of the Ulla, half of the estate of Quintalna in Salnés, and the estate of Ruvinum in Taberiolos. Desiring to imitate her with all the ardor of his mind, he likewise granted the estate of Sautum Longum in Deza, the estate of Dadin in Cusanca, Villa Nova in Deza, and another estate beside the bridge of the Ulla [Col. 0926B].

Within the district of Salinas, Oduarius Didacides gave the estate of Ovar; Ovecus Cresconides, the estate of Portal; and Nuno Pelagides, another Sautum. As they gave them with great devotion together with their wives, so we received them with the highest affection of heart.

But because this shepherd was always zealous in acquiring possessions for his Church, he diligently obtained from Aria Aloitides, together with her slaves, a fourth part of the church of St. Verissimus of Arcubus, half of the church of St. George of Villa Nova, and, on the bank of the Ulla, the church of St. John of Coba [Col. 0926C]. Having acquired them, he guarded them with yet more vigilant care. For just as the prudent recognize it as a supreme virtue justly to acquire another’s possessions, so they believe it a virtue no less great cautiously to preserve what has been acquired.

Finally, we ourselves saw that, on Mount Zebruario, after he had obtained the borough of Paturnelo from Ovecus Sancho, Didacus Viliulfides gave a third part of the monastery of Novallis on the bank of the Tambre.

Moreover, in the district of Faro, we know that Cresconius Petrides gave an estate; likewise, we know that Sandinus Alfonso granted his share of the estate of Benviver in Dubria.

Further, the bishop, with the subtle intelligence of his mind, as though most certain of future events and foreseeing evils from afar [Col. 0926D], lest the poor be oppressed by the intolerable burden of one of our parishioners, namely Count Peter, who was accustomed to devastate all things in the manner of enemies, exchanged with the count’s brother García an estate acquired from Onega Ectaz by the terms of a testament, for another at Aona. There, at Aona, he acquired for a fitting price the estate of Peter Petrides, which the aforesaid count, burning like a furnace with the thirst of greed, had desired to buy. The bishop then bought that estate, named Ova, from Peter Petriz, whose right it was, for the price of six hundred solidi, and so it escaped the count’s injustice.

At about the same time, the bishop had long sought the estate of Jacob in Montanos from Martino Pelagides. In the Vaniensis affinity, Gunza Eriz, clearly perceiving Aria Gundesindides by manifest evidence—who had bestowed a fourth part of the monastery of St. Pelagius of Circitello—gave to our Church with complete permanence her share of that monastery and an eighth part of St. Eulalia of Bando [Col. 0927A].

Meanwhile, Ildoncia Froilaz, being advanced in years, meditating in holy contemplation upon things never bounded by any end, and realizing after the shipwrecks of this life that she could do no further work, was strongly moved by the holy example of Geloyra Martinides and Alfonso Munio. The former had granted forever to the Church an estate within the bounds of St. Eulalia of Ovorio; the latter, the estates of Olveira, Cirues, and Neorma in Pistomarci. She, cherishing a like intention, hastened without delay to bring to the effect of good devotion what her mind desired concerning the monastery of Argentario in Cornato, when by a formal document, in the presence of clerics, she subjected her own portion to our Church [Col. 0927B].

Having acquired at Taberiolos Villacobas from Baraguntia Sisnandiz, and at Villa Plana one sixth, and at Lagaztene one sixth of the upper portion and one tenth of the lower portion, he bought, by payment of a price, two shares at Villa Bella in the lordship of Salinas.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Again, concerning the restoration of churches

Moreover, just as the provident fatherhood of the aforesaid bishop, through the brilliant diligence of his intelligence, carefully acquired from the woman Aria Savariquiz, Guina Oduariz, two estates—Pausata and Fusim, one of them in Lagartones and the other on the bank of the river Ulla in the lordship of Sacro Monte [Col. 0927C]—so too, when Pelagius Gundesindides departed from this present light, it obtained no less diligently another of his estates at Santa Xpina de Noya.

Finally, his fatherly discernment obtained churches which he carefully restored upon the properties of Blessed James at Nemitos together with a certain honorable man, John, archdeacon of our Church; and, having restored them, he diligently consecrated them without omitting our presence: namely Barbarios, Pravella, Avegundo, Toiobre, Degio, Aumentarias, and Moralias. We exclude these from the present discussion.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. [Col. 0927D] Concerning the building of the castle of Honesti

We insert these matters because, when the cruelty of the Ishmaelites had raged more fiercely in the devastation of our country through continual incursions, the bishop himself, with the prophet, set himself as a strong wall for the house of Israel. When men from different regions customarily assembled every year to repair the castle of Honesti, so that the multitude of those coming might restore what had been destroyed and needed repair, he took counsel with the king. The king ordered him, since the castle was badly repaired, to destroy it wholly [Col. 0928A], lest perhaps the concealed cunning of the Ishmaelites should seize it by some stratagem or by the heat of lamentation [the reading is uncertain], and from there devastate to the ground all its surrounding territory and the neighboring region on every side.

> **Note:** [Col. 0927D] (54) See the preceding volume, under Bishop Cresconius, no. 5.

When he had heard this counsel, the bishop pondered worthy sighs within the lodging of his mind. Since it pleased his prudence always more to strive toward the building up of useful things than to yearn utterly for destruction, he ordered a solidus of royal coinage to be paid from every household throughout his bishopric for the castle’s support. When these payments had been received, he freed, through the formal insertion of a document, the men subject to this service from that servile custom. With their small sum of money—since the coinage at that time was thin and weak both in weight and in legal standard—he could not bring even one whole tower to its full height [Col. 0928B]. But from his own resources he fortified the castle of Honesti with a building of walls, defensive works, and the height of towers, so that, should either Moabites or Ishmaelites somehow approach that castle from elsewhere, they would either be overwhelmed by stones and sharp stakes hurled down from above, or would without doubt be exposed to danger of capture or death from the soldiers who remained there in the guardianship of peace.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the archpresbyterates of Bisancos, Trasancos, and Salagia

Before all these things were done, the aforesaid bishop, recalling that the bishop of Mondoñedo had held from his predecessors, namely the bishops of Compostela, two archpresbyterates and a half under the title of a *praestamen* [precarial grant], requested them peacefully from him, lest the Church of Compostela should at some future time lose them under some pretext [Col. 0928C]. Since he scorned to restore them, the bishop made a complaint at the council of Carrión, which the blessed archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church celebrated, and he repeatedly sent his envoys to the lord pope concerning the matter.

> **Note:** [Col. 0927D] (55) Namely, from the year 1102, as is clear from the following number. But because in 1108, which is now under discussion, the dispute was again litigated [Col. 0928D], matters pertaining to it, though done at different times, as he says, are not inappropriately recalled together.

Although the letters which he brought back had been issued at different times, since they concerned one matter we have not inappropriately joined them together. Therefore Archbishop Lord Bernard, having learned from several of the bishops of the province that the aforesaid archpresbyterates—Bisancos, Trasancos, and Salagia—belonged by right to the Church of Compostela, sent the following letter to the bishop of Mondoñedo [Col. 0928D].

### Concerning the same matter

Bernard, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his dearest lord G., bishop of Mondoñedo, greeting.

> **Note:** [Col. 0928D] (56) His name was Gundisalvus.

We learned through your envoys of the necessity of your illness, by reason of which your brotherhood was unable to present itself at the Council of Carrión (A.D. 1102). At that council, among the other complaints raised against you, the Church of St. James laid before our ears a serious complaint against you: namely, that you violently usurp two archpresbyterates and a half which are known once to have belonged by right to the aforesaid Apostle [Col. 0929A].

Therefore we command you, under obedience, not to refuse, putting aside every other evasion, to restore whatever the aforesaid Church is said to have possessed by lawful documents, as is contained in the Roman privilege; lest, as a transgressor of the Roman privilege, you be struck by the sword of anathema. Finally, after restoring these things to the aforesaid Church, we shall intercede with the venerable brother and fellow bishop D., that he may, by our intervention, grant them or other things to your brotherhood for a time, condescending to you. Farewell.

> **Note:** [Col. 0929D] Perhaps the same as the common *condescendendo*, that is, “indulging his will.”

Given at León, the second day before the Nones of February, Era 1111 (A.D. 1103).

When the bishop of Mondoñedo did not obey these letters [Col. 0929B], the bishop of Compostela sent two envoys to the lord pope and informed him through them of this matter litigated at the Council of Carrión. The lord pope, seeing letters of such authority and attentively considering the command of the whole council, sent the following letters to the bishop of Mondoñedo:

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.  
> “Of our venerable brother,” etc. See above, no. 94.

### Again concerning the same matter

Having received these letters, he did not wish to answer us, but sent his clerics, Gundisalvus and Munio, to the presence of the lord pope. Through them he brought the following letter to Bishop D. of Compostela:

[Col. 0929C]

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.  
> “To those requesting,” etc. See above, no. 98.

### Again concerning the same matter

By the command of these letters, both we and they went with great haste to Rome at the Kalends of October. We received this judgment from Lord Pope Paschal II: that five of the oldest persons of the Church of Mondoñedo should go to Astorga and, before the bishop of Burgos, Lord G., who was to come with the pope’s mandatory letters, swear that they had possessed the aforesaid dioceses without disturbance for forty years, on the condition that they should thereafter not be troubled.

When the bishop of Mondoñedo heard the aforesaid judgment, though he was unable to bear exertion because of the weakness of old age, he entered Astorga with the clerics of the Church of Compostela to undergo judgment. When he was there and did not find the bishop of Burgos, who was prevented by illness, he could not complete the judgment, both because of that bishop’s absence and because of a lack of persons. Therefore they agreed that, wherever he might be, they would present themselves before him and settle so great a matter.

As they left there, they came with all haste to the castle of Soria, where Lord King A. was, and found the bishop of Burgos in his court. There, just as previously at Astorga, he wholly refused to carry out the pope’s judgment before that bishop’s presence and that of many noble men [Col. 0930A]. The bishop of Burgos, seeing that they had failed, reported the matter to the lord pope in his letters. The pope, having taken counsel with the cardinals, sent the following letter to the bishop of Mondoñedo:

### Again concerning the same matter

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.  
> “As from our fellow bishop,” etc. See above, no. 160.

### Again concerning the same matter

When they had seen these letters written above, they scorned to obey, as though bound by the chain of ignorance. Therefore, when the archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church held a council at León, the same bishop of Compostela attended; in the presence of the king and the whole council, he personally set forth in Latin his complaint concerning their fault of disobedience [Col. 0930B].

Once the complaint had been heard and debated for a long time by both sides, the legate of the Holy Roman Church entrusted the decision of this matter to certain bishops. They withdrew separately, discussed the arguments of both sides with one another, and by common counsel decreed that the dioceses taken from the bishop of Mondoñedo should remain under the rule of the bishop of Ourense, until they should go to Rome with letters from the whole council and bring an end to this matter, litigated for so long.

Having received letters both from the archbishop of Toledo and from the whole council, the same bishop sent his archdeacon, named Geoffrey, to Rome concerning this matter. Because the envoys of the Church of Mondoñedo were absent, the lord pope did not determine the case, but entrusted its decision to the archbishop of Toledo through the following letters [Col. 0930C].

## CHAPTER XXXV. Decision of the same matter

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.  
> “The letters of your affection,” etc. See above, no. 187.

Because, after these letters had been brought, we could not obtain justice through the archbishop of Toledo, legate of the Roman Church, we rested from this dispute for a short time, though not without distress. During this delay, the clergy and people of that diocese, recalling that those dioceses had been and ought to be subject to the Church of Blessed James both by lawful records and by legal title, and knowing this without any doubt [Col. 0930D], moreover having heard the judgment of the archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, came of their own accord to the eminence of the aforesaid bishop. They confessed aloud that they had erred, and, having undergone the penance of so prolonged an error, rendered perpetual obedience to him and to his Church. Their submission and names are set down below in the text of the documents.

### Obedience of the abbot of St. Martin of Trasancos

I, Nuno, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin, situated in the territory of Trasancos beside the river called Juvia, promise canonical subjection and every obedience in Christ, on behalf of the parish of the Church of Compostela, to Lord Didacus II, bishop of the Church of St. James the Apostle [Col. 0931A]. I shall henceforth forever be faithful and obedient, with the aforesaid monastery and the men belonging to it, to him and to his successors canonically advanced, for the diocese of St. James; and so shall my successors who are to be placed over the same monastery.

I, Abbot Nuno, made this profession in Era 1118, on the seventh day before the Ides of February (A.D. 1110).

> **Note:** [Col. 0931D] Although the narrative is now about events of the year 1108, he rightly attaches the aforesaid obediences, although they were made at another time, as he had stated, because they brought the matter to its present conclusion. See Book II, chapter 56.

### Concerning the subjection of others

Not long after receiving this abbot’s obedience, in Era 1118, on the Nones of March, we devoutly received this profession and obedience from the persons written below.

### Obedience of monks, abbots, clerics, and laypeople

[Col. 0931B]

We, inhabitants of the dioceses of Bisancos, Trasancos, Lavacencos, and Arros—abbots, archpresbyters, monks, and all the rectors of those churches, as well as counts, knights, ladies, and all the people whose names and subscriptions are recorded below—truthfully confess to you, venerable lord D. II, by God’s grace bishop of St. James the Apostle, and to your Church, that the aforesaid dioceses were once subject by canonical institution to the see of Iria, according to their proper and ancient boundaries; and that they were removed from it for a certain unjust cause.

Since we recognize that both we and our predecessors have erred against the decrees of the canons, having recognized the path of truth we voluntarily submit ourselves, promising obedience to you and to your Church [Col. 0931C]. Henceforth, gathering at Blessed James, we and our successors shall faithfully pay each year to you and to your successors the rents and dues belonging to the right of the see or diocese, under the direction of your prelate, whom you and your successors shall unanimously elect with us and with the consent of our successors. We shall pay them with every reverence.

Before God and Blessed James, we unanimously affirm this covenant: neither we nor our successors shall ever at any time withdraw from this promise and subjection. Rather, casting aside the precedence and lordship of other pontiffs, we shall, as stated above, cleave forever with our strength and all our effort to the obedience and commands of you and your successors, so that, being guided with you in this age [Col. 0931D], we may live justly and piously and happily attain the kingdoms of heaven through your prayers and the intercession of Blessed James.

If anyone through unbelief should hereafter resist or seek to annul what has been established, whoever that person may be, unless he comes to repentance, let him be struck by the sword of perpetual anathema. But upon all who observe this agreement may there rest the blessing of our Lord and Redeemer and of Blessed James, full remission of their sins, and happy dwelling forever with all the saints. May this document of confession and subjection possess complete force through all ages. Amen.

### Confirmers

[Col. 0932A]

Peter Froylaz, count: I confirm by my own mark.  
Countess Lady Mayor, wife of the same count: I confirm.  
Nuno, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin of Juvia: I confirm with my own hand.  
Munina Froylaz, sister of the aforesaid count: I confirm by my own declaration and subscription.  
Visclavara Froylaz, sister of the same count, and Munia, consecrated to God: they confirm.

### Names of the knights of Bisancos

These are the names of the knights dwelling in Bisancos, recorded below:

Menindus Holmiz confirms.  
Feruens Holmiz confirms.  
Histrarius Holmiz confirms.  
Ovecus Froylaz confirms.  
Rudericus Pelaiz confirms.  
Vistrarius Pelaz confirms.  
Gundisalvus Menendiz confirms.  
Muninus Oduariz confirms.  
Veremudus Rageliz confirms.  
Joannes Vimaraz confirms [Col. 0932B].  
Veremudus Asmodi confirms.  
Petrus Veremudiz confirms.  
Fernandus Suariz confirms.

### Names of the priests

These are the names of the clerics dwelling there who solemnly vowed and confirmed this subjection to Blessed James, both for themselves who were present and for all their absent companions, and for the whole people:

Pelagius Almondiz, priest of the church of St. Peter of Cervalles, confirms.  
Didacus Fulgentiz, priest of the church of St. Eulalia of Juvia, confirms.  
Vimara, priest of St. James of Francia, confirms.  
Rudericus Sisnandiz, priest and head of the monastery of St. Vincent, confirms.  
Pelagius Veremudiz, priest of the church of St. John of Pinnario, confirms.  
Gutierre Osoriz, priest of the church of St. Saviour of Magnios, confirms.  
Rudericus Muniz [Col. 0932C], priest of the church of St. Vincent of Mediano, confirms.  
Oduarius, priest of the church of St. Eulalia of Caurio, confirms.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. To confirm this obedience
Having received the obedience both of the clergy and of the people, the aforesaid bishop promptly dispatched to Rome two of his clerics—Gaufrid, namely, archdeacon of that church, and Peter the chaplain—concerning all these matters. From the lord pope they brought back the following letters, which brought this business to an end.

**Instrument concerning those matters which pertain to the Church of St. James.**

[Col. 0933C]

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

Likewise Peter, chaplain of our Church, laid before the lord pope, in Latin, a complaint concerning a certain bastard named Suarius, who was more conspicuous in secular power than occupied with the office of subdeacon. For Suarius, fortified by the strength of his kinsmen, without any claim of right, seized from him with the utmost violence a third share of the church of St. Michael, before the month of January had ended. Unable to bear the assault of this storm, he fled for refuge to the exalted presence of the lord pope. Seeing that Suarius was enveloped in the mist of injustice, we received, concerning the restoration of that church, the following letter fortified by the seal of Roman authority.

**On the restoration of that church.**

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Confirmation concerning the cardinals and other matters

“Finally, we have thought it not inappropriate to collect into one place the letters which we remember having received before the king’s death: those concerning the confirmation of your cardinals, whom, God helping, we established in the Church for the honor of your Church; concerning the investiture of the monastery of Cines; concerning those who bind their daughters in incestuous marriage; and concerning various other affairs. But before we proceed to other matters, as we previously received letters concerning knights who, because of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, left your lands exposed to devastation by Moorish incursions, so we rightly place them first in the sequence of this book.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the integrity and learning of King Alfonso, peace in his kingdom, and the oath sworn by the Galicians at León to Alfonso, son of Count Raymond, while he was still a boy

[Col. 0935A]

Accordingly, with great prudence the bishop acquired, through watchful care and immense labor, the inheritances, churches, and estates which we have noted above without observing their proper order; and, having acquired them, he permanently devoted them to the rights of his Church. He added many others, omitted by us because unknown to us. Whoever wishes to know them, we direct to consult the documentary records deposited and preserved in the treasury of the church of Blessed James. All the aforementioned possessions were justly acquired by the bishop before the death of our Catholic king Alfonso, of blessed memory.

This king, illustrious for the power of remarkable holiness and admirable for the capacity of his ardent mind—how severely he struck down the backs of his enemies by repeated blows and continual attacks, we know beyond doubt, because we have seen with our own bodily eyes those places which he freed from the dominion of the Ishmaelites by his unconquered sword. The kingdom of Toledo, the castles, cities, and towns known to lie beyond the course of the river Douro, in which the religion of the Christian profession is maintained and observed, he utterly cleared of the worship of nations that venerated vain gods. There he labored in building churches and devoted those which had been consecrated to divine worship.

Moreover, although he was exceedingly powerful in governing his subjects, he displayed such discernment, wisdom, and humility [Col. 0935C] that human ingenuity could by no means describe it, even if it wished to do so. For he did not delight in the singularity of his exalted rank, but reflected within himself upon the equality of the human condition. He knew that, if he despised subjects equal to himself by nature, or failed to govern them as was fitting, he would in every way offend the ruler of all creation, under whom all are equal by nature. How justly and temperately, therefore, he exacted the due obligations of authority from his subjects, and how peaceably he treated them, was shown in part after his death by the ruin of noble men and the wars that subsequently broke out more frequently.

When fate wholly removed his son-in-law Count Raymond from the sight of this present light, and Raymond’s son—who had not yet completed his third year—was presented to the most pious king, the king’s inmost affection of pity stirred within him. He addressed all the nobles, counts, and princes of Galicia who had gone with the boy to León at his command in these words:

> “Indeed, the boy’s father possessed the whole government and jurisdiction of Galicia. Therefore I present all of you who held his rights and honors while he lived, and still hold them after his death, without doubt as servants to his son, my grandson; and I grant him all Galicia. If his mother Urraca wishes to take a husband, I shall demand from him no further service even for myself. And so that, without any scruple of doubt, they may place faith in all these things which I declare in the hearing of your presence, I command you, in the presence of the archbishop of Vienne, the uncle of the aforesaid boy, to swear the following oath into the hands of Lord Didacus, the second bishop of the Church of Blessed James by divine dispensation, a discerning man: that you shall receive the boy now present as your lord; that you shall guard him, once received, more cautiously and vigilantly; and that you shall defend with all your strength the honor which I confer upon him in your presence, even against myself should I prove unjust toward him.”

After the oath had been sworn within the walls of León, as we have heard, and received with diligent care by the bishop of the Church of Compostela, everyone returned home under the authority of so great a ruler.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the death of King Alfonso, and the discord and other evils that were impending

[Col. 0936B]

After nearly two years had passed, this King Alfonso died under the weight of illness. He had been the light and shield of the peoples of Spain, in the Era 1117, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] “The second day before the Kalends of July” should be read, Era 1147—that is, the last day of June in the year 1109.]

When he died, faith was set aside as though it had never existed, and peace, which had long held mastery, was lost together with its ruler. Then war, sedition, and famine arose throughout the whole extent of his kingdom. The land was deprived not only of its due cultivation but, stripped of all justice, was left desolate.

Therefore great discord sprang up between Count Peter and certain Galician nobles, who disregarded the oath which they had sworn to their lord and set aside the bond of peace.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Peter Froylaz, Count of Trava, guardian of the royal boy Alfonso VII, concerning whom much occurs in this work; consult the places indicated in the general index.]

The count, to whose guardianship the boy’s father, while still alive, had entrusted him, wished to avert this. At one time with gentle speech, at another with threats, he attempted to curb their obstinacy, so that he might remove them from the darkness of ignorance and diligently bring them back to the state of justice which they had rashly abandoned. But because a heart weighed down by iniquity, when heavenly grace is lacking, is enlightened neither by abundance of words nor by a profusion of speeches, they were carried away by the cloud of error and inflamed with excessive rage; they refused to believe the count’s words.

For they were bound together by an alliance of a contrived brotherhood: they were to aid one another’s hostile strength with mutual and tireless force and to endure every adversity unanimously. Protected by this security, they turned their minds away from the union of concord. The bishop of Compostela, urgently invited and repeatedly entreated by them, accepted the assistance of this great brotherhood with the intention of preserving the Church’s peace and stability, watching with tireless concern over the welfare of the whole Galician kingdom, and reconciling them with the count by every means in his power—dissuading them and showing them the danger of violated faith.

Having therefore entered into the fellowship of the aforesaid alliance, and after no long interval, the aforesaid nobles of the land, having recognized in every respect and through all things that the bishop of Compostela was distinguished in ability, prudent in counsel, discerning in judgment, truthful, and fervent in zeal for justice, invited the care of so great a bishop in connection with the castle of Biti and swore an oath of fidelity to him. Yet many of the foremost men of Galicia had, before this new brotherhood was devised, rendered homage to the aforesaid bishop because of the *soldatae* and benefices which they had received abundantly from his generosity—such as Arias Petriz, Peter Gudesteiz, John Didacides, Pelagius Gudesteiz, and many other outstanding knights whom he had strongly bound to himself by the bond of homage.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] A letter of the pope, brought without a title, concerning the illicit marriage of Queen Urraca and the king of Aragon, which is discussed immediately below.]

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“To this end Almighty God,” etc. See under Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the unlawful marriage of the king of Aragon and the queen, and the war that thereby arose among the Galicians

[Col. 0937B]

Meanwhile, after the king of Aragon had been taken as husband—the same king to whom Queen Urraca had joined herself in an incestuous marriage—the queen swiftly sent her messengers into Galicia on behalf of her son. Since she burned utterly with the desire to raise that son to the heights of royal rank, she summoned all the nobles of Galicia to his elevation, lest they be deprived of so great a joy. They carried out her commands without delay and set out with all speed.

But when they had safely passed through León, they learned by a completely trustworthy report that the queen had been reconciled and reunited with the king of Aragon, her husband—if indeed he ought to be called her husband, when he was joined to her in a close degree of kinship. Deeply distressed, they swiftly summoned Count Henry, the aforesaid boy’s uncle, and carefully sought his counsel about what they should do in this turn of events. Strengthened by his prudent advice, Count Peter seized on the road near the castle of Sorices certain men among those who were betraying the oath sworn to the count’s son, and returned with them to Galicia at speed.

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Today Castro Xeriz.]

For their subsequent release he received the castle of the Minho.

[Note: [Col. 0938D] The castle of the Minho is today Santa María de Castrelo, on the bank of the Minho, about four leagues below Ourense.]

There he swiftly brought, as though under safe protection, the woman known to be his wife, together with her son and lord, whom she herself had reared in her lap. The inhabitants, unwilling to tolerate the harm caused by this admission, drove the count out of those territories with immense disgrace. Continually violating the binding obligations of their pledged faith, together with those who shared their wickedness, they shamelessly besieged in the castle of the Minho their lord—as it is sacrilegious even to say—and his nurse.

When those besieged could no longer endure the hardship of the siege because of scarcity of food and drink, nor the besiegers because of their prolonged watch, both now suffering hunger beyond measure, they accepted a mutual agreement, confirmed by an oath sworn on both sides by eight men. They unanimously decreed that the besieged should surrender the castle and a certain man whom they held captive, namely Oduarius Ordonides, to the besiegers without any ransom; and that, under the escort of those same leaders, the countess, with all who were inside, should return safely to her own people without incurring any loss.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the siege of the castle of the Minho

But the distinguished men who, together with the countess, were rendering more diligent service to the royal boy, hesitated somewhat about their opponents’ faith, as though foreseeing what was to come. They utterly refused to leave the castle if the presence of the bishop of Compostela were lacking, for in him alone at that time the abundance of fidelity fully resided. Accordingly, having sent an embassy to him concerning all these matters, both parties invited him twice and three times with every earnestness. When he received this embassy, he immediately sent messengers to them and promised that he would come quickly. For he strove both to rescue his lord from so unspeakable a distress of hardship, to bind those in conflict with the ties of concord, and to restore the peace of the land completely.

When the aforesaid bishop had proceeded by the direct road and arrived at the river Ernego with a few of his knights, he found the messengers whom he had already sent ahead. Although there he learned from the report of certain persons that he had received a deceitful embassy, he nevertheless refused to withdraw his foot from the course he had begun in good intention. Confiding greatly both in his undertaking, inspired by pious devotion, and in those whom he had bound to himself by the privilege of homage, he sent two messengers to them a second time for different reasons: Munio, namely his *couterinus* [fellow-countryman], to learn from the bishop’s enemies and from the countess what they intended to do; and Peter Gutierriz, who at that time was regarded as an enemy of the count, to discover from the enemies of the aforesaid count whether, by chance, they had laid snares of treachery.

Returning swiftly, they said not only that they had found no ambushes, but also caused Arias Oduariz to come to meet the bishop, so that he might precede him more safely and remove from him any doubt of treachery. Trusting in his companionship, the bishop reached the bank of the Minho while conversing with him.

There, after the solemn celebration of Mass, and after his knights had pitched their tents, they were struck by reports of a wicked betrayal. Setting before the bishop many reasons why he should not cross the river, they forbade him to do so. Although A. Petriz’s knights and other worthy men confirmed the warning, he scorned to believe it. He trusted too much in them: both because of their mutual brotherhood and the homage which they had afterwards voluntarily rendered to him, and because almost all belonged to his diocese and had received *soldatae* and benefices from his generosity.

Thus persuaded by this confidence, he received at close quarters two other messengers who urgently invited him: Sancho Ramiriz on the countess’s side, and Rudericus Sanchiz on the other. He therefore did not fear to enter the boat. As he was boarding it, his knights diligently sought, according to the custom of the country, for vain omens. They carefully observed a larger eagle crossing in the opposite direction; all were further struck by this one omen and for a third and fourth time rebuked him more vehemently, urging him not to go there. Because their words had proceeded not so much from abundance of understanding as from the mother of errors, namely ignorance, the aforesaid bishop received them with the kindly ear of his heart and is said to have given this answer:

> “Do not, dearest sons, disturb the purpose of a good intention by such trifles and empty omens. Know that the Almighty Lord, governor of all creation, has by no means entrusted the secrets of his counsel to birds and brute animals of this kind.”

## When the bishop went to the castle of the Minho

[Col. 0939B]

Overcome by this unanswerable reasoning, all the knights restrained their mouths as with a bridle and fell silent. Then, accompanied by three companions—Peter Anaides, his cleric and canon; M. Gelmiriz; and Peter Gutierriz, who is said, and is beyond doubt, to have disclosed this very betrayal—he crossed safely to the other side of the river. There he held a private conference with his betrayers, Peter Arias and the others.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] The principal authors of the betrayal were Arias Pérez, Peter Arias, Ferdinand Sánchez, and Oduarius Ordoñez. From chapter 66.]

At that place he wisely set before them the dangers threatening the land and questioned them with watchful concern and utmost diligence, so that, if they reported the matter, the truth about the fraud which had repeatedly troubled his ears might somehow become clear to him as well. But because heavenly truth hides itself from a mind oppressed by its own iniquity, and because they harbored the wound of betrayal in their breasts, they hastened to heap iniquity upon iniquity. With an oath, they utterly denied to his eminence that they would in any way commit treachery:

> “For we,” they said, “have submitted our necks to your fatherhood under a sure obligation of homage; and after all this, infected by no gall of malice, could we have devised any disgrace against you? Indeed, if perhaps we should see any disgrace inflicted upon you by anyone, let your discernment confidently know that, out of love for you, we shall expose our bodies to dangers even unto death.”

## CHAPTER L. [Col. 0939D] That, after swearing an oath, the traitors invited him to dinner

Enticed by these false words and promises, the bishop began slowly to ascend to the height of the tower in which the countess sat with her lord. When those standing above saw his approach nearby, they received him with such gladness of heart and joy of mind as those rejoice whom heavenly charity, by its presence, has visited after they had been plunged into the abyss.

[Note: [Col. 0940D] I would not wish you to imitate this manner of flattery.]

There, after reciprocal discussion of many matters, they confirmed before the bishop, outside the castle fortifications, an agreement sworn on both sides by twelve men. Its condition was that on the following day the castle should be entirely restored to them, and that they should conduct the countess herself, together with the noble boy, namely their lord, and all her troops and household goods, safely to her husband without loss.

After this compact had been confirmed and, as day receded, night was already drawing near, he told those around him that he would go beyond the river, where he had left the whole company of his troops and where he had ordered necessary provisions to be prepared for himself and them. But those who had fixed the dreadful missile of treachery within the bosom of their minds, and had already unanimously conspired to complete their disgrace, earnestly entreated his fatherhood not to cross the river in the deep stillness of night. Yielding to their flattering words, the bishop immediately granted them what they requested.

Then Ferdinand Sanchiz, by whose lordship the province of Lemos was at that time oppressed, undertook to entertain him that night with these deceitful words:

> “Most holy father and lord, you must today dine with me at such a dinner as you have never yet had.”

## CHAPTER LI. The contrivance of treachery

How great and what sort of a preparation for dinner it was, the betrayal of the following day made clear. And because the mind is often foreknowing of future things, the bishop passed almost the whole night sleepless. When morning came, certain natives of that province fled to him as to a fountain of mercy. He received their confession with an open ear and, opening to them the bowels of mercy, imposed upon them the fitting form of penance.

The aforesaid Ferdinand, more heated than the others with the prospect of carrying out the betrayal, boldly rebuked the bishop by deceitful guile, together with certain accomplices, in order that he might more quickly complete the business of the begun surrender. Since the day was advancing toward the fulfillment of works of goodness, Ferdinand feared that he could not achieve the result of his wicked will. But the pious father, armed on right and left, endured his insolence, overflowing with the ardor of charity:

> “First, my son,” he said, “in accordance with the voice of Truth, I must preach the kingdom of God; then I must attend to the concerns of this world.”

## CHAPTER LII. On the countess

Having first attended, according to the solicitude of pastoral care, to the flock entrusted to him, he entered the castle to carry out the surrender, amid the great joy of those standing around. To him, sitting within the castle entrance as though at a harbor of salvation, the countess descended from the summit of the tower, where she and the royal boy were being held as though in the depths of the sea, accompanied by no small company of nobles. There she remained close at the bishop’s side with the royal boy until all her household goods had been brought out.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the capture of the boy king and the countess

While she imagined herself protected there by the presence of so great a father, a band of traitors, equipped with swords and shields and terrible in every kind of weapon, shamelessly burst through the castle gate. They ran in haste, all together, to take the boy, whom she was already holding in her lap, almost lifeless because of the unexpected assault and the clamor of arms. Since she struggled to rescue him from their hands, they raged at her like lions and threatened her terribly: unless she immediately released him, they would without doubt—horrible to relate—dishonor her down to her very excrement.

When these fiercely uttered words violently struck the bishop’s ears, the bishop himself, with the utmost skill, gently took the nearly lifeless boy from the countess’s hands and entrusted him to the careful custody of his fosterer Ordonius. Thereafter they led the countess, violently tearing at her cheeks and pouring out tears like a swelling river, captive and with grievous disgrace back to the height of the tower from which she had descended of her own accord, together with her lord and certain others.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the plundering of the bishop’s property

[Col. 0941C]

After these things had thus been done, the aforesaid bishop saw noble and distinguished knights who had been serving the royal boy with the countess grievously beaten, dishonored, and stripped of their own possessions. Accompanied by only two clerics, overwhelmed by the excessive anguish of his heart and as though for a while forgetful of himself, he sat down sadly on the ground.

They had also seized his *couterinus*, Munio, whom he had sent outside the castle on an embassy to Arias Petriz, by a like fraud and betrayal while he was carrying out that embassy. Moreover, following John’s saying, “Let the evildoer still do evil, and let him who is filthy still be made filthy” (Revelation 22), they hastened to add crime more vehemently to iniquity. They sent Pelagius Martin and Leovegild Luz, accomplices in their malice, with the greater part of their troops and the entire brotherhood of that territory, beyond the river to invade the bishop’s tents and greedily plunder the spoils of his knights. Going under the pretense of peace and remaining with them in deceitful conference, they terribly assaulted their lodging and camp with armed force.

Intoxicated with the gall of betrayal and darkened by the gloom of their blindness, they carried off not only all the bishop’s household goods but also—an outrage terrible to human ears—laid their sacrilegious hands upon his chapel. They tore his chasuble into pieces among themselves with the insatiable rapacity of wolves and did not shrink from preserving it for their wicked use.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Other manuscripts read *infulam*, “a mitre,” which among writers of that age means the same thing as *casula*, “chasuble.”]

From that very chasuble they disgracefully adorned, without delay, the borders and fringes of their garments—as if by embellishing them. They likewise divided into three parts the golden vessel in which the Lord’s body, that is, our saving victim, is offered: one fearlessly claimed the lower portion, another the upper, and a third the remaining part for himself in most execrable fashion. They divided in the same way a silver chest and a crucifix wondrously fashioned by a goldsmith’s hand. What more need be said? We pass over, to spare the tedious labor of writing, not only almost all the horses and the equipment of the entire military force, but even packages of no small consequence.

When these things had been carefully learned, such fear and such unexpected horror struck the whole military force of the Church of Compostela that, abandoning the shorter road and traveling through wooded mountain summits, it reached home only with great difficulty.

## CHAPTER LV. When the traitors crossed the Minho with the bishop

After the betrayal described above, Peter Arias and his son, leaving the castle that same day with the bishop and certain other nobles, spent the night resting beside the monastery of St. Stephen on the bank of the Sil. Throughout the whole night they had the captives guarded with watchful care and an armed company of knights. When that night had passed and Phoebus had risen, as usual, from the waters of Ocean, they swiftly arrived at the crossing-place of the Minho commonly called Ambas Mixtas and crossed without encountering any obstacle of harm.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] Today Ambas Mestas, where the Sil and Minho meet.]

There the aforesaid bishop called Arias Petriz aside and, with two of his clerics present, addressed him as follows:

> “I am astonished that you, formerly a noble and excellent man, whom I regarded as a brother by blood and almost as half of my own heart, should have devised and carried out such treachery. From your very childhood I had been joined to you by the privilege of exceptional affection; moreover, I trusted you with fuller confidence as a friend close to my heart, both because you had received benefices and most abundant *soldatae* from my generosity, and because you had made me trust you under the bond of homage, confirmed by oath not once but twice and three times. I grieve more deeply over the folly of you and your associates, and over your deceitful youth, than over my own disgrace: unless you take better counsel, the name of your most wicked treachery will be published and cursed throughout the whole world.”

## CHAPTER LVI. Arias’s response to the bishop’s words

Arias replied to these most wisely tested words with this speech:

> “These things, most holy father, which your fatherhood tells me with the utmost ardor of charity, I perceive by the eye of my judgment to be true—and beyond doubt worse than you yourself maintain. Yet you inspired such intense fear in our party that, had we allowed your exalted person, so abundantly supplied with prudence in counsel, such a great host, and so many friends, to return safely to your own lands, we ourselves would without delay have been deprived both of our honors and of our possessions because of the capture of the others which we carried out in the presence of your venerable person. Although this deed appears detestable and blameworthy to human reason, because it can no longer be undone, we cannot discover in our minds by what means it might be dissolved.”

## CHAPTER LVII. The words of Peter Anaides

[Col. 0943B]

Peter Anaides, the cleric of the aforesaid bishop, breaking silence as if in indignation, addressed him thus:

> “When I consider your words with continual reflection of mind, I am filled with extraordinary indignation and sharply afflicted in heart with grief, because I perceive that counsel has wholly failed you in actions such as these. You, in whom only lately the vein of intelligence was thought to leap in the left side [an uncertain figurative expression], how could you seize by evil cunning and the fraud of your dreadful crime a man so excellent and so powerful—the governor of all Galicia—without first devising, through tireless deliberation, by what agreement the deed might afterward be undone? Finally, if you labor to provide for your own advantage, you must now, without any delay, consider whether, for his release, he should make you rich by a gift from his own resources or remove the uncertainty of your fear by venerable hostages. But if, as you assert, you seized him on account of fear, then receive for the time being either an oath from Munio, his *couterinus* brother, or the castles of Honesti and Santa María de Lanciata, lest what you fear should happen to you.”

He had proposed the castles deliberately and with shrewd ingenuity, because he knew without hesitation that, if the bishop were released under this agreement, his lord would recover his castles within about three days.

> “I see that neither you yourselves nor your descendants will in any way escape the danger of so dreadful a crime, and that you will incur forever the reproach of this most wicked betrayal, unless you hasten to release him as soon as possible.”

Before his words had even ended—for they were spoken as a rebuke—Peter, abbot of Termas, known to be a companion of his lord in that same captivity, interrupted him and continued in this manner.

## CHAPTER LVIII. The words of Peter, abbot of Termas

“You know, dearest brother, that the providence of this our father has enlarged the Church of Compostela abundantly in both honors and possessions. He more fully adorned and more firmly strengthened it with the number of seventy-two canons, whom his fatherhood had rendered well disciplined within the bosom of his affection. This Church, afflicted by the suffering of so great a father, will be utterly laid waste; and, because you are the cause of its ruin, it will be destroyed and reduced to nothing.”

## CHAPTER LIX. On the agreement for the bishop’s release
Accepting these and the aforesaid reasons with kindly feeling, Arias Petriz said: “In return, I mean, for receiving the castles, I shall hasten without delay to set your lord free.” Accordingly, that same day, coming by a swift route to a certain estate, namely Amoarium, we confirmed the aforesaid agreement—lest it should be shaken or weakened—by pledges received from their side; and concerning all this we sent Munio Eriz and Froila Menendiz to Compostela. When, moreover, the arrival of the second dawn drove the darkness from the face of the world, we entered the castle of Saint John of Peña Corveria [Note: [Col. 0943] Cornaria should be read, as below, ch. III, no. 4. Today commonly Peña Corneira.]; then, on the third day, leaving P. Arias there with the royal boy and certain others in bonds, we travelled through the trackless, bushy heights of the mountains and, not without great labour, reached the castle of Luparia [Note: [Col. 0943D] Between Compostela and Iria.]. There we received, with the utmost joy of heart, the above-named messengers whom we had already sent ahead to the Church of Compostela, together with two canons of that same church and several other fellow citizens. From their report we learned that all the clergy of Compostela had bound themselves by a sacred oath to work unanimously for the release of the aforesaid bishop, and that, once he should breathe the air of life again, they would accept no other lord [Col. 0944C]. Moreover, not only the citizens but also the knights of the whole land had, with deliberate care, bound themselves by the bond of sacred faith, so that, proceeding with all speed, they might free their lord from the prison of so wicked a captivity; for by the unanimous judgment of all, the whole treasure of the Church and the entire public wealth were being offered for the raising of troops.

This report, which raised us heavenward with intense joy, struck Arias Petriz with still more violent dismay. Therefore he took counsel with some of his followers, intending to withdraw from the promise of the aforesaid compact and, without any delay of time, to take the aforesaid bishop to another castle where he might be held more firmly and securely. Since this counsel was by no means concealed from the bishop [Col. 0944D], he promptly called A. Petriz to account before the force then at his disposal, because he wished unreasonably to withdraw himself from the agreement which he had previously made. When the barons of that land perceived this, not without grief of heart, they sternly rebuked him and prohibited him in every way from daring to do anything other than what had been settled between them. Compelled, therefore, by their irresistible argument, A. Petriz entrusted the bishop to their custody on this condition: if the aforesaid castles were delivered to him that day, they should immediately release the bishop. Gladly receiving him under their protection, they moved him a league away from the castle [Col. 0945A]. From that place he sent his brother M. and P. Anaides to deliver the castle of Honesti; and, once it had been delivered to Froila Menendiz, who was to receive it on Arias’s behalf, he ordered it to be surrendered under every authority.

## CHAPTER LX. On the liberation of the bishop

While this was taking place, A. Petriz, reflecting within the secret chamber of his heart that he could in no way retain the aforesaid castles, adopted the better and more advantageous counsel and addressed his barons thus:

“I judge it very useful and necessary for myself that, abandoning the castles, I should permit the bishop to go free and willingly render whatever justice he may demand from me for the dishonour inflicted upon him. Yet, lest what I fear should happen to me [Col. 0945B] in this crisis, let him not delay to send me, as quickly as possible, three of his brothers as hostages for a time: namely Munio, treasurer of the Church of Blessed James, and Peter Gelmiriz, and his brother John. Meanwhile, until they come, let Archdeacon O., P. Anaides, and P. Vimariades remain with me.”

Since all his knights approved this sound and excellent counsel with one accord, the aforesaid bishop, accompanied by the greater part of them, entered that same day his castle of Honesti, intending to surrender it with great ceremony. As he entered, a vast multitude of his own knights received him with exceeding joy of heart. This multitude, equipped with lances, swords, and shields, had prudently concealed itself in certain hidden places beside the road, so that, if by chance Arias’s soldiers should seize the castle, they might come with all speed, prevent the castle from being filled with slaughter, surround it on every side, and unanimously storm it once besieged [Col. 0945C]. When the rejoicing of that night had ended, protected by the strength of his knights, on the following day he was received at Iria with no less honour. From there he swiftly sent his three brothers to Arias, in accordance with the terms of the aforesaid undertaking, so that Arias might without delay release the other three who had remained with him in their stead. The venerable presence of the bishop received these men, as though freed from chains, with every expression of joy.

## CHAPTER LXI. The joy of Compostela at the bishop’s arrival

[Col. 0945D] When the dawn of the third day was reddening, as he prepared his journey to Compostela, a vast multitude of both sexes, gathering from different quarters as though wholly converging upon the protector of the entire province, accompanied his longed-for presence as far as the milestone from which the desirable site of the holy city comes into view. When, by the helping grace of God, he reached those places, as we have briefly mentioned above, the whole throng of the Compostelans came out to meet him, singing with drums, zithers, and various musical instruments, and offering praises to heavenly mercy for the safety of their recovered shepherd. For an innumerable company of young men sang with such rejoicing [Col. 0946A] that, were one to attempt to express it, the power of our speech would fail beneath so great a task of description. The remaining multitude of youths, rejoicing at his desired presence with hymns and sweet-flowing melodies of harmony, came singing with him as far as the church of Compostela.
