In that church, if previously he had watched less diligently than he ought over the care of those subject to him, thereafter, strengthened by divine protection, whatever he perceived required correction among his subjects he corrected with the staff of pastoral care, by the generous grace of divine God, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the restoration of peace after his liberation

[Col. 0946B] Therefore, after, in the Era 1148 [Note: [Col. 0945] Two manuscripts read VIIII instead of VIII, but wrongly; for in the following year they write Era 1149, ch. 73.], the venerable D., bishop of the Apostolic See—as has already been said—was, with the Lord’s help, brought forth from the captivity of the aforesaid traitors: a man conspicuous for immeasurable goodness, discerning in prudence, proved in temperance, steadfast in courage, strict in justice, and eminent in every moral virtue—the clergy and people of the city of Compostela, women and little children, received him as he came from treacherous captivity with as much joy as Lazarus’s sisters deserved to receive their brother, four days dead, when the Lord and Saviour raised him. For although he was held in custody by his betrayers for only five days—alas for the crime!—wherever news of his betrayal was heard, prayers, outbursts of anger, and anxious disturbance arose at once.

Indeed, in the city of Compostela those to whom zeal for uprightness is especially accustomed always to be hateful had suddenly risen to such insolence that they dared to attack the religious persons of the Church in a wicked conspiracy and did not hesitate, through any reverence or fear, to assault clerics [Col. 0946C]. Thus it came about that certain gluttonous villains of the city, having surrounded in his house an archdeacon of Saint James—a Catholic and noble man—wished to kill him on false suspicion. Yet Truth, which was accustomed often to cherish the archdeacon Munio, did not wish to abandon her lover in so great a danger, but mercifully freed him from the impious hands of the sacrilegious. Nevertheless, it was decreed that those who raged in such drunken madness should be subjected to the continual service of the clerics [Col. 0946D]; and this was established by decree of royal authority and confirmed by a privilege of apostolic authority, as may be found written in the lawful register of the blessed Apostle.

But once the bishop had, by divine grace, been restored to the chair of his see, prosperity immediately followed for a while, and the warlike turbulence of Galicia and the frequent tumults of the city subsided somewhat. We believe that this happened because evil-doers feared to experience the real vengeance of the bishop, while good men feared to lose his favour. Indeed, the affairs of the counts and other leading men of Galicia were referred to the bishop, to be settled by his counsel and judgment; and whatever the bishop prudently ordered was unanimously approved by all [Col. 0947A].

That bishop, however, lamented and sighed deeply for the royal boy, the grandson, that is, of the glorious King Alfonso, solemnly to be remembered for the sanctity of his rule. The boy, delivered up together with the bishop, was still held in that same captivity; and the bishop feared all the more that he whom he unquestionably hoped would reign might perish through poisonous treachery. Terrified by this fear and apprehension, the venerable bishop directed all the purpose and effort of his mind toward securing a worthy release for the queen’s son, who had been shamefully captured. He believed that through the boy’s liberation Galicia could be restored to the union of peace and concord. Accordingly, having summoned the chief persons of his church [Col. 0947B], he disclosed the purpose which he had been turning over in his mind; and, having taken useful counsel with them, he sent his envoy for Count Peter, whose wife and sons were held captive for the royal infant, so that he might take counsel with him as to how the boy could be raised to the kingdom.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the release of the boy, son of the queen

Count Peter and the aforesaid bishop accordingly met beside the river called Tamar. There, after many arguments and varied assertions had been multiplied, they finally came to the conclusion that so great a matter ought by no means to be undertaken without the joint counsel and assistance of the queen, who was his mother. Therefore envoys from the bishop and the count went to the queen and openly disclosed to her the secret which the bishop had long pondered in his mind. Having heard them attentively and examined the matter with careful inquiry, the queen rejoiced with a solemn joy beyond what can be believed [Col. 0947C]: both because she heard of the elevation of her own son to the kingdom, and because through his exaltation she could confidently believe that the overthrow of the Aragonese tyrant, or at least his swifter expulsion from the kingdom, might more easily come about.

She immediately summoned Count Ferdinand, a vigorous and prudent man, whom Queen Lady U. addressed with the following entreating words:

## CHAPTER LXIV. The queen’s words to Count F. concerning the elevation of her son to kingship

[Col. 0947D] “Noble and wise Count F., whom not only the bond of kinship but also the prerogative of the ample honour which I have always shown you binds most strongly to me with an indissoluble chain: I earnestly request counsel from your generosity as to what at last should be decided concerning my son, whom the venerable bishop of Blessed James is striving with all zeal to raise as king. For it is known to you and to all who inhabit the kingdoms of Spain that my father, Emperor Alfonso, when the hour of his death approached, entrusted the whole kingdom to me at Toledo, and Galicia to my son Alfonso, his grandson; and he declared by testament that, if I should take a husband, after my death the dominion of the whole kingdom would belong to him by hereditary right [Col. 0948A].

“He ordered before him almost all the consuls and the other holders of authority in Spain, who at that time had assembled at Toledo while setting out on an expedition against the Moors. Of these men, he had brought some up from childhood, abundantly enriched others from poverty, and ennobled still others, raising them from low birth. He kindly subjected their service to my rule, diligently commended my person and kingdom to their faithful protection, and threatened and warned me not to presume in any way to determine anything grave or difficult apart from their will and common counsel. Thus it came about that, after my father’s death, according to their disposition and judgment, I was unwillingly married to the bloodstained [uncertain reading: *pialtico*] Aragonese tyrant, and unhappily joined to him in a shameful and accursed marriage [Note: [Col. 0947D] Below, ‘phantastical.’] [Note: [Col. 0948D] See ch. 79, no. 3.].

“No one knows better than your prudence what and how great insults, pains, and torments I endured while I was with him. For not only did he continually dishonour me with shameful words, but—to the grief of all nobility—it must be said that he often struck my face with his filthy hands and kicked me with his foot. This man, his mind polluted by sacrilege and formed by no principle of discernment, trusting in auguries and divinations, irrationally believes that ravens and crows can do harm. As though ashamed, he avoids wise and noble men; having become the companion of worthless buffoons, he is stirred by every commotion of frivolity. He zealously honours the execrable fellowship of apostates [Col. 0948C], and, despising all divine worship of the Church and religious persons as nothing, holds them in contempt. Hence he violates and destroys the churches of God without pity, despoils their ministers, and seizes their possessions. Hence, by the violence of his tyranny, he expelled the bishops of Burgos and León from their sees. He also laid hands upon the bishop of Palencia, whom he had ordered to come to him under the guarantee of Christian faith, and thus seized him through fraud and deceit. He kept the archbishop of Toledo—a religious pillar of God’s Church and legate of Roman holiness—away from his diocese for two years; and he drove the abbot of Saint Facundus from his own monastery, installing in his place his sacrilegious brother, with all religion and justice set aside.

“Moreover, he had burned with such fury and hatred against my little son Alfonso that he strove with all his strength to destroy him, believing that he would securely possess the kingdom if the boy could somehow be handed over to death [Col. 0948D]. For this reason he sought by a dreadful plot to bring the warlike Count Peter—most steadfast in firmness of faith—to ruin, because Peter, the faithful guardian of the infant, could not be separated from his loyalty by any tribulation or trouble. At my father’s command he had sworn allegiance to the child’s lordship in the city of León.

“Accordingly, the savage Celtiberian entered Galicia in fury. How many and how great were the crimes he committed in that region is plainly shown by the slaughter of nobles; the soldiers cruelly killed at Mount Irsoum [Col. 0949A]; the castle thrown down; the land laid waste and stripped of every good; the violation of churches and the dishonouring of their priests; respectable women stripped naked; virgins shamelessly violated; Count Peter’s hereditary estates destroyed; houses and palaces burned; herds of mares and cattle, partly carried away from Galicia and partly cut to pieces; the groans of the afflicted and the tears of the poor. In addition, the fearful anathema of the lord pope, and the condemnation of the archbishop of Toledo and of the most religious pontiff of the Apostolic Church, incessantly denounced the shamefulness of our marriage.

“Therefore, when I knew that I had been deeply contaminated by the contagion of sacrilege and could no longer endure the sharp sword of justice [Col. 0949B], I took care, with deliberate resolve, to separate myself from that phantastical idolater. But after the separation had been made and my shameful marriage dissolved, fires, massacres, plunder, murders, betrayals, and wars immediately sprang up everywhere through the countryside and Castile. While he shamefully enjoyed union with me, he had deceitfully occupied certain cities and entrusted them to his officers to guard. Now his wicked robber-bandits emerge from them and plunder the whole province; they burn my royal estates and palaces, and mercilessly demolish and ruin the boroughs on the public road and the hostels where pilgrims of Saint James used to lodge.

“Finally, the fields are uncultivated, the land unploughed, famine and want press hard; farmers once abounding in ample wealth, to whom nothing at all remains save light straw, which they hold against their naked bodies to cover the shameful parts of their frailty, are found dead everywhere in streets and fields from cold and hunger [Col. 0949C]. The modesty of virgins is violated without shame; mothers are dishonoured, widows lament, orphans are desolate, and places once inhabited stand deserted and ravaged—all openly attest our pitiable misery. In short, no corner of Iberia is untouched by the noise or disturbance of so great a frenzy. Now, therefore, most illustrious count, since I have set forth all my reasons and disclosed my inner concerns, it becomes your nobility to give counsel to my wavering mind according to what seems best to you.”

## CHAPTER LXV. The reply of Count Ferdinand

[Col. 0949D]

Count F. is reported to have given this reply: “Mighty and glorious queen, I have weighed with the greatest care the account you have presented on true grounds and have wholly committed it to firm memory. In it you have shown that the king of Aragon is the cause of all evil and the ruin of Spain, and that no hope of salvation is to be looked for in him. You must therefore be especially vigilant lest what the apostolic man is undertaking at divine prompting, and has communicated to you through his envoys, should appear to be delayed in any degree through you. Rather, setting aside every delay, strive to bring it to completion with diligent care; entrust yourself, your son, his cause [Col. 0950A], and his undertaking to the judgment and direction of the aforesaid bishop; and henceforth presume to do nothing apart from his counsel. Indeed, if it should please your will, I shall convey this embassy to that bishop, and at your command I shall faithfully obey him in all matters whatsoever he commands, and willingly furnish such assistance as I can by every means.”

Since the queen approved this counsel with the greatest favour, Count F. at once set out and hastened to the aforesaid bishop. He found him seated at Saint James in his court, surrounded by clergy and knights. Kissing his hand on the queen’s behalf, he conveyed to him many kindly greetings. He then recounted privately and individually to the bishop the reasons for his coming and everything the queen had told him [Col. 0950B]. Afterwards Count F. was conducted to lodging and, after the labour of the journey, gave his limbs to welcome sleep.

That night the bishop could sleep little or not at all. With anxious consideration he considered how—as scarcely or never could be accomplished—his own dishonour and that of his Church might not remain unavenged, and how he might free the infant from captivity. For it was the intention of those who held the boy to make him the price of the enmities which, because of their own wrongful acts, they had incurred against that bishop and Count Peter. The bishop therefore adopted sound and useful counsel: he preferred not to avenge his own injury rather than allow the infant to be detained in shameful captivity [Col. 0950C]. Accordingly he sent messengers to his traitors and enemies, asking them to release the infant and not to fear that vengeance for the crime they had committed against the bishop would fall upon them. On hearing this, the traitors eagerly promised to do so, provided that Count Peter, by a similar agreement, remitted the hatred arising from their injuries.

Therefore, on a fixed day and at a fixed place, the oft-mentioned bishop summoned both the traitors and the count to the bridge over the river Ulla, called that of Cessuris [Note: [Col. 0949] Read “bridge of Gessuris,” which still retains that name today, over the Ulla near Iria.]. He had first bound them firmly by an oath of faith that they would not attempt to plot any harm against one another at that meeting. We cannot now set forth the many settlements of disputes and the various public and private statements then discussed; but we must not pass over in silence what took place before our eyes [Col. 0950D].

## CHAPTER LXVI. The release of the boy and his installation as king

Since the bishop wisely perceived that forgiving the captivity and dishonour inflicted upon his own person belonged to the common safety of the entire land and to public benefit, he not only wholeheartedly remitted and allowed to remain unavenged the injury of his betrayal and the disgrace inflicted upon him by P. Arias, Arias Petriz, Fernando Sanciade, Oduario Ordoniz, and the other impious traitors, but also persuaded Count P., with gentle speech, likewise to set aside his own injuries and the enmities arising from them. Thus, when every accusation concerning offences and every hatred of enmity had been ended [Col. 0951A], the count and the above-named men entered into a covenant of friendship, secured by oaths, while preserving fealty and loyalty to the queen and the infant; and they were restored to concord in a firm peace.

Having become faithful friends after peace was established, the bishop, full of immeasurable goodness, and all the others unanimously fixed a day upon which they would raise the infant as king. Accordingly, on the following Sunday, when the Introit of the Mass is sung, “You are righteous, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0951] Namely, the seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost, which in the year 1110 fell on 25 September.], they brought the boy who was to reign to Saint James, amid great and noble ceremony and universal rejoicing. The bishop, clothed in pontifical vestments, and the other clerics, fittingly adorned in ecclesiastical garments, received him in a glorious procession. Taking him, the bishop led him joyfully before the altar of Blessed James the Apostle, where his body is said to rest [Col. 0951B]; there, according to the religious ordinances of the canons, he anointed him as king, gave him a sword and sceptre, crowned him with a golden diadem, and caused him, established as king, to sit in the pontifical seat.

Then, after Mass had been solemnly celebrated according to custom, the bishop led the new king to his palace and invited all the leading men of Galicia to a royal banquet. At it the most illustrious Count Peter acted as royal steward; his son Roderic, as standard-bearer, held shield and spear at the king’s shoulders; Munio Pelagides acted as royal offertory-bearer; and Veremudus Petrides ordered wine and *sicera*—strong drink—to be supplied abundantly to all the tables. Thus, when all had been carefully satisfied with diverse dishes, that day passed in hymns of rejoicing and songs of songs [Col. 0951C].

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the subjection of the city of Lugo to the rule of the boy-king

On the next day, the first to dawn after his elevation, all assembled before the bishop and took counsel to lead their king to León; and, after installing him there with his mother, to strive to subject the whole kingdom to his authority, together with all the leading men of Castile. But because certain men, gathered at the city of Lugo from different regions, still upheld with foolish presumption the injustice of the Aragonese tyrant—wicked robbers, murderers, transgressors, adulterers, fornicators, bloody despoilers of the possessions of the wretched, violators of churches, who feared bodily punishments and torments for their abominable crimes [Col. 0951D]—it seemed fitting to the bishop, count, and other princes that the city should first be purged of all criminals and subjected to the king’s rule before they began to consider any other business. Proceeding therefore to the city, they sent envoys ahead to the people of Lugo, ordering them either to surrender the city to the king or to prepare, if they could, to defend themselves. When they heard the terrible embassy and that the king’s army was coming against them, they preferred to surrender the city to the king rather than commit anything against their natural lord that might disturb his will [Col. 0952A].

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the battle fought at Angos

Once the city had been pacified and the realm restored to the boy, the bishop and count, with a few of the nobler men, directed their journey straight toward León, as they had determined at Compostela. When they reached the place called the Fountain of Angos, they pitched their pavilions and tents all around. Ignorant that the treacherous Aragonese had hidden scouts or ambushes along the route, they rested there that night with all fear removed and enjoyed safe quarters and sleep. Yet they numbered only 266 men [Col. 0952B], and no more.

When the treacherous Aragonese learned this from his scouts, he assembled an army of 660 armoured knights and 2,000 foot-soldiers equipped with bows, swords, clubs, and weapons; and, springing forth from concealment, he came to meet them. At dawn the Galicians rose; hearing that the wicked enemy was coming upon them, they immediately sprang to arms, swiftly armed themselves, formed their battle-lines, and, awaiting battle with few fighters—one against ten, ten against a thousand—boldly occupied the field. Yet when they saw the enemy approaching from afar with grim faces, they began to advance step by step against so great an army. When they were already near, wielding their lances with strong arms and urging their swift horses with spurs, they attacked the first battle-line in a terrible clash [Col. 0952C], wounded nearly all of it, and cast it to the ground; and at once no small multitude of Aragonese was slain. But when, fighting and courageously laying their enemies low, they had penetrated into the immense troop of knights and the innumerable mass of infantry, exhausted by battle, they were surrounded on every side by dust and enemies. Wounded from behind and at the flanks, they could not withstand the blow of fortune. Some therefore died in the bloody battle; others were captured, not without great loss of blood.

The courageous Count Peter, who had broken into the midst of the enemy’s battle-lines, after exacting most fierce and prolonged vengeance upon the enemy, preferred to be captured fighting rather than shamefully abandon the field [Col. 0952D]. Count Ferdinand also died in the battle, and many others fell.

When the bishop learned that the fortune of war was turning to the adverse side, he was troubled with greater fear and concern for the king whom he had newly anointed than for his own bodily person. For he feared not only the king’s death or capture, but also the destruction of all Spain. With diligent effort and prudent skill, therefore, he arranged to withdraw the little emperor from so great a danger of war and restored him safe and sound to his mother, Queen Lady Urraca, in the strong castle of Orzilion—which castle is in Castile [Col. 0953A]. He himself withdrew to the city of Astorga, where for three days he gathered up those wounded and scattered in the battle, becoming a haven of common safety and a singular comfort to all. After three days, with all whom he could collect from the battle, he returned by long routes to the city of Compostela of Saint James. He found it not merely grievously disturbed when it heard of the unlucky outcome of the battle; almost all Galicia was now shaken by such disasters and warlike turbulence that, nearly broken, it despaired of safety. The bishop therefore summoned all the leading men of Galicia and compelled them by firm assurances under oath to show fidelity and service to the queen and her son. Thus he restored tranquillity and peace to Galicia.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the *infantaticum* between the Tamar and Ulla given by the queen to Blessed James

[Col. 0953B]

When the queen received her son Alfonso, the little king, coming—as has been said—from the unhappy battle, the magnitude of her joy of heart can more openly be known to mothers of royal sons than expressed in writing. First, she rejoiced because she had received her son safe; next, because through him she not unreasonably hoped that the Aragonese tyrant could be expelled from the kingdom. Therefore, in the strong and impregnable fortress of Orzilion, the queen committed her son to be guarded. Leaving with him faithful guards from among the leading men of that land, she resolved to travel to Galicia.

Accordingly, beginning her journey through the harsh Asturian mountains and stony heights, she passed through Oviedo [Col. 0953C]. When she reached the city of Lugo, divine compunction moved her inwardly to strive, in penitence, to visit the threshold of Blessed James. She therefore came to Compostela; entering the apostolic church, she prostrated herself on the pavement between the iron doors of its vestibule and the most holy altar. Stretching out her hands, she poured forth to the Lord with devout feeling this prayer:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who, by the dispensation of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, deigned to restore by your own blood the world lost through the transgression of the first parent: I humbly implore and beseech you that the kingdom of Spain, happily possessed by my father A., but now grievously desolated by his death and disturbed on every side by the schism of the Aragonese tyranny [Col. 0953D], you, our most merciful Saviour, may deign, through the sweet intercession of your apostle James—whose most glorious body rests venerably in this present place—to grant and bring into peace for the lord to whom it belongs by right, so that your faithful may be able to dwell there in tranquillity and become fit to serve you, the living and true God, through infinite ages of ages.”

After making the sign of the cross and rising from prayer, the venerable bishop of that place and the venerable persons of his clerics received her as befitted her and led her to the episcopal palace, where she was suitably lodged. On the following day, inspired by the divine Spirit [Col. 0954A], with a heart contrite in the Lord and humbled in supplicating devotion for the salvation of herself and the whole kingdom, for the remedy of her soul and those of her parents, she charitably offered to Blessed James and his ministers the royal courts in that city, other residences which were hers by right, the whole *infantaticum* between the Tamar and Ulla, and whatever seemed to belong to the royal right. What she had offered she confirmed by a charter of privilege for the honour of that Church.

## CHAPTER LXX. Names of the houses and estates which the queen gave to Blessed James

We set down these estates, courts, or residences by name: namely, that estate which had belonged to Lord F., king; in Quintana [Col. 0954B], which had belonged to Gundisalvus Adefonsiz, four houses, namely two *solia* and two ground-level houses; and elsewhere one house which had belonged to Maior Didaciz, beside that of John Struariz; and two *solia* which she had from Froila Didaciz’s portion; and one ground-level house in the valley of Milvori; and another house beside the house of Arias Didaciz; and the estate of Siceranes; and one estate of Erimar; and the estate called Figueirola; and one mill which had belonged to Novales.

Likewise, in the land of Pistomarci, in the royal domain: Saint Vincent of Sispalona, Trenonzum, Ferrarios [Note: [Col. 0953D] Another manuscript: Hispatona, Trevonium.] with their appurtenances; the *monumenta* of Sanderezum; the new estate of Masiti; Rama, the inheritance of Odorio; Monumenta; Sarra; the castle of Malladas; Corronium; the meadows of Lord Pepi [Col. 0954C]; Juncarias [Note: [Col. 0954D] Read *Juncarias*.], Villafredi; Listas; Canales; in Nogia, Verrimes of Jusano; again Villafranca; half of Lovium; in Auzonio, her share; in Alvariza, one plot of land within its boundaries; in Pastoriza, her share; a fourth part of the water-rights of Jusano; in Circites, the revenues of Arumde; the house of Arias Exemeniz; a third part of the estate of Palatios; the estate called Dara with its inhabitants; and in Villiestro, Figeirola.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On resources from the treasury given to the queen

All these above-mentioned estates, which lie between the Tamar and Ulla, together with the men belonging to the royal domain and to the *infantaticum*, she bestowed upon that same Church for the same reason. This action wonderfully kindled the minds of all the clerics toward the queen’s benefit and greatly encouraged them to carry out justly all her will. But the queen had spent nearly her whole father’s treasury in prosecuting war against the Aragonese, and therefore lacked resources sufficient for a prolonged campaign. Accordingly, by the common counsel of the canons and decree of the entire senate, it was judged that assistance and counsel requested by the queen from their Church ought not to be denied her. Thus, in order to defeat the worst devastator of Spain and expel the disturber of the whole kingdom, they ordered, of their own free will, that one hundred ounces of gold and 200 marks of silver from the treasury of Saint James should be given to the queen at her request [Col. 0955A].

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the siege of Luparia and the capture of Arias Petriz and his accomplices
Meanwhile the queen remained at Compostela for fifteen days and summoned all the magnates of Galicia and her whole court for the approaching Easter, which was to fall on 2 April. Immediately the leading men of Galicia assembled from every side: the valiant and faithful Count P., Munio Pelagides, Vermudo Petrides, Rodrigo Vela, M. Gelmirides, and the rest who appeared to hold some principality or lordship in Galicia. Among them was also Arias Petrides, who had indeed been the chief of the wicked treachery deceitfully perpetrated at the Castle of Miño against the lord bishop D. and against the queen’s son, the infant A. (as related above, ch. 49), and who at the same time had fraudulently seized the castle of Lupa. Yet although Arias was an infamous traitor, of such obstinacy and guile that scarcely anyone—or no one—could endure him, the prudent and restrained queen received and treated him kindly and honourably.

But because he was carried away by the familiar tempest of his savagery, feared no little the deserved penalties and torments for the crimes he had committed in his pride, and was openly marked by his infamy, he was terrified and despaired. On the night after Good Friday he secretly left Compostela and withdrew to Lupa, intending to rebel against the queen and her son and, if possible, to commit another act of treachery. That same night, at Matins, this was reported in church to the queen. She immediately took counsel with the bishop and the other nobles and rightly resolved that, after the Lord’s Easter had been gloriously celebrated, they should go out together to crush Arias’s pride and fraud. Accordingly, on the second day of Easter the queen set out with the bishop and her army, and besieged Arias, traitor and arrogant man, at Lupa.

The stubborn Arias, now under siege, struck by overwhelming terror and made unsteady and trembling by the tumult of his fury, utterly despaired of safety. Lacking discernment and reason, he did not know what to do. At length, blinded by the foul darkness of his malice and forgetful of himself, he obtained no treaty of protection for himself in respect of the crimes he had committed, but surrendered himself and the castle to the queen and rode with her. His accomplices, participants in the aforesaid treachery, when they heard that Arias was with the queen, supposed that he—who had been, as it were, the head of their conspiracy—had secured some agreement for their safety. They came to him at court and spoke with him. But when they found nothing advantageous for themselves, they earnestly wished to absent themselves from court because of the disgrace and confusion of their offences; yet they could not depart. For the queen ordered them all to be seized and kept bound in iron fetters until they surrendered all the castles they held.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the Siege of Astorga

Having thus received from the faithless traitors the castles, in the Era 1149, the queen assembled the army of Galicia and set out to attack the king of Aragon. Through difficult roads, laborious mountains, and country cold with the snows and ice of the previous winter—which had raged with exceptional severity that year—they came as far as the city of Astorga. While the foot-soldiers and servants refreshed there what had been weakened on the journey and prepared the necessary provisions, the queen, by the common counsel of her nobles, sent messengers for the Castilians, Asturians, and her other faithful men throughout the Campos. On hearing the queen’s summons, they gathered very quickly. Leaving their castles, they pitched their tents and pavilions on the plain; yet they did not at once come directly to the queen or encamp beside her.

Meanwhile the impious enemy of Aragon had secretly gathered an innumerable army. There assembled men of Nájera, Burgos, Palencia, Carrión, Zamora, León, and those who had unanimously come out from San Facundo. Their hearts had been so goaded by diabolical persuasion that they willingly followed a man who had resolved to spend his life without the law of Christian faith and justice, and gladly obeyed his commands.

> [Note: Col. 0955D: The manuscripts read *Nazareni*, that is, inhabitants of the town then called Nazara in Rioja, now Nájera. For this reason *Najareni* has been substituted, as we noted above in the Preliminary Notice, no. 18; Col. 0956D.]

All these, I say, and another rabble were with him: men who, because of the grave disgrace of their crimes—murderers, evildoers, fornicators, adulterers, thieves, criminals, ravishers, sacrilegious persons, enchanters, diviners, hateful robbers, accursed apostates—had shamefully abandoned their native places and attached themselves to him as the prince of all the guilty. The wicked Aragonese was surrounded by such an army. Advancing against Astorga, he suddenly appeared among the thickets of the mountains visible from Astorga between the river Órbigo and the city, with a great multitude of soldiers. Approaching near the city, he pitched camp and made his quarters there. Since he had experienced at Fuente Angos that the Galicians were strong in war even when few in number, he did not dare attack them at the city, especially since he had certainly learned that their force was greater than on that earlier occasion.

Having sent envoys into Aragon, Martín Muñiz was bringing by his command three hundred mailed Aragonese knights; with their help he expected either to take the city or to make frequent assaults upon it. The Castilians, however—whom we mentioned above as having pitched their tents on the plain—heard that the Aragonese were hastening to assist the hostile army. They immediately ran to arms, mounted their swift horses, and fiercely occupied the road by which the enemy would come. When they saw them approaching from afar with grim eyes, raging within themselves through an excessive desire to fight, they turned their whole battle-line upon them at once. Spurring their swift horses with sharp spurs, grasping stout lances in strong arms, they attacked terribly; striking hard blows, they spilled their enemies’ entrails beneath shields and mail-shirts. The wounded were cast down, and the spoils of the impious were seized. The Aragonese fell; Martín Muñiz and very many others were immediately captured. All the rest, except the prisoners and those who died in battle, took flight or hid among the thickets.

When he heard this, the savage Aragonese, frustrated in the vain hope he had entertained and, like Herod deceived by the Magi, trembled in anxious fear, worn out by distrust and sleepless care. With night coming on, he secretly withdrew his army from the siege and fled to Carrión.

At daybreak the queen went out onto the plain with the faithful Galician magnates. Sending her envoys, she ordered the Castilians and Asturians to come to her, together with all whom she considered loyal to her throughout the Campos and Extremadura. She no longer remained in castles or cities, but lived in tents; and she assembled a very large and powerful army. She pursued the cruel little king of Aragon, surrounded his camp, tents, and army, besieged him at Carrión, and held him under siege for a long time.

> [Note: Col. 0957D: Formerly *Extrema* and *Extremitas* denoted the regions lying at the extremities of the Duero, from the river’s source to its southern bank, of which Segovia was the chief place; see ch. 117. Now Extremadura extends from Salamanca to Mérida and beyond the river Anas; Col. 0958D.]

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the Restoration of Peace in Galicia by the Bishop

Meanwhile the venerable bishop of the Church of St James returned to his own lands. He had left the aforesaid expedition at Triacastela, by the counsel of the queen and all the leading men of Galicia, in order to restore peace and concord in Galicia while the queen hurried to war against the Aragonese tyrant.

At that time Pelagius Gudesteides and Rabinatus Muñiz, having heard that the queen had crossed the mountains and would not easily return to Galicia, completed no small portion of their journey back to their castles and plotted how they might rebel against Queen Urraca and her little son, King Alfonso, whom the aforesaid bishop had anointed king in the church of St James. Then they approached Arias Petrides, P. Arides, Oduarius Ordonides, and their accomplices. These men, because of the aforesaid treachery against the lord bishop Didacus and against the queen’s son, the little King A., had been seized and put in chains by the queen. After hostages had been placed in the queen’s power and all their fortresses surrendered, they had fled as exiles to the ports and furthest borders of Galicia. With them P. Gudesteides and R. Muñiz took counsel and discussed disturbing the kingdom.

Alas, wretches! They made light of the oath they had sworn to the queen and her son, King A. Having assembled forces on both sides, they invaded Deza, Tabeirós, and all the other territories. Plundering and devastating the surrounding country, they seized for themselves, by the violence of their tyranny, the whole land lying between the Miño and the Ulla, except the castle of Lupa. They bound nobles and peasants alike by oath to be faithful to their lord—that is, the Aragonese tyrant, whom by their wicked act they had chosen as lord.

When the aforesaid bishop learned that the fierce rage of the traitors had broken out, he was pierced with great grief. Yet, relying boldly upon prudent counsel, he assembled a great army and hurried to destroy them, although they were supported by an innumerable host of warriors. For he knew that one who strikes down evil men insofar as they are evil is a minister of God. But the utterly depraved traitors, conscious of their guilt, scattered when they heard of the bishop’s arrival. One party, namely P. Gudesteides and R. Muñiz with their soldiers, fled to fortified castles. Another party, led by Arias Petrides and P. Arides together with the participants in the aforesaid treachery, deprived of the protection of castles, climbed steep mountains and hid there.

The bishop, therefore, as a man of the highest prudence, turned everything they had gained to the queen’s advantage. Annulment having been made of their former oath, he compelled the men of the aforesaid conspiracy to swear that they would be faithful to Queen Urraca and her son, the little King Alfonso—the bishop’s godson—whom the bishop had consecrated king after rescuing him from the captivity of A. Petrides, Peter Arides, and Oduarius Ordonides. Having expelled and put the enemies to flight, the bishop restored peace; and, so that they should not dare return, he left the greater part of his soldiers to protect those lands.

## CHAPTER LXXV. The Queen’s Request to the Bishop Concerning the Siege of the Rebel Castles

After this, when some time had passed, Queen Urraca sent a letter in the following terms to the aforesaid protector:

> “To the most reverend and most holy lord DIDACUS, bishop of the Church of St James, Queen URRACA sends greeting. It has become clearly known to me how, by the grace of your valour and by your prudence, you have defended the kingdom of Galicia; how you have expelled from my kingdom and from the kingdom of my son, King A., those who were usurping it—P. Gudesteides, Rabinatus Muñiz, A. Petrides, and the other traitors; how, after expelling the traitors from Galicia, you have restored peace and tranquillity; and how many and how great evils you have suffered in defending my kingdom since I left you. Therefore I render the highest thanks to almighty God, to St James, and to you; and I rejoice in having so reverend a protector.
>
> “For the future, I humbly entreat your clemency and most earnestly beseech your prudence to go and besiege the castle of St Pelagius of Luto, Daravum, and the other places that are refuges of Pelagius Godesteides, Rabinatus Muñiz, and the other wicked men. If, with God’s consent and St James’s intercession, you can drive the enemies from those castles and take them by force of arms, then, as seems best to your prudence, either retain them for yourself or give them to certain of my leading men who will faithfully keep them for the service of myself and my little son, King A. Farewell; and bring the aforesaid matters to completion as soon as you can.”

Hearing this, the aforesaid shield of his country—that is, the venerable bishop of the Church of St James—immediately issued an edict that no man of full age or manly spirit in his lordship should withdraw from the expedition. He also gave a certain castle to his brother M. Gelmirides, so that he might provide assistance. Then, having assembled an innumerable host of horsemen and foot-soldiers, he hastened as quickly as possible to extirpate the rage of the wicked men and to subdue the aforesaid castles.

First, however, he decreed and ordered that the people of Iria and all who, in the honour of St James, lived along the shores of the Ocean should prepare a fleet and make for the same siege, so that the castle of St Pelagius of Luto—situated on the seashore and protected on one side by its position, on the other by the force of the sea—might be enclosed by siege from every direction. Upon hearing their lord’s decree and command, the people of Iria promptly prepared a fleet in their customary fashion, loaded their ships with arms and every necessity, and, rowing past the castle of Honesti, went to the people of St Mary of Lanchata. For these men, skilled in the same craft, lived on the shore and were accustomed to practise naval service. Thus the men of Iria, with a dense company of young men, undertook the intended voyage, committed themselves to the deep, and with favourable conditions headed for the ordered siege.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Pirates of England

At the same time P. Godesteides and R. Muñiz had hired pirates to assist them. These had come from the regions of England, intending to go to Jerusalem, and had reached Spain. They had therefore taken them into their service, so that, fortified by their aid, they themselves might trouble the neighbouring regions through plunder and devastation, while the English pirates—being a people seasoned with no honey of mercy—might ravage remote places and those near the sea and exercise the fury of their cruelty. And this is exactly what happened. The English suddenly invaded the coastal districts in a swift sail; they slaughtered some, stripped others, and deprived all of their goods. Others, as though they were Moabites, they captured and chained, forcing them to pay ransom. Indeed, blinded by excessive greed for money—an abomination!—they violated churches; guilty of so great a sacrilege, they carried off whatever necessary things they found there, and even persons. But the intercession of St James did not permit his province to be ravaged and depopulated by that wicked people with impunity, nor did it allow so great an outrage to remain unavenged.

Meanwhile, as the sailors of Iria and the men who had come from St Mary of Lanchata were making for the aforesaid siege, the said raiders happened, in their accustomed manner, to have come for plunder. They had destroyed a certain church and were carrying the spoils to their fleet. When the men of Iria and the others saw them in a distant part of the coast, they had no doubt that they were English pirates. They then took up arms, readied shields, swords, and missiles, and eagerly hastened to battle, yet did not cease from rowing. The English did the same; but, impeded by their guilt, they scarcely had time enough either to arm or to row.

What more need be said? Battle arose on both sides. Missiles were thrown like hail, and the struggle was waged especially with stones carried for this purpose in the ships’ hulls. At last, with St James’s help, the men of Iria and the men of St Mary of Lanchata attacked the enemy more fiercely and, in a swift leap, boarded the enemy vessels. They pierced some with missiles, overwhelmed others with stones, and allowed others to live after binding their hands behind their backs. Entering the English pirates’ two-oared vessel and two other ships which Pelagius Godesteides and Rabinatus Muñiz had supplied to the English as assistance, they completed their intended journey. Rejoicing in so great a triumph, they took prisoners with them and proceeded to the aforesaid siege.

When this report of what had happened reached the ears of their lord—the venerable bishop of the Church of St James—he rejoiced greatly and gave the highest thanks to almighty God, who had deigned to defend and protect the province of His apostle James from wicked raiders. When the aforesaid victors had brought their ships to shore, the bishop saw the captured Englishmen weeping and wailing. Moved by paternal compassion, he felt mercy; for he had written in the treasury of his memory: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Matthew V), etc. He then addressed his sailors as follows:

> “Brothers, you know that by right a fifth part of everything you have gained in this victory, with God’s help, belongs to me. Although these things are many and valuable, I do not wish to take anything from you, but give me only the captives as my share.”

He said this because he wished to free them from their chains and rescue them from the yoke of captivity. Having received the captives as his portion, the bishop bound them by oath that they would no longer trouble Christians, nor presume to do against Christians any such thing as has been described above. He then released them from their chains and allowed them to depart free.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the Siege and Surrender of St Pelagius of Luto, and of Daravum

Meanwhile the castle of St Pelagius of Luto was besieged and surrounded on one side by the great tumult of warriors, on the other by naval warfare. Then the aforesaid bishop selected certain companies, both foot-soldiers and horsemen, and ordered them to go quickly and besiege Daravum, where R. Muñiz was hiding with a band of traitors. He himself took part in the aforesaid siege with an innumerable army.

Once both castles had been besieged, siege-engines were prepared: ballistas and the other machines for attacking castles were erected. But the band of rebels occupying the castle of St Pelagius of Luto, after seeing that the bishop’s determination did not in the least abandon its undertaking, that he wished to carry his purpose through to completion, and that they despaired of being able to resist him, considered all their affairs to be on the brink of ruin. Now they were terrified; now they promised surrender. Why delay with many words? Stupefied by so great a tumult of war and shaken by overwhelming fear, they surrendered the castle to the bishop.

On the very day on which the castle of St Pelagius of Luto was given to Lord Didacus, the venerable bishop of the Church of St James, R. Muñiz heard of his accomplices’ surrender and feared that the whole tempest of war would turn upon him and his own position. Therefore he surrendered the castle of Daravum—his hope and confidence—to the bishop’s soldiers, who, as we said above, had besieged it. When both castles had surrendered, the bishop entrusted them to certain leading men, who were to hold and protect them faithfully for Queen U. and her little son, King A., the bishop’s godson.

When the aforesaid traitors—A. Petrides, P. Arides, and the rest—heard this (for they had hidden in the mountains and, trusting in the assistance of those who had been defeated, had planned once more to trouble Galicia), their hopes frustrated, they were confounded and terrified and fled to the ports of Galicia. At last, after the aforesaid traitors had been driven out and extirpated, and after the castles had been acquired and fortified, the venerable bishop returned joyfully and gladly to his own lands, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honour and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the Bishop’s Prudence

After the aforesaid bishop had calmed the rage of the aforesaid traitors and taken their strongholds by siege, he returned to the church of his patron, St James the Apostle, and devoted unwearied care to it. Although, as stated above, he was hindered by so many and such great affairs and occupied by the manifold turmoil of concerns involved in restoring peace, he nevertheless laboured continually in the worship of the Church and strove with all the affection of his mind for the exaltation of ecclesiastical affairs.

After returning from the aforesaid expedition, he ordered the demolition of a very ancient little church which, within the vast capacity of the new church, threatened collapse through impending ruin. It extended in length to the altar of St James from the pillar beside the principal wall of the church and next to one of the four principal pillars, which is left behind on the left when one enters the upper part of the choir; it stands directly opposite those entering the church by the doors of the episcopal palace. On the other side, that is, on the right, it extended from the pillar opposite the aforesaid pillar to the same altar. Its width was the same as that of the present choir.

After that church was destroyed in Era 1150—a structure that seemed like a shade cast over the whole church—he constructed there a sufficiently suitable choir, which to the present day, by God’s grace and St James’s aid, is splendidly adorned through the industry of that same bishop and the excellence of its outstanding clergy. The bishop himself, like a wise architect, built a raised pulpit at the right end of this choir, in which the singers and subdeacons perform the order of their office; and another on the left, where the lessons and Gospels are read. The special and splendid new church of St James was begun in Era 1116, on the fifth day before the Ides of July (1078).

> [Note: Col. 0961D: If you compare the Era with the statements in Book III, ch. 1, read not XVI but XX—that is, the year 1082, not 1078.]

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the Arrival of the Abbot of Chiusa in Spain

Meanwhile the aforesaid bishop, seeing the tumult of discord growing ever greater and the Aragonese tyrant, in the violence of his savagery, devastating almost all Spain, repeatedly sent letters to the pope of the holy Roman Church. Concerned for the peace of the whole country, he admonished and entreated him—as one who held authority over the whole world and was shepherd and ruler of all Christendom—to extend his counsel to the western regions, troubled by the excessive tumult of discord. That is, he asked him to send one of his cardinals or another venerable person of ecclesiastical rank, who, having examined on both sides the rule of justice, might either invite the warlike Aragonese to a treaty of peace or strike him with the sword of anathema if he refused.

Moreover, he showed him what and how much the aforesaid Aragonese had done in those regions from ambition for kingship; how many and what great evils, inflamed by the rage of tyranny, he had inflicted upon Spain: divine and human things boldly violated by him; the churches of Spain grievously disturbed; the treasures of churches violently plundered; their inheritances and estates dispersed; dukes and all the nobles of Iberia, some bound by him in fetters and iron chains, others slain by the sword; the poor delivered over to death by iron, hunger, and cold; the very priests of the Lord and the very bishops, teachers of the churches, captured like thieves and robbers, expelled from their sees, and afflicted by various insults. He further reported that the venerable archbishop of Toledo, legate of the Roman Church, had been grievously harassed by him and expelled from his diocese for two years; that the bishop of Palencia had been seized by treachery, as had the bishop of Osma; that the bishops of Burgos and León had been expelled; and that the abbot of St Facundus had been taken from his monastery. Beyond this, he described such persecution of the Church and such devastation in Spain as even the Saracens, had it been within their power, could not have inflicted.

Thus repeatedly and humbly urged by the bishop of the see of Compostela in these and other matters, the Roman pontiff sent to the Spaniards the venerable person of the abbot of Chiusa.

> [Note: Col. 0962D: Read *Clusensis*, not *Cluniacensis*. Chiusa is an abbey in the diocese of Turin.]

The abbot brought letters from the same teacher of the law, directing that all the bishops of Spain should assemble in the pope’s presence by the next feast of Blessed Mary, bringing with them envoys of the Aragonese king and the noble Queen U. Thus, after the causes of both sides had been more fully investigated, an end might, with God’s aid, be imposed upon such calamities and peace and tranquillity restored to the lands of Spain.

The same venerable father ordered the aforesaid bishop of the Church of St James to abstain from this assembly. For he knew him to be the firmest shield of the whole country, an impregnable wall opposing himself to enemies amid unceasing concern for his country’s defence and the restoration of peace. He also knew that, for this reason, the Aragonese tyrant was excessively hostile to him and wished, if he could, with all the intention of his mind to devise a snare for him. Alas, unhappy Aragonese! In the storehouse of his mind he did not possess the saying: “He who digs a pit for his neighbour shall fall into it; and he who sets a stone for his neighbour stumbles over it” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII, XXIX). And elsewhere: “Touch not my anointed ones,” etc. (Psalm CIV).

The aforesaid abbot of Chiusa entered the western regions and saw far more and more wicked things than he had heard; he found all Spain disturbed by the spur of discord. He then approached the impious Aragonese and, by the authority of St Peter the Apostle, of the holy Roman Church, and of the pope of that apostolic see, forbade him, as he had been commanded, henceforth to return to an unlawful union with his kinswoman. He further forbade him to presume any longer to disturb, through the tempest of his savagery, the kingdom of Spain, which the most noble King A., in fulfilment of the laws of nature, had given to his daughter Queen U. and to his grandson, the little King A. If he should refuse to do any of these things, he was to fall under the sword of anathema.

What then did he do? Precisely what is written: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom I). The same abbot then approached Queen U. and reported the same matters to her. She replied fittingly, as befitted her: after the death of her father King A., the Aragonese tyrant had rushed into her kingdom; and, lest the kingdom of Spain, recently bereft of so great a king, should be shaken by some tumult of discord, the Iberian magnates had compelled her against her will into union by marriage with him. Therefore, since divine law and human laws forbade such things, she did not resist satisfying Roman authority. For she knew that to offend God under hope of repentance is to deny oneself the way of repentance.

The abbot of Chiusa also delivered to the bishops of Spain the letters sent by the Roman pontiff and summoned them at the appointed time to the aforesaid synod, so that they might discuss more fully, in the pope’s presence, the affair of the king and queen and the question of peace and concord.

### The Same Abbot Came to Galicia and Took Counsel from the Aforesaid Bishop

After arranging these matters, the abbot set out for Galicia and entered it through the narrow and rough mountain passes. At last he reached Compostela, the apostolic city, and was honourably received by the bishop of that place. Since the abbot of Chiusa knew the venerable bishop of the Church of St James to be an abundant fountain of prudence, the firmest shield of his country, a cultivator of justice, and a lover of peace, and since he rightly thought that treaties of peace, if they could in any way be made, would most of all be restored through him, he urgently requested him to explain fully the entire sequence of events: the causes of all discord between the impious Aragonese and Queen U., daughter of the noble King A.; what and how much the Aragonese had done in the western region; and how, once the leprosy of discord had been eradicated, peace and concord might be restored in Spain.

The venerable bishop is said to have given this answer:

> “Indeed, most venerable brother, in the time of the most noble King A., the kingdom of Spain flourished exceedingly, more than exceedingly, in the glory of wealth and in no small fertility. While he ruled, peace, faith, laws, and rights flourished. But after his death, when King A. of Aragon fell into an unlawful union and took in marriage his kinswoman Queen U., daughter of the aforesaid King A., all the things just mentioned were turned into their opposites.
>
> “Why should I recount the glory of the Spanish magnates turned into toil and misery, and the poor oppressed by hunger, nakedness, and every calamity? Why should I recount the churches of Spain violated and destroyed by that Aragonese, and divine and human things violated by him? Why should I recount the most venerable metropolitan of Toledo and legate of the Roman Church both expelled and captured—an abomination!—and moreover the bishops of Osma, Palencia, and Ourense likewise captured; the bishops of León and Burgos, and even the abbot of the church of St Facundus, expelled and dishonoured by various insults? What more? By his violence laws and justice have departed; fraud, perjuries, and other such things have entered in.
>
> “Therefore let us humbly entreat almighty God and with all devotion of mind beseech St James that He may deign to put an end to so many and such great evils, rescue Spain from the mouth of the bloodstained lion, and—since division and discord exist between the aforesaid king of Aragon and Queen U., his kinswoman—ensure that they are separated from one another, as is just. We must strive and resist with all strength of mind and body lest a reconciliation in unlawful union occur between them again. It is surely ours to labour for this for many reasons. For if that unlawful marriage of the Aragonese wolf and our Queen U.—may it not be so!—should be confirmed, the dreadful crime of unlawful union will undoubtedly henceforth become habitual in the western regions through following those authors of it; and holy mother Church will be uprooted and destroyed to its very foundations.
>
> “Alas for sorrow! The ministers of the Lord will be oppressed by many intolerable insults; princes, dukes, and all the magnates of Spain will be reduced to disgrace. Finally, while the Aragonese tyrant rules in Spain, peace and concord will utterly flee. In this matter, most venerable brother, whom our mother the holy Roman Church has sent to determine and examine this question, exhort the Aragonese king and, by exhorting, compel him to fear further defilement by the guilt of consanguinity. Let him cease troubling the kingdom of Spain, which the most noble King A., while still alive, entrusted to his daughter Queen U. and to his grandson, the little King A., son of that same queen. Let him keep what is his and leave what belongs to others. If he refuses, let him be excluded from the threshold of the holy Church and from fellowship with all Christians.”

Hearing this, the abbot of Chiusa greatly praised the bishop’s prudence; and, having received his counsel, he departed from the apostolic city.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the Reconciliation and Subsequent Separation of the King of Aragon and the Queen

At the same time the Aragonese tyrant and Queen Urraca, again under a pretence of peace, established between themselves agreements of concord, so that each might by a certain cunning contrivance take castles and strongholds from the other. Dukes, princes, men of Burgos, men of Nájera, Carrión, Palencia, and León, and many others took part in that deceitful agreement. Most of them bound themselves by the firm chain of an oath on this condition: if the king of Aragon injured Queen U., as he had been accustomed to do, and seemed to violate the agreement established between himself and the queen by breaking the peace treaty, the aforesaid magnates and all others were to support the queen’s party and not delay unanimously to avenge her wrongs. Moreover, they were to place their castles, towns, and all their fortresses in the queen’s hands and expel the lying and perjured Aragonese king from the kingdom. If the queen acted injuriously toward him, the matter was to be reversed.

Yet the fierce Aragonese could not conceal the snares of his fraud for long, and by his deceit he took from the queen whatever castles and fortresses he could. At length, having broken the agreement, he wished to expel her from her kingdom. Therefore the men of Burgos, Nájera, Carrión, and León, together with other Spanish magnates, assembled with the aforesaid Aragonese at San Facundo and pointed out to him that he was violating the agreement previously settled and wholly wronging the queen. But he put forward many excuses and, postponing the matter from one day to the next with crafty words, was proved by all to have broken the agreement in the execution of his fraud. Refusing to reform, he secretly left San Facundo as though fleeing.

Then all who had come to San Facundo to investigate the aforesaid wrongs immediately handed over their castles, towns, and all their fortresses to the queen, and congratulated their lady, the daughter of their lord, the most noble King A. Nevertheless, although the tumult of discord was greatly checked by the absence of the aforesaid tyrant, he still troubled a large part of Spain. For when the aforesaid Aragonese departed, he had left his soldiers in the castles and fortresses which he had previously held or later taken from the queen; and they disturbed, devastated, and plundered in hostile fashion the neighbouring regions.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the Election of Munio as Bishop of Mondoñedo, and of Hugh of Portugal
In the time of Lord Diego, the most reverend bishop of the church of Blessed James, of whom we have spoken above, that church of the same apostle flourished happily with a senate of canons [Col. 0966A] and shone with a venerable assembly of clerics. For it was fitting that, above all the churches of Spain, that church should shine forth in the excellence of its clergy and the distinction of its persons—the church which the presence of Blessed James the Apostle illumined throughout the whole western world. Yet, if it is permissible to proclaim true things truthfully, the aforesaid bishop adorned the apostolic church of his patron by organizing its canons and by the bright lamp of its excellent clerics. For after, with God’s assent, he had been raised to the episcopal dignity in the church of the aforesaid apostle, he cultivated the clerics living there, like brute beasts, with the ploughshare of discipline; he adorned their conduct with decency; and, having humbled those oppressed by the severity of the yoke, he compelled them to labour earnestly in scholarly study. Moreover, he not only drew them out of the darkness of ignorance [Col. 0966B], but also, raising each according to his deserts to the height of honour, richly endowed him from ecclesiastical resources. Why say more? The aforesaid householder prudently cultivated the vineyard entrusted to him and took care to bring profit to his Lord from the talents committed to him.

And since it pleased Blessed James that the sons of his church should be exalted, two of the canons whom the aforesaid bishop had trained ascended to the summit of the episcopate. One of them, Hugh, namely archdeacon of St James, was raised to the Portuguese see; the other, Munio Adefonsiades, treasurer of the same church, to the see of Mondoñedo. After the election of both, Lord Maurice, archbishop of Braga, determined that their consecration should take place at Tui. [Col. 0966C] Thereafter he asked the bishop of the church of Blessed James to come to that consecration; for those whom he was to consecrate were the bishop’s beloved sons, and they embraced one another in a very close bond of affection. Indeed, the archbishop had been a canon of St James and received benefits and prebends from that bishop: namely half of Braga and half of Corneliana with their appurtenances, which belonged to the royal right and pertained to the bishop of St James. But what belonged to the canons of St James was by no means entrusted to the archbishop. The venerable bishop of the church of St James had, moved by the grace of the highest affection, entrusted these things temporarily as a fief to the archbishop of Braga—that is, to his venerable person, not to his church—so that whenever he wished [Col. 0966D] he might take them back and cause what was his to return to him.

### On the Archbishop of Braga

Maurice, archbishop of Braga, made this document for the aforesaid bishop of St James in the city of Tui, when he received from him the benefice written below, in the Era 1147 [Note: [Col. 0965] In the year 1109. See the preceding volume, in the *Life of D. Gelmírez*, no. 63.], on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

“I, Maurice, archbishop of the church of Braga, receive from the hand of our friend and brother, Lord Diego II, venerable bishop of the church of Compostela, as a benefice or fief, half of the possessions and inheritances which the church of St James has in the Portuguese land, from the river Lima to the Douro: namely [Col. 0967A] half of the church of Saints Victor and Fructuosus with all its appurtenances, and half of the estate called Corneliana, with everything belonging to it, and of the other estates known to pertain to the aforesaid church of Blessed James. I shall hold and possess these from him; and whenever he wishes to recover them, I shall peacefully surrender or restore them to him or to the church of St James.”

I, Maurice, the aforesaid archbishop, confirm with my own hand. Present were:

Hugh, archdeacon of St James, confirms.  
Munio Adefonsi, treasurer of the same place, confirms.  
Peter Didaci, canon of St James, confirms.  
Vimara, prior and archdeacon of the church of Braga, confirms.  
Bernard, master of the same church, confirms.  
I, Diego II, though unworthy bishop of the church [Col. 0967B] of Blessed James, confirm with my own hand.  
Munio Gómez, archdeacon and notary, confirms.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On the ordination of the aforesaid elects

The bishop of the apostolic see had given all these things to the archbishop without the consent or counsel of his canons; therefore, they could have been regarded as void. Yet the aforesaid bishop did not venture at all to go to the appointed place, both because a winter harsher than usual had set in and because he saw all Galicia disturbed by the tumult of discord, and feared that on the journey the rebels and traitors of Galicia might presume either to dishonour or to trouble himself or his people. He therefore sent there with the aforesaid elects certain of his canons—distinguished and venerable persons—who might both accompany the elects honourably and fully explain to the archbishop the reason for his absence. [Col. 0967C]

When the archbishop heard of the bishop’s absence and drew nearer on the aforesaid grounds, he did not refuse to come to the church of Lérez [Note: [Col. 0967D] Today, Lérez.], which lies in the diocese of Blessed James. He sent envoys to the bishop, asking that his graciousness not refuse to attend the forthcoming consecration, especially since he himself, broken and weakened by the suffering of a long illness which he had endured, had come from the see of Braga to the church of Lérez through the heights of mountains and the hollows of valleys, and desired with all his heart to see him, so that he might discuss more fully with him the removal of discord, the restoration of peace, and the tranquillity of the churches. For since discord had prevailed for no short time, bishops dared neither to assemble for the holding of councils nor even securely to visit their own dioceses. If they attempted this, traitors, criminals, perjurers, and others trained in the following of the Aragonese tyrant—something wholly unfit to recount—would, if they could, lay hands upon the ministers of Christ.

Nevertheless, when the venerable bishop of the apostolic see heard that his brother, the archbishop of Braga, had come near, he took counsel from his canons concerning this matter and set out. At last he reached the church of Lérez, and the archbishop greatly rejoiced at his arrival.

[Col. 0968A] On that same day—that is, on the Saturday before Passion Sunday, on which the bishop of St James entered Lérez—the archbishop celebrated Mass and raised Lord Hugh the archdeacon to the rank of priesthood. On the following day, namely Passion Sunday, the canons of St James assembled in the church of Lérez: the aforesaid bishop, father of the canons and himself a canon; the archbishop of Braga; the bishops of Ourense and Tui; the elect of Mondoñedo; and the elect of Portugal. All these were canons of the church of the apostle St James, together with other venerable canons. O fathers, with what great and venerable a light did the church of Lérez shine through the canons of St James, since on that day it received so memorable an honour!

Thereafter the archbishop solemnly celebrated Mass and, with the aforesaid bishops standing by, consecrated the elects after sufficiently examining the matters pertinent to the act. When Mass had been celebrated, the bishop of the apostolic see returned to one of his estates, called Geogildum, situated in the pleasant setting of a valley near Lérez, and brought the bishop of Ourense with him. In the church of Lérez, however, he ordered that the archbishop, the two bishops newly advanced to episcopal dignity, and all others whom they wished should be cared for most attentively. For he well knew: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). On that same day the archbishop and the bishop of the church of St James, taking counsel concerning a pact of peace, the welfare of the churches, and also matters belonging [Col. 0968C] to the dioceses of Ourense and Tui, over which there was disagreement between the bishops of the two sees, discussed these things at length.

On the next day the bishop of Blessed James did not delay in returning to Compostela, accompanied by the bishops of Ourense, Mondoñedo, and Portugal. When they had come to the milestone from which the site of the city of Compostela can be seen, the venerable father ordered certain men to go ahead and announce to the clergy of the apostolic see the arrival of the bishops. Therefore, as the aforesaid patron entered the apostolic city, the whole city came out to meet him. Little children, youths, men, old men, virgins, married women, and matrons assembled for the spectacle, so that they might see the canons of St James, whom he had trained with him from the first rudiments of childhood [Col. 0968D] and who had now been advanced to the summit of the episcopate. Giving thanks to God and to Blessed James, they also magnified their own shepherd, who had displayed such diligent and earnest paternal affection toward his sons as to raise them to the height of honour.

After they came to the church of the apostle St James, the canons, clothed in surplices and silk copes, and the clergy of the whole city received them in procession and, singing a responsory, conducted them with the highest reverence as far as the iron doors of the altar. The reverend prudence of their father had indeed arranged and commanded that this should be done. Thereafter, because it was the feast of the Annunciation of St Mary, Lord Hugh, bishop of Portugal [Col. 0969A] and archdeacon of the church of St James, reverently celebrated Mass upon the altar of that apostle. He had lately, as we said above, risen to the rank of priesthood and to the summit of the episcopate; and he rightly offered the first-fruits of his dignity, with the fullest thanksgiving, to his most gracious father, Blessed James, who had deigned to promote him to so great a height of honour.

O how great and how splendid is the mercy of the blessed apostle, who gloriously and happily exalts his sons by making them blessed! O how greatly the apostle adorned his church! What great and memorable distinction he bestowed upon his church when, on the same day, he raised two of its canons to episcopal honour! Therefore, most beloved brethren, let us beseech almighty God [Col. 0969B] and earnestly implore the mercy of the apostle Blessed James, that he may deign happily to govern and protect the worthy shepherd of his see and the aforesaid bishops, and cause them to ascend from virtue to virtue; and may our Lord Jesus Christ, who willed that they should be exalted and become his chief ministers, deign to choose and exalt still others from the same church of his apostle, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0969] What has been written thus far I ascribe to the bishops mentioned, namely Munio and Hugh; the rest to the canon Gerald. See preliminary notice, no. 7.]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the war of the king of Aragon in Castile

While Queen U. ruled over the cities, towns, and very many castles of her realm, and, after the expulsion of the Aragonese by those who had wished to incur the guilt of perjury, as we have said above, had subjected no small part [Col. 0969C] of Spain to her authority, the Aragonese tyrant with an armed band of soldiers invaded now Castile, now the Campos, now Extremadura. With sword and fire he devastated everything: some peasants he pierced with the sword; others he captured and led away with their hands bound behind their backs. Why say more? In armed rage he even violated churches; and whatever the frightened people had brought into the bosom of their mother church as a refuge of safety, that wicked tyranny carried off, having drenched the altar and the walls of the temple with human blood. Alas for the dreadful greed of possession, which never knows how to be sated and plunges, thirsting for money, into the pit of destruction!

Then that sacrilegious man returned to his castles and filled them with no small abundance of pay, trained and incited his men for the clamour of war, and [Col. 0969D] sometimes laid snares for his enemies, sometimes, girded with martial boldness, made an attack upon them, capturing some and forcing others to turn their backs in flight. But the Castilians, terrified at the very name of the Aragonese, could defend neither themselves nor their possessions, utterly refused to labour amid the tumults of war; and, since I have begun to speak of them, I shall not pass over their cowardly soldiery.

### On the Castilians

In the time of the most noble King A., son of King Ferdinand, the Castilian soldiers laboured most earnestly in the practice of war; they endured danger and hardship, and the more frequently they engaged in military affairs, the more spirited and ready for arms they rushed into battle. By overthrowing enemies and seizing enemy spoils, they won triumph, praise, and the renown of soldiery for themselves. Spain had chosen them as its most distinguished men and did not fear to send them as its strongest men to war. At that time King A. was their leader and prince, and he strove to impart the pattern of his courage and excellence to them as to heirs especially dear and close to his heart. He was the first to rush upon the enemy, the first to overthrow their formations, and he encouraged his soldiers to do the same. He trained them, by his own example, to meet the Agarenes and to labour manfully in martial exercise.

But after King A. died—he who was the lamp and shield [Col. 0970B] of Castilian excellence—everything turned to the worse for them. The Castilians gave themselves over to indolence and cowardice; luxury and greed wore down their courage; and their former spirit lay hidden as fearfulness came upon them. The more necessity summoned them to the clamour of war, the more they wished to absent themselves from battle and hide farther away. They strove neither to defend their own possessions nor to acquire those of others through warfare. For although a greater multitude of soldiers was found in Castile, and although they could easily have expelled the Aragonese from Castile if courage had not failed them, their former spirit did not spring up in them at all. Therefore the Aragonese and certain Trans-Pyrenean soldiers who were present in aid of the king heaped reproaches and mockery upon the Castilians, called them womanish soldiers, and declared that they were no longer fit either to guard camps or to be stirred by the tumult of war, since fifteen hundred yielded to them and one hundred triumphed over two hundred.

### How the Galicians hastened to take the field

Accordingly Queen U., seeing that the realm of herself and of her little son King A. was being devastated to its foundations and laid waste by her enemies with sword and fire, was pierced with deep grief of heart and mourned. For she was a woman alone, without a husband, supported by the aid of few, and in so great a tumult of affairs she did not know what to do. She saw her son, King A., still subject to the first stages of childhood; she observed that the Castilians, whom she had formerly known as vigorous in war and powerful in courage, were now indolent and inflamed by scarcely any praise of valour [Col. 0970D]. She had distributed to them the boundless treasure of her father, so that even her own household resources now failed for necessities, and she had no lavish gifts to give to her townsmen.

Moreover, she saw the enemies making frequent assaults daily before the gates of the city; she grieved exceedingly—more than exceedingly—to see cattle, sheep, beasts of burden, and other such things carried off, crops and vineyards destroyed, houses burned, and people killed. Without ceasing she sent envoys to the Castilians to bring her help. Yet she saw some stay away and others greatly fear the sight of the Aragonese, and in the excessive indignation of her mind she often turned them into laughter. At last, having taken prudent counsel, the queen sent envoys to the Galicians, begging and imploring them to come as swiftly as possible and rescue her from the jaws of those who gaped after her, from the hands of the Aragonese. She placed great confidence in them, because they had reared her son and loved him with all the affection of their hearts. She did not at all doubt that they were vigorous in war and would always be faithful to herself and her son.

Among them she addressed the venerable bishop of St James especially in these words. He had baptized her little son King A. and anointed him king in the church of Blessed James. For he was the lamp of all Galicia, extending protection to all; the queen knew beyond doubt that his counsel would be acceptable to the Galicians, and that whatever he advised the nobles of Galicia would scarcely, or never, be done otherwise.

[Col. 0971B] “Most venerable Father, may it please your holiness to come upon campaign with a gathered force of soldiers, and to exhort and admonish all the nobles of Galicia to hasten swiftly to assist me and my son, King A. For the Aragonese tyrant grievously ravages my realm, and there is no one able to resist his tyranny. Therefore may your fatherhood compel the Galicians to come speedily to war; and may you not only compel the councillors, magnates, and other soldiers of Galicia to come upon campaign, but also not refuse to come with them at the head of your assembled troops.
