For if that impious man can fortify his castles with pay, arms, and every necessary thing before Galicia sends me its soldiers, their arrival afterwards will be of no use, and in the following year the castles cannot be compelled to surrender by siege.”

When he heard this, the venerable bishop summoned the nobles of Galicia to the court of Blessed James: namely Count P. R. Velaz, Count Gutierre, M. Pelagides, M. Gelmirides, P. Pelagides, and many others. With them he discussed fully the matter of the campaign. He urged and admonished them, setting every excuse aside, to hasten with an army gathered from every side to aid their lady the queen. He showed them that the queen, at so great a height of royal power, was almost bereft of everyone’s assistance; that her son was still subject to the cradle of childhood; that the Aragonese tyrant was hostile to her; that the Castilians were fearful and weak in every martial endeavour; that the enemies were present and devastated her realm on every side. [Col. 0971D] He further declared that the queen had placed the fullness of her hope and trust in the Galicians and that they had been dearer to her from her childhood. Since in so great a danger she begged their help so earnestly, he affirmed that it must by no means be delayed.

Why say more? Thus admonished by these and other arguments, the Galicians obeyed their patron. Knowing that he would be their leader and that he was marching to assist the queen and her son A., to restore peace to the realm, and knowing that he bore with him the breastplate of righteousness, they were kindled by certain incentives of courage and no longer delayed to hasten to the work of war. They greatly desired to expose themselves for the defence of the realm and to restrain the rage of the Aragonese tyrant.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On the Galicians’ campaign and the queen’s stratagem

[Col. 0972A]

Accordingly, on the third day before the Kalends of June, the venerable bishop of Blessed James, Count Peter, and all the soldiery of Galicia set out on campaign and marched toward the Campos. Yet after no small part of the journey had been completed, messengers came to the bishop of St James and to all the leading men of Galicia, saying that the queen was hostile to the Galicians and, because they had not advanced to war quickly enough, was exercising grave enmities against them; and that, if they approached her, some would be stripped of their honours and others held in fetters. Others and still others came saying the same things. Hence many of the Galicians became greatly disturbed and wished to withdraw from the undertaking.

Then the bishop’s admirable prudence removed from them this cloud of schism, and, showing them the path of sound counsel, called them back to their purpose, saying that all these things had been invented by informers and contained nothing true. Then, after several days had passed, when they had already left the passes of Galicia, all unanimously wished to return; cursing the queen, they resolved neither to give her aid nor to proceed further toward her. For messengers frequently came to them, reporting the same things and asserting that the matter was indeed so.

But the aforesaid bishop, restraining the disturbed nobles by his eloquence, sent envoys to the queen and inquired whether the messengers had reported the truth. When they had come to Astorga and found the aforesaid reports to be true, the bishop’s remarkable prudence summoned the leaders of the army [Col. 0972C] and discussed with them what these matters signified. Thereafter he showed by many arguments that the queen would never devise such things, especially since she loved the Galicians exceedingly and needed their aid most of all at that time. But when the aforesaid nobles would not assent to the bishop, he sent two of his venerable clerics—namely Cardinal P. and P. Pelagides—as envoys to the queen concerning the aforesaid affair, charging them with what they should report to her, how they should rebuke her, and how they should investigate the course of the aforesaid matter.

Departing, they found the queen at Carrión; instructed by their father’s admonitions, they addressed her thus:

“Whoever does not recompense anyone’s favour or the fullness of his due reward according to his merit, as is just, demands that help be denied him in time of necessity. For who is so mad as to blame anyone for a good deed, or return hatred in recompense for service? Indeed, O queen, since the king of Aragon began to trouble the realm of Spain which your most noble father King A. left to you and to your little son King A., the Galicians have remained more faithful than others to your party, and, compelled by no onset of discord, they have stood firm against the rage of the enemy. For when the Castilians, Leonese, and the countless people of the Campos and Extremadura had yielded, and, following Fortune’s favour, had set the Aragonese tyrant over themselves as king, the Galicians continually rendered faithful service to you and to your renowned offspring, and endured much greater and graver hardships.

[Col. 0973A] “Why recount how much they suffered at Fonte Dangós? With what extraordinary boldness they attacked the countless battle-lines of the Aragonese enemy? Moreover, that same Aragonese besieged the Galicians at Astorga; but after his siege was broken, it is known to all that they besieged that same Aragonese at Carrión [Note: [Col. 0973D] Above, ch. 73.] and held him under siege for a long time. Behold, again: because they heard that the plunderer of Aragon was ravaging Castile, the Campos, and the neighbouring regions, and was fortifying his castles with arms and pay, repeatedly summoned by your supplicatory messengers, they were coming with an assembled army to aid you and your son, rejoicing to pour out their blood for the defence of the realm.

“But after it was reported to them that you gave heed to bearers of idle tales and informers, that you held their soldiery—who until now have been the protectors of your whole realm—in contempt, that their service and praise were turned into blame, and that, in return for the favour of their good deeds and as recompense for their merits, you were threatening to deprive them of their honours and put them in fetters, for this reason they withdraw from the undertaking and refuse to receive evil in return for good. They wish to return to Galicia and defend themselves and their own land; they will remain faithful to you and your son. But once they have returned, they will not cross the Galician mountains to come forth on campaign from there. Do not doubt that we have said this to you on behalf of them all and that, unless you come to your senses, they will carry it out. For your most noble father King A., when he summoned the Galicians, Asturians, Castilians, and whatever soldiers of his realm to military exercises, enriched some with honours and won the goodwill of others. Would he have been troublesome [Col. 0973C] to those who caused him no trouble at all and carried out all his commands? Far from it!”

When the queen heard this, tears sprang up, and she began to protest and swear that she had never planned such things nor wished to devise a fraud of this kind against the brave soldiers of Galicia. Thereafter the queen asked the envoys humbly to beseech their lord, namely the bishop of the church of St James, that he himself might exhort and admonish the nobles of Galicia not to take empty reports for truth and not to delay their coming any longer.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. How the pacified Galicians went to Burgos

At that time Arias Petrides, Ferdinand Sanchiz, and certain of their accomplices were at the queen’s court; and because they were hostile to Count P. and certain nobles of Galicia, they instilled into the queen’s ears every evil thing they could concerning the Galicians. For these men, as we said above (from chapter 49), had raised a sedition at the castle of Miño against the bishop of St James, against the queen’s little son King A., against the countess, wife of Count P., and against many leading men of Galicia; and they held them captive.

Accordingly, the aforesaid envoys departed, came to the Galician camp, and reported to their lord the bishop all that the queen had told them. Then the bishop summoned the nobles and, with paternal admonitions, urged them not to take upon themselves the title of cowardice or wish to abandon their undertaking; for all the reports concerning the queen’s hatred were doubtless false. At last the Galicians accepted their father’s admonitions and set out toward the queen. When they came to Carrión, where the queen was staying, they pitched their tents along the river called Carrión, in green meadows. But because they were doubtful and afraid of what they had heard again and again, and because there was no firm friendship between Count P. and many of the Galician nobles on the one hand and the queen on the other, they refused to go immediately to court. Therefore envoys were sent ahead to seek from the queen a pledge of security, for they feared that the queen, giving too much heed to what the informers had instilled in her ears, might dishonour them either in their persons or in their honours.

While these matters were being fully discussed and the sun was sinking toward its setting, behold, a messenger arrived reporting that the king of Aragon would come to Burgos the next day with a great force and would fortify the castle, which that tyrant still held, with men, arms, and pay. If this happened, the Galician army would hasten fruitlessly to besiege it, and the Aragonese plunderer would not lose his customary refuge for a long time. The city of Burgos, situated on the side of a mountain, favoured the queen. Nature had also formed two summits on that mountain: Jews inhabited the lower one and likewise supported our party; on the upper one stood the castle, seen to be sufficiently fortified on the one side by the nature of the site and on the other by wall and towers. There the rebel Aragonese, together with Saracens whom the king had sent there, ravaged both the city subject to them and the neighbouring districts.

When these things became known to the queen, after giving a pledge of security she humbly begged the Galician party, for her sake, to hurry to Burgos and terrify the coming of the savage enemy. Therefore, in the silence of the late night, the vigorous soldiers set out and reached Burgos in rapid march; they occupied the mountain and pitched their tents beside the castle. Meanwhile, the bishop of St James restored a bond of friendship between the queen and Count P. and many nobles of Galicia, binding them in a bond of firm affection, namely by an oath.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. How the bishop celebrated Mass in the church of St John near Burgos

[Col. 0974D]

On a certain day the same bishop visited the church of Blessed John near Burgos, and, because it was the feast of Blessed John the Baptist, he determined to celebrate Mass. Then the citizens of that city, the Castilians, and the whole army of Galicia assembled; the queen also attended with all her nobles (24 June). During the solemnities of Mass the venerable bishop of Blessed James refreshed the people standing by with the nourishment of the divine word and sufficiently expounded matters belonging to the joys of so great a feast. Then, considering the frail lot of Spain, he began to speak at length of the condition of Holy Church and of the weakness of the Spaniards, saying:

### Sermon of the bishop on the condition of the realm of Spain

[Col. 0975A]

“You know, dearest brethren, that the most noble King A. was a cultivator of justice and that, as long as he governed the realm of Spain, the condition of Holy Church flourished happily in its strength. At that time laws, rights, peace, and justice especially prevailed, and cultivators of virtue were found everywhere. In the time of that king the Moabite Moors and the other neighbouring enemies yielded to us, and we subjected their strongholds to our dominion. But after King A., paying the debt of nature, transferred his realm to his daughter Queen U. and to his little grandson King A., and the sceptre of imperial rule rightfully passed to them, discord immediately began to spring up. At once the rights of the Church were completely violated; dukes, princes, and all the nobles of Spain were broken and reduced to the condition of cowardice. Their former courage lay wholly hidden.

“We know indeed that Queen U. and her son King A. ought rightfully to possess the realm granted to them and that, while they live, this sovereignty cannot lawfully be transferred to others. Yet although we are supported by the patronage of a just cause, although we desire—as is just—to expel the enemies from the borders of our native land, we who were once conquerors are now defeated, though many, by a few. We should inquire and investigate why such courage and such glory in war have been blunted in us and lost their strength.

“Now, now, dearest brethren, we are weighed down by so great a burden of sins, we have submitted our necks so greatly to the yoke of Satan, that, although we take up arms by the grace of justice, courage, crushed within us by the mass of sins, cannot exercise its strength. Though surrounded by an innumerable multitude, we cannot bear the attack of our enemies. So that you may understand this better, listen to what happened under the old law.

### On the vengeance taken upon the tribe of Benjamin because of a woman violated by rape

“A certain man of the people of Israel came with his wife to a city inhabited by the tribe of Benjamin. As he sat in the public square and found no one to offer him lodging, behold, a poor man from the outskirts, seeing him a stranger and in need of hospitality, took him, his wife, and his little baggage into his house. That traveller was handsome and comely in appearance; his wife too was of a most elegant figure. But when twilight came, men of that city came to the house and demanded that the traveller with his wife be given to them. For they wished to imitate in the man the vice of Sodom and to defile the woman by adultery. When the master of the house heard this, he began to entreat and admonish his fellow citizens not to attempt so horrible and lawless a crime. Since they would not yield and wished to use force, he gave them the woman, scarcely obtaining by prayers that they should at least let the man go. Then the wicked men took the woman, oppressed her by intercourse throughout the whole night, and killed her; they threw her corpse before the door of the man from the outskirts.

“When morning came and the man wished to depart, he found his wife dead before the door. He cut her into pieces and sent individual pieces to every tribe of Israel. When the eleven tribes of Israel saw that pieces of the woman had been sent to them, marvelling at the most wicked portent, they anxiously began to consider what it signified. Finally, all the tribes of Israel chose ten men to investigate fully the course of this affair as the significance of a dreadful portent. Once what had happened in the tribe of Benjamin had been disclosed, all immediately rose unanimously to avenge so great a crime. Therefore forty thousand soldiers were sent, the most courageous and strongest in war, to destroy the tribe of Benjamin from the least to the decrepit and to raze their city to the ground.

“But the men of Benjamin, learning of the enemies’ arrival, gathered for war twenty-five thousand horsemen and seven hundred archers, most skilled in the art of archery, and joined battle against the innumerable enemy. Yet those who had taken up arms for the cause of justice and wished to avenge the aforesaid crime, though, as we said above, far more numerous, yielded on the first day of battle, and twenty-two thousand of them fell. Afterwards they advanced to war again and again, and all except five thousand were killed by the tribe of Benjamin. They were amazed and astonished that they defended the cause of justice and were defeated by a wicked enemy.

“At last, when the Israelites had assembled, a certain old man arose among them and explained why so many misfortunes had befallen them. He showed that, devoted to vices and oppressed by the burden of sins, they were unarmed and weak and could not resist their enemies. But if they withdrew their necks from the yoke of sins and, undertaking repentance, came to their senses, then, girded with courage—which had previously lain hidden, stifled by vices—they would undoubtedly overthrow their enemies and fully avenge the enemies’ injury. Hearing this, the Israelites, undertaking repentance, raised their heads and, having laid aside the burden of sins, attacked their enemies. Why say more? The five thousand of them who remained overthrew the twenty-five thousand horsemen and seven hundred archers of the tribe of Benjamin; they killed all except four hundred who had hidden among the rocks, and razed their city to the ground. Moreover, all agreed that no more marriages should take place between the eleven tribes of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, and that the tribe of Benjamin should be wholly separated from the other tribes (Judges 19–20).”

You also, brethren, awakened by a like example, come to your senses. Withdraw your necks from the yoke of wicked domination; root out from yourselves the clouds of such great enticements; take up the shield of courage; put on the breastplate of righteousness, so that you may defend your realm, restrain the rage of your enemies, and attain the joys of paradise, through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On the surrender of the castle of Burgos.

After the aforesaid Father had more fully unfolded the doctrines of sacred eloquence, restored to hope of virtue the minds of all who marvelled at what they had heard, and solemnly celebrated Mass, he returned to the camp. Since the castle, as has been stated above, was besieged by the Galicians, the king of Aragon gathered an army, prepared pay, and did not at all fear to come to the castle through the midst of his enemies; for if he lacked the refuge of this castle, he would be excluded from the whole of Castile.

When this was reported to the queen, she immediately sent envoys to the Castilians, to tell them that the king of Aragon was at hand with a great army and to urge them to hasten to the exertion of so great a war. But the Castilian soldiers, hearing of the Aragonese king’s approach, promised that they would come to battle on the following day. For they had long learned by experience with what force of daring the Aragonese rushed into battles, and therefore took care to withdraw themselves from so great a contest. Alas! The valiant soldiers of Castile saw enemies invading their borders, yet, although supported by the protection of others, they feared to go out against them.

But when the news was brought to the Galicians, they suddenly took up arms, hastened to go out against the aforesaid enemy, rushed forward boldly, reached Atapuerca, and, when twilight came, gave their limbs to rest, intending to march out to battle on the following day and attack upon the enemy’s arrival. Oh, how different was the cause that summoned these men and those men to war! Laws, rights, peace, and justice called the Galicians to arms; their opposites drove the Aragonese headlong into every wickedness.

When it was reported to the Aragonese king, sitting at table in Villafranca, that the Galicians were at hand and were rushing to meet him in love of Mars, he was afraid. For that fierce man had experienced at the Fountain of Angos, although they had been few, that the soldiers of Galicia were distinguished in warfare and vigorous in martial zeal; and he had learned by experience with what boldness they thirsted for the blood of their enemies. [Note: Above, ch. 68.] Thus the warlike yielded to the warlike, and he who was fierce in war feared men fiercer than himself.

On hearing this, the Galicians returned to their camp in a triumph of highest praise. But those who were rebels in the castle, when they saw that their lord had withdrawn and could not give them assistance, approached the queen and, having given hostages, concluded with her the following agreement: if the king of Aragon did not furnish them with aid and pay within fifteen days, they promised without doubt to surrender the castle to the queen; and it was settled that, once the surrender had been made, they themselves should depart unharmed with all their possessions.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On holding a council at Palencia.

At the same time B., Archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, came to Burgos. The bishop of St James approached him and implored his reverend fatherhood to deliberate upon the condition of the Church, which was being utterly overthrown, and upon the restoration of peace.

Then the most venerable Father, assenting to him, summoned the bishops who were present, namely those of Ourense, Oviedo, and Mondoñedo. The archbishop and bishop of St James met with them, and after prolonged discussion they lamented together the thorough violation of the Church’s rights and Spain’s devastation and desolation on every side under Aragonese tyranny.

But because, amid the outbreak of discord, the time did not then permit these matters to be more fully settled—both because many bishops of Spain were absent and because the queen was entangled in the manifold business of wars—they resolved to defer the determination of so great a matter and to hold a general council in the future. To this all the bishops, abbots, dukes, princes, counts, and other leading men of Spain were to be able to assemble in the city of Palencia eight days before the coming feast of All Saints, in order to investigate more carefully the cause of the king and queen, and to restore to sees and monasteries the dioceses, towns, dwellings, fields, and vineyards which they had lost during this time of discord. [Note: 25 October.] This plan pleased the queen and all the princes of Spain exceedingly.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On the king’s envoys to the queen concerning reconciliation.

Meanwhile the king of Aragon, seeing that his fury accomplished nothing and that the towns which he held in Castile, in Campania, or in Extremadura were in some cases being captured by his enemies and in others shut up under a prolonged siege, sent envoys to the queen and sought treaties of peace. He pretended that he wished to return to his unlawful marriage with the queen and to fulfil the sworn agreement which had existed between himself and her. Alas for such deceitful cunning, by which he might at least acquire the sovereignty of the realm!

One day, after the Archbishop of Toledo and the bishops of Ourense, Mondoñedo, and Oviedo had departed from Burgos, it happened by chance that the venerable bishop of St James came to the queen, according to his custom, to advise her concerning so many and such important affairs. He found the Aragonese envoys in the midst of the palace. They were urging the queen toward the king’s abominable marriage, and the people of Burgos were inviting her, under the name of a feigned peace, to that same union. Many assented to their sacrilegious arguments, especially the Franks; for Galicians, Asturians, Leonese, people of Campania, Castilians who were inhabitants of that city, and many others had assembled.

When the most venerable Father learned this and saw them all rushing with shameless purpose toward destruction, he rose, armed with the shield of virtue, although it seemed most difficult to raise any objection against their perverse obstinacy. When all had assembled in the cloister of St Mary and, with the queen present, had received with favourable ears the words of the envoys of the Aragonese king, the bishop ordered silence; and silence was made. Indeed, all especially revered him as bishop of St James and wished to hear his judgment on the substance of this affair. For they thought that he would assent to the envoys of the king of Aragon and that his prudence too would approve what the irrational clamour of so great an assembly had universally resolved.

But the aforesaid Father did not yield to the senseless crowd. Rather, wishing to turn them back from showing such perverse favour, he began fearlessly to preach to them as follows.

### Words of the Bishop of Compostela.

“Until now you have given assent to the envoys of the king of Aragon and have listened with the whole affection of your minds to their report; now hear the messenger of the almighty King, and store his commands in the treasury of your minds. He will assuredly proclaim to you the teaching of eternal salvation and will preach before our Lord what is good and just.

“Those envoys have told you things most harmful and tending toward the pit of destruction; they have proclaimed what is contrary to your salvation both here and eternally, and what right and law also forbid. But I, brothers, a minister and messenger of almighty God, and an interpreter of justice appointed beforehand to defend the rights of holy Church, shall set forth for you the things that bring salvation and shall show you what, in this affair, you must uphold and what you must reject.

“You know, dearest brothers, that our Lord and Redeemer commanded in the Old Law that priests be appointed to preside over his people and to instruct the people subject to them in the Lord’s commandments. At the beginning of the New Law likewise, the Lord himself chose apostles for himself and appointed them stewards of his ministries. He entrusted to them the sacraments of the Church and gave them the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, saying: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 18).

“We, though unworthy, hold their place; and, having been given the same power, we have ascended to the height of pastoral care. We bishops are called the chief stewards of the ministries of God; we are God’s more special and intimate sons. Therefore Truth says: ‘Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zech. 2). Christ entrusted to us his bride, namely the Church, and gave us her children to instruct.

“What more need be said? He committed to our care what is most intimate and precious to the King of kings in the world: namely, the care of souls and the protection of the sheep entrusted to us from the rage of the savage wolf. If they should go astray and rush into the downfall of the broader way, it is surely ours to call them back to the way of truth and to feed the flock entrusted to us in the pastures of discipline. The kings of the earth, dukes, princes, and every people reborn in Christ are subject to us, and we bear the care of all.

“In this matter, dearest brothers, I beseech you, and in beseeching I admonish you: do not in any way wish the king of Aragon and Queen U., fellow countrymen and related by a line of blood, to return to an unlawful marriage. For it is wickedness and a very horrible crime for such things to occur. If, however, you declare that you have sworn an oath concerning the agreement between the king and queen and do not wish to incur the guilt of perjury, and that for this reason, as though compelled by an oath, you wish to bring both back to the union of their former bond, know certainly that oaths of this kind must be broken. For Scripture says: ‘An oath is not to be kept when evil is rashly promised’; for example, if someone should swear to commit murder, or should promise an adulteress a perpetual pledge of remaining with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfil an oath than to perpetrate murder or to remain in the disgrace of fornication.

“Therefore, having been warned, repent, and prevent so great a wickedness from entering the borders of Spain. Whoever shall either contract such a marriage or consent to its being contracted, we excommunicate and anathematize him by the authority of God the almighty Father, and separate him from the thresholds of holy Church.”

Moreover, in order not only to call them back from participation in the aforesaid crime, but also to compel them to cease from the destruction of churches, slaughter, robbery, and arson, he showed them the letters written below, sent by the lord pope to all the bishops of Spain:

“P., bishop, servant of the servants of God,” etc.

“The calamities of your regions,” etc. See Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. 163.

### How the bishop escaped the uproar by flight.

After the aforesaid bishop had ended his speech, the whole people suddenly roared, and a discordant murmur arose among them. Some, who were concerned to examine more effectively what was fair and just, praised the reverend Father’s words. Others, however, whom a worse cause, not weighed by the standard of justice, was driving headlong—whose band was the more numerous—wanted to throw stones or make an attack upon him.

But the soldiers of the prelate, stirred by such an uproar, came up and on every side protected their lord with armed force. Then the prelate, surrounded by the crowd of his soldiers, departed unharmed and quickly returned to the camp.

## CHAPTER XC. On the surrender of the castle of Burgos and the return of the Galicians.

When the fifteen appointed days had elapsed, the Aragonese surrendered the castle to the queen. Oh, what great and splendid praise in warfare that day bestowed upon the Galicians, when the warlike Aragonese yielded to them! Yet much more splendid and much more pleasing was it when Galicia’s vigorous valour protected Castile and its soldiers from the enemy’s attack, and compelled the Aragonese to surrender the castle.

Shame! The Castilians need the strength of others and are protected by Galician boldness. What will become of these timid soldiers when the army of Galicia, their shield and wall, has departed? The Galicians now resolved upon the day of returning home; they rejoiced to leave and go back to their own country. When this became known to the queen, she came to the camp and earnestly tried to turn them back from their purpose of departure. For she wished to send them to the castle of Barlanca, which the Moabites were besieging.

But all of them, unanimously unwilling to comply with their lady’s entreaties, hastened all the more eagerly to depart. Then the venerable bishop, addressing the queen, advised her not to delay the Galicians’ return any longer, lest, by prolonging their wish, what they had done well should remain without glory. Therefore the queen, guided by the reverend Father’s counsel, ordered the Galicians to return home and permitted the bishop himself to return with them to the church of St James.

Yet first, rendering him the highest thanks and binding herself to him by a bond of firm affection—for although the queen had previously both loved and revered him as so great a protector, she embraced him with greater reverence and firmer love after she had learned that the eloquence of such wisdom benefited her, and after she had seen him, by following the path of justice, labour with all his heart in her aid—and she carefully observed his commands. Accordingly, she made this agreement with him and granted him the following charter.

Era 1151, 8 Ides of July [8 July].

“I, Queen U., make to you, lord D., bishop of the church of St James, this promise in pledge of faith: henceforth I shall be your faithful friend; while I live, I shall exalt your honour and put down evil; and I shall not fail you, to the best of my power and understanding, in promoting your welfare. If I learn of any evil contrary to your honour or person, I shall not keep it concealed from you, but shall reveal it to you at a fitting time and, to the best of my power, destroy it. But if any evil concerning me is said to you or arises, it shall be determined by the judgment of those who stand between you and me, if they are my friends; and if they are lacking, it shall be done by the judgment of other friends of us both.

“I grant that your person shall no longer come on campaign unless he wishes; only send me your soldiers as aid, according to custom. Witnesses present at this agreement: M., bishop of Mondoñedo, and P., cardinal of St James.”

### On the return of the bishop and the Galicians.

At last the Galicians departed and, setting out for their homeland, rejoiced that the aforesaid bishop, their leader and protector, was accompanying them. But Count Peter with a portion of his soldiers, Count R. and M. Pelagiades, as well as M. Gelmirides, brother of the bishop of St James, with a portion of his own and his brother’s soldiers, and many other Galician magnates, advanced to Barlanca against the siege of the Moabites; and, not finding them there, returned.

After the Galicians reached Carrión, the people of Carrión, having heard the aforesaid anathema, sought to seize the bishop. But, protected by divine grace, he escaped, covered with a red cloak and shaded by a cap in the Lombard manner. Alas for wickedness! Because he had preached the rule of justice and the rights of the Church, he was hated by an impious people.

On the following day the same bishop, in order that he might travel more safely, had some companies of soldiers go ahead, others follow behind all those who went before, and placed the baggage between the two; and he directed everyone to proceed cautiously. Moreover, how gracious and kindly he was toward all on that journey; how he refreshed everyone with the nourishment of instruction; how he taught them beforehand to avoid the ambushes of enemies lying in wait on every side; and how many and how great supports he afforded the whole army—I shall not be able adequately to unfold this, hindered by the barrenness of my little talent. For although I was present and saw it with my own eyes, I pass over some things in the record of memory and omit others for the sake of brevity.

He also made Nezanus Gudesteides, who, because of injuries inflicted upon him, wished to seize and dishonour the soldiers of Count P. and M. Pelagiades, peaceable, and bound him to them by a bond of very great affection. He held the castle of St Mary of Octaris, and was able to bar passage, through mountain defiles and the hollows of valleys, to all who entered the highlands of Galicia. [Note: Read *Autares* more correctly; it overlooks the gorge of Valcarce, and its ruins are still visible today on the summit of those rocks.] But the aforesaid Father was the leader and guardian of the Galicians and conducted them unharmed as far as their homes. He himself also was received by the clergy of his holy mother Church and by all the people with joy and gladness and with the honour of a procession; and the whole assembly rejoiced at his arrival.

### On the death of Cardinal Gundesindus and the promotion of P. Gundesindiz in his place.

At the same time, one of the cardinals of the Church of St James, named Gundesindus, paid the debt of death and distributed the inheritance of his mother, namely of the aforesaid Church, which is called Holegium. Of his houses, which he possessed apart from the houses of the palace, he gave one half to the hospital of St James and the other half for the work of building that same apostle’s church. Peter, prior of the aforesaid church, purchased these in the assembly and with the consent of all the canons.

When the aforesaid cardinal had died, P. Gundesindiz, who had been chaplain to the bishop mentioned above, was raised by canonical promotion to fill his place and obtained the title of cardinal.

## CHAPTER XCI. On the exchange of the estates of Arias Exemeniz for half of Dena.

During the aforesaid campaign, when the magnates of Galicia were besieging the aforesaid castle of Burgos, Arias Exemeniz and his fellow-countrymen approached Queen U. and earnestly begged her to contrive somehow to obtain from the lord D., the aforesaid bishop of that apostolic see, the estates that had belonged to Mayor Didaciz between the rivers Ulla and Tambre, which the queen herself had granted to St James by charter.

The queen, complying with their requests, yet ashamed to inflict any hardship upon Galicia’s valiant young men amid the outbreak of war, spoke with the bishop about these matters. She asked and begged him to restore the named estates to A. Exemeniz and his fellow-countrymen and to receive in exchange for them half of Dena.

After taking counsel with certain of his canons who were present, the prelate did not refuse to make the exchange and prudently chose to comply with the queen’s entreaties. This was both because a portion of the estates of the town of Dena, given in exchange, lay within the boundaries of the honour of St James, and because, in the land of St Mary of Lanchata, he was striving to remove from royal jurisdiction certain estates belonging to Dena which were subject to royal right, and earnestly desired that they should belong to the church of St James. Moreover, it did not seem fitting to him that the queen’s request in this matter should fail.

The exchange was therefore made between the aforesaid bishop and Queen U.: the estates of Mayor Didaciz between the Ulla and Tambre were given to Arias Exemeniz, and half of Dena was received. This transaction is believed beyond doubt to have been very useful and advantageous to the church of St James.

## CHAPTER XCII. On the council held at Palencia and the return of the Bishop of Compostela.

In the year 1113 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, held a synodal assembly at Palencia on 8 Kalends of November, that is, 25 October, and discussed at length the oppressions and afflictions of Spain and the overthrow and disasters of the churches. [Note: Some manuscripts wrongly have XIV instead of XIII. Pulgar, vol. II, p. 150, printed 1118, which is wholly unacceptable; for the entire course of the narrative concerns the year 1113, designated at the end of this chapter as Era 1151.]

The bishops of Galicia were present. But the bishop of the Church of St James—at whose counsel and urging the aforesaid archbishop had resolved to hold the council—could not attend the council because, amid the outbreak of discord, he was detained by a most difficult obstacle. For in the previous summer, having assembled an army from every side, he had gone into Campania to make war upon the Aragonese king.

If he dared to go again into those parts, he would either have had to take with him companies of soldiers to protect and defend him—a course forbidden by the season and the continual exertion of warfare—or he would nevertheless have had to fear that the aforesaid man’s shameful fury, a thing monstrous to report, might lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed. For a destructive hand, at times of war, incited by desire for plunder and riches, does not shrink from rushing into every wickedness.

Nevertheless, as the aforesaid bishop set out for the general synod, he reached Tres Castillas. But Count R. and Count M., together with many leading men of Galicia, approached him and urged and begged him to abandon his intended undertaking, saying:

“We know well, most venerable Father, that if you presume to go into Campania without the shield of armed force, you will be grievously harassed by the savage violence of your enemies—or, to speak more truly, dishonoured by capture at the hands of any robber—and that Galicia will be oppressed by manifold assaults of discord. It is beyond doubt that we too, in your absence, shall fall into peril to our safety.

“It is your concern to bear care and solicitude for us and for all Galicia. Therefore we urge and advise you to desist from what you have undertaken and, what is most important, to provide for yourself and us all. If you choose to oppose us, then, before you are dishonoured or captured by others—which is most certain—you will be seized and held by us, lest you rashly attempt so great a thing. It is better for you to be forbidden by us permission to depart than for us, by unwise favour, to give our assent to your descent into such a precipice.”

Accordingly, the bishop assented to these and other arguments and sent two of his clerics to the aforesaid council. Pleading to the Roman legate the necessary cause of his absence, they carried the letter written below.

### Letter of the legate of the Holy Roman Church to the Bishop of Compostela.

“BERNARD, Archbishop of the see of Toledo and, by God’s grace, legate of the Holy Roman Church, sends greeting and blessing to the bishop of the Church of Compostela.

“We have seen the envoys whom you sent to us, who said that you were unable to attend the council which we held at Palencia chiefly at your counsel, being detained by unavoidable necessity. Truly, because you withheld from us your comfort, aid, and counsel, we took it ill, to confess the truth to you. But because of the long-standing friendship which exists between you and me, and through the intercession of your clerics, we endure it and pardon you.”

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the town of Pianela given to M. Froylaz.

After this, the aforesaid bishop, eagerly striving more watchfully to increase the possessions of his Church, with the counsel of all the canons granted a town called Pianela, together with its church, to a certain nun, namely M. [Munina] Froylaz, sister of Count P., so that while she lived she might possess, inhabit, build up, and plant it as best she could.

When the course of her life had ended, the aforesaid town, with all its appurtenances, was to revert to the right of the church of St James. She too, not unmindful of so great a benefit, conveyed to the church of St James the following estates: namely, the town called Rus, with its little church, in Nemitos; the shares which she held in Figariola; the town of Marín, half reclaimed from wilderness; in the territory of Salinas, the town of Marañes; and half of the estate which had belonged to her mother-in-law Goda. She granted all these, with everything pertaining to them, to St James.

That the agreement and compact in this matter might be more valid and secure on both sides and not be erased by the passage of encroaching time, it was confirmed by a charter, which you will find in the *Register of St James*. It was made in Era 1151, on 8 Ides of November [6 November].

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the other half of Dena and on other estates or churches.

Count P., whom the aforesaid bishop, as his spiritual son, instructed with the nourishment of spiritual teaching and admonished to bestow fully upon churches and the ministers of churches the tithes of everything that he possessed and his other benefactions, also granted to the Church of St James the other half of the town of Dena mentioned above.

He also gave the following estates: in Prucios, his share in the church of St Saviour of Pernis; St Julian of Carantonia; St Peter of Grandal; the entire St Mary of Castro in Bisancos; St James of Francia; St Stephen of Erens; St Eugenia of Trasancos; the church of St Saturninus in Abbati; the church in Nendos; the church of St Mary of Olarios in Salto; St Tyrsus in Selaya; in Nemancos, St Stephen of Lires; St Mary of Mauri; likewise St Mary of Ozia in Nemancos; half of St Mary of Mour for the present, and after his death the estate which is there.

Moreover, he granted to St James Amaranti and Nimia, and whatever he possessed between the Ulla and Tambre, or whatever he should thereafter acquire there in those estates, and the court at Patrono, apart from the houses in Compostela.

## CHAPTER XCV. For removing the oppressions of the people.

At about this time the aforesaid protector of Galicia, looking with an eye of compassion upon the oppressions and afflictions of the poor, the common people harassed by accusations and injuries, and the province of St James grievously overwhelmed by the continual disturbance of rapacity, employed the solicitude of paternal mercy and devoted himself earnestly to relieving the unjust oppressions of the people.

For after the death of the most noble Emperor A., amid the outbreak of so many wars, soldiers had to be enriched with greater payments and broader possessions, which was a cause of oppression and poverty for the people. For money was in one way or another taken away from the weaker and less powerful and lavishly distributed to nobles and others labouring in military service. Indeed, in time of war circumstances require that soldiers who resist the enemy’s assaults and bravely defend their own should be fully rewarded with generous gifts by the guardians of their country.

But the aforesaid bishop, contemplating with merciful compassion the tribulation of oppression and the calamity of want among his subjects, and sharing their suffering with paternal mercy, took diligent care to remove the causes of such great evils. In order to relieve and restore all the people of the honour of St James, everywhere afflicted by public and private accusations and robberies, he established, with the counsel of all the canons of the apostolic Church, decrees to be observed most firmly in the honour of St James. He ordained that in these decrees, without evasion, what was fair and just should be maintained.

So that they might be more secure and not shaken by any assault, he bound by oath all the magnates who held authority in the honour of St James or were subject to his lordship to observe them more diligently; nor did he leave the others exempt from the same oath. Then, lest they should be erased by the passage of time, he handed down the following brief written provisions for us to read and observe.

## CHAPTER XCVI. The decrees of Didacus II, bishop of the Church of St James, for the protection of the poor, begin.

“By the ordering mercy of God, I, DIDACUS II, bishop of the Church of St James, with the judgment of the canons of the same see and the counsel of the other noble men, reviewing the ordinances of my predecessors, establish and, in establishing, confirm the following decrees for the protection of the people and for the administration of the rule of justice throughout the whole honour of St James—excepting the city of Compostela and all boroughs, where newcomers and many others flocking together could not at all be capable of observing these statutes:

1. **On churches.** Beginning from the beginning, we command that no one break into or forcibly enter a church’s boundaries. But if anyone wishes, while justice is pending and demands it, to seize anything within a church’s boundaries or to seal it up for himself, he shall first apply to the bishop’s vicar so that permission may be granted him.

2. **On the houses of nobles and non-nobles, pledges, and accusations committed.** In the houses of nobles, or wherever their wives or unarmed sons are present, we withdraw from vicars and all others permission to distrain. We command that the same be observed in the houses of all others, except where there is a case of theft, homicide, the forcible violation of a woman—commonly called *raptum* [abduction or rape]—or a Lenten due.

“If livestock or other such things that may be seized for an accusation committed are not found outside peasant houses, the vicar, with neighbours and lawful witnesses called in, shall seal up the house or remove a pledge from it. Whatever has been distrained, as stated above, shall be kept intact until eight days are complete; it shall be entrusted to neighbours for safekeeping and shall remain unharmed and free from every use until the appointed term. If all the animals are required for agricultural labour, they shall be kept free from all work.

“At last, if the person charged does not come at the appointed time for the examination of justice, unless detained by a necessary cause, the examiners of justice shall retain a portion of the pledge corresponding to the amount of the accusation; the remainder shall be restored to its owners. If anyone presumes to distrain another person unjustly or without first seeking permission from his lord, he shall restore double and pay sixty solidi to the bishop. Nevertheless, whoever has distrained with a vicar after first seeking justice before suitable witnesses shall not restore double.

3. **On judges.** Cases concerning estates and churches shall be determined only by the magnates and judges of the apostolic see. Judgments in cases involving surety for accusations shall, according to the custom of our predecessors and to the exclusion of other judges in the honour of St James, be referred to the judges of the apostolic see.

4. **On accusations against the poor.** The poor and weak shall satisfy accusations mercifully, so that they may not be wholly deprived of their livelihoods.

5. **On traitors and robbers.** Let no one presume to protect or defend traitors and robbers. Indeed, those who protect them shall bear the damages or penalties which the traitors or robbers deserved to bear.

6. **On thieves.** After a thief has been convicted or apprehended as guilty of theft for the third time, he shall be delivered to the rulers of the land and the examiners of justice. They, as justice dictates, shall exact punishment from him according to his deserts and shall heed the purpose for which the sword has been entrusted to them. For they should know that: ‘He who strikes the wicked because they are wicked is a minister of God’; and elsewhere: ‘To punish the wicked is not the shedding of blood.’

7. **On charters.** We command that charters be made before the assembly of the whole Church or before a public council, and we prohibit charters made otherwise from having force.

8. **On *fossataria* and *luctuosa*.** To those who bear the yoke of servile condition, or who pay Lenten dues, we remit the customary payments called *fossataria* and *luctuosa*, provided that they inhabit the estates of their fathers or parents.

9. **On Sunday.** On the Lord’s Day we prohibit country people from going to the city for trade.

10. **On agreements and other documents.** Agreements and other documents of this kind shall be made by authorized clerics, just as by judges, or by the archdeacon, or by the archpriest of the place itself. Otherwise, they shall be deemed void.

11. **On the cases of the poor.** If any powerful person has to conduct or determine a judicial case against a poor person, he shall introduce a person of equal rank, who may determine his case in person, lest the poor person’s justice be stifled by someone’s power.

12. **On Lent.** During the days of Lent, we forbid the making of charters, the determination of cases of accusation, the exercise of judicial proceedings, and the collection of *fossataria*, unless a great necessity of campaign arises. This prohibition applies to our own men, not to outsiders, who are dealt with according to their lords’ wishes; cases of theft, *raus* [uncertain reading], homicide, and Lenten dues are excepted.

13. **That cases of accusation be heard on the Kalends.** On the day of the Kalends, archpriests, priests, soldiers, and peasants shall assemble in the manner of their predecessors on the Kalends. Then, if any complaint or injury has arisen, it shall be truthfully investigated and remedied by the archpriest and other discerning men. If they cannot determine it, then on the following day, after a true investigation of the matter, it shall be referred to the bishop and the leading men of the apostolic see and determined.

14. **On cases to be conducted on the sixth day.** Every week on the sixth day [Friday], the doors of the episcopal palace having been opened, every complaint and injury shall be reported and determined in the presence of the bishop, judges, and canons.

15. **On driving out wolves.** On every Saturday, except Easter and Pentecost, priests, soldiers, and peasants, free from every other occupation, shall pursue wolves and prepare for them the pits which the common people call *fogios*. Every church shall also pay seven iron rods. Whoever delays in going to this task, if he is a priest—unless detained by visiting the sick—or a soldier, shall pay five solidi; if a peasant, he shall pay a sheep or one solidus.

16. **On vicars.** Soldiers and all who hold pre-eminent authority shall appoint to their administrative offices such vicars as have means from which they may satisfy penalties if they act contrary to the justice of these decrees. Otherwise their lords shall bear the penalties for the damage and violation of justice committed by them.

17. **On robbers.** Whoever captures a robber shall hand him over to the steward of the land; and whatever the steward takes from him, the captor shall receive one third of it. The same shall apply to traitors.”

18. That no one shall plunder or disturb the property of the dead.—Whenever anyone has paid nature’s due, his inheritances and other holdings shall remain intact and undisturbed for ten days, exactly as he left them. When the ten days have ended, while the possessions and other holdings remain under the same legal right under which he fell to death’s dart, and as he left them, any contentious disputes concerning them shall be determined by the judges of the apostolic see and by other learned men. Moreover, lest any inheritance-hunter or sycophant make a wrongful claim, the matter shall be investigated fully by the proofs of justice [Col. 0988B].

19. That officials shall not have leave to distrain on Sunday.—From the ninth hour on Saturday until the first hour on Monday, no *sajo* [royal or judicial officer] shall have leave to seize pledges, except from murderers, thieves, violators of virgins, violent abductors, and traitors. If anyone from a foreign land seeks justice, he shall receive justice within the aforesaid period.

20. That assemblies of litigants shall not be held in a church.—We forbid the council of the *sajones* or an assembly of knights from being held in a church or within its bounds.

21. That clerics shall not become laymen’s stewards or tutors.—Clerics shall neither become stewards for laymen nor fosterers of their children; nor shall they be dishonoured by a lay person or have their goods taken from them. Whoever acts otherwise shall make the prescribed canonical satisfaction and, being excommunicated, shall be excluded from the fellowship of the faithful [Col. 0988C].

22. Concerning the goods of captives.—The goods of those captured by the Moors shall be kept wholly unviolated and intact for a year, so that, if perhaps they are able by chance to ransom the captive, they may ransom him. But if not, once the year is completed, their goods shall be distributed according to the judgment of their relatives.

23. Concerning merchants and pilgrims.—Merchants, *romarii* [pilgrims to Rome], and pilgrims shall not be distrained upon. Whoever acts otherwise shall restore double what he has taken, shall be excommunicated, and shall pay sixty solidi to the lord of that jurisdiction.

24. Concerning clerics.—Clerics shall not pay the *fossataria* [a levy connected with military service]. We forbid abbots and clerics coming to a synod, or bringing a vow [offering] or third-part dues, to be distrained upon [Col. 0988D].

25. Concerning measures.—We forbid all other *talegas* [Note: [Col. 0987D] Read *talegas*, that is, a kind of measure, which among the Galicians is a fourth part of that called *fanega* among us [Col. 0988D].] to be bought or sold, whether in this city or outside it, unless according to the measure of that stone which stands in the field of Compostela. Whoever acts otherwise, being excommunicated, shall pay sixty solidi, until he comes to repentance.

## CHAPTER XCVII. Concerning the council at Palencia, and the election of the queen’s chaplain as bishop of Lugo

At the aforesaid council of Palencia [Note: [Col. 0988D] In the year 1113, as we noted at the beginning of chapter 92.] the archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, together with very many bishops and abbots of the Spanish kingdoms, while more profitably setting forth an examination of justice suited to the circumstances and time [Col. 0989A], lamented that robberies, burnings, killings, and the other calamities of Spain were becoming more frequent day by day. Having shared the counsel of all, they all besought the ineffable mercy of God with most humble devotion, that He might deign more promptly to provide remedies for so many and such great evils.

Finally, grieving over the ruin of churches and over things divine and human alike being more boldly violated, they took anxious care to provide relief and, with God’s help, to impose an end upon such great calamities. Nor did they delay to bring the help of paternal consolation to the Church of Lugo, concerning whose distress a public discussion had arisen. For it had long been deprived of a protector and was almost bereft of a shepherd; it was being driven by very great storms, as happens in time of war [Col. 0989B].

Peter, bishop of that Church, wholly aspiring to heavenly blessedness and free from the concerns of this world, refused to bear the burden of so great an office. He could not, as was necessary, protect the honour of the Church of Lugo, exercise care for souls, and labour amid many and diverse affairs. Moreover, illness afflicted him, and he could no longer be equal to that office. Therefore that Church, deprived of patronage, was gravely troubled by the force of storms and was especially oppressed, having been subjected to the lordship of Count R.

Accordingly, it was decreed by the general assembly that, since the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Lugo utterly refused to bear the care of government and was in no way able to fulfil the ministry of a bishop, another should be canonically advanced to the episcopate, lest the Church be uprooted to its very foundation [Col. 0989C]: one who would both protect the Church from the bites of those gaping after it and exercise care for souls.

Therefore the clerics of the Church of Lugo approached the archbishop and humbly requested that, providing for the desolation of their mother church, he would mercifully accede to their petition. The aforesaid man of the highest religious devotion likewise earnestly laboured by prayers to obtain that he might cease from so great a burden and that another might be chosen bishop—one who would protect the Church and hold the office of shepherd, which he himself could in no way fulfil.

Accordingly, by the aforesaid persons of the Church of Lugo and the other venerable persons, Peter, chaplain of Queen U., was designated bishop and requested with the greatest earnestness. He was then sent to the city of Lugo to be canonically advanced to the episcopate [Col. 0989D]. The archbishop himself sent the following letter concerning his election and consecration to Bishop D. of Compostela, A. of Tui, D. of Ourense, and M. of Mondoñedo.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. Concerning the examination and consecration of the bishop-elect of Lugo

> BERNARD, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops in Christ, Lord D. of Compostela, Lord M. of Mondoñedo, Lord A. of Tui, and Lord D. of Ourense: entrance into the heavenly kingdom.
>
> We wish it to be known to your brotherhood that, as we have learned, the clergy and people of the Church of Lugo have chosen for themselves as shepherd Lord Peter, chaplain of the queen [Col. 0990A]. But because we do not know whether the election was canonical, we command you in charity—and, in commanding, request—that you investigate the matter more carefully. If you find the election canonical, then, because the archbishop of Braga, so long as he remains disobedient and rebellious to the Holy Roman Church, as you know, and suspended from episcopal office, cannot consecrate anyone: either take care to bless him with the lord of Compostela acting in our stead, or send him without doubt to us with your letters to be consecrated.
>
> So long as Maurice perseveres in this wickedness, no bishop, no abbot of the province of Braga, nor even cleric or layman, shall render him the obedience he deserves. Farewell.

When these letters had been seen, a most prompt inquiry was held concerning his election; and because it had been canonically made, the consecration was not delayed. Therefore Didacus, bishop of Saint James, acting in the archbishop’s stead, consecrated the bishop-elect of the Church of Lugo as bishop in the church of Saint James, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April], in the presence of D., bishop of Ourense, and M., bishop of Mondoñedo; and he was appointed shepherd of the Church of Lugo [Col. 0990B].

The aforesaid archbishop likewise sent the following letter to Didacus, bishop of the Church of Saint James.

## CHAPTER XCIX. To signify friendship between the archbishop of Toledo and the bishop of Compostela concerning the excommunication of M., archbishop of Braga

> BERNARD, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop in Christ, Lord D. of Compostela: may you be happily joined to the citizens above [Col. 0990C].
>
> With great affection of mind and much desire of heart, I would wish, if it were possible, to see your friendship, in order to speak with you concerning the common welfare of this greatly disturbed kingdom. But since the disturbance is so great that we are deprived of seeing one another in person, let charity and letter join those whom bodily absence separates.
>
> Let your belovedness therefore know that M. of Braga, because he refused to make satisfaction for his invasion of the Church of León, and thereafter, having been suspended by us from both offices, presumptuously presumed to celebrate episcopal and priestly offices, received from the lord pope the following letter:
>
> “Among the other complaints brought to the apostolic see concerning you, the invasion and devastation of the Church of León has grieved us more heavily. Though warned concerning it by our letters and summoned to a council by our vicar B. of Toledo, you scorned both to come and to make satisfaction. Moreover, after being forbidden by him, on account of such wickedness and disobedience, from both priestly and episcopal office, you stubbornly presumed to celebrate those same offices. Therefore we, by God’s authority avenging so great a crime of wickedness and pride, forbid you those same offices and the obedience of the Church of Braga, until, coming to repentance, you obey and make full satisfaction.” Given at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction (in the year 1114) [Col. 0990D].
>
> We therefore request your friendship to show this letter to all the suffragan bishops of the Church of Braga and to admonish them not to render obedience to the aforesaid M., according to the command of the lord pope. Send also to the Portuguese infanta, for your sake and out of affection for us, this other letter. Farewell.

## CHAPTER C. Concerning churches and inheritances acquired by the same bishop for the Church of Saint James

At the same time the aforesaid bishop of the apostolic Church, striving everywhere with tireless concern for the dignity and increase of his Church, built churches, acquired inheritances and possessions, and constructed buildings and fortified places.

He acquired for his Church the following inheritances: the monastery of Saint Pelagius of Circitello, with its household and its villages—namely Villamayor Maurentani, Castro [lacuna]racto, Salamir, Cesari, Anserice, Quintanas, Villar Rubi, and Salimes with the church of Saint Martha; and, in the district of Molnes, Ango; in Deza, the villages of Trauca, Occa, and Ordiale; in Siaonia, other villages, with all the charters and appurtenances of the aforesaid monastery, wherever they may be found [Col. 0991B].

Likewise, the daughter of Count Peter Froylaz, named Enxemena, granted to the Church of Saint James an eighth part of Saint Mary of Transmonte, with its household and all its appurtenances. Likewise, the brother of the same Count P., named Rudericus Froylaz, granted to the Church of the same apostle an eighth part of Saint Pelagius of Lenes, with its household and all its appurtenances, and a certain estate beside Avegundi, namely the village of Saint James [Col. 0991C].

Furthermore, the same bishop built certain churches: the church of Saint James of Patrono, the church of Pilonio, and the church of Saint Saviour of Cherua in Pistomarcis. He also fortified the castle of Honesti with towers, surrounded it with a wall, adorned it with a bridge and other works, and erected very many buildings in honour of Saint James.

Likewise Rabinatus Muniz gave the Church of Saint James Villa Aquilon, Vilar, and Rial, with their household and appurtenances. Count Peter likewise, with his wife Countess Lady M., granted there at Ventosa half of one church, Saint Christopher’s, and in the territory of Faro a third part of another church, Saint Mary of Aoso. Likewise, in Coronato Suarius Froylaz gave a village named Bausendi [Col. 0991D], and two other villages there.

At approximately the same time Queen Lady U., daughter of King Adefonsus of venerable memory, maintained that certain clerics of the Church of Saint James—namely Didacus of Ludanense [Note: [Col. 0991D] Read *Budanense*, as the following passages show.], and his brothers Pelagius and Peter, together with all their descendants and all their inheritance—were subject to capitation dues, and she wished to establish by many assertions that they were bound to serve her in servile condition.

But since they were canons of Saint James, Bishop D., greatly grieved by their disgrace and loss, persistently and tirelessly implored the lady queen that, for love of God and Saint James, she would wholly abandon such a claim and allow the aforesaid clerics and their descendants to remain undisturbed and to enjoy the right of freedom in the service of God and for the remission of her sins [Col. 0992A]. Yielding to his petition, the queen not only ceased, at the bishop’s intercession, to trouble them under her own claim, but from that time determined to hold them all among her household retainers and special friends.

After two of the aforesaid brothers, Pelagius and Peter, had died, while the third, Didacus, was alive but insane—he who, prompted by the devil while mad, killed his uncle—Nuno Budanensis, with his brother Froyla, his maternal uncle Didacus Dulcitii, and other kinsmen, conveyed by charter to the Church of Saint James the monastery of Budanense, established in the territory of Coronato, which was their own hereditary possession. They confirmed with their own hands the charter which they had made as evidence and confirmation of this conveyance; and, confirmed, they delivered it to the lord bishop, to be kept and held in the treasury of Saint James, with joyful hand and glad heart [Col. 0992B].

They made this conveyance upon the following terms and agreement: for as long as they lived, they should possess the aforesaid monastery for their livelihood, and they should be subject and obedient to the Church of Saint James. This was also added: if any of their descendants should become clerics and wish to hold it in secular tenure, they should possess the aforesaid monastery on the same terms.

After this charter had been made and received from them, the lord bishop acquired, without any evil artifice or bad contrivance, almost all the charters which they had concerning the aforesaid monastery, and deposited them in the treasury of Saint James as evidence of the aforesaid condition [Col. 0992C].

Peter Vimaraz likewise, together with his wife, gave the Church of Saint James a sixth part of the church of Tabladella between the two bridges. He also gave the village of Tabladella with its dependent holding. Besides this, the same aforesaid bishop restored, renewed, and consecrated the church of Saint Thomas the Apostle of Ojames.

Likewise Count Ovecus of Galicia and his wife Eila gave Saint James, on the bank of the Pisuerga, their share of the village of Bovadella and of the village of Pisata; and they commended to the protection of Saint James all their servants, freed from the yoke of servitude. Count Peter likewise, with his wife Countess M., gave the apostle half of the offspring [dependants] of the church of Saint Tyrsius of Avegundo, with its charter, which church they had already long before granted there [Col. 0992D].

Likewise the Gelmirides, brothers of the aforesaid bishop, granted Saint James their shares in five churches: Saint Peter of Orvego, Saint Michael of Castanella, Saint James of Ripa de Sar, and Saint Antoninus of Castro, on condition that each year, on their anniversary—namely, the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene—the canons should be splendidly provided for from them. Likewise Arias Petrides gave Villa Viridis. Likewise Visclavara Froylaz, sister of Count Peter, gave Saint James half of Saint Peter of Crendes in Nemitos.

Count Munio and his wife Countess Lupa granted Saint James their share of the church of Saint Eulalia of Aria; at Salceta, one dependent holding with its inheritance; at Amunio, another dependent holding with its inheritance; in Decia, the village of Vellegio with its dependants; and at Aviancos, Saint Martin of Olarios, as Queen U. had given it to them [Col. 0993A].

Likewise Rannemirus Muninz gave the aforesaid apostle his whole share of Saint Martin of Severana with its appurtenances, namely Saint John of Bojon with villages and inheritances: that is, the village of Forno, the village of Cerquitu, with all other inheritances; likewise, as a share pertaining to Saint Martin of Severana, half of Saint Mary of Coleirsi, half of Saint Peter of Sena, half of Saint Eulalia on the bank of the Umia, half of Saint Leocritia of Sicana, half of Saint Martin of Meix, and his share of the monastery of Calogo with its appurtenances—that is, the village of Callario, and likewise Callerii, and three [uncertain: perhaps a place-name] Callarius; likewise his share in Deiru, and in the village of Usa, the village of Curbellion, the village of Unio, the village of Portas, the village of Loix, and Saint Mary of Vesomanio [Col. 0993B].

Likewise Marina Fredenandiz gave Saint James her share of the church of Saint Saviour of Sobradello. Likewise Peter Arias gave Saint James his share of Villa Nova. Likewise Gundesindus Cidiz gave Saint James at Taberiolos a fourth part of the church of Saint John of Santellas, with its appurtenances and dependants. Munio Didaz likewise granted Saint James his share of Saint Mary of Carredecello, with appurtenances and a certain estate.

Likewise Queen Urraca gave Saint James half of the monastery of Ledesma, with its appurtenances and dependants, and likewise half of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caneda, with its appurtenances and dependants [Col. 0993C]. The queen likewise gave Saint James, by testamentary charter, Caldas de Cuntes, a certain inheritance in the wood of Lide, and another in Veja.

### Friendship between the archbishop and Count P.

> I, Count Lord P. Froylaz, together with those named below, swear to you, Lord Didacus II, bishop, by God the almighty Father, and by all His saints and the powers of heaven, that—saving fidelity to the lord Infante A., or to another lord whom we may accept by common counsel—I shall be your faithful friend, without fraud or evil contrivance. I shall guard and defend your life and limbs, and the honour which you now have or shall hereafter have, in every way suppressing your dishonour in all things and through all things [Col. 0993D], and likewise exalting your honour, against all men according to my power, judgment, and discretion.
>
> Likewise I swear that I shall help and protect your kinsmen whom you entrust to me and who associate themselves with me, as I would some of my own good men. I shall defend and protect, for your advantage and benefit, the men and estates of Saint James which are in my land, so that through me you suffer no hindrance or loss in them. If I or my men commit any injury there, I shall make redress, either personally or through the judgment and award of our friends and men, with all my will and power.
>
> If perhaps by chance you lose your honour [Col. 0994A], I shall grant you half my own honour; and I shall defend and protect you and your canons who are your friends and mine, as myself. Concerning the advancement of the lord Infante A. and the giving and conferring of his honours, while we have him in our power we shall act in accordance with your command and counsel.
>
> If I lie in this oath, may I be perjured. And those who swear with me, if they wish to commit perjury, shall stand with you, together with their benefices and honours, excepting castles, and shall aid you without deceit or evil contrivance. Concerning these persons who are included in this agreement, as they shall examine and judge concerning all matters conducted between us, so shall I do. This oath shall be dissolved if we dissolve it.
>
> [Col. 0994B] Those who swear with Lord Count P. to that bishop are these: his wife, Countess Lady Major; his son Veremudus Petriz; his son Fernandus Petriz; Arias Nuniz; Arias Exemeniz; Froyla Petriz; Arias Sesmondiz; Sarracenus Muniz; Froyla Afonso; and Joannes Gutierrez.

## CHAPTER CI. Concerning the council to be held at León

Not long afterwards Bernard, archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, sent the following letter to the aforesaid bishop, commanding him to come to the council which he was to hold at León on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October].

> BERNARD, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop, Lord D. of Compostela: everlasting blessedness.
>
> Let your belovedness know that I have spoken with the king [Note: [Col. 0993D] That is, the king of Aragon.] and queen concerning the common peace. But since, because the king refused, we were unable to make any agreement between them, we have decreed to hold a council at León on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], at which we wish and command your belovedness to be present [Col. 0994C]. For you will be greatly necessary to us there, and we do not wish you, under any pretext, to withdraw your presence from the aforesaid synod. Farewell. We command you also to bring with you the abbots and provosts of your diocese.

### Concerning the condition of Holy Church and the rigor of justice established by the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Saint James with the bishops named below

> We, ministers of the Church of God by divine dispensation—Didacus of the see of Compostela, A. of Tui, Munio of Valibria, Peter of Lugo, Didacus of Ourense, and Hugh of Portugal—by the will of Lord Bernard, archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, assembled at Compostela on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December [17 November]. With the abbots of the monasteries of Galicia and the other religious prelates, we held a council, the Lord consenting [Col. 0994D].
>
> At this council we caused the counts and other magnates of the land, who could not go to the council of León, to be admonished that they should keep with inviolable observance the decrees enacted at that council:
>
> 1. No layman shall presume to commit any violence against the churches of God, their goods, or their ministers; and inheritances and testamentary gifts unjustly taken from those churches shall be wholly restored to them [Col. 0995A].
> 2. No layman shall have any authority within the sanctuary of a church, which we commonly call *passales* or *dextros*.
> 3. No layman shall dare either to receive or touch the tithes, first-fruits, or offerings of the living or the dead belonging to churches; and no ordained person shall receive a church from a lay hand.
> 4. Traders, pilgrims, and labourers shall be at peace and travel safely through the lands, so that no one may lay hands upon them or their goods.
> 5. A lawful marriage shall in no way be violated; and those joined by consanguinity or kinship shall be completely separated or deprived of communion.
> 6. Traitors and notorious perjurers, and their testimony, shall be received by no one, because they are infamous [Col. 0995B].
> 7. No person shall sell, buy, or convey by charter any church to a layman, because that is simoniacal.
> 8. No cleric shall have a woman in his house except those whom the canons permit.
> 9. Monks or clerics who have abandoned their habit shall be deprived of communion until they repent.
> 10. Monks shall live under the authority of their abbot, shall possess no private property, and shall not perform public offices as parish priests do.
>
> May those who endeavour to observe and fulfil these decrees according to the direction of their bishops merit the grace of almighty God. But those who neglect them, whether in the Campos, Castile, Portugal, Galicia, Extremadura, or Aragon [Col. 0995C], shall be subject to anathema; and in their land or lordship the divine office shall in no way be celebrated, except penance and baptism.
>
> We have also made a confraternity among ourselves, that each may love the other, that each may assist the other according to his power if necessary, and that we may mutually maintain charity among ourselves. Whenever any one of us dies, the others shall unanimously aid his soul by alms, prayers, and sacrifices, so that it may attain eternal blessedness. To confirm this confraternity, we have decreed that every year, in the middle of Lent, we shall assemble at Compostela and correct the wrongs that have come to our hearing.

The following were likewise sent to the Roman pontiff by that same bishop of Compostela, who was anxiously labouring for the exaltation of his Church [Col. 0995D]. [Note: [Col. 0995D] The bishop of Compostela was seriously and most eagerly considering the transfer of the metropolitan see of Emerita to his own Church. This was his principal concern; the pope’s answer below concerns this matter, although it says nothing expressly about the petition.]

### Reply to the bishop’s petition

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.
>
> “Although we are far distant from you,” etc. See Paschal, under the year 1118, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 393.

The following was likewise sent to him by John Gaietan, cardinal and chancellor, who later became Pope Gelasius.

> To his dearest brother and sweetest friend, D., bishop of Compostela: Brother John, by the grace of God deacon, greeting in the Lord.
>
> We thank your kindness because what had been done inadequately by your other envoys you are now completing through others [Col. 0996A]. I was unable to discuss at greater length with the lord pope the matter which you communicated to me, because, while I was staying in the City, he had gone far away; nevertheless, he returned on the day before the vigil of Saint John. For the time being, however, I did what I could. But at this time, amid so great a conflict, neither he nor we think it suitable to deliberate upon such a transfer. For the small part of the province of Emerita which the Christians hold is possessed by the bishop of Toledo; and to disturb him at this time, amid so great an oppression, would be sinful.
>
> In any case, you know that whatever service lies within our capacity has always been ready for your affairs. Therefore remember us. May He who keeps Israel keep you. Amen.
