## CHAPTER CII. Concerning the queen’s plot against the bishop and their reconciliation

[Col. 0996B]

Meanwhile Queen U. returned to Galicia and arrived at Compostela. The aforesaid bishop of Saint James, knowing that she readily listened to whisperers and slanderers; knowing that, being a woman and unarmed, her spirit was unequal to governing the kingdom of Spain in peace and justice; and knowing that, if justice prevailed as it ought, the kingdom of Galicia should be subjected to the rule of her son King Ildefonsus—had somewhat withdrawn his mind from favouring that queen.

The queen, however, at the counsel of the bishop’s enemies, strove to capture him if place or time should require it. Meanwhile words were exchanged between them [Col. 0996C], the queen laying a trap and the bishop guarding himself more shrewdly. When, her first purpose having failed, the queen was staying in the district of Salinas and the surrounding region, she considered in what place, in what manner, and with what helpers she might capture the bishop. She desired it but did not dare; she considered it but was afraid.

At last she decided that the bishop, who was then at Iria, should meet her as she returned from those parts and thus be seized unexpectedly. For she would not dare to lay hands upon him at Compostela, or where he was protected by his own men. Count P. Froylaz, the intimate friend of the aforesaid bishop, having learned of this treachery from the queen herself and her counsellors, was greatly alarmed. Through his own messenger, secretly and under a solemn pledge of trust, he faithfully disclosed to the bishop the day and hour [Col. 0996D], what he ought to do, and how he might better guard and faithfully protect himself.

Having heard of the treachery of this wicked plot, the bishop returned to Compostela, first instructing his stewards to receive the queen honourably at the shrine of the patron. Afterwards he summoned together his magnates, canons, and citizens, and publicly set forth all that had been revealed to him and how the queen was plotting against him. All were astonished and unanimously condemned the motives of so wicked a scheme.

Having then taken counsel, the bishop was surrounded by an armed force of horsemen and foot-soldiers [Col. 0997A], so that his enemies might not rashly dare anything against him or bring their plot to effect. When the queen learned that the deceit of her scheme had failed and that she could proceed no further, she abandoned the plan and strongly asserted that she alone had not devised such things. She concealed her fault entirely beneath tears and swore that she wished to love, honour, and protect the bishop, her patron, as herself. For it is written: “The heart of fools will be unlike” (Prov. 15:7).

Nevertheless the bishop received the queen carefully and rendered her the service due to royal honour; indeed, surrounded by arms, he was formidable to his enemies. The counts of Galicia and the other magnates came to Compostela, grievously distressed by the discord between the queen and bishop. They called all accomplices in such a plan wicked traitors and laboured earnestly to restore peace between them.

At last the queen summoned the bishop and his magnates to an alliance, and with twenty of the leading barons of Galicia, Castile, and Campania made the following agreement and oath.

### The queen’s oath

> I, Queen Lady U., swear to you, Lord D., bishop, by God the almighty Father and by all His saints, that from this day forward I shall be your faithful friend concerning your person and the honour which you have or shall have, without evil artifice or evil intent, to the extent of my power. You shall not lose your honour through me, my counsel [Col. 0997C], or my contrivance.
>
> The counsels which you tell me and command to be concealed I shall not disclose where it may turn out badly for you. I shall help you rightly to defend and protect your honour against all men. If anyone says evil to me about you, I shall not heed it or reproach you for it. If any wrong has been done by me against you, I shall make amends according to the judgment of M., bishop of Valibria, Lords A. and P. Muniz, and A. and P. Anaiaz; and if these are insufficient, we shall appoint others pleasing to us.
>
> If I violate this oath, you and your oath-takers shall be released; and I shall be perjured if I refuse to make amends within ten days, if we are in Galicia, or, if we are outside it [Col. 0997D], within three months after I have been summoned in my kingdom. We further add to this oath that, if I am perjured, all my oath-takers shall be on your side.
>
> We, the oath-takers on behalf of Queen Lady U., swear to you, Lord D., bishop, that Queen Lady Urraca shall carry out what is written above. If the queen refuses this command, we shall enforce the judgment prescribed above. We shall attest this in council once or twice, at a suitable place and time, in her kingdom; otherwise, according to her concession, we shall be perjured. Count Lord M. Adefonsus Ruderiquiz, Fredenandus Joannes, Joannes Didaci, and those whom the bishop releases shall be released from this oath.

## CHAPTER CIII. Concerning the bishop’s ships and the booty taken from the Saracens by them

[Col. 0998A]

At the same time the Saracens of Seville, Saltes, Castile, Salvia, Lisbon, and others dwelling along the maritime borders from Seville to Coimbra were accustomed to build ships and to come by sea in armed force. They ravaged and laid waste the coastal districts from Coimbra to the Pyrenees: namely Portugal, Morracios, the borders of Salinas, Pistomarchos, Gentines, Nemarcos, Sonaria, Salagia, Bregantinos, Nemitos, Prucios, Bisancos, Trasancos, Vivarium, Duvios, Navia, the other coastal territories of the Asturians, and the land of Saint Juliana.

They especially devastated on every side the shores of the sea lying nearest to the province of Saint James [Col. 0998B]. Setting their course for the nearby islands—namely Flamia, Aonios, Salvara, Arouca, Crevia, and Monte Lauros—they established their base there and refreshed themselves and their ships from the labour of the journey. From there they made frequent assaults on Christians, sometimes secretly and sometimes openly.

Why should I dwell on many details? They utterly destroyed churches and dug up altars—an unspeakable thing. They burned the palaces of noblemen, villages, and huts; felled trees; slaughtered herds; placed aboard ship as much of them as they required; and captured some men, women, youths, and children, while delivering others to death. [Note: [Col. 0997D] On this again, book II, chapter 21.]

Why say more? They captured Fredenandus Arias and Menendus Didacides, most noble and very powerful men; and these men gave sixty Christian captives—yet persons of servile condition—to the captors as ransom for themselves [Col. 0998C]. Moreover, they delivered many nobles, some into captivity and others to death; for the Saracens themselves pitched their tents on the seashore. Therefore the farmers of the Ocean coast abandoned the shores from mid-spring until mid-autumn, or hid in caves with all their household.

Against so many and such great persecutions by the pagans, the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Saint James had often taken care, with the magnates of Galicia, to extend a helping hand. Yet the Galicians were not accustomed to build ships, except cargo-vessels, or to cut through the deep sea in sailing biremes [Col. 0998D]. Therefore the bishop thought that he could in no way put an end to so many and such great evils.

Now, as has been said, he had issued decrees by which the common people might remain secure from the powerful and by which, justice dictating, each person might have what was his. He also vigorously administered peace to the country so far as lay within his power. But what counsel or protection could he offer where neither counsel nor protection was of use? Only the ineffable mercy of God, only His inestimable wisdom, could provide for its own work.

The aforesaid bishop, therefore, supported by the boundless providence of God and moved with pity for the captivity of Christians, sent his messengers to Pisa and Genoa. [Col. 0999A] There, indeed, were found excellent shipwrights and most experienced sailors, who yielded in natural talent to no Palinurus of Aeneas; the aforesaid messengers overawed them by promises of many gifts and persuaded them to set out for Galicia to build ships. Without delay, shipwrights from the city of Genoa came to Compostela to the bishop, and, having first agreed with him upon a fixed price, undertook to build him two biremes.

How great the joy and rejoicing of the inhabitants of the coast—indeed, of all the Galicians—was may be judged from the usefulness of the undertaking; for they rejoiced at the liberation and defence of their homeland. For how could the Saracens, arriving in a multitude of ships, be prevented from plundering and carrying Galicia into captivity unless they were met in turn by naval force? [Col. 0999B] Thus, at very great expense, two biremes were made, which the common people call *galleys* [Note: [Col. 0999D] Today, *galeras*.]. The men of Iria, having summoned another Palinurus—that is, the craftsman of those ships, named Eugerius—went, by the bishop’s command and exhortation, to repay the Saracens in kind.

Why say more? Two hundred men, ready for war by sea and land, with swift sail invaded the land of the Ishmaelites. For the injuries and insults formerly received, they repaid the Ishmaelites in equal measure and more. They burned houses and crops on the threshing-floors—for it was the season of threshing [Note: [Col. 0999D] About the month of July.]—cut down trees and vineyards, and their sword spared neither great nor small. They did not blush to burn and demolish their temples and to do within them deeds foul to relate. They captured, destroyed, and burned their cargo-ships and sailing vessels, accustomed to carry off Christian captives. [Col. 0999C] At last, when the sword had had its fill and their ships had been laden with gold, silver, and booty, they returned joyfully to their own country, singing praise to God and to St James.

Ah! What joy for the worshippers of the Christian faith, to see Saracens brought in captivity, their hands bound behind their backs, in their own ships. Of all these things the men of Iria gave the bishop a fourth share, together with other dues owed to him by right of ownership in their ships. They also gave captives to St James, to carry stones and other materials for the construction of his church. Would that the unbelief of the Ishmaelites were thus more often crushed! Would that good things more often befall the faithful and evil things the unbelievers!

## CHAPTER CIV. [Col. 0999D] The oath of Counts M. and R. to the aforesaid bishop.

At about this time Count M. and Count R. made the following oath to the aforesaid bishop of St James:

> “I, Count M. Pelagides of Monterroso, and I, Count R. Velaz of Sarria, swear to you, Lord D. II, bishop of St James, by God the Almighty Father and by all His saints, that we shall be your faithful men and your friends, without evil contrivance or evil intent; and that against all men [Col. 1000A] we shall assist you in defending your person and your honour, which you now possess or shall hereafter possess. Namely, the land called Montanos and the castle of St George—these which we name—and all that you now possess and all that you shall possess, we shall help you to acquire and defend, according to our power and understanding, by every means while we live.
>
> “Moreover, we shall bring to you Queen Lady U., so that she may swear to you, and we again with her and with others whom you shall choose, that she shall be your faithful friend; and that you shall never lose your honour through her, but that she shall help you against all men to preserve for you your person and your honour while she lives. And if she should wish to rise against you, or deal with you otherwise than she has sworn, then by whatever means we could, we would help you to regain or recover [Col. 1000B] her favour while preserving your whole honour. But if we could not do this consistently with your honours, we shall abandon those honours for your sake and remain with you until we recover for you both the queen’s favour and your honour.”

### The oath of Queen U. to the same bishop

> “I, Queen Lady Urraca, swear to you, Lord D., bishop of the church of St James, by God the Almighty Father and by all His saints, that from this day forward I shall be your faithful friend and lady, without contrivance or evil intent; that I shall defend and assist you and your honour against all men; that I shall thwart your dishonour by every means; and that in my days you shall not lose your honour, neither through me [Col. 1000C] nor through my counsel or design. If I learn of any evil directed against you or your honour, I shall disclose it to you at a suitable time for your advantage. And this oath shall remain firm so long as you observe the oath which your men made to me on your behalf; and if I wrong you, I shall correct myself by the judgment of those who are parties to this agreement.”

These are the names of those who swore: Count Froyla Didacides; Count R. Velaz; Count Munio Pelagides; Veremund Nuniz, son of Count Nuno.

These preceding and following oaths were made in the time of war, through the initiative of the aforesaid bishop and with the counsel of his canons, lest the Church of St James in any way be weakened or deprived of its possessions, and so that it might recover the honours which the predecessors of that Church had unjustly lost. They were made after the death of King Lord A., of blessed memory, in the eighth year after his death, in the Era 1153. [Note: [Col. 0999D] The Era and the year after the king’s death do not agree. For above, ch. 47, the king is said to have died on the third day before the Kalends of July, Era 1147; from this to 1153 six years, not eight—or seven if begun years are counted—had elapsed. Perhaps the original read “in the seventh year,” and someone carelessly added “eighth,” which another person, wishing to express it in Latin, rendered *octavo*.]

### The oath of M., bishop of Vallibria

Besides this, the same bishop of the Church of St James received this oath from M., bishop of Vallibria [Note: [Col. 1000D] Today, bishop of Mondoñedo.], who had formerly been treasurer of St James:

> “I, M., bishop of Vallibria, swear to you, Lord [Col. 1001A] D. H., bishop of St James, that from this day forward I shall be your faithful friend, without contrivance or evil intent; that I shall exalt your honour and diminish your harm; and that, during your lifetime, I shall in no way seek from another the honour of the altar which you give me justly and canonically. I shall faithfully serve you during your life in those matters in which I am summoned as advocate. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels.”

## CHAPTER CV. That the bishop of Portugal was sent to Rome with an embassy.

Although the aforesaid bishop, with the counsel of his canons, laboured with such great exertion for the elevation of the Church, he nevertheless did not fail to send his envoys to Rome: namely Hugh, bishop of Portugal [Col. 1001B], who had formerly been archdeacon of the Church of St James, and his cleric L. They brought back from the lord pope letters of the following kind.

### Concerning the liberty acquired during war

> “Paschal, bishop, etc.”
>
> “The disturbance of your kingdom,” etc.

See Paschal II, *Patrologia*, vol. CXIII, no. 435.

## CHAPTER CVI. Concerning the general council to be held at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] The council proclaimed in 1115, which was held at Rome in March of the following year.]

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc.
>
> “From the Fathers of the Church,” etc.

See above, no. 432.

## CHAPTER CVII. Concerning the discord and reconciliation of the bishop and the queen.

At about this time the seedbed of discord began to sprout between the aforesaid bishop and Queen U. [Col. 1001C] The Galicians, moreover, are especially prone to whispering and to pouring into the ears of rulers things now true, now false. Through their continual insinuations the bishop began to be alienated from the queen, and the queen from the bishop.

Therefore, in order to reconcile the bishop to herself, the queen hastened to go into Galicia. For she knew that through the bishop she might either retain or lose the kingdom of Galicia; indeed, the bishop and the Church of St James are the head and mirror of Galicia, and the hope of that kingdom rests in him. After the queen had reconciled the aforesaid bishop to herself through her dukes, counts, viscounts, and marquises, rejoicing in the success of her arrival, she granted him Termas by decree, [Col. 1001D] which was then royal property; and she confirmed her gifts by a written privilege, preserved to the present day in the cartulary of the Church of St James.

Moreover, the queen came to Limia in order to curb the arrogance of Menendo Nuniz, who, in rebellion against her, was laying waste Limia. Having accomplished this, she returned to Luparia.

### Concerning the queen’s plot against the bishop and their reconciliation

Meanwhile certain evil associates, rivals, and slanderers—lovers of discord rather than peace—did not cease to urge the queen to seize the bishop and strip him of power and honour. [Col. 1002A] A woman’s mind is weak and unstable and quickly goes astray, as it is written: “Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman doing good” (Ecclesiasticus 42:14). The queen’s mind was already wavering, already preparing to commit the crime; in many ways she prepared the bishop’s capture and laid snares to seize him.

But since she neither dared nor could lay hands upon so great a man without enlisting the assistance of the more powerful men of Galicia, she sent envoys to Count P. Froylaz and begged him to lend a helping hand to so great a crime. She promised him a share in the honour of St James—that is, the price of the crime. He, however, did not presume to undertake the audacity of so great an outrage. Indeed, that count, a man who feared God and abhorred so great a crime, wholly refused to lay hands on the Lord’s anointed; [Col. 1002B] he greatly feared to become an accomplice in such an abominable betrayal. For he was a count of great power, foster-father of the son of Lady Queen Urraca, spiritual kinsman of the aforesaid bishop, bound to him by a bond of the highest affection, and accustomed to confess his sins to him.

Accordingly, through John Vistruariz, a citizen of St James, he revealed to the bishop every device of the abominable betrayal and advised him to beware the snare of iniquity. The bishop’s capture was being prepared either at Iria or at Compostela.

The bishop recoiled at the report of such wickedness and could scarcely give credence to what he heard. He returned from Iria to Compostela, in order to reveal the snares of the wicked design to the canons and citizens. He summoned his leading men from both places and publicly disclosed the woman’s abominable design. [Col. 1002C] The bishop surrounded himself with cavalry and infantry, so that the woman’s snares might fall to no effect.

The queen came to Iria. Although the bishop knew the whole evil plot, he nevertheless, being prudent and wise, ordered that she be served: “For weapons that are foreseen strike less severely.” Had the bishop not foreknown the deceit, he would easily have fallen into the snare. But when the queen learned that the bishop had discovered her fraudulent contrivances and that she could no longer bring to completion what she desired, she repented of her undertaking. She wished she had not yielded to whisperers; she denounced the accomplices in such wickedness and, so far as she could, suppressed the report of so great a crime. She publicly declared on oath that she had neither planned nor desired such things, strove by tears to win belief, [Col. 1002D] and condemned and hated so great a crime. At last she returned to Compostela.

The bishop, though avoiding conversation with her, nevertheless ordered that she be honourably served. Guarded by arms, he avoided speaking with her for two or three days. At length, softened by earnest entreaties, he came to speak with the queen in the choir of the Church of St James, with many persons present. Yet the greater part of the armed men were the bishop’s, because he greatly feared her. The queen, recalling the benefits which her father, King Lord A., and she herself had conferred upon the Church of St James and upon the bishop, earnestly begged him, saying:

> “Reverend [Col. 1003A] Father, upon whose protection the kingdom of Galicia depends, whom alone I have as patron after the death of my father King A., I humbly beseech your holiness not to bring yourself to believe the words of idle tale-bearers or give assent to whisperers. For I would rather be deprived of my kingdom than lay hands upon you, my lord and patron. Who could be so criminal and depraved as to afflict the bishop of St James with even the least dishonour, or—to forbid it!—incur the infamy of an abominable betrayal and leave to posterity an example of such wickedness?
>
> “Certainly, if you think that I planned or wished such things, I shall have a hundred nobles whom you select in my kingdom—or more—swear to you that these accusations were falsely fabricated and invented against me. Let us return, I beseech you, dearest Father, let us return [Col. 1003B] to our former compact, and let no cause of discord be sown between us. Let the devices of false suspicions be far from us, and let the work of slanderers, together with their envy, perish among us. For what patron shall I have in Galicia, what counsellor, if the bishop of St James exercises hostility toward me? He ought to preside over Galicia on my behalf and uphold the rights of justice. If any discord arises among the dukes or princes of Galicia, he will call them back to peace. Him I embrace; him I venerate above all the bishops of my kingdom.”

To this the bishop replied:

> “Your most noble father, King A., embraced the Church of St James and its bishop with the greatest love, and how many and how great benefits he conferred upon it is sufficiently evident. But if you lend your mind to slanderers and do not accept the counsel of upright men, your kingdom will be scattered, each person will look to himself, and the path of fools will prevail. Fearing the assault of my enemies, [Col. 1003C] I go attended by armed force—not in rebellion against you, but to make my enemies’ teeth tremble.”

After this the bishop returned to his palace, attended by no small armed force. Then, with envoys sent by both sides two and three times, negotiations for peace took place and efforts were made to ensure that the bishop should not be hostile to the queen. The queen made a substantial compact with the bishop: setting aside every ground for suspicion, she would have the bishop as her patron and, as it were, lord, a man of such reverence and prudence. She also promised him the primacy of Galicia.

This compact further provided that the queen would not give her assent to slanderers, evil-speakers, or the bishop’s other enemies. The queen swore to the bishop that she would not violate this agreement and would fulfil it to the best of her power, as appears in what follows. Moreover, so that the agreement might be considered firmer and more indissoluble, the queen promised the aforesaid bishop twenty of the more powerful men of Galicia, León, Campania, and Castile, to be chosen by the bishop, who would swear the same oath. The bishop carefully stipulated this condition: if, before she left Galicia, the queen did not furnish ten chosen Galicians to swear, and likewise as many chosen men of León, Campania, and Castile by the appointed term, then [Col. 1004A] the aforesaid agreement should be dissolved and the queen considered guilty of perjury.

Once the oath of peace had been taken and the compact established between bishop and queen, the queen returned to Lugo. Certain of our canons went there for this purpose and received the oaths of some princes, because she had not fulfilled what she had promised. Later, when the queen had crossed the Pyrenees, the aforesaid bishop, mindful of his compact, sent his canons and knights to the queen to receive the oath of the selected princes of León, Campania, and Castile. But cursed is the land where a boy reigns and a woman holds supreme authority: a kingdom must be governed not by entreaties and blandishments but by laws and command. For which of the princes beyond the mountains did the queen not implore and summon by entreaty to confirm that agreement by oath? Yet soft measures suit the soft, harsh measures the harsh.

After the bishop had twice and three times sent envoys to the queen and had received neither the aforesaid guarantors by the appointed time nor afterward, he made known to the queen through messengers that the covenants of the said agreement were dissolved and would no longer be observed by him. [Col. 1004B] But no one can fully set forth how many and how great blandishments, or how many and how great promises, the queen then made to the bishop—unless he knows the inventions of women. She promised him many things through many different persons.

## CHAPTER CVIII. Concerning the discord between the queen and her son, the king.

At the same time and in the same circumstances great discord sprang up between the queen and her son King A. Count P. [Col. 1004C] Froylaz, together with no small part of the nobility of Spain, followed the boy while he was staying in Extremadura. This greatly troubled the queen, for she feared that, as he rose in this way, he might obtain the sceptre of the whole kingdom against her will; for there is no faith among partners in royal power.

### Concerning the peace compact between the bishop and the king

When the boy learned that the agreement which the queen had made with the aforesaid bishop had been dissolved, he sent envoys to the bishop with these words:

> “Most reverend Father and lord, I do not believe that your holiness is unaware that, at the death of my father, namely Count Raymond, my most noble grandfather King A., when I was still an infant, summoned the nobles of all Galicia to León and commanded them to render homage and swear an oath to me. Having received an oath from each of them, [Col. 1004D] he gave me lordship over all Galicia.
>
> “My grandfather, King Lord A., moreover, imposed this condition: if my mother the queen remained content with the bed of widowhood, the kingdom of all Galicia should be subject to your authority and to that of my uncle, the archbishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 1003D] He later became Pope Callixtus.]. But if she entered a marital union, the kingdom of Galicia should revert to me. This my mother herself and all the nobles of Galicia ratified by oath. I rejoice that you, most holy Father, were present. It is plain to the bleary-eyed and barbers alike” (Horace, *Satires* I.7.3) “that my mother has enjoyed the marriage bed. Therefore I now rightly demand the rights of my kingdom. If any of the Galician nobles seeks to take Galicia away from me, he unquestionably incurs the guilt of perjury; and may God, the righteous and mighty judge, judge between him and me.
>
> “But you, whom above all such men I embrace and venerate as my lord and patron—you who regenerated me at the font of baptism and, not long afterward, anointed me king in the church of St James, in whom the anchor of my confidence is placed—deign to give assistance [Col. 1005A] for the recovery of my kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 1005D] Above, ch. 66.]

Hearing this, the bishop, moved on the one hand by compassion and compelled on the other by justice, sought to choose the better course. He considered the woman’s unstable faith, her weak rule, and the kingdom already almost ruined, with truth and justice now far departed. [Col. 1005B] On the other hand, he weighed the boy’s tender age: a boy supported by the aid of few, seeking what was his own, not another’s; and he considered the Galicians, fickle and companions of fortune. If he whose duty it was to uphold justice should violently undertake to take justice away from the boy, a most just and deserved outcry would arise against him.

Having consulted his elders, he promised aid to the boy, lest he lose the kingdom which was his by right. Clergy and people proclaimed that the bishop was acting justly and mercifully and that the boy’s kingdom ought to return to him. The matter was publicly proclaimed—for this is the way of peoples: the one who is to come is always loved. With what longing was the boy’s arrival desired! Clergy and people favoured him, and he was blessed by all; they denounced the queen as despoiler of the kingdom and enemy of peace and justice.

But what shall I say of the ways of very many Galicians? [Col. 1005C] They are companions of fortune: raised up in prosperity, broken in adversity, driven by every light breeze. They consider it the height of freedom to change lords and rebel against their lords. They follow money, not justice; and for each person to possess only his own is, in their view, a crime. They are ready to whisper some novelty into the ears of the powerful, to slander and gnaw away at their lords and friends; the art of flattery is well known to them; they love perjury and betrayal. But I would have said this with due respect to the worthy Galicians. [Note: [Col. 1006D] See what was said in the prefatory no. 12.] Yet if I persisted in recounting such customs, time would fail me before material did.

## CHAPTER CIX. Concerning the discord between the bishop and the queen, and their reconciliation.

Meanwhile the aforesaid boy returned to Galicia from Extremadura with Count P. Froylaz, his tutor, and was honourably received by the aforesaid bishop at Iria. Then he came to Compostela amid the greatest rejoicing and gladness. When the boy king entered the city, the whole population came out to meet him with the greatest joy; greeting him, they congratulated him on his arrival according to Galician custom, as their lord. Indeed, all the men went forth armed to meet him, in order to render honour to the king. Then it was most pleasing to see the racing of swift-footed horses, [Col. 1006A] ranks of armed infantry, and dances of chanting women. Meanwhile the bishop went ahead to the church with the canons who were with him and prepared a procession for the approaching king. Why say more? The king was received reverently with procession and honoured by all.

When the queen learned that her son had come to Galicia and had been honourably received as king at Compostela by the bishop of St James and the other barons of the province, she was greatly distressed. Distrusting herself, she feared that she had wholly lost the kingdom of Galicia. Thereafter she hastened into Galicia, gathering about herself such nobles as she could obtain. She found Counts R. and M. almost already pressed into a corner, expecting themselves and their possessions to be ruined by the king. Having therefore assembled an army [Col. 1006B] on this side of Triacastela, the queen came to Melide with the aforesaid counts, her nobles, and certain persons who had already deserted the little king and attached themselves to the queen—as is the custom in Galicia.

Then she sent skilful envoys to the aforesaid bishop of St James with these words:

> “Reverend Father, although my wickedness and incompetence may deserve that I be deprived of the kingdom of Galicia and it be transferred to another, yet my sex should be spared. Let your fatherhood remember my most noble father King A., who raised you from your very youth and conferred upon you so many and such great benefits. I too, if you remember well, after I came into power through kingdom and riches, did not prove ungrateful to the honour of St James and to you. May it please your holiness not to take my kingdom from me.
>
> “If you complain that I did not fulfil the agreement between you and me, and that I was hostile to you, I shall make satisfaction as you yourself direct, provided that through you I do not lose my kingdom. For this purpose I shall grant to the Church of St James and to you the honour of Luparia with its castle, the honour of Ferraria with its castle, and Montana, that I may have you reconciled to me.”

To these words she added prayers and tears. But the bishop, shaken neither by prayers nor promises nor tears, declared that he would in no way depart from justice to the extent of his ability. [Col. 1006C] He called perjured any Galician noble who had sworn the kingdom of Galicia to the boy king, if he did not assist him to acquire and retain that kingdom.

[Col. 1006D] Yet, as I have said above, the Galicians, companions of fortune, came by night to the queen; those who had lately belonged to the boy king promised their aid to the queen. The citizens of Compostela too, whom the aforesaid bishop—knowing them to be such—had bound to himself by oath, secretly approached the queen. In a joint assembly of clergy and people they greeted her, called her their lady, promised to give her aid and the city of Compostela. Yet, to tell the truth, this was not done with the counsel of all the Compostelans. Certain citizens, in whom the leprosy of betrayal was naturally implanted, devised these things.

Meanwhile the citizens of Compostela came to the bishop—many with fraudulent intent, some perhaps with good intention—and earnestly entreated him [Col. 1007A] to compel the boy king and Countess M., wife of Count Peter, tutor of the king, to leave Compostela with their cavalry. If he did this, they unanimously asserted on oath that they would assist the bishop against all men, as their lord. Now the boy king and the aforesaid countess had fortified the towers and palaces of the bishop and the work of St James with no small troop of knights and with other necessary supplies. The Compostelans greatly feared this and therefore secretly devised certain plans.

Count Peter, moreover, was outside the city with a great army, intending to make war upon the queen. But when he learned that the support of Compostela was lacking and saw not a few knights flocking to the queen, he yielded. The aforesaid bishop, [Col. 1007B] acquiescing in the prayers of the canons and Compostelans, could scarcely obtain from the boy king that he should leave the city with his cavalry. When the king had thus left the city with the countess and his knights, while the bishop remained there with certain knights and his household, the Compostelans quickly sent word to the queen, without the bishop’s knowledge, to hasten to Compostela.

Nevertheless, certain Compostelans came to the bishop and urged him to conclude a peace compact with the queen. Others plotted that, when the queen entered the city, the bishop, as hostile and rebellious to her, should be expelled, deposed, and deprived of the honour of St James. Some of the citizens whom the bishop himself counted as familiar associates took part in these schemes. But, as Boethius says: “No pestilence is more effective in doing harm than an intimate enemy.”

[Col. 1007C] Meanwhile the queen, with a great army of cavalry and infantry, came to Compostela without the bishop’s knowledge. Some Compostelans went out to meet her, begging and entreating her to enter the city without delay. When this was disclosed to the bishop, the queen’s cavalry and infantry appeared on every side. He learned the loyalty of traitors and saw that neither assistance nor counsel was available to him. What was he to do? He saw that the citizens, except for a few, were hostile to him; and he perceived that those whom he had believed his helpers and wholly united with him were in fact most strongly opposed to him. Yet, steadfast in adversity, he ordered the towers and the work of St James fortified, so that at least there he might resist his enemies.

At last the queen entered Compostela. [Col. 1007D] Everything belonging to the bishop, wherever it could be found outside the towers and the church, was given over to plunder. The bishop and all who helped him were treated as rebels. The queen and the citizens threatened him; the army threatened him. From one day to the next it was said that they would assault and destroy him and all who were with him. Indeed, to tell the truth, I myself, because I was with him, was afraid, and would rather have been at Beauvais—though not in his absence. In short, I saw his friends become enemies, his intimates most hostile, and the people of Galicia opposed to him.

Meanwhile Count M., Fredenand John’s son, and certain nobles, at the queen’s request, went to the bishop, urging him at least now to make peace with the queen and enter into a [Col. 1008A] substantial peace compact with her. At one moment they threatened the bishop with war and capture; at another they brought prayers and promises. But internal enemies zealously strove to prevent the queen from making peace with the bishop and to deprive the bishop of his honour. O how ruinous is feigned friendship! What a deadly wound is internal hostility! Weapons from afar are more easily guarded against than those from near at hand.

At last the bishop, constrained by force and yielding to the counsel of his nobles and friends, when he saw his cause brought into a narrow pass and many friends and others withdrawn, communicated terms of peace to the queen’s envoys and delayed a peace compact no longer. Yet a serious difficulty disrupted everything. Fredenand Petrides, son of Count P. Froylaz, the king’s tutor, had, with the assistance of the aforesaid bishop, besieged the castle of Luparia, which belonged to the queen. [Col. 1008B] This Fredenand was a vassal of the aforesaid bishop; the bishop had given him in benefice Dubria, Ventosa, Viniones, and half the island of Laonia. Once discord had arisen between bishop and queen, Fredenand Petrides, supported by the bishop’s power, had invaded and laid waste all around the land of Salinas. Moreover, for nearly three months he had besieged the castle of Luparia and repeatedly assaulted it. Finally, unless the queen had hurried into Galicia, that castle was already compelled to surrender. This greatly distressed the queen. Accordingly, she was unwilling in any way to reconcile herself with the bishop unless he restored to her what Fredenand [Col. 1008C] had destroyed and carried off in the land of Salinas; for this reason the settlement between them was delayed.

## CHAPTER CX. Concerning Prior Peter, the bishop’s nephew, and his brother Gundesind, and the conspiracy at Compostela.

At last, by the counsel of the counts and princes, a peace compact was sanctioned between them and the former state of peace was restored. Meanwhile certain citizens more powerful than the rest—who, as I said above, bore ill will toward the bishop, though they had been unable to bring their earlier schemes to effect—when they saw their plans had collapsed, turned their minds to another course. Stirring up the people and conspiring against the bishop, they expelled from the city some of the bishop’s kinsmen: namely P., his nephew, canon and prior [Col. 1008D] of our Church, and Gundesind, his brother, with the queen’s consent. They said that through their counsel and instigation the bishop had withdrawn from the queen and thus discord had arisen in Galicia; further, that through G., who had been steward of the city, many evils had befallen the city.

After expelling them in order to diminish the bishop’s power, they formed, at the prompting of those whom I called the bishop’s internal enemies, a conspiracy [Note: [Col. 1007D] The conspiracy lasted a whole year, as we learn from ch. 113, §2.] which they called a *germanitas*, “brotherhood.” To confirm and strengthen this conspiracy, all bound themselves by oath: namely, that they would help one another against all men, unanimously look after and defend themselves, and, if anyone should suffer damage or injury from any powerful person or from another outside that conspiracy, the other accomplices would assist him to the best of their ability. [Col. 1009A] They added many other provisions, too lengthy for me to recount. But in plotting everything to the bishop’s harm and to break his power, they made Lady Queen U. and the abbess of that conspiracy. She afterward dealt with them according to their deserts and gave their accomplices a fitting recompense, as is recounted below.

## CHAPTER CXI. That the queen was besieged at Suberoso.

At that time the queen left Compostela and went to Torania [Note: [Col. 1009D] Alternatively, Toronia.]. There was Gumesi Nuniz, who favoured the boy king and rebelled against the queen, [Col. 1009B] powerful through the location and fortification of his castles and through his multitude of cavalry and infantry. When the queen wished there to besiege those who rebelled against her, she was herself besieged by them. Count P., the king’s tutor, and the Infanta Theresa, the queen’s sister and lady of all Portugal, besieged the queen in the castle of Suberoso with a great army. But the queen, having summoned her army, escaped and returned to Compostela.

On her return, certain citizens of Compostela met her, saying that the aforesaid bishop was the queen’s enemy and foe, had broken the agreement between them, and alleging other matters harmful to the bishop. But all these things had been fabricated and invented by the bishop’s internal enemies, so that they might now achieve what they had previously been unable to accomplish. When the queen returned to Compostela and saw that what had been reported to her [Col. 1009C] was false and invented, she regarded those men as idle tale-bearers and no longer wished to comply with them as if they were traitors. At last, after remaining a little while at Compostela, she returned to León.

### Concerning the conspiracies of Compostela

Meanwhile the aforesaid conspirators, having joined clergy and people to themselves, oppressed some and exalted others, as though for the protection of justice. They renewed laws and popular ordinances, assumed lordship over the whole city, destroyed palaces, and even threatened certain people with death. The bishop, content with the mere shadow of his title and yielding to circumstances, did not approve their actions and counsels, but neither did he condemn them. It was enough for him to be called lord and to be consulted by these conspirators in certain matters. [Col. 1009D] For outside the city he retained only his customary lordship; within the city, circumstances and the time did not permit him to exercise lordship. So strong had the conspiracy of the traitors become! If I wished to unfold their deeds and counsels, time would fail me before material did.

### Concerning the battle fought in the harbour of Macenaria.

At that same time Count P., the king’s tutor, together with his sons Vermudo and Fernando and his supporters, was troubling Compostela and making frequent assaults upon people and livestock. Now fortune favoured him; now he turned his back to arrows, as is the way of war. But how it befell him at the harbour of Machanaria, and how many men, horses, and weapons he lost, would take long to relate. [Col. 1010A] For the aforesaid bishop, who in time of peace devoted himself to ecclesiastical affairs, when he saw his city and its surrounding districts being disturbed and plundered, judged it worthwhile to defend the honour of Blessed James by arms.

How difficult it is to guard oneself against enemies both within and without! The bishop had continually to restrain the audacity of external enemies and guard against the snares of his own household. But I shall pass these over in silence: the men through whose hands the bishop’s plans and business were conducted, and by whom he was betrayed. For the bishop had selected certain men of the city whom he himself had reared from their cradles, together with other closest associates, intimate to his heart and to his counsels. Yet whatever they could draw from him, they poured out to everyone. For they were “full of cracks” [HORACE], and were preparing a trap for their lord. They added falsehoods to truths; and, in order to stir clergy and people to hatred of the bishop, they declared that the bishop bore infinite hatred toward clergy and people.

O wickedness! Those whom the bishop had brought up from their cradles, enriched with benefices and honours, loved with a father’s affection, and made his most intimate confidants—these men most earnestly desired his destruction. Yet the bishop, because he knew the character of certain Galicians, had bound them to himself by oath. But it is written: “Let the one who does wrong continue to do wrong, and let the filthy continue to be filthy, and let the holy be made holy” (Rev. 22). Why should I linger over these matters? The outcome proves the deeds.

Meanwhile the aforesaid traitors repeatedly sent embassies to the queen, saying that the bishop was [Col. 1010C] deceitful, hostile to the queen, attached to the queen’s enemies, and an oppressor of her friends. The bishop, however, though he foresaw no small part of their conduct, was benevolent toward all, gracious to all, a comforter of those who had fallen, and, insofar as he could, a helper of the poor. Within himself he said: “I will bear the wrath of God, which I have deserved, until He vindicates my cause.”

### On the flight of Count P. and the acts of the conspirators

About that time the aforesaid Count P. was proceeding with his cavalry to one of his castles, namely Saint John of Pena Cornaria, passing through the borders of the land of Blessed James. When this became known to the bishop, he summoned his army, pursued the count, and forced him to flee through the mountains of Deza. The bishop indeed struck external enemies with a twofold sword, spiritual and material, and was wholly intent upon defending his country—truly courageous in adversity.

To say nothing further, the enemies and plunderers of the city and province of Saint James were daily struck with the spiritual sword in the church of that apostle; this greatly weakened their spirits. Thus and thus the bishop, triumphing over his enemies, strove both to protect his own people and to overcome his adversaries. Yet he was regarded with suspicion by the traitors of Compostela. For since the bishop loved the boy-king with such affection, and such friendship had existed between the bishop and Count Peter, men could scarcely believe that the bishop was truly opposed to the king and the count.

Therefore the bishop, not pursuing hatred against them, but protecting his own and defending the queen’s party, oppressed the enemies more vigorously. Yet this did not bring him praise from the traitors. Whatever prudence he possessed, whatever good he did, they secretly distorted in the manner of the populace. At that time the bishop’s party in the city of Compostela was so diminished by the accomplices of treachery that it had no power either to command or to order.

Certain members of the bishop’s household, who were also traitors, daily summoned clergy and people to assembly in the bishop’s absence; they handled laws and judgments, and weakened the bishop’s party as far as they could, saying that they were striving for liberty. They drew some to themselves by oath, others by gifts, and others by threats. Moreover, they either diminished the bishop’s rights or retained them for themselves. [Col. 1011B] Alas, wretches! They had wholly forgotten the oath which twice or three times they had sworn to the bishop, pledging fidelity and homage.

But if anyone happened to favour the bishop’s party, he had either to hide or impose silence upon his mouth. For, by the contrivances of the traitors and their promises, nearly the whole multitude of clergy and people had been divided from the bishop. The bishop, in his own palace as though in hiding, dared neither to oppose their enactments nor, if they asked anything of him, to resist their petition. He ate his bread in silence; what was set upon his table was first bought in the market by his servants. Scarcely anyone would serve him; scarcely anyone would accompany him. Believe one who experienced it: I saw and testify that the bishop’s vessels and clothes were often pawned for food. He had almost no rights and no household service in the city. The accomplices of treachery possessed everything and commanded everyone.

One day, when clergy and people had been called into assembly, one of his traitors delivered a speech to the people in his customary fashion, and stirred them all so strongly against the bishop that the bishop’s palaces were almost razed to the ground; part of those palaces had already been destroyed. By the arguments of those accomplices, this same most wicked man demanded from the bishop, through the people’s violence, an office and ecclesiastical dignity; the bishop wholly refused. For it was unjust that one whom the people, by violence and against the bishop’s will, had made should be honoured in the Church of God.

But when the bishop learned that, unless he made him honoured, either his palaces would be destroyed down to their foundations or perhaps graver things would be done against himself, then, being excessively compelled by the people of the city, he called the wiser and more eminent persons of the Church. Taking their advice, he yielded for the time being. He therefore granted the ecclesiastical dignity—not to that man, but to those mediators—on condition that he should receive it back from them whenever he wished. The man was made not honoured but dishonoured; a slight tower easily falls when it has been founded upon sand.

O abominable treachery of Galicia! Those whom the bishop regarded as closest to his heart, who ate with him at one table, were striving with all their heart for his uprooting.

## CHAPTER 112. How the queen gave the head of Blessed James to the bishop

[Col. 1012A]

At that time the bishop, seeing Galicia on one side defiled by the pestilential disease of traitors, and on the other destroyed by the storm of discord, resolved to visit the queen. Popular opinion then held that the bishop did not dare to approach the queen, nor even to leave Compostela. Therefore, setting out, the bishop visited the queen at Campania. Contrary to some people’s expectation, she received him attentively and honourably.

The people of Galicia said that the queen would seize and imprison this bishop if she could take him. But the event was altogether otherwise. The queen both received him honourably and thereafter regarded him as her truest protector. For in him lay the anchor of the entire kingdom of Galicia, as was by no means hidden from the queen.

When the queen learned from the bishop the state of all Galicia and the continual disturbances of war caused by her son, she took counsel with her princes and discovered that every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste. Peter, prior of the church of Saint James and nephew of the aforesaid bishop, having been expelled from the city of Compostela by the traitors, was most carefully received by the queen for the bishop’s sake.

After they had come to León, the queen honoured the aforesaid bishop with a most precious gift: namely, the head of James the Apostle. Let us relate the history of this matter more fully.

### On the discovery of the head of James

Maurice, bishop of Coimbra, later archbishop of Braga, now Pope Gilbert [Col. 1012C], had long ago gone to Jerusalem and remained there for a considerable time. He was building a certain church near Jerusalem. While he stayed there, an old man who lived near that place began frequently to visit him. Maurice questioned him about various things, for he was a native of that place.

At last Maurice asked him why the little church in which the old man lived was held in such reverence among the inhabitants. The old priest replied, as he had received the tradition from his predecessors, that the head of Blessed James the Apostle was in that church. When Bishop Maurice heard this, he began more often to summon the old man to himself, to win him over with words, and by gifts to make him his friend and familiar; then he investigated the matter more carefully, such being the cunning of men.

[Note: “Now” indicates that the author wrote this between 1118 and 1121, when Burdinus was captured, as we read below at [Col. 1012D], chapter 41. He was called not Gilbert but Gregory by his followers.]

[Col. 1012D] The bishop also began to frequent and venerate that little church, and often to attend its vigils. But when he saw that his devices made no progress—for guards were continually present there—he directed his mind to another course. He summoned those of his clerics whom he knew to be more faithful and more ready for such a task, and disclosed to them his intention.

Having taken their advice, two of them deliberately began to feign sickness and fever; carrying lamps and candles, they frequently visited that church and spent the night there. At length, on a suitable night, when the others were absent and the door of the church was shut, they attacked the altar with mattocks, which they had secretly brought with them. Digging deep beneath the altar, as they had heard, they found an ivory vessel, and inside it another, of silver, full of relics. Taking it, they departed by night with the bishop and fled to the holy city of Jerusalem.

At dawn a certain hermit saw them passing along the road, called them to himself, and said:

> “I know indeed, dearest brothers, what you are carrying and what precious treasure you have stolen. Go: may the grace of God accompany you. For where the body of this apostle is, there too must be his head.”

When Bishop Maurice heard this, he understood that what he had done had been revealed by the Holy Spirit to the servant of God. Yet he feared that rumour of the matter would swiftly spread everywhere; and as soon as he could, he crossed the sea. At length, when he came to Spain, he reverently placed those relics at Carrión, in the church of Saint Zoilus. For he saw Spain disturbed by the continual tumult of discord, and feared that by some chance he might be deprived of so great a treasure.

[Note: The head brought by Maurice, bishop of Coimbra, is not that of the apostle whose body is buried at Compostela, but that of James the son of Alphaeus, bishop of the people of Jerusalem. See the preceding volume, in the Life of this prelate, no. 80.]

After a considerable period had passed, Queen U. was received at Carrión and the king of Aragon was expelled. When she learned that the head of Blessed James, which Bishop Maurice had brought from Jerusalem, was in the church of Saint Zoilus, she ordered it, together with the other relics, removed from there. She carried it to León and placed it in the church of Saint Isidore. Thus she gave to the aforesaid bishop of Saint James this great treasure: namely, the head of Blessed James, a fragment of the Lord’s tomb, a certain bone of Saint Stephen, the other relics, and the silver vessel.

### How the bishop brought to Compostela the head of Blessed James given him by the queen

[Col. 1013C] Among her other affairs, the queen most earnestly requested the bishop’s wisdom to labour at reconciling her little son, the king, to her. This did not displease the bishop. For he knew that Spain could not have peace so long as discord remained between the queen and her son.

The queen also sent envoys to the people of Compostela, both clergy and laity, and commanded them to honour and love their bishop and not to take from him the rights or authority of his city. She also ordered them to restore to his former honour the bishop’s nephew P., prior of the church of Blessed James.

At length the bishop returned to his homeland in Galicia, bringing with him the precious treasure. When he reached the settlement called Ferriarios, [Col. 1013D] he sent messengers ahead to Compostela to announce his arrival and report the queen’s precious gifts which the bishop was bringing with him. This greatly displeased the accomplices of the aforesaid treachery. For they had supposed that the queen would neither receive nor love the bishop, nor honour him with such a precious gift; indeed, they expected worse things. The contrary happened beyond their expectation.

When the bishop arrived at Mount of Joy, that is, at the Humiliatorium, the clergy and people of the whole city came to meet him and, with the greatest joy, venerated the precious treasure. The bishop himself entered Compostela barefoot, chanting psalms with the canons. [Col. 1014A] O what shame for clergy and people! I myself, returning with the bishop, burst into tears from excessive joy. Yet some took it ill, because it contributed to the bishop’s praise and honour.

The prior of the church entered the city with the bishop and the rejoicing crowds. From the promontory of Mount of Joy to the church of Blessed James, the procession both preceded and followed. At last the bishop entered the apostolic church and, taking that precious treasure in his hands, offered it upon the altar of Blessed James. After Mass had been celebrated according to custom, and rejoicings and praises of God had been solemnly completed—for it was Sunday—he returned to his palace.

On the following day, after clergy and people had been summoned, the queen’s commands and the other matters pertaining to the affair were publicly reported. Yet the aforesaid accomplices continued no less to desire the bishop’s destruction.

## CHAPTER 113. On the reconciliation of the queen and her son

Not long afterwards, the aforesaid bishop summoned the boy-king, the queen’s son, and Count P., his tutor, to a conference. With them he dealt concerning the reconciliation of mother and son, determining how a true reconciliation should be made between them, how much of the kingdom each should hold, and what pledges of genuine reconciliation should exist between them.

When these matters had been discussed and settled, the bishop left Compostela and set out for the queen with the envoys of the boy-king: namely Fernando Pérez, Count Gutierre, and the others who supported the king’s party. He explained to the queen what he had discussed with her son concerning their reconciliation and true peace between them. Hearing this, the queen rejoiced exceedingly and gave the bishop profound thanks. For reconciliation between the queen and her son could not be achieved through another; and unless it were achieved, the kingdom of Spain and Galicia would be lost.

O with what boundless hatred the wicked regard the good! What a man of great skill, able to restore so great and such a peace! The bishop was hated by many because he strove for peace, because he laboured to restore peace to the kingdom of Spain, now almost lost.

Therefore the queen summoned to Saint Facundus the neighbouring bishops concerning this business: namely, the bishops of León, Astorga, Oviedo, Mondoñedo, and the bishop of Granada, who was present; also Counts Pedro González, Munio Peláez, Count Suero, and the other princes, too numerous to list. Having taken their counsel, a treaty of reconciliation between the boy and his mother was settled.

Pedro González, consul of Castile, was sent with the bishop of Saint James and the other envoys to the boy-king, to be witnesses of the agreement determined and guarantors of so great a treaty. When they had reached Galicia, the aforesaid bishop of Saint James approached the boy-king with the aforementioned envoys on the bank of the Tambre. He reported to him his mother’s words; [Col. 1015A] he also reported how affectionately his mother loved him, that she assigned to him all her kingdom, what treaty of reconciliation she wished to enter into with him—as a mother with her son—and that she wished to provide witnesses and oath-takers for this treaty.

He was believed, as so great a protector who always strove for peace was worthy of belief, as were the other envoys. Treaties of reconciliation were made, and the agreement of this concord was confirmed by oath. Oath-takers were provided on both sides: thirty on this side and thirty on the other, the best men found in Galicia or Campania. They swore a most firm covenant of fidelity, friendship, and mutual assistance between the queen and her son for three years. It was also determined how much of the kingdom the queen was to hold for herself and how much the boy was to hold as his own; and that they should help one another according to their ability, as either might need.

Finally, after the treaty of peace had been established and confirmed by oath, the envoys returned to the queen and reported what they had done with her son. Spain rejoiced at the reconciliation of mother and son and welcomed the coming peace. In hope of peace, bishops, consuls, princes, knights, citizens, and peasants rejoiced; they believed that they would now recover what they had lost after the death of King A.

All desire King A., though he is a boy, and earnestly wish him to reign in the place of his grandfather and father, so that he may imitate the paths of peace and justice of the most noble King A. and Count Raymond. They curse the king of Aragon and promise that they will be hostile to him if they have this King A.

2. After no small part of spring had passed, [Col. 1015C] the queen came to Galicia on account of her son. For unless she herself had been present, the aforesaid treaties of reconciliation could in no way have been consummated, nor could she have led the Galicians on campaign except with her son.

[Note: Since, as is immediately said here, the tyrannical domination of the Compostelans endured for a whole year and had arisen in the preceding year, 1116, the following detestable rebellion is rightly assigned to 1117. The events related after it belong to 1118, as will appear below.]

When the queen entered Compostela, terror struck the traitors. For throughout the whole year they had plotted the bishop’s ruin, though he strove for peace. They had deprived him of the rights and authority of the city; they had not obeyed the queen’s commands as far as they were able; they had inflicted no slight injuries upon the princes and knights of Galicia; and they had acted like kings—uprooting, destroying, renewing, and exalting—as is the custom of servants and peasants after power to rule is given them. Because they had done all these things with impunity and without permission, they feared that they would not escape punishment.

But when they saw the queen and her son reconciled, and the aforesaid bishop held by them in the highest honour and affection, they bore it more bitterly and lost confidence in themselves. They took counsel as to what they should do or devise if the queen or bishop should wish to harm them, or seek redress from them for injuries caused by their misdeeds and for so many and such great wrongs. They had no hope or confidence except in their treachery. They ran about, consulted, renewed walls and fortifications, and aroused in the queen and her son, who was now with her, suspicion that they intended rebellion.

Alas, wretches! They undertake things beyond their strength and will fall from on high. The bishop and the queen then, together with her son and the princes of all Galicia, endured them and, as though unaware of the designs of so great a treachery, concealed their awareness.

## CHAPTER 114. On the attack of the conspirators upon the bishop and the queen, the burning of the church, and other events

Meanwhile the queen went to Luparia and, returning thence, was received by the bishop at Iria. Afterwards she returned to Compostela with a great army of knights. For the queen had taken counsel with the bishop, her son, and the nobles of Galicia as to how she might avenge the injuries of the traitors of Compostela and curb their arrogance. For this purpose she had assembled no small companies of armed men. One part of them was to enter Compostela with her and the bishop, as had been arranged; another was to remain outside the city with her son. When the people of Compostela observed this, they were greatly afraid.

For they were conscious of guilt and saw that their dominion was already tottering. At last they saw themselves and their possessions placed in distress, and too late repented of what they had done. Why say more? The utterly lost companions of Judas: some fled to the church of Saint James, others to other churches, and others hid in their hiding places. One man, who was among the leaders of the treachery, deceitfully assumed a monastic habit so that the abbot and other monks might save him in the church of Saint Martin from danger of death; thus, as a monk, he escaped the queen’s wrath.

While the rest remained in the church of Saint James, the queen summoned the bishop and said:

> “Reverend Father, may it please your holiness that these most dishonourable traitors be removed from the church and repaid according to their deserts. Let so great a stench of treachery be removed from the church, and let this filthy dungheap be cast out from it.”

To this the bishop replied:

> “Queen, it is not lawful to remove from the church anyone who has taken refuge there—whether thief, perjurer, traitor, or criminal. Yet all their property outside the church may become plunder and be seized by our people.”

The queen said:

> “If the church gives them protection and they are secure in it, why do they retain arms in the church, when through the church they are protected and defended? Why do they arm and fortify themselves with other weapons? It is unfitting that those held sufficiently safe in the church should adopt any protection besides the church. I order this forbidden: either let them lay down their arms and be safely kept in the church as is fitting, or let an equal or greater number of our own armed men remain in the church with those armed men, lest they dare to do anything insane.”

The bishop and the others present approved the queen’s counsel, and it was forbidden that weapons should be borne in the church. When this became known to those traitors, they raged. Pursuing through the church the messengers of the bishop and queen, who had told them to lay down their arms in the church, they began hostilities. The envoys fled to the higher parts of the church. The criminal traitors raised war-cries; the clamour reached the ears of all; the traitors’ rebellious spirit broke forth, and they revealed what they had long plotted.

The whole city resounded. Men ran to arms and hurried to battle. Rumour, than which no evil is swifter [VIRGIL, *Aeneid* IV.173], reported that the bishop’s and queen’s soldiers had attacked the Compostelans. A few persons, both canons and citizens, remained outside this abominable madness and wished to restrain the enormous audacity of their frenzied kinsmen. But what could a few do against so many thousands?

The accomplices of treachery rushed to battle and, summoning their acquaintances and friends, wished to destroy the bishop and queen, because they had wished to destroy them. When the bishop and queen, in the bishop’s palace, heard the city’s cries and tumult and learned how the companions of Iscariot had incited the city against them, they were afraid. For they saw the traitors’ audacity increasing, war being stirred up more boldly, the church of Blessed James and the bishop’s palace besieged by armed hands, and attacked more fiercely.

They did not know what counsel to adopt against such abominable attacks. The apostolic church was assaulted by repeated attacks; stones, arrows, and missiles flew over the altar, and the traitors waged their wicked battle. What would those criminal hands not dare? The most abandoned attackers set fire to the church of Blessed James and burned it on both sides. For no small part of the church was roofed with tamarisk and boards.

O wickedness! A church so venerable and worthy of the apostle was burned, and no honour was rendered to so precious a patron. O grief! The flames of the apostolic church rose high and offered a dreadful spectacle on every side. All who stood by—men and women fearing God—wept and lamented, cursing the perpetrators of so great a crime. How great was the mourning of pilgrims who had come from different regions to the apostle’s body!

When the bishop and queen saw the burning of the church and the aforesaid accomplices, with such a multitude ready for every crime, they did not dare trust themselves to the bishop’s palace. They fled with their company to the bell-tower. The Compostelans, however, climbed to the upper parts of the apostolic church and entered the bishop’s palace. They ran, seized, and threw down things. Clothes, gold and silver vessels, and everything belonging to bishop and queen were taken, plundered, and made booty for the wicked enemies.

The Compostelans climbed the church of Blessed James and the tower of the bishop’s palace, preparing to attack the bell-tower, in which the bishop was with his companions and soldiers and the queen with hers. Some attacked from atop the church, some from the towers, and some, gathered on the ground around it, attacked that tower. They cast stones and arrows at the bishop, queen, and their companions, and threatened them with death.

But those in the tower with bishop and queen protected themselves no less vigorously, given their position and their inferior numbers, and returned the blows of battle. Here the fighting lasted for some time. Finally, seeing so few men resisting so great a multitude and exchanging blows with them, the Compostelans rushed together to bring fire. Linking their shields over their heads, they sent fire through a window in the lower part of the tower. Having applied fire, they also fed it. Why linger longer? A fire was kindled within the tower and attacked those inside it.

When the bishop saw that neither he nor the queen was spared and that so great a multitude thirsted for their death, he addressed the queen and those within:

> “Dearest brothers, we are now surrounded by the impious hand of criminals; now confined in a narrow place, we have no refuge. God alone, who is the refuge of the oppressed and the consolation of the sorrowful, is our refuge and consolation. Let us place our hope and trust in God, who can rescue us from the hands of the wicked and deliver us from so great a peril. For He delivered Daniel from the lions’ den; He delivered the three youths, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, from the burning fiery furnace. Let us turn to the Lord with all our heart, and He will turn to us. For He says: ‘Turn to me, and I will turn to you’ (Zech. 1:3). Let us repent of our iniquities and sins. Let us confess our sins to one another and pray for one another that we may be saved. Let us call upon God’s mercy, that He may forgive us our sins and deign to grant us His mercy, He who lives for ever and ever.”

At this the queen and all present burst into tears and made confession to the bishop.

[Col. 1018C] Then the queen, turning to the bishop, said:

> “Go out, Father, go out from this fire, so that I may dare to go out with you. They will spare you as their protector, their bishop, their lord.”

Then the bishop said:

> “This is not sound counsel. They hold me and my companions as enemies and especially thirst for our death.”

But those outside cried:

> “If the queen wishes, let her leave. To her alone we grant permission to depart and the possibility of life. Let the rest perish by arms and fire.”

When she heard this, as the fire within was now gaining strength, the queen, compelled by the bishop and having received from them a pledge of safety, left the tower. When the rest of the mob saw her come out, they rushed upon her, seized her, and threw her to the ground in filth. Like wolves they dragged her about and tore her clothes; her body was stripped from the breasts downward, and before everyone she lay long upon the ground in dishonour. Many also wished to stone her to death. Among them an old woman of Compostela struck her severely on the jaw with a stone.

Meanwhile, as the bishop prayed inside and the fire rose higher, the abbot of Saint Martin came to him carrying a certain crucifix, which he gave him. Receiving it, the bishop made his confession and, as if about to go forth to martyrdom, left the tower. Having cast off his pallium and received from someone a very poor cloak—marvellous thing!—he set the crucifix before his face. Through the battle-lines of combatants, the ranks of his bitterest enemies, and the weapons of more than three thousand criminal traitors, he passed, recognized by only one person.

[Col. 1019A] Then he came to the place where the queen lay in filth, trampled by the rushing mob. Seeing her so shamefully stripped and thrown down, he was pierced by extreme sorrow and passed on. Passing through the church of Blessed James, he reached the church of Saint Mary with a certain canon, Michael González, who later stood by him in adversity. Then he received the body and blood of the Lord and rested there more securely.

Meanwhile certain canons came there, having learned of his departure, as though to investigate whether the bishop had escaped the danger of fire and armed men or had remained in the tower to perish. But the bishop, having experienced others’ treachery, begged the aforesaid Michael and others who seemed to be guarding him near the altar to remove them from there. Since they could not be driven away before the bishop’s safety and escape had been disclosed, they swore that they would reveal nothing to anyone about the bishop’s welfare. Thus it was disclosed to them what had happened to the bishop and how; and they departed.

At length the queen, her hair torn, her body stripped, and herself thrown into mud, escaped and reached the same church in which the bishop was hiding, though she knew nothing of the bishop.

Those who remained in the tower, when they saw that the force of the fire had overcome the tower’s height, partly threw themselves down from above and thus escaped; others burst into the midst of the armed ranks. Peter, prior of the church of Blessed James—whom we mentioned above, the bishop’s nephew—leapt among the armed men and escaped by his agility; so did many others.

Gundesind Gelmírez, the bishop’s brother, leapt into the midst and was pierced by lances and swords. Roderic Oduariz, the bishop’s major-domo; Rademir, his steward; and Didacus Strabo, the city’s reeve, were killed there. Others, wounded, stripped, and half-dead, escaped.

A secret order from the bishop was conveyed through an envoy to the queen, sitting in the church of Saint Mary, that the bishop had escaped the fire and was hiding in that same church. When she learned this, although she mourned her own disgrace and suffering, she nevertheless rejoiced greatly at the bishop’s escape. But she feared that it might become known to the persecutors, and therefore concealed the cause of her joy.

After this the people of Compostela assembled around the queen in the church of Blessed Mary. Pretending to rejoice at her safety, they attended her and filled the church with armed bands for her protection. Fearing these groups both for herself and lest anything about the bishop’s presence become known to them, the queen addressed them thus:

> “Go, most wicked men; go, most criminal men; go, utterly lost men, to the tower in which your bishop is perishing by arms and fire. Remove him from danger as quickly as you can, lest you be held by posterity to be an example of such great wickedness and infamy. Go, I say, rebels and faithless men, and prevent so great a crime from being done.”

She said this in order to remove them, lest they suspect anything about the bishop. At these words the crowds who had gathered departed and went as far as the tower. They drove back the armed men still attacking the tower and feeding the fire. With one voice they called for water and threw it inside; they extinguished the fire as much as they could and strove to save the bishop.

Some of the canons, widows and orphans, the poor, and no small number of citizens wept for the bishop. But the fire had become so fierce in the tower that, had the bishop still been there, he would have been reduced to ashes. The tower itself, its beams, and its flooring were burned. The bells, made from fifteen hundred pounds of bronze, were burned and collapsed.

After the aforesaid queen had by this stratagem diverted the assaults of the people from the church of St Mary, she herself departed, fleeing to the church of St Martin, that she might be safer there. The bishop, meanwhile, secretly and stealthily leaving the church of St Mary because of the crowd and attacks of the people, accompanied by the aforesaid Michael and two Frenchmen, crossed over walls and rooftops and entered, through a window, the house of a certain man named Maurinus, the others entering with him. In a corner of this house the bishop lay concealed with the aforesaid companions, covered with cloths and other such things. While he was hiding there, behold, four armed men of the traitors’ party came seeking him and said: “Who is hiding here? What is happening here? Have you seen the man whom we seek—that is, the bishop?” At this the bishop and Michael concealed themselves amid a mass of cloths and garments; for, had they not hidden, the bishop would immediately have been pierced through by their weapons. When these men arrived, however, the two Frenchmen stood up, saying that they had returned from the tumults of war and were resting there, wearied by such exertion. The mistress of the same house was also present. Knowing that the bishop was concealed there, she loudly rebuked the men as invaders and spies upon her house, and compelled them to leave. The two aforesaid Frenchmen went out with them as well, that they might remove them more quickly and shield their bishop.

How great was the ineffable mercy of almighty God, who delivered the bishop from the aforesaid danger and snatched him from the very hands of these most wicked men! Once they had gone, Gundisalvus, the son-in-law of the aforesaid woman, came and said: “Father and lord, flee from here and hide yourself as quickly as possible. Behold, the accursed band of traitors—stained with the blood of others and still thirsting for yours—is seeking you everywhere. I saw them hurrying here with swords and clubs. Go quickly, and delay no longer. God is able to deliver you from the hands of the wicked, from their gaping jaws.” At these words the bishop arose; and, after the floor of the adjoining house had been broken through by Gundisalvus, then that of another, and then of a third, he reached the house of Froyla Rodesindiz, which stood in the middle of the city. The mistress of the house began to cry out that invaders were destroying and entering her home. Michael answered that a certain acquaintance and friend of her husband, named Froyla Menindiz, the queen’s steward, had escaped the internal sedition and tumults of war and had fled to this house.

Not long afterward the master of the house arrived, namely Froyla Rodesindiz. When he learned that the bishop was there, he ran to him and said through tears: “Thanks be to God, dearest Father, who delivered you from so great a peril and caused you to come here unharmed.
