Yet the attack of the enemies must be feared, lest, running hither and thither, they find and kill you; for they are ready for every crime. Come with me, then.” And he led him, with Michael, down into a very dark storeroom; there they long gave way to tears.

Meanwhile, the aforesaid Frenchmen prepared four very swift horses for the bishop, so that, when the sun had declined, he might cross to the other side of the street and then, by way of the fields of St Martin, he, Michael, and the others might mount them and flee. But the event turned out very differently. When these preparations had been made, P., abbot of St Pelagius, arrived with one of his monks, Pelagius Didacide; likewise P., prior of the canons and nephew of the bishop himself. They said: “We come to you, sent by the clergy and people of the whole city. They repent of having acted badly toward you; they love you as their lord, their bishop, and are ready to make satisfaction to you. A thousand or five hundred, clergy and laity alike, await you in the cloister of St Pelagius, ready on behalf of all the others to swear to you an oath of love and fidelity; and they request your presence. Leave these hiding places, therefore, and come to them, reconciled. Never have you had them more subject to you than today, if you comply with us.”

But the traitors had fabricated all this, in order that through these messengers they might at least thus deceive the bishop into being found, and, once found, destroy him. When the bishop was urged by these messengers to come out, and was strongly pressed by them, he recognized beforehand the deceit and contrivance of the traitors and said to the messengers: “Go to those thousand or five hundred whom you mention, and report to them that I am sound and unharmed. Tell no one where I am. If matters are as you report, let only one hundred of them, on behalf of all the rest, make the oath you describe. I shall come to them tomorrow.” O how great was the man’s prudence, by which, through God’s grace, he foresaw what, and in what manner, those wicked men had devised! The aforesaid messengers departed, but found no one to ratify what had been promised. Then at last the fabrication of deceit and treachery became clear to them: if the bishop had complied, he would unexpectedly, through their plan, have fallen into the hands of his enemies and perhaps been killed by them. The aforesaid prior, recognizing their deceit and treachery, was astonished and terrified; he remained safely there in the church.

The abbot, however, returned to the bishop with the aforesaid monk and reported the traitors’ fraud and falsehood, and that the bishop had prudently perceived their schemes. Then, once twilight had already fallen, the abbot and the aforesaid monk secretly brought the bishop with Michael to their church, namely the church of St Pelagius, and led him into that church’s treasury, without the other monks’ knowledge, except that of the treasurer. After this the abbot addressed the bishop: “Take courage, Father, and be strong. Take food, that you may be refreshed”—for the bishop was still fasting. To this the bishop replied: “It is not fitting,” he said, “that I break my fast when tomorrow I am to die fighting at the hands of my enemies. The compassion and mercy of God alone, which delivered me today from so many and such great dangers, will also act tomorrow, if he wills.” Yet, yielding to the abbot’s earnest entreaties, he tasted a little bread and wine, and thus rested. It is clearer than daylight that that night the bishop did not yield his limbs to deep sleep, but found consolation in psalms and prayers. When the monks rose for Matins, he too rose; through a window in that treasury he heard the monks’ morning office.

At length, when day dawned—it was Sunday—all the accomplices in the treachery assembled in the house of the canons, having summoned clergy and people, partly by threats, partly by gifts. They believed that the conspiracy of their wickedness would succeed, and they exercised authority over all things as though they were kings. At their head was a certain impious and very wicked man, who had remained at Compostela throughout the period of the treachery and, as chief of the traitorous accomplices, had urged very many into the conspiracy. He embraced in hope the lordship of the church of St James, and with all his heart longed for it. Indeed, the servants had already divided the whole estate or honour of St James among themselves, and had determined what and how much each should possess.

After they had assembled in the canonical house, the aforesaid wicked man urged them in many words to preserve fraternity among themselves and maintain it firmly; to be of one mind; to fortify their city with wall and rampart; and to drive out whatever enemies might still remain among them. They also resolved to reconcile the queen to themselves and, after making satisfaction to her for the public disgrace and injury inflicted upon her, to enter into a covenant of most secure peace with her. They sent men to the queen, who was hiding from fear of them in the church of St Martin, to settle these matters with her; first, however, they were to ask whether the bishop had escaped, where he was hiding, and what course regarding him pleased the clergy and people.

Then a certain man arose among them, one loved and reared by the bishop, in whom the bishop had placed great confidence, and declared these words to all: “Until now, brothers, we have had over us a lord and bishop whom henceforth it is not fitting that he should rule over us or be our bishop. For he has diminished the dignity of your church and grievously oppressed you beneath the yoke of his lordship. Moreover, lest any one of you demand him as lord or bishop, I confess before God and St James and before you that henceforth he shall be neither my lord nor my bishop. For I am ready to prove that these things have justly happened to him, and that he ought to be deprived of every honour that he possessed.”

The aforesaid bishop had reared this utterly wicked man from childhood in his palace, had made him honoured in the church of St James, and, when he had grown up, had sent him to France to study grammar, providing him with no small sum of money. Afterward, when he returned, the bishop had made him his most intimate and beloved familiar and, loving him with a father’s affection as though he were lord of his own household, had also given him substantial sums of money. Although he had received scarcely any service from him, he had granted him a good benefice: namely Asnoios, half of Sarantes, Ceia, half of St Christina of Noia, and many other things. O most ruinous faithlessness of Galicia! The bishop had reared, loved, and enriched with honours and benefices this utterly wicked man as a son; yet he, as though forgetful of all this and returning evil for good, thirsted for the bishop’s ruin and death.

When he had finished the aforesaid proclamation, a party of clergy and people, imbued with the same poison, praised his words and judged that matters ought to be no otherwise. Those who had not shared in that treachery or conspired against either bishop or queen, and who hated such counsels, although such great wickedness displeased them and although they thought differently concerning the bishop and all the rest, nevertheless did not dare either to contradict or even to mutter. For if, among so many accomplices of Judas, they had presumed to say or do anything other than what the traitors wished, their houses would immediately have been demolished, their property would have gone as plunder, and they themselves perhaps would have been buried beneath a heap of stones. “For,” as Solomon says, “there is a time to speak, and a time to be silent” (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

Then those most wicked traitors, after taking counsel with their accomplices and being wholly filled with evil, cleverly and artfully sent to the queen, Lady U., utterly depraved envoys in this conspiracy and treachery. They addressed her as follows: “We confess, O queen, that in the violence of anger we inflicted dishonour and disgrace upon you, and that we dared what ought not have been dared against the church of St James and against you. We deeply repent of this; therefore we have come to make satisfaction to you on our own behalf and on behalf of our other companions. Forgive us, then, and we shall restore all that is yours to you. We also wish you to have peace with us and that the surest oaths of reconciliation be made between us.”

When the queen heard this—she had feared their coming like a lamb among wolves—she was rightly and shrewdly delighted, and most graciously gave them a feigned answer: “What you say greatly pleases me; and whatever offence you have committed against me, so far as it concerns me, is forgiven you. It pleases me that covenants of peace be made between you and me, and that former evils be remembered no more.”

Then the messengers added: “Peace and concord between us will readily be achieved hereafter, but we make one exception: namely, we do not wish to have D. as bishop, and we are altogether hostile to him, for he has hitherto oppressed us and reduced the dignity of our church and city to nothing. Therefore we all hate him, and do not wish him to reign over us.”

Then the queen said: “What is your bishop to me? Judge him according to your own will. Whatever pleases you on this matter will please me also; whomever you put forward, I too shall put forward. For henceforth I differ from you in nothing.” She said this in order that she might somehow escape their hands.

On hearing this, the messengers returned to their accomplices, reporting what they had heard from the queen and much else besides. The accomplices in that accursed conspiracy rejoiced together and congratulated themselves that the queen herself had not thwarted the designs of their fraud. But this joy would turn into sorrow.

A certain wicked man who had previously taken monastic habit, when he heard that his accomplices were ruling, that the bishop was being cast aside, and that the queen was being reconciled to them, laid aside his monastic habit and left the monastery as an apostate. Since he had been a companion in the conspiracy, he wished to share in the rule; and this happened to him beyond his expectation.

Certain cardinals and canons of the church of St James, after hearing that the queen was being reconciled to the Compostelans and that the latter had told her that all hated the bishop and that he was no longer worthy of the episcopate, went to the queen, prepared neither to conceal the truth even for fear of death nor, abandoning the bishop, to favour the traitors’ party. They said to her: “Queen, although the accomplices in this conspiracy, which you know, have reported evil to you concerning our bishop, and although they have said that he is by no means worthy of the episcopate, nevertheless they must not be believed. They wish to rule, but by treachery; they wish to command, but by violence. We are prepared to answer all who accuse him and to defend his cause. What has he done that he should be deposed? What has he done abroad that he should be deprived of his honour? If anyone accuses him, we are ready, even in his absence, to answer that person. Since they lie about everything concerning him, they ought not lightly to be believed.” At these words the queen rejoiced, and because they proved faithful to their bishop, she rendered them no small thanks. In truth the conspirators had no cause to deprive the bishop of his honour except violence for the moment.

## CHAPTER CXV. How the queen escaped from Compostela

Meanwhile the bishop, concealed in the church of St Pelagius, had heard that peace was being made between the queen and the Compostelans. On hearing this, he sent to the queen a monk, Pelagius Didacide, to learn from her everything—how and on what terms these things were being done. The queen secretly questioned the monk concerning the bishop and where he was, and addressed him in these words: “Faithful confessor, go quickly from here and report to the bishop on my behalf that he should make peace with the Compostelans as quickly as he can, if he can, and leave the city. But if he cannot leave in this way, let him at least hasten to depart secretly in the silence of night and escape the hands of the wicked. For I too shall leave Compostela as quickly as I can, and I shall repay the traitors evil for evil, as they have deserved. To escape their hands, I am, as it were, entering into covenants of peace and reconciliation with them; for the present I shall give them guarantors to confirm them, whom I shall make guilty of perjury. In no other way can I escape or leave the city.”

Having heard this, the monk returned to the bishop and reported every detail. Hearing it, the bishop rejoiced. On that same day, Sunday, the Compostelans, still full of the frenzy of madness, came after dinner to the queen in the church of St Martin, demanding that a covenant and peace between themselves and the queen be ratified by oaths. They demanded that guarantors be given to them on the queen’s behalf and that their pact be put in writing. They themselves had already installed their steward in the city, but with the queen’s advice, so that he might favour them for a time, while nonetheless arranging and ordering everything according to the traitors’ counsel. They had appointed one man as prior, another as provost of the canonical house, another as lord of the altar, and so on for the rest.

The queen is said to have given them this answer: “Why do we delay any longer in this discord? Receive from me an oath to establish and maintain peace and reconciliation between you and me. On my behalf let Fredenandus and Veremudus, sons of Count Peter, and Fredenandus Joannides swear to you. Then I shall give you those whom you especially wish to participate in this oath: my son and Count Peter, who are outside the city and dare not enter because of these tumults of discord, together with the other consuls and princes of Galicia.” For the queen’s son, with his tutor Count Peter and the other magnates of Galicia, was near the city with a large body of cavalry, watching to see whether the queen might escape. But when they heard that what seemed a peace was being made between the queen and the Compostelans, they waited there still more attentively for her.

Then Fredenandus and Veremudus, together with the other Fredenandus, who had fled from the church with the queen—the aforementioned guarantors—swore to the Compostelans that peace and reconciliation between the queen and the Compostelans would be as had been determined. In truth they swore this so that the queen might escape and they themselves might be regarded as perjurers; for this was what they had already agreed in secret conference with the queen. The Compostelans, joyful and believing themselves to have attained their desire, accepted the oath and gave the queen and her people leave to depart the city, so that she might cause her son, Count P., and the others to swear to them and ratify that pact. O foolish audacity of traitors! O blind madness of conspirators! They imagine that so great and abominable a crime will go unpunished, and that they will bear with impunity what they have wickedly done—which is to be king.

The queen left the city and escaped the traitors’ snares: like a dove, she fled the talons of the hawk; like a lamb, the mouths of wolves. A certain foolish and mad man, with some of his Compostelan accomplices, accompanied her as far as the pass. But after the queen had withdrawn from the city, when they heard and learned that she would not return to Compostela or keep peace with the Compostelans, they quickly returned. The queen went to her son and her nobles, and now secure, recounted to them what had happened to her. She also ordered a declaration of defiance to be conveyed from her to the Compostelans, that they should beware, fortify themselves, and prepare for war; for, she said, so great a crime as they had committed would not remain unpunished. On hearing this, the Compostelans became as if half-dead; seized with overwhelming terror, they saw themselves hemmed in. They had neither confidence nor counsel; they saw vengeance for their crime beginning to spring up, and they despaired of themselves. Nevertheless, they fled to the church and carried there the most precious things they possessed.

## CHAPTER CXVI. How the bishop escaped from the hands of the traitors

On that same day, Sunday, as the sun was declining, the aforesaid bishop sat in the treasury of St Pelagius, considering what he should do, how he might escape, and by what route he might depart. Behold, a great crowd of traitors came running swiftly into the cloister of St Pelagius, all armed and seeking the bishop. Not finding him there, they entered the church, inclined to sacrilege; they searched for the bishop in every corner of the church, behind the altars, and even beneath the altar-veils, intending to kill him if they found him.

Then the treasurer-monk, who was with the bishop, turned to him and said: “Father, do you see your traitors rushing about armed?” To this the bishop said: “What do you say?” The monk answered: “Behold, they seek you inside and outside the church, thirsting for your blood. They will be here presently. Take thought for yourself, lest they find and slaughter you here. See how great a crowd is entering, and how swiftly.” Then the bishop turned to Michael: “Let us flee, Michael! Let us get out of here quickly. Put on this cloak, and I this very poor cape. Let us run among those who run about; let us hasten among those who hurry; let us go out among those entering and leaving. God alone, if he wills, is able to deliver us.”

Accordingly, the bishop left with the aforesaid Michael, placed between death and life. Passing through the frequent crowds seeking him, he reached the cloister of the same monastery, then another cloister; surrounded on both sides, he vaulted over the wall near the church of St James, where the altar of St Peter stands. Thus, with the aforesaid Michael, he came by the rooftops to the dormitory of our canons and rested there a little. Afterward, opening the dormitory door, he went out into the *quintana* of the palace before the refectory. There was a very bright radiance of moonlight, providing sufficient light for all those running to the church of St James and carrying their possessions there. For the entire city was terrified, fearing an assault by the queen’s soldiers; conscious of so great a crime, they flocked to the church night and day.

Yet the bishop, passing through their midst as though he were one of them, reached the house of Peter Gundesindidez, canon and cardinal of the church of St James, who had not withdrawn from either loyalty to his bishop or the path of justice amid so many and such great storms. Then Michael knocked at the door, while the bishop remained hidden behind him because of the bright moonbeams and the many movements of people. Once the door had been opened, the bishop entered the chamber of the aforesaid cardinal and hid there until certain canons whom the cardinal had invited to supper—and whom the bishop suspected—had gone away. After they had left, the bishop, with the aforesaid cardinal and Michael, passed through the cardinal’s house to the other side of the street.

Then the cardinal said to the bishop: “Father, the sound course for you is to put on arms and pass through the guards who stand watch here and around the rampart as though you were one of them.” The bishop replied: “Far be it from me to put on any arms other than the arms of Christ, which I have with me. Protected by the arms of Christ, I escaped yesterday’s fire; strengthened by those same arms, and with God helping and protecting me, I shall pass through other perils no less fearful in the midst of my enemies. Yet provide me with two other armed men, with whom I may pass through so many guards as though I were one of them. Come: we must delay no longer. For our enemies are at hand; they pursue us and thirst for our blood.”

Without delay the cardinal obeyed his counsel and surrounded the bishop with two armed men, Michael also being armed with one man’s lance. Thus they proceeded. When the sentries standing watch on either side between the Fagarian street and the Valley of the Miliorum saw them passing, they cried out: “Who are you? Where are you going? What do you seek?” Then one of the bishop’s companions, instructed by the bishop what to answer, said: “We are going outside the city to keep watch and to ensure that enemies do not attack the city secretly. It is time for you to keep watch and stand guard; it is time to run here and there. But you sluggards, why do you stay here? Why do you give your limbs to rest here? Rise, run about, keep more vigilant watch.” While these words were being spoken, they passed by and vaulted the rampart. But to recount what and how great evils the bishop suffered that night, and through what places he went on foot, would be a long labour for me and requires a work of its own.

At length the aforesaid bishop reached the Oak Spring on the road to Padrón, weary from the labour of the journey and accompanied by Michael and several others. He sent two of them ahead to a certain steward of his who was staying nearby, ordering him to come and bring mounts with him. When these had been brought, the bishop mounted with his followers; now protected by a considerable troop of soldiers, he came to Iria. Like one fleeing captivity, like one rising from the dead, he was received by his friends.

Meanwhile the aforesaid cardinal, through whose house the bishop had passed and who had delivered him, was captured by the traitors, and all his property was seized by them. The next day they led him into public, demanding either that he hand over the bishop or suffer the penalty of death himself. But almighty God, the just and mighty Judge, delivered him from the hands of the wicked. Meanwhile, at Iria, once his own escape and that of the queen had become known, the bishop struck with the sword of anathema all those dwelling in Compostela and suspended them from the thresholds of holy Church. This wounded the Compostelans to the marrow and utterly weakened them. The bishop also summoned all the men of the province of St James, both horsemen and foot-soldiers, and, yielding to the queen’s earnest entreaties, hastened to besiege the Compostelans. The queen likewise sent her envoys in every direction and commanded all—consuls and princes, horsemen and foot-soldiers alike—to come for the siege and destruction of Compostela.

The queen’s son A. besieged Compostela from the side of the Rocky Mount with a considerable army of cavalry and infantry. With him were his tutor Count P.; the latter’s sons Fredenandus, Veremudus, and Rudericus; his brothers-in-law Count Guterius and Gumiesse Nuniz; and the other magnates. From the side of Iria the bishop besieged it with a great army of horsemen and an innumerable host of infantry. From the side of the Sacred Mount, Count A. besieged it with an army of the Limian people, joined by Castilians—[Note: That is, from the territory of Castile, in the diocese of Ourense]—the people of Deza, and many others. From the side of the monastery of St Peter, Count Munio besieged it with all his army. From the side of Penellas, Count Rudericus besieged it with a very large army.

At daybreak the pride of the Compostelans was broken, on one side by the multitude of besiegers and their repeated assaults, and on the other by the sword of anathema. For although the accursed crowd of conspirators encouraged the other Compostelans not to accept the bishop’s anathema or recognize him as bishop, others—canons and citizens alike—adopting the sounder counsel and observing justice, obeyed him as their bishop and accepted his excommunication. The sons of Iscariot ran hither and thither and fortified the city with rampart, hedges, heaps of stones, and wooden defensive works; they encouraged and exhorted the people, but in vain. For when no small part of the Compostelans, uninvolved in the accursed treachery, saw the city besieged on every side, trees cut down, crops gathered, heads, feet, or hands cut off, and the bodies of the dead left unburied; when they saw also that the queen’s forces increased each day while their own diminished, they judged it worth while to adopt another course. Indeed, a large part of the Compostelans fled every night, fearing that the city would be wholly destroyed and that the Compostelans would receive what they deserved for their deeds.

The traitors were now hated by the rest; their counsel was now esteemed at nothing; curses were now pronounced against those who had been the authors of such wickedness and who had conspired against the bishop and queen. For, supported by no patronage, they saw that the city could easily be taken if attacked, and that armies on every side were eager to storm it. Who would not eagerly rush upon traitors? Who would not extirpate these accursed men who conspired against their own bishop? Who would not destroy those wishing to destroy kingdom and priesthood? Who would not burn the violators and burners of the Apostolic Church? All Galicia regarded the authors of so great a crime as enemies; all Galicia thirsted for their blood.

At length, despising the traitors’ counsel and rejecting the madness of the conspiracy, certain canons and citizens—who had neither participated in the aforesaid treachery nor been able to prevent it—went out to the bishop in the hope of supplicating him and requesting mercy. They said: “Most reverend Father, we come to the fountain of your mercy. We implore your watchful compassion: let the bosom of your mercy be opened to us. Stretch out to us the hand of help. The whole city, except the traitors, begs you: let the diseased part be cut away and removed, that the rest may live. Spare us, Father—Father, spare your children. Do not strike with the hostile sword those whom you have been accustomed to cherish in the bosom of pity and mercy. Have mercy upon us and be our arm, for we flee to you, as to our father, to our bishop.”

When the bishop yielded to their prayers and, in fatherly fashion, had pity on his children, he went to the queen and her son, reporting the Compostelans’ supplication and their recourse to mercy. When the queen heard it, she said: “Far be it that traitors who have committed so many and such great crimes should be spared! My judgment stands firm: all the traitors and criminals of Compostela are to be destroyed by fire or sword. For just as they spared neither the church of St James, nor you, nor me, so neither should they be spared. I beg that punishment be inflicted upon them according to their deserts and that they perish from the book of life. You too, Father, ought to desire their destruction. For it concerns you to abominate and destroy so great a crime.”

When the bishop saw that the queen’s mind was bent upon vengeance for her injury and could be moved by no entreaties, he summoned the boy-king, Count P., his tutor, Count Rudericus, Count Munio, and the other more prudent men of Galicia, asking them to soften the queen’s mind by prayers, that she might have pity on the apostolic city and, while destroying the traitors, spare the rest.

Then they went to the queen and sought, by the most earnest and innumerable prayers, to bend her to mercy. The queen wept because she saw that she could not avenge the conspirators’ crime according to her will or utterly extirpate the traitors and their offspring. At last, yielding with difficulty, as if compelled, to the prayers of the bishop and the others, the queen consented that covenants of reconciliation be made with the Compostelans.

Accordingly, the Compostelans covenanted under oath, first, utterly to destroy their *germanitas*, that is, their conspiracy, and they gave its written instrument to the bishop to be destroyed. They further covenanted to pay eleven hundred marks of silver and to restore everything whatsoever that they had taken from the bishop or his men, and from the queen or hers. The traitors, both canons and citizens, were to be proscribed—that is, made exiles and deprived of inheritances, buildings, and other benefices. Thus one hundred persons, canons and citizens alike, were proscribed and made exiles.

After these had been expelled and proscribed, the rest who remained, canons and citizens alike, came to the bishop and queen at the *alterium pullorum* [Note: Here, as above, ch. 15, no. 5, *auterium* should be read], their arms now laid aside; the Compostelans now released from anathema; the covenant of peace now ratified; and the bishop’s soldiers holding the church and the towers. They came after hostages had been given for the silver and the other obligations—namely fifty sons of the leading men of Compostela. They came, I say, and swore fidelity and obedience to the bishop and queen, and swore that they would not gather together the proscribed men except by command of the bishop and queen. Therefore the penalty for participation in and consent to the conspiracy and crime was remitted to them; they obtained mercy from the bishop and queen and from all the princes of Galicia.

The bishop entered Compostela and was received with great joy. He regained the summit of his honour; the hatred of the conspirators having been expelled, he sat upon his throne. He ordered the church of St James, which had been burned, to be rebuilt; the bells that had melted to be remade; and his palaces to be restored. Silver was given by the Compostelans, and what had been taken was restored to the bishop and queen.

## CHAPTER CXVII. That the bishop went on campaign as far as Segovia in order to recover the estate of St James in Portugal
Not long afterward, when the queen set out on an expedition against the king of Aragon, the bishop departed with her, having assembled his own army, together with all the counts and all the princes of Galicia. Her son, the king, followed her with his tutor, having in his company Count Adefonsus of Limia, Count Guterius, Fredenandus and Veremudus, sons of Count Peter, Gumiz Nuniz, and very many barons of Galicia with a large body of troops. At last they reached Campania; and, having assembled the men of León, the Campesinos, Castilians, and Asturians, they advanced into Extremadura.

The aforesaid bishop, however, remained at Palencia, having given his army to the queen, both because he was suffering in his leg and because he did not wish to take part in the plundering and robbery of the poor. Yet, after taking counsel with the clerics who were with him, he went to Segovia for a definite reason. For this bishop had formerly made Maurice, bishop of Braga, a canon of the church of St. James, and had granted him as a prebend one half of the estate of St. James which lies at Braga and in its district. When that Maurice, through the violence of the king of the Germans, had been made pope, another was elected in his place at Braga—namely Pelagius Menindiz, an unlearned man—who was forcibly holding that same estate of St. James.

The archbishop of Toledo had set a day on which the aforesaid elect of Braga was to come to Segovia to be consecrated there by the archbishop himself. The aforesaid bishop of the church of St. James came to this consecration so that he might recover, before the archbishop and the other bishops, the aforesaid estate of St. James. But since the matter was deferred by the archbishop and no judgment concerning that estate was rendered before the consecration of the elect of Braga, and since a sedition arose in the same city of Segovia against the queen and her army, the affair was postponed.

It was determined by the archbishop and the other bishops who were present—namely, the bishops of Salamanca, Osma, and Portugal—that a hearing between the bishop of St. James and the bishop of Braga concerning this matter should take place at Tuy on the Kalends of the coming September. The bishops of Ourense and Lugo were also appointed judges; and although all had assembled at Tuy on the appointed day for settling this affair, the entire matter nevertheless remained undecided. [Note: [Col. 1029D] See the following book, chapter 6.]

Therefore, when our bishop returned from Segovia and came to Compostela, he took counsel with his canons about how, with God’s help, he might exalt the church of St. James. For from the time he became bishop he had earnestly sought this end: that the apostolic church might possess an archbishopric or some greater dignity. [Col. 1030D] But so great and difficult a matter can be gained only through hardships, and in its proper time and place.

How the church of St. James, through the aforesaid bishop and by the assisting grace of God, obtained an archbishopric, I consider it neither superfluous but indeed most useful to make known to contemporaries and posterity through the style of our composition. This is made most plainly clear by the book which follows. All these things I saw with my own eyes and, for the benefit of our Church, composed in my own style with God’s help; and what I did not see with my own eyes, I learned wisely and faithfully from the bishop himself and from many trustworthy men.

# IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

How the Church of Compostela was made a metropolitan see through the aforesaid Bishop Didacus II. Outline of the second book.

[Col. 1031]

# THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 1031A]

We do not at all think it worthwhile that human praises should be covered by the cloud of oblivion. For those among posterity whose minds incline toward virtue, such praises are a kind of elementary instruction in virtue. Indeed, since a later day is the pupil of an earlier one, how much more do the good deeds of former times furnish instruction to those of the present!

In this matter, because of the teeth of detractors, who do not fear to gnaw away the glory of good men, I do not shrink from making the praises of our predecessors clear. For I do not wish that what has been well accomplished, and desires the light and demands the pen of memory, should become obscure through the long interval of time.

Therefore, obedient to the exhortation of your holiness, most reverend Father Didacus, bishop of St. James, we have endeavored to continue in part the narrative of the preceding book. For the earlier portion of that book had been written by Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo, and Hugh, bishop of Portugal—men, that is, prudent and venerable. Applying the small spark of my own talent to their style, we have set forth in writing what you did in the aforesaid church and in what manner: how, like a good cultivator in a vineyard, you labored; and how, before becoming bishop and while bishop, you governed it.

Next we shall undertake to tell how that same apostolic Church, with God’s help and through your industrious effort, became a metropolitan see; and how, while exalting it in other respects, you defended it against the most savage attacks of impending persecutions. May the Giver of all good grant that you live long and happily, preside long and happily over your Church, and grant also to me the grace to write your praise.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE REGISTER OF DIDACUS II, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF ST. JAMES, BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1031B]

Accordingly, nearly all those who had presided over the episcopal chair in the church of St. James up to the time of the aforesaid bishop had been not merely bishops but, as it were, princes, except Dalmachius, the Cluniac monk of blessed memory, and a few others.

For ever since the body of St. James had been revealed there and had become illustrious through great and innumerable miracles, the kings of Spain, out of love for so great an apostle, honored the church of St. James above the others and granted to the aforesaid apostle, throughout the surrounding regions, the authority of royal jurisdiction. Thus, just as that Church surpassed the other churches among the Spaniards through the presence of so great an apostle, so it should surpass them in its power over estates, inheritances, and all other things that had belonged to royal jurisdiction. [Col. 1031C]

Therefore, endowed with so lofty a summit of honor, the bishops of the Church of St. James possessed from kings a royal power above that of the other bishops of Spain. When the king of the Spaniards invaded with his army to extirpate the race of the faithless Ishmaelites, the bishop of the church of St. James was never absent with the whole army of his realm.

Indeed, to state the truth more fully, the bishops of the church of St. James had been accustomed to go forth to war protected by military arms and to check more sternly the boldness of the Saracens. Hence among the Galicians this proverb became current: [Col. 1032B] “The bishop of St. James: staff and crossbow.”

Nor is this surprising, since at that time almost the whole of Spain was uncultivated and illiterate. No Spanish bishop then rendered any service or obedience to our mother, the holy Roman Church. Spain followed the Toledo law, not the Roman law. But after King A., of blessed memory, gave the Roman law and Roman customs to the Spaniards, from that time onward the powers of the holy Church began to flourish among them, as a certain cloud of ignorance was gradually erased.

Why should I mention that the earlier prelates of the church of St. James were uneducated and ignorant? In the time of the Toledo law, a certain cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church came into Spain to see what learning, what religion, and what ecclesiastical custom existed there. When he came into Galicia, he duly sent his messengers in advance to the bishop of that place at Compostela.

Then the bishop of Compostela summoned one of the treasurers of the church of St. James and said: “Behold, a cardinal of the Roman Church is here. Go, and render him at Compostela as much service as Rome rendered you there; let the Church of Compostela serve him as much as the Roman Church served you.”

That saying, seasoned with no salt but rather stuffed with a great weight of haughtiness, the Roman Church has kept before its eyes and remembered down to the present day; and, frequently recalled, it has harmed and still harms the church of St. James. Yet, with the Lord’s help, that same Church will soon shake the yoke from its neck, although it had already shaken it off in some measure in the time of Lord Dalmachius, bishop of Compostela. At the council of Auvergne at Clermont, he obtained from Pope Urban the liberty of the church of St. James, in the presence and with the consent of three hundred bishops.

This Dalmachius, taken from the Cluniac community, presided as bishop of the church of St. James for only two years and died. After him Didacus II succeeded as bishop of the same Church. It is not unfitting, we have judged, to recall some matters concerning him.

## CHAPTER II. On the Character and Habits of Bishop Didacus II

[Col. 1033B]

He was a native of Galicia, born of parents respectable by worldly standards. His father, named Gelmirius, was a knight and a very powerful man in the time of Didacus Pelagides, bishop of Compostela. From that bishop he received and administered a castle called Honesto, together with the surrounding estate attached to it: Iria and its dependencies, Amaea, and Pistomarcos.

The aforesaid King Alfonso expelled that bishop from the church of St. James and kept him for a long time in fetters, branding him a traitor. For certain enemies of his, moved by jealous envy, said that he was striving to betray the kingdom of Galicia to the king of the English and Northmen and to take it from the king of the Spaniards. Whether this report, spread everywhere, was true or not is not now the subject of our work. [Col. 1033C]

During the episcopate of this Bishop Didacus, the Didacus of whom we speak was a good young man, educated in letters in the church of St. James and brought up in the household of that bishop. But after, as we have said, that bishop was deprived of his office, and Dalmachius, succeeding him as bishop, paid the debt of nature, King A., of blessed memory, and Count Raymond, the king’s son-in-law—who then possessed and governed Galicia, the Portuguese land, and their estates—seeing this young man to be discerning, adorned with good morals, and endowed with quick intelligence, appointed him, with the counsel of the canons, provost over the church and estate of St. James.

He held authority and ruled [Col. 1033D] for five years, so that he rose from rank to rank, from good to better, from virtue to virtue. [Note: [Col. 1033D] Only four are mentioned in Book I, chapter 7, and below, chapter 91: a four-year period. Perhaps the fifth year, begun but not completed, was counted [Col. 1034D].]

When afterward the clergy and people of the church of St. James chose a bishop for themselves, the aforesaid Didacus was elected bishop by the counsel of that same King A., Count Raymond, and the princes of Galicia. Yet before he received from a lay hand the church and estate of the church of St. James, he rendered [the object is not specified in the supplied text] to the blessed archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Roman Church, in the presence of the bishops of Galicia who attended his election—namely D. of Ourense, P. of Lugo, A. of Tuy, G. of Mondoñedo—as well as the princes of Galicia, clergy, and people of Compostela.

Although the course of our narrative has partly recounted above what and how great things he accomplished in his episcopate, we nevertheless do not think it superfluous to recall certain matters now.

## CHAPTER III. How the Same Bishop Sought to Obtain an Archbishopric

He was a man of exceptionally keen intelligence in ecclesiastical and secular affairs. Since the church of St. James was uncultivated and undisciplined in those times, he directed his mind toward establishing there the customs of the churches of France. This was exceedingly laborious for him.

Yet, just as a good farmer uproots thorns and thistles, tears out ferns and nettles, and plants useful seeds, so he established a fixed number of canons—namely, seventy-two—who should enter the choir of St. James only in surplices and copes. Previously the church of St. James had clerics like knights: with unshaven beards, torn and multicolored copes, pointed shoes, and the like. [Note: [Col. 1034D] Book I, chapter 20.]

When they met together in the refectory, some went hungry while others feasted splendidly; each man, according to the abundance of his wealth, consumed larger and more costly dishes. But the aforesaid bishop ordained that an equal portion should be given to every canon, and thus removed from them their customary schism.

Previously there were seven or twelve weekly ministers who presided at the altar of St. James, and all offerings pertaining to the clerics flowed to them as though to lords. But the bishop himself assigned each canon his own week at the altar. Why linger over these things? The abundance of his deeds exceeds our pen.

But although, with God’s help, he exalted the church of St. James in many and various ways, I shall not pass over in silence what he chiefly sought from the time he became bishop, what he desired with all the strength of his soul.

He observed that wherever in the world the body of an apostle rested, there was either a papacy, a patriarchate, or at least an archbishopric—except at the church of St. James. This appeared to him almost shameful and unjust, especially because St. James was the Lord’s kinsman and one of the Lord’s closest and most intimate disciples. [Col. 1034D]

For when our Lord took Peter, James, and John as His more special and intimate friends, He was transfigured before them on Mount Tabor. And when the mother of the sons of Zebedee asked the Lord that her two sons, James and John, might sit, one at His right hand and the other at His left, in His kingdom, a dispute arose among His disciples as to which of them seemed to be greatest (Luke 22:24), especially whether Peter, James, or John.

But those who had formerly been bishops in the church of St. James, with the near exception of Dalmachius of blessed memory, who lived there at a critical time, had not labored to obtain an archbishopric or the Church’s other dignities; rather, they were occupied with arms and warfare. Therefore it was necessary for this aforesaid bishop to labor more abundantly and more attentively, so that the church of St. James might shine with its due honor. [Col. 1035A]

Moved by this purpose, he had formerly gone to Rome and pressed Pope Paschal with earnest prayers to confer an archbishopric upon the church of St. James. But because he could not then obtain this, he scarcely secured the pallium and only with great exertion—as is written above in this Register—which was already a sign and pledge of the future event.

Finally Pope Paschal said to him: “Your purpose is indeed worthy, dearest brother; your petition is great and ought to be granted, if the Lord gives us time and opportunity. For it is fitting that the church of St. James should be adorned with an archbishopric or even with a greater dignity.” [Col. 1035B]

Yet one thing greatly impeded the obtaining of this request. The Romans who opposed the petition said: “Up to now the church of Compostela has been proud and arrogant toward us; up to now it has regarded the Roman Church not as its mistress but almost as its equal, and has served it unwillingly. But since this bishop displays so much humility and so much obedience toward us, and since humility conquers all things, if he perseveres in his humility and obedience, he may in future obtain the fulfillment of his wish with our consent.”

For the Roman Church feared that the church of Compostela, supported by so great an apostle, after acquiring the rights of ecclesiastical dignity, might assume for itself the primacy and privilege of honor among the western churches; and that, just as the Roman Church presided and ruled over the other churches because of the Apostle, so the church of Compostela might preside and rule over the western churches because of its own apostle. The Roman Church feared this greatly then, fears it even now, and takes precautions against it for the future. [Col. 1035C]

But how many times and in how many ways the aforesaid bishop, together with his canons, removed the spurs of that hatred and envy when he was in Rome; how many times and in how many ways he afterward visited the Roman curia through his messengers; and how much humility and obedience he showed to the lord pope and the cardinals of the Roman Church—the outcome of the matter will disclose.

Accordingly, he obtained cardinalates for the church of St. James and other ecclesiastical dignities. Yet his mind continued always to aspire to an archbishopric.

After the death of the aforesaid Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 1035D] 1118, 21 January], John of Gaeta, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, was elevated to the papacy [Note: [Col. 1035D] 25 January] and was called Gelasius. The aforesaid bishop nevertheless put his purpose out of mind.

At that time two canons of our Church were going to Jerusalem: Peter Didacides and Peter Anaiades, one a cardinal and the other treasurer. The bishop instructed them to negotiate with Pope Gelasius concerning the acquisition of an archbishopric. [Col. 1036A] For Gelasius, when he had been a cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church, had often discussed this business with his predecessor and understood what was appropriate for each church in Spain.

When the aforesaid canons came to him and spoke with him about this matter, he began the conversation, saying: “I know, brothers, I know what you seek: you wish to strip the church of Braga of its archbishopric and exalt the church of St. James. I myself often discussed this very matter with my predecessor. If it can ever be done justly, and by whatever means, now the time has come. For the church of Braga has given birth to a scandalous offender against the Roman Church—namely Maurice—who defiled the bed of his mother, the Holy Roman Church, and, agreeing with the sacrilegious emperor of the Germans, was set up by him in the Church as an idol, for his own ruin and confusion.” [Col. 1036B] [Note: [Col. 1035D] From 9 March 1118 Maurice—also called Burdinus—was intruded into the apostolic see [Col. 1036D].] “The whole Catholic Church abominates and detests him.

“But you have come here not on account of this embassy, but because of your pilgrimage. Go to the Lord’s tomb, whither you had intended to go. And if your bishop sends us his messengers concerning this matter, we shall answer him fully and according to his desire. Nevertheless, report to your lord what you have spoken with me and what disposition you have found in me concerning this business. I too do not refuse to send him my letters.”

Accordingly, in these terms Pope Gelasius sent his letter to the aforesaid bishop.

### Letter of the Pope

[Col. 1036C]

“Gelasius, bishop,” etc.

“Although occupied with weightier affairs,” etc. See Gelasius II, *Patrology*, vol. CLXIII, no. 11.

## CHAPTER IV. How the Prior and Cardinal, Sent to the Pope, Were Captured on the Road

When the aforesaid bishop saw such a letter from Pope Gelasius, it will become clear how greatly he rejoiced and how much more eagerly he longed for the fulfillment of his hope. For he rejoiced that John of Gaeta, called Gelasius, formerly cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church and most expert in Roman customs, had been justly and canonically elevated to the Roman pontificate. [Col. 1036D]

This Gelasius knew the churches and pastors of almost the entire world, and understood well what was suitable for each; above all, he held the churches of Spain and their rulers ready in the treasury of his breast. Among these he loved and revered the church of the Apostle St. James as the worthiest and most outstanding of all the others, and wished to exalt it with greater dignity, as would be fitting and just, both because of the presence and love of so great an apostle and for other reasons. He also embraced its pastor, the aforesaid bishop, with a special privilege of affection and wished readily to grant his request. [Col. 1037A]

Therefore the aforesaid bishop summoned the chief and wisest canons of his Church, publicly read out the aforesaid letters of Pope Gelasius, took counsel with them concerning the matter to which he aspired, and said:

“You know, brothers, how long and how laboriously I have toiled to exalt the church of St. James. You also know what I have chiefly desired for a long time: namely, that the church of St. James should be exalted to archiepiscopal dignity. Yet this desire of mine, so great and so worthy, will not lack fulfillment when God wills it.

“Now, brothers, it is time to ask and receive, seek and find, knock and have opened. I would most gladly go in person to Pope Gelasius, who is a friend both of our Church and of ourselves; and I believe I should obtain from him an archbishopric for our Church. But the way is blocked for me on both sides. On this side, pirates of the Ishmaelites are blockading our Ocean Sea with no fewer than twenty ships; on that side, because of the wars and disturbances of the kingdom of Spain, no access by land lies open to us. Moreover, King A. of Aragon is hostile to our Church and to us and forbids permission to pass through his kingdom. [Col. 1037B]

“Therefore we must deliberate which of our canons we should send secretly to Pope Gelasius under the appearance of pilgrims.”

After counsel had been taken, Peter, prior of our Church and nephew of the bishop, and another Peter, cardinal of St. Felix, received the office of embassy. [Note: [Col. 1037D] Ambrosius de Morales: “cardinal of St. James of the fortunate embassy,” etc. *Jacobi* is absent from the manuscripts, where both here and below, chapter 7, Peter is called cardinal of St. Felix; nor does the word *legationis* (“of the embassy”) occur there, though it occasioned the correction here [Col. 1038D]. See the preceding volume, in the *Life of Lord Gelmirez*, no. 94.]

They were forbidden to disclose their journey to anyone in any way, but were to prepare themselves carefully and secretly for the road. And because so great and difficult a matter could not be accomplished without great expense and the fruit of most lavish benefaction, by the counsel of the bishop and his canons the golden panel that had belonged to the former and lesser altar was broken up.

They took particular care at that time that this should not become known. For the bishop and canons feared that those canons and citizens who had been exiled from the city of Compostela because of the aforesaid sedition and were living in the regions of Campania and Castile might learn of it; and that, in order to harm the church of St. James and its bishop and to obstruct the envoys’ journey, they might disclose the affair as it was being conducted to the brigands of the king of Aragon. [Col. 1037D] For many delight in harming others even when it brings them no advantage, so long as they may stifle another’s benefit. This is what Galicians do especially.

Finally, the aforesaid envoys, having prepared what was necessary for so great a journey and having been given by the bishop and those canons who were present one hundred and twenty ounces from the golden panel to carry, began their journey. A report circulated among the people that they were going to Queen U., who at that time held the kingdom of Spain, and that these things were done with her consent and counsel.

Yet “nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known” (Matthew 10:26). Someone fully privy to that plan announced the matter, as it had been done and was being conducted, to the aforesaid exiles. They immediately made it known to the men of the king of Aragon, who held a castle named Castrum Soricis, through which the aforesaid envoys had to pass. It stands in the middle of the public road. [Col. 1038A]

Why say more? When the envoys—both Peters, one the prior of our Church and the other the cardinal—reached Castrum Soricis, although they were traveling under the guise of pilgrims, the Aragonese brigands at once laid hands upon them. The one hundred and twenty ounces of gold were taken from them; their mounts, clothes, silver, coinage, and everything they had prepared as necessary for the journey were taken away.

The prior, because he was more powerful and more renowned, being the nephew of the bishop of St. James, was bound in fetters. But the cardinal, because he was a priest and less powerful, was detained for three or four days and then allowed to depart. He went to Zaragoza to the king of Aragon and reported the capture of the prior and himself, and what they had lost.

At that time the king of Aragon was besieging Zaragoza with an army of Franks. Afterward he began to take it, when the Saracens had been forced by famine to surrender. [Note: [Col. 1038D] Zaragoza was captured on 18 December 1118.]

Finally, when he could not obtain the prior’s release from the king either through his own intercession or that of others, he crossed the Alps and went to Pope Gelasius, whom he had heard had arrived at Maguelone, recounting the misfortunes of himself and his companion.

Why that Pope Gelasius had left Rome and crossed by ship into the regions of Gaul is as follows.

## CHAPTER V. Why Pope Gelasius Fled Rome

After John of Gaeta, called Gelasius, had been elected and consecrated Roman pontiff by the Roman clergy and people, Henry, king of the Germans and emperor of the Romans—whom Pope Paschal had excommunicated because he had dared to lay hands upon him and had inflicted many injuries upon the Roman Church—heard that Paschal had paid the debt of nature and came quickly to Rome.

For he was striving to seize and hold in his own hand the royal and ecclesiastical powers until a pope should be established there according to his counsel and will. When he heard that John, cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church, was already pope under the name Gelasius, he took it badly, but nonetheless hastened to the City. [Col. 1038D]

When it was reported to Pope Gelasius and the cardinals of the Roman Church that the tyrant of the Germans was unexpectedly flying to Rome with such speed, fear fell upon them. They knew his tyranny and impious persecution and feared lest he dare to devise some evil against the Roman Church.

Yet the aforesaid tyrant of the Germans, having heard of Pope Gelasius’s election and consecration, sent messengers to him under the guise of peace and friendship, pretending that Gelasius’s canonical election and consecration pleased him greatly. But he was plotting something else. He was preparing snares for him in order to lay hands upon him, so that he might either drive him from the papacy or, having captured him, compel him to enter an unjust compact with him.

When this became known to Pope Gelasius, leaving the aforesaid tyrant in Rome, he embarked upon a ship with some of the cardinals and other Romans and, by way of the Tiber, committed himself to the high sea, fulfilling what the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23). [Col. 1039A]

He then landed at Maguelone, on this side of the Rhône. Having taken counsel with the cardinals and provincial bishops, he determined to hold a council at Clermont in Auvergne on the Kalends of March. Accordingly he sent messengers into Aquitaine, France, Normandy, Flanders, England, and the surrounding regions; and he sent one of his cardinals, named Deusdedit, into Spain, to invite the bishops of Spain to the aforesaid council. [Col. 1039B]

## CHAPTER VI. How He Intended to Send Bishop D. of Ourense and Giraldus to Pope G.

After the aforesaid bishop of St. James had been told of the capture of the prior and cardinal, he was almost overcome with grief, both because the envoys’ mission had failed and because so great a sum of money had been lost.

At that time the bishop himself had gone to Tuy to undergo a judicial examination with Pelagius, bishop of Braga, concerning half of Corneliana and the remainder of the estate of St. James in Portugal around Braga. The judges present were the bishops Didacus of Ourense, P. of Lugo, and A. of Tuy, by the order of the blessed archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Roman Church. [Col. 1039C]

For the aforesaid bishop of St. James had granted as a prebend to Maurice, archbishop of Braga, the half which was his own. At that same time Maurice, having been raised up as an idol by the aforesaid tyrant of the Germans, was defiling the bed of his mother, the holy Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 1039D] See above, Book I, chapter 81, no. 3; and chapter 117 on the dispute between the bishops of Compostela and Braga [Col. 1040D].] His successor Pelagius, supported by force, retained that half.

Though he came for this examination, he nevertheless refused to submit to judgment or even to cross the Minho. Coming as far as the bank of the Minho, [Col. 1039D] he said: “Let him who now holds it, hold it. For I shall neither cross to Tuy nor submit to the judgment of those bishops.” Returning thence to Braga, he seized by violent hand the other half of the aforesaid estate, which belonged to the canons of St. James.

After this, as our bishop was returning, he took counsel with the bishop of Ourense, the bishop of Tuy, and certain canons of our Church, so that, although his nephew the prior and Peter the cardinal had been captured and detained with such great losses, he should by no means abandon the undertaking.

It was therefore determined that Bishop D. of Ourense and I, Giraldus, canon of the church of St. James—who had been present at the earlier affairs and have woven together the sequence of this narrative—should go to Pope Gelasius to obtain archiepiscopal dignity. [Col. 1040A] We did not yet know, however, that Pope Gelasius, fleeing the tyrant of the Germans, had landed on this side of the Rhône, at Maguelone.

We were given the aforesaid one hundred ounces of gold and, with this blessing, began our journey to the lord pope. Yet great care had to be taken lest this affair become known. For some of our canons, only outwardly devoted and friendly to the bishop, would pass on to the aforesaid exiles anything they learned about it. Hence Boethius says: “No pest is more effective for harm than an enemy who is familiar.”

When these men learned of our journey, they sent letters to Castrum Soricis, Villafranca, Nájera, Logroño, Estella, Puente la Reina, Pamplona, and Jaca, so that they might prepare a trap for us also, as they had done for the earlier envoys. The letters said:

“Whoever holds the approaches to the kingdom of the king of Aragon; whoever seeks the advantage of your king: behold, Didacus, bishop of Ourense, and Girardus, teacher of the bishop of St. James, are going to Pope Gelasius with an immense sum of money. Take care that they do not pass through the kingdom of Aragon in any way. It was well done that the earlier envoys were captured at Castrum Soricis; and it will be much better and more advantageous for you if these men are captured too, since they are endeavoring to cross the Alps to the harm of the king of Aragon.” [Col. 1040B] [Note: [Col. 1040D] See below, chapter 56, no. 3.]

Encouraged by these and other messages, the Aragonese brigands watched the approaches to the roads with such vigilance and diligence as would be hard to believe. But when we had completed only a small part of the journey and had arrived at Sahagún, we heard and learned that ambushes were being prepared for us so obstinately day and night. We therefore decided it was better to turn back from our undertaking than to go, together with our possessions, to destruction into the jaws of our gaping enemies. [Col. 1040C]

We were nevertheless trying to pass by side routes in poor clothing; and because we had now heard that Pope Gelasius had arrived at Maguelone, we did not refuse, for love of St. James, to undertake so arduous and laborious a journey. But when we shared our plan with Queen Urraca, she utterly forbade it.

We were almost distressed that so great a matter entrusted to us should remain altogether unaccomplished. At last, after counsel had been taken, the blessed prior of Carrión was summoned by the queen and the course of our affair was explained to him. Why say more? By the prayers of the queen and ourselves, we scarcely obtained his agreement to go in our stead to Pope Gelasius, explain why we had abandoned the undertaking, and, insofar as he could, bring the affair of our Church—namely the archbishopric—to completion. [Col. 1040D]

For he could pass freely through the kingdom of the king of Aragon, as though going to Cluny. The monastery of St. Zoilus, over which he presided, lay under the power of the king of Aragon. Yet before he undertook that journey, he had first to endeavor to free Peter, prior of the church of St. James and nephew of our bishop, who was still held captive at Castrum Soricis. For he and his monks could safely approach Castrum Soricis, where there was a den of thieves—indeed, a dwelling-place of demons—and negotiate for the prior’s release.

When he had drawn him from those bonds by giving sixty marks of silver for him, we gave the aforesaid prior of Carrión at Palencia the letters we were carrying, fifty ounces of gold, and my mule. Thus he set out on his journey to Pope Gelasius. We, however, returned home. [Col. 1041A]

## CHAPTER VII. On the Arrival in Galicia of the Roman Cardinal Deusdedit

At the same time the aforesaid cardinal, Deusdedit—whom, as we have said, Pope Gelasius had sent to invite the bishops of Spain to the council in Auvergne—was approaching the church of St. James. With him came Peter Didacides, cardinal of St. Felix, who had formerly escaped from the capture at Castrum Soricis and had gone to Pope Gelasius, recounting to him the misfortunes of his journey.

Cardinal Deusdedit was honorably received by the aforesaid bishop of St. James with a procession in the church of that apostle and was carefully provided for. Finally the cardinal showed him privately the letter which Pope Gelasius was sending to the bishop of St. James. It was as follows:

“Gelasius, bishop,” etc.

“By the affection of our ancient love,” etc. See Gelasius II, *Patrology*, vol. CLXIII, no. 21.

## CHAPTER VIII. On His Preparations for the Council, the Cardinal Made a Canon, and the Death of Pope Gelasius

[Col. 1041C]

On seeing these letters, and having taken counsel for their interpretation, our bishop resolved to set out, together with the Roman cardinal and some of his canons, for the council which Pope Gelasius had arranged to hold at Clermont in Auvergne on the Kalends of March. For the bishop himself was most earnestly striving to obtain the archbishopric for the Church of St James, and therefore did not at all refuse to undertake anything harsh or laborious. He thought that, if he could attend the aforesaid council, Pope Gelasius would grant his request; consequently neither the tumults of wars and discord in Spain [Col. 1041D], nor the hostility of the king of Aragon, turned him back from the journey. Nevertheless, he first sent letters to the bishop of Jaca and to the prior of Nájera, asking them to obtain for him from the king of Aragon permission to pass through his kingdom.

Meanwhile the bishop prepared what was necessary for so great a journey, and invited those of his canons who were more prudent and were to travel with him to share the labour of the road. In the meantime we made Cardinal Deusdedit a canon of the Church of St James together with our bishop—since he was a cardinal of the Roman Church and the envoy of Pope Gelasius, whom the bishop intended presently to approach on account of so great a matter—and granted him his weekly altar-duty, as to another canon; for we perceived that this would be greatly advantageous to our Church [Col. 1042A] and to our bishop. For this is a common proverb: “He who loves me loves mine as well.”

These are the canons appointed to travel with the bishop to the Council of Auvergne, well supplied with garments and wealth and with all else necessary for so great a journey and undertaking: namely, Lord [D.] bishop of Ourense, our canon; Peter Gundesindides, cardinal and *primicerius*; P. Cresconides, archdeacon; B., treasurer; and his brother P. Stephanides; M., brother of D., bishop of Ourense; and I, Girard. With us also were those who were not canons: namely Master Raucelin, Robert of Salerno, physician, and other clerics, with their company of knights and retainers.

[Col. 1042B] After our bishop had come with us to St Facundus, the Roman Cardinal Deusdedit, who was to await him there, had already gone ahead. For he had heard that the king of Aragon was in no way granting the bishop of St James permission to pass through his kingdom, and he had hastened ahead so that he might obtain it as cardinal. Yet the result was contrary to his hope: not only did he fail to obtain the stated permission, but he even feared for himself. For, as the cardinal himself later told me, scouts of the king of Aragon seized his baggage and packs, saying:

“We have learned that the bishop of St James wishes to cross the Alps, and that he will carry with him an immense quantity of money, some of it personally and some of it already entrusted to this cardinal for transport. Therefore, whatever money of the bishop [Col. 1042C] of St James you are carrying with you—as our king commands—hand it over to us, lest you lose your own.”

When the cardinal maintained that he was carrying no money but his own, the scouts scarcely accepting his word, he passed rapidly through the kingdom of the Aragonese tyrant. Already at that time Rumour—“an evil than which none is more swift in active motion” (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.173)—was flying everywhere that Pope Gelasius had paid the debt of nature.

> [Note: Col. 1041D. He died 29 January 1119.]

This thoroughly filled the cardinal with fear and recalled our bishop from the journey to the council of Auvergne.

Nevertheless, since this bishop had already reached the Campos, he judged it fitting to visit Queen U. She was then at Burgos [Col. 1042D], and the road from St Facundus to Burgos was considered quite dangerous and full of bands of robbers. Therefore, after staying for some time at St Facundus, he took a force of knights from the neighbouring province and came to Palencia. Having remained there for nearly a month, he reached Burgos under the escort of the bishop of Palencia and the queen’s knights, and was honourably received by the queen.

At the same time Gutierre Fernández had captured Count Pedro González.

> [Note: Col. 1042D. Of Lara.]

He was holding him captive in the castle of Mansilla. This Count P., according to report, was accustomed to serve Queen U. in a most firm bond of affection; and he held from her Castile and no small part of the Campos. For this reason his capture had caused the queen grief [Col. 1043A] and sorrow.

Moreover, while we stayed at Burgos for some time, behold, B., prior of Carrión, whom, as I said above, we had sent to Pope Gelasius in our place, arrived and reported Pope Gelasius’s death. He also told us how Guy, archbishop of Vienne, brother of Count Raymond, had been elected and consecrated Roman pontiff.

## CHAPTER IX. The Election and Consecration of Pope Calixtus

For when Pope Gelasius had died and his body had been brought to Cluny, the bishops of the neighbouring provinces gathered there to render the rites due at his funeral. While the cardinals of the Roman Church who were present, together with the bishops of the Roman curia—of Ostia and of Porto—and many of the Roman people, were fully considering whom they should elect Roman pontiff, [Col. 1043B] the aforesaid archbishop of the Church of Vienne arrived. Pope Gelasius, still living but already at the threshold of death, had foretold to the Roman clergy and people that either he or Pons, abbot of Cluny, son of the countess of Mergueil, should be elected Roman pontiff.

This archbishop, of royal descent, was distinguished by prudence, humility, chastity, and every other excellence of character. Moreover, in the time of Popes Paschal and Gelasius, he had remained steadfast in defending the rights of Holy Church against his kinsman, the emperor of the Germans. Formerly, too, because Pope Paschal was accommodating himself to the aforesaid tyrant of the Germans [Col. 1043C] and had not excommunicated him as guilty of sacrilege, he had resisted the pope to his face together with the bishops of Gaul. Unless Paschal should at last strike the emperor with the sword of anathema, as justice required, this archbishop and legate of the Roman Church, having enlisted the bishops of Gaul, would rise more severely against Pope Paschal himself with the drawn sword of justice.

Accordingly, it seemed to the cardinal bishops and the others that this archbishop of Vienne was fit to preside over the Roman Church, to protect and preserve it by God’s aid from the many and such great storms converging upon it, and, while keeping the bounds of justice, neither to be broken by adversity nor exalted by prosperity. But because he was surrounded by an innumerable troop of horsemen—namely, the princes of Burgundy, his fellow-countrymen—it was necessary that he be elected Roman pontiff without his retinue knowing it.

Therefore the cardinals of the Roman Church, the bishops, and the other Romans present separated him from his company and addressed him with a few words; though resisting and loudly declaring himself unworthy, he was unanimously elected pope.

> [Note: Col. 1043D. On 1 February 1119.]

When this became known to his countrymen and knights who had come with him to Cluny, they rushed in a violent armed assault, broke down the doors, came to the place where these matters were being conducted apart, and forcibly carried him away. They tore to pieces the cope, stole, and other pontifical vestments in which he was clothed, saying:

“Shame! Why do the Romans attempt to take our shepherd and lord from us, and to deprive not merely the Church of Vienne [Col. 1044A], but all Burgundy and France, of so great a protector? Let them elect anyone they please as Roman pontiff; we do not give them our pontiff. Otherwise, let them beware.”

Indeed, to confess the truth, on that day the cloisters of Cluny were almost drenched with Roman blood. At length, after the crowd had passed and the men of Savoy had been calmed, their archbishop having been vindicated, the cardinals and others who shortly before had hidden while fleeing the sword gathered at the church of St Peter and deliberated what they should do in these circumstances. Afterwards, having taken counsel, they excluded from the thresholds of Holy Church all the perpetrators of that wicked violence unless they made satisfaction.

When the men of Savoy heard this, their anger now cooling and recognizing themselves guilty of violence, they returned that same day, as though unwilling and compelled, to make satisfaction. They restored what they had taken and approved what they had previously rejected altogether. The Romans joyfully received their pontiff and consecrated him pope, calling him Calixtus. Afterwards the bishop of Porto was sent to Rome with certain others to announce the death of Pope Gelasius and to inform the Catholic brethren of the Roman Church of the election and consecration of Pope Calixtus. When this became known to the Roman clergy and people, it greatly pleased them; they praised and confirmed what their brethren had so beneficially provided for the Roman Church and that they had chosen for themselves so fit a shepherd.

After the aforesaid prior of Carrión had explained these and similar matters to us [Col. 1044C]—for he himself had been present at the death of Pope Gelasius and at the election of Pope Calixtus—the aforesaid bishop of St James, although, as we have said, he was already earnestly seeking the elevation of his Church, strove much more eagerly for it after hearing of the election and consecration of Pope Calixtus.

For a close bond of affection had existed from earlier times between the aforesaid archbishop of Vienne and this bishop of the Church of St James: first, because they had once gone together to Rome and mutually fulfilled the teaching of the blessed apostle Peter: “Each, as he has received a grace, administering it to one another” (1 Peter 4:10); secondly, because his brother Count Raymond, whom he loved greatly, was buried in the church of St James; and thirdly, because the aforesaid bishop had baptized in the church of St James and anointed as king his nephew, King A., son of Count Raymond. For these and other reasons Pope Calixtus embraced the Church of the blessed apostle St James and the bishop of that place with paternal affection, and, if place and time permitted, intended to elevate it.

At the same time, while we were still remaining at Burgos, a powerful man of Savoy, named Robert and surnamed the Frank, brother-in-law of Pope Calixtus, came to the Church of St James for prayer. Through him Pope Calixtus sent the following letter to the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Compostela, in the year 1119:

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“This noble man,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 2.

## CHAPTER X. How Girard Was Sent to Pope Calixtus

[Col. 1045A]

The following shows with what joy the aforesaid bishop of St James rejoiced at seeing Pope Calixtus’s letter, and with what desire he yearned to greet Pope Calixtus through his envoy. Having taken counsel with the queen, the bishop considered which of the clerics who were with him he should send. Yet the journey through the kingdom of the king of Aragon—indeed, through the midst of Scylla and Charybdis—was so difficult and perilous that they could scarcely obtain by many entreaties the consent or courage of the man whom the bishop and queen had chosen to go there.

Finally, when our bishop returned with the queen to Palencia and thence to St Facundus, it was definitively settled that I, Girard, whose appointment had previously been determined, should set out for Pope Calixtus. And I undertook so dangerous and arduous a task boldly, especially from love for St James and at the exhortation of our bishop. We entrusted to Bernard, sacristan of the church of Carrión, for transport beyond the Alps, the money needed for this business: namely, a golden chest worth nine marks, one hundred *morabitini*, 211 Poitevin solidi, sixty solidi of Milanese currency, twenty solidi in Toulousain coin, and other things.

But I, having entrusted my horses to the aforesaid brother-in-law of Pope Calixtus, who was now returning from St James and was returning from St Facundus to Palencia, and having discussed the relevant matter with the queen, set out by byways, concealed in poor clothing, taking with me two pilgrims as companions in hardship and counsel. [Col. 1045C] Afterwards we came to St Dominic; and from there, making our way over the rugged mountains, through the hollows of the valleys, past the steep cliffs of Caracena, and through the valleys of Anguiano, we regained the main road at Citerón. Then, hiding by day and travelling by night, we escaped and crossed the Alps by the passes of Cize.

When I remember how great was the labour of my body and the anguish of my spirit that I endured in escaping this Charybdis, as the Lord lives and as my soul lives, I tremble wholly within myself and, trembling, shudder. Far be it from me to set down with my pen matters which my mind scarcely dares recall because of the measure of hardship and anxiety!

[Col. 1045D] At last, arriving at Morlaas, I waited there for a long time for the aforesaid sacristan Bernard and Stephen, chamberlain of Cluny. Although Cluniac monks, they feared to pass through the kingdom of the Aragonese tyrant. So great was the inhumanity practised by the Aragonese robbers! Since the aforesaid monks were indulging excessively in delay, I took up the road and went to Pope Calixtus with the bishop of Maguelonne, whom I found at Montpellier. He was returning from Auvergne, where he had conferred with William, duke of Aquitaine, by the mountains lying between Le Puy and Nîmes.

After I had greeted him on behalf of the bishop of St James, Queen U., and his nephew King Ildefonsus, I carefully explained to him, thirsting to hear it, the situation of each. Concerning his nephew, since he loved him almost beyond measure, and since he eagerly inquired how he was and whether he had yet taken Alcalá—which he had once besieged and had now taken—an adequate answer was given. Among other matters, frequent mention was made of the Church of St James and its bishop.

What more need be said? As far as I could, I repeatedly discussed with Pope Calixtus the elevation of our Church and our bishop. The Roman cardinals Boso and Deusdedit also assisted me as they could. For they loved the Church of St James and its shepherd with his flock.
