But our request was greatly hindered because Pope Calixtus was still, as it were, a novice; and although for various reasons he wished to elevate and adorn the Church of St James, he did not venture, in the absence of our bishop in person [Col. 1046B] and of the bishops of the neighbouring provinces, to transfer an archbishopric from one place to another. Nevertheless, he deferred his response to our petition until the council which he intended to hold at Toulouse on the Kalends of July.

Another obstacle to our request was that friendship between Pope Calixtus and Pons, abbot of Cluny—upon whom the success of our Church’s affair partly depended—was not especially firm. For this reason the pope did not at all comply with the requests of the aforesaid abbot in many matters.

Meanwhile a monk, Spanish by nation and named Burgundio, sent by Bernard, archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, came to the lord pope and said that he had letters from King Ildefonsus, the pope’s nephew. The archbishop of Toledo had ordered those letters [Col. 1046C] to be composed in the name of the boy King A.; in them he made many complaints against the Church of St James and many against its bishop. Under this feigned pretext, the boy king complained to his uncle the pope, saying that he, a boy without father or guardian, was losing the kingdom of Spain through the bishop of St James, who opposed him in every matter in which he could; unless therefore the lord pope, as his uncle and as his patron and protector, mercifully extended to him a helping hand, he would quickly be cast down from the summit of his kingdom by the bishop of St James. He added other matters which I think it more useful to pass over in silence.

It is not part of the present business to relate with what sorrow the pope remained alone with himself until the fourth day after seeing those letters, or how many tears he shed, moved by compassion for his nephew. [Col. 1046D] These letters were shown to no one except those most intimate with the pope. On one occasion, when the abbot of Cluny happened to retain them for his own inspection, he showed them to me also. From them I learned sufficiently what disposition the archbishop of Toledo had toward the Church of St James and its bishop; and I likewise explained their meaning to my companions and assistants, P. Anayade and A. Didacides, whom I had found at St-Gilles, returning from Jerusalem, in the court of the lord pope.

## CHAPTER XI. Pope Calixtus’s Reply Concerning the Archbishopric

At last, after the council at Toulouse had been held, on 6 June 1119, and after we, together with the abbot of Cluny and [Col. 1047A] the bishop of Lescar, pressed the lord pope to explain to us what he had decided concerning the purpose of our request, we finally heard this from him:

“The Roman Church, dearest sons in Christ, has long been wearied by many distractions and shaken by many adversities. By God’s authorisation, though unworthy, I rejoice almost exceedingly to preside over it amid these adversities and to bring aid to its oppressions. Let your prudence remember to ask and admonish, on our behalf, the bishop of St James, your lord, to take care to assist the Roman Church from his resources, with which, thanks to God and St James, he is abundantly supplied.

“We also ask him to aid our nephew King Ildefonsus manfully and steadfastly, as he has done from his earliest years, [Col. 1047B] and henceforth at least to secure for him the kingdom of Galicia, which his grandfather King Aldefonsus granted him at the city of León, in the presence of myself and your lord. If he supports him openly, we too shall comply openly with his requests. But, as has been reported to us, he opposes him as much as he can. If this is so, hatred of him arises in us and in our friends.

“Formerly, indeed, I embraced the Church of St James and its aforesaid bishop with paternal affection. Therefore, so that our former love may gain greater strength between us, let him furnish the power of assistance to our aforesaid nephew, as his father and protector. But at present we can in no way comply with his request that we confer the archbishopric of the Church of Braga upon St James; [Col. 1047C] for, in the absence of his person and of the bishops of the neighbouring provinces, so great a matter cannot at all be accomplished. Yet if he had attended the council of Toulouse, we would have granted this request of his.

“Therefore, if he desires the Church of St James to be elevated, advise him to hasten to come to us; and, so that his desire may be fulfilled more completely, let him hasten to attend the council which we have resolved to hold at Reims on the feast of St Luke the Evangelist.”

After Pope Calixtus had disclosed these and other matters to us, we gave him twenty ounces of gold, lest we return without having greeted him. We entrusted the golden chest, with the aforesaid *morabitini* and the rest, to the abbot of Cluny for safekeeping. Then we returned, having received from Pope Calixtus letters of the following kind:

## CHAPTER XII. Invitation of the Bishop to the Council of Reims

[Col. 1047D]

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Before undertaking,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 19.

### On the Bishop’s Preparations for the Council of Reims

After the bishop, together with the canons of the Church of St James, had seen these letters of Pope Calixtus, he resolved to go to him with certain of his canons; indeed, he was eagerly striving for the elevation of his Church. But because it was not expedient for him to pass through the midst of Spain’s bands of robbers, through the strongholds of tyrants, and through the kingdom of the king of Aragon—although the lord pope had commanded the Aragonese tyrant, through the bishop of Lescar [Col. 1048A] and other envoys, to grant the aforesaid bishop of St James permission to pass through his kingdom—he judged it fitting to sail to Gaul.

Accordingly, he ordered two ships, which the common people call galleys, to be prepared for the journey. The ships were prepared, and we too prepared ourselves to undertake the voyage. Yet it was not proper that so great a business should be undertaken without consulting the queen. Therefore two of our canons were sent to her, namely P. Gundesindides, cardinal, and P. Judex, to tell her of the bishop’s journey to the pope, to communicate his plan to her, and to ask to whom the bishop should entrust the honour of the Church of St James and its castles.

Some of our canons urged the bishop not to undertake this journey. The queen too, after she heard of the journey’s preparations [Col. 1048B], reflecting that nearly all Galicia would be laid waste by the absence of the bishop of St James, and that, in the absence of so great a guardian and protector of peace, Galicia would be torn apart by the bites of savage fury, utterly dissuaded and forbade the aforesaid bishop from undertaking the aforesaid journey. Some had also suggested to the queen that the bishop wished to go to Gaul in order to bring with him fellow-countrymen of King A. and contrive to hand over the kingdom of Spain freely to King A., the queen’s son; and the queen greatly feared this. This dissuasion and prohibition greatly troubled the bishop and many canons of our Church.

Furthermore, twenty Saracen ships, which had come to take Christians captive and slaughter them, had at that time reached the province of St James. From the river Douro to the Ulla, from the Ulla to Asturias, and beyond, they ravaged all the coasts of the Ocean Sea; they killed some Christians and took others captive, and possessed the maritime borders everywhere as though they were lords of the sea. [Col. 1048C] At last, yielding to the queen’s dissuasion and that of certain of our canons, and fearing also that he might fall into the hands of the Ishmaelites, our bishop withdrew from the journey to Gaul which he had intended to make.

Yet it was by no means right to disregard or allow to come to nothing Pope Calixtus’s summons to the Council of Reims and his promises. No canon of the Church of St James, however famous a reputation might have made him, dared in any way pass through the jaws of those gaping dangers, through the midst of Spain’s Charybdis. By chance, at that time Hugo, bishop of Portugal, who had formerly been archdeacon of the Church of St James, had come to Compostela and was constantly discussing our Church’s affairs with our bishop. When he saw the aforesaid letters of Pope Calixtus and learned that our bishop’s plan of going to the council at Reims had been frustrated, he was stirred by a certain boldness of spirit and, yearning for the elevation of the Church of St James, fearlessly promised that he himself would go to the pope through the midst of the robber fleets.

But first, because the archbishopric of the Church of Braga could not in any way be obtained in the absence of our bishop, who was making the request, and of the bishops of the neighbouring provinces, who were to consent to it, it was determined after consultation with the aforesaid bishop of our Church and certain canons that he should seek, for the elevation of the Church of St James, [Col. 1049A] the metropolitan see of the Church of Mérida or another ecclesiastical dignity. How the aforesaid bishop of Portugal passed through the kingdom of the Aragonese tyrant concealed in poor clothing, and what he afterwards did, the following page will show, God helping.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the Bishop of Portugal Was Sent to Pope Calixtus

Accordingly, the aforesaid bishop of Portugal, not refusing so great a hardship and such abasement of his person, clothed in ragged and most mean garments [Col. 1049B], set out for Pope Calixtus. He had as his companion in the journey and undertaking A. Petrides, a canon of the Church of St James, whom the aforesaid bishop of Compostela had assigned to him.

But the bishop of Portugal, as a man of cautious and shrewd counsel, boldly presumed to go in advance and hurry on more quickly with his two retainers. Now on horseback, now on foot, he passed through cities and fortified towns; now blind, now lame, now with his face distorted as if by palsy, now changed in other ways as seemed useful to him, he deceived the eyes of his enemies. Both his friends and enemies saw him and did not recognize him, considering him poor, a beggar, and contemptible. O happy man, whom the blessed apostle James so protected [Col. 1049C] that he was seen by his enemies yet not recognized by them! He passed through the midst of enemies and most wicked robbers, and no one harmed him.

But the aforesaid A., when he came to Burgos, was captured and detained there [perhaps *retentus*, “held”], and the things he carried were taken away. The bishop of Portugal, however, had fortunately passed through two days before, while they were secretly preparing an ambush for him.

> [Note: Col. 1049D. Here *perendie* means not “the day after tomorrow,” but “on the day already past.”]

For when it became known that he had already passed Burgos, those who were eager to capture him were greatly distressed.

Afterwards the same bishop came to Logroño.

> [Note: Col. 1050D. We also read above of Gronium in chapter 6, between Nájera and Estella; it is now Logroño.]

Concealed among other pilgrims, he lodged with a certain citizen of Burgos. This man looked at him more attentively, for he had known him during his archdeaconry and episcopate [Col. 1049D] and had often served him. He called him apart to a more secluded place and said:

“Who are you, hiding beneath this ragged garment? Are you not H., bishop of Portugal?”

When the bishop denied that he was a bishop and pretended to be someone else, the Burgos man said:

“I recognize you, Father Bishop. Neither a disguised face nor the meanest garment can make you someone else to me. I formerly knew and loved you as so worthy and honourable a bishop; now too, do not fear to make me the servant of your affection. Tell me the purpose of your journey. Why are you concealed in poor dress? It is perfectly clear to me that you do so in order to pass by like a beggar: you fear what is to be feared, and not without reason you pretend to be another person. For our king of Aragon has forbidden all clerics of the Church of St James to cross through his kingdom and has threatened his gatekeepers that none of them may pass this way. But you, trusting in the aid of the blessed apostle James, and taking counsel from me, will pass through safely, with God’s help.”

After the aforesaid citizen of Burgos had said these and other things to the bishop of Portugal, the bishop saw that he had been discovered and that the fiction of his poverty and pilgrimage was open to the man. He replied:

“I am indeed H., bishop of Portugal, and formerly, if you remember well, I was your intimate and heartfelt friend. But since the proof of love is the performance of a deed, because my affection has benefited you too sparingly until now, henceforth, while life remains, it shall make fuller amends. [Col. 1050B] And since I have long found you most faithful in matters entrusted to you, I shall not hesitate to disclose to you in good faith the secrets of my journey.

“With God’s help, I am going to Pope Calixtus, sent by the bishop of Compostela for the purpose of elevating the Church of St James: namely, that the metropolitan see of Braga or of Mérida may be transferred to the Church of St James. Furthermore, I shall petition Pope Calixtus on behalf of my see, the Church of Portugal, from which the bishops of Braga and Coimbra are taking parishes belonging to its own diocese, that it may be restored, as justice dictates, in the parishes unjustly taken from it.

“Moreover, as the Lord lives and as my soul lives, I am not journeying to France or Burgundy at the behest of Queen U., her son King A., or the infanta of Portugal. For this is what your king of Aragon fears, and for this reason he has forbidden the clerics of St James to pass through his kingdom. [Col. 1050C] He fears that an army of Franks may enter his kingdom and claim the sovereignty of the realm for itself.”

As the bishop and the citizen of Burgos secretly exchanged these and similar words, the bishop, aided by great discernment of mind, gave the friend and host a mark of silver which he had with him, receiving from him a pledge that he would reveal nothing to anyone about his journey or his business. Then, taking counsel from him, he departed rejoicing but still fearful. And just as a dove, startled by the claws of a hawk, cleaves the air in swift but fearful flight, so the bishop hastened through the kingdom of the Aragonese tyrant—indeed, through the midst of Charybdis.

[Col. 1050D] After he came to Morlaas, he refreshed himself there for two days, like one escaping shipwreck. Yet that refreshment almost became his ruin. For after he had already departed, behold, on the following day Aragonese pursuers, having heard that the bishop of Portugal had passed through the kingdom of Aragon without the king’s permission, sought him in order to capture him. But He who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den and the three youths from the fiery furnace delivered the bishop of Portugal from the hands of his Aragonese persecutors.

Afterwards the bishop of Portugal came as far as Cluny and found Pope Calixtus there. He delivered to him [Col. 1051A] the letters of the aforesaid bishop of Compostela and, openly and privately, added besides whatever it was necessary to add. He also gave the aforesaid abbot of Cluny letters and credentials that were necessary. Certainly it was necessary that the abbot of Cluny should know that Hugo, bishop of Portugal, was the envoy of the bishop of St James, so that he might hand over to him the money which we had entrusted to the abbot for safekeeping. And so it was done.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Estrangement and Reconciliation of Pope Calixtus and the Abbot of Cluny

Between Pope Calixtus and P., abbot of Cluny, there had long been, as it were, an appearance of feigned affection.

> [Note: Col. 1051D. He is called Pons above, chapter 9.]

For after Guy, archbishop of Vienne, had been elected and consecrated pope Calixtus at Cluny, and while all who had been present—Roman, Savoyard, and Aquitanian clergy and laity alike—approved his election and consecration, the aforesaid abbot of Cluny would neither praise nor reject that election or consecration. Instead he said:

“Let envoys go ahead to Rome to notify our brethren in Christ of Pope Gelasius’s death, and let them also make known to them what has been done at Cluny concerning our fellow brother, the archbishop of Vienne, by the Roman cardinals, bishops, clerics, and even laymen. If the Roman clergy and people approve his election and consecration, then it is for us to approve it after them and to obey their authority.”

Many bishops of Gaul approved this judgment of the abbot of Cluny. Therefore, after the Roman clergy and people had approved Pope Calixtus’s election and consecration and had execrated Maurice, the idol of the German tyrant, the abbot of Cluny and the other bishops and abbots of Gaul revered Pope Calixtus as one justly raised to the dignity of the apostolic summit.

For this reason, however, Pope Calixtus had not until that time regarded the aforesaid abbot of Cluny as especially close to his heart, nor had he ever assented to his requests. Why should I mention the dispute over the church of Mergueil between the abbot of Cluny and the bishop of Maguelonne, in which Pope Calixtus inclined more favourably toward the bishop of Maguelonne’s side? [Col. 1051D] Or why mention the cemetery of the metropolitan church of St Mary at Auch, granted by Pope Calixtus and established for the future by the authority of privileges, although it had anciently belonged to the monastery of St Orens of Cluny? And so in these matters, and in many others besides.

When Pope Calixtus came to Cluny in the second year of his pontificate, he was received with the highest honor by the abbot himself and by the community of Cluny; and, remaining there from the Nativity of the Lord until the Epiphany of the Lord, he celebrated those feasts solemnly. On the day of the Lord’s Epiphany, Pope Calixtus came into the chapter-house, where the abbot was present, together with so great and glorious a company of monks. Then, pierced by a great impulse of charity, he prostrated himself upon the ground in tears before the abbot and the community of Cluny. The abbot and monks likewise prostrated themselves, mercifully entreating the pope to rise. At length the pope raised himself; the abbot also rose with the monks.

Then the pope, indicating silence with his hand, said: “Brothers and dearest sons in Christ: ‘Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity’ (Ps. XXXII). It is good and salutary for us to live together in the one grace of charity; it is good that we, as diverse members, should serve one head, namely Christ, and should be one body in Christ with one heart and one soul. For, as the blessed apostle James says: ‘Where jealousy and contention are, there are inconstancy and every evil work’ (Jas. III.16).—‘Let us,’ moreover, as the blessed apostle Peter says, ‘not be idle nor without fruit in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ; but let us have patience, and in patience godliness, and in godliness brotherly love, and in brotherly love charity’ (II Pet. I.8). And the blessed apostle John says: ‘We have this commandment from God: that he who loves the Lord should also love his brother’ (I John IV.2).

“I have said these things, brothers, because for some time I have not fully shown you the grace of affection, nor have I given you satisfaction in certain matters as I ought. But now, having experienced the untiring services of charity which you have rendered more fully to the Holy Roman Church out of the highest affection, and having seen the bowels of charity which you show to all Christ’s faithful, I desire to become a participant in your rejoicing of charity and to be counted your brother and fellow-soldier. For I see that the excellence of your charity has brought almost the whole world under its sway. If, by loving you too little, I have hitherto offended in any way against your party, I now repent. I wish the abbot of Cluny to be most dear to my heart, and the monks of Cluny to be my closest friends. Let the greater affairs of the Roman Church that must be settled in these regions be decided chiefly by your counsel; let my person be placed at the disposal of your judgment and counsel.”

While Pope Calixtus spoke these and other such words before the abbot and the community of Cluny, he placed himself in the hands of the abbot and of the whole community, and requested to become a brother and participant in the prayers and benefactions of the Cluniac community. Pope Calixtus was received into the fellowship and participation of the prayers and benefactions of the monastery of Cluny. Thus there arose between Pope Calixtus, P., abbot of Cluny, and the Cluniac community such a union of affection and bond of charity that they became one heart and one soul.

Indeed, to confess the truth, among all the churches of Gaul the monastery of Cluny surpasses and excels in holiness and charity. Therefore it was worthwhile for Pope Calixtus to hold the monastery of Cluny most dear to his heart, as his own chamber and seat; for, in order to confound the ravisher of mother Roman Church, namely Burdinus, the idol of the German tyrant, to restrain that tyrant’s tyranny, to confirm the ordinance of Holy Church, and to extirpate the image of pestilential heresy, the abbot of Cluny and the community of the monastery of Cluny were useful and necessary to the Roman Church.

## Chapter XV. On obtaining the archbishopric

When the bishop of Portugal saw this covenant of mutual affection and charity between Pope Calixtus and P., abbot of Cluny, he rejoiced with great joy. For the hope and anchor of his undertaking lay in the abbot of Cluny; he perceived that Calixtus would now readily grant the abbot’s petition—indeed, even his counsel [Col. 1053B]. He therefore came to the aforesaid abbot and said:

“Now, now, most reverend Father, is the time to exalt the Church of blessed James, while Pope Calixtus is in your hands. Let his ears be assailed with prayers; while we have time, let us act swiftly. For blessed James has obtained this for us.”

Certainly, before so great a bond of affection had been formed between pope and abbot, the bishop of Portugal would scarcely have dared even to utter a word about conferring an archbishopric upon the Church of Compostela. Before he came to the papal court, the Romans, cardinals and others alike, awaited the arrival of the aforesaid bishop of Compostela with excessive longing, expecting to receive from him great and innumerable gifts. But after the bishop of Portugal arrived and reported that the bishop of St. James was utterly unable at that time to come in person to Pope Calixtus—both because the tyrant of Aragon would by no means grant him permission to pass through his kingdom, and because twenty ships of Ishmaelite pirates held the Ocean Sea under blockade—the Romans took it badly that their aforesaid expectation had come to nothing [Col. 1053C].

They said: “The bishop of Compostela, powerful in the height of wealth and honor, holds the Roman court in contempt. Although he asks the lord pope to transfer so great a thing as an archbishopric to his church, he would not attend the Council of Reims when invited so that his petition might be granted. Moreover, he has declared himself unable to come to the pope either by ship over the waves or on foot by land. Indeed, through his envoy the bishop of Portugal, while he himself is absent, while the suffragan bishops are absent, and without royal consent, he demands that the archbishopric of Braga be transferred to the Church of Compostela—a thing which he could scarcely obtain even with great humility and great service.” Pope Calixtus himself, too, had somewhat withdrawn from the former degree of affection which he had held toward the bishop of St. James.

But the covenant of affection made between him and the abbot of Cluny favored our cause and produced the fruit of benefit for our Church. For when the abbot of Cluny had heard the bishop of Portugal’s argument, he approached Pope Calixtus and said:

“I pray and beseech your holiness, most holy Father, that you deign to exalt the Church of the blessed apostle James and to yield to the just desire of its bishop, your dearest friend [Col. 1054A]. What your predecessors Paschal and Gelasius would have accomplished, had time or place not failed them, do you, with God as author, complete. Blessed James himself asks you for a metropolitan see for his Church. If you will not yield either to my prayers or to my counsel, at least yield to the petition of blessed James. Moreover, the Church of every apostle, wherever on earth it may be, flourishes and glories in ecclesiastical dignity. The Church of blessed James alone, lying hidden in the western region, is content with a mere bishopric. The other co-provincial sees, situated on the soil of his inheritance and subject to him on that account alone, surpass him by right of inheritance, not by any ecclesiastical dignity.

“But if it does not seem right in your sight to transfer the metropolitan see of the Church of Braga to the Church of Compostela, or to confer upon the aforesaid Church of blessed James the archbishopric which the Church of Lugo formerly possessed in the time of Teodemir, king of the Goths, then at least deign henceforth to grant to the Church of blessed James at Compostela the metropolitan see of the Church of Mérida, which, devastated by Saracen ferocity, has lost the worship of the Christian faith; and deign to exalt the apostolic Church with the dignity of an archbishopric.”

After the abbot had softened the pope’s mind by these and other arguments, he took the bishop of Portugal with him and turned to the cardinals, promising some and entreating others with persuasive words that they should all unanimously beseech Pope Calixtus to exalt the Church of blessed James [Col. 1054C]. There were at the papal court certain Allobroges, powerful and noble men, compatriots of the pope: namely Guido of Albione, duke of Burgundy, and many others, brothers of the Church of blessed James, who had formerly visited blessed James and subjected themselves to that apostle. Therefore they greatly loved the Church of blessed James and its bishop.

When they heard of the metropolitan see to be obtained for the exaltation of the Church of blessed James, they all, with the abbot of Cluny and the bishop of Portugal, fell prostrate at the pope’s feet, compassionately petitioning him to deign to adorn the Church of blessed James with the archbishopric of Mérida. They further declared that they would not be torn from his feet until he yielded to their petition. Who could be so hard-hearted as not to assent to the worthy prayers of the abbot of Cluny, the bishop of Portugal, and so many princes of Burgundy prostrate upon the ground? The cardinals themselves also, earnestly beseeching the lord pope, prayed that the metropolitan see of Mérida might be transferred to the Church of Compostela [Col. 1054D].

Then the pope opened his mouth and said: “Rise, dearest sons in Christ, rise. Great indeed is what you ask, but it is fitting that you obtain it. By God’s agency, the Church of Compostela shall be adorned with the metropolitan dignity of the Church of Mérida.”

On hearing this, the abbot of Cluny rose, the bishop of Portugal rose, and the other princes of Burgundy rose. Joyfully they kissed the pope’s foot and gave thanks. Nearly all who were at that court rejoiced when they heard that Pope Calixtus was raising the Church of blessed James to an archbishopric [Col. 1055A].

## Chapter XVI. On other envoys and the benediction sent to the lord pope

Meanwhile the aforesaid bishop of the Church of blessed James sent P. Fulconides and A. Petrides, canons of that same church, to Pope Calixtus, so that together with the bishop of Portugal they might transact the affairs of his Church. For he was troubled that the bishop of Portugal had crossed the Alps, as it were alone. The aforesaid A., who had once been captured at Burgos, had by then escaped captivity.

These two, disguised as pilgrims, passed through the kingdom of the king of Aragon amid the severe onset of winter weather and reached the papal court. There they found the bishop of Portugal joyful and cheerful, and almost in possession of his desire [Col. 1055B]. For although the pope had already granted the metropolitan see of Mérida to the Church of Compostela, the bishop of Portugal was still striving to ensure that the aforesaid bishop of the Church of blessed James should exercise a legation over the provinces of Mérida and Braga. In order to obtain this metropolitan dignity and legation, the aforesaid envoys worked with the bishop of Portugal as best they could.

Once these had been obtained, the two men, P. and A., were sent back as swiftly as possible to the Church of blessed James, reporting that Pope Calixtus had transferred the metropolitan see of Mérida to the Church of Compostela and had entrusted to the bishop of St. James a legation in his stead over the provinces of Mérida and Braga. When this became known to the bishop of Compostela and to the canons of the Church of Compostela, my pen is insufficient to describe how joyfully they exulted [Col. 1055C]. Yet this was made known only to the greater and more influential canons. Letters of the abbot of Cluny and the bishop of Portugal were also shown to them, in which they called the bishop of St. James “archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church.”

The bishop of Portugal remained at the papal court, awaiting the benediction to be sent from the Church of blessed James to the pope and cardinals. He already had the aforesaid golden casket with one hundred morabitins, fifty Poitevin shillings, and another hundred morabitins that he had brought with him as a gift; but, to complete the benediction, two hundred and sixty marks of silver had to be added. Accordingly, after counsel had been taken by the bishop of St. James and his aforesaid canons, it seemed good to them to take these from the treasury of St. James [Col. 1055D].

Thus, with very few accomplices in this plan, a round silver table commonly called an *intremissa*, which had belonged to Almostam, king of the Saracens, containing forty marks of silver; a golden cross; a golden chasuble which King Ordoño had given to blessed James; and a golden crown were broken up in order to supply the gift of the aforesaid benediction. Since all these things did not suffice to make up the two hundred and sixty marks of silver, the bishop himself added forty marks of silver from his own resources.

How so many and such valuable things might be sent required exceedingly subtle ingenuity. At that time a ship of Norse merchants, which, driven by the wind, had wandered into the Ocean of the Agarene barbarians, had put in at the castle called Honesto and was hastening to return to Normandy. The aforesaid bishop of St. James pretended that he would send the aforementioned money through these merchants, employing a prudent plan. For the Galician people are eager to learn the secrets of plans of this kind, and very few of them faithfully keep what is entrusted to them. It was therefore a wise plan to show them one thing in appearance and do another.

After the Norsemen had departed, Rumor, the frequent herald of falsehood, asserted that the bishop had sent the aforementioned money by ship to Normandy, and from Normandy to Cluny. Thus the deceitful intention of certain of our fellow canons was frustrated; if they had learned the matter as it was actually done, being “full of leaks” (Horace), they would have let it flow out more quickly [Col. 1056B].

At last, when many Galicians were going to Jerusalem after receiving the cross, the aforesaid bishop, a man of most discerning intelligence, entrusted this money for transport to two subtle and exceedingly crafty men: P., the brother treasurer, and P. Joannides, who afterwards became our canon. By the bishop’s counsel and instruction, they distributed it in trust, under the pretext of penance: to one, ten ounces of gold; to another, eight; to another, seven; to another, five; and so on. For as many ounces of gold as they entrusted to each man to carry, so many years of penance they remitted for him. What a contrivance of a pope of most subtle and discerning intelligence!

Thus they passed safely through the kingdom of the tyrant of Aragon and carried the aforesaid money as far as Montpellier [Col. 1056C]. There the monks of Cluny received it and, as had been arranged, conveyed it to Cluny. When the two aforesaid men, both named P., found there the abbot of Cluny, the bishop of Portugal, and Stephen of Besançon, chamberlain of Pope Calixtus, they gave the aforesaid benediction to that chamberlain Stephen in the pope’s stead.

After this, when the bishop of Portugal wished to return to Spain but did not dare to travel back through the kingdom of the tyrant of Aragon—for ambushes had been prepared in many places—he sent to our Church, carried by the aforesaid bearers of the benediction, the privileges transferring the metropolitan see of Mérida to the Church of Compostela and entrusting the legation to the bishop of St. James. They are as follows.

### Privilege concerning the archbishopric of the province of Mérida

[Col. 1056D]

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“By the disposition of the Almighty,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 79.

## Chapter XVII. On the suffragan bishops

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Entrusted to us,” etc. See above, no. 82.

## Chapter XVIII. On the legation of the provinces of Braga and Mérida

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

[Col. 1057A] “The ancient [authority] of the Apostolic See,” etc. See above, no. 80.

### Special letters of Pope Calixtus to the archbishop of Compostela (27 February 1120)

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“And your person,” etc. See above, no. 81.

## Chapter XIX. That from this day he was called archbishop

These transferred privileges were received at Compostela with the greatest joy on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, and on that very feast of the passion of blessed James they were read aloud in the Church of that apostle before all the clergy and people. From that day the aforesaid bishop of the Church of blessed James was regarded and called archbishop of the Church of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 1057B].

For from the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1104, when he had obtained the pallium at Rome from Pope Paschal, he had aspired by every means in his power to obtain an archbishopric for the Church of blessed James. By frequently approaching the Roman court through his friends and envoys, he had rendered the most distinguished service to the Roman pontiff, the cardinals, and the entire Roman court, as has partly been written above. Why should I recount how much and how great a sum he expended from the treasury of blessed James, and much from his own resources, in order to bring his most holy and just desire to fulfillment? Or why recount the many and severe labors and dangers of his canons [Col. 1057C], whom he repeatedly sent to the Roman court in order to obtain this? I, Gerald, have myself experienced no small part of these.

In short, the aforesaid archbishop of the Church of blessed James and legate of the Holy Roman Church showed such humility to the Roman Church that, although his Church excelled all the other churches of Spain in honor and wealth, it nevertheless surpassed them all in humility and service toward the Roman Church. Therefore, as Scripture testifies when it says, “Humility conquers all,” and elsewhere, “He who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV.11), the apostolic Church of blessed James was exalted through humility.

Indeed, the Almighty, by whose will all things are ordered, willed this arrangement: that he who had planted this vineyard should himself eat of its fruits and delight in its glory. For the aforesaid archbishop had long ago planted this vineyard and frequently cultivated it with great labor; and in his time the Church of blessed James, glorious through the fruit of this vineyard, was raised to metropolitan dignity [Col. 1057D]. The archbishop himself also attained the summit of greater dignity, as legate of the Holy Roman Church over the provinces of Mérida and Braga.

O that divine mercy may grant a longer span of life to so ready and useful a cultivator, so that, with God as author, the Church of blessed James, through the counsel and labor of that same cultivator, may in his own time be raised to still greater dignity! O that the Church of Compostela may obtain, while his life endures, what he still purposes and desires! Amen.

## Chapter XX. On the return of the bishop of Portugal and the granting of the cross

At about this time the aforesaid bishop of Portugal, wishing to return to Spain with Cardinal B., legate of the Roman Church, whom Pope Calixtus had sent to the Iberians, returned as far as the city of Oloron, where, seized by fevers, he remained for some time.

> Note: [Col. 1057D] He was called Boso.

At length, restored to health, as he was returning to Spain through the Alps, he learned that traps had been laid for him in many places. For spies sent for this purpose by the king of Aragon and the bishop of Jaca accompanied him, in order to announce his arrival at Jaca, at Estella, or elsewhere, so that he might be captured [Col. 1058B]. The aforesaid cardinal encouraged him to come with him into Spain. But the bishops of Pamplona and Lascuarre, to whom the tyranny of the king of Aragon was very well known, dissuaded the bishop of Portugal from knowingly falling into the hands of his enemies.

Indeed, neither the presence of the Roman cardinal nor that of the other bishops, nor his episcopal rank, would save him from capture; for the king of Aragon hated the clerics of the Church of blessed James beyond measure. The bishop of Portugal therefore adopted a prudent course and immediately reversed his journey, returning to the city of Auch, and from Auch to the city of Labourd [Col. 1058C]. Then, having laid aside his episcopal garments, he entered the Alps with two servants and a local guide who knew both the barbarous language of the Basques and the way through trackless regions.

> Note: [Col. 1057D] I read *Vasconum* (“of the Basques”) rather than *Blasconum*. Although Blascon is in Gaul, this is irrelevant, since it is an island off the route and does not possess, as the Basques do, a distinctive language, but rather the vernacular of the Gauls.

From there, through Gipuzkoa, Navarre, Biscay, and Asturias, along the sea that beats against the farthest rocks of Spain, he travelled now on horseback and now on foot. In those remote and pathless mountain regions live fierce men of an unknown language, ready for every crime; nor without reason are men considered savage and unrestrained in places so harsh and inhospitable. For this trackless path led through rocks, thickets, and desert places. Moreover, there the sea had stretched out certain arms to divide the provinces, making for those travelling that way a great and established abyss [Col. 1058D].

Yet the bishop of Portugal, fearing neither the harshness of the places, nor the savagery of the inhabitants, nor the swollen violence of the arms of Ocean spread about him, but trusting in the aid of the blessed apostle James, arrived at last, through the byways of mountains, valleys, and seas, at Carrión. Restored thus to the public road, and guided by God’s grace, he returned safely as far as Compostela. There he was honorably received in procession by the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, and by the canons of that Church [Col. 1059A].

He then offered upon the altar of blessed James the sealed aforesaid privileges of the archbishopric and legation. For Pope Calixtus had committed his own authority to the aforesaid bishop of Portugal: namely, that the bishop of Portugal, acting in the lord pope’s stead, should invest the archbishop of the see of Compostela with the cross, on the presentation upon the altar of blessed James of the privileges of the metropolitan see of Mérida and of the legation over the provinces of Mérida and Braga. This was done accordingly. One point alone had escaped our notice: that Pope Calixtus had granted to the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church the right to carry the cross before himself. But it then became known to us.

Moreover, before the archbishop and his canons, the bishop of Portugal related how he had spent the year in obtaining the archbishopric and legation, and how much and what great things he had endured [Col. 1059B]. He also stated how much still had to be added in order to complete what had been deficient. The aforesaid golden casket of nine marks, when it was given, had been accepted and received by Pope Calixtus from the bishop of Portugal and the abbot of Cluny as though it were entirely of gold; but its inner part was silver. When this was discovered, the bishop of Portugal had promised to give twenty ounces of gold to make up the deficiency.

Moreover, one fourth of the gold which Stephen of Besançon, the pope’s chamberlain, had received—namely two hundred ounces—had been found false. Therefore fifty ounces of gold had to be given, as well as the expenses of travel and labor which the bishop of Portugal had incurred, namely thirty ounces of gold. All this—that is, one hundred ounces of gold—the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church had to give to complete the payment, and did give [Col. 1059C].

Furthermore, the archbishop rewarded the bishop of Portugal generously for so great a labor. He gave garments to him and his servants; he also bestowed upon him a pontifical ring, benefices, and other recompense. For ever since the aforesaid archbishop had obtained the pallium from Pope Paschal, he had distributed much gold, silver, and other precious things so that the Church of blessed James at Compostela might have an archbishopric. By repeatedly distributing great and innumerable gifts to the Roman pontiff, Roman cardinals, others at the Roman court, and also to his canons and friends laboring again in this cause, he brought to fulfillment what he had long desired. The aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church also frequently distributes very much, in order that he may possess what has been obtained and obtain the other things still to be acquired [Col. 1059D].

Would that, through God’s mercy and with a longer life granted to him, he may, as a faithful steward, expend and distribute very much upon a similar work, so that in his time the Church of blessed James at Compostela may be raised to greater dignity!

## Chapter XXI. On Saracen ships captured by the people of Iria

From the time of King A., of good memory, Saracens from Seville, Almería, Lisbon, and other places bordering the sea had been accustomed to sail into Galicia. They had it readily within their power to destroy and burn churches; carry off whatever they could take thence; slaughter some people; lead others away in chains; capture women and children; bear away as booty whatever else was necessary to them; cut down vineyards and trees; set fire to houses; and assault and force entry into castles by repeated attacks, as happened at Santa María de Lancata and San Pelayo de Luto [Col. 1060A].

For this reason, from the middle of April until the middle of November, the shores of the Galician sea lay deserted and devastated. Such was the frequency of Saracen audacity. Therefore the aforesaid archbishop of blessed James and legate of the Holy Roman Church, pierced with fatherly grief because in the regions of Galicia there were no men skilled in the art of navigation, sent his envoys to Arles, Genoa, and Pisa, to bring from there the most skilled shipbuilders.

Why say more? A Genoese named Augerius, a most expert shipwright, built two ships at Iria, commonly called *galeae* (“galleys”); in their construction the archbishop spent much money and many resources [Col. 1060B]. In the same year in which they were built, the men of Iria, armed and accompanied by their aforesaid mariner Augerius at the archbishop’s command and exhortation, boarded the ships, went to the land of the Saracens, and in return slaughtered, captured, burned, and cut down. At last, after they had captured, destroyed, and burned certain Saracen vessels, they returned home, bringing other vessels with them and carrying abundant gold, silver, captives, and garments.

From that time the Ishmaelites did not dare invade the province of blessed James except with a multitude of ships. At a certain time, Saracens of Seville and Lisbon invaded the province of blessed James in twenty ships; surrounded by their own multitude, they ravaged the country on every side. Yet they captured few people, for the rest had fled to the mountains. Finally, when the others returned home, four ships remained, lingering around the islands of Ouras, Salvara, and Flamia.

> Note: [Col. 1059D] In Book I, chapter 103, it is called *Aonios*; in Pliny, *Aunius*; commonly, Ons. Salvara is today Sálvora, at the mouth of the river Ulla. In chapter 109, no. 5, Laonia is added, which is perhaps the Flamia mentioned here.

When the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church learned this, he hastened to Iria, summoned the people of Iria, and ordered and urged them to go and destroy the Saracens with the ships of the archbishop and their own ships. He also exhorted his soldiers to test their strength against the Saracens together with the people of Iria [Col. 1060D].

Then the people of Iria, having equipped the ships, launched themselves upon the high sea and sought the Ishmaelite vessels through the islands. When they found them below the castle of San Pelayo de Luto, they saw that they had put in to shore and were carrying provisions aboard their ships. As twilight was already thickening, the people of Iria took possession of the approaches to the sea, keeping watch so that the Saracens might not escape by night.

At dawn, the people of Iria, united in zeal and prepared for battle, formed their line and attacked the Saracen ships. When the Saracens saw them coming swiftly toward them from afar, they bent to the oars, ran to their weapons, and prepared for battle no less promptly [Col. 1061A]. But the people of Iria, as the attackers, rushed more boldly against the Hagarites; with mighty force they struck, damaged, and shattered the ships of the pagans with the iron beaks of their own vessels, and in the same encounter leapt aboard the enemy ships. They slaughtered some, cast others into the deep, and spared others as captives. Among the Ishmaelites, some tried to fight, others to row away, and others to escape by swimming.

Meanwhile one Saracen vessel, swifter than the rest, escaped from the ships of the people of Iria and fled; but the other three were held by the Christians. Sixteen Saracens were killed there; ninety-eight were captured, besides weapons and spoils; and Christians whom the Saracens were carrying away as captives were also freed. At last the people of Iria returned joyfully to their homes with the three captured vessels, the Ishmaelite captives, and a multitude of spoils [Col. 1061B]. They gave the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church, as their lord, a fifth part of all these things, together with what was owed to him by right of ownership of his ships.

Would that more and more Saracens might frequently come to capture Christians under such an omen, so that what they had been accustomed to do to Christians may henceforth be turned against the Hagarites!

## Chapter XXII. On the *cautum* between the Ulla and the Tambre

At the same time Queen U. came into Galicia in order to extinguish certain fires of discord already kindled to no small degree. This she partly brought to effect through the patronage and counsel of the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church. Meanwhile, while the queen remained at Compostela, the archbishop, striving earnestly for the exaltation and increase of the Church of blessed James in both secular and ecclesiastical matters, took counsel with the queen that she might grant to the aforesaid Church the *cautum* between the Ulla and the Tambre [Col. 1061C].

For the Church of Compostela possessed authority and jurisdiction on every side, but had not yet possessed the *cautum* between the Ulla and the Tambre.

> Note: [Col. 1061D] Another reading: *Uliam*.

This was a great and difficult thing to obtain. Therefore, in order that the Church of blessed James at Compostela might henceforth possess the *cautum* between the Ulla and the Tambre, the aforesaid archbishop of the Church of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church gave Queen U. from the treasury of St. James a silver table of sixty marks, and ten marks of silver from his own resources.

The queen, in turn, granted such a *cautum* to the Church of blessed James between the Ulla and the Tambre by firm and indissoluble written instruments: namely, if anyone coming from elsewhere should seize a pledge between the Ulla and the Tambre without the *sajón* of the archbishop of Compostela, in order to carry away booty from it, or should violate the *cautum* in any other way, he should pay six thousand shillings to the archbishop of the see of Compostela and his canons [Col. 1061D]. But if any of those dwelling between the Ulla and the Tambre should seize a pledge there without the *sajón* of the archbishop of Compostela, or should otherwise violate the aforesaid *cautum*, he should pay five hundred shillings to the aforesaid archbishop and his canons. You will find this written more firmly and fully in the text of the charter issued on this matter by Queen U.

Furthermore, the same queen gave to the Church of blessed James—that is, to its archbishop and canons—the land of Dormiana with its boundaries, its inhabitants, and her own *character* [mark or jurisdiction], as is set forth in the written instruments concerning these matters [Col. 1062A]. She also granted, by a firm and indissoluble writing, to the Church of blessed James—that is, to its archbishop and canons—both halves of the island of Laonia: one half, which Bishop Didacus, her predecessor of good memory, had lost; and the other half of the same island, which the Church of blessed James had lacked during these times of war. The writings and charters concerning all these matters are preserved in the Cartulary of blessed James. May the Church of blessed James as swiftly obtain these things, and others like them, through the counsel and prudence of the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church.

## Chapter XXIII. On the building of Honesto

[Col. 1062B]

Although the aforesaid archbishop, legate of the Holy Roman Church, devoted all his efforts to the building up and exaltation of his Church, as we have stated above, he nevertheless attended, as was fitting, to secular affairs as well, namely so that he might order ecclesiastical matters with his whole intention of mind and apply such care as lay within his power. He also abolished, so far as he could, wicked customs among secular people which ought to be abolished. For by command of the king of Spain the peasants from Triacastella to the Ocean Sea were required to assemble to build the walls of a castle called Honesti; these, constructed without mortar, of small stones with timbers inserted between them, continually threatened to collapse. The Spaniards indeed feared lest [Col. 1062C] Englishmen or Northmen, or other barbarian peoples, might attack Galicia by sea from that direction. For Honesti is, as it were, a key and seal of Galicia: if foreign peoples seized this place for themselves and established a fortification there, Galicia would lie ready to hand for invasion and devastation.

Fearing this, the king of Spain issued an edict that the farmers from the bank of the river called Issi to the sea should, twice yearly according to custom, assemble at a fixed time to rebuild the walls of Honesti, which were liable easily to fall and were ruinous. This was exceedingly laborious and difficult for those compelled to rebuild them—indeed, more than exceedingly so. Yet Cresconius, bishop of the Church of St James, of good memory, had partly fortified this same castle with lofty towers [Col. 1062D] and an exceedingly strong wall; and his successor, Bishop Didacus, had built part of the same castle. Nonetheless, the aforesaid settlers were still compelled at stated times to gather in order to rebuild its walls and towers. Therefore the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church, deeply sympathizing with them, took counsel with Adefonsus, the Catholic king of Spain, with his son-in-law Count Raymond, lord of all Galicia, with the canons of St James, and with the princes of Galicia; and he enclosed the aforesaid castle with a most solid wall and fortified it with lofty towers, as the structure shows even to this day. O how mercifully, how gloriously he acted, who freed the settlers of Galicia from so great a burden of labour [Col. 1063A] and abolished the customary work imposed by the royal edict!

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the Saracens wished to attack Honesti, and concerning the construction of the greater tower

At a certain time a multitude of Saracens attacked Galicia by sea; having defeated, captured, and destroyed the castle of St Mary of Lanzada, they turned their minds to besieging and taking Honesti. So great was their bold multitude. When this became known to the aforesaid archbishop, during the very solemnity of the passion of St James, while Matins were being chanted, he mounted a very swift horse at full speed and, accompanied by only three knights, went to Honesti, so that he might enter the castle before the Saracens [Col. 1063B] invaded or besieged it. The other knights and citizens of Compostela followed him. This blunted the boldness of the Ishmaelites.

Yet on the following night their leader, called *Alcaida* in his own language, boarded a light vessel with twenty highly skilled and experienced men and came to reconnoitre the site, the castle’s defences, and the number of its warriors, so that if he found anything insufficiently secure, he might hasten at dawn with his army to besiege the castle. But after he had thoroughly reconnoitred the whole area and learned that the archbishop had arrived there with a multitude of warriors, he returned and abandoned his design, not daring to attack the aforesaid castle.

Accordingly, from that day the archbishop considered and planned how he might fortify the aforesaid castle more securely. [Col. 1063C] For he feared lest either the Saracens or other peoples might unexpectedly enter the castle and wickedly lay waste the province of St James round about. Taking counsel, therefore, with his canons and the princes of Galicia, he constructed in the middle of the castle a tower surpassing all others in height and strength. He made very great expenditures on its construction; indeed, he made it pre-eminent above the others, as the head and mistress of the entire castle. For as the eagle surpasses and rules all other birds, so that tower surpasses and rules the other towers of that castle. A wise plan indeed: that tower will defend the other towers and the whole castle, if necessary, and will not fear the assaults of Saracens or other peoples. And [Col. 1063D] if at any time the archbishop of St James or his canons should come to the aforesaid castle, or if—may it not happen!—they should flee to it from an enemy attack upon their city, dwelling in that tower, as lords and possessors of the estate, they shall preside over and rule the whole castle. For Fortune’s wheel is changeable: now it flatters, now it threatens hardships. Therefore let each man strive to do what concerns his own interest.

## CHAPTER XXV. How he built new palaces

The aforesaid archbishop greatly exalted, enlarged, and enriched the Church of St James, both in ecclesiastical and secular matters. He was a man of great prudence and great discernment, skilled in ecclesiastical affairs [Col. 1064A] and sufficiently provident in secular ones, as is evident even to this day. Furthermore, since his palace at Compostela, where he lived, was rather unsuitable—for kings, consuls, and other great men from every quarter gathered there whenever they came to the city of Compostela—it was fitting that, as archbishop of St James and legate of the Holy Roman Church, he should possess a suitable, indeed a royal, palace. Accordingly, beside the church of St James he built spacious and lofty palaces, suitable and royal, sufficient, as was fitting, to receive a multitude of princes and peoples.

In a pillar of this palace he also caused a very deep well to be made by remarkable workmanship, as the structure shows. For it is customary for royal palaces to have water readily available for drawing, useful for many purposes. And because the choir of the church of St James was far from these [Col. 1064B] palaces, and it was very burdensome for him constantly to go down and up, back and forth, he built his chapel above, over the portico in front of which coinage is struck, on the front of the church of St James, to the right for those departing from that apostolic church. He then consecrated that chapel in commemoration of St Paul the Apostle, St Gregory, St Benedict, and St Antoninus. For previously, before the present church of St James was built, altars of St Benedict and St Antoninus had stood in the towers which Bishop Cresconius had built to fortify the apostolic church before the old little church of St James. The aforesaid archbishop had destroyed these towers while building this distinguished apostolic church. Therefore he made due recompense of honour to St Benedict and St Antoninus [Col. 1064C]: since he had destroyed their altars, their commemoration was to be observed in the aforesaid chapel. And so it was done.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the council held at Compostela

After some time had passed, the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church determined, by command of Pope Calixtus, to hold a council at Compostela on the fifth Ides of the next January [9 January], in the year 1121. He therefore summoned by letter to the council the bishops and abbots, together with the princes over whom he exercised the legation of the Holy Roman Church: namely P. of Lugo, M. of Mondoñedo, P. of Astorga, D. of Ourense, A. of Tui, P. of Braga, G. [Col. 1064D] of Coimbra, G., bishop-elect of Salamanca, P., bishop-elect of Ávila, and their abbots. Since some of these neither attended the aforesaid council nor sent representatives in their stead, he pronounced sentence against them at the same council and prohibited them from performing episcopal and priestly office until they had made satisfaction to him.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the lord pope’s letters

At the same time Pope Calixtus, out of an affection of love, sent the following letter to the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church:

> “Calixtus, bishop,” etc.
>
> “To the special brotherhood,” etc. See under Paschal II, no. 144.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the patriarch’s letter

[Col. 1065A]

Vermundus, patriarch of Jerusalem, also sent the following letter to the same archbishop.

### Concerning the oppression of the city of Jerusalem

> “VERMUNDUS, by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem, and G., prior of the most glorious Sepulchre, and the community of canons of the same place, to DIDACUS, by God’s providence archbishop of St James and legate of the Holy Roman Church, and to the venerable college of canons of the same see, together with all abbots, clergy, barons, and people subject to him: may you see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.
>
> “The fame of your goodness and prudence has often reached our ears; but recently, when our brother R. arrived and told us the same things, and greater things besides, love for your holiness took deeper root in our hearts. Because you received our messengers, treated them honourably, and bestowed benefits upon them, and, in our place, for the love of God and reverence for the glorious Sepulchre, benefited others by word and deed as a merciful Father, we humbly supplicate you; we render countless thanks to God and to you; and, prostrate at your feet, [Col. 1065B] we humbly ask that you continue to do the same.
>
> “But because we cannot repay you for these things, we have resolved to pray continually for you and for the condition of your Church; and we entreat that we may receive the same from you. We ask to be protected by your prayers and temporal arms, and that the hungry may be sustained by your alms and by the holy exhortations which you offer to the other faithful. Nor have we written this without great grief. For, because of our sins, we are afflicted more frequently than usual by various scourges, God permitting it. For the sky has withheld its rain for four years, and our land has not yielded its fruit as it was accustomed to do. Whatever the land did produce, though little, locust and caterpillar, innumerable in number, consumed, ears and stalks alike.
>
> “What shall we say of hostile incursions? We are surrounded everywhere by Saracens. Babylon lies to the east, Ascalon to the west, Assur on the seacoast, Damascus to the north. Why recount the treacherous kingdoms and the countless other enemies who assail us without ceasing? We are attacked daily, slaughtered daily, taken captive; deprived of our heads, we are handed over to wild beasts and birds; we are sold like sheep. In short: for the name of Jesus, before [Col. 1065D] we abandon the holy city of Jerusalem, the Lord’s Cross, and the most holy Sepulchre of Christ, we are prepared to die. Therefore, moved by pity, consider what is necessary for persons placed in such peril.
>
> “Most illustrious archbishop, prostrate at your feet and shedding tears—alas, how many!—we implore you: come to our aid. O most glorious champion of God! Let our prayers move you; let the lamentable cry of monks and canons move you; let the tears of widows and orphans move you. Hear the groans of the fettered; let the mournful lament of the poor, lying in the streets of Jerusalem, reach you; let the incomparable toil of the soldiers—alas, so few!—sink into your heart’s depths. What can we say of the sufferings of the foot-soldiers? They are shut up [Col. 1066A] in the towers and walls of Jerusalem and in caverns of the earth, praying daily for you and awaiting your help, like doves at their windows, devoted only to the Lord.
>
> “With whatever eyes you can, look above all upon the most holy places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, and the rest. Let these stir your minds! Venerable Father, why is there hesitation to die at Jerusalem for the name of Jesus, where the Son of God did not hesitate to be spat upon and crucified for us? We believe that God has preserved you to accomplish His work. Therefore, dearest brother, labour with the clergy and people entrusted to you, that you may come to Christ’s army and speedily aid us; or, if you cannot come yourself, send those whom you can. God is witness that we have not written this without great grief.
>
> “For no one dares leave the walls of Jerusalem or the other places, except with an armed force of knights or foot-soldiers, even for a distance of one mile—and less. We are compelled to share with them what we ourselves used to eat. Indeed, the Saracens scarcely fear to come as far as the gates of Jerusalem. Therefore, if you delay coming, we fear that you will lament with great mourning over the dead of Jerusalem—alas, too late!—because there was no one to help. Nor will you be free from responsibility for our death, since, though called upon as advocates, you were unwilling to bring aid. Nothing now remains for us but to undergo death or, if it be permitted, to flee across the sea—which may it not happen! Consider what must be done. For if you had not heard our cry, or had not seen our messengers or letters, perhaps you would have had some excuse; but what excuse will you have henceforth? Come, come.
>
> “All who come [Col. 1066C] to our aid, we release, by God’s help, from the bonds of all sins for which they have received penance, and lay them upon the shoulders of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Consider with what great blessing those ought to be filled who help those coming or wishing to come, who give them sound counsel to come, or who preserve their possessions in peace; and observe, as a just judge, with what sword of anathema those who hinder them or seize their possessions ought to be struck. Farewell.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the discord and reconciliation of the archbishop and the queen

At that time Queen U. came into Galicia to suppress the rebellion of certain princes and to calm Galicia, inflamed by the frenzy of discord. She seized Count M. and held him in fetters until, through the hand of the aforesaid archbishop of the Church of Compostela, he restored castles to her and paid immense sums of money. After this, while the queen lingered for a long time at Compostela, a spark of discord began to arise between the archbishop and the queen. For it was said that the queen was deceitfully plotting the archbishop’s capture or death, if she could accomplish it. On account of this rumour the archbishop was surrounded by an armed force of knights and citizens. A certain member of the queen’s household, having by chance heard evidence of this plot when he entered more private parts of the court—as one belonging to the inner circle—had seriously related it to a close associate of his in the archbishop’s household.

[Col. 1067A] When the report of this became widespread, inquiry was made into the source of so great an evil. Then that man of the archbishop’s household, a knight, stepped forth into the midst and disclosed what he had heard, from whom, and in what manner. For he preferred to reveal the plot rather than betray his lord. But the man who had first disclosed the evidence of the royal plot, seeing that he would deservedly incur punishment if he agreed with his accuser and acknowledged himself author of so grave a charge, began more vigorously to deny it and to swear that he had never uttered such things.

What more need be said? Though the archbishop neither ordered nor forbade it, a judicial duel was entrusted to the queen’s judgment. The archbishop’s knight finally won the triumph of victory, and the queen’s knight—despite the archbishop’s prayers being rejected—was justly blinded. Thus what had previously been reported under a veil concerning treachery was openly revealed once suspicion had been removed. [Col. 1067B] Yet the queen asserted by every means she could that she had neither devised nor wished such things.

Then, to remove entirely the cloud that stood between herself and the archbishop, she began to entreat the archbishop with prayers, enlisting as helpers Henry, abbot of St John of Angély, and Stephen, chamberlain of Cluny, men of great learning and authority. Through them the queen earnestly sought the renewal of a pact of peace between herself and the archbishop. For she knew that without the archbishop she could in no way retain the kingdom of Galicia. Therefore, both in person and through the said helpers and others, she strove not to be deprived of the archbishop’s protection.

At the intercession of these and others, the archbishop yielded to the queen’s requests. In the presence and testimony of the abbot of Angély and the chamberlain of Cluny, who were then at Compostela, the queen established a covenant of concord with the archbishop and promised before the aforesaid witnesses that she would be faithful and friendly to him. She also granted the aforesaid archbishop lordship over all Galicia. She ordered all her princes to perform homage to him, and so it was done. In obedience to the queen’s command, Arias Petrides, prince of Lupaia; Fredenandus Joannis; Veremudus Suarizi; Joannes Didacides; and the other princes of Galicia performed homage to the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 1067D] and faithfully subjected themselves and their possessions to his dominion. They acknowledged him as lord, patron, king, and prince, while preserving their fidelity to the queen, by whose will these things were done. They further added that if the queen presumed to inflict injury or violence upon the archbishop, they would all oppose the queen as rebels, in whatever manner the archbishop commanded them, and, rendering faithful homage to the archbishop, would faithfully obey him. That they would do so was established by their oath.

At the queen’s request, this condition was also added to the covenant: if the queen should by any deceit be found guilty of these acts, the abbot of Angély and the chamberlain of Cluny, persons of such great reverence [Col. 1068A] and learning, should proclaim to the lord pope, the abbot of Cluny, bishops, kings, and princes of the land the terms of so great a covenant and the abhorrent crime of so great a betrayal, so as to make all men hostile to the queen as a violator of so great a covenant. Compelled also by the queen’s own prayers, they established the same covenant and gave the kiss of peace to the archbishop, agreeing that, if the queen were guilty of this breach, they would strive by every means in their power, as though acting for themselves, to avenge so great a crime and give the archbishop such assistance as they could.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the destruction of the castle of Raneta, and another on the bank of the Issi

[Col. 1068B]

As a result of this covenant between the archbishop and the queen, the bond of fidelity and friendship became so strong that the archbishop rescued the kingdom of Galicia from the fury of rebellious tyrants. He also razed to the ground castles that were useless to the Church of St James and hostile to the queen. In Taberolo, Federnandus, son of the consul Peter, had built a castle called Raneta; and because he opposed the church of St James in certain matters, it was destroyed by the archbishop.

Furthermore, Count M., who through the archbishop’s intervention had escaped the queen’s chains, was inflamed by ambition for the kingdom. He strove, prone to every crime, to regain what he had been compelled to surrender when captured by the queen. Thus he disturbed with the provocations of war Castellam—[Note: That is, a territory so named in the diocese of Ourense.]—Decia, Mount Rosus, Lemavos, and the adjacent districts; [Col. 1068C] and he violently seized no small part of them. He also built a castle on the bank of the Issi, which, like a robber in a forest, lay in wait against the honour of St James and travellers on the public road, being a dwelling-place of plunderers and bandits.

When, at the archbishop’s instigation, a covenant of peace and affection was restored between the queen and her son, King A., the mother came with her son into Galicia to eradicate the rebellion of Count M. They then sent entreating letters to the archbishop, asking him to extend a helping hand to subdue the cruelty of the aforesaid tyrant. The archbishop therefore gathered a multitude of the citizens of Compostela, summoned the princes of Galicia subject to his lordship, and hastened with countless knights and foot-soldiers to besiege and destroy the castle on the bank [Col. 1068D] of the Issi. Nor did this lack its effect. On the very day on which it was besieged, the men of Compostela, attacking repeatedly, yielded neither to wounds from weapons or stones nor spared the boldness of those under siege. They pressed on, rushed in, and thirsted for the blood of the besieged.

At last, after very many within had been wounded and killed, the Compostelans burst through the castle gates and walls in a single assault and entered the castle. They captured the enemies, seized their spoils, and utterly destroyed the castle. The archbishop made the outcome of this affair an example to the other princes of Galicia, lest they presume to build castles near the honour of the church of St James [Col. 1069A] or become rebels against him whom they ought to obey. [Note: Here, through I know not what carelessness of copyists, the agreement of Mauritius of Braga, placed in Book I, chapter 81, no. 3, p. 145, has been inserted.]

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning later oaths made contrary to earlier ones

Because the queen had repeatedly compelled the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church to make later oaths contrary to earlier ones, he thought it worthwhile to obtain from Pope Calixtus letters of this kind, which would confirm the earlier oaths and render the later ones void, as oaths extorted by force.

### Concerning confirmation of the earlier oath and annulment of the others

> “Calixtus, bishop,” etc.
>
> “Illefonsus, king of illustrious memory,” etc. See [Col. 1069B] under Calixtus, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 84.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Counsel of the cardinal B. of Rome

> “BOSSO, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, servant and legate of the Apostolic See, to A., archbishop of Compostela, greetings.
>
> “Having seen the letter of your affection and heard the words of the bishop of Portugal, we earnestly desire what he has reported to us. But you must take the utmost care not to begin rashly, because snares are being laid for you on every side. Therefore make especial use of our counsel, as our venerable brother, the bishop of Portugal, will inform you on our behalf.
>
> “As for the cross which, through him, we instructed you to have made for us, we repeatedly ask you to ensure that it is made carefully and quickly. We advise you to make concord and peace with the queen, while preserving your rank and honour. The reason we commanded you to send legates to the council is that through them we might communicate to you the counsel which we are sending through the bishop of Portugal. Farewell.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the friendship of D. [Note: Deusdedit, mentioned above, chapter 8.] the Roman cardinal

> “To DIDACUS, by God’s grace most reverend archbishop of St James, enemy of every vice, D., cardinal of St Lawrence in Damaso, sends greeting and pure friendship.
>
> “I think it is not unknown to you, dearest lord, how faithful I have been to your dignity in all things, and how diligently I have laboured for your advantage; and, although bodily absence separates us, I shall continue to labour devotedly so long as I live. This has been so since you deigned to number me as a brother in your holy [Col. 1069D] fellowship.
>
> “But now, because some expanse of lands separates us and we cannot see your long-desired face, do not disdain to inform us by letters sent concerning your welfare. Do not hesitate to send your affairs, in which I may supply counsel or aid, to your canon; for I shall most willingly give my service. Furthermore, as one brother entreats brothers, a canon canons, and a friend friends, I humbly beseech you to do, through the bearer of this little letter, what I entrusted to you, according to your customary kindness [Col. 1070A] toward me, and to show him honour for the sake of our friendship. Greet Cardinal Peter and Robert of Salerno.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the friendship of P., abbot of Cluny

> “To the most reverend Father, lord D., archbishop of St James and legate of the Holy Roman Church, whom I embrace with all my heart, Brother P., unworthy servant of the brothers of Cluny, offers devoted service of will and faithful prayers.
>
> “Your faithful devotion and sincere affection toward us place us greatly in your debt. For our brothers returning from you tell us that we are always in your heart and on your lips. Therefore we pray that almighty God, who inspired this desire in your heart, may grant us, through the prayers and merits of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and of St James, before whose most sacred body you preside, the means of seeing you and may allow us, before we depart this life, to speak face to face.
>
> “Accordingly, both we and our whole congregation always remember you in prayers, alms, and every other benefaction; and we humbly pray that almighty God, author and lover of peace, may grant you peace and prosperity. We wish you to know that in place of our dearest brother Lord Dalmacius, whose loss deeply grieves us, we have sent to you the bearer of this letter, Lord Hugh, whom we love greatly. Through [Col. 1070C] him also, since he is most dear to our heart, you will be able to send us every indication of your favourable disposition. May Christ Jesus, the supreme pontiff, deign to govern and exalt your episcopate in peace. Farewell.”

### Concerning the friendship of G., duke of Aquitaine, and others

> “G. [Note: William VIII, duke of Aquitaine], by the grace of God duke of the Aquitanians, to the archbishop of St James: may you be crowned with glory and honour.
>
> “I do not wish your prudence to be unaware that the queen has fulfilled none of the things which she promised me in your presence and, as you know, said she would do; therefore I hastened to return home. On my return journey I did not dare come to you and speak with you, both from fear of the queen herself and of the king of Aragon; and I bore this with sorrow.
>
> “Now I ask your vigilant care—whom I love greatly, as you will be able to prove by experience, you who surpass all those whom Iberia contains in dignity and power of your order—that, first for God’s sake and then for mine, and because it is just, you support and defend the queen’s son and prevent his disinheritance. For it has been reported to me that the king and queen have made peace and joined together in a plot to destroy him.
>
> “Therefore gain eternal glory by assisting that orphan, and speak concerning this matter with Count Peter of Galicia and all the friends of the aforesaid boy. If, after taking counsel with us and them, you wish to defend him, I approve that he should remain [Col. 1071A] in your hand and custody. But if your judgment sees that he can have neither refuge nor such assistance as would keep him safe and in honour, I humbly entreat your friendship to endeavour to send him to me by ship. For if I live, I shall ensure that he becomes his grandfather’s heir.
>
> “Therefore, concerning one of these two alternatives—whether you will retain and protect him until I come, or whether, after hearing the counsel of those whom I have named, seeing that it is not good for him to remain with you, you decide he should be sent to me—inform me as quickly as possible by letter. May your dignity and worth flourish.”

### Likewise, concerning the friendship of B., Roman cardinal

> “BOSSO, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and dearest friend D., archbishop of St James, greeting.
>
