> “We have found your most intimate friendship to be sufficiently useful and honourable to us and to the Roman Church. Therefore we preserve it with inward affection and lasting remembrance. Through our messenger we have sent faithful reports to the lord pope concerning the generosity, affection, and reverence which you have shown to St Peter and to us. The lord pope received this most gratefully and, as your cleric Laurentius, who was present at the curia, can tell you, gave abundant thanks before his whole court and promised to show the fullness of his benevolence toward you and toward your Church.
>
> “Concerning the progress of our undertaking and God’s army, and also concerning the council which, God willing, we propose to hold at Toulouse on Sexagesima Sunday, [Note: A day entirely different from that of the other published Council of Toulouse, and especially a different year. Bosso the cardinal therefore indicates another Council of Toulouse after the year 1119, of which alone there is mention among the authors.] [Col. 1071C] the venerable brother Maguelonne bishop, bearer of this letter, will report to you as one familiar to us reports familiarly to us. We ask you to take care to show him, for our sake, honour and the kindness of service. When he returns, we ask that through him you communicate to us by your letters all your wishes and whatever you may desire from us through your diligence.”

### Letter sent by the countess of Flanders to the archbishop on behalf of her nephews

> “To the archbishop of St James, her special lord, C., countess of the Flemings, sends greeting with the service of affection.
>
> “If you enjoy prosperity, I rejoice with you; if you suffer any adversity, I grieve with you. For the Apostle says: ‘Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep’ (Romans 12:15). Beloved lord, I offer manifold thanks to your nobility because, as has been reported to me, you are bringing up with especial kindness and mercy the children [Note: namely, Alfonsus and Sancha, children of Count Raymond and Urraca.] of our brother Count R., in a manner fitting to their youth and to your own distinction. I now entreat your goodness to inform us by writing, if it pleases you, concerning everything that bears upon their childhood.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Consecration of M., elect of San Andrés de Espinareda, as abbot

[Col. 1072A]

At the same time Martin, elect of the monastery of St Andrew of Espinareda, situated in the diocese of Astorga, came to the church of Compostela to be consecrated abbot by the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church. The bishop of Astorga was hostile to the aforesaid elect; therefore he maintained that Martin’s election should be annulled and that he was unworthy of ecclesiastical prelacy. But the elect fled to the church of Compostela.

Then the archbishop, so as not to appear to inflict an injury upon the bishop of Astorga, sent him letters announcing the arrival of the elect of Espinareda and the reason for his arrival. Finally, he added that if the bishop of Astorga, or anyone else, [Col. 1072B] whether cleric or layman, had a charge to bring against the aforesaid elect of Espinareda, he should come before the archbishop at an appointed time, where the cause of both parties would be examined with the utmost justice. But when neither the bishop nor another person appeared to challenge the elect—although the bishop sent letters that he should not be consecrated—since no one may accuse by letters, the aforesaid elect was consecrated abbot by the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the queen’s arrival in Galicia

At the same time the same archbishop urged the queen, both by letters and messengers, to return to Galicia. Certain princes, lovers of discord rather than peace, had fomented rebellion [Col. 1072C] against the queen and her supporters. They had also built fortified places and, as their power enabled them, had turned concord into discord. But the archbishop everywhere opposed them, crushed their unbridled audacity, and restored peace as far as he could.

When the queen came into Galicia with her son—for they were then joined by a covenant of peace—the archbishop, with his army and the men of Compostela, besieged and destroyed the castle which Count Munio had built on the bank of the Issi. The other castles held by the tyrannical rebellion of that count or of others were likewise captured, and some were destroyed. At last the queen came to Compostela with her son and the princes of Galicia.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the arrival of Cardinal B. at Compostela and the consecration of the elect of Ávila

[Col. 1072D]

At that time Bosso, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, visited the thresholds of St James and was honourably received by the archbishop, as was fitting; with him came G., bishop of Lescar. The other bishops also assembled there: namely P. of Braga, A. of Tui, D. of Ourense, P. of Lugo, M. of Mondoñedo, H. of Portugal, P. of Segovia, and S., elect of Ávila, so that he might be consecrated bishop by the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela, as his suffragan. [Col. 1073A] Since they maintained that he had been elected by lot, the matter of his election was discussed at length and determined in the presence of so many worthy pillars of the holy Church. With the assent of the aforesaid cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, the aforesaid elect was consecrated bishop by the archbishop of Compostela and the other bishops.

At his consecration he promised the following obedience to the church of Compostela and its archbishop:

> “I, Sancius, to be ordained bishop of the church of Ávila, promise that I shall perpetually render to the church of Compostela and to its rulers, in the presence of Lord Archbishop D., the subjection, reverence, and obedience established by the holy Fathers, in accordance with the precepts of the canons; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning the council to be held at San Facundo

[Col. 1073B]

After his consecration, the Roman cardinal and legate, the archbishop and legate of Compostela, together with the other bishops, the queen and her son King A., and the princes of Galicia, deliberated at length concerning the condition of the holy Church and the kingdom of Spain. To confirm more sacredly the arrangements of this matter, it was determined that the same cardinal should hold a council at San Facundo on the eighth day before the Kalends of the next September [25 August]. All bishops and abbots from Burgos to the Ocean were summoned to that council. But why the archbishop of St James, together with many others, was absent from this council will be indicated by what follows.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the covenant of the archbishop and the queen

[Col. 1073C]

Between the aforesaid archbishop of the see of Compostela, legate of the Holy Roman Church, and Queen U., how often bonds of concord had been ratified by oath we have repeatedly indicated briefly. For fear and suspicion lest a woman’s mind should resort to its customary weapons, namely fraud, the archbishop, repeatedly urging the bonds of peace between himself and the queen, had renewed them again and again by oaths, and had confirmed them when renewed. In this way he had drawn almost all the princes of Galicia, Campania, and Castile to his side, and had bound them to himself by oath: if the queen should either seize the aforesaid archbishop or attempt to expel him from his honor, all who had sworn that this should not happen were unanimously to assist the archbishop [Col. 1073D] and oppose the queen. But who in Galicia loves truth and holiness? Who there follows justice and the other virtues? There almost all the followers of fortune pursue things contrary to virtue; very few are accounted faithful. There is none who follows good, not even one. Fearing their treachery, and taking such precautions for the future as lay within his power, the archbishop had taken as witnesses and guarantors of this compact, pledging their faith, En., abbot of Angoulême and compatriot of the queen herself, and S., chamberlain of Cluny. [Note: [Col. 1073D] Above, ch. 29.] A certain monk of Cluny also, named Gerard, had recently ratified the union of these compacts between the archbishop and the queen, so that he had made the archbishop, formerly fearful, courageous, and, formerly suspicious, steadfast. What does female folly not dare? What does the serpent’s cunning not presume? What does the most wicked viper not undertake? The examples of Eve, our first parent, sufficiently show what womanly contrivances dare, presume, and undertake. The exceedingly bold womanly mind rushes into what is forbidden; it violates sacred things and confounds right and wrong.

## CHAPTER XL. How the archbishop went into Portugal at the queen’s request

When, therefore, the aforesaid queen had resolved to go to Tuy in order to crush the forces of her sister, the queen of Portugal, she approached the aforesaid archbishop [Col. 1074A]—as her lord and protector, as her most faithful [Col. 1074B] helper and defender—with most flattering entreaties, asking that he not refuse to go there with her, taking with him his own army and the Compostelans. It was indeed difficult to compel the Compostelans, contrary to their laws and popular enactments, to undertake an expedition as far as Tuy. Yet they yielded to the archbishop’s prayers and gifts, and all came with him as far as Tuy. The archbishop labored especially to bring this about, both that he might render the queen faithful and useful service and that, after her enemies had been defeated, he might restore peace to Galicia.

For the queen of Portugal had formerly invaded Tuy and the surrounding region and had made them her own. When she learned of the arrival of the archbishop of Compostela, the queen, and her army, she immediately gathered her army and encamped on the other bank [Col. 1074C] of the Minho. On this side sat the army of the archbishop and queen; on the other, that of the Portuguese. Then the archbishop said: “If an opportunity is given us to attack the Portuguese army, victory is in our hands. But the Minho separates the two armies, and is like a wall to our enemies. Therefore let the Compostelans and Iriense men attempt to cross the river by boat and hasten to occupy the island which lies nearer to the Portuguese—for there was an island in midstream. Some should cross the river in boats, others by swimming.”

This counsel certainly pleased the queen and her princes. Without delay the Compostelans and Iriense men, with selected soldiers, board vessels. They attack the Portuguese boats moving along the Minho [Col. 1074D] and boldly seize the aforesaid island. When the Portuguese saw this, astonished at the unrestrained boldness of the Compostelans, they abandoned their camp and turned to flight. Then the army of the archbishop and queen crossed the river, entered the borders of Portugal, and set about plundering. Why say more? They burn, they pillage, and they invade the enemy’s land in hostile fashion.

At length the archbishop urged the queen to return with the Compostelans to his city. “Since,” he said, “we have overcome the ranks of our enemies and scattered them after overcoming them, since we have entered the borders of Portugal beyond expectation, the situation itself requires that I return home with the Compostelans; for it is not my concern to take part in plundering and [Col. 1075A] burning. I must attend to ecclesiastical affairs.” To this the queen replied: “Most holy and most reverend Father and lord, your counsel and help have brought us to so great a prize of victory, that we have both recovered what was ours and possess what belonged to our enemies. Your presence alone terrifies and weakens the strength of our enemies. If, therefore, you depart for your own lands and are absent, we certainly have reason to fear. For our enemies will recover their strength, and the end of our victory will be inglorious. Let the Compostelans—for citizens ought not to remain longer in camp—return home; but let the present right hand of your counsel and assistance protect and defend us.”

Yielding to these and other entreaties of the queen, the archbishop remained [Col. 1075B] in Portugal with his soldiers after the Compostelans had returned. At that time B., cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, sent him the following letter:

## CHAPTER XLI. Invitation to the council

“BOSSO, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his venerable brother and dearest friend D., archbishop of the Church of Compostela, greetings.

“Having gratefully received the letter of your affection concerning the successful outcome for the king and queen, we give thanks to Almighty God. Our mind is likewise stirred, to the increase of your honor, by your exertion, right, counsel, and assistance in their affairs. Moreover, do not let it escape your memory that, in order to settle ecclesiastical matters and correct the many abuses in the regions of Spain [Col. 1075C], we came especially to the counsel of Blessed James and to yours, and fixed the place and day of a council. As we invited you face to face in person, so now by these letters, invoking apostolic authority, we invite your presence and ask and exhort you, in fidelity to the Roman Church, that no occasion whatever keep you from that council. Know that, if you should not be present and the council should remain [void] through your absence, so great a loss to the Church will without doubt be imputed to you, and we fear that this will harm you in the future. We have heard from those who testify that they saw it that Burdinus, captured by the lord pope [Note: [Col. 1075D] In April, in the year 1121.], has been carried to Rome as he deserved.”

## CHAPTER XLII. On the capture of the archbishop while returning from Portugal

[Col. 1075D]

After this, when no small part of Portugal had been reclaimed, the archbishop and queen besieged the queen of Portugal herself in a castle called Lanhoso, and extended their camps as far as the Douro. In those same days the archbishop recovered in Portugal the honor of Blessed James, namely Braga, half of Corneliana, and the rest; and he distributed what he had recovered among his stewards.

While the archbishop of Compostela remained in Portugal in camp, a rumour, foreboding future evil, whispered that Queen U. was contriving the archbishop’s capture. When the archbishop heard this through the reports of many, he shrank from believing so great and abominable a crime [Col. 1076A]. The queen of Portugal herself also informed him through her messengers of the capture and its manner, saying: “Let the archbishop beware; for unless he does, my sister will without doubt seize him. Those intimate with her who participated in the planning of this crime have themselves explained to me the manner of his capture. Therefore let him flee to any one of my castles, that he may not be seized. Or let him return to his city in my ships; otherwise, once he crosses the Minho, he will be delivered into captivity.”

When the archbishop heard these and similar things, he would not bring himself to believe them or withdraw himself from the queen’s service. Rather, he said: “To remove this cloud of suspicion from me, the queen has bound herself to me by oath in many compacts of peace and affection. Moreover [Col. 1076B], she has employed between herself and me so many and such great witnesses and makers of this compact that it is the mark of a mad mind to believe such things. Certainly, from the time when I made a compact of concord with her, I have served her earnestly and faithfully, and will serve her. Why, then, should she break out into so great a crime? Why should she incur the deed of Judas Iscariot? Why should she make God and men hostile to her? But if she has firmly resolved to lay hands on me and, like a second Jezebel, persecute the members of the Church in both lands, behold, it is better for me without fault to fall into her hands than to seem to transgress the compacts which I established with her; for God is able to deliver me from her hands.”

At last, as the archbishop and queen returned with their army from Portugal, they came to the Limia and, by way of Celanova, [Col. 1076C] to Castela, which lies on the bank of the Minho. Then the queen, being an artisan of deceit and a mistress of crime, ordered the archbishop’s soldiers at daybreak to cross the Minho; but she herself remained behind with her son the king and the archbishop. This they contrived so that, when she laid hands on the archbishop, the soldiers might not be able to resist so great a crime.

Accordingly, when the army had crossed the Minho and tents had been pitched on the opposite bank of the river, the aforesaid Jezebel immediately laid hands upon the archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church. Alas for the crime! A mind smeared with pestilential poison fears nothing, is ashamed of nothing, and recoils from no abomination. At first the archbishop began to warn her not to undertake so great a crime, nor so depart from faith and truth [Col. 1076D]. But “wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul” (Ps. I, 4); and: “Let him who does harm continue to do harm, and let him who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Rev. 22:11).

When the most wicked capture of the archbishop became known, the archbishop of Braga and the bishop of Ourense, who were with him, terrified, took flight. The queen had as accomplices and helpers in this most criminal betrayal Count Roderic, who had returned from Jerusalem the day before yesterday; Fernando João; João Diáquez; João Ramírez; Odoário Ordóñez; Arias Pérez; and others, all of whom held benefices from the archbishop after having sworn that they would be his friends and faithful men. They had also rendered homage to the archbishop [Col. 1077A] in this manner: if the queen presumed to lay hands upon him or expel him from his honor, all alike, with whatever means they could, were to aid the archbishop—their lord and patron—against the queen. From the injury done to their very head anyone may infer how great a spoil these traitors made of the archbishop’s clerics, knights, and servants. Captured with the archbishop were his three brothers, Muño Gelmírez, Peter, and another Peter, together with many others. Vermudo Suárez was also captured with him.

The archbishop was then taken to the castle of João Diáquez, called Orzilion; and from there, under the custody of that same João, now separated from his clerics and soldiers except for two or three, he was transferred [Col. 1077B] to a castle called Cira. This Vermudo had built, with the permission of the archbishop and the canons of Blessed James, in the land of that apostle; but, forced by his captivity, he had now surrendered it to the queen.

After the rumour of so great a crime flew through Compostela, it shook all minds while the solemn rites of Mass were being celebrated on the feast of St Mary Magdalene. My pen is plainly insufficient to tell how great the grief and sorrow were in the church of Blessed James. At once the whole city rushed to the church; they weep and lament at the fraud inflicted upon the Lord and their archbishop, calling the queen an apostate, a violator of peace and faith, and a disturber of all Spain. Some virtually [Col. 1077C] threaten her unless she frees the archbishop. Finally, clergy and people having assembled together, they take counsel, and by common agreement four canons and as many citizens are delegated to inquire of the queen why she had seized the archbishop and what she intended concerning his freedom.

But her heart was hardened like Pharaoh’s heart. She thirsts for money; her bloody rage thirsts and pants to destroy the honor of Blessed James. Yet God protects those who hope in him. After the clergy and people of Compostela had been told what the queen intended concerning the archbishop, the canons immediately assembled in the canonical house. They bound themselves by oath to labor in every way for the archbishop’s release and, if necessary, to give both their inheritances and their possessions for him. This strongly encouraged the laity to do the same. [Col. 1077D] Who can count the tears of the whole city? Who can adequately recount the groans and entreaties daily made in the church for the archbishop? Who does not know that clergy and people alike were in mourning and distress? You could see all things full of tears, all desolate, all bereft of their shepherd.

After the queen entered Compostela by night, on the following day, which was the solemnity of Blessed James, all the canons laid aside their festive expression and dress, clothed themselves in black capes, and, displaying grief, comported themselves mournfully. This greatly displeased the queen and her accomplices. For such tumult among clergy and people often arose in the apostolic church [Col. 1078A] that the authors of so great a crime feared punishment might return upon their own heads. Then the canons and citizens approached the queen with great supplication and entreaty, asking her to state what answer she would give concerning the archbishop.

She had already acquired the castles of Blessed James, namely Honesto and St Mary of Lanzada, from Muño Gelmírez, the archbishop’s brother, whom she had captured with the archbishop. Then Jezebel, as though satisfying clergy and people, answered: “Behold, the archbishop may choose to enter into a compact with me and settle his release: either, concerning all matters for which I summon him to answer, let the archbishop answer and satisfy me fully; or let him, after the accusation concerning his captivity has been buried by his own oath and that of the canons, submit to the examination of my mercy [Col. 1078B]. Let him choose one of these; otherwise he shall remain in captivity.” But she said this deceitfully, in order meanwhile to have him transferred to the castle of St Mary of Oteres [Note: [Col. 1077D] At Autares, as we noted in Book I, ch. 90, no. 3.], to overthrow the honor of Blessed James utterly, and to endeavor to consign some canons and citizens to chains, strip others of all possessions, and expel others from the church.

The canons, together with citizens, were sent to the archbishop as bearers of this twofold proposal. The queen forbade them to have any discussion with the archbishop on other matters, or to be granted leave to speak with him about anything beyond the aforesaid two-part proposal. She also sent with them a spy, namely her clerk Fernando Pérez, to be present at their conversation and to observe that they did not hold more or less conversation with the archbishop [Col. 1078C] than permitted.

When the archbishop heard the queen’s most impious proposal, he said: “We need counsel in these matters.” “But,” they said to him, “you are granted no leave to take further counsel or to hold further conversation.” Then the archbishop said: “The Almighty, who looks upon the broken and afflicted, will provide us counsel and aid. The things you have reported to me are evil: namely, that, either while held captive and stripped of my honor and possessions, I should enter into judgment with the queen contrary to laws and canons; or, after the complaint concerning so great a crime committed against me has been suppressed by an oath, I should accept the queen’s punishment—called mercy—as undefined and without appeal. Such mercy ought rather to be called impiety, indeed crime [Col. 1078D]. For what sort of mercy she has toward holy Church and its members, no distant examples need be sought: the effect of this matter in my own case bears witness. Neither alternative, therefore, is useful to me. It is not the act of a sound mind either to suppress by oath, contrary to the canons, the complaint concerning so great a crime committed against holy Church, or to regard the manifest impiety of Jezebel as mercy.”

While these things were taking place, B., cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, sent the archbishop the following letter.

### A letter of consolation to the archbishop in captivity

“B., cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his venerable brother and friend, most dear in Christ, D., archbishop of the Church of Compostela [Col. 1079A], legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and liberation.

“At first the report of your capture was not believed; but later, when heard on certain testimony, we were made sad by vehement grief, and we are no less astonished at the sudden and disgraceful perpetration of such deceit. For so great an injury done in your person to Blessed Peter and the Roman Church, we wished, as soon as we heard it, to exercise the justice of ecclesiastical vengeance with fitting punishment. But at the urging of certain of your friends—who are deeply grieved at this misfortune and, holding hope for your liberation, are laboring for it—we have deferred this punishment until the council. Henceforth, confidently put your confidence in him who said, ‘Take courage; I have overcome the world’ (John 16:33) [Col. 1079B]; for the prayer of the Church and your own prayer to God is and shall be for you. Write quickly, through the bearer of this letter or through any of your people, what you wish us to do in this matter.”

### On the release of the archbishop

Meanwhile the queen’s son, King A., deeply grieved at the treacherous capture of the archbishop—since the archbishop had baptized him and anointed him king—considered how he might free him. He had participated in so great a crime, but had not been able to prevent it. Chains were also being prepared for the king himself, but only after the archbishop’s capture had been accomplished. Therefore, after holding discussion with Count P., his guardian, Count M., and certain other princes of Galicia, he left Compostela and went to their camps, which were pitched on the bank of the Tambre. For they had foreseen between themselves [Col. 1079C] between themselves that, if the king separated from his mother on account of rebellion, the archbishop would immediately be released, whether the queen wished it or not; and the outcome proves that it was so.

For once it was announced in the city of Compostela that the son had departed from his mother because of discord and had gone to the tents of the counts, the boldness of maternal tyranny was immediately broken and confounded. Jezebel, guilty of so great a crime, fled with her accomplices to the church of Blessed James. Thus the wheel of fortune turns: those who were encouraged lose heart; those who had lost heart are encouraged. The queen’s party is confounded and trembles; the party of the king and archbishop is exalted and rejoices. How great the tumult, the rush, and the eagerness of all to pursue, despoil, and capture the queen’s men were, scarcely could even an eyewitness adequately recount. All run [Col. 1079D] to the church against the queen, hurling insulting words at her and threatening worse unless she frees the archbishop; with one mouth and one voice all unanimously cry out that the archbishop be released at once.

Why say more? The queen bursts into tears—partly from fear, partly because her treachery has been defeated. She swears that she had been compelled to commit so great a crime and transfers the blame for the whole deed to her accomplices. She cries out that the archbishop should be released and that the authors of the most criminal capture ought to be consigned to chains.

While this was so, behold João Diáquez, in whose custody the archbishop was held captive. Having brought with him certain captured compatriots of the archbishop, he had come to the city to confer with the queen [Col. 1080A] about how the archbishop should be taken captive on the following night to the castle of St Mary of Oteres, which is in the valley of Carcer. But the mercy of the Almighty ordained otherwise; human wickedness had expected otherwise. Therefore clergy and people, surrounding João and leading him as though a captive, urgently demand of the queen that, without evasion, willing or unwilling, she order the archbishop released; otherwise she herself and João would succumb to danger. Then the queen, compelled and unwilling, ordered the archbishop’s release. João, surrounded by the multitude of people and bound by oath not to flee, they hastened away to release him.

Thus, against the will and under compulsion of the queen and her accomplices, the archbishop was released. When he entered Compostela, although he had been held captive for no more than eight days [Col. 1080B], the joy and gladness among all were such that even the eloquence of Maro would fail in recounting them. Persons of every sex and age come to meet him; with tears poured out for joy, they eagerly desire to see and speak with their patron and archbishop. Him whose removal they had lately mourned, they now rejoice to have restored. The whole city rejoices and dances as though it had escaped the shipwreck of Charybdis. The entire clergy likewise, solemnly prepared and with the highest honor of procession, received him most honorably.

At length, after completing prayer before the apostolic altar and kissing the brethren, he approached the queen, who had concealed herself within the enclosure of the altar, and said to her: “I know indeed, queen, that compelled by the counsels of very wicked men you undertook this crime [Col. 1080C]; but what cause you had in this wickedness is unknown to me. Yet the merciful and compassionate Lord, with whom nothing is impossible, has freed me from this captivity. Following his example—for he says, ‘Forgive, and you shall be forgiven’ (Luke 6:37)—so far as concerns me, if you repent, I forgive and pardon you what you did against me. May God also grant you the disposition to restore to us the castles of Blessed James which you violently and unjustly extorted from our men, and to have peace with us.”

After this had taken place and a day or two had passed, the archbishop began more frequently to urge the queen to make peace with him and restore the castles of Blessed James. But the queen thirsted intensely for money and burned to retain the castles of Blessed James [Col. 1080D]. This was the principal reason why discord sprang up between them and the greater part of Galicia was ruined by the thorns of war. Yet the archbishop repeatedly appealed to the queen for peace and concord. But, such being the untamed mind of a woman, now she demanded that a thousand men, clerical as well as lay, be given to her as sworn guarantors; now she demanded the clergy and people of the entire city and suburb. Neither this nor that came about, because no immense sum of money was owed to her.

When the archbishop observed the queen’s disposition and understood that she would neither restore the castles nor be appeased without an immense sum of money, he immediately established peace with her young son, the king, and applied himself as strongly as he could to recovering the honor of Blessed James. Moreover, he attached to himself several princes of Galicia [Col. 1081A], namely Counts Pedro Froilaz, Muño, Gutierre, and Gómez; Arias Pérez, lord of Lupa, who had rendered the archbishop an oath and homage against the queen and for that reason adhered to him; Vermudo Suárez and others; as well as Queen T. of Portugal and Count Fernando. These and others the archbishop had as helpers in recovering and defending the honor of Blessed James.

Meanwhile Pope Calixtus of the Holy Roman Church sent this letter to the same archbishop:

## CHAPTER XLIII. On bishops suspended because they had not attended the council, and on the archbishop of Braga deprived of the legation

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Dignity and honor,” etc. See Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 137 [Col. 1081B].

## CHAPTER XLIV. Familiar letter of the lord Roman cardinal to the archbishop

“To DIDACUS, by God’s grace archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, from D. [DEUSDEDIT], cardinal of the Holy Roman Church: greeting and prosperity.

“Know that, on seeing your messenger, we rejoiced exceedingly, and for the Church of Blessed James, as was fitting, we have labored much with our associates and friends. Henceforth I direct you, as your brother and in every respect your most faithful friend, to serve our lord C. and the curia in such a way that you retain what you hold and acquire what you do not yet have [Col. 1081C]. Do not doubt that I labor unceasingly and faithfully for the Church of Blessed James. As for the revenues of my week, which I left in your power, I ask that you send them to me through the first pilgrims who come to us. Do not doubt that your canon Peter has labored greatly in the curia on behalf of you and his Church. For this reason we ask that you hold him dearer henceforth. Farewell. Do not hesitate to lend me, through him, seven gold pieces to pacify the curia, which he found exceedingly angry.”

### On the friendship of P., abbot of Cluny

“To the most reverend Father, joined to us in the charity of Christ, lord D., archbishop of St James and legate of the Holy Roman Church: Fr. P. [Pontius], unworthy servant of the brethren of Cluny [Col. 1081D], the service of most devoted goodwill and faithful prayers.

“Charity, which burns especially in your heart, has by no means learned to grow lukewarm or cold toward us and our entire congregation; rather, it continually endeavors to love us with a certain privilege of special affection. For although you are distressed by many tribulations, wearied with anxieties and most savage wars, and your glorious mind is struck and made anxious by the pressures of innumerable cares, nevertheless you most graciously and devoutly embrace us with particular pious love. Since this love is firmly founded upon the most solid rock, which is Christ, we rejoice, dearest Father, from the heart, to possess you as a singularly dear and faithful friend [Col. 1082A].

“Therefore we humbly and sincerely implore the most glorious excellence of your highness that, as you have already begun to love, you may love with diligent zeal the house of God and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose ministry we have undertaken through God’s authorship; and that, loving it with the devotion of piety, you may sustain it, so that through the intercession and merit of that same patron you may obtain the everlasting fruit of eternal reward. Nor should your venerable nobility doubt that we are wholly your heartfelt and singular friend, joined and united to your affection in the charity of Christ; and that we are always mindful of you in our prayers and other benefactions. Though absent from you in body, we are nevertheless present in spirit [Col. 1082B]. We also desire—and, if God grants it, earnestly ask—that you deign sometime to visit the house of Cluny, for we wish to see and embrace you. We desire that we, who love one another, may see one another; and that our whole congregation may be yours, since by benefits and outstanding devotion you show yourself wholly ours.”

### Again, the aforesaid cardinal to the archbishop

“To the venerable lord D., by God’s grace archbishop of Compostela, from D., cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso and of the Holy Roman Church: an indissoluble bond of love.

“How much affection and how much diligence, dearest one, we have devoted to the business entrusted to your messengers, the newly arrived messengers can adequately relate in order. We therefore direct you that, whenever any affairs press upon you, do not hesitate to send to our brethren [Col. 1082C], because we are always ready to obey your commands and diligently attend each day to your affairs as though they were our own. We therefore humbly entreat your kindness to take care to send what of our Week is with you through the bearer of this little letter or another trustworthy messenger; and we earnestly request that you treat this man with great honor. Moreover, we urgently ask your greatness to greet our most beloved brethren on our behalf.”

### Familiar letters of Pope Calixtus to the archbishop

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“This knight,” etc. See Paschal II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 140.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the decrees of the council held at Saint Facundus

[Col. 1082D]

“B., cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his venerable brother and dearest friend D., archbishop of Compostela, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting.

“By the letter which we sent to your affection through the bishop of Portugal, and now by the bearer of this letter, the Roman knight who comes from the lord pope to St James for the sake of prayer, we again transmit this letter to your brotherhood, so that through him you may write to us concerning both your will and that of the young king, and concerning what is to be reported by us to the lord pope. Command that the decrees of our council [Note: [Col. 1081D] Of the council proclaimed for 25 August of this year 1121; see ch. 38.] at Saint Facundus, which we transmitted to you through the Portuguese bishop, be maintained and observed throughout the regions of your jurisdiction, just as they were confirmed by us at the council through apostolic sanction [Col. 1083A].”

## CHAPTER XLVI. On P., archbishop of Braga, made a canon in the Church of St James

At about this time P. [Pelagius], archbishop of Braga, came to Compostela. As noted above [ch. 43], he had for a time been removed from the legation of the archbishop of Compostela. For after he had sent his clerics to Pope Calixtus and they had reported, by a certain crafty argument, hostilities between the archbishop of Compostela and the archbishop of Braga, the archbishop of Braga was temporarily removed from that legation, as stated above.

The pope also commanded the archbishop of Braga by letter [Col. 1083B] to restore the honor of Blessed James in Portugal—namely, that which his predecessor M., archbishop of Braga, had held in benefice from the same archbishop of Compostela and which this man was violently retaining. Therefore the archbishop of Braga established a compact of friendship with D., archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church; and, having been made a canon of the Church of Blessed James, he received in benefice from the same archbishop of Compostela half of the aforesaid honor, so that he might defend the other half to the best of his ability, as this document declares:

“I, P., archbishop of the Church of Braga, in my own person and not on behalf of the Church, receive from you, lord D., archbishop of the Church of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, and from your Church [Col. 1083C], as a benefice, half of the church of St Victor, which is called Braga; half of St Fructuosus with the estate of Montelios; and half of the estate of Corneliana with all their appurtenances. I receive them upon this condition: that I hold all the aforesaid things during my lifetime, and that, at my death, your Church receive them and possess them peacefully from my successors; and that I aid, defend, and protect, for the benefit of your Church, the other half of all these possessions which you currently hold. I, P., by God’s grace archbishop of the Church of Braga, confirm this with my own hand. Hugh, bishop of Portugal. O. Peter, prior of the Church of Braga. O. Nuno, deacon and canon of the Church of Braga, wrote and confirmed [Col. 1083D]. You have another similar instrument.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning G., bishop of Salamanca

“G. [Gerald] likewise, elected of the Church of Salamanca, consecrated bishop at Rome by Pope Calixtus, ratified this submission of obedience to the aforesaid archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church:

“I, G., bishop of the Church of Salamanca, promise that I shall perpetually render to the Church of Compostela and its rulers, in the presence of Lord D., archbishop, the submission, reverence, and obedience established by the holy Fathers according to the prescriptions of the canons; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar [Col. 1084A].”
