## CHAPTER XLIX. On the reconciliation of the archbishop, the queen, and the young king
Pope Calixtus had sent these letters to Boso, Roman cardinal and legate; to Bernard, archbishop of Toledo and legate; to the other bishops throughout Spain; and also to the queen, author of so great a crime, and to [Col. 1084C] her son the king, concerning the deliberation and restoration of the aforesaid archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church. For the archbishop himself, now consigned to that shameful captivity, had sent messengers to his nephew P., dean of the church of blessed James, who was studying philosophy in France, and had informed him of his captivity, its manner, and its cause. Taking with him certain canons who were studying with him, he came to Cluny. Thereafter, by the counsel and assistance of the abbot of Cluny and the community, and also of the princes of France and Burgundy, who embraced the archbishop of Compostela with the greatest affection, he approached Pope Calixtus and showed him the outrage which Queen Urraca of Spain had committed against [Col. 1084D] the archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church.

Accordingly, at his prompting and that of his companions, and because an indissoluble and fruitful charity of affection flourished between Pope Calixtus—both before and during his papacy—and the archbishop of Compostela—both before and during his archiepiscopate—and moreover because justice required it, the pope dispatched the aforesaid letters throughout Spain. When she had seen them, the queen, author of so great a crime, strove to make satisfaction and be reconciled with the archbishop. By flatteries and promises—such being a woman’s device—she laboured to win him over. But when she could not change him either by entreaties or promises, she immediately resorted to arms: she assembled an army, came to the castle of Cira, and thence to Taberolos, as though intending to invade the district of Salinas; then, ascending Mount Sacrum in rapid march, she encamped there with her army. With her were Count R., Count M., Menendus Nunizi, and many princes of Galicia with their companies.

When the archbishop learned this, he immediately assembled an army of cavalry, infantry, and men of Compostela, and encamped at the foot of the same mountain. The boy-king also, the queen’s son, together with Count Peter, Varemundus Petrides, Arias Petrides, and many princes of Galicia, had an immense multitude of cavalry and infantry, twice as great as the queen’s. The armies stood on either side: the one holding the mountain summits which they had occupied; the other preparing to cast them down from the crest of the mountain by fighting. This, indeed, was exceedingly difficult and [Col. 1085A] dangerous. Moreover, what supplied incentives for war to the king, the archbishop, and their army was that the queen was contriving to build a castle upon the slope of that mountain.

Thus armed companies on both sides first met one another in battle; and, when the twilight of night intervened, after some had been struck down on either side, they desisted from their undertaking. Yet battle was proclaimed for the next day, and each army was encouraged for war. Then the archbishop, seeing that war was to arise between mother and son and that very many people on both sides would perish, was moved by fatherly compassion. He turned his mind toward terms of peace and considered how the battle-lines of both might be dissolved. He begged the boy-king for peace and begged him to be reconciled with his mother. He also sent [Col. 1085C] messengers to the queen and advised her not to bring herself and her followers to ruin. He showed her the greatest dangers immediately before her unless she repented, and by strongly frightening her sought to incline her toward reconciliation and peace. But her heart was hardened and unrepentant.

Then the archbishop summoned the powerful and experienced men of both armies; and, having taken counsel with them, he urged them by every means toward peace. Why say more? From both sides he bound two hundred men by oath, that they should strive to the best of their ability to restore peace and eliminate the war then imminent. Great was the archbishop’s prudence, to avert the slaughter of so many men on either side and to turn discord into its opposite. These two hundred, by the archbishop’s counsel and assistance, appointed ten judges, who should more certainly examine under oath the matters of justice between the king and [Col. 1085D] the archbishop and between the queen, and, after examining them, decide them as justice dictated. It was also decreed that whoever—whether king or queen—refused to submit to their judgment or failed to carry out what they decided should be regarded as a violator of justice. Therefore they were to oppose every person who evaded justice, but aid the pursuer of justice as they would the Lord. This was established by oath.

Accordingly, in their first judgment the aforesaid judges ordered the queen, without delay, to restore to the archbishop the castles of blessed James—namely Honestum and St Mary of Lanzada—which she was holding by force. They further added that the queen should recover Lord Archbishop Diego and the honour of blessed James, which she had lost because of [Col. 1086A] the archbishop’s capture. But because the archbishop had little confidence in the queen’s faith and truth, an oath and written bond were obtained between the archbishop and queen, as it were an anchor of truth, lest she withdraw from the judgment’s sentence. The following is that document and agreement between the archbishop and the queen.

### The Queen’s Oath

“Era 1159. I, Queen Lady Urraca, give you, Lord Diego, archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church, my faith, by God the Almighty Father and by all His saints: that throughout my life I shall be your faithful lady and friend, as a good king is to his good archbishop; that I shall increase [Col. 1086B] your advantage and destroy your harm; and that, to the best of my power, I shall defend your life, your limbs, and the honour which you possess or shall possess, against all men and above all men, without deceit or evil intent. Neither through me nor by my counsel shall you be captured or expelled from your honour. Nor shall I ever make an agreement with any person to your detriment or to that of the city of blessed James throughout my life. If any evil be said to me concerning you, either I shall pay it no heed, or I shall bring you to answer it; and I shall accept concerning it the judgment which those who are parties to this agreement, both your men and ours, shall give me. Having received satisfaction at a suitable time and place, I shall stand by the aforesaid agreement throughout my life. You shall never come upon our military expedition [Col. 1086C] or into my court unless you wish to do so. And on Friday, within the octave of this Nativity of the Lord, I shall give you, the aforesaid Lord Archbishop D., your castles—namely Honestum and St Mary of Lanzada. And whatever you release me from under this pact shall stand released.”

“We, sixty barons and knights of Queen Lady U., swear to you, Lord Archbishop Diego, by God the Almighty Father and by all His saints, that if Queen Lady Urraca does not fulfil toward you what has been said above, we shall stand with you without deceit or evil intent.”

### On the Restoration of the Castles

As the queen had agreed in this document, she partly fulfilled it. For she restored the castle of Honestum to the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church on the aforesaid [Col. 1086D] Friday. She did, however, restore the castle of St Mary of Lanzada on the following day.

## CHAPTER L. On the Miracles Which Occurred During the Archbishop’s Captivity in the Presence of Saracens, and on One of Them Restored to Health

I consider it not unfitting to recall what happened during the aforesaid captivity of the archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church. The king of the Saracens, named Ali, who held sway over the Hagarenes on both this side of the sea and beyond the sea of Iberia, had sent Ishmaelite envoys, men distinguished and illustrious, to Queen Urraca and her son [Col. 1087A] on an embassy. As they made their way westward, having heard that the queen was staying with her son in the regions of Galicia, they saw very many Christian pilgrims going to and returning from blessed James for prayer. Astonished, they asked a centurion named Peter, whom they had as a Christian guide and protector among Christians and who was well skilled in their language:

“Who,” they said, “is this man whom so great a multitude of Christians visits with devotion? Who is this so great and such a one, whom innumerable Christians both beyond and on this side of the Pyrenees seek out for prayer? So great is the multitude going to and returning from him that scarcely is there open to us a free road westward.”

They were answered that this was blessed James, apostle of our Lord and Saviour, brother of John the apostle and evangelist, both sons of Zebedee; that his body lay buried in the regions of Galicia; and that Gaul, England, Latium, Germany, and every land of Christians, above all Spain, venerated him as its patron and protector. [Col. 1087B] The Ishmaelite people further learned that this same James had suffered under Herod in Jerusalem and had been brought to Galicia.

When they had arrived at Compostela, those who had previously marvelled at what they had heard were struck with great amazement upon seeing the apostolic basilica. “Ah!” they said, “how noble and glorious is the pre-eminent building of your James! On this side of the sea and beyond our sea, we have not seen anything comparable to it. By Muhammad, great glory has been bestowed upon him, if he is as mighty in heaven as you hold him to be illustrious on earth. What patronage, then, what help does he impart to those who honour and venerate him?”

To this the centurion replied in the Ishmaelite tongue: “By his merits and intercessions he obtains from our Lord Jesus Christ such grace that, through God’s mercy, he grants sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and health to lepers and to others afflicted by various kinds of disease. He succours and aids all who devoutly ask him; both beyond and on this side of the Pyrenees he is powerful through innumerable miracles. For he has freed persons bound and consigned to prison; he has healed others held by long illness; he has brought aid to some in their greatest difficulties. Everywhere on earth Almighty God displays His miracles through the merits and intercessions of blessed James. Therefore so great a multitude visits his body; therefore innumerable persons ask his aid with unwavering confidence.” [Col. 1087C]

At this the Ishmaelites were astonished and marvelled, and said nothing; they admitted that their Muhammad could do nothing of the kind. The centurion, indeed, being a most eloquent and prudent man, continually confounded the unbelief of the pagans and extolled the Christian faith by praises and assertions of truth. By the truest and most evident arguments, he demonstrated that the pagans were blinded by a cloud of ignorance and deceived by manifold error. The Ishmaelites did not dare in any way to oppose this, since they had before their eyes evidences of the truth and were amazed by so great a glory of blessed James.

Meanwhile the aforesaid archbishop was captured by the queen; [Col. 1088A] the church of blessed James sat in sorrow. Clergy and people were afflicted with excessive distress; peaceful conditions were disturbed; the apostolic province mourned at so great a crime; joyful things were exchanged for sad, and prosperity was darkened by adversity. Then the Ishmaelites—who had previously scarcely dared to mutter against the arguments of truth—heard that the archbishop of the apostolic see and legate of the Holy Roman Church had been treacherously captured by the queen. Mockingly they said:

“The archbishop of the apostle James and Roman legate, shepherd and protector of the apostolic church, is held captive by a woman. A great and abominable crime! If the apostle James, who, as you confess, restores sight to the blind and walking to the lame, is powerful, let him free him from womanly bonds. If he is powerful to loose the fettered, restore the sick to health, and bring aid, as you asserted, to all who ask him, let him aid his minister, who aids those beyond the Pyrenees. He who aids all, let him, if he can, aid his own bishop. Let him show the strength of his power in his bishop, whom so great a multitude of Christians visits and prays to. Let him free him, return him, and restore him to his church, that he may preside over, protect, and pacify his church and province as he did yesterday and the day before. Let him free him, lest his church waste away in sorrow and, wasting away, sink into eclipse.” [Col. 1088B]

Why linger over many words? The ingenious eloquence of the pagans in turn attacked the Christians; and unless the apostle had then and there brought aid, they crushed the faith of Christ as though a pestle striking from above were pounding barley-gruel. Yet the centurion confidently affirmed that blessed James’ patronage never failed those who devoutly sought it.

“What use,” he said, “is it to speak merely in words, or to dispute about God’s predestination? The depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge permits many things to occur, so that in them He may show the glory of His power through the merits and intercessions of His saints. He permits the ungodly to rage against God’s saints and permits the devices of their wickedness to take effect, so that the ungodly may perish in his ungodliness and the righteous, by God’s grace, may receive the fruit of his righteousness. Thus the Psalmist says: ‘I saw the wicked greatly exalted and lifted up; and I passed by, and behold, he was not’ (Ps. 36:35).” Likewise: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (ibid., v. 25).

[Col. 1088D] While the prayer of the faithful was continually prolonged with these and other words, after eight days the archbishop was freed from the queen’s captivity, as we have outlined above (ch. 42). Clergy and people of Compostela came out to meet him as he returned from captivity; the cloud of sorrow having been removed, joy and exultation arose. The church of Compostela rejoiced at the freeing of its shepherd, and the whole city celebrated in great joy.

At this the Ishmaelites said: “What is this? Why does such joy course through the minds of all? For whom is the glory of so great a procession being prepared?”

They heard from the centurion: “Blessed James the apostle has freed his archbishop from a woman’s bonds and restored him sound and unharmed to his church.”

On hearing this, the Ishmaelites, utterly astonished, marvelled exceedingly. “Truly,” they said, “the apostle James [Col. 1089A] has freed him and protected him from his persecutors; truly divine power has annulled devilish arguments and destroyed the serpent’s cunning. Foolishly we formerly assailed the Christians’ arguments; foolishly we hurled insults against the apostle James. Rightly is he held and praised by Christians as patron and protector, since he does not cease to aid them, being a pious and timely helper. Now the judgment of Christians and pagans [Note: [Col. 1089D] Supply ‘minds,’ or something similar.], though they differ in faith, nevertheless agrees; and manifold praise is rendered to blessed James by both. Both pagans and Christians become admirers and praisers of so great a miracle, and none of them doubts that it was done through blessed James.”

After this, while these same Ishmaelites remained longer at Compostela, a swelling abscess arose upon one of their necks. It appeared wholly incurable and deadly, for such a condition commonly closes the entrance to life. A widow regularly visited the same house in which they were lodging; she daily visited the apostolic thresholds with tapers and offerings, and, persisting in prayer, often spent the night there. Seeing this, the Ishmaelites asked whither and why the widow brought the aforesaid things with such care. They were answered [Col. 1089B] that she was entreating the mercy of blessed James the apostle by these and other offerings for the salvation of her own soul, of her parents, and of the other faithful. Perhaps the unbelief of the pagans would have dared to reproach and ridicule offerings of this sort, had they not seen the most evident miracle of apostolic power in the deliverance of the aforesaid archbishop and legate. Now, however, they dared neither to disparage the miracle nor to diminish the apostle’s glory.

Then he upon whose neck the abscess was swelling said: “I beg you, intercede for me with your apostle, whose patronage we see is at hand for those who seek it. Pray that he may deign to be merciful also to me, since through God’s mercy he is powerful. Carry also to his altar on my behalf this candle”—and he gave it—“and beseech him to restore me unharmed from the swelling of this abscess.”

At this the widow, smiling with joy, said: “I give thanks to God and blessed James, who has revealed to you the wonders of His power and the light of truth; yet He has not shown them to you fully.” Taking the candle, she touched his abscess with it and [Col. 1089C] made the sign of the cross over it. Then she went to the church and, as was her custom, offered her offerings and prayed. When her prayer was ended, she offered the candle which she had received from the Ishmaelite; she added prayer to prayer, begging blessed James to restore the aforesaid Ishmaelite to health and, through God’s mercy, to free him from the deadly plague of the abscess.

Hardly had the prayer been completed when the abscess’s swelling was emptied, and the Ishmaelite was restored to health. A scar remained, namely a sign of the emptied disease. Great and ineffable is God’s mercy, which does not refuse, through the sign of the cross—which according to the Apostle is foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:23)—to impart remedies of salvation even to the Gentiles themselves. Great also is the mercy of blessed [Col. 1089D] James the apostle, who never ceased to entreat his Lord for all who sought his help and to aid them with the grace of salvation.

After the Ishmaelite had experienced blessed James’ patronage and the removal of the deadly plague of his abscess, he and his companions rejoiced in astonishment at the excess of their joy and marvelled at the power of so great a miracle. They told the centurion and the other Christians what had happened and how, and declared that the apostle’s power had anticipated the aid of medicine. Why say more? Blessed James the apostle was praised and magnified by believers and unbelievers alike as a most merciful protector; all publicly professed the apostle James’ wondrous power through God’s grace and extolled him with fitting praises.

At last the Ishmaelites said: “As report had told us, we have seen the great mercy of this apostle in the freeing of your archbishop and likewise his wondrous power in our companion’s abscess. We bear witness that he is rightly sought in prayer by Christians beyond and on this side of the Pyrenees; rightly is he invoked with such devotion by the multitude of Christians; rightly is he called and regarded as patron and protector by Christians. We wondered at the multitude of pilgrims going and returning; we wondered at the great glory bestowed upon this apostle on earth; we wondered at what ought not to be wondered at, and were amazed at what ought not to amaze us. It is therefore not right to shut up in silence the many miracles of the apostle James. [Col. 1090B] These things will surely be made known throughout every province of our people, and this apostle’s acts of patronage will be related among our nation. Far and wide we shall proclaim his glory and power; we shall be heralds of truth and truthful reporters of what we have seen. We shall extol the apostle James as is fitting; made evangelists of the magnificence of Almighty God and of the mercy of His apostle, we shall report his mighty deeds.

“O how great is God’s compassion, who through His apostle displays miracles of His power even to unbelievers! O how great is God’s kindness, who does not disdain in a time of necessity to grant His mercy to believers and unbelievers, concerning which it is written: ‘Beautiful is the mercy of God in the time of affliction, like a rain-cloud in a time of drought’ (Ecclus. 35:26). May we too deserve to have that mercy ready for us [Col. 1090D] in all things and everywhere, through the favour of Him who is the fountain of mercy!”

## CHAPTER LI. On the Recovery of the Castle of Pharo

Meanwhile the archbishop, although detained by the pressure of grave affairs in so troubled a time, turned his mind toward recovering the castle of blessed James named Pharo. For he judged it very advantageous, now that the other castles had been recovered, that this one also should be recovered—the one which the queen had formerly wrested from him by treacherous contrivance and, as an instrument of the hatred she had exercised against the archbishop, had entrusted to one of her nobles. Yet that official, at the queen’s command, had sworn an oath and done homage to the archbishop: namely, that he would faithfully hold the same castle on behalf of and in service to blessed James.

Not long afterward, Varemundus Petrides, son of Count Peter, treacherously seized that lord and possessor of the castle, binding him in fetters and restraining him under the harsh penalty of imprisonment, in order by this wrong to extort the castle from him. When the man delayed surrendering the castle, Varemundus placed a beam upon his chest and threatened outright to put out his eyes unless the castle were quickly given up to him. Thus Petrides achieved his purpose by treachery and acquired the aforesaid castle.

Upon learning this, the archbishop began at one moment to promise Varemundus much, at another to threaten him much, so that he might obtain from him the castle of blessed James. But Varemundus listened neither to the archbishop’s promises nor to his threats; he feared neither his spiritual nor his temporal sword. For he judged it advantageous to retain so great and such a stronghold. At last, when the archbishop saw that Varemundus would not at all desist from his treacherous usurpation of the castle, he assembled an army and marched to besiege it.

When this became known everywhere, Fredenandus, Varemundus’s brother, and Count Munio, his brother-in-law—both inhabitants and faithful men of the archbishop’s jurisdiction—approached the archbishop and entered into discussion with him concerning Varemundus’s reconciliation and the restoration of the castle. On the one hand, kinship of blood compelled them; on the other, loyalty and usefulness in the archbishop’s service. In many and varied conversations they argued between the archbishop and Varemundus, that Varemundus should restore the castle and have the archbishop as his benefactor and friend. But Varemundus’s tyrannical boldness utterly refused this.

For this reason the archbishop, more greatly provoked to anger, threatened a siege—unless the castle were returned to him quickly and without delay—and prepared to continue it until surrender. Why say more? Varemundus, unwilling and compelled, returned the castle to the archbishop. The archbishop gave it for safekeeping to an archdeacon of the church of blessed James, named Peter, whose patronymic was Cresconides. Having been reconciled with Varemundus, the archbishop appeased him by gifts and other benefices, while Varemundus’s brother Fredenandus and Count Munio, his brother-in-law, negotiated his cause with the archbishop and interceded for him.

Afterwards, having taken counsel with the canons, the archbishop gave the same castle to Fredenandus, Varemundus’s brother. This man served the archbishop as commander of his military force and received very many benefices from him. Yet the same Fredenandus swore an oath and did homage to the archbishop, namely that he would hold this castle for the right and service of blessed James and would return it to the archbishop or the canons, without dispute, whenever they demanded it.

Finally, when the same Fredenandus went to Portugal, he entrusted the same castle to Count M., his brother-in-law, having received from him [Note: [Col. 1091D] “faith,” or “security,” is lacking.] an undertaking that, when he should be ordered to return it, he would return it without any objection to the archbishop or his canons. After some time had passed, the archbishop, eagerly longing to recover the castle, urged the aforesaid Fredenandus—now count in Portugal—both by letters and messengers to restore it. Mindful of the oath and homage he had made to the archbishop, Fredenandus ordered Count M. to return the castle to the archbishop.

But Count M. took it badly to be deprived of the castle, being attached to such a stronghold. At last the archbishop thundered at Count M., who had received very many and most generous benefices from him: either return the castle without delay or have the archbishop as an enemy, with the abundance of blessed James’s benefices taken away from him—something that would cause him most grievous loss. Therefore Count M., unwilling—indeed, compelled—returned the castle to the archbishop. [Col. 1092A] The archbishop entrusted it to one of his nobles. Thus it came about that, with the aid of blessed James, the archbishop recovered both those castles which he had lost during his captivity and the others which he had acquired after his release; and they remain to this day under the protection and safeguard of that archbishop, belonging by right and ownership to blessed James.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Council Held at Compostela

At the same time the aforesaid archbishop and legate, though beset on every side by the tumults of persecutions, summoned the bishops and abbots of the provinces of Braga and Mérida to a council, eager for the service of God and for strengthening the condition of holy Church. This council was attended by D., bishop of Ourense; A., bishop of Tui; G., bishop of Coimbra; H., bishop of Portugal; M., bishop of Mondoñedo; S., bishop of Ávila; and their abbots. The bishop of Salamanca had been driven from his see and was a fugitive. For the king of Aragon had expelled him and set up in his church idolaters and violators of holy Church. This bishop of Salamanca, after remaining a long time at Compostela with the aforesaid archbishop, had departed two days earlier with the queen by that archbishop’s permission; he had also received gifts from the archbishop and a chapel for celebrating the episcopal office.

The bishop of Lugo, however, who at that time was serving the queen while she stayed in his city, sent [Col. 1092D] the abbots and clergy of his diocese to the council to excuse his absence. All the abbots and clergy of Astorga attended, their see being without a pastor, for their pastor had recently paid the debt of nature. Since the archbishop of Braga was then staying in the territories of Numantia and could not attend this council, he sent abbots and clergy of his metropolitan church there; and in that place he disputed at length with the bishop of Portugal concerning the boundaries of his church.

This council was held at Compostela, by the counsel of king and queen, in mid-Lent, in the Era 1158, on 8 March, by the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the see of Compostela. So great a multitude of clergy, people, and princes of Galicia assembled that they could scarcely be contained in the apostolic church, though it was of great size. At that council discussion was diligently held concerning the condition of holy Church, then greatly shaken by the tumults of persecution, and concerning the establishment of peace. [Col. 1093A]

## CHAPTER LIII. How the Lord Delivered Him from the Hands of the Saracens While He Was Still Young

Great is the compassion of Almighty God; great the mercy of the Lord, “who knows those who are His” (2 Tim. 2:19), who, as has been related above, delivered the archbishop of Compostela and legate from the hands of Jezebel through the patronage of blessed James the apostle. For by the right hand of God’s power this same archbishop escaped very many and most difficult snares of distress, as we have partly said above. I judge it worthwhile to recall these and the rest together; I do not wish my pen to be accused of idleness.

Therefore, when the same archbishop, “before his episcopate”—that is, after his first appointment as provost of the honour of blessed James [Note: [Col. 1093D] About the year 1095.]—was on campaign with Count R. and the nobles of Galicia to extirpate the unbelief of the pagans, the Saracens, having gathered forces from every side, surrounded the Christian camp near Lisbon and besieged it with an immense multitude of warriors. So great a multitude of the unbelieving people had flocked together; so great were the barbarian forces assembled to make an attack for the destruction of the Christians. Finally, while they killed some Christians and consigned others to fetters, he himself, though unarmed, escaped free and unharmed from the storm of missiles, from so great an effusion of blood—indeed, from the very hands of the Saracens—being protected by the right hand of the Almighty. [Col. 1093C] For he had in heart and mouth that Davidic saying: “The Lord delivered me from the midst of my enemies” (Ps. 17:18); and that saying of Solomon in the Song of Songs concerning the divine protection and ineffable grace of the Lord: “His left hand is under my head, and His right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6; 8:3).

### How, When Others Fell from the Building of Blessed James, He Remained Unharmed in His Seat

After a considerable interval, when he was already bishop [Note: [Col. 1093D] After the year 1100.], one day he sat high upon scaffolding in the construction works of the church of blessed James, together with a great multitude of people. While there the cases of many persons were being decided, as was natural in the presence of the bishop of blessed James, among other matters the bishop accused a certain knight of the crime of theft. For he had always especially hated those guilty of this offence and seems to have wished utterly to root out such predatory conduct among the Galicians.

While the aforesaid knight was brought before the bishop and charged with committing theft, suddenly the scaffolding, under excessive weight, collapsed to the ground. The crowd itself fell; he saw some half-dead, others with broken thighs, shins, or arms, shattered by so great a fall. But the bishop, hanging as though in the air upon part of the beams with only one companion, remained unharmed, divine grace protecting him. [Col. 1094A] All the others fell battered. He remained seated in his place with but that one companion.

Afterward ladders and supports having been set in place, the bishop and his companion were brought unharmed down to the ground; to the amazement of all, he had remained uninjured in such danger. The knight whom we recalled above as brought before the bishop on a charge of theft was brought to the bishop badly battered, with thigh and shin broken. When the bishop saw him scourged by the grievous impact, he said:

“It was done by divine vengeance. I indeed wished to punish you for the accusation of theft; but God, the just Judge, has exercised His sentence upon you. Far be it from me that, after divine vengeance upon you, you should be struck by the scourge of human judgment. For it is written: ‘He shall not be judged twice for the same thing’ [according to the Septuagint; Nahum 1:9]. Cease, therefore, brother, from this wickedness.”

[Col. 1094B] And he said: “May He who struck you with the rod of His correction console you, as a most loving Father, with the staff of fatherly support. Let us both give thanks to God for the ineffable magnificence of His counsel: the mercy of the most loving Father preserved me unharmed in so great a danger; He injured you so that henceforth you may repent of the wickedness you had begun. Great is God’s compassion, great His patience, who wishes no one to perish but desires all people to be saved!”

### How He Escaped Unharmed When the Hall at Iria Collapsed
Moreover, one day [Note: [Col. 1094D] About the year 1107], the same bishop was seated at Iria on a lofty throne and, justice speaking through him, was examining public cases. A very great multitude of people had gathered there, as was fitting for the presence of so great a man: some in order to receive just redress for injuries they had suffered; [Col. 1094C] others as advocates, to make satisfaction; others to receive the determinations of laws and decrees of the people and the workings of justice. A certain very powerful knight was also present. Because of an incestuous union with a blood-relative, the bishop had struck him with the sword of anathema and excluded him from the thresholds of the church. Intending to call him back from so great a crime of incest, the bishop preached to him words of life and discipline. At one point he terrified him with the fires of Gehenna, declaring that, unless he repented, he would be consigned to everlasting torments; at another, if he repented, he promised him the blessedness of eternal life and a happy dwelling in heavenly glory.

While this was taking place, and while the knight was being rebuked by the prelate for his consanguineous union, the throne-room’s roof and [Col. 1094D] walls suddenly collapsed as their joints came apart. All fell into the abyss, crushed beneath the weight of beams, tiles, and stones. Amid so great a heap of ruin they were dashed about: some had broken legs or arms; others, their whole bodies battered, were half-dead. At the sound of this immense collapse crowds gathered; people ran from both sides to the precipice of the episcopal palace. Some, weeping and wailing, sought parents; others friends; others children beneath the mound of stones and heap of fragments; and, when they found them half-dead, drew them out. But that part of the throne on which the bishop alone was seated upon his bench remained firm and wholly unharmed, not in any degree shaken by the destruction of the falling palace.

It was, moreover, the established custom that the bishop of St James, [Col. 1095A] because of the surpassing eminence of his dignity, should sit alone upon his seat unless another bishop, a king, or some other distinguished person was present. On that day the aforesaid bishop had celebrated the Mass of the Lord’s Resurrection. Therefore, in this great danger he found propitious toward him the one to whom he had offered praise and prayers in presenting the most holy sacrifice. For, protected by divine grace while the palace collapsed on every side and the others were cast down, he alone remained unhurt and safe in his seat, only that portion of the throne upon which he sat being preserved. For it is written: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144 [145]:18). And: “The Lord guards all who love him” (ibid., 20).

The knight whom we mentioned above, after escaping gravely injured from the heap of ruins, immediately prostrated himself at the bishop’s [Col. 1095B] feet, renounced his unlawful union with a blood-relative, and, having become penitent in the matter in which he had formerly been incorrigible, begged and entreated that penance be given him. The bishop said to him:

“You know, dearest son, how great the Lord’s mercy has hitherto been toward the hardness of your heart. For he ‘does not wish the sinner to perish, but rather that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. 33:11); and likewise ‘whom the Lord loves he chastens; he scourges every son whom he receives’ (Heb. 12:6). Therefore, son, so that over you, a sinner doing penance, ‘there may be greater joy in heaven than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance’ (Luke 15:7), receive penance and turn to the Lord your God, and he shall turn to you. Indeed, he has chastened you because he loves you; he has scourged you because he receives you as a son. These are the scourges of paternal mercy; these are the blows of divine correction. Do not regard them as scourges of wrath, lest you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath.”

Why say more? Having received penance from the bishop, the knight was recalled from his unlawful consanguineous union. This day supplied us with two trophies; it brought two joys to the Church: the bishop’s preservation in so great a danger, and the knight’s repentance from an unlawful union.

### How he escaped the captivity of Arias Petriz

The same bishop also, after some time, when Galicia had been set ablaze by the torches of discord, plainly showed—more clearly than light itself—how earnestly he laboured for the restoration of peace. For after the death of King Alfonso, lord of blessed memory [Col. 1095D] [Note: [Col. 1095D] In the year 1110], certain accomplices in wickedness, desiring to throw Galicia into the turmoil of war, had besieged in the castle of Miño the boy-king, son of Count Raymond and Queen Urraca; the countess, wife of Count Pedro, the king’s guardian; and many leading men of Galicia. As was said in the earlier book (ch. 49), the bishop intended both to free them and to restore the delight of peace. Further, judging it necessary [Note: [Col. 1096D] One should read *ducebat*, or else admit that something is missing.] to cut away the stings of enmities, the contrivances of conspiracies, and the incentives to treachery, the bishop was nevertheless, together with those besieged, consigned to captivity through the detestable treachery of Arias Petriz and his accomplices.

When he had been captured, kings, princes, dukes, and marquises strove to usurp the pre-eminence of his [Col. 1096A] honour. Many—both the authors of the treachery and others—were roused to vindicate for themselves the honour of St James. But it belongs to us to marvel at the boundless clemency of God and his wondrous mercy by which he freed him from the hands of perjured traitors; such deeds belong to divine providence. He who said, “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33), rescued him from the hands of his enemies and set him high above them. These matters have indeed been written briefly above; yet I think it fitting that they should be noted here with the rest, so that, seeing from how great dangers the Lord delivered him, others may place still greater confidence in the mercy of the Lord.

### How he escaped the battle of Angos

[Col. 1096B] Finally, after the bishop had been released and the others at last set free, and after he had anointed the aforesaid boy king at Compostela, and thus bound the Galicians together in peace (in the year 1111), the same bishop hurried into the field with the boy-king and the princes of Galicia. He judged it just and holy to expel the Aragonese king from no small part of the kingdom on this side of the bridge of the Gronio, which he had violently and fraudulently usurped; for it is the part of justice to render to each person what is his own.

But when they arrived at the fountain of Angos, near the city of León, the Aragonese met them with a great multitude of cavalry and infantry. Battle was joined on both sides, and very many Galicians were overthrown: some killed, some captured, and some [Col. 1096C] put to flight. Before his battle-lines engaged, the warlike Aragonese had entrusted this task to ten of the bolder and stronger men in his force: they were to look about and discover in what part of the battle the bishop of St James was stationed. He further commanded and ordered that they should pursue him until they captured him. For if the bishop of the Church of Compostela were captured, the Aragonese hoped that he would easily invade Galicia and immediately reclaim it for his own jurisdiction.

And why should he not? The bishop was Galicia’s guardian, protector, and patron. While others rushed into the tumults of discord and stirred up wars and seditions, he steadfastly remained the reconciler, the lover of peace, justice, and truth. Though divided in part, he consoled and strengthened the kingdom of Galicia. [Col. 1096D] Therefore he was hated by those who desired everything to be disturbed and ruined; but loved as father and lord by those who pursued the contrary course.

When the tyrant of Aragon had won the palm of victory, those whom the king had assigned eagerly searched everywhere for the bishop and pressed forward more boldly to capture him. Yet he who does not forsake those who hope in him (Ps. 33 [34]:23), who loves those who love him (Prov. 8:17), came promptly to his aid. He protected him from his pursuers, rescued him from gaping jaws and from lions’ teeth; through the midst of the enemy’s ranks, through the midst of the battle formations, through the very swords of those pursuing him, [Col. 1097A] protected by divine power, he escaped unharmed. Accordingly, attributing this great protection to him from whom every good proceeds, the bishop said: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. 117 [118]:7). At last, after gathering those who had escaped from the battle—though many had been lost—he returned home, as is evident in the first book (ch. 73).

### How he escaped the burning of the tower and the midst of his enemies

Moreover, after no little time had passed, the clergy and citizens of Compostela conspired and swore an oath against the bishop. They often attempted to drive him from the bishopric; they often devised plans of treachery against him with the queen; kings and princes often rose against him. But [Col. 1097B] the Lord was his helper, and he did not fear what man might do to him (Ps. 55 [56]:5).

When the seditious men of the conspiracy and conjuration, accomplices in their iniquity, grieved that their snares had been wholly frustrated, they rose in assault against the bishop and the queen, hurling stones, missiles, and fire at them, and threatening death by every means. But how the mighty right hand of the just Judge, to whom all things are possible, delivered him from the siege and burning of the tower; how it led him through the wedges of surrounding enemies; how it freed him from the daggers of those pursuing him and thirsting for his blood; how it drew him from the midst of his enemies, even through the midst of their watches; and how it afterward set him high above his enemies—human [Col. 1097C] capacity and ingenuity are insufficient to understand, much less fully to describe. Nevertheless, as much as the small vessel of my intellect can contain, the course of the history indicates in the earlier book (ch. 114).

These are the Lord’s words: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move yourself,’ and it will move” (Matt. 17:19). Since the righteous lives by faith (Heb. 10:38), possessing all things and abounding, there is no doubt that he lives in him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He directs the way of his servants toward peace; he protects and guards those who pursue truth; he protects on the right and on the left those who live this life. The bishop held this way, loved this truth, and desired this life. Therefore he was loved by him whom he loved; he was protected by him; [Col. 1097D] and by him he was made high above his enemies.

The queen likewise had plotted many things against him, both during his bishopric and during his archbishopric. She had, indeed, stripped churches throughout her kingdom of gold, silver, and every kind of precious thing; she had ruined cities, towns, castles, and villages, as the facts show down to the present day; and had driven away peace and justice and their companions. When her tireless greed had laid waste the Iberian kingdom, the church of St James and its honours remained—the possessions which that Jezebel burned to plunder. Therefore covenants of peace were often broken between her and the shepherd of this Church, for she constantly thirsted for plunder and destruction. The archbishop [Col. 1098A] laboured manfully, like a vigorous shepherd, to keep wolfish fury from his fold and to remove the beastly teeth from the body of his Church.

But since the designs of a woman’s mind were repeatedly thwarted, and since this wild-haired beast could satisfy her frenzy neither by force nor by fraud, she turned her mind to greater devices of wickedness. For it is written: “The instability of desire perverts the understanding” (Wis. 4:12). At last the queen entered into so great a covenant of friendship with the archbishop, and bound herself to him by so many and such solemn oaths, that every advantage of deceit was thought to have disappeared; indeed, she made herself exceedingly subject to the archbishop. The archbishop, believing every fern of wickedness to have been utterly uprooted from her, trusted her. Yet true is that saying of the poet:

> A vessel once steeped in its youth will long retain its scent.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 1, line 69)

[Col. 1098B]

He complied with her more readily and assisted her more attentively, both in Galicia and within the borders of Portugal, as I have set forth more fully above in this book (ch. 40). Why linger over many details? As they returned from Portugal, the queen, scorning so many treaties and so many oaths and fearing neither lordship nor men, seized the archbishop by a most wicked treachery and shut him up in her fortresses. After this, now confident of attaining her desire, she was encouraged to plunder and destroy the canons, citizens, indeed the entire honour of St James. She believed that, once the head was captured, nothing could hinder her and all things would be in her hands. Her mind was polluted by the sacrilegious purpose of most wickedly despoiling God and men. For St Augustine says: “A fully formed will to act is reckoned as the deed itself.” Likewise: “You willed it but could not do it; God thus reckons it as though you had done what you willed.” She fastened crimes together with perjuries and heaped sacrileges upon sacrileges.

But he who delivered the three youths from the furnace of blazing fire, and who rescued St Peter from Herod’s prison, himself drew the archbishop out of the queen’s accursed captivity. He was freed in a wondrous and ineffable manner, despite her will and resistance. To the astonishment both of those present and of those absent who heard how his unexpected and unforeseen liberation occurred, divine providence willed it to happen thus: on the eighth day he was freed from the prison [Col. 1098D] of captivity. God did not wish that what had belonged solely to the highest power should be ascribed to human boldness.

The archbishop himself marvelled—as we often heard from his own mouth—that God’s power had shown itself so effectively and so swiftly propitious toward him, attributing this not to his own merits but to divine compassion. The gracious and merciful Lord, who had delivered him from so many and such great afflictions, did not wish to abandon his servant in the bonds of the Babylonian woman; he did not wish the Church of his apostle to be deprived of such a prelate; he did not wish it to be torn apart by the teeth of lions and wolves; he did not wish sacred and non-sacred things alike to be destroyed by the utterly depraved.

Wonderful and ineffable is God’s dispensation: he permits his servants to be oppressed and afflicted by the wicked, in order to show forth in them the arm of heavenly power; he loosens the reins of the wicked so that [Col. 1099A] the reward of merit may increase for his faithful. For as the struggle of persecution increases, the palm of victory also increases. Hence it is written: “No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). And elsewhere: “To the conqueror I shall give to eat from the tree of life” (Rev. 2:7).

Strong and effective was your arm, O Lord, in the archbishop’s deliverance. It was indeed a great and abhorrent crime that such things should be done to the Christ of the Lord; the more abominable and accursed the deed, the more effective and wondrous in him was the miracle of miraculous omnipotence. Therefore, because this more excellent and admirable protection was displayed amid a more wicked and execrable crime, I have wished to recall to memory the other matters mentioned above. Let all, therefore, who trust in the mercy of the Lord hear and understand [Col. 1099B] the magnificence of heavenly protection shown toward the archbishop, and glorify the Father who is in heaven and on earth.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the waterworks by which water flows before the porch of the church of St James

Among the other works of the aforesaid archbishop and legate, one noble and illustrious work ought not to be obscured by oblivion. For the admirable usefulness of the work itself demands that, in proportion as it is of itself delightful and not without glory, so it should be fully extolled by my praises. Things worthy of praise ought, by proclamation, to be committed to memory.

When the archbishop, ever watchful in untiring care, discovered that the pilgrims of St James suffered an excessive shortage of water, he was moved with paternal compassion and grieved. He knew the Apostle’s saying: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12). He suffered with the pilgrims who came to the apostolic church and sought water day and night for drinking or other necessary uses, but did not find it. Necessity often compelled them to buy water from their hosts or others at a price, and what they had reserved to buy food was partly spent for water. Those whose purse lacked money very often endured a most severe scarcity of water. Certainly so great a multitude of pilgrims flocked to the church of St James!

For a long time the archbishop devised a remedy, but the task was difficult—indeed most difficult. At last, by his urging, counsel, command, and direction, Bernald, treasurer of the Church of St James, began to construct aqueducts. Thus, for almost a mile beyond the suburb of Compostela, aqueducts and underground channels were made. With great labour and the expenditure of very great sums, the watercourse was directed toward the church and brought in through an excavated and constructed channel. When it reached the vicinity of the church of St Martin, namely beside the house of Pedro Anaiade, wooden conduits strengthened with iron and lead received the torrent of water. They discharged one part before the porch of the apostolic church and another into the cloister of St Martin, for the use of the monks.

In that same monastery there had been so great a lack of water that they had none even for washing [Col. 1100A] their hands unless it were carried from elsewhere. But such an abundance of this water now flows that it suffices for the monastery of St Martin and pours in a rushing stream before the church of St James. Through these wooden conduits it is discharged into an excavated stone of extraordinary size, which the archbishop himself had long ago ordered made for this purpose—indeed, for this purpose, but in another place, namely in the cloister of the canons of St James.

For this indefatigably vigorous labourer in the Lord’s field desired with all the effort of his mind to build for the apostolic canons a cloister, an illustrious and elegant work, and to bring water through underground channels into the cloister for the canons’ use, just as to this day it is brought and flows before the porch of the church of St James. But impeded by the tumult of wars, because that work was deferred—although in his own time he had ardently desired to construct it—he assigned that useful, necessary, and beneficial stone to receive the water. Thus the stone receives water brought through underground channels and unfailingly provides it to all who need it.

The pilgrims rejoice exceedingly in the abundance of so much water. They call it the water of St James, as though sanctified, most healthful, and divinely prepared for human use. Yet no one who has not seen it can adequately marvel at the usefulness it provides or at the excellence of its astonishing spectacle. So that it might flow forth colder and clearer, the archbishop caused its channel to be covered with stones and overlaid with earth, from the point at which the spring [Col. 1100C] rises to the source from which it is drawn. Thus, flowing forth cold and most clear, it was most beneficial for pilgrims’ drinking and for other people’s use.

We have in the Gospel: “Two shall be in one bed: one shall be taken and the other left; two women grinding: one shall be taken and the other left; two in the field: one shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. 24:41). The person who labours in the field—that is, in the ministry of holy Church—as in the Lord’s field, is the one who gives such attentive care to the Church over which he presides and cultivates the field entrusted to him with such concern as is fitting: cultivating what ought to be cultivated, uprooting what ought to be uprooted, renewing what ought to be renewed, and building what ought to be built. Such a worker indeed, like a faithful and prudent servant, when night comes—that is, the adversity of the age—remaining constant in faith and in the practice of good works, is taken into eternal life, while others fall away and are left for punishment.

May the aforesaid archbishop, who, both in ecclesiastical and secular matters, so far as concerns him and as our capacity permits, has shown such solicitude and manfully cultivated the Lord’s field, after happily completing at last the course of this life, himself be taken with those who are taken into eternal life.

## CHAPTER LV. On the building of churches and palaces

The same archbishop also built the church of St Pelagius before the altars beside the church of St James, after demolishing the most ancient and undistinguished little church that had formerly stood there. Likewise, in Compostela he completely renewed [Col. 1101A] the church of St Michael, the church of St Felix, and the church of St Benedict.

Above the porch of the church of St James, by which one goes to the Village of the Blackbirds (*Villare Milvorum*), he built an altar in honour of blessed Benedict, and also of blessed Paul—whose commemoration was rarely observed in the churches of Spain—of St Antoninus, and of St Nicholas. Above the porch leading to the stream of water beside the mint, he had built an altar. He strove to render due honour to blessed Benedict and St Antoninus, whose altars had been in a certain tower beside the old little church of St James, as has been written more clearly above (ch. 25).

He also demolished the most ancient little church of St Thomas of Ouria, which wholly threatened collapse, and built another new one there. At the castle of Honesto, besides the other buildings he erected there, which we have noted above, he built excellent palaces. Since the church which he had made in that same castle was low and small and was trodden underfoot by those walking along the castle walls, he ordered it demolished. Then he built there another church, larger, higher, and more imposing. He judged it useful and fitting that such a church and such palaces should be built at Honesto, where the archbishop of St James might honourably stay at times, as befitted him, with his clerics and knights.

In time of war Honesto is, as it were, the treasury and storehouse of the archbishop of Compostela and his canons. It was therefore proper that lofty and distinguished dwellings should be built there, so that God might be worshipped worthily and reverently in his dwelling-place, and that in [Col. 1101C] the other buildings the ministers of St James might rest with dignity.

At Iria there were spacious and large palaces built by his predecessor, Bishop Diego, lord of blessed memory. The archbishop himself used to lodge in them before becoming archbishop. But when the tumult of wars arose and the trap of treachery became more frequent throughout Galicia, he recalled that long ago a bishop of St James named Gudesteus had been killed there by the deceit and treachery of the princes of Galicia. That bishop had observed the Lenten fast at Iria, separated from his knights and household, in order to devote himself and serve God more freely. In the silence of the deep night, therefore, the most wicked band of traitors burst into the dormitory adjoining the church walls, where he rested with the canons—alas for the crime!—and cut down the bishop with swords.

Remembering these things, the archbishop judged in wartime that it was worthwhile to go to Padrón, where there was a populous multitude of houses. For whenever he lodged in the aforesaid palaces, his knights and household went to the nearby houses of Padrón and left their lord with only a few clerics and chamberlains, as though in solitude. One must trust experience. I was there with him many times, and I saw what I attest in writing; I very often feared a sudden attack by enemies.

For this reason the archbishop, having adopted sound counsel, went to Padrón and moved [Col. 1102A] his residence there. Since it was not fitting for him to live in unsuitable buildings, he constructed suitable palaces beside the church at Padrón, which he himself had built through a certain priest, Pelagius, steward of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 1101D] Book I, chapter 2]. In these palaces, surrounded as it were by a multitude of fellow residents and attended by his own knights, the archbishop often lives to this present day, through God’s mercy and with health as his companion. May he so dwell, so build, and so prosper for a long time, by God’s gift!

## CHAPTER LVI. On the agreement concerning the archpresbyterates of Salagia, Bisancos, Trasancos, Lavacencos, and Arros, between the archbishop and M., bishop of Mondoñedo

Between the aforesaid archbishop, the canons of the Church of Compostela, and the bishop of Mondoñedo [Col. 1102B] and the clerics of the Church of Mondoñedo, a dispute concerning certain archpresbyterates—namely Bisancos, Trasancos, Salagia, and Lavacencos—had often been debated in the time of King Alfonso of blessed memory. For the Church of Compostela maintained that these archpresbyterates belonged to its diocese, while the Church of Mondoñedo maintained that they belonged to its own.

In this matter our archbishop, in order to obtain what was asserted to belong to his Church, had frequently sent his clerics to Rome and spent no small sums of money. The question had often been brought forward and debated in the presence of Pope Paschal; the pope himself had often sent letters concerning this matter to the Churches of Compostela and Mondoñedo and also to the neighbouring bishops, as has been written more fully in the first book (ch. 34). The matter was also often addressed in many councils held throughout Spain in the presence of Roman cardinals and legates, but it was not decided.

Finally, by sentence of the Roman pontiff, it was decreed that the clerics of Compostela and Mondoñedo should meet at Astorga to settle the matter. The bishop of Burgos was appointed judge in this case; but since the Mondoñedans failed to appear and alleged that they suffered violence from the Church of Compostela, the question remained undecided. Nevertheless, the canons of the Church of Compostela maintained that the Mondoñedans had been defeated in judgment and that, justice speaking, they had vindicated the aforesaid archpresbyterates for themselves.

The decision of this matter remained dormant for many years because of the outbreak of war throughout Spain. Now the Church of Compostela, now that of Mondoñedo claimed these archpresbyterates, but Compostela did so more often, being supported more strongly by the pillar of justice and by ecclesiastical and secular power. The clergy and people inhabiting that part of the diocese likewise strayed into a certain haughtiness of disobedience, because they boasted of having two mothers.

At last, after M. [Munio], treasurer of the Church of Compostela, had become bishop of the Church of Mondoñedo, and after no small passage of time, the question of the aforesaid affair began to be discussed between our archbishop and that bishop. But the archbishop, seeing that the matter, formerly undecided, was being prolonged for too long and that spiritual harm to both churches was multiplying more and more, exercised paternal stewardship in this matter. Having summoned M., bishop of Mondoñedo, he resolved to impose a firm settlement upon it.

Therefore, by the good pleasure of both parties—namely, the archbishop and legate of Compostela with his canons, and the bishop of Mondoñedo with his canons—it was established and agreed that the Church of Compostela should henceforth hold peacefully and without disturbance the two archpresbyterates of Salagia and Bisancos; while the Church of Mondoñedo, or Valibre, should henceforth hold peacefully and without disturbance the archpresbyterates of Trasancos, Lavacencos, and Arros. And so that this might never in any manner be disturbed or shaken, it was confirmed on both sides by the strongest authority of a written instrument, as follows.

### Agreement between the archbishop and the bishop of Mondoñedo

[Col. 1103B]

> “We, whose names are written below, seeing Lord Diego, archbishop and legate of the see of Compostela, and Lord Munio, bishop of Valibre, in disagreement and dispute with one another concerning certain archpresbyterates, namely Salagia, Bisancos, and Trasancos as far as Lavacencos and Arros—concerning which a complaint had often been debated between the aforesaid Lord Diego, archbishop, and Lord Gonzalo, bishop of Mondoñedo, predecessor of the aforesaid Bishop Lord Munio, in the time of King Alfonso of blessed memory, namely in general councils and also in the presence of Lord Pope Paschal—have judged it worthwhile, in compassion for the prolonged weariness and dissension of our brethren, to put an end to so great a matter.
>
> “Requested and invited by them and by their canons, we came together and, with their consent, undertook to examine this matter in a spirit of brotherly love. For it is our duty to destroy the seedbed of schism and, by diligent care, to plant among those at discord the nursery of charity. Having therefore examined the claims of both Churches, we establish between them this agreement with enduring and perpetual firmness: henceforth the Church of St James shall hold by perpetual right, and possess without any claim for restitution, the two archpresbyterates of Salagia and Bisancos; and Valibre, or Mondoñedo, shall henceforth hold by perpetual right, and possess without any claim for restitution, the archpresbyterates of Trasancos, Lavacencos, and Arros.
>
> “We further add to this agreement that, out of the honour of St James, the Church of Valibre or Mondoñedo shall hold in perpetuity all offerings throughout the entire bishopric of Valibre or Mondoñedo, and shall possess them quietly and freely for ever, except for a candle valued at one hundred pounds, at the rate of twenty-five solidi per pound, which it shall pay annually to the church of St James.
>
> “Likewise we add that the Church of Valibre shall by no means exact throughout the whole archbishopric of Compostela the church dues which we call *terciae* [thirds]; and conversely, the Church of Compostela shall by no means exact throughout the whole bishopric of Valibre the church dues which we call *terciae*.
>
> “We therefore confirm this agreement of settlement by our letters and strengthen it with our own seals, so that henceforth and forever the aforesaid complaint between the Churches of Compostela and Valibre may be silenced in perpetual quiet. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this document of our settlement, then, after a second or third warning, if that person does not make fitting amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But for all who observe this, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1104B] and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.
>
> “This agreement of settlement was made in the era 1159, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. A document of the same kind is kept in the treasury of the Church of Valibre.”

> “I, Munio, unworthy vicar of the Church of Valibre, confirm this writing with my own hand. I, Peter, archdeacon of the Church of Valibre, confirm. I, Arias Sisnandiz, who at that time was archdeacon of the Church of Valibre in Salagia, confirm. Peter, prior, confirms. Veremund, archdeacon and priest of whatever worth, surnamed Alfonso, confirms. I, Alderetus, confirm. I, Peter, confirm. Pelagius confirms. Martin confirms. Peter, priest, confirms. Froyla, priest, confirms. Peter, priest of the first [Col. 1104C] clergy, confirms. Diego Oduariz confirms. Julian, archdeacon, confirms. Guido, archdeacon, confirms. Peter John confirms. Peter, abbot, confirms.”

### Pact of M., bishop of Valibre

> “I, Munio, bishop of Valibre, promise you, Lord Diego, archbishop of the Church of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, in the faith of Christ and in the truth of the matter, that from this hour onward I shall be your faithful friend: defending your life, limbs, and the honour which you have or shall have; opposing your harm in all things and through all things, without trickery or evil intent, according to my power. But if—may it never be!—exile should befall you by any force or violence, or expulsion from your office, I shall either bodily accompany you wherever you go or arrange myself according to your counsel. With God’s grace assisting, I shall observe this toward you while you live, as long as I live. So may God help me and these holy Gospels.
>
> “Whatever you release from this pact established in the faith of Christ shall be released. The counsels which you tell me I shall not disclose to your injury.”

> “I, M., unworthy bishop, confirm this writing with my own hand. Peter, archdeacon of Valibre, confirms. Arias Sisnandiz, of the Church of Valibre and archdeacon, confirms. Those canons of St James who were present: Arias Gundisalvides likewise confirms; Peter Gundesind likewise confirms; Peter Eliae, archdeacon, confirms; Peter Cresconides, archdeacon, confirms; Peter Anaiades confirms; Peter Astruarides confirms; Arias Munionides [Col. 1105A] confirms; Master Giraldus confirms. [Note: [Col. 1105] This is the very author who wrote these things. In Latin he is called *magister*; in Greek, *didaskalos* [teacher]; above, ch. 6.] Bernald Bernaldici confirms; Alfonso likewise confirms; Peter Stephanici confirms; Peter Fulco confirms; Peter Pelagides confirms; Pelagius Muniz confirms.”

## CHAPTER LVII. Inventory of vestments, books, and other ornaments of the church which the archbishop provided
The things which the archbishop himself bought, gained, acquired, or caused to be made for the internal uses and adornment of his Church—namely vestments and other ornaments—are not unfitting to commemorate in the course of this work. For to bury in oblivion things which deserve the memorial light through themselves or through their author is evidence of fault. Indeed, in caring for his Church the archbishop expended much, as circumstances and advantage required; but he acquired more, and greater things, as the truth of the matter attests. One must consider in what times, and amid how many and what persecutions, he protected his Church, Saint James assisting, with the shield of patronage; how much and how great an expenditure he made in overcoming the causes of persecutions; and how much and how great he acquired.

These, therefore, as the following account reveals, the aforesaid archbishop and legate of the Holy Roman Church gained, bought, or caused to be made as vestments and ornaments for the Church: namely, four citharas constructed in Greek fashion; four pontifical copes, and twelve other costly copes of silk fabric; two sets of pontifical vestments with all that pertains to them [Col. 1105B–C]. He gave away three others: one to Hugh, bishop of Portugal, formerly archdeacon of the Church of Saint James; another to Munio, bishop of Mondoñedo, formerly treasurer of the Church of the same Apostle; and the third to G., bishop of Salamanca, his suffragan.

Furthermore, two dalmatics; one black chasuble of purple; three Gospel-books, two of silver and one of gold, the latter already ruined and restored by the archbishop himself; a silver missal; a silver epistolary; a silver *syon* [reading uncertain]; a golden belt; two silver caskets, in one of which the head of Saint James is said to be; another casket of ivory; another gilt metal casket, of remarkable workmanship, carved with glass; another very precious golden casket, which the archbishop bought for three thousand solidi [Col. 1105D] and afterwards gave to Pope Calixtus; a silver reliquary of the Wood of the Lord, given to him by Queen U., daughter of King Adefonsus; a golden cross which he himself gave to Boso, Roman cardinal and legate, afterwards bishop in the city of Turin; three silver chalices; and one golden chalice, which likewise he gave to the pope for the advantage of his Church; a golden thurible which likewise he expended for the advantage of his Church; and another golden thurible which he afterwards restored to the pope in place of the former.

Three silver ewers; one antiphonary; one service-book; one missal; three breviaries; one Lenten book; two benedictionals; a pastoral book; a book *On the Lives of Bishops*; canons; another book containing diverse opinions; another book *On Faith in the Holy Trinity* and on other opinions; and another larger book for the whole cycle of the year [Col. 1106A].

## CHAPTER LIX. How Queen [Urraca] plotted against the archbishop.

[Col. 1106B]

Many arrangements for reconciliation had been made between Archbishop Didacus, legate of the Holy Roman Church, and Queen U.; many compacts of peace had preceded, as is written in the earlier and in this following book. Yet after the queen, at the prompting of certain wicked persons, had dared that most detestable deed—alas for the crime!—namely, to lay hands upon the Christ of the Lord, there remained between them, as it were, the appearance of friendship, while a cloud of suspicion hovered on either side.

Though the archbishop had experienced so great a sacrilege, and though he and the queen had entered into the aforesaid compact, he nevertheless did not wholly trust the queen, nor did he place confidence in her manifold assurances [Col. 1106C]. Yet he in no way withheld from her royal rights and the service due to her, in accordance with the Gospel: “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

The queen, however, conscious of so execrable an offence, strove in every possible way to erase the written record of this guilt. Now with honeyed words, now with boundless promises, she enticed the archbishop, subjecting the kingdom of Galicia to his authority and making its counts and princes obedient to his command. For although she had already made a peace compact with her son King A., and although she held him, with all his power, subject to herself as her son, she recognized that the archbishop’s prudence was exceedingly necessary to her; and she saw that, without his assistance, she could not wholly restrain Galicia under her rule.

Moreover, she had cast Count P. Froylaz and his sons into chains, and she especially needed the archbishop’s counsel and aid in recovering the honours of those imprisoned men and the castle of Luparia, in which Arias Petriz was in rebellion. She could neither besiege that castle nor compel it to surrender, nor crush the other Galician conspirators, except through the archbishop, whose wisdom and power stood pre-eminent [Col. 1106D]. If they began to oppose the queen, almost the whole of Iberia would be shaken by rebellion.

Compelled by this circumstance, therefore, the queen returned to the western regions of Galicia. Before doing so, however, she repeatedly sent messengers—bishops, counts, princes, and citizens—to the archbishop, with these words:

“I have learned, reverend Father, from the reports of some and from certain indications, that your mind has become alienated from me because of the deed which, at the persuasion of the worst men, I presumed to commit against you; and that the excellence of your prudence distrusts my good faith. Therefore I come to the bosom of your fatherhood to make satisfaction, and, as you shall command, to efface the guilt of that sacrilege. I set you before myself as father and protector above all the bishops and wise men of the West. I see that your counsel and aid are altogether necessary to me; nor, unless you are my friend and helper, can I subdue the Galicians, partly inflamed with the torch of treachery and rebellion” [Col. 1107A].

She adorned these and other statements, again and again, with boundless promises; and finally, through the cooperation of the envoys’ prudence, she somewhat softened the archbishop’s mind.

Why say more? They considered and established by what compact of alliance the cloud of fear and suspicion might be removed from the archbishop; how the accusation arising from the former crime might be buried; and how the archbishop might have no need henceforth to fear or guard against a similar undertaking by the queen. Accordingly, between the archbishop, the queen, and their men, a compact of alliance so great and of such a kind was sanctioned that the archbishop need no longer fear the queen’s plots or devices, nor the queen despair of the archbishop’s aid; and that, should she wish to evade her obligation—as is a woman’s disposition—she would be unable to set a snare for the archbishop.

For the queen gave all the bishops of her kingdom to the archbishop as a bond of faith, on this condition: if the queen should hereafter attempt to violate or contrive anything against the archbishop other than what is stated in the following document, or should presume to attack either his person or his honour, the aforesaid bishops should pronounce a sentence of anathema upon the queen and her realm, utterly prohibiting divine service everywhere, except baptism and penance, until she came to her senses and made satisfaction to the archbishop [Col. 1107B–C].

The queen also bound all the counts and princes of her kingdom to this compact by oath, in this manner: if she should presume to act against the archbishop otherwise than appears in the following document, all of them, together with their castles, towns, and honours, should oppose the queen and rise in rebellion for the archbishop until the queen made satisfaction to him.

In sanctioning this compact of alliance, it was determined and decreed that letters of the bishops, secured by the seal of each, containing the terms of the alliance, should be conveyed to the lord pope and confirmed by his writing and seal. His sentence was also to be added: whoever transgressed the faith of the aforesaid alliance should be punished by an apostolic sentence until satisfaction had been made. But whoever observed and fulfilled the terms of the alliance was to be endowed with perpetual blessing. This was the compact of alliance between the archbishop and the queen.

### Form of the assurance furnished by the queen to the archbishop

“In the Era 1161, six days before the Kalends of April. I, Queen U., promise and affirm to you, D. Didacus, archbishop of Saint James, by God the Father Almighty [Col. 1108A], and by all His saints, that from this day I shall be your faithful lady and friend, as a good king is to his good archbishop: throughout my whole life, advancing your good and resisting your evil; and I shall defend your life, limbs, and the honour which you possess or shall possess, to the extent of my power, against all men and above all men, without deceit or evil design.

“Neither through me nor through my counsel shall you be captured, killed, or deprived of your honour. I shall never make a pact with any man to your detriment. And if any evil is said to me concerning you, either I shall pay it no heed, or I shall bring you to judgment and accept concerning it the judgment given me by those who are in this pact and who desire concord between me and you, concerning my men and yours. Once restoration and amends have been made at a suitable place and time, I shall stand by you in the aforesaid agreement, and shall fulfil all this without deceit or evil design.

“And if—God forbid—you should be captured by anyone, I shall strive by every means and exert myself for your release, for the restoration of your honour, and for the recovery of your possessions. To confirm this fidelity, I give you Count Lord P. Gunsalviz and those written below, so that, if I do not observe this pact, they shall stand with you together with their honours until I have made amends. And if these men die or are expelled, those who succeed them shall give you [security] for carrying out the aforesaid pact” [Col. 1108B].

“We archbishops and bishops written below promise and affirm that, if the queen—God forbid—does not observe the aforesaid pact, we shall stand with the archbishop to the queen’s detriment and harm; we shall immediately excommunicate her, and her land, and our bishoprics, excepting baptism and penance, until she makes amends.

“Whatever has hitherto occurred between me and you shall henceforth be forgiven and released; and whatever you release from this compact shall be released.”

The queen holds a similar document.

Bishop Munio of Valibre confirms.  
Bishop Alo of Astorga confirms.  
John Ramiriz swears.  
Guterre Horca swears.  
Peter Guterriz swears.  
John Didaci swears.  
Federnandus Joannes swears.

It was determined that all other documents and agreements which had preceded this compact between the archbishop and the queen were to be held null and void [Col. 1108D]. This alone was firmly to be retained; this alone was decreed to be faithfully observed.

## CHAPTER LX. Letter of Pope Calixtus sent to the archbishop concerning the grant of the legation

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Having examined the affairs of the Church of Lugo,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 205.

## CHAPTER LXI. That things acquired by a prelate should be committed to the memory of writing.

[Note: Col. 1107D. Words of the archbishop.]

Our Lord and Redeemer, desiring to direct the course of our work with unharmed foot, teaches us that we, who by pastoral care ought to instruct others through the example of good action, must not at any time, by concealing the good deeds which we do, be convicted of hiding a lamp under a bushel: “No one,” he says, “lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Matt. 5:15).
