For just as a lamp placed under a bushel illuminates no place except that in which it stands, so one who does good secretly forms no one but himself through his own example [Col. 1109A].

Again, lest, if our good works are displayed before human eyes, the wind of self-exaltation should extinguish them like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, he taught us to avoid arrogance when he added: “When you have done all good things, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10).

Therefore, wishing to walk in the path in which he taught, and as he taught, we judged it fitting to compile, in the sequence of this book for the edification of those who follow, whatever worthy of remembrance occurred to us or to our predecessors in bishopric or archbishopric, and likewise how much each of us benefited the Church over which we preside, lest it become obsolete beneath the soot of oblivion. The function of this book accords well with the etymology of its title, since it is rightly called a *Register* because it contains past transactions or deeds performed [Col. 1109B].

May the Lord grant that we, the husbandmen to whom He has leased His vineyard, may not, like the barren fig tree occupying the ground uselessly, be struck by the sentence of this severe judgment: “He will miserably destroy the wicked” (Matt. 21:41), etc.; but that, faithfully bringing to the Lord the doubled talent, we may be comforted by this word of the Lord: “Well done, good servant” (Matt. 25:21), etc.

Now, finally, the following document must show what our Church has newly acquired through us.

Urraca, by God’s ordinance queen of the Spains, granted to our Church, to possess by hereditary right, all the inheritances which Lady Tigria had bestowed upon her, so that, because she had made the Apostle heir to so great and such an inheritance, she might receive remission of her sins. The aforesaid Tigria, emulating this deed with godly emulation, established that after her death she would likewise leave to this Church the other half which she had reserved for herself.

### Acquisition of certain inheritances

[Col. 1109D] These are the names of the inheritances which Queen Lady Urraca and Tigria Enxemeniz give to the Church of Saint James and to you, Lord Archbishop D.: Bastavales, Dayam, Neruimes, Cirquites, Dorma, Queygido, Gandera, Saint Julian, Saint Eulalia, Saint Vincent, the monastery of Villarino, which is on the bank of the Minho, with its inheritances; in Salnés, our portion of the monastery of Supratelio, of Saint Mary of Tralegio, of Saint Mary of Cendam, and of Saint Mamete of Alamir; and likewise I command and give you other inheritances which I ought to have in return for my other inheritances which my brother Peter Enxemeniz sold in Salnés, Superata, Guldreganes, and Truanes, without my counsel and consent. For these, I, Tigria Enxemeniz, must first restore myself in full, and afterwards divide other possessions with my brothers [Col. 1110A].

Of all these aforesaid inheritances, I, Queen Lady Urraca, and Lady Tigria give and grant our portions to the Church of Saint James and to you, the archbishop.

Marina Rabinadiz gave Saint James, the lord archbishop, and his canons a certain estate with its people and inheritances, called Savardes.

## CHAPTER LXII. The queen’s oath which she rendered to the archbishop.

After Queen Lady U.—alas for the crime!—had caused the venerable lord D., then the first archbishop of the see of Compostela and likewise legate of the Holy Roman Church, to be held in custody, the people of Compostela, anxious for the liberation of their pastor, strove unanimously to make her release, whether willing or unwilling, him whom she had wickedly captured [Col. 1110B].

Though he had long before known that her snares were being laid for him, he nevertheless did not in any degree withdraw from her service. Obeying her commands, he followed her with his army as she set out against the Portuguese enemy, hoping that, since she could not capture him in her own land, she might do so more freely in Portugal, where his resources would not be so great.

Once, as we have said, he had been delivered from her hands through God’s mercy, since it was unworthy that he should be consigned to prison custody when God had granted him the power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, it remained to reconcile peace between him and the queen. She complained also that, in releasing him, she had endured forcible compulsion from her own men.

When at last every grievance between them had been permanently silenced, so that no further complaint concerning these matters might disturb their faith, she nevertheless kept the wound of a hidden hostility concealed in her breast [Col. 1110C]. But who does not believe that an evil woman wounds when she swears weeping? For she is unconcerned with perjuries.

Some time afterwards, when she came to visit Galicia, she accused before the royal majesty certain persons who had used force against her in freeing the archbishop, maintaining that, because with rash daring they had conspired against her, they ought not merely to be deprived of their inheritances but also punished by capital sentence. Then, because it was just that his aid should not fail them in whatever cause they were attacked, he held before those violently assailed by the queen the shield of just defence, ready himself, one man for all, to receive the darts of adversity which might be aimed, as indeed they were aimed, against them [Col. 1110D].

Finally, redeeming at his own expense their exile, the forfeiture of their inheritances, and whatever similar penalties royal severity demands for vengeance, for three hundred marks and more, he strove to win back the queen’s favour for himself and his men. Thanks be to God, for from that time until now the queen has cherished him so deeply within the bosom of her affection that she has no one to whom she more willingly entrusts the secrets of her counsels, or in whom she more confidently trusts. For to find favour in the eyes of kings is nothing other than God’s gift.

After peace had meanwhile been concluded and confirmed between them by the strength of an oath, Arias Petriz, commander of the castle of Luparia, revolted because the queen had cast his father-in-law, Count Lord P., together with his sons and wife, into chains [Col. 1111A]. While the queen scattered her soldiers in every direction to besiege this castle, because it did not readily yield to assault, she determined to fortify another castle close before it.

While she was energetically occupied with this work, certain knights of the archbishop approached to speak with her, hoping that she had not altered her former attitude toward him and believing that they would find in her a woman devoted to their cause; but they found a most resolute man. “Behold, queen,” they said, “unless it displeases your majesty, we shall hand over that lord archbishop, ever opposed to your will, either captured or slain.”

Looking at them with a grim countenance, the queen not only denounced the sacrilegious crime she had heard, but, calling the witnesses who stood there, compelled one of them—Peter Garcio, who had been spokesman—to repeat before them what he had said to her alone, so that his confession might make him guilty [Col. 1111B]. Convicted by his own mouth of having uttered an abominable proposal, he was seized, chained, and thrust into prison; thus he fell into the pit which he had set. The others, because they steadfastly denied it, were reserved for satisfaction to military justice.

Questioned by the queen herself as to what plan he had devised for committing this disorderly deed, he explained:

“When, returning from his castle of Honesto, he had set out for Iria with few companions, as is his custom, we had resolved by common consent to consign him to death rather than capture. But if, in the place where we hoped, neither the one nor the other should occur, I request that leadership of this undertaking be assigned to my courage. For in the middle of the night, when he and his chamberlains had surrendered to sleep, I should secretly enter his chamber with an armed band by places which I knew well, and beyond doubt accomplish my intention” [Col. 1111C].

After the queen had considered such a detestable crime and the manner in which it was to have been committed [perhaps: “had been reported”], she said: “Are you the man whom, only the day before yesterday, he had appointed chief of his household, whom he loved above the rest, and to whom he was accustomed to entrust his most intimate counsels? Truly, ‘a man’s enemies are those of his own household’ [the citation is printed Matt. 7:6], because ‘he who ate his bread has lifted up treachery against him’ (Ps. 40:10).”

Although the queen had sought first through Bernald, treasurer of our Church, and Fernandus Petriz, the queen’s own chancellor, to notify the archbishop who and what sort of men had conspired against his death, and to urge him to guard against them; and although she had again warned him, in her usual kindness, through Count Lord R., nevertheless the benefits which the archbishop had conferred upon each of them did not allow him to believe such things about them [Col. 1111D].

For he had received some of them from the earliest beginnings of childhood to be reared with paternal affection until they attained military maturity; he had armed others once they were grown, providing horses and arms and whatever military service required; to some he had committed himself and his court to be directed at their discretion. Yet since it belongs to the perfect to repay good for evil, and human frailty does not yet permit us to rise to the summit of perfection, he nevertheless did not depart from the path of justice in refusing to repay evils with evils.

For Augustine says: “God will repay evil for evil, because He is just; good for evil, because He is good; good for good, because He is good and just; evil for good, never, because He is not unjust.”

Accordingly, inflicting temporal vengeance upon them as far as possible, he ravaged and overthrew their houses and inheritances, utterly destroying them. Since the destruction of their inheritances did not satisfy vengeance, he caused such accomplices and conspirators in so great a crime as he could capture to be thrown into prison; but those who escaped by flight he bound with the bond of anathema until they made satisfaction [Col. 1112A].

Behold, while I have tried to be brief, I remember that I have omitted the causes and their names. But this fault easily deserves pardon, since the truest reasoning proves that it is no fault. If it is established that it is a fault, behold, the pen is at hand, and the tongue obeys the service of the mind that dictates, so that what has not been included may be added without disfiguring the account. Although neither of them is designated by his own proper name, the enormity of their crime would nevertheless allow their infamy to be proclaimed among the ears of the people. Would that they had never wished to undertake so great a crime, nor supplied us with such sorrowful matter concerning themselves!

How greatly the inception of a wicked intention differs from the completion of an act may be gathered from Augustine’s words, who says: “A perfected will shall be reckoned as the deed of the act” [Col. 1112B–C].

[Note: Col. 1111. St Augustine, Appendix, Sermon 147, §7, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIX.]

And if, according to John, one who hates his brother unto death is bound by the guilt of homicide (1 John 3:15), how much more are these men, wishing to bring their intention to effect so far as lay in them, stained by the blot of a double guilt: they incur both parricide against their Father and the mark of treason against their Lord.

I should certainly wish, if I could, not to recall so great a grief to memory, a grief which forces me and all others of sound judgment to burst into groans and tears. For who could pass with dry eyes and unstinted tears over the attempt, with sacrilegious daring, to murder their own Lord—he in whom alone the safety of their country consists, and through whom the condition of the Church is strengthened? Their intention aimed at this outcome: since there was no other to set himself as a wall for the house of Israel (Ezek. 13:5), once the shepherd had been removed, they would find the Lord’s flock without a head and could then more freely join house to house and extend their inheritances [Col. 1112D].

O truly like Judas! If they had brought about what they wished, their sin would in no respect have differed from his, except that he plotted against God, whereas they plotted death against a man. I wish, however, to explain the cause for which each of them dared this act, since men frequently accuse themselves when questioned while wishing to excuse themselves; and thus they appear the more contemptible, the more they had intended death against so eminent a man for so trivial a cause.

Let us suppose, however, that a just cause of conspiracy had provoked them—which nevertheless would not have afforded them an occasion for just defence, since one loses one’s right there, in the cause of justice, where one rashly seeks to stretch out one’s hand against the defender of justice. For we read that those passing by wished to raise the Ark of the Lord when it was about to fall, but because they rashly laid their hands upon the kicking oxen, they perished (2 Sam. 6:6). If those who strove to raise it as it fell were sentenced to death, what punishment do those deserve who wished to dash down the Ark of the Lord while it stood firm? [Col. 1113A]

Behold, while in pursuit of closely investigating the truth I greatly desire to avoid the sea of opinions, the anchor must be cast, lest, when I wish, I should be unable to swim with the strength of my eloquence to port.

Since, therefore, as we have said, Peter Garcio was held by the archbishop among the dearest of the dear—and afterwards deserved so much greater hatred because, beyond expectation, he had become an enemy from being the most intimate friend—he received from the archbishop’s hand, as a benefice, the land called Cordarium. When he had turned this power into tyranny and had been unable in any way to satisfy the dropsy of his greed from the property of the poor, the archbishop, seeing that his admonitions had achieved nothing, chose to endure this until his rule should become oppression of the poor [Col. 1113B].

Without delay, once his honour had been taken away, he began to rage and grow mad more inhumanly, and unceasingly to seek accomplices and helpers for his faction. Convicted of so great a crime, he was first captured by the queen; then, by the counsel of the Galician nobles and as the rule of justice required, he was handed over by the queen herself to the lord archbishop and sent to the prison called Honesto, where fitting penance was imposed upon him and his companions by the archbishop [Col. 1113C].

At last, after long wasting in prison, he paid two thousand solidi to the lord archbishop for his redemption. The archbishop then reconciled him to himself by this oath:

“I, Peter Garcio, swear with twelve oath-helpers, first by Almighty God, and by all else by which common practice requires the faith of an oath, that I shall in no way attack, by word or deed, the land or men of Queen Lady U.; nor the land of the present lord archbishop D., under whose power I am; nor the land of Fernandus Joannes or of his brother Peter Mariscot, nor their men, whether land inhabited or depopulated. From this Nativity of the Lord, which falls under Era 1162, until another Nativity—that is, for a complete year—I shall neither seek nor hold the lordship of anyone who makes war upon your land.

“After this year has ended, if I should have a lord who makes war against all of you or against any one of you, and if that war should find me with him, I shall come against you with my lord in such a manner that, while preserving faith toward my lord, I shall, so far as I can, seek your honour and advantage as those of my lords, without fraud or evil design [Col. 1113D].

“Moreover, I give Arias Petriz as surety, so that, if I prove perjured concerning the aforesaid pact, he shall not receive me into his land; rather, in opposing me, he shall assist you. I, moreover, shall henceforth be perjured, together with all who swear with me; and in addition I shall pay three thousand solidi, for which I have already given sureties.”

[Note: Col. 1113D. “1161” should be read, namely the year 1123, as the preceding and following material confirms.]

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the confirmation of the legation

Although Archbishop D. was harassed amid so many storms of tribulation and surrounded on every side by the difficulties of secular affairs, he was nevertheless greatly concerned for the benefit and exaltation of his Church. He therefore sent to Rome his envoys P. Fulconis and P. Heliae—the one chaplain of the Church of Saint James, the other its archdeacon—with his blessing, namely with four hundred gold coins, with letters of supplication from himself and from the king and queen, and with the necessities for their journey supplied to them [Col. 1114A–B].

Through them, with the king and queen petitioning and with his own friendship and service assisting, he obtained confirmation, by letters sent to him by the lord pope, of his legation, which the archbishop of Toledo had disturbed.

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Anciently, of the Apostolic See,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 238.

Through the same envoys the lord pope also sent such a privilege to the archbishop of Compostela that, by its authority, out of reverence for Blessed James the Apostle, for the special love of his nephew King Ildephonsus, and for his special affection for the archbishop of Compostela himself, he granted and confirmed that the Church of Saint James should hold peacefully, without litigation, and possess in perpetuity the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida, which had first been granted to it temporarily [Col. 1114C].

Behold the privilege confirming the translation to the see of Saint James of the metropolitan dignity that had belonged to the see of Mérida:

“Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela, and to his successors canonically promoted, forever. The power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth [Col. 1114D],” etc.

[Note: A bull has been inserted here out of its proper place. You will find it in the following chapter, together with the manner in which it was obtained.]

## CHAPTER LXIV. Celebration of the council

[Col. 1114D] Therefore, after the archbishop of Compostela had seen and received the letters of Pope Calixtus confirming his legation, he invited to a council the bishops and abbots established throughout the provinces of Mérida and Braga. All except those of Braga and Coimbra gladly assembled at Compostela in response to his invitation. There, in mid-Lent, he held a council, with Lord King Ildefonsus, the princes, and almost all the powers of the land present.

At this council he himself wisely and laudably dealt, according to the authority given him by the Lord, with the benefit and honour of the Holy Church, assisted by his venerable brethren, the bishops of Astorga, Valibre, Ávila, Lugo, Salamanca, and Tui [Col. 1115A]. Since the bishops of Braga and Coimbra were unwilling either to attend the council or to send representatives bearing excuses, he granted them, by the common counsel and request of the aforesaid brethren, canonical delays within which they were to come into his presence and make satisfaction for their fault. Because they were unwilling to do this, after those delays had elapsed he punished them with canonical sentence.

After the celebration of this council, at the following Pentecost, the aforesaid king, now a young man, received new arms from the altar of Saint James, on the counsel of the archbishop of Compostela and with the archbishop himself blessing the arms. He restored to the archbishop of Compostela and his Church half of the honour of Montani, which the Church of Compostela had long lost. He also made a privilege concerning this half, confirmed it with his own hand, and offered it upon the altar of Saint James [Col. 1115B]. In the hand of the lord of Compostela and upon the altar of Saint James, with clergy and people seeing and hearing, he firmly promised that, as his honour and power increased, he would restore the other half to the same Church.

When the archbishop of Compostela received this gift from the king, he cheerfully gave the king ten marks of silver, not as a price, but solely from charity and affection. He also bestowed, with a generous hand, a great weight of money upon the king’s counsellors, who had helped and supported his cause in this affair. He gave the king himself thirty marks of silver and one thousand solidi, together with three excellent chargers; but he did this secretly because of the queen, who at that time was wholly hostile to her son the king. For he feared that the queen might detect these gifts and thereby become hostile and angry toward him [Col. 1115C].

Meanwhile, the same archbishop, having had the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida conferred upon himself and his Church for the time being—until, that is, the see of Mérida should be restored to the power and dominion of Christians—began, after the example of a good and prudent shepherd, to consider with himself and to concern himself over how he might claim and retain that aforesaid dignity for his Church in perpetuity. For he had stored away in the cabinet of his mind that saying of the Wise Man: “It is altogether better not to acquire honour than to lose through idleness and negligence an honour once acquired.” He knew also that it was a most grievous and intolerable fall: from precedence into subjection, from [Col. 1115D] lordship into servitude, from rich adornment into nakedness. And therefore, fearing lest his Church, stripped and deprived of the aforesaid dignity, should become a suffragan instead of a metropolis, he sent his envoys, Peter Fulconis, cardinal, and Peter Heliae, his archdeacon [Note: [Col. 1115D] See the preceding chapter.], to Rome with his blessing—that is, with four hundred gold pieces—having fully provided both of them with everything necessary for the whole journey. By his letters he humbly and suppliantly asked the lord pope to grant to that Church, for the reverence of Blessed James, to hold and possess in perpetuity the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida which, as has been said, he had granted temporarily to the Church of Compostela; and to sanction and confirm the grant by a privilege of his authority [Col. 1116A]. He also earnestly begged, by letters sent to the friends and intimates whom he then had in Rome, that they should endeavour to be his supporters and helpers in this business.

Thus, after the immense hardships of the journey and many anxieties, the envoys finally reached Rome. First, kissing the lord pope’s feet and humbly greeting him on behalf of Lord Archbishop Diego, they presented to him the greater part of the four hundred gold pieces; then they distributed the lesser part among the cardinals and leading men of the Roman curia, as they knew best how it should be distributed. Finally, they set forth orally how great and extensive was the affection borne by the archbishop of Compostela toward the lord pope and the Roman Church, and how devoted and [Col. 1116B] ready he was to carry out their service and will and to render obedience to the Roman Church. Thereupon they submitted for reading in the curia the letters which they had brought with them to the lord pope on the said archbishop’s behalf. When the letters had been read and the envoys’ words heard, the will and petition of the lord of Compostela became known to all. His will and petition were that the aforesaid dignity should be transferred permanently to the Church of Compostela, and that, once transferred, it should be sanctioned and confirmed by a privilege of apostolic authority.

Therefore the lord pope, having taken counsel with the cardinals and the leading men of the Roman curia, decreed, with the common assent of all present, that the lord of Compostela ought to be heard in his petitions [Col. 1116C], because of reverence for Blessed James and because of the fidelity and affection which he bore toward the Roman Church. Having summoned the envoys, he disclosed to them in order, in the following words, the decision he had taken with the cardinals:

> “How great is the affection, and how devoted the will, which your lord, the archbishop of Compostela—our special friend—bears toward us and the Roman Church, is sufficiently clear to all persons of the Roman curia. For although he is very far removed from us in place, he nevertheless makes himself present to us through the affection of his heart and the frequent bestowal of blessings. He has therefore indeed deserved to be heard by us and to obtain his petition, difficult though it be, since all the good men of the Roman curia unanimously will and advise this. Accordingly, we grant in perpetuity to the Church of Compostela, for reverence toward God and Blessed James and for love of him, the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida which we had granted to that Church temporarily; and, by the common counsel of our brethren, we firmly and steadfastly sanction and confirm that grant by a privilege of our authority [Col. 1116D].
>
> “You shall carry that privilege, however, to your lord unsealed, so that he and his worthy clerics may read it and inspect it carefully to determine whether anything ought to be added, removed, or improved for its stability and firmness. If they find anything in it that should be corrected or improved, let them correct and amend it according to their judgment [Col. 1117A]. Thereafter let your lord take care to return it to us corrected and amended, and we shall seal that privilege with the impressed seal of our authority, perpetually transferring by apostolic authority the aforesaid dignity to the Church of Compostela.”

On hearing this, the envoys of the lord of Compostela humbly kissed the lord pope’s feet, rendering immense thanks to his majesty on behalf of the lord of Compostela and promising him, on behalf of the Church of Compostela, faithful obedience with reverence in return for the bestowal of so great a benefit. A few days later, having received the promised privilege from the lord pope’s hand, they returned joyfully to their own country and gladly presented the unsealed privilege to their lord [Col. 1117B].

When the lord archbishop expressed no small astonishment at the absence of a seal, the envoys explained to him in these words why they had brought the privilege unsealed:

> “Venerable Father, as we plainly perceived from his own words, the lord pope embraces you and your Church in the arms of inward affection. Because of the goodwill and faithful obedience which you endeavour to show to him and to the Holy Roman Church, he certainly counts you among his most intimate friends and most special sons. And so that it may be evident to you by the performance of a deed that his affection for you is genuine and sincere, he has sent you this privilege unsealed, so that, if you see anything which ought to be added or removed in order to make it firmer and more stable, you may have it added or removed [Col. 1117C] as you wish. After you have corrected it according to your pleasure, take care to return it to him without delay; and whatever form you return to him, in that form it shall be sealed and confirmed for you by him, out of reverence for God and Blessed James and because of his especial affection for you.”

Upon hearing this, the man of Compostela, filled with no little joy, immediately ordered his best and most intimate clerics to be summoned. When they gladly assembled at his invitation, he instructed them carefully to examine whether they saw anything needing addition to the privilege, such that, if added or omitted, the privilege might become more stable and firm. Obeying his command, they read and reread the aforesaid privilege; and, as best they could, they amended what they found there that needed correction and improvement [Col. 1117D].

After the privilege had been corrected and amended, the lord of Compostela, recognizing from the conferment upon himself and his Church of so great a benefit and dignity that the lord pope’s affection and goodwill toward him were great, recalled with mindful heart that Gregorian saying: “The proof of love is the showing of the deed.” [Note: [Col. 1117] St Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 30, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI.] He sent three hundred ounces of gold, out of affection and goodwill, to the pope himself and to the other Romans who were his friends. He also sent back to Rome with the privilege his envoys: P. Fulconis, cardinal, who had brought the privilege unsealed, and Adefonsus Petrides, canon of Blessed James. He did not entrust the aforesaid blessing to those envoys to carry, but rather to known and faithful pilgrims [Col. 1118A], fearing that if the envoys themselves carried it, they might lose it entirely should they be captured on the road. For the king of Aragon was extraordinarily hostile to the lord of Compostela on account of Lady Queen U., whom he held in his power and with whom he was then allied; and he caused all whom he could catch on the road from Galicia or Castile—except pilgrims to Jerusalem—to be harshly treated and despoiled.

Yet one of the pilgrims lost twenty-seven ounces of gold, sewn into the cloak which he was wearing, when robbers stripped him of the cloak on the road. The loss of this gold afterward proved a very great hindrance and disturbance to the envoys of the lord of Compostela. For when they reached Rome and the aforesaid privilege had been sealed and confirmed by the lord pope [Col. 1118B], they distributed to the lord pope and to the others among whom it was to be apportioned the money which they had safely received from the pilgrims. But they had no means of making up the twenty-seven ounces lost on the road; and because they did not dare return to their lord until those twenty-seven ounces had been replaced, they remained in Rome, troubled and anxious, for nearly a month. Their lord the archbishop had charged them under obedience to distribute intact those three hundred ounces of gold to the lord pope and his other friends.

At that time there were in those regions two canons of Blessed James, P. Astrarides and Pelagius Joannides, who had gone to Apulia and Sicily two years earlier to seek from the faithful assistance for the work of the Church of Blessed James. These two canons, having traversed the districts of those provinces in seeking what has been described [Col. 1118C], had already resolved to return to their homeland, and on their return had now reached Pavia. When the aforementioned envoys of the lord of Compostela, who were staying in Rome for the said reason, learned this, they took counsel together and decided that one of them—namely Peter Fulconis, the cardinal—should remain at Rome, while the other, namely Adefonsus Petrides, should go to them at Pavia to extract from them, by loan or some other means, the twenty-seven ounces of gold lacking from the three hundred ounces.

When he had arrived in the aforesaid city, he found his fellow canons there at once. He related to them in detail the whole matter as it had occurred and the reason for his coming [Col. 1118D]. They, doubting nothing of his words, decided that one of them should go with Adefonsus Petrides to the aforesaid cardinal at Rome and should do whatever the envoys asked. When Adefonsus Petrides returned to Rome with his fellow canon, he and Peter Fulconis, the cardinal, received twenty-seven ounces of gold from him and distributed them to the lord pope and the others among whom they were to be apportioned. Thus the three hundred ounces of gold which the lord of Compostela had sent to the lord pope out of affection and goodwill were made complete. Two hundred ounces came from the treasury of Blessed James, and one hundred from the property and private resources of the lord of Compostela. Thereupon, having received from the lord pope’s hand the privilege for the perpetual transfer [Col. 1119A] of the dignity of Mérida to the Church of Compostela, together with the pallium belonging to that dignity, they returned joyfully to their own country. A copy of that privilege is set down below in this form.

**The Church of Compostela, a metropolis in perpetuity.**

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“The power of binding,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 270.

## CHAPTER LXV. Dispute between the archbishops of Toledo and Compostela

At the time when the above-mentioned envoys went to Rome to have this privilege sealed and confirmed, a very great disagreement had arisen between the lord of Compostela [Col. 1119B] and the lord of Toledo. The man of Toledo had long held the legation over all Spain; but Pope Calixtus had at that time taken part of that legation from Toledo and conferred it upon the lord of Compostela, out of reverence for Blessed James and because of the faithful obedience which he had continually rendered to the Roman Church. He entrusted to the man of Compostela the exercise of his office in two provinces, namely Braga and Mérida.

Whereupon the man of Toledo, inflamed with no small anger and afflicted by vehement grief, pursued such serious hostilities against the man of Compostela that he both disturbed and attacked his legation by every means he could, and violently and shamelessly usurped the dignity of Mérida already granted to him by the lord pope. For he consecrated and ordained the bishop of Salamanca, whose ordination and consecration belonged by canonical institution to the lord of Compostela because he was his suffragan, without the counsel and consent of the bishops of the province and contrary to the enactments of the holy Fathers and decrees of the sacred canons [Col. 1119C]. He forbade bishops, abbots, and ecclesiastical persons who wished to obey the lord of Compostela as legate and metropolitan, disregarding the rule of justice and driven by unconsidered ambition. He also sent letters to Braga and Coimbra, in which he absolutely forbade each of them in any way to obey the lord of Compostela. By letters of this kind he also commanded and forbade the man of Compostela to hold a council without his advice.

## CHAPTER LXVI. The letters of the man of Toledo to the man of Compostela, forbidding the council, begin

[Col. 1119D]

> “BERNARD, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop in Christ, DIEGO of Compostela: greeting.
>
> “We have seen the letters sent to us by your affection, in which you informed us that you had resolved to hold a council at Compostela in mid-Lent and had summoned our consecrated bishop, namely the bishop of Salamanca. We are greatly astonished that the judgment of your cunning should act so presumptuously, especially since we do not believe you ignorant of the letters of Lord Pope Calixtus, sent generally to the archbishops established throughout [Col. 1120A] Spain and to bishops, abbots, provosts, and the clerical and lay orders. In those letters he exempted neither your person nor that of anyone else from rendering obedience and reverence to me, as legate of the Roman See and vicar of the Roman pontiff; and he directed that, when summoned to a synod, they should unanimously come in order to correct, by our counsel, whatever required correction. Up to this time we have received no decree from the lord pope contrary to the authority of this institution.
>
> “Moreover, it seems to us that you act against the determinations of the holy Fathers and the enactments of venerable laws, and violently annul the commands of the sacred canons; for you presume, uncommanded and unasked, to usurp within the sphere [Col. 1120B] of our legation something which is not yours and does not even pertain to you. Therefore, on behalf of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we forbid you to presume in any way to hold a general synod without our advice and our prior command. Finally, we entirely forbid the bishops and abbots subject to the jurisdiction of the Church of Braga who wish to share our communion to attend your synod.
>
> “You charge us in your writings with having wronged and injured you and your Church in the consecration of the bishop of Salamanca; yet our conscience does not accuse us of having wronged you in any respect. What we did, we did by the authority of the Roman pontiffs—namely Lords U. and P., as well as Gelasius, and Lord C., who now presides over the whole Christian world. Among other things, in the privilege which he sent and granted us, he inserted this statement: ‘We likewise subject to your jurisdiction the dioceses of those cities which, when the Saracens invaded, lost their proper metropolitans, on the condition that, so long as they remain without their own metropolitans, they shall be subject and obedient to you as to their proper metropolitan.’ [Col. 1120C]
>
> “Strengthened by this authority, we raised the said bishop to pontifical honour, since he was under our authority, inflicting no injury upon you or your Church. It is clear, indeed, that you have done us a far greater injury. While pretending to be our friend, you have exerted all your strength secretly and stealthily to diminish, and indeed to encroach upon and, if possible, take away the dignity and honour of our Church. Furthermore, you consecrated the bishop of Ávila, who belongs to the jurisdiction of our Church, against right and against law. We rejected and canonically annulled his election, which was made by lot—not canonically by clerics, but rather by utterly unlearned laymen [Col. 1120D]. How great an injury we have suffered in this is plain to everyone.
>
> “Accordingly, we inform and, in informing, command your excellence that you come to León on the first Sunday after the Octave of Easter, prepared to make satisfaction to us for all these matters and to render us, as primate, the obedience which the sacred canons command to be rendered by metropolitans to their primates. But if you disdain to come to us on the appointed day, know beyond doubt that we shall enforce against you a canonical sentence.”

Having received these letters, swollen with pride and full of arrogance and loquacity, the lord of Compostela did not depart from the path of truth but carefully observed the rule of justice and reason. In the manner of an upright and wise man, he replied with the following humble and reasonable letter.

**The letters of the man of Compostela to the man of Toledo begin: a reply to the prohibition and to the other charges made against him.**

[Col. 1121A]

> “To his beloved brother in Christ, Lord B., by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church: D., by divine appointment archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of that same Holy Roman Church, [wishes him] more closely to examine what ought to be done, and more diligently and steadfastly to observe what has been examined.
>
> “Having carefully examined the letters of your prudence, we have most clearly perceived by what a wind of inconstancy and fickleness the maturity of your judgment is stirred. For your chamberlain, Lord P., a monk of Cluny, recently brought us certain letters from you, which we still possess, containing the assurance that whatever he should promise and affirm to us on your behalf we should regard as certain. Among other things which he conveyed and promised us on your behalf in the presence of Lady Queen [Urraca] and Lord Munio, bishop of Valibre [Vallibriense], he affirmed in their presence two matters in particular: namely, that you wished to make just and canonical satisfaction to us concerning the less-than-canonical consecration of the bishop of Salamanca, and that that bishop of Salamanca would come to make to us, as the one directing and deputing him, the profession owed us [Col. 1121B].
>
> “Persuaded by the sweetness of this embassy, by the requests also of your nephew Lord B., who had come to our court with the chaplain of the lord pope, but above all by affection for you, we granted the consecrated bishop a respite from the interdict imposed upon him, until the feast of Saint Stephen. But now we have received from your messenger other letters, far different from and wholly contrary to the former ones. They plainly show that not only do you not yet repent of your wrongful deeds toward us, but that you also wish importunately to defend those very wrongs. How absurd this is in word and deed for a person of your standing, and how completely contrary to the rule of justice, is clearer than daylight even to the less learned.
>
> “We therefore wonder, not without reason, at your prudence, which strives with all its might, despite the decree of the lord and pope, to disturb our legation [Col. 1121C], and does not cease to usurp the rights of our dignity; for you have often been made fully certain both concerning the archiepiscopal dignity conferred upon us and concerning the confirmation of our legation by the letters of the lord pope long since sent to us.
>
> “We also wonder with what face you dare make a sound concerning the consecration of the bishop of Ávila, for which you rebuke us, since he too is a suffragan of our Church, and since his election was canonically examined by nine bishops and two archbishops, as well as by the Roman cardinal Boso, who had come to us as legate of the Roman Church; it was found canonical and was canonically approved by all.
>
> “Having said this, we make a brief reply to you concerning the prohibition [Col. 1122A] of our council, neither bombastically nor unreasonably. Since it is established by the privileges and authorities of the Roman pontiffs Lord U., Lord P., and Lord C. that we and our Church are exempt and wholly free from the jurisdiction of all prelates, save only that of the lord pope, know beyond doubt that we shall obey you neither as primate, nor as legate, nor as archbishop.
>
> “We further remind you that we were about to go, at the time fixed, to the conference between ourselves and you arranged at León through the mediation of the lady queen, and there, with the counsel of wise men, to restore peace and our former friendship with you. But, having heard the bombast of your letters and their false accusations, we have resolved neither to attend your conference nor to restore any friendship with you, unless you first endeavour to make satisfaction to us concerning the consecration of the bishop of Salamanca and the other manifest injuries [Col. 1122B]. We rightly ascribe the blame for these trifles and false accusations not to you, who formerly were accustomed to show such discretion and discernment, but to your counsellors, who through ambition impel your dignity toward unlawful acts.
>
> “Finally, we remind your discretion, and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and on behalf of Lord Pope Calixtus, in reminding command, that you presume no further to disturb or usurp our legation or the dignity of our archbishopric.”

At about the same time that D., the man of Compostela, sent the aforesaid letters [Col. 1122C] to the man of Toledo, he sent envoys to Rome to lodge before Pope C. a just and reasonable complaint against that same man of Toledo: namely, that in consecrating the bishop of Salamanca he had usurped the boundaries of his dignity against the decrees of the sacred canons, and that in withdrawing Coimbra and other bishops and abbots he had openly and manifestly injured him. When the lord Pope Calixtus had heard his letters and complaint, he promptly sent his letters to the bishop of Salamanca. By apostolic authority he directed and commanded, and in commanding directed, that the bishop of Salamanca, setting aside every excuse, should show affection and faithful obedience to the Church of Compostela as his metropolis and to the archbishop of Compostela as a suffragan to his metropolitan [Col. 1122D]. A copy of the letters sent by the lord pope to that bishop of Salamanca is written below.

## CHAPTER LXVII. The letters of Lord Pope Calixtus to the bishop of Salamanca begin, concerning obedience to be rendered to the lord of Compostela

“Calixtus, bishop,” etc.

“Since in the regions of Spain,” etc. See under Calixtus II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 271.

After seeing these letters, the bishop of Salamanca came to Compostela and, upon the altar of Blessed James, promised faithfully and reverently to the lord archbishop and to the Church of Blessed James and its rulers the fidelity and obedience canonically due. He confirmed this promise in his own hand with these words [Col. 1123A]:

> “I, M., bishop of the Church of Salamanca, promise that I shall perpetually render the subjection and obedience, with reverence, established by the holy Fathers according to the precepts of the canons, to the Church of Blessed James and its rulers, in the presence of Lord Archbishop D.; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar.”

Likewise he sent other letters to the bishop of Coimbra, in which he similarly directed by apostolic authority that he should endeavour in every way to render faithful obedience to the lord of Compostela as legate of the Holy Roman Church and as his metropolitan. We have also set down below a copy of those letters in this form.

**The letters of Lord Pope Calixtus to the bishop of Coimbra begin, concerning obedience to be rendered to the lord of Compostela as legate and his metropolitan.**

[Col. 1123B]

“CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G. [Gundisalvus], bishop of Coimbra: greeting,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1123D] As above, no. I.]

## CHAPTER LXVIII. How the archbishop laboured greatly to acquire the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida, and how he compelled the citizens of Compostela to swear to uphold justice

If I should attempt to explain individually and recall to memory how much the lord of Compostela laboured to acquire the aforesaid dignity for the benefit and honour of his Church, and how much and how great were the sums he expended from his own resources and from the treasury of Blessed James, or irrecoverably lost when his envoys were captured on the Roman journey, neither Maronian nor Tullian eloquence, were it mine, could possibly suffice for the task [Col. 1123C]. For he was beset by many difficulties, through which he was hindered both in this matter and in other ecclesiastical affairs. The war of the king of Aragon troubled him beyond expression; from fear of that king, his envoys did not dare go to Rome except at the greatest peril and with the utmost fear. There was also the conflict between King A. and Queen U., in whose service he had to spend much; as well as the discord of the nobles of Galicia and the devastation of that land, which had reduced almost to nothing all the revenues of the honour of Blessed James.

Yet although the lord of Compostela was hemmed in by so many and such great difficulties, he did not neglect ecclesiastical matters for secular ones, nor secular matters for ecclesiastical ones [Col. 1123D]. Rather, with watchful care, he strove prudently and wisely to conduct and order both, as he knew them to be beneficial for himself and his Church.

Seeing therefore that the city of Compostela was entangled and corrupted by wicked and perverse customs, and that it would utterly perish unless some remedy were supplied, he summoned together the leading clergy and people of that city and made the following address in their presence:

> “I, D., although unworthy, first bishop of this see and then—whether by God’s command or permission—after much sweat and much labour made archbishop of that same see, have long laboured in governing this honour. I reasonably injured many whom it was proper to injure, and, persuaded by the obligation of charity, I assisted many whom it was proper to assist. Yet, by ennobling and exalting the unworthy, and by debasing and oppressing the worthy, I have erred by transgressing the boundary of justice [Col. 1124A]. I therefore confess myself guilty in the sight of the divine majesty and in the presence of you all.
>
> “Now, through God’s mercy, I should like to correct and amend my life and conduct for the better, and to observe and uphold justice whole and inviolable. But because I cannot do this alone without your assistance, I most earnestly beseech all of you, both clergy and people, to assist me in this matter for the salvation of your souls and the reward of eternal life; and, just as I promise you, promise into my hand that you will observe and uphold justice, and have an oath made out for me concerning that promise.
>
> “I wish you to swear to justice and uphold it once sworn because I see faith, integrity, and all other good practices disappearing from our citizens, and I see fraud, deceit, robbery, violence, and the nettles of other crimes increasing. These cannot possibly be uprooted without the sickle of justice.”

Having heard this address, the men of Compostela present—both clergy and people—unanimously replied that in this and in other matters which they did not doubt would be beneficial to them, they would give him their assent and obey him. They therefore swore to uphold justice and caused the following document to be drawn up concerning that oath.

**Concerning the observance of justice in the city of Compostela**

[Col. 1124C]

> “Diego, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, wishing wholly to destroy and eradicate the wicked customs which he saw practised in the city of Compostela, promises before all, in truth and in the faith of Christ, that, maintaining and observing justice at Compostela, he will in no way depart from it for money, favour, or hatred. And, so that this justice may be observed without fail, he commands that the reeve of the city shall affirm upon oath that he will uphold justice and will not depart from it through affection, hatred, money, or the request of any person.
>
> “Likewise, in mutilating, blinding, and hanging, as justice requires, he shall in no way depart from it; but with an even balance and just judgment he shall render to each person what is just [Col. 1124D]. He shall always preserve and maintain in force this document, confirmed by our lord, and the other good laws of our city.
>
> “Likewise, I command and direct that the judges of the holy place shall affirm under oath upon the altar that they will uphold justice, observe the good customs of the city, and depart from justice neither for favour, hatred, nor money; and that in judgments they shall consider neither persons nor the countenance of the powerful (Leviticus 19:15), but shall decide justly and courageously between rich and poor. But if the reeve of the city or the judges depart from this promise of truth, after being summoned twice and three times, let them make fitting satisfaction. If they refuse, let them incur perjury, forfeit their office, and make double compensation for what they have contaminated.
>
> “And let this judgment apply to all parishioners and tithe-payers of the Church of Blessed James, that is, within a mile of the city, on the stated day, in the era 1162 [Note: [Col. 1125D] The reading must without doubt be era 1162, that is, the year 1124 (not 1125); for it is evident from what follows [Col. 1126D] that Pope Calixtus was alive, though he died on 13 December of that same year.], and on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.”

> “We, the people of Compostela, affirm by oath that we shall uphold and defend the justice established by our lord, and by his reeve and judges: so that neither money nor kinship shall cause us to depart from the aforesaid justice, and that in judicial proceedings, whether helping or hindering one another, we shall in no way accept offerings.”

Likewise the senior members of the canonical community promise this in truth and in the faith of Christ, while preserving the rights of the order of our lord and of all the canons:

> “But if we, the people of the city, depart from this promise, after a second and third admonition we shall make amends. Otherwise, let us incur perjury and make double compensation for what we have contaminated [Col. 1125B]. And let the custom of this promise descend to all my successors and yours, so that it may be observed in perpetuity.”

## CHAPTER LXIX. Concerning the sacrilege committed by Count P. in the church of Compostela and his satisfaction for it

Count Peter, inflamed by the heat of anger and instigated by the devil, struck Count Adefonsus before the doorway of the altar of Blessed James and by that wicked act brought great dishonour upon God and the apostle himself. Afterwards, led by repentance, he came with his wife into the presence of the lord archbishop. He disclosed to him the great dishonour which he had inflicted upon God and Blessed James the apostle, along with many other crimes which he had committed at the devil’s prompting [Col. 1125C], and asked him for penitence and counsel for the salvation of his soul.

The archbishop, wisely providing for the benefit of his soul, imposed upon him a fitting penance according to the decrees of the sacred canons. By salutary admonition he urged him to confer some honour upon God and Blessed James as a remedy for the aforesaid dishonour and his other sins. The count and his wife, accepting the archbishop’s counsel, granted to Blessed James and his church, to possess in perpetuity, the monastery of Corispindo with all its appurtenances and the whole village; and, by the lord archbishop’s command and advice, they confirmed with their own hands the privilege drawn up concerning it.

## CHAPTER LXX. The arrival of the Roman legate in Spain

[Col. 1125D]

After some passage of time, when the venerable archbishop had obtained from Pope Calixtus, by the rendering of very many services and by a promise of steadfast fidelity, that he should transfer in perpetuity to the Church of Compostela the metropolitan dignity of the see of Mérida, and should confirm that perpetual transfer by a privilege of his authority, a certain cardinal of the Roman Church, Deusdedit, delegated from the pope’s side, came into the regions of Spain, intending diligently to visit the churches of the Spanish land and wisely to provide for their welfare and benefit. To this visitor the aforesaid pope entrusted the envoys of the Church of Burgos [Col. 1126A], who were then at Rome; and by apostolic authority he commanded him, under obedience, to provide for the welfare of the Church of Burgos, which, bereft of the support of a pastor, had long remained in great hardship and tribulation, and to see to it that its elect, whose election was already five years old, should be consecrated bishop.

Accordingly, the aforesaid cardinal, entering the Spanish regions, came to the city of Burgos, accompanied by the envoys of the Church of Burgos; and he found that church worn down by great persecutions and tribulations and almost deserted. Therefore, deeply affected with sorrow and filled, after the example of a good father, with pious compassion, he judged it necessary to improve the condition of that church and to order that its elect be consecrated bishop, for the honour of God and the benefit of that church [Col. 1126B]. But because this consecration could not take place in those parts for fear of the king of Aragon, who was opposing the elect himself, he enjoined the elect to go to Compostela, there to be ordained by command of the lord of Compostela. For the cardinal himself was going to Compostela, in order, by command of Pope Calixtus, to confer with the lord of Compostela about his consecration and many other affairs. Having visited the Church of Burgos and the others lying along his route, he finally reached Compostela, where he was kindly and honourably received by the lord of Compostela; remaining there for eight days, he was splendidly entertained by him.

When, therefore, the cardinal and the lord of Compostela had come together for consultation [Col. 1126C] and had dealt diligently with the condition of the Spanish churches, the cardinal, grieving for the calamity and misery of the Church of Burgos, commanded the lord archbishop by apostolic and his own authority, and charitably requested him, to take care to consecrate the elect of the Church of Burgos as bishop. He also explained why the pope had entrusted this business to him rather than to another. When these and other matters had been settled at Compostela, and having received a blessing from the lord of Compostela, he left Compostela, went to Braga, and proceeded through the Portuguese regions into the region of Campos. At Valle Oliti he celebrated a council, divine grace going before him, after summoning the brethren. At this council the elect of the Church of Burgos was present with the other brethren [Col. 1126D]. After the council was ended, the cardinal, accompanied by the elect himself, went to the castle of Setpúlveda, and there delivered to the elect of Burgos the following letter concerning his consecration, addressed to the lord of Compostela.

### The letter of the Roman cardinal Deusdedit to the lord of Compostela concerning the consecration of the elect of Burgos begins

“DEUSDEDIT, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Spains, to DIDACUS, by God’s grace archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church: greeting and pure friendship.

“We do not believe that your prudence is unaware of the great hardship and misery in which the Church of Burgos has hitherto been [Col. 1127A]. Therefore, by the fraternal affection and the obedience which you especially owe to the Holy Roman Church, we direct you that, having summoned your brother co-bishops, you consecrate lord Simeon, elect of the Church of Burgos, as bishop, with whichever bishops you please, saving the reverence due to our holy mother, the Roman Church, to which the Church of Burgos belongs in all matters, on whatever day after the Purification of Saint Mary he shall come to you. Receive from him the oath of fidelity, as ancient custom requires. Farewell.”

When the lord archbishop had seen such letters, he ordered the better and more prudent persons of his church to be summoned into his chamber. Showing them the letters and the command of the Roman cardinal, he asked what they advised him concerning that command [Col. 1127B] and the request of the elect of Burgos. These wise and prudent clerics, since the archbishop was shortly to celebrate a council, praised and advised that he should keep the elect of Burgos until the council and consult the bishops who would gather at the council concerning the cardinal’s command and his consecration. Following their advice, the lord archbishop retained the elect until the celebration of the council at Compostela and assisted him generously in many needs.

When therefore the appointed day of the council had arrived, and the venerable brethren—the bishops of Asturias, Mondoñedo, Lugo, Salamanca, Zamora, Portugal, and Tuy—had assembled, the lord archbishop celebrated a council at Compostela on the Sunday of the Mercy of the Lord [Col. 1127C], that is, 20 April 1124, the second Sunday after Easter. With the assent and unanimous approval of the aforesaid brethren, he enacted and confirmed at it the following chapters.

## CHAPTER LXXI. Celebration of the council

Didacus, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, celebrated a council at Compostela on the Sunday of the Mercy of the Lord—20 April 1124, the second Sunday after Easter—having summoned the brethren, the bishops of Asturias, Lugo, Valbrie, Tuy, Portugal, Zamora, Salamanca, and Burgos. In it he dealt, according to the power granted him by God, with the honour and benefit of Holy Mother Church, while the aforesaid brethren, together with their twenty-seven abbots [Col. 1127D], religious persons, and worthy clerics, worked unanimously with him. And because he saw that, through sins demanding it, the kingdom of Spain was so disturbed that even the Church of God, Christian religion having been destroyed, was in danger and was almost reduced to ruin, it pleased him, in a general synod, for the condition of the Church and the tranquillity of the kingdom, to subscribe and, having subscribed, confirm the following chapters:

“Therefore we command and establish by apostolic authority that, with heavenly mercy helping, the Peace of God observed among the Romans, Franks, and other faithful peoples shall be inviolably maintained by all Christians throughout the whole kingdom of Spain: namely, from the first day of the Advent of the Lord [Col. 1128A] until the octave of Epiphany; from Quinquagesima until the octave of Easter; from the Rogation Days until the octave of Pentecost; during the fasts of the Four Seasons; on vigils and feasts of Blessed Mary, Blessed John, and the apostles; and on the feast of All Saints, celebrated on the Kalends of November. Thus no one, even if he has a homicide-case or any other enmity against another, may presume to kill, seize, or in any way harm him.

“Bishops, priests, abbots, monks and nuns, every ecclesiastical order of the Church, ecclesiastical property, and oxen, whoever may own them, shall remain in peace on all days. Pilgrims and merchants shall not be seized or distrained, except through their own fault. The days and appointed periods of peace shall be determined as stated above and confirmed by oath [Col. 1128B].

“Whoever refuses to confirm this peace by oath shall be excommunicated until he swears. Whoever presumes to violate it, the bishop with his whole bishopric shall proceed against him for the destruction of himself and his goods until he makes satisfaction; and his lord, whose man he is, shall take away his benefice, and no one else thereafter may receive him until he has made just and canonical satisfaction for violation of the peace.

“If any of those proceeding against him dies in this obedience, he shall be absolved from all his sins for which he has already received, or shall receive, penance, as though he had died on the journey to Jerusalem, unless he is excommunicated. Likewise, if anyone who has renounced arms for obedience and for observance of the aforesaid peace is killed by his enemies [Col. 1128C], he shall have the aforesaid remission. Whoever kills him shall pay double wergild to the lords of the land, his penance shall be doubled, and he shall never perform penance in his homeland, but shall go into exile. Whoever seizes, mutilates, blinds, or does him any other harm shall make double compensation for what he had previously been liable to pay.

“If anyone dies in such sin without penance, he shall not be buried, but shall rot in his own house and shall not be taken away from it. The princes of the lands, knights, and foot-soldiers shall not presume to take up arms on the aforesaid days, except against pagans, invaders of the homeland, or violators of the aforesaid peace. We again confirm the other chapters which we established in the previous council [Col. 1128D].”

### Confirmation of the elect of Burgos

In the same council he also questioned all the bishops present concerning the consecration of the elect of Burgos, showing them the lord cardinal’s letters and setting forth the labours and tribulations of the Church of Burgos. The bishops, grieving for the Church of Burgos, which had so long remained bereft of a pastor, unanimously approved and advised the lord archbishop to provide mercifully for the welfare of that church and to consecrate its elect bishop for God’s service and the salvation of his own soul [Col. 1129A].

Complying with their request, three days after the end of the council he solemnly consecrated the elect of Burgos bishop, with the bishops of Asturias, Mondoñedo, and Portugal assisting. He caused him to promise obedience and fidelity to the Holy Roman Church, as ancient custom requires, and to confirm this with his own hand upon the most holy altar. Then the newly consecrated bishop, having received leave from the lord archbishop, returned joyfully to his own country.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Acquisition

Meanwhile, the archbishop, unceasingly concerned for the welfare of his church, very diligently acquired for the use of his church the estate called Sinales, situated beside Saint Christina of Noia, with all its appurtenances and household—not the whole estate, however, but half of three fourths—from the lady Aurodona Didaci. In exchange, he granted her half of another estate, namely Lustris, which half she was to hold only during her lifetime [Col. 1129B]. After her death, that half of the aforesaid estate was to revert by hereditary right to the Church of Blessed James.

### Acquisition

A certain provost named Didacus, priest of this venerable archbishop, at that time held the stewardship at Saint Mary of Nevar. Since this priest had already grown weary of holding that stewardship, he came of his own free will to the lord archbishop and agreed with him that he would grant in perpetuity to the lord archbishop and the Church of Blessed James half of all the goods and inheritances which he had acquired in that stewardship; the other half he would retain for himself to possess by hereditary right [Col. 1129C].

He had acquired in the aforesaid stewardship the church of Saint Michael of Rozuan, adjoining the church of Saint Mary of Nevar, and other inheritances situated in the boundaries and environs of that church. The archbishop, wise and prudent, wishing these acquisitions to remain secure and unshaken, caused deeds of purchase concerning them to be drawn up, ratified and confirmed by those who had concluded these agreements with him, and deposited in the treasury of Blessed James.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. Concerning the reconciliation of the king and his mother the queen

[Col. 1129D]

At about that time, after the death of the lord B., archbishop of Toledo, with whom the lord of Compostela had maintained a bitter and prolonged struggle for the advancement of his church, King A. and Queen U., his mother, who had long disagreed with one another, became reconciled and friends through the mediation and diligent efforts of the same lord of Compostela and his friends. Once this reconciliation had been made, at the instigation and contrivance of certain rivals, they sent the following letter to the lord of Compostela.

### Letter of the king and queen to the lord of Compostela

“A. and U., by God’s grace king and queen of Spain, to their dearest lord D., archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church: may you live in Christ.

“Let your holiness know that we are bound together by an indissoluble bond of friendship. As for the honour of the Church of Toledo, which you have laboured over a long time to diminish or annihilate by disturbing it, we say and admonish that you must henceforth by no means disturb it, lest the aforesaid church be deprived—God forbid—of its honour through your interference [Col. 1130A]. Farewell.”

### Reply of the lord archbishop to the aforesaid letter of the king and queen

“DIDACUS, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his venerable lady the queen, Lady U., and to her son, Lord A., the king: may you so govern the earthly kingdom that you do not lose the eternal one.

“We have received the letters of your highness with glad hand and examined them carefully. Just as the discord which, through our sins demanding it, has arisen between you until now was the destruction of the poor and of all churches, so the concord which, through God’s prevenient grace, we have learned has newly been made between you is the strengthening of holy peace and the foundation of Christian religion [Col. 1130B]. Because this is what we have always desired openly and secretly, and now know is being accomplished with God’s help, we render countless thanks to God and to Blessed James, who inspired your hearts to this. Therefore let not your clemency deign to doubt that we also rejoice, exult, and congratulate you exceedingly.

“Concerning the diminution of the Church of Toledo, which by these same letters you have informed us that we should not wish: God knows that we have never wished, nor do we wish, the rightful honour of that church or of any other church to be diminished. If our rivals or those of our church, by attacking and tearing us to pieces, make accusations about us before your nobility, do not willingly lend your ears to the bites of our detractors for their sake [Col. 1130C]. But if they assert anything which they profess to perceive, let them come before your royal judgment, and according to your counsel we shall answer their importunities.

“Remember also that, among other things which your royal prudence told us, it promised to do this: never to diminish our church, but always to defend, exalt, and increase it, being ever supported by our aid and counsel. If, moreover, we have obtained, now possess, or shall obtain anything, God willing, from the dignities of the Roman Church, we have done and shall do so always supported by your aid and counsel [Col. 1130D].

“We are sending you Suario Froilati, steward of our household, so that he may report orally to your excellency what is not contained in the letter. Through him reveal to us your heart and will, for we are ready to do and fulfil, to the best of our ability, whatever you command us. May almighty God, through the love and intercession of the most blessed apostle James, preserve your person and kingdom and bring you to everlasting life. Amen.”

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Letter sent by the cardinal to the archbishop

At about the same time Deusdedit, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 1131A], sent the following letter from Rome to the lord archbishop:

“To the venerable D., archbishop of Compostela and faithful legate of the Holy Roman Church, D., unworthy cardinal of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus: inquiry after the happiness of your prosperity.

“Let your supreme dignity, dearest friend, know that, by the favour of divine mercy, we are sound and safe; and that, while we live, our presence will be beneficially at your service. We wish you to know this especially in the imminent matter of improving your legation, most merciful lord, and renewing your privileges. Therefore we send this letter, so that you may promptly dispatch envoys to the Roman curia through us to attend to these matters without delay.

“Furthermore, most fortunate lord, we beseech your unfailing kindness that you faithfully send us, by these same envoys or by other envoys, the chasuble concerning which we have very often asked you [Col. 1131B], so that we may be able, as we ought, jointly to oblige your friends in your service. Moreover, most pious father, we ask you to greet on our behalf the whole congregation devoted to God and to receive the bearer of this little letter honourably. Farewell.”

### Reply of the lord archbishop to the aforesaid cardinal’s foregoing letter

“To the venerable lord and reverend father, Deusdedit, by God’s grace cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, D., humble servant of the Compostelans: faithful prayers and devoted service with reverence.

“That the excellence of your industry lives, flourishes, and, through the favour of divine grace, enjoys prosperity and safety, gives our heart joy beyond what can be believed. Your prudence should not doubt that we and our church rejoice at your successes as at our own, in pure truth and with every pretence removed, and render devoted thanks for them to divine omnipotence [Col. 1131C]. For we and our church remain steadfastly in the goodwill and affection of your holiness; and, with divine grace helping, we shall remain so that no intervening occasion can ever tear us away from it.

“Therefore we most earnestly beseech your venerable highness to repay us and our church with the gift of reciprocal love and, after the example of a good father and faithful friend, to deign, for the love of God and Blessed James, to love us and hold us as dear and special sons [Col. 1131D]. Furthermore, we inform the blessed memory of your lordship that our devotion has faithfully sent to your holiness, through envoys whom we recently sent to Rome, the modest provision for your week. We most earnestly ask your prudence kindly and honourably to receive them and diligently to conduct our business before the lord pope.

“As for the chasuble which you mentioned in your letter, what you request cannot be done at present, because when the letter of your holiness reached us our envoys had already set out for Rome long before. For your sake, remember us who are not forgetful of you. May your fatherhood flourish.”

## CHAPTER LXXV. Concerning the construction of a galley against Saracen incursions

After obtaining the archbishopric, the same archbishop saw that the warfare of the Almoravids was doing great annual harm to his land in its coastal parts. For the advancement of Christians and the humbling of Saracens, he adopted a wise and very useful plan: at great expense he had a bireme built, commonly called a *galea*, or galley. When built, he entrusted it to a certain young man named Fuxon, a native of the city of Pisa, an upright man highly skilled in seamanship, so that with it he might harass the land of the Almoravids by sea [Col. 1132A].

The aforesaid young man, having received the galley and sworn fidelity to the lord archbishop, began to harass the land of the Saracens by sea; with divine grace helping, he brought back from it much spoil and many captives. Thus, by the foresight and counsel of the lord archbishop, the coastal land which had previously been plundered and devastated each year by the Saracens remained completely secure; and the Saracens, who had annually been the plunderers and devastators of that land, by God’s grace became the prey of Christians [Col. 1132B].

During his episcopate he also had two galleys built with the same purpose. Yet through the fault and negligence of the inhabitants of Padrón, to whom they had been entrusted by him for guarding, they were destroyed and rendered useless. Before they were destroyed, however, they inflicted many losses on the Almoravids and conferred very many benefits upon Christians [Col. 1132C].

## CHAPTER LXXVI. At that time D., cardinal of the Roman Church, sent this letter to the lord of Compostela

“DEUSDEDIT, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Lawrence, to DIDACUS, most reverend and most glorious archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church: the desired greeting in Christ.

“I first make haste to signify what your admirable kindness desires affectionately to hear from me. Let your charity know, dearest friend, that I am sound and safe, and that Calixtus of blessed memory has undoubtedly departed honourably from this life [Col. 1132D]—on 13 December 1124. Therefore the glorious divine goodness did not permit His Church, bereft of its pastor, to remain long so; but quickly appointed Honorius its bishop. To him, venerable friend, I advise you to send honourable envoys promptly, so that through me and our friends you may renew your privileges, indeed from good to better.

“Furthermore, most merciful father, we seek to urge your greatness to take care to send us at once, through the same envoys or through others whom you know to be trustworthy, the chasuble long desired by us, so that you may have our faithful service for the honour of yourself, the blessed apostle James, and all the canons together.”

### The lord of Compostela replied to the aforesaid letter as follows

[Col. 1133A]

“To the venerable lord and reverend father, by God’s grace legate and cardinal of our mother the Holy Roman Church, D., DIDACUS, humble servant of the Compostelans: the desired happiness of this present and future life.

“You should not doubt that we and our church rejoice, in pure truth and without any pretence, at your welfare and prosperity as though they were our own; and that we would likewise grieve at your adversity and tribulation, should they occur—God forbid—for your prudence is by no means unaware of how great and what kind of affection our devotion bears toward you. Persisting faithfully in your goodwill and love, and devotedly girded to carry out, to the best of our ability, your service and will [Col. 1133B], we earnestly beseech your clemency to look not to the rarity or smallness of our service but rather to the expenditure of pure and true love, and to conduct the business of us and our church at the curia and before the majesty of the lord pope after the example of a good father and patron.

“Furthermore, we inform the blessed memory of your lordship that our modest self received the letters of your highness on the fourth Nones of August [2 August] and read them with glad and joyful heart. We had sent our envoys to Rome with our blessing and the revenue for your week fifteen days after Easter had passed, because we had already heard of the death of our lord and reverend father of venerable memory, Pope Calixtus [Col. 1133C]. Therefore, until those envoys return and we send others, we cannot at present comply with your request. Meanwhile, for your sake, remember our smallness, which is never forgetful of your dignity. May your fatherhood flourish.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Concerning the making of the greater and lesser bells

Meanwhile the venerable archbishop, being very greatly concerned for the benefit and honour of his church, strove with vigilant and unwearied care to acquire or purchase the ornaments which he perceived to be necessary and fitting for it. Seeing, therefore, that his church needed good and suitable bells, he engaged, from beyond Porto, a certain master highly skilled in the craft, on agreed terms and pay; and he ordered two larger and two smaller bells to be made for the honour and benefit of his church [Col. 1133D].

O prudent and wise man, who never neglected ecclesiastical affairs when secular business arose, nor through concern for ecclesiastical affairs left unattended secular matters belonging to him!

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. Celebration of the council

Likewise, the venerable archbishop grieved greatly that the kingdom of Spain was being troubled and devastated through the discord between King A. and his mother Queen U. In fatherly concern he provided for the benefit and honour of Holy Church. Having invited bishops, abbots, and other religious persons, and summoned counts and princes also, he celebrated a council at Compostela on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January], in the third year of his archiepiscopate [Col. 1134A].  
[Note: The fifth year was already passing since 25 July 1120, when, as appears above in chapter 19, he began to be called archbishop.]

At the council he dealt first prudently and wisely with ecclesiastical affairs, and then with peace between the aforesaid King A. and his mother the queen, as also among the other princes who were mutually at variance.
