Finally, he proclaimed, commended, and praised orally at that council an expedition against the Moors, for the humbling and confusion of paganism and for the advancement and building-up of Christianity. By the authority of almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and James, and of all the saints, he granted full absolution of all their sins to all who, after receiving penance, would go on that expedition [Col. 1134B].

He also sent the following charter concerning that full absolution to kings, counts, other princes, knights, and foot-soldiers, so that, when they had seen the full absolution, they might go more willingly and devoutly upon the aforesaid expedition for God’s service and remission of their sins. He ordered archbishops, abbots, and other prelates of Holy Church to preach, commend, and explain this charter to all the people and by every means to encourage them toward the aforesaid expedition.

“DIDACUS, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to the venerable and beloved brethren in Christ—archbishops, bishops [Col. 1134C], abbots, and all prelates of Holy Church—as also to kings, counts, other princes, and all Christian people: may you use temporal things so soberly, justly, and piously that through God’s grace you may deserve to attain eternal things.

“Your charity, dearest brethren, hears the Apostle crying out and calling us in this way to avoid sleep: ‘It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep’ (Rom. 13:11). It is fitting and most salutary that we obey this voice: both because by living wickedly we have lied concerning what we promised in baptism, and because we see our end and the day of strict judgment approaching.

“Behold, dearest brethren, the Lord stands at the door and cries: ‘If anyone opens the door to me, I will enter and dine with him, and he with me’ (Rev. 3:20) [Col. 1134D]. Therefore let us not harden the ears of our heart against his voice, lest he say to us terribly and justly: ‘I called and you refused’ (Prov. 1:24); I knocked at your door, and you did not open to me.

“Therefore, casting away the works of darkness and the unbearable yoke of the devil, let us apply ourselves to works of righteousness and unanimously put on the armour of light, according to the Apostle’s admonition (Eph. 6:11). As the soldiers of Christ and faithful sons of Holy Church opened the road to Jerusalem with much labour and the shedding of much blood, so let us become soldiers of Christ; and, having defeated his most wicked enemies, the Saracens, let us open, through his assisting grace, the way to that same sepulchre of the Lord through the regions of Spain [Col. 1135A], a route shorter and much less laborious.

“Whoever wishes to share in this warfare should remember all his sins and hasten to true confession and true penance. Then, having taken up arms, let him not delay in proceeding to the camp of Christ for God’s service and the remission of his sins. If he does this, we and our venerable brother co-bishops, abbots, and other religious persons, sitting with us in the council which, according to the lord pope’s decree, we celebrated at Compostela by God’s authorship on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, absolve him from all sins which, from the font of baptism until this present day, he has committed at the devil’s instigation, by the authority of almighty God, the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and James, and all the saints [Col. 1135B].

“To those unwilling or unable to join these camps of Christ, we command and forbid under obedience that they presume by rash daring to inflict any harm upon the lands, honours, or other goods of those who remain in God’s service, or in any way to seize or trouble their persons or possessions. If they despise our decree in this matter, by the authority of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and James and all the saints, we excommunicate and anathematize them and exclude them from the thresholds of Holy Church. Thus, if they are ill, they shall not be visited until they make satisfaction; and if they die, they shall not be buried [Col. 1135C]. If any prince or lord grants them fiefs or other benefices, both giver and receiver shall be anathema.

“If any man or woman cannot go to the aforesaid camp, but, according to his or her means, sends armed knights or foot-soldiers in his or her place, after receiving penance as stated above, we grant that person the same full absolution in the Lord’s name. Whoever, observing our command, honours, assists, and gives support to Christ’s champions as they go to the Lord’s army or return from it, may receive during the course of this present life the fruit of good action and deserve to obtain in the future the rewards of eternal blessedness.

“May divine omnipotence visit you with the grace of its blessing [Col. 1135D] and inflame and inspire your hearts to go into this army of God, through him to whom belong honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

“Whenever prelates of Holy Church see this charter, let them take the greatest care to preach, commend, and explain it orally, for God’s service and the remission of sins, to kings, counts, other princes, knights, and foot-soldiers. We and the whole synodal assembly also command that whoever undertakes this expedition, so great and so salutary, for the remedy and salvation of his soul, shall not presume to return from it without the leave and counsel of bishops and princes.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Letter of the lord pope sent to the archbishop

[Col. 1136A]

After the celebration of the aforesaid council, Honorius, pope of Rome, successor of Pope Calixtus of venerable memory, sent the following letter to the lord of Compostela:

“Honorius, bishop,” etc.

“Your …,” etc. See under Honorius II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, no. 17.

## CHAPTER LXXX. How F. Joannides attacked the people of Compostela and, summoned by the king, went to his court

After a not long interval, F. Joannides, lord of Saint Pelagius of Luto, driven by tyrannical savagery and the goads of avarice, treacherously seized the burgesses of the city of Compostela [Col. 1136B]. Having shut them up in prison, he began inhumanely and intolerably to compel them to ransom themselves by the infliction of various tortures. He alleged as a pretext for their seizure a certain false and fabricated cause: namely, that he had suffered very great injuries and numerous insults from the Compostelans, which, he said, he could not leave unavenged.

When he learned of their capture, the lord archbishop—highly skilled in all matters, secular as well as ecclesiastical, and most renowned among illustrious men—sent prudent and wise envoys to him twice, three times, and four times. He demanded of him why he had inflicted such an injury and so great an affront upon Blessed James and himself; through these envoys he instructed and earnestly requested him, for the love of God and Blessed James, to call to mind the homage and fidelity which he had rendered and confirmed by oath, and, observing the limits of justice, to release his captives unharmed and without any payment [Col. 1136C].

But he was deafer than iron and stones to these commands. He neither feared the Lord, avenger of crimes and impieties, nor showed reverence to Blessed James or to the archbishop; for he was unwilling either to release the captives or to correct his wrongs. Therefore the lord archbishop, no little stirred, first excommunicated him, all subject to him, and his entire territory by the authority of almighty God and all the saints; and throughout his land he prohibited all divine offices except penance and baptism [Col. 1136D].

Then, when he, deceived by diabolical fraud, utterly despised the excommunication, and the lord archbishop was unwilling, out of fear of him, to do nothing, the archbishop, defender and upholder of reason and justice, gathered an immense army of knights and foot-soldiers and invaded his lordship by land and sea in hostile fashion. He attacked the fortifications of the castles with the utmost severity; he utterly devastated by plunder and fire his villages and inheritances and the whole lordship belonging to him. Moreover, he caused the whole army to take up quarters and remain in that land until the aforesaid tyrant, compelled by necessity, restored peace with him and allowed those whom he held captive to depart freely and unconditionally, without any ransom. In addition, he confirmed his former homage and former friendship with the lord archbishop [Col. 1137A], and promised that he would come to Compostela into his presence to make satisfaction.

While the archbishop was engaged in such an expedition for the protection of justice and the vindication of his own dignity, he had already learned, through messengers and public report, of the death of Queen Urraca, who had paid the debt of nature on the sixth Ides of March, in the era 1163 (A.D. 1126), in the district of Campaña. Returning nevertheless from that expedition, having attained his purpose and triumphed over his enemy, to Compostela, he received certain news of the queen’s death. For there he found in his court royal messengers—the bishop of Mondoñedo, namely, and other worthy men—reporting to him that the queen’s death was true, and earnestly and humbly entreating him, by the king’s command, that, having hastened his journey, he should proceed to León, in order to crown the king there and give him counsel concerning the administration, reconciliation, and ordering of the kingdom, for the honour and advantage of Holy Church. For the city of León was at that time already under royal jurisdiction, since the king had acquired it by the counsel and aid of the citizens and princes of the land.

Having heard the message of King A., the lord archbishop, after procuring abundantly everything he knew would be necessary for the journey, set out joyfully for León on the Friday before Palm Sunday, accompanied by the chief and most distinguished persons of his church. Departing thus from Compostela, he reached the city of Lugo on Saturday, where he was kindly and fittingly received in procession by Lord Peter, bishop of Lugo, and by the clergy and people of that city. There he solemnly celebrated Palm Sunday. On the following day, departing from Lugo, he reached the city of Astorga on Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper. There he was likewise received with a most splendid procession by Lord Alon, bishop of that city, and by the clerical and lay multitude; and, with chrism and consecrated oil, he himself completed in ecclesiastical fashion the whole office belonging to that day. Then, leaving Astorga with the bishops of Mondoñedo, Astorga, and Lugo accompanying him, he at last reached León on the vigil of the Sunday of the Resurrection. There he was graciously and honourably received with an eminent procession by Lord D., bishop of that city, by the bishop of Oviedo, who was then present there, by clergy and people, [Col. 1137D] and by the leading men of the whole country; and there he celebrated the Paschal solemnity with joy. On the following day, after the vigil and Mass for the soul of Queen Urraca, who lay buried there, had been celebrated, he put on his pontifical vestments and came to her tomb with crosses and censers, performing the due obsequies for the remedy and salvation of her soul according to ecclesiastical custom.

The king, however, who was then absent from León through necessity, upon hearing of his arrival sent his envoys to him with all speed, most earnestly and tirelessly begging him to deign to come to him as far as the city of Zamora, and not to be burdened by the labour or length of the journey. Having heard the king’s embassy, on the third day after the Sunday of the Resurrection the archbishop left León with the bishops of Mondoñedo, Lugo, Astorga, and Oviedo and undertook the journey to Zamora with an innumerable military and clerical retinue. As he approached that city, King A., the archbishop of Toledo, all the bishops who were present at the king’s court, and also the clergy and people of the city went out to meet him. He was received with a great and remarkable procession, most magnificently and honourably, and at the king’s command was lodged in the royal palaces. For the king loved him with the special affection due to his godfather, patron, spiritual father, and coronator, so greatly that he wholly subordinated his own honour to the archbishop’s honour, [Col. 1138B] and ordered all the servants of his court to serve and please the archbishop more than himself. He held him in such favour and honour that he never allowed him to come to the royal court; rather, the king himself came to the archbishop’s court twice or three times daily. So long as he remained at his court, the king everywhere granted him his own palaces for lodging; and, as stated above, he always came to the archbishop’s lodging, both to show him reverence and to settle matters in his presence and according to his counsel and judgment. The archbishop of Toledo, the bishops of Segovia, Palencia, Salamanca, and Ávila, and all the others mentioned above also came daily to his court, both because he was legate of the Holy Roman Church and because, through his intercession with the king, they obtained from the king the petitions they sought.

## Chapter LXXXI. How he bought the castle of Cira from Queen Urraca

Lest we pass over the truth in silence, we have thought it necessary to record with the foregoing that the lord of Compostela had always had a bitter lawsuit and a most serious quarrel with Queen Urraca after the death of her father, King A., of venerable memory—sometimes secretly, sometimes openly. Incited by the prompting and counsel of certain of his rivals, the queen secretly longed for his humiliation and removal; and, in order to extort money, she was greatly eager to replace and substitute another in his office. [Col. 1138D] He, however, like a prudent and wise man, guarded himself most carefully against her plots and treacheries; and, lest she should prevail against him in any manner, he constantly kept the protection of friends and dependants around him. Although he was incessantly harassed and troubled by her, this man of supreme prudence and remarkable foresight strove with sleepless and untiring care to increase and enlarge the honour of his church.

Seeing, therefore, that a certain castle named Cira, with its dependencies, was highly useful and advantageous to his church, being situated and founded in the middle of the honour of St James, he took counsel with his friends and bought that castle from her for the hereditary possession of St James for 150 marks of silver. He extracted from her a written deed of the sale and purchase [Col. 1139A] of that castle; and she herself, having received the aforesaid money, confirmed and ratified that document with her own hand. Afterwards, when the dispute and dissension between them, as mentioned above, had continued for some time, the queen asked the lord archbishop for that castle as a fief. He acceded to her request and granted her the fortress she sought, on this condition and agreement: whenever he or his successor wished to recover his castle, Queen Urraca was to restore peacefully and without any resistance to the lord archbishop, or to his successor, what was his and what he had bought.

After a long time, it happened that the lord of Compostela sent his envoys, the archdeacon Arias Muñiz and Cardinal Arias González, into the district of Campaña to the queen. When they arrived there, [Col. 1139B] they found her very ill and at the point of death. Before the envoys’ arrival, she had already put her household in order; and, remembering the agreement which she had made with the lord of Compostela concerning the castle of Cira, she had ordered that castle to be restored to St James and the lord archbishop, with every pretext set aside. When she also saw the envoys, wishing her command to remain valid and unshaken, she invested the aforesaid envoys publicly with the castle and its dependencies. Through those envoys and through a certain knight, Juan Díaz, who was then present at her court, she commanded Juan Díaz himself, under whose right and lordship the aforesaid castle was held, not to delay peacefully and without any opposition [Col. 1139C] in restoring the castle to the lord archbishop.

Accordingly, after receiving from the queen letters to Juan Díaz concerning this embassy, the aforesaid envoys of the lord of Compostela came to the lord king at San Facundo and related to him, fully and truthfully, what the queen had commanded concerning the castle and honour of Cira. The king, trusting without hesitation the words of the envoys, willingly granted and confirmed what his mother the queen had ordered concerning that castle. He also sent a messenger with his own letters to Juan Díaz, commanding and most earnestly requesting him to restore without delay the castle of Cira to the lord of Compostela, in accordance with Queen Urraca’s decree. He likewise ordered the lord of Compostela by letter that, if Juan Díaz should presume to oppose him in the surrender of the castle, he should gather an army, attack him, [Col. 1139D] and take the castle from him by force.

Juan Díaz, however, upon seeing the king’s letters and messenger, would neither fulfil the queen’s decree nor carry out the king’s command. Instead, retaining the castle contrary to law, he wholly despised the will and decision of king and queen. Therefore, when the lord archbishop wished to invade him by armed force and compel him to submit to justice, Juan made homage and swore fealty to the lord archbishop, promising and swearing that he would go into the presence of the lord king and, if the king commanded it, would restore the castle to the lord archbishop without fraud. Having received his homage and fealty, the archbishop answered that it pleased him that Juan should go into the king’s presence, [Col. 1140A] and that he himself would never wish to possess the castle unless the king ordered it.

At the same time when the lord of Compostela went to León at the king’s invitation, intending to crown the king and give him counsel concerning the administration and ordering of the realm, as stated above, Juan Díaz preceded him on the journey. Coming into the king’s presence while the lord of Compostela was unaware and absent, he had obtained from the king, both personally and through his friends, that the king should grant him the castle of Cira as a fief; and he had already made and sworn homage and fealty to the king for that castle. Therefore, when the lord of Compostela subsequently came into the king’s presence, he had a great conflict and most bitter dispute with both the king and Juan Díaz. For when he asked the king for the castle which was his own, and which Queen Urraca, at her death, had restored to St James and to him, the king answered that he had already granted that castle, with the court as witness, to Juan Díaz as a fief; nor could he take away from him any longer what he had already received from Juan in homage and fealty for that castle.

On hearing this, the lord of Compostela presented many grounds and arguments, both publicly and privately, to the king, by which it was quite manifest to all the barons of the court that St James and he had been wronged and burdened. Then, both personally and through friends, he began earnestly to beg and entreat the king to fear divine omnipotence, the avenger of wrongs, following the example of a good and just king; to show reverence to St James for the remission [Col. 1140C] of his sins; and not, through the counsel and persuasion of evil men, to depart from the path of truth and justice. The good shepherd knocked at the door, that the pastures of his sheep might be enlarged and that they might not be devoured by wolfish rapacity; he cried at the door, but was in no way heard, the counsel of malevolent and greedy men preventing it. For the king answered him as he cried and knocked that he would never strip his knight, Juan Díaz, by taking away that castle, nor would he in the manner of an inconstant and frivolous man annul what he had done in the presence of all the chief men of his court.

Having recognized and seen the king’s obstinacy and unyieldingness, the lord of Compostela, deeply afflicted with grief, began anxiously to consider and devise [Col. 1140D] how he might soften and overcome the king’s heart, hardened against him, and recall him from so great a stubbornness. He therefore bribed the king’s attendants and intimates with money: he promised ten marks to the steward of the royal household, and another ten to another counsellor, adviser, and manager of all the king’s affairs, so that they might favour him in this matter and assist him in seeking justice. Having thus attracted and enlisted them, he likewise approached the king with money and, promising him fifty marks of silver, requested only justice for the injury inflicted on him by the king, with the aforesaid supporters helping and pleading for him.

The king, partly changed by the promise of money and partly swayed by the counsel and entreaties of the aforesaid supporters of the lord of Compostela, answered him thus: [Col. 1141A] “Reverend father, I should very much wish that St James and your holiness should have your justice; but I greatly fear offending my knight. I also fear the reproach of the populace and of the whole court if I should so quickly annul what I established so recently. Yet if your discretion could give me such counsel as to show how I might restore your justice to you and keep my knight at peace, I would most willingly do it for love of God and St James.”

The lord of Compostela answered these words of the king: “With the help of divine omnipotence and St James, in whose merits we trust, we shall indeed give you such counsel.” Having said this, he explained that counsel to him in these words: “Order all the pontiffs, princes, and leading men of the entire court to come into your presence tomorrow. When you and they have assembled together, I shall make my complaint before everyone concerning you and Juan Díaz, and demand redress for the injury inflicted upon me by you and by him. Once my complaint has been made and my argument and his have been heard, order the pontiffs, councillors, and powers of the court to withdraw apart, so that they may carefully examine our arguments and, after examining them, render a true judgment. Thus I shall be able to obtain my justice from you without blame, for they will indeed find that I was wronged in the taking of my castle.”

This counsel greatly pleased the king, and it was accordingly carried out on the following day. When the lord of Compostela and Juan Díaz had each presented his case before the full court, [Col. 1141C] the pontiffs, councillors, and princes present withdrew apart at the king’s command. Examining the arguments of both parties, they found that the lord of Compostela had been unjustly and unreasonably deprived of his castle. They therefore ruled unanimously that the king should satisfy his knight in another way and wholly restore his castle to the lord of Compostela. This judgment pleased the king sufficiently, both because it was just and because he saw that his knight could not lawfully bring an accusation against him. Accordingly, after granting that knight another hereditary honour and paying him 1,500 solidi in Jaca currency, he satisfied him and restored the castle to the lord of Compostela in perpetuity.

In the same city, the lord of Compostela acquired, by his prudence and shrewdness, for the hereditary possession of St James and his church, a certain village named Archilinos, an excellent place highly suitable for cultivation, from the king’s sister, the lady Infanta Geloira, with the king confirming and approving the transaction. [Col. 1141D] Thus the lord of Compostela, having recovered his castle with its dependencies and triumphed over his rivals and adversaries, returned joyfully home. May the guardian who gives strength to the wise be praised.

## Chapter LXXXII. Exchange of the castle of Faro for the land of Taberioli

At the same time, while the lord of Compostela was staying with the king in the royal court, the king earnestly requested him at a castle named Tierra [Note: [Col. 1141] Today Castro-Tierra, in the kingdom of León, on the western bank of the river Esla.] that, by making an exchange with him, he should grant him the castle of Faro [Col. 1142A] with its dependencies in return for the land of Taberioli, with its ancient boundaries and the honours pertaining to it.

Having taken counsel with the chief persons of his church who were present with him, the lord of Compostela assented to the king’s request. He did so partly because the aforesaid castle of Faro was very remote from the honour of St James and brought almost no benefit to the lord of Compostela except its name; indeed, for its guarding and watch, he paid out large sums every year to mercenary soldiers. He also did so because he knew that the land of Taberioli and its appurtenances were useful and advantageous to him, being adjacent to the honour of St James and situated about the river Ulla; and because that land, with its ancient boundaries and its *character*, was much better and much larger than the territory pertaining to the castle of Faro. Concerning this exchange, he obtained from the king a charter, at the king’s earnest request, confirmed and ratified by the king’s own hand before all the courtiers.

The lord of Compostela also acquired from Vermudo Pérez the church called St Anastasia, which is in the land of Gentines, because Vermudo, son of Count Peter, granted that church in perpetuity to St James and the lord of Compostela, for the remedy of his soul and the reward of eternal life.

He also received two estates in the land of Salnés from his kinswoman Lady Mayor Arias. At her death she likewise bestowed them permanently upon St James and his church for the salvation and remedy of her soul. The lord of Compostela generously granted the aforesaid church and those [Col. 1142C] two estates as a fief to one of his cardinals, Peter Foulques, because that cardinal had laboured greatly and faithfully in his service and on the Roman journey.

## Chapter LXXXIII. How he visited the Roman court through envoys

A long interval before the aforesaid exchange, the lord of Compostela had sent to the curia his envoys Pelagius Astrariz and one of his clerics named Sesnandus. One of them fell sick on the journey and could not reach it; the other, after reaching the curia, was ill there for a long time and obtained nothing whatever in the matter [Col. 1142D] for which he had been sent. For at that time he found the entire curia disturbed against the lord of Compostela, because his rivals—the archbishop of Toledo and the bishop of Coimbra—were then present there and had poured many fabricated and false allegations concerning the lord of Compostela into the ears of the pope and throughout the whole curia.

When the lord of Compostela learned of their illness and impediment, he sent other envoys there with his blessing: Peter Foulques, cardinal and chaplain, and Pelagius Díaz, canon. They likewise found the curia disturbed against him; nevertheless, with much exertion and through the intervention of certain friends of the lord of Compostela, they appeased the pope and the whole curia. When they had appeased them, they brought to the lord of Compostela letters of this kind on the pope’s behalf:

> “Honorius, bishop,” etc.
>
> “The envoys with letters,” etc. See under Honorius II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, no. 33.

Other envoys, returning from the curia after obtaining nothing, brought these other letters to the lord of Compostela:

> “Honorius, bishop,” etc.
>
> “Although concerning your person,” etc. See above, no. 34.

The following letter was sent by A., cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor:

> “To his dearest friend DIDACUS, by the grace of God venerable archbishop of Compostela, A., cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Roman Church, and L., [Col. 1143B] may you enjoy the bread of salvation.
>
> “We give you thanks as to a father and friend for the gifts bestowed upon us by your fatherhood. We have laboured for your honour and service, and, so far as the power which God has given us permits, we shall by no means cease to labour until the end which you request. Farewell.”

## Chapter LXXXIV. How he captured the tower of Taberioli

After Queen Urraca had died, and her son Alfonso had been elevated as king and was now equipped with military arms, many Galician princes feared that, as he removed them, they would lose the royal honours which they held; and they rebelled against him contrary to law and right. All of them, however, except Arias Pérez—who had been a traitor and rebel against the aforesaid queen, [Col. 1143C] and had treacherously seized the king himself in his childhood—were reconciled to the king through the mediation and counsel of the lord of Compostela and made homage and fealty to him.

Arias Pérez, however, presumed to rebel against the king in the royal castle of Lupaia, together with the entire honour attached to that castle, and in other castles—namely, St John of Peña Cornaria and the tower of Taberioli, which this traitor had built there. He neither deigned to make homage to the king nor to render him any service. The king, angered because more important affairs prevented him from coming into Galicia to subdue him, most earnestly requested in letters and through messengers the lord of Compostela, his godfather and faithful supporter, whom he himself had placed over all Galicia. [Col. 1143D] He likewise commanded and ordered by letter Count G., to whom he had granted the entire honour of the aforesaid traitor, that they should rise together against that traitor, take away the honours which he held, and, gathering all their forces, besiege the fortresses mentioned above until they compelled him to a genuine surrender and utterly destroyed and disinherited him.

Having heard the king’s commands and seen his letters with the messengers, the lord of Compostela and the aforesaid count, having taken counsel, unanimously resolved that the lord of Compostela, after gathering a great army of infantry and cavalry, should keep the tower of Taberioli under siege until he captured it and, when captured, completely destroyed it. The count himself was to keep the castle of Lupaia—fortified by nature and art—and the other castles under such siege that no one could enter them or leave them, nor could provisions or weapons be brought in. The lord of Compostela therefore summoned all his knights and infantry, and also admonished and ordered the citizens of Compostela not to delay in taking part in this enterprise. He besieged the tower of Taberioli, fortified by rampart and ditch, and attacked it most fiercely with iron and fire. He also caused a military engine to be made, which the common people call a *gatus* (“cat”); bringing it against the tower, he ordered the tower to be undermined all around and the squared stones removed from beneath it. [Col. 1144B] Thus, with great labour and difficulty, he finally captured the tower and entirely destroyed it after its capture.

Thirty-six of Arias Pérez’s knights who were rebelling inside were all captured. Their military equipment, wheat, and everything else contained there were all made booty for the soldiers. Thus, having captured the tower, the lord of Compostela returned home victorious and having attained his purpose, with joy and gladness. In the aforesaid tower he lost in death two very noble knights from among his own retainers; accordingly, he was sorrowful and grieved for a long time.

Before the destruction of the aforesaid tower, he had utterly and completely destroyed two castles: one named Grallaria, built by Count M. on the bank of the river Iso to attack and devastate the honour of St James; the other built by Count F., son of Count Peter, in the land of Taberioli near Raneta [Col. 1144C] for the same purpose.

After a short interval, the aforesaid pope, namely Honorius, sent letters of this kind to the lord of Compostela. Their bearers were Peter Foulques, cardinal and chaplain, and Peter Gudesteiz, canon:

> “Honorius, bishop,” etc.
>
> “Noble and famous,” etc. See above, no. 50.

## Chapter LXXXV. How he went into Portugal with the emperor, and of that emperor’s ingratitude toward him

A full year and a half after the death of Queen Urraca had passed, in the era 1164 (A.D. 1127), on the sixth Ides of March [Note: [Col. 1143D] The era and date of the month indicate when Queen Urraca died—as is clear from chapter 80, no. 2—not what had elapsed [Col. 1144D] since her death. Or else era 1165 should be substituted.], King A., her son, now twenty-one years old, having violently expelled and put to flight the king of Aragon from a castle, had an immense quarrel with his aunt, the Portuguese queen named T.

For she, puffed up with proud arrogance, exceeded the bounds of justice and deigned to render the king no service from the kingdom which she ought to have held from him. Indeed, powerful in men, arms, and resources, she invaded the borders of Galicia with an armed army and violently subjected to her own right and lordship the cities and castles adjoining Portugal—namely Tui and others. [Col. 1145A] She also caused new fortresses to be built in that land in order to disturb and devastate the country and to rebel against the king. Therefore King A. and almost all the princes of the Spanish lands who supported his side were greatly angered. The king came into Galicia and summoned the princes and powers of the entire land for an expedition against that queen. He also earnestly appealed to the lord of Compostela, who possessed greater power than all the leading men of Galicia, to assist him in recovering his kingdom and overthrowing his enemies.

The lord of Compostela, assenting out of zeal for justice to this request, summoned together all knights and infantry who were under his jurisdiction; and he compelled the citizens of Compostela, partly by force and partly by entreaties, to join him in that expedition. Having therefore assembled a great army, he accompanied King A. into Portugal against the aforesaid queen. There, for six weeks, he remained with all his forces in great labour and danger, devastating villages and besieging and taking castles and cities. Nor did he return from there, nor permit his army to return, until nearly the whole land had been devastated and he had restored concord between the king and queen through his own counsel and skill.

Once the whole land had been pacified and a stable and firm agreement restored between them, the lord of Compostela returned home with great joy. For, in all truth and without any pretence, he considered the king to be his closest friend and intimate, both because he had rendered so great a service and many earlier services, and because he was the king’s godfather, had anointed him king, and had armed him with his own hands as a knight before the altar of St James. [Col. 1145C] The lord of Compostela thought thus within himself; but the king had another purpose in mind. Whisperers and slanderers, driven by ill will and envy, rose unanimously against the lord of Compostela after making a conspiracy. Accusing him before the king of deadly and false crimes, they advised the king first to seize him and, having seized him, strip him of all honour and money; then to divide all his honour into five parts.

The king, however, clearly perceiving their treachery and ill will against the lord archbishop and having no doubt that their slanders were fabricated and false, was unwilling wholly to consent to their counsels and persuasions, out of fear of God and St James. He answered that he would never stretch out his hands to commit so great a crime, nor allow his soul to be polluted by the seizure of his godfather and spiritual father. He added that he would never take away the archbishop’s honour during his lifetime unless he committed some act against the king for which he ought justly and reasonably to be deprived of that honour.

Upon hearing this, those whisperers and traitors, greatly saddened, advised the king at least to demand from him an enormous sum of money. The king promised that he would assent to their counsels and wishes, not so much at their prompting as compelled by financial necessity; for he was in urgent need of money, which at that time was greatly necessary to him for paying mercenary soldiers. [Col. 1146A] O envy! What and how great are the crimes which you devise and contrive—neither tongue can express them nor mind conceive them. Envy brought the disaster of death upon the first human being; whence the Apostle says: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Rom. 5:12; Wis. 2:24). Under envy’s prompting, the Jews dared to condemn their King, namely Christ, to a most shameful death. Under envy’s prompting, whisperers and slanderers rose with poisonous mouths against the lord of Compostela, who had deserved no evil from them.

Some of them were noble knights dwelling outside the city, his own fosterlings, enriched and ennobled by him; others were citizens of Compostela, bound to him by oath, upon whom he had bestowed many benefits; still others were clerics and canons of the church, whom he had raised in his court as spiritual sons and, after raising them, had promoted at the appropriate time to honours and dignities. Through them, therefore, the proverb of Pygmalion was fulfilled in the lord of Compostela: “Many necks have been broken because of good deeds.”

## Chapter LXXXVI. How the emperor violently extorted money from the archbishop

Meanwhile, after King A., as stated, had acquired and pacified the Portuguese district through the prudence and counsel of the lord of Compostela, he came swiftly to Compostela. The archbishop received him carefully and honourably: he summoned together all the clerics of the whole city, the abbots with their [Col. 1146C] monks, clothed them in silk copes, made for him a splendid and distinguished procession, and showed him great honour and reverence. Afterwards, he provided for him magnificently and abundantly until the third day.

On the third day after his arrival, the king came with a few men into the treasury of St James and privately addressed the lord of Compostela as follows: “Reverend father, as I well know and have now very often proved in deed, your ability has loved me greatly from the beginning of my reign; it has steadfastly remained in goodwill and love toward me, with every pretence removed; it has diligently resolved to serve me and obey my commands. Those whom I loved, it loved; and those whom I hated, it hated also. Why say more? It has been my foot and my eye; with fatherly affection it has provided in every respect for my advantage. Therefore I return the greatest thanks due to your merits, O your magnificence, and most earnestly beseech your clemency to persevere firmly in these things. I also desire and earnestly ask that, as you have helped and sustained me hitherto, so you may now help me and grant me some of your money at present, because I am surrounded by great necessities and weighty affairs which I cannot manage without the counsel and assistance of your discretion.”

When the king had finished speaking, the lord of Compostela, although he had no doubt that the king had spoken deceitfully and had learned through his friends of the treachery noted above, nevertheless answered him graciously. [Col. 1147A] He said that he wished always to remain in the king’s love and favour, and that on no account would he ever turn away from loyalty and service to him. Then, with the counsel of his brethren, he promised him 300 marks of silver, by which he might relieve his needs and settle his affairs.

At the offer of this gift, the king was silent for a long time and would then give him no reply, because he considered the proposed gift insignificant. After much intervening conversation, he finally answered that he would leave the treasury in order to consult with his confidential advisers, who were hostile to us, concerning the offer of that gift. Then the lord of Compostela, perceiving his intention and showing reverence to royal dignity, addressed him thus: “Lord king, if it please your highness, I shall withdraw apart, and you may take counsel with your confidential advisers concerning what you ought to answer me.”

When the king replied that this pleased him, the lord of Compostela left the treasury and entered the choir of St James. There, with certain persons of his church and a few other men, he awaited the royal reply for a long time. The king then took counsel with the adversaries and traitors of the lord of Compostela and sent word to him through those same adversaries that he should give him 600 marks of silver and allow him to seize whomever he wished from the city. The lord archbishop then sent word to the king through the same messengers that he should name individually those whom he wished to seize. The king named Lord Bernald, treasurer of St James; Peter Estébaniz, his brother; and Gonzalo Peláez, his nephew—friends, that is, and most intimate associates of the lord archbishop—whom he would by no means allow to be seized or consent to have seized.

Hearing their names, the archbishop, greatly distressed, replied that he would permit neither them nor anyone else from the city—whether cleric or layman, not even the humblest peasant of the whole jurisdiction of St James—to be seized, nor would he give the king permission to seize them. On hearing this, the king became angry; urged on by accomplices in the nefarious treachery, he sent him word that he must pay him a thousand marks of silver, or surrender the whole jurisdiction of St James. Yet he said that he would leave him some part of that jurisdiction in which he could live well [Col. 1147D] and maintain himself honourably.

Then the archbishop summoned to himself all the officials and canons of his Church. He set out before them in order the king’s message and demand. As they were astonished and amazed at the royal demand, the lord archbishop spoke as follows:

> “Dearest brothers, observe that the king is seeking an occasion against us, because we have ill-wishers and traitors in his palace, at whose prompting and counsel he wishes to injure us, deprive us of this jurisdiction. And you, brothers, must henceforth take thought for your Church: choose yourselves a shepherd, for I will resign from this jurisdiction before I pay such a sum of money, since I do not know where I could obtain so great a sum of money. Nevertheless, I shall not abandon my dignity [Col. 1148A] or my order, whether for the king or for any power; rather, in them I shall serve almighty God for as long as I live.”

Then all present, both canons and others, began at these words of the archbishop to weep and say:

> “Why, Father, do you wish to abandon us? Why do you wish to leave us desolate? For a ravening wolf will invade your flock and plunder it for himself; he will stretch forth the hand of his cruelty over your sheepfold and utterly strip it of all its resources. Of two evils the lighter must be chosen: it is evil for you to promise so great a sum to the king, but it is worse for you to abandon your jurisdiction. For if you abandon it, all whom you have hitherto nourished, supported, and enriched will now be reduced to nothing, and your church will be destroyed. Therefore set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel [Col. 1148B]; resist the wolf that is coming, lest you seem to be a hireling and not a shepherd. Labour for your sheepfold; console your Church; labour for justice. Attend to Truth itself, preaching thus in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution’ (Matt. 5:10), and so forth. Attend to the prophet, who threatens negligent shepherds thus: ‘Woe to you, shepherds who feed yourselves and not the sheep’ (Ezek. 34:2). Therefore gird on your sword, Father: ‘Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord’ (Ps. 26 [27]:14). Place confident trust in him who said, ‘It is I; take courage’ (Mark 6:50), for he has never yet forsaken you, and already many times has assisted you in our great necessities. Promise the money demanded of you; with God’s consent we shall all help you to repay it [Col. 1148C], since it is better that we voluntarily contribute some portion of our own means to you than that, when the king takes everything by force, we lose the whole.”

While all were saying these and similar things and encouraging their lord to retain his jurisdiction, his adversaries, sent by the king, came into the choir and said:

> “Lord Archbishop, either give the king an answer quickly, or he will immediately send his officers to seize and appropriate the city for himself.”

Hearing this, the lord archbishop, by the common counsel of all, changed his mind with unanimous consent and promised the king a thousand marks of silver, on this condition and agreement: that he should seize no one [Col. 1148D] in the whole jurisdiction of St James or in the city, nor injure him in any respect.

Once this agreement between king and archbishop had been established and confirmed, his adversaries and traitors—both clerics and laymen, but especially clerics—seeing that he remained in office and grieving exceedingly over it, approached the king in the house of a certain burgess of Compostela and sought to compel him to annul the aforesaid agreement, saying:

> “Lord King, you have been deceived and utterly deluded. The archbishop and his advisers have deceived you by marvellous art and cunning. For the small sum which he promised, he could give you in a single moment, and three times as much if he wished. Therefore accept our counsel, hasten to annul the agreement which you made with him, and in return for the jurisdiction that you have left him [Col. 1149A], we shall provide you with three thousand marks of pure silver and thereafter remain steadfast in your service and fidelity. If you wish to do this, great advantage will result for you: once you have obtained so great a sum of money, you will be able to acquire and pacify your kingdom, reward your knights honourably, and tame and humble the pride and obstinacy of your enemies.”

As they said these and similar things and urged the king to annul the agreement, the king replied:

> “Leave me now, and I shall take counsel with one of my faithful men as to what answer I ought to give you concerning this advice of yours.”

They answered:

> “With whom do you wish to take counsel? All the princes and powers of your court favour his side more than yours; they labour more to free him from your hands [Col. 1149B] than to extort from him what profits you. For he has already corrupted them all, either by money given or promised, and bound them to himself for his own advantage against you. Do, therefore, as we advise you, and accept the money which we promise you.”

The king replied:

> “Although everything you say seems true to me, I shall nevertheless not accept your counsel until I have received advice on this matter from one of my faithful men.”

Having said this, the king withdrew and called aside a certain count, a worthy and honourable man from Jerusalem. Through the faith, friendship, and homage which the count owed and had rendered him, he asked and urged him to give sound and upright counsel [Col. 1149C] concerning a certain affair, and not to depart from the path of truth on any pretext. The count promised and swore to the king that this would be so. Then the king spoke as follows:

> “I have already made an agreement with the archbishop for a thousand marks of silver and left him his entire jurisdiction. But there are certain adversaries and ill-wishers of his, hostile to him, as I well know, who wish to compel me to annul that agreement. For this they promise me three thousand marks of pure silver, if I take from him the entire jurisdiction of St James and bestow it upon them. I replied to them that I would never do this until I had taken counsel with one of my faithful men. Now I wish you to consider my advantage and determine in your mind whether I ought to annul that agreement, or keep it as I have begun [Col. 1149D] and promised.”

To this the count replied:

> “My lord king, whoever gives you such advice desires that you be dishonoured and infamous. Those traitors advise you thus not in order to provide for your advantage, but rather to injure the archbishop, whom they would greatly harm if they could. Do you not know that he who persecutes the archbishop persecutes the Lord, St James, and his Church? I saw your mother, Queen Lady Urraca, persecuting him, wronging him in many ways, and even handing him over to a treacherous imprisonment. But God and St James drew him from her hands against her will and visibly delivered him from many other dangers. Afterwards she lost almost her entire kingdom because of that sin, since she had presumed to stretch forth her hands to so great a crime [Col. 1150A]. Therefore set God before the eyes of your mind; show reverence to St James; if you can, amend and improve the agreement which you have already made and confirmed with the archbishop, for it is indeed far too harsh and intolerable. But if you are unwilling to amend and mitigate it, at least do not make it worse, for I fear that God may be angry with you and avenge upon you so great an injury.”

Having heard this, the king recognized the counsellor’s advice as sound and useful to himself; and, not doubting that the traitors were inflamed against the archbishop by envy and ill will, he accepted the count’s advice and refused to annul, at their prompting, the agreement he had made with the archbishop. Indeed, as though angry, he went to those traitors and forbade them with threats to urge such things upon him any further, saying:

> “I do not wish to act according to your advice, because it would bring me more disgrace and condemnation than salvation and honour. I fear to offend God and St James and to incur infamy and reproach from both nobles and common people. Be quiet, therefore, and do not urge so great a crime upon me any longer.” [Col. 1150B]

The man of Compostela, therefore, having learned the king’s disposition, paid him the aforementioned money, partly from his own resources and partly from those of others. He received a portion of the money from the canons of his Church, who voluntarily contributed it to assist him, as they had promised. The burgesses also gave him another portion, some freely and others as a loan. But when neither his own resources nor the gifts or loans of the canons [Col. 1150C] and burgesses sufficed to complete the total of a thousand marks, the archbishop, by the common counsel and assent of the brethren, procured, by requesting it throughout the jurisdiction of St James from both nobles and non-nobles, whatever was lacking for completion of that number. Thus he paid the king the full amount promised, namely a thousand marks of silver.

He did this not because he feared imprisonment of his person or loss of his jurisdiction, but because he feared that the king might stretch forth the hand of his cruelty to a new and unprecedented crime, presume to invade and lay waste the church of St James, and distribute its jurisdiction to lay powers, as he had already planned with the traitors.

## Chapter LXXXVII. How the archbishop induced the emperor to make satisfaction for the aforesaid offence

[Col. 1150D]

Before the king departed from the city of Compostela, while the archbishop was in great tribulation and severe distress because he could not pay the aforesaid money, which the king, at the traitors’ prompting, was demanding without delay, the archbishop reflected and pondered in his mind and heart upon the king’s impiety and wickedness. He clearly perceived that the king would incur the eternal damnation of his soul if, in such a great sin, he paid the debt of nature—that is, died—without repentance and due satisfaction.

Therefore, recalling before the eyes of his mind the Lord’s command, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 19:19), he had compassion on the king’s perishing soul [Col. 1151A]: both because he had always loved him, having baptized him, anointed and crowned him king, and later armed him as a knight with his own hands before the altar of St James when he had become an adult; and because he was the grandson of King Alfonso and the son of Count Raymond and Queen Lady Urraca, who had conferred many benefits upon the archbishop before their death.

For these reasons, and especially compelled by brotherly charity, he called the king aside and earnestly urged him in these words to repent and reform himself:

> “By your sins, deceived through the devil’s cunning, you have brought great dishonour in the sight of the Lord and great injury upon God and St James. Following the counsels of wicked men, you have violently invaded and despoiled the church of the most blessed apostle without any justification. Come therefore to your senses and do penance [Col. 1151B], for unless you repent and correct your errors, you will suffer the eternal ruin of your soul by God’s just judgment. Do you not know that, as God is the rewarder of every good, so he is the just and strict avenger of every injury?”

Hearing this, the king was struck with fear, because he knew that what the archbishop said was true and beyond doubt. He gave this reply:

> “Lord Archbishop, how can I repent? I cannot relinquish this money, though I do not doubt that I receive it unjustly from you. For if I relinquish it, I have nothing with which to relieve my necessities or pay my retainers. Therefore I neither see nor can see how I may repent; for I have heard from you and from other ecclesiastical persons that sin [Col. 1151C] is not remitted unless what has been taken is restored.”

The archbishop replied:

> “Come into the chapter-house in the presence of myself and the brethren, and, with God’s help, we shall give you counsel concerning what you can do as a remedy for so great a crime.”

The next day the king came into the chapter-house with a few leading men and retainers of his court. In his presence and that of all the brethren, I and other worthy and authoritative men heard with our own ears the archbishop speak as follows:

> “Lord King, I have always loved you, and still love you, for the sake of your grandfather King Alfonso of venerable memory, your father Count Raymond, and your mother Queen Lady Urraca. Therefore I desire to give you sound and upright counsel. Other kings, your predecessors—God-fearing and devout men—loved, honoured, and exalted this place and this church above [Col. 1151D] all other places and churches in Spain, out of love for God and St James. They richly endowed this church with public and private gifts. They bestowed upon this church castles, jurisdictions, towns, and estates in the service of God and for remission of their sins. For the salvation and remedy of their souls, they gave this church gold and silver vessels, precious crosses, silk copes, silk and gilded hangings, and other ornaments belonging to the honour of God and the adornment of holy Church.
>
> “But you have not only negligently failed, in rash presumption, to follow their footsteps and imitate their examples: you have even violently taken away the alms and benefactions which they gave to this Church [Col. 1152A], your nurse, from which—and from me, though unworthy, and from the brethren—you have received many benefits. You have neither set God before the eyes of your mind nor shown reverence to St James, whose venerable body is buried in this church. Consider, therefore, and weigh how great a gate of hell you have opened for your soul. Consider how greatly you have erred and what crime you have committed at the devil’s prompting. If death overtakes you unrepentant and making no satisfaction for so great a crime, you shall by no means see God face to face. Even in this present life, divine vengeance will bring bodily harm upon you unless you hasten to make satisfaction to God and St James through repentance.
>
> “Therefore accept my counsel. Hasten to repent, and by repentance reconcile God and St James to yourself. And as you have dishonoured the church [Col. 1152B] of St James by inflicting so great an injury upon it, so honour and console it by conferring some gift or benefaction. Honour him with your body: promise and grant us that your body shall be buried in it, following your father’s example. If you accept this counsel of ours and are willing to do so, we and the brethren shall forgive you so great a crime and unanimously intercede for you with God and St James.”

Then the king, without hesitation understanding that the archbishop spoke truth and asked what was just, gave this brief answer:

> “If I knew and were assured that you and this Church would show me such and so great mercy, and such honour, as you showed my father, I would most willingly consent to your request [Col. 1152C] and commend my body and my soul into your hands.”

The archbishop replied:

> “Whatever honour we render your father with respect to his body, and whatever benefits and prayers we offer for his soul, we shall do all this for you and for the salvation of your soul—and more besides, because you require greater benefits than your father. Although you are young and have lived only a little while in this world, in your recklessness you have incurred greater sins than your father, even though he had remained longer in this life. For your father [Note: [Col. 1151D] Count Raymond.] was a good, devout, and wise man, fearing God in all his actions and fulfilling his commandments; and therefore I certainly believe that he rests in Abraham’s bosom in paradise. He confessed his sins to me both in health and in sickness [Col. 1152D], and I imposed penance upon him. And as you have committed greater crimes through the devil’s deception, greater benefits are more necessary for you than for him.
>
> “We therefore promise you, beyond what we do for your father, a third part of the Masses which clerics ordained by me and by my successors shall celebrate; that in general synods we shall make mention of your soul and offer a special prayer to God for it; and that after your death a Mass for the remedy of your soul shall be specially celebrated in this church each week.”

Hearing this, the king answered with joy:

> “Everything that you say and promise seems good and useful to me [Col. 1153A]. Yet there is one thing over which I would rejoice greatly, if I could obtain it from you. I should like, if it pleased the Lord, St James, and yourselves, to become a canon of this Church, and in all its alms, Masses, prayers, and other benefits to become, both in life and in death, a fellow sharer and participant as one of the canons. For if I become a canon of this Church, I shall be able more steadfastly and reasonably to crush and humble my rivals and adversaries and, with God’s help, defend its rights.”

Then the archbishop and the canons present in the chapter approved the king’s request and granted it him with unanimous assent. Thus in that chapter the king was made a canon of the Church of St James, and they granted him bread in the canonical household, a week of service at the altar, and [Col. 1153B] the other benefits of the Church, just as each canon possesses them.

Having received the canonry and the Church’s benefice, the king commended his body and soul into the hands of the archbishop and canons. Before the archbishop and the entire chapter, he promised that, wherever he died, he would have his body carried to the church of St James for burial.

When this had been done, one of the canons, not prompted by the archbishop or by any other canon, stood up in the middle of the chapter and said:

> “Lord King, you have received a benefit of our Church in its chapter; behold, you have become as one of us. We shall have to celebrate your anniversary yearly if we wish to follow and observe the rule of justice and the examples of the holy Fathers [Col. 1153C]. You too ought diligently to follow in the footsteps and imitate the examples of your father and mother, and of good kings and princes who have commended their bodies and souls to ecclesiastical persons and Churches. For good kings and good princes promise and grant to the Church in which they are to be buried something from their resources or jurisdictions for the celebration of their anniversary. We therefore wish, and ask you, that for the benefit and salvation of your soul you follow in their footsteps and promise this Church some jurisdiction or inheritance for the celebration of your anniversary.”

The king replied:

> “Leave me for now. I see that your request is just, reasonable, and useful for me. I shall take counsel [Col. 1153D] with myself and my retainers, and consider what I can promise and give you and your Church for my anniversary; afterwards I shall give you an answer.”

### How the emperor granted the castle of St George to the Church of Compostela

Then the archbishop and the others present in the chapter began to conduct other business and discuss other matters, introducing many and varied conversations, as commonly happens in such a gathering. But after the king had long remained silent while they spoke thus, without being addressed or questioned by anyone in the assembly, he spoke as follows:

> “Lord Archbishop, I have now considered and taken counsel for myself, and I have found what I can give you and your Church for the annual celebration of my anniversary. [Col. 1154A] For that purpose I promise and grant you the castle of St George with all its appurtenances, to hold and possess in perpetuity peacefully and free from every claim. Count Roderic, who now holds that castle from me, shall render you homage and fealty for it, so that at my death he may leave it to you in every respect free and unencumbered. And if Count Roderic dies or loses the castle in any manner, and another lord receives it from me, before receiving it he shall likewise render homage and fealty to you and your Church, so that he may deliver that castle to you without any rebellion.
>
> “If Count Roderic or another, at the devil’s persuasion, should do otherwise—may it not be so!—let them be held as traitors to me, their lord, and let all regard them as perjurers and traitors. I earnestly ask your fatherhood to excommunicate and curse them and exclude them from the thresholds of holy Church until they fully restore the aforesaid castle, as stated above, into your hands and into the right of yourself and your Church. If from fear of excommunication they refuse to reform and restore the castle, you and your friends, having gathered an army and your forces, invade and pursue them until they restore the said castle with its appurtenances to you and your Church. I shall order my notary to make for you a testament concerning that castle; I shall confirm it with my own hands and, once confirmed, offer it upon the altar of St James into your hands.”

On the following day Count Roderic, though unwilling, under compulsion from the king rendered homage and fealty concerning that castle [Col. 1154C] and its appurtenances to the lord archbishop. Afterwards the king, in accordance with his promise, offered upon the altar of St James and into the archbishop’s hands, before the canons and many others, the testament concerning the aforesaid castle, drawn up by his notary and confirmed by his own hand.

He also ordered two documents to be made concerning the promise of his body, his canonry, and his reception of the ecclesiastical benefice. One he delivered to be kept in the treasury of St James with the castle’s privilege; the other he had carried with him in his own archives.

### Promise of half the land of Montanos

After making this promise concerning the castle, the king spoke in the same chapter before the whole assembly as follows:

> “I have already given you and your Church half of the land of the Montanos [Col. 1154D], and have made you a testament concerning the whole of it. Now I promise the other half, as I have already promised; and as I have already given you the one half, I shall give you the other as soon as I can. For I shall love and do love this Church, whose canonry and benefice I have now received and possess, above all the Churches of Spain; and to the extent of my power I shall defend and maintain it against its adversaries and rivals.”

After the archbishop heard such words from the king and perceived that the king’s goodwill towards himself and his Church was great, he made the following address:

> “Lord King, before we entered Portugal with our army to march against Queen Teresa, you and I held a private conference in the land of Taberioli. In it you fully gave your person and household into my right and power: those whom I wished expelled were to be expelled, and those whom I wished received were to be received. You also deprived my adversaries and traitors of honour, and bestowed their offices—namely the chaplaincy and chancellorship—upon me or whomever I wished. Now, unless it displeases your majesty, I should like to know whether you did this falsely, deceitfully, or in genuine truth and without any pretence.” [Col. 1155A]

To these words of the archbishop, King Alfonso replied:

> “However I acted then, whether falsely or not falsely, whatever I then granted you I now gladly grant and confirm. Dispose of my kingdom and household as you wish; possess the offices of your adversaries, namely the chaplaincy and chancellorship, and grant them to whom you please.” [Col. 1155B]

Then the archbishop gave thanks before all to the lord king for the grant of so great a gift. He restored the chaplaincy to his own control, but conferred the chancellorship upon Lord Bernard, treasurer of St James and his familiar associate.

I who wrote this saw some of these things with my own eyes, and heard others from the lord of Compostela and from other worthy and honourable men by truthful report. As they were done at that time, so I have set them down in order in my style, according to the measure of my ability. For I added nothing there on my own part, and knowingly omitted nothing of what I saw or heard.

I also, together with many others, afterwards saw him oppressed by the burden of great sorrow and distress, and repenting of the agreement which he had made with the king concerning so great a sum of money, because he could not pay it as he had promised [Col. 1155C]. For he always took greater care to provide for the public good than for private interest. Therefore he was greatly praised by all and is to be diligently imitated by his successors.

## Chapter LXXXVIII. The emperor’s sister chose burial in the Church of Compostela

When the lord archbishop had obtained from the king, through earnest entreaties, the grant that his body should be buried in the Church of St James, as stated above, he approached the king’s sister, the infanta Lady Sancha, who had then come to him to secure and receive the honours pertaining to her. He earnestly asked her to grant that her body likewise be buried in the church of St James, following the example of her royal brother [Col. 1155D]. She gladly assented to his request, understanding it to be just, reasonable, and especially beneficial to herself.

She also promised to the Church of St James, for her *tricennarium*—the thirty-day commemoration—and her anniversary, the prosperous monastery of St Michael of Escalada, adjoining the city of León and possessing great estates, to be held and possessed perpetually.

## Chapter LXXXIX. The promise of Queen T. of Portugal to choose burial in the Church of Compostela

After the archbishop saw that he had obtained the two aforementioned concessions, one from the king and the other from the infanta his sister, he sent his letter to the Portuguese queen, Lady T., the king’s maternal aunt [Col. 1156A], in the following terms:

> “Venerable Queen, by this communication we make known to your nobility that our lord King Alfonso and the infanta his sister, providing for their souls on our counsel, have granted that their bodies be buried in the church of St James and have promised to the same Church a portion of their jurisdictions for the salvation and remedy of their souls. Therefore we exhort and request your wisdom to promise that your body shall be buried in the aforesaid church after their example, and to grant what you have promised.”

When she had read this letter, the aforesaid queen greatly rejoiced, regarding the archbishop’s request as just, reasonable, and especially beneficial to herself. In the presence of one of the cardinals of St James and many other persons, with joyful heart and cheerful countenance, she granted what the archbishop had asked of her by letter and promised publicly that at her death she would give a large part of her jurisdiction to the same Church [Col. 1156B].

## Chapter XC. On the recovery of the monastery of St Pelagius of Cercedello

Desiring with utmost zeal to increase the jurisdiction of his Church, the man of Compostela carried on a serious and lengthy conflict with Veremudus Suariz, Alfonso Oduariz, and their kin concerning a certain monastery of St Pelagius of Cercedello. Veremudus and his kin wished to hold and possess that monastery as their inheritance, so that the Church of St James should have no right in it. But the archbishop would not consent to this [Col. 1156C], because he knew that the monastery belonged to the Church of St James, not wholly but in part.

They therefore came many times before worthy and discerning men, both clerics and laymen, so that they might settle the affair, but were never able to settle it. At last, however, since the archbishop recognized that they possessed some right in the monastery, he did not wish, as one who feared God, utterly to dispossess and burden them concerning it. Rather, he made an agreement and reconciliation with them: he granted them half of the monastery and its appurtenances, while retaining the other half as an inheritance for the Church of St James. A document made and confirmed by them on this matter is kept in the treasury, and they possess another document made and confirmed by him.

## Chapter XCI. Privilege concerning the non-seizure of goods upon an archbishop’s death

[Col. 1156D]

As I who wrote this heard not once but very often from the lord of Compostela, it was the custom of the kings of Spain, when the bishop of the church of St James died, to appoint their deputies in the city of Compostela and throughout the apostle’s entire jurisdiction. During the election of the succeeding bishop, they would hold that jurisdiction arbitrarily for three or four years, as they pleased.

That same man of Compostela, as I learned from him, held and governed the Church and the entire jurisdiction of St James for a full four years before his own election, with the kings’ consent [Col. 1157A] and approval—not tyrannically, however, but canonically. Yet the royal *majorini* [royal officials], disregarding the rule of justice and confusing right with wrong, violently plundered the villages, oppressed the poor and needy contrary to right and law, treated nobles and commoners as they pleased, and stripped them of their goods and inheritances. In short, they reduced the whole land to their right and power, and once they had reduced it, they utterly devastated it.

Wishing to abolish and eradicate this wicked and intolerable custom, the man of Compostela worked very hard in the time of Queen Lady Urraca, both personally and through his friends, by giving, promising, serving, and entreating, to obtain from her a privilege concerning the liberty of the Church and the whole jurisdiction of St James. She, yielding to his entreaties [Col. 1157B] and remembering the many services he had rendered her, ordered a certain cardinal of the Church of St James, named P. Didacides, to write that privilege so that she might confirm and ratify the document. But before it was written, that queen was overtaken by death, and thus the man of Compostela could not obtain that privilege in her time.

In the time of King A., the queen’s son, he likewise endured many inconveniences and losses and spent an immense sum of money in order to obtain the aforesaid privilege from him. The king, perceiving his purpose to be good and just, at length assented to his petition for many reasons. For the man of Compostela, having given him an incalculable sum of money, addressed him as follows:

> “I baptized you, and I am and have been your godfather. At a fitting time I anointed and crowned you king; with my own hands I armed you as a knight before the altar of St James. From your childhood until your exaltation I served you faithfully, always preferring your advantage to my own. I have many times incurred enmities through the service and loyalty which I maintained toward you. In the manner of a discerning and wise man, you ought to remember all these things and somehow recompense me for at least some of these services. Even if I had rendered you no service at all, and asked such a thing of you for the service of God, remission of your sins, and the salvation of your parents, I ought to have obtained it from you.” [Col. 1157C]

When the king heard this reasoning of the man of Compostela, so just and reasonable, he ordered that such a privilege concerning the liberty of the Church and the entire jurisdiction of St James be made for him, and he confirmed and ratified it with his own hand [Col. 1157D].

## Chapter XCII. Text of the privilege
“By the generosity and devotion of my predecessors—the Catholic kings of venerable memory, my grandfather Alfonso and others—the church of the blessed Apostle James is known to have been founded and built, enriched and exalted by the bestowal of many honours, and perpetually entrusted into the right and power of its bishops and canons, without any participation or lordship of a lay person. But because, in the times of certain of my kinsmen and predecessors, those things which had been well established and ordered for the honour of God and of Saint James were being destroyed through wars and the evil, deeply rooted customs of men, and the canons of that holy place, as well as the poor dependent upon its honour, suffered very great loss and damage to their property; and because, what was worse, when the bishop of that see died, an official sent by the king invaded all the possessions of the Church and destroyed them without mercy: therefore I, Alfonso, by the grace of God Emperor of the Spains, together with my consort Queen Lady Berengaria, at the prayers of Lord Diego, the present archbishop, and at the request of his canons, desiring utterly to destroy and eradicate the aforesaid evil customs, and reasonably following the good examples and institutions of my predecessors, have resolved, of my own free will—not under compulsion—to make and confirm the security of this privilege, to the honour of God and of the Apostle Saint James [Col. 1158A–B], in God’s service, for the benefit of the soul of my father, whose body lies honourably buried in that same church; for the salvation of my own soul and the remission of my sins, since my body, as I promise, is to be buried in that church itself; and for the refreshment and absolution of all my kinsmen, whom may God mercifully absolve from all their sins committed in this matter.

“I decree that, when the present archbishop named Diego, or any one of his successors, has paid the debt of nature, neither I nor any of my successors, nor any secular person, shall have—or permit anyone to have—any right or authority in the whole church of Saint James, or in its castles and honours belonging to it [Col. 1158C]. Rather, the entire Church and all its honour shall remain and continue peacefully, without any invasion, under the judgment and disposition of the canons of that Church, until a worthy, holy, and religious election of an archbishop is made by those canons.

“But if I or any of my successors should presume to oppose or contravene this charter of our ordinance, let him be excommunicated and anathematized by the authority of Almighty God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of the Apostle Saint James, and of all the saints; let him be made a stranger to participation in the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; let him be buried in hell with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive; and let him share the lot of Judas, betrayer of his Lord [Col. 1158D], until he repents and returns to fitting satisfaction. But for all who observe this, may there be peace, salvation, and joy, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

“May this writing, sanctioned and confirmed by our authority in the manner stated above, remain unshaken through all ages of ages. This privilege was drawn up at Segovia, in the era 1166, and on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.”

I, A., by the grace of God Emperor of Spain, confirm by my own authority what I ordered to be done.

Count Peter of Lara confirms. Count Rodrigo of Asturias, the king’s standard-bearer, confirms. [Col. 1159A] Count Bernard confirms. Count Suero confirms. Rodrigo Martínez confirms. Pedro López confirms. Rodrigo Vermúdez, the king’s steward, confirms. Ramiro Froilaz confirms. Raymond, Archbishop of Toledo, confirms. Peter, Bishop of Segovia, confirms. Bernard, Bishop of Sigüenza, confirms. Bertrand, Bishop of Osma, confirms. Sancho, Bishop of Ávila, confirms. Pedro Díaz confirms. Pedro Braóliz confirms. Frederick Fernández confirms. Gutierre Ermeíldez confirms. [Col. 1159B] Fernando Pérez confirms. Bernard, treasurer of the church of Saint James and the king’s chancellor, confirms. Cidi, witness; Velidi, witness; Belidi, witnesses.

## CHAPTER XCIII. Again concerning the monastery of Cersedello

After the aforesaid affair concerning the monastery of Saint Pelagius of Cersedello had been settled between the archbishop and Vermudo Suárez and the other knights, a certain abbot named Vermudo, to whom that monastery belonged, took his charters and approached the royal presence. Before all the barons attending the court, he bitterly complained against the archbishop of Compostela and the aforesaid knights, affirming openly that he had been unjustly and unreasonably expelled from his place and inheritance [Col. 1159C]. But when the king saw that he was already old, weak, and beset by many hardships, he took pity on his misery and sent the following letter to the lord of Compostela, ordering that the abbot be restored to his monastery: namely, that he should possess it throughout his life, while after his death it should remain as had already been decided.

“A., by the grace of God Emperor of Spain, sends abundant greeting to the venerable lord DIEGO, by the same grace Archbishop of the see of Compostela.

“Know that I have seen this Abbot Vermudo with great grievance concerning his inheritance. He showed his charters to me and to my barons, and we saw that he has suffered a great wrong.
