And now know that he has given me that inheritance and its charter; and if Vermudo Suárez or anyone else should bring a claim against that inheritance, let him come before me and have judgment with that abbot and with me. But now I send him to you, so that you may receive, in my stead, all the charters concerning that inheritance from him, and place him in his inheritance. Let him live in it throughout his entire life; make restoration for all that they have taken from him; and protect and defend him, in my place, against all persons. And if you are unwilling to protect him, I shall entrust him to another who will protect him well, together with his kinsmen and all his inheritances. And let this matter not fail, for it is justice, if you love me. Farewell.” [Col. 1159D]

Afterward the abbot, repenting of his action and complaint, returned from the king and, coming before the archbishop [Col. 1160A], bestowed upon the lord archbishop all the charters which he held concerning that monastery, earnestly asking and entreating him to grant the aforesaid monastery to him for his lifetime, so that he might have there food, clothing, and the other necessities. After his death, the monastery was to return to the church of Saint James, as had already been decided.

The archbishop, having received from him all the charters, gave him the monastery to hold during his life and to draw necessities from it. But after his death, the church of Saint James was to recover it free and released from him and all his kindred, and, once recovered, possess it peacefully and without any claim. Upon this promise and agreement he caused an instrument to be drawn up; he confirmed it with his own hand, and, once confirmed, delivered it to the lord archbishop to hold and possess as testimony and confirmation of this pact [Col. 1160B].

## CHAPTER XCIV. The privilege made by the lord archbishop for the canons concerning their anniversaries and revenues

Since it belongs to prelates everywhere to exercise the rights of justice, to confirm for the honour of Almighty God and the common good, to preserve and increase good institutions, and to uproot and annihilate their opposites, therefore I, Diego, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church, by divine clemency, of my own will and with my full judgment, together with the counsel and assent of all our canons, reasonably decree and perpetually establish by this writing of confirmation [Col. 1160C] the following: after the death of each one of our canons, their goods shall not be forcibly seized and dissipated by anyone; rather, as the aforesaid canons themselves shall have ordered in their directions, so, as far as possible, shall these be fulfilled, and no one shall be harmed.

Moreover, whatever I have canonically assigned, or shall with God’s help assign, to an anniversary to be devoutly celebrated each year for the benefit of my soul; or whatever the canons themselves, burgesses, or any others have similarly assigned or shall henceforth assign for their anniversaries: this shall be administered and held irrevocably, free from hatred, favour, gift, and kinship, according to what the assembly of canons in chapter shall suitably ordain for the common good, or direct one of our canons to hold, with the counsel of the archbishop and dean [Col. 1160D].

If kings, counts, princes of the land, or knights should grant great honours to the church of Saint James for their anniversaries—such as castles, estates, or the like—then, after the canons have first been provided each year from those same honours with a good meal, what remains shall be divided equally between the archbishop and the canons. This is on the condition that, if any *sajo*, whether mine or the king’s, should presume to violate any such gift given to God, then, if he breaks in and escapes unharmed, he shall pay 500 solidi to you and to us. If, however, he dies there, nothing shall be paid for him. If he is beaten, he shall gain everything. If, from outside, he insolently invades anything without seeking legal justice, he shall pay sixty solidi [Col. 1161A] to us and to you, and make double restitution for the robbery. And this shall always remain firm after the canonical share, with no person hindering or compelling it; it shall remain valid and unshaken.

But if we, or our successors, or any person should attempt to violate this writing made for the common good, let him incur the loss of his honour, lie under anathema, be removed from the sight of Almighty God, and be eternally punished in the torment of everlasting damnation with Judas, betrayer of the Son of God. For the audacity of his presumption, let him pay twenty thousand solidi to the canonical portion of Saint James, and make double restitution for whatever he has put under claim. And let this writing remain perpetually in force. Amen. The charter was made in the era 1166.”

Diego, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Compostela [Col. 1161B] and legate of the Holy Roman Church, in the twenty-eighth year of his pontificate, confirms this writing by his own authority.

> [Note: [Col. 1161] Some manuscripts here are corrupt; yet they are readily and securely corrected from the following document, where the era 1166 and the twenty-eighth year of the pontificate agree with one another.]

He also transferred the church of Saint Mary of Argalo, already dilapidated and close to ruin, and founded in an unsuitable place, to a more fitting and better location. Having transferred it, he built it from the foundations and made it considerably better.

The same archbishop, with the common assent and counsel of the brethren, also caused this charter of confirmation and deed of gift to be made for the Hospital of Saint James, concerning a certain plot of land situated in the palace orchard, for the construction there of a church for the burial of the poor and pilgrims [Col. 1162A].

“I, Diego, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Compostela, together with the assembly of canons of that same church, for the honour of God, the Apostle Saint James, and all the saints, have made this instrument of confirmation and deed of gift concerning a certain parcel of land belonging to our Church, situated in the palace orchard. By our spontaneous will, through this charter of confirmation, we give and grant it to the church of the Hospital of Saint James, in order that a church may be built for the benefit and salvation of the poor and pilgrims already buried there, and for the burial of others yet to be interred there. From this present day onward, the poor of the aforesaid hospital, both present and future, shall have and possess that little church forever through all time [Col. 1162B].

“If anyone should act against this our deed, let him pay one thousand solidi to the Hospital’s party, make double restitution for that which he has claimed, and let this our writing always remain firm. The document was made on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the era 1166.”

The aforesaid Archbishop Diego, who ordered it to be done, confirms it by his authority in the twenty-eighth year of his pontificate.

# IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF LORD DIEGO OF COMPOSTELA

[Col. 1161]

[Col. 1161C] “Since the deeds and virtues of illustrious men are by no means protected from the destruction of oblivion unless they are commended to memory by writing or in some other way, the lord of Compostela ordered a register to be made, in which are contained, for the most part, written accounts of everything that he accomplished well or acquired through the enterprise of his Church. He divided that register into three books. The first is reasonably entitled the Book of the Bishopric, and the other two [Col. 1162C] the Books of the Archbishopric. For the deeds which he accomplished or acquisitions which he made during his episcopate or archiepiscopate are, as has been said, described in that register. It pleased him, moreover, that the three books should be entitled in this way, so that anyone seeking anything in them might find it more easily from the title itself.”

# THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1161]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the counsel taken by the archbishop with the brethren for building cloisters and workshops

[Col. 1161D]

Forty-six years had passed since the beginning of the new church of Saint James.

> [Note: [Col. 1161] Therefore it was begun in the year 1082, under King Alfonso VI, by Diego I, bishop of Compostela.]

By God’s grace, the greater part of that church had already been completed. Yet it still had no cloister and no suitable workshops, nor was it adorned or embellished with buildings like the churches beyond the passes, [Col. 1162D] which are of lesser dignity and have fewer revenues.

Pilgrims, both clerical and lay, flocking to the thresholds of the most blessed Apostle to pray, asked their hosts and the clergy where the cloisters and workshops of the church of Saint James were. They wandered about the whole circuit of the Church, seeking where its cloisters and workshops might be found; and because they saw no cloister there and found no fitting workspaces, they openly disparaged the prelates and administrators of the Church [Col. 1163A].

When this came to the ears of the lord of Compostela, he was deeply grieved. He summoned the entire assembly of brethren in chapter and made the following address:

“Brethren, our church is of the greatest and most celebrated renown, not through our own merits but through the grace of God and the merits of our patron, the most blessed Apostle James. Both beyond the passes and on this side of them it is reputed most wealthy and noble; yet it still has no cloister and no good workshops. Every see beyond the passes has buildings more beautiful and more substantial than ours, as I saw with my own eyes in many different places, both before and after my episcopate, when the interests of our Church required that I travel abroad. And you who have travelled abroad know just as well as I that what I say is most true [Col. 1163B]. Surely it is a very great disgrace both to me and to you that so holy, rich, and famous a place should lack buildings and facilities.

“Therefore I earnestly beg the affection of your brotherhood that we promptly take unanimous counsel concerning how we may build suitable cloisters and workshops for the honour of God and our Church, so that by good works we may more readily obtain mercy from God and may not be reproached with justice either by neighbours or strangers. And I, if you are willing to agree with my counsel, promise one hundred marks of pure silver to begin that work: thirty of these I shall give now with my own hand, and the rest when one year is completed. In whatever ways I can assist that work, whether through myself or through my friends, I shall assist it, preserving the bounds of justice [Col. 1163C].

“At my death, moreover, I shall leave in perpetuity to that work, for the benefit of my soul, the hundred cows which I possess, so that it may have them and their offspring peacefully and without any claim, and may never lose them through anyone taking them away.”

When the lord of Compostela had finished this address, the entire assembly of brethren unanimously commended his purpose and intention, and promised willingly to assist in beginning and completing that work. The archbishop, greatly rejoicing in their response, chose from among them two approved and prudent men—namely, Lord Peter Helias, the dean, and Lord Peter Gundesind, cardinal and first of the clergy—and entrusted them with the care of beginning and managing the work [Col. 1163D]. They, cheerfully rendering obedience to their prelate, undertook before all to begin and arrange the aforesaid work. This having been established and confirmed, all departed from the chapter in joyful spirits.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Arias Petrides

Arias Petrides was one of the energetic and capable knights of Galicia. He was not, however, of great nobility, but was very bold and eloquent, so that he could turn white into black and black into white. He was also deceitful and a most wicked dissembler; he always acted treacherously against the king and queen and the other princes of Galicia, and persisted in rebellion against them.

It happened that he married the daughter of Count Peter, named Ildaria. When her mother, Countess Lady Mayor, Arias’s mother-in-law, had paid the debt of nature and was brought to Compostela for honourable burial, the aforesaid Arias came, dressed in mourning according to the custom of the people, among the other princes and knights attending her burial [Col. 1164A]. When the archbishop, who had always been his enemy because of Arias’s wickedness, saw him, he called him aside and addressed him in this way, desiring, like a good and provident shepherd, to invite him to amend and correct his life:

“Arias Petrides, there are few vices into which, through your sins and the deception of the devil, you have not fallen. You have been perjured, a false witness, greedy, a robber, deceitful, a dissembler, sacrilegious, and criminal; you have lived too luxuriously and too worldly. You saw the things that were right with the eyes of your mind, and, once seen, wholly neglected them. I therefore fear that if you depart this life in such a state, you will lose eternal life and incur the perpetual damnation of your soul. I very much desire, then, that by repenting and making satisfaction to Almighty God, you should provide for the welfare of your soul and reconcile God himself to you by a manner of life more worthy, so that at the end of your life you may obtain mercy from him and be worthy to possess eternal life” [Col. 1164B].

By urging these and similar things upon him, he finally moved him to repentance and compunction. Following the counsel of the lord archbishop, Arias left at his death to the church of Saint James, as an inheritance for the salvation and benefit of his soul, the castle of Saint John of Penna Cornaria with its dependencies, and half of a certain monastery named Arcos, situated in the district of Salnés, with its appurtenances. He entrusted the burial of his body in the cemetery of that Church, and the care of his soul in life and death, to the hand of the lord archbishop and the brethren.

He also gave six estates belonging to the inheritance of that monastery to the present lord archbishop, so that the archbishop himself and his Church might begin to have, while Arias was still alive, a rightful interest in that monastery [Col. 1164C]. Concerning all these things—both the aforesaid castle and the monastery—he ordered a privilege to be made. He confirmed it with his own hand, placed it once confirmed upon the altar of Saint James, and afterward delivered it into the hand of the lord archbishop for safekeeping [Col. 1164D]. The archbishop received that privilege and deposited it, once received, in the treasury of Saint James to be preserved.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the death of Count Peter de Trava and what he left to the Church

Count Peter, a prudent, wise, and very powerful man, and his wife Countess Lady Mayor, likewise wise and prudent, had customarily been parishioners of the church of Mondoñedo. They made confession to the bishop of that place, received their penance from him, and obeyed him as subjects. They also bestowed upon the aforesaid Church and its bishop alms and benefactions to be administered and distributed for the benefit of their souls.

They did this, however, contrary to the authority of the sacred canons and the ordinances of the holy Fathers; for, as the sacred canons testify, no bishop or priest may receive the parishioner of another bishop or priest without that person’s consent. Since the lord of Compostela saw that the aforesaid count and his wife were plainly in error and had ignorantly abandoned their mother, the church of Compostela, he held many and various discussions with them. He preached to them until he caused them to leave the church and bishopric of Mondoñedo and become parishioners of the church of Compostela [Col. 1165A].

Thus, through the saving preaching and admonition of the lord of Compostela, they became children of the church of Compostela, and entrusted their bodies and souls into the hand of the lord of Compostela, so that he might advise them for their salvation and benefit.

It happened that the aforesaid count fell ill at Compostela unto death. Seeing death imminent, he made disposition of his household in the presence of the lord of Compostela, the count’s wife, and his children [Col. 1165B]. That disposition and his entire testamentary direction were entrusted into the hand of the lord of Compostela, his wife and children jointly authorizing it. One part of this direction was carried out at the count’s death, but another part remained to be carried out until the death of the countess.

It happened that the countess herself, not long afterward, paid the debt of nature. At her death, the whole direction of the count was fully carried out, just as the count himself, his wife the countess, and their children had granted and confirmed [Col. 1165C].

The count and countess left, for the salvation and benefit of their souls, villages, estates, churches, monasteries, and many other things in the hand of the lord of Compostela and of Cardinal Peter Gundisalvez, to be disposed of and distributed according to his will and judgment. The names of these villages, estates, churches, and monasteries are written down and recorded in their directions, which the aforesaid cardinal holds. Whoever wishes sufficiently and fully to know what and how much the aforesaid count and countess entrusted to be distributed at their death for the benefit of their souls should consult their directions, and there he will find everything. We do not wish to append those directions to this book, in order to avoid excessive length [Col. 1165D].

The aforesaid count and countess wished to give all the things mentioned above to the church of Saint James in God’s service and for remission of their sins. But the lord of Compostela, seeing that this would be unjust and contrary to reason, beneficially advised them to leave to the bishop of Mondoñedo and his Church, for the salvation of their souls, the churches and other property acquired in the bishopric of Mondoñedo; what they had acquired in the bishopric of Lugo, to the church of Lugo; what they had acquired in the bishopric of Ourense, to the bishop of Ourense; similarly, what they had acquired in the parish of Tui, to the bishop of Tui; and so with the rest.

## CHAPTER IV. The recovery of what had been lost in Asturias

[Col. 1166A]

After the death of King Alfonso of venerable memory, so many troubles and discords arose throughout the whole kingdom of Spain that the entire land was utterly thrown into turmoil, and from being most excellent and abundant was turned into the worst and most wicked condition. As a result, the church of Saint James lost for many years the honour which it possessed in the bishopric of Asturias, and derived almost no benefit from it.

When, by divine mercy, that calamity had been turned into tranquillity, the lord of Compostela exerted himself in many ways to recover that honour. At last, after much labour, he recovered it and entrusted it for tenure and possession to John Cidiz, who lived in the borough of Saint James called Cacabelos [Col. 1166B], under the following written condition:

“In the era 1166, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, I, John Cidiz, and my wife Maria Constantiz, and my son Giraldus, a cleric, make with you, Lord Diego, Archbishop of the see of Compostela, and with all the canons of your Church, a pact or agreement by this most binding writing: while dwelling in the houses and courts of Saint James, we shall work, build up, and plant the estates of your Church situated in the bishopric of Asturias which you grant to us. From both your estates and our two estates, Lower Roboredo and Upper Roboredo, which we give and grant to you and your Church in perpetual hereditary right, and also from all your other estates which we hold today and which are in our right, we shall give you one third of the bread, wine, and everything which we have there or may, God granting, acquire; two thirds being reserved to us [Col. 1166C].

“You shall have two parts of the offerings of Saint James, and we one part. We shall hold the aforesaid estates throughout our lives, so long as we faithfully serve you and your Church as lords, without another lord, showing obedience and reverence. If, after our death, our son is fit for this service, he shall hold all the estates throughout his life, with the aforesaid condition observed.

“From all other estates which we may thereafter acquire, with God’s help, whether from produce or inheritance, we shall perpetually give one third to you and your Church and reserve two thirds to ourselves. But if we prove false and violate this agreement, let us pay to your party [lacuna]; and let this writing always remain firm.”

We named above, who ordered this to be made, confirm it with our own hands. [Col. 1166D]

## CHAPTER V. The sending of envoys to the pope

After the death of the most blessed Pope Calixtus II, the lord of Compostela sent his envoys to Calixtus’s successor, named Honorius. They returned without accomplishing the business for which they had gone. Nevertheless, he received them kindly and honourably, and through them informed the lord of Compostela that he would send into Spain a legate from his own side, to conduct and arrange both secular and ecclesiastical affairs in accordance with the will and counsel of the lord of Compostela [Col. 1167A].

When the lord of Compostela saw that this legate was delaying beyond the promised time, he sent other envoys to the aforesaid Pope Honorius and to his friend A., his chancellor, Aimeric. They brought to the lord of Compostela the following letter on the chancellor’s behalf.

### Letter of the cardinal to the archbishop

“To his dearest friend DIEGO, Archbishop of Compostela, A., cardinal-deacon and chancellor, greeting.

“Thanks be to God, we are well and safe. The condition of the lord pope and of the Holy Roman Church remains in due stability, and his disposition toward you has not changed [Col. 1167B]. We hope, indeed, that he will shortly send from his side a legate into your regions, who will explain his will more fully to you.”

## CHAPTER VI. This privilege was caused to be made by the lord of Compostela for the procurator of the Hospital of Saint James, in testimony to his promise, which promise is contained in the privilege written below

“Certain citizens dwelling in the city of Compostela spread rumours among the people that I, Diego, by the grace of God Archbishop of Compostela, install a procurator in the Hospital of Saint James upon receiving money and remove him at will. Since many believed this to be true, they often withheld their alms and benefactions from that Hospital [Col. 1167C].

“But I, wishing that their suspicion should be entirely removed from me, cause this writing to be made. In it I promise Almighty God, the Apostle Saint James, and all the saints that I shall never install or remove a procurator in that Hospital upon receiving money. Rather, with the counsel of the brethren and of certain God-fearing and God-loving citizens, I shall consider and choose a wise, prudent, religious person necessary to the management of the poor. Into his hand and authority I shall commit the whole house with its revenues, to be held and administered as long as I live.

“From now on I establish and pray that my successors, who after me shall govern and administer the honour of Saint James [Col. 1167D], should strive to follow my footsteps in this matter and should never promote or appoint a procurator in the aforesaid house for money received or promised. Instead, as has been said above, let them choose a suitable and religious person and put him in charge of that house without any payment.

“If any ecclesiastical or secular person, deceived by diabolical fraud, should wish to oppose this writing and this ordinance of mine, let him be cursed and excommunicated, and made a stranger to the most sacred body and blood of our Lord. Let him incur without remedy that sentence imposed by Saint Peter upon Simon Magus, when he said: ‘May your money be with you unto perdition’ (Acts 8:20). Let him suffer without end the infernal punishments with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive because their sins required it [Col. 1168A], and let him have fellowship with Judas, betrayer of his Lord and Master, unless he repents and without partiality corrects his errors with fitting satisfaction.

“But all those who observe this ordinance of mine and act accordingly, let them receive ‘blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his saviour’ (Psalm 23[24]:5); let them deserve to become sharers with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the heavenly paradise; let them here receive, by the Lord’s bounty, the fruit of good action; and before the strict Judge let them find the rewards of eternal peace.

“This writing and privilege of the aforesaid ordinance was made by me, Diego, first Archbishop of the see of Compostela, in the era 1166, on the [uncertain date] before the Kalends of December, while King Alfonso, son of the duke Raymond of venerable memory and Queen U., was reigning in the city of León and at Toledo [Col. 1168B]. At that time the procurator of that Hospital was Lord Peter, whom the common people called ‘king’s slave.’ Diego, the aforesaid archbishop, who ordered this to be done, confirms it by his own authority in the twenty-eighth year of his pontificate.”

## CHAPTER VII. Departure for the council

Alfonso, king of the Spains, grandson of King A. of venerable memory and son of the illustrious Queen Lady U. and the distinguished Duke Raymond, saw that almost all Spain had been thrown into disorder after the death of his grandfather and his mother. He therefore decided to hold a council in the city of Palencia during the first week of Lent in the era 1167 [Col. 1168C].

He invited to that council all the bishops, abbots, counts, princes, and territorial powers of Spain, so that, according to their counsel and judgment, he might root out with the sickle of justice the nettles of wickedness which had arisen in Spain after the death of his aforesaid grandfather the king and after the death of his aforesaid mother the queen, and might turn what was crooked into what was straight.

When the lord of Compostela heard of this invitation, he quickly prepared what was necessary for his journey; having made these preparations, he set out as soon as possible. While already on the road, he heard from certain reports that the aforesaid council had been postponed until mid-Lent. He therefore returned home and sent his envoy to the king to learn from him the fixed day on which the council was to be held [Col. 1168D]. The messenger, detained by various hindrances on the way, was delayed for a long time.

Meanwhile, the lord of Compostela received another messenger from the king, announcing on the king’s behalf and earnestly requesting that he hasten to Palencia for the council, setting every excuse aside. On hearing the king’s messenger, he prepared what was necessary for the journey, as well and honourably as he could in the shortness of time; and, having prepared these things, he cheerfully took the road.

When the king, the Archbishop of Toledo, all the bishops and abbots, the counts, princes, other powers, and the whole council learned of his arrival, they resolved to await him. As he proceeded with haste, he was received at Astorga,

> [Note: [Col. 1167D] Understand Asturica.]

at León, and at Saint Facundus with splendid procession and great honour [Col. 1169A]. When he drew near to Palencia, the king, with his counts, princes, all the powers, and a great escort of knights, went out to meet him and received him with honour and careful ceremony. Meanwhile the Archbishop of Toledo and all the bishops present, together with the abbots and clergy, prepared a distinguished procession and received him joyfully and exultantly.

Once he had been lodged, and the king wished to go to his own quarters, the man of Compostela said to him: “Lord king, go gladly to your lodging and rest in peace; after I have taken my meal, I shall come there to discuss matters privately with you and to set forth [Col. 1169B] those things which must be spoken and enacted in the council.” The king replied: “Venerable father, I think it better and more fitting that I should go to your lodging than that you should come to mine, since you have now arrived weary from the journey.” On hearing this, the man of Compostela answered: “Lord king, let your will be done.” Accordingly, after taking his meal, the king came to his lodging with a few companions; and, after speaking briefly with him, he entrusted the entire jurisdiction and authority of the council into his hand and power, so that whatever he might deliberate and order should remain enacted and binding. Then he invited the man of Toledo and the other bishops present to his lodging and took counsel with them concerning the forthcoming business of the council. On the following day, when the king came to him, the man of Compostela disclosed the plan concerning the council’s proceedings which he had formed with the man of Toledo [Col. 1169C] and the bishops. The king, approving and confirming their enactment, asked him, together with the man of Toledo and the other bishops, that, after Mass had been celebrated, he should deliver an address in the general council and make the council’s acts known to all. In accordance with the counsel of the king and bishops, he did all this and communicated the acts of the council to everyone. Those acts are contained below on this page.

## Decrees of the bishops

“Since we see many evils being committed in the Church of God and against Christ’s poor, and grieve that the realm of our lord Emperor A., son of Count Raymond and Queen Lady U., is being torn apart, diminished, and corrupted in diverse ways by certain wicked persons, therefore [Col. 1169D] I, Raymond, archbishop and primate of the see of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, together with the bishops whose names are written below, and with our Emperor A. present and giving his support, have judged it beneficial to establish among ourselves a firm stability of unity. In this indissoluble bond of charity, we decree that henceforth, united by the strength of concord, we shall labour as is fitting for the salvation of the faithful and, by God’s aid, shall watch with prudent care over our aforesaid emperor and his realm.

“Therefore, in celebrating a council at Palencia for the welfare of the Holy Church and the safety of the whole kingdom, among other things we unanimously decree the following: no one shall keep with himself or retain in his household a known traitor, robber, ravager, perjurer, or excommunicate person. [Col. 1170A] We also command that no one shall possess a church by hereditary right within eighty-four paces, nor exercise any authority there without the deputy of his bishop. The offerings and tithes of excommunicated persons shall not be accepted. The rulers of territories shall not despoil the people subject to them without just judgment. Churches shall not be granted to laymen as benefices or for administration. Openly kept concubines of clerics shall be expelled. Churches, estates, and dependent households which belonged to sees and monasteries, wherever they may be, shall be restored to them. Wandering monks shall be compelled to return to their own monasteries, and bishops shall not retain them without their abbots’ permission. No excommunicated person of another jurisdiction shall be received. We command adulterers and incestuous persons to be separated altogether. Clerics shall neither receive nor possess churches through lay hands, [Col. 1170B] nor shall bishops’ deputies consent to this. Bishops, by virtue of their office, shall compel those at variance to make peace. If anyone assaults clerics, monks, travellers, merchants, pilgrims seeking the holy shrines, or women, he shall be assigned to a monastery or to exile. No one shall levy portaticum, a toll on goods in transit, except in the places where it was customarily taken in the time of Lord King A.; likewise, no one shall seize, distrain, or steal oxen, but they shall remain in peace throughout the whole kingdom. All shall faithfully obey the king without deceit, evil device, or counsel; whoever does not do so shall be excommunicated. No one shall presume to exact from clerics military service, the bearing of arms, or anything contrary to the canons. Laymen shall under no pretext possess the thirds of churches or any offerings whatever; rather, everything belonging to churches shall remain under the bishops’ disposition. [Col. 1170C] Here. Those who make counterfeit coin shall be excommunicated and shall suffer the king’s punishment of having their eyes put out.”

After the council had been celebrated and *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”) sung according to synodal custom, the man of Compostela, by counsel of the brethren, asked the king to grant him, for the honour of God and Saint James, those rights in the city of Mérida which pertained to himself and his successors. The king willingly assented to his just and reasonable request and caused this privilege concerning that grant to be made for him, as is contained in the following document.

[Col. 1170D] “Since, by the deliberation of the Holy Roman Church and, as is fitting, through the dispensatory ordering of the heavenly disposition, my uncle of blessed memory, Pope Calixtus, transferred in perpetuity to the Church of Compostela the dignity of the archbishopric of the Church of Mérida, in consideration of the merits and reverence of the most blessed apostle James, therefore I, Adefonsus, by the grace of God Emperor of Spain, together with my consort Queen Lady Berengaria, by the counsel of the archbishops, bishops, and princes of the land who attended the Council of Palencia, have judged it beneficial, for the honour and due exaltation of God and of the most blessed Apostle James, our patron, to make this charter concerning the city of Mérida, now possessed by the Saracens. By God’s helping power, we believe that we shall shortly possess it, once the unbelieving filth of the Saracens has been conquered [Col. 1171A] and expelled. In this charter I give and with devout intent confirm, for the salvation of my soul and those of my grandfathers and parents, to you, Lord Diego, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Compostela, to your Church, and to your successors, to possess forever by hereditary right, all things of the aforesaid city which pertain to royal right, together with all its ancient lands, its due castles, and its other appurtenances. And just as my grandfathers and great-grandfathers earnestly endeavoured, by magnificent gifts—namely castles and various other revenues—to enlarge and increase the church of Saint James for the salvation of their souls, so, trusting in God’s mercy, I desire and promise, in imitation of them, to raise and exalt the aforesaid seat of the apostle. But if anyone should attempt to act against this [Col. 1171B] my deed, let him be excluded from participation in the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and let him have fellowship with Judas, betrayer of his Lord and Master. But upon all who observe this, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and may find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. This charter was made in the era 1167, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March 1129]. I, the aforesaid Emperor Adefonsus, together with my consort, confirm by my own authority what I commanded to be done.”

When these matters had been completed, the man of Compostela at once wished to bid the king farewell and return home. But the king earnestly asked him to accompany him as far as Carrión. Gladly complying with his wish, [Col. 1171C] he went with him to Carrión, where he was received by clergy and people with a great and distinguished procession. From there he returned joyfully and happily to his own country, and on Palm Saturday he entered his see with his travelling companions in exultation and honour.

## CHAPTER VIII. Acquisition of a Golden Chalice

The treasurer of the Church of Saint James, named B., resolved to go to Jerusalem in God’s service and for remission of his sins. As, having prepared what was necessary, he was about to undertake the journey, the man of Compostela saw that his church would suffer many losses through his absence and did not doubt that the church’s work had great need of his supervision. He therefore decided altogether to recall him from that journey and, once recalled, to retain him. He advised him to send through trustworthy messengers to Jerusalem everything which he intended to offer with his own hand at the Holy Sepulchre and the other holy places adjacent to it; and, from the expense which he would have incurred on the journey, to buy some honourable and precious ornament for the honour and service of God and Saint James, and, once bought, to place it in the treasury of that Church. This was on the condition that it should never be removed thence for any reason, sold, or given away. While the archbishop was considering this matter by counsel of the brethren, it happened that Lord King A. sent to Compostela, through a certain servant of his named Albertinus, a fine and precious golden chalice, containing seven hundred *morabitini*, to be sold. The king had acquired it from the archbishop of Toledo [Col. 1172A] in a time of pressing need. He did this because he knew there was no place in all Spain where it could be sold more advantageously. When the man of Compostela saw how good and precious the chalice was, he advised the aforesaid treasurer to buy it for the honour of God and Saint James and as a redemption for his journey, and thereby adorn the church of the apostle, his mother. The treasurer, recognizing his lord’s counsel as sound and useful, did not dissent. Rather, cheerfully obeying his command, he bought the aforesaid chalice for one hundred marks of pure silver and adorned his church with it, according to the counsel of the lord of Compostela and the brethren. [Col. 1172B] When this had been done, he absolved him in a full assembly from all sins, just as those labouring on the Jerusalem journey are customarily absolved; and, for remission of his sins, he entrusted to him the whole work of the Church of Saint James, to be managed, ordered, and advanced. O provident and venerable man! Neither in prosperity nor adversity did he ever forget the honour and exaltation of his Church; but in pure truth, with every pretence set aside, he always strove, both personally and through his friends, for its protection and honour.

## CHAPTER IX. Acquisition of an Aquamanile

While the aforesaid treasurer was staying at the royal court on the counsel of the lord of Compostela, before planning the Jerusalem journey, and was at Toledo, he saw in the church of Toledo a precious and exquisitely worked crystal aquamanile, or hand-washing vessel. Because he knew that the man of Toledo loved this aquamanile greatly, he did not dare to ask him for it, fearing that his request would be refused. He therefore quietly suggested to the king that he ask the man of Toledo for it and grant it to him as a gift. The king willingly agreed, asked the man of Toledo for the aquamanile, and obtained it. He then gladly gave the acquired vessel to the treasurer, who at that time was the king’s chancellor through the hand of the lord of Compostela. The treasurer adorned his mother church of Saint James, for God’s service and the remedy of his soul, with the gift of the aforesaid aquamanile and another smaller vessel [Col. 1172D] of the same kind. At about the same time the man of Compostela likewise gave his church, as he had formerly given many other ornaments, a precious and excellently worked chalice of the same kind, whose workmanship surpassed its material.

## CHAPTER X. The Slander of the Lord of Compostela by Many Persons

After Pope Calixtus of venerable memory had died, Honorius succeeded him in office at the demand of the curia. Before him, rivals and detractors, led by envy and ill will, grievously accused the lord of Compostela, maintaining that he imprudently followed apostolic custom in his vestments and in receiving pilgrims’ offerings. [Col. 1173A] The apostolic lord was consequently moved to anger and was somewhat disturbed against the man of Compostela. But when he had learned the truth of the matter—which he investigated through neighbouring bishops adjacent to the see of Compostela and through pilgrims—he also sent his own legate from Rome to Compostela, without the man of Compostela’s knowledge, to inquire into the affair. By the testimony of the bishops and of that legate, he proved the rivals’ accusations wholly false. His mind was thereby calmed, and he withdrew from the indignation he had held against the man of Compostela.

When the man of Compostela learned, from many reports, of his adversaries’ fabrications and slanders, and perceived that they had grievously accused him before the lord pope, he sent as his envoys the canons and cardinals Peter Fulconis and Martin Petrides: partly to counter the detractors’ accusations, and partly to request from the lord pope the legateship of all Spain for himself. [Col. 1173B] On arriving at the curia, these envoys wisely distributed the blessing which they had brought with them—namely three hundred *almorabitini*. They gave two hundred and twenty *morabitini* to the lord pope and spent eighty to pacify the curia. Besides this offering to the apostolic lord and the pacification of the curia, fourteen marks of silver and ten gold coins were expended, partly on the maintenance of the aforesaid envoys and partly on matters pertaining to their journey. After they had explained the reason for their journey and demonstrated in many ways that the detractors’ imposture was wholly false, the lord pope replied graciously that it would greatly please him for the man of Compostela to have the Spanish legateship, but that this could not then be done. For, he said, that legateship had been granted in the curia to a Roman cardinal, and that cardinal had already long since set out for Spain. He nevertheless promised that, when the cardinal returned, he would take counsel regarding the man of Compostela’s request, and he sent him the following letter through the aforesaid messengers.

“Honorius, bishop,” etc.

“Concerning the matter that we,” etc. See Honorius II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, no. 97.

He also directed another letter to King A., who had requested this legateship for the man of Compostela in his own written petition. [Col. 1173D] A copy of it was as follows.

### Letter of the Pope to the King

“Honorius, bishop,” etc.

“With what affection,” etc. See above, no. 98.

He also commanded Archbishop P. [Pelagius] of Braga by another letter to be at the curia on the Sunday *Misericordias Domini* (“The mercies of the Lord”), prepared to answer for the usurped consecration of the bishop-elect of Coimbra.

> [Note: [Col. 1173D] The same as above: namely, “I am the good shepherd,” the Second Sunday after Easter.]

For the aforesaid envoys of the lord of Compostela had made a serious complaint against him on this matter before the whole curia: he had presumed to consecrate the bishop of Coimbra, a suffragan of the Church of Compostela, [Col. 1174A] while disregarding the rule of the sacred canons and despising the privilege of the Holy Roman Church.

And this is the pope’s letter to the man of Braga.

“Honorius, bishop,” etc.

“It pleased the Roman pontiff,” etc. See above, no. 96.

## CHAPTER XI. Construction of the Monastery of Canogio

From the time when the lord of Compostela was enthroned, by the ordering grace of God, in the summit of pontifical office, he diligently sought throughout the whole honour of Saint James and throughout [Col. 1174B] Galicia, in the manner of a prudent and wise shepherd, a suitable and fitting place for nuns. He did this because at that time there was no monastery, either in his entire pontificate or indeed in all Galicia, in which holy and religious nuns lived. Since he could find no better place to his liking, he demolished to its foundations the church of Saint Mary of Canogio, which was small and almost ruined by age, and rebuilt there at his own expense a larger and better church.

> [Note: [Col. 1174D] See Book I, chapter 21.]

During his archiepiscopate he installed in it women of good repute, who were to serve God as nuns, having supplied them with every necessity for food and clothing. He judged that place suitable for those nuns both because [Col. 1174C] it was near the city and under the protection of the apostle Saint James, and because he considered that the nuns ought to be aided and supported by the benefactions and alms of citizens dwelling in the city. At the command of the man of Compostela, these nuns entered the aforesaid monastery in the era 1167, in the month of September, for the honour of God and Saint James.

## CHAPTER XII. Exaction of Money by the King

After King A. of Spain, grandson of King A. of venerable memory—with whom the man of Compostela had enjoyed steadfast peace and faithful friendship—obtained the kingdom of Spain upon the death of his mother Queen Lady U., he never ceased, following his mother’s example, to attack and trouble the Church of Compostela. When, after the despoiling of that church fully described above,

> [Note: [Col. 1174D] Book II, chapter 86.]

he had come from the Castilian regions into Galicia because of urgent affairs, he found the man of Compostela suffering from so severe an illness that no one believed he would recover from it. Nevertheless, prompted by greed and constrained by lack of necessities, he secretly demanded money from him through his intermediaries: Albertinus of León, his secretary, and Roderic Vermúdez, his *maiorinus* or royal steward. When [Col. 1175A] the archbishop could not turn his mind away from that demand by repeated entreaties, and saw that he could not otherwise escape unless money were given to him, he gave him seventy marks of pure silver. Afterwards, before the aforesaid men, he finally established this agreement with him: that he would give him one hundred marks annually, on condition that the king neither attacked nor troubled him or his church, nor asked anything further from him; and that, when all wars were ended and he possessed his kingdom settled and at peace, he would restore to the man of Compostela, should he be alive, or to his successor and the Church of Saint James, in money or honour, down to the very smallest farthing, all the money which he received annually from him under this condition. When this secret agreement between king and archbishop had been confirmed, the archbishop at once placed the aforesaid Albertinus, his faithful friend, into the king’s hand, that he should answer to him annually for the hundred marks and be his debtor. The man of Compostela made this agreement with the king because he judged it better and more honourable to pay one hundred marks of silver annually than continually to endure the disgrace and despoiling of his church.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the King Wished to Deprive the Archbishop of the Coinage and of the Privilege Granted Him for the Work of the Church of Saint James

At about the same time, the aforesaid King A., induced by the prompting of certain wicked counsellors, wished violently to take away from him the coinage of the city of Compostela. His grandfather, King Adefonsus, the exalter and patron of the Holy Church, had granted this coinage forever for the building and completion of the work of the Church of Saint James, for his own soul and those of his parents. He had made a privilege concerning this grant to the Church of Saint James, confirmed it with his own hand, and, kneeling, had delivered it at the city of Segovia into the hand of the lord of Compostela, to be offered on his behalf upon the most holy altar of Saint James.

> [Note: [Col. 1175D] Book I, chapter 29.]

But the lord of Compostela, seeing his wicked intention and resisting manfully against the approaching wolf not as a hireling but as a good shepherd, produced before all present the aforesaid privilege which he kept deposited in the treasury of Saint James, and had it read in his presence in the Church of Saint James. The king, after seeing and hearing [Col. 1175D] the privilege, abandoned his wicked purpose. Thus the coinage remained wholly under the right of the lord of Compostela, for the support of the work of the Church of Saint James; and the king confirmed and ratified by his own hand the privilege granted and enacted by his grandfather, King A. Thus the dispute between king and archbishop regarding the coinage of the city of Compostela was completely settled.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Creation of Honorius as Pope, the Sending of a Legate into Spain, and the Celebration of a Council

After Pope Calixtus of venerable memory had died, [Col. 1176A] Honorius, a man of remarkable ability and great integrity, obtained the episcopal office of the Roman see at the curia’s demand. He sent Humbert, a venerable man, cardinal and priest, from his side into the Spanish regions, so that, having gathered the brethren together, he might celebrate a council there and, with their common counsel and assistance, confirm what had been well established, while correcting wrong practices by changing them for the better.

This cardinal came to Compostela, where he was graciously and carefully received by the lord of Compostela and was treated with diligence and honour. He remained there for eight days. Departing from there, he went into Portugal and, turning his route, finally arrived at Carrión. There he had previously arranged to celebrate a council with the archbishop and the king, who had stayed five weeks at Compostela with the lord archbishop. Both the king and the cardinal first invited the lord of Compostela in person and then through their letters and messengers, earnestly asking him to endeavour to attend that council. [Col. 1176B] They did so because they knew beyond doubt that the council would carry little weight in the absence of the man of Compostela. But at that time he was suffering from a serious illness, over which clergy and people grieved deeply. Yet although he was held by a severe infirmity which could have sufficiently excused him from the burden of the council, he resolved to attend, not so much because of the king’s and cardinal’s invitation as for the honour and benefit of the Holy Church.

Having prepared what he knew necessary for the journey, he gladly set out with the leading men of his clergy, cardinals and archdeacons, and many other honourable persons. As he approached León, attended by a great multitude of clergy, King Adefonsus, having been informed of his arrival by travellers, went out to meet him with councillors, officials, and a great company of soldiers, and received him with great joy and honour. Meanwhile the bishop of León and his clergy made their preparations and received the archbishop with a distinguished and splendid procession. When the procession was ended, the king personally invited him to his palace and that day entertained him magnificently and abundantly. After the meal, the king and the man of Compostela [Col. 1176D] entered a chamber alone and discussed many matters there. In this conversation, the king earnestly asked the lord of Compostela to give him counsel and assistance for acquiring and holding his kingdom, and to treat in council with the archbishops, bishops, and powers of the land regarding the state of that kingdom. Since he knew that he did not lawfully have his wife, because she was his relative, he earnestly begged the lord archbishop that, if the matter should be raised in the council, he would support and uphold him personally and through his friends.

> [Note: [Col. 1175D] There is no mention of this relationship among other writers of that age; nor, had it been known to the prelates, would they have kept so profound a silence about it, as the dissolution, despite their opposition, of his mother's unlawful marriage demonstrates.]

The man of Compostela, [Col. 1177A] having heard his request and plea, promised that it would be so.

On the next day, the abbot of Saint Facundus and the monks of that place, with the clergy present there, made a great procession for him and rejoiced greatly at his arrival. The following day, having left the borough of Saint Facundus, he at last reached Carrión. There he was received with honour and rejoicing by the bishops who had gathered for the council, by the clergy, and by the prior of Saint Zoilus with the monks of that monastery, after a great procession had been made. He was lodged there for as long as the council lasted. On the next day King Adefonsus and the man of Compostela, with the Roman cardinal and legate and with the archbishop of Tarragona, entered a certain private house, where they carefully considered and discussed what they were to establish and enact in the council. [Col. 1177B] Once these matters had been considered and discussed, they celebrated the council in the monastery of Saint Zoilus on 4 February, the second day before the Nones of February, after the brethren had assembled.

> [Note: [Col. 1177D] The Council of Carrión was celebrated on 4 February, era 1168, in the year 1130, as is evident from the original document in Colmenares, *Historia Segoviensis*, p. 116.]

At this council they established and confirmed many things concerning the honour and benefit of the Holy Church and the Spanish kingdom. Three bishops—the bishops of León, Salamanca, and Oviedo—and the abbot of Sahagún were deposed. Lord Arias, cardinal and canon of the Church of Saint James, was appointed in place of the bishop of León, at the counsel and with the approval of the lord of Compostela, into whose hand and authority the whole council had been placed by the grant of the king and Roman cardinal. Adefonsus Petrides, canon of the same Church, was appointed to Salamanca, through the action of the same man of Compostela with the king [Col. 1177C] and Roman cardinal. King Adefonsus and the Roman cardinal showed the lord of Compostela such honour that they placed the whole council in his hand and power, so that he might establish and confirm whatever he wished to order, and might wholly annul and invalidate whatever he reasonably wished to annul.

After the council had been celebrated, before the man of Compostela departed from the king, he prudently provided for the honour and welfare of his Church in accordance with the custom of a good shepherd. He asked the king to secure to him the two villages that belonged by right to the Church of Saint James, Cacabelos and Léndicos, so that neither Sagio nor any other person might presume to enter them in order to inflict violence or injury upon their inhabitants. [Col. 1177D] He also asked the king to grant him, for the salvation and remedy of his soul, an estate near Talavera, a city adjoining Toledo, from which sufficient oil might be obtained to provide abundantly for the illumination of the Church of Saint James during winter. For in winter few pilgrims visit the shrines of the apostle Saint James, fearing the difficulty of travel and the severity of winter; and the wax that they bring cannot suffice for illuminating the church. Recognizing his requests to be just and reasonable, the king firmly secured the aforesaid villages according to the man of Compostela’s wishes and granted to the Church of Saint James, to possess forever, the oil-producing estate near the aforesaid city. [Col. 1178A] Then the lord of Compostela placed two canons, P. Stephanides and F. Petrides, into the king’s hand, to receive the promised estate from the king and, once received, entrust it to some inhabitant of that city, who would hold and guard it and ensure that oil was brought annually to the Church of Saint James. Having obtained these and many other things from the king which are not written here, he returned home joyfully. The clergy and people of his see received him with inexpressible exultation and a distinguished procession.

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 1178B] Deposition of Certain Bishops and Appointment of the Bishop of Salamanca

At the Council of Carrión, when the legate of the Roman see, Lord Humbert, cardinal and priest, had gathered the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of Spain together, with Adefonsus, king of Spain, many counts, and other powers also present, three bishops—as we have already said—were solemnly, justly, and reasonably deposed: the bishops of Oviedo, León, and Salamanca. The bishop of Salamanca was a suffragan of the Church of Saint James. To prevent the Church of Salamanca from remaining long bereft, neglected, and without a patron, King Adefonsus and the lord of Compostela took counsel to relieve its widowhood with paternal affection and appoint for its governance and [Col. 1178C] salvation a pastor. With the assent of the king and lord of Compostela, and with the approval and counsel of the entire synodal assembly, they elected as bishop Adefonsus Petrides, canon of the apostle Saint James, a worthy man of honourable repute. The clerics of Salamanca rejoiced greatly at his election.

When the council had ended and that election had been made, the lord of Compostela returned honourably and exultantly home with the king’s leave and friendship. The king immediately sent him letters through his messengers, earnestly requesting and urgently beseeching him to consecrate the aforesaid bishop-elect. On hearing the royal request and understanding his will, the man of Compostela, since the consecration of the bishop-elect of Salamanca, his suffragan, belonged to him, invited by letter the bishops of Mondoñedo, Lugo, Ávila, Porto, and Tui, together with the abbots of the entire province. In response to his invitation, all of them came gladly and cheerfully to Compostela. First, in the presence of the bishops and abbots and an innumerable multitude of clergy and people, he consecrated the bishop-elect on the Sunday on which is read, “I am the Good Shepherd.” In his consecration, in the presence of the aforesaid bishops, he promised fidelity and devoted obedience, as ecclesiastical custom requires, to the metropolitan Church of the apostle Saint James and to the lord of Compostela, [Col. 1179A] and swore it with his own hand before all upon the altar of the apostle Saint James.

After the consecration had been completed, a council began the next day and lasted three days. At that council he publicly proclaimed, enacted, and confirmed orally all the acts of the Council of Carrión. On his own authority he also added and instituted many matters pertaining to the honour and benefit of the Holy Church. The whole synodal assembly unanimously approved and authorized them all, as useful and honourable measures. When the council ended, the bishops, abbots, and clerics present sang *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”) with joyful hearts according to ecclesiastical custom; afterwards each one, having received the lord of Compostela’s blessing and leave, returned to his own place rejoicing and cheerfully.

## CHAPTER XVI. Capture of an Archdeacon by Count R. and the Archbishop’s Punishment of Him until He Made Satisfaction

[Col. 1179B]

A certain archdeacon of the Church of the apostle St James, named A. Munincides, held his archdeaconry in the lands of St George, Trava, and Ferraria, belonging to the castles, under Count Roderic, son of Count Peter. Because he preached the truth sternly to the clergy and people of those lands—who were unlearned and almost undisciplined—and wished, as a good and discerning man, to instruct and enlighten them by the precepts of Holy Scripture, many persons from those lands, both knights and peasants, goaded by diabolical prompting, rose against him. They seized him, dishonoured and beat him, stripped him and his followers of their mounts and clothing, and cruelly shut them in prison. [Col. 1179C]

When the lord of Compostela heard this, he was greatly grieved. Having convened a chapter with his canons and taken counsel from them, he ordered every crucifix in the whole church to be laid upon the ground. He caused the canons, clothed in black and afflicted with intense sorrow, to descend from their seats and celebrate the divine office silently in choir. In vengeance for so great a crime, he excommunicated and anathematized the lands dependent upon the aforesaid castles, in which the wrongdoers lived.

The count, however, greatly fearing both the excommunication and the enmity of the lord of Compostela, immediately ordered that the captive archdeacon be released and restored in all the possessions that he had lost. He then came to Compostela, intending to clear himself of so great a crime [Col. 1179D] and to render full justice to the lord of Compostela and the aforesaid archdeacon. When they had met for discussion, and after they had long disputed and contended concerning the dishonour done to the church and the wrong suffered by the archdeacon, the count, in accordance with the judgment and counsel of the distinguished men present, swore with his own hand upon the text of the Gospels in the choir of St James, before clergy and people, together with eleven other nobles—García Petrides, Peter Gutierrides, Peter Diacus, Pelagius Curvus, Salvator Nunicides, Arias Munincides, Peter Munincides, Martin Sanciades, John Gutierrides, Nuno Pelagides, and Saracenus Municides—that he had neither known of, advised, nor commanded the seizure of the archdeacon. [Col. 1180A]

He also promised and likewise swore that he would hand over to the lord of Compostela, with all their possessions and inheritances, those peasants who had taken part in the aforesaid seizure and dishonoured the archdeacon, so that he might exact from them whatever justice he pleased. Concerning the knights, who were noble and powerful, he promised and swore that he would entirely take away the benefices which they held from him and exclude them from his service until they had rendered full justice to the lord of Compostela and his church.

When this had been done, the count and the lord of Compostela were reconciled to one another and became good friends. The lord of Compostela, indeed, wished to exact such severe justice from the count and those wrongdoers that he himself, his Church, and his canons might thereby be [Col. 1180B] honoured, and that others, terrified, might thereafter not dare stretch forth their hands to so great a crime.

## CHAPTER XVII. An ordinance concerning the state of the land, made by the archbishop and the barons of Galicia

The aforesaid count, namely Roderic Petrides, and another count of Sarria, named Roderic Velaz, having been released from the imprisonment of Count Roderic of Asturias by the intervention and release granted by the lord king of the Spains; likewise García Petrides, brother of the aforesaid count—these three, with their barons and other magnates, assembled at Compostela in the presence of the lord of Compostela by the king’s command.

When their arrival had been heard and learned, F. Joannides, for himself and his father-in-law Count Gómez, and many other princes of the lands, also gathered there. [Col. 1180C] When the lord of Compostela saw them all assembled in his presence, and saw that all the lands of Galicia were oppressed and burdened by cruel tyranny, he preached to them, counselled them, and admonished them in many ways to confirm good ordinances throughout their lands and correct what was evil for the better, wishing to root out the nettles of crimes with the sickle of justice.

They all assented to his counsel and admonition, and promised and swore in his hand that they would act according to his counsel and amend for the better what had been done unjustly and violently. The lord of Compostela in turn promised before them that he would do the same throughout all his land. Upon these promises and oaths, by common consent [Col. 1180D] and unanimous will, they made the following decree, a copy of which is written below.

Archbishop Lord Diego, Count Roderic Petrides, Roderic Velaz, Count García Petrides, and F. Joannides, with their barons and magnates, ordained in the court of the apostle St James that all distraints and seizures made throughout their lands, whether justly or unjustly, by their vicars and officials, should be remedied and restored within ten days from the day on which this decree was made by them. Concerning distraints made thereafter, they were to enforce and receive right through their *sagiones* [officials charged with execution].

If anyone sought justice from those *sagiones*, and the *sagiones* themselves were unwilling to bring them to justice, those *sagiones* should settle and make good the whole claim [Col. 1181A] from their own property. They further ordained that whoever should make a distraint without a *sagio* from that day forward should restore the whole distraint twofold and pay sixty solidi. Whoever requested a *sagio*, if he were so endowed with rent and inheritance that he could obtain his right, should be given a *sagio* for making the distraint. But if he were unstable and wholly without rent, he should provide a surety; and if he could not obtain a surety, the pledges should be placed in the vicariate for up to nine days, so that each person might obtain his full right.

They also added that merchants should not be distrained upon in their lands unless they were proved to be debtors or sureties; whoever acted otherwise should restore those pledges twofold and pay sixty solidi. In addition, they unanimously decreed that if anyone should denounce a known and convicted thief in the house of any person, together with his stolen goods, he should either obtain justice from him or answer to the accuser concerning that charge. If he were a peasant, he should swiftly summon his neighbours to seize him; and if they held that peasant under suspicion, the peasant himself should clear himself of that suspicion according to the judgment of worthy men.

If the son of a knight entered another knight’s house with theft or robbery, the lord of the house should retain that theft and robbery by his right, or receive from him a surety for them, so that the injured party might obtain full justice. Once this had been done, he should let the knight’s son depart free. If they should make accusation against him elsewhere, the knight’s son himself should answer for the whole charge.

In the lands of Pistomarcos, Noya, and Amaia, on the archbishop’s side, D. Saniz, O. Martiniz, and P. Didacidi, a canon, [Col. 1181C] were appointed governors and judges. In the lands of Montaos, Dubria, and Lajas, A. Alvitiz, G. Froiaz, and O. Gutierrez were appointed governors and judges of justice. In the land of Coronato, P. Froiaz, O. Muniz, and the cardinal Lord P. Gund. were appointed; and over Vereda, U. Suariz, O. Vimarazi, and P. Pelaiz of Sindili. In the city of St James: the lord dean P. Anajaz; judges P. and P. G.; A. Palaez; and Ad. Arias.

Both the aforesaid counts, their barons, and the other magnates who were present promised and swore in the hand of the lord of Compostela that they would likewise appoint governors and judges throughout all their lands who, following the archbishop’s example, would judge and uphold justice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The restraint of certain plunderers

[Col. 1181D]

After the aforementioned counts, with their barons, García Petrides, Fernandus Joannides, and the other magnates had sworn, by promising justice in the hand of the lord of Compostela and promising by oath, García Petrides, brother of Count Roderic Petrides, incurred the guilt of perjury before three days had passed after the oath. For he utterly neglected to observe what he had sworn before all.

English and Lotharingian merchants had come by ship to the harbour of the apostle St James with goods for sale. García attacked them with an armed multitude on the road which leads travellers from Padrón to Compostela, and stripped them entirely of their pack animals and the merchandise which they were bringing to Compostela to sell. [Col. 1182A] When this was reported to the lord of Compostela, he was deeply grieved. Yet, having a courageous heart and not despairing that the Lord and the apostle St James would avenge so great an injury, he immediately commanded his court’s *majorinus*, Pelagius Curvus by name—whose wife was the archbishop’s niece—together with all the burgesses of the city and the knights of his court, to arm themselves and swiftly pursue that robber and his followers, so that, after recovering the plunder, they might avenge such disgrace upon him.

The aforesaid *majorinus* and all the others, both burgesses and knights, obeyed his commands without delay and armed themselves unanimously. They encountered him as he was already entering the mountains with all the plunder, attacked him fiercely and courageously, and, with the help of God the Lord and the apostle St James—upon whom the robber had inflicted such dishonour—won the victory. [Col. 1182B]

They took from him, as he fled, all the booty he was carrying, worth nearly twenty-two thousand marks. They also captured twenty mounts—mules, she-mules, and horses—together with shields, swords, and many other spoils customarily won in such a victory. One part of his force withdrew from the battle grievously wounded; another part was captured and brought to Compostela. Thus the aforesaid *majorinus* and the people of Compostela, having gained so great a victory, returned home with great rejoicing and gladness. At the lord of Compostela’s command, everything belonging to each merchant was restored and secured to him.

The lord of Compostela rejoiced greatly in such a victory, both because he deeply sympathized with the wretched merchants who had lost their property and because of the justice so recently sworn and so quickly violated. [Col. 1182C]

## CHAPTER XIX. Acquisition of the castle of Faro

At about the same time as the battle described above was fought, Count Roderic, son of Count Peter Froila and the Countess Lady Mayor, at the exhortation, admonition, and preaching of the lord of Compostela, granted to the church of the apostle St James the castle called Faro, in God’s service and for remission of his offences, together with all its dependencies. This was upon the condition that during his lifetime he should hold the castle from the archbishop as though in fief; but at his death he should leave the castle free and unencumbered, to be possessed and held forever by the church of that apostle. [Col. 1182D]

He added that, should he be unable to have a legitimate son, he would likewise grant to that Church and its archbishop for possession and holding another castle called Spelunca. He ordered a privilege to be drawn up concerning this gift. Fortified and confirmed with legal force, he offered it with his own hand upon the altar of the apostle St James, in the presence of the lord of Compostela and many others of the canonical community, as testimony of his donation. He also compelled his vicar, who at that time held the castle under his authority, to perform homage and fealty to us for that castle.

## CHAPTER XX. Visitation of the monastery of St Pelagius of Antealtares

[Col. 1183A]

Among the other honourable and praiseworthy acts which the lord of Compostela wisely and sagaciously established and confirmed during his archiepiscopate, he did one thing by which my mind does not doubt that he pleased the divine omnipotence beyond expression. He converted the monastery of St Pelagius of Antealtares—dead to God and living to the world—from the shameful and monstrous life it had led to an honourable and regular life, through the keenness of his diligence and the assiduity of his skill.

There was in that monastery an abbot named P. In his youth, while he wore the monastic habit and observed the Rule of St Benedict, he was sufficiently worthy and industrious; and by the good self-restraint which seemed to be in him [Col. 1183B], he was promoted to the dignity of the abbacy with the community’s will and counsel. But once he had obtained the honour of the abbacy, he became more wicked and incontinent than any man. He was greedy for goods, lavish toward prostitutes, gluttonous, and so lustful that he begot sons and daughters while wearing the monastic habit and holding abbatial dignity. The resources of the monastery, from which the community ought honourably to have lived and been maintained, he squandered upon gluttons for empty praise and upon his concubines to attract them.

> [Note: [Col. 1183D] See the preceding volume, p. 24.]

When the lord of Compostela learned of his wickedness from the reports of several people, deeply grieving at the damnation and destruction of his soul, he rebuked and admonished him seven times—publicly and privately, personally and through others, and in a general chapter—to change and amend his life, so foul [Col. 1183C] and so infamous, for the better. But he always promised verbally what the lord of Compostela required and never put it into effect.

Therefore, seeing that he was wholly incorrigible and intractable, and grieving greatly over this, the lord of Compostela held a general chapter in that monastery. In that chapter, the aforesaid abbot was publicly accused by lawful and qualified witnesses and convicted of having had seventy concubines. The lord of Compostela deprived him of the dignity of the abbacy and of the order itself, he having condemned himself and judged himself unworthy; and he ordered a benefice from the revenues of that abbacy to be granted him for the necessities of life.

When this had been done, he ordered another monk, a young man worthy, honourable, and of good reputation, named R., to be elected, with the whole community approving and consenting. He compelled the elect to swear that, according to the measure of his ability, he would observe the monastic order and the Rule of St Benedict, and would cause the monks subject to him to observe them as well as he could. [Col. 1183D] He then compelled the monks themselves to swear fealty and obedience in his hand to the elected abbot, and to swear that they would never possess private property or wear irregular caps upon their heads, contrary to customary usage, but only such as befit regular monks.

Thereafter he consecrated the elect as abbot before the altar of the apostle St James. He made the consecrated abbot swear to him fealty and obedience upon the altar of the apostle St James, as the order of reason requires. Thus the lord of Compostela rooted out the evil customs and damnable enormities of the aforesaid monastery and planted regular observance and moral decency in it. Thus Diego, a man of the greatest integrity, did deeds so great and such as no one had done before.

> [Note: [Col. 1183D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the other copy; [Col. 1184D] another copy reads differently: “Let there therefore be praise for the man of integrity,” etc.]

## CHAPTER XXI. The schism of Anacletus II

After the death of Pope Honorius of blessed memory:

> [Note: [Col. 1184D] On 14 February, in the year 1139.]

two elections were held in the Roman Church: one catholic and canonical, the other violent and schismatic. Since the lord of Compostela was wholly ignorant which of the elected men was catholic and canonically elected, he sent his envoys to the curia to ascertain which of the aforesaid elections was catholic: P. Fulconis, chaplain and cardinal, [Col. 1184B] and M. Petrides, cardinal. Those envoys visited and greeted Pope Innocent, whose election was good and just. Returning home, they brought the following writings to the lord of Compostela and greeted him kindly on the pope’s behalf.

The lord of Compostela did all this because he wished to know which of the elected men was catholic, so that he might support his party and render him the obedience due.

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“Our dearest brother,” etc. See under Innocent II, for the year 1143.

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“Our predecessor,” etc. See above.

## CHAPTER XXII. Papal confirmation of the royal privilege, that property should not be seized while the Church is vacant

[Col. 1184C]

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“Holy Mother Church,” etc. See above.

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“Because of submission,” etc. See above.

Privilege concerning confirmation of vows.

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“Kings, princes, and other faithful of God,” etc. See above.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Anacletus’s intrusion into the papacy

After the death of Pope Honorius of blessed memory, a very great disagreement arose in the city of Rome concerning the appointment of another pope. For when the greater and better part of clergy and people had assembled and, by common consent and unanimous will, elected as pope a certain cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, an honourable man of approved reputation and a good cleric, named Gregory, a certain schismatic priest and cardinal, son of Peter Leo, enlisted and associated with himself, through his power, nobility, and abundance of paternal money, the bishop of Porto alone and other schismatics, clerical as well as lay. By their favour and goodwill, acquired through money given and promised, he caused himself to be elected pope. [Col. 1185A]

That fashioned idol drove the aforesaid elect from the city and remained in the Apostolic See as though pope, because he clearly knew that he would need the favour and goodwill of the lord of Compostela in order to retain the papacy, and that through him, his counsel, and his power, he would gain the other bishops of the Spains for his support. Therefore, unasked and without any prior notice of an embassy, he sent the lord of Compostela through his own envoys the following letters of entreaty.

But the lord of Compostela, knowing him to be schismatic and not canonically elected, utterly despised his letters and, without even reading them, refused to depart from the path of truth.

And here are the letters which he sent to the lord of Compostela for the aforesaid reason.

> “ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “You have always aided the common mother, the holy Roman Church, with the highest devotion, and have diligently taken care to assist our predecessors in their most urgent necessities. Therefore our lord and fosterer, Pope Paschal of holy memory, and the Roman pontiffs after him loved your brotherhood above others and adorned you with splendid returns of favour. We therefore, mindful both of your merits and of the old friendship which you especially maintained with my father Peter Leo of good memory, desire chiefly to love and, God granting, to honour, after the Church of the apostles Peter and Paul, your person and the Church of the apostle St James entrusted to you.
>
