> “Let your vigorous zeal therefore, according to custom, now also gird itself for the service of St Peter. Persevering in your former affection and steadfastness of faith, let it endeavour to love the Roman Church more fully for our sake and assist it more earnestly. Moreover, we have sent to your brotherhood letters containing an account of our election and of the scandal perpetrated by false brethren. We ask you, therefore, to have them read publicly before all those in your regions and to send them to other regions to be copied. Furthermore, do not delay in any way to send the envoys of your brotherhood to us.
>
> “Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.”

He sent the lord of Compostela another letter concerning the proceedings of his election, so that it might be sent throughout the Spains to be read. [Col. 1185D]

> “The whole clergy and people of the city of Rome to DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, and to all faithful persons to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord, and the spirit of faith and understanding.
>
> “Although news of the death of Pope Honorius of good memory has reached you by report, nevertheless, lest you be deceived by anyone lying, compelled to accept uncertain things as certain, or remain uninformed of what occurred in the City after his death, we have thought fit to make these matters known to your affection in writing, as we saw and heard them.
>
> “While the aforesaid pope lay ill in the Lateran, when we could hope more for his death than for his recovery, he was carried, by the counsel of certain persons, to the monastery of St Gregory. Since his illness then appeared to be tending toward death, it was determined by common counsel of the cardinals and bishops that, because the City was torn by many hatreds and enmities and the hearts of all the Roman clergy were disturbed by great bitterness, we ought to consider the appointment of a Roman pontiff if he should die. [Col. 1186A]
>
> “Some, approving this counsel, asserted that, according to the decree of the canons, while the Roman pontiff lived and had not been buried in the customary manner, there ought to be no discussion of electing a successor. Although a party of the brethren opposed this view, alleging the need of the time, the hatreds of the City, party interests, and dangers to the Church, and saying that the canons ought to be moderated for necessity and time, nevertheless after this and other matters all determined under a strict anathema that, while the pope remained unburied, there should be absolutely no mention of the election of any person.
>
> “The next day, while many rumours and diverse opinions of men were violently boiling up in the City, the people ran together, believing the pope either already dead or then dying. We assembled in the secretarium of the same monastery and began to consider what we ought to do in these circumstances. At last all the brethren thought it best that eight persons should be chosen to deliberate concerning the election and elect the person of the next pontiff, provided that, if they could not agree unanimously among themselves upon a person, some of the brethren should be added who, God granting, would bring them to agreement on a person. [Col. 1186B]
>
> “There was also a lengthy dispute about the place in which the election should be held. At length it was agreed among us that, after all the brethren had been summoned, we should meet with the electors at St Adrian’s, if the fortifications adjoining that church were surrendered into the power of the cardinals. Two cardinals were then sent to receive the aforesaid fortifications. But when they already had them in their hands, this was forbidden by certain bishops who, limping on the right—indeed on both—knees, were turning toward the other party. Since our brethren took this to be an indication of evil intention, the greater and sounder party no longer dared return to the aforesaid monastery. [Col. 1186C]
>
> “Accordingly, when the pope died on the fourth weekday after Ash Wednesday, about sunset, all the doors were shut and no cardinal was permitted to enter him.
>
> > [Note: [Col. 1185D] The manuscripts vary concerning the weekday: one has the fourth, another the fifth; although it was in fact the sixth, namely 14 February 1130, two days before the First Sunday of Lent.]
>
> “When morning came, four bishops, who had no or very little authority in an election, and very few cardinals assembled in the aforesaid secretarium. There it was again decreed under anathema that no discussion of an election should take place unless the pope had been honourably buried and all the other brethren, especially those elected for this purpose, had been summoned from every side. Yet while they were still proclaiming that the pope lived, he was suddenly brought in dead, miserably borne by lay hands. The bier was not set down, no rites were performed for him; but he was dragged at once, like a most worthless beast, into the cloister and plunged into a most vile grave.
>
> “Thus, with his body not covered, and their very oath and anathema despised, intoxicated by the tricks and cunning of Aimeric, the former chancellor, they assembled deceitfully in excessive haste, as they had arranged among themselves. They neither summoned nor consulted the brethren; and although Cardinal P. of St Susanna, the Pisan, who was then present, objected, they gathered apart, as has been written, at the altar, desiring to elect another into darkness and the title of curse. By the rash audacity of zeal, they fashioned the deacon of St Angelo for themselves into an image and an idol. [Col. 1187A]
>
> “And since such a thing has indeed never been heard of from the beginning of the world and is horrible to all, a small number of laymen, fleeing from the often-mentioned monastery of St Gregory, suddenly carried the dead pope, snatched from the grave, before the fashioned idol to the Lateran, so that the dead man and the living man entered the Basilica of the Saviour together. There, with the pontiff’s body unburied—indeed, wickedly placed in the narrowness of a vile tomb without covering or rites—they brought the fashioned idol to the palace in most miserable haste. There the spirit of error lay hidden until Leo Frangipane, with his son Otto and his brother Cencio, having made fealty, returned to the unity and obedience of the Roman Church in the service of Lord Pope Anacletus.
>
> “But thanks be to God, who [confounded] those enemies—
>
> > [Note: [Col. 1187D] ‘Confounded,’ or something similar, must be supplied.]
>
> “—for from that time they have not dared appear in the City but lie miserably concealed across the Tiber. Moreover, apart from five who wished to have their own pope, the senior cardinals together with the remaining cardinals—upon whom, with the clergy, belongs the election of the Roman pontiff—the deacons with the subdeacons and all orders of the Roman Church, the archpriests and abbots, with all the clergy and people of the city of Rome who had assembled at St Mark’s awaiting the pope’s death so that, according to custom and the ancient norm of Roman order, they might honourably bury him: when they heard that Pope Honorius had already died and been buried, after mature counsel, at the people’s request, and with the agreement of the honoured men, they elected with equal and common vote, unanimously, harmoniously, and happily, God granting, as Pope Anacletus, Lord Peter, son of Peter Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of St Callistus. [Col. 1187C]
>
> “They led him to the basilica of the apostle St Peter with hymns and praises, by the Sacred Way, as is the custom of the Church. Having placed him upon its most holy chair, on the second Sunday of Lent the venerable old man P., bishop of Porto, and many bishops from various regions solemnly consecrated him Roman pontiff at the altar of St Peter. Hence, according to the ancient norm of Roman order, the City was crowned; there was joy among the clergy, exultation among the people, and sweet consolation for the wretched and oppressed.
>
> “This pope, canonically elected and lawfully installed, the Roman Church recognizes; she knows no other, utterly rejects and repudiates any other. Furthermore, we wish it to be known to you all that our lord Pope Anacletus, repeatedly assembling with our brethren—P., bishop of Porto, other bishops of neighbouring cities, cardinals, and all the Roman clergy—summoned for the fourth time, through honourable persons among laymen and clerical nobles, those former brethren who had caused the scandal heard of among us in the Roman Church, to the bosom of Mother Church and the unity of fraternity. But they, persisting with obstinate spirit in the perfidy of their hearts, not only despised our admonitions and those of the Church but advanced into schism and the defence of error, which is heretical. [Col. 1188A]
>
> “Therefore, when a full assembly of our brethren, bishops and cardinals, together with all the orders of the palace, all abbots and priors in Rome, the archpriests, and all the clergy had assembled, all approving, we pronounced by the judgment of the Holy Spirit the sentence of excommunication against those schismatics. We therefore admonish and exhort you, as sons and faithful people of St Peter, to avoid them in every way as schismatics and excommunicates, and to take care, God granting, unanimously to hold valid and observe what has been done by us and by the Church.” [Col. 1188B]

## CHAPTER XXIV

> [Note: [Col. 1187D] The manuscripts lack a title; but for the sake of distinction, and because the subject differs, we assign and add a chapter number. [Col. 1188D]]

The Portuguese infante, son of Count Henry, named A., having acquired the Portuguese country and forcibly deprived Fernando Petrides, son of Count Peter—who, having abandoned his lawful wife, was at that time committing adultery with the mother of the infante himself, Queen Teresa [Col. 1188C], and ruled all that land—had a great dispute and great war with King A., son of Count Raymond and Queen Lady U.

> [Note: [Col. 1188D] See the preceding volume, in the Life of Lord Diego Gelmírez, no. 222.]

The infante, puffed up by the vice of pride, refused to submit to the king’s lordship, but, having acquired honour, swelled arrogantly against him. Since the king, detained in the regions of Campania and Castile by various affairs—being about to fight the king of Aragon and Count P. Gundisalvides of Lara, who had adulterously lain with the king’s mother and begotten adulterine sons and daughters by the same queen—could not come to Galicia to defeat him, he sent his envoys to the lord of Compostela, the counts, princes, and other magnates of the land, commanding them to go against the infante and attack him by whatever means they could. [Col. 1188D]

The counts, princes, and other magnates, obeying the royal order, gathered their armies and marched against him. Yet, through the obstruction of certain persons’ treachery, they did not fight him. The lord of Compostela, suffering at that time from grave illness, could not go on that expedition. He therefore commanded his *majorinus* and all his knights to go with the knights and other princes in aid of the king. He also requested, and by requesting commanded, the citizens of Compostela, both on his own behalf and on the king’s, to set out upon that expedition. But they proved rebellious and would obey neither his command nor the king’s. [Col. 1189A] Therefore the king was deeply stirred against them and very angry.

After returning from that expedition, the king sent his envoys for the lord of Compostela, the counts, and the other magnates of the land, and summoned them to him at the city of León, in order to discuss with them the state of the kingdom and the pacification of the lands.

When the lord of Compostela saw the king’s envoys, he promptly prepared what he knew necessary for his journey. Once these things were ready, he set out with the chief persons of his Church. When he approached León, the king, informed of his arrival, went out to meet him with a great retinue of magnates and received him gladly and honourably. Lord Arias, bishop of León, who had been a canon and cardinal of the Church of St James, showed him great honour. Having summoned clergy and people, he received him in a great procession. When the procession was completed, he vacated his own palace for him and gave it to him as a dwelling for as long as he remained there with the king. [Col. 1189B]

The next day, the lord of Compostela rose very early and went to the king’s palace with a great retinue of clerics and knights. When he came into the king’s presence, the king, somewhat displeased, said to him:

> “Venerable father, I ought to go to you, visit your palace, and yet you come to me. Do not come again to my palace as long as you remain here. For I shall go daily to your palace, to make private use of your conversation and counsel, and I shall arrange everything according to your will. I ought indeed to honour and love your person, because you are my spiritual father: you regenerated me at the font of baptism, anointed me king, adorned me with military arms, and of your own free will bestowed upon me many benefits in your Church.”

Having heard the king’s wish, the lord of Compostela never went to the royal palace; rather, the king came every day with the counts and magnates to his palace. There the king publicly discussed his affairs and the pacification of the lands with the lord of Compostela, the counts, and the other magnates. He firmly commanded all who were present that each should maintain and administer justice within his own honour, and should in no way oppress or injure the poor or churches. [Col. 1189C] Should anyone presume to do so, he would be neither in possession of his right nor remain in his honour, but, like a traitor, would lose that honour irrecoverably.

This edict proceeded from the king, with the lord of Compostela separately approving and counselling it. The burgesses of Compostela who had gone with the archbishop appeased the king’s anger, which they had incurred through their failure in the aforesaid expedition, by the counsel and request of the archbishop, through a promise of three hundred marks of pure silver. Of these, the lord of Compostela promised one hundred out of affection for those citizens, and the burgesses promised that they would give two hundred.

When these matters had thus been arranged and confirmed, the archbishop returned home with joy and gladness and in the king’s friendship. [Col. 1190A] His Church received him gladly and honourably.

Meanwhile, a certain knight named M. Petrides, who had built a certain castle in the land of St. James, seized a citizen of Compostela and kept him captive in that castle. Whereupon the people of Compostela, not a little angered, resolved to go and destroy that castle. When the lord of Compostela heard of the capture of his citizen, he was greatly enraged, and ordered his steward, all his knights, and the citizens of Compostela to assault that castle, utterly destroy it by fighting, and free the captive citizen. Obeying his command and besieging the castle, they pressed the attack until they took it by force. Having taken it, they left not one stone upon another in it. [Col. 1190B] Therefore the whole land rejoiced and rendered thanks to Almighty God for its destruction; for from that castle many injuries and evils were daily inflicted upon the neighboring country, and the poor dwelling round about were intolerably oppressed.

## CHAPTER XXV

According to the judgment of human deliberation, it seemed to those who do not wish truth to be propped up by falsehood that Innocent, Roman pontiff, had been installed by canonical election after the death of Pope Honorius; while another, the antipope P., son of Leo, driven by the spurs of ambition and envy, through the violence of his supporters—who remained in the city in greater number and wealth—utterly disregarding the rule of justice, had seized not a chair of honor but [Col. 1190C] one of pestilence. After this, Lord Innocent, unable to resist the fury of the wicked, came by ship to Genoa, accompanied by nearly his entire court. There the envoys of the archbishop of Compostela first met him joyfully, bearing a voluntary gift, namely forty marks of pure silver. Having received them honorably and lent a gracious ear to their petitions, he dismissed them kindly.

After some time, with Louis, king of the Franks, favorable to him, and with all the archbishops and bishops devoted in their obedience to his service in France, it happened that he entered the regions of Gaul. There, for a second time, the lord of Compostela took care to send ambassadors to him concerning the affairs of his Church. After the passage of a certain interval, when the envoys wished to return [Col. 1190D] home, Lord Innocent wished by the present letters to communicate to the man of Compostela, as to a special son and familiar friend of the Apostolic See, his own condition and that of the whole curia. He also summoned the archbishop of Braga, concerning whose injury the lord of Compostela had complained, to reply by his letters.

These letters Lord Innocent sent to the archbishop of Compostela.

> “Innocent, bishop,” etc.

> “Our predecessors,” etc. See under Innocent II, for the year 1143.

To the archbishop of Braga.

> “Innocent, bishop,” etc.

[Col. 1191A]

> “For the transgression and contempt,” etc. See above.

## CHAPTER XXVI

At about the same time, the patriarch of holy Jerusalem, together with the entire convent of the Lord’s Sepulchre; P., abbot of the Cluniac brethren; and the holy congregation of that place, returning thanks to the archbishop of Compostela for benefits frequently bestowed upon them in a cheerful and charitable spirit, sent the following letters.

> “S. [STEPHEN], by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem, and the entire convent of canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, to DIDACUS, by the same grace archbishop of St. James, his brother and friend: greeting, together with the faithful offering of prayers.
>
> [Col. 1191B] “To your fatherhood we render deserved praises and thanks for the aid and benefit that you have often charitably bestowed upon us; and now we beseech your piety that you open the bowels of your mercy to the bearer of these presents, Aymeric, our brother and fellow canon, and receive him and his companions honorably for as long as he remains among you. For know without doubt that what we require you to do for him, we shall repay to you and yours, if need should arise. We likewise ask that you cause the church of Nogueres, which is in your diocese, with all its appurtenances, and also the alms which are bestowed upon us within your jurisdiction, to be placed under his charge, with due regard for your authority; and that you commend him to your leading men, both clerical and lay. Farewell; pray for us, who [Col. 1191C] pray for you.”

From the Cluniacs.

> “To our most reverend and beloved lord DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, brother P. [PETER THE VENERABLE], abbot of Cluny: greeting and spiritual affection—not as we ought, but as we are able.
>
> “Again and repeatedly greeting your reverence, we give thanks to such sweetness, to such most fervent and most steadfast affection, by which you cherish and sustain us and our possessions, and daily inflame the heart of our entire congregation ever more with longing for your love. Therefore know that we are mindful of you in all things, asking that you too may always be mindful in the Lord of us and of our brethren, [Col. 1191D] and may not cease to extend the customary kindness to our concerns in your vicinity.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

After the matters set out above had been completed, Pope Innocent did not delay in going to Liège to address Lothair, king of the Romans, and his magnates concerning the peace of the Church and the welfare of the realm. A solemn conference having been held there, and the matters which he recognized as pertaining to the advantage of the Church and the honor of God having been considered, he returned joyfully to Gaul. Then, after taking common counsel with his brother cardinal-bishops to preserve the unity of the Church and cut off the schism, he proclaimed a general council to be held at Reims.

Accordingly, he took care to send into Spain from his side a subdeacon of the Roman [Col. 1192A] Church named G., to summon archbishops, bishops, and abbots to celebrate so great an assembly; through him he again sent the following letter to the lord of Compostela as a Catholic and prudent man. Since it was unbecoming for a legate of the Roman Church to depart unrewarded from a man of so great a name, the lord of Compostela charitably gave the departing man ten marks of pure silver for expenses. Considering the many needs of the lord pope and wishing to relieve his difficulties opportunely, he generously sent him, through the aforesaid legate, the assistance of twenty marks.

These are the letters of the lord pope to the man of Compostela.

> “Innocent, bishop,” etc.

[Col. 1192B]

> “For the unity of the Church,” etc. See under Innocent II, for the year 1143.

Concerning the chancellor.

> “To his dearest father and friend DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, A., deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church: greeting and affection.
>
> “We love your person with sincere charity, as we have loved it purely from former times, and we gladly devote ourselves to the honor of the Church of Compostela and to yours. Therefore, prompted by confidence in this affection, we earnestly commend to your kindness our very dear G., subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, whom the lord pope has deemed fit to dispatch to the regions of Spain for the service of St. Peter. For by showing him your goodwill, you will be able to secure the service of many who are in the curia [Col. 1192C].”

Letter from Cardinal Humbert.

> “To his dearest brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, most greatly beloved in Christ: HUMBERT, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, greeting and affection.
>
> “We exhort your brotherhood with so much the greater confidence as we embrace your person in the arms of a closer affection. We therefore earnestly commend to your love our very dear nephew, the bearer of these presents, G., subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, whom the lord pope, trusting in his integrity, sends from his side as a member of his household to the regions of Spain. We ask you, and firmly entreat you by that love which exists between us, [Col. 1192D] to treat and honor him kindly, and, to speak presumptuously, to show effectively in his person how much you love us. For whatever honor and goodwill you show toward him, we shall receive as pleasing, as though done to ourselves; and he, since he is esteemed there, may well, by the Lord’s grant, render service to you and your Church.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the construction of a ship

After the death of King A. of good memory, while Lord Didacus held the archiepiscopal throne of Compostela, as we wrote in the preceding volume, the violent hand of the Saracens began to invade the borders of Galicia with pirate vessels and was accustomed every year to undermine seriously the condition of the Christian religion. [Col. 1193A] Moved mercifully by compassion for so great an affliction, the aforesaid Father hired skilled craftsmen at no small price and did not delay to equip two ships of remarkable speed, at the cost of immense labor and great expenditure of money. When these had been carefully equipped, the lowly Christians, recovering strength and courage, bravely repelled those frequent assaults of the enemy and, often attacking them, successfully defeated them.

After a long period, however, the ships having fallen apart, partly through enemy neglect and partly through the decay of their timbers, hostile fury rose more fiercely, adding worse things to worse; and it did not delay in harassing by naval war the Christian people devoted to the service of St. James. Attacking the coastal districts by stealthy raids, [Col. 1193B] they gave men and women, after plundering all their goods, partly to slaughter and partly to captivity; and, spurred by lust, they shamefully violated women, both virgins and married women.

Therefore the prudence of the aforesaid man, desiring to turn away so great a rage of enemies, engaged a certain young man then thought to excel all others in shipbuilding, together with craftsmen from various regions, who were rewarded liberally. They labored with the utmost care to complete an excellent ship, fashioned by subtle workmanship, endowed with exceptional beauty, and suited to winds and waves. For its most complete fitting-out the lord of Compostela did not refuse to spend sixty marks of the purest silver out of love for his neighbors. Nevertheless, he continued to obtain many important fittings for the ship without charge. Thus the ship, manned by valiant warriors, put the enemies to flight, seized booty, and boldly invaded their kingdom as far as the Atlantic Sea. Having captured an innumerable multitude of Saracens, the ship was loaded with precious riches and pure gold—namely, 1,700 morabitinos—and with other furnishings of great value; through the grace of the Apostle it returned safely and triumphantly to port. When the time came for the regular division, thirteen marks of silver were given to the lord archbishop for the tenth share which he was to receive under the division; and, in honor of his person, he charitably accepted from the common stock certain gifts of no small weight which befitted a man of such dignity. [Col. 1193D]

## CHAPTER XXIX. These are the letters of the archbishop of Braga

> “To the venerable lord DIDACUS, archbishop of the Church of Compostela, P., by the grace of God minister of the Church of Braga: greeting in Christ and the affection of love.
>
> “With what inward affection of love we love you, and how we wish the advantage of you and of your friends to increase, we cannot explain to you by letters. Yet, if a suitable place or fitting time were granted us, what we affirm in words would, without evasions, be proved in your service. Since you have entrusted the revenues of the archbishopric of Braga to your cleric, Lord P. Ferdinand, and to your [Col. 1194A] canon, we consider this very pleasing and highly commend it. Leaving this aside, we ask whether you are entrusting to the aforesaid P., together with the other revenues, the revenues from the land of Ferdinand Menendiz, which we once received from you as a benefice, or whether you wish to retain them. Let us know by your letter what seems good to you in this matter; for the Portuguese bishop has never held those revenues [from] the land of Ferdinand Menendici. Farewell.”

After a short interval, the aforesaid pirate ship, commonly called a galley, which the lord archbishop had caused to be built and equipped with diligent care and at great expense, manned by valiant young men, hastened across the sea to attack the lands of the Saracens. Having captured a multitude of enemies, taken an immense weight of gold, and violently seized silk garments and other spoils of no small value, it returned safely with triumph and joy to its customary port of Iria. After a just and orderly division had been made, the lord archbishop received, according to the rule of equity, twenty-five marks of silver and one Moor, to be redeemed for a great price, as his share. [Col. 1194B]

> “Having considered the [letters] of your brotherhood,” etc. See under Innocent II, for the year 1143.

Letters through the provinces.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Didacus, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, went to the king and obtained this privilege from him

> “It befits royal majesty to defend the churches of God, enrich them with gifts, enlarge them with benefices, and raise the dignities of persons. Therefore I, Adefonsus, by the grace of God emperor of Spain, reasonably following the custom of my predecessors, together with my wife, Queen Lady Berengaria, make for you, Lord Didacus, archbishop of the Church of St. James, and for all the lords and senior canons of that same Church, present and [Col. 1194D] future, out of reverence for the most glorious Apostle James and for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, this charter of confirmation: namely, that no one may rashly presume to assail the dignity of your persons; that no one may dare to violate the houses in which you regularly reside, or carry anything off from them; that no one may attempt to invade or take away anything from your canonical anniversary revenues and common honors, or from the benefices of individual persons. Even if anyone has a cause of injury against the archbishop, or endures the gravest injury from any citizen, knight, or any other person, he shall nevertheless in no way dare to invade or despoil the aforesaid revenues of the canons.
>
> “If anyone attempts to infringe any of the aforesaid provisions, [Col. 1195A] he shall, according to his offense, be punished by canonical judgment and pay five hundred solidi to the injured party and to the Church. I exempt all other inheritances and possessions of all the canons from every subjection to the *sagiones* (royal officers); no one may presume to seize their property and means, even if he is a debtor or surety, unless he has first, once and twice, publicly been summoned to come to justice and has refused. Otherwise, whoever seizes anything or takes a pledge before public summons shall make double restitution for a simple offense and moreover pay sixty solidi to the injured party.
>
> “I likewise confirm in every respect the wills of my predecessors and parents, and the grants of counts, knights, and any persons whatsoever, which they have bestowed or shall bestow from their own property or from my royal domains upon the Church of St. James, in its established condition. [Col. 1195B] This testamentary charter was made at Palencia on the Kalends of April, era 1171. I, Adefonsus, by the grace of God emperor of Spain, with the assent of Lord Didacus, archbishop of the same Church, of the other prelates of Spain, and of all counts and princes, confirm by my own authority. Didacus, archbishop of the same Church, confirm by my own authority. M., bishop of Ourense, confirms. P., bishop of Palencia, confirms. A., bishop of León, confirms. P., bishop of Lugo, confirms.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. When the archbishop was at the court of King A.

It happened that Lord Didacus, archbishop of the see of Compostela, went to the court of King Adefonsus in order to discuss with him the affairs of his Church. While he was staying with him at Carrión, the following dispute arose between the archbishop and Bernard, the king’s chancellor, a canon and treasurer of the aforesaid see. Bernard maintained that he had acquired that office, namely the chancellorship, through himself and King A., not through the archbishop. The archbishop, on the contrary, said that the king had generously bestowed upon him the two offices of chaplaincy and chancellorship, and that Bernard, canon and treasurer of the aforesaid Church, held that dignity chiefly and principally from his hand.

Then Lord Bernard, though kindly and amicably admonished by his lord archbishop in the presence of his brethren and the other fellow canons present, [Col. 1195D] would not desist from that injury. At last, after counsel had been taken in the king’s presence, with the counts and barons of Spain present and with the canons and citizens also hearing the case, the arguments having been set forth on both sides, Lord Bernard, justly and reasonably convicted, abandoned his unjust position and, with the king present and consenting and others favoring the just side, invested his lord archbishop with the right to that office. Afterwards the archbishop, having consulted his brethren, entrusted that dignity—the chancellorship—to Lord Bernard, his cleric and canon, for a time, according to the good pleasure of his own will; and thus that controversy ended.

Thereafter the king, in the presence of his barons and also of the canons and citizens who were in the archbishop’s retinue, again granted and confirmed by the authority of his word the two offices, chaplaincy and chancellorship, as he had already granted them to the lord archbishop, in era 1171, on the fourth Ides of March, in the thirty-third year of his pontificate. [Col. 1196A]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. This decree was issued

This is the decree which the canons of St. James the Apostle, and the judges and citizens of Compostela, by the authority and confirmation of King Lord Adefonsus and Archbishop Lord Didacus, decree shall be observed, all evil customs having been abolished and good ones restored for perpetual observance.

For good Castilian wine brought into the city, no fewer than eight quarts shall be given for a mark; [Col. 1196B] for other good wine brought by boats, no fewer than twelve quarts shall be given here for a mark, and the purchaser shall profit by one quart from each mark’s worth, selling the rest honestly and without any admixture according to the measure established for them by the council. Whoever wishes to buy wine of our own land shall pay four solidi for a large *carrega*, and shall sell it to us without admixture, four [measures] for two solidi, retaining a half-quart as profit.

A peasant or citizen who brings that *sicera* [cider or fermented drink] without admixture shall sell it himself and give four full *canadas* for the iron-bound *canada* of Ferdinand Velasco, or its equivalent. Of good *sicera* from the cask in this city, he shall give three *canadas* for a nummus; and no one may presume to keep a tavern of this *sicera* by the cask or jar. Regraters (*magulanes*) and forestallers (*untiquitariae*) [Col. 1196C] shall be wholly driven out, both within and without. No one shall buy fish, meat, seafood, octopus, lobsters, lampreys, bait-fish, apples, or fruit in order to profit and resell them, but only in order to eat them; the person who brings them shall sell them himself openly. Merchants of this town who go to the coastal places and river-mouths for any fish shall not sell it to a regrater, but shall themselves sell it publicly both to citizens and strangers.

Likewise, those who go into those regions for cattle, pigs, and various meats shall not sell to other regraters, except to citizens or butchers. The butchers shall buy by order of the council, handle [the meat] daily in the market, and sell it without dishonest contrivance by the lawful weight established for them by the council according to ancient custom [Col. 1196D]—except oxen, which we do not permit them to handle, except old oxen unfit for the plough. [Col. 1196D]

We further add that no one may dare to buy horses, mares, oxen, or cows from royal officers, thieves, robbers, or an unknown man without a surety. Cheese and butter shall be sold by weight according to ancient custom. We also decree concerning fish that no fewer than five large *vesugos* [sea bream] or mullets shall be sold for a nummus; and of the smaller kind, ten forming a large *tema* for a nummus; a lobster for a nummus; a large octopus for no more than two denarii; a good medium-sized one for no more than a nummus; fresh or salted *pexotas* [fish, uncertain species] no fewer than three for a nummus; [Col. 1197A] large oysters no fewer than fifty; sardines no fewer than ten; an eight-palm conger eel for no more than seven denarii; good medium-sized ones for no more than three nummi; lampreys for no more than three nummi; the largest *ircim* [fish, uncertain species] for no more than ten nummi; a good *cordarium* [fish, uncertain species] with white skin for no more than six denarii; a good *effolatum* [uncertain fish] for three nummi; a hen, duck, or partridge, each for a nummus; a good hare for two nummi; eggs, no fewer than thirty for a nummus; a good kid with its skin for no more than three nummi; a good goose for no more than four nummi; and the best ram for no more than eight nummi.

Baker-women who possess houses or property sufficient for carrying out their office shall buy at the true assessed rate and, without fraud, make [Col. 1197B] good, *salgatum* [term uncertain], and clean bread worth one nummus or a *mealia*, by the weight assigned to them by the council; when they have met their dues, they shall make no more than four nummi of profit. Innkeepers, moneyers, money-changers, and citizens shall not possess false marks, false pounds, or false weights; nor shall innkeepers keep women bakers in their houses or elsewhere. Wax, spices, cumin, and incense shall be sold by true pounds.

Smiths shall sell the best horseshoes and mule-shoes for no more than two nummi a pair; medium ones for three *minuti*; a good axe for no more than eight nummi; a good hoe for no more than four; an excellent ploughshare for no more than three, and a medium one for two; an excellent clearing-sickle for no more than three, a medium one for two; a harvesting sickle for a nummus; a *saxium faucinum* [uncertain tool] for individual [uncertain units], and *medaculas* [uncertain item].

[Col. 1197C] Concerning footwear: the best goatskin clogs, without fraud, for no more than eight nummi; good *osas* [boots or leggings] for no more than two solidi. The best women’s *zapatones* [large shoes] for no more than twelve nummi. Good cowhide *zapatones* for *barraganes* [uncertain type or users] for no more than five nummi; other kinds for four or three according to their value; the best *suffurtas* for no more than three nummi; the rest for a nummus, three obols, or two nummi according to their value. The best *liadizos* goatskin *zapatones* for no more than twelve nummi. We also order and jointly confirm that none of our merchants shall sell oxhides, cowhides, billy-goat skins, or goatskins to those boats.

[Col. 1197D] Royal officers, thieves, and bad men shall not be admitted to the hearing of cases. The accuser and defender, with only one or two friends each, shall come before the judges or the city’s deputy to complete judgment or furnish surety, lest one entrap his brother in litigation. If need requires, the judges shall call to their assistance from clerics or laymen those whom they deem useful for maintaining or obtaining justice. Innkeepers shall not go beyond the boundary of the Minho in any of the aforesaid selling or buying. No one shall use force or fraud against a seller—by “force” I mean injury. Both buyer and seller who act contrary to the aforesaid decree shall pay five solidi; sellers shall be liable to flogging [Col. 1198A] and deprived of their office. We declare and confirm that no house or hiding-place shall shelter anyone publicly guilty of this offense.

The whole council selected suitable men: for setting the wine measure, namely Pelagius Astrarici with Pelagius Albus, Aloytus Candanatici, and Stephen Pelaizi; and for assessing bread, Froila Rodesindii, Michael Martinizi, and Arias Guntadici. They shall conduct that assessment of bread and establish its weight. Likewise, for meat: Pelagius Astrarici, Ferdinand Justilaci, John Arias, and Pelagius Viliulfici; and according to the assessment, we shall establish that weight and that stone-weight for pork and beef. When there is need to increase or decrease [the assessment], it shall neither be increased nor decreased except by the consent, command, and judgment of the canons, judges, citizens, and rector of the city. In era 1171, on the [uncertain number] Nones of May. [Col. 1198B]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. After the death of Lord Sancho, bishop of the Church of Ávila, of good memory, the people of the city sent this letter to the lord archbishop

> “To DIDACUS, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, the whole council of Ávila, both clerical and lay: greeting and devoted submission.
>
> “The Church of Ávila, your daughter, deprived of her pontiff and thereby cast down into mourning, awaits the consolation of your fatherhood and implores the help of your authority. For, after our prelate Lord S. had been buried, all of us unanimously chose as bishop our archdeacon, Lord Eneco, who for a considerable part of his life has served innocently in [Col. 1198C] our Church; with your confirmation, we sought the assent of the king and princes, and all granted it and sent us to your protection. Therefore, in all humility we pray that your assent and confirmation may be present, that you may consecrate without delay him whom we recognize as necessary for us, and that you may notify us of your assent, confirmation, and the time for consecration. May the sorrow of our desolation move the bowels of your compassion, so that you may consecrate him for us as quickly as possible and not allow so many sheep subject to your command to remain long without a shepherd. For the page of the Old Testament also testifies that, if one of the loaves of offering was removed, another was to be put in its place with the utmost speed (Exod. XXV; Num. IV). Farewell; and, if you love our welfare, [Col. 1198D] as we most certainly believe, consecrate him without delay.”

The bishop-elect of the Church of Ávila likewise sent this letter to the archbishop of Compostela.

> “To DIDACUS, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, E., elected bishop of the Church of Ávila with his authority consenting: faithful service and the obedience of due submission.
>
> “After God saw fit to call our shepherd, Lord Sancho, from this age, the whole clergy assembled and elected me bishop, the people requested it, and the king consented. Yet, if the authority of your judgment commends it, and since there is one God, one baptism, one Church, and because I have learned that all are of one mind and preserve unity in electing me, I have consented to their election, provided that the consent of your holiness be present. Therefore I seek the counsel of your fatherhood and ask the aid of your authority, that you may write back to me the appointed time at which I am to come to the Church of Compostela, my mother, and there, commended to the judgment of your wisdom, receive from God through you the episcopal dignity of order. Farewell, and write back to me what pleases your holiness.” [Col. 1199A]

Reply of the lord archbishop to the clerical and lay sons of the Church of Ávila.

> “DIDACUS, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, to the clerical and lay sons of the Church of Ávila: greeting, aid, and protection in Christ.
>
> [Col. 1199B] “Having considered your benevolent letters, by which you did not neglect to set before our sight that the Church of God, namely your mother, was bereft of its own pontiff, we cannot explain to you how much grief and sorrow they have stirred in the depths of our compassion. For just as the life of so great a pontiff, our son and brother, held and retained no small ardor of our fatherhood and affection for his person, so his death cannot be borne by us without the deepest compassion of our heart. Almost everyone knows and proclaims what great labor—indeed, what immense and various calamities—he steadfastly underwent for his Church, and to what high estate he at last manfully raised it.
>
> “[Col. 1199C] But because you humbly request the authority of our aid and earnestly desire to be refreshed by the compassion of our consolation, we cannot reasonably refuse what, at your request, has seemed just and right, according to the Gospel saying: ‘Ask, and you shall receive’ (John XVI), etc. Nor do we deem it fitting that sheep granted by God to our jurisdiction should remain long without a ruler’s governance. Yet when your envoy reached us, we were unceasingly laboring throughout the bounds of our archbishopric at the work suited to our office, for the praise and honor of God. Therefore, since at that time our resources were not available for accomplishing so great a matter so suddenly, we command you with the utmost goodwill [Col. 1199D] that, for the feast of St. James chiefly celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, he be presented, as is fitting, to our Church and presence together with authoritative persons, clerical and lay, from your Church. We do not propose this in order to cause you trouble, but suitably defer the time meanwhile so that what is fitting for the honor of your Church, for him himself, and for us may be prepared. May Almighty God, by the intercession and merits of St. James, keep you, fortify you, and defend you from all adversities. Amen.”

Reply to the bishop-elect.

> “DIDACUS, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Compostela, to his beloved son E., bishop-elect of the Church of Ávila: greeting and paternal affection in the Lord.
>
> “Because we loved your brother, the shepherd of the Church of Ávila [Col. 1200A] and our son, most deeply in life, we bear his death with no small sadness. Therefore, since your person is especially adorned by life and character, do not doubt that it is held by us in a double affection; for we do not wish you to be deprived of that heartfelt regard which we showed him while he lived. Thus we rejoice not a little at the election of your person, if it is as the letters sent into our presence state and their bearer affirms.
>
> “We therefore exhort and admonish you in the Lord, as a special son of our Church, not to delay in coming, with some of your canons and worthy citizens, to your mother Church of Compostela and before our person for the feast of St. James, celebrated with the greatest reverence on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. Meanwhile we shall summon, as our means permit, our brethren and neighboring fellow bishops, so that, after they have assembled and been consulted in brotherly love, your consecration, if it ought to take place, may, God consenting, be performed justly and canonically on the aforesaid day and time.” [Col. 1200B]

King Adefonsus sent this letter through the same bishop-elect to the lord archbishop.

> “ADEFONSUS, by the grace of God emperor of Spain, to the venerable Father Lord DIDACUS, archbishop of the Church of Compostela: life in Christ.
>
> “I notify your affection that Sancho, bishop of Ávila, has died, and that in his bishopric his brother, named Eneco, has been elected by clergy and people and presented to me. Whom, once confirmed by the scrutiny of your discernment, do not delay to consecrate for the sake of justice and out of regard for me; for we have recognized that at present he is very useful and necessary to his subjects for governing them. Farewell.” [Col. 1200C]

This is the record of the election of Lord Eneco, archdeacon of the Church of Ávila, promoted to episcopal dignity. When Bishop Sancho had been honorably buried by Lord P., bishop of Segovia, and by a great assembly of clerics and laypeople, he was elected without opposition, by the equal consent of all present. For all the clerics of that city, and many others from the surrounding districts who had gathered for the burial of their shepherd, assembled separately [Col. 1200D] and began zealously and carefully to investigate and inquire among themselves whether someone might be found in their assembly who was fit to succeed in the place of the deceased predecessor.

But after many and diverse opinions, by the grace of Almighty God’s granting, all at last unanimously agreed upon the aforesaid Eneco. Because he was worthily and commendably discharging the office of archdeacon and seemed to surpass the others in the excellence of his religious life and character, they judged that the good brother, imitating the praiseworthy life of his good brother, ought likewise to become his successor in pontifical dignity. This election, first made by the clergy, greatly pleased all the people assembled in the church. There was no one in the entire assembly of the people who opposed or resisted the establishment [Col. 1201A] of the election; rather, all cried out together with one heart and one voice that they wished him and desired him to become their shepherd and bishop. And while the clerics sang *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God”—they joyfully glorified the almighty power and mercy of God with the greatest devotion, hands raised to heaven.

Concerning his consecration.

After the death of Sancho, bishop of Ávila, of blessed memory, the clergy and people, having deliberated carefully, unanimously chose Eneco, brother of the deceased, who was serving as archdeacon in that same Church, to govern the same Church, with the king’s assent and on the advice of the bishops of the province. With one voice and common consent they presented him, elected by all, to Lord Diego, archbishop of the see of Compostela, [Col. 1201B] to whose metropolitan jurisdiction it was known to belong, that he might be consecrated, as was fitting.

The metropolitan, having carefully investigated the election and determined, from the lawful testimony of those present and the common written testimony of those absent, that it was worthy and canonical, and having learned by letters of the king’s assent, invited his brother bishops and the canons—namely Munio of Valibre, P. of Lugo, M. of Ourense, and P. of Tui—to the consecration of the elect. Out of reverence for St James and in honour of the archbishop, they willingly hastened to assemble for the principal feast of that apostle, celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July]. Thus, when these brethren had gathered at Compostela, the lord archbishop, after holding a holy and devout [Col. 1201C] consultation with them, solemnly and honourably consecrated the aforesaid elect on the feast day itself, according to the ordinances of the canons.

Once consecrated, he did not refuse to promise, as he ought, the obedience due in subjection to the metropolitan prelate to whom he was subject as a suffragan; and, in the presence of the aforesaid bishops and of all who attended the consecration, he bound himself firmly by a subscribed oath of fidelity.

This is the oath.

> “I, Eneco, now to be ordained bishop of the holy Church of Ávila, promise that I shall forever render the subjection, reverence, and obedience established by the holy Fathers, according to the precepts of the canons, to the Church of St James and to its rulers [Col. 1201D], in the presence of Lord Diego the archbishop; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. The whole clergy of the Church of Salamanca sent this letter to the lord archbishop.

> “To the venerable lord and most beloved father of all, DIEGO, archbishop of the see of Compostela: all the clergy of the Church of Salamanca, obedience with faithful service.
>
> “Behold us, your servants, ready to obey the commands of your magnificent mercy, reverend Father. Placed under unbearable anxiety, we beseech with suppliant heart and humble voice the discernment of your dignity: have mercy upon us, and allow us to live in peace.
>
> “Now, merciful Father, we wish to report to your graciousness concerning Munio’s first arrival, when he came from Idanha. We received him on this condition: that within a few days certain clerics, with their own purses, should come with him into your presence, so that we might see what you approved concerning his election; and this pleased him. Yet, without our knowledge, he secretly departed when he came here. But, on leaving your holiness, he declared before us and the laity that he had obtained your letters and blessing. To tell your fatherhood the truth, we were displeased that he had summoned none of us, as he had agreed to do; and some of his companions said: ‘You have not done, lord, what we arranged as right; do not go to Rome without some of us.’ Yet he departed without our knowledge, accompanied only by [Col. 1202B] a certain squire.
>
> “When he returned, he assured us in vague words that he bore honour and dignity, and he represented himself, though not with truthful words, as free and subject to no authority except that of the Apostolic See. Soon afterward he ordered many barons to be endowed with benefices of churches. When this crime was reported to our ears, we judged that he had not been lawfully granted to the see of Salamanca. On a certain day we came to him and asked for the Church’s privilege and dignity. Hearing this, he was moved to anger and more and more openly delivered clerics and churches into the hands of laymen.
>
> “Know that we have said these things of him not from envy, not from swelling pride, nor from any hatred, but because we cannot endure so great an injury to God’s holy Church. Therefore, good Father, do not leave us like a flock [Col. 1202C] without a shepherd; rather, have mercy upon us. Take counsel even from the lowly concerning what you should do regarding the distresses of our Church. For whatever your loving goodness commands, know that, in the truth of the matter, we shall be faithful and steadfast to you as to our own father. Farewell.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the restoration of the canonry to a better condition, since it had been diminished.

To all who survey the course of events with the eye of discernment, certain and manifest indications make clear how solicitously and diligently Lord Diego, first archbishop of the see of Compostela, strove to exalt his Church and raise it to the rank of higher dignity. For if, by a proper method of comparison, we wish to set present circumstances beside past ones, even the envious will not cease to praise his prudence and [Col. 1202D] deeds. But because it is long and difficult to recount all his benefactions, let us not refuse to commit at least one among many to the memory of posterity.

Let us begin a little further back by recalling Bishop Cresconius, his predecessor, a famous man of distinguished nobility, who flourished as a vigorous warrior in the time of King Fernando. In his time, although the Church of Compostela was rich in wealth and abounded in honours, only seven canons served in it. They observed no rule of any order, nor even a distinctive habit; they did not wear the tonsure of the crown, nor did they wish to shave their beards. Thus they lived less than canonically.

To offer a still more recent example: Lord Diego Peláez, bishop, who flourished greatly in the time of King A. of pious memory and was afterward deprived of the dignity of that same office, established in that Church twenty-four canons wholly ignorant of the ecclesiastical office. But Lord Diego, first archbishop of the same see, thereafter devoted seventy-two [Note: [Col. 1203D] See Book I, chapter 20.] canons—educated in literary studies, skilled in the ecclesiastical office, and adorned in life and morals—to the Church’s service in perpetuity. He placed at their disposal and under their administration common revenues sufficient for honourable sustenance and clothing. Once these matters had been established and firmly ordered, the whole community of canons remained for a long time in peace and security, with all necessities supplied.

But after the passage of a long [Col. 1203B] period, the aforesaid provision for the common good, partly through the wrongful acquiescence of others, began gradually to decline from that excellent and agreeable condition. The common sustenance was diminished and reduced almost to nothing. When the pious and kindly shepherd learned this—he who ought to consult and provide for the welfare of all in temporal and spiritual matters—he convened the brethren according to custom and diligently sought to remove the seedbed of so great a scandal. Having first held useful and honourable deliberation with the dean and the other leading men, he decreed that, besides bread, anniversaries, and other things customarily bestowed upon canons out of charitable concern, twelve marks should be given each month for the daily provision of the kitchen. He confidently promised that he would improve matters further according to circumstances. Thus, when the loss sustained by the common resources had been partly repaired, the murmuring and scandal that daily disturbed fraternal concord wholly ceased: in the Era 1172 [A.D. 1134].

### On completing the cloister.

On the same feast day on which the lord archbishop, as stated above, consecrated the bishop of Ávila and improved the condition of the canonry, he also held a united and unanimous deliberation with his brethren, after careful consultation with the bishops present, concerning the beginning and completion of the cloister. He had long ago entrusted the undertaking to the oversight of certain brethren; but because of other intervening causes it had been neglected and interrupted. Then, seeking to devote more earnest care and greater [Col. 1203D] diligence to the work, he charged two brethren—the archdeacon P. Cresconiz and Cardinal Lord P. Gundesindiz—with its execution, by the authority of the whole community, through their counsel and solicitude. And so that this resolution might be confirmed by the actual undertaking of the work, the lord archbishop promised, out of charitable devotion, to give one hundred marks toward the construction of the cloister, according to fixed intervals of time. To prevent delay in beginning so great a work, he did not hesitate to give thirty marks at once.

### On restoring the church and canonry of the patron.

It is known and manifest to all, with every scruple of doubt removed, that the see of Compostela [Col. 1204A] had originally been founded and established in ancient times at Iria, before the discovery of the apostolic body. But after the most glorious body of St James was discovered in the time of Bishop Theodemir, through the guiding revelation of divine grace, the aforesaid see, then called Iria, was fittingly transferred by royal privilege, episcopal counsel, and the assent of all the people to Compostela, where the precious drachma had been found.

After this transfer of the see had been made by common counsel, the Church of Iria, deprived of the dignity of so great an honour, declined entirely from religious observance and was greatly diminished in temporal resources until the succession of Lord Diego, the first archbishop. Indeed, that place had fallen into such poverty that the few clerics living there, wholly unskilled in the clerical office, could scarcely share even poor sustenance except during Lent and the season of the Lord’s Advent. [Col. 1204B] The lord archbishop, pitying the destitution of that Church, since it had formerly shone in the highest rank of honour, sought partly to restore it. He appointed there twelve clerics, with their prior, adequately instructed in the exercise of their office, to celebrate divine worship; and out of pious charity he granted them common revenues sufficient for food and clothing.

Having carefully accomplished this, and since good ought always to advance toward better, he did not cease to undertake another work of virtue. He decreed that a very poor and small chapel, founded on the bank of the Sar, where the glorious [Col. 1204C] apostle’s body had been deposited when it was brought ashore from the ship, should be restored with the greatest care in honour of so great a guest. Since things well begun are wont to be brought to a joyful completion, he did not delay to have the body of that church founded with three apses, through the deliberate initiative of his kindness.

He established that three altars should be built there and celebrated with honour: the middle one in honour of the most glorious apostle James, whose body had been received there as a guest; and the two corner altars, one for Blessed Mary, his mother, and the other for his brother, the blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist, in the affection of holy devotion. Once these arrangements had been carefully made, he strove in pious charity to honour and adorn the church with excellent candelabra, hangings, and other ornaments appropriate to ecclesiastical worship. [Col. 1204D]

And because a twofold good is commonly stronger than a single one, the lord archbishop distributed by a just rule of division the revenues of both churches—namely, that of Iria, which he had first restored, and this one, which he had afterward decreed should be built. He assigned twelve canons to each, to serve to God’s honour; and so he laboured that both churches, suitably restored in temporal and spiritual matters, should thereafter devote themselves solely to religious worship.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the dispute between the archbishop and Count Fernando.

After a short time had passed, although the lord archbishop and Count Fernando observed between themselves the bond of friendship they had confirmed, a grave and irreconcilable conflict arose. It happened that a knight of the archbishop came to the court of that count. The count accused him of certain charges and, without the archbishop’s knowledge, seized him and placed him in chains. When he heard this, the lord archbishop, angered by so great an insult, ordered two of the count’s knights to be seized and held in custody.

After these things had occurred, the aforesaid count, driven by an outburst of rage, violently attacked a certain archdeacon, P. Cresconiad, to whose oversight the administration of the count’s lands had been entrusted. He seized him, placed him in chains, and held him in one of his very strong castles. When this execrable crime became known to the archbishop and his Church, he summoned [Col. 1205B] the aforesaid count once, twice, and three times, according to the rule of the canons, to make satisfaction for so great an injury. But because, though so often summoned, he scorned to make satisfaction, the lord archbishop, with the whole community of the Church, pronounced a public sentence of excommunication against him.

Thereupon the count, moved by repentance, at last came to his senses; and, after conferring with the archbishop, he restored the archdeacon whom he held captive. Thereafter, wishing to make satisfaction in the presence of the archbishop and all the canons, he came humbly to his mother Church, which he had offended. First, in settlement for the sacrilege, he gave hostages according to the custom of the country; then, as an expression of humility, he humbly offered himself, as though a captive, into the power of the archbishop and all the canons. [Col. 1205C]

Then, for fuller satisfaction, the lord archbishop and the entire community delivered the count himself into the lordship and power of the archdeacon. The count also swore before all that he would not again commit such an act.

There still remained between them an unresolved matter concerning the *hombres de creación* (“men of creation/settlement”), whom the aforesaid count claimed between the Ulla and the Tambre. On this issue there had very often been bitter contention, not only between them but also between their predecessors. That dispute, they say, was also the principal reason why Bishop Lord Gudesteus was killed at Iria by the hand of certain violent men. Many nobles likewise, because of the same cause, were mutilated or slain by the sword and suffered loss of body and property.

Therefore, lest the seedbed of so great a hatred should sprout again, the lord archbishop, wishing to settle that dispute completely, with the advice of the canons and the king’s assent, granted to the aforesaid count a certain estate called Lubre, on this condition: neither he nor anyone of his kin nor his heir should henceforth claim that *creación*, its right, or its inheritance, apart from the estate of Savardes with fifty men, held in the honour of St James. This exchange was confirmed in perpetuity by a lawful charter and royal authority. [Note: [Col. 1205D] A charter concerning this matter appears below, chapter 40.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Letters of the pope and the antipope.

[Col. 1206A]

At that time, while the matters mentioned above were occurring, the schism that had long been growing in the Church of God had by no means subsided, but had increased from bad to worse. Peter, son of Leo, supported by Duke Roger and partly by the proud power of his lineage, had obtained the chair of the first see and sought, through many constructions of words, to establish the justice of his cause. The other, Innocent, violently expelled from the City and residing at Pisa, did not cease to weaken his adversary’s party and to commend his own as plausible.

Each strove to defend his own party. On the same day, by separate messengers who knew nothing of one another, they simultaneously sent letters of this kind to Lord Diego, archbishop of Compostela, who at that time was stationed at the castle of Honesto with a great army of knights and an innumerable multitude of foot-soldiers to repel the fury of the Saracens. [Col. 1206B]

> “Innocent, bishop, etc.
>
> “Concerning your prudence and integrity,” etc. See Innocent II, under the year 1143.

> “Anacletus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Diego, archbishop of St James: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Because of the exceeding affection of charity with which we love your person, and from which we likewise believe ourselves to be loved in return, we have already sent you letters from the Apostolic See rather frequently, having such confidence in you that you ought also frequently to visit us by your letters and messengers. Yet, dearest brother in Christ, we do not know by what sluggishness you have been held back, but we have never deserved to receive any reply from you. Therefore, though we are greatly astonished and somewhat grieved by this, we do not cease to visit you again by our letters and to inform you concerning what has been done or is being done among us.
>
> “For after Lothair’s departure—whom, as we believe you have already learned, with divine power cooperating, we compelled to return disgracefully and most shamefully, not without great slaughter among his men—the heresiarch G. [Note: [Col. 1206D] He had formerly been called Innocent, now Gregory.] whom he had intruded within the houses of our perjurers in the first nest of his faction, fled by ship to Pisa at night, since, with clergy and people protesting against him, [Col. 1206D] he could not remain in the City. There he lurks, living somehow in utter misery.
>
> “By God’s grace, however, we are safe and prosperous with our brethren and sons—the bishops, cardinal priests and deacons—the entire clergy and people of the City, who adhere to us, as they have from the beginning, with undivided charity. In the Lateran palace, following the ancient custom of our predecessors, with all the patricians of our city, we have celebrated the Easter solemnities, together with the other feasts of the year, quietly and peacefully, honourably and devoutly.
>
> “We have recently recovered and retain in our power the basilicas of St John and of St Paul the Apostle, together with certain other fortified places which they had seized at the coming of Lothair, our enemy, [Col. 1207A] and of which they greatly boasted. By God’s grace, with the aid of our faithful ones, especially our most beloved son R., king of Sicily, we are preparing wholly to uproot from the midst of the Church those perjurers of ours, the Leofraiapani, and one brother of theirs—who, as the third, was most rashly bold in every wickedness, and with almost sixty fighting men was crushed and killed beneath the collapse of a church bell-tower that they had undermined at night.
>
> “For we are besieging them so vigorously while they are enclosed that they will soon either surrender themselves into our hands or, as we have said, perish root and branch. Therefore, dearest brother, join us in giving due thanks to the Lord, giver of all good things; reject, through the wisdom granted you, the lies of our enemies; and pray Almighty God that our eyes may see our purpose brought to completion. By frequent letters sent to us through the bearer of this letter and through other messengers, inform us of your condition and of the good will and disposition you bear toward us, lest, according to the Apostle’s saying, we seem to love more than to be loved. Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April].”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the seizure of Bernald and the dean, and their release.

It is known and evident to very many that Lord Diego, archbishop of the see of Compostela, had from childhood nourished and educated Bernald and Peter Helias with great diligence, and cherished them with such affection that he made the one, namely Bernald, treasurer, adding many useful and honourable benefices and dignities of the Church of St James; and he unexpectedly appointed the other, namely Peter Helias, who was archdeacon of the aforesaid Church, as dean. But, to compress much into few words, he showed them such affection that whatever he intended to do or say he hastened especially to entrust to their counsel and judgment.

To Bernald, whom he loved wonderfully above the others, he also honourably gave the chancellorship, counsel, familiarity, and favour alike of King Lord A., as well as of the counts and his princes, just as a spiritual father entrusts such things to a spiritual son in whom he has confidence. For so great a power had been granted by Almighty God to the aforesaid archbishop that he held both the king’s chaplaincy and chancellorship, [Col. 1207D] and disposed at will of every cleric of the court.

When they saw themselves placed at such a height of dignity and honour, swollen by the breath of pride, the dean in the city and Bernald at the royal court—both kinsmen—secretly devised against him certain hostile and unsuitable schemes, by every means they could, repeatedly raising the necks of their arrogance against him.

As this execrable crime of plotting gradually became known to the archbishop through circumstantial indications, he bore it grievously, pitying rather their foolish and empty notions. Having learned and repeatedly pondered these things, he watched daily, considering whether the memory of his most honourable upbringing of them and of the benefits they had received might easily recall them to amendment and correction. But because diabolical cunning does not cease to flatter a person in persuasion, their pride, alas, grew more frequent and more manifest.

It happened, therefore, that the archbishop went to Carrión to discuss with the king certain matters that had arisen for him. There he instructed Bernald in counsel that he should without delay surrender the chancellorship which he had given him to hold for his fidelity and service; and that, returning to the Church of St James, which had nurtured and honoured him, he should strive faithfully to serve Almighty God and the aforesaid apostle with the other persons of that Church. In this way the archbishop desired that the hidden things of Bernald’s heart and the obligations of his fidelity should [Col. 1208B] be fully revealed.

Bernald, conscious of his evil intent and being the contriver of so great a deceit, received this most sorrowfully. He asked the archbishop for time to take counsel about what he should do, openly showing already what the subsequent outcome proved to be true. During the three days’ delay, he urgently begged his acquaintances and friends, through their counsel and assistance, to obtain from the king permission that he might retain, against the archbishop’s will, both the chancellorship and everything the archbishop had given him, offering thanks to God and the king alone.

At their intervention the king gave some assent, and immediately sent two envoys to the archbishop, namely Albertinus and Fernando Joanniz, to ask him on the king’s behalf not to remove the chancellorship from Bernald, but thereafter to love him as he had loved him the more. The archbishop, however, whose knowledge was prudent, now plainly and openly discerned Bernald’s deceitful machinations. He is said to have given them this answer: if it pleased the royal dignity, the king should take back the chancellorship which he had entrusted to Bernald; afterward he should dispose of it, according to his own counsel and will, as seemed fitting and honourable.

The king, seeing that the archbishop followed the path of constancy and reason, promised to come to him that same day at the cloister of St Zoilus and to bring Bernald to make satisfaction and to enter the archbishop’s favour and service. On the appointed day, the king came to the archbishop as he had said, gloriously attended by his counts and princes. [Col. 1208D] Courteously and respectfully, he called upon him to explain the matter, earnestly wishing to know how the seedbed of discord that seemed to exist between the archbishop and Bernald had arisen. For, when he considered in order what the archbishop had shown Bernald from his very childhood, and what he had endured for love of him, he wondered greatly how such a disagreement had unexpectedly come between them.

The archbishop, wishing to set forth in sequence the course of events by which the aforesaid dispute had arisen, showed the king that certain things had been reported to him about Bernald which were not fit to be heard, much less believed. Wishing to test these matters gently and without scandal, and to bring Bernald back from error to the way of salvation and amendment, he had judged that no method of testing and correction could be more useful or less offensive than that Bernald, having surrendered the chancellorship into his hand, should return to the Church and serve God and His glorious apostle there in a devout spirit.

When the king recognized that the archbishop had spoken so justly and reasonably, he took Bernald aside and, as the king afterward confessed, is reported to have addressed him in these words:

> “No corner of Spain is ignorant how great was the bond of affection with which the archbishop embraced you, how lovingly he reared you long ago, what he has shown toward you, and what he has endured for you until now. Therefore it is just and fitting that you should always obey him humbly and never, on any pretext, wish to withdraw your heart from his service and fidelity. Come then: recalling these things, return wholly to obedience; present yourself, wherever you can, humble and obedient, to carry out his service and will. For what I have freely bestowed upon so great and honourable a man, I cannot take away without cause, nor can I in any way support you against him.”

Bernald, recognizing that he had been reasonably defeated on every side and that the matter he had been turning over in his heart had turned out very differently from what he had expected, returned with the king, greatly saddened, to the council from which he had come. In the presence of the king, his counts and barons, and fifteen canons of the Church of St James who were present, he immediately invested his lord, the archbishop of Compostela, with the right to that dignity, namely the chancellorship. The archbishop, thus justly and honourably invested, after consulting his brethren, entrusted that prerogative—the chancellorship—to Bernald for a time, and so ended the various turns of that dispute as he wished.

### On the same matter.

Thus, having gained victory over his enemies and the king’s favour, Lord Diego, archbishop of Compostela, returned most honourably to his own place, with Bernald and many other persons of his Church returning cheerfully and gladly with him. Meanwhile, as the king had already determined by the counsel of his barons, he set out in imperial fashion on an expedition against the Saracens, with a great and innumerable company of princes, knights, and foot soldiers.

As he afterward recalled one by one the acts Bernald had committed against his lord, and as certain enemies of Bernald suggested it, the king considered it just and highly advantageous that Bernald should be seized: partly because he had grievously erred and acted proudly against his lord, so that he might learn the price of his error and pride; partly in order that he might be wholly stripped of everything he appeared to possess. Desiring this to be carried out as quickly as possible, the king immediately sent ahead to the archbishop one of his princes and officers, Fernando Joanniz, ordering him to have Bernald seized without delay and all his money brought before the king—but first, for the Church’s part, to have the castle of Honesto and all [Col. 1210A] the honours of St James that Bernald held, with their full appurtenances, placed in the lord archbishop’s hand.

The king further added that, if anything contrary or harmful should ever happen to the archbishop as a result, he himself would bear the consequences and would always be the author and guarantor of the act he commanded, fearing that, once this pretext had been found, the archbishop might refuse to do what he had ordered. When this was presented to the archbishop, he took it badly and entirely denied that he would do it.

The king, seeing that what he had ordered had not been carried out in any respect, sent three further messengers to the archbishop in succession, each repeating and affirming more forcefully and effectively what the first had said. Although the archbishop heard them and their report made the king’s order and will plainly known to him, he nevertheless appeared to have done nothing to Bernald beyond what he had done in response to the first envoy.

Finally, not long afterward, when the king saw that his command had by no means been carried out, he was moved to great anger and sent back to the archbishop a fifth envoy, not long after those he had sent before. This time he was not merely ordering but terrifyingly threatening the following: unless the archbishop placed Bernald under arrest and in custody in the manner in which he had now informed him five times through his messengers, he himself would pay from his own resources every penny of Bernald’s wealth, down to the last farthing, and perhaps would not escape something worse.

When the archbishop recognized that great and irremediable danger and loss threatened him and his Church unless he immediately carried out the royal will, he at last, sorrowful and most unwilling, had Bernald seized, together with his kinsman the dean, and caused them, once seized, to be guarded honourably and respectfully. It should be noted, however, that the dean was captured for no other reason—although he had often acted covertly and in some matters openly against his lord—than because the city, which was somewhat disturbed, might at that time be more seriously disturbed through his counsel and contrivance and stirred violently against the lord archbishop. Once the archbishop discovered that no uprising of the citizens against him had arisen because of their seizure, he immediately released the dean and restored him honourably and fully to all his possessions.

### Again, on the same matter.

[Col. 1210D]

Meanwhile, after not many days had passed, Lord Guido, cardinal and legate of the Roman See, happened to come to Compostela. With great indignation he called the archbishop to account, wishing to know why he had allowed so wicked and dangerous a kind of offence to be committed, especially since he ought to have been a pattern and example to others.
