The archbishop, being innocent of this offence, replied freely that the act for which the cardinal reproached him had been done not by his own counsel or prompting but by that of the king, as has been stated above; and he affirmed before all, in the cardinal’s presence, that it could be remedied by no one but the king. After the words of the two sides had been exchanged, [Col. 1211A] the cardinal promised that he would go to the king and do what he could with him to secure Bernald’s release.

When he had spoken with the king and earnestly asked him, with many prayers, to order Bernald released, the king, greatly angered, ordered Bernald immediately to be delivered into the hands of Munio, bishop of Valibre, and faithfully guarded. He declared that Bernald would never be released by the archbishop, by the cardinal, or by anyone else, but only by himself. For he considered it shameful and dishonourable that Bernald should be released at another’s request and entreaties, rather than solely through the king’s own favour, since he had ordered Bernald’s seizure.

After the king’s order and will had been carried out as he directed, a council was held not long afterward at León by the aforesaid cardinal. There it was decreed that the lord archbishop should restore to Bernald everything he had lost in the seizure and, once so restored, should judge him justly and canonically in his own church as his canon and cleric. Once this had been pronounced and approved as a judgment, the archbishop carried it out completely. Although the king had cleverly and ingeniously kept all Bernald’s money that had been taken from him, the archbishop nevertheless, like a pious and merciful father, reconciled Bernald to himself and faithfully and without reproach fully restored him in all those things in which, according to the command of the cardinal and his council, he ought to have been reinstated.

When this affair had thus been concluded, every variation of controversy, every discord, and every contention that had existed between them, as stated above, was so calmed and put to rest that Bernald himself acknowledged and declared that after God he had no father or lord but Lord Diego, archbishop of Compostela, remembering all the benefits that the archbishop had bestowed upon him from childhood.

## CHAPTER XL. Charter of counter-exchange.

> “I, Count Ferdinand, son of the lord Count Pedro Froilaz and Lady Urraca Froilaz [Note: [Col. 1211D] First wife of Count Pedro de Trava], together with all who have a claim through me, make to you, Lord Diego, archbishop of the see of Compostela, and to the clerics and canons of the same church, this deed of exchange and instrument of confirmation and transfer: of my share in the church of St Mary of Transmonte, and likewise of another share in St Pelagius of Lene(s), of which you already possess [Col. 1211D] another share from my sister Enxemena Pérez, who gave it to the blessed Apostle James for the salvation of her soul.
>
> “That is to say, our aforesaid eighth share, with all its appurtenances, wherever you may be able to find them within all their ancient boundaries, and with all the dependent holdings in Transmonte, Amaea, Valeyrón, the land of Noia, Navaria, Pistomarcos, and from St James as far as the sea—which I hold by succession from my mother Lady Urraca, from my grandfather Count Froyla Arias, and from my great-grandfather Arias Tedóniz; and which I divided with my siblings Vermudo Pérez and Countess Lady Lupa, and with my nephew Sancho Sánchez, who received their shares and divisions [Col. 1212A] in other lands, while I alone received this entire portion. And now, before the whole council and in their presence, I exchange and transfer it to you in its entirety for your own estate and inheritance called St Eulalia of Lubre, and St Tyrsius, and St Marina, and St Peter of Cerverales, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, except for fifty villager households, of both sexes, whom I retain for myself in order to populate my estate of Savardes.
>
> “From this present day onward, may you and all your successors forever have and possess these things, and do with all that I give you whatever you wish. But if anyone—which I least believe will occur—should come, or if I should come, to violate this deed of exchange and instrument of transfer, whoever he may be, let him, or let me, pay to you, Lord Archbishop Diego, and to the clerics and canons of the same Church, or to those representing you, that same inheritance and its dependent holdings doubled or tripled; and let him be excommunicated and accursed, and pay to you or to those representing you ten talents of gold. And may this my act always remain firm.
>
> “The charter of exchange was made on the third Nones of October, in the era 1172. I, Count Ferdinand, confirm by my own authority what I freely give, transfer, and exchange. Count Lord Munio Peláez confirms. Countess Lady Lupa Pérez confirms. Vermudo Pérez confirms. Sancho Sánchez confirms. Urraca Pérez confirms. Countess Lady Geloira Pérez confirms. Ilduara Pérez confirms. Lord Suario, abbot of Cinis, confirms. Lord Martin, abbot of Moirame, [Col. 1212C] confirms. Pedro Gutiérrez confirms. John Gutiérrez confirms. Froyla Atánez confirms. Sarraceno Muñoz confirms. Arias Muñoz confirms. Gonzalo Menéndez confirms. Roderic, abbot of the monastery of Antealtares, confirms. Pedro, abbot of the monastery of St Martin, confirms. John, abbot of the monastery of St Peter Outside-the-Walls, confirms. Pedro, abbot of Monsontio, confirms. Vermudo, archdeacon of Vallibria, confirms. Gonzalo, prior of Nemenio, confirms. Aloitus, abbot of Villar Romazi, confirms.”

This is the agreement concerning the deeds and boundary-markers of St Mary of Transmonte.

> “In the era 1172, and [reading uncertain], on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, I, Count Ferdinand Pérez, with my sons and daughters and all who have a claim through me, make to you, Lord Diego, by God’s grace archbishop of St James, and to the clerics of the same church [Col. 1212D] or to those representing you, a most binding pact and agreement concerning the deeds and boundary-markers of St Mary of Transmonte and St Pelagius of Lene(s), and likewise concerning our dependent holdings there in Transmonte, Amaea, Valeyrón, St Christina of Noia, Pistomarcos, and from St James as far as the sea. These came to me in the division and partition among my brothers and sisters, and I transferred and exchanged them with you for the inheritance, churches, and dependent holdings of Lubre, except for one villager whom I reserve for myself in order to populate my estate of Savardes.
>
> “Accordingly, we give you the deeds which we possess, and I make this agreement further: if I can find more, [Col. 1213A] I shall faithfully give it to you; and if I cannot find it, but at some time such deeds are found, they shall either be given to you or be held invalid against you and remain without force. If I should prove false and fail to fulfil this agreement, I shall pay to you or to those representing you double whatever I place in dispute, and in addition ten talents of gold. May this document always remain firm.
>
> “I, Count Ferdinand, and all who have a claim through me, confirm this my act. Pedro Gutiérrez confirms. Sancho Sánchez confirms. Count Munio confirms. Countess Lady Lupa Pérez confirms. Vermudo Pérez confirms. Suario, abbot of the monastery of Cinis, confirms.”

### Concerning Pedro Infanzón

At about the same time the lord of Compostela prudently and shrewdly obtained from Pedro Infanzón, then about to leave for Jerusalem, a certain share of the church of St Mary of Transmonte—[Col. 1213B] namely, six whole parts of two fourths—to the honor of God and of his Church. In confirmation of the testamentary donation, he generously and willingly granted him three marks of pure silver, in the era 1172, on the second day before the eighth Kalends of December.

### CHAPTER XLI. On the death of Bernald

After the archbishop of Compostela had been reconciled with Bernald and all the animosities arising from their offences had been ended between them, and after everything belonging to Bernald had been restored to his rightful possession and faithfully made whole, as we mentioned a little above, Bernald at once unhappily entered the regions of Champagne. Swollen, as before, by the breath of pride, [Col. 1213C] he again secretly opposed and attacked the lord of Compostela by every means. Yet everyone without doubt regarded as false and untrue all that Bernald alleged from hatred of the archbishop. When he had come swiftly to Burgos, still troubled at heart against the archbishop, he paid the debt of death in that city itself, by divine judgment—alas!

### CHAPTER XLII. At that time the lord of Compostela sent his messengers to Rome; and they brought back to the lord of Compostela these letters.

> “Innocent, bishop,” etc.
>
> “Because a dutiful son,” etc. See under Innocent II, [Col. 1213D] for the year 1143.

### CHAPTER XLIII. These are the letters of the elect of Salamanca to the lord of Compostela.

> “To his most reverend lord, DIEGO, archbishop of Compostela: BERENGARIUS, archdeacon and chancellor of the emperor, greeting and obedience.
>
> “Let it be known to your fatherhood that I have been honorably received by the clergy and people of Salamanca, and lawfully and canonically elected, in the presence of the archbishop of Toledo and two bishops, namely those of Segovia and Zamora, whom the emperor had sent there with me. It remains, therefore, that I should come to you on an appointed day to be ordained and consecrated; or, should you perhaps approach our regions on some business, please take care to notify me by letter. Farewell.”

These are the letters sent by the clergy and people of the Church of Salamanca to Compostela.

> “To their most reverend lord, DIEGO, archbishop of Compostela: the clergy and people of Salamanca, greeting.
>
> “Lest our recent action escape your prudence, we have judged it right to inform you that we have elected lawfully and canonically Lord Berengarius, archdeacon and chancellor of the emperor, whom the emperor sent to us with the archbishop of Toledo and two bishops, namely those of Segovia and Zamora. We did this because that Peter, not daring to place confidence in his own election, withdrew. At length we recognized him as altogether useless [Col. 1214B] for governing the Church. We had already long been unanimous in Berengarius’s lawful election, and at León we requested him from the emperor, the cardinal, and the archbishop of Toledo; having granted him to us, they entrusted him to us. But what we had then not dared to do through fear of Count Pedro López, we have now accomplished through the mercy of divine goodness.
>
> “We therefore send him to your fatherhood, so that, receiving him kindly, you may ordain and consecrate him. Farewell.”

Letters of the archbishop of Toledo to Compostela.

> “To the reverend—would that he were graciously disposed!—R., primate of the Spains and archbishop of the see of Toledo, together with his fellow bishops P. of Segovia and B. of Zamora, to Lord DIEGO, metropolitan of Compostela: greeting and affection.
>
> “We have thought it right to report to your affection what was done in your Church of Salamanca [Col. 1214C] in our presence and under our witness: how, after its so long and pitiable widowhood, the Dayspring from on high visited it. You ought especially to rejoice at so necessary a benefit to your special suffragan. Know, therefore, that no interpretation of words can sufficiently convey to you the depth of calamity and the grievous oppression under which we found that Church of yours when, delegated by the emperor—who, having heard of the many and great misfortunes of that Church, sent us to the city with the elect Berengarius—we arrived there.
>
> “The Salamancans themselves had elected him in the city of León through their elected envoys, namely the archdeacon, the prior, and the schoolmaster, with the consent of the emperor [Col. 1214D] and the approval of G. [Guido], the Roman legate. Having received him from me, whose archdeacon he was, we brought the elect to the city. The aforesaid electors received him honorably, and the whole council of Salamanca escorted him with the Ambrosian hymn to the altar. The only exceptions were a certain utterly simple man—of such a kind as we do not now seek to explain to you—and a very few of his accomplices, who had enthroned him under the shadow and semblance of a usurping and sacrilegious election, in order under that pretext to possess the goods and patrimony of the Church.
>
> “But, thanks be to God, the larger and sounder number prevailed—indeed, we should not say ‘part,’ for had you been present, as we greatly wished, you would have seen the whole city agreeing in its entirety. Furthermore, although we knew that that lay and fictitious election was wholly a shadow and falsehood, nevertheless, to satisfy the lay intruders and the utterly simple intruder, we offered him judgment in your court or in the Roman court. Although at the first meeting he had replied that he would appear for a hearing—he who had concealed himself for a year and more—yet in the end he wholly failed to appear. When clergy and citizens saw this, they rejected him and received the man whom they had elected.
>
> “Therefore, since we have fully learned the entire matter, we advise your affection to receive this man and, as necessity requires of us, to ordain and consecrate him. Farewell. We sealed this letter with the seal of Zamora, because we did not have our own there.”

Letter of the emperor addressed to the archbishop.

[Col. 1215B]

> “A., by God’s grace emperor of the Spains, to the venerable Father Lord DIEGO, archbishop of Compostela: may you be so occupied with Martha that Mary may be free for prayer.
>
> “You have very often heard both of the long oppression of the Church of Salamanca and of its calamitous deprivation of its own shepherd; and it is certain that this has happened through the negligence of none but you and me. For at the council of León, the more distinguished members of the clergy and people of Salamanca, with the agreement of the others, earnestly requested from me, the cardinal, and the archbishop of Toledo, Lord Berengarius the archdeacon as ruler of their Church; and we willingly granted him to them.
>
> “But because the matter did not then take full effect, Count P. López preventing it, at last, unable any longer to endure the pitiable cry of that Church which my father had built, I sent the aforesaid Berengarius—my familiar, as you know, and my chancellor—to Salamanca: an honorable and prudent man, and one whom, as could be inferred from his character, I found useful for restoring and governing the Church. [Col. 1215C] I send him to your discretion, having been lawfully and canonically elected by the Salamancans, to be ordained and consecrated. Consider, therefore, who he is and from whom he is sent; receive him kindly and honorably, and send him back more honorably, for you should not rejoice only a little that he remains in your college.”

These are the names of the bishops who subscribed and were then present with Lord Archbishop Diego at his consecration in the church of Blessed James: G. of Lugo, P. of Tui, Eneco of Ávila, B. of Zamora.

This is the oath which he made upon the altar of St James.

> “I, Berengarius, bishop-elect to be ordained of the holy Church of Salamanca, promise that I shall forever show submission, reverence, and obedience, established by the most holy Fathers according to the prescriptions of the canons, to the rulers of the Church of St James and to that Church itself, in the presence of Lord Archbishop D.; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar.”

### CHAPTER XLIV. On the altar-panel made behind the altar

[Col. 1216A]

Desiring with the utmost zeal to increase and adorn the honor of his Church, both in prosperity and adversity, the lord of Compostela at that time wonderfully began, and still more wonderfully completed, a certain panel behind the altar of St James. It was precious and most excellently wrought in ancient style, its workmanship surpassing its material; just as he had previously bestowed other ornaments upon the same Church.

### CHAPTER XLV. Letter sent from Rome to the archbishop of Compostela [Note: [Col. 1215D] 27 December 1135.]

> “Innocent, bishop, etc.
>
> “Let your affection know,” etc. See under Innocent II, [Col. 1216B] for the year 1143.

Letter of a cardinal sent from Rome to the archbishop of Compostela.

> “G. [GUIDO], cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and friend DIEGO of Compostela, greeting.
>
> “How often and how devotedly P. Fulco, chaplain of the Church of St James, has labored as a good and useful son in your service is plainly known to us, and you have been able more fully to experience through the evidence of his work. Since reason therefore requires that one who renders welcome service to another should receive from him a fitting benefit, we ask your affection that the same P., because—[the remainder is lacking].”

### CHAPTER XLVI. On the conspiracy made

Among the other harms and adversities which the Church of Compostela endured in its shepherds continually serving God, Archbishop D., of venerable memory, adorned with good character and likewise distinguished by learning, suffered very many—especially from the thirtieth year of his archiepiscopate onward, when he offered all his members to God as weapons of righteousness. Hence a certain philosopher says: “Those who try to live unlike the pursuits of wicked men can scarcely be peaceful and happy in the world.”

This man adorned and instructed his Church so successfully that, as the moon is brighter than the stars, so by God’s grace he most gloriously exalted it above every Church on earth in pilgrimage, except the Roman Church, its mistress, [Col. 1216D] and other churches like it. Likewise, finding the canons without good discipline and lacking every seasoning of wisdom, he watered their uncultivated minds with the rain of teaching; and divine mercy made some who obeyed him conspicuous in learning and conduct.

He committed these harms and adversities inflicted upon the aforesaid archbishop to memory and writing so that, since they might perish from frail memory, they might be preserved by enduring letters, and that his successors might carefully beware; for, according to Gregory [Note: [Col. 1215] St Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 35, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI], “weapons that have been foreseen strike less severely.”

[Col. 1217A] It is beyond doubt—indeed, it has been made known to many—that certain canons, deceived by a zeal like that of the patriarchs against their brother, plotted, as though against Christ, to depose the aforesaid outstanding archbishop, their lord and spiritual father, without any reason requiring it. These were not just any canons, but especially those whom the Father of venerable memory had adopted as sons and had advanced so far in honors and dignities that none of their order in Spain equalled them in temporal prosperity.

Concerning them it was without doubt believed that no changeability of human circumstance, no duration of time, however prolonged, could cause the memory of his kindness to fade from them. But as one diseased sheep contaminates the flock, so by wicked and abominable counsels they almost corrupt the fellowship of the lesser canons. Since they could not accomplish what they deceitfully turned over under their tongues, they enticed with flattering and fraudulent words a great part of the citizens, and, in the manner of sirens, “against the Lord and against his Christ,” according to the custom of Jews and Gentiles, “they assembled together” (Psalm 2:2), so that what the greater men had devised in counsel the citizens might bring to completion in deed.

And as, in the betrayal of Christ Jesus, priests and Jews first took counsel, and then the Gentiles carried the counsel into effect—because the Pharisees crucified the Lord with the sword of the tongue at the third hour, and the Gentiles by deed at the sixth—so these greater men first acted through gifts and counsel, and the citizens performed the deed. The event itself later proved this, [Col. 1217C] as shall be related in order below.

Then, overturning ancient rights and proper institutions and imposing self-made laws upon the city, they warned a certain municipal steward not to receive what was his and had been granted by lawful judgment unless they had decreed it by common counsel. Every Friday, going armed to the church anciently called the “augmentation of puldrorum” [Note: [Col. 1217D] See col. 909, note 40], with various kinds of weapons, they regarded the guilty as innocent and spared them, while pressing down the necks of the innocent.

They did this because they were bound together by such an oath that they would not only have made the steward undergo a capital sentence, but would also have unanimously stoned their reverend lord and Father, according to the conspiracy made against him. After this, in the square of the palace, they forced him—though unwilling and resisting in every way—to swear that he would not break their decrees and self-made laws, but would keep them in force at their appointed time. The condition was added that, if the citizens forcibly retained rights and all things belonging to him, then, after the archbishop had summoned them two or three times in council, unless they made amends, they would incur perjury and bodily punishment, and his steward would exact without further summons everything due to him. Conversely, if the supreme pontiff did not keep the written oath and retained what belonged to them, he too would not escape the bonds of perjury.

The supreme pontiff, however, kept the oath in every respect and remained free from perjury. They, on the other hand, became bound in the chains of perjury, because not long afterward they retained their rights and dues as before, broke the sworn oath they had given, and thus, as their deserts required, justly fell into worse things. As Scripture says: “Let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22). The most merciful Father, as befits a good shepherd intent upon the gain of souls, summoned them ten and twenty times in council and called them to account, that they might remember so great an oath and not deny him what was his, as they had sworn. Yet they not only retained what was his, but, by breaking the oath, sinned most grievously. What more is there to say? He bore the title of archbishop, but was deprived of its honor.

[Col. 1218B] Having done this, they swiftly went to the emperor, held a secret conference with him, and—horrible even to contemplate, let alone to recount as an act!—fraudulently promised the emperor immense gifts, namely three thousand marks of silver, so that this most illustrious father and staff of many needy persons might lose his office and be banished into perpetual exile.

Hearing this, the emperor, inflamed by the great quantity of gold and silver, summoned the nobles and counts of his court and long deliberated anxiously about his removal and deprivation of honor: by what means, in what manner, and with what help he might expel him. Then the counts and bishops present advised the emperor to send without delay, removing every pretext, for Cardinal Guido, legate of the Roman Church, whom he already knew well and who had visited [Col. 1218C] Spain less than two years earlier [Note: [Col. 1217D] Namely in 1134, as is clear from chapter 39, no. 5], and who had no wish to come into the regions of Spain for ten years.

When this had been done, the cardinal came at the emperor’s command, Apostolic authority having urged it, and visited the western Church. The emperor honorably received him at his court and diligently discussed with the members of that court the stripping of the archbishop’s honor and his fraudulent deposition; day and night he held prolonged counsel with the cardinal.

The cardinal, considering within himself that this affair could not be done lawfully unless the Apostolic See commanded it and the leading members of the Roman curia supported it, said that he would not dare lay hands on a person so eminent and honorable, since he had as yet found no cause worthy of deposition; and, even if he acted rashly, nothing had been entrusted to him without the pope’s knowledge.

The emperor heard this with displeasure and, after consulting with the cardinal, resolved to send to Rome a certain eloquent cleric of his, named Boso, known to the pope and his household, to seek the pope’s counsel concerning this affair. Though vexed by this, the emperor accepted his words and approved the arrangement proposed by the cardinal.

Meanwhile the emperor told the cardinal to travel through all the churches of Spain until Boso returned from Rome, and to admonish the shepherds charged with the governance of souls to attend [Col. 1219A] a council. The cardinal agreed to this proposal and began to visit bishoprics and archbishoprics as well as abbeys. Thereafter he entered Compostela with great pomp and a long train of attendants. He remained there for fifteen days, and the archbishop, worthy of most serene memory, humbly and with great reverence provided for him with innumerable banquets and royal dishes.

But certain canons, filled with most foul thoughts and stricken by devouring envy, whispered continually to the cardinal, by day and by night, about the archbishop, so that they scarcely allowed the legate of the Roman Church to take food. All the archbishop’s friends wondered what those great and prolonged deliberations portended.

### CHAPTER XLVII. On the violation of the church

[Col. 1219B]

Meanwhile, after the cardinal had departed, certain laymen were incited by the counsel of certain canons—whom, among the other canons, the archbishop had adorned with dignities and honors, as was said above, and regarded as most beloved sons, and who had long contemplated a conspiracy against the archbishop. Since they could no longer conceal the pestilential design that had arisen from the aforesaid canons, the abominable design which they had devised with great treachery, they brought it forth in abominable deeds. They left a wicked example to posterity and successors; they came into God’s inheritance, namely into the church of Blessed James; and, as David says, by violating the temple of God, [Col. 1219C] they defiled it (Psalm 78:1). Those who ought to have been the watchmen and defenders of the church became its destroyers and invaders.

For one day, while the aforesaid Father, burdened by illness and old age, was resting in bed after dinner, on the fourth day before the Ides of August, in the era 1174 [Note: [Col. 1219D] The manuscripts have era 1175, year 1137. But the preceding and following era-dates support 1174, year 1136; for the council called in that year by the cardinal (preceding chapter) was held in that same year. [Col. 1220D] It is discussed immediately afterward in chapter 49. The same follows from the consecration of the bishop of Zaragoza at that council, in 1136], William Siginiz, the chief instigator of this betrayal, thought that while he slept he could more freely suffocate him unawares, together with the other villains, and that no one would be in the city to resist the conspiracy.

Having gathered together a savage band of feasters, gluttons, and drunkards, and a great part of the citizens, he came armed through the middle of the city with all the others, carrying javelins, clubs, swords, and countless weapons. He burst into the church with threats, [Col. 1219D] terrifying by tongue and hand. Some of the canons, not knowing why they had come armed or what they were bent on doing, were alarmed by the uproar of their arrival and the assault of the armed men, and questioned some of them. They answered that they had assembled to storm the archbishop’s court by force, stone him while he slept and did not know of his own destruction, put to the sword all who supported him, and raze the houses of his supporters to their foundations.

[Col. 1220A] Then someone came suddenly, awakened him from sleep, and told him that his body was to be torn apart and cut with swords unless he escaped. But he, aware that he had never harmed those executioners thirsting for his blood and had benefited them in every way, not only refused to believe the messenger but rebuked him in words. Again another came breathlessly and reported a message like the first. At this, he promptly returned and ordered the door to be shut behind him.

As he was returning, the aforesaid William, that utterly wicked contriver of great deceit, encountered him beyond the gate, disgracefully seized him by the hair, and struck with a sword the head of the ordained cleric. Wounded and battered, he scarcely managed to escape from the hands of those striking him and flee to the altar of St James.

Then they came to the door of the palace with axes, adzes, swords, and every kind of weapon. They thrust and battered the door so fiercely that their sweat began to run like a river, yet they could never gain entry. They raged and gnashed their teeth against the venerable Father no differently than lions which, having endured a long hunger, are shut in caves and bound with iron chains, roar at the sight of animals and desire to fill their jaws with their flesh.

But when they could not enter through the lower door of the palace, they went up through the church of St James, broke the upper palace doors with double-headed axes and swords, and descended into the upper rooms. The floors resounded under the weight and multitude of the armed men with such a terrible noise as that of lightning and the greatest thunders of heaven.

[Col. 1220C] Then a certain venerable canon, sent by heavenly mercy, warned the archbishop to flee or take refuge at the altar of the Apostle St James, otherwise he would suffer the fiercest fate at the hands of executioners and drunkards that very day. Hearing this, he quickly rose; hearing the sound of feet walking above him, he believed the aforesaid canon and the others who were bringing similar reports. As he had been lying in bed, covered only with that canon’s cloak and supported by the hands of two canons, he unwillingly began to depart.

But those dishonorable men, made members and food of the devil, saw the archbishop leaving and fleeing through the square. All those standing above on the floors [Col. 1220D] unanimously hurled stones at him and pursued the venerable old man as far as the entrance to the altar of St James with a dense shower of stones and multitude of rocks. Stones and rocks flew after the glorious chief pastor from the hands of the criminals with such cruelty and savage ferocity that, striking and breaking the stones of the choir of St James, they reduced them to sand. One of those wicked men struck the holy Father on the shoulders; from the force of that blow he fell pitifully from the hands of the canons carrying him.

Lamenting, they quickly lifted him and carried the archbishop to the venerable altar of St James, where the apostle’s body lies buried, glorious and wondrous throughout the world. Placing him beneath the altar canopy, they firmly shut the altar doors, and there, besieged and enclosed, he was afraid. Nevertheless, he wisely placed confidence in God’s mercy, because he had not forgotten Augustine’s saying, which he had stored in the treasury of his heart: “Whatever is inflicted on the righteous by the wicked is not punishment for sin but a test of virtue; for the good person is free even though he serves, and the evil person is a slave even though he sometimes fulfils his own will” [Note: [Col. 1221D] St Augustine, *Appendix to the Sentences*, part III, 53, p. 1863, *Patrologia*, vol. XLV].

#### On the plundering of the vestments

While this was taking place, some of the traitors went down into the archbishop’s chamber and plundered his vestments and those of the canons living with him. The rest [Col. 1221B] went on to stone the archbishop beneath the altar of St James. Having quickly carried out this deed, clapping their hands and rejoicing in heart, they reached the altar gate. But after all had assembled with their weapons before the iron doors of the altar, and found the doors bolted and firmly barred with beams, they could not enter the altar at all.

Raging and gnashing their teeth, they climbed onto the fabric of the church itself, so that the man whom they could not kill from below they might hurl to his death by casting stones from above. While he remained besieged beneath the altar, certain burgesses, feigning concord and pretending to regret their treachery, asked the most merciful Father—after sending honorable canons who were with him facing death—to come to the gate [Col. 1221C] and hold discussion with them concerning the restoration of peace and the calming of so great a war.

Then, at the intervention and with the consent of good men grieving over his impending death, the archbishop came to the gate and conferred with them. In gentle and honeyed words he begged them by any means to restrain the assaults and anger of the traitors and firmly obtain an agreement of peace. But while the archbishop was humbly addressing them, some of the wicked men deceitfully tried to kill him with daggers and missiles through the iron altar doors. Foreseeing this, the archbishop promptly withdrew and wished to hide beneath the altar.

When the wicked men standing above on the structure saw him return, they cast stones after him and struck the venerable old man’s ear. After this happened, he sought refuge at the altar and hid himself between the altar cloths and the altar-table itself, lamenting, weeping, and uttering bitter sobs. When he had hidden himself, they hurled showers of stones from every side upon the archbishop, the altar, and its surroundings; and they broke part of the canopy of the venerable apostle, of the altar-table itself, and of the altar vestments.

In winter, when the west wind blows and the north wind accompanies it, drops of water do not pour down more thickly or densely than stones were poured upon the altar, the supreme pontiff, and the canopy. Those who were with the archbishop had nowhere to hide and nowhere to avoid the cast and downward fall of the stones; therefore they exposed their bodies to blows and strikes, concealing only their heads.

[Col. 1222A] The most devout Father could never find rest around the altar; everywhere death from stones and rocks was present. If I wished to disclose all the multitude and magnitude of the things that William, that wicked traitor, and the multitude of perverse men did against the archbishop, God is my witness that the account would be longer than the text of the Psalms and Acts of the Apostles.

What else can I say? God’s mercy alone, favorable to all, protected him through certain canons grieved by the treachery and rescued him from the hands of his enemies; so too did the intercession of the glorious apostle, whose Church he had loved from the beginning of his life and fittingly adorned in many ways.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. On the escape from the church, when the archbishop escaped from the church

[Col. 1222B]

Meanwhile a great part of the citizens, and also of the canons who had not assented to the counsel and actions of the profane men, entered the church; and together with the married women and widows they unanimously wept most bitterly over the persecution of their distinguished shepherd. Kneeling, weeping, and striking their breasts harshly, they begged God that their gentle pastor, the marvelous comforter of orphans and widows, might be rescued from the hands of those rising against him and preserved unharmed from so great an assault.

When this had been done, casting off fear, they exposed themselves to the battle and to the attack of stones flying down around the altar of St. James. Lamenting, they said to his blood-thirsty executioners [Col. 1222C] that this impiety would recoil upon them and that divine providence would exact upon their offspring vengeance both bodily and spiritual. For the Lord had said through the prophet: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20:5).

Then, compelled by the lamentation and grief of the canons and citizens mourning their father’s death, and by the women drawing long sighs from the depths of their hearts, the attackers, though unwilling and exhausted, ceased throwing stones. Descending from the work of St. James, and hearing sobbing and cries from all parts of the church, they left the church. Wearied from persecuting the venerable old man, they returned to their homes from the victory of their great war, grieving because they had left him half-alive rather than slain [Col. 1222D] and cut into pieces, as they had deceitfully planned among themselves; yet rejoicing and exulting because, with no one resisting, they had gained the victory and had nearly fulfilled their desires by sinning with impunity in the present—a condition which the saints judge to be especially the wrath of God, as Augustine testifies: “Nothing is more unhappy than the prosperity of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and evil will is strengthened as though it were an enemy.” [Note: [Col. 1222D] St Augustine, *Sentences*, appendix, part III, 42, p. 1862, *Patrologia*, vol. XLV.]

But after the executioners, gnashing their teeth, had withdrawn from the house of God, the aforesaid citizens and their devout wives, together with a certain part of the canons, immediately opened the iron gates of the altar. They bore the archbishop [Col. 1223A] honorably into his court and, magnifying God, praised him who had preserved their guardian from death and had not allowed him to expire amid the multitude of stone-throwers.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the council held at Burgos

In that court he rested a short while after the persecution, since the time of the general council was drawing near. When it arrived, accompanied by a body of canons and taking with him all the chief persons of his Church, he set out—more honorably than the other bishops of Spain—for the appointed council to be held at Burgos, though sick and having been stoned by wicked men at the altar of the most holy apostle. His purpose was to report to the emperor the insults most shamefully inflicted on him, and that the legate [Col. 1223B] of the Holy Roman Church, together with the other bishops, might excommunicate these criminals.

On the first day of the council, one of the canons arose, signaled silence with his hand, and tearfully made a public accusation against William and the other executioners, stone-throwers in the church of the holy apostle. They had stoned the venerable old archbishop, the staff of the clergy and sustainer of very many poor people, around the body and altar of the glorious apostle; they had wounded certain canons; and they had broken the altar-table together with part of the ciborium.

After the accusation had been made, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, clergy, and all the counts with the knights present at the council were deeply grieved at so great a crime inflicted upon so great a person. Without delay they quickly rose before the emperor [Col. 1223C] and, together with the legate of the Roman Church, excommunicated not only William, the originator of this wickedness, and the crowd of evildoers, but also anyone who should defend them by perverse arguments, eat with them, associate with them, or aid them in counsel or in any other manner—unless they assisted toward satisfaction for their sins. Moreover, they established among themselves an edict that was in no way to be broken: even if the offenders should at some time wish to repent, unless death intervened first, they should never presume to receive them to satisfaction; rather, they should seek a hearing before Rome, with letters from the archbishop of Compostela, concerning so great a crime.

After they had pronounced the prohibition with uplifted hands, while the others answered “Amen,” they most shamefully expelled William, that utterly wicked deceiver, and his followers from the council, driving and excommunicating them. They earnestly commanded the emperor not to decline in any way to do what was his duty: namely, to inflict bodily punishment, and not to hear with a deaf ear Augustine’s saying: “What priests are unable to correct by the rigor of words, the powerful should accomplish by the severity of punishments.”

The aforesaid William, endowed with diabolical cunning, had attended the council with a certain faction of sacrilegious men constantly clinging to his side. When he saw himself excommunicated, the people favoring him, and all the others shamefully expelled together with him, he did not repent of what he had done; rather, deprived of standing, he sinned more grievously. Of such men [Col. 1224A] Solomon says: “When the wicked man comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). Thus, after his excommunication, he began to promise greater things and to adhere more zealously to his purpose of treachery.

On the following day all attended the council according to custom, and they pronounced a similar, indeed a harsher, excommunication against William and the others. On that same day, when the council had ended, behold: a certain bishop and the prior of Cluny, abundantly endowed with the brilliance of learning, adorned with good character, and persons of distinction, arrived. Without the archbishop’s knowledge, they secretly handed to the Roman cardinal certain letters sent by the abbot of Cluny, instructing him to treat the archbishop of Compostela most honorably on account of the shepherd of the Cluniac monastery and his community [Col. 1224B]—the archbishop having long since been received into their fellowship through prayers and benefactions—and to show him, among others, great reverence with humility out of love and affection for them; otherwise, he should make a complaint about him to the pope if he did not show the customary goodwill and service. Then, entirely without the archbishop’s knowledge, they delivered to the emperor other letters containing similar matter.

After the emperor and cardinal had read the letters addressed to them, deeply troubled in heart and moved by great anger, the aforesaid Boso arrived, having long before been sent by the cardinal and emperor with letters bearing the pope’s seal, directing that the archbishop be humbly regarded as the apostolic representative, that everything in the council be arranged according to [Col. 1224C] his counsel, and that, setting aside all pretense, he be assisted with counsel and aid. Having read these, the emperor and cardinal were most violently indignant and disturbed in mind, because their schemes, prolonged through many days and nights, were being frustrated to no avail and they would never obtain the immense sum promised by the traitors.

When these matters had been completed, the emperor sent certain of his household retainers to the archbishop, his godfather. Sent thus, they had a private conversation with him on the emperor’s behalf and said that innumerable insults against him and the cardinal had been reported by the traitors. On hearing this, the archbishop rose and said that he would speak with the emperor face to face, through no intermediary. When he came, the emperor rose and received him honorably. Dismissing everyone else, he related in order everything that had been said about him and told him that they had promised him three thousand marks of silver if he would depose him from his office and banish him into perpetual exile. But he himself had refused to do so, because the archbishop had bestowed many benefits upon him, regenerated him at the font of baptism, armed him before the body of the most holy apostle, and finally subjected all Spain to his rule. Yet, because very great wars and armies were threatening daily, which he could not carry through without an abundant treasury of money, since he lacked the means to satisfy the soldiers, he affectionately begged the archbishop to help him with an annual [Col. 1225A] subsidy by whatever means possible.

Then the archbishop promised four hundred marks of silver, in order that the inheritances granted to St. James by his forefathers might be confirmed by documentary privileges, and that the emperor might not lose his honor—which was rather a burden—but protect Spain in tranquillity and peace. After this, now secure and reconciled with the emperor, and made one heart and soul with him, he went to his lodging.

### On the pardon granted by the archbishop

On the following day, accompanied by his canons and with the traitors following behind him, he arrived for the final day of the council. When bishops with clergy and counts with knights saw these traitors following the archbishop, they began to cry out:

> “Behold wolves following the lamb; behold Pharisees crucifying Christ; behold excommunicated heretical traitors of the Church promising gifts against their own father.”

At this they were stunned; their tongues clove to their throats, and bloodless and utterly discomfited they went to the council. The gracious Father reproved those shouting and assailing the traitors on every side, and humbly begged them not to bark at them, because, if they had sinned, they could be amended and corrected.

But when the treacherous canons saw themselves shamefully disgraced and deceived in their schemes, they ran swiftly, once the council was ended, to the emperor and cardinal, with whom they had contrived their accursed treachery, so that they might intercede for them with the archbishop and establish peace with him. [Col. 1225C] Then the venerable Father, knowing no reserve of hatred, spared them through the intervention of the cardinal and emperor and made peace with them on the condition that they should no longer disparage him or devise such deeds, horrible as these, against him. If they should attempt it again, he would not forget their former acts, and, deprived of their office, they would undergo the fitting sentence for treachery.

### On the return of the Compostelan

After this the cardinal spoke privately with the archbishop, begging and imploring that he, who was accustomed to extend a hand to all who came to him in need, should not deny help to the cardinal in his need, but should extend to him something from the abundance of his riches, so that by his support the cardinal might return honorably to the Roman [Col. 1225D] court.

Then, for the honor of the Roman Church, so that it might always magnify the see of Compostela, and because he never ceased from the goodness of generosity, the archbishop charitably assisted the cardinal from his own resources with three hundred gold pieces. Thus aided, and made a son through affection and service, the cardinal withdrew from Spain. When all these matters had thus passed, the enemies had been laid low and those who had raised their heel were crushed; and the archbishop returned happily to his see with dignity and honor, with the trampling down of his enemies, and with pomp and magnificent glory.

### On the consecration

While the synod was being held, the canons of the Church of Saragossa, who had been deprived of their shepherd, stood pleading before the cardinal of the Roman [Col. 1226A] Church together with their elect. They asked him to permit the elect, whom they had canonically chosen among themselves, to receive episcopal orders, and to approach the archbishop of Compostela and devoutly ask him, together with the other archbishops and bishops, to advance the elect to priestly order.

Then the archbishop, moved by the requests of the cardinal and emperor, assented to the petition of the archbishops and bishops. In the council, with honor and reverence, he most honorably consecrated the elect in the see of Burgos, in the presence of bishops and also many clergy, powerful men, and nobles.

It happened indeed that before the general council was held, a certain Pisan, coming to the thresholds of St. James, was returning from pilgrimage. He reported to the pope in order what he had seen with his own [Col. 1226B] eyes at the altar of St. James, what he had heard concerning the persecutors of that altar and the stoners of its shepherd, the conspiracy of certain citizens against the archbishop, and the emperor’s contemplation of the archbishop’s deposition, motivated by the greatness of gold and silver.

The pope, having summoned the cardinals and leading men of the Roman curia, openly set forth all these things in the same order before everyone, not without great contrition and sorrow of heart. When this had been said, the cardinals and other leaders grieved beyond expression, and weeping and drawing sighs, cried out with the pope: “Until now the Roman Church has endured countless adversities and afflictions, and now at last it has lost its right arm.”

After this, the cardinal returning [Col. 1226C] from Spain recounted in sequence to the pope and all the Roman curia these same things that had been described. Then the pope wished to rise terribly against the emperor and the same traitors; but because at that time the Roman Church was constrained by persecutions and adversity, he delayed action lest a greater scandal arise in the Church, so that when the appropriate time should arrive he might exercise the terrible vengeance of excommunication. For truth, as Scripture says, is sometimes to be concealed so that richer seeds may spring up. The governor of Damascus seized Paul, but Paul escaped when the brethren lowered him in a basket through the wall (2 Cor. 11); and, as the Evangelist testifies, when Jesus saw the crowds of Jews stirred against [Col. 1226D] him because of the truth, he hid himself and went out of the Temple (John 8). Thus the pope, amid the persecution of the Roman Church, rightly refused to excommunicate without result, so that afterward, in tranquillity, he might more justly impose a fruitful excommunication.

These are the letters of the lord pope sent to the archbishop.

## CHAPTER L

“Innocent, bishop,” etc.

“The whole Roman curia,” etc. See under Innocent II, at the year 1143.

These are the letters sent to the archbishop by the chancellor and cardinal:

> “To the dearest Father and friend DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela [Col. 1227A], to the chaplains [Note: [Col. 1227D] The chaplains named before the archdeacons denote the cardinal’s chaplains, who are properly apostolic chaplains.], archdeacons, and other canons of St. James: A., by the grace of God deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, greetings and affection.
>
> “From the time of Pope Calixtus, from which time, by the Lord’s gift, I have served the Roman Church, I have gladly performed what I learned to pertain to the honor of the Church of Compostela. These words are not a reproach, but a renewal of mutual affection. It therefore befits your honor to take care to respond proportionately to our requests. By these present letters we ask your unanimity to receive kindly, for our affection, Aria, the bearer of this letter, as he returns to you, since he is known to have conducted himself honorably among us; and to grant him, for our sake, a fixed [Col. 1227B] benefice from which he may live honorably, so that by one benefit bestowed you may have two persons, namely myself and him, obligated to you.”

Letters sent to the archbishop by Cardinal G.

> “To the dearest brother and friend DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, to the chaplains, archdeacons, and other canons of St. James: GUIDO, deacon-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, greetings and affection.
>
> “We do not wish your charity to be unaware that Aria, the bearer of this letter, is greatly loved and held dear both by our friends and by us, because he has conducted himself well in Italy. We are accordingly very glad concerning him, both because of his friendship and because he was nurtured in your [Col. 1227C] Church. We therefore earnestly commend him to your affection, asking that henceforth you hold him dearer among yourselves and, so that in your affairs, when occasion requires, you may more readily experience the counsel and assistance of us and our friends, grant him, at the request of our intercession—and especially of Lord A., the chancellor, who asks for him—a fixed benefice in the Church of Compostela.”

## CHAPTER LI. On the dissolution of the council

After the conclusion of the general council and the return of Lord D., the supreme and incomparable archbishop, not yet a year had passed when the Portuguese infante, who had made a conspiracy against the emperor with King García of Aragon, heard that the emperor was being troubled by that same King García and learned that grave affairs pressed upon him. Not content with the kingdom of Portugal, he prepared his army, entered the emperor’s territory, forcibly seized the city of Tui by military force, and secretly took certain castles through a count.

Then a certain duke most faithful to the emperor and ignorant of every treachery, seeing the emperor’s land plundered, castles seized by treachery, and the infante devastating the emperor’s kingdom and attempting still greater things, went swiftly to the emperor [Col. 1228A] and reported in order everything that had happened. Hearing this, the emperor traveled continuously by day and night and, with a small number of his knights, entered Tui from the city of Zamora within three days. He sent envoys to the counts and princes of his realm, ordering them not to delay in coming as quickly as possible with their whole force of horse and foot, so that at the beginning of harvest, in the summer season, they might enter Portuguese territory and utterly devastate it.

But the counts and princes, treating the emperor’s orders lightly, delayed going as soon as they had seen his messengers; indeed, they rejoiced more at the prospect of war than in a time of peace and tranquillity. The aforesaid envoys, returning from Compostela, earnestly urged the archbishop to proceed with all his cavalry and demanded funds for the emperor’s use. Then the distinguished Father, namely the archbishop, sent two thousand solidi for the emperor’s expenses through these same messengers and secured his princes and knights for raising an army by stipends.

But on the following day, on which he had intended to depart, certain envoys of the emperor came to the archbishop and said that the emperor had made peace with the infante and that they were bound by great affection and a bond of concord for the whole of their lives; they further said that the emperor would come to Compostela that same day. Hearing this, the venerable old man, solicitous for the welfare of friends and enemies, desisted from the expedition. With bells ringing and cymbals sounding, he received the emperor reverently at Compostela [Col. 1228C] with great pomp, utmost joy, and exultation of heart—the abbots and monks of the whole city, then the priests and canons, all resplendent in gold, purple, and silken garments. He provided for him most abundantly with splendid and most delicate foods and with a great allowance, namely five marks of silver on each day for twelve days, apart from the bishops, counts, and princes.

The poverty of my talent cannot express what kindness, what inward affection of his whole heart, and what friendship the emperor began to show to his godfather. Great indeed was the friendship between them, of which the supreme philosopher Cicero speaks in his book: “Friendship [Col. 1228D] surpasses all human things: it gathers what is scattered, preserves what is gathered, and increases for the better what is preserved.”

## CHAPTER LII. On the emperor’s promise to the archbishop

After these things, one Sunday, when the archbishop was sitting in chapter according to custom and the other canons and worthy and honorable persons of the Church were present, the emperor suddenly arrived, accompanied by the counts and princes of his realm. In a clear voice, before all who heard, he promised his spiritual father, the venerable old man and staff of all the needy, never to depart in any way from his direction and counsel, [Col. 1229A] and throughout all Galicia to do whatever the reverend Father himself should advise him.

Then he added something that ought not to be concealed in silence, but whose testimony should remain forever in the following account as evidence of his promise, removing every doubt. In his times a wicked and detestable custom had become established which had most shamefully dishonored the Church of the most glorious apostle, revered throughout the whole world: whatever the circumstances, the archbishop was to pay money annually to the emperor.

Then the emperor, perceiving that the Church of Compostela, the sceptre and head of his empire, had been oppressed by so great a burden of wicked custom—and that the Church which they ought to have adorned, exalted, and treated more reverently than the other Churches of Spain had, in a remarkable manner, been trampled down—was moved by divine grace, reverence for the blessed apostle, and affection for the archbishop. In the presence of the counts and powerful princes of his empire, with all the canons of this Church listening, he promised henceforth not to extort the customary payment from the Church, nor to demand anything from its offspring.

After making this promise, he took the cap of a certain count and, having kissed his godfather’s hand, humbly gave it to the archbishop with bowed head as a sign of confirmation. He completely granted that he would shortly restore the land of the Montañeses, which he had taken from St. James; and what he promised in words, he devoutly carried out in deed. Further, that divine mercy might pardon him for so wicked a custom, he promised to give two hundred gold pieces [Col. 1229C] each year, so that the cloister of St. James might be built.

Hearing this, the archbishop joyfully magnified God inwardly and began to rejoice with inexpressible delight: both because God, through his old man and shepherd of souls, had greatly exalted the Church of Compostela on that day, and because the emperor, by God’s prompting, had abandoned so great a crime.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the expulsion of the evildoers

After these matters had thus been transacted, the emperor, remembering the great sacrilege committed against the archbishop at the altar of the most glorious and most venerable apostle—a deed abominable to tell and horrible to hear—exacted vengeance from the executioners. Some, after their houses and inheritances had been confiscated, he compelled to go into exile with their offspring. Others he shamefully seized and left stripped of their possessions and all goods. Others still, though abounding in gold and silver, he allowed to beg from door to door. He made the rich and wealthy poor and needy and afflicted them with various privations.

Concerning those who had fled, he ordered all the barons of his empire that whoever found them first should either punish them, without ransom, by every most severe kind of death, or bring them captive to him. After this, the emperor considered that not all the citizens were free from guilt in the sacrilege: some executioners had perpetrated the detestable crime; but the rest had consented to the wickedness and counsel of the sacrilegious men and, allowing the archbishop to be stoned when they could have defended him, had not delivered him. Thus both parties were guilty: some had stoned him, while others had not defended him, Paul testifying that those who commit such acts and consent to wickedness are worthy of death (Rom. 1:32). He therefore wished the burgesses who shared in the sacrilege by deed and consent to share also in its punishment.

When he brought them all to account and, as they could not defend themselves by any argument, wished to extort an immense sum from them, the archbishop immediately came and humbly begged the emperor to pardon them, remember the natural precept, “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another,” and show mercy and clemency to uncultivated mountain men, who lived without rational judgment and were deprived of all understanding. [Col. 1230B]

Why recount individually how great was the mercy in which the holy man, the venerable Father, abounded? In every respect he showed himself a disciple of him who, on the cross, prayed to God for his executioners in these words: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Then the aforesaid emperor, bent toward mercy by the intercession and words of his godfather, reluctantly spared the citizens; and those whom he had planned to reduce to begging he left untouched by any monetary penalty.

When all this had taken place and the archbishop’s enemies had been crushed from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, the emperor, joined to the archbishop by an indissoluble bond of affection and made with him one heart and one soul forever, happily departed from Compostela.

[Col. 1230C] After these events the emperor left the city of Compostela. As he departed, before the counts and princes of Spain, all the canons of St. James who were present, the cardinals of that Church, and others too numerous to enumerate individually, he most firmly promised and granted to the most reverend Father Didacus, archbishop of the Church of Compostela—as the foregoing course of narrative declares—that throughout his lifetime no flattery would ever estrange him from affection for his godfather, nor would he, at the urging of the pious Father’s enemies, break the aforesaid pact.

But before scarcely two years had passed, when he had come into the region of the Campani [Note: [Col. 1229D] In the autumn of the year 1138.], he consigned all his promises and honeyed words to oblivion and the winds. For he admitted to counsel and intimacy the profane executioners and crowd of wicked members of Antichrist, whom the legate of the Roman Church had condemned in the synod and whom the entire assembly of archbishops, holy bishops, abbots, and all orthodox Christians had repudiated and struck with the bond of anathema. The same emperor had shamefully expelled them from the council; and moreover the aforesaid legate had decreed, according to the judgment of the canons, that anyone who gave them not merely a kiss but even association or aid, or any bishop or archbishop who presumed to admit them to penance, should incur and undergo the sentence and fellowship [Col. 1231A] of excommunication.

But, as Scripture says, “The actions of superiors are examples for subjects”; and the Apostle says: “When one member suffers with another, the other members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). Who would dare reject the bloody traitors when the emperor himself summoned them to his own court, furnished counsel and aid at their pleasure, and daily, without ceasing, lent his ears to whisperers and detractors against the glorious archbishop, the venerable old man—he who had brought him forth from the laver of holy regeneration, had been his godfather at the sacred font, had fittingly and manfully armed him in distinguished arms before the altar of the glorious apostle James, and, placing the diadem on his head, had anointed him king?

What more? With so willing, voluntary, and spontaneous a heart did he burn with desire for money and to hear their whispering, just as a religious man, whose manner of life in spirit is in heaven, is accustomed insatiably to hear the honeyed words of divine Scripture, than which nothing beneath the sun is dearer to him. For Scripture says: “Every head is sick and every heart sorrowful. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him” (Isa. 1:5–6).

These aforementioned traitors, both lay and clerical, gathered to themselves certain men everywhere considered familiar associates of the archbishop. They went together to the emperor without delay and promised infinite gifts—namely two thousand marks—in order that he might deprive the archbishop of office and dignity and bring low his friends and all connected to him by blood.

[Col. 1231C] When the emperor had often heard them, burning with love of money no less than Crassus, the Roman dictator, whose practice was to extort money from all whom he captured and to sell justice for gold and silver, he quickly sent a certain deputy of his to Compostela to the archbishop. The deputy was to ensure that the offerings of the altar and the treasury of St. James remained untouched and that, in the archbishop’s absence, it should not be opened at all. From this treasury there had constantly been spent funds for the work of that Church, something never remembered to have been done by any of the emperor’s forefathers, not even in the time of King Alfonso of venerable memory and good fortune, or of Count Raymond, his father.

When this was privately reported to the most reverend old man, he outwardly feigned a cheerful countenance; but inwardly—as we learned from him—the deepest darkness of sorrow occupied his mind. This was because the magnificent work of St. James would fail, and because the throng of Romans and pilgrims seeking the thresholds of St. James would for this reason fail to assemble and refuse to visit, bringing the various alms and gifts by which he himself, with the canons and likewise with the poor, widows, and orphans, lived abundantly and had food and clothing for the common benefit. [Col. 1231D]

After these things, all the canons having been assembled in chapter, he notified them in sequence, not without considerable groaning and sorrow of heart, of the emperor’s mission directed toward the humiliation and injury of their Church. He most kindly instructed each one to advise him according to the resources and capacity of his own judgment.

Meanwhile, while these deliberations were being conducted, after a short time had passed a certain imperial envoy suddenly entered to the archbishop and announced, leaving no doubt, that the emperor would shortly arrive at Compostela. As he departed, another approached and told the archbishop much the same. Then a third hurried up without delay and, setting aside all ambiguity, emphatically declared that the same emperor would come to Compostela and would discuss with the archbishop, before many persons standing by, all matters concerning himself and his Church.

But the Father—religious, endowed with clemency and gentleness, kindly disposed both toward his own people and strangers, a shield and strong staff for the clergy of every order toward all—did not delay most graciously to await the emperor as his lord and king, ready for every service. He prepared with the greatest joy and reverence everything that might honorably be furnished to him. Yet the contrivers of the aforesaid fraud, continually maligning their father before the emperor’s counts and princes, despite the benefits bestowed upon them by him almost from their cradles, and whispering against the archbishop, turning white into black and black into white, considered with fraudulent and subtle ingenuity, devising deceit under their tongue and in their tongue, that if the archbishop were removed from his office and dignity as they had planned and shortly before advised the emperor, and another succeeded in his place, then not only would he suffer loss, but each one of them [Col. 1232C] would quickly lose the offices, dignity, and riches bestowed on him from the Church; their offspring would mourn day by day over their lost goods; and, loving cursing and fleeing blessing, they would incur the psalmist’s curse concerning Judas and men like him: “He loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Ps. 108:8).

Concerning these affairs and those accursed schemes—schemes to be avoided even by decree, not yet in action, which would be worse—they again went to the emperor and cunningly and deceitfully advised him to reconcile and make peace with the archbishop and to establish with him a concord and indissoluble friendship to be maintained forever. They said that the archbishop sincerely and without pretense loved him strongly in all things, with all men, and above all men who bear corruptible flesh, as his lord, king, and emperor, and would faithfully perform whatever was pleasing in his sight. Even if he wished violently to deprive him of office, it could by no means be done, no reason requiring it; otherwise, the archbishop would strike him and his whole kingdom and empire, together with his suffragan bishops, most severely with the bond of anathema and just excommunication, utterly turn away the pilgrims and diverse foreign nations visiting St. James for the remission of sins, and the earth would receive no dead person.

The emperor immediately understood that they were advising him for the advantage of his own honor and dignity; assenting to their counsel, he gave it his faith and support. Then, inflamed by the torches of cupidity and avarice and insatiably burning with love of money, he sent these same men and a certain deputy of his, familiar to the archbishop, to persuade him to give something from the abundance of his generosity for the needs of his soldiers and for securing the government of his realm; to open the treasury of St. James, long untouched and held under interdiction by the deputy; to pay generously, from the solidified funds [reading uncertain: *de solidata*] of offerings and alms of the Church, as reason required, the masters and craftsmen constantly laboring on the work of St. James; and to exercise everywhere, as before, according to his own will, rightful power over the Church’s revenues and its jurisdiction, both within and without. [Col. 1233A]

## CHAPTER LIV. On the counsel given to him

[Col. 1233B]

Upon hearing this embassy, he summoned to chapter the cardinals and the greater and lesser members of the Church. With no little grief and contrition of heart, he set forth in order all that had been sent to him; and he most earnestly commended to each of them that they advise him according to the measure of his ability and judgment. Hearing this, and carefully investigating the matter inwardly in counsel, they advised him to excommunicate most severely the emperor, his honour, and his metropolitan city; and that his Church should no longer daily endure from that emperor so many persecutions, compelled by no justice. They themselves, leaving all that was theirs, would unanimously cleave to him wherever he chose to go, whether to Rome or into [Col. 1233C] exile, in order to obtain justice in this affair; and, not abandoning him even in death, would lay down their lives together with him.

But he, prudently and wisely choosing the lesser of two evils, and long and constantly considering and recalling with the chief men of his Church that, if he struck the emperor of the kingdom of Spain with the sword of excommunication, the Church would thereby suffer loss; that the whole multitude of the faithful would refuse to visit St James as pilgrims; that every dead person would lie unburied, without the commending rites of burial; and that still worse things would arise in Spain, which could scarcely all be enumerated, so that green wood would perish with dry, and dry with green [Col. 1233D]—rejected the counsel already mentioned.

Then, provident for himself and his people, flourishing in discernment and wisdom, and reflecting upon the common saying that “the king’s anger is the messenger of death,” he chose a sounder and more useful counsel: namely, to allay with immense money the emperor’s jaws, ever thirsting for gold and silver, so that thereafter the Church might have rest for a time. For he was not unmindful of the deeds of the Redeemer, but stored them in the treasury of his heart. For when the Jews took up stones and wished to cast them at Christ, he withdrew himself from their sight and departed from the Temple, foreseeing that, if he allowed himself to die there, so great a harvest of believers, both from Jews and Gentiles, would not thereafter rise up through his preaching.

## CHAPTER LV. Concerning Money

[Col. 1234A]

While the Church of Compostela was suffering such a rupture with its head, the archbishop sent to the emperor those same adversaries of his, as well as other members of his household; and through them he promised that a large sum of money from his own resources and from the property of his Church—namely, five hundred marks of silver—would be given as soon as possible to meet the need and restore peace to his whole empire. This was on the following condition: that he should everywhere diligently promote the exaltation and honour of the Church, together with the dignity of his person; and that, whenever with penetrating mind and faithful spirit [Col. 1234B] he discerned any persons hostile either to himself or to his Church, he should overthrow them according to his power and resources, and should manfully give aid and support to him and to his Church, with his favour and assistance accompanying them.

When the emperor attentively heard this aforesaid promise through the same messengers, and recalled the benefits shown to him by the archbishop, his godfather, almost from his earliest years, and always bestowed upon him at times of need, he was beyond measure delighted and rejoiced exceedingly in mind and body. He promised to establish forever an indissoluble bond of love toward himself, the Church, and its city; and, although separated from him bodily by interval of time and distance of place, he would nevertheless never be separated from him in affection of mind, neither through flatterers nor through sowers of discord. Concerning the government of his empire and the ordering of his honour, relying upon counsel, prudent discernment, and wisdom, he would henceforth deliberate watchfully with him; and his spirit should now rest, since the emperor’s mind would unceasingly watch on his behalf. What he promised the aforesaid envoys by speech and words, he made more certain by sending the following letter through one of his own messengers.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Letter Which the Emperor Sent to the Archbishop

“To the venerable lord, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Compostela: ADEFONSUS, by the same grace Emperor of the Spains, greeting and a perpetual bond of affection. [Col. 1234D]

“How great is the love with which our heart embraces you, neither pen can write nor voice express. Whenever we hear news of your prosperity and welfare, nothing more joyful can reach our ears. Because we are bound by so great a bond of affection, we faithfully promise you that we shall always maintain you and your possessions; that we shall defend them against hostile attack to the extent of our power; and that we shall compel your wrongdoers to undergo the punishment of vengeance sufficient for due satisfaction. For we grieve no less at the devastation of your possessions and at what is done contrary to you than if an enemy were ravaging and disturbing our own inheritance [Col. 1235A] and our own tranquillity.

“Therefore let your mind be at peace and free from all anxiety, because our mind shall watch diligently for you. Do not come to the conference which we have decreed shall take place at Palencia on the feast of St Luke the Evangelist, because of the approaching winter cold and the grievous labour of a long journey; but wait in your town, since we shall shortly be coming to you. Farewell.”

The emperor sent this letter to the canons and citizens:

“ADEFONSUS, by God’s grace emperor of all Spain, to the whole convent of canons of St James and to all the burgesses of the same town: increase of salvation, love, and faith.

“I have taken care to send this letter to your beloved selves, so that you may not fail to know that I love the venerable Archbishop Lord Didacus with my whole affection, with my whole heart. For this reason, by imperial command I order you to behave toward him in such a manner that you do not violate the fidelity and love owed by you to him; and that you always remain obedient to him in all things and in every respect, as is fitting. Whoever rashly rises against his just will shall receive such punishment of vengeance as if he had acted against me. Take care, therefore, that you presume to do nothing against him deserving vengeance. Farewell.” [Col. 1235B]

## CHAPTER LVII. Concerning the Council

[Col. 1236A]

When these matters had been concluded, the Bishop of Lascuar, legate of the Roman Church and sent into Spain from the side of Pope Innocent, unexpectedly entered Compostela. He most earnestly invited the archbishops, the bishops of Spain, religious abbots, and especially Lord Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela, head of Spain and chief of the bishops subject to him, to come to the city of Rome for a council, setting aside every excuse, on the Sunday in Lent when the whole Church sings *Laetare, Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”)—provided that he was not hindered by some bodily impediment and could travel without harm.

[Note: [Col. 1235B] From this one may ascertain the exact date of the Second Lateran Council, held in 1139. For when, with the death of Anacletus in 1138, the Church received its long-desired tranquillity, a council was proclaimed in that year for the following year, [Col. 1236B] in which Laetare Sunday, that is, the fourth Sunday in Lent, fell on 2 April. Easter fell on the twenty-third of the same month.]

This invitation was on the condition [Col. 1236B] that, because the Roman Church, long troubled and trampled by an ungrateful people, was now, by the help of divine mercy, established in peace and beloved tranquillity, the venerable pope was diligently summoning the pastors of the holy Church, entrusted by God with the care of souls, in order that, with God’s favour and assistance, he might unanimously deliberate with them concerning the state of God’s holy Church, its welfare, the restoration of all Christendom, and the suppression of the Moabites; and that, illuminating the darkness of ignorance by deed and word, he might show forth the way of truth and holy religion.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1134

# SAINT NORBERT, FOUNDER OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG

[Col. 1235]

# PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY ON THE LIFE OF SAINT NORBERT, BY DANIEL PAPEBROCH, OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS

*(Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, June, vol. I, p. 809)*

## § I. Chronological Synopsis of the Life; His Cult Authorized by Gregory XIII and Enlarged by His Successors

[Col. 1235C]

If many peoples of Asia—the Colophonians, Chians, Salaminians, and Smyrnaeans—have thought it glorious to claim Homer, renowned for poetic praise, as their fellow-citizen, and have not improperly contended, each above the others, that he was theirs: how much greater ought to be the glory of Europeans, who claim Norbert, more eminent than Homer and illustrious with a holier praise of virtues [Col. 1236C], either as their fellow-citizen, like the people of Xanten; or acknowledge him as founder of a most religious order, like the Premonstratensians; or venerate him as an apostle, like the people of Antwerp; or sent him as their archbishop to heaven, like the people of Magdeburg; or devoutly preserve his mortal remains, like the people of Prague.
