The French, Belgians, Germans, and Italians, who once marvelled as he travelled through their lands teaching for the salvation of many, now adore him triumphant in heaven.

The city of Xanten, distinguished by a college of canons, a magnificent church building, and the birth of St Norbert, lies in the duchy of Cleves near the Rhine. Prémontré lies in Picardy, a province of France, three leagues west of Laon, more flourishing in the cultivation of religious virtues than in fertility of soil. Here are the cradle of the Order of Prémontré, which took its name from the place. Antwerp, Magdeburg, and Prague indicate places too well known to require explanation.

Norbert, therefore—many write *Nortbertus*, undoubtedly following the origin of the word, which signifies “prince of the north”; but the softer pronunciation of the majority has worn away the *t*, just as Lambert is said instead of Lantbert, that is, “prince of the land,” and Suibert instead of Suitbert, which may be interpreted “southern prince” [Col. 1237B]—Norbert, I say, was born at Xanten, the city mentioned above, of noble stock, about the year 1085.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] See June, vol. VI, part I, p. 21, col. 2.]

He began to inhabit Prémontré and laid the foundations of a religious order in 1120. Four years later, summoned to Antwerp to destroy the heresy of Tanchelin, he received the church of St Michael for himself and his companions, to possess in perpetuity. He was then made Archbishop of Magdeburg in 1126. Finally, in 1134, on 6 June, he departed for heaven to receive the eternal reward of his labours, commanding that his body be buried “among his brethren and sons, in the church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg. There it was buried for some years [Col. 1237C] before the altar of the Holy Cross in the middle of the monastery. But his good sons (as the *Acts*, no. 115, relate), who loved to keep him, so that their memory might be commended without forgetfulness, transferred him before their eyes into the choir.”

At last, in 1627, when the Lutheran plague prevailed at Magdeburg, he was translated with greater glory to Prague. John de Pruetis, Abbot General of the Premonstratensians, had been working toward this from 1596 onward, as appears from his letters to the Abbot of St Michael’s, Antwerp, on this subject.

2. But the author’s further statement in the same place—that “Norbert had already been canonized in the time of Innocent III, and that this is evident from ancient martyrologies in the Vatican Library, read daily in the Roman churches, especially St Peter’s”—proceeded from less certain information or from information less sincere. Yet John Le Paige, syndic of the Order, afterwards wrote the same in book II, chapter 43, of the *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, published in 1633. He even distinctly specified about the seventeenth year of the pontificate, namely 1214, as the year in which that canonization occurred.

For apart from the fact that no writing on the matter by that Innocent, or by any other pope earlier than the sixteenth century, exists or is recorded by any writer as ever having existed, we—though as eager as anyone to confirm the aforesaid opinion concerning the canonization—examined with earnest attention at Rome many manuscript martyrologies, including some belonging to the very Vatican Church of St Peter. We regret that [Col. 1238A] we could draw from them no confirmation of the desired kind.

The authority of other writers opposes that opinion: they assign Norbert’s canonization to times much later, and speak from their own memory. Among them Peter of Opmers, or Cratepolius, a Franciscan and bachelor of theology, in his *Catalogue of Almost All the Archbishops of the Whole World*, published at Cologne in 1596, says on p. 232, when dealing with the Archbishops of Magdeburg and Norbert, that he “was canonized in his own times by Gregory XIII in the year of the Lord 1582”—only fourteen years before that bachelor of theology printed his work.

Aubertus Miraeus says the same in his *Monastic Origins*, p. 371: “Norbert was enrolled among the saints by Gregory XIII in 1582, and the pope’s diploma is found in his *Premonstratensian Chronicle* under that year.” Lucas Castellanus, Procurator General of the entire Dominican Order, likewise says in his treatise *On the Certainty of the Glory of Those Canonized*, printed at Rome in 1628, p. 441, that Norbert “was solemnly and certainly enrolled among the saints,” but that it is unknown by whom. Had he applied a little more diligence and inquiry to the matter he was treating, he could easily have learned of the diploma issued by Gregory XIII, mentioned by Miraeus—the sole foundation known to us for enrolling Norbert among the canonized.

By that document the pope grants the Premonstratensians, among other things, “that they may freely and lawfully celebrate forever, in all and each of the monasteries, churches, and places of the said Order, with annual solemnity, the feast of St Norbert, confessor and bishop, on 6 June [Col. 1238C], the day on which the same St Norbert passed from this life to heaven, with its octave and with a double office of one confessor and bishop; that they may make commemoration of the same saint whenever the other customary commemorations must be made according to the institution or rite of the Order; and also that they may freely and lawfully enter and note the aforesaid St Norbert, who is found described and noted under that sixth day of June in many martyrologies received into the usage of the Catholic Church, in the calendar of the same Order only, under the same sixth day of June, as a double feast with its octave.”

3. For the pope to be moved to make these determinations, the ancient and immemorial cult of Norbert as a saint first had to be established. For that purpose the martyrologies alone, or chiefly, appear to have been adduced, since only their authority is alleged in the bull just quoted. But the Premonstratensians gratuitously assumed that these were Vatican martyrologies. It would have been better said of French and German martyrologies, into which Norbert was more likely to have been entered.

Nevertheless, I think I can discover from Miraeus’s *Premonstratensian Chronicle* why some imagined Vatican martyrologies. Explaining under the year 1582 the occasion for requesting and obtaining the Office, he says:

“When John Molanus, doctor of theology at Louvain, eminently deserving in ecclesiastical history, had published Usuard’s Martyrology with an index of the saints of Belgium—this was the Louvain edition of 1573, revised eight years after the first and often reprinted thereafter—it was not without divine providence that he wrote the following concerning St Norbert in that Index: ‘Norbert of Xanten, founder of the Premonstratensian Order and Archbishop of Magdeburg, has not yet been entered in the catalogue of saints; not because he lacked merits, which were most abundant, but, I think, because the Order neglected to request this from the Roman See.’

“These words so stung the Reverend Lord Ambrose Loots, Abbot of Parc monastery outside the walls of Louvain, that he sent a very full letter to John de Pruetis, then Premonstratensian abbot and therefore head of the entire Order, urging him to remove this mark of negligence. The result was that the said Lord John de Pruetis diligently negotiated at Rome, through the most illustrious Cardinal Philip Boncompagni, protector of the Premonstratensian Order, for the canonization, as they call it, of Blessed Norbert—that is, his enrollment in the catalogue of saints by Pope Gregory XIII. Thus, while archives and libraries were searched and eminent testimonies of holiness sought, a very extensive document was discovered at Rome in the Vatican Library, prepared many years before for his solemn canonization, as they call it. After it had been carefully examined, Pope Gregory XIII issued a diploma for solemn celebration of St Norbert’s feast on 6 June, and another granting indulgences obtainable among the Premonstratensians on the same day.” [Col. 1239C]

4. Thus far Miraeus, citing Molanus’s Index, the only source relevant to the matter, and its complaint about neglect of promoting the cult. In the same place follows an account of “how much the people of Antwerp owe him.” All this is also found in the *Nativities of the Saints of Belgium*, together with a brief account of the rest of his life. That work was composed in the decade following publication of the Index, but was not published until another decade later, after its author’s death, namely in 1595.

I add this so that one may not wonder why Molanus, who had not yet seen Norbert venerated as a saint, but had seen his anniversary observed annually in Belgium with funeral rite—which was subsequently better altered, so that on the day after the feast such a service should be performed for the dead of the same religious family—never anywhere uses a more religious title for him. The omission of that title in the *Additions to the Martyrology* also indicates to us that Molanus had seen no manuscript or printed work which he himself could follow in using the title of saint.

We nevertheless do not doubt that such works existed long ago, although we ourselves have seen none except a single Cologne edition of 1521, where he is simply noted: “Commemoration of Norbert, of holy memory, Archbishop of Magdeburg and confessor, founder of the Premonstratensian Order”; and a manuscript *Florarium*, where one reads: “On the same day, of Blessed Norbert, bishop and confessor.” Such works, I say, undoubtedly existed long ago; but we do not think that they prove an explicit [Col. 1240A] and formal canonization by anyone.

What then? They prove for us a cult from time immemorial, confirmed by the long-standing knowledge and toleration of the Apostolic See or of the ordinaries, and therefore sufficient to ground a declaration of unquestioned holiness for the whole Church, such as Gregory promulgated, citing the martyrologies. These martyrologies also appear to have been the only, or chief, authorities cited in that lengthy document which, according to Miraeus, moved the pope.

It would nevertheless be worthwhile to possess the document itself. Therefore I wrote to Rome to the most illustrious Schelstrate, keeper of the Vatican Library; and I urged the Premonstratensians to press the matter there through their representatives. This might perhaps be useful if what is sought is found: so that it may be known who sent it to Rome and when, and before which pope the cause was either instituted or to be instituted, and through what intervening obstacles it was left aside until Gregory.

5. Meanwhile Michael Malcorpius, attributing St Norbert’s canonization to that decree as though it were contained in it, in his elegiac Life of the saint, printed at Liège in 1599, after noting in the margin, “Canonized in 1582, 5 Kalends of August,” concluded his poem thus:

> Although blind posterity for a long time  
> Wrongly defrauded its native saint of honour deserved,  
> Yet he has hitherto tasted, and shall taste forever,  
> Perennial nectar—a new divinity upon Olympus’ height.  
> All the greater, therefore, is the eternal praise possessed  
> By Gregory, the thirteenth heir of this name.  
> For he, justly and piously, decreed that this Norbert also,  
> Dwelling in heaven’s golden temples, should be venerated throughout the world.  
> Now altars, now churches, rise in his name;  
> And, duly invoked, he brings sure help to the devout.

6. Gregory himself increased this established cult, as we have already begun to hear from Miraeus, by granting “a plenary indulgence for the feast-day of St Norbert, until the Jubilee year exclusively.” “Clement VIII granted the same for seven years”; “but Paul V made it perpetual in 1606,” and then in 1617 “permitted its transfer with the feast.” Later, “Gregory XV approved and confirmed in 1621 the prayer and lessons of the second nocturn to be recited on the feast of St Norbert. Urban VIII also approved transfer of the feast to 11 July by a diploma granted in 1625,” printed by Chrysostom Vander Sterre in the *Echo of St Norbert*, p. 173.

Meanwhile, when Urban VIII inserted the feast into the Roman Breviary and Missal and wished it to be celebrated with the semidouble rite, he transferred that solemnity back from 11 July to 6 June, the saint’s true natal day. On that same day, in the present Roman Martyrology, the commemoration of St Norbert is placed before all others. Pope Clement X decreed in 1672 that the Office itself should thereafter be celebrated by all with the double rite.

When the Reverend Father Charles Alexander of Manderscheit, then penitentiary at Rome for Belgium and formerly my instructor in the novitiate of the Society, sent me a copy of the decree, he added the following words in a letter:

“If this affair was not completed by me, it was at least begun and initiated by my persuasions and counsels. I was the first, some years ago, to suggest that they attempt a matter which would involve very little difficulty. I wrote to you that, through the Abbot of St Michael’s, you should move the others to hope for attaining what almost every other order had already obtained for its founders. Finally, I induced our Norbertines here to obtain, through the Abbot of Strahov at Prague, letters of recommendation from the Emperor. When these had been obtained, and Cardinal Landgrave had undertaken the recommendation of the whole matter, the business was at last brought most happily to completion through the great diligence of the Procurator General of the Premonstratensians.” [Col. 1241A]

7. Thus he wrote. Afterwards, when the Vatican colonnade, extended to its upper enclosure, was being adorned with statues of saints, and he heard that the founders of most religious orders were counted among them, he was the first to suggest to those overseeing the work that a place should be given to St Norbert. By arguments and every influence he possessed with them, even with the intervention of Father John Paul Oliva, our General, he persuaded them accordingly. No Italian would otherwise have thought of Norbert, because his Order is now known among them only through a few younger members of the monastery of Tongerlo in Brabant, who reside in Rome in turns for study under a superior sent from there and, like themselves, foreign in that place.

The Order had anticipated these honours paid to St Norbert by adapting for its founder what is now common to abbots and bishops: namely, an armorial shield with a motto, representing the saint’s life in separate parts. In the penultimate section, Norbert lies composed in a bier, from which a funeral pall flowing down the sides is adorned, according to the custom of this age, with the shield mentioned. The shield is so composed as to contain a summary of all that must be more fully explained concerning the blessed man.

The whole field of the shield is red, first divided by a white cross. Above it, on either side, branches of palm and olive emerge and surround in the middle the sacred Host and eucharistic chalice. The motto indicates the meaning of all these things: **BY FAITH AND PATIENCE**. These were indeed the saint’s chief virtues, by which he constantly bore the cross of the Lord; gloriously triumphed over visible and invisible enemies; and proved an outstanding restorer of peace wherever he went. He restored to its due veneration the mysteries of the Christian faith, despised or even trampled underfoot elsewhere and at Antwerp.

He so well united the pursuits of the active and contemplative lives—which are also jointly represented in the preliminary image to the aforesaid pictures—that he steadfastly maintained their highest summit until he reached that place where, laborious action having ceased, the blessed vision alone occupies him: the vision of mysteries firmly believed and constantly preached. [Col. 1241D]

## § II. The Life Written Under the Direction of Hugh, the Saint’s First Companion and Successor in the Government of Prémontré, with Supplementary Extracts

8. As regards the Life, my predecessors had long begun to collect the primary *Acts* from various manuscript codices. They had also received the *Acts*, printed in 1608 with the Lives of certain other Fathers of the Premonstratensian Order, at the press of the monastery of Louka on the river Dyje—of the same Order, near Znojmo in Moravia, close to the Austrian frontier—by Sigismund Kohel, abbot there.

But as this Life seems to have been mutilated in many places and altered elsewhere at the editor’s discretion, we set it aside and refer to the primary text. The most illustrious and reverend Lord John Chrysostom Vander Sterre, Abbot of the church of St Michael in Antwerp, Vicar General of the Premonstratensian Order in Brabant and elsewhere, our singular friend and patron of studies, spared both his own people and us the trouble of more careful inquiry into this text.

He did so by communicating the Life of his holy founder as he had caused it to be printed, though he did not yet permit it to be published. His most worthy successor, Norbert van Couwerven, ordered it published in 1656. That edition had been prepared by comparing no fewer than fifteen manuscript codices: “those of Antwerp, Grimbergen, Parc, Averbode, Trunchien, Ninove, Bern, Heylissem, Nijmegen, Morin, Steinveld, Knechtsteden, Chotěšov, Marchtal, Wilten, and others, so that its text might be presented throughout pure and uncorrupted.” [Col. 1242B]

The author of this Life was a canon of the Order, probably of the chief monastery of Prémontré, assisted by several others. For, as he says near the end of the prologue, “it was secured by careful examination that, when certain persons who had constantly lived with him from the beginning had assembled together, every detail should be written in that manner and order which the agreement of the greater number approved.”

9. The first person present from the beginning may be considered Hugh, Norbert’s companion before the Premonstratensian settlement was begun, and afterwards his first successor at Prémontré during Norbert’s own life and with his support. Hugh survived him by thirty years, though he did not succeed him as Archbishop of Magdeburg, as Baronius inadvertently wrote under the year 1134, at the end.

It is probable that Hugh was still alive when these *Acts* were written. This appears from no. 118, after the saint’s apparition to Hugh and the prayer made for him: “May almighty God grant that, according to the meaning of the promise, he may come to him; and may He make him a companion in the joys of eternal happiness and in the gifts of God’s received blessing, whom he left behind as companion, successor, and sharer in the miserable and penal tribulation of this age.”

Therefore these *Acts* were written at Hugh’s prompting, or with his favour and help, according to matters “which,” as the author says in the prologue, “we have either read written by others, or have in great part seen and do see”; and below: “I shall briefly set down those things which I have learned and know concerning him from what others have related on lawful and trustworthy testimony.”

Gregory XV approved as the first lesson for the second nocturn a passage taken from this Life, as though it were the Life “written by Blessed Hugh of Prémontré,” the saint’s successor. I believe this was more easily assumed by those who suggested it than it could have been proved. Certainly no one afterwards accepted it as probable; and the praise of “pious and holy conduct,” inserted in no. 27, prevents us from believing that a humble man wrote thus about himself. [Col. 1243A]

10. Moreover, that the Life was written with Hugh’s favour and help, as I have said, may be attested by the verses placed by the author at its end, beginning:

> Happy Norbert, first Father of this Order:  
> I rejoice, Father Hugh, that you favour his merits.

Yet I cannot persuade myself that the report is true which came from France to Peter de Waghenare, subprior of Veurne: that another Life exists there, “written thirty years after the death of St Norbert, containing many things generally unknown,” as he wrote to our Bollandus about the year 1657. For how could Pagius have been unaware of such a Life in the Library?

I therefore believe that the many things generally unknown are contained in this very Life which we publish and which then had not yet been made public, but was still hidden in manuscripts. Yet it is evident from the writings of the men of Cappenberg and from other materials which we add under the title of *Supplementary Extracts*, that some matters could have been stated more fully or new material added. These extracts are from the book of Herman the monk, *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon*, addressed to Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon—the very man who first received and fostered St Norbert in France. The book would better be entitled, as its editor Lucas d’Achery or some older copyist did entitle it, *On the Deeds of the Venerable Bishop Bartholomew and St Norbert*. For the author also introduces it thus:

“After those miracles, I added how divine mercy, in your days, caused nine—indeed ten—monasteries to be built through your labour, by Lord Norbert and Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.”

I shall also give, as the third chapter of the *Supplementary Extracts*, material concerning the foundations of two monasteries: one promoted by Norbert while still a secular cleric in his native Cleves, the other in the metropolitan see of Magdeburg, with the original documents produced.

11. The same Chrysostom Vander Sterre, who ordered the primary Life mentioned above to be printed, had intended to add his own annotations, as he indicated in the final gathering. But death overtook him on 27 July 1652. What he left unfinished was accomplished by Polycarp de Hertoge, a canon of the same monastery, who composed very extensive notes, strengthened with sayings of the holy Fathers and at times reinforced by theological dissertations.

The kindly reader may consult these in the edition mentioned above, as well as the various readings added by Chrysostom. I have been content, according to our custom, to note certain matters bearing on history and to indicate a few variations in readings of some importance. I judged that longer digressions should be avoided, lest the bulk of the work grow excessively.

[Note: [Col. 1243D] See June, vol. VI, part I, p. 22, col. 1.]

## § III. Praises Bestowed upon St Norbert and His Order by Writers of His Own Age

[Col. 1244A]

12. We rightly name St Bernard first in this paragraph. Although he did not wholly approve St Norbert’s opinion in the question concerning Antichrist (*Epistle* 56), he nevertheless congratulates himself that on such an occasion “he deserved to see his face and to draw many things from the heavenly pipe—that is, from Norbert’s own mouth.”

Writing in his eighth letter to Bruno, Elect of Cologne, who had sought counsel on whether he ought to accept his election, Bernard concludes thus: “You have Lord Norbert, whom, being present yourself, you can better question in person on such matters. For the more ready that man is for us in opening the divine mysteries, the nearer he is known to be to God.”

The year when Bernard wrote this was 1132, the third-to-last year of St Norbert’s life. After Norbert had long been dead, Bernard wrote to a Premonstratensian abbot in *Epistle* 252: “I have always fostered and advanced your Order, as far as lay in me.” He then proves this by clear arguments. Finally, after excusing all that had occasioned complaints, he professes that his friendship with them was and would remain indissoluble:

“I shall cling to you, even if you do not wish it; I shall cling to you even if I myself should not wish it. Long ago I bound myself by a strong bond, by unfeigned charity, that charity which never fails. With those who are troubled I shall be peaceful; to those who trouble them I shall also give place to anger, lest I give place to the devil. I shall be conquered by quarrels; I shall conquer by service. I shall render service to the unwilling, add benefits to the ungrateful, and honour even those who despise me. And now my soul is sorrowful [Col. 1244C] because I have offended you on any occasion; and it will remain sorrowful until you relieve me by your forgiveness. If you delay, I shall go and make excuse; I shall persist in knocking at the doors; I shall press on, opportunely and inopportunely, until I either merit or wring from you a blessing.”

13. So deeply had the friendship contracted with Saint Norbert taken root in the heart of that holy man, especially from the time when they had joined the weapons of sacred preaching against Peter Abelard. Although in the year 1120 or 1121, at the Synod of Soissons, Abelard had himself consigned his own book to the flames with his own hands, at the command of Cono, legate of the Apostolic See, he nevertheless continued to complain that the judgment was, as it were, perverse, and to teach and defend the same doctrines as before. Meanwhile, repeatedly wielding a pen dipped in the gall of bitterness against both saints, he turned their genuine praises into insults. Thus he did nothing other than bear witness to their virtue when, in Letter 1, he complains that his enemies had stirred up against him “new apostles, in whom the world placed great confidence: one of whom boasts that he has restored the life of regular canons, the other that of monks.” And when, in his sermon on John the Baptist, he slanders them because, “coming forth from solitude to the crowds, just as they swelled with the feigned name of religion, so by the pretence of miracles they desired, through favor, to appear wonderful,” he is shown from their own Acts, from the infallible judgment of the Church commanding that they be venerated as saints, and finally from the sentence delivered by Innocent II in 1140 against Abelard’s errors, to have been mistaken regarding both men and in both charges—if indeed not to have lied. That judgment approved that the saints had acted not “imprudently,” but most prudently, in “running through the world preaching, publishing him abroad as much as they could, rendering him by no small degree contemptible in the eyes both of ecclesiastical and secular powers,” and in spreading unfavorable reports concerning both his faith and his earlier life, disgraced by notorious lusts—though these may perhaps then have been corrected—“to such an extent that they turned away from him even his closest friends.”

14. Far from deserving belief, therefore, is his assertion that “those greatest miracles, including the raising of the dead, had been attempted in vain,” although he himself had marvelled and laughed that Norbert had recently done this. For that very reason we should believe the event to have been truly reported, although the author of the Life passed it over in silence. His sole concern, because of “the obstinate shamelessness of certain unbelievers and ungodly persons,” was, as he professes in the prologue, “briefly to touch upon matters known to all, which even they themselves would not dare, with any dishonesty, to deny.” I would say that Abelard is being censured here, were I not persuaded that this Life was written after his death at Cluny in 1142. Peter of Cluny testifies, writing to Innocent II, that Abelard “came peacefully to an agreement with Saint Bernard, after their earlier complaints had been laid to rest”—and therefore after his heresies too had been retracted. Without doubt he would have done the same with Norbert, had he lived, and would have withdrawn the calumnies laid upon him. For he spent the remaining three years of his life most holily and died most devoutly, as may be read in the letter of the aforementioned Peter to Heloise, then an abbess and equally holy, but formerly Abelard’s pupil and mistress.

15. But I turn to the more distinct and fully developed praises of Norbert and of the Premonstratensian Order by various authors. The earliest in date of composition is Hermann, Abbot of Saint Martin at Tournai. At Rome, about the year 1141, he composed a lengthy account of the restoration of his monastery, full of information on various matters, such as is printed in volume XII of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*. Having narrated there the deceitful seizure of Pope Paschal II, carried out by Henry IV in 1111 in order to extort approval of the investitures, he says:

> “A certain cleric named Norbert, who had been the emperor’s chaplain in that same seizure, seeing the great wickedness of his lord the king, was moved by repentance and prostrated himself at the feet of the lord pope. Having received absolution from him, he was converted at least to this extent: in 1113 he refused the bishopric of Cambrai offered to him, since it could not be held without the stain of imperial investiture. But not long afterwards he was struck from heaven after the manner of Paul; and, abandoning secular life, he came into France. Finding in the bishopric of Laon a certain solitary place called Prémontré, he began there to serve God under the Rule of Saint Augustine—indeed, under one much stricter and more austere. Thus, by God’s grace, in a short time he made such progress that we see no one after the apostles today to have produced so much fruit in the Church. For, although the thirtieth year since his conversion has not yet come, we have already heard that almost a hundred monasteries have been founded by his followers in various parts of the world, so that their rule is observed even as far as Jerusalem. To say nothing of other places: in the city of Laon, the lord Bishop Bartholomew entrusted to him a certain poor church built in honor of Saint Martin. Norbert placed there a few of his brethren and set over them as abbot a religious man named Walter. God bestowed upon him such grace that almost five hundred brethren now seem to live in that very church, and nearly ten other monasteries have already sprung from it. Norbert himself, afterwards made archbishop in the city of Magdeburg, died in the time of Emperor Lothair, who succeeded Henry.”

16. Let Lawrence of Liège follow Hermann, a Benedictine by profession as Hermann was, in his *History of the Bishops of Verdun*, written for Bishop Albero before the latter’s death in 1144, and to be found in the same aforementioned volume of the *Spicilegium*. There he relates how that same Bishop Albero, after long attempting in vain to restore monastic rigor in certain places,

> “uprooted the degenerate and barren planting with the sword of severance, and planted there a new shoot of clerics of the monastic order, whom Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, a great man in the Church, had selected for him from among the professed members of his own order.”

There is also there a letter of Albero himself to Pope Innocent, in which he explains why,

> “in the church of Saint Paul, near the city, which through the neglect and irreligion of the few monks living there had been reduced to such infamy that it was called no longer a house of God but a brothel, he had placed the poor of Christ from the church of Prémontré, living praiseworthily according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine.”

17. After reporting this letter, the author also treats of the Cistercians introduced by the same bishop. Speaking of the reform of ecclesiastical and monastic order, he first says that “simoniacal greed was cut down by Peter’s sword”; then he compares the new religious way of the Carthusians to “an eagle flying into heaven.” He continues:

> “That we may have the creature of the calf, laboring and offering sacrifice to God, and likewise that of the man wisely reasoning about divine and human things, there followed those two cherubim, spreading their wings in the midst of the Church and, with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, looking upon one another; that is, two most illustrious orders, protecting the Church by their devotion and, with hearts turned toward God, emulating one another in mutual charity. One of these, the Cistercian, led by Bernard, abbot of most holy name, restored the monastic order, now almost fallen, to the first standard of apostolic life. The other, rightly and by name Fore-shown by God [*Praemonstratus*], begun under the leadership of Norbert, bishop of Parthenopolis, shook the ecclesiastical order free from the mud of worldly vanity. You might believe these two orders to be the two prophets in the Book of Revelation, sent by God near the end of the world and clothed in the sackcloth of repentance; the two olive trees of heavenly mercy and the two lampstands of divine grace. So they afflict themselves in all things; so they water the world with the word of life; so they enlighten it with the light of merits. These two, with God’s cooperation and the aid of all the devout, have already advanced so greatly that the Cistercian Order, within the space of thirty years, has grown into two hundred abbeys of great name, worth, and number, and has begun to spread even among the barbarous Sarmatians and the farthest Scythians; while the Premonstratensian has, during these twenty years, grown to almost seventy abbeys.”

18. Such are those ancient authors, though only recently printed. But the books of the *Antikeimenon* (“Objections”), dedicated to Pope Eugenius III and therefore written before 1153, have not yet seen the light. Their author was Anselm, bishop of the Church of Havelberg in Lower Saxony, under the metropolitan of Magdeburg. The original manuscript codex—perhaps the only one in the entire world, and worthy of publication in an enlarged library of the holy Fathers—is owned by our most friendly Henry Julius, Baron von Blum, imperial councillor in the appellate tribunal at Prague. From him was also sent to Florentius another copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology, which we frequently praise. He had entrusted this codex to our Hermann Horst, confessor of the Empress Dowager Eleanor, to read; Horst gave it for examination to Reinold Dehnius, likewise a learned priest of our Society and well known for his books. May God receive the souls of them both. Dehnius transcribed with his own hand, for us, from Book I, chapter 10, the following fragment concerning our subject.

19. “There arose in the same profession—that is, the canonical profession—and in imitation of the apostolic life, a certain religious priest named Norbert, in the time of Pope Gelasius. On account of his religious life, and because of the many enormities and schisms then occurring in the Western Church, he received from Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, letters and authority to preach. In his time most illustrious and renowned for religious life, he travelled through diverse provinces preaching; he gathered no small multitude of religious persons, established many communities, and formed them by word and example to the perfection of apostolic life. He also possessed such favor before God and men that those who could attach themselves to him truly called themselves blessed. Afterwards he was made archbishop in the Church of Magdeburg. His holy and venerable body rests in the church of Blessed Mary in his metropolitan city, where he himself had established brethren of his religious order. Thus the religious life renewed through him began to grow greatly and spread throughout the earth, so that there is scarcely any province in the western regions where a community of that religious order is not found: France, Germany, Burgundy, Aquitaine, Spain on this side of the Pyrenees, Lesser Brittany, England, Denmark, Saxony, Leutecia [perhaps Sweden?], Poland, Bavaria and Swabia, Pannonia and Hungary, Lombardy, Ligniagia [perhaps Liguria?], Etruria, and Tuscany. All these provinces indeed have communities of the aforesaid order, and continually trust to be helped by their examples and prayers. This same holy society also extended its branches into the regions of the East: for there is one community at Bethlehem and another at the place called Saint Habakkuk.”

20. These, then, may stand for a few among the many authors of whom the author of the *Life* says in his prologue that “they wrote the life and deeds of Saint Norbert, but did not pursue the matter fully and in order.” Nor does the author of the *Deeds of Bishop Bartholomew* do so. He too was a contemporary writer, about the year 1150, less than thirty years after the saint’s arrival in the city of Laon. That author is not produced here because excerpts from him will make up chapter 2 of the *Analecta*, after the material appended by the Cappenberg writers. The latter alone has thus far been printed, while the former has been sampled piecemeal and in parts by Pagi and Polycarp. It appears to be the work which André du Chesne, in his *Bibliotheca Historiae Francicae*, p. 248, calls the manuscript *History of the Restoration of the Church of Laon under Bishop Bartholomew*.

> [Note: Col. 1247D. See vol. VI of June, part 1, p. 22, col. 2.]

### § IV. Testimonies of Certain Authors of the Following Century. The Ancient Discipline of the Order of Nuns

21. We first give a place in the following century to Robert of Mont, continuator of Sigebert of Gembloux, who writes under the year 1131:

> “In those times the canonical Order of Prémontré and the monastic Cistercian Order, like two olive trees in the presence of the Lord, ministered to the world the light of piety and the richness of devotion. Like fruitful vines, they propagated branches of religious life in every direction; and, as the fragrance of their good repute gradually spread through nearly all the bounds of the Christian world, they founded new abbeys where previously there had been no worship of God. Thus brethren from Prémontré were also sent into Syria and Palestine, where they built several abbeys.”

So he, comprehending much in a brief encomium. Somewhat more diffuse is the author of the *Annals of Laon*, plainly contemporary with Robert. He is that anonymous canon of Laon, apparently English by nationality, whose work is praised by André du Chesne in the *Bibliotheca* and on the page cited above under the title of a manuscript *Chronicle from the Nativity of Christ to the Year 1218*, dealing especially with Belgian affairs. Pagi gives reason for this opinion when he transcribes for us from the *Annals*, as he calls them on p. 10, Book III, chapter 1, under the year 1121. For such a chronicle as we have just heard of could easily—and indeed should—have filled two books before reaching the time of Bishop Bartholomew. Receive, therefore, his words here, until someone publishes this *Annals* or *Chronicle* in full—which we also desire for the *History of Bishop Bartholomew*.

22. “After a few years, that discoverer and founder of a new light and a new conversion—not only of outward brightness, but also of inward radiance—the lord Norbert, coming from Germany into France, with divine grace preceding and accompanying him, planted in the bishopric of Laon that first vineyard, namely the Premonstratensian. Rooted and founded in charity, it extended its shoots like a fruitful vine from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth. With the wine of its strength, which gladdens the heart of man, it has now abundantly intoxicated many princes and judges of the earth, young men and virgins, old men together with the younger, so that, powerfully intoxicated, they seek nothing else than to praise the name of the Lord and sing to him a new song. For, putting off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new man, created according to God, they utterly cast away fleshly allurements; and, like water changed by the Lord into wine at the wedding, they forget the things behind and stretch forth to those before them. Thus, though bodily present on earth, they set their minds on things above, not on things upon the earth, saying with the Apostle: ‘But our commonwealth is in heaven’ (Phil. 3:20), where Christ is at the right hand of God. Joined in mind to the heavenly seraphim, they burn continually with love for Christ alone. To him they also offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, displaying in their outward clothing the brightness of virtue in which they shine inwardly.”

So he writes, and perhaps much else in the progress of his history worthy of being brought to light, if someone would act as its midwife.

23. Let James of Vitry complete the group of three authors of the thirteenth century who more fully praise the Premonstratensians or their founder Norbert. More do not presently occur to us, though we scarcely doubt that there are more. He was bishop of Acre in Palestine and Cardinal-Bishop of Tusculum of the Holy Roman Church. We could not omit him, if only because we are to give his own Life—he died in 1224—on 23 June, as a noble corollary to the Life of Saint Mary of Oignies published by him, on account of certain grounds for the cult common to them both. Pagi held in such esteem the polished praise of the white-robed order, or chapter 22 of the *Western History*, “On the Canons of the Premonstratensian Order,” that he judged it worthy of extensive commentaries. Omitting those, it will suffice to add a few notes left by Henschenius, who had undertaken to illustrate the entire Life of Saint Norbert with notes, to be enlarged by me in a second revision insofar as need might require. The words of Vitry are these.

24. “A certain just and God-fearing man, a true worshipper of God, abiding in his innocence, named Norbert, after teaching many by his preaching, like a heavenly pipe and silver trumpet, and after encouraging those divinely inspired and converted to the Lord to bear the fruit of a better life, at length established in the place called Prémontré a peaceful dwelling for the work of himself and his disciples.

> [Note: Col. 1249C. Vitry had treated in the preceding chapter 21 of regular canons, to which he appends this.]

“Having assumed the regular habit, in order to serve the Lord according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, he tightened for himself and his disciples the customary manner of life which the aforementioned regular canons had observed more loosely down to those times, adding certain new institutions and modifying certain old ones.

> [Note: Col. 1249C. Pagi, Book I, chapter 3, explaining Vitry’s text, states that their ‘essential habit is a woollen, snow-white tunic with a white woollen scapular.’]

> [Note: Col. 1249C. In chapter 4, Pagi says that the supreme pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, Innocent, and Honorius—each the third of his name—likewise Gregory IX, Innocent IV, Urban and Gregory X, and others, confirmed this Rule of Saint Augustine for them. Pagi sets forth the Rule in chapter 4 of Book I and explains it in nineteen sections. In Book III he presents their privileges; in privilege 105, Gregory X invokes the example of several predecessors.]

“The canons and lay brethren of the Premonstratensian Order never eat meat, except in sickness.

> [Note: Col. 1249C. The perpetual abstinence from meat was relaxed by Pope Pius II in 1460, and later by Sixtus IV, Alexander VI, and Julius II. See chapter 6 of Pagi.]

“From the Feast of the Holy Cross until Easter they fast.

> [Note: Col. 1250C. The fasting was later modified by the authority of the same pontiffs and reduced to Advent, Quinquagesima, Fridays throughout the year, the vigils of the Virgin Mother of God, and similar days, as Pagi teaches in chapter 7.]

“They eat two cooked dishes in the refectory, in the Cistercian fashion.

> [Note: Col. 1250C. Pagi reports in chapter 8 that, by the authority of Clement VI, the use of woollen garments next to the skin was left to the judgment and dispensation of prelates.]

“They do not wear linen shirts; they use goatskins. They sleep clothed in white tunics and shod with hose. They are clothed in white woollen cloaks, without any dye. On feast days, according to the custom of other canons, they read nine lessons; on other days, only three at Matins. After the night office they return to the dormitory to sleep and rest. At designated seasons and fixed hours they go out for manual labor.

> [Note: Col. 1250C. Namely, to avoid idleness; but it is evident that literary studies are preferred to manual labor.]

“They personally undertake parish churches and the care of secular souls. All monasteries of this institution and religious order are contained under the one head of the monastery of Prémontré, to which all the abbots of this order assemble every year for the general chapter.

> [Note: Col. 1250C. The general chapter was changed from annual to triennial in 1605, under Francis of Longpré, Abbot of Prémontré.]

“They have estates and priories not only for men but also for women, in which clerics and lay persons live according to what their superiors enjoin.

> [Note: Col. 1250C. *Curiae* are courts, granges, villages, or estates in which, if two or more priests are stationed, they are called priories.]”

25. “But at the beginning of the Order and of the new planting, while they still abounded in the precious treasure of poverty, intoxicated, as it were, by the new wine of new religious life and burning with that fire which the Lord sent upon the earth to burn, they were so inflamed that they went not only to neighboring regions but to remote provinces throughout almost the entire world; they enlightened them and called them onward by the example of their way of life. Hence, in a short time, many monasteries of this order and profession, both of clerics and of nuns, were built everywhere and, by the gifts of princes and alms of the faithful, enlarged beyond measure with abundant revenues and broad possessions and sufficiently endowed.

> [Note: Col. 1251D. The monasteries were distributed through thirty *circariae*, or provinces; Pagi indicates these from p. 318 onward. Relevant here is what Miraeus recites, at the end of the index of monasteries appended to the *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, from a Steinfeld manuscript, as having been read in the monastery of Oberzell near Würzburg: ‘This is the total of cloisters or monasteries of the Premonstratensian Order: one thousand abbeys, three hundred provostries, and five hundred convents of nuns. Moreover, in the aforesaid order there are sixteen episcopal sees: of these, seven are archbishoprics and nine diocesan bishoprics.’ I believe this total was gathered within the first century, or century and a half, of the Order. For, as the same Miraeus testifies, this is inscribed upon the walls of the hall at Schlägl in Austria: ‘Before the year 1200, the monasteries of this white family, counted throughout the world, were 1,300 for canons and 500 for nuns, apart from priories and other lesser houses.’]

“For chaste matrons, holy widows, and virgins devoted to God, like precious stones suited to the adornment and beauty of so holy and honorable a religious life, were joined like two walls of men and women by one cornerstone. Thus a dwelling pleasing to God was built, like the structure of another ark completed by a cubit. In it the untamed animals and bestial impulses of sensuality were subdued with such severity by fasts, vigils, prayers, and various other disciplines that, their tumult restrained and peace attained, they did not greatly trouble the governors of the ark. And if at any time they rose against them without discipline, they killed all the sinners of the earth at morning—that is, at the beginning of the devilish suggestion—by dashing their heads against the rock.

“For the nuns were kept so enclosed within the boundaries of the monastery that no entrance was open to any men. Since they did not sing in choir or church but devoted themselves only in silence to prayer, reading their psalters and privately reciting the canonical Hours or the Hours of the Blessed Virgin Mary with all humility and devotion, priests and clerics of the same order lived separately—men tested and religious—who ministered to them in divine offices, heard their confessions through windows, and took care at fixed times to instruct and form them with the words of the divine Scriptures.”

26. The author of the *Deeds of Bishop Bartholomew*, chapter 2 of the *Analecta*, speaks thus of them: “We see in a remarkable way that women hasten to the monasteries of that institution, so that we believe more than ten thousand women are contained in them.” The manuscript chronicler of Parc Abbey near Louvain observes that Saint Norbert himself placed them at Prémontré; and that this is clear from a diploma of Celestine II given to Abbot Hugh on 11 December 1142. Among other monasteries where they were maintained, he names Oberzell near Würzburg, Weissenau near Ravensburg, Saint Michael’s at Antwerp, and finally his own Parc. Its second abbot, Philip, writing to Saint Hildegard, says: “Pray, venerable Mother, for me and for the congregation of brothers and sisters which I have to govern, that the Lord may grant us peace and concord.”

Concerning them the same chronicler writes: “They lived apart from men, and gave themselves not to singing in choir or church but only to prayer in silence, reading their psalters and the canonical Hours or the Hours of the Blessed Virgin privately and with all humility and devotion, and serving in other works of the Church and of the brethren—sewing, spinning, weaving, and washing.”

27. All this continued in complete innocence, until, as Vitry adds, “when the first fervor cooled, heedless security began to introduce torpor and negligence; and it converted the windows”—through which speech alone had at first been permitted—“into doors.” Therefore, as he concludes, “wisely the Premonstratensians unanimously decreed in general chapter that henceforth women should not be received into their Order.” Pagi teaches, at this passage, p. 352, that this chapter was held in 1138; and he further explains that it was not decreed that there should be no women at all, but rather, as Bartholomew says—Saint Norbert having been the first to receive them—“it seemed good to remove them and place them farther away for the service of God.”

Perhaps the chronicler of Parc derives from the statutes of the Order a somewhat more fitting and clearer qualification. There, distinction 4, chapter 15 says: “No woman shall be received into our Order as a sister, except in those places which from ancient times have been assigned to sisters who sing.” Therefore the Fathers intended to exclude only lay sisters (*conversae*), who almost did not live in the monasteries themselves, such as the chronicler described above; they did not intend wholly to extinguish the monasteries of those women to whom attendance in choir and sacred singing had been permitted. These have endured down to the present times, according to the bulls of the supreme pontiffs Innocent II, Celestine II, and Eugenius III. The last-named, in 1152, said:

> “We have also considered this according to the principle of humanity, and by the present decree, to remain in force forever, we enact that the sisters who, through the labor of our brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, and through your exhortation, came to the service of almighty God and offered themselves to the Lord, shall now and always receive, without anyone’s opposition, from the goods of your church—for no small part of these is known to have come to that place through them—the necessities required for their temporal support.”

28. Thus far I had written and prepared for the press when the most illustrious Lord Jacobus, Baron Le Roy—renowned for published accounts of the marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire and of Gallo-Brabant—brought me the happily recovered *Chronicle* of Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines. In it he showed me a passage to read, also copied by André du Chesne among the proofs to Book VI of the *Genealogical History of the Families of Guînes, Ardres, Ghent, and Coucy*, p. 333. It explains the beginning of the Order under the year 1119 in these words:

> “The Premonstratensian Order began at this time through the wonderful man Lord Norbert, a Teuton by nation. The church was founded in the diocese of Laon under Bishop Bartholomew, in the presence of the noble man Thomas of Coucy and his son Enguerrand. This order had three hundred and fifty abbeys.”

This author, most trustworthy in matters of his own century, ceases writing in 1241. He then proceeds to set forth genealogically the antiquity of those nobles under whom that Premonstratensian house was founded, which is not the purpose of our undertaking here.

[Col. 1253]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT NORBERT, BY A CONTEMPORARY PREMONSTRATENSIAN CANON

*(Prepared from several manuscripts, especially by Dom Chrysostom, Abbot of Saint Michael’s at Antwerp.)*

## PROLOGUE

1. Beyond doubt, every faithful and devout soul approaches more nearly to winning the love and glory of almighty God in proportion as it more readily believes the good it hears about another person, and desires and hopes that the same Lord God may grant it to itself. Whoever does not believe does not imitate; whoever does not imitate will never arrive. For just as the homeland which we seek in the exile of this life is true, so likewise the road by which we travel is true and singular. On this road, so greatly and variously obstructed by errors and hardships, there have not been lacking for us, from the beginning of the world, among the other benefits of divine providence, examples of holy men. Following their footsteps, we might seek more eagerly and attain more surely the joys of eternal blessedness.

Some of these examples are things past, which we read as recorded by others; others are things which we ourselves have in great measure seen and still see. Therefore, since nothing is so advantageous to the Christian person in this pilgrimage, or so necessary for attaining the rewards of everlasting glory, as to form one’s life by honorable morals and occupy oneself with praiseworthy pursuits, one gladly and with every devotion receives whatever concerning such men may be found worthy of committal to memory. For those whose virtue one endeavors to emulate, one should also strive to recall their merits in continual meditation.

But unbelievers and ungodly persons, whose god is their belly and whose highest good is bodily pleasure, do not fear immediately to judge as false and invented whatever they read or hear that is alien to their pursuits and manner of life. And because they bear a foul and unclean conscience, hating righteousness and suspecting truth, they do not cease to turn simple people away from the way of salvation and overthrow them with their corrupt and ruined morals.

2. Therefore, in order to turn aside the obstinate shamelessness of these people, although I have resolved to write concerning Premonstratensian men whose merits of every religious and holy life have been approved before God and among men in our own times, I am compelled to omit much, touching briefly only those things known to all and which even they themselves would not dare to deny through any dishonesty.

As I considered the works of these men and observed their growth, I discovered in a marvellous way not human power but God’s. Remembering therefore the Gospel saying uttered by the good Master and Savior of all, Jesus Christ: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:16), and that “a bad tree cannot bear good fruits” (ibid., 18), I set myself to investigate the tree from which so many and such great fruits had sprung. And when I sought somewhat more carefully into the origin and root of the matter, Father Norbert, of pious and venerable memory, came before me. Concerning him, as the logic and order of the narrative may suggest, I shall briefly and summarily set down some things which I have learned and know from the lawful and trustworthy testimony of others to have been related about him.

And lest an unbroken and lengthy discourse produce weariness in the reader, I shall take care, insofar as I can diligently do so, to arrange this matter distinctly in chapters and mark it with titles. I shall take a fitting beginning for my narrative from the aforesaid Father himself, who was the first of this congregation. Moreover, it should be known that, although many have written his Life and deeds, I have found none at all who pursues the matter fully and in order. To prevent this from occurring here also, careful inquiry has been made, so that, when certain persons who had lived continually with him from the beginning had come together, each matter might be written in the manner and order approved by the agreement of the majority.

[Col. 1257]

## Chapter I. Birth; secular life; conversion to a better life

[Col. 1257A]

**3. [Chapter I.]** In the days of [Note: **[Col. 1257A]** Henry, Emperor IV and King of Germany V, **[Col. 1257B]** called the Younger in relation to his father Henry the Elder, whom he succeeded, after the latter had been deposed by authority of the Apostolic See, on 25 December 1105; he died on 23 May 1125.] Henry the Younger, Augustus Caesar, while [Note: **[Col. 1257B]** Paschal II held the see from 14 August 1099 until 20 January 1118.] Paschal, Supreme Pontiff, administered the governance of the Apostolic See, in the year 1115 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, there was a certain man named Norbert, a German by nationality, from the town of [Note: **[Col. 1257B]** Xanten, or Sancten, a town of Cleves, so called from the holy martyrs Victor and his companions, killed there under Diocletian on 10 October. In 1028 the place received a college of canons, among whose number Saint Norbert himself was later included. Hence, in a calendar of that church, at 6 June, D. Crasius reports that he read in Polycarp: “Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, our brother.” Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, likewise mentions him in a charter of 1144, to be given under Chapter 3 of the *Analecta*, as “then a canon of Xanten,” when the monastery at Fürstenberg was founded, and “afterward bishop of Magdeburg.” Therefore, when the equally contemporary monk Hermann, in Chapter 2 of the *Analecta*, calls the Saint “a canon of Cologne,” he must be understood to have named the diocese for the particular church within it.

Moreover, the house now shown at Xanten as the birthplace of Saint Norbert, in the street commonly called Mar-strate, “is no longer one house but three adjoining houses,” as R. P. Lambert Buren wrote to us. For many years he had been senior of our residence at Xanten and confessor to most of its canons, and was nearly seventy years old. Having diligently questioned individuals, he says that “this is the tradition of all alike, inhabitants and neighbours.” In 1692, the year in which he wrote that letter, he found that “the first of these three houses toward the market-place, bearing the sign of the Three Merchants, was occupied by a woman merchant; a baker inhabited the second; and a blacksmith the third. The latter’s father, an eighty-year-old man, reported that these three houses had been a single house, but that all of it except the walls had perished in a fire. The same is confirmed by another old man, older than eighty, born and raised in the house now occupied by the baker. He adds that he had heard from his own father, likewise an octogenarian, that Saint Norbert had once been born in the place where he himself was then living.” At the vicarage of Saint Peter there still remains a chalice said to have belonged to Saint Norbert or to have been given by him.] Xanten, which in antiquity [Note: **[Col. 1257D]** It is believed to have been built from the ruins of Trajan’s Cologne; perhaps this gave certain persons occasion to invent that the place had formerly been called Troy or Trojana.] was called Troy; born of an illustrious line of Frankish and German [Note: **[Col. 1257D]** On 1 February, before the Life of Saint Sigebert, king, we treated of the origin of the Franks, both Ripuarian and Salian, and showed that they originated in the territories of Zutphen and Overijssel, migrated thence into Betuwe **[Col. 1258B]** and Brabant, and finally established the ancient Frankish kingdom. His descent is thus traced from these Salian Franks. Polycarp indeed believes that his mother Hadwig was a daughter of Eudes, Duke of Burgundy, son of Robert, King of France; while Herbert, Count Palatine of the Rhine, was a great-grandson through his mother Matilda of Otto I. But we should wish to read these matters confirmed by ancient testimony.] Salians; endowed with wealth, handsome in appearance, slender and somewhat tall in stature, a grown man; instructed in letters as well as in courtly and worldly affairs; polished in speech; a cleric by office, a subdeacon by order, [Col. 1258A] but in life and character, considering his age and worldly habits, exceedingly frivolous.

His father was named Herbert, from the castle near the forest of Kettela [Note: **[Col. 1258B]** Gennep, a town of Cleves, formerly *Genapum*, whence “Gennepians”: it lies on the river Rur, beyond which stretches the forest called in old writings Kettelensis, today Kesselensis, from the ancient castle of Kettel, now Kessel, namely the castle of the Gennepians, situated about half a league above their town, where the forest begins. Below the same town, at the confluence of the said Rur and the Meuse, lies the court of the Gennepians, commonly called Genepper-Huys, itself turned during the preceding century into a very strongly fortified castle, now levelled to the ground.

That it was formerly written *Kettel*—just as Hassum, between Gennep and Goch, was formerly called and written **[Col. 1258C]** *Hattum*—was taught me by John Michael van der Ketten, prior of the Bridgettines of Kalkar in the same Cleves. Thus the father of Saint Norbert is understood to have taken his name from the castle of the Gennepians itself—for *Kettel* or *Kessel* in our language means the same as *Castellum*, and has similarly remained from that word commonly used by the Romans—and that castle was his own hereditary possession, since nobles in that age commonly took their names from their lordships.

That the family of Gennep was noble is clear both from the brothers Heribert and Erebert of Gennep, named in the aforementioned charter of Fürstenberg and probably kinsmen of Saint Norbert, who are there also recorded to have had a brother Heribert; and from William of Gennep, Archbishop of Cologne, whose highly ornamented monument with epitaph is in the metropolitan church; he died on 15 September 1362.

Henschenius further suggested in his *Diatribe on the Trajectensians* that the German Menapii—whom Julius Caesar says “sent a great part of their cavalry across the Meuse **[Col. 1258D]** to the Ambivareti, for plundering and foraging”—should rather be called Gennepians; Tacitus called them Gugerni, we call them Gochenars, and now Cleves-men, the name being taken in different ways from those three principal neighbouring towns, Gennep, Goch, and Cleves.] named Gennep; and his mother was named Hadwig. While she carried him in her womb, having asked for him from the Lord, she heard in a dream one saying to her: “Be of good courage, Hadwig [Note: **[Col. 1258D]** Variant manuscripts: “For he whom you carry in your womb will be an archbishop”; and he is said to have been born about the year 1080.], for he shall be great before God and before men.”

**4.** Since in all things the prosperity of this present life complied with his wishes and temporal success smiled upon him, it came about, among other things, that he was also conspicuous in the courts of great men: first in the court of Lord Frederick, [Note: **[Col. 1258D]** Frederick held office from the year 1100 until 25 October 1131. Norbert is said to have been with him about 1112, and in the following year at the emperor’s court.] Archbishop of Cologne, and then in the emperor’s household. In the latter, indeed, because of his clerical [Col. 1259A] office [Note: **[Col. 1259D]** Hermann, Abbot of Saint Martin at Tournai, calls him the Emperor’s chaplain.] and his learning; in the former because of his nobility of spirit and refinement of manner; and in both because of his agreeable way of life and elegance of manners.

Here distinguished, there noble; vigorous in both places; loved and honoured no less by his lords than by the entire household; welcome to all and suited to everyone; great among the great and small among the small; illustrious among nobles and rustic among the low-born; eloquent among the learned and, as it were, foolish among the uneducated, he made himself lovable to all. In short, having become all things to all, he accommodated himself to the pursuits of all among whom he moved.

For he was cheerful in appearance, serene of countenance, pleasant in speech, gentle in intercourse, agreeable in company, generous to his own people, peaceable toward strangers; lavish in giving, modest in receiving; master of his own counsel and keeping his purposes before his eyes; employing his own judgment according to reason and conducting life according to his will. He denied himself nothing and left unattempted nothing that the appetite of his own will suggested; giving no thought to what was permitted, nor guarding against what was unfitting, provided only that what pleased him was available and what displeased him did not obstruct him. He swallowed up the past, devoured the present, and forestalled even the future: an outstanding citizen of this world and celebrated colonist of Babylon, walking with his eyes closed and his head turned backward, knowing neither what was ordained for him hereafter nor what the coming day would bring him—or rather, what was worse, caring absolutely nothing for it; impatient of religion and peace, [Col. 1259C] a slave of restlessness and impatience.

**5.** Moreover, the continuous succession of favourable events and the breath of popular favour enlarged in all these things the hope of his ambitions and expanded the desires of his heart. From every side people applauded with sweet-sounding cries and a voice honeyed to a man thus disposed: “Well done! Well done!” In comparison with its sweetness and pleasantness, the promise of the heavenly kingdom, the threat of burning Gehenna, and matters like these sounded in his ears like slow and sleepy words, noisy and tumultuous, full of vexation and annoyance—like senile ravings and childish absurdities. Indeed, every song that did not echo a double “Well done!” all around him seemed to him empty speech and a fabulous tale.

**[Chapter II.]** Thus goaded by these spurs and troubled by such a sting, Norbert was swept about in the midst of Babylon: through manifold twisting turnings, along laborious and difficult paths, always going and never returning; wandering without knowing, a vagrant and fugitive; tossed about without feeling it, in danger yet secure; [Col. 1260A] exhausting himself for the wind and hunting vanity. Then it happened—and behold, suddenly and unexpectedly—a swift word and a mighty hand bore down upon the fugitive’s back, casting down the rider and raising up the bent man.

**6.** For it happened that, alone except for one boy whom he had taken with him, he hurried toward a certain place called [Note: **[Col. 1259D]** In the aforementioned charter of Fürstenberg there is named “Agnes, abbess of Frethena,” which I have no doubt is here called Freden in a softer dialect. I find near the river Borkel in Westphalia, six leagues from Xanten, the small town of Vreden, and understand that there is there a noble monastery of canonesses, with canons to minister to them in sacred matters and in the divine office, as in many other places in the Low Countries. Norbert therefore may have travelled there for vain social intercourse rather than spiritual profit when he was divinely touched. Yet on the same road, after the second league from Xanten, one comes to Marien-Vreden, a place now occupied by Augustinian hermits. Some elderly citizens also assert that a place once called Vreden, now destroyed, lay nearer.] Freden. But why he went secretly or alone, he knows who said: “I will hedge up your ways with thorns” (Hosea 2:6).

As he proceeded amid the pleasantness of a green meadow, with splendid equipment both for riding and in silken dress, the clouds suddenly thickened, storms arose, thunder frightened him, lightning flashed, and tempests raged. The refuge of villages was far away; the spirit that has power over tempests instilled terrors and dreadful intimations of death. What more need be said? The unlettered man did not cease to cry out and preach to the learned, the servant to his lord, [Col. 1260B] the boy to his elder: “Norbert, where are you going? Lord, what are you doing? Return, Father, return! For the mighty hand of the Lord is against you.”

The servant cries out, the ass speaks—but more usefully than Balaam’s ass. For the merciful Lord above, eager to call back and not slow to convert, seemed to say: “Norbert, Norbert, why do you persecute me? I prepared a body for you; I provided the riches with which you display yourself. You ought to have served me: why do you hasten to ruin others also? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

At these words, a bolt suddenly sprang forth before the horse’s feet, consuming the grass and splitting open the earth deeper than the height of a man, so that no mortal in sound mind could have heard it. And, as was said above, the mighty hand of the Lord cast down the rider; but his mercy, giving life, immediately raised up the man bowed down and humbled. The boy stood stunned; the lord lay prostrate, and the horse lay prostrate; he was almost beside himself unto death. A sulphurous stench, like the fire of hell, filled the place and the man’s garments.

**7.** After the space of an hour, the man rose as though from a heavy sleep. Coming to himself and inwardly touched by sorrow of heart, he began to say within himself: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” And immediately, as though an answer were given: “Cease from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.” He went no farther and did not cross the ditch which the Lord had dug for him. But reflecting upon the mercies of the Lord—“for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever”—he returned [Col. 1260D] by the road by which he had come.

From that time, gradually increasing the fire of divine love conceived within him, he did not at once change his clothing or immediately leave the world. Instead, beneath soft garments he subdued his limbs by the harshness of haircloth, and began to rise up against himself. Then, little by little, the inward sword of God’s word, penetrating the depths, burning the reins, and searching [Col. 1261A] hearts, began from within, by a reversal, to reform what had been falsely deformed: uprooting and destroying, rebuilding and planting; casting out the serpent by the very way through which it had crept in. Suddenly and in a moment it turned and changed the wild, rapacious hawk into a simple, gentle dove.

Thus it came about, as the Apostle says (Romans 5:20), that “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.” And because the Holy Spirit knew the measure and order of his own operation, he forgot nothing. After inspiring love, he further added and opened understanding, and instilled in the mind, now inwardly renewed, that it should still endure for a short and suitable time before putting off the outer man with his deeds; and that it should choose a fitting and appropriate place publicly to renounce this world, its prince and master the devil, and all his pomps—where the mercy of divine loving-kindness might appear more evident and prove more welcome.

**8.** Therefore, in the meantime the man of God gathered his strength to himself, [Note: **[Col. 1261D]** The Nijmegen manuscript: “and remaining at home.”] returned inwardly into himself, strengthened his spirit, and pondered higher counsels. He wholly changed and redirected every pursuit of his life onto paths utterly different and entirely opposed to his former ones.

Now taught to fight against the enemy, he immediately withdrew his foot from the court; and, remaining at home or dwelling in the abbey of Siegburg with Conon, [Note: **[Col. 1261D]** Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, dedicated his books *On the Victory of the Word of God* to Canon, or Conon, Abbot of Siegburg. He became Bishop of Regensburg in 1126 and died in 1130. He seems to have governed the abbey, third in order according to Bucelinus, in 1115 or the following year. That abbey is beyond Cologne, across the Rhine, about three German miles away, **[Col. 1262D]** and is also commonly called Siburg.] abbot of blessed memory, who then ruled that monastery, a man of remarkable holiness, he committed the divine Scriptures to memory. As Solomon says, he waited wisely until the time; and, practising certain preliminaries of his future conversion, he smoothed by tireless premeditation whatever poverty he planned for himself and whatever sufferings and struggles might come upon him.

And lest the ardent spirit of a novice recruit and soldier still untrained should be distressed in any measure by the suspense of careful delay, he was strengthened by the example of his Lord, Master, and Redeemer of all, Jesus Christ. For he read that Christ waited until his own time and hour came, as the Gospel account reports, saying of the Jews: “And they did not seize him, because his hour had not yet come” (John 7:30); and elsewhere, in his own person: “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4); and again: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready” (John 6:7); and again the Evangelist says: “When the feast-day of the Passover of the Jews was drawing near, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 6:4; 13:1), and so forth.

Thus imbued with the new grace of inward virtue but not yet stripped of the garment of outward oldness, [Col. 1262A] he soothed his desire with the hope of more abundant fruit. He wished rather to receive simultaneously both the clothing and the adornment of the new man: the former in the habit of religion, the latter in the dignity of the priesthood. The conferred gifts would thereby be more joyful in proportion as each gift was greater when joined with the other; and thus the malignant spirit would fall more grievously before the eyes of those around him, in proportion as the magnificent King triumphed more gloriously in Norbert.

## Chapter II. Holy orders received; the word of God preached; injury patiently endured

**9. [Chapter III.]** When the long-desired time had now arrived and holy orders were, according to custom, to be celebrated in the Church, the man of God, filled with devout exultation, hastened with every devotion to Lord Frederick, [Col. 1262B] Archbishop of Cologne, asking that he might be ordained first among the others.

On hearing this, the archbishop was greatly astonished that the man now sought of his own accord what he had often declined when offered by others. Yet he willingly and gladly agreed to do what he asked. Norbert immediately added: “I wish to be made both deacon and priest at the same time.”

At this the archbishop, greatly astonished and alarmed, asked what was the reason for a will so sudden and unexpected. He replied: “It is thus in my mind; you cannot know now, but you shall know afterward.” When the archbishop, wishing to know the reason, pressed him more vigorously, the man of God considered within himself that the archbishop was in every way a worthy and fitting person to whom he could and ought to disclose the knowledge of his secrets. Falling at his feet with tears and groaning, seeking and receiving pardon for his sins, he confessed to him the firm and unchanging purpose of his will.

The archbishop therefore saw that the man had resolutely decided upon what he sought. Fearing to violate the welcome and pleasant friendship of one familiar to him, considering also the good which could very easily arise from so praiseworthy a man, and understanding that such things did not happen without divine prompting, he finally consented, although [Note: **[Col. 1262D]** This shows that, before Celestine III, Honorius III, and Innocent III, whose decrees prohibiting it remain extant, this prohibition existed but could be dispensed with by bishops. Below, at no. 24, he “obtained pardon” from Pope Gelasius II for this act.] it was not permitted for these two highest orders to be conferred or received together by anyone—having nevertheless made a dispensation in view of the circumstances and the time.

[Col. 1262D]

**10.** When the hour came for celebrating the office, all who were to be ordained were clothed, according to ecclesiastical custom, in sacred white vestments and arranged in their places. Norbert too stood amid the crowding people: known, as was thought, to all, but unknown, as the truth of the matter stood, to everyone; wondrous before men, but more wondrous before God.

As all looked on and waited, and the sacristan offered him blessed garments for putting on, as the others did, in order to receive holy orders, the man in whose breast the Holy Spirit had already begun his temple turned his hand toward one of his servants standing beside him and signalled that he should bring him a sheepskin garment, which he had deliberately ordered prepared for this purpose.

When it was brought, and all watched with closer attention, he stripped off the varied and many-formed devil—that is, the garment of remarkable value, abounding in costly vanity, purchased from unrighteous mammon, such that no like could be found in the streets of Babylon—and, before them all, put on the one and simple Christ: namely, a garment wholly unusual for worldly people, especially nobles in that region, of the most contemptible price and almost no value. To the companions of his former frivolity it displayed rather a token for ridicule than any evidence of conversion; but to the man of God it was more precious than purple and fine linen.

Then at last he turned his other hand toward the sacristan and put on in addition the garments offered to him, which, as custom required, he would use in receiving holy orders. He paid no attention whatever to what men thought or said about him.

**11.** Having therefore received, according to the vow and desire of his heart, holy orders, and having despised and set aside human judgment of himself, he immediately turned aside and went to the great and renowned monastery of Siegburg. There, among monks religious and devout in all holiness, he might learn the exercise of the priesthood he had received and obtain sure instruction in religious living.

When he had completed about forty days there, he returned to his native soil, going to the church of which he had been, and was still said to be, a secular canon. **[Chapter IV.]** On the following day, his dean and fellow canons offered him, as it is customary in many places to offer the newly ordained, the celebration of the mysteries of the conventual High Mass. He humbly agreed that he would do so.

When the appointed hour arrived, he approached the altar, and all that the service required was solemnly performed as far as the Gospel. Once the Gospel had been read, the man of God, inflamed with zeal of divine fervour and with the fire of the Holy Spirit growing warm in his heart, [Col. 1263D] turned toward the church porch.
