Applying the ministry of his voice and the office of his tongue to the word of God, he began, as divinely inspired, to bring forth from the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge devout counsels for the life to come and salutary exhortations to eternal blessedness.

He further added and showed how all pleasures of this life are fluid and perishable: brief in duration, cheap in worth, neither worthy of love nor fit for possession; glory unstable, ambition blind, riches fleeting, delight momentary, rest untrustworthy, security uncertain, joys vain, prosperity false. He showed, finally, how in all these things biting cares and wearying anxieties spur on the desiring person and harass the possessor. For whatever is greedily possessed in this life is not lost without pain, since what is desired is neither acquired without difficulty nor kept without danger.

He bent and directed the whole force of his discourse toward his fellow canons, without expressly identifying anyone, yet repeatedly dwelling especially upon matters that would more sharply pierce their consciences. He threatened sternly and heightened the vengeance, affirming and establishing—and with many necessary arguments incontrovertibly asserting—that the severity of divine strictness allows no dishonourable deed to remain unavenged and leaves no unlawful act unpunished; for “those who do such things,” as the Apostle says, “shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:21).

Afterward he returned to the altar and carried the begun mysteries of the most holy Mass through to their conclusion.

**12.** Again, the following day, when all had taken their seats in chapter as customary, he first took up a book and began to address the dean. He showed from the words of [Note: **[Col. 1263D]** At the Council of Aachen, held in 816 under Louis the Pious, a pattern for the institution of canons was prescribed from the holy Fathers, principally from the rules handed down by Saints Isidore and Gregory: from the latter in the book *Pastoral Care*, and from the former in the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* and *On the Highest Good*. This is clear to anyone consulting the said council, which in all editions has the relevant passages of each Father indicated either in the margin or in the headings. The same could have been done in those martyrologies in which we find, appended to each day, some sentence drawn from the said rule—in the Paris editions of Usuard of 1490 and 1536. It would be very useful to restore this wholesome practice for clerics, who often have no supply of instruction suited to their state. Moreover, Part II, p. 197 of Holstenius’s edition of the *Code of Rules* contains the Rule of the Monks of Saint Isidore. Whether this was seen by the Fathers at Aachen has not yet been possible to determine through comparison.] the blessed Gregory and Isidore, whose rule they claimed to observe, that he, who was set over all and their teacher, ought to call them back to the straight path of honourable and holy life.

The elders and prelates, hearing this, silently considered the matter, as wise men, according to what is written: “The wise man delays and reserves [his answer] for later” (Proverbs 29:11); and because they did not presume in any way to resist the truth and the Spirit who was speaking. But the younger men, who are accustomed to give less heed to the things of God, murmuring to one another and mocking apart, attributed it to his former frivolity. Consequently, they departed from there, showing him only outward [sole] reverence, both because his authority carried weight among them and because he displayed the badge and habit of some religious order.

But he, somehow discerning and observing from afar the approaches and byways of each one, on the next day, when they had gathered again, began to cry out against them, identifying each by name: who had done or said what was wholly unlawful, where, at what hour, and with whom.

**13.** As he continued in this manner for very many days, he seemed already intolerable to them. And because, as the divine saying declares, “no prophet is accepted in his own country,” while God more deeply ordered his path for the salvation of many, a malignant spirit, by God’s hidden permission, crept into their hearts—the spirit “that works in the children of unbelief” (Luke 4:24), such as they then were. They stirred up against him a most undistinguished cleric, of lowly rank and humble fortune.

As this man spoke against him with rash and audacious presumption and overwhelmed him with the roughness of insults, he even, seized by incredible madness, befouled Norbert’s face with spittle. The man of God, receiving so great an outrage, restrained himself and kept silent. Having wiped his face and attributed the matter to his own sins, he chose to give way before God to tears rather than vengeance.

In this deed, as may be understood, he learned by experience how much strength, through God’s grace, remained in him for enduring greater things for righteousness’ sake. Indeed, from the testimony of many we have learned that the cleric by whom he was insulted with spittle was such a person that, had Norbert himself ordered him dragged through the mud and plunged into it by the cooks of his kitchen, no one would have said anything but: “It was well done.”

These and similar matters are related about him chiefly for this reason: visible miracles are marvellous to the simple and unlearned, but the patience and virtues of the saints are to be admired and imitated by those who gird themselves for Christ’s warfare. Thus those who have shared in the labour and endurance may also share in the recompense; and thereby the reward may not be unequal for persons whose cause in their purpose is not dissimilar.

## Chapter III. Why and how the saints suffer evils; steadfastness of faith in Saint Norbert

**14. [Chapter V.]** For [Note: **[Col. 1265D]** The following matter through no. 20 is absent from some manuscripts and from Surius, because it is a doctrinal treatise with little bearing on the Life; it is nevertheless retained, lest **[Col. 1266D]** the work be thought mutilated.] if, as the divine saying declares, “Nothing happens on earth without a cause” (Job 1), and if the highest and principal distinction of a rational creature is to know the causes of things that happen, then surely no one doubts that the adversities which saints suffer in this world are worthy both of being related and of being understood—not whether they exist, but whether they are adversities of saints. For the cause of things cannot be known when their outcome is unknown.

Once a cause has been understood and known, then at last each person is readily moved, from within himself and as though by a spontaneous, voluntary impulse of his own, toward the end, as the consideration of advantage or loss dictates, and toward imitating or avoiding what is set before him. For in every matter carefully considered, two things chiefly present themselves: namely, the cause, by knowledge of which the inward faculty of the mind is nourished; and the effect, by use of which the outward sense of the body is assisted.

Hence there is a twofold apprehension of things: one by experience according to use, pertaining to the outward bodily sense; the other by knowledge according to understanding, pertaining to the inward faculty of the mind. Since the nature and motion of these two—the soul and the body, and again reason and sense—are different and opposed, it often happens either that reason, when exercised, weakens sense and removes its obstinacy in feeling; or, conversely, that sense, when strengthened, overwhelms reason and blunts the keenness of understanding.

Accordingly, when reason is exercised toward virtue with bodily sense subjected to it, a person acts courageously; but when sense is nourished toward pleasure with reason overwhelmed, a person endures in a bestial way. This is why persons devoted to the senses of the flesh and accustomed to bodily things neither seek reason nor attend to cause, supposing that everything comes about through chance and unforeseen movements. But those in whom reason flourishes and the light of intellect shines forth inquire diligently and readily perceive that nothing ever happens, nor indeed can happen, without a definite and rational cause.

15. Therefore, if you see a man entangled in visible things, [Col. 1266B] relying upon the judgment of the senses, caring for the flesh, asserting chance, defining fortune, blaspheming Mercury, do not ask him why holy, righteous, and good men suffer so many evils in this world although they do none of these things; for such a man counts it as nothing either to know what they suffer or to imitate what they do. But he for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:22), who can truly say with Paul, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14), bearing a devout concern for his salvation—such a one undoubtedly observes anxiously and considers carefully what the saints suffer for a time, in this life alone, by the debt of the human condition, and to what end they are brought by such suffering through the mercy of divine compassion.

But [Col. 1266C] in this distribution three things must especially be considered: namely, what each person suffers, why, and finally what follows from it. This may be stated more briefly as punishment, cause, and end. Of punishment the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21); and again: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:28). Of cause it is written: “It is not punishment that makes the martyr, but the cause” (St Augustine, Letters 61 and 167). Therefore the Gospel speaks in the person of the Lord: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). Finally, of the end it is written: “God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Rev. 21:4). And again in [Col. 1266D] the Book of Wisdom: “These are they whom once we held in derision” (Wis. 5:3), and the rest which follows there.

Of these three, punishment comes first in knowledge, and then follows the end. Yet [Note: [Col. 1266D] Some manuscripts read “change” or “alteration of the end.”] in imitation the end comes first and punishment follows. The end persuades us to will; punishment proves whether we can; while the intervening cause distinguishes between the children of the kingdom and the children of Gehenna, as between chaff and wheat—between those who suffer for righteousness and those who are punished according to righteousness.

16. For this reason God, by whose providence the whole [Col. 1267A] world is governed and administered, in order to show himself the most powerful maker and the most just disposer of all things, did not [Note: [Col. 1267D] “He did not prohibit” here means “he did not prevent.”] prevent there being any wicked person. Rather, subjecting to the laws of his rule those who are such through their own wrongful and iniquitous will, by his omnipotence he brings it about that, just as something was made from nothing by him and through him, so likewise by the same one and through the same one either the wicked become good, or those who desire and strive to be good are perfected through the wicked as through suitable instruments. He does not separate or divide them, but permits them to exist intermixed and together.

For these four things—good and something, nothing and evil—are in a sense set apart from one another by degrees, both in the order of consideration and by the condition of their nature. For as much as nothing differs from something, [Col. 1267B] so undoubtedly is evil lower through punishment, because it is nothing, and good higher through merit, because it is, without qualification, something. Accordingly, God, like a king in his commonwealth, disposing and ordering by a wisdom that reaches everywhere throughout the universe of things (Wis. 8), opens the desire of the wicked, or blocks their way, according as he judges fitting, toward attaining what they crave; but he prepares the will of the good by prevening it, and afterward assists their ability.

That what is said may be more certain, both points must be proved from the divine Scriptures. In Psalm 103, after certain works of God have been recalled, the Holy Spirit speaks and says: “How greatly have thy works been magnified, O Lord! Thou hast made all things in wisdom.” And, having again briefly enumerated a few things, it adds: [Col. 1267C] “This dragon, whom thou hast formed to play with it; all things wait upon thee, that thou mayest give them food in due season.” To give food is plainly to open the way toward attaining what they crave. That passage also accords with this meaning which we read in the Gospel: that the demons asked the Lord Jesus Christ to let them enter into the swine (Matt. 8:31). For what the prophetic utterance says, “They wait,” the evangelist Matthew expresses as “They begged”; and what this one says, “When thou givest to them,” that one says, “Go”; and what this one says, “They shall gather,” that one says, “They went.”

After this the Prophet continues and says: “But when thou turnest away thy face, they shall be troubled.” This is to block the way, restraining a perverse will [Col. 1267D] and binding it with certain invisible bonds. Something similar to this is found in the Book of Tobit: “Then the angel Raphael seized the demon and bound him in the desert of Upper Egypt” (Tob. 8:3).

17. Concerning prevening mercy, Psalm 58 says: “And his mercy shall go before me”; concerning following mercy, Psalm 22 says: “And his mercy shall follow me.” The remaining words of both psalms, from beginning to end, bear witness to this sense. For the former begins with adversity and proceeds to describe his tribulation, as one not yet forestalled; but the latter, beginning from prosperity, describes God’s benefits toward him as one already forestalled. Therefore [Col. 1268A] the former prays with groaning: “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God”; but the latter relates with joy: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing.”

Thus the good share, promiscuously and without distinction, these temporal advantages and disadvantages with the wicked—sometimes in greater measure, the better they are found to be. But these good things happen to the good so that they may be believed to come from God and be distributed by him; whereas they happen to the wicked so that those who are good, or wish to become good, may not esteem such things greatly. Likewise these temporal evils fall upon both good and wicked persons: upon the former, that they may be proved, cleansed, or exercised; upon the latter, lest their crimes and iniquities be thought unknown to God or neglected by him. Thus the depth of the divine counsel is worthy of greater reverence, in proportion as it is more incomprehensible to human [Col. 1268B] understandings.

Therefore we also, who fear the punishments of the wicked and desire the rewards of the good, ought not, having heard and understood these things, to harden our hearts. Rather, stirred by the examples of both, as by divine voices, we should strive, with the help of our Lord, to attain what we desire: to amend our life, correct our actions, instruct our character, and always advance our understanding, will, and purpose toward better things.

18. [CHAP. VI.] Thus the man of God Norbert, tested as was said above and now found in every respect worthy in one thing, was still sought out and examined by a greater trial, so that the working of divine providence upon him might appear more clearly, according to what is written: “He who loves his son [Col. 1268C] is diligent in chastising him” (Ecclus. 30:1). For after these things, while he was wearing himself down by incredible fasting and abstinence, persisting day and night in vigils and prayers, it happened once, as he was customarily celebrating Mass in a certain crypt, that a spider fell into the already consecrated chalice. At the sight of this the priest was stunned, having life and death before his eyes; for the spider was of no small size. What was a man to do whose faith was now firmly established in the Lord? Lest he waste any part of the prepared sacrifice, he chose rather to undergo the danger, and drank all that was there.

The sacrifice having been completed, he expected to die immediately. Therefore, while he stood unmoved from his place before the altar, commending to the Lord in prayer the end he expected, he was provoked by an itching of the nostrils; and, as he scratched, a sudden fit of sneezing expelled the spider whole through his nostrils. Behold, God again did not yet will the death of his priest, whom he foresaw would be useful to him, but rather his faith. In this event it was most plainly discovered both how great this man’s faith in the Lord was, and how great the Lord’s kindness toward him. For two things were necessary to him for what was being prepared: patience and faith—patience as weapons, faith as strength; patience, lest he yield unarmed; faith, lest he fail through weakness.

Accordingly, he acquired such faith that throughout all the days of his life he was readily preferred, by the common judgment of all, to all then living. Moreover, that man was without any doubt commendably endowed with the gift of the other virtues; but faith is so carefully praised in him above the rest because it was undoubtedly through it that he accomplished so many things, according to what we read in the Gospel, where the Lord says to his disciples: “If you had faith as a grain of mustard seed, and said to this mountain, ‘Move,’ it would move” (Matt. 17:19). And again: “All things are possible to him who believes” (Mark 9:22). The Apostle also agrees in these words, saying: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought…” (Heb. 11:33), and the rest which follows there, undoubtedly commending faith.

Hence, when someone was saying in what respect each outstanding man of his own time excelled, he said: “In Norbert faith is eminent; in [Note: [Col. 1269D] St Bernard praises St Norbert in Letter 8 to St Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne; Letter 38 to Prince Theobald; Letter 79 to Luke, Abbot of Cuissy; Letter 56 to Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres; and Letter 126 to Pope Innocent II.] Bernard of Clairvaux charity; in [Note: [Col. 1269D] Milo, disciple of St Norbert, first abbot of the Church of St Judoc in the Wood, now called the monastery of Dommartin, situated in the territory of Artois near Hesdin. In 1131, on 15 February, he was made bishop of Thérouanne; he died on 16 July 1159. We discussed him among those omitted on 15 February, for there are those who call him blessed or even saint. Polycarpus offers a lengthy defence of him against Peter of Cluny’s bitter letter, as having been carried away by excessive zeal—also, in St Bernard’s judgment—in the affair of the monastery of St Bertin, on whose behalf Milo stood.] Milo of Thérouanne humility.” Therefore, if anything be said of him which exceeds the ordinary condition of human custom, it ought not seem incredible to one who is not such a man; rather, he should refer it at once to him who gave this man, through grace, faith, and through faith the power to do such things.

## CHAPTER IV. Persecutions endured; pilgrimages undertaken. Authority to preach obtained.

19. [CHAP. VII.] Therefore, protected by the shield of patience and strengthened by the power of faith, preaching to all and proclaiming the word of God “in season,” as it is said, “and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2), and making himself better each day, he lived for three years in the same garb. When he was persecuted by those to whom his preaching was unwelcome, he sometimes withdrew to a certain monastery of monks at Siegburg, three leagues from Cologne; sometimes to the monastery of regular canons called [Note: [Col. 1269D] The monastery of Rode, in the diocese of Cologne and duchy of Limburg, is mentioned by Caesarius, book XI, chapter 42, and is indicated to have been near the town of Wurm. Although no town of that name now exists, there is nevertheless a river so called, either named from it or giving it its name; rising near Aachen, it descends to the Rur in Jülich territory and meanwhile passes through the notable town of Herzogenrath, French Rolducq. Beside it stands the abbey of regular canons, commonly called Kloster-rath, whose abbot and monks, when writing Latin, call themselves Rothenses or Rodenses. The abbey lies roughly halfway between Jülich and Maastricht on the Meuse, and is no less distant from the saints than from Cologne. See 5 June, Life of St Gurlach, chapter 7, note d.] Rode; but more frequently to a certain hermit named Lidulphus, [Note: [Col. 1270C] Also called Ludolfus and Ludulfus. He is otherwise still unknown to us, except that Gelenius, in *Sacrarium Coloniense*, book III, Syntagma 22, says that the parish church of St Mary on the Shore, otherwise Liskercken, was called by the ancients the church of St Lisolphus. Since he finds no trace elsewhere of a St Lisolphus, he conjectures that this is the Lidolfus named in the Life of St Norbert. And on p. 752, compiling a register of saints and venerable persons whose feast-days are unknown, he says: “The Venerable Ludolfus, or Lovo, Count of Cleves, is said to have taken a wife about the year 755, and, after raising an heir by her, to have embraced the life of a hermit on Mount St Joachim near Bedburg,” by the Erft River, four leagues west of Cologne. The name is suitable, but the date and place disagree—perhaps through the confusion of two persons into one.] a man of remarkable holiness [Col. 1270A] and abstinence who lived the clerical life. He fled to men of this kind in order to refresh his spirit whenever he was persecuted by those to whom the words of truth were tiresome. He stayed among them in order both to learn from them the rules of holy life and to receive an increase of heavenly hope. Yet sometimes, returning home from the holy men, he tirelessly persisted in the task of preaching which he had begun.

[CHAP. VIII.] While matters stood thus, it happened that a certain council was held in the German lands, near the town called Fritzlar, [Note: [Col. 1270D] Urspergensis mentions this council at Fritzlar in Hesse, held in 1118, and adds that another was then held at Cologne, at which he writes that Norbert was present. But, taking one for the other, he is mistaken.] before Lord [Note: [Col. 1270D] Conon, or Kuno, a German and Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina, created by Paschal II.] Conon, legate of the Apostolic See. Taking occasion from this, bishops, archbishops, abbots, and many other persons who had assembled there to deal with matters concerning themselves, after taking counsel [Col. 1270B] summoned the man of God. When he was present, they began, by the common agreement of all, to rebuke him before the aforesaid lord with accusations: namely, why he had usurped the office of preaching; why in that preaching he attacked them so sharply with words and reproaches, although he had been sent by no one and had not been appointed their superior; why besides he displayed a religious habit, when religion and possession were in no respect compatible; and on what grounds he had cast aside costly garments, when the custom of the country did not allow this—especially among nobles such as he was—that while they remained in the world they should wear garments of lambskin or goatskin.

20. To all these charges the wise man, taught by God, answered wisely, saying: “If I am accused concerning religion: ‘Pure and undefiled religion before God [Col. 1270C] and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself unspotted from this world’ (Jas. 1:27). If concerning preaching: it is written, ‘He who causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way shall save his soul from death and shall cover a multitude of sins’ (Jas. 5:20). If concerning authority: it is given to us in the reception of the priesthood, when it is said, ‘Receive authority, and be proclaimers [Col. 1271A] of the words of God.’ If, finally, concerning dress: the first shepherd of the Church teaches us that a precious garment is not acceptable before God (1 Pet. 3:3); John the Baptist was clothed in camel’s hair; and Cecilia wore a hair-shirt next to her flesh; and, greater than all these, almighty God at the beginning of the world made and gave to the first-created Adam not a purple garment but a tunic of skins” (Gen. 3:21).

Thus undefeated, assisted by divine grace, he departed from them, because their testimony against him was not admissible. Deprived, therefore, of every comfort and supported only by divine help, he continually devoted himself to prayers and psalmody, being wholly opposed to the vanity and pleasure of worldly people. Thus he was against all, and all were against him.

[Col. 1271B] 21. [CHAP. IX.] Then, having resolved to pass the whole following night without sleep and to pray to God that he who is the giver of right counsel and helper of good works would, according to the good pleasure of his will, direct his counsel and assist his purpose, he spent the night in prayer. At earliest dawn, resting his cheek a little upon his hand, behold, the adversary appeared, hoping to accomplish something by himself, although previously he had been able to do nothing through the bodily members by which he had plotted against him. Mocking and jeering, he said: “Come now, come now; you have proposed much. But to what end do you hope to arrive, when you could not even persevere in your resolution for one night?”

The man awoke and, not ignorant of the snares of the ensnaring enemy, replied: “Who would believe your threats, when from the beginning, as Truth bears witness, you have been a liar and the father of lies?” (John 8:44.) Thus the evil spirit departed from him in confusion.

But the man of God, seeing that all were against him and that truth, to which he bore witness, was now being choked by the overflowing falsehood of many—especially because their sin became greater through the proclamation of the words of God, according to the Lord’s saying, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22)—and understanding also that they would assail him even with the bringing of a false accusation, grieved and feared more for their loss and destruction than for any harm they could inflict upon him. He came to his archbishop and [Col. 1272A] resigned to him whatever benefices and revenues he had acquired in the Church, in which he had been greatly enriched.

22. Moreover, he sold his houses and all other things [Note: [Col. 1271D] Chrysostomus Vander Sterre, in his Life written in the Brabant vernacular, states that he bestowed a large part of his possessions in founding a monastery on the high hill of Firstenbergh near the town of Xanten. This is indeed proved by a charter to be published in chapter 3 of the *Analecta*; but it must have occurred immediately at the beginning of his conversion, if not earlier. The place afterward passed to Cistercian nuns, who migrated to Xanten after it was destroyed in war. There still remains a rustic village with a small chapel and a round stone turret, visible for three leagues or more because of its elevated position. Our Stephen Pighius, describing the journey of Prince Charles of Neuburg, says it was also called Varesberg, that is, Mount of Varus: namely, of the man who guarded the Rhine entrusted to him by Augustus for three years and afterward became still more famous through his own disaster and that of the Roman legions.] which he possessed either as patrimony or by another hereditary right. Distributing all his household equipment to the poor and keeping nothing for himself except ten marks of silver, one mule, and one chapel for celebrating Mass, he took with him only two lay companions for his journey and, following the example of the patriarch Abraham, undertook a voluntary pilgrimage.

When he came to a certain castle called Huy, [Note: [Col. 1271D] Huy, a renowned town in the territory of Liège, [Col. 1272D] situated on the Meuse between Liège and Namur.] situated on the River Meuse, he considered within himself that he ought, being naked, to follow the naked cross. There he distributed to the poor that very property which he had kept for himself, [Col. 1272B] retaining only the chapel in order to celebrate the mysteries of the most holy Mass.

[CHAP. X.] Thus, having completely laid down and cast off the burden of temporal possessions, with the strength of a mind now well ordered and prepared to endure utter poverty and want, he entered upon the arduous and lofty path of holy life. Barefoot, therefore, wearing a woollen tunic and a cloak sufficient for him, without roof and without fixed dwelling, overcoming terrible winters and harsh ice by strength of spirit, with Christ alone as guide, he set out with the two companions of his exceptional purpose toward [Note: [Col. 1272D] The town of Saint-Gilles, in Occitania and the diocese of Nîmes, where there was formerly a famous Benedictine abbey, later transferred to the Knights Hospitaller.] St Gilles. When he arrived there and, by the ordering grace of God, who does not forsake those who hope in him, found Pope Gelasius, successor to [Col. 1272C] Paschal, [Note: [Col. 1272D] Fleeing the rage of the schismatics in 1118, Gelasius “under the Lord’s guidance arrived safe and unharmed, with all his companions, at the harbour of the town of Saint-Gilles.” So says Pandulf the subdeacon, who was present, in his Life; see it in the *Propylaeum* for May, and Baronius under the year 1118, no. 16, where he adds that “Norbert obtained from the pontiff the office of preaching.”] he confessed to him the will and purpose of his heart. He then requested and obtained from the said pontiff pardon especially for having received simultaneously the two highest orders contrary to the ordinances of the canons.

23. The Pope, seeing his prudence and the Spirit of God dwelling in him, wished to keep him with himself. But Norbert begged and implored him not to bind him by this obedience. He explained how he had squandered himself in indulgence at the courts of kings and pontiffs, and that what the Pope invited him to do was wholly unsuitable to his youth [Note: [Col. 1272D] From this some think they can determine the year in which the saint was born, though they differ according to their differing definitions of the limit of youth. Polycarpus believes that he was thirty, the canonical age for priesthood, when he was ordained about 1115, and consequently that he was born about 1085.] or to the penance he had undertaken. If the Pope commanded him to be a canon, monk, hermit, or even a travelling pilgrim, he would gladly [Col. 1273A] obey wholly in every respect.

[CHAP. XI.] But the holy pontiff, seeing the man’s steadfastness and the good devotion of his mind, and having heard and learned of the persecution which he had suffered for the word of truth, granted him permission and authority to preach the word of God not merely where he had previously preached, but wherever in the world he might wish and be able. He imposed this upon him, exhorting and commanding him in his own person. Moreover, he prohibited those who had earlier opposed him from envy from hindering even the simple folk, should they judge his preaching superfluous or less useful. And, in order that this might be valid and stable, he confirmed it by letters and seal of his authority.

[CHAP. XII.] Having therefore received, by apostolic command, the obedience to preach, he began to return in the midst of the severe rigour of winter, again barefoot as he had gone. For that man burned with such love of God—something which must not be passed over—that neither the severity of cold, nor hunger, nor bodily weariness recalled him from what he had begun. On the journey the snow sometimes reached his knees and at other times his thighs; yet it could not detain him even for a single day.

24. Except on Sundays, he took no food other than Lenten food and then only in the evening; indeed, he used fish or wine very rarely. His body had no rest by day, while his spirit had no rest either by night or by day; for that man was of singular faith and great strength. As he proceeded in this most honourable and praiseworthy vigour of body and mind, passing through Orléans, a certain subdeacon joined his company. Thus, with three companions, he came to Valenciennes on the Saturday before Palm Sunday.

On the next day he preached to the people, scarcely yet knowing or understanding anything of that language, [Note: [Col. 1273D] He means the poor, uneducated, untaught, and rustic people. “The Roman language” was what is now called the Gallic or French language. This is said below, no. 27, to have happened in June 1118; Palm Sunday then fell on 7 April and Easter on the 14th.] namely Romance, because he had never learned it. Yet he did not doubt that, if he began the word of God in his native tongue, the Holy Spirit—who had once taught the diversity of one hundred and twenty languages—would make the barbarous German tongue or the difficulty of Latin eloquence understandable to his hearers. By God’s grace he was so well received by all that they compelled him to refresh somewhat his exhausted and weakened limbs there.

Since he would not consent by any argument—for his face was set toward the diocese of Cologne, because of his knowledge of the people and language [Col. 1274A] there—it happened by God’s dispensation that, when his companions were struck by a sudden illness, he could not then proceed farther. The man therefore remained in order to care for his sick companions, who within the octave of Easter in the following days rested in the Lord with a blessed end. Two of the laymen lie buried in the suburb near Valenciennes, in the church of Blessed Peter beside the marketplace, on the left side toward the west. The subdeacon, having become a monk, lies buried in the church of St Mary, situated in the same town. [Note: [Col. 1273D] Peter Doutremannus, recounting the same matter from the *Chronicle of Prémontré* in his history of Valenciennes, p. 120, says that the church of St Peter stood near the marketplace—which now occupies the middle of the city but was then a suburb—and near the chapel of the leper-house. He calls the other church, of the Blessed Virgin, the principal church of the place, as it still is, under the title “Major,” in distinction from another church of the same name belonging to an abbey in that city, from which one of the gates takes its name.] 

## CHAPTER V. Conversation with the Bishop of Cambrai. Hugh taken as companion. Sermons preached.

25. Meanwhile, while he remained there to care for his companions, [Col. 1274B] it happened that Lord [Note: [Col. 1274D] Burchard, made bishop in 1115, later gave the church of St Foillan in Hainaut to the Premonstratensians and confirmed the Church of Tongerloo to the same order.] Burchard, Bishop of Cambrai, a man of pious and venerable memory, was passing through that place on Wednesday, the day immediately before the Lord’s Supper. On hearing this, the man of God—because they had known one another while still living in the world—went to speak with him.

Coming to the door of the house in which the bishop was staying, he found there, before the entrance and by God’s will, one of the bishop’s clerics standing. In a low voice he asked him to introduce him to the bishop, for frost lay upon the ground and the man went barefoot. The said cleric entered, spoke with the bishop, and brought the man in. As they spoke together for a while, they recognized each other and immediately remembered their former familiarity. The bishop [Col. 1274C] looked at the man, marvelled and was exceedingly astonished within himself, and burst into tears; he could not restrain himself, for his heart was moved toward him. Throwing himself upon Norbert’s neck and crying out in pious lamentation, he said with a sigh: “O Norbert, who would ever have believed or imagined such things of you?”

The cleric who had introduced him stood there and saw the bishop’s affection for the man, but did not understand their conversation because they were speaking German. Venturing forward, he asked what this meant. The bishop immediately said: “This man whom you see thus was brought up with me at the royal court, a nobleman and so abounding in luxuries that he refused my bishopric when it was offered to him.” [Note: [Col. 1274D] The bishopric had been vacant, after the death of Blessed Odo, for a year and a half or more from 19 June 1113. Norbert seems to have refused the bishopric offered within that period because, though not yet converted from the world, he nevertheless abhorred investitures; he knew that the privilege extorted by them, but annulled by the pope and council in 1112, was null.]

[Col. 1274D] 26. Hearing these things, that cleric was immediately bathed in tears, both because he saw his lord weeping and because his mind and spirit overflowed in honey-sweet charity toward the love of so great a [Col. 1275A] man. He himself also had the desire to leave the world, and had long since chosen in his heart this manner of life which he saw in that man; with excessive devotion he desired daily to follow him. Yet, speaking no word of this, he kept the matter only within the secret of his conscience, silently considering it because his ways were about to change.

Meanwhile the man of God, remaining in that same place, awaited the end of his companions. When those by whose comfort he had frequently overcome many journeys, the severity of the roads, and the cold snow, were received by God—as stated above—for the merit of their holy life, he himself was next seized by a severe sickness. The bishop waited to see what end the illness which had befallen him would have, and visited his friend through a certain archdeacon and certain other persons of his household. The aforesaid cleric, ardently attached to him in love, anxiously inquired from day to day whether and when he would recover.

After he had recovered, the cleric came to him; and, having confessed the vow and desire of his heart and promised that he would go with him, the man immediately stretched his hands to heaven and, giving boundless thanks, said: “Lord God, today I asked you to give me a companion.” For he supposed that the cleric would remain with him at once and return nowhere further to settle any affairs. But the cleric had not decided this; rather, he first wished to arrange his matters. Therefore, after [Col. 1275C] saying, “I have matters of my own to put in order,” the man was saddened at such words and, in a tone expressing tender feeling, said: “Come, brother: if this is from God, it will not be dissolved.” The other at once replied: “You have bound me with an indissoluble bond, Father.”

Thus he departed and, having arranged his affairs as best he could—or left them unarranged—returned shortly afterward, as quickly as he could. Thereafter he followed the man of God Norbert without turning back, judging it wicked and unworthy to permit, for the sake of any temporal matter, any delay in things pleasing to God, or to allow any interval of postponement amid so great an ardour of devotion.

27. [CHAP. XIII.] Therefore, in the year one thousand one hundred and eighteen after the incarnation [Col. 1275D] of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the month of June, while the man of God was still at the castle of Valenciennes, deprived of all the consolation of his companions mentioned above, so that divine mercy toward its servant Norbert might appear more manifest and become more welcome, after they had departed this life Lord Hugh approached him. This was the name of the aforesaid cleric, who succeeded him next in the government of the [Note: [Col. 1275D] Hugh died in 1164, on 10 February. On that date we gave some notice of him among those omitted, because we then learned from our Premonstratensian brethren that no ecclesiastical cult existed for him. Later, however, in a certain chapter attended by many abbots, his body was elevated, and certain relics were brought to Antwerp by Abbot Norbert van Cauwerve and placed in the same shrine with the relics of St Norbert. Therefore, if more certain documents concerning his cult, life, and miracles are produced, they will be given in a supplement.] Church of Prémontré. [Col. 1276A] Leaving all things, he joined Norbert in the same life and poverty, being indeed a man of devout and holy conduct.

The man rejoiced and gave boundless thanks to God; comparing inward inspiration with God’s outward gift, he was encouraged to preach. Now knowing and confidently trusting in the will of God, he went about castles, villages, and towns, preaching and reconciling those wickedly at variance, restoring long-standing hatreds and wars to peace. They were true poor men of Christ, freely giving their labour to others and asking or receiving nothing from anyone, even for food or clothing, unless something was offered them for Mass. Whatever it was, they distributed it all to the poor, mindful of the Holy Spirit and the Prophet, who [Col. 1276B] praises the man “who has scattered abroad and given to the poor, whose righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9).

For they were secure in the grace of God, who would provide for his servants what was necessary. Holding firmly that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth (Heb. 11:13), they could be touched by no mark of ambition, since all their hope depended upon heaven. For it seemed base to a generous spirit that one who had despised all things for Christ should, like a dog returning to its vomit, employ any contrivance in the pursuit of mean plunder and pant after contemptible payments.

28. He was therefore brought into such admiration and affection in the hearts of all that, wherever they turned while travelling and approached villages or fortified towns, even the shepherds, leaving their flocks, would run ahead in haste and cry aloud to the people that the servants of God were coming. [Col. 1276C] Then bells were rung; then crowds of people of every sex, age, and condition flocked in groups to the church, gladly heard the solemnities of the Mass, and still more gladly received the exhortations and admonitions of the words spoken. After the sermon, moreover, considerable discussion was held concerning frequent confession, the performance of penance, married persons, possessions, and how those who die in such conditions ought to be saved. After questions and answers had been given and received on all these matters, they were finally led to lodging toward evening.

For a man counted himself greatly fortunate and worthy before God if he deserved to receive him as a guest. Sometimes one person led the little donkey, another seized its halter, another forcibly detained the young man whom they had alone to look after the donkey. For who would not marvel that men should lead such a new manner of life upon earth, possessing nothing from the earth and seeking nothing? For if, as Solomon says, “It is joy to the righteous to do justice” (Prov. XXI, 15), the man of God especially rejoiced that he had fulfilled that evangelical command in carrying out his preaching: that he should carry neither bag, nor sandals, nor two tunics (Mark VI, 8), except a staff, [Col. 1277A] a chapel-kit [capella] for celebrating Mass, and a psalter or some other little book, I know not which.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] *Capella*: that is, the equipment of a chapel—for example, a chalice and the other necessities of Mass. Thus above, no. 22, the saint is said to have reserved for himself “one chapel-kit.”]

Nor did the holy man permit a seat to be prepared, or a table to be set for his refreshment. The ground was his seat and his knees his table; his dishes were seasoned with salt, and with nothing else; their drink was water—unless perhaps they were constrained by invitations from bishops, archbishops, or abbots in cities, abbeys, and similar places, where, for the peace of those dining together, they did not wish to exceed their hosts’ measure and custom.

29. For these persons, showing them every kindness, even assembled them in their chapters with fear and reverence so that he might address them; and after the sermon, when opportunity was given, they assailed him with many questions [Col. 1277B]: concerning orders, rules, dress, and the various institutions of the holy Fathers; concerning the life and conduct of prelates; the subjection and obedience of subjects; the heavenly sacraments and heavenly life; the recompense and blessedness of the elect; the glory of the everlasting age and the felicity of good spirits; the indiscriminate occurrence in this world of tribulations among good and evil alike; and the end to which the deeds of each will come when the Judge appears at the end of the ages.

Indeed, questions of this sort, so numerous and various, could not have been without the prompting and deceit of the enemy who lay in ambush. This was afterward proved, since some surrounded the man with their many questions in order to test him, others in order to deceive him, though most in order to learn, [Col. 1277C] so that they might catch him in speech and discover whether he truly preached a manner of life so unfamiliar in modern times. But although the holy man knew for certain, from their own admissions, that they were plotting against him, he feared none of this. Rather, crying out and lifting up his voice as a trumpet, he declared the crimes of sinners; what he preached with his mouth he demonstrated by deed; and what he performed he confirmed by signs and miracles.

Thus, travelling everywhere, he recalled many from error; by urging penance, he restrained many from crime; and he brought many who were at variance back to harmony. For these and similar reasons God bestowed upon him such love and favour among the people that scarcely anyone could be satisfied with seeing and speaking with him. And he himself had such charity toward the people that, for a long time, leaving the lodgings of churches, he preferred to lodge in the midst of cities and fortified towns, where he gladly received all who came to him. Moreover, in all these things he was, beyond what can be spoken or believed, patient in vigils, diligent in labour, gracious in speech, pleasing in appearance, kind toward the simple, and severe against the enemies of the Church. In those times none of those who seemed religious obtained such favour among the people or such frequent attendance.

30. [CHAPTER XIV.] The holy man, therefore, who had newly received Hugh, newly a novice, [Col. 1278A] as the companion he had asked from God, addressed him with words of this sort and sustained him with many admonitions, lest he should falter amid so great an austerity of penance. And lest he should shrink from poverty, he set before him the example of Blessed Lawrence, who scattered the treasures of the holy pontiff Sixtus. He desired that Hugh, gradually putting aside the parching heat of the secular world, should draw from the fountain of heavenly refreshment and sweetness. He promised him likewise what Truth itself has promised: that whoever drinks from it shall never thirst (John IV, 13).

He also taught him how a sinner ought to be reconciled and draw near to God; by what pursuits, labours, and virtues any righteous person may attain the fellowship of good spirits. He showed how great is the power of humility, [Col. 1278B] by which heaven is reached; of simplicity, by which it is entered; what obedience is like, by which one comes to knowledge of God’s hidden things; what patience is like, by which strength of soul is possessed; what chastity is like, which makes one near to God; what virginity is like, which walks with him; and what poverty is like, which causes one to possess the kingdom of heaven. The man of God, filled with these things, repeated these and similar teachings many times from day to day for the sake of exhortation.

## CHAPTER VI. Discords removed and peace established.

31. [CHAPTER XV.] Therefore, to relate specifically some matters which have been stated generally: it happened one day, as he passed through a certain fortified town called Fosses,

[Note: [Col. 1278D] Fosses, a town in the territory of Liège, where St Ultan rests, as we said in his Acts on the Kalends of May.]

that crowds of people, clergy and laity alike, assembled, marvelling at this unfamiliar way of life—especially because they knew the companion whom he had received. Understanding from the grace granted him by God that he was a minister of concord and peace, they began earnestly to beg him to rest with them for a little while. They declared that in that region there was a very great conflict born of deadly hatred, from which, they affirmed, no fewer than sixty persons had been slain; and that, although many religious and powerful persons had long laboured over it, it could not be pacified.

As many said much concerning the matter, it should not be thought accidental, but ordered by divine grace, that a certain man was passing by whose brother had been killed that very week [Col. 1278D] in the same feud. When those standing by saw him, they said: “See, here is one of those of whom we are speaking among ourselves.” Having summoned him, the man of God immediately put his arms around his neck and said:

“My beloved, I am a traveller passing through, and in these parts I have so far asked or received nothing from anyone. But because I see you a young man, well armed and finely appointed, I wish to ask and receive from you my first gift. In view of your evident generosity, I beg you not to refuse me.”

At once that man, moved by a divine prompting and by an impulse of compassion, his eyes filled with tears, replied: “What is there, reverend Father, that could be refused to you by me or by anyone?” When the man of God asked him to forgive the killer of his brother, forgiveness was granted without delay. Nor was it merely granted: from then on he rendered service to the man of God, showing how everything might be pacified and the hostilities wholly reconciled. It was Friday,

[Note: [Col. 1279D] Surius and certain manuscripts read “the second day”; more read “the third.” But from the immediately following Saturday it is clear that “the sixth” must be read. The text was probably VI, which is very easily changed into III, and, by the erasure of one stroke, into II.]

when the matter was first reported to the man of God.

32. On the morning of the following Saturday, both parties of the adversaries met in the village called Monastery,

[Note: [Col. 1279D] Monasterium, commonly Moustier, so called from the monastery founded there by St Amand, two leagues from the city of Namur, as we said on 6 February before this Life, no. 62; and as will again be said on 17 July in the Life of St Fredegand, whose relics rest there.]

and a great multitude from the surrounding district also assembled: partly to see the man of God, of whom unusual things were being reported, and partly to summon the disputants, by whom the whole region was troubled, to reconciliation.

By the command of divine Truth, that man remained praying in a certain room with the door shut almost until the third hour. [Col. 1279B] The people, overcome—as often happens—with weariness and a certain curiosity, began to wonder greatly and murmur; and in their murmuring said to one another: “Why have we assembled? We thought that he would come out, sow the seeds of God’s word, and soften the hard hearts of those at variance with the streams of the fountain of life. Yet he lies hidden away, sleeping and resting, or doing something else according to his own will.”

When they became so impatient that they would endure no longer, they compelled his companion, who had come out to them, to enter and tell him that all were about to leave unless he came out. That companion, being timid, knew that he was praying; he delayed to enter, lest he disturb him in his prayer. [Col. 1279C] But pressed by their importunity, he finally entered and, standing trembling before him, said in a low voice: “Father, the people are waiting, and because you do not show them your presence, they wish to depart.”

He answered: “Be silent, my son. It is not ours to serve God according to the will of men, but according to the will of God.”

Yet not long afterward he rose from prayer and entered the church. Prepared in sacred vestments, he first celebrated the Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary, as is customary on Saturdays; then the Mass

[Note: [Col. 1280D] St Aybert, a priest ordained by Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, at this same period celebrated two Masses each day, one for the living and the other for the dead, as Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant, writes in his Life, published by us on 7 April, no. 14.]

for those dead persons whose deaths had caused the hatred which he desired to pacify. When these had been most devoutly completed according to custom, he came out to preach. But because the hour for dinner had already passed—it was nearly the ninth hour—and many had gone out to eat, [Col. 1279D] he found few to whom he could preach.

For it was his custom, from the abundance of the depths of his charity, to speak to each person according to that person’s measure and capacity, whether few or many, rich or poor. After making a brief prayer, [Col. 1280A] he began to speak and drew breath; and, in a wonderful and ineffable manner, that spirit of charity became like a voice spread abroad, a sound in the hearts of those who had left through weariness. At the sound of the trumpet, each one left food or drink and rushed swiftly to the church from the places and booths where they had sat, as though about to receive a better feast.

33. When the man of God saw the church filled, he shortened his sermon and addressed them thus:

“Men and brethren, when our Lord Jesus Christ sent his disciples to preach, among other commands he gave them this command: that, upon first entering whatever house, they should first say, ‘Peace to this house’ (Matt. X, 12); and if a son of peace were there, their peace would rest upon him [Col. 1280B] (ibid.). We too, made imitators of them not by our merits but solely by the superabundant grace of God, proclaim to you that same peace, which is not to be despised by an unbelieving mind, for it makes one attain everlasting peace.

“You do not, therefore, fail to know why we have assembled. This is not ours, nor from us, since I am a passing stranger and foreigner; it belongs to the power and will of God. But it is yours wholly to yield to his will with devout affection.”

To this all spoke with one voice: “Let the Lord command us through you what is pleasing to him. We have no objection to whatever the Lord, through your direction, may wish to do with us in this affair.”

What more need be said? Both opposing parties went out on either side into the courtyard, with relics placed in the middle; and after a short interval the discord was renounced, concord was made, and peace was confirmed by oath. [Col. 1280C]

34. [CHAPTER XVI.] Since he was not sluggish in such work, nor in the other works of God which, by the office laid upon him and in penance, he had undertaken through divine mercy, he rose at first light the next day and went apart to another village not far away, called Gembloux,

[Note: [Col. 1280D] Gembloux, a town in French Brabant, in the same region as the places mentioned above, where there is a distinguished abbey, discussed by us on 23 May in the Life of St Guibert its founder.]

to preach to the people. There he was received with the greatest devotion, because they had heard that he was both a reporter of God’s words and a bearer of gentle peace.

But in that same region two princes were very bitter enemies; and, as often happens, the whole region had been reduced to devastation [Col. 1280D] and desolation by plundering and fire. Hearing this, and moved by the cries of the people and by compassion for their misery and poverty, the man of God approached the princes with whatever effort he could: first one, then the other. Speaking to the first, he said:

“You are great and powerful, and you ought not to be ignorant that power has been granted you by God. I am the servant of him who sent me to you; you ought to hear me, I say, not for my sake but for the love of him. For your benefit and that of many I have come to you. Hear, therefore, a poor pilgrim; receive the commands of the Lord your God, sent to you through him. Receive, that you may be received by him. Forgive him who harmed you; forgive, that you may be forgiven. Let this be for your own benefit and for the aid of the poor and needy: let your profit be the remission of your sins, relief for the poor, and the restoration of their possessions that have been scattered.”

On hearing this, the prince looked upon the man, whose face was angelic; he considered the humility of his dress and bearing, the eloquence of his speech joined with the simplicity of a dove and the prudence of a serpent. Then he trembled altogether—for all his inward parts were stirred—and, softened in his reply by compassion, said: [Col. 1281B] “Let what you wish be done. There is no sound argument that anyone can raise in contradiction or resistance to your request.”

35. Having thus brought about what he sought through such a disposition, he went from him to the other prince. But the sower of discord, who set his throne in the north, had gone beforehand and so hardened the man’s heart, sown in it the root of his own seed, and closed the eyes of his mind, that no ray of true light was in his mind, no warmth of charity in his heart, by which he might offer the man of God even a small measure of a gracious response.

Seeing the cruelty of that man’s expression, the rolling of his eyes, the savagery of his words, and the hardness of his heart, the man of God at once fell silent lest he cast pearls before a swine. Turning to the companion whom he had with him, he said: “This man is mad; but it will shortly come to pass that he falls backward and is handed over to his enemies to be captured, ensnared, and trampled underfoot.” [Col. 1281C]

He said this, and in that same week the effect followed his words: for he was captured and held by his enemies. Let the hearer know that this has been related so that, in this also, the man of God may be believed to have possessed the spirit of prophecy.

36. [CHAPTER XVII.] Departing from there, he came to a neighbouring village called Colrois.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Colrois, called *Coteri* by Surius, appears to be Couroy, a town not a full league from Gembloux.]

Since his fame had already spread everywhere, people of the neighbouring district gathered to hear the sermon. [Col. 1281D] After Mass had been celebrated and the sermon heard and concluded, he began, as was his custom, to inquire whether there was any dissension among them concerning peace and concord. When they named certain persons among them who were at variance, he began gently to exhort them to withdraw from the conflicts of their old hatred.

One of them, though asked with many prayers, would in no way agree to his request or that of all those standing around. He leapt outside, mounted his horse—for he was a knight—and attempted to flee. But although he savagely spurred the horse again and again, it could not advance even one pace. [Col. 1282A] The others who had remained in the church came out, and people ran together from all sides in immense astonishment and wonder. Some began to cry out mockingly; some, with compassion, to weep; yet all praised God with one voice, who is glorious in his saints and there displayed that same glory before the eyes of sinners.

Confounded with no small shame by the voices of those crying out, the man returned to the church before the man of God. Prostrate, he asked forgiveness; and he promptly and gladly agreed to what had previously been asked of him. He asked for and received absolution because he had offended God’s holy man. Thus was fulfilled in him what is written: “Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek thy name, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXII, 17).

## CHAPTER VII. Praemonstratum begins to be inhabited through the favour of Pope Callixtus and the patronage of the bishop of Laon. Diabolical temptations overcome.

[Col. 1282B]

37. [CHAPTER XVIII.] If, then, the truth of the matter and the order of events according to truth are joined to the preceding causes, this ought in no way to produce weariness or an occasion for disparagement in readers and hearers. For even if some matters appear superfluous to the weary or to any envious persons, they are nevertheless unfolded truthfully by those who saw and heard them, and they cannot be omitted, because the course of events cannot otherwise proceed in sequence and satisfy those who desire to know.

All that has been set forth above is but a little of the many things he did [Col. 1282C] before he gathered brothers. Now there remain very many things for which he laboured in gathering, settling, and preserving them: how he preserved those whom he had bound together by the word of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit in the bond of unity; and how he taught them to be lovers of voluntary poverty and imitators of Christ in complete obedience.

In that same year it happened that Pope Gelasius of blessed memory,

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Gelasius died at Cluny on 29 January [Col. 1282D] 1119; Callixtus II succeeded him in February.]

from whom he had received authority to preach, departed from the world. He was succeeded by Callixtus, bishop of Vienne, a man of pious and holy life and worthy memory. It is established that he was elected at Cluny and, by the common election of all, received in the see of the universal Church the authority, summit of honour, and dignity.

For the aforesaid Pope Gelasius had crossed over with [Col. 1282D] the sounder part of the cardinals in order to visit Holy Mother Church in her members. Sitting at the head, he had heard much of these matters, as one who had been chancellor for many years in the time of Pope Paschal and others; and whatever had happened throughout the world, whether on the right or the left, could not have been unknown to him. Deprived of so great a father, the cardinals and the other sons of the holy Roman Church who had assembled for Gelasius’s funeral sought and received counsel from him who said, “I will not leave you orphans” (John XIV, 18). To complete what his predecessor had begun, Callixtus, [Col. 1283A] giving a favourable beginning upon his arrival, convened a council at Rheims,

[Note: [Col. 1283D] The Council of Rheims began to be held on 20 October 1119.]

where the Church confirmed his accession, and he approved and strengthened what had been well done; and what was found amiss and needed correction, he both corrected by Roman authority and commanded to be corrected.

38. When the man of God heard that the dignity of the apostolic see had been renewed—it was autumn, when the first wintry season begins to grow cold—he went barefoot to Rheims. There he was joyfully received by the bishops and abbots who had assembled, though they were greatly astonished at the excellence of his preaching and answers, and at the severity and harshness of the penance he had undertaken. Although very many of them asked that it be moderated and that indulgence be granted him, he would accept no relaxation whatever as concerned the affliction of his body. [Col. 1283B]

Nevertheless, lest his sound doctrine should be undermined by any detractors—such persons are apt to appear in novelties of this kind—he asked that the letters of apostolic authority which, as stated above, he had received from Pope Gelasius should be renewed. [CHAPTER XIX.] Having received them, the lord pope commanded Bartholomew, venerable bishop of Laon,

[Note: [Col. 1283D] Bishop Bartholomew was consecrated in 1113. He resigned his bishopric in 1150, became a monk at Foigny, and died there on 26 June, on which day we treat of him among the omitted saints. For Hugh, etc., see vol. VI of June, p. 25, col. 2.]

to undertake his care. For the man of God had certain relatives, descended from his mother’s family, in the bishopric and in the same city. Their hearts were moved with compassionate affection for him, and at their prompting the bishop was urged, though unwillingly, to extend him a helping hand for some time. [Col. 1283C]

When the council had been completed and concluded, the pope soon afterward came to Laon. The bishop, having taken counsel with the pope concerning how he might retain him, offered him the church of St Martin, situated in the suburb, where a few brothers lived under the rule of canonical profession. He resisted in every possible way.

39. At last, when compelled lest he incur the offence of the supreme pontiff and the charge of disobedience, he agreed to what was requested, provided that the canons living there would not refuse to observe the manner of life which he would teach them according to the Gospel and apostolic institution. But when, upon inquiry, he showed them the way of evangelical observance—how they ought to be imitators of Christ and despisers of the world; how voluntary poor persons; how patient under reproaches, insults, mockery, hunger, thirst, nakedness, and other such things; [Col. 1283D] and how obedient to the commands and rules of the holy Fathers—they were immediately terrified at his speech and appearance and said: “We do not want this man over us, because neither our own custom nor that of our predecessors knows such a master. Let us be allowed to live as we do.”

God indeed wishes to chastise, but not to kill; thus the man both obeyed and, released from obedience, did not depart from it. He therefore remained there. His companion, mentioned above, had gone with Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, for he had certain unsettled matters concerning the possessions he had recently abandoned. Because they were being plundered otherwise than he wished—for he was indeed a novice—he could not bear it patiently. [Col. 1284A]

Meanwhile the bishop tried to restore the limbs of his guest, weakened and exhausted by fasting and cold; but he himself was daily refreshed by his guest with the spiritual, honey-sweet refreshment of God’s word. For this reason, inflamed toward him with intense love and the fire of charity, the bishop continually urged him, adding whatever prayers he could, to remain in his bishopric. Every day he led him about and showed him churches which might please him, solitudes, deserts, cultivated or uncultivated land, for building and dwelling.

At length, overcome by the prayers of the bishop and of many others, religious persons and noblemen alike, he chose a place very deserted and solitary, called of old by the inhabitants Praemonstratum. There he promised that, if God should ever grant him companions to gather, he would remain.

40. [CHAPTER XX.] When winter had passed and the cold of snow and ice had been somewhat dispelled by spring warmth, the man of God, as was his custom, girded with the strength of divine consolation, [Col. 1284C] went out to preach. Coming alone to Cambrai and delivering a sermon to the people, the seed fell on good ground: namely, into a young man called Evermode.

[Note: [Col. 1283D] Blessed Evermode, later bishop of Ratzeburg in Wendenland, or Lower Saxony, lived until about [Col. 1284D] the year 1178; he died on 17 February, on which date we illustrated his Acts.]

He was so drenched with the dew of the Holy Spirit in receiving the word of God that, through the grace of love, he stood praying to the Lord his God in that same place and at the same steps where he had carefully observed the man of God standing while preaching. What, then, did the youth—taught by the Holy Spirit in the Word—do except believe that he was that same Word,

[Note: [Col. 1284D] That is, in the spirit, as St John the Baptist was called Elijah by Christ, and under a certain representation and power.]

which was made flesh, and adore him where his feet had stood? He did not delay, but at once left everything and followed him.

He was bound to him by so great a bond of inward love that, throughout his life, the spirit of the man of God rested in him; and after his departure, he entrusted to Evermode the place of his burial, giving him this command: never to depart from him unless he was to return. Arriving at Nivelles,

[Note: [Col. 1284D] Nivigella or Nivella, famous for the life and burial of St Gertrude, as was said in her Life on 17 March.]

he received another young man, Anthony by name, given him by God. These two, together with the third whom he had earlier received, were, so far as human judgment can discern, [Col. 1285A] the roots and foundation of the multitude that followed.

It must be left to God’s providence where he gathered other companions and how God gave them to him, for this is hidden from human eyes by reason of the surpassing height of his wisdom and knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] Peter of Waghenare gives the names of these men; Polycarp de Hertoghe does not credit him.]

It is nevertheless known that during that Lent he had so many that, in Passion Week before Easter, he returned with thirteen and took possession of the aforesaid place, namely Praemonstratum.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] How the saint began to possess Praemonstratum is clearly explained by the *Deeds of Bartholomew* below, and by the documents produced in the annotations to chapter 2 of the *Analecta*. From one of these he here gives the first boundaries and rights of the place: “We wish it to be known that I, Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, have given to Norbert and his successors living in the holy purpose a place which was under our jurisdiction, wholly free and released from every exaction of any person, at Humbert’s Bridge, from the place called Halierpret as far as the Valley of Robert, with the three adjoining valleys: the entire freehold, from the stream Vois, as the valleys are divided and extend, for the construction of a church for God and in honour of the Mother of God. And, as we possess the whole as a freehold, so we grant it to them to possess in every respect freely.

“The pastures or meadows from Humbert’s Bridge [Col. 1287D] as far as Monandi’s neighbour, on this side and beyond the stream, shall be common to their animals at all times. Beyond the stream, on the side of the church, they shall be enclosed for the use of the same brothers until the hay and crops are gathered; afterward they shall be common, provided only that no person be troublesome to their religious life on any pretext. The country people of the neighbourhood are nevertheless permitted to collect, from the wood on the mountain ridges, material for a plough-head, plough-handle, or axle.

“In all the labour of the brothers performed in these places, no one shall exact from them either tithe or land-dues; nor shall any person disturb their peace. We declare them, wholly released from every parish, and all its subject hermits, to remain so.” This charter was given in 1121, since in the preceding year, as Bartholomew himself states elsewhere, Norbert had come with him to Laon.]

41. [CHAPTER XXI.] Therefore, when the foundation had been placed in Christ Jesus—as the Apostle says, “the foundation laid is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11)—the building gradually grew out of living, well-cut and polished stones, and the house of God was enlarged [Col. 1285B] to receive pilgrims who undertook voluntary pilgrimage and hastened to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Yet the snares of the tempting enemy and opposing foe were not absent. By manifold deceit and diverse cunning he laboured to uproot what had been planted, tear up what had been founded, scatter what had been gathered, and hand over what had been scattered to death. Observing in each person individual and particular dispositions—for example, in some an inclination toward the highest contemplation, in other, unlearned men a desire for greater wisdom, in others fasting, and in others the forgiveness of enemies—he opposed himself in every way. And he who had presumptuously wished to be like the Most High did not fear to transform himself into an angel of light in order to deceive God’s new recruits.

Therefore, to recount for the ears of willing hearers a few of these very many occurrences: one night, it happened that a certain brother, standing at Matins, contemplating and thinking of that glorious and ineffable Trinity, saw the ancient adversary visibly standing before him. He said: “O how happy you are, and how praiseworthy in your good purpose! You have begun well and intend to persevere in so great an affliction. Therefore you shall deserve to see the Holy Trinity, toward which you sigh with the whole affection of your mind.” Having said this, he appeared bearing three heads and asserted that he was the Trinity.

The brother was terrified and greatly astonished. Yet, after reflecting briefly, he sensed not “the sound of a gentle breeze” (III Kings XIX, 12), but the foul wind of a whirlwind, and said: “O wretched and unhappy being, worse than all creatures! You, I say, who were the seal of the likeness of God and by pride lost the knowledge of this truth—how dare you claim not merely to know the Trinity, but to be the Trinity itself, when from now on you have not been granted the power even to will to know it? Depart, depart, and do not presume any further to trouble me, who will not obey your deceits.” He immediately departed, but was thereafter to return to the same man.

[Col. 1286A] 42. That brother was indeed ready for obedience, devoted in prayer, and constant in fasting, so that he fasted throughout the whole year, in summer as in winter. No one could compel him to take a second meal in a day except on Sundays; and even then he took something uncooked, not any cooked food.

But while everyone marvelled at him and the strength of such abstinence and self-restraint was everywhere praised in his honour, Satan again came, secretly laying snares in order to overthrow the new soldier. For he was young, and Satan might resent that he had at one time resisted him. On the Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, when Lenten abstinence is prescribed for the devotion of all the faithful, such hunger and gluttonous craving seized him that he said he could in no way fast, and that he would utterly die if he were compelled to abstain even from milk and cheese.

When he was told: “What is this, brother? It is the sacred annual fast, and it is not lawful for anyone—not even a layperson—to take refreshment twice, or for any little child to break abstinence from milk and cheese,” he answered with a grim expression and wolfish rage: “Does God wish a human being to die by withholding from him, at any time, whatever he created for that person’s use and for reception in time of necessity?” [Col. 1286B]

What more need be said? Father Norbert was absent, and the brothers were still inexperienced, unaccustomed to take up arms against assaults of this kind. By many entreaties they finally obtained from him permission to eat Lenten food twice and in whatever quantity he wished. They feared lest the reproach should arise that their religion, so strict and so suddenly established, did not preserve in its converts even the customary practice of laypeople. [Col. 1286C]

43. When, therefore, the days of Lent had passed and the man of God returned to Prémontré to celebrate Easter with his brethren, at the entrance to the valley a great terror seized him, and a whirlwind surrounded him, as though a wind were coming from the north. Immediately perceiving this, he foretold to those accompanying him that an evil temptation was at hand. But when he reached the brethren, trembling, they related in answer to his questions what had happened. Grieving, he said repeatedly: “Alas for me! To my misery, to the harm of the brother’s soul, and to the disclosure of our folly, you have consented to this; and thereby, unless he is resisted manfully, you have given the devil an opportunity for destruction. [Col. 1286D] Where is he?” When the man was brought in, he could scarcely support himself because of excessive fatness; swollen like a bladder and filled with the spirit of gluttony, he could do nothing but look with grim eyes at the master whom he had been accustomed to love above all things. The man of God, therefore, to whom God had given discernment of spirits, saw that this was not a human infirmity but a diabolical temptation; [Col. 1287A] he immediately forbade that anything whatever should be given to him. After he had fasted for several days, when he was restored a quarter of a coarse loaf and a measured vessel of water, he reckoned this the height of luxury; and thus, with God’s help through his master, he returned to his former practice of living well and moderately.

## Chapter VIII. Various companions acquired. A demoniac woman delivered. Relics received.

44. [Chapter XXII.] The ancient enemy having been defeated by the young man, the fear of the faint-hearted flock driven away, and peace restored, the man of God went out to preach, as was his custom. But, as commonly happens when the standard-bearer is absent from the battlefield, enemies lying in ambush attack their opponents; so likewise the most wicked [Col. 1287B] plotter “bent his bow and prepared in it instruments of death” (Ps. 7:14), considering both the wavering flock and the leader of the battle, the protector against frequent arrows, to be absent.

For the moment, however, we must leave aside the adversary, in order first to relate what the man of God did on this journey. “The man went forth unto his work” (Ps. 103:23). Passing through the country, he received back his first companion, who had gone away to settle his affairs; and, having restored very many persons encountered on the road from discord to concord, they arrived at Nivelles. Since from the beginning of his preaching he had been exceedingly beloved in that town, as soon as he took up residence at Prémontré, certain men from among them ran to him for the sake of religious life (*conversatio*). [Note: Col. 1288D: Perhaps “for the sake of conversion” should be read, rather than “for the sake of religious life.”] Yet, unable to bear the severity of the order and of the rule imposed upon them, [Col. 1287C] they returned, “like a dog to its vomit” (2 Pet. 2:22). As often happens, wishing to conceal their own wickedness, they sowed, to the disgrace of the man of God and to the rejection of the seed of his preaching, tares over the field of the householder—as the hostile man had done—so that people neither wished to see him nor cared to hear his preaching.

But he, who was accustomed to drink such draughts, was not in the least dismayed by the malice of those who had stirred up this hostility. Rather, he trusted that it was material for victory against the demons who strove to oppose his preaching and the salvation of believers which God wrought through him.

45. While he was thus held in little esteem among that people, God raised for His soldier [Col. 1287D] a battle, in which, through God’s gift, he fought bravely and gained victory.
