Restored to his former favor, he obtained not only the affection of the people of Nivelles but also, before [Col. 1288A] all who heard of it, the esteem and grace of a most sweet fragrance.

For there was there a certain father whose daughter had already for a year been tormented by a demon and was kept in chains and confinement. Weeping bitterly and sighing, afflicted by his daughter’s suffering, he began to beg him at least to deem her worthy to be seen and touched by him. A great work—but faith in the deed was no less great. “Bring her to me,” he said. The girl, then twelve years old, was brought, and a very great multitude of people assembled.

Then the priest of God, seeing the time, place, and occasion, took greater confidence so that God might be glorified. Clothed in stole and alb, he began to perform an exorcism and began to read various Gospel passages over the girl’s head. To these the demon answered: “I have often heard such lyres, [Col. 1288B] and neither for you nor for all these people will I today depart from this dwelling. For whom should I depart? The pillars of the Church have fallen.”

When the priest multiplied the exorcism, the demon replied: “You accomplish nothing, because you have not yet adjured me by the radiant blood of the martyrs.” Then the demon, being truly proud and wishing to display his knowledge, uttered through the girl’s mouth the Song of Songs from beginning to end; and, repeating it word for word, interpreted it into the Roman language to the end; and, again repeating it word for word, rendered the whole in Teutonic, although the girl, while still healthy, had learned nothing but the Psalter.

[Note: Col. 1288D: Just as that part of Brabant in which Nivelles lies is commonly called Roman Brabant because of the vernacular language there, namely Walloon, so the demon is said here to have translated into no language other than that vernacular what he had first uttered in Latin from the sacred Song of Songs, and then to have used the Teutonic language for the sake of the other Brabanters who spoke Teutonic.]

46. Nevertheless, the priest of God pressed on; and while [Col. 1288C] he persisted and commanded the demon to depart from God’s creature, the demon was forced to reply: “If you compel me to go out from here, permit me to enter that monk”—for a certain monk was standing there—and he named him.

Then Father Norbert, to whom God had given discernment of spirits, cried out to the people: “Hear, hear the malice of this demon! In order to defame God’s servant, he has demanded that he be tormented, as though he were a sinner and deserving of this punishment. But do not be scandalized by this; for such is his wickedness that he wishes to disparage all good persons and, so far as he can, render them infamous.”

Having said this, he resumed the office and began to press more sharply. Then the demon said: “What are you doing? Neither for you nor for another [Col. 1288D] will I go out today. But if you presently see me cry aloud, such a multitude of mine—that is, of the black ones—will come to battle. To battle! To battle! Now I shall make these arches and vaults fall upon you!”

At these [Col. 1289A] words the people fled, but the priest remained unafraid and undaunted. Then the girl put her hand upon his stole, so as to tighten it around his neck. When those present wished to pull her hands away, he said: “Do not do so; allow her. If she has received authority from God, let her do what she can.” Then her boldness, struck down by this saying, relaxed her hands of her own accord, as though showing reverence.

Now, when a great part of the day had been spent, Father Norbert decided to place her in exorcised water. And so it was done. Because she was fair-haired, the priest feared that the devil might retain power over her by occasion of her hair, and ordered her to be shorn. Stung by this injury, the demon began to retaliate against the priest with curses, saying: “Foreigner from France, foreigner from France, [Col. 1289B] what have I done to you? Why do you not allow me to rest? May every evil and misfortune, and every adverse event, come upon your head—you who torment me so greatly!”

47. It was now evening; and Father Norbert, seeing that the demon had not gone out, was somewhat saddened. He ordered the girl returned to her father and brought again on the following day for Mass. He himself began to remove his alb and other vestments. When the wicked demon saw this, he began mockingly to clap his hands and say: “Ha, ha, he! Now you are doing well. Today you did not do a deed that pleased me so much; you spent the day today and accomplished nothing!”

Angered and indignant at this, Father Norbert went to his lodging and resolved in his heart not to taste food until she was healed. Thus he passed [Col. 1289C] that day and night without food. The next day had now arrived; the priest of God prepared himself to celebrate the mysteries of Mass, and the girl was again brought. Again a great crowd of people gathered, to see the contest of priest and demon. He commanded two brethren who were with him to hold her nearby, not far from the altar.

When the service had begun and had reached the Gospel, she was brought to the altar, and many Gospel passages were read over her head. The demon again began to repeat mockingly that he had often heard such lyres. But when the point was reached at which the priest elevates the host before the Lord, the demon cried out: “See, see how he holds his little god in his hands!” [Col. 1289D] The demons confess what heretics deny.

Then the priest of God shuddered; and, filled with a spirit of power, he began, in the very course of his prayer, to assail and torment the demon. Forced and tortured, it cried through the girl’s mouth: “Behold, I burn! Behold, I burn!” Again and again it cried: “Behold, I die! Behold, I die!” A third time also it said in a loud voice, repeating it frequently: “I want to go out! I want to go out! Release me!”

But the two brethren held her firmly. The unclean spirit, unable to endure any delay, fled, leaving behind foul traces of most fetid urine, and abandoned the vessel it had possessed. The girl, freed from her tormentor, collapsed and weak, was carried to her father’s house; and shortly afterward, having taken food, she appeared [Col. 1290A] completely sound, in possession of her senses, and perfectly healed. This was done publicly, with the whole people as witnesses; together they proclaimed God’s praises and confessed Father Norbert to be a truly apostolic man.

48. [Chapter XXIII.] After this he came to Cologne, where he was gladly received and heard still more gladly in preaching and confession, because they had formerly known him as a young man and now saw him wonderfully changed. Since people are usually imitators of novelties, many clerics and laypeople, flocking to his word and exhortation, became imitators of Christ’s poverty and followed him.

He already intended to build a church in which he might receive those gathered together. For this reason he asked [Col. 1290B] Archbishop Frederick and the other faithful that he might be deemed worthy to receive the patronage of some holy relics, with which blessed Cologne had from ancient times been richly furnished and endowed. The bishop consented, the clergy consented, and the people also, judging the request just.

He, however, prescribed a fast for the brethren whom he had with him and those whom God had given him there, and commended this precious gift to God, that He might grant them to discover a venerable patron. That same night, by a vision, a virgin from among the eleven thousand virgins was indicated to someone, together with the virgin’s name and the place where she lay; and on the following day, according to the order of the vision, her body was sought there and found entire. Having received it with hymns, praise of God, and thanksgiving, they filled for him two small vessels, fashioned like biers, with [Col. 1290C] relics also of other virgins and of certain other martyrs—namely Gereon, the Moors, and the two Ewalds.

[Note: Col. 1289D: Saint Ursula and her companions are commemorated on 21 October.]

[Note: Col. 1290D: Saint Gereon and his companions, 10 October; and the two Ewalds, the 3rd of the same month.]

49. On the following day, when he likewise petitioned the provost and canons of St. Gereon to give him relics, permission was granted him to seek and take whatever in their church might please him. The man rejoiced, and, as was his custom, commended this promise more earnestly to God through prayer throughout the whole night.

When morning came, he ordered digging in the middle of the monastery, where no sign of any grave was visible. There a whole body was found, lacking only the brain, and was reverently and most carefully [Col. 1290D] placed. When the canons and the innumerable crowd that had gathered saw this, they said: “Behold our lord Saint Gereon, our venerable protector, whom we and our predecessors have diligently sought for many years and, our sins demanding it, were unable to find.”

With great cries of joy they gave immense thanks to God, proclaiming the man worthy of God, through whom such a great treasure, long desired, had been granted to be found. And, lest anyone doubt that it was he, let him know for certain that the true mark of his identification was this: it was read of his death and martyrdom that a part of his head, not the entire head, [Col. 1291A] had been cut off. They possessed that part, but did not know where the rest of the body was.

The holy body was therefore received and elevated with the honor due to it; and a portion of it was given to the man of God. What remained was magnificently reinterred by clergy and people. Not long afterward, having taken the relics and assembled a company of brethren, both clerics and laymen, whom he had begotten for God by the word of preaching, he set out to return. Everywhere he was received magnificently with procession in churches and religious communities.

Hearing of his passage, a noblewoman named Ermensendis, countess of Namur, hastened to meet him and earnestly begged him to accept her former little church in the village of Floreffe for the installation of brethren and religious life. For she had long desired, for the remedy of her own soul and those of her predecessors, to promote religious life in that church. Seeing the woman’s ardent devotion, he regarded her favorably and accepted what she requested. Leaving there the other [Col. 1291B] vessel of relics, he hastened to Prémontré, for the feast of the Nativity was near at hand. He had about thirty novice brethren, clerics and laymen.

[Note: Col. 1291D: Countess Ermensendis, wife of Count Godfrey of Namur, who himself offered the Abbey of Floreffe to Saint Norbert in fief in 1121 and later, having become a convert—as they say—rests there before the high altar with his wife Ermensendis, his son Henry, and Henry’s wife Agnes. This abbey is situated nearly two miles from Namur on the River Sambre. Document, etc. See vol. VI of June, p. 25, col. 2.]

[Note: Col. 1292D: Relics of the saints mentioned above are there, especially the arm of Saint Gereon, fittingly enclosed in a gold-covered shrine.]

## Chapter IX. Profession according to the Rule of Saint Augustine. Prescribed exercises of the virtues.

50. [Chapter XXIV.] Having assembled nearly forty clerics and a very large number of laymen, he fostered them with continual consolation evening and morning, and exhorted them in many [Col. 1291C] sermons not to abandon the blessed purpose and voluntary poverty they had undertaken. What he taught, like an eagle urging its young to fly, he demonstrated by works.

For his exhortations and sermons were not of the earth, nor did they display any earthly flavor; rather, like a dove, having taken wings, he flew. He flew indeed in mind and speech toward rest, and made his hearers fly also, so that he seemed to say with the Prophet: “I shall take wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest” (Ps. 54:7). Accordingly, some brethren sitting by, caught up in so great an ecstasy of mind, rose from the places where they sat and thought they were finding wings around themselves, immediately imagining that they would fly and be at rest.

Indeed, [Col. 1291D] they believed him to such an extent and clung to him with such affection of familiarity that they sought no order, no Rule, no institutions of the holy Fathers for attaining the glory of eternal blessedness, except what they heard from his mouth or learned had been said by him. The man, discerning in all things and provident in all matters, knew this. Lest the holy planting might later be uprooted and the foundation which he had determined to set upon firm rock might be shaken, he instructed them concerning order, [Col. 1292A] rule, and the institutions of the holy Fathers, without which the apostolic and evangelical institution could not be observed in its fullness—the institution by which God’s sure commandments stand, together with the end of all perfection and the blessing of all the faithful.

They, like sheep following their shepherd in simplicity, did not reject what he urged or what he advised. Rather, they embraced what he taught and, in longing for eternal pasture, obeyed in all things.

51. Therefore the man feared all the more that he might fail to show what pertained to salvation to the little flock seeking God with its whole heart in simplicity. This was not because he did not know the diverse rules and institutions of the holy Fathers, but because many religious persons, both bishops and abbots, gave diverse counsels: one urged the eremitic life, another the anchoritic life, another that the Cistercian order should be adopted.

But he, whose work and counsel depended upon heavenly things, who commended his beginning not to himself or to men but to Him who is the beginning of all things, pondered everything in his heart. Like one wise and swift to hear, he delayed and reserved judgment for the future. At length, lest he seem to inflict an injury upon the canonical profession to which both he and all who wished to live with him had been assigned from childhood, he ordered that the Rule instituted by Blessed Augustine for his followers be brought. For he now desired to live the apostolic life which he had undertaken in preaching, a life which he had heard was ordered and renewed after the apostles by that same blessed man.

When he had carefully examined the Rule brought to him, compact in few words but well ordered in many respects, he immediately, on the approaching feast of the Nativity of the Lord, according to the image of the Lord’s census, caused each one, by the same act of stability in place and profession, to enroll himself for that city of blessed eternity. Then, because very many asserted very many expositions of that same Rule and diverse opinions of interpretation, since they saw its prescriptions as not agreeing with the customs and practices of other religious orders—and because they brought some to fear, others to doubt, and others to lukewarmness, as with a planting not yet firmly rooted—the man of God said: “Why are you surprised, or why do you hesitate, when all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth? And if they are diverse, are they therefore opposed? If practice and institution change, [Col. 1292D] ought the bond of charity, which is love, to change?”

52. The Rule indeed says: “First let God be loved, then one’s neighbor.” The kingdom of God is not achieved by rule alone, but by truth and the observance of God’s commandments. Therefore this Rule expressly determines matters of love, labor, abstinence from food and fasting, clothing, silence, obedience, mutual precedence in honor, and honoring one’s Father. [Col. 1293A] What more, then, could be expedient for any religious person to obtain salvation?

But if there is among spiritual persons any contention concerning the color, coarseness, or fineness of clothing, let those who on this account take occasion to disparage speak—let them speak, I say—of this Rule, of the Gospel, and of the institution of the apostles: let them say where whiteness, blackness, fineness, or coarseness is prescribed by a command; then they may be believed.

There is, however, one point: the angels, witnesses of the Resurrection, are recorded as appearing in white; while by the authority and practice of the Church penitents wear wool. Likewise, in the Old Testament they went out to the people in woolen garments, but in the sanctuary, by command, they customarily used linen. Since the exposition of the holy Fathers and of our predecessors teaches [Col. 1293B] that holy preachers and those in the canonical profession represent in type the place of these angels, they should not cause scandal by white garments. And if they are penitents and their duty compels them to go out to the people, let them not shrink from woolen garments; but if they are about to enter God’s sanctuary, let them not omit linen.

The just man did not teach this in order to disparage the institutions of other Fathers, which are very numerous; for he had become all things to all people, that he might gain all.

[Note: Cols. 1293C–1294D: Although, for Norbert, the multitude of men clothed in white, seen running toward the Cross while he prayed at Prémontré in the little church of St. John the Baptist, might have been sufficient reason for choosing a white garment—as will be read from Hermann the monk, ch. 2 of the *Analecta*, §2—nevertheless the constant tradition of the order maintains, and more recent writers report without hesitation, that, while praying there on another occasion, the saint saw the Queen of Heaven in heavenly splendor with many angels. She declared that his prayers had been heard, showed him the place for founding the first monastery, approved his going to the Roman pontiff for confirmation of the order, and moreover presented him with a white habit, adding in a honeyed voice: “Son Norbert, receive the white garment.”

Thus John Chrysostom van der Sterre, book II of the *Life*, ch. 2; John le Paige, book II of the *Bibliotheca*, ch. 12; Gerard van Hardegom, book I, ch. 2 of his work entitled *The White Blessed Virgin, Mother, Patroness, and Lady of the White Premonstratensian Order*; and others. I wish that their assertions could be strengthened by more ancient authorities. Yet, however these matters are understood, they establish nothing except that the Virgin prescribed the white color while leaving unchanged the form already in use. What garment, moreover, would the canons have worn except the canonical garment of their own time—a garment in which nothing of worldly pomp overflowed, but austerity appeared?

[Col. 1293D: See vol. VI of June, part I, p. 2, col. 2, no. 11.] Thus I find that at the beginning the Premonstratensians used neither linen garments or undershirts next to the skin, nor bedcovers of linen; that they went barefoot; and furthermore that they maintained perpetual abstinence from meat. Although these observances have now prudently been relaxed, there are nevertheless even today in Lorraine persons who, out of love for a more severe life, have returned themselves to the former practice, as those who know and praise them in this time affirm.]

53. [Chapter XXV.] He was severe in discipline; and when many were already flocking to him, he exhausted their whole spirit, with the Holy Spirit teaching, so that, the spirit of pride emptied out, that same Holy Spirit might find a better dwelling-place in them. Nor was the grace of God lacking, which furnished the strength of divine consolation to hearts however unruly, lax, and utterly withered. Concern and solicitude for bodily matters were scarcely present; they had devoted their whole effort to spiritual things, following the divine Scriptures and having Christ as their leader.

For that spiritual Father also considered this: those who wished to remain with him could never stray if they made and fulfilled their profession according to the Gospels, the sayings of the apostles, and the purpose of Saint Augustine. He perceived this and judged that these professions should be made in the manner already stated. [Col. 1294A]

Thus the minds of those gathered from the beginning were so disposed that they would rather choose an old, patched tunic than any new and intact garment. Hence some, embracing poverty in no small measure, blushed when new garments were given to them; and, to show how worthless worldly pomp is and to restrain pride, they sewed old rags over new clothing. No task was so contemptible that they rejected it. Their obedience was so ready that, if a burning oven were set before them or any death offered itself, they would fear the one commanding them more than death.

There was continual silence in every place, at every time, and in every condition, so that even those who accompanied him, although mingled with the densest crowds, could scarcely have a single word forced from their mouths. [Col. 1294B] If he reproved any one of them for even the smallest offense, that person immediately fell at his feet to make satisfaction and was not ashamed before the eyes of the people standing around. If any of his followers responded to wrongdoing with bitterness in deed, word, or expression, he immediately underwent the penalty of satisfaction.

54. He wished them to fast at all times, content with one meal a day. He also wished them to ride on little asses for as much as four or five leagues; but this could not be observed because bodily weakness opposed it. He commanded his brethren always to use breeches, because the man always abhorred the weakening of masculine strength of soul by effeminate softness; yet he did not approve more precious material on this account before the eyes of the inward Judge. [Col. 1294C] How religious was that order which, by its rule and purpose, was free of such things!

He commanded them to use wool next to the skin and woolen garments for work, without any dye, although he himself was continually clothed in a most rough hair-shirt. In the sanctuary, however, and wherever the divine sacraments were to be handled or celebrated, he wished linen to be used, for purity and manifold propriety; and he decreed that it should be used at all times.

Three matters, however, which he especially commended must not be omitted. Repeatedly, day after day, he urged that these be observed: purity around the altar and in the divine mysteries; correction of excesses and negligences [Col. 1295A] in chapter and everywhere; care for the poor and hospitality. For at the altar each person displays faith and love for God; in purification of conscience, care of oneself; and in receiving guests and the poor, love of neighbor. He constantly maintained that a house which diligently endeavored to observe these three things could never lack more than it was able to bear.

For in words and deeds he proclaimed that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. In all his actions he attended to the governing reason before him, so that, supported by reason and established by authority, it might stand.

[Note: Col. 1294D: The Rule of Saint Benedict permits the use of breeches for those going outside the cloister. Since the Cluniacs also used them within it, Peter the Venerable defends this practice in book I, letter 28, as honorable, useful, necessary, and therefore in no way contrary to the Rule, which forbids nothing of the kind.]

[Note: Col. 1294D: The manuscripts read “these statutes,” which appears to make no sense and ought to have been corrected.]

## Chapter X. The hypocrisy of one companion exposed; a church built.

55. [Chapter XXVI.] One day, at last, as he was returning [Col. 1295B] from Reims with certain companions and two novices whom the divine word addressed to them had drawn from the world, they walked silently along the road, meditating upon their God. A voice from a cloud sounded in their ears in this manner: “This is the fellowship of Brother Norbert.” Another voice from the other side answered: “Of these two novices, one is not of the fellowship of the others.”

The man himself and those accompanying him heard this and silently considered the matter, suspecting no evil; yet they wondered what ought to be done. Father Norbert, upon whom greater solicitude rested, knew that it was not superfluous for these voices to be heard by divine permission. With every urgency of prayer he sought to discover to what end [Col. 1295C] this response had been given, observing day by day the character and acts of the persons of whom it had been spoken.

When he had observed that one of them was less devout in confession, frivolous in speech, restless in body, inconstant in character, lukewarm in prayer, negligent in obedience, and undisciplined in everything—for he was an Englishman—he said: “What is it, brother? What is it that you carry in your heart? Reveal what lies hidden. If you seek God, no creature is invisible before Him; for, as the Apostle says, all things are naked and open to His eyes” (Heb. 4:13). “We seek truth and strive, insofar as human frailty permits, to walk in truth. There is no communion of truth with falsehood, nor any participation of the faithful with the unfaithful.”

But the other, shaking his head and displaying frivolity [Col. 1295D] of speech, said: “Do you think, good Father, that I wish to steal anything from you? You are poor; but ‘to everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away’” (Matt. 25:29).

56. He said this and fulfilled his words by deed. For at that time a certain person had perhaps come for conversion and had brought a little silver along with his small property. It lay cast behind the altar of the poor oratory which they then possessed as their only one. But one night [Col. 1296A] that Englishman, seeing an hour suitable for his purpose, seized the silver and fled.

Thus that deceiver, full of fraud and a servant of the devil, thinking them poor in heart, while Christ’s poor suspected no deceit, increased their poverty to such a degree that no resources remained from which the expenses of even one day could be provided. What then? They had first to be tested in bodily sustenance—the people who had heard that possessors of the kingdom of heaven are those known to become poor, not in possessions and riches, but in the spirit of poverty. They had to be tested in lesser matters, so that they might learn to stand firm in the storms and tumults they were to encounter, as the following narrative will show.

Therefore, to make known the divine work, great and exquisite, in which He works great things in small things by the secret counsel of His ordering—He who, looking upon the lowly, knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 137)—it seems fitting to say a few words about the place called Prémontré and its situation. Thus may praise in all things, at all times, be given by all who hear to Him who, from eternity and before all times, knew it only in His foreknowledge and revealed it in the last time.

57. Now at that time, to continue the sequence of events, very many persons were frequently joining themselves to the discipline, life, and purpose of the often-mentioned man, leaving everything behind. Since there was now a crowd, they sought, by settled counsel, where in that same wilderness they should prepare a fixed place suitable for dwelling and building.

For the place was exceedingly rugged and entirely uncultivated, occupied by thickets, marshes, and other inconveniences. [Col. 1296C] Nothing suitable for habitation was visible except a small chapel, an orchard beside it, and a small pool, which is known even now to be filled only in rainy weather by waters descending from the mountains and by the seepage of marshes.

There the man of God had settled with his small fellowship, joining the anchor of hope to unshaken faith and, with our patriarch Abraham, hoping against hope. So much was this the case that nearly all religious persons testified, and the people cried out, that what the man had begun could not stand; because of the harshness of extreme poverty and subsistence, they expected flight after a few years rather than any foundation of stability.

[Note: Cols. 1295D–1296D: (72) Peter de Waghenare, §27 of the *Life*: “The church and monastery built there by Saint Norbert were constructed not without a miracle, since angels were evidently laboring alongside, advancing the work much more at night than all the workmen did by day. This is attested by the most reverend lord Goswin van Weirdt, doctor of sacred theology and prior of Floreffe, as the archives of that same monastery of Floreffe declare.” Would that, for greater credibility, the archives of Prémontré also contained the same account, or that those of Floreffe set it forth more distinctly!]

But what could he do by human reasoning, deprived of rational assistance? Knowing that Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), he also set his face to await death there—he who had come to die to the world and live to Christ. He cried that those live—he cried that they truly live—who do not live for themselves but in whom poor Christ lives: “Yet I live, no longer I,” says the Apostle, “but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). He had heard this and taught it; and: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:15).

Nevertheless, lest the little flock should despair, lest he might gladden the hearts of his friends who awaited not the outcome but the condition of the undertaking, [Col. 1297A] and lest he might remove an occasion of disparagement from rivals, he himself began to traverse and examine, and commanded others to examine, whatever suitability there could be in such a place. He added that continual and earnest prayer should be offered to almighty God, that He might show the place in which divine worship was to be celebrated at all times.

58. [CHAPTER XXVII.] And when many persons, with many prayers, and persevering persons with persevering prayers, commended this plan to the Lord, earnestly seeking, through excessive affliction, fasting, and prayers, the good pleasure of His will, a certain revelation appeared to someone: sufficiently plain and clear, it openly announced, by an evident signification, the place, what was in that place, and what was to come from that place. [Col. 1297B] For there, where the church now stands, our Lord Jesus Christ was seen as upon the cross, above whom shone seven rays of the sun of wondrous brightness; and from the four sides—just as the entrances of that place are known to be four, in the form of a cross—a great multitude of pilgrims hastened with wallets and staffs; and, having bent their knees in worship before their Redeemer and kissed His feet, they turned back as though about to depart with permission. When this was reported to the man of God, he gave thanks to the Lord his God, who gives His servants—those who seek Him in truth and obey Him in faith and righteousness—confidence concerning things past and knowledge of things future by secret revelation. And after this, his face brightened and, taking courage, [Col. 1297C] he said: “Come then, come, most beloved brothers: gird yourselves and be strong men. Very many kinds of warfare are prepared for you, which will come from enemies both visible and invisible. But those new recruits who came in the vision shall come visibly; and, having received command and obedience from Him who was obedient to the Father, they will fight with you until the consummation.”

Who can doubt that this word was true and prophetic? It was indeed true, as the subsequent action daily demonstrates in those who, leaving everything behind, come as pilgrims and, after making their profession—as if giving a kiss—depart for diverse nations to gain the battle-lines of conflict. From sea to sea the multitude resounded, and their voice was heard; in it the works of God are manifest, and “sought out according to all His desires” (Ps. 110:2). Thanks be to Him who does not abandon those who hope in Him.

59. [CHAPTER XXVIII.] Since, then, the spiritual building and temple had been well arranged and put together, material labor also had to be applied, so that all things might be done with a blessing. With Bishop Bartholomew summoned, the foundation having been dug out and consecrated, he caused the church to be founded with consecrated stones. Lord Thomas of Coucy was present, who feared the man of God and revered him for God’s sake, knowing him to be a just man and worthy of every honor; his son Ingelram, still a little boy, was also present, as were many noble clergy and laymen, and an innumerable multitude of people, wondering and watching as though at a spectacle, and saying among themselves: “Who [Col. 1298A] do you suppose this man is? What sort of faith does he possess, that he employs no practical calculation? Do you suppose this work will stand, being set in so great a wilderness? Its foundation is laid neither on rock nor upon firm ground, but in a marsh.”

For the marsh there was so deep that it could scarcely absorb the great heap of stones thrown into it. Yet it ought not to waver, nor could it be uprooted, because “the planting which my heavenly Father plants shall not be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13). Moreover, some of the masons were Germans—for certain men of Cologne, friends of the man of God, had hired them—while others were natives, now friends of the Premonstratensians; and they competed in the work, some hastening on one side of the church, others on the other. The building grew with the greatest speed, and within nine months the church was completed and brought to perfection, and [Col. 1298B] consecrated by the aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew.

60. But because sorrow is accustomed to be mixed with joys and adversity with prosperity, a certain misfortune occurred on the very day of the consecration. For when the innumerable multitude that had assembled from distant regions for the feast rushed competitively, as is customary, to make offerings and to go around the altar, the high altar was moved, one stone came loose, and the consecration was invalidated, as authority prescribes; thus all the labor was reduced to nothing. The man was alarmed and saddened, yet he feared the scandal of the little ones more than he distrusted the works of God, which do not happen without cause.

But what did that man do? At last, renewing in the Lord [Col. 1298C] the strength of consolation—he who was accustomed to drain and swallow such temptations—he secretly arranged with the bishop that the church should again be dedicated on the octave of St. Martin. And so it was done. As long as he lived, he maintained for this reason that another renovation would have to be undertaken in future times. Those who were present then saw this, and some who followed them; and those who follow will see still more, because, as Truth testifies, “he who believes does the works which I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14:12). And elsewhere: “If you believe, you shall see greater things than these” (John 1:50).

Let what has been said about the material building suffice. But what the man did meanwhile, and what befell the little flock, must not be passed over in silence. Yet since no one can narrate in due order, at the same instant, both what happened to him and what happened to them at the same time, no reader should wonder if the pen now turns in alternation to matters concerning the acts of individuals and the countless occurrences that must not be omitted.

## CHAPTER XI. Temptations Overcome. The Possessed Delivered.

61. [CHAPTER XXIX.] At last the man went out to preach; he went out again to sow seed—not his own, but the Lord’s seed. He left persons in charge of the work begun, persons in charge of all other affairs and of preserving everything intact, and persons in charge of the community of clergy and laymen; appointing two by two to the several offices. At his final farewell he taught them concerning peace and unanimity, saying that no assembled multitude could go astray when the concord of its prelates had preceded it.

But when the shepherd departed, the wolf with raging mouth plotted against the sheep. Truly I have called them plots, because, digging into their sheepfold from the opposite side, he entered secretly: first to strike terror; then, to cast down those terrified by the hammer of his tail; to slaughter those cast down; and afterward to devour and destroy the slaughtered with gaping mouth. Yet because his arrogance is greater than his strength, he rightly began by striking terror. For to certain brothers, as though they were enemies of mortal hatred whom they had left behind in the world, he appeared with his attendants, armed as though to kill them, even in daylight. Terrified by the appearance of an armed army, the display of weapons, and the neighing of horses, they resisted by whatever means they could; so that, while fleeing, they hastened to defend themselves with sticks and stones snatched up in haste, their arms wrapped in whatever supports or tunics they could find. But—strange and incredible as it may seem—the battle was so fierce that they believed themselves to be hurling and receiving missiles, striking and being struck, wounded and wounding, killing and being killed. When many other brothers ran to them and reproved them for such madness, they replied: “Do you not see that we are being crushed by our enemies, and that we are almost cut to pieces in vain, dying in irretrievable disgrace?” [Col. 1299A–B]

62. Then the brothers, knowing that they were deluded by the assault of demons, sprinkled holy water and made the sign of the cross. When the band of evil spirits withdrew, those men, as if their enemies had been defeated and put to flight, pursued them at a rapid run, shouting loudly: “Come then, come! Turn and resist; fight bravely, or else you shall die a most disgraceful death if from now on you presume to approach us and bring threats and death upon us.”

But after returning to themselves, some of them recognized that they had been deceived and thereafter persevered bravely, having conquered bravely. Others, unable to endure the shame of such mockery and despairing of perseverance, withdrew, struck by the demon’s tail-sting. But this evil and false spirit was not satisfied—nor is it surprised if it swallows the sea, but it strives to drink up the whole Jordan as well. Since it could not openly seduce them utterly, it did not fear to return, presumptuously undertaking more hidden snares.

For in that same poverty a multitude had assembled from diverse nations and of varied rank: noble and ignoble, rich and poor, older and younger, learned, simple, and uneducated people; for the man was accustomed to receive them, thus becoming an imitator of the Gospel: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37). [Col. 1299C–D] Among them the deceptive spirit observed certain uneducated persons, recognizing them as vessels that had formerly belonged to him, in whom he had been accustomed to find a dwelling-place for his own repose and will. He filled them with such false wisdom of deception that those who previously could scarcely read in any book now spoke great things from books and, prophesying about the future, preached greater and astonishing things.

63. One of them even declared that he knew Daniel’s prophecy, and under the guidance of falsehood said certain things about that passage in which the prophet writes of four, seven, and ten horns and kings, and of Antichrist. By these means he had already made some of the simpler brethren attentive and, had it been possible, would have drawn even the man of God and the venerable Simon, abbot of St. Nicholas, into error. For his arrogance had advanced so far that, while they sat present, he presumed even to deliver an address in chapter. One who saw and heard bears witness to this matter; and this is its sign, that he gives the opening of the discourse. For the discourse was: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent.” This lying spirit uttered it through the instrument it had assumed, but it could not proceed at all to the truth that follows, namely: “and you shall receive the eternal kingdom.” [Col. 1300A–B]

Therefore, when Father Norbert indicated to someone what he thought of the matter, that person replied: “Good master, it will soon become evident.” Then, when the false spirit saw that those who heard truth and sweetness had partly detected it, being an artificer of a thousand devices, it more cunningly sought other forms of deception. Since it could not overthrow the cooperators in manifest activity, it tried at least to cut off some contemplatives from contemplation. For that same cleric, minister of this wicked undertaking, was seized by a sudden and very grave illness. He who formerly gave answers concerning visible things now presumed to set his mouth toward heaven concerning invisible and ineffable things.

64. [Col. 1300C] The brothers ran together, as is customary, to anoint him; they ran together also to hear what he said. He made great assertions about himself, and still greater ones about many bystanders. Of himself he said that that evening he would either be with the angels in heaven or would stand sound among the other brothers in choir. Of others, observing the aptitude of each, he spoke as if prophesying and divining: “When I was recently caught up in ecstasy to the higher regions, I saw this man summoned to eternity; that one already set in the seat of blessedness; this man’s bed prepared in that same blessedness. This man is to be a bishop; that one is to be appointed ruler and master of many religious; this one will persevere in his good purpose; that other will fail and withdraw.”

Having said this, he threw himself down as though about to breathe his last, lying on the ground for the space of an hour, as those who are immediately dying usually do. Then, on hearing the first sound of Vespers, he rose and entered the choir at a rapid run with the others. When the bystanders saw this, each confessing his own scandal to the other, they declared that they had been deceived. Yet even then that ancient and most malignant plotter did not cease—he who was devoid of all goodness and truth and the most wicked inventor of every crime. For he stirred up another cleric in the same way. As the first had drawn a deceptive spirit from the prophet Daniel, so this one professed no less that he understood, and ought to investigate, the gifts of the heavenly secrets in the Apocalypse of John the Apostle.

When one of the priors brought him into chapter, he said: “Behold, at last the Dayspring from on high has visited us, [Col. 1301A] because no long exercise in the schools instructed this man, nor did labor measured by years teach him; rather, an angelic revelation labored throughout the whole night, in the silence of darkness, diligently to instruct him and, through him, us. Let us therefore hear him, that from him we may learn what he learned from on high in the Apocalypse through ecstasy of mind.”

65. Hearing this, certain brothers, to whom the subtlety of deceptive spirits had already become partly known, prohibited it altogether, saying: “From now on we are willing to hear neither this man nor any other in a discourse before Father Norbert returns.” The most deceitful spirit therefore saw that its splendor, by which it transforms itself into an angel of light, had been repulsed. Like a roaring lion, hungry and prowling about seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8), as if roused to anger and no longer able to hide, it began openly to exercise its cruelty and the fuel of hatred that it bore against the congregation and its well-ordered battle-line.

First, between those two whom it had thus deceived and through whom it had tried to ensnare others by mockery, it placed such discordant enmity that, if either could catch the other anywhere, he would kill him; and unless they had been restrained with bolts and chains, neither would have found an opportunity to escape. [CHAPTER XXX.] Then that most troublesome plotter, who adds iniquity to iniquity in order to place an aggravated heavy burden upon the innocent, seized a young man, the son of a certain lay brother, and, wickedly entering him, began to torment him. [Col. 1301B–C] Since he could not overthrow the entire flock by his manifold artifice, he strove by every means at least to leave it ruined.

What could the flock do without its shepherd, when the wolf so laid snares for it on every side? They stood astonished and bewildered at the assaults so frequent, since they were unaccustomed to bear arms of this kind. Nevertheless, they shut up the possessed man in bonds until a decision could be made about what ought to be done.

66. When the silence of night had come, the prior who then presided over the others wished to enter to him. While he was still standing outside, some distance from the house—all doors having been shut, with no opening through which he could be seen, and moreover it was dark—the demon within began to shout loudly: “He is about to come in to me! He is about to come in to me! He is coming, he is coming—that master in his studded tunic! A curse upon him! Fasten the door tightly; fasten it as quickly as possible!” But the prior did not yield for this reason; he went forward and, knocking at the door, entered.

Standing before him, he said: “Tell me, I beg you, what is it that you are saying?” He replied: “Do you ask what I am saying, or who I am that speaks? I shall reveal neither to you. Are you this man’s master or guardian, or the leader of others? Go away, go away as quickly as possible, lest you depart from me shamefully abused.” But he, certain that it was an evil spirit and that it had very often come to deceive, though now at last it had entered to destroy, said: “I adjure you by Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who conquered your snares upon the cross, and justly and mightily recovered the authority which you had seized unjustly and deceitfully over this man: do not presume to conceal who you are.” [Col. 1301D–1302A]

It said: “Will you compel me in this way?” He answered: “Not I. He compels you who, as has been stated, conquered you on the other occasion by the cross.” And that evil demon cried out: “Alas, alas! What shall I do? I am,” it said, “that same one who was in the girl of Nivigella, before Norbert your master, in the form of a white dog. Cursed be the hour in which he was ever born!”

67. Thus certain concerning his own and the others’ troublesome persecutor, the prior summoned the whole community and, recounting all these things, asked what ought to be done. Having taken counsel, though fearful as novices unaccustomed to such things, they undertook bodily discipline, appointed fasts and prayers among themselves, blessed water in a vessel suitable for this purpose, and went in procession to the place where the demon was praying. It began to rage and cry out with great uproar: “Let our people come to this battle, for we are more numerous; and we shall crush them as grains of wheat are crushed by a stone, and we shall utterly destroy them.”

When the prior replied: “You will do so if you have received authority from God,” it turned toward him and, stretching out its hands as though it wished to tear the garments in which it was clothed, said: “Do you think that you are the master of these people?” And, pointing at the cross which the boy held there, it said: “He is the master, not you. I shall do nothing for you; but he is the one by whom I am tormented.”

Demons confess and fear Jesus Christ crucified; Jews possessing the Law, and false Christians, do not acknowledge Him, but abhor and mock Him. [Col. 1302B–C] The man in whom the evil spirit was was unbound; but since he could scarcely be held by many bystanders, a young cleric of the community, taking up a humble boldness from true obedience, to which he was wholly devoted, said: “Let it be commanded me under obedience, and I will hold him—not with my own hands and bonds, but with those of obedience.” When the command had been given to him and the others had withdrawn, he held him alone and led him as far as the holy water. But the demon trembled at the sight of him, as any little child is accustomed to tremble before rods set out for whipping.

68. He was placed in exorcized water; exorcisms were read, adjurations performed, and the Gospels read, while some brothers wept, others prayed, and others were occupied with bodily disciplines or other afflictions. Yet all marveled at the useless and jesting answers of his words. What more need be said? At last, after the excessive and innumerable exhausting ordeals of the wretched little body, the demon, sitting upon the possessed man’s tongue, assumed the form of a grain of very black *leaticula* [reading uncertain]; and, with its mouth open and tongue drawn out, displayed itself to all those standing by, saying: “See, here I am; but I shall not go out today for the sake of all of you.”

When it was answered: “You are a liar, and from the beginning you did not stand in the truth; no believer ought to trust you,” not long afterward it went out with a sound of most foul stench, leaving behind traces intolerably disgusting. Immediately the body, freed from its torturer, fell down; laid upon a little bed, it scarcely recovered from that illness after a long period of restoration. [Col. 1302D–1303A]

[CHAPTER XXXI.] The brothers having thus been extraordinarily and repeatedly exhausted and disturbed by the cunning artifice of this demon, the demon itself, impatient of all repose and in no way consenting to the peace of quiet, found no place among the simple for its deception. Flying easily, as it is light by natural swiftness, it hastened to Trajectum, where Father Norbert was, and seized a man who was the steward of a certain prince. Since it could not dissolve the battle-line which he had left well arranged, it sought at least to strike at the standard-bearer and, through the standard-bearer, to minister missiles of death within the battle-line.

69. For in that town there was a day of annual celebration, when people ordinarily assemble for such a solemnity. Many had gathered there, and the priest of God Norbert was celebrating in the principal church, where the crowd was greatest. There also was the man who had been seized by the demon during the Secret of the Mass, and he was scarcely held bound amid great commotion and raging. When the solemnities of the Mass had ended, he was brought before Norbert with a great concourse of people standing around and awaiting the contest between Christ’s soldier and the demon.

Norbert, still clothed in sacred vestments—indeed girded with the power of the Holy Spirit, armored with the breastplate of righteousness and the shield of faith and truth—advanced to fight that most troublesome enemy. Some brothers standing nearby urged him to spare his weakness, because evening had come, this occurrence was accidental, and not every contingency could be remedied. But he was moved, and rebuked them sternly in expression and reply: “You do not understand, brothers; you do not understand, I say, that through the devil’s envy death entered the world, and still persists in it; nor will he ever have the will to repent. For this one intrudes himself so frequently and persistently in order both to make me odious and to make the word of God, ministered through me, seem worthless in the hearts of those who hear it. And from those who have received it, though he cannot secretly take it away, he nevertheless strives openly, from arrogance innate to him, to remove it. Has not the exposition of truth sounded in your ears, which says: ‘The devil comes to take away the seed of the word of God from their hearts’?” (Luke 8:12.) [Col. 1303B–D]

70. Having said this, he placed the possessed man before the altar and began the exorcism, commanding the demon to depart. When he put exorcized salt into the man’s mouth, the demon spat with great force into the priest’s face and eyes, saying: “You have already given the counsel that I should be put into water, so that there I might be beaten with the harshest whips, almost to death. You strive in vain: your whips do not hurt me, your threats do not frighten me, death does not torment me, nor do the bonds of death bind me.”

The counsel had indeed been given, as stated above, that he be put into exorcized water, but while that madman was absent. Therefore, as clergy and people stood around—some from curiosity, others from compassion—the most wicked demon, through the mouth of the invaded man, began to reveal the most wicked lives, adulteries, and fornications of many persons, exposing with its malicious mouth whatever had not been covered by confession. On hearing this, all began to flee here and there, only a few remaining with Father Norbert. When the day was already declining and evening had come, those who were present, exhausted by fasting and by the vigils of the preceding night, compelled him to go to his lodging, so that he might take a little rest, refresh his weakened limbs with some food, and be restored by sleep. [Col. 1304A]

While he was seated at supper with his brothers and certain guests, word was brought to him that the sick man was sitting quietly, unbound before the altar, and begging forgiveness for the wrongs he had committed and the curses he had disgracefully uttered. They gave thanks to God; for that night and on the following day he appeared to be healed. [Col. 1304B]

71. There existed among the citizens of that town a certain deadly hatred. The next day Father Norbert labored throughout the day to make peace; and, with grace assisting, he had fully settled everything in peace and quiet. Immediately the devil, who had been expelled from their hearts, gladly departing from there, entered again into that same wretched man who seemed healed, and he at once began again to shriek and rage.

When the priest of God returned from church, the bystanders said: “Do you not know that the possessed man of yesterday is mad? Unless he is helped and healed as quickly as possible, he will perish, consumed by his own madness.” The man of God replied: “No, he cannot now be delivered from his torturer, because this has happened to him as his sins demand it—for he also held the office of the town’s procurator—and by his own desert he has been handed over to his torturer. Let him be for the present, so that after the demon has tormented him for several days, and satisfaction has been received, that most wicked demon may be expelled more easily.”

A wise man, trained in the contest to be waged with unclean spirits, he allowed him to be tormented and vexed for three days; afterward, through divine mercy, he was healed, so that, restored to his senses and sound, he returned to his own home. [Col. 1304B–C]

## CHAPTER XII. Blessed Godfrey of Cappenberg Converts; The Same Man Persuades Count Theobald to Consider Marriage.

72. [CHAPTER XXXII.] At that time, as the fame of the remarkable deeds of so great a man spread very widely and gloriously, a most powerful count of Westphalia, named Godfrey, was pierced by the spirit of poverty.

> [Note: Col. 1303D (73)] This is Blessed Godfrey of Cappenberg, a count who became a canon of the Premonstratensian Order. He died on 13 January 1127; his various *Acta* have been elucidated under that date.

He came to Norbert because he had heard much about him; but when, through the instruction of the Holy Spirit who worked through Norbert, he found things still greater, he opened to him all his plan and intention. Although he had already inwardly devoted his whole self to God, he was without delay instructed outwardly concerning renouncing all things and embracing voluntary poverty. For he was rich, powerful in arms as a young man, and abundantly endowed with many estates, male servants, and female servants. Immediately renouncing all these, [Col. 1305A] he entrusted himself and all his possessions to God, to be disposed of through the hands of the man of God, under this agreement: that he would redirect the resources of his own house—that is, Cappenberg Castle—to its consecration, so that, where the abomination of vices had reigned, the consecration of divine blessing might there establish a place for virtues.

> [Note: Col. 1305D (74)] Cappenberg, in the diocese of Münster, is situated at a town on the river Lippe and is nearly one mile distant from Lünen.

What was the young man to do, about to wage a most severe contest? Truly I call it a most severe war, because he had a wife and a younger brother, who opposed by every means whatever he had resolved to do. His feudal men, male and female servants, and all his ministeriales also opposed him. Count Frederick, [Col. 1305A] his wife’s father, opposed him as well, declaring that a great part of the alms he had given belonged to the dowry of his daughter.

> [Note: Col. 1305D (75)] Frederick, Count of Westphalia, of Arnsberg, is called by Gobelinus, sixth age, chapter 48, under the year 1123, a most ferocious man. His grandson afterward founded at Arnsberg a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order; that place now belongs to the jurisdiction of the Elector of Cologne.

What more shall I say? His hand was against all of them, and the hand of all of them against him. A war was waged, not with material arms but with faith; not with quarrels but with reason; not with an armed multitude but with the aid of angels. He was helmeted with heavenly hope and armored with supernal power. At last humble persistence conquered, planted at the opportune time and accompanied by hope of heavenly blessedness and perfect humility. It conquered, indeed, because his wife consented, and his brother, laying aside leonine fury, assumed lamb-like gentleness; and both took the religious habit which they knew Count Godfrey himself wished to take.

> [Note: Col. 1305D (76)] Countess Jutta of Bonneburgh lived as a recluse on the left side of the mountain, until she was summoned to Herford and appointed abbess over its distinguished community of noble women.

> [Note: Col. 1305D (77)] Otto, after Blessed Godfrey and another Otto, was the third provost of Cappenberg. He died in 1171 or the following year. We have also treated him among those omitted, under 23 February.

Father Norbert rejoiced, and the count rejoiced also. Having rendered to Caesar all that was Caesar’s and retained for God what was God’s, he built, at Father Norbert’s direction, three churches on his own freehold estates. [Col. 1305B–C] Having installed brothers in them and established religious life, so that God’s service was carried out fittingly, temptation and the persecution of evil spirits did not fail to arise.

73. For Count Frederick, the count’s wife’s father, indulging his ambition because Cappenberg Castle had held the lordship of Westphalia—while claiming that it was his daughter’s dowry—threatened the brothers that, unless they departed from it as quickly as possible, he would kill them all. He even came there several times with his cavalry, threatening Father Norbert that, if he caught him, he would hang him together with his donkey, so that the balance might prove which of them was the heavier. Bishops and other princes present contradicted such proud speech and, for those words also, threatened him with God’s wrath.

For Father Norbert was now more highly esteemed by everyone around and beyond the Rhine, [Col. 1305D–1306A] and they could not bear with equanimity that anyone should threaten or curse him. The brothers at Cappenberg, pressed hard and having no deliverer except God from the hand of the powerful and wicked man, sent to their Father for help, reporting at the same time the arrogant man’s words. On receiving this message, Norbert gathered the strength of faith and hope in Him and through Him who said, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). He gave himself wholly to the matter and publicly declared that he would enter Frederick’s land with his donkey and place himself at his disposal.

What more need be said? Although the journey was long, he refused to exchange his donkey. But, having crossed the Rhine, as soon as he entered Count Frederick’s land with his donkey—unarmed and weak—Frederick himself, seated at dinner, burst apart in the middle, his abdomen having split open.

> [Note: Col. 1306D (78)] In three manuscripts the words enclosed here in brackets are omitted; they occur in others and seem altogether necessary for the completeness of the sense.

Not long afterward that most cruel enemy, seized by illness, died; he brought an end to his malice and to his life at once. Therefore one should observe who this soldier was and whose soldier he was: seated upon a donkey, he brandished from afar the sword of God’s wrath, pierced the enemy in vengeance for himself and his brothers, and gained triumph over a monstrous tyrant.

Thus, when everything had been pacified and brothers fearing God had been chosen, he established, as stated above, the service of God to be performed perpetually in three churches upon that same freehold: namely, Cappenberg, Elophstadt, and Varlar.

> [Note: Col. 1306D (79)] Elophstadium, or Elfstat—more commonly Ilmstadt—in the Wetterau, five leagues from Frankfurt, is celebrated for the death of Blessed Godfrey.

> [Note: Col. 1306D (80)] Varlar is one league from Coesfeld, the residence of the bishops of Münster.

In these places a community of many brothers and sisters flourishes to the present day, and honorable religious life prospers in divine worship. [Col. 1306B–C]

74. [CHAPTER XXXIII.] Many things might be told about so great a Father, but very many are nevertheless omitted, because no single person can know all that God worked through him. He was indeed a burning lamp, conspicuous enough for modern times: a light placed not under a bushel but upon a mountain. His name was great and renowned in both Germany and France.

Therefore, when he was returning to France and the news of the conversion of the aforesaid prince was widely spread, to the wonder of many—because he had exchanged his secular habit for religious life, dissolved his castles, the soldiery of his castles, and his whole county, and devoted everything to God’s service—a most noble prince of France, namely Count Theobald, was moved and pierced by this example.

> [Note: Col. 1306D (81)] Theobald of Blois, whose extensive county along the Loire is represented in a separate geographical map, was also Count of Chartres and Champagne. He died on 10 January 1251 and was the son of Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror. Of him the continuator of the Monk of Jumièges says: “Theobald, a man praiseworthy in every respect, though a layman, who venerated and supported religious men with extraordinary affection, succeeded his father Stephen in the county of Blois; having bought the county of Troyes from his uncle Hugh, he possessed it together with the county of Chartres.” Robert of Auxerre, under the year 1136, adorns him with this same praise: “At this time Theobald, Count of Champagne, flourished: father of orphans and judge of widows, eye of the blind, foot of the lame, singularly generous in sustaining the poor, and incomparable in liberality in constructing monasteries and toward every kind of religious person. How lavishly he bestowed alms, and how eminent a lover and promoter of religion he was, the tongue can scarcely explain.”

[Col. 1307A] He approached the man of God, seeking in like manner counsel concerning his salvation and the remission of his sins. Considering the man of God’s eloquence, the dignity of his appearance, and the maturity of his speech and replies, his mind was so filled through the affection of piety with love for the sweetness of God and all gentleness that he at once subjected his entire self, together with all his possessions, to the authority of the man of God. For he too was prudent and well instructed; he wisely gathered in his heart sound doctrine and the wisdom of God’s words, and did so commendably.

But the man of God, on the other hand, seeing the noble heart of this high-born prince and the noble and devout offering which he was making from his own substance—together with the holocaust he was making of all his possessions and wealth—asked for a brief delay before replying, [Col. 1307B] and commended this matter more attentively to the Lord God.

75. For he had understood that this prince possessed very extensive resources and a great many castles, and that they could not all easily be destroyed and made over to some religious order, both because of the diminution of the realm and because of the ruin of many other noble princes who held fiefs under the same prince. He had also heard that he was exceedingly generous in giving alms, in building churches, cloisters, and other establishments for religious persons, and in adding substantial assistance for their other needs. Likewise, he had heard that this man was a father to orphans, a spouse to widows, a steward to the poor, and moreover a consolation to lepers. [Note: [Col. 1307D] (82) Even now in Belgium lepers are called *Lazari*, because their communal dwellings are numerous, especially at Jerusalem. Indeed, outside Rome, as a Lapide testifies, there are foundations under the invocation of St. Lazarus, the poor man of the Gospel whose sores dogs licked.] Therefore the man, discerning in all things, did not presume to prescribe another manner of life for one whom he regarded as chosen by God to be the minister of all these things.

But the prince awaited an answer concerning contempt of the world and the renunciation of everything. The man of God, having received divine counsel after the delay granted for deliberation, said: “It shall not be so. For, as you have begun, you shall bear the Lord’s yoke together with the yoke of married society; and your offspring, with the blessing of your forefathers who preceded you, shall possess your most bountiful land. For it is not lawful for us to destroy in you what the divine dispensation willed, before all ages, to ordain through you in these latter times.”

To this the prince replied: “If, reverend Father, you affirm that this must be so by God’s will: ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness’ [Col. 1308A] (Ps. 23:1), and no one ought to obtain anything from it except through him. Since you command this from him, I have no objection. But let this be certain to you: I shall take no woman in marriage except one whom the Lord God shall wish to join to me through you.”

Let every hearer, therefore, weigh how great was the virtue of discernment in this man, who caused one of two princes to abandon everything, while commanding the other to possess everything as though possessing nothing. For he observed in the one that he plundered even what belonged to the needy; but in the other he observed that he never ceased to give his own goods generously to those in need.

[CHAPTER XXXIV.] At that time, finally, the man of God had planned a journey to Rome, in order to establish the rule of his brethren and to secure confirmation of the possessions bestowed upon them by God. Taking with him the count’s envoys, [Col. 1308B] he led them as far as Regensburg. For the bishop of that city was of most noble birth, and had a very powerful brother, namely Engelbert, a certain margrave, whose daughters were of marriageable age. One of them, having been sought in marriage, was to be granted to Count Theobald as his wife.

[Note: [Col. 1307D] (83) Hartwic, son of Engelbert, duke of Carinthia, presided from 1105 to 1126.]

[Note: [Col. 1308D] (84) Engelbert, margrave of Craiburg. Concerning these men consult Wiguleius Hund in his work on the bishops of Regensburg.]

[Note: [Col. 1308D] (85) Frankish writers call her Matilda. The continuator of the Monk of Jumièges calls her “the daughter of a certain count of Bohemia, who had many sons and daughters.” Our Labbe, in his *Genealogical Tables*, table 6, under the counts of Champagne, lists five sons and six daughters, all noble with great titles. Some wrongly confuse her with Matilda of Flanders.]

## CHAPTER XIII. A blind woman and a demoniac cured. The heresy of Tanchelin extirpated at Antwerp.

76. The envoys returned with this report; and Father Norbert, undertaking the journey he had begun, reached Rome. There he was honorably received by Pope Honorius, of blessed memory, and willingly obtained from him whatever he justly requested. [Note: [Col. 1308D] (86) Honorius II, created pope late in 1124, lived until February 1130. A bull issued in 1126, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [17 February], is addressed: “To the beloved sons Norbert, brother in Christ, and the canons of the Church of St. Mary at Prémontré, and their successors, who have professed the regular life in perpetuity.” It begins: “Following the footsteps of apostolic discipline, they renounce worldly pomp and possessions [Col. 1309C] and serve the Lord with their whole strength.” Having thus praised and confirmed their purpose, the pontiff says: “We decree that in your churches, [Col. 1309D] in which brethren professing the canonical life dwell, no person may change the order established there according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine. Nor may any bishop in future times dare to expel brethren of this religious order from your churches; nor may any person professing the canonical life dare to depart from the same churches or cloisters without the permission of the common congregation. No bishop, abbot, or monk may receive one who has departed without a letter of authorization from the community. We also confirm by the authority of this present written decree the goods and possessions which you justly and lawfully possess, among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of St. Martin of Laon, in the diocese of Laon; the church of St. Mary of Vivarais, in the diocese of Soissons; the church of St. Mary of Floreffe, in the diocese of Liège; the church of St. Mary and of the blessed Peter and Paul at Cappenberg, in the diocese of Münster; the church of St. Mary at Waller in the same diocese; the church of St. Mary at Elostat [Col. 1310C] in the diocese of Mainz; the church of St. Annalis—perhaps *Salinaevallis* should be read—in the diocese of Metz; and the church of St. Michael at Antwerp in the diocese of Cambrai.”

Here, then, eight abbeys had already been founded. The possessions assigned to the chief monastery of Prémontré may be read in the remainder of the bull in Pagius, fol. 392. I merely observe here that the privileges noted above are identical in substance with those which, in the preceding year, 1124, had been issued in fuller language and with a remarkable encomium upon the new foundation by “Peter, cardinal priest of the Apostolic See, and Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo,” both legates of Pope Calixtus II in France. See their diploma in the same Pagius, fol. 390. I have inspected it, etc. See vol. VI of June, p. 25, col. 2.]

When everything had been completed and he was already considering his return, one night at the first light of dawn, while he himself and certain of his companions—whom he had as the solace of his journey—were meditating upon God, they plainly heard a voice announcing that he himself would be bishop of Parthenopolis. On hearing this, they stood amazed; nor did any of them dare confess to another what he had heard.

For he had sent one of his clerics ahead to announce his return to the count and to receive an answer concerning the marriage which, through the count’s envoys, he had heard was being sought. But as he himself returned, he happened to pass through a certain city named Würzburg, which at that time lacked a bishop. The people and clergy—for it was Easter—compelled him to celebrate the feast with them.

[Col. 1309A] While he was detained there, on the holy day, as he celebrated the principal Mass and they had come to the reception of the most holy Body and Blood of the Lord, a blind woman, known to all, approached him. After the breath of the Lord’s Blood, newly poured forth, had been breathed upon her eyes by him, she received sight. Therefore, while all the people present raised their voices in admiration and praise, extolling the majesty of God, it happened that certain wealthy men among the leading citizens, pierced with contrition and inflamed with love for God, gave themselves and their possessions to God through the hands of the man of God. From their property and possessions a church is known to have been built there, which shines in divine worship even to the present day.

But the man of God and his brethren remembered the voice they had heard at Rome. Since both names of cities, Parthenopolis and Herbipolis, ended in *polis*, they feared that he might be made bishop by those who praised him beyond measure because of the magnificent work of God which had occurred there. They therefore hurriedly left the city.

77. [CHAPTER XXXV.] Having received authority from the Roman pontiff concerning the intended foundation and the established rule, when he had returned to the place of his poverty, namely Prémontré, he immediately confirmed what he had earlier done: namely, the church of Blessed Marinus, situated in the suburb of Laon, which he had organized under its abbot while he was still in extreme poverty.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] (87) Namely Walter, afterwards bishop of Laon, who died on 5 October 1153. On that day he is entered with the title of Blessed in the *Natales* of the Premonstratensian Order and is included among the devout by Saussaye.]

How greatly it grew in spiritual and temporal building, and in what soil it was planted and set down roots, let the trees grafted from it among the various nations of the earth declare; let the fruit most sweetly fragrant from them proclaim it; and let those who saw it and became fellow workers bear witness to their successors, unto eternity, as successors follow successors.

He also caused an abbot to be appointed in the church of Vivarais, which he had received in the district of Soissons. [Note: [Col. 1310D] (88) The monastery of Vivarais, now Vallis Serena, where the saint installed Henry as abbot. Le Paige, p. 454, gives his eulogy under the title of Blessed; Saussaye enrolls him among the devout on 30 August.] There, when the brethren entered, a demon which had been pursuing him immediately entered a certain man, as it is written: “Assyria also has come with them” (Ps. 82:9). Father Norbert, with God’s cooperation, delivered him in this manner.

[Col. 1310A] The man had, as was his custom yesterday and the day before, gone out to work his farm. While, exhausted by the double heat of labour, he became thirsty, he approached a nearby spring. As he bent down to drink, he saw in the water itself a huge and terrifying shadow. Terrified by that sight, he restrained himself from tasting the water; but, raising himself, he saw what seemed to be the great figure of a man, who asked fearfully: “Whose man are you?” When it had vanished after saying this, he was immediately seized by a demon and began to rage.

78. It was about the afternoon hour and near the village; thus he was found toward evening, bound, and brought in. Father Norbert looked attentively at him and said: “Do you see how the malignant spirit, which envies all good things, strives to make us hateful even in this place? For it labours to spread such a rumour—that this mark of disgrace follows upon our arrival—and this sign is intended to make people think that these evils precede us. Yet, by God’s grace, it shall not prevail.”

Then he began to sign and exorcise the man, until he became quiet and spoke sound words. In prayer he begged the holy Mother of God, in whose honour the church had been consecrated, to have mercy on him. Seeing this, those standing by rejoiced greatly, giving thanks to God and saying: “Come, blessed be God! Now our Father can rest a little in every respect, for he arrived here weary, having newly come from a long journey.”

But he who, as has often been said, possessed discernment of spirits, drew nearer. When he sensed a most foul stench issuing from the nostrils of the possessed man, he said: “[Col. 1310C] It is not as you suppose. This wicked spirit has never departed; rather, it lurks in this reed and speaks composed words, out of fear of divine power, so that it may not be expelled. When we depart, however, it may torture this wretched man more fiercely. Yet he has not been handed over to this hostile power without cause. Let us leave him this night, so that by this affliction he may pay the punishment due; let us pray for him, and perhaps tomorrow God will more readily have mercy upon him.”

And so it happened. But the truth of the matter, and the signs of truth which followed, proved the priest’s words to be true. For when they withdrew from him, the possessed man began to shriek and rage far more wickedly than he had done before. On the following day, however, the man of God returned to him; and before an innumerable crowd standing as though for a spectacle, the sick man was restored whole by God’s grace and returned to his own house with all his faculties unimpaired.

79. [CHAPTER XXXVI.] These things concerning this demoniac have been related by way of digression, so that the events which occurred may, as far as possible, be discussed in their proper order and place. For it must not be passed over why he was called to take charge of the church at Antwerp.

There was, and is, at Antwerp a place, a very large and populous town, in which there was only one priest responsible for the care of all the people dwelling there. But because of the excessive multitude and his frequent negligence, he could not manage it; nor was he trusted, since he himself had openly made his niece, related to him in the third degree, his partner in crime, as though in marriage and carnal union. For this reason that people, like a flock without a shepherd, wandered into many vain errors.

Thus it happened that a certain heretic, a seducer of remarkable subtlety and cunning, named Tanchelin, [Note: [Col. 1311C] (89) Tanchelin is called *Tanchelmus* by the clergy of the church of Utrecht-on-the-Rhine in their letter to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; *Tanquelmus* by Peter Abelard, a contemporary of Saints Norbert and Bernard, in book II of his *Introduction to Theology*; *Tandemus* by Robert of Monte in his supplement to Sigebert’s Chronicle; *Landelinus* by William Heda in his *History of the Bishops of Utrecht*; and by some also *Tandericus* and *Tauchelinus*. I judge the latter readings entirely corrupt and attribute them to the carelessness of copyists. Between *Tanchelinus* and *Tanchelmus* I do not know which to prefer, since *Dankeling* and *Dankhelm* are equally German names: the former derived from *Dank, Danken*, that is, “grace,” “to give thanks,” and the latter compounded from it. For where we Belgians now use D in our softer dialect, our forefathers, like the other Germans who still speak somewhat more harshly, used T.
