The passage of Abelard, in the Paris edition of 1616, p. 1066, reads thus: “A certain layman, Tanquelmus, recently in Flanders . . . raised himself to such madness that he caused himself to be called and celebrated as the Son of God, and, as is said, caused a temple to be built for himself by the deceived people.” We shall shortly give the Utrecht letter in full, as it was published among ancient monuments against schismatics at Ingolstadt in 1612 by Sebastian Tengnagel, imperial librarian at Vienna. Robert of Monte says almost everything that the *Life* says, at times even in the same words; with this special addition, that he asserts he was “of extreme subtlety, although a layman, yet keener in speech than many eloquent clerics”; and that, at times, “with three thousand followers, he raged with slaughter against those who resisted him.” He also adds some details concerning Tanchelin’s death, more conveniently to be set forth below, after the Utrecht letter.] arrived there and found among that people a place for his deception.

He was, in fact, the most wicked of all men, an enemy of God and all his sacraments, and an opponent of all religion and the Christian faith. He said that the ministry of bishops and priests was nothing, and denied that reception of the most holy Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was beneficial to eternal salvation. He led that people—who for many years had not had the truth of these matters proclaimed to them—into the same error.

They believed him, and approximately three thousand fighting men followed him. There was no duke, bishop, or any prince who dared resist or confront him, or appear before him unless he followed [Col. 1312A] his sect. He went about in costly display, clothed in garments embroidered with gold, with his hair braided by a triple cord and bound with a threefold band of gold embroidery. By persuasive words and lavish banquet arrangements he expended their goodwill in order to seduce them.

A strange and astonishing thing! They drank his bathwater and carried it away, storing it as though it were a relic. When he seduced daughters in the presence of their mothers and brides while their husbands looked on, he declared it to be a spiritual act; indeed, a woman who had not merited to be joined in that nefarious union called herself unfortunate. This most foul and detestable abomination of seduction could in no way be extirpated even after the heretic’s death, although a community of twelve clerics was stationed there by the bishop to assist the priest who was alone in the church of St. Michael.

80. Then the clerics, prompted by charity and compelled by this evident necessity, entrusted the church to Father Norbert and his brethren.

[Note: [Col. 1312C] (90) Polycarp says in more than one place that there were twelve of them. The same is read in a certain vernacular writing on the origins of Antwerp, composed about the year 1400 and preserved in the city archive; it is cited more fully in the particular Commentary on those origins and on the affairs of Antwerp. I refrain from bringing other evidence to light. For the present it will be enough to take from the same work the first part of the second Commentary after the Acts of Norbert, to explain the beginnings of the churches of St. Michael and St. Mary, their separation from one another, and the particular advances and growth of the church of St. Michael.

### Letter of the Church of Utrecht to Frederick, bishop of Cologne, concerning Tanchelm the seducer

To its lord and venerable Father FREDERICK, archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne: the humble Church of Utrecht, from sincere affection, offers most devoted prayers together with the obedience due in submission.

1. “We give thanks, reverend Father, to your holiness, because in fatherly compassion you grieved for our condition and restrained the course and onset of our Antichrist, the disturber and blasphemer of Christ’s Church. He opened his mouth against heaven and dared to stir up against the sacraments of the Church a heresy long ago slain by the judgments of the holy Fathers. For, swelling with the spirit of pride—which is the root of every [Col. 1313B] heresy and apostasy—he declared pope, bishops, archbishops, priests, and clerics to be nothing. Shaking the pillars of God’s Church, he even dared to divide the rock of our faith, that is, Christ. He maintained that the Church belonged only to himself and his own followers: the Church which Christ received from the Father, the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession. This man tried to restrict it to the Tanchelmists alone.

2. “But now, holy Father, receive the complaints of our affliction and consider this forerunner of Antichrist, who runs before him in the same form and along the same tracks which he himself will follow. First, in maritime districts, he mingled the poison of his unbelief among a rude people of weaker faith. Through matrons and little women—whose familiar company, private conversation, and secret lying together he most gladly enjoyed—he began gradually to scatter his errors; then through them he entangled their husbands also in the snares of his perfidy. No longer preaching in darkness or chambers, but beginning to preach upon the rooftops, he addressed the widely spread multitude in open fields. Like a king about to address the people, surrounded by attendants bearing a banner and a sword before him, as if with royal insignia, he customarily came forth to deliver his discourse.

“The deceived people listened to him as to an angel of God. Indeed, he was truly an angel of Satan. He proclaimed that God’s churches ought to be regarded as brothels; that what was performed through the priestly office at the Lord’s table was nothing; that it should, on account of ministers’ merits, be called defilement rather than sacraments; and that the efficacy of sacraments depended upon the holiness of their ministers. Yet St. Augustine says (*On Psalm* 10.6, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVI): “The Lord [Col. 1313D] Christ sent his betrayer—whom he called a devil (John 6:72), who before betraying the Lord had not even been faithful with the Lord’s money-box (John 12:6)—together with the other apostles to preach the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 10:5), in order to show that God’s gifts reach those who receive with faith, even if the person through whom they receive is like Judas.”

Likewise Augustine (ibid., 5; ibid.): “If, in receiving sacraments, the merit of giver and receiver must be considered, it is the merit of God the giver and of my conscience, the receiver. For these two things are not uncertain to me: his goodness and my faith. Why do you interpose yourself, of whom I can know nothing certain? Do not play physician: ‘In the Lord I trust’ (Ps. 10:2). For if I trust in you, how do I know that you did no evil last night?”

Declaring sacrilegiously against these and similar judgments, he dissuaded the people from receiving the sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood, and forbade tithes to be paid to the ministers of the Church. This he readily persuaded people willing to accept it, because he preached only what he knew would please them either by its novelty or by the people’s strong inclination toward it.

3. “Through such successes in wickedness, so great an audacity of crime came upon the wretched man that he even called himself God. He asserted that if Christ was God because he possessed the Holy Spirit, then he himself was God no less and in no different a sense because he had received the fullness of the Holy Spirit. In this presumption he went so far in his deception that some worshipped divinity in him, so that he distributed the water of his bath for the most foolish people to drink as a blessing, as though it were a more sacred and effective sacrament, beneficial to the salvation of body [Col. 1314C] and soul.

“At one time, moreover, while he was contriving through a new invention a new kind of gain, he ordered an image of St. Mary—one’s mind recoils to say it—to be brought into the midst of the crowd. Approaching it and touching the image’s hand with his own, he betrothed St. Mary to himself under the representation of that image. With sacrilegious mouth he uttered in full the sacramental and solemn words of betrothal, as is commonly done: ‘Behold, most beloved, I have betrothed the Virgin Mary to myself. You shall provide the betrothal gifts and the expenses for the wedding.’

“He set out two chests, one on the right and the other on the left of the image. ‘Let men offer here,’ he said, ‘and women there. I shall now see which sex burns with greater love for me and for my bride.’ And behold: the utterly crazed people rushed forward in rivalry with gifts and offerings. The women threw earrings and necklaces; and thus, not without most monstrous sacrilege, he amassed an immense sum of money.

4. “A certain blacksmith, moreover, named Manasses, whom we heard had been detained by you together with that wicked man, following the example of his most evil master established a certain fraternity commonly called a *Gilda* [guild]. In it he appointed twelve men in the figure of the twelve apostles, and a single woman in the figure of Blessed Mary. She, as they say, was led around among each of the twelve; and, in insult to the most holy Virgin, was joined to each of them in nefarious indecency, as though to confirm the fraternity.

“A certain priest also, named Everwacherus, apostatized from priestly dignity and adhered to the teaching of that abominable man. He followed him to Rome and attempted, by the authority of the lord pope, to attach the maritime districts—that is, the fourth part of our diocese—to the bishopric of Thérouanne in the kingdom of France. We heard that he too had been detained by your holiness, and rejoiced. This priest, Tanchelm’s supporter in all things, seized the tithes belonging to the brethren of the Church of St. Peter and drove out their priest from altar and church by armed force. Their crimes are infinite, Lord; [Col. 1315B] we have suppressed very many of them because a letter must be brief. Let it suffice to say in sum that divine things have come into such contempt that whoever despises the Church more is considered holier.

5. “Therefore, holy Father, since divine mercy, no longer enduring that its Church should remain in peril, has delivered them into your hands, we ask and beseech you in the Lord that by no means may they escape from [Col. 1315C] your hands. If they do escape, we announce and attest to you without any ambiguity that irreparable loss to our Church and the destruction of innumerable souls will follow. Truly, lord, our Church will suffer a most grievous fall if those men should somehow escape, whose speech, according to the Apostle, spreads like a cancer (2 Tim. 2:17) and destroys the minds of the simple by flattery.

“Even now our Antichrist, pretending to be a monk, after the example of that head of whom he has become a member, has transformed himself into an angel of light, so that he might deceive more securely by more cunningly assuming a counterfeit appearance of holiness. We ask, lord, that you be moved by righteous indignation against these detestable destroyers of the Church.

“Augustine (*Tractate* 11 on John 13:14, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV): ‘When God wishes to stir up authorities against schismatics, against heretics, against destroyers of the Church, against those who puff at Christ in scorn, let them not wonder that God stirs them up, so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah. Let Hagar recognize herself, bow her neck, and return to her mistress. Why do they wonder that Christian authorities are moved against detestable destroyers of the Church? Should they then not be moved? And how would they render account for their authority? It pertains to Christian kings that they should wish, in their own times, their mother Church—by whom they were spiritually born—to be at peace.

“We read the visions of Daniel and the prophetic acts. The three boys praised God in the fire. King Nebuchadnezzar marvelled at the boys praising God and at the fire, harmless around them [edition: “not harmful”]. Though he had set up his own statue and compelled everyone to worship it, he was nevertheless moved by the boys’ praises; when he saw the majesty of God present in the fire, he said: “And I will issue a decree to all tribes and tongues throughout the earth: whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be destroyed, and their houses laid waste” (Dan. 3:96).’ If Nebuchadnezzar praised and proclaimed and gave glory to God, so as to send a decree throughout his kingdom, how should Christian kings not [Col. 1316C] be moved against the blasphemers of Christ’s Church?’ Thus Augustine.

“Accordingly, we beseech you in the Lord that your holiness deal with these men in such a manner as to provide aid for our Church, which has long been in peril.”

I judge that the maritime districts—the fourth part of the diocese of Utrecht, belonging to the German Empire—which the impious Everwacherus attempted, by authority of the lord pope, to attach, that is to annex, to the bishopric of Thérouanne in the kingdom of France, were the land of the Four Offices, commonly called *de vier Ampten*, in Flanders, in the district of Rijen, whose head was Antwerp, situated across the Scheldt together with the islands of Zeeland.

These were possessed by Robert, count of Flanders, surnamed the Frisian; the counts of Holland claimed them as belonging to their jurisdiction, supported by the aid of Emperor Henry. But the Flemings, as Meyer writes under the year 1108, “seemed invincible under such a leader; and Henry returned ingloriously, having achieved nothing memorable; and, when peace was made at Mainz, the Fleming retained” what he possessed. Hence Robert may have conceived the desire that these disputed lands should be subject rather to the bishopric of Thérouanne than to that of Utrecht. Everwacherus, offering himself to the pope as promoter of this undertaking, could readily have gained both the favour of the count of Flanders and that of John, bishop of Thérouanne.

From this, furthermore, there seems to arise an occasion for ascertaining the date at which the letter was written: namely, by observing that the clergy write it without any mention of their bishop, and therefore most probably after his death, while the see was vacant. This was “Burchard, a devout, pious, and peaceable man,” as John of Beka describes him; in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, in 1112, [Col. 1317A] he died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [18 May].

But I read in Meyer’s *Annals of Flanders* that in 1113 Tanchelin the heretic, falsely glorying in monastic dress and condemned by anathema, was expelled from Bruges by clergy and people; and under 1115, that “in the same year the heretic Tanchelin is killed.” Robert of Monte explains this more distinctly: “After many errors and many slaughters,” he says, “while sailing, he was struck in the head by a certain priest and died.”

I therefore conceive the affair to have happened as follows. Having set out from the islands of Zeeland, Tanchelin scattered his poisons through imperial Flanders, together with the Four Offices themselves, which were subject to the diocese of Utrecht; he infected Antwerp too and the whole district of Rijen, from the beginning of the twelfth century until its eighth or ninth year. Then he betook himself to the Flemings, vassals of the French kingdom, and to the Morini, having laid aside secular dress and “pretended to be a monk.” He even dared to go to Rome under a show of holiness. On his return in 1112, he and his companions were detained at Cologne, doubtless because of the evil reputation he had left behind at Rome and everywhere along the route.

But, having escaped from custody, he returned to Bruges, soon to be anathematized by clergy and people. He then wandered through the maritime districts which he had chiefly infected, until he was cut down by a priest who sought, in no good manner, to avenge an injury done to his order. The phrase “even now” certainly indicates that this deceitful man, clothed in monastic habit, had appeared not [Col. 1317C] long before the letter was written: that is, after the many massacres of souls perpetrated in the diocese of Utrecht and in neighbouring Antwerp, although Antwerp belonged to Cambrai, while he wore secular dress. To repair these ravages, Burchard of Cambrai restored canons to St. Michael’s at Antwerp; nor is it credible that either the bishop of Utrecht or Burchard likewise had ceased his efforts.

Both men, on learning of the most wicked man’s journey to Rome, would have done nothing foreign to their duty if they took care to inform Paschal II, then occupant of the Apostolic See, about that evil man’s doctrine and conduct. The pope, compelled amid the gravest disturbances in Italy to purchase peace from Henry on most unjust terms, may have been less attentive to such reports. Yet the criminal found at Cologne the prisons he had escaped at Rome, with the result we have seen, Burchard of Utrecht having already died.

Whether he escaped from there before the denunciation of the Utrecht clergy reached Cologne, and was therefore guarded more negligently and gained a readier opportunity to flee—or whether he escaped otherwise—let each decide as he pleases. I do not believe that he preached at Antwerp after 1108 or 1109, since the *Life of St. Norbert* makes no mention of his assuming monastic dress. Yet I say that there remained there a leaven of wickedness which could not be purged except by a new sprinkling of the white order.

Anselm of Gembloux—or whoever else added certain matters to the first exemplar of Anselm in Miraeus’s edition, printed in a distinctive type on the authority of several manuscripts—writes under the year 1115: “Tanchelin the heretic, who had infected Antwerp, Walcheren, the surrounding islands, and the maritime districts in those parts with many heresies, is killed”: namely, in the manner Robert of Monte has taught us. And upon him a poet, by no means witless, cited in *Coenobiographia*, p. 8, played as follows, thereby confirming the form of the name used by the people of Utrecht:

[Col. 1318A]

> What madness burns in Tanchelm’s raging breast?  
> Does he suppose that God forgets his crime?  
> Let him not exult too greatly in earth’s open cleft:  
> If earth refuses this head, the wave will take it.

There are those who suspect that he was a man of wealth in these regions and powerful through some secular office. Yet when, in the histories of the preceding century, I read how a contemptible tailor, John of Leiden, obtained and exercised an Anabaptist kingdom in a monastery of Westphalia [Col. 1318B], and how in our own age at Naples a certain Thomas Agnellus, raised from the dregs of the fishing populace, acted against the nobility and the king, I seek in Tanchelm no distinctions of birth or fortune.

As for Burchard of Utrecht, I should not dare to entertain such favorable expectations of his effort against the heresiarch, if I believed true what Beka wrote of him: namely, how, when he was to clear himself before Hildebrand, legate of the Apostolic See, of the charge of simony by which he was defamed, and was ordered to pronounce the verse, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,” he named indeed the Father and the Son without fear, but could not call upon the Holy Spirit until he had been deprived of the episcopate, in the purchase of which he was convicted of having been a partner of Simon Magus. If, I say, I believed that these things were truly said of Burchard of Utrecht, I should also judge that he had done nothing worthy against Tanchelm; indeed, I should think it rather his fault that the heresy prevailed, and that his canons wrote that the see had stood vacant for perhaps rather more years through the deposition, not the death, of a simoniacal bishop.

But how could Beka have failed to see—not to say how little this suited a man whom he praises as devout and pious—but how absurdly it was applied to one first created bishop in 1099, that is, forty-four years after the time of Hildebrand’s legation to Gaul for abolishing the treachery of simony? I pass over the fact that he could in no way have been judged in Gaul, since he had nothing whatever in common with Gaul. Paul of Bernried, who wrote the Life of Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, and relates the affair as done at the Synod of Lyons, no. 11, from the frequent account of Pope Callistus and from Hildebrand’s own mouth; Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, later Pope Victor III; and St Peter Damian, name neither bishop nor episcopate.

If, contrary to probability, it were otherwise established that this person was from Utrecht, he ought to be named William, brother of Wichard, governor of Guelders, “a man wholly given to war,” says Beka [Col. 1318D], who succeeded Bernulf after his death on 19 July 1054. Arnold Buchelius, Beka’s scholiast, taking no concern to establish Burchard’s innocence from the chronology, confidently declares that the entire “account” “seems fabricated, in order to forge hatred against the emperor, whom they alleged to be stained by the vice of simony because he insisted on the investiture of prelates by staff and ring, received from his forefathers.”

Is this, then, the presidency of a heretical spirit: to call into suspicion of slander authors most worthy of all trust, who openly accuse the crime of sacrilegious purchase and make no mention at all of investiture, the right concerning which was still then under dispute—merely because of the shameful lie of a fabricated miracle? I do not know, moreover, whether even in the very purchase of an episcopate a Calvinist would acknowledge anything criminal: one accustomed, from Tanchelm’s doctrine through Calvin, to despise the sacrament of Orders and to assign to the civil magistrate all authority in sacred matters, if that sect has any sacred matters.

], through the bishop’s hands they gave this same church, with certain revenues, trusting that through the merits of Norbert himself and his brethren God would remove the savagery of the deadly plague and, with the darkness of ignorance driven away, restore the light of truth. The church was accordingly received; and the clergy built another for themselves in the same town. Both remain to the present day, devoted to God’s service.

But Father Norbert, having installed experienced brethren who would apply a life-giving remedy to the mortal wound, began with them also to sow the word of God and to pour forth sayings sweeter to their throats than honey and the honeycomb [Col. 1312C], giving sweet nourishment to the sick and proclaiming to the weak the bread which strengthens the human heart and bestows eternal life. For he said: “Brothers, do not wonder, and do not be afraid. Through ignorance you followed falsehood, thinking it truth; if anyone had taught you this earlier, then, as you proved ready for destruction, so you would have proved readier to receive salvation” [Col. 1313A].

Some, therefore, hearing the word and seeing the works that followed, were struck with reverence; men and women brought back the Lord’s Body, which they had stored in chests or holes for ten, fifteen, or very many years. Who would not be amazed at this detestable deed? Who would say that it ought not to be commended to memory and posterity: that a most wicked deceiver fraudulently misled this people, and that the pious preacher Norbert, both personally and through his followers, brought them back to the way of truth and righteousness? This narrative may seem superfluous to hearers; yet the transition to what follows cannot be plainly understood unless the testimony of the preceding work teaches this at some point [Col. 1313B].

## CHAPTER XIV. Demons repeatedly repelled. Wolves tamed.

**81. [CHAP. XXXVII.]** Among other matters, this must not be passed over [Col. 1314A]. One night at Prémontré, in the house of poverty, he had remained longer than usual with certain sickly and weak brethren, discussing heavenly hope and the glory of blessedness, and listening to their discussion. In the silence of the secret night, some of them grew thirsty, and someone was sent to the spring to bring water.

When those who had been sent returned, as soon as they entered the door of the cell, he said: “Why, men of God, have you brought unclean water here?” Astonished, they were afraid; they protested that they had brought a well-washed vessel and the purest water. As it was poured from the pot into the cup, once and twice he made them throw it out of that same cup, absolutely forbidding anyone to taste even a little of it. When for the third time the whole contents were poured out down to the bottom of the little pot, and, with a light brought near, they looked more clearly and carefully, they saw an extraordinarily large toad crawling in the cup and were astonished.

They could indeed be astonished and marvel exceedingly, both because it was winter, when creatures of this kind do not usually appear [Col. 1315A], and because they remembered that the spring was most pure and the vessel thoroughly clean.

> **[Note: Col. 1315D] (91).** This spring, even today called that of St Norbert because he and his first companions drank from it, is visited as efficacious in driving away fevers. This was learned at Prémontré and related at Antwerp by the Reverend Josephus Dappiano, of blessed memory, as Polycarpus describes it at length in his very words in *Analecta*, book II, chapter 2, to be cited below [Col. 1316D].

Seeing them stunned, Father Norbert said: “Why do you marvel, brothers? That wicked spirit who persecutes us in enmity is ingenious in a thousand devices. But cast it out, for the arrogance of his cunning and subtlety is greater than his strength.”

What, then, O reader, ought one to observe concerning this man? Could he have opposed unclean spirits by this subtle discernment unless the infusion and superabundant grace of the Holy Spirit had taught him?

**82. [CHAP. XXXVIII.]** On another occasion, when certain brethren had gone into the forest to cut wood, they found a wolf devouring a roe-deer. Shouting, they drove it away; and taking with them the prey [Col. 1315B] which the wolf’s rapacity had seized, they brought it home and, suspecting no harm, hung it in a certain corner.

But the wolf, as though protesting the injury done him, followed them and sat at the door of the house they had entered, like some domestic dog, seeming to demand back what had been taken from him. Those who arrived, not knowing what had happened, shouted at him, as people usually do, to drive him away [Col. 1316A]. But he looked at them with a tame expression and remained motionless.

When this was reported to the man of God, he assembled all the brethren and asked what had occurred, saying that so savage an animal would not without cause have assumed the appearance of such gentleness. The brethren who knew themselves guilty, fearing, came forward publicly; and, asking pardon as though for a grave offence, they recounted what had happened and the injury which they thought they had done the wolf.

Hearing this, the man of God said: “Give him back what is his; for you acted unjustly in taking what was not yours.” When the wolf had received his prey, he went away in peace, harming no one.

**83. [CHAP. XXXIX.]** A certain boy, a shepherd of sheep, asked what he should do if, having no dogs, some wolf carried off a sheep from him [Col. 1316B]. He was jokingly told to command it, in the name of his master, not to dare carry her away or harm her.

Not long afterward it happened that the same boy was, as usual, guarding the sheep in the field. A wolf came, seized one of them, and fled carrying it away at full speed. The brother saw it from afar and, mindful of the command, began to cry out loudly: “Where are you fleeing, most malicious robber,” he said, “swifter than usual? Put down the sheep; put her down, I say. I command you this in the name of my master: do not hurt her, nor presume to carry her farther” [Col. 1317A]. The wolf immediately put her down unharmed; and the boy quickly lifted her onto his shoulders and carried her back to the others.

**84.** Whether this was the same boy or another is unknown. It is known, however, that on another day a certain clerical brother was sent into the field to guard the animals. A wolf remained by them throughout the day while he was present; and, as though affording assistance in the watch, it displayed no savagery. When evening drew near and it was time for the flock to be brought in, the brother drove the flock in from one side and the wolf from the other.

When the flock had been brought in and the brother had shut the door, leaving the wolf outside [Col. 1319A], the wolf, as though complaining of the injury done it and demanding its due wages, struck the door with its paw as best it could. It struck repeatedly, showing that it wished to enter and receive some portion of food.

When the man of God heard this, he said: “Why do you not open to the guest who is knocking?” They answered that it was not a guest but a wolf forcing itself in impertinently, and that it would not depart for all of them together. He summoned the brethren and asked on what occasion it had come there. But since all were silent, he called the cleric whom he had sent that morning to guard the flock and asked who had helped him in guarding it.

The man, afraid to disclose what had happened to him but not daring, when questioned, to conceal it, said: “That beast is knocking at the door [Col. 1319B]. It was with me today and preserved the flock entrusted to me together with me, as though it had been entrusted to it, until it was shut within the door.”

Hearing this, the man of God said: “Give it some fodder, for it is asking payment for the service it has rendered; the laborer is worthy of his food.” When meat was thrown to it at the man of God’s command, it seized it as its wages and went away. Not long afterward, it once received bread from the hand of a boy tending calves.

What is this, brothers? Savage beasts devoid of reason become tame and obey human beings; rational man shuts his ear and does not obey—as though he who formed the eye did not see (Psalm 93:9). Wretched man does not go on his way [Col. 1319C], although “when his ways please God, all his enemies will be at peace with him” (Proverbs 16:7), and elsewhere: “The whole world shall fight against the senseless” (Wisdom 5:21). The man of God preached this to all, taught this to his own followers, and, as if flying before them, demonstrated it by deed.

**85. [CHAP. XL.]** By manifold art, as has often been said, that envious enemy persecuted the company arrayed to fight him [Col. 1320A], so that scarcely any of them dared go anywhere after the darkness of night returned.

But one upon whom he laid many snares said that he was of little faith. Rebuking himself, he took courage and went alone to attend a private need. A demon stood before him, having assumed the appearance of a very terrifying man, advancing with a most black aspect, threatening as though he would carry the man away through the air.

But he, gathering the strength of faith and recovering vigor of mind, said within himself: “How long shall I endure the falsity and phantoms of this most importunate enemy?” Rising, he wished to seize it; the demon turned to flight. He swiftly pursued it and, coming to a nearby tree, began to wrestle against it, wishing to hold and bind the demon.

> **[Note: Col. 1319C] (92).** Having stated that at Prémontré there was “an orchard beside the little chapel,” he nevertheless says it is uncertain whether the tree here in question stood there or elsewhere. Then, from Peter de Waghenare, he relates concerning “a certain tree at Prémontré, planted by St Norbert in the middle of the cloister, which never put forth green foliage, but, superior alike to cold and heat, unfolded luxuriant leaves for five centuries. The tradition of the elders was added: on the feast days of the holy Father, as though it felt the hands of its cultivator, it was accustomed to surpass itself in such verdure that it captivated those looking upon it [Col. 1319D]. But this too provokes wonder: the tree is said to have been the holy Father’s staff; and likewise that this wood is described as related to cedar, of pleasing fragrance and inherent power. And though it is cause for sorrow that, through neglect, this tree was uprooted, yet there is joy in this, that certain small branches taken from it are said to revive and grow elsewhere.”

After a short interval, looking back, he recognized that this was the tree which he knew stood there. Thus, with this courage of mind, the illusion of the venomous serpent was overcome, and thereafter he suffered no fear.

The demon also presumed to attack another in a similar way, instilling the same terror. It stood visibly before him while he sat attending a private need; and neither moved from his place, from the beginning of Matins until the end. But at last the brother’s timely steadfastness conquered the demon’s shameless importunity. Rising and making the sign of the cross, he sprang out through the door which appeared to be occupied by the demon; finding no one obstructing him [Col. 1320C], he learned that such an illusion could harm neither him nor anyone else. He remained free from this false fear; having grasped the liberty of the Holy Spirit, he did not afterward depart from it.

> **[Note: Col. 1319D] (93).** In the Morin manuscript a chapter, omitted by the others, was inserted here under this title: “How the evil spirit, rebuked by a certain brother for its degradation, departed in confusion.” Receive now this chapter, as it was transmitted to us by Waghenare:
>
> “At that time a brother of sufficiently proven holiness was stationed to guard the gate, to give alms there, and to receive guests with prayer, according to the statute of the order. One night, as he lay upon a bed which was likewise made of stone for them all [Col. 1320C], Satan came to him. The brother was not sleeping but praying. Satan roared and sometimes grunted like a pig, rolling the stone about the brother’s feet.
>
> “When it had done this on the first night and the following one, and was not slow to return on the third, the brother—having already received counsel from his prior concerning what he should say or do—addressed it thus when it came the third time:
>
> “‘Alas, wretched and most wretched one! You were once that Lucifer who rose in the morning [Col. 1320D]; you were in the delights of God’s paradise. But because these did not suffice for you, and you said, “I will set my throne in the north; I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14), you lost what you were. You exchanged light for darkness, blessedness for misery, and the place of delights for stench with swine, which you chose. Behold a worthy exchange, a fitting barter! Come now: this is not your place. Roll yourself in the stench of sewers, and make yourself like swine.’
>
> “He departed confused, and thereafter, until the day of that brother’s death, did not come to tempt him in any visible form. For the wicked spirit is thus put to shame and confounded when the delights he has lost are cast in his teeth; just as he fears and trembles when, in exorcisms, the threats and terrors of the coming judgment are set before him. Hence the Church’s custom arose that the conclusion of all exorcisms should sound thus: ‘I exorcize you by him who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Amen.’”

**86. [CHAP. XLI.]** If these were the struggles due to the members, what struggles were due to the head? If these befell subjects, what befell their master? Greater ones, certainly. Greater, indeed, because he had inflicted greater damage upon the enemy himself and foresaw that he would yet inflict exceedingly great damage upon him in the future.

Therefore, after the man of God had spent one entire night without sleep in prayer, standing before the altar of the poor oratory which he had undertaken at Prémontré at the beginning of his conversion, Satan stood behind him in the shape of a dreadful bear, presenting a terrible aspect with teeth and claws. When the man turned and wished to go forward to restore his weakened limbs by a little sleep, he suddenly saw the beast standing there and was frightened. But immediately recovering himself, observing that the door of the oratory was shut and recalling that he had heard no sound of anyone entering, he recognized the snares of his persecutor.

After praying briefly and regaining his strength, he said: “What are you waiting for, bloody beast? Your claws are empty; your dreadful teeth are wind; your shaggy hide is smoke and vapor passing vainly away, like a shadow that vanishes when the sun departs. You, who were the seal of God’s likeness, when you were light, deserved darkness through pride. Depart now: I command you, for there is no accord of Christ with Belial; no fellowship of light with darkness; no share of the faithful with the unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6:12). Depart quickly. You know that you can harm no one unless permitted; and then only those who, because their sins demand it, have been made subject to your power.” At these words the liar, unable to bear words of truth, vanished.

**87. [CHAP. XLII.]** By then the time had come when Count Theobald, mentioned above [Col. 1321C], was to meet, on a day arranged through messengers and in a place likewise appointed, his future wife, her father, and a great company of their relatives. He had invited Father Norbert, who had given the counsel for this union, and brought him with him to that place.

When they arrived, they did not find her, for she had remained on the road, detained by a grave illness. The count and all who were with him wondered at this, suspecting some cause of repentance or deception. After consultation, Father Norbert was earnestly entreated to go forward to meet her and report whether the reason for this delay was genuine [Col. 1322A].

The man acceded to those who begged him, considering it also a reproach to himself if he did not carry through to the end the care he had undertaken concerning this marriage. He received eight marks of silver and sent them to his brethren at Prémontré. In his absence they had undertaken to feed five hundred poor people, because it was a time of famine and they were buying food for themselves and the poor.

Since he had been angry with them for this, he commanded that in his name they should add another hundred and twenty poor people, so that one hundred should receive a full meal from the common food, thirteen should be refreshed in the hospital house with bread, meat, and wine, and seven should be with the canons in the refectory. He believed that the offence which he had committed against God and the brethren—because the humanity and work of mercy which they had undertaken in faith in Jesus Christ for the poor had displeased him—would thus be remitted and expiated. For he did not expect ever to return to live among them, nor did he wish to leave any mark of offence upon those whom he knew to be gathered in the love of God, of himself, and of all the faithful, following in this the example of the true Master, who “having loved his own, loved them unto the end” (John 13:1) [Col. 1322B].

> **[Note: Col. 1321C] (94).** Abbot Chrysostomus left written testimony in his own hand that, while residing at Saintes, he read and ordered the following copied in an old breviary there:
>
> “St Norbert, after staying for some time at Antwerp, finally took leave of the brethren there and departed, having established so large a sum of money as would suffice permanently to maintain one hundred and twenty poor persons” [Col. 1321D].
>
> The saint may have made the same provision on different occasions and in different places; therefore I would have no scruple remain here. For at Magdeburg also, in 1130, when he had established brethren there, he “handed over in perpetual right the hospital house, founded by Archbishop Adelbert, for them to govern and administer,” because he “had found it so ruined and almost annihilated that those who ought to have received their daily support there were begging shamefully and miserably.”
>
> Another ordinance left by the same saint concerning the poor at Prémontré is likewise worthy to be read here in full, as it is reported by Pagius, folio 304:
>
> “Let a tithe be given to God, for the hospital, from every possession and offering of the brethren, for the use of the poor. Thus, if a sum of money is worth ten solidi, or if an offering up to ten solidi has been made, from these ten, eight poor persons shall be clothed each year: in winter, namely, one on the feast of All Saints, one at the Nativity of the Lord, one at the Circumcision of the Lord; likewise one at the Epiphany of the Lord, at the Purification of St Mary, at the Annunciation of St Mary, at the Burial of the Lord, and at the Resurrection of the Lord. They shall be clothed in new garments: namely, shirts, breeches [Col. 1322C], stockings, socks, shoes, a tunic, and a hooded cloak or furs.
>
> “In summer, namely at the Ascension of the Lord, during the seven days of Pentecost, at the passion of the apostles Peter and Paul, and at the Assumption of St Mary, one person shall be clothed at each feast with a new mantle or cloak, shirt, breeches, socks, and shoes. From the day on which a poor person receives clothing until the eighth day, if he wishes to remain, bodily refreshment shall be provided for him there. The remainder shall be spent for the use of poor persons arriving or passing through.
>
> “On the Lord’s Supper, moreover, every priest or deacon, after washing the feet of the beggars and with the counsel of the provost, shall charitably give them one of his own garments—whether cloak, furs, tunic, or stockings. Having received this charity, they shall by no means remain for seven days as above, but shall depart immediately after their meal” [Col. 1322D].

## CHAPTER XV. Entry into the Archbishopric of Magdeburg. Establishment there of a monastery of the Order.

**88.** From there he proceeded to the place to which he was being sent. Coming to Speyer, he found the Saxons and, for the most part, the clergy of the city of Parthenopolis gathered before King Lothair to choose an archbishop [Col. 1322C]. Hearing that this man had arrived, whom the people proclaimed a holy man throughout diverse nations of the earth, they called him both to make a discourse, in which he was gladly heard, and to hear his counsel concerning certain affairs, as the need of some among those assembled required.

The affair of the Parthenopolitans, who had been deprived of their father, was first considered. There was present a certain cardinal, newly arrived from the Roman See, and an innumerable multitude of other princes [Col. 1323A]. In the election, three were named by their counsel, one of whom was Father Norbert, though he did not know it.

> **[Note: Col. 1322D] (95).** Gerard, later Pope Lucius: so Robert of Monte. In chapter 2 of his *Annals*, Peter is added as his fellow legate [Col. 1323D]. At Gerard’s exhortation, because of his longstanding goodwill toward the new Order, Stephen, bishop of Metz, in 1136 confirmed a gift made by the abbot of Saint-Trond—who had a share in the allod of Averbode—to the Premonstratensian church founded there, in respect of the right which the bishop himself held over the men of Saint-Trond. This shows that the beginnings of that foundation should properly be referred to 1128, when Gerard was a legate in Germany, even if it was not fully completed before 1135.

When they hesitated and, of the three, strove toward the better choice, Albero, primicerius of the church of Metz—the man who later became archbishop of the church of Trier—secretly signaled to them with his finger from the opposite side that they should choose the man of God, Norbert.

> **[Note: Col. 1323D] (96).** Albero of Trier, elected in 1132.

They immediately seized him by the hands and, crying out again and again, exclaimed: “We elect this man as our father; we approve him as our shepherd.”

> **[Note: Col. 1324D] (97).** Our ancient Saxon manuscript: “In the year of the Lord 1126, Norbert succeeded Ruker in the see of Magdeburg.”

**89.** The weak man could not defend himself. He was not allowed to think, nor, even by thinking, to arrange anything concerning himself. But as soon as he was seized, he was praised by the king and approved by all who stood by; he was also confirmed by the legate of the Roman Church himself [Col. 1323B].

> **[Note: Col. 1324D] (98).** This was Lothair, duke of Saxony, elected king on 24 August 1125. Having gone to Rome with St Norbert, he was crowned emperor on 4 June 1133.

The man was led away, carrying with him an aggravated heavy burden; he was led to a place he did not know. He was drawn, I say, to a people of a crooked and perverse nation, namely among Slavs and Saxons.

> **[Note: Col. 1324D] (99).** Slavia formerly extended from the right bank of the Elbe, beside which Magdeburg lies, as far as the Baltic Sea and Wagria, a province of Holstein. Ancient Saxony lies on the left bank.

Each people derives its name from a reality: the former, because the sharpness of the Slavs had been taken away, suggesting the sting of unbelief; the latter, attesting the weight of stones and the blindness and savagery of a stony heart. And he who, for the sevenfold service which Laban had rendered, had expected Rachel—or Mary’s “better part,” which he himself had chosen, though weak in body (Luke 10:42)—found instead Martha’s work and Leah’s labor. For “there is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30).

Therefore he who had neglected the unbelieving nation of pagans, to which he had purposed to go at the beginning of his conversion in order to recall any from the error of unbelief, was now forced, bearing authority and office with him, manifestly to submit to the obedience from which he had thought to escape the divine disposition [Col. 1323C].

**90. [CHAP. XLIII.]** At his entry, according to the custom of peoples, there was an innumerable concourse. All, the older and the younger, rejoiced: the older because they had chosen a person of fame and high name; the younger because they had been granted to receive one who sympathized with their infirmities.

Seeing from afar the city to which he was being led, he walked barefoot. Barefoot he entered the sanctuary in procession; barefoot he was led into the palace [Col. 1323D]. Yet, as a poor man, poorly clothed in a cloak, while others entered he was rejected by the doorkeeper, who did not recognize him. The doorkeeper said to him: “Other poor persons were admitted long ago. It is not fitting for you to force yourself in importunately, crowding this multitude of princes” [Col. 1324A].

Those who followed cried out: “Wretch, what are you doing? Let him be, wretch! What have you done? Do you not know that this is our bishop and your lord?”

But Father Norbert called back the man, who had quickly fled and hidden himself behind, and said with a smile: “Do not fear or flee, my brother. You know me better and see me with a clearer eye than those who compel me to these lofty palaces, to which one who appears so poor and insignificant as I do ought not to be exalted.”

**91. [CHAP. XLIV.]** Having thus been consecrated and made bishop and raised to the episcopal chair, he did not forget the apostolic precept commanding a bishop to be the steward of his own house (1 Timothy 3:4). Summoning the provosts of the household and all the ministers [Col. 1324B], he investigated what the revenues of the episcopal table were, where they lay, and who were those who ought to preside over each.

When all had been counted and entered in writing, together with the expenses required from them, scarcely enough was found among all of them to suffice for four months of the year. The priest of God, exceedingly astonished, carefully asked whether the Church had in former times been enriched by a larger possession of estates, or whether things belonging to its right had been dissipated because some who had previously held the administration had guarded them too negligently.

When he learned the truth—that the Church had been noble, founded and exalted by royal power, endowed and enlarged by generosity—he said: “Where are these things? Or by what means have they been alienated from it and from you, to whom they belonged?”

They replied: “Some of your predecessors, indulging their flesh too greatly, granted one estate to their carnal brothers and bestowed another on certain relatives and kinsmen. Others who succeeded them did likewise, giving some things in fief. Others, more lax and oppressed by powerful men, were unable to defend what belonged by right to the Church and lost certain things. Thus all the possessions which were accustomed to serve this dignity and honor were diminished and reduced utterly to nothing” [Col. 1324C].

**92.** Hearing this, the man remembered that “cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17:5). Gathering strength in him and through him by whom he did not doubt that he had been called to administer this office, and fearlessly assuming the splendor of authority, he sent emissaries in every direction. He commanded that whoever unjustly possessed the property of the Church over which, by God’s authorship, he presided should by no means dare thereafter to lay hands upon it, unless they first showed it to be their hereditary right and an ancient paternal possession [Col. 1325A].

Hearing this, those robbers and sacrilegious men were greatly indignant that an unarmed and poor man, who had been brought in riding an ass, should dare to issue so powerful and prompt a command. They counted it as nothing, thinking they would lose none of what they had violently possessed through him.

But he pursued them with the spiritual sword with which he was girded. Sitting in his own quiet, he attacked, struck down, and cast down; and, having cast them down, he bound them with the bond of anathema. They recognized this persecution as light for the bishop but long-lasting and grievous for themselves, since authority commanded that those who endure an anathema for one year are, after that year, outside the law and may receive no hearing in legal matters. For the most part, therefore, they relinquished what they had unjustly seized for themselves by usurping the Church’s benefices. Yet they did so unwillingly and therefore secretly supplied fuel for enmity and hatred against the bishop wherever and however they could [Col. 1325B].

**93.** But he who had undertaken the way of justice and the course of the straight path before his elevation to the episcopate remained unmoved by them. He preached the word, proclaimed the kingdom of God, and made peace within his borders. He exalted religious houses and built new ones where none existed; he embraced and set in order religious persons; and he inflicted continual persecution upon the undisciplined and irreligious unless they repented.

He said that deans, priests, those charged with governing the people, and all promoted to sacred orders must in every way maintain chastity. He compelled them either to keep it or, if publicly exposed, to leave all ecclesiastical benefices [Col. 1325C].

All this was the beginning of sorrows and the occasion of persecutions. For day after day each person, confessing the grievance which he bore with difficulty, said: “Why did we wish this newcomer, whose customs we did not know, to reign over us? He is opposed to our works and customs beyond what we can bear.”

This complaint was circulated among the greater and the lesser alike, among the rich and also the poor: some being burdened, others fearing burden, still others merely yielding to common rumor from others. Thus he who had formerly been exalted with great praises was now cast down by blame, reproaches, and words alone, without even knowing it himself [Col. 1325D]. Yet he nevertheless advanced outwardly in his work, through the ordering of him who customarily arranges inwardly all outward things before they come to pass.

94. [CHAP. XLV.] Before the episcopal palace stood, not far away, a church dedicated to Saint Mary, Mother of God, in which there were twenty secular canons, established from ancient times under a provost. Since the priest of God had foreseen that this church was necessary to him—so that, after placing his brethren there, he might sometimes recover his breath a little from the tumult demanded by the office laid upon him—he frequently made it clear both to the king, to the canons of the Greater Church, and to the canons of that church, that, if elsewhere they received revenues from him on equal or better terms, they should freely grant that church to him. All with one voice objected, declaring that a church of so great a name ought not to be altered, nor its dignity, being subject to royal authority, diminished; nor ought a people of another order and custom to be imposed upon it, a people ignorant of royal rights and of the subjection and service due according to their custom.

For several years he endured this refusal from them all; but at last he prevailed, persevering humbly in his petition. He prevailed indeed through the argument by which he pressed them; he prevailed also through the constancy by which they knew that, from good beginnings to the end, he would never be willing to desist. Having removed those clerics and resettled each one as he wished, he placed brethren of his own order in that church, as he had long desired. There he ordained that the service of God should be maintained, both while he lived according to the instituted order and, after his departure, forever.

> [Note: Col. 1325D (100). Thus all the manuscripts. The single Parc manuscript writes more distinctly: “And each one having been placed where he wished.” Honorius II, approving the change in a brief document—which Polycarp reports as brought to Magdeburg in his *Annotations*, p. 415—says: “The clerics who had been living insufficiently religious lives in the church of St Mary, providing like a pious father for their needs in other places, you have placed elsewhere.” Robert of Monte assigns this event to the year 1129. For Norbert’s own charter, see chapter 3 of the *Analecta*.]

## CHAPTER XVI. Persecutions endured. The first abbots appointed.

95. [CHAP. XLVI.] The number of the brethren increased; they multiplied in Saxony, where religious life had grown cold, and in Slavonia, where it had not existed, they took root, flowered with fruitful growth, and multiplied like the Hebrews. The Saxons raged; the people of Parthenopolis raged. As hatred and envy against the man of God grew stronger, he, placing hope and trust in God, did not cease to enlarge this congregation and those of other customs.

For this reason wolves raged against the lamb, sheep against the shepherd: the wolf shared its savagery with the sheep under the guise of gentleness; the sheep shared its gentleness with the wolf in savagery, so that, agreeing on both sides, they might exercise cruel ferocity in the shepherd’s killing. You might see a remarkable kind of persecution. Those who stood at his side secretly pierced his sides; friends, turned near at hand into enemies, hurled missiles at him from afar; his counsellors, his neighbors, carried arrows in their quivers to be discharged at the suitable time and place, and sharp swords beneath their tongues, laying ambushes everywhere in secret in order to kill the innocent.

“They became corrupt and abominable against him; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps was beneath their lips. There they trembled where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5).

They feared that they would lose through him the kingdom for which he labored so that they might reign without end. They feared becoming poor; yet they acted perversely, wishing to extinguish the one through whom they ought—and, if they wished, were able—to become rich. Perhaps the hearer is weary of hearing blasphemies so often, while the writer brings forward no charge of blasphemy. Let the world, then, hear and judge; let the old hear, let the young discern and learn, and let them tell and teach their successors whether anything was done in ancient days such as was done in those days.

96. For the day had now come—the day, I say, most holy and most celebrated, the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper—on which the authority of the holy Fathers decreed that penitents should be reconciled to God; and on which that innocent Lamb, in order to reconcile the enmity between God and humankind, was seized and led away to be sacrificed. And behold, at the door of the place where the priest of God received the confessions of penitents, there stood a man clothed in a cloak, in the likeness of a penitent, earnestly begging the doorkeeper that he might be permitted to enter and make confession to the bishop.

When the doorkeeper informed the man of God of this, he said: “Do not admit him.” And while the doorkeeper, by his lord’s command, said that he ought to wait a little, the man pressed more and more insistently to be brought in. Thus he continued knocking, and was not admitted until the other crowd that had assembled for confession had withdrawn; then at last he was given leave to enter. When the man of God carefully observed him from a distance, he said: “Do not come any nearer, but stand still, and see that you do not move your foot.”

Calling some of the palace servants who were outside, he ordered them to strip the young man standing there of the cloak in which he was wrapped. When he had been stripped, a sharp dagger appeared, bound to his side, nearly a foot and a half in length. At the bishop’s command he was brought before him with the dagger, while all present watched. When he was asked why he had come armed in this fashion, trembling and astonished—as one conscious of unspeakable and wicked cruelty—and fearing death, he fell at the bishop’s feet and confessed that he had been sent to kill him. Naming those by whom he had been hired, and at whose urging and counsel he had come to perpetrate so execrable a crime, the others present, and those flocking together for this unprecedented spectacle, were exceedingly astonished that the authors of this treachery were those accustomed to deliberate with the bishop about the greatest affairs and the most secret counsels.

97. But the righteous man, as was his manner, with cheerful face and serene expression looked toward them and said: “Why do you wonder if the ancient enemy recognized his own vessel and endeavors to perform his work in his own members—a work which, on this most sacred night, he did not fear to perform upon our holy Head, Jesus Christ? O how blessed would be the man who, at some hour of this day, were betrayed and died not merely by enemies, but even by friends, such as those whom you have heard named!”

“This,” I say, “is the day on which mercy is given to the despairing, pardon to sinners, and life restored to the dead. In preventing this death of mine on this day, you have prolonged my sorrow and imposed labor upon me, but you have also deferred my rest. These men were and are friends; and yet they do not deserve thereby to become enemies. For it is fitting that we imitate our Head and Beginning, Jesus Christ. For he says: ‘Do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you’ (Matt. 5:44); and elsewhere: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34).”

Nevertheless, the betrayer was confined in custody, not in order that he might be punished, but so that the counsel of his abettors might be exposed, and so that in them the ignominy of so great a crime might inflict the punishment which no penitence or grief of heart had made them feel. What then? Could the man of God have known what the man who came under the pretext of confession and penance was carrying, unless superabundant grace had taught him? Those who armed themselves with shameful wickedness and manifest injustice are defeated and fail before an unarmed man.

98. [CHAP. XLVII.] Envious wickedness did not cease in secret, though openly it feigned gentle justice; and it was so much more grievous and evil because it was practiced by members of his household and by intimates. It was indeed intimacy worthy of the name. For at a certain hour of the night, when he had risen as usual with his clerics to celebrate Matins, one of the household clerics came and stationed himself in ambush behind the door, full of wickedness and cruel malice, armed with suitable weapons by which he could cautiously and treacherously strike and kill the innocent man.

When the chaplains who went before had come out—as is the custom in that land, for chaplains precede their lords—the man sprang from ambush. Thinking that the bishop was last, he struck one of the clerics and tore his garment down the middle. When the cleric cried out, saying, “Who is hurting me?” the assailant recognized from the sound of his voice that he was not the man he sought. “I thought,” he said, “that this was the last man, whom I intended to deliver to death.” For the bishop had gone ahead unnoticed among the others, fearing this very event as though he knew beforehand what was to come.

But the assailant turned to flight at a swift run; and when others pursued him to capture him, the man of God said: “Let him flee, and do not return evil for evil. He has done what he could and what God permitted him to do; for my hour has not yet come. But those who sent him shall neither sleep nor rest until they are glutted with their reproaches and either deliver me to death or, if the work being done through me is divine, make it manifestly proved.”

99. [CHAP. XLVIII.] Although deprived of so great a father, the little flock of the church of Prémontré nevertheless waited patiently for two years, following the example of him who said: “I shall not leave you orphans; I go and I come to you” (John 14:18). Some of them, together with certain secular persons, said: “We shall by no means be able to endure; for when the shepherd departs, the sheep are accustomed to scatter.” Others wanted no master except him; others, despairing of his return, wanted to elect another. Thus they contended, each side advancing a cause that appeared alike in truth and reason, and having no consolation from faithful exhortation; being still but slightly rooted, they wavered rather than could conceive any stability in themselves.

When this was reported to the man of God, fearing that what God had planted through him might wither if it were not still watered with the dew of divine counsel, he summoned certain brethren among the priors who possessed greater and sounder judgment. He asked them what needed to be done, investigating each person’s wishes separately, so that he might be more certain in every respect in determining the course of his work. When he learned that some wished to live with him, others to live elsewhere by his counsel, and others to keep the vow of their chosen poverty, but that most wished under a definite master and discipline to observe that same manner of poverty, he sent them back to their place, retaining a few with himself. Again and again he urged upon them the rule of peace and unanimity, so that, when he granted them the power to choose a father, the harmony of Christ Jesus and the love that he taught might be found among them.

They departed; and the good Father, not forgetful of the children whom he had begotten in Christ, sent faithful messengers to them before long, lest they remain too long without a teacher. These messengers both announced that they had leave to elect and declared his own will concerning the election. It is unnecessary here to linger over how and what was done in the election, since those who had been well taught by their master had no need to be further instructed by the delegates sent to them.

100. Therefore, once the election had been approved by the sons, as the Father had granted his consent, those who had been sent returned to him and announced that the command expressing his will had been fulfilled. He himself had the elected man with him.

> [Note: Col. 1329C (101). This is Hugh, his first companion, discussed above in connection with chapter 5.]

Yet he ordered the matter to be concealed for several days; nor was it disclosed to the man elected, so that the curiosity of certain persons who were with him—who also eagerly awaited this answer—might be observed. For it was his custom, whenever events of this kind were to be considered, changed, or confirmed, and whenever other matters arose through various practical circumstances, to draw out fully the spirit of every person around him concerning each affair, so that he might make no abrupt determination in matters without first, insofar as a human being could, seeking the will of God and receiving the better judgment from those about him.

The counsel was concealed for a time. Yet the man elected did not fail to know what had been done concerning him, so that, taught by divine revelation, he might consider the matter silently. For he declared that, on the morning of the day on which the election concerning him was made, he had stood in a vision before Jesus Christ, the Son of God, together with his father and master Norbert. Jesus stretched out his right hand and received from the hand of the man of God that brother whom the other brethren had elected, while the man of God said: “Lord, I present to your most holy majesty this man entrusted to me by you.”

101. By this, without doubt, he could know what else divine mercy was ordaining concerning him. Why say more? The day came on which it pleased the man of God to complete what he had begun; and, having summoned the brethren who were with him, he disclosed his counsel to them. Calling the elected man, he said: “You shall succeed me, by the election of your brethren, in the house of our poverty.”

And when he replied: “It is necessary to obey you, and especially the Father of all. I shall go and consider the courses and advances of God’s mercy. If I can proceed and make progress in them, thanks be to him; but if not, may I be permitted without offense to return to you, whom after God I have chosen as my father and guardian of my soul.”

“Go,” he said, “for the hand of the Lord shall be with you until the end.”

Having received this blessing, he departed with two companions assigned to him. The man of God commanded that he should establish one as father in the church of Antwerp, and the other likewise in that of Floreffe.

> [Note: Col. 1329C–D (102). This is Waltmann, who died on 15 April 1138. Chrysostomus vander Sterre enrolled him among his saints on their feast days, and we mentioned him among those omitted. Le Paige, p. 455, and Sanderus in his description of this monastery collected the notices of him published by various writers. It pleased them to append the commemoration printed after the litanies of St Norbert.  
> Antiphon: “This man, despising, etc.”  
> V. “The righteous shall spring up like the lily.”  
> R. “And shall flourish forever before the Lord.”  
> Prayer, compiled from the collects for St Francis and St Charles Borromeo: “We beseech you, Lord, may heavenly grace enlarge your Church through the merits of blessed Father Waltmann, so that, as pastoral solicitude made him glorious, so his intercession may always make us fervent in your love.”]

> [Note: Col. 1329D (103). This is Richard, whose eulogy with the title “Blessed” is given by Le Paige, p. 439. Saussaius places him among the Pious on 30 August. Floreffe was discussed in chapter 8.]

And so it was done. He was installed and consecrated under the title of Father in the church of Prémontré, and those two in the other two churches named above. Two others had already been consecrated in two other churches: that of Blessed Martin at Laon, and that of Viviers.

> [Note: Col. 1329D (104). Walter and Henry, concerning whom and whose monasteries chapter 13 has spoken.]

These five, together with a sixth whom the abbot of Prémontré, immediately after entering office, had installed at the place called Bonne-Espérance, seeing the imminent dissolution of the order in many places and fearing a greater one to come, assembled on an appointed day in a designated place. Cutting away whatever then appeared superfluous in their own houses, they resolved thereafter, after the likeness and example of the Cistercians, to return there together annually in order to correct the defects of their order.

> [Note: Col. 1329D–1330D (105). The monastery of Bonne-Espérance is in Hainaut, near the town of Binche. Its first abbot was Odo, a disciple of St Norbert, though appointed by Hugh. Le Paige, in his usual manner, also calls him Blessed and gives his eulogy on p. 463. Since Saussaius did not know his feast day, he placed him in an appendix of such persons, p. 1228.  
> The practice of all these men was that, after receiving the blessing, they performed pontifical functions while being content with ring and staff, although Benedictines commonly used both mitre and gloves. The Premonstratensians agreed that their own members should not gradually assume these insignia. Therefore application was made to Innocent III to forbid them such use, as he did on 12 May 1198, “lest perhaps one of them take upon himself the arrogance of pride, or appear exalted in his own eyes when he sees himself using things granted by the Apostolic See to bishops and the greater prelates of churches.” This prohibition was later relaxed, no doubt for just reasons. One reason may have been that provosts of canons and archpriests of bishops might perhaps contend with these abbots for a superior rank, as some now contend with abbots who do not wear mitres.]

> [Note: Col. 1330D (106). Pagius adds that St Norbert himself commanded that such a chapter should be celebrated every year “on the feast of St Dionysius,” 9 October.]

When this became known in other places, there were six in the first year, nine in the second, twelve in the third, and eighteen in the fourth. From then on they multiplied throughout the world, as their words, actions, and works testify down to the present day.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Saint obtains confirmation from Innocent II of the privileges of his church. In a sedition he maintains constancy and is miraculously preserved from death.

102. [CHAP. XLIX.] Then Pope Honorius of blessed memory was called to his predestined eternity, and Innocent was installed by canonical election in the holy Roman See.

> [Note: Col. 1331D (107). On the death of Honorius II in the year 1130, Innocent II succeeded him. Peter Leonis, the antipope called Anacletus, opposed him.]

Since Innocent could not hold the see because of the intrusion of Peter Leonis and the sedition of his faction, he left Rome and went to France, where he was honorably received, as was fitting. When a council was convened at Reims, bishops from diverse nations assembled from every side; Father Norbert also came, and there they excommunicated that intruder Peter. Approving Innocent’s election, they delivered Peter Leonis to the roaring lion to be devoured unless he repented.

> [Note: Col. 1331D (108). The council of three hundred bishops and abbots began at Reims in October.]

In this account, treating of the Roman pontiffs may seem superfluous to someone; but certain matters that ought not to be omitted concerning the soldier of Christ—matters known to have been magnificently and laudably accomplished by him in modern times—cannot otherwise be narrated in due sequence. For he had brought with him the very ancient privileges of his church, nearly consumed by worms, and caused all of them to be renewed and corrected under Roman protection, annexing what he had recovered from the hands of those who had unjustly and violently seized it, as noted above. Moreover, he secretly obtained another privilege, so that, when an opportunity arose, strengthened by Roman authority, he might propagate the order of his religious life in the episcopal church.

When the council had ended and he was returning to his own see, what he had done had already become partly known—namely, how he had armed himself against them with the spiritual sword and with the walls and defenses of fortresses. They raged more fiercely, saying to one another: “Our kingdom shall not stand, and our glory is nothing; indeed, the honor of all of us and the dignity of our predecessors shall be destroyed unless we remove him from among us as soon as possible and take this subtle power of his from our land.” From that time they sought an opportunity to act cautiously, in accordance with their disordered and foolish plotting.

103. But when it pleased him who had chosen and taken Norbert into the work of his ministry to test the man’s constancy—he who, as has been said, had proved faith and patience—he did not delay long, but brought about an occasion and time both to glut with blood the rage of those hungering for it and to purify his recruit in the fire of manifest tribulation.

At the same time, an incident occurred in the Greater Church.

> [Note: Col. 1331D (109). This is the church of St Maurice, built by Otto I, concerning which see more fully chapter 1 of the *Analecta*.]

It had been secretly revealed to the man of God. When he informed the senior members of the church and declared that, because of such an event, the church ought to be expiated according to canonical authority, they refused to agree with him, saying that a church known to have been consecrated by the authority of many kings and pontiffs ought not to be consecrated anew. They forbade this; but he, on the contrary, asserted that he would never be willing to celebrate the divine mysteries in it unless they allowed the demonic infestation in which it had been ensnared to be removed from it.

They disputed in this fashion. Yet the man, who did not fear their cunning so long as God’s cause was at stake, made the outcome of the matter known to all the people from the pulpit.

> [Note: Col. 1332D (110). Antwerp manuscript: “in public.”]

He also showed that he was being forbidden to do what was authoritative and what the practice of the holy Fathers had established in such occurrences.

104. Having said this, on the following night he took with him two bishops then staying with him, the provost of that church, who supported him in this matter, and a great many of his clerical brethren. They entered the church, and, clothed in sacred vestments and using consecrated water, completed with sincere devotion the rite required by the affair described above. They consecrated, with the divine blessing and by the office properly due, the place for consecrating the Lord’s body and blood.

> [Note: Col. 1332D (111). Bern manuscript: “the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.”]

But the aforesaid adversaries, detesting this deed, hastened to fill their hands with the blood of the innocent priest. These men kept vigil to gather the blood of the Lamb; those men kept vigil to shed innocent blood. For as soon as the rite was completed, while all who were present were still in sacred vestments, a great shout and a violent uproar of people were heard outside. The whole city had been stirred by no small and indescribable frenzy, because certain adversaries had made to the people a cruel and astonishing allegation: that the bishop had broken the altars, opened the sacristy, dismantled and taken away the shrines and reliquaries for himself, and intended, under cover of that same night, to flee with all these things and with all the church’s treasure.

Those who were with the man of God heard this and were afraid, some more and some less. But he, undaunted, wished to go out to them and ask what was happening. The others, however, forbade this in every possible way, saying that such a popular tumult could not easily be calmed by anyone at such an hour. They compelled him to ascend a certain fortified structure, built there long ago by Emperor Otto in place of a tower of the church which he had begun to build but, prevented by death, had not completed.

> [Note: Col. 1332D (112). *Municipium*, as though *muricipium*, “that which is enclosed by a wall”; thus here the word means only what elsewhere it signifies, a town surrounded by walls.]

105. There the man withdrew, together with those who were with him, still clothed in sacred vestments, awaiting a shameful death of the body rather than life. The cries of those assaulting and rushing upon them became stronger. They repeatedly cried, “Theid-ut, theid-ut”—that is, “Go out, go out.”

> [Note: Col. 1333D–1334D (113). Thus three manuscripts, consistently according to the language of the people, though with some variation: some also write *Thieduss* or *uet*. Many read *Thiedur* or *Theidur*; but this would have to be translated “go away.”]

But those above in the tower, during the solemnities of Matins, sang praises to God in response, resounding with immense voices, with hymns and songs of exultation, praises to God in honor of the outstanding preacher Paul. Meanwhile the others increased their taunting cries with disorderly shouts, proclaiming that the priest of God deserved death.

It was, indeed, the night immediately after the day on which the Church celebrates the martyrdom of the blessed Peter and Paul. As the Church celebrates on the preceding night for one of them, blessed Peter, so on the following night it celebrated the solemnities for the other, Paul, according to the Church’s custom. Those who were besieged sang of the man whom his history tells was himself besieged; and they regained strength against fear of martyrdom when blessed Paul’s deposit, which he affirms is reserved for him in glory, sounded in their ears: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that the just Judge is able to keep my deposit until that day” (2 Tim. 1:12).

In this confidence some of them stood without trembling. But others, still clinging too firmly to the world and to their flesh, groaned with no small lamentation and said: “Alas, alas! Why have we followed this man here, to die with him in our sins?” The holy man encouraged them as best he could with honey-sweet consolation: “Do not be frightened, dearest brethren, do not be frightened. For what has been done by us belongs to God; what is being done belongs to God; it is God’s permission when some good work of his is attacked by his enemies.”

At times he said these things; at other times he prayed more earnestly for them, lest they lose heart and despair. As they grew weaker, his desire to pray increased; and, as he himself later declared, he feared death less than he feared that they might fail through despair.

106. Throughout the night the hostile party assembled. In this moment of such necessity, the holy priest and the company assembled with him multiplied their prayers. At morning, when daylight began to break with the earliest dawn, some pressed the attack on the tower, while others assailed the bishop and his clerics with arrows and javelins.
