Certain men, said to have sworn his death, being keener seekers of that cruel slaughter, forced an entry by whatever means and boldly reached the upper part of the tower.

When the man saw them rush in with drawn swords, he went forward to meet them, lest they vent their fury upon the death of others. Following the example of his Master, he said: “You seek one man; behold, I am he. Spare these men, who have deserved no sentence of death.”

But when they saw him still clothed in his purple episcopal and priestly vestment, they were terrified; and, retreating a little, in an instant God, at whose command all things are ordered, having made manifest the constancy of his martyr insofar as it depended on him, so pierced the minds of those persecutors with a change of heart that they fell at his feet, sought and received pardon for so great an outrage, and came forth from adversaries as defenders.

Others, however, pursuing them swiftly, found one of his chamberlains—who loyally adhered to him—defending a certain entrance. Thinking that the bishop had already been beheaded by those who had gone before, they hated that same chamberlain because he loved his master; they struck him with the sword and, cutting his neck almost to the throat, left him half alive, though believing him dead.

Seeing this, the man of God sprang, against the wishes of everyone, into the middle of the crowd; giving his enemies power over him, he offered himself to death, choosing rather to die than that anyone else should die while he remained alive.

107. But the very man who had struck his servant, seeing him, still full of diabolical rage and wickedness, holding his bloodied sword drawn, stretched out his hand against the bishop and with bold presumption delivered him a heavy blow upon the shoulders. But the sword rebounded as though it had struck an adamantine stone, and from the fresh blood with which it was stained it dyed the fringes of the episcopal mitre that he wore on his head. As long as the man lived, that mitre remained visibly sprinkled with the same blood.

Some who stood by awaited the outcome from the opposing side—those who awaited human blood more than the man himself. When they saw, I say, that he did not die, because some spared him while others struck him without injuring him, they ran and swiftly brought relics of the saints, placing them in the middle. They declared that it was a great impropriety for a shepherd to be so disgracefully attacked by his sheep. This was their pretext, a feigned humanity; for in this crisis they too compelled him to remove from the church of Blessed Mary the brethren whom he had placed there, as was said above. But he refused, affirming that, as long as he lived, this action would never be annulled by them—an action confirmed, to their grief, by royal power and Roman authority.

108. While these things were taking place, the count of that city arrived upon the road. As though ignorant of the event, he ran into the midst of the rioters, divided them from one another, and named a fixed day on which all who had a just complaint against the bishop should come, to administer and receive justice. At the judge’s command they therefore withdrew.

But the priest of God entered that same church, for which the whole disturbance had arisen, intending to celebrate Mass and render boundless thanks to his God. When he approached the altar, he called those around him and said: “Behold, all things are whole, safe, and sound—those things that had been reported as broken and carried away.” He therefore celebrated Mass in the same place; he himself also read both the Epistle and the Gospel, for all his ministers had withdrawn, overcome by weariness and fear. Thus it could truly be said of him, as of our supreme Head Jesus Christ: “Leaving him, they all fled” (Matt. 26:56).

When Mass had ended, he came to the palace, his face bearing a purple hue in a wondrous and ineffable way, as one well drunk from the cup of his Lord, so that he could say with the Prophet: “I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:13). He had retained this color in the very danger of death; and those who had been with him testified that no one saw him grow pale even for a moment. He himself, on the contrary, declared the constancy of martyrs to be light and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

Thus the Lord delivered him, fulfilling the promise of him who said: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord delivered them” (Ps. 33:20), testing the faith of his soldier but in no way thirsting for his blood.

> [Note: Col. 1335C–D (114). Our Saxon chronicler relates the whole event briefly as follows: “In the same year”—namely, 1129 of Lothair IV—“on the Commemoration of St Paul there occurred a very great disturbance of the citizens of Magdeburg against Archbishop Norbert, because he had purified the Greater Church at night after it had, as had been reported to him, been polluted. As the tumult increased, he went up into the upper part of the older monastery with the bishops of Meissen and Havelberg—of these, Gumbert had succeeded Hemo in 1120; I have not yet discovered the other’s name—and with the provost of the Greater Monastery. There he was besieged for a long time, while the enraged adversaries reproached him for having broken the altars and stolen away the relics of the saints. But divine grace marvelously delivered him from their snares; and, excommunicating those who persisted in evil, he brought them into subjection.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Another conspiracy exposed. Journey to Rome. Illness and death.

109. [CHAP. L.] It is the customary way of the envious that, when they have been somewhat provoked on some occasion by those whom they envy, they do not immediately disclose all that they resent and that pains their hearts; but after withdrawing from them, swelling with sharper pain, they reserve for a later time, more embittered and given a better opportunity for greater vengeance, whatever they might have said or done to their opponents’ disgrace. Thus the aforesaid adversaries, to whom the justice preached to them by the unconquered bishop was hateful, [Col. 1335C] again convened their perverse assemblies. Each set forth his own grievance, saying that they had been deceived and that their minds had been ensnared by magical art and the darkness of obscurity, since they had left this man alive—a man who would not yield to them and did not fear in the least to alter their rite and honour or the dignity due to the city. Truly they were deceived and foolish [Note: [Col. 1335D] (115) This seems unquestionably to be the sense that should be read, having been corrupted by copyists into the following form: “Truly deceived, and no wonder, since deceitful, deceitful and astonishing.”], nor was it surprising, since they were deceitful and had, indeed, met to devise astonishing things.

For they had also firmly decreed there that, when they were to assemble on the appointed day, [Col. 1336A] each should drink a denarius-worth [Note: [Col. 1335D] (116) *Denariata*: that is, to the value of one denarius.] of wine or mead [Note: [Col. 1335D] (117) *Medo*: hydromel, or mead. This drink commonly supplies the lack of wine where wine does not grow, and, when it has been boiled for a long time, equals the most generous wines. Therefore, in these regions of ours Spanish and other sweet wines are excluded from the sacrifice of the Mass, because fraudulent wine-merchants sometimes substitute for them a mead so made that even the more expert can scarcely distinguish real from counterfeit wine.], so that, if anything contrary to their wishes should occur in the hearing of their complaints, they might make good, by killing their shepherd, what they had previously failed to do; and thus the deed might be attributed to drunkenness rather than premeditation. It was also decreed that whoever did not obey this resolution should have his house subject to demolition and all his goods to plunder by the judges of that entire council.

When this action was reported to the ears of certain princes of the land, who in some measure loved the man of God because they knew that he was a holy and righteous man, they urged him to withdraw for a time, following the example of his Master, who hid himself from the face of those persecuting him, as it is written: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John [Col. 1336B] 8:59). When he refused and joyfully awaited the palm of martyrdom, they compelled him by many entreaties to depart.

110. The day previously named arrived; at the signal, the city began to resound with immense cries. When the man of God asked what was happening, he was told that a great multitude of people had gathered and wished to drive the brethren out of the church of Blessed Mary. But he smiled and said: “It is not so, because the planting which the heavenly Father has planted cannot be uprooted.” Nevertheless, they compelled him to leave; and, after mounts had been prepared, he went out to a certain abbey of monks dedicated to St John [Note: [Col. 1336D] (118) But this same abbey now occupies approximately the middle of the city, which stretches along the Elbe, and has a distinguished church; for the city has since been enlarged fourfold in length, not only by the addition of the suburb of St John [after which addition I do not know whether any trace remains of the formerly narrower walls] and by levelling the ditches that separated the suburb from the city, but also by building the Jews’ quarter on one side and the “new city,” as it is called, on the other. This is how Marianus depicts the city in an elegant engraving in his *Topography of Lower Saxony*.], situated in a suburb of the city above a certain hill. Having there arranged everything with sufficient room, he went on to a certain castle belonging to him, called [Col. 1336C] Halle [Note: [Col. 1336D] (119) Halle, a town on the river Saale, twelve leagues distant from Magdeburg; at that time under archiepiscopal jurisdiction, it later became independent.], that he might there rest from so great a tumult. But he found that place shut as well: his enemies had gone before him and occupied all the fortification.

What was a man to do who found nowhere that his foot might rest? What was he to do, deprived of human help? He betook himself to a certain church of regular canons [Note: [Col. 1336D] (120) Perhaps at Petersberg, or St Peter’s Hill, on the southern side of the city, where, according to Marianus, a church or chapel may still be seen.], which was nearby. There he prayed to his God for several days, that He might deign to direct his way according to the good pleasure of His will. But He who said through the prophet, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, [Col. 1337A] and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5), seeing the humility and constancy of His recruit, regarded the prayers of His truth; and, as He willed and from whom He willed, peace was granted to affairs. For as the enemies had eagerly assembled to kill him, so they hastened to assemble in order to make amends. They offered every form of satisfaction and a great quantity of money. But he, who had come to seek souls for God rather than money, rejected the money, lest he incur the offence of the Lord his God, so that he might gain their souls, which through this transgression stood in danger of destruction.

Finally, he said that the offence was theirs, not his: by sinning, they had harmed themselves, not him; and they had rather harmed the one whom they had left wounded and lying half-dead. He sought satisfaction for [Col. 1337B] that man, not at all for himself, following the example of his Head, who said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34); and that Apostle’s example: “Repaying no one evil for evil” (Rom. 12:17). With inward sorrow he grieved for that man who had deserved nothing worthy of death, yet lay condemned to death and held fast by a grievous wound.

111. [CHAP. LI.] Therefore, seeing by what grief the man of God was most deeply distressed, the adversaries strove to comfort him in the matter in which they perceived him to be burdened. For they rebuilt in full the house of that wounded man which they had demolished, and, to heal the wound they had inflicted upon him, they contributed forty marks of silver. After this, the gates of the castle, which they had earlier shut at his arrival, were opened; and he entered [Col. 1337C] with every honour, surrounded by a great company of nobles and by a multitude of common people praising God for the constancy of so great a bishop. They declared him worthy of the episcopate, since Almighty God had delivered him from the hands of so many persecutors and, in so evident a danger of death, he had remained unconquered, with the integrity of his faith and the safety of his body.

Thus humility prevailed, with the grace of humility going before it, so that in him the marks of Truth might shine forth—the Truth which says: “He who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:14). Therefore the praises of so great a man must not be passed over in silence, because God is glorious in His saints. And when the great deeds of the Fathers who went before are related, the works of their sons who follow are stirred to imitate them. These events took place in the fifth year of his episcopate; afterwards he occupied the see for three further years, day by day giving honour to the ministry entrusted to him by God, [Col. 1338A] advancing in all religious devotion and uprightness. He preserved the unity of the holy Church; he pursued and detested all its disturbers and schismatics; he embraced the good; gave counsel to the desolate; supported the poor, orphans, and widows; fostered and extended religious communities; taught the pattern of religious life; and, insofar as the dignity of his office permitted, showed himself approachable to both lesser and greater persons. Mindful of divine bounty and grace, each day he offered to the Lord his God a conscience of good repute, inward sweetness, and delight.

112. [CHAP. LII.] There was at the holy Roman see a most serious schism, exceedingly difficult to settle, concerning two pontiffs, as has been stated: Innocent and Peter Leo. One of them—Innocent—had been [Col. 1338B] canonically elected; he was Catholic and was accepted and approved by all Catholics. The other, Peter, had been intruded; nevertheless, he had occupied the holy see, not through God or the holy Church, but through secular power. For he himself, though not distinguished by nobility, was powerful in the city through the multitude of his kin; and, blinded by the passion of his ambition, he was destroying the holy laws, the order, all the ordinances of the Fathers and of the holy Church, and the rule of Christian faith. Demolishing some towers and fortifications of the city and fortifying others, he prepared to obtain every secular principality and the object of his own covetousness.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] (121) All commonly consider this to refer to that schism and to its author Anacletus—for that was the name he chose to be called. St Bernard, in Letter 56 to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, declares that he had this from the saint’s own mouth, beginning thus: “What you ask me concerning Lord Norbert—whether, namely, he is going to Jerusalem—I do not know. For when, a few days ago, I deserved to see his face and to draw many things from the heavenly pipe, that is, from his own mouth, I did not hear this from him. But when I asked him what he thought concerning Antichrist, he declared that he knew with complete certainty that Antichrist would be revealed during the generation now living. When he wished to explain to me, as I asked, whence he had this certainty, after hearing his answer I did not think that I ought to believe it as certain. Yet, in summary, he maintained this: that he would not see death unless he first saw a general persecution in the Church.” In a certain way he may indeed be said to have seen this, when he saw the aforesaid most scandalous schism; and he foretold that Anacletus would be Antichrist. Bernard plainly understood him in this sense in Letters 124, 125, and 126, where he writes concerning him. Baronius, under the year 1106, no. 26, thinks that all this refers to the fact “that, since holy men had often foreknown immense future persecutions of the Church, they thought that the very magnitude of events meant that the times of Antichrist were at hand.”]

For this reason, after King Lothair and the princes of the holy faith had taken counsel, lest the knowledge and strength of the faithful Christians in these present times should perish through [Col. 1338C] that deadly pest, they organized an expedition into Italy, so that the material sword might at least pierce that sacrilegious man whom the spiritual sword, by which he had already been struck very often, could not penetrate. By the command and obedience of Innocent, the Catholic shepherd, Bishop Norbert set out with him and with other bishops and archbishops. Passing through camps and cities [not] without intolerable disturbance, with a great host marching before and following after, they reached Rome, bringing with them the venerable Pope Innocent. Entering with a great assault and a strong hand, they placed this same pope in the holy see, despite all enemies and adversaries.

[Col. 1338D] 113. The pontiff, once placed in the see, and the others who had come with him, also consecrated King Lothair as [Col. 1339A] Roman emperor.

[Note: [Col. 1339C] (122) It seems good to set out the whole course of this journey from our Magdeburg Chronicle, where the following is read under the year 1132: “King Lothair celebrated the Assumption of St Mary at Würzburg, and from there entered Lombardy with an army. Since the archbishop of Cologne was absent—Frederick having died and Bruno not yet having been consecrated—although by right he ought to be chancellor in these regions, Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, was assigned to that office. In the year of the Lord 1133 the king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Italy, at the castle called Meduina,” at the confluence of the Meduna and Livenza, on the border of the districts of Treviso and Friuli. “The king then proceeded from there and celebrated holy Easter, 26 March, at St Flavian,” about twelve Roman miles from the city near Mount Soracte, now called St Orestes or even St Sylvester, where, they fabulously say, he lay hidden while Constantine persecuted the Church. Virgil and Silius called the place Flavian; it has now been completely destroyed, probably an ancient Roman colony, whose name seems later to have passed into that of St Flavian the martyr, commemorated on 28 January. “Then, coming to Rome on the Kalends of May, he was honourably received at St John Lateran by the pope, clergy, and Romans; there he celebrated Pentecost, and on that holy day was crowned in procession on the Aventine Hill at St Sabina. Having remained there for six continuous weeks, he finally, by the counsel and will of the princes and through the mediation of Archbishop Norbert, [Col. 1340D] received the imperial blessing from Pope Innocent in the aforesaid basilica of Constantine, together with his wife, on the second day before the Nones of June, a Sunday, which that year was the third after the feast of the coming of the Holy Spirit. These things having been done,” it says, “the emperor crossed the Alps and celebrated the Nativity of St Mary at Würzburg [lacuna]. He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne [lacuna]. He celebrated Pentecost, 3 June, at Merseburg” in Swabia; but “Norbert” had already departed from him, and “died within the fourth week” of that Pentecost season; “and within the following fifth week was buried in the monastery of St Mary.”]

For this man was a vigorous leader in war, eminent in arms, prudent in counsel, terrible to the enemies of God and the holy Church, a friend of truth, an ally of justice, and an enemy of injustice. His probity was made manifest in Sicily and flourished also in Saxony. While he lived, the whole Roman Empire, entrusted to his guardianship, could not totter. He too loved the man of God, Norbert, because he constantly used his counsels, which were powerful in courage and foresight; and because he drew from him the drink of heavenly sweetness and was daily refreshed by the bread of divine nourishment.

That man was very weak in body, worn down by long and severe penitential austerity; but his infirmity increased far more when the toil and [Col. 1339B] pain of travel, the occupation of territories, the burden of domestic affairs, the change of diverse climates, and continual unrest were added to it. It is impossible for one person to recount everything he did there or elsewhere, because it was not possible for one person to know or learn everything. Yet it is known that, after returning from Italy to his city, Parthenopolis, he was soon seized by a grievous sickness and suffered from it for a time, namely, for four months. Having administered the episcopate wisely and faithfully for eight years, full of the Holy Spirit and with all his faculties unimpaired, after giving a blessing to those standing by, he rested in a blessed end. For, as Augustine says, he could not die badly who had lived well.

It was the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1134, the Wednesday of Pentecost week, the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], in the fifth year of Pope Innocent’s reign and the ninth of Lothair.

## CHAPTER XIX. Burial of the body. Three apparitions. Epilogue.

114. [CHAP. LIII.] When Father Norbert, of blessed and worthy memory, had died, his spirit having been called to the eternity of supreme blessedness, and his holy body having been left lifeless, no small dispute arose between the cathedral church and the church of St Mary [Col. 1340A] concerning the place of his burial. Some wished—and declared it fitting and just—that, since he had been head of the churches of that city, his bones should be conveyed with honour to the principal church, and that there he should await the coming of the supreme Judge, where his title was fixed and without end, if he had happened to live in the flesh without end.

But the other party—the brethren of St Mary—asserted that he belonged to them by right, because through him they had been reconciled to their Creator and had chosen him as their father; through him they had returned themselves and their devotion to the Lord their God, from whom they had turned away. Above all, they urged that, while still living, the man had commanded—and had until the end shown that the devotion of his will demanded—that he should be buried and rest among his brethren and sons, whom he had begotten for God by God’s word in the time of his poverty. [Col. 1340B] Such was the dispute; and on each side an evident answer based on a just and certain argument was advanced.

A remarkable matter! They contended to keep the lifeless body of this man, thinking that his presence in death would benefit them, though, while he lived and could benefit them, they had in every way sought his absence. At last, those who stood between the parties, who endured the dispute equally on both sides, saw that they were invincible and that each party asserted the superior justice of its own claim. They advised that messengers be sent as quickly as possible to King Lothair, and that whatever he commanded or judged should be held ratified. So it was done.

115. Meanwhile the body lay unburied, and day after day it was carried through each of the city’s monasteries. [Col. 1340C] In each, vigils and the observances due to departed believers were carefully celebrated, until, on the eighth day, those who had been sent returned. Then, by the emperor’s command, the holy man’s body was buried among the brethren in the church of St Mary. This too was remarkable and should not be passed over in silence: although the summer was so severe that in that same year no hay was cut in the meadows because of the extreme drought, no corruption producing any stench issued from his body during all those days.

[Note: [Col. 1340D] (123) Polycarp adds in his Notes: “Even after many centuries, the marvellous and extraordinary fragrance exhaled from it struck religious awe and terror—indeed, sudden death—into a certain provost infected with the impious Lutheran pest, when he attempted to break open the tomb, as authorities report.” I wish that he had named those authorities.]

From this one may understand how the superabundant grace which cleansed him from the corruption of mind preserved his body from corruption, while it had to be handled and prepared for burial with the customary offices of funeral humanity. He was therefore buried before the altar of the Holy Cross, in the middle [Note: [Col. 1341C] (124) By “monastery” one might understand the cloister, in the open area of which was the common cemetery of the brethren, as is the custom in various monasteries. But Pagius persuasively argues that the church must certainly be understood here: the saint was buried in its front portion, assigned to the laity. He describes the place thus precisely: “He was first buried in the middle of the church before the altar there dedicated to the Holy Cross, at the entrance to the choir, between the stone stairways by which it is approached from either side in pairs.”] of the monastery for several years. But his good sons, following the command of Truth, as it is written, “Honour thy father, that thou mayest be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20:12), and mindful of the kindness he had shown them, wished to keep him before their eyes, that his memory might be commended without forgetfulness. They transferred him into the choir, where he awaits the last day, in hope of the certain resurrection and glory, in a tomb carefully fitted out according to the convenience of the place.

[Note: [Col. 1341D] (125) “Then indeed,” says the same Pagius, “some years later—perhaps after the fire of 1188, mentioned in Corollary 1, no. 61—the body had not yet begun to decay so much that it could not conveniently be removed and transferred to another shrine, in the clothing and position in which it had first been laid [lacuna]. It was transferred to the choir itself and placed beneath the altar mentioned above, in a monument or stone of white marble, set upright to the height of the man.” Thus the head of the tomb entered beneath the hollow of the altar, so that the sacrifice was performed directly above the dead man’s head, while the rest [Col. 1342C] projected into the choir where it could be seen by all, as will appear from the history of the translation.]

[Col. 1341B] 116. [CHAP. LIV.] Evidence of his salvation and hope ought not to seem unbelievable to any faithful person’s judgment, especially since, after his departure, he appeared in that form to certain persons whom one had every reason to believe; and, when they asked concerning his condition, by divine permission he gave such an answer that no one who considers it carefully ought to doubt that it is true and certain.

For on the same day and hour on which his soul was separated from his body, a certain brother saw him in a white garment and of beautiful appearance, holding an olive branch in his hand. When, being afraid, he asked him whence he came or where he was hastening, he answered: “I have been sent from paradise, whence I have brought this flowering olive branch; and I am going swiftly to transplant it in the place of my poverty, that is, in the church of Prémontré.” [Col. 1341C] The brother awoke from this most unusual vision and began to consider within himself what it signified. Reporting the vision to certain persons at the church [Note: [Col. 1342D] (126) I understand the church of Prémontré, namely, the same church to which the saint showed that he was transplanting the olive branch, and which was almost two hundred leagues distant from Magdeburg. Thus it is not surprising if news of the death arrived there so late. But I do not understand what the transplantation of the branch meant, since neither was the deceased’s body brought there nor did the brethren return there from Magdeburg.], for he was at an estate of that church, they committed to memory the day and hour of the vision, waiting to see what it portended and what events would follow so manifest an apparition. When at length they heard of their master’s death, they found that it was the very day on which his soul had been released from the flesh.

Likewise, he appeared in his own form to another brother [Note: [Col. 1342D] (127) Here *curia* means a court, estate, or property. It is probable that this occurred at Prémontré.], who was a priest, standing before him. But immediately the appearance of the man changed [Col. 1342A] into a flower of marvellous whiteness, like a lily flower; angels received it and carried it into heaven. At earliest dawn the brother awoke and ran to his prior to receive permission to celebrate Mass and thereby commend to God the soul of his pious father Norbert. When the prior asked what sign there was for so sudden an attestation, he explained the sequence of events. The prior commanded him to remember that day. It was then found that this day was the day of the burial of the man of God.

117. There was also another man [Note: [Col. 1342D] (128) Chrysostom van der Sterre understands this to be Hugh, abbot there; rightly so, since below the saint is said to have left to the man who saw him “a successor,” namely, in the government of the monastery.] among those whom God had given him at the beginning of his conversion. He adhered to him faithfully and affectionately, and inwardly grieved at the departure of his master; yet he grieved more because [Col. 1342B] he had no certainty of his salvation. With every urgency of prayer he entreated his God to receive some answer concerning the mercy which, from unmerited grace, He had bestowed upon His soldier and a sinner truly penitent. One night Norbert appeared to him in a most beautiful house, brightly illuminated by the splendour of the sun.

Recognizing his master, whose vision he fervently desired in whatever way he might enjoy it, the man quickly fell at his feet and humbly begged him to deign to disclose something concerning his condition and the mercy received from God. Raising him from the ground and embracing his neck with his arms, Norbert said: “My son, you ask a difficult thing. Yet because it is opened to him who knocks without ceasing, [Col. 1342C] come, let us sit down.” There was there a most beautiful seat prepared. When they had sat down upon it, he said: “It was said to me: ‘Come, my sister, rest.’ I am in peace and rest; but I have not yet escaped the dreadful fear of judgment, at which even angels will tremble.”

Filled with this honey-sweet and longed-for answer, the brother feared that he would depart, for he knew that in the vision he saw what he had asked to see. “I beg you,” he said, “most loving Father, tell me whether you took it ill that I did not come to you when, while you were still alive, you commanded me to come.” He answered: “You will come.”

[Note: [Col. 1342D] (129) Hugh did indeed go to him when he died thirty years later. Moreover, the following prayer and the information stated below concerning the saint, before the author left homeland and property, would make the Premonstratensians’ opinion plausible: that Hugh himself was the author, and therefore suppressed both his own name and those of his companions—if only he had done so also in no. 27, or at least without the encomium, “of holy manner of life.” Let it therefore suffice to maintain that this Life was written, under Hugh’s direction and with his contribution of materials, within the first twenty or thirty years after the saint’s death, since Hugh is said to have survived until 1164, and the body is said below to have remained buried “in the middle of the monastery for several years.” Yet, remarkably, no mention is made of miracles performed at the tomb before or after the translation. One might therefore suppose that, owing to their absence, God permitting this for hidden reasons, no thought was given to pursuing canonization. The opposite occurred in the cause of St Bernard, who died nineteen years after St Norbert and, because of the frequency of miracles, was canonized within twelve years.]

Then he disappeared. And it proved true: [Col. 1343A] that brother had intended to go to him, but another matter intervened and he did not arrive.

[Note: [Col. 1344C] (130) It would be remarkable if Emperor Conrad, who had loved him so greatly while alive, had paid no honour to him after death; but the author omitted to note this. For, as the Saxon Chronicler testifies: “The emperor celebrated the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul at Magdeburg, and Conrad, a canon of that same church, was made archbishop with the consent of the general election of clergy and people.”]

118. May Almighty God grant that, according to the meaning of the promise, he may come to him; and that the man whom he left as companion and successor, sharing the wretched and penal tribulation of this age, may be made his fellow partaker in the joys of eternal blessedness and in the gifts of blessing received from God, through Him who lives for ever, preserves mercy, and gives it to all who obey Him in good works and walk in the way of salvation, justice, and truth.

And what more? Should any of the faithful despair of the salvation of so great a man, who, as has been stated, both lived and, after death, being permitted by God, showed these signs of his salvation? But someone will say: “I hear what is written; but I doubt whether [Col. 1344A] this writing is true, because it is uncertain to me.” Believe, if you will: in Christ’s truth the writer attests the truth of the event. For he either saw the things he wrote about him, or heard them from truthful reporters who had seen them and were still living when he committed the foregoing work to remembrance by this writing—apart from certain things which he learned from Norbert himself before he left his land and kindred and laid aside the burden of property.

Therefore let successors live on and strive to commit to memory what was done and narrated by him and by the brethren of the same order who went before them. For although some may not accept everything in every respect, and these things may not please everyone completely, they cannot harm the well-disposed, even if it should happen that they do not benefit the ill-disposed and detractors.

[Col. 1343]

# NORBERTINE ANALECTA

## CHAPTER ONE. Additions by the brethren of Cappenberg to the Life.

[Col. 1343B] 1. [CHAP. I.] We too, the sons of Cappenberg, gladly add what has come to our knowledge concerning our common Father, lest, in recounting paternal merit, we should seem, as ungrateful men, to fail your holiness. There is among us a little book containing the Life of our Founder, worthy of God, in which it is thus written:

“In those [Note: [Col. 1344D] (131) These words are contained in precisely the same form in the earlier Life of Blessed Godfrey of Cappenberg, under 13 January, no. 9.] days there appeared in the regions of Westphalia a certain eminent luminary of the Church, that memorable herald of God, Norbert: a man indeed of admirable grace, most sweet eloquence, supreme self-restraint; an instructor and propagator of canonical religious life; a gatherer of Christ’s servants; founder of not a few monasteries; most vigorous both in bearing and voice; a preacher of true repentance; and in every respect an executor of that prophetic command which says, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; [Col. 1343C] make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God’” (Luke 3:4).

[CHAP. II.] “Nor do I judge it fitting to pass over in silence two of his great works which were performed in this place. [Note: [Col. 1344D] (132) These are also related there, nos. 14 and 15.] At one time he foretold in the spirit that a famine would come upon Westphalia and would also chastise the brethren for a while. In accordance with the foreknowledge of the man of God, it came to pass so severely that the dreadful calamity of [Col. 1344B] hunger destroyed very many. Thus, one day, when the brethren were about to go to their meal and were distributing to guests and poor persons whatever they had withheld from themselves through abstinence, bread for food failed them, so that it could not be found anywhere from which bread might be made. The man of God had often declared what is written: ‘The Lord will not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger’ (Ps. X, 3). And behold, the Lord suddenly sent through His faithful such an abundance of bread that the brethren were sufficiently refreshed and offered it cheerfully to those arriving. From that day onward, suitable provisions never failed the brethren.”

2. [CHAP. III.] “At another time, [Note: [Col. 1344D] (133) There also, no. 16.] when the holy man wished to send one of the brethren on monastic business, he found him laid low with a violent [Col. 1344C] fever. Using only the word of command, he laid upon him the cause of obedience through Christ’s power: ‘Go,’ he said, ‘and return; and do not suffer fever any longer.’ Immediately the brother recovered his strength and carried out as quickly as possible what the holy Father had commanded. Thus the word of the man of God both accomplished the business and suddenly put the protracted illness to flight.”

[CHAP. IV.] “There is likewise written there [Note: [Col. 1344D] (134) There also, no. 11.]: It pleased [Col. 1345A] the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in the herald of truth and, speaking through him, deigned to produce wonderful fruits in the Lord’s field—it pleased Him, I say—that the brethren living in the aforesaid monasteries, namely Cappenberg, Varlar, and Elofstat, should profess the Rule of Blessed Augustine, on the condition that they should observe that Rule somewhat more strictly than had hitherto been customary: specifically, by abstaining from the eating of fat and meat and by displaying the rigour of penance also in a more austere habit. For John, the friend of the Bridegroom, was fed not on elaborate but rather on natural and wild foods; and the Saviour himself, before the crowds flocking to the wilderness, praised him for the austerity of his clothing. And behold, our Order, with divine mercy accompanying it, spreads far and wide; and, as we truly trust, it will spread much more widely in the future. Therefore we must not doubt that it was both begun at the prompting of the Holy Spirit and promulgated by the direction of divine ordination. [Col. 1345B] For did not the Lord himself, the guide of the journey, transplant this vine from Egypt upon a lofty arm?”

There is also added there:

3. [Note: [Col. 1345B] (135) In the same place, no. 13: the author says, “I heard,” in the singular; they suppose this occurred in the year 1121.] [CHAPTER V.] Nevertheless, we heard the same champion of orthodox truth continue in the common chapter as follows:

“I know,” he said, “one of the brethren of our profession who, while investigating our Rule rather diligently, saw blessed Augustine—not indeed through his own merits, but through the prayers of his fellow brethren. Augustine handed him the golden Rule, brought forth from his right side, and made himself known to him in eloquent speech, saying: ‘The one whom you see is I, Augustine, bishop of Hippo. Behold, you have the Rule which I wrote. If your brethren, my sons, serve well under it, they will stand secure before Christ [Col. 1346B] amid the terror of the Last Judgment.’”

He indeed related these things humbly, as though concerning another; nevertheless, we have no doubt that he himself was the one to whom this was revealed. [Note: [Col. 1345B] (136) The author of the Life of Blessed Louis of Arnstein, who departed to heaven on 24 September 1185, and whose work was written in the same century, also referred to this matter when he was about to relate Louis’s entry into the Premonstratensian Order: “In the year 1119,” he says, “Norbert of blessed memory . . . came to Prémontré; and he gave the brethren to observe the habit which he had received not from man nor through man, confirmed by apostolic decrees, as it is uniformly kept in the churches of that profession. Living irreproachably in it upon the seat of his pontificate, in the year of grace 1137, assured of the crown of righteousness, he happily completed the course of his life; [Col. 1345C] and, buried with due honour, he rests in the church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg.” How important it is to possess and consult the uncorrupted monuments of the ancients with one’s own eyes, rather than those of others! By “habit” the author plainly means that of the mind, not of the body: namely, the rule or standard of life received by Saint Norbert from Saint Augustine in a vision, confirmed for Norbert by papal decrees, and observed in all his monasteries. Herdegomius, in *Virgo Candida*, book I, chapter 7, §3, strays into questions of the colour and shape of clothing; and from this he thinks he has established “how true and ancient is the story of that apparition”—that is, of the Virgin handing over a white garment. I therefore continue to wish, as above, that narrators of a revelation of this sort may be found who are as ancient as possible. Meanwhile Gaspar Bruschius will lead our company, the more acceptable because he is less partisan and is a full half-century earlier than the Premonstratensian writers of this age, whom I mention elsewhere. [Col. 1345D] For he flourished in 1550, famous for a poetic laurel and many published books. When only seventeen years old, he composed a praise and history of Ursberg monastery, such as the elder author inserted into his *Monasteriology*; and there, among other things, he wrote that the Mother of God wished the Premonstratensians, whose monastery this is,

> To be marked by a pure garment and its whiteness . . .

And:

> Therefore she once sent this down from highest Olympus;  
> She spoke: “Take this as a pledge of my affection.”

From this we may understand that even then the words customarily read were those which the Mother of God is said to have used in addressing Norbert. Similar words seem also to have been read by the man who prefixed these verses, cited by Pagius, p. 21, to the Breviaries of 1498 and 1512:

> Norbert is borne away by a heavenly voice;  
> Angels provide a snow-white garment;  
> At last the gracious Lady reveals herself  
> To the religious man.

[Col. 1346B] This poet, however, earlier even than Bruschius, states more clearly than he that an angelic vision came first and a Marian vision followed. He thus warns us that the matter was not customarily told or read by everyone in the same manner. Antonius Trumelius, a French poet, departed still further from the others; his poem is printed before the Breviary published at Paris in 1574 and 1598:

> When Father Norbert had set his heart on things above,  
> And in prayers asked with what garment he should be clothed,  
> An angel hastened down, sent from lofty heaven,  
> And clothed him in a tunic gleaming with snowy whiteness.

[Col. 1346C] Yet from this varied narration of the same event, which began to be written down only three or four centuries later, it is apparent how ill those persons serve traditions who, while striving to preserve every minute point of writers of this sort in all its circumstances, often bring the very substance of the matter into the peril of perplexing hesitation among people from whom they demand more belief than is necessary. Content, therefore, to retain the fact, let us not dispute whether the garment shown to Norbert from heaven differed from the common form of canonical dress then in use by more than its colour. Rather, let us judge that it differed either not at all or very little. This is indicated by the statutes of the Order themselves. From a manuscript of Parc, Ferreolus Locrius, *Maria Augusta*, book III, chapter 11, gives this title:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and to the praise and glory of the most glorious Mary, Mother of God, under whose holy auspices and manifestation our Order is believed to have taken its origin in a white habit; and of blessed [Col. 1346D] Father Augustine, under whose Rule the same Order is acknowledged to have been established, the statutes, ordinances, and regulations happily begin and follow.”

Moreover, Herdegomius gives in the preface the reason why “the holy man, when the most holy Virgin presented it, took up a white but nonetheless canonical habit . . . . . and decreed that his followers should wear it perpetually: namely, that by their own habit they might recognize and present themselves as canons, or preachers—as he himself interprets this from the teaching of the holy Fathers [no. 52].” Thus, just as from the form of the garments used by clerics of our Society of Jesus we know what, a century and a half ago, in Italy and Spain, where that Society began, was considered the modest dress of honourable clerics and priests, to whose use the Jesuits were deliberately accommodated: so from the habit of the Premonstratensians we should understand the canonical habit, even as used by secular clergy in the diocese of Laon. Although, in the course of almost five centuries, there has been a great change among secular clergy and some change among religious, [Col. 1347C] by which there now appears an immense difference.

Nor should the scapular trouble us. We see no secular or regular canons using one except the Premonstratensians. Yet Pagius writes in *Bibliotheca*, book I, chapter 3, that “as certain ancient canons—certainly those of Laon—so Premonstratensian canons devoutly wear and cherish the scapular as the habit of the Virgin Mother of God.” For my own part, I do not see what special commonality Mary can be said to have with a scapular, whether clerical or monastic—a garment by which we know that patience and the bearing of the Lord’s cross are signified—such that this part of religious dress should rather than another be called a token of Marian [Col. 1347D] patronage. If, however, there is something to this—which I would gladly accept—I shall congratulate the Premonstratensians for having possessed from the year 1119 that prerogative of which the Carmelite Fathers first began to boast in 1251.

But I return to the Premonstratensian habit, by which they are commanded to remember that they “present themselves as canons or preachers.” I observe that the force of this expression lies especially in the scapular, insofar as it is itself a figure of the cross. Nor was its use so peculiar to those of Laon that it could not also be found elsewhere. For those who were called “Preachers” by their proper title, instituted in the thirteenth century by Saint Dominic, canon of Osma, probably retained from the canons of Osma in Spain a similar form of their own dress, and thus of the scapular too; from which one may reasonably infer the same of many others. Indeed, as varied as the habit of regular canons is in different regions, so varied also was that of the secular clergy among whom this regular life had its origin at different times and through different founders. To pass over examples more commonly known in Belgium and elsewhere, consult vol. II of the English *Monasticon*: on p. 367 see the Hospitallers of Saint John Baptist; on pp. 755 and 783, the Gilbertines of Sempringham. Both are Augustinian canons, yet their habits differ from each other and from others more than those of the Premonstratensians and the Preachers do. Although, etc. See Appendix, p. 982, ch. 2.]

[Col. 1347A] 4. [CHAPTER VI.] Thus far material from the little book concerning our founder has been inserted. Now, if it please you, let us briefly and affectionately set forth those things which are recorded neither in your little book nor in ours, according to what we have truthfully learned.

The event occurred at Floreffe. For when the memorable Father was there perhaps celebrating the divine mysteries, in the performance of which he was accustomed to show himself most devout, suddenly, before receiving communion, he saw in the middle of the paten a fairly large drop, red with the Lord’s blood. Calling our brother Rudolph, the sacristan, then his deacon, he said: “Brother, do you see what I see?” “I see it, lord,” he replied; and at the greatness of so great a thing he began to weep abundantly. [Note: [Col. 1348C] (137) Polycarpus relates a similar miracle, performed in the same place on the feasts of the Finding of the Cross in 1204 and 1214, when abundant blood dripped from a particle of it. Caught upon strips of cloth, it is reverently preserved to this day.] After the manifestation of this miracle, taking occasion from it, as we believe, we were thereafter commanded to wash the paten; and the observance of this custom began among us, [Col. 1347B] although until then it had been unknown to us. [Note: [Col. 1348D] (138) In answer to the question whether this rite still obtains today, it was said that it has fallen out of use.]

5. [CHAPTER VII.] We read in the Life of Blessed Servatius [Note: [Col. 1348D] (139) We illustrated the various Acts of Saint Servatius on 13 May, mentioning this veil at no. 24. We rightly doubt the truth of the miracle because of the frivolity of the author; indeed we fear that the tale about the angel may be invented. Yet we judge the veil no less worthy of veneration, because that it was preserved incorrupt in the tomb, whoever may have placed it there, is miraculous; and even the touch of the sacred limbs alone is sufficient to require that it be held in honour.] that, after that most holy bishop’s death, a certain silk cloth was brought by angelic hands, before the eyes and to the great astonishment of the people, and placed over his venerable body. Accordingly this silk is honoured with the highest reverence in the church of Maastricht, and is kept and locked away with especial care.

When, therefore, the man of God came to Maastricht, he requested that this silk be shown to him. But they all began together to make excuses, especially since no one dared even to look inside the very chest in which it was deposited. But why say more? At last the request of the man of God prevailed. When they had opened the sacred repository in his presence, suddenly, behold, that silk cloth—what I am about to tell is marvellous—rose up and flew forth by a certain wonderful and divine impulse. Circling the basilica itself for some [Col. 1347C] time, it finally remained spread out near the ceiling at the summit of the church, and there poised itself, as if sustained by some rowing motion of wings. [Col. 1348A] At this sight some cried out in astonishment, while others mournfully feared that it would be wholly taken away from them. The man of God, silently considering the matter, began the solemnities of Mass. While he performed them, behold, the silk folded itself together again and gently lowered itself upon the priest’s outstretched arms. He received it reverently and restored it to its place. In this act, therefore, I do not doubt that God showed both the glory of merit in Bishop Servatius and the faith and power of prayer in His servant.

6. [CHAPTER VIII.] At a place called Bonlandt [Note: [Col. 1348D] (140) I have so far found neither Bonlant nor its alternative form Boulant on topographical maps.], where a monastery of our brethren also flourishes, there lived a powerful invader of other men’s property. [Col. 1348B] Among the other evils of his violence, he had for some time held by unjust usurpation certain wine revenues which properly belonged to the church of Magdeburg and were especially intended for the celebration of divine worship.

When the archbishop happened to come there, as a brother of that place testified to me, he did not remain silent on behalf of the church entrusted to him. Summoning the robber, though he caused fear to many, he spoke freely: “Why, man, do you dare inflict this injury upon Blessed Maurice [Note: [Col. 1348D] (141) The metropolitan church of Magdeburg was dedicated to Saint Maurice, leader of the Theban Legion, by Tagino, the fourth archbishop, when “Emperor Otto I, as Dresserus, though a heretic, writes, carried his relics barefoot in the bitterest cold from the Benedictine monastery of Saint Benedict at Bergen into it, and reverently placed them upon the high altar”], by holding through rash invasion and expending upon your own uses the annual revenues established for the celebration of divine worship?”

When the swollen man replied that this was not an invasion but the lawful possession of his inheritance, the man of God answered in a prophetic spirit: “Know, brother, that in the coming year you will be driven away from this plundering by God’s judgment.” He spoke, and it happened. For in that same year the unhappy man was killed by his enemies.

7. [CHAPTER IX.] At another time, while on the expedition of King Lothair, he came with the king to Augsburg in Vindelicia. There he foretold in the following manner the famous uprising that broke out between the people of that city and the king. Whenever this thrice-blessed man entered a church for prayer, he used always to say at the very threshold of the basilica, with bowed knees: “Peace to this house and to all who dwell in it.”

When, therefore, entering the church of the aforesaid city, he had finished his prayer, he called his deacon—through whose account we know these things—and revealed to him what he had learned through the Spirit, saying: “Brother, I prayed peace for this place; I desired peace. Yet I have found here a repulse of peace. I therefore entrust our pallium [Note: [Col. 1349C] (142) Did the saint, then, customarily carry his archiepiscopal pallium with him even through Germany? For the concern of the person giving the command does not permit us to think of some ordinary cloak. I would rather believe this than Polycarpus’s opinion that it happened when Norbert accompanied Lothair to Rome to be crowned, as though he would use it there in this solemn act—a thing I do not know whether even an archbishop may do in the presence of the supreme pontiff.] and all else that is under your charge to your most attentive care, because confusion and a great conflict threaten this [Col. 1349B] place.”

So it happened. For on the following day, after many had been struck down and wounded by the king, the citizens paid the penalty for their rashness; and only after many losses were they at last restored to the king’s favour.

[CHAPTER X.] At another time, when a demoniac was brought to him, to state the matter briefly, he exorcised water mixed with salt. As he went forward and began sprinkling it, before he reached the man the evil spirit departed. [Note: [Col. 1349C] (143) To these it is pleasing to add that Maurice du Pré, in his brief Annals of the Premonstratensian Order, writing under the year 1134 concerning the death of Saint Norbert, calls him “a distinguished raiser of three dead persons.” Peter of Wagenaar tries to prove this “from the Nanceian *peristomata*, in which he is depicted raising the same number of dead persons one by one.” He adds “the authority of Richard the Italian, protonotary of the supreme pontiff, in his synopsis of the evangelical Fathers,” hitherto unknown to us. Nor is the argument without force that may be drawn from Abelard the heretic, the bitterest enemy of Saints Bernard and Norbert. While he slanders them both “for pretence,” by which “they sought to appear wonderful through the grace of miracles,” he blasphemously declares that “that supreme attempt at raising the dead also had been vainly made” by them: “For,” he says, “we marvelled and laughed that Norbert lately presumed this, as did his fellow-apostle Fursitus.” We are little moved by this laughter, and we regret that the author was compelled, “because of the obstinate and shameless impudence,” of Abelard himself and those like him—an impudence to be turned away—to omit much, and to touch only briefly upon matters known to everyone and which they would not dare deny by any wickedness. But who is this Fursitus, called by Abelard Saint Norbert’s fellow-apostle? I suspect it is an insult rather than a name. Should any useful identification occur, I entrust its explanation to some happier conjecturer; for among Saint Norbert’s disciples there is no one whose name approaches it.] These are a few things out of many which have come to our knowledge, and which we have judged it would not be pious to keep silent, because both the Law and the Gospel admonish us not to neglect the honour of our Father. He also, who leaves us examples of such great perfection, will not cease, as we confidently trust, [Col. 1350A] to intercede for us with Christ, so that here we may imitate the footsteps of so great a predecessor and, when the term of this misery is ended, may be received with him into eternal glory, enriched by the profit of merits. Amen. [Note: [Col. 1350D] (144) I leave the following verses as I found them printed after the Appendix, since they may have been composed at Cappenberg after the Life had been read there. Yet if anyone prefers to think that they were appended by this author, I shall not object.]

8.

> Blessed Norbert, first Father of this Order:  
> I rejoice, Father Hugh, that you favour his merits.  
> Blessed indeed is he who scorned the heights of the world,  
> And, subjected to Christ’s yoke, sowed holy seed;  
> From which a wondrous fruit has sprung up everywhere—  
> Fruit by which the cloistered Rule saves many;  
> Fruit that happily fills the granaries of heaven.  
>
> A distinguished spirit, the fire of God’s gift,  
> Enlightened him and made him illustrious by teaching,  
> Inflaming him from heaven and matching him with great teachers.  
> Illustrious in merits, he bears an indelible name:  
> [Col. 1350B] For he steadfastly loved true poverty;  
> By the strength of faith he put to flight the assaults of the devil.  
>
> This vessel of the eternal Word, this minister of peace,  
> Established peace and reconciled the discordant.  
> Raised by advancement to the pontifical office,  
> He was a notable man: a cross to the wicked, a model to the kind,  
> And a bright star in the affairs of the churches.  
>
> Blessed is he who could safely confront swords,  
> Conscious of no guilt, growing pale at no fault,  
> Nor doubting death, joined in love to Christ.  
> Blessed shall be his sheaves when the Lord comes,  
> Whom the good Judge will receive from our Order.  
> May grace protect us at this judgment. Amen.

Here ends the Life of our glorious Father Norbert.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1349]

From Book III of Herman the Monk, *On the Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon*.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVI, col. 990.)

## CHAPTER III. On monasteries founded by Saint Norbert near Xanten and at Magdeburg

[Col. 1349]

[Col. 1349C] 9. When I read in the Life of the saint, no. 11, that after being ordained priest he “went to a certain monastery of Siegburg, of great and distinguished renown,” and again in no. 19 that, to take some breath from the attacks of his persecutors at the beginning of his preaching, “he sometimes went to a certain monastery of monks at Siegburg, three leagues from Cologne,” I wondered at this *certain*, as though it were superfluous. Yet I thought of no place other than the monastery of Siegburg itself, which, though four travelling leagues away, lies only three German miles from Cologne.

But after I came upon the charter of Arnold, first archbishop of Cologne of that name, issued in the final year of his pontificate, A.D. 1144, “on Mount Vurstenberg,” I understood that a monastery had been built there which was subject to the abbot of Siegburg, who had received the foundation and placed there monks selected from his own house. Thus I understood how far from idle *certain* is in that passage, and that perhaps several other houses had likewise been subject to that quasi-archmonastery, each of which could be called “a certain Siegburg house,” that is, one belonging to the order or jurisdiction of Siegburg.

Such also may have been the other house mentioned without a proper name in no. 19. It should be sought not beyond Cologne, as Siegburg is, but near it; and therefore seven, or at least four, leagues nearer Xanten than that house, which is fully twenty leagues away. In another sense, it might be understood of some monastery three leagues from Cologne but thirteen or sixteen leagues from Xanten—although none such is now found, probably because it has been destroyed. Closest to these is the place of which the cited charter says that it was situated on a mountain only two thousand paces away, called Vurstenberg, and which anyone coming from Cologne, as Norbert came in no. 11, and travelling toward Xanten, had to pass.

Since Saint Norbert had a considerable part in its recent foundation, it is readily understood why he went there [Col. 1351C] out of his way: to prepare himself over several days for the due offering to God of the first fruits of his priesthood. I have therefore thought it fitting to present here a copy of the charter itself, sent to our Bollandus by a certain Justus Dudink, lord of Cleves. It shows how seriously the saint, immediately after his conversion, applied his mind to advancing divine worship, contributing there no small part of his resources; and that he had as companion in this pious work his brother Heribert, otherwise unknown to us. From him probably descended a numerous posterity, to share in the propitiatory sacrifices said on the saint’s anniversary or the following day, as the practice still continues, for the consolation of the deceased members of that family. Probably related to this are also Heribert and [Col. 1351D] Erebert of Gennep, brothers of Saint Norbert, perhaps cousins, here likewise named among the benefactors of the aforesaid monastery. The text of the charter is as follows.

10. “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Arnold, called—not by merit but by the calling grace of God—archbishop of the holy church of Cologne, wishes perpetual peace and eternal salvation to all who have received the common faith with us.

“We wish it to be known to you how the monastery of Blessed Mary on Mount Vurstenberg near Xanten was begun, and how, desiring to advance it in every respect both before God and before men, we have decreed that a general record be made of all things hitherto reasonably offered there: namely, to encourage the devotion of the good and to restrain thereafter the cunning of the wicked. Let us therefore show our favour toward that place, and faithfully offer to the Lord Jesus Christ and to His holy Virgin Mother this document, filled with the varied gifts of the faithful like a little crown woven of diverse flowers.

“Henry of Alpheim, a ministerial of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1351D] (145) That is, of the cathedral church of Cologne, which Gelenius, *Syntagma*, book III, section I, §4, says was built by Archbishop Willibert in the year 873 and whose principal choir was dedicated to Saint Peter. It stood until about 1248, when it was burned; then this new church began to be built, and its choir was crowned with vaulting in 1320.], [Col. 1352B] being a man of proven integrity, with the counsel and assistance of Norbert, then canon of Xanten and later bishop of Magdeburg, obtained by earnest requests from Lord Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, that, in hope of eternal recompense, he should convey by lawful donation to the church of Siegburg the benefice which had come to him on the aforesaid Mount Vurstenberg by paternal—indeed ancestral—succession. This was done on the condition that he should summon some brethren of that monastery to establish monastic life upon the land of that benefice.

“The archbishop, readily and willingly disposed toward such matters, confirmed the fief before suitable witnesses to the church of Siegburg. The brethren were brought in; [Col. 1352C] divine religion gradually began to flourish there; and it was firmly decreed that the place should remain perpetually subject to the monastery of Siegburg.

“The same Henry likewise offered to God and Saint Mary an allodial estate which he possessed in the village of [Note: [Col. 1351D] (146) Geist Castle lies roughly midway on the road between the monastery of Westphalia and the city of Paderborn, as I myself have seen. Our Society now has there a house of third probation, from the bequest of its last owner. [Col. 1352D] Yet I scarcely believe that this is the place meant here, since it is farther from the town of Xanten; rather, it is another place, which I find nowhere recorded. As with many other places successively to be named, I shall not linger over searching for it, but leave the investigation to those curious about Westphalian and Cologne affairs.] Geist: one *mansus*, paying seven solidi yearly, excepting two denarii; eight malders [Note: [Col. 1352D] (147) A *maldarium*, otherwise *maldrum*, is as much as is normally carried at once to a mill, from the German *malen*, ‘to grind’; hence a miller is called a *malder*.] of mixed grain, that is, half barley and half oats; two pigs worth four solidi and six denarii; and a house-plot lying at Xanten, whose rent is twelve denarii.

11. “Following this man’s example, the aforesaid Norbert and his brother Heribert offered the estate of Egre with all its appurtenances. To make the grant firmer and the offering more pleasing to God, they also willingly gave to the same place little estates donated from elsewhere. The annual revenues of this estate [Col. 1352D] are six malders of wheat, three of rye, twelve of barley, eight of oats, and one of legumes—a total of thirty malders; eleven solidi for transport on the Rhine; and, if any salmon is caught in that stretch, one half of it.

“They also offered a small field at Wedreke, paying two malders of rye and one and a half of barley; likewise a small field there [Col. 1353A] paying three malders [Note: [Col. 1353D] (148) *Brasium* is grain soaked in water until it begins to sprout and then dried; after it is ground, beer is brewed from it.] of malt, and four solidi less two denarii. Another at Meitreke pays eighteen denarii.

“Cuno, first abbot of the Siegburg monks, ever ready for every good work, received in exchange from Rudolph of Bart an estate at Birtine and transferred it to Blessed Mary, with the consent of his entire convent, together with all pertaining to it—woods and fields, arable land and meadows, cultivated and uncultivated land.

“The right pertaining to that estate extends through every wood belonging to the count’s estate in the same village: when after acorn-feeding pigs are assessed—what they call *cranna* [Note: [Col. 1353D] (149) I have not yet been able to learn what *cranna* was, although I had several persons inquire in Cleves.]—the official of the brethren is to receive a tenth of all the pigs, or money in place of pigs. And within the jurisdiction of either estate, if any offence requiring punishment occurs, such as theft, the shedding of blood, [Col. 1353B] or the like, whatever profit arises from it shall be divided equally between the count’s officials and the brethren.

12. “Alward and Wolthildis, appearing before the court with their sons, offered an estate at Walheim; and at Erpete eight *jugera* of arable land, four *jugera* of vineyard, and a house-site at Pielcheim, paying four solidi in the currency of Soest [Note: [Col. 1353D] (150) Soest, commonly Soust, is in the territory of the Mark; after the monastery of Westphalia it was considered most wealthy, and it remains so even now.], together with fifteen serfs, of whom males shall pay nine denarii and females four.

“Agena, abbess of [Note: [Col. 1353D] (151) Frethena, commonly Vreden; see what is said in the Life, no. 6.] Frethena, and her brother Stephen gave an allodial estate at Mereheim which pays one mark of heavy coinage, three *statuae* [Note: [Col. 1353D] (152) A *statua* is the same as a grain measure called a rod. For in the Saxon Mirror, in Cange, where the text reads, ‘a heap of wheat of twelve rods,’ the margin notes: ‘A heap of wheat having twelve *statuae* . . . and each *statua* contains twelve pegs . . . in the height of a man’s stature up to the shoulders.’ Thus its derivation is apparent. Below, however, at no. 146, three *statuae* are interpreted as three nights’ lodging.] with ten [lacuna].

“Reinbert of Wiscele and his son Theodorus gave at Velwig two and a half *mansi*, with all their appurtenances; eight dependent persons [Col. 1353C] paying a wax rent [*ad censum*] of wax; and at Nereibich a house and plot paying twelve denarii in the currency of Deventer. [Note: [Col. 1354D] (153) Deventer, or Daventria, commonly Deventer, is a town in Overijssel, in the diocese of Utrecht, one of the three principal towns together with Zwolle and Kampen.]

“At Birte, Bertrudis gave a *mansus* paying four and a half solidi in the currency of Duisburg. [Note: [Col. 1354D] (154) By Dusberg I believe either Duisburg in Cleves on the Ruhr is meant, or Doesburg on the IJssel in Zutphen.] At Lengele, land paying three Deventer solidi; at Diedeheim, thirty denarii of the same currency. Hubert of Oie gave at Magellheim half a pound. Razo of Birte, at Hungese, gave three Deventer solidi. From the same village Rutger, at Ore, gave five serfs subject to a wax rent. Volmar, priest of [Note: [Col. 1354D] (155) Rees, a strongly fortified town of Cleves on the right bank of the Rhine, is three leagues from Xanten.] Rees, gave at Wetzevelt four malders of rye and one of beans. At Boemelwig Bernard of Wisse gave three malders of rye and the same quantity of barley malt. Vietpold of Recken, at Pellheim, [Col. 1353D] gave one *mansus*, paying three solidi in the currency of Dortmund. [Col. 1354A] Wiedekint of Duisburg gave an allodial estate at Hile, paying ten denarii. Trimintrudis, handmaid of God, bought at Riencheim land yielding half a mark.

13. “At Butreche an allodial estate was offered for Vertlero, yielding four solidi. In the same place Frederick of Butburge gave a small piece of land paying fourteen denarii in Deventer currency; one pound, and three [Col. 1354B] Dortmund solidi. [Note: [Col. 1354D] (156) Dortmund is a large town in the diocese of Cologne, between the rivers Ruhr and Lippe. The ancient power of this and the other places already mentioned is evident from their right to strike their own coinage.]

“In the same place the brethren themselves bought an allodial estate yielding four solidi in Cologne currency. Gertrude of Nervenich gave, for the soul of Count Adalbert, a property paying three and a half Dortmund solidi and one serf. At Wiscele, Bertrad of Hogeslotrehiem offered an allodial estate from which four solidi and six denarii in Cologne currency were due [Col. 1354B] for the light of the church. Likewise, a certain woman offered goods from which eighteen denarii would begin to be paid after her death.

“A certain Megfrid, during the term of his office, gave at Kierbruch four serfs with an allodial estate paying twenty-seven solidi in Cologne currency and three *statuae*, that is, three nights’ lodging. Excepted is the reception due to the person who carries the rent thence: namely, a supper, lodging for the night, and breakfast in the morning. At Kasle, a certain Hugh gave, for his daughter, twenty-five denarii in Duisburg currency. At Hulse the brethren bought an allodial estate whose annual revenue is twelve denarii.

14. “Bertolf, count of Stromberg [Note: [Col. 1354D] (157) Stromberg, with the title of burgraviate, now belongs to the bishopric of Münster, between the Lippe and Ems; it is believed that Quintilius Varus lost his legions there.], lawfully offered to the monastery of Siegburg five *mansi*, which [Col. 1354C] the aforesaid Cuno, abbot of that place, with the consent of that whole church, assigned to the use of the brethren serving God on the holy mountain. These *mansi* pay fifteen solidi in Deventer currency, ten pigs, and five sheep. No advocate of this allodial estate shall exist except the archbishop of Cologne alone; and the inhabitants themselves shall enjoy the same rights as the other men of Saint Peter at that holy place in meadows and fields, woods and waters.

“A certain Arnold of Kempen surrendered a fief which he had held from Almar, advocate of Cologne. At Arnold’s own request, Lord Frederick the archbishop gave it to Blessed Mary, in commemoration of his anniversary. This benefice at Kempen originally paid three [solidi?]; but afterwards, upon consultation, two women were given in place of the solidi; their descendants shall give what [Col. 1355A] is just.

“Before Cleves, Renizo of Strale gave five *jugera*, whose rent is two solidi in Deventer currency. Imo gave, for his daughter, a small field yielding three sextaries of barley. Gerbergus of Seleheim gave one *mansus* at Alfene. Azela of Bumele gave six *jugera*. In the same place Gela of Kalkar gave a *truta* in the measure of two malders of barley [reading and sense uncertain]. Heribert [Note: [Col. 1355D] (158) If it were certain that this was the same man as the Heribert mentioned above, Saint Norbert’s brother, we should here have another brother, Erebert. Perhaps both had the common surname “of Gennep” from the same family as that brother.] of Gennep gave, for his brother Erebert, who had been killed, one *mansus* at Brakele, paying seven Deventer solidi. At Remagen, Manegald, canon of Xanten, and the above-named Bertad bought five *jugera* of vineyard. One half, while the aforesaid cleric lives, and the remaining part after his death, shall belong to the brethren on the mountain.

[Col. 1355B] 15. “Lord Hildolfus, Archbishop [Note: [Col. 1355D] (159) No Hildolfus after Fridericus is found in Gelenius or the Sammarthani. Correct them accordingly, and understand that Hildolfus II succeeded Hugo, who died in Italy, in the year 1138, besides Hildolfus, successor of St Anno, who died in 1079; he held this see for some time before Arnold, whom they make Hugo’s immediate successor [Col. 1356D].], when dedicating the oratory of St Martin on the mountain itself, gave nine holdings of houses at Sanctis; their rents, some greater and some smaller, amount together to five solidi, for the light of that chapel. On the mountain, Count Arnold gave one jugerum; the religious woman Adelheidis, three jugera. In the field of Mageneete are seven jugera belonging to the mountain: of these: Volmarus and his wife, one; Wilhelmus, two; Videricus of Eile, one; Rudolfus of Mageneete, one; Amizia of Budweche; Rudolfus of Lo; Bezela of Megeneete, two. At Wentervelde, Henricus, having professed as a monk, gave one jugerum. At Ebbecheren, Grunzelinus of Bevenburch gave a small holding worth twelve denarii. Gebehardus, priest of Brutine, gave half a jugerum below the mountain. Amelune gave one, Snedo two, jugera [Col. 1355C] on the mountain. In the wood called Hiese, the people of both estates at Britine shall have equal rights in every respect. Cuno, a cleric at Wissele, bought at Rimagen a jugerum of vineyard and gave it to Blessed Mary. Heribertus of Britine gave the allod which he possessed on the mountain, amounting to five jugera of land; and he conveyed it with the consent of his people. In Lappesdal, one jugerum was received from a certain Ingelgerus, who was setting out for Jerusalem, on the right-hand side of the mountain. Rurgerus and his brother Hermannus gave a field, thought to measure one jugerum. Gerhardus of Lattingen gave two jugera to the saints.

16. “These things, and whatever other gifts there are, which at different times and in different places have been lawfully offered by diverse persons of either sex to the Lord Jesus Christ and to his holy Mother, the perpetual Virgin Mary, for remembrance of all the faithful living and dead, on the oft-mentioned mountain, and have been lawfully received, we have confirmed by our episcopal authority. We invoke the eternal judgment of God and judicial sentence [Col. 1356A] upon every human soul that, by whatever means or device, shall defraud any part of these things, or consent to their being defrauded: while he lives, let him be excluded from all prayers which are made on that mountain or throughout the whole Church; and when dying, let him receive a portion with those whose worm does not die and whose fire is not quenched. For their sin shall never be blotted out before God unless he repents and makes worthy satisfaction to God. Done on Mount Vurstenberg, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1144, in the seventh indiction, in the first year of the apostolic lord Lucius [Note: [Col. 1356D] (160) Mabillon found in some necrology that this Pope Lucius died in the same year, on 25 August. I, however, think that I have demonstrated in the *Paralipomena on Papal Chronology* that he did not die before 13 February of the following year; this is also proved by the present document.], in the seventh year of Conrad III, emperor of the Romans in the West; and in the second year of Emmanuel Comnenus in the East [Note: [Col. 1356D] (161) Chrysostomus van der Sterre wrote in his vernacular *Life of St Norbert* that this monastery was afterwards handed over to religious women, who, compelled by the adversity of the times, finally migrated to the town of Santen, as I have already said above.].”

17. How closely the end matched these most praiseworthy beginnings, so far as the establishment of monasteries is concerned—to pass over the intervening period—will be shown by Norbert’s own charter, sent to us by Abbot Vitus of Strahov, under this title: “How Norbert restored the Church of the Blessed Virgin from secular clergy to brethren of his own order. Likewise, concerning the poverty of the place and how he newly provided for the brethren.” The tenor of the charter is as follows: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Norbert, by the grace of God Archbishop of the Church of Magdeburg. Let it be known to all, both future and present, that, considering the condition of the Church of Magdeburg and desiring to exalt it in religious life, to restore what was diminished, and to reform what was insufficiently corrected or change it for the better, I found in that city a church dedicated to Blessed Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, so reduced in its internal and external resources [Col. 1356C] that the fabric and roofing of the church itself had almost entirely fallen into ruin, and the food supplies were insufficient for the twelve clerics appointed there to serve God. For much of what belonged to that church had even been distributed to knights as benefices; some lay uncultivated through neglect; some had been appropriated to the uses of others, so that the church was almost irrecoverably despoiled.

18. “We therefore, moved by compassion for their poverty and frequent complaint, and desiring the church rather to grow than to decline, obtained this from them by admonition, exhortation, and persuasion: that, leaving that church, they should yield it to religious men living the common life under the Rule of Blessed Augustine [Col. 1356D], and should entrust themselves to our provision without any condition. So that they themselves might live, as before, in cloistered discipline under a dean, we assigned them to other churches in the city.
