We placed some in the church of Blessed Nicholas; we supported some from the goods of that church [Col. 1357A]. But we endowed our brethren, substituted in the church, with the church’s former possessions and rights; and, for their fuller peace and quiet, we decreed that they should owe regard to no one except us and our successors. Therefore, that these arrangements may remain forever unshaken, we confirm them under the ban of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and under our own. Peace and remission of sins be to those who observe them. But if a person of any rank shall presume to annul the work of our zeal, or with rash daring disturb Christ’s poor, or seek by any pretext to remove them, let him be anathema maranatha until the day of the Lord. I, Elinderus, subscribe. I, Uwernus, subscribe. I, Wernerus, subscribe. I, Sidagus, subscribe. I, Anselmus, subscribe. I, Theodericus, subscribe. I, Sigebodo, subscribe. I, Godescalcus, subscribe. Done in the year 1129 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the seventh indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the suburb of the city of Magdeburg, in the abbey of Blessed John the Baptist.”

[Col. 1357]

## TWO SERMONS OF ST NORBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG, TO THE PEOPLE

### SERMON I

[Col. 1357B]

(HUGO, *Life of Saint Norbert*, Luxembourg, 1704, quarto, notes, p. 354.)

I had departed from you in sorrow, brethren; but now, through the gracious mercy of God, I return to you joyful and, as it were, dancing. The enemy, that inveterate devil, sower of hatred and quarrels, had torn us from you by a dreadful schism, so that he who had begun to establish his dominion through divisions might extend it by dissensions; and, by separating the shepherd from the flock, might drag the sheep—wandering at the voice of a hireling and without a sure guide—into the abyss. This was the ancient fraud of the envious enemy; this also was the origin of the present evil, by which he shattered concord, no less necessary to the public welfare than to the safety of the sheep and the office of the shepherd. Almost overwhelmed by the storm, [Col. 1357C] we had to evade by flight the waves which could not be calmed by prayers. But thanks be to God: Christ, who had seemed to sleep amid the raging tempest, at last awakened by the cries of those in peril, commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. The peace which the devil had snatched away, the God of peace restored to us. I beseech you, brethren, love it ardently, seek it unceasingly, and guard it prudently. Let our hearts cleave together in the bond of charity; and, as it is written of the first worshippers of the Christian faith, “there was one heart and one soul,” so henceforward let us all walk in unity of spirit. Do not fear, little children, whom I again travail to bring forth, that the evils by which you have assailed your shepherd will make the shepherd harsh toward you. For although you inflicted violence, not upon me, but upon the priesthood [Col. 1358B], yet I hope, through the mercy of him who forgives our iniquities, that the abundance of your tears has blotted out the crime you committed. Therefore let us pray now to the Father of mercies and God of all consolation that he may preserve anew, for those who become worthy, the peace which he gave to the unworthy. Let us strive by good works to redeem evil deeds and make our calling sure, so that with one voice God may be glorified, now and always. Amen.

### SERMON II

On preserving concord.

(LE PAIGE, *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, Paris, 1633, folio, p. 370.)

Brethren, when our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1358C] sent his disciples to preach, among other things he gave them this command: that, upon entering any house, they should first say, “Peace to this house”; and if a son of peace were there, their peace would rest upon him. Now we too, made their imitators not by our merits but by the overflowing grace of God alone, proclaim to you that same peace, which must not be despised by an unbelieving mind; for it leads to everlasting peace. You therefore do not fail to know why we have assembled. It is not ours to accomplish this, nor does it proceed from us—for I am a pilgrim and passing stranger—but it belongs to God’s power and will; ours, however, is to submit wholly, with devout affection, to his will.

[Col. 1357]

## CHARTERS OF ST NORBERT

(Year 1129.) I. For the Church of St Mary at Magdeburg.

[Printed above in the *Norbertine Analecta*, chapter 3, nos. 32–33.]

II. He transfers a certain hospice to the Premonstratensian brethren established in the Church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg.

(HUGO, *Life of St Norbert*, p. 362, notes.)

[Col. 1358D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, we, NORBERT, by the grace of God Archbishop of the holy Church of Magdeburg.

Whereas, through the bountiful generosity of our predecessor of pious memory, Adalbert [Col. 1359A], a certain hospice had been built beside the church of most blessed and glorious Mary, we found it, contrary to our expectation, almost destroyed, so that those who were to receive their daily allowance there were begging shamefully and miserably. Moved by compassion for their need and misery, with the counsel and consent of our chief men, we have transferred that same hospice, with all things belonging to it, to our brethren established in the church of Blessed Mary, perpetual Virgin, to govern and administer in perpetual right.

Done in the suburb of the city of Magdeburg, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130.

Witnesses to this matter are Lindolphus, Bishop of Brandenburg [Col. 1359B]; Gombertus, Bishop of Havelberg; and Hartuicus, Bishop of Meissen.

III. Charter of St Norbert in support of hospitality for the poor.

(HUGO, *ibid.*, p. 250.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

Tithes shall be given to God for the hospice, from every possession and offering of the brethren, for the use of the poor. Thus, if the sum of money is worth ten solidi, or offerings amount to as much as ten solidi, eighteen poor persons shall be clothed from these resources each year [Col. 1360A]: eight in winter and ten in summer. In winter, namely, one shall be clothed at the feast of All Saints; one at the Nativity of the Lord; one at the Circumcision of the Lord; and likewise one at the Epiphany, at the Purification of St Mary, at the Annunciation of St Mary, at the Burial of the Lord, and at the Resurrection of the Lord, with new garments—namely, shirts, breeches, hose, socks, shoes, a tunic, and a cloak with a mantle or furs. In summer, at the Ascension of the Lord, during the seven days of Pentecost, at the Passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and at the Assumption of St Mary, one person shall be clothed at each feast with a new cloak or cape, shirt, breeches, socks, and shoes.

[Col. 1360B]

From the day on which a poor person receives clothing until the eighth day, if he wishes to remain, bodily refreshment shall be provided for him there. The remainder shall be spent for the use of poor persons arriving or passing through. At the Lord’s Supper, however, each priest or deacon, after the washing of beggars’ feet, shall, with the provost’s counsel, charitably give one of his own garments—whether cloak, furs, tunic, or hose—to one of them. After receiving this charity, such persons shall by no means remain for seven days, as above, but shall depart after refreshment.

[Col. 1359]

## PIOUS DONATIONS MADE TO ST NORBERT AND THE PREMONSTRATENSIANS BY BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF LAON

(HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred and Canonical Premonstratensian Order*, Nancy, 1734, folio.)

(Year 1121.) I. Charter of the donation of Prémontré by Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon.

[Col. 1359C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

We wish it to be known to both present and future persons that I, Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, have given to the venerable man Norbert, distinguished for religious life in our times, and to his successors living in the holy purpose, a place that was under our jurisdiction, wholly free and released from every exaction by any person, at Huberti-Pont (Huberpont), from the place called Halieprest (Près-prieur) as far as Rohard Valley (*vallée Rohard*), with the three adjacent valleys [Col. 1359D], entirely as an allod, from the stream toward Vois, as the valleys divide and lead onward, for the building of a church in honour of God and the holy Mother of God. As we possess the whole as an allod, so we grant it to them to possess wholly and freely in every way. The pastures and meadows, from Pont-Huberti as far as neighbouring Mormand, on this side and beyond the stream, shall at all times be common to their animals. Beyond the stream, however, on the side of the church, they shall be protected for the use of those brethren until the gathering of hay and crops [Col. 1360C]. Thereafter they shall be common, provided only that no one harass their religious life on any pretext. The peasants living nearby are nevertheless permitted to gather from the woodland on the mountain ridges timber for a plough-head, plough-stilt, or axle. In all work done by those brethren in the same places, no one shall demand from them either tithe or *terragium* [land-rent], nor shall any person inflict trouble upon their peace; and we decree that they and all hermits subject to them shall remain wholly released from every parish jurisdiction. We further wish it known that the church and place of Prémontré were given and confirmed to the Church of St Vincent by our predecessor Helenand, as is also contained in the privilege; but now, because the whole had been reduced utterly to solitude, Abbot Scifridus and the convent of that same Church of St Vincent judged it useful [Col. 1361A] to restore it into our hand and leave it to our disposal, which was done. Therefore, considering that nothing was better in this matter, we likewise freely granted that same church, with all that the aforesaid monks possessed there, to the venerable man Norbert and to his successors living in the holy purpose, to possess forever free from every exaction. They shall admit among themselves no assemblies of laypeople, but only persons living under the same provost. And that they may possess these things more freely, we established for the aforesaid brethren at our mill called Burdellum (Bordet) an annual rent of six *galetae* of grain. The brethren of the Church of Prémontré shall henceforth render nothing to them on this account. We assigned two *galetae* of grain at the same mill to the canons of St John at Laon, to whom the tithe of the Church of Prémontré belonged; and the brethren of the Church of Prémontré shall henceforth render them nothing in respect of matters belonging to the parish tithe [Col. 1361B]. We decree that all the surrounding valleys leading down around the site of Prémontré, and the slopes of the mountains on every side, shall remain freely and perpetually possessed as an allod by the brethren living a religious life there; and that none of the surrounding parishes shall impose any harassment upon their religious life, whether in tithes or in any other matter. This was done with the assent and will of Thomas, from whose fief two parts of the tithe descended; he himself, and those who held from him, surrendered them into our hands for the use of the aforesaid brethren. Moreover, whatever right or customary claim Thomas and his foresters under him—namely Girelmus of Valsalione (Vausaillon), Radulphus of Quinciaco (Quincy), and the elder Radulphus of Cociaco-villa (Coucy-la-Ville)—had, they gave wholly free and unencumbered for the use of the aforesaid brethren [Col. 1361C]. Thomas himself also gave the aforesaid brethren a ploughland at the place Rosiers. With the consent of all, we also caused to be closed the road by which neighbouring inhabitants had been accustomed to go through the middle of the valley of the Church of Prémontré.

Robertus of Anlerio also surrendered into our hand, for the use of the aforesaid brethren, the allod which he possessed in the adjoining wood. Further, we gave the aforesaid brethren [Col. 1361D] three ploughlands: one near our town of Aniliacum; another near Larciniacum (Vercigny near La Fère); and a third near Capriniacum above the mountain (Mount Chevergny), beyond the stream Aquila (the river Aigle, now the Elle), free of tithes on those three ploughlands. Whoever attempts to violate or disturb this charter and instrument of our ordinance shall be anathema and incur the wrath of almighty God on the Day of Judgment.

The mark of Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon. The mark of Guido, dean and archdeacon. The mark of Radulphus, archdeacon. The mark of Sifridus, abbot of St Vincent. The mark of Simon, abbot of St Nicholas of the Wood. [Col. 1362A] The mark of Bilihardus, cantor. The mark of Drogo, priest. The mark of Herbertus, priest. The mark of Erhardus, deacon. The mark of Godefridus, deacon. The mark of Eliardus, subdeacon. The mark of Guido, subdeacon. The mark of Robertus, acolyte. The mark of Robertus, dean of St John. The mark of Jusfridus, cantor. The mark of Hemmo, treasurer. The mark of Henricus. The mark of Valerius. The mark of Gundrannus. The mark of Hugo. The mark of Robertus, priest of the Church of St Martin. The mark of Helbertus, viscount. [Col. 1362B] The mark of Clarebaldus of the Market. The mark of Nicholas, castellan.

Done at Laon in the chapter of the Church of Blessed Mary of Laon, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, fourteenth indiction, no epact, fifth concurrent, in the reign of Louis, King of the Franks, who granted to Brother Norbert and the other brethren living religiously in the aforesaid place that they should hold forever whatever is given and shall be given to them that belongs to his fief.

I, Radulphus, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

(Year 1121.) II. Charter of Bishop Bartholomew transferring Prémontré to Blessed Norbert.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I [Col. 1362C], BARTHOLOMEW, by the grace of God bishop of Laon.

Since the Church of St Vincent possessed, by the gift of our predecessor Bishop Elinand, the place called Prémontré, which belonged to the bishop’s own table, as is contained in that church’s privilege, the monks long inhabited that place and, through much labour, obtained little or no profit. Seeing this, I asked Abbot Adalberon and the monks to grant me the aforesaid place freely, so that I might dispose of it according to my will. The abbot and monks assented to my petition and freely granted me, without contradiction, all that they possessed in that place. In return, not ungrateful for their willingness [Col. 1362D], I granted to the Church of St Vincent in perpetual possession the altar of Bariacum, subject to synodal right. I also gave them half a *modius* of grain at the mill near the village called Broincurtum. But seeing that the aforesaid place called Prémontré was most useful for religious men, I granted it freely and without contradiction for perpetual possession to Brother Norbert and his subjects and successors. Brother Norbert, however, being by no means covetous of another’s property, at first refused to receive it, until Seifridus, Abbot of St Vincent, and his monks confirmed that gift to him in chapter by common assent. To ensure that this grant could not thereafter be altered in any way, we took care to confirm it by the impress of our image, by the seal of the Church of St Mary of Laon, and by the seals of Seifridus, Abbot of St Vincent [Col. 1363A].

The mark of Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon. The mark of Seifridus, Abbot of St Vincent. The mark of Simon of St Nicholas of the Wood. The mark of Guido, dean and archdeacon. The mark of Rodulphus, archdeacon. The mark of Bilhardus, cantor. The mark of Robertus, dean of St John. The mark of Gaufridus, cantor. [Col. 1364A] The mark of Robertus, provost of St Martin. The mark of Herbertus, viscount. The mark of Clarembaldus of the Market. The mark of Nicholas, castellan.

Done at Laon in the chapter of the Church of St Mary of Laon, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, fourteenth indiction, no epact, fifth concurrent.

I, Radulphus, chancellor of the Church of Laon, wrote and subscribed.

ONE BOOK ON THE WILL OF GOD. 437  

Preface. 437  
CHAP. I.—That this division is impious and foolish: “one will approving evil, another permitting it.” 437  
CHAP. II.—That God’s permission is the same as what Paul calls God’s goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering. Also, what is meant by: “God gave them up to the desires of their hearts,” and similar expressions. 438  
CHAP. III.—That God permits evil unwillingly, yet not under compulsion. 438  
CHAP. IV.—That when God hardens someone, He does not will evil, but wills that the person be punished according to His justice. 439  
CHAP. V.—Certain scruples of curious persons who argue that God wills evil. 440  
CHAP. VI.—That it is not the part of a sound mind to raise questions of this sort concerning God’s will. This is treated through the comparison of a potter and his vessel. 440  
CHAP. VII.—That God made no creature exempt from suffering and vices because this nature belongs to Himself alone. 441  
CHAP. VIII.—He teaches by comparison that something unchangeable could indeed be begotten by God, but could not be created. 442  
CHAP. IX.—That God wished to make a creature comparable to Himself, and did so by mingling in the one Christ the substances of His birth and of His creaturehood. 443  
CHAP. X.—That it is an argument for God’s omnipotence that He assumed human nature, which nothing other than He Himself could have assumed. 443  
CHAP. XI.—That this creature of God’s omnipotence was such that it could not sin. Also, how God Almighty cannot do evil. 444  
CHAP. XII.—That angels possess the inability to sin not by nature but by grace received. Further, why God did not establish them firmly when He established them, or at least before evil occurred. 444  
CHAP. XIII.—He refutes the impiety of the flesh, which reasons that God imposed a law upon Adam because He wished him to become a transgressor. 445  
CHAP. XIV.—That God imposed a command upon humankind so that His goodness might make humanity blessed and truly living. [Col. 1388] 446  
CHAP. XV.—That those are mistaken who think the command not to eat the fruit was slight; he teaches this by comparison with the sun. 446  
CHAP. XVI.—That faith, hope, and charity, in which eternal life consists, were required in that first commandment. 447  
CHAP. XVII.—That the command concerning the fruit of paradise was sufficiently great, since at that time there was no need for another to be laid down, and Adam’s faithfulness or iniquity could nevertheless be tested by this command, whatever its kind. 447  
CHAP. XVIII.—That this tree was especially forbidden because, though beautiful, it would all the more easily ensnare the man, who had already begun to neglect God. 448  
CHAP. XIX.—That those are slanderers of God for whom the fact that He always forbids evil is not proof of His good will. 448  
CHAP. XX.—That humankind had to be prohibited from the tree of life for a different reason than from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because death resulted from the latter in one way, while life was to be expected from the former in another. 449  
CHAP. XXI.—That, just as God willed obedience, so He also fulfilled it in Christ crucified and dying for us. 450  
CHAP. XXII.—That God accomplished what He willed not through another, but through Himself. 450  
CHAP. XXIII.—That if God had willed evil to occur, so that He Himself might correct it to His glory, He would have suffered in assumed flesh not freely, but as a matter of obligation. 451  
CHAP. XXIV.—That, as God does not unjustly destroy the substance of a creature already corrupted, so He did not unjustly condemn the foreknown wickedness of the future human being. 451  
CHAP. XXV.—That the prophetic words, “I, the Lord, make peace and create evil,” refer not to the evil of sin but to the evil of affliction, since doing and suffering differ from one another. 452  
CHAP. XXVI.—That those through whom the evil which the Lord creates comes about are not excusable, since the Lord neither willed nor made them evil; rather, when they were evil, He used them as a rod of discipline. 453  

ONE BOOK ON THE OMNIPOTENCE OF GOD. 453  

Prologue. 453  
CHAP. I.—That God’s omnipotence has two ways, mercy and truth, and likewise two hands, right and left, by which it advances toward God’s glory. 455  
CHAP. II.—When it is asserted that God does not will evil, the impious argue that He is not omnipotent. This, therefore, is the reason why he also discusses omnipotence. 456  
CHAP. III.—That the beginning and cause of an evil will in a good creature was nothing. 456  
CHAP. IV.—That true knowledge for confession consists in recognizing that evil comes from nothing and tends toward nothing. 457  
CHAP. V.—That a creature of evil will tends toward nothing in two ways: first through the error of ignorance, and second through the falsehood of malice. 457  
CHAP. VI.—That good will is not naturally inherent in human being or angel, but is given from God’s gift and grace. 458  
CHAP. VII.—That God did not give good will to all creatures, not because He willed otherwise or could not do so, but because they did not receive it. 459  
CHAP. VIII.—That God must act with the other hand, that of judgment, where there is an evil heart of unbelief. 460  
CHAP. IX.—That the objection of certain persons—that no one can resist God’s will—is defective; for one must understand: “and have peace.” 461  
CHAP. X.—That unbelievers do indeed resist God’s will, but do not prevail, since they themselves are rather overcome. 462  
CHAP. XI.—That there are two ways and hands of God, mercy and judgment, shown through the law for conquering a city which the Lord Himself gave. 462  
CHAP. XII.—That it is God’s will that all receive peace and be saved; yet the stiff-necked do not approach, but rather object to God’s mercy when it has been made known. 463  
CHAP. XIII.—That it would have been better not to have known the truth than to hold the truth once known in unrighteousness. 464  
CHAP. XIV.—That the Lord did not make the truth known to certain persons, not because He did not wish them to repent, but because He foreknew that they would not undertake true repentance. 465  
CHAP. XV.—That God is nonetheless omnipotent even if not all accept the peace He offers, provided that He conquers and strikes all; demonstrated from the example of Joshua. 466  
CHAP. XVI.—That, in the usage of Scripture, God’s omnipotence is especially proclaimed in His punishing sinners and casting down the proud. 466  
CHAP. XVII.—That the hand of mercy is equally—indeed, more—marvellous than the hand of judgment, if one considers it thoroughly. [Col. 1389] 467  
CHAP. XVIII.—That evil persons are born daily through the fault of their parents, not because God wills evil. 468  
CHAP. XIX.—That one who does not assent to the impious subtlety of opponents is judged simple and rustic. 469  
CHAP. XX.—That those who maintain that God wills evil wrongly defend themselves with Augustine’s authority. 469  
CHAP. XXI.—That it is falsely attributed to Augustine that God wills evil to occur unless one adds “by permitting”; only then is the statement complete, if it is said that God wills evil to occur by permitting it. 470  
CHAP. XXII.—He teaches from Augustine’s example that one who rightly refutes error should not be wrongly censured, whatever the source from which he has acquired the doctrine. 471  
CHAP. XXIII.—That the opponents, while seeking to defend their division of the will of evil by saying that some things are mediate and others immediate, have fallen into a more absurd error. 473  
CHAP. XXIV.—That God so completely does not will evil to occur that He does not permit it in every way. For He permits it not by consenting, but by not opposing evil effects. 474  
CHAP. XXV.—That, just as the evangelical father of the household did indeed let his son go but did not wish him to perish, so God permitted sin to occur but did not will it. 475  
CHAP. XXVI.—That he answered the foregoing late because at first he did not know that the opponents had taken their opinion from Augustine; thus it must be rejected as water polluted with the filth of baths is rejected from a clear spring. 475  
CHAP. XXVII.—That with God no word is impossible—namely, whatever He Himself has spoken in Scripture, not whatever some impious buffoon may utter against God’s justice. 476

## ST NORBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG

Preliminary Commentary.

§ I.—Chronological synopsis of the Life; his cult authorized by Gregory XIII and enlarged by his successors. 1235 § II.—The Life, written under the direction of Hugh, the saint’s first companion and successor in the government of Prémontré, with *Analecta*. 1241 § III.—Praises bestowed upon St Norbert and his order by writers of his own age. 1244 § IV.—Testimonies of certain authors of the following century. The ancient discipline of the order of canonesses. 1248

## LIFE OF ST NORBERT

Prologue. 1253 The Life begins. 1257 CHAP. I.—Birth; secular life; conversion to a better life. 1257 CHAP. II.—Holy orders received. The word of God preached. An injury patiently endured. 1262 CHAP. III.—Why and how saints suffer evils. St Norbert’s constancy in faith. 1265 CHAP. IV.—Persecutions endured; pilgrimages undertaken. Authority to preach obtained. 1269 CHAP. V.—Conversation with the bishop of Cambrai. Hugh summoned as a companion. Sermons delivered. 1274 CHAP. VI.—Discords removed and peace established. 1278 CHAP. VII.—With the favour of Pope Calixtus and the patronage of the bishop of Laon, Prémontré began to be inhabited. Diabolical temptations overcome. 1282 CHAP. VIII.—Various companions acquired. A possessed woman delivered. Relics received. 1287 CHAP. IX.—Profession according to the rule of St Augustine. Exercises of virtue prescribed. 1291 CHAP. X.—The hypocrisy of one companion exposed; a church constructed. 1295 CHAP. XI.—Temptations overcome. Demoniacs delivered. 1298 CHAP. XII.—Blessed Godfrey of Cappenberg converted; he persuaded Count Theobald, who was considering it, to marry. 1304 CHAP. XIII.—A blind woman and a demoniac healed. Tanchelin’s heresy eradicated at Antwerp. 1308 CHAP. XIV.—Demons repeatedly repelled. Wolves tamed. 1314 CHAP. XV.—The archbishopric of Magdeburg entered upon. A monastery of the order founded there. 1322 CHAP. XVI.—Persecutions endured. The first abbots ordained. 1326 CHAP. XVII.—The saint obtains from Innocent II confirmation of the privileges of his church. In a sedition he remains steadfast and is miraculously preserved from death. 1331 CHAP. XVIII.—Another conspiracy exposed. Journey to Rome. Illness and death. 1335 CHAP. XIX.—Burial of the body. Threefold apparition. Epilogue. 1337 *Norbertine Analecta*. 1343 CHAP. I.—Additions by the brethren of Cappenberg to the Life. 1343 CHAP. II.—From Book III of the monk Hermann’s *Miracles of St Mary of Laon*. 1349 CHAP. III.—Concerning monasteries founded by St Norbert near Saintes and at Magdeburg. 1349

Sermon I. 1357 Sermon II.—On preserving concord. 1358
